## Volume front matter

## Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III;** a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost diligence; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, and also with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; amplified by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever any one of the Fathers has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, by which the reader may readily discover which Fathers have commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture, and in which places of their works. An extremely accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection, single, methodical, and chronological, of six hundred fragments and short works previously scattered here and there, but now gathered for the first time in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. — One thousand two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; one thousand three hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition are sold for eight hundred francs. — The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are given in it only in Latin translation.

# In the year of the Lord 1001. Benedict, monk of Saint Andrew

[Column 0009]

## Notice concerning Benedict and his Chronicle

*(From D. Pertz, Monuments of German History, Writers, vol. III.)*

[Column 0009A] This Chronicle, hitherto unpublished, is owed to Benedict, a monk of Saint Andrew on Mount Soracte, a man in whom I do not know whether stupidity or negligence was greater. He lived during the time of John XII, and, as the tenth century was drawing to a close, endured the yoke of John XVI and Crescentius. Led by love and vanity concerning his monastery, he undertook to write history.

He was not entirely without books by which he could be assisted in producing his Chronicle. He made use of the *Lives of Saint Pigmenius, Saint Martin, and Saint Barbatus*, the *Translation of Saint Bartholomew from the island of Lipari to Benevento*, Bede’s *Chronicle*, the complete *Annals of Lorsch*, Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne*, the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs* [Note: [Column 0009C] He calls it the “episcopal book” in chapter 39], the edicts of the Lombard kings, the charters of the archive of Saint Andrew, and notices relevant both to the history of the monasteries situated on Mount Soracte and to that of the Lombards and Romans.

But the work itself shows that he used even the best sources very badly. He omits many sentences, indeed entire pages, of the annals; without hesitation he joins the latest events to earlier ones as though they were identical; he brings together men separated from one another by immense distances of time and place—Narses with Rothari, Romuald with Sicard and Sykinollus, Charlemagne with Aaron, Nicephorus, and Michael—and he transmits many fables.

Almost none of these fables is more ridiculous than the story that he repeatedly brings emperors and kings to Italy so that they may grant privileges to the monastery of Saint Andrew and insert them into the Lombard edicts. In addition, lacking command of Latin, he knew neither how to understand what he read nor how to write what he understood. He used a style which is so extreme a sign of the barbarism of the Romans of his age that one is astonished and horrified.

It is therefore self-evident that such a man was entirely unsuited to writing history, and that the portion of his work whose sources are unknown must be used only with great distrust. Even so, I frankly acknowledge that some material worthy of belief, and capable of shedding new light on history, is found in the accounts of Ratchis and Tassia, of Prince Alberic, and of Roman affairs in the tenth century. I have also indicated in my *Annals* [Note: [Column 0009C] Volume V, pp. 148–149] that this work contains the earliest trace here of the legend of Charlemagne’s journey to the Holy Land.

The work is defective at the beginning and lacks an ending, since only a parchment leaf survived in the codex [Note: [Column 0009C] In the Chigi Library, shelfmark F. IV. 75]. Its handwriting, executed around the year 1000, shows that it is an autograph. In editing the book, I introduced a division into chapters; I prohibited the reprinting of certain passages transcribed word for word from Bede and the *Annals of Lorsch*; the remainder I reproduced literally.

It is fitting to append to the Chronicle a short treatise on imperial power in the City, edited by Flacius from an ancient codex in which it was found after Eutropius, or the *Miscellaneous History* [Note: [Column 0009C] In the *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth*, p. 158, and repeated by Godastus in *The Monarchy of the Empire*, vol. I]. I suspect that its author was our Benedict.

The time and place support this: the author wrote around the year 1000 in Rome or its vicinity [Note: [Column 0009C] From a diploma of Otto III, *Monuments of Law*, vol. II, 162 (Patrology, vol. 138), whose wording he had before his eyes and annotated below. Since earlier editors did not notice this, and thought that the author had written around the year 900, they called him “Eutropius the Lombard,” because the treatise was read after Eutropius’s work. Muratori, in his *Annals* under the year 964, guessed the author’s date, but without taking Otto’s diploma into account], and there is mention of the monastery of Saint Andrew; complete sentences are repeated from the Chronicle [Note: [Column 0010C] See below, column 52]; there is the story of Pope Zachary’s journey to Francia; and the style of writing is uncultivated, although I believe Flacius made it highly polished and corrected.

If this is so, the treatise deserves the same degree of confidence as the Chronicle, so that one should rely on none of its statements without carefully weighing the matter and calling upon the primary sources. The author wrote partly, as one may reasonably believe, for the use of the emperor Otto III, and therefore between the years 998 [Column 0010C] and 1001.

[Column 0009]

# Chronicle of Benedict the Monk

[Column 0009C] **1.** The priest Pigmenius [Note: [Column 0010C] This is excerpted from the acts of the saint. Compare *Acta Sanctorum*, May III, p. 482] said in a loud voice:

> “Almighty God, how is it that I do not see you, nor in this way hear you, and that you utter words especially against God, whom you have denied, Julian, sacrilegious and most impious man?”

He ordered him to be thrown from the middle of the stone bridge into the river, together with a little boy who was dragging him with his hands. Not long afterward, in the meantime [Note: [Column 0011D] “In the meantime … all his possessions” is taken from Sulpicius’s *Life of Saint Martin*, chapter 3], when barbarians invaded the Gauls [Note: [Column 0011D] That is, Gaul], the most impious emperor Julian assembled the army at the city of the Vangiones and began distributing a donative to the soldiers.

As was customary, the names were read out one by one until Martin was reached [Note: [Column 0011D] That is, until they came to Martin]. Julian ordered him to be presented to him. He addressed him, saying:

> “Did both your father and you serve among the schoolmen in the palace under King Constantius?”

The man of God Martin replied:

> “I am a soldier of Christ; I may not fight.”

At these words the tyrant roared:

> “Do you refuse military service for the sake of religion?”

He therefore ordered Martin to be confined. Martin then signed himself with the sign of the cross in the name of the Lord Jesus. Protected not by shield or helmet [Note: [Column 0011D] That is, “or”], I shall safely penetrate the battle-line in a wedge formation [Note: [Column 0011D] Thus written instead of *penetrabat*. In Sulpicius Martin himself says this].

On the following day the enemy sent envoys to ask for peace, surrendering themselves and all their possessions [Note: [Column 0012D] Namely, surrendering themselves]. Thus the man of God was freed from the tyrant’s persecution. Julian returned to Rome as emperor.

In the end, such wickedness existed in his time that I cannot describe it. He began to close the churches of the saints, open the temples of idols, and cause the property of the churches to be placed in the imperial treasury. After deliberation with his officials, he ordered that the church of Saint Sylvester on Mount Serapti and its dependencies—which had been built from the foundations of this church—and the property of that church be placed in the treasury, so that, as though through hatred of the emperor Constantine, what had been accomplished might be destroyed.

At that same time, by the will of almighty God, war arose between the Persians and the impious emperor Julian. He marched into Persia. What wickedness he exercised [Note: [Column 0012D] That is, “practiced”] against blessed Basil, archbishop, when he marched there, we shall now pass over.

When he had advanced and reached that place, the Romans engaged the Persians in battle. Julian, the most impious emperor, was defeated and held fast, and was grievously afflicted by the Persians. Julian himself was flayed from the crown of his head to the nails of his feet. His skin, dyed scarlet, was kept there for all time by the king of the Persians; whenever there was peace, they sat upon Julian’s skin and rejoiced together.

Julian reigned two years and eight months.

**2.** When Jovian became a most Christian emperor, the churches were opened and the Christian religion began to rejoice. Jovian reigned eight months.

Damasus [Note: [Column 0012D] From Bede, who took part of it from the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*], bishop of Rome, built a basilica beside the theater [Note: [Column 0012D] That is, “beside the theater”] for Saint Lawrence, and another basilica in the catacomb where the bodies of the holy apostles Peter and Paul lay. In that place he adorned with verses the *platoniam* [Note: [Column 0011] *Platoniam* in the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*], the very spot where the holy bodies lay.

That same year, after Auxentius’s death and the appointment of Ambrose as bishop at Milan, all Italy was converted to the true faith. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, died; Martin succeeded him as bishop.

Concerning him the Apostle says:

> “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19).

And concerning him the Lord says:

> “And I, if I be lifted up, will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).

Pope Damasus built the church of Saint Sylvester on Mount Serapti with the utmost care, and restored whatever of its property and adjoining possessions had been taken away.

While praying in the basilica at the consecration of the most blessed bishop Sylvester, he gave thanks to the Lord, saying:

> I return thanks to you, hope of the life of the good,  
> who granted me to know the sacred rite,  
> which the impious apostate Julian destroyed,  
> and to overcome the wicked through love of the heavenly kingdom.  
>   
> I ask and entreat you, God: permit me to fulfill blessed things,  
> and grant me to behold the holy joys I desire.  
>   
> Almighty Lord, by whom the structure of the world stands,  
> who rule heaven and earth and send forth lightning,  
> without whom no created heaven or earth flourishes:  
> may heaven and earth praise you, powerful through eternity.  
> Let every human being bless you, praise you, and move about in your honor.  
>   
> For that stone is approved at your feet,  
> and Peter, raising it by your right hand, established it upon the waters.  
> And the Israelites once, with you as their guide,  
> crossed the Red Sea upon dry ground [Note: [Column 0012D] That is, “the seas”].  
>   
> To you, together with the Father and the holy Spirit,  
> be glory, majesty, and power, equal throughout the ages.

He composed these verses on stone at the body of the holy one.

Many Roman nobles began to abandon the world and devote themselves in the aforesaid church to a life of holy discipline [Note: [Column 0012D] That is, “zeal”].

In the meantime, I must not remain silent about the glory of this apostolic church. Although all the apostles are believed to have been chosen by the Lord before the ages, as the Apostle teaches:

> “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless in his sight” (Ephesians 1:4),

our Redeemer and Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, before triumphing over the destruction of Satan, rejoicing as victor, and entering the realms of heaven, founded and immovably fortified this holy church—which he acquired with his precious blood—through the blessed apostles and apostolic men.

The emperor Constantine wonderfully strengthened and solidified it, so that it might always remain inviolate and glorious and, through the building of those men and their new offspring [Note: [Column 0013D] “Offspring”], gather very many sons.

**3.** What happened afterward: Valens, together with Gratian, son of his brother Valentinian, for four years [Note: [Column 0013D] What follows through chapter 6, concerning the plundering of the city, is all taken from Bede].

Valens issued a law that monks unwilling to serve in the army were to be killed with clubs. The nation of the Huns and Vandals [Note: [Column 0014D] “And Vandals” is absent from Bede], which had been shut away in mountains inaccessible for a long time [Note: [Column 0013] Bede has “long inaccessible”], suddenly, roused and inflamed by savage fury, attacked the Goths. They were scattered [Note: [Column 0013] Bede has “scattered here and there”], thrown into confusion, and expelled from their ancient dwellings.

The Goths crossed the Danube in flight. They were received by the emperor Valens without laying down their arms, but soon, compelled by hunger through “the great tribe of the Avars, [of] a leader” [the corrupt text; Note: [Column 0013] Bede has “through the avarice of Maximus”], they were driven to revolt. After defeating the emperor Valens, they sent their army through Thrace, and, mingling together [Note: [Column 0013] Bede has “mixing together”], poured everything into slaughter, fires, and plunder.

**4.** Gratian, with his brother Valentinian, for six years. The emperor Theodosius defeated those Scythian peoples—namely, the Alans, Huns, and Goths—in many great battles, and so forth.

**5.** The emperor Arcadius, son of Theodosius, together with his brother Honorius, for thirteen years. The Goths entered Italy; first the Vandals and Alans, afterward the Goths, and so forth.

**6.** Honorius, together with the younger Theodosius, son of his brother, for fifteen years. Alaric, king of the Goths, invaded Rome and burned part of it, on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, in the year 1164 from the foundation of the city. On the sixth day after he had entered and plundered the city, they began to devastate the kingdom of Italy with fire and sword.

Pages 3 through 6 are written by Anastasius, a monk under Nonossus, superior of the monastery of Saint Sylvester.

## Miracles in the monastery of Saint Sylvester

A lamp was broken and, through prayers, was found whole again. Thus his fame grew throughout the kingdom of Italy; even the Goths, bold though they were, were in no way able to approach that church.

Other miracles:

> “Pope Symmachus, hearing of the holy man, established by an official grant in the aforesaid church the entire estate of Transpaitano, together with the male and female tenants living and residing there.”

The author continues:

**7.** At the time of which we have spoken, Theodoric, king of the Goths, had Symmachus the consul and patrician murdered at Ravenna. Symmachus had only one daughter, named Galla. She was given to a husband while still in the period of youth, but within the space of one year she was widowed by his death.

Although the abundance of the world, together with wealth and age, called her to renew the marriage bed, she chose instead to be joined to God in spiritual marriage, by which one begins in mourning but reaches eternal joys.

Accordingly, she ordered all her possessions—her inheritance and marriage-property from her husband [Column 0014A]—to be used in building holy churches.

She possessed an estate with a mountain called Campana, situated in the territory of Collina. On one side were the boundaries of Cusia; on the second side, streams with water called the Cava, which the inhabitants of the region call Carba; on the third side was a stream called the Grifianellus; and on the fourth a great river. Beside the water she ordered walls to be built from the foundations.

Upon the whole mass of the walls she constructed a church in honor of Saint Andrew the Apostle, beside the river itself. Near that church was a harbor called Bonus.

In the estate of Pontianellus she built a church in honor of Saint Lawrence, martyr and Levite.

When she had transferred the estate with the mountain of Campana and its appurtenances to the monastery of Saint Sylvester, called Mount Serapti, by means of chartered documents, she built a church of Saint John the Baptist near the place called Tarega, in Nepi territory, together with all her property, and established it within the church of the holy Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, our Lady, and within the bishopric of the city of Nepi.

The most excellent patrician Galla also constructed two churches in Collina territory, in honor of the prince of the apostles Peter: one basilica called the Mother Church, and another called Ascuto [Note: [Column 0013] “Ascuto” agrees with the codex]. Together with all their property, she established them in full within the bishopric of Nepi.

Likewise, in Sabina territory, within the estate called Cornicle, commonly known as Septimiliana, she established a basilica in honor of Saint Valentine, bishop, together with all the possessions belonging to that church, within the bishopric of Sabina [Note: [Column 0013] The abbreviation “S. q. e. e. i. c. q. d. F.” is written by another hand or at another time, but in the same period], which was built in the city called Forum Novum.

In the aforesaid territory of Sabina she also established the church of Saint Peter at Tarano, with all its possessions, within the aforesaid bishopric.

After completing the work of constructing the churches of God and making these endowments to the venerable places, she cast off secular clothing and devoted herself to the service of almighty God in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, entering the monastery.

There, for many years, devoted to simplicity of heart and prayer, she generously performed works of almsgiving for the needy.

When almighty God had nearly decided to repay her labors with her reward, she was struck in the breast by ulcers of cancer. One night, while she lay exhausted by this illness, she saw the blessed apostle Peter standing before her.

She said to him:

> “What is it, my lord? Have my sins been forgiven me?”

The prince of the apostles graciously inclined his head and answered with a nod:

> “They have been forgiven; come!”

When these things had thus ended, the vision of the apostle standing beside her and speaking with her was taken away.

On the third day, however, she died from the illness mentioned above.

What happened remains, even to this day, as a memorial of her in that same monastery. These events took place in the time of Alaric, king of the Goths.

**8.** When Alaric died, Totila, the most impious king of the Goths, succeeded him in the kingdom. During his time, many wicked deeds were committed in the kingdom of Italy, and Roman territories were brought under subjection.

The holy confessors of God were seized, beaten, afflicted, and killed for Christ. Many churches in the kingdom of Italy were destroyed, and cities were burned with sword and fire.

He also caused the bridges over the Tiber on the Salarian Way to collapse from their foundations. The river had previously been called the Albula; it was called the Tiber after Tiberinus, a king and son of King Capis, and bridges had been built across it.

Justinian, nephew of Justin (the text reads *uxore*). Narses, patrician of Rome, was summoned and chosen by all the Roman people. His appearance was unusual, but he was exceedingly wise. His voice was sweet, and he was perfectly suited to investigate and govern the Roman empire.

Then wicked men arose from the Roman territories, together with the Goths, who were laboring and plotting the destruction of the patrician Narses, seeking how he might be expelled and driven from the Roman empire.

**9.** When Justinian himself died, Justin the Younger succeeded him in the kingdom. Narses had defeated and killed Totila, king of the Goths, in Italy. Afterward the Goths had no king in Italy.

The account of Narses’s quarrel with the Romans and of the empress “Sufficia” follows.

John, bishop and pontiff of the Roman Church, built and dedicated the church of the apostles Philip and James, which his predecessor Pelagius had begun. The faithful people call it “Saints Apostles” [Note: [Column 0015D] “John … dedicated” is taken from Bede].

Concerning Alboin, Narses, and his being summoned to Italy, from Bede’s *Chronicle*, the author continues:

Narses the patrician made an amicable agreement with the Lombards, and they established a pact and understanding among themselves concerning the kingdom of Italy.

When Alboin, king of the Lombards, died, Rothari succeeded him as king [Note: [Column 0015D] “By no means”]. Narses and Rothari then became, as it were, brothers in the kingdom, and they took counsel about how the kingdom of Italy might be snatched from the emperor Justin [Note: [Column 0015] “Justinian” corrected to “Justin”] and his successors.

Rothari, an excellent and most warlike man, became strong; no one in his time was like him.

Narses gave him advice concerning the ports in the kingdom of Italy, that he should destroy all of them. This was done, and the kingdom of Italy was freed from the yoke of Constantinople. From that day onward, the Romans no longer paid tributes to the Greek emperors.

Narses the patrician built a church with a monastery for the blessed apostle Paul, called “at the Salvian Waters,” where the relics of the blessed martyr Anastasius are venerated.

He constructed a bridge over the Tiber and restored it better from its foundations. He also established many endowments for all the churches within the city of Rome.

He made an agreement with King Rothari concerning the Pentapolis and the territories of Tuscany: just as Constantine had established them for the holy Roman Church, so they were to remain secure.

After a written instrument had been received from King Rothari in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, the Lombards proceeded to the city of Ticinum. Thus the kingdom of Italy became the dwelling place of the Lombards.

Narses therefore caused the monastery of Mount Serapti to receive these things, and established for it endowments and possessions. Peace was made between the Lombards and the Romans, though it did not last long.

Afterward Rome was ruled by patricians.

The emperor Tiberius Constantine [Note: [Column 0016D] What follows is from Bede].

Gregory, sent as *apocrisiarius* of the holy Roman Church to Constantinople, later composed books expounding Job. Eutychius, bishop of that city, had fallen into error; Gregory corrected him in the presence of Tiberius, and so forth, from Bede.

**10.** Soon the Lombard nation, drawn out from the sheath of its dwelling, grew thick upon our neck. The human race that had risen in this land in vast numbers, like a dense field of grain, withered after being cut down.

Cities were depopulated, fortresses overturned, and churches burned. The monasteries of men and women were destroyed. Estates were deserted by everyone and deprived of every cultivator; the land lay empty in solitude.

No owner lived there. The monastery of Mount Serapti was reduced to solitude [Note: [Column 0015] That is, “brought down”], and all its estates were destroyed.

Wild beasts occupied places formerly held by crowds of people. What may be happening in other parts of the world, I do not know.

Rothari, king of the Lombards, slippery in body and very much addicted to wine, held a synod with the bishops [Note: [Column 0015] “Held a synod” agrees with the codex] and composed the laws of the Lombards in edicts [Note: [Column 0016D] That is, “edicts”], so that the Lombards might live in Italy according to law.

But they did not abandon the ancient practices of their paganism. In the Lombard manner they sacrificed a goat’s head to the devil, running around it while fighting and chanting wicked incantations. Anyone who did not consent to this was undoubtedly punished by death, without further questioning.

Rothari, king of the Lombards, died and was buried by the Lombard people in the city of Ravenna.

Pope Sergius found in the sacristy of the blessed apostle Peter a silver chest that had lain for a very long time in an exceedingly dark corner. As the Lord revealed it, he found within it a cross adorned with various stones.

After removing four petals from it, in which gems of extraordinary size were enclosed, he saw that a portion of the life-giving wood of the Lord’s cross had been placed inside.

From that time onward, every year in the basilica of the Savior, called Constantiniana, on the day of its Exaltation, the people kissed and adored it [Note: [Column 0017D] That is, “by all”].

Gysulf, king [Note: [Column 0017] “Duke” in Bede] of the Lombards, devastated Benevento in Campania with fire, sword, and captivity at the beginning of his reign [Note: [Column 0017] The words “at the beginning of his reign” are absent from Bede].

When there was no one able to resist his assault, Pope John, who had succeeded Sergius, sent priests and many gifts to him and redeemed all the captives, causing the enemies to return home.

But, by the marvelous favor of God, that tyrant Gysulf, king of the Lombards, was killed by his own men.

**11.** Ereberectus [Note: [Column 0017D] For what follows through “the apostle Peter,” compare Bede, whom our author interpolated] was strengthened as king of the Lombards. He began carefully to inquire into the patrimonies of the Cottian Alps, considering very seriously, out of love for Peter, prince of the apostles, how they had been taken away by his predecessors and how they belonged to the apostolic see, though they had long been held by the Lombards.

He restored them to the jurisdiction of that see and sent the donation, written in letters of gold, to Rome.

John was pope. Among many illustrious works, he built an oratory of the holy Mother of God, executed with splendid workmanship inside the church of the blessed apostle Peter, at the place called “at the Veronica.”

When Ereberectus, king of the Lombards, heard of the destruction of the monastery of Saint Sylvester on Mount Serapti, a request was made by John of this apostolic see that he retain it in his royal hands. When this had been done, the monastery was restored with all its possessions, and the government of the holy life of discipline remained peacefully in the monastery, together with the territories of Tuscany.

**12.** When Ereberectus, king of the Lombards, died, Liubrandus [Note: [Column 0017D] “Liubrandus … confirmed” is from Bede] succeeded him as king of the Lombards.

He confirmed, at the admonition of the venerable Pope Gregory, who had succeeded John, the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps [Note: [Column 0017D] That is, “of the Alps”], which King Ereberectus had made and he had reclaimed [Note: [Column 0017] “Ereberectus” in the codex].

King Liubrandus died during his reign.

### 12*

King Grimuald succeeded to the kingdom and governed the reins of the Lombard realm. His son Romuald ruled the Samnites. The distinguished priest Barbatus, whose name I have mentioned above, shone by the will of the Redeemer; his activities at Benevento were celebrated [Note: That is, “celebrated”] and resplendent with miracles.

Although the Lombards in those days were washed in the sacred waters of baptism, they nevertheless retained the ancient rite of paganism and lived as though with a bestial mind. They worshiped the image of a beast commonly called a viper.

King Grimuald, Romuald’s father, held a synod with the Lombard bishops and judges in the city of Milan, before the body of Saint Ambrose, and added to the laws in the edicts that King Rothari had formerly established. King Romuald bowed the necks that ought properly to have been bowed to their Creator. Indeed, not far from the walls of Benevento, as though on a solemn day, they worshiped a sacred tree, on which they hung a hide, and so on, as is related in the Life of Saint Barbatus.

### 13

When all the Lombards in the kingdom of Italy had abandoned error and been converted under Christ’s guidance, they held to the faith of the Holy Trinity.

Meanwhile, Gisa, Romuald’s sister, inflamed with love for Christ, in no way sought the embrace of a man. She was beautiful and of elegant form, and the fame of her beauty spread throughout the whole world.

For it had been reported to Florentius, king of Palermo [Note: That Romuald was besieged by the Greeks, but certainly not by the Saracens, is established from Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards V.7.], how beautiful the girl was. A barbarian host was gathered from Africa, Palermo, and Babylon; fleets and ships hastened in rivalry [Note: That is, “filled out” (*impletum*).] and reached Amalfi, covering the land like locusts. They rushed [Note: That is, “charged upon” (*irruentes*).] upon the city of Benevento, and Romuald saw the barbarian army, because it was numerous, and they were greatly afraid.

Romuald said to the Lombards:

> “Let us rise and go up against our enemies.”

The Lombards replied:

> “We cannot go up against so great an army. It is better for us to seek refuge in our city and save our lives, and to send messengers to our king Grimuald, your father, so that we may fight against them; for we are few.”

Romuald said:

> “Far be that from us. Since the days when King Alboin, our predecessor, led the Lombards out of Pannonia, nothing of this kind has been found among the Lombards. And if the end of our people has come, let us die bravely for our homeland, and let us not abandon victory to our fathers!”

Then there arose a great mourning among the Lombard people, because they were few, especially among the inhabitants of ancient Benevento. Radelchis and the other kinsmen of Prince Romuald were secretly conducting negotiations with the barbarian host. All the princes and the men of their several principalities, including those who seemed strongest, groaned.

Then the glorious prince Romuald went out from the city of Benevento. Suddenly he fell upon the barbarian host; the Lombard army drew near and stood against the barbarian army. Those who were with Romuald sounded the trumpets. The earth was shaken by the voice of both armies, and battle was joined from morning until evening.

Forty thousand men of the barbarian host fell that day. King Florentius fled and, reaching the seashore, went aboard a ship.

Prince Romuald became strong in his deeds like a lion and was like a lion’s cub roaring in battle. He pursued the wicked, chasing them, and victory was delivered into his hands. Then he returned to the city of Benevento, and many peoples spoke of him.

This same prince Romuald built a glorious church where the Lombards had previously worshiped trees, in honor of Saint Felix. There he placed the body of Saint Felix and those of several other saints; he adorned and gilded the church, whose memory remains to this day.

The same Romuald fathered three sons by Theuderada. The first was called Aroald, the second Maroald, and the third Sycardus; the last was Sikinolfus.

The events I relate occurred in the time of Romuald, when the body of the holy apostle Bartholomew was transported from Upper India and arrived at the island of Lipari [Note: That is, “to Lipari.”]. It remained there for several years.

Then, by God’s will, the people of the Hagarenes came [Note: The codex reads *agarorum*.]. They consumed the whole island with fire and sword and razed its walls to their foundations. Thus they reached the little shrine [Note: That is, “the little place”] where the most blessed apostle lay.

When the little shrine had been broken open, the apostle’s bones were found, as it is written:

> “The Lord guards all their bones; not one of them shall be broken” (Psalm 33:21).

That same night the Lord appeared to the apostle’s guardians, saying:

> “Go, gather the apostle’s bones.”

One of them replied, in distress and agitation:

> “Alas! How many years have I persevered in his service, and how many troubles have happened to me. Now all his bones have been broken and mixed with other bones. How can I recognize them among my own bones?”

The Lord said to them:

> “Look for the bones shining like flames among the others; collect those carefully.”

And so it was done. The apostle’s relics were gathered into a clean shroud.

It is the custom of the Hagarenes to ravage Apulia. When this report spread, Romuald sent an army to guard the harbors and the boundaries of the sea.

Thus the Lombards came to the desolated island of Lipari. They saw the man of God and asked him:

> “Whose relics do you venerate here?”

He replied:

> “The body of the most blessed apostle Bartholomew was torn apart by the Hagarenes; now, by God’s wondrous will, it has been gathered again. The Hagarenes are coming once more; I do not know what to do!”

When the Lombards heard this, they rejoiced greatly [Note: The reading is *nimiappreenderunt*.] and took the man, together with the venerable body of the apostle, aboard a ship; then they set sail.

And behold, a large fleet of Hagarenes drew near. When the Lombards saw that their hope was gone, they prostrated themselves devoutly before the apostle’s body with tears and said:

> “Holy apostle Bartholomew, if we are delivered from these dangers and return in peace, in your name we shall make a golden and silver altar within the church of Holy Mary, Mother of God.”

After saying this, they rose from prayer. Then such a great dark confusion arose that no one could see anything between the Lombards and the Hagarenes.

Thus they entered the city of Benevento rejoicing. They brought with them the treasure that they had taken, and delivered it to Prince Romuald. The merits of that apostle’s body, together with the signs associated with it, remain there until the end of the age.

### 14

After some time had passed, the glorious prince died.

His sons, Arud and Maroald, prudent princes and brothers, ruled in his place [Note: Grimoald, son of Romuald, succeeded him.]. Separated from their brothers, they began to live in the city of Nocera [Note: Nocera?]. They left Sycardus and the boy Sykinolfus in the city of Benevento [Note: A fable. Compare Erchempertus.], and their power grew throughout all the territory of Apulia.

Radelchis, their cousin, entered into a conspiracy with the inhabitants of the city of Nocera, and they acted secretly. When the day of the Paschal Epiphanies came, they slaughtered the supreme prince by night in the church of that city.

When Prince Sycardus heard of his brother’s death, he remembered the valor of his fathers and of his own Lombard people. He gathered an army in hostile fashion and came to the city of Nocera.

Nocera was a large and very strongly fortified city. The Lombards began to besiege it, devastating its settlements with fire and sword, and destroying its fortifications. They surrounded the city with a circuit of defenses, so that the inhabitants of Nocera could not raise their hands against the assault of the warriors.

The Lombards fought against them for many days and constructed siege engines. Prince Sycardus sent envoys from the city of Benevento to the boy Sykinolfus, his brother, asking him to come to him.

Sykinolfus the prince went out with a multitude of men and attacked the city of Nocera. He killed many people. They captured the city and burned it with fire, together with its people and women, so that not one of them remained. He overturned the walls and demolished the fortifications of the city from their foundations.

Sycardus returned to the city of Lavello. Sykinolfus entered the city of Benevento, and they began to administer justice to the people and kill the wicked.

For Radelchis’s plan was vain and most evil. He sent envoys to the city of Salerno, to Bishop Leo, asking that Sykinolfus the boy be sent to the city of Salerno so that he might be instructed in the art of letters. This was carried out, and their request was fulfilled.

The same Sikinolfus ruled in the city of Salerno [Note: That is, “while he ruled.”]

The Beneventans, united in plotting the death of Prince Sycardus, sent messengers to Leo, bishop of Salerno, asking him to put out Sykinolfus’s eyes, so that they themselves might exercise authority over the principality of Benevento and take possession of the city of Salerno.

Bishop Leo did not consent to their plan.

Then the united Beneventans went to the city of Lavello and began peacefully to relate to Prince Sycardus the matters they had in mind. The prince received their words kindly and treated them honorably.

Then one of them seized a sword and struck the prince, whereupon they began to cut his whole body to pieces with iron. They burned the city of Lavello and returned to the city of Benevento.

They swore among themselves that they would no longer submit to Prince Sykinolfus.

Then Prince Sykinolfus rose up, together with all the brothers who had joined him. They fought great battles, extended his power over his Lombard people, clothed himself in a cuirass like a giant, girded on his weapons of war, and prepared himself for battle.

When he came from the city of Benevento, the unhappy Beneventans sent messengers to Sykinolfus, saying:

> “These men are murderers; we place them in your hands. The land is under your authority.”

Sykinolfus, prince of Salerno, took vengeance for his brother. Forty-six men from Benevento were slaughtered and hanged.

He went to the city of Salerno as a victor. A great division then arose between Benevento and its successors, and Salerno and its successors, and that division continues to the present day (A.D. 712).

### 15

Liuprandus, king of the Lombards, fought against the people of the Avars in the region of Aquileia. He trampled down Aquileia and Venetia, as well as the islands of Sardinia and Corsica, and enlarged the kingdom of the Lombards.

Having become a most Christian and Catholic king, he held a synod of canons with the bishops and clergy concerning the faith of the Holy Trinity. The king of the Lombards admirably arranged matters that had previously been left unsettled.

This same king ruled honorably for many years, and the kingdom of the Lombards and Romans was at peace.

### 16 (A.D. 743)

This same king fathered two sons [Note: Not at all; compare Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards VI.56]. The first was called Rachis, the second Astulphus.

Rachis was established in the kingdom by his father and became king of Italy while his father was still alive. King Liuprandus died (A.D. 744, September).

Rachis took as his wife Tassia, from the city of Rome, and broke the paternal Lombard law concerning *morgincap* and *mithio*, which had been fixed in their laws; he did not fulfill it.

He made written donations to the Romans, just as the Romans themselves had requested. Because of this the Lombards were angered against King Rachis and began negotiations with Astulphus concerning his kingdom.

King Rachis went to the ancient city of Pinna, which had been destroyed. There were Lombard inhabitants there, including a man named Lupo, who had died without heirs. It is established in the laws of the Lombards that when a Lombard dies without heirs, his estate succeeds to the royal fisc.

King Rachis therefore took possession of all Lupo’s property under his royal authority.

Queen Tassia asked Rachis, her husband, to go with her to the monastery of Saint Silvester on Mount Soracte for prayer, since it was the custom of the Romans to visit there frequently.

The king consented to his wife’s request and came with his retinue to the mountains of Soracte. As he hastened to the place called “At the Arch,” such a great burning arose in his nostrils that nothing like it had ever before or afterward afflicted him—not only the king and queen, but also all the Lombards who followed them.

When they entered the church beside the body of the most holy Nonnosus, whose memory I mentioned above, not far from the body of Saint Silvester, one of the king’s Lombard parasites was there. He belonged to a Lombard family from the city of Benevento whose members had been afflicted by a demon from generation to generation, because of the curse imposed by the most blessed Bishop Barbatus on Theodora, the wife of Prince Romuald, whose story we mentioned above.

The demon began to cry out through this Lombard:

> “O Nonnosus, why do you trouble me? Now I will not leave here, because we shall succeed to this family from generation to generation. O Bishop Silvester, your power sets me on fire. And if you drive me out from here, I shall return to Benevento, to the kinsman of this man.”

After saying this, the demon tore at him and departed from him. For this reason that Lombard family of Benevento has been called “*tempta-demonium*” (“tempted/demonic”) to the present day.

Such great joy came upon King Rachis, his wife, and all the Lombards who followed them that the ferocity they had formerly possessed was changed into the humility of grace. It would take too long to relate how many tears the Lombards shed in prayer and how many gifts they offered there.

King Rachis and Queen Tassia, his wife, by a written deed of donation, granted to the venerable monastery of Saint Silvester and the most blessed Nonnosus one estate called Ustriciano, in the territory of Spoleto, in the district called Pinna. A church in honor of Saint Silvester had been built within that estate, together with all the adjoining and appurtenant properties belonging or pertaining to it, just as Duke Lupo had held them in his own hands.

The king remained on that mountain for three days, giving thanks to God, and then returned from the city of Spoleto.

The Lombards, inflamed with fury, as was the custom of their people, unanimously demanded that Astulphus break the written donations made by King Rachis, so that they would no longer belong to the Lombards [Note: Benedict’s narrative is supported by a previously unknown law of Aistulphus, which it is useful to present here from the Parisian codex of the Lombard edicts, no. 4613:

> “First of all they decreed concerning those donations that were made by King Rachis and his wife Tassia, that none of those grants which were later made after Aistulphus had been made king by Rachis should in any way remain valid, unless Aistulphus should again grant them to the person to whom they had been given.”

].

The Lombards also asked Astulphus to meet with the bishops, abbots, superiors of hospices, and guardians of the churches, and to have this fixed in the edictal laws.

Astulphus swore and promised that he would do this if the Lombards granted him the kingdom.

### 17

Astulphus was crowned in the city of Milan (A.D. 749, June), within the church of Bishop Saint Ambrose, and was elected king in the month of June [Note: Thus we have the date of Aistulphus’s accession precisely established; compare Brunetti, *Codice diplomatico toscano* I, 387], in the tenth indiction [Note: Tenth in the codex; “second” should be read].

At that time such great wickedness flared up as had never been found among his predecessors.

He held a synod with Valerius, archbishop of the city of Ravenna, and Conaldus, archbishop of the city of Milan, together with the surrounding bishops [Note: That is, “the neighboring bishops”], abbots, judges, and Lombard officials remaining in the kingdom of Italy. He drew up chapters as the Lombards had requested and ordered them affixed to the edicts.

Then wicked Roman men arose and told King Astulphus to come, seize the territories of Tuscany, and usurp the Roman Empire.

His heart was exalted, not in God or in honor of the churches, but in war, plunder, fire, and the sword.

When they came into the city of Spoleto, he sent Robert, count of the palace, from Savina, to guard the roads and harbors and prevent the Romans from using the route.

He sent Grimuald from Centucella to guard the Roman roads and the sea harbors. He sent a message to the city of Terracina to guard the maritime and land routes, so that nothing might be sold to any Roman and no property obtained.

King Astulphus went into the Tiburtine plain with six thousand Lombards, and great fear arose among the Romans. They made agreements with the city of Tivoli and with the city of Pristina, so that the Romans would have neither intercourse nor friendship with him.

The Lombards burned the churches of the saints, where their bodies rested. They ravaged all Tuscany with fire and sword, while the city of Nepi remained under their authority. The many attacks that he now launched against the Romans cannot be related one by one. The fortresses of the Romans were destroyed, and monasteries and towns were ravaged; they could find no hope of recovery.

Stephen was pontiff in the city of Rome [Note: The following should be compared with the Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs concerning Zacharias and Stephen]. Seeing himself placed in such desolation, he said:

> “Alas, what shall I do? The Italian kingdom has been oppressed by many peoples: first by the Medes and the Lanes, afterward by the Gauls, third by the Goths, fourth by the Lombards. Since possession was established in Italy, finally, by the great bishop Zacharias, my predecessor, whom by God’s authority I serve, calamities have overwhelmed it. The impious Lombards have devastated the city; they have destroyed the monasteries of men and women throughout the territories of Tuscany; the basilicas of the saints have been burned. He has condemned himself to exile because of the work of God’s churches.

> “Pipin, one of the Franks, who came from Francia, came. King Pipin received him joyfully and honorably, inviting him into Italy so that he might establish the Lombard people under his authority. This Pipin ruled the Frankish people together with Charlemagne. We shall explain below the order and origin of these events.

> “A dispute arose between Pipin and Charlemagne concerning the Frankish kingdom. Pope Zacharias was asked by Charlemagne to grant the monastery of Saint Silvester on Mount Soracte, by pontifical decree, in perpetual right. The supreme pontiff willingly granted this, and he established by fixed right all its appurtenances, just as they had been arranged in earlier times.

> “Pipin and Charlemagne sent envoys from Pope Zacharias to King Astulphus, and found them in the city of Ticinum. They made known everything and how it had been carried out. Astulphus, the most wicked, impious, and crafty king of the Lombards, composed his words honorably and restored to the Romans all the Pentapolis, the territories of Tuscany, and whatever seemed to belong to the holy Roman Church.

> “Nevertheless, they did not depart from their evil custom. After taking counsel with the bishops and those who feared God about what they ought to do concerning the persecution of the Lombards—whether the Italian kingdom and Roman Empire should fall to the Greek people, or whether the Franks should enter Italy—they concluded: ‘It is better for us to be subject to the rule of the Franks than to that of the Greeks.’”

### 18

Robert, count of the Lombard palace from Savina, went out to fight against the Romans. Thus he came to the city of Lubria, where battle was joined with the Romans. Many Romans, both commoners and nobles, fell.

Robert the Lombard took up his position in the field and had a strong force. Then the bishop, in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, addressed the people, saying:

> “May help from heaven be with you. Choose to fight against the Lombards; do not be afraid!”

The Romans went against Robert the Lombard. And behold, the Lombard army was crossing the river Lubria. The Romans pursued them, and nearly two hundred Lombards were slaughtered and killed by the sword. Robert, count of the palace, was also killed, and the Romans returned as victors.

After this, the most holy Pope Stephen set out on the road for the sake of the Roman people and the defense of that holy Church. He came to Francia, to the palace at Aachen, seeking help and consolation for the rights of Saint Peter.

King Pipin received the apostolic envoy honorably. They went together to Saint-Denis.

Pipin said to the apostolic envoy [Note: From the *Annales Laurissenses*, A.D. 74.]:

> “Your predecessor Zacharias informed me through my envoys, Bishop Burgardus and the chaplain Folradus, about the kings in Francia who at that time did not possess royal power, asking whether this was right or not. Pope Zacharias instructed me that it would be better for me to be called king, since I possessed the power, rather than for the man who remained without royal power, so that the order might not be disturbed through apostolic authority.

> “Accordingly [Note: That is, “thence” (*inde*).], I, Pipin, was elected king according to the custom of the Franks and anointed by the hands of the blessed Archbishop Boniface. I was raised by the Franks to the kingship in the city of Soissons. Ilderic the Saxon, who was falsely called king, was tonsured and sent to a monastery.

> “After the death of our father Charles, I divided the Frankish kingdom with my brother Charlemagne at the place called Poitiers [Note: *Annales Laurissenses*, A.D. 742]. In that same year my brother Charlemagne devastated Alamannia. Then [Note: *Ibid.*, A.D. 745.] Charlemagne confessed to me, his brother Pipin, that he wished to abandon the world, and that year he would undertake no warfare; nevertheless, I sent him away honorably with gifts.”

When the apostolic envoy heard these things, he confirmed Pipin as king through holy anointing, and with him anointed his two sons, Lord Charles and Charlemagne, as kings [Note: “King” corrected to “kings”] [Note: *Annales Laurissenses*, A.D. 754].

Then Charlemagne went to Rome to the threshold of the apostles [Note: *Annales Laurissenses*, A.D. 746]. After this he entered the monastery on Mount Soracte, where he was tonsured and became a monk.

### 18*

Let us now hear what great glory he established there.

Seeing that it was arduous for the brothers to toil on the mountain, he built at the foot of the mountain, at the place called “At Marianum” [Note: That is, “At Marianum”], a monastery in honor of Saint Stephen the martyr. He joined all the brothers to it except the abbot and left several brothers there for the use of the earlier monastery.

He remained for some time in the monastery of Saint Stephen, but his spirit was not at ease in that place.

One day, while traveling through the fields belonging to that monastery toward the church of the apostle Saint Andrew, beside the river, he was investigating the church’s properties below Mount Grifianellus. He found the ancient fortress called Aquari, which sends forth waters at the foot of Mount Grifianellus.

He examined it carefully for a long time, observed all the buildings that seemed suitable for the work of a monastery, and then returned to the monastery.

After taking counsel with the brothers concerning the fortress of Bahiano—how and in what manner a monastery should be built beside the fortress, dedicated to the Lord Prince of the Apostles Peter, to Saint Benedict, and in commemoration of the apostle Saint Andrew—it has remained there to the present day.

The man of God Charlemagne purchased the aforementioned field, one estate called Saint Vitus, with the woodland [Note: That is, *silva*, “forest”; *wald*] called Corgitu.

Likewise, the estate of Saint Gregory, with its male and female tenants; the estate of Petronianus and that of Asinianus; the estate of Saint Heristus and its appurtenances; the estate of Fanianus, six *unciae*; the estates of Priscianus, in which is the church of Saint Victor, with its male and female tenants; the estate of Flabianellus; the estate of Robellus; and the estate of Corbianus; the estate of Magere with its appurtenances; the estate of Cotteanus, in which is the church of Saint Benedict, or whatever other name it bears, with the male and female servants residing there, the huts and the farmstead; the estate of Clarano; the farmstead of Cerole; the farmstead of Rufianus Grassus, with male and female tenants; the estate of Carpinianus; the estate of Cossanus; the estate of Torritula; the estate of Sentianus, three *unciae*; the estate of Folianus; and the estate of Bassanus, with the church of Saint Valentine, with its male and female servants; the estate of Aurelianus; six *unciae* of the estate of Celedranus; the estate of Cecilianus, with male and female tenants; the estate of Laurianus; the estate of Grazzanus; the estate of Marianus, with male and female servants; the estate of Forianus; four *unciae* of the estate of Terrentianellus; the estate of Marcellianus; the estate of Pulbina; the estate of Bersianus; the estate of Grifianus; the estate of Belgarolus; six *unciae* of the estate of Ofianus; the estate of Maturis; the estate of Patinara; the estate of Montone, with its male and female servants; the estate of Salvianus; the estate of Cerbinarola; the estate of Pattialis; three *unciae* of Casaventoli; eight *unciae*; the estate of Antiquus; the estate of Priscianus; the estate of Quarazzanus; the estate of Pontinianus; the estate of Catonianus; the estate of Ciminianus; the estate of Matitianus; eight *unciae* of the estate of Paonis; the estate of Terlata; the estate of Barbarica; the estate of Casa Crisciani; the estate of Vallescura; the estate of Rupiliano; the estate of Damianus; the estate of Asterius; the estate of Martunianus; the estate of Serianus, with two watermills and the cell of Saint Silvester; the estate of Saint Prosperus, called Cacahelli; the estate of Munitioni; the estate of Junianus; the estate of Proniamus; the estate of Mitilianus; the estate of Ruscianus; the estate of Plaga Montes; the estate of Pollianus, with the church of Saint Mary and its male and female servants; the estate of Scatianus; the estate of Carianus; the estate of Manianus; the estate of Occisus; and six *unciae* of the estate of Rutilianus.

### 19

Again, a complaint was made to King Pipin and his sons Charles and Charlemagne concerning King Astulphus of the Lombards and the violence he was inflicting upon the holy Roman Church and the Roman people.

When King Pipin heard these words from the apostolic envoy, he was deeply saddened on account of the apostolic journey and swore, saying:

> “I shall come in person.”

A summons went out from the king to the Frankish people, to Saxony, the regions of Aquitaine, Bavaria, Wasconia [Note: That is, Wasconia], Alamannia, and all his kingdoms, ordering everyone to take the field on the Kalends of May against King Astulphus and the Lombard people.

Charlemagne the monk, Pipin’s brother, having completed the monastery of the apostle Saint Andrew and all that belonged to the use of the monastery, saw that he was not united in customs with the people and with his brothers’ monasteries [Note: *conjunctus* corrected to *conjunctum*.]. He therefore departed from there [Note: Compare *Annales Laurissenses*, A.D. 746, and Einhard, *Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 2] into the province of Samnium, to Mount Cassino, to the monastery of Saint Benedict, and remained there.

When the Lombard king Astulphus heard that King Pipin of the Franks was coming against him with the transalpine peoples, King Astulphus quickly came from the monastery of Saint Benedict on Mount Cassino. He asked and entreated the abbot of that monastery, promising many gifts, to send the monk Charlemagne to his brother King Pipin, so that he might thwart Pope Stephen’s plans and prevent the Franks from entering Italy.

After receiving the blessing of his abbot and the brothers, Charlemagne willingly set out and thus came to Francia [Note: Compare the *Life of Pope Stephen*, chapter 30, and *Annales Laurissenses*, A.D. 753].

The monk Charlemagne told Pipin everything that had happened in order. King Pipin refused to follow his counsel.

King Pipin, responding to the apostolic invitation, set out for Italy to seek justice for the blessed apostle Peter [Note: Compare *Annales Laurissenses*, A.D. 755].

King Astulphus of the Lombards, resisting the aforesaid justice, sought the Lombard fortifications. Pipin the king and the Franks came against him, and the Franks and Lombards entered into battle.

The Lombards were put to flight, with the help of the Lord and through the intercession of the blessed apostle Peter, and King Pipin with the Franks emerged victorious.

That same year Pope Stephen was brought back to the holy see by the envoys of Lord King Pipin, Bishop Folradus and the others who were with him.

King Astulphus was shut up in the city of Pavia and promised to carry out the justice of Saint Peter. Therefore King Pipin, having received forty hostages together with their oaths, returned to Francia.

The monk Charlemagne remained in the city of Vienne together with Lady Queen Berta [Note: Bertrada, the queen]. He languished in illness for many days and died in peace.

When King Pipin saw that what King Astulphus of the Lombards had previously promised concerning the rights of Saint Peter was not true, he once again set out for Italy with Pope Stephen’s envoys. He besieged Pavia and shut up King Astulphus of the Lombards. He confirmed more and more strongly the rights of Saint Peter, so that those things which Astulphus had previously promised should remain firm. In addition, he took Ravenna together with the Pentapolis and the entire Exarchate, and by decree he handed them over to Saint Peter.

He also ordered, through the apostolic envoys, that no one should dare to damage or violate the monastery of the apostle Saint Andrew.

When King Pipin returned, the aforementioned wicked King Astulphus wished to deny what he had previously promised, release the hostages, and break his oaths. One day he went hunting, but, struck by God’s judgment, he ended his life.

### 20

The Lombards took counsel about how they might save themselves from the Franks and raised Desiderius to the kingship. How and in what manner this happened afterward we shall relate.

Pope Stephen, seeing that he was victorious on every side and that the glory of the bishop and of the Roman people was triumphant, began to build a church in the city of Rome, near the Via Flaminia, in honor of Saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius. It stood opposite [Note: Opposite the Campus Martius?], not far from the monument of Augustus [Note: That is, the mausoleum of Augustus], and decorated with beautiful architectural forms, as he had seen in Francia.

The emperor Constantine sent King Pipin, from Constantinople, an organ among other gifts, which reached Francia [Note: This account through “preserve it” is from the *Annales Laurissenses*, A.D. 757.].

King Pipin held his assembly at Compiègne with the Franks. There Tassilo, duke of the Bavarians, came and commended himself to him by placing his hands in his, swore many and innumerable oaths, placed his hands upon the relics of the saints, and promised fidelity to King Pipin and to his sons Charles and Charlemagne, with a right-minded heart and firm devotion, as a vassal ought to act toward his lord.

The aforementioned Tassilo confirmed this upon the bodies of Saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, as well as Saint Germanus and Saint Martin, promising that he would preserve it throughout all the days of his life.

King Pipin went into Saxony [Note: This account through “died” is from the *Annales Laurissenses*, A.D. 758.], and the strength of the Saxons was broken by his power at the place called Simnia. A great slaughter was made among the Saxon people.

Then they promised Pipin to fulfill all his wishes and to present honors at his assembly, even up to three hundred horses every year.

A son was born to King Pipin [Note: This account through “died” is from the *Annales Laurissenses*, A.D. 759.], and the aforementioned king gave him his own name, so that he would be called Pipin like his father. He lived for two years and died in the third.

That same year King Pipin went to Rome [Note: It is certain that Pippin never went to Rome.]. Pope Stephen and all his clergy, together with the sacred orders and the Roman people, went out to meet the king with hymns and praises and came to the church of Saint Peregrinus.

King Pipin observed the Roman people and their actions and joyfully arrived at the church of the Prince of the Apostles. His solemnity of Masses was celebrated, and it would take too long to relate how many alms he gave to the poor and what gifts he made to the churches.

King Pipin remained in the city of Rome for one month. Lord Pope Stephen then began to fall ill. King Pipin was troubled and afraid for the apostolic man’s death. On the appointed day, Stephen died.

An assembly of the Roman people was held with King Pipin concerning Paul, the brother of Pope Stephen, so that he might preside over the apostolic chair. He was elected by the Roman people and clergy, by King Pipin, and by the Frankish people, and was elected to the most holy see of the blessed apostle Peter.

He established all the Roman territory, the territories of Tuscany, the entire Pentapolis, and the mountains of the Goths in the church of the blessed apostle Peter.

Giving thanks to God and to the Prince of the Apostles, he returned to Francia.

21. Then King Pippin, seeing Waifar, duke of the Aquitanians, etc. What follows is taken from the *Annals of Lorsch*, for the years 760, 761, and 762, up to: “Pippin … returned to Francia through Legemodica.” And the people became powerful. He proceeded to Italy [Note: There is no doubt that what follows was found by our author.] to arrange the Italian kingdom. He wintered the whole season in the monastery of Saint Andrew the Apostle, Saint Silvester the Confessor of Christ, and Saint Stephen the Martyr; moreover, in the territory of Tuscany he established, by a charter issued in his own name, all the property of the monastery that had been acquired by his brother Charlemagne. He also granted to the venerable monastery the cross of the Lord that hung around his neck; likewise he established under his oath the principality of Benevento, Salerno, Capua, and the whole territory of Naples, together with whatever had been abandoned in Campania. He granted the whole Pentapolis and all the territory of Tuscany to the apostolic [see] of Paul and to his own jurisdiction. Rejoicing and glad, he came to Francia.

Then [Note: “Then … Tassilo,” from the *Annals of Lorsch*, year 764.] King Pippin held his assembly at Worms, and undertook no other expedition, but remained in Francia. The mildest king was dealing with the matter between Waifar and Tassilo, because Tassilo was his kinsman. Then King Pippin sent his envoys to Bavaria, to Tassilo, speaking these words to them:

> “King Pippin of the Franks has sent us to you, so that we may make known to you the benefit and honor that King Pippin has assigned to you. Because you are my kinsman, he has given you all Bavaria, and you have promised by oath to preserve your allegiance.”

Now Tassilo, moved by this, refused to see the king’s face. Then, etc., as in the *Annals of Lorsch* for the years 766, 767, and 768, up to Pippin’s death. There he died and ended his life on the eighth day before the Kalends of October.

22. Thus Lord Adrian, a Roman by birth, from the district of the Via Lata, of the order of the *scrinium* of the holy Roman Church, was elected pope by the entire Roman people in this seat of the most blessed prince of the apostles.

It is necessary to recount the origin of the Frankish kings through their genealogy: how the most gentle king Charles reached the summit of royal power. Let us now tell it.

The race of the Merovingians was the one from which the Franks were accustomed to create their kings. The first was Pippin, who fathered a son by a concubine named Charles; this was the first Charles called “the Advocate.” Charles fathered two sons, Pippin and Charlemagne, who, claiming dominion over the whole of Francia, subdued it. When this first Charles died—the one who had been deposed from office together with Childeric the Saxon—his brothers Pippin and Charlemagne [Note: Or “brother,” according to one manuscript.] held Francia as though by hereditary right.

This Pippin and Charlemagne, in complete harmony with one another, divided the Frankish kingdom between them. Charlemagne, having been clothed in the habit of holy conduct, while Pippin, through the authority received from the apostolic Stephen, was made king. Pippin fathered two sons, Charles and Charlemagne, who were anointed kings together with their father Pippin by Pope Stephen. When Pippin died, Charles, the glorious, most gentle, and beloved king, succeeded him, together with Charlemagne.

Not long afterward, when King Charlemagne died, his wife and sons, together with certain nobles who agreed with them [Note: That is, “optimates,” leading men.], fled to Italy and placed themselves and their children under the protection of Desiderius, king of the Lombards. Charles, however, was made king by the agreement of all the Franks.

Lord Pope Adrian, unable to endure the persecution of the Lombards, sent envoys with the apostolic blessing. Peter crossed the sea as far as Marseille and then traveled by land to Lord Charles, inviting him, as in the *Annals of Lorsch*, year 773, up to Easter, likewise in Rome.

Lord King Charles was honorably received by Pope Adrian and by the entire Roman people, and in the church of the blessed Apostle Peter he was honored with the praises of the schools. Who could recount the extent of the pestilence, lamentation, and devastation inflicted by the Lombards upon the Roman people? After receiving the blessing and absolution of the blessed Apostle Peter, Lord Charles again captured the city of Pavia, as in the *Annals of Lorsch* for the years 774, 775, 776, 780, and 781, though much is omitted, up to Aquitaine.

On his return, Lord King Charles stayed in the monastery of Saint Andrew the Apostle with his wife, Queen Hildegard, and his entire retinue. He granted to the monastery all the property of the churches [Note: The manuscript originally read *monasteria*; corrected to *monasterii*.] that his cousin Charlemagne had granted to that monastery, as well as the monastery of Saint Silvester with Mount Soracte and the monastery of Saint Stephen at Mariano, together with all their estates, by a charter of his royal power; he also established very extensive gifts there.

After receiving a blessing from the venerable place, he reached the city of Milan, etc., as in the *Annals of Lorsch* for the years 781, 783, 786, 787, 788, and 794, though much is omitted. For the year 786 it adds the reasons why Charles undertook the Italian expedition: he held an assembly concerning their agreements under the laws of Italy, which had not previously been written down by the kings, their predecessors, although they had long before been proclaimed to them. This was done.

For the year 796 it continues:

> It was also announced to him that Adrian, Roman pontiff, whom he held in the highest affection, had died. He wept as though he had lost a brother or a dearest son. For he was very well balanced in his friendships, so that he did not admit them readily, but retained them with the greatest constancy.

Leo immediately succeeded him. He sent envoys with gifts to the king, and also sent him the keys of the confession of Saint Peter and the banner of the Roman city.

He sent to Lord King Charles at the palace of Aachen a treasure gathered over the long duration of many ancient centuries [Note: *Annals of Lorsch*, year unspecified.]. After receiving it, and giving thanks to God, the giver of all good things, that same most prudent and generous man and steward of God sent a large part of it to Rome, to the threshold of the apostles, through his beloved abbot Agilbert. He distributed the remaining portion as gifts to his nobles, clergy, laymen, and other faithful.

The king, having gathered them, etc.—excerpts from the *Annals of Lorsch* for the years 796 and 799—up to: “to Norlaud the Saxon in Bardengau … and there, awaiting Leo the pontiff, he honorably dismissed Charles, his son, just as he had been received.”

Leo immediately set out for Rome. The king returned to his palace at Aachen, and the holy Pope Leo was received there by the aforementioned Charles with the highest honor. The king caused Charles, son of Charles, to exact vengeance upon the Romans, and assigned all the territory of Tuscany, Ravenna, and the Pentapolis to the supreme pontiff. He established the monastery of Saint Silvester on Mount Soracte and the church of Saint Stephen at Mariano by charter in the aforesaid monastery of Saint Andrew, and made more extensive gifts.

After this Lord Charles returned to Aachen. In the middle of November it was reported to him, etc., as in the *Annals of Lorsch* for the year 804, concerning the great gifts bestowed. Lord Pope Leo recounted how great a civil revolt the Romans had raised against him and how the property of the churches had been taken away. The most gentle emperor heard these words and pondered them in his heart.

Then the emperor, intending to go through Bavaria, etc., as in the *Annals of Lorsch*, up to: “He remained with him for nine days; and, as had been said and arranged, he returned to Rome.”

After arranging and putting in order everything that was necessary and required for the holy Roman Church, and for the whole territory of Tuscany, the Pentapolis, and Ravenna, he installed Leo in apostolic authority. He granted the monastery of Saint Andrew the Apostle immunity and ordered it to be affixed in the edicts of the Lombard laws. From there he returned to Francia.

The excerpts from the *Annals of Lorsch* for the years 805, 808, 810, and 814, and from Einhard’s *Life of Charles*, chapters 15 and 16, follow, up to “they declared.”

23. He ordered [Note: The following bracketed passage is an editorial insertion.]

[Since at this point the beginnings of the tale of Charles’s expedition to the Holy Land are read, it seems worthwhile to add to it the beginnings of the fabulous account of his Spanish expedition—namely, a fragment written in the tenth century, which I found inscribed on three leaves at the end of manuscript no. 921 in the Royal Library at The Hague, containing the *Deeds of the Frankish Kings:

“and in the outcome, just as a crafty smile of proud fortune promises itself almost entirely. A rain of weapons hisses, suspended in the air; and the attack presses forward with all the greater force as it is driven by hand. The higher rank turns in the trench, wounded by its own injuries, and inflicts heavy falls upon those behind; and the one who falls announces that the danger is increased by the weight of his companions.

Nor yet had either side perceived the unexpected deeds of misfortune, their senses bound by deep fear and equal numbness, while he restored his breath, already sufficient for his wearied limbs. From afar, alternating fury strikes and presses on with other blows, against which every access through skill and arms had been denied, although valor was everywhere employed, and although impatience for heroic deeds had accomplished marvelous things in war. He moves more freely through the defenses and the hidden passages of the walls.

The winged seed of missiles rebounds upon the coverings of the shields like hail. Iron serves as its companion, and the recalled strength of his men, now ignorant of a dry belly and savage throat, which he had endured so badly, had never satisfied their minds more fully with slaughter—as pious vows deserve.

The sword almost makes all right hands intent upon it; the soldier returns to the nearer walls, and the overflowing trench desires to rise upward. From above a sharpened stake drips and scatters wounds; a heavy millstone crushes the bodies that approach under confused arms. Now the commander is thrust from the fortress by force and driven outside amid vast slaughter. He destroys and kills, since a thousand hands provide assistance to one man.

Before the gates is displayed a chosen and greater crown of men, to guard the entrances and deceive the attackers, so that they may have their backs secure and confidence. There Gradivus [Mars] laughs, marking bloody arms.

And the battle alternates evenly, committed with all its strength, in many and marvelous ways within and without, wherever it can display itself with a threatening horn.

Meanwhile, amid the weight of circumstances and wavering life, the fourth day brought its morning, while the star fled through torn darkness. The solar circuit had made the bright sphere glorious, reddening toward its setting, as it itself announced the rise of the messenger of truth. It is clear that the approach of the distinguished youth had become known, with the report of the common people borne beforehand from afar on the breeze.

There was no delay: as though the eager opening of his spirit were competing, they arrived, exhausted on their war-horses and armed with keys, having conquered the world in many regions. Immediately the fiery soldier of Ernaldus thundered against the walls. Holding his spear, he skillfully gasped before his men; sweat poured everywhere from the commander, his eyes shone, foam gathered around his mouth, and fierce veins beat in his chest. Now his knee faltered; now he stood firmer than an oak.

§ The youth of Bernard, tested in adversity, vomits forth its full strength, and resists whatever may oppose it. Fortune favors his desire and strives to make him prevail.

§ The heavy roar of Bertrand advances where the stronger part of the city rises above ditch and wall, promising in his mind whatever is subject to him, and slaughtering the fighters. With that sound an unbearable blow falls from heaven. Weapons threatening sudden death have driven neither backward nor forward, not even a little; nor has the most dreadful shower of arrows done so. He advances his step still farther, seeing his fate bristle. He takes joy in proving the more difficult danger and counts himself to be something in it.

Already the vigorous hand of the youth moves the walls, and now the iron bars of the gates are broken together with the entire doorpost. A passage is opened, and ruin is revealed everywhere to better advantage. Iron is joined against the enemy. Strengths are stirred on their own behalf, and every right hand acts. The sluggish becomes active; the terrified becomes fierce. Here the spear has no room, but the sword alone fights.

For every blow is useless unless secretly delivered into the belly or breast, since the press was so tight that no hand could be suspended for a stroke. It is uncertain where Mars more fully brings forth men pale with death, or where he strikes the air more gloriously with groaning. He traverses the entrance of the city, its center, and its farthest end. No other figure is seen across such vast spaces, nor does anything retain the color of a greater fate.

Courtyards, fields, houses, boards, thresholds, and doorposts float in blood; in deep corruption the high stones grow wet. Blood lies spread everywhere. Pools redden everywhere. The air swells. Black night settles over the city.

Soon each attendant ran to the war-horses, as the hardened stream of blood crept up to their knees and their submerged footprints held the men who pressed upon them. The kings likewise came together and challenged Mars with all their strength, since it was rightly believed that they could grant the whole world a single day. Each returned more fiercely to the labor of his purpose, and many surrendered their wounds to fate.

O treaty of weapons, never to be satisfied! The quarrel of Mars falters toward the fields of the sword. For nothing more can remain standing with strength in the city, which now prevails; nor does it wish to loosen all necks freely to the sword, receive open movements, and rejoice in the assisting spear as it vibrates.

The earth is astonished, and the hidden fields beneath the gathering, that the city could contain so many men and drive them outside. Here is the question: into whose hands could victory have come, if a fortunate vein had survived?

O bearer of the heavens and the world, whom I have moved by prayer, grant me, as I ask, permission to say something, and stand by me, most holy bishop, with your aid.

Behold, the untamed frenzy of kings surges and swells throughout the immense circles of Mars, and constrains fortune, which by itself neither turns back nor slips where it wishes.

But Emperor Charles restrains himself more greatly, brave and steadfast in reverence for the Thunderer, whom he always knew to be present and generous. He urges his ardent hands toward the love of war. Fear does not compel him to follow so powerful a king; rather, his mind compels him to advance.

He raises his eyes to the stars, his eyes loosened [Note: That is, “his eyes,” according to the manuscript.] by the flowing moisture of tears, and wets his cheeks, lest the offended people should triumph over the heavenly king, and lest the proud should receive spoils.
