§ The lofty commander, mounted on the horse he had purchased through much slaughter, controls the middle ranks with a sword skilled in punishment and scatters death here and there. Thus the weakened right hands withdraw their weapons, which they are unable to hold upright. The outcome of war labors, and the rival order of fate strives to bring upon the clever man Borel, father of a man who was experienced amid the fires of battle, a bitter old age.

There was no delay: the guest remaining in the body [Note: That is, “the soul,” according to the manuscript.] was drained away through the protections of the shield and the triple-woven tunic [Note: *Tonicam* corrected to *tunicam*.]. He lowered his head, but his legs turned upward as he fell; now his broken necks opened upon the ground.

Wibelinus [Note: So the manuscript.] breathes again, nimble and bold, a boy equal to his father in courage but inferior in size, to be balanced in all things by the judging sword. He saw one of Borel’s sons surrounded, roaring from afar, while a thousand men endured the right hand. Intent upon him, he breaks through the path, urging on his horse with a signal from his heel, and immediately comes before him, placing his burning sword between the middle of his temples.

He cuts out the neck according to his accustomed practice, to which he clung more closely, and divides the whole marrow on both sides. His tongue protruded more than a foot as he fell.

§ The thirsting desire for praise reveals how great Ernaldus is and with what achievement he shines. Whatever Bellona prepares, he tears and drags away like a lion whatever he finds, while the savage jaws had long tasted the entrails of the slain and no spoils had satisfied them.

He is able to recognize another of the fraternal line before his own eyes and bends the pliant edge of his spear toward the blow.

The insatiable desire for human praise declares how great the courage of Ernaldus is and with what achievement it shines. Whatever the nature of war requires in the service of valor, he completes without sluggishness. As hungry leonine rage rages over prey encountered by it, so Ernaldus’s courage rages through battles.

After many deeds successfully performed, he sees someone guilty of the slaughter of his brother. Without delay, he hurled a spear at him, and the flying weapon found the enemy’s breastplate passable. By that blow the soldier’s body was driven ten cubits farther. Thus shaken from his horse, he surrendered his life to the underworld.

Moreover, Bertrand’s dreadful hand enters the battle. It struck great fear into the enemy and, with savage weapons, gave harsh fates to many mortals. The right hand of the palatine was accustomed to spare none of the enemy; it immediately left the man who begged for mercy lifeless.

By chance three bodies of youths were presented to him. The first, resisting briefly, had met a hard death there. The terrible lightning of the sword passed through the middle of his head, his throat, his chest, and his navel. His entrails, torn out, fell warm into his lap. The triple-woven tunic refused to place an obstacle before the sharp edge.

Nor was it enough to have killed the human body; the horse, too, was found deprived of life. The sword had split the horse’s spine; at last he was found driven halfway into the earth. Bertrand, dragging him back, turned the remaining parts against the enemy.

There was no delay: the inner fluid became visible and was added to the air. The strong fastenings of the horse’s trappings also burst, together with the belts rattling with metal plates.

Bernard’s terrible boldness likewise swept through the expanses of the fields. Serving Mars fiercely, he deprived many mortals of the light of day. He rejoiced in the honor of a successful victory, by which the chance of fortune thus raised him.”]

This fragment seems to belong to the account of the siege of Pamplona undertaken in 778, which Turpin is also known to describe. It deals with a war against pagans, that is, the Saracens, who with the Franks were masters of the world. Ernoldus or Ernaldus [Col. 0035D] seems to be Arnold, whom the author of the *Life of Louis* reports to have been appointed by Charles as governor of the kingdom of Aquitaine in 781. The same man is called Arnold of Bellanda by Turpin in chapters 11, 14, and 30; according to Turpin, chapter 14, he played a leading part in the capture of Pamplona. Borel, or Burellus, count and prefect of Ausona in 798, took part in the Spanish expedition in 809. Wibelinus may perhaps be understood as Turpin’s Willerin, in chapters 29 and 11, unless William, duke of Toulouse, is intended. In any case, readers will easily notice that complete verses have been inserted into the text.

On the same parchment we read these verses:

> And now the birds in the forest  
> joyfully resound with their voices;  
> let them humbly praise God;  
> let them solemnly proclaim high things.  
> You, Christ, have mercy.
>
> When the first day, Sunday, is spoken of,  
> the turtledove moans in the air;  
> the dove calls upon Christ with its throat;  
> it calls upon God in its breast.  
> You, Christ.
>
> When Monday is named,  
> the kite calls upon God with its neck;  
> the sparrow gradually shakes itself;  
> from the heart it loves God.
>
> Tuesday is the third day:  
> the birds sing in harmony;  
> the swallow flies boldly;  
> they do not cease praising God.

[The fragment resumes:]

[lacuna] The most powerful king ordered that a fleet be constructed, with Norman ships being built, and ships by the river, from Gaul and from northern Germany [Note: Einhard’s *Life*, chapter 17.], so that he ordered them to be stationed with such fortification in every harbor and river wherever ships could be found. He ordered them to be gathered by the Adriatic Sea in the province of Venetia.

Then throughout Italy, in the territories of Venetia and Aquileia [Note: That is, Aquileia.], and in Ravenna, Rimini, and Ancona, as well as along the entire coast of the Adriatic Sea, up to Traversus, he ordered ships to be gathered. From the whole Tyrrhenian Sea [Note: That is, the Mediterranean.], Liguria [Note: Perhaps Liguria.], Corsica, Sardinia, Pisa, Centumcellae, Rome, and whatever belonged to the territory of Apulia [Note: In the manuscript: “in the territory of Apulia.”], a great multitude of ships was assembled at Traversus, as much as could thereafter be found down to the present day.

The most gentle king, having received the apostolic blessing from Leo, ascended to the holy archangel [Note: Saint Michael on Mount Gargano.], worshiping and beseeching God to direct his journey in peace. Having set out, he began his journey and reached Mount Gargano; there he offered many gifts.

Proceeding through the territory of Naples, he reached Lower Calabria [Note: That is, “lower.”] and then Traversus. It extends for a length of more than one thousand Roman miles. He ordered bridges to be made over the sea. He commanded all the Franks, Saxons, Bavarians, Aquitanians, Gascons, Pannonians, Avars, Alemanni, and Lombards to go before him—the multitude of those peoples cannot be contained in number. All the nations of the Greek lands were also mobilized, so that their strength was counted as nothing.

They praised and blessed God, who directs Charles, the servant of the prince of the apostles Peter, along the right road.

When Aaron, king of the Persians, heard this—he held almost the whole East except India [Note: The manuscript has “penetrated.”] [Note: From Einhard’s *Life of Charles*, chapter 16.]—he formed such friendship and concord with him that he preferred Charles’s favour to the friendship of all other princes in the world, and judged that Charles alone was to be honoured by him with such generosity.

Afterward, when he had reached the most sacred sepulchre of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and the place of the Resurrection, he adorned the holy place with gold and gems and also set upon it a golden banner of marvelous size. He not only adorned all the holy places, but also granted King Aaron authority over the Lord’s manger and sepulchre, which Aaron had requested [Note: The manuscript reads *petierant*; corrected to *petierat*.] [Note: Compare Einhard, cited above.].

What immense garments, spices, and other great riches of the eastern lands did he grant to Charles as gifts!

When the year turned, the most prudent king traveled with King Aaron as far as Alexandria. Thus Franks and Hagarenes rejoiced together as though they were kinsmen. King Aaron was dismissed by Charles the Great in peace and returned to his own country.

The most pious and powerful king then reached the imperial city of Constantinople. Nicephorus [Note: Compare Einhard, cited above.], Michael, and Leo were greatly afraid that he wished to take the empire from them and were deeply alarmed beneath their scepter. When the king learned of their fear, he established between them a most firm pact and treaty, so that no opportunity for discord should remain between either party.

For the power of the Franks had always been suspect to the Romans and Greeks. Hence the Greek saying became proverbial:

> ΤΟΝ ΦΡΑΚΟΝ ΦΙΛΟΝ ΕΧΙϹ, ΙΤΟΝΑ ΟΥΚ ΕΧΙϹ.  
> “Have a Frank as a friend; do not have him as a neighbour.”

The Latins say:

> “Have the Franks as friends.”

Then the emperor returned to Italy, having received from the emperors of Constantinople many gifts and presents, as well as a portion of the body of the holy Apostle Andrew.

Coming to Rome, he established very extensive gifts for blessed Peter. Having set the city in order, he granted the whole Pentapolis, the territory of Ravenna, and all Tuscany to apostolic authority.

Giving thanks to God and to the prince of the apostles, and having received the apostolic blessing, he was called Augustus by the entire Roman people. Together with the pontiff he proceeded as far as Mount Soracte, to the monastery of Saint Silvester.

Then he went with the supreme pontiff to the monastery of Saint Andrew. The emperor was asked by the pontiff to establish in this monastery a portion of the relics of the body of the holy Apostle Andrew as a consecration. What was placed in its stead in the venerable church of this monastery is unknown to us.

The victorious, triumphant, crowned king returned to Francia.

He, who stood firm in such occupations while enlarging his kingdom and subjecting other nations, was continually engaged in such matters. To recount all this at length and in order would take much time; let us now touch upon it briefly.

Then, when he took the daughter of Desiderius, following his mother’s advice, etc.—excerpts from the *Life of Charles*, chapters 18, 19, 20, 22, 30, 31, and 32, up to the year and indiction: “the sixth indiction, the fifth day before the Kalends of February” (814).

> These little verses in praise of you, greatest prince,  
> Benedict, your suppliant servant and monk [Note: That is, *monachusque*, “and a monk.”], composed for your eternal remembrance:  
> with kindly mind he raised your illustrious name to the stars.  
> Prudent reader, know that he wrote this record.

24. At this time Lord Louis sent his envoys, Bishop Norbertus, to Emperor Leo at Constantinople, to renew their friendship and to confirm the aforesaid pact.

After leaving Aachen, etc.—excerpts from the *Annals of Lorsch* for the years 814–824, 826, 827, and 829, with the following additions:

**Year 815** [Note: In the year 814 he writes “three hundred gold solidi” instead of “seven thousand.”]: Meanwhile certain leading Romans … were slaughtered. There were three hundred Romans who were killed in the Lateran field. Among the leading men was Pope Leo IV, who established the whole Pentapolis and the territory of Tuscany under pontifical authority.

**Year 819:** “In this matter many things concerning the condition of the churches and monasteries were discussed and arranged. He also ordered the chapters that had long ago been written in the edicts to be affixed. When this had been completed—Count Ubaldo took Judith as his wife.”

**Year 824:** “When two men had been elected through the disputes of the people to the pope’s place, Eugenius, archpriest of the title of Saint Sabina, was one; the other’s name is not preserved. A civil revolt then arose among the Romans, and, when the party of the nobles prevailed, Eugenius was installed and ordained.”

He joins the years 827 and 829 in this way:

> The emperor’s envoy came to Rome and examined what the election of the people was like. There he celebrated the Mass of Saint Martin, the feast of the blessed Apostle Andrew, and also the holy day of the Lord’s Nativity itself, with great joy and rejoicing.

In February an assembly was held there, and he set out for Italy [Note: It is certain that Louis did not go to Italy; this seems to concern Emperor Louis II, son of Lothair.]. Entering Rome, and having celebrated the solemnity of Mass in the church of the prince of the apostles, he proceeded into the territory of Apulia, to the city of Bari. He ordered four towers to be built.

He arranged for ships of the Adriatic Sea, carrying whatever was necessary, to be guarded by a Frankish force in the city of Bari, at Scalaoria of Lower and Upper Calabria [Note: That is, Calabria; the letter *s* of *custodientes* has been repeated in the word *calaoria*.], and in whatever maritime cities were situated there, so that they would not be devastated by the Hagarenes.

The Romans imposed this upon Emperor Louis the Pious, and his memory therefore remains forever.

Emperor Louis displayed such great strength in Italy that he was unable to rescue the Roman pontiff’s kinsman from the laws [Note: That is, “kinsman.”] [Note: Compare the *Annals of Lorsch*, year 823.].

In the Lateran palace he had judges appointed in advance, for each day, at the place called the Wolf, which is the mother of the Romans, so that they might investigate the Roman people through a formal hearing conducted by the duke of Spoleto, named Aciprand.

Emperor Louis granted to Pope Gregory of the holy apostolic see whatever Emperor Constantine had previously granted to the church [Note: That is, “to the church.”].

He granted the monastery of Saint Benedict on Monte Cassino in the province of Samnium; the monastery of the holy Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary [Note: Farfa.], on Mount Acutianus in the territory of Sabina; the monastery of the Lord Savior in the territory of Reate, near the mountains of Letinianus and Bugoianus; and the monastery of Saint Silvester on Mount Soracte together with the monastery of Saint Andrew the Apostle, as fortified possessions for the defense of his palace and imperial treasury.

He also ordered that the notices set out in the laws [Note: That is, “written above.”] be affixed to these monasteries in the edicts of the Lombard laws.

He established the whole kingdom of Italy under the prior arrangement of his son Lothair, who was his partner in the kingdom. After receiving the blessing in the church of the prince of the apostles and absolution from the apostolic authority, he returned to Francia. Not many days afterward he died (840).

25. From this arose a dispute among the king’s sons—Lothair, Pippin, Louis, Charles, and Charlemagne—concerning their partnership in the kingdom. They divided the kingdom among themselves, beginning at the city of Füssen [Note: Füssen?], which is the center [Note: Perhaps “navel.”] between the Adriatic Sea and the Tyrrhenian Sea, and extending as far as Aquitaine. The Italian and Roman people were separated from the rule of the Franks.

The Frankish kings began to fight among themselves. As a result, news reached Córdoba and all Africa, including Carthage. The Saracens began to renew their evil plan, so that they might usurp the kingdom and plunder the church of Saint Peter.

King Charles [Note: Nonsense.]—son of Louis the Pious of blessed memory—because of some offense of his own which is not now relevant [Note: That is, “not.”], renounced the kingdom in favor of his brothers and received the habit of holy conduct in the monastery of Saint Benedict on Monte Cassino.

The Lord granted him such humility that he washed the feet of all the brothers [Note: The manuscript originally seems to have read *lavaretur*; the editors thought *lavaret* was written.], and considered himself the least among them [Note: The phrase is written twice.].

Beginning with the Saxons, who were in conflict with the kings Pippin, Charlemagne, and Louis, Lothair—who was called Augustus—ruled the kingdom of Italy. The Saxons fought daily and began to diminish the Frankish kingdom.

After that Charlemagne died [Note: Louis the Pious.], the Saxons entered Francia, devastating it with sword and fire. King Pippin [Note: Lothair.] made peace with the Saxons. King Louis of Aquitaine [Note: Germany.] fought against the Saxons. The Aquitanians formed assemblies among themselves. As a result, the kingdom of Aquitaine was taken away from the Franks, and it has remained so down to the present day.

### 26

When that same Lothair died (855), his son Charles [Note: [Col. 0038D] Louis II] succeeded him in the kingdom, but not for a very long time (846). Persecution arose among the Romans themselves; wicked men came out and sent messengers to the king of Babylon, asking him to come and possess the kingdom of Italy.

[Col. 0038D] At last so great a multitude of Hagarenes entered Italy from the port of Centumcellae that they filled the face of the land like locusts—or like a crop in a field. Such fear seized the Romans [Col. 0039A] that no one dared go out beyond the gates. Rome was besieged; the Leonine City was seized; the church of Saint Peter was captured and stripped; and throughout the monasteries belonging to that church he ordered their horses to be stationed.

The mother of all churches was turned into an object of disgrace, and all her ornament was torn away. The barbarians came near the altar, dancing in a circle and clapping their hands. One of them seized a small lance and struck the face of the Lord, depicted in mosaic in the apse, with the weapon—not only breaking the mosaic but also pouring out the material of which it had been made. Blood began to flow, as though He were a living man in the body; and this remains there forever.

Its adornment, as we said above, together with all its monasteries and churches in the Leonine City, was destroyed. The province of Tuscany was laid waste, and its cities were brought to disgrace; the Romans were afflicted with grief, and the apostolic church was in mourning. Gregory [Note: [Col. 0039D] Leo IV] had succeeded to this apostolic see (847). Inspired by the Holy Spirit, he daily strengthened the Roman people by the power of the Holy Spirit; and they took counsel about how almighty God might remove the savage barbarian nations and rescue the church of the holy apostle Peter, who is the head of all the churches, from those pestiferous peoples.

A messenger was sent to King Louis (816), son of Louis [Note: [Col. 0039D] Lothair], of pious memory, asking him to come and defend the church of Saint Peter and the Roman kingdom. Just as his father Pippin, Charles, and Louis had established the kingdom of Italy through the triumph of victory, so he too was to obtain the Roman kingdom according to his promises.

King Louis did not delay long, but set out for Rome with the Franks. Pope Gregory sent messengers to the marquis Guido, asking him to come to the aid of the Roman city and the holy church, for whose love the Lord had shed his blood, and promising him very generous gifts.

The marquis Guido therefore set out with the whole army of his Lombard people and entered the city of Rome. They began the battle at the bridge of Saint Peter and at the gates of the Leonine City. Many of the barbarian people were killed through the power of Saint Peter; and the pestiferous people said among themselves: “For we have seen the blood of the God of the Christians!”

The Hagarenes and their leader were routed, and they [Note: [Col. 0039] I have supplied the punctuation here.] scattered among themselves. King Louis came in hostile fashion as far as Mount Mario [Note: [Col. 0039D] Monte Mario], where the church of Saint Clement is. When he saw their multitude, his heart began to fear, because his courage was not like his father’s.

The Franks made an assault and sounded the trumpet. Their voices and the trumpets became like thunder, while the uproar of the Roman city and the voices from the churches grew especially loud. The Franks came to the arch called the Arch of the Soldiers; who could number that tribulation?

When King Louis came from the ditch [Col. 0040A], not far from the arch, he raised his hands toward the Franks, so that, when the Franks saw him, they might turn their feet backward behind themselves [Note: [Col. 0039] The manuscript lacks the punctuation.]

The Hagarenes provoked one another and came out of the Leonine City and from the church of the prince of the apostles; they fell upon the Franks. So many were killed that no one could count them [Note: [Col. 0040D] Prudentius, under the year 846, and the Chronicle of Monte Cassino also report Louis’s defeat.]

The marquis Guido and the Roman people pursued them to kill them. The Hagarenes advanced and fled, and thus they came to the port of Centumcellae; nevertheless, not even a tenth part of them remained. After boarding ships, the Hagarenes entered the sea with all the ornaments of the holy church.

The marquis Guido with his retinue and King Louis with as many Franks as had escaped returned to Rome. Because of this, the Roman people held the Franks up to ridicule down to the present day. [Col. 0040B] The marquis Guido, having received very generous gifts and the thanks of the Roman people, returned to his own country.

King Louis entered the city of Pavia, with the kingdom defrauded from Charles, his nephew (875).

### 27

The Romans, acting still more deceitfully against the Franks, sent embassies to Palermo and Africa, asking them to come and possess the kingdom of Italy. Then the people of the Hagarenes came out like water-buckets, hastened to Amalfi, and filled Upper Calabria. When they came to the river called the Garigliano [Note: [Col. 0040D] Garilianus], they seized the towers and made their dwelling there.

They began to ravage all Campania with iron and fire. The territory of Ciculus, Savina, the city of Narni, the city of Orte, and the city of Nepi were reduced under their dominion. Because of this, no more king of the Franks ruled in Italy down to the present day.

The Hagarenes ruled in the Roman kingdom for thirty years. The land was reduced to solitude, and the monasteries of the saints were without praises. Nevertheless, this happened because of the sins of the people. As it is written: “From heaven the Lord looked upon the sons of men, all who dwell upon the earth; from his prepared dwelling-place” (Psalm 32:13).

As we said above, the Hagarenes usurped the Roman kingdom over the course of thirty years (904–911). At that time Sergius III was presiding over the supreme see [Note: [Col. 0039] *Sedes* corrected to *sedis* in manuscript c.] of the holy apostolic church. In his time a great ruin shook the church of the Lateran patriarchate of Saint John, which is called the Constantinian church; it was broken from its foundations. The apostolic Sergius immediately restored it more fully from its foundations. How many gifts he offered in this patriarchate, in the same basilica, on the two sides before the altar, is written in the account of the restoration of the paintings.

### 28

Among the Lombard people, a king named Guido ruled in the city of Pavia. During his reign the Lombard kingdom was reduced under his royal authority [Col. 0041A] (888–894). This same Guido held a synod with the bishops, abbots, and faithful Lombards, composed laws in chapters, and ordered them to be affixed to the edicts.

During his reign hostility arose between the Lombards and the Franks concerning the kingdom of Italy. The Lombards closed the fortified passes and guarded the roads to Gaul.

### 29

Pope Sergius died on the ninth day before the Kalends of May [Note: [Col. 0041D] The dates are uncertain: October 913 or April 914]. Lando succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0041D] Anastasius III from August 911 until October 913; then Lando] by birth a Sabine. He sat in the chair of the holy apostolic see for six months, and then died.

Formosus succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0041D] Formosus sat from September 891 until April 896; John X succeeded Lando]. Pope Formosus restored the entire church of the prince of the apostles Peter with paintings. How great and what sort of hostility there was between the Romans and Pope Formosus, let us now be silent.

That same Formosus died, and John the Tenth succeeded him as pope [Col. 0041B] (April 914). He took counsel with the marquis Alberic concerning the Saracens. At that time Akyprandus of Rieti, together with many others from among the Lombards and Sabines, came out and prepared for battle with the Saracens, at the walls of an old city worn away by age, called Tribulana [Note: [Col. 0042D] Trevi?].

When the battle had been joined, through the intercession of blessed Peter the apostle the Saracens were killed. Another battle took place between the men of Nepi and Sutri and the Saracens in the field of Baccani [Note: [Col. 0042D] Baccano]; many Saracens were slaughtered and wounded.

The Saracens who were in the territory of Narni [Note: [Col. 0041] *Inarnienses* in manuscript c.], in Orte, and in the region of Ciculus heard of this. They all prepared themselves together under their leader, who was at the river Garigliano, making ready for the journey and recognizing especially that destruction would come upon themselves.

The heart of Pope John the Tenth was anxious, together with the glorious marquis Alberic. They gathered a multitude and came in hostile fashion to [Note: [Col. 0041] *Ha* corrected to *a* in manuscript c.] the river Garigliano. The marquis Alberic became like a most powerful lion among the Saracens (916).

The Beneventans heard of the battle, came out of Benevento, and went to the tower. They fought a great battle, and the Saracens were crushed before the Romans. Pope John the Tenth and the marquis Alberic were victorious, and the Roman people received the marquis Alberic with honor.

That same marquis Alberic was deformed [or “had an elongated form”; the reading is uncertain]. He took one of the noble Roman women, whose name survives, the daughter of Theophylact—not as a wife, but in an evil union. He fathered a son by her and, out of love for his father, gave him the name Alberic. How this Alberic later came to power, we shall relate afterward.

Pope John the Tenth therefore renovated three structures in the Lateran palace, wonderfully arranged and decorated with paintings, and ordered them to be inscribed on both sides.

Hostility arose between Alberic’s mother and the pope, and the Roman people were divided among themselves. The marquis Peter, brother of the pope mentioned above, was indeed involved; such hatred arose from the quarrel between the Romans and the marquis that he was not permitted to enter the city of Rome.

The marquis Peter entered the city of Orte and built a very strong fortress at the head of that city. The Romans raged still more, and the marquis Peter no longer dared enter the city of Rome.

Immediately he sent a messenger to the Hungarian people, asking them to come and possess Italy. When this had been done, the entire Hungarian people entered Italy. At the same time the marquis Peter entered the city of Rome.

The Hungarian people ravaged all Tuscany, consuming it with fire and sword [Note: [Col. 0041] *Vastata* was deleted here]. They carried away many people, together with women, and whatever their hands could seize. Since there was no one capable of resisting their assault, they returned to their own country.

The Romans, enraged, hurried unanimously [Col. 0042B] to the Lateran palace. They killed the marquis Peter, but no one touched the apostolic official. From then onward the custom arose that every year [Note: [Col. 0041] That is, “years”] the Hungarians ravaged the Roman territories.

### 30

Pope John the Tenth died (May 928) [Note: [Col. 0042D] He was followed by Leo VI, Stephen VII, and then John XI]. The lady senator mentioned above appointed her kinsman John to the most holy see, and for this reason he was called the Eleventh (20 March 931).

Rome was subjected to the power of a woman, just as we read in the prophet: “Women shall rule Jerusalem” (Isaiah 3:4).

Again the Hungarians came near Rome by the gate of Saint John. The Romans came out and fought with the Hungarian people. Noble Romans fell, just as they lie buried and at rest by the gates of that church [Col. 0042C] (937?).

Then, when the Hungarian people came from the city of Rieti, Joseph the prudent Lombard came out with a huge Lombard army. He killed some of them with the sword and captured others alive. Seeing that they were being attacked from every side by the army, the Hungarian people returned to their own country and no longer entered Italy to plunder.

Alas for the Italian people! How many disasters and how great a slaughter have foreign peoples inflicted upon you! Leonine City [Note: [Col. 0041] *Leonianiana* in manuscript c.], which Centumcellae built, you were captured by the Saracens and foreign peoples; indeed, also by the people of Bavaria, by the peoples of Gaul, and by a king named Arnulf. For they say that you were captured from the saddles of horses.

In the time of Pope John the Tenth, whose memory was mentioned above, signs appeared, whose sequence is recorded in this little book. From his days there was shown what would come to pass in later times.

### 31

In the year 921 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the first indiction—the ninth indiction—during the time of Lord John the Tenth, in the seventh year of his pontificate, signs were seen.

Near the city of Rome, many stones appeared to fall from heaven. In the city called Narni they were so dreadful and gloomy that it was believed they had been brought from infernal places. One of those stones was so enormous that, after falling into the river Nera, it could still be seen to this day rising one cubit above the waters of the river.

Many fiery torches were also seen by all the Roman people in this city, coming from heaven, so that they almost touched the earth. Some fell near the house of Theophylact; others near the church of the holy apostles James and Philip, which we call the church of the holy apostles; others ran here and there.

Likewise, at the same time, the sky appeared to burn near the port of this city, eighteen miles [Note: [Col. 0043] *Miliariario* in manuscript c.] from the city of Rome. In that flame three columns were seen together, in the form of the columns now placed in buildings. Upon these three columns three doves [Note: [Col. 0043] That is, *columbae*, “doves”] appeared to sit, one upon each column.

One of them, raising its wings, wished to extinguish the flame but could not. Then the second and the third likewise tried, but accomplished nothing. Soon afterward, however, one of them came from another direction with its wings spread, and beat its wings against the flame until it extinguished the whole fire.

After this, near the gate of this city called the Salarian Gate, before the church of Saint Susanna and the martyr Cyriacus, a certain woman, on a Sunday in the month of March, during the Passion of the Lord, was returning from the station at the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, on the seventeenth day of that month, and was cooking a stew.

When she had first taken some of the stew, she ate it. Then, wishing to lift the pot from the place where she had set it, she was completely unable to do so. The pot contained a porridge made from millet.

When she left the house, she began to weep and made the matter known to her neighbors and relatives. They all ran up, but none of those who came could pull it away from the marble on which it rested.

Again and again crowds of the people of this city—both clergy and the whole Roman community of both sexes—came, but no one could free it. It clung so tightly to the marble that it seemed to have been carved from the marble itself.

This continued for nearly four hours, from the ninth hour until night. They stood over the vessel, making the sign of the cross and praying many litanies to God that the vessel might be freed from the place where it sat; but even this did not help.

Finally, when other clerics came and likewise performed litanies, one of them extended his hand, made the sign of Christ, and offered prayers. Immediately the vessel was lifted up unharmed.

In the same way, in the church of Saint Agatha, which is called a deaconry, during the vigil of that martyr, a wooden image on which the face of the revered martyr was painted leapt from its proper place, where it stood fastened with ropes. It remained suspended for almost an hour, then returned to its proper place. Afterward it leaned over and remained as though lying down for a considerable time [Col. 0044A], and then stood upright again as it had been before.

In the church of Saint Angel, near the river Tiber, where the churches of Saints Abbacirus and John and of Saint Barbara are situated, the doors of that church remained closed for almost the entire day. No one could open them that day, either by force or through litanies. On the following day, after a litany had been performed and prayers offered, they opened, as they had customarily done before.

After this, a form like a beast was seen high in the air, like a monstrous dragon. Its length could be seen extending from the church of Saint Eusebius, near the small market, almost to the Salarian Gate. Many people saw it for a very long time; then, when a cloud covered it, it disappeared completely.

Rome began to afflict itself, troubled by the grief of its people.

### 32

The mother of the Roman prince Alberic sent messengers from the city of Pavia to a certain Hugh, king of the Lombards, asking him to marry her. This was accomplished (932). After the marriage had been celebrated, the king ascended with the queen into the castle of Saint Angelo. The king conceived an evil plan: to blind Alberic, his stepson, and reduce the Roman kingdom under his own power.

When Alberic learned of the king’s treachery, he pledged his faith to the Romans. They began to sound the trumpets; the voices of the churches rang out loudly. Clad in armor and united as one, they made the earth resound with their voices.

The king’s heart began to fear, together with the queen, and he returned to Lombardy.

The prince Alberic shone in the face of all the Romans like his father, and his strength was great. He was exceedingly terrifying, and the yoke upon the Romans was made heavier, as was also the yoke upon the holy apostolic see (942–946). When Marinus was elected pope, no one dared undertake anything beyond the command of Prince Alberic.

### 33

The glorious prince Alberic remembered—I believe that this was given and determined through the power of the Holy Spirit—and began to become a patron of monasteries.

He built the monastery of Saint Lawrence in the field of Verano and the monastery of Saint Paul the Apostle. He restored the property of the monasteries that had previously been taken away by wicked men.

He heard of the desolation of the monastery of Saint Andrew the Apostle and of Saint Sylvester on Mount Soracte, which had been captured by the Hagarenes. He also heard that the servants of this monastery were living carnally and that the property of the churches had been granted to the prince’s faithful as a benefice.

Someone came forward and said: “Alas for me! What disasters have befallen the monastery of Saint Andrew, which was once so great, built and magnificently arranged by Charles the Great! With all its property and tenants, it has been reduced to nothing!”

When the glorious prince Alberic heard this, he began to reflect more deeply. There was a venerable presbyter and physician named Leo, magnificently adorned with holiness, whose reputation was not unknown to the prince. Alberic immediately summoned him from the church of Saints Philip and James and made him father of the monastery.

He sent his messenger named Leo, whom the Romans called the chamberlain, to recover all the monastery’s property and tenants, including the colonists living and remaining there, together with the aforesaid monastery of Saint Sylvester on Mount Soracte, the monastery of Saint Stephen in Mariano, and all their appurtenances belonging to the monastery of Saint Andrew the Apostle described above. He invested and restored these possessions to Leo, the venerable abbot, just as they had been granted in ancient times.

Let us now relate how great a favor God bestowed upon Leo, the venerable abbot. He built a fortress on both sides of the monastery and constructed three towers at its entrance, completing them strongly and securely.

When Prince Alberic saw this, he willingly offered them gifts and commended himself to their sacred prayers. He added to them the monastery called Acutianum, which is dedicated to holy Mary, the Mother of God and ever-virgin [Col. 0045B], in the territory of Sabina.

A certain Campo was abbot in this monastery, together with his brothers, who were dissolute in their bodies [Note: [Col. 0045] Cf. *Chronicon Farfense*, pp. 457–458 (Muratori II, B).]. Leo governed it for two years.

This venerable abbot Leo bought two estates in the territory of Sabina: the estate of Similjanum, where the church of Saint Clement is, six ounces; the estate of Tezzanum, where the church of Saint Mary is, in its entirety; the estate of Villalena; the estate of Peculiaris, in its entirety; the estate of Terria, in its entirety; the estate of Carpinianus, in its entirety; the estate of Granianus, where the church of Saint Andrew the Apostle is; the estate of Porcanus, in its entirety; the estate of Agellus, three ounces; the estate of Calbianus, in its entirety; the estate of Antiscianus, six vineyard plots—all in the estate of Toccia, in the place called Salina; three plots of land from the estate of Antiscianus, from the monument to the bank, in the territory of the fortress of Summa Villa; the estate of Antiquus, with its other names, in its entirety; the estate of Casale, where the church of Saint Valentine is, together with the estate of Carpinianus; the estate of Musinianus with all its appurtenances; the estate of Cazza, in its entirety; the estate of Cesarnonus, in its entirety; and the estate of Castellione, where the church of Saint Lawrence is.

Within the city of Nepi, he acquired the cell of Saint Gratillianus with its appurtenances; the estate of Urbanella, in its entirety; the estate of Rotilganus; in the territory of Nepi, the valley called Cupa; and property in the territory of Campania.

Within the city [Note: [Col. 0045] That is, “within the city”] of Rome, not far from the church of Saint Apollinaris, he acquired one useful cell at the temple of Alexander; one excellent meadow at Aquintus; one meadow belonging to Saint Peter at the place called the Arch of the Soldiers; and two strips of land in the saltworks at Artheula.

In the estate of Septemiliana, in the territory of Sabina, from the public road to the river, he acquired the estate of Brutrucus, with land and vineyards; and the estate of Ascletus, all of it in every respect.

In the monastery of Saint Andrew he built, within that same monastery, a church of Saint Mary and joined it to the cenobium. He restored from its foundations the church of Saint Andrew the Apostle beside the river. He restored the church of Saint Michael on the Grifian Mountains. I judge that his memory will endure forever.

### 34

Let us return to the section concerning Prince Alberic, and explain how in his time no power of the kings of the Lombards or of Transalpine lands entered the Roman territories by force.

By a concubine he fathered a son who was to become prince, and gave him the name Octavian.

Alberic the prince took counsel [Note: [Col. 0045] That is, “entered into a plan”] to associate with himself in marriage a wife from the bloodline of the Greek emperors. Benedict was sent from Campania to Constantinople to arrange everything necessary for the alliance.

The Romans, following their wicked custom, plotted to kill the prince. Alberic learned of their plans. The bishop Marinus and Bishop Benedict, together with several others, acted secretly [Note: [Col. 0045] That is, “secretly from there”] to kill Prince Alberic; they formed a very evil conspiracy among themselves.

Their plans, however, were futile. The glorious prince had sisters who were senators. Secretly [Note: [Col. 0045] That is, “secretly from there”] they discussed among themselves the death of their brother.

Then one of them, abandoning the plot as though grieved in the burning of her heart, informed her brother the prince what disturbance was being prepared against him and how it was occurring.

Prince Alberic immediately seized the bishops mentioned above. Some of the others he handed over to the sword, others he had beaten, others he had wounded, and others he shut up in prison. Thus the prince was delivered from the Roman sedition.

Afterward he planned that one of the most beautiful noblewomen of Rome should be placed in authority over the servants of his household, so that he might grant gifts to his wife of Greek descent in the presence of the Greeks during the wedding celebrations. This was accomplished.

The woman was not only from the city of Rome but also from Sabina. This was accomplished; nevertheless, he did not reach the bridal chamber.

There was then a man named Agapitus in the holy apostolic see. Not long afterward the glorious prince began to grow weak. He hastened to the church of the prince of the apostles and sent messengers throughout Rome, summoning all the Roman nobles to him.

All swore by oath that after his death they would elect Octavian, his son, as pope, after the death of Pope Agapitus.

Having arranged the affairs of his sister and of his son Octavian, he ended his life within the confession of blessed Peter the apostle (946–955).

### 35

Meanwhile, not long afterward, Pope Agapitus died (January 956). Octavian was received into the most holy see and was called Pope John the Twelfth [Col. 0046D].

He became so licentious in his body and so bold as was formerly practiced among pagan peoples [Note: [Col. 0045] That is, “not now”]. He frequently made a practice of hunting, not like an apostolic man but like a wild animal.

His thoughts were vain. He loved gatherings of women; he hated the churches; he loved savage young men. He burned with such great lust of the body that we cannot now recount it [Note: [Col. 0045] That is, “we cannot”].

There was in the city of Rome a deacon of the holy Roman church named John, and Azzo, the chief notary. They were hostile to the pope because of his frequent wickedness [Note: [Col. 0047D] That is, “of the pontiff”]. Let us now relate how the Saxon kings came into Italy and the Roman kingdom [Note: [Col. 0047D] It is easy to understand that Otto’s history has become badly confused].

John the deacon and Azzo, chief notary, were chosen as strong allies. They were of one heart and one soul, intending rather to remove the pope from life than to preserve him alive, so that the Roman empire might be granted to the Saxon king and a benign prelate might preside over the holy church.

They sent messengers to Otto, first king of the Saxons, asking him to come and possess Italy and the Roman empire.

When the pope learned of this treachery, he seized John the deacon and ordered the hand with which he wrote the document to be cut off. He also had John the deacon’s nose cut off.

As time passed, Otto, the first king of the Saxons, and his son Liudolf entered Italy, repeatedly making their way through Gaul and the Saxon kingdom [Note: [Col. 0047] *Protelando*, that is, “by prolonging”]. How they dealt with the Lombards and with Liudolf we shall not now relate; thus, by shortening the account, let us now reach the summit of the kingdom.

### 36

When King Otto came to the kingdom of Italy, almost so great a multitude of peoples was in Italy that they filled the face of the land like water-buckets.

He had with him peoples of various nations whose languages the people did not understand. Moreover, he had a people called the Guinula, carrying baggage [Note: [Col. 0047] *Sarracinas* corrected to *sarracins* in manuscript c.], carts, and machines for transport.

Their appearance was terrifying. They hastened in curved vehicles [Note: [Col. 0047] That is, “carts”], cutting their way through the roads, and stood ready for battle with iron.

As the king and his men moved through the Italian kingdom, peoples came from both sides toward the city of Rome. The Roman people, together with the pontiff, went out to meet him, and he was received with honor. Masses were celebrated in the church of the prince of the apostles, and he was praised with apostolic praises [Note: [Col. 0047] That is, “apostolic”] and honorably acclaimed as Augustus [Note: [Col. 0047D] Concerning Otto’s arrival, Georgius cites the following from a catalogue of Roman pontiffs in Vatican manuscript 1340, in his notes on Baronius’s *Annales*, Mansi edition: “John of the region of Via Lata [read: *lata*], whose father was Alberic, prince of the Romans; he sat eight years and four months. In his time, namely in the year 962 of the Lord’s incarnation, Otto the emperor first came to Rome with Adelaide, in January, on the thirty-first day, a Friday, and remained there fifteen days; he departed from there on 14 February, the feast of Saint Valentine.”]

Thus the Italian kingdom and the Roman empire were subjected to the Saxon king (2 February 962). Concerning the Lombard kings and the marquis Hubert, how they were captured while fleeing and expelled from the Italian kingdom, let us now be silent.

King Otto became powerful in the kingdom and returned to Gaul. Again the king came near Rome with the queen, named Adelaide, and they stood crowned in the church of the prince of the apostles. They sent many gifts throughout all the holy churches of Rome.

Then great poverty began to increase in the Italian kingdom; pestilence, famine, fire, and the sword ravaged Italy. Oxen and cows fell to the ground. The land was reduced to solitude, and an increasingly severe famine spread (963).

Because of this, great disputes arose between the apostolic official and the emperor; we shall not now relate them.

[Col. 0048A] The Romans began to turn against the apostolic official, and a great disturbance [Note: [Col. 0047] That is, “an annulment” or “irritation”] arose: discord between the apostolic official and the emperor. Let us briefly explain how the conflict began.

Pope John withdrew into the regions of Campania, abandoning the apostolic see because of fear of the emperor. The Romans, raging still more among themselves, appealed to the emperor to elect Leo, the chief notary, as pope.

The emperor approved. Leo was elected and installed in the most holy see (6 December). After arranging everything in Tuscany and within the borders of the Pentapolis at the church of the prince of the apostles, the emperor granted it to Pope Leo and returned to Gaul.

### 37

In the year 964, the Romans, following their ancient custom, were divided among themselves. Pope John was summoned from the regions of Campania. He entered Rome with great force; and when he seized the emperor’s messengers and some Romans who supported Pope Leo, Pope Leo fled and withdrew into distant regions.

They say that he hastened as far as the Transalpine mountains.

Not long afterward the emperor returned to Italy with a great army, together with the apostolic official. When Pope John heard of the king’s attack and fury, he abandoned Rome and entered Campania again.

The Romans raged among themselves. Willingly or unwillingly, they submitted to Benedict, a subdeacon of the holy Roman church, who was elected and summoned from the schools and whom they established over the holy apostolic see.

He was a most prudent man, trained in the grammatical arts. Hence the Roman people called Benedict “the Grammarian.”

When the emperor heard of this schism, he became exceedingly angry and swore by the power of his kingdom that he would besiege the city of Rome from every side unless he brought Pope Benedict under his authority [Note: [Col. 0047] That is, “besieged”].

So great a multitude of Lombards, Saxons, and Gauls surrounded Rome on every side and for such a length of time that no one dared go outside the walls.

A great famine afflicted the Romans, together with fire and the sword, as it is written: “Affliction alone gives understanding, even through hearing” (Isaiah 28:19).

They began to weaken among themselves, and the powers they had formerly possessed were reduced to nothing. With one accord, from the least to the greatest, and compelled by necessity, they seized Pope Benedict and handed him over to the emperor.

They said to one another: “It is better that this one man should die for all, so that we may be freed in our minds from the torments of famine.”

The emperor sent the pontiff into exile in the regions of Saxony.

Pope Leo returned to the most holy see [Col. 0049A], and the entire Roman people honored him with praises. There was great rejoicing between the Saxon king and the pontiffs concerning Pope John the Twelfth [Note: [Col. 0049] That is, concerning his death]. His deeds and death are found in the episcopal little book.

### 38

That same emperor Otto, the Saxon, fathered a son, who was named Otto out of love for his father’s name. This same Otto the Second was crowned by the supreme pontiff, and his father’s kingdom was joined to him (25 December 967).

The emperors made a law and combined Roman law and Lombard law within the legislation; he ordered it to be affixed to the edicts of the Lombards (29 October 968).

Immediately he sent a messenger to Constantinople to join his children to those of the royal blood. This emperor possessed very firm power, and his authority in the Italian kingdom was strong.

The words of the Greek emperor pleased him. He rejoiced, and they sent immeasurable gold and silver with the girl into the land of Romania. In the church of the prince of the apostles a crown was placed upon her head; the wedding was celebrated and adorned with praises. She became empress of the Romans and, in the Greek language, was called “Pyphanu.”

They proceeded to Saxony with great joy (972).

39. Pope Leo died (A.D. 965). John, bishop-elect of the city of Narni, was installed in the most holy see; for this reason he was called Pope John XIII. But the Romans, according to their wicked custom, drove the pope from the Lateran palace. Some struck his head, others slapped his face, while others tortured his buttocks with knots [Note: [Col. 0049] perhaps “with knots” (*nates nodis*)]. Thus, after beating and abusing him, they confined him in the territory of Campania. They said among themselves to the Romans: “May the Saxon kings not come and destroy our kingdom, and our children fall into captivity, with the apostle Peter interceding!” His see had remained widowed.

[Col. 0050A] Pope John escaped from custody in the region of the Marsi and, proceeding hostilely, entered Sabina; then, passing through the borders of Tuscany, he returned to Rome. The Roman clergy and people went out to meet him with hymns and praises (A.D. 966). After celebrating Mass in the church of Saint Peter, he entered the Lateran palace. The pontiff frequently greeted the people; he rejoiced with the Romans and feasted daily. I think that, with deceitful intent, he disgracefully sought to avenge the injury done to him.

The pontiff sent envoys in a cloak [or: “with a message”] to the emperors in Saxony, asking them to come and defend the holy Roman Church. So many men from Gaul entered Italy that none had previously or subsequently been seen in such numbers. Woe to you, Rome, because you have been oppressed and trampled by so many peoples (A.D. 967, January); you who were also seized by the Saxon king, whose people were put to the sword and whose strength was reduced to nothing! They carry your gold and silver away in their purses. You were a mother; now you have become a daughter. What you possessed, you have lost. You have been stripped of your former power: in the time of Pope Leo you were trampled by Julius the First.

You once triumphed over the lofty nations of the earth; you trod down the world and slaughtered its kings. You held the scepter and possessed the greatest power. You were violently stripped and made menstruous—that is, defiled—by the Saxon king. As certain wise men say, and as is found written in your histories: formerly you fought foreign peoples and conquered the world on every side, from north to south; seized by the peoples of Gaul, you were exceedingly splendid.

All your walls, towers, and fortifications, as are now found, numbered 381 towers, 46 castle-towers, 6,800 fortifications, and 15 gates. Woe to you, Leonine City! Formerly you were captured; now you have been abandoned by the Saxon king [Note: [Col. 0049] Here the author appears to have brought his writing to an end.]

[Col. 0049]

## A Short Treatise on Imperial Authority in the City of Rome

[Col. 0049D] In ancient times imperial glory flourished at Rome. Under its domination stood various kingdoms, and all peoples bowed their own necks to it. It therefore established consuls, who by daily practice arranged the reins of government through deliberation. Offices were distributed among senators and magistrates, according as each person’s ministry required him to perform his duty. Imperial glory, however, was exalted by everyone solely with praises and honors.

After the coming of the only-begotten Son of God and the glory of his ascension, the Roman Empire transferred itself to Byzantium, which was called Constantinople after the great Caesar Constantine. Because it gloried in the Roman Empire, it was called New Rome, [Col. 0050D] though ancient Rome was still gloriously preferred above the others.

As the apostles and their successors went through the whole world preaching the Gospel according to the divine command, the Caesars returned to Rome, inflicting various tortures upon the saints in order to please their gods. Thus it happened that blessed Peter, whom Jesus Christ our Lord had placed above the others, came to Rome for the sake of preaching. Rome was proclaimed the mistress of all nations. Just as she had previously been deceived by many images of idols, so through the many preachings of the apostles and the exhortations of other martyrs she was converted, together with the rest.

There blessed Peter and Paul, the teacher of the nations, [Col. 0051A] were crowned with martyrdom, so that just as Rome, through her ancient walls, had been the head of many peoples in the division of images, so she might be called the head and mistress of all Christians in the unity of true faith and undivided Godhead. She possesses primacy over all Christianity by the privilege received from Jesus, who said: “You shall be called Cephas” (John 1:24); and elsewhere: “I shall pray for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32).

When the Roman Empire was divided, because the imperial seat that had customarily been at ancient Rome had been transferred to Constantinople, the peoples of many nations rebelled against the city. Hence, as Orosius bears witness, great and numerous wars arose against it. At that time Rome was ruled by patricians. Yet she remained so subject to her emperor that if an emperor was ever found to be cruel in the manner of the pagans, he would crown the most holy prelates of Rome and other Christians with martyrdom through various punishments, by means of his legates.

As the Christian religion grew, such a fervor of faith blazed among the patricians until the Lombards [Note: [Col. 0051D] “Longobards” in the edition] entered Italy. When they approached the Po, word was brought to Rome—Pope Silverius was then presiding over the Roman Church—to the patrician Narses, whose wife was called Polyxiana. They were informed that the aforementioned pontiff had sent to the Lombards, inviting them to Rome so that Greek power might be abolished and the rights of the Church raised under the authority of the pontiff, who was burdened by such necessity that he cared for nothing except the churches and clergy.

His daily sustenance was therefore supplied from the palace according to custom, together with annual gifts for the restoration of churches and the emperor’s alms as a mark of honor; and this was done solely out of reverence for the apostles Peter and Paul. Whenever an imperial legate was sent by the prince so that the Roman pontiff might travel to Constantinople to the emperor, he went, neglecting every other consideration, even if he knew for certain that he was being sent into exile.

On one occasion a messenger was sent by the patrician Narses to Pope Silverius. When he went to the house where the pope lay sick, his wife said to him: “Lord pope, what have we done to you, that you wished to bring the Lombards against us?” After saying this, she had him seized and tonsured, made him put on a monastic garment, and had him led, seated on a donkey, to the monastery of Saint Sabas. When he had gone out and was sitting outside on the donkey, one of the bystanders said: “Alas, the lord pope is dead.”

Furthermore, when the Lombards invaded Italy and converted to the faith of Christ, the Greeks were driven out, and imperial rule ceased from the city of Rome as far as the Franks. The Lombards were ruled by kings. After the regions of Italy had been divided, the duke of Spoleto was established at Rome in place of the king, on the condition that whenever the apostolic ruler died, the aforesaid duke would take part in the election of the future pontiff, receiving many gifts for the royal share.

If disputes arose among the Romans, a messenger from the king’s leading men would come with the same duke to deliberate cases and legal judgments. Those who incurred criminal guilt were punished by royal authority or sent into exile, even without consulting the apostolic ruler. This continued until Bishop Zacharias, who deceitfully set out, as though on the pretext of some personal friendship, [Note: [Col. 0051D] On Zacharias’s pretended journey to Pippin, see above, *Chronicle*, no. 17.] to Charles, king of the Franks, because that same Charles had as his wife the daughter of Desiderius, king of Italy.

He invited Charles to Italy, sowing discord among the kings, praising and presenting before him the imperial scepters. He received from him a guarantee concerning the time when he should enter Italy. After they had sworn to one another, he returned.

As he passed through the borders of Desiderius’s kingdom, he separated some of his men from him, giving some very large gifts and promising others that similar gifts would be given. When Charles received this kingdom, he went to Rome and gave many gifts there, through which the Roman dominion still holds property from the borders of this kingdom to the present day. He made a pact with the Romans and their pontiff concerning the appointment of the pontiff: a legate was to be present, and he himself was to settle contentious disputes.

They established annual gifts to be brought to the palace at Pavia: ten pounds of gold, one hundred of silver, and ten excellent cloaks, apart from private gifts. Whenever the emperor or his legate came to Rome, judges were sent from the palace each year. Throughout all the Roman territories they claimed legal jurisdiction, compelling the inhabitants of those places to come to court, while their judges administered the proper law in the presence of the imperial judges. If inhabitants of another nation were found there, they were judged according to royal law [Note: [Col. 0051D] “even if” (*etsi*) for *et*].

There were monasteries in Sabina belonging to the Lord Savior and to holy Mary, Mother of God, as well as the monastery of blessed Andrew the apostle near Mount Soracte, along with other fiscal estates within Roman territory, for imperial use. Monks also traveled not only through the Italian kingdom but through Francia, carrying tribute, wines, and other gifts according to their ability.

Thus, while the Romans were glorying in their security, their hearts were lifted up according to their custom, and they wished to claim imperial authority for themselves. When Pope Leo resisted, [Col. 0052D] they seized him and wished to tear out his eyes. They tore out one, but could not tear out the other, because divine mercy delivered him. They expelled him from the city as though both his eyes had been destroyed.

Fleeing to Francia, he reached Charles. Consequently Charles came to avenge the apostolic ruler. After seizing the Romans, he had three hundred of their leading men beheaded in one day in the Lateran field [Note: [Col. 0052D] Compare the *Life of Leo III*, chapters 21 and 26; the *Lorsch Annals*, A.D. 800.]

[Col. 0053A] Therefore it was decreed that all the leading men of Rome, bishops and laymen alike, should be imperial subjects, and that the entire populace should likewise swear fidelity to the emperor with them. The emperor’s own envoy was to remain at Rome at all times to settle contentious disputes.

He lived in the palace of Saint Peter, and it was established what daily stipend, and of what kind, was to be given him from the palace. Whatever remained from the aforementioned monasteries and estates was brought to him in abundance.

Imperial authority was so powerful there that if the case of a minor or uninstructed person was set aside in a legal judgment, and that person, on someone’s advice, held the feet of the emperor’s envoy, asking him for justice, and the envoy adjured the Roman leaders, saying: “By the fidelity that you owe the lord emperor, administer justice to this man,” no one dared to deviate either to the right or to the left, even if the injury had been inflicted by relatives of the pontiff [Note: [Col. 0053D] See above, *Chronicle*, no. 24].

Very often they did not settle cases before the apostolic ruler, but in the judicial place *lateratus ad* [Note: [Col. 0053] I have corrected this to *lateratus ad*], where there was a place called “At the She-Wolf,” which was called the mother of the Romans [Note: [Col. 0053D] See above, *Chronicle*, no. 24]. There they concluded judicial cases.

The compositions that used to be paid by wrongdoers [Note: [Col. 0053D] “were paid” (*solvebantur*)] were divided equally between the emperor’s envoy and the apostolic ruler. If the offense was such that the criminal property was to be assigned to the public treasury, it did not pass under ecclesiastical authority unless by an imperial act of gift.

If a bishop or Roman judge incurred the emperor’s anger, and it was permitted for the Caesar to come to Rome, he came. Otherwise, the duke of Spoleto was sent; the offender was seized and led into exile. His house was sealed with the king’s ring until the emperor’s decision, so that if he ever returned to favor, he would have his property preserved; otherwise, by imperial commands, it was distributed among the soldiers.

If someone was referred to the authority of a judge and appealed to the Caesar’s clemency, a legate was sent by the emperor for that business. He carefully examined the truth of the matter; and if the expelled person was found to be at fault, he had to endure the injury.

The Romans followed this custom until the emperor Louis the Great [Note: [Col. 0053] It appears that “who is otherwise called II” was added by Flacius], son of Lothair. Because he preferred to live in Italy, he became closer to Rome. There he also exercised a somewhat greater authority, having with him strong men of that city who knew the ancient custom of the emperors and reported it to the Caesar.

They advised him to recover the ancient dominion of the emperors and assured him that, unless he abandoned the attempt out of reverence for the blessed apostles, he would certainly accomplish it.

This prince also entered the territories of Benevento and the whole of Calabria for two reasons. First, because the province belonged to Italy and he wished to claim the borders of the entire kingdom under his authority; second, because the extremely savage people of the Hagarenes had already reached those borders. They had captured a certain city called Bari, fortified it, and filled it with provisions, keeping it as a place of refuge. For that reason he was kindly received by the inhabitants of that region.

The aforementioned Caesar therefore proceeded with a multitude of people to attack those same peoples. So as not to burden those who had been plundered by the Hagarenes, he sought assistance from Ravenna. He also sought assistance from nearby Venice, so that, supported by naval aid, he might be able to reach Apulia in abundance.

At that time John was presiding over the Church of Ravenna, an archbishop who was especially close to the emperor because he served him. Moved by envy, the Roman pontiff named Nicholas [Col. 0054B] became enraged against him. He deceitfully summoned him to Rome, so that he might condemn him in what appeared to be an ecclesiastical judgment and appoint another in his place.

When the archbishop heard this, he fled to Queen Engelberga. She sent her legates to the apostolic ruler, asking him to restore his favor to the archbishop. When she could not obtain this, she humbly informed her lord, asking him to extend his protection and favor to the archbishop and forbidding the apostolic ruler to cause him any disturbance.

Because the apostolic ruler, without the emperor’s knowledge, pronounced excommunications against him, a serious enmity arose between them. At last royal honor was raised against apostolic dignity, with the ancient statutes of the Fathers being brought forward: that a prelate was not permitted to excommunicate [Col. 0054C] a bishop without consulting a synodal council, and that a synod ought to be summoned not by the pope but by the emperor.

Many further measures were taken against the Roman pontiff on this account. In the Pentapolis he distributed benefices among his own men, ordering that no administration be supplied to Rome except aid transported by sea. The emperor’s loyal men received many kinds of assistance.

He also caused certain estates in the regions of Campania to be seized for royal use and for the use of his loyal men. From the monasteries mentioned above, daily services were also demanded for the king’s table [Note: [Col. 0054D] That is, for the table], through various provisions.

Finally, with the advice of the Roman leaders, he appointed in the city of Rome a certain bishop named Arsenius, adorned with holiness and learning and serving as representative of the Roman see. He gave him as an assistant John the deacon and archchancellor, his own secretary, who later became bishop of Rieti, for which office he had already been chosen.

At the appropriate time, therefore, the emperor came to Rome (A.D. 864) [Note: [Col. 0054D] For what follows, compare the *Deeds of Nicholas I*, chapters 21 ff.; but our author depends neither on that work nor on the *Annals of Hincmar]. He was received honorably by everyone, both great and small. The aforementioned archbishop of Ravenna came with him, fearing none of the pontiff’s threats.

Thus a greater dispute arose between the pope and the emperor. The emperor was in the palace of the apostle Saint Peter, while the pope was at the Church of the Holy Apostles. When all the pope’s plots against royal dignity were treated as worthless, he established monks and virgins consecrated to Christ from the monasteries of Rome, so that, under the pretext of religion, they might celebrate daily litanies around the circuit of the walls and sing Masses against evil-doing princes.

When the king’s leading men heard this, they approached the pope humbly and asked him privately to prohibit such actions. When they could obtain nothing from him, they returned in sorrow.

One day certain soldiers of the aforementioned prince were going to Saint Paul’s and were returning when they happened to encounter such litanies. At the prompting of the ancient enemy, they were inflamed with anger and took vengeance on those people for their lord’s allegiance, striking and severely beating them with the clubs they carried in their hands.

Those people fled, throwing down the crosses and images they were carrying, as is the custom of the Greeks. Some of these were trampled, others broken. The emperor was consequently moved to great anger, and for this reason the apostolic ruler became more conciliatory.

At last the pontiff went to Saint Peter’s and pleaded with the emperor on behalf of those who had carried out such actions; he could scarcely obtain pardon. Thus they became close to one another again. Nevertheless, royal dignity remained at Rome and in its territories until the end of the emperor’s days, as was stated above.

When he fell ill and approached the end of his life, because he had no son he wished the Great Charles to succeed him in receiving the imperial scepters. While these events were taking place, the Roman pontiffs continually sent letters by envoys [Note: [Col. 0055] The editions read “letters”] inviting Charles the Bald, king of the Franks, secretly to come. Because he was almost a philosopher in his letters, they asked him to come to blessed Peter and restore his Church from the yoke of servitude to its own liberty, as though it had been oppressed by force by someone.

After these machinations had unfolded, Louis died (A.D. 875). A legate was immediately sent to the same Charles at the summons of John, who was then presiding, by the pope [Note: [Col. 0055] This appears to require deletion]. Charles delayed nothing in coming, entered Italy, and made for Rome (A.D. 876).

Another envoy was sent by the emperor’s wife, Engelberga, or by his leading men, to the Great Charles, informing him of the dead man’s wishes. Because the journey was longer, he did not wish [Note: [Col. 0055] Perhaps “was unable”] to come so quickly that he could prevent Charles the Bald’s journey.

When Charles the Bald came to Rome, he renewed the pact with the Romans, granting them the rights and customs of that kingdom. He assigned them revenues from the three monasteries mentioned above: the monastery of the Lord Savior, that of blessed Mary ever-virgin in Sabina, and that of Saint Andrew near Mount Soracte, as well as from many other monasteries and fiscal estates.

He also granted them the territories of Samnium and Calabria, together with all the cities of Benevento. In addition, for the adornment of the kingdom, he granted them the entire duchy of Spoleto with two cities of Tuscany that the duke himself had customarily held, namely Aricia and Chiusi, so that the man who had previously presided in place of the king might thereafter appear subject to the Romans.

He also removed from them the royal legations, their regular attendance, and their presence at the apostolic election. What more is there to say? He granted them everything they wished, just as things are given that are acquired neither rightly nor with hope of being possessed [Note: [Col. 0055C] From a diploma of Otto III. See *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Leges*, II, B, 162, line 26; *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXVIII].

After this Charles had been driven away out of fear of the other Charles [Col. 0056C] [Note: [Col. 0056C] Namely, Charles the Fat], who was coming, he fell ill before leaving the Italian kingdom. He had scarcely departed when he died (A.D. 877).

From that day onward none of the emperors or kings acquired the honorable customs of royal dignity, because either strength was lacking or knowledge was lacking amid the many conflicts and continual divisions of the kingdom. Hence there were many battles, accusations, and acts of plunder in the kingdom.

# IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 1003. POPE SYLVESTER II (GERBERT)

[Col. 0057]

## Historical Notice on Pope Sylvester II

*(Natalis Alexander, Tenth Century, p. 36.)*

[Col. 0057A] Gerbert, a Gaul by nation and an Aquitanian by homeland, succeeded Gregory V. Born of humble parentage, he was a monk of Aurillac, then abbot of Bobbio, tutor of Otto III and Robert, king of the Franks, archbishop of Reims, and afterward archbishop of Ravenna. Through the favor of his pupil, the emperor Otto, he was raised to the apostolic see and, changing his name, was called Sylvester II.

The story that he learned magic arts and necromancy at Seville, kept a demon as a familiar, and, after becoming pontiff, consulted it about the length of his life—receiving from it the answer that he would not die before celebrating Mass in Jerusalem—together with other absurd and foolish tales, was invented and committed to writing by Benno, a pseudocardinal and schismatic.

Sigebert [Col. 0057B] repeated this fable in his *Commentaries* under the year 998, although he speaks of it doubtfully; so did Martin of Troppau, Saint Antoninus, *Chronicle*, vol. II, title 16, §18; Vincent of Beauvais, book XXIV, chapter 88; Werner Rolewinck, in the *Fasciculus temporum*; William of Malmesbury, book II of *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*, chapter 10; the Magdeburg Centuriators; and Platina, in his book *Lives of the Pontiffs*, under Sylvester II.

But contemporary writers destroy this invention of the schismatic author, which historians who were too credulous and insufficiently careful accepted, since they adorn Gerbert, or Sylvester II, with praises and proclaim his outstanding merits.

Concerning him, Thietmar, bishop of Merseburg, writes in book VI:

“Above, when discussing the universal pope Bruno, I mentioned only his successor Gerbert. Since I am now going to write something more extensively about him, this will not be inappropriate. He was born in the western regions, educated from childhood in the liberal arts, and eventually promoted to govern the city of Reims justly. He was exceptionally skilled in discerning the courses of the stars and surpassed his contemporaries in knowledge of various arts.

“At last, expelled from his own country, he sought the emperor Otto and remained with him for a long time. At Magdeburg he made a clock, setting it correctly after observing, through a certain tube, a star that guided sailors. After the aforementioned pope had died, he succeeded him through the emperor’s favor and sat until the time of King Henry, being called Sylvester.”

Concerning him, Helgaud, a monk of Fleury, writes in the *Life of Robert, Most Christian King*:

“That king was exceedingly wise in letters. Gifts of perfect knowledge, given by God, were implanted in his most wise heart. For his most pious mother entrusted him to the school at Reims, and he was given to Lord Gerbert for instruction. Gerbert taught him the liberal disciplines sufficiently, so that in all things he might please almighty God through virtuous works.

“And so it happened. For Gerbert, because of the supreme merit of his wisdom, by which he shone throughout the world, obtained the episcopate of Reims through a gift from King Hugh and, for not many years, adorned it magnificently in all things necessary to the holy Church. After leaving it, he was made ruler of Ravenna by Otto III.

“From there he hastened upward to the apostolate of the most holy apostle Peter and performed many distinguished works of virtue in it, especially in the holy almsgiving that he firmly maintained while he lived faithfully. Among other things, he cheerfully and joyfully played upon the letter R as follows:

> Gerbert climbs from R to R; afterward, as pope, he flourishes in R.

“This clearly demonstrates that the honors of the three bishoprics which he assumed, governed, and held after becoming a monk under the rule of our father Benedict were indicated at the beginning by the sign of this letter R—namely, Reims, Ravenna, and Rome.”

[Col. 0058C] Concerning the same pontiff, Rudolf Glaber writes in book I of his *History*:

“The emperor summoned Gerbert, archbishop of Ravenna, and appointed him chief pontiff of the Romans. This Gerbert was of Gallic origin and belonged even to a humble lineage, but he was extremely sharp-minded and fully trained in the study of the liberal arts.

“Accordingly, he had also been appointed by Hugh, king of the Franks, as pontiff of Reims. But because he was very shrewd and prudent, and understood that Arnulf, archbishop of that same city, in whose lifetime he had been ordained with the consent of that king, was striving to be restored to his former see, he cautiously set out and came to the aforementioned Otto.

“Otto received him with considerable honor and immediately raised him first at Ravenna and then in the city of Rome to the pontificate.”

Concerning Gerbert, the bishops of the province of Reims wrote as follows in the decree of his election to that same archbishopric:

“We, the bishops of the diocese of Reims, in accordance with the constitutions of the Fathers, with the favor and consent of both our princes, Lord Hugh Augustus and the most excellent King Robert, and also with the agreement of those who belong to God among the clergy and people, elect for ourselves as archbishop the abbot Gerbert, mature in age, prudent by nature, teachable, affable, merciful . . .

“We have known his life and character from childhood; we have experienced his zeal in divine and human matters. We desire to be formed by his counsel and instruction, and by subscribing to this document we confirm his election.”

The excellent pontiff Gregory V, most devoted to ecclesiastical discipline, raised him to the archbishopric of Ravenna and adorned him with many privileges because of his outstanding merits.

Sylvester II honored Stephen, the most holy king of the Hungarians, who had brought Pannonia to the faith of Christ, with the title of king and a royal diadem. He ordered that a cross be carried before him as a sign of the apostolate. He left the churches established in Stephen’s territories to be organized by Stephen himself; at his request he established the Church of Esztergom as a metropolitan church; and he confirmed the other bishops and the entire nation with apostolic blessing, as Bishop Chartuitius testifies in the *Life of Saint Stephen, King of the Hungarians*, in Surius, under August 20.

Sylvester II confirmed the restoration of Arnulf, archbishop of Reims, with such skill and prudence that he did not derogate from the things which he himself had written against Arnulf in a spirit of rivalry and contention, nor from the Acts of the Synod of Reims in which Arnulf had been deposed, while safeguarding the authority of the apostolic see. Thus, in a letter addressed to Arnulf, he mentions the guilt of his conscience and asserts that Arnulf had been deprived of pontifical honor because of certain excesses. He says that he is coming to his aid, so that, because his abdication lacked Roman consent, it may be repaired through the gift of Roman mercy.

[Col. 0059D] Sylvester II died on May 12 in the year of Christ 1003, after having occupied the see for four years and three or four months.
