Pope Sergius IV, Supreme Pontiff, placed this epitaph upon him. It completely overturns the slander of Benno, which had been accepted by other writers who were simpler and excessively credulous:

> Here lies the body of Sylvester, light of the world,  
> To be restored at the sound of the coming Lord.  
> The most learned virgin who gave him to the world  
> And the Roman heights, head of the world,  
> Gerbert the Frank first merited  
> The metropolitan see of the people of Reims, his homeland.  
> Then he deserved to ascend the highest  
> And noble governance of the Church of Ravenna, and thus, powerful,  
> [Col. 0060A] After a year, under a changed name, he received Rome,  
> So that he might become a new shepherd of the whole world.  
> Caesar Otto the Third, faithful in kindred spirit,  
> Was exceedingly pleased with him and offered him this honor.  
> Both men were adorned with the virtue of wisdom;  
> Every age rejoices, and every guilt is broken.  
> Like the bearer of the keys, he possessed the seat of heaven,  
> And was appointed shepherd in the place of three.  
> After he assumed Peter’s office, he drove away  
> The ages of his life within a five-year span.  
> The world grew cold; peace was shattered in triumph;  
> The wavering Church forgot her rest.  
> Sergius, the priest, his successor,  
> Arranged this tomb with gentle devotion and love.  
> Whoever turns lowered eyes toward this tomb,  
> Say, “Almighty Lord, have mercy on him.”

The occasion for inventing the story that he was devoted to magical arts was his supreme expertise in mathematics, his exceptionally inventive genius in devising new clocks and other machines, and his skill in completing works that, in an unrefined age and among uneducated people, seemed impossible without the aid of a familiar spirit and a demon.

The foolish rumor was increased by his extraordinary good fortune: namely, that a man of obscure origin had passed from the cloister into the court; that he had easily insinuated himself into the friendship of princes; that he had obtained the two foremost archbishoprics of Gaul and Italy; and that he had finally been raised to the pontifical see.

“These things were popularly invented,” to use William of Malmesbury’s words, “because the people commonly injure the reputation of learned men, saying that a man speaks with a demon when they see him outstanding in some work. Thus Boethius, in the book *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, complains that he was branded with such accusations because of his devotion to wisdom, as though he had polluted his conscience with sacrilege through ambition for office.

“He says: ‘It was not fitting for me to seek the aid of the basest spirits, when you were preparing me for such excellence that you might make me like God. Yet for this very reason we seem akin to wrongdoing: because we are imbued with your teachings and formed by your character.”’”

Sylvester II left several monuments of his genius and learning: namely, a book on Geometry, which Onuphrius Panvinus testifies that he read in the Farnese Library in his annotations on Platina; a book on Numbers addressed to Constantine, a monk of Fleury; and many short letters, some of which are extant in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, published from the manuscript of Papirius Masson, and others in volume II of André Duchesne’s *History of the Franks*.

They were written before his pontificate, and some are rather severe toward Pope John XV [Col. 0060D]. P. Mabillon published Gerbert’s letter to Constantine, monk of Fleury, *On the Construction of the Sphere*, and an excellent sermon, *On the Instruction of Bishops*, in volume II of the *Veterum Analecta*.

The *Short Treatise on a Passage of Porphyry* should also be attributed to him, in the judgment of Mabillon. Its preface, addressed to the emperor Otto III, was published in volume I of the *Analecta*. Mabillon also testifies, in volume II of the *Analecta*, p. 215, that Gerbert’s *Geometry* and *Rhythmomachia* exist in a manuscript of the Thuane Library.

[Col. 0061]

## Literary Notice

*(From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. III, p. 44.)*

[Col. 0061A] Gerbert, scholasticus of Orléans, of the Benedictine order in the monastery of Fleury; tutor of the emperor Otto III and of Robert, king of the Franks; from abbot of Bobbio and of Saint Columban, archbishop of Reims and thereafter of Ravenna; and finally Pope Sylvester II, from April 2, 999, until May 12, 1003.

His letters are extant in the volumes of the councils:

1. To Ascelin (Azolinus), or Adalbero, bishop of Laon, summoning him to come to a Roman synod after being accused;

2. To Arnulf, whom he restored to the archbishopric of Reims; and

3. To Robert, abbot of Vézelay, whose privileges he confirms.

Another 161 letters, written by Gerbert while he still used that name as archbishop of Reims, and which Baronius used from the manuscript of Nicolas Fabri, were first published by Jean-Baptiste Masson, brother of Papirius, Paris, 1611, in quarto; and thereafter in André Duchesne’s *Scriptores Francici*, vol. II, pp. 789–827; in the *Bibliothecae Patrum*, Paris, 1644–1654, vol. III; Cologne, 1618, vol. X; and Lyon, 1677, vol. XVII, p. 669.

The last of those 161 letters is addressed to Constantine, whom Gerbert placed before his still unpublished book *On the Division of Numbers* as its preface. Duchesne also published, from the Sirmond manuscript, in volume II of the *Scriptores Francorum*, Paris, 1636, pp. 828–843, another 55 letters of Gerbert, which I do not find repeated in the *Bibliothecae Patrum*.

A letter to the same Constantine, a monk of Fleury and later abbot of Saint Maximinus: *On the Construction of the Sphere*, in volume II of Jean Mabillon’s *Analecta*, p. 212 (new edition, p. 102).

A sermon *On the Instruction of Bishops*, in the same work, p. 103.

A preface to the emperor Otto III on a passage of Porphyry that Gerbert had elucidated, in volume I of the same work, p. 110 (new edition, p. 106).

Bernard Pez published Gerbert’s own book *On the Rational and on the Use of Reason*, preceded by the same preface, in volume I, part II, of the *Anecdota*, p. 149. Fr. Benzonius refers to this work when he says:

> When you turn over Logic, what do you resolve, Gerbert?  
> Hence Otto the Third prefers you to the whole world.

After receiving the solution concerning the use of reason and the rational, Otto gave Gerbert, the solver, Rome after Ravenna—that is, an imperial gift. Benzonius records this in book I, chapter 15, of his *History*, in Joan. Peter Ludewig’s *Relics of Ancient Monuments*, vol. IX, p. 249, and in Menckenius’s *German Writers*, vol. I, p. 980.

Letters written to Salla, bishop of Urgell, in A.D. 1001, and to Odo, bishop of Girona, in A.D. 1002, in Baluze’s appendix to *Marca Hispanica*, p. 957 ff.

[Col. 0062A] A letter to Adelbold concerning the cause of the difference between areas in an equilateral triangle, treated geometrically and arithmetically, in the aforementioned Pez, *Anecdota*, vol. III, part II, pp. 82–84.

*Geometry*, divided into 94 chapters, in the same work, pp. 7–82.

*Booklet on the Blood and Body of the Lord*, same source, vol. I, part II, pp. 133–148. Incipit: “Just as a certain wise man said before us.” Ludovicus Cellotius had published it without the author’s name in the appendix to his *History of Gottschalk* (Paris, 1655, fol.); Mabillon published it under the name of Heriger, abbot of Lobbes, in the prolegomena to part II of the fourth century of the Benedictines. But Pez restored it to Gerbert on the authority of the Göttweig manuscript.

Acts of the Synod of Reims, A.D. 992, in the Magdeburg Centuriators, century X, chapter 9, p. 246; attacked by Baronius under that year, no. 9 ff.

*Apologetic Sermon*, delivered at the Council of Mouzon in A.D. 995, published in the acts of that council and in the Magdeburg Centuries, vol. III, p. 279. Baronius, under the year 995, and the eminent Cave erroneously counted it among the unpublished works.

*Rhythmomachia*, published at Leipzig in 1616, fol., together with the four German books of the most illustrious Prince Augustus, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, *On the Game of Chess*.

*Life and Passion of Saint Adalbert Ursinus*, Count of Rosemberg, bishop of Prague, archbishop of Gniezno, and martyr in A.D. 967, apostle of the Bohemians, Hungarians, Poles, and Prussians. It was published by Abraham Bzovius from a Cassinese manuscript (Rome, 1629, fol.), together with *Sylvester II Caesio Aquitano Vindicated from Magic and Other Calumnies* [Col. 0062C] [Note: [Col. 0061] This defense of Sylvester II was reprinted at Rome in 1678, fol. See the *Paris Ephemerides of the Learned* for that year, p. 331.], and in the appendix to volume XX of the *Annals* (Rome, 1641, fol.). George Henschenius, however, who published the same *Life* from a Prague manuscript in the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. III, April 23, p. 178, denies that it is Gerbert’s, although he does not deny that it was written at Gerbert’s prompting and dedicated to him by a monk of Saints Boniface and Alexius. Bohuslav Balbín holds the same opinion; he offers this *Life* for reading in *Sacred Bohemia*, *Historical Miscellanies of the Kingdom of Bohemia*, decade I, book IV (Prague, 1682, fol.). Canisius also published it anonymously in vol. V, part II of the *Ancient Readings*, p. 332 (new edition, vol. III, p. 45).

A twelve-line poem in praise of Severinus Boethius, in Baronius, under the year 526, no. 18.

[Col. 0062D] But the *Altercation with Leo, Nuncio of Pope John XV*, which Baronius likewise mentions under the year 992, no. 9, has not yet, as far as I know, been published; nor has the book *On Rhetoric*, or the work *On the Composition of the Astrolabe*, as Ludovicus Jacobus testifies, p. 214 of the *Bibliotheca Pontificia*. On the study of the mathematical sciences, in which Gerbert blossomed to a miraculous degree for his age, see John Wallis, chapter 4 of his *Algebra*, vol. II of his *Works*, pp. 16 ff.; there he also discusses Gerbert’s *Abacus* and *Algorithm*, or the book *On the Division of Numbers*, which he wrote for his teacher in Spain, the learned Joseph, who himself had composed a little book on multiplication and division. William of Malmesbury says more about Gerbert in book II of his *History of the English*, pp. 64–65, including the following:

> “In the astrolabe he surpassed Ptolemy; Alkindus [Note: [Col. 0063B] Read this with Wallis instead of *Aleandraeum*.] in the intervals of the stars; Julius Firmicus in matters of fate. There [in Spain] he learned what the singing and flight of birds portend. There he learned to summon subtle figures from the underworld; there, finally, whatever human curiosity has discovered as either harmful or beneficial. For the lawful arts—arithmetic, music, and geometry—there is no need to speak: he absorbed them so thoroughly that he showed them inferior to his own intellect and brought them back to Gaul with great effort, where they had long since become entirely obsolete. Certainly, he was the first to seize the *Abacus* from the Saracens and to provide rules that the abacists, even when sweating over them, can scarcely understand.”

Besides all the letters listed here, Baluzius published another in his little book *On the Correction of Gratian*. It was addressed to a certain abbot and excuses Gerbert from the charge of simony of which he was accused when he obtained the Roman pontificate. See Baluzius in the same work.

[Col. 0063]

## Inquiry into the Writings of Gerbert, Later Sylvester II

(*Literary History of France* by Benedictine monks of Saint-Maur, vol. VI, p. 577.)

[Col. 0063B] Although a large number of writings by Gerbert have come down to us, we are by no means certain that we possess all the works of his pen. Nor can we flatter ourselves that we have been preserved a knowledge of all those that are lost, since he wrote so much during the course of a long life. Let us examine the matter. To proceed in an orderly fashion, we shall begin with his works on the liberal arts, as the earliest that he wrote. We shall then turn to those dealing with ecclesiastical subjects.

**1.** No one is unaware that Gerbert’s predominant field of knowledge was mathematics. Since arithmetic and geometry are the two wings of the mathematician, according to Plato, Gerbert devoted particular attention to them, although, departing from the opinion of that ancient philosopher, he ranked music second after arithmetic (*Preface to the Geometry*). He wrote extensively on this first branch of mathematics; yet almost nothing of his work on the subject has been printed [Col. 0063D], perhaps with good reason.

Dom Bernard Pez, while visiting the libraries of Bavaria, found in that of the abbey of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg a treatise on arithmetic which he had no difficulty believing to be by Gerbert (PEZ, *Anecdota*, vol. I, dissertation, p. 38, no. 63). What persuaded him was that it follows Gerbert’s *Abacus* in an in-quarto manuscript six hundred years old, and that the author’s name is indicated by a capital G at the head of the title, as follows: “G. *The Most Subtle Book on Arithmetic*” (*G. Liber subtilissimus de arithmetica*).

The work is dedicated, in a preface or dedicatory epistle, to one of Gerbert’s teachers, whose name likewise is designated only by a capital S. It would be difficult to guess who this patron was. Gerbert’s letters offer no clarification on the matter [Col. 0064B]. If conjecture may be permitted, it seems very likely that one of the teachers Gerbert had in Spain is meant here. For it was there that he learned arithmetic particularly well.

Whoever he was, Gerbert, from the opening of his epistle, expresses great esteem and respect for him: “To the Teacher and Father”—these are his words—“Theosophus J. G., his son, though less worthy; whatever salvation there is in Christ, from son to father.” The epistle begins with the words, “Since every one of the liberal arts even today…” (*Cum omnis hodieque liberalium artium*); the body of the work begins with: “In Greek, arithmetic; in Latin, the science of numbers” (*Graece arithmetica, Latine dicitur numerorum scientia*).

In manuscript no. 3413, in-quarto, from the library of John Selden (CAT. *MSS. Angl.*, vol. I, part I, p. 124, no. 1), there was formerly found, together with Boethius’s *Arithmetic* and *Music* and other writings, a work by Gerbert with its preface, under the title: “Gerbert’s *Theory*, with a prologue to the same” (*Gerberti Theorica cum prologo in eamdem*). Oudin understood this to mean a treatise on the theory of arithmetic (OUD., *Writers*, vol. II, p. 512). If so, it could very well be the same work just described, although it does not bear all the same identifying features as it does in the Saint-Emmeram manuscript.

**2.** Another work of Gerbert on arithmetic is his famous *Abacus* (PEZ, ibid.). It is found in the same Regensburg manuscript, but its beginning is missing. In the subscription it is addressed to Otto III and also bears the title *Algorithm*. The letter of that prince to Gerbert (GERB., *Letters*, part I, letter 153), asking him to teach him all the refinements of arithmetic, suggests that Gerbert composed it on that occasion.

It should therefore not be confused, as some writers seem to have done (OUD., ibid.), with other works on the same subject addressed to Constantine of Fleury. The reason for the confusion is that this treatise, together with the work on multiplication and a letter to Constantine, occurs in one of the manuscripts that Joseph Scaliger bequeathed to the library of the University of Leiden; thus the two works may have been made into one.

There is another copy of this *Abacus* in an eleventh-century manuscript preserved in the King’s Library, under no. 5366.5 (LE BEUF, vol. II, p. 84, note). We have said elsewhere that this work is nothing other than tables of arithmetic, in which Gerbert traced the various combinations of the Arabic numerals.

Vignier mentions another work of the same kind, on the same [Col. 0065B] subject and under the same title, composed by a certain Bernelin, otherwise unknown, although he is presumed to have been Gerbert’s disciple [Note: [Col. 0065D] Since Bernelin is regarded as Gerbert’s disciple and may have been French, readers may not object if we add here that his treatise *On the Abacus*, which consisted of four books in the library of Pierre Pithou (MONTF., *Bib. bib.*, p. 116, no. 2), is also found, together with several other unspecified writings, in manuscript 4539 of the Vatican Library (app. 24, no. 2). Manuscript 480 among the manuscripts of Christina, Queen of Sweden, which form part of the same library, also contains the same work, together with treatises on Music, Arithmetic, and Geometry by the same author.]

William of Malmesbury and those who copied him (MALM., *On the Kings of England*, book II, chapter 10, p. 65; ALBER., *Chronicle*, part II, p. 30) clearly say that Gerbert took from the Saracens of Spain the *Abacus* just described. They agree, however, that the rules prescribed in it are unintelligible even to those who make the greatest effort to understand them.

Nothing, moreover, is more amusing than the idea they formed of this book. It is clear that they did not know it, since they represent it as Gerbert’s book of magic. Still more ridiculous is the way they seriously relate that Gerbert stole it from his teacher [Col. 0065C].

In addition to the three copies of Gerbert’s *Abacus* already noted, there are two more in two manuscripts of the King’s Library, nos. 2231 and 4312 (MONTF., *Bib. bib.*, pp. 955, no. 2, and 987, no. 1) [Note: [Col. 0066D] It can be seen from this that the treatise *On the Division of Numbers* is not lost, as a modern scholar complains (GOUJ., *State of the Sciences*, p. 54).]

It is also found under the title *The Abacus Composed by Gerbert the Scholastic* (*Gerberti scholastici Abacus compositus*) in the Vatican Library (app. 88, no. 1), among the philosophical manuscripts of Christina, Queen of Sweden. It is impossible to say precisely whether the two works by the same author found among these manuscripts—one entitled *Rules of the Abacus* (*Regulae Abaci*), the other *On Numbers* (*De numeris*)—are the same as the *Abacus*. Perhaps they are only the work that Heriger, abbot of Lobbes, composed on this famous treatise and entitled *Rules of Numbers for Gerbert’s Abacus* (*Regulae numerorum super Abacum Gerberti*) (ALBER., *Chronicle*, part II, p. 32).

**3.** Gerbert also composed various other treatises on the same subject, which most writers have confused with one another but which it is important to distinguish. We have just seen that the Scaliger manuscript containing the *Abacus* also contains the treatise on multiplication, the *Little Book of Multiplication* (*Libellus multiplicationum*). This is apparently the same work that Abbé Le Beuf says he saw in the King’s Library, manuscript 5436.3.

This treatise is addressed to Constantine of Fleury, whom the author calls his “Theophilus,” and it prescribes rules for multiplication with the fingers—a method of counting much used among the ancients, which Gerbert revived in his own century.

**4.** This treatise on multiplication is doubtless different (GERB., *Letters*, preface, p. 2) from the work on the division or fraction of numbers, *On the Division of Numbers* (*De numerorum divisione*), which the first editor of Gerbert’s letters kept in manuscript in his own collection (CAT. *MSS. Angl.*, vol. II, p. 69, no. 2), and which bears the title *Rules on Divisions* (*Regulae de divisionibus*) in a manuscript of Isaac Vossius.

According to Le Masson’s copy, Gerbert’s letter to Constantine of Fleury stands at the beginning. It is letter 160 in the first edition and 161 in du Chesne’s edition. At the end of this letter, Le Masson published the opening words of the treatise, which begins as follows: “On the simple [number]. If you multiply a single number…” (*De simplici. Si multiplicaveris singularem numerum, etc.*). These words do not appear in the second edition.

In this letter Gerbert announces to his friend the work he is sending him and presents it as a work of geometry rather than arithmetic. Thus one may doubt whether the letter concerns the treatise *On the Division of Numbers*, and consequently whether its position at the head of that treatise is arbitrary rather than natural [Col. 0066C]. The work of which the letter speaks, whatever it may have been, was short in words but prolix in its propositions: “Brief indeed in words, but prolix in meaning” (*Brevem quidem verbis, sed prolixam sententiis*).

**5.** To all these writings on arithmetic Gerbert added another, entitled *Rhythmomachia*—that is, according to the force of the Greek term, “the battle of numbers” or “the battle of figures.” This treatise is found in a manuscript formerly belonging to the library of M. de Thou and now in the King’s Library, manuscript 4001 among the Colbert manuscripts (MAB., *Annals*, vol. II, pp. 215–216).

Abbè Le Beuf, who examined it, says that this little work occupies only four pages and that the game of figures whose rules it gives closely resembles chess. It indeed concerns pyramids and other pieces of different colors—black, white, and red—and mentions captures. John of Salisbury, bishop of Chartres, knew of this game of figures, although the title is somewhat distorted in the letter in which he mentions it [Col. 0067A] (letter 235). What little he says, moreover, confirms the idea just given. Gerbert cites only Boethius; but there is no doubt that he also drew something from Pythagoras, as Wibold, bishop of Arras and Cambrai, had done for his game of virtues, which we have discussed.

Casimir Oudin asserts (*Writers*, supplement, p. 313) that Gerbert’s *Rhythmomachia* was printed together with the four German books on chess that the duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg published under the assumed name Gustavus Selenus, at Leipzig in 1616, in a folio volume that has become very rare.

A modern scholar (LE BEUF, ibid., pp. 85–86, note), reporting this fact from Oudin, has given it a meaning foreign to Oudin’s statement. He does not say, as this scholar asserts, that the prince merely published Gerbert’s work in German, but only that the work was printed together with the illustrious prince’s German work.

It cannot be determined precisely whether all these writings of Gerbert on arithmetic, which were known to Trithemius (*Hirsau Chronicle*, vol. I, p. 142), are gathered together in two different manuscripts of the Vatican Library, among those that belonged to Queen Christina, under the simple title *Arithmetic of Gerbert the Scholastic* (*Arithmetica Gerberti scolastici*) (MONTF., ibid., pp. 24, no. 2, and 58, no. 1), or whether only one of our philosopher’s treatises on the subject is present there.

Since, however, one of these manuscripts announces the works of Bernelin, Gerbert’s disciple, on the same subject, together with the arithmetic of his master, it might be understood as containing everything Gerbert wrote on the topic, collected into one volume and supplemented with Bernelin’s works.

**6.** If Gerbert did not publish as many writings on geometry as on arithmetic, the single treatise of his that remains to us on this first discipline surpasses everything he left on the other. This treatise on geometry is indeed as admirable for its brevity and clarity as for the matters it contains, and for the method and manner in which they are treated. With good reason one may doubt whether, from the first decline of letters until their final restoration [Col. 0067D], anyone handled this subject more successfully.

Gerbert begins his work by explaining the origin of geometry and the two principal uses to which it has been put. He then defines it and demonstrates its usefulness. In doing so, he does not forget to point out that it serves especially to reveal and inspire admiration for the ineffable power and supreme wisdom of God, who made everything according to number, weight, and measure.

Proceeding from there to establish the principles and prescribe the rules of this science, he first touches upon its excellence by recalling the praises bestowed on it by Saint Augustine in his various works, especially in his treatise *On the Quantity of the Soul*. To make his work accessible to everyone, and particularly useful to beginners, whom he has especially in view, he first apologizes to the learned and then applies himself to giving clear notions of the terms, the figures, and, in short, everything pertaining to geometry. He goes so far as to explain the measures of the ancients, which he knew thoroughly.

He goes still further. To make the matters perceptible and, so to speak, allow them to be touched with the finger, he gives examples of every discovery he proposes and teaches how one must proceed to achieve it. For this purpose, he places before his readers every kind of figure used in the practice of this science. He teaches them the various operations required to measure an oblong, square, or triangular field; to determine the height of a tree, tower, or pyramid; to ascertain the quantity of water in a well; to make accurate divisions; and to find the meridian for the construction of sundials.

Boethius, Gerbert’s favorite author, was apparently one of the guides he followed in this treatise. But there is no reason to doubt that he also drew great illumination from the beautiful geometrical figures he acquired during one of his journeys to Italy (Letter, part I, letter 8). He gave such breadth to this science that he subjected even the numbers used for counting to its authority (letter 134).

This treatise by Gerbert, formerly found in the Farnese Library under the title *Book of the Art of Geometry* (*Liber geometriae artis*) (BZOV., *Life of Sylvester*, chapter 7, p. 23), and also preserved in manuscript in the King’s Library, was printed through the efforts of Dom Bernard Pez (ANECD., vol. III, part II, pp. 1–82; dissertation, pp. 7–8). The manuscript from which he took it is approximately six hundred years old and is preserved in the abbey of Saint Peter at Salzburg. It does not reproduce the original text accurately, nor does it accurately reproduce the geometrical figures with which it is filled; the editor nevertheless took care to have them engraved on wood as well as possible.

**7.** Trithemius informs us that Gerbert composed two further treatises, one on the construction of the astrolabe and the other on the manner of constructing the sundial, or quadrant, another mathematical instrument. This twofold treatise is found in manuscripts 1246 and 1269 of the Sorbonne Library, and Abbé Le Beuf reports its beginning. Gerbert also treats there of sundials.

**8.** The work he composed on the sphere has been printed. Trithemius calls it an equally beautiful and necessary work, *pulchrum et necessarium opus*. It is, however, only a letter to Constantine of Fleury, Gerbert’s friend. Nor is it long [Col. 0069A]. Dom Mabillon (ibid., pp. 212–215), having unearthed it in a manuscript of the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, published it in the second volume of his *Analects*.

In few words, though with fairly great detail, the author describes the method of constructing spheres; this detail, moreover, shows that their use was not very common in France. To obtain everything Gerbert wrote on the subject that has come down to us, the preceding letter must be joined to the one he addressed to Remy, a monk of Trier, in which he also discusses the construction of the sphere, representing it as arduous work. This letter shows that a lathe was used to shape the sphere and horsehide to cover it. Our philosopher worked on it himself, despite all the other duties occupying him.

**9.** Gerbert also wrote on one part of dialectic. But he did so only incidentally, as will be seen, and not as a professor giving instruction in the discipline. We possess a short treatise he composed on a difficulty drawn from Porphyry and concerning the categories (PEZ., ibid., vol. II, part II, p. 151). The precise question is whether “the rational” (*rationale*) and “the one using reason” (*ratione uti*) have the same extension, or, in the language of dialecticians, the same power (pp. 149–150). This is what led to the title of the work: *On the Rational and on Using Reason* (*De rationali et ratione uti*).

It is dedicated to the emperor Otto III in an epistle that tells us when and on what occasion it was composed.

During the summer of 997, while this prince was in Italy preparing for war against the Wends, whom Gerbert calls Sarmatians, he had several learned men in his retinue, among them Gerbert, and took pleasure in proposing subtle and difficult philosophical questions to them (MAB., ibid., vol. I, at the end). Since no one had answered satisfactorily, he ordered Gerbert to resolve the question concerning the rational and the one using reason. Gerbert could not carry this out immediately because of illness. After recovering his health, however, he did so in the little work under discussion.

He enters into a long and serious discussion, supporting it both with the authority of the ancient philosophers and with his own reasoning, as well as with a figure to make the matter more perceptible. But it must be admitted that the difficulty was not worth the effort. Gerbert therefore considered himself obliged, at the end of his work, to apologize for undertaking a subject scarcely appropriate to the episcopal dignity with which he was invested. If he did so, it was only from a desire to please the emperor, who was then occupied with a kind of study to which the question under discussion was not unrelated.

The finest passage in the entire work is the dedicatory epistle. Besides the historical details just reported, some of which are highly honorable to the memory of Otto III, it reveals the author’s skill in courting the great [Col. 0070A]. It is also the only part of the work that Dom Mabillon (ibid., pp. 121–123) considered worthy of the public’s attention. Although he possessed the entire work, he limited himself to printing the epistle alone.

Since his copy gave the name of the author and that of the patron only by their initials, he thought that the work might belong to Gebhard, bishop of Augsburg, who had also been part of the Italian journey mentioned above. Later, having acquired more information on the matter, he recognized that it was a work of Gerbert (ibid., at the end of vol. II, p. 215).

This has since been confirmed by the edition Dom Bernard Pez prepared of the complete work from a manuscript of the abbey of Tegernsee in Bavaria, approximately six hundred years old, in which the names of Gerbert and the emperor Otto are written out in full (PEZ., ibid., dissertation, p. 69, no. 3). They are expressed in the same manner in another manuscript of the same age, belonging to the abbey of Saint Emmeram, which contains the same treatise.

**10.** At the end of the work, in this latter manuscript, there are twelve elegiac verses, which the editor printed at the beginning (ibid., vol. I, part II, pp. 149–150). They are a prosopopoeia in which the poet makes Philosophy deliver high praise of the work as something capable of advancing one swiftly along the paths of wisdom.

Dom Pez has no doubt that these verses—tolerable, and better than an infinitude of others from that period—are by Gerbert. We shall take this opportunity to discuss the other poems of our philosopher, insofar as we can know them.

There is another epigram of his, in twelve heroic verses, on the portrait of the celebrated Boethius, which skilled judges regard as a very elegant piece (CAVE, p. 512; OLEAR., *Bibliography*, part II, p. 181). They are not wrong; and one may add that it would not dishonor the poets of the better centuries to count it among their productions.

For good taste, energy, nobility of expression, and the other beauties of poetry, this epigram alone is worth more than all the other pieces of verse produced by Gerbert’s century and the two following centuries. It was therefore not considered unworthy of a place in the *Collection of Short Poems of the Ancients*, where it was printed (EP. ET POES. VET., book II, p. 65). From there it passed into the later editions of Baronius’s *Annals*, to complete the praise of Boethius. It is expressly included in the 1658 edition, under the year 526, p. 117.

The portrait of this philosopher, which occasioned the epigram, was the one Otto III kept in his study. It can be seen from this that the author composed it after he had withdrawn to the court of that emperor.

It was doubtless unknown to a modern scholar who speaks of Gerbert’s versification with supreme contempt (GOUJ., *State of the Sciences*, p. 72). He is no more accurate when he makes our philosopher speak as follows: “I have never composed verse; now I am taking a liking to it, and as long as this taste lasts, I shall send you as many verses as there are distinguished men in France.” It is not Gerbert who speaks in this way, but Otto III, his pupil, then king of Germany and later emperor.

The letter cited, which is the 153rd among Gerbert’s letters, proves this completely. In it Otto begs his dear teacher, then archbishop of Reims, to teach him arithmetic and Greek thoroughly, and, in the enthusiasm he felt for versification, promises to send him as many verses as there were men in France at that time.

This is admittedly a hyperbolic expression, but it must be allowed its full extent, without restricting it by the phrase “distinguished men,” which imposes extremely narrow limits on it and is not found in the original text.

As for the other pieces of verse by Gerbert, we know only four, all epitaphs, each consisting of four long verses. They were composed to adorn the tombs of the emperor Otto II, Lothair king of France, a duke named Frederick, and the scholastic Adalbert. They are printed among the author’s letters, where they occupy the places of letter 66 and the three following letters.

These epitaphs, moreover, possess no superiority over the other poetry of the period beyond the terseness ordinarily found in Gerbert’s other writings.

**11.** From his poems we must pass to his proses, or sequences [Col. 0071C], which have much in common. An author of a *History of the Popes*, writing toward the end of the twelfth century, whose manuscript is preserved in the abbey of Zwettl, asserts that the prose beginning *Ad celebres, Rex caeli*, and so forth, in honor of the angels, is by Gerbert (PEZ., ibid., vol. I, part II, pp. 380–381). Alberic of Trois-Fontaines, who may have drawn this fact from the preceding author, attests the same thing (ALB., *Chronicle*, part II, p. 36).

We do not know, after all, whether this prose still exists anywhere. It is not found in the collection of Josse Clichtove, who gathered so many others.

**12.** We have no greater certainty about the existence of the *Treatise on Rhetoric* that Gerbert composed, as he himself tells us in one of his letters to Bernard, a monk of Aurillac (GERB., letter 92).

From what he says about it, it appears to have been the first, or at least one of the first, works he published after returning from Italy to France, as soon as he found himself entrusted with directing the schools of Reims. It was a volume of respectable size, since it contained twenty-six sheets, or membranes, as they were then called. The author’s opinion of its merit should make us regret its loss.

Gerbert devoted such care to the composition of this work that he hoped the most learned men would receive it with admiration and that it would be of great use to students in entering into the understanding of, and grasping, what is most subtle and obscure in the art and writings of rhetoricians.

**13.** Until now, the anonymous work on the Eucharist published by Father Cellot had been regarded as a work of Heriger, abbot of Lobbes, dating from the end of the tenth century or the opening years of the eleventh. Dom Mabillon, who held this opinion, seemed to have established it with a firmness matched by his modesty (ACT. BEN., vol. VI, prologue, nos. 47–48; *Annals*, book LII, no. 99).

But even the most learned men are never infallible in criticism. Discoveries may easily escape their insight in which others will be more fortunate. This is what happened concerning the true author of the work in question.

Dom Bernard Pez, having recovered it under the name of Gerbert, later pope, in a manuscript of the abbey of Göttweig in Austria dating from the same period as the manuscript attributing it to Heriger, undertook to restore it to the first of these two writers (ANECD., dissertation, p. 69, no. 2; vol. I, part II, p. 132).

It must be admitted that the title, written in red by the same hand as the body of the work, is already strong evidence in favor of Gerbert. This evidence, combined with the identity of style between this work and the others by the same author, outweighs all Dom Mabillon’s arguments. In abandoning Mabillon on this point, however, one does not deny that Heriger also wrote on the Eucharist.

The work under discussion is entitled *Treatise on the Body and Blood of the Lord*. Gerbert appears to have been moved to undertake it by two principal motives.

The first was to show that those who, like Paschasius Radbertus, maintained that Christ’s body in the Eucharist is the same body that was born of the Virgin, died, and rose again, and those others who, like Rabanus of Mainz and Ratramnus of Corbie, maintained the contrary, did not in fact hold different opinions about the underlying basis of the mystery.

The second motive that induced our writer to take up his pen was to demonstrate the absurdity of the imaginary error of the Stercoranists. It can be seen from this that even at the end of the tenth century these questions concerning the Eucharist were still being debated.

Following this plan, Gerbert divided his work into two parts. The first, which is the more extensive, is devoted to proving the first point of his purpose by means of a large number of passages drawn from the Greek and Latin Fathers, almost all very well chosen. He strengthens these proofs with various arguments taken from arithmetic, dialectic, and geometry, supported by figures; the first of these was omitted in the latest edition of the work.

This manner of reasoning reveals Gerbert unmistakably. Throughout everything he says about Paschasius, he speaks of him and his work only with great praise. Similarly, this entire first part is filled with invincible proofs of the real presence of Jesus Christ in the Eucharist.

[Col. 0073A] Gerbert is very brief in the second part. He devotes himself particularly to exposing what he himself calls the absurdities of those who, in support of the Stercoranist opinion, abused these words of the Gospel, in verse 17 of chapter 15 of Saint Matthew: “Everything that enters the mouth goes down,” and so forth. This gives him occasion to recall the blasphemy of certain heretics who maintained on this subject that Jesus Christ had been ignorant of physics. Gerbert himself also plays the physicist to some extent, explaining digestion. Finally, he concludes that it is absurd that a spiritual food, such as the body of Jesus Christ in the Eucharist, should be subject to digestion and its consequences. It is therefore, he says, nourishment for the inner man. But if [Col. 0073B] it has an influence on the outer man, piety requires us to believe that this is in order for it to be the seed of his resurrection on the last day. In this short treatise the author displays considerable precision and soundness of mind. Nothing else, however, can be discovered in it that would indicate whether he undertook it before or after his episcopate.

We have two editions of it. The first was prepared by Father Cellot, who published the work anonymously in the Appendix to his history of Gottschalk, together with a very extensive commentary of his own. Nearly eighty years later, Dom Bernard Pez (ibid., pp. 131–146) had it reprinted from the manuscript mentioned above, which assigns it to Gerbert as its true author.

[Col. 0073C] 14. Nor is it known at what time our writer composed a hymn on the Holy Spirit which, together with its commentary, formerly formed part of the manuscripts of Thomas Bodley, under the numbers 1406–10 (Cat. ms. Ang., vol. I, part I, p. 124, no. 1). The inscription does indeed give him the title of pope; but this circumstance is ambiguous and is insufficient to establish the date of the work. In any case, only those who have it in their hands can give us fuller information about it and tell us whether this hymn concerns the procession of the Holy Spirit, his divinity, or his divine operations.

15. The acts of the famous council held at Saint-Basle in 991, for the deposition of Arnoul, archbishop of [Col. 0073D] Reims, are counted among Gerbert’s writings. It was indeed Gerbert who committed them to writing in his capacity as secretary of the assembly. It does not otherwise appear that he contributed anything to them except their style, which is far superior to that of many other writings from the same period. Nevertheless, he has not escaped accusations of having inserted several things of his own. This would be very difficult to prove, given the care taken in such assemblies to have their acts recorded in their entirety. Baronius nevertheless supposed (An. vol. X, pp. 869, 874, 881) that Gerbert had allowed himself considerable freedom in the acts in question. This put him in such a bad temper against Gerbert that he treated him [Col. 0074A] in a manner equally offensive to courtesy and charity. His criticism of the acts, as bitter as it was vigorous, doubtless caused the collectors of councils to omit them from their compilations. They are nevertheless printed not only in the Magdeburg Centuriators but also separately in a duodecimo volume, published at Frankfurt in 1600 by the heirs of André Wechel, under the title: *Synodus Ecclesiae Gallicanae habita Durocorti Remorum sub Hugone A. et Roberto Francorum rege* — “Synod of the Gallican Church held at Reims under Hugh and Robert, king of the Franks.” An apology for this same council was added, consisting only of several curious letters by Gerbert. The du Chesnes also inserted most of these acts among their *Historians of France* (du Chesn., vol. IV, pp. 101–114).

[Col. 0074B] 16. Gerbert has a discourse (Conc. vol. IX, pp. 747–749) that he delivered at the council of Mouzon in 995 and of which he left a copy with Abbot Leo, the pope’s legate. It has been said that this assembly concerned the deposition of Gerbert, who then occupied the see of Reims, and the restoration of Arnoul. The discourse is an eloquent and well-written defense in which Gerbert explains in what manner and for what reasons he had accepted the government of this church. He says that he had been destined for it upon the death of Archbishop Adalberon, but that Arnoul had then excluded him by resorting to simony.

It is entirely surprising that Mr. Cave (p. 512) doubted whether this work existed anywhere. We [Col. 0074C] have at least four editions of it in as many collections. Baronius included it in his *Annals* (under the year 995, pp. 893–895); Abraham Bzovius (Bzov. *Vit. Silv.*, ch. 21, pp. 76–78) inserted it into the life of our pope; Dom Marlot included it in his *History of the Church of Reims* (vol. II, book I, ch. 16); and Father Labbe included it in the general collection of councils (Conc., ibid.).

17. The preceding discourse is accompanied by a dialogue or conference between Gerbert and the legate Leo at the same council. It is mentioned (Cave, ibid.; *Rom. pont. Vit.*, vol. I, p. 757; Du Pin, *Tenth Century*, p. 148), perhaps without having been seen, as a very fine work, distinct from the discourse, which is not in dialogue form. Gerbert would therefore have produced two different works concerning the council [Col. 0074D] of Mouzon; and it appears, from the characteristics attributed to the work now under discussion, that this cannot reasonably be doubted. Hugh of Fleury, a writer of the eleventh century (Du Chesn., vol. IV, p. 143), knew this dialogue by Gerbert, which he calls a disputation, and says that it was found in full among the acts of the archbishops of Reims. Three other authors (ibid., vol. III, p. 353; Conc., ibid., p. 750; *Spic.*, vol. II, p. 735), who followed Hugh of Fleury closely and perhaps copied him—a chronicler of the same century, the continuator of Aimoin, and Clarius, a monk of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif at Sens—attest the same thing and add that this disputation was *valde utilem* (“very useful”). But there is every [Col. 0075A] appearance that it is lost, as is also that part of the history of the archbishops of Reims in which it had been inserted; this is therefore a double loss.

Before bringing this article to a close, the reader will not be displeased to see in it an example of those striking errors into which even the most learned men can fall when they neglect to exercise their full attention. It is known what was at issue at the council of Mouzon between Gerbert and the legate of the Holy See. Nevertheless, Mr. Du Pin did not fail to assert that the subject of their conference was the construction of the astrolabe. Surely they had matters of an entirely different and more important kind to settle. This learned bibliographer’s error probably [Col. 0075B] arose from his having read, concerning these two different works by Gerbert, only what Mr. Cave says about them. In announcing them together, along with two others, under the same entry, Cave may have caused the confusion. Here is the way he speaks of them, which will justify our conjecture: “A most beautiful dialogue between him and Leo, the apostolic nuncio; *A book on the construction of the astrolabe*; *Book I on rhetoric*; *A speech at the synod of Mouzon*, etc.”

18. Another disputation is attributed to Gerbert (Bib. Bodl., part II, p. 163, no. 2; Oud., *Script.*, suppl., p. 313), one that took place at Rome and was printed in that city in 1544 in a quarto volume. This work, entitled *Disputation of Christians and Jews, held at Rome* (*Disputatio Christianorum et judaeorum Romae habita*), appears to be very rare, and it has not been possible for us to see it ourselves. We are therefore unable to provide a fuller description of it, or even to say whether the author was already pope when he wrote it, or whether he composed it during one of his visits to Rome before his pontificate.

19. There is almost the same uncertainty regarding the time when Gerbert composed the treatise or discourse *The Ideal or Portrait of Bishops* (*De informatione episcoporum*). It is clear from the whole course of the work that the author was then invested with the episcopate. But nothing in it shows that he was already occupying the Holy See. What he says there applies equally to a simple archbishop and to a pope. Gerbert [Col. 0075D] first delivered it orally at an assembly of bishops, whether in a council or otherwise (Mab., *Annal.*, vol. II, p. 210): “Placed in the midst of priests, I shall address the priests themselves” (*In gremio sacerdotum positus, ipsos alloquar sacerdotes*). In any event, whatever capacity he held when he wrote this work—whether as archbishop of Reims or Ravenna, or as pope—it can be regarded only as a venerable monument to his zeal to see the episcopal order shining with the virtues appropriate to its character.

The author has two aims. First, he demonstrates the excellence of the episcopate; then he establishes the obligation incumbent upon those invested with it to lead a life corresponding to this high dignity. Everything revolves around these two points, which are treated fairly well [Col. 0076A] for the period. Gerbert includes a brief but fine exposition of the qualities that Saint Paul, in his First Epistle to Timothy, attributes to the episcopate. After this he launches a vigorous attack on simony, which was then so common, comparing it with the leprosy of Gehazi. The manner in which he combats it is all the more capable of making an impression because it is more direct and more fully detailed. In enhancing the dignity of the episcopate, he says that all bishops, together with Saint Peter, have received the charge of shepherding the sheep of which Jesus Christ speaks in the final chapter of Saint John’s Gospel. This passage is noteworthy if the author was already pope at that time. He concludes this fine discourse with a short prayer in which he implores the Holy Spirit to come to the aid of [Col. 0076B] all bishops, so that they may put into practice what he has inspired him to say to them.

What contributes further to giving a favorable impression of this work and its author is that so many beauties were discovered in it that people wished to honor Saint Ambrose with its authorship, Saint Ambrose being the most polished and eloquent of the Latin Fathers. In the very century in which Gerbert died, Cardinal Humbert, unaware of the true author of this little work, copied a very long fragment of it under the name of that Father; it forms chapter 16 of the first book of his work against the simoniacs (Humb., *In Sim.*, book I, ch. 16). Likewise, Giles Charlier, in his reply to Nicolas Thaborite at the Council of Basel, again cites this work under the name of Saint Ambrose (Mart., *Am. Coll.*, [Col. 0076C] vol. VIII, p. 460).

It is on the authority of these writers, and of others who followed them on this point, that the little work bears the name of this holy doctor in several manuscripts and was consequently printed among his works, where it appears under various titles (Amb., vol. II, appendix, pp. 357–364). Dom Martène (*Anec.*, vol. V, preface, p. 2) says that he searched for it there in vain; but this was because he was looking for it only under the title *On the Life and Ordination of Bishops*, the same title under which Humbert quotes the passage mentioned above. He would have found it under the title *On Priestly Dignity*, as it is listed in volume IV of the Paris edition of 1642, or *On the Formation of Bishops*, as it is entitled in the appendix to the latest edition. It has thus been classified among the works falsely attributed to Saint Ambrose since Dom Mabillon restored it to its true author, Gerbert, on the authority of an ancient manuscript from Saint-Martial of Limoges (Mab., ibid., p. 215). It was from this same manuscript that he had it reprinted in the second volume of his *Analecta*. There are nevertheless several variants between the text of that edition and the text of the same work as it appears among the works of Saint Ambrose. Besides the inscriptions already noted, it also bears in various manuscripts the title *Pastoral*; and this is how Alger and Giles Charlier cite it.

[Col. 0077A] 20. The most interesting of Gerbert’s works is unquestionably the collection of his letters. Jean le Masson, archdeacon of Caen in the Church of Bayeux, published one hundred and sixty of them, together with the letters of John of Salisbury and Stephen of Tournai, all in a quarto volume published in Paris by Macé Ruette in 1611. This editor based them on the manuscript of Papire le Masson, an advocate in the Parliament of Paris and his brother, who had directed the edition and who was the author of the Life of Gerbert found after his letters. They were soon afterward incorporated into the various collections of the Fathers.

In 1636, André du Chesne printed a much fuller collection at the end of the second volume of his *Historians of France* (vol. II, pp. 789–844). It is [Col. 0077B] divided into two parts. The first, which contains only one more letter than Le Masson’s collection, was revised against a manuscript through which the new editor corrected several errors that had crept into the first edition, particularly in letter 134. The second part was taken from a manuscript belonging to Father Sirmond and comprises fifty-five letters that had never before appeared. This edition of Du Chesne should have been taken as the model when people undertook to incorporate Gerbert’s letters into the libraries of the Fathers published after 1636. But this was not even done with regard to the Lyon edition, which was nevertheless intended to be more complete and extensive than the earlier ones.

[Col. 0077C] In that edition, only what Le Masson had published was printed from these letters (Bib. PP., vol. XVII, pp. 669–691).

In neither part of this collection of letters has any chronological order been observed. As for the order of subjects, it was impossible to establish one, since the topics are so varied and are sometimes multiplied within the same letters. Most of them are very short and rarely interesting, although one nevertheless finds in them historical and literary details that help to clarify what was happening at that time in the state and sometimes in the Church, as well as the cultivation of letters. Others contain excellent observations and sound advice; but the predominant characteristic of the majority is a talent for politics and intrigue. Accordingly, several are [Col. 0077D] addressed to popes, emperors, kings, empresses and other princesses, and to archbishops who had a major role in public affairs; or they were written in the name of those same powers, who often employed Gerbert’s pen. One is somewhat vehement, written in the name of Thierry, bishop of Metz, to Prince Charles, brother of King Lothair (letter 31); and another (letter 32), even more vehement, was written in Charles’s name in reply to the prelate. They apparently caused a stir, since Gerbert felt obliged to write to Thierry (letter 33) to explain to him in what spirit he had been moved to compose this reply.

[Col. 0078A] These two vigorous letters, when compared with another (letter 75) that breathes nothing but tenderness, show that Gerbert knew how to adapt his style to the different subjects he undertook to address. The latter was written in the name of Emma, queen of France, concerning the death of King Lothair, her husband, to the empress Adelaide. One of the most interesting as well as one of the longest [Note: [Col. 0077D] This letter is also printed in the General Collection of Councils (p. 745–747), but with a false inscription according to which it is addressed to the Empress Adelaide, whereas it is written to the queen of France of the same name.] in the first part of the collection (letter 159) is the one Gerbert addressed to another Adelaide, queen of France and wife of Hugh Capet, and to all the suffragans of the Church of Reims. In it the author defends his ordination as archbishop of this metropolitan see, from which it was then proposed to expel him [Col. 0078B] in order to restore Arnoul. He discusses the reasons that people believed they had for doing so, according to what he had learned from public rumor.

The letters in the second part inform us particularly about what occurred as a result of the election of Arnoul and of Gerbert in his place. They contain the records of this double election together with Gerbert’s profession of faith. A few are written in Arnoul’s name; but most are in Gerbert’s name as archbishop of Reims, although he does not use that title, and rarely even calls himself a bishop in general terms. The last two (letters 54 and 55), which were inserted into the Collection of Councils (vol. IX, pp. 777–779), were not written until he was pope. We have already given an [Col. 0078C] account of the last, by which Sylvester confirms Arnoul’s restoration, a circumstance that makes it noteworthy. The penultimate letter, which Le Masson had already published at the head of his collection but outside the body of the work, is written to Azelin or Ascelin, the same person as Adalberon, bishop of Laon. It is extremely vigorous and filled with a great many reproaches. Sylvester then summons this prelate to Rome to be judged in a great council that was to be held there during Easter week.

In general, Gerbert rarely gives himself any title at the head of his letters. Those that occasionally appear there are the titles of Scholasticus and schoolmaster abbot, *Scholaris abbas* (letters 7, 12, 142, 148, 161).

He calls himself abbot of Bobbio only once [Col. 0078D] (letter 14), although he retained that abbey until his pontificate.

Two things in particular make his letters obscure and prevent them from providing all the assistance they might otherwise offer: the laconic manner in which they are written and the absence of an address at the head of a great many of them. At other times, the names of the persons to whom they are addressed or of whom they speak are designated only by initials. All this shows how necessary good notes would be to clarify them. The observations made by Dom Mabillon [Col. 0079A] on several of these letters shed considerable light on them (An., book XLIX, no. 63).

Not all the letters belonging to Gerbert were included in the collection we have just described. There are many others scattered through various collections, of which it is important to provide an account.

The first of this class to present itself is the one Gerbert wrote to Séguin, archbishop of Sens, who had attended the Council of Saint-Basle, where Arnoul’s deposition had been decided (Conc., ibid., pp. 744–745). It appears to have been written immediately after France learned what Pope John XV had done in favor of this deposed prelate and against Gerbert’s election. It may therefore date from the year 993. Since [Col. 0079B] this pontiff interdicted all the bishops who had taken part in this important affair, Séguin feared that he would be included in the censure, although he had consistently refused to consent to Arnoul’s deposition. In his letter Gerbert undertakes, by several arguments, to show him that his fear was vain and unfounded. Assuming—something he perhaps ought to have proved—that the judgment rendered by the bishops at Saint-Basle was canonical and consequently the judgment of God himself, he maintains that the pope’s judgment cannot be greater. On this subject he cites the passage in the Acts of the Apostles where it is said that one must obey God rather than men, as well as the eighth verse of the first chapter of the Epistle to the Galatians. He adds several maxims of Saint Leo and Saint Gregory [Col. 0079C] the Great. After establishing as further principles of his system that the common law of the Church is the Gospel, the writings of the apostles and prophets, the canons dictated by the Holy Spirit and consecrated by the respect of the whole world, and finally the decrees of the Holy See that conform to them, he concludes that anyone who has departed from these laws through contempt must be judged according to these laws. But those who observe them must always remain at peace. Séguin must therefore take care not to abstain from the holy mysteries, for otherwise he would make himself guilty.

Gerbert did not expect to become pope when he wrote this letter, which directly opposes the modern claims of the Roman court, claims that had already [Col. 0079D] struck deep roots. For this reason Baronius went to considerable lengths to refute it and reports it in his *Annals* only for that purpose (Bar., *An.*, 992, pp. 882–884). It had already been printed following the acts of the council held at Saint-Basle, in the Frankfurt edition mentioned above (*Rem. Conc.*, pp. 143–146). Later, Fathers Labbe and Cossart included it in their general collection of councils (Conc., ibid., pp. 744–745).

Another letter by Gerbert, which is not found in Du Chesne’s collection and follows the [Col. 0080A] preceding one closely, is the one he wrote to Vildebold, bishop of Strasbourg (*Rem. Conc.*, pp. 113–148). This prelate, who was Gerbert’s friend, had asked him to inform him about his great affair. Gerbert did so in this letter, which is very lengthy and perhaps the most interesting of all his letters. He discusses two points, one historical or factual, the other dogmatic or juridical. After recounting the history of Arnoul, his rival, and reporting what preceded and followed his ordination, he undertakes to answer those who said that the pope had been wronged when this prelate was deposed without the authority of the Holy See. Here Gerbert speaks as a canonist and treats the matter concerning the distinction among crimes and judicial procedure.

[Col. 0080B] At the end of his letter Gerbert (Mart., *Am. Coll.*, vol. I, p. 352) tries to persuade his reader that it was impossible for a man without birth, without possessions, a stranger in the country, such as he was, to have been preferred to so many others who were powerful in the world and distinguished by their illustrious alliances, in order to occupy the see of Reims; it must therefore have been through a special disposition of the one who raises the poor from the dust to make him sit among the princes of his people. He then asks Vildebold to act as the interpreter of his innocence and to justify him before the king and the prelates known to him against the calumnies directed at him, as though he had usurped the see of Reims and had Arnoul arrested. Finally, he [Col. 0080C] ends this long letter by complaining of the sad condition into which the conduct of Rome had plunged the Gallican Church. “Rome,” he says, “has until now been regarded as the mother of all the Churches. Now it is thought to give curses to good men and blessings to the wicked.”

This letter, being little known, required a sufficient account. Du Chesne had published its beginning (vol. IV, p. 114), which Dom Marlot later reprinted from him (*Hist. Rem.*, vol. II, book I, ch. 16, pp. 51–52). Subsequently Dom Martène [Note: [Col. 0079] This editor assigns the date of Gerbert’s letter to Vildebold as late as 995; but it is beyond dispute that it was written no later than 993.] having found a fuller version among Dom Mabillon’s papers, inserted it into his large collection (vol. I, pp. 351–352) of ancient monuments, believing that he was giving it in full. But more than three [Col. 0080D] quarters are missing. What he published beyond the portions supplied by the other two contains almost nothing but the end of the letter. Even the final two or three lines are missing from it. Thus this rare piece is found complete only following the acts of the Council of Saint-Basle, together with the letter to Séguin (*Rem. Conc.*, ibid.).

We have another letter by Gerbert, newly discovered through the efforts of Dom Bernard Pez (*Anec.*, vol. III, part II, pp. 81–84), who found it following the same author’s treatise on geometry in the Salzburg manuscript mentioned above. It is a reply [Col. 0081A] to a difficulty that Adalbold the Scholastic [Note: [Col. 0081D] We do not know on what basis a scholar of our own day (Le Beuf, ibid., p. 86) gives this scholastic the name Ethelbald and the status of bishop of Wittenberg.] had proposed to Gerbert concerning a geometrical operation discussed by Macrobius in his commentary on the *Dream of Scipio*. The letter is entitled: *On the reason for the diversity of areas in an equilateral triangle, considered geometrically or arithmetically* (*De causa diversitatis arearum in trigono aequilatero, geometrice arithmeticeve expenso*). Gerbert was already pope when he wrote this reply, as appears from Adalbold’s letter, which gives him both the titles of sovereign pontiff and philosopher. It cannot be said (Montf., *Bib. bib.*, pp. 24–2, 88–1) whether what two Vatican manuscripts among those belonging to Christina, queen of Sweden, announce under this vague title—*Some things of Gerbert to Adalbold* (*Gerberti ad Adalboldum nonnulla*)—contains anything other than the reply in question. Adalbold, who is generally considered to be the same person as the bishop of Utrecht of that name, had not yet been elevated to the episcopate, since Sylvester does not call him a bishop and he himself uses only the title Scholasticus.

There are still other letters by Gerbert that were not included in the collections published of them. But since they are not of equal value to the preceding ones, we shall merely indicate them. Such is the letter to Theotard, bishop of Le Puy-en-Velay (*Gall. Chr. nov.*, vol. II, appendix, p. 226), by which Sylvester confirms his election and ordination. There are also the letters he wrote to Salla, bishop of Urgell, and to Odo, bishop of Girona, one dated to the year 1001 and the other to the following year (Marca, *Hisp.*, appendix, pp. 957–959). Fathers Labbe and Cossart published another to Robert, abbot of [Col. 0081C] Vézelay, in favor of the privileges of his monastery (Conc., vol. IX, pp. 779–780). Dom Martène (*Ampl. Collect.*, vol. II, p. 54), for his part, published another under the title of a bull, addressed to Ravanger, abbot of Stavelot and Malmedy, declaring these two abbeys to be under the protection of the Holy See. At the head of this letter Sylvester takes the title of universal pope and vicar of Saint Peter. He also wrote to Saint Odilo, abbot of Cluny, and to his entire congregation, to resolve the doubt concerning certain ordinations performed by a bishop who had formerly been a monk of Cluny. This letter forms part of the *Bullarium* of that order.

We have no difficulty believing that the two letters [Col. 0081D] to Pope John XV, under the name of Hugh Capet, king of France, were written by Gerbert. What persuades us is that he is the author of another letter from the same prince to the emperors Basil and Constantine, which is the one hundred and eleventh among those in the first class. Besides, Gerbert’s style is sufficiently recognizable in them. Both are found in Du Chesne’s collection of historians, in Baronius’s *Annals*, and in the general collection of councils. The first asks the sovereign pontiff to render justice against Arnoul, archbishop of Reims. In the second, the king invites him to come to France and indicates the city of Grenoble, where the popes and kings [Col. 0082A] who preceded him had been accustomed to meet, so that he might more easily acquaint himself with the dispute between Arnoul and Gerbert. Gerbert was then in possession of the see of Reims and consequently Hugh’s great chancellor; this confirms the view that these two letters are his work.

There is no doubt that Gerbert, whether as archbishop of Reims or Ravenna, as sovereign pontiff, or even as a scholar before being raised to all these dignities, wrote several other letters that are still either buried in obscurity or entirely lost. The one he addressed to Constantine of Fleury has not been published by name; in it he calls him his Theophilus, as was mentioned above. Nor does the letter appear [Col. 0082B] that he wrote to the suffragans of Sens in favor of Leotheric, their metropolitan, in whose place Count Fromond wished to have Brunon, his own son, ordained (Spic., vol. II, pp. 737–738).

21. As for the bulls of our pope, they belong to the class of his letters, and we know of none other than those mentioned in the preceding article. We shall add here only that Oldoini (*Rom. pont. Vit.*, vol. I, p. 757) attributes to him one that he calls admirable, for establishing the commemoration of the faithful departed on the day after the feast of All Saints. It is known that this pious ceremony, fixed for that day, owes [Col. 0082C] its origin to Saint Odilo, abbot of Cluny, who instituted it, as is generally believed, in the year 998 (Mab., *An.*, book LI, no. 85). Pope Sylvester may very well have issued a bull confirming this holy institution. But it appears nowhere; and if it still existed in manuscript in Rome in Oldoini’s time, how was it overlooked in the new and very extensive collection of papal bulls published in 1692? That collection in fact begins with those of Leo IX, and contains none of Sylvester II or of the preceding pontiffs.

22. What remains of the acts of the councils that Gerbert convened and presided over, whether as metropolitan or as pope, should naturally be counted among his writings. But what has [Col. 0082D] come down to us amounts to very little. Of all those he held while governing the Church of Reims, nothing has been preserved of what took place there except what is found in his collection of letters. The fortieth letter of the second class, for example, contains a warning issued in council against those who seized church property; and it was consequently included in the General Collection of Councils (Conc., vol. IX, p. 740). It is thought to date from the year 993. What we have from the Council of Mouzon, held in 995 by order of Abbot Leo, the pope’s legate, consists chiefly of the discourse [Col. 0083A] Gerbert delivered there, of which we have given an account elsewhere.

He himself convened another as soon as he occupied the see of Ravenna (Conc., ibid., p. 766). The year 997 is assigned as the date of this council; but it is beyond dispute that it belongs to the following year, as we have already shown by establishing the time when Gerbert ascended to the see of that church. Nearly all the suffragans, together with the priests and deacons of Ravenna, attended this council. The regulations made there have been preserved, divided into three articles, to which various bibliographers (Ugh., vol. II, pp. 351–352), in the catalogue of Gerbert’s writings, give the title *On the Celebration of the Council*, as though it were a treatise on how to convene and hold a council.

We have evidence that Gerbert convened several councils during the four years and several weeks in which he occupied the see (Conc., ibid., p. 124; Gerb., letters, part II, letter 54). But care was not taken to preserve their acts for us. There were once, however, very detailed records of the councils held concerning the dispute between Willigis, archbishop of Mainz, and Saint Bernward, bishop of Hildesheim, over the abbey of Gandersheim. We infer this from the fact that the priest Thangmar inserted them into the Life of Saint Bernward, his bishop. Apart from this, all that remains of the other councils is the act in favor of the immunity of the Abbey of Saint Peter at Perugia, dating from the year 1002 (Conc., ibid., pp. 1246–1248).

[Col. 0083C] 23. Abraham Bzovius, who wrote a rather unusual history of Gerbert, also published under his name, as a work unquestionably by him, the Life of Saint Adalbert, bishop of Prague and martyr. It was printed in Rome in the type of the Apostolic Chamber in 1629, in a quarto volume, and subsequently most bibliographers had no hesitation in counting it among Gerbert’s writings. Even Mr. Cave followed this opinion, as did Mr. Olearius after him (Rom. pont., ibid.; Jacob., *Bib. pont.*, p. 214; Olear., *Bib.*, part II, p. 181; Cave, p. 512).

[Col. 0084A] Nevertheless, highly skilled critics (BOLL. 23 Apr., p. 176, n. 9; MAB. ibid., vol. VII, p. 847, n. 3) have shown that this is an untenable error. The work belongs to an anonymous monk of the monastery of Saint Boniface and Saint Alexius in Rome, and our pope’s only connection with it is that he may perhaps have encouraged the author to undertake it. Certainly, M. Basnage has no grounds for bringing a kind of literary lawsuit against these critics because they stated that Bzovius had published the Life in question as a work of Silvester (CANIS. B., vol. III, p. 44, n. 2). On the contrary, he claims that this editor merely says that it was accurately written by one of Saint Adalbert’s friends. Let our readers judge for themselves. Here is one of the titles that Bzovius [Col. 0084B] placed at the head of the work:

*Passion of Saint Adalbert, bishop and martyr, published by Lord Silvester, pope of the city of Rome.*

Could any work be attributed to an author more expressly? The first title on the volume’s title page—which may perhaps have occasioned the error into which M. Basnage fell because he did not read it in full—is nevertheless neither less clear nor less explicit. We copy the portion relevant to our purpose:

*The Life and Passion of Saint Adalbert, published by his contemporary and familiar friend Silvester II, Supreme Pontiff.*

When one undertakes to censure another person’s opinion, one ought to be more certain of the evidence one advances in order to oppose it.

24. Oldoini (Rom. pont. ibid., p. 757) also attempted to transfer to our pope the honor of having composed [Col. 0084C] the Life of the holy empress Adelaide, on the ground that he was perfectly familiar with her history. We possess various editions of this work, at the end of which are found a hymn, a collect, and other prayers for the Mass and Office of this saint, as this supplement to Ciaconius presents them here. But far from any of these editions bearing the name of Gerbert or Silvester, the dedicatory epistle prefixed to one of them (Clun. bib., p. 353) visibly shows that this Life is one of the works produced by the pen of Saint Odilo, abbot of Cluny, to whom all scholars today agree that it belongs.

# The First Part of the Works of Gerbert, Later Pope Silvester II: On the Mathematical Disciplines

[Col. 0085]

## A Short Book on the Division of Numbers

Previously relegated among the spurious minor works of Venerable Bede (*Works*, vol. I, col. 681), now restored for the first time to its author and reviewed according to the evidence of Scaliger Codex XXVIII, preserved in the library of Leiden.

*(From the papers of D. Pitra.)*

## Preface

[Col. 0085C] Gerbert the schoolmaster to his Constantine.  
[Note: [Col. 0085D] Edition: “To his Constantine.” The rest is lacking.]

The power of friendship turns almost impossible things into possible ones. For how could we undertake to explain the principles of numbers on the abacus unless you, Constantine, encouraged us, sweet solace of my labors? Thus, although several lustrums have now passed since we possessed either a book or practice concerning these matters, we bring forward some things with the same words, having recalled them to memory, and others with the same meaning. Let no philosopher without letters suppose that these things are contrary to any art or to philosophy itself. For what will he say that digits, articulated numbers, and minutes are, if he disdains to be an auditor of his elders? Yet he wishes to appear to know alone what he does not know with me, as Flaccus says.

What of the fact that the same number is sometimes simple, sometimes composite; now a digit, now constituted as an articulated number? You therefore have, diligent investigator of such matters, a path of reasoning concise in words but extensive in meaning, fully adapted both to the collection of intervals and their distribution in the practical operations of the geometric radius according to inclination and elevation, and, both in theoretical and practical work, to the measurement of heaven and earth with complete confidence.

## Chapter I. On the Simple Number

[Note: [Col. 0085D] Edition: “On the simple number.” “If you multiply a simple number by a simple number, you will assign a simple number to each digit and ten to every articulated number, both directly and conversely. If you multiply a simple number by ten, you will assign ten to each digit, and so forth.”]

[Col. 0086C]

If you multiply a simple number, [you will assign to each [Note: [Col. 0086D] We add this from the editions.]] digit only up to three, or to an articulated number five times two. From then on, you will place digits among the simple numbers and articulated numbers among the tens, both directly and conversely. If you multiply a simple number by ten, you will assign ten to each digit and one hundred to every articulated number.

If you multiply a simple number by one hundred, you will assign one hundred to each digit and one thousand to an articulated number.

If you multiply a simple number by one thousand, you will assign one thousand to a digit and ten thousand to an articulated number.

If you multiply a simple number by ten thousand, you will assign ten thousand to a digit and one hundred thousand to an articulated number.

If you multiply a simple number by one hundred thousand, you will assign one hundred thousand to a digit [Col. 0086D] and one million to an articulated number.

## Chapter II. On Ten

[Note: [Col. 0086D] The title of this and the following chapter is lacking in the manuscript.]

If you multiply ten by ten, you will assign one hundred to a digit and one thousand to an articulated number.

If you multiply ten by one hundred, you will assign one thousand to a digit and ten thousand to an articulated number.

[Col. 0087A] If you multiply ten by one thousand, you will assign ten thousand to a digit and one hundred thousand to an articulated number.

If you multiply ten by ten thousand, you will assign one hundred thousand to a digit and one million to an articulated number.

If you multiply ten by one hundred thousand, you will assign one million to a digit and also ten million to each articulated number.

## Chapter III. On One Hundred

[Note: [Col. 0087D] Edition: “On one hundred.”]

If you multiply one hundred by one hundred, you will assign ten thousand to a digit and one hundred million to an articulated number.  
[Note: [Col. 0087D] Edition: “and one hundred thousand to an articulated number.”]

If you multiply one hundred by one thousand, you will assign one hundred thousand to a digit and one million to an articulated number.

If you multiply one hundred by ten thousand, you will assign one million to a digit and ten million to an articulated number.

If you multiply one hundred by one hundred thousand, you will assign ten million to a digit [Col. 0087B] and one hundred million to an articulated number.

## Chapter IV. On One Thousand

[Note: [Col. 0087D] Edition: “On one thousand.”]

If you multiply one thousand by one thousand, you will assign one million to a digit and ten million to an articulated number.

If you multiply one thousand by ten thousand, you will assign ten million to a digit and one hundred million to an articulated number.

If you multiply one thousand by one hundred thousand, you will assign one hundred million to a digit and one hundred billion to an articulated number.

## Chapter V. On Ten Thousand

[Note: [Col. 0087D] Edition: “On ten thousand.”]

If you multiply ten thousand by ten thousand, you will assign one million to a digit and one hundred million to an articulated number.  
[Note: [Col. 0087D] Edition: “one hundred million to a digit and one billion to an articulated number.”]

[Col. 0087C] If you multiply ten thousand by one hundred thousand, you will assign one billion to a digit and ten billion to an articulated number.

## Chapter VI. On One Hundred Thousand

[Note: [Col. 0087D] Edition: “On one hundred thousand.”]

If you multiply one hundred thousand by one hundred thousand, you will assign ten billion to a digit and one hundred billion to an articulated number.

## How a Simple Number Is Divided by a Simple Number, or One Hundred by One Hundred, or One Thousand by One Thousand

In the division of numbers on the abacus [Note: [Col. 0088D] The editions add *abaci* and read *dicat* instead of *sic*.], just as simple numbers stand in relation to simple numbers, so, in a certain manner, ten stands in relation to tens, hundreds to hundreds, and thousands to thousands, as follows:
