If you wish to divide simple numbers by simple numbers, or ten by ten, or one hundred by one hundred, or one thousand by one thousand, you will subtract simple numbers from simple numbers according to their denomination.

## Chapter VII

### How Simple Numbers Measure Tens, Hundreds, and Thousands by Their Quantity

In the division of numbers, just as simple numbers stand in relation to tens, hundreds, and thousands, so tens stand in relation to hundreds and thousands, hundreds to thousands, and thousands to composite tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands beyond them, as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0088D] Edition: “so tens stand in relation to hundreds.”]

If you wish to divide by a simple number a ten, a hundred, or a thousand, whether all at once or intermittently, you will multiply the difference from the simple number to ten by the complete denomination of the dividend. You will reduce the articulated numbers according to their own denomination and the stated difference, but add the digits to the digits. If articulated numbers result as above, you will reduce them until only digits remain. A thousand, indeed, will have articulated numbers in the thousands, digits in the hundreds, and digits in the tens; ten will have articulated numbers in the tens and digits in the simple numbers.  
[Note: [Col. 0088D] Edition: “intermittently, you will multiply the difference of the division from the simple number.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0088D] Scaliger Codex: “and thousands indeed”; “digits.”]

## Chapter VIII

### How Ten Measures a Hundred or a Thousand, or a Hundred Thousand, or a Thousand and Higher Numbers

[Col. 0088B]

If you wish to divide a hundred or a thousand by the number ten, or a hundred thousand or higher numbers by ten, or subsequent numbers by a thousand, you will multiply the difference of the divisor—as from a simple number to ten—by the complete denomination of the dividend; that is, by the terms of the simple number. You will reduce the articulated numbers and digits until you reach the final divisor, just as happened when simple numbers divided each number.

## Chapter IX

### How All Simple Numbers, Together with Tens, Measure Tens, Hundreds, and Thousands, Whether Divided Together or Intermittently

[Col. 0088C]

If you wish to divide by a composite number consisting of ten and a simple number, or by a simple ten or a ten combined with a simple number, consider what portion of the divisor the simple number occupies. For the second simple number has the ratio to the second places of the dividend, the third to the third, the fourth to the fourth, the fifth to the fifth, and so on. That is, the difference from the simple number of the divisor to ten will be multiplied by the denomination of the second, third, fourth, and fifth places. Whatever exceeds the second, third, fourth, and fifth places you will add; and if there are more such places than in the divisor, they will be reduced by the same rule. Composite simple numbers will likewise be added to the dividend.

You will do the same with hundreds and thousands, except that you will distribute one hundred or one thousand among the other places—a situation that does not arise with one ten—and the articulated numbers will take their places, being advanced from one hundred or one thousand and obtaining positions from the several dividends.  
[Note: [Col. 0088D] The editions omit “to be divided.”]

## Chapter X. Another Division of a Hundred or a Thousand and Thereafter by the Same Divisors

If you wish to divide a hundred or a thousand, and thereafter, by a composite number consisting of ten and a simple number, you will first divide the hundred as above, taking the difference of the divisor from the simple number to ten; then you will multiply whatever remains by the denomination of the proposed hundred. If a simple number is added to the hundred to form a composite, or if ten combined with a simple number is involved, you will reduce or add in the tens and simple numbers, as stated above. The first articulated numbers are in the sum nearest to and less than the dividend; when increased, however, they take the places of the other articulated numbers of the dividends.  
[Note: [Col. 0089D] Edition: “if the simple number is added to the hundred.”]

## Chapter XI. How Tens Joined to Hundreds, or Hundreds to Thousands, Measure Hundreds, Thousands, or Higher Numbers

If you wish to divide by a composite number consisting of a hundred with a ten, or a thousand with a hundred, either a hundred or a thousand, consider what portion of the divisor the ten, the hundred, or the thousand occupies, and multiply the difference of the divisor by the denomination of those portions, as you did with simple numbers joined to tens.  
[Note: [Col. 0089D] Edition: “tens.” The edition reads “five-hundreds or hundreds”; the manuscript has the uncertain reading *ce tenus*.]

## Chapter XII. Another Division of a Hundred or a Thousand, and Thereafter, by the Same Composite or Simple Divisors

If you wish to divide a hundred or a thousand by ten, or a thousand by a hundred, take the difference of the divisor according to the ratio of simple numbers to ten and multiply it. Do this either by the whole denomination of the dividend, if the divisor is a simple ten or hundred, or by the second, third, fourth, or fifth places if it is composite, observing what portion of the composite divisor the ten or hundred occupies.  
[Note: [Col. 0089D] Edition: “divisors and simple [numbers].”]  
[Note: [Col. 0089D] Edition: “the same.”]

## Chapter XIII. How Two Joined Extremes, with One Intermediate Number Omitted, Measure the Others

If you wish to divide a hundred or a thousand by a composite hundred or thousand, with one intermediate number omitted, you will take one of the dividends to form the minutes and compare the largest divisor with the remaining part. If anything is left over, you will set it aside among the remainders. You will multiply the minute by the denomination by which the divisor is made equal to the dividend. The difference will be placed in full among the digits. Before the articulated numbers, however, there will be another difference, one less, as though it bore a ratio to the adjacent numbers when they are digits and articulated numbers. [Col. 0089D]

For an articulated number alone—that is, without digits [Note: [Col. 0089D] Lacking in the codex]—sets forth its complete difference of the digit, or, if it alone is present, supplies the whole difference [Note: [Col. 0089D] Edition: “the difference. A digit alone supplies the whole.”]. And when the digit is alone, or when it is always accompanied by an articulated number, the complete difference will be advanced to the one set apart for forming the minutes. These differences, and anything that may have been set apart from the largest divisor, will indicate what remains from the dividends.

## Chapter XIV. How a Hundred with a Simple Number Measures a Thousand and Higher Numbers, or a Thousand with Tens Measures Tens of Thousands and Higher Numbers

[Col. 0090A]

If you wish to divide a thousand or higher numbers by a composite number consisting of a hundred and a simple number, you will distribute one thousand among hundreds. Then you will set aside one hundred to form the minutes, and compare the largest divisor with the remaining part. If anything is set aside, you will place it among the remainders. You will multiply the minute as in the preceding chapter, and arrange all the remaining numbers, whether those set aside or those used as differences. Again you will multiply the same differences, and anything that may have been set aside, by the denomination of the proposed dividend. You will proceed by the same rule [Col. 0090B] to the final differences; and with thousand-divisors combined with tens, extending to tens of thousands and higher numbers, you will preserve essentially the same procedure.

## Chapter XV. How Many Divisors There Are in Each Dividend

If you wish to know how many divisors there are in each dividend, advance the articulated numbers from which the denominations of multiplication arise toward the digits; and if articulated numbers result from their increase, turn back toward the articulated numbers. If equal divisors arise among the simple numbers, add an equal number of units to the sums.

Thus, both in the denominations proceeding from the whole and in those proceeding from the parts—that is, from the second, third, and fourth places, and thereafter according to the same rule—you will establish one unit for the final divisor. Just as, with hundreds and thousands, whatever exceeds one is multiplied by the denomination of the whole sum, so [Note: [Col. 0090D] Edition: “is multiplied thus”] the divisors will be multiplied by the denomination of the entire dividend.

But it is not only to hundreds and thousands that the simple divisor ten sends the denominations of a hundred or a thousand, and of composite numbers beyond them, to the third place—that is [Note: [Col. 0090D] Edition: “the same”], to the third place from the one being divided—in collecting the divisors. A hundred, as the divisor of a thousand, sends its divisors to the fourth place; a thousand sends them to the fifth; and a hundred or a thousand, together with their composite divisors, leaving one place aside, send their denominations to the final digits.  
[Note: [Col. 0090D] Edition: “a hundred or a thousand as divisors; its divisors.”]

## Chapter XVI. On the Extension of Certain Measures of Land

[Col. 0090D]

A digit is the smallest part of rural measures.

An ounce contains three digits.

A palm extends to four digits.

Sixteen digits measure a foot.

A pace has a measure of five feet.

A perch, also called a ten-foot measure, extends to two paces, that is, ten feet.  
[Note: [Col. 0090D] Edition: “extends.”]

[Col. 0091A] One hundred and twenty-five paces make a stade.

Eight stades make a mile.

One thousand paces, that is, one and a half miles, make a league, which contains one thousand five hundred paces.

Two leagues, or three miles, make a *resta*.  
[Note: [Col. 0091D] Edition: Edition: *leuvae*.]

Some read *leuca* instead of *leuva*.

The circumference of the whole earth is 252,000 stades. This makes 21,000 Gallic leagues, when those stades are divided by twelve; and 31,500 miles, when they are divided by fifty. It makes 31,000,000 paces and 500 feet (the same stades having been multiplied by 125); 157,000,000 [in paces] and 500 ounces (when multiplied fivefold); 1,800 [in feet]; 90,000,000 (when multiplied twelvefold); and 1,000,000. Digits: 5,671,000; the ounces being multiplied by three. [The latter numerical sequence is corrupt as printed.]

The remainder is lacking in the manuscript.

# Geometry

## Notice of the Reverend Father Bernard Pez on the Following Short Work

*(The Most Recent Treasury of Unpublished Materials, Preface to vol. III.)*

Both ancient and modern writers report that Gerbert, later called Silvester II, was highly accomplished not only in theological and philosophical studies but also in the mathematical disciplines. Among learned men it is a settled opinion that Gerbert came under suspicion of magic among certain people for no other reason than that he mastered the mathematical disciplines and the liberal arts so thoroughly that he almost resurrected them in France, where they were nearly dead.

Yet the absurdity of this story is demonstrated by his epitaph alone, composed by Sergius IV, Silvester’s successor, and reported much more accurately by the Anonymous of Zwettl, vol. I, p. III, in the *History of the Roman Pontiffs*, than it appears in Baronius and Papebroch.

Moreover, although Gerbert’s reputation in mathematics has hitherto been so certain, very few specimens of his work in this field have been brought to light. Mabillon alone, in vol. II of the *Analecta*, p. 212, published a letter of Gerbert the schoolmaster to Constantine the monk on the construction of the sphere. Since it is extremely brief, there is no reason why William Cave—and G. Olearius following him, vol. II of the *Bibliotheca Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum*, p. 181—should call it a book on the sphere.

In a note to the aforementioned letter of Gerbert, Mabillon observes that Gerbert’s *Geometry* and *Rhythmomachia* are preserved in a manuscript of the Thuane Library, marked no. 283. The codex later moved to the Colbert Library, as Casimir Oudinus informs us in the *Supplement to Bellarmine*, p. 313. He also notes that an ancient book of *Rhythmomachia* was published together with four books, in its own German language, on the game of chess, at Leipzig in 1616 in folio, by the most illustrious Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg, under the name Gustavus Selenus; this edition is now rare.

Cave, in his *Literary History*, p. 512, Geneva edition, records that a manuscript book of Gerbert’s *Geometry* was formerly also held in the Farnese Library.

We found another codex—written by a hand approximately six hundred years old and containing Gerbert’s *Geometry*—in the Petrine Library at Salzburg. After we had returned home, the most reverend and illustrious lord Placidus, abbot of the celebrated Petrine monastery, most graciously shared it with us.

In this codex, Gerbert’s text, which is not marked by divisions into chapters, was accompanied here and there in the margins by notes from an anonymous writer. We used for our edition only those notes that could shed some light on the ancient signs for geometrical measurements, wholly unknown in our own age, by having them carefully engraved here in wood just as they were written in the codex.

For the rest, the text is corrupt in more than one place, and the geometrical diagrams are not everywhere sufficiently exact. Nevertheless, we judged that it would be wrong for us to depart from the fidelity of our codex. Let those to whom fortune offers the Colbert manuscript and other manuscript codices restore the defective passages.

In the meantime, even from this book of Gerbert’s *Geometry* it can be understood that mathematical disciplines and other distinguished arts were by no means so neglected in the tenth century as certain modern writers have imagined. Perhaps not many people, even in our own highly polished age, have discussed geometry more elegantly, concisely, and clearly than Gerbert.

But it is not our purpose here to institute comparisons between periods and individuals.

[Col. 0091]

# Geometry

## Here Begins the Prologue to Gerbert’s Geometry

*(In the work of the Reverend Father Bernard Pez, The Most Recent Treasury of Unpublished Materials, vol. III, part II, p. 5.)*

[Col. 0091B] Among the four disciplines in the order of mathematical studies, geometrical speculation naturally occupies the third place, after the treatment of arithmetic and music. Since the rationale of this order is presented sufficiently clearly in the very principles of arithmetical instruction by Boethius, the most learned and eloquent expositor of the liberal arts, we pass it over in silence as something familiar.

[Col. 0092B] This discipline, to speak simply, received its Greek name from the measurement of the earth: for in the Greek language γῆ (*gē*) means “earth,” while μέτρον (*metron*) means “measurement.”

The Egyptians are said to have been its first inventors. Because the overflowing of the Nile repeatedly confused the boundaries of fields by inundating them, they devised the ingenuity of such an art, through whose practice each person could more easily separate the extent of his own small plot from the surrounding land. Although it was first invented for the useful measurement of the earth and took its name from that purpose, later investigators, examining its principles more carefully, adapted its speculation also to several other matters that seemed either useful to know or pleasant to practice.

Some have accordingly assigned it the following definition: Geometry is the discipline of magnitude and of forms that are contemplated according to magnitude. It may also, if I am not mistaken, be defined in this way: Geometry is the science of probable measurement, traced out through the reasoning of proposed rational magnitudes.

The usefulness of this discipline is extremely great for all lovers of wisdom. It is highly subtle for exercising the powers of the mind and intellect and sharpening the understanding; delightful for investigating by certain and true reasoning many things that appear astonishing and unexpected to most people; and fully supplied with subtle speculations for contemplating, admiring, and praising the marvelous power of nature, the power and ineffable wisdom of the Creator who ordered all things by number, measure, and weight (Wisdom 11:21).

Since we shall gather from various sources some material concerning its principles and rules, insofar as our modest intellectual ability permits, so that we may lead the mind of the learner more orderly toward subtler matters, let us take our beginning from the elements of the art itself, which they call a “term.”

[Col. 0093] The Prologue ends.

# Here Begins Gerbert’s Geometry

[Col. 0093]

## Chapter One. What Is a Solid Body? What Are a Line, a Point, and a Surface? What Are a Solid, Square, and Other Feet?

[Col. 0093B]

The beginnings, and as it were the elements, of this art appear to be the point, line, surface, and solidity. Boethius and other writers on both secular and divine learning discuss these subjects sufficiently and more than sufficiently in many passages of their works. The blessed and most eloquent doctor of the Church, Augustine, also treats them at length in several of his books, especially in the one entitled *On the Quantity of the Soul*. There he shows that an eye dulled by such powerful images of bodily things can, through the exercises of these arts, be cleansed and sharpened to some degree for contemplating spiritual and true realities.

But for prudent readers, if any should perhaps deign to consider this, it should not be tedious if, beginning in reverse order with the solid body—which is more familiar to ordinary human perception—I attempt briefly to show what each of these things is, proceeding from the more complex to the simpler.

A solid body is anything extended through three intervals or dimensions; that is, anything spread out in length, breadth, and height, such as anything that can be grasped by sight or touch—for example, this tablet on which I am writing. In Greek this is called *stereon*. The boundary of this, or the plane spread over its surface, has received among us the name “surface”; in Greek, *epiphaneia*. It must be understood in such a way that it claims no height, that is, no thickness, for itself, but extends while confined solely to length and breadth. For if you add height to these, it is no longer a surface but a part of a body and therefore a solid body.

The extremity or boundary of a surface is a line, or in Greek *gramma*. You must conceive it mentally as extending in a straight course without breadth and possessing length alone, lest, when breadth is added, it become not a line but a surface.

A point determines the beginning and end of a line. It contracts itself according to intelligible reasoning so that, existing merely as the end of a line, it possesses no quantity of a part or of any magnitude whatsoever. Thus, to define each item according to the foregoing account:

A point is the smallest indivisible mark. In Greek it is called *sēmeion*. Taking the place of the unit—which is the beginning of all numbers, though it is not itself a number—it is the source of all measurements, while itself being capable of no measure or magnitude.

A line is length without breadth, and it admits division only along its own length. A surface is breadth without height.

These, the line and the surface, cannot subsist in nature apart from bodies; nevertheless, they are understood mentally as incorporeal and as possessing, so to speak, a being apart from bodies. Solidity, defined above as remaining in solid bodies, can also be grasped by the senses; it is subject to divisions of every kind in length and breadth, as well as in height.

For the time being, this brief account of the matters mentioned above will suffice for simpler readers. Those more learned, who have elsewhere been adequately instructed about such things, should not be detained in them longer.

Accordingly, whatever is proposed to be measured rationally through the three dimensions of a solid body is measured by the guidance of reason according to a geometrical theorem. What is investigated by measurement is either length, breadth, or thickness, which geometers customarily call height.

Length is measured in lines enclosing the area of some figure or field; in the distances of journeys; in the heights of trees and buildings; and in the measurement of rivers, courts, and other things laid out in a straight line up to a fixed limit. This is called linear measurement.

Breadth is measured in the quantity of the area or plane itself, enclosed by lines with definite boundaries; when measured as a square or plane, it is called square measurement, and in Greek *epipedon*.

Height is measured in the thickness or density of structures of a defined measure, or in the capacity of vessels of a defined quantity. This is called solid measurement.

Hence we customarily call certain measures feet—sometimes linear, sometimes square, and sometimes solid.

A linear foot, by which we measure lines or some length while paying no attention to height or breadth, is as follows: [Col. 0095B] A square or plane foot, by which a surface, plane, or area enclosed by lines is measured, is equal and square in length and breadth but lacks height, thus: [diagram].

A solid foot is equal and square in length, breadth, and height. By it solid bodies are measured; it retains the form of a cube or die. It cannot be plainly represented by the equality of a plane, but it can easily be conceived mentally or formed in wax, wood, or another material of that kind, although Calcidius, in explaining Plato’s *Timaeus*, described both a solid body represented on a plane.

Other measures, which we shall discuss shortly afterward, are likewise distinguished in three ways, as has already been said of the foot. They are understood either as linear, square, or solid. It is especially important to know that square measures are determined through linear measures. For if linear measures are multiplied by themselves or against one another, square measures arise; and if square measures are likewise multiplied by linear measures, solid measures are found.

To make this clear, let a line be extended lengthwise in place of a linear foot and be divided into four linear palms in this manner: [diagram]. If this linear foot, with a breadth of equal size added, is described equally into a square, a square foot of this kind is formed: [diagram].

[Col. 0095D]

If, therefore, you multiply four linear palms of length by the same number marked in breadth—that is, four by four—you will find, on the plane of the square foot, sixteen square palms in this manner: [diagram].

If, again, forming the same solid foot, you impose upon its length and breadth an equal height, and multiply it by four linear palms of the superimposed height—that is, by the sixteen square palms of the plane—you will find, in the solid foot, sixty-four solid palms. Anyone will understand this more easily than it can be represented in a palm.

Thus a linear foot contains four linear palms, a square foot sixteen square palms, and a solid foot sixty-four solid palms. The same rule of multiplication should be observed in the other measures according to the quantity of each.

## Chapter Two. On the Names and Quantities of Measures Invented by the Ancients

The names of measures invented by the ancients and preserved in the usage of later generations down to the present are approximately these: the digit, ounce, palm, sixth—which is also called the *dodrans*—foot, small tile, cubit, step, pace, perch—which is also called the ten-foot measure—smallest *actus*, *clima*, *porca*, square *actus*, which is also called the *agripennus* or *aripennus*, *jugerum*, or *juger* or *jugus*, *centuria*, stade, mile, and league.

Let us first consider the quantity of each according to linear measures, so that afterward they may be more conveniently converted into square and solid measures.

A digit is the smallest measure that the ancients used in measuring fields. It contains four grains of barley, arranged lengthwise in a continuous line. You must not simply take the fingers of just any people, which are certainly very unequal, but must uniformly regard as the definite geometrical length of a digit the space occupied transversely by the breadth of a digit belonging to an average person of that period. The same must be done with the palm, foot, cubit, and the other measures of this kind.

An ounce, according to the ancients, contains three digits. But because one twelfth of anything is called an ounce, later writers assigned only one digit and one-third of a digit to the ounce, so that it could be one-twelfth of the foot, which consists of sixteen digits. For *as* and *triens* together make sixteen.

A palm, however, the fourth part of a foot, contains four digits and three ounces. It is called a palm from *palma*, that is, from the extended hand, which consists of four digits.

A sixth, also called a *dodrans*, contains twelve digits, nine ounces, and three palms. It is called *dodrans* because it consists of a whole foot with a quarter subtracted.

A foot contains sixteen digits, twelve ounces, four palms, one sixth, and one-third of a sixth. This measure is more commonly used in measuring all kinds of things.

[Col. 0097A] A small tile cannot be understood in length alone, as the preceding measures can, but also has breadth, so that it becomes square. It has one foot in breadth and one foot plus eleven-twelfths of a foot in length; in breadth it has twelve ounces and in length twenty-three. In its entire area it contains 276 square ounces. It is called *laterculus*, a diminutive of *later*, “tile,” because tiles of this measure were customarily made for covering or flooring buildings.

A cubit contains one and a half feet, two sixths, six palms, eighteen ounces, and twenty-four digits. In some places it is also used for the stature of human beings.

A step contains two cubits, three feet, four sixths, twelve palms, thirty-six ounces, and forty-eight digits. It is called a step because people walking commonly measure just so much space by alternating their steps.

A pace contains one step and a *bisse* (two-thirds; the Old Gloss in the codex explains it as a *bisse*, elsewhere as a *dodrans*), three cubits and a *triens* (one-third; the same Gloss), five feet, six sixths and [a fraction missing in the printed source], twenty palms, sixty ounces, and eighty digits. It is chiefly used for measuring distances on journeys. It seems to be called *passus* from *patere*, “to extend,” because it is formed by legs extended across an interval of five feet; hence hair spread out is also called *passi*.

A perch, also called a ten-foot measure, contains two paces, three steps and one-third, six cubits and a *bisse* (two-thirds), ten feet, thirteen sixths and [a fraction missing in the printed source], forty palms, 120 ounces, and 160 digits. It is called *pertica*, as though from *portica*, from carrying. For the surveyor carries a measuring rod in his hand for measuring fields.

A smallest *actus* is considered only as a quantity of the surface of fields. It has four feet in breadth and 140 in length. When these are multiplied together—that is, four times 140—they show 560 square feet over the whole surface of the field. It seems to derive its name from working the land.

A *clima*, likewise designating the quantity of a field, has sixty feet both in length and in breadth. When multiplied together, these complete 1,600 square feet.

Porta, nevertheless indicating a measure of land, has 80 feet in length and 36 in breadth. Multiplied together, these indicate 2,400 square feet.

The square actus, also called the agripennus or aripennus, by which we distinguish the extent of land, contains 12 perticae along each of its four sides, that is, 120 feet. Multiplied by itself, it shows in the agripennus 144 square perticae and 14,400 square feet.

The jugerum, or juger, or jugus, which is formed by joining two aripenni and takes its name from *jungere*, “to join,” likewise [lacuna] the measure of land, has in length 24 perticae, that is, 240 feet, and in breadth 12 perticae, that is, 120 feet. When this breadth is multiplied by the length, you will find on the surface of the jugerum 288 square perticae, but 28,800 square feet. Its fourth part is called a *tabula*, containing 72 square perticae.

A centuria is land containing 200 jugera; it is so called because among the ancients it was reckoned only in hundreds of jugera. These measures, however, which indicate the quantity of land, should be considered more by the quantity of their area and the plane enclosed by lines than by the length of the lines themselves by which they are enclosed. For it makes no difference what length of lines encloses an area, provided that the area itself does not lose its proper quantity, as in the case of the jugerum. Whether, therefore, it has 24 perticae in length and 12 in breadth, as stated above, or 18 in length and 16 in breadth, or 32 in length and 9 in breadth, or whether length and breadth are exchanged in some other way, if by their mutual multiplication they can produce 288 square perticae, they will nevertheless constitute a jugerum. The same understanding should be applied to the agripennus and the other measures of land.

**[Col. 0098B]** A stadium, which is more commonly used for measuring journeys, contains 125 passus, 208 and one-third gradus, 416 and two-thirds cubits, 625 feet, 933 and one-third sextae, 2,500 palmi, 7,500 unciae, and 10,000 digits. The stadium is said to take its name from *stare*, “to stand”: either because young men, having run this distance, would stand at the finish, or because Hercules was the first to mark out this distance by standing after traversing it in a single breath.

A mile contains 8 stadia, 1,000 passus—from which it also received its name—1,600 gradus, 61 [uncertain], 3,300 cubits, 33 [uncertain], 5,000 feet, 6,600 sextae, 66 [uncertain], 20,000 palmi, 60,000 unciae, and 80,000 digits. By permission of the ancient law, this was the distance of the Sabbath journey.

A leuca contains one and a half miles, 12 stadia, 1,500 passus, 2,500 gradus, 5,000 cubits, 7,500 feet, 10,000 sextae, 30,000 palmi, 90,000 unciae, and 120,000 digits. The leuca is said to derive its name from *levare*, that is, “to relieve,” because the body is relieved after so long a journey. Hence among the Teutons it is also called a *Rasta*, from resting.

## CHAPTER III. On the threefold description of the quantity of these same measures

Since what has been said so far about linear measures—that is, measures indicating length alone—has been stated somewhat loosely, let us now also briefly record, on the following little page if you please, the quantity of these same measures when they become square or solid, in passus, feet, and digits; namely, omitting those which, as we stated earlier, indicate only the quantities of the surface of fields.

A leuca has 1,500 linear passus, [in square measure] M.I.CC.L, [in solid measure] three times MMM, and three times CMM, and LXX, es MM, and Ves II.

A mile has 1,000 linear passus, MI square, MM solid, and two thousand thousands.

A pertica has two linear passus, four square, and eight solid.

A passus has five linear feet, 25 square, and 125 solid.

A gradus has 3 linear feet, 9 square, and 27 solid.

**[Col. 0099A]** A cubit has one linear foot and one half. [Note: **[Col. 0099D]** The old Gloss explains this as one half.] It has two and one-third square feet, and three solid feet.

[Note: **[Col. 0099D]** The same Gloss explains this as a half-uncia or semi-uncia.] A foot has 16 linear digits, 256 square, and 4,096 solid.

A sexta has 12 linear digits, 144 square, and 1,728 solid.

A palm has 4 linear digits, 16 square, and 64 solid.

An uncia has one linear digit, one square, and two solid. [Note: **[Col. 0100D]** The same Gloss explains these signs in this manner: *duella*, half-uncia, *obolus*, *siliqua*.]

A digit has 4 linear grains of barley, 16 square, and 64 solid.

And thus, concerning the measures handed down to us by our predecessors, enough—and, as I think, not more than enough—has been said. **[Col. 0099B]** If anyone needs the earlier divisions for measuring, every diligent person will be able to possess each of the measures mentioned above, as necessity requires, in various ways, whether through the customary fractions or through conceptual subdivisions.

## CHAPTER IV. On plane figures

Now we must consider the figures enclosed by the linear measures mentioned above. A figure, called *schema* in Greek, is a space enclosed by definite boundaries. There are two kinds of figures: they are either plane or solid. We shall deal with solids later; for now let us examine planes.

Plane figures are those which lack depth—that is, height—and are considered only in length and breadth. When these are presented according to reason, they are either bounded by straight lines, which in Greek are called *euthyae*, and are angular; they are then called *euthygramma*. Or they are enclosed by curved or surrounding lines, which the Greeks call *cyclic* or *cycloid* (the Codex has *licoid*) or *capella*; these figures are round or oblong and are called *campylogramma*. Or else they are composed of both kinds, that is, straight and curved lines, and are partly angular and partly crescent-shaped or round; this kind is called *micton* by the Greeks. Each of these will be described more clearly below, as seems convenient and useful.

The space or plane enclosed by the lines of plane figures is called *embadum* by the Greeks, which our people have translated as *area*. For investigating the quantity of this *embadum*, or area, various rules are reported in scattered form, according to the variety of figures and theorems. We shall attempt to take up some of them—those which our diligence has been able to reach and which seemed more useful—in a somewhat more orderly arrangement, after first establishing a few points about the kinds of angles and certain other matters necessary for what follows.

Thus plane figures, which we said are bounded by straight lines and are angular, are necessarily formed from three kinds of plane angles. **[Col. 0100A]** A plane angle is the meeting at a single point of two lines drawn in different directions on a plane. Or, stated otherwise: an angle is the space contained beneath two lines touching one another. Distinguished, in fact, into three kinds, it is either right, obtuse, or acute.

A right angle, also called a normal angle, is formed in this way: when a standing straight line meets another straight line lying horizontally, it makes equal angles on both sides:

**[Col. 0100B]**

This angle, as though occupying the middle course of virtue and always equal and uniform to itself, neither expands beyond what is proper nor contracts below what is just.

An obtuse angle, also called greater-than-normal or blunt, is an angle which, in the manner of *pleonasia*, once it has exceeded the right angle, can be widened and expanded by an uncertain and indefinite amount until it falls away into a straight line. It is formed when one line, inclined away from a line lying horizontally, is joined to it in this manner:

**[Col. 0100C]** An acute angle is one which, imitating *neomesia* and remaining below a right angle, can repeatedly be narrowed by an indefinite amount until it reaches a straight line. It is formed when another straight line touches a straight line lying horizontally, inclined toward it, in this manner:

These angles, then, being made from straight lines—called *euthygrammi* in Greek—may be called *rectilinear* in Latin. Yet the same three kinds of angles can in some fashion be represented by straight and curved lines, and also by curved lines alone.

## CHAPTER V. Every composite figure is constituted from these three kinds of angles

In all plane figures, therefore, as has been said, and particularly in angular figures, you necessarily find one, two, or all of these kinds of angles. You find one kind when all the angles are right, or all obtuse, or all acute; two kinds when some angles are right and others acute, or some obtuse and others acute, or some right and others obtuse; and all three kinds when a figure contains a right, an obtuse, and an acute angle—although this occurs more rarely in a single figure. **[Col. 0103D]** The whole matter will become clear later in the adequate construction of these figures. Now we shall attempt to address what seems appropriate concerning the triangle, which naturally occurs first among plane figures.

## CHAPTER VI. On the primacy of the triangle

The triangle, as Boethius sufficiently demonstrated in his arithmetical works, is the principle of plane figures because three straight lines can first enclose a surface or some breadth. Two straight lines can enclose no space. And because the triangle, stretched out by three lines, is the first to produce angular and plane figures, it rightly holds the position of primacy among those figures.

It is also the principle and, as it were, the element of angular figures because every such figure is composed from it and resolved into it. For if you mark the surface—that is, the central area—of a triangle, quadrilateral, pentagon, hexagon, or any of the other succeeding polygons with a point, and draw straight lines from that point to the angles, you will observe that each figure is composed of and divided into as many triangles as it itself has angles. In the same way, the triangle is divided into three triangles, the quadrilateral into four, the pentagon into five, and the succeeding figures into triangles according to the number of their angles.

Here a subtle consequence also follows: since each of them is divided into triangles, the area of each can be found by the rules of triangles by those who apply themselves diligently. Thus it can be sufficiently demonstrated to anyone that the triangle is the principle of all plane figures.

## CHAPTER VII. On the kinds of triangle

A triangle, also called a *trigonus* or *tripleurus*, is a plane figure bounded by three straight lines or sides and the same number of angles. There are three kinds: the orthogonius, the ampligonius, and the oxygonius.

An orthogonius is a triangle having one right angle and two acute angles, in this manner:

It takes its name from the right angle that it contains. For in Greek *orthon* means “straight,” while *gone* means “angle.” Hence *orthogonius* means “right-angled.”

An ampligonius is a triangle having one obtuse angle and two acute angles, as follows:

**[Col. 0104D]** It too receives its name from its obtuse angle.

An oxygonius is bounded by three entirely acute angles, as follows:

Hence it is named from the acute angle, since *oxya* means “sharp.” It can also have angles of a single kind and equal sides; this is entirely impossible in the preceding type, as anyone can easily understand and confirm by looking at their figures.

These triangles also have three other terms distinguishing them. One is called *isopleurus*, another *isoceles*, and another *scalenos*.

An isopleurus is contained by sides that are all equal. For *isos* means “equal,” and *pleuros* means “side.”

An isoceles has two equal sides and, as it were, stands upon two legs, while its third side is unequal. Hence it is called *isoceles*, as if “equal-legged.”

**[Col. 0105B]** A scalenos contains sides that are all unequal to one another. It is called *scalenos*, as if “stepped,” because, like steps, one side passes from one level to another. But only the isopleurus, that is, the equilateral triangle, can be an oxygonius triangle; isosceles and scalene triangles can be orthogonius, ampligonius, or oxygonius. Each of them can be formed either with two equal sides and a third unequal side or with all sides unequal.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the nature of triangles

One should also observe in these triangles that, according to the quantity of angles described above, in every ampligonius triangle the exterior, that is, obtuse angle, is greater than either of the interior, that is, acute angles, which are situated opposite it in the ampligonius triangle. Those two angles are proved to be smaller not only than the exterior angle but also than a right angle, as in this figure:

In every triangle, any two angles taken together are less than two right angles.

In every triangle, the smaller side produces the larger angle, while the larger side produces the smaller angle.

If, from the endpoints of any side of a triangle, two straight lines are inclined inward so as to form an angle, those lines themselves are shorter than the other sides of the triangle, while they form a larger angle, as follows:

**[Col. 0105D]**

In every orthogonius triangle, the single right angle is proved equal to the other two interior, that is, acute angles. In an oxygonius triangle, each of the three interior, that is, acute angles, is equal to two right angles, and in every triangle the same is entirely true: its three angles together are equal to two right angles. For in an ampligonius triangle, by as much as the exterior, that is, obtuse angle, exceeds a right angle, by that much the two interior, that is, acute angles, fall short of a right angle. In an orthogonius triangle there is one right angle, and the interior, that is, acute angles, together complete one right angle, as has been said.

In an oxygonius triangle, two acute angles together exceed one right angle, but they fall short of two right angles by as much as the third angle can supply. According to this reasoning, if I am not mistaken, what Boethius stated in his Commentaries on Aristotle’s *Categories* should be understood: “Many have often been accustomed to raise a difficulty: we know that a triangle has three interior angles equal to two right angles.”

Having disposed for the present of these matters concerning the nature of triangles, let us briefly say how each angle may be discerned as either right, obtuse, or acute, so that we may more certainly determine whether a given triangle is orthogonius, ampligonius, or oxygonius.

## CHAPTER IX. How the three kinds of angle can be distinguished

If you are uncertain about an angle, whether it is right, obtuse, or acute, you may use the following experiment. From the angle about which you are uncertain, mark off on each of the two lines meeting there an equal measure of any length, marking the two endpoints. Draw a straight line from one point to the other, divide it into two equal parts, and mark its midpoint with a point. If this midpoint is at the same distance from the angle in question as the measure by which you found the half-line, the angle will be right. If it is farther away and cannot be reached by that measure, the angle is acute; if the stated measure passes beyond it because it is nearer, it is recognized as obtuse, that is, blunt.

For example, let the angle about which you are uncertain be *a*. On each of its lines let equal measures terminate at *b* and *c*. The midpoint of the line drawn from *b* to *c* is *d*. If, therefore, points *b*, *c*, and *a* are equally distant from point *d*, angle *a* is right. If *d* is nearer to *a* than to *b* and *c*, the angle is obtuse. **[Col. 0106D]** If it is farther away, there is no doubt that angle *a* is acute.

Or use another method, according to Pythagoras’ discovery. From the angle about which you are uncertain, measure off three equal lengths—feet, for example—along one of its lines, and four equal lengths along the other. Mark the endpoints on both sides, and draw a straight line from one endpoint to the other. If this line is five feet of equal length, the angle in question will be right; if more than five, obtuse; if less, it will appear acute.

For example, let the angle itself be *e*. From *e* I measure three units, as it were feet, along one line as far as *g*, and four from *e* along the other as far as *f*. If, therefore, I find five measures of the same length in the line between *f* and *g*, I have no doubt, compelled by nature, that angle *e* is perfectly right. If it is more than five, I hold it to be obtuse; if less, it must certainly be counted among the acute angles, as is clear in the following diagram.

The straight lines by which triangles, quadrilaterals, and certain other plane figures are bounded are generally designated by the following terms.

## CHAPTER X. On the names of lines in figures

**[Col. 0107B]**

A line which lies directly, and not obliquely, on one side of a figure receives the name *basis*, because the figure is founded upon it. A line drawn similarly and directly at the top, as it were at the summit of the figure, is called the *coraustus*. A line hanging directly downward from the top like a perpendicular, where it joins the basis or coraustus, forms a right angle and receives the name *cathetus*, or perpendicular. But the line which, drawn obliquely downward or upward, appears to produce an obtuse or acute angle is called the *hypotenusa*, that is, the oblique line, or *podismus*.

From the measurement of these lines, and especially of the cathetus and the basis or coraustus, which determine the length and breadth of the figure, we must investigate the square measure of its *embadum*, as we mentioned above. Although some place the ampligonius first because of its larger angle, and consider the oxygonius more primary because of its isopleurous form, which enjoys equality both of angles and sides, we nevertheless judge that the orthogonius should rightly be preferred to these, both because of the primacy of the right angle and because its method is clearer and more certain, and because the ampligonius and oxygonius appear to receive their rules from it.

## CHAPTER XI. On Pythagorean right triangles

Among all triangles with different sides, the orthogonius which is called Pythagorean after its discoverer Pythagoras seems in some way to possess a special privilege and distinction. Why this is so will be made clear below. It is contained by such proportions among its sides that the basis is to the cathetus in the ratio of one and one-third, the hypotenuse to the basis in the ratio of one and one-quarter, and likewise to the cathetus in the ratio of one and two-thirds. The cathetus has feet—or other smaller or larger measures—in these same proportions, as follows.

## CHAPTER XII. How fractions are added to figures

Since sometimes certain or all of the sides of such orthogonal triangles are customarily presented with fractions added—for a skillful geometer ought not to be ignorant of the art of fractional calculation—it is appropriate to record examples of this also:

In these and other orthogonal triangles constituted according to the same proportions of their sides, namely Pythagorean triangles, you can find the other sides from the cathetus in the following way.

Triple the cathetus; subtract a ninth from it; take half of what remains as the basis. If you add to the basis thus found the same ninth that you subtracted, you will have the hypotenuse. Thus, in the first example I gave, a cathetus of 3, multiplied by 3, produces 9; after subtracting a ninth, that is, one, the remainder is 8, and half of it produces the basis, which is designated by 4. If you restore to this basis the ninth previously subtracted, that is, one, the hypotenuse is completed, marked as 5 units.

The same result is found in the other examples that follow, whether with whole numbers or with numbers composed of fractions. Thus, in the case where the cathetus is 4, four multiplied by 3 makes 12. After subtracting a ninth of this, that is, one and one-third, the remainder—10 and two-thirds—when halved gives the basis as 5 and one-third. When that same ninth is added to the basis, it shows that the oblique side is 6 and one-half.

Or find the same result another way. Triple half the cathetus, subtracting a ninth from it, and take the result as the basis. Add its ninth to the same triple quantity, and the hypotenuse is produced. Thus, when the cathetus is 6, half of it, namely 3, multiplied by 3 produces 9. After subtracting a ninth, the basis is 8. When the ninth is added to the 9 itself, the hypotenuse becomes 10.

Similarly, in the case where I assigned a quarter to the cathetus, half of it—namely 2 and one-half—when multiplied by 3 produces 7 and one-half and [uncertain notation]. Subtracting its ninth, that is, [uncertain notation], leaves 7 as the basis. When it is added, it gives 8 to the hypotenuse.

**[Col. 0109C]** Or otherwise: multiply half the cathetus by six; subtract a ninth from it; take half the remainder as the basis. Add the same ninth to the basis found, and the hypotenuse is produced. Thus, in the case where the cathetus is 9, half of it, namely 4 and one-half, multiplied by six makes 27. After subtracting a ninth, namely 3, the remainder is 24; half of it, namely 12, is the basis. When the 3—that is, the previously mentioned ninth—is added to it, the total is 15, which constitutes the oblique side.

Likewise, in the case where the cathetus is given as 6 and [fraction], half of it, which is 3 [a quarter], multiplied by six makes 19. After subtracting a ninth, which is 2 (the old Gloss interprets the sign *z.* as a *siliqua*), [uncertain fractional notation] are subtracted, leaving 16 and five [uncertain]. Half of this, namely 8, together with a sextula, completes the basis. When the aforesaid ninth is added to it, it makes the oblique side, namely 10 and one-half, with five [uncertain sign] set aside amid considerable uncertainty.

There is also another rule, worthy of much more careful examination, which is entirely true in these Pythagorean right triangles and either wholly true or close to the truth in all other right triangles.

By this rule, in almost every orthogonius triangle the quantity of the third side can be investigated from any two sides with complete certainty according to the constitution of nature, as follows:

To find the hypotenuse, multiply the number of the cathetus by itself, so that it becomes a square, and add to it the number of the basis similarly multiplied by itself. The square root of this total, composed of the two squares, should be understood as the number of the hypotenuse.

**[Col. 0110A]** A square, as is well known from arithmetic, is a number produced by multiplying one number by itself: for example, 4, produced from 2; 9, produced from 3; and 16, produced by multiplying 4 by itself. Twice two creates 4, three times three creates 9, and four times four creates 16. The number which, multiplied by itself, produces a square is called the square root of the square produced from it.

To determine the quantity of the basis, subtract from the number of the hypotenuse multiplied by itself the number of the cathetus likewise multiplied by itself, and assign the square root of the remainder to the basis as its naturally inherent quantity.

To investigate the measure of the cathetus, subtract from the number of the hypotenuse likewise multiplied by itself the number of the basis multiplied by itself, and take the square root of the remainder as the cathetus.

To make each of these points clear by examples, I shall take the smallest of the preceding right triangles and find its hypotenuse from its cathetus and basis in this way. The cathetus, namely 3, multiplied by itself produces 9, a square. Likewise the basis, namely 4, multiplied by itself produces 16, a square. These two squares, 9 and 16, when joined, make 25, again forming a square. Its square root, which is 5—for five times five completes the number 25—is the hypotenuse.

From the cathetus and hypotenuse you will find the basis as follows. From the number of the hypotenuse, namely 25, I subtract 9, the cathetus multiplied by itself; the square root of the remainder, namely 16, is 4, which I assign to the basis. To find the cathetus, from the same 25, the hypotenuse multiplied by itself, I subtract the basis multiplied by itself, namely 16, and assign the square root of the remaining 9, namely 3, to the cathetus.

Again, to provide a larger example, I take a triangle whose cathetus is 12 and whose basis is 16. I join the numbers produced by multiplying each by itself, namely 144 and 256; the square root of the 400 produced from these is 20, which I assign to the hypotenuse. If from the same 400 I subtract the cathetus multiplied by itself, namely 144, the square root of the remaining 256, namely 16, is assigned to the basis. If from the same 400 the basis multiplied by itself, namely 256, is subtracted, the remaining 144 has 12 as its square root, which is assigned to the perpendicular, that is, the cathetus.

And lest I avoid providing an example also with fractional quantities, I take the triangle for which above I posited 6 and [fraction] in the cathetus. I multiply the cathetus by itself in the regular manner, which is very easy for an abacist, and obtain a square of 40 and one-half. Likewise, the basis, which is 8 and [fraction], when multiplied by itself produces a square of 71 and two [fractions] and one-third. These two squares joined together make a square containing 101 and two *siliquae* and one-third of a *siliqua*. Its square root, found to be 10 and one-half and [uncertain notation]—for when this is multiplied by itself it restores the same quantity—shows the quantity of the hypotenuse.

If from the same hypotenuse number multiplied by itself, namely two *siliquae* and one-third of a *siliqua*, you subtract the cathetus multiplied by itself, namely 40 and one-half, the square root of the remainder, namely 71 and two *siliquae* and one-third of a *siliqua*, will be the basis, namely 8 and [uncertain notation]. If the basis multiplied by itself is subtracted from the same hypotenuse number, the remainder is 408, whose square root is 6, restoring the cathetus. This rule never fails anyone wishing to test it in the other right triangles as well, provided that one wishes to find the linear measures of the sides.

For finding the square *embadum*, that is, the area, in these Pythagorean right triangles, use the following rule: add together the quantities of the three sides—the cathetus, basis, and hypotenuse. Take half of this, and subtract the basis from it. Multiply what remains by the cathetus, and double the resulting sum. Multiply the doubled quantity by one quarter of itself, and take the square root of the resulting sum as the *embadum*.

For example, I add together the numbers of the three sides of the smallest of the preceding right triangles, namely 3, 4, and 5; the result is 12. Half of this is 6. From it I subtract 4, the basis; the remainder, 2, multiplied by the cathetus, namely 3, makes 6. When doubled, this becomes 12. Multiplying this by one quarter of itself, namely 3, produces 36. If I take its square root, namely 6, I have the area of the right triangle.

Likewise, in the first example that I gave with fractions, if you add the sides, namely 4, 5, and 6, you obtain 16. Take half of this, namely 8; subtract the basis, namely 5; multiply the remainder, namely 3, by the cathetus, namely 4, and you have 10. When doubled, this becomes 20. Multiplying it by one quarter of itself, namely 5, gives 113 [the printed calculation is uncertain]. If I take its square root, which is 10 [uncertain fraction], I obtain the area of the entire *embadum*. The same applies in the other cases.

A much simpler, easier, and more efficient rule for finding the *embadum* in all right triangles—and indeed a universal rule for every triangle—is to multiply the cathetus by half the basis and take the resulting product as the *embadum*. The same result is obtained if, conversely, the whole basis is multiplied by half the cathetus and the resulting product is called the *embadum*. Or, if the whole basis is multiplied by the whole perpendicular, half of the resulting number is assigned to the area.

For when the basis is multiplied by the cathetus, or the breadth by the length, the quantity of the square’s area is found. When I divide it diagonally from one angle to the opposite angle, I produce two triangles equal to one another, because in each of them I find half the area of the quadrilateral.

To add examples of this rule, let me take from the preceding right triangles one whose cathetus is recorded as 15 feet and whose basis is 20 feet. I multiply the basis by the cathetus in this way: 15 times 20 makes 300. Half of this, namely 150, indicates the number of square feet in the entire area.

Likewise, in the fractional example, whose cathetus is 6 [fraction] feet and whose basis is 8, multiplying the basis by the cathetus in the ordinary manner produces 53 square feet and 9 *siliquae*. Half of this, namely 26 feet and [uncertain notation], together with half a *siliqua*, indicates the quantity of the entire area. The same applies in the other cases.

If you also wish to know how many smaller measures than the foot—such as palms, unciae, and digits—are contained in the *embada* mentioned above, look back at how many of each of these measures a square foot contains. A square foot contains, as stated above, four times four palms, that is, 16; twelve times twelve unciae, that is, 144; and sixteen times sixteen digits, that is, 256. Multiply the area of the preceding right triangles by each of these numbers. In the first area, which contains 150 square feet, you will find 2,400 square palms, 21,600 unciae, and 38,400 square digits.

**[Col. 0112B]** In the subsequent example, whose area contains 26 square feet and [fraction], you will find 427 palms and two *siliquae*; 3,850 unciae and five [uncertain]; and 6,863 digits, five [uncertain], and two *siliquae*. The same procedure applies to the others.

If a field having the form of such a right triangle is proposed—for example, one whose cathetus measures 60 perticae, whose basis measures 80, and whose hypotenuse measures 100—and one asks how many jugera or agripenni it contains, first multiply the basis, 80, by the cathetus, 60: the result is 4,800. Take half of this, namely 2,400, as the number of square perticae in the entire field. Then investigate how many times this number contains the 288 square perticae of one jugerum or the 144 square perticae of one agripennus. In 2,400 there are eight times 288, plus one-third of 288; and 144 is contained in the same number sixteen times and two-thirds of another 144. Therefore there is no doubt that the proposed right-triangular field contains 8 jugera and one-third of a jugerum, or 16 agripenni and two-thirds of an agripennus.

But since enough has been said about finding the quantity of the *embadum* in these right triangles, we think we should append another rule by which, from the numbers of the hypotenuse and the *embadum*, people find the cathetus and basis. It is as follows:

The square of the hypotenuse is added to four times the area, and the square root of this total is taken; this is undoubtedly understood to comprise together the numbers of the base and the cathetus. But in order that each of these—namely, the base and the cathetus—may receive its own distinct number, I subtract four areas from the square of the hypotenuse and take the square root of the number that remains. I add this to the number found above, which contained the base and cathetus indistinctly, and assign half of their combined total to the larger of them, namely, the base. If, however, I subtract the square root itself from that same number, which contains the base and cathetus together, and take half of the remainder, I find the lesser side, namely, the cathetus. Or alternatively: from the number that contains the base and cathetus equally, I subtract the base found, and the cathetus remains; or I subtract the cathetus found, and the remainder will be the base.

To confirm all this by clear examples, let it be tested in any of the right triangles given above. I therefore take one whose hypotenuse is 10 and whose area is 24 feet. The hypotenuse multiplied by itself proceeds as follows. When four times the area is added to it, 196 results. The square root of this number, namely 14, contains together the numbers of the base and cathetus. In order that I may determine them, from the square of the hypotenuse, namely 100, I subtract four areas, namely 96; and adding the square root of the remaining four, namely 2, to the common number of both, namely 14, I obtain 16. I assign half of this, namely 8, to the base. But if I subtract the square root itself, namely 2, from the common number of both, namely 14, twelve remain. Half of this, namely 6, represents the cathetus. The same result follows if I subtract the base found, namely 8, from the common number of both, which is 14, or if I subtract the cathetus found, namely 6, from that same common number, which is 14.

Likewise, I take one whose *podismus* is 6 and whose area contains 10. The *podismus*, namely 6 multiplied by itself, produces 44 [uncertain reading]. To this I add four areas, namely 42 [uncertain reading], and I complete 87 [uncertain reading]. The square root of this, namely 9, comprises together the quantities of the cathetus and base. In order to separate them, from the number produced by the *podismus* multiplied by itself, namely 44, I subtract four areas, namely 42, and 8 remain. If its square root, namely 1, is subtracted from the common number of both, which is 6, the half of the remainder, namely 4, determines the cathetus. The same square root, namely 1, added to the same common number, which is 9, makes 10. Half of this, namely 5, undoubtedly gives the base. These rules concerning the Pythagorean figures are, for the present, sufficient—such as we have been able to find.

Other figures are also formed from the Pythagorean figures mentioned above. They are called *tripleuri* if the quantity that the base had above is taken by the cathetus, and the quantity that the cathetus possessed is alternately assumed by the base, as in the figures written below. I do not think it necessary to linger longer over the rules of these right triangles. For all the rules that were given above—whether for determining alternately the quantities of the sides or for finding the measure of the area—and that were clarified by examples, are likewise shown to preserve the same correspondence in these figures, except that where in some of those rules a particular matter seems to pertain to the cathetus, here it is attributed to the base, and what there pertained to the base is here attributed to the cathetus. (An old glossator notes here: “The wording is false. But this is the sense: they differ from the Pythagorean figures in that the base of the Pythagorean figures is the cathetus of these, and conversely.”) To avoid the appearance of repeating myself at length, I have preferred to leave this to the reader’s diligence and verification.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the geometry of the aforesaid triangles

I by no means think that the following observation, which nature herself offered me to contemplate while I was writing these things, should pass in silence. Whenever you wish to compare any one of the right triangles above with another, in accordance with what Plato sets forth concerning plane figures in the cosmogony of the *Timaeus*, and what Boethius demonstrates by an example concerning squares in his works on arithmetic, you will marvel to find one geometric mean between them, joining the two by a single proportion.

The first of the right triangles prescribed above fills an area of 6. If you compare it with the second, which contains 24, you can find only one number between them, namely 12, which contains both in a single proportion, that is, in the double proportion.

Likewise, between the second and third, namely 24 and 54, the middle number 36 is found; it is compared with each by a sesquialteral relation. Between the third and fourth, namely 54 and 96, you find the middle number 72, continuing both by a sesquitertial proportion. And whichever figures you compare with one another, even with others intervening, you will recognize the same thing without error. For if you likewise compare the first with the fifth, namely 6 with 150, you will nevertheless find in the middle 30, which continues both by a fivefold comparison. Likewise, if you compare the second and sixth, namely 24 and 216, you will recognize 72 as the middle number joining both by a triple proportion.

Nor should you fear that any difficulty will trouble you if you wish to compare whole figures with fractional ones, and fractional figures likewise with one another. For if you compare the first, namely 6, with the one that contains an area of 10, you will at once see 8 in the middle, joining both by a sesquitertial relation. Likewise, if you wish to compare that same figure, which contains 10, with the following one, which contains 18, the middle number 14 is shown to possess the properties of a geometric mean between them. For the number 14 contains 10 and five sixteenths of it; and, in the same way, 14 contains 18 and five sixteenths of it. This proportion is called “exceeding by five parts of sixteen.” Thus, not to linger longer, whatever such triangles you compare with one another, you will be able, without hesitation, to find one number between them, as stated, which preserves all the properties of a geometric mean. But this number, which produces geometric proportionality, is to be found in the following manner:

The cathetus of the first right triangle is multiplied by the base of the second, or, which amounts to the same thing, the base of the first is multiplied by the cathetus of the second; half of the number produced is taken and regarded as the geometric mean between the two right triangles, as between 6 and 24. The cathetus of the first, which is 3, is multiplied by the base of the second, which is 8, and 24 is produced. Half of this, namely 12, is placed as the geometric mean between 6 and 24. Or alternatively:

The areas of the right triangles themselves are multiplied together, and the square root of the resulting number is placed between them as the geometric mean. Thus, in the examples mentioned above, which contain 28 and 57 in their respective areas, the areas multiplied together produce 1606 [the following printed symbol is uncertain: φ]. The square root of these is found to be 4 and [uncertain reading], and it is recognized to preserve the properties of a geometric mean between the two right triangles.

You should also consider that the right triangles themselves are continued by the same proportion through the geometric mean of which I have spoken, namely, the proportion by which their corresponding sides—cathetus to cathetus, base to base, *podismus* to *podismus*—are compared with one another. For if their sides are double one another, the right triangles themselves are likewise joined by a double comparison through the intervening mean; if sesquialteral, by a sesquialteral proportion; and similarly in the other cases. But enough of this. Now let us consider the remaining right triangles.

There are also other right triangles, joined not by the same proportions of sides as those above, but nevertheless distinguished by corresponding numerical relations in their sides, so that the cathetus multiplied by itself and the base likewise multiplied by itself produce two squares which, when joined together, form a third square. The square root of this third square, according to the rule given above, constitutes the *podismus*, as in the examples below; they are related to one another by a single proportion of sides.

[Note: These five are Pythagorean figures, but reversed.]

These are all connected by this proportion of sides: the cathetus and the base, each multiplied by itself, produce two squares; the two joined together produce a third, whose square root constitutes the hypotenuse. The following figures, however, are each connected with the others by a different proportion of sides; nevertheless, as in the examples just mentioned, the cathetus multiplied by itself and the base multiplied by itself, when these two squares are joined together, produce a third whose square root is the hypotenuse.

## CHAPTER XIV. What benefits does the art of geometry promise?

Before treating the varieties of geometrical figures, it is necessary to demonstrate what benefits the study of this art promises, so that the reader’s intellect, stimulated by a threefold method of introduction, may more readily approach the reading and examine more diligently the treatment of the work that follows. For this discipline is described with painstaking precision, yet it is a rich description, both in the investigation of every dimension and in the usefulness of those investigations. Although it is difficult to attain, whoever labors in it with tireless dedication will be capable of doing so. And, so that we may attain it more easily, as has been said, every theorem should have its own figure appended to it.

## CHAPTER XV. The names of the measures used by geometers

The names of the measures that we use are these: the digit, ounce, palm, sixth, which is also called the *dodrans*, foot, brick, cubit, degree, pace, ten-foot measure, which is also called the perch—almost as though *portica*, from carrying—climate, *actus*, which is also called the *aripennus*, *jugerum*, *centuria*, stadium, and mile.

The digit is the smallest part of agricultural measures.

According to some, the ounce contains three digits; according to others, and this is more correct, one digit and a third of a digit.

The palm contains four digits and three ounces.

The sixth contains twelve digits, nine ounces, and three palms.

The foot contains 16 digits, 12 ounces, 4 palms, and one sixth plus a third of a sixth.

The brick is one foot in width and 23 ounces in length.

The cubit contains a foot and a half, 2 sixths, 6 palms, 18 ounces, and 24 digits.

A degree contains 2 feet; a pace, 5 feet; a perch, 9 feet; a climate, 60 feet.

An *actus* is 110 in width and 120 in length.

A *jugerum*, which is made by joining two *actus*, is 240 in length and 220 in width.

A *centuria* is 200.

A stadium is 625 feet, or 125 paces.

A mile is 1,000 paces, or 8 stadia.

## CHAPTER XVI. Measuring height with an astrolabe

If a height is situated on level ground, it can be measured by the following observation. Take an astrolabe from the height-measurer and place the *mediclinion* at the midpoint of the square drawn on its reverse surface, so that, in this position, the *mediclinion* on the other side of the astrolabe stands at the number of degrees 45. Then proceed forward or backward from it, estimating the distance, until the summit of the height is seen through both openings of the *mediclinion*. After observing it, mark the place where the measurer stood, and add the measurer’s height to this marked distance. Then carefully mark the place itself, and measure the entire level ground from there to the foot of the height. However many feet that level ground contains, so many feet, without doubt, will the height contain.

But if the *mediclinion* does not stand at the midpoint of the square, but at the first, second, third, or some other degree of the square, then, when the degrees are compared with 12, whatever the relation is between those degrees of the square and 12, the same will be the relation between the level ground and the height being measured, with the measurer’s height added.

## CHAPTER XVII. Measuring an inaccessible height with the *horoscopus*

Let any height be inaccessible because of the obstruction of a river or valley, as from a to b, and let the obstruction of the river or valley be from b to c. Take the *horoscopus* while standing on the bank at c, and carefully observe the summit a through both openings of the *mediclinion*. Consider the number of degrees in the measurement of the square, which, for example, is marked by the number four. Divide the total of the square, namely 144, by this number, and write down the quarter found, namely 36. Then measure a definite amount of space from c to d; for the example, let it be 40 feet. Again take the *horoscopus*, standing at the end d, and observe the summit a through both openings as before. Consider again the number of degrees in the square, which is marked by the number three; once more divide the total of the square by it, and write down the third part, namely 48, beside the quarter, which is 36. Subtract the smaller number from the larger, namely 36 from 48, and compare what remains, namely 12, with the side of the square, which is 12. Declare the remaining number and the side of the square equal; and just as the final remainder, 12, is considered equal to the side of the square, so let the space d–c be declared equal to the space a–b. And whatever fraction the number three, which is the final number of degrees in 12, represents, let that same fraction of the space a–b undoubtedly be declared to exist in the space d–b.

Thus a–b is 40, just as c–d is 40; the whole b–d is 160, and b–c is 120.

[Col. 0117]

## CHAPTER XVIII. Again on the same subject

If some inaccessible elevated object is to be estimated with the *horoscopus*, let the height-measurer stand at the instrument used for measuring the elevation and look through both openings of the *mediclinion* until he sees the summit of the height to be measured. After observing it, count the degrees of the square; for example, let them be counted as 3, which is contained four times in the side of the square, 12. Having done this, proceed forward and backward until the summit of the height already seen is seen again. When it is seen, inspect the number of degrees of the square again; let it, for example, be 2, which is undoubtedly contained six times in 12, that is, in the side of the square. Let the interval between the measurer’s stations be 12 feet. Having done this, subtract the smaller containing number, namely four, once from the larger containing number, namely six; keep in mind the two that remain, and let the interval between the measurer’s stations be said to be twice the inaccessible height.

And so that what we have said may be understood in every case, let a universal rule, wavering in no instance, be established: after the containing numbers have been subtracted, if one remains, the interval between the measurer’s stations will equal the height; if two remain, it will be double; if three, triple; and so in the following cases.

This is made clear by the following diagram.

## CHAPTER XIX. Measuring a height with the *horoscopus*

If you wish to measure any level surface with the *horoscopus*, direct your gaze through both openings of the *mediclinion* until your line of sight ends at the boundary of the quantity being measured. Then inspect at which degree of the square the *mediclinion* stands, compare that number of degrees with 12, and whatever the relation of the degrees to 12 may be, such will be the relation of the measurer’s height to the whole level surface.

For example, let the measurer’s height be a–b, and the level surface b–c; let the number of degrees be 3, which, when compared with 12, is found—without doubt—to be a quarter of it. Therefore a–b, which is the measurer’s height, is to b–c, that is, to the level surface, as the number three is calculated to be a quarter of 12.

## CHAPTER XX. Measuring a well with the *horoscopus*

First, the geometer must carefully determine whether the circular outline of the well is truly circular, as assessed with a plumb line. Then the size of its diameter must be ascertained. Once the diameter has been found, the measurer, standing on the rim of the well, should look downward through the *mediclinion* toward the endpoint of the opposite side of the astrolabe. After seeing it, compare the number of degrees at which the *mediclinion* stands in the square with 12. In whatever relation the number of degrees in the square stands to 12, the diameter will stand in the same relation to the depth of the well and to the measurer’s height.

Let the degrees, for example, be 4, and the diameter 4 feet. Therefore, just as 4 is contained three times in 12, so the diameter is related to the depth of the well and to the measurer’s height. Subtracting that height, regard what remains as the depth of the well.

Let us therefore set out a figure of the well marked with definite letters. Let a–c be 4 feet, that is, the diameter; let the depth of the well be a–b; let its diameter be a–c; and let the geometer’s height, c–d, be 4 feet. Now let us establish a–c as 4 feet, that is, the diameter, and direct the gaze through the *mediclinion* from a–d to b. Then let us compare the degrees—which, for the example, are 4—with 12 in a triple proportion, and place a–c, which is likewise 4, in the same comparison with d–e. Thus a–c is 4 feet, d–e is 12 feet, and a–c, which is the measurer’s height, is 4 feet. When these 4 are subtracted—namely, d–c from d–e—c–e, eight feet, remain; this is the depth of the well.

## CHAPTER XXI. Finding the height of a tree, column, or tower by its shadow with an astrolabe

If you wish to find the height of any tree, column, tower, or any similar object standing on level ground, suspend the astrolabe and direct the sun’s ray straight through both openings of the *alhidada*. Observe at which part of the side of the square, which is divided into 12 parts, the straight line of the *alhidada* stands. Whatever proportion the number of parts appearing above the *alhidada* bears to 12—that is, to the entire side of the square—the same proportion, without doubt, will the height you wish to find bear to the shadow that it casts on the ground.

For example: if two parts appear above it, to which 12 has a sixfold proportion, the shadow will likewise have a sixfold proportion to the height; if three appear, quadruple; if 4, triple; if 5, double plus two-fifths; if 6, double; if 7, one and five-sevenths; if 8, sesquialteral; if 9, sesquitertial; if 10, sesquiquintal; if 11, sesquiundecimal; if all appear, the height and shadow will be equal.

In every case, whatever proportion the triangle formed by the *alhidada* in the square has, a triangle of the same proportion will be formed by the shadow of any upright body standing on the ground. In this triangle, the shaded ground itself is the base, the upright height is the cathetus, and the sunbeam that transversely limits the shadow is understood to occupy the place of the hypotenuse.

## CHAPTER XXII. Again on the same subject

If you wish to discover the relation of a shadow to a body at any hour of the day, take the *astrolapsus*, and, with the sun’s ray passing through the openings of the *mediclinion*, observe at which degree of the square the *mediclinion* stands. Whatever the relation of that degree to 12, such will be the relation of the shadow to the body. One point must be observed: when the *mediclinion* stands on the right side of the *clima*, the shadow is greater than the body; but when it stands on the left, the body is greater than the shadow.
