## CHAPTER XXIII. Measuring a height with a mirror or basin

Having marked a center on a mirror, or in the middle of a bowl full of water, set it on level ground. The geometer should then move back and forth until, through the central point, he sees the summit of the object being measured. Once the summit has been found, carefully measure the distance between the measurer’s feet and the center of the mirror, or the middle of the vessel filled with water; then compare it no less carefully with the measurer’s height. Whatever relation that distance bears to the measurer’s height, the same will be the relation of the line from the center of the mirror to the foot of the object whose height is being measured. For example, let a plane figure be added.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Estimating the height of anything in sunlight

Whatever object is placed beneath the open sky casts a shadow, but not always one equal to itself. Therefore choose whatever fraction of its shadow you wish. Then place on the ground a rod equal to that fraction, and divide the shadow cast from it into feet, palms, or ounces. If the shadow is found to be greater than the rod, subtract from each of the units measured by the rod an amount equal to the excess of the shadow over the rod. But if the shadow is smaller, add to the aforesaid units the amount by which the rod exceeds it. Whatever has increased in the shadow by addition, or remained after subtraction, take as the measure of the object.

Another instrument is also constructed for finding a height without difficulty. It is thought to have been invented by a wise man (gloss: Pythagoras) for this reason: since it was considered difficult for the measurer to bring his line of sight down to the ground, and inconvenient for the observer, the instrument takes its dimensions from the height of the measurer.

Let us make a rod of such a size that it is twice the length of the measurer; at its midpoint let another rod be joined orthogonally, one equal in length to the measurer’s height and therefore half as long as the rod to which it is joined. This instrument, once assembled, should be carried by the measurer across the level ground until, through the ends of these rods, the summit of the object to be measured is seen. Once it has been observed, let the height be declared equal to the distance measured from the place where the measurer stands to the foot of the height, with the measurer’s own height added.

For example, let the measurer’s height be a–b; let c–d be a rod twice his height; let another rod, a–e, be joined orthogonally to its midpoint and be half its length; let the height to be measured be f–g; and let the distance from the measurer to the foot of the height be b–g. In this matter the measurer must never forget to attach to this measurement, and to every plumb line, a counterweight of equal weight, prepared geometrically for measuring. For example, let a plane figure be supplied below.

## CHAPTER XXV. Finding a level surface with a rod or reed

Set up a rod, made equal to the measurer’s line of sight, at the endpoint of the visible surface. Join to it another rod of any size by an orthogonal arrangement; this second rod should be moved upward and downward by the surveyor until, through the summits of both rods, the opposite boundary of the level surface can be seen. After observing it, carefully mark the junction of the rods, compare the upper part of the fixed rod from the junction with its total length, and unhesitatingly declare the same comparison between the hanging rod and the level surface as was stated above between the upper part from the junction and the total length of the fixed rod.

To make clearer what we calculate through the bending of letters, let us place before the eyes of readers a picture that displays the matter more plainly, though obscurely.

Let the standing rod, made equal to the measurer’s line of sight, be a–c; let the level surface to be measured be c–d; let the rod hanging orthogonally be b–e. Thus let a–b be the midpoint of a–c, and b–e will be the midpoint of c–d.

## CHAPTER XXVI. A figure for measuring height

If anyone carefully examines the force of the preceding figure, set out above, by which we measured a level surface, the force of this figure also, by which we measure heights, cannot remain wholly hidden from him. For this differs little from the preceding figure, except that the former operates on a level surface, while this one operates in measuring a height.

Let the height to be measured be a–b; the measurer’s height c–d; and the rod with which the height is measured, e–f, longer than the measurer’s height. Let a line be drawn orthogonally from the measurer’s eye through the rod to the height, g–b. Once this has been done, compare d–g with g–f, and declare the same comparison between d–b and b–a as was declared between d–g and g–f.

For example, let d–g be double g–f; likewise, let d–h be indubitably double h–a. If h–h [uncertain reading] is compared measurably with h–a, which is considered equal to the measurer’s height d–c, the entire height a–b is undoubtedly measured. But because it may happen that c–b is sometimes impassable, h–a is not altogether known to us, although it is proportional. For this reason the level surface b–c must be measured backward, and another figure must similarly be constructed from the preceding one.

## CHAPTER XXVII. A figure for measuring a level surface

Let the level surface to be measured be b–i, and let the measurer’s height be i–k. Let the rod equal to the preceding one be l–m. Let a line be drawn orthogonally from the measurer’s eye, extending upward through the rod k–n. Then compare k–n with n–l in a quadruple proportion, and likewise declare the whole k–h and h–a to be quadruple.

Since above it was learned that d–h and h–a were double, whereas now k–h and h–a are declared quadruple, subtract d–h from the whole k–h; k–d remains, which is measurably double h–a. If a–d, h–a, k–i (the measurer’s height, which is equal to n–m), and d–c, g–e, and h–b are added in measurable relation, the whole b–a, which is the measured height, should in no way be doubted.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Measuring a level surface by means of a reed

Standing at the extremity of the level surface to be measured, let the measurer set up for himself a reed shorter than his own height. He should place it upright in various places on the level surface until, over the top of the reed, the other extremity of the level surface is seen opposite him. Having done this, direct an orthogonal line from the top of the reed to the measurer’s height, carefully mark the place on that height where the line ends, and compare the portion of the height from that mark to the eye with the orthogonally drawn line. Whatever comparison this portion of the height bears to the whole orthogonal line, the same comparison shall be declared between the whole height and the entire level surface.

For example, let the measurer’s height be a–b, the level surface to be measured b–c, the cane with which it is measured d–e, and the orthogonally drawn line d–f. Whatever fraction a–f is of f–d, the same fraction a–b will be of b–c. Let a–f be one quarter of f–d; in the same way, let a–b be one quarter of b–c.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Measuring a well

As was said in the preceding figure of the well, the geometer must first carefully determine whether the circumference of the well is circular; then he must ascertain the size of its diameter. Once this has been found, the measurer, standing above the top of the well, should place beneath his feet a *scorpio* of any length (old gloss: any rod), and move it forward and backward step by step until, over the top of the *scorpio*, he sees the other extremity of the well’s depth. Having done this, he must carefully mark the portion of the *scorpio* that projects over the well, using the mark made by the measurer’s feet, and compare it no less carefully with the measurer’s height. Whatever relation this portion bears to the measurer’s height, the same relation will the diameter together with the measurer’s height bear to the entire depth of the well.

For example, let the depth of the well be a–b, its diameter a–c, the measurer’s height a–f, and let a–e be the rod compared with his height and by which the depth of the well is investigated; let the other part of the well be c–d. Let a–f be quadruple a–e; therefore b–f is quadruple a–c.

Subtract the measurer’s height from the measure of the well, if you wish to remove it.

## CHAPTER XXX. Measuring a height with a right triangle

The geometer should construct a right triangle composed of a base and cathetus of the same number, while disregarding the proportion of the hypotenuse, which in this right triangle is judged entirely useless for investigating height. The instrument, once constructed, should be dragged by the measurer across the level ground until, with his eye placed near the ground, he sees the summit of the height to be investigated over the top of the cathetus. Once it has been seen, the level ground should be measured from the place where the line of sight rested to the foot of the height; whatever its length, that shall be declared the height.

To make this more clearly understood, let the right triangle together with the height being measured be placed before the eyes in a diagram.

## CHAPTER XXXI. A Pythagorean right triangle for measuring a height

There is also another right triangle for estimating height, called Pythagorean after its inventor. It is composed, according to natural relations, of a cathetus, base, and hypotenuse: the cathetus is marked with three, the base with four, and the hypotenuse with five. If you wish to mark the cathetus with four and the base with three, the same result will follow in reverse: the base will be in a sesquitertial proportion to the cathetus, and the hypotenuse will be compared with the base by a sesquiquartal proportion.

Everything said in the preceding figure applies to this one: it should be dragged until the summit of the object is seen over the top of the cathetus. There is only this difference: in the measured quantity of the level surface, one quarter must be subtracted, because the horizontal base exceeds the upright cathetus by one quarter of itself.

To make this more clearly noticeable, let another right triangle be drawn below.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Measuring a height inaccessible to us

To measure an object inaccessible to us, even though the procedure is laborious, let us construct a figure in the following manner. Let the quantity of the object to be measured be a–b, and let us suppose that we wish to know how many cubits, ells, feet, digits, ounces, or any other measure it contains.

With the object set up orthogonally, let there be impassable space between us and the object, namely g–b. Let us erect a right triangle d–g for ourselves, and let a line be drawn upward from g to d, as was first said concerning a–b. Let a level line be drawn from d to z, just as the line from g to d lies level, and let the lengths of g–d and d–z be known, since we make them ourselves.

Let us erect a line orthogonally upward from z to u, and place the eye on the orthogonally erected line z–u, so that our line of sight passes through d to b. Let the place on this line where the eye stood be marked by the point u, and let us measure the length of z–u. After this, let us place the eye again on the line z–u, so that we are able to see through d to a; let the place at which the line of sight stood be marked by the point b. Let us see where this line touching the ground joins the line g–b, and let that point be e, so that g–e is straight.

After this, let us note the length between z and h. Whatever fraction z–h is of z–d, and z–d of d–g, the same is d–g of g–e. The lines h–z and z–d are known, because we made them. Therefore the length of g–e is known. And whatever relation u–z bears to z–d, the same is d–g to the line g–b. Since the lines u–z, z–d, and d–g are known to us, the fourth line, g–b, will therefore be known.

And because we already know the line g–e, and from it know the line g–b, we can know the length of b–e. Whatever relation d–g bears to g–e, the same is n–b to b–e; and the lines d–g, g–h [uncertain reading], and b–e are known. Therefore the line a–b is known, and this is what we were seeking.

To summarize more briefly what was stated above at length, let the concise statement be given that philosophy delights in: whatever comparison z–u bears to h–u, the same will g–d bear to b–a. If z–u is double h–u, then g–d will be double b–a.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Measuring a plane surface by any proposed method

If we are required to measure a plane surface in any manner, let us take a piece of wood one cubit in length and attach to it three other pieces of equal dimension in such a joining that, when joined, they appear to assume the definition of a square, being right-angled at its four corners. At the ends of one of its sides let two half-foot rods be erected and fixed; these, pierced at their upper ends, should appear to admit the measurer’s line of sight through both openings.

Then let the *mediclinion* be attached to the *horoscopus* at the extremity of the opposite side in such a way that, while it is drawn along the opposite side, which is marked with definite measurements, it imitates—or appears to imitate—the form of a Pythagorean right triangle.

For example, let the square be a–b–c–d; let the two half-foot rods placed at the ends of one side be e–f; and let the *mediclinion*, placed at the summit of the opposite side and running along the side opposite it, d–g, proceed in the following manner.

The square figure, assembled in this way, should be placed lying at the extremity of the level surface to be measured. The measurer should raise it on the other side until, through the openings e–f, he sees the opposite boundary of the surface, and he should place a mark at the spot where his line of sight rested. Then he should direct his gaze through the *mediclinion* positioned opposite until the already marked boundary is seen. Having done this, let the place where g stood be marked, and compare c–g with g–b. Whatever relation c–g bears to g–b, the same relation will a–b bear to the entire level surface.

For example, let the whole level surface be called a–h, and let c–g—that is, from the top of the upper part of the square to the lower part of the *mediclinion*—be made equal to g–b, that is, from the *mediclinion* to the lower angle of the same side. Therefore a–b, that is, the width, will undoubtedly be equal to b–h, that is, from the square to the boundary of the level surface. The same method should be used for all the other proportions of c–g to g–b.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Measuring the depth of a well or ditch

You will test the depth of a well or any ditch as follows. Take a straight piece of wood and place it over the mouth of the well. Observe its shadow in e–f, that is, in the depth of the well; let the piece of wood be four cubits [the text has a lacuna] longer, and let another straight rod, similar to it, extend beneath its feet. Let the depth of the well be a–e and the straight rod a–d; let another rod, a–c–b, lie across the mouth of the well and cut d–e at right angles. Look into the water of the well at the shadow a–c, from d to f, and you will find that a–c is contained as many times in a–c–b, or e–f in a–e–d. For example, if a–c is one palm and d–a is three, a–c is contained three times in d–a, just as a–c–b is contained three times in d–a–c. Subtract a–d; a–e remains.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Finding the height of a mountain
When you seek the height of some mountain, place [Col. 0129B] before you, on level ground before the mountain, a staff longer than yourself: let the staff be **a b**, and yourself **c d**. Then, moving this way and that, look along the straight line of sight through **a** until you see **f**. Consider then how much **g c** is in relation to **g a**; by that same proportion, **c b** is to **b f**. Thus, for example, if **g c** is double **g a**, **c h** is double **h f**; and whatever the proportion of **g c** to **g a**, beyond doubt the same is the proportion of **c h** to **h f**. Conversely, whatever **a g** is in relation to **g c**, the same is **f h** in relation to **h c**. **h f** is the mountain; and whatever **d b** is in relation to **h g**, the same is **d i** in relation to **f i**.

But if there is a river or some other obstacle between **c** and **h**, so that you cannot reach the mountain’s foot in order to find the measurement described above, take **a g b**, that is, the staff, and walk backward thirty cubits, or whatever distance you choose. Then look again along the straight line from **m**, through **n**, until **d f**, which is the summit of the mountain. Next observe the proportion of **m c** to **c n**; the same is the proportion of **m h** to **h f**. Subtract **c h** from **m h**, and what remains is the height of the mountain.

For example, if you find **c h** to be double **h f**, and afterward **m h** to be quadruple **h f**, subtract **c h** from **m h**, that is, two from four; two remain, which is **m c**. You will say: since **m c** is double **h f**, add thirty—or twenty—cubits to **m c**, and fifteen—or ten—to **h f**; thus **c h** is three times **h f**, and **m h** seven times **h f**. Subtract **c h** from **m h**, that is, three from seven; four remain. Therefore **m c** is four times **h f**. The same procedure applies in other cases.

[Col. 0129D]

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the same subject

If you seek to do this without moving the staff, proceed as follows. Let the mountain be **a b**. Take a staff two cubits longer than yourself and place it before you on level ground. Then observe the staff, which is **c d e**, and direct your gaze straight from **f**, through **d**, to **a**, dividing the staff at one cubit; observe how much **f e** is in relation to **e d**. The same proportion is **f g** to **g a**.

Walk backward until you see from **h**, through **c**, to **a**, where the mountain’s summit is. Observe how much **h e** is in relation to **e c**; the same is **h g** in relation to **g a**. Suppose you had previously found **f g** to be four times **g a**, and **h g** ten times **g a**. Subtract **f g** from **h g**, that is, four from ten; six remain. Thus **h f** is one and a half times **g a**, or **g a** is one and a half times **f h**.

[Col. 0130B]

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Finding the height of towers, etc., by means of a mirror

If you wish to know the height of towers or mountains by means of a mirror or a bowl full of water, take a mirror and place it on level ground near the mountain. Move yourself, and only the mirror placed on the ground, this way and that until you see **a** in **b**, that is, the summit of the mountain in the middle of the mirror. Observe the relationship and proportion between **d c** and **c b**; the same relationship and proportion exist between **b e** and **e a**.

If there is an obstacle preventing you from carrying out the measurement, walk backward with the mirror, place it on the ground, and, moving yourself, see **a** in **z**. Whatever proportion **p r** and **r z** have to one another, the same proportion exists between **z e** and **e a**. Subtract **b e** from this, and **b z** remains.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Finding the width of a river or field, etc.

[Col. 0130D]

If you wish to know the width of a river, or of some field, courtyard, or anything else, take a staff that reaches to your eyes—according to some authorities, one cubit less—and place it on the riverbank. Stand close to it. The staff is, as shown below, approximately **a b**. Place another staff upright upon the first, as **c d**.

Then look along the straight line of sight through **a d** until you see **e**, that is, the bank on the opposite side; for **b e** is the river, and **a e** the straight line of sight. Next observe the proportion of **a c** to **c d**, or conversely that of **d c** to **a c**; the same is the proportion of **a c b** to **b e**. Thus, if **d c** is double **a c**, **b e** is double **d c a**; if it is triple, it is triple, and so forth.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Another method for the same purpose

If you wish to find this out by another method, take a staff shorter than yourself, approximately reaching your chest, and place it on the riverbank. Take another staff reaching to your eyes, as **c d**, and walk backward as far as you wish. Place this staff, and move only yourself this way and that until, looking from **c** through **a** to **e**, you see the opposite bank of the river.

Then subtract **a b** from **c d**; **f c** remains. Observe the proportion of **a f** to **f c**; the same is the proportion of **b e** to **b a**. If **a f** is three times **f c**, then **b e** is three times **b a**.

## CHAPTER XL. Measuring height with arrows and a cord

[Col. 0131C]

Since, intent upon geometric figures, we have now grown weary of adhering to the discoveries of the philosophers, let us refresh our minds with military exercises, lest we become wholly exhausted. Just as a body wearied by daily fare is restored by unfamiliar food, so the mind burdened by philosophical austerities is relieved by the conjectural invention of poets. Therefore, to refresh our minds, let us set down a military invention after the foregoing material.

If you wish to investigate the height of anything, you can investigate it in the following way, using the skill of an archer. Take a bow with an arrow and a cord. Attach one end of the cord to the end of the arrow, while the other end remains in your hand. Let the arrow, shot from the bow, strike the summit of the height being measured.

Afterward, in the same way, tie the end of another cord to the arrow or to some projectile, and let this projectile strike the foot of the height, as the first struck its summit. When this has been done, draw back both cords, and carefully measure how many feet or cubits each contains.

Then multiply each cord’s number by itself, and consider the sum of the two multiplications. Subtract the smaller sum from the greater, and carefully find the side of the square corresponding to the number that remains from the greater sum. Once this has been carefully sought and wisely found, the height being investigated is to be stated as having as many feet or cubits as the side of that square contains.

To make what we have said clearer, let the height and the cord be represented below by letters and figures. Let the height being investigated be **a b**. Let the length of the first cord, which reached the summit of the height, terminate in the number five, **a c**. Let the length of the other cord, which struck the foot of the height, be defined by the number four, **c b**.

The number of the first cord, multiplied by itself, produces 25; the number four of the second cord, multiplied by itself, produces 16. When the smaller number is subtracted from 25, 9 remains. The side of the square of 9 is found to be 3, because three multiplied by itself produces 9. Therefore the height **a b** is three feet high.

But since it may happen that the side of the square of the remainder cannot be found as an integer, the subtlety of fractions must necessarily be employed. Since it would take too long to discuss this, we omit it and append a diagram with the numbers and letters.

[Col. 0132B]

## CHAPTER XLI. Finding the projection in an oblique triangle, and determining its size

Given the three lines of an oblique triangle—namely, the greater hypotenuse of eighteen feet, the base of eight, and the lesser hypotenuse of ten—seek the projection upon which the perpendicular falls as follows.

From the sum produced by multiplying the greater hypotenuse by itself, subtract the combined products of the two lesser lines, namely the base and the lesser hypotenuse, each multiplied by itself. Take half of the excess that remains. Divide this by the number of the base; as many units as the quotient contains, so many units shall be assigned to the projection.

Find the perpendicular as follows. Subtract the projection multiplied by itself from the lesser hypotenuse multiplied by itself; take the side of the remainder. That number will be the perpendicular.

If you wish to find the area of this oblique triangle, multiply the base by the perpendicular. Take half of the product; this will unquestionably be the area of the oblique triangle.

## CHAPTER XLII. How the perpendicular and base are found in a right triangle

[Col. 0133A]

In a right triangle whose hypotenuse is twenty-five feet and whose area is 150, find the perpendicular and the base as follows. Multiply the number of the hypotenuse by itself. Add to the resulting sum four areas, which make 600; the total is 1225. The side of this sum is 35.

Next, to find the difference between the two straight sides, namely the perpendicular and the base, multiply the hypotenuse by itself, producing 625. Subtract four areas from this; 25 remains. Its side is 5. Add this to the side of the preceding number, namely 35; the result is 40. Half of this constitutes the base of the triangle. Subtract from it the number five, which had been added to the preceding number, 35, in order to establish the base; the result is the perpendicular.

## CHAPTER XLIII. Finding separately the base and perpendicular of a triangle

If a triangle is given whose perpendicular and base together are twenty-three feet, whose area is 60, and whose hypotenuse is seventeen, find the base and perpendicular separately as follows.

Multiply the number of the hypotenuse by itself; the result is 289. Subtract four areas, that is, 240. From the remainder, 49, take the side, which is 7. Add this to the sum of the base and perpendicular, 23; the result is thirty feet. Half of this is the base of the same triangle.

Subtract this from 23, that is, subtract the base from the number representing the base and perpendicular together; eight remains, and this constitutes the perpendicular. In this figure, when half the perpendicular found is multiplied, and one is subtracted from the resulting sum, the base is found; when the two are taken together, they produce the hypotenuse.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Finding the perpendicular and projections in an acute triangle whose sides have unequal numerical measures

Given an acute triangle whose sides have unequal measurements distributed as follows—the lesser hypotenuse 13, the base 14, and the greater hypotenuse 15—if you wish to find its perpendicular and determine each projection, multiply the lesser hypotenuse by itself, namely 13, and the base by itself, namely 14; combine the two products, which produce 395.

Then subtract the greater hypotenuse multiplied by itself, namely 225. From the remainder, 140, take half, namely 70. Divide this by the base, 14; you will find five times 14 in 70. This quotient is the number of the lesser projection.

Likewise, to find the perpendicular, subtract the lesser projection multiplied by itself from the lesser hypotenuse multiplied by itself. After this subtraction, the side of the remaining number will be the perpendicular.

## CHAPTER XLV. Finding the base from any given perpendicular of a right triangle

From any given perpendicular of a right triangle you may find the base as follows. Multiply the perpendicular by three, remove a ninth, and take half of the remainder; this will be the base. Restore to the base what was removed; it will be the hypotenuse.

Or proceed thus: take half, multiply it by three, and subtract a ninth from the product; the remainder is the base.

Or multiply half the perpendicular by six, subtract a ninth, and take half of the remainder; this is the base. Restore the ninth to the base; the result is the hypotenuse.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Finding the area of a right triangle

[Col. 0134C]

If the area of a right triangle is sought, combine the numbers of its three lines—the perpendicular, the base, and the hypotenuse—into one, for example 6, 8, and 10. Joined together, these produce 24. Take half of this. Subtract the base, namely 8; multiply what remains, namely four, by the perpendicular, 6. Double that product, and the result is 48. Multiply this by one quarter of itself; the side of the resulting sum is to be taken as the area.

[Col. 0134D]

In oblique or acute triangles the rule just given is applicable, but not even in right triangles except those governed by a sesquitertian or sesquiquartan proportion. In other triangles, including right triangles, the universal rule is sufficient: multiply the base by the perpendicular and take half of the product as the area. For multiplying the base by the perpendicular means nothing other than filling the area of a square or rectangle—“a figure longer on one side” [Old Gloss: that is, longer on one side than on the other]. When you divide it from corner to corner, you produce a triangle.

## CHAPTER XLVII. Finding the base from the perpendicular

[Col. 0135A]

If you wish to find the base from the perpendicular, multiply the perpendicular by itself; for example, 5 produces 25. Subtract one from this and take half of the remainder, 24; this is 12, which is the base. Add back the one previously subtracted, and you will find the hypotenuse.

If you wish to find the feet of the area, multiply the base by the perpendicular, namely 12 by 5; the result is 60. Take half, namely 30; this is the area.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Finding the area of a trapezium

A trapezium has a base of forty feet, a perpendicular of thirty, and a **coraustus** of twenty-five. If you wish to determine its area, multiply the coraustus by the perpendicular: thirty times twenty-five gives 750.

Then multiply the remaining part of the base by the perpendicular: thirty times fifteen gives 450; take half, 225, and add it to the preceding number; the result is 975. This is the area.

## CHAPTER XLIX. Determining the area of an equilateral triangle whose sides are each thirty feet

If you wish to determine the area in feet of an equilateral triangle whose sides are each thirty, first find the perpendicular as follows. Multiply one side by itself; the result is 900. Multiply half of the other side by itself; the result is 225. Subtract this from 900; 675 remains. Add one to this; the result is 676. Its side is 26.

This is the perpendicular. Multiply it by half the base, namely 15 by 26; you will find 390 feet as the area.

[Col. 0135D]

In every right triangle, the perpendicular and base together produce the hypotenuse; the hypotenuse and perpendicular produce the base; and the hypotenuse and base again produce the perpendicular. For when the perpendicular is multiplied by itself, namely 5, producing 25, and the base, namely 12, producing 144, are combined, they make 169; taking the side of this gives the hypotenuse.

If the hypotenuse is multiplied by itself, namely 13, producing 169, and the perpendicular is subtracted from it multiplied by itself, namely 25, 144 remains; taking its side, namely 12, gives the base. If you multiply the hypotenuse by itself and subtract the base from the resulting sum, namely 144, 25 remains; the side of this is the number of the perpendicular.

In the same right triangles, the perpendicular and base may be used to determine the area as follows. Multiply the perpendicular, 5, by the base, 12; the result is 60. Half of this, namely 30, is the area. The same result would be obtained by multiplying the base by half the perpendicular, or the perpendicular by half the base.

[Col. 0136B]

## CHAPTER L. Finding the perpendicular or area of an isosceles triangle

In an isosceles triangle—[Codex: *isoscelis*]—whose individual sides are twenty-five feet and whose base is fourteen, if you wish to find the perpendicular or the area, multiply one side by itself, namely 25; the result is 625. Subtract from this half the base multiplied by itself, namely 49. The remainder is 576; take its side, 24, and this is the perpendicular in feet. Multiply it by half the base, and you will find the area, 169.

[Col. 0136C]

## CHAPTER LI. Finding the perpendicular of a scalene triangle

For finding the perpendicular of a scalene triangle whose lesser side is fifteen feet, whose base is twenty-five, and whose greater side is twenty, use the following rule.

Multiply the lesser side by itself; fifteen produces 225. The base, 25, produces 625. Combine these two sums; they produce 850. Subtract the greater side multiplied by itself, namely 400. From the remainder, 450, take half, namely 225. Take the part of that number denominated by the number written over the base, namely 25; you will find one ninth of the said number, and it will be the lesser projection in feet. Multiplied by itself, it produces 81. Subtract this from the product of the lesser side multiplied by itself, namely from 225; the remainder is 144, whose side is the number of the perpendicular.

## CHAPTER LII. Finding the diagonal in a square

[Col. 0137A]

If you wish to find the diagonal in a square, as we have already said in the case of right triangles, multiply one side, which here is 4, by itself; the result is 16. Multiply the other side by itself, namely 3; the result is 9. Combine these; they produce 25. If you take its side, you have found the diagonal.

If you wish to find the area by means of it, multiply it by itself; the result is 25. Take half of this; it is the area. But what is closer to the truth, and applies to every square, is to multiply the length by the width; the result gives the square feet of the area.

[Col. 0137B]

## CHAPTER LIII. Finding the number of trees in a field

A field whose length is 120 feet and whose width is 70, in which trees are planted five feet apart: if their number is sought, take the number contained in each dimension—namely 24 for the length and 14 for the width. Multiply these together; they produce 336. This is the number of trees.

There is also another rule for finding it: multiply the length by the width; the result is 8400. Divide this by five times five, that is, by 25; the result is 336, and that is the number of trees.

If, with the length and the number of trees known, the width is sought, divide 120, the length, by 5; the result is 24. The number of trees, 336, contains this number fourteen times, producing 14; and 14 multiplied by 5 gives 70, which is the width of the field.

## CHAPTER LIV. Finding the perpendicular of a rhombus

[Col. 0137D]

For a rhombus—[Codex: *cumbi*]—whose individual sides are ten feet and whose diagonal is twelve, find the perpendicular as follows. Multiply half the diagonal, namely 6, by itself; the result is 36. Subtract this from the product of one side multiplied by itself, namely from 100. The remainder is 64; take its side, 8. This is the perpendicular of the rhombus in feet.

Multiply it by the diagonal, namely 12; the result is 95 [textual number apparently corrupt]. This is the area in feet.

## CHAPTER LV. How the triangle, square, hexagon, etc., fill their equilateral areas

Every equilateral triangle multiplies one side by itself, adds the side itself to that product, and takes half of the result; thus it fills its area.

Every square having equal sides multiplies one side by itself; that single multiplication fills its area.

A pentagon bounded by equal sides requires three multiplications of one side by itself; from the resulting product, subtract the area once and take half of the remainder.

A hexagon requires four multiplications of the side by itself; from the resulting product, subtract the area twice and take the remainder’s half.

A heptagon requires five multiplications and the area three times.

An octagon requires seven multiplications and the area four times.

[Col. 0138B]

A nonagon requires seven multiplications and the area five times. The remaining figures follow this pattern.

## CHAPTER LVI. Finding the diameter and area of any round figure or circle

If you wish to find the diameter and area of any round figure or circle, proceed as follows. Subtract 22 units from the circumference itself; take a third of what remains. This will be the diameter.

If you wish to find the area, either multiply the entire circumference by the entire diameter and then take a quarter; or multiply half the circumference by the entire diameter and then take half; or multiply a quarter of the circumference by the diameter and take the whole result. The same result would be obtained by multiplying half the circumference by half the diameter.

## CHAPTER LVII. Finding the area of a semicircle

[Col. 0138D]

For a semicircle whose base is twenty-eight feet and whose diameter is eighteen, find the area as follows. Multiply the base by the diameter; the result is 392 feet. Multiply this by eleven; the result is 312 feet [the printed calculation appears corrupt]. Take one fourteenth of this; the result is 398 [the printed figures appear corrupt]. This is the area of the semicircle in feet.

## CHAPTER LVIII. Calculating the area of a sphere

For a sphere whose length is four feet and whose width is three, calculate the area as follows. Add the length and width together; the result is 7. Take half of this, 3½. Multiplied by itself, it makes “12 and .” [the printed text is incomplete]. Multiplied elevenfold, it makes “434. SS.” [the printed numerical notation is uncertain]. Take one fourteenth of this; the result is 9 feet, 7 ounces and half an ounce—that is, seven-twelfths and a half-ounce. This is therefore the area of the sphere.

This rule is valid for every sphere, whether round or oblong.

## CHAPTER LIX. Finding the diameter of a circle inscribed in a right triangle and tangent to each side

In a right triangle containing a circle inscribed so that it touches each side, subtract the number of the hypotenuse from the combined numbers of the perpendicular and base; you will find the diameter.

But if you wish to determine how much of the triangle’s area remains occupied by the portions extending beyond the circle, first find the area of the whole triangle according to the rules given above. Subtract one twenty-first of it; multiply that fraction by eleven and assign the result to the area of the circle.

Whatever remains—namely 140—take as the area of the portions extending beyond the circle, as the diagram below shows. That is: take one twenty-first, multiply it by eleven, and it becomes the area of the circle. Multiply by ten, and you obtain the excess portions of the triangle.

## CHAPTER LX. A rule for constructing pyramids in all equilateral many-sided figures

For constructing pyramids in all figures proceeding from many angles and having equal sides, the following rule is sufficient. Once the area of any such figure has been found, multiply it by two. Add to this sum the number of one side. Multiply the resulting combination by the number that is one unit greater than the number of sides, and take one sixth of the sum. This produces the pyramid of the previously doubled surface.

To give an example for each, let us first consider an acute, equilateral triangle whose individual sides are designated by the number ten and whose area is 55. Multiply this by two; the result is 110. Add one side, namely 10; the result is 120. Multiply this by the number one greater than the number of sides, namely eleven; the result is 1320. Take one sixth of this, namely 220; this becomes the pyramid of the acute triangle just described.

## CHAPTER LXI. Finding the pyramid of a square whose individual sides are ten feet and whose area is 100

For a square whose individual sides are ten feet and whose area is 100, find the pyramid as in the triangle described above. Multiply its area, 100, by two; the result is 200. Add one side to this sum; the result is 210. Multiply this by eleven for the reason stated above; the result is 2310. Take one sixth, namely 385; this is the pyramid of the square described.

## CHAPTER LXII. Finding the pyramid of an equilateral pentagon with sides of ten

In a pentagon likewise, bounded by equal sides and marked with the number ten, you will find the same rule for constructing the pyramid without variation. Its area, namely 145, multiplied by two gives 290. Increased by the number of one side, it produces 300. Multiplied by eleven, this produces 33 [the printed figure appears corrupt]. After taking one sixth, namely 550 [the numerical sequence is corrupt], the area already mentioned is added to its pyramid.

Therefore no one should doubt that this rule applies likewise to the remaining figures—hexagons, heptagons, octagons, nonagons, decagons, and all figures proceeding from many angles and having equal sides—not only when marked by ten, but with any number.

## CHAPTER LXIII. In a circle bounded by two squares, determining how much one exceeds the other

[Col. 0141A]

In any circle bounded by two squares, one inside and the other outside, if you wish to determine how much the outer exceeds and surpasses the inner, multiply its diameter by itself. In doing this, you obtain the product of the perpendicular of the square mentioned above multiplied by the base, and that multiplication fills its area.

To find the area of the circle, subtract three fourteenths from the entire sum of the square. After this subtraction, if, by the rule given above—multiplying half the circumference by half the diameter—you find the area of the circle, you should understand that the circle is exceeded by the outer square by three fourteenths of that same amount.

From the same area of the square mentioned above, take half, and add four fourteenths of the same quantity from which the preceding whole amount was taken; you will then obtain the area of the circle.

When you do this, understand that the half taken from the entire area of the greater square was the area of the smaller square, and that the circle exceeds it by four fourteenths, since the same area is increased by those four fourteenths to complete the area.

To make this clearer in a diagram, let the circle be shown together with the squares.

What remains from the parts of the greater square extending beyond the circle? **42.**

What remains from the parts of the circle extending beyond the smaller square? **56.**

## CHAPTER LXIV. Finding the acres of a mountain

[Col. 0141D]

If the acres of a mountain are sought, where the circumference at the summit is 300 feet, the ascent 800, and one circuit 1000, join the two circumferences, namely 1300. Take half of this, namely 650. Multiply this by the ascent, 800; the result is DXX [the printed Roman numeral is evidently incomplete or corrupt]. This is the number of feet of the whole mountain; divide the aforesaid number by XXVIII, DCCX. When this has been done, 18 acres are found in the mountain, with 1600 feet remaining.

## CHAPTER LXV. How squares and the sides of triangles, squares, pentagons, etc., are generated

[Col. 0142A]

Every triangle, when multiplied by eight and increased by one, produces a square. The side of that square, after one has been subtracted and the stated second part taken, produces the side of the triangle.

Every square, multiplied by sixteen, produces a square. The side of that square, after the stated fourth part is taken, produces the side of the square.

Every pentagon, multiplied by twenty-four and increased by one, produces a square. The side of that square, after one has been added and the stated sixth part taken, produces the side of the pentagon.

Every hexagon, multiplied by thirty-two and increased by four, produces a square. The side of that square, after two have been added and the stated eighth part taken, produces the side of the hexagon.

Every heptagon, multiplied by forty and increased by nine, produces a square. The side of that square, after three have been added and the stated tenth part taken, produces the side of the heptagon.

Every octagon, multiplied by forty-eight and increased by sixteen, produces a square. The side of that square, after four have been added and the stated twelfth part taken, produces the side of the octagon.

Every nonagon, multiplied by fifty-six and increased by twenty-five, produces a square. The side of that square, after five have been added and the stated fourteenth part taken, produces the side of the nonagon.

Every decagon, multiplied by sixty-four and increased by thirty-six, and with the stated sixteenth part taken, produces the side of the decagon.

Every undecagon, multiplied by seventy-two and increased by forty-nine, produces a square. Its side, after seven have been added and the stated nineteenth part taken, produces the side of the undecagon.

Every dodecagon, multiplied by eighty and increased by sixty-four, produces a square. Its side, after eight have been added and the stated twentieth part taken, produces the side of the dodecagon.

Observe the pattern: the multiplication increases regularly by eight, while the additions beginning with the pentagon naturally proceed through odd numbers. The triangle is multiplied by eight, the square by sixteen, the pentagon by twenty-four, and the hexagon by thirty-two, corresponding to eight times eight, sixteen times sixteen, and so on. No one should doubt that a difference of eight is always present between these denominations, and likewise in the remaining figures.

Beginning with the pentagon, it is clear that the additions in all the multiplications differ naturally by odd numbers. The pentagon’s multiplication is increased by one only, the hexagon’s by four, the heptagon’s by nine, and the octagon’s by sixteen. Among the first figures—namely, 5 and 4—the first odd number occupies the place of the difference, namely 3 between 4 and 9; the second, namely 5, between 9 and 16; the third, namely 7 [the printed sequence is incomplete or corrupt].

## CHAPTER LXVI. Finding the perpendicular and area of an acute triangle

In an acute triangle whose lesser side is thirteen feet, greater side fifteen, and base fourteen, find the perpendicular and area as follows.

Multiply the lesser side by itself; the result is 169. Multiply the base by itself; the result is 196. Together they make 365. Then multiply the hypotenuse by itself; the result is 225. Subtract this from 365; 140 remains. Half of this is 70. One fourteenth of it, namely 5, is the lesser projection on which the perpendicular falls. Multiplied by itself, this produces 25. Subtract this from 169; 144 remains. Its side, namely 12, is the perpendicular. Multiplying this by half the base gives the area.

In every equilateral square, know that the diagonal has, in its length, one side and doubles the area of the square. If you wish to find the greater side, use the diagonal of the smaller square [the final wording is textually uncertain].

## CHAPTER LXVII. Placing sheep in a field so that each occupies a definite space

In a field 200 feet long and 100 feet wide, if you wish to put sheep so that each has five feet in length and four in width, proceed as follows. Multiply 5 by twenty, or take one fifth of 100; the result is 40. Then divide 100 by 4; one quarter of the hundred is 25.

Thus, whether you multiply 40 by twenty-five or 25 by forty, you will obtain 1000, which is the number of sheep placed in the field.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. Finding how many *agripennis* a sloping field contains

A sloping field has 100 *perticae* on each side, 50 on each front, and 60 in the middle. If you wish to know how many *agripennis* it contains, proceed as follows.

Add the front, 50, and the middle, 60; the result is 110. Take half, namely 55, and multiply it by the length, 100; the result is 5500. These are the *perticae* of the whole field.

To find the *agripennis*, divide 5500 by the *perticae* of one *agripennis*, namely 144, according to some authorities, who say that an *agripennis* has twelve *perticae* on each side. You will find 144 thirty-eight times in 5500, with 28 *perticae* remaining. Thus you should understand the number of *agripennis* to be 38.

[Col. 0144A]

But if the division is made by 72—for some say that an *agripennis* is twelve *perticae* long and six wide, and six times twelve is 72—there will be 72 *agripennis*, with the same *perticae* stated above remaining.

If you wish to test this rule, test it as follows. Multiply the long side separately and say: fifty times 100 produces 5000. Then, if you wish to determine the areas of the curved portions, multiply the perpendicular of each curve, namely 5 and 5; if you have not forgotten the stated rule for right triangles, you will find the area of one curve to be 250 and of the other equally 250. Together they make 500. Thus the number of *perticae* of the sloping field is 5500.

## CHAPTER LIX. Determining the *agripennis* in a quadrangular field

[Col. 0144B]

In a quadrangular field having thirty *perticae* on one side, thirty-two on the other, thirty-two on one front, and thirty-four on the other, determine how many *agripennis* it should contain as follows.

The two lengths of the field together make 62. Take half of 62; the result is 31. The two widths of the same field together make 66. Take half of 66; the result is 33. Multiply these two halves together; the result is 1023. This is the number of *perticae* of the entire field.

Divide this by the number of *perticae* in one *agripennis*, namely 144; you will find that the field contains 7 *agripennis*, with 15 *perticae* remaining.

## CHAPTER LXX. Finding the *agripennis* in a triangular field

In a triangular field having thirty *perticae* on one side, the same on the other, and eighteen on the front, take the number of *agripennis* it should contain as follows.

Join the two lengths; they make 60. Take half of 60; the result is 30. Since the front has eighteen *perticae*, take half of 18; the result is 9. Multiply 30 by 9; the result is 270. Within this number there is one *agripennis*, with 54 *perticae* remaining.

You should understand that throughout we take an *agripennis* to be twelve *perticae* on every side.

## CHAPTER LXXI. Knowing the number of *agripennis* in a round field

In a round field whose circumference is 418 *perticae*, you can determine the number of *agripennis* as follows. Subtract from 418 its twenty-second part, namely 19. Take a third of the remainder as the diameter, namely 133.

Then take half of this third, namely 66½, and multiply it by half the entire circumference, namely 209. You will thereby certainly fill the whole area, 14,898½ *perticae*. Divide this by 144; the result is 96½ *agripennis*, with two and a half *perticae* remaining; or 96½ [the printed notation is corrupt], with nothing remaining.

## CHAPTER LXXII. Placing houses of fixed length and width in a quadrangular city

In a quadrangular city having 1100 feet on one side, 1000 on the other, and 600 feet on one front and the same on the other, if you wish to place houses so that each is forty feet long and thirty feet wide, proceed as follows.

Join the two lengths of the city; together they make 2100. Likewise, if the two widths are joined, they make 1200. Take half of 1200; the result is 600. Again take half of 2100; the result is 1050.

Since each house is forty feet long and thirty feet wide, take a fortieth of 1050; the result is 26, with 10 remaining. Then take a thirtieth of 600; the result is 20. Multiply twenty by twenty-six; the result is 520. That is the number of houses the city can contain.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. The same matter in a triangular city

In a triangular city having 100 feet on one side, 100 on the other, and 90 on the front, if you wish to know how many houses it can contain, with each house twenty feet long and ten feet wide, proceed as follows.

Take half of the joined sides, namely of 200; the result is 100. Likewise take half of the front, namely of 90; the result is 45.

Since the length of each house is twenty feet and its width ten, take a twentieth of 100; the result is 5, and a tenth of 40; the result is 4. Multiply five by four; the result is 20. This kind of city can contain that many houses.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. Placing houses of fixed length and width in a round city

[Col. 0146A]

In a round city whose circumference is 8008 feet, if you wish to place houses thirty feet long and twenty feet wide, proceed as follows. Subtract a twenty-second part, namely 364. From the remainder, 7644, take a third, namely 2548; take this as the diameter.

Take half of this diameter, namely 1274, and multiply it by half the circumference, namely 4000 and 4. The entire area is thereby filled with quinquies millies ICMXCVI feet [the printed numeral is corrupt]. Divide this by 600, that is, by twenty times thirty; the result is 8501 houses, with 496 feet remaining.

## CHAPTER LXXV. How many bricks are required to pave a basilica

To determine how many bricks are needed to pave a basilica whose length is 240 feet and width 120 feet, proceed as follows [Col. 0146C]. Multiply the length by the width—that is, 120 by 240—giving 28,800. Multiply this by twelve times twelve, that is, by 144 (for a square foot contains 144 square unciae), and you will obtain 4,147,200 square unciae. If you divide this by twelve times 23, that is, by the 276 square unciae contained in one brick, you will obtain 15,026, with 24 square unciae remaining. Thus 15,026 bricks can cover the pavement of the aforesaid basilica.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. To lay out a road of a fixed width in a trench, canal, and so forth

In a trench, canal, or *cavana* [Old Gloss: *cavana*, that is, a cellar], which is 100 feet long and 64 feet wide, if you wish to place vessels 7 feet long and 4 feet wide in such a way that a passage 4 feet wide runs lengthwise, proceed as follows [Col. 0146D]. See how many times 7 is contained in 100 and 4 in 64: you will find fourteen times 7 in 100, with 2 remaining, and sixteen times 4 in 64. But 4 of these are assigned to the passage. Since, therefore, there are fifteen times 4 in 60, and fourteen times 7 in 100, the result is 210. Thus you can place 210 vessels in the aforesaid *cavana*.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. To find the area of a circle

For a circle whose diameter is 14 feet, find its area as follows. Multiply the diameter by itself, giving 196. Multiply by eleven, giving 2,156; take one fourteenth of this, giving 154. This is the area in square feet.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. To determine a circle from its diameter

Determine a circle from its diameter as follows: take the diameter—for example, 14—and multiply it by 22, giving 308; take one seventh of this, giving 44. This is the circumference.

## CHAPTER LXXIX. To find the area of a semicircle

For a semicircle whose base is 10 feet and whose line to the center is 5 feet, find the area as follows: multiply the diameter by itself, giving 100. Multiply this by eleven, giving 1,100. Take one twenty-eighth of this; the result will be 39 feet, with two sevenths remaining, that is, 8; and this is the area.

The same result would follow if you multiplied the base by the line drawn to the center, multiplied the product by eleven, and then took one fourteenth of it. This is true of every exactly bisected sphere.

For a circle whose area is 616 square feet, find the diameter as follows. Multiply 616 by fourteen, giving 8,624. From this take one eleventh, giving 784. The square root of this number is 28; this will be the diameter.

## CHAPTER LXXX. In a right triangle whose perpendicular is represented by an even number, to find the base and hypotenuse

In a right triangle whose perpendicular is marked by an even number, for example 8, find the base and hypotenuse as follows. Take half the perpendicular, namely 4, and multiply it by itself, giving 16. Subtract 1 from this; the remainder is the base. Add 2 to it, and the result is the hypotenuse.

## CHAPTER LXXXI. To find acres on a *strabo* mountain

On a *strabo* mountain [Old Gloss: one which is precipitous on one side and has an extended slope on the other], whose circumference at the foot is 1,400 feet, whose circumference at the summit is 200 feet, whose height on the right side is 850 feet and on the left 750 feet, find the number of acres as follows [Col. 0147D]. Take half of the sum of the upper and lower circumferences; this gives 800 feet. Multiply these halves by one another, giving 640,000. In this you will find twenty-two times the number of square feet in one acre, namely 28,800, with 6,400 remaining.

## CHAPTER LXXXII. To make a column, to thicken a circle, and to find the height of objects

For making a column, use one seventh of the lower circumference and one eighth of the upper circumference [Col. 0148A].

If you wish to thicken a circle, cube its diameter, multiply the cube by eleven, and take one twenty-first of the resulting sum; this will be the thickness of the sphere.

There is also another method for determining height, as follows. Take a right triangle whose perpendicular is 6 feet—or 3—and whose base is 8 feet—or 4—and whose hypotenuse is 10 feet—or 5. Set it upright so that its base rests on the ground: the perpendicular must stand opposite the object whose height is to be measured, while the hypotenuse extends from the top of the perpendicular down to the ground and reaches the end of the base [Col. 0148B]. Lying on the ground, place your eye directly at the point where the base and hypotenuse meet. Then move backward or forward, while keeping your eye in position, until the top of the perpendicular appears level with the summit of the object whose height you seek. When this has been done, mark the place where your eye was, and measure from that mark to the foot of the object. Divide this distance by 4 and subtract one quarter of it; take the remaining three quarters as the height of the object in question. This is the most reliable method of measuring height, provided that the ground over which the perpendicular is moved is neither mountainous nor hollowed, but level.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. To determine the amphorae of a well

A well whose diameter is 7 feet and whose height is 40 feet will hold as many amphorae as result when the area of this diameter is multiplied by the height, provided that each amphora is 1 foot long and 1 foot high [Col. 0148C].

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. To find how many cubic feet a vessel contains and how many amphorae it holds

For a vessel whose lower width is 3 feet, upper width 2 feet, middle width 5 feet, and height 12 feet, determine how many cubic feet it contains and consequently how many amphorae it holds as follows. Multiply the middle width by itself, then triple this amount, and multiply the upper and lower diameters separately by themselves; when all these are added together, the result is 88 [Col. 0148D]. Multiply this by eleven and then take one fourteenth of the resulting sum: the result is 69 and two fourteenths, that is, one seventh. Multiply this by one third of the height, namely by 4, and the number of amphorae is 276 and eight fourteenths, that is, four sevenths.

If the vessel has a lower width of 5 feet, an upper width of 3 feet, and a height of 9 feet, determine how many amphorae it holds as follows. The lower width multiplied by itself gives 25, and the upper width multiplied by itself gives 9; the product of the two is 15. Adding these three sums together gives 49. Multiply this by eleven, giving 539. One fourteenth of this is 38 [S; the abbreviation is unclear]. Multiply this by one third of the height, giving 115 [S]. This is the number of amphorae, or cubic feet.

After carefully examining these three rules—concerning a well and the two vessels—there will scarcely be any well, vessel, or vat whose depth cannot be determined, unless its proportions are exceptionally irregular [Col. 0149A].

## CHAPTER LXXXV. From the addition of all the numbers produced in natural order, to determine how much the depth increases, and so forth

If you wish to know how much the depth increases from the addition of all the numbers produced in natural order, this rule will suffice, provided that the addition begins with unity and proceeds continuously by the rules and in the proper order. If an even number is accumulated, multiply the next number by half of the last [Col. 0149B]. For example, for 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6—or if you wish to know their sum—multiply the following number, namely 7, by half of 6, namely 3, and the result is 21; the aforesaid addition likewise produces this sum.

If, however, an odd number of numbers is gathered, multiply the last number gathered by its greater part, as in 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. Multiply 7 by its greater part, namely 4. Four times 7 gives 28, which encloses all the terms written above.

If only even numbers are involved, as in 2, 4, 6, 8, multiply half of the last number gathered by the number that follows it; and if they are odd, as in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, multiply the greater part of the last number by itself.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. To find the gilding of a circle

Find the gilding of a circle as follows: multiply the diameter of the circle by itself and then multiply it by 22. Take one seventh of the resulting sum; this will be the amount of gilding for the circle. The same result would follow if you multiplied the circumference by the diameter [Col. 0149C].

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. To find the cubic feet of an irregular column

If there is an irregular column whose lower width is 13 feet, upper width 5 feet, and height 30 feet, find its cubic feet as follows. Multiply the lower width by itself, and the upper width by itself, and multiply the two by one another; when these three sums are added together, the result is 259 feet. Multiply this by eleven and take one fourteenth of the resulting sum; the result is 203½, namely the sum of the areas of the upper, middle, and lower sections [Col. 0149D]. Then multiply this by one third of the height; the result is 2,035 cubic feet.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. To make a hexagon

If you wish to make a hexagon whose side is 10 feet, make a line 10 feet long and fix a compass at its end; draw a circle. The distance from the center of the circle to its circumference is equal to the line. Draw six such lines from the circumference, and you will have a hexagon.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. To inscribe an octagon within an equilateral square

If you wish to inscribe an octagon within an equilateral square, take the middle diagonal [Col. 0150A]. Open the compass to this distance [Old Gloss: extended] and fix it at a corner of the square. Mark a point on each side as far as the circle reaches, and proceed in this manner around each corner and along each side. Then draw a line from point to point, cutting off the corners of the square, and you will have an octagon.

## CHAPTER XC. To find the cubic feet of a structure placed around a well

If there is a well whose diameter is 5 feet and around it is a structure 20 feet high and 2 feet wide, find the cubic feet of the structure as follows [Col. 0150B]. Multiply the width of the structure by itself, giving 4. Add the diameter of the well, giving 9. Multiply this by itself, giving 81. Subtract the diameter of the well multiplied by itself; 56 remains. Multiply this by eleven and take one fourteenth of the resulting sum; the result is 44 square feet. Multiply this by the height, namely by 20, giving 880. Thus the structure contains 880 cubic feet.

## CHAPTER XCI. To find the cubic feet of a prism on a right triangle

If a prism is based on a right triangle whose perpendicular is 19, base 12, and height 20, find its cubic feet as follows [Col. 0150C]. First find the area of the right triangle from its perpendicular and base; this will be 54. Multiply this by the height, namely 20, giving 1,080. This is the number of cubic feet in the prism.

If you wish to gild it, multiply the circumference of the right triangle, namely 36, by the height, namely 20, giving 720; this is the number of square feet of gilding.

## CHAPTER XCII. To find the diagonal in every quadrilateral, and so forth

In every quadrilateral, whether equilateral or oblong, find the diagonal as follows: multiply the width and length separately by themselves, and find the side of the sum of the resulting quantities. Take this as the diagonal [Col. 0150D].

From the perpendicular of a right triangle you can find the base as follows: multiply the perpendicular by three, subtract one ninth, and take half of the remainder; this will be the base. Restore what was subtracted from the base, and the result will be the hypotenuse.

Or as follows: take half the perpendicular and multiply it by three; the remainder is the base.

Or multiply half the perpendicular by six, subtract one ninth, and half of the remainder will be the base. Restore the ninth to the base, and the result will be the hypotenuse.

## CHAPTER XCIII. How many stadia on land correspond to the divisions of the zodiac, and so forth

There was a philosopher named Eratosthenes, also a most exact geometer, who, wishing to learn the size of the terrestrial globe, is said to have used the following argument from this art [Col. 0151A]. With the assistance of the surveyors of King Ptolemy, who ruled the whole of Egypt, he determined the number of stadia from Syene to Meroë. He set up, at intervals along the places from north toward south, as many learned men skilled in gnomonic computation as there were vessels, placing at each location sundials formed with equal dimensions and gnomons of equal length. On a single day he had them all observe the midday shadow and record the length of the shadow cast by each gnomon.

In this way he discovered that, over a distance of 700 stadia, the shadow did not correspond to a gnomon of the same length. From this test he concluded that the 360 divisions into which the entire circle of the zodiac is divided extend down to the earth, and that the portion which there is not possible to discover or measure occupies on the earth no more than 700 stadia, or slightly less. Having determined on earth the length of one division belonging to the zodiac, and multiplying this measurement 360 times, he established without hesitation the circumference and measurement of the earth in thousands of stadia. For he declared that the circumference of the entire terrestrial globe was 25,000 stadia. If this sum is divided equally into 360 parts, it will be clear how many stadia each portion must occupy on earth, even though on the celestial circle it admits no measurement by human conjecture [Col. 0151B].

It is therefore best to determine the shadow at the sixth hour and begin the boundary from it, so that the lines are always arranged at midday. It follows that the line from east to west should meet this line at right angles. First draw a circle on level ground and place a *sciotherum* at its center, whose shadow sometimes extends outside the circle and sometimes enters it [Col. 0151C]. For it is certain that both the eastern and western shadows can be detected. We must therefore observe how, from the first rising of the sun, the shadow is restrained. Then, when it reaches the line of the circle, we shall mark that place on the circumference [Col. 0152A]. We shall mark it similarly when the shadow is leaving the circle. After marking the two places on the circle where the entering and departing shadow falls, draw a straight line from one mark on the circumference to the other, and mark its midpoint. Through this point a straight line must be drawn from the center of the circle; by this line we shall determine the cardinal direction. From it we shall draw the *decumani* at right angles, and wherever on that line we find the appropriate right angle, we shall establish the *decumanus* correctly.

## CHAPTER XCIV. Another method of tracing the meridian

[Note: [Col. 0151C] The text of this chapter is confused and obscure.]

There is also another method by which we can trace the meridian by means of three shadows [Col. 0152B]. On level ground we shall set up a gnomon, *a b*, and mark its three shadows, *c b e*. We shall determine these shadows at right angles, observing how far one is separated from another. If we are establishing the meridian, the first shadow will be the longest; if it is after midday, the last will be the longest. We shall then represent these shadows on a board in proportion to their multiplication and preserve them on the ground in this manner.

The gnomon therefore stands *a b* on the surface *b*. Let us take the greatest shadow on the surface and mark it with the sign *d*. Likewise mark the ground with the sign *e*, so that in the vessel there is a proportional relation of lengths, without *b e d c e* [the wording is uncertain]. We count the hypotenuses from *c* to *a* and from *d* to *a*. Now, with *a* as the point and *e* as the radius, we draw a circle [Col. 0152C].

# GERBERT’S LETTER TO ADELBOLD  
## On the cause of the difference between the areas of an equilateral triangle, examined geometrically and arithmetically

*(In Pez, as cited above.)*

To Adelbold, hitherto beloved and always worthy of love: the integrity of faith and the steadfastness of integrity.

Among the geometrical figures that you had received from us was a certain equilateral triangle whose side was 30 feet and whose perpendicular was 26. According to the comparison of the side and the perpendicular, its area was 390. If you measure this same triangle arithmetically, without taking account of the perpendicular, according to the arithmetical rule—so that one side is multiplied by itself, the number of one side is added to that product, and half of the sum is taken—the area will be 462. Do you see how these two rules disagree?

But I have also examined more closely that geometrical rule which measured the area as 390 feet by means of the perpendicular. I allow its perpendicular only 25 and five sevenths, and its area is 385 and five sevenths. Let this be a universal rule for finding the perpendicular in every equilateral triangle: always subtract one seventh from the side and assign the remaining six parts to the perpendicular.

To make what is being said clearer, I shall give an example in smaller numbers [Col. 0153B]. I give you a triangle with a side of 7 feet and a perpendicular 1 foot long. I measure it by the geometrical rule as follows. Take one seventh from the side; I assign the remaining 6 to the perpendicular. I multiply the side by this and say: six times seven gives 42. Half of this, 21, is the area of the triangle.

If you measure this same triangle by the arithmetical rule and say: seven times seven gives 49; add the side, making 56; divide it to obtain the area, and you will find 28. Thus, in a triangle of one and the same size, the areas are different—which cannot happen.

But, so that you are not delayed any longer, I shall disclose the cause of the difference. I believe you know which feet are called linear, which square, and which solid, and that, when measuring areas, we customarily admit only laid-out squares [Col. 0153C]. Whatever portion of these a triangle touches, the arithmetical rule counts them as whole units. I shall draw it so that what is being said may be clearer [Col. 0154A].

Behold, in this little drawing there are 28 feet, although they are not complete units. Hence the arithmetical rule, taking a part as a whole, includes halves together with the complete units. The precision of the geometrical discipline, however, casts away the portions extending beyond the sides and joins together the half-sections remaining within the sides; it counts only what is enclosed by the lines.

For in this little diagram, where the side is measured by 7, if you seek the perpendicular, it is 6. Multiplying this by 7, you fill out what is virtually a square whose front is 6 feet and whose side is 7 feet, and you establish its area as 42. If you halve this, you leave 21 feet as the triangle’s area [Col. 0154B].

To understand this more clearly, look carefully, and always remember me [Col. 0154C].

---

# GERBERT, LATER POPE SYLVESTER II, LETTER TO CONSTANTINE, MONK OF FLEURY  
## On the construction of the sphere

*(In Mabillon, new edition of the* Analecta, *p. 102 ff.)*

## Mabillon’s Prefatory Notice

This letter of Gerbert, which is absent from the printed books, has been recovered from a manuscript in our library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. It is addressed to Constantine, a monk and teacher at Fleury, to whom Gerbert also sent letters 87, 142, and 161. He mentions him as well in Letter 92.

I consider Gerbert to be the author of a little book on a passage of Porphyry, whose preface to Otto III, emperor, was published in volume I of the *Analecta*. In notes to that preface I had conjectured that this little work was by Gebehard, bishop of Augsburg; but, after more mature consideration, I thought it should be assigned to Gerbert in the additions to volume I of the *Analecta*. The same author wrote the sermon *On the Ordination of Bishops*, which, at my request, our Peter Trelius copied from a manuscript in the library of Saint-Martial at Limoges; I have already mentioned him. Gerbert’s own *Geometry* and *Rhythmomachia* are preserved in a manuscript of the Thuane Library, marked no. 283.

## Gerbert to Constantine

A sphere, my brother, such as the one about which you ask, for displaying the celestial circles or signs, is round on every side. A line drawn around it divides its middle equally into 60 parts [Col. 0155A]. When, therefore, you establish the beginning of the line, fix one foot of the compass there, and place the other foot opposite it at the point where 6 of the 60 parts of the aforesaid line end. When you turn the compass around, you enclose 12 parts.

Then, moving the first foot, extend the second foot to the place where the eleventh part of the aforesaid line ends, and turn it around so that it encompasses 12 parts. In the same way, extend the foot again to the end of the fifteenth part of the aforesaid line; by this movement, having 30 parts, the middle of the sphere is cut [Col. 0155B].

Then transfer the compass to the other side of the sphere, where you had fixed the first foot, taking care to place it opposite the first point, and observe the aforesaid method for measuring the arcs and combining the parts. There will be only five arcs, the middle one of which is equal to the line divided into 60 parts.

Take one of these hemispheres, hollow it out on the inside, and wherever you had fixed one foot of the compass on the aforesaid line in order to draw the arc, pierce a hole, so that the arc passes through the center of the hole. At the poles of the sphere also, where you first placed the foot of the compass, make individual holes, so that the middle of those holes terminates the aforesaid hemisphere.

There will thus be seven holes, in each of which you place a half-foot-long tube [Col. 0156A]. The two outermost tubes are positioned opposite one another, so that through both you can see as though through a single tube. To prevent the tubes from wobbling this way and that, use an iron semicircle measured and pierced according to the size of the aforesaid hemisphere, by which you restrain the upper ends of the tubes.

These tubes differ from organ pipes in that they have the same thickness throughout, so that nothing obstructs the sight of anyone contemplating the celestial circles through them. The semicircle should be approximately two fingers wide and should preserve the same proportional division by which it is pierced to receive the tubes, since the entire hemisphere has a length of 30 parts.

After marking our northern pole, place the constructed hemisphere under the open sky in such a way that you can see that northern pole freely through the two outermost tubes mentioned above [Col. 0156B]. If you are uncertain about the pole, place one tube in a position where it will not move during the entire night, and through it observe the star that you believe to be the pole. If it is the pole, you will be able to observe it throughout the night; if it is another star, it will soon disappear from sight through the tube as it changes position.

Once the hemisphere has been placed in the manner described, so that it cannot move in any way, you will be able to measure first, through the lower and upper first tube, the northern pole; through the second, the arctic circle; through the third, the summer circle; through the fourth, the equinoctial circle; through the fifth, the winter circle; and through the sixth, the antarctic circles.

As for the antarctic pole, since it lies beneath the earth there is no sky: only the earth presents itself to anyone looking through both tubes.

# GERBERT, LATER POPE SYLVESTER II, BOOKLET ON THE RATIONAL AND THE USE OF REASON

Recovered from a manuscript of the distinguished monastery of Tegernsee in Bavaria by the Reverend Father Alphonsus Hueber, Benedictine monk of that place.

*(In R. P. Bernard Pez, newest* Thesaurus Anecdotorum, *vol. I, part II, col. 147.)*

## To the Reader

Among Gerbert’s works is listed the *Rhythmomachia*, published at Leipzig in 1616 in folio together with the four books of the most illustrious Prince Augustus of Lüneburg, under the pseudonym Gustavus Selenus, on the game of chess. This is what the Benedictine authors of the *Gallia litteraria* say; so does Fabricius; and so do all who during the past two centuries have written about ecclesiastical authors.

Whether they have rightly been trusted up to now had to be investigated from the book itself which Selenus published after the labors of Faber Stapulensis, Buxerus, and Barrozzi. But it shed no light: the entire book is devoted to explaining various exercises connected with the game of chess. On page 443, however, we read the title: “*Rhythmomachia*, a noble and most ancient Pythagorean game, which Francisco Barrozzi, a noble Venetian, wrote in the French language and which Gustavus Selenus rendered into German.”

Is not Gerbert’s *Rhythmomachia* the source of this little work? But Gerbert is mentioned only in the following passage, among other material found in Buxerus, folio 42a, and in Selenus, page 494:

> “Thomas Topcliff, an Englishman, supplied me with a certain little book which, as he reported, was extracted from an ancient Chaldaean book and rendered into the English language; it contains a certain method of playing *Rhythmomachia*, which I did not wish to omit from this little book of mine, especially since I hold the opinion that this form of progression, which corresponds to chess, is the perfection of our game, and that the ancients followed it in playing. From this I conjecture that the progress and movement of chess derived their origin from the same source.
>
> “From this it is sufficiently clear how severely and stoically certain ancients described this game: while they were content with contemplation of the game, they neglected in its practice what would have been neither unpleasant nor disagreeable to the players. These are Pope Gilbert, Hermannus Contractus, Castrensis, and Nicolaus Orestinus. In our own time they were imitated by Orontius Fineus, Delphinas, and Jacobus Faber Stapulensis; nor have I hitherto departed from their footsteps.
>
> “But when I saw that this contemplation was separated from recreation and was sometimes burdensome, I was very glad to have recovered what had long ago been cut off and separated, which seemed most conducive to the exact completion of this game.”

The book of Jacobus Faber Stapulensis, mentioned above by Buxerus, might perhaps shed some light; but thus far we have not succeeded in seeing this work.

Here, learned reader, you have what we have been able to conjecture about Gerbert’s *Rhythmomachia*. We leave the dispute itself to be decided by you.
