## Pez’s Notice

*(Introductory dissertation in volume I of the* Thesaurus Anecdotorum.)*

We have already spoken of this little work, which is purely dialectical. It now emerges, complete, from the library of Tegernsee. Immediately after it there was preserved there a sermon delivered by Gerbert at the council of Mouzon, which Guilielmus Cave included among works not yet published in his *Literary History*, although it has been very widely published and almost single-handedly constitutes nearly all the acts of that synod, which Cave reviews shortly afterward.

Moreover, Gerbert’s dedicatory letter had already been published by Mabillon in volume I of the *Analecta*. Mabillon had conjectured in notes to that letter, or preface, that the whole work was by Gebehard, bishop of Augsburg. But, as he says in volume II of the same *Analecta*, p. 215, after more mature consideration he thought it should be assigned to Gerbert in the additions to volume I of the *Analecta*.

In the same place Mabillon published, under Gerbert’s name, a sermon *On the Formation of Bishops*. Deceived by the difference in title, as Itigius notes in the preface to the *Treatise on Libraries and the Chains of the Fathers*, p. XCIII, he believed it had never previously been published, although it had already been published many times among the works of Ambrose.

But we return to Gerbert’s little work *On the Rational and the Use of Reason*. We have seen it not only in the library of Tegernsee but also in the contemporary—or nearly contemporary—manuscript of Emmeram, written by a similar hand. If I am not mistaken, it is also preserved in the Imperial Library at Vienna. In the Emmeram manuscript, several verses followed the entire little work; we have restored them in their proper place.

---

# VERSES IN GERBERT’S BOOK ON THE RATIONAL AND THE USE OF REASON

[Note: [Col. 0157] These verses are absent from the Tegernsee manuscript, but in the Emmeram manuscript, written around the eleventh century, they are appended after a few short pieces to Gerbert’s work *On the Rational and the Use of Reason*.]

Whoever wishes to climb the shadowy realms of Wisdom,

Drink the cups of this book in its meadows.

Having drunk, you will bend your swift step through the grasses

Where the instruments of learned men adorn their camp.

And, arriving, you will take with praise the glittering throne,

And Wisdom will grant you such a destiny:

“Sweet friend, you have always hastened to my halls;

Now let us rule the scepters there together without end.

Let us equal the proud empire with its attendant splendor,

And continually carry your name with me to the stars.

Loftily, however, see how many, with the oar of the tongue,

Draw new sails across our waters.”

---

# HERE BEGINS THE WORK ON THE RATIONAL AND THE USE OF REASON, EXTRACTED FROM THE MOST WISE LORD GERBERT, SUPREME PONTIFF OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE, AT THE REQUEST OF OTTO AUGUSTUS III

## Gerbert, bishop, to his lord and glorious Otto, Caesar, ever Augustus, emperor of the Romans: the service owed in obedience

While we were staying in Germany during a particularly fervent season of the year, bound, as we always are and always shall be, to imperial service, I do not know what movement of the mind, silently reconsidering within itself the measure of divine mysteries, resolved itself into words and brought forth matters that had been described by Aristotle and the highest authorities in very difficult propositions. It would have been astonishing that, amid the wars being prepared against the Sarmatians, any mortal could have possessed such recesses of the mind, from which such subtle and splendid thoughts flowed like streams from a purest spring.

You remember—and we too can remember—that many noble scholars and learned men were then present, among them several bishops distinguished for wisdom and renowned for eloquence [Col. 0159B]. Yet we saw none of them who could adequately explain any of these questions. Some were too remote from ordinary usage and had never previously been subject to doubt; others, though often debated, could not be resolved.

Your divine providence, judging ignorance unworthy of the sacred palace, commanded me to examine the matters that different people proposed in different ways concerning the Rational and the Use of Reason. At that time bodily weakness and more serious business postponed the task. Now that health has returned, while occupied with public and private affairs and established on this Italian journey, I, who shall remain your inseparable companion in every service for as long as life endures, briefly set down what I have conceived concerning this question [Col. 0159C].

I do this so that Italy may not think the sacred palace has grown numb, and so that Greece may not boast that she alone possesses imperial philosophy and Roman power.

[Note: [Col. 0159D] In the margin the manuscript gives this gloss on these words: “Italy is fertile in producing crops; Gaul and Germany are noble in nourishing soldiers. The Italians do not know what the Gauls know. The Italians accumulate denarii; the Gauls scrape together wisdom.” These remarks are recorded here without injury to anyone.]

The Roman empire is ours—ours. Productive Italy supplies strength through her crops, and Gaul and Germany through their soldiers; nor are the strongest kingdoms of Scythia lacking to us. You are our Caesar, emperor and Augustus of the Romans. Born from the highest blood of the Greeks, you surpass the Greeks in empire; by hereditary right you rule the Romans; in intelligence and eloquence you surpass both.

Therefore, before so great a judge, we shall first discuss certain preliminary exercises of the scholars—or rather, sophistical arguments. Then we shall pursue the discoveries of the philosophers in these matters. Finally, dialectic, manifold and thorny, shall complete the proposed question [Col. 0159D].

### I

They ask what Porphyry means when he says that a differentia is predicated as though it were related to a kindred differentia, as “to use reason” is predicated of “rational”; for the greater is always predicated of the lesser, but the lesser never of the greater. Thus “animal,” because it is greater than “horse,” is predicated of what is a horse, and “human being” is likewise predicated of what is a human being. How, then, can “to use reason” be predicated of “rational,” when “rational” appears to be greater than “to use reason”?

Everything that uses reason is rational; but, they say, “rational” concerns a capacity without its exercise, whereas “to use reason” concerns a capacity together with its exercise. Capacity together with its exercise is more than capacity alone. Therefore, they say, “to use reason” is rightly predicated of “rational,” as the greater of the lesser [Col. 0160A].

### II

The answer is as follows. How are the things that descend in a straight line from the most general to the most specific—whether subordinate genera or differentiae, whether placed among substances or among accidents—related? They are such that what is stated of a lower level universally receives the names and definitions of all the higher levels.

For example, “sensible,” since it is a differentia placed under “animate body,” when stated universally receives the name and definition of the higher terms. Everything sensible is an animate body, and is also a substance, and every virtue, habit, and quality.

But if “rational” is placed beneath “to use reason” in the same manner, how will “rational,” when stated universally, receive the name of its predicate, namely “to use reason”? For not everything that is rational is thought to use reason.

Therefore, if “rational” signifies capacity alone, while “to use reason” signifies capacity and exercise, “to use reason” will be predicated of “rational.” Conversely, if “rational,” when universally stated, does not receive the name of the aforesaid predicate, namely “to use reason,” then “to use reason” will not be predicated of “rational.” There would thus be two contraries—being predicated and not being predicated—in the same subject, which cannot happen [Col. 0160C].

### III

Let us likewise establish other differentiae according to accident, and let an accidental differentia be predicated as though it were related to a kindred accidental differentia, as “to walk” is predicated of “capable of walking.” Let this be done according to the nature of accident: since accidents are first considered in individuals, and afterward in species and genera.

Let us say that Cicero walks because he is capable of walking; and again, because Cicero is a human being, walks, and is capable of walking, let us say that both the human being walks and is capable of walking. Likewise, since an animal walks, it is capable of walking.

In these matters we must consider, they say, lest the relation of cause and effect appear to apply to living things [Col. 0160D]. For just as the cause is said to precede the effect—for example, “because he saw, he loved”—so capacity necessarily precedes exercise. And because things that precede in this way not only precede but also, when removed, remove what follows along with them, once the capacity has been taken away, the exercise must also be removed.

For if Cicero is not capable of walking—that is, if he cannot walk—he does not walk at all; that is, he does not perform the exercise of walking, which cannot be understood without the capacity. But if “to use reason” is exercise together with capacity, while “rational” is capacity alone, then, once capacity alone has been removed—which is prior by nature—exercise together with capacity cannot exist.

Therefore what is later by nature will not be predicated of what is earlier by nature. Capacity is earlier by nature, and exercise later; therefore, “to use reason” will not be predicated of “rational” according to the relation of capacity and exercise [Col. 0161A].

### IV

But, they say, “to use reason” is more numerous than “rational” by the dignity, excellence, or power proper to it [Col. 0161B]. Yet the nature of genera, species, and differentiae does not admit this. Human being and ass are equally subordinate to animal, and God and human being equally participate in the differentia “rational.” Therefore, they say, “to use reason” is not predicated of “rational” according to dignity, power, or excellence.

### V

I see that many objections can be raised against these propositions. Therefore, setting aside sophistical—that is, captious—controversy, something must be explained about the nature of power and act, and about the category in which “Rational” and “to use reason” are situated. We must also examine the nature of what is prior, whether it is appropriate to predication; and, as though by a certain thread, the discussion must be led from several points concerning the nature and order of predications to the matter at issue—namely, the predication of “to use reason” of “Rational” [Col. 0161C].

### VI

I judge that this should be done according to the tradition of the ancients, and especially of Aristotle, whose relevant words and statements I shall interpret briefly and clearly.

“Some powers,” he says, “are equivocal.” He speaks correctly in saying “some,” because not every power is equivocal. For a power that produces species from itself is not equivocal but univocal. A power is equivocal when it is predicated both of an act and of that power which can proceed to act. It receives no definition that is common to both; rather, the power that exists in act gives its name and definition to its own species. Aristotle speaks of this as follows:

“It is clear from what has been said that what exists necessarily exists according to act. Therefore, if what is prior is eternal, and what exists in act is prior in power. Some things exist in act without power, such as the first substances. Others exist in act together with possibility; these are prior by nature but posterior in time. Others never exist in act, but only in power.”

Things that are necessary, he says, exist in act—in that act, namely, which they cannot relinquish, as heaven and the sun possess their proper motion. Again, things that are necessary are eternal, and things that are eternal are prior to those powers that have not yet come into act. Therefore, the act that always exists is prior to the act that does not yet exist. For the act that always exists does not arise from power, since, whenever that thing existed, the act was not absent from its substance.

Thus, in necessary things, in which the act is eternal, the things themselves must also be eternal, as is understood in the case of heaven and the sun, which philosophers have held to be not only eternal but divine and immortal [Col. 0161D–0162A].

### VII

There are likewise non-necessary acts, whose species are twofold. Some of them have proceeded from power into act; others have received their substance together with the act itself.

Those that have proceeded from power into act are of this kind: when Cicero sits, before he sat he was able to sit; for he would not have sat if he had not previously possessed the power of sitting. Cicero therefore sits—that is, he exercises the act of sitting—because the act has proceeded from power.

The other act does not proceed from power, but always subsists together with the subsisting thing. It is of this kind: when fire is hot, no power of becoming hot preceded the existence of the fire itself; rather, what belonged to its substance did not cease to be hot—that is, it did not abandon the act of being hot. In this it shares a common nature with the higher and heavenly substances [Col. 0162B].

The difference is that those higher things belong to the necessary class, and, since their substance is incorruptible, they have not only never abandoned their act but are themselves never destroyed. Fire, however, belongs to a non-necessary class. So long as it subsists, it does not abandon its act; but because it is not of the necessary class, it loses the act together with its substance. For necessary things always exist necessarily and can never fail to exist. Fire, however, does not exist necessarily, though it necessarily possesses the act of being hot for as long as it exists [Col. 0162C].

Aristotle therefore rightly said: “What exists necessarily exists according to act.” For, according to necessity, all higher things that exist and subsist can never be destroyed and will never abandon their act.

“Therefore,” he says, “if what is prior is eternal, and what exists in act is prior in power.”

He derives the truth of these propositions from the nature of things. Since everything that exists is either simple or composite, it is clear that simple things are prior to composites. In divine and higher things there is nothing composite, but everything is simple. Otherwise, every composite thing would necessarily be resolved into the things from which it was composed. But divine and heavenly substances, and the elements of all things, are not resolved, because they are simple and uncompounded [Col. 0162D]. Things that are joined together from the first elements are again resolved into those same elements.

The eternal things, therefore, which are the principles of all other things, are prior to those that are not eternal. But eternal things do not exist, nor have they ever existed, without act. Therefore act is prior to power.

### VIII

Again, Aristotle, wishing to establish the genus as though from the nature of the things lying before us, determines its differences and species after making a division:

“Some things exist in act without power, such as the first substances. Others exist in act together with power; these are prior by nature but posterior in time.”

He says that some things exist in act without power, while others exist in act together with power; and those that exist in act without power are the first substances [Col. 0163A]. They are called “first” because they are the principles of things.

They are without power in the sense that they cannot be otherwise. Heaven and the sun cannot fail to move; fire cannot fail to be hot; water cannot fail to be wet.

Those things that exist in act together with power arise from a movement of the mind. Thus, when I sit, I have approached this act through a movement of the mind; the act was preceded by the power of sitting. I would not have sat unless I had first possessed the power of sitting.

Although this power precedes the act in time, Aristotle nevertheless says that the act together with the power is prior to power alone: “Those things that exist in act together with power are prior by nature but posterior in time.”

This happens because power, being the beginning of act, is something incomplete; but the complete is prior to the incomplete. Things that surpass others through the nobility of their nature are likewise prior, since goodness and virtue are equal in this respect. Equality is prior to inequality, for every inequality proceeds from equality [Col. 0163B].

Therefore the act in which power is consummated and perfected is prior to power, which before the act is curtailed and imperfect. Although power precedes the act in time, it has nevertheless flowed from the perfect by nature, as something possessing less than perfection [Col. 0164A].

### IX

“Others,” he says, “never exist in act, but only in power.”

Number is infinite in power; but when you specify any number, it is finite in act. The same reasoning applies to time. Time is infinite in power; but when you specify a day, a month, a year, or anything else, it is finite in act.

A description of all these matters must therefore be made, so that what has been said may become clearer when its figure is set before the eyes. In this first description nothing is demonstrated except the equivocation of act and power; for they participate only in the name [Col. 0164B].

[Col. 0163]

### X

As for power, the matter is clear: it is called “power.” Act, however, is called “power” because whatever exists can exist.

The second description contains a division of the genus. Act is a genus, and its species are two: necessary and non-necessary. It has already been said that the necessary is found in the higher substances, which always remain in their integrity.

The non-necessary produces two species from itself: one that has proceeded from power into act, and another that has burst forth into act not from power but from the nature of subsistence.

If we wish to include in the preceding formula that species which never exists in act but only in power, we may divide matters as follows: some things exist in act; others in power, with “act” signifying that which has been placed in the position of genus. Let us divide power again into that which can exist in act and that which can never exist in act.

With these points established, we must ask what kind of power the Rational difference possesses: whether it is one that can never come into act, or one that can come into act; and what act together with power is proposed in the other difference, namely “to use reason.” Is it an act preceded by power, or one accompanied by power?

The nature of a power that follows an act is entirely different from that of one that precedes it. These powers are so separated by the property of their nature that wherever one is present, the other cannot be.

In mutable things there is therefore a power called “either-way” power, preceding and following the act. Thus, when Cicero walks, before he walked he was able either to walk or not to walk; and because he walks, it follows that he can walk, though not necessarily, for he can also not walk.

In higher things, in simple elements, no power is found that can be either way, nor any power that precedes the act. Their act contains an unmoving, fixed, and therefore necessary power, which can do one thing but not either alternative. Since the sun moves, it is clear that it can move; and it necessarily cannot fail to move [Col. 0165A].

Since we assign different powers to different classes of things—namely, mutable and immutable things—we must ask where the Rational difference and “to use reason” can be situated.

### XI

I see that the Rational difference exists in eternal and necessary things, whose substance never ceases to exist. Substantial differences, species, and genera also always exist.

Some things are forms of things—or, so to speak, forms of forms; others are acts; others are certain powers.

Rational, therefore, insofar as it exists among intelligible things, belongs to the necessary class of act, where there is not a power that can choose either alternative, but a power that is fixed, immovable, and necessary [Col. 0165B].

But because these intelligible things, when they are applied to corruptible things, are changed through contact with bodies, they all pass again into that power which can proceed to act. For Rational—or, to speak more generally, genera, species, differences, propria, and accidents—exists in one way among intelligible things and in another way among natural things.

Among intelligible things there are also forms of things; among intelligible things some are passions and others acts. Since they exist in the soul while they are understood, they are passions of the soul, because every act of understanding is a passion of the soul. But when they come to knowledge through careful and perfect study, they are acts of the soul, because all knowledge is an act of the soul [Col. 0165C].

Rational is therefore considered in one way in the eternal species of human beings, whether among intelligible or intellectual things, and in another way among natural things. There, forms or acts are eternal; here, there is a power that can come into act.

Thus, since Cicero is a human being, and a human being is called rational, Cicero is rational in the sense that he can use reason—that is, exercise that act—because he proceeds from a power that admits either alternative. Cicero can use reason, and he can fail to use it.

Therefore, because the Rational difference is present substantially in Cicero or in a human being, while “to use reason” is present accidentally, “to use reason” is rightly said to be predicated of Rational as an accident of a subject. For whatever is present and absent without the destruction of the subject is an accident.

We see that “to use reason” can be absent from a human being or from Plato, and from Rational things, without the destruction of the subject. It is therefore an accident [Col. 0165D].

Furthermore, “to use reason” is an act of doing. For whoever uses reason does something—that is, exercises a certain act of reasoning. Doing is one of the most general genera of accidents. Therefore “to use reason” is an accident.

### XII

That “to use reason” is an accident of Rational is inferred as follows: what is Rational can use reason; and what can use reason does use reason. Therefore “to use reason” is an accident of Rational, and is predicated of Rational as a difference akin to itself.

Just as we differ by the Rational difference from the other animals that are not rational, so, because we use reason, we differ from those that cannot use it [Col. 0166A].

Again, a human being is always rational, but does not always use reason. Therefore “to use reason” is not a substantial difference.

### XIII

Perhaps, however, someone will ask what this very “to use reason” is, and why this difference is akin to the Rational difference.

“What,” Boethius says, “is to use reason other than to use judgment?” Everything else is common to us with the other living creatures; we are separated from them by reason alone.

If the only difference between us and the other animals is judgment, why should we hesitate to identify “to use reason” with “to use judgment”? If someone removes this from things, he removes human reason; and once human reason has been removed, humanity itself will not remain.

If, therefore, according to Boethius, we differ from the other animals by using reason, just as we do by the Rational difference, “to use reason” is rightly predicated of Rational as a difference akin to itself, and as an accident of a subject without which it cannot exist.

For if you remove the subject—that is, the Rational—there will be no one who uses reason. But if you remove the accident—that is, “to use reason”—you have not thereby removed the subject, Rational. A human being can exist who is Rational even while asleep, but does not use reason [Col. 0166B].

### XIV

“But,” they say, “the term that is predicated must be greater than or equal to the subject; it cannot be lesser. Yet ‘to use reason’ appears to be less than Rational. For Rational encompasses the whole species of human beings and of God, whereas ‘to use reason’ applies not to all of them but only to those who exercise the act of reason.”

Since, therefore, the lesser is being predicated of the greater, this is an appropriate place to say a little about the nature of predication.

Some may think that the same difficulty appears in other predications, as when we say, “A human being is a philosopher.” “Human being” is the subject term; “philosopher” is predicated, and does not appear capable of being equal to it. A term is predicated of the subject, but is much less than it. For not all human beings are philosophers.

But the force of predication is not correctly understood in this way. Predication occurs either of substance of substance, as in “A human being is an animal”; or of accident of accident, as in “Dialectic is a science”; or of accident of substance, as in “A human being is white.”

Since an accident always exists in a subject, while a subject is always either universal or particular, an accident too will be universal or particular according to the nature of its subject.

Thus, science, although it is a universal accident because it is predicated of many, is particular and individual when it exists in Plato, just as Plato himself is. But when it is said to exist in a human being—that is, in a universal reality—it is understood to be universal as well, as in “A human being is learned” [Col. 0166C].

Again, since accidents are considered principally in individuals—that is, in the first substances—individuals are called first substances, either because they are receptive of accidents or because they are the first things to come to knowledge.

Therefore, their understanding in second substances will correspond to the nature of the first substances. Thus, because baldness exists in Socrates, Socrates is called bald; and because Socrates is a human being, an animal, and a substance, Socrates is also called a bald human being, a bald animal, and a bald substance [Col. 0166D–0167A].

### XV

No one should think that I mean to say that the predication of lesser things extends to greater things, since greater things are always predicated of lesser things, while lesser things are never predicated of greater things.

It is one thing to predicate general things of special things, and likewise special things of individuals, whether in the category of substance or in the categories of accidents, according to the nature of each. It is quite another thing to refer the nature of accidents to the property of substance.

In the former case, one considers which substance is predicated of which substance and which accident of which accident. In the latter, one considers how an accident is related to substance and in what subject it is first found, as was said here concerning the baldness of Socrates [Col. 0167B].

For although Socrates, being bald and also being a human being, is a bald human being, it does not follow that every human being is bald. This will become clearer from the division of propositions.

Some propositions are universal, such as “Every human being is an animal”; some are particular, such as “Some human being is an animal”; and some are indefinite, such as “A human being is an animal.”

If universality had force by itself in the terms of propositions, the determinative words that determine universality would not have been added. Since “human being” is universal, the addition of a determination expresses whether it has been stated universally or particularly in the proposition.

The determinations are “every,” “no,” and “some” [Col. 0167C].

Since “human being” is universal, when, without any determination, you say of it, “A human being is a philosopher,” no necessity compels the statement to be understood as meaning that every human being is a philosopher. Since Socrates is a philosopher and is also a human being, it will be true when you say, “A human being is a philosopher.”

Indefinite propositions that have a universal subject therefore contain the force of particular propositions. When I say, “A human being is a philosopher,” it is equivalent to saying, “Some human being is a philosopher.”

Since the Rational difference, when “to use reason” is predicated of it, is a universal subject, the proposition concerning it will be indefinite and will contain the force of a particular proposition. Thus, in saying, “Because something is Rational, it uses reason,” the proposition is equivalent to saying, “Some Rational thing uses reason” [Col. 0167D].

Whoever says, “Everything that is Rational uses reason,” has enunciated a universal reality universally, and the affirmation is false. Its negation—“No Rational thing uses reason”—is likewise found to be false.

### XVI

Furthermore, in things that are predicated substantially according to a universal affirmation and negation, one of the two is always true and the other false. If the affirmation is true, the negation is found to be false; and if the affirmation is false, the negation is found to be true. Thus: “Every human being is an animal”; “No human being is an animal.” Again: “Every human being is a stone”; “No human being is a stone.”

But if predication is made universally according to an accident, both propositions must be found false, as in: “Every human being is a philosopher”; “No human being is a philosopher” [Col. 0168A].

Since, therefore, “to use reason,” when predicated universally of Rational, makes both enunciations—affirmation and negation—false, it will be predicated of Rational not substantially but accidentally.

For the person who says, “Everything that is Rational uses reason,” is speaking falsely, since someone who is asleep is Rational but does not use reason. Conversely, “No Rational thing uses reason” is false, since many do use reason.

Therefore “to use reason” is predicated of Rational not substantially but accidentally, as an accidental difference of a substantial difference. Just as rationality separates us from the other animals that are not rational, so “to use reason” causes us to differ from those animals that do not use reason [Col. 0168B].

“To use reason” will also be predicated of Rational according to the nature of indefinite predications, which contain the force of particular predications, not according to the property of determinations, which indicate the quantity of the subject terms.

Nor will the universal subject “Rational” receive the name and definition of the predicate, as happens only in substantial predications.

By “substantial predications” I mean those that proceed from the most general genera through the most specific species, whether they occur in substances or in accidents. Thus, when “rational, mortal animal”—the definition of a human being, namely “rational, mortal animal”—is predicated of a human being, the predication is substantial.

For every definition is predicated of the thing it defines. When I say, “Dialectic is the science of arguing well,” I predicate this definition of dialectic. Both predications are substantial, just as both are definitions; for every definition that begins from a genus and proceeds through differences to the species that it defines is substantial [Col. 0168C].

### XVII

Since, as I think, it has been clearly demonstrated how “to use reason” is predicated of Rational, I have not considered it necessary to answer those who have devised such foolish predication as cannot be found in the nature of predications.

It does not follow that, because act and power are greater, and greater than power alone, “to use reason,” in which both are present, should therefore be predicated of Rational. “He walks,” in which act together with power is present, is not said of “able to walk,” that is, of power alone; rather, conversely, “he does not walk” may be predicated of “able to walk.”

Nor is one predicated of two merely because it precedes them; nor are the first substances predicated of the second substances. Rather, the second substances are predicated of the first [Col. 0168D].

I, Gerbert, have written this, although it is removed from priestly gravity, yet not alien to imperial study; and I have preferred to displease others rather than fail to please you, both in this matter and in all affairs worthy of your command.

You will therefore read these things among the exercises of your mathematical studies. Whether I have brought together material worthy of the sacred palace, the studies of noblemen will answer. Logic will not remain silent after consultation, nor will I fear being rightly censured if I have labored to accomplish what could please sacred ears.

**THE END**

## THE WORKS OF GERBERT, LATER POPE SYLVESTER II, PART TWO  
### ON ECCLESIASTICAL MATTERS

[Col. 0169]

## A Sermon on the Formation of Bishops

*(In Mabillon, New Analecta, new edition, p. 103.) (C)*

[Col. 0169A] If, brothers, anyone recalls the saying in which he reproved the thrifty servant concerning the money kept back for himself which he had received to put out at interest, saying, “You should have put my money with the bankers, and when I came I would have collected it with interest” (Luke XIX, 33), he will no longer reserve the grace of the divine gift bestowed upon him solely for his own use while remaining an idle hearer.

Rather, by making it available to all and investing it more abundantly, he will possess it more securely, so that through it he may offer the fruit of edification to many and, like a beautiful tree laden with fruit, may not be proved to occupy the ground without fruit while he lives. The tree itself is adorned with its fruits, and all who receive fruit from it are nourished.

The blessed Apostle also invites us to this very thing: “Do not seek what is yours, but what belongs to others” (1 Corinthians X, 24); and elsewhere: “I do not seek what is useful to me, but what is useful to many, so that they may be saved” (ibid., 3).

Therefore, we to whom the administration of the Lord’s word has been entrusted, and who have undertaken to feed and nourish Christ’s flock, believe that we shall not escape without suffering the harm of great danger if not only [do we not] live according to these principles, but also do not preach them at all [Col. 0169B].

Although the wickedness of our life delays us from preaching these things, the necessity of the command nevertheless summons us. And just as “Woe is me if I do not preach” applies to me, and as I shall be condemned if I keep the treasure I have received buried in the earth and conceal it for a long time in my heart, or if I keep the lamp of the divine word pressed down beneath a bushel rather than placing it on a lampstand before the eyes of all, so also shall I be condemned if I do not unlock, with those keys of the kingdom of heaven which all we priests received in the blessed Apostle Peter, the barriers of human ignorance, so that I may deserve to hear, in proportion to my tongue’s capacity: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much” (Matthew XXV, 21) [Col. 0169C].

Therefore, fearing these reproaches and punishments, almost struck down under the fear of God, and invited by fraternal love, I shall no longer address the subordinate populace, whom I am accustomed continually to admonish. Rather, I shall turn my words to the preachers of the populace themselves, and, like an obedient servant—that is, a bishop—to priests who are my fellow servants, I shall not hesitate boldly to preach the duties of salvation [Col. 0170A].

Nor shall I claim any privilege of conscience because I offer these things to my fellow priests out of charity; nor do I declare myself to be perfect in life when I admonish others concerning the perfect life. Rather, when I dare to speak these things to them, I shall hear together with them the things I say.

With divine assistance, I shall now begin, to the extent of my ability. Aided by the prayers of those to whom our discourse is directed, I shall take the desired path and, as though placed in the midst of the priests, address the priests themselves.

Hear me, most blessed fathers, and, if you deem me worthy, most holy brothers. Hear me, Levitical stock, priestly offspring, consecrated lineage, leaders and rulers of Christ’s flock. Hear me as I both entreat and fear, as I carefully concern myself with our common interests, and as I wish to demonstrate the honor of the episcopate, so that, once I have shown its prerogative of honor, we may also seek the corresponding merits [Col. 0170B].

We cannot go astray in our work if we know the truth. For it is fitting that the priestly dignity should first be known by us, and then preserved by us, so that the saying of the psalmist may not be directed against us: “When a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Psalm CXLVIII).

The honor and sublimity of the episcopate, brothers, can be equaled by no comparisons [Col. 0170C]. If you compare the insignia of kings and the diadems of princes, they will be far inferior, as though you were comparing leaden metal with the radiance of gold. For you see the necks of kings and princes being bowed before the knees of priests, and, after kissing their decrees, they believe themselves strengthened by their prayers.

What should I say now about the multitude of the people, over which the bishop has merited not only to be set by the Lord, but has also been commanded by evangelical precepts to protect it by paternal right?

Thus the Lord certainly said to the blessed Peter: “Peter, do you love me?” And he replied: “You know, Lord, that I love you” (John XXI). When he had been questioned a third time and had followed with a threefold response, the Lord repeated to him three times: “Feed my sheep.”

What sheep, what flock did the blessed Apostle receive then? Not only did he receive them at that time, but he received them together with us, and with him we all receive them. Therefore they are entrusted to priests to govern, and they are rightly said to be subject to their rulers, because, while the evangelical command shines forth, we nevertheless see this fixed in place: “A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his lord; but it is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher, and for the servant to be like his lord” [Col. 0171A–B] (Luke VI, 40).

You should understand, brothers, that I have prefaced all these matters for this reason: to show that nothing in this world is more excellent than priests and that nothing more sublime than bishops can be found.

When we demonstrate the dignity of the episcopate, we should recognize before the eyes of bishops what we are, and demonstrate by our actions rather than by our name what we profess to be. Let the name correspond to the action, and the action answer to the name. Let there not be an empty name and an enormous crime; a sublime honor and a punishable life; a godlike profession and an unlawful action; a religious garment and an irreligious conduct; an exalted rank and a disgraceful transgression [Col. 0171B–C].

Let there not be a higher chair in the church while the priest’s conscience is found to be much lower. Let us not simulate the speech of doves while possessing the mind of dogs. Let us not display a sheep-like profession while harboring a wolf-like ferocity. Thus the Lord may rightly answer us through the prophet: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah XXIX, 13).

For, brothers, just as a cloak identifies a senator, agriculture a peasant, weapons a barbarian, skill at rowing a sailor, and the quality of their work identifies individual craftsmen as its makers, so a bishop is marked only by episcopal works. He is recognized more by his conduct than by his profession, and is called a bishop by his merits rather than by his name [Col. 0171C].

For just as we say that nothing is more excellent than a bishop, so nothing is more pitiable if a bishop is endangered by his life, if a priest is held in crime, or if a pontiff is stained by the marks of vice. And just as it is easier to fall from level ground, so one who falls from a height incurs a grave ruin.

The episcopal honor is indeed great before human beings; but after a fall—which may God forbid!—the grief is great. The rank in the Church is high; but if one slips from it through negligence, he is miserably marked out by all. Great sublimity demands great vigilance; greater honor requires greater care [Col. 0171D].

To whom more is entrusted, from him more is required. “The powerful will suffer powerful torments”; and “for the one who knows the law and does not do it, it is sin.” The servant who knows his lord’s will and does not do what is fitting will be beaten with many blows.

[Col. 0172A] For God requires one thing of a bishop and another of a presbyter; one thing of a deacon and another of a cleric, and something else of a layman. Although he requires the work of each one individually, nevertheless more will be demanded from him to whom greater care has been entrusted; the greater the number of peoples committed to his governance, the greater the penalties he will pay if the administration entrusted to him has been neglected.

And, to depict for our fellow priests the measure and pattern of the episcopate, we must review the apostolic rule in its entirety, since it distinguishes each feature of the episcopate individually, lest some talkative priests complain that in this work they have been rebuked by my inventions rather than reproved by apostolic judgments.

Thus the blessed Apostle says to all bishops: “This is a faithful saying” (1 Tim. 3:1), as though he were saying: “What I am about to say, I declare truthfully, so that no one may think that I have lied.” “If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work”—that is: Do you wish to be a bishop? What you aspire to is great; but it is also a good work, if you embrace it. Otherwise, you cannot be a bishop if you choose to despise episcopal duties.

Again he introduces the matter and says: “It is necessary that a bishop be blameless.” He says “blameless,” for if you are blamed, you are subjected to the disgrace of guilt. Indeed, guilt brings one to liability; whoever is subjected to liability is bound to punishment; whoever is bound to punishment is subject to servitude; and whoever is subject to servitude loses freedom. Behold what episcopal freedom becomes through the criminal stages we have described. But so that you may not be blamed, preserve blameless conduct in every respect.

After this he adds: “The husband of one wife.” If you attend to the literal sense, he condemns bigamy, so that the man who desires to attain the rank of bishop may not know a second union. But if it is understood allegorically, he forbids a bishop to have two wives—that is, he must not, after Catholic doctrine, adopt heretical belief; rather, he must associate himself only with the faith of Christian sincerity, so that he may be called the husband of one wife alone—that is, of the Church.

It follows: “Sober.” By “sober” he means not merely sparing in wine, but moderate in conduct, so that he does not indulge in wine beyond measure and may rejoice in a sober mind. If he does not do this, he will not be a bishop.

And, adding what follows, he says: “Prudent” (1 Cor. 3:19). He means not worldly prudence, of which it is said that it is foolishness with God, but spiritual prudence—one that is circumspect in action and skilled in speech—so that he may be “wise as a serpent and simple as a dove.” If he is not such a man, he is not a bishop.

Again he introduces: “Well adorned.” If we attend only to the surface of the letter, we will seek for the priest no other adornment than a more splendid garment—for example, we will seek beaver or silk clothing—and that man will believe himself holier among bishops who has the brighter garment [l., vestem]. But the holy Apostle does not wish to be understood in this way. He desires to adorn the bishop not in the flesh but in the mind, so that the priest may please God who has arranged his soul for God.

Whoever does not do these things will not be a bishop; and the unjust man incurs infamy who despises the holy Apostle.

After this he adds: “Hospitable,” so that, out of regard for humanity, he may receive in his lodging one who has no lodging, and bring the needy man without a roof into his own house. He must not merely consume the gifts of Christ, which Christ’s goodness has bestowed upon him.

“Teachable”—that is, he must possess wisdom, so that he may not only adequately instruct the people entrusted to him, but also be able to repel the contradictions of every heresy, lest through his ignorance he fail to teach the ignorant. Otherwise what is written may happen: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit” (Matt. 15:14).

Let the man who does not know himself to be such as we have described not seek the priesthood, lest he deprive another of the place who could illuminate all by the radiance of his wisdom.

He says likewise: “Not given to wine”—that is, not devoted to much wine. The bishop must drink in such a way that it is impossible to know whether he has drunk, lest after abundant drinking he take pleasure in womanish lust, since, as the Apostle says, every kind of wantonness is nourished by wine. If he cannot do these things, he cannot be a bishop.

Finally he continues, saying: “Not a striker, but moderate”—that is, he must not have hands ready for violence, nor strike the consciences of others with wicked suspicions, lest, when he is found insolent, he be judged more an athlete of violence than a bishop. Rather, he must patiently endure injuries inflicted by others, so that through steadfast patience he may display the calm moderation of his mind.

Again he says: “Not contentious”—that is, he must not loosen his tongue for abuse, so that the man who proclaims the praises of God and offers divine sacrifices may not utter the poisons of quarrels. For God cannot be blessed by the mouth of a priest while man is cursed, since man is known to possess the image of God; nor can evil and good in any way belong together in him. If he does not do these things, he will not be a bishop.

Next he continues: “Not greedy”—that is, the bishop must not be overcome by the desire for profit in anything. For the sake of shameful gain he must not become liable to sin and nourish avarice, the root of all evils. Being content solely with the allowances of the Church, he must not seek at all what he understands to be superfluous; rather, by distributing those very things to Christ’s poor, he should purchase for himself the kingdoms of heaven.

He then joins what follows and says: “One who rules his own household well, having his children submissive with all chastity.” He says that he must preside well over his own household—that is, he must govern the household of his body by authoritative right. He must not himself be subjected to the body, nor be driven headlong, without restraint, into the reins of lust, so that he may guide his own children to the rule of chastity by the example of purity.

If he does not do these things, he cannot be called a bishop.

Then he says: “If anyone does not know how to rule his own household, how will he take care of the Church of God?” This is precisely what we said above: if he cannot cultivate the household of his own heart, how will he take care of many others? And if he cannot remove the beam of sin from his own eye, from whose eye will he remove the speck? Whoever does not do this will not be a bishop.

Again it follows, and he says: “Not a novice”—that is, he must not hastily receive the rank of priesthood if he has recently come to the faith from paganism or has been transferred from secular military service to clerical office, lest, being lifted up in pride, he fall into the snare of the devil. For what he has not learned over a long period he will not be able to observe in a short time; instead, having fallen and being ignorant, he will receive the judgment that the devil, in his pride, deserved to receive.

And, bringing the rule and episcopal pattern to a conclusion, he finally says: “He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside”—that is, from heretics and schismatics who, outside the holy Church, establish profane gatherings. Yet even among them, the Apostle says, a bishop must have a good testimony concerning his spotless and holy life, [lacuna], whence they may take an occasion for slander and begin to defame the Catholic doctrine of the holy religion. If he cannot be such a man, how can he be a bishop?

[Col. 0174A] As I think, in this work we have perceived ourselves to have been freed from a great debt, since we have opposed not our own testimonies against bishops, but those of the Apostle, lest, like a cloud [lacuna]. But when the authority of the holy Apostle has supported us in each matter, let them dare to criticize the Apostles rather than us, if they are so bold.

Although the length of this little book may constrain us to hasten toward its end, nevertheless concern born of fraternal love delays us—especially concern for those priests who, dulled by the torpor of their minds, bring disrepute upon priestly honor and lament that in these times a new rule has been discovered so lavishly.

Following the example of the leprous Gehazi and Simon the magician, they bought the grace of the Holy Spirit for a price and sold it, fearing not at all that, having bought the honor of the priesthood, they had been condemned together with Simon by the blessed Apostle Peter: “May your money be with you unto perdition, because you thought that the gift of the Holy Spirit could be possessed for a price.” They also judge that they have received leprosy from the holy Elisha together with Gehazi, when they estimate that the priestly rank too should be sold for a price.

And just as, when the head is corrupted by more powerful diseases, it is necessary for the rest of the body to be fatally drenched by the flood of the disease above, so these men, who appear to be the head of the Church, corrupt the fraternal body with a pestilential disease, so that nothing in the structure of the whole body can escape uninjured from the virus of negligent priests’ depravity.

You may see throughout the Church priests whom not merit but money has advanced, foolish and unlearned men who have seized the priestly rank. If you wish to ask them truthfully who appointed them priests, they immediately reply: “I was recently ordained bishop by the archbishop, and I gave a hundred solidi for him to confer the episcopal rank upon me. If I had not given them, I would not be a bishop today. Therefore it is better for me to reduce the gold in my little chest than to lose so great a priesthood. I gave gold and received the episcopate; yet, if I live successfully, I do not doubt that I shall quickly recover it. I ordain a presbyter and receive gold; I make a deacon and receive a quantity of silver; and likewise from each of the other orders, and from blessing abbots and churches, I confidently expect monetary profit. Behold, I have the gold that I gave, untouched in my little chest.”

[Col. 0175A] I answer: This is precisely what grieves me about you, because the archbishop made you a bishop in the flesh. Money ordained you spiritually leprous. You gave money and thought that you had acquired the grace of God, and by this means you received leprosy itself. Again, you accepted money and did not fear to sell the grace of God for a price; at the same time you handed over leprosy and carried out a wretched commerce at the expense of souls.

For the sake of money you appointed an abbot over monks, and exalted a leprous man to the death of monks. And ignorant people cry out at your ordinations: “He is worthy and just,” while the wretched conscience cries out: “He is unworthy and unjust.”

Such a bishop pronounces: “Peace be with you,” while inwardly he has no peace with himself. To carnal eyes he appears a great bishop, but in the sight of God he is greatly leprous. Through money he acquired an illicit rank and lost God in his inner man. The flesh receives dignity, and the soul loses honor. The servant-flesh has been made master, and the soul, which was master, has been made servant; the lower part rules over peoples, and the higher serves demons. He purchased the priesthood for the flesh and prepared ruin for the soul.

And what will it profit such a man if he gains the whole world and suffers the loss of his soul? What you gave when you were ordained was gold; what you lost was your soul. When you ordained another, what you received was money; what you gave was leprosy. These are your commercial dealings, which you have carried out to your own destruction.

Nevertheless, I will question my fellow bishop for a little while, since I am a bishop and am speaking with a bishop.

Tell me, brother bishop, when you gave money, what did you receive?

“What?” he says. “The episcopal grace.”

“And why is this grace called by such a name?”

“Why?” he says. “I suppose because it is given freely, and for that reason it is called grace.”

“And if grace is given freely and is not valued in gold, why do you purchase it with money?”

“But,” you say, “it would not have been given to me if it had not been bought with coins; nor would I have been ordained bishop if I had not given money.”

“As your answers show, when you were ordained you did not receive grace, because you did not merit it freely. And if you did not receive grace, brother, how could you become a bishop? If the Lord says to the disciples, ‘Freely you have received; freely give’ (Matt. 10:8), why did you suppose that you could possess freely given grace for a price? As I see it, when you gave gold, you both lost it and failed to acquire holy grace.”

[Col. 0175D] Adding one more question, I examine my brother bishop, lest we appear to have omitted anything from our truthful proofs:

“Who gives episcopal grace, brother bishop—God or man?”

“Without doubt, God, but through man. Man lays on the hand, and God bestows grace; the priest serves God with a supplicating right hand, and God blesses with a powerful right hand; the bishop initiates the rank, and God grants the dignity.”

“O justice! O equity! If money is given to man, who performs no greater service in the ordination than the service granted to him, why is everything denied to God, who bestows the very rank upon you? Does it seem just to you that the servant should be honored while God suffers injury, and that the priest should unjustly receive money while God suffers injury from man?

“But since God expects nothing from you for the rank he has granted, why does the priest shamelessly expect money from you? God, in his goodness, wished to grant it freely to man, while the rapacious bishop demands money from man! God, as a benevolent giver, bestowed it freely upon him, while the priest, as a malicious man, took him captive!

“For what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?”

Behold to what evils the divine order is brought down. Behold to what disgrace those have fallen who deserved to hear from the Judge of the world: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14).

Behold those to whom the nations are subjected, those to whom the Lord said: “You are the salt of the earth” (ibid., 13). If you have been established by the Lord as the light of the Church, so that with the radiant eloquence of your preaching you may illuminate the darkness of consciences caused by ignorance, why are you yourself held fast and bound by palpable darkness through the transgressions mentioned above?

And not only do you perish deservedly because you do these things; you also undeservedly destroy others with yourself. If you have deserved to possess the flavor of salt, so that you may season the fields of the foolish, why, having been made tasteless by such a disgrace of vices, do you offer yourself to be trampled by filthy swine, so that after this you can season neither others nor yourself?

As a sensual man, you sought the office of the eyes in the body—that is, in the Church—so that through you the rest of the body might have the guidance of light. But now, because you are darkened by bleary vision in the gloom of vices, you provide no light yourself and take light away from others.

Of these eyes the Gospel says: “If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light.” That is: if the bishop, who has deserved to preside as the light in the body, is adorned with the innocence of simplicity, the whole Church will shine with the splendor of light.

“But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark.” That is: if the bishop, who appeared to provide light for the body subject to him, is clouded by the blindness of wickedness, what will the other members do, since the light of their eyes has been taken away? That is: what will the secular multitude do when the bishop has provoked the multitude toward a similar abyss of crimes through illicit pleasures and forbidden actions, so that nothing now appears illicit which the bishop perpetrates as though it were lawful?

Rather, everyone believes that whatever the bishop finds pleasurable is more praiseworthy, and no one fears doing what the pontiff does not hesitate to do.

[Col. 0176D] The name by which you are designated condemns you yourself. You are unhesitatingly called “bishop” by everyone; and what else does “bishop” mean than “overseer”? Since you rightly look upon everyone from the more exalted seat of the Church, and everyone’s eyes look toward you, so that you may give them food at the proper time, why do you display yourself like a foul mirror before the eyes of all, so that they cannot adorn themselves by your darkness?

Let it suffice that we have extended our discourse this far for a little while concerning our fellow priests, in which we have shown both their excellence and their fall, lest, trusting in the sublimity of their honors, they fail to seek perfection of conduct and fail to believe themselves priests if they are called so only by name and not by deed.

And although I know that many priests who neglect to embrace these things will maliciously disparage me because of this distinction, I nevertheless believe that even more—those who strive to attain these things—will faithfully pray for me. But just as we are not weighed down by the tearing attacks of detractors, so we are helped by the prayers of approved men.

Come now, holy Spirit, who have assisted us in this work through divine inspirations: assist all priests, so that they may do what you yourself have commanded in this little book, and so that you may rightly grant them the kingdoms of heaven which you promised. You live and reign with the Father and the only-begotten Son, God, in Trinity and Unity, through all ages of ages. Amen.

GERBERT’S, LATER POPE SYLVESTER II’S, LITTLE BOOK ON THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD, RESTORED FOR THE FIRST TIME TO ITS AUTHOR FROM A CODEX OF THE FAMOUS MONASTERY OF GÖTTWEIG IN AUSTRIA, OF THE ORDER OF ST. BENEDICT, BY THE REVEREND FATHER HIERONYMUS PEZ, BENEDICTINE OF MELK.

(In R. P. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum novissimus*, vol. I, part II, col. 131.)

[Col. 0177]

NOTICE OF THE REVEREND FATHER PEZ.

(An introductory dissertation in vol. I of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*.)

Long ago this little work was published as that of an anonymous author by the learned Cellot. Concerning its genuine author, the most learned Mabillon, in the second part of the preface to the fourth Benedictine century, § 3, speaks as follows:

“Although this anonymous author was plainly endowed with only moderate talent and ordinary learning, nevertheless it must be acknowledged that his testimony is of no small value for illuminating the controversies of the ninth and tenth centuries, especially if it is established, as some have thought, that he lived in the tenth century.

“For this author, commonly called the Cellotian Anonymous because he was first published by the learned Cellot in an appendix to the *History of Gottschalk*, teaches four principal things concerning these controversies.

“First, that Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz, and Ratramnus wrote against the opinion of Paschasius, who asserted that in the Eucharist the body is the same as that which was born of the Virgin Mary; and this Anonymous also attacks that view.

“Second, that the authors of the Stercorarian doctrine are Heribald, bishop of Auxerre, who presented the matter disgracefully to Rabanus, and Rabanus himself, who takes it up even more disgracefully and concludes it most disgracefully. The author also attempts to refute them.

“Third, that this invention revived in the time of the Anonymous himself.

“Fourth, that nevertheless the true body and blood of Christ are contained in the Eucharist.”

Mabillon adds:

“No one fails to see how important these matters are. I therefore thought it worthwhile, before treating of the opponents of Paschasius, to indicate the name and age of this Anonymous—both of which are disputed among scholars.”

Then, in §§ 47 and 48, partly by conjectures and partly on the authority of the Gembloux codex, which is five hundred years old, he shows that Heriger, abbot of Lobbes, was the author of the Cellotian book.

It is widely known how much applause this most diligent investigation has won for Mabillon among all learned men. Yet the matter is by no means settled. Whether we consider Mabillon’s conjectures or the codices he cites, equally strong arguments arise against his position.

As for the conjectures, we admit that from the continuator of the Chronicle of Lobbes, Sigebert of Gembloux, and Gerard, abbot of La Sauve-Majeure, it is certain that Heriger, abbot of Lobbes, composed a work *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. But since Gerard the abbot expressly calls it a letter, whereas no trace whatever of a letter is found in the Cellotian Anonymous, there is no reason why this little work should be attributed to Heriger.

Moreover, to the Gembloux codex, which displays the name of Heriger, we oppose a remarkable codex of the same age from Göttweig, in which, besides Ratramnus’s book *On the Body of the Lord*, there appears the little book of the Anonymous under the name of Gerbert, written very distinctly in red by the first hand.

Indeed, we have no doubt that learned men will rather adopt our opinion than Mabillon’s. Those who know Gerbert’s bold style and his intellect, steeped in dialectical and mathematical disciplines, could arrive at the same suspicion from the little work itself, even if no codex supported it.

This was also the reason why, following Gerbert’s little book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, we appended another work of his, *On the Rational and Reason*, from a six-hundred-year-old Tegernsee codex. Although the latter may seem slight in itself, it is nevertheless highly suitable for forming a judgment that the same author wrote both little works.

The style is the same in both, as are the brevity and confidence in disputation, the same skill in constructing dialectical figures, and so forth. When these features are joined with the testimony of the Göttweig codex, they scarcely leave room for doubt that the genuine author of the Cellotian little work was Gerbert—who in the tenth century paved his way to the Roman pontificate by his reputation for learning—and not Heriger, abbot of the monastery of Lobbes in Belgium.

[Col. 0179]

GERBERT, ON THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD. (G)*

[Col. 0179A] I. As a certain wise man said before us, whose opinion we approve although we do not know his name: “Observing the Apostle’s statement that ‘the natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God,’ we hesitate greatly, lest, living less spiritually, when we prepare answers concerning spiritual matters—answers concerning things we perhaps have not yet perceived—we fall upon a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.

“But again, when we direct our inward gaze toward him who said, ‘Open your mouth, and I will fill it’ (Ps. 80:11), while the integrity of faith remains intact, we are urged to respond concerning a subject about which it is fitting not to remain silent—namely, the mystery of the body and blood of the Lord.

“Some say that what is taken from the altar is the same as that which was born from the Virgin; others deny this and say that it is something else; while some, inspired by the devil, even blaspheme by saying that it is subject to excretion.

“Concerning these matters it would be dangerous to respond to anything, and rather we should close our ears, unless it were more dangerous that they had proposed such things. For this is like drawing butter or blood from the breasts instead of milk.

“‘Have you found honey?’ says Wisdom. ‘Eat as much as is sufficient’ (Prov. 25:16). And again: ‘Do not be an excessive investigator of majesty, lest you be overwhelmed by glory’ (ibid., 27).

“Let a place for answering be reserved for those who said that it is subject to excretion—something never before heard of—namely, Heribald, bishop of Auxerre, who proposed the matter disgracefully, and Rabanus of Mainz, who took it up more disgracefully and concluded it most disgracefully.

“But for those who have said that it is the same as that which was born from the Virgin, or that it is something else, let various statements of the holy Fathers be set forth. They appear different to these men, but they could be sufficient if they were understood fully and distinctly.

“I mean Paschasius Ratbert, abbot of Corbie, who, when asked—or perhaps challenged—wrote a little book on the same matter, useful enough, in nearly one hundred chapters. Having sprinkled it with much authority from many Fathers, he quotes in the name of St. Ambrose: ‘The flesh which is taken from the altar is plainly none other than that which was born of the Virgin Mary, suffered on the cross, rose from the tomb, and is still offered today for the life of the world.’”

[Col. 0179D] Against him Rabanus, in his letter to Abbot Egilo, and a certain Ratramnus, in a book composed for King Charles, argue sufficiently, saying that it is something else—whether by the testimony of Jerome, who says that the body of the Lord is spoken of in two ways, or by the authority of St. Augustine, who says that it is spoken of in three ways.

And because they contend that this is not found in Ambrose’s books in precisely those words, let us set forth not only his immutable statements, but also those of the blessed Augustine and Jerome and the others, exactly as they have been found. Thus, when these have been carefully examined, it may become clear to whom God, or through whom God, has deigned to open the truth: namely, that such great men do not disagree, that everyone in the Catholic Church ought to hold one and the same opinion, and that there is no schism.

But when we come to those who in our own time have not feared to serve these disputes, and who for this reason have deserved to define nothing worthy or have been able to satisfy posterity in what was to come, let us not hesitate to repeat the words of the blessed Hilary (*On the Trinity*, book VIII):

“‘One must not speak of the things of God according to human or worldly understanding; nor must perversity be extorted by force or by an imprudent proclamation of heavenly sayings into an alien and impious interpretation. Let us read what has been written, and let us understand what we have read; then we shall fulfill the duty of perfect faith.’”

These words are directed against those who think that Christ categorized foods when he said, “Everything that enters into the mouth,” and what follows; or against those who teach that whatever is said about the body of the Lord is said either in truth or in figure, and therefore in shadow. But more on these matters later. For now, let us set forth the statements of the holy Fathers as they stand.

II. Ambrose, in the book *On the Sacraments*:

“‘This food which you receive, this living bread which came down from heaven, supplies the substance of eternal life; and whoever eats this will not die forever. And it is the body of Christ.’

“Again: ‘It is therefore clear that the Virgin gave birth contrary to the order of nature, and that this which we consecrate is a body from the Virgin. Why do you seek the order of nature in the body of Christ, when the Lord Jesus himself was born from a virgin contrary to nature? It is truly the flesh of Christ that was crucified and buried; therefore it is truly the sacrament of that flesh.’

“Again: ‘Just as our Lord Jesus Christ is truly the Son of God—not as men are sons through grace, but as a Son from the substance of the Father—so too the flesh which we receive is true flesh, as he himself said, and the drink is true.’”

Pope Leo: “You ought to communicate at the sacred table in such a way that you have absolutely no doubt concerning the truth of Christ’s body and blood.”

Augustine: “Christ took earth from the earth, because flesh is from the earth, and he took flesh from Mary’s flesh. And because he walked in that very flesh, he gave us that flesh to eat for salvation.”

Basil: “O miracle! O benevolence of God toward us! He who sits above at the right hand of the Father is nevertheless held in human hands at the time of the sacrifice, and is handed over to those who desire to lick him and embrace him with blessing; and all this takes place before human eyes.”

Again he himself says: “When, he says, the priest has also invoked the Holy Spirit and has sacrificed that revered victim and then touched the common Lord,” and so forth.

Gregory: “Christ, rising from the dead, although he no longer dies and death will no longer rule over him, nevertheless, living immortally and incorruptibly in himself, is again sacrificed for us in the mystery of the sacred offering.”

These statements have been set down here so that perhaps through them the simplicity of Paschasius Ratbert may be excused from the charge for which Rabanus and Ratramnus appear chiefly to disparage him (the text has *loquentibus*, perhaps to be read *obloquentibus*, “detractors”; the codex reads *Ratmanno*): namely, because he said that the flesh taken from the altar is the same flesh that is born from the Virgin and that is still sacrificed daily for the salvation of the world.

Although nothing pleases and delights us more than whatever can be said more sublimely about this mystery, nevertheless, because his opponents assert the contrary—that it is not the same—we shall briefly set forth their position.

III. Jerome:

“‘The blood and flesh of Christ are understood in two ways: either as that spiritual and divine flesh of which he himself says, “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink”; or as the flesh which was crucified and the blood which was poured out by the soldier’s lance.’”

Augustine, writing that the body of Christ is spoken of in three ways—that is, the Church, which is Christ’s body and which we are, and the mystical body which is consecrated from the substance of bread and wine through the Holy Spirit—added the following:

“‘Moreover, that body which was born from the Virgin Mary, into which that body is transferred which hung on the cross, was buried in the tomb, rose from the dead, entered heaven, and, having become priest forever, intercedes for us daily—to him, if we communicate rightly, we direct our mind, so that from him and through him we may receive his body, his flesh, while he remains whole. This is truly that very flesh, and the fruit of that flesh, so that he may always remain the same and feed all who are in the body.’”

Fulgentius:

“‘Hold firmly and doubt in no way that God the Word himself, the only-begotten, having become flesh, offered himself for us as a sacrifice and offering to God for a pleasing aroma. To him, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, animals were sacrificed by patriarchs, prophets, and priests in the time of the Old Testament. And to him now—that is, in the time of the New Testament—the holy Catholic Church throughout the entire world does not cease to offer, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, with whom he has one divinity, the sacrifice of bread and wine in faith and holy love.

“‘In those carnal victims there was a sign of the flesh of Christ, which he himself, sinless, was to offer for our sins, and of the blood which he was to pour out for the remission of our sins. But in this sacrifice there is thanksgiving and remembrance of the flesh of Christ which he offered for us, and of the blood which that same God poured out for us.

“‘Of this the blessed Apostle Paul says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to rule the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood.”

“‘In those sacrifices, therefore, what was to be given to us was signified figuratively; but in this sacrifice what is now to be given to us is shown plainly.’”

Eusebius:

“‘Because Christ was about to remove from our eyes the body he had assumed and carry it among the stars, it was necessary that on this day he consecrate for us the sacrament of his body and blood, so that what had once been offered as the price might be continually honored through the mystery. Since the redemption of humanity was proceeding daily and without ceasing, the offering of redemption also had to be perpetual; that enduring victim had to live in our memory and always be present in grace.

“‘It is truly a unique and perfect sacrifice, to be judged by faith, not by appearance; not to be assessed by the sight of the outward man, but by the affection of the inward man. Hence the heavenly authority rightly confirms that “my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.”

“‘Let every ambiguity of unbelief therefore depart, since the one who is the author of the gift is himself also the witness of its truth.’”

IV. We could also set forth statements of other men, both ancient and modern, as well as statements of Ambrose himself that agree with these, if we did not think that these were sufficient—namely, that this may be called figurative and yet the body of Christ may truly be present.

But those who do not understand these things and cannot distinguish them clearly, and who instead introduce greater error into minds less capable of understanding, fail to attend to what Hilary said above: “One must not speak of the things of God according to human or worldly understanding.” They argue either that the matter is wholly figurative and that there is no truth in this mystery, or that, if there is truth, it is no longer a figure.

But just as Paschasius Radbertus usefully treats many other matters in the same book beyond human estimation, so he strongly confronts this sophism, saying: “A figure is not always a shadow, and by right this mystery can simultaneously be called both figure and truth.”

If anyone wishes to know this more fully, he can draw it from his volume, supported by complete authority. But we, “not being wise in high things, but consenting to the humble” (Rom. 12:16), should simply confess that it is a figure, insofar as bread and wine are seen outwardly; but that it is truth, insofar as the body and blood of Christ are truly believed to be within.

And, as a certain wise man said in our own time:

“Just as we believe all things in Christ to be true—true divinity and true humanity, the true Word and true flesh, true God and true man—so, in the mystery of his body and blood, which by the power of heavenly blessing and the divine Word is consecrated into that which it was not, let us hold nothing false, nothing frivolous, nothing unfaithful.”

But what are we, in our littleness, to judge concerning the disagreement of such great men, whose statements have been cited, though they agree in the eyes of those who understand them?

Perhaps almighty God, aware of our humility and concerned even more for the salvation of his faithful who do not impiously doubt, and for the healing of their hesitation, will deign to disclose the matter through the labor of our inquiry, so that the fruit of such great usefulness, which is contained in the same book, may not perish because of one word, and so that the authority of blessed Ambrose himself—whose books need an interpreter more than those of the others, since no Latin writer appears to have followed the Greeks so closely—may deservedly carry the palm.

### V. Cyril

“Therefore we necessarily add this as well: announcing the death, according to the flesh, of the only-begotten Son of God, that is, Jesus Christ, and likewise confessing his resurrection and ascension into heaven, we celebrate in the churches the bloodless service of sacrifice. Thus also we approach the mystical blessings and are sanctified, becoming participants in the sacred body and precious blood of Christ, and thereby made the redemption of us all—not receiving ordinary flesh (God forbid!), nor flesh such as that of sanctified men joined to the Word according to a unity of dignity, or as though it possessed a divine indwelling; but flesh truly life-giving and made the very flesh of the Word himself. For, since he naturally exists as Life, being God, because he is joined to his own flesh, he declared it to be life-giving. And therefore, although he says to us, ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood,’ we must not regard it as the flesh of an ordinary man from among us—for how could human flesh, according to its nature, be life-giving?—but as flesh truly made his own, since for our sake he became and was called the Son of Man.”

Great is the authority of so eminent a man, who said both that Christ’s flesh is truly life-giving and that it was made the very flesh of the Word, and that life exists naturally as God. By the authority, therefore, of this great man, every ambiguity is resolved which blessed Ambrose left implicit: namely, that the flesh of Christ which is taken from the altar is naturally the same flesh that was born of the Virgin. And for that reason, whether with Jerome it is said to be twofold, or with Augustine threefold, Christ’s body ought in particular to be said to be one, since it is naturally one.

Hence Augustine also says: “That we may take from him and through him, while he remains whole, we who are his body, his flesh.” How well the distinction is made! It is constructed in this way: “That we,” he says, “who are the body of Christ, that is, the Church, may take from him who was born of the Virgin Mary, from him—that is, his flesh, which is consecrated on the altar—while he remains whole.”
