But in order to demonstrate more certainly that blessed Cyril regarded this threefold distinction according to Augustine as specifically expressed but naturally one, he says: “Not as flesh such as that of sanctified men joined to the Word according to a unity of dignity, or as though it possessed a divine indwelling; but truly life-giving flesh, made the very flesh of the Word.”

For the Arians, who denied that the Father and the Son had one substance, asserted that what the Son himself says—“I and the Father are one” (John 10:30)—was to be understood as referring to harmony of will. Hilary, the true Lucifer of the Romans, refutes them more explicitly; and his argument is of great value for understanding what Cyril had said.

### VI. Hilary

*(On the Trinity, VIII)*

“I now ask those who introduce a united will between the Father and the Son: Is Christ in us today through the truth of nature, or through harmony of will? For if the Word truly became flesh, and if we truly receive the Word made flesh as food in the Lord’s meal, how can he not be considered to remain naturally in us? He who, when born as man, assumed the nature of our flesh, already inseparable from himself, and mingled the nature of his flesh with the nature of eternity under the sacrament of the flesh to be communicated to us.

“For thus we are all in God: because the Father is in Christ, and Christ is in us. Therefore, whoever denies that the Father is naturally in Christ must first deny that he himself is naturally in Christ, or that Christ is naturally in him; for the Father in Christ and Christ in us make us one in these realities.

“If, therefore, Christ truly assumed the flesh of our body, and if that man who was born of Mary is truly Christ, and if we truly receive under the mystery the flesh of his body, and through this become one—for the Father is in him and he is in us—how can unity of will be asserted, when the natural possession effected through the sacrament is itself the sacrament of perfect unity?

“For he himself says: ‘My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.’ No room for doubt has been left concerning the reality of the flesh and blood. For now, both by the Lord’s own declaration and by our faith, it is truly flesh and truly blood; and, once received and consumed, they bring about this result: that we are in Christ and Christ in us.

“Is this not truth? Let it plainly not be true for those who deny that Christ Jesus is true God. He himself, therefore, is in us through the flesh, and we are in him, while that which we are is with him in God.”

A little later he says:

“This, then, is the cause of our life: that we have Christ remaining in us bodily through the flesh, so that we may live through him under the condition by which he lives through the Father. If, therefore, we live naturally through him according to the flesh—that is, if we have obtained the nature of his flesh—how can he not have the Father naturally in himself according to the Spirit, since he himself lives through the Father?”

### VII.

Here we must see how he wished to prove, by means of what was indisputable to the heretics, what was doubtful. They doubted that the Father and the Son had one substance, because they tried to refer the statement “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30) to agreement of mind, so that the unity would be one of will and not of nature, just as “the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32).

But it was indisputable that the Word had truly become flesh. Nevertheless, because God, having been born as man, assumed the nature of our flesh inseparable from himself, and mingled the nature of his flesh with the nature of eternity under the sacrament of this flesh to be communicated to us, and because through this we become one body in Christ, therefore through this we are all one in God the Father and the Son, since the Father is proved to be in Christ and Christ in us, let us examine the distinction.

Christ assumed the nature of our flesh when he came forth as man, born of the Virgin. Behold the flesh from the Virgin! Under the sacrament of flesh to be communicated, behold what is taken from the altar! He united us to the nature of eternity. Behold our body, which is the Church!

I believe that it is now clear what blessed Ambrose had said: that the word “naturally” must finally be understood implicitly. Augustine, Jerome, and Fulgentius imply the word “specifically.”

And because the practice of justice is piety, or because wisdom is the fruit of piety, at times certain simple and uneducated people, yet fervent in good works and piety, advance better through pure faith than through affected speech. Those elders in the *Life of the Fathers* compelled another elder, equally old and a holy man but doubtful concerning this mystery, to believe—not by dialectical arguments but by simple words and prayer—that what we take from the altar is naturally the Lord’s body, and is truly so, not figuratively.

Behold how much faith accomplishes where speech fails!

And we ourselves, before being instructed by the authority of such great men—Cyril and Hilary, I mean—were once considering how to resolve the disagreement of the saints mentioned above, which seemed so to later writers, by means of some dialectical argument.

For that art which divides genera into species and resolves species into genera was not made by human contrivance; rather, it exists in the nature of things, established by the Author of all arts, which are true arts, discovered by the wise and employed for the benefit of diligent investigation of things, as it is written: “Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds” (Genesis 1:24).

But first it occurred to us to introduce some middle term of arithmetic, according to one of the proportionalities of numbers which we contemplate in the ratios and differences of terms. Yet this too was not made by human contrivance, because in it there is the steadfast wisdom of ineffable and divine power, to which it is said: “You have ordered all things by measure and number and weight” (Wisdom 11:20).

Let two highest terms be established, with a middle term between them, differing by equal differences but proportionally. In the same way, let two highest terms again be established—a predicate and a subject—with a subordinate middle term between them, so that just as the first is predicated of the middle, so the middle is predicated of the last, and consequently the first of the last.

Therefore, do not doubt that the last is contained in the first—that is, that the first is predicated of the last—since, if the last is contained in the middle and the middle in the first, then most certainly the last is contained in the first.

By this likeness, too, the structure of the universe—that is, the making of the world—has been consolidated: namely, the two extremes, fire and earth, have been indissolubly bound together by the two middle elements, air and water.

These are likenesses which, not in their entirety but in part, like many others in the divine Scriptures, are applied according to Augustine to the threefold character of the Lord’s body. For in these likenesses a greater and a lesser term, a predicate and a subject, are found. But in the sacrament of the Lord’s body, what is there of the human in relation to the divine? Nothing greater or lesser is found, nor predicate and subject.

For there is no difference where there is one thing: there are not two or three bodies, but one. “One bread,” says the Apostle, “we, though many, are one body in Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:17). And again: “The two shall be one flesh” (1 Corinthians 6:16). “This mystery,” says the Apostle, “is great; but I speak with reference to Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5:32)—that is, in us, who are the body of Christ, which is the Church, and in the flesh of Christ, which was born of the Virgin Mary. Between these, or between which, stands the middle element that benefits both: the flesh taken from the altar, worthily received.

### VIII.

David signified this threefold but united reality in the books of Kings, where he was carried in his own hands. No one can literally be carried in his own hands. But the true David, that is, Christ, was carried in his own hands when, reclining at supper with the whole body that had been born of the Virgin—the body that was to be laid in death, to rise again, and nevertheless, glorified, to be borne up into heaven and placed at the right hand of the Father—he offered to his disciples for communion the body that we now take from the altar, in his hands, that is, made naturally related and conformed to his true body, and offered to his disciples, that is, to his body, which is us, or the Church.

“For no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13). But flesh ascended which had not descended, since it had already been united to the Godhead.

Hence blessed Mary deserved to become not only *Christotokos* (Χριστοτόκος), “Mother of Christ,” but also *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος), “Mother of God.”

Therefore this must be understood as follows: No one ascended into heaven with flesh except the one who descended with divinity.

For this reason he became a participant in our humanity by assuming our flesh from the Virgin: so that he might unite us—namely, the Church—who had become participants in his divinity, to his body, taken from the Virgin, with the Eucharist, which is taken from the altar, mediating and confirming the union.

For he himself transformed the body of his humility.

Therefore, just as the Father is naturally in the Son through divinity, and just as the Son is naturally in us according to the assumption of humanity, and just as we are naturally in him through the union of flesh, while that which we are is with him in God, so he mingled the nature of his flesh with the nature of eternity under the sacrament of the flesh to be communicated to us.

As Christ himself says: “That they all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, so that they too may be in us” (John 17:21). And again: “That they may be one, just as we are one, I in them and you in me” (John 17:22).

Behold the evident and manifest distinction previously set forth from the words of Christ our Lord himself!

And in order that the distinction of this sacrifice too may shine forth more clearly, let us present it figuratively. It may be constructed as follows:

Christ, imperishable, incapable of being eaten. The Eucharist, to be taken, to be eaten, given from him. The Church, taking and eating his body, receives what was given by him.

Unless it is constructed in this way, someone might think that the word is in the accusative case. But we say that *Ecclesia* is nominative, since it is his body.

Christ therefore assumed our flesh, not phantom flesh but natural flesh. Therefore our flesh too is natural, from which that flesh was taken. But that flesh which unites both and makes them naturally related is itself also naturally related.

Yet, as a certain wise man says, this does not mean that there are several fleshes or bodies, just as there are not many sacrifices, although it is offered by many people in different places and at different times. For the divinity of the Word of God, which is one, fills all things and is wholly everywhere; it makes the sacrifices not many but one, although it is offered by many, and makes the body of Christ one with that body which he received in the Virgin’s womb.

“How watchfully, how openly,” he says, “one body of Christ is made with that which he received from the Virgin’s womb!”

For it must truly and without hesitation be believed that at the very hour of the offering, at the priest’s prayer, heaven is opened, and that which is the altar itself—Christ, both priest and victim—is carried upward by angelic ministry and becomes one through contact with it.

“O what kind of hands,” as Saint Basil says, “ought the priest to have, ministers of such great things, hands which repeatedly touch the common Lord, brought back again by angelic service!”

But let Paschasius Radbertus now be sufficiently excused, and let his book be defended for the benefit of many. He erred in this one respect only: in treating the statement of blessed Ambrose, he expressed not word for word but sense for sense.

As for the further objection that he said, “Christ suffers as many times as Masses happen to be celebrated daily everywhere,” I certainly have not found this in his book. Augustine and the others say that Christ remains whole. Saint Andrew likewise says: “The Lamb remains whole and alive in his kingdom.” Blessed Peter says: “Christ died once for our sins” (1 Peter 3:18). And Paul says: “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more” (Romans 6:9). Nearly the entire text of the Epistle to the Hebrews says the same thing.

### IX.

Now we must answer the absurdities of those who think that matters concerning God should be discussed according to human or worldly understanding.

Our Lord was speaking not about spiritual food but about bodily food when he said: “Everything that enters the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled into the latrine” (Matthew 15:17).

But in all the Scriptures it is not always to be understood with the strict precision of a categorical syllogism. For although, as the same Lord says, evil thoughts come out of the heart (Matthew 15:19), surely good thoughts cannot also come out?

The heretics calumniated the Lord on the basis of this saying, claiming that he was ignorant of natural science. Natural science, they say, works as follows: the fiery power, whose seat is in the heart, distributes the subtle vapor of food and drink through hidden pores into the various parts of the body, while separating the coarse matter into the latrine.

And we often see not only the sick but also the healthy reject through vomiting what they have taken in through the mouth, and some have lived for long periods without digestion [perhaps supply: “life”]. Even though what they had taken was expelled through nausea of the stomach, a subtler juice nevertheless spread through the limbs as far as the nails.

Therefore one must say either that the Lord did not speak with strict precision, or that every bodily channel through which the subtle vapor of food spreads was called a latrine—and this so that no heretic may chatter.

Furthermore, because we truly believe that not only our soul but also our flesh is renewed by this mystery—for he assumed the whole human being who healed the whole human being on the Sabbath—flesh is spiritually transformed into flesh, so that Christ’s substance may be found in our flesh, just as he is established to have assumed our substance into his divinity.

Thus whoever eats his flesh and drinks his blood may live through the soul both now and forever, and flesh, raised from the dust of the earth, may be made alive on the last day.

Therefore, just as by the powerful efficacy of the one who causes this, the ordinary bread that we eat daily, although white, is changed within us into the color of blood or into another flowing liquid, so by his power the flesh and blood of Christ, once received, ought to be preserved—not as harmful and superfluous humors, but conformed to the flesh that is truly to be raised again.

And because everything we have said was not taken from ourselves, let us also state what a certain wise man has determined concerning this matter:

“We know that this sacrament must in every respect be distinguished from ordinary foods by its mystery and reverence, foods which are taken by natural and necessary use. Thus all have explained what the Apostle said: ‘Not discerning’ the body of Christ—that is, not distinguishing it from other foods, or failing to consider its excellence—for it is one and the same thing.”

For he does not reverence its excellence if he says that it is subject to the latrine just like other foods.

Nevertheless, insofar as eating and drinking are concerned, it is received in the same manner: it passes through the mouth and is sent into the stomach.

What the Lord wished to accomplish with his mystery, we know to be known only to his will. We know that it can be consumed by spiritual power; we know also that it can be preserved in imperishable perpetuity, because whatever Christ has chosen among these possibilities, he accomplishes through his sacrament.

Yet far be it that so great a mystery should become subject to the latrine! For if perhaps the order of nature is preserved, the mystery, which is perceived by faith alone, would be humbled.

If body preserves its order in body, the mystery established by the sacrament of divinity is not violated; nor does the spirit lose what it has received spiritually, with complete faith, in a bodily reality.

### X.

But let us now conclude by the firm syllogism we proposed above.

We said that the Lord spoke not of spiritual foods but of bodily foods: “Everything that enters the mouth,” and so forth.

There is an external human being who is corrupted, and there is also an inner human being who is renewed. The body of Christ is spiritual nourishment, belonging rather to the inner human being, for whom digestion is not predicated.

But if it belongs to the external human being, it is pious and salutary to believe that it is diffused through the limbs, for the benefit of those who are to be raised in the general resurrection.

It is therefore clear that it is not subject to the latrine.

## SELECTED AUTHENTIC MATERIALS FROM THE COUNCIL OF BASLE

*(Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims, vol. I, p. 635.)*

[Col. 0189]

### THE COUNCIL OF SAINT-BASLE

The city of Laon, in which Arnulf had taken refuge with Charles of Lorraine, was delivered to Hugh Capet by the bishop Adalbero-Ascelin. Charles and Arnulf were sent as prisoners to Orléans. The king summoned a council to have the archbishop judged. This assembly met in June 991 at the abbey of Saint-Basle [Note: The abbey of Saint-Basle, at Verzy near Reims, was destroyed after the suppression of religious orders in France.], near Reims [Note: We had considered reproducing verbatim the acts of this council, drafted by Gerbert. But the more one reads these acts, the more suspicious they appear. First, the writer is the man who took the place of the deposed prelate and who had an interest in presenting the council’s decisions in a favorable light. Moreover, this writer admits in his preface that he made additions and suppressions in the original acts and that he commented upon and paraphrased the speeches, etc.; this does not speak in favor of his fidelity. In addition, the only editions we possess of this work of Gerbert were issued by heretics: the continuators of Magdeburg and the heirs of A. Wechel; and these editors are not beyond suspicion of interpolation. We shall therefore content ourselves with a simple analysis.].

Two archbishops were present: Seguin of Sens and Dacbert of Bourges; and eleven bishops: Guy of Soissons, Adalbero of Laon, Herveus of Beauvais, Gotesman of Amiens, Ratbod of Noyon, Odo of Senlis, Walter of Autun, Bruno of Langres, Milo of Mâcon, Arnulf of Orléans, and Herbert of Auxerre, along with a large number of abbots. Arnulf, taken from prison, was brought forward to be judged by the council.

The presidency was assigned to the archbishop of Sens, the senior of the metropolitans. Arnulf of Orléans was appointed prosecutor. After some preliminary proceedings, the prosecutor presented the case. The president declared that, in accordance with the canons [Note: Council of Toledo, in the year 633, canon 31.], he would proceed to judgment only if it were promised that the accused’s life would be spared if he were convicted. The trial then began.

Against Arnulf they produced the oath of fidelity that he had sworn; the testimony of the priest Adalger, who stated that he had opened the gates of Reims only on the archbishop’s orders; and the sentence of excommunication that Arnulf had pronounced against the perpetrators of the plundering, which, in light of his conduct, was now regarded merely as a stratagem to conceal his treachery.

The defenders—John, head of the school at Auxerre; Roaulhe, abbot of Senones; and Abbo, abbot of Fleury—argued in Arnulf’s favor:

1. that he could not answer, and consequently could not be judged, before being restored to his see;
2. that the canonical admonitions had to be made;
3. that the case had to be notified to the Holy See;
4. that the accusers and the accused had to appear before a larger council.

To these defenses it was answered that the accusers were persons of such character that they could not be challenged; that Arnulf had been summoned several times and had always refused to appear; that he could be judged without being restored, since this had been done in the case of Ebbo of Reims and Hildeman of Beauvais; and finally that the pope had been consulted, with the letters of the king and the bishops produced as evidence.

The prosecutor sought to establish the council’s competence in a highly immoderate denunciation of the Roman court [Note: This speech alone betrays the unfaithfulness of the account. Some authors have tried to see in this attack the principles of the Gallican Church; the latter strongly rejects such an accusation. No Catholic could ever have uttered what is here placed in the mouth of a bishop, and Gerbert himself, however interested he may have been in exaggerating the faults of the Roman court, could not have written the heretical principles with which this speech is filled. Certainly the whole Church lamented the scandals caused by certain pontiffs, but it never occurred to any Catholic to say that a vicious pope loses his authority and no longer possesses the prerogatives of Saint Peter. This doctrine has too clearly the character of Wyclif and his like not to reveal the source from which it proceeds.].

Arnulf was then brought in and took his place among the bishops. The prosecutor reproached him for disloyalty to the king. The archbishop tried to deny the charge and to accuse the witnesses testifying against him of imposture.

At the proposal of several abbots, he withdrew to a separate place to confer with certain prelates whom he chose as advisers: the archbishop of Sens and the bishops of Orléans, Langres, and Amiens. There, kneeling before them, he confessed himself guilty. This confession was repeated in the presence of the bishops and abbots.

Such was the first session.

The following day they assembled again. The minds of those present were more favorably disposed toward Arnulf: some were moved by his birth and youth; others saw in his person the entire episcopal body compromised. Everything seemed to promise a favorable sentence.

But the two kings, Hugh and Robert, came to the council and had an account given to them of what had been done. Arnulf was brought before them. Intimidated by their presence, he answered the questions put to him only with embarrassment and finally confirmed his confessions of the previous day.

“Prostrate yourself, then,” said the bishop of Orléans to him; “prostrate yourself before your masters, whom you have offended.”

Arnulf prostrated himself with his arms extended in the form of a cross and begged for his life with groans that drew tears from the eyes of all those present. The archbishop of Bourges threw himself at the king’s feet and asked for mercy.

Hugh allowed himself to be moved, on condition that the accused remain in his custody. Then the bishops proceeded to his deposition. He was stripped of the insignia of his rank and made to subscribe to an act of abdication copied from that of Ebbo [Note: We do not cite this document, which reproduces Ebbo’s act of resignation.]. After he had signed it, they repeated to him what had likewise been said to Ebbo: “According to your profession and your subscription, cease from office” [Note: It is true that Arnulf had failed in the fidelity he had promised Hugh Capet in order to embrace the party of legitimacy; but such a fault was quite excusable in a prelate who himself belonged to the deposed family. The severity of the sentence can therefore be attributed only to the king’s influence; and the assembly of Saint-Basle should be regarded as a political faction rather than as a true council.].

Adalger wished to appeal to the royal clemency and to place upon his archbishop the blame of which he had been the instrument and instigator. The bishops indignantly reproached him for having ruined Arnulf by his counsel. He was given only the choice between deposition and perpetual excommunication. He chose deposition and was reduced to lay communion.

Finally, the council again pronounced excommunication against the perpetrators of the plundering who had not yet given satisfaction [Note: We believe it appropriate to set alongside Gerbert’s account, which we have analyzed, the narrative of the continuator of Aimoin concerning the same council:

“In those days there was in the city of Reims an archbishop, a good and modest man, the brother [son] of King Lothair by a concubine, named Arnulf. King Hugh, however, envied him, wishing to destroy the offspring of King Lothair. He therefore assembled a synod in the city of Reims and invited to that place the archbishop of the city of Sens, named Seguin, with his suffragans. In that council the same Hugh, by the deceit of his nephew [uncle], whom he held in prison, caused Lord Arnulf, archbishop of Reims, to be degraded, saying that one born of a concubine ought not to be a bishop.

“In his place he caused Lord Gerbert, a monk and philosopher, to be consecrated. This Gerbert was the teacher of King Robert, the son of this Hugh, and of Lord Leotheric, archbishop and venerable successor of Seguin. But he had Arnulf committed to custody in the city of Orléans.

“The venerable archbishop Seguin did not consent either to Arnulf’s degradation or to Gerbert’s ordination; but the king’s command pressed upon him. The other bishops, though unwilling, nevertheless degraded Arnulf and ordained Gerbert out of fear of the king. Seguin, however, fearing God more than an earthly king, refused to consent to the king’s wickedness and instead rebuked the king as much as he could. For this reason the king’s anger against him blazed up.

“With great disgrace he ordered Arnulf to be expelled from the church of Blessed Mary the Virgin at Reims and, bound in this manner, to be thrust into prison.”]

Once Arnulf had been deposed, another archbishop had to be elected. Hugh Capet caused the choice to fall upon Gerbert, who had been his son’s tutor. An act of election of the new prelate was drawn up, and he immediately made his profession of faith.

[Col. 0191]

## ACT OF THE ELECTION OF GERBERT

[Col. 0191A]

“Beloved brothers, the judgments of God are always just, though sometimes hidden. For behold: after the death of blessed Adalbero, we placed over ourselves and over the Church of Reims a man sprung from royal stock, driven by the cry of the multitude, Scripture saying, ‘The voice of the people is the voice of God,’ and following the institutions of the holy canons, which seek the desire and votes of clergy and people in the election of a bishop.

“The vision of our mind was darkened because we followed the letter incautiously and investigated too little the harmonious judgment of the divine Scriptures. For the voice of the people crying, ‘Crucify, crucify,’ was not the voice of God.

“Therefore not every voice of the people is the voice of God, nor are all the votes and desires of clergy and people to be sought in the election of a bishop, but only those of the simple and incorrupt—that is, those not at all enticed by hope of gain.

“The statements of the Fathers must be expounded. ‘It is not permitted,’ he says, ‘for the crowds to make the election of those who are called to the priesthood; rather, the judgment must belong to the bishops, so that they themselves may test the one who is to be ordained, whether he has been instructed in speech, faith, and episcopal conduct.’”

[Col. 0192A]

“We, therefore, the bishops of the diocese of Reims, in accordance with these constitutions of the Fathers, with the favor and concurrence of both our princes, the august Hugh and the most excellent King Robert, and also with the assent of those in the clergy and people who belong to God, elect for ourselves as archbishop the abbot Gerbert, mature in age, prudent by nature, teachable, affable, and merciful.

“We do not prefer to him wandering youth, self-exalting ambition, or one who administers everything rashly; indeed, we cannot patiently endure hearing that such men should be placed over us, men whose wisdom and counsel we know cannot administer ecclesiastical and civil law.

“Since this must be examined in every bishop, it must especially be examined in him who presides over the others, the metropolitan.

“We therefore elect this Gerbert, who . . . . . was. We have known his life and conduct from childhood; we have experienced his zeal in divine and human affairs; we seek to be formed by his counsel and teaching. By subscribing to his election, we confirm, establish, and strengthen it with the common deliberation of all good men.”

[Col. 0191]

## GERBERT’S PROFESSION OF FAITH

[Note: For Gerbert’s text, see the Magdeburg Centuries and the *Administrative Archives of the City of Reims*, by M. Varin, vol. I, p. 100. For the criticism, see Longueval’s *History of the Gallican Church*, book 19, and Marchetti’s criticism of Fleury, vol. I, p. 177.]

[Col. 0191B]

“I, Gerbert, by the prevenient grace of God soon to become archbishop of Reims, affirm above all the articles of faith in simple words: I confirm that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. I proclaim the whole Godhead in the Trinity to be coessential, consubstantial, coeternal, and omnipotent. I profess each person in the Trinity to be true God, and all three persons to be one God.

“I believe that the divine Incarnation occurred not in the Father nor in the Holy Spirit but in the Son alone: he who was the Son of God the Father in divinity himself became the son of his mother in humanity, true God from the Father and true man from his mother. Having flesh from his mother’s womb and a rational human soul, he is simultaneously both natures—that is, man and God—in one person, one Son, one Christ, one Lord.

“I confess him, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, to be both the author and the Lord and governor of all creatures that exist; to have suffered with true suffering of the flesh; to have died with the true death of his body; to have risen with the true resurrection of his flesh and the true [lacuna] of his soul, in which he will come to judge the living and the dead.

“I believe that the same one is the author, Lord, and God of the New and Old Testaments. I believe that the devil became evil not by creation but by choice. I believe in the resurrection of this flesh that we bear, and not of another.

[Col. 0194A]

“I believe that judgment will come and that each person will receive punishments or rewards for the things he has done. I do not forbid marriage; I do not condemn second marriages; I do not censure the eating of meat; I confess that the reconciled penitent ought to be admitted to communion.

“I believe that in baptism all sins are forgiven, both original sin contracted and those committed by the will; and I confess that no one can be saved outside the Catholic Church.

“I confirm the four holy synods which the universal mother Church confirms.”

[Note: Gerbert, letters 25 and 26 bis; Labbe, vol. IX, col. 739; Hardouin, vol. VI, part I, col. 724; Marlot, vol. II, p. 49, etc.]

[Col. 0193]

## SELECTED MATERIALS FROM THE COUNCIL OF REIMS

*(Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims, vol. I, p. 641.)*

[NOTE.]

In 993 Gerbert assembled the bishops of the province in council in order to condemn Herbert III, count of Vermandois, and other lords who were plundering the property of the Church. The council addressed the following admonition to the guilty parties:

### MONITORY LETTER

Gerbert and all the bishops of the diocese of Reims to the perpetrators of the same offenses.

[Col. 0193B] Gerbert, by the grace of God bishop of Reims; Guido of Soissons; Adalbero of Laon; Ratbod of Noyon; Rotard of Cambrai; Odo of Senlis; Fulco of Amiens; Framericus of Thérouanne; Heriveus of Beauvais—bishops through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

To you, Gerbert [Note: [Col. 0193C] Gerbert, Herbert, count of Vermandois.], and to the invaders, executioners, and tyrants named below: the long-suffering patience of priests has endured the raging fury of your madness, and still awaits you with forbearance. How long, then, will your insanity oppose our sound understanding? You inflict devastation upon the clergy; you do not cease your plundering of the clergy, monks, and poor. Therefore we, all the bishops of the diocese of Reims, summon your conscience and invite you to make satisfaction, granting you a period for repentance until the coming Kalends. Then we shall either recognize you as fruitful branches of the Church, or cut you off from God’s field like useless wood with the sword of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0194C] Gerbert, letter 40, twice; Labbe, vol. IX, col. 740; Hardouin, vol. VI, part I, col. 725; Marlot, vol. II, p. 49, etc.].

[Col. 0193]

EXCERPTS FROM THE COUNCIL OF MOUZON.

[NOTE.]

Leo, abbot of Saint Boniface in Rome, was sent to France by the pope as legate, to settle the affair of Arnulf. A council was announced at Nouzon for June 993; only four bishops attended, and even they were not from France. They were Liudulf, archbishop of Trier; Aimon of Verdun; Notger of Liège; and Sigefroi of Münster. Gerbert, summoned to the council, sat facing the bishops to give an account of his ordination. The bishop of Verdun presented the facts in a speech delivered in the vernacular, so that the laypeople might understand it. He then read aloud a letter from the pope addressed to the metropolitans of Gaul concerning this affair. Gerbert himself delivered his defense and submitted it in writing to the legate. After the council’s deliberation, Gerbert was ordered to abstain from every function and to remain under suspension until the next council, scheduled to be held at Reims in the following July. Gerbert wished to protest; but, following the representations of the archbishop of Trier, he consented to abstain from celebrating Mass.

GERBERT’S SPEECH.

[Col. 0193C] Most reverend fathers, I have always kept this day before my eyes and directed my hope and desire toward it, from the time when, warned by my brothers, I undertook this burden of the priesthood, not without danger to my life. The salvation of the perishing people mattered greatly to me, and so did your authority, [Col. 0194C] by which I believed I would be kept safe. I remembered your past kindnesses and your gentle, approachable goodwill, which I had often enjoyed with great praise. But suddenly, an adverse report suggested that you were offended and labored to attribute blame to what had plainly been prepared with great courage among others. I confess that I was horrified, and because of your indignation I put aside even the swords I had previously feared. Now, since divine favor has brought before me those to whom I have always entrusted my salvation, I shall briefly set forth my innocence and explain by what counsel I was placed over the city of Reims.

After the death of the blessed Emperor Otto, I had resolved not to leave the service of my father Adalbero. Yet, without my knowledge, he selected me beforehand for the priesthood, and when he departed to the Lord, he designated me before illustrious men as the future pastor of the church. But simoniacal heresy, finding me standing upon the firmness of a rock, thrust me aside and preferred Arnulf. I nevertheless offered him a loyal obedience beyond what was proper, [Col. 0195B] until I openly recognized, through many witnesses and through myself, that he had apostatized. Then, having issued a letter of repudiation, I abandoned him and all his apostates—not, as my rivals say, in the hope or expectation of obtaining his dignity, but terrified by the monstrous works of the devil concealed in human form. I abandoned him, I say, not for that reason, but lest I incur the prophetic condemnation: “You give help to the wicked and join friendship with those who hate me, and therefore you deserve the wrath of the Lord” (1 Chronicles 19).

Then, after the ecclesiastical sanctions had been carried out over a long period and the peremptory law had been completed, when nothing remained except that he should be restrained by the prince’s judicial authority and removed from the principal [Col. 0195C] see as a seditious and rebellious man, I was again summoned and admonished by my brothers and by the chief men of the kingdom, according to the law of the African council, to take charge of the people who had been divided and torn apart, once the apostate had been excluded. I delayed this for a long time and afterward consented with less than full willingness, since I understood in every way what kinds of torments would accompany me. This is the simplicity of my conduct, this the purity of my innocence; before the Lord and before you priests, my conscience is clean in all these matters.

But behold, the accuser confronts me from the opposite side and, by introducing novel expressions to increase resentment, cries out: “You betrayed your lord, handed him over to prison, seized his bride, and invaded his see.” Did I betray a lord whose servant I had never been, to whom I had never rendered any kind of oath [Col. 0195D] (sic)? If I served him for a time, this was done at the command of my father Adalbero, who ordered me to remain in the church of Reims until I could discern the conduct and actions worthy of a bishop consecrated there. While I waited for this, I became the spoil of enemies, and the violent hand of plunderers took away what your generosity and the liberality of great leaders had bestowed in an illustrious and distinguished manner; they grieved that I had been torn away from their swords almost naked. Finally, after I abandoned that apostate, I did not follow his ways or journeys, nor did I communicate with him in any manner. How, then, did I betray him, when I did not know where he was at that time? Nor did I hand him over to prison, for only recently, in the presence of faithful witnesses, I confronted my senior so that, on my account, he should not be held in custody even for a moment [Col. 0196A]. If your authority depended upon me, Arnulf would become so insignificant that he could scarcely harm me. But if your contrary judgment—God forbid!—were to decree it, what would it matter to me whether Arnulf or another were established as bishop of Reims?

As for the seized bride and the invaded see, what is said is ridiculous. First, I say that she was never his bride: instead of making the lawful gift of spiritual dowry, he stripped her of the benefits previously bestowed, abused her, and tore her apart. He had not yet been marked with the priestly ring, and already the agents of Simon had ravaged everything that appeared to belong to the marked bride. I say further: even if it were granted that she had in some way been his bride, she ceased to be so after he prostituted her to his plunderers—polluted, violated, and, so to speak, adulterated [Col. 0196B]. Did I therefore seize from him either a bride whom he never possessed or one whom he lost through his own crime?

How could I, a newcomer and stranger, relying on the resources of no one, invade a see filled with a multitude of peoples? But perhaps the apostolic see is being brought against us, as though this supreme matter had been examined either without consulting it, through ignorance, or in defiance. Certainly nothing was done, nor was anything to be done, that was not reported to the apostolic see; its judgment was awaited for eighteen months. But when no counsel could be obtained from human beings, recourse was had to the supreme utterance of the Son of God: “If your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it away from you” (Matthew 5). And he decrees that a sinful brother who has been admonished before witnesses and before the Church, but does not obey, is to be treated as a pagan and a tax collector.

Arnulf was therefore summoned and admonished by letters and legates of the bishops of Gaul to desist from the fury he had begun and, if he could, to clear himself by some means of the crime of treason. Since he despised salutary warnings, he was treated as a pagan and a tax collector. Yet he was not thereby judged as a pagan, out of reverence for the apostolic see and the privileges of the sacred priesthood; rather, since the sentence of condemnation had been pronounced by him against himself, it was judged that this was the only praiseworthy thing he had done throughout his life. For if, when he condemned himself, the bishops were to absolve him, they would incur the penalty of his crime.

“If all priests and the world,” says Pope Leo the Great [Col. 0196D], “agree with those who are to be condemned” (sic), “condemnation involves those who consent; agreement does not absolve them from transgression.” For God, who destroyed the sinful world by a universal flood, made this clear to all.” And Pope Gelasius says: “An error once condemned together with its author carries its own execration and punishment into anyone who becomes a participant in its wicked communion.”

Thus, after he had been excluded from the church of Reims, this priestly burden was imposed upon me by my brothers, the bishops of Gaul, under an appeal to the divine name. I resisted and greatly feared what I had suffered and was still suffering. If, perhaps, anything was done contrary to the sacred laws, it was not malice but the necessity of the time that caused it. Otherwise, in a time of war, to observe every right and everything lawful—what is that other than to lose one’s country and bring about its destruction? The laws are silent amid arms, and at this time that savage beast Odo abused them so completely that he seized the most reverend priests of God as though they were worthless slaves, did not even spare the most sacred altars, and blocked the public supply routes.

I return to myself, most reverend fathers. For the salvation of the perishing people and the care of the entire commonwealth, furious death has descended upon me with all its forces. [Col. 0198A] On one side there is dreadful poverty: armed hands seize the granaries and storehouses; on the other, the strong sword; within, fear has made both days and nights sleepless. Only your authority has been awaited as a remedy for such great evils. It is believed to possess such power that it can bring assistance not only to Reims but also to the whole church of the Gauls, desolated and almost reduced to nothing. This we await with divine favor, and we all pray together that it may come to pass [Note: [Col. 0197D] Labbe, vol. IX, col. 747; Hardouin, vol. VI, part I, col. 733; Marlot, vol. II, p. 54.].

[Col. 0197]

COUNCIL OF RAVENNA HELD BY GERBERT, ARCHBISHOP, IN THE YEAR 997, CONCERNING VARIOUS MATTERS PERTAINING TO ECCLESIASTICAL DISCIPLINE [Note: [Col. 0197D] Rubeus says that Emperor Otto attended this synod, Histories, book V; but these acts prove that assertion false. The synod at Ravenna which Rivesius reports in his History of the Councils as having been held in this same year under Gerbert’s presidency, at which he says that Hugh, abbot of Farfa, who had entered unjustly [Col. 0198D] and simoniacally, performed penance, and that Arnulf of Milan was deprived of the papacy, leaves no trace of itself in this year. Nor was there then any Arnulf who was archbishop of Milan and could have been deprived of the papacy. For the first Arnulf died in 975, while the second Arnulf did not assume the archbishopric until 999. Gabriel COSSART.].

(From Labbe, Councils, vol. IX, p. 769.)

[Col. 0197B] With our Lord Jesus Christ reigning forever, in the time of the pious Caesar Otto III, in the second year of his empire, indiction 11, beneath the image of the Savior, inside the doors of the greater church of Ravenna, Gerbert, prelate of that church, seated with several bishops and priests of the aforesaid church, with the deacons and the entire clergy standing by, said:

I.

“In the holy Church of Ravenna, which divine providence has wished me to govern, a highly reprehensible custom has arisen for some time: the subdeacon sells to the bishops themselves, at the time of their consecration, the body of the Lord, which they call the formed host; and he sells the chrism annually to the archpriests of your parish. In these practices the sale of the Son of God and the sale of the Holy Spirit are evident. Therefore, by the present decree I establish that henceforth this shall no longer occur in this see and in all matters belonging to us.” All approved this decree as they established it. And he said: “If anyone should dare to attempt anything contrary to this decree, let him be anathema.” And they all replied: “Amen.”

II.

“We also establish that, annually, on the feast of Saint Vitalis, all the archpriests belonging to us shall, out of respect for the see, pay our subdeacons an annual census of two solidi; and whoever grants [this] by way of a census shall suffer punishment at the discretion of the leading men of this Church.” This was approved by everyone.

III.

[Col. 0197D] “Although it was established in ancient times that no bishop should receive another bishop’s cleric without a letter from that bishop directing him to do so, or dedicate a church [f. missing: ‘dedicate’] in another’s diocese, whether for money received or promised; nor should he promote [f. missing: ‘promote’] someone whom he does not find suitable for office, or whom immature age or crime excludes; nor someone whom ignorance disqualifies, whom the laws condemn for infamy, or whom bodily weakness or mutilation prevents; nor someone marked by degraded offices or dishonorable ministries; nor someone rejected by an appetite for shameful profit; nor anyone prohibited by the laws; nor any of those called neophytes, bigamists, curials, or laymen, or any of those restricted by the canons and laws—we therefore do not doubt that it is fitting for us, by this present council, to uphold and confirm the sanctions of the ancient Fathers.

“No one among us shall presume to dedicate a church or even an oratory in another’s diocese [Col. 0198C] without the permission and consent of the bishop to whom that diocese belongs. Nor shall anyone presume to receive, promote, or retain persons from another diocese or parish without canonical letters, in the form which the Council of Nicaea, assembled in Bithynia, decreed should be read according to Latin custom. No one shall admit anyone to sacred orders unless age, life, learning, conduct, canonical authority, and legal standing commend him.

“So that this sanction may remain firm in every respect, and so that such things may not be granted to the unworthy, we bind ourselves under the obligation of anathema, as well as our successors, the bishops who should presume to act contrary to these decrees. And if anyone of sacred order receives anything for the burial of the dead—except what may perhaps have been freely contributed to the Church by the friends or relatives of the deceased—let them be held subject to this curse.”

[Col. 0199A] Everyone approved together, acclaiming that it pleased them, and they shouted: “Let it be done, let it be done.”

These acts were promulgated in the year 997 of the Lord’s incarnation, on the Kalends of May, indiction 2, under the most merciful rule of the aforementioned prince Otto, specifically the third. The bishops who were present and the cardinal priests of the Church of Ravenna subscribed and confirmed them.

G. A. R. Ubertus of Livy. Albardus of Sarzana. [Col. 0200A] John of Bologna. Raimbald of Comacchio. Hildeprand of Faenza. George of Comacchio. George of Cesena. Leo of Ficodens. Teupert of Pupilium. Christopher and Guinizo, envoys of the holy Church of Parma. John, John, and Vannius, priests. Anastasius, Deusdedit, Paul, and Leo.

[Col. 0199]

ROMAN COUNCIL HELD IN THE YEAR 1002 UNDER THE PRESIDENCY OF SYLVESTER II, SUPREME PONTIFF, AT WHICH, AMONG OTHER MATTERS, THE IMMUNITY OF THE ABBEY OF PERUGIA WAS AFFIRMED.

(From Labbe, Councils, vol. IX, p. 1247.)

[Col. 0199B] Whatever disputes are settled by judicial decision should best be entrusted to the office of a writer, lest, with the passage of time, they succumb to oblivion and, arising again, cause the former error to begin anew.

Accordingly, while Lord Sylvester II, pontiff of the Roman see, was presiding at a synod held in the sacred Lateran palace, in the fourth year of his ordination, on the third day of December, indiction 1, Peter, archivist of that same sacred palace, stood forth and delivered this speech before the entire synod, saying:

“Lord pope, your abbot of Perugia brings a complaint against Conon, bishop of Perugia, because he was dragged away by armed force by the bishop’s retainers from beneath the altar of your monastery, which the abbot himself governs, and pulled out through the doors of the church and the cloisters of the brothers. Everything found there was handed over to plunder [Col. 0199C], for the benefit of the brothers, and the bishop is known to have received a share of it, since he participates in these sacrileges and is in no way believed to be free from the same crime.”

The bishop replied to him: “I am prepared to clear myself according to the judgment of these brothers of mine, since this was done neither at my command nor by my will. If the abbot had brought any complaint against me, I would either have compelled him to make satisfaction or, if I could not do so, would have defended my favor toward him together with every benefit. But, Father of all pontiffs, I implore your mercy and that of this entire assembly, so that no prejudice may be inflicted upon me today. You entrusted the Church of Perugia to me and made me swear that I would neither diminish it nor consent to its diminution. That monastery, which this abbot holds, properly belongs to my bishopric and is subject to no other jurisdiction. If a law were made concerning it, your apostolate would have no special claim over it.”

The reverend pope added: “I have neither withdrawn that monastery from your Church nor had it withdrawn. I found it under the jurisdiction and dominion of our Church, and have held it possessed in that manner until now. Let the privileges of our predecessors, the popes, be brought forward, and, after they have been read, let our brother bishops judge what the uprightness of equity requires.”

The privileges of Pope John and Pope Gregory, his predecessors, were then produced, placed before the assembly, and read aloud before the entire synod. The bishop said: “I do not reject these privileges, but I say that they were made without the consent of my predecessor, in whose time the earlier privilege was first issued. If I saw only his consent, I would maintain perpetual silence concerning it.”

In reply, all the clergy of the holy Roman Church said to him: “We have all seen the letter of your predecessor, in which there was both consent and an earnest request from the bishop that this be done [Col. 0200C]. We are witnesses of this matter, and we establish that it was true according to canonical sanction.”

Finally, the Gospels were brought forward, and the clerics stood ready to swear. The bishops delivered this judgment: either the bishop should accept those testimonies and pay the penalty stipulated by the privilege, or he should renounce the monastery. The aforesaid bishop Conon of the holy Church of Perugia therefore renounced to his lord, Pope Sylvester, the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter, situated not far from the city of Perugia, together with everything belonging to that monastery and named in the aforementioned privileges. He gave the aforesaid abbot the kiss of peace and promised that henceforth he would assist him.

After this, the same most reverend pope, together with the Roman judges [Col. 0200D], decreed that if any bishop of the Church of Perugia should attempt to reopen the dispute settled here against this abbot or his successors, he should pay ten pounds of the purest gold to the Lateran palace. May this judgment remain valid forever.

PART III OF THE WORKS OF GERBERT, LATER POPE SYLVESTER II—LETTERS AND DIPLOMAS.

SECTION I.

[Col. 0201]

Letters written before the supreme pontificate. EDITED BY ANDRÉ DUCHESNE.

(History of the Franks, vol. II, pp. 789–841.)

LETTER ONE. TO THE EMPEROR OTTO.

[Col. 0201A]

To his lord Otto Caesar, ever Augustus, Gerbert, formerly free.

While I weigh the public affairs of kingdoms, I fear to occupy the ears of my most serene lord with my own letters. Let my lord speak to his servant by letters of his own, according to the customary practice, so that the performance of his service may be made clear and the ambiguity of letters removed—letters which, although we often find them expressing the gravity of our Caesar, do not represent it to us as we conduct our affairs. In short, it will be a sign to us that you wish or do not wish something, depending on whether the decision has been issued favorably or unfavorably. For, insofar as it lies with us, whatever can be done must be accomplished if we learn your wish.

O, let Lord Bishop Gerbert state the verdict concerning our innocence in the matter of Brovingus [Col. 0201B] and Isimbard; let Litefred and Gerard say why Rodulf received their benefice. Let no one be called guilty of treason who always considered it glory to stand on Caesar’s behalf and disgrace to stand against Caesar.

LETTER TWO. TO THE SAME CAESAR.

I would rather report joyful than sad matters to my lord’s most serene ears. But when I see my monks wasting away from hunger and being oppressed by nakedness, how can I remain silent? This evil would indeed be bearable if at the same time a better hope had not also been taken away. By means of certain documents, which they call libelli, the entire sanctuary of the Lord has been sold. The money collected is found nowhere; the storehouses and granaries have been emptied, but there is nothing in the purses. What, then, am I, a sinner, to do here? If it could be done with my lord’s favor, it would be better for me alone to suffer want among the Gauls than to beg among the Italians together with so many needy people.

Rainerius the Frank, our intimate friend and eager for your honor, entrusted to my confidence many matters concerning the condition of your empire for me to report to you [Col. 0202A]—not, however, to be entrusted to a messenger, nor even inserted in letters without your consultation.

LETTER THREE. TO GERBERT, BISHOP OF THÉROUANNE.

O hope of our counsel, it is foolish to conceal the state of the present evil, and dangerous to speak of it, lest we appear to be acting from hatred of persons. If an abbot is permitted to hand over the immovable property of a monastery to any persons under the name of a libellus, and its movable property under the pretext of almsgiving, and, if anything should perhaps remain, to make a monk his heir, what specifically concerns the appointment of a new abbot?

Everything is said to have belonged to Petroald, nothing to the abbot; and it is clear that this is so, since nothing has been left to us except the buildings and the common use of the simple elements. My lord’s letter orders that Petroald be honored and retain what he held. The burden placed upon the parents on the same scale is doubled. Weigh the strength of the case; consider what I have lost and what I have pursued, apart from my lord’s favor. Take up the burden of a friend with counsel and assistance, and write back what should be done.

LETTER FOUR. TO BOSO.

GERBERT sends Boso greetings in Christ.

Let many words be dismissed, and let us follow deeds. We give you neither by money nor by friendship the sanctuary of my lord, nor, if it has been given by anyone, do we consent to it. Restore the hay that your men took from blessed Columbanus, if you do not wish to discover what we can accomplish with the favor of our lord Caesar and with the counsel and assistance of our friends. On these conditions we do not reject the laws of friendship.

LETTER FIVE. TO PETER, BISHOP OF PAVIA.

[Col. 0202C]

We give no Italian any thanks for the fact that we appear to possess the abbey of Saint Columbanus. If we have been praised by you before our lord, we have not returned to you undeserved praise. You ask for mutual conversations, yet you do not cease plundering our Church. You divide our property among soldiers as though it were your own, although you ought to have restored these things in their entirety. Plunder, pillage, shake the strength of Italy against us. You have found an opportune time. Our lord is occupied in the contest of wars; we shall neither hold back hands prepared to help him nor rashly usurp what belongs to his office. If we can make use of peace, we shall serve our Caesar both in person and in absence. Otherwise, his presence alone will console our poverty. And since, as the poet says, “nowhere is trust secure,” and since things neither seen nor heard are fabricated, we reveal our intention to you only in writing, and will accept yours in no other way.

LETTER SIX. TO ADELAIDE, AUGUSTA.

[Col. 0203B]

Regarding benefices and libelli, we have partly carried out our wishes in accordance with the desire of our lord Caesar. Let my lady remember that she indicated to her servant that she would pray for more things than can be done. Since we departed from you, we have seen neither Grifo nor his messenger. How shall we take away tomorrow the land that we permitted to be granted to our faithful men? But if everything that everyone orders is done, what are we doing here? And if we give everything, what shall we retain? We grant Grifo no benefice wherever we have the power to do so.

LETTER SEVEN. TO AIRARD.

[Col. 0203C] Gerbert, formerly a teacher, sends greetings to his Airard.

We have agreed to your requests and urge you to carry out our affairs as though they were your own. Pliny is to be corrected; Eugraphius is to be received; the works which are at Orbais and at Saint Basolus are to be copied out. Do what we ask, so that we may do what you ask.

LETTER EIGHT. TO ADALBERO, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS.

What I have done at Mantua concerning your affairs I shall explain better in person by word than in writing from a distance. I did not know which keys to the books I should send, because of the common use of similar locks. Obtain for us from Lord Azo, abbot of Der, the History of Julius Caesar for us to copy, so that you may have it—you with whom we have [a textually uncertain phrase follows]—and may hope for what we have found: namely, eight volumes of Boethius on astrology, as well as outstanding geometrical figures and other things no less worthy of admiration. Only your absence disturbs our fortunes, night and day.

LETTER NINE. TO GISILBERT, ABBOT.

If you are well, we rejoice. We regard your need as our own and ask you to relieve the need we are suffering. The philosopher Demosthenes published a book on diseases and remedies of the eyes entitled Ophthalmicus. If you have its beginning, we have it, as well as the end of Cicero’s speech For King Deiotarus. Farewell.

LETTER TEN. TO THE CAESAR.

[Col. 0204A]

Two brothers from the monastery of Principiano, like exiles and strangers, have been received by us. They bitterly complain of the desolation inflicted upon their place by the bishop of Laon and a neophyte abbot, and they also report that they ought not to be subject to any Church at all. It will therefore be a matter for your prudence and piety to ensure that neither the Church of Laon is deprived of its due honor because of hatred for its pastor, nor the monastery subjected to the tyranny of its devastator.

LETTER ELEVEN. THE SAME TO THE SAME.

Why do the foxes’ mouths and tails flatter my lord here? Let them leave the palace, or let them produce their retainers, who despise Caesar’s edicts, attempt to kill his envoys, and compare Caesar himself to an ass [Col. 0204B]. I say nothing of myself, whom they whisper, in a novel mode of expression, to be a spare horse, having a wife and children because part of my family has been gathered back from France. The defeated lack shame. O times! O customs! In what part of the world am I living? If I follow my homeland, I abandon the most sacred faith; if I do not follow it, I am an exile. Yet it is better to be an exile in the palace with faith than to reign in Latium without faith.

LETTER TWELVE. TO HUGH, THE TEACHER.

Gerbert, formerly a teacher, to his Hugh.

In accordance with the greatness of my spirit, my lord has enriched me with the greatest honors [Col. 0204C]. For what part of Italy does not contain the possessions of blessed Columbanus? This is indeed the result of the generosity and goodwill of our Caesar, but fortune has arranged matters otherwise. In accordance with the greatness of my friend, he has burdened me with the greatest enemies. For what part of Italy does not have enemies for me? My strength is unequal to the strength of Italy. This is the condition of peace: if I serve while stripped, they will cease striking me; if clothed, they will pursue me with drawn swords; where they cannot strike with the sword, they will assail with verbal darts. Imperial majesty is despised, both in me and in itself, through the division of the Lord’s sanctuary made according to the laws of the libelli. Because I do not wish to consent, I am called treacherous, cruel, and tyrannical. Caesar himself, the most distinguished of all men, is compared to an ass by gallows-birds [Col. 0204D]. O most faithful of friends, do not abandon your friend in counsel and assistance. Remember that I asked you to prefer my being a soldier in Caesar’s camps to my being a king among foreigners.

LETTER THIRTEEN. TO ECBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER.

We consider your happiness to be our own glory. If you suffer any hardship, we suffer it together with you. You have come to know the greatness of spirit of our lord Caesar, his purpose, and his desire for good men, which surpasses all others. Therefore, if you are deliberating whether to send scholars to us in Italy, our counsel is openly stated: whatever you praise, we shall praise; whatever you endure, we shall endure.

LETTER FOURTEEN. TO POPE JOHN.

[Col. 0205A]

To the most blessed Pope John, Gerbert, abbot in name alone and by virtue of the office of the monastery of Bobbio.

Where shall I turn? Shame upon me! If I appeal to the apostolic see, I am mocked. Because of enemies, I cannot come to you, nor do I possess the freedom to leave Italy. It is difficult to remain, when nothing has been left to us either in the monastery or outside it, except the pastoral staff and the apostolic blessing. We love Lady Imiza because she loves you. Through her, by messengers and letters, you will make known to us whatever you wish us to do; and through her we shall inform you of whatever we learn concerning the condition and designs of kingdoms that may be of interest to you. Farewell.

LETTER FIFTEEN. TO PETROALD, THE MONK.

[Col. 0205B]

Brother, let unstable circumstances not disturb your great understanding. Those who once proclaimed you a flourishing lord and father now disdain to have you as a fellow servant and equal. Fortune turns everything upside down. In giving and receiving, use our permission as befits a monk and as you know how to do. Do not neglect what we agreed upon, so that we may have a more frequent remembrance of you.

LETTER SIXTEEN. TO GERALD, ABBOT OF AURILLAC.

It is dead, it is dead, my Father—the condition of the Churches of the Lord. The commonwealth has perished, the Lord’s sanctuary is invaded, [Col. 0205C] and the people have become the spoil of enemies. Advise me, Father, where I should turn. My soldiers are ready to take up arms and fortify the camps. But what hope is there without a leader for the country, when we know the faith, morals, and dispositions of certain Italians? We have therefore yielded to fortune, and we now resume, with our minds still fixed upon them, the pursuits interrupted by the times. If it pleases you, we wish our former teacher Raimund to take part in them, while in the meantime we set out on the journey to Rome at the December Kalends.

LETTER SEVENTEEN. TO THE SAME.

My father Adalbero, archbishop of Reims, wishes you good health. The reason he did not visit you in person was the disturbance of the kingdoms, especially the uprising against his Church by Heribert of Troyes and Count Otto, son of Tedbald [Col. 0205D]. He wishes to know from you what the condition of the kingdoms is and whether Hugh, whom in your language you call an abbot-count, has taken a wife. Consider what belongs to him as belonging to us, and, so that he may not desire what belongs to you without payment, indicate what of his you would like.

As a sign of this, he is sending you an elaborate linen cloak, like the one he once sent through your Airard, though that one was plain. Abbot Guarnerius left with you a book on the multiplication and division of numbers written by Joseph the Spaniard; we ask for a copy of it for common use. If you are given the opportunity to see the thresholds of the blessed Remigius and Denis, we shall be able, after sending a messenger ahead, to share the delight of your conversations.

LETTER EIGHTEEN. TO THE BROTHERS OF BOBBIO.

[Col. 0206A]

Holy Scripture says: “May those who seek the Lord deceitfully never deserve to find him.” You professed the Rule of Saint Benedict, yet by abandoning and rejecting your pastor you willingly placed your necks beneath the yoke of tyrants. I do not speak of all your tyrants or leaders. How do you wish to appear before the tribunal of Christ?

I write this not as a means of retaining the honor, but, speaking what must be spoken, I free my soul from blame through pastoral care; I do not involve those who refuse to listen. Review the apostolic privileges; recall the anathemas you show me; and further understand what the sacred canons say: “Whoever in any way joins himself to the excommunicated, let him be excommunicated.” Consider how great the danger in which your affairs are placed. May the heavenly Judge cause you to recognize his commands and fulfill them in action.

LETTER NINETEEN. TO RAINAUD, THE MONK.

You are right, brother, to complain about the deprivation of your abbot. There are sheep in the valleys before the mouths of wolves, without a shepherd; monks in the monastery, without an abbot. According to your knowledge and ability, I exhort and urge you to desire and do what is good. The three different governments over you in a single year teach you what you see: deceit and instability. Lament the desolation that is to come, not so much of walls as of souls, and do not despair of the Lord’s mercy.

LETTER TWENTY. TO ADELAIDE, THE EMPRESS.

[Col. 0206C]

I have many sins before God, but against my lady—whose promised loyalty I have never violated, nor betrayed what was entrusted to me, even when she sought to drive me from her service, and toward whom I thought I had shown devotion without greed—I have none. If I made some slight error regarding your will, it was due to lack of foresight, not deliberation. May the long continuation of your penance during Lent now be sufficient for you; I confidently believe that it is.

For a time the blind greed of certain noble paupers prevailed; now may your piety toward justice, which has always been yours, prevail. Divine providence favors this, reconciling kingdoms to you and subjecting powerful kings to your rule. [Col. 0206D] This is my position: the loyalty I kept toward my lady’s son A., I shall keep toward his mother. If I cannot do so in person, at least I shall do so in absence by speaking well, wishing well, and praying well.

LETTER TWENTY-ONE. TO ECEMANNUS, A PALATINE MONK.

Feeling your goodwill toward me, my brother, I rejoice in the friendship of so great a man. I have clearly discovered that you are truly steadfast in faith, both toward me and toward those who have entrusted themselves to you *. Indeed, the admirable woman would not hold you dear in any other way. You will therefore take up the burden of your friend, offer good words, interpret my letters kindly, and regard my affairs as your own.

LETTER TWENTY-TWO. TO LADY IMIZA.

[Col. 0207A]

I consider myself fortunate to have gained the recognition and friendship of so great a woman, whose firm loyalty and enduring constancy my Gauls cannot admire sufficiently. And although your prudence has no need of admonition, nevertheless, because we perceive that you share our labor and grieve with us over our misfortune, we wish the lord pope to be approached by your messengers and letters, as well as by ours; and, if we have supporters and helpers both individually and collectively, let us, who grieve together, rejoice together when God is favorable. Approach my lady, the empress Theophania, in my name. Tell her that the kings of the Franks favor her son and are attempting nothing else than to destroy, under the pretext of advocacy, the tyranny of Henry, who wishes to make himself king.

## LETTER XXIII. TO LORD JOHN, POPE.

I bear with deep grief and indignation that the sanctuary of the Lord, entrusted to me by the holy Roman and Apostolic Church, is being invaded and plundered. Moreover, what will henceforth be established if what was enacted with the consent of the prince, by the election of the bishops, the will of the clergy and people, and finally the consecration of the most excellent of all men, the pope, is dissolved? What if commands are violated, privileges despised, and divine and human laws overthrown? Do not disdain to indicate by sacred letters with what hope I may risk approaching you. Otherwise, do not be surprised if I attach myself to those camps where there is the greatest share of human law and none of divine law: for humanity comes first in practical matters, divinity second in contemplative ones. This will happen because of my faintheartedness, if your magnanimity ceases.

## LETTER XXIV. TO LUPITUS OF BARCELONA.

Although I have no merits in your eyes, your nobility and affability nevertheless lead me to trust in you and to have confidence in you. Therefore send me, as I request, the book on astrology translated by you; and if you wish to ask anything of me in return, demand it without hesitation.

## LETTER XXV. TO BONI’S DAUGHTER, BISHOP OF GERONA.

[Col. 0207D]

The great authority of your name moves me in many ways: to come to see and address you, and also to obey you. The freedom long denied to me postponed this, though it was granted with grief. Since my lord Otto Caesar is no longer among the living, it is now lawful both to speak with friends and to obey their commands. If you wish to communicate anything to us, we shall be at Reims until the Kalends of November, and at Rome on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, if we are able to enjoy peace. My father Adalbero, archbishop of Reims, desires, through your efforts, to possess certain opinions which the wise Joseph has published concerning the multiplication and division of numbers.

## LETTER XXVI. TO ECBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER, IN THE PERSON OF ADALBERO.

[Col. 0208A]

See volume CXXXVII of the *Patrologia*, under ADALBERO OF REIMS, letter 1.

## LETTER XXVII. TO WILLIGIS, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, IN THE PERSON OF THE SAME.

See the same work, letter 2.

## LETTER XXVIII. IN THE PERSON OF JERUSALEM, LAID WASTE, TO THE UNIVERSAL CHURCH.

To the universal Church, which rules with the scepters of kingdoms, from her who is in Jerusalem.

While you flourish in good health, immaculate bride of the Lord, whose member I confess myself to be, I have through you the greatest hope of raising my head, now almost crushed. Or would I distrust you in anything, mistress of all things, if you acknowledge me as your own? Should anyone of your members think that the notorious disaster inflicted upon me does not in the least concern him, and that he ought to recoil from the lowest condition of worldly affairs?

Although now cast down, I once possessed the best portion of the whole world. With me are the utterances of the prophets and the insignia of the patriarchs. From here came forth the apostles, the bright lights of the world; from here the world received the faith of Christ; here it found its Redeemer. For although he is everywhere in his divinity, here he was born in his humanity, suffered, and was buried; from here he was taken up into heaven. But when the prophet said, “His tomb shall be glorious,” while the pagans overturn the holy places, the devil is attempting to render it inglorious.

Therefore strive, soldier of Christ; be standard-bearer and fellow-warrior; and what you cannot accomplish by arms, provide through the help of counsel and resources. What is it that you give, and to whom do you give it? Surely, a little from much, and to him who freely gave all that he has, yet did not receive it back from the ungrateful as he deserved; here he multiplies it, and in the future rewards it. Through me he blesses you, so that by giving you may increase and he may forgive your sins, so that you may live and reign with him.

## LETTER XXIX. TO WALON AND HIS OBSTINATE FOLLOWERS, IN THE PERSON OF ADALBERO.

See volume CXXXVII of the *Patrologia*, under ADALBERO OF REIMS, letter 3.

## LETTER XXX. TO NOTEGER, BISHOP OF LIÈGE, IN THE PERSON OF THE SAME.

[Col. 0208D]

See the work cited above, letter 4.

## LETTER XXXI. THE CONTROVERSY OF DIETERIC, BISHOP OF METZ, AGAINST CHARLES.

**DIETERIC**, servant of the servants of the Lord, lover of emperors, and most faithful guardian of their offspring, to **CHARLES**, his nephew by blood but most shameless violator of faith.

The loyalty which, as you know, has never been violated by any good man, was pledged in sacred words before the altar of blessed John, in the presence of the venerable bishop Noteger, of yourself, and of men who, though not nobler, were nevertheless more eminent in truth. You, a most frivolous deserter, placing faith in neither one side nor the other, allowed a blind love of ruling to weaken you and compel you to disregard it. And what wonder if you vomited forth upon your nephew the plague of your most filthy heart, when with a bloody hand—always most ready for every crime—and with a band of robbers and a troop of thieves, you sought by evil deceit to seize from your noble brother, the king of the Franks, his city of Laon—his, I say, certainly never yours—and to defraud him of his kingdom, while disgracing and befouling with your lies the imperial sister, his partner in the kingdom?

You have never considered anything worthy of care: “enlarge, fatten, make fat”—you who, unlike your fathers, have abandoned the Lord your maker. Recall how often I restrained your shameless mouth with my finger, while you poured out vile accusations against the archbishop of Reims and still viler ones against the queen, babbling with a serpent’s hiss. You yourself know better what you did to the bishop of Laon, while hiding for a short time in a corner of the kingdom of Lotharingia and boasting with an empty arrogance that you presided over the whole realm.

Recall your niece, a woman better than you though you are a man, together with her son of noble disposition; recall the vicars of the apostles, the shepherds of the holy Church’s flock, whom you strive to gnaw night and day with a dog’s tooth; recall also the other princes, who owe nothing to your jurisdiction and possess, by the same Lord as author, what they possess. Then, at last, shaking off your empty dreams and cleansing your forehead, drunk with the most false potion, you will be able to measure how insignificant is what you are doing, and how impossible, by divine will, is what you are plotting.

Therefore, though scarcely enrolled among their number according to merit, yet endowed with the honor of binding and loosing, I am to defend with the pastoral staff committed to me, unworthy though I am, the Church: I mean no other Church than that redeemed by the blood of the supreme Shepherd, which you, despising divine law, strive with your accomplices, so far as you can, to rend and tear to pieces. You disregard that terrible word of the Lord: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye”; and likewise the other saying: “Whoever despises you despises me.”

Until now, striving to heal your wounds, I have poured in oil and wine, secretly mixing gentleness with severity in public through our friends. From now on, unless you come to your senses, I shall cut you away with the sword of the Holy Spirit entrusted to me, together with your putrefying members, and hand you over to unquenchable fire. Thus, just as your faith, had you not despised it, would have been with those above, so, because you despise it, may it be forever with those below.

When the bars have been firmly secured and the gates of the heavenly Jerusalem closed, the Son of the Virgin, the bridegroom of that city, will say to the rejected: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels,” as it is written: “Woe to him who plunders! Will he not himself be plundered?” Beware lest you be found among that plunder, for whoever is found there is made an exile from the eternal inheritance.

May the Lord confound the counsel of Ahithophel.

## LETTER XXXII. GERBERT IN THE PERSON OF CHARLES.

**CHARLES**, whatever he is by the sole grace of God, to **DIETERIC**, the model of hypocrites, most faithless toward emperors, murderer of their offspring, and public enemy of the commonwealth.

It would have been fitting for my dignity to suppress your curses in silence and to take no account of what the insolence of a tyrant, rather than the judgment of a priest, produced. But lest silence toward your conspirators seem to constitute a confession, I shall touch briefly upon the sum of your crimes and report the least of the greatest. I shall also omit some points of my argument, so that you, swollen like an empty wineskin, may deflate when pressed beneath the weight of the words “fattened, made sleek, enlarged,” in which, as you rave, you are described.

Why do you claim that the lady Duchess Beatrice, together with her son and the chief men of the kingdom, has been deceived by us? Miserable man, you do not understand that scarcely anyone is a participant in your conspiracy. I do not affirm the utterly faithful loyalty of our Caesar’s son alone, nor from some corner, as you belch forth after drinking at night. The princes of Gaul are with me, the kings of the Franks, and, whether you like it or not, the most illustrious Lotharingians, devoted in faith.

They are concerned for the Caesar’s son; they seek neither to seize the kingdom, as you do, nor to establish a fellow-ruler. You have confused divine and human laws, and, inattentive to the laws, you imagine yourself, like a snail with horns in its own shell, to be in charge of everything.

Why do you direct threats from your pastoral office?
