As though you were a shepherd rather than a ravening wolf—or rather another Judas, if Judas was an apostle who betrayed his Lord for thirty pieces of silver—and you a bishop who, in hope of the most notorious profit, deprived your own lord, the king and heir of the kingdom, of his kingdom. This was too little for you: you exacted from him, as from an enemy, punishments that, so far as you were concerned, had no end. Is this how the benefits of the Ottos deserved to be repaid? In the end, it is evident that you never kept faith with them, and not merely because of the son.

When you hated Lothar, the king of the Franks whom you call glorious, when you drove him from the kingdom and compelled me to reign, were you keeping the faith promised to him and to me? I say the faith promised to me before the altar, which you shamelessly name. Surely you understand what you did. You urged me to take up arms against my brother and your lord’s sister, so that you might stab our entire royal family with mutual wounds, substitute tyrants in the name of kings, and, once the priesthood had been despised, recline in empty palaces with them.

Do you think you injure me if you say that you have injured those whose glory is my glory and whose dishonor, in the contrary view, afflicts me? But the truth is otherwise: the enormity of your crimes does not allow you to conceal your own offenses. And although you wish to employ a defense, the pallor that repeatedly comes over your face through the agitation of your person, and then the blush; sudden silence while speaking; sudden words that do not cohere with what came before—even when no one is asking—reveal the immense torment of your conscience.

Blush, miserable man, and recognize that what you thought only you knew has come to everyone’s attention. Do not stain the innocent with your sins, and do not measure the most shameful of your vices by the hands so often polluted by perjury. Stop violating the sacred things, and you who prescribe the remedy of repentance to us first, seek it publicly.

You have committed perjury; you have drained your own city through plunder; you have devastated the Church entrusted to you, as you say. I agree: then return what you abused—the guardianship of your lady, whom you humbled by taking away her freedom and imposing servitude. And you, who are described as the Lord’s pupil, built your table through the luxury of the rich man of the Gospel upon the tears of the orphan and widow; through such miseries you have heaped up mountains of gold.

Over these things, unhappy man, groan privately and publicly. Otherwise hear what is directed against you: “For days will come upon you, and they will surround you and hem you in on every side, and they will cast you down to the ground, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.”

“We have heard of the pride of Moab: he is exceedingly proud. His pride and his arrogance exceed his strength.”

## LETTER XXXIII. GERBERT’S DEFENSE CONCERNING THE CONTROVERSY HE DESCRIBED.

To the lord and most reverend bishop **DIETERIC**, G., the faithful servant of Caesar.

O glory of the Roman Empire! Shall we say that so much reason has perished from the former father of the state that the people, together with their shepherd, should be prey for enemies like a sluggish flock? Set your generosity, magnanimity, and prudence, like three most powerful legions, before the house of Israel; appoint divinity as their commander, lest we who have considered your prosperity our glory, if we lose the splendor of the empire, be made inglorious in turn.

We say this not because you need admonition, but so that we may interpret the concern of our mind for you. We recently employed this kind of interpretation in the controversy with your most bitter enemy, who was provoking your majesty, where we fear that we incurred the fault of an unfaithful interpreter by failing to match his speech to the movements of his mind. But if this intention is pleasing, henceforth we shall labor to express more carefully the feelings of friends and enemies, so that through us you may learn in complete faith what you ought to follow and what you ought to avoid. In this matter we are glad to have poured light upon you and darkness upon the enemy. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIV. TO WILLIGIS, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ.

We do not entrust to writing many matters which we commit to messengers. Thus my father Adalbero, archbishop of Reims, wholly faithful to you, has entrusted many things to this abbot Airard, his intimate associate, concerning the condition and peace of the kingdoms to be maintained with you. Moreover, he calls God to witness that the matters he communicated to you by letter are truly so. Believe the messenger as you would him, and, if writing is unsuitable, repay him in living words with whatever you deem appropriate.

But, O my father, with what words shall I address one who grieves over the same cause as I do? Deprived of Caesar, we are prey for enemies; we thought that Caesar survived in his son. O who betrayed us, who took away our second light? The lamb ought to have been entrusted to his mother, not to the wolf.

For my part, the enormity of my grief does not allow me to advise myself. Now my spirit rushes headlong against the Italian enemies who are utterly plundering my possessions; now, as though deliberating on better things, it seeks distant lands. But while Otto returns, while his features remain fixed in my heart, while his Socratic discussions repeatedly come to mind, the impulse is broken, and the weariness of my exile is somewhat relieved among the Gauls.

Advise me, Father. Although I have no merits toward your majesty, neither has my loyalty been absent nor will it be absent, if fortune once again smiles as before. When you have found the opportune time, you will recall from exile, in consultation with the empresses and with those to whom you think the matter should be referred, me, the faithful servant of Caesar, who have done nothing wrong except remain faithful to Caesar. You alone, therefore, bear my burden, which I did not wish to share with friendly princes until I had tested what could be accomplished through the man whom I judge most highly.

## LETTER XXXV. TO GERALD, ABBOT OF AURILLAC.

The many occupations with which our—so to speak—trustee, my father Adalbero, archbishop of Reims, is detained are indicated both by the delay of this messenger and by his present absence from the city of Reims. The matter occupying him concerns the condition of the kingdoms. While he receives hostages from the leading men of the Lotharingian kingdom, while he compels them to obey the emperor’s son under the protection of the king of the Franks, and while he prevents Henry from reigning in Gaul, he had nothing suitable to your name to send.

But if he perceives that it would please you, he will replace with a new one the gold-woven garment which he sent, modestly describing it as old, something which the shortness of time did not permit; he will add a stole of Phrygian workmanship, together with other things of the same kind. Through you he wishes to learn the condition of our kingdom and what that Hugo, son of Raimund, is doing and planning. In common we hold this opinion: what is approved by you is of the greatest value to us.

## LETTER XXXVI. TO WIDO, ABBOT OF GHENT, IN THE PERSON OF ADALBERO.

See volume CXXXVII of the *Patrologia*, under ADALBERO [OF REIMS], letter 5.

## LETTER XXXVII. TO ROBERT THE PALATINE.

I think you remember me very much, since I weave you into my private concerns day and night. Therefore make my lady Theophania remember me as well; I always wish her good health and a happy reign with her son. I keep her memory frequently, as is right, and Gaul bears witness that, for her assistance, I have stirred up very many advocates, as you know.

It will therefore be your duty to discover and write back whether I should remain in Francia as a reserve soldier for Caesar’s camp, whether, prepared to undergo every danger, I should come to you, or whether I should rather prepare myself for the journey which you and my lady know well, as was arranged at the palace in Pavia. At the same time, do not fail to say where, when, and what you think about this matter.

I also wish you to know that whatever I entrusted to safe ears in that same palace concerning the loyalty, devotion, and steadfastness of that famous archbishop Adalbero toward the son of our lord Caesar, you may confidently regard as being so, according to his knowledge and ability.

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO ECBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER, IN THE PERSON OF ADALBERO.

See above, letter 6.

## LETTER XXXIX. TO NOTEGER, BISHOP OF LIÈGE.

Do you not see, Father, whether you ought to keep watch for the Caesar’s camp, in defense of the most famous former loyalty, or whether, under blind fortune and ignorance of the times, divine and human laws are simultaneously being brought to ruin? Look: the man to whom, because of his father’s merits, you vowed your loyalty is being openly abandoned, although you ought to preserve the loyalty you vowed.

The Germans of Breisach on the bank of the Rhine now secretly approach the kings of the Franks. Henry, called an enemy of the state, appeared on the Kalends of February. Advise me, Father: resistance must be made by every means, lest they unite against the Lord and against his Christ. A ruling multitude, a disturbance of kingdoms.

If it is difficult to exclude the whole party, choose the better one. For my part, I, who owe great loyalty to Otto because of his benefits, immediately deliberate in this way concerning his lord’s son. We know Henry’s lofty designs and the advance of the Franks. But we do not fail to recognize what end it will have. Do not make a partner in the kingdom of one whom, once admitted, you may be unable to expel.

## LETTER XL. TO STEPHANUS, DEACON OF THE ROMAN CHURCH.

The uncertain times of the state, my brother, have compelled me to return to Gaul. All Italy seemed to me to be Rome; the world shudders at the customs of the Romans. In what condition Rome now stands, who are its pontiffs and masters of affairs, and what outcome has that man of mine had—my own, I say, especially my own—to whom I entrusted you? Do not hesitate to report these matters, and whatever good things, obstacles notwithstanding, concern you.

For me and for our archbishop A., you will discreetly and without dispute return, through Guido, count of Soissons, the Suetonius Tranquillus, the Quintus Aurelius, and the other works you know, identifying what belongs to whom; and you will learn what we are preparing appropriate to your name. Nor should you, as our friends, conceal from us whatever certain information you have learned concerning the Greek empire, the kingdom of the Franks, and the enterprise of the Italians. What an abundance of words lacks is contained in the weight of the thoughts.

## LETTER XLI. TO ADALDURON, BISHOP OF VERDUN.

Do not consider the number of lines in this letter. Weigh much in a few words. Dangerous times have taken away the freedom to say clearly what one wishes. Since the fortune of Francia is advancing in deed and action, we have taken advantage of the moment to meet with the most faithful messengers.

On behalf of Godefrid’s men, we promised that you wished to renew the pact once agreed between them and our Caesar Otto, adding to the pact the son in whom he alone rejoices. We persuaded them that Caesar, as he lay dying, had desired this very thing through Godefrid’s most beloved son.

Thus this matter appeared to belong jointly to us alone and to the Caesar’s son. If you wish to advance what has been begun, or to abandon it, write back promptly. Whether in this matter we are exposed to danger for someone, despite our safe leisure, and what schemes or attacks may have been quieted by this course, is not easy to say.

## LETTER XLII. TO NOTEGER, BISHOP OF LIÈGE, IN THE PERSON OF ADALBERO.

See volume CXXXVII of the *Patrologia*, under ADALBERO OF REIMS, letter 7.

## LETTER XLIII. TO THE SAME, IN THE PERSON OF GODEFRID.

[Col. 0214A]

In accordance with the promises of the archbishop of Trier, we shall go to inspect the arrangement of our A. on the third day before the Nones of January. Wherever he may still have decided upon the leader of your journey, we shall send word five days before the Kalends and announce whatever more certain information we have learned. We are uncertain whether our brother will come there.

## LETTER XLIV. TO ECBERT, ABBOT OF TOURS.

Since I have learned from many honorable messengers that you frequently remember me and, by right of kinship, proclaim a great friendship, I think myself blessed in your estimation if I am found worthy of being loved by the judgment of so great a man.

But because I am not one who, like Panaetius, sometimes separates the honorable from the useful, but rather one who, with Cicero, combines the honorable with every useful thing, I do not wish these most honorable and sacred friendships to be without their respective usefulness in any respect. And since the study of conduct and the study of speech are not separated from philosophy, I have always joined the study of speaking well to the study of living well.

Although living well alone is superior to speaking well, and once the cares of government have been discharged, one may suffice without the other, both are necessary for us who are occupied in public affairs. For speaking suitably in order to persuade, and restraining the spirits of the enraged from their assault by gentle speech, are of the greatest usefulness.

To prepare for this, I am constantly acquiring a library. Just as formerly at Rome and in other parts of Italy, so also in Germany and Belgium I have bought writers and copies of authors at the cost of much money, aided by the goodwill and zeal of my friends and fellow provincials. Allow me to have the same thing done repeatedly among you, through you, so that I may obtain what I request. We shall specify at the end of the letter which works we wish to have copied.

We shall send parchment and the necessary expenses to your authority for the copyist, while not forgetting your additional kindness. Finally, lest by saying more we abuse the laws of the letter: the reason for so much labor is our contempt for treacherous fortune—a contempt produced in us not by nature alone, as in many people, but by cultivated learning. Therefore, in leisure and in business alike, we teach what we know and learn what we do not know.

## LETTER XLV. TO RAIMUND, MONK OF AURILLAC.

The Latins and barbarians who share in the fruit of our labor know how much love we bear you. Their wish seeks your presence. For it is evident that we are full of cares and will not remain in a place of study on account of anyone else’s business.

For these cares, philosophy alone has been found to be the one remedy. From its studies we have often received many advantages; by it, in this turbulent time, we have broken the movement of fortune, which rages severely both against others and against us. For when the condition of the state in Italy was such that we would shamefully have had to submit to the yoke of tyrants if we professed our innocence, or if we attempted to rely on our strength, we would have had to secure clients everywhere, fortify camps, and practice plunder, arson, and murder.

We chose the certain leisure of studies over the uncertain business of wars. And because, while following the traces of philosophy, we do not attain it, we have not suppressed every impulse of our turbulent spirit. At one moment we return to what we left behind; at another, moved by the exhortation of our intimate friend, Abbot Guarinus, we approach the princes of Spain. We shall be torn away from our earlier undertakings by the sacred letters of our lady Theophania, empress, ever Augusta, ever to be loved, ever to be revered.

Amid such instability of affairs, Gerbert, the special son of the most faithful father Gerald, whom these matters do not touch, asks for his judgment concerning the courses to be followed, amid fear of sorrow and desire for joy.

Farewell; may Father Gerald be well; may Brother Airard be well; may the most holy order be well, my nourisher and instructor, and may it remember me in its holy prayers, as well as Father A., archbishop of Reims, wholly devoted to it.

## LETTER XLVI. TO GERALD, ABBOT.

I do not know whether divinity has granted mortals anything better than friends, provided that they are people whom one may rightly seek and rightly regard. Happy was the day, happy the hour, when I was permitted to know a man whose name, whenever remembered, has turned all our troubles aside. If I sometimes enjoyed his presence, I would not think myself happier without reason.

To make this possible, I had established for myself no ignoble residences in Italy. But blind fortune has enveloped the world in darkness; it presses me down and leaves me uncertain whether it is driving me forward or guiding me, as I now aim here and now there. The features of my friend remain fixed in my heart: I mean him who is my lord and father, Gerald, whose deliberation will become our execution.

## LETTER XLVII. TO ADALBERO, DESIGNATED BISHOP OF VERDUN, AND HERMANN, BROTHERS.

Happy are those for whom paternal virtue is an example worthy of imitation. Your father requests this of you. Let the sudden event not frighten you. Keep inviolate the loyalty you promised to the Caesar’s son; defend all the fortresses against the enemies; finally, do not surrender to the Franks either Scarpone, or the castle of Haidon, or anything else that he left to you—whether enticed by the empty hope of his liberation, by fear of his torture, or by fear of Frederick’s son.

These are the commands that your magnanimous father gave to his noble sons. Let the enemies perceive that they have not captured all of Godefrid in you. Gather aid from everywhere; present yourselves as liberators of your homeland, resembling your father in everything. On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, he wished me to become the interpreter of his wishes, as one most faithful to him and to his own.

## LETTER XLVIII. TO AN UNNAMED RECIPIENT.

We conclude briefly an obscure and unnamed letter. Lothar, king of Francia, is first in name alone, whereas Hugo is so not in name but in deed and action. If you had sought his friendship for the common good and joined his son to the Caesar’s son, you would long ago have ceased to experience the kings of the Franks as enemies.

## LETTER XLIX. TO NOTEGER, BISHOP OF LIÈGE.

[Col. 0216A]

The present times make your name worthy of respect: in them the probity of the few is praised, while the wickedness of the many is proclaimed. Your friend Godefrid is now watching to see which of his friends have loved him more than their own interests, and which would have remained faithful to wife and children if the final day had carried him away.

And because so great a man thinks so highly of you, this alone can show how greatly virtue shines in you. He urges and admonishes those who love him and belong to him to remain faithful to his lady Theophania and to her son, not to be broken by the strength of the enemies, and not to be frightened by any misfortune. A joyful day will come, which will truly distinguish and separate the betrayers and liberators of their homeland through punishments and rewards.

You must not in any way make Adalbero, archbishop of Reims, who is wholly faithful to you, aware of these matters. The letters sent to your archbishops testify to how greatly he is oppressed by tyranny: in them he has written none of what he wished, but only what the tyrant, while he was inattentive, extorted.

## LETTER L. TO MATHILDA, COUNTESS.

Let my lady Mathilda lay aside every complaint. Your illustrious husband Godefrid, foremost among his peers and formidable even to the victors themselves, has commanded this. Cheer your mind, because a sorrowful spirit dries up the bones and disturbs counsel.

Keep the purest faith with the lady Theophania, empress, always Augusta, and with her son, always Augustus, together with your sons. Make no pact with the enemy Franks; shun the kings of the Franks. Hold and defend all the fortresses in such a way that your adversaries have no part in them—neither through hope of your husband’s liberation, nor through fear of his execution, nor through fear of Frederick’s son.

On the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, at the river Marne, he entrusted this to my faith, and I have reported it to you in complete faith.

## LETTER LI. GERBERT TO SIGIFRID, THE COUNT’S SON.

Because of the great love you bear your parents, who are now exiles, we addressed them at the river Marne on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. We have informed our lady Theophania by letter of what they wished her to know concerning their loyalty.

And because, through the goodwill of Otto and Heribert, whose custody protects them, we are able to speak with them, you will inform us in writing of whatever you or our lady may wish to entrust to them. We also commit this to your loyalty: if you bind Hugo to yourselves in friendship, you will easily be able to avoid every attack of the Franks.

## LETTER LII. TO THE LADY THEOPHANIA, EMPRESS.

Although I wished to approach you in accordance with your command, divinity did not oppose this without reason. For on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, after addressing the captured counts Godefrid and his uncle Sigifrid, I alone among the ranks of the enemies was found to be on your side; to me they entrusted, confidently, their opinions concerning the condition of your empire.

I therefore wrote letters of exhortation, according to their understanding, to their wives, children, and friends: that they should persevere in loyalty to you, be frightened by no assault of the enemies, and, following their example, if fortune required it, choose exile rather than their homeland with treachery, in order to preserve their loyalty to you.

I hold these men especially dear. What weighs more heavily upon them is that they are unable to carry out your affairs than that they appear to have been handed over to the captivity of the enemies. But since discord among princes is the destruction of kingdoms, the concord of your princes seems to us likely to be the remedy for such great evils. For “a threefold cord is not easily broken.”

You should also know that the kings of the Franks do not look upon us with favorable eyes, because we hold opinions contrary to them concerning your loyalty, and also because we enjoy great familiarity with Adalbero, archbishop of Reims. For the same reason they persecute him and consider him utterly faithless to them.

In all these matters, clearly inform us what you wish us to do. And if any route should open among the enemies by which and at what time we might approach your presence, let us know more certainly; we are prepared in every way to obey you.

The matter has progressed to the point that it is no longer a question of his expulsion, which would be a tolerable evil, but of life and blood. I share this with him, as though I were urging him on against royal efforts. Finally, the burden of oppression is so great, and hatred of your name so intense, that he does not dare to communicate his miseries to you in any reply.

But if this tyranny prevails and a route for fleeing to you opens to him, he will not have thought better of you without reason or held a secure hope, since he has been considering what support he might obtain from you and your son, in whom your influence has prevailed.

## LETTER LIX. TO THE LORD DIETERIC, BISHOP OF METZ.

What the royal action or plan presently is was disclosed by Henry’s messenger on the Ides of May. On his return, his eagerness to ask questions and investigate many matters indicated that he was displaying one thing in his expression while carrying another in his mind.

Duke Hugo is said to have gathered about six hundred soldiers. This report suddenly dissolved and dispersed the assembly of the Franks held at the palace of Compiègne on the fifth day before the Ides of May. Among your men were Duke Charles and Count Reinharius; among ours, Herbert of Troyes. Otto, however, was excluded through sharper vigilance. Gibewin was also present, the bishop of Laon and brother of Gocilo, who escaped after the son of his brother Bardo had been given as a hostage for peace, on the condition that he should do whatever Sigifrid and Godefrid might do.

What is this? For the Franks, mere hope; for us, a certain reality. It remains only that you should not wish to hand over to enemies, deprived of counsel and assistance, the homeland which you hold in your hands by counsel, aid, and strength. I bear it with restless and indignant mind that the city of Verdun should be quietly defended against a few robbers—unless perhaps this is deferred for a greater plan, so that they may waste away in sudden ruin from the quarter from which they expect nothing.

## LETTER LX. GERBERT TO AN UNNAMED RECIPIENT.

[Col. 0218B]

A matter that is to be concealed does not wish to be entrusted to many people. What is written to us in a different style is not unjustly thought to be handled adversely. The silence of your friend Adalbero indicates both his own condition and that of the Churches of the Lord and the palace of the Franks. I shall address this briefly, as I can.

I have not forgotten Caesar’s loyal men. A conspiracy against the Caesar’s son and against you has both been formed and is being pursued—not only by the princes, among whom Duke Charles is no longer acting secretly, but also by soldiers whom it is possible to attract through hope or fear.

On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, Duke Hugo finally kissed the king and queen through the cunning of certain men, so that it might be thought that the name of so great a man would be included in the conspiracy. It is not, however, nor do we think it will be in these circumstances.

Count Sigifrid has returned to his own lands. Count Godefrid, if he were to return Castrilucium together with Hainaut to Renier, and deprive himself and his son of the county and the bishopric of Verdun, might perhaps be able to return to his own lands after displaying unbroken loyalty to the kings of the Franks and giving hostages.

The end of Dieteric concerns Duke Hugo; Heribert concerns Otto. A mediating peace now at last reconciles Adalbero the archbishop, who is faithful to you, on the condition that it may in due course be made perpetual. In this matter, nothing can be arranged concerning you and your people, in whose name he is placed first, that could obstruct the safety of you and your people.

A hidden and furtive expedition is suddenly being directed against some of your men. You will not conceal from us, who rejoice in your safety, what you have accomplished across the Rhine.

## LETTER LXI. GERBERT TO ADALBERO, ARCHBISHOP.

As you wished, the matter has been arranged; your delay until the appointed conference has been generally commended. Hugh’s friendship must be sought earnestly, and every effort must be made lest we misuse what has begun well. For this is indeed the understanding, but I do not know by what arrangement your brother Godefridus and Rainherius told my Gobtherus—whom I had sent to Tours—that you would be present, so that, if Odo sent you any message, you might both speak with him and fulfill by your actions whatever he indicated. Moreover, Duke Hugh, taking advantage of the disagreement between the bishop of Paris and Abbot Gual—[Col. 0219A]—asks our abbot Airardus, among others, to come to him. We are confident that he can be persuaded to do this. Once the conference is over, put an end to all delays and return yourselves to the city and to your people.

## LETTER LXII. TO BEATRICE, DUCHESS, IN THE PERSON OF ADALBERON

See *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXVII, under ADALBERON OF REIMS, letter 14.

## LETTER LXIII. TO THE SAME

See above, letter 15.

## LETTER LXIV. TO THE SAME

See above, letter 16.

## LETTER LXV. TO NITHARDUS, ABBOT OF MEDELECENSE

[Col. 0219B]

One must always look to the advantage of the greatest number, and public interests must be preferred to private benefits. You compel Brother Gaud. to return suddenly, with all his household possessions prepared and still to be prepared, without any consideration of the time involved. Have you alone not felt the great upheavals of civil war? We who seem to be masters and princes of the world, traveling constantly with exhausted horses, have fewer and fewer companions. When you said that he was unwilling to return because of weariness with the monastery, you are nevertheless keeping him back by every means, so that this may not prove true. It follows, therefore, that we must discover whether you value the advantage of a few or that of many more highly in this matter.

## LETTER LXVI. TO NOTEGER, BISHOP OF LIÈGE

[Col. 0219C] See *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXVII, under ADALBERON OF REIMS, letter 17.

## LETTER LXVII. TO THE SAME, IN THE PERSON OF THE SAME

See above, letter 18.

## LETTER LXVIII. TO ABBOT RAINERUS

Although your understanding does not fail to recognize that the government of souls is the art of arts, nevertheless it seemed useful to make this suggestion to you, despite your heavy involvement in public affairs. We have persuaded Brother Menig.—whom, through your gentle eloquence and paternal affability, you compelled to change his abode overseas—while he remained hesitant and uncertain, to experience your gentleness, of which he already knows. Therefore, like a good physician, a learned man will have to offer honeyed remedies, [Col. 0219D] lest, if bitter antidotes are administered at the first taste, he begin fearfully to dread for his own health. Receive him on this condition, if it pleases you; if it displeases you, bear calmly whatever he wishes concerning his return, lest we perhaps perform the office of a betrayer.

## LETTER LXIX. TO ECBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER

The fact that we did not carry out what we had ordered from the city of Verdun concerning the return of Brother G. was brought about by the sharper demands of the present time: necessity both imposes what we do not want and removes what we do want. Now, at last, lest we appear ungrateful toward those who have deserved well, we send him back to your clemency as best we can, asking only this from your customary benevolence: that, because of our recommendation, he may experience your affability [Col. 0220A] and, if it can be done with your consent, not be deprived of the studies to which he has resolved to devote himself with especial zeal.

## LETTER LXX. TO MAIOLUS, ABBOT OF CLUNY

Although you are constantly occupied with vigilant care over your own flock, it is nevertheless a greater charity if you sometimes heal the contagion of another flock. In the monastery of Fleury, an invader, as they say, has occupied the highest place among the monks, out of reverence for Father Benedict. If you remain silent, who will speak? If this is not corrected, what wicked man will not hope for something similar? We say these things out of zeal for divine love, so that, upon our examination, if he is upright he may be received, but if he is wicked he may be deprived of the fellowship of all abbots and of the monastic order, [Col. 0220B] to the punishment of his condemnation. Your approval of this, expressed in a letter to us, will be most welcome.

## LETTER LXXI. TO GERALD, ABBOT OF AURILLAC

Most beloved of God, you see the world burning with wars, yet you do not raise your hands to the Almighty for the condition of the churches of the Lord! You wish us to undertake a health-bringing and charity-filled journey to the shrine of blessed Gerald; may God grant success to this desire! But how difficult this is to accomplish is easily understood, unless your merits prevail. You ask what view should be taken of King Louis and whether the Frankish army will bring aid to Borellus. We should by no means inquire into the former from our own standpoint, since, as Sallust says, [Col. 0220C] all men who deliberate about doubtful matters must be removed from anger, hatred, and pity. As for the latter, although by its own nature it inclines equally toward being and not being, our judgment seems rather to incline toward its not being. The instruments, moreover, and the things you ordered to be sent to you, are being kept in Italy, to be presented to your sight once peace has been established among the kingdoms. Regard as your own whatever belongs by right to the enemy. Show your longed-for presence as a pious father to sons who desire it, even for the sake of blessed Remigius, apostle of the Franks, so that our impossibility may be resolved by your ability.

## LETTER LXXII. TO STEPHANUS THE DEACON, GIVEN ON 2 March

Occupied with the funeral rites of Lord King Lothar, we replied briefly to the many things about which you had asked. All the Lotharian captives have long since escaped, except Count Godefridus, concerning whom better things are shortly expected. Write back what is happening among you and your people, and through this envoy return to us, with complete charity, the books copied for us through your industry.

## LETTER LXXIII. TO NITHARDUS, ABBOT OF MEDELECENSE

Because we do not sometimes enjoy your presence, the troubled condition of the state is to blame. You think that you alone endure hardships, and you do not know what is most harsh for others. But while men are being driven by uncertain fortune, and while a certain dwelling is being sought for me—not for our people—in an uncertain place, why do you hoard for so long beside me the treasures of faithless Fortune, deposited in your care? And since I speak as the most faithful to the most faithful, [Col. 0221A] hasten your journey. For either the imperial court will soon gather me to itself, or I shall return as quickly as possible to Iberia, which has been neglected for too long.

## LETTER LXXIV. TO ECBERT, ARCHBISHOP, IN THE PERSON OF ADALBERON

See *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXVII, under ADALBERON OF REIMS, letter 20.

## LETTER LXXV. IN THE PERSON OF QUEEN EMMA, TO HER MOTHER

To the Lady Adelaide, Empress, ever Augusta: Emma, once queen, now deprived of the light of the Franks.

The times of my delights have passed, the times of my beauty, O my lady and sweet mother: the man through whom I flourished when he flourished, and reigned when he reigned, has made his wife a widow forever. O bitter day, the sixth day before the Nones of March, which robbed me of my husband and plunged me into these miseries! May my pious mother understand the lament and anguish of her daughter, filled with sorrow. I would prefer not to exist at all, unless God had left me a mother as a consolation. O when shall I see you, when shall I speak with you! Our people wish me and my son to meet you and King Conrad near Mount Romaricus, where the kingdoms share a boundary, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June. But this delay is a thousand years to me. Meanwhile, know that the princes of the Franks have confirmed their loyalty to me and my son together by oath. In this matter, and in the other matters that must be pursued or avoided, we shall follow your judgment, so that you may be called not merely the mother of two queens but the mother of all kingdoms. [Col. 0221C] Remember also your words: that you loved my husband more than you loved me, and that he himself loved you more than he loved me. May these sweet affections benefit his soul; and what you cannot provide temporally, repay spiritually through the holy fathers—that is, bishops, abbots, monks, and all the most devout servants of the Lord.

*(Numbers 76, 77, 78, and 79 contain epitaphs of Lothar, king of the Franks; Duke Frederick; Adalbert the Scholastic; and the Emperor Otto. We have given these separately above.)*

## LETTER LXXX. INVECTIVE AGAINST THE CHURCH OF VERDUN

What remedy shall we find for your diseases, accursed city of Verdun? You have torn apart the unity of the holy Church of the Lord; you have severed the most sacred fellowship of the human race. For what else have you done, when you still stubbornly refuse to recognize your shepherd, elected by the will of your hereditary king, with the agreement and support of the bishops of the neighboring provinces, and moreover endowed with episcopal blessing? You attempt, like a mutilated and deformed limb, without unity with the body, to graft yourself from the cultivated olive onto the wild olive. You do not recognize your shepherd because you are plotting to deprive your king of his kingdom. It is not your right to create new kings and princes—that is, to pass under unfamiliar yokes. Your sin is exceedingly grave, impious city.

No battering ram has shattered your walls; your soldiers have not been weakened by hunger; they have not been struck by any kind of weapon. You have corrupted the sanctuary of the Lord; you have invaded and now possess the sanctuary of the Lord. You have become a den of thieves. Enemies of the human race, your friends, forgetful of virgins, of the sanctity of the marriage bed, of kinship and office, have now made you a dreadful brothel in holy days and holy places. The altars of the Lord have been battered by kicks and dug up with mattocks. The wealth of religious people and of the poor has been exposed to plunder and fires.

Return, return to the peace of the churches and to the unity of the kingdoms, city that drives out virtues and welcomes vices. And you, whoever you are who belong to the better part of the Lord, return and separate yourselves like sheep from goats. We know the ringleaders of the polluted city; we know its bands of armed followers, whom until now we have endured with divine patience, though they deserve to be struck by the divine sword. Now, weighed down by blindness of mind and lulled into the darkness of death, we strike them, by a sentence of condemnation promulgated from the divine laws, with the common judgment of all good people. [Col. 0222B]

## LETTER LXXXI. TO ECBERT [Note: Below he is called Ewrardus and Ebrardus.] ABBOT OF TOURS

Where the supreme rule of religion ought to have been, the appearance of the gravest crime has rightly moved and terrified us. But who will be the author of this correction, while all the leading men of your order remain silent? We have written a few things about this to the venerable Abbot Maiolus, because we know that a wise man understands much from a few words. He has been appointed by us as the leader for avenging this great affair—or, to speak more truthfully, this great act of audacity. Whoever among us first learns his decision will communicate it to the other without delay.

## LETTER LXXXII. TO ADSON, ABBOT OF DER

Break all delays, my father, and on the third or second day before the Kalends of July depart from Ur of the Chaldeans. One must obey veteran friends, long tested in loyalty. Our father Adalbero, father of his country, once faithful to you and now most faithful, impatient of delay, seeks your presence. It is wrong to communicate in your absence what we wish to say in person. The beloved volumes of books belonging to you and to us have accompanied your journey. Let this much that I have said suffice.

## LETTER LXXXIII. TO THE PEOPLE OF BOBBIO

[Col. 0222D]

Gerbert, by the grace of God, if he is anything, offers the fullest greeting to his most beloved sons, the people of Bobbio of both orders.

You have done something wholly worthy of you and suited to your name by seeking and visiting your father, for you have proved yourselves truly his sons by right. Therefore, both for your diligence and for your constant loyalty toward me, though absent I now give you thanks, and, if God is favorable, when present I shall offer you the thanks that are due. Although I am now almost safely in harbor, I nevertheless bear with displeasure that you are tossed by hostile waves. But we know that the Lord can do all things, and we trust that, moved by the prayer of the poor, he will immediately bring aid to the afflicted.

## LETTER LXXXIV. TO HUGH, MARQUIS

[Col. 0223A]

I do not value you highly without reason, and I exalt both you and yours with my prayers and praises, since you deign to remember me despite your many occupations. We place this among honorable things, and therefore among the foremost; accordingly, we have the greatest confidence in you. We earnestly ask that the memory of us not fade, and we pour out, though absent, whatever prayers we can, asking you to assist the already weary affairs of blessed Columbanus.

## LETTER LXXXV. TO CONON THE ITALIAN, MARQUIS

Although we have earned your favor through none of the merits of service, nevertheless the virtue and nobility both of your lineage and of your own character lead us to think well of you and to hope for better things. If the greatest can be aided by the least, our efforts will not be lacking to your honor at the proper place and time. By offering counsel and good words, we shall ensure that, when Fortune smiles upon you, our modest position may find rest beneath your wings.

## LETTER LXXXVI. TO THE EMPRESS THEOPHANIA, IN THE PERSON OF ADALBERON

See *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXVII, under ADALBERON OF REIMS, letter 20.

## LETTER LXXXVII. TO CONSTANTINUS THE SCHOLASTIC OF FLEURY

That man of God wisely and expertly judged that the invader ought to be condemned, but he stated the matter less fully than he might have. He carefully and prudently explained that the man himself was infamous even before the insignia of honor, that his supporters would increase his infamy among religious men, and that he should be deprived of the fellowship of the saints. Therefore, hasten your journey and visit us on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, so that through you we may be more fully informed about all these matters. At the same time, you will rejoice in our punishment of the invader, and the man who thought you were mud in our nostrils should consider the words directed against himself and dread that you may smell, like incense, after being perfumed. Let Cicero’s little works accompany your journey: *On the Republic*, *Against Verres*, and the many works that the father of Roman eloquence composed in defense of others.

## LETTER LXXXVIII. TO MAIOLUS, ABBOT OF CLUNY, IN THE PERSON OF ADALBERON

[Col. 0223D] See *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXVII, under ADALBERON OF REIMS, letter 22.

## LETTER LXXXIX. TO ECBERT [EBRARD], ABBOT OF TOURS, IN THE PERSON OF ADALBERON

See above, letter 23.

## LETTER XC. TO THE EMPRESS THEOPHANIA AND TO HER SON OTTO

See above, letter 24.

## LETTER XCI. TO RAYMUND, ABBOT OF AURILLAC

Deprived of the illustrious Father Gerald, I seemed not to survive as a complete person. But when you, whom I desired greatly, were appointed father according to my wishes, I was born again whole as a son. Nor do I alone rejoice in your honor: Father Adalbero rejoices as well, offering himself and all that is his to you from the heart, all the more closely as you shine more brightly with the light of religion and knowledge. For love of him and because of his merit, I spent almost an uninterrupted three years in Francia. While there I endured the anger of kings, the tumults of peoples, and the heat of kingdoms at odds with one another; I was afflicted by such weariness that I almost regretted having undertaken pastoral care.

But since my lady Theophania, Empress, ever Augusta, orders me to depart with her for Saxony on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, and I have ordered some of my monks and soldiers to come from Italy to meet me there, I do not now have anything certain to write concerning the instruments placed in Italy or concerning the monk who is to be sent to transport them, especially [Col. 0224B] since, without the presence of my lady Theophania, I do not dare trust the loyalty of my soldiers, because they are Italians. Nor do I know sufficiently whether I shall lead an army into Italy before autumn or whether we shall remain in Germany, so that we may gather as many troops as possible against King Louis of the Franks, unless he keeps quiet. He is most troublesome to his friends but not very troublesome to his most destructive enemies; a speedy outcome will show who he is and what should be understood about him.

The illustrious character of the divine-memory Emperor Otto, once peace had been restored among the dukes and princes, led legions of soldiers the following summer against the Sarmatians, whom in that language they call Wends. There he captured, destroyed, and devastated forty-six strongly fortified cities by his own presence and the strength of his soldiers.

The Archbishop of Reims, Adalbero, greets you and Airardus, as does the entire community of the monastery of Aurillac, with me added as one wholly devoted to you. Farewell again and again.

## LETTER XCII. TO BERNARD, A MONK

You ask, most beloved brother, what sort of things I am doing and whether they are advantageous or disadvantageous. I doubt whether I can satisfy this request in a few words, since, when examined more deeply, they seem to contain no advantages at all—or, if they possess any in some manner, they drag most disadvantages along with them.

First, involvement in public affairs is now an act of recklessness, since divine and human laws are confused there because of the immeasurable greed of utterly depraved men. It has been decided that the only law is whatever lust and force have extorted in the manner of wild beasts. In private affairs, however, I count it to my credit that, even when crushed by no misfortune, I do not abandon friends in adversity.

Whether this deserves to be remembered I leave to the judgment of others. I also count it to my credit that I left Italy so that I would not in any way be compelled to negotiate with the enemies of my lord and elder son, D. M. Otto; and that I sometimes offer the sweetest fruit of the liberal disciplines to the most noble scholars for their enjoyment.

For love of these studies, in the late autumn I published a certain work in the art of rhetoric, laid out on twenty-six sheets joined and linked together in the form of a number longer than the preceding one, which is made from twice thirteen. The work is truly marvelous to those who understand it, useful to students, and designed to grasp and place in the mind the fleeting and most obscure matters of rhetoricians. [Col. 0225A]

Therefore, if any of you is moved by concern for such matters, both for mastering music and for the things produced from instruments—matters that I am unable to complete myself—if I learn that Lord Abbot Raymund wishes this firmly, I shall arrange for them to be supplied through Constantius of Fleury. He is a noble and exceptionally learned scholar, and he is my closest friend.

Farewell, most beloved brother, and always share reciprocally in my affection; consider our possessions to be held in common.

## LETTER XCIII. TO ADALBERON, ARCHBISHOP

It is characteristic of a most corrupt age that it cannot be decided, according to popular opinion, what is more useful. What you are doing is useful in the judgment of many; it is more useful when more people judge that you should remain in the city and restrain the small and most worthless band of brigands, both by your presence and by the number of your soldiers. They think that you ought to speak with your brother and hear what Otto and Heribert want, since they are suddenly demanding mutual conferences. Although there is no trustworthiness in them, they must nevertheless be dealt with according to their circumstances. Certainly, while they are afraid, their danger will demand from them what their own loyalty would not have demanded.

## LETTER XCIV. TO THE SAME

On the eighth day before the Kalends of October, Reinherius returned from Reims with the reply, to carry out your business. His view is this: if you wish to learn a definite conclusion concerning your brother’s situation, a matter to be disclosed to no mortal except you, meet your brother and his companions at Altovillare on the fourth day before the Kalends, and do not again allow your nephew Hecilo and the leading kinsmen of your family to depart anywhere. A serious matter is being dealt with seriously.

Fortify Mosomum and Maceriae with a large number of soldiers. Duke Cono is plotting an ambush on behalf of his Otto, but an easy remedy will be found among us. The bishop of Laon, with Otto and Heribert supporting him, has gone to the duke at the place they call Dordingum. Return; let there be no delay.

## LETTER XCV. TO THE BROTHERS OF FLEURY, IN THE PERSON OF THE ABBOTS OF REIMS

We rightly profess that we belong to one community, since your good fortune raises us up and your misfortune humbles us, even in the estimation of the most distinguished men. The ambition of certain people, their wantonness, and their detestable audacity defile this most holy fellowship and purest friendship, since through faction a man has been placed over you whom the truest Fathers do not hesitate to condemn.

And since there is one Catholic Church and one fellowship of all the faithful, we have resolved not to depart from the judgments of those who shine in the Church of the Lord like the brightest stars through everlasting ages. Is not the revered Father Maiolus a most radiant star? Is not Father Ecbert [Ebrard] a brilliant constellation?

In a letter that the latter recently sent to our venerable father Adalbero, archbishop—his judgment had been sought concerning the appointment of your father—he says, among other things:

“Indeed, the man had long been notorious among you for his infamous conduct, but that he should obtain such a position by your decision was beyond expectation. Again, after some further remarks in the same letter: Since it is therefore our concern, we have tried to exhort our neighbors and fellow citizens. If they cannot eliminate this sacrilege, they will proclaim that he must be deprived of the fellowship of the saints; nor will there be any faithful Christian to whom this ambitious audacity will not become detestable. We cannot praise what has been done; we do not know what will happen.

“Another cries out, and at the same time marks us out, saying: ‘We are no less burdened by the fact that that monastic superior, whom we believe to stand at the summit of religion, dares, while he serves under you and is at odds with you, to judge us mistaken.’ And who would dare approve a man raised up by fraudulent ambition, when Father Benedict says that every exaltation is a form of pride?

“Again, at the end of the same letter: ‘Even if this does not seem foolish to you, we shall condemn his access to us to perpetual closure. Let the leaders act and judge as they wish; we, the poor of Christ, shall not be turned from this judgment by favor or fear of secular powers.’”

Pay attention to these words, companions and fellow soldiers. Separate yourselves, as Christ’s sheep, from him who is not a shepherd but a wolf that ravages sheep. Let him parade before himself the kings, dukes of the world, and princes by whose favor alone he made himself the leader of those monks, and let him not blush to thrust himself forward when, in humility, he ought to have withdrawn.

Let it be enough that until now ignorance has caused us to go astray. Let the man who is condemned by the judgment of such Fathers lack our fellowship. Then let him be joined to us, when he has been reconciled by the judgment of those whose decision has now deprived him of our fellowship.

## LETTER XCVI. TO THE BROTHERS OF BLANDINIUM

You who adopted me as your brother have made us feel your orphanhood most deeply; and that man of venerable memory has made us mindful of him forever through honorable services. Therefore act quickly and seek a father worthy of you, lest the Lord’s flock wander without a shepherd. If you need our help, use it—our counsel and assistance—according to our strength and knowledge. Return our books as quickly as possible; and if that which was to be copied by Claudianus is also sent, it will be a thing most worthy of you and of your charity.

## LETTER XCVII. IN THE PERSON OF QUEEN EMMA, TO HER MOTHER

[Col. 0226D]

My grief has grown heavier, O my lady, O sweet name of mother, since I lost my husband. My hope was in my son, but he has become an enemy. My once sweetest friends have withdrawn from me, to my disgrace and that of my entire family. They have fabricated the most wicked charges against the bishop of Laon. They persecute him and strive to strip him of his rightful honor, so that everlasting disgrace may be branded upon me—disgrace that may appear to be an entirely just cause for my losing my own honor.

Come to me, pious mother, to your daughter filled with sorrow. My enemies boast that I have no brother, relative, or friend left who can bring me aid. Let the pious lady attend to these matters; let your daughter-in-law return to favor. Let her be reconciled to me through you, and let it be permitted me to love her son, whom I suffer as my own enemy. Counts Otto and Heribert, most powerful men, will be with me in your counsel.

If it can be done, free us from our cares so that we may enjoy mutual conversations. If not, gather your ancient wisdom from every quarter; prepare for the Franks an unexpected counterstroke, so that the force with which they rage against us may recoil upon them. Meanwhile, indicate both in writing and through a most faithful messenger what you think should be done.

## LETTER XCVIII. IN THE PERSON OF THE BISHOP OF LAON, TO THE BISHOPS

Although, through the faction of certain men and by royal power, I am at present excluded from my own see, I have by no means been deprived of my episcopal office. Nor do falsely alleged crimes condemn a man whose innocent conscience does not reproach him in this matter.

Let the flock therefore feel the absence of its shepherd, and let me also feel that you grieve on my behalf. Therefore I admonish, ask, beg, entreat, and, in the name of the ever-living and awe-inspiring Lord, solemnly adjure you: grant holy chrism to my church in whatever manner and through whatever person you can, but do not perform episcopal blessing or the solemnities of the Mass in my parish, because it is written: “Whatever you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.”

But if you despise divine and human laws and do not heed our admonitions, know that, although you deserve to be struck by divine vengeance, you will nevertheless be summoned before a greater hearing under ecclesiastical law.

## LETTER XCIX. IN THE PERSON OF ADALBERON, ARCHBISHOP, TO THE BISHOP OF BEAUVAIS

[Col. 0227C]

See *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXVII, under ADALBERON OF REIMS, letter 25.

## LETTER C. TO ECBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER

How much benefit a firmly established peace between our kings has brought, and how much it will bring, is demonstrated by the city of Verdun, restored in its entirety to your authority without slaughter or bloodshed, without hostages, and without payments. Cologne will also bear witness when the matters long withheld from it are restored in full.

This would have happened sooner if the sharper concerns of the kingdoms had not recently detained us longer in the making of peace, because of the perverse conduct of certain of our people. Now, therefore, having found an opportune time, we place ourselves at your service. We advise that Dudo and Count Gesilbert, invaders of the property of your Church, be excommunicated without delay.

Let your brother be warned that your friend Adalbero, archbishop of Reims, concerning Dudo, and Guido, bishop of Soissons, concerning Gesilbert, must not permit them to injure the sons of their Church with impunity. Rather, let them excommunicate those whom you have excommunicated until they obtain forgiveness from you through worthy satisfaction—those who have attempted to possess the sanctuary of the Lord as an inheritance.

We earnestly ask that you inform us, in complete confidence, what our lady Theophania, Empress, ever Augusta, will undertake in public affairs in the time ahead, in what places she will remain, and whether the Saxon army, victorious, has returned from its accustomed enemy. We shall receive whatever concerns you and yours with an averted and sorrowful face, but we shall accept and carry forward whatever is favorable with the greatest joy. [Col. 0228A]

## LETTER CI. TO THE SAME

Pressed by the multitude of our concerns, by the haste of the embassy, and also by the length of the roads, we were deprived, with great sorrow, of the conference we desired with you. But the presence of the distinguished man Folmar refreshed us. Through him your virtue became evident, since you employ as your minister one who praiseworthily fulfills the Lord’s will even without being instructed.

We are therefore devoted to your service, both because of this matter and because of the great affection that our senior Adalbero bears toward us; he wished you in every respect to be participants in the things we have done.

On the fourth day before the Kalends of April, Lady Duchess Beatrice had arranged at the palace of Compiègne that on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, at Montfaucon, Lady Adelaide the Empress, Duke Charles, King Louis, Queen Emma, and Duke Henry should meet to conclude peace. But because this had been arranged without the knowledge of Lady Theophania, Empress, ever Augusta, we understood that deception lay behind it. We therefore advised that peace should instead be made through her own agency, and that you should first investigate through your own efforts what the terms of peace would be.

This was approved, and your companions on the journey were named; on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June we were to meet for a conference with the Franks. If there our senior has concluded peace with the king, he will work with all his strength for peace among the kingdoms. It is enough to have offered a few suggestions to your great intelligence.

As for the land that is being forcibly taken from you in our regions, we advise you to remain silent for the present. Later we shall show you what you ought to do about it.

## LETTER CII. TO ADALBERON, ARCHBISHOP

Consider with what confidence and caution you ought to seek conferences with Otto and Heribert, lest, because of the present siege of Chèvremont, new plans be prepared against you through new deceptions from every direction. Remember the fate of Guifridus [Godefridus], and of the bishop of Verdun, because of the seizure of the castle of Luxembourg.

## LETTER CIII. TO LADY THEOPHANIA, EMPRESS, IN THE PERSON OF ADALBERON

See *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXVII, under ADALBERON OF REIMS, letter 26.

## LETTER CIV. TO ECBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER, IN THE PERSON OF ADALBERON

[Col. 0228D]

See above, letter 27.

## LETTER CV. TO THE BROTHERS OF BLANDINIUM, IN THE PERSON OF ADALBERON

See above, letter 28.

## LETTER CVI. TO ECBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER

Because we have long been unable to enjoy your eagerly desired counsel, we do not endure it with sufficient patience; we press forward and labor to overcome our difficulties amid the din of events. A synod has reportedly been summoned in the regions of the Rhine. Both the increasingly serious illnesses of our bishops and royal affairs are disturbing the synod that we wished to hold together.

But, lest we meanwhile languish in idleness, we intend for the present to seek the intercession of blessed Otto. Through you we plan to obtain a return, so that we may punish our prolonged separation by that reunion. Since our route takes us through Verdun, send there, if possible, on the Kalends of November, the cross that, as we hope, has been fashioned through your knowledge; let this be a pledge of friendship. As the pleasing work is more frequently brought before our eyes, our undivided love will increase day by day.

## LETTER CVII. IN THE PERSON OF KING HUGH, TO SIGUINUS, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

Since we do not wish to abuse royal power in anything, we arrange all affairs of the state through the deliberation and judgment of our faithful men, and we judge you entirely worthy to share in their counsel. Therefore, with honorable and benevolent affection, we warn you to confirm before the Kalends of November the loyalty that the others have pledged to us, for the peace and harmony of the holy Church of the Lord and of the entire Christian people.

Otherwise, if—something we do not desire—you pay insufficient attention to what must carefully be carried out at the persuasion of certain wicked men, you will have to endure the harsher judgment of the lord pope and the bishops of the neighboring provinces, and our gentleness, known to all, will assume through royal power the most just zeal for correction.

## LETTER CXI. TO BASIL AND CONSTANTINE, ORTHODOX EMPERORS  
HUGH, BY THE GRACE OF GOD KING OF THE FRANKS

Both the nobility of your lineage and the glory of your great deeds urge and compel us to love you. You seem to be men whose friendship could not be considered more worthy among human affairs. We seek this most holy friendship and most just fellowship in such a way that we do not seek your kingdoms or your wealth through it.

But this arrangement makes those things that belong to our authority belong to you, and, if it pleases you, our union will be of great use and will produce great fruits. For, while we stand in the way, neither a Gaul nor a German will assail the frontiers of the Roman Empire.

Therefore, so that these benefits may become permanent, since we have one son, who is himself king, and cannot arrange a marriage for him with someone equal to him because of the kinship of the neighboring kings, we seek with special affection a daughter of the holy Empire. If this request pleases your most serene ears, inform us with imperial letters or with trustworthy messengers, so that whatever has been spoken may be fulfilled in fact through our envoys worthy of your majesty. [Col. 0230A]

## LETTER CXII. IN THE PERSON OF KING HUGH, TO BORELLUS, MARQUIS

Since the anticipatory mercy of the Lord has granted us a most peaceful kingdom of the Franks, we have decided to come to the aid of your unrest as quickly as possible, with the counsel and assistance of all our faithful men.

If, therefore, you wish to preserve the loyalty that you have so often offered to us and to our predecessors through intermediaries, lest we be deceived by a vain hope of your support when we come to your region, then, as soon as you learn that our army has spread through Aquitaine, hasten to us with a few men. In this way you will both confirm your promised loyalty and show the army the roads it needs.

But if you prefer to remain where you are and have chosen to obey us rather than the Ishmaelites, send envoys to us by Easter. They will both gladden us concerning your loyalty and make you entirely certain of our arrival.

## LETTER CXVI. TO ROMULF, ABBOT OF SENS

By God’s favor we are well, and we wish you to be even better. We are using, as we have always used, the grace and goodwill of princes, awaiting in due time the conversion of a good hope into reality. Where we shall remain for the future is uncertain because of these uncertain times.

Since you wrote that our work would be of no small size, but we did not know the measure of the volume, we sent two solidi through the cleric whom you sent. We shall do the same if you indicate it, until, when the work is complete, you say: “It is enough.”

## LETTER CXIX. EMMA, ONCE QUEEN, TO LADY THEOPHANIA, EMPRESS
May the piety of your name come to the aid of one afflicted and captured by brigands. I once possessed both lineage and dignity, and the royal name. Now, as though without lineage or dignity, I am subjected to every insult, made the captive handmaid of the cruelest enemies. And how could that impious Charles hear my voice, when he scorned to hear yours? Yet you held me worthy of your remembrance, and ordered what you wished to be done on my behalf [Col. 0231A]; while he occupied the royal city. He does not think that obedience to anyone accords with his name. I do not wish to explain to him the spirit with which he vainly promises himself kingdoms. I ask only this: let him not strike a woman in me, while he is beaten back among men.

## LETTER CXX. TO THE LADY AUGUSTA THEOPHANIA, IN THE NAME OF KING HUGH. V. I. D. K. V. A. Z.

Feeling your benevolence and affability toward us, and wishing to receive hostages from Charles and to lift the siege according to your will, we desired to preserve our most faithful alliance and holy friendship. But this Charles, despising your envoys and authority [Col. 0231B], neither acquiesces in these matters, nor releases the queen, nor accepts any hostages from the bishop. Let him see for himself what benefit his obstinacy brings him. Wishing, however, to confirm your friendship toward us forever, we have decided that A., associate and participant in our kingdom, should come to meet you at the estate of Satanicum on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September. Whatever you establish among yourselves as good and just, we shall preserve forever, without deceit or fraud, between ourselves and your son.

## LETTER CXXI. TO [AN ADDRESSEE] OF TREVES. V. V. D. K. A.

See volume CXXXVII of the *Patrologia*, in ADALBERON OF RHEIMS, letter 38.

## LETTER CXXII. ADALBERON, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS, TO DUKE CHARLES.

[Col. 0231C]

See above, letter 39.

## LETTER CXXIII. TO THIETMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

Exhausted by the labor of the siege against Charles and severely tormented by the force of fevers, I am not sufficiently able to express my sincere affection toward you, dearest brother. I signify only this: command, and we shall obey; and let our friendship consist in willing and refusing the same things. And since, amid the grave heats of cares, philosophy alone can be like a remedy, wherever we possess incomplete portions of it, let your diligence supply what is lacking.

For the present, write back only what is missing for us in the first volume of the second edition of Boethius, in the book *Perihermenias*: namely, from the place where it is written, “But ‘does not run’ and ‘does not labor’”—the words “when it signifies time” included—up to the place where it says, “the words spoken according to themselves are indeed names, and signify something” [Col. 0231D]. For this portion of the deficient commentary, we shall not be forgetful of your kindness; we shall not abandon the faith conceived in our mind, and whatever you wish we shall carry out to the best of our ability.

## LETTER CXXIV. A. H. C. H. J. V. B. Z.

My ancient palaces having been demolished down to their foundations, even the palace that, as it was rising again, you undertook to build for me has almost been swallowed up by your flood [Col. 0232A]. We are pressing on, and at our own expense we are embellishing the construction of so great a work with new craftsmen, lest, upon your arrival, we be forced to move into suburban quarters. Grant this enormous undertaking another fifteen days, and send back your architect A., who can complete what has been begun without expense to me; and so await us with all your forces, if that is your pleasure, for the breaching [variant: breaking] of the fortress and the tearing up of the mountain from its very roots.

## LETTER CXXV. TO AN UNKNOWN RECIPIENT

Since nature joins many people to us through kinship, and many through affection, no fruit of friendship is sweeter than that which rests upon the foundation of charity. For whose services have we ever found more refined or more pleasing than yours? Finally, amid such great disturbance of our commonwealth, while we continually suffer the treachery of soldiers, we continually turn our eyes toward you, certain that we shall not return without bringing back consolation [Col. 0232B].

And since we do not wish you to be burdened or exhausted except in the greatest necessity, Z. Z. Q. M. B. and, if you judge it so, any other person, with the strength of soldiers, aid, and V. Q. O. V. E. X., on the second day before the Kalends of October, so that both our terrified deserters may return and our enemies may waste away before new and unexpected forces.

## LETTER CXXVI. TO AN UNKNOWN RECIPIENT

Because you have been restored from impaired health, you rightly lessen our prolonged sorrow. For we rejoice if you rejoice, and grieve if you grieve. Thus the holy fellowship remains, feeling one and the same thing. Nor do we alone feel your sweet affection toward us: those also feel it who, with no small delight, behold the marvelous work of the cross that you have fashioned in our name, in which the pledge of friendship claims eternity for itself [Col. 0232C].

## LETTER CXXVII. TO AN UNKNOWN RECIPIENT

We devise, we attempt; we do what we wish, and what we do not wish we cannot do. Behold, Rai. and G., whom you indicated would be sent to you, have been unable to carry out your command: one is worn down by his usual illness, the other by an unusual one, though it has ended with weariness of himself [Col. 0232D].

R. will carry it out very soon, having been changed for the better; and it has long been in his mind that Count Hermann should be present through his services [variant: “formerly following”]. And since you know with how much silence and fidelity we have entrusted our secrets, we ask you to act in our place and in the place of our legate with Count Heribert, doing whatever you decide by wiser counsel. When the court is concluded, we beg you to confer with us what you have heard, reported, and discovered, intending to use your wise counsel in everything.

## LETTER CXXVIII. TO ADELAIDE, MOTHER OF KINGDOMS

The letter of the former lady Hemma, sent long ago to D. Q. V. M. H. E., bears witness to the straits in which she is afflicted and the anguish under which she is pressed [Col. 0233A]. We have sent you a copy of it, both so that you might know what has happened and how it has benefited her not at all, and so that you might investigate the cause of the deceit—if indeed it is deceit.

Certainly it is clear that you have hitherto been a most illustrious lady and mother of kingdoms. We have believed that, if dangers should arise for us, you would wish to come to our aid; how much more distressing, then, if you do not help your once-beloved daughter, whether her power has been taken from her or not. Nevertheless, we urge you to inquire of Charles, through powerful envoys, whether he wishes to return her to you or to entrust her to your protection. For he seems to retain her with such obstinate purpose for this reason: lest he appear to have taken her without cause.

## LETTER CXXIX. V. V. D. A. H. G. I. D. V. I. D.

Although I know that you are sufficiently occupied with your own affairs, the common danger ought to make you more solicitous. You know what agreements we made with Counts Odo and Heribert, and why we gave hostages. They are pressing us and demanding the friendship that was promised. Therefore I must answer their messengers concerning my will and yours on the third day before the Nones of September [Col. 0233B].

You know the customs, designs, deceit, and fraud of those among whom I live. Return, then, as far as Bublion, so that I may speak with you about matters that I cannot commit to writing. They are important matters and greatly concern you. And because I cannot leave the city without grave danger, if you wish, the count’s men [Manac., Count] will come to meet you and bring you to us with complete security [Col. 0233C]. Farewell, and send back as quickly as possible whatever is in your heart.

## LETTER CXXX. TO THE MONK RAINAUD

Do not suppose, dearest brother, that it is through any fault of mine that I have been deprived for so long of the presence of my brothers. Since I departed from you, I have pursued the cause of my father Columbanus to the best of my ability, through frequent journeys. Ambition for kingdoms and these dreadful and pitiable times have turned right into wrong; no one’s loyalty is repaid according to justice. Yet, knowing that everything depends upon the judgment of the Lord, who at once changes the hearts and kingdoms of the children of men, I patiently await the outcome of events. I both advise and urge you to do the same.

Meanwhile, I ask one thing most earnestly—something that may be done without danger or harm to you and that will bind me to you most closely in friendship [Col. 0233D]. You know with what zeal I seek copies of books from everywhere; you know how many scribes are found here and there in the cities and countryside of Italy. Come, then, and, with no one but yourself aware of it, arrange at your own expense for the following to be copied for me: Manilius’ *Astronomica*, Victorinus on rhetoric, and Demosthenes the ophthalmologist. I promise you, brother, and hold it as certain, that I am keeping this faithful service and this praiseworthy obedience under holy silence; and whatever you spend, I shall send back in full, according to your instructions and at the time you command. Only indicate to whom we should deliver both your gifts and our writings, and more frequently gladden us with your letters. Do not fear that whatever you deposit under our trust will come to the knowledge of anyone [Col. 0234A].

## LETTER CXXXI

We rejoice greatly that we continually enjoy your benevolence in accordance with the dignity of your name, both for our advantage and for the advancement of your honor. We are now glad at the presence of our nephew Adalberon, bishop of Verdun, who has promised that, taking account of place and time, he will be present with forces.

Therefore, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, you will display to the city of Rheims a greatness equal to his in affection of mind. You will also conceal this from the monk who carries the letter and cover the matter with safe silence, so that your arrival may be secret and unexpected to us [Col. 0234B].

## LETTER CXXXII

How much counsel and reason you turn over in your prudent mind, the outcome of Charles’s journeys has made clearer than anything else. But unless you are able to drive him from your province as an enemy, you ought to have remembered your friends, Queen Hemma and Bishop Adalberon. And if he wishes to raise a friend to the kingdom, he nevertheless ought not to forget them; moreover, among the faithless evil deeds are not overcome by benefits.

Inform us, then, whether any of these matters can be changed for the better through you; why the conference announced for peace between the kings was neglected; and whether at least future peace between them is assured. Meanwhile, if we have earned anything through your benevolence, we ask and implore you earnestly that no prejudice be done to our soldier We. on behalf of Ber. For they have a common estate in litigation with the Church, and B. wishes that a share of the chapel of the new construction be ceded to him—something that cannot lawfully be held except by an equitable division [Col. 0234C]. Farewell in good health, and, if you please, return our codex through a faithful messenger.

## LETTER CXXXIII. Z. R. B. I.

For a long time now we have anxiously been deprived of your presence, and we reserve many matters to be arranged by your counsels. You know to how few people the affairs of the commonwealth should be entrusted. Therefore we desire, advise, and beg with every affection of charity that you be present at Rheims on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, both because of the most important considerations that it is lawful for you alone to know, and also for arranging the appointment of O., the designated bishop of Senlis [Col. 0234D].

## LETTER CXXXIV. TO REMIGIUS, MONK OF TREVES

You understood very well the matter concerning the number D., namely how it measures itself. For once one is one, but not for that reason does every number measure itself, as you wrote, because it is equal to itself. For although four, taken once, are four, it does not follow that four measure four; rather, two does, for twice two is four.

Moreover, the letter I that you found marked beneath the figure X signifies units; these, distributed into six and four, produce a sesquialteral proportion. The same can also be seen in six and two, where unity is the difference. We have sent you no sphere, nor do we presently have one; nor is it a matter of little labor for people so occupied with civil affairs [Col. 0235A]. If, therefore, concern for such matters holds you, send us the volume of Statius’ *Achilleid*, carefully prepared, so that by your gift you may obtain the sphere which, because of its difficulty, you cannot have for free.

## LETTER CXXXV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP

Just as the report of your journey brought us sorrow, so the changed report of your delayed journey brought, as it were, the fruit of joy. We were anxious both because of your absence and because honors did not correspond to the merits of so great a person.

We are therefore making every effort, and assigning to a period of time what the brevity of the season did not allow; we are also preparing gifts according to our means. I say “means” because you know among whom we live and by how much treachery of certain people we are harassed. The siege of the city of Laon, interrupted during the intervening peace, must also be resumed on the tenth day before the Kalends of November [Col. 0235B].

Therefore, as we have advised, we advise again: come both for the relief of the soldiers, if we should need it, and for the assistance of our captive fellow-brother A., and so that B. and G. may present themselves as brothers more worthy of your exhortation, amid such great danger to affairs.

## LETTER CXXXVI

Do not bear heavily or with an unjust spirit the Lord’s most just correction, dearest brother. For the Godhead does not deem the impious worthy of chastisement by his scourge, reserving them to be punished with eternal torments. Learn to preserve steadfastness in adversity. And if you cannot imitate Job and the ancient priests of our order, at least take as your model a layman of our own time, and one related to you: Count Godefrid [Col. 0235C].

We shall not be forgetful of your salvation, nor shall we leave unattempted anything that ought to be done for you. Let I. V. Q. know everything that concerns you, so that he may make our legate completely informed in every respect at Paris on the feast of Saint Dionysius, so that, if a siege is to take place—and if it is not—one plan after another may be broken.

Farewell happily, and attend to this one thing: do not cast yourself headlong, so that it would be better to have perished in another way than, through your destruction, to leave eternal disgrace to yourself and your descendants. Farewell again, and beware greatly of I. V. I. Q. Z. II. Z. A., as of a treacherous and deceitful man [Col. 0235D].

## LETTER CXXXVII

Because of the absence of our soldiers, the matter you requested did not achieve its full effect; nevertheless, it remains our intention, and upon their return we shall carry out whatever we can. But if you desire perpetual peace for the peasants of Asinetum, let Count Cen. come to us as soon as possible, so that the plans may be compared on their merits and your military force may bring us worthy assistance, according to what we shall signify through him. We entrust these matters to trustworthy ears because of the enemies’ manifold ambushes.

## LETTER CXXXVIII
