We congratulate you on the restoration of your improved bodily condition, and at the same time because you wished to know about ours. By the Lord’s favor we are well, and we wish every good thing according to our prayers. We neither knowingly strive to violate the friendship begun, nor to repel the injury inflicted by our people; rather, from the Kalends of January until the beginning of Lent, we are ready to meet you at the borders of our France, Burgundy, and the kingdom of Lotharingia, as soon as you designate a fixed day and a place described by its proper name, so that the peace and concord of kingdoms and of the Lord’s Churches may not be abandoned through our fault [Col. 0236A].

## LETTER CXXXIX

To a learned man, steadfastly holding to pure faith, which belongs to few today, we shall disclose two sayings of Christ, together with our counsel, and answer the question proposed. We say: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s”; and: “Let the dead bury their own dead.”

Having considered these things, pursue honorably what has been lawfully enjoined by the bishop. You shall avoid whatever is brought forward by anyone against divine law. Let the sons of darkness, the sons of Belial, use their time dishonorably; but we, sons of light and sons of peace, do not place our hope in man, who withers like grass. Let us await patiently what the Prophet says: “I saw the wicked exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; I passed by, and behold, he was not there; I sought him, and his place was not found” [Col. 0236B].

## LETTER CXL

We are not sufficient to repay with fitting thanks the benefits of our liberator. We rejoice also that our members, which seemed in you to have been swallowed by hell, have been snatched from its jaws by Christ the victor.

But, as is appropriate to the present time, we advise you to learn through conversation with us what you should seek and what you should avoid before you join the assemblies of the princes of our kingdom. At the same time, by letter or through a faithful messenger, indicate whether you presently consider the journey of A. II. and Ra. to Count Otto safe, and where they should meet [Col. 0236C].

## LETTER CXLI

After longer deliberation, nothing safer for the common good has been found than to abstain for the present from an interview with your lord, if this can be done honorably. But if you cannot touch upon the substance of greater causes, it is good to decide nothing except what is clearly useful.

Meanwhile, relying on the good faith of all, Ra. will await your legate at Senlis on Thursday, or will proceed to Chartres if you approve, and return to Compiègne if you so indicate [Col. 0236D].

## LETTER CXLII. ADALBERON, BISHOP OF R., AND SCHOLARIS, ABBOT, TO THEIR CONSTANTINE

We congratulate you, dearest brother, that the invader and enemy of monastic religion has been removed from human affairs, to the salvation of many. Press on, then; and if you already have a Father worthy of your love and that of your brothers, let us also have him present through your efforts very soon, on the feast of Saint Remigius, so that our affection—having been somewhat estranged from the monks of Fleury through your agency—may through your agency be greatly reconciled.

But if all this cannot easily be done, let us at least be permitted to enjoy your presence, if we have ever done anything that pleased you, and if you deem it worthy to do something that may please us [Col. 0237A].

## LETTER CXLIII

If you now show, in minor matters, the benevolence that you bestowed without partiality in the greatest matters, you ought to expect no small praise and no slight reward. You labored so that we might be freed from the enemy, but now you have been disregarded because the Lord freed us from the lion’s mouth.

Continue your customary service, so that, by the command of your lord and lady, that violent brigand may at least be compelled to return our household goods. We do not seek gold or masses of silver, but things whose absence is disgraceful. We mean tapestries, carpets, and similar objects. At the same time, we ask that our trust not be judged by the trustworthiness of one who has never promised anything that he had decided to make binding [Col. 0237B].

## LETTER CXLIV

As the letter in the royal name that we sent you states, we advise, ask, and implore you to take care to carry this out, both because of your benevolence toward us and because of the peace of the Church of the Lord that will arise from peace among the princes—unless, perhaps, we are frustrated of your desirable presence and are regarded among the faithful as faithless and suspect.

## LETTER CXLV. GERBERT TO THE BISHOP OF PARIS

Although the whole Catholic Church is one and the same, a certain measure has nevertheless been prescribed for each priest, within which he should extend himself and beyond which he should place boundaries. Therefore, concerning the case of Abbot Rotbert, because of the loyalty that we maintain and always wish to maintain toward you, we propose these three points for deliberation [Col. 0237C].

First, that it is not our right to place the sickle in another’s harvest; for this we return manifold thanks, since you have deigned to honor us even beyond what is owed.

Second, that the monastery of Saint Dionysius possesses such reverence and dignity that no magistrate there should be removed or appointed without the consent and solemn approval of the provincials whose concern it is.

Third, if you postpone the matter, we propose that it be suggested to your gentleness that we shall discover whatever is more honorable and useful together with the most religious and distinguished men.

## LETTER CXLVI

On the tenth day before the Kalends of January, we sent to your fraternity, through R., the namesake of his father, a letter received from the king, in which your arrival and that of my brother in the city of Rheims were requested, so that we might go to meet the king’s legates on the fifth day before the Kalends of January. They indeed came as agreed, but they did not find you.

We now send a copy of our earlier letter, requesting that an immediate reply be given concerning both your own will and your action [Col. 0237D].

## LETTER CXLVII. EMMA, ONCE QUEEN OF THE FRANKS

These are bitter times, priest of the Lord, in which the most holy faith is everywhere growing scarce. But remember that faith which you have always promised and which I would rather believe you will preserve. Let my captivity and the hands of brigands move you.

I speak to one who knows [Col. 0238A]: I am that Emma, once queen of the Franks, who ruled over so many thousands. Now I do not even have native-born companions with whom I might at least approach the assembly of so great a duke as Henry, nor am I permitted to enjoy your desirable presence for the sake of obtaining safety and counsel.

Come, then, to assist our case—not to decide it, but to defer it until we may speak with one another. We speak of the castle of Q. G. R.; and do not allow your brother to be called a traitor, whom until now we have found to remain in unfeigned faithfulness.

Meanwhile, since, as you know, the agent of our affairs has neither returned nor have we heard what has happened to him, do not return empty-handed. Bring back in your purses the money for which we have long been waiting; you will receive payment and favor for your worthy services, both for this and for the others that you have often rendered.

## LETTER CXLVIII. TO REMIGIUS, MONK OF TREVES

[Col. 0238B]

**GERBERT, SCHOLARIS AND ABBOT, TO REMIGIUS, MONK OF TREVES**

Your affection, most loving brother, weighs heavily upon the work of the *Achilleid*, which you did indeed begin well, but abandoned when the exemplar failed. Therefore, mindful of your kindness, we too have begun a very difficult work: a sphere, which has already been polished on the lathe and skillfully wrapped in horsehide.

But if you are wearied by an excessive desire to possess one decorated with plain coloring, expect it around the Kalends of March—unless, perhaps, you wait for one adorned with a horizon and the beauty of various colors, and dread a year’s labor [Col. 0238C].

As for what was given and received among our dependents, the law has been so established that he who owed nothing should return nothing.

## LETTER CXLIX

We bear your absence with considerable annoyance, but we are weighed down by even greater concern because we do not know what is happening around you. For since we share in your concerns, we certainly ought not to be ignorant of the progress and outcome of your affairs.

Hasten, therefore, and make clear by letter what you have subsequently done, are doing, and soon intend to do concerning public and private business; at the same time, indicate what you wish us to do. On the second day before the Ides of February, when the election of the bishop is to be held—and preferably on the preceding day—we shall await your replies: what Ansel has done among the counts; why we have still not seen his messenger; whether we ought first to meet the king and the counts; whether we ought to postpone the journey to the appointed conference at Cale; whether you will come there; and through whose favor these and similar matters are to be accomplished. Deposit all this in full faith with those who have complete confidence in you [Col. 0238D].

## LETTER CL

We answer your freely given benevolence with no merits of our own. For what have we ever contributed worthy of the embassy of Roderic? This alone remains for us to understand: what was meant when it was said that we should not prefer the interests of any king or bishop to those of you and your lord.

For it is not sufficiently clear whether you command us, abandoning everything we possess, to follow you and your interests, or whether, in a certain manner of speaking, you merely wish to relieve us with consoling hope from the attack of raging fortune [Col. 0239A].

King Hugh, the neighboring bishops, and those who seek the see of Rheims offer very much. But we have accepted nothing from them so far, nor do we attempt to do anything without your counsel. For this reason we have delayed approaching the king, lest, having been carried off by him, we seem to have rejected your commands. Because the sweetest affection of my dear father Adalberon is to be preferred above all mortals, it is desirable somehow to discern that affection in you.

I have carefully entrusted to Roderic the execution of the remaining matters that were in our mind and that we wished to have done concerning you.

## LETTER CLI. GERBERT’S GREETING TO ONE WHO WROTE TO HIM UNDER THE NAME OF THE REVEREND FATHER ADALBERON, BISHOP OF VERDUN

If you ask about my condition, whoever you are who claim familiarity with me, I may answer—by your leave—that I am placed amid adversities with a good disposition, following a strong man but not overtaking him.

As for the affairs of the commonwealth, I do not report them, since I do not know what to write. I would have explained more fully the private matter of my brother suffering from stone, if it were permitted me to see what had been discovered by those before us. For now I am content with a small portion of the antidote *philoanthropos* and its written account. Blame yourself if you turn what has been prepared for health into destruction by failing to observe a regimen.

Nor should you wish, with me as your authority, to handle matters belonging to physicians, especially since I have only aspired to their knowledge and have always avoided their practice [Col. 0239B].

## LETTER CLII. TO REMIGIUS

[Col. 0239C]

**GERBERT TO HIS BROTHER REMIGIUS**

Such was the importance and power of my lord and father Adalberon in affairs hanging upon eternity that, once he had been dissolved into the origins of things, the world seemed likely to fall back into primordial chaos. In so great a disturbance and, so to speak, confusion, you looked too incautiously into what you might wish and what you might ask, forgetting the duties owed by mortals.

Was it necessary, in such a crisis, with the commonwealth abandoned, to turn to the commentaries of philosophers—at times unnecessary ones? I say nothing of myself, against whom no threats of death were directed, and whom Father Adalberon had designated as his successor with the favor of the entire clergy, all the bishops, and certain soldiers, while they insisted that I had been the author of everything that displeased them [Col. 0239D].

For the friends who had enjoyed the companionship of the blessed Father Adalberon with me and had labored with me were about to abandon me for the sake of a turned piece of wood.

Bear patiently, then, with the delays imposed by necessity, and await better times, in which studies that have long since died out in us may be revived.

## LETTER CLIII. OF THE EMPEROR OTTO TO GERBERT

**To G., most skilled in philosophy and crowned with the laurels of its three branches, OTTO, as befits him.**

[Note: [Col. 0239D] Alternatively, “Emperor Otto to his teacher Gerbert.”]

We wish your excellence, venerable to all for its most loving attachment, to be joined to us, and we adopt for ourselves the everlasting constancy of so great a patron, because the disciplined eminence of your teaching has always been an authority not disdainful of our simplicity [Col. 0240A].

Nevertheless, so that, every ambiguity removed, we may enjoy from you the speech of naked truth, we have judged and firmly resolved that this letter should make our will clear to you: in this matter, the essence of our adoption and the singularity of our request is that your skillful foresight should, in writing as well as in speech, apply itself to correcting us, unlearned and badly trained, beyond its customary measure, and to counsel of the highest loyalty [variant: felicity] in public affairs.

In conveying this will of ours, which we do not wish to be refused, we want you to recoil from Saxon rusticity, but to be summoned all the more to this pursuit by our Greek subtlety. For if there is anyone who can awaken it, some spark of Greek industry will be found among us [Col. 0240B].

For this reason, having abundantly applied the flame of your knowledge to our little fire, we humbly beg you, with God’s help, to awaken the lively Greek intellect and teach us the book of arithmetic, so that, fully instructed by its teachings, we may understand something of the subtlety of those who came before us.

Let your paternal authority not delay informing us by letter what you think should be done in this matter and what should not. Farewell.

I have never composed verses, nor have I cultivated them. When I have them in use and flourish in them [variant: am strong in them], however many men Gaul contains, so many poems shall I send you.

## LETTER CLIV. GERBERT TO OTTO CAESAR

[Col. 0240C]

**To the lord and glorious Otto Caesar, ever Augustus, Gerbert, by the grace of God bishop of Rheims, whatever is worthy of so great an emperor.**

For your surpassing benevolence, by which we are judged worthy forever of your service, we may perhaps answer with our prayers, but we cannot answer with merits. For if we are kindled by any small spark of knowledge, all of it was produced by your glory, nourished by your father’s virtue, and acquired through your grandfather’s magnificence.

What, then? We do not contribute our own treasures to yours; rather, we return those we have received. That you have partly attained them and will very soon partly attain them is shown by the honorable and useful petition worthy of your majesty [Col. 0240D].

For unless you held firmly and fixedly that the power of numbers either contains within itself the beginnings of all things or pours them forth from itself, you would not hasten with such zeal toward full and perfect knowledge of them. And unless you embraced the gravity of moral philosophy, the humility that guards all virtues would not have been so impressed upon your words.

Yet the subtlety of a mind conscious of its own excellence is not silent, since you have taught its rhetorical power—which, so to speak, flows both from yourself and from the source of the Greeks—in a rhetorical manner. Here something almost divine is expressed: a man Greek by birth and Roman in imperial power, as though by hereditary right reclaiming for himself the treasures of Greek and Roman wisdom.

Therefore, Caesar, we obey the imperial commands, both in this matter and in everything whatsoever your divine majesty decrees. For we cannot be lacking in obedience [Col. 0241A], since among human affairs we see nothing sweeter than your rule.

## LETTER CLV. OF OTTO TO GERBERT

**Otto Augustus, emperor, to the most reverend pope Gerbert.**

[Note: [Col. 0241] Alternatively, “Otto, by the grace of God emperor Augustus, to the most reverend pope Gerbert.”]

Since, by the favor of the Godhead, we are connected not only by a line of blood but also, among all mortals, by a certain excellence of our kind, we ought not to be unlike one another in our devotion to the worship of the Lord.

Therefore, concerned in our mind for your character, we commend this Abbot Peter to your apostolate, so that whatever you learn should be done by him or by our legate concerning what is honorable and useful for his monastery, you may strive to carry out with every diligence. Thus, while we honor the memorials of the martyrs together, may we together experience their benefits. Farewell [Col. 0241B].

## LETTER CLVI. OF THE EMPEROR OTTO TO COUNT R.

**Otto, by the grace of the Lord emperor Augustus, to Count R., greetings.**

The various affairs of the kingdom sometimes compel us to issue different commands. For this reason, because of the necessity of certain matters, we recently gave the abbey of Saint Vincent at Capua to the monk John, without either judging Abbot Rothfrid or deposing him.

Therefore, out of consideration for mercy, we grant to that same Abbot Rothfrid the cell of Saint Mary, with everything belonging to it, in the county of Marsi, in the place called Apininici, together with the remaining property of Saint Vincent situated in the same county. We also grant the cell of Saint Mary in the territory of Benevento, where the place is called Sanus locus, with all the property of Saint Vincent situated in the land of Benevento [Col. 0241C].

Accordingly, we command you and the prince of Benevento that, since these properties are near you, you assist Abbot Rothfrid in holding them, out of loyalty to us, without any contradiction.

## LETTER CLVII. OF OTTO TO ADELAIDE AUGUSTA

**To the lady Adelaide, empress, ever Augusta, Otto, by the grace of the Lord emperor Augustus.**

Since, according to your prayers and desires, the Godhead has bestowed upon us the rights of imperial power with fortunate success, we worship the Godhead and render thanks to you. For we know and understand your maternal affection and your devoted efforts; for these reasons we cannot fail in service to you [Col. 0241D].

Therefore, since, as we are advanced, your honor is raised, we earnestly pray and desire that the commonwealth be advanced through you and, once advanced, be happily governed in its proper state. Farewell.

## LETTER CLVIII. OF OTTO TO GERBERT

**To the most reverend pope Gerbert, Otto, by the grace of God emperor Augustus.**

Because, constrained by the difficulty of the times, I cannot satisfy your wishes, I am afflicted with vehement sorrow. I am moved by affection and devotion toward you, but the necessity of nature, constraining everything by its own right, sets the qualities of the Italian air against the qualities of my body in a certain natural opposition [Col. 0242A].

We therefore change our place only in body, while remaining with you in mind. We leave with you, for your comfort and assistance, the leading men of Italy: Hugh the Tuscan, wholly faithful to you; Count S., prefect of the Spoleto and Camerino territories, to whom, out of love for you, we have granted the eight counties that are under litigation; and we have appointed him our legate over them for the present, so that the peoples may have a ruler and may render you, through his agency, the services owed to you.

## LETTER CLIX. OF GERBERT TO ADELAIDE AUGUSTA

**To the lady and glorious Adelaide, queen, ever Augusta, Gerbert, by the grace of the Lord bishop of Rheims, and to all his fellow-brothers and fellow-bishops of the diocese of Rheims, health in Christ [Col. 0242B].**
The letter brought a happy beginning under your name, contained salutary admonitions, but ended in sadness. For it showed your mind’s gracious affection toward me and urged me to hasten my return to my proper see. But what did so bitter an ending mean? For it says this: “Know that, if you now make light of these admonitions, we shall use both the resources and the counsels of our own people without incurring blame on your account. While I preside over the city of Rheims, when has it not been, is it not, or will it not be lawful for me to use your counsels and the resources entrusted to me? Was it more lawful when Arnulf held it? But he took it from you by deceit and fraud; I, on the contrary, preserved it for you, against the deceits and frauds of many, by many vigils and much labor. It is exceedingly strange that you do not perceive the ambushes of your enemies. For those who seek to restore Arnulf to his see for the confusion of your kingdom do not think this safe for themselves unless they first destroy me by some opportunity. We take this to be very probable for two reasons: because, when I had recently been placed at Rheims, you resolved to absolve him; and because Leo, the Roman abbot, obtained his absolution in order to confirm the new marriage of my lord King Robert, as has been reported to me by letter from the people of Rheims. To this is added the danger that the loyalty at the present court of Calmiciaca has been undermined by Guibinus, the nephew of Guibinus. The number of estates was, I believe, limitless, and the people of Rheims could not have been sufficient to possess them unless the people of Châlons had been invited to occupy them as colonies. What then? If Arnulf is to be absolved, or if Guibinus, or anyone else, is to be enthroned in my see, it is impossible to understand my return without danger to my head. I cannot doubt that this is so, although you pay too little attention to it. For I know your endeavors, which ought to be proclaimed to all mortals; I know your mind’s sweetest affections toward me. If I cannot answer them with corresponding merit, I shall answer them with my prayers.

“Therefore, so that I may intrude less upon you and speak about myself not at all—since divine grace has freed me from the immensity of dangers and, insofar as concerns me alone, arranges and preserves me in complete happiness—I beg and implore you by the dread name of almighty God to come, if you can in any way, to the aid of the desolated and battered Church of Rheims. Since it is the head of the kingdom of the Franks, if it perishes, its members must necessarily follow. But how can it not perish when, placed under the name of two men as though between hammer and anvil, it approves neither of them as ruler and therefore drifts like a rudderless vessel amid the waves of the sea? What, moreover, do you think will happen if a third is added to their number without the judgment of the Church? I do not speak these things as a soothsayer or prophet. I remember that not only my soldiers but also my clerics conspired so that no one would eat with me and no one would attend the sacred rites. I say nothing of the baseness and contempt, and nothing of the most serious injuries often inflicted upon me by many. To these things you summon me back, and the letter adds threats so that I may suffer worse. What is this, O divine majesty? Do they think me so foolish, or so alienated from you, that I do not see the swords hanging over me, or that I would plunge your Church into schism? I, however, clearly perceive the tricks of the wicked and, against every schism, defend the unity of the Church with my death, if this has been decreed.

“Therefore I ask you, my lady, ever Augusta, and likewise my brothers, my fellow bishops, who have been placed under anathema—whether justly or unjustly—for the cause of the traitor Arnulf, to bear patiently with me as I await the judgment of the Church. For I do not wish to abandon the Church, which I received to govern by the judgment of bishops, without the judgment of bishops. Nor, again, when a greater authority is present, do I intend to retain it by force against the judgment of the bishops. While I await these judgments, I endure my exile—which many consider fortunate—not without great sorrow.”

## EPISTOLA CLX

The bright face of my lord King Robert comes before me: his joyful countenance, the conversations in which I visited him, your speeches filled with wisdom and gravity, and then the gracious affability of princes and bishops. When these are taken from me, life itself is somehow burdensome.

My only consolation is the piety, benevolence, and generosity of the illustrious Caesar Otto, who loves you and what belongs to you with such affection that day and night he confers with me about where and when he might see you familiarly: my elder, King Robert, his equal in age and similar in pursuits, whom he wishes to address and embrace.

Therefore, if the journey to Rome—which the business of the synod is delaying me from undertaking—has been postponed at this time, you will expect me around the Kalends of November, as the most faithful interpreter of these matters and one entirely obedient to you.

## EPISTOLA CLXI. TO CONSTANTINE THE SCHOLASTIC

“The power of friendship reduces almost impossible things to possible ones,” and so forth. It appears above, prefixed to the little book *On the Division of Numbers*.

## OTHER LETTERS OF GERBERT

First published by André Duchesne from the manuscript copy of Jacobus Sirmond of the Society of Jesus.

(*Historiæ Francorum Scriptores*, vol. II, p. 828.)

## EPISTOLA CLXII. ELECTION OF ARNULF AS ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS, EDITED BY GERBERT

[Col. 0243C]

The sons of the metropolitan city of Rheims send greetings to the holy and universal Catholic Church.

When our father A., of divine memory, abandoned his bodily senses, we lost the bright light of our shepherd and became the prey of enemies. Therefore we set about and strive to repair the ruins of so great a man. The canonical period has elapsed; the laws have been violated, although they provide that no see may remain vacant for more than thirty days.

Now at last, when we were knocking, the divine light appeared and showed us the way we should follow: the Antichrist having been driven away and the heresy of simony condemned. We, I say, who are called the bishops of the diocese of the metropolitan city of Rheims, together with all the clergy, while the people of different orders acclaim us and our orthodox kings give their consent, choose for ourselves as prelate a man outstanding in piety, distinguished in faith, wonderful in steadfastness, prudent in counsel, and capable in the conduct of affairs. In him, these virtues, which shine so brightly, show that the others cannot be absent.

We mean Arnulf, the son of King Lothair. Although his noble blood was stained by some contagion through the fault of the times and placed him under anathema, nevertheless Mother Church, purifying him, washed him with her mystical sacraments. Him, I say, we call the son of the Church of Laon and, to speak more truthfully, of Rheims. For that city belongs to the territory of Rheims and to the parish of Rheims; nor was it so separated from blessed Remigius that it became alien. Indeed, that man, full of God, seeking unity and not desiring division, divided it in such a way that it might remain joined, like a part within the whole. Understanding what kind and how great a man he would become, he blessed his native soil with the dignity of the priesthood.

Therefore we choose this Arnulf, born here and educated here, free from the heresy of simony, removed from tyrannical faction, restoring to each person his due rights, and not laying waste to the sanctuary of God. Let fraud and [lacuna] be far from our election; and let not the sons of Belial think that it concerns them. Let the sons of peace and concord make it stable and firm forever by confirming, strengthening, and subscribing to it.

## EPISTOLA CLXIII. IN THE PERSON OF ARNULF, BISHOP OF RHEIMS

Although as yet we possess no merits, either in public affairs or in private life, our mind is nevertheless by no means lacking in them; rather, in a special way, we burn to win and retain your affection.

For this reason we patiently endure Gerard, your old soldier, using force and taking possession of the benefice of our faithful Gueniric, and we ask you to order him to be quiet. If he should perhaps disregard this, let him experience the most just defender of each of the two as his admonisher.

## EPISTOLA CLXIV. TO E., BISHOP OF TRIER, IN THE PERSON OF THE SAME MAN

Knowing your benevolence, or rather your piety, which you always showed toward my predecessor of blessed memory, I consider myself fortunate if I receive it in such a way that its acceptance knows no end.

Therefore, beginning with the abundant charity shown by you, we rejoice and desire to enjoy mutual love indissolubly. And because the tumult of divided kingdoms and the novelty of our ordination prevent us from deciding and completing matters—those who act boldly obstructing the direction of our affairs—we entrust these matters to your prudent judgment. At the same time, we ask that, if possible, it be definitely prescribed where and when we may meet after your return from the palace, and that for the present we may be certain of anything new you have learned, so that afterward we may be more fully instructed in what you will come to know more clearly.

It is a great proof that we shall remain forever in the holiest friendship and firmest fellowship when we use as interpreters the same authorities that you always employed with my predecessor, both in leisure and in business.

## EPISTOLA CLXV

I understand very well that you understand the movements of my mind, and for that reason I love and embrace you all the more carefully. I remember the most honorable admonition by which you suspended me for a sufficiently long time from communion with certain princes; you indicated what you intended.

Therefore I beg you by the venerable name of my father and by the inviolate faith with which I have always honored him and his own, not to force me to forget those men whom, for love of him, I have always loved especially, neglecting my own interests.

May the faith preserved toward my lady Theophana and her son prevent me from becoming the glory of their enemies, whom, for her sake, whenever I was able, I drove into disgrace and contempt. Again, I ask and implore you jointly not to be displeased with the service of one to whom your rule, honor, and power have until now been pleasing.

By your generosity, see to it that I do not become, in the absence of what is honorable and in the flight of the best arts, a follower of Catiline, whose teacher Marcus Tullius’ precepts I diligently carried out both in leisure and in business.

## EPISTOLA CLXVI

It is not foreign to your humanity or to the sacred priesthood to give counsel to those who seek it.

I have never given an oath to any mortal except Lord Otto of blessed memory. I have considered that oath to have extended to my lady Theophana and her son Otto Augustus, since in some way I understood the three as one.

How long, then, do you think this faith must be maintained? I say that, although stripped of the most ample possessions conferred by imperial gift and confirmed by apostolic blessing, I have not been granted even one little estate either for having kept faith or for retaining it.

I say that, placed among your gravest enemies, I have not been swayed by any of their gifts, however great they were. How long, then, shall I practice this kind of friendship? Give counsel and offer comfort to one who implores it—not because of my merits, but nevertheless because of the benefits that you have always deservedly received praise for bestowing upon all.

## EPISTOLA CLXVII

The joy I had conceived at the journey to Rome—which your company and the prospect of speaking with my lady Theophana, ever Augusta, had made greater—is disturbed by my lord’s prohibition.

Therefore, as a friend of a friend, take my place: so that through you we may obtain the pallium from the lord pope and retain through you the favor toward our lady that you began. By God’s assent, we shall be in her service at Easter, and no one will be able to prevent you from remaining faithful and devoted to her and to her son.

## EPISTOLA CLXVIII. TO RAINARD, MONK OF BOBBIO

A certain Tetbald, who called himself a monk of Bobbio, came to us last summer. Through him we sent you our letter, to which your letter does not sufficiently respond. Therefore we are sending back a copy of the earlier letter and addressing your request in this way.

If you take pleasure in serving under the rule of our father Benedict and under a spiritual abbot in another monastery, use my permission; and let neither the fact that the transfer is for the sake of religion nor that it was made by the command of your abbot be an obstacle to you.

For the rest, in giving and receiving, we partly loosen and partly tighten the reins of permission. Let discretion be preserved in this manner: give and receive whatever ought to be given and received lawfully and without offense against the divine laws. Do not think that it falls within my permission if you willingly give anything to, or receive anything from, a tyrant or an impious man.

## EPISTOLA CLXIX. TO REMIGIUS, MONK OF TRIER

Your repeated petition, sweetest brother, sufficiently shows through what waves we are being tossed. You do not know—you do not know—what shipwrecks we have endured since we departed from you.

For through the gravest labors of summer, sustained without interruption, we contracted illnesses that the pestilential autumn almost made fatal. To these things violent fortune was added, demanding back everything it had given through the plunderers who devastated the city of Rheims.

Now we mourn the captivity of our friends and deliberate with sleepless care whether our sees ought to be exchanged. Our homeland is in such grief and sorrow. Fear and trembling surround the walls; want presses upon the citizens. The clergy of both orders groans because of the devastation that is to come.

Therefore it is your duty to raise your hand to the Almighty on our behalf. And if the Divinity should lessen the punishment of our sin, we shall in every way remember your kindness.

## EPISTOLA CLXX. GERBERT TO RAYMOND

To our most reverend father Raymond, duke: his son.

You should know, sweetest Father, in what harbor I am to steer my ship after losing its pilot, and what is the condition of the Frankish commonwealth.

When I had resolved not to depart from the patronage and counsel of my father, the blessed Adalbero, I was suddenly deprived of him in such a way that I feared for my own survival. Since we were of one heart and one soul, and his enemies did not think him transferred while they saw me surviving, they pointed me out with a finger as an object of hatred to Charles, who was then and is now harassing our homeland, saying that I deposed kings and appointed kings.

And because I was entangled in the commonwealth, I suffered when the commonwealth suffered; like the greatest portion of the spoil in the destruction of our city, I was seized along with it. This entirely delayed my journey to Italy, where even the organs and the best part of my furnishings are being kept.

For we could not resist rushing fortune, nor has the Divinity yet revealed at what harbor it wishes me to stand. Therefore those who will rejoice over me and over my fortunes await the outcome of the fortune now pressing upon us.

I shall do everything in my power and omit nothing that ought to be done until I enjoy the dwelling I desire and render my vows to God in Zion. Farewell, most loving Father. May brother Ariardus fare well; may the most holy community subject to you fare well; and remember me in your contemplative prayers with my father Adal.

## EPISTOLA CLXXI. GERBERT TO A STILL VENERABLE BISHOP

Have you trusted so greatly in negligence and doubtful circumstances that you do not see the swords hanging over your neck, or feel the battering rams and siege sheds striking your flanks?

Remember, I beg you, what happened, O once fortunate and dear friend, under the rule of my father Adalbero. The brother of the deified Augustus Lothair, heir to the kingdom, was expelled from the kingdom. His rivals, as many believe, were made kings. By what right was the legitimate heir disinherited? By what right was he deprived of the kingdom? And by what right did he return to his father’s house?

What decrees of the Roman pontiffs forbade infants to be baptized? What sacred canons removed innocent priests from the altars? Abraham pleads with God over whether He ought to destroy the righteous man together with the wicked in Sodom, and you, shepherd, do not hesitate to consign the guilty and the innocent alike to punishment?

But why do I speak of these lesser matters, when I know that your accusation has been drawn up by the priests of God and is full of crimes, pregnant with wickedness? Judges have been chosen; if you fail to appear before their judgment, you will gain nothing from your absence. And if you appear, you will cease to be a bishop. Someone has been found to take your place.

Run, then, while some leisure remains, and do not place your hope in the Loire and the Seine, for this will profit you nothing. I, being aware of the factions, conspiracies, lawyers, and advisers, have said these things to you out of an old friendship, in faithful silence, so that I might rouse you from your lethargy. It is for you to seek a fuller remedy, since you also seem to have fallen into an epileptic seizure. Farewell.

## EPISTOLA CLXXII

We return immense thanks for your immense benevolence, or rather piety, toward us. You have clearly shown by your compassion how highly you regard us.

Therefore we too declare what we are planning for the future, not only from what we spend the nights discussing with a very few people, but also from the anathema already pronounced against the plunderers of the city of Rheims. We send you a copy of it so that you may fully understand what kind of mind we possess, and at the same time that we are about to undertake greater things, which we reserve for their proper time.

Everything has its time. We say what must be kept silent; we keep silent about what must be said. We do what we do not wish to do; what we wish to do, we cannot. Everything is therefore full of disturbance, or rather confusion; desirable things do not present themselves in the way that things to be avoided do.

For if a reasonable opportunity had been offered, we would long ago have sought your conversations. We would have revived the royal name, which is almost dead among the Franks, by great counsels and great strength. But because of these impious times and the wicked schemes of the most depraved men, we act secretly in matters that we cannot conduct openly.

The day will come—the day will come, I say, and it is near—on which the thoughts, words, and deeds of each of us will be tested. Meanwhile, recognize the limits prescribed for you. Do not wish to determine the greater affairs of the kingdom without the metropolitan’s knowledge, and do not hasten to pronounce judgment on matters whose purpose you do not know.

Reserve your prudence and strength; then expose your strongest hearts to the enemy on our behalf, when you see the victorious standards being carried before us as leaders.

## EPISTOLA CLXXIII

Having entered a tossing sea, we are shipwrecked and groan; nowhere does a safe shore appear, nowhere a harbor. In you we seek rest. Certainly, in you there is something which, once you have given it, is not lacking and remains in abundance for the recipient.

Therefore, with every affection of charity, we ask you to be present at Rheims on the second day before the Kalends of April, if we have earned anything by the right of friendship or think that we can earn it.

## EPISTOLA CLXXIV. TO ROMULF, ABBOT OF SENS

You have fulfilled, through your gifts, the duties of giver and receiver. For nothing in human affairs is more important to us than knowledge of illustrious men, which is certainly unfolded in the many volumes of books.

Continue, then, as you have begun, and offer the streams of Marcus Tullius to one who thirsts. Let Marcus Tullius enter into the midst of the cares with which, after the destruction of our city, we are so entangled that, although we are considered fortunate in the eyes of men, in our own judgment we are unfortunate.

We seek the things of the world, find them, and complete them; and, so to speak, we have become leaders in wickedness. Bring help, Father, so that the Divinity, excluded by the multitude of our sins, may be moved by your prayers to return, visit us, and dwell with us. May we rejoice, if possible, in your presence, we who grieve at the absence of the blessed Father Adalbero.

## EPISTOLA CLXXV. TO E., ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER

The sword has reached the soul, most blessed Father; we are hemmed in on every side by the swords of our enemies.

On one side we are pressed by the faith promised to the kings of the Franks. On the other, subjected to the power of Prince Charles, who is reclaiming the kingdom for himself, we are forced either to exchange masters or to become exiles.

This alone remains as a hope: that divine foreknowledge has bound you to us by a kind of kinship and has made us bear one another’s burdens. Therefore we flee to you as to a reliable defense, as to an altar of prudence, and as to interpreters of divine and human laws.

The counsels you deliver will be heavenly oracles to your sons.

## EPISTOLA CLXXVI. G. SENDS GREETINGS TO R., HIS BELOVED

You ask for great things, sweetest brother, but things not undeserved in view of your merits. For what is so desirable that your benevolence would not deserve it? What is so humble that these times permit it to be bestowed upon friends?

Therefore, since you lack a physician and we lack the material for remedies, we have refrained from describing what the most skilled physicians would judge useful for a diseased liver.

You call this disease *postuma* [as printed] in a corrupted form; we call it an abscess. Cornelius Celsus says that the Greeks call it **ἡπατικόν**, “hepatic.”

## EPISTOLA CLXXVII. TO ROMULF, ABBOT OF SENS

We think that we shall be relieved in an instant from the great burden of our cares by our deliberations, directed equally toward what is useful and what is honorable. This must certainly be completed, just as it was begun, through your pure affections in the contemplation of divine things.

And so, in a more suitable place, we shall enjoy mutual charity.

## EPISTOLA CLXXVIII. TO BRUNO, BISHOP OF LANGRES

Our most serene Augustus, our lord, has long desired your welcome presence for the purpose of consultation. Therefore I advise and beg you, for the sake of the safety of the entire commonwealth, to hasten your journey as soon as possible.

And since I heard you speak at Roceium on behalf of my safety, may I now deserve to be heard at Senlis on behalf of the liberation of all good men.

## EPISTOLA CLXXIX. TO ECBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER

Although I have tested your prudence in many matters, I understood it especially well recently, when you sharply rebutted with a subtle reply the complaint that I had contrived in the person of Archbishop A.

Therefore, with my conscience serving as witness, I feared that I had displeased you, since I had already begun to displease myself because I was being judged not a companion of vices but the chief of the greatest crimes.

I am the man who, under the rule of my father Adalbero, of blessed memory, served in the school of every virtue; now I inhabit the royal court, discussing words of life with the priests of God. Neither for love of Charles nor of Arnulf have I allowed myself any longer to become an instrument of the devil by declaiming against the truth in defense of a lie.

Therefore I beg to be found worthy of your ancient benevolence. Indeed, I have exposed my conscience to your judgment so that from me you may fully learn what you ought to understand concerning the destruction of Rheims.

## EPISTOLA CLXXX. TO ADALBERO, BISHOP OF VERDUN

I shall not use many words with one who shares in and knows all my counsels. For after the departure of my blessed father Adalbero to the Lord, it is sufficiently clear why I remained at Rheims for so long and why I sought to leave both before and after the destruction of the city.

You have also often repeated that Terentian saying: “If what you want cannot be done, want what you can.” And now, not unmindful of your kindnesses and piety toward me, I preserve my conceived love for you and your people, and I judge myself happier because of it.

For how could I not love those who love me? I perceive that you rejoice with me because I escaped the gatherings of wicked men and was restored to ecclesiastical communion.

Therefore conduct the cause of your friend in the customary manner: that is, let Laelius return from the Helvetii or Suebi; let a fitting companion be sought for the beloved Aquila, so that the end of our works may be perfected charity.

## EPISTOLA CLXXXI

While we embrace your exceptional and singular friendship more closely, we endure the envy of many men, especially of those who disturb the counsels of your lord against us.

The evil increases daily. Our enemies multiply and grow bolder through hope in divided kingdoms. Therefore, if you possess the virtue that we believe and desire you to possess, let us feel that it does not harm us that we have placed your affection before the affection of King Otto.

Let our enemies learn through you that the concord of the kingdoms is stable, although they deny that it can be achieved without their consultation. And because the road is difficult for credible envoys among enemies, perform the role of our envoys and pledge on our behalf whatever you judge honorable.

Assume responsibility for us in our absence as though we were present. If you discover anything salutary, inform us as soon as possible by letter or messenger, so that, while our rivals remain unaware, the friendship begun between both parties may be strengthened through the most faithful intermediaries.

We say this because we do not wish to send envoys of greater authority at great peril to themselves without a definite reason, and because a meeting of kings is laborious and at this time entirely useless on account of the ill-will of both parties.

But if you perceive that the counsels of wicked men have prevailed and that an honorable and useful friendship cannot be achieved, first of all we implore from you both the greatest counsel and the greatest aid. Do not allow us to be deceived by a vain expectation, us whom until now you have considered worthy of every kind of friendship and kinship.

## EPISTOLA CLXXXII

Your happiness brings us glory and consolation at the same time. For where there is one flesh and one blood, there also is one affection.

That day has passed and may it never return—the day on which your sorrow brought us inescapable pain. And now, in peace as then in distress, we entrust ourselves and what belongs to us to your service, so that, if you attempt anything great and worthy of your memory, whether by force or by skill, you may use our labor, diligence, counsel, intelligence, and strength.

But if you pursue quiet and silence, may we both now and forever be permitted to rejoice in you, in peace and quiet. Let not the rivals of your name boast that they can do more harm than you can do good.

If it can be done, let there be between us and your lord an honorable form of friendship. Prescribe what must be followed and what avoided, and do not allow us, who have resolved to pursue the friendship of no one against you, to be surrounded by deceits and frauds.

## EPISTOLA CLXXXIII. THE BISHOPS OF THE DIOCESE OF RHEIMS SEND GREETINGS TO THE MOST REVEREND FATHER R.

Since our brother and fellow bishop A. has been captured within his own Church and, because of the violence of the enemy, as is reported, is unable sufficiently to carry out what belongs to his jurisdiction, we, mindful of our duty, have repeated what we once did by his counsel against the most notorious plunderers.

We added this: that, in food and drink, we showed no mercy, contrary to divine and human law, as he did; moreover, we condemned the leaders, counts, and accomplices of the entire faction with anathema and suspended that Church from the divine office, judging this sufficient for the rest of the Christian faithful.

Therefore we are sending you a copy of the decree and anathema, and we urge, admonish, and ask you to favor our judgment and do the same.

## EPISTOLA CLXXXIV. TO GARINBERT, ABBOT

Because you care for us and rejoice in our welfare, we return due thanks. Nor are we so separated by distance, nor do we enjoy such a situation, with God’s favor, that we cannot practice our old friendships.

I shall therefore carry out what you ordered and, insofar as I can, using the persuasion or favor of the Augusti, I shall drive the army far from the neighborhood of Rheims until you have stored in the city whatever you still possess in the fields.

You too must take care of my son Aquila until you send him back to me through friends who are entirely trustworthy. And so that you may not be unaware of what the synod of the bishops of our diocese has decreed, I am sending you and our associates a copy of the proceedings, so that from it you may fully learn what you ought to follow and what to avoid.

## EPISTOLA CLXXXV. GERBERT’S BOOK OF RENUNCIATION TO ARNULF, ARCHBISHOP

After long and repeated reflection upon the unhappy condition of our city, and after finding no way out of its evils without the destruction of good men, I finally approved a decision that would remedy the present troubles and guard our friends against those of the future.

Therefore we exchange soil for soil and lordship for lordship, and, freed from your benefices, we leave them to you and to our rivals as an object of envy, so that we may not be accused here of the fidelity we promised, and there be assailed on account of relationships of friendship somehow extending to your uncle.

For under the arrangement by which we live, nothing is owed to one party when faith has been pledged to the other. For if we wish you to be safe, how can we preside over your uncle? Again, if we preside over your uncle, how can we wish you to be safe?

We resolve this dispute by moving elsewhere, owing neither you nor him anything except gratuitous goodwill. If you embrace this arrangement, reserve for me and my people, together with our furnishings, the houses that we built through our own labor and at great expense.

We also ask that the churches which we obtained through solemn and lawful donations according to the custom of the province not be touched by any prejudicial action. Beyond this we shall not ask much.

Once this has been done, you will honorably invite me, who once bore a free neck, to your service. But there can be no doubt that, if you overstep these limits, you will have transferred under oath to our rivals everything we possessed, just as we received it from many people, at the very time when, in accordance with your wishes, we were dictating the sharpest counsels for you.

Nor shall we be able to forget the evils of the past when the judgments of the present remind us of them.

## EPISTOLA CLXXXVI. ELECTION OF GERBERT AS ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

[Col. 0252B]

Beloved brothers, the judgments of God are always just, but sometimes hidden.

For after the death of our father A., of blessed memory, we placed over ourselves and over the Church of Rheims a certain man descended from royal stock. Driven by the shout of the multitude—for Scripture says, “The voice of the people is the voice of God”—and by the institutions of the holy canons, which require the desire and wishes of the clergy and people to be sought in the election of a bishop, we followed the letter incautiously and, with our mind’s vision clouded, investigated too little the harmonious judgment of the divine Scriptures.

For the voice of the people shouting, “Crucify, crucify,” was not the voice of God. Therefore not every voice of the people is the voice of God, nor should the wishes and desires of every member of the clergy and people be sought in the election of a bishop, but only those of the simple and incorrupt—that is, those not elected in hope of gain.

The judgments of the Fathers must be set forth. “It is not permitted,” he says, “for the crowds to make the election of those who are summoned to the priesthood; rather, the judgment must belong to the bishops, so that they themselves may test the one who is to be ordained, whether he has been instructed in the faith and in episcopal life.”

Therefore we, the bishops of the diocese of Rheims, in accordance with these constitutions of the Fathers, with the favor and assent of both our princes, Lord Hugh Augustus and the most excellent King Robert, and also with the agreement of those in the clergy and people who belong to God, choose for ourselves as archbishop the abbot Gerbert, mature in age, prudent by nature, teachable, affable, and merciful.

We do not prefer to him an unstable youth, ambition that exalts itself, and one who administers everything rashly. Indeed, we cannot patiently endure even hearing that we should be subjected to such men, whose wisdom and counsel we know cannot administer ecclesiastical and civil laws.

Since this must be examined in every bishop, it must especially be examined in one who presides over the others as metropolitan. Therefore we choose this Gerbert, who [lacuna in the source: ***]. We have known his life and character from childhood and have tested his study of divine and human matters. We seek to be instructed by his counsel and teaching.

By subscribing, we confirm, establish, and strengthen his election with the common counsel of all good men.

## EPISTOLA CLXXXVII. PROFESSION OF FAITH OF GERBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

[Col. 0253A]

I, Gerbert, by the prevenient grace of God soon to become archbishop of Rheims, first of all affirm in simple words the documents of the faith: I confirm that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, and I proclaim that the entire Godhead in the Trinity is coessential, consubstantial, coeternal, and almighty.

I profess that each person in the Trinity is the true God, and that all three persons are one God. I believe that the divine Incarnation took place not in the Father or in the Holy Spirit, but in the Son alone: he who was the Son of God the Father in divinity became the son of a mother in humanity—true God from the Father and true man from his mother.

I confess that he possessed flesh from his mother’s womb and a rational human soul, and that in him the two natures, namely man and God, are one person, one Son, one Christ, one Lord. Together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, I confess him to be the author, lord, and ruler of all creatures that exist.

I affirm that he suffered with the true suffering of the flesh, died with the true death of his body, and rose again with the true resurrection of his flesh and with the true resurrection of his soul [asterisk as printed], in which he will come to judge the living and the dead.

I believe the author, lord, and God of the New and Old Testaments to be one and the same. I believe that the devil became evil not by creation but by his own will.

I believe in the resurrection of this flesh that we bear, and not of another. I believe that judgment will take place and that each person will receive either punishments or rewards for what he has done.

I do not prohibit marriage; I do not condemn second marriages. I do not censure the precept concerning meats. I confess that the reconciled penitent ought to be admitted to communion.

I believe that in baptism all sins are forgiven—that is, both original sin, which has been contracted, and those sins that have been voluntarily committed. I confess that no one can be saved outside the Catholic Church.

I confirm the four holy synods that the universal mother Church confirms.

## EPISTOLA CLXXXVIII. GERBERT TO CAESAR OTTO

To the glorious lord Otto, Caesar, ever Augustus, Roman emperor, Gerbert, bishop, offers the inadequate service of his obedience.

We are deeply distressed by your absence, separated as we are by the length of the lands between us [Col. 0253D]. And as for the fact that an exceedingly misleading report has brought you none of the splendid achievements accomplished by you, as always, this is a matter of great concern. At present it is foreign to me to speak about the life and character of Count Harmandus; therefore it is of the greatest importance to me to make known to you the groans and sighs of his brother. For that nobleman complains that his brother is being starved to death at Gorze, contrary to the dignity of his own birth and that of his family, and he considers this an everlasting disgrace. But if this is true, what purpose do such dreadful punishments serve? What kind of death is more bitter than starvation? Hunger alone surpasses every kind of punishment; it scorns death itself and, contrary to nature’s order, calls death upon itself. Remove, I beg you, so monstrous a crime, and return to his brother, who asks for him, the brother who, as he says, is still breathing [Col. 0254A]. Remember only the condition of those who capture and are captured, lest captives, after their liberation, be able either themselves or through their captors, or through the friends of their captors, to injure those responsible for their captivity.

## LETTER CLXXXIX. GERBERT TO OTTON

To the most excellent lord Otto, ever Augustus Caesar, the least of his bishops, always and everywhere, offers the services of due servitude.

Since among human affairs we see nothing sweeter than your rule, you could signify nothing sweeter to those anxious for you than the supreme glory of your rule and its supreme steadfastness joined with dignity. And what glory, surely, is greater in a prince? What steadfastness in a supreme commander is more praiseworthy than to gather legions, invade hostile territory, withstand the enemy’s attack by your presence, and expose yourself to the greatest dangers for your country, for religion, and for the safety of your people and the commonwealth? These deeds have had how fortunate an outcome.

We are less troubled by the embassy of Abbot Leo sent to you concerning that Arnulf; yet that embassy, which is altogether false, has not lodged in my mind. Rather, he thought that what Abbot Leo demands as promised by my Gauls would prove true. Or, if the matter is so, I know your innate benevolence: you both wish and are able to resist such audacity. And since our Leo directed his journey to you by flying, as he himself wrote, on 8 September, when the letter first arrived—carried, I believe, by hostile winds—nothing has been decided concerning Arnulf [Col. 0254C].

But he brings with him other matters, just as they were conceived by great minds, so they must be brought to completion by great counsels. May your G., your servant, enjoy eternal health. And because you have magnificently bestowed magnificent Sasbach, your Gerbert dedicates himself eternally to your eternal rule. And because R. S. V. D. binds himself to your eternal service, your G. [does likewise]. Your G. has asked that what was liberally bestowed by you but, for some reason, taken away by someone unknown to me, be restored to him. May the final number of your abacus determine it.

## LETTER CXC

To the lord and most reverend father, the illustrious G., from his son.

In a brilliant speech you expressed how sweet and useful the holiest friendships and firmest partnerships are, and you deigned to make me a participant and partner in divinity through so great a benefit [Col. 0254D]. For what else is true friendship except the chief gift of divinity? Trusting, therefore, in your friendship, confidently expecting good from it, and hoping for better things in the future, I am not afraid of Arnulf’s return to the city of Reims. But if he has arrived as Hungerius, who wished it, reported, I trust that for this reason I shall be freed from Hur the Chaldean and shall not fail in your service.

And what I have always wished and always desired will make me an inseparable companion to this cause, and we call this its solemn command. What, therefore, could be sweeter or more excellent? You consequently ought not, and will not, have to sigh on behalf of your friend’s cause, since everything has arisen—and will arise, with divinity propitious—from complete and common deliberation and decision: you giving counsel, your friends giving assistance, and your rule happily executing and managing everything [Col. 0255A].

Farewell, and rejoice with me over the successful and prosperous affairs of our Caesar. Farewell again, and in greater numbers.

## LETTER CXCI. GERBERT TO OTTO CAESAR AND ALSO AUGUSTUS EMPEROR OF THE ROMANS

To the lord and glorious ever Augustus Otto Caesar, Gerbert.

I know that I have offended, and do offend, the Divinity in many things; but I do not know in what I am accused of having offended you or your people, or why my service has suddenly become so displeasing. Would that what was conferred upon me by your munificence with such glory had either not been permitted me to accept or, once accepted [Col. 0255B], had not been lost with such disgrace! What am I to think this means—something that you certainly gave, or could have given, or could not have given? If you could not, why did you pretend that you could? But if you could, what unknown and nameless emperor commands our most renowned emperor, famous throughout the world? In what darkness is that gallows-bird hiding? Let him come into the light and be crucified, so that our Caesar may be free to rule.

Many have believed that I was able to assist many in your piety’s presence. Now it is worthwhile to have patrons whom I once undertook to defend; greater confidence must be placed in my enemies than in my friends. Friends have taught me all that is healthful and everything prosperous. Enemies have foretold that neither commands nor benefits will help me, and that sweet beginnings will have bitter endings—whether by a prophetic or a fanatical spirit [Col. 0255C]. These things are indeed more grievous to me than I wish, but less fitting for an imperial person.

For three, so to speak, ages of the world, before you, your father, and your grandfather, I have displayed the purest loyalty amid enemies and weapons. For your safety I have exposed my insignificant person, such as it is, to raging kings and maddened peoples. Through trackless places and deserts, through the attacks and encounters of brigands, tormented by hunger and thirst and by the violence of cold and heat, I remained unbroken amid so many storms, so that I would rather have chosen death than fail to see the emperor’s son, then held captive, ruling. I saw him and rejoiced; and would that I might be permitted to rejoice to the end and finish my days in peace with you!

## LETTER CXCII. TO ADALBERT, ARCHBISHOP AND ABBOT OF THE GREATER MONASTERY

[Col. 0255D]

Nature keeps its cycles, and the good earth, long unfruitful—not by its own judgment—bears forth marvelous flowers and fruits. For behold, the little cell of blessed Martin now revives the long-dead ranks of monks. Martin’s virtue is recognized in his disciples. Among them we rejoice that we have received Osulf, a pupil of blessed conduct, as a model of life and character. We offer his most holy affections to be joined with your own, so that he who opposed the ancient enemy in a singular struggle may emerge victorious beneath the shield of your prayers. Let us therefore be relieved by your merits, we who are weighed down by our own offenses.

## LETTER CXCIII. GERBERT TO ARNULF, BISHOP OF ORLÉANS

[Col. 0256A]

Divinity has bestowed much upon mortals, O guardian of my spirit: it has given them faith and has not denied them knowledge. Hence Peter recognizes Christ as the Son of God and faithfully confesses him once recognized. Hence it is that the just person lives by faith. We therefore join knowledge to this faith because fools are said not to possess faith. That you possess this faith is indicated by the splendid knowledge of your generous spirit; the sequence of your speech makes this clear, since you desire it to be everlasting among us.

I therefore give and return thanks to the giver of such great gifts: both that he has preserved for me a friend who differs from me in nothing, and that he has placed less trust in our rivals, who tell plausible but untrue stories. This is your gift, good Jesus, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house. This I, your priest, confess before you: that your venerable craftsman [*artificem*], A., honors, cherishes, and loves me, and that he brings to mind with heart and mouth all those of my order whom I know today [Col. 0256B].

Away, then, with every fraud and deceit; let peace and brotherhood be present here, so that whoever injures one of us may have injured both. While the power of Christ protects me, no tyrannical force will deter me from this undertaking—not even the threats of kings, which we endured as grave ones during this Paschal feast. For we were accused of having unjustly condemned the monks of Saint-Denis. We were pressed to celebrate the divine offices in the presence of the condemned and told that we ought not to oppose the privileges granted to the monastery of blessed Dionysius by the Roman Church.

We were further told that we would give our assent to privileges promulgated with canonical authority [Col. 0256C] and that, if anything had been decreed contrary to ecclesiastical laws, we would not accept it as law. But when the burden of the case was directed especially against me, I said that it did not belong to my jurisdiction, and that I would not, as I was accused of doing, rush into an injury against my lords, but would observe whose interest it was that the same fault be brought forward.

When the judgment of the secular monks had prevailed in favor of the party [lacuna]—your blessedness’s son Fulco is witness that this was so; he learned the bitterness of my spirit, not without a shedding of tears. For I grieved, and grieve greatly [lacuna]. Moreover, you were accused by some unknown informer as though you were plotting against royal honor, and as one who [lacuna].

It was not therefore, as was reported to you, my strength that raged against you, nor did harsh speech disparage an absent friend. But while I tried to excuse you, I nearly cast myself as an accused man before the palace hounds [Col. 0256D]. Let there therefore be among us, as you wish, a “yes” only, not both “yes” and “no”; let there be assistance and counsel held in common. I also judge that this should be confirmed in sacred matters by written words, if it pleases your sublimity, so that, once every movement of suspicion has been removed, we may have one heart and one soul.

## LETTER CXCIV. GERBERT TO CONSTANTINE, ABBOT OF MICY

I was sufficiently, indeed exceedingly, astonished by the embassy of the venerable A. For he reported [lacuna]. But all these things are not pains themselves, but the beginnings of pains. What is sought and desired is greater than I, humble and insignificant though I am; and the true proverb says: “Your own affair is at stake when your neighbor’s wall is burning” [Col. 0257A]. There is also the divine saying: “Begin from my sanctuary,” that is, from the foundation of the kingdom and from the citadel.

What acts of deceit accompany this deed is obvious. For once this is conceded, sacerdotal dignity—or rather its gravity—is thrown into confusion, and the condition of the kingdom is endangered. But if this is done without consulting the bishops, the authority, gravity, and dignity of the bishops are annulled. They neither could nor ought to deprive a bishop, however wicked, of his priesthood. But if they acted after consultation, they themselves are witnesses of their own condemnation, since they judged that they themselves should not judge. And they dared to act contrary to their own profession and their own subscription, made by themselves in the document of abdication.

His capture, his prolonged imprisonment, the appointment of another to his seat, the appointing authorities, the appointed man, and those ordained by him will be recalled to memory and will be subjected to accusation [Col. 0257B]. The kings themselves, too, will appear as sinners in each of these sins. Let no one flatter himself that, once anything has been shaken, he remains unharmed; nor let anyone be deceived by the false name of a pledge, since matters and acts depend not on the indulgence of judges but on the firmness of the cases.

## LETTER CXCV. TO NOCHERIUS, BISHOP OF LIÈGE

Although we are not unaware from what source the movements of your spirit toward us have flowed, nevertheless, in accordance with our office, we ought to provide—without a serious dispute and insofar as it concerns you—that this source dry up and this movement cease. Therefore, at the request of the venerable VV., bishop of the city of Strasbourg [Col. 0257C], I recently set out in writing the substance of the evils of our time, disclosed what was agreed and disagreed between the parties, and sent it to you as judges whose probity has been tested.

And now, to fulfill the desire of my enemies—since it cannot be done from the whole world, at least from the entire government of our princes—I am laboring by every means available to me to have a universal council convened. At it, the opportunity to assemble and debate will be freely granted not only to the curious but also to our enemies. So far are we from wrongdoing, and so greatly do we trust in our innocence, that we not only do not avoid a regular judgment but pursue it as though it were fleeing from the whole world.

Behold, now that they have been warned for the third time, if they do not present themselves, both the appeal and the reopening of the case will be silenced by a peremptory law [Col. 0257D]. In this matter it is yours to take heed, since the Lord’s anger threatens the one of whom he says: “Woe to him through whom the scandal comes!” For although the apostle Paul says: “We preach Christ Jesus, a stumbling block indeed to the Jews and folly to the Greeks,” the woe is not therefore Paul’s, but belongs to those who, as the prophet says, call good evil and evil good.

The Lord knows who are his; he knows whose zeal is stirred on his behalf. But if God is for us, who can be against us? I therefore beg and implore you, by whatever piety there is in you, not to believe more about me from my enemies than from yourselves. Test whether I am what I have been toward you in every respect: devoted and obedient, faithful to my friends in common, an ardent lover of equity and truth, without deceit [Col. 0258A] and pride, one who has enjoyed the friendship of you and your people, and who seeks from your virtue what was lost—not through my fault. If it is denied me, I shall grieve greatly; if restored, I shall likewise rejoice greatly.

## LETTER CXCVI. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT GERALD AND THE BROTHERS

Because of the duty of my position and order, distracted among many matters by the demands of great affairs, I have until now not wished to inform you, either through envoys or letters, about what is happening around me. Now, since a brother [lacuna], just as I had written through an older [lacuna] messenger, while I was fleeing the city of Reims for the sake of God, by the grace of God I was placed over the city of Reims. This circumstance has aroused nations and peoples against me in envy. And because they cannot avenge themselves by force, they seek to do so by law.

A struggle of arms is more bearable [Col. 0258B] than a legal dispute. Although I have satisfied my rivals, insofar as it concerns me, through skill in speaking and lengthy interpretation of the laws, they have still not abandoned the hatreds once begun. Therefore, revered Fathers, by your witness and through your pupil, offer help with prayers poured out to God. The victory of the disciple is the glory of the teachers.

I give thanks to all of you collectively for my instruction, but especially to Father R. To him, if there is any knowledge in me, I return thanks, after God, above all mortals. Now [lacuna] may your holy college prosper [lacuna]. May those once known to me or joined to me by kinship prosper, if any remain, whose appearance alone I recognize, and not all of them sufficiently—not because I have forgotten any of them through arrogance, but because I have been worn down by the savagery of barbarians [Col. 0258C] and, so to speak, wholly transformed.

What I learned as an adolescent I lost as a young man; what I desired as a young man I despised as an old man. Such are the fruits I bring myself. O pleasure! Such joys do the honors of the world produce. Believe me, who have experienced it: insofar as glory raises princes outwardly, so far does suffering distress them inwardly.

## LETTER CXCVII

You consulted us whether the man who polluted his wife’s sister by adultery ought, after completing penance, to return to the former union or take another woman. One is permitted, while the other is completely forbidden. In the African councils, under title 49, it was decided that, according to evangelical and apostolic discipline, neither a woman dismissed by her husband nor a man dismissed by his wife should be joined to another, but that they should remain so that they might be reconciled to one another [Col. 0258D]. If they despise this, they are to be reduced to penance.

If the woman takes another husband, she is not to receive communion before the man whom she left has departed from this world—unless the necessity of illness should compel communion to be given. Let the man therefore perform penance to the end according to the law for those who have polluted themselves with incest, namely, ten years. The woman likewise, being related by blood, should, if possible, profess chastity, since she is pressed by the heat of youth and there is fear that she may be tempted by Satan.

We know nothing better in this matter than what Pope Leo says about similar cases: “A young man,” he says, “if he cannot remain continent, can be sustained by the remedy of a wife.” In this manner it may be said that if this adulteress cannot remain continent, she should marry, as the Apostle says, only in the Lord [Col. 0259A].

## LETTER CXCVIII. GERBERT TO POPE LEO

Knowing your great benevolence toward me, I consider myself fortunate in the friendship of so great a man. Indeed, because our service has not been as obedient to you as it ought to have been, this should be attributed not to ill will but to necessity. Amid the various disturbances by which we are constantly shaken, scarcely anyone suitable can be found to whom the secrets of the heart may safely be disclosed.

Thus deceit and fraud, simulation and dissimulation, have successively occupied the citadel of virtue. Hence it is that, after you departed from me, we have had no mutual exchange of letters, except for the letter we sent you under the sign of the triple cross [Col. 0259B]. Accordingly, we place ourselves and all that belongs to us under your direction in such a way that whoever should perhaps injure us may be seen to have inflicted an injury upon Lord Leo the pope.

Henceforth it will not be our jurisdiction to determine what is prepared, how much, for whom, or when; rather, diligent service will be rendered to Lord Leo by his minister. I salute the lord bishop, a friend worthy of reverence in every respect, placing great confidence in his wisdom and eloquence and in his singular moral integrity, and thereby making myself bound to serve him.

## LETTER CXCIX. TO POPE JOHN

I am afflicted with intense grief [Col. 0259C] and groan from the depths of my being that it could have been insinuated to your most holy apostolate that I might appear guilty of some usurpation. Until now I have conducted myself in the Church of God with such an attitude that I have benefited many and harmed no one. I did not therefore expose Arnulf’s sins; I merely withdrew from a man sinning publicly—not, as my rivals say, in the hope of obtaining his honor, God and those who know me are witnesses, but so that I would not share in another’s sins.

## LETTER CC

Because we do not at times enjoy your conversations, we do not bear it with a sufficiently even mind. Through such mutual exchanges charity remains, separated things come together, harshness grows mild, hostilities perish, and many advantages of the present are obtained. But since, through the movement of the times, we achieve this less than we should, and since the brevity of a letter can scarcely express our affection between us, we ask your benevolence [Col. 0259D] on behalf of a brother [lacuna], so that our intercession may benefit him with you, and our letter may obtain more for him than gifts offered by chance from someone or other.

Bound by the difficulties of the times, we have until now not been sufficiently able to meet regularly and seek the things of God. Now, because by God’s mercy we are permitted to breathe again, we judge that you ought to be present, and we warn and beg you to set aside every avoidable excuse.

Although the form of discipline is proposed equally to all priests, namely, to know and observe the sacred canons established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, nevertheless it is more strictly enjoined upon us that what we have received from pastors as a model of conduct and life be graciously passed on to the flock entrusted to us. Since, then, we place money before facts [Col. 0260A; *in facte*], why do we trample upon the rights of the sacred laws through unlawful greed?

You should weigh, distinguish, and judge these matters—and the outcries that we constantly endure—not according to the prejudice of tyrants, as a tyrant among tyrants, but according to the judgment of priests, as a priest among priests. Restrain these movements; silence these complaints; overcome them by the gravity of your conduct and the tenderness of your years. Continuous reading and constant questioning will sharpen your mind.

Why did the judgment [lacuna] escape us? Why, when he appealed to a higher hearing, was he deprived of his possessions? But if he was despoiled not while appealing but in silence, why was the judgment pronounced against him not reported to us? If you did these things knowingly, the law applies against the contumacious; if unknowingly, forgiveness must certainly be granted on this condition: that what was unlawfully taken from the priest be legally restored [Col. 0260B].
