Afterward, if it seems appropriate, let the judgment be renewed according to the laws, lest you think that my son R. distrusts his case because he has not now appeared as agreed.

Occupied with many affairs, we cannot send him to your examination before the fifteenth day before the Kalends. We earnestly beg, by your supreme benevolence toward us, that these delays not harm him. If you do these things gently and judge his case without partiality toward persons, you will make us greatly indebted to your service.

## LETTER CCI. GERBERT AND ALL THE BISHOPS OF THE DIOCESE OF REIMS TO ITS USURPERS

Girbert, by the grace of God bishop of Reims; Guido, bishop of Soissons; Adalbero, bishop of Laon; R., bishop of Noyon; Rot., bishop of Cambrai; O., bishop of Senlis; F., bishop of Amiens; B., bishop of Meaux; Her., bishop of Beauvais—bishops through the grace of the Holy Spirit—to you Girbert and those who are listed below, usurpers, executioners, and tyrants.

For a long time the moderation of priests has endured the raging fury of your madness, and it still waits patiently. How long, then, will your insanity resist our sound understanding? How long will the dissimulation of the wicked disturb the quiet of the simple? You inflict slaughter upon the clergy; you do not cease from plundering the clergy, monks, and poor.

Therefore we, all the bishops of the diocese of Reims, summon your consciences and invite you to satisfaction, granting you a period for repentance until the coming Kalends [Col. 0260D]. Then we shall either recognize you as barren branches of the Church or cut you off from God’s field with the sword of the Holy Spirit as useless wood.

## LETTER CCII. TO ERVEA, BISHOP OF BEAUVAIS

The reason we have retained D., who is so dear to us, for so long was not ill will but your greatest advantage, so that his return might prove honorable and useful both to you and to him. And now, as you request, we send him to your charity, though he is abandoning his homeland, his parents, and every kind of friend out of love for us. We transfer him like an inestimable treasure from our bosom into your keeping.

Receive him, then, learned in the liberal arts, instructed in the mastery of crafts, sought by many for a great price [Col. 0261A] but obtained by us. We wish him to be treated and guarded in such a way that your indulgence may alleviate the grief caused him by our absence. Hold him with that munificence and generosity which befit G., archbishop of Reims, when giving, and the bishop of Beauvais when receiving.

## LETTER CCIII

You, notable virgin, ought to have praised and confirmed your father's agreements and arrangements. But since you have dissolved them and persist in denying what you have additionally done, we invite you to acknowledge your sin.

We also order you, R., to cease from the seizure of property [lacuna] and to restore what you have wrongly usurped. Nor should you think that you [lacuna] may be passed over: you are, I say, a cleric by tonsure, but in life and conduct * for three years with your accomplice N. [Col. 0261B]

All of you, I say, will either show the Catholic Church worthy fruits of repentance, or, like pagans and publicans, you will be driven from the Catholic Church by the sword of the Holy Spirit.

## LETTER CCIV

Having received your complaint, reverend father, we wrote with our brothers and fellow bishops concerning the same matter, and we also sent letters of warning to those who despise you. It will therefore be the task of your prudence, for the preservation of peace and charity, to receive them gently as wayward sons if they repent.

But if, God forbid, they persist in wickedness, we order that the writing of our summons be publicly displayed for reading in a prominent place in the Church. Then let a reasoned excommunication, formally composed and solemnly celebrated by you, be affixed in a prominent place, and let a copy of it be sent to us, so that the same may be done in our churches [Col. 0261C].

And since you have asked that a learned cleric be sent to you who might be of assistance in these and other matters, when my D. returns, we shall endeavor to have him serve your needs.

## LETTER CCV

Your fraternity knows how much moderation must be exercised in caring for the salvation of souls, and this must be carefully considered, so that nothing be done to excess. For while you exercise, that is, within the Church, the severity of judgment, you have gone beyond the measure established by the Fathers. What councils or decrees have forbidden little children to be baptized or the faithful to be buried in cemeteries?

But if that place is legally bound by your interdict—and, to speak solemnly, by your ban—it would be lawful for innocent parishioners to move to other places and make lawful use of their sacred rites [Col. 0261D]. I therefore admonish your fatherhood to temper the measure of your judgment and to handle the entire matter in such a way that you may please the divine Majesty before your eyes and not displease the judgment of your fellow bishops.

Having long endured the various disturbances of an evil time, I flee to your comfort as to the safest harbor. Otherwise, either we shall find comfort through your help, or we shall have to seek assistance from abroad.

## LETTER CCVI. GERBERT TO EMPRESS ADELAIDE

Again and again considering with myself where faith, truth, piety, and justice have made their dwelling, I could find only your piety and majesty, in which manifold virtue has always lived and held possession [Col. 0262A]. To you, therefore, as to the special temple of mercy, I suppliantly flee, and I ask again for your ever-healthful counsel and assistance.

For because [lacuna] rage bitterly against me alone and demand my life together with my blood. To the heap of evils is added [lacuna]. Even Rome itself, which ought to have been a source of consolation, rages.

I therefore beg and implore you: may kingdoms be softened by you and by your imperial authority. For I am wholly and everywhere yours, awaiting your examination and relief. I know only this to be certain: that I wish what you have judged pleasing.

## LETTER CCVII

Although Divinity has always shown human affairs to be governed by the counsel of the eternal King, it especially wished, in your time, to make you the material of its counsels [Col. 0262B]. For it exalted and humbled you; then, moderating and diminishing that humility through its goodness, and with the supreme favor of many peoples following, restored you to your seat and ordered you to shine more brightly in its house like gold tested in a furnace.

I therefore praise and glorify his mercies and compassions, both in you and in me, whom, a stranger and, so to speak, an exile throughout the whole world, he eventually ordered to find rest and stand upon a firm land. I am sending you one whom you wished to receive from me at the sacred font. But whether you ought to send him to us to be educated is not for us to decide. If we refuse, we may perhaps appear ungrateful; if we praise him, there is something unfavorable for the boy. Whatever the difficulty of the times may bring will be attributed to our fault [Col. 0262C].

## LETTER CCVIII. GERBERT TO FULCO, BISHOP OF AMIENS

Amid the various occupations of great affairs, no annoyance afflicts us more than the frequent reports of your excesses. Although the care of the entire metropolitan church of Reims has been entrusted to us, it is especially the care of you, who, because of the tenderness of your affections and the lightness of your character, have not yet learned to bear the weight of the priesthood.

Why, then, contrary to the agreement established in common, did you carry out a usurpation in your own parish before the time appointed for the council? You are not relieved in this matter even if the things you seized belong to the Church, since this may not be done except according to the laws [Col. 0262D]. To this was added the unlawful presumption of arms and a violation of the Church, as though everything were permitted to a priest in churches.

But the Apostle says: “Everything is lawful for me, but not everything is beneficial.” These things are lawful through free choice, which you have used badly; but they are not beneficial according to the divine laws, which you have despised. We therefore admonish your fraternity to correct your errors and, if you are willing, to make satisfaction to us whom you have offended, so that acknowledgment of these excesses may become the abolition of many sins.

## LETTER CCIX. GERBERT TO ARCHEMBALD, ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS

We have received your complaint with fraternal compassion. Therefore we do not delay counsel and assistance, insofar as it concerns us [Col. 0263A]. Since the clergy, as you say, has rejected your blessing, let it happen as it is written: “He refused the blessing, and it shall be far from him.” In return for the injury of rejection, the Lord teaches that the dust of one’s sandals is to be shaken off against them.

## LETTER CCX. GERBERT TO EMPRESS ADELAIDE

I have been afflicted by such grief at a report almost beyond belief and exceedingly wicked that I have nearly wept away the light of my eyes. But since you order me to come to you and provide consolation, you command something good but impossible. My days have passed, dear and glorious lady; my old age threatens me with my final day.

Pleurisy occupies my sides [Col. 0263B]; my ears ring, my eyes stream, and my whole body is pierced by continual stings. This entire year has seen me lying on my bed from pain, and now, scarcely rising, I have relapsed as pains hurl me down on alternate days.

But if any respite from the pains is granted, I shall not be able to forget your benefaction. Although what the Council of Nicaea has defined concerning communion for those deprived of it may seem sufficient—that those rejected by others should not be received—we obey every command of yours, both in this matter and in any honest and appropriate affairs.

But because the salvation of souls must be handled with great moderation, and no one should be removed hastily from the body and blood of the Son of God, through which mystery true life is lived and by which the person justly deprived, while still alive, has died, we judge that the military man should first be approached by our admonition, in case he may repent and satisfy your reverence [Col. 0263C].

We indeed removed him long ago from the thresholds of the Church alone, together with certain others, on account of these and other excesses. Later we shall separate him from the body of the Lord, and then from the communion of the faithful, so that by these successive stages he may be warned concerning his salvation, and so that, through the contagion of one person—because of the necessary military association of this evil time—the people of God may be infected less, while he alone bears his wickedness, disgrace, and ruin in the meantime.

## LETTER CCXI. TO THE CANONS OF SAINT MARTIN, IN THE NAME OF THE BISHOPS

[Col. 0263D]

All the bishops who came to the council in the church of Saint Paul, to all the clerics of the monastery of Saint Martin.

Having heard the report of your rebellion against our brother, the bishop of the city of Tours, we have sent this letter, jointly decreeing that you either return to harmony with your bishop or come to the hearing to be held at Chelles, to render an account of the discord you have long maintained, on 9 May. If you do not do so, know that you will be struck by the censure of canonical severity.

## LETTER CCXII. GERBERT TO ARNULF, BISHOP OF ORLÉANS

[Col. 0264A]

I cannot express by any kind of speech the feeling of our spirit toward you, since I would risk my very head through any pretense. You have taught, warned, and instructed me about what I ought to avoid and what I ought to pursue. And now, with every effort and every exertion, according to my knowledge and ability, I return such thanks as I can and commit myself and all that is mine to your patronage and direction, entertaining no doubtful hope that splendid beginnings will have happy outcomes.

And since the council [lacuna], I earnestly beg that the immense cares which at present wholly claim me may not harm our Church. For when, after a little while, by God’s favor, we are permitted to breathe again, we shall await your judgment concerning these and other matters in your presence [Col. 0264B].

## LETTER CCXIII. GERBERT TO THE BISHOP OF METZ

Although the virtue that is in us has previously become known in many ways, now, more than abundantly revealing its feeling in words and judgments, it has shone forth even above the candlestick. Since the Apostle says, “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep,” you received with joyful spirit the news that I had been freed from the unjust persecution of my brothers, and you grieved that you had now been involved in my dangers.

Therefore, while absent, I return thanks, and, if you wish, I accept the debt of service in person. For the rest [lacuna], we do not yet possess other matters worthy of report that have been sufficiently established [Col. 0264C].

## LETTER CCXIV. GERBERT TO THE BISHOP OF VERDUN

Our common sons R. and D. have gladdened us through the pleasant exchange of affairs. Since, as the Apostle says, “Bad conversations corrupt good morals,” you, delighting in simplicity, could not suddenly detect the varied and tangled dispositions of certain Gauls—sweet in speech, bitter at heart; and you were not without good reason disturbed by all their fabricated devices, full of bewilderment.

But since your inborn prudence could not be deceived for long, we rejoice that you have fully understood their simulation and dissimulation. Therefore we shall be able to have our son D., learned in much knowledge of affairs, as a faithful interpreter of everything that may be agreeable to us in common. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXV. TO AZELIN, BISHOP OF LAON

(See below among the letters and diplomas written after the assumption of the supreme pontificate.)

## LETTER CCXVI. TO ARNULF, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

(See in the same place.)

[Col. 0265]

# SUPPLEMENT TO THE LETTERS OF GERBERT IN THE EDITION OF DUCHESNE

*(Acts of the ecclesiastical province of Reims, vol. I, p. 645 ff.)*

## FIRST LETTER. TO VILDEROD, BISHOP OF STRASBOURG. On Arnulf’s deposition

[Col. 0265A]

Gerbert to Vilderod, bishop of the city of Strasbourg.

A chaste fellowship, well conceived and better preserved by an outstanding service . . . when, though I was far away and scarcely known even by name, you refreshed me with the sweet address of a faithful interpreter, and by that outstanding service openly demonstrated to whom, and to how great a priest, Helvetia is obedient.

Arnulf, King Lothair’s son, as is reported, after ensnaring his own bishop by deceit and fraud and taking him captive together with his city, after shedding much human blood, and after plunder and arson, was condemned in the assembly of all the bishops of Gaul [Note: See the Council of Reims of the year 987.]. Then, after Adalbero’s death, he was reconciled by Adalbero alone, bishop of Laon, in hope of obtaining peace; he was granted the metropolitan church of Reims after receiving from him terrible oaths and a written profession, to preserve his fidelity to his kings, which he recited aloud in the assembly of the Church [Note: See Arnulf’s oath.] and confirmed by signing with his own hand.

Not yet had six months elapsed since his ordination when, behold, an enemy invaded the city which he had betrayed, polluted God’s sanctuary, carried off its spoils, and took the clergy and people captive. After this Arnulf placed his own plunderers under anathema and commanded the bishops of Gaul to do the same. He removed the estates of the Church which he had given by oath to his soldiers and handed them over to the enemy; he led the conspirators’ force against his king and his army into battle under Charles’s standards.

Meanwhile [Col. 0265C] the Roman pontiff was admonished by envoys and synodal letters to come to the aid of the troubled Church; but he did not heed either Catholics or clergy who offered counsel. Therefore, after a serious consultation among the bishops, Arnulf was summoned by envoys, synodal letters, and a threefold admonition over eighteen continuous months, so that he might desist from the madness he had begun and regularly purge himself of the crime of treason and rebellion with which he was charged. He refused. But when he perceived that the supporters of his wickedness were withdrawing from him, he went in fear to the king and, through new oaths and new conditions, became a participant at the royal table. Thus, once the king’s anger had been appeased, he believed himself freed from every charge. Returning from there soon afterward, however, he broke his oath and failed to observe the conditions; [Col. 0265D] but those whose interests were involved, unable to bear being deceived so often and deprived so often of their goods, occupied the fortress at Laon.

Arnulf [Col. 0266A] was found among the king’s enemies, brought before the synod, and required to give an account of so many and such great crimes. After deliberating at length with himself and with his accomplices, he voluntarily burst forth into a confession of his sins; he produced other witnesses to corroborate his confessions, set down his crimes in a written declaration, and signed it after it had been read aloud before the Church. He laid aside the insignia of the priesthood and renounced them, while his confessors and witnesses testified and replied:

“According to your profession and subscription, withdraw from office . . .”

They replied that the king had granted Arnulf pardon, and that afterward he had committed nothing deserving pardon; that an injury had been done to the Roman pontiff, since Arnulf ought not to have been deposed without his authority and without the restoration of his rights . . . . .

In the epilogue: [Col. 0266B] I, tossed about upon land and sea, while I pursue the discoveries of philosophers, while I flee uncivilized peoples and do not escape them. I, I say, who was no small part of the betrayed city of Reims and of its captive and plundered people, flee to you as to the safest harbor. Therefore extend a saving hand to me as I struggle amid the waves; raise me up when I am weary. Malignant envy has spread the report that I invaded another’s see, that by my instigation a pastor was captured, accused, and deposed. That this is not so is attested by the dignity of the Gallic priesthood; kings and nobles are witnesses. Why was a poor man and exile, supported neither by birth nor by wealth, preferred to many rich men and those distinguished by the nobility of their parents, unless because this is your work, good Jesus, who raise the poor from the dung heap so that he may sit with princes?

You know that I have always honored Germany [Col. 0266C] as a mistress and cherished Belgium as a mother . . . And now I ask you to restore to me the gracious affections which I lost; I beg that your bishop William become the reconciler of the grace which I undeservedly lost, and the interpreter of my innocence before the prelates and before our king, to whom, by favoring him during the reign of King Lothair, I was handed over to the swords of the enemy. And now evils are repaid to us for good by those whom we had considered lovers of peace and protectors of the innocent.

The whole Church of the Gauls lies crushed beneath tyranny, although salvation was expected not from the Gauls but from these men. Yet you, Christ, are the one salvation of humanity. And Rome, hitherto regarded as the mother of all the Churches, is said to curse the good and bless the wicked, to associate with those to whom one ought not even say “Hail,” and to condemn those who zealously observe your law, abusing the power of binding and loosing which she received from you [Col. 0266D] [Note: Marlot published a fragment of this letter (vol. II, p. 51). The editors of the Council of Saint-Basle, and after them M. Varin, in his *Administrative Archives of the City of Reims* (vol. I, p. 179), added it to the purported acts of that council. Their version is much longer than the one given here, but bears obvious signs of alteration; it is overlaid with passages from Hincmar, evidently added to Gerbert’s work. The text presented here, despite its lacunae, seemed to us more authentic and therefore preferable; we took it from the collection of D. Martenne, vol. I, col. 351.] . . . .

## LETTER II. TO SEGUINUS, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

*(Year 993.) On the interdict issued against the fathers of the Council of Basle* [Note: Pope John XV, informed by several bishops of what had occurred at the Council of Saint-Basle, annulled the acts of that council and suspended from their functions all the bishops who had taken part in Arnulf’s deposition. Gerbert, whose election was thereby annulled, made every effort to induce the bishops to despise the censure. This is the purpose of the present letter, whose immoderate language betrays the writer’s irritation. We should nevertheless observe that this letter passed through the same hands as the acts of the Council of Saint-Basle.]

[Col. 0267A]

It would indeed have been fitting for your prudence to avoid the wiles of crafty men and to hear the voice of the Lord saying: “If they say to you, ‘Behold, here is Christ,’ or ‘There he is,’ do not follow them” (Matthew 24). It is said that there is someone in Rome who justifies what you condemn and condemns what you regard as just; and we say that it belongs to God alone, and not to man, to condemn what appears just and to justify what is thought evil. “God,” says the Apostle, “is the one who justifies; who is he that condemns?” (Romans 8). It follows, therefore, that if God condemns, there is no one who justifies.

God says: [Col. 0267B] “If your brother sins against you, go and reprove him between you and him alone” (Matthew 18), and so forth, “until he is as a heathen and a tax collector.” How, then, do our adversaries say that in Arnulf’s deposition the judgment of the Roman bishop ought to have been awaited? Can they teach that the judgment of the Roman bishop is greater than the judgment of God?

But the first of the Roman bishops—indeed, the prince of the apostles themselves—cries out: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5). And Paul himself, teacher of the whole world, cries out: “If anyone announces to you anything beyond what you have received, let him be accursed, even if it is an angel from heaven” (Galatians 1). Because Pope Marcellinus burned incense to Jupiter, was it therefore necessary for all bishops to offer incense?

I declare firmly [Col. 0267C] that if the Roman bishop sins against a brother and, after repeated admonition, does not listen to the Church, then this Roman bishop, I say, must by God’s command be regarded as a heathen and a tax collector. For the higher the rank, the more serious the fall.

If, on that account, he considers us unworthy of his communion because none of us agrees to think contrary to the Gospel, he will not thereby be able to separate us from the communion of Christ. Even a presbyter ought not to be removed from office unless he has confessed or been convicted, especially since the Apostle says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?” And again: “For I am certain that neither death nor life, etc.” (Romans 8). What greater separation is there than to remove any of the faithful from the body and blood of the Son of God, who is sacrificed daily for our salvation, [Col. 0267D] any of the faithful? If the man who has taken away bodily life from himself or another is called a murderer, then [the corresponding statement about] the man who has taken away eternal life from himself or another follows. The following clause is corruptly ordered in the source: “Nor indeed can Gregory’s judgment, [III?], be referred to bishops under a designation applied to the people.” “Whether justly or unjustly,” he says, “the pastor binds, the pastor’s sentence must be feared.” For it is not the bishop who is called the flock, but the people. For just as the pastor’s life differs from the flock, so the pastor’s life ought to differ from the common people.

You ought not, therefore, to have been suspended from sacred communion as though you had confessed or been convicted of crimes, nor as though you were rebels and deserters, since you have never avoided the most holy councils—especially since both your conduct and your conscience are pure, no legal sentence of condemnation has yet been issued against you in this matter, and none can be imposed according to the laws. It has not been legally imposed because Gregory [Col. 0268B] says: “A sentence pronounced without writing does not even deserve to bear the name of sentence.” It cannot be imposed according to the laws because Pope Leo the Great says: “The privilege of Peter is not upheld wherever judgment is not rendered according to equity.”

We must not, therefore, give our adversaries an opportunity to make it appear that the priesthood, which is everywhere one just as the Catholic Church is one, is subject to a single man, so that no priest may exist unless money, favor, fear, or ignorance—once corrupted—has commended him to that man. Let the common law of the Catholic Church be the Gospel, the Apostles, the Prophets, the canons established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, and the decrees of the Apostolic See that do not dissent from these. Let the one who deviates from them through contempt be judged by them and rejected by them. But let perpetual and everlasting peace belong to the one who observes these things and carries them out to the best of his ability.

We wish you well. XXCCV. Farewell again, and do not suspend yourselves from sacred and mystical things. For whoever, accused before a judge, remains silent, confesses; and whoever, when the judge is judging, subjects himself to punishment, confesses. Confession is made either for salvation or for destruction: for salvation when someone confesses the truth about himself; for destruction when he fabricates false and deadly crimes about himself or allows them to be fabricated against him. To remain silent before a judge is therefore to confess. To confess false and deadly crimes is the act of a murderer, because anyone who becomes the cause of his own death is a greater murderer. And the Lord says: “By your own mouth I judge you.” False accusation must therefore be rejected, and illegal judgment despised, lest, while we wish to appear innocent before the Church, we become guilty [Col. 0268D] [Note: Baronius, *Annales*, under the year 993; Labbe, vol. IX; Hardouin, vol. VI, etc.].

[Col. 0269]

# OATH GIVEN BY PETER, ABBOT OF CLASSIS OF SAINT APOLLINARIS, TO GERBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA

*(Year 998, 30 November.)*

*(Camaldulian Annals, vol. I, p. 147, from the authentic document in the archive of Classis.)*

[Col. 0269A] A copy of the document, whose wording is as follows:

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. In the third year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of the lord Gregory V, supreme and universal pope, in the most holy apostolic see of blessed Peter the Apostle; and in the third year of the reign of the lord Otto III the Younger; on the thirtieth day of the month of November, in the tenth indiction, at Ravenna.

The pastoral care and foresight of the lord and most holy and most blessed Gerbert, archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna, my prelate and ordainer, who, although I am your unworthy servant, supported by no merits, in the clemency of his praise and piety—as also toward all his subjects—deigned, through divine power breathing upon him, graciously to extend over me the overflowing bowels of his merciful kindness, and deigned to appoint me, though unworthy and undeserving, in the monastery of Saint Apollinaris, martyr of Christ, to preserve the rule of Saint Benedict and to guard it according to my understanding and ability, by the working of divine grace, and to constitute me abbot.

Therefore I, a presbyter and monk, elected by the congregation of the monastery of Saint Apollinaris called at Classis, promise by this holy altar, by the holy relics deposited here, and by these four holy Gospels of God, that from this hour onward I am and shall be faithful throughout all the days of my life to my holy lady, the Church of Ravenna, and to you, my lord Gerbert, archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna, in true faith, and to your successors forever. I promise that, according to my ability, I shall fulfill every command, will, or custom of the holy [Col. 0269C] Church of Ravenna.

I shall never join myself with your enemies to the detriment of the holy Church of Ravenna or through infidelity toward you; rather, with all my strength I shall stand against them for your fidelity. Whatever I may learn from them, either personally or through my messenger, I shall strive to report promptly, as soon as I can, to you or to your faithful servants. I promise faithfully that throughout the days of my life I shall never go, nor send a messenger, to the pope, or to a greater or equal patriarch, or to the emperor, or to a king, or to any person, great or small, acting against your holy lady, the Church of Ravenna, or against your will or that of your successors, by any device and without your permission or that of your successors.

At the festivals of the holy martyrs Apollinaris and Vitalis, moreover, I promise to attend the synod every year according to ancient custom, [Col. 0270B] except in case of illness or travel. And concerning the property of the monastery of Saint Apollinaris, in which you intend to ordain me, from this hour onward I shall not presume to make any writing or charter that diminishes it, except only through leases or emphyteusis for the renewal of its goods, as they have been firmly established by our predecessors, or as I may arrange them better.

I shall renew all the property and possessions of that monastery for its improvement, and, with all my strength, I promise to gather the produce from those places which have been leased, after the complete inheritance of the contracting parties has been acquired according to the law of payment, insofar as I am able to administer it. So that this may truly be believed by all and observed by me in the future, I have written it with my own hand.

I, Peter, monk, presbyter, and abbot of the monastery of Saint Apollinaris at Classis, have written this promise with my own hand. [Col. 0270C]

And I, Artusinus the notary, have copied it.

# SECTION TWO

[Col. 0269]

# LETTERS AND PONTIFICAL DECREES

## [GENUINE]

### I. Sylvester II confirms the monastery of Saint Lambert at Seon, at the request of its founder, Count Aribo, and the Emperor Otto III, and enriches it with rights, on the condition that the monks pay twelve denarii each year to the Roman See

*(Year 999.)*

*[Monumenta Boica*, Munich, 1763, quarto, vol. II, p. 123.]

[Col. 0269D]

# SYLVESTER, BISHOP, SERVANT OF THE SERVANTS OF GOD

[Col. 0270D] If we endeavor, by our pontifical authority, to strengthen and exalt places or monasteries constructed for religious persons and devoted to God, we undoubtedly believe that this will contribute to our reward in both blessednesses. Therefore, let the diligence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, know how Count Aribo, for the remedy of his soul and those of his parents, constructed with generous benevolence a monastery in honor of the holy martyr Landpert on a certain place belonging to him, formerly called Burgili but [Col. 0271A] now called by the inhabitants Seuva Cella of Saint Landpert the Martyr. He requested that, for the increase of the reward of his salvation, it be confirmed as free by the authority of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles.

Accordingly, persuaded by the pious interventions of the most glorious Emperor Augustus Otto III, our apostolic authority has granted the aforesaid monastery of Saint Landpert the Martyr, through the text of this privilege, the freedom to choose for itself, and has granted that the monks serving God there may, according to the rule established by blessed Benedict the abbot, choose an abbot for themselves. Moreover, it pleased our authority to grant that the aforesaid founder may exercise the advocacy of the monastery as long as he lives; but after his death, the abbot, with the brothers, shall freely choose for themselves as advocate whomever they judge most useful.

The monastery shall possess and administer peacefully and securely, without any opposition whatsoever from any person, all urban or rural places, various estates, cultivated or uncultivated, with all their appurtenances, which have been or shall be granted by Christians; and after him all his successors, the abbots, shall possess them forever.

For this reason we confirm the aforesaid monastery, through the protection of the holy Roman Church and the liberality of our privilege, so that neither we nor any of our pontifical successors, nor any emperor or king, shall have the power to sell, grant as a benefice, or transfer it. No duke, archbishop, bishop, count, or any other person shall dare to disturb or molest it, or to usurp for himself anything from its possessions without the abbot’s will.

And as a token and testimony of the liberty granted, twelve denarii, in honor of the twelve apostles, shall each year be brought to the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul. If it should be impossible to present them each year, they shall be paid within a period of twelve years. And from now on one collect shall be said each day at Mass for the living Roman pontiff, and likewise for the dead.

But if anyone, with rash audacity—which we do not believe will happen—should attempt to contravene or act against the terms of this apostolic confirmation, let him know that he is bound by the chain of the anathema of our lord Peter, prince of the apostles, and that he is to be burned eternally with the devil and his most atrocious pomp, and with Judas, the traitor of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ; and, cast down together into the Tartarean abyss, let him perish with the impious.

Let it be fully known to all the faithful of Christ that if this my decree should not be able to remain eternally in such stability—which God forbid—then, immediately and without opposition from all rulers, this abbey, under the honor of the aforesaid freedom, shall freely return as property to the nearest heir from the family of the aforementioned Count Aribo. Yet even he shall not use it as his own property, but shall be its faithful custodian until it is again graciously treated like the other free abbeys that are to be provided for by royal protection.

Whoever proves to be the guardian and observer of this our privilege shall obtain from the Lord the grace of blessing and eternal life. [Col. 0272A]

Written by the hand of Peter, notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year 999 of the Lord’s incarnation, in the twelfth indiction.

### II. Pope Sylvester II confirms the privileges of the monastery of Fulda at the request of Abbot Erkanbald

*(Year 999, 31 December.)*

*[Dronke, *Codex Diplomaticus Fuldensis*, p. 341.]*

[Col. 0272B]

# SYLVESTER, BISHOP, SERVANT OF THE SERVANTS OF GOD, TO HIS BELOVED SON ERKANBALD, VENERABLE ABBOT OF THE SACRED MONASTERY OF OUR SAVIOR JESUS CHRIST, AND TO ALL YOUR SUCCESSORS, THE ABBOTS OF THAT MONASTERY, FOREVER

The care of our pontificate urges us to favor the interests of all the holy Churches of God and, so that each may remain in its proper condition, to provide them suitable assistance. Therefore, dearest son, we perpetually confirm to you and to your successors everything that your predecessors rightly and reasonably requested from our predecessors.

We therefore grant and confirm to you, by the enactment of our privilege, the monastery of Fulda, which the most holy martyr of Christ Boniface originally built and magnificently endowed through the gifts of kings and princes and through his own resources, together with all its cells, churches, estates, and everything belonging to it. No future abbot shall ever presume to receive consecration except from this apostolic see. Among all the monasteries of Germany, we grant to you and your successors the first rank in sitting or judging and in holding council.

No bishop, archbishop, or patriarch may rashly celebrate the solemn rites of Mass upon the altar of your patronage without permission received from you. Let no prince presume to subject either all or part of the monastery’s possessions to any mortal, or to grant anything under the name of a benefice; rather, let the Church of Fulda always serve the Roman See alone, specially, in freedom and security.

If, God forbid, any abbot of your monastery should have become infamous through some crime, we establish and command that he shall not undergo judgment upon an accusation until he has been heard and examined by our apostolic see. [Col. 0272D]

It shall also be permitted to you, dearest son, and to your successors, the abbots of that monastery, following the custom of bishops, to appeal to the apostolic see for the defense of yourself and your Church, and to defend yourselves against all your adversaries with the shield of Roman majesty.

We decree this also after deliberation: at suitable times it shall be reported to our vigilance how monastic discipline is directed according to the rule and how the brothers’ harmony is preserved through ecclesiastical diligence, lest, God forbid, under cover of this privilege, your minds and steps of righteousness be turned away from the norm of justice.

We forbid—and this in accordance with the decree of our predecessor Zacharias—that any woman enter the same monastery. We also earnestly command and admonish that no one take or grant to anyone anything from the revenues, lands, tithes, or other offerings of the faithful offered there to the holy martyr Boniface and to many other princes, beyond the lawful benefits of the officials. Rather, just as that blessed patron of yours established, let everything remain valid and ordered, both what appears to belong to the poorhouse and the guest gate and what belongs to the needs of the brothers.

Above all these things, we establish by the page of this decree, which we confirm by the authority of the prince of the apostles, that if anyone should dare to violate this charter of our privilege, let him be anathema, incur the anger of almighty God, and be excommunicated from the assembly of the saints; nevertheless, the dignity of the aforesaid monastery, granted by us, shall remain perpetually inviolable. [Col. 0273B]

Written by the hand of Antonius, notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church. Farewell.

Given on the second day before the Kalends of January, by the hand of John, bishop of the holy Church of Albano and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the first year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of the lord Sylvester the Younger, pope; while the lord Otto III the Peaceful was emperor, in the third year of his empire, in the thirteenth indiction.

### III. Pope Sylvester II grants Arnulf of Reims—“deprived of pontifical honor for certain transgressions, because his abdication lacked Roman consent”—permission, after receiving the staff and ring, to exercise the archiepiscopal office and enjoy all the insignia in the customary manner. He also confirms the privileges of the Church of Reims

*(Year 999.)*

*[Duchesne, *Historiæ Francorum Scriptores*, II, 843.]*

[Col. 0273C]

# SYLVESTER, BISHOP, SERVANT OF THE SERVANTS OF GOD, TO HIS BELOVED SON IN CHRIST ARNULF, ARCHBISHOP OF THE HOLY CHURCH OF REIMS

It belongs to the apostolic summit not only to care for sinners, but also to raise up those who have fallen and to restore those deprived of their proper rank by furnishing them with the insignia of recovered dignity, so that Peter may possess free power to loose and so that the dignity of Roman authority may everywhere shine forth.

Therefore, Arnulf, archbishop of Reims, since you had been deprived of pontifical honor for certain transgressions, we have deemed it right to assist you, so that, because your abdication lacked Roman consent, you may be believed capable of being restored through the gift of Roman mercy. For Peter possesses that supreme power to which no mortal felicity can be compared. [Col. 0273D]

Accordingly, by the provisions of this privilege of ours, once your staff and ring have been returned, we grant you the right to exercise the archiepiscopal office and to enjoy, in the customary manner, all the insignia belonging to the holy metropolitan Church of Reims. You shall use the pallium on the appointed solemnities, obtain the blessing of the kings of the Franks and of the bishops subject to you, and exercise, by our apostolic authority, every jurisdiction that your predecessors are seen to have possessed.

We also command that no mortal presume, in a synod or anywhere else, to bring against you in any way the charge of your abdication, [Col. 0274A] or on this occasion to burst into words of reproach against you. Rather, our authority shall protect you everywhere, even if the guilt of conscience should come forward.

Moreover, we confirm and grant to you the archbishopric of Reims in its entirety, with all the bishoprics subject to it, together with all monasteries, parishes, titular churches, chapels, estates, castles, villages, small holdings, and all possessions belonging to the Church of Reims, subject to and without violation of the testament of blessed Remigius, apostle of the Franks.

Establishing this by apostolic censure, under invocation of the divine judgment and prohibition by anathema, we decree that none of our pontifical successors, nor any other person, great or small, shall ever be permitted to violate this privilege of ours. If anyone, God forbid, should attempt to violate this Roman decree, let him be anathema. [Col. 0274B]

### IV. Letter of Pope Sylvester II concerning the election of Theotard as bishop of Anicium

*(Year 999.)*

*[Mansi, *Concilia*, vol. XIX, col. 244.]*

# SYLVESTER, SERVANT OF THE SERVANTS OF GOD, TO HIS BELOVED SON IN THE LORD THEOTARD, BISHOP OF THE HOLY CHURCH OF VELAY

Whenever disputes arise between opposing parties, an end ought to be sought through synodal deliberation, and whatever has been established ought to be carried out according to the synodal decision.

Therefore, since it is established from the general synod held [Col. 0274C] at Rome that Stephen, the invader of your Church, was rightly condemned by our predecessor Gregory V and removed from every priestly office—because he had been elected while Guido, the bishop, his uncle and predecessor, was still alive, without the will of the clergy and people, and after Guido’s death had been ordained bishop by only certain bishops—and since at that synod permission was first granted to the clergy serving God in the Church of Velay to elect another bishop, it was decreed that their chosen candidate should be ordained bishop by the Roman pontiff; and since we have learned that you were elected by them, therefore, with apostolic authority favoring their election, we ordain you bishop.

With pastoral concern we exhort you, dearest brother, to guard with diligent care the flock entrusted to you and to order yourself in good works, etc., so that if any bishop should rashly presume to excommunicate you or attempt to ensnare you in the bond of anathema, relying on our protection you may disregard that excommunication. [Col. 0274D]

[Note: Sylvester had subscribed this synod when he was then archbishop of Ravenna, under the name Gerbert.]

### V. Pope Sylvester II sends the sacred crown to Stephen, duke of the Hungarians, whom he also honors with the royal title; and, granting various privileges, establishes the Church of Esztergom as the metropolitan church of the kingdom

[Note: I would not dare to add the name of bull to this most celebrated document; nevertheless, I thought it should be included here, since it is a great testimony to the apostolic concern of the Roman pontiffs for spreading the orthodox religion, and an illustrious demonstration of the filial devotion of the kings of Hungary toward the Roman Church, which has never been like that found among other kingdoms and kings.]

*(Year 1000.)*

*[Cocquelines, *Amplissima Collectio Bullarum Romanorum Pontificum*, I, 399.]*

# SYLVESTER, BISHOP, SERVANT OF THE SERVANTS OF GOD, TO STEPHEN, DUKE OF THE HUNGARIANS: GREETING AND APOSTOLIC BLESSING

The envoys of your nobility, and above all our dearest brother Astricus, venerable bishop of Kalocsa, brought our heart so much greater joy and accomplished their office with so much less labor, inasmuch as, divinely forewarned, they had awaited with the most eager spirit the arrival of those from a people unknown to us.

A blessed embassy: anticipated by a heavenly message and conducted through angelic service, it was concluded by God’s decree before it had been heard by us. Truly, it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but, according to the Apostle, of God who has mercy (Romans 9:16): he who, as Daniel testifies, changes times and ages, transfers kingdoms and establishes them, reveals deep and hidden things, [Col. 0275B] and knows what is set in darkness (Daniel 2:21–22), because with him is the light which, as John teaches, enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1:9).

First, therefore, we give thanks to God the Father and to our Lord Jesus Christ, who in our times found for himself David, the son of Géza, a man after his own heart, and, having irradiated him with heavenly light, raised him up to shepherd his people Israel, the chosen nation of the Hungarians.

Next, we praise your highness’s devotion toward God and your reverence toward the apostolic see, over which, by the mercy of God, though supported by none of our merits, we preside. Then, with worthy praise, we commend the generosity of your liberality, by which you have offered to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the kingdom, the people whose duke you are, and all that is yours, including yourself, through the same envoys and letters. By this noble deed you have openly testified, and have truly shown yourself to be by merit such a person as you earnestly desired us to declare you.

But we shall be brief. It is not necessary for us to commend further one whom so many and such great deeds accomplished for Christ proclaim publicly, and whom God himself commends. Therefore, glorious son, everything requested from us and from the apostolic see—the diadem and royal name, the metropolitan church of Esztergom and the remaining bishoprics—we have gladly granted, grant, and bestow, with the apostolic blessing of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, the authority of that same almighty God going before and so commanding. [Col. 0275D]

We accept under the protection of the holy Roman Church the kingdom offered by your munificence to Saint Peter, together with you, your people, and the Hungarian nation, present and future; and we return and confer it upon your prudence, your heirs, and your legitimate successors, to have, hold, rule, govern, and possess.

All such heirs and successors of yours, after they have been legitimately elected by the leading men, shall likewise be bound to show due obedience and reverence to us and to our successors, either personally or through envoys; to demonstrate that they are subject to the holy Roman Church—which receives all its subjects not as slaves but as sons—and to persevere firmly in the Catholic faith and in the religion of Christ our Lord and Savior, and to promote it.

And because your nobility, emulating the glory of the apostles, has not disdained to perform an apostolic duty by preaching Christ and spreading his faith, has striven to supply our role and that of the priesthood, and has honored the prince of the apostles above all others with singular devotion, therefore we also, by a special privilege, wishing to honor your excellence and your heirs and legitimate successors on account of your merits, now and in all future ages, grant, will, and request—once you and they have been duly crowned with the crown we are sending, according to the formula delivered to your envoys—that you may and can have a cross, the emblem of the apostolate, carried before you, and that they likewise may and can do so; and, according as divine grace shall teach you and them, we likewise grant by apostolic authority that you may arrange and regulate the present and future Churches of your kingdom in our name and that of our successors.

All these matters are explained more fully in another letter, addressed jointly to you, the leading men of the kingdom, and all the faithful people, and delivered through our envoy whom we are sending to you. [Col. 0276B]

We pray almighty God, who called you from your mother’s womb by your name to the kingdom and the crown, and who commanded that the diadem made by us for the duke of Poland be given to you, to increase the fruits of his justice in you; may he generously water his new plants, your kingdom, with the dew of his blessing; may he preserve your kingdom for you and you unharmed for your kingdom; may he protect you from visible and invisible enemies; and, after the troubles of your earthly kingdom, may he adorn you with an eternal crown in the heavenly kingdom.

Given at Rome, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the thirteenth indiction.

### VI. Letter of Pope Sylvester II to Count Darferius and his sons and grandsons

*(Year 999.)*

*[Contatore, *History of Terracina*, 41.]*

[The supplied source ends here.]

[Col. 0276D] To Count Darferius and his sons and grandsons, “especially on account of the military service” promised to him, he grants “in the name of a benefice the upper and lower city called Terracina, with all its district and the County of Terracina.” “And since,” he says, “it is well known that the pontiffs of the holy Roman Church, in the name of a pension payable at specified indictions, have indiscriminately granted these and many other properties to certain persons, while they pursued profit and, under a very small census, were losing the Church’s greatest possessions, we wholly change this kind of gift for the better, so that the things which we grant through this page of our decree [Col. 0277A] under the name of a benefice are also military stipends. For we consider this kind of pension worthy, so that soldiers may contend in peace by their service and in war by their arms for the honor and safety of the holy Roman Church. But lest ecclesiastical possessions be able to pass into anyone’s possession or ownership, in the name of a pension we establish from this present fourteenth indiction that three gold solidi be paid to the agents of the holy Roman Church, namely in the month of January.”

## VII. Letter of Pope Sylvester II to Azelinus, Bishop of Laon

He summons Azelinus, accused of many crimes, to the next synod at Rome. (Year 1001.)

[At Mansi, *Concilia*, vol. XIX, col. 241.]

[Col. 0277B]

**SYLVESTER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **AZELINUS** [variant: Ascelinus], Bishop of Laon.

As for your well-being and the apostolic blessing, there is nothing you can wonder at, since, under the pontifical title, you have ceased even to be a human being in character. If faith joins a mortal being to God, faithlessness nevertheless makes a rational being equal to brute animals. Since it is clear that you understand all this, we are greatly astonished that you have abandoned your natural condition and perpetrated new and unheard-of crimes with such inhumanity.

The letter of King Robert and his bishops has been presented to apostolic and imperial hands; it accuses you before the entire clergy and people of the following public crimes. When you had been invited by the archbishops of Reims and Tours [Col. 0277C] and the other brethren to the synod held at Compiègne, after receiving from some of them and from others oaths guaranteeing the security of your life, limbs, and freedom from captivity, you are said finally to have come. Since you rightly dreaded the severity of the synod, being conscious of your own guilt, you came to plead for mercy, as that same letter attests.

You made it clear that you could not answer the charges under the law, and you did not deny that you had offended your lord, the king. Asking only for pardon throughout the synod, you obtained the king’s favor by renewed perjuries. Having given hostages—namely your archdeacon and another soldier—you promised to return the towers of Laon. Taking your master, the archbishop of Reims, with you under the pretext of receiving the towers, you wished to capture him; for the imprisonment of the others [Col. 0277D] exposed the deceit of the plot you had conceived against him.

O Judas, renewing the betrayal of your master and defiling pontifical glory in our times! If you wished to hand over the archbishop, you would not spare the lord king either, if you could. You keep the soldiers who were handed over in prison, and you are not afraid to deceive the king.

How often have we admonished you by letters of entreaty, and labored to rescue you from these dangers! But since, with the heaps of your sins rushing upon you, we have been unable to restrain you, we command you to be present at Rome in the coming Holy Week and admonish you to appear there at the synod that is to be held generally. Therefore, do not violate or delay this summons of ours on any pretext; for, unless you are present, you will be subject to synodal authority in that council [Col. 0278A], and you will gain nothing from your absence.

Let no excuse concerning the roads weigh upon you, since no ambushes await you in the kingdom of Lothair, while Italy presents no cause for fear. Unless you are detained by bodily illness, no other excuse can exist. But witnesses must be sent who can confirm your illness, answer your accusers, and clear you under the law.

## VIII. Pope Sylvester II Confirms the Possessions and Rights of the Church of Urgell

(Year 1091.)

[Cocquelines, *Bullarum seu pontificum amplissima Collectio*, I, 301.]

[Col. 0278B]

**SYLVESTER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend bishop of the holy Church of Urgell and to his successors forever.

The desire that is shown to endure through the appointment of religious superiors and the stability of holy places must, with God as its author, be supported without any delay. Whenever our assent and the protection of holy apostolic authority are sought for measures advantageous to their own interests, it is fitting that we willingly come to their aid out of benevolent regard and properly secure them, by reason, in complete safety, so that from this the Creator of all, God, may inscribe for us above all a reward in the heavenly realms.

And therefore, because you asked us to strengthen by a series of apostolic authority the aforesaid bishopric of the holy Church of Urgell, and to confirm that everything belonging to it which it appears justly and lawfully to possess or hold should remain there inviolably by perpetual right, we have yielded to your prayers. By this privilege of our authority, establishing and decreeing, we order that all urban or rural places—that is, estates, manses, halls, castles, farmsteads, vineyards, lands, and various properties, cultivated or uncultivated, with their tithes and first fruits, and with their male and female tenants, female servants, and *aldiones*—which have been granted to that bishopric by any faithful Christians; whether in the County of Cerdanya, the districts of Libia, Berguedà, Pallars, Ribagorça, Jesta, Cardós, Navia, and Turb; and the place of Santa Deodata with its boundaries; likewise the castle of Sanaugia with its boundaries; Calbicià, Feners, Submont, Letone, and Clopedera [Col. 0278D] with their woods and boundaries; in the district of Osona, Castellato and Turizella with their boundaries; in Marfà, the allod itself that belonged to Bishop Guisad; in the County of Girona, the estate of Adeiz with the whole allod or parish itself; likewise in Urgell, the estate called Baschara with its boundaries, the parish of Alasse itself, and the estate of Boxedera, Nocolone, Sardina, and Sallellas, with their fief and comital allod; in the estate of Saint Stephen, the fief and comital allod; in the valley of Andorra, all the comital allods, and that of Montanicello or le Cubilare itself with their boundaries; the castle of Catorbite with its boundaries, the estate of Salente with its boundaries, and the fief of Archavelle itself; and the monastery of Saint Peter at Schalas [Col. 0279A] with all its appurtenances.

Also the tower that belonged to Marchuz, and another tower within the boundaries of Celsima that belonged to Bellone; likewise a third part of the toll with the appurtenances of the market; and everything that appears through any documents to belong to the same pious place; and whatever from now on and in the future you and your successors shall lawfully acquire—you must possess, hold, and own all these things forever, in great security, peacefully and quietly.

No king, prince, count, margrave, judge, or any person, great or small, shall ever presume to inflict any force or invasion upon that bishopric or its appurtenances. If anyone, with reckless boldness—which we do not believe will happen—should attempt to act against the terms of this apostolic confirmation of ours, let him know that he is bound by the anathema of our lord, the prince of the apostles, Peter, and that he is to be burned in everlasting fire with the devil and his most dreadful pomp, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ; and, sunk together with the impious into the Tartarean abyss, let him perish.

But whoever proves to be the guardian and observer of this privilege of ours shall obtain from the Lord the grace of blessing and eternal life.

Written by the hand of Peter, notary and registrar of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the fourteenth indiction.

## IX. Letter of Pope Sylvester II to Robert, Abbot of Vézelay

He confirms the privileges of Vézelay. (Year 1001.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, vol. XIX, col. 243.]

[Col. 0279C]

**SYLVESTER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son **ROBERT**, devout abbot of the holy monastery of Vézelay, and to the entire congregation of that monastery, forever.

Whenever people hope that we will grant what unquestionably accords with reason, it is fitting for us to concede it willingly and to offer appropriate assistance to the desires of those who ask. And therefore, because you asked us to grant the monastery of Vézelay, over which you are known to preside, a privilege of the apostolic see—this monastery, which was formerly built in the kingdom of Burgundy, in the parish of Autun, in the district of Avallon, by Gerard, a most noble and Christian man, and by his wife Bertha, in honor of the Lord and [Col. 0279D] our Savior Jesus Christ and in veneration of his most blessed mother Mary; and which was bestowed by the aforesaid founders upon blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, through generous devotion and the page of a testament—we have willingly decided, moved by your prayers, that this should be done, just as it was done long ago by our predecessors, Pope Nicholas of pious memory and Pope John.

By this privilege of apostolic authority we confirm and establish that no emperor, no king, no prelate, no person endowed with any dignity, nor anyone else may, under any pretext or occasion, diminish, remove, or apply to his own uses any of all the movable or immovable possessions [Col. 0280A] granted and conveyed to that monastery by the founders already named or by any other persons, or that may in the future be lawfully donated from anyone’s own property. Rather, we wish and command that everything offered there, or that may happen to be offered from the time of the present fourteenth indiction onward, be possessed intact and without disturbance for the support of the aforesaid monastery and for the use of the abbots and monks serving God there under the rule of Father Benedict.

This is on the following condition: no future pontiff of our successors in this holy see, which by God’s authority we serve, shall ever or anywhere allow any of those possessions to be granted as a benefice to anyone, exchanged, or conceded under any census. Instead, our successors, receiving only the census assigned in the testament of the founders’ gift—by which they made this holy Roman see heir to the same monastery—namely one pound of silver each year, shall diligently strive, with pastoral care, to provide the monastery, and you and your successors, and the monks living there under the rule of the aforesaid Father, with the support of pious fatherhood against all who attack them.

We likewise establish that, when the abbot of the said monastery dies, no one else shall be appointed there by any trick of concealment, except the person whom the consent of the monks, in accordance with the fear of God and the institution of the rule of blessed Benedict, has chosen and whom the pontiff of this apostolic see has provided to be ordained [Col. 0280C].

Therefore we establish, decree by apostolic authority, and confirm through this apostolic privilege of ours that no king or pontiff, abbot or count, or any person, great or small, corrupted by the desire of avarice or deceived by diabolical suggestion, dare or presume in any way to rise against your honor, venerable Abbot Robert, or to inflict trouble upon you in your place or on account of your office, or to inflict any invasion, plunder, or violence concerning all the monastery’s possessions granted and confirmed to you and your predecessors by us and our predecessors through the page of a privilege. If anyone does so, let him know that, by the authority of God, Saint Peter, and our apostolic excommunication, he is separated from the body and blood of our Lord [Col. 0280D] Jesus Christ and from entry into the church.

We add this clause to the present document in order to exclude the place of avarice: no king, no bishop or priest, nor any of the faithful, either personally or through a substitute, may ever presume to receive anything, under any pretext whatsoever, as a gift in connection with the appointment of the same abbot, or of clerics or priests, or with the donation of chrism, or the consecration of the basilica, or any other matter pertaining to the same monastery; nor may the same abbot give anything for his appointment.

Nor may the bishop of that city and parish celebrate public Masses there unless invited by the abbot of that monastery, nor announce stations in [Col. 0281A] the same monastery, lest the peace of God’s servants be disturbed in any way by a popular gathering; nor may he presume to exact lodging dues from it. We do not merely deny the reception of the faithful or religious men, and the beneficence that the Apostle commands to be shown to all, insofar as the place and its resources permit; rather, we expressly recommend that these things be done there.

If any king, bishop, priest, abbot, judge, count, or secular person attempts to act against this page of our institution, struck by apostolic anathema, let him lose the dignity of his power or honor and recognize himself as guilty before the divine judgment. Unless he mourns what he has wrongly done, let him be separated from the most sacred body of our Lord Jesus Christ and subjected to the strict vengeance of eternal judgment [Col. 0281B].

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who rightly observe the same place’s rights, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the eternal Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

## X. Letter of Sylvester II to Odo, Bishop of Girona

(Year 1002.)

[Flórez, *España Sagrada*, XLIII, 419.]

**SYLVESTER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son **ODO**, bishop of the holy Church of Girona, and to his successors forever.

The desire that, and so forth. And therefore, because you asked us to strengthen the aforesaid bishopric of the holy Church of Mary of Girona through the protection of apostolic authority, and to confirm that everything belonging to it should remain there inviolably by perpetual right—namely, whatever it appears to possess within the walls of the city of Girona or in its county, together with the church of Saint Felix the Martyr and Saint Narcissus, which is beside the gate of the city of Girona, with all their appurtenances; and the church of Saint Mary, which is called [in the vernacular] Labisbal, the episcopal church; together with the allod itself, or the fisc, called Fontanetus and Fonte Edeta, and Apiliares and Ventinaco, and the wall and smaller wall of Palatiolo, and the fountain itself.

All these things, with tithes, first fruits, offerings, and fiscal service; and the allod called Parietes Rufini with its boundaries and adjoining lands; and all the parish churches [Col. 0281D] and dependent churches throughout the entire County of Girona, with the tithes, first fruits, and offerings of the faithful, and the allods belonging or appearing to belong to those churches; and a third part of the coinage of the city of Girona, together with the census of the Jews; and a third part of the toll from the markets of the aforesaid city or its county; and a third part of the pasturage dues of the aforesaid county.

And in the County of Besalú, the allod called Bascara and the allod of Crispianus, with their boundaries and adjoining lands; and the cell of Saint Lawrence, which is above the castle of Bobeta, in the manner in which Fredolo holds it by royal decrees; and the church of Saint Martin, which is in the place called Calidas, with everything it appears to possess [Col. 0282A]; and all the parish churches and dependent churches in the aforesaid County of Besalú that belong or ought to belong to the aforesaid see, with tithes, first fruits, offerings, and the allods belonging to those churches; together with a third part of the toll, its markets, and its pastures.

And in the city of Empúries, everything that the aforesaid see possesses there, together with the census from the sea; and in the aforesaid County of Empúries, the allod called Uliano, with its boundaries and adjoining lands and with fiscal service; and the churches founded there, with the tithes, first fruits, and offerings belonging to those churches; and the church of Saint John, which is in Bederga, with its tithes, first fruits, and offerings [Col. 0282B].

And all the parish churches with their dependencies in the aforesaid County of Empúries, together with their tithes, first fruits, offerings, and allods belonging to those churches; and in Potralata, the church of Saint Martin, with its tithes, first fruits, and offerings; and in the County of Peralada, the church of Saint Mary, with its tithes, first fruits, offerings, and allods; and all the parish churches with their dependencies in the aforesaid County of Peralada, with their tithes, first fruits, offerings, and allods; and a third part of the toll from the markets and a third part of the pasturage dues.

And so that we might secure it through the page of our privilege, established without the yoke or authority of any person—therefore, yielding to your prayers, by this privilege of our authority we establish and decree that all places, and so forth, so that no judge, no margrave, and so forth. But whoever is its guardian, and so forth.

Written by the hand of Peter, notary and registrar of the holy Roman Church, in the month of December, in the first indiction. Farewell.

## XI. Bull of Pope Sylvester II by Which He Takes Both the Monastery of Stavelot and That of Malmedy under His Protection and Orders That, in the Election of an Abbot, One from Stavelot Be Chosen If a Suitable Candidate Is Found There

(Years 999–1003.)

[Marten, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 54.]

[Col. 0282D]

**SYLVESTER**, supreme and universal pope and vicar of blessed [Col. 0283A] Peter, servant of the servants of God, to Ravenger, venerable abbot of the Stavelot and Malmedy monasteries, and to all who desire to live devoutly in Christ: true love in the Lord Jesus and unanimous brotherly charity.

Since it is evident that, after the transgression of our first parents, the human race was subjected to that sentence through the abuse of free will—so that, in the Psalmist’s words, one human being might be set over the heads of others, in order, namely, to restrain the illicit desires of human pleasure, and so that we might be controlled not only by civil laws but also by ecclesiastical rules and principles—the institution of authorities has advanced to such a point that holy places of holy things, founded by the devotion of the faithful and devoted to divine worship, which have received many distinguished endowments from various persons, seek decrees of immunity not only from kings but also from emperors; indeed, they desire privileges of our authority for their stability.

Therefore, at the request of the venerable Notger, Bishop of Liège, we receive the abbey of Stavelot and Malmedy, nobly built through the generosity of ancient kings and emperors and always defended both by the authority of our predecessors and by royal immunity, under the protection of this same immunity of ours.

Let them always have an abbot, with this provision prevailing for the peace of the people of Malmedy: since blessed Remaclus, founder of both monasteries and formerly bishop and pastor of the Tungrians, preferred to choose a place of burial for himself in one of them—namely, Stavelot—the people of Stavelot shall have the first turn in the election, if a man better in merits and more learned in letters is found among them. But if a better man is found not there but at Malmedy, he shall be placed over both establishments rather than admitting an outsider.

## XII. Letter of Pope Sylvester II to Odilo, Abbot of Cluny

(Years 999–1003.)

[Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. IV, p. 134.]

[Note: [Col. 0283D] Since quite a few bishops, having renounced their dignity, were withdrawing to the monastery of Cluny in order to profess the monastic life, it happened that one of them, with the consent of his fellow bishops and his abbot, conferred ecclesiastical orders upon certain clerics. From this a doubt arose among some as to whether those ordinations were valid; some bishops appear to have disapproved of them and deposed those who had been ordained. These men, nevertheless, [Col. 0284D] had advanced to higher grades. It seemed appropriate to consult Sylvester II about them, through a letter written to him by Abbot Odilo and delivered by the monk Gerbald, who, I think, later became abbot of the monastery of Saint Christina at Olonna in the territory of Milan. To this letter the pontiff replied as follows.]

**SYLVESTER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Odilo, beloved son and distinguished abbot, and to the entire congregation entrusted to him: affectionate greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0283C] We continually commend ourselves to your most holy prayers and pray, in faithful petitions, that you may deign to receive us; for, whatever may be the extent of our ability, your advancement will in no way experience a lack.

Regarding the matters you have presented for examination by our authority through your monk Gerbald, we respond to you with the following judgment, by **APOSTOLIC AUTHORITY AND THE COUNSEL OF OUR FELLOW BISHOPS**.

We recognize that that bishop was canonically ordained and had reasonably received the episcopal office. But after he had been led by divine love to renounce secular honors and offices, it was no longer lawful for him to perform the same functions that he had previously performed in the ordinary life.

Therefore, since he did what he did neither rashly nor contrary to Catholic authority, but exercised it obediently and simply with the permission of his fellow bishops and his own abbot; and since a good intention is not contrary to God, we wish and judge that all whom he led and blessed for promotion to any ecclesiastical grade shall be blessed and shall exercise their proper grade by our permission and blessing.

But those who, proudly and presumptuously, refuse to remain in the same grade in which he ordained them shall be suspended from the grade they received after his [variant: on account of his] deposition; they may nevertheless lawfully enjoy the grade they previously held. The bishop just mentioned must not presume to do similar things hereafter.

Farewell.

## XIII. Letter of Pope Sylvester II to [lacuna], Abbot

(Years 999–1003.)

[At Theiner, *Disquisitiones criticae in praecipuas canonum et decretalium Collectiones*, p. 318, from Vatican Codex no. 1363, fol. 207.]

**SYLVESTER**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to [lacuna], abbot: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We delayed replying to you about the matter on which you consulted us because we have no authority for it in the Roman volumes. We remember, however, that the books in which we read a specific ruling were left in Gaul. Nevertheless, we retain in our memory something that we believe may suffice for your request.

In those same books it is written concerning bishops promoted through money that, if anyone of this kind is found, he is to be deprived of episcopal office for two years, abstain from wine and cooked food two days each week, and eat only after completing the Psalter. We see this to agree with the traditions of the earlier Fathers, who decreed that bishops of this kind should be deposed.

Suspension from office is to be equivalent to deposition. For one who is deposed is not deprived of communion. A two-year suspension with penance is certainly equivalent to deposition alone. Whoever, after a two-year suspension and penance, is restored to his office is mercifully reconciled as though after deposition.

Begin the aforesaid two-year period, therefore, after the octave of Pentecost, and by that arrangement you shall be restored to your office. If you can entrust the care of the brethren and the burden of the entire monastery to one of the brothers until you have completed your penance, entrust them to him. If not, then, although you are burdened, you must patiently bear the whole burden yourself. Thus, repeated heat pours the metal more purely from the furnace.

## XIV. Fragment

Sylvester II takes under his protection the church of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, built in the County of Gévaudan by Stephen, vice-count, and his wife Angelmoda, and offered to blessed Peter. (Years 999–1003.)

[*Histoire de Languedoc*, vol. II, proofs, p. 154.]

[Col. 0284D] **SYLVESTER**, bishop, to all worshipers of the Christian faith.

We wish it to be known that Stephen, vice-count, and Angelmoda, husband and wife, donated to our holy Roman Church, by a deed of gift, the church of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, built from their own property and situated in the County of Gévaudan, and so forth.

Therefore it pleased us [Col. 0285A] to place the aforesaid church [lacuna] under our protection, and so forth. We order that no king, margrave, duke, count, vice-count, or other person of high or low status dare disturb or molest that church in any way, and so forth.

## XV. Sylvester II Adorns with Privileges the Monastery of the Holy Trinity and Saint Peter of Bourgueil, Founded by Emma, Countess of Poitiers

(Year 1003.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, first edition.]

**SYLVESTER**, pope, to Emma, Countess of Poitiers.

You have made known to our ears that, by God’s gift and at the urging and exhortation of the venerable Abbot Gaubert, you founded at the place called Bourgueil a monastery in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity and of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles [Col. 0285B], enriched it with lands, and endowed it with possessions. Moved by your prayers, we willingly grant our assent.

Therefore, with Raynald, Bishop of Angers, consenting, we establish that no bishop of any city may presume to hold a council in the same monastery without the consent and will of the abbot and monks of that place.

The monks of that place may conduct the election of an abbot, choosing not someone from outside but one from among themselves, whose life and conduct are according to God. Once he has been elected, they shall present him to the Duke of Aquitaine and his sons, and the duke shall grant him the investiture without any opposition or resistance.

But if any abbot, inflamed by desire or fortified by secular power, should wish to enter this abbey by force and dare to disregard the writing set forth above, let him fall under the dreadful judgment of God.

The churches of that monastery, wherever they are situated, shall remain free from disturbance by any bishop, archdeacon, or other person, except for the synodal dues or those called in the vernacular *circada* or *parada*, and so forth [Col. 0286B].

Written by the hand of Peter, notary and registrar of the holy Roman Church, indiction I. Farewell, Sylvester, also called Gerbert, pope.

# DOUBTFUL WORKS

[Col. 0285]

## XVI. Letter of Pope Sylvester II to the Emperor Otto III

He states that he has entrusted to the Bishop of Pavia the monastery of the Pavia nuns called Senator’s monastery, and asks the emperor to confirm this arrangement. (Year 1001.)

[Muratori, *Antichità Italiane*, V, 991.]

[Col. 0285B]

[Col. 0285C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, **SYLVESTER**, servant of the servants of God, humble bishop of the apostolic see, to **OTTO**, emperor.

It is fitting always to watch and labor with pastoral care for the salvation of the flock, so that, supported by your protection, our administration may strive to protect, guard, and defend our churches, lest the unrestrained violence of wicked people, free from every fear, prevent those serving God from performing their duties.

We know that this was known to your predecessors and to your imperial majesty: Senator built at Pavia, for the remedy of his soul and that of all the faithful, a monastery in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin. He gave it to our jurisdiction on the condition that, at the appropriate time, we should consecrate as abbess there one elected from that congregation to govern the holy nuns, and that we should defend that place from the molestation of wicked men.

Now, however, [lacuna], while the worst slander was oppressing the abbess and the holy nuns serving God, we were unable to defend them from a distance as was fitting. Through the intervention of our vicar Wido, the bishop of that place, and also at the urging of your imperial majesty, we granted that monastery to the church of Saint Syrus—not for dominion through subjection, nor through external [lacuna] dominion, nor under any condition, but solely for consecration and defense. Thus the pastor and bishop of that place might defend the present abbess and the holy nuns from every disturbance.
