This was on the condition that if the aforesaid bishop, or any of his successors, should cause any of my successors or of the emperors to establish anything by writing or by any device [lacuna], the monastery should immediately return to our consecration [Col. 0286C] and your protection.

Since neither we nor anyone else dares to act otherwise than Senator of blessed memory acted when he made his arrangement concerning it, we beg your imperial clemency to strengthen our constitution by your decree, and we ask you to confirm it. If any bishop or any person, great or small, should presume to diminish or devastate the possessions of that church, or to exact any tribute, let him know that, unless he repents, he is bound by the bond of anathema on behalf of Saint Mary, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, all God’s elect, and ourselves, and is condemned forever with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord.

To make this still more firmly established, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and marked it with our seal.

Sylvester [lacuna], bishop, and of holy Mary, Virgin and Mother of God [Col. 0286D], we have confirmed with our own hand.

The sign of Emperor Otto.

Written by the hand of Peter, scribe of the holy Roman Church.

Confirmed by the hand of Gregory, secretary of the holy apostolic see.

Done at Rome in the year 1001 of the Lord’s incarnation, in the thirteenth indiction, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Sylvester, universal pope.

A leaden seal is attached.

[Col. 0287]

# POEMS OF SYLVESTER II

## I. Epigram of Gerbert, Bishop of Ravenna, Later Roman Pontiff

It bears the following inscription, addressed to the image of Boethius.

[Baronius, *Annales ecclesiastici*, vol. VII, Appendix, p. 5.]

[Col. 0287A]

While powerful Rome declares her laws throughout the world,

You, father and light of your country, Severinus Boethius,

As consul, guide the reins of affairs;

You pour light into studies and refuse to yield

To the intellects of the Greeks; but, divine mind, restrain

The empire of the world. When the sword of the Goths rages,

Roman liberty perishes. You, consul and exile,

Leave behind illustrious titles through a glorious death.

Now Otto the Third, the honor of the empire,

Who surpasses the highest arts, judges you worthy of his court,

[Col. 0287B]

And establishes monuments to your labor forever,

And adorns the well-deserving man with honorable distinctions.

## II. Epitaph of Lothair, King of the Franks

[In Duchesne, *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. II, among the letters of Gerbert.]

To whose service the dukes assembled, whom every good man revered,

Offspring of the Caesars, O Caesar Lothair, you display monuments of grief

In a second light,

Because you were seen in the star of dreadful Mars.

## III. Epitaph of Duke Frederick

[Same source.]

By the decree of the Franks this man bore the name Frederick;

His forefathers, dukes sprung from royal blood, begot him;

Last sleep carried off one equal in office and merits,

When the lofty house of Mercury lay open to you, O Phoebus.

## IV. Epitaph of Adalbert the Scholastic

[Same source.]

Born of nobles and having attained the study of reason,

Belgium says that you were Adalbert in the flower of youth.

Fortune, not allowing you to remain long,

Carried you away,

When Apollo had brought forth twice six days of February.

## V. Epitaph of Emperor Otto

[Same source.]

The dukes trembled at whose command;

The enemy bore away the man

Whom they had known as their lord and the father of his people.

Otto, glory of the gods, dearest Caesar to us,

The seventh light of December snatched you away undeservedly [the printed text reads: “mmeritis”].

# SPURIOUS OR BY ANOTHER AUTHOR

[Col. 0287]

## ACTS OF THE COUNCIL OF REIMS AT SAINT-BASLE, BY GERBERT, ARCHBISHOP

[At Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. III, p. 658.]

### THE PROLOGUE OF THE SYNOD OF REIMS BEGINS

[Note: [Col. 0287] Reading: “G. papae” (“pope”), edition 1.]

[Col. 0287C] Although my rivals sharpen their teeth against me and prepare to tear apart my words and deeds, I am moved more by the service of my friends than by the hatred of my enemies. For I have not learned to fear where there was no fear, nor to leave unfinished the affairs of my friends. I shall therefore gird myself and briefly touch upon the principal classes of cases presented at the Council of Reims, so that both the truth of what was done may become known and what was reconsidered by the most eminent men may be recognized.

I ask the leaders of this sacred assembly that, if I express anything insufficiently weighty or inadequately polished, it be attributed not to any injury done to them but to my ignorance; and I ask the hearers not to mark me down as having said something irrelevant or too little. For I judge that three kinds of interpretation must be employed [Note: [Col. 0287] “indum” corrected to “utendum” in 2.]: namely, that some things should be transferred literally from one language into another; in other cases, the gravity of the meaning and the dignity of the eloquence should be shaped according to the manner of expression [Note: [Col. 0287] “ita” in 1 and 2.]; and in still others, a single expression should provide the occasion both for investigating what is hidden and for bringing the very sentiments plainly into the light. Although I may not be able to achieve these things fully, I shall nevertheless try by these methods to interpret the opinions of the most learned men.

But I shall to some extent restrain their amplifications and digressions, if there are any of that kind, lest I seem to be moved chiefly by hatred of certain persons, and especially of Arnulf the traitor, as though I desired to appear to have legitimately obtained the episcopal see of Reims through his legitimate deposition. This will belong to another work and will be entangled with other questions, when I shall discuss at greater length, as I have conceived in my mind, the proper, common, and distinguishing powers of bishops, archbishops or metropolitans [Note: [Col. 0289] “metrapolitanorum” in 1.], patriarchs or primates, and even of the Roman [Col. 0290A] bishop.

[Col. 0289A] THE PROLOGUE ENDS [Note: [Col. 0289] “End of the prologue of the Synod of Reims” in 2.].

THE CHAPTERS BEGIN.

[Col. 0290A]

1. Who the bishops were, where they came from, and from which provinces they assembled.  
2. Arnulf the bishop’s introductory statement concerning the examination of Arnulf’s case [Note: [Col. 0289] “Odo” in 2.].  
3. Archbishop Siguin’s response concerning the cognizance of the judgment.  
4. The objection of Archbishop Daibert and Bishop Herveus.  
5. Bishop Bruno’s complaint.  
6. The prosecution of Bishops Gotesmann and Bruno concerning the examination [Note: [Col. 0289] “discusione” in 1.] of Arnulf.  
7. Bishop Ratbod says that the bishops of Lotharingia criticize Arnulf’s written pledge.  
8. Arnulf’s written statement.  
9. Bishop Arnulf partly censures and partly praises the same written statement.  
10. A copy of the written statement of a certain heretic who had converted.  
11. The confession of the priest Adalger.  
12. Bishop Odo introduces Arnulf’s admonition and anathema.  
13. Bishop Gualterius censures these things.  
14. Bishop Guido introduces another anathema.  
15. Archbishop Siguin argues that Arnulf and his accomplices appear to have been condemned.  
16. Examples from the canons concerning condemned men who minister.  
17. The admonition of Bishop Arnulf in defense of Arnulf.  
[Col. 0289C] 18. Archbishop Siguin’s anathema concerning the same matter.  
19. Those who tried to defend Arnulf, and the examples they used.  
20. Archbishop Stephen’s letter to Pope Damasus.  
21. Damasus’s reply to the same.  
22. Bishop Ratbod presents a decretal volume to the synod in defense of Arnulf.  
23. A brief note on Arnulf’s accusation and defense.  
24. That he was justly captured, according to the African Council [Note: [Col. 0289] “africano” in 2.].  
25. A copy of the king’s letter addressed to the Roman pontiff concerning Arnulf’s case.  
26. Likewise, the bishops’ letter to the same.  
[Col. 0290A] 27. What the king’s and Bishop Bruno’s envoys did at Rome.  
28. Bishop Arnulf’s lucid speech containing the force of the entire synod.  
29. Examples from the canons against Arnulf.  
30. Arnulf, brought before the synod, contradicts the bishops’ opinions; but, unable to endure Rainerius’s sentence [Note: [Col. 0289] “retineri” in 2 and in the Frankfurt (1b) and Flacius (2b) editions.], he asks to withdraw.  
31. After Arnulf’s departure, the synod records chapters concerning his crimes.  
32. Concerning priests from border regions subject to enemies who undertake embassies without the king’s permission.  
[Col. 0290B] 33. Concerning those who do not keep the faith promised to kings.  
34. Concerning clerics who commit capital crimes.  
35. Concerning those who flee to the enemy.  
36. Concerning those who, while the king is still alive, arrange a kingdom for themselves or for others.  
37. Concerning the protection of princes’ lives.  
38. Concerning clerical or lay refugees and traitors.  
39. Concerning clerics or monks who perjure themselves against the king.  
40. The bishops’ collection, Arnulf’s confession, and the question of his deposition.  
41. Concerning the deposition of Bishop Maximus.  
42. Concerning the priest Euticetes.  
43. Concerning Ratherius and Peter, who were expelled.  
44. Concerning those unjustly deposed.  
45. How Arnulf ought to be deposed.  
[Col. 0290C] 46. The example of Archbishop Potamius, who was deposed.  
47. Concerning Egidius and Ebo, who were deposed.  
48. Concerning the judgment not being reopened.  
49. The synod of the following day.  
50. The entrance of the kings into the synod.  
51. Bishop Arnulf briefly recapitulates the proceedings of the previous day.  
52. Bishop Arnulf embellishes Arnulf’s confession against Count Brochard [Note: [Col. 0289] “c. b.” in 2.].  
53. Arnulf asks the kings for pardon, receives it, and acknowledges the manner of his abdication.  
54. Arnulf’s written abdication.  
55. The priest Adalger’s protest and deposition.  
56. The African Council in which the status of the Roman bishop is ascertained.

THE SYNOD OF REIMS BEGINS [Note: [Col. 0289] “1. s. r.” is absent in 2.].

[Col. 0289]

[Col. 0289D] 1. In the year [Note: [Col. 0289] absent in 2?] 991 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the fourth indiction, in the fifth year [Note: [Col. 0289] absent in 2; “V. regni” in 1b.] of the reign of the lord Hugh Augustus and of the most excellent King Robert, in the fourth year [Note: [Col. 0289] omitted in 1 and 1b; in 2b: “in the ninth year of the reign of the lord Otto Augustus and the fourth year of the most excellent King Hugh.”], a synod was assembled in the territory of Reims.

This was arranged with great diligence by the princes, because all the bishops of Gaul could not assemble there on account of certain necessities of the kingdom. Those were therefore to assemble especially who were their provincial colleagues [Note: [Col. 0289] “provintia” is consistently written in 2.]; then, from neighboring provinces, those more distinguished in reputation and dignity, and those who seemed worthy to represent their provinces and able by their presence to sustain the absence of their brethren.

Accordingly, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, [Col. 0291A] they assembled in the basilica of the lord Basolus the confessor. From the diocese of Reims itself were Guido, bishop of Soissons [Note: [Col. 0291] “suessionicae” in 2.]; Adalbero of Laon; Herveus of Beauvais; Gotesmann of Amiens; Ratbod of Noyon; and Odo of Senlis. From the province of Bourges, which is considered part of Aquitaine, came Archbishop Daibert. From the first province of Lyon came Gualterius, bishop of Autun [Note: [Col. 0291] “Gualterus” in 1b and 2.], Bruno of Langres, and Milo of Mâcon. From the province of Sens, which is the first metropolitan province of the Sequani and borders the province of Reims, came Archbishop Siguin, Arnulf of Orléans, and Herbert of Auxerre.

In addition, very many abbots from various cities were present; after the bishops’ private discussion they were ordered to remain. When the whole structure of the synod had been considered, the dignity of presidency and judicial authority rested, as it were, with Archbishop Siguin, whom both his age and the merit and learning of his life commended. Arnulf, however, the venerable bishop, was appointed guardian of order and interpreter of all that was to be done, because he was regarded as more distinguished in wisdom and eloquence than all the bishops of Gaul.

After he had presented the allegations of those priests who could not be present, and after the entrance of the entire clergy, certain opinions having been examined, we received the following introductory statement from him:

2. “It is indeed as you say, most reverend fathers: no tumult, no insolent accuser, and no unjust judge ought to disturb this holy council. Let each person’s place and due [Col. 0291C] reverence be preserved; and let no one think that either he or another is being burdened by prejudice, since there is free opportunity both to bring forward proposals, to inquire, and to respond. Let consultations or deliberations be placed before us in such a way that no one complains that something he does not wish has been imposed upon him, or that something he does wish has been taken away.

“Since you have wished me to speak first, I shall say what I think in your presence and in that of the clergy recently admitted [Note: [Col. 0291] “ammissi” is written consistently in 1.], and I shall go back a little further so that matters properly arranged may become more clearly known.

“For while, amid various disturbances of war, I was striving with all my strength for the peace of the Church, which by God’s authorship I serve, I was so suddenly shaken by the report of new messengers and the rumor of an unheard-of crime that even in trivial matters my tongue faltered and my understanding grew dull. It was being reported that that noble city of Reims had been opened to the enemy through the deceit of treachery, had been surrendered to plunder and devastation, and that the Holy of Holies had been polluted by armed soldiers. The instigator and author of all these evils—something I cannot report without great pain of heart—was said to be Arnulf the bishop, the very man who ought to have protected it.

“The priestly dignity was being attacked on his account, and scarcely anyone refrained from insulting our order. Now, since we have assembled through love and zeal for religion and for our most serene king, our lord Hugh, we must ask [Col. 0292A] how we can free ourselves from so great a disgrace, and whether our brother and fellow bishop Arnulf seeks to clear himself of the crimes laid against him [Note: [Col. 0291] corrected from “queat” to “quaerat”; “queat” in 1b.], or to ward off the charge of lèse-majesté.

“For you all know that we are accused of the reproach [Note: [Col. 0291] “probo,” corrected by a later hand, in 2.] of disloyalty and treachery because of one man. ‘If,’ they say, ‘the bishops use just laws and are most faithful to their kings, why do they not punish an utterly impure man according to their own laws?’ Surely they are trying to conceal the crimes of others so that [Note: [Col. 0291] perhaps “an” in 1?] they themselves may be permitted to sin with impunity. May this be far from your most holy assembly! May it be far from us to try to defend or condemn anyone contrary to divine and human laws!

“Let those who know the sequence of events speak [Note: [Col. 0291] “sique,” corrected by a later hand to “sicque,” in 2.], and let those who, as they themselves assert, have suffered serious injuries set out their cases. Then, if any contradiction arises, let judgment be pronounced [Note: [Col. 0291] “promultetur” in 2.] with the authority of the canons after the parties have been examined.”

3. Then Siguin said: “I shall not permit an examination to be made of one who is said to be liable to a charge of lèse-majesté [Note: [Col. 0291] “obnixius” in 2.], unless perhaps indulgence from punishment is promised to a convicted man.”

At the same time, chapter 31 of the Council of Toledo, concerning the same matter [Note: [Col. 0291] “exadem,” corrected to “eadem,” in 2.], was brought forward:

“Often princes entrust their affairs to priests against any persons liable to a charge of lèse-majesté; and because priests have been chosen by Christ for the ministry of salvation, there they may consent to become judges with the kings where indulgence from punishment is promised by oath [Note: [Col. 0291] “promittetur” in 2.], not where a sentence of danger is being prepared. If any priest, contrary to this common decree, should act as examiner in another person’s danger, let him be guilty before Christ of the blood shed, and before the Church let him lose his own rank.”

4. “It is very serious indeed,” said Daibertus, “that you offer yourself as judge in another’s affairs so that, when you convict the accused, you may fall with him; when you give judgment, you may depart condemned yourself [Note: [Col. 0291] “habeas” in 1.].”

“If this is dangerous,” said Bishop Herveus, “see that it is not more dangerous for ecclesiastical judgments thereafter to be withheld from secular persons. For it follows that we are dragged before secular courts if we seem in any respect to resist the divine laws. But how will what is established to have been committed be left without judgment? Or why shall we complain against our prince if what we dare not touch is restrained by judicial authority [Note: [Col. 0291] “conceditur” in the editions.]?”

5. Bishop Bruno said: “Certainly none of you is as greatly disturbed as I am by the examination of so grave a danger. For I alone am being tossed about on everyone’s lips on account of this most unhappy affair. I seem to have plunged him into these miseries who, contrary to the wishes of all good men, gave myself as a hostage and pledge in hope of preserving loyalty; such [Note: [Col. 0291] “Tanta,” corrected by the same hand to “Tanti,” in 1.] were King Lothar’s merits in my eyes, and so greatly did our kinship move me.

“And although I knew that this usurper of the city of Laon and leader of the entire tyrannical faction had been, nevertheless under the pretext [Note: [Col. 0291] “optentu” in 2.] of this honor I tried to draw him toward a better state of life [Note: [Col. 0291] “visus” in 1.], so that he who had been an instigator of discord and wars might himself lay the foundations of peace and charity.

“Consider the beginnings of peace; consider the man who repays good with evil. He delivered men very dear to me and greatly necessary for the conduct of my life—namely, my only brother, Count Gislebert, and my cousin, Count Guido, together with the others whose friendship was my pride—over to genuine captivity by means of a feigned captivity [Note: [Col. 0293] corrected from “contra dedit” to “contradidit” in 2.]. He abandoned me, the sponsor of peace, to the danger of death. And oh, the shameless audacity of a man who, though the murderer of me—or rather of himself—and of the whole Church, still with brazen face denies what cannot be denied!

“Certainly, from what he confesses we shall extract what he is ashamed to disclose. Certainly, in the presence of the kings and bishops, before the faces of clergy and people, he willingly bound himself by oath to be of assistance to his princes, in counsel and aid, according to his knowledge and ability, against Charles; and likewise to give neither counsel nor aid to the enemies of his lords, knowingly contributing to their disloyalty; nor, because of any oath already taken or to be taken, to abandon the side of his lords.

“Was not Charles an enemy, since he was trying to invade the kingdom? Were not Rotger and Manasses enemies, since they had seized his clergy and people in his own church with armed soldiers? He himself had made these men his fellow consecrators and chief friends; he had enriched them with the goods of those who had chosen him and conferred the principate upon him—men from whom he could take nothing without perjury, whom he necessarily ought to assist unless they sinned against him. But what did they do wrong? Did they perhaps persuade themselves to keep the faith they had promised?

“Forgive me, brothers, if excessive grief has detracted somewhat from the gravity proper to a priest, and if it does not allow me to finish the speech which your understanding has fully grasped from what preceded.”

6. Here Gotesmann [Note: [Col. 0293] “Godesmann” in 2.], bishop of the Church of Amiens, added: “The venerable Father Bruno has pursued [Note: [Col. 0293] “propersecutus” in 2; “persecutus” in 2b.] many points which, the more they lend credibility to doubtful matters, the more they prove him guilty of lèse-majesté and conclusively show him unworthy of the priesthood. But since a little earlier there was talk of a dangerous examination, I should like to know what Father Bruno thinks about it. For it is not right that we should become authors of bloodshed, when we ought to be authors of salvation.”

And he replied: “I believe, reverend fathers, that you understand what you say, and that you are ashamed of something else which you keep silent about. For the divine laws move you [Note: [Col. 0293] “nos,” corrected to “vos,” in 1.], and so does a man joined to me by close blood relationship [Note: [Col. 0293] perhaps “carius” in 1?], being the son of my maternal uncle, King Lothar. I have, and I return, many thanks for your kindness.

“But may it be far from me to prefer love of blood to the love [Note: [Col. 0293] “amore” in 2.] of Christ, or to allow the Church of God to be polluted, as far as lies in me, by my blood. Therefore, let us proceed: let us undertake [Note: [Col. 0293] “aggediantur,” corrected to “aggrediatur,” in 2.] both the examination and the judgment, and do not recoil from bloodshed, since it is not difficult to obtain what is justly requested from the benevolence of the princes.

“For this above all must be feared: that while we perhaps wish to spare one person, as our brother and fellow bishop Herveus reported a little earlier, we may leave both him and the entire ecclesiastical order in danger of bloodshed. Therefore, if it pleases you, let that priest who opened the city gates be admitted and disclose the sequence of events.”

Everyone said: “It pleases us.”

7. “Since,” said Ratbodus, bishop of the Church of Noyon, “I hear many of our brethren saying that the written pledge of loyalty issued by Arnulf in the form of a chirograph may suffice for his condemnation, and since there is a report that certain Lotharingians are disputing against this document, I should meanwhile like to submit this matter to the judgment of so many fathers and learn what ought to be thought of it.”

The synod said: “Let it be brought forward.”

The chirograph was therefore brought forward in the following form:

8. “I, Arnulf, by the prevenient grace of God archbishop of Reims, promise the kings of the Franks, Hugh and Robert, that I shall preserve the purest faith, and shall provide counsel and aid, according to my knowledge and ability, in all matters; knowingly I shall assist neither their enemies by counsel nor by aid toward their disloyalty.

“I make this promise in the sight of the divine majesty, of the blessed spirits, and of the whole Church standing by, and for faithfully keeping it I shall receive the rewards of eternal blessing. But if—which I do not wish and may it be far from me—I should deviate from these things, may all my blessing be turned into a curse; may my days be few, and may another receive my episcopate. May my friends depart from me and be forever my enemies.

“Therefore, as testimony to my blessing or curse, I subscribe this chirograph issued by me, and I ask my brothers and sons to subscribe it. I, Arnulf the archbishop, have subscribed.” [Note: [Col. 0293] The words were supplied from Richer.]

9. When this had been read [Note: [Col. 0293] “perfecto” in 2; “peracto” in 2a.], Arnulf, the venerable bishop of the Church of Orléans, added:

“This document, I say, possesses the greatest force for accusation; it also possesses subtle powers of defense, if the persons involved are taken into account. For its author Arnulf is detestable, because through his boundless ambition for an honor he sought he has left behind an unheard-of and detestable memorial of himself in the world.

“Those, however, who composed the document seem to have done something useful and necessary, so that, if he should ever wish to deny the faith he had promised, the document might stand as a witness against him; and if he himself should deviate, acting contrary to his profession and subscription, he might deprive himself of his honor. Moreover, lest he be defended for too long under the name of supreme pontiff while sinning, the supreme pontiff himself appears to have pronounced the sentence of his own condemnation against himself.

“But since the priest is present, I shall stop speaking, so that room may be made for him.”

Meanwhile, as a place for the priest to stand was being chosen, he indicated to those sitting beside him that a certain bishop, converted from heresy to the Catholic faith, had presented the blessed Gregory with a similar written statement. The difference was that this Arnulf had been moved by considerations of evil causes—that is [Note: [Col. 0295] “. . . id” in 2.], by treachery and greed—whereas the other had been moved by the best causes [Note: [Col. 0295] “opt.” corrected to “obt.” in 2.], namely, the Catholic faith and the love of possessing God. The document was written there, among other things, as follows:

10. “And therefore, after discovering the snare of division by which I was held, and after prolonged deliberation within myself, I have returned, under the guidance of divine grace, to the unity of the apostolic see with willing and spontaneous resolve [Note: [Col. 0295] “nec” in 1.]. And lest I be thought to have returned not with a pure mind but dissimulating, I promise and pledge to you, and through you to Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and to his most blessed vicar Gregory and his successors, under penalty of the loss of my rank and the obligation of anathema, that I shall never, through the persuasion of anyone or in any other manner, return to the schism from which I have been rescued by the mercy of our Redeemer; rather, I shall always remain in every respect within the unity of the holy Catholic Church and in communion with the Roman pontiff.

“Therefore I swear by almighty God, by these four holy Gospels [Note: [Col. 0295] “quattuor” in 2.] which I hold in my hands, and by the welfare and genius of our lords, Mauricius and Theodosius, governors of the republic, that I shall remain in the unity of the Church, as I have said, to which by God’s favor I have returned, and in the communion of the Roman pontiff always and without doubt.

“But if—which may it be far from me—I should separate myself from this unity by any excuse or argument, I shall be found bound by eternal punishment as one guilty of perjury, and in the age to come I shall share the portion of the author of the schism.”

11. Adalger said: “I know, most reverend fathers, that I shall not have great expectation of success in speaking, since everything I shall say in my defense may perhaps seem to speak against me. I understood this at the outset also, when Dudo, a soldier of Charles, contrived that I should become the author of this treachery.

“When I asked him why, from so great a mass of people, I—a cleric and priest—should especially be chosen to betray my senior and bishop on behalf of Charles, with whom I had nothing to do, he first said that he knew the sluggishness and stupidity of men; but he extolled my talent, prudence, and greatness of spirit with extraordinary praises. Finally, he said that my very senior wished this and had ordered it.

“Although I had seemingly promised him my faith, I nevertheless considered it insufficiently safe unless I myself, without an interpreter, recognized the instructions as coming from the mouth of that senior, whose words had not been properly believed. His love and his command plunged me into these miseries.

“I nevertheless asked him, relying on whose assistance I was to carry out the orders, and whether he himself would have anything to fear [Note: [Col. 0295] absent in 1.]. When he said that Charles was his uncle and that Manasses and Rotger had given him whatever oaths he wished [Note: [Col. 0295] “Manassen” in 2.], he identified his own uncle Robert, Charles’s servant, as his most faithful count, together with certain others.

“And so that this deed might be concealed under the appearance of honor, I gave my hands and oaths to Charles as well—but at his command; I received the keys of the city—but from his hand; I opened the gates—but at his order.

“If any of you thinks otherwise, and considers me unworthy of belief, let him believe fire, boiling water, and red-hot iron; let the tortures testify, since my words are not sufficient. My very enemies, to whom I have lately begun to be hateful, will bear witness, since they will prove that I live through their favor. For, shuddering at your anathema and terrified by this confession of mine, I then scarcely escaped, through their compassion, the swords of Richard, the bishop’s brother.”

[Col. 0296B] 12. To this Odo, bishop of Senlis, replied: “Now, as I say, the anathema returns to our memory. Father Arnulf said that he had condemned our Arnulf in the chirograph. We, however, received from him at that very time, through the hands of the venerable Bishop Guido, a certain written statement in which both a confession of his deed and its condemnation seemed to be contained. Let Your Holiness order it to be read now.”

The synod said: “Let it be read.”

It was therefore read as follows:

“Arnulf, by the grace of God archbishop, an admonition [Note: [Col. 0295] “commonitorum” in 2.] to the plunderers of Reims.

“What do you want, you criminal hand of the plunderers of Reims? Do the tears of orphans and widows move you not at all? And does not their advocate, whether you wish it or not, your Lord himself, who is both witness and judge and stern avenger, move you—he whose [Col. 0296C] judgment you will not escape?

“See what you have done before his eyes: you were not ashamed of the holy chastity of virgins; you left even matrons, who ought to be revered by barbarians, naked; you showed no regard for the orphan and the fatherless. Was this too little for you? You approached the temple of the Mother of God, revered by all mortals. You broke through, polluted, and violated its courtyard. Whatever the eyes there saw, you desired [Note: [Col. 0295] “concupisti” in 1; “concupivisti” in 2.]. Whatever the hands were able to touch [Note: [Col. 0295] “attractare” in 2.], you seized.

“And indeed, while abusing mercy contrary to divine and human law, we do not forgive you what you stole of food and drink, but because of these impious times we do not demand it. We do demand everything else that you seized and retain with polluted hands [Note: [Col. 0295] “eam” in 1.]. Therefore restore it, or receive upon yourselves the sentence of condemnation promulgated by the sacred canons against invaders of ecclesiastical property, a sentence pronounced against you and to be pronounced many times:

“ANATHEMA AGAINST THE PLUNDERERS [Note: [Col. 0295] “A. I. P.” is absent in 2.].

“By the authority of almighty God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, with the intervention and assistance of blessed Mary ever-virgin, and also by the authority and power handed down to the apostles and left to us, we excommunicate, anathematize, curse, condemn, and separate from the thresholds of holy mother Church you—the instigators, perpetrators, accomplices, and supporters among the plunderers of Reims, and those who alienate their own lords’ goods under the name of purchase.

“May your eyes, which desired these things, be darkened; may the hands that seized them wither; may all the limbs that assisted be weakened [Note: [Col. 0297] This sentence is absent in 1.]. May you always labor and find no rest, and be deprived of the fruit of your labor. May you fear and tremble before the face of the pursuing and non-pursuing enemy, so that you may waste away and perish.

“May your portion be with Judas, the traitor of the Lord, in the land of death and darkness, until your hearts are converted to full satisfaction. Let this be the manner of full satisfaction: that you restore in full to their rightful owners everything unjustly taken, except food and drink, and that you humble yourselves in repentance before the Church of Reims, which you did not reverence as the holy Church of Reims. Nor [Note: [Col. 0297] “ne” in 1.] may these curses, persecutors of your crimes, cease from you as long as you remain in the sin of invasion.

“Amen. So be it. So be it.”

13. When this had been read, Gualterius, bishop of the Church of Autun, said: “What sort of portent is this [Note: [Col. 0297] “quodnam” in 2.]? Is this bishop of sound enough mind, since he condemns the guilty for the loss of the most worthless household goods [Note: [Col. 0297] “supp.” in 2.], yet says nothing about the captivity of himself, the clergy, and the people?

“Perhaps he pronounces an anathema over the huts of the poor because they are more likely to collapse from rot [Note: [Col. 0297] A gloss in the margin of 1 says, ‘that is, decay’; the word itself was erased and appears as ‘carie’ in 2.] than from force, while he says nothing about the temple of God, most famous throughout the world. Surely every earthly creature is less valuable than man, and every man-made building is less valuable than the temple of God.

“But because [Note: [Col. 0297] “f. q.” in 2.] the Apostle perhaps says, ‘If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink’ (Romans 12:20), he indulges the plunderers in food and drink as though acting out of piety, yet warns them away from gold and silver. What does this have to do with Christ’s poor? Certainly they did not lose gold and silver, because they did not possess them; but they did lose the food and drink which they had acquired for the necessities of life with no small labor.

“Behold, brothers, you have heard the argument of a ruined man, a murderer of the poor, and a nourisher of plunderers. You have understood that he wished to be captured for this purpose: so that his feigned captivity might bring about the genuine captivity of the nobles. For this reason he does not keep sacrilegious persons from communion, because he knows himself to be the author of sacrilege.

“Yet even so [Note: [Col. 0297] absent in 1.] he does not escape, while he mixes together the instigators, inventors, perpetrators, accomplices, and supporters. For he himself is the instigator, by whose counsel and command the treachery was carried out; he himself is the perpetrator and accomplice, so that, as a certain wise man says, ‘Those companions of yours were your hands’; he himself is the supporter, who to the present has consented by remaining silent and, as is reported, has moreover heaped great benefits upon them.

“This matter tends toward infinity, but I shall contract my speech as briefly as I can, lest I seem to be dictating a criminal indictment.”

14. Bishop Guido said: “If Arnulf was so injured in his own written statements, where he could have taken precautions for himself, how was he not condemned at the recent synod held at Senlis?

“For we, all of us who are present here and belong to the diocese of Reims, had assembled to complain that the holy Church of Reims, the mother of us all, was being desolated. Our metropolitan was being reported to be held by the enemy together with the clergy and people. Yet the rumor that he had committed the treachery was widespread.

“Therefore, by the common counsel of our fellow provincials, we decreed an anathema against the guilty, so that no one could in any way evade it by hiding himself. If it pleases you, let a copy of it [Note: [Col. 0297] “exe” in 1.] be brought forward.”

It was brought forward in the following form:

“INVECTIVE SPEECH OF THE BISHOPS OF THE DIOCESE OF REIMS, DELIVERED AT SENLIS IN PLACE OF A DECREE.

“‘How far will your unrestrained license extend, satellites of the other traitor Judas? To what end will the audacity begun by your leader in crimes proceed? We mean your leader, the priest Adalger, who has polluted the name of priestly dignity with his own name.

“‘Therefore we address you, deadly priest: what did you have in mind after those bloody arms with which you acted at Laon, so that once again, having become a worthless apostate, you might betray Arnulf, archbishop of Reims, when previously you lay beside him like a most faithful guardian, were his constant companion at table, arranged his counsels, and administered the sacred things?

“‘Did you think that you could escape the severity of ecclesiastical discipline or the judgment of almighty God? You opened the city gates and introduced the enemy; you attacked, as though it were an enemy camp, the venerable temple of the Mother of God, revered even by barbarians.

“‘And will you also escape divine laws, you great multitude of plunderers, who were bound to the Church by immense benefits, who say, “Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as an inheritance,” who, wearing armor and helmets and carrying shields and spears, brought military standards before the altar of the blessed Mother of God; who, with polluted hands, seized the shepherd together with the clergy and people within the Holy of Holies, assigned them to custody, committed them to prison, and still retain them?

“‘And you as well, through whose deceit and fraud, counsel and assistance, so great a crime was committed: you are to be joined with those who were the leaders of so great a crime, so that you may suffer the punishment of the sin together, since you conspired together in [Note: [Col. 0297] absent in 1.] the cause of the sin and sold the property of the citizens of Reims like the most impious plunderers under the auctioneer’s spear.

“‘Nor should you be absent, who carried out no less trivial acts against Adalbero, bishop of Laon. And to cut out the heresy that is sprouting [Note: [Col. 0297] “pulul.” in 2.], which declares that everything is permitted to Charles even in sacred places, we remove from sacred offices both the Church of Reims and the Church of Laon, each polluted by sacrilege, though in different ways, until both are legitimately reconciled.

“‘And lest anyone think that we will favor such human monsters or consent to such actions, we confirm, establish, and strengthen our sentence in this way, exposed to every danger for the faith by which we live:

“‘ANATHEMA AGAINST THE GUILTY.

“‘By the authority of almighty God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, with the intervention and assistance of blessed Mary ever-virgin together with all the saints, and also by the authority and power handed down to the apostles and left to us, we excommunicate, anathematize, [Col. 0299A] condemn, and separate from the thresholds of holy mother Church Adelger the priest, a member of the devil, betrayer of the bishop, clergy, and entire people of Reims; and likewise those who were the inventors, instigators, perpetrators, accomplices, and supporters of this betrayal, the despoilers of citizens, and those who alienate their own lords’ goods under the name of purchase.

“‘To these we add the invaders of the bishopric of Laon and the most grievous torturers of that bishop. May it happen to them as Scripture says:

“‘“Those who said, ‘Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as an inheritance’—my God, make them like a wheel and like straw before the face of the wind. As fire burns the forest and as flame consumes the mountains, so may you pursue them in your storm and trouble them in your wrath. Fill their faces with disgrace, [Col. 0299B] and they will seek your name, O Lord. Let them be ashamed and troubled forever and ever; let them be confounded and perish. And let them know that you alone, whose name is Lord, are the Most High over all the earth” (Psalm 82:13–19).

“‘And because they did not pity the orphan and widow, nor reverence the temples of God, and usurped dominion over the churches for themselves, may their sons become orphans and their wives widows. May the creditor search out all their substance, and may strangers plunder their labors. May their sons be driven away as they stagger and beg; may they be expelled from their dwellings [Note: [Col. 0299] “de habitationibus” is absent in 1.]. May their days be few, and may another receive their office.

“‘And crush them with a double crushing, O Lord our God, unless they repent and make satisfaction to the Catholic Church through fruitful penitence.

“Amen. So be it. So be it.’”

[Col. 0299C] **15. Archbishop Siguinus:** “Has this document come to Arnulf’s notice?”—It was said that it had. He added: “Did he afterward [Note: [Col. 0299] *hab* in 1.] suspend himself from the communion of those whom he had rightly condemned?—On the contrary,” they replied, “he considered them worthy of the full communion of the faithful.”—“I cannot sufficiently marvel,” he said, “at his audacity [Note: [Col. 0299] *hujus*, ‘of this man,’ in 2.]. First, he himself removed his plunderers from communion and prescribed the terms of their condemnation: that they should restore everything unjustly taken [Note: [Col. 0299] *restituerant*, ‘they had restored,’ in 2.] and humble themselves before the church of Reims, since they had not revered the holy church of Reims. And, as was recently reported to me by certain brothers, the restoration of the lost property has either scarcely been made at all or not at all; and no one has publicly undertaken penance [Col. 0299D] for a crime publicly committed. But secretly—whoever was able [the source is elliptical]—although it is written: ‘Let the one who sins publicly repent publicly.’ Or how, as our brother and fellow bishop Gualterius recently reported, did he condemn them as guilty for a worthless piece of household property [Note: [Col. 0299] *supp.*, abbreviation in 2.], yet remove no one from communion for the violated church? Or did he consider it a trivial crime that the divine laws do not think they can avenge entirely by themselves unless they transfer it to human jurisdiction? For it is written in the Council of Toledo, chapter 10 [Note: [Col. 0299] *toletanio*, variant in 2.]: ‘Those who have entrusted themselves to be defended by the Lord’s cloisters shall not, under any circumstance, be held by obligations [Col. 0300A]. But if anyone attempts to violate this decree, let him both incur ecclesiastical excommunication and be struck by the sentence of royal severity.’ Here it is plainly said that these sacrilegious men are to be excommunicated by the bishops and punished by the king with a penalty proportionate to their deserts. But what bishop can absolve anyone unless he is penitent [Note: [Col. 0299] *poenitentia*, ‘penance,’ in 2.] and seeks pardon with worthy satisfaction? When, then, did these men make satisfaction so that they could be absolved, since they truly allowed no one whom they had captured to depart free?

“But let it be granted that Arnulf absolved them. Why, then, was his cleric Raineri [Note: [Col. 0299] *reineri*, variant in 2.], son of the vicedominus, kept in detention? If this was done by force and against Arnulf’s will, then, since they remained guilty of sacrilege, they could not have been absolved even by a suitable bishop. But if it was with his consent, they received from the person bound a bond for absolution [Col. 0300B]. Again, let it be granted that Arnulf absolved them. How could he have done this without the presence of his clerics? Yet it must be established that they were not present when the men were absolved. They were present, however, when the bond was imposed. Therefore the absolution, which ought to have been solemn, must be regarded as invalid if it was carried out in secret. For it is written in the Council of Carthage, chapter 23, that a bishop must hear no one’s case without the presence of his clerics; otherwise the bishop’s sentence is invalid unless confirmed by the presence of the clerics.

“And because it is written: ‘When the wicked comes into the depths of sins, he despises’ (Prov. XVIII, 3), this man, conscious of so many crimes, was not ashamed to handle sacred matters in the church from which our brothers and fellow bishops of the diocese of Reims, acting on our advice [Col. 0300C], had suspended him from communion for the most just reasons. Therefore, if it pleases you, let the canonical chapters concerning these matters be examined, so that no one may claim that this man was condemned by our judgment, but rather by the judgment of the holy Fathers.”

The synod said: “It pleases us; let them be examined.” Accordingly, the following rulings were brought forward:

**16. On the condemned who attempt to minister, from the Council of Antioch, chapter [Note: [Col. 0299] *kapitulo*, variant in 2.] 4:** “If any bishop condemned by a synod, or presbyter or deacon condemned by his bishop, should dare to touch anything belonging to the sacred ministry—whether the bishop according to the preceding custom, or the presbyter or deacon—he shall in no way be permitted either to have hope of restoration or a place for satisfaction in another synod. Moreover, all who communicate with him shall be expelled from the church, especially if, after learning that sentence had been pronounced against the persons mentioned, they have attempted to communicate with them.

“Likewise: If anyone who has been excommunicated presumes to communicate before a hearing, he has pronounced condemnation upon himself.”

**From the Council of Carthage, chapter 29:** “It pleased the whole council that anyone who has been excommunicated for his own negligence—whether a bishop or any cleric—and who during the time of his excommunication has presumed to receive communion before a hearing, be judged to have pronounced upon himself a sentence of condemnation.”

**From the Council of Carthage, chapter [Note: [Col. 0299] one chapter is missing.] 13:** “A bishop who acts contrary to his profession made in council is to be deposed. If anyone acts contrary to his profession or subscription in any matter, he shall deprive himself of his office.”

[Col. 0301A] **17. Bishop Arnulf said:** “Although these matters stand thus, most reverend Fathers [Note: [Col. 0301] *reverendissimi*, ‘most reverend,’ in 1?], and although it is certain that this Arnulf is condemned by the unanimous judgments of all the Fathers, nevertheless, lest we be brought into disrepute, let those who are zealous for his defense be summoned [Note: [Col. 0301] *admoneantur*, ‘let them be admonished,’ in 2.], and let them have an opportunity to contradict and to defend their Arnulf in whatever way they can. Let this be our decree under ecclesiastical discipline, so that from now on no opportunity for excuse may remain. Let the one who thinks he has just causes offer his defense now. Here is his clergy; here are abbots not insignificant in knowledge and eloquence. Let them raise up the fallen and lift up the humbled; and if they believe that he was unjustly cast down, let them explain by what justice he ought to be restored. For it is not lawful for us to rejoice in the ruin of our brother and fellow priest, nor will anyone regard it as an injury [Note: [Col. 0301] *in i.* in 2.] to himself [Col. 0301B] if he learns that the things said or done against Arnulf have been refuted by truthful assertions.”

**18. Archbishop Siguinus said:** “As our venerable brother and fellow bishop Arnulf has pleaded, by the authority of God the almighty Father, and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, with the assistance of blessed Mary ever-virgin and of all the saints, and also by the authority of this sacred assembly, we command that no one in this synod conceal in silence whatever he considers suitable for Arnulf’s defense, or whatever he thinks deserves censure in the matters done concerning him. Nor shall anyone henceforth have license [Note: [Col. 0301] *scientia*, ‘knowledge,’ in 2.] to criticize or reproach the decision of this most sacred council if he now withdraws from the defense, since he certainly had sufficient time to come forward [Col. 0301C] and now has every opportunity to speak.

“Nor should anyone flatter himself on the pretext of ambushes, since we know that our princes have granted everyone permission to come without injury and to set forth whatever cases they wished. Let the testimony of conscience—which will judge each person at the final examination—be present for both present and future accusers or detractors, whether against Arnulf or against us. Let the image of Christ judging at the last judgment be present to us who judge; and let the defenders have as their model the mercy by which mercy must be shown to the merciful.”

**19.** When all the Fathers had declared, “It pleases us, it pleases us—this decree of Father Siguinus!”, astonishment seized many who had thought that Arnulf would have to be condemned by the resolute decision of the bishops [Col. 0301D]. But the hope of defending him led some to great eagerness of spirit. The sons of his own church, moved by shame, did not wish to accuse him; yet they did not dare to defend him at all, being bound both by conscience and by the anathema. There were, however, very determined defenders, distinguished for their knowledge and eloquence: John, the scholar of Auxerre; Romulf, abbot of Sens; and Abbo, head of the monastery of Fleury. They were weighed down by ignorance of the earlier proceedings [Col. 0302A] and summoned to speak by the anathema.

When silence had been established, numerous volumes of books from the various parties suddenly appeared. Many things were brought forward, many compared among those seated together [Note: [Col. 0301] *consedentes*, variant in 2.], and they presented an impressive spectacle. Above all, the letter of Archbishop Stephen and the three councils to Damasus was read, followed by Damasus’s reply, in this form:

**20. [Note: [Col. 0301] The division is found only after *referendae* in 2.] On the fact that the cases of bishops and the greater ecclesiastical affairs must always be referred to the apostolic see.**

“To the most blessed Lord, exalted to the apostolic dignity, the holy Father of fathers Damasus, pope and highest pontiff of all prelates: Stephen, archbishop of the Council of Mauritania, and all the bishops of the three councils of the African province [Col. 0302B].

“We make known to Your Blessedness that certain brothers living near us are attempting, without consulting you, to cast certain of our brothers—namely, venerable bishops—from their proper rank. Yet the decrees of all the Fathers reserve to your see, in honor of the most blessed Peter, the judgments of bishops and the conclusion of the greatest ecclesiastical affairs, so that the whole judgment concerning the investigation of the matters of God—which we ought to observe with every care and diligence—may be referred to it.

“Most especially, such matters ought to be examined by the apostolic summit itself, whose ancient concern it is both to condemn what is evil and to restore what is worthy of praise. For ancient regulations have decreed that whatever of this kind is done, even in remote or distant provinces, must not be handled or accepted before it has been brought to the knowledge of your nourishing see, so that it may be confirmed by its authority according to the judgment pronounced, and so forth—together with the many other provisions established concerning these and similar matters.

“If anything has been done unlawfully, then, as has always been the custom of your see, hasten to meet it [Col. 0302C], and stand firm, fighting valiantly on their behalf like a father for his sons. As was rightly said to Jesus son of Sirach [Note: [Col. 0301] *sirach*, variant in 2.]: ‘Fight for the truth unto death, and the Lord God will fight for you always’ (Eccli. IV, 33). For it is not good to show partiality to the wicked, so as to turn aside from the truth of judgment.

“If, on the other hand, these things are not unlawful, let such licence be open to us all, most blessed Father; or let it be made clear whether it is lawful to summon to a synod or condemn these men—or even clerics of lower rank—when they have not been canonically summoned at the proper time, or when there are no legitimate accusers or true and innocent witnesses, or unless they have manifestly been convicted according to the canons or voluntarily confessed, or when they have been driven from their sees or stripped of their goods. For we read that they cannot canonically be summoned to a synod before their restoration, after they have fully resumed the rights of their sees, which they are to hold and govern for a long time [Note: [Col. 0301] *s. vocari a.* in 2; *deest* in 2.], and after all their possessions have been most completely restored to them by law [Note: [Col. 0301] absent in 1.]; nor may they be commanded to come to synods unless they wish to do so voluntarily [Note: [Col. 0301] 2 reads, corruptly, *et sit imperare ut veniant ad synodus nisi sponte voluerint*, ‘and it is to be commanded that they come to synods unless they wish voluntarily’], and the rest.”

**21. Likewise, Damasus’s letter to the same Stephen and to the African councils, stating that the judgments of bishops and the greater cases must be concluded only by the authority of the apostolic see.**

“Damasus, servant of the servants of God and, by his grace, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, to Stephen, archbishop of the Council of Mauritania, and to all the bishops of the African province [Col. 0302D].

“After reading the letters of your fraternity, I first give thanks that I have been deemed worthy to enjoy the blessing of so many brothers; then I give thanks that I have found you concerned for the brothers and bearing with them the cross of the Lord, who says: ‘Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me’ (Matt. XVI, 24), together with the other words pertaining to this matter.

“Therefore, since on the present occasion Your Blessedness, moved by apostolic compassion, has urged us, in the consultation concerning these proceedings, to extend apostolic protection to the brothers and to assist their wrongs—and since you evidently say with the Apostle, in fellow-feeling: ‘Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?’ (II Cor. XI, 19)—we must strive to ensure that none of those entrusted to us is torn apart or captured by savage beasts.

“For this reason, in accordance with your prudent admonition, and still more according to the divine command of the Lord, we who have undertaken episcopal ministry over his household—that is, over the universal Catholic Church—must vigilantly watch lest, while we sleep, anything belonging to his sacred offices, namely apostolic jurisdiction, the successors and ministers of the apostles, be suppressed or unjustly condemned without our consultation [Col. 0303B].

“You know, dearest brothers, that God established the apostolic see as the firm and immovable foundation and the most luminous title of his priests, that is, of all bishops, and as the summit of the churches. For, as the divine and truthful word declares, you are Peter, and upon your foundation the columns of the churches—by which bishops are understood—have been firmly established. To you I have entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and I have proclaimed the power to bind and loose what is in heaven and what is on earth [Note: [Col. 0303] *commissi*, ‘I entrusted,’ or *commissi*, variant in 1?].

“You are, as prince and teacher of the orthodox and undefiled faith, the chief of profaned men and of my members, especially of my disciples. In his place, by the grace of God, we today serve as ambassadors for Christ; and all the prelates of this holy see have acted, act, and will act in his place.

“Therefore I would not have commanded that all the matters you have reported are unlawful unless I knew that you were so fully instructed that you do not doubt that everything about which you seek counsel is unlawful [Col. 0303C].

“For metropolitans, together with all their comprovincial bishops, may examine bishops and the most important ecclesiastical cases, provided that none of them is absent and that all agree concerning each individual case. But it is by no means permitted to them to decide the major disputes and cases of bishops and churches, or to condemn bishops, without the authority of this holy see. If necessary, all must appeal to it and be strengthened by its assistance.

“For, as you know, a synod held without its authority is not Catholic; nor can a bishop be definitively condemned except in a legitimate synod, convened at the proper time by apostolic summons. Nor are any councils ever read to have been valid that were not supported by apostolic authority.

“Accusers and witnesses of clerics, concerning whom you have inquired, must be entirely free from infamy, suspicion, and manifest stain, and fully instructed in the true faith [Note: [Col. 0303] *suspicione*, repeated in 2.]; they must be such as divine authority commands to be chosen for the priesthood. For, as ancient authority has handed down, priests cannot be accused or testified against by persons who neither ought nor can be advanced to the same honor [Col. 0303D].

“The summons of the person accused to the synod, according to the canonical decrees of the Fathers, must be made within a suitable and canonical period, both by his presence and by writings and messengers [Note: [Col. 0303] *impetitur*, ‘is accused,’ in 2.]. For unless he has been canonically summoned at the proper time and in canonical form, even if he comes to the assembly for whatever reason, he shall in no way answer his plotters unless he wishes to do so voluntarily. For if worldly laws do not permit this, how much less do divine laws?

“Concerning those who have been expelled and stripped of their possessions [Col. 0304A], I can tell you nothing more truthful than what the holy Fathers have defined and our predecessors have confirmed by apostolic authority. This is how the matter stands: the holy canons have decreed that bishops who have been expelled and stripped of their possessions must first recover their own churches and have all their property legally restored to them; only afterward, if anyone wishes to accuse them, have the canons sanctioned that he do so at equal risk. They decree that right-thinking bishops who desire justice are to be judges at the proper time, after those men have for a long time resumed their rights and are freely enjoying their possessions, and have assembled in church, taking counsel with wise men who are friends and servants of God, where there are witnesses for each of those who appeared to have been oppressed. There are other provisions pertaining to this order which, to avoid excessive length, we have not inserted here, since we believe these are sufficient. If anyone is not satisfied with them, let him read them, and he will be satisfied.

“For we know that unarmed men cannot properly fight armed men. In the same way, those who have been expelled or stripped of their goods cannot properly litigate with those who remain in their own position and enjoy their friends and possessions [Col. 0304B]. Nor do the laws of the world permit this to be done to secular persons. They command that those who have first been expelled, oppressed, or stripped of their possessions be restored with everything belonging to them, and afterward, at the proper time, be ordered to come to court, as their law provides. They do not permit an appellant to be prevented by imprisonment. For, as you know, earthly things teach in part the things of heaven.

“Accusers and accusations which the laws of the world do not admit must in no way be admitted in these cases, because the Catholic Church defends everything that is irreproachable [Note: [Col. 0303] *in manu recentiori*, ‘in a later hand,’ in 2.], and there is no doubt that this was established by our predecessors because of the plots of wicked men.

“It is fitting that the priests of the Lord handle the cases of the brothers piously and attend to them reverently [Note: [Col. 0303] *attendere*, ‘to attend to,’ in 2.], arranging their judgments with regard to sacrifices, so that they may carry out everything not arrogantly or with tyrannical domination, as is reported of certain persons, but charitably, for God and in fraternal love. No one should presume to inflict upon another what he does not wish done to himself according to the Lord’s word [Col. 0304C]; ‘With what measure you measure, it will be measured to you’ (Matt. VII, 2).

“We must always hold fast to what we have learned through the preaching of the apostles and the instruction of the Fathers, lest we seem to devise something new or to be continually intent on harming our brothers. Rather, let us bear one another’s burdens, so that, according to the Apostle, we may fulfill the law of the Lord (Gal. VI, 2).

“A suitable time must be foreseen when the case of each accused person may most properly be brought forward, so that its gravity and its consistency may be recognized [the following clause is textually corrupt: ‘which against the decrees of the Fathers, or a synod, is least known to be disclosed by confession’], and so that all may attend to it in an orderly way, answer it rationally in every respect, and openly show that they desire justice.

“No one, however, is to be introduced in person; rather, accusers and accused are to be heard with equal fairness, according to what the order of the proceedings requires. Accusers and judges must not be the same persons: accusers by themselves, judges by themselves, witnesses by themselves, and accused by themselves [Col. 0304D], each in his own orderly role.

“First, a written indictment must always be made, so that the false accuser may receive the punishment of retaliation; for no one ought to be judged or condemned before an indictment, since the laws of the world also preserve this same rule. In all these matters true equity must always be maintained, so that they may receive the reward of accusation, judgment, and testimony according to the truth of the proceedings.

“For it is written: ‘Lying lips are an abomination to the Lord’ (Prov. XII, 22); and: ‘A false witness who utters lies and sows scandals and quarrels among brothers’ (ibid. VI, 19). He himself also admonishes and says: ‘You shall not slander your neighbor, nor oppress him by force; you shall not do what is unjust, nor judge unjustly; you shall not consider the person of the poor, nor honor the face of the powerful; judge your neighbor justly’ (Lev. XIX, 13–15); and: ‘What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another’ (Tob. IV, 16), and many other things of this kind.

“Since we have also received the apostolic command to watch over ourselves and over the flock in which the Holy Spirit has placed us as bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired through his own blood (Acts XX, 28), it is fitting for us to do so [Col. 0305A]. ‘Beware of wolves; beware of evil workers,’ who do perverse things and speak hostile words, so that they may always slander and disgrace the Lord’s disciples. It is of the greatest importance that you and all the priests of the Lord correct such men, for there is no worse evil than that citizens envy citizens and priests or clerics plot against priests or bishops.

“The voice of truth also testifies: ‘Whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye’ (Zech. II, 8); and: ‘Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him that an ass’s millstone be hung around his neck and he be drowned in the depths of the sea’ (Matt. XVIII, 6); and again: ‘Blessed is the one who is not scandalized in me’ (Matt. XI, 6). Without doubt, the one who scandalizes the Lord is the one who scandalizes his bishop or priest [Note: [Col. 0305] *deum*, ‘God,’ in 2.].

“There are many other such matters which are not inserted here, lest the letter become excessively long. You must also admonish and instruct your aforesaid neighbors to withdraw from such actions and promptly correct what they have unlawfully done against the brothers mentioned above. Those whom they have injured without consulting us, they must, without consulting us, heal with complete satisfaction, and they must quickly reconcile themselves with them if they do not wish to incur the censure of the apostolic see.

“For if anything had arisen in them or against them, they ought to have awaited our examination, so that, as has always been granted as a privilege to this see, they might either be condemned by our authority or supported by our assistance. They ought not, according to their own pleasure, to invade our rights without a disposition issued by the apostolic see [Col. 0305C].

“From now on, let all priests abstain from such conduct, lest they be excluded from the solidity and priestly honor of the apostolic rock upon which Christ, as has been said, built the universal Church, to which the supreme judgments of bishops and the major cases [Note: [Col. 0305] *causas*, ‘cases,’ in 1 and 2.] have been reserved, as was mentioned above.

“Accused bishops in criminal cases must be granted a delay of six months, or more if necessary. For this is also permitted to laymen, as no one trained in secular disciplines is unaware; how much more, then, to priests, who are unquestionably superior to them?

“It is also established in the decrees of the Fathers that no one may canonically judge or condemn a priest before the accused priest has the canonically examined accusers present and receives an opportunity for defense—that is, ecclesiastical delays for cleansing the crimes and other matters [Note: [Col. 0305] *id*, ‘that is,’ in 2; *item* may be read in 1?]. Nor may an accusation first be examined outside the accused person’s own province without apostolic command, to which reverence must be shown in every case. For the ancient rule of the Fathers also teaches this, and imperial statutes agree with it:

“‘The examination of crimes must take place where the crime was committed; for elsewhere the accused person is forbidden to be heard, and elsewhere the canons prescribe that whatever cases arise must be concluded in the places where they originated,’ and so forth.

“Such matters and others like them must be observed, while the apostolic authority is preserved in everything, so that nothing in these matters may be settled before it is known to please that authority, by which all ought to be supported. And if anything burdensome or intolerable should happen to them, its judgment must always be awaited.

“For no one should presumptuously, or driven by the spur of his own thinking—as we have often learned has happened—slander or accuse any priest [Col. 0306A]. Their injury concerns Christ, in whose place they serve as ambassadors for the people redeemed by Christ’s blood. Their cases, because they are God’s cases, must be reserved for his judgment—he who can kill the body and cast the soul into Gehenna, who says: ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay’ (Rom. XII, 19), and before whom conscience lies exposed, since nothing hidden is concealed from him.

“Everyone must also be instructed that through us Christ has thundered to them that it is not for sheep to anticipate the ambushes of wolves, but for the shepherd. Therefore blessed Paul the Apostle warns that no one should rashly and lightly presume to judge those whom no one can judge more truly or better than God: ‘But you,’ he says, ‘why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise him? For we shall all stand before the tribunal of God. For it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bend to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.” Therefore each of us shall give an account of himself to God’” (Rom. XIV, 10–12) [Col. 0306B].

“Let no one, then, arrogate to himself rash boldness in this matter, doing anything beyond what pertains to concord, whereby the unity of the Church might be destroyed. Let no one lightly assent to the slander, judgment, or condemnation of brothers, especially of priests, who are nearer to God and who make Christ’s body by their own mouths. For this reason the wrath of God comes upon the sons of transgression, who persecute Christ in his members.

“Do not, brothers—do not become participants with such men, nor share in their sins or unprofitable words. Rather, rebuke the gatherings of such men, who strive to stretch their tongues against the brothers as though they were a bow. Defend the brothers, then, and admonish everyone to arm themselves against the persecutors of the brothers.

“We are confident of better things from you, and of things nearer to salvation, because neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither things present nor things to come, neither power nor height, neither depth nor any creature, as the Teacher of the Gentiles declares, will be able to separate us from the love of our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom. VIII, 38–39), which is especially perfected in priests and in his other members.

“Therefore do not abandon your confidence, which has a great reward. For behold, the judge stands before the door, joyfully promising crowns to those [Note: [Col. 0305] *promitens*, ‘promising,’ in 2.] who, for his sake, bring aid to their brothers, assist the oppressed, and labor together in charity.

“But if anyone withdraws, he will not please God, but will fall [Note: [Col. 0305] *cadit*, ‘falls,’ in 2.], because he did not lift up the fallen but withered away.

“And somewhat later: ‘He judges rashly if anyone condemns a bishop without the authority of the apostolic see, since, as was stated above, this special privilege has been reserved to it.’

“Again, somewhat later: ‘Without doubt, the one who commits iniquity in judgment is the one who claims for himself what he is not permitted to claim. For this reason these rights have been granted to this see, so that no one may presume to usurp them without consulting it [Note: [Col. 0305] this phrase is absent in 1.]—he who does not wish to be judged unworthy of ecclesiastical honor or held in contempt [Col. 0306D].

“Therefore it is necessary to drive away the negligent, but in such a way that the guilty are not strengthened; and the good must resist the wicked and those who plot against the brothers, lest, overcome by the torpor of sloth, we be held liable for silence. Accordingly, whoever can oppose and disturb the perverse but does not do so does nothing other than favor impiety. Nor is the one free from the stain of secret complicity who ceases to oppose an evident crime,” and so forth.

**22.** A volume was also brought [Note: [Col. 0305] *Ablatus*, corrected to *oblatus* in 2.] from the kingdom of Lotharingia through the hands of Ratbodo, bishop of Noyon, containing the following:

[Col. 0307A] **From the decrees of Pope Saint Clement, on the accusation of bishops:** “The permission to accuse or testify must be denied to those who have neglected the dignity of the Christian religion and name, and the rule of their own law or profession, or the things regularly prohibited. For transgressors of their own law and its voluntary violators are called apostates. Every apostate must be rejected and, before his return, must not be admitted either as an accuser or as a witness.”

**From the decrees of Pope Stephen:** “No bishop, while he has been stripped of his possessions or expelled from his own see for any reason, ought to be accused, nor may any crime be brought against him by anyone, before he has been completely restored, everything taken from him by whatever means has been legally returned, and he himself has been regularly restored to his own see and former status.”

**Likewise, from the same pope [Note: [Col. 0307] ‘I from the same,’ in 2.]:** “We reject accusers and accusations which the laws of the world do not admit and which our predecessors prohibited. No foreigner is to become either an accuser or a judge of bishops. Hence it is written concerning Lot: ‘You came in as a stranger; do you now presume to judge?’ (Gen. XIX, 9.) No servant or freedman is to be their accuser, nor any suspect or infamous person. Those who live with the enemies, and all laymen, are also to be rejected.”

**From the decrees of Pope Sixtus:** “Let no pontiff presume to excommunicate or judge a bishop who has been stripped of his possessions or expelled from his see, since there is no privilege by which one who has already been stripped can be stripped again.”

**From the decrees of Pope Julius:** “If anyone from this day forward presumes to condemn a bishop or expel him from his own see contrary to the sentence of this holy see, let him know that he is irrecoverably condemned and will forever lack his own honor. And those who have been expelled or condemned without the sentence of this see, know that by the authority of this holy see they are to recover their former communion and be restored to their own sees [Col. 0307C].”

**Likewise:** “Injuries to bishops are prohibited, so that those who attempt such things or presume to harm them, if they are clerics, shall fall from their own rank; but if they are monks or laymen, they shall be anathematized.”

**From the decrees of Pope Symmachus:** “Let the man who, while any pontiff is alive, is convicted of having sought or attempted in any way to obtain his episcopate be deprived of the dignity of his order and of communion; and we have decreed that all equally guilty of this offense are to be punished by the penalty of anathema.”

**Likewise:** “No one may lawfully wish or be able to transgress the commands of the apostolic see, nor the ministry of its disposition, which everyone must follow in charity. Let whoever wishes to oppose the apostolic decrees lie prostrate in grief at his own ruin. From that point onward let him have no place among priests, but let him be expelled from the sacred ministry. Let no one afterward concern himself with his judgment, since it is beyond doubt that he has already been condemned by the holy and apostolic Church, by its authority, by his own disobedience, and by his presumption. He must be removed by the greater excommunication, because the discipline of the holy Church has been entrusted to him: he ought not merely to have obeyed the commands of the prelate of the holy Church, but also to have warned others not to pass them by. Let the one who refused to obey the apostolic commands be alien from divine and pontifical offices [Col. 0307D].”

**From the decrees of Pope Eusebius:** “The sheep entrusted to their shepherd must neither rebuke him, unless he has strayed from the right faith, nor accuse him in any way. For the deeds of shepherds are not to be struck down by the sword of the sheep, although they may appear rightly subject to rebuke.

“We say this because in your letters we have found that certain bishops in your regions have been accused by their own sheep—some, evidently, on suspicion, and others for a definite reason—and that, for this reason, some have been stripped of their possessions and others driven from their own sees. Know that these men cannot be summoned either to a provincial synod or to a general synod, nor judged in any matter, before everything taken from them has been legally restored to their authority [Col. 0308A].

“Likewise, from the same pope: ‘Correct your error, brothers, and guard yourselves from every stain of error, so that you may be able to offer God a pure gift. Do not persecute the servants of God; do not defame or accuse bishops, because God has willed to reserve them for his own judgment.’”

**From the decrees of Pope Adrian:** “Murderers, sorcerers, thieves, sacrilegious persons, robbers, poisoners, adulterers, those who have committed abduction or given false testimony, and those who have run to diviners and magicians, are in no way to be admitted either as accusers or as witnesses [Col. 0308B]. When someone brings a charge, it must be established that he himself was not previously a criminal, because it is dangerous and inadmissible for a guilty person’s accusation to be accepted against anyone.”

**From the decrees of Pope Fabian:** “It has likewise been established, and we, confirming the same statutes, decree that if any cleric is hostile to or plots against his bishops, attempts to accuse them, or is a conspirator, he is to be immediately removed from the clergy before a judicial examination and handed over to the curia. He shall serve it throughout the days of his life and remain infamous, without any hope of restoration. Nor may anyone ever presume to be both accuser and judge at the same time.”

[Additional textual-apparatus notes: Col. 0301, §18: *sacrosancto* in 1; *occurrere*, ‘to come forward,’ in 2; *juditio*, ‘judgment,’ in 2. Col. 0301–0302, §20: heading, *Quid* in 2?; *i. a. p.* in 2 at ‘without consulting you’; *juditia* in 2, repeatedly; *reservarunt* in 2 at ‘reserve’; *Sin* in 2. Col. 0302D, §21 heading: *aucteritate*, corrected to *auctoritate*, in 2. Col. 0303C: *episcopos* in 2? Col. 0304A: *Judicetur* in 1?; *viribus* in 1. Col. 0304C: the words beginning *o. i. ut ed.* are absent in 1. Col. 0305A: 2 adds, ‘And again, beware of wolves.’ Col. 0305C: *sacerdotum* in 2. Col. 0307A: *dignitate* in 1. Col. 0307B: *se depulsum* in 2. Col. 0307C: *dampnanti* in 2. Col. 0307D: *non*, corrected to *ne*, in 2.]

From the decrees of Pope Marcellus:

“If any bishops have been expelled or stripped of their possessions, first everything that was taken from them by their enemies or persecutors must be legally restored [Note: [Col. 0307] lacking in 1.], and their own sees, together with all that belongs to them duly assembled, must be restored [Col. 0308C]. Only afterward, at a suitable time, should they be summoned—or rather, we decree that a synod should be regularly convened. Before these things have been done, they may not answer concerning themselves according to the statutes mentioned above, or give an account of the charges against them if they find themselves overwhelmed by them. But once these matters have been duly completed and all their possessions freely placed at their disposal, then, if it seems just, let them answer their accusers. And if it should be necessary for them, let them receive a substantial postponement, so that they may investigate the matters alleged against them and not, deceived by some fraud, fall culpably.”

From the decrees of Pope Anacletus:

“Accusers,” he says [Note: [Col. 0307] *inquid* for *inquit*, 2.], “cannot also be witnesses if, before yesterday or three days ago [Note: [Col. 0307] *esternum*; corrected by a later hand, 2.], they were enemies, lest they desire to cause harm in anger or wish to avenge themselves for having been injured. The disposition of accusers and witnesses must therefore be sought as free from hostility and not open to suspicion.”

From the decrees of Pope Damasus:
