“Whoever chooses to accuse another must accuse him in person and not through someone else. Nor should anyone ever be judged before he has legitimate accusers present and has been granted an opportunity to defend himself and clear away the charges” [Col. 0308D].

Pope Silverius, making a complaint about his fraudulent arrest, said, among other things:

“Those who have done such things against me I have anathematized; and together with the bishops, by apostolic and synodal authority, I have decreed that no bishop should ever be deceived in this way, while such a presumptuous offender should be made *anathema maranatha*—‘accursed at the coming of the Lord’—in the sight of God and the holy angels” [Note: [Col. 0307] *maranata*, 2.].

### 23

In all these matters, those who were striving for Arnulf’s defense [Note: [Col. 0307] *defensione*, 2.] repeatedly advanced four principal points [Col. 0309] [Note: [Col. 0309] *ingerebantur*, “were advanced,” 2.]. First, that he should be restored to his see, since one who had been stripped of his possessions ought not to be required to answer; next, that there should be legitimate summonses and that the case should be reported to the Roman pontiff; then, that the accused, the accusers, the witnesses, and the judges should be distinguished in a great synod [Note: [Col. 0309] *discernos*, 1.]; and that, according to the reasoning of the canons, the case could not otherwise be regarded as properly constituted.

After all these points had been carefully considered, the opposing side replied that almost everything had been completed according to the order of the decrees.

“For, to begin with the latest matters,” they said, “his accuser is sufficiently qualified for this case: he was neither previously an enemy nor induced to accuse by fear or reward, but was moved solely by religious zeal; and, if he had not known him, he could be considered worthy of the presbyterate which he holds. His summonses to the synod, moreover, through canonical letters and through *apocrisiarii*, extend beyond not merely six months but even a year” [Col. 0309B].

They added that he could by no means be restored to his see, because even if restored he would have no voice with which to speak. For this is contained in the African Council, title 12:

“If clerics have refused to clear themselves of their case within a year, let their voice afterward be heard no more at all.”

And because his arrest was thought to be odious, the same practice was found to be neither unusual nor foreign to the sacred laws. For it was clearly recorded in the history of the bishops of Rheims that Hildemannus, bishop of Beauvais, detained [Note: [Col. 0309] *decentem* corrected to *decentum*, 2.] in the monastery of Saint Vedastus, awaited a synod because he was accused before Emperor Louis of having wished to flee to the emperor Lothar. Ebo, archbishop of Rheims, was likewise attempting the same thing and, through Rothadus [Note: [Col. 0309] *Rothardum*, 1.], bishop of Soissons, and Erchenradus, bishop of Paris, suffered similar treatment for similar reasons in the monastery at Vuld. (Flodoard, *History of Rheims*, II.20.)

It therefore seemed just that one who, being accused [Note: [Col. 0309] *inp.* for *impetitus*, 2.] of a crime against royal majesty, had not obeyed the summons of the bishops should be brought before the court by judicial authority; and they maintained that this was confirmed by the African Council, title 38:

### 24

Cresconius, bishop of Villaregia, having abandoned his own people, invaded the church of Tuburnia and, to this day, although admonished according to what had been decreed, has refused to leave the people whom he invaded, contrary to the statutes that had been promulgated. We have indeed heard that these statutes were confirmed, but we ask, according to the instructions given to us, that you deign to give us assurance that, when necessity itself compels it, it may be lawful for us to approach the governor of the province against him according to the statutes of the most glorious rulers [Col. 0309D], so that he who refused to yield to the gentle admonition of your holiness [Note: [Col. 0309] *nolunt*, “they refuse,” 2.] and to correct what is unlawful may immediately be excluded by judicial authority.

Bishop Aurelius said:

“When the form of discipline has been preserved, it will not be considered an act of aggression if, after being courteously summoned by your charity, he refuses to withdraw, since, through his contempt and obstinacy, he will also have been summoned by judicial authority.”

Likewise, from the same council, title 43:

“There are many who conspire with their own peoples, whom they deceive, as has been said, by scratching their ears in order to seduce men of vicious life; or certainly, puffed up and separated from this fellowship [Col. 0310A], who think that they ought to cling to their own people and sometimes, when summoned, refuse to come to the council, perhaps fearing that their [lacuna] *gitia* may be exposed. I say, if it pleases you, that in their case not only should the dioceses not be preserved for them, but every effort should also be made against the church itself that has wickedly favored them, so that they may be rejected even by public authority and removed from those principal sees. For one who has adhered to all the brethren and to the whole council ought to possess not only his own rights intact but also the dioceses. But those who think their own peoples sufficient for them, having despised fraternal love [Note: [Col. 0309] *per aeterna*, “for eternal things,” 1.], should not only lose the dioceses but, as I have said, should also be deprived by public authority of their own churches, as rebels.”

### 25

They said that the case had been brought before the Roman pontiff in the following documents [Note: [Col. 0309] lacking in 1.]:

“To the most blessed Pope John, Hugo, by the grace of God king of the Franks.

“Moved by new and unprecedented circumstances, we have decided to seek your counsels with the greatest zeal and care, since we know that you have devoted all your time to human and divine studies. Consider, therefore, what has happened and prescribe what must be done, so that both the sacred laws may receive their due honor and royal authority may not be annulled.

“Arnulfus, said to be the son of King Lothar, after the grave enmities and crimes that he practiced against us and our kingdom, was adopted by us in place of a parent and was freely given the metropolitan church of Rheims. He swore an oath valid against both past and future oaths. He composed, read aloud, and confirmed a written pledge of fidelity under the name of a *chirograph*, and caused it to be confirmed. He compelled the soldiers and all the citizens to swear that they would remain faithful to us if he should ever fall into the power of his enemies [Col. 0310C].

“Against all these commitments, as the most reliable witnesses clearly testify, he himself opened the gates to the enemy and delivered the clergy and people entrusted to his faith into captivity and plunder. But let it be granted that he is subject to another’s power, as he himself wishes to appear: why does he compel the citizens and soldiers to perjure themselves? Why does he prepare arms against us? Why does he fortify the city and the military camps against us? If he has been captured, why does he not allow himself to be freed? If he has been overwhelmed by the force of his enemies, why does he not wish assistance to be brought to him? And if he has been freed, why does he not return to us?

“He is summoned to the palace and scorns coming. He is invited by the archbishops and fellow bishops and replies that he owes them nothing. Therefore, you who hold the place of the apostles, determine what should be done with another Judas, lest the name of God be blasphemed through us [Note: [Col. 0309] *vos*, “you,” 2.], and lest, perhaps, moved by just grief and provoked by your delay, we undertake the destruction of the city and the burning of the entire province. Nor will you be able to offer an excuse before God the Judge if, when we ask and are ignorant of the proper form of judgment, you refuse to provide it to us.

### 26

Likewise, the letter of the bishops to the same pontiff [Note: [Col. 0309] “the letter of the bishops to the same”; the remainder is absent in 2.]:

“To the lord and most reverend [Note: [Col. 0309] *revendissimo*, perhaps for *reverendissimo*, 1?] Pope John, the bishops of the diocese of Rheims.

“We are not unaware [Note: [Col. 0309] a second hand adds *o*, 2.], most blessed Father, that long ago we ought to have sought the counsels of the holy Roman Church on account of the ruin and collapse of the priestly order. But oppressed by a multitude of tyrants and separated by the vastness of the lands, we have until now been unable to fulfill our desires.

“Now, therefore, we bring before your judgment, not without great sorrow, the new and unprecedented crime of Arnulfus, archbishop of Rheims. He has become a notorious apostate and now occupies in the Church the place once held by Judas the betrayer. Formerly a son of the church of Laon, after seizing his bishop through deceit and fraud and invading his church, he has, to crown his own condemnation, taken captive the church of Rheims entrusted to him, together with its clergy and people.

“He is moved neither by our summons—or rather, by our most salutary exhortation [Note: [Col. 0311] *exortatio*, 1.]—nor by the repeated admonition of the archbishops of the province, nor by the profession made canonically before God and his angels, nor by the written document of the *chirograph* read aloud in the presence of the Church, nor by the numerous oaths devised through extraordinary deliberations. Many churches stand deprived of their pastors through his fault [Note: [Col. 0311] omitted in 2.]; countless peoples perish without priestly blessing and confirmation. He himself, by a tyrannical faction and scorning divine and human rights, exercises tyranny. He plots the destruction of our kings, from whom he freely received such great honor.

“Therefore, at last awakened by the monstrosities of this most abandoned man, we have followed the judgment of the Lord, who says: ‘If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between yourself and him alone. If he listens to you, you have won your brother. But if he does not listen, take with you one or two more, so that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses [Note: [Col. 0311] reading abbreviated *d. t.*, 2.].’ If he does not listen to them, tell it to the church. But if he does not listen even to the church, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector” (Matthew 18:15–17).

“Stand by the falling Church, Father, and pronounce against the accused the sentence promulgated from the sacred canons—or rather, spoken by Truth herself. Let us perceive in you another Peter, defender and confirmer of the Christian faith. Let the holy Roman Church pronounce a sentence of condemnation against the accused, whom the universal Church condemns.

“Let your authority support us both in the removal of this apostate and in the new appointment of an archbishop who may worthily preside over the house of God; and, with our fellow bishops summoned and promoted as necessity requires, let us know and understand why we ought to prefer your apostolate above all others.”

[Col. 0311D]

### 27

After these letters had been read aloud in the middle of the synod, the defenders of Arnulfus were asked about the date on which they had been sent and about the embassy they reported. Concerning the first, the eleventh month was found; concerning the second, nothing worthy of record was discovered, except that the envoys had presented the documents to the Roman pontiff and had initially been received courteously. Later, however, after the envoys of Count Heribert had offered the pontiff a horse distinguished by its excellent build and snowy color, together with other gifts, they said that they had been exhausted for three days before the palace gates and, not having been admitted, had returned with their business unfinished [Col. 0312A].

The clerics present with Bishop Bruno also supported this account. They said that they had approached the Roman pontiff on account of Bruno’s arrest [Note: [Col. 0311] *Romanorum*, “of the Romans,” 1.]. When they requested from him, by apostolic authority, curses against the accused, his ministers judged that ten solidi should be paid. After they had been mocked for this—for if [Note: [Col. 0311] *se*, perhaps for *si*, 1?] the matter could be redeemed with money, not even a thousand talents would delay it—they finally received this reply from the pontiff himself: that the person for whose sake he had been captured should look after him well.

The apostolic see therefore did not prejudge this judgment. The African bishops had also been rightly disturbed by this Roman precedent. In the synod of 217 bishops begun in the time of Pope Zosimus, prolonged through the time of Boniface, and finally completed under Celestine, they definitively established in eternal records what they wished to be thought about the authority of the Roman bishop. Since this council is distinguished, illuminated by the presence of blessed Augustine, refined by carefully devised consultations, and provides this synod with the force of many arguments, we have judged it useful to append its proceedings in full.

### 28

Father Arnulfus spoke publicly at length about these matters and discussed many points with those who sat beside him alone. Since his words might have less charm if left scattered as he delivered them, we preferred to gather them together, so that a continuous speech might provide greater benefit to the diligent reader.

“We, most reverend Fathers [Note: [Col. 0311] *reverend.*, perhaps for *reverendissimi*, 1?],” he said, “decree that the Roman Church must always be honored for the memory of blessed Peter, and we do not seek to oppose the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, while nevertheless preserving the authority of the Council of Nicaea, which the same Roman Church has always venerated.

“We also decree that the statutes of the sacred canons [Note: [Col. 0311] *canonicum*, ‘of the canon,’ 1.]—established in different places and at different times but by the same Spirit of God—remain valid forever, and we judge that they must be observed by all.

“There are, however, two matters that we must carefully foresee [Note: [Col. 0311] *pervideri*, 2.]: namely [Note: [Col. 0311] *idem*, 1.], whether the silence of the Roman pontiff or a new constitution can prejudice the laws promulgated in the canons or the decrees of earlier authorities [Note: [Col. 0311] *praejudicari*, perhaps ‘be prejudiced,’ 1?]. For if silence prejudices them, then, while he remains silent, all laws and all the decrees of earlier authorities must necessarily be silent. But if a new constitution does so, of what use are established laws when everything is directed according to the will of one person? You see that, once these two possibilities are admitted, the condition of the churches of God is endangered; and while we seek laws through laws, we have no laws at all.

“What then? Shall we diminish the privilege of the Roman pontiff? By no means. But if the Roman bishop is one whom knowledge and merit of life commend, neither silence nor a new constitution need be feared. If, however, he is estranged by ignorance, fear, or desire, or if his position gives rise to envy—as we have seen happening in these times, when tyranny prevails at Rome—then still less should silence or a new constitution be feared. For one who is in any way opposed to the laws cannot prejudice the laws.

“But, O Rome, worthy of lamentation! You who once brought forth for our ancestors the illustrious lights of the Fathers have in our times spread monstrous darkness [Note: [Col. 0313] *monstruosas*, 2.], destined to be famous for a future age. Formerly we received illustrious Leos and great Gregories. What shall I say of Gelasius and Innocent, who surpassed all worldly philosophy [Note: [Col. 0313] *philosophiam*, 2.] by their wisdom and eloquence? Their succession is long: men who filled the world with their teaching.

“To the governance of such men—who surpassed all mortals in merit of life and knowledge—the universal Church was rightly entrusted, although even in this very prosperity the African bishops opposed this privilege to you, fearing, I believe, the miseries that we suffer more than the appearance of domination. For what have we not seen in these times?

“We saw John, surnamed Octavianus, immersed in a whirlpool of lust and even conspiring against Otto, whom he had created emperor. After John was driven out, Leo, a neophyte [Note: [Col. 0313] *neophitus*, 2.], was made pontiff. But when Emperor Otto departed from Rome, Octavianus returned, drove out Leo, mutilated the deacon John by cutting off his nose, the fingers of his right hand, and his tongue, and, after raging through the city with the slaughter of many leading men, soon died.

“The Romans substituted for him the deacon Benedict, surnamed the Grammarian. Leo the neophyte, together with his emperor, soon afterward attacked him as well, besieged and captured him, deposed him, and sent him into perpetual exile in Germany.

“Otto the emperor was succeeded by Emperor Otto, who in our age surpasses all rulers in arms, counsel, and knowledge. At Rome, the pontificate was succeeded by the dreadful monster Boniface [Note: [Col. 0313] another hand has *Malifacius*, 2; *Malefacius*, 2a.], surpassing all mortals in wickedness and stained even with the blood of his predecessor. But after he too had been driven out and condemned in a great synod, he returned to Rome after the death of the divine Otto. There he cast down from the citadel of the City, deposed, and killed through the filth of imprisonment the distinguished apostolic man Peter, formerly bishop of the church of Pavia, despite the pledge of faith given under oath.

“Is it therefore decreed that innumerable priests of God throughout the world, distinguished by knowledge and merit of life [Note: [Col. 0313] *conspicuis*, 2.], should be subjected to such monsters—men full of human disgrace and empty of knowledge of divine and human matters? What is this, most reverend Fathers? Or by what fault are we to believe that it has happened that the head of the churches of God, raised on high and crowned with glory and honor, has been cast down so low and disfigured by disgrace and dishonor?

“This is our sin, our impiety: that we seek what is ours and not what belongs to Jesus Christ. For if, in anyone elected to the episcopate, the gravity of his character, the merit of his life, and his knowledge of divine and human matters are carefully investigated, what should not be investigated in one who desires to appear the teacher of all bishops?

“Why, then, is he established in the highest see so basely that he is found unworthy of holding any place even among the clergy? What do you think this man is, reverend Fathers, seated upon a lofty throne [Note: [Col. 0313] *sublimo*, 1.], radiant in purple and gold? Surely, if he lacks charity and is puffed up and exalted by knowledge alone, he is Antichrist, seated in the temple of God and displaying himself as though he were God.

“But if he is founded neither on charity nor raised up by knowledge, he is in the temple of God like a statue, like an idol: to ask answers from him is to consult marble.

“Where, then, shall we go for counsel? The Gospel teaches that someone sought fruit three times from a fig tree and, because he found none, wished to cut it down, but, having been admonished [Note: [Col. 0313] *adm.*, 2.], waited. Let us therefore wait for our primates as long as we can, and meanwhile let us investigate where the nourishment of the divine word may be found [Col. 0314B].

“Certainly, in Belgica and Germany, which are near us, there are chief priests of God outstanding in religious devotion, as certain witnesses at this holy assembly testify [Note: [Col. 0313] *d. in* deleted, 2.]. Therefore, if the hostility of kings who disagree did not prevent it, judgment from the bishops of those regions ought rather to be sought than from that city which is now exposed for sale to purchasers and weighs judgments according to the quantity of money.

“If someone should say that, according to Gelasius, the Roman Church judges the whole Church, that it is subject to the judgment of no one, and that no one may ever judge its judgment, then let the person who says this establish for us in the Roman Church the one whose judgment cannot be judged [Note: [Col. 0313] corrected reading: *ut de ejus iudicio*, 2.]—although the African bishops themselves judge this impossible. ‘Unless perhaps,’ they say, ‘there is someone who believes that the Lord our God can inspire justice in the examination of one person while denying it to innumerable [Note: [Col. 0313] *innumberabilius*, 1.] priests gathered in council’ [Note: [Col. 0313] *deum*, ‘God,’ 2.].

“But since at this time, as rumor has it, there is scarcely anyone at Rome who has learned letters—without which, as it is written, a man can scarcely become a doorkeeper—with what confidence will any of them teach what he has not learned [Note: [Col. 0313] *didicitur*, ‘is learned,’ 1.]?

“Compared with the Roman pontiff, ignorance in other priests is in some measure tolerable; but in the Roman pontiff, who must judge concerning the faith, life, morals, and discipline of priests and concerning the universal Catholic Church, it may appear intolerable.

“For he is, as some maintain, the one who, according to the prophet Ezekiel, dwells in the treasury, which faces the southern road, and keeps watch in the temple’s guardrooms [Col. 0314D]. Why should one who is higher in position but lower in knowledge not willingly accept the judgment of one lower in position but superior in knowledge?

“Certainly the prince of the apostles himself did not reject the judgment of Paul, although Paul was lower in position and superior in knowledge and resisted him to his face, because the teaching of the master did not appear sound.

“And when Pope Gregory says, ‘If any fault is found in bishops, I do not know who is not subject to the apostolic see,’ he adds: ‘But when fault does not require it, all are equal according to the rule of humility.’

“Let the man entangled in crimes recognize that the Roman pontiff presides over him; and let the man who is burdened by no more atrocious deeds understand that he is equal and that, in any matter, he may deliver a judgment worthy of himself and of the Roman pontiff.

“But let us suppose that Damasus is now at Rome: what has been done contrary to his decree? If I remember correctly, the first chapter was that the cases of bishops and the most important ecclesiastical affairs must always be referred to the apostolic see.

“Indeed, they were referred—not only by the bishops but also by our most serene prince. Free authority was granted to the apostolic see to investigate, learn, and judge the truth, after intervals of time that were far too long; and we did not approach the case until we had been driven to despair of its judgment.

“The Roman bishop was therefore consulted as was proper, both concerning the deposition of this Arnulfus and concerning the substitution of one who could worthily preside over the house of God [Note: [Col. 0315] *posset*, ‘could,’ 2.]. But why he gave no reply, let those concerned see to it themselves.

“We, however, apply the Council of Sardica—which strongly supports the privilege of the Roman Church—to this case in such a way that we believe what it says about a lone bishop remaining in any province applies to the Roman bishop. For it is stated in title 6:

“Bishop Hosius said: ‘If it should happen that, in a province where there are many bishops, one bishop alone should remain, and he should through negligence refuse to ordain a bishop, while the people gather bishops from a neighboring province, that bishop who lives in the same province must first be summoned and shown that the people are asking for a ruler for themselves, and that it is just that they themselves should come and ordain a bishop together with him.

“‘But if, when summoned by letters, he remains silent, dissembles, and gives no reply, then the people must be satisfied, so that bishops may come from neighboring provinces and ordain a bishop.’

“According to the meaning of this decision, the bishops and the prince were summoned at the request of the people, so that Arnulfus might be deposed by their authority and another substituted.

“Therefore, because he remained silent when summoned by letters, dissembled, and gave no reply, I judge that the people must now be satisfied: the bishops who have gathered from neighboring provinces should depose this Arnulfus if he is worthy of deposition, and, if someone who can preside over the house of God should be found, they should appoint him bishop [Col. 0315D].

“And since Damasus permits the chief affairs of bishops to be examined by metropolitans and assigns the determination of them to their authority, we do not resist Damasus. But we bring forward the writing of blessed Gregory:

“‘The bearer of this letter, Nemesion, coming to us, reported that Paulus, bishop of the city of Deaclina [Note: [Col. 0315] so in 1 and 2; *Tentinae* in 1a and 2a.], among other evils, had fallen into a bodily crime, had been accused by his own clerics, and, after an inquiry had been held, had proved himself guilty in such a way that we cannot speak of it without sorrow. Moreover, after he had been convicted, he presented a written statement in which he confessed that the matters of which he had been accused were true.

“‘For this reason, after he had been deposed by episcopal judgment, a bishop was ordained in his place with the agreement of your fraternity.’”

“Behold, here Paul the bishop is deposed without Gregory’s knowledge, and another is substituted in his place; the case, together with its consequences, is reported to Gregory by the bearer of the letter. Gregory does not take vengeance on those who deposed him, but proceeds further against the man deposed; for after a little he says:

‘If he should perhaps—which we do not believe—after his deposition, shamelessly and with a perverse mind, speak anything about the episcopate, and again attempt with any presumption to aspire to it, let the vigor of your fraternity be wholly aroused against his wickedness, and take care that, deprived of participation in the Lord’s body and blood, he be confined in a monastery to perform penance there until the day of his death, so that he may learn by worthy lamentation to cleanse the stains of the crime he committed, which he desires wickedly to increase still further to the destruction of his soul.’

How, then, has the decree of Pope Eusebius been observed? For a little earlier, in the decretal volume, we read:

‘The sheep, therefore, entrusted to their shepherd ought neither to rebuke him—unless he has strayed from the true faith—nor can they accuse him in any way; for the deeds of shepherds are not to be struck down by the sword of the sheep’s mouth [Note: [Col. 0315] “of the mouth,” 2?], although they may rightly appear to require rebuke.’

Certainly this Paul was rebuked and accused by his own sheep, that is, by his own clergy—not concerning the faith, but concerning a bodily crime. In this variety of decrees and canons, therefore, the following must be observed: that the outcomes of cases reach their conclusion according to equity [Note: [Col. 0315] lacking in 2?], without rashly introducing disturbances of mind.

And since we have learned that the examination and determination of so important a case was made by the metropolitan of First Justiniana, let us now also show that bishops are permitted to examine the most important cases of their own metropolitans.

Gregory likewise writes to all the bishops of the Council of Vizacium:

‘Just as it is praiseworthy and discerning to show those who hold precedence the reverence and honor that are owed, so it is a matter of uprightness and fear of God, if they require any correction, not to put it off through dissimulation; lest, God forbid, disease begin to invade the whole body if the illness is not cured in the head. Some time ago, indeed, certain matters concerning our brother Clementius, your primate, were brought to us—matters that would pierce our heart with no small grief. But because we were oppressed by various tribulations, and especially because enemies were raging all around us, we had no opportunity to investigate them. Since, however, they are so serious that they must in no way pass without examination, we exhort your fraternity in these words: you ought, with every care and alertness, to investigate the substance of the truth in many ways; and, once the matters have been heard, either let them be cut away by canonical punishment, or, if they are false, let the innocence of our brother not long lie torn apart under an infamous accusation.

‘Therefore, lest anyone’s sluggishness prevail in the investigation, we admonish you [Note: [Col. 0317] “admonish,” 2] that neither regard for any person, nor favor, nor flattery, nor anything else should soften any of you toward the matters reported to us or shake you from the path of truth. Rather, gird yourselves as priests to investigate the truth for God’s sake. For if anyone should presume to be sluggish in this matter or show himself negligent, let him know that he is a participant before the almighty Lord in the crimes alleged, because he is not moved by zeal to scrutinize carefully the causes of the unspeakable deed [Note: [Col. 0317] “to examine beforehand,” 2].’

Here, clearly, we understand that no sinful person is exempt from the judgment of the universal Church. For everyone who sins criminally is judged, so to speak, as altered and diminished in rank as though under the law.

Lucillus, bishop of the city of Malta [Note: [Col. 0317] “Mellita,” 2; [Col. 0317D] “Malta”], is accused before blessed Gregory, and he learns from the letters of his fellow bishops that the crimes brought forward are true. Therefore, he says:

‘Because the punishment of so great a crime must not be delayed at all, let your fraternity take to yourselves three or four of our brothers and fellow priests, so that, with them also present and the truth stated and established, you may undertake without ambiguity to depose the aforementioned Lucillus from the episcopal order, which the contagion of this crime has stained.’

He proceeds further and directs a sentence worthy of the Roman pontiff against those conscious of the crimes:

‘Since certain priests or deacons are said to have been aware of and participants in the revealed iniquity, let your Holiness examine the matter with careful investigation; and if you find it to be so, let them likewise be cast down from the rank of their honor and assigned to monasteries, where they may worthily perform penance.’

This is still not enough, because he knows what was said to the prophet Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0317] “to Ezekiel,” 2]:

‘Son of man, pierce through the wall’ (Ezekiel XII).

But, he says:

‘Since many are reported to have fallen through these men into the stain of this sin, it is appropriate for you to deprive all who are clearly found guilty [Note: [Col. 0317] corrected from “regi,” “guilty,” 2] of participation in the Lord’s body and blood.’

Here Gregory does not nourish vices but cuts them off. For what else is it to remain silent about manifest sins than to nourish crimes?

But let it be so; let us be silent about matters in which no one complains that he has been injured. What shall we do if armed commanders discover the nocturnal thefts of the marriage bed? If angry kings convict one of us of treason? What, I ask, shall we do if they perceive that they have been deceived by some collusion, through long circumlocutions and intricate quibbles? Do you suppose that they will redeem the form of judgment at Rome with money, and that there will be no accused person who, if he hopes to be ransomed by money, will offer mountains of gold and silver to the Romans [Note: [Col. 0317] “Roman,” 1]?

But if you think that the matters we propose are remote from practice, custom, and distance of place, take examples from nearby. Certainly Egidius, archbishop of Reims, because he was convicted of having used the friendship of King Hilperic [Note: [Col. 0317] “Chilperic,” written by another hand after other words were erased, 2] against the fidelity owed to his own king Childebert, was deposed in the city of Metz by the bishops of Gaul and condemned to perpetual exile at Argentoratum, which is now called Strasbourg. Soon Romulfus, son of Duke Lupus, already a priest, was substituted for him. Nor is it found that the great Gregory, the most zealous defender of the privilege of the Roman Church, said anything either in favor of these proceedings or against them.

Ebo also, metropolitan of the same Church of Reims, was deposed by the bishops of Gaul at Thionville [Note: [Col. 0317] “Theodonisvilla,” 2] on account of the crime of lèse-majesté; much later his deposition was investigated and established by Pope Nicholas, and afterward confirmed by Sergius.

What, then? Shall we condemn the decrees of Damasus? By no means. But in hidden cases, and in those in which a rightful appeal is made because of their seriousness, we shall have recourse to a universal council or to Damasus—if, that is, we hear that he is residing at Rome. Yet even appeal to Damasus is prohibited to Africans by African councils, as was said above and will still be said.

But in evident cases, and in those in which no appeal is made to the Roman bishop, we shall use provincial or conprovincial councils. The Council of Antioch also seems to wish this in its fourteenth chapter:

‘If any bishop has been accused in the judgment of bishops on some criminal charges, and it happens that the bishops of the province who have assembled hold differing opinions about him—some declaring him innocent, others guilty—then, in order to remove such a controversy, the holy synod has decreed that the metropolitan bishop of another neighboring province, together with several other bishops, should be summoned. They shall sit together and settle whatever the question may be, so that the judgment promulgated by the bishops of one province may be firm.’

Although this council, which concerns the private case of our fellow bishop, ought also to be regarded as universal, since it contains the judgments of several provinces.

And lest we seem to speak merely to please ourselves and to interpret the judgments of the ancients incorrectly, hear what Hincmarus, archbishop of Reims and most learned in the law of God, thinks about this. Writing to Pope Nicholas, he says:

‘Far be it from us to disregard the privilege of the first and highest see, that of the pontiff of the holy Roman Church, to such an extent that we should burden your supreme authority with controversies and quarrels both of the higher and the lower order, which the canons of Nicaea and of the other holy councils, together with the decrees of Innocent and of the other pontiffs of the holy Roman See, command to be settled in provincial synods by the metropolitans.

‘But if perhaps a case concerning bishops should arise for which we have no certain and explicit judgments in the sacred rules, and which for that reason cannot be determined in a provincial or conprovincial examination, then we must have recourse concerning it to the divine oracle, that is, to the apostolic see.’

Concerning appeals, the same Hincmarus agrees with us that a legitimate appeal may be made from suspect judges and judges of lesser authority to judges of greater authority; but from elected judges, and where the accused has had his case decided, no appeal at all can be made. Concerning this, the African council likewise says:

‘THAT IT IS NOT PERMITTED TO APPEAL FROM ELECTED JUDGES.’

‘If an appeal has been made, let the appellant choose judges, and let the person against whom he has appealed choose with him; thereafter no one may appeal from those judges.’

Again, in the same councils, concerning the same matter, chapter 22:

‘If clerics think that they ought to appeal from bishops, let them appeal only to the African councils or to the primates of their provinces, just as has often been decreed concerning bishops. But those who think that they should appeal overseas are not to be received into communion by anyone in the land of Africa [Note: [Col. 0319] “within Africa,” 2].’

By “overseas,” they plainly wished the Roman Church to be understood. Thus the African bishops confirmed that a case ought to be determined where it arose.

Let anyone who can consider, however, that what was read shortly before was not without a certain difficulty. Damasus says:

‘As you know, it is not catholic for a synod to be held without its— that is, the Roman See’s—authority.’

What, then, if barbarian swords rage all around and the freedom to travel to Rome is cut off? Or if Rome, serving some barbarian, is carried by his caprice into some kingdom? In the meantime, will there either be no councils, or will the bishops of the whole world await the councils and counsels by which the losses or destruction of their kings by enemies are to be arranged?

And certainly the Nicene canon—which, according to the testimony of the Roman Church itself, surpasses all councils and all decrees by the excellence of its authority—says that councils ought to be held twice a year, and prescribes that nothing concerning this belongs to the authority of the Roman bishop. Indeed, as the African synod interprets it, it greatly diminishes his privilege.

The same African synod prescribes, in chapter nine of the Council of Milevis, that private cases are to be judged in a provincial synod, but common cases in a general council.

For our part, once the quarrel of controversy has been set aside, we honor the Roman Church, because of the memory of the chief of the apostles, as we have received from our ancestors, as much as we are able—more than the Africans do. Whether it is about to produce something worthy or unworthy, if the condition of kingdoms permits it, let us seek responses from it, as was clearly also done in the case of Arnulfus.

If it promulgates a just or unjust form of judgment in matters to be sought or avoided, in the one case the peace and unity of the churches will be preserved; in the other we shall hear the voice of the Apostle saying:

‘Whoever announces to you anything beyond what you received, let him be accursed, even if he should pretend to be an angel from heaven!’ (Galatians I, 8–9.)

But if it remains silent, as now, the laws consulted will speak with the voice of their authors.

But O unhappy times, in which we are frustrated of the patronage of so great a Church! To what city shall we flee hereafter, when we see the mistress of all nations deprived of human and divine support? To speak more plainly and openly: after the fall of the empire, this city has lost the Alexandrian Church and the Church of Antioch; and, to say nothing of Africa and Asia, Europe itself is now departing. For the Constantinopolitan Church has withdrawn, and the inner regions of Spain know nothing of its judgments.

There is therefore a falling away, according to the Apostle, not only of nations but also of churches (II Thessalonians II, 3). Since the Antichrist appears to be at hand, whose ministers have occupied Gaul and oppress us with all their strength, and as the same Apostle says:

‘The mystery of iniquity is already at work; only let the one who now restrains it continue to restrain it until he is removed from the midst, so that that son of perdition may be revealed, the man of sin, who opposes and exalts himself above the name of God and the worship of God’ (II Thessalonians II, 7–8).

This is already happening openly. Roman power has been shaken, religion has been overthrown, and the name of God is humbled with impunity by frequent perjuries; even the worship of divine religion itself is despised by the highest priests [Note: [Col. 0319] “held in contempt,” 1].

Moreover, Rome itself is now almost departing from itself, since it neither provides counsel for itself nor for others.

Therefore, if it pleases your charity, since we know that Pelagius the patriarch was heard by twelve bishops, as blessed Augustine writes in a certain book against the same Pelagius [Note: [Col. 0319] lacking, 2], and since the Roman Church, consulted by us, has promulgated no form of judgment, let chapters from the sacred laws be brought forward: by how many bishops a bishop detained in a crime ought to be heard, and what sentence should be imposed on those who refuse to be present to state their case.”

Accordingly, at the command of the synod, the following judgments were read aloud:

**29.** [Note: [Col. 0319] In Codex 2, chapter 29 begins with the word *Felix*.]

From the Council of Carthage, title 10:

Bishop Felix said:

“I propose, according to the statutes of the ancient councils, that if any bishop—which may we never desire—should fall into some accusation, and should be under such pressing necessity that he cannot assemble many, then, so that he may not remain under accusation, he should be heard by twelve bishops; a presbyter by six bishops together with his own bishop; and a deacon by three.”

From the Council of Carthage, chapter 7:

Bishop Aurelius said:

“Whoever accuses a bishop shall bring the case to the primate of that province; and the person against whom the crime is alleged shall not be suspended from communion unless, having been summoned by letter to state his case before the chosen judges on the appointed day, he fails to appear—namely, within the space of a month from the day on which it is established that he received the letter [Note: [Col. 0319] ‘judgment’ 1?].

“But if someone proves genuine causes of necessity that clearly prevented him from appearing, he shall have a full opportunity to state his case during the following month; nevertheless, after the second month he shall not communicate until he has been cleared. If he refuses to appear at the annual universal council, so that his case may be settled there, he shall be judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation upon himself. During the period in which he does not communicate, he shall not communicate either in his own church or in his parish.”

Concerning contempt of judgment [Note: [Col. 0319] “contention,” 1], from a letter of Pope Boniface:

“He proves that the things said against him are true who is wholly unwilling to be present to refute them. No one doubts that the guilty person thus evades judgment, just as the innocent person seeks to be acquitted. But the crafty quibbling of those who think that matters must be managed by cunning devices will never receive the name of innocence.

“For whoever thinks that he can evade judgment by delays confesses everything. Nevertheless, the person said to be such will at some time come into the open; and it does him no good to have hidden and evaded judgment so often. Wherever he flees, his acts and deeds pursue him, if the crimes brought against him are true. If he wishes to be present, let him answer the charges, if he has confidence; but if he neglects to appear, let him not gain a postponement of the sentence through his absence.

“For it is clear that a person confesses the crime when, despite being granted judgment and being summoned to it so many times, he does not use the opportunity to clear himself. For it makes no difference whether everything alleged is proved in a hearing at which he is present, since his repeated absence, itself procured as a confession, is established as such.”

**30.** After all these matters had been examined, Arnulfus’s defenders requested pardon—both because they had previously investigated his affairs less carefully than they should have and because they had wearied the council with long delays. They then added that they had not been led by any kind of controversy to undertake the work of defense, but that the bishops’ anathema had imposed upon them the necessity of speaking.

The bishops, however, including those who appeared to have stood against Arnulfus, said that they had received the charges with equanimity. They too approved the view that a legitimate judgment could now be held in common, and that nothing remained except for Arnulfus himself to be brought forward and to answer concerning the character of his conduct as he wished.

Accordingly, at the command of the synod, he took his seat among the bishops.

Father Arnulfus then recalled, in a mild address, the king’s benefits toward him and also his own wrongs against the king. Arnulfus denied that he had done anything against the king’s safety, but said that, for the sake of the loyalty he had preserved toward him, he had been captured by enemies in his own city together with the clergy and people. He had received no assistance from the king in return; indeed, his benefits had been repaid with injuries.

Father Arnulfus brought forward the presbyter who was present. He asserted that, after receiving the keys from Arnulfus’s hand, he had opened the city gates to the enemy at Arnulfus’s command.

Arnulfus replied [Note: [Col. 0321] “replied,” 2] that the presbyter was making long-prepared statements and reporting falsehoods as truths; his own innocence ought not to be made suspect by the presbyter’s fabricated accusations.

The presbyter, in turn, pressed the point that no one had compelled him to accuse; that the path of flight had been open to him; that he had always been utterly faithful to Arnulfus; and that he had no other motive in accusing him than to free himself from the charge of treason, since he had obeyed Arnulfus’s command. If the synod doubted anything in his confession of the truth, or attributed it to his own fault, he promised to submit to the synod’s decrees—provided only that he be restored to ecclesiastical communion.

At this Arnulfus complained that he was being held by the enemies [Note: [Col. 0321] “bones,” 2] and that he had never seen a bishop treated in such a way; therefore, he said, he did not know how to answer.

Nor, he added, had his monks, clergy, or abbots been left to him, so that he could command them to do whatever he wished. This statement was thought to be that of a foolish man.

“And what,” said Father Arnulfus, “should be commanded to them? Should they exempt you from your faults? [Note: [Col. 0321] “think that they exempt you,” 2] Indeed, if you say that you are speaking in testimony, here are your bishops, who frequently urged you, for your own sake, to come to the synod; here are your abbots, and your clergy together with their superiors. All these are permitted to defend you—not merely voluntarily, but under an imposed obligation.”

At this he returned to his earlier statements, saying that he had never seen a bishop treated in such a way and that he did not know how to answer concerning his own treatment. He added that a learned man could appear foolish among so many wise men.

“Why, then,” said Bishop Guido, “when you had been treated according to your wishes, and had so often been summoned by the bishops and by your own lord the king, did you refuse to answer?”

He replied:

“I had been denounced to the king, and therefore I did not dare to go where I was summoned.”

“It is not so,” said Bishop Guido. “When I met you near the city of Laon, at Cavignon, before trustworthy witnesses, clerics and laymen, I invited you for the third time to the assembly of your brothers, calling upon you under the testimony of the divine name, by the authority of the canons and by the fellowship of all the faithful. I also urged you to go into the presence of your lords, by the fidelity that you had promised them and by all the oaths that you had given them.

“Therefore you cannot deny that you are a perjurer, as shown by the *chirograph* to which you subscribed and made all of us subscribe. But when you replied that you could not go without Odo and Heribert as guides, because you feared that force might be used against you, I offered you my brother Gualterius as a hostage. I promised that I and my father, Count Gualterius, would guide you on the journey, so that you could return to your own home without danger to your life or limbs and without the danger of capture.

“At that very moment I was also ready to confirm this under oath with my own hand. When you claimed that you had been captured by Karolus and had given him oaths and hostages, and therefore could not go without his permission, I asked you which hostages seemed more valuable to you: your brother Richard; Bruno, your cousin the bishop; and the son of his sister, who were in the power of kings; or your soldiers Sehardus and Raynoldus [Note: [Col. 0321] ‘Rainoldus’], who were permitted to depart after giving boys as hostages, and whose benefices you assigned to your supposed captors—openly revealing how great was the care taken by both the giver and the receiver of the hostages.

“I also asked which oath you ought rather to keep: the one you had freely given to the king and your lord, or the one you had been compelled to give to an armed enemy.

“There were three oaths that you could escape by no art or ingenuity. The first was the oath by which you bound yourself not to withdraw from loyalty to our lords on account of any oath you had taken or might take. The second was that, if you had been intercepted by enemies, as you were then pretending, as soon as a path of flight opened to you, you would not delay returning to your lords in true fidelity. I was urging you to do this at that very moment, when only a few men were with you, whereas I had troops of excellent soldiers [Note: [Col. 0323] ‘excellent,’ 2].

“What shall I say about the third, when you are guilty of as many perjuries as you make people perjure themselves? For all your citizens and soldiers, at your command, swore that if you were ever captured by enemies, or if you yourself voluntarily withdrew from fidelity to the king, they would preserve their loyalty to the king and retain the city and the fortress under his authority.

“Yet when you withdrew from fidelity to the king, you ordered them to swear oaths to you against all mortal men; you closed the city gates against your lord the king; you opened them to Karolus whenever it pleased him; and you refused to heed the declaration in your *chirograph*, while you supplied the enemies of your lords, according to your knowledge and ability, with counsel and assistance.

“Will you also attempt to deny these things?”

He also added that agreements and arrangements had been made with Arnulfus in the vernacular language, by which Arnulfus had, as it were, emancipated the bishops from their subjection if he departed from the conditions of the *chirograph*; and that he had already achieved this at Cavignon on his own behalf and on behalf of the other bishops.

At this Arnulfus was ashamed of the fact that he had not observed the conditions of the *chirograph* and the oaths; nevertheless, by whatever means he could, he minimized these same matters.

The bishops therefore asked that one of Arnulfus’s household be admitted as a witness, someone whose conscience he would fear.

Raynerius [Note: [Col. 0323] “Rainerus,” 2] was admitted. He was fully aware of Arnulfus’s secrets and publicly declared that Arnulfus had been perjured, among other perjuries, even against Raynerius himself, his wife, and his son.

When the holy assembly told him what Arnulfus denied concerning his infidelity to the king, he addressed Arnulfus in these words:

“Why are you destroying the whole people through your error? Do you not remember what you told me beside the river Axona before the surrender of the city? And so that you may remember everything better, do you not know that you preferred the love of Ludovicus, son of Karolus, to all mortal men, and that you wanted me to consider his safety?

“Go, then, and confess your crimes to the bishops, so that, since you have lost your body, you may at least save your soul through penance, and release the people who still doubt your crimes from this error.

“But if you refuse, before the bishops and before the whole multitude standing outside the doors, I shall reveal your sins, which are still uncertain, and bring forward your crimes, which are not part of the people’s suspicions, so that all may know and understand what they ought to think about you.

“And so that my words may be believed forever, after I have finished speaking I shall confirm with an oath by my right hand that they are true, and shall hand over my servant to the bishops; he shall walk across burning plowshares and, by manifest signs, declare that God is judging you.”

At this some of the abbots said that Arnulfus ought to be given a secluded place in which to deliberate with whomever he wished, so that he might be able to answer on his own behalf with greater prudence.

To them Father Arnulfus said:

“Who is preventing him? Let him rise and bring into his consultation whomever he chooses.”

He then rose and led the venerable bishops into the more secluded part of the crypt, after carefully fastening the doors: Siguinus of Sens, Arnulfus of Orléans, Bruno of Langres, and Gotesmannus of Amiens.

**31.** During their absence, many chapters from the canons were brought forward in the synod, and much was discussed among those present. They were ignorant of everything being done in secret, but they were not unaware that Arnulfus had sought conversations with the Empress Theophanu and with the king’s enemies against the king’s will and interest; that he had stationed troops of his soldiers under Karolus’s standards in battle against the same king; and, in addition, that he was guilty of the crime of lèse-majesté.

He also appeared to be entangled in various kinds of oaths, to such an extent that no priest enveloped in so many perjuries could lawfully fulfill the episcopal ministry.

The following judgments were found to bear, as it were, upon these matters from nearby:

**32.** [Note: [Col. 0323] In 2, chapter 32 begins with the word *Confitemini*.]

From the Council of Toledo, chapter 30:

“[The opening reading is uncertain: perhaps ‘confidants of enemies’:] priests, except for those who have received permission from the royal power, must not presume secretly to receive or send a message from any outsider.” Whoever is discovered or convicted of doing so shall be denounced to the prince and punished in the council with a fitting penalty.”

Again, from the same title, chapter 75:

**33.** “After certain institutions of the ecclesiastical order or decrees concerning the discipline of some persons, the final judgment for all of us priests is to issue, under God the judge, a final episcopal decree for the strength of our kings and the stability of the Gothic people.

“For, as is reported, there is among many nations such great treachery of mind that they disdain to preserve the faith promised by oath to their kings. With their mouths they pretend to profess the oath, while in their minds they retain the wickedness of disloyalty.

“They swear to their kings and violate the faith they promise; nor do they fear that book of judgment by which a curse and many threats of punishment are brought upon those who swear falsely in the name of God.

“What hope, then, will such peoples have when laboring against their enemies? What trust can thereafter be placed, in peace, in dealings with other nations after a treaty that must not be violated? [Alternatively: ‘what covenant?’; Note: [Col. 0323] the words *a. q. f.* are absent in 1.] What rights will remain in such a pledge among enemies, when they do not preserve sworn faith even toward their own kings?

“For who is so mad as to cut off his own head with his own hand? Yet they, forgetful of their own welfare, kill themselves with their own hand, turning their strength against themselves and against their own kings.

“Although the Lord says, ‘Do not touch my anointed ones!’ (I Chronicles XVI, 22), and David says, ‘Who has stretched out his hand against the Lord’s anointed and remained innocent?’ (I Samuel XXVI, 9), they neither fear perjury nor hesitate to bring destruction upon kings.

“Faith in a treaty is given to enemies and is not violated. If faith is maintained in war, how much more must it be preserved among one’s own people? It is sacrilege if peoples violate the faith promised to their kings, because in them there is not only a breach of a treaty, but also an offense against God, in whose name the promise itself is made.

“For this reason heavenly anger has changed many kingdoms of the earth, so that, on account of the impiety of their faith and morals, one kingdom was dissolved from another [Note: [Col. 0323] ‘one from another,’ 1].

“Therefore we too must beware of the downfall of such peoples, lest we likewise be struck by a sudden blow and punished by a cruel penalty. For if God did not spare the angels who transgressed against him, who lost their heavenly dwelling through disobedience—and therefore he says through Isaiah, ‘My sword is drunk in heaven’ (Isaiah XXXIV, 5)—how much more must we fear the destruction of our salvation, lest we perish under the same raging sword through disloyalty?

“If we wish to avoid divine anger and desire to move his severity toward mercy, let us preserve toward God the worship and fear of religion; let us guard toward our rulers the faith and pledge we have promised.

“Let there not be among us, as among certain nations, impious subtlety of disloyalty, treachery of a deceitful mind, the wickedness of perjury, or the abominable schemes of conspiracies. Let no one seize the kingdom presumptuously; let no one incite mutual seditions among citizens; let no one plot the destruction of kings.

“Rather, when a ruler has died in peace, let the leading men of the nation, together with the priests, establish his successor to the kingdom by common counsel, so that, while the harmony of unity is preserved among us, no division of the fatherland and people may be stirred up through the force of ambition.

“But if this admonition does not correct our minds and does not lead our heart at all toward the common salvation, hear our sentence.

“Therefore, whoever among us or among all the peoples of Spain, by any conspiracy or design, violates the oath of faith that he has promised for the safety of the fatherland, the condition of the Gothic people, or the preservation of the king’s safety; or assaults the king with deadly violence [Note: [Col. 0325] ‘attrectaverit,’ ‘lays hands upon,’ 1, in some copies]; or strips him of royal power; or usurps the height of kingship through tyrannical presumption—let him be anathema in the sight of God the Father and the angels. Let him be made an outsider from the Catholic Church, which he has profaned by perjury, and an alien from every assembly of Christians, together with all his accomplices in impiety, because it is fitting that one punishment hold those bound whom a similar error has found entangled.”

This we repeat a second time, saying:

“Whoever from now on, among us or among all the peoples of Spain, by any deliberation or design, violates the oath of faith that he has promised for the safety of the fatherland, the condition of the Gothic people, or the preservation of the king’s safety; or assaults the king with deadly violence; or strips him of royal power; or usurps the height of kingship through tyrannical presumption—let him be anathema in the sight of Christ and his apostles. Let him be made an outsider from the Catholic Church, which he has profaned by perjury, an alien from every fellowship of Christians, and let him be held condemned at the future judgment of God, together with his accomplices, because it is fitting that those who are joined to such men should also be held liable by sharing in their condemnation.”

This also we proclaim a third time, saying:

“Whoever from now on, among us or among all the peoples of Spain, by any purpose or design, violates the oath of faith that he has promised for the safety of the fatherland, the condition of the Gothic people, or the security of royal power; or assaults the king with deadly violence; or strips him of royal power; or usurps the height of kingship through tyrannical presumption—let him be anathema in the sight of the Holy Spirit and the martyrs of Christ. Let him be made an outsider from the Catholic Church, which he has profaned by perjury, alien from all communion with Christians, and let him have no share among the righteous. Rather, let him be condemned to eternal punishments with the devil and his angels, together with those who strive through the same conspiracy, so that an equal punishment of destruction may bind those whom a wicked association joins in ruin.

“Therefore, if it pleases all of you who are present, confirm this third repeated sentence by the agreement of your voices” [Note: [Col. 0325] “confirm,” 2].

The whole clergy and people said:

“Those who presume to act against this your definition [Note: [Col. 0325] lacking in 1]—anathema maranatha, that is, let them be destruction at the coming of the Lord—and let them, both they and their companions, have a share with Judas Iscariot. Amen.”

Therefore we ourselves and all the priests admonish the Church of Christ and the people, so that this dreadful and so often repeated sentence may condemn none of us in the present or eternal judgment. Rather, let us preserve the faith promised toward our most glorious lord Sisenandus the king and serve him with sincere devotion. In this way we may not only call forth the mercy of divine kindness upon ourselves, but also deserve to receive the favor of the aforementioned ruler.

Again, from the Council of Agde [Note: [Col. 0325] “Agathensis,” 2], title 50:”

### 34

If a bishop, presbyter, or deacon commits a capital crime, falsifies a document, or gives false testimony, he shall be deposed from the dignity of his office, confined in a monastery, and there alone receive lay communion for as long as he lives. [Column 0326B]

Likewise, from the Sixth Council of Toledo, chapter 12:

### 35

The audacity of depraved minds often seeks refuge among enemies, either through the malice of their thoughts or on account of their crimes. Therefore, whoever has been the perpetrator of such deeds, possessing the power to defend the adversaries and having inflicted losses of property upon his country or nation, shall be brought under the authority of the king and the nation, excommunicated, and confined; he shall be subjected to the rules of prolonged penance.

But if, first remembering his own wrongdoing, he flees for refuge to the church, then, through the intercession of the priests and out of reverence for the place, the king’s mercy shall be preserved toward him, together with justice.

Likewise, from the same council [Note: absent in witness 2], title 17:

### 36

[Note: XXXV. 2 in witness 2.]

Although a judgment concerning such a matter was promulgated at the preceding council, which was held in the first year of our glorious ruler, nevertheless it pleases us to repeat what ought to be observed.

Therefore, so long as the king lives, no layman of whatever dignity, nor anyone consecrated to the rank of bishop, presbyter, or deacon, nor anyone devoted to any other clerical office, shall by any action or deliberation designate a future king for himself against the welfare and, without doubt, the will of the living king. For the sake of that hope, he shall neither draw others to himself by flattery or persuasion, nor himself yield to another.

For it must be considered unjust and utterly detestable among Christians to look toward unlawful events of the future and to arrange what is to come while those whose lives are at stake know nothing of it.

If anyone has already deliberated upon such wicked matters with anyone else, he shall know that priestly moderation grants him this: if he asks pardon, he should make every effort to disclose the matter without delay to the ears of the present ruler.

But if he keeps silent and refuses to reveal the schemes of his deliberation, let him be punished with the worst anathema.

Likewise, from the same council, title 18:

### 37

At the preceding universal synod, provision was certainly made for the safety of our rulers; but we wish to repeat what was well enacted and to strengthen with worthy authority what has been salutarily ordered. [Column 0326D]

Therefore, before God and the entire order of angels, before the company of the prophets and apostles and the whole choir of martyrs, before the entire Catholic Church and the assembly of Christians, we testify that no one shall plot the destruction of the king; no one shall attack the ruler’s life; no one shall deprive him of the government of the kingdom; no one shall usurp the summit of the kingdom through tyrannical presumption; and no one shall, by any scheme whatsoever, join his hand to the hands of conspirators against him.

If anyone among us should dare to attempt any of these things [Note: witness 2 reads *temerario*, “rashly”], let him be struck by divine anathema and held condemned by eternal judgment, with no place of remedy.

But the one who has attained his throne, if he wishes to be cleansed from so great a sacrilege, must avenge the death of that man as though he were his own father. [Column 0327A]

Likewise, from the Council of Toledo, in the era 684:

### 38

It contributes greatly to the correction of many if matters that have been established are recalled to memory through fraternal discussion [Note: witness 1 reads *consolationem*, “consolation”], and if those matters are also added that seem to be lacking or that are thought properly to require establishment.

For who does not know how many unlawful acts have thus far been committed [Note: witness 2 reads *actenus*, “thus far”] by tyrants and fugitives who transferred themselves into foreign regions, and how frequently their unspeakable arrogance has been displayed? These acts brought about the diminution of the homeland and imposed unceasing labor upon the Gothic army.

If this madness had indeed been committed by laymen, it might perhaps sometimes appear tolerable to us. Yet what is more astonishing—and worse—is that so many who had embraced religion have sometimes been carried headlong into this presumption, so that it would be no slight disgrace to us if a matter that both secular law and ecclesiastical discipline ought promptly to correct were left unpunished in any respect.

Therefore, by unanimous decision, it has now seemed right to define that whoever, established in the clerical order from the highest rank to the lowest, transfers himself [Note: witness 1 perhaps reads *traduxerit*] for any reason into the territory of a foreign people, so that from there, in his arrogance, he appears to seek either his return or anything else, or so that under this pretext he may harm, plan to harm, or in any way actually harm the Gothic people, the homeland, or the kingdom—

and likewise whoever is found to have been aware of such acts and is known to have supplied them with advice or assistance, whether so that they might seek flight to a foreign people, persist in the evils they had begun [Note: witness 2 reads *coeceperant*], or inflict any injury after their flight upon the Gothic people, the homeland, or the ruler, and persist in that same wickedness—

whoever is known to have done this shall unquestionably be deprived of every degree of his honor, so that another may immediately and permanently receive the place in which he had served, to govern it. [Column 0327C]

But the transgressor himself, placed under penance, if, remembering the evil he had done, he truly performs penance until the day of his death, shall receive communion only at the very end of his life. If, before the time of his end arrives, any priest, even at the ruler’s command, agrees to communicate him, he shall become a participant in that crime and be anathematized forever; he shall be condemned with the same sentence as the person whom he communicated. For no priest ought in this matter to give assent to the ruler’s power [Note: witness 2 perhaps reads *potestate*], lest he appear to incur perjury—or, God forbid, lest, if any ruler who is a traitor to the Catholic faith should arise, a priest be compelled, whether by the ruler’s favor or by fear, to return from the light of right belief [Note: witness 1 reads *recto*, “right”] into darkness.

Thus, neither the provisions appended above ought ever to be annulled [Note: witness 1 reads *evocari*, “summoned” or “called forth”] by the commands or threats of rulers.

For we know that nearly all the priests of Spain, as well as all the nobles, judges, and other men of the palace office, have sworn, and that it has now been decreed by law [Note: witness 2 reads *degibus*, corrected by another hand to *de regibus*, “concerning kings”], that no fugitive or traitor who is found to have acted against the Gothic people, the homeland, or the king, or to have transferred himself into the fellowship of another people, shall in any way be restored to possession of his property—unless perhaps the ruler wishes to grant such persons some act of humanity. Even then, he shall have the power to grant the traitor no more than a twentieth part of his property, taken from whatever possessions the king chooses. [Column 0327D]

But because the perversity of reckless levity sometimes so exalts many clerics that, setting aside the gravity of their order and forgetting the oath they have promised, they rashly consent to the elevation of another while the ruler to whom they had promised to remain faithful is still alive, this license ought to be entirely abolished and utterly eradicated from our fellowship.

Thus, if any layman, while still within the boundaries of the Gothic homeland, should arrogantly attempt to seize the summit of the kingdom, and any cleric should offer him assistance or favor, and it should happen through the power of his offense that the cleric be seen to have aided this man who appears to be acting arrogantly in his ambition for the kingdom, then from that very day and moment the bishop or cleric of whatever order must remain perpetually excommunicated, from the time when he entangled himself in such a crime. [Column 0328A]

Nevertheless, if, because of the wickedness of the ruler—the ruler to whom he wickedly gave his consent—the priestly authorities are unable to suspend him from communion, then, at least if he survives until after the death of that king, he shall be subjected to the correction of the earlier anathema.

And whoever agrees that the grace of communion should be bestowed on him otherwise than at the very end of his life [Note: witness 2 reads *ultima*, “final”], provided that he has been shown to repent lawfully [Column 0328B]—meanwhile, it has seemed good to us to decree by this synodal constitution the following:

Whoever, even among the laity, is subsequently found guilty of violating the chapters prohibited above—that is, by going into foreign regions in hostility to the people, homeland, or royal power, or by giving assistance to such persons—shall not only, as has been said, be deprived of all ownership of his property, but, condemned to perpetual excommunication, shall never be given communion except at the final moment of his death, unless the remedy of his communion, or the entreaty of the priests concerning the persons specified above, has been obtained from the ruler.

For if anyone is found wickedly to speak in disparagement or insult of the ruler, or to plot or give assent to the killing of the king or the seizure of his property, we judge such a person worthy of excommunication. Whether communion should ever afterward be granted to him [Note: witness 2 reads *t. si sit*; the reading is uncertain], however, we leave to the ruler’s mercy to decide; for it is unquestionably within his power to temper the faults of his subjects by a judgment of mercy and justice. [Column 0328C]

We admonish the most merciful rulers and, invoking them unanimously by the ineffable sacrament of the divine name, earnestly entreat them never, without a just priestly petition where necessity requires it, to suspend this sentence of excommunication against traitorous clerics or laymen who transfer themselves into foreign regions or give assistance to such persons.

For this appears to provide more effectively for the common welfare: that the form of our constitution be preserved.

And let any king henceforward who believes or permits the severity of this canon to be violated in any respect become an execrable anathema and remain forever guilty before the Lord as a betrayer of the Catholic faith.

Likewise, from the Council of Toledo, in the era [Note: witness 1 has *era*; above it is written “that is, chapter”; witness 2 reads “era … chapter II”] 668:

### 39

[Note: witness 1 perhaps reads *Frequentiam*, “frequency.”]

The harmful pressure of frequent troubles may indeed be despised because of the gravity of the speaker’s authority; but since honorable concern hastens to restrain what repeated custom does not take care to avoid, and since this matter has been guarded both by the sanctions of certain ancestral decrees and by legal enactments, so that no one may attempt to plot against the safety of the rulers, the people, or the homeland, this one point is now specifically brought forward for observance:

If anyone among the religious—from the bishop down to the lowest rank of clerics or monks—is found by profane will to have violated the general oaths sworn for the safety of the king, the people, or the homeland, he shall immediately be deprived of his own dignity and held excluded from both place and honor. [Column 0328D]

[Column 0329A]

### 40

While each person was repeating these and similar matters to himself or to another, the bishops who were sitting in the synod were summoned by those bishops [Note: witness 2 has *iis*, corrected in another hand to *his*, “these”] who had accompanied Arnulf into the more remote regions. When they had assembled [Note: witness 1 omits “they had”], they learned the reason for their arrival amid no little weeping and much lamentation.

Arnulf’s case was similar to that of the presbyter Apiarius. Concerning him, just as the African bishops reported to Pope Celestine of Rome, so here the bishops appeared to report concerning Arnulf to the bishops in the following manner:

“The just, strong, and patient God the Judge cut short, with great dispatch, Arnulf’s evasions by which he was trying to conceal unspeakable disgrace. For the more hideous and putrid obstinacy by which his shameless denial sought to bury so great a mass of livid filth was suppressed; while our God pressed upon his conscience and disclosed even to men the hidden things that, as though in a cesspool of crimes, He had already condemned in his heart.

Suddenly, in confessing all the disgraceful deeds laid before him, he burst forth as a deceitful denier; and at last, of his own accord, he himself convicted himself of all the unbelievable infamies. He turned into lamentation even that hope of ours by which we both believed and desired that he could be cleansed from such shameful stains.

He mitigated our grief by this one consolation: he freed us from the labor of a longer examination and provided some kind of remedy for his wounds, although his confession was reluctant and resisted by his own conscience.”

The confessing bishops further added that he had thrown himself at their feet and, with tears and groans, had declared his crimes under the name of confession, and that he wished to be removed from the priestly office which he had until then unworthily exercised.

But the bishops who, with Arnulf’s consent, had been admitted as witnesses to his confession said that they preferred to hear it from his own mouth.

When this had been done, the bishops adjured him by the fearful name of almighty God, under a terrible anathema, not to utter anything false [Note: witness 1 perhaps reads *false*] about himself under the pressure of any fear. They promised that they would bring him every consolation and would recover his former honor even against the will of the kings, provided only that he wished to establish his innocence by an equitable and useful account.

But he, thanking the bishops for their concern for his salvation, confirmed that what he had entrusted to their faith was true. He said that he did not wish to lie to God, before whose presence he stood and whose judgment he feared to face.

The bishops therefore, since the matters he had brought forth in confession appeared to them extremely serious, requested permission to admit the most learned and most devout of the abbots [Note: witness 2 reads *ac*, “and”] and clergy [Note: witness 2 reads *et*, “and”]. Bound by an oath or anathema, these men would faithfully conceal his sins, jointly determine what ought to be done, and become utterly trustworthy witnesses for future ages of what had been said and done.

After considering this for some time, he permitted it to be done.

Accordingly, nearly thirty men were admitted [Note: witness 1 reads *ammissi*] from the entire college of abbots and clergy. Under the condition of anathema, Arnulf’s confession was publicly disclosed in his presence at his own command [Note: witness 1 reads *prolata*, “produced,” instead of *propalata*, “publicly disclosed”].

He was then removed, and after lengthy consultations it was decided how his secret should be concealed and how the absent clergy and people should be satisfied concerning his deposition.

For it was already certain that the man who had chosen judges for himself could not proceed to another judgment. It also appeared that the bishops were deprived of the privilege of Rome through envy, since Arnulf had appealed neither to other judges nor to the apostolic see—neither before the hearing of the chosen judges, which would certainly have been permissible had he thought his case just, nor after the sentence of those judges, which was plainly not permissible.

Rather, as a defendant convicted by the conscience that tormented him and, as it then appeared, confessing of his own accord, he had demanded the procedure of a trial as a wicked accuser of himself.

It was therefore asked how his deposition could be carried out so that it would conform to law and custom.

As for the law [Note: witness 2 reads *quid*, “what,” for *quidem*], it was clear that one and the same law always looks toward equity. As for custom, it was clear that custom is neither one nor uniform [Note: absent in witness 2], nor does it always aim at equity; nevertheless, that custom should prevail which is close to law or equity.

The law and custom governing the deposition of bishops or archbishops were therefore sought. This law was found in the African councils, but without the ceremonial practice and custom of deposition [Note: witness 2 adds: “Concerning Maximinus the bishop”]:

### 41

Concerning Maximinus of Bagai, and concerning him and the people themselves, it was decided that a letter should be sent from the council, so that he might withdraw from the episcopate and they might seek another for themselves.

### 42
