Likewise, when the presbyter Eutyches was deposed at the Constantinopolitan synod, he received no other ceremony of deposition than that anathema was proclaimed against him by all, followed some time later by a sentence pronounced by Bishop Flavian in this manner:

“Eutyches, formerly presbyter and archimandrite, has been found, from the matters previously conducted and from the questions put before him, to suffer from the perversity of Valentinus and Apollinaris and to follow their blasphemies unalterably. He neither respected our exhortation and teaching nor wished to consent to the correct doctrines [Note: witness 1 has *docmatibus*, an orthographic form of *dogmatibus*].

Therefore, lamenting his complete destruction [Note: witness 1 reads *perdictionem*, “destruction,” for *perditionem*], we have decreed, through Jesus Christ our Lord [Note: witness 2 abbreviates “our Lord Jesus Christ”], whom he has blasphemed, that he is excluded from every priestly office, from our communion, and from the primacy of the monastery.

Let those who afterward speak with him or come to him know that they too will be liable to the penalty of excommunication if they do not avoid his conversations.”

### 43

Likewise, the practices or customs that arose concerning Ratherius, bishop of Verona, and concerning Peter, archbishop of Ravenna, have been abolished by everyone.

Each man had received a successor without presenting a document of abdication or laying aside the insignia of the priesthood: Ratherius received Milo, and Peter received Honestus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Apollinaris.

The lord Pope John, surnamed Bonus, saw Honestus, who had first been presented to him for consecration, before he learned of Peter’s deposition, whether by report or by rumor.

The law and custom, or ceremonial practice, of deposition was therefore brought forward from the Council of Toledo, chapter 28:

### 44

If a bishop, presbyter, or deacon is unjustly removed from his rank and is found innocent at a second synod, he cannot remain what he was unless he recovers the rank he lost from the hand of the bishops before the altar.

If he is a bishop, he shall receive the stole, ring, and staff; if a presbyter, the stole and chasuble; if a deacon, the stole and alb; and likewise the other ranks shall receive, for their restoration, those things that they had received when they were ordained [Note: witness 1 reads *eas*, “those,” instead of *ea*, “those things”; witness 1 also reads *qui* instead of *quae*]. [Column 0331B]

### 45

From this sentence it was therefore understood that whatever each person had received at his promotion, he ought to return at his deposition.

At his promotion Arnulf had received a ring and staff, as well as a certain kind of stole which, by distinction, is called a *palleum* [Note: witness 2 reads *pallium*, “pallium”]. He therefore ought to return these things.

Nor would this act prejudice the Roman primate, since Arnulf had not appealed to him, nor had any necessity of deposition been imposed upon Arnulf. Moreover, when the Roman bishop was summoned by the bishops and the ruler, he had refused to answer, although he ought rather, as executor of the sacred canons, both to condemn the guilty by his own authority and to urge on the bishops who were delaying judgment, just as Gregory did with the bishops of the Council of Bizacium concerning the crime of their primate.

Likewise, the decree concerning Potamius, archbishop of Braga, was established as valid by the law and custom of the Council of Toledo. It was as follows: [Column 0331C]

### 46

“We might have taken up the canonical flute in a song of fraternal joy, because divine mercy had summoned our assembly to the pursuit of concord. We might have been obliged to avoid grief, since through the visitation of discipline we appeared to have renewed the rules of our fathers.

Yet we take up a heavier sistrum instead of a cymbal [Note: witness 2 reads *cimbalo*, “cymbal”], and sing a funeral instead of a song. Mourning, we say with Jeremiah’s lamentations: ‘The joy of our heart has been dissolved; our chorus [Note: witness 2 reads *corus*] has been turned into mourning’ (Jeremiah 5:15).

Therefore we see woe before us, because we see that the crown of our head has fallen, when so noble a man has collapsed into the lowest condition, although his eminent holiness had stood as the best.

For while we were peacefully discussing ecclesiastical rules, a letter of confused confession and a subscription requiring erasure was brought before our assembly. Potamius, bishop of the church of Braga, had written it concerning his own deeds, in his own words and in clauses written by his own hand.

When it was opened, the sorrowful assembly recounted with tears rather than words what the page that had to be obliterated and the letters that had to be erased disclosed [Note: witness 2 reads *recensuit*, “reviewed,” instead of the corrected reading *resensuit*, “recounted”].

Then, after the bishops of God had been gathered together in solitude and secrecy, we caused the aforesaid bishop to appear before us. We confronted him with sobs more than with words and placed before him the document that disclosed his deformity and our disgrace [Note: witness 2 has the possibly corrupt form *deformidatis*].

He took it and read it again. When we asked whether it contained a statement of his own work and his own writing, he asserted that what he saw there upon rereading was the work of his own action, the speech of his own mouth, and the authority of his own fingers.

Again, calling him to account by an oath invoking the divine name, we adjured him to state truthfully whether he was voluntarily speaking a lie about himself or was being pressed by someone’s violence and, terrified, recounting such things.

He immediately cried out in a mournful voice, his eyes wet with tears, amid weeping and the crashing of sobs [Note: witness 2 reads *pl. m.*—probably *ploratu multo*, “with much weeping”], swearing by the name of the one God that he truly confessed these same evils about himself [Note: witness 1 reads *vera*, “true,” instead of *vere*, “truly”] and that no violence had forced him to confess them.

He further declared that for nearly nine months he had voluntarily abandoned the governance of his church and had shut himself up in a kind of prison to perform penance for the crime he had committed.

Then, through his faithful confession, the admission was disclosed that he had been defiled by sexual contact with a woman.

Although the ancient rule of our fathers decreed that he should be removed from his honor, we, nevertheless preserving the rights of mercy, did not take away the name of honor that he himself had already taken from himself by confessing his crime. Instead, by firm authority we decreed that he should serve perpetual penance in duties and hardships.

We judged it better that he should travel through the harsh solitude of penance and eventually reach a dwelling of refreshment than that, left to the freedom of his own will, he should be cast headlong into eternal damnation. [Column 0332B]

Then, by the common election of us all, we appointed the venerable Fructuosus, bishop of the church of Dumium, to retain the governance of the church of Braga. He was to assume the care of the entire metropolitan province of Galicia, of all its bishops and public assemblies, and of all the souls entrusted to the church of Braga, and was to arrange and preserve everything in such a way that he would glorify our Lord through the uprightness of his work and provide us joy through the church’s safety.

But since it is fitting to look to the future, lest some disturbance of litigation arise in a state of peace, our vigilance has undertaken to attach to this decree the sentence of the Fathers that condemns the aforesaid Bishop Potamius for the sake of rectitude.

‘From the Council of Valencia, title 4.’ [Column 0332C]

Nor did we judge it foreign to the usefulness of the church to write this, brothers, so that you might know that whoever, under ordination to the diaconate, presbyterate, or episcopate, says that he has been polluted by a mortal crime must be removed from the aforesaid orders—liable either through the truth of his confession or through the lie of falsehood.

For he cannot be absolved in these matters if he says of himself what would be punished if said of others. Since everyone who is the cause of his own death is a greater murderer.”

Many other sentences could indeed have been attached to this decree, requiring that the aforesaid Bishop Potamius be expelled with the utmost severity. But from all of them we preferred to insert this one written sentence [Note: witness 1 has an abbreviated reading meaning “we preferred to place”], lest, if we repeated so many decrees of condemnation, we should appear to be authors of an excessively severe punishment.”

### 47

After the removal of this Potamius, the depositions of the archbishops of Reims, Egidius and Ebo, appeared valid both by law and by custom. [Column 0332D]

Since this had been done for the third time without being censured, and had moreover been handed down in eternal memorials, they judged that it should have the force of law and custom.

They did not consider it proper that any bishop, at his deposition, should be mutilated in the Roman manner, since this was supported neither by law nor by any custom found recorded in historical memorials.

Following the African council, therefore, they decided to spare Arnulf’s modesty, both on account of the church’s disgrace and on account of the insolent attacks of secular people, so that priestly dignity would not be polluted and so that he might not perhaps be publicly convicted of the matters concerning which he had been and was still to be accused. [Column 0333A]

They therefore judged that a document of his deposition should be dictated, written before him at his command, confirmed by his own hand, and attested by a confession in his living voice, so that his abdication would not appear to have been sought, unwilling, or extorted, since a man entangled in so many crimes could not stand at the sacred altars.

If a bishop weakened in body can receive a successor after presenting a document of abdication, according to Gregory, then much more can a man who is dead to God in soul receive a successor after presenting a document of abdication.

They further added that if these matters were determined in such a ceremonial and solemn manner, this judgment could not be renewed at all. They held that this was confirmed by the Council of Antioch, chapter 15: [Column 0333B]

### 48

“If a bishop accused of a criminal offense has received one harmonious and unanimous sentence from all the bishops who are within the province, he cannot afterward be judged by others. The sentence pronounced by all must remain in force and be held firm and ratified concerning him, as one that was properly agreed upon.”

When these matters had been settled, they then departed [Note: witness 2 omits *tum*, “then”].

### 49

On the following day, while the bishops were seated [Note: witness 2 abbreviates *consedentibus*] in the basilica of the lord Basil the Confessor and the entire clergy had been assembled in due order, a few civil matters but many ecclesiastical affairs were discussed.

Again Arnulf of Reims returned to their memory. Since his case was now being treated not as a defense but chiefly as a complaint, some pitied him because of his lineage and others because of the flower of his youth. Yet the bishops were more deeply provoked by the ruin of their brother and the disgrace of priestly dignity. [Column 0333C]

Each person measured his downfall by his own circumstances and believed that he would be freed from infamy if the man who was being publicly accused were free of crimes [or would be endangered if he lost his case; this sentence is absent in witness 1].

### 50

But while they prolonged these complaints, behold, the kings of the Franks, together with the leading men of the palace, entered the sacred assembly.

They thanked the bishops for having demonstrated their devotion with complete faith by deliberating so long for the safety of the rulers. They praised them because they had not only withdrawn from the conspiracy of wicked men but had also shown by their own efforts that they had been inwardly alien to it.

At the same time, they asked that the sequence of events be briefly explained and that they be told at what conclusion the matter had come to rest. [Column 0333D]

### 51

Father Arnulf said:

“It ought not to be attributed to us that which it is clear we have not deserved. Although it is always necessary to deliberate for your safety, we devoted this entire period to the safety of our brother, who had been placed in danger.

If the matter was not brought to the outcome we desire [Note: witness 2 reads *voluimus*, “we desired,” instead of *volumus*, “we desire”], this was certainly not done out of love and goodwill toward you or hatred of him, but because of the difficulty of the case. If any resemblance of a defense had appeared in the charges, we would have brought forth powerful mechanisms of argument and the strongest darts of our sentences for his protection. [Column 0334A]

Such compassion moved us; such fervor of charity set us ablaze. In the end, we not only sharpened those who were prepared to defend him on his behalf, but also compelled those who appeared to attack him to hesitate before our anathema [Note: witness 2 reads *vestro*, “your,” instead of *nostro*, “our”].

Thus, numerous sentences of the Fathers were pronounced on both sides, but he received no help from any of them.

He was also brought into the midst and questioned. At first he denied everything, but when the forms of the charges were presented to him one by one, he had to confess what was known to have been done publicly.

Since from what he confessed there followed the very matters he had denied, he also brought into question those matters which he had tried hardest to conceal.

While he was caught in these evasions, he was advised to consider his own interests. Asking for a withdrawal, he led the bishops into the more remote regions. There, while it was thought that they were going to discuss the character of his purgations, his conscience urging him on, he suddenly burst into a confession of his sins and left everyone present astonished. [Column 0334B]

Although the bishops promised him safety and assured him that he would suffer nothing serious if he dispelled the adverse rumors [Note: witness 2 reads *aversos*, “hostile,” instead of *adversos*, “adverse”], he nevertheless persisted in confessing against himself and requested to be deprived of the priesthood.

Some of the abbots and many of the clergy were present at this confession and will remain witnesses of Arnulf’s secrets for long ages.

But if it pleases you, let him be brought into the presence of everyone and, before the multitude, let him himself, as both witness and judge, set forth his case and at the same time free the accusers, witnesses, and judges from reproach, bearing the role of all of them in his own person.”

[Column 0334C]

### 52

When he entered with the entire people, after a brief silence had been called, Father Arnulf addressed Arnulf:

“Do you see that everyone’s face is turned toward you alone? Why do you not speak for yourself?”

Since he was uttering poorly arranged words and could scarcely be understood, Father Arnulf said:

“Are you still of the opinion in which we left you late yesterday?”

“I am,” he replied.

“Do you wish to abdicate the honor of the priesthood, which you have until now abused?”

And he replied:

“As you say.”

Then Count Brochard said:

“What does this mean—‘as you say’? Let him speak openly; let him confess openly, so that afterward he may not claim that the bishops fabricated whatever crimes they wished, or deny that he confessed them.”

And he replied:

“Openly I say and profess that I have erred and have deviated from royal fidelity. But I ask you to believe Lord Arnulf, who is speaking for me, and in your presence I myself beseech him—since he knows my circumstances and since it pleases him—to set forth my case in that manner.” [Column 0334D]

Father Arnulf said:

“He is by nature silent, and moreover he is ashamed to confess openly the things that he committed and that, under Christ’s testimony, he entrusted to our faith to be concealed.

Let it be enough for you to know this much: he publicly confesses that he did not at all preserve the oaths that he publicly gave to his kings [Note: absent in witness 1], and that he publicly acted against his profession and the subscription he made in the form of a written bond.” [Column 0335A]

Count Brochard said:

“It is not enough for me unless he openly admits or openly denies, under your testimony, that he committed a betrayal, so that another person may have free opportunity to succeed in his place.”

Father Arnulf replied:

“Indeed, today you will not be equal to the priests, to whom alone a pure confession is owed.

Suppose that one of the soldiers were accused before the king of the stated crime, but denied that offense while confessing that he had sinned in other matters to such an extent that he could possess neither an estate nor a benefice, and pleaded for nothing but his life.

If, I say, his estate or benefice were offered to you by royal generosity, would you refuse to accept it? What difference does it make among all deadly crimes whether someone is punished for murder, adultery, or poisoning?

Therefore, let it be enough for you that he has disclosed his sins to us through confession, that he publicly declares himself unworthy of the priesthood, and that he confesses before the kings and in the sight of the church that he sinned in such a way that he is worthy of no honor in this world.

For it does not appear relevant whether he deprives himself of the priesthood on account of this crime or that one.”

### 53

Then, turning to Arnulf, he said: “What do you say to these things that I have said on your behalf up to now?”

“I say and profess,” he replied, “that it is so, just as you have said.”

“Prostrate yourself, then,” said Father Arnulf, “before your lords and before your kings, whom you have inexpiably offended; confess your own guilt and plead for your life.”

When he had prostrated himself in the form of a cross and pleaded for his life and limbs with all the lamentation he could summon, he moved the entire synod to tears and sighs. Immediately Daibert, archbishop of Bourges [Col. 0335C], throwing himself at the feet of the princes, offered the most humble prayers of all for the man’s safety. They, moved by compassion, said: “Let him live by your favor and remain under our custody, fearing neither sword nor chains—unless perhaps he places his hope in flight.”

This statement did not please the bishops sufficiently, since they thought that the young man could easily be persuaded to flee, and that for this reason he would again become subject to the laws of death. They therefore repeated their prayers and again obtained [Note: [Col. 0335] “they repeated” in witness 1], that the young man should not be struck by the sword unless he should again commit some deed worthy of an avenging sword.

Thus lifted from the ground and fearing nothing serious any longer, he waited in astonishment for his deposition. He was therefore asked whether he wished his abdication to be solemnly carried out on the authority of the canons. When he had entrusted this to the authority of the bishops [Col. 0335D], he was persuaded to descend by degrees from the summit of honor to which he had risen by degrees.

He therefore resigns to the king what he had received from the king [Note: [Col. 0335] “which” in witness 2]; and he also lays down before the bishops the insignia of priestly dignity—not because they were demanding them or wished to retain them, but because they intended to preserve them for those to whom the matter would belong in the future. Then he asks that a document of his abdication be written according to the model of the abdication of his predecessor Ebo; and, once it had been written, he reads it aloud in the midst of the assembly as follows:

### 54

“I, Arnulf, formerly archbishop of Reims [Col. 0336A], recognizing my frailty and the weight of my sins, have appointed as witnesses and confessors of my sins—and as judges of my offenses—Siguin, archbishop; Daibert, archbishop; Arnulf, bishop; Gotesmann, bishop; Herveu, bishop; Ratbod, bishop; Gualter, bishop; Bruno, bishop; Milo, bishop; Adalbero, bishop; Odo, bishop; Guido, bishop; and Heribert, bishop. To them I gave a pure confession, seeking a remedy through repentance and the salvation of my soul, so that I might withdraw from the office and ministry of the pontificate, of which I recognize myself to be unworthy, and that I might render myself alienated on account of my crimes, in which I confessed privately to them that I had sinned [Note: [Col. 0335] absent in witness 2], and concerning which I was publicly accused [Col. 0336B]. This I did in such a way that they might be witnesses to another person’s succeeding to and being consecrated in my place—one who might worthily preside over and benefit the Church, over which I have hitherto presided unworthily. And so that thereafter I might be able, by canonical authority, to make no further claim or appeal, I have confirmed this by signing it with my own hand.”

After it had been read, I signed it in these words: “I, Arnulf, formerly archbishop, have signed.”

The bishops present were witnesses to this document of Arnulf; when he asked them to sign it, they signed, and they said to him individually: “According to your profession and signature, cease from office.” After this he released the clergy and the people from the bond of their oaths, so that everyone would have free opportunity to pass over into the rights of another.

### 55

When these matters had been solemnly completed, behold, the priest Adalger [Col. 0336C] prostrated himself at the feet of the kings and complained that he was being deprived of communion because he had obeyed the command of his lord and archbishop, whom it was not permissible to resist.

Father Arnulf said to him: “Did you open the gates of the city [Note: [Col. 0335] “of the city” in witness 2] to the enemy?”

He replied: “I opened them.”

Father Arnulf said: “Did you enter the temple of God in a hostile manner?”

Then the priest said: “I cannot deny it.”

Father Arnulf said: “From your own mouth I judge you. Your blood be upon your own head!”

Bishop Gualter added: “When a commanding bishop has been punished in this way, you, who obeyed and carried out his orders with your own hands, shall pay the penalty that follows.”

Father Bruno said: “You and those like you destroyed the young man through evil counsels and evil actions. Are you therefore to sing while he weeps? Or how shall I restrain my complaints if those who have cast my uncle’s son into these miseries suffer no punishment?”

Accordingly, the priest was ordered to choose what he preferred: either perpetual anathema or lawful deposition from his office. For he had come voluntarily, on the condition that he suffer no violence. After deliberating with himself for a long time, he preferred to be deposed rather than remain under perpetual anathema.

The bishops, however, moved by no pity toward him, dressed him in priestly vestments. Then, without reverence, they removed from him one item after another down to the subdiaconate, adding each time, individually: “Cease from office!” [Col. 0337A] Thereafter, through a lawful reconciliation to the laity, they granted him communion only and subjected him to penance.

But those sacrilegious men and betrayers of the city who had come neither voluntarily nor under compulsion to make satisfaction, they condemned again by anathema. After this the council was solemnly concluded.

**THE SYNOD OF REIMS ENDS** [Note: [Col. 0337] “of Pope Girbert” in witness 1].

### 56

**Here begins the Council of Carthage of the African bishops, joined by Girbert to the preceding synod, insofar as material from it was useful** [Note: [Col. 0337] “The African Council of Carthage VI, held in the year 457 of the era, by 217 bishops” in witness 2].

In this council it was arranged that the Council of Nicaea should be requested from the eastern bishops. A legation of the Roman Church attended that synod, namely Bishop Faustinus and the priests Phylippus and Asellus.

1. Address of the holy Bishop Aurelius to the synod [Col. 0337B].
2. Response of Faustinus, bishop and legate of the Roman Church, concerning matters established partly by canon and partly by custom.
3. Concerning the reading of the memorandum of the Roman pope.
4. Response of Pope Alippius concerning the search for authentic copies of the Council of Nicaea [Col. 0338A].
5. Where Bishop Faustinus said that the synod’s search for the truth of the Nicene synod should be reported to the Roman pope.
6. Concerning the sentence of the Council of Sardica, read aloud by the petitioner, Bishop Novatus.
7. Where Bishop Augustine promises, together with the synod, to preserve the Council of Nicaea.
8. Where Bishop Faustinus requests that the Roman pope be written to because of uncertainty about the chapter that was read.
9. Where the synod decreed that copies of the Council of Nicaea should be sought especially from the eastern bishops.
10. Profession of the faith of the Council of Nicaea.
11. Letter of the African council to Boniface, bishop of the city of Rome.
12. Reply of the bishops of Rome, Alexandria, and Constantinople, sent to the African synod together with copies of the Council of Nicaea [Col. 0338B].
13. Letter of the African council to Celestine, bishop of the city of Rome.

We have omitted the text of the Council of Carthage.

[Col. 0337]

## Letter of Leo, abbot and legate [Note: [Col. 0337D] I found it written in a contemporary hand in the royal Brussels codex marked no. 503, formerly a parchment manuscript of the Abbey of the Golden Valley of St. Mary, tenth century, fol. 219 and following; see [Col. 0338D] *Archivum*, VII, 812. Since it is relevant to the history of Arnulf and Gerbert, I present it here, copied by the distinguished scholar Ludovic Bethmann.]

**To Hugh and Robert, kings.**

(Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. III, p. 686.)

[Col. 0337C] **L.** [Note: [Col. 0337] That is, Leo.]

After we sent our legate from Mouzon to your charity, so that the case of Arnulf and Gerbert might be brought to an end canonically, with the fear of God and according to rule, within your kingdom, on the holy day of Pentecost a document was brought [Note: [Col. 0337] “carried,” “brought,” or “presented” should perhaps be read] to us containing the proceedings of your synod held against Arnulf—or rather, against the Roman Church—wholly filled with insults and blasphemies.

When we saw it, stunned with amazement and astonishment, we immediately considered returning to the apostolic lord and carrying that apostate document to him. But when you reported to me that you wished to settle everything canonically, we were compelled to come and learn the truth of this matter.

For, to speak more truly to your charity, the prophecy of the blessed apostle and evangelist John has come to pass in you. He says: “Many antichrists have arisen; hence we know that it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18). And what is the Antichrist except one who is opposed to Christ?

Behold, Christ, who is truth and could not lie, said that the Church of the blessed apostle Peter is the foundation of all the churches. And where ought we to hope to find the summit of the Church, except where its foundation has been placed? There, without doubt, remain both the summit and the whole Church.

But your antichrists say that there is a marble statue there and that it is a temple of idols. Far be it, far be it that any Christian should willingly hear this insult against Peter—or rather against Christ—and that his heart should not be inflamed by zeal for God against such heresy!

And because the vicars of Peter and his disciples do not wish to have as their teacher Plato, or Virgil, or Terence, or the other beasts among the philosophers, who, flying proudly like birds through the air, plunging into the depths like fish through the sea, and walking like cattle upon the earth, described these things—you say that they ought not even to be doorkeepers, because they have not been imbued with such poetry.

In this matter, know that those who said such things have lied. For Peter knew nothing of such matters, and he was made the doorkeeper of heaven when the Lord himself said to him: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:19). Therefore his vicars and disciples were instructed in apostolic and evangelical teachings, not in ornament of speech but in the reason and meaning of words; for it is written: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27).

From the beginning of the world, God did not choose orators and philosophers, but the unlettered and the rustic. Yet it is no wonder if the vicars of Peter hear from pseudo-bishops what he himself heard from the scribes and Pharisees, who, to his insult, said that he was “uneducated” [Note: [Col. 0339] “thus” in witness c.] and without learning, and who mocked them by saying: “These men are full of new wine” (Acts 2:13).

For this reason the prophet Joel rebuked their blindness [Col. 0339B], saying among other things: “Indeed, upon my male servants and upon my female servants I will pour out my spirit” (Joel 2:28)—not upon scribes and Pharisees or false priests, who say that they know God but deny him by their deeds.

And since you have accused the Roman pontiff because he accepted gifts offered to him [Note: [Col. 0339] “accounts” in the manuscript], by this you have disparaged not only him but all the apostles and their successors, indeed the Lord himself, who is the head of all the churches, because he likewise did not reject gifts offered to him.

Moreover, since in your council you took care to mention pontiffs who had already died—a practice contrary to everything Christian, namely, rashly judging those who have departed to God—you will be able to find the relevant matter in the second chapter of Pope Anastasius’s letter addressed to the emperor Anastasius [Col. 0339C], and you will more easily recognize how contrary to proper order you have acted.

Thus it is clearer than daylight that you have separated the Roman Church, your mother, from yourselves, since you did not fear to write such an insult against it. Therefore such profane and perverse words against the Roman Church have never proceeded from a pious heart or mouth.

Nevertheless, if the words written in contempt of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles—or rather of God, whose ordinance you resist—and composed as though to disparage the most sacred Church were indeed yours, I confess that you had not diligently read the sacred rules, the acts of the venerable synods, or the canons of truthful and approved men, when you attempted so uselessly [Col. 0339D] and improperly to introduce such matters in disparagement of the Roman Church.

Finally, if Ham, the son of Noah, saw his father’s nakedness, mocked him, and did not cover it, he is said to have received an everlasting curse. How much more, then, those who not only fail to cover their spiritual fathers but, by mocking them and falsely provoking people to derision [Note: [Col. 0339] “from” in the manuscript], incite others according to their own custom! For it is written: “The eye that mocks a father and scorns obedience to a mother” and what follows (Proverbs 30:17).

Knowing this, Archbishop Athanasius and all the bishops of Egypt, the Thebaid, and Libya, when they sought counsel against the heretics from the holy pontiff Felix—now a martyr—who at that time was regarded by men like you as an invader, received it by God’s will. They sought what concerned them; what did not concern them they left to God; and they remained silent about disparaging the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0339] “concerning the petition” in witness c.].

There was a certain Dioscorus, archbishop of Alexandria, whose example you have imitated. He presumed to write against Pope Leo and against the Roman Church. But the holy Fathers at Chalcedon detested his presumption to such an extent that they condemned him without any restoration.

They did not investigate whether Dioscorus had dictated anything against the Roman Church justly or unjustly, or in any manner whatsoever; without controversy, they avenged this in him because, although he was inferior, he had attempted to assail his predecessor and teacher with insults. They wished, certainly, that nothing confused and nothing disorderly should occur in the house of God.

Yet Father Arnulf thought little of these matters when he and his—who knows what—apostate son [Note: [Col. 0339] Gerbert is meant, later the supreme pontiff, who at that time apparently had not yet acknowledged himself to be the writer of the Synod of Reims] dared to write so much against the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0339] “to write” in the manuscript]—things which even the Arian heretics had never presumed to write (above, Council of Basle, no. 28).

Certainly it is written that poisonous children are born from poisonous parents. Against this the most blessed Pope Boniface says: “No one has ever boldly raised his hands against the apostolic dignity, whose judgment may not be reconsidered; no one has rebelled in this matter except one who wished to be judged concerning himself.”

For even if the Roman Church has sometimes faltered in some matter, with the help of the apostle Peter it has raised itself up and has always given assistance to all the churches. It itself, however, has never sought assistance from another—not by its own strength, but by the assistance of God, who said to Peter: “And you, once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32).

These privileges, then, of the Roman Church, as the blessed Pope Nicholas testifies, were granted by Christ, not by synods, which merely celebrated and venerated them. They cannot in any way be diminished, broken, or changed, because no human effort can remove the foundation that God laid; and what God established remains firm and strong.

The one who attempts to resist God’s ordinance is, above all, the one who sins. These privileges of the Roman Church can be struck, but they cannot be transferred; they can be dragged, but they cannot be torn out: they remain undefiled [Note: [Col. 0339] “thus” in the manuscript]. As long as the Christian name is preached, they will not cease to endure, unimpaired [Note: [Col. 0339] “mutilated” in the manuscript].

And since you have set the canons against the Roman Church, hear what Gelasius, destroyer of many heresies, says in the memorandum given to Faustus, the master who was feigning a legation to Constantinople. Among other things he says:

“They bring forward the canons against us, although they do not know what they are saying. They reveal themselves to be transgressors of the very canons because they refuse to obey the first see when it gives sound and upright counsel.

“The canons themselves decreed that appeals from the whole Church should be brought before the judgment of this see, while they established that no appeal should be made from it anywhere at all. Thus they ordained that it should judge the whole Church, that it should go before no judgment, and that it should never be judged by any judgment; nor ought its sentence to be annulled.”

And since you wrote whatever you were able to vomit forth in disparagement of the Roman Church, while secretly withholding what constitutes its honor and glory, you hid the medicine of the soul and displayed the poison by which you might kill the unwary and the simple.

Indeed, whatever Aurelius, Augustine, Alippius, and the other bishops established in Africa sent to Pope Boniface by way of inquiry, as sons to fathers, you set forth insolently and arrogantly. But you did not wish to say that, because of the tribulation and distress threatening him from Eulalius—who had been ordained on the same day as the aforesaid Boniface, had always been in opposition to him, and lived for three years and five months—he was entirely unable to write to them, as Pope Celestine testifies.

You also did not wish to display the letter of the aforesaid Pope Celestine, which praised them and embraced their opinion concerning free will [Note: [Col. 0341] “judgment” in the manuscript], while reproving the fact that the eastern churches had been consulted about the Council of Nicaea. For during thirty years and more the eastern heretics had so devastated the eastern churches that they left almost no book on the Catholic faith which they had not falsified or burned.

Moreover, only a few people were able to conceal the written creed of the Council of Nicaea. For this reason many of the aforementioned eastern churches asked the Roman Church to have that creed written out for them. Archbishop Athanasius of Alexandria, who had attended the Council of Nicaea while still a deacon, sent a supplication to Pope Mark asking that it be written out for him.

And since, later, in the time of Constantius and Julian, that pestilential disease reached the Roman Church itself—which is the head of all the churches—the aforementioned Celestine, gathering together in one place the aforesaid synod as well as the decrees of the pontiffs dispersed among various Roman churches, especially those of Pope Miltiades, sent back to Aurelius the same things that Isidore reports [Note: [Col. 0341] “asserts” in witness c.]. But by remaining entirely silent about these matters, you concealed them [Note: [Col. 0341] “you concealed it” in the manuscript].

As for the Council of Antioch about which you wrote: if it was held with legates of the Roman Church, they themselves held primacy there as judges; and, as in all synods, they signed, and they confirmed Pope Leo’s letter addressed to them as though it were the Gospel.

But if, as you have heard, they inflicted punishment upon Dioscorus, patriarch of Antioch, I beseech you by God, do not conceal it, because God is truth, and whoever conceals the truth certainly denies God.

And since you disparaged the blessed Gregory, saying that he did not inquire into the deposition of bishops, consider rationally and establish that in his time he had either his defensor, notary, subdeacon, or vicar, as you will be able to find in his life; this representative arranged and administered everything in his place, praising and confirming what they did rightly, and correcting and amending what they did disorderly.

Thus he restored to Bishop Menne, after he had cleared himself in his presence, both the dignity of his honor and the grace of communion [Col. 0342B]. Similarly, he had Bishop Januarius and Bishop Stephen heard and restored to their order through his defensor John.

Indeed, he restored not only bishops but also priests who had been irregularly deposed [Note: [Col. 0341] “placed” in witness c.]—restoring them likewise to their order and dignity. You can find these matters partly in his life and partly in his register.

Thus you brought Pope Nicholas forward as a witness for your cause, because he had remained silent against the Roman Church in the deposition of bishops. How sternly he acted against Photius, the invader of the Church of Constantinople, until he restored Ignatius to his own see, you can find in his letters.

Also consider more carefully how stern he was at the Synod of Metz against kings and bishops in excommunicating and refusing to reconcile them. It has always been characteristic of the Roman Church to justify the just, condemn the impious, expel enemies, and refresh its children.

And since you reproached it because the eastern, African, and Spanish churches had separated themselves from it, recognize that in this you spoke falsely. For now Theodore, archbishop of Egypt, and Orestes of Jerusalem sent their legates to the apostolic lord in the preceding year [Note: [Col. 0341] “they sent” in witness c.; “they sought” in the manuscript], asking his counsel whether converts from the heresy of the Jacobites ought to enter the clergy. Since, moreover, through fear of the Saracens they could not consecrate an altar in any church, they asked that they be permitted to consecrate a cloth for them.

Likewise, from Africa, the clergy and people of Carthage, in the time of Pope Benedict VII [Col. 0342D], chose a certain priest named James and sent him to Rome so that he might be consecrated there. The letter he brought with him contained, among other things, the following:

“To the most blessed lord and apostolic pope, the clergy and people of Carthage, a city protected by God.

“We ask your Blessedness to come to the aid of the wretched and desolate city of Africa, which has been reduced to such nothingness that, where once it was a metropolis, scarcely any priests are now found. And just as our predecessors fled to your predecessors, so now we, however few and unworthy, flee to you. Therefore we have sent you the priest James, so that by ordaining him for us you may provide us consolation.”

The aforesaid pontiff sent him to our monastery until his Catholic faith could be tested. When he found him orthodox, he consecrated him archbishop and sent him back to his own people with a privilege.

Likewise from Spain, in the time of Pope John, the son of Alberic—whom you unjustly disparaged—Julian, archbishop of Córdoba, sent a letter with legates concerning many and very difficult matters, asking counsel. He did not inquire who or what sort of man the pope was, but, showing veneration to the apostolic see, sought what was useful to him.

From this, recognize that the Roman Church is still honored and venerated by all the churches, and that only you disparage and dishonor it [Note: [Col. 0343] “honor it” in witness c.].

You say that you entrusted the matter to God, not to the apostolic pope, and that he gave you no answer. It is known to everyone that, in such tribulation and oppression from Crescentius, he was placed in such circumstances that he could give no answer to you or to anyone else, whenever and however he wished [Col. 0343B]. Nevertheless, as soon as he could, he sent us to investigate and inquire into your case.

But when we arrived at Aix, we found him already deposed, and we could obtain no answer from you [Col. 0344A]. When we had returned home, the apostolic lord invited you to Rome; yet you did not wish to come to him [Note: [Col. 0343] Compare Hugh’s letter to the pope from the Lyon codex in the Frankfurt edition of the Synod of Reims, p. 149].

And because, while on the journey, we wrote not as we wished but as we were able, we now return to your synod—a synod honored and praised by you, but corrupted and reviled by all who hear of it.

Who among the faithful can listen with impartial ears to the story of an archbishop deceived through his faith, long tormented in prison, then brought naked and bound, amid a multitude of shouting soldiers, to the synod, and condemned on the testimony of one man?

Who, hearing such things, does not curse your synod? Nor, as your document states, did any of you wish to hear him when he denied three or four times that he was guilty [Note: [Col. 0343] the letter *a* has been worn away]. Instead, you condemned him together with one priest [Col. 0344B]—something prohibited by every authority.

It is forbidden to believe the testimony of a single person against even a layman of no honor or dignity; how much more is this forbidden against an archbishop!

But since you say that he accused and confessed against himself, consider whether such a confession ought to have been accepted. For, as your document records, you said to him: “Ask forgiveness so that your life may be granted to you.”

O useless confession! It was as though he had been told: “Unless you say what we want, you will not be able to live.”

Behold, Arnulf, the archbishop, like the patriarch Joseph, captured and thrown into a pit, denied it because he feared death [Note: [Col. 0343] The second manuscript ends here; the following, final page contains certain theological material written in another hand].

[Col. 0343]

# Proceedings of the Council of Mouzon by Gerbert, archbishop

(Ann. 995, June 2.)

[In Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. III, p. 690.]

[Col. 0343C] **Council of Mouzon** [Note: [Col. 0343] “Mouzon” in witness c.]

In the year 995 from the incarnation of the Lord, in the eighth indiction, a synod was announced by Pope John to be held in the parish of the metropolitan church of Reims. Accordingly, on the fourth day before the Nones of June, when the most venerable bishops had assembled at Mouzon—Liudolf of Trier, Aymo of Verdun, Notker of Liège, and Suitger of the city of Minigardevurda—Leo, abbot of the monastery of Saint Boniface in the city of Rome, acting in the place of Pope John, sat among them in the church of Blessed Mary, Mother of God.

In their presence Gerbert, archbishop of Reims, was also present to give an account of his ordination. Abbots of various cities also attended this council, men not undistinguished but eminent among their own people in life, conduct, and learning. Laymen too were admitted, including Count Godefrid and the others [Col. 0344C].

When silence had been established and all who were present had taken their seats, Bishop Aymo rose and preached in French. He said that Pope John had invited the bishops of Gaul to Aachen Palace on account of the synod, but that they had not wished to go there. He had likewise invited them to Rome, but they had not come. Now, out of his concern, he had established a council in the province of Reims and wished, through his vicar, to learn what was being said contrary to him concerning Arnulf’s deposition and Gerbert’s advancement.

After this he produced a letter sealed with lead. Breaking the seal, he read it aloud before everyone. It began as follows:

“John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the archbishops of Gaul: greeting and apostolic blessing, and the rest.”

After the letter had been read, Gerbert, archbishop of Reims, rose and added the following address:

**Exordium:** “Indeed, always …” (see *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXVIII, col. 166), continuing to “we pray together.”

When Gerbert had finished this address, he produced the letter written to Abbot Leo [Note: [Col. 0345] “he handed it over” in the margin], received the pope’s letter, and sat down again.

Then the bishops withdrew from the council and admitted Count Godefrid to their consultations. After this they summoned Gerbert and asked him to arrange for John, the monk of Abbot Leo, to be escorted with every honor to the kings of the Franks; they obtained this request.

Next they announced that a synod was to be held at Reims on the Kalends of July [Col. 0345B]. The synod already seemed to have been dissolved when, behold, Bishop Gerbert [Note: [Col. 0345] “Girbert” in witness c.] received episcopal legates as though from Leo’s party, ordering him to abstain from the divine office until the announced synod.

When he refused, the matter proceeded in Leo’s presence. There he briefly stated that no bishop, patriarch, or apostolic could remove any of the faithful from communion unless that person had voluntarily confessed, had been convicted, or had refused to come to a council.

None of these conditions applied to him, since he had neither confessed nor been convicted, and he alone from Gaul had come to the council. Therefore he would not condemn himself by his own judgment, since he was conscious of no wrongdoing in any of the matters alleged against him.

But after being approached with the moderation and uprightness of Lord Liudolf, archbishop of Trier, and fraternally admonished not to give his rivals an opportunity for scandal—as though he wished to resist the commands of the apostolic lord—he yielded, in the name of obedience, to abstaining only from the celebration of Mass [Col. 0346B] until the approaching Kalends of July, when another synod had been convened. And so they departed.

[Col. 0345]

# Proceedings of the Council of Causey by Gerbert, archbishop

(Year 995.)

[In Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. III, p. 691.]

[Col. 0345C] **Address of the bishops delivered at the Council of Causey in the presence of Leo, abbot and legate of Pope John**

**Exordium.**—Our wishes have been fulfilled, most reverend Fathers, because, with the bishops of all Gaul joined together in charity, the apostolic see presides over our assembly through the venerable abbot and monk Leo.

We are confident that in him, and likewise in us, there is such prudence and uprightness of conduct that we may rejoice that the matters we have demonstrated as probable and necessary have been weighed not on a deceitful and unjust scale, but on an equal and rational balance, in accordance with what blessed Augustine says in the second book *On Baptism*:

“Let us not offer deceitful scales on which we may weigh what we wish and, according to our own judgment, all day long declare: ‘This is heavy; this is light’ [Col. 0345D]. Rather, let us bring the divine scale from the Holy Scriptures, as from the Lord’s treasuries, and weigh on it what is heavier—or rather, let us not weigh it ourselves, but recognize what has been weighed by the Lord.”

Clearly, this holy and wise man seems to understand that sins are to be regarded as greater or lesser not according to human preference but rather according to divine judgment.

For if, by concealing it, we remain silent about any sin, does that mean that the sin is not a sin? Or if we refuse to judge it, is it therefore less before the eyes of the divine majesty? No.

Therefore, venerable fathers and brothers, weigh what ought to have been judged by us in the case of Arnulf. It was evident that before the eyes of God and men he had fallen into an enormous abyss, since he condemned himself with his own mouth, and because, on account of his rebellion and obstinacy, the African councils had deprived him of every right [Col. 0346C].

Consider, I say, what could have been done more suitably and beneficially for the salvation of the perishing people, who were exposed to danger throughout the kingdom, than that, once the tyrant had been excluded, a pastor useful to the people and the kingdom should be appointed. This was followed both by the people’s peace and by the stability of the kingdom.

But behold, from the opposite side the enemy of the human race speaks through his instruments: “This could not lawfully be done without the authority of the apostolic see, without the presence of a legate, and only after the Church had been received back from Arnulf.”

### Reproof and Confirmation Arranged Alternately

[Col. 0346D] Is this authority, that an innumerable multitude of people should continually perish? That no Roman should come to their aid, even when invited and earnestly entreated? And that no one may or dares do anything unless a Roman is present? We pass over the difficulties of travel, the lack of funds, and the shortage of a prudent legate; and, once Rome has been reached, the Apostolic See will not be free to deliver its judgment, but only whatever measure of gold can obtain favor with Crescentius, a member of the devil. [Col. 0347A] We are not speaking of unknown matters. The king’s envoys and ours went to Rome, presented letters to the pontiff, and were received by him with due honor. But, as we believe, because they offered no little gifts to Crescentius, they were excluded from the palace for three days, and returned without receiving any reply. There is no doubt that this has come about through our sins: that the Roman Church, which is the mother and head of all churches, should be oppressed by tyranny, and that all its members should be weakened.

These matters, I say, we pass over; yet even amid such great difficulty we show that the sacred laws were obeyed, so that the Apostolic See could neither honorably nor usefully have added or altered anything in Arnulf’s case, nor can it do so now. For if some decrees of the pontiffs are so authoritative, and some councils so confirmed by the Apostolic See, [Col. 0347B] that nothing ought thereafter to be changed, those who carry out these decrees and councils are in every respect worthy of praise and reward, while their disturbers deserve reproach and to be subjected to every kind of punishment.

Again, if under the most blessed pontiffs there occurred cases resembling that of Arnulf, whatever was judged in those cases ought to have been judged in Arnulf’s case. Now Bishop Cresconius, because he was rebellious and contumacious—not against the prince but against the bishops—was judged by the African synod to be restrained by the prince’s power and excluded from the Church. Likewise, that synod judged universally that bishops who conspired together and refused to come to the assembly of their brethren—perhaps fearing that their crimes would be exposed—were to be restrained by the prince’s power, removed from the principal sees, and deprived even of their own sees, by public authority as rebels and by apostolic authority, through the priests Faustinus, Philippus, and Asellus. [Col. 0347C]

What the Apostolic See did in the case of Cresconius, and taught should be done in the case of others, was observed with the greatest care in Arnulf’s case as well. For since he had disdainfully refused, for more than a year, to come to the assembly of his brethren, although repeatedly invited, and since he had additionally proved rebellious against his prince and a traitor to his city and homeland, he was brought before the necessary synod by the prince’s authority. After the inquiry had been held, he was found by his own declaration to be such as he had been reputed to be.

But the rival says: “He could not be judged; let him receive the church, regain his strength and retain his long-held friends, and then let him be summoned to judgment.” What does it mean to remove a tyrant from his arms? Indeed, he could not be judged otherwise than as one stripped of his power. But an equally armed tyrant, surrounded by weapons, could never be brought to judgment. What is the restoration to the Church, the recovery of his strength, and the retention of his friends, except the resurrection of extinguished tyranny against our kings, vengeance for injuries, relief for the wicked, and the oppression of every good person?

“But,” he says, “let him be bound by hostages and by many kinds of oaths.” Can more numerous or stronger oaths be found than those already offered? Can the hostages of his brother Richard be preferred to Bishop Bruno [Col. 0348A] and the son of his sister? By what right, then, will the decree of Pope Boniface be declared void, when he thunders that, if the accused neglects to appear, he is not to gain an extension of the sentence or any advantage from his absence?

Clearly, these apostolic decrees neither protect one who flees nor restore to the Church one who has confessed or been convicted. Therefore, one who has been justly deprived will not receive that church which he governed not as a bishop but devastated like a most savage plunderer. Let the supreme pontiffs Leo and Zosimus, and the great Gregory, say what they established by apostolic authority concerning those who have confessed or been convicted in this way.

“Such persons,” says Leo, “having fallen, are deprived of the Church in order to obtain God’s mercy; they must seek withdrawal, where, if their satisfaction is worthy, it may also be fruitful.”

And Zosimus [Col. 0348B] relates that Lazarus, long before condemned in the Council of Turin by the sentences of very grave bishops as a false accuser, after he had attacked the life of the innocent Bishop Brictius with false accusations, later obtained the priesthood from that same Proculus, who among the others in the synod had consented to his condemnation. Subsequently, conscious of his own life, he voluntarily removed himself from office by submitting a letter of resignation.

And Gregory writes to John, archbishop of First Justiniana:

“Dearest brother, the bearer of this letter, Nemesius, came to us and reported—as the copies of the proceedings that he brought here also contained—that Paul, bishop of the city of Diocletiana, had offered, shortly afterward, a written petition in which he confessed that the charges of which he had been accused were true. Therefore, after he had been deposed by episcopal judgment, it was decided, with the consent of your fraternity, that another should be ordained bishop in his place.”

And Pope John writes to all the churches established throughout Gaul:

“We judge that you should give the aforesaid Bishop Contumeliosus a petition granting him leave to do penance, in which he shall clearly acknowledge his error and publicly make profession on a specified day and under a specified consul.”

“No,” says the accuser, “Arnulf could not condemn himself without a legate of the Apostolic See.” How, then, could Lazarus, Paul, and Contumeliosus do so—and, to come closer to the case in hand, how could Ebo, archbishop of Reims? For if it was not permitted to Arnulf, it was not permitted to them either. But it is clear that it was permitted to them. For it is permitted to abandon evil and do good without a legate and authority of the Apostolic See. [Col. 0348D]

Now it is evil for a criminal to remain in the episcopal order, and good for him to withdraw from it. Arnulf therefore acted well if he withdrew from the episcopal order, in which he could not remain as a criminal. He rightly abandoned what he had obtained by deceit, against divine and human laws.

“Why, then,” says the accuser, “is he detained after being stripped of every power, rather than being allowed to go wherever he wishes?” Evidently because the emperor sent the archimandrite Eutyches, after he had been deposed in a synod; but the great Pope Leo ordered that he be taken to a more remote place, lest the raging disease in him should corrupt others by its contagion.

He is therefore justly detained, since he is still plotting the destruction of his homeland and inciting his followers through frequent embassies not to abandon the fury they have begun. You see, most reverend Fathers, that the apostolic and ecclesiastical laws stand with us.

But what shall we do with wicked men for whom no reasoning is sufficient unless their bodily senses too are satisfied? Let us yield to the importunity of such people and show that nothing was done in Arnulf’s case without the presence of a legate of the Apostolic See.

Certainly, Seguinus, archbishop of Sens, venerable for his life, renewed at Rome the authority of Pope John entrusted to him throughout Gaul. Thus, coming from the side of the Apostolic See with a decree of privilege, he has exercised that authority down to the present with the consent of all the bishops of Gaul.

In his presence, therefore, Arnulf divested himself of the priesthood; and, in accordance with the decrees of the apostolic men Zosimus, Leo, [Col. 0349B] and Gregory, he laid down the priestly insignia after presenting a petition—whether one prefers to call it a petition of confession or, so it may be said, of resignation.

For this are we summoned to judgment, as though we had oppressed an innocent man? We did not oppress him at all; rather, for eighteen months we tolerated him while he contrived wars, seditions, and divisions within the kingdom. Yet the African councils removed him from communion after the second month following his summons, judged that by failing to appear at the annual council he had pronounced the sentence of condemnation upon himself, and ruled that after a year his voice should no longer be heard at all.

But, O Christian faith, O Christian religion! Who will ever be considered guilty if today a traitor to his homeland is acquitted as though innocent? Let the laws henceforth be silent; let the rights of kings be hushed, if no one may be touched by judicial proceedings except one whom the tyrant Crescentius, hired for payment, wishes to acquit or punish. Let the traitor to his homeland receive a reward, and let the man who freed it be driven into exile.

But the Holy Spirit did not sing thus through the mouth of David: “God has spoken once”—that is, unchangeably—“these two things I have heard” (Psalm 61:12): namely, that power belongs to God in condemning the reprobate, and mercy in glorifying [Col. 0350A] the elect. He adds: “For you will render to each according to his works” (ibid. 13)—that is, according to what he is, he says, not according to what he is not. The prophet says: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness” (Isaiah 5:20).

If, therefore, the decrees of the blessed pontiffs Gregory, Leo, and Zosimus, as well as the African councils, are to be regarded as authoritative, then those who murmur that Arnulf was irregularly deposed and accuse our simplicity before the Apostolic See must be censured and utterly disregarded. They act as though we had deposed him because of his innocence when he appealed to the Apostolic See, although in fact he himself fled to judges whom he himself had chosen and, after his confession, requested from them a method of doing penance.

This brings an end to the disputes by the authority of the African council. [Col. 0350B]

### Epilogue

Now we turn to you, Abbot Leo, who exercise the role of Lord Pope John in this synod. If any compassion moves you, we urge you to make the disturbers of peace cease by apostolic authority. They do not strive for Arnulf’s restoration because they have been prompted by zeal for God or fraternal charity; they know that, by the judgment of God and of the universal Church, he has been permanently deprived of the priestly office. Rather, delighted by novelty and by changes in affairs, they incite the holy and apostolic Church against us, so that, when there is no one who dares to oppose them, they may be permitted to sin with impunity.

Your Holiness recognizes how much hatred this brings upon the Roman Church. The judgments of the people are not so blunted that they cannot sometimes understand what is more equitable and just. When any bishops rashly resist this matter, the gravity and dignity of the priesthood are discredited through our fault.

Through you, let the apostolate of blessed Peter join itself to us; through you, let the net of the Church, already torn, be restored, so that when you return to Rome after having brought this matter to a good conclusion, the bishops of Gaul may once again recall you by their hope, desire, and prayer.

The Council of Causeium is concluded.

In the year of the Lord 995–1003. Purchard, monk of Reichenau.

[Col. 0349]

### Historical Notice

(From John Egon, *On the Illustrious Men of Reichenau*, in Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum* I, III, 685.)

Under the flourishing and numerous direction of Witegowo, among others there blossomed forth the monk Burcard, outstanding in talent and eloquence, a serious and excellent poet. Among other works that he wrote, at the command of the Reichenau community he sang in heroic verse of the illustrious deeds of his abbot Witegowo. His poem survives, together with a picture of the monastery prefixed to it, in an ancient manuscript whose beginning is as follows:

“Here begins this text, written in poetic words.”

[Col. 0351]

### Purchard’s Poem on the Deeds of Witegowo, Abbot

(From Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. IV, p. 621.)

### Preliminary Notice

[Col. 0351A] Abbot Witegowo ruled the wealthy monastery of Reichenau after Ruodmann, who was hostile to the people of St Gall, from 985 to 997. [Note: [Col. 0351C] He is called Witego in the catalogue of the abbots of Reichenau, *SS.* II, 38.] Purchard the monk undertook, by decree of the Fathers of Reichenau, to write of his deeds at home and abroad. Begun in 993 or 994 and brought down to that point, he enlarged it in 996 by adding a continuation that briefly touched upon Otto III’s journey to Rome. The book, written in hexameter verse in the form of a dialogue between the Poet and Reichenau, recounts the abbot’s efforts to recover the monastery’s scattered possessions, to build and adorn churches, his journeys undertaken in the king’s service, and his journey to Rome, which it treats only briefly; it also records the privileges brought back from there. Each verse, as we have seen above in the works of Hrotsvit, consists of two parts ending in almost the same sound. [Note: [Col. 0351C] For example, *felix* and *fidelis*, *opibus* and *beatus*, *faceret* and *notarent*, *laudes* and *clemens*, *refers* and *merens* do not correspond exactly to one another.]

The unique manuscript, brought from the library of the monastery of Reichenau to the Karlsruhe library, became known to us through the report of the highly learned and most deserving associate, the distinguished Molter, privy councillor and director of the library. [Note: [Col. 0352C] *Archiv* II, 393. Neugart cites our work from Egon’s *On the Illustrious Men of Reichenau*, ch. 24, in *Episcopatus Constantiensis* I, p. 321, yet he himself did not see the poem.] [Col. 0352A] At the command of His Serene Highness Leopold, Grand Duke of Baden, it was sent to me at my request and will now be reproduced in our edition. It is a parchment autograph in quarto, written in the hand of the late tenth century, corrected here and there by the author himself, and completed toward the end with a somewhat finer pen. The poem is preserved in manuscript no. CCV, formerly so designated, folios 71–84. It follows Alcuin’s questions on Genesis and *Chapters of Propositions for Sharpening the Minds of the Young*, and the interpretation of Solomon’s parables precedes it; the poem fills the reverse part of the first page of that work. But since the book was rebound again a few centuries ago, the order of the pages was disturbed, so that the pages now incorrectly marked with the consecutive numbers 71, 72, 73, and 84 should, as the sequence of the sense shows, be numbered 71, 72, 79, 80, 81, 82, 77, 78, 73, 74, 75, 76, 83, and 84. Of these, 71–78 make up a quire, 79–82 a binion, 83 is half a leaf, and 84 displays on its reverse the beginning of the *Parables*. Now that the proper order has been restored, let us hear our poet.

## On the Deeds of Witegowo, Abbot

[Col. 0351]

[Col. 0351B] To the most reverend senate of the Fathers of Reichenau, possessing the spiritual life in the love of Christ: Purchard, wishing to obey the will of such sublime authority as an inferior in all things.

“Since the whole fountain of wisdom seems to flow forth by derivation from the streams of your hearts and diligently to irrigate the green meadows of your offspring according to apostolic regeneration, I wonder why you should deign to choose me, the most foolish of all these people, who in no way can be compared even with a little flower of withering hay, to write so sublime a work, as appears in what follows.

“But, as I believe your fatherly affection knows, always overflowing with compassion, it grieved you to see me given over to the sleep of laziness and sunk in the depths, never raising myself by urging myself toward the mature studies of others. For that reason, I believe, not because of any expertise in a suitable art but so that some remedy of work might be provided for one idle, you imposed upon me the obedient task of explaining the sequence of the following matters—though it is a master’s command, yet impossible for me, being less eloquent.

“For I wrote, compelled by your command, when and how our venerable lord Abbot Witegowo flourished in this office through the pursuit of virtues; how, at the beginning of his rule, he restored in full our estates, which during the peaceful period of Abbot Ruodmann had been seized by invaders, carried off, and utterly devastated; and with what ardor, burning in the service of God, he established temples of churches, of whatever kind and size, in certain places belonging to us for the celebration of the divine offices, and endowed them most richly from his own resources.

“For whatever he accomplished in this place during the ten years of his administration, beneath the structures of churches, in the varied carvings of arches and columns of different workmanship, and also in altars and crosses fashioned in gold and silver, those precious ornaments adorned with marvelous interweaving of gems, the pen of the writer does not leave untouched. Whatever he is known to have done year by year is individually declared in the completion of each work.

“Accordingly, under a certain designation of place, I have caused a personage to respond to my assertions; and, writing in smoothly flowing hexameter verse, I have striven, with God’s help and your prayers, to complete everything to the end.

“But because I am bound by your command, although I know that I cannot persist through any increase of usefulness, and yet have attempted to expose myself boldly to matters that others of stronger intellect have neglected out of fear, I ask that in these bold undertakings you do not regard the proud estimation of my impudence, but rather the humble intention of one who obeys. [Note: [Col. 0353] *humillam* in the manuscript.] If any fault—of which I do not deny there are many—of hidden defect should appear to you in this little work, deign to correct it quietly, lest it become an obstacle to those who wish to know the truth. [Note: [Col. 0353] End of folio 71. The following page shows how the ‘rustic poet,’ prostrate on the ground, addresses Reichenau, with St Mary the Virgin and the infant Christ present, while Abbot Witegowo and St Pirminius the bishop stand nearby; then he continues: ‘Here begins,’ etc.]”

[Col. 0353] HERE BEGINS THIS TEXT, WRITTEN IN POETIC WORDS:

“May fortunate Reichenau flourish in all the ornaments

Of this structure, which the noble abbot made,

Giving his devotion to Christ, whose name is Witegowo.”

### The Poet

[Note: [Col. 0353] The speaker’s name is absent.] [Col. 0353B]

Tell what has been sought: why do you weep, mother Reichenau,

Originator, by the Lord’s gift, of all good things?

Why do you try to tear out the curls from your head,

Or to lacerate your tender cheeks?

[5] And why, watering your cheeks with tears, do you seem to sit

With downcast face, as though beneath a prison vault?

Why, pious mother, do you lament your years in this way,

Your branches of peace ever green with golden foliage?

Do you wish to appear so ungrateful for the Lord’s gifts,

Or do you remember with what garland of light you shine?

He himself granted you such honor,

A place in the world of which no one boasts.

For, by his piety so disposing it, withdrawn

[Col. 0353C] From all lands, you rest in special peace,

Powerful in freedom, scorning earthly business,

Joined only to the love of the Lord,

Which is believed to be the everlasting glory of freedom.

Burning with devotion in the service of holy Mary,

You yourself are called her worthier bridal chamber on earth;

For the gracious one himself bestowed this special distinction upon you:

him whom the Virgin, inspired by the Holy Spirit, bore.

Why do you not rejoice, overflowing with abundant resources?

Whatever flies above the stars, whatever the wave of the sea supplies,

Whatever the earth produces, is provided for your uses.

### Reichenau

[25] Son, what are you saying? You are a child; you speak childish things.

Why do you falsely claim that I am troubled by empty grief?

My spouse despises me and leaves me alone,

As though captive, supported by no consolation.

### The Poet

If, as is the custom of a child, I now speak childish things,

[30] I must speak them; there is no reason to remain silent.

One must never place confidence in women’s complaints;

But tell the petitioner what it is that seems to cause you contempt.

### Reichenau

I believe such presumption is not in your heart.

Yet, secure in the consolation—I do not know whose—you dare

[35] Send blasphemous words against me.

Still, I do not wonder at this, since, despised by my spouse and left behind,

I am held cheap in the judgment by which all things are valued.

But I am not a woman clamorous with empty complaints;

I wish to submit to the law of perfect faith,

[40] Which apostolic teaching praises beautifully,

Saying: “A man such as cannot be found faithful

Ought to be saved, relying upon a faithful woman” [Note: [Col. 0353D] 1 Corinthians 7:14.]

“And the time will come when my conquered spouse,

Languishing with love for me, will return; and, remaining steadfast,

He will rejoice with me and restore his own joys to his bride.

And you and those like you, mere servants after such great agreements,

Have not dared to challenge me with an insulting voice.”

### The Poet

[Col. 0354C] I live under your authority in servile chains.

If I have deserved it, I ought, at your command, to be struck;

[50] For it is fitting that you yourself should enjoy your own dominion,

And govern what must be governed, rather than an alien power.

### Reichenau

These rights cannot seem alien to me,

Since I myself am powerful, taking up my spouse’s scepters,

If only I were able to keep with me, steadfast,

[55] This teacher radiant with the flower of virtues,

Who shines as my entire sacred love and as the author of my governance;

Without him, therefore, I have no life.

For the more I drink, the more I burn with holy thirst.

### The Poet

[Col. 0354D] Since you have been wounded by the foolish words I poured forth,

[60] My understanding began to diminish with fear,

And, because I am deaf, my ear is not open to what you say.

I beg you, then, do what your mother Wisdom

Advises and commands: let your right hand spare the guilty;

Let correction be sweet to me among the gifts of pardon.

### Reichenau

[65] Be confident, since the virtue of patience

Has taught me to disregard every insult truly [Note: [Col. 0353] That is, *truly*.];

Nor, in adverse circumstances, would the prosperous condition of my mind be absent [Note: [Col. 0353] *prosera* in the manuscript.]

If only my spouse wished to live with me alone,

Continually and steadfastly, never departing from this place.

### The Poet

[70] Trusting in your piety, excellent lady,

I hope to deserve forgiveness for what I have said.

Now I attempt to ask you about matters I do not know.

Tell me: after the death of Ruodmann, your beloved father,

Who increased your endowment with various honors,

But because of his death you wore the garments of widowhood,

Why is it that you now enjoy being joined again in marriage?

Who is he, and how great, whom your fire consumes in this way?

Or when, tell me, I beg you, did you celebrate such a marriage?

What obscure hiding places then held me,

[80] So that I was not permitted to be present at such great festivities?

[Col. 0355B] ### Reichenau

If you wish to know these things, I order you to revisit

The innermost chamber of your mind; let what my speech confirms be revealed to you.

You see me bound by a second marital covenant,

after I had been deprived of my beloved father,

[85] Ruodmann, who, rich in abundant treasure,

Increased my endowments with honor,

So that you may not be surprised when you are warned by the words that follow.

For when men lurking beneath an evil plague perceived

That I had been left alone, without any guardian,

[90] They took up arms against me, since I had no avenger,

Depriving me of my paternal possessions, utterly overturning my fields,

Reducing me to plunder—dreadful to say!

And, laying me low, their savage greed leveled me to the ground,

Me who had once been raised above the stars of heaven.

[95] [Col. 0355C] Captive in their hearts by equal ambition,

They obtained the estates that had been conveyed to me by an ancient written document.

Observing no justice for themselves, they took possession of them.

While they raged with such madness and raged with impunity,

I sat lamenting, staining my breast and hands with blood.

[100] For the increase of grief was the doubling of misfortunes:

The death of my father and the robber’s disastrous plunder.

Yet I endured very much amid so great a loss.

Amid so many calamities, while no defender stood by me

By whom I might overcome such a burden,

[105] My tenants, summoned with troubled hearts,

Came to me [Note: [Col. 0355D] The manuscript punctuates it in this way.] and offered counsel,

Which reason confirmed by clear signs.

For, when I recounted our common hardship,

The losses they had suffered through my misfortunes,

[110] [Col. 0355D] They said: “Mother, use our counsel.

If lawsuits and the furies of war harass you,

And no complete security is available either to you or to us,

Nor any hope of a supporter who might offer consolation,

We desire all the more that you, as we judge more honorably,

[115] Be betrothed to one under whose authority you can be protected,

Rather than remain as food for the gaping robber.

Then our possessions too, made safe by his protection,

Will be guarded for us beneath the flower of the former peace.”

Seeking him, I began to utter these words:

“Tell me, my sons, if a single man can be found

[Col. 0356A] Who lives in this world,

Such and so great, surrounded on every side by virtues,

That I may obtain peace and marry him in a firm covenant,

And that, driving away the enemies who have harmed us until now,

[125] He himself may bear the strength of my former spouse.”

Then the man who now seems to survive was pointed out to me:

A man of great merit, worthy of every praise,

Beloved of Christ, called Lord Witegowo,

Effective in speech, with holy wisdom as his teacher.

[130] Heaven had made him a teacher for the whole world,

And he practices in his deeds all the good things he teaches in words.

No pen of any tongue, no instrument of speech,

Nor any writing that resounds with accounts of blessed deeds,

Can recount how great the piety is

[135] Of this lord and father, who, made the temple of the Holy Spirit,

[Col. 0356B] Is a seat both of divine wisdom and of the Spirit.

Therefore, obtaining such great defenses of counsel,

Through the king’s gift and through the senate of the pontiffs,

I was handed over as spouse to a man chosen for such merits,

[140] Who soon restored all honor to me with a new endowment.

Indeed, under his right authority, my entire left side,

Being weak, could have no power against me,

If only he wished to live at home with me,

As I have just said, ceasing to wander here and there.”

### The Poet

[145] If what has just been said about you is proved true,

You ought now to enjoy yourself more, putting aside your sorrows,

Since this senator remains your protector,

Whose deeds bear such great and such worthy praises.

But those things which you sing with tears and turn over with great lament,

[150] His restless movements and wandering steps—

Unless I am mistaken, I believe, nor do I conceal it in an uncertain mind—

Show that the journey of this man who is departing is not without purpose.

Tell the one who asks where his continual passage is directed;

Let the matter itself immediately prove, through clear reasoning,

The direction in which he travels.
