### Reichenau

My wandering spouse often strikes out in every direction

Along a well-worn road, by various paths and through byways.

More often, look, he keeps frequent course to the king,

Where, delaying for many days,

[160] He rejoices with the king, because the king rejoices with him.

For when Wisdom made him eloquent,

He is said to be the king’s mouth, the beneficial tongue of the peoples,

Shining among the foremost Catholic pillars.

[Col. 0356D] He teaches rulers of kings, counts, and their cohorts.

At the king’s command, everything obeys his words.

No one turns back in opposition to his will;

For all the people proclaim that he is the king’s hand.

Thus delaying there and standing beside the royal scepters,

He does not wish to remember at home the bride he has left behind.

[170] At last, when he slowly leaves the scepter-bearing court,

Returning to his homeland, he finally comes like another guest.

He remains beneath my wings, with loathing in his mind,

Scarcely one night, since the same journey compels him.

From there, his mind is again seized by the desire to depart,

[175] [Col. 0357A] To pray with submissive mind at the apostolic shrines;

He wishes to visit Rome to fulfill his vow.

He delays nothing on the journey, as though always suffering me

To cry out behind him with my customary complaints.

Continuing on his course, he delays for a long time,

And returns only after many days have come to an end.

Coming to me, he says: “Greetings, dearest!”

Then, having said this, he says: “Farewell quickly!”

His first word becomes “Farewell,” before kisses can mark it with “Greetings.”

From there he travels throughout the whole world on various journeys,

Carefully investigating whose heir each tract of land is,

And discovers that many estates are held from me.

Then, making a stay, he sits there properly administering everything

That is recognized to be broken and dissolved,

Restoring deserted seats and ruined buildings.

[190] [Col. 0357B] He gathers the fruits produced by the grassy earth,

Unwilling that uncultivated fields should lie without produce [Note: [Col. 0357] That is, *uncultivated*.]

Thus he always rejoices in the rich fields he possesses.

From their abundant revenues he labors tirelessly,

Seeking that the churches dedicated to the honor of the Lord

Be adorned with varied patterns of metal and gems,

And that he increase them through polished structures.

I shall briefly reveal to you, my son, a little of his zeal.

Purchard the leader [Note: [Col. 0357D] Duke of Alamannia.], a lover of the highest integrity,

Gave us the royal fisc called by the name of Sleitheim [Note: [Col. 0357] In the margin: *Schleytem*, in a sixteenth-century hand.],

For the praise of the Mother who created all things.

Yet, when granting it, he stipulated that it should remain in his possession

During the lifetime of his present wife, and afterward become ours.

Then it remained for many years without serving our needs.

[Col. 0357C] For after the duke himself had ended his life,

[205] His wife [Note: [Col. 0357D] Hadawiga.] possessed it according to the agreement,

And she lived many years afterward in the world.

But when I entered into the rights of the lord who now survives,

It was fitting that, ready with generous gifts, he should serve

Such a matron, descended from a royal line,

[210] Hoping through his efforts to gain such a great return,

So that by entreating her in love

He might join her to himself continually in a firm covenant.

And when she was conquered by his prayers, prompted by his gifts,

She granted him the previously mentioned place under his own rights [Note: [Col. 0357] That is, *her own*.]

Why should I recount many things? He soon came there,

To the walls and all the buildings newly and skillfully prepared,

Which antiquity itself had dismantled in various parts.

The church, neglected in its revenues and buildings, groaned.

Surrounding it and broadly enlarging its grounds,

[220] He made a splendid work, a temple most noble to the Lord,

Adding, behold, every fitting adornment.

Now the ecclesiastical use of its resources

Suffices for the place; let Christ be praised in it.

There is also another village of ours called Funginga,

Beautiful in appearance, fertile in cultivation,

Which the blessed Bishop Pirminius first gave me

[Col. 0358A] As a fixed endowment, when he had begun to love me,

Still a tender girl in my first bloom,

According to the norm of justice, under the love of sobriety.

[230] My husband Witegowo, because of his love for him [Note: [Col. 0358D] Pirminius.],

Loves him so greatly, unless I am mistaken,

That he would put him before me, if fortune and circumstances allowed.

For, as I have said, lamenting that he leaves me behind as before,

He never ceases to remain in that place.

And when he saw a small chapel standing there,

Which the garrulous voice of the common people proclaims to be a memorial

Because of the merit of the venerable bishop who gave it,

So that it might be first among my endowments in due order,

[240] He enlarged this little building on every side

And completed it as a noble, lofty temple.

[Col. 0358B] Around the site he built monastic dwellings,

And added cells suitable for those serving the Lord,

So that they might live here securely, without the world’s turmoil,

Adding from his resources whatever their needs required.

Such a monastery, dedicated to the honor of Christ,

My man Witegowo accomplished through his zeal.

Yet this is only a slight shadow, as it were, of his works;

For his more serious achievements terrify anyone who attempts to speak of them,

Even if he is wise and unfamiliar with such matters.

In many regions, wherever the breadth of the world extends,

The service of the Lord is celebrated with faithful hearts

In the holy houses that he himself, in his goodness, made.

### The Poet

[Col. 0358C] Mother, you tell of marvelous things while grieving in a woman’s heart.

May the joys of happiness wipe away the sadness of your life;

This is more fitting beneath the praises of this father.

It is not contempt but increased honor that is being attributed to you.

He rightly intends to preserve the secrets of kings,

So that he may be a perfect friend to princes alike;

Hence your defender is truly powerful everywhere.

[260] Tell me whether he ever brought you consolations

In royal gifts when he returned from the king.

### Reichenau

He had certainly brought them before; I cannot deny it.

For, when he returned some time ago, he carried a testament

That had been secured by a royal seal,

[265] [Col. 0358D] In which my freedom and authority were confirmed.

### The Poet

For these things the assembly of our people ought to give him thanks,

Since these writings are a most free charter of common salvation.

Let this move you to rejoice, not to mourn sadly,

Since in this way your scepters shine.

[270] Tell me also what sort of gift he brought you after visiting

The apostolic patrons in Rome.

[Col. 0359A] ### Reichenau

What he himself gave me, although I was sad at heart,

Was a gift such that none was more precious:

By placing my hope in it, I fear no dangers—

A crystal vessel filled with the blood of Christ.

### The Poet

I say joyfully: Rejoice now, mother Reichenau,

Because of such a gift, since you are happier than the whole world.

Happy also is your faithful one,

Whom he joined to you in such subtle honor,

In whom, lady, you can wipe away the filth of sins;

And, believe me, you need fear neither of the two enemies.

Even if that blessed father did not make you illustrious

By his other resources, these gifts that he bestowed would still show

[Col. 0359B] That he surpassed all his predecessors in merit.

[285] Merciful God, receive the praises of so many works!

For in what is sung here, your glory and praise are rightly proclaimed:

You are the one who deigned to send such a father

To the mother Reichenau, so that her children might applaud the gift.

But since our conversation proceeds by turns,

Please tell me, in answer to my request,

Who made the structure of these temples of yours

For the praise of the Lord.

The sky is painted as though in a varied arrangement of stars;

So too you yourself are star-like, crowned with your chapels.

I did not see such splendor in you in former times,

[295] When Father Ruodmann lived in this world,

Although you stood exceedingly rich in his possessions.

I marvel that such great walls could be completed by one man

In so short a time—twice five years—

The number that the course of the sun now contains since his death.

Who, I ask, changed this entire place for the better,

Renewing it beautifully and adorning it with shining gems?

[Col. 0359C] ### Reichenau

All this that you see shining more beautifully in these buildings

Was done by the man who recently occupied the place next to me.

For, as you yourself sing, the sun’s course has now ascended

To its tenth year since the death of my former lord,

During which this learned Witegowo ruled me.

And, as I sang before, although he never ceased to wander here and there,

though he was always seldom with me,

[310] he nevertheless diligently let no year pass without wishing to close it with the accomplishment of this one work;

and when he began it, or when he completed what had been begun,

now he shows you by open discourse with me.

When, in the first year in which he began to rule me (985),

[Col. 0359D] [Note: That is, Witigowo.] he had built the left side of the church of the blessed Mother,

[315] founding with devoted mind an outstanding chapel,

which he wished to be dedicated under the patronage of Januarius,

who, through love of the heavenly homeland, endured

the victorious confession of martyrdom for Christ. [Note: The reading is *confesio* in c.]

Within it, with the altars arranged for divine worship,

[Col. 0360A]

[320] one altar was erected for you, blessed Stephen, Christ’s protomartyr,

so that you yourself, mercifully, might receive the prayers

which the assembly of devoted brothers pours forth to you;

another, Laurentius, is seen to be dedicated to you,

so that you too may rightly be present to those praying to you in their vows.

[325] Between these, Witigowo, model of goodness,

erected a lofty altar with ardent zeal,

adorning it with a panel prepared with gems and gold,

in which he enclosed the bones of blessed Januarius.

In such work he had brought the first year to completion.

Let voices of every kind say: “To you be glory, Christ!” (I) [Note: The author wrote the number of the ending year in the margin.]

When the course of the second year had arrived (986),

that blessed man, mindful of divine worship,

began to lay the foundations of a beautifully designed chapel,

at the monastery gate, through which the passage of the cloister opens,

[335] [Col. 0360B] showing everyone the way in and the way out,

which he consecrated in honor of blessed Pirminius,

who first guided me with paternal affection.

Then, delaying nothing in the work, he joined the cloister walls,

where the circuit had not previously been properly completed,

on the upper side of the church of blessed Januarius,

whose roof he had then himself completed,

and afterward made steps of polished stone,

by which one climbs to the church threshold and gate.

A painted image of the Mother remains upon the wall,

bearing Christ in her lap, the pledge of her love;

the brothers, lying prostrate above the high steps,

touch it in prayer and kiss it with holy devotion.

On the right side the painting marks the blessed

[Col. 0360C] Evangelist Mark, with his beautiful face,

and Januarius is painted beneath the left border.

Our devotion prays to both of them as patrons.

For this reason Lord Witigowo wished them to be painted,

so that such defenders might defend us everywhere

from the snares of the enemy opposing us.

[355] He also ordered the entire cloister to be painted;

those are the panels painted across the ceilings,

recording the deeds and memorials of the fathers who came before.

Whatever life amid wars, whatever peaceful way of life

they had at that time, the painting represents in full.

At the entrance to the cloister, which I mentioned earlier,

he ordered it to be adorned with representations of my fathers,

whom his prelatial office made worthy to be my prelates,

so that, in whatever place, those who first come to the temple

may see what a place has been prepared for the Lord:

[365] “You too are becoming lowly, deprived of so great an adornment;

[the opening reading, ‘Un,’ is corrupt:] you do not have even one house suitable for the service of Christ and the lay congregation,

nor does it contain a space in which that congregation may gather as one.

As far as I can, I now willingly desire

to join walls equal in form and extent on every side

to the old structure, which now consists only of part of the chapel.

[Col. 0361A] Let our work, together with what ancient structure still remains, be covered by a single roof,

and thus let us strengthen the lofty roof of the great church.”

Then, I confess, I brought forth joys from my glad heart,

because I had been permitted to converse with him in sweet words;

for he rarely exchanged any word with me.

“Thanks to you, lord!” I said, bending my knee,

[380] “you who, with wondrous workmanship and varied adornment,

make me an ornament in different regions of the world.

Whatever things your wisdom reveals as pleasing to you,

do them, I ask; do them gladly, leaving none of them undone.”

Why should I relate so much, already delaying my speech too long?

[385] [Col. 0361B] Everything he said, he himself accomplished in three years,

making, with an elegant construction of equal form,

such a temple for God as had none more spacious.

Supported throughout by varied ornament,

he himself, hastening as the lord had commanded, prepared

for it curved arches [Note: That is, *camuros*, “curved”] and overlaid them everywhere with stucco,

with varied figures and springlike flowers.

He had made them support columns cut from beautiful, variegated, polished stones.

When he had brought the whole work completely to its finish,

with great joy he had the solemn temple dedicated

in honor of holy Mary,

and of the virginal choir, bowed in prayer for us,

[Col. 0361C]

and beneath the apostolic crowns of Peter and Paul.

Praise be to you, Christ, giver of such zeal, who willed it: for six years you thus granted him the rights of authority. [Note: The reading is “O Christ.”]

[400] (VI)

As soon as the circle of seven years had been completed (991),

he built a hall raised higher toward the sky,

dedicated to you, holy Michael, archangel of Christ, [Note: “oc” added.]

which likewise shines with the beautiful blessed Otmar.

[405] That benevolent man strengthened it on either side

with a twin tower, made in rounded form,

with curved vaults and receding passages around it,

to which a stairway shows the ascent to be by a rising course.

[Col. 0361D] Between these, having purchased them at great cost,

[410] he hung bells whose signals sounded sweetly. [Note: Written in an erased place.]

After this he cultivated, before the threshold of holy Mary’s house,

a beautiful garden, though of small extent.

Enclosing it everywhere with walls and curved arches,

he made an earthly paradise gleaming with light,

[415] from which the beauty of the temple shines and gleams far away,

offering new spectacles to the people who come there.

[Col. 0362A] In the middle of this church, which he himself also built,

he raised upon steps a lofty altar,

opposite the front of which the entrance doors look out,

as is customary; upon it he then placed a panel

shining with a solid mass of gold worth talents.

Through its middle, behold, a clear mirror is visible,

which remains at once green and of glasslike color,

in which everyone can aptly see his own face.

[425] If anyone enters the church or passes through it,

then bows forward, as nature requires,

behold, all that is set behind him gleams brilliantly.

In such works, this great adornment of the loving elder

closed his seventh year. (VII)

[430] To you, Christ, be praise, author of such blessings!

[Col. 0362B] When the sun had then completed the boundary of the eighth year (992),

he founded, before this paradisiacal garden,

a very beautiful church of Saint Bartholomew,

and nearby he built a temple of salvation

[435] for you, Erasmus, and likewise for you, martyr Heraclius. [Note: “O Christ” is written above the text.] [Note: Written above.]

Lord Witigowo established this purpose for it:

that every place in the sacred buildings, shining with light,

might be a refuge, hope, and secure salvation for those who pray,

so that Christ might cleanse all their impurities,

[440] through the intercession of the saints themselves,

by whose names each chapel shines.

[Col. 0362C] Thus, flourishing in virtues from his eighth year (VIII),

he entered the ninth (993), which he undertook in its entirety,

adorning each altar with little golden ornaments and gems.

Before your altar, Mary, most noble virgin,

[445] beneath the single ascent of the steps, wondrously furnished,

it gleams, clad in gems and gold.

He also had silver-plated panels prepared,

with which he encircled the covering of its sides everywhere,

which he carried all around the altar itself in the form of a bed. [Note: The reading is *speciae*, that is, *specie* (“in appearance”).]

And it is called by our speech the holy Confession.

[Col. 0362D]

[455] Behind it stands close to the Lord’s altar a water jar,

from which he commanded flowing water to become wine;

it still bears gifts of salvation to the vows of those who pray.

Then, rejoicing, he again made an altar for blessed Mark,

and at the same time one in honor of the holy Cross,

which he completely clad in beautiful refined gold

and embellished variously with gems and a necklace. [Note: The reading is *variae*, that is, *varie* (“variously”).]

POET. [Note: The speaker-label is absent.]

Since by his care you have been raised from the dungheap,

[460] pray rather that he may have a long lifetime.

In such prayers, invoking the power of the Thunderer.

[Col. 0363A] For since you are permitted to retain such a father,

it is clear that you always rule in the queen’s citadel;

but—may this not happen!—if that pious man abandons you,

you will always be disgraceful, like a worthless little maidservant.

AUGIA.

When someone is saddened, held captive in mind,

he seeks and finds repose through one who consoles him;

so I, believe me, through your consolations, son,

casting away sadness, raise up the joys of my mind;

[470] for the promise of your true declaration confirms them.

While the rule of the elder who now lives governs me,

meanwhile my rights flourish and stand firm;

afterward, if I am not mistaken, when I am deprived

[Col. 0363B] of the crown of so great a head,

I immediately become a common subject of gossip,

wandering like a sheep that has slipped from the back of its shepherd.

Therefore, O son [Note: “O” written above.], give yourself eagerly with me

to pour out prayers to Christ, lest fortune with an unlucky foot

strike us down and take away from us the joys

of so great a shepherd, filled with heavenly love!

[480] Holy Mother of God, Virgin, offer frequent prayers

to your Son, for us and for the life of our ruler!

And all you saints, under whose honor he dedicated

the temples of God that he prepared on every side,

may they remember him before the Lord without end throughout the ages,

and may they obtain for him rights of authority flourishing

with the flower of peace, for Christ’s consolation;

and after the shadow of his mortal body has been laid aside,

[Col. 0363C] may he become their companion, placed in a heavenly seat!

May the God himself will this, who is three and one,

so that Father Witigowo may prosper and rule with power,

and may his name, Amen, live through the ages!

This concluding passage brings the poem to an end and gives rest

to the care of the writer, since all labor is fleeting,

but rewards will always stand powerfully without end. [Note: These three verses were written in red ink. From this point another hand, but of the same period, continues.]

[495] + Afterward, when he had happily entered his eleventh year,

guiding the souls entrusted to him with even governance,

he restored the buildings of the church dedicated in honor of Christ’s martyr,

Pelagius, as Scripture calls him.

They had been enclosed and hemmed in by a narrow boundary,

[500] erected within by an earlier, unsuitable structure,

which none of the wise had viewed in a fair light, judging it to be supported by insufficiently skilled workmanship. Thus the same father restored it, though so ill-formed; levelling the piled mass of dusty sand,

[Col. 0363D]

[505] he made the church honorable with a spacious border.

Not far from here is a house gleaming with royal ornament,

made sufficiently magnificent by its resources and craftsmanship,

[Col. 0364A] since he built it in honor of the emperor himself.

Not many days had elapsed since this man had first led into the Latin world the king whom sweet Swabia nurtures (996).

Holding him to that man’s authority with threatening terror,

and then boldly advancing toward the citadels of Romulus

with the many soldiers whom he had brought with him,

he amassed the imperial forces in broad array.

The Italians, struck by sudden fear, said:

“What do you suppose this man is, of such great power?

No one ought to resist this sceptered man,

who, behold, carries such great columns of men!”

[Col. 0364B]

[520] When they had said this, others replied:

“Augia sent this man to us; he teaches and governs her.

He will likewise be the foremost golden abbot of the Swabians.

It is to our advantage that we serve him.”

Then the Roman nobles, giving themselves and everything they had,

[525] soon placed the imperial crown upon the king;

after this he was called Caesar and Augustus.

When these matters had thus been completed, the shepherd returned

to the embrace of his bride, refreshing his limbs in rest. (IX)

What kind of man he is, or how great, his piety will rightly prove;

if you wish to know it now,

drink it in with the ears of your heart.

For he lives chastely, kindled by a twofold love,

and fortified by the seal of the Gospel in his heart.

[Col. 0364C] A snowy dove cherishes a serpent without fear,

and every pallor of envy flees from him everywhere.

[535] He always hates quarrels and seeks tranquil silence;

but, as the matter is well known from many examples,

the glory of the righteous is the fury and anger of the wicked!

Christ’s permission allows him to be tested in this way

by adverse circumstances, though harmful only in the slightest degree.

For when he has suffered something distressing in mind through loss,

he arms himself with the weapons supplied by steadfast patience,

and invokes God, who immediately redeems him.

I have often seen him tossed about in such great danger,

when the hostile hand cried out in a mocking voice:

[545] “If you are wise, rejoice! That man is already wretched and lost;

to his delighted enemies he becomes bitter mourning to his friends!”

Meanwhile, crying to the Lord from his ready heart,

he endured everything and dealt with it patiently within himself.

After a short while the Lord came, and he was redeemed;

[550] glory came to him, and the proud soon blushed.

This blessed man is among those who patiently endure losses,

whose blessed realms in heaven are with the Lord.

## Around the Same Year. Gozpert, Abbot of Tegernsee

[Col. 0365]

## Letters of Gozpert

(From R. P. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. V, part I, p. 121, from a contemporary Tegernsee manuscript.)

### Notice

Gozpert’s letters are full of good fruit. He was abbot of Tegernsee near the end of the tenth century. The fourth, fifth, and sixth letters are addressed to Meginhelm, a famous count descended from a family of the highest nobility, to whom he commends the Tegernsee community, suffering from severe famine in the East, in these words:

“We ask that you open to us the hand of your customary generosity and order a little grain to be given to us, as your alms, for the sustenance of those in the eastern region over which you rule, lest we see them completely consumed or die from hunger and starvation.”

From this passage it is perfectly clear that “the East” and “the eastern region” mean Austria, where even today certain estates belonging to Tegernsee are situated, as the Reverend Father discusses at greater length, concerning the ancient nomenclature of Austria, in the preliminary dissertations to volume I of the *Scriptores rerum Austriacarum*. Yet concerning this very famous count, who once ruled in Austria, there is, so far as I know, profound silence in our ancient annals.

## Letter I. To Ramuold, Abbot of Saint Emmeram

[Col. 0365A]

He announces that he will be at Regensburg on the feast of Saint Emmeram and asks that the book of the complete collation be copied and sent to him.

To Abbot R., most clear mirror of monastic religion, G., wholly submissive in the affection of his mind to the service owed by a disciple.

We thirst with ardent desire for the presence of your fatherhood. We wish, in your company, to revive somewhat our limbs, growing feeble and scarcely able to bear the burdens of old age and labors; we desire to be refreshed for a little while by the most delightful conversation of the brothers, because our sighing heart does not cease to reveal, with frequent grief, that we have been separated from you for so long a period.

At the next meeting with our duke we hope to be presented to your sight; but if some hindering circumstance prevents this, or if some matter cancels it, nevertheless, supported by your prayers, we do not doubt that we shall attend the feast of Saint Emmeram, our patron.

The book of the complete collation, which we requested some time ago because it is not held in our library, we again ask for on bended knees: order it to be lent to us. As quickly as we can, we shall have it copied, and at the appointed time we shall not delay either returning it to you ourselves or sending it back through a messenger. Farewell.

## Letter II. To Count Arnold

He gives him abundant thanks for the favors he has bestowed and declares his grief at the death of the empress Adelheid, recording what his monks have offered for the repose of her soul.

[Col. 0365C] Abbot G., appointed provider of monastic worship in name alone, to Count A., ennobled by a distinguished lineage and no less by noble rank: the happiness of supreme salvation in the Lord.

By no worthy treatment of words can we write adequate thanks to your most beneficent highness for the manifold kindness that you continually and unwearingly bestow upon us, unworthy as we are, and upon our household. And since we have never earned anything of this kind by any service, we beseech God to repay you with a hundredfold gift.

Above all, I, who bear the name of abbot, and the devoted company of our fellow monks have until now kept remembrance of you in diligent prayers. From now on, however, we have firmly resolved to perpetuate your name memorially in our monastery, day and night, in our prayers.

The mournful news of the death of our most beloved lady, Adelheid, [Col. 0366B] disturbed us exceedingly and . . . ours, as was fitting in the case of such a person. From that time until now we have completed the customary observances of prayers for her, and we know that at every annual return of the season we must hold vigils and Masses with offerings.

Order the day of the Kalends to be written on parchment and sent to us by the bearer of this letter. Farewell.

## Letter III. To the Same

He gives the greatest thanks for the finely made windows provided for the Tegernsee church and sends back the boys whom he has hitherto raised in the monastery for the purpose of learning, so that they may give evidence of their education.

To the most worthy Count A., everywhere renowned for the glory of manifold virtues, Abbot G. and the assembly of the brothers subject to him: diligence in prayers and salvation in the Lord.

[Col. 0367A] May God, the rewarder of all, deign to repay before the heavenly assemblies, with rewards multiplied a hundred times over, the exercises of your most faithful devotion, which for so long a time you have tirelessly bestowed upon us and our people through the diversity of your labors and the greatness of your services.

We rightly beseech God for you, since you have exalted our place through such honorable works as we have neither known in the days of our predecessors nor hoped that we ourselves would see. Until now the windows of our church had been closed with old cloths. In your fortunate days, the golden-haired sun first shone upon the floors of our basilica through glass of many-colored paintings; and the hearts of all who look upon them are deeply touched by manifold joys, as they marvel among themselves at the variety of this unusual work.

Therefore, as long as this place is seen adorned with such ornament, your name is inscribed day and night in the celebrations of our prayers. And so that the memory of all your relatives may henceforth be kept here, have the names of as many as you wish written on parchment and sent to us by the present messenger.

We leave the boys to your judgment, to be tested whether they have been taught that work so well that it may be honorable to you and necessary to us; or, if I find that something is lacking in them, may I be permitted to send them back to you for improvement. Farewell.

## Letter IV. To Count Meginhelm

He asks that he be granted some grain for the sustenance of those who serve his monastery in Austria.

[Col. 0367C] G., abbot of the monastery of Saint Quirinus, to the illustrious and venerable count: greeting in the Lord.

In the greatest need, faithful friends are rightly sought, and, as it is written, they are undoubtedly proved when they bestow the consolation of assistance. Since we have always had your consolation in all our affairs, we therefore now, as though speaking to our one and proper father and lord, make our complaint to your compassion concerning our household in the East, which this year is exposed to the grave danger of famine because of the shortage of grain.

For our part we cannot assist it as we ought, since in this year Ceres has not yielded good fruit for us in our lands. But we ask that you open to us the hand of your customary generosity and order a little grain to be given to us, as your alms, for the sustenance of those in the eastern region over which you rule, lest we see them entirely consumed or die from hunger and starvation. Farewell.

## Letter V. To the Same

He gives thanks for the husons, a kind of fish, and explains how many prayers the people of Tegernsee offer to God for the soul of his wife.

To the most famous Count Meginhelm, descended from a family of the highest nobility, Abbot G., with the monastic flock subject to him: greeting in the Lord.

The pressing need compels us to trouble you by asking every year; and it is your customary and annual generosity that has allowed us to learn what sort of fish those called husons are, since we could scarcely have known otherwise except through your alms.

We also wish you to know that we omit no year in paying the tribute of prayer that we promised you, apart from those prayers that we celebrate jointly for all who give us alms. In particular, for you and your friends who are still living or have already died in Christ, and for your wife of blessed memory, we sing forty-three Masses and ten psalters.

Moreover, your names are written among us for perpetual remembrance. Farewell.

## Letter VI. To the Same

He asks that husons be sent to him and his monks, since they abstain from meat according to monastic custom.

[Col. 0368B] To Lord M., everywhere renowned for the glory of a good name, Gozpert, abbot, with his fellow brothers: greeting in the Lord.

Having no gift of service in our hands, we approach you asking for great things, yet boldly, because we regain confidence from our awareness of your complete goodness toward us.

Living in the southern region, as you know, and abstaining from meat according to the monastic custom, as is fitting, we are rarely nourished by the catch of fish, because we have scarcely any fish-bearing waters. But if God has made the catch of husons abundant this year, we ask that you order some to be shared with us as a gift, so that thereafter we may keep remembrance of you before God in our prayers. Farewell.

## Letter VII. To Gebhard, Bishop of Augsburg

[Col. 0368C]

He praises his religious devotion and piety and promises that he will visit him when the season of the year permits.

To Lord Bishop G., deservedly exalted to the apostolic see through the merits of holy predecessors, G., the least of God’s servants, and the humble monastic congregation entrusted to him: the diligence of their service and prayers in Christ.

We rejoice with you in the virtues of your praiseworthy reputation, which pious report spreads everywhere throughout Mother Church. We have most often learned of these through the repeated account of our venerable bishop G. [Goteschalk, bishop of Freising], who loves you greatly in Christ.

Through the favor or intimacy of your predecessor bishops, we have been very fully engaged in their almsgiving; they loved us for the love of God and of holy Quirinus, our patron. With still greater spiritual desire we long to enjoy your favor above that of others, because we perceive that you adorn, through your conduct and way of life, the name and religious character of Benedictine life, placed as you are in apostolic dignity.

Because we were nourished from childhood in the bosom of the Augsburg church, we ought very often to visit that holy place. Next summer, when the grass can suffice for travelers, we wish to see you within, supported by your prayers, and to be enlivened by your presence, as our spirit desires at every moment.

Therefore, venerable bishop, we ask that henceforth you remember us, [Col. 0369A] when we forget you and do not remember ourselves. Farewell.

## Letter VIII. To Bruno

That he order the tithes from the village of Tatinhusa to be paid to the church of Tontinhusa.

To Bruno, most beneficent lord, your devoted servant, the abbot.

A certain little village of your inheritance, called Tatinhusa, possessed by a colony of two *hubae*, had, within the memory and lifetime of all who still survive, always paid its tithe to our church called Tontinhusa.

We complain to your compassion that this endowment has been unjustly taken from us, and we ask that, with your judges weighing everything justly and willingly under your authority, you order the same tithe to be granted to us until, in the council of the archpresbyters and before the lawmakers, what is most just may be judged.

Afterward we neither wish nor are able to oppose whatever you order to be done concerning it. Farewell.

## Letter IX. To Count Otto

He commends a certain servant to him and asks that two little cloaks belonging to the man be returned.

To the venerable Count Otto, Gozpert, abbot, with the brothers entrusted to him: devoted service and diligence in prayer.

Trusting exceedingly in your compassion day and night, we commend to you this servant of ours, deprived of every consolation, after God, his only comforter, in the tribulation now pressing upon him.

We ask that you order the two little cloaks that remained in your possession to be returned to him, for the love of God and Saint Quirinus and as your alms. If you deign to console him, know that we shall certainly rejoice greatly on that account. Farewell.

## Letter X. To Countess H.

He asks for money for the redemption of certain relatives of his.

To Lady Countess H., everywhere renowned for her good reputation: your devoted servant offers constancy in diligent prayer.

I lament to your compassion the cause of my pressing need, since, as we hear, you kindly console those who are in distress. Certain people related to me by blood, who were free, were sold by wicked men and are being harshly oppressed in servitude.

But our lord Duke Henry has ordered, as an alms of his, that they return free if we repay him the price. For this purpose we ask that you provide us some assistance for the love of God, always remembering that those who rescue the oppressed deserve eternal rewards. Farewell.

## Letter XI. To Abbot Otpert

That he permit an exchange to be made between the servants of the two parties.

Abbot Gozbert, with his brothers, to his beloved lord and fellow brother Otpert: greeting in the Lord.

We ask you, for the love of the friendship that exists between us, concerning the transaction made between our servant and your servant, to order that an exchange of the same transaction be made, and that it be completed in good faith on both sides.

This is so, however, only if you wish and order that our servant testify under oath that the property of your servant has not been made worse in his possession through any fault of his.

## Letter XII. To the Brothers of the Church of Eichstätt

That they write to him the day of his brother’s death.

G., abbot, though unworthy, of the Tegernsee monastery, to the beloved brothers of the Church of Eichstätt, as though to brothers born from the same womb in Christian kinship.

Although we are separated from you by bodily distance, we are nevertheless continually joined to your affection by the bond of special remembrance. A mournful report disturbed us to the depths of our heart, because we heard that our brother had already departed to God. While he lived, he was half of my soul.

We ask that the day of his death be written in the calendar and sent to us. We have resolved to give this one thing to our living brother, but we hope that he rejoices in Christ. We ask that you order it to be offered among you in memory of his blessed soul. Farewell.

## Letter XIII. To Lord H.

That he grant him the third part of the *Tripartite History* for use and copying.

Abbot G., though unworthy, to Lord H.: greeting [Col. 0370C] in Christ.

Remember, we ask, the faith and charity that each of us promised to the other; and, lest it grow cold in any way between us, if you command me to perform any service for you, I shall strive devotedly to fulfill it.

We have two written parts of the *Tripartite History*. The third part is lacking because we cannot acquire another copy, unless you deign, out of regard for us, to send it to us.

## Letter XIV. To Count R.

He proves that the maidservant Imma and her children are owed to him by law and asks that they be returned.

To Lord R., highly worthy of the honor of countship, Gozpert, abbot, with the brothers subject to him: greeting in the Lord.

We have always heard that in all the authority of your office you act wisely and decide everything according to law. Therefore we grieve that our maidservant Imma, with her children, has been unjustly taken from us by your authority.

For we know that, if she possessed the law of her fathers, her children would be your servants. But she lost the law of her fathers because she was violated while under our authority and bore a son before taking a legitimate husband. All who know her and saw that same infant are witnesses to this matter.

Therefore we ask that you order the same maidservant, with her children, to be returned to us, lest it also be a sin for you if you delay returning her, and lest it become necessary for us to make a complaint about this matter to our lord duke. [Note: The printed text has *non sic* (“not thus”); with the negation it is contrary to the sense.]

## Letter XV. To P., His Kinsman

That he persist in his excellent intention of helping the Tegernsee community and protect certain servants expelled from the city.

G., in every respect your devoted servant, to P., his most beloved kinsman and dearest lord: diligent prayer and devoted service.

May God, who leaves no one who acts well without reward, restore to you the gift of recompense for what you have constantly, devotedly, and faithfully done for us, when we fled to your aid [Note: Something appears to be missing.] to seek the justice of God for our monastery.

We ask you, for the love of God and of holy Quirinus, to continue in faithful assistance as you have begun, and, as we trust you will, to bring it to a faithful conclusion. Whatever we or our messengers have promised to give you for this business, we shall present without delay whenever and wherever you wish, provided that, through your help, our *curtlia* (farmsteads or enclosed holdings) are restored to us.

We send these servants of ours to your compassion. The townsmen had expelled them from the city because of the men who had been despoiled, as you well know, since they had presumed nothing in this matter before they had your permission and that of Lord Tagin.

Therefore we ask that you do not release them from your authority until you have enabled them to remain peacefully and without fear in the city. Farewell.

## Letter XVI. To the Same

[Col. 0372A]

He complains of being neglected and forgotten and asks that some copper, tin, and lead be sent for casting a bell, together with some incense for the worship of God and Saint Quirinus.

Abbot G. and the other brothers to P., whatever fathers owe to a beloved brother and dearest son.

Several years have been counted since you left your native soil and went to unknown regions, in which, as we have gladly heard, you have also become quite abundantly enriched. But we wonder and grieve that you have so completely forgotten us that you have never sent us even a word of greeting through the messengers who frequently travel back and forth, although you have been joined to our mind and heart by love ever since you were a little boy.

In memory of our friendship, which must not be forgotten, we ask that you send us some copper, tin, or even lead. For, if God goes before us, we wish to cast a great bell in honor of God and Saint Quirinus. The cities of our land have been exhausted of all these materials, and we cannot obtain anything of this kind at any price.

For burning incense also in the house of God and at the altar of Saint Quirinus, we ask that you send us some incense or some other kind of aromatic substance. If you send us any message through the present messengers concerning something we can do in your service, we shall gladly fulfill it with every devotion. Farewell.

[Col. 0371]

## Other Letters of Gozpert

(From Mabillon, *Analecta*, new edition, p. 434.)

## Letter I. To Uto, His Nephew

[Col. 0371C]

Abbot Gozpert, humble servant of God, to his beloved nephew Uto: greeting in God.

We ask you, for the love of God and of his martyr Saint Quirinus, to order the tithe to be rendered which the tenants of Saint Quirinus owe, so that his service may be maintained and the poor who come daily to his monastery may have sustenance.

For it is greatly to be feared that, when you unjustly take away the alms of God’s Church from Christ’s poor, what you may lawfully and without danger of sin possess will be taken away from you by God. May God grant that you avoid this. Farewell.

## Letter II. To Count Adalp

[Col. 0371D] To the most noble Count Adalp, Gozpert, abbot, with the monks entrusted to him: a pledge of heavenly greeting in Christ.

Although we live in the farthest regions, in rocky and wooded places, the celebrated reputation of your piety, which you have shown toward us and our little community, has very often reached us through the reports of many people.

Since we are neither able nor sufficient to repay it by any other service, we have your name written among us in the book of life, and daily beseech God to reward you, since you do such things for us and our people for his love.

Living in such places, as we have said, we suffer a great shortage of fish. Therefore, if the fishing has prospered in your hands this year, we ask that you order some to be shared with us in your customary kindness. Farewell.

## Letter III. To Arnold, His Nephew

Gozpert, called abbot, though unworthy, to Lord Arnold and to our niece, your wife Adelheid: greeting in the highest God.

Compelled by the greatest need, we earnestly request the faithful assistance of our friends, because this year the nourishment of our provisions has been entirely insufficient, choked by the barrenness of the fields.

In all matters we hope that you will show us compassion from the depths of your kindness. Therefore we ask that you help us in this present danger; and if you order some grain to be given for our sustenance or that of our household, we shall honorably receive it as a precious gift of gold or silver. Farewell.

## Appendix to the Letters of Gozpert

[Col. 0373]

## Letters of the Tegernsee Community

(From Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, V, I, p. 130.)

## Letter I. To Their Abbot Gozpert

[The supplied source ends here, with the opening heading of this letter.]

[Col. 0373A]

On the intention of the duke, who wished to restore certain things taken away, and on a tithe formerly given to a certain recluse.

To our lord and elder, Abbot G., from the brothers subject to him—whatever is due to a beloved Father.

Our brother Nonnus Eigino, having returned from the journey on which he had been sent to the monastery, reported to us concerning our lord the duke that he had promised willingly to restore what had been taken from our monastery in the East. He ordered Brother Meginh. to wait there so that he might remind him of whatever things might be required there, and this when our lord the duke should next return there. For Brother Meginh. is still waiting there, compelled to remain through the ripening of the vintage and by the expectation of our lord the duke’s return. I beg you to send word to me, your servant Froumund, whether you have given the recluse at Niunpurc the tithe which she formerly received from our abbot. For I fear that it may entirely perish from us, since it had never come into our investiture, but had always wandered here and there through benefices.

## LETTER II. TO HENRY, DUKE OF BAVARIA

Concerning the death of the same Gozpert and the election of a new abbot, which they earnestly ask him to allow them to make freely.

To our lord the duke H., the congregation of the monastery of Saint Quirinus, your poor alms-seeking community, offers day and night its earnest prayer for your well-being.

Our blessed Father Gozpert rested in the Lord in the sleep of peace on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February. For his death we wretched people can find no consolation unless you, who after God are our one and only lord, deign also, with the compassion of loving fatherhood, to have pity on us. First, prostrate at your feet upon the ground, we humbly beseech you not ever to grant the place and monastery of Saint Quirinus to the authority of anyone other than yourself, lest in your time we should see the things which your father and your other relatives granted to this monastery as alms being taken away or distributed by others, and lest we and our descendants should thereafter always grieve over these losses.

When we complained to you about the illness of our abbot, we held firmly, as though spoken by the mouth of God, what you promised us concerning the election. We ask you again, for the love of God and Saint Quirinus, not to appoint any abbot for us outside our petition. Finally, when you return happily to your homeland, we shall assemble before you and, by your command and permission, elect the man whom we believe to be a guardian of regular religious observance and in no way forgetful of your service, insofar as is sufficient.

## THIETPALD, MONK OF TEGERNSEE, AROUND THE SAME YEAR

[Col. 0373]

## LETTER OF THIETPALD TO SAINT ADELBERT, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF PRUSSIA

He announces that, having rejected Aristotelian philosophy, he is devoting himself to sacred matters, and wishes that everything may turn out for him according to his heart’s desire.

(Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum novus*, V, I, 131.)

[Col. 0373C] To ADALBERT, presiding over the episcopal throne of the holy Church of Prussia, bishop of unique devotion to you, THIETPALD, though the least of the poor in spirit, sends the sprinkling of Christ’s blood and whatever that may be which the distinguished preacher testifies to be hidden with Christ in God [Col. 0374C].

[Col. 0375A] I know, reverend prelate, that your holiness demands no philosophical compilation from my feebleness; but if there is anything to be done, you would rather fashion it from simple truth, scarcely remembering that God made the wisdom of this world foolish after he dried up the rivers of Ethan. For, through the sweetness of David’s ten-stringed instrument and of God entering in, so far as depended on me I have almost forgotten Aristotle’s ten Categories. Therefore I have chosen to present to my Lord things apparently lowly and mediocre—things whose lips have not been moistened to the utmost by the Pegasean spring—rather than toil more anxiously over matters in which I would fall all the more dishonorably.

If I am called a fool, biting back the circuitous expression, I give thanks [Col. 0376A]—and deservedly so, provided that I acknowledge myself refreshed by Plato’s bran and recognize you, Father, as satisfied at Solomon’s banquet. What more is there to say? Know for certain that I rejoice above all in your well-being and in your prosperity in every respect, because, as is fitting in the Lord, I regard my own advantage or misfortune according as the sum of your well-being—or, God forbid, your ineptitude—may turn out. As for the nature of my voluntary servitude toward you, why is there any need for words, when, according to the greater extent of my means, you can find no cleric or dependent subject to you more ready and at the same time more devoted than I am in every place [not]?

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1004. SAINT ABBO, ABBOT OF FLORIACUM

## LIFE OF SAINT ABBO, BY AIMOIN, A MONK

(In Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. VIII, pp. 30–58.)

[Col. 0375]

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[Col. 0375B] 1. It is not easy to judge which was more fortunate: Aimoin, in having Abbo as his teacher and instructor, or Abbo—or Abo himself—in having obtained Aimoin, a monk of Floriacum and his own disciple, as the writer of his life. For Aimoin’s work on Abbo is of such a kind that it brings Abbo himself before us and admirably represents his qualities and rightly performed deeds. It was first printed by John de Bosco Coelestinus from a manuscript codex of Floriacum. We have again compared the printed books with that manuscript, restoring certain passages which in Bosco’s edition were considerably damaged or defective because of the difficulty of the writing, or were left blank.

2. Besides Aimoin, various authors have extolled Abbo with praise, whether while he was alive, such as Fulbert [Col. 0375C], later bishop of Chartres, or after his death, such as William of Malmesbury, the monk Orderic Vitalis, the authors of the *Deeds of Saint Oswald, Bishop of Worcester*, cited above, and many more recent writers. William and Orderic especially celebrate Abbo’s mission to England. That mission was indeed illustrious, both because monastic discipline was restored through it and because the study of letters was newly revived in the English monasteries. William says in Book III of *On the Bishops of the English*, where he is speaking of Oswald:

“Moreover,” he says, “he generously took care to summon men distinguished in letters to England, lest he deprive his homeland of that good without which the other goods seem to me almost empty. One of these was Abbo, a monk of Floriacum, who brought much fruit of learning into England and, at the command of Archbishop Dunstan, added the Passion of Edmund the Martyr to the fullness of literature. Later, having returned home and been appointed abbot there, he diligently upheld the strictness of religious observance. When he attempted to practice this custom in a certain cell of the monastery of Floriacum, situated in Gascony and still called ad Regulam (“at the Rule”), Gascony could not endure it; they sent him, lifeless from a lance, to the heavenly ones.”

This is what William wrote about his studies. Orderic Vitalis wrote as follows about monastic discipline in Book IV, p. 517:

“At their prayers”—namely, those of Dunstan, Æthelwold, and Oswald—“Abbo of Floriacum, a wise and religious cenobite, was sent across the sea and taught monastic practice at Ramsey and in other monasteries of England, just as it was observed in Gaul at that time.”

Thus Gaul, which had once received the teaching of literary studies from the English—Alcuin and others—first through Grimbald and John, monks trained in the monasteries of Gaul, and then, on this second occasion, through Abbo, poured the same light of learning back into England; and a third time it was to do so through Lanfranc, Anselm, and others, all fellow soldiers of the Order of Saint Benedict [Col. 0377A].

3. Nor did Gaul fail to claim for itself a considerable share of so great a light, which Abbo spread everywhere through both learning and piety. For not only Floriacum but also the surrounding monasteries were illuminated by him. Hence Fulbert addresses Letter 21 to “the most beloved Father Abbo, filled to overflowing with virtue and grace,” and implores his assistance in settling the factions that had arisen in the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres over the election of an abbot. At the end he says:

“Therefore, now returning to you, reverend Father, whom I believe and see to have been provided by the Lord for our splendor, together with my lord and your faithful servant Rodulf, I beg and beseech you, by the charisms of holy wisdom given to you, by the sweetness of brotherly charity, if you can do anything, attack the enemies of the Lord, restore your stricken brothers, and do not allow those for whom you believe Christ’s blood was poured out to perish for lack of your assistance” [Col. 0377B].

For this reason Odolric, abbot of Saint Martial of Limoges, said at the Council of Limoges concerning the apostleship of Saint Martial that he had been “trained for many years in the liberal arts” at the monastery of Saint Benedict. He then asked what “the father of that place, Abbo, a most flourishing philosopher, whom many of you,” he said, “know, and the most famous teacher in all France in every divine and secular authority, and afterward crowned with martyrdom by the sword of persecution in Gascony,” had said about Saint Martial.

Nothing, however, contributes more to Abbo’s praise than a speech delivered at the same Council of Limoges on the dedication of Saint Peter. Stephen Baluze, a man of great learning, who communicated to me a fragment of it from a Colbert manuscript, suspects that this speech was by Ademar of Angoulême. The fragment runs as follows:

“It would be a very long task to bring forward in detail the established testimonies of so many Fathers concerning his—that is, Saint Martial’s—… Nevertheless, it is enough to recall one matter from the ancient authors. You know certainly, if not by sight then by hearing, that most renowned Father who succeeded him in pastoral governance, that man of complete learning and grave authority, the archbishop of Bourges, defender of orthodox faith and cultivator of Catholic piety. For he went long before us, crowned with martyrdom and having suffered through the shedding of blood by the impious. We have already heard that miracles shine forth at his tomb, confirmed by the testimony of trustworthy men; his martyrdom too is solemnly celebrated in many churches according to the custom of the holy martyrs.

“In this martyr, Wisdom had made for herself so great a dwelling that, although the learned men of his age flourished in countless numbers, his authority was nevertheless held above all others. Thus throughout Gaul and Germany and among the English—for there too he was held in the highest fame—whenever any question was debated, if someone said that he had heard the decision from him, no further authority was required. Everyone judged that whatever had been heard from the mouth [Col. 0378A] of so great a man was established; he surpassed them in authority like another Solomon. Although by residence or birth he was a Frank, he was nevertheless illustrious in Roman eloquence, and was judged as though he were another Cicero.

“In councils of the Fathers, before kings and princes, he alone distinguished the matters proposed; alone, as master of all, he brought doubt to an end in a few words. Everyone, even the most expert among the learned, depended upon his mouth; in his presence they placed a finger upon their lips. So great was he in wisdom—besides being supported by the seven pillars of the liberal arts—and so full of authority and grace that he was an ornament to the whole Church. He adorned gatherings of bishops, approved all his statements by the authority of the divine Scriptures, and whatever proceeded from his mouth sounded, as it were, not human but divine” [Col. 0378B].

“In one of his treatises he could not keep silent about the truth concerning Martial, saying:

‘This supreme Father Martial was altogether a sufficiently mystical guest of Christ at the supper, taking the remnants of the heavenly bread; and when afterward he rose and wiped the company of the disciples, he himself gladly offered the linen cloths. Nor did he ever withdraw from the sacred fellowship, the one among the pious company who was without Thomas because of fear. Indeed, when Christ was ascending to heaven, he deserved to be blessed among the crowds standing by. Nor did he reject the choirs of those praising him, but with them at that time received the gifts and many-tongued languages of the Holy Spirit. Supported by these, he finally reached Antioch with Peter as his companion, and from there the city of Rome. Leaving it, he crossed into Gaul, a great part of whose clear and noble province is Aquitaine; arriving there, he became the apostle of the entire province for all ages’” [Col. 0378C].

Nothing more illustrious than this eulogy can be brought forward in praise of Abbo. But now at last let us come to his particular deeds, after we have set forth the state of the monastery of Floriacum as it was in the tenth century and the succession of its abbots.

4. After Saint Odo the abbot, whom we saw above in his acts to have restored the discipline that had collapsed at Floriacum, Archembald—or Ercambold—governed Floriacum from the year 942. According to the *Life of Saint Oswald*, he clothed Oswald, who had come there from England, in the monastic habit. Goslin, bishop of Toul of the Leuci, came to Floriacum and received from this abbot the Rule together with a carefully ordered manner of life. He also gave Saint Cadroes the monastic habit; likewise, “he restored the monastic Rule in the monastery of Saint Remigius at Reims, appointing as abbot there Hincmar, a monk of that place,” as Frodoard testifies in Book IV, chapter 32, of his *History of Reims*.

The same was done in the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres by his successor Wlfaldus, who sent twelve monks there with Abbot Alveus. He is praised in Book II, chapter 2, of the *Life of Saint Odo*. Under these two men lived the monk Drogo, later distinguished for his piety as a hermit, as Aimoin testifies in Book I, chapter 4, of *The Miracles of Saint Benedict*.

When Wlfaldus was transferred to the see of Chartres, Richard succeeded him from the year 962. In his time, namely in the year 974, the monastery of Floriacum was consumed by fire, according to Aimoin; he restored it within three years. In Richard’s time Adalelmus [Col. 0379A] the knight granted blessed Benedict a splendid silver cross engraved with the face of our Savior, together with an estate in the Senonais district called Villari, for the salvation of the soul of his lord, the illustrious Hugh, duke of the Franks; for his father Rotbert and his mother Berta; and for his cousin Burchard and his other relatives and friends.

After Adalelmus and Burchard, the document is subscribed by Hugh, duke of the Franks; Count Odo; Alberic; Emmo; Drogo; Anselm; Walter; Erveus; Walter and another Walter; Hugh; Corbo; Gausbert; Rotrocus; Countess Adela; and Count Milo, her son. It was enacted publicly at Paris in an assembly of nobles, on the sixth day before the Ides of September, in the twenty-first year of the glorious King Lothair, indiction III—that is, in the year of Christ 975.

After Abbot Richard, Amalbert succeeded him—these are Aimoin’s words—“who was kind by nature and proved still kinder through the greatness of the humility implanted in him.” Aimoin testifies that he received the religious habit from Amalbert in his tender years. Amalbert was succeeded by Oilboldus, in whose time Arnulf, the second bishop of Orléans of that name, harassed the monks of Floriacum greatly because of the subjection he demanded from them, as we shall soon explain.

Finally, in the year 988, Oilboldus had Abbo as his successor, the man whose works we now have before us. Aimoin writes of him as follows in Book II, chapter 1, of *The Miracles of Saint Benedict*:

“Therefore, when Oilboldus, abbot, rested in Christ, Abbo, a man beloved by God and human beings, was elected by the brothers with King Hugh’s approval and succeeded to the office of monastic governance. In the year preceding that in which we are writing these things, which was the thousand and fourth from the Lord’s incarnation [Col. 0379C], he was innocently killed in the regions of Gascony by faithless men of that nation, and, crowned with the laurel of martyrdom through his blood, was called by Christ to the eternal kingdoms. In his days we shall set out in writing the wonderful things performed by almighty God through our most eminent Father Benedict …”

After Abbo, Gauzlin was placed over the monks of Floriacum. He was the bastard son of the most noble prince of the Franks, as Ademar calls him in his *Chronicle*, p. 172—that is, illegitimate—“nourished from childhood in the monastery of Saint Benedict.” Although the monks opposed him as abbot because of his birth, and later the people of Bourges likewise protested against him as archbishop, King Rotbert imposed him upon them. The beginning of the preceding speech about Abbo is to be understood as referring to him. The monk Tortarius enumerates Gauzlin’s successors as abbots in his book *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict* [Col. 0379D].

5. Aimoin mentions two journeys by Abbo to Rome in chapter 11 of the following book: one to Pope John XV and the other to Gregory V. Aimoin marks John with the stain of simony. Baronius, however, in the additions for the year 992 after volume XII, argues that this crime should be charged not against Pope John but against Crescentius, the tyrant who dominated the pope in Rome.

Whatever the truth may be, Abbo himself, in a letter to L., abbot of Fulda, bears witness to Aimoin concerning his first journey. I have not yet been able to learn who this L., abbot of Fulda, was, since Brower contains no abbot of that period whose name begins with L. The letter was written in the year 996, as the learned Stephen Baluze correctly noted when he published it in volume I of his *Miscellanies*—that is, in the very year in which Gregory succeeded John after the extinction of the antipope Boniface. It begins as follows:

“To the most beloved of the most beloved, the lord L., abbot of Saint Boniface, resounding wonderfully with the distinction of eloquence, the merit of life, and the teaching of wisdom, Abbo, humble abbot of the monastery of Floriacum, sends the Spirit of the Lord, who filled the world, to fill his knowledge and understanding.

“While charity, which is the bond of perfection, joined us both together at Reims in private conversation, your tongue, moved by a good zeal, poured forth in public and in secret so many streams of prayer and so many honeycombs of Holy Scripture [Col. 0380B] that, exclaiming, I am compelled to say: ‘Grace has been poured upon your lips,’ and so forth.

“Among the private secrets of our conversation, one particular saying of your magnificence distilled into our ears. I am as eager to fulfill it, if God wills, as I am to obtain eternal life through a vow. You asked that distinguished relics of Saint Father Benedict be sent to you, because it was wholly certain that the presence of his most holy body was retained by us; and therefore you desired most earnestly that an oratory be built in his honor, and likewise that we be compensated with something from Saint Boniface or from the sacred limbs of the other saints.

“Your incomparable goodness added that, if any desire concerning domestic affairs urged us to strengthen our privileges through the apostolic style of Roman authority, you would be our most faithful collaborator in every respect. It was my intention to accomplish all these things when I approached humbly the magnificent limbs of the prince of the apostles; but, alas, to my great sorrow, I found the Roman Church bereft of a worthy shepherd.

“I confess that your absence affected me as a hen’s chick is accustomed to be affected when it laments with hoarse cries that the one protection of its mother has been taken away. But recently I heard news that made me rejoice more than over gold and topaz: that the apostolic dignity had been raised up through a certain man of imperial blood, completely endowed with virtues and wisdom.

“Your return sounded in our mind like the ineffable harmony of a return to paradise [Col. 0380D]. Now therefore, just as we spoke to one another, and as this letter presents itself to your sight, may it please you to hear through these monks of our holy Father Benedict and to carry out what you hear, as you promised, with the greatest faith and devotion.

“May that same Spirit who inspired Gregory with every flower of eloquence inspire the venerable apostolic bishop of this holy Roman Church, and grant you to be his most beloved secretary, for the strengthening of the fallen apostolic authority. Farewell.”

6. Three points in this letter deserve attention. First, relics of Saint Benedict were requested from Floriacum, where even the Germans at that time were persuaded that his body rested. Second, it records Abbo’s first journey to Rome, whose see, he complains, was deprived of a worthy shepherd. Third, it records the election of Pope Gregory V from the imperial line. Concerning him, the manuscript *Saxon Chronicle* says under the year 996:

“Meanwhile Pope John died. Therefore King Otto, already in Italy, stirred by the report, sent certain princes ahead and, by public agreement and election, had his nephew Bruno, son of Otto, who governed the Verona march, ordained as pope, giving him the name Gregory.”

7. Abbo was therefore sent by King Rotbert to this Gregory. “The principal one of the causes for which he was sent,” Aimoin says later in his *Life*, “was this: because Arnulf, archbishop of Reims [Col. 0381B], had been deprived of his see and committed to custody without a lawful hearing. For this reason Gregory threatened that he would bring an anathema upon the entire kingdom of the Franks.”

While Abbo diligently carried out this public business, he also thought about the private interests of his monastery and obtained from the pope a privilege, the substance of which Aimoin reports.

8. This embassy especially reveals how great Abbo’s authority was with the king. It is also clearly shown by the freedom with which he rebuked King Rotbert for his union with Bertha, his own blood relative and relation by marriage. Helgaud compares Abbo’s action in the *Life of Rotbert* with the action of the prophet Nathan. He says that, just as David was corrected by Nathan, so “this man was likewise harshly rebuked privately and publicly by the lord and venerable Abbo, the abbot of Floriacum chosen by God, now, by the favor of Christ’s grace, shining with miracles, without fear of death. The rebuke of this holy man continued until the most merciful king recognized his guilt, completely abandoned the woman whom he had wrongly joined to himself, and washed away the stain of sin by a satisfaction pleasing to God.”

The same authority is evident from the collection of canons presented to Kings Hugh and Rotbert, “in which,” he says, “I have expressed the substance of your office and have not been silent about how the nobles of the kingdom ought to preserve faith toward you.” This collection may be found in volume II of the *Analecta*.

How highly King Hugh esteemed Abbo is made clear by a diploma granted by him, which we have drawn from the original as follows:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Hugh, by the grace of God king of the Franks. It has always been the custom and practice of our royal predecessors to exalt the churches of God, to favor with kindness the just petitions of the servants of God, and to relieve their oppressions benevolently, so that they might have God propitious, for whose love they had done these things.

“For this reason, having heard the complaints of the venerable Abbo, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary, Saint Peter, and Saint Benedict at Floriacum, and of the monks living under him who had come into our presence, concerning the evil customs and continual exactions which Arnulf of Château-sur-Eure, in the capacity of advocate and vicar, was receiving from the estate called Eure, which lay in their power and which no one had ever previously done, I sent my son Rotbert the king to that place, so that he might restore it under our protection and defense, so that none of his men, whether slave or free, might presume to take anything there. He himself carried this out without delay.

“Meanwhile a dispute arose between Count Odo and me. Among the other dependents and faithful men whom we summoned to our service, we also called Arnulf, bishop of Orléans, to our assistance. For this reason he asked that we restore to his nephew, the aforesaid Arnulf, the customary payments, just as he himself had previously held them, although by force. Unwilling to offend him because of his service, I summoned the aforesaid abbot and asked him to pay thirty modii of wine from the vintage of that estate [Col. 0382B] to Arnulf himself, for as long as his uncle the bishop lived, for our safety, on the condition that none of Arnulf’s men, slave or free, should thereafter exact anything there.

“After his death, however, neither Arnulf himself nor any of his successors may dare to demand either this same payment or anything else from that estate, or presume to enter it or take anything further. Therefore, for the stability and public knowledge of the matter, I issued this writ of immunity concerning the aforesaid place and confirmed it below with my own hand; I also had my son Rotbert the king confirm it and sealed it with the impression of my ring.

“Thus no person ever afterward—bishop, abbot, duke, count, viscount, vicar, toll-collector, or any public exactor—may enter it in our time or in that of our successors to demand anything, or presume to exact anything; but let the abbot and congregation of the aforesaid place possess that estate in peace under the protection of our immunity. And just as the other possessions of the aforesaid place continue fortified and defended by the charters of our predecessors, the kings of the Franks, so let this possession also remain fortified and irrevocable by the authority of this present charter, for the alms of my soul and that of my son and for the perpetual stability of our rule.

“Enacted publicly in the city of Paris, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 993, indiction VI, year VII, while the most glorious King Hugh and his illustrious son Rotbert were reigning. Sign of the most glorious King Hugh. Sign of the illustrious King Rotbert.”

9. The Arnulf who is mentioned here is Arnulf, bishop of Orléans, the very man who had serious quarrels with our Abbo and opposed him in the synod concerning Arnulf, archbishop of Reims.

It is useful here to present the succession of the bishops of Orléans during the tenth century, since the published accounts, even that of Saussey, are less accurate. We shall repeat it chiefly from Letald of Micy, a monk, in Book I of *The Miracles of Saint Maximinus the Abbot*, published in the first volume.

Agius governed Orléans during the reign of Charles the Bald and had Walter as his successor. After Walter came Trohannus, Berno, Anselm, Theodoricus for four years, Ermentheus, and his nephew Ernulfus, who governed the bishopric. This is taken from Letald.

This Ernulfus or Arnulf entered the see in the year 963, as is clear from a diploma of Hugh, duke, surnamed the Great, restoring to the church of Orléans the suburban abbey of Saint John in the year of the Lord 975, indiction III, when Arnulf was bishop in the twelfth year of his episcopate [Col. 0383A]. The diploma is subscribed by Duke Hugh and his son Rotbert; Count Gauffred and his son Fulco; Count Henry; Count Wauter; Walter and his son Radulf; and Count Burchard, together with Burchard, the scribe of this transaction.

Ernulfus or Arnulf was succeeded by Manasses, who attended the Synod of Sens in 981. It is necessary to admit after him a second Arnulf, unknown to Saussey and others—namely, the one mentioned in the diploma above. Aimoin discusses this second Arnulf at the end of Book I of *The Miracles of Saint Benedict* and reports a miracle that occurred on Arnulf’s account during the time of Abbot Oilboldus, who surrendered the governance of the monastery of Floriacum to Abbo by his death, around the year 988. Aimoin’s words, from chapter 19, are as follows:

“Arnulf, bishop of Orléans, otherwise a good man who observed ecclesiastical rules very well in knowledge and practice, never truly loved the abbots of this place of Floriacum, chiefly because they, obeying only the royal authority, by no means depended upon his command in the subjection to which he was excessively devoted. For this reason he permitted the vineyards of Saint Benedict, situated in the suburb of the city of Orléans, in a place called Boaria, to be overrun by his satellites,” and so forth.

Aimoin’s moderation and fairness are praiseworthy here: he wrote without bitterness about Bishop Arnulf, although he knew that Abbo had suffered unworthy treatment from him, indeed insults and injuries from his satellites [Col. 0383C].

10. It must be examined what this subjection was, and of what kind, which Arnulf demanded from the monks of Floriacum. I find that bishops formerly used to demand a twofold subjection from monasteries. One was that by which a newly ordained abbot professed solemn subjection to his bishop in spiritual matters. The other was that by which monasteries, in temporal affairs, were subject not to royal authority but to the authority and jurisdiction of the diocesan bishop. A more suitable place for discussing this twofold subjection seemed to be the preface to this volume, where we examine the dispute between Abbo and Arnulf.

11. But another matter, no less liable to provoke hostility, occupied Abbo: namely, the controversy over tithes, debated at the Dionysian synod near Paris. The bishops wanted to take these tithes not only from laypeople but also from monks. Abbo resisted on behalf of the monks. But the laypeople, rushing upon the bishops, scarcely—or scarcely at all—refrained from striking them.

The odium of this action was cast upon Abbo through Arnulf of Orléans, who was hostile to him, so that Abbo himself was compelled to defend himself in an *Apology* before Kings Hugh and Rotbert. The synod was held during their rule, that is, before the year 998, as Aimoin describes at length in chapter 9 of the following *Life*. From this single account we have our knowledge of that synod.

Anyone who is the author of the brief treatise in volume IX of the Councils edited by Labbe, col. 771, is mistaken when he says that Abbo “incited the monks of Saint-Denis and their other dependents against the bishops” [Col. 0384A]. It is established that this was done by the laypeople who were present, whose chief interest was to assert their claim to the tithes.

This *Apology* of Abbo, together with other letters of his, was recently printed in the royal press under the care of the illustrious Claude Pellé, administrator of the kingdom. A letter of Gerbert—[in] Chesney, vol. II, p. 836—to Arnulf, bishop of Orléans, seems to refer to this matter, in which he says that the monks of Saint-Denis had been placed under an interdict, perhaps because of those disturbances.

12. But at last we must come to Abbo’s death. According to Aimoin, it occurred “in the thousand and fourth year, indiction II, on the thirteenth day of the month of November.” Aimoin says that he was martyred; he was killed by the rioting inhabitants of the town of La Réole, not by monks, as some relate. I say that he was called a martyr according to the custom of those times, when anyone who led a pious and innocent life and was killed was regarded as a martyr, as we have observed more than once elsewhere.

The authors contemporary with or close to Aimoin speak in the same way. Glaber writes in Book III, chapter 3:

“When these things had taken place, it happened that the venerable Abbo, father of the monastery of Saint Benedict, called Floriacum, crossed into the province of the southern Gascons for the sake of defending monastic religion. When he arrived there and stayed in a certain monastery, diligently carrying out the things of God according to his customary manner, he was greatly revered by all. It happened one day that, in the courtyard of that monastery, when the sparks of anger among certain quarrelsome men had burst into flame, an exceedingly violent disturbance arose.

“When the most reverend man, the aforesaid Abbo, learned of this and came forward to calm the disturbance, carrying in his hands writing tablets with a stylus, one of the crowd, inspired by a diabolical spirit, rushed upon him and pierced his side with a lance, making him a martyr of Christ. He too, as is said, was shortly afterward seized by a demon and miserably ended his life. The body of the aforesaid Father was honorably buried there by both his own people and the other faithful of that province. There, too, the Lord afterward bestowed many benefits upon people to the praise of his name.”

The *Chronicle of Anjou*, in Labbe, volume I of the *Library*, p. 286, says:

“In the year 1004 the lord Abbo was martyred in Aquitaine, in the monastery at La Réole, near the palace once belonging to the kings at Cassinogilum. He wrote nineteen cycles.”

At the Council of Limoges already mentioned, Odolric, abbot, is said to have been “crowned with martyrdom” in Gascony—namely, in the district of Bordeaux, which at that time belonged to the duchy of Gascony.

Ademar writes in his *Chronicle*:

“Abbo came to Saint Peter’s church at La Réole, which is a possession of the monastery of Saint Benedict of the Franks. There he was killed in a Gascon tumult and buried there, and he began to shine forth through miracles. His pastoral staff was sent back to France.
