Bernard, duke of Gascony, punished the killers for the death of so great a man, handing some over to hanging and others to the flames [Col. 0385A]. He also secured without dispute for the Frankish monks of Saint Benedict the whole possession of La Réole, which had previously been held in dispute by invading parties.”

In the necrology of Silviniacum it is recorded: “On the Ides of November: the death of the lord Abbo, abbot.”

13. In the first volume of the *Baluze Miscellanies* there is an encyclical letter of the monks of Floriacum concerning the killing of the same Abbo. I shall not hesitate to transcribe that letter here.

“ To all abbots and faithful of Christ, wherever they dwell: the little community of Floriacum, cast down and bereft of its father. Almost swallowed up by weeping and crushed by grief, extend to us the hand of spiritual assistance, most holy fathers, through the affection of brotherly charity. Fed with the bread of sorrow and the drink of bitterness, may we deserve to be refreshed by your prayers—those whose joy-bringing lyre has been turned into the mourning of sadness, whose organ sounds a mournful lament, and whose delight is only the voice of weepers. The sword of grief has pierced even to our soul as we mourn that, for his zeal on behalf of holy religion, our lord and abbot Abbo has departed from this world, crowned with martyrdom; by the swords of the Gascons he happily deserved to become a happy companion of the blessed martyrs. May your prayer wipe away the stains of his soul—he who was ever your lover and a true admirer of all who serve Christ. Come also to our aid, through fraternal prayers, us whom he has left orphaned, and appease almighty God with the sacrifices of your prayers, so that in his grace he may deign to console the flock deprived of its head and bereft of its pious father. He died on the Ides of November, the feast day of Saint Brictius.”

14. Baronius, following Sigebert, assigns the year of his death to 1003, since he had not yet seen Aimoinus’s little book on Abbo’s life. But after this book was published by Jean du Bois—where the fourth year of the Incarnation and the second indiction are expressly given—he thought the matter could be reconciled by saying that Aimoinus had reckoned the year from the Incarnation and the second indiction from September, whereas Sigebert had calculated the year from the Nativity, which is nine months later than the Incarnation. Yet, with all due respect to so great a man, I would say that Aimoinus’s years of the Incarnation are none other than the years commonly reckoned from the Nativity; and that Sigebert’s calculation—or rather that of his interpolator—must be corrected (for in Miraeus the date of Abbo’s slaughter is printed in a different type), since he put the third year in place of the fourth.

15. It is remarkable how quickly Abbo’s cult was accepted in sacred observances, to such an extent that at the time of the Council of Limoges, that is, in 1031, “his martyrdom was also solemnly celebrated in several churches according to the custom observed for holy martyrs,” as is clear from a sermon delivered then, a fragment of which we quoted above, no. 3. Hence in a very old Floriacum calendar the following words, written by a second hand, are found: “The Ides of November: in Gascony, at the monastery called Squirs, the passion of blessed Abbo, abbot of Floriacum”; and in another: “The Ides: Abbo, abbot and martyr, four lessons.” His office is still celebrated in the monastery of Floriacum and at Regula, where his body is preserved.

16. As for the priory of Regula [La Réole], its founders were Gumbaldus, bishop of Bordeaux, and his brother Willelm, son of Sancho, duke of the Gascons. A document concerning this matter was printed in volume II of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca nova*, p. 543. It is said to be situated “in the regions of Gascony, in the district of Aliard, above the bank of the river Garonne,” namely, ten leagues above Bordeaux. The document is dated “in the year 977, indiction V,” and was drawn up for Richard, abbot of the monastery of Floriacum, to whom this place has been attached ever since; it was anciently called Squirs and in modern times Regula.

Appended to this charter in Labbe are “the customs of the church of Regula,” among which it is established that “no one is to draw a knife, sword, lance, spear, axe, besogium, or any sword in a quarrel.” This statute seems to have been occasioned by Abbo’s killing, since he was pierced by a lance during a quarrel. The priory of Regula still exists, even now as a conventual house under the Congregation of Saint Maur.

17. A few words remain to be said about Abbo’s writings, most of which have perished. Aimoinus lists various works in the following little book: on syllogisms; on computation; on the courses of the sun, moon, and planets, in chapter 3; and a collection from the Fathers, which, Aimoinus says in chapter 7, could not in his time be found at Floriacum because it had been stolen by outsiders. I think this is the collection of canons that we published from a manuscript of Saint Martial at Limoges in volume II of the *Analecta*. In addition, Abbo wrote an *Apologeticus* to Hugh and Rotbert, fragments of which Aimoinus reports in chapters 8 and 9.

He also mentions various letters of Abbo: two to Bernard, abbot of Bellilocus, in chapter 10; one to Gregory V in chapter 12; and another to Odilo, abbot of Cluny, in chapter 13. There, besides acrostic verses addressed to the emperor Otto III, mention is made of Abbo’s work *On the Paschal Cycles*, dedicated to his fellow monks at Floriacum. This work itself had certainly already been published by Bede before Dionysius’s cycles, with a preface in which Abbo mentions “the passing of our most holy father Benedict,” as Aimoinus notes in the same place.

Two other letters by Abbo on the same subject are extant in volume III of the *Analecta*. To these must be added his letter to L., abbot of Fulda, printed by the illustrious Baluze in volume II of the *Miscellanea*; a fragment of this letter was quoted above, no. 5. Papirius Masson had seen a manuscript containing Abbo’s letters; this is the very manuscript from which several of Abbo’s letters, together with his *Apologeticus*, were recently published, as we have already observed.

Let us now examine Aimoinus’s little book on Abbo, whose title in the manuscript is as follows:

# [LIFE OF SAINT ABBO]

## THE LETTER OF AIMOINUS, A MONK OF FLORIACUM, TO HERVEUS, TREASURER OF SAINT MARTIN, BEGINS

### On the life and martyrdom of Saint Abbo, abbot of the monastery of Floriacum

To the most reverend man, lord Herveus, cleric and treasurer of the holy bishop Martin [Note: Concerning this Herveus, see the dialogue of Hugh, archdeacon of Tours, in volume II of the *Analecta*, p. 357 onward, and Glaber, book III, chapter 4.], Aimoinus, the least in understanding among the monks of blessed Father Benedict, sends the unfailing treasure of eternal life.

Because, through the grace of the heavenly Redeemer, you, most beloved lord, have chosen for yourself a chaste and peaceable life, we all whose hearts are devoted to your kindness rejoice with no little joy. For we remember the pleasing disposition of your youth: how gentle you were toward your companions, how gracious toward your elders, and—what is more—how pleasing to God and to all the saints. Your holiness has also shown itself mindful of the examples of goodness that you saw or heard in this sacred monastery of Floriacum. As you daily reflect on the ways by which one may walk the paths of the higher life, you diligently remember the instructions and constant admonitions of your teacher, our holy father Abbo.

It seems superfluous to repeat his diligent care of your generosity in affection, since it is evident that your kindly mind never forgets it. Therefore, struck by the hand of holy charity, because you were loved by him himself and because your devotion is proved to have loved him, one day you deigned to admonish my smallness to undertake, for the benefit of many, to commit his life to writing, or the manner in which he reached martyrdom.

But I understood that this work would displease the minds of many. Nevertheless, eager to obey your affection, which has always been sweet to me from childhood, I strove to complete what you commanded, though in an ineffectual style. I disregard the tongues of those who disparage me and flee for refuge to the assistance of your prayer, which I know to be pleasing to God, so that through your intercession his mercy may grant me eternal joys for this work, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with God the Father, and so forth.

## THE PREFACE TO THE LIFE OR MARTYRDOM OF SAINT ABBO, ABBOT, BEGINS

It was once the practice of ancient paganism to commit to writing in memorials even the dishonorable deeds of those whom its adherents had loved above all, and to report to its gods the praises owed for their worthy achievements. But we, who through Christ’s grace have escaped their error, must maintain the same zeal with a different purpose: namely, to reveal in our writings the lives of the holy Fathers and the victories of the martyrs to the generations that will come after us.

Yet we must refer these very things to the praise of our Creator, through whom they were able either to live well or to receive the crown of martyrdom. Therefore, let us undertake to write, even in rustic speech, the life of one beloved lord—namely, our holy father Abbo—or the manner in which he attained martyrdom.

No one ought to doubt that he was truly a martyr [was], since it is clear that he endured death for the sake of the Truth, which is Christ. Although he did not recall people from the worship of idols, he nevertheless labored to free them—which is the greater thing—from slavery to vices; for those who are continually devoted to such vices are shown to serve not God but demons.

The fact that he was not tortured for a long time inflicts no loss upon his glory or praise, since it is clear that certain martyrs, by confessing the name of Christ alone, even without receiving baptism, deserved the heavenly kingdom after their own blood had been shed by a capital sentence.

But if anyone should think that he must be disparaged because in his life he scarcely performed any wondrous sign, let him read the lives of the outstanding teachers Augustine and Jerome. In them he will find praised not prodigies of temporal signs—for such things are often performed by wicked men—but purity of life, the eloquence of wholesome teaching, and constancy of faith. Nevertheless, this thrice-blessed man was not deprived during his life of the glory of miracles.

Having said these things beforehand against detractors, should they perhaps arise, let us, with the help of Christ’s grace and the prayers of this saint, undertake the work we have proposed.

# THE BOOK BEGINS

## CHAPTER I. Abbo, a citizen of Orléans. He studies at Floriacum. He is entrusted to Saint Benedict.

The venerable Abbo was born in the district of Orléans. His father was called Laetus and his mother Ermengardis. Their bloodline did not nourish them with a vain, swollen, and proud nobility, but they were ennobled by the freedom inherited from ancestors and forebears; and, surpassing every other distinction, the fear of the Lord adorned them with honorable morals.

Born, therefore, to such parents, Abbo was entrusted to the monastery of Floriacum, to be instructed in letters at the school of the clergy serving the church of Saint Peter. Divine providence, as we certainly believe, had predetermined this, so that he might take the beginnings of his literary education there where later he would abundantly offer the streams of learning to minds thirsting for wisdom, and would return to them—or to their descendants—the fruit of the capital entrusted to him doubled, from those by whom he had received only the simple rudiments of the elements.

There were in the same monastery two outstanding men whom kinship of blood had made relatives of his mother. One was called Gunboldus, who, having abandoned the vanities of this world for fear of God, had assumed the habit of the monastic order. The other was called Christianus, who under a clerical garment strove to serve Christ, fearing that a grave loss threatened him if he did not follow, to the best of his ability, the commandments of the one from whom he also derived the mark of his own name.

Both burned with the fire of love for the Lord; both were in the priestly order and, together with the sacrifice of our redemption, offered themselves also to God upon the altar of the heart. At their fervent urging, the parents mentioned above handed over the boy Abbo to serve Christ and the holy father Benedict.

## CHAPTER II. Under Abbot Wlfaldus. He joins piety to study.

At that time the most reverend abbot Wlfaldus, beloved by God and by all the people, was exercising the pastoral care of this most sacred place at Floriacum. The boy Abbo, already mentioned, was therefore handed over by his parents to him, so that, instructed under his direction, he might become a servant of Christ.

When he had been brought before the assembly of the brothers, Wlfaldus asked him by what name he was called. He immediately answered the questioner and declared that he was called Abbo. Then the holy man Wlfaldus, at once inspired by a prophetic spirit and playing upon the name, said: “Abbo, if the last letter is changed, it means ‘father’ in the language of the Achaeans.””

Then, turning to the boy, he said: “From now on, sweetest of boys, present yourself to Christ in such a way that you may be found worthy of the designation of your name. May the almighty Father grant this—the one from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named (Ephesians III, 25)—and make you observe his commandments, so that you may attain eternal joys.”

After saying this, and after his parents had first made a solemn offering of him according to the most discerning institution contained in the rule of the holy father Benedict, he gave him the monastic habit. Once handed over to the schools, he seemed burdensome to none of his companions. He possessed dove-like simplicity joined to serpentine shrewdness, so that by gentleness he might soften the well-disposed and by the acuity of a prudent mind avoid the deceitful.

Even as a young boy he probed the depths of the literary arts with such intense application that whatever he heard once from his teachers he stored firmly in the hidden chambers of his heart. When he had passed beyond childhood, he sought through frequent meditation to restrain the vices of adolescence, knowing that it is written: “Frequent meditation is an affliction of the flesh” (Ecclesiastes XII, 12). For this reason he endeavored to subdue the flesh by continual exercise in letters, so that he might compel it to serve the spirit.

Yet, as often happens with certain young men, he did not abandon the intention of devoted prayer because of his zeal for reading. He loved with complete devotion of mind the purpose of monastic religion, which he proclaimed by wearing its habit; and, as though for a certain relief, after offering the libations of prayers sent to the Lord, he took up the exercises of the liberal arts.

His chief practice was to cling to the sides of the elders. Although at appointed hours he rejoiced in the company of his fellow students, at unsuitable times he made himself closer to the seniors. [Note: Saint Benedict, in chapter 48 of the Rule, forbids a brother to associate with another brother at unsuitable hours; this passage refers to that provision.]

## CHAPTER III. Master of the schools at Floriacum. He visits the academies. He publishes writings.

When he had already attained such a height of knowledge that he was able to distribute to others the gift of the talent he had acquired, he was placed in charge of instructing the students. For several cycles of years he taught them both reading and song with such care that he openly showed his joy at being able to increase the profits of the money entrusted to him.

But, still eager to investigate the greater secrets of knowledge, he visited the workshops of wisdom in various places. Since he had already reached a full understanding of grammar, arithmetic, and dialectic, he continued to add the remaining arts to his intellect. Therefore he went to Paris and Reims to those who professed philosophy, and made some progress with them in astronomy, though not as much as he desired.

From there he returned to Orléans and, although secretly because of envious people, purchased the sweetness of the musical art from a certain cleric for a considerable sum of money. Thus, thoroughly instructed in five of what are called the liberal arts, he surpassed all his contemporaries in the greatness of his wisdom.

Rhetoric and geometry remained. Although he did not attain their fullness as he wished, he nevertheless did not remain entirely unacquainted with them. From the abundance of rhetorical eloquence he read Victorinus, whom Jerome, the interpreter of divine law, proudly declares to have had as his teacher; and he learned no small amount about the multiplicity of geometrical numbers.

Once he had vigorously attained all these things through the lively talent of his mind, their application was easy for him. Finally, he unraveled certain dialectical knots of syllogisms with the greatest clarity and composed various pleasing calculations of computus, in the manner of secular tables. He also committed to the knowledge of posterity, in writing, discussions that he had composed concerning the courses of the sun, moon, and planets.

## CHAPTER IV. He is sent to England. He escapes shipwreck. At that time he was a levite.

Meanwhile a delegation of the English nation came to the monastery of Floriacum, requesting that one of its learned men be granted to them. That nation had been drawn especially to the love of the holy father Benedict and of the aforementioned place for two reasons.

First, because blessed Pope Gregory, when he sent preachers to convert it to the faith of Christ, had particularly impressed upon it the observance of the rule of the same beloved lord Benedict. Second, because a man of great nobility among them, called Oswaldus [Note: The acts of Saint Oswald are given above under the year 992, where the monastery of Ramsey, discussed below, is mentioned], had rejected the world and converted to serve Christ in the aforesaid monastery of Floriacum. On account of the merit of his good life, he was raised by the king of that province to the rank of archbishop and built a monastery in the English region for God and for his patron Saint Benedict.

The envoys whom the preceding account reported as having come to Floriacum were from that monastery. At that time the holy Floriacum community was governed by the reverend father Oylboldus, a man illustrious in lineage and conduct according to worldly rank. By the gentleness of his words rather than by commanding authority, he prevailed upon the blessed man Abbo not to refuse to go and instruct the minds of the people of that nation with the divine and human wisdom in which he was exceptionally gifted.

Abbo, becoming a diligent executor of the command, did not delay setting out for the place to which he was sent, out of regard for the obedience that was familiar to him. Although envious people and calumniators tried to persuade the man of God that the abbot, inflamed by evil intent, wished to send him across the sea so that he would never be able to return, Abbo, trusting in God’s goodness, continually turned over in his heart the apostolic saying: “For those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans VIII, 28).

The preparations for the journey, however, which the lord Oylboldus magnificently provided for the departing man, showed that the matter was otherwise. When they had reached the Morini, from whom the shortest crossing to the English is made, he remained on the shore for nearly a month, the sailors preventing him from entering the rough sea.

Weary of the tedious delay, one day he went to the harbor and summoned the shipmaster, asking whether he could safely enter the sea. The shipmaster replied that it would certainly not be advisable at that moment, but that from the blowing of the winds he understood that favorable sailing would not be long delayed.

Then the man of God said: “If it pleases almighty God, through the merits of our most holy father Benedict, that I cross this sea for the benefit of others, let the sea be made calm at daybreak tomorrow. But if it pleases the supreme Creator otherwise, on that day I shall begin to turn back by the route I came.”

Returning to the lodging, he urged a certain monk named Riculeus, who was in charge of the envoys escorting him, to pray together with him to the Lord: if the Lord did not disapprove of their plan, may he deign to prosper the journey; but if he rejected it, may he inspire their hearts with the desire to return home.

With Riculeus’s agreement, after they had rendered the evening synaxis to God, both prostrated themselves on the ground to pray. When the prayer was finished, they gave their limbs to rest. And behold, at dawn of the following day, the shipmaster’s messenger arrived, calling loudly for them to set out.

They boarded the ship, and with eight other ships accompanying them, proceeded into the open sea. Suddenly they saw porpoises and swordfish playing in the waves, and whales raising their backs like the roofs of enormous buildings. Hearing from the sailors that all these were signs of an approaching storm, the man of God resorted again to the familiar protection of prayer.

The effect of his prayers was not lacking. When the storm arose, the ship in which the man of Christ was staying, together with two others that had followed it, was carried safely into port. The remaining six, along with their crews, were battered by the storms and by the thrusts of the fish and perished. The Lord deigned to perform this sign through him while he was still serving in the office of levite.

## CHAPTER V. He teaches at Ramsey for two years. Beloved by all.

At last, after long journeys by land and sea, he entered the territory of the English. First of all he visited the monastery of Saint Benedict at Ramsey; that was the name of the place founded in those regions by the venerable Oswaldus, whom we mentioned above.

The man who held the office of abbot there was called Germanus, and he too had been raised to that dignity from this sacred monastery of Floriacum. While the holy servant of God Abbo stayed there for nearly two years, he instructed some of the monks in literary knowledge.

During those same years he visited the king of the English and his duke Hebelguinus [Note: More concerning this duke, the founder of the monastery of Ramsey, is found in the acts of Saint Oswald. We possess Abbo’s letter to the monks of Ramsey and others concerning grammatical matters.]. From the king he received only words, but from the duke he received gifts worthy of his holiness, and for as long as he remained with him he was held in great honor.

He also enjoyed friendly intimacy with the venerable bishops already mentioned, Oswaldus and the blessed Dunstan. The former was archbishop of York, the latter of Canterbury. Christ’s grace showed that it had found good pleasure in their lives and conduct by even now illuminating their tombs with the glory of miracles.

They held this blessed man in such admiration that, in seeking to retain him, they disagreed with one another in a charitable—and, so to speak, harmonious—discord.

## CHAPTER VI. He is recalled to Floriacum. Enriched with gifts and made a priest.

At that time he received a letter from his venerable abbot Oylboldus, filled with the anxious tenderness of a father. Among other things, it urged him to hasten his return to his own monastery and to present himself to the sight of those who longed for him.

We have inserted in this volume the beginning of the letter and certain other passages selected from it. The letter began as follows:

“Abbot Oylboldus, through the foreknowledge of God, and the entire harmonious congregation of Father Benedict, to the sweetest brother Abbo: whatever a father says to a son, whatever a friend says to a friend.

Thanks be to almighty God, who inspired your heart so that in Babylonian captivity you would remember most beloved Sion. We offer a sacrifice of jubilation because your letters have gladdened our heart and driven from our memory and mind what we feared most concerning you.

Truly, your lips are a dripping honeycomb: they have poured forth streams of words sweeter to our throat than honey and the honeycomb, and we have received and preserved them among us as more precious than gold and silver.

And a little later:

‘As long as you, a burning and shining lamp, and the other suns as well, have illuminated the house of the Lord with the mirror of prudence, justice, and temperance, the fathers rejoiced in their sons, and our father Benedict rejoiced in his pupils, whom he had raised from their very cradles on the nourishment of philosophy.’”

At last the man of God Abbo, following the admonition of his honorable father Oylboldus and setting his face toward revisiting his native land, was honored with magnificent gifts by the bishops mentioned above.

From the venerable Dunstan he received splendid gifts in silver, to be carried to the holy father Benedict. From the lord Oswaldus he received, together with the grace of the priesthood, all the ministries appropriate to that rank.

Returning, therefore, he brought with him a varied treasure, whose individual forms conveyed a fitting meaning concerning his life. For the golden bracelets and necklaces signified the appropriate recompense for his benefactions and words; the priestly garments foretold the splendor of present and future glory. The golden chalice and the numerous silver coins foreshadowed the innocent purity of his life and the radiance of his eloquence.

After his return to the monastery of the flourishing name, he possessed all these things so remarkably that he became known to many who had previously been unaware of him.

## CHAPTER VII. He is made abbot of Floriacum. He instructs his monks with excellent admonitions and urges them to study and write. His writings.

Afterward, when the venerable abbot Oylboldus had departed this life, the common election of the brothers of Floriacum reached the point of choosing Abbo, as they requested him for themselves as father. At that time a prince named Hugh presided over the royal court of the Franks, and he did not delay giving his consent.

Although, as commonly happens in such matters, some of the brothers stubbornly resisted this election [Note: On this opposition and the disturbances that followed from it, compare what was said above in the *Eulogy of Saint Maiolus*, p. 776 of the preceding volume], nevertheless the authority of the majority—and, as later became clear, of the sounder counsel—prevailed.

The man worthy of God, Abbo, therefore undertook the pastoral office and, as one who understood what he had undertaken, strove to administer it irreproachably to the best of his ability. He admonished his subjects to cast away the thorns of vices and to sow the spices of virtues in the little gardens of their hearts.

He used to say that a continual battle must be maintained against the vices of the flesh, and that one must investigate with every effort by what weapons one might resist its allurements. To accomplish this, after the vows of prayer and the manly struggles of fasting, he considered the study of letters—and especially the practice of dictation—of great benefit.

Since he himself was exceedingly devoted to these pursuits, he scarcely allowed any time to pass without reading, writing, or dictating. Many distinguished writings of his remain that would require a volume of their own. For now we insert a few of them briefly in our pages, for the benefit of future generations.

After clarifying, as we said earlier, the dialectical syllogisms; after setting down calculations of computus; and after explaining the dimensions of the paths of the sun and moon, he also turned his mind to the divine Scriptures. Taking statements from the authorities of many Fathers and, like a most prudent bee, composing honeycombs from various flowers, he drew out a work full of honey.

Although it is not presently found [Note: I think this is the collection of canons published in volume II of the *Analecta*, p. 248 onward], partly through the negligence of our own people and partly because outsiders removed it out of greed, it is nevertheless certain that he excerpted it so that he would have at hand defenses against the bishop of Orléans, who was demanding certain things from him that were not right.

## CHAPTER VIII. Bishop Arnulf is hostile to him. Abbo’s apologetic book to the kings.

Finally, although this man of God was prepared, according to the apostle’s command, to submit to every human creature for God’s sake (I Peter II, 13), he nevertheless understood that the place he governed could later be harmed if he rendered, at the bishop’s pleasure, the forms of submission that the latter required. Therefore he refused to do so throughout his life.

Consequently, when the same bishop, named Arnulfus, realized that Abbo could be convicted neither by reason nor by the words of divine law [words], he openly showed himself hostile to him in controversy. It happened that the satellites of the aforementioned bishop attacked this man of God by night as he was traveling to Tours for the feast of Saint Martin and inflicted serious insults upon him, even wounding some of the men who served him to the point of death.

Although the aforementioned prelate had always shown himself to possess honorable conduct in his other actions, he did not bear this indignantly, as he should have done. Instead, for the sake of public opinion, he brought before Abbo some of those who had committed this crime, as though for satisfaction, so that they might be beaten with rods.

But the servant of God, perceiving that this was not being done with a righteous intention and remembering the Lord’s statement in Scripture, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Romans II, 22), refused to accept what was offered. Because he refrained from taking vengeance himself, he deserved to have the Lord avenge him.

For we learned from widespread report that some of those men were found dead in their beds, carried off by sudden death, while others had been driven mad. Indeed, because it is difficult to be free from envy in prosperity, he was also torn by the envious tooth of certain other prelates and men of our order—namely, monks—whom we now think it unnecessary to identify by name.

Therefore, he wrote an apologetic book to the lords of the realm, the illustrious kings of France, Hugh and his son Rotbert, who loved him greatly because of the path of supreme equity and truth that this servant of God himself followed harmlessly and faithfully. The book begins as follows:

“It often happens that, while the excessive horror of disasters rising around us exhausts the mind, the mind, disturbed by that very horror, does not bring forth what it ought to say. Instead, carried elsewhere by a phantasm of thoughts, it says what ought to be kept silent and, consequently, keeps silent about what ought to be said.

For the one who desires to arrange the secret of truth through reasoning always loves the repose of the highest tranquility. Therefore, from the very rudiments of learning, ‘As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs’ (Psalm XLI, 2) for the laborious spiritual leisure of philosophy.

When I was turning this leisure into an honorable occupation for the benefit of many, I abandoned it because of my sins and was, in a manner of speaking, led back to the anxieties of the world. Under the care of pastoral government, I am daily sustained by the water of anguish and the bread of tribulation.

The treacherous cunning of my rivals gnaws at me with a dog’s tooth; the frequent bitterness of my adversaries surrounds me with barking. They murmur nothing else against me except that I wish the senate of monks to remain safe. I sought the advancement of our commonwealth and, with whatever authority I possessed, opposed the quibbling of those who plotted against it.

‘I have not altogether hidden mercy and truth from the great assembly’ (Psalm XXXIX, 11).

Because of such evils they lie in wait for my blood and pursue me with re-enlisted hatreds, to such a degree that even royal majesty does not deter them from secretly murdering me if opportunity or time should favor them. Therefore, assiduously in my prayers I beseech the Lord to judge and discern my cause as usual and to rescue me from the unjust and deceitful man (Psalm XLII, 1).”

In the same book, when mentioning heretics, he inserts the following after several other passages:

“Our Fathers so persecuted all heresies that, after first setting forth the faith, they examined in their councils whether anyone held an opinion contrary to the apostles themselves. Whoever was found to do so was either immediately brought back to the body of the Church or, until he renounced his error, struck with anathema and deprived of Catholic communion.

The orthodox were no more careful to avoid touching a serpent than to avoid associating with those contaminated by such leprosy. Hence the canons forbid us, if we know ourselves to be Catholics, even to pray with them.

For under the emperor Marcian, at Chalcedon, a session lasting fifteen days and more was held concerning this matter, with six hundred bishops present, or twelve hundred, as some prefer to say. The pious emperor abundantly supplied all of them from his own resources with whatever was needed, until they had rejected all heretics—that is, those who in word or deed had held opinions different from the holy apostles.

When this had been done, the purity of the faith so pleased the pious emperor that he himself, together with his wife, publicly professed it in writing before that great council. Imitate his pious religion, our most beloved kings Hugh and Rotbert, if you wish to be heirs and coheirs with Christ in the land of the living; drive every heretical depravity from your kingdom, so that God may preserve you in eternal peace.”

And a little later, after lamenting that, among the other heresies, the desolation [possibly: prayer] of churches had also risen in these regions, he adds:

“Let whoever wishes to be saved beware of believing that she—namely, the Church—is the possession of anyone other than God alone. Hence it is said to Peter, the chief of the apostles: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church’ (Matthew XVI, 18). He says ‘my,’ not ‘your.’

And Christ says elsewhere: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer’ (Matthew XXI, 13). The Psalmist also says: ‘Holiness befits your house, O Lord’ (Psalm XCXII, 5).

If, therefore, the Church is not Peter’s, whose will it be? Or will Peter’s successors dare to claim for themselves a power that Peter, the chief of the Church, did not possess?

Certainly, most beloved princes, we neither live nor speak as Catholics when I say that the Church is mine and another says that it is his. And, like certain beasts—compared with beasts without understanding—we sometimes offer both churches for sale, and do not fear to buy those put up for sale by others.

There is also another most serious error: it is said that the altar belongs to the bishop and the church to some other lord, although from the consecrated building and the altar one single thing is formed, which is called a church, just as one human being consists of body and soul.

See, most equitable princes, where greed leads us while charity grows cold.”

## CHAPTER IX. The Council at Saint-Denis concerning tithes. Abbo composes a defense.

In those days, at the monastery of Saint-Denis, not far from Paris, a council of a very large number of bishops was assembled. Although they ought to have spoken about the purity of the faith and the correction of the evil conduct both of themselves and of their subjects, in accordance with the common proverb they turned their entire discourse to the tithes of the churches [Note: In the tenth century controversies likewise arose in Germany concerning the tithes of monasteries; see *Ex saeculi III*, part II, p. 29], which they sought to take away from laymen and from monks serving God. When the venerable worshiper of God Abbo resisted them in this matter, they stirred up the undifferentiated force of the populace against him; and when a sudden riot arose, such fear seized the bishops that, abandoning the public assembly, each fled in every direction.

Among them was Sewinus, archbishop of Sens, who had arrogated to himself the primacy of Gaul at that synod and seized also the primacy in flight. While fleeing, he was struck with an axe between the shoulders, smeared with mud by the townspeople, and escaped only with difficulty. Fear likewise gave such swift wings to one of the bishops as he fled that, abandoning the lavish preparations for the banquet he had arranged for himself, he made his way in terrified flight toward the walls of the nearby city of Paris.

Therefore, perceiving that the whole charge for so great an injury was being cast upon himself by the aforesaid Arnulf as well as by the other bishops, this devoted servant of God Abbo, in the same *Apology*, clears himself not only of this accusation but also of certain others, in these words:

> “I do not, he says, withdraw myself from your examination, O kings, and from that of other wise men, because I suspect that I have thought contrary to the canons. I am accused of having laid violent hands on bishops through monks; I am denounced as having transferred your goodwill to your own bishop; I am charged with having associated with certain excommunicated persons. But let it be so: what canonical judgment did I contradict, when at that council I could scarcely see an open book? Or was that truly a council at which men arrived reconciled and departed unreconciled, when those who were at variance ought either to have been reconciled there or punished with canonical severity? What had the bishops committed against me personally, so that I should have wished to harm them even in thought—especially since it happened that a man who was not my enemy, but most friendly to me in faith and action, endured graver dangers?
>
> “Behold, before God in Christ I do not lie: when I heard the outcry of those pursuing them, I grieved beyond what can be expressed, remembering the former friendship and the benefits of so great a man, whose snow-white hair showed his venerable head, apart from the prerogative of primacy and the episcopal insignia. By what persuasion did I deceive you, so that you would withdraw your goodwill from the best and bestow it upon those who had deserved ill? Am I God, who changes minds, changes hearts, changes kingdoms and times? I openly confess that I know nothing of magic and have learned nothing of evil arts.”

A little later he adds:

> “Finally, when he asserts that I mixed with excommunicated persons, I certainly acted according to the example of the man who received the sons of Belial when, under cover of night, they advanced to murder me, after their own archbishop—Sewinus, a man of singular merit—and Odo, bishop of Chartres, as well as other men of great life and religion, had anathematized them. Indignant that unjust judgments should arise, he cries out in the voice of one who curses: ‘O the times! O the morals!’ Certainly those who wish to carry out their perverse desires in the workshop of falsehood themselves strive to establish unjust laws.”

Finally, since he was not unaware that his writings displeased many, he commends himself to the kings, especially to lord Rotbert, whom he knew to be learned in letters and therefore attentive to students, writing as follows:

> “Moreover, although I familiarly address my lords and advise what is good, I know that the minds of many are aroused against me, in accordance with the saying of the comic poet:
>
> “ ‘Obsequiousness wins friends; truth gives birth to hatred.’  
> “ *(Terence, Andria* I.1.41.)
>
> “I am not greatly troubled by their hostility, my sweet glory, Rotbert, whom divine goodness, born from royal ancestors, has brought to the summit of the kingdom, if, after the Lord and his saints, I am especially sustained by your help and counsel—whose mention I never omit in my daily prayers.”

## CHAPTER X. Bernard, abbot of Bellilocum, of illustrious family and bishop of Cahors; Bernard of Bellilocum, of illustrious family and bishop of Cahors; Abbo gives him excellent advice. He attacks simony. The first pilgrimages to Jerusalem. Bernard’s journey to Rome, etc. Another letter of Abbo to him. Laws must be interpreted according to the circumstances of cases.

To Bernard, abbot of Bellilocum, among other things he sent the texts of two letters, whose contents we have thought should not be passed over. This Bernard, in fact, had been offered to God by his father Hugo, who was born of a distinguished—though not the highest—rank among the nobles of Aquitaine. From a numerous company of sons, Hugo had dedicated him to service and sent him to the monastery of Saint Benedict at Fleury to be instructed in letters.

Abbo, who was full of every virtue, received Bernard, at the command of his venerable abbot Richard, as his foster-son; he loved him greatly and, whenever the opportunity of time permitted, instructed him in the liberal arts. But after no long interval of years Bernard was recalled by his father and given the abbey of Solignac, which Saint Eligius had once built. Not long afterward he obtained Bellilocum, a place which his father had acquired by right of war and victorious arms.

When Count Willelmus of Toulouse intended to entrust him with the bishopric of Cahors, which he now governs, both the count himself and the archbishop of Bourges, under whose jurisdiction that church lies, demanded from him a considerable sum of money. For this reason the holy Abbo sent a charitable letter to his foster-son, who was asking what ought to be done. It ran as follows:

> “Since divine goodness has raised you, his servant, to very many honors, which you cultivate so greatly through the distinction of your virtues that you make yourself an example to many good men, I exhort and admonish you, mindful of your profession, to seek those degrees of excellence in which you will not offend the Lord.”

After some further remarks, speaking of those who either sell or buy the grace of the Holy Spirit, he says:

> “Such buyers weave certain webs, as it were webs of spiders, with which they defend themselves by saying that they buy not a blessing but the possessions of the Church. But whose possession is the Church, if not God’s alone? Who is its lord, if not God? For although the present Church needs two advocates, one in temporal matters and the other in spiritual matters, it nevertheless possesses neither as lord—neither of whom can sell or buy the Church, which Christ redeemed with his blood.”

Giving him counsel, he concludes the letter with this sentence:

> “Therefore, never consent in any way to become a heretic, because the man who attacks the faith that the catholic Church held under the holy apostles performs penance for his sins in vain.”

But Bernard, at last wearied of the goods of this life, seeing the charity of many growing cold and therefore iniquity abounding, resolved in his mind to leave everything he possessed and seek Jerusalem. His father had begun and undertaken that journey in fulfillment of a vow of penance before almost all the inhabitants of Gaul of that period.

Yet Bernard did not intend to accomplish this without the judgment or counsel of his teacher. He came to the monastery at Fleury, intending to disclose the secrets of his heart to this master of his, who was complete in every virtue. Abbo, however, forbade the journey to Jerusalem; but, so that he would not appear altogether to oppose Bernard’s will, he permitted him to travel to Rome and visit Mount Garganus. With fatherly affection, he assigned some of his own men to accompany or serve him and allowed them to depart with a brotherly blessing.

Compelled by the complaints of his relatives, who were likewise going to visit the thresholds of the apostles and said that, after his departure, clandestine wars had broken out among them, he sent back to him from the journey the priest Constantine, whom the pious master himself had assigned to Bernard for his service. He instructed Constantine to tell him that he had been compelled by the needs of his people to return home; yet he would do nothing without Bernard’s command, and indeed would obey him in all things, as he had previously promised.

At the same time Constantine was to raise the question whether it would be better to abandon everything or, in order to provide protection for his people, to serve the world outwardly, at least in appearance. Abbo, a lover of truth, sent him a written reply in which he explained what seemed more right to him, while granting Bernard the freedom to choose what he himself preferred.

In this letter Abbo mourns and laments, not only for Bernard the abbot but also for all his companions on the journey, because they had either suffered serious hardship or died. Among them was lord Remigius the monk, who later presided over the cell in which the blessed Abbo now rests, buried in body. Abbo had sent him to serve the aforesaid abbot, now bishop; he was severely afflicted by a violent fever.

We have thought it worthwhile to insert the letter in its entirety into this volume, to demonstrate the benevolent affection of this man of God. In his other letters we shall provide abbreviated accounts. It is as follows:

> “To my lord, the most beloved of abbots, BERNARD, ABBO, servant of the servants of God.
>
> “I have received, venerable father in Christ, the living letter of your pilgrimage, and from a priest almost dead I have learned what you, half-alive amid the waves of your thoughts, are mourning: the calamity of your homeland has presently made you powerless to fulfill the vow you conceived and, as I believe, has delayed your innate devotion but has not extinguished it entirely.
>
> “When I heard this, I confess that I grieved exceedingly and satisfied my sorrow with tears, since the great multitude of brothers around me groaned out of longing for you. As all groaned together, there returned to our memory the fact that Hugo, a man of great gravity, your companion on the journey and partner in labor, died amid many good men’s tears—more grievously to none than to you, for whose love, after the Lord, he left his homeland and parents and ended his life in exile.
>
> “After I had given sufficient expression to my grief, at last I took counsel for myself, since I could not do so for you in your absence. In my prayers during the day I seem to see you, while I do not cease to offer to almighty God the sacrifice of a contrite spirit.
>
> “For I was exceedingly afraid of what the bearer of your message disclosed: namely, that your face had so withered that you could scarcely remain standing, deprived not only of the sobriety and friendship of the deceased but also of the strength of your own body.
>
> “I fear, therefore, that the snares of the devil—which are many and hedge in the paths of God’s servants with thorns—may turn you away from the way of God’s commandments and compel you to look back before you arrive at Segor, the little city in which, by saving your soul, you may be saved (Genesis XXII).
>
> “For I know that now herds of relatives, phalanxes of soldiers, and crowds of friends are clamoring around you; and those who have been brought in as reinforcements persuade you with declamatory arguments of what they judge useful for themselves, not for you. But, with the calves tied up at home, you know what the cows did that carried the ark of the covenant while lowing: without turning aside to the right or to the left, they brought it to Beth-shemesh (1 Samuel VI.12).
>
> “Mindful of this deed, remember that the tail of the victim is commanded to be offered in sacrifice, and let no thought of household affairs creep in that may turn you aside from the straight path.
>
> “For I remember what you said to me in familiar conversation when you had decided to depart for Rome, asking whether the pastoral care once undertaken ought to be abandoned and whether we should give a bill of divorce to the brothers and sons who oppose us on the way of God. When I replied that I knew this to be certain on the authority of the Fathers, and perceived that death was gaining mastery over the sheep entrusted to you, I neither dared nor ought to persuade you to regard yourself as unfruitful, even for yourself, setting before you the example of Paul fleeing from Damascus and of the blessed father Benedict, legislator of monks.
>
> “Finally, in many cases an occasion presents itself which makes the difficulty of a contrary law better by a good outcome. Who would not praise the care of pastoral governance if it is beneficial? Who, again, would not praise the shepherd’s benevolence toward himself if it does not benefit others?
>
> “There is often something in the divine commandments that is also found in ancient edicts. There is a law: ‘If any male enters the temple of Venus, let him be punished with death.’ A certain young man, passing by the temple of Venus, saw his mother being beaten inside; he entered and rescued her. He was accused of having acted contrary to the law. He defended himself by saying that he had obeyed the law; and, while the parties disputed, if ignorance does not benefit the one who struck her, the circumstance of compassion helps him.
>
> “The same is found in our Gospels, where we are commanded not only to leave a wife but even to hate her, with the reward proposed that whoever does this will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life. Again, the man who has dismissed his wife is written to be worthy not of a reward but of the punishment prescribed for adulterers.
>
> “Moreover, both the man who rescued his mother and the man who dismissed his wife suffer prejudice if they are punished, since each thinks that he pleases the author of the law in the very matter through which he is judged to have offended.
>
> “Therefore, dearest father, do not regard good as better than evil, but believe that one good is better than another good. From contrary judgments choose the one by which you may renounce vices and grow through the moral exercises of the virtues.
>
> “Finally, while you ought to bear the burden of an abbot, you are uncertain whether you ought to lay it down. Take discretion, which you especially need, as the mother of the virtues; ascend the tribunal of conscience and examine by judgment what is more useful or honorable for your soul.
>
> “To fulfill the office of abbot and seek the profit of souls is most honorable for one to whom it is not impossible. But for the man to whom the wickedness of his subjects makes it impossible, what remains except that he should think it more honorable to obey the divine oracle in which it is written: ‘My son, have mercy on your soul by pleasing God’? (Ecclesiasticus XXX.24.)
>
> “Certainly, in Ezekiel also, the watchman who cries out but is not heard frees his own soul; and according to father Benedict, the despised and rejected shepherd is absolved if he has shown every care toward the sheep entrusted to him.
>
> “For the rest, venerable father, at least on the feast of our father Benedict, let us know what pleases you, so that we may soon be certain of the salvation we desire for you.”

## CHAPTER XI. Abbo’s two journeys to Rome. Pope Gregory’s reply to him.

Meanwhile the distinguished Abbo set out for Rome with suitable preparations, intending to strengthen—or rather renew—the privileges of the church entrusted to him. He found, however, not the kind of pontiff of the apostolic see whom he wished or ought to have found, a man named John. He discovered him to be eager for shameful profit and venal in all his actions [Note: That is, John XV, who died in 996 after eleven years of pontificate; Gregory V succeeded him, to whom Abbo was sent as Rotbert’s envoy].

After cursing him, Abbo visited the holy places for the sake of prayer and returned to his own monastery, having purchased several silk cloaks of excellent appearance, suitable for ecclesiastical adornment.

A few years later an occasion arose for him to return to the Roman city, at the request and entreaties of the glorious king Rotbert. The principal reason for which he was sent was this: Arnulf, archbishop of Reims, had been deprived of his see and committed to custody without a lawful hearing. For this reason Gregory, who had succeeded John in the apostolic see and was distinguished not only by nobility of birth but also by integrity of mind, threatened to bring an anathema upon the entire kingdom of the Franks.

Thus the servant of Christ and of God was compelled to return to Italy. Although he was burdened by the weight of his body—for in the regions beyond the sea the unusual quality of the pilgrims’ food and his drinking of cooked beverages had made his body heavy—he was nevertheless in no way wearied by the labor. Nor did his very corpulence bring upon him any stain of disgrace. Since he was eager for peace, he considered every kind of fatigue light, provided that he might find the man whom, as rumor had told him, he had heard could restore the discipline of religion to its former condition.

Setting out, he once again reached the walls of Rome. When he did not find there the man whom he sought, he searched through hollow valleys and across rugged mountains and at last found him in the territory of the men of Spoleto.

When the two lights of the Church saw one another, they rejoiced with a joy beyond belief and rushed into each other’s arms. Abbo, the guardian of true humility, first delivered words of greeting on behalf of the king. Then the truly apostolic priest, having returned the greeting with a blessing, said to the blessed man:

> “I rejoice that you have arrived safely, son, most fervent guardian, as I have learned, of the Church and of truth. A deafening report about you has filled my ears: that you possess both divine and human wisdom and cannot be drawn away from the right of justice by any friendship.
>
> “I confess that I have long desired to behold your face and have yearned to enjoy your friendly conversation. Let us therefore enjoy the conversations we have desired, and for a while refresh our minds with alternating readings of divine and worldly books.
>
> “Moreover, I want you to know one thing: I willingly receive your embassy, and I shall do whatever you advise. It will be your task to ask, and mine to grant your requests as far as possible. For I know that you will ask nothing contrary to right and justice, and therefore I know that it would not be proper for me to oppose you.”

After these words, he provided him with everything necessary for sustenance and allowed him to depart to his lodging. He kept him there for about eight days, frequently inviting him to his table, and willingly assented to everything for which he had come.

## CHAPTER XII. The privileges and gifts granted to Abbo by him. The substance of the privilege. The restoration of Archbishop Arnulf.

Then the careful shepherd Abbo, mindful of the welfare of the place he governed, asked that an apostolic privilege be granted for it. The pope, worthy of God, bestowed it so favorably that he not only sought no financial profit but also gave Abbo incense and a chasuble for use during the solemn celebration of Mass, and sent the joyful servant of God back to his own home.

Among other provisions, that privilege stated that the bishop of Orléans was not to visit the monastery at Fleury unless invited, and that no bishop was ever to prohibit divine service in that monastery, even if the entire kingdom of Gaul were struck by the punishment of anathema from the apostolic see because of the sins of the people.

But lest anyone think that the apostolic lord and holy Abbo had acted here contrary to the rules of the holy Fathers, it seemed necessary to us to insert a few examples from the many letters of Pope Gregory the Great. In seeking out such examples, this blessed man always had a pious purpose. He knew that Gregory had never either thought or written anything contrary to the decrees of the canons.

That distinguished Pope Gregory therefore writes to Maximian, bishop of Ravenna, among other things:

> “Whenever an abbot wishes to come or send someone to the Roman pontiff for the benefit of his monastery, he must be permitted to do so in every way.”

He also frequently wrote, both to the pontiff mentioned above and to his predecessor John, that monasteries ought not to be harassed by bishops and clergy. To the abbot Luminosus, concerning the same matter, he says, among other things:

> “By our command sent to Castorius, our brother and fellow bishop, and to his successors, we have entirely removed the power of inflicting any injury upon you and your monastery, so that he might neither henceforth burden you, nor inventory the property of the monastery, nor permit a public procession to take place there.”

To the same Castorius, after some intervening remarks, he writes:

> “We absolutely forbid public Masses to be celebrated there by a bishop—that is, plainly, in the monastery—lest in the retreats of God’s servants any opportunity be given for public gatherings, and lest the more frequent entry of women, God forbid, usually draw simpler minds into scandal.”

That divine service ought not to be forbidden to monasteries he asserts in a letter to John, bishop of Orvieto:

> “Agapitus, abbot of the monastery of Saint George, has informed us that he is suffering many burdens from your holiness. Not only are you preventing those things by which the monastery might receive some assistance in time of need, but Masses are also forbidden to be celebrated in the monastery, and you even prohibit the burial of the dead there.
>
> “If this is so, we exhort you to withdraw from such inhumanity and to permit the dead to be buried there and Masses to be celebrated without any further objection, lest the aforesaid venerable man be compelled to lodge another complaint concerning the matters just mentioned.”

Enough, however, has been said about these matters; let us now return to the order of the narrative we began.

When the honorable Abbo returned to the king who had sent him, he announced that everything for which he had gone had been accomplished. He released Arnulf of Reims from custody and restored him to his episcopate; he returned to him the pallium sent by the lord pope [Note: Cossartius correctly infers from this that Arnulf was not restored immediately after the Council of Reims of 995, under John XV, but only under Gregory V, during whose pontificate this embassy took place. See vol. IX, cols. 757–758].

Afterward, through messengers, he sent a friendly and fully respectful letter to the venerable apostolic lord Gregory, informing him that he had completed everything as Gregory had ordered. Its opening is as follows:

> “To the lord ever venerable in Christ, prelate of the holy Roman and apostolic see, and therefore teacher of the universal Church, his own Abbo, rector of Fleury, sends greetings in Christ.
>
> “It often happens that the judgment of complete truth falters because of the interpretation of a malicious intermediary. To avoid this, venerable father, I faithfully and simply conveyed the thoughts of your mind, as you commanded, and I did not fear the king’s anger while keeping in full the faith I had promised you, since I added nothing, subtracted nothing, changed nothing, and omitted nothing.
>
> “Arnulf himself is a witness to all these things, having been freed and released from custody. I presented your pallium to him in the same condition in which I had received it from your holy hands” [Note: This passage must be restored here from a difficult manuscript; Vossius read, “I presented the pallium covered.”].

At the end of the letter he also remembers the chasuble given to him by Gregory, saying:

> “For, mindful of your generosity, as a servant I give thanks to the Lord, and when I use your gift, the chasuble, during the solemn celebration of Mass, I can in no way forget you in my offerings. For the rest, I have resolved always to obey you; may God preserve your apostolate in everlasting peace.”

## CHAPTER XIII. Some letters and writings of Abbo.

He also composed a letter in hexameter verses to the emperor Otto, incomparable in the poetry of the learned men of that time. He took his model from a book of Porphyry and made the following verse the subject and, as it were, the foundation of the whole work:

> “Otto, mighty Caesar, yield to our buskin.”

This verse ends with the same letter with which it begins. Thus, since it occupies both the beginnings and the ends of all the verses, it also stands upright through the middle of the letter and proceeds transversely in the form of a cross; nevertheless, it becomes the concluding line of the poem. In this way it can be read six times in different arrangements, and it makes four quadrangles in the letter [Col. 0404A]. In those quadrangles four names are read, placed upright: in two of them, Otto and Caesar; in the others, Abbo and abba. Although these are written in red and sound as separate words, they are arranged in sequence together with the other letters of the verses. See below.

The same venerable Abbo also wrote to Odilo, the venerable abbot of Cluny, a man of sound and religious life, explaining clearly why the chapter divisions or annotations found in the Gospels differ among themselves and what should be understood concerning the sign ·:. [Note: *Erae* or *herae* sometimes signify divisions of chapters; see *Analecta*, vol. II, pp. 458–459.]

There are also other writings of this holy father addressed to other persons, which, lest they cause the reader weariness, we shall for the moment conceal in silence.

One matter must not be omitted: he corrected the cycles of the years of the Lord’s Incarnation, from the beginning of the Incarnate Word down to his own times, according to the true testimony of the Gospels, and extended them afterward to approximately the year 1595. He entrusted the preface of this work to his brothers and sons, namely to us, the monks of Fleury, and mentions the year of the passing of our most holy father Benedict [Note: This little work is discussed in the preliminary observations].

## CHAPTER XIV. A leper healed by him.

It is enough now to have brought forth, as far as possible, the praise of his faithful tongue and the elegance of his polished style. But it is eminently worthy of being proclaimed by renowned report among the peoples that this blessed man was not left by God without miracles while he still dwelt in the world present in the flesh. Rather, God showed that he had been pleased with his life by making it distinguished through miracles.

At that same time there was a certain man whom a dreadful stain of leprosy had covered. He was instructed in a dream to seek from this man of God the help of his health. Fearing to approach him personally, he went to a monk named Elisiernus [Boscius incorrectly reads “Elizerius”], a man of good reputation and excellent conduct, who was especially close to this holy man.

He explained to him the cause of his need and the manner of the vision that had been revealed. He said that it had been disclosed to him that the servant of Christ ought to wash his hands in exorcised water, and that the sick man himself should receive this water and pour it over his diseased limbs.

At first, on hearing this, the monk refused to believe his words and began to rebuke him:

> “Why, O man, do you come to test us by presenting the delusions of your dreams as truth? Do not, do not seek to seduce our minds with your false flatteries.”

Then the sick man solemnly swore that he was presenting no cloud of deceit but was asserting the truth.

The brother therefore went to the thrice-blessed and divine man of whom we are speaking and disclosed to him the oracle he had heard from the sick man. Abbo, however, became somewhat agitated and, with an expression of indignation, almost in tears, said:

> “I have not hitherto given you such examples that anyone should think I desire the attentions of flattery. Therefore, if you wish to be called and to be my beloved, take care that I never hear this word from your mouth again—especially since I know that I am in no way capable of such things [the text reads *fore*; read *esse*, “to be”] and that deeds of this sort belong to holy men.”

When the brother objected that he ought not to conceal a grace divinely bestowed upon him, which might be believed capable of helping those who sought healing—especially since the sick man was persuading him by a straightforward and simple faith, not by the desire of flatterers—Abbo at last allowed himself to be overcome.

Water was brought and blessed; he washed his hands in it, gave it to the aforesaid monk, and commanded him to carry it to the sick man who had requested it.

The monk brought the water to the leper and said to him:

> “Now your infirmity is apparent to all. If, therefore, you wish us to give credence to your words, after you have poured these waters over yourself, present yourself to our sight on the third day.”

The sick man did as he had been commanded. Before the appointed period had elapsed, behold, the man who had long appeared discolored was seen by everyone to have been clothed again in his natural appearance [reading: “clothed again,” masculine].

When this seemed clearly credible to the observant brother, he immediately took care to report to the man of God what had happened. Abbo, invoking the name of Christ with terrible solemnity, forbade him to make the matter known to anyone, either by himself or through the man who had been healed, as long as the holy man remained in the body.

In this matter he imitated the example of the Lord Christ and our Redeemer, who, addressing the leper he had healed, said: “See that you tell no one” (Matthew VIII.4).

After the passing of this most holy man, the aforesaid lord Elisiernus reported these events to us under oath as a witness to their truth. We have endeavored to recount them simply, without diminishing the truth or increasing falsehood. That venerable Elisiernus died a praiseworthy death before a year had passed from the time when he told us these things.

## CHAPTER XV. The church ornaments made by him.

It is not believed to depart from a proper kind of praise if our account explains what was done under him or through him for the adornment of the house of God, which is the Church—especially since, among the praises of Solomon, this is chiefly celebrated: that he built the Lord’s temple at magnificent expense.

Although his limited resources could not equal the wealth of wealthy Solomon, nevertheless what was accomplished, insofar as the poverty of the place he governed and the harshness of the times permitted, ought not to be hidden in silence.

He completed the front panel of the altar of holy Mary, Mother of God, which his predecessor, lord Oylbold, had begun to construct in gold. He had two adjoining panels enlarged and covered with silver. To summarize much in few words, six altars—both his own and those belonging to the monks living under his rule—shone with silver plates fastened to them through devout care: one dedicated to God under the name of Father Benedict; another under the name of the supreme and undivided Trinity; and also altars of Saint Stephen, Saint Anianus, Saint John the Evangelist, and his brother, blessed James.

A wooden screen placed around the tomb of the renowned confessor of Christ, Benedict, was likewise adorned with a similar appearance of metal; upon it certain miracles of that beloved Lord are visibly represented by the art of engraving.

These things, and several others, were completed at the monastery of Fleury under the distinguished father Abbo through the diligence and administration of the honorable monk Gauzfred, to whom Abbo had entrusted the custody of the sacred treasures. Through Gauzfred’s care a stone treasury was also built, sufficiently suitable for warding off the violence of fire, should it break out—which God forbid! The venerable father Abbo whom we are discussing supplied the expenses.

Since we have related many things about his way of life and writings, lest we weary the reader with excessive talk, let us turn our style to recounting his passing.

## CHAPTER XVI. He visits the monastery of Regula to reform it. He leaves some of his men there.

Thus, when this Abbo, beloved by God and venerable among men, had labored energetically for sixteen continuous years in the pastoral office entrusted to him by God, he departed for Gascony.

In that region there is a certain monastery formerly called, as is said, Squirs; by people of the present time it is called by the opposite name, Regula. No rule of religion and scarcely any traces of good conduct had appeared in that place down to those times.

Guillelmus, son of Sancho, count of Bordeaux and duke of all Gascony, having heard the reputation for religious life of lord Richard, abbot of Fleury, had long before entrusted that place to him and his successors to govern. This has been explained more fully in the book we wrote about the life and deeds of the abbots of our monastery [Note: It is regrettable that this book has been lost, or at least remains hidden somewhere even now].

At that place, both the venerable Richard himself and two of his successors, Amalbert and Oylbold, labored long and hard so that the place might truly deserve, through the conduct of its inhabitants, to bear its proper name. Nothing useful, however, was accomplished.

After them, when this blessed man Abbo had attained the rank of abbot, certain people persuaded him to go there. He replied jokingly that he would go there when he had grown weary of life. Although he said this in jest, the outcome of events afterward was indeed so.

It was said, finally, that none of his predecessors had been permitted to live long after traveling to Gascony.

At last Abbo went to the aforesaid region. He visited the counts of that land, the sons of the aforementioned Guillelmus, Bernard and Sancho, and arranged that the place should be governed not according to his own will but according to theirs.

At that time he returned safely to his own monastery, leaving some of his men behind, as though for the protection of the place. But those whom he left behind, fearing the treachery of the Gascons, remained unwillingly. Later, after suffering many injuries at the hands of the Gascons, they returned to him together with those whom he had sent to them as assistants.

When Abbo found that their negligence was to blame [the text reads *fore*; read *fuisse*, “to have been”], he sent others to correct what the first men had neglected. Those men suffered similar treatment, sent messengers to him, and informed him of what they were enduring. They threatened that, unless help were brought to them quickly, they would abandon the place and return to their own homes.

They also reported to him one thing known from the decision of the counts [the text reads *fore*; read *esse*, “to be”]: if he once came to them, they would have freer authority over the place than before. He should declare verbally to both the counts and the viscount Amalguinus, whom he had given them as their advocate, what he himself wished. Those whom he decided should remain would remain; those whom he judged should leave, the aforesaid princes promised to expel by force.

## CHAPTER XVII. His second journey to Regula through Poitiers, etc.

At last, driven by such arguments, and with the final day of his calling already approaching, he undertook the journey for a second time, taking as companions from among the monks the aforementioned Remigius, myself—Aimoinus, who write this—and William, who, according to the custom of abbots, was then his attendant.

[**Note:** The abbot’s attendants were his household officials, such as the chaplain, steward, and keeper of the seal. See the *Glossary* appended to Matthew Paris. Here the abbot’s attendant seems to have been the bearer of the seal, on which the abbot’s image was represented, or certainly the chaplain, who customarily carried the pastoral staff before him. Indeed, Abbo’s staff was sent back to France—that is, to Fleury—after his death, as the monk Ademar bears witness in his *Chronicle*.]

Once he had set out upon the road, he ordered the envoys who had come on his behalf to go ahead of him, to inform the counts and the advocate of his arrival, and to arrange that they should not delay the conference while he was coming to them. He himself, neglecting nothing that might benefit the monastery he governed, proceeded to Poitiers and visited William, count of that city, intending to ask his assistance concerning his monastery’s estate called Salx, which had been grievously oppressed by the claims of its advocates. After the count had promised that, once Abbo had returned, a fair hearing would be granted him, he lingered there for a short time on another matter.

Perhaps the abbot of the monastery of Saint Cyprian, situated in the suburb of Poitiers and related by blood to that saint, a man named Gislebertus, was being falsely accused of a crime. He detained Abbo with the most humble entreaty, asking him to deign to take part in his case, which he thought would shortly be brought before the court. But when the shameless accuser withdrew, fearing that the truth might become evident, the man of God Abbo—who wished, insofar as he was able, to aid all who suffered injury—gave his kinsman a letter to carry on his behalf to Odilo, abbot of the Cluniacs, to whom that monastery was subject. These letters are evidently the last of his correspondence, and they are preserved among us with the rest.

[**Note:** Here Jean du Bois mentions Papirius Masson, who possessed Abbo’s letters and kept them concealed, to the great loss of the republic; but now we have them in print from the Pithoean manuscript.]

He hastened to bring the journey he had begun to completion. Accordingly, on the fifth day after we had arrived there, having celebrated the solemnity of All Saints, we departed on the following Thursday and, passing through the monastery of Charroux, reached the little monastery of Nantolium, founded in honor of the most holy father Benedict. Departing from there on Saturday, we arrived at Angoulême.

[**Note:** He lodged at the monastery of Saint Eparchius, commonly called Saint Cybard, at Angoulême, as Ademar, a monk of that place, bears witness.]

We left that city on Sunday. As we walked along uncertain where we would find lodging for the coming night, and therefore saddened, the Lord showed us that He had by no means forgotten that holy man in whose service we were making this journey.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Received at home by Giraldus and by Aimoinus’s mother

For, while we had decided to make for the castle called Aubeterre, suddenly the noble lord of that castle, named Giraldus, appeared, having come swiftly up behind us. When he asked who we were and learned that our blessed father Abbo was present, he rejoiced at his arrival and said to him:

“By God and my faith, I declare, my lord, that I rejoice exceedingly that I have been found worthy to see you. For your goodness and wisdom are famed throughout the whole world. Therefore, if it pleases your kindness, I shall be a most generous host to you this night, providing everything necessary for your sustenance.”

He did as he had said and, remaining until nightfall, even performed the duties of a servant in waiting upon him. When he had provided lodging for us beside a certain church belonging to him, he went away without eating to the aforementioned castle.

On the following day, still preserving the benevolence he had shown the day before, he came out to meet him. He sent ahead, through intermediaries, gifts of fish and escorted him for several miles; he also supplied guides for the road both to the man of God himself and to those who accompanied him for the sake of lodging. At last, after asking for and receiving his blessing, he returned joyfully to his own home.

We have related this so that it may be clearly evident that divine assistance was never lacking to this holy man when human help seemed likely to fail him. Nor was this true only on that occasion: on all his journeys, and especially along the entire road that he traveled at that time, his welcome arrival was eagerly awaited by all through whose lands he passed, just as masters are awaited by servants.

Moreover, on the very day on which we departed from Aubeterre, after crossing the river Isle, we lodged together with blessed Abbo in a village called Ad-Francos. There my mother, Aunenrudis by name, a kinswoman of the aforementioned knight Giraldus, received us with every display of hospitality in her power. Burning with the fervor of devotion and service toward that same man of God, she earnestly begged him to remain with her for two days.

He strongly refused, however, and, when the day had been appointed, ordered his men to hasten their preparations for departure. At that point, as though foreseeing the future, he first declared that he was suffering pain in the arm in which he was later struck.

## CHAPTER XIX. At last he reaches Regula

From there they came to the banks of the Dordogne; after crossing the river, they entered the borders of Gascony. As they crossed the Dronne, before reaching the aforementioned monastery of Regula, they encountered a torrent called the Droth.

[**Note:** This is how it is read in the manuscript used by Jean du Bois, although he printed *Aroth* or *Codrot*, being uncertain which reading should be adopted.]

Since it was necessary to cross it, the man of God climbed into a boat, extremely small for that little stream. As the boat slipped backward toward the muddy bank, he nearly fell into the water up to his belt. Wonderful to relate! Although his feet were slightly wet, scarcely any moisture appeared on the rest of his clothing.

After crossing this most unfortunate torrent, they reached the monastery of Regula on the following day. On the first day they remained there quietly. On the second, however, a quarrel arose toward evening between our men and the Gascons over fodder for the horses, and was scarcely settled by their superiors.

When the venerable father Abbo learned of this on the following day, he severely rebuked his men for starting a fight while unarmed and among a people hostile to them. He advised them to preserve their patience until he could confer with the count and the advocate of the place, whom they expected to arrive at any moment. Then, he promised, he would avenge at will the injuries suffered by his own men and by those whom he had originally left there.

With these and similar words he tried to calm the fury of his men.
