That day the solemnity of blessed Martin, bishop of Tours, was being celebrated throughout the world, and the holy man celebrated the festal rites of Mass with great joy of heart and body. On that day and on the next, which was Sunday, the same servant of God Abbo, after offering the holy sacrifice himself and taking bodily nourishment, surveyed the mountain on which the monastery stood on every side. He began to praise and admire not only the strength of the site but also the foundations of the enormous buildings that had once stood there.

We therefore think it appropriate to commit briefly to writing the character of these places, as praised by the holy man.

## CHAPTER XX. The site of Regula. Cassinogilum. The faction of the people of Regula against Abbo. Abbo’s wound. His death. The fury of the rioters. Abbo’s funeral. Burial in his customary clothing

The monastery of Regula, dedicated to God in honor of the prince of the apostles, is situated on a mountain. This mountain is enclosed on three sides—east, north, and west—by other mountains; on the south it is defended by the river Garonne and by the chasm of a dangerous valley.

To the east, between it and another mountain, there is a very narrow valley through which a spring flows, called by the inhabitants the Mosella. In the same way, on the west, it is washed by the swift current of another spring called the Mosa. These names are thought to have been given them by the Franks who were left there by Charlemagne to defend the province.

Not far away—about three miles—stands the palace of that great prince, Cassinogilum. There the same emperor left his wife, the mother of Louis the Pious, pregnant, while he was conducting an expedition against the Saracens in Spain. Heinardus, the narrator of his life, also records this, and we briefly mentioned it in our book of the miracles of the holy father Benedict.

Because of the position described above, the site of Regula would not easily have been accessible to enemies, unless a small plain had adjoined it on the north. Opposite this plain the founder of the settlement—or, as some prefer, of the city—built a tower of squared stones, which now displays nothing but the traces of its own ruins.

When the man of God saw and admired both the ruined walls of this and of the other buildings, hanging down along the slopes of the entire mountain because of the strength of their cement, he smiled at us with a joyful face and said:

“I am now more powerful than our lord, the king of the Franks, within these boundaries, where no one fears his authority, since I possess such a house. But alas, what grief! The possession of this place was being prepared in a way very different from what would have been useful to him and to us.”

For the faction of the wicked men who had inflicted injuries upon those whom the holy father himself had sent to that place had by then conspired to create a disturbance on any pretext and to subject his servants to such murderous outrage that neither he nor anyone else would dare approach them again.

It is not certainly known whether they had plotted his death amid their schemes, except that the man who is said to have struck him was reportedly heard to say during the quarrel with our men that he would consider it nothing if he pierced his belly with a lance.

Accordingly, on the Monday when the feast of the holy confessor Brictius was being celebrated, our holy father Abbo began to rebuke a monk who was said to have devised these plots, because he had left the monastery without permission and dared to eat outside. His proper name was Anezan; both his people and his name were barbarous.

While he pretended to endure the holy man’s rebuke patiently, he answered the bystanders with insolent words. Suddenly a cry of women was heard, shouting according to the custom of that people whenever a riot breaks out or a man dies.

[**Note:** The distinguished Pierre de Marca observes from the Pithoean manuscript that this cry was called *Biahore*.]

Then that treacherous man, a monk in name only, said to those standing around him:

“Now it will be said that this disturbance arose at my instigation.”

One of those present replied:

“If you fear that, come with us to calm this commotion.”

But when he delayed, the man who had given this advice hurried forward to restrain our people.

The cause of the disturbance was as follows. Both Franks and Gascons were assailing one another with insults. One of the Franks, excessively angered by the insult directed against his lord, struck the insulter with a stick between the neck and the shoulders and knocked him to the ground. Once he had been felled, both our men and the rioters began throwing stones at one another.

Meanwhile, the man of God Abbo was sitting inside the monastery cloister, reciting some little calculations of the computus. When he heard the uproar of the rioters, he went out from the lower part of the mountain. Hurrying to restrain his own men, who had occupied the higher ground, he was struck by a soldier of the opposing side with a lance so forcefully in the left arm that the iron pierced through to the interior of his ribs.

When struck, he neither cried out nor staggered, nor did he move from the spot like one who is falling. He merely said:

“This man has done this deliberately.”

Then he began to climb toward the house where his servants were lodging. A certain brother named William, whom we mentioned above, supported him.

I followed in his footsteps and saw, on the threshold of the house into which the holy man had already entered, a portion of clotted blood. When I asked where it had come from, I received this answer from the man of God:

“It is from me, as God is my witness.”

Immediately my hair stood on end; horror spread through my body and gave my voice a hoarse sound. No one had yet noticed that he had been wounded in the flesh. We had thought only that his clothing had been pierced.

I therefore said to him:

“Where, my lord, has the wound been inflicted?”

When he raised his arm to reveal the injury, suddenly a stream of blood burst forth from the innermost recesses of his ribs and was caught by the loose sleeve of his leather garment.

Yet he himself was no sadder, nor did the color of his face change. When he perceived that I was becoming increasingly terrified, both from the alteration of my expression and from my words of distress, he said with a cheerful face, almost seeming to smile:

“What would you do if you yourself were wounded? Nevertheless, do not be afraid. Rather, go outside to our men and make them come to me, so that this disturbance may be calmed.”

When I had done this and they had entered in obedience to him, he, already drained of blood, gave up his spirit on the Ides of November, supported in the arms of his disciples and servants.

Those who were privileged to witness his holy end reported—although I had remained outside to calm the rioters—that these were his final words:

“Have mercy, almighty God, on my soul and on the place and community which, with your permission, I have governed until now.”

After uttering these words, as has been said, he breathed out his soul.

But the rioters surrounded the house in which the blessed father, now dead, was being mourned by his men, and cut down the bolted door hinges. The furious crowd then burst in. After wounding several people, they battered the man of God’s chamberlain, named Adelardus, who was watering his lord’s head with tears while it rested upon his own knees. They struck him with sharpened clubs and lances until he was near death.

Dragging out his weakened life until dawn on Tuesday, he finally collapsed and died. He was buried in the monastery cloister, and beside him the keeper of the holy man’s horses was later buried. The latter, though wounded at that time, lingered until the feast of Saint Andrew and then died.

When the perpetrators of so great a disaster recognized with certainty that blessed Abbo had died, they all vied with one another in fleeing, so that, when daylight returned, not even the women could be found in any of the houses throughout the village.

We remained there for four days after the holy man’s death. A certain honorable man named William, son of Oriolus, stayed continually with us to protect us. This William had come there that same day with some others in order to see the blessed man; after seeing him, he had withdrawn to his lodging, about a mile and a half from the monastery. When he heard the news of our misery, he quickly hastened to our aid with his men.

These men carried the blessed body—which still lay in the house where he had returned his soul to the Creator, almost upon the bare ground—upon a carpet and brought it to us. Our own men, because of the darkness of night, had not dared to leave the monastery cloister.

For some time there was doubt about where the body should be placed. At last it was unanimously decided that, since he had been killed innocently and for the sake of the Truth who is Christ, he should be placed in the church. There we kept him unburied until dawn on Wednesday—two nights and one day—with all the devotion of psalms and tears that we could muster.

It cannot be described what mourning and what groans were uttered by those who came from neighboring places to see him, when they saw dead the man whom they had longed to behold alive. They gazed upon his face, still not covered by a shroud, which in its redness looked more like the face of a sleeping man than of one dead, and they were filled with tears.

It seemed almost incredible, while he was alive, that after his death he would receive so great a lamentation, not only from his own people but also from strangers in tears. For whoever came, known or unknown, broke immediately into tears upon seeing his body or, after the burial, his tomb.

At dawn on Wednesday he was buried, still wearing the clothing in which he had been dressed, as is customary when those who have been killed are buried, and without being washed. He was placed in a stone sarcophagus in the inner part of the crypt, before the altar of the most holy father Benedict.

The burial was sufficiently seemly, had so unexpected an end of life not befallen him. But we know from the testimony of Scripture that “the righteous, though he be taken before his time, shall be in rest” (Wisdom 4:7).

## CHAPTER XXI. The return of his companions to Fleury. The mournful death of Abbo. The celebrated feast of Saint Benedict in December

On the fourth day after the burial of the holy body, we departed from there. For two days we were detained by the viscount Amaluinus and his wife Rosemberga, who showed us charitable affection. As we approach the conclusion of this volume, it is fitting briefly to recall that woman’s most gracious compassion toward our company.

She herself persuaded her husband to retain us even though we were wounded. Once we had been detained, she supplied everything necessary, not only for the sick but also for those who served them and for the horses, of which there were sixteen in all.

[**Note:** This was the retinue of an abbot in those times; it was later increased beyond all measure.]

She herself sought out a physician and paid him for treating the sick. She also demanded that I remain with them, not only by gentle entreaty but with a certain authoritative force arising from kinship.

Those who recovered safely were honorably received, at her command, by her stewards throughout all her estates that lay along the road. Spreading the sad news of so great a grief along the entire journey, they finally brought it to the monastery of Fleury.

No speech is sufficient to explain the mourning and grief that then seized our entire holy community, since even those to whom his strictness had seemed burdensome mourned him inconsolably.

This immense grief was increased by the arrival of many abbots who were gathering for the approaching solemnity of the holy father Benedict, which is celebrated in the month of December. Some had been summoned by Abbo to arrange certain matters; others had come to consult him for definite reasons connected with their own needs. Among them was the venerable Odilo, abbot of Cluny, who throughout Abbo’s life had been closely united with him by the honorable bond of charitable familiarity in the Lord.

The presence of such men, and the absence of the one for whose sake they had come, caused sadness and added to our grief, because we had been left bereft of such a shepherd, while the abbots of the monasteries had looked to his prudent counsel.

These things concerning the life, character, deeds, and martyrdom of our most holy father Abbo—some heard from faithful men, others witnessed by us—we have written to you, most reverend among the clergy, Hervé, in a truthful account insofar as we were able, as your holiness requested.

Now we ask your kindness to implore the Lord’s mercy on our behalf, so that, if in our account we have in any way offended him, He may deign in His most loving compassion to forgive us; and that He who deigned to glorify Abbo’s tomb with miracles may grant me the ability, in the following volume, to make these miracles known to the faithful for the praise of His name.

## MIRACLES OF SAINT ABBO

By the same author, Aimoinus

### 1

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1004, in the second indiction, on the thirteenth day of November, the venerable abbot Abbo was martyred. The day of his passion is distinguished both by his swift passing, by the feast of Saint Brictius, and also by the feast of a certain saint named Herardus. The head of this saint is preserved buried in the monastery of Regula, while the rest of his body lies buried in a certain cell of that monastery.

Concerning who he was or what he did, we have been unable to find anything written down to this day except the day of his passing.

We have thought it worthwhile, however, to commit to writing for the knowledge of posterity the miracles that the Lord determined to perform through our honored father after his death.

While his body was still being kept unburied in the church, a certain weak man, whom a long period of fever had worn down, was shown in a vision that, if he wished to be well, he should ask that Abbo’s right hand be washed with water and should himself drink that water.

When he had asked this of the monk Remigius, later head of that place, and had obtained it, he drank the water and was restored to his former health.

### 2

Then, on the second day after the holy man’s death, one of the women who had stirred up the riot with her shouting became insane and rolled about the church with her entire body naked.

Afterward she was struck with leprosy and expelled from human society, and she was never cleansed until the end of her life.

### 3

On the fourth day, the church warden, having lit two candles each half a foot in length after the completion of Compline, placed one before the altar of Saint Peter and the other before the tomb of the martyr Abbo.

[**Note:** Here the word *lucerna* means a candle.]

When he rose at Matins to designate the hymns, he found that the one he had placed before the altar of Saint Peter had burned down, whereas he confessed that he found the one he had placed at the head of the holy man’s tomb almost entirely intact. It appeared to have continued burning until the morning of the following day.

### 4

There was a certain blind man from the region of Périgueux. In a vision he was shown that, if he wished to see, he should seek the tomb of this saint, so that through the saint’s intercession he might receive light from the Lord.

When he had gone to the site of Regula in accordance with the vision shown to him and had spent several nights keeping vigil beside the saint’s tomb, he recovered his sight.

Therefore, after giving part of his inheritance to Saint Peter, blessed Benedict, and the holy martyr Abbo and to those who served them, he returned to his own home.

### 5

Another blind man, from the region of Bordeaux, was likewise warned in a vision to visit the monastery of Regula: there was a saint whose merits would move the Lord to grant him light.

Obeying the command, he went to the place and spent nearly eight days sleeping before the saint’s tomb.

[**Note:** Thus the custom of what are called novenas had not yet been established.]

One night, when the brothers were rising for the hymns of Matins, he awakened a boy lying before him and said:

“Rise, so that together we may attend the morning offices.”

The boy replied that he had no light with which to kindle a lamp. The man said:

“I see a lamp burning before the altar of the Holy Cross.”

The boy answered:

“If you see it, go and bring it here.”

The man went, seized the light, and climbed without a guide to the upper part of the crypt, to those who were occupied with the chanting of the psalms.

On the following day, when he related to the brothers everything that had happened to him, he kindled their hearts to give thanks to God. His words were confirmed by the beauty of his white hair, by his countenance, and by the honorable bearing of his entire body.

He who always adorns his chosen friends with merits,  
and grants the patrons of Fleury to flourish in heaven,  
bestowing perpetual life after the death of the flesh.  
Amen.

## LITERARY NOTICE ON SAINT ABBO

*(In Oudinus, Ecclesiastical Writers, vol. II, p. 509.)*

Saint Abbo, abbot and martyr of Fleury, or of Saint Benedict beside the Loire, in the diocese of Orléans, was a learned and holy man. The many works he wrote demonstrate his learning, while his blood, poured out and offered to preserve the observance of the order, bears witness to his sanctity.

Sigebert, in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 139, and in his *Chronicle* under the year 990, mentions this Abbo, as we shall also say below. So too does Senatus Bravonius, a twelfth-century writer, in the *Life of Saint Oswald*, in Surius under 15 October.

From this we learn that, at the urging of Saint Dunstan, while he was staying in England, Abbo wrote the *Passion of Blessed Edmund, King and Martyr*. We possess it in Surius, volume VI, under 20 November. It also exists in manuscript in the private Lumley Library in England and in the Royal Library of France, manuscript 3861, folio 66.

Some works of this Abbo have been printed; others have perished through the passage of time. He wrote books on dialectic and astronomy, as Aimoinus testifies in his *Life*, chapter 3, but the injury of time has taken them from us.

His commentary on Victorinus’s Paschal Canon, by which he corrected the cycles of years from the Lord’s incarnation down to his own time in accordance with the true faith of the Gospels, also perished through the passage of time. Sigebert preserved its memory in his book *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 139, in these words:

“He showed how great his ability was in both sciences when he commented upon Victorinus’s computation, extending it to his own time and afterward lengthening it by approximately 1,595 years.”

Abbo’s *Apology* to Hugh, king of the Franks, concerning the immunities of the monastery of Fleury, also perished.

[**Note:** See below, column 417.]

Fragments of it survive in Aimoinus’s *Life of Abbo*, chapters 8 and 9.

Let us now turn to the printed works. There exists an *Epitome of the Lives of Ninety-One Roman Pontiffs*, compiled from the papal history of Anastasius the Librarian and printed together with that history at Mainz in 1602 in quarto, through the study and labor of Jean Busée of Noyon, theologian of the Society of Jesus.

The *Life of Saint Edmund, King and Martyr of the English*, which Abbo wrote at Dunstan’s request while he was staying in England, exists in Surius under 20 November.

There is also an *Epitome or Little Collection of Canons* arranged under specific subject headings, edited by Jean Mabillon in volume II of the *Analecta*, pages 248 and following. There he gives various preliminary remarks on the writings of Abbo, both published and lost; he also discusses him at greater length in the sixth volume of the *Lives of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*.

We have included him here because of the *Epitome of the Canons*, which Labbe omitted, since it had not yet been published.

I have recently heard from Placide Porcher, librarian of the Benedictines of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, that several letters of Abbo have been found in certain Pithoean manuscript codices formerly preserved in a Parisian library. Undoubtedly the learned men of that royal city would not long tolerate their remaining unpublished.

One of these, addressed to the abbot of Fulda, was published by Étienne Baluze in volume I of the *Miscellanea*, page 409. Aimoinus supplied fragments of others in the *Life of Saint Abbo*: fragments of two letters to Bernard, abbot of Belloc, in chapter 10 of this *Life*; another to Gregory V, Roman pontiff, in chapter 12; and finally a letter written in hexameter verse to the emperor Otto, in chapter 13.

John Bale, an Englishman, had formerly seen these letters of Abbo, since he mentions them by assigning their titles in his work *On the Writers of England*. Concerning Abbo he writes as follows:

“Abbo, abbot of the monastery of Fleury, a Gaul from the region of Orléans, wrote a two-book *Life of Edmund the Martyr*; one book of an *Apology* to the kings of the Franks; one book *On Victorinus’s Computation*; one book of additions to the same; one book *On the Movements of the Stars*; one book *On the Course of the Planets*; one book of *Astronomical Demonstrations*; one book *Against the Bishop of Orléans*; one book of *Elementary Lessons for Boys*; one book of *Spiritual Categories*; one book *On Computation*; one book of *Homilies on the Gospels*; one book *On the Lord’s Supper*; and letters to Gregory V, King Robert, the emperor Otto, Bernard of Belloc, and Odilo of Cluny. He published one sequence on Saint Stephen the Protomartyr and several responsories. He corrected the cycles of the years of the Lord’s incarnation down to his own time. He died in the year 1004, killed by his own monks, and his life was written by Aimoinus of Fleury.”

This is what Bale says. Perhaps he inserted this Gaul among his Englishmen because he had found all these works of Abbo together in manuscript in England.

These letters, together with the *Apology* to the king of the Franks, were published and issued this year, 1687, in the *Posthumous Works of Pierre Pithou of Troyes*, which appeared from the royal press of France in three folio volumes, to the great honor and regret attending this distinguished man, who had died approximately a hundred years earlier and had left many manuscripts.

This *Apology* of Abbo, together with various letters, is found in volume I, page 393, continuing through page 429.

What we have said about his date can be established from the fact that he wrote his *Apology* to Hugh Capet and his son Robert, kings of France. It is sufficiently clear that these men and the emperor Otto III were συγχρόνους—contemporaries.

The same is indicated by several letters of Abbo to Gregory V, supreme pontiff, and to others, which now exist in print.

The life and most holy death of this Abbo, which took place on 13 November, in the second indiction, in the year 1004 of Christian salvation, in the monastery of Squirs or Regula on the Garonne, in the diocese of Bazas, have been recorded by Aimoinus, a monk of Fleury, his disciple and companion, who was present there. They are found in the *Fleury Library*, page 299, together with several miracles of the same man, edited by Jean du Bois, a Celestine, in 1605 at Lyon, by Horace Cardon.

Sigebert, however, in his *Chronicle*, less accurately assigned his killing to the year 1003, and led other eminent chronologists into error as well.

One should also consult Ralph Glaber, book III, chapter 3; Jean Trithemius and other more recent writers; Labbe, in his historical dissertation *On the Ecclesiastical Writers Listed by Bellarmine*, volume I, page 22; Jean Mabillon, in the work cited; Gerardus Johannes Vossius, book II of *On Latin Historians*, chapter 41, page 354 of the latest edition and page 331 of the first edition; Jacobus Philippus Bergomensis, book XII of the *Supplement of Chronicles*, under the year 982, where he wrongly calls him Albo; Charles Saussey, in his *Orléanais Annals*, book IV, chapter 8; and especially the preserver of Abbo’s letters, Pierre Pithou, in his *Collection or Compilation of Ancient Writers of Frankish History*. There one finds, copied from an ancient parchment, the *Life of this Abbo*, which the aforementioned Bale attributes to Aimonius, or rather to Aimoinus, a monk of Fleury, as Labbe writes.

Among other things, it explains how, when a riot arose between the Vascones and the Franks, Abbo was killed by a lance. This occurred in the year 1004, on the Ides of November, the birthday of Saint Brictius, a day that is also celebrated by the monks in Abbo’s honor.

He is therefore entirely different from that Abbo, a monk and poet of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, who is said to have flourished in the years 886 and 887.

Jean Mabillon, in the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, sixth century, part I, page 39, Paris edition, printed by Charles Robustel in 1701, folio.

## ENCyclical LETTER OF THE MONKS OF FLEURY CONCERNING THE KILLING OF ABBOT ABBO

*(In Baluze, Miscellanea, vol. II, p. 114.)*

To all abbots and faithful Christians dwelling in every place:

The little community of Fleury, cast down and deprived of its father, sends greetings.

Almost swallowed up by weeping and crushed by grief, extend to us the hand of spiritual assistance, most holy fathers, through the affection of fraternal charity.

Fed with the bread of sorrow and the drink of bitterness, may we deserve to be refreshed by your prayers. The harp of those whose joy has been turned into mourning sounds with lamentation; their organ sounds mournfully with grief, and their gladness is nothing but the voice of those who weep.

The sword of sorrow has pierced to the soul, as we mourn that, for the sake of devotion to holy religion, our lord and abbot Abbo has departed from this world crowned with martyrdom. Through the swords of the Vascones he happily deserved to become a happy companion of the blessed martyrs.

May your prayer wipe away the stains from his soul; for he was always a true lover of you and a true lover of all who serve Christ.

Come also to our aid, whom he has left orphaned, with fraternal prayers, and appease almighty God with the sacrifices of your prayers, so that by His grace He may deign to console the flock that has been left headless and deprived of its loving father.

He died on the Ides of November, the birthday of Saint Brictius.

## LETTERS AND APOLOGY OF SAINT ABBO, ABBOT OF FLEURY

Published in the *Posthumous Works of Pierre Pithou*, *Code of the Ancient Canons of the Roman Church*, Paris, Royal Press, 1687, at the end of volume I, page 393, from the library of the illustrious Claudius Lepelletier, lord, administrator of the kingdom, prefect of the royal treasury, and honorary president of the supreme senate of France; and in Galland’s *Library of the Fathers*, volume XIV.

## NOTICE OF THE PARISIAN EDITOR
Here, learned reader, are brought forth various works of the brothers Peter and Francis Pithou, among which are found the little works of Abbo of Fleury, formerly its most celebrated abbot. Until now, only fragments of these had appeared, inserted by Aimoinus into his Life of Abbo. You will not demand more elegant polish and ornament in them, provided you remember the age in which they were produced—an age not very fertile in the liberal arts. You will consider yourself fairly treated, I think, if the fruitfulness of their subject matter compensates for blemishes, or even defects, of expression. Abbo did not write to display eloquence or learning. Firmly devoted to his religious vocation, he desired nothing more ardently than, freed from worldly cares and removed from tumult, to enjoy blessed leisure. But when he had been summoned to administer the monastery, he became entangled and constrained by many affairs, and was sometimes forced to contend most bitterly with powerful men and bishops over some trifling matter, a small estate, tithes, or other rights, and to invoke against their force and intrigues the authority of most Christian kings and supreme pontiffs. He accomplished this especially in the Apologeticus and in several of his letters. But why should we say nothing about Abbo himself? The reason is the testimonies of ancient and recent writers concerning him, which we append.

[Col. 0419]

## TESTIMONIES OF ANCIENT AND RECENT WRITERS CONCERNING SAINT ABBO

### Letter 21 of Fulbert, Bishop of Chartres

[Col. 0419A]

To Abbo, my dearest Father, full of virtue and surrounded by grace, from his Fulbert. With what form of greeting should I honor you, holy abbot, great philosopher?

### Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, in *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 140

Abbo, abbot of Fleury, showed how much he was capable of in both branches of learning when he wrote a commentary on Victorius’s computus. He died a martyr.

### The same author, in his *Chronography*, under the year 994

Abbo, abbot of Fleury, who wrote a commentary on Victorius’s computus.

### Senatus Bravonius, in the *Life of Saint Oswald*

Moreover, he wished the monk Abbo of Fleury to reside in the monastery of Ramsey, distinguished for the holiness of his conduct and exceedingly learned in letters, so that he might teach the monks, preside over the schools, and advance both regular, or monastic, discipline and knowledge of letters. This Abbo, at Dunstan’s urging, carefully composed the passion of the blessed King and martyr Edmund. At last, having returned to Fleury and become abbot there, he was killed by his own monks.

### Abbot Trithemius, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Abbo, abbot of the monastery of Fleury, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man trained in the divine Scriptures through constant reading and study and exceedingly learned in the secular disciplines, also distinguished in life and conduct, and proved worthy even of the crown of martyrdom. [Col. 0420A] While preaching the word of God in Gascony, he became a witness to the Christian faith through the shedding of his blood. He wrote one book on Victorius’s computus, one book of additions to it, and certain other works. He flourished in the time of Otto I, in the year of the Lord 970.

### Jacobus Philippus Bergomatis, *Chronicles*, book XII, under the year 982

Also Abbo, abbot of Fleury: a man exceedingly well versed in the divine Scriptures and exceedingly learned in the secular disciplines, likewise distinguished by remarkable conduct, and so forth, as Trithemius says.

### Conrad Gesner, in the *Bibliotheca*

Abbo, abbot of the monastery of Fleury, a Gaul from Orléans, wrote two books on the Life of Eadmund the martyr; one book, an apology, addressed to the kings of the Franks; one book on Victorius’s computus; one book of additions to that work; one book on the movements of the stars; one book on the course of the planets; [Col. 0420B] letters to Gregory V, the Emperor Otto, King Robert, Bernard of Beaulieu, and Odilo of Cluny; one book of astronomical demonstrations; one book against the bishop of Orléans; one book of spiritual categories; one book on Computus; one book of homilies on the Gospels; one book on the Lord’s Supper; one sequence on Saint Stephen the martyr; and certain responsories. He corrected the cycles of the years of the Lord’s Incarnation down to his own time. He died in the year 1004, killed by his own monks. Aimoinus of Fleury wrote his Life.

[Col. 0419]

# THE LETTERS OF SAINT ABBO

## LETTER I. TO GREGORY V, SUPREME PONTIFF

[Col. 0419C]

To the ever-venerable lord Gregory, prelate of the holy Roman and apostolic See, and therefore teacher of the universal Church, from his Abbo, rector of the men of Fleury: greetings in Christ.

It often happens that the purity of an undivided truth is made to waver by an ill-faithful interpreter. Guarding against this, venerable Father, I have faithfully and plainly set forth the thoughts of your mind, as you instructed me; nor did I fear the king’s anger while I kept in full the faith I had promised you. For I added nothing, diminished nothing, changed nothing, and omitted nothing. The archbishop Arnulf of Reims himself, released and absolved from custody, is witness to all this; to him I presented your pallium in precisely the form in which I had immediately received it from your holy hands. My lord Robert, illustrious king of the Franks, is also called as witness—indeed, your spiritual son in Christ—who has resolved to obey you as though you were blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose place you now hold on earth.

Moreover, I urge your majesty to teach the aforesaid archbishop how he ought to conduct himself with his clergy, how he should draw the sons of his Church away from their former errors, and how he should restore the estates or possessions that Saint Mary has lost. For, as one of the secular poets says:

> Whatever kings rave, the Greeks suffer punishment.  
> *(Horace, Epistles I.2.11.)*

So it has happened to the Church of Reims: whatever evil Arnulf and Gerbert committed has been exacted upon the possessions of Saint Mary. And because I honor and have honored both of them as friends, whenever I found anything in them deserving of reproach, I did not keep silent, though it displeased them. Yet I have learned of nothing they did more blameworthy than that, through their dispute, they reduced the noblest of all the Gallican Churches to poverty, degradation, worthlessness, and desolation. Come to its aid with your unanswerable authority and restore it to the former condition in which it is known to have been left by Adalbero of blessed memory.

Furthermore, I suggest to your holiness that you remember what Count Fulco conveyed to you through me: namely, that he preferred to restore ancient monasteries that had been ruined rather than to build new ones from their foundations. How frivolous and entirely empty this is, the neighboring monastery of Saint Peter, called Ferrières, makes clear. In former times, through royal munificence, it was a most magnificent member of the Roman Church; now, through the favor of its own vassals, it has been so consumed that scarcely anything remains for the support of a few brothers.

These and other matters are what the tears of the oppressed request. Extend to them the hand of consolation, which the Lord has looked upon from heaven in order to release the groaning of the fettered, when he made you the head of us all.

Finally, let it become known what I myself am suffering. There is a certain Qauz, nephew of Wal, count of the castle of Nanton, who is ravaging the possessions of our monastery. I beg you, if I have found favor in your eyes, to speak about him with Wal, who is now in Rome, threatening his nephew with the rod of excommunication unless he repents. For, mindful of your generosity, I give thanks to the Lord as a servant; since, fully enjoying your gift amid the solemnities of the Mass, I cannot possibly forget you in my prayers.

For the rest, I have always resolved to obey you. May God preserve your apostolate in eternal peace. Farewell.

## LETTER II. GREGORY V TO ABBO

*(See Gregory V, in volume 137 of the *Patrologia*.)*

## LETTER III. ABBO TO GREGORY V, SUPREME PONTIFF

[Col. 0421C]

To the ever-venerable lord Gregory, prelate of the holy Roman and universal Church, from that Abbo, rector of the men of Fleury.

Many intrusive people thrust themselves forward, supposing that I possess some influence with your clemency. They fall on their knees and implore the help of your intercession for their sins. I believed their opinion so far to be true that, as a matter of prudent administration, I brought their declamatory appeal to your ears, judging it useful to your Church, which is desired by all who wish to live devoutly in Christ (2 Tim. 3:12). But I shrank from the petitions of certain people who make much of themselves, lest I provoke to anger one whom I ought to have appeased.

If I approach you as an unscrupulous or even importunate intercessor, remember that Moses, at the waters of contradiction (Num. 20:24), when he wished to benefit a rebellious people, received the sentence of divine punishment, although he was the meekest man above all others. Therefore I took thought for myself and for the needs of my friends. Before your majesty, insofar as I was able, I neither said what ought to have been left unsaid nor kept silent about what ought to have been said.

Thus, having benefited from your goodwill, I learned by experience that your mind has compassion for the misfortunes of the wretched, the calamities of the afflicted, and the lapses of human weakness. For while I conversed with you about the passions of the soul, what else did I discover but the moral teaching of Gregory’s eloquence and the severity of paternal indulgence?

Attracted by these qualities, I returned joyfully to Fleury and made known to everyone whom my speech could reach the fullness of holiness and reverence in your conduct. Thus what happened to me was like what happened to the queen of the East, who came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom and, returning to her own land, blessed the king and his servants (1 Kings 10:1 ff.). Although I lived with you in Italy only for a moment, I can scarcely, for as long as the spirit rules these limbs, recount the marvelous things I heard and saw.

Accordingly, a certain venerable woman named Hildegard, astonished at these matters, was preparing to go to Rome when she tearfully entreated me, by right of kinship, to commend her to you in my letter. She is both sinful and noble—not noble because she is sinful, but sinful because she is noble. For, while the enemy of the human race was acting as her procurer, this secular woman committed many offenses in the world, for which she sought the remedy of penance. On the advice of good men, she built from her own property and possessions two monasteries, one for canons and the other for nuns. In each of them, nearly nine miles apart from one another, she assigned such great revenues that they could suffice even for many more souls than belong to both communities.

She wishes to place one monastery under the patronage of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and the other under that of the apostle Saint Andrew, as tributaries of the Roman Church, and to have them fortified by the privilege of your unanswerable authority. Therefore I earnestly beseech your serenity, more than usual, to follow the custom of your predecessors and, as a new authority, confirm these new monasteries with new books of privileges, so that the communities themselves may serve the Lord in peace, free from every worldly disturbance, especially under the penalty of excommunication.

## LETTER IV. TO GREGORY V, SUPREME PONTIFF

To the ever-venerable lord Gregory, prelate of the holy Roman and universal Church, from his mindful Abbo, rector of the men of Fleury.

I have learned by experience that “whoever adds knowledge adds pain” (Eccles. 1:18). When, through understanding of divine law, I separate the precious from the worthless, the memory of past evils pierces my heart, because it recognizes that it has served virtue too little. Thus knowledge puffs up against the allurements of human frailty, while charity builds up (1 Cor. 8:1). I experienced this in the conversation we had together, when, speaking about the passions of the soul in the province of Spoleto, we turned the leisure of our journey into an honorable undertaking.

Remembering that conversation, I ask and implore your fatherhood that, aided by your prayers, I may deserve to attain fellowship with those who please the Lord. May this faithful servant of yours, Humbold, also experience toward himself and his own need the goodness which the whole world desires to obtain for its perpetual peace.

Finally, you asked how the body of Benedict, legislator of the monks, was transferred to Gaul, and what events are historically recorded as having taken place in Cisalpine regions. After I had disclosed the history to you, I did not delay sending it, as you ordered, for the Transalpine peoples to read. By this little booklet I have satisfied your request.

I also sent two Manzerine vessels, on which Charity and Ethics are represented in relief work. One of them, namely Charity, holds the Old and New Testaments in both hands, in separate compartments; Ethics embraces history and allegory with her wings. Thus each virtue—Charity and Ethics—displays four virtues around the several rims of the vessels, worked by the engraver.

> When we see the children of the City stripped of their offices,  
> Rome rages, subjected to foreign masters.  
>   
> Nor is this surprising, since the stage becomes harsher toward them,  
> and has something cruel [the reading is corrupt], through which it will become bloodstained.  
>   
> Whom should you beware more than Gregory, now at last the fifth,  
> ever watchful at the sentry-posts of the world?  
>   
> Free through love of him, I crossed the Alps bowed down,  
> I, Abbo, following snowfalls equal to those of the Eridanus.  
>   
> The ashes of the Father, called by the name of Benedict,  
> are entrusted to the West—and to you, holy man of God.  
>   
> We Franks joyfully venerate them together in this reliquary;  
> you too should venerate them, to whom I have given these deeds to read.

## LETTER V. TO THE MONKS OF SAINT MARTIN

To these fathers and brothers, my fellow soldiers in the monastery of Saint Martin, especially Heriveus, a mirror of good character, from Abbo, lover of the lovers of Christ.

An appropriate opportunity is ordinarily sought for carrying out the effectiveness of any undertaking, since nothing can be accomplished without it. I mention this to your charity because you delayed beyond measure in sending the little document of your embassy. For this reason it was impossible for me to obey you, although I desire in every way to please you and shall never appear disobedient to the instructions of good men, unless compelled by a religious obligation or by the pressure of time.

But when you charitably urged me to set out on the journey, I was greatly surprised that you did not state in your letter the reason for the advancement you seek. For I have at hand everywhere the authorities of the holy Fathers which you specifically ordered to be brought forward, lest I be deceived by the seductive guile of rivals who dig a pit for a brother and perhaps fall into it themselves (Eccles. 10:8).

I learned one thing, as though from popular opinion: namely, that the lord archbishop AR. opposes the privileges of Saint M., our common patron. But what madman would believe that a man of such authority and gentleness would wish to oppose the decrees of the Roman pontiffs and the institutions of the holy canons?

The Roman Church, by its excellence over all Churches, possesses this privilege: just as the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom holds primacy at the apostolic summit, so the same Roman Church grants authority to all those Churches, as though they were its members, throughout the four regions of the whole world. Whoever therefore contradicts the Roman Church, what else does he do than withdraw himself from its members and become part of Christ’s adversaries?

That great and inviolable Council of Nicaea certainly commands that every Church’s privilege be preserved. The most holy Pope Gregory declares that he venerates it as though it were the holy Gospel. Concerning privileges, the same venerable pope also writes to Bishop John, saying:

> It is exceedingly grave and plainly contrary to the priestly vocation to disturb the privileges once granted to any monastery and to attempt to invalidate what has been arranged for its peace.  
> *(Book VII, letter 33.)*

And further:

> Therefore we exhort your fraternity with earnest words to refrain, without any excuse, from troubling the monastery, and not to attempt to tear away through the usurpation of any pretext what has long been safeguarded for it, but to strive to preserve everything inviolate and without any resistance. Let him know that he is not permitted to do more in that monastery than was permitted to his predecessors.

Far be it, then—far be it—that the writings of holy men, and especially of the ancient Roman pontiffs, should endure the prejudices of modern men and that the opinions of later generations should make light of those whose memories they venerate!

For if those younger in time scorn the decrees of the ancients, to which they ought to have given assent, what remains but that lead should float upon the waters while wood sinks and splits to the bottom—especially since it is written: “Do not move the ancient boundary-stone that your fathers established” (Prov. 22:28).

I advise only this: investigate the merits of the bishops of Tours and of the Roman pontiffs, one of whom issued the decree and the other recorded it; then determine whether, under the weight of the opposing party’s efforts, you can judge that the matter stands otherwise than they declared.

Farewell.

## LETTER VI. TO ROBERT, KING OF THE FRANKS

[Col. 0424C]

To Robert, illustrious king of the Franks, from Abbo, servant of God’s servants, remembering the salt that I once ate in the palace.

I am exceedingly astonished at the source from which these salts of eloquence have burst forth. Their bitterness, my lord king, I unexpectedly found abhorrent; and, though I abhorred it, I could not conceal it in silence. For until now I have made use of palace eloquence, and from almost the very cradle I learned the truth as a boy in the monastery—a truth which the secretary claims I have lost.

Now that the snow of my head is turning white, I give thanks to him, because he has brought me back to myself. For he has made known that I am a man, subject to the changes of mutable fortune, as he both said and wrote. Scripture says: “Every man is a liar” (Ps. 115:11). But perhaps the Prophet uttered this in ecstasy—a statement I too would have received kindly, were it not written: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. 5:7).

For what else did my friend accomplish by turning the Apostle’s words against me, when he declared that in my speech something both is and is not (James 5:12), unless he wished to reproach one who confessed either that what is does not exist, or that what does not exist does exist? You should know that I am in no way guilty of this offense here, since, before this letter in which I am accused of lying, I had seen no one with whom I could converse concerning such a matter as being and not being.

As for what he added—“but let it be”—I considered the limit of my weakness and preferred to be like men rather than like God, rejecting the pride of him who was the seal of God’s likeness (Ezek. 28:12).

Moreover, just as no one is good except God alone (Mark 10:18), so nothing among created things is unchangeable. For there is nothing in them that is not mutable; and if every creature is mutable, how can his word not be mutable? He alone reserved this as his proper possession, concerning whom it was said in the Old Testament: “He who is has sent me to you” (Exod. 3:14).

Behold, venerable king, my apologetic speech before your majesty. And, lest you be deceived by the foolishness of this manner of expression, I wish—and have always wished—that you be cautious.

Farewell.

## LETTER VII. TO ODILO, ABBOT OF CLUNY

To the ever-venerable lord Odilo, father of the congregation of Cluny, from his fellow in the same office, Abbo, unworthy servant of Christ’s servants.

It often happens that we prepare, according to our modest ability, banquets for our friends from the dishes of spiritual philosophy, hoping through this introduction to share in their delights. For, as Scripture says, “all things are common among friends.” Therefore no one takes pleasure in using his studies alone, and the feast of charity is willingly tasted when, among those who pursue the same knowledge, one is not deprived of the gift by which he wins lovers of truth.

Accordingly, venerable father, disregarding the madness of rivals, I resolved, in the manner of a commentator, to write something pleasing to friends and useful to posterity, and I wished to share it with you, whom, once I came to know, I have always loved and continue to love in all things with devoted affection.

Nor am I ashamed to have you as judge of the question I have undertaken—one whom the charm of the sweetest affability recommends, adorned, as it were, by a lineage of ancient nobility, together with eloquence beautified by frequent and humble wisdom. I experienced this wisdom more than usual on a short journey, when we stayed together both at our monastery and at the monastery of the man of God. There one of your brothers, as it seemed to me sufficiently well disposed, attentive, and teachable, asked about the repetition of similar numbers found so frequently in the canons of the Gospels.

In explaining this question, I could not satisfy him fully, partly because of its difficulty and partly because neither place nor time was sufficient for a matter of this kind. Now, however, having found the opportunity, I shall explain how the accumulation of numbers occurs in the aforesaid canons, after first setting out the system by which numbers are prefixed threefold in each of the books of the Gospels. Some designate chapters, others sections, and others annotations—both common and particular.

The chapters and sections, both written in vermilion, appear to differ in this respect: the chapters are expressed in larger characters, while the sections nowhere exceed ten and do not follow one another in order below ten, except where circumstances require it. The annotations, written in ink, begin with one in each Evangelist and increase in ordered numerical progression to a great plurality, whether as the first numbers or as the only numbers.

This will be more easily understood if the annotation of one Evangelist, as must be done for the others, is set out as an example. Thus, in Matthew there are twenty-eight chapters, among which are 355 annotations, each accompanied by its own section-number, by which one can determine in which canon that annotation is found.

The fact that there are ten canons and no more, in which the Evangelists are compared with one another only nine times, is due to this: Mark preserves a particular relationship with John, with whom he never agrees to stand alone. Nor does Mark stand alone with another Evangelist except Matthew. For when there is agreement among all four, there is one mode; but if one differs, four modes are found. If any one is compared with two, there will ultimately be six; if, in the manner of a single combat, one stands separately against each of the others, there are the remaining individual cases. [Col. 0426B]

It should also be observed in these same canons that they are divided by straight lines, from the reader’s left to right. Between these lines, up to the end, four annotations are made, one for each of the Evangelists arranged at the head of each canon.

Among the first lines of the first canon, therefore, there are twenty annotations. Their order presents no difficulty: in Matthew VII, in Mark II, in Luke VII, and in John X.

The question concerning the others arises because John wrote in scattered places what the others, gathering their material together, each stated once in his own work. For example, let the words of the Evangelists be arranged as they occur in the text, with their particular and differing annotations:

[Col. 0426C]

“I indeed baptize you in water for repentance; but he who is to come after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.”

“And John was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist, and he ate locusts and wild honey. And he preached, saying: ‘The one mightier than I is coming after me, whose sandal-thong I am not worthy, stooping down, to untie. I baptized you in water, but he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit.’”

“I baptize you in water, but one mightier than I will come, whose sandal-thong I am not worthy to untie. [Col. 0426D] He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.”

“John bears witness concerning him and cries out, saying: ‘This was he of whom I said, “He who comes after me has been made before me; he was before me.”’”

“I baptize in water, but in your midst stands one whom you do not know.”

[Col. 0427A]

“This is he of whom I said: ‘After me comes a man who was made before me, because he was before me; and I did not know him. But in order that he might be revealed to Israel, for this reason I came baptizing in water.’”

“You yourselves bear witness on my behalf that I said: ‘I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.’”

With these passages set out beforehand, the sober reader understands that John touched now here, now there, upon what Matthew and the others collected in the order of a single annotation of their own. Thus, in the Gospel of John itself, after the first annotation, a repetition of similar numbers occurs four times: once concerning the man who was to come and the baptism of John, where John reported one matter and omitted the other; again elsewhere, where he stated both together; and finally concerning the aforesaid man who was to come, whom he called Christ.

Let us therefore examine the beginning of the first canon, after this one agreement of all the Evangelists. After the second line, John repeated one annotation a third time, while the others repeated theirs a second time. After the third line, John himself varied five times what each of the others explained once in its proper place.

This principle is observed in the other canons that are included in the comparison. Nor should this be left unsaid: the progression of the annotations is one and equal, but in the canons a number is sometimes omitted, while in the individual Gospels the order of the numbers remains regular.

Care must nevertheless be taken to avoid disagreement where there ought to be no difference at all. To speak of Matthew, who holds the principal place in the aforesaid canons: apart from two exceptions, from the beginning of his book to the end, the first section-number maintains the sequence of the first canon; similarly, the second maintains that of the second, the third that of the third, and so on with the rest.

Hence the annotation in Matthew’s text numbered LXXXVI is wrongly thought to have the first section-number. For after examining very many volumes of the Gospels, and finding nowhere in any canon an annotation between LXX and XCVIII, you will find this annotation of Matthew—namely LXXXVI—only in the sixth canon and nowhere else. Therefore the first section-number should not be written there, but rather the sixth, as the examined sequence of one ancient volume has shown.

For what Matthew arranged under the latter section-number, he himself repeated as annotation 244 under the first section-number. Accordingly, in reciprocal correspondence, the others agree with it; in this correspondence Mark has set forth nearly the same material under annotation CXXXVIIII.

It must therefore be repeated that, although an annotation may be omitted, the progression of the Evangelist who is regarded as first in any canon nevertheless advances in an ordered increase. For example, in Matthew, after annotation eight comes eleven; in John it is found after the fourteenth annotation. But among the others who agree with that first Evangelist, an omission sometimes occurs because of the agreement.

If any doubt arises in such matters, one should take up the book of Augustine on the agreement of the Evangelists, the uniquely subtle interpreter of all ecclesiastical questions. After Ammonius, who made one Gospel out of the four, following the model of the book called the *Harmony of Rules*, Augustine extracted all the doubtful propositions of the Gospels and arranged them in one codex, shedding the greatest light upon their obscurity.

After Ammonius, Eusebius of Caesarea also permitted the books of the Gospels to remain as they were, and distinguished them by a system of corresponding numbers, which he called the canons of the Gospels. Jerome, interpreter of the divine law, followed him and made the work Latin from the Greek. He also wrote to Damasus explaining how the arrangement of these canons should be understood:

> It must be known, lest the ignorant be entangled in error by the similarity of the numbers, that, just as in the annotations of the distinct canons, in any given canon three Evangelists have the same number noted in sequence twice, three times, four times, or even more often, while the fourth has differing numbers, so what those three say once in that place the fourth places in the body of his book as many times as different numbers are set down in his canon, contrary to the continued similarity of the aforesaid numbers.
>
> Likewise, if in one or even two of them the same number is found placed in sequence twice, three times, or more often in that canon, while a different number is found in the others, there can be no doubt that what the former Evangelist or Evangelists have said once in their book is represented by their canon or canons through numbers repeated twice or three times; while the others speak as many times in one and the same sense as they have displayed a difference in the annotation of the numbers. This rule will be observed throughout the comparison of all nine canons. In the tenth, however, since it contains only the particular material of each Evangelist, comparison with what exists alone is impossible.

Finally, venerable Father, because I transferred these matters to you by disentangling them from the commentary of the aforesaid man, and sent them not as a prejudgment but as a considered judgment, I feared that, wishing to satisfy that well-disposed brother’s intellectual curiosity, I might seem to you verbose or excessively talkative. Out of fear of saying too much, I therefore refrained from saying more.

One point remains for him, perhaps because he has not learned it: what *aera* properly means, since Isidore, whom I followed, uses the term very frequently in the canons. An *aera* is the reckoning of individual years. It is called *aera* from the bronze payment that was rendered each year to the Roman republic; for this reason, in Spanish usage, a hundredth year, or any other year, is called the hundredth *aera*, or another corresponding *aera*.

Let that familiar questioner of mine know that I devoted attentive work to him and built for him a palanquin from the woods of Lebanon, by means of that charity which the Apostle desires: “May the God of patience and consolation grant you to think the same thing among yourselves according to Jesus Christ” (Rom. 15:5).

For you are both a consolation to me, and I desire you both to think the same thing that I think according to that Christ, so that, united in mind and with one voice, we may together glorify him in the integrity of the catholic faith.

Farewell.

## LETTER VIII. TO G. . . ., ABBOT

To the most beloved lord in Christ, brother and fellow abbot G., from the humble rector of the men of Fleury, Abbo.

My desire had been to investigate the zeal and character of good men, to imitate them once investigated, and to describe them once imitated—not to examine the life of wicked men, full of vices, and, after investigating it, to expose it with many tears. The matter over which I groan compelled me to do this: that in the final hour the charity of many grows cold, especially of those who outwardly profess that the world has been crucified to them (Gal. 6:14), although by simulation—and even by dissimulation—they provoke God’s anger. Venerable Father, beware their deceits; do not listen to their fraudulent words, for “their throat is an open tomb” (Ps. 5:9): they consider the disturbance of the commonwealth the greatest gain.

Under a sheep’s skin, wolves flee to the monastery’s asylum; they hide themselves in the stalls as in hiding places, and whenever they find an opportunity to do evil, they do it. They harass simpler brothers with false deceptions, deceive the unwary by the seduction of flattering destruction, and, having corrupted them with the poison of their iniquity, plunge them into the labyrinth of their error. They disparage the better men and invent crimes horrifying to hear. Their god is their belly, “and their glory is in their shame” (Phil. 3:19), because, being earthly-minded, they have not tasted how sweet the Lord and his Christ are, in whom “we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28).

I write this to your holiness, applying like things to like, because in the monastery of Saint Martin Major, quite near you, the report of such deeds has become known. These may be charged to your administration—not because you have assented to the malicious, but because you neglected to correct an unheard-of crime by your unchallengeable authority. For when legates had come from different parts of the world, it was necessary for lovers of sacred religion to assemble as judges, to determine the criminal accusations by their sentence, and to establish whether the man said to be guilty had deserved rejection by a just judgment before the sight of the divine Majesty.

[Col. 0429D] For that most holy and great pope Gregory did not wish abbots to be treated in this way on the basis of newly arisen rumors. Concerning Bishop Siagrius of Autun, he writes among other things to Lupus, priest and abbot, instructing that the bishop of the city alone should not presume to judge the cases of an accused abbot; rather, after summoning several fellow bishops, he should bring the matter before a council, so that by the common and equal decree of all, the innocent might be acquitted or the guilty condemned.

I also thought that the same principle should be inserted into our privilege, which, though unworthy, I have earned in our time by receiving it from the holy hands of the lord Gregory, the most holy pope, under the authority of Saint Peter. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, I appeal to you—not declamatorily but administratively—you whom I love greatly: do not believe suborned witnesses; do not suddenly believe false accusations, perhaps fabricated, for the devil too, in order to deceive the good, sometimes transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11:14).

Remember the testimony of the priests whom he convicted of speaking falsely, using as his argument that a crime once committed could not have taken place in different locations. From this comes what is found in the canons: in an appeal involving men of sacred order, some are to be accusers, others witnesses, and others judges, and the life of each must be examined, lest they be plotting vengeance or wish to exercise against an innocent man the savage fury of their indignation. Indeed, in accordance with the saying of Sallustius (Speech of Caesar in the Senate), it is necessary that all be free from anger, hatred, favor, and compassion.

Tell me, I ask, where has it been read that sheep have judged their shepherd? Or where Judas betrayed his Teacher? Yet Judas himself neither accused nor judged him. David, though placed within the rite of circumcision, refused to lay hands upon Saul, his lord. Nevertheless, he cut off the edge of his cloak (1 Sam. 24:5), clearly teaching that subjects should touch the faults of prelates with the hand of the humblest correction, while refusing to destroy their name. For “there is no authority except from God,” and “whoever resists authority resists what God has appointed” (Rom. 13:1–2).

Let the monks of the Major congregation therefore consider what they have done against the abbot. Their rule was to pass their life in silence, to disparage no one, hate no one, to keep silent not only from evil but even from good, and not to return curses for curses but rather to bless. Who released them from the yoke of the rule, so that they proclaim peace with clattering mouths while biting with their teeth, run freely through the streets, and serve as informers—when informers are punished by death, or, if preserved alive in greater humanity, corrected by a seven-year remedy of penance?

Who taught men, followers of the contemplative life—men who ought to have watered his feet with tears like Mary and, within the enclosure of their cloister, ascended the tribunal of conscience, neither exposing nor publishing their own or others’ sins, but rather mourning them—to proscribe people and condemn the guilty in public courts?

Behold, the report has spread that, contrary to divine and human laws, the abbot wished to purge himself by red-hot iron, yet he is denied a hearing, excluded from the privilege of judgment, carried away after suffering public prejudice; the examination is given to laymen and withdrawn from monks. Their sounder mind and sounder counsel notwithstanding, the regular order has been confused among the unsound for the space of one lustrum.

But let it be so: let a prelate conscious of crime be silenced, worthy of the fork, and miserably overwhelmed by tortures. Will he therefore entrust his neck to the chains of his subjects? Will he fail to be torn apart by the hands of his own men? Perhaps that former Frederick of ours, the rival of good brothers and the worst of plotters, established such schools among you, so that, just as from Arius came the Arians and from Gnatho the Gnathonics, so his disciples are Frederickians after Frederick!

Certainly, venerable Father, such a handle for calumny must be avoided, as must the unpunished manufacture of lies by wickedness, lest those who have hitherto been a good odor of God in every place deceive you in any way. For I am judged by them to be worse than the worst, and am called a parricide; if I pleased them, I would not be Christ’s servant (Gal. 1:10). But I thank you, because you grieved in my place and could not endure the curses inflicted upon me, though I am your least brother.

For the rest, I would like to learn from your letter whether the rejected abbot sent his brothers a document of repudiation, or whether, having been prejudged, he suffered violence. For with me the standard-bearer of the whole religious order, Odilo, is despised, and, as we have been informed, the brothers of the monastery of Cluny were expelled dishonorably from Major Monastery. We have learned that only two leaders of the faction carried this out; their boldness in attempting every crime was all the greater because the power of their supportive assembly was greater.

For often, as we have learned from the evidence, silence introduces the same forces as eloquence, which gathers the necessity of an allegation. Indeed, it is evil both to keep silent about what ought to be said and, worse still, to say what ought to remain silent.

Therefore, most loving of all, admonish as many good brothers of that congregation as possible to advance toward better things. Correct the murmurers and double-tongued, so that they may cease from their most wicked vice. Set before them the example from the ancient law: “A vessel,” Moses says, “which has no covering is unclean” (Lev. 11:53), because that mouth defiles the soul which, without the barrier of moderation, lies open to utter every disgrace.

Let them remember their profession and learn that subjects must obey their prelates, not command them; that they must request anything from the prior with humble submission, not, in pride, contradict his commands. Those who strive to shake their neck from beneath the yoke of the rule endeavor not to entreat their elder but to rebuke him; they seek scandal for him, not peace; they are always eager to serve conspiracy or insurrection. Nor do they fear the punishments appointed for conspirators, which deserters from military service or offenders against imperial majesty endure.

Nor does our discourse proceed with the intention of withdrawing from the examination of holy men and chosen judges a father who is said to be incestuous or sacrilegious. Rather, I counsel the piety and compassion of his sons, lest, like Ham, they uncover their father’s nakedness, but instead hide it with averted faces (Gen. 2:22–23). For who does not know that Ham afterward suffered his father’s curse in his descendants, and was not the servant of his brothers but the servant of servants?

Finally, having prefaced these matters, I appended one conditional proposition concerning the same issue, from which arise syllogisms based on antecedents, consequents, and contradictories. Even if your charity has not drawn them out, authority will be able to suggest the force of the necessary conclusion. For when you assume what is true concerning the case of Bernerius, you will make clear, without any ambiguity, what must follow. The proposition is this: If an abbot is openly guilty of the crime alleged, he is unworthy of the office of the fatherhood granted to him.

Certainly, one of two alternatives must be true of an abbot: either this or that. For he cannot both be openly guilty of the crime alleged and not be unworthy of the office of the fatherhood granted to him.

Finally, I urge you not to spare, with excessively loose reins, that second rival of ours in fraternal slaughter; for, as I have recognized in his foolish letters, this loquacious man either disparages the good or crawls with hands and feet toward evil like a serpent.

Farewell.

## LETTER IX. TO BERNERIUS, ABBOT

Would that ecclesiastical authority passed over nothing in the case of Abbot B., but openly taught how prelates ought to live and conduct themselves with their subjects, and how both prelates and subjects ought to be judged for what they have done. I do not suppose that you are ignorant of this, since from your very cradle you were raised among teachers of sacred religion, nor have you escaped the judgment by which those accused of crimes are condemned or acquitted.

You also know that God shows no partiality (Deut. 10:17), and that a monastic profession found blameworthy condemns rather than frees the accused from the charges brought against him, and is of no value as a defense of crime. Why, then, should you wait for the sentence of good men, when your own conscience accuses you and the reputation of a most shameful action defames you? So much so that, as I have learned from truthful informants, you disclose that you have confessed part of the abomination, while, under the name of some wondrous deed, you conceal another part as a dissembler of vices.

But what does it matter whether you possess part of the deed or the whole deed, when everyone praises and considers wisely spoken that verse:

> He who has begun half the deed has it . . . . .  
> (Horace, *Epistles* 1.2.40.)

Nor does that rhetorical device known as the transference of the charge help you, nor the altered name of the deed, when a crime committed in a brothel with someone’s wife is named differently by the man and by the accused: the former complains of adultery, while the latter admits not adultery but that what he did in the brothel was permissible. Neither alternative, however, supplies a firm defense, least of all for you, who became an instigator of vices after being chosen to become a teacher of virtues.

You are said to have contaminated many members of the flock entrusted to you with your disease; you are convicted of having destroyed them by the leprosy of the foulest contagion. You say nothing except that you did it but did not complete it: you pierced with a sword your companion—indeed, your son—and the man who had chosen you as guardian of his life; you gave him poison; you set fire to sacred buildings. If the man pierced by the sword escaped, if the poison he drank did not kill him, if the fire did not prevail, you deny that you sinned and affirm that it is of no concern to you.

Repent, repent, I say, and return to yourself. If you are conscious of the charges brought against you, do not bring infamy upon abbots and monks with yourself, since not only you but all of your order are believed to be such. In Christ I confess the truth: all who are such as you are said—and, as I have heard, acknowledge yourself to be, since you do not contradict the informers—all, I say, are unworthy both of the monastic habit and of the office of abbot.

Yet may this be far from you! We seek your defense, if it can be made, as we seek our own; with you grieving we shall grieve, and with you rejoicing we shall rejoice. Do not delay a hearing, I beg you, if you are defending your innocence. If not, satisfy your brothers by sending a document of repudiation, and, after returning the pastoral governance to the bishop, let another who is worthy succeed as soon as possible.

Farewell.

## LETTER X. TO [LACUNA], BISHOP

Abbo, lover of the lovers of Christ, to N., bishop.

The usefulness of literary knowledge is recognized from the difficulty of the questions. When the ignorance of the common people cannot untangle them, it strives to investigate their meaning from a learned person—provided, of course, that some doubt about unheard-of matters has touched the ignorant.

For when anything whatever in the nature of things is sought—whether it exists, what it is, why it is, and how it is—and when even the ignorant multitude does not pass over these questions, it is certain that no one asks anything at all about matters wholly unknown. Philosophy exercises its labor even upon things that do not exist, so that nothing of nature and nothing of morality escapes it; concerning these it conducts subtle investigations.

Therefore a question is proposed concerning the observance of an oath, and the path of inquiry is not unknown, since an abundance of arguments is available. For to swear is nothing other than to pray lawfully. He who prays, insofar as the opinion of truth and falsehood is concerned, treats only one kind of statement, even though it must be subject to an oath. Dialecticians call this statement enunciative: confined to the present, it looks to the past through the action of a deed, but to the future through a promise concerning a deed.

The action of a deed can be expressed under oath so that it is definitively true or false for someone who knows the matter definitively. A promise concerning a future action, however, just as it does not fall under definite knowledge, so an oath concerning promised matters is not known to be definitively true or false, except in matters which the necessity of nature compels—for example, that immortal God exists and that human beings die. For it is definitively true that everything born will die.

But what happens by contingency, since it need not happen and is largely a matter of opinion, cannot rationally be affirmed or denied definitively under oath. For in contingent matters the promising mode often deceives us, and a thing comes about by chance or necessity otherwise than we think.

When someone swears, therefore, the question is whether he prays lawfully, and what the circumstances of an oath are. Place, time, and person are considered. If the oath lacks a lawful place, time, or person, the one who swears will not be held liable for the oath. Hence, in the Old Testament, the Lord commands through Moses that if a girl who is still in her father’s house makes a vow or takes an oath, she is not to be bound by the vow or oath if, as soon as it comes to the parent’s knowledge, she is forbidden by the exercise of paternal authority.

Likewise, the vow or oath of a woman who is under a husband’s authority is to be void if the majesty of marital authority refuses its consent, or rather if, on the day when he learns of her foolishness, he prohibits it with the strictest correction (Num. 30:4 ff.). For, as Solomon says, the vows of fools must be broken (Eccl. 5:2).

Moses continues there that the woman herself, who was thought to have incurred the guilt of perjury, merits the Lord’s pardon. It is also written that God did good to the Hebrew midwives, who, by their lie, are said to have saved the Israelite boys destined to be killed from death (Exod. 1:20).

The cause of a lie and of perjury must therefore be weighed, since by it we sometimes commit a lighter sin and sometimes a more serious one; yet we never lie without sin, since every sin is said to be from the devil (1 John 3:8). Elsewhere too the Lord commands through the Prophet: “Do not love a lying oath” (Zech. 8:17). And what is it to swear falsely except to commit perjury?

He forbids loving this, as though he allowed unwilling perjury, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I do not want. If I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (Rom. 7:19 ff.). Therefore he is forced to cry out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:24).

To this statement agrees Tobit, who, instructing his son in naturally good conduct, says: “Do not lie any lie.” This command means: one must not use a lie—that is, one must not use any particular lie. Yet the truth of the Gospel makes known that one must not use not merely every lie but any lie at all, since it declares that every lie is from the devil.

Whatever is from the devil is evil; no evil is to be used; therefore nothing that is from the devil is to be used. Every lie is from the devil; no lie is good; therefore nothing that is from the devil is good.

Moreover, Scripture says: “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. 115:11), since the devil corrupted human nature by this vice, so that it is both mortal and lying—neither lying except insofar as it is mortal, nor mortal except insofar as it is lying.

In perjury, therefore—that is, in a lying oath—the vice of lying must be considered, as well as the taking of the Lord’s name in vain, since that alone is sufficient for death, according to what is written: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11). When another evil is added to it, a graver sin is produced: sometimes committed through fear of death for the preservation of bodily life, sometimes through hope of profit for the acquisition of earthly goods. This has been judged properly to be called perjury.

But human compassion does not regard a sin committed for the preservation of bodily life as a great matter, in accordance with the comedian’s saying:

> For a great sin, it is enough to suffer a little punishment.  
> (Terence, *The Woman of Andros*, act 5, scene 3.)

Fear and pity move the judge’s mind equally toward mercy, while he distinguishes the measure of a lighter and a graver fault by the scales of just examination. For no one disregards the chapters of the same law, though they may seem contrary to one another, except as a transgressor of the law; yet fear or filial duty sometimes acquits him.

Finally, the law ordered that a male who entered the temple of Venus should be punished by death. It also ordered that anyone who saw his mother being beaten should be punished by death unless he rescued her. A certain young man therefore saw his mother being beaten in the temple of Venus and, entering the temple, rescued her.
