The question is what he ought more properly to have observed when he saw his mother being beaten. Whether he entered or did not enter, he was to be punished by death. But filial duty takes precedence: out of affection for his mother, and with usefulness and honor, it clears the accused.

Moses’ law concerning the circumcision of a boy is similar if his eighth day from birth occurs (Gen. 17:12). In the New Testament too, the wife is commanded in one place to be loved and in another to be hated (Luke 14:26). The sword of discernment separates all these matters—a sword unknown to the Jews, who, when questioned by Jesus about John’s baptism and fearing to be struck from either side, became dull-witted (Matt. 21:25–26).

Since we have begun speaking about oaths, it must be said that, once greed has been removed, no one willingly takes pleasure in swearing; rather, an oath is often “from evil,” as the Gospel says (Matt. 5:34). A wicked rich man oppresses the poor; a wicked robber strips the traveler; a wicked accuser brings a case against the innocent. Thus the wretch cannot escape the enemy’s snares, for he suffers beyond measure because he is of low estate.

When, through the violence of an exactor whom we cannot avoid, we are compelled to swear, we sometimes fall into perjury under the compulsion of necessity, or are enticed by the misguided favor of certain people. Thus the adulterer, in fleeing temporal death, acquits himself by an oath that he is not guilty of adultery, and in this way consigns himself to eternal death.

Someone else, during a tumult or military conspiracy, swore to the death of an excellent emperor. And what shall I say? He has already killed his own soul, although the Truth says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28).

Another man, however, is still deliberating in the affection of sin and, during the stages of deliberation, considers what is more useful or honorable. Let the deed of that strong-handed man serve as his example: after swearing to kill Nabal, a foolish and wicked man, he preferred, through repentance, to erase his perjury rather than, having committed murder, to obtain the fulfillment of his evil vow (1 Sam. 25).

Therefore, if someone’s habit of swearing inclines toward the outcome by which he knowingly sees that many have offended God, we advise him to place his foot lightly elsewhere rather than seek such a precipice, from which hope of rising again may be more difficult.

Thus, those wishing to escape from the shipwreck of a besieged city seek that part of the wall which they know to be shorter. Always surrounded by the enemy’s wedges, we avoid grave danger while seeking a way of escape. Many cannot avoid perjury in the labyrinth of error, since one person affirms under the obligation of an oath the very thing that another, in turn, strives to deny by oath, and each takes this as a statement. Yet one side of the contradiction is always false, without any doubt.

It is also asked whether a man who has been compelled under torture to swear that he will not reclaim his property unjustly taken from him ought nevertheless to reclaim it. The argument from the associated term resolves this question very easily, since to swear is to pray lawfully. For whoever prays, whether falsely or truthfully, speaks lawfully or unlawfully. He prays lawfully who does not depart from the truth; unlawfully, he who is compelled to involve the truth in a lie. Nor does the man who has lawfully received what he possesses lawfully endure the violence of the robber.

He ought therefore to reclaim whatever he lawfully possessed and unjustly lost. “Yet he swore,” someone says. It may nevertheless be defended that the man who did not pray lawfully did not swear, since juridical clemency and divine law make room for his defense and for the removal of charges.

But if a hearing is withheld, innocence is condemned not by law but by cruelty. For just as the sin of Judas, who betrayed Christ, was greater than that of Pilate, who crucified him, so the sin of the one who compels perjury is greater than that of the innocent man who commits perjury through fear of death. Peter denied Life because he feared to die.

Yet, taking pity on human weakness, the Lord looked upon Peter and upon his bitter tears. Scripture does not say that he looked upon those whose terror caused him to fail in confessing Christ. Such a denier and a perjurer fall, in similar fashion, into the pit of sin: the one is ashamed to confess the Lord’s name, while the other takes it in vain—so far as lies within him, either through fear or through greed; through greed, like a merchant, and through fear, like an unwilling betrayer of the faith.

Hence divine Scripture forbids swearing, and adds the reason: lest one perhaps commit perjury. For it is perjury, not swearing, that is sin. Elsewhere too it is written: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent” (Ps. 109:4), because an oath—only a false one—is followed by the remedy of repentance.

Writing these things concerning oaths freely uttered and forcibly extorted, I have distinguished them for your fraternity and gathered their differences, so that, once they have reached the sanctuary of your knowledge and have pleased your brothers after your examination, they may be recited openly before all.

The man compelled to swear does not differ from the man baptized by force, if both are regarded as violators of the sacrament. For, as Augustine says:

> A person may be dragged unwillingly to the Church; he may unwillingly approach the altar; he may unwillingly receive the sacrament; he cannot believe unless he wills to; he cannot preserve faith in his heart unless he wills to. Therefore let anyone beware of compelling an unwilling person to the sacraments of faith, lest he bind himself more tightly with the fetter of condemnation than the person whom he considers guilty of violated faith. For both the giver and the drinker of poison die: the former in soul, the latter through the violated nature of his body.  
> (Augustine, *Tractate XXVI on John*.)

Thus I am weary of my life, and sometimes shed very many tears as I behold the calamities of the innocent. With them, having suffered violence, I am compelled to cry out: “Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips, for I was peaceful with those who hated peace; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause” (Ps. 119:2).

Farewell.

## LETTER XI. TO THE MONKS OF MICIACUM

The rector of the men of Fleury sends greetings in the Lord to the brothers of Miciacum, especially to their dean Constantine.

Since charity is good will, I marvel that you were not ashamed to lack that good in whose absence you openly confess the rancor of your evil will—not merely in words but in the letters you sent to our brothers. You certainly ought not to have done this.

For their benevolence does not willingly receive preachers of crimes, betrayers of the accused, and accusers of brothers, especially where [something, namely a substantive, seems to be missing] no hearing is granted and the accused is denied an audience, although it is written that no one absent can be condemned.

I truly confess, brothers, that you wished to stain our brothers with your praises, joining them to your calumny as though they were accomplices, making them supporters, judges of detraction, and leaders of accusation. But how far their innocence is from such a plague is attested by the ignoble scribe Frederick, now exiled in Jerusalem because of his fabrication of lies and his unheard-of history of vices invented about his brothers.

Indeed, in our profession also, the singular Odilo, rector of the men of Cluny, recently expelled from his monastery such historiographers when they were exposed, beating them with whips and terribly branding them with the iron of amputation. For Christians must pursue the Saterrici whom the pagans pursued; their number has now increased. May the mercy of divine compassion exterminate them from beneath heaven!

Finally, the heresy of the Acephali, which has now arisen, must be condemned together with the Saterrici, because they rule without a head and without a spiritual father; contrary to the law and right of nature, they tear their brothers apart, and, while biting, proclaim peace. No species of animal rages except against those unlike itself.

Therefore, remembering your profession, return to yourselves. Remember what you vowed before God and his saints. Desire that the abbot whom you expelled with his one little sheep should preside over you according to the rule. Leave the faults of his brothers to his judgment. And if the rule of Benedict, the legislator of monks, displeases you, at least let the Apostle’s sentence please you: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master; and he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand” (Rom. 14:4).

Finally, if you lay the hand of correction upon your shepherd, know that Jesus Christ, the Shepherd of shepherds, contradicts you; your abbot imitates his example in that he left you, as though needing no one, in the mountains and seeks to bring back to the flock the one sheep that had gone astray.

I also found this most serious matter in your conspiracy: you provoked the kindness of the lord Fulco, bishop of Orléans, against your abbot; by your council you brought him to harshness and armed him against an innocent man, contrary to the authority of the canons.

I call him innocent because, as he asserts, he makes use of a good conscience and endeavors to respond to the charges. This, he testifies, one of you has at some time read. Hence we infer that the envy of the devil—through which death entered the world (Wis. 2:24)—is devouring the mind of the ambushing troop of substitutes, since they block his opportunity for defense, something which until now has been permitted to no one in the Catholic Church.

Finally, my speech is addressed to you, my once-familiar Letaldus. Elsewhere my smallness embraces your singular knowledge and strives to exalt it with the highest praises. What interest did you have in gnawing away at the life of one wretched man and marking the nonexistent faults of one little person, when it is written that a wise man does not commit acts for which he must repent?

Perhaps you do not repent of your deeds. Yet who has willingly taken up the ministry of the devil, marking the faults of men, sitting in the seat of pestilence (Ps. 1:1), and constructing assemblies of the malicious?

I exhort and implore you, dearest brother: remember your weakness; take up the entrails of mercy; rebuke, entreat, and admonish your brothers with all patience and instruction (2 Tim. 4:2)—in such a way that neither correction drags them into despair nor patience yields to the fuel of their vices.

For you are said to be the head of this conspiracy. You presumed to take upon yourself the office of your abbot, lord Rotbert—an unspeakable thing to say—and you did not dread the punishment of an informer. May almighty God restore him, free from every evil and without any rebellion, to the unanimity of his father and brothers.

Farewell.

## LETTER XII. TO ODILO

The lover of the lovers of Christ, Abbo, rector of the men of Fleury, sends greetings in the Lord to Odilo, father of the men of Cluny, distinguished by prerogative.

As I was traveling into Gascony for the establishment of monastic religion, I happened to come to the monastery of Saint Cyprian the Martyr, situated in the suburb of the most famous city of Poitiers. After I discovered that this place was subject to your authority, I considered it ours, since, according to the opinion of some, all things are common among friends.

For this reason I was deeply grieved by the reputation then circulating among the ears of the common people. Examining it in turn, I groaned beyond measure over you, because the devil’s envy creeps into men of our profession through the undisciplined; because those who are called monks become satirical accusers, slanderers of their brothers, instigators of vices, and, with a viper’s tooth, gnaw at the entrails of Mother Church.

Venerable Father, their madness must be restrained, lest the profane trample holy things and the precious stones of the sanctuary become cheap. For the charity of many is already growing cold (Matt. 24:12), and evil men in cowls join themselves together for mutual aid and counsel, as is written of the feathers of Leviathan: one is joined to another, and not even a breath passes between them (Job 41:7).

Informers are punished by the laws of the world with the death penalty. With what boldness, then, do wretches dare to open their mouths for the death of a brother and the disparagement of a neighbor, assuming the office of a betrayer? Their profession is to remain silent, even about good things.

Wisely, dearest brother, beware the cunning of these men. They bite the simple life of the good while, like wolves in sheep’s clothing, proclaiming peace.

At what [time], certainly, has it been read that monks and priests of the Lord were condemned on the accusation of a prostitute? Which monk, by the authority of the Fathers, compelled his abbot to a secular court? Which cleric or bishop subjected him to a council?

I truly confess that such presumption must be struck with the severest rigor. For, as Benedict, the most discerning legislator of monks, says, a man who forgets his profession ought to disclose his own sin and another’s to his abbot or spiritual elder, not expose and publish it. This does not remove from you the power to judge your brothers, since he entrusted that power to another.

Finally, since, by the authority of Gregory the Great, in an accusation of crime some are accusers, others witnesses, and others judges, act, most prudent man, so that the innocent may rejoice, freed from the charge, and the rash accuser may recognize himself as guilty, lest he laugh at the punishments of the innocent.

Farewell.

## LETTER XIII. OF ALBERT, ABBOT OF MICIACUM, TO POPE JOHN XVIII

To the holy and venerable lord Pope John XVIII: Albert, abbot of the abbey of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr and of M., confessor of Christ, and the entire congregation of monks of that same place, namely Miciacum, send greetings in Christ.

We know that you, reverend Father, have been appointed on earth as vicar of the universal Church in the place of blessed Peter, so that you may support those who are unjustly oppressed and, by the authority of blessed Peter, oppress those who exalt themselves excessively. Therefore we have taken refuge in your reverence through this letter, so that you may assist us and do what we ask.

The place in which we live is called Miciacus. The most holy men, namely blessed Euspicius and his nephew, the venerable Maximinus, founded it through a royal grant of Clovis I, the first Christian king of the Franks; and thereafter many others built it at their own expense. That same place once flourished so greatly in spiritual and temporal prosperity that one hundred and forty monks were gathered there to serve God continually. Later, however, it was so devastated by the invasion of wicked men that no monk could live there. Now, with the help of Christ’s grace, the same place has gradually begun to rise from the degradation of its ruin, like a revived sick man recovering from a long illness, through the alms of good men and women. Among these is a good woman named Lady Regina, who has offered many gifts to the aforesaid place, for her own salvation and for the relief of the souls of her husband and children, now deceased, presenting them in reverence to God and the saints worshiped there.

She fears, however, that after her death one of her relatives or some outsider may attempt to take away anything from all that she has given to God. For this reason we suggest to Your Holiness that you confirm by your authority, with the inscription of the seal bearing your name, the two volumes that we have written in your name: one contains the title to the property granted by this venerable woman, while the other establishes the total inventory of the substance of our monastery. We shall pray continually to God for you, both while you live and after your death.

For it is fitting, venerable Father, that you follow the custom of your predecessors and confirm for monasteries new books of inventories, by which the communities themselves may serve God peacefully, free from all worldly disturbance, especially under the penalty of excommunication. May God preserve your apostolate in eternal peace. Farewell in Christ, blessed Father.

## LETTER XIV. ABBON’S LETTER TO G. . . .

To his dearest brother G., Abbo, abbot of the men of Fleury, lover of Christ’s lovers.

Often it happens that hatred increases on account of truth; the mind of the wise man endures this most patiently while the business at hand promises a useful and honorable outcome. For that end he bears it, and by bearing it he mercifully prays for his enemies. I do not deny that you have done this: because of the injustice you suffer, you cry out to God from the depths, and you contradict, as far as your ability permits, all those whom you can address in denunciation. You endure as enemies those whom you ought to have had as friends, since Christians who break out into hostility forget their own profession when they reap fields that are not theirs, invade the property of others, and seize the stipends of God’s servants.

And what shall I say? It is not the uneducated who do this, but Christian teachers, rulers of the peoples, and, blinded in a manner by the root of all evils—namely, pride [Note: [Col. 0439D]—that is, pride]—they reduce Christ’s poor to destitution. They would surely do this least of all if they dreaded the divine Scripture’s prohibition: “You shall not move the boundaries that your fathers established” (Prov. 22:28); “You shall not defraud your neighbor, nor oppress him by force” (Lev. 19:13). And the Lord says through the prophet Moses: “Woe to the wicked man who moves his neighbor’s boundary!” (Deut. 27:17.) And again through Isaiah: “Woe to you who join house to house and add field to field!” (Isa. 5:8.) He adds below: “Woe to those who enact unjust laws and, when writing, write injustice, so that they may oppress the poor in judgment!” (Isa. 10:1–2.)

Indeed, they enact unjust laws in order to oppress the poor in judgment. They do not leave the endowments of churches to the churches to which those endowments belong, so that the poor may be supported from them; instead, they distribute them to their soldiers either as gifts or as benefices. They invent an unprecedentedly good fiction for the world, claiming that these endowments belong not to the churches but rather to the altars, although the largest altar could be restored for one tremissis, whereas a church requires the expenditure of many solidi.

Nor should you wonder, dearest brother, that this heresy has grown in our own time, when justice has departed from the earth. For now new expressions are pleasing—expressions which the Apostle forbids (1 Tim. 6:20)—and in the temple of God what is sacred is made secular. Altars are handed over into the possession of laymen. The sins of the people are not “eaten” by monks or clerics (Hos. 4:8), who intercede with God for the sins of that same people; instead, by the judgment of bishops, the offerings of the church benefit the horses and dogs of laymen more than pilgrims, orphans, and widows, or the restoration of churches.

They assert that these are their own altars, which they separate from the church without any authoritative basis, led by the same error that held the heretics captive: they attempted to divide the one person of Jesus Christ into two natures by multiplying persons, contrary to the saying, “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). The Apostle declares the crucified one to be the very one whom he revealed by his confession as the Lord of glory. For just as soul and flesh together constitute one human being, so God and man together constitute one Christ. He consecrated his holy bride—namely, the entire Church—to himself and united it to himself once consecrated.

If you consider the buildings of the churches, a foundation, walls, and roof without Christ’s table constitute a house, not a church, just as a corpse is called a body without a soul. I have said this so that no one may wish to divide what is indivisible, calling one thing the church and another the altar. For the foolish man who attempts what is impossible is consumed by labor that is of little use.

No one contradicts the priests of the Lord when, on the authority of the canons, they affirm that the endowments and tithes of churches are in their hand, provided that by “hand” one understands authority. For the aforesaid things are in the bishop’s hand just as a kingdom is in the king’s hand, so that by their authority and judgment equity may be preserved for each person in obtaining what belongs to him.

But so that no one may falsely suppose that I have assigned this meaning to “hand,” let him remember that the fearful sinner repeatedly prays to be rescued from the hand of death. Finally, Christ himself makes clearer whose the Church is: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18). He says, “my,” not “your.” Therefore, if the whole Church belongs to Christ and belongs neither to Peter nor to anyone else, it follows that there ought to be no human quarrel over its pastures or goods, since the portion belongs to the one to whom the whole belongs. If anything from its temporal goods must be divided, it ought especially to benefit those who serve the Church spiritually by day and by night.

Nevertheless, I am considerably troubled by the fact that, although all tithes are in the bishop’s hand, the authority of the canons grants the bishop a third, or rather a fourth, part. For to whom the whole has been granted, the part has also been granted; but if the part is granted separately, it is useless to maintain that the whole was granted—unless perhaps that whole refers to the bishop’s administration, and not to the transfer of ownership, so that he might be able to give, sell, or retain it for his own uses.

Who is unaware that clerics and ecclesiastical property are under the bishop’s hand, while he has received authority to distribute those same goods through stewards? As for the third, or rather the fourth, part, he may do whatever he wishes with it, insofar as it pleases him to act as an ecclesiastical steward: he has been granted the power to give it away, sell it, and possess it. Yet when there are sometimes a thousand churches in a single bishopric, it is astonishing if the greed of priests is so great that the third part—or, which is less, the fourth part—of their churches cannot satisfy them.

The Council of Braga, foreseeing this, says: “The bishop shall not demand a third part of any offering of the people in parish churches; rather, that third part shall be reserved for the lights of the church or its restoration, and an account of it shall be rendered to the bishop each year.”

Since, then, this has been written concerning the portion of churches, where, I ask, does any written authority transmit, concerning endowments or tithes, that an account must be rendered to the bishop each year? Or can anything belonging to the church, especially immovable property, be alienated? Alienation of property is precisely such a transfer under law that, after it, no lawful recovery remains, because possession no longer belongs to the former owner. There are as many witnesses that this alienation cannot be made from the property of the Church as there are authors of laws and canons.

One of my predecessors therefore built a church on the property of our monastery and granted it an endowment. Did the monastery thereby lose possession? Or could the abbot alienate it? Accordingly, when the administrative books of our monastery, dating almost from the time of Charles the Great and nearly consumed by age, were examined, they revealed what the built church owes to me and my brothers; and the diligence of the steward there assesses what it pays in return under the name of an endowment, with its own burdens.

As for what once disturbed you in my presence, when it was said that monks could not hold churches, remove it from your mind. Know that a monk, unless promoted to the clerical state, cannot serve a church while retaining its ministries, nor ought he or can he live from its revenues or offerings [Note: [Col. 0441] This passage is certainly obscure; at first glance anyone might judge it mutilated or corrupt].

In writing all this to your fraternity, I wished to make you attentive and cautious against those who speak against you, by setting out certain chapters concerning the Church, so that the man who attacks our interests might not find you unprepared. For the one who advised us to possess the simplicity of a dove first instructed us to maintain the cunning of a serpent (Matt. 10:16), lest the evil deeds of some feigned friendship lure us through kindness, or crafty cleverness oppress the innocent.

For in the Song of Songs we are commanded to catch the foxes that destroy the vineyards: “For flowers have appeared in our land” (Song 2:15). These are the prerogatives of divine grace by which we are nourished, like young goats that feed among the lilies (ibid., 16), conscious of our sins under the teaching and rule of the lawgiver Benedict. We also groan because we endure the savage jaws of those whose having suffered more serious things at the hands of others we do not fail to recognize. They do not dare to turn their vengeance against those others, but direct persecution against us, the least of all, and against our innocence, in accordance with Virgil’s saying:

> The grim lioness pursues the wolf, and the wolf himself pursues the she-goat;  
> The wanton she-goat pursues the flowering cytisus.  
> (Virgil, *Eclogues* 2.63.)

Do not be angry that I have compared you to a she-goat, which sometimes obeys the wolf, mutters, and plaintively laments its misery in mournful bleating. You too, because you are compelled to abandon the sweet fields after losing them (Virgil, *Eclogues* 1.3), are accused of impatience and reproached for silence. Yet sometimes the she-goat is rescued from the very jaws of the wolf by tearful complaints, whereas by remaining silent it is hurried headlong to death.

Therefore, if you can, strive and resist evil. Since you are a Christian, do not allow a Christian bishop especially to sin against you. Do not offer him the other cheek, and do not surrender your cloak to one who wishes to take it away (Matt. 5:39–40), lest you lose it through your patience. Remember the proverb that is written: “For a bad knot in a tree, a bad wedge must be sought.”

I do not say this so that you, as a monk, should transgress your profession by attacking anyone with your hands, but so that you may pierce and correct him with the sword of the divine word and with the statements of the holy Fathers set out below. He has forgotten the Christian profession and strives to become an extorter of property and a distorter of laws, while attempting to take from the founders of churches or their heirs what belongs to them. In this way, by saving your own soul and his, you will save both.

Pope Gregory the Great resists, in many letters, bishops and clerics who opportunistically seek control over monasteries on the pretext of governance. Writing on this matter to John, bishop of Ravenna (*Epistles* 4.1), he says:

> It has come to my attention that in some places belonging to your fraternity, once consecrated to monasteries, there are now dwellings of clerics or even laymen. Those who are in the churches pretend to live religiously, seek to be placed over monasteries, and through their way of life monasteries are destroyed. No one can both serve ecclesiastical duties and remain properly within the monastic rule, so that the one who holds the discipline of a monastery is compelled each day to remain in ecclesiastical service. Therefore let your fraternity hasten to correct whatever of this kind has occurred in any place, because I will in no way tolerate the holy places of monks being destroyed through the ambition of clerics.

Likewise, to Marianus, bishop of Ravenna (*ibid.* 6.40):

> That a bishop ought not to trouble a monastery. Some time ago, through the reports of many people, it came to us that the monasteries established in the territories of Ravenna were being excessively burdened by the domination of your clerics, so that, on the pretext of governance—something grievous to say—they possessed them as if they were their own property. Deeply grieving over this, we sent letters to your predecessor, so that he should correct the matter in every respect. But since he was soon overtaken by the end of his life, lest this burden remain upon the monastery, we recall that we wrote the same things to your fraternity. And because, as we have learned, correction of this matter has until now been neglected, we have judged it necessary to send these written instructions to you again.
>
> We therefore urge you, once every delay and every excuse has been removed, to strive to relieve the monasteries themselves from such a burden, so that thereafter no cleric, nor anyone constituted in holy orders, may have permission to enter them for any reason except to pray, or, if they have been invited to perform the sacred mysteries of the Mass. But lest they perhaps suffer any burden through the promotion of any monk or abbot, we must ensure that, if anyone from any monastery should proceed to the clerical office or sacred order, he should no longer have any authority there, as we have said, so that monasteries may not be compelled under cover of this pretext to bear the burdens we prohibit.
>
> Your holiness has now been warned a second time to correct all these matters with vigilant care. Do not delay, lest, if we should afterward discover that you have been negligent—which we do not believe— we be compelled to provide for the peace of monasteries by another means. For you should know that we will no longer tolerate the congregation of God’s servants remaining subject to such a necessity.

Concerning unjust excommunication, he writes after other matters to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari [Note: [Col. 0443D] Read “Calaritanus,” that is, “of Cagliari”], saying (*ibid.* 2.34):

> Among many complaints, the most distinguished man Isidore has complained that he was unjustly excommunicated and anathematized by your fraternity. When we wished to learn from your cleric, who was present, why this had been done, it became clear that it had been done for no other reason than that he had insulted you. This greatly distressed us, because, if it is so, you show that you think of nothing heavenly but indicate that your conduct is worldly, since, for the sake of avenging a personal insult—a thing forbidden by the sacred rules—you have brought upon him the curse of anathema.
>
> Therefore, from now on, be entirely watchful and careful, and do not again presume to inflict such things on anyone in defense of your own insult. For if you do anything of this kind, know that afterward it will be avenged upon you.

To Luminosus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Thomas at Rimini (*ibid.* 4.14):

> We have gladly received your petition and that of your congregation, giving a faithful response to your requests in accordance with the statutes of the Fathers and the form of the law. By a directive sent to our brother and fellow bishop Castorius, we have completely removed from him and his successors the power to inflict any injury upon you or your monastery, so that he may neither continue to burden you, nor make an inventory of the monastery’s property, nor conduct a public procession there. We have left him only this jurisdiction: to appoint, in place of a deceased abbot, another whom the common consent of the congregation has chosen as worthy.
>
> These matters having been completed, be diligent in God’s work and devote yourselves to constant prayer, lest it appear that you have sought security of mind in prayer while, instead—God forbid!—you have wrongly avoided episcopal discipline.

Gregory to Castorius, bishop of Rimini, concerning the same matter (*ibid.* 4.43):

> Luminosus, abbot of the monastery of Saints Andrew and Thomas, situated in the city of Rimini, has poured out tearful prayers to us. The text of the petition he submitted explains the matter. We therefore exhort your fraternity that, when the abbot of that monastery church dies, your administration should in no way interfere with recording and safeguarding the property of that monastery, whether acquired or to be acquired.
>
> We wish you to appoint as abbot of that monastery not someone else, but one whom the entire congregation, by common consent, has demanded as worthy in character and in the discipline of monastic conduct. We absolutely prohibit public Masses from being celebrated there by the bishop, lest in the retreats of God’s servants any opportunity be offered for popular gatherings, and lest the more frequent entrance of women should often—God forbid!—draw simpler souls into scandal.
>
> We establish this page of our writings as a rule for all future time and for bishops who are to be appointed thereafter, and we order it to be preserved inviolate: that you and your Church, with the Lord’s help, should be content with your own rights alone, and that this monastery, serving no other or general or canonical jurisdiction, should complete its divine work with the greatest devotion of mind, free from molestation and every burden. Given in the month of July, in the fourteenth indiction.

That a bishop ought not to prohibit a monastery from Masses or burial:

> Gregory to John, bishop of the Old City (*Epistles* 1.12). Agapitus, abbot of the monastery of Saint George, has informed us that he is suffering many burdens from Your Holiness, and not only in matters [“for,” or “against”] which a monastery might be able to sustain as assistance in a time of necessity, but also that you prohibit Masses from being celebrated in the monastery itself and forbid the dead to be buried there.
>
> If this is so, we urge you to withdraw from such inhumanity and to permit the dead to be buried there and Masses to be celebrated without any further opposition. Nor should the aforesaid venerable man again be compelled to lodge a complaint concerning these matters.

That a bishop ought not to prohibit a monastery from Masses.

Likewise, to Martinianus, bishop (*ibid.* 7.18; first indiction):

> How necessary it is to provide for the peace of monasteries and to consider their perpetual security is shown by the office you previously held, when you governed a monastery. Therefore, since we have learned that the monastery of the blessed John and Stephen, situated in the city of Classe and known to be governed by our common son Claudius the abbot, has suffered many wrongs and burdens from your predecessors, your fraternity’s foresight ought to arrange their future peace by a salutary ordinance, so that those living there in God’s service may, with his grace assisting them, remain free.
>
> But lest, according to a custom that ought rather to be corrected, anyone at any time presume to inflict any trouble upon them, it is necessary that the matters we have taken care to enumerate below be guarded by the zeal of your fraternity in such a way that no opportunity for further disturbance may arise from them.
>
> Therefore let no one henceforth dare to diminish by any kind of exaction the revenues, property, or documents of the aforesaid monastery, or any place belonging to it in any manner whatsoever; nor let anyone impose levies or practice any deceit. But if any dispute should arise between Ravenna and the aforesaid monastery and cannot be settled peacefully, let it be resolved without deliberate delay before chosen men from both parties who fear God, with the holy Gospels interposed.
>
> When the abbot dies, let no outsider be appointed. Let the congregation itself freely choose from within its own body the person whom it wishes, and let the chosen man be appointed without fraud or any form of bribery. If they cannot find a suitable person among themselves, let them likewise choose a diligent man from another monastery to be appointed.
>
> No person, on any pretext, is to be placed over the incoming abbot in his monastery, except in the event—God forbid—that there are crimes of the kind which the sacred canons show must be punished.
>
> It must likewise be guarded that, against the will of the abbot of that monastery, monks may not be taken from there to govern other monasteries, to receive sacred orders, or to enter the clerical office. But if there are enough monks to sing God’s praises and fulfill the needs of the monasteries, let the abbot devoutly offer from those remaining whoever he considers worthy before God. If, though having enough, he refuses to give them, then the bishop of Ravenna may take from those remaining men to govern other monasteries.
>
> No one from there is to be advanced to ecclesiastical office unless the abbot of the place, after being asked, offers him of his own will. Whoever proceeds from the aforesaid monastery to ecclesiastical office must thereafter have neither authority nor permission to live there.
>
> It must also be observed that, whenever circumstances require it, an inventory of the property or documents of that monastery is not to be made by ecclesiastical persons. The abbot of the place is to make the inventory together with other abbots.
>
> Whenever the abbot may wish to come or send someone to the Roman pontiff for the benefit of his monastery, he must be permitted to do so in every respect.
>
> Moreover, although monasteries ought eagerly to await the arrival of bishops, since we have been informed that the aforesaid monastery was burdened under your predecessor on the pretext of providing hospitality, Your Holiness ought appropriately to regulate this matter, so that the bishop of that city may visit the monastery whenever he wishes for the purpose of visiting and exhorting it, but in such a way that the monastery incurs no burden.
>
> The aforesaid abbot not only does not fear Your Fraternity’s frequent visits to the monastery, but even ardently desires them, knowing that through you the monastery’s substance cannot in any way be burdened.

That the privileges, ordinances, and decrees of blessed Gregory and the other saints should be observed without any opposition:

> To Boniface, the defender (*ibid.* 7.17): Those who labor faithfully for ecclesiastical interests ought to be assisted with appropriate benefit, so that we may rightly appear to have answered their services, and so that they may become more useful through the grace granted to them.

And after some other matters:

> We establish that these decrees of our ordinance, which have been arranged for the privileges and administration of defenders, are to be observed with perpetual stability and without any opposition, whether they are matters we have decreed in writing or matters that appear to have been arranged in our presence. We decree that no pontiff may tear them up or alter them, either in whole or in part, or on any pretext.
>
> For it is exceedingly harsh and especially contrary to the good character of priests for anyone, under any excuse of reason, to strive to rescind what has been properly arranged and, by his example, to teach others that what they have established may at some time be dissolved.

To John, bishop of Scillium, likewise concerning the same matter (*ibid.* 7.32):

> It is exceedingly serious and clearly contrary to the priestly profession either to disrupt privileges once granted to any monastery or to attempt to invalidate arrangements made for its peace. The monks of Castellum—which is situated in your city—have complained to us that you are hastening to introduce into that monastery certain things which were permitted by your predecessors and preserved by long custom, and that you are disturbing the ancient arrangement by a novel prejudice.
>
> Therefore we exhort your fraternity in these words: if this is so, refrain from such molestation without any excuse, and do not attempt to tear away by usurpation on any pretext what has been preserved for them over so long a time. Rather, strive to preserve everything inviolate and without any opposition, and know that you are not permitted to claim more in that monastery than your predecessors were.
>
> Since they have also complained that you took certain things from the monastery under the appearance of a gift, it is necessary that, if you remember having accepted anything improperly from there, you restore it without delay, lest the charge of greed severely condemn you, when priestly generosity ought rather to have shown you to be generous toward monasteries.

And shortly afterward:

> The monks also reported that the fortress called Scillacium was founded on land belonging by right to their monastery and that, for this reason, the inhabitants there, having drawn up written instruments, used to expend a contribution each year as a form of support; but afterward they disdained to pay it and needlessly withdrew themselves from that obligation.
>
> Let your fraternity carefully ascertain the truth, and, if you find that this is so, earnestly ensure that they do not delay providing what they promised, since reason itself demands it. In this way they may peacefully possess what they hold, and the rights of the monastery may suffer no prejudice.
>
> Furthermore, the aforesaid monks of the monastery have complained to us that their abbot granted you, within the fortress of Scillium—which extends for six hundred feet—a piece of land under the pretext of constructing a church, by way of a donation. We therefore wish that as much of the land as can be enclosed by the walls of the church that has been built should be vindicated to the church’s right.
>
> Whatever may lie outside the walls of that church must return without difficulty to the rights of the monastery, because neither the statutes of secular laws nor those of the sacred canons permit the property of a monastery to be separated from its right under any title. Therefore restore, without any opposition, the donation of that land, which was made contrary to reason.

Likewise, the law of equity demands that what was restored by our predecessors after the truth had been ascertained should not now be retained by our church, lest what is plainly contrary to the religious profession appear to have been restored not truly but only in appearance and with greater deceit.

Therefore, since Stephen, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mark, known to be situated beside the walls of the city of Spoleto, has complained to us that the estate called Massa Veneris, situated in the province of Campania in the territory of Minturnae, which we know was restored to him by an order of our predecessor, Benedict, of blessed memory, is now being unjustly retained by our church, we order you by this authority that, if it is plainly being held by men of our church, you restore it to the right of the aforesaid monastery without any delay or dispute.

But if it is being held not by our men but perhaps by certain outsiders, we wish you to act with vigorous care so that it may in every respect be restored to the right of the aforesaid monastery, so that, through your diligence, it may receive what is its own without any weariness, and another person may not unjustly profit from the monastery’s loss.

(*Ibid.* 2.39.)

> As for ecclesiastical privileges, let Your Fraternity hold this without hesitation: just as we defend our own rights, so we preserve the rights of each individual church. I shall neither grant anyone, through favor, more than he deserves, nor, prompted by ambition, diminish for anyone what belongs by right to him. But I wish to honor my brothers in every respect and strive to advance their honors before the eyes of others, provided that there is nothing which one person may lawfully set against another.
>
> I rejoice greatly in the character of your envoys, in whom it has been shown to me how much you love me, since you have sent to me chosen brothers and sons.

(*Ibid.* 6.32.)

> Although we believe that your fraternity is diligently concerned, with pastoral vigilance, for the care of monasteries, nevertheless we considered it necessary to report to you what we have learned concerning a monastery situated in the province of Africa.
>
> Abbot Concodeus, the bearer of this letter, complains that whenever he wishes to restrain under regular discipline the monks whom he is known to govern, they rashly abandon the monastery and wander wherever they wish, existing as though this were permitted to them.
>
> Since this is altogether harmful to them and presents an example of perdition to others, we urge your fraternity, if this is so, to exercise ecclesiastical correction upon them and, with severe punishment, unquestionably restrain them from such presumption. By a salutary provision, subject their proud minds to the yoke of discipline in order to make them obey, so that those whom the example of their conduct might have encouraged to such an excess of depravity may be recalled from their fault by correction and taught, as is proper, to obey their superiors.
>
> Since he also says that certain bishops defend monks who transgress, let your fraternity be diligent in this matter and, by every means and through threats, suspend them from such defense.

(*Ibid.* 7.115.)

> Since the desire of a pious will and the intention of praiseworthy devotion ought always to be assisted by priestly efforts, care must be taken that what has been arranged for the peace of religion and religious conduct may not be neglected through dissimulation or disturbed through some presumption [Note: [Col. 0449] Something appears to be missing from these last two clauses]; but just as what reason demanded ought to have been determined in no other way, so what has been determined ought not to be violated.
>
> Therefore Childebert, king of the Franks, of glorious memory, inflamed by love of the Catholic religion, established within the walls of the city of Arles, as we find recorded in writing, a monastery for men for the sake of his reward, and granted certain things there for the support of its inhabitants. Lest his will ever be rendered void, and lest what had been arranged for the peace of the monks be disturbed, he asked by letters that what [or, “whatever”] he had granted be confirmed by apostolic authority in the right of that monastery.
>
> He added this also to his request: that certain privileges should likewise be granted to the same monastery both in the administration of its property and in the appointment of its abbot. For he knew that the faithful show such reverence to the Apostolic See that what has been arranged by its decree is thereafter not shaken by any unlawful usurpation.
>
> Therefore, because both the royal will and the matter greatly desired required fulfillment, our predecessor Vigilius, bishop of the Roman See, sent a letter to your predecessor Aurelius. In it, everything required by the earnestness of the king’s desire was gladly confirmed by apostolic authority, since a matter so requested could not endure obstruction.
>
> But so that your fraternity may know what was decreed at that time, we have taken care to append to this letter the writings of our aforesaid predecessor. After reading them, we urge you to preserve everything inviolate with priestly zeal, as is fitting, and to permit there nothing of what has been forbidden, nothing of what is unlawful.
>
> Nevertheless, as an excess of caution, we again confirm by our authority in every respect all that our predecessor established for the peace of this matter. Therefore let your fraternity conduct itself in guarding these provisions in such a way that it both excludes every opportunity for disturbance and strives to bring others to do the same, showing itself properly diligent and devoted in preserving the most pious will of the deceased.

Item, on preserving privileges, Gregory to all bishops:

“No one has the right either to wish or to be able to transgress the commands of the apostolic see, nor the administration of its disposition, which it is fitting that the charity of all should follow. Let anyone who wishes to oppose apostolic decrees therefore be prostrated by grief at his own ruin, and let him henceforth have no place among priests; but let him be expelled from the holy ministry, lest anyone afterward undertake responsibility for his judgment, since it is beyond doubt that he has already been condemned by the holy and apostolic Church, by its authority, and by his own disobedience and presumption. For he must be removed by the greater excommunication, to whom the discipline of the holy Church has been entrusted, who ought not only to obey the commands of the Church set over him, but also to admonish others lest they transgress them. Let him be excluded from divine and pontifical offices who was unwilling to obey apostolic commands.” [Col. 0449D–0450A]

Words of blessed Jerome to Jovinian: what sort of man ought to be chosen as bishop (Book I, *Against Jovinian*):

“The Apostle does not say: ‘Let a bishop be chosen who takes one wife and fathers children’; but ‘who has had one wife and children subject in every discipline.’ Certainly you admit that a man cannot be a bishop who fathers children while he is a bishop; otherwise, if he is discovered, he will not be treated as a husband but condemned as an adulterer. Either permit priests to perform the works of marriage, so that virgins and married men are the same; or, if priests may not touch wives, they are holy in this respect because they imitate virginal chastity. [Col. 0450B] But this too must be added: if a layman, or any believer, cannot pray unless he abstains from marital duty, then a priest, who must always offer sacrifices for the people, must always pray. If he must always pray, therefore he must always abstain from marriage. For under the old law, those who offered sacrifices for the people were not only absent from their homes, but were purified for a time by being separated from their wives, and they did not drink wine or strong drink, which commonly arouse lust.”

On bishops who live with women:

“No bishop is to live with a woman under any circumstances. If he is proved not to have observed this, let him be deprived of the honor of the episcopate, because he has shown himself unworthy of the priesthood.”

On clerics who have women in their houses:

“According to the divine rules, we forbid priests, deacons, and others in the clergy who are not recorded as having wives to have a woman in their house. We permit only a mother, daughter, sister, or other persons who avoid every ground for accusation. But if anyone, contrary to this observance, has in his house a woman who can give rise to suspicion of sexual misconduct, and if he hears from his fellow clerics that he is living with such a woman but refuses to drive her from his house, or if, when an accuser appears, he is proved to have behaved dishonestly with such a woman, then the bishop, according to the ecclesiastical canons, must expel him from the clergy.” [Col. 0450C]

On the marriages of clerics:

“If a future deacon or subdeacon does not have a wife joined to him, according to what we explained above, he is not to be consecrated unless, after being questioned beforehand by the consecrator, he promises that after consecration he can live chastely without a lawful wife. The consecrator must not, at the time of consecration, grant the future deacon or subdeacon permission to take a wife after consecration. If he permits this to happen, let him be removed from his episcopate. But a priest, deacon, or subdeacon who takes a wife is indeed to be expelled from the clergy, but he is to be handed over, together with his property, to the curia of the city in which he was a cleric. If a lector contracts a second marriage, or even a first marriage but marries a widow or a woman separated from her husband, or one rejected by the canons or sacred laws, let him not advance to another grade of the Church. But if he has somehow been promoted to a higher grade, let him be removed from it and restored to his former rank.” [Col. 0450D–0451A]

On clerics who cannot contract marriages:

“A cleric above the rank of lector and cantor, such as a subdeacon or deacon, must not dare to contract any marriage; otherwise let him fall from the priesthood. A lector who contracts a second marriage must likewise be forbidden to ascend to a higher grade of the ecclesiastical order. A layman also, if it appears that he has joined himself to a wife who had another husband, or if he is not lawfully joined, or if he himself has had another wife, cannot become a subdeacon, deacon, or priest. Even if he has infiltrated his way into consecration by clandestine means, his honor falls. Likewise, anyone who has contracted two marriages is forbidden to become a deacon or priest. And if anyone has taken as his wife a woman separated from the husband whom she herself left, he cannot become either a deacon or a priest. The same applies if he has had a concubine, since such men ought to live in chastity. A chaste man, however, is one who has or has had a chaste wife, and has received her as a virgin, herself a virgin.

“But if any priest, deacon, or subdeacon takes a wife, or has a concubine, whether secretly or openly or under any pretext, let him fall from the honor of the clergy, be deprived of it, and become a layman. Likewise, the provisions we have stated concerning clerics are also to apply to deaconesses. The constitution orders that deaconesses be created if they are fifty years old, provided that they are virgins or have had only one husband. If, however, a woman is made a deaconess before the age of fifty because of some necessity, she may live nowhere except in the monastery of consecrated women, where no males reside and where she may not live as she pleases. Deaconesses must live by themselves and admit no one else to live with them except, in truth, a brother. But if there is any suspicion that a so-called brother is living with her under false pretenses, either she must not be consecrated from the beginning, or, if she has been consecrated, she must lose her honor.” [Col. 0451B–C]

On clerics:

“No one is to become a cleric unless he has both a good reputation and learning. For one who does not know letters cannot be a cleric. Priests and deacons must also be taught the sacred prayers and ecclesiastical canons. They must be consecrated without reproach, without opposition, and without the payment of money, freed both from official and curial status, except perhaps according to the observance that we explained in the first chapter of the present constitution.

“Likewise, whether a lector, subdeacon, or priest, if he despises the honor of the clergy and passes into another way of life, let one of two things happen: either he is subjected, together with his property, to curial status, or, if he possesses several curial cities, or so that he may be made more degraded, he is dragged into official status—that is, into the *taxiotic* condition.” [Col. 0451D–0452A]

On bishops:

“This constitution speaks in its first chapter on the consecration of bishops about how the process ought to proceed. It is necessary first to examine the bishop’s life, whether it is good or blameworthy, and again whether he is fortified by good testimonies or not. If he belongs to official or curial status, he is forbidden to become a bishop, unless perhaps he has been in a monastery from early childhood. In that way he has been freed from the conditions mentioned above, but only so that he pays a fourth part of his substance to the curia, according to the observance of the law.

“Nor is it permitted to rise immediately from the lay state to the episcopate, nor is it sufficient to have deceptively held the honor of the clergy. A man who is to be a bishop must have neither a wife nor a concubine, neither sons nor grandsons, whether legitimate or unknown to the laws. If anyone acts contrary to these provisions, both the man who has been made bishop and the man who made him are to be expelled from the honor of the episcopate.

“Let it not be permitted to become a bishop by the payment of money. The man who becomes a bishop must be either a monk or a cleric, but in such a way that it is evident that he has been in the clerical order for not less than six months. He must also read the sacred canons. At the time of his consecration, the consecrator must ask him whether he can perform and preserve everything that the divine canons command. If he denies that he can preserve them, let him not be consecrated. But if he promises that he will observe, insofar as is possible for human beings, the holy precepts of the canons, then the consecrator must admonish and declare to him that, if he does not observe the holy canons, he will be alien from God and will not be numbered among religious bishops. For the canons of the Fathers must possess the force of laws.

“If anyone gives money and is created bishop in this way, not only will he himself not be among the bishops, but the man who consecrated him will not be among them either. The money or property given for the sake of the consecration is to be assigned to the holy Church, whether it belongs to the bishop or to the one who gave it. The man who accepted it must not only lose the property but also the rank and honor of the clergy.

“Likewise, if the recipient is a layman who has accepted money or property, he must lose what he received and be compelled to pay to the holy Church another amount equal to what he accepted as money. If he holds public office, he must cease to hold office and be condemned to irrevocable exile. If a constituted priest or deacon reaches the episcopate by a payment of money, he must not only cease to be a bishop but also lose his former rank of priest or deacon.

“The consecration of a bishop must take place before the entire Christian people, so that everyone may have the opportunity to object if he wishes. If an objection is made before the consecration, the man must not be consecrated bishop until the objection has been examined and he has appeared blameless in every respect. But if the man who objected proves a false accuser by abandoning the judgment concerning the objection and not carrying his case through, the man who consecrated the bishop must forbid him holy communion for the whole of his life.” [Col. 0452B–D]

It was decreed concerning the appointment of priests:

“That priests may neither be appointed nor expelled in any churches without the authority or consent of the bishops. If laymen present to the bishops clerics of approved life and doctrine to be consecrated and appointed in their churches, let the bishops reject them on no pretext whatsoever.” [Col. 0453A]

In the Council of Carthage:

“That no strange women cohabit with any clerics at all, but only mothers, grandmothers, maternal aunts, paternal aunts, sisters, and the daughters of brothers or sisters.”

Again, in the same council:

“That continent clerics not approach widows or virgins except by order and permission of the bishops, and that they not do so alone, but with clerics or with those whom the bishop orders. Nor should bishops or priests themselves approach such women alone, but either where clerics are present or where some serious Christians are present.”

In the Council of Ancyra:

“When deacons are ordained, if at the ordination itself they protest, saying that they wish to have wives and cannot remain continent, then, if afterward they enter into marriage, they are to remain in the clergy only and be removed from the ministry. But all who kept silent, accepted the laying on of hands, and professed continence, and afterward entered into marriage, must cease from the ministry and the clergy, receiving only lay communion.” [Col. 0453B]

In the Decretals of Pope Leo:

“That carnal marriage is denied to subdeacons. For although those outside the clerical order are free to devote themselves to marital partnership and the begetting of children, nevertheless, in order to exhibit the purity of perfect continence, carnal marriage is not granted even to subdeacons, so that those who have wives may be as though they had none, and those who do not have wives may remain unmarried. If this is rightly preserved in this order, which is fourth from the highest, how much more must it be observed in the first, second, and third, so that no one may be judged fit for Levitical, priestly, or episcopal dignity who is found not yet to have restrained himself from the pleasure of a wife.” [Col. 0453C]

Pope Innocent:

“That those who have fathered children while in the presbyterate must be removed from office. One who, instructed by zeal for the faith and discipline, does not tolerate the Church’s being polluted by unworthy priests whom he asserts to have fathered children while in the presbyterate—I would explain that this is not permitted if I did not know that your prudence possesses knowledge of the whole law. Therefore, dearest brothers, after examining the contents of the petition that has been submitted, order those who are said to have committed such acts to be brought into the midst. After the objections brought against those priests have been investigated, if they can be convicted, let them be removed from priestly office; for those who are not holy cannot handle holy things, and they become alien from the ministry which they have polluted by unlawful living. We are astonished that their bishops conceal these matters, so that they appear either to connive at restraining them or to be unaware that they are unlawful.” [Col. 0453D]

At the Council of Nicaea, concerning women introduced into clerics’ households:

“The great synod entirely forbade a bishop, priest, deacon, or anyone at all in the clergy to have a woman introduced into his household, except perhaps a mother, sister, aunt, or only those persons who avoid suspicion.”

Blessed Ambrose greatly extols this Council of Nicaea in his book *On the Trinity* in these words:

“Of the councils, or especially of the council, I shall follow the judgment of the three hundred and eighteen priests who, chosen like those of Abraham, victorious through the harmony of their faith, raised a trophy throughout the whole world after the wicked had been subdued. It seems to me that this is divine: that, in the same number, we possess in the councils an oracle of faith and, in the history of piety, an example.” [Col. 0454A]

In the Decretals, on which women may live with clerics:

“We do not permit any other women to live in the houses of clerics except those whom the Council of Nicaea permitted to live with them solely because of necessary family relationships.”

In the Council of Laodicea:

“Baths are not to be taken by men and women together. Those devoted to sacred offices, whether clerics or continent persons, and every Christian layman must not bathe with women, because among the gentiles this is the first reproach.”

That clerics may not attend entertainments and spectacles:

“Ministers of the altar, or any clerics, ought to attend no spectacles that are presented either at weddings or at banquets, but before the *thymelici* enter, they must rise from the banquet and depart.” [Col. 0454B]

[Note: *Thymelici*, that is, flute players.]

In the Synod of Neocaesarea, chapter 1:

“A priest who has taken a wife must be deposed from his order. If he has committed fornication or adultery, he must be expelled from the Church and, reduced to the rank of laymen, perform penance.”

In the same synod, chapter 12:

“This rule is observed among clerics, especially since the ancient rule requires that anyone who, having been corrected and baptized, wishes to become a cleric must promise that he will under no circumstances take a wife.” [Col. 0454C]

In the Council of Carthage, concerning continence, Bishop Aurelius said:

“When, in the previous council, the regulation of continence and chastity was discussed, it pleased us that these three grades, which are joined by a certain written obligation of chastity through consecration—namely, bishops, priests, and deacons—should be continent in all things, as befits holy prelates and priests of God, as well as Levites and those who serve the divine sacraments, so that they may obtain simply what they ask from God; and that what the apostles taught and antiquity itself preserved, we too should preserve.” [Col. 0454D]

In the same synod, concerning abstinence from wives by the various orders, Bishop Faustinus of the Church of Potentia in the province of Picenum, legate of the holy Church, said:

“It is pleasing that bishops, priests, and deacons, or those who handle the sacraments, guardians of chastity, abstain from their wives.”

All the bishops said:

“It is pleasing that chastity be preserved in all things and by all who serve at the altar.”

Furthermore, when the incontinence of certain clerics toward their own wives was reported, “it was decreed that bishops, priests, and deacons should, according to the earlier statutes, also abstain from their wives. If they do not do so, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office. Other clerics, however, are not to be compelled to this, but it is to be observed according to the custom of each Church.” [Col. 0455A]

At the Roman synod presided over by blessed Pope Sylvester with two hundred and eighty-four bishops:

“No priest may take a wife from the day on which he receives the honor of the presbyterate. If anyone acts otherwise in disregard of this, we declare that he is to be deprived of his honor for twelve years. If anyone acts against this written declaration, which has been made publicly and in his presence, he is to be condemned forever.”

Ambrose, in his letter to Titus, says among other things:

“A husband of one wife: although it is not forbidden to have a second wife numerically, nevertheless, if someone is to be worthy of the episcopate, he must reject even what is lawful because of the exalted nature of that order, since the man who desires that office ought to be better than the others. He must be sober, chaste, well ordered, hospitable, teachable, not addicted to wine, not violent, but moderate; not quarrelsome, not harsh; ruling his household well; having children subject to him with complete charity. He says that such a man, who preserves the good qualities he enumerates, ought to be made a bishop, for these are marks of episcopal dignity.

“If anyone has pursued higher things and has dedicated body and soul to God so as not to join himself in marriage, he will be all the more worthy. For this reason he placed the lower condition first, so that no one would doubt the superiority of the higher. Let the bishop be chaste, whom the Greeks call *sōphrona* (σώφρονα), while the Latin translator, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, translated it as ‘prudent’ instead of ‘chaste.’

“If laymen are commanded to abstain from intercourse with their wives for the sake of prayer, what must be thought of the bishop, who must offer unblemished sacrifices to God every day for his own sins and those of the people? Let us reread the Books of Kings, and we shall find that the priest Abimelech was unwilling to give the loaves of the Presence to David and his young men until he had asked whether the young men were clean with respect to a woman—not, of course, a strange woman, but a wife—and until he had heard from them that they had abstained from marital activity since yesterday and the day before, he never granted them the loaves that he had first refused.

“How great is the difference between the loaves of the Presence and the body of Christ? What difference is there between shadow and substance, between image and truth, between representations of future things and the things themselves that were prefigured through those representations? Therefore, just as gentleness, patience, sobriety, moderation, abstinence from profit, hospitality, and kindness ought especially to be found in a bishop and ought to make him eminent among all laymen, so too must there be a distinctive chastity—so I may say, a priestly purity—so that his mind, which is to make the body of Christ, may abstain not only from unclean action but also from the casting of the eye and the error of thought.

“A bishop must also be just and holy, so that he may exercise justice among the peoples over whom he presides, rendering to each what he deserves and showing no partiality in judgment. The difference between the justice of a layman and that of a bishop is that a layman can appear just in a few matters, whereas a bishop exercises justice in as many matters as he has subjects.

“Let the bishop also be abstinent—not merely, as some think, from lust and the embrace of a wife, but from all disturbances of the soul: so that he is not provoked to anger, not cast down by sadness, not agitated by fear, and not lifted up by excessive joy. Abstinence is also numbered by the Apostle among the fruits of the Spirit.” [Col. 0455B–456A]

Isidore, Bishop of Seville, in the book *On Sacred Offices*:

“He who presides over peoples in educating and training them toward virtue must necessarily be holy in all things and be considered blameworthy in nothing. For he who rebukes another for sins must himself be free from sin. With what face could he rebuke his subjects when the one corrected could immediately say to him: ‘Teach yourself first what is right, O bishop’?

“Therefore, let him who neglects to do what is right cease teaching what is right. He who strives to admonish others to live well must first correct himself, so that in all things he may offer himself as a pattern of life and urge everyone toward good work both by teaching and by action.

“Knowledge of the Scriptures is also necessary for him. If a bishop’s life alone is holy, he can benefit only himself by living in this way. But if he is also learned in doctrine and speech, he can instruct others, teach his own people, and strike back at adversaries. Unless these are refuted and convicted, they can easily pervert the hearts of the simple.

“His speech must be pure, simple, and suitable. His special duty above others is to read the Scriptures, review the canons, imitate the examples of the saints, devote himself to vigils, fasts, and prayers, keep peace with his brothers, despise none of his members, condemn no one unless he has been proved guilty, and excommunicate no one unless he has been examined. He must excel equally in humility and authority, so that by excessive humility he does not allow the vices of his subjects to grow strong, nor by immoderate authority exercise the power of severity; rather, let him act toward those entrusted to him with greater caution, the more fearfully he dreads Christ’s judgment.” [Col. 0456B–C]

The same author, in the same book:

“Let bishops therefore also be virgins, chaste and pure, and let them proceed along the way of sublimity. Let them follow Christ with the foot of humility, perseveringly holding what they ardently vowed, so that, having professed this and preserved their integrity, they may also be consistent in their other conduct, without which virginity is undoubtedly idle and empty.

“Those are shown to be virgins who serve continence in such a way that they are weighed down by no crimes and by no honor connected with earthly concerns. For the care of the world is produced by marital union, as Paul teaches when he says: ‘I want you to be free from anxiety. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife’ (1 Cor. VII, 32–33). Hence it is recognized that a vow of continence of this sort cannot please God when it is obstructed by worldly cares.” [Col. 0456D]

The same author, in the same book:

“Bishops themselves ought therefore to be so perfect and so learned in priestly offices that, in the holy place, in the courts of the tabernacle of testimony, by not sinning themselves they may consume the sins of the people.

“What does it mean to eat sin in a holy place? The place to which Moses came was holy, according to what was said to him: ‘The place on which you stand is holy ground’ (Exod. III, 5). Likewise, in the Church of God the holy place is perfect faith and charity from a pure heart and a good conscience.

“Let bishops see and learn what kind of touch makes one unclean and what kind of touch makes one clean. The Apostle says: ‘It is good for a man not to touch a woman’ (1 Cor. VII, 1). This touch is unclean; it is what the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart’ (Matt. V, 28). For the vice of desire has touched his heart, and his soul has been made unclean.

“If anyone touches anything in this way, whether through desire for a woman, through greed for money, or through any other sinful desire, he has touched something unclean and has been defiled. Therefore, if you have touched anything of this kind, you must know how to offer sacrifice, according to what we mentioned above, so that you may be made clean.” [Col. 0457A–B]

Ambrose, on the Epistle to the Romans, chapter VIII:

“Brothers, all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. If the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God, and those who are in the flesh cannot please God, I think that those who serve marital duty love the wisdom of the flesh and are in the flesh. Drawing us away from it and joining us to the Spirit, the Apostle afterward says (chapter XII): ‘I appeal to you, through the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God.’”

The same author shortly afterward:

“See, brother, how much chastity is required of a bishop, so that if his sons are unchaste, he himself cannot be a bishop, and by the same vice with which Eli the high priest offended God he too will offend. Eli had indeed rebuked his sons, but because he had not expelled the offenders, he fell backward and died (1 Kings IV).

“In every rank and sex, chastity holds the chief place. You see, therefore, that a bishop, priest, or deacon is not blessed merely because he is a bishop, priest, or deacon, but if he possesses the virtues of his names and offices. Otherwise, if a deacon is holier than his bishop, he will not be worse before Christ because he is in a lower rank—just as Stephen the deacon, who was crowned first with martyrdom, will not be lower in the kingdom of heaven than many bishops, nor than Timothy and Titus. I would not dare place them beneath him, just as I would not dare place him before them (1 Tim. III, 2–3).

“A bishop must therefore be irreproachable, so that he is enslaved to no vice of luxury: a husband of one wife, one who has had one wife, not one who has one; sober—or, as it is said in Greek, watchful—namely *nēphanton* (νηφαντόν); chaste, for this is what *sōphrona* (σώφρονα) signifies; well ordered in both chastity and conduct; hospitable, so that he may imitate Abraham and receive Christ with strangers, or rather in strangers; a teacher—for it is of no benefit to enjoy the consciousness of virtues unless he can also instruct the people entrusted to him, so that he may be able to exhort in doctrine and rebuke those who contradict.

“He must not be addicted to wine, because he is always in the Holy of Holies and offers sacrifices, and he does not drink wine or strong drink; not addicted to wine, because in wine there is lust; not addicted to wine—let the bishop drink in such a way that no one knows whether he has drunk.” [Col. 0457D–0458B]

Ambrose, on the Epistle to the Romans:

“What happiness it is not to be a wife’s servant but Christ’s; not to serve the flesh but the Spirit! For he who clings to the Lord is one spirit with him (1 Cor. VII, 17).

“And lest, in what he had said above—‘Were you called as a slave? Do not let it concern you; but if you can become free, make use of it rather’ (ibid., 21)—he might seem to have mocked continence and delivered us into servitude to wives, he adds a statement that cuts off every quibble: ‘You were bought at a great price; do not become slaves of human beings’ (ibid., 23). We have been redeemed by the most precious blood of Christ; do not become slaves of wives either.

“Christ truly loves virgins, because they freely offer what was not commanded of them. It is a greater grace to offer what one does not owe than to return what is demanded.

“When the apostles considered the burden of a wife, they said: ‘If such is the situation of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry’ (Matt. XIX, 10). Approving their judgment, the Lord said: ‘You rightly judge that it is expedient for a man striving toward the kingdom of heaven not to take a wife. But the matter is difficult, and not all receive this word, but only those to whom it has been given’ (ibid., 11).

“And shortly afterward this statement must be considered: ‘There are those who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven’ (ibid., 12). Therefore, those who have not made themselves eunuchs cannot receive the place of eunuchs. ‘Let him who can receive it receive it’ (ibid.).

“It is a matter of great faith and great virtue to be a most pure temple of God, to offer oneself entirely as a holocaust to the Lord, and, according to the same Apostle, to be holy in body and spirit. [Col. 0458C] These are the eunuchs who, thinking themselves a dry tree because of their barrenness, hear through Isaiah (Isa. LVI) that a place has been prepared for them in heaven in place of sons and daughters.”

Jerome:

“He cannot serve in the Lord’s army who is the servant of a wife.

“On the mirrors of fasting women, as though they were the purest bodies of virgins: the *luter* [probably an uncertain OCR reading] in the tabernacle, and within the sanctuary the cherubim, the mercy seat, the ark of the testimony, the table of the Presence, the lampstand, and the censer are all of the purest gold. For silver could not be brought into the Holy of Holies.

“As a worm in wood, so a wicked wife destroys her husband. But if you assert that this was said about wicked wives, I shall briefly answer you: What necessity compels me to run the risk of whether the woman I take will turn out to be wicked or good? It is better to live in a deserted land than with a quarrelsome and angry wife.

“He who has taken a wife knows how rare it is to find one without these vices. Hence Varius Geminus, a distinguished orator, aptly said: ‘He who does not quarrel is unmarried.’ ‘It is better to dwell in a corner of the roof than in a common house with a cursing wife’ (Prov. XXV, 24). For by continual quarrels and daily chatter she makes his house rain through and drives him from his dwelling—that is, from the Church.

“I think that, as long as a man who has a wife returns to the same marital relation, Satan does not tempt him, because he sows in the flesh and not in the spirit. But the one who sows in the flesh will reap corruption—not I, but the Apostle says this (Gal. VI, 8).
