“God the Father chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and blameless before him (Eph. I, 4). We walked in the desires of the flesh, doing its will and the will of our thoughts, and we were children of wrath like the rest. But now, when he raised us up and made us sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus (Eph. II, 3, 5–6), we must put off, according to our former way of life, the old man who is corrupted according to the desires of the flesh (ibid., IV, 22). Whatever things are true, whatever things are chaste, whatever things are upright, whatever things pertain to chastity—let us be joined to these and follow them.” [Col. 0458D–0459A]

The blessed Ambrose to Pammachius:

“It follows that, according to the image of him who gave the priesthood of the Church, the ministers and priests of the Church should also take upon themselves the sins of the people and, imitating the Master, grant the people remission of sins. The priests of the Church themselves ought therefore to be so perfect and so learned in priestly offices that, in the holy place, in the courts of the tabernacle of testimony, by not sinning themselves they may consume the sins of the people.

“What does it mean to eat sin in a holy place? The place to which Moses came was holy, according to what was said to him: ‘The place on which you stand is holy ground’ (Exod. III, 5). Likewise, in the Church of God the holy place is perfect faith and charity from a pure heart and a good conscience. Whoever stands in these things must recognize that he stands in the Church, in a holy place.” [Col. 0459B–0460A]

Again, shortly afterward:

“Let the priests of the Lord who preside over the Churches learn that their portion is given together with those whose offenses they have reconciled (Hebr. II, 17). What does it mean to reconcile an offense? If you take a sinner and, by admonishing, exhorting, teaching, and instructing him, bring him to repentance; if you correct him from error, amend him from his vices, and make him such that, once converted, he becomes pleasing to God, you are said to have reconciled him for his offense.

“If, therefore, you are such a priest, and such is your teaching and your speech, a portion is given to you of those whom you have corrected, so that their merit may be your reward, their salvation your glory.” [Col. 0460B]

## Epistle XV. To Leo, Abbot of the Roman Monastery of Saint Boniface

(In Mabillon, *Annales Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, vol. IV, Appendix, p. 691.)

[Col. 0459]

[Col. 0459B] To Lord L., abbot of Saint Boniface, dearest of the dearest, wonderfully resounding with the distinction of eloquence, the merit of life, and the teaching of wisdom: Abbo, humble abbot of the monastery of Fleury, wishes that the Spirit of the Lord, who has filled the world, may fill his very knowledge and understanding.

Charity, which is the bond of perfection, when it joined us both together at Rheims, caused your tongue, in private conversation, to pour forth publicly and in private so many oratorical streams and such great honeycombs of Holy Scripture, in a fervor of righteous zeal, that I am compelled to exclaim: “Grace has been poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever.” While I stood astonished at the flashes of such thunderous strokes, I was thereafter compelled everywhere to confess that you are the thunder of the Holy Spirit, who descended upon the apostles in fiery tongues, and that he has also fittingly polished you into a flaming sword for cutting down the wicked from his temple, with the seven gifts of grace.

Meanwhile, at last, raising the eyes of my mind, I wished with eagle eyes to behold the sunlike rays of your eloquence; and, as Ecclesiastes says, “A brother helping a brother is like a fortified and strong city,” I resolved, if it pleases you, to have you forever as a staff of strong assistance and a column of inseparable friendship. For this reason I bend my knees to the Father, that through our Lord Jesus Christ he may grant you to be of one mind, so that your honeycomb-dripping lips may possess our memory as an inheritance throughout the everlasting ages.

Amid the intimate secrets of our conversation, your magnificence let fall into our ears a certain expression which I am no less eager, if God wills, to fulfill than to obtain eternal life as the object of my vow. You asked that the distinguished relics of Saint Benedict, the holy Father, be sent to you, since it was entirely certain that the presence of his most holy body was being retained by us, and therefore you earnestly wished an oratory to be built in his honor; likewise, you wished that we should receive from Saint Boniface, or from the sacred limbs of the other saints, an equivalent recompense for ourselves.

Moreover, your incomparable goodness added that, if some desire concerning domestic affairs pressed upon us, requiring us to strengthen our privileges through the apostolic instrument of Roman authority, you would be our most faithful collaborator in everything and through everything. It was my intention to accomplish all these things when I approached, as a suppliant, the magnificent limbs of the prince of the apostles; but, alas, to my grief, I encountered the Roman Church deprived of a worthy shepherd.

In your absence, I confess, I was affected as a hen’s chick is accustomed to be affected when, complaining with hoarse throat, it laments that its mother’s sole protection has been taken away. Recently, however, I heard news that gladdened me more than gold and topaz: that the apostolic dignity had been raised up by a man of imperial blood, wholly endowed with virtues and wisdom. Your return resounded in our mind like the ineffable harmony of a return to paradise.

Now therefore, just as we discussed with one another, and as this letter presents itself to your sight, may it please you to hear through these monks of Saint Benedict, and, having heard, to accomplish what you promised, with complete faith and devotion. May that same Spirit who inspired Gregory with every flower of eloquence inspire the venerable apostolic shepherd of this holy Roman Church, and grant you to be his sweetest confidential secretary, so as to strengthen the abasement of apostolic authority. Farewell.

## LETTER XVI. TO BERNARD, ABBOT OF BELLUS LOCUS

[Col. 0461]

(See above in the Life of Saint Abbo, no. 10.)

[Col. 0461]

## THE APOLOGETIC OF SAINT ABBO, ABBOT OF FLEURY, TO HUGH AND ROBERT, KINGS OF THE FRANKS

[Col. 0461B]

It often happens that, when the excessive terror of rising calamities wearies the mind, the mind, disturbed by that very terror, does not bring forth what it ought to say; rather, carried elsewhere by the phantoms of its thoughts, it says what ought to have been kept silent and, as follows from this, keeps silent about what ought to be said.

For the person who has undertaken to arrange the secret of truth through reasoning always loves the repose of the highest tranquility. Therefore, from the very beginnings of my studies, just as the deer longs for springs of water (Psalm XLI, 1), so my soul longed for the laborious leisure of spiritual philosophy, which I might turn into an honorable occupation for the benefit of many. But, because my sins stood in the way, abandoning that pursuit I was in a certain sense brought back to the cares of the world, where I am daily sustained under the charge of pastoral government by the water of distress and the bread of affliction (3 Kings XXII, 27).

The treacherous cunning of my rivals gnaws at me with a dog’s tooth; the frequent bitterness of my adversaries barks around me. They murmur nothing else against me except that I wished the senate of monks to be safe, sought the enlargement of our commonwealth, opposed the quibbling of those lying in wait with whatever authority I could command, and did not entirely conceal mercy and truth from a great council.

For such things they lie in wait for my blood and pursue me with hastily assembled hatreds, to such a degree that not even royal majesty deters them from secretly murdering me, if place and time should favor them. Hence, assiduously in my prayers I beseech God to judge and discern my cause as usual and to rescue me from an unjust and deceitful man (Psalm XLII, 1). And if I am granted an opportunity to defend myself before my lords the bishops, whom I have learned to be orthodox in the Catholic faith, I believe that I shall be innocent of the charge, provided they examine the origin of the quarrels without respect of persons.

For who, by his own prejudice, would proceed to the point of alienating some possession, however small, of a monastery? Who would dare, as an extortioner of property and a distorter of laws, to entangle and confuse the cords of ecclesiastical inheritance by mixing them together, when it is written: “You shall not move the boundaries that your fathers established”? (Proverbs XXII, 22.)

Behold, in accordance with the rules of the holy Fathers, I do not evade a hearing, subject to the judgment of the bishops, prepared to render an account of my stewardship, provided only that I receive assurance that I will not suffer harm by being seized by those lying in wait. I am prepared to die if ever I have committed anything worthy of death.

And first I desire that my faith be examined, without which I cannot be saved, so that others may profit from my examination, or by my protest recognize that they have fallen into heresy and strive to be rescued from it as quickly as possible—lest by remaining in it until death they become the devil’s stubble. For whoever believes about God, religion, or the common condition of the holy Church otherwise than Christ taught, or than the Catholic Church held under the holy apostles and handed down to their successors to be held, is not Catholic or faithful, but plainly a heretic.

Indeed, our fathers persecuted all heresies in such a way that, once the faith had first been set forth, they investigated in their councils whether anyone held anything contrary to the apostles themselves. Whoever was found was, without any delay, either restored to the body of the whole Church or struck with anathema until renouncing his error and deprived of Catholic communion. Nor did the orthodox avoid touching a serpent more carefully than they avoided clinging to those contaminated with such leprosy.

Therefore the canons forbid us, if we know ourselves to be Catholics, even to pray with them. For under the emperor Marcian, at Chalcedon, a session lasting fifteen days and more was held concerning this matter, with two hundred bishops sitting, or, as some prefer, one thousand two hundred; and the pious emperor generously supplied all of them with expenses from his own resources, so that they might reject all heretics from themselves—that is, those who had thought or acted otherwise than the holy apostles.

When this had been done, the purity of the faith pleased the pious emperor so greatly that, together with his wife, he publicly professed it under his signature before that great council. Imitate that council’s pious devotion, our lords Hugh and Robert, most illustrious kings, if you wish to be heirs and coheirs with Christ in the land of the living, and drive every heretical depravity from your kingdom, so that God may preserve you in eternal peace.

For it must be understood that during the solemn celebration of Mass the priest daily supplicates God and intercedes not for heretics or schismatics, but only for the orthodox and for the worshipers of the Catholic and apostolic faith. Anyone who proudly separates himself from their unanimity in word or deed is thereby excluded from that supplication. But whoever humbly confesses himself subject to sins or uncertain in faith must be borne with and corrected, not as an outsider but as a brother, since he has not yet placed his portion with the hypocrites—especially since Peter, the prince of the Church, denied God, and Thomas doubted in faith.

Indeed, we know that within the holy and universal Church there are three orders, as it were three degrees, of the faithful of both sexes. Although none of them is without sin, the first is good, the second better, and the third best.

The first order, in both sexes, is that of married persons; the second, that of the continent and widows; the third, that of virgins and consecrated women. Among men alone there are likewise three degrees or orders: the first is that of laymen, the second that of clerics, and the third that of monks.

But since I have proposed to explain the differences among these degrees, and have judged it right to call one better or holier than another, I have thought it necessary to explain briefly how each awaits the reward of eternal recompense in its own vocation, and how, by the authority of the holy Fathers, people may be promoted from one degree to another.

Marriage is permitted solely by way of indulgence, lest an age more inclined to decline should fall into worse things through the weakness of the flesh. Marriage is forbidden to no one except the person who, in order to earn the joys of the heavenly homeland, has freely chosen lifelong continence. If such a person has failed to observe it, then, although the devotion was concealed, the hidden crime must be erased by more secret penance; nevertheless, the person must remain in the degree in which he or she laments having committed the evil.

But if someone wishes to justify it for himself by the example of the priests of the Old Testament, he falls from his own degree and washes away the fault with tears. Here is the principle: if the person belongs among those to whom it is permitted, he or she is not punished, but is even considered worthy of reward, because by obedience the person has remained content with the chastity taught by the Apostle.

The qualification “if the person belongs among those to whom it is permitted” has been added because, in both sexes, there are people who bind themselves by a vow so that, if they are virgins, they may remain in virginity; and, if they are not virgins, they may reject intercourse with the flesh and live perpetually in celibacy. There is also kinship or family relationship, from whose carnal union all who are under the Catholic faith are prohibited.

Moreover, among those who bind themselves by a vow, or among those who have not yet crossed the seventh degree of kinship, a detestable marriage must immediately be dissolved by the remedy of penance. But what does not require penance, because it is permitted by authority, must never be dissolved except either by the death of one spouse or by the profession of celibacy by both.

From here we pass to the more excellent order of the continent and widows. If they remain in it, according to the Apostle, they will deserve a greater crown of eternal reward in proportion to the heavier penalty they endure after having experienced the pleasure of the flesh. To these, too, he granted second marriages by way of discernment, saying that it is better to marry than to burn (1 Corinthians VII, 9).

As for third or fourth marriages, or even more numerous marriages, I do not remember having read whether Catholics ought to celebrate them. But this presents itself without any doubt: if such an act is a serious offense in women, it is much more serious if it occurs in men.

No one is ignorant of how great is the glory of virgins. Who knows a human being to seek, by a privilege of grace, what an angel possesses by nature? When the virtue of virginity is strengthened by humility, it will be rewarded with a recompense of singular merit, because God promises virgins that they will follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Revelation XIV, 4). By this virtue the venerable fellowship of consecrated women is adorned, and many rejoice that they have earned it throughout all the orders of men, within the bosom of their mother, the Church.

But setting these matters aside, we must first speak of the order of men, that is, of laymen. Some are farmers, others are combatants. The farmers labor in agriculture and in various crafts of rural work, from which the entire multitude of the Church is sustained. The combatants, content with the pay of military service, do not clash with one another in the womb of their mother, but with every skill attack the adversaries of the holy Church of God.

Next comes the order of clerics, which is specifically distinguished into three degrees: deacons, presbyters, and bishops. For all who belong to the lower degree are called clerics by a misuse of the term, while, like laymen, they are permitted by indulgence to associate with wives. It is established that the apostles and their successors prohibited clerics—that is, deacons, presbyters, and bishops—from having wives.

Κλῆρος, in Greek, is called sors in Latin, “lot.” Hence clerics, chosen by lot for God to sacrifice or to minister, should strive to beget children not carnally but spiritually, so that they may always remember the lot of the saints in light. For they, having undertaken the daily care of all the churches (2 Corinthians II, 28), labor in the active life with Martha, who is anxious about many things (Luke X, 41).

The monks, however, having attained in the contemplative life that one thing which is necessary, rejoice with Mary all the more in watering Jesus’ feet with tears and wiping them with their hair (Luke VII, 38), the farther they are removed from the disturbance of all the world’s affairs.

Indeed, the order of clerics, situated midway between laymen and monks, is as much above the lower as it is below the higher, since, insofar as it differs from each of the two orders, it is joined to the other. The former are bound to wives, devoted to the care of household affairs, and occupied with the activities of the world. The latter are alienated from the activities of the world, renouncing their own will and obeying the commands of a spiritual father. They live both by the alms of good men and by the labor of their own hands, and they can say with Peter: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Matthew XIX, 27).

Finally, the irreproachable life of clerics is a mirror of the entire Church, just as the habit and firm profession of monks is an example of the whole perfection of penance. And although clerics who are worthy of reproach, lest the profane handle holy things, are degraded for specific causes, monks are never entirely deprived of the communion of their brothers except on account of pride. They receive even criminal laymen or clerics, and when they are discovered in a crime they correct themselves according to regular discipline.

Finally, let anyone ordained a presbyter from among monks, or made a monk from among clerics, know that he does not serve ecclesiastical offices in the manner of clerics, but celebrates Mass in the community according to the institution of the Gregorian privilege.

But since what seemed necessary to say about the individual orders has been said, it must not be left unsaid how promotion from one order to another takes place. People are promoted from laymen or clerics to monastic life, and from laymen or monks to the clerical order. When and how this ought to happen the authority of the holy Fathers clearly makes known. Those who have not followed that authority have strayed from the faith outside the Catholic Church.

Therefore, in the canon, while prayers are being offered for the orthodox and for the worshipers of the Catholic and apostolic faith, they must take the greatest care concerning what Pope Gregory reports in his synod: “There is one faith, one baptism, one Catholic Church, in which alone sins can be forgiven.” If there is no remission of sins outside it, why does a heretic or schismatic fast? Why does he give tithes? Why does he worship God as a suppliant?

For just as the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul (Acts IV, 32), so throughout the whole world there is one Church of all those who, according to the teaching of the apostles, hold one understanding in God. The word “church” is translated from Greek into Latin as convocatio, “assembly,” because we are all called to one faith and one baptism.

Therefore every house where, with an altar erected, the people gather to entreat God, so long as it bears the name of a church, is worthy of reverence and the highest honor among every nation, because in it we are reborn from water and the Holy Spirit (John III, 5); in it the divine mysteries are celebrated; in it confession and the remission of sins take place.

Let anyone who wishes to be saved beware of believing that it is the possession of anyone except God alone. Hence it is said to Peter, the prince of the apostles: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew XVI, 18). He says “my,” not “your.” And Christ says elsewhere: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matthew XXI, 13). The Psalmist also says: “Holiness befits your house, O Lord” (Psalm XCII, 5).

If the Church is not Peter’s, whose will it be? Or will Peter’s successors dare to claim for themselves a power that Peter, the prince of the Church, did not possess? Certainly, dearest princes, we neither live nor speak as Catholics when I say that one church is mine, another says that another church is his, and, made like beasts of burden and compared with foolish animals, we sometimes put both up for sale and do not fear to buy them after others have put them up for sale.

There is also another gravest error: it is said that the altar belongs to the bishop and the church to some other lord, although from the consecrated house and the altar one thing is formed that is called a church, just as one human being consists of body and soul.

See, most just princes, where greed leads us when charity grows cold (Matthew XXIV, 12). From the gifts of almighty God, which are received freely, we become merchants and try to sell what we certainly do not possess. For scarcely anything seems to belong to the Church, which belongs to God alone, unless a price is given for it: the episcopate, the presbyterate, the diaconate, and the remaining lower degrees; also the archdeaconate, the deanery, the provostship, the custody of treasures, the baptistery, burial, and whatever similar things there may be.

Such merchants customarily assert by a deceitful reply that they are not buying the blessing through which the grace of the Holy Spirit is received, but the properties of the churches or the possessions of the bishop, although it is certain that in the Catholic Church one cannot exist without the other.

Has anyone used fire without the fuel by which it is nourished? Or has anyone ever held fire and been without heat? Who has found honey without sweetness? Who has detected wormwood without bitterness? Yet it is possible for the same water to be found sweet and bitter under different conditions. Because this happens contingently, it sometimes deceives our judgment, so that what is believed to be sweet proves bitter.

So too such a transaction is considered good when it is certainly evil, because it occurs for the sake of shameful profit. The practice has become so widespread that this is now believed to happen without sin. But the Holy Spirit, through the mouth of blessed Pope Gregory, says: “Because the blessing is turned into a curse for the person who is promoted in order to become a heretic, no outsider is free from that curse who, out of greed for profit, rejoices that he has invaded ecclesiastical ministry” (Book VII, Letter 3).

I am greatly astonished at how the practice arose whereby laymen sell bishoprics, since blessed Ambrose, in a pastoral sermon, adds the following after much else, with tears rather than laughter:

“See,” he says, “throughout the Church those whom not merit but money has advanced to the episcopal order: a frivolous and ignorant people who have chosen such a priest for themselves. If you wish to ask them truthfully who appointed them priests, they will immediately answer and say: ‘I was recently ordained by the archbishop, and I gave him one hundred solidi so that I might deserve to obtain episcopal grace. If I had not given them, I would not be a bishop today. Therefore it is better for me to bring gold into the treasury than to lose so great a priesthood. I gave gold and purchased the episcopate; nevertheless, if I live, I do not doubt that I shall immediately recover those solidi. I ordain presbyters, consecrate deacons, and receive gold; and from the other orders as well I trust that I shall extract monetary profit. Behold, I have received in my treasury the gold that I gave; therefore I received the episcopate for free.’

“Indeed, this is what I lament: the archbishop made the bishop according to the flesh; for the sake of money he specifically ordained a leper. ‘May your money perish with you,’ he said, ‘because you thought to purchase the gift of the Holy Spirit for a price, and you carried out a miserable commerce to the destruction of souls’” (Book On the Dignity of the Priesthood, chapter 5).

From what precedes and follows it is easily understood with what intention this holy man spoke these words.

As for the fact that those called Simonians have brought laymen into their curse, this was done after the example of the priests who joined Pilate and Herod, the rulers of their own people, to themselves for the ministry of the Lord’s passion.

Nor are we unaware that, on account of such bishops—who are chosen not for the merit of their life or the teaching of their wisdom, but rather for the greatest sum of money—the seed of discord and harm increases in the kingdom. Gregory bears witness to this in the letter written to the kings Theudebert and Theuderic:

“It is reported,” he says, “that the Simoniac heresy, which first crept against the Church through the devil’s planting and was struck and condemned at its very origin by the weapon of apostolic vengeance, dominates within the boundaries of your kingdom, since in priests faith ought to be chosen together with life.”

And shortly afterward:

“From this, not only is a lethal wound inflicted upon the soul of the ordainer and the ordained, but even your Excellency’s kingdom is weighed down by the fault of bishops, by whose intercessions it ought to have been helped.”

And afterward:

“Therefore greater calamity must be feared in those places where such intercessors are brought to the place of governance—men who provoke God’s wrath against themselves more than they ought to appease him on behalf of the peoples. Nor can our concern negligently omit this further evil: certain men, enticed by the prompting of empty glory, suddenly seize the honor of the priesthood from the lay state and—what one is ashamed to say and finds grievous to keep silent—become rulers who ought to be governed and teachers who ought to be taught; yet they neither blush to be seen nor are afraid” (Book IX, Letter 110).

Thus far Saint Gregory.

And since such prelates, intent upon avarice, allow the churches to be utterly ruined and destroy by their example the morals of their subjects, whom they ought to correct, it remains that the defenders and founders of the churches, and the heirs of their founders, should withdraw from their communion, lest they become participants in the curse.

Nevertheless, if the pontifical dignity and royal majesty are Catholic, the authority of each is weighed on an equal scale, so that they may benefit the Church which Christ redeemed with his blood. The dignity of the one proclaims the law of the Lord spiritually to the peoples; the majesty of the other, when necessary, protects it by arms. Therefore care must be taken lest those whose ministries correspond to one another recoil from one another.

Their harmony in different offices benefits each of them to the extent that, by consulting together with one mind, they think about the common good. For this reason the names of emperors or consuls are placed at the head of the pages of ancient councils, through whose favor the deliberations of great bishops were held; those bishops had first carefully examined the purity of the faith and whom they should find worthy of the council according to their order.

Therefore, most merciful princes, following the custom of your royal predecessors, give your assent to those councils through which the commonwealth is improved and enlarged by reconciliation. For if, in some kind of council, one person wishes to assign to himself another’s estates or small possessions for private dealings, and thus, at his brother’s loss, to extinguish the thirst of his avarice by accumulating money in chests and coffers, without observing the thirty-year law that arose from imperial constitutions or the authority of the canons, know without doubt that this evil concerns you, since you hold the summit of the kingdom for the very purpose of rendering just judgment to all.

For you, indeed, our lords, every one of your subjects cries out to God and says: “Give the king your judgments, O God, and your justice to the king’s son; judge your people in justice and your poor in judgment” (Psalm LXXI, 1–2).

Although the sense of these verses can be referred to God the Father of all and to his only-begotten Son, nothing prevents us from understanding them as a prayer concerning an earthly king: that he judge the people not by his own judgment but by God’s, since he will have to render an account even for an idle word.

Nor do I withdraw myself from your examination or that of other wise men. I am suspected of holding views contrary to the canons; I am accused of having raised my hand against bishops over the monks, of having taken your goodwill away from your own bishop, and of having participated with certain excommunicated persons. But so be it.

Which canon’s judgment did I contradict, when scarcely any council permitted me to see an open book? Or what council was it where people came reconciled and departed unreconciled, when the dissenting parties ought there to have been reconciled or punished by canonical discipline?

What had the bishops individually done to me, that I should have wished to harm them even in thought—especially since it happened that one who was not an enemy but most friendly in faith and conduct endured greater dangers?

Behold, before God in Christ I do not lie (Galatians I, 20): when I heard the outcry of those pursuing him, I grieved beyond what can be expressed, remembering the former friendship and the benefits of so great a man, whose snow-white head showed him to be worthy of reverence, apart from the privilege of primacy and the priestly mitre.

By what suggestion did I deceive you, so that you would take your goodwill away from the best and give it to those who deserved ill? Am I God, who changes minds, kingdoms, and times? I openly confess that I know nothing of magic and have learned nothing of evil arts.

Therefore the man who complains against me on this matter seems to accuse no one but you, who, abandoning the path of equity, neglected to repay his benefits in kind. Or perhaps I despise the authority of royal majesty! However little he has exasperated you, by exasperating he provoked you, by provoking offended you, and after offending delayed to appease you; yet he marvels that gifts of just recompense are being bestowed upon him for such benefits. He does not blame himself for what he deserved, but attempts to transfer the guilt to the destruction of an innocent man.

For if, when he took what was ours, he thought that he had done you no harm, he certainly did not believe you to be lords of our possessions or their defenders. If he did believe it, he injured you along with me and did not fail to know that he had injured himself.

Why, then, does he accuse me rhetorically? Why does he alone attribute to me what burdens him? Can I know how often I sent envoys, how often I asked for peace, how often I offered myself as a suppliant? God is my witness that, with the rights of our monastery preserved, I was prepared to obey everything that he might regularly command. And if I have deserved any evil, while the abundance of our possessions remains undisturbed, let the just sentence of the bishops be hurled against me, because he alone, as he ought, will never rage against me beyond justice except through clandestine execution.

I know how severe he was toward Letaldus, a monk of Micy, whom, forgetting priestly reverence, he treated insultingly and without any legal process. If he had read Gregory’s letter to Abbot Lupus, he would certainly never have committed so great a crime:

“Since,” he says, “many opportunities are sought by wicked men there, as is reported, for deceiving religious persons, we judge that the presbyter of the aforesaid Church should in no way be deprived or deposed, unless the specific cause of a crime requires it. Therefore, if any such complaint should arise against him, it is necessary that the bishop of the city not examine the case alone, but that, having summoned his fellow bishops, he investigate it with careful scrutiny, so that, with all judging together in agreement, the rigor of canonical discipline may be able either to strike the guilty or absolve the innocent.”

Finally, when he asserts that I associated with excommunicated persons, I certainly did so following his example. He received the sons of Belial, who were advancing by night robbery to kill me, after their archbishop Siguinus, a man of singular merit, had anathematized them, as had Odo, bishop of Chartres, and other men of great life and religious character.

He openly asserted before everyone, with the authority he possessed, that no one could excommunicate a person who was intent upon correction and satisfaction—especially since he himself and the other bishops extended the sentence of the curse until suitable satisfaction had been made.

Moreover, I do not remember ever having read anywhere how many or which persons ought to take part in the binding of the guilty, or how many or which in their absolution, except in the degradation of a priest.

The Gospel, however, plainly says that if your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother; if he does not listen, tell it to the Church. And if he does not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector (Matthew XVIII, 15, 17).

Behold the rule of divine mercy, by which we are commanded to rebuke some of the guilty who listen through pious correction in private, and to reprimand others who do not listen through public denunciation, up to the ears of the Church.

But did public denunciation remove private indulgence, or did private denunciation take away public indulgence? Does public denunciation require public indulgence, and private denunciation private indulgence?

Moreover, when someone brings his offering to the altar, will he not be reconciled there with me concerning the crime because he has been exposed to the Church? (Matthew V, 23.)

O times! O customs! Certainly those who wish to carry out their perverse desires in the workshop of falsehood strive to establish new laws. But the Apostle, advising us, meets them:

“If anyone,” he says, “preaches to you anything other than what you received, let him be anathema” (Galatians I, 9).

How greatly this anathema must be feared the Book of Judges shows, where it is written: “Anathema is in your midst, O Israel; you will not be able to stand before your enemies” (Joshua VII, 13).

That excommunication must not be imposed lightly, and that a member of Christ must be cut away from the body only with grievous pain, is made clear in a chapter of the African Council:

“As long as,” it says, “his own bishop has not communicated with the excommunicated person, no other bishops should communicate with that bishop, so that the bishop may be more careful not to pronounce against anyone what he cannot prove by other evidence.”

Indeed, whatever is done in the Church, unless it is supported by the authority of the Fathers, is judged to be pretense, not truth. And we know that if certain hypocrites and crafty men provoke God’s anger, can a presbyter or bishop be considered properly ordained if he is ordained against the authority of the canons? Or will a presbyter or bishop cease from the duty of his office without an authentic degradation?

Are we to believe someone excommunicated when his conscience does not reproach him with the crime for which he ought to be deprived of communion? Excommunication by a pastor is then just, when a canonical summons has first been issued to the guilty person, and he has refused to correct his guilt under the judgment of the Church. In this way he separates from the healthy sheep the man puffed up with pride, whom he knows must be separated by divine judgment.

And because the excommunicated man had sinned against his own pastor, another neither ought nor could absolve him.

But whoever hurls excommunication at my brother who sins against me does not forgive him his sin. I do—the one against whom he sinned. Most serene princes, cleanse your kingdom from this evil of excommunication, because scarcely anyone in it is not, at least for this reason, excommunicated: that he has clung to an excommunicated person at a banquet or in the kiss of peace.

Moreover, when I speak familiarly with my lords and advise what is good, I know that I arouse the anger of many against me, in accordance with the saying of the comic poet:

“Compliance wins friends; truth breeds hatred.”

(TERENCE, *The Girl from Andros*, Act I, scene V, line 1.)

I am not greatly troubled by their hostility, my sweet glory, Robert, descended from royal ancestors [Note: [Col. 0469D] Horace, *Odes* I, 1.] [Col. 0470D], whom divine mercy has brought to the height of the kingdom, provided that, after God and his saints, I am specially sustained by your help and counsel. I never fail to mention you in my daily prayers.

Finally, I shall append in outline to this little index the matters that most urgently require correction in your realm—not in my own words, however, but in the authoritative sayings of the saints—so that afterward you may move the bishops to correct them canonically in their councils.

First I thought it necessary to speak of the faith, which I have heard varied by alternating choirs both in Francia and in the Church of the English. Some say, as I judge, according to Athanasius: “The Holy Spirit is neither made, nor created, nor begotten by the Father and the Son, but proceeds”; others say only: “The Holy Spirit is neither made nor created by the Father and the Son, but proceeds.” By omitting “nor begotten”—that is, the point at issue—they believe that they are following the synod of Lord Gregory, where it is written: “The Holy Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten, but only proceeds.”

I also heard, when I was a young man, a sermon preached before the people in the Church of Paris concerning the end of the world: that immediately after the number of a thousand years had been completed Antichrist would come, and that the universal judgment would follow not long afterward. I resisted this preaching with all the force I could, from the Gospels, the Apocalypse, and the Book of Daniel.

Finally, my abbot, Richard of blessed memory, vigorously drove away the error that had arisen concerning the end of the world after he received letters from the Lotharingians, to which he ordered me to reply. For rumor had almost filled the whole world with the claim that, when the Lord’s Annunciation had occurred on Good Friday, the end of the age would certainly follow without any doubt.

There was also, at one time, a very serious error concerning the beginning of Advent, which is observed each year before the Lord’s Nativity: some began it after the fifth day before the Kalends of December, others before that date, although Advent never contains more than four weeks, though it has at least one day [beyond the four full weeks]. Since disputes of this kind commonly grow within the Church, the matter should be determined by a council, so that all of us who live in it may hold one opinion—a result which your diligence may secure, since you wish us to be united in your house.

# Collection of Canons of Saint Abbo, Abbot of Fleury

*(In Mabillon, Analecta, new edition, p. 133.)*

## Notice

Abbo, or Abo, abbot of Fleury and author of this collection of canons, and the kind of man he was, is described by Aimoinus, his monk, in the book on his life; in that work he records that Abbo’s death occurred in the year 1004. This author lists various works of Abbo: *On Computation*, and on the courses of the sun, moon, and planets; a collection of defenses against the bishop of Orléans; an *Apology* addressed to Kings Hugh and Robert; a metrical letter to the Emperor Otto; a short book on the calculation of Victorius; another short book on the Gospel chapters addressed to Odilo, abbot of Cluny; and, in addition, several letters.

After mentioning these works, Aimoinus adds in chapter 13:

“There also exist other writings of this holy Father addressed to other persons; lest they weary the reader, let them for the present be concealed in silence.”

In all this he makes no mention of the earlier *Collection*. Nor does the monk Sigebert, when speaking of Abbo in chapter 139 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

“Abbo, abbot of Fleury, showed how capable he was in both branches of learning when he wrote a commentary on the calculation of Victorius.”

Both authors likewise omitted, in addition to the collection of canons, the book *On the Life of Saint Edmund, King of the English*. Yet it is beyond doubt that Abbo was the author of that book as well as of the aforesaid collection.

The *Book of Canons*, which our Peter Trelius brought out of the library of the collegiate church of Saint Martial at Limoges, seemed to me by no means unworthy of the light of day, both because it can contribute considerably to restoring the readings and lacunae of the ancient canons, and because the condition of the Frankish commonwealth at that time can easily be inferred from these canons. Abbo collected them to remedy the ills and misfortunes of the kingdom and presented them to King Hugh and his son Robert, who was reigning jointly with his father, before the year 997, the final year of Hugh’s reign.

It is also significant that the compiler cites none of the spurious letters of the Roman pontiffs, although at that time such counterfeit documents were admitted with blind reverence. This collection of canons may properly be reckoned among the capitularies of the Frankish kings. Its title, which I have faithfully reproduced from a parchment manuscript, seems more correctly to be formulated as follows:

**HERE BEGIN THE CANONS OF ABO, ABBOT, ADDRESSED TO HUGH AND ROBERT HIS SON, KINGS OF THE FRANKS**

## HERE BEGIN THE CANONS OF THE LORD ABO, ABBOT, AND OF KING HUGH AND ROBERT HIS SON, KING OF THE FRANKS, EXCERPTED FROM OTHER CANONS

## Preface

To my most glorious lords, the kings of the Franks, Hugh and his son Robert, bearing an appearance worthy of imperial power: the humble Abo, rector of the men of Fleury, offers the gift of perpetual salvation in Christ.

After divine clemency had caused you to assume the summit of royal power, you endured many misfortunes, by the hidden but not unjust judgment of God, for your testing and benefit. These misfortunes came not from foreign peoples but from the leading men of the kingdom, so that the beginnings of your rule might be leavened.

**Note ([Col. 0473B]).** On these leading men, who were hostile when Robert entered upon the kingdom, Glaber Rodulfus treats in *Histories*, book III, chapter 2.

But because the almighty Lord rescued you from all these things, remember the goodness and mercy of God; remember your predecessors, the good kings; remember just judgments; and always keep in mind that you must spare your subjects and subdue the proud.

Indeed, most serene lords, because I have found you favorably disposed toward our order, I have arranged the chapters written below from books of canons and laws, partly from my own opinions and partly from those of others, in a single continuous composition. Dedicating them to your name, after having employed an *Apology* against my rivals, I have briefly set them out, gathered into one volume. In it I expressed the substance of your office and did not conceal how faithfully the nobles of the kingdom ought to serve you.

I also assembled many provisions for the defense of the monastic order, which I have always wished to remain safe, and of which you are most devout defenders and advocates. Therefore, together with the monks, take pity on your Abo, so that God may grant you to find his mercy here and forever with the holy kings.

Farewell.

### Note

**I had used an *Apology*.** Aimoinus reports fragments of this *Apology* in chapters 8 and 9 of his *Life of Abbo*, and Baronius reports them at the beginning of volume 11 of the *Annals*. In this work the author clears himself of the calumnies of his rivals, who were even plotting against his life; he dedicated the work to Kings Hugh and Robert, whom he urged to drive heretical depravity—especially simony—from their kingdom.

Aimoinus says:

“Finally, since he knew that many people disliked his writings, he commended himself to the kings, especially to the lord Robert, whom he knew to be learned in letters and therefore devoted to students, writing in these words:

‘Moreover, when, speaking familiarly to my lords about their good qualities, I know that I stir up the minds of many against myself, in accordance with the saying of the Comic poet:

> Compliance produces friends; truth produces hatred.

I am not greatly troubled by their hostility, my sweet glory, Robert, whom divine goodness, descended from kings through your ancestors, has brought to the summit of royal power,’”

and so forth.

Here Abo imitates Horace in praising Robert as descended from kings through his ancestors. Glaber Rodulfus explains this in book 1, chapter 2, and the following chapters, and more fully at the beginning of book 2. The most distinguished Hadrian Valesius discusses it in his notes on the poem of Adalbero, bishop of Laon.

Furthermore, Charles, called the Simple, in letters granted to the monastery of Utica, calls Count Hugh, who was Robert’s grandfather, his kinsman.

Although Abo was so highly esteemed by King Robert, he nevertheless did not hesitate to rebuke him for his illicit union with Bertha, as the monk Helgaud testifies in his book on Robert’s life. That freedom of speech did not provoke the most pious prince to anger but to repentance.

### Note

**I wish the senate of the monks to remain safe.** From this statement the conspirators—haters of the monks of that period—took material for attacking and harassing Abbo, as Abbo himself complains in his *Apology*, reported by Aimoinus:

“Cunning that seeks to undermine me gnaws at me with a dog’s tooth; the frequent bitterness of my adversaries barks all around me. They murmur nothing else against me except that I wish the senate of the monks to remain safe. I sought the increase of our commonwealth and, with whatever authority I possessed, opposed the quibbling of those lying in wait. Nor did I altogether hide mercy and truth from extensive counsel. Because of such evils they plot against my blood and pursue me with hastily assembled hatreds, to such an extent that not even royal majesty deters them from secretly murdering me, if opportunity and time should favor them.”

Aimoinus’s *Life of Abbo*, chapter 8, proves this by the event itself.

### Note

**You are defenders and advocates.** How devoted Hugh, Robert’s father, was to Saint Benedict and his order is attested by the monk Helgaud, who reports Hugh’s final words to his son Robert as he was dying, specifically urging him “under no circumstances to allow the father of all, Benedict, to be separated from him.”

Hugh demonstrated this inclination toward Saint Benedict not only by restoring to the monks many monasteries that had previously been occupied by secular canons, but also by granting them the free power to elect abbots. Robert imitated Hugh’s devotion; Helgaud says that he “always clung with all his heart to Father Benedict and his followers,” so much so that Adalbero, bishop of Laon, reproached the king for it, using poetic license.

## I. On the Honor of Churches and Monasteries

That honor with which the Church, the temple of the living God, ought to be held is testified by the Lord himself in the Gospel, where he says to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18).

Since it is itself the oratory of which the blessed Father Benedict says, “Let this place be called an oratory, and let nothing else be done or stored there” (Saint Benedict, *Rule*, chapter 52), care must be taken that the place whose foundation is Christ not be transferred to secular uses because of the plundering of its property. For Christians are said to inflict violence, within or outside, upon the courts and precincts of the house of God.

Therefore the Augusti Theodosius and Valentinian, in book 9 of the laws, chapter 34, addressed to the prefect Antiochus, say:

“Let the temples of the most high God stand open to those who fear him. We decree that not only the altars and the space surrounding the temple-oratory—which encloses the churches within by a four-sided circuit of walls—are to be established as places of refuge for those fleeing for protection; rather, extending as far as the outermost doors of the church, which the people eager to pray enter first, we command that the altar of salvation be available to those seeking refuge, as well as the entrance to the temple that we have described as enclosed by the circuit of its walls.

“Beyond the public places, whatever lies between the first doors of the church and the temple, whether in small cells, houses, gardens, baths, open spaces, or porticoes, shall protect refugees in place of the interior temple. Let no one attempt to lay sacrilegious hands upon them in order to drag them out. Nor, when he sees that he is placing himself in danger, let anyone who dares such a thing seek aid for himself by fleeing to the same places.

“We grant this breadth of space so that no one may be allowed to lie down or spend the night in the very temple of God or at the most holy altars, with the clergy themselves forbidding this for reasons of religion, whether in the morning or in the evening.”

### Interpretation

Churches are places dedicated to God. Therefore they are to protect those guilty persons who, compelled by fear, have taken refuge there, so that no one may presume to bring violence or lay hands upon the holy places in order to seize their property. Whatever space belongs either to the porticoes or to the open areas adjoining the church, we command to be guarded as though it were part of the interior of the temple, so that the pressure of fear may not compel the accused to remain around the altars and pollute the venerable places.

Certainly, if anyone has taken refuge in a holy place, he must immediately lay down any weapons he may have brought with him. They must not imagine that they are defended more by the protection of weapons than by reverence for the holy places. If they refuse to lay down their arms and do not trust the priest or clerics, they should know that they will be dragged out by armed forces.

If, however, anyone attempts for any reason to extract a guilty person from a holy place, he is to be condemned to capital punishment.

## II. On the Defenders of Churches and Monasteries

Those who are called defenders of churches today defend for themselves, against the authority of laws and canons, what belonged by right to the churches. By thus inflicting violence upon clerics and monks, they plunder the property of churches and monasteries under the pretext of usufruct; they reduce the tenants to poverty; they do not enlarge the possessions of the churches but diminish them; and they ravage those whom they ought to have defended.

They leave an abundance of property exposed as prey to every enemy. They do not even prepare themselves, or oppose the enemy in words, so as to resist them. They think that they are no longer advocates but lords, since after the enemy’s departure they consume whatever remains, in accordance with the prophetic saying: “The locust ate what the young locust left, and the caterpillar ate what the locust left,” and so forth (Joel 1:4).

For this reason, finally, we see churches destroyed, some monasteries ruined, and others reduced to the greatest poverty—churches and monasteries that once flourished in great glory through the almsgiving of good men. Many people voluntarily put themselves forward under the pretext of advocacy and intercept the greatest portion of the possessions, revenues, and offerings that the ecclesiastical authorities ought to have received.

Therefore, so that such presumption might cease, it was provided in the African council, chapter 64:

“It was also agreed that the envoys Vincent and Fortunatius, who are to proceed in the name of all the provinces, should ask the most glorious emperors to grant permission for the appointment of defenders from among the learned advocates who are active in the practice or office of defending cases. Thus, in the manner of the priests of the province, those who undertake the defense of the churches themselves shall have authority to act in the churches’ affairs whenever necessity demands it, whether to resist those who creep in or to present what is necessary by entering the secretariats of the judges.”

## III. On the King’s Office

What the king’s office is, the title of his function itself reveals, and the care undertaken for the whole kingdom makes it known. Nothing so greatly raises the king’s mind toward doing good as the clemency of different princes held up as examples. The gentleness of the Emperor Constantine is praised among divided bishops, and the pure faith of Marcian among heretics and orthodox believers.

But why should I speak of foreign examples, and delay in speaking of them, when Charles and his son Louis displayed such great piety and prudence in administering the commonwealth and promoting the welfare of the churches? Certainly both knew, according to the time and circumstances, how to spare the humble and subdue the proud.

Accordingly, from the books produced from the councils of their time, together with the submissions of the bishops, one may easily find the following statement, expressed in book 2, chapter 1 of the Sixth Council of Paris, after some other material:

“The justice of the king is to oppress no one unjustly through power; to judge between a man and his neighbor without respect of persons; to be a defender of strangers, orphans, and widows; to restrain thefts; to punish adulteries; not to exalt the wicked; not to maintain the immodest and the actors; to remove the impious from the land; not to allow parricides and perjurers to live; to defend the churches; to feed the poor with alms; to place just men over the affairs of the kingdom; to have as counselors old, wise, and sober men; not to attend to the superstitions of magicians, diviners, and prophetesses; to defer anger; to defend his country bravely and justly against adversaries; to live in God in all things; not to let prosperity raise his spirit; to endure all adversity patiently; to hold the Catholic faith in God; not to allow his sons to act impiously; to devote himself to prayers at appointed hours; and not to taste food before the proper hours.

“Woe to the land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning” (Ecclesiastes 10:16). These things bring prosperity to the kingdom in the present life and lead the king to the better kingdoms of heaven.”

## IV. On Loyalty to the King

Since the king’s office is to examine thoroughly the affairs of the entire kingdom, so that no injustice may lie hidden in them, how can he sustain so great a burden unless the bishops and leading men of the kingdom assent to him?

And since the Apostle says, “Fear God; honor the king” (1 Peter 2:17), how will he exercise the responsibilities of his office against the rebellion of the disobedient if the leading men of the kingdom do not offer him the honor he deserves, with all reverence, through their aid and counsel?

He alone is not sufficient for all the useful affairs of the kingdom. Therefore, since he shares the burden with others whom he considers worthy of honor, he himself must be honored with sincere devotion. No one should oppose him in any way, because “whoever resists authority resists the ordinance of God” (Romans 13:2).

Just as it is better not to make a vow than not to fulfill it after making it, so it is better not to subscribe to the prince’s election than, after subscribing, to despise or proscribe the one elected. In the one case love of freedom is praised; in the other, servile rebellion is rightly condemned.

We know of three general elections: the first is that of a king or emperor, the second that of a bishop, and the third that of an abbot. The first is carried out by the harmony of the whole kingdom; the second by the unanimity of the citizens and clergy; the third by the sounder counsel of the monastic community. Each is to be conducted not for the sake of secular friendship or money, but according to its proper vocation, on the basis of wisdom or merit of life.

Moreover, once a king has been ordained, he demands from all his subjects an oath of loyalty, so that discord may not arise in any part of his kingdom.

Thus we find written in the Fourth Council of Toledo:

“After certain regulations of ecclesiastical order and decrees pertaining to the discipline of particular persons, finally we all, the priests, have judged that, for the strength of our kings and the stability of the nation, we should issue a final pontifical decree before God, the judge.

“For, as is reported, there exists among many peoples such great treachery of mind that they disdain to keep the faith promised by oath to their kings. They pretend with their mouths to make the profession of an oath, while retaining in their minds the impiety of treachery. They swear to their kings and violate the faith they promise, nor do they fear that book of God’s judgment by which a curse and many threats of punishment are brought upon those who swear falsely in the name of the Lord.

“What hope, then, will such peoples have when struggling against enemies? What faith may thereafter be trusted with other peoples in peace? What pact will remain inviolate? What sworn pledge among enemies will endure, when they do not preserve the faith they have sworn to their own kings?

“For who is so insane as to cut off his own head with his own hand? Yet they, as is evident, forgetful of their salvation, kill themselves with their own hand by turning their own strength against themselves and their kings.

“And when the Lord says, ‘Do not touch my anointed ones’ (Psalm 104:15), and David says, ‘Who can stretch out his hand against the Lord’s anointed and remain innocent?’ (1 Samuel 26:9), they neither fear perjury nor hesitate to bring destruction upon their kings.

“Faith is given to enemies in a treaty and is not violated. If faith has force even in war, how much more must it be preserved among one’s own people? It is sacrilege if peoples violate the faith promised to their kings, because by this they transgress not only a treaty but also against God, in whose name the promise itself is made.”

## V. On Privileges

The authority of the Roman and apostolic see shines throughout the universal Church of the whole world, with Christ the Lord showing favor. Nor is this surprising, since the pontiffs of that see appear to exercise the functions of blessed Peter, who is the prince of the whole Church.

Christian emperors also granted this same see such exceptional distinction that, once they had founded episcopal churches or monasteries of men or women, they never afterward revoked the law they had imposed under the anathema of excommunication, unless necessity intervened.

Thus it is written in the Council of Nicaea, chapter 6:

“Let the ancient custom be preserved throughout Egypt, Libya, and the Pentapolis, so that the bishop of Alexandria shall have authority over all these regions, since a similar custom exists for the bishop of the city of Rome. Likewise, in Antioch and in the other provinces, let the privileges belonging to their churches be preserved.”

Likewise, Gregory to John, bishop:

“It is exceedingly serious and contrary to the priestly vocation to disturb the privileges once granted to any monastery and to attempt to invalidate arrangements made for its peace. The monks of your diocese have therefore complained to us that you are hastening to introduce certain measures into their monastery contrary to what your predecessors permitted and long custom preserved, and that you are disturbing the ancient order by an innovation prejudicial to it.

“Accordingly, we exhort your Fraternity in the strongest terms that, if this is so, you should refrain without any excuse from troubling the monastery and should not attempt to tear away by any usurpation the rights that have long been preserved for it. Rather, strive to keep everything inviolate and without any resistance, and know that you are not permitted more in that monastery than your predecessors were.”

Likewise, in the laws, chapter 510:

“Possessions belonging to religious houses shall not be subject to any assessment, except for the construction of roads or the building of bridges, and even then only if they possess property within the territory of the city in which the assessment is sought. They shall enjoy immunity from extraordinary levies and from the assessment of profitable revenues.”

## VI. On Royal or Imperial Commands

The power of the most glorious kings has wished whatever it establishes by command, whether in word or deed, to be stable and firm—especially whatever, at the suggestion of their leading men, they have judged ratified for the benefit of the Church.

Therefore, whoever contradicts royal commands shows that he neither loves nor fears the king, especially when the command is supported by the assertion of ancient men, which he knows to be authoritative. For the Lord says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my words” (John 14:23). Whoever therefore hates the king hates his command and seeks to criticize words that cannot be reproached.

But from where does this arise except from the king’s excessive gentleness? Everything excessive is harmful. For this reason we are commanded to possess both the simplicity of the dove and the cunning of the serpent, so that the mind may not be excessively inclined in either direction and, being too anxious, fail to preserve moderation.

Charles therefore established the following decree—not concerning an imperial command, but concerning the little letters of his own correspondence—in the fourth book of his capitularies:

“If anyone despises our letters—that is, the summons sent for the reception of our envoys—let him lose the honors he possesses; or let him remain in the place where he ought to have received the aforesaid envoys and receive there the delegations coming to him from his own property, until he has satisfied our mind.

“Anyone who in any way [acts concerning] our letter shall come to the palace at our command and receive, according to our will, a punishment appropriate to his foolishness.” [The verb is absent or corrupt in the supplied text.]

“If a free man—that is, a count’s minister—has done this, let him lose whatever honor or benefice he may have held. If he is an unfree servant, let him be beaten at the stake and let his head be shaved.”

## VII. On the Difference between Testaments and *Precariae*

Since some testaments are made in the name of a dowry, others as donations of inheritance, and others concern Church property, which is difficult to alienate and is called *precaria*, apart from these there are royal—that is, imperial—commands, strengthened by the authority of the command, to which the privileges of the Roman pontiffs agree when decreed under the anathema of excommunication.

But among *precariae*—which are made by agreement and obtained through petitions—some are held by various persons by way of a rent-bearing usufruct, while others are held through the emphyteutic exchange, that is, by contract. This is done in the manner set out in the third book of the Councils, chapter 22:

**Note ([Col. 0479D]).** This occurs in chapter 22 of the Council of Meaux, held in 845. That decree was taken from the chapters of the synod of Beauvais, and was reported by Regino in book I of *On Ecclesiastical Disciplines*, chapter 363, and likewise by Burchard and Gratian. Since Abbo cites it from the third book of the Councils, he perhaps indicates that in the manuscripts of his time the Council of Meaux was assigned the place of book III among the councils held from the reign of Charles the Bald to that year.

“No one shall presume to make a *precaria* from Church property unless, according to the quality of the property agreed upon, twice as much is received from Church property as is given from one’s own property, and only in the name of the person who has given it, if he wishes to hold both his own and the Church’s property by usufruct.

“If, however, he has presently relinquished his own property, he may take usufruct from Church property only in his own name, because whoever holds such property must protect it in such a way as to be its steward, not its giver as though it were his own.

“No authority may compel anyone to make a *precaria* from things dedicated to God and the saints, since reason and practice establish that no one who does not wish to do so should be forced, contrary to usefulness and reason, to make a benefit from his own property.

“Nor does reason permit royal commands to be issued concerning ecclesiastical *precariae*, nor does authority of any kind allow it, since royal majesty must judge it improper to confirm commands in ecclesiastical law unless they are requested by an ecclesiastical ruler.

“The guardian of the Church must therefore take the greatest care not to forget his rank and ecclesiastical communion and request, out of any desire to please, that a royal command be issued against authority. If he does so, he must not be heard; and if he obtains such a command, it must be rescinded by royal discretion and episcopal judgment, and the unjust petitioner must be suitably corrected for his unjust suggestion to the prince.”

## VIII. On the Fact that Necessity Excludes Laws and Canons

Ecclesiastical rules, which the Greeks call *canons*, were devised by the holy Fathers so that we might walk along the path of justice without any winding detour of error.

It makes no difference by which canonical institution someone is instructed for the proper profession of the Christian faith, provided that, having entered the way of truth with an unimpeded step, he does not depart from the divine oracles under the guidance of the Gospel.

Not every invention is accompanied by necessity, so that it would be impossible for what someone has usefully devised to be done in another way. Thus, in the African council, Hosius of Córdoba discusses many matters according to his judgment, and the Church willingly accepts them as very sound canonical instruction.

Therefore the configuration of the lands, the character of the times, human weakness, and other necessities of circumstances must be considered; these things commonly alter the regulations of different provinces. Many matters have also been changed by authority for the common benefit of the churches, and no faithful person condemns this.

Why should this be surprising, when canons are sometimes found to contradict one another, and what is commanded in one council is prohibited in another? Those who never wish, for the convenience of temporal life, to turn from virtue to vice or from truth to falsehood do not consider this to have happened without reason.

The same principle exists in the decrees of the pontiffs. Their authority is so great that the judgments of many await the decision of a single Roman pontiff.

In such matters, therefore, usefulness and propriety always prevail—not the seductive pleasure of desires, which holy men avoid.

But lest we seem to speak of such things without support, we offer examples. The transfer of bishops was prohibited in the Nicene and Chalcedonian synods; it was permitted by necessity or usefulness in the Council of Antioch.

It was permitted by necessity because Silvanus, whose weak body could not endure the cold, was transferred by Atticus from Philippopolis to Troy.

By the authority of the Roman pontiff, Perigenes, ordained bishop at Petra, was received and enthroned at Corinth after its bishop had died.

Nor should these cases seem surprising, since Christ taught that a wife must be hated, whereas the Apostle commanded us to love a wife. Gregory also restored to their former ranks bishops condemned by other bishops through the privilege of his authority, reconciled bishops, and appointed successors to bishops (Gregory, book 3, letter 20).

Gregory excommunicated Maximus, bishop of the city of Salona, because, having been ordained through money, he had fallen into the heresy of simony. Although excommunicated, Maximus celebrated Masses. Nevertheless, after seven years, Gregory restored him when repentance had moved him to conversion and granted him the pallium, after receiving an oath concerning the prohibitions, before the body of Saint Apollinaris (book 7, letter 82, indiction 2).

## IX. On the Difference between Law and Custom

Just as a king is named from ruling, so law is named from reading. Therefore the promulgation of laws is extended through the edicts of kings, and each ruler exercises Christian rule piously within the boundaries of his kingdom.

Custom obeys this rule. If it is not obstructed by public interests, custom takes the place of law. Cicero, in his rhetorical works, did not fail to set forth the similarity and difference between these matters by the following definition (Cicero, *On Invention*, book 2):

“Customary law is thought to be that which antiquity has approved by the will of all without a written law.”

Legitimate rights, however, must be known from laws, and they are more remote from ordinary understanding. They must often be introduced by way of comparison or to amplify a matter.

Thus, if I remember correctly, law and custom are species of right. Law is the written constitution of princes; custom is a usage approved by antiquity but not written.

Did antiquity agree so completely with evil that no one ever wished to practice moral discipline? We have learned this nowhere among any people, since all human beings, even when acting badly, love the good of nature.

All human beings therefore must use either good laws or good customs. Yet we have found some who think that they are subject neither to good customs through established usage nor to any laws. Those who live without law will perish without law.

## X. On the Fact that Priests Must Not Send a Commission to a Foreign People

From the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 30:

“Priests living near the enemy, except those who have received permission by royal authority, must not presume secretly to receive or send any commission to a foreign people. Whoever is discovered and convicted of this, after being denounced to the prince before the council, shall be punished with a severe and appropriate penalty.”

## XI. On Clerics Chosen by the Builders of Venerable Places or by Their Heirs

In the laws, chapter 456:

“If anyone has built a house of prayer, and he himself or his heirs wish to consecrate clerics in that house, the administrators of the house shall be heard if they nominate clerics who are worthy. But if those men are such that they are not approved by the divine canons, it will belong to the bishop to choose other suitable clerics.”

## XII. On the Ordination or Degradation of Priests
From the Second Council of Seville, chapter 6:

“The presbyter Fragitanus of the Church of Córdoba [variant: ‘of the Church, as we have learned, Fragitanus of Córdoba’] was once unjustly expelled by his bishop and, though innocent, condemned to exile. By our subscription we have decreed that, in accordance with the synodal judgment of the ancient Fathers, no man should dare to depose any presbyter or deacon without examination by a council. For there are many who condemn people without investigation, by tyrannical power rather than canonical authority; and just as they exalt some through the favor of grace, so they abase others, moved by hatred and envy, and condemn them on the basis of a light breath of opinion, although they do not establish their crimes. [Col. 0483B]

“For a bishop alone can confer honor upon priests and ministers; he cannot take it away. If those who, in the secular world, have received the honor of freedom from their masters are not returned to the bond of servitude unless they have been publicly accused before leading men in a tribunal and court, how much more is this true of those who, consecrated to the divine altars, are adorned with ecclesiastical honor? Such persons certainly cannot be condemned by one man, nor can they be stripped of the privileges of their honor by a single judge. Rather, after being presented for synodal judgment, the matter must be determined according to what the canon has prescribed concerning them.”

### XIII. — That Bishops Are Not to Be Ordained for Money

[Note: [Col. 0483D] “That bishops are not to be ordained for money.” At that time the crime of simony was rampant. Abo himself addressed this subject in his letter to Bernard, abbot of Bellus-Locus, preserved by Aimoinus in the Life of Abo, chapter 10; so too did Rudolfus Glaber in Book II, chapter 6, of his Histories, along with other writers of that period. Gerbertus had preceded them in the sermon printed above, where he laments that this evil had revived in his own age—that is, had become widespread. See Liutprand of Ticinum, deacon, in his History of His Own Time.]

From the Book of Laws [Note: [Col. 0484D] By the title “Book of Laws,” Abo means the book of the Novels. This passage is found in Novel 6, chapter 8, and Novel 123, chapter 1.], chapter 430:

“Above all, we enact that this be observed: no one is to be consecrated bishop in return for gold or any other thing. If anything of this kind has been done, those who receive or provide the money lose themselves and their souls, and their intermediaries are subjected to condemnation according to the divine rules and sacred canons. Therefore the giver, the recipient, and the person who acted as intermediary are all to be removed from the priesthood or the honor of the clerical order. Whatever was given for this purpose is to be claimed for the church whose priesthood he wished to purchase. If, however, the person who accepted something for this purpose, or acted as intermediary, is a layman, twice the amount given is to be exacted from him and claimed for the church. We command not only that what was given be claimed, but also enact that every security and every other action whatsoever be rendered void, so that the person who received the promise must not only return the security but must also be required to give the Church another sum equal to what the security contains.” [Col. 0483C–D]

Also from the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 11:

“If any bishop performs an ordination for money, reduces to a price a grace that cannot be sold, or ordains for money a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone numbered among the clergy; or if he promotes for money an administrator or anyone subject to the rule, for the sake of his most shameful profit, the person proved to have attempted this shall be subject to the peril of his own rank. The person who was ordained shall gain nothing from this ordination or promotion, which was made by commercial dealing, but shall be a stranger to the dignity or office that he purchased with money. If anyone acts as intermediary in such shameful and abominable payments, whether given or received, then, if he is a cleric, he shall fall from his own rank; but if he is a layman or monk, he shall be anathematized.” [Col. 0484A]

### XIV. — On the Election of an Abbot

In the Laws, chapter 480:

“It remains for us to speak of monks. Therefore we enact that an abbot, or archimandrite, be placed over each monastery—not according to the rank of the monks, but one whom all the monks, or those of better reputation, shall have elected. With the holy Gospels set before them, they are to declare that they have elected him not because of friendship or favor, but because they know him to possess sound faith, chaste conduct, and the competence and ability to preserve usefully the discipline of the monks and the entire condition of the monastery. If he has been elected in this manner, he is to be confirmed in every respect by the bishop to whom the monastery is subject. What we have said concerning monasteries of monks is likewise to be observed in monasteries and archisteria of women.” [Col. 0484B]

### XV. — On the Ordination of an Abbot and the Bishop’s Access to the Monastery

GREGORY to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna (Gregory, Book VII, Letter 18, indiction 1):

“How necessary it is to provide for the peace of monasteries [Col. 0484C] and to concern oneself with their perpetual security is shown by the service you formerly rendered in governing a monastery. Since we have learned that the monastery of the blessed John and Stephen, situated in the city of Classe and presided over by our common son Claudius the abbot, has suffered many prejudices and burdens from your predecessors, it is necessary that your fraternity’s foresight arrange their future peace through a salutary ordinance, so that, living there in God’s service and aided by his grace, they may persevere with a free mind.

“But lest anyone, at any time, presume to inflict any trouble upon them through that custom which rather needs correction, it is necessary that the matters listed below be guarded by your fraternity’s diligence [Col. 0484D], so that no further opportunity for causing disturbance may arise from them. Therefore no one is henceforth to dare, in any manner or under any pretext, to diminish the revenues, property, or documents of the said monastery, or anything belonging to it, nor to make any deceitful encroachments. If some matter should arise between the Church of Ravenna and the aforesaid monastery and cannot be settled peacefully, let it be resolved without voluntary [Col. 0485A] delay before chosen God-fearing arbiters from both parties, with the holy Gospels as means.

“Upon the death of the abbot, no outsider is to be appointed, but only someone from the same congregation whom the congregation has freely chosen for itself; and whoever is elected is to be ordained without fraud or any form of venality. Nor is any person to be set against an abbot who comes to his monastery on any pretext, unless—God forbid—there are established crimes of the kind that the sacred canons are shown to punish.

“It must likewise be guarded that, against the will of the abbot of that monastery, monks are not taken from it to set over other monasteries, or for sacred orders or clerical office.
