If, however, there are enough monks to suffice for celebrating God’s praises and completing the needs of the monasteries, let the abbot devoutly offer from those who remain whichever he judges worthy [Col. 0485B]. If, while having enough, he refuses to provide one, then the bishop of Ravenna may take from those who remain someone to govern other monasteries. No one, however, is to be brought from there into ecclesiastical office unless the abbot of the place, after being admonished, offers him of his own will. Whoever from the aforesaid monastery reaches an ecclesiastical order is thereafter to have there neither any authority nor permission to reside.

“It must also be observed that, whenever circumstances require, an inventory of the property or documents of the same monastery is not to be made by ecclesiastics; rather, the abbot of the place is to make an inventory of the property together with other abbots. Whenever, for the benefit of his monastery, the abbot should wish to come or send someone to the Roman pontiff, he is to be permitted to do so in every respect.

“Furthermore, although monasteries ought eagerly to await the arrival of bishops, we have nevertheless been informed that the aforesaid monastery was burdened in the time of your predecessor on the pretext of providing hospitality. Your holiness must therefore appropriately moderate this, so that the bishop of that city may visit the monastery as often as he wishes for the purpose of visitation and exhortation, but may fulfill the duty of charity there in such a way that the monastery incurs no burden. The aforesaid abbot does not fear your fraternity’s frequent visits to the monastery; indeed, he earnestly desires them, knowing that through you the substance of the monastery cannot be burdened at all.” [Col. 0485C]

And again to the same man in another letter, after some intervening material (Book VI, Letter 40):

“We exhort you, removing every delay and every excuse, to strive to relieve the monasteries of Ravenna from the burden of yourself and your clergy [Col. 0485D–0486A], so that henceforth neither clerics nor those constituted in sacred orders may have permission to enter them for any reason except solely to pray, or perhaps when they have been invited to perform the sacred mysteries of the Mass. But lest they perhaps have to bear any burden because of the promotion of a monk or abbot, you must take care that, if any abbot or monk from any monastery proceeds to clerical office or sacred order, he thereafter have no authority there, as we have said, so that the monasteries may not be compelled, under cover of this pretext, to bear the burdens we forbid. Your holiness, already admonished a second time, must not delay correcting all these matters with vigilant care.”

[Col. 0486B] Likewise Gregory to John, bishop of Orvieto (Book I, Letter 12):

“Agapitus, abbot of the monastery of Saint George, has made known to us that he suffers many burdens from your holiness—not only in matters that, in a time of necessity, could provide some assistance to the monastery, but also because you prohibit Masses from being celebrated in that same monastery and forbid the burial of the dead. If this is so, we exhort you to desist from such inhumanity, and to permit the dead to be buried there and Masses to be celebrated without any further opposition, lest the aforesaid venerable man be compelled again to lodge a complaint concerning these matters.”

### XVI. — That an Abbot Must Be a Priest

Pope Eugenius [Note: [Col. 0485D] Specifically, at the Roman synod held in 826. Abo does not reproduce the words of that synod exactly, but in abbreviated form, both in this chapter and in chapter 37. It is therefore clear that in Abo’s time some abbots of our order lacked the priesthood. Such were Nicholas of Normandy, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Ouen near Rouen toward the end of the eleventh century, who was only a deacon, and likewise Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, who was ordained priest only after attaining the dignity of cardinal. See Observation 33 in the first preface to the Third Age of the Benedictines.] chapter 27 (Eugenius II, at the Roman synod):

“Such abbots are to be ordained in monasteries as can rule well those subject to them; they must also have attained priestly honor.” [Col. 0486C]

### XVII. — What Is to Be Done with an Accused Abbot

GREGORY to Lupus, abbot [Note: [Col. 0485D] In the published editions: “To Luponus, presbyter and abbot,” namely of the monastery of Saint Martin in the suburb of Autun. The same letter is also cited by the old author who wrote the booklet on the life of Saint Hugh, a monk of that place, although the authenticity of this letter is challenged by some, as is that of the two preceding letters, because in them the author threatens kings, bishops, and others with certain punishments that they consider foreign to Gregory’s mind. Nevertheless, Frodoardus, who lived almost a century before Abo, praises in Book III, chapter 27, of his History of Reims the privilege of the hospice of Autun, according to the form of which the letter addressed to Lupus was dictated.], (Gregory, Book II, Letter 12):

“Since many opportunities for deceiving religious persons are sought by wicked men there, as is said, we judge that the presbyter of the aforesaid church should in no way be deprived or deposed unless the specific cause of a crime requires it. Therefore, if any complaint of this kind has arisen against him, it is necessary not only that the bishop of the city examine the case, but also that, calling his fellow bishops to his assistance, he investigate it carefully, so that, with all judging in agreement, he may, by the judgment of canonical strictness, either strike the guilty person with censure or absolve the innocent.” [Col. 0486D]

### XVIII. — On Monks and Nuns, That They Should Live According to the Rule

[Col. 0487A]

(From the First Council of Verneuil, chapter 5.)

“Monasteries of both men and women that disdain to live regularly according to the rule are to be corrected by the bishop in whose diocese they appear to be situated. If the bishop cannot correct them, the matter is to be reported to the metropolitan. If he too cannot correct them, they are to come before a public synod; and if they disdain the public synod, they are either to lose their rank or to be excommunicated by all the bishops. A person of such character is to be appointed in their place at that synod, by the will of the lord king or with the consent of the servants of God, to govern that congregation according to the rule.”

### XIX. — On an Abbot Subject to the King

[Col. 0487B] From the Council of the Palace of Verneuil (same source, chapter 20):

“At another synod you granted us this: that the property of those monasteries where monks or nuns live regularly should be left to them, so that they might have the means to live. If the place were royal, the abbot or abbess was to give an account to the lord king; if episcopal, to that bishop.”

### XX. — On the Superior of Fleury

In the Council of Toul [Note: [Col. 0487D] Namely, at Savonnières, a place in the suburb of Toul in the territory of the Leuci. In chapter 11 of this synod, which is Abo’s chapter 12, this decree is found. Abo, as is his custom, omits some of its wording, for he generally does not cite the canons word for word.], chapter 12:

“At last the general synod prostrated itself to the ground before the glorious King Charles and Radulfus, archbishop of Bourges, beseeching and adjuring them by the cross and blood of Christ to strive to preserve as valid and unshaken the privilege of the monastery of Saint Benedict, which the aforesaid king had confirmed with his consent and which the same Radulfus had subscribed. If the abbot should be found by direct emissaries to be negligent and unsuited to the sacred rules, let him be removed by that paternal authority and another, found to be worthy, substituted; and let the authority of the privilege not be withdrawn from that monastery on any pretext.” [Col. 0487C]

### XXI. — On the Priesthood of a Monk

GREGORY to Lucius [variant: Lucidus], bishop (Gregory, Book X, Letter 54):

“Our son John, abbot, has requested that a presbyter be ordained for him in his monastery from that same congregation. Therefore we have deemed it necessary to exhort your fraternity by this present authority, so that you carefully investigate the man whom he offers from his congregation for consecration, examining, as is customary, whatever matters require examination; and if nothing is found in him that could stand in his way, [Col. 0487D–0488A] let him be consecrated canonically, as is customary. Granting him no other privilege, except that in his own congregation, whenever appropriate, he is to celebrate only the sacred mysteries of the Mass.”

And Saint Benedict in his Rule, chapter 62:

“Once ordained, let him beware of exaltation or pride, and presume to do nothing except what is commanded him by his abbot, knowing that he is much more subject to regular discipline,” and so forth. [Col. 0488A]

### XXII. — On Monks Who Do Not Keep Their Vocation

In the Laws, chapter 490:

“If anyone leaves his monastery or transfers to another monastery, his property is to belong to the first monastery, into which he had previously entered.”

Likewise, chapter 16:

“If anyone establishes himself in a monastery [Col. 0488B] and, after putting on the religious habit, leaves the monastery, all his goods that he brought into the monastery are to belong to that monastery.” The same is stated in another constitution: “Even if he did not bring them in. For all property is with its master, the monastery.”

Likewise, chapter 18:

“If anyone enters a monastery and, after leaving the religious habit, departs, enters military service, or simply becomes a layman, he is to be stripped of his military belt and is not to enjoy a free life, but is to be compelled to serve the governor of the province. His property, however, is to remain in the monastery.”

Likewise, the examples of Pope Siricius to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, chapter 6:

“Furthermore, you report that some monks and women religious, whether nuns or others, having abandoned their profession of holiness, have sunk into such wantonness that at first, secretly and as though under the pretext of monasteries, they became involved in illicit and sacrilegious intercourse; later, driven into the abyss by despair of conscience, they openly produced children from illicit unions. Both the public laws and ecclesiastical laws condemn this. Therefore we command that these shameless and detestable persons be expelled from the community of monasteries and from the assemblies of the churches, so that, confined in their own prisons and lamenting such a great crime in continual mourning, they may purge it in the cleansing fire of repentance; thus, at least at death, mercy alone may come to their aid through the grace of communion.” [Col. 0488C]

### XXIII. — On Clerics Who Wish to Become Monks, and on the Insolence of Bishops Toward Monks

[Note: [Col. 0487D] “On the insolence of bishops.” This title might seem too harsh unless the Fathers of Toledo had previously used the word “insolence” in the same matter, in chapter 2 of the Ninth Council of Toledo. Abo may perhaps have been led by their example; he cites the same passage below in chapter 32 and appears to have used the same word, although he would have moderated the title more correctly in this form: “On the insolence of certain bishops toward monks.” Certainly Regino, in the first appendix to his collection of canons, chapter 33, where he cites the same chapter 51 of the Fourth Council of Toledo, gives it the title: “On the discretion of the power that bishops may exercise in monasteries.”]

[Col. 0488D]

Chapter 52 [reading: 50] of the Fourth Council of Toledo:

“Clerics who seek the monastic profession [Note: [Col. 0488D] If Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, had had this passage of the Toledan synod before him, he would have used it most opportunely in Letter 29 to Guenilo, bishop of Sens, who was attempting to prevent two presbyters of his parish from adopting the monastic profession. Guenilo denied them permission to leave their titular churches unless Lupus could prove by authoritative evidence that this could be done without fault. Lupus undertook the task, although he admits that he had never seen or read this matter brought into dispute. A letter of almost the same argument is Gregory the Great’s Letter 39 of Book X, to Desiderius, bishop in Gaul. Desiderius wished to recall to the Church the cleric Pancratius, formerly his own, who had subsequently become a monk, although Gregory admonished him not to continue attempting this. There is also an important letter on this subject from Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, to Atto, bishop of Troyes, in Book II, Letter 50.] because they desire to pursue a better life: the bishop must freely grant them entry into monasteries, and the vocation of those striving to pass over to the desire for contemplation must not be obstructed.” [Col. 0489A]

Likewise, chapter 51:

“It has been reported to the present council that monks are subjected to servile labor by episcopal command and that the rights of monasteries are usurped through illicit presumption, contrary to the decrees of the canons, so that nearly the whole monastery becomes property [variant: ‘nearly the whole property of the monastery is made’], and the glorious portion of Christ is brought into disgraceful servitude. Therefore we admonish those who preside over churches not to presume such things any longer, but to claim for themselves in monasteries only what the canons prescribe: namely, to admonish monks toward holy conduct, to appoint abbots to certain offices [variant: ‘abbots and other officials’], and to correct acts performed outside the rule. If they presume to do anything forbidden by the canons against monks, or attempt to usurp any part of the monastery’s property, the sentence of excommunication will not be lacking against those who thereafter do not withdraw themselves from such unlawful acts.” [Col. 0489B]

### XXIV. — On Clerics Who Become Monks Because of Vanity

From the Council of Zaragoza, chapter 6 (Council of Zaragoza, under Damasus):

“If any cleric, because of presumed luxury and vanity, voluntarily withdraws from his office and prefers to appear to be a monk, as though an observer of the law, rather than a cleric, he is to be expelled from the church and not received back unless, by asking and entreating over a very long period, he has made satisfaction.” All the bishops said: “Let it be so.” [Col. 0489C]

### XXV. — On Church Possessions

From another Council of Toledo, chapter 4:

“If any of the clergy is proved to have made for himself little fields or vineyards on church lands for the purpose of sustaining life, let him possess them until the day of his death. After his departure from this life, however, let him restore his right to the church, in accordance with the provisions of the earlier canons, and let him leave it by testamentary or hereditary right to none of his heirs or successors, unless perhaps the bishop should wish to grant it to someone for services rendered to the church.”

GREGORY to JOHN, BISHOP (Gregory, Book VII, Letter 33, indiction 1):

[Col. 0489D] “The monks of your diocese have complained that you have taken certain things from the monastery under the appearance of a gift of hospitality. Therefore, if you recall having accepted anything improperly, you must restore it without delay, lest the charge of avarice severely condemn you, whom priestly generosity ought rather to have shown to be generous toward monasteries. The monks have also complained that their abbot granted you land as a donation under the pretext of building a church. Therefore, except for the portion enclosed by the church walls [Col. 0490A], we wish it to return without difficulty to the rights of the monastery, because neither the statutes of worldly laws nor those of the sacred canons permit monastery property to be separated from its right under any title. Therefore restore, without any opposition, the donation of that land, which was made contrary to reason.”

Likewise, in the Laws, chapter 404:

“If anyone, possessing another’s property in bad faith, sells, gives, or alienates it in another manner, and the person who considers himself its owner, knowing this, gives formal notice to the recipient of the property—within ten years if they are present, or within twenty years if they are absent—the property is nevertheless to remain securely with the purchaser, the person who received the gift, or the person who acquired it by another form of alienation. But if the possessor alienated it in bad faith without the owner’s knowledge, this shall not prejudice the owner unless a period of thirty years has elapsed, even if the purchaser or the person who acquired it by another form of alienation has been a possessor in good faith.” [Col. 0490B]

### XXVI. — On a Monk or Nun Summoned to Court

From Constitution 2, chapter 74 (Novel 79, chapter 1):

“If anyone has a lawsuit with monks or nuns, he must not dare to accuse or drag them before a civil judge while they are established in an archisterium or monastery, but should rather approach the bishop of the city. He shall determine whether the principal person ought to be produced, or whether the case should be defended through a representative, abbot, or apocrisiarius, in every respect with due propriety, so that the bishop may deliver a judgment consistent with the laws [Col. 0490C] and the canons.”

On Transgressors, chapter 4:

“If anyone violates this constitution, then, if he holds a magistracy, he shall be fined a penalty of ten pounds of gold; an officer appointed to execute litigation, however, shall be confined in the deaconries of the churches to undergo the appropriate penalties, and thereafter shall not be permitted to hold the office of executor.”

### XXVII. — On What Is Offered by the Faithful in Basilicas

From the Council of Orléans, chapter 11 (First Council of Orléans, chapter 15):

“Concerning whatever the faithful offer to parishes in lands, vineyards, slaves, or livestock, let the statutes of the ancient canons be observed, and let everything remain in the bishop’s power. Of what is brought to the altar, however, let one third be faithfully delivered to the bishops.” [Col. 0490D]

### XXVIII. — On Bishops Who Invade Churches While Bypassing a Synod

From the Council of Carthage, chapter 66 (African, or Carthaginian, Council, chapter 87, under Boniface I and Celestine I):

“It has been decided that bishops who believe that certain churches or congregations belong to their see must not reclaim them without bringing their cases before judging bishops, and then invade while another holds them, whether the congregations wish it or not; otherwise they shall suffer loss in their case. Whoever has already done this, if the dispute between the bishops has not yet been concluded but is still being contested, is to withdraw, once it has been established that he invaded while bypassing the ecclesiastical judges.

“Let no one flatter himself because he has requested [variant: obtained] letters from the primate authorizing him to retain the church. Whether he has letters or not, he must approach the person who holds it and receive his letters, so that it may appear that he has held peacefully the church belonging to him. If the other person raises any question, let the case be concluded by episcopal judges—either those whom the primates assign to them or those whom they themselves select from among their neighbors with the primate’s advice [variant: ‘with the consent of the primate’].” [Col. 0491A]

### XXIX. — On the Thirty-Year Limitation

[Col. 0491B] From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 17:

“The rural parishes of each church, or those situated on estates, are to remain undisturbed with the bishops who are known to retain them, especially if they have governed them under their administration for thirty years while holding them without force. If a dispute concerning them has arisen or arises within thirty years, those who claim to have been injured are permitted to contend before the holy synod of the province. If anyone is injured by the metropolitan, let judgment be rendered before the primate of the diocese or before the See of Constantinople, as stated above. If a city has been newly established by imperial authority, or is immediately newly established, let the ecclesiastical arrangements of the parishes likewise follow the civil and public arrangements.”

### XXX. — On the Endowment of Churches

[Col. 0491C] From the Third Council of Toledo, chapter 19:

“Many, contrary to the decrees of the canons, request that the churches they have built be consecrated in such a way that they consider the endowment of the church not to belong to the bishop’s administration. This practice was displeasing in the past and is forbidden for the future; rather, everything is to belong to the bishop’s administration and authority, according to the ancient constitution.”

### XXXI. — On the Bishop: What He Ought to Receive from a Church

From the council mentioned above, chapter 2 (Third Council of Braga, canon 2):

“It has been decided that no bishop, while travelling through his diocese, may take anything from the churches beyond the honor of his see, namely two solidi, nor demand a third part of any offering of the people [Col. 0491D] in parish churches. Rather, that third part is to be preserved for the lights of the church or for repairs, and an account of it is to be rendered to the bishop each year. For if the bishop takes that third part, he has taken away the church’s light and its repairs. Likewise, parish clergy are not to be compelled to serve bishops in certain works in servile fashion, because it is written: ‘Not as domineering over the clergy’ (1 Peter 5:3).”

### XXXII. — On Church Property and the Relatives of Its Founders

From the Ninth Council of Toledo, chapter 1:

“Therefore, the whole quantity of ecclesiastical property, just as it grants the remedy of forgiveness to the donor, so rightly prepares punishment for the defrauder. [Col. 0492A] Therefore, let no priest or minister take anything from the property of the church that the faithful have bestowed in any place, or convert it to his own right or to the advantage of his own see. For just as each person’s devotion gratefully offered a vow to the Lord, so it determined that the fullness of the vows should be preserved in the place where they were made. If the gifts are retained there, the grace of the offerer remains; if they are frustrated, the ruin of the defrauder threatens.

“Yet, so that greater stability may be secured in this matter, the worthy sons, grandsons, and more honorable relatives of the person who built or enriched the church may lawfully exercise this well-intentioned vigilance: if they discover that the priest or minister has defrauded anything from the gifts, they may either restrain him through an honorable agreement of admonition [Col. 0492B] or report the matter to the bishop or judge for correction. If the bishop attempts such things, they are to take care to report them to his metropolitan. If the metropolitan does such things, they must not delay bringing them to the king’s attention.

“Nevertheless, the heirs themselves may not assert control over these properties as though they possessed a proprietary right; they may not introduce robbery, fraud, or any violence whatsoever. They may exercise only a salutary vigilance, without engaging in any harmful action or appropriating either a large or any part of the salutary recompense. If anyone thereafter wishes to violate these admonitions, let him restore with shame what he has wrongfully seized and suffer the sentence of annual excommunication.”

Likewise, chapter 2 (same source):

“Since it has often been customary to extort even what is not owed by entreaty and, in a certain sense, by force born of grief [Col. 0492C], how much more ought those things not to be surrendered without resistance which are exacted both by the order of law and by the pain of compassion? Since it is often known to happen that parish churches or sacred monasteries, through the insolence or negligence of certain bishops, fall into such a terrible ruin that the sorrow arising among the builders is heavier than the joy that had existed in the labor of construction [variant: ‘building’], therefore we decree with pious compassion that, as long as the founders of those churches survive in this life, they be permitted to exercise watchful care over those places and to bear their principal responsibility; and that those same founders offer principal or suitable rectors in those basilicas for the bishops to ordain.” [Col. 0492D]

In the Laws, chapter 456:

“If anyone has built a house of prayer and he himself or his heirs prefer to consecrate clerics in that house, let the administrators of the house be heard if they have nominated clerics who are worthy. But if those men are such that they are not approved by the divine canons, it will belong to the bishop to choose other suitable clerics.”

### XXXIII. — On the Provision of Episcopal Assistance

Chapter 37 (Fourth Council of Toledo):

“Whenever bishops, through the support of anyone, make some provision for an ecclesiastical benefit, and promise any small thing in remuneration for it, they must discharge what they promised, so that, when it has been brought before the provincial council, it may be confirmed by their agreement; for, as the apostle Paul says, ‘They will receive their reward’ (1 Corinthians 3:8).” [Col. 0493A]

### XXXIV. — On the Poverty of Those Who Have Given Their Property to the Church

Chapter 38 (same source):

“Priests must provide the necessities of life to the poor, especially to those toward whom a return is owed. Therefore, if any of the faithful have contributed something from their means to the church out of personal devotion, and if they themselves or their children should subsequently be reduced to poverty, let them receive from that same church assistance for living, according to the needs of the time. If ecclesiastical property is generously given to clerics, monks, pilgrims, or anyone suffering necessity, solely out of regard for religion, how much more ought provision to be made for those to whom a just repayment is owed?” [Col. 0493B]

### XXXV. — On the Avarice of Priests

Chapter 33 (same source):

“Avarice is the root of all evils, and its thirst also possesses the minds of priests. Many of the faithful, out of love for Christ and the martyrs, build basilicas in the dioceses of bishops and record offerings; but the priests take them away and convert them to their own uses. Hence worshippers of sacred things decline, while they lose their stipends. Hence the buildings of basilicas that are collapsing are not repaired, because everything is taken away by priestly avarice.

“Therefore the present council has decreed that bishops govern their dioceses in such a way that they presume to take nothing from their rights, but, in accordance with the authority of earlier councils, receive a third part both of offerings and of dues and revenues. If they should presume to take more, let it be restored through the council, upon appeal either by the founders themselves or, if they have already departed from this world, by their relatives. The founders of basilicas must nevertheless understand that they have no authority over the property they contribute to the same church; rather, according to the provisions of the canons, just as the church itself, so also its endowment belongs to the bishop’s administration.” [Col. 0493C]

GREGORY to LEO, bishop (Gregory, Book VII, Letter 8, indiction 1):

“We wish that whatever may have come to your church from revenue or under any other title, you should set aside a fourth portion of it without any diminution [Col. 0493D] and divide it discreetly, according to the fear of God, among the presbyters, deacons, and clergy as you see fit, giving to each according as the merit of his labor requires.”

That four portions ought to be made from the property of the church [Col. 0494A] is stated by Gelasius in his decretals, chapter 27:

“Four portions,” he says, “both from revenue and from the offerings of the faithful, insofar as the resources of each church permit, should be made, as was long ago reasonably decreed: one for the pontiff, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth to be applied to the fabric of the church.”

Simplicius, bishop, to Florentinus, Equitius, and Severus, bishops (Simplicius, *Decrees*, chap. 2):

“Concerning the revenues of churches or the offerings of the faithful, let no one who does not know what is proper be permitted to do anything; but only a fourth portion of these is to be remitted; let two parts, beneficial for church buildings and for distribution to pilgrims and the poor, be administered by the presbyter Bonager at the peril of his order. The final part shall be divided among the clergy according to the merits of each.”

XXXVI.—On those who have been unjustly excommunicated

From the African Council, chap. 100 [Note: [Col. 0493D] From the African Council, chap. 100. This chapter is absent from the published editions of the African, or Carthaginian, Council. The collection consists of one hundred different chapters from councils of the African province, followed by five further chapters drawn from certain episcopal letters. In the most recent edition of the councils, the conclusion of the council is cited as chapter one hundred, in the words of Bishop Aurelius: “According to the statutes of the entire council assembled, and according to the judgment of my mediocrity, it pleases us to make a conclusion concerning all matters,” and so forth. This in no way corresponds to the heading of chapter one hundred, which is placed at the beginning of the council: “That a bishop should not rashly deprive anyone of communion.” This chapter, however, corresponds excellently to that heading in Abo and should be supplied from this passage in the published editions.]: “As long as his own bishop communicates with an excommunicated person, the other bishops shall not communicate with that bishop, so that the bishop may be more careful not to say of anyone what he cannot prove by other evidence.”

Likewise, from the Council of Cologne, chap. 56 [Note: [Col. 0494D] From the Council of Cologne, chap. 56. This passage is absent from the published editions. It appears to be a decree of the Council of Cologne, held in 870 concerning ecclesiastical discipline. From this we infer that that council had many decrees, of which Abo cites chapter 56.]: “Let no bishop deprive anyone of ecclesiastical communion without a certain and manifest cause of sin. Moreover, let him impose an anathema on no one without the consent of the archbishop and the bishops, even after evangelical admonition, unless there is an authority from the canons teaching that it should be imposed; for anathema is a condemnation to eternal death and should be imposed only for a mortal crime and upon one who could not otherwise be corrected.”

Likewise, in the *Laws*, chap. 441: “Let no bishop and no presbyter excommunicate anyone before the cause for which the ecclesiastical canons command this to be done has been proved. But if someone excommunicates another person against him, let the one who has been excommunicated return to the grace of holy communion by the authority of the greater priest; but let the one who excommunicated him unlawfully abstain from holy communion for as long a time as seems appropriate to the greater priest, so that he may justly suffer what he unjustly did.”

XXXVII.—On churches and their presbyters

From the Third Council of Toledo, chap. 20: “The complaints of many have demanded this constitution, by which we have learned that bishops rage through their parishes not as priests but cruelly; and, although it is written, ‘Be examples to the flock, and not as those who lord it over the clergy’ (1 Peter 5:3), they inflict exactions or losses upon their dioceses. Therefore we decree that, except for what the constitutions of the Fathers command bishops to receive from parishes, they shall be denied the other things that have hitherto been arrogated. That is, they shall not burden presbyters or deacons with forced labor, nor weary them with any exactions, lest they appear in the Church of God to be exactors rather than bishops of God.

“Those clergy, both local and diocesan, who discover that they are being burdened by the bishop shall not delay to bring their complaints to the metropolitan; and the metropolitan shall not delay to restrain such presumptions.”

Pope Eugenius, chap. 21 (Roman synod): “A monastery or oratory canonically constructed shall not be taken away from the ownership of its founder against his will; and he may commend it to whichever presbyter he wishes, with the consent of his bishop, so that he may not be an evil man, provided that the priest obediently returns to the bishop whenever the bishop requires.”

Likewise, chap. 24: “Bishops shall ordain presbyters in their own churches. But if any other person, in his own basilica, does not send a presbyter within three months after being admonished by the bishop, let the bishop report this to the ruler so that he may correct it.”

Likewise, chap. 25: “If destroyed churches cannot be rebuilt from their own resources, let the people of the parish assist them.”

Likewise, chap. 26: “Let no bishop demand from any cleric subject to him donations beyond what the statutes of the Fathers prescribe, nor impose forced labor.”

XXXVIII.—That the bishop has a third part of the church’s property and may give it to whomever he wishes

[Col. 0495C]

Chapter 6 (from another council): “We have thought it opportune to decree that the bishop may confer the third part which he knows has been assigned to him from the church’s property by the sanction of the Fathers, either upon the church whose property it is clearly shown to be, or upon another church which he has chosen and determined to benefit; so that the decision he makes may remain lawful and possess irrevocable force.”

Likewise, from the Third Council of Toledo, chap. 3: “No bishop shall be permitted to alienate the property of another church, since this is also prohibited by the ancient canons. But if they give anything that does not burden the church’s interests, for the support of monks or of churches belonging to their parish, let it remain secure; and, without prejudice to the rights of the church, they are permitted for the time being to provide whatever they can for the needs of pilgrims, clergy, and the poor.”

XXXIX.—On the holiness of the clergy’s life

Pope Siricius, in letter, chap. 7 (Siricius, *Decrees*): “We have learned that very many priests of Christ and levites, after long periods since their consecration, have fathered offspring both from their own wives and even from shameful intercourse, and defend their crime by this argument: that in the Old Testament the priests and ministers are read to have been granted the ability to beget children. But those men were chosen through the succession of their lineage from the single tribe of Levi, to whom God says: ‘Be holy, because I am holy’ (Leviticus 19:2). Hence they were also ordered to live far from their homes in the temple during the year of their service, so that they could not engage in carnal intercourse with their wives.

“But all of us who are priests and levites are bound by an unbreakable law: from the day of our ordination we must dedicate both our hearts and our bodies to sobriety and chastity, provided that in all things we please our God in the sacrifices that we offer daily. Therefore, to those who lament that they have fallen through ignorance, we declare that mercy should not be denied on this condition: that, without any increase of honor, they remain throughout their lives in the office in which they were found, provided that thereafter they strive to show themselves continent.

“But those who, following the example of the ancient priesthood, use marriage as though it were lawful must know that, by the authority of the apostolic see, they have been deposed from every ecclesiastical honor which they unworthily held, and that thereafter, by no indulgence of ours, may they touch the divine mysteries—whether they are bishops, presbyters, or deacons.”

XL.—On the sons of presbyters, bishops, or deacons

From the Ninth Council of Toledo, chap. 10: “But whoever among the clergy, from a bishop down to a subdeacon, thereafter begets children from either a slave woman or a disgraceful union with a freeborn woman while holding ecclesiastical office, let those from whom they are proved to have been begotten be condemned by canonical judgment. But the offspring, alienated [variant: born] through such pollution, shall not only never receive their parents’ inheritance, but shall also remain in perpetual servitude to the church from whose priest or minister’s disgrace they were born.

“Let the sons of priests who were born before the priesthood not put on secular spectacles, nor even attend them, although this is forbidden to all Christians; and let them not go where there are blasphemies, as you have in the Council of Carthage, chap. 15.”

XLI.—On the administration of church property

From the Council of Eastern Bishops, chap. 14, concerning a bishop’s presumption in matters of church property: “If any bishop, compelled by no necessity of ecclesiastical administration, presumes to sell anything from the church’s property among his clergy, or where there happens to be no presbyter, let him be compelled to restore the property itself to its own church; let him be deposed unheard in the judgment of the bishops; and, as one guilty of theft or robbery, let him be deprived of his office.”

Likewise, chap. 16: “Let the bishop have authority over the church’s property, so that he may administer it to those suffering need, with all reverence and fear of God. He ought to share whatever is necessary, if he himself or the brothers who are with him should need something or suffer need in any way, according to the holy Apostle’s saying: ‘Having food and clothing, with these we are content’ (1 Timothy 6:8).

“But if the bishop wishes to seize the church’s property for his own purposes, and consumes the church’s profits and the produce of the fields without the counsel of the presbyters or deacons, or gives power to his brothers, sons, or any relatives so that through them the property may secretly be damaged, he must be held liable before the council. Presbyters and deacons likewise must be rebuked if they do the same.”

XLII.—That no one should choose a bishop as his successor

From the Council of Antioch, chap. 25 (the Council of Antioch under Pope Julius I): “A bishop may not appoint another as his successor in his place, even if he approaches the end of his life. But if anything of this kind has been done, let such an appointment be invalid. Let the ecclesiastical law that governs this matter be preserved: it ought to be done only with the synod and judgment of the bishops, who, after the death of the bishop who has died, have the power to promote whoever proves worthy.”

Likewise, Gregory to Anatolius, subdeacon of Constantinople [Col. 0497B] (Gregory, book 9, letter 41):

“Nowhere do the canons prescribe that a bishop should be succeeded on account of illness. It is altogether unjust that, if bodily sickness falls upon him, the sick man should be deprived of his honor; and therefore this cannot by any means be done through us, lest my soul incur sin through his deposition.

“But it should be suggested that, if the man who is in charge is ill, an administrator should be sought for him who can undertake all his care and, without deposing him, fulfill his place in governing the church and in safeguarding the city. Thus neither almighty God will be offended, nor will the city be found neglected.

“But if that most reverend John should perhaps ask, on account of his illness, to be relieved of the honor of the episcopate, this should be granted once he has submitted his request in writing. Otherwise, through fear of almighty God, we cannot do this in any way.

“If he does not wish to ask this, whatever pleases the most pious emperor, whatever he orders to be done, lies within his authority. Let him himself provide as he knows best; only let him not make us participate in the deposition. Whatever the emperor does, if it is canonical, we follow it; but if it is not canonical, we bear it insofar as we can without our own sin.”

XLIII.—On communion

Augustine, in the *Ecclesiastical Rules* [Note: [Col. 0497D] Augustine in the *Ecclesiastical Rules*. The author means the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, which at the beginning of the ninth century was falsely attributed to Augustine by some and was soon afterward rejected as his by learned men, especially by the clergy of Lyons, who wrote concerning the case of Gottschalk against John Scotus, who was abusing the authority of this book as though it were Augustine’s.] chap. 23 (the author of the *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*):

“Whether one should receive communion of the Eucharist daily, I neither praise nor condemn. Nevertheless, I encourage communion on every Sunday, provided that the mind has no inclination to sin. For I say that one who still has the will to sin is burdened more by receiving the Eucharist than cleansed by it.

“Therefore, although someone is tormented by sin, if thereafter he has no will to sin and, when he is about to communicate, makes satisfaction with tears and prayers, then, having done these things and trusting in the Lord’s mercy, which is accustomed to forgive sins to a devout confession, let him approach the Eucharist without fear and securely. But I say this concerning one who is not burdened by capital sins.

“As for one who is weighed down by mortal sins committed after baptism, I first urge him to make satisfaction through public penance, and then, reconciled according to the priest’s judgment, to be joined to communion, if he wishes to receive the Eucharist not for judgment or condemnation.

“Nor do we deny that mortal crimes may be absolved through secret satisfaction, but first the secular habit must be changed, so that through devotion to religion, through correction of life, and through continual—indeed perpetual—mourning, he may obtain pardon by God’s mercy. This is on the strict condition that he do nothing contrary to the sins for which he repents, and that he humbly receive the Eucharist on every Sunday until death.”

Gregory (Gregory, in the tenth response to Augustine’s questions):

“The mystery of holy communion should not be forbidden to a woman during her menstrual period. If, however, out of great reverence she does not presume to receive it, she is to be praised. But if she does receive it, she is not to be judged. It is characteristic of good minds to recognize their faults in some way where there is no fault, because often something that proceeds from fault is done without fault.

“Thus, when we are hungry, we eat without fault, although our hunger came about through the fault of the first man. Menstruation is not a fault for women, since it occurs naturally; but because nature itself has been corrupted, so that what appears to be polluted even without the intention of the will derives from fault, the human person recognizes in it what human nature has become through judgment. Thus the human being, who willingly committed the fault, bears the guilt of fault unwillingly.

“Therefore women should examine themselves; and if, during their menstrual period, they do not presume to approach the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, they are to be praised for their sound judgment. But when, out of the practice of a religious life, they are carried by love of that same mystery toward receiving it, they are not, as we have said, to be restrained.”

And below:

“It must be carefully considered that, when the Lord was about to speak to the people on Mount Sinai, he first commanded that same people to abstain from women. If there, where the Lord spoke through a creature subject to human beings, such bodily purity was required that those who were to receive the words of God were not to be mingled with women, how much more ought women who receive the body of almighty God to preserve purity of flesh within themselves, lest they be burdened by the greatness of that immeasurable mystery?

“Hence the priest is also told concerning David and his young men that, if they were clean from women, they could receive the bread of the Presence; they would certainly not receive it unless David acknowledged them to be clean. But a man may receive the mystery of holy communion after intercourse with his wife once he has washed with water, when, according to the previously established judgment, he is also permitted to enter the church.”

Likewise, concerning pollution in sleep (response 2):

“The Old Testament calls such a man polluted and does not permit him to enter the church until evening unless he has washed with water. But the spiritual people, understanding this differently, receive it according to the same interpretation: one is deceived as though in a dream when, tempted by impurity, he is defiled in thought by empty images.

“But he must be washed with water, so that he may cleanse the faults of his thought with tears; and, unless the fire of temptation has first withdrawn, he should recognize himself as guilty, as it were, until evening.

“Yet in this same deception a very necessary discernment is required, which you must weigh carefully: from what cause it has happened to the sleeping mind. Sometimes it comes from overeating, sometimes from an excess or weakness of nature, and sometimes from thought.

“When it has arisen from an excess or weakness of nature, this deception is not at all to be feared, because the mind, which has suffered it unknowingly, is more to be pitied than blamed for having caused it.

“But when the appetite for food is carried beyond measure in taking nourishment, and therefore the receptacles of the bodily fluids are weighed down, the mind has some guilt from this—not, however, to the point of forbidding the reception of the holy mystery or the celebration of the solemnities of the Mass, when perhaps a feast day requires it, or necessity compels the mystery to be offered because another priest is absent from the place.

“For if others are present who can fulfill the ministry, the deception caused by overeating should not prevent reception of the sacred mystery; but, as I think, one should humbly abstain from offering the sacred mystery, provided that the sleeping person’s mind has not been shaken by an impure imagination.

“For there are people in whom such a deception often arises without their mind, even while their body lies asleep, being defiled by an impure imagination. In this matter one thing is shown: that the mind itself is not then guilty but is free in its own judgment, since, although the body was asleep, it remembers having seen nothing, yet while awake it remembers having fallen into gluttony.

“But if the deception of the sleeper arises from an impure thought entertained while awake, the mind’s guilt is evident. For the person sees from what root that pollution proceeded: what he knowingly thought, he unknowingly suffered.”

When monks and other penitents ought to communicate is made clear by Saint Eucherius [Note: [Col. 0499C] Saint Eucherius. I have not found this passage in the published writings of Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, nor in the sermons published under the name of Eusebius of Emesa, which learned men reasonably believe should be attributed to Eucherius of Lyons. Here Eucherius establishes a distinction between those who undertake the monastic life and other penitents: penance must be required of the latter before communion, but not of the former. “For one who renounces the world,” he says, “public penance is not necessary, because, having been converted, he has groaned and entered into a covenant with the eternal God.”

“Since penance before communion was instituted chiefly to test the penitent’s will—whether it is alienated from the desire to sin—no doubt about this remains in those who, bidding farewell to the world, sincerely profess the difficult exercises of monastic life in approved monasteries. For in this way they enter into a covenant with the eternal God to satisfy divine justice throughout the whole course of their lives.

“‘From that day,’ says Eucherius, ‘the offenses he committed in the world are not remembered, from the moment he has promised God that thereafter he will practice righteousness.’

“On the occasion of this passage, I recall what I remember reading in Peter Damian, *Opusculum* 13, chapters 6 and 7, against certain heads of monasteries ‘who, attributing more to the monastic rule than is appropriate, impose no other penance on anyone coming from the world, even if he has fallen gravely, than that he observe the monastery’s common order.’

“Peter condemns this on the ground that ‘those who come to conversion in childhood, as well as those who come after being guarded from serious offenses, can murmur and complain justly if they are compelled to follow the same way of life as those burdened with crimes.’

“Nevertheless, this teaching is opposed by the example of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, who imposed no other penance on a man guilty of capital crimes and freed from the extreme penalties than profession of the monastic life at Clairvaux. Indeed, if life had been organized in all monasteries as it was at that time among the monks of Clairvaux, that would be a just form of penance for all penitents, however gravely they had fallen.

“Nor was any other penance once required of priests and other persons who had fallen into more serious crimes than confinement in a monastery. Although some in monasteries are guilty and others innocent, the same form of penance can nevertheless suit both, since what the former perform out of obligation, the latter perform solely out of love of righteousness.”]:

“Let secular penance be given to one whose neck still hangs beneath the yoke of the world; and let the period be fixed for him according to the enormity of his sin or offense, since he still serves time.

“But why should one who renounces the world and its service, and promises to serve God throughout all his days, delay penance? Let every such result pursue the wasteland of the desert like a wild ass, as Job says: ‘Who has let the wild ass go free in the desert?’ (Job 39:5).

“Let him carefully beware of the lion and be nourished in the desert by a scant drink of dry grasses. Let him raise his head into the air, and let the breeze of the Holy Spirit restrain the excessively burning heat of thirst, lest, while greatly desiring pleasant green places, he be hindered by excessive delights and incur danger to his salvation.

“Therefore public penance is not necessary for one who renounces the world, because, having been converted, he has groaned and entered into a covenant with the eternal God. From that day, the offenses he committed in the world are not remembered, from the moment he has promised God that thereafter he will practice righteousness.

“Therefore, concerning the written bond by which the monk has promised in complete faith that he will fulfill the debt he has undertaken—even if, after becoming a believer, he sinned in the world—once he has again made his renunciation, let him not hesitate to receive the Lord’s body, nor, under the pretext of excessive humility, let him be kept away from the body and blood of the one to whom he has joined himself in order to become one body.

“Let the one who has ceased to sin not cease to communicate—only let him not sin thereafter. For just as visible fire has two powers within itself, namely, to burn fragile things and to illuminate darkness, so that fiery body of the Lord, when it is received with fear and great reverence, consumes the sins of the body and illuminates the understanding of the soul. For this reason he ought to communicate more frequently.

“But if, as it is written, there is leprosy on the skin, it will be unclean—that is, sin in the monk, since Scripture signifies that the monk is the skin, mortifying his members upon the earth. Ashes have clung to the bones, the flesh is changed because of oil, it is weakened by fasting, and the knees dry up like grass. Therefore, if leprosy appears on this skin, it will be unclean; and unless it is hyacinth-colored or pure red, it will not be suitable for the adornment of the tabernacle.”

These are the judgments of the holy Fathers, full of discernment, by which men and women are instructed when and in what condition they ought to approach communion of the Eucharist.

Of the sins on account of which we are commanded to abstain from the Eucharist, some draw us through the defect of nature even against our will, while others draw us voluntarily. Against his will was the man led by the law of sin who lamented: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members” (Romans 7:23).

Accordingly, Gregory, singularly magnificent in discernment and eloquence, by showing indulgence toward human weakness and granting such persons access to the church and communion of the Eucharist, consoles one who is grieving, because sometimes a man is polluted unwillingly by nocturnal sleep, and a woman by her menstruation.

From his authority we learn that one who alone is conscious to himself of the act of sin will also be his own judge, even after confession, in receiving communion of the body and blood of Christ.

But the one who is voluntarily seized by the law of sin is not so much saddened by the recollection of sins as delighted by it, because he deliberately sins with consent. Therefore, as Augustine says, “in the communion of the Eucharist he should be considered more burdened than cleansed,” since he remains wholly in the desire to sin.

“For every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Corinthians 6:18). It must therefore be understood concerning one who willingly sins either against himself or against another that he ought to be kept from communion, lest we appear to cast our pearls before swine and become participants in another’s destruction.

Yet the example of Christ comes to mind: he gave dipped bread to Judas the betrayer, of whom it is written that “after the morsel Satan entered into him” (John 13:27). But Christ, who was not ignorant of secret things, offered the bread to reveal the lost disciple; we, however, conscious of our sins, should offer the Eucharist to a brother not for display but in remembrance of Christ.

Hence Augustine (*Tractate 61 on John*) says:

“Why are you surprised if Christ’s bread was given to Judas, through which he was to be handed over to the devil, when, on the contrary, you see that the angel of Satan was given to Paul, through whom he was to be perfected in Christ? Thus what is good harmed the wicked, and what is evil benefited the good.

“It is written: ‘Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord’ (1 Corinthians 11:27). If the one who does not judge—that is, does not distinguish—the Lord’s body from other foods is rebuked, how is the one who approaches his table as an enemy while pretending to be a friend condemned?

“If the negligence of a guest is touched by rebuke, with what punishment is the betrayer of the host struck? What was the bread given to the betrayer other than a demonstration of the grace toward which he was ungrateful? After that bread, Satan entered the Lord’s betrayer, so that he might possess more fully the one already handed over to him—one into whom he had previously entered in order to deceive him.”

XLIV.—How the accusers of priests are to be examined, and whether a judgment has been pronounced in writing between the parties

Gregory to John the defensor, among other matters (Gregory, book 2, letter 52):

“Since Bishop Stephen complains that certain things were fabricated out of hatred against him, and that he was accused on the basis of false charges, and asserts that nothing was done in an orderly manner but that he was condemned unjustly, it must first be carefully investigated whether the trial was properly conducted, and whether the accusers were different from the witnesses.

“Next, the nature of the charges must be examined: whether they were worthy of exile or deposition; whether testimony was given against him under oath in his presence; whether the proceedings were recorded in writing; and whether he had the opportunity to respond and defend himself.

“Furthermore, the persons of the accusers and witnesses must be carefully investigated: what their status and reputation were; whether they were poor; whether perhaps they had some hostility toward the bishop; and whether they gave testimony from hearsay or testified that they knew the matter personally. It must also be determined whether the case was judged in writing and whether the judgment was read in the presence of the parties.

“But if these matters were not formally conducted, and if no charge worthy of exile or deposition was proved, he must by all means be recalled to his own church. Those, however, who condemned him contrary to the fear of God and the statutes of the canons must be excommunicated and sent to a monastery to perform penance for six months—yet in such a way that, if the danger of death should threaten any of them, the blessing of the viaticum is not to be denied.

“But the man who rashly sought his position while he was still alive must be deprived of the priesthood and excluded from every ecclesiastical ministry; and he must be handed over to that most beloved brother and our fellow bishop, so that he may either bring him to us for ecclesiastical judgment or keep him in custody with himself.

“As for the bishops who dared to ordain him or consented to his perverse ordination, let them be deprived of communion and assigned to a monastery to perform penance for six months.

“But if the bishops confess that they consented to the condemnation or deposition of the aforementioned Stephen through fear of the judge, and that they did these things not of their own accord, their period should be shortened and the measure of their penance moderated.”

Likewise, concerning a certain bishop accused of a crime, and whether it is harmful if a confession has been extorted.

Gregory to Constantius of Milan (book 8, letter 30):

“After rereading the letters which you sent to us through Marianus, the bearer of this letter, we wrote back that we were pleased by your concern, because you did not tolerate disregarding what had reached you concerning our brother and fellow bishop Pompeius, who must still be called by that name.

“But if the care shown in investigating the matter had been matched by equal precision in examining it, nothing that was said about him would have remained ambiguous; it would have become clear whether it was true or fabricated, since, as we have learned, a similar inquiry had already been raised against him in Sicily before our brother of revered memory, Maximianus.

“Because his case was investigated with the utmost precision, however, he who had been accused of the crime was found innocent.

“Now, since the charges made against him were not investigated with the strictness that was appropriate, and since the proceedings prepared from them before your Fraternity are shown to be sufficient neither for his condemnation nor for his acquittal, this is not a trivial matter to be decided carelessly or in passing. For it is a very serious and improper thing to pronounce a certain judgment in a doubtful case.

“These proceedings could have been suitable for deciding the matter if the accused’s confession had followed them—provided, however, that the precision of the examination had drawn that confession out of hidden facts, rather than violent affliction having extorted it. For such affliction frequently causes even the innocent to be compelled to confess themselves guilty.

“Therefore, since the aforementioned bishop asserts that, as is said, he was tortured in custody and burned by hunger, you must determine whether it is harmful if a confession was extorted in this way.

“When such cases come to judgment and an appeal is made to the apostolic see, is not the person being judged present? Is not the truth then sought with the utmost strictness and from every side, so that it may be decided whether the judgment ought to stand?

“Moreover, if the aforementioned bishop wishes to appeal to the apostolic see, his case must be examined internally and with every diligence.

“Therefore, since the person is absent and the proceedings that you sent to us, as we have said, do not seem adequate to satisfy us, we ought not and cannot rashly decide anything concerning the bishop’s person, lest—God forbid—we be found blameworthy in matters in which we have the lawful duty to reconsider the judgments of others.”

Likewise, concerning a bishop whom he rebuked for not sending useful men to represent his case, and for having returned to favor after giving an oath.

Gregory to Maximus, bishop of Salona (book 2, letter 13):

“We had previously written other letters to your Fraternity; and, when we wished to release the men whom you had sent to us, I find that you wrote to certain of our people that you had not sent the presbyter Veteranus and the defensor Optatus to represent you in the case at that time, and that therefore the proceedings conducted with them ought not to stand.

“But Thomas, the defensor of your church, testified that you had not said this. For this reason, we now judge that we cannot even trust the bearers of the present letter, lest the same thing be said of them after these men.

“Since this has caused us great doubt and warned us that we must be cautious, if you wish your case henceforth to be properly prepared, send a representative with a legally executed mandate, strengthened by the signatures of yourself, the presbyters or deacons, and the witnesses, together with proceedings drawn up according to custom, so that whatever has been done for the case may be legally upheld.

“For we are prepared, with God’s help, to preserve what is just and lawful in every respect not only for you but for everyone—provided only that you do not omit to do what the law prescribes.”

Likewise, Gregory to Castorius, notary and chartularius of Ravenna (book 7, letter 81, indiction 2):

“The more you see that we trust you and that necessary cases are being entrusted to you, the more energetic and diligent you must show yourself to be.

“Therefore, if Maximus of Salona confirms under oath that he is not involved in the simoniacal heresy; if, when questioned only about other matters before the body of Saint Apollinaris, he answers that he is innocent; and if he performs the penance we assigned for his disobedience, we wish you, in order to console him, to give him the letter that we wrote to him, in which we stated that we had restored both our favor and communion to him.

“For just as it is fitting that we be severe toward those who persist in obstinacy, so we must not deny a place of pardon to those who have humbled themselves and performed penance.”

A certain bishop cleared himself by oath of a charge before the body of blessed Peter. GREGORY to JUSTINIAN [or JUSTIN] (Book II, Letter 23):

“The ancient enemy’s envy has this characteristic: those whom, while God resists him, he cannot deceive into perpetrating wickedness, he tears apart for the present by falsely fabricating accusations against their reputations. Since, therefore, an unfavorable rumor had spread concerning our brother and fellow bishop Leo, contrary to the purpose of the priesthood, we made a strict and prolonged inquiry to discover whether these things were true; and we found no fault in him with respect to what had been reported. But lest anything appear to have been omitted that could leave doubt in our heart, we had him give an oath before the most sacred body of blessed Peter. When this had been done, we rejoiced with great exultation, because his innocence clearly shone forth through this test.

“For this reason let Your Glory receive the aforesaid man with every kindness and show him the reverence proper to a priest. Let no doubt remain in your heart concerning matters that have been cleared up; rather, you ought to adhere most devotedly to the aforesaid bishop in all things, so that you may be seen properly and suitably to honor God in his person, since he is God’s minister.”

XLV.—Concerning bishops summoned to court to give testimony.

From Constitution, chapter 9:

“No bishop shall be compelled to come to court for the purpose of giving testimony; rather, the judge shall send his officials to the bishop, so that, with the holy Gospels set before him, the bishop may state what he knows, in accordance with what is proper for priests.”

XLVI.—Concerning accused bishops.

Chapter 10:

“No bishop, whether in a civil or a criminal case, shall be brought or presented before any judge, whether civil or military, unless an imperial order has been issued. Any magistrate who dares to order this shall be punished by loss of his military belt and condemnation to pay twenty pounds of gold; these twenty pounds shall be assigned to the church whose bishop was ordered to be brought or presented. The officer executing the action, after losing his belt, shall be subjected to torture and sent into exile.”

XLVII.—Concerning those who have a case against a bishop.

Chapter 37:

“If a cleric or anyone else wishes to be heard against a bishop for any reason whatsoever, their metropolitan shall first decide the matter according to the holy canons and our laws. If anyone contradicts the judgment, the matter shall be referred to the patriarch of that region, and he shall bring it to an end according to the canons and the law. If anyone wishes to proceed against a metropolitan, the patriarch of that region shall decide the case.

“Whatever bishop is accused before any judge shall absolutely not be compelled to give any security or undertaking in the litigation; nevertheless, he shall make every effort to refute the claims and charges of the plaintiff.”

XLVIII.—Concerning the testimony of clerics.

Chapter 33:

“If a priest or deacon gives false testimony in a pecuniary case, he shall not be subjected to torture, but shall be separated from the divine ministry for three years and handed over to a monastery. If he gives false testimony in criminal cases, he shall be stripped of the honor of the clerical state and subjected to the penalties prescribed by law.

“Other clerics of a lower rank, for any false testimony whatsoever, shall be stripped of their ecclesiastical order and subjected to the legal forms of punishment.

“If anyone has any action against a cleric, monk, deaconess, monastery, or arch-monastery, he shall first approach the most religious bishop to whom each of them is subject; and that bishop shall decide the matter concerning them. If one of the litigants contradicts the judgment, and the bishop is acting by imperial or judicial order, the matter shall be referred to the emperor or to the judge who issued the order.

“If the same canonical matter should arise from an ecclesiastical judgment, it is not the magistrate but the religious bishop who shall bring the case to an end according to the sacred canons.”

XLIX.—How beneficial frequent offering of the sacrifice is.

Gregory, in Homily 37 on the Gospels:

“Consider, brothers, how merciful it is that he who is able to destroy by his coming delays his arrival. Let us send an embassy to him by weeping, giving, and offering sacred victims. For, uniquely for our absolution, the victim of the sacred altar, offered with tears and a kindly disposition, comes to our aid, because he who, having risen from the dead, dies no more, still suffers for us through this mystery in himself. For as often as we offer him the victim of his Passion, so often do we renew his Passion for our absolution.”

[Col. 0506A] The same teacher added an example of this matter when he described a certain man bound in captivity and released whenever an offering was made for him:

“His wife, thinking him dead, offered the sacrifice for him every week; and, as he himself later learned after returning home, he was released as often as the saving victim was offered for him.”

L.—Concerning soldiers.

Augustine, On the Words of the Lord, Homily 19:

“To serve as a soldier is not a crime, but to serve as a soldier for the sake of plunder is a sin. Nor is administering the republic criminal; but to administer the republic in order to increase one’s private fortune seems condemnable. For this reason, pay has been established for soldiers by a certain providence, lest, while expenses are being sought, plunder should prevail.

“But what sort of thing is it when, after being reproved by their superiors for some wrongdoing, and when someone is asked why he was drunk, why he seized another’s property, or why, in his disorder, he committed murder, he immediately replies: ‘What were a secular man and a soldier supposed to do? Surely I have not professed to be a monk or a cleric?’ As though everyone who is not a cleric or monk might lawfully do what is unlawful.”

LI.—Concerning soldiers’ pay.

“It is said according to the Gospel: ‘John and the soldiers asked him: “And what shall we do?” John said to them: “Shake no one down, accuse no one falsely, but be content with your pay”’ (Luke 3:14).

“Here the soldier ought to recognize himself. Scripture does not speak only of those soldiers who are occupied in armed service; rather, whoever wears the belt of his service is reckoned a soldier of his rank. This statement may, for example, be applied to soldiers, protectors, and all governors. Whoever receives the pay publicly assigned to him, if he seeks more, is condemned by John’s sentence as an accuser and extortioner.

“This evil, however, has become so widespread that now, as if by custom, laws are sold, rights are corrupted, judgment itself is for sale, and no case can any longer exist without a cause.”

LII.—Concerning clerics who serve as soldiers, and their pay.

“This statement, which addresses soldiers, can also be applied to clerics, because, although they may not appear to serve the world as soldiers, they nevertheless serve God, as the Apostle says: ‘No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs’ (2 Timothy 2:4).

“We seem, I say, not to serve as soldiers, with our tunics loose and flowing; but we have the belt of our service, by which we bind the inward parts of chastity. Concerning this belt the Lord says: ‘Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands’ (Luke 12:35).

“For the Catholic cleric too is held by this sentence. If he is not content with the pay that, at the Lord’s command, he receives from the altar, but conducts business—

[Note: [Col. 0505D] ‘He conducts business.’ Jerome has almost similar things in his letter to Nepotian, against clerics who are merchants and devoted to avarice, and against those who, through disgraceful services to widows, lay siege to their inheritances. [Col. 0506D]]

“—if he sells intercessions to the Lord and willingly embraces widows’ gifts, he may be considered more a businessman than a cleric.

“Nor can we say: ‘No one accuses us of violent seizure; no one brings a charge against us.’ As though at times flattering approaches did not lure greater plunder from widows than tortures. Nor does it matter to the Lord whether someone seizes another’s property by force or by deception, provided that he possesses what belongs to another by whatever means.”

[Col. 0507]

## LIFE OF SAINT EDMUND, KING OF THE ENGLISH AND MARTYR, BY SAINT ABBON, ABBOT OF FLEURY

(From Surius, *Acts of the Saints*, for 20 November.)

## AUTHOR’S PREFACE TO DUNSTAN, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 0507B] To DUNSTAN, lord archbishop of the holy metropolitan Church of the Dorobernians, mature in character and age, ABBO, a monk and deacon of Fleury, though unworthy: from Christ the Lord, the upper and lower irrigation.

After I had departed from you, venerable Father, with great joy of heart and hastened back to the monastery that you know, those with whom, bound by fraternal charity, I have until now lived as a guest began earnestly to press me, by the hand of Saint Desiderius, to set down in writing the passion of Edmund, king and martyr and performer of wonders. They asserted that this would benefit posterity, please you, and provide no useless memorial of my littleness among the churches of the English.

For they had heard that your holiness, having gathered it from the memory of antiquity, had recounted it historically—though it had already been forgotten by many and written by no one—in my presence to the lord bishop of the Church of Rochester, to the abbot of the monastery called Malmesbury, and to other brothers standing around, as is your custom: brothers whom you never cease nourishing with the food of the divine word in Latin and in the vernacular.

You confessed to them, your eyes suffused with tears, that when you were younger you had learned it from a certain decrepit old man who simply and fully related it in good faith to the most glorious King Æthelstan, asserting under oath that on that very day he had been the blessed man’s arms-bearer, when the latter fell as a martyr for Christ.

Because you placed such faith in this man’s assertion that you stored his words whole in the treasury of your memory, later pouring them forth to younger men with honeyed speech, the brothers began to press my feebleness even more urgently, so that I might satisfy their fervent desire and, as far as my strength allowed, not permit the sequence of such great deeds to perish.

Since I did not wish, out of reverence for you, to refuse their request, I set aside for a while the study of secular letters and turned, as it were, to the soul’s inner philosophy, when I proposed to write the virtues of him who truly philosophized upon the throne of the kingdom. I intended especially to recount those deeds which, after his death, became unheard-of in the world—deeds no one would believe unless the unassailable authority of your testimony had confirmed them.

Indeed, when you—whose white hair compels belief—were speaking of the king’s present incorruption, someone made a more careful inquiry whether such a thing could be true. Wishing to remove the uncertainty of that question, you opened the sanctuary of your vast learning and added, as an example, something that shook the astonished hearts of your hearers even more: namely, that Saint Cuthbert, the incomparable confessor and bishop, not only still awaits the day of the first resurrection with an incorrupt body—

[Note: [Col. 0507D] Note, reader, a matter most worthy of admiration. Moreover, in our own age the body of this Saint Cuthbert was found intact. (See Alan Cope, *Dialogue* III, chapter 29.) [Col. 0508D]]

“—but is also suffused with a certain gentle warmth.

“I admired this and took it as an argument by which I might proceed with greater confidence to labor over the deeds of the holy king. I trusted in his incomparable merits and in yours, and, consecrating to you the first fruits of my labor, I humbly beg you to turn your leisure toward an honorable task for even a single day: cutting away what is superfluous here and filling what is incomplete. For, apart from the sequence of the final miracle, I have faithfully arranged everything according to your truthful account, urging all people toward the death of so great a martyr.

“Farewell, Father in Christ.”

## THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 0507]

[Col. 0507D] I. At one time three peoples of Germany—namely, the Saxons, Jutes, and Angles—were summoned into Britain through a precarious arrangement and for disastrous assistance. At first they served the Britons as a daytime defense [perhaps: “as defenders”]. When the Britons were repeatedly harassed in war and bravely defended themselves and their people, while the newcomers devoted themselves to idleness and sat at home like proletarians intent only on pleasure, trusting in the invincible courage of the mercenary soldiers whom they had hired, they resolved to drive the wretched natives from their homes and fatherland.

An agreement was made, and, having excluded the Britons, the victorious foreigners decided among themselves to divide the island, exceedingly fertile in all its resources. They judged it unworthy that an island capable of providing sufficient sustenance both for its own defense and for excellent men should remain under the dominion of the idle.

On this pretext, the Saxons obtained by lot the eastern part of the island, which to this day in the language of the English is called East Anglia, while the Jutes and Angles turned toward other regions in which they might obtain their share, so that there would be no dispute over possession among their companions, since there was enough land to bring them the profit of kingship.

Thus it came about that, divided into regions and provinces, one and the same Britain was sufficient first for leaders and then for kings.

II. The aforesaid eastern part is considered noble among other things because it is washed by waters on almost every side: toward the southeast and east it is enclosed by the Ocean; toward the north, by the wetness of immense marshes. These marshes, arising because of the level character of the land near the middle of almost the whole of Britain, descend for a hundred miles and more, together with very large rivers, into the sea.

On the side where the sun turns toward the west, the province is joined to the rest of the island and is therefore passable. But, lest it be attacked by frequent incursions of enemies, an embankment resembling a higher wall is strengthened in front by a ditch dug into the earth.

In its interior the land is sufficiently rich and very fertile, delightful in the beauty of its gardens and woods, distinguished by the hunting of wild animals, and far from unproductive in pastures for cattle and beasts of burden.

We say nothing of its fish-filled rivers, since on one side, as stated, the tongue of the sea laps it, while on the other an immeasurable multitude of broad pools, stretching for two or three thousand [units—perhaps acres or miles], flows past through the expanded marshes.

These marshes provide desirable retreats for solitary life to many communities of monks, who, enclosed within them, do not need the solitude of the desert. Among them are the celibate coenobites, holy monks of the father Benedict, in a place celebrated in our time.

[Col. 0509D] III. But to return to the subject: this province had a very fierce king [text uncertain], descended from the noble lineage of the ancient Saxons and, from the earliest period of his life, a most sincere worshiper of the Christian faith.
