Born of royal ancestors, and outstanding in good character, he was chosen by the unanimous favor of all his fellow provincials—not so much through hereditary succession as seized upon by them—to preside over them with sceptered power. For he possessed an appearance worthy of rule, which tranquil devotion continually adorned with the serenity of his heart.

He was approachable to all through gentle speech, distinguished by the grace of humility, and among his contemporaries he remained a lord of wondrous gentleness, without any arrogance of pride. The holy man already displayed in his face what was later revealed by divine will, for as a boy he seized with all the force of virtue the path which divine mercy knew would end in martyrdom.

IV. Once he had attained the height of rule, it is beyond our ability to unfold how great was his kindness toward his subjects and how great his discernment toward the perverse; we cannot adequately express even the smallest of his qualities in fitting language.

For he tempered the cunning of the serpent with the gentleness of dove-like simplicity in such a way that he was neither deceived by the fraudulent simulation of the ancient enemy nor induced to accept, contrary to justice, the judgments of wicked men. He investigated with the utmost care matters of which he was ignorant, walking upon the royal road. He did not turn to the right by exalting himself because of his merits, nor to the left by yielding to the vices of human frailty.

He was also generously liberal toward the needy and a most merciful father to orphans and widows, always keeping before his eyes the saying of the Wise Man: “They have appointed you ruler? Do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclesiasticus 32:1).

Although he stood out conspicuously in Christ and the Church through the adornment of good works, the enemy of the human race—who envies people’s good deeds all the more when he himself is deprived of the appearance of good will—undertook to test his patience, as he had tested that of holy Job.

V. Therefore he sent against him one of his own members, who, after removing everything he possessed from every side, would force him, if possible, to break into impatience, so that, in despair, he might bless God to his face.

This adversary was called Inguar. Together with another man of the same perversity, named Hubba (Stubba), he attempted, unless divine mercy intervened, to bring the whole territory of Britain to destruction.

Nor is this surprising, since they came hardened by the cold of their wickedness from that region of the earth where he established his seat who, through pride, desired to be like the Most High. Indeed, it is established according to the prophet’s prediction that every evil comes from the north, just as those who have suffered more than enough have wrongly learned this from the adverse throws of a falling die, having experienced the savagery of the northern peoples.

They are certainly so cruel by natural ferocity that they do not know how to be softened by human misfortunes. Indeed, some peoples among them eat human flesh; from this practice they are called by the Greek designation *Anthropophagi*—“man-eaters.”

Many such nations abound below Scythia, near the Hyperborean mountains. As we read, they will follow Antichrist before all other nations, feeding without any compassion upon the tortures of human beings who refuse to bear the mark of the beast upon their foreheads.

Hence, having already begun to trouble Christians, they are unable to maintain peace with them—especially the Danes, who are excessively close to the regions of the West, since they practice piracy around them through frequent acts of plunder.

From their people, therefore, the aforesaid leaders Inguar and Hubba first attacked the province of the Northumbrians (or Nordanhumbrians), and ravaged the whole region in succession with grievous devastation.

None of the provincials could resist their most evil efforts without being punished by the wrath of deserved heavenly indignation. Hubba, the minister of iniquity, carried this out. After Inguar had made his plunder, he left Hubba there as his partner in cruelty, then suddenly came from the northern side and, arriving with a large fleet, secretly landed at one of its towns.

Having entered while the citizens were unaware, he gave it over to be burned by fire. He slaughtered children and old men, together with the young, whom he encountered in the streets of the city, and ordered that the modesty of matrons and virgins be delivered over to mockery.

Husbands lay dead or dying with their wives on the threshold. An infant was torn from its mother’s breast and butchered before its mother’s eyes, so that the wailing might be greater.

The impious soldier raged through the city, now searched and set ablaze, toward every outrage by which he might please the tyrant who, moved solely by a passion for cruelty, had ordered the innocent to perish.

[Col. 0511B] VI. When he had already satisfied, not so much his Achaemenian fury [text uncertain], by the multitude of those he had killed as postponed it for the future through exhaustion, he summoned certain commoners, whom he considered unworthy of his sword. He diligently investigated where their king was living at that time.

For word had reached him that the same glorious king, namely Edmund, in the flower of his age and possessed of robust strength, was in every respect vigorous in war. Therefore he hastened to deliver indiscriminately to death as many as he could find all around, lest the king, surrounded by a troop of soldiers, be able to resist him in defense of his people.

At that time the king was staying far from the city in a village called in their language Hagislidun. A nearby body of water and a nearby wood were also called by the same name.

The most impious man reasoned—as the truth of the matter showed—that the more people his deadly agent could seize and bring to destruction in advance, the fewer would be gathered into the army to meet the king if battle had to be joined.

Nor did he dare leave the fleet without a strong force, because this Danish and Alan nation was accustomed to behave like evening wolves: secretly descending onto the open ground and returning as quickly as possible to familiar hiding places in the woods. Although it always sought to live by plunder, it never openly engaged an enemy in declared battle unless, after ambushing them, it had removed all hope of returning to the ships’ harbor.

VII. Therefore, exercising the greatest caution, he summoned one of his fellow soldiers and sent him to the king, who was free from such a tumult of cares, to discover the extent of his possessions. If the king refused to obey his savage commands, he was to seek to subdue him by torture, taking him unawares, as happened.

He himself, supported by a large retinue, followed at a slow pace and ordered the bearer of the wicked embassy, free from any danger of fear, to attack the unsuspecting king in these words:

“Your lord Inguar, king most invincible and feared by land and sea, has subjected diverse lands to himself by arms and has landed with many ships on the desired shore of this province, intending to winter here. Therefore he commands you to divide with him the ancient treasures and paternal wealth, and to reign under him.

“If you scorn his power, supported by countless legions, you shall be judged unworthy both of life and of your kingdom, to your own detriment. And who are you to dare insolently oppose such great power?

“The storm of the sea serves our oars, nor does it remove us from the purpose of our directed intent. Neither the immense roaring of heaven nor the frequent surges of the rivers have ever harmed us, with the elements’ favoring grace.

“Therefore be, with all your people, under this greatest ruler. The elements serve him because of his inborn clemency, for this most merciful man knows how to spare his subjects in every affair and to conquer the proud.”

VIII. When he heard this, the most holy king groaned with deep anguish of heart. He summoned one of his bishops, who served as his confidential adviser, and consulted him about what response he ought to make.

The bishop, fearful for the king’s life, urged him by many examples to consent. The king, however, bowed his head and fixing his eyes upon the ground, remained silent for a little while. At last he opened his lips and spoke:

“O bishop, we have lived to see what we have never feared! Behold, a barbarian foreigner threatens the ancient settlers of our kingdom with drawn sword, while the once-happy native, sighing and groaning, remains silent.

“If only everyone were now groaning while alive, so that they might not perish in bloody slaughter; then, even if I should fall, they could survive upon the sweet fields of their homeland and later return to the glory of their former happiness!”

The bishop replied:

“Whom do you wish to survive for their homeland, when the hostile sword has scarcely left anyone in the whole city? With axes blunted upon the corpses of your people, they are coming to bind you, deprived of soldiers, with leather thongs.

“Therefore, O king, half of my soul, unless you take precautions through the protection of flight or the ill-omened refuge of surrender, torturers will be here at once, and you will suffer punishment through their infamous service.”

To this the most blessed king replied:

“This is what I desire; this I place before all other wishes: not to survive my dearest faithful people, whom the savage pirate has destroyed by stealing their souls in their beds, together with their children and wives.

“And what do you advise? That, at the end of my life, abandoned by my own guard, I should bring disgrace upon our glory by fleeing? I have always avoided the slander of informing accusations and have never endured the reproach of abandoning my army, since it was honorable for me to die for my country. And now shall I become the voluntary betrayer of my people, when, because of the loss of those dear to me, life itself is loathsome?

“The almighty arbiter of all things stands as witness that no one, whether alive or dead, shall separate me from the love of Christ. In confessing him at baptism I received the ring of faith, renouncing Satan and all his pomp.

“Through this renunciation it came about that, for the praise and glory of the eternal Trinity, I was deemed worthy to be consecrated a third time, anointed with the chrism of sanctification for the sake of eternal life.

“First, I received the stole of the saving bath; second, through confirmation bestowed with the greater pontifical sign; third, when, amid the acclamation of you and the whole people, I assumed this passing power of kingship.

“Thus, thrice sprinkled with the oil of mystical consecration, I resolved to benefit the commonwealth of the English more than to rule it, refusing to submit my neck to any yoke except the service of God.

“Now, under a pretense of benevolence, that cunning man holds out the snare of his scheme, by which he intends to entangle Christ’s servant, especially since he promises what heavenly generosity has granted us.

“He offers life, of which I am not yet deprived; he promises a kingdom, which I possess; he wishes to confer riches, of which I have no need. For these things, then, should I now begin to serve two masters, when I have vowed before the present nobles to live under Christ alone and reign under Christ alone?”

IX. Then he turned to the man whom the most impious Inguar had sent to speak about the terms of the kingdom:

“Wet with the blood of my people, you have become worthy of the punishment of death. But, clearly following the example of my Christ, I do not wish to stain my pure hands; for, if it should so happen, I am gladly prepared to fall beneath your weapons for his name.

“Therefore return swiftly and carry these answers to your lord without delay:

“‘You imitate your father well, son of the devil. Swelling with pride, he fell from heaven, and, desiring through his lie to ensnare the human race, made many liable to his punishment.

“As his chief follower, you can neither frighten me with threats nor deceive me by luring me with the blandishments of a gentle destruction. You will find me unarmed according to Christ’s commands.

“Let your insatiable greed seize and consume the treasures and riches that merciful divinity has until now bestowed upon us. For even if you shatter this fleeting and fragile body like a clay vessel, true freedom of spirit will never be yours, even for a moment.

“It is more honorable to defend perpetual freedom, if not with weapons, then at least with one’s throat, than to demand its recovery through tearful complaints. For one man it is glorious to die, while for the other servile obstinacy stands opposed: since a servant ought to serve whatever conditions his master has imposed. If he rejects any of them, however unjust, he is judged guilty of treason and assigned servile punishments.

“Granted, the practice of this servitude is grievous; but more grievous is the wound that usually arises from such misfortune. For, as those who more frequently reason in attendance upon legal cases know, a conclusion follows from a combination of opposing propositions: if freedom is sought, there is no doubt that the master is injured by contempt.”

“Therefore, whether willingly or unwillingly, when my free spirit flies from its prison to heaven, it will be contaminated by no form of emancipation or alienation. A Dane shall never see a king diminished by decapitation survive to celebrate a triumph.

“You tempt me with the hope of kingship after killing all my people, as though I had such a fierce desire to reign that I would wish to rule over empty houses, without a noble inhabitant or precious furnishings.

“As your savage ferocity has begun, after the servants, let it tear the king from his throne, drag him away, spit upon him, strike him with blows, and finally slaughter him. The King of kings sees these things in pity and, as I believe, will transfer him to eternal life, where he will reign with him.

“Know, therefore, that for love of temporal life the Christian king Edmund will not submit to a pagan leader unless you first become a member of our religion. He prefers to be a standard-bearer in the camp of the eternal King.’”

X. The holy man had scarcely finished speaking, and the soldier who was to carry back the reply had scarcely stepped out of the house, when Inguar met him and ordered him, in brief words, to reveal everything concerning the king’s final secrets.

When the soldier reported these things, the tyrant ordered his entire troop to surround the interior and the king alone to be seized, since he now knew him to be rebellious against his laws.

Then the holy king Edmund, like a member of Christ, was seized in the palace after casting aside his weapons. He was bound and restrained with tighter chains, and, innocent, was brought before the impious leader, as Christ had been brought before Pilate the governor. He desired to follow the footsteps of him who was sacrificed as a victim for us.

Bound, he was mocked in many ways and at last, beaten with savage persistence, was led to a nearby tree. Tied to it, he was tormented for a very long time with cruel whips, yet was not overcome, continually invoking Christ in plaintive cries.

Therefore the adversaries, driven mad, pierced him throughout his body with arrows, as though in sport, as at a target. They multiplied the severity of his torment with repeated blows of the thongs, for they impressed wounds upon wounds while giving arrows a place among arrows.

Thus it happened that, pierced all around by the sharp points of the darts, he shuddered and writhed like a rough hedgehog or a thistle bristling with spines, resembling the outstanding martyr Sebastian in his passion.

When Inguar the forked one saw that even then the man did not yield to the torturers, but continually cried out to Christ, he immediately ordered the executioner to cut off his head.

The executioner hastily tore the half-dead man, whose vital warmth still throbbed in his warm breast, from the bloodied stake. Then—after the recesses of the ribs had been laid open by repeated pricks, as though he had been snatched from the rack or the savage claws of torturers—he ordered him to extend the head that had always been distinguished by a royal diadem. [The transmitted syntax is disordered.]

When the gentlest man stood there like a ram chosen from the whole flock, willing in a blessed exchange to trade worldly life, intent upon divine benefits, he was already refreshed by the vision of the inward light, which, placed in the contest, he desired to enjoy more fully.

Thus, while he was speaking words of prayer, one of the executioners seized a dagger and deprived him of this light with a single blow, decapitating him.

And so, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, Edmund, a holocaust most pleasing to God, exhausted by the fire of his Passion, entered, as king and martyr, the senate of the heavenly court with the palm of victory and the crown of righteousness.

XI. With such an end he completed, following the footsteps of Christ his Lord, the mortification of the cross which the king had continually borne in his body.

Christ, pure of crime, poured out blood upon the column to which he had been bound, not for himself but for us, leaving behind the marks of his scourging. Edmund, for the attainment of imperishable glory, suffered similar punishments upon a bloodstained stake.

Christ, perfect in life, most graciously endured the sharpness of the immense nails in his hands and feet to wipe away the rust of our sins. Edmund, for love of the Lord’s name, bristling with heavy arrows throughout his body and torn to the marrow by the harshness of his torments, remained steadfast in his confession and brought it to an end when he received the sentence of death.

The Danes, ministers of the devil, left his body mutilated and bristling with barbs. With their leader they carried away the holy head, which had not been anointed with the oil of the sinner but with the sacrament of a certain mystery, and, departing, hid it by throwing it farther away among the dense thickets of a wood called Hagdesdum.

They worked with every cunning to prevent the Christians—of whom they had scarcely left a few—from giving the martyr’s most sacred body, together with its head, an honorable burial according to the capacity of those who would bury it.

A certain member of our religion secretly witnessed this horrifying spectacle. Having, as we believe, been withdrawn from the swords of the pagans, he was preserved by divine providence so that the investigation of this matter might be revealed, although he had no knowledge at all of what had happened to the head, except that he had seen the Danish executioners enter the inner forest with it.

## XII

Therefore, as soon as some measure of peace had been restored to the churches, Christians began to emerge from their hiding places, diligently searching so that they might find the head of their king and martyr, reunite it with the body, and bury both again with fitting honor according to their means.

For when the pagans had departed and were everywhere engaged in devastation—particularly in the region of the Estranguli—the most holy body, still lying in the open, was very easily found in the same field where the king had fallen after completing the course of his struggle. Because of their ancient memory of his benefactions and the king’s innate clemency, people flocked freely from every direction and began sorrowfully to lament that they had been deprived of so great a part of his body.

To their minds heavenly benevolence offered encouragement after they had heard the useful testimony of the man who, as has been said, had witnessed so great a vision. A great multitude therefore gathered and searched in every direction through the pathless woods, to see whether they might happen upon the place where the holy man’s head lay.

For all truly wise people were convinced that the worshipers of another sect, envying our faith, had carried away the martyr’s head and had hidden it somewhere not far within the thick forest—either buried beneath a poor covering of turf, or left to be devoured by birds and wild beasts. After they had taken counsel, all hastened toward the search with equal zeal. Each person carried either a horn or a trumpet, so that, as they wandered around the whole area, they might signal one another by their voices or by the sound of the trumpets, lest they return to places already searched or abandon places not yet examined.

When this had been done, something happened that is marvelous to relate and unheard of throughout the ages. The head of the holy king, although far removed from its body, burst forth in a voice without the assistance of fibers or the service of the arteries within the chest. While many were slowly exploring the trackless places in the manner of gravediggers, the head, once it could be heard speaking, answered the voices of those encouraging one another and calling alternately, as companions to a companion, “Where are you?” It indicated the place by saying in the language of its homeland, “Her, her, her,” which the Latin tongue renders: “Here, here, here.”

It never ceased crying out and repeating the same words until it had drawn everyone to itself. The plectrum of the dead tongue quivered within the passages of the throat, revealing in itself the mighty deeds of the Word-begotten One, who fitted human speech to a braying she-ass in order to rebuke the prophet’s folly.

The Creator of all things attached another marvel to this one when he gave the head an extraordinary guardian from his heavenly treasury. For a huge wolf was found in that place by divine mercy. Embracing the sacred head between its forelegs, it lay prostrate on the ground and kept watch over the martyr. It permitted no beast to harm what had been entrusted to it; lying stretched upon the ground, it guarded the inviolable relic with even greater attentiveness, its voracity forgotten.

Those who had gathered and witnessed this were astonished. They declared the most blessed King and Martyr Eadmund to be like in merits to the man of desires, who, amid the gaping jaws of hungry lions, remained unharmed and despised the threats of those lying in wait.

## XIII

Taking up with unanimous devotion the pearl of inestimable value that they had found, they carried it back to its body amid abundant showers of joyful tears, blessing God with hymns and praises. The wolf, guardian and bearer of those same relics, followed them all the way to the place of burial.

Keeping close behind them and mourning as though for a lost trust, it harmed no one even when provoked and caused no one annoyance. It returned unharmed to the familiar secrets of its beloved solitude. After that, no wolf of such terrifying appearance was ever seen again in those places.

When at last it had withdrawn, those to whom the task had been entrusted fitted the head to the holy body with the greatest care and every exercise of ingenuity. For the time being, they placed both, joined together, in a suitable mausoleum.

At that place a basilica was subsequently built above it, in poor workmanship, and he remained buried there for many years. At last, when the fires of war had been completely extinguished and the violent storm of persecution had subsided, the religious devotion of the faithful began to breathe again, having been delivered from the pressures of tribulation.

When it found a suitable opportunity, it revealed in many works the devotion it felt toward the most blessed King and Martyr Eadmund. For the same saint, beneath the humble shelter of the consecrated house, repeatedly manifested through signs of miracles what merit he possessed before God.

Moved by these events, the population of that province—not only the common people but also the nobility—built an immense church in the royal settlement called in the English language Bedricesgueord (Beodricheswort), and in Latin Bedrici curtis, “Bedric’s court.” It was constructed with wonderful wooden paneling, and they transferred him there with great glory, as was fitting.

## XIV

But—marvelous to relate!—although the martyr’s precious body was thought to have putrefied because of the long passage of time, it was found so sound and whole that, not only had the head been restored and joined to the body, but no wound or scar whatsoever appeared upon it.

Thus the holy king and martyr Eadmund, worthy of reverent mention, whole and exceedingly like a living man, was transferred to the aforesaid place. There he still awaits, in the same form, the blessed joys of the resurrection that have been promised.

Only on his neck, as a sign of martyrdom, one exceedingly fine red line appeared in the form of a scarlet thread. A woman of blessed memory named Osuven was accustomed to testify to this. Shortly before our own times, she spent many years beside his sacred tomb, occupied with fasting and prayers.

With regard to this venerable woman, whether through divine revelation or excessive devotion, the following custom grew up: whenever the sepulchre of the blessed martyr was opened, every year on the Lord’s Supper she would cut off his hair and nails. She carefully gathered all these things and stored them in a little casket. As long as she lived, she did not neglect to venerate them with extraordinary affection, placing them upon the altar of the same church, where they are still preserved with the honor due to them.

## XV

The religious bishop Theodredus, of the same province, also of blessed memory and called “the Good” because of the excellence of his merits, learned by the following experience what we have said concerning the incorruption of the holy king.

As we began to relate, many religious people had contributed numerous gifts to the aforesaid place, suitable for the burial of the martyr, including ornaments of the greatest value in gold and silver. Some men of evil mind, utterly forgetful of every good thing, attempted under cover of night to break into the same basilica for the purpose of robbery.

There were eight of them. Without any reverence for the saint, they had resolved to satisfy their mad desire by secretly carrying off whatever they found useful within the enclosure of the monastery. Accordingly, they took machines and every kind of tool they needed to accomplish the deed. One night they undertook the crime they had planned, and, standing in the church courtyard, each applied himself to the evil he had conceived by a different method.

One placed a ladder against the doors so that he might enter through an inserted window; another worked at the bolt or latch with a file or a smith’s hammer; others attempted to undermine the wall with mattocks and spades.

When the work had been arranged and each man strove competitively with all the strength he possessed, the holy martyr bound them in the very act of attempting it. They could neither move their feet from the spot nor abandon the task they had undertaken. One hung high in the air with his ladder; another remained openly bent over as a digger, although he had come secretly to perform this work.

Meanwhile, one of the matricularii, who was lying inside the basilica, was awakened from sleep. Yet he remained unwillingly prostrate upon his bed, for the power of the martyr had bound him in his effort, lest he, who was close at hand, should encounter these marvelous events, and the repeated sound of the disturbance should strike the inner ears of the watchman.

But what need is there to say that he could not rise, when he could not even break into speech?

At last, when morning came, the thieves still persisted in the work they had begun. They were seized by many people and handed over to tighter bonds, and finally were brought before the judgment of the aforesaid holy bishop Theodredus.

He pronounced a sentence without reflection, and afterward regretted throughout the whole of his life that he had issued it. For he ordered all of them to be fastened to gallows at once, because they had dared to enter secretly the courtyard of Saint Eadmund the martyr.

He did not call to mind what the Lord warns through the prophet: “Do not cease rescuing those who are led away to death” (Prov. 24:11). Nor did he remember the deed of the prophet Elisha, who fed the raiders from Samaria with bread and water and sent them back to their own people, saying to the king, who wished to strike them immediately, that he had not captured them with his sword and bow (IV Kings 6:22).

Nor did he remember the command of the Apostle, which says: “If you have secular lawsuits, appoint as judges those who are contemptible in the Church,” that is, secular men (I Cor. 6:4).

For this reason the authority of the canons forbids any bishop, or anyone from the clergy, to perform the office of informer, since it is exceedingly disgraceful for ministers of heavenly life to consent to the death of any human being.

Accordingly, the aforesaid bishop came to his senses and grieved deeply. Imposing penance upon himself, he devoted himself for a long time to heavy lamentation.

When this penance had finally been completed, he instructed the people of his diocese. By instructing them he summoned them; by summoning them he humbly persuaded them to remove and turn away the anger of divine indignation through a three-day fast. He hoped that the Lord, appeased by the sacrifice of a contrite spirit, would grant him his grace, so that he might dare to touch and lift the body of the blessed martyr, which, although it had flourished with such great virtues in the world, was still contained in a humble and unsuitable mausoleum.

And so it happened. He found the body of the most holy king—previously torn apart and mutilated—united and incorrupt, as we have already related. He touched it, washed it, and once again placed it, clothed in new and excellent garments, in a wooden chest, blessing God, who is wondrous in his saints and glorious in all his works (Psalm LXVIII).

## XVI

It is not burdensome to relate the story of a man of great power named Leofustan. Unable to restrain the impulse of his youthful age, he plunged into such a disgrace through wantonness that, relying on the authority of his singular power, he ordered the body of so great a martyr to be shown to him.

Although many people, especially his own retainers, tried to prevent him, his command prevailed, for, because of the arrogance of his nobility, he was a source of terror to everyone.

When the chest had been opened, he stood there and looked. At that very moment God turned him over to a debased mind and drove him into madness (Rom. 1:28). Through his punishment he learned that he had presumed to do what was not permitted.

When his father heard this, a deeply religious man named Alfgarus, he was horrified at the most shameful deed, gave thanks to the martyr, and removed his son from his presence. The son was eventually reduced to the greatest poverty and ended his life by God’s judgment, consumed by worms.

Thus the holy King and Martyr Eadmund made it known to everyone that he was not inferior in merit to the blessed levite and martyr Lawrence. As the blessed Father Gregory relates, when some worthy and unworthy people attempted to lift Lawrence’s body, seven of them suddenly died on the spot.

O how worthy of reverence that place has proved to be, since beneath the appearance of one who sleeps it contains so great a witness of Christ, and in it such great miracles occur—and are reported to have occurred—as we have nowhere else heard of among the English in our own time!

I pass over these miracles for the sake of brevity, lest I incur the displeasure of some tedious person by becoming more prolix than is proper. I believe that what has been said can suffice for the ardent desire of those who, apart from God, prefer nothing to the patronage of this martyr.

It is established concerning him, as concerning all the other saints now reigning with Christ, that although his soul is in heavenly glory, he is not far removed, through visitation, day and night, from the presence of the body with which he earned the joys of blessed immortality that he now enjoys.

For, while in the eternal homeland he is joined to Him who is wholly present everywhere, he has from Him the power to do whatever he wills, except only for that which he desires with tireless longing: to be clothed through the resurrection in the garment of transformed flesh. For then the blessedness of the saints will be perfect, when, by Christ’s gift, that state has been attained.

## XVII

From this holy martyr it is possible to estimate what holiness he possesses in this life, since his dead flesh displays a certain glory of resurrection without any defilement of its own.

Catholic Fathers, in their brief accounts, exalt those who have been granted such a gift because of the singular privilege achieved through virginity. They say that, by just recompense, even here they rejoice unusually in the incorruption of the flesh—those who preserved it until death, not without the powerful persecution of continual martyrdom.

For what is greater, under the charity of Christian faith, than for a human being by grace to attain what an angel possesses by nature?

Therefore the divine oracle promises, as a singular gift, that virgins will follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev. 14:4).

We must therefore consider who this man was who, at the height of kingship, amid so many riches and luxuries of the world, strove to conquer himself by trampling down wantonness—as his incorrupt flesh demonstrates.

Let those who serve him with human devotion strive to please him with the purity that his incorrupt limbs plainly show to have pleased him perpetually; and if they cannot do so with the virginal flower of chastity, then at least through the continual mortification of pleasures they have experienced.

For if that invisible and unlocatable presence of the holy soul should be offended by the filthiness of any of its servants, we must fear what the prophet terribly threatens: “In the land of the saints he has acted wickedly, and therefore he shall not see the glory of the Lord” (Isa. 26:10).

Moved by terror of this sentence, let us implore the patronage of this holy King and Martyr Eadmund, so that he may cleanse us, together with those who serve him worthily, from the sins by which we deserve punishment; through him who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## [Col. 0519]

## The Acrostic Poem of Saint Abbo to the Emperor Otto

*(In Fabricius, Bibliotheca Latina, vol. III, book IV, chapter 1.)*

**Otto, valiant Caesar, give place to our poetic buskin.**

Blessed in your ancestors, as many as the stars shine in heaven.  
The Saxon has accepted you as lord, and Rome has marked you.  
The world itself receives you, content with its sole fosterling.  
By the titles of your virtues you are recognized as an active man.  
A conqueror of your country and a pursuer of peace at court.  
A light flashing everywhere, a radiance shining like the sun.  
Therefore, by God’s kindness, the customary sacred things shall be restored;  
nor shall any virtue be lacking by which grace climbs the summit  
and, through hidden causes, [lacuna] pardon.  
Certainly we all, Caesar, unknown to you even now,  
[know] what land, rich in grain, awaits the Austrasians,  
and what fruitful soil is sufficiently abundant in harvest,  
dear to the greatest men and full of fierce cultivators.  
May the Ishmaelite not be absent from his father’s rule,  
when the skilful ruler governed, reigning as emperor.  
Now, Augustus, I shall set forth your venerable name.

**Otto, valiant Caesar, give place to our poetic buskin.**

For he alone reigns while absent, O heir of Caesar,  
wholly like his grandfather, if new life restores you.  
That king was mighty, a lover of Roman law,  
the entire glory of his homeland, born of an ancestral throne.  
There were times of peace while he flourished under such rule.  
So great a man was he whom I have undertaken to describe in verse.  
Why then do you restrain your birthright, and why now  
do you defer amid an exile’s wars the pious ceremonial honors due?  
While I, the good poet, desire that this wondrous gift be bestowed,  
you will enlarge the work, yourself hence responsive to mine.  
Caesar, that, diminished by an invincible shield and from this  
made more useful to all, you may be granted a marvellous triumph beforehand;  
terrible yet merciful, he smiled beneath a secure diadem.  
The illustrious countenance of your grandfather and father is clothed upon you.  
Again each was a victor under a dreadful time.  
Now, living, you are one worthy name with your father.

**Otto, valiant Caesar, give place to our poetic buskin.**

## [Grammatical Questions]

## [Col. 0521]

### Notice concerning the following booklet and Saint Abbo’s journey to England

*(In Mabillon, Annales Benedictini, book XLIX, vol. IV, p. 29.)*

“An embassy of the English people was sent to the monastery of Fleury to ask for one of the wise men who might instruct the English monks in piety and letters.

Aimon says in his book On the Life of Saint Abbo that this happened for two reasons. The first was that blessed Gregory, when he sent preachers to that people to convert them to the faith of Christ, especially urged them to observe the rule of the beloved Lord Benedict.

The second was that a man of great nobility named Oswald, despising the world, turned to serve Christ in the aforesaid monastery of Fleury. Because of the merit of his good life, he was raised by the king of that province to the rank of archbishop, and in the English region he built a monastery for God and his patron Saint Benedict—namely, Ramsey, which had been founded by the aforesaid Oswald, archbishop of York. It was therefore from that monastery that the envoys just mentioned were sent.

They arrived at Fleury when Oilboldus first assumed the office of prefect. He persuaded his monk Abbo—then a deacon—not so much by commanding authority as by gentle words, not to avoid the task of instructing the people of that nation, since Abbo possessed great skill in divine and human letters.

Abbo, accustomed to obedience, immediately complied with the will of his abbot. He rejected the malicious counsels of certain whisperers, who secretly suggested that their abbot wished by evil deceit to drive him overseas so that he would never be able to return.

But the magnificent preparations for the journey that Oilboldus supplied to Abbo at his departure showed that the matter was quite otherwise. This was confirmed especially by Abbo’s return to Gaul, since Oilboldus himself recalled him from England after two years.

On that journey, when they had reached the Morini, who are separated from the English by a very narrow strait, Abbo was forced to remain there for almost a month while the sailors hesitated to cross because of the rough sea.

Wearied by the boredom of such a long delay, he warned and encouraged a certain monk named Riculeus, who was in charge of escorting the envoys, that they should pray together to the Lord. If the Lord did not disapprove of their plan, he should deign to prosper their journey; but if he did not approve it, he should inspire them with the desire to return to their own country.

Without delay, after the evening service, both threw themselves upon the ground in prayer.

God, in his mercy, granted their prayers. At the first twilight of the following day, a message from the shipmaster arrived, loudly calling them to cross. They immediately boarded the ship. When they had gone out to sea, accompanied by eight other ships, marsuppae [a marine creature; the term is uncertain], porpoise-fish playing in the waves, and whales raising their backs like enormous roofs suddenly appeared.

When Abbo learned from the sailors that all these were signs of an approaching storm, he immediately returned to the accustomed protection of prayer and obtained what he asked. For when the storm arose, his ship and the two others following it were carried unharmed into port. The remaining six, together with the people in them, were battered by the storms and the thrusts of the fish and perished.

The Lord deigned to perform this sign through him while he was still serving in the office of levite.

At last he entered the land of the English and went to the monastery of Ramsey, which was governed by an abbot named Germanus, who had been taken from the monastery of Fleury. Abbo remained there for two years and instructed certain monks of the place in literary knowledge.

During this period the man of God won great esteem. He was especially welcome to the leading men of the kingdom, above all to the most holy archbishops Oswald and Dunstan, who competed with one another to retain him among themselves.

While he was staying there, his disciples consulted him about certain small grammatical questions, and he wrote them an answer. Since it is absent from the printed editions, it must be presented here from the Peleterian manuscript.

The questions are put to Abbo below, followed by his own answers. In these he praises God’s *Palinodia*, composed by Hilary, bishop of Poitiers—that is, the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*, attributed to Augustine—which Abbo assigns to Saint Hilary.”

## [Col. 0521]

# Grammatical Questions of Saint Abbo, Abbot of Fleury

*(Mai, Classici Auctores, V, 329.)*

### Notice

“This little work comes from a royal Vatican manuscript whose age appears to be nearly contemporary with the author himself.

Mabillon published a very brief portion of this work in the *Annales Benedictini*, vol. IV, appendix, p. 631. But since by far the greater part had until now remained unpublished, I present it here.”

## [Col. 0521]

### 1

“To the most beloved brothers in Christ, the English—especially those who regularly live in the monastery of the holy Father Benedict under the school of virtues—from the monastery of Fleury, the same Father’s little servant, Abbo, a Frank by birth, a monk by profession, a deacon by office: the gift of perpetual salvation in him who is essentially good.

The omnipotence of the divine majesty, which changes and orders the times, has permitted me, from the beginning of my life, to be tested in many ways and by various means, according to its will, until the strength of youth became accustomed to adversities, and misfortune in the form of exile eventually increased that strength as a final addition to virtue.

Although, by God’s agency, I endure this among so many men of religious life who, as I infer from their actions, love me as they love themselves, I cannot recall without pain—and therefore not with the fulfillment of my desire—that I am now deprived of the bodily presence of my spiritual fosterling, whose presence once seemed sweeter to me than life itself.

Now, since this has happened through obedience, which is better than sacrifices, I desire not only to serve the commands of the brothers with whom I live, but also, according to the measure of my small ability, to benefit the people of this island. For it is clear that by no accident but under divine governance I came, after the waves of the sea-storm had been calmed, to this exile across so vast an expanse of ocean with wonderful tranquility.

While I am detained here by certain scholarly occupations, the misery of the calamity I endure is lightened, since the goodwill of those with whom I live compels me not only to wish, as far as I can, to assist the needs of the brothers, but even to wish to do so beyond my strength.

Therefore I have resolved to answer the questions put to me by all those living among the English, wherever they may be, so that you, dearest brothers, may have some memorials of your exile, upon which you may exercise the acuity of your trained minds.

Nor will I deprive you of questions answered, which all manner of students raise either by testing or by speaking. And even if some rival objects to me, ‘Do not carry wood into the forest,’ I am nevertheless certain that the barrenness or poverty of your intellect is not unworthy of the abundance of my banquet, which is offered in this form.”

### 2

“In the first question it was asked whether the penultimate syllable of *salubris* should be said or considered short or long. I presented to them what I had certainly read in the ancient authorities on the Latin language, and, lest these matters slip from your memory, I also set them down in writing.

First of all, Donatus says that in words of three syllables, four syllables, and more, if the penultimate syllable is long by position, it receives the acute accent and the antepenultimate is pronounced with the grave accent, as in *Catellus* and *Metellus*. This applies when the syllable is long by position, but not when the long position arises from a mute and a liquid; in that case the accent changes, as in *latebrae* and *tenebrae*.

From this it has become established that if the penultimate syllable of any word ends in a short vowel followed by two consonants, the first a mute and the second a liquid, that word—whether of three or four syllables—will never receive the accent on the penultimate. Rather, the accent shifts to the antepenultimate, although in poetry either practice may be permitted according to the poet’s will.

For if such words are verbal feminines, or any others naturally long, they cannot in any way be shortened because of a mute and a liquid. This is what the attached condition means: if such a syllable is long by position, the accent is shifted to the antepenultimate.”

### 3

“But some people hold that the penultimate syllables in the examples are long by nature. They think the words are derived from second-conjugation verbs, specifically from the second-person imperative, which is long: *teneo, tenes, tene, tenebrae*; *lateo, lates, late, latebrae*. The accent therefore does not shift before the penultimate.

They likewise think that forms from first-conjugation verbs arise in the same way: *lavo, lavas, lava, lavacrum*; *aratrum*; *ventilabrum*. From the third conjugation they derive *terebrum* and similar forms.

They pronounce these in the same way without any rule, whether they are Greek or Latin: *theatrum, feretrum, pharetra, cathedra*. If the penultimate syllables of all these nouns and similar words are long by nature, they cannot even be shortened in meter.

But Donatus proves that what precedes is false; therefore what follows is also false.

Those words similar to these that lose one letter through syncope always preserve, according to Martianus, the accent they previously had in the same syllable, as in *manipulus, maniplus* and *venabulum, venablum*.

Finally, concerning words formed from nouns, Priscian states that the final letter of the primitive nominative is sometimes removed and *-bris* is added, as in *mulier, muliebris* and *salus, salubris*. The ancient form *saluber* in the nominative is also shown by this verse:

> Phoebe saluber ades.  
> Healthy Phoebus, be present.

From this it may be inferred that its penultimate is quite regularly long, since only the form derived from the long nominative is retained.

I do not remember ever having read a syllable that is naturally long shortened in meter, except through the figure called systole—apart from cases in which a vowel before another vowel is lengthened, as in *illius, unius, diei, speciei*.

Indeed, verbal feminines whose penultimate syllables are long, as I said above, will in no way be found with their final syllable shortened, since they have *t* before *-rix*, from the past participle ending in *-tus*.”

### 4

“I shall show you the rules governing the verbal forms derived from these words.

With the exception of four participles—*satus, ratus, status, datus*—all the remaining participles that have *a* before *-tus* in the past are lengthened, as in *amatus*, from which come *amator* and *amatrix*.

Participles with *e* before *-tus* are also found lengthened, such as *recensetus*. Thus Prudentius writes in the *Passion of the Martyr Hippolytus*:

> Cumque recensetis constaret partibus ille.  
> And when that man was evident in his renewed parts.

If a participle has *i* before *-tus*, its penultimate is everywhere shortened, unless it comes from a fourth-conjugation verb, as in *domo, domas, domitus*; *moneo, mones, monitus*; *audio, audis, auditus*; *condo, condis, conditus*. Hence the masculine forms *domitor, monitor, auditor, conditor*, and from them the feminine forms *domitrix, monitrix, auditrix, conditrix*.

In the third conjugation, *oblitus, quaesitus, tritus, petitus,* and *cupitus* are lengthened, together with forms compounded from them. It must nevertheless be noted that *oblitus* is shortened when it is compounded from the verb *lino*.

In the fourth conjugation only two forms are shortened, namely *queo* and *eo*, together with forms compounded from them: *eo, itus; exeo, exitus*. I have not read verbal forms derived from these.

Finally, if the same past form has *u* before *-tus*, its penultimate is short when it is compounded from the verb *ruo*: *eruo, erutus; obruo, obrutus*. In all other cases it is long: *induo, indutus; exuo, exutus; adjuvo, adjutus*, whence *adjutor* and *adjutrix*.

If *o* occurs before *-tus*, it is always long: *moveo, motus; foveo, fotus; lavo, lotus*, and *lautus* behaves likewise.

From these rules you can finally understand that naturally long penultimate syllables are not shortened by metrical necessity because of a mute and a liquid, since all such syllables can be lengthened when naturally short.

Therefore I advise you to attend to the rules of Donatus and especially Priscian rather than to the sudden inventions of younger men. In prose, pronounce *candelabrum, delubrum, aratrum, lavacrum* and similar forms with a shortened penultimate, except for those that have been excluded, and for the one noun *October*, so that afterward you may lengthen them when metrical necessity requires it.”

### 5

“You asked with what accent the genitive of *mulier* should be pronounced. You should know that although its penultimate is short, it is customarily accented for the sake of euphony, just as with the verbs *calefacio, calefacis*.

Since every disyllabic noun and every longer noun ending in *-er* is shortened, if its genitive exceeds two syllables, it always shortens the penultimate, unless there is position or the penultimate of the nominative is naturally long, as in *October, saluber, equester*.

Concerning the pronoun *alter, alterius*, as some prefer to classify it: although it follows the rule of pronouns ending in *-ius*, which lengthen the penultimate in prose, this word alone is excepted because its genitive has only two syllables more than its nominative.

You should also know that in the fifth declension the penultimate of the trisyllabic genitive of *fides, fidei* is shortened in prose, because it does not have *i* before *e*, as the other trisyllabic genitives of the fifth declension do.”

### 6

“Concerning the verbs *irrito, assevero, persevero, radico* and the compound *eradico*, as well as *relego, allego, instigo,* and *subrepo*, note that their penultimate syllables are always long.

Of *irrito* Virgil says in Book X:

> Irritatque virum telis et voce lacessit.  
> He provokes the man with weapons and challenges him with his voice.

Some people read this corruptly as *irritat atque virum telis*. That cannot be correct, as the position of the prepositive conjunction shows.

The same Virgil writes in Book IV:

> Illam terra parens ira irritata deorum.  
> Her, the mother earth, provoked by anger against the gods.

Nor should it trouble you that we pronounce *irritus, irrita, irritum* with a shortened penultimate. Virgil has the following in Book V:

> Ante locum et variis assultibus irritus urget.  
> He presses before the place, ineffectual, with various assaults.

And in Book X:

> Irrita deflexit partim stringentia corpus.  
> In vain he turned aside the weapons partly grazing his body.

That *assevero* is a ditrochee, as is *persevero*, can be recognized from the noun *severus*, from which it appears to be derived. *Severus* is an amphibrach, as Prudentius testifies in the *Psychomachia*:

> Fronte severus adhuc, et multo funere anhelus.  
> Still stern in countenance and breathless from much slaughter.

Concerning *radico*, you should know that verbs are formed from the oblique case of neuter nouns in the following way: *munus, muneris, munero, muneras*; *decus, decoris, decoro, decoras*. Hence Horace writes:

> Ac bene nummatum decorat suadela Venusque.  
> Persuasion and Venus adorn the man well supplied with money.

The same applies to *index, indicis; indico, indicas*; *fornix, fornicis; fornico, fornicar*; *cornix, cornicis; cornico, cornicar*. Hence Persius writes:

> Nescio quid tecum grave cornicaris inepte.  
> I do not know what serious nonsense you are croaking with yourself.

Likewise *radix, radicis; radico, radicas*. Hence the verse:

> Radicet altis sensibus.  
> May it take root in deep feelings.

This is an iambic dimeter, which in the Ambrosian hymns [Note: [Col. 0525D] that is, in the hymns.] is always content in the first foot with either an iamb or a spondee.

The authority of Phocas led people to think that its penultimate should be shortened, since he includes the noun among the shortened forms, although it can be found everywhere with a long penultimate, as in Virgil:

> Aut Ida in magna radicibus eruta pinus.  
> Or a pine uprooted by its roots on great Ida.

Of the four words I have mentioned, two shorten the penultimate of their genitive: *index* and *fornix*; two lengthen it: *cornix* and *radix*.

As for *relego* and *allego*, note that if they are taken from a first-conjugation verb, their penultimate is always long. But if they belong to the third conjugation, they admit shortening [Note: [Col. 0526D] the manuscript reads “lengthening”], as in:

> Unde est, culpam releget lubricam.  
> From which it is that he may banish slippery guilt.

This too is an iambic dimeter, whose second foot always claims an iamb.

For *lego, legas*, meaning ‘to perform a legation,’ the *e* is long, whence *legatus*, ‘sent.’ But *lego, legis*, in every other meaning, is shortened, as is *ligo, ligas*, whence *religatus*, that is, ‘bound again.’

Virgil shows how *instigo* should be pronounced in Book V:

> Instigant studiis, resonat clamoribus aether.  
> They spur them on with zeal; the sky echoes with their cries.

The same applies to *investigo, castigo,* and *inspico*.

*Subrepo* too is lengthened if it is compounded from the verb *repo*; but if it comes from *rapio*, it is shortened. The former has the past form *subrepsi*, while the latter has *subripui*.”

### 7

“*Exaro* and *denoto* shorten their penultimates, as in Virgil’s first *Georgic*:

> Nudus ara, sere nudus.  
> Plough naked; sow naked.

And Horace:

> Paterna rura bobus exarat suis.  
> He ploughs his ancestral fields with his oxen.

This verse is a wholly iambic iambic trimeter, composed entirely of iambs.

*Demeto* and *demoror* have shortened penultimates. Horace writes:

> Accidit ut quidam testes caudamque salacem  
> demeteret ferro.  
> It happened that someone cut off with iron the testicles and the wanton tail.

Virgil has in Book X:

> Turne sed infelix Teucros quid demoror armis.  
> Turnus, unhappy man, why do I delay the Teucrians with weapons?

Concerning *exhalo*, Lucan writes in Book IV:

> Exhalat nebulas quidquid concrescere primus.  
> Whatever first condensed, it exhales mists.

Concerning *mano*, Virgil writes in Book III:

> Tum gelidus toto manabat corpore sudor.  
> Then cold sweat poured from his whole body.

Concerning *infidus* and *Getulus*, Lucan writes in Book IV:

> Infidusque novis ducibus dubiusque priori.  
> Treacherous toward the new leaders and doubtful of the former.

And:

> Inculto Getulus equus.  
> The Getulian horse in the uncultivated land.

*Diffidit* and *discidit*, when compounded from *findo* or *scindo*, shorten their penultimates. Horace writes:

> Diffidit urbium  
> portas vir Macedo, et subruit aemulos.  
> The Macedonian man split open the gates of cities and overthrew his rivals.

*Diffidit urbium* is a choriamb followed by a pyrrhic; what follows is an Asclepiad verse.

The same Horace writes in a glyconic verse:

> Nequidquam Deus abscidit.  
> In vain has God cut off.”

## [Col. 0527]

8. Nor are you unaware that all past participles ending in *-sus* lengthen their penultimate syllable and derive from verbs of the second and third conjugations. From the second-person present form one can determine whether the penultimate syllable of the corresponding participle is long by nature or by position: unless the penultimate syllable of that second-person form is long by position, it will never be so in the aforementioned participle. The exceptions are *sedeo, fodio, quatio, patior, pateo, careo, maneo,* and *cedo* in the sense “I give a place,” together with compounds formed from them.

The following are lengthened by position: *mordeo, morsus*; *findo, fissus*. By nature, however, the following are lengthened: *caedo, caesus*; *fido, fisus*; and many others. I have therefore set these out so that you may distinguish them not only in writing but also in sound: *fisum* and *fissum*, *caesum* and *cessum*, *ferum* and *ferrum*, *pyrum* and *Pyrrhum*, and any similar forms. For every consonant repeated in the middle of a word sounds stronger than when it is single.

But *s*, when it stands alone in the middle of a word, never closes a syllable before a following consonant—just as neither *c* nor *p* does, unless those letters precede themselves—and is everywhere pronounced so lightly that among the Greeks, according to Priscian, an aspiration is sometimes written in its place: ἥμισυ (*hēmĭsy*) for *semis*, ἓξ (*hex*) for *sex*, ἑπτὰ (*hepta*) for *septem*. Between two words also, when *s* comes first, as in *Deus summus*, so that there may not be too much hissing, the first *s* loses its sound; in that position, when followed by a vowel, it sometimes produces synaloepha. Virgil, in Book XII:

> *Inter se coiisse viros, et decernere ferro.*  
> “To have come together among themselves and contend with iron.”

By contrast, that canine letter *r* always sounds harsh, except when, in the middle of a word, it begins a syllable after a vowel.

9. Concerning the mute consonants, which can terminate any syllable or part of a word in every language, it may generally be said that those who assign them at the ends of words the same sound which they can have when they precede themselves are quite right. Examples are *Obbaob, Job, occidit, haec, illac, addo, ad, illud, agger, Agag, merop, attinet, amat,* and *docet*.

But *t*, in the same syllable when preceded by a consonant, is distinctly sounded, as in *fest* and *est*; and sometimes it is so sounded without a preceding consonant to mark a distinction, especially when a vowel follows in the next word. Since the human breath makes three of these letters light without aspiration and harsh with aspiration—namely *c, p,* and *t*—while the remaining three occupy the middle position among the medial sounds in words, we pronounce them with the sound of the light letters when they occur at the ends of words. This is not surprising, since there is such proximity between these letters and the others that, for the sound of *c* and *g*, the tongue’s plectrum strikes the palate almost identically; for the sound of *p* and *b*, the movement of the lips makes the impact scarcely distinguishable; and for the sound of *t* and *d*, the tongue’s tip rebounds from the teeth with very little difference. Thus these letters can even be found written by themselves, since we say *quingenti* for *quincenti*, *actus* for *agtus*, *scriptus* for *scribtus*, and *attinet* for *adtinet*, along with very many similar forms.

10. It is therefore clear from what has been said that *c* and *g* are pronounced almost alike before any vowel. But it is well known that, before the three vowels *a, o,* and *u*, they sound in the throat.

When *e* or *i* follows the letter *c* in the same syllable, it is usually pronounced in three ways. Sometimes it almost appears to sound like *g*, especially when preceded by *s*, as in *suscipio, suscepi, suscepit*. Sometimes it is pronounced with a kind of hissing, as though an *s* were attached to it, as in *cujus* and *coepit*. This occurs especially where *t* is pronounced with the sound of *z* at the beginning of a syllable, as in *laetitia* and *justitia*.

Finally, those who add a third manner of pronunciation decree that these same syllables should be pronounced with the sound of *que* or *qui*, producing *susquipio* for *suscipio*, *susquepit* for *suscepit*, and *quivis* for *civis*. How frivolous this is will be clear to every truly wise person. For why do the Latins consistently write *sequor, sequeris* or *sequere, sequitur*, rather than *secor, seceris* or *secere, secitur*, when *secutus* derives from it? And why do they write *qui, cujus*, or *quae, cujus*, changing the first letters of the nominative and genitive, if, as these chatterers claim, *ce* and *ci* have the sound of *que* and *qui*—especially when *g*, which is extremely similar to that letter, is distinguished by a change of vowel?

Thus we say *vinco, vinci, vince, vincam*, changing the sound along with the vowels, just as we say *lego, legi, lege, legam*. If anyone makes the same alteration after *g*, we thereby expose his conspicuous ignorance. It is foolish to say *pingue* for *pinge*, *lingue* for *linge*, and, as Servius maintains in the ninth book of the *Aeneid*, *ungue* for *unge*; hence he also says that *ungentum* is written without *u* when it contains *g*.

Likewise, *q* has a thick sound only when *v* is attached to it before another vowel. Once that *v* is removed, *g* remains, but *q* cannot remain; indeed, it changes into *c* as soon as it loses *u* before another vowel, as in *sequor, secutus*.

11. Finally, since all consonants, and especially the mutes, lie like a lifeless body until the individual vowels animate and move them according to their own will, it is certain that the Romans sometimes judge certain letters to be superfluous because they lack this movement, such as *h, k,* and *q*. Yet *k* and *q* differ from *c* in form and name, although they agree with it in vocal sound through *a* and *u*. As for *h*, which is useful only for meter, we always place it before vowels without any sound wherever it seems it ought to be written; with consonants to which it should be attached, we place it afterward, so that it may proceed from a fuller breath within.

There is one semivowel, *r*, and three mutes which are aspirated, as has been said. No one doubts the sound of any of them, except perhaps when a mark of aspiration is inserted between *c* and *e* or *i*, as in *Chereas* and *parrochia*. On this matter it should be known that, as we learn from Latin manuscripts, when our interpreters incorporated Greek words into Latin and represented a Greek *kappa* with their own letter *c*, they changed the sound along with the spelling, in accordance with the properties of each language. Thus Κύρος (*Kýros*) becomes *Cyrus*, κοινὸν (*koinon*) becomes *coena*, and κῆρας (*kēras*) gives *primicerius*. This is not surprising, since Θεὸς (*Theos*) is changed and pronounced *Deus*. Likewise πορφύριος (*porphyrios*) becomes *purpureus*.

When our writers use *ch* for χ (*chi*), just as they use *ph* for φ (*phi*) and *th* for θ (*theta*) in certain words, it is certain that these words are not Latin. We therefore pronounce them with the sounds of the Greek letters, although some, deceived by the similarity of the written forms, pronounce *x* for χ and say *arxe* for ἄρχη (*archē*), and *maxaera* for μαχαίρα (*machaira*).

Accordingly, when Χηρηας (*Chēreas*) is written in Greek, it is pronounced as though it were written *Kereas*, and παροιχία (*paroichia*) as though it were *parroechia*. Yet *sigma* changes this sound when it is placed before χ, as in σχῆμα (*schēma*). The letter *s* preserves this force among the Latins as well. Among them, *ti* is always pronounced with the sound of *ci* when a vowel follows it in the next syllable, unless *s* itself precedes it, as in *lectio, quaestio, testium, legentium*.

[Note: Hence the mixed spellings *otium, ocium*; *vitium, vicium*, and so forth.]

The ancients also doubled *s* for the letter *z*. Wherever this occurs at the end of a word’s final syllable, its penultimate syllable is lengthened in prose, although in verse it is treated as common.

12. Concerning the letter *g*, know that if *u* does not follow it, it is not made thick by a diphthong, as in *lagoena* and *tragoedia*. But you, Englishmen, can clearly perceive the aspirates: they have the sound of your own letter, and you more often write *b* for θ (*theta*), just as you pronounce *l* for the digamma.

Before a consonant in the same syllable one also finds *par sest* for *pars est*, and *feli xes* for *felix es*. Do not overlook that *pupugit* and *tutudit* have short penultimate syllables.

From *tundo*, *tunsus* loses its *n* in composition, producing *obtusus* and *retusus*, just as *nanciscor* produces *nactus*. *Dissero* likewise loses its *s* in the past tense, producing *disertus*. Horace:

> *Fecundi calices quem non facere disertum*  
> “Abundant cups—whom do they not make eloquent?”

Priscian states that the past tense of *cedo* is written in the same way as that of *cado*, namely *cecidi*. He teaches that all verbs which grow in their past forms repeat not only the first consonant but also the first vowel of the first syllable.

13. Finally, it must be said that one must carefully avoid the collision that tends to occur either in pronunciation or in writing, as in *ve [lacuna] t rex* [Note: Several words have been lost because the membrane of the codex was cut away.], for the present-tense form of *venit* and for the first as well as the second syllable of its past tense, unless the first vowel of the present tense is *a*. Thus: *tendo, tetendi*; *posco, poposci*; *tundo, tutundi*; except *pello, pepuli* and *spondeo, spopondi*.

For when the present tense contains the letter *a*, the first syllable of the past tense always ends in *c*; the second syllable, however, is sometimes *e* lengthened and sometimes *i* shortened, as in *fallo, fefelli*; *parco, peperci*; *tango, tetigi*; *cano, cecini*. By analogy, *cedo* ought to have produced *cecidi*, but by the authority of the ancients only the penultimate diphthong is changed into a lengthened *i*, while the preceding syllable remains short—having grown before it—as in all past forms of this kind.

Regarding these forms generally, one must observe that, when they are compounded according to the discretion of scribes, they are found either to preserve or to lose the preceding syllable; nevertheless, we must consider which form is more commonly used. Horace:

> *Spectatum* [Note: The manuscript reads *speratum*.] *meritis diram qui contudit hydram.*  
> “He who crushed the dread Hydra, worthy of being seen.”

14. Since you have asked about the verbs *fulgeo, mulceo, ferveo, strideo, oleo, tueor, coniveo, sedeo, pendeo, cieo, frendeo, degeo,* and *excelleo, tergeo*, which are found among poets as verbs of the second and third conjugations, and about which of these conjugations it is more appropriate to follow in prose, I want you to know that the first eight preserve the rule of the second conjugation in the present tense; the remainder belong to the third conjugation, except *cieo* and *pendeo*.

The first of these, whether simple or compound, now belongs to the second conjugation and now to the fourth. This is shown by the past forms of the passive, whose penultimate syllable is either short or long. *Pendeo*, when simple and meaning “to hang,” belongs to the second conjugation; when meaning “to loosen,” it belongs to the third. Yet its compound is never said in prose to belong to the second conjugation, nor is *sedeo* ever assigned to the third, except in *consido*.

It should also be noted that *sedeo*, whether simple or compound, enjoys, under the third conjugation, a lengthened penultimate syllable ending in *s*, as in *sido*.

15. Concerning the first and second persons plural of the perfect past and of the future subjunctive—which, if I remember correctly, I have read only once in verse, and that in Virgil—you should know this rule: except in the present indicative of the fourth conjugation and the second-person plural of its perfect, *i* is everywhere short in every mood and conjugation before the final letter in the second-person singular and before the last syllable of the first- and second-person plural, except only in *sis, simus, sitis, velis, velimus,* and *velitis*.

This is not surprising, since all verbs containing *a* or *e* in those positions have a long vowel, except one: whether simple or compound, *do* always shortens the vowel before the penultimate syllable, as in *damus* and *circumdamus*. Another exception is *es* and its compounds, which have a short vowel in the second person.

Nevertheless, we attach little importance to this rule in the aforementioned subjunctive tenses, because Servius teaches that, when found once in meter, it is to be read by systole.

Finally, I am not ashamed to explain to you my own rebuke. Once, when I had assented to one of your fellow brothers who was reading *myrmicoleonta* from the moral books, I kept silent after receiving a mocking response. Yet if he had noticed the genitive *myrmicoleontis* in the same book, he would not have denied that the common noun ends in *-on*, whose genitive, as in the simple Greek form, also takes *t*, as in *leon, leontis*.

16. Greek words ending in *-on*, which among the Greeks lengthen or shorten the penultimate syllable of the genitive, sometimes end among us in *-o*, following the usage of Latin nouns. They then preserve the same letter and lengthen it in the oblique cases; if they did not follow this pattern and shorten it, they would appear to derive from nominatives ending in *-on*, as *Simon* and *Simo*, *Sidon* and *Sido*.

Virgil, in Book I:

> *Sidoniam puer ire parat mea maxima cura.*  
> “The boy, my greatest concern, prepares to go to Sidon.”

The same poet, in Book IX:

> *Cratera antiquum quem dat Sidonia Dido.*  
> “The ancient bowl which Sidonian Dido gives.”

I find *cratera, statera,* and *panthera*, whether declined as Greek or as Latin, with their penultimate syllables lengthened, as in the preceding verse of Virgil. The Greek accusative of the third declension frequently ends in *-a*: *aera, aethera*.

Likewise, according to Priscian, all Greek words ending in *-a* and preceded by a diphthong, if inflected according to Latin declension, retain that same diphthong, lengthened either in *-ei* or in *-i*: *Calliopeia, Calliopea*; *comoedeia, comoedia*. Although *i* is shortened in verse, in prose it preserves its natural quantity, except in the single name *Alexandria*, which also produces *Alexandrea*. Thus we say *psalmodia* and *melodia* with a lengthened penultimate syllable, so that at least from this feature they may be recognized as Greek. For the sake of meter, however, they are short. Horace, in the *Art of Poetry*:

> *Effutire leves indigna tragoedia versus*  
> “Tragedy, unworthy to pour forth trivial verses.”

Let the same be understood of *spondaeus, Matthaeus, platea,* and *Nicaea*, and of similar words; their pronunciation itself shows that they are not Latin. *Ecclesia* and *neomenia*, together with any similar forms, are outside this rule.

The same applies to *Heliodorus* and *Polydorus*. Virgil, in Book III:

> *Fas omne abrupit, Polydorum obtruncat et auro.*  
> “He broke every divine law, and cut down Polydorus, even for gold.”

Juvenal:

> *Tonsoris Licini damno rapit Heliodorus.*  
> “Heliodorus snatches away the loss of Licinus the barber.”

[Note: Let us note the excellent reading *Licini*, in place of the spurious and absurd reading that crept into the sixth satire of Juvenal, line 372.]

The same is true of *Pandorus* and *Gassiodorus*. But names ending in *-or* have the proper penultimate syllable of their genitive short, as *Castor, Castoris* and *Nicanor, Nicanorus*.

17. Concerning *bos*, know that the plural dative and ablative of the third declension are formed from the singular genitive by inserting *bu*, as *pater, patribus*; similarly, *bos, bovis, bovibus*. Its first syllable is short, but when syncope occurs it is lengthened. Virgil:

> *Ille meas errare boves.*  
> “He makes my cattle wander.”

Horace, in a Sapphic verse, whose second position is a spondee:

> *Quaeque vos bobus veneratur albis.*  
> “And she venerates you with white oxen.”

It is nevertheless thought that the *o* changes into *u* when it is lengthened; hence *bucula* and *bucolica carmina* should be written with a lengthened *u*.

The ancients declined *os, ossis* and *ossum, ossi*; therefore, to distinguish singular from plural, modern writers spell the latter with a double *s*.

This is not surprising, since Virgil, solely for the sake of meter, said in Book VIII:

> *Alituum pecudumque genus sopor altus habebat.*  
> “Deep sleep held the race of winged creatures and cattle.”

Nor should you forget that trisyllabic and longer nouns whose final syllables begin with *n* have a penultimate syllable ending in long *a*, *e*, or *u*, as *Garganus, tribunus,* and *terrenus*. The only exceptions are *sagana, lagana, orphanus,* and *Satamon*.

[Col. 0532A]

18. A question commonly arises in the Book of Maccabees concerning the construction of the phrase: “and he remembered his covenant which he spoke to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, his faithful servants,” as though it ought to have said, “to Abraham and the rest of his faithful servants.” We say, however, that this is a zeugma, so that the construction is: “he remembered his covenant which he spoke, and so forth,” and, separately, “he remembered his faithful servants.”

The construction “the word which you hear is not mine” is likewise comparable to “the city which I establish is yours” and “the teaching which you heard benefits you.” Although it is marked by solecism, it requires the rhetorical figure of hypallage, as in:

> *Caesarie caput ille niger, Pie, talia dicta,*  
> “That black-headed man, O Pius, [spoke] such words,”

> *Cui relegendo placent quos facit ille modos.*  
> “To whom, when reread, the rhythms he produces are pleasing.”

19. Grammarians say that the comparative degree always governs the ablative case. But in Augustine’s little works I have read that, if a comparative joins the things being compared in the same case, the thing introduced by that degree will be outside those things themselves. For example, suppose there are three learned men: if you ask which of them is more learned, you plainly desire a fourth to be supplied; but if you ask through the genitive which of them is more learned, you wish to know which one of the three is the more learned.

Therefore, as the same teacher says, when three virtues are named—faith, hope, and charity—it is better to say, in the neuter form, “charity is the greater among these” (*major horum*) rather than “charity is greater than these” (*major his*), so that you do not introduce a fourth but distinguish which is greater among the things already proposed. Hence Martianus, in *The Marriage of Philology*, says: “Progna’s greater than her sons.”

In the *Palinody of God*, composed by Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, one should read, not according to the error of certain ignorant people, *suscepistis* (“you have received”), but rather *suscepturus* (“about to receive”): “You, about to receive a human being for liberation.”

For the future active participle, when joined to a verb of the same meaning, suggests the consequence of a certain fitting order conditionally, so that it is scarcely possible for one thing to occur unless the other has preceded it. Thus: “About to visit the English brothers, Os—, the archbishop, I did not fear the danger of the sea,” and so forth.

20. [Note: I do not see how this article 20 relates to grammatical questions.]

Just as *lustrum* denoted a period of five years, during which the city was purified and tribute was paid by all nations, so *olympias* denotes a period of four years. This period, instituted in the time of the priest Ozias, required that, after it had elapsed, games should be paid to Olympian Jupiter.

Hence the Lord is said to have been born in the 193rd Olympiad; and in the book *On the Praise of Virgins* we learn that Diocletian was the persecutor of Christians in the 267th Olympiad. From the first Olympiad onward, whenever something is said to have happened, the total number is revealed by multiplying by four, as is said in the chronicles.

21. In the Catholic creed issued by Athanasius, the defender of truth, who after many persecutions was found wholly orthodox, one verse should be read as follows:

> “The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son: not made, nor created, nor begotten, but proceeding.”

Although many, out of the simplicity of their understanding, attempt to remove the words *nec genitus* (“nor begotten”), because among other Catholics one often reads, “the Holy Spirit [is] not begotten, but proceeding,” while many read, “not unbegotten, but only proceeding.”

If these correctors returned to the inner consideration of logic, they would certainly perceive a firm stability of faith in both assertions. This same faith holds, concerning the divinity of the Trinity, that the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. Catholics define these persons by their properties, not as diverse in times or places.

The fact that the Father is neither made nor created is shared by him with the Son and the Holy Spirit. The fact that he is not begotten is shared with the Holy Spirit but not with the Son. The fact that the Son is begotten distinguishes the Father and the Spirit from him. Since, therefore, the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten, it is clear that the Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son, since he possesses neither of the distinguishing characteristics of those persons.

But if the Holy Spirit is not begotten, someone may say, then without doubt he is unbegotten. This is not so. Ordinary usage, in agreement with Aristotle’s judgment, rejects it. We tolerate even our enemies saying that we are not less wise than foolish, and that we are not just rather than unjust, when everyone openly confesses the same thing for the sake of humility.

For what sick person, knowing that he is not healthy, would patiently hear that he is insane? Thus certain things denied without privation are true, although, when affirmed privatively, they cannot be true. Yet if a negation is added hyperbatonically to such privative expressions, it sometimes restores them to truth.

When it is said of someone, “He is not healthy,” someone may wonder whether “insane” is intended; that consequence is possible, and therefore the speaker must necessarily add that he is neither healthy nor insane. Likewise, when I say that the Holy Spirit is not begotten, this is sufficient with respect to truth.
