But to remove the occasion for slander, it is useful for the discussion to make clear that he is neither begotten nor unbegotten.

Privative language requires negation, whereas negation does not necessarily require privation. For not everything that does not see is blind, although everything blind necessarily does not see; and not everything that is not just is unjust, although everything unjust is necessarily not just.

[Col. 0533D]

22. Finally, since many such arguments are available, it is enough to have shown these things through numbers, whose doctrinal significance provides physical explanations in many ways.

Certainly God delights in an odd number, for he established all things in number, measure, and weight. I therefore judge that the nature of the Trinity’s difference should in some manner be examined through three odd numbers following one another, with even numbers omitted between them. The first is five, the second seven, and the third nine.

The two omitted numbers signify the twofold nature of the one Jesus Christ. For the former—six—exists as a perfection produced from the first odd number doubled; the latter—nine—receives diminution from the first even number multiplied fourfold, under the appearance of cubic quantity, so that it may indicate the perfect God made somewhat lower than the angels in the form of a servant.

Since, below ten and with the exception of seven, all numbers either generate or are generated, the first of these prescribed odd numbers generates but is not generated; the second neither generates nor is generated; the third is generated but does not generate. No faithful person doubts which persons these correspond to, especially since the philosophers of the nations, for the reason stated above, attributed seven to Minerva, and we attribute it to that wisdom which, as is evident from counting, is never simple.

23. But since I seem to have discussed these matters sufficiently in the little book which, compelled by the requests of the brothers, I formerly published on Victor’s calculation, *On Number, Measure, and Weight* [Note: This work of Abbo is lengthy and has not yet been published. I myself read it in an ancient manuscript and intend to publish it at some point. In reading it, I meanwhile gained excellent information—namely, that Abbo had before him the grammarian Virgil, now published by me [*Classical Authors*, V, at the beginning], and that he knew his native place to be Toulouse, a fact he most gratefully disclosed to us, who had been unaware of it. For Abbo writes: “A scruple is weighed at sixteen lentil grains, although VIRGIL OF TOULOUSE asserts in his little works that it is weighed at seventeen barley grains, counting three grains in each husk.” As this testimony does not occur in the grammatical letters of Virgil published by me, there is no reason for surprise, since we know that Virgil also produced other writings on grammar.], I have refrained from saying more here, lest excessive length impose weariness upon the reader’s negligence in a letter of charity.

Therefore, having briefly dissected the innermost substance of the questions presented—questions which your brotherhood may examine by reading and read by examining—I have decided to bring them to an end, especially since, by disputing, I have reached him who is both beginning and end.

Farewell.

Mabillon adds:

> O company of Ramsey, which are enclosed by broad waters,  
> You strive to shine for God purer than refined gold.  
>   
> The vast, exceedingly fish-filled marsh displays its heights,  
> So that new barriers of the wilderness may be found for you.  
>   
> For where the traitor of the raven-bearing hydra rises,  
> A fair island gleams amid a wooded pool.  
>   
> And where the reins of the shining Ox plunge themselves,  
> From there a bridge lies open to its Englishmen.  
>   
> Where the Cynosure of heaven guides the fixed circuit on every side,  
> The eel-filled marsh knows no bounds.  
>   
> Whence the wandering Phoebean light casts shadows to the left,  
> The land lies open, uninterrupted by any ford.  
>   
> By chance I gave myself here, unknown among unknown pupils,  
> Whom, blessed Father Benedict, you prepare rightly to protect.

[Col. 0535]

# Epitome of Saint Abbo on the Lives of Ninety-One Roman Pontiffs

Drawn from the book on the lives of the Roman pontiffs attributed to Anastasius the Librarian, and now for the first time brought to light from an ancient manuscript codex.

(From the edition entitled: *History of the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs by Anastasius, Librarian of the Holy Roman Church, from the blessed apostle Peter to Nicholas I, hitherto never printed; followed by the Life of Hadrian II and Stephen VI, by William the Librarian; from the Augsburg library of the illustrious Marcus Welser. Various readings, etc., were added.* The edition was published at Mainz in 1602, at the press of Johann Albin.)

## Excerpt

From the deeds of the Roman pontiffs, from the little book which contains the deeds of the Roman pontiffs—deeds which Albo [thus; *Floriac* had been erased in the Munich manuscript, or perhaps *abbot*] judged useful for posterity concerning each of them in due order—he briefly and usefully excerpted [them], following the truth of Damasus, pontiff of the Roman Church, who wrote the same little book at the request of Jerome, interpreter of the divine law.

### I. Peter

[Col. 0535A]

Blessed PETER, prince of the Apostles, an Antiochene, son of John, from the province of Galilee and the village of Bethsaida, brother of Andrew, first held the episcopal see at Antioch for seven years, and afterward in the city of Rome for twenty-five years, two months, and three days. He ordained three bishops: Linus, Cletus, and Clement. Of these, Linus and Cletus personally supplied every priestly ministry in the city of Rome to the people who came, while Peter himself devoted himself to prayer and preaching. To Clement, however, he entrusted the chair, or the ordering of the whole Church. After this he was crowned with martyrdom together with Paul, thirty-eight years after the Passion of the Lord, and was buried on the Via Aurelia, in the temple of Apollo near the place where he was crucified, in the Vatican, on 29 June [three days before the Kalends of July].

### II. Linus

[Col. 0535B]

LINUS, an Italian by nation, from the region of Tuscany, son of Herculanus, sat for eleven years, three months, and twelve days. He decreed that a woman should enter church with her head veiled. Crowned with martyrdom, he was buried beside the body of Blessed Peter in the Vatican, on 23 September [nine days before the Kalends of October].

### III. Cletus

CLETUS, a Roman by nation, from the district of the Vicus Patricius, son of Aemilianus, sat for twelve years, one month, and eleven days. Crowned with martyrdom, he was buried beside the body of Blessed Peter on 26 April [six days before the Kalends of May]. The episcopate was vacant for thirty days.

### IV. Clement

[Col. 0536A]

CLEMENS, a Roman by nation, from the Caelian Hill district, son of Faustinus, sat for nine years, two months, and ten days. He wrote two letters called Catholic. While writing certain books through zeal for the faith of the Christian religion, he was banished into exile, crowned with martyrdom, and buried in Greece on 24 November [eight days before the Kalends of December]. The episcopate was vacant for twenty-one days.

### V. Anacletus

ANACLETUS, a Greek by nation, from Athens, son of Antiochus, sat for nine years, two months, and ten days. He constructed the memorial of the blessed Apostle Peter, where he himself was also buried beside Peter’s body. The episcopate was vacant for thirteen days.

### VI. Evaristus

[Col. 0536B]

EVARISTUS, a Greek by nation, son of a Jew named Judas, from the city of Bethlehem, sat for nine years, ten months, and two days. He divided the titular churches in the city of Rome and ordained seven deacons to guard the preaching bishop on account of the style of truth. He was buried beside the body of the blessed Apostle Peter. The episcopate was vacant for eighteen days.

### VII. Alexander

ALEXANDER, a Roman by nation, son of Alexander, from the district of Caput Tauri, sat for ten years, seven months, and two days. He decreed that water for sprinkling, with salt, should be blessed in human dwellings. He was buried on the Via Nomentana, where he was beheaded, seven miles from the city of Rome, on 3 May [five days before the Nones of May]. The episcopate was vacant for thirty-five days.

### VIII. Sixtus

[Col. 0537A]

SIXTUS, a Roman by nation, son of Pastor, from the district of Vialata, sat for ten years, two months, and one day. He decreed that sacred ministrations should not be touched except by ministers, and that any bishop summoned to the Apostolic See, upon returning to his parish, should not be received except with a letter of authorization. He too was buried beside the body of Blessed Peter on 3 April [three days before the Nones of April]. The episcopate was vacant for two days.

### IX. Telesphorus

TELESPHORUS, a Greek by nation, one of the anchorites, sat for eleven years, three months, and twenty-one days. He decreed that a fast should be observed for seven weeks before Easter; that masses should be celebrated by night at the Nativity of the Lord; that no one should ever celebrate masses before the third hour; and that the angelic hymn should be sung before the sacrifice. Crowned with martyrdom, he was buried beside the body of Blessed Peter on 2 January [four days before the Nones of January]. The episcopate was vacant for seven days.

### X. Hyginus

HYGINUS, a Greek by nation, a philosopher from Athens, whose genealogy I have not found, sat for fifteen years, three months, and four days. He was buried beside the body of Blessed Peter on 11 January [three days before the Ides of January]. The episcopate was vacant for two days.

### XI. Pius

PIUS, an Italian by nation, son of Rufinus, brother of Pastor, from the city of Aquileia, sat for ten years, nine months, and three days. During his episcopate Hermes wrote a book which states that an angel of the Lord, in the guise of a shepherd, commanded him that Easter should be celebrated on the Lord’s day. He decreed that a heretic coming from the heresy of the Jews should be received and baptized. He was buried beside the body of Blessed Peter on 11 July [five days before the Ides of July]. The episcopate was vacant for fourteen days.

### XII. Anicetus

ANICETUS, a Syrian by nation, son of John, from the village of Humisa, sat for twelve years, four months, and three days. He decreed that a cleric should not grow his hair. He died a martyr and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on 20 April [twelve days before the Kalends of May]. The episcopate was vacant for seventeen days.

### XIII. Sother

SOTHER, a Campanian by nation, son of Concordius, from the city of Fundi, sat for nine years, six months, and twenty-one days. He decreed that no nun should touch the sacred cloth or place incense in the holy church. He was buried beside the body of Blessed Peter on 24 May [nine days before the Kalends of June]. The episcopate was vacant for twenty-one days.

### XIV. Eleuther

ELEUTHER, a Greek by nation, son of Habundius, from the town of Nicopolis, sat for fifteen years, three months, and two days. He received a letter from Lucius, king of the Britons, asking to be made Christian. He further confirmed that no rational and human food should be rejected by Christians, especially by the faithful. He was buried beside the body of Blessed Peter on 24 May [nine days before the Kalends of June]. The episcopate was vacant for fifteen days.

### XV. Victor

[Col. 0538A]

VICTOR, an African by nation, son of Felix, sat for fifteen years, three months, and ten days. He decreed that, in case of necessity, a pagan should be baptized wherever found, and that holy Easter should be observed on the Lord’s day from the fourteenth moon of the first month through the twenty-first. He was buried beside the body of Blessed Peter on 28 July [five days before the Kalends of August]. The episcopate was vacant for twelve days.

### XVI. Zephyrinus

ZEPHYRINUS, a Roman by nation, son of Habundius, sat for eight years, six months, and three days. He decreed that a cleric, levite, or priest should be ordained in the presence of all clergy and faithful laity, and that a presbyter should receive the consecrated crown to distribute to the people. He was buried in his own cemetery, beside the cemetery of Calixtus on the Via Appia, on 27 August [six days before the Kalends of September]. The episcopate was vacant for six days.

### XVII. Callistus

CALLISTUS, a Roman by nation, son of Domitius, from the city of Ravenna, sat for six years, two months, and ten days. He decreed that the fast on Saturday should be kept three times a year. Crowned with martyrdom, he was buried in the cemetery of Calepodius, on the Via Aurelia, at the third mile, on 13 October [three days before the Ides of October]. The episcopate was vacant for six days.

### XVIII. Urbanus

URBANUS, a Roman by nation, son of Pontianus, sat for nine years, one month, and two days. By his teaching he led Valerian, spouse of Saint Cecilia, and many others as far as martyrdom. Having become a confessor, he was buried in the cemetery of Praetextatus on the Via Appia, on 25 December [eight days before the Kalends of January]. The episcopate was vacant for thirty days.

### XIX. Pontianus

PONTIANUS, a Roman by nation, son of Calpurnius, sat for nine years, five months, and two days. He and the presbyter Hippolytus were deported into exile by Alexander to the island of Butiana in Sardinia. There he died and was crowned with martyrdom on 30 October [three days before the Kalends of November]. Blessed Fabian brought him back by ship with the clergy and buried him in the cemetery of Calixtus on the Via Appia. The episcopate was vacant for ten days.

### XX. Antherus

ANTHERUS, a Greek by nation, son of Romulus, sat for twelve years, one month, and twelve days. He diligently investigated the acts of the martyrs and deposited them in the Church. Crowned with martyrdom, he was buried in the cemetery of Calixtus on the Via Appia, on 3 January [three days before the Nones of January]. The episcopate was vacant for thirteen days.

### XXI. Fabianus

FABIANUS, a Roman by nation, son of Fabius, sat for fourteen years, eleven months, and ten days. He divided the districts among the deacons and appointed six deacons to supervise the seven notaries. At that time Novatus came from Africa and divided the Church. Fabian, however, was crowned with martyrdom and buried in the cemetery of Calixtus on the Via Appia, on 20 January [thirteen days before the Kalends of February]. The episcopate was vacant for six days.

### XXII. Cornelius

[Col. 0539A]

CORNELIUS, a Roman by nation, son of Castinus, sat for two years, three months, and ten days. He was driven to Centumcellae, and there received a letter written in prison by Cyprian the martyr. In that same place he was beheaded and became a martyr. Blessed Lucina collected his body by night with the clergy and buried it in a crypt beside the cemetery of Callistus on the Via Appia, on her estate, on 14 September [eighteen days before the Kalends of October]. The episcopate was vacant for thirty-five days.

### XXIII. Lucius

LUCIUS, a Roman by nation, son of Porphyrius, sat for three years, seven months, and six days. He was in exile, but afterward returned unharmed to his Church and decreed that, everywhere, two presbyters and three deacons should not leave the bishop, on account of ecclesiastical testimony. He too was beheaded by Valerian on 5 March [three days before the Nones of March] and buried in the cemetery of Calixtus on the Via Appia on 25 August [eight days before the Kalends of September]. The episcopate was vacant for thirty-five days.

### XXIV.

STEPHANUS, a Roman by nationality, son of Jobius, held office for 6 years, 5 months, and 2 days. He established that priests and Levites should use sacred vestments only in the church. Crowned with martyrdom, he was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, on the fourth day before the Nones of August. At that time there was a great persecution under Decius.

XXV.

XISTUS, a Greek by nationality, son of a philosopher, held office for 1 year, 10 months, and 26 days. Crowned with martyrdom under Valerian on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, he was followed in suffering three days later by blessed Lawrence, the archdeacon. [Col. 0539C] Finally, blessed Xistus was buried in the cemetery of blessed Calixtus on the Appian Way. The episcopate remained vacant for 35 days.

XXVI.

DIONYSIUS, from among the monks—whose lineage we were unable to discover—held office for 6 years, 2 months, and 4 days. He assigned churches and cemeteries to the priests and established the parishes of the diocese. His deposition was on the sixth day before the Kalends of January, in the cemetery of Calixtus on the Appian Way. The episcopate remained vacant for 5 days.

XXVII.

FELIX, a Roman by nationality, son of Constantius, held office for 4 years, 3 months, and 25 days. He established that Masses should be celebrated above the memorials of the martyrs. He built a basilica on the Via Aurelia, where, after being crowned with martyrdom, he was buried [Col. 0539D] on the third day before the Kalends of June, at the second milestone from the city of Rome. The episcopate remained vacant for 5 days.

XXVIII.

EUTHICIANUS, a Tuscan by nationality, son of Marinus, from the city of Luna, held office for 1 year, 1 month, and 1 day. He established that only produce—beans and grapes—should be blessed upon the altar. He was buried in the cemetery of Calixtus on the Appian Way, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August. The episcopate remained vacant for 8 days.

XXIX.

GAIUS, a Dalmatian by nationality, from the family of the Emperor Diocletian, son of Gaius, held office for 11 years, 4 months, and 12 days. He established that all the orders should ascend in the church in the following manner [Col. 0540A]: if someone were deemed worthy to become a bishop, he was to be successively doorkeeper, lector, exorcist, then subdeacon, deacon, priest, and thereafter be ordained bishop. Fleeing the persecution of Diocletian and living in the crypts, he was crowned with martyrdom and buried in the cemetery of Calixtus on the Appian Way, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May. The episcopate remained vacant for 11 days.

XXX.

MARCELLINUS, a Roman by nationality, son of Projectus, held office for 9 years, 4 months, and 16 days. At that time there was a great persecution, so that within 30 days 17,000 people of both sexes were crowned with martyrdom throughout the various provinces. Among them Marcellinus himself was brought to sacrifice and burn incense, which he did. A few days later, moved to repentance, he was beheaded by that same Diocletian [Col. 0540B] for the faith of Christ. His body lay in the street for 25 days. Then Marcellus the priest collected it by night and buried him on the Via Salaria in the cemetery of Priscilla, beside the body of Saint Crescention, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May. The episcopate remained vacant for 7 years, 7 months, and 25 days.

XXXI.

MARCELLUS, a Roman by nationality, son of Benedictus, from the Vialata district, held office for 5 years, 7 months, and 21 days. He established a cemetery on the Via Salaria and, after being arrested, was condemned to the *catabulum*. When nine months had elapsed in prayer and fasting, his clergy came by night, stripped him [of his confinement], and led him to the house of the widow Lucina, which he dedicated as a title-church of the holy Church. When Maxentius heard this, he ordered him to serve the animals there. [Col. 0540C] Thus, while serving the animals, he died naked and clothed in sackcloth. Blessed Lucina collected his body and buried him in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February. The episcopate remained vacant for 30 days.

XXXII.

EUSEBIUS, a Greek by nationality, from the physicians, held office for 6 years, 1 month, and 3 days. During his time the Lord’s cross was discovered, on the fifth day before the Nones of May, by Judas, who was baptized afterward. He found heretics and reconciled them through the laying on of hands. He too was buried in the cemetery of Calixtus on the Appian Way, on the sixth day before the Nones of October. The episcopate remained vacant for 7 days.

XXXIII.

MELCHIADES, an African by nationality, held office for 4 years. He established that Sunday and the fifth day of the week should in no way be observed as fast days; and he arranged that the sacred offerings—that is, the *fermentum* from the bishop’s consecration—should be sent throughout the churches. He was buried in the cemetery of Calixtus on the Appian Way, on the fourth day before the Ides of January. The episcopate remained vacant for 16 days.

XXXIV.

SILVESTER, a Roman by nationality, son of Rufinus, held office for 23 years, 10 months, and 11 days. He was in exile on Mount Soracte. Later, returning with honor, he baptized Constantine Augustus, whom the Lord had cured of leprosy. During his time, at his command, the Council was held at Nicaea in Bithynia, and 318 Catholic bishops assembled [Col. 0541A]; they condemned Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius. In the city of Rome as well, he himself, with the emperor’s approval, assembled 277 bishops and again condemned Calixtus, Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius.

He also established that, after baptism, a priest should anoint the baptized person with chrism after he had been lifted from the water, because of the possibility of death; that no layman should dare to bring a charge against a cleric; that deacons should use dalmatics in the church; and that no cleric should enter the court for any reason or plead a case before a judge except in the church.

He further established that the altar sacrifice should not be celebrated on silk or dyed cloth, but only on linen, just as the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was buried in a clean linen shroud. If anyone desired to serve or advance in the church, he was to be a lector for [Col. 0541B] 30 years, an exorcist for 30 days, an acolyte for 5 years, a subdeacon for 5, a deacon for 7, and a priest for 3; he was to be approved in every respect and have a good testimony from those outside, and be the husband of one wife blessed by a priest; then he might proceed to the order of the episcopate.

He was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria, at the third milestone from the city of Rome, on the day before the Kalends of January, and rested there as a Catholic and confessor. The episcopate remained vacant for 21 days.

XXXV.

MARCUS, a Roman by nationality, son of Priscus, held office for 2 years, 9 months, and 20 days. He established that the bishop of Ostia, who consecrates the Bishop of the City, should use the pallium, and that the Bishop of the City of Rome should be consecrated by him. He died on the Nones of October and was buried [Col. 0541C] in the cemetery of Balbina on the Via Ardeatina. The episcopate remained vacant for 20 days.

XXXVI.

JULIUS, a Roman by nationality, son of Rusticus, held office for 15 years, 2 months, and 5 days. He was sent into exile for 10 months by the heretical Emperor Constantine. After Constantine’s death he returned. He established that no cleric should conduct any case in public; that records of events, which are necessary for all because of the faith of the Church, should be collected by notaries and kept in the church by the clergy. He too was buried on the Via Aurelia, in the cemetery of Calepodius at the third milestone, on the day before the Ides of April. The episcopate remained vacant for 25 days.

XXXVII.

[Col. 0541D] LIBERIUS, a Roman by nationality, son of Augustus, held office for 6 years, 4 months, and 8 days. Because he refused to consent to the Arian heresy, he was in exile for 3 years. On his advice FELIX, the venerable priest, was ordained bishop in his place. Felix found two priests, Ursacius and Valens, who had agreed with Constantius Augustus, an Arian, and condemned them in a council of 48 bishops.

After a few days Ursacius and Valens, moved by zeal, asked Constantius to recall Liberius from exile. He agreed with them that Liberius should meet with the heretics in communion only once, provided that he was not rebaptized. After this Constantius held a council with certain men who were from the dregs of the Arian party, expelled Felix from the episcopate [Col. 0542A], although he was a Catholic, and recalled Liberius.

Felix, deposed on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, lived on his small estate on the Via Portuensis. Liberius entered the city on the fourth day before the Nones of August and consented to the heretics, though he was not rebaptized. He held the basilicas of blessed Peter and Paul and the Constantinian basilica for 7 years. There was also a great persecution in the city of Rome. Thus all the years of Felix are counted as part of this ordination. Liberius, however, was buried on the Via Salaria in the cemetery of Priscilla. The episcopate remained vacant for 7 days.

XXXVIII.

FELIX, a Roman by nationality, son of Anastasius, held office for 1 year, 3 months, and 2 days. He declared Constantius, the son of Constantine, a heretic, and said that he had been rebaptized a second time by Eusebius, Bishop of Nicomedia, in a village [Col. 0542B] called Aquilon. For this act he was beheaded with many clerics and faithful Christians secretly beside the walls of the city, near Trajan’s aqueduct, on the third day before the Ides of November. Thereafter Christians, together with the priest Damasus, carried off his body and buried it peacefully in the aforementioned basilica on the Via Aurelia, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December. The episcopate remained vacant for 38 days.

XXXIX.

DAMASUS, a Spaniard by nationality, son of Antonius, held office for 18 years, 3 months, and 10 days. Ursinus was ordained with him in the same [contention; literally, “intention”]. After a council of priests had been held, Ursinus was expelled from the city and established as bishop at Naples. Supported by a very great multitude, Damasus remained bishop in the Apostolic See.

At length he was accused and charged with [Col. 0542C] adultery, but in a synod he was cleared by 44 bishops. They also condemned his accusers, Concordius and Callistus, and expelled them from the Church. He sought out many bodies of saints, found them, and adorned their memorials with verses. He also established that psalms should be sung day and night throughout all the churches. He was buried on the Via Ardeatina in his basilica, on the third day before the Ides of December, beside his mother and his sister. The episcopate remained vacant for 31 days.

XL.

SIRICIUS, a Roman by nationality, son of Tiburtius, held office for 15 years. He established that no priest should celebrate Mass throughout the entire week unless he had received what had been consecrated by the bishop, called the [Col. 0542D] *fermentum*. He also hated all heretics, especially the Manichaeans, whom, when discovered, he had deported into exile. He decreed that if anyone converted from the Manichaeans returned to the Church, he should not receive communion in any way unless, confined to a monastery until the end of his life, fasting and devoted to prayers, he were given the viaticum.

He also established that a heretic should be reconciled through the laying on of hands in the presence of the entire Church. He was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May. The episcopate remained vacant for 20 days.

XLI.

ANASTASIUS, a Roman by nationality, son of Maximus, held office for 3 years and 10 days. [Col. 0543A] He established that whenever the holy Gospels were read, the priests should not sit but stand bent forward; and that no one should receive a cleric from overseas unless he produced a letter from his own bishop, because Manichaeans had been discovered in the city at that time. He was buried in his own cemetery at the Bear with the Cap, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May. The episcopate remained vacant for 21 days.

XLII.

INNOCENTIUS, an Albanian by nationality, son of Innocentius, held office for 15 years, 3 months, and 21 days. He encountered Pelagius and Coelestius and condemned the heretics. He established that one born of a Christian should be born again through baptism—that is, should be baptized—which Pelagius condemned. He also established that the Sabbath fast should be observed, because the Lord was placed in the tomb [Col. 0543B] on the Sabbath and the disciples fasted. He was buried in the cemetery at the Bear with the Cap, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August. The episcopate remained vacant for 22 days.

XLIII.

ZOZIMUS, a Greek by nationality, son of Abraham, held office for 7 years, 4 months, and 24 days. He established that deacons should have the left shoulder covered with cloaks of linen mesh, and granted permission throughout the parish for candles to be blessed. He also established that no one should offer a public drink to a cleric except in the room of the faithful, especially of clerics. He was buried on the Via Tiburtina beside the body of blessed Lawrence the martyr, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January. The episcopate remained vacant for 11 days.

XLIV.

BONIFACIUS, a Roman by nationality, son of Jocundus [Col. 0543C] the priest, held office for 3 years, 8 months, and 6 days. He was ordained on the same day as Eulalius, in a contested election. There was great dissension in the clergy for 15 days and 8 months.

When Augusta Placidia heard this, while she was residing at Ravenna with her son Valentinian Augustus, she reported it to Honorius Augustus at Milan. At their command both men were expelled from the city. But Eulalius, because he had been ordained in the Constantinian basilica, presumed to enter the city and baptize; he celebrated Easter in the aforementioned basilica. When the Augusti heard this, they sent men and expelled him to Campania, while they recalled Bonifacius to the city and established him as bishop.

After Bonifacius died, the clergy and people requested that Eulalius be recalled, but he refused to return. Finally, Bonifacius established that no woman or nun should touch the sacred [Col. 0543D] pallium or place incense, and that no slave should become a cleric, nor anyone liable to civic office. He too was buried on the Via Salaria beside the body of Saint Felicitas the martyr, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November. The episcopate remained vacant for 9 days.

XLV.

CAELESTINUS, a Campanian by nationality, son of Priscus, held office for 9 years, 10 months, and 17 days. He established that the 150 psalms of David should be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice. Previously, only the epistle of blessed Paul and the holy Gospel had been read. He was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria, on the eighth day before the Ides of April. The episcopate remained vacant for 20 days.

XLVI.

[Col. 0544A]

XISTUS, a Roman by nationality, son of Sixtus, held office for 8 years and 19 days. After 1 year and 8 months, he was accused by a certain Bassus. When Valentinian Augustus heard this, he ordered a synod to be assembled, in which Xistus was examined by 46 bishops and cleared, while Bassus was condemned, so that even on his final day the viaticum was not denied him.

Against Bassus, Valentinian Augustus, moved by holy zeal, joined his estates and property to the Catholic Church; Bassus died three months later. Bishop Xistus handled his body with his own hands and buried it beside blessed Peter the Apostle, in the chamber of his parents. Xistus himself was also buried on the Via Tiburtina, in a crypt beside the body of blessed Lawrence. The episcopate remained vacant for 22 days.

XLVII.

[Col. 0544B]

LEO, a Tuscan by nationality, son of Quintianus, held office for 21 years, 1 month, and 13 days. He encountered two heresies, the Eutychian and the Nestorian. Concerning these he sent word to MARCIANUS Augustus, an orthodox and Catholic ruler, asking him to assemble a council of bishops.

This was immediately done. There assembled 256 priests and 408 other bishops. A letter was circulated together with the letter of holy Bishop Leo—that is, the *tome*, in which the faith of the Apostolic Church of Rome was contained. Thus, in the presence of the Catholic ruler Marcian, a council of 630 bishops was held at Chalcedon, in the shrine of Saint Euphemia. They set forth the Catholic faith, saying [Col. 0544C] that in the one Christ, God and man, there are two natures.

There the most devout Augustus, together with his wife, Augusta Pulcheria, laying aside their royal majesty, set forth their faith in writing before all the bishops. The bishops condemned Eutyches and Nestorius and sent their statement to Leo, the most blessed pope.

Leo established that a nun should not receive a blessed veil upon her head unless she had been tested in virginity for 60 years; and that during the action of the sacrifice it should be said: “The holy sacrifice,” and so forth. He was buried beside blessed Peter the Apostle, on the third day before the Ides of April. The episcopate remained vacant for 7 days.

XLVIII.

HILARIUS, a Sardinian by nationality, son of Crispinus, held office for 6 years, 3 months, and 10 days. He confirmed three synods [Col. 0544D]—the Nicene, Ephesian, and Chalcedonian—or the *tome* of holy Bishop Leo—and condemned all the founders of heresies and their followers. He also confirmed the authority and primacy of the Catholic and apostolic see of the Roman Church. He was buried at Saint Lawrence, in a crypt beside the body of blessed Xistus the bishop, on the fourth day before the Ides of September. The episcopate remained vacant for 10 days.

XLIX.

SIMPLICIUS, a Tiburtine by nationality, son of Castorius, held office for 15 years, 1 month, and 7 days. During his time a report came from Greece from Acacius, Bishop of Constantinople, asserting that Peter of Alexandria had become a heretic and an Eutychianist, and that he had been implicated [Col. 0545A] in the death of a certain Catholic priest. When Bishop Simplicius heard this, he made no reply to Acacius but condemned Peter, awaiting a period for repentance. He was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle, on the sixth day before the Nones of March. The episcopate remained vacant for 6 days.

L.

FELIX, a Roman by nationality, son of Felix the priest of the title-church of Fasciola, held office for 8 years, 11 months, and 17 days. At that time a report again came from Greece that Peter had been recalled by Acacius, Bishop of Constantinople. When Felix, the Roman bishop, heard this, he sent a defender with the counsel of his see and, in a council, condemned Acacius together with Peter.

Three years later a report again came from the Emperor Zeno that Acacius should return as a penitent. Then Pope Felix sent two [Col. 0545B] bishops, Mesenus and Vitalis, so that, if they found Acacius an accomplice of Peter, they might condemn them again; otherwise, they were to offer him a written statement of repentance.

When they entered Constantinople, they were corrupted by money and did not do what the Lord Pope had commanded. After their return, he held a council at Rome, examined both bishops—Mesenus and Vitalis—and rejected them as guilty from communion. But Mesenus did not conceal his sin, and for this reason he was granted time for repentance. Felix was buried in the basilica of blessed Paul the Apostle. The episcopate remained vacant for 5 days.

LI.

GELASIUS, an African by nationality, son of Valerius, held office [Col. 0545C] for 4 years, 8 months, and 18 days. He found Manichaeans in the city and ordered them deported into exile and their books burned. In a synod, with tears and after the submission of a written satisfaction, he restored Bishop Mesenus, who had been cleared, and returned him to his own church.

A report again came from Greece that Peter and Acacius were committing many evils and murders. At that time John, the Catholic Bishop of Alexandria, fled and came to Rome. Blessed Gelasius received him with honor and granted him the second see. After holding a synod, he sent word throughout the East and again condemned Peter and Acacius perpetually unless they sought repentance with a written statement of satisfaction.

He also composed the prefaces and prayers of the sacraments in carefully guarded language. He was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter [Col. 0545D] on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December. The episcopate remained vacant for 7 days.

LII.

[Col. 0545D]

ANASTASIUS, a Roman by nationality, son of Peter, from the fifth district, Caput Tauri, held office for 1 year, 2 months, and 24 days. Because he had communicated with a certain Thessalonian deacon named Photinus, who was in communion with Acacius without the counsel of the bishops, priests, or clerics of the Catholic Church, they suspended themselves from communion with him.

When he later wished to recall Acacius secretly but was unable to do so, he was struck by divine judgment and buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December. The episcopate remained vacant for 4 days.

LIII.

[Col. 0546A]

SYMMACHUS, a Sardinian by nationality, son of Fortunatus, held office for 15 years, 7 months, and 27 days. He was ordained on the same day as Laurentius, in a contested election: Symmachus in the Constantinian basilica, and Laurentius in the basilica of Saint Mary. For this reason the clergy separated and the Senate was divided.

After the dispute had arisen, both parties decided that the two men, once ordained, should go to Ravenna for judgment by King Theodoric. When this had been done, the king judged that the one ordained first, or the one supported by the greater part, should hold the Apostolic See. Thus Symmachus became bishop, and, out of mercy, he appointed Laurentius bishop of the city of Nuceria.

Four years later, however, certain members of the clergy and Senate, especially Festus and Probinus, moved by zeal, accused the same pope before Theodoric of the gravest crime and suborned false witnesses, whom they sent to Ravenna. Meanwhile they secretly recalled Laurentius. The clergy was again divided.

Then the accusers of Symmachus asked the king to appoint a visitor to the Apostolic See. This was done, and he appointed Peter, Bishop of the city of Altinum, contrary to the canons. Therefore the aforementioned pope assembled 115 bishops and, after a synod had been held, was cleared of the false charge. Peter of Altinum, invader of the Apostolic See, was condemned, as was Laurentius of Nuceria, because, while the bishop was alive, they had laid claim to his see. Symmachus was restored with honor to his see by all his own people.

For this reason Festus and Probinus, enraged, began fighting within the city, especially against Faustus the former consul and all who were in communion with Symmachus. Clerics, nuns, and virgins were killed by the sword; the latter were dragged naked from their monasteries. Only Faustus the former consul fought on behalf of the Church.

After all this, the same pope found Manichaeans in the city, burned their books, and sent them into exile. Every year throughout Africa or Sardinia he supplied money and clothing to bishops who had been confined in exile, and he ransomed captives in various provinces.

He too was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle as a confessor, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August. The episcopate remained vacant for 7 days.

LIV.

HORMISDA, a Campanian by nationality, son of Justus, from the [Col. 0546D] city of Frisinone, held office for 9 years and 17 days. In accordance with the decree of a synod and with the counsel of King Theodoric, he sent envoys to Greece, showing consideration for the Apostolic See, because the Greeks were bound under the bond of anathema on account of Peter of Alexandria and Acacius of Constantinople under Bishop John.

He sent Ennodius, Bishop of Ticinum; Fortunatus, Bishop of Catinum; Venantius, a priest of the city of Rome; Vitalis, a deacon; and Hilary, a notary, to Augustus Anastasius. They accomplished nothing, because Anastasius himself was in communion with the Eutychian heresy.

A second time he sent Ennodius and Peregrinus, Bishop of Mesenus. When Anastasius wished to corrupt them with money, they refused absolutely [Col. 0547A] unless he carried out the satisfaction required by the Apostolic See. Then the emperor, filled with rage, expelled them through a small gate and placed them on a dangerous ship, ordering Heliodorus and Demetrius that they should not enter any Greek city.

The envoys, however, more secretly, set forth throughout all the cities the 19 holy letters of the faith through the hands of orthodox monks. The bishops who were accomplices of Augustus Anastasius because of the crime sent these letters to Constantinople. Filled with rage, Anastasius wrote among other sacred statements: “We wish to command, not to be commanded.” After this, struck by divine judgment with lightning, he died.

Justinus the Orthodox succeeded him in the empire. He sent his authority to Hormisda, the Roman pope, so that peace might be restored to the churches. The pope accepted this authority and, with the counsel of King Theodoric, sent Germanus, Bishop of Capua; John and Blandus, priests; Felix and Dioscorus, deacons; and Peter, a notary, equipped with the faith and the text of a written statement of repentance.

When they came near Constantinople, such grace of faith shone forth that a multitude of orthodox monks and distinguished men—and the Emperor Justinus and the consul Vitalianus as well—came together to meet them at the Round Castle, which leads toward the city. They were received with honor and great joy by the clergy and Bishop John.

When the accomplices of Anastasius perceived this, they shut themselves inside the greater church called Hagia Sophia. After taking counsel, they sent word to the emperor, saying: “Unless an explanation is given us why our bishop Acacius was condemned [Col. 0547C], we will in no way consent to the Apostolic See.”

He also condemned Peter and Acacius, as well as all heresies, and found Manichaeans, whom he deported into exile after an examination involving blows; their books he burned. At the same time a gift adorned with precious gems came from Clovis, the Christian king of the Franks, to blessed Peter the Apostle.

Hormisda was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle, on the eighth day before the Ides of August, in the consulship of Maximus. The episcopate remained vacant for 6 days.

LV.

JOANNES, a Tuscan by nationality, son of Constantius, held office for 2 years, 9 months, and 17 days. He was summoned by King Theodoric to Ravenna, and Theodoric sent him as envoy to Constantinople to the orthodox Emperor Justin, who, acting on his counsel and out of love for the Christian religion, wished to remove the heretics, so that he might consecrate the churches of the Arians as Catholic churches. On account of this the heretical King Theodoric blazed with anger and wished to destroy all Italy by the sword.

Then Pope John, ill, set out weeping, with senators and consuls—namely the importunate Theodorus and the patrician Agapitus—having received instructions that the churches should be returned to the heretics in the eastern regions; otherwise Theodoric would destroy all Italy by the sword. As he travelled, the whole city met him with candles and crosses in honor of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul. The Emperor Justin rejoiced to receive Pope John of Rome in the Greek regions, just as the Emperor Constantine had received Bishop Silvester.

Justinus, giving honor to God, bowed himself down and worshipped the most blessed John, beseeching him with great tears that the embassy might be acceptable in his sight. Once John had obtained from Justin what he had gone to obtain, at Justin's request, as vicar of the blessed Apostle Peter, he placed the crown upon him with his own hands and with honor. At the same time the heretical King Theodoric seized two illustrious senators and former consuls, Symmachus and Boethius, and killed them by the sword.

When the venerable Pope John and the senators accompanying him returned from Constantinople, the aforesaid heretical king received them with great guile and hatred. He wished to kill them by the sword, but did not dare, fearing the indignation of the Emperor Justin, although he allowed them, afflicted in custody, to be tortured and burned. The pope himself, afflicted in custody, wasted away and died a martyr on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June. The same heretical King Theodoric immediately followed him in death. The body of blessed John was transferred from Ravenna and buried in the basilica of blessed Peter on the sixth day before the Kalends of June. The episcopate remained vacant for 58 days.

LVI.

FELIX, a Samnite by nationality, son of Castorius, held office for 4 years, 2 months, and 13 days. He was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle, on the fourth day before the Ides of October. The episcopate remained vacant for 3 days.

LVII.

[Col. 0548C] BONIFACIUS, a Roman by nationality, son of Sigebald, held office for 2 years and 26 days. He was ordained in the basilica of Julius, in a contested election, together with Dioscorus, who was being ordained in the Constantinian basilica. There was dissension in the clergy and Senate for 28 days. But Dioscorus died in that same year, on the second day before the Ides of October. Bonifacius, moved by zeal, anathematized him with great bitterness in a written document and consigned it to the Church archive; but no one was willing to subscribe to it.

Having assembled a synod in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle, he exacted from the priests, by their written documents, an oath before the confession of the Apostle Peter concerning the deacon Vigilius, that he should succeed him. Therefore, when another synod had been held, all the priests determined, out of reverence for the holy See, that this had been done contrary to the canons and that blame attached to him who had appointed his own successor. Accordingly Bonifacius confessed himself guilty because he had made, by his subscription, a written document concerning the deacon Vigilius before the confession of the Apostle Peter; and, in the presence of all the priests, clergy, and Senate, he consumed that document in the fire.

Then a report came from the African bishops concerning the constitution, requesting that the Bishop of Carthage should do everything by the counsel of the Lord Pope. He was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle, on the seventeenth day of October. The episcopate remained vacant for 15 days.

LVIII.

JOANNES, also called Martyrius, a Roman by nationality, son of Projectus, from [Col. 0549A] Caelian Hill, held office for 2 years, 4 months, and 6 days. At that time the Emperor Justinian, a religious man with the highest love for the Christian religion, sent his faith set down in his own handwriting to the Apostolic See through the bishops Epatius and Demetrius. Pope John was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June. The episcopate remained vacant for 6 days.

LIX.

AGAPITUS, a Roman by nationality, son of Gordianus the priest of the title-church of Saints John and Paul, held office for 11 months and 18 days. The letters of anathema which Bonifacius had extorted through envy and deceit from priests and bishops against the canons and against Dioscorus, with everyone assembled in the midst of the church, he burned in the fire [Col. 0549B] and absolved the entire Church.

Finally, he was sent by Theodatus, king of the Goths, to Domnus Justinianus Augustus. The emperor was angry with that same king because he had killed Queen Amalsuentha, who had been entrusted to him—the daughter, namely, of King Theodoric, who had made him king.

Agapitus therefore entered Constantinople on the tenth day before the Kalends of May and was received with honor. He began a dispute with Justinian Augustus concerning religion and gave a most steadfast answer concerning the Lord Jesus Christ, God and man: that in the one person of Jesus Christ there are two natures.

During this dispute he discovered that Anthemius, the Bishop of Constantinople, was a heretic. The emperor therefore said to Agapitus: “Either consent to us, or I shall send you into exile.” He replied [Col. 0549C]: “I desired to come to Justinian, the most Christian emperor, but now I have found a Diocletian. Know, however, that neither you nor your bishop are fit for the Christian religion unless you confess two natures in Christ.”

Finally, at the emperor’s command, Anthemius was summoned. After an investigation, he never wished to confess the doctrine of the Catholic response. But Saint Pope Agapitus convicted him, and for this reason he was glorified by all Christians.

Then the emperor, filled with joy, humbled himself and worshiped the most blessed Pope Agapitus, because he expelled Anthemius from communion and sent him into exile. In his place he consecrated a Catholic bishop named Moenas.

After obtaining everything for which he had been sent [Col. 0549D], Agapitus died at Constantinople from an illness, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May. His body was transferred in a lead coffin to the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle, where it was buried on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October. The episcopate remained vacant for 58 days.

LX.

SILVERIUS, a Campanian by nation, son of Hormisdas, Bishop of Rome, sat for 1 year, 5 months, and 11 days. He was elevated by the tyrant Theodahad without deliberation or decree. Having been corrupted by money, Theodahad instilled such fear in the clergy that anyone who did not consent to his appointment would be punished by the sword. For this reason the priests did not subscribe before his ordination, according to ancient custom, but afterward.

After two months, by divine providence, Theodahad was extinguished, and King Witigis was elevated. Coming to Ravenna, he took for himself as wife the daughter of Queen Amalasuntha. At this the Emperor Justinian, angered, sent the patrician Belisarius with an army to free all Italy from Gothic captivity.

Then, when the patrician came into the regions of Sicily, he heard that the Goths had made themselves a king and proceeded from there through Campania to Naples, which he began to besiege because the Neapolitan citizens had refused to open the city to him. He entered the city by fighting and, carried away by fury, killed both the Goths and all the Neapolitan citizens, sparing no sex or age, nor priests, servants of God, or consecrated women.

After waging a great war against Witigis, he entered the city of Rome on 10 December and fortified it. On the very night when he entered the city, those who were inside it and those outside fled to Ravenna, leaving all the gates open. Then King Witigis, gathering a multitude of Gothic troops, returned against Rome on 21 February and pitched camp at the Milvian Bridge. For one year the Roman city was so closely besieged that no one had the opportunity either to leave or to enter.

Within the city there was a great famine, so that water was sold at a price, unless the [remedy] of the Nymphs—*rechedus*, an uncertain reading—had come to the rescue. There were also very great battles, while Belisarius defended the Romans and the city; and he freed it from the Goths, whom he afterward forced to flee to Ravenna.

At that time Vigilius was deacon and *apocrisiarius* in Constantinople. He knew of the Emperor’s grief concerning Anthemius, the patriarch who had been deposed by the most holy Pope Agapitus because he had been found to be a heretic, and in whose place Agapitus had installed Maenas, a servant of God.

Finally, at Vigilius’s counsel, the Emperor sent letters to Rome, to Pope Silverius, asking and imploring him: “Either do not delay coming to us, or at least recall Anthemius to his place.” When blessed Silverius had read these letters, he groaned and said: “Now I know that this matter has brought about the end of my life.” Nevertheless, placing his confidence in the Lord, he wrote back to the Empress:

“Lady Empress, I shall never do this thing: recall a heretical man condemned in his wickedness.”

Then the indignant Empress sent orders to Belisarius through the deacon Vigilius:

“Find some pretext against Pope Silverius and depose him from the episcopate, or at least send him to us without delay. Behold, there you have Vigilius, our most beloved archdeacon and *apocrisiarius*, who promised us that he would recall the patriarch Anthemius.”

Having received the order, Belisarius said: “I shall indeed carry out the command, but let the man who is involved in the death of Pope Silverius himself give an account of his deeds to the Lord Jesus Christ.”

Under pressure from the order, certain false witnesses came forward and said: “On one occasion we found Pope Silverius sending written messages to the king of the Goths, in which it was stated: ‘Come to the gate called the Asinarian Gate, near the Lateran, and I will hand over the city and the patrician Belisarius.’”

When Belisarius heard this, he did not believe it, knowing that they were saying these things out of envy. But when many persisted in the same accusation, he became afraid. He had Silverius come to him in the Pincian palace and ordered the entire clergy to remain outside.

When Silverius had entered with Vigilius alone, the patrician Antonina, lying on her bed, saw him and said: “Tell me, Lord Pope Silverius, what have we done to you and to the Romans, that you should wish to hand us over to the Goths?”

While she was still speaking, John, a regional subdeacon of the first ecclesiastical region, entered, removed the pallium from Silverius’s neck, and led him into a chamber. There he stripped him and clothed him in a monastic garment.

When Xystus, a subdeacon of the sixth region, saw him as a monk, he went outside and announced to the clergy: “The lord Pope has been deposed and has been made a monk.” When they heard this, they all fled.

Vigilius the archdeacon then received him under the appearance of faithfulness and sent him into exile at Ponza, sustaining him with the bread of tribulation and the water of distress. Failing, he died as a confessor and was buried in that same place on 20 June; the sick are healed there. The episcopate was vacant for 5 days.

## LXI

VIGILIUS, a Roman by nation, son of John the Consul, sat for 17 years, 6 months, and 26 days.

At that time Belisarius waged war against Witigis, king of the Goths. When Witigis was fleeing by night, John, the *magister militum*, surnamed “the Bloodthirsty,” pursued him, captured him, and brought him to Belisarius. Belisarius, under oath, brought him safely to the Emperor Justinian in Constantinople. The Emperor made him patrician and count and sent him near the Persian frontier, where he ended his life.

The Emperor and the Empress gave thanks to Belisarius and sent him back to Africa, which was restored to the imperial government after the Vandal king [Gundar], Vuimarith, had been killed by treachery under the pretext of peace.

At that time the Empress Theodora wrote to Pope Vigilius: “Come and fulfill for us what you willingly promised concerning our father Anthemius, and restore him to his office.”

Vigilius wrote back: “Far be this from me, Lady Empress. Earlier I spoke wrongly and foolishly; now I will in no way consent to you, so as to restore a heretical and anathematized man. But if I am an unworthy vicar of blessed Peter the Apostle, how were my predecessors, the most holy Agapitus and Silverius, who condemned him?”

Then the Romans reported that Silverius had been deposed at Vigilius’s counsel, declaring that Vigilius was treating the Romans, your servants, and your own people badly. For he was so furious that he struck his notary on the face, and the man immediately fell at his feet and died.

Likewise, he gave his niece Vigilia to Astherius, a consul and the son of a widowed woman; he had him seized at night and beaten until he died.

When the Empress heard this, she sent Anthemius the *scribo* to Rome with a large force, saying: “Except in the basilica of Saint Peter, spare him. But if you find Vigilius in the Lateran, in the palace, or in any church, put him immediately on a ship and bring him to us. If you do not do this, I shall have you flayed alive by Him who lives forever.”

Anthemius the *scribo*, coming to Rome, found Vigilius in the church of Saint Cecilia on 22 November, for it was her feast day. He was found distributing gifts to the people. He was taken down to the Tiber and put on a ship, while the common people followed him, crying out that they wished to receive his prayer. After he had given the prayer, all the people said, “Amen,” and the ship began to move.

When the Romans saw that the ship in which Vigilius was sitting had begun to move, the people started throwing stones, clubs, and cooking pots after him, saying: “Your hunger go with you; your pestilence go with you. You have done evil to the Romans; may you meet evil wherever you are going.”

His supporters did indeed follow him from the church.

When he entered Sicily, he was permitted to ordain priests and deacons in the city of Catania during the month of December. From among them he sent back to Rome Ampliatus, his *vicedominus*, Valentinus, Bishop of Saint Rufina, and Secundus, to guard the Lateran and govern the clergy.

After bidding farewell to everyone, he entered Constantinople on the vigil of our Lord Jesus Christ. The Emperor came to meet him, kissed him, and began to weep, while that people sang before him all the way to the Church of Saint Sophia:

“Behold, the Lord who rules has arrived,” and so forth.

For two years there had been disputes concerning the patriarch Anthemius, and they displayed a written undertaking in his own hand by which Vigilius had promised to restore him to his place. But Vigilius, desiring death more than life, would not consent to them in any way and said: “As I see it, it was not Justinian and Theodora who caused me to come to them, but Diocletian and Eleutheria. Do as you wish, for I receive what my deeds deserve.”

Then someone struck him in the face, saying: “Murderer, do you not know what you are saying? Do you not know that you killed Pope Silverius and killed the son of a widow with kicks and clubs?”

Vigilius then fled into the basilica of Saint Euphemia and grasped the altar column. They dragged him away from it, threw him outside the church, had a rope placed around his neck, and dragged him through the entire city until evening.

He was then sent into custody, where he was given only a little bread and water. The Roman clergy who were with him were sent into exile to various mines.

Then the Goths, with their king Bandua, who was called Totila, descended upon Rome and besieged it. A famine arose in the Roman city, so severe that the people even wished to eat their own children.

One day the king entered Rome through the gate of Saint Paul, in the thirteenth indiction, and lived among the Romans like a father among his children.

Certain senators, however, fleeing, entered Constantinople and came before the Emperor distressed and desolate. The Emperor consoled them and sent Narses the eunuch, his chamberlain, into Italy. When Narses fought the Goths, God granted him victory: the king was killed, and a multitude of Goths was slain.

Then the assembled clergy asked Narses, together with his own petition, to ask the Emperor that, if Pope Vigilius were still alive, or if any priests, deacons, or clergy who had been exiled with him were still living, they might return.

When Narses’s report was received, the Emperor and all his illustrious officials rejoiced because God had granted rest to the Romans. He immediately sent to the various places where they had been exiled, at Gypsum and Proconnesus, and ordered them to come before him. He said to them:

“Do you wish to receive Vigilius as your Pope, or your archdeacon Pelagius? My hand will be with you.”

They all replied: “May God command your piety to restore Vigilius to us now. When God wishes him to pass from this world, then, with your command, let our archdeacon Pelagius be given to us.”

Then he released them all with Vigilius. They came to Sicily, to the city of Syracuse, where Vigilius, afflicted by the pain of kidney stones, died. His body was brought to Rome, and he was buried at Saint Marcellus on the Salarian Way. The episcopate was vacant for 3 months and 5 days.

## LXII

PELAGIUS, a Roman by nation, son of John Vicarianus, sat for 11 years, 10 months, and 18 days.

Since there were no bishops to ordain him, because a multitude of religious, learned, and noble persons had withdrawn from communion with him, saying that he had involved himself in the death of Pope Vigilius and that he had therefore been subjected to such punishments, he was ordained by two bishops—John of Perugia and Bonus of Ferentino—and by Andrew, a priest of Ostia. For there was no one in the clergy or the monasteries who could be promoted.

Then Narses and Pope Pelagius, having taken counsel together, set out from Saint Pancratius with a litany, hymns, and spiritual songs, and came to Saint Peter the Apostle. There the same Pope, holding the Gospels, with the Lord’s cross above his head, ascended the ambo and gave satisfaction to the people, declaring that he had done no wrong against Vigilius.

He also asked that it be confirmed that, if anyone in the holy Church—from the doorkeeper to the rank of bishop—should advance either through influence or through any promises, he should make no progress, because that is simony. He died and was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle. The episcopate was vacant for 2 months and 25 days.

## LXIII

JOHN, son of the illustrious Anastasius, sat for 12 years, 11 months, and 26 days.

At that time the Heruli came into Tharsia, having raised Sindald as their king, and oppressed all Italy. Narses went out against them, killed their king, and subjected the entire people.

Afterward, in the same way, the Frankish commanders Immingus and Bucellenus oppressed Italy; but, with the Lord’s help, they too were killed by Narses.

When all Italy rejoiced at this outcome, the Romans, moved by envy, reported to Justinian and [Sophia], saying that Narses, the eunuch who ruled, had preferred that the Romans serve the Goths rather than the Greeks.

When Narses heard this, he came from Rome to Campania and, indignant, wrote to the Lombard people to come and take possession of Italy.

When Pope John learned all this, he came quickly to Naples and prevailed upon Narses to return to Rome. Narses had decided to leave Italy, for which he had labored greatly, and return to Constantinople. Thus both of them returned.

The most holy John lived for a long time in the cemetery of Saints Tiburtius and Valerian. Narses, however, entered Rome and died after a long time. The most holy John also died and was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle. The episcopate was vacant for 10 months and 3 days.

## LXIV

BENEDICT, a Roman by nation, son of Boniface, sat for 4 years, 1 month, and 29 days.

At the same time the Lombard people invaded all Italy, and there was also such a severe famine that even the inhabitants of many fortified places surrendered themselves to the Lombards so that they might escape the shortage of food.

Placed amid these labors and afflictions, the most holy Pope died and was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle, in the sacristy. The episcopate was vacant for 3 months and 10 days.

## LXV

PELAGIUS, a Roman by nation, son of Unigildus, sat for 10 years, 2 months, and 10 days.

He was ordained without the Emperor’s command, because the Lombards were besieging the Roman city and harassing Italy with great devastation.

During his time there were such heavy rains that everyone said that the waters of the Flood had overflowed. There was such a disaster as no one in the world remembered ever having occurred.

He died and was buried at blessed Peter the Apostle. The episcopate was vacant for 3 months and 25 days.

## LXVI

GREGORY, a Roman by nation, son of Gordianus, sat for 13 years, 6 months, and 10 days.

He expounded homilies on the Gospels and added many other things that we cannot enumerate, including these words in the canon: “Dispose our days in your peace,” and so forth.

He also sent preachers to the people of the Angles to convert them to the Lord Jesus Christ. He made his own house into a monastery.

He died and was buried at blessed Peter the Apostle, before the sacristy, on 12 March. The episcopate was vacant for 5 months and 19 days.

## LXVII

SABINIAN, a Tuscan by nation, from the city of Blera, son of Bonus, sat for 1 year, 5 months, and 9 days.

At that time there was a severe famine in the Roman city. Having made peace with the Lombard people, he ordered the Church’s granaries to be opened and grain to be sold at one solidus for thirty *modii*.

He increased the lamps in the church of blessed Peter the Apostle. He was buried in the Church of blessed Peter the Apostle. He was deposed on 22 February. The episcopate was vacant for 10 months and 26 days.

## LXVIII

BONIFACE, a Roman by nation, son of John, sat for 8 months and 22 days.

He obtained from the Emperor Phocas that the Apostolic See of blessed Peter the Apostle should be the head of all the churches, because the see of Constantinople was writing that it was first among all the churches.

He also convened a synod in the Church of blessed Peter the Apostle, at which 72 bishops, 30 priests, 3 deacons, and the entire clergy were present. Under threat of anathema, it was decreed that no one should presume, while the Pope was alive, to call himself the bishop of the city or to form a faction for his election, except on the third day after his death. Then, once the clergy and the sons of the Church had assembled, an election was to be held, and each person would have the freedom to elect whichever priest he wished.

After his death he was buried in the Church of blessed Peter the Apostle on 12 November. The episcopate was vacant for 10 months and 6 days.

## LXIX

BONIFACE, a Marsian by nation, from the city of Valeria, son of John the physician, sat for 6 years, 8 months, and 13 days.

During his time there were extremely severe famine, pestilence, and floods.

He asked the Emperor Phocas for the temple called the Pantheon, in which he established a church of blessed Mary, ever-Virgin.

He died on 25 May and was buried at blessed Peter the Apostle.

## LXX

DEUSDEDIT, a Roman by nation, son of Stephen the subdeacon, sat for 3 years and 23 days.

He greatly loved the clergy. He recalled the priests and clergy to their former places.

During his time the patrician and chamberlain Eleutherius came from Ravenna and killed all those who had been involved in the death of John, the exarch and judge of the imperial government.

After he had been received most favorably by the most holy Pope Deusdedit, he left Rome and came to Naples, which was held by John Consinus, the usurper. Fighting against him, he killed that tyrant and entered Naples, killing many others with him. He then returned to Ravenna, where, after a military payment had been made to the soldiers, great peace was established throughout Italy.

He established that a second Mass should be celebrated among the clergy.

At that time there was a great earthquake in August, in the sixth indiction. After this came an outbreak of scabies among the people, so severe that no one could recognize his own dead.

He died on 8 November and was buried at blessed Peter the Apostle. For his service he left one complete military payment to the entire clergy. The episcopate was vacant for 1 month and 16 days.

## LXXI

BONIFACE, a Campanian by nation, from the city of Naples, son of John, sat for 5 years.

He decreed that a testament should be valid according to the Emperor’s command; that no one should be dragged from a church; that an acolyte should not presume to remove the relics of holy martyrs unless he were a priest; and that at the Lateran an acolyte should not baptize with a deacon, but that the succeeding subdeacons should do so.

At that time, before the day of his ordination, Eleutherius, the patrician and exarch, the usurper, seized the kingdom. When he came to the Roman city, he was killed by the soldiers of Ravenna in the fortress called Luciolus, and his head was carried to Constantinople to the most pious Emperor.

The blessed Boniface died and was buried at blessed Peter the Apostle on 25 October. The episcopate was vacant for 13 days.

## LXXII

HONORIUS, a Campanian by nation, son of Petronius the Consul, sat for 12 years, 11 months, and 17 days.

He established and decreed in the Church that every week, on Saturday, a litany should go out from Saint Apollinaris to blessed Peter the Apostle, and that the entire people should meet it with hymns and songs.

He was buried in the place mentioned above on 12 October. The episcopate was vacant for 1 year, 7 months, and 18 days.

## LXXIII

SEVERINUS, a Roman by nation, son of Abienus, sat for 2 months and 4 days.

During his time, while he had only been elected and had not yet been ordained, the Lateran episcopal residence was devastated by Mauritius the *chartularius* and Isacius, the patrician and exarch of Italy. After taking counsel against the Church of God, they incited the Roman army, saying:

“What benefit is it that such great sums of money have been gathered in the Lateran episcopal residence by Pope Honorius, when none of it is used to support the soldiers, although the payments that the Lord Emperor has periodically ordered to be given to you are kept there by the holy man?”

When they heard this, all armed men, from child to old man, came to the aforesaid Church. Nevertheless, they could not break into it, because those who were with the most holy Severinus resisted them.

Therefore Mauritius, unable to accomplish by force what he wished, did it by deceit. He entered the wardrobe of the Lateran episcopal residence and sealed everything that Christian devotion had left to Saint Peter for the redemption of souls.

Afterward he sent letters to Ravenna to the patrician Isacius, who immediately came to Rome and ordered all the leading members of the Church to be sent into exile, so that no one would remain to obstruct his affairs.

Then, after several days, he entered the Lateran episcopal residence and plundered it for eight days. He sent most of its contents to the Emperor Heraclius in Constantinople.

Thus the most holy Severinus was ordained. He too was buried at blessed Peter the Apostle on 2 August. The episcopate was vacant for 4 months and 29 days.

## LXXIV

JOHN, a Dalmatian by nation, son of Venantius the Scholastic, sat for 1 year, 9 months, and 19 days.

He sent large sums of money throughout Dalmatia and Histria through the most holy and faithful Abbot Martin, for the redemption of captives who had been carried off by foreign peoples.

He was buried at blessed Peter the Apostle on 15 October. The episcopate was vacant for 1 month and 10 days.

## LXXV

THEODORE, a Greek by nation, son of Theodore, Bishop of the city of Jerusalem, sat for 6 years, 5 months, and 18 days.

During his time Mauritius the *chartularius*, through whom Isacius had perpetrated many evils, conspired against Isacius. He joined to himself all those who, while living in the forts around the Roman city, had devastated the Church of God, wishing to assume the title of king.

When Isacius heard this, he sent Donus, his *magister militum* and *sacellarius*, to the Roman city. After abandoning Mauritius, the entire Roman army went out to meet Donus.

Mauritius himself fled to Saint Mary at the Crib. From there he was dragged out, a halter was placed miserably around his neck, and he was sent, together with all his counselors who had been similarly bound, to Ravenna at the hands of Marinus the *scribo* and Thomas the *chartularius*.

Near Ravenna, at a place called Ficudæ, twelve miles from the city, they beheaded him, as Isacius had ordered. His head was brought to Ravenna. When Isacius saw it, he rejoiced greatly and, as an example to many, ordered it to be carried around the city and then placed on a stake.

As for those who had been sent with him in fetters, Isacius kept them under strict guard while considering by what death he should punish them. But by God’s will he was struck down and died, and those men returned from prison to their homes.

When the Emperor heard of Isacius’s death, he sent Theodore the patrician and exarch, surnamed Calliopas, to govern all Italy.

At that time Pyrrhus, who had been Bishop and patriarch of Constantinople, came from Africa to the threshold of the Apostles. He presented the Apostolic See with a document bearing his signature, condemning everything that he or his predecessors had written or done against our immaculate faith.

The Lord Pope honored him as a priest of the imperial city and had a chair placed for him beside the altar.

But when he again returned, like a dog, to his own vomit of impiety, the most holy Theodore summoned all the priests and the clergy and condemned him under the bond of anathema in the Church of blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles.

Then he regularly rebuked Paul, patriarch of the imperial city, and also admonished him through the *apocrisiarii* to correct his own formulation and return to the orthodox faith and the Catholic Church.

When he finally could not recall him from his undertaking, he struck him with the penalty of deposition, according to Apostolic authority.

Blessed Theodore was buried at blessed Peter the Apostle on the day before 15 May.

## LXXVI

MARTIN, from the city of Todi in the province of Tuscany, sat for 6 years, 1 month, and 26 days.

During his time Paul, Bishop of Constantinople, inflamed with the spirit of pride, strove not only in words but also in writings and through the opinions of most wicked heretics to weaken Catholic doctrine. He defined that one should confess in Christ the Lord neither one nor two wills or operations.

Through this presumption he reached such madness that he overturned the altar of the holy Roman See, which had been consecrated in the house of Placidia, and forbade our *apocrisiarii* to offer the immaculate offering there.

Because they consistently called him a heretic, those *apocrisiarii* were detained and thrown into custody; others were sent into exile, and some were afflicted with beatings.

When the most holy Bishop Martin heard this, he sent for and gathered 105 bishops in the city of Rome. He held a synod according to the institutions of the orthodox Fathers in the Church of the Savior beside the Lateran episcopal residence. The bishops and priests were seated, while the deacons and the entire clergy stood by.

There they condemned, under the penalty of anathema, Cyrus of Alexandria, Pyrrhus, Sergius, and Paul, patriarch of Constantinople.

During those same days the Emperor sent Olympius, his chamberlain and exarch, to Italy to govern the whole country. He instructed him, as Paul had advised, to make all the bishops of Italy subscribe to the *Typos*, the document issued by Paul.

If it could in any way be done, he was to seize Pope Martin himself, because then the bishops of Italy would more easily subscribe. If the Roman or Ravennate army opposed him, he was to remain silent for the moment until he had obtained the whole province.

Obeying these orders, Olympius came to Rome and found the holy Roman Church most firmly established in the Catholic faith. He wished, armed with his army, to introduce schism, but, prevented by God’s power, he was forced to abandon his evil intention openly.

Therefore, in the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, at the Crib, while the Lord Pope was offering him Communion during the solemn celebration of Mass, he wished to kill him. He had commanded this to his *spatharius*, but Almighty God blinded the man so that the blood of the most holy Bishop would not be shed and the Catholic Church would not be subjected to heresy.

For that armed man himself confessed under oath that this was what had happened.

When the exarch Olympius saw that God’s hand was protecting the most holy Pope Martin, he made peace with him. He then gathered his army and went to Sicily against the Saracen people, where most of the Roman army perished and the exarch himself died of illness.

He was succeeded by Theodore the exarch, sent by the Emperor, who was surnamed Calliopas, together with Theodore the imperial chamberlain, also called Pellurius.

They took Pope Martin from the Church of the Savior, which is called Constantiniana, brought him to Constantinople, and even there he did not yield to them.

Therefore he was sent into exile, to a place called Cherson, where, as God willed, he ended his life in peace on 17 September. As a confessor, he performs many miracles to this present day.

## LXXVII

EUGENE, a Roman by nation, from the first region of the Aventine, a cleric from the cradle, son of Rufinianus, sat for 2 years, 9 months, and 24 days.

During his time Peter, patriarch of Constantinople, sent a Synodical letter to the Apostolic See according to custom, but it was exceedingly obscure and did not declare the operations or wills in our Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore the people and clergy, inflamed with even greater uproar, cast it out of the holy Church of God. They would not even allow the same Pope to celebrate Mass in the basilica of Saint Mary, Mother of God, at the Crib unless he promised that he would by no means receive it.

He too was buried at blessed Peter the Apostle on 2 June. The episcopate was vacant for 1 month and 28 days.

## LXXVIII

VITALIAN, a Segnian by nation, from the province of Campania, son of Anastasius, sat for 14 years and 6 months.

He sent his representatives with a Synodical letter, according to custom, to the imperial city, to the most pious Emperors, announcing his ordination.

During his time Constantine Augustus came to Rome. The same Pope received him and went out to meet him at the fifth milestone from the city, in the sixth indiction.

After remaining in the Roman city for twelve days and offering many gifts in various places, Constantine removed all the bronze objects that were there for the city’s adornment.

He also stripped the Church of Saint Mary at the Martyrs of its bronze roof tiles and sent them, together with the other objects, to the imperial city.

Afterward he returned to Sicily and lived at Syracuse. There he imposed upon the peoples of the provinces of Calabria, Sicily, Africa, and Sardinia such afflictions through *diagrapha*, that is, head taxes and ship levies, as had never been heard of in the world. He also removed the sacred vessels and treasures of the holy Churches of God.

Later, on 15 July, in the twelfth indiction, he was betrayed and killed in a bath.
