The death of the most holy Vitalian immediately followed. He was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on 27 January. The episcopate was vacant for 2 months and 13 days.

## LXXIX

ADEODATUS, a Roman by nation, from the monks, son of Jovianus, sat for 4 years, 2 months, and 5 days.

During his time Mezentius, who was in Sicily with an eastern army, seized the kingdom and “intarzizavit” [an uncertain reading, apparently indicating that he tyrannized or usurped power]. The army of Italy fled in different directions until, with God’s help, he himself was killed and his head was brought by *intarta* [an uncertain term] to Constantinople.

After his death the Saracens took possession of Sicily. After killing many people, the population fled to the mountains or to fortified places. The Saracens then returned to Alexandria, carrying with them the goods that had been transported there by ship from the Roman city.

The aforesaid most holy man also acquired rural estates and, during his lifetime, established an abbot and a community there.

After his passing there were such rains and thunder that no age remembered their like. Unless the Lord had been appeased by the litanies that were performed daily, human beings and cattle would have perished.

Although legumes grew again in the fields, because of the excessive rains people could store no grain from the threshing floors in the granaries.

The most blessed Adeodatus was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on 10 July. The episcopate was vacant for 4 months and 15 days.

## LXXX

DONUS, a Roman by nation, son of Mauricius, sat for 1 year, 6 months, and 10 days.

In the city of Rome, in the monastery called Boeziana, he found Syrian Nestorianist monks. He distributed them among various monasteries and established Roman monks there.

During his time the Church of Ravenna, which had separated itself from the Roman Church on account of autocephaly, again subjected itself to its former Apostolic See.

The bishop of that Church, named Reparatus, immediately ended his life, as God willed.

While Donus was elected in the month of August, a star appeared in the east and remained visible from cockcrow until morning for three months; its rays penetrated the heavens. Afterward it turned back upon itself and disappeared, and a great mortality of human beings followed in the eastern region.

He was buried at blessed Peter the Apostle on 11 April. The episcopate was vacant for 2 months and 15 days.

## LXXXI
AGATHO, a Sicilian by nation, held the see for 2 years, 6 months, and 3 days. During his pontificate, Theodore, Archbishop of Ravenna, after the passage of many years, presented himself again to the Apostolic See. He received the imperial command of the most devout rulers, the Augusti Constantine, Heraclius, and Tiberius, through Epiphanius the glorious *a secretis* official. This command had been sent to his predecessor, Pope Donus, exhorting him to send priests or his representatives to the royal city for the unification of the holy Churches of God. He did not delay in doing so, and sent bishops, priests, and devout monks there as quickly as possible.

At that time the moon underwent an eclipse, on 18 June, in the eighth indiction. A most grievous mortality followed during the three succeeding months and ravaged the City both within and without to such an extent as is remembered not to have occurred in the times of any other pontiffs.

Finally, the legates of the Apostolic See entered the royal city on 10 November, in the ninth indiction. With the Lord accompanying them, they were received in the oratory of the blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, within the palace, and presented to him the Pope’s letters as well. When he had received them, he admonished them that, setting aside philosophical assertions, they should satisfy him through synodal decrees with the pure faith of the holy Fathers, confirmed by the Scriptures—not through anger, but through a peaceful disposition—and he granted them a postponement for reconsideration, providing them with everything necessary for their support in the house called Placidia.

On the Lord’s Day, therefore, they were summoned to the holy Mother of God at Blachernae with such great honor that he even sent horses with attendants for them from the palace. On 22 November also, in the basilica called the Trullus, the Emperor sat in royal attire, together with George, Patriarch of Constantinople, and Macarius of Antioch, and with the representatives of the Apostolic See and the bishops of the eastern regions, 150 in number.

After this they brought in various books and volumes, as well as synods which the heretics had falsified, believing that they could prevail not by truth but by deceit. They said that Christ had not two wills and operations but one; this became clear before the Prince and the Synod.

Then the devout Prince ordered the representatives to sit in the Synod, occupying the place of the most holy Pope Agatho. They were told to bring before the Synod all the books which they knew to pertain to the matter of faith, and this was done. [Col. 0561A] George the deacon and keeper of the archives of the Church of Constantinople was then summoned, and he was ordered to bring forth from the Church’s library, according to their information, the books relevant to the matter.

In these it was found that Christ had two natures and two wills or operations. Macarius, by contrast, was found to have confessed falsely. Then the imperial piety forbade George the Patriarch to receive Macarius and his followers in his own Church.

Next, so that the light of truth might appear, the statements of the venerable Fathers John of Constantinople, Cyril, Athanasius, Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Dionysius, Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, and Leo were brought before the Synod. These statements affirmed that Christ had two natures and two wills or operations, to satisfy the Prince and the Synod.

On the following day the synodical letter of the most holy Pope Agatho was reread. It had been approved by the Catholic Fathers and subscribed by 120 Western bishops.

After this everyone urged Macarius to state his opinion concerning Christ’s will or operation. Since he refused to say either that Christ had one or that he had two wills or operations, the most serene Prince brought forth Macarius’s own volume, in which he had most plainly affirmed one will in the Lord and had subscribed it with his own hand, together with Theodore and the Patriarchs.

But George, the most holy Patriarch, repented of his error and professed that he believed and preached as the Apostolic See teaches. Therefore, together with the other Catholics, he anathematized all the heretics and Macarius himself. After Basil, Bishop of Crete, had removed Macarius’s *orarium* at the command of the Synod and the Prince, they anathematized him outside the Synod and cast him out together with his throne. Stephen, his disciple, was expelled from the presence of the holy Synod by the Roman clergy.

At that same hour such a quantity of exceedingly black spiderwebs fell in the midst of the people that everyone marveled. Thus, after the filth of the heresies had been expelled, the holy Church of God was united.

Theophanius, abbot of the monastery of Pagias on the island of Sicily, was appointed in Macarius’s place and became patriarch of the Church of Antioch. Macarius and his supporters were sent into exile to the city of Rome. It was decreed that the names of the Patriarchs should be removed from the diptychs of the Churches and from paintings or doors wherever they might be found: namely, those of Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul, and also that of Peter, through whom this error had sprung up.

The Catholic people, however, received such a great favor that, for the joy of the holy Council being held in the royal city, John, Bishop of Porto, who was one of the legates, celebrated public Masses in Latin on the Lord’s Day of the octave of Easter in the Church of Saint Sophia before the Prince and the Patriarch, and everyone with one voice acclaimed all the praises and victories of the most devout Emperors.

He also received an imperial command, according to his request, by which the amount customarily paid for the ordination of a pontiff was reduced, with the proviso that, if an election should take place after his death, no one was to be ordained unless a general decree had first been introduced from the royal city according to ancient custom.

The holy Agatho was buried at the blessed Peter the Apostle on 10 January. The episcopate remained vacant for 1 year, 7 months, and 5 days.

## LXXXII

LEO the Younger, a Sicilian by nation, son of Paul, held the see for 10 months and 17 days. He was highly eloquent, adequately trained in the divine Scriptures, learned in the Greek and Latin languages, outstanding in song and psalmody, and refined by the most subtle practice in understanding them.

When he received the holy Sixth Synod, which had been held in the royal city under the Emperor Constantine by the two Patriarchs, of Constantinople [Col. 0562B] and Antioch, together with 150 bishops, he translated it most carefully from Greek into Latin.

Although he condemned the other heretics, he absolved only two: namely, Anastasius the priest and Leontinus the deacon, on the holy day of the Epiphany, when they set forth their faith in their own writings according to what the holy Synod had determined.

During his pontificate, when the imperial command of the most devout Prince was carried out, the Church of Ravenna was restored under the authority of the Apostolic See. It was decreed that, after the death of the archbishop, the person elected should come to the city of Rome to be ordained, and it was established what he ought to pay for the use of the pallium or for various services of the Church.

They also restored, in order to remove scandals from the Apostolic See, the practice that neither the anniversary nor the *Agenda* of the former Bishop Maurus should be celebrated, as well as the charter of autocephaly which they had secured for themselves.

During his pontificate also, the moon underwent an eclipse on 15 April, in the eleventh indiction. After the Lord’s Supper, almost the entire night was turned into blood.

He too was buried at the blessed Peter the Apostle on 3 July. The episcopate remained vacant for 11 months and 22 days.

## LXXXIII

BENEDICT the Younger, a Roman by nation, son of John, held the see for 10 months and 12 days. From childhood he was highly learned in the Scriptures and in song, and was kindly.

He received the imperial commands of the great Prince Constantine addressed to the venerable clergy and people, and to the most fortunate army of the city of Rome. Through them it was granted that whoever was elected to the Apostolic See should immediately and without delay be ordained bishop.

Together with the clergy and the army he received locks of hair from the lord Justin and Heraclius, sons of the most merciful Prince.

At that time a star appeared at night like the moon beneath a cloud, between the Nativity of the Lord and the Epiphany. Likewise, near the end of February, a star emerged during the day in the west and moved toward the eastern regions.

After this, Mount Bebius, which is in Campania, erupted throughout the day in March, and all the surrounding places were destroyed by the dust.

He was immediately seized by illness, died, and was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on 8 May. The episcopate remained vacant for 2 months and 15 days.

## LXXXIV

[Col. 0563A]

JOHN, a Syrian by nation, from the province of Antioch, son of Cyriacus, held the see for 1 year and 9 days. He was exceedingly energetic and endowed with learning.

When he was a deacon, he had been sent by Pope Agatho, of holy memory, to the royal city with other priests, and represented the Apostolic See at the holy Sixth Synod. After obtaining from the most merciful Prince the things for which he had gone, he returned and was elected in the Constantinian Church.

At that time Justinian Augustus was reigning, having succeeded his father at the beginning of September, in the fourteenth indiction. Immediately, with God’s help, he established peace with the Saracen people for ten years, on land and sea.

The province of Africa was also brought under the Roman Empire and restored.

After the passage of many years, he reinstated and confirmed under the jurisdiction of the same Church the bishop of the Church of Turris, whom Citonatus, Archbishop of Cagliari, had made without the authority of the Roman Pontiff.

This most holy man, after being held by a long illness, died and was buried at the blessed Peter the Apostle on the second day of August. The episcopate remained vacant for 2 months and 18 days.

## LXXXV

CONON, born of a Thracian father and raised in Sicily, later came to Rome to serve that Church and attained the dignity of the priesthood. He held the see for 11 months.

The clergy and people agreed upon his election, although a considerable dispute had arisen because the clergy supported Peter the archpriest, while the army supported his successor, Theodore the priest.

The clergy kept watch before the doors of the Constantinian basilica, while the army occupied the basilica of the blessed Stephen the Protomartyr. Since neither side would yield to the other, the priests and clergy entered the Lateran Episcopium unanimously and elected the aforesaid pontiff. He truly had an angelic appearance, venerable gray hair, and truthful speech.

When the army saw this, after several days it yielded, subscribed together with the clergy, and, as was customary, sent legates to the excellent Theodore, the exarch.

Conon received an imperial command from the Prince Justinian, which stated that the acts of the Sixth Synod were in his possession—acts which his father, the lord Constantine, of pious memory, had carried out with God’s help.

During his pontificate, the imperial piety remitted two hundred measures of grain which the Bruttii and Lucania had paid annually.

Beyond custom, and without the consent of the clergy, he appointed Constantine, a deacon of the Church of Syracuse, rector of the Sicilian patrimony. He was a harsh and deceitful man, whom Conon permitted to use *mappulae* for riding.

After the Pontiff’s departure, an uprising arose against him among the citizens because of disputes over the patrimony. He was confined under strict guard by the provincial judge, because he was found to be involved in the judges’ dissension.

When the most holy Pontiff died after being held by a long illness, he left much gold to all the clergy and monasteries, just as his predecessor, Pope Benedict, had done.

His archdeacon, seeing him grow ill and driven by greed, refused to distribute the gold. Instead, he wrote to John, the glorious new exarch residing at Ravenna, promising him gifts if, through his faction, he himself were elected to the pontificate. The exarch sent instructions to Rome that this should be done.

The most blessed Pontiff was buried at the blessed Peter the Apostle on 22 September. The episcopate remained vacant for 2 months and 23 days.

## LXXXVI

SERGIUS, a Syrian by nation, born in the region of Antioch to a father named Tiberius, in Palermo of Sicily, held the see for 13 years, 8 months, and 23 days.

He came to Rome under Pope Adeodatus, of holy memory, and was enrolled among the clergy of the Roman Church. Since he was diligent and capable in the office of song, he was entrusted to the prior of the singers for instruction. He was made an acolyte and advanced through the ranks up to the priesthood, in which he was consecrated by Pope Leo at the title-church of Saint Susanna.

When Conon, of holy memory, died, as usually happened, one part of the Roman people supported the election of Theodore the archpriest, and another part the election of Paschal the archdeacon. Since both sides persisted fiercely in their positions, the chief judges, the army of the Roman military, and a large part of the clergy went to the sacred palace and deliberated how the quarrel might be brought to an end.

With God’s consent they settled upon the person of the aforesaid Sergius. Taking him from the midst of the people, they brought him into the oratory of the blessed Caesarius, martyr of Christ, which was inside the palace, and from there led him to the Lateran Episcopium with acclamations of praise.

When he entered the palace, one of the two elected men—namely, Theodore the archpriest—immediately yielded, humbled himself, saluted him, and kissed him. Paschal, however, did not yield at all at first, though he eventually saluted him.

Nevertheless, secretly he did not cease sending messages to Ravenna, persuading John Patricius and exarch to come to Rome. John came out of love for the promised money. When he found that everyone had agreed upon Sergius, he was unable to aid Paschal, and therefore inflicted a loss upon the Church of the blessed Peter the Apostle from its own funds, demanding one hundred pounds of gold from the aforesaid Pontiff—the sum which the wretched archdeacon had promised him.

After a long time, because of the incantations and the *loculi* [or *lucos*, according to the variant] which he worshipped, and the lots which he practiced, he was stripped of office and confined in a monastery. After five years he died unrepentant because of the hardness of his heart.

Finally, during the pontificate of Sergius, the Emperor Justinian ordered a council to be held in the royal city. There the representatives of the Apostolic See were deceived and subscribed to certain chapters issued outside ecclesiastical custom, and they sent them to the Roman Pontiff, as the head of all priests, asking him to subscribe.

But the most blessed Pontiff absolutely refused. He would not receive those volumes or allow them to be opened for reading; instead, he rejected and cast them aside as invalid, choosing to die rather than consent to the errors of novelties.

Therefore, in anger, the Emperor sent Magistrianus to Rome to transfer John, the God-beloved Bishop of Porto, and Boniface, the Pope’s counselor, to the royal city. Then he sent his *protospatharius* Zacharias, ordering him to do the same with the Roman Pontiff.

But by God’s mercy the heart of the army of Ravenna was stirred, as was that of the Duchy of the Pentapolis, and they prevented this from happening. They entered through the gate of the blessed Peter with arms and with a crowd from the Lateran Episcopium, wishing to see the Pontiff, whom rumor had said had been taken away by ship during the night.

The most holy Pontiff Sergius therefore went out to meet the soldiers before the doors of the basilica called that of Pope Theodore. With a gentle reply he soothed their hearts and rescued Zacharias from their hands, for they wished to expel him from the city of Rome with insults and abuse; he had hidden beneath the Pontiff’s bed.

At that time the man who had sent him was, by God’s repayment, deprived of his kingdom, and the state of the Church was preserved under Christ’s governance.

Moreover, the blessed man found in the treasury of Saint Peter the Apostle a silver chest lying in the darkest corner. He removed its seal and opened the small container within. There he found a silk covering placed over the contents, called a *staurarium*. After removing it, he saw beneath it a cross adorned with various precious stones.

When four petals were removed from it, within which gems of marvelous size had been enclosed, an ineffable portion of the saving wood of the Lord’s Cross was found. For the salvation of the human race, he established that it should be kissed and adored by all the Christian people on the day of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross in the basilica of the Savior called the Constantinian.

After many other things which he did, renewed, or bestowed in the Churches of God, he established that at the time of the breaking of the Lord’s body the clergy and people should sing: “Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world,” and so forth.

He also established that on the days of the Annunciation of the Lord, the Dormition and Nativity of holy Mary, Mother of God, and Saint Simeon’s feast—which the Greeks call the *Hypapante*—the litany should go out from Saint Hadrian’s, and the people should meet at Saint Mary’s.

This blessed man was buried in the basilica of the blessed Peter the Apostle on 8 September, in the fourteenth indiction, under Tiberius Augustus. The episcopate remained vacant for 1 month and 20 days.

## LXXXVII

[Col. 0565D]

JOHN, a Greek by nation, held the see for 3 years, 2 months, and 12 days.

During his pontificate Theophylact, the chamberlain, Patricius, and exarch of Italy, came to the city of Rome from Sicily. Wishing to strip certain inhabitants of the City of their property, he provoked a most serious uprising against himself.

The Pontiff quelled it with salutary admonitions. He placed himself between the parties, closed the gates of the city, and sent priests to the ditch where they had assembled.

Then, when Gisulf, duke of the Lombard people at Benevento, came with all his forces, setting fires and carrying out much plundering in Campania, and taking not a few captives, he dug a ditch as far as the place called Horreas. Since no one was able to resist him, the aforesaid Pontiff sent priests with Apostolic gifts and redeemed all the captives from his hands, causing him and his army to return to their own territory.

After his death the episcopate remained vacant for 1 month and 18 days.

## LXXXVIII

JOHN, a Greek by nation, son of Plato, held the see for 2 years, 7 months, and 17 days. He was a most learned man and eloquent in speech.

During his pontificate Aripert, king of the Lombards, wrote a donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps in letters of gold and restored it to the right of the Roman Church. That patrimony had been held for a long time by the same Lombard people.

At that time also the Emperor Justinian came from the regions of Khazaria through the lands of Bulgaria with Trebellus to the royal city and recovered his own kingdom, from which he had been expelled.

He captured Leo and Tiberius, who had usurped his position, and had them slaughtered in the middle of the Circus before the entire people.

He also sent to Rome, through two metropolitan bishops, the volumes which he had previously sent under the lord Sergius, of Apostolic memory. They contained various chapters opposed to the Roman Church. He adjured them to have the Apostolic Church convene a council, confirm what had been removed, and reject and annul whatever was contrary.

This man, however, timid through human weakness, did not correct them at all but sent them back to the Prince. Not long afterward he departed this life and was gathered to his fathers. The episcopate remained vacant for 3 months.

## LXXXIX

SISINNIUS, a Syrian by nation, son of John, held the see for 20 days. He was so constrained by gout in his feet and hands that he was unable to bring food to his mouth with his own hands.

Therefore he died a sudden death. The episcopate remained vacant for 1 month and 28 days.

## XC

CONSTANTINE, a Syrian by nation, son of John, held the see for 7 years and 15 days. He was exceedingly gentle.

During his pontificate a great famine occurred in the city of Rome for three years. It was followed by such abundance that the profusion of fertility caused the scarcity of sterility to be forgotten.

He ordained Felix Archbishop of Ravenna. Following the custom of his predecessors, Felix refused to provide the required guarantees and, through the power of the judges, acted as he wished.

Therefore the Emperor Justinian sent Theodore Patricius, first officer of the army of the island of Sicily, with a fleet, and he captured Ravenna. He seized the arrogant archbishop, bound him in a ship, deprived him of the light of his eyes, and sent him into exile beyond the Pontus. All the rebels whom he found there he bound in chains, took away their wealth, and sent them to Constantinople.

At that time, by sacred imperial command, the aforesaid Pontiff Constantine was ordered to ascend to the royal city. He did so on 5 October, in the ninth indiction.

He was followed by Nicetas, Bishop of Silva Candida; George, Bishop of Porto; Michael, Paul, and George, priests; Gregory, a deacon; George, the *secundicerius*; John, first of the defenders; Cosmas, the treasurer; Sisinnius, the *nomenclator*; Sergius, the archivist; Dorotheus and Julian, subdeacons; and a few clerics from the other ranks of the Church.

When he reached Naples, he found there John Patricius and exarch, surnamed Rizocopus. While stationed at Rome, this man had beheaded Sajulus the deacon, Peter the treasurer, Sergius the abbot, and Sergius the ordainer. After returning to Ravenna, he died a most shameful death.

Finally, while the supreme Pontiff and his companions were traveling toward Sicily, Theodore Patricius and the *stratigos*, who was suffering from illness, met him. The Pontiff received him with great reverence, and he quickly obtained healing.

Crossing by way of Reggio, Croton, and Callipolis, he came to Hydruntum, where Bishop Nicetas died. He delayed there because it was winter. There he received the imperial seal through Theophanius the regional official. It stated that all judges should receive the Pontiff as though he were the Emperor himself.

From there they departed by way of the island of Chios and came to the seventh milestone from the royal city. There Tiberius, the Emperor, son of Justinian Augustus, came out to meet him, together with Cyrus the Patriarch, the clergy, and a multitude of people, all rejoicing and celebrating a feast day.

Using an imperial saddle, the Apostolic Pontiff entered the city with a *camelaucum*, as he was accustomed to proceed at Rome.

When the Emperor Justinian heard this, he was filled with joy and sent from Nicaea in Bithynia a sacred letter full of thanksgiving, asking that the Pontiff meet him at Nicomedia while he himself came from Nicaea. This was done.

The most Christian Augustus prostrated himself, kissed the Pontiff’s feet, and they rushed into one another’s arms. Then, with him, he celebrated Mass for the Emperor on the Lord’s Day with such joy that, after communicating from the Pontiff’s hands, the Prince obtained from him prayers for the forgiveness of his sins. He thus renewed all the privileges of his Church.

Returning to Rome from the city of Nicomedia after frequent voyages, and with the Lord granting him safety, he reached the port of Gaeta unharmed. There he found a very large crowd of Roman people, and on 24 October, in the tenth indiction, he entered Rome.

After three months, however, a mournful message arrived reporting that Justinian the orthodox Emperor had been massacred and that Philippicus the heretic had been raised to the imperial power. Constantine received his imperial letter, written together with its corrupt doctrine, but rejected it in agreement with the Council of the Apostolic See.

At the same time Felix, Archbishop of Ravenna, was brought back from exile. Moved to repentance, and although deprived of the light of his eyes, he nevertheless returned to his own throne and, after confessing the expositions of the faith, earned absolution through reconciliation.

At that time also two kings of Saxony came swiftly to Rome out of love for the Apostles and ended their lives there as they desired.

Benedict, Archbishop of Milan, also came to fulfill a vow of prayer and presented himself to his Pontiff, putting aside the dispute concerning the Church of Pavia, whose bishop was to be consecrated by the lord Pope.

Finally, the Roman people decreed that they would in no way receive the name of the heretical Emperor, whether in documents or on coins or images, nor commemorate him during the solemn celebrations of Mass.

It happened that a certain Peter was sent to Ravenna for the Duchy of the city of Rome and had recorded the name of the heretical Emperor in his appointment. Therefore the Roman people refused to accept this duke, and so violent a civil war arose with Duke Christopher that they engaged one another on the Sacred Way before the palace. More than thirty men of both sides were scourged so severely that they died.

The disturbance did not cease until the Pontiff sent priests with Gospels and crosses to calm it.

Not many days afterward a messenger came from Sicily announcing that Philippicus the heretic had been expelled from the imperial throne and that Anastasius the orthodox had assumed the imperial scepters.

Scholasticus the chamberlain, Patricius and exarch, came to Rome and declared to everyone that Anastasius was a confessor of the holy Sixth Council and a preacher of the true faith.

After the death of so great a Pontiff, the episcopate remained vacant for 40 days.

## XCI

GREGORY, a Roman by nation, son of Marcellus, held the see for 15 years, 8 months, and 24 days.

He lived during the reigns of the Augusti Anastasius, Theodosius, Leo, and Constantine. As a child he was brought up in the patriarchate under the lord Pope Sergius, of holy memory, and was made treasurer, with responsibility for the Library entrusted to him.

Later, when he had been promoted to the order of the diaconate, he went with the holy Pontiff Constantine to the royal city. There he gave an excellent answer to each question put by the Prince Justinian concerning certain chapters.

He was a chaste man, learned in the divine Scriptures. John, the bishop of Constantinople, sent a synodical letter to him, and the same Pontiff subscribed it.

Among the many good works he performed, he preached the word of salvation in Germany through Bishop Boniface and converted that people, which sat in darkness, to Christ through the teaching of light.

At that time Luitprand, king of the Lombards, confirmed the return of the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps which King Aripert had made, at the admonition of so great a man.

A sign also occurred in the moon during the fourteenth indiction: it appeared full of blood until midnight.

Theudo, duke of the Bavarian people, was also the first from that nation to come to the threshold of the blessed Peter the Apostle as a pilgrim for prayer.

After this the Emperor Anastasius sent a prepared fleet of ships from Alexandria against the Agarene people. They, having turned to another plan, returned from the middle of their journey to the royal city, elected Theodosius the orthodox Emperor, and compelled him to accept and confirm the imperial throne.

Anastasius therefore fortified the city of Nicaea with its citizens and with as many of the army as he could, and fought with the fleet in which Theodosius had been. Nearly seven thousand of the army were killed.

After Anastasius’s side was defeated, he himself requested a promise of immunity. After giving an oath, he became a cleric and was consecrated a priest.

Theodosius then immediately entered the royal city, restored to their former state the things which had been overthrown by Philippicus, and greatly benefited the Church through the fervor of his faith.

At that time the river Tiber left its bed and rose beyond measure, so that in the Via Lata its waters rose to a height of one and a half human stature. The waters spread from the gate of the blessed Peter the Apostle as far as the Milvian Bridge.

The greatest tribulation therefore threatened the Romans, because they were unable to sow. For this reason litanies were frequently held by the lord Pope.

At last, on the eighth day, they ceased, in the fifteenth indiction.

At the same time the fortress of Cumae had been seized by the Lombards through the treachery of a supposed peace. Since the lord Pope was unable to recover it either by prayers or gifts, John, Duke of Naples, entered its walls silently by night with Theodinus the subdeacon and rector, together with an army. They killed nearly three hundred Lombards and their *castaldus*, and brought the rest of the captives to Naples.

In this way they recovered the fortress. For its redemption the most holy Pope paid seventy pounds of gold, as he had promised.

At that time also the wicked race of the Saracens, after having held the province of Spain under occupation for ten years, attempted in the eleventh year to cross the Rhône River and occupy Francia, where Eudo was in command.

After issuing a general summons to the Franks, Eudo surrounded and destroyed the Saracens. Of them, 365,000 were killed in a single day, as the letter of that same Eudo, Duke of the Franks, sent to the aforesaid Pontiff records. Of the Franks only 1,050 died in that battle.

More of them did not perish because, in the preceding year, the same Duke Eudo had received three sponges as a blessing from the aforesaid Pontiff. At the hour when the battle was joined, whoever managed to obtain a small piece of one of them was neither wounded nor killed.

At the same time, in the regions of Campania, burned wheat, barley, and legumes fell from the sky in a certain place as though it were rain.

This Pontiff established that the fast and celebration of Mass which had not previously been observed on Thursday during Lent should be held.

Meanwhile, Constantinople was besieged by the Saracens for two years. But since God opposed them, the greater part of them were killed there by famine and war, and, with the consent of the Emperor Leo, they withdrew in confusion.

It was also said that nearly 300,000 people of different sexes and ages in that city were destroyed by the necessity of pestilence.

At that same time the Pope’s mother, a woman certainly honorable in character and in name, was taken from this life. After her death he built anew, from the foundations, his own house in honor of Saint Agatha, martyr of Christ, adding dining rooms and whatever was necessary for a monastery of monks. He endowed it with urban and rural estates.

The fortress of Narnia was also seized by the Lombards. After several days Basil the Duke, Jordan the *cartularius*, and John the subdeacon, surnamed Lurion, formed a plan to kill the Pontiff. Martin, the imperial *spatarius*, gave his assent to them.

[Col. 0569] The remainder is missing. Whatever had been added very briefly in a manuscript by someone else concerning the next twenty-two Roman pontiffs, I judged unworthy of the light, both because it had not been excerpted from the book on the Roman pontiffs attributed to Anastasius the Librarian, as all the preceding material had been, and because it was mutilated and full of lacunae.

[Col. 0569]

## PREFACE OF SAINT ABBON TO HIS COMMENTARY ON THE CYCLE OF VICTORIUS

(Dom. Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 118.)

[Col. 0569D] When I was once giving the computation of Victorius to brothers who were knocking at the innermost recesses of my heart with the hand of holy desire, and when, bound to them by heartfelt love, I was serving them in true obedience according to the measure of my small ability, I was compelled by their earnest entreaties to undertake a task for which my strength is scarcely sufficient. What I had been explaining simply by word of mouth, they enjoined me, out of charity, [Col. 0570D] to commit to pages in the manner of a laborious commentary and, by adding many statements, to elucidate somewhat more clearly.

For when words are lacking, memory sometimes recovers what has been lost through signs standing for words; and, as though awakening from deep sleep through a pleasing sequence of melody, it attains what it desires and, repeated again and again in the mind, establishes it firmly. Therefore, [Col. 0571A] although weak shoulders succumb beneath the burden imposed upon them, nevertheless, trusting in God’s assistance, I shall strive with all my strength and shall attempt to disclose, though I scarcely dare to attempt it, what I accede to at the request of those whose welfare, together with that of my studies, I diligently desire to advance.

For since they served me generously and without envy, not for show, but so that one might prefer another in my service, as sons serve their father, I could have been ungrateful if, spurning their suggestions, I had appeared forgetful of the benefit I had received. Ever since I became attached to them from the heart, I have always secured my own advantages from their advantages. Through them I obtained leisure and silence for study, and it pleased me to turn this into an honorable undertaking. I have impressed upon my mind that the greatest gain is to serve as fully as possible the interests of all good people, especially since I regard it as useful to myself and consider nothing in life more agreeable than to study or teach with attention.

For from the apprenticeship of my earliest years I have continually lamented that the disciplines of the liberal arts were weakened through the carelessness and negligence of certain people and reduced to scarcely a few, who set a miserly price upon their art. Therefore, lest anyone should see me, through a singular office—which would be pride—or, tormented by another’s happiness—which would be envy and the height of folly—affecting the minds of the less learned by calculating the value of teaching, I earnestly desire in many ways to benefit those for whom, under the form of an exposition, I am constructing a bridge to an introduction to arithmetic.

But Victorius, having used a preface, abuses the function of a prologue, [Col. 0572A] since he does not first bring out the arguments of his narrative, although he proposes many matters from the work that follows, which I have decided to make clearer individually for the instruction of beginners, so that no idle person, hungry for the fruit of reading, may labor in vain.

Here one must first observe that, just as is usually sought in the beginnings of narratives, the hearer’s goodwill, attention, and teachability are won here; these matters will be discussed in the context of the preface itself. For the present, however, Victorius’s purpose was this: that, when the reader was confused, he might multiply or divide the sums of numbers, or that something might be proposed concerning the arts that depend upon the principles of numbers—arithmetic, geometry, music, and astrology—or that there might be a question concerning measure and weight, all of which belong to the calculator’s responsibility.

Finally, anyone who has acquired even a small understanding of such matters could recognize from what was said previously how great the usefulness of this computation is, even if, because of the difficulty of multiplication, he has in no way labored over every possible calculation of times. But since all created things have been established in number and weight (Wisdom 11:21), I am pleased to establish speculation concerning each of these matters, so that, once their nature has been understood, the individual things in which they are present may more easily be perceived. From this, an appropriate beginning is taken here.

**The preface ends.**

## The Commentary on the Same Work Begins

“Love of wisdom, which is called philosophy by the Greeks, is held to be tripartite in its character, etc.”

[Col. 0571]

## On the Nineteen-Year Cycles Ascribed to Bede the Venerable

(*Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. VII, p. 177, under Abbo of Fleury.)

Abbo also worked on the Easter Cycle of Victorius, which we discussed in the fifth century; and his work still exists in various libraries of Europe (MONTF., *Bibl. bibl.*, p. 23, 87; MART., *Voy. lit.*, vol. I, part II, p. 210). It is found by name in two manuscripts of the Vatican Library, one of which formerly belonged to Christina, Queen of Sweden, and the other to Alexandre Petau, and in a third manuscript of the Abbey of Laubes. It is from the latter that Dom Martène and Dom Durand published the author’s preface (MART., *Anec.*, vol. I, pp. 118–119).

It appears that he was already abbot when he undertook this work. He was persuaded to do so by the request of his brothers, who found great difficulties in Victorius’s work. Abbo undertakes to clarify and correct it; in his view, this required as much insight as application, because one had to employ the knowledge supplied by arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy. Nevertheless, after work of this kind, Abbo had enough modesty to regard his commentary only as a path toward understanding arithmetic, which is the title it bears in one of the manuscripts mentioned.

Sigebert (*Script.*, chap. 139) does him greater justice and is not afraid to say that this commentary shows how deeply versed its author was in both kinds of literature. It appears very likely that this is the same commentary of which the author of a chronicle of Anjou intended to speak (LAB., *Bib. nov.*, vol. I, p. 286), when he says, in obscure and perhaps corrupt terms, that Abbo had written nineteen-year cycles: “Who wrote the nineteen cycles.” This work was indeed very well known in the following centuries. Alberic of Trois-Fontaines, Trithemius, and the other later bibliographers mention it (ALB., *Chr.*, part II, p. 34; TRIT., *Script.*, chap. 303; POSS., *App.*, vol. I, p. 35).

Although Aimoin does not name Victorius, he nevertheless clearly designates the writing of Abbo that is at issue here when he says (*Life of Abbo*, chap. 13) that this abbot corrected, according to the truth of the Gospels, the cycles of the years of the Incarnation of the Word, and carried them from the point of that celebrated epoch down to his own time.

Aimoin adds that Abbo subsequently carried his work much farther by drawing up cycles for approximately 1,595 years. According to the same historian, the preface of this new work was addressed to the monks of Fleury, and the author spoke in it of the year of the death of Saint Benedict of Monte Cassino. This is the work that Trithemius, James Philip of Bergamo, and others knew under the title *Additions to the Commentary on the Cycle of Victorius*, which they know how to distinguish from it (TRIT., ibid.; POSS., ibid.).

The notice that Aimoin gives us, when compared with the work on the same subject printed in the first volume of the works of the Venerable Bede (vol. I, p. 823), shows that this is the work of Abbo that we are undertaking to discuss. His name, in truth, does not appear there, nor does the inscription by which he addressed it to his brothers at Fleury; but one need only read the preface to recognize in it the preface mentioned by Aimoin, as well as one of Abbo’s manuscript letters that Dom Mabillon says he had held in his hands.

Besides the fact that the character of the writing is the same in both pieces, as it is also in the notice given by Aimoin, the title of the work, which is entitled *Nineteen-Year Cycles*, announces, in accordance with what we read in Aimoin, that they extend over 1,595 years. It is difficult to understand how this work was attributed to the Venerable Bede, who is cited in it at least twice. The expression of the chronicler of Anjou quoted above—“who wrote the nineteen cycles”—which he uses in speaking of Abbo, might well designate the writing under discussion here rather than the commentary on Victorius. For this writer may have intended to express the term *decennovales* by the number nineteen that he uses.

Whatever the case may be, what Abbo accomplished in the preceding work with respect to Victorius, whose errors he corrected, he undertakes in this one with respect to Dionysius the Little, whose computations he proposes to rectify. After his preface, in which he speaks twice of the death of Saint Benedict, he reports in full the Cycle of that famous Roman computist and then gives two examples or models of the way in which he ought to have proceeded in his chronological calculations. After these come two further examples taken from the Cycle of Saint Cyril of Alexandria, followed by the author’s complete nineteen-year Cycle.

The final part of the work consists of calculations for finding, in each year, the day of the moon that is to determine the feast of Easter throughout the course of this cycle. According to the title, these calculations were intended to serve from the year of the Incarnation through the year 1,595.

At the beginning there is also, under the name of the priest Bede and with the title “Preface,” a brief explanation of what is meant by the Easter cycle. But some manuscripts in which this explanation appears under the title “Letter” attribute it to Abbo (MONTF., ibid., p. 23); this is consistent and confirms what we have just established.

Our learned abbot clearly explains there the eight columns that ordinarily enter into the construction of an Easter cycle. After them follow eight long verses, in which there is considerable artistry; Abbo appears to have composed them so that the rules of his explanation, which he skillfully managed to incorporate into them, might be remembered more easily.

One must not confuse with the two preceding works a treatise on Computation by Abbo, although this work concerns almost the same subject as the others. The historian of his life himself clearly distinguishes them, and they are likewise distinguished in the manuscripts (AIM., ibid., chaps. 3, 7; MONTF., ibid., pp. 23, 87). There are two copies in the Vatican Library; in one this treatise bears the title *On the Method of Calculation*, and in the other, *Letter and Treatise on Computation*. Aimoin, undertaking to leave posterity some account of it (AIM., ibid., chap. 3), says that the computations Abbo includes in it are varied and agreeable, and more or less similar to the calculation tables that people were accustomed to draw up for temporal affairs.

[Col. 0573]

## Preface on the Cycles of Blessed Cyril and Dionysius the Roman, and on Those of a Certain Student of Bede

[Col. 0573A] Dionysius, an abbot who was Roman by birth, composed the Easter cycles with remarkable brevity, being distinguished, as he was, by knowledge of both languages. As he himself says, he began them with the year 248 of Diocletian, the tyrant rather than the emperor. But, deciding to commemorate the Incarnation of the Lord rather than that same tyrant, he published five nineteen-year cycles, in which he marked the years of Christ.

For Saint Cyril had included the observance of Easter up to the time of Dionysius in five nineteen-year cycles. Dionysius placed the fifth of these before his own five and, thus beginning from the year 532 of the Lord’s Incarnation, carried them, according to his arrangement, through the year 722.

But since these cycles, once completed, could in no way return upon themselves—those that had been encompassed by Saint Cyril in ninety-five years could not do so, nor could those that Dionysius himself had arranged over the same span of time [Col. 0574A]—for the entire computation of the sun and moon is never found again in its entirety, without some confusion, until the great year has been completed, as he himself acknowledges—he therefore instructs the sober reader, after the six years remaining at that time from the fifth cycle of blessed Cyril have been completed, not to repeat those same years, but to understand that one must begin with his own first cycle, which is headed by the 532 years.

To these five nineteen-year cycles, twenty-three others were added, completing the great year, which is fulfilled in 532 years and consists of twenty-eight nineteen-year cycles. This year therefore revolves through its own traces without any confusion, because the solar cycle is completed in twenty-eight years and the lunar cycle in nineteen years, and they end in the same sequence in which they began together.

The great year of 532 years is repeated so that the Easter reckoning concerning the sun and moon may be repeated without error. Thus, [Col. 0575A] since it contains twenty-eight nineteen-year, or lunar, cycles, it also contains nineteen solar cycles. In these cycles of Dionysius, the solar cycle begins in the ninth year of its own cycle and ends in the eighth. The nineteen-year cycle, however, plainly governs the entire reckoning of the moon in them.

Therefore it is certain beyond doubt that nineteen times twenty-eight, or twenty-eight times nineteen, produces 532. By this number of years, as has been said, the great year called the Easter year is completed. For in the epacts and in the concurrent days, whether in the nineteen-year or lunar cycle, and likewise in the Easter term and in Easter Sunday with the moon of that day, whatever the year 532 of the Lord’s Incarnation was, such will be the year 1,064; and whatever was the first year of the Incarnate Word and the year 533 after it, such will also be the year 1,615. Thereafter, in the same order, throughout the end of the threefold series of the Lord’s years, this agreement is preserved everywhere. The first of these series has entirely passed; the second, as though it were a second great year, still lies ahead; how much of the third remains in the future—although I have included it in these cycles—God alone knows.

Since these things are so, a question arises concerning the year of the Lord’s Passion. This year, the thirty-fourth from the Nativity, causes the Easter term—the fourteenth moon, that is, the moon on which God was handed over for sacrifice—to occur according to the concurrent days and regulars of the same line, although the Catholic faith holds that he was handed over after the meal on Thursday and crucified on Friday, the fifteenth day of the moon.

In the obscurity of this question, the much-respected Lord Bede contributed no light, except that he preferred the truth of the Gospels to this man’s authority. He appears in some way to have followed blessed Theophilus, who says that the Lord was handed over on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, although the aforementioned man adds one day and writes that it was on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April and that the moon was then fourteen days old.

He also differs from all ecclesiastical teachers in this: he demonstrates that the Lord was crucified under a nineteen-day-old moon. For Theophilus, like the others, asserts that he was crucified under a fifteen-day-old moon, since he reports that he rose from the dead on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, after the many matters he had discussed with his fellow bishops concerning the origin of the world.

Thus, later generations forgave this one error of so great a man in such a way that they followed him in all the churches. But another matter occurs to me, which I ought not to consign to oblivion. In the year 529 from the Incarnation of the Lord, under the emperor Justin, the most holy father of monks, Benedict, shone forth in Italy through his virtues, as Victor, bishop of Capua, or Paul, monk of Cassino, bears witness; he was a contemporary of this Dionysius. This Father Benedict, namely, departed from this life on Holy Saturday of Easter, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, as is read in the most reliable Acts.

[Note: [Col. 0575] He died in the year 543, as Leo of Ostia asserts, in solar cycle 20, on 21 March, a Saturday.]

The year sought in the cycles of Dionysius, which are mentioned so frequently, in which Holy Saturday falls on the aforementioned Kalends, can be found three times in the entire great year: only in the three nineteen-year cycles numbered 4, 22, and 27.

But since Father Benedict, after the year 529 of the Lord, lived on in Cassino, shining through miracles, it is clear that he did not depart from this world in either the twenty-second or the twenty-seventh cycle. Since Pope Gregory, the marvelous narrator of his life, died in the year 605 from the Incarnation of the Lord, it is certain that Benedict did not pass from the troubles of this life in the fourth cycle either. Indeed, his monastery had already been overrun by the Lombards after his death.

Therefore, unless the reliability of the Acts were complete, the cycle mentioned above would bring an accusation concerning the passing of both the Lord and the servant. Driven by this accusation, I began to investigate what such a controversy might produce, [Col. 0576B] and first I turned from the years of the Lord to the statements of the chronicles—especially those of Eusebius of Caesarea and Jerome, interpreter of the divine law—in order to determine how many years there were from the Incarnation of Christ to the reign of Diocletian, since from that point to the first year of the cycles of Dionysius I had found 248 years.

After laboring over the matter for a long time, I found that the interval from the birth of one to the accession of the other was 286 or 287 years, since Christ was born in the third year of the 194th Olympiad and Diocletian usurped the empire in the second year of the 266th Olympiad. Since seventy-one Olympiads had passed in between, making 284 years, two or three years are gathered from the two outer Olympiads.

When these are taken together, all the years from the Incarnation of the Lord to the first cycle of Dionysius—whether those years fell before or after the accession of Diocletian—amount in total to 534, or rather 535.

In saying this I neither prejudge nor condemn the opinions of others; rather, investigating what is true from authoritative books, I affirm, in accordance with the faith of the Council of Nicaea, that no year of any nineteen-year cycle corresponds to the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection unless it has a fourteenth moon on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

A year of the kind sought for the passing of Father Benedict never occurs except in the sixteenth year of the same cycle, having a fourteenth moon on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. For the Easter term to fall on Thursday, five concurrent days combine with seven regulars; for the other to fall on Holy Saturday, three concurrent days appear with four regulars.

From the Passion of the Lord to the passing of holy Father Benedict, 497 years elapsed. When these are divided by thirty, with the thirtieth part doubled, it becomes clear that, apart from the third, no concurrent day can occur in the year 497 after the Passion of the Lord.

Anyone who desires to know this rule of division more fully should read chapter 55 of Lord Bede on the return of the concurrent days. That same holy priest ought to have taken it into account in his addition to the cycles, by which he could have avoided the negligence of another. Although he touched upon it, he leaves it to later authors to solve, while they think that no calculation escapes him and therefore value his authority so highly, preserved through so many passing years, that it can scarcely be corrected because so many considerations oppose it.

Nevertheless, we have added two cycles to all these twenty-eight nineteen-year cycles, so that we might demonstrate to the diligence of the reader what we have said Dionysius ought to have done. After examining these, a skilled calculator will have no doubt concerning the remainder throughout the great year—if he is willing at least to entertain doubt.

Finally, it must be understood that in these cycles of Dionysius the years of the Lord proceed in their sequence, and, after fifteen years have elapsed, the indiction returns. These belong neither to the sun nor to the moon, and therefore, when the year is completed, they do not return in the same manner in which they began.

**John of Nijmegen, greetings to the diligent reader.**

Bede wrote eighty-four nineteen-year cycles for the years from the birth of Christ [Col. 0578A] through 1595—or, if you prefer, which amounts to the same thing, twenty-eight cycles repeated three times. Some of these had been corrupted, partly through the ravages of time and partly through the ignorance of copyists, while others had perished altogether. We restored some of them elsewhere and corrected others so that they might be complete through the year 1595. A later age, when the endpoint of these years arrives, will add more.

It must nevertheless be understood that these eighty-four cycles can be reduced to twenty-eight, each cycle consisting of a threefold series of years, for everything returns identically in the 531st year as well. For the great cycle consists of the same number of years; once they have elapsed, because of the courses of the sun and moon, everything that belongs to the nineteen-year cycles must return in the same order and manner, except for the indictions and the letters of the Lord’s day.

Farewell, and judge our work favorably.

[Col. 0577]

## The Nineteen-Year Cycles of the Priest Bede Follow

Together with those written by Dionysius the Roman, surnamed the Little, and by blessed Cyril, through the year 1,595 of salvation; these contain three great cycles.

(See among the works of Bede the Venerable, vol. I, col. 823, *Patrologia*, vol. XC.)

[Col. 0577]

## Preface of the Priest Bede on the Easter Cycle

[Col. 0577B] The Easter cycle is enclosed by eight lines.

The first order contains the years from the Incarnation of the Lord, increasing by one in each successive year.

The second contains the indictions of the Romans, which continually revolve within themselves in a course of fifteen years.

The third contains the eleven lunar epacts, which increase with each solar year according to the course of the moon and are always added when the moon of the Kalends is sought; they are placed at the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.

The fourth contains the concurrent days of the week, which, being placed at the ninth day before the Kalends of April because of the loss caused by the leap year, necessarily complete twenty-eight years. Their reckoning requires twenty-eight nineteen-year cycles to be written, so that each set of concurrent days may begin one cycle and the entire sum of the Easter computation may be explained in 532 years.

The fifth contains the lunar cycle, which is itself included in nineteen years, preceded by three years of the nineteen-year cycle. [Col. 0577C]

The sixth contains the fourteenth moon, by which the ancients observed Easter. It wanders in varying progression from the twelfth day before the Kalends of April to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, and takes the time of *incensio* [“burning”; the reading is uncertain] from the seventh day before the Ides of March through the ninth day before the Kalends of April. From the fourteenth moon to the fourteenth moon of the following year there are 354 days if it is a common year; if it is an embolismic year, 384.

The seventh contains the days of Easter Sunday, found from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April [Col. 0578B] through the seventh day before the Kalends of May, extended freely because of the reckoning of the embolisms.

Finally, the eighth contains the moon of the Easter feast, varying from the fifteenth to the twenty-first day because of the Lord’s day. For the leap removes a night but adds age, which has increased throughout the entire cycle. In this respect the night is removed because the moon wanes before it is thought to do so. Naturally, however, that very night remains; this night is the beginning of the coming year and the starting point of the cycle that is beginning. For this reason, the final year, while then retaining epact 18, assigns to the first year not 11 days, as usually happens in the other years, but 12; and because the cycles turn at the end of thirty days, no zero epact is placed at the beginning of the cycle.

## Poem on the Same Matter

The first line, Christ, contains your years,

[Col. 0578C]  
And the second holds the cycle’s indiction.  
The third will preserve the certain numbers for the epacts.  
The fourth counts the seven days of the leap year.  
The fifth computes for you the lunar cycle of the year.  
Now the sixth marks the fourteenth moons.  
For the seventh displays the time and day of Easter.  
The final order shows the moon’s age.

[Col. 0579]

## The Cycles of the Priest Bede for Discovering the Paschal Moons of Each Year, from Year 1 through the Year of Christ 1595

## Fragment on Saint Martial

(Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, VIII, 31, no. 3.)

## Notice

(*Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. VII, p. 181.)

The author of a sermon preached at the dedication of the church of Saint Peter of Limoges, believed to be Ademar of Chabannes, copies in it a fairly long passage from another work of Abbo. This passage concerns the alleged apostleship of Saint Martial and is found in none of Abbo’s works that have been printed. Nor does it appear that it could have found a place in the others that still remain in manuscript. The work in which it occurred must therefore be numbered among those that have been lost. In any event, what Abbo says in this passage he had taken from the false Acts of Saint Martial, as is easy to establish by comparing the one with the other.

[Col. 0579A] This supreme father Martial was altogether a sufficiently mystical guest of Christ at the supper, receiving the remnants of the heavenly bread; and when, rising afterward, he wiped the company of the disciples, he himself gladly supplied the linens. Nor did he ever shrink from holy companionship, being the only one of the pious company who was without Thomas because of fear.

Indeed, when Christ was departing for the heavenly places, he deserved to be blessed among the throngs standing by. He did not spurn the choirs of those giving praise, [Col. 0580A] but with them he then received the gifts of the Holy Spirit and the many-forked tongues. Supported by these, he eventually reached Antioch in the company of Peter, and from there the city of Rome. Leaving it, he crossed over to Gaul, of which the clear and noble province of Aquitaine is a large part; when he arrived there, he became the apostle of the entire province for all ages.

## Appendix to Saint Abbo

[Col. 0579]

## Catalogue of the Abbots of Fleury

(Baluze, *Miscellanea*, Lucca edition, I, 19.)

Here begin the names of the abbots of Saint Mary, Saint Peter, and our lord Benedict’s monastery of Fleury, after it was first built.

The first abbot, Rigomarus, held office for five years. The second abbot, Mumolus, for thirty years. Within these thirty years, the body of Father Benedict was brought from Monte Cassino by the monk Aigulf in the year 660 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the time of King Clovis, son of Dagobert.

The third abbot, Leobardus, held office for ten years.

The fourth abbot, Ido, for one and a half years.

[Col. 0580A] The fifth abbot, Auderannus, held office for half a year.

[Col. 0580B] The sixth, Flatbertus, for three years.

The seventh abbot, Adalbertus, for twenty-nine years.

The eighth abbot, Geilo, for nineteen years.

The ninth abbot, Medo, for twenty-one years.

The tenth abbot, Rodulfus, for nineteen years.

The eleventh abbot, Ido, for nine years.

[Col. 0581A] The twelfth abbot, Magulfus, for sixteen years.

The thirteenth abbot, Fulradus, for one and a half years.

The fourteenth abbot, Theodulfus, for nineteen and a half years. The most glorious emperor Charles brought him from Spain into Gaul because of the learning in which he excelled, and appointed him abbot of Fleury and bishop of Orléans.

Since, as we have said, he was regarded as outstanding in learning and renowned for his teaching, he published an explanation of the holy Creed of Athanasius, which the monks sing every day at Prime after the three regular psalms. He also set forth, in a concise but very lucid account, what mystery is contained in the sacrament of the Mass and in the things performed during it.

Nor was his zeal any less for works of the most elegant buildings. There is, in short, a villa called Germaniacus, three miles distant from our monastery. Most of this had been given or sold to the abbots who preceded him by faithful men whose inheritance it was. At this place, therefore, the same Theodulf, abbot and bishop, built a church of such marvelous workmanship that, before it was consumed by fire, no work of building in all Neustria could be found equal to it.

For, constructing the entire basilica with vaulted work, he adorned its interior with plaster flowers and mosaic, and decorated the marble pavement with an emblematic design, so that the eyes of those who looked upon it could scarcely be satisfied with its pleasing appearance. Moreover, in the masonry of the tower from which the bells hung, he inserted the following verses, expressed in silver-colored lettering:

[Col. 0582A]

“I, Theodulf, have consecrated this temple in God’s honor.

Whoever you are who stand here, I beg you: remember me.”

[Note: [Col. 0581] See Letaldus, chapter 3, *On the Miracles of Saint Maximinus of Micy*.]

In this deed he imitated Charles the Great, who at that time had built at Aachen palace a church of such great splendor that in all Gaul it had no equal. But that prince ordered the temple he had built to be dedicated in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God.

Theodulf, however, consecrating the hall he had constructed to God, creator and savior of all things, adorned it with a representation of the cherubim overshadowing the mercy seat above his altar, executed with the greatest artistic skill, and embellished it with these verses:

“Behold here the holy oracle and the cherubim, as you look upon them;

And behold, the ark of God’s covenant shines forth.

Seeing this, and striving to strike the Thunderer with prayers,

Join Theodulf, I ask you, to your petitions.”

[Col. 0582B] But since the wise are always envied and it is difficult to escape envy in prosperity, he was accused by rivals before the emperor Louis of having been involved in a conspiracy made against him. He was exiled to Angers and also placed under guard. There, on Palm Sunday, in the presence of the king himself, he sang from the tower in which he was detained the beautiful verses he had composed, proclaiming the glory of Christ’s praise and now sung by clergy throughout all Gaul. Their beginning is:

“Glory, praise, and honor be to you, Christ the King, Redeemer,

To whom the children’s noble praise brought forth a devout hosanna.”

[Col. 0581]

## Annals of Fleury

(Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores II, 254.)

## Note

These notes were added to a manuscript of the nineteen-year cycles of Dionysius, covering the years 532–1063 and now preserved in the Royal Library of Paris under no. 5443. It is a parchment quarto, written in the ninth century, and contains annotations added after the year 854 by various hands of contemporaries. Here I present them again after Chesne (vol. III, pp. 355–357), corrected and enlarged by me from the original, while omitting nearly everything preceding that year, since those materials are taken from the *History* of Paul the Deacon, the Annals of Saint Columba, and the Annals of Saint-Amand.

## In the Year of the Lord’s Incarnation

[Col. 0581D]

**626.** | Leodelodus, founder of the monastery of Fleury, died. |

**849.** | In the eighth year of King Charles, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, there was an earthquake, at about the tenth hour of the night. |

**853.** | Adalbertus, a monk of good memory, died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January. |

**864.** | A comet appeared around the Kalends of May for twenty days. |

**866.** | During the reign of Charles, son of Louis, two of his sons died: Hlotharius, the abbot, and Charles, king of Aquitaine. His uncle also, Rhodulfus, counselor and chief officer of the palace, died. Likewise Rhodulfus, archbishop of Aquitaine. And two Aquitanian princes, Landricus and Imino, fighting one another, killed each other. Rhothbertus and Ramnulfus also, men of extraordinary power and skilled in arms, themselves among the foremost leaders, were killed by the sword of the Northmen. |

**877.** | Charles, son of Louis, died on the second day before the Nones of October, and Louis, his son, assumed the kingdom on the sixth day before the Ides of December. |

**878.** | Pope John came into Gaul and remained for a long time at the city of Troyes. In the same year, on the Ides of October, there was an eclipse of the moon when it was fourteen days old, and an eclipse of the sun followed in the same month, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, when the moon was twenty-eight days old; both heavenly bodies having undergone eclipse within fifteen days. |

**879.** | King Louis died on the fourth day before the Ides of April. |

**880.** | Louis and Karloman assumed the kingdom at Amiens and divided it in the month of March. |

**882.** | Louis, the brother of Karloman, died. |

**905.** | In this year, in the middle of May, on Thursday, a star appeared near the north itself, emitting from the region of the circinus a great ray toward the south-southeast, like an extremely long spear, between Leo and Gemini, across the zodiac; and it was seen for approximately twenty-three days. |

**917.** | A memorable battle took place near Soissons, in which King Robert fell, although his army won the victory; in the same year, Rudolf was raised to the kingship. |

**936.** | The glorious king of the Franks, Rudolf, died. The first incursion of the Hungarians into all Gaul. |

**952.** | In this year Hugh, duke of the Burgundians, and Alan, ruler of the Bretons, died. |

**954.** | Louis, king of the Franks, died, and his son Lothair was nobly raised as king at Reims. |

**956.** | In this year, on the fourth day before the Nones of September, the moon was turned to blood. In the same year, in the month of June, a marvelous sign appeared in the sky, namely a great dragon without a head. Immediately afterward came the death of Hugh the Great, prince of the Franks, Burgundians, Bretons, and Northmen. A solar eclipse occurred on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January, and stars appeared from the first hour until the third. |

**974.** | In that year the monastery of Saint Benedict at Fleury was burned. But through God’s providence, within a short period of three years it was restored to better condition under Lord Abbot Richard, the organizer. It was burned on the octave of Saint Lawrence. |

**969 or 970.** | Lothair, king of the Franks, died. |

**979.** | Louis was raised by the Franks as king at Compiègne. |

[Col. 0583D] **987.** | Louis, king of the Franks, died. In the same year Hugh, duke and king of the Franks, was raised at Noyon; [Col. 0584A] he also raised his son Robert as king at Orléans. |

**988.** | [Note: [Col. 0583] Tironian notes, among which *abbas* (“abbot”) is written plainly; perhaps to be expanded as “Abbo, abbot of the monastery of Fleury,” or something of that kind.] |

**991.** | Hugh (?). |

**997.** | King Hugh died. And in another hand: King Hugh died, and his son Robert reigns in his place. |
1003. | The winter was longer than usual, and the flooding from the rains was more severe; in various regions the rivers overflowed their banks beyond measure. Above all, however, the Loire exceeded its limits to such an extent that it terrified everything situated around it with the danger of death: it penetrated embankments, uprooted huts together with their inhabitants, tore out strong bridges and hedges, and drowned oxen with their herdsmen, sheepfolds with their sheep and children, so that it was thought to be a universal flood. In that same year, near the city of Orléans, in a place called Porcaria, many people reportedly saw a phantom city constructed from the third hour of the day until the ninth hour, surrounded by meadows and water with mills and fully supplied with soldiers and necessary equipment. We also heard, as rumor spread, that an infant had been born with the feet of all animals, but resembling a human being in its single head and one foot and hand. Its parents, overcome by grief and shame, concealed it in the earth two or three times; when they were unable to destroy it, they took counsel and drowned it in the river. Such a great uproar of voices followed its death that the whole region was thought to have lamented. In that same year Pope Girbertus died. The following year [written by another hand]: Abbo the abbot was crowned with martyrdom. |

1029. | Gauzlinus the abbot died. |

### Letter of Albert to Pope John XVII

**On the Antiquity and Customary Number of the Monks of the Monastery of Micy**

*(It is printed above among the letters of St Abbo, the thirteenth letter of this volume, col. 439.)*

[Col. 0585]

### Charter of Albert Confirming Certain Estates for the Monastery of Jumièges, in Which He Had Put on the Monastic Habit

[Col. 0585A] In the name of Christ, I, Albert, abbot of the abbey of the holy Stephen, the first martyr, and of Christ’s confessor Maximinus, wish it to be known to all who have charge of the holy Church of God that, before I undertook the monastic order, I possessed a certain allod inherited from my mother, not received as anyone’s benefice. I gave it to St Peter in the monastery of Jumièges, where I received the habit, for the salvation of my soul, of my son Arnulf, archbishop of Tours, and of my parents, so that the saint named above, as intercessor, might plead for us before God.

This allod is in the county of Bellême, in a place called Domna-Maria, [Col. 0586A] and I gave it to St Peter with all its appurtenances. I ordered this charter to be made so that, after me, no one might be able to take it away from St Peter. If anyone should presume to do so, may he receive condemnation together with Judas the betrayer, Annas, and Caiaphas.

To make this little charter more secure, I have confirmed it below and presented it to my parents for their confirmation.

Signature of Albert, abbot.  
Signature of Radbod, bishop of Sées.  
Signature of Arnulf, archbishop of Tours.  
Signature of Ribald.  
Signature of Gislebert.  
Signature of King Robert.  
Signature of William of Bellême.  
Signature of Richard, count of the Normans.

## About the Same Time. Rorico, a Monk of Moissac in the Region of Cahors.

[Col. 0587]

### Historical Notice

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini, vol. VI.)*

[Col. 0587A] Rorico, a monk of Moissac in the region of Cahors, lived, judging from his style, in the eleventh century. He wrote the *Deeds of the Franks* from the origin of the nation up to the death of King Clovis I. They appear in the writers on Frankish affairs edited by André du Chesne, vol. I, p. 799, and in the new collection of Frankish writers by Martin Bouquet (Paris, 1741, fol.), vol. III. The work is written in a crude style and is full of fables.—Jacques le Long, *Bibliotheca historica of France*, p. 315.

Everything concerning this historian of Frankish affairs is uncertain. He nowhere states his monastic profession. He never indicates that he lived at Moissac, and he is believed to have been a monk of Moissac for no other reason than that this work was extracted from a manuscript of the monastery of Moissac. This work is merely a bare epitome of a much older anonymous author, who published a historical work under the same title; it should be read in du Chesne, vol. I, p. 799 and following. See the *Literary History of France*, vol. VII, p. 146.

[Col. 0587]

### Second Notice

*(Literary History of France, vol. VII, p. 136.)*

[Col. 0587B] Roricon, whose abbreviated history is much more famous than it is interesting, is otherwise almost unknown to us. It is customary to call him a monk (Du Chesne, vol. I, p. 799; Le Long, *Bibliotheca Francica*, p. 315), but no proof is offered, and we find no basis for this designation other than the pious tone in which he wrote—a tone that could equally belong to a devout ecclesiastic. There is, in any event, no difficulty in regarding him either as a cleric or as a monk. In his century it was extremely rare to find laymen who were literate and capable of writing as he did.

A Roricon, bishop of Laon until 976, is known (Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. III, appendix, p. 594, no. 26); he was regarded as a prelate possessing every kind of fine learning, *totius scientiae lumen*—“the light of all knowledge.” But no one has thought of attributing the work about to be discussed to him, and we ourselves do not claim to honor him with its authorship. Apart from the fact that only the identity of the name could authorize such an opinion, and that is highly uncertain, a prelate so learned would presumably have succeeded better in carrying out his undertaking.

If certain expressions of our historian were taken literally (*preface to Book I*), one would believe that he had worked as a shepherd and tended flocks in the countryside. But it is clear from other passages of his work (*Books II, III, and IV, prefaces*) that this is merely a fiction which seemed ingenious to him and suited his genius. He says, moreover (*Book I, preface*), quite clearly that he belonged to the nation of the Franks. He provides us with nothing precise for fixing the time at which [Col. 0588B] he wrote. Nevertheless, his style leads one to judge that he did so only in the eleventh century (Le Long, ibid.). The foundation is very slight, but what gives this opinion greater weight is that the author mentions Perpignan (*Book IV*, p. 18), which was not known until the tenth century.

Roricon’s work is entitled *Gesta Francorum*, “The Deeds or Exploits of the Franks.” It is an imposing title that promises much; nevertheless, the work is almost nothing more than an epitome of an anonymous historian who left us another, much fuller work under the same title, published by du Chesne, vol. I, p. 799. Roricon set out to abridge this historian from the origin of the nation through the death of Clovis, inclusive, and he copies all his fables and errors. He divided his work into four books and placed a preface at the beginning of each, in which he left traces of his poetic genius. The body of the work, after all, is not badly written. It is only unfortunate that its author did not work from better material.

André du Chesne was the first to print this abridgment (Du Chesne, ibid., pp. 799–817), from an ancient manuscript of the abbey of Moissac, and he also seems to have been the first to give Roricon the designation “monk.” Dom Bouquet subsequently included it, based on the earlier edition, at the beginning of the third volume of his new *Collection of the Historians of France*, with brief preliminary remarks.

[Col. 0589]

# The Deeds of the Franks, from the Origin of That Nation up to the Death of King Clovis I

**By Roricon the Monk**

*(Du Chesne, *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, I, 799, from an ancient manuscript exemplar of the monastery of Moissac, which the most distinguished man Innocentius Ciron, canon and chancellor of the church and university of Toulouse, had transcribed.)*

## [Book One]

### Prologue

[Col. 0589]

[Col. 0589A] Since the edge of my pen seems to have been eaten away by a certain rust, which idle inactivity, the enemy of every good thing, has wrought upon it, lest sloth similarly bind the tongue’s plectrum or stiffen it with some sluggishness while we linger in the care of the sheep, while the she-goats browse on cytisus, and while a little of the day still seems to remain, I shall recount, as you request, in a brief narrative some small deeds of my nation, as our predecessors have related them, remembering my homeland. Let it not be charged to loquacity if I have raised the deeds of my ancestors with certain praises, since devotion toward one’s parents is bound by both order and nature to exalt the deeds of prudent forebears.

## Book One

[Col. 0589]
