Since your intention demands that I explain to you why my fellow countrymen are called Franks, a matter worthy of narration if you will grant me leisure, I shall disclose as much as the monuments of the ancients have transmitted to us and as much as I have been able to retain in memory. If any of you knows the deeds of the Trojans, if, as Virgil relates, you have heard even lightly of their destruction discovered through Ulysses’ deceit, there is no need to recount here individually why Agamemnon’s madness blazed forth to conquer that most ferocious people. It is neither suited to my ability nor is it my intention to weave a history; rather, I have undertaken to relate a brief tale.

After Hector’s death and the destruction of Ilium, all hope for the homeland perished. Everyone’s hearts trembled, and, with their strength exhausted, they abandoned the pleasant fields: some sought unknown hearths by land, while others, rowing across the sea, entrusted the hope of life to treacherous waters. In order to provide for either necessity, they resolved to seek not neighboring but distant and unknown nations, so that they might in some measure escape the stigma of such great infamy.

Among them, Priam and Antenor, entering the banks of the river Tanais with a vast multitude from the Trojan army, sought by ship the borders of Pannonia beside the Maeotian marshes. After sending scouts around the region, they discovered nearby a place suitable for their settlement, remote from the common dwelling places of human beings: a land untilled by any plow and surrounded on every side by the sea. There they fixed their tents and, recovering their courage, built a city which they called Sicambria.

These men, strong and valiant and supported by their customary ferocity, took up arms against their neighbors, ravaging the surrounding territories and spreading the fame of their name everywhere. Whenever the people of Pannonia wished to drive them from their own borders, their efforts were frustrated and they were cut down by the strangers’ swords; nor could they rise against them by any means to defeat them. Since they could expel them from their own little fields neither by arms nor by strength nor by any other assistance, they finally ceased pursuing them. Those whom they had previously persecuted as enemies, they afterward began, against their will, to cultivate and honor as lords and neighbors.

Thus they grew into a great nation and inhabited Sicambria until the time of the emperor Valentinian. They had dukes, leading men, and every rank of nobles; and although they did not possess the same breadth of honor, they eagerly retained, at least in name, the pride of their former dignity. If they happened to choose certain leaders, preserving the names of their earlier fathers as though by hereditary right, they permitted no one else to be imposed upon them except one whom the dignity of the name had elevated.

The emperor Valentinian ruled the citadel of the Roman Empire. He was a most vigorous man and a lover of the commonwealth, a generous patron of the poor and humble, and a most savage destroyer of rebels. Against him the exceedingly fierce nation of the Alans took up servile arms, recklessly raising rebellious hands to devastate the empire or stir up seditions, and ravaging everything it could seize.

The emperor met them with a very large army above the river Danube. Drawing up his battle line against them, he suppressed their servile insolence by an imperial decree: he defeated many of them in battle and forced others to flee headlong. Those who escaped by flight entered the Maeotian marshes, where they fortified themselves and gathered whatever aids they could for defense—or rather, resistance.

After examining the difficulties of the place, the emperor, unwilling to weary his entire army, bound them by an imperial oath that tribute would be remitted for ten years to whoever could thereafter expel this rebellious nation by deceit or by arms. The Sicambri, whom we have already said came from Troy, eager to test their courage, set ambushes in hidden shelters within the marshes. Then they made a sudden attack upon the Alans and, slaughtering them in great numbers, finally brought them bound as enemies before the emperor.

After accomplishing this victory, he both subdued the rebels with a fitting punishment and ordered that our Trojans—namely, the Sicambri—be called Franks. When the ten years had elapsed, the same emperor sent a leading man, together with tax collectors from the Roman people, to collect tribute from the Franks. But the Franks indignantly bore the fact that men who, escaping the cruelty of the Greeks under the same fate, had fled from their own borders should now provoke their own blood to pay tribute. Without delay they rose against the leading official and deprived him of life, and likewise the envoys whom the emperor had sent.

Corrupted by the counsel of their young men, they discussed these words among themselves: “The emperor, with the Roman army, could not drive the rebellious nation of the Alans from its hiding place in the marshes; why, then, should we, who defeated them, pay tribute?”

When he heard this, the emperor, boiling with anger, marched against the Franks, taking with him Aristarchus, the commander of his army. Aristarchus, attacking the Franks with an innumerable multitude, killed one of their leaders, named Priam, with his sword. After crushing the others in a great slaughter, though at heavy cost to the Roman army, he finally defeated them and forced them to turn their backs.

The Franks realized that they could not long endure the emperor’s anger and feared losing the liberty they had acquired by arms. They therefore chose to live in exile all the days of their lives rather than allow the dignity of so great a name to be stained any longer by servile disgrace.

Abandoning Sicambria, half of them, with their wives and children, wandered through Europe, wavering here and there without fixed homes or any firm place of settlement. Through the various winding paths of their journey they defended themselves and their descendants with the sword whenever, while seeking the means of livelihood, they were forced to go somewhere and encountered inhuman people who tried to prevent them from obtaining necessities.

Wherever they advanced, the terror they spread everywhere compelled peoples to assemble in one place, countless nations to unite, and every fortification of the homeland to be defended with every kind of device and weapon. Moreover, the entire populace, as though the hope of the homeland had perished, searched out hidden places and carried themselves and their little children into the retreats of the mountains. From every side, with trumpets sounding, the townspeople drove the passing people away from their fortifications with spears and arrows, as though they knew that the strangers had come to conquer their homeland.

But the nation had come not to fight but to travel onward, and it proceeded along the direct route, unless the necessity of obtaining food forced someone to go elsewhere. The common army, marching swiftly, reached the banks of the Rhine without great impediment. There they pitched their tents in the towns of the Germans and lived peacefully with the rulers of that land.

Those who had remained at Sicambria, inhabiting the banks of the Danube, chose a king for themselves named Torcat; hence they were also called Torci.

After a short time had passed, the Franks entered again with renewed strength and recovered from their weariness. Those who, as we have said, had reached the banks of the Rhine attempted to build a city after the model of Troy. But abandoning the unfinished work, they jointly chose a king for themselves, as did the other nations, named Faramund, son of Marchomir, son of Priam. Raising him to the throne, they began to honor him with due reverence.

When he died, they raised his son Clodio to his father’s throne. For a few days he lived in the territory of the Thuringians, in the fortress of Dispargum. The Franks were always suspicious and uncertain, wavering in doubt while diligently investigating whether some place might perhaps be found somewhere that seemed suitable for their settlement.

While they were troubled by this anxiety, scouts reported to them that Gaul was nobler than all other regions, filled with every kind of distinction, planted with fruit-bearing groves, and a fertile land suited to everything that could relieve human needs. Encouraged by this message, they seized courage and weapons. To avenge the injuries they had suffered from the Romans, they sharpened their hearts along with their swords—not in order to flee, but to exterminate them—and they inflamed each of their people with harsher words.

At about this time the Romans inhabited the land from the river Rhine to the river Loire, while from the Loire toward Spain the Goths held dominion. The Burgundians were also Arians and lived beside the river Rhône.

King Clodio therefore sent his advance forces as far as the city of Cambrai. He himself followed with a very large army, crossing the Rhine. Entering the Carbonarian Forest, he seized the city of Tournai and then hastened as far as Cambrai. After remaining there for a short time, he ordered all the Romans found in the city to be killed by the sword.

Having retained the city, he advanced from there and occupied the territory as far as the river Somme. Entering the city of Amiens, he established the seat of his kingdom there and thereafter rested under a peaceful rule. He reigned for twenty-two years and died.

After his death, Merovech was chosen to govern the people and was raised to the royal throne in the same city of Amiens. This Merovech, from whom the Franks were first called Merovingians, was held in such great veneration among the Franks because of his usefulness and prudence that all honored him as a common father.

He fathered Childeric, the father of the most excellent King Clovis. At that time the Franks were heathen, worshiping idols and not acknowledging the king of heaven who created all things.

Merovech died, and his son Childeric reigned in his place. Since King Childeric was excessively lustful and ruled over the Franks, he violated their daughters by force. Greatly indignant at this, they jointly and unanimously resolved either to kill him or drive him from the kingdom.

When Childeric realized that the minds of the Franks had turned against him, he divided one gold coin into pieces, summoned his counsellor Viomad, and said to him: “I perceive that this people intends to rise up against me, and I ask your united assistance: pacify the Franks for me as far as you are able. When you know that they have been calmed, command me to return, and this division of the gold coin shall be the sign between you and me. When I see the portion that I leave with you, I shall return in peace. Otherwise, I shall remain with Sisinius [elsewhere called Bisinus], king of the Thuringians.”

Having said this, he secretly fled to the Thuringians and lived with Sisinius and his wife Basina. After he had been expelled, the Franks, following an ill-advised and useless plan, set the Roman soldier Aegidius over themselves. He ruled them for eight years, and Viomad joined him in a feigned friendship out of loyalty to his lord Childeric.

Viomad urged the king to oppress certain Franks harshly. The Franks, worn down by the madness of King Aegidius, sought Viomad’s advice and asked what they should do. He said to them:

“Do you not remember how the Romans crushed your ancestors? How they expelled them from Sicambria? And you expelled your useful and vigorous king and raised over yourselves this cruel and arrogant Roman soldier? You did this without counsel, and now you rightly drink from the cup that you yourselves served.”

They replied: “Without law he was then permitted to abuse our daughters. Now we regret having done this, and would that we might deserve to find him, so that he might reign over us in peace.”

When Viomad heard this, he sent swift messengers to Childeric, telling him to return in peace and sending reliable signs of the divided gold coin in advance. When Childeric realized that the Franks desired him, he gladly returned [Col. 0593C] to his kingdom.

The Franks received him with joy and expelled Aegidius in disgrace. Basina, the wife of King Sisinius, with whom we have already said that Childeric had hidden, repeatedly left her husband’s bed and experienced the companionship of our king. For this reason she followed him to Francia not long afterward, wishing to live with him in the place of a wife.

When Childeric unexpectedly saw her and asked what purpose had brought her to him from so distant a province, she is said, in accordance with her excessive lust, to have given this reply:

“Because I know your usefulness and beauty, and that you are capable and vigorous, I have come from my home to live with you. For if I had known someone more useful than you even at the ends of the earth, I would have sought him no less.”

The woman’s witty speech pleased the king, and he joyfully took her as his wife. She conceived and bore a son and called him Clovis.

This was the most powerful king of all the Frankish kings, an outstanding and most vigorous man, a most warlike conqueror, an enlarger of the empire, and a lover of every kind of justice.

At this time King Childeric gathered the Frankish army and attacked the city of Agrippina on the river Rhine. Surrounding it with every apparatus of war, he finally defeated its people after devastating them in a great slaughter. Retaining all the fortifications of that city for himself, he ordered it to be called Cologne. The Roman Aegidius, whom we mentioned above, governed it. Unable to resist so great an army, he left the city and sought safety in flight, thus escaping the king’s fury.

Advancing from there, the Franks ravaged and captured the city of Trier on the river Moselle.

At that time Aegidius, the Roman tyrant, died, and his son named Syagrius was raised to his father’s throne in the city of Soissons. King Childeric once again gathered his army and reached Orléans, ravaging with extreme ferocity all the lands around it.

From there he advanced to Angers to meet Adovagrius, duke of the Saxons, who had conquered and devastated that same Angers, leaving Count Paul to guard the city. When King Childeric unexpectedly burst into the city and resolved to cut down Duke Adovagrius, Adovagrius escaped by ship; Paul was killed by the king’s sword, and the city’s principal building was burned with fire.

After achieving this victory, while he wished to return to his own territory, namely the city of Amiens, he was seized by a fever and breathed his last. He left the government of the people to his son Clovis. King Childeric died in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, and his son Clovis reigned in his place.

## [Book Two]

### Prologue to Book Two

[Col. 0593]

[Col. 0593D] It has been related, as I believe, sufficiently briefly and in a manner suited to the brevity proposed, why the people of the Franks were brought to these regions and why they are called by that name. But since I see you attentive while we still await the setting of the sun and lead the well-fed flocks back to the sheepfold, I shall explain in only a few words how this people traversed all Gaul and how it took the country away from the Romans.

For I ask you not to find it burdensome if, to complete the history or dispel the boredom of those who dislike lengthy narration and enjoy always hearing something new, I touch upon certain matters from the little works of neighboring peoples, drawing them from the side [or: “from the margin”; the reading is uncertain]. For one who always overflows with his own pleasures is pleased even when he touches upon foreign matters.

## Book Two

[Col. 0593]

[Col. 0593D] In the fifth year of his reign, therefore, Clovis took up arms against Syagrius, the son of Aegidius, and ordered all the Franks to assemble in an army to drive him from his father’s throne.

Syagrius likewise gathered forces from every quarter and prepared the courage of his people for defense, recalling the brave deeds of the Romans and continually declaring that their swords were exceedingly sharp for despising their enemies.

When both battle lines stood facing one another and spears were launched everywhere amid the blaring of trumpets, the Franks fought the Romans with all their strength. Remembering the earlier injury—how the Romans had expelled them from Sicambria—they spared no age and slaughtered everyone alike by cutting off their necks with swords. What is even horrifying to say, they threw many of them to the beasts to be torn apart.

When Syagrius saw his army cut down, he alone fled from the battle. As he tried to withdraw himself from death, he was instead destined for death. For while he was fleeing to Toulouse, to Alaric, king of the Goths, and Clovis, victorious, was rejoicing over the spoils he had stripped away, messengers arrived and reported to Clovis that Syagrius was being concealed by Alaric.

After Syagrius’s entire kingdom had been overrun, Clovis sent his envoys to Alaric, ordering him to surrender Syagrius; otherwise, he should prepare for war. Fearing to test the swords of the Franks, Alaric sent Syagrius to King Clovis by the same envoys, humbly requesting that he return to his enemy the man whom he had sought.

When Syagrius was presented to the king, Clovis ordered a swordsman to cut off his head. Then, after the tumult had subsided and the enemy had been put to flight or partly decapitated, Clovis retained for himself alone Syagrius’s kingdom, all his treasures, and the entire royal furnishings. He ordered the booty and spoils of the slain to be divided equally among all the soldiers.

For they had ravaged not only certain villas or fortresses, but also many churches, plundering them with such greed that, while each person hid away whatever gold or silver utensils he could find, they also cut up with their fingernails objects that served no useful purpose or threw them into the flames and burned them.

Among the other ornaments of the churches, they had taken from one church a vessel of extraordinary size and remarkable beauty. The bishop of that church followed them through envoys, humbly begging King Clovis to deign to return the vessel that had been taken.

He replied to them: “Even if everything we have taken from the churches of Christians were required to be returned, nevertheless, if the bishop seems not to deserve anything else, I shall not refuse the vessel if it falls to our share.”

Having said this, he hastened to the place where the whole booty was to be divided and said to all the soldiers:

“I beg you, dearest soldiers, for the love of God, to assign that vessel to my portion, so that I may return it to the bishop who is asking for it, lest his poor church be wholly laid waste by our violence.”

Everyone approved the king’s request and, with joyful hearts, resolved to return the vessel. But one of the Franks, to his own ruin, raised an axe and struck the vessel, saying: “Let whatever the lot has given him be granted by the king to anyone; let him leave us our own share.”

While everyone stood astonished and disturbed by the novelty of the deed, the king’s indignation temporarily submitted to patience, and he ordered the vessel to be returned to the bishop.

When the year had elapsed, he assembled the army and, according to custom, went around inspecting everyone and carefully examining the equipment of each man. At last he caught sight of the man who had struck the vessel. Recalling the aforementioned insult, he marveled at the man’s rustic weapons and began to rebuke him for having disfigured an assembly of noble men with such a dreadful appearance.

Taking up each weapon, he dashed it to the ground with the greatest indignation. When the man bent down to extend his hand to gather up his weapons, the king raised his axe, struck his head with a deadly wound, and said: “Thus did you strike the vessel at Soissons last year.”

After he had died, Clovis led the same army against the Thuringians. Overthrowing them in a great slaughter, and after countless killings, after the reduction of the entire people, and after the devastation of the homeland, he finally ordered the survivors who had preserved their lives by flight to return, and he made them tributaries of the Franks.

In those days Gundobaldus and Godegisilus, kings of the Burgundians and sons of Gundeveus, who was descended from the line of King Athanaric, were led by excessive ambition to kill their brother Chilperic with the sword. They drowned his wife in the waves with a stone tied around her neck.

This Chilperic had two daughters. One was named Chronna; the other was called Crochildis. Gundobaldus, changing Chronna’s clothing, condemned her to exile, but kept Chrochildis at home.

King Clovis had then ordered his envoy Aurelian to find for him a noble girl adorned with good morals and distinguished in bodily appearance, whom he could take in marriage.

Aurelian had frequently gone to Burgundy, and therefore knew Chrochildis’s prudence and elegance well. He approached the king and began to praise the girl’s prudence with extravagant encomiums. The king’s desire for her was inflamed, and through his envoy he addressed the virgin, asking whether the noble and orphaned girl might wish to be joined to the king of the Franks.

Aurelian set out to carry the king’s message, traveling toward Burgundy. He went on foot to the place where he knew the girl to be, carrying a bag and staff, covered with patched tunics, and hiding Clovis’s gifts in a basket.

When he arrived, on a Sunday he mingled with the other poor people seeking alms, so that he might say a few words to Chrochildis as she returned from church. For she was a Christian.

When she returned home from church and, in her customary generosity, distributed alms to each of the poor, she came to Aurelian and offered him a gold coin, entirely unaware of the affair. When he had received it, he discreetly drew aside the girl’s cloak, indicating that he wished to speak with her.

They came to the palace, and the virgin, followed by Aurelian, entered the dining room and sent a maidservant to summon the stranger. Aurelian presented the king’s gifts and, holding out a ring from Clovis’s hand, gave it to the girl, saying:

“Please, my lady, let your servant speak something secretly into your ears, so that I may lawfully disclose the commands of my lord the king.”

She replied: “Speak.”

Taking the betrothal ornaments from the basket, he offered them to the girl and said:

“My lord King Clovis commands that, if you grant him the consent of your will, he will receive you as his wife without delay.”

The girl marveled at the man’s ingenuity and, with great joy of heart, accepted the king’s gifts. She put the other objects away for herself but placed the ring alone among her uncle’s treasures, and gave the bearer this reply:

“Give greetings to Clovis. Although it is not lawful for a Christian woman to marry a pagan, nevertheless, if the will of the Lord God whom I serve, confess, and adore should be present, I shall give thanks to the divine majesty and follow the will of the one who commands. And you, faithful helper of our secret, go in peace.”

The girl’s words were conveyed to Clovis. Clovis again sent Aurelian as envoy to Gundobaldus, commanding him to give his niece to him in marriage if he wished to keep the Franks at peace; otherwise, he should either pay tribute or take up arms to fight him.

When Gundobaldus heard this, he was thrown into confusion of mind. He summoned his friends and counsellors and said to them:

“You all know, my counsellors and friends, that Clovis, king of the Franks, is seeking pretexts against us, requesting through an envoy my niece Chrochildis, although he has not yet seen her face. This is the origin of the quarrel, this is the cause of discord, this is the boundless ruin of our destruction. The whole affair is directed toward this end: that he may deprive us all of life and then strip our nation of its liberty. I have therefore summoned you, so that, with common counsel, you may seek a sounder outcome and, looking to the common good, decide by your authority what must be done.”

Having thus concluded his speech, his Burgundian councillors, fearing to incur Clovis’s anger, unanimously resolved that the girl should be given to so great and powerful a king, lest on this pretext the ferocity of so great a nation be sharpened against them for their destruction. For they feared the Franks, as did the other peoples who saw them spreading everywhere; and they believed that no one could withstand their swords. They therefore ordered the matter to be hastened, lest a delayed response turn into resentment.

Gundobad then summoned Aurelian and began to address him as follows:

“Since you have come to investigate our homes and country under the pretext of seeking a wife for your lord the king, report these answers of our people to Clovis. He has vainly supposed that he could have my niece as his wife; he has uselessly desired the beauty of my Chrochildis.”

Enraged by this, Aurelian replied:

“Since you think that I have brought the commands of some rustic, know that no one has issued this command except Clovis, your lord and mine—your lord, I say, your lord, so that you may send him his betrothed, Chrochildis. If you delay, you must either pay tribute to him or defend your freedom with the sword.”

Gundobad, irritated, answered Aurelian only this:

“Let your lord Clovis come, let him come, for he will find swords prepared to defend the freedom of the Burgundians. With the Lord God helping us, his boldness will fall to destruction, and the blood of many peoples, which has been shed by his hands, will be avenged.” [Col. 0598A]

After saying more, his madness was at last calmed by the counsel of prudent men, and he handed Chrochildis over to Aurelian. Aurelian received her with immense joy, led her with him as far as the city of Soissons, and presented her to Clovis. Delighted by her beauty, the king summoned the nobles of his kingdom and, according to royal custom, took her as his wife.

Late that day, when they were to recline together according to the marriage custom, she first addressed Clovis:

“May my lord the king, I beg, hear his handmaid and deign to grant his servant a little request, if I have found favor in his sight.”

Clovis replied: “Ask what you wish, for your request will be granted.”

Then the queen, filled with the Spirit of God, began to address the king in these words:

“First, your handmaid asks this of you, my lord the king: believe in the Lord of heaven, the almighty Father, who created you. Next, confess that the Lord Jesus Christ, who redeemed us, was sent by the Father from heaven for the salvation of believers. Third, acknowledge the Holy Spirit and the illumination of all the righteous; and, acknowledging this, venerate together the majesty of the one Godhead. In the three persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, suspect nothing earlier, nothing later, nothing less; rather, embrace eternity and co-equality with your whole mind.

“Burn the idols that are not gods but mute images, rebuild the churches of my God that you have burned, and receive baptism in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Finally, I ask that you seek the treasures of my father and mother, whom my uncle Gundobad wickedly killed, and whose blood the Lord will avenge.”

The king said: “For the present it seems difficult to me to abandon my gods and worship your God; but the rest I shall do as I am able.”

She replied: “This is the greatest and singular request I make: worship the Lord of heaven, through whom, whether you wish it or not, you reign, and in whose name you will easily overcome the camps of your adversaries.”

Having thus concluded, they entered the bedchamber and reclined together. Celebrating their wedding, they spent an entire year in joy and gladness.

When the year had passed, Clovis again sent Aurelian to Gundobad, ordering him to send him the treasures of Chrochildis, his wife. Burning with anger, Gundobad could scarcely endure Aurelian’s words and finally burst out:

“Will my kingdom—or my treasures—now be placed in Clovis’s hands? Did I not warn you, Aurelian, and tell you not to come again to investigate the wealth of our kingdom or the prosperity of our princes? I call upon the safety of our people as witness: unless you quickly return and withdraw from me, I will kill you.”

Aurelian replied:

“My lord King Clovis and the chief men of his kingdom live, and I do not fear you while my lord lives. Your own and my lord Clovis gives this command: he is coming to meet you in order to receive his wife’s treasures.”

When they heard this, the leading Burgundians advised their king to return without delay everything that had belonged to Chrochildis’s father or mother. They said that the king was ferocious, that the people were without God, and that a pact ought to be secured with such men, lest they invade them unanimously and destroy both their land and their people.

What more is there to say? Gundobad returned to the king’s envoy all Chrochildis’s belongings, together with objects of the purest gold and exceedingly valuable works of silver from his own treasury. He said to Aurelian:

“What remains, except that I must give my entire kingdom to Clovis? Return quickly to your lord the king, since you have many gifts to bring him. He reaps a harvest that he did not sow and gathers what he did not scatter.”

Aurelian replied:

“Your son is my lord Clovis. Do not be saddened if I have brought him this small amount; from this moment onward everything that belongs to you will be held in common.”

The Burgundians said: “Long live the king who has such envoys!”

Aurelian returned to his lord and restored to him everything that Gundobad had handed over.

In those days Clovis extended the kingdom of the Franks as far as the Seine. After taking the fortress of Melun, he handed it over to his envoy Aurelian and appointed him duke of that province. Then, advancing as far as Aurelianis, he extended the boundaries of the Franks to the river Loire.

Meanwhile the queen urged her lord to worship God and remove the mute images from his entire kingdom, if he wished to be victorious against the impiety of all his enemies. Clovis mocked and ridiculed her; yet he rejected her counsels of life not by reproaching her but rather by gentle words.

At length it came about that the queen conceived and bore a son, and ordered him to be taken into the church, according to Christian custom, to be washed in sacred baptism. He was baptized, signed, and anointed with sacred chrism. Those who received him from the sacred font called him Ingumer. The infant soon died, and what had happened was reported to Clovis.

The anxious father grieved, seeing his firstborn unexpectedly carried to the tomb, and rebuked the queen because she had marked the infant, as he said, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. For the madman insisted that, if the child had been dedicated to his gods, he would not so quickly have been deprived of this light. But the queen gave thanks to God because he had raised her firstborn to heavenly glory.

After this she bore another child. Having been washed in the baptismal font, he was called Clodomir. When he too began to fall ill, Clovis rebuked the queen in harsher words, asserting that this child likewise could not possibly live, since the other had lived no differently. But while the queen prayed, and the Lord’s mercy went before him, the infant was restored both to life and to health.

The king therefore continued to delay believing and did not wish to hear the counsels of salvation, until at last he made war against the Alemanni and the Suebi. In that conflict he was compelled to confess that God alone can grant help to one who believes.

For when both battle lines stood against one another, and javelins were hurled at close quarters amid the blaring of trumpets, and the strength of the Franks was insufficient to crush their enemies, the Lord looked down from above. Marveling at the labor of the woman who desired to save her unbelieving husband, he sent his fear upon the Franks. They were already preparing to turn their backs when Aurelian, calling upon the Lord’s name for help, firmly addressed the king:

“Believe only, my lord the king, in the Lord of heaven whom Chrochildis proclaims; and, having called upon his name, you will quickly crush your enemies.”

Encouraged by these words, the king raised his eyes to heaven and prayed to the Lord with tears:

“Good Jesus, whom my queen Chrochildis proclaims to be the Son of the living God, who come to the aid of those in tribulation and give help to those who hope in you, I devoutly ask your help. Do not refuse me alone what has been granted to many. If you give me victory, and I experience your power in this matter, I shall believe in you and be baptized. For I called upon my gods, and they withdrew from me; and I suspect that they possess no power, since they neither come to my aid nor bring help when invoked. I invoke you, I confess you. At your command may our army be strengthened and the boldness of our adversaries be crushed, so that, even if I do not deserve victory, I may at least be freed from them.”

When he had thus concluded and called upon the Lord’s name with an inward groaning of the heart, the Alemanni, their strength exhausted, turned their backs and placed their hope of life in flight. But when they also saw that their king had been killed, they turned back and begged Clovis to order an end to such slaughter, surrendering themselves and all that they possessed. When he had stopped the blow that threatened them, he devastated their lands with excessive plundering and placed them under tribute.

Having won this victory, he returned to Gaul and told his wife how, by invoking the name of Jesus Christ, he had deserved to obtain victory. Chrochildis immediately rejoiced and, drenched in tears, hastily summoned Saint Remigius, archbishop of Reims, so that he might complete in her husband what the Lord had already begun to accomplish through her.

The bishop opened the door of salvation and refreshed the sinner’s thirsty soul with a torrent of Scripture. The king’s madness was softened, and he was changed from a wolf into a sheep. Fearing to come to the Lord empty-handed, he prepared a thousand sacrifices to offer to his Creator.

Although he had not yet been initiated into the sacred rites, he became an apostle to his people. He proclaimed the Lord’s name to the nations and threatened the army lest they bow any longer before images. What more is there to say? Suddenly the people came together; all the soldiers joined right hands and offered equal hearts to the Creator. Whoever was slower to run to the font was reproached by the others as more sluggish.

Seeing the ranks hastening to the church with linked hands, while they wished to be baptized even out of love for the king before they knew the ordinances of baptism, the king entered the church that he was destined to conquer, surrounded by this great throng.

When he perceived the fragrance of the smoking incense and sweet-smelling frankincense, and marveled that the walls were covered with curtains and hangings and that the entire floor had been strewn with various flowers, he asked the bishop whether this was paradise, or the future glory that he had promised him in his preaching.

The bishop replied:

“No, this is not the paradise that I promised my lord the king. It is the Church of God, through which and in which, by good works, that unfailing glory of the heavenly kingdom is obtained which the Lord prepared from the beginning of the world for those who love him.” [Col. 0601A]

The Lord supplied such great grace among the people that one would no longer have thought that groups of twenty or a hundred were coming to the place of baptism, but that almost the entire city had rushed together as one, given one judgment, and offered equal hearts to the Creator.

Thus united in inward joy, they applauded together and encouraged their king with these words:

“Our lord the king should continue what he has begun, for we too reject mortal gods, despise worthless things, drive out objects made by human hands, and receive with undefiled faith the true God whom Remigius proclaims. We embrace him with the reverence of faith. We believe and worship this God of Christianity, and we are prepared to remain in this religion to the end of life.”

What more is there to say? He came to baptism like a new Constantine, having renounced the pomp of the devil and humbled his fierce spirit before the Creator.

The bishop rejoiced with this devotion and, stretching out his hands on high, praised God’s power. He exhorted the king with these words:

“Bend your neck gently, Sicamber; burn the various idols and venerate divine worship. Abandon your former errors and former shrines, and from this moment strive to renew the holy sanctuaries.”

Thus the king, confessing the almighty Lord in the Trinity, was baptized by Saint Remigius in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and was anointed with sacred chrism, bearing the sign of the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.

More than three thousand of his army were baptized; his sisters Albofledis and Landechildis were also baptized, as was the entire people of the Franks. For our Lord Jesus Christ abundantly poured his holy grace upon them.

On this occasion he spread the grace of his faith throughout the Gallic land. Behold, we have restored the king renewed; it is necessary that we likewise renew the page. But first, having rested our limbs for a little while, let us regain our breath, so that tomorrow we may more easily relate the matters that follow in our narrative.

# [BOOK THREE]

## PROLOGUE OF THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0601]

Before the darkness of night has been wiped away, you press me to discharge my debt, for you are importunate lenders: you shake my sluggish limbs and rebuke my laziness in bed with harsher words, asking why, still almost asleep, I have not yet stretched out my fingers to write, although each of you knows the condition under which one is burdened when, hired for wages, he is compelled to serve others.

First we shall lead the little sheep back to pasture; first we shall give the lambs a little milk to drink; first we shall shelter them under a small roof. And when I have laid my limbs beneath a leafy tree, if you are present and, casting clods or stones, drive away the wolf with us so that he does not lie in wait for the small flock, then perhaps I shall be able to discharge more freely and conveniently what you demand.

And lest I seem to be weaving delays for you: while we wait for the south wind’s breath to remove the noxious cloudy mists of the air, or to tear apart the spiders’ webs by which the grasses are accustomed to be infected, let us now move to the other side, stand together as one, and lighten your boredom with this brief account.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0601C]

After our king Clovis had been baptized, as we have said, and his entire army had been anointed with sacred chrism, the queen is said to have rejoiced with such exultation that, falling prostrate before all the people and drenched in tears, she blessed the majesty of the Lord, because he had deigned to fulfill in her what she had read written in the Apostle, who says: “The unbelieving husband will be saved through the believing wife.” [Col. 0601D]

From that time, by the Lord’s providence, the power and glory of the Franks are reported to have been so magnified that not only neighboring peoples but even those far away sought their friendship and desired to be joined or allied with them through kinship.

Thus it came about that Theoderic, king of Italy, who ruled the Goths and Romans in Italy, sought and took Landechildis, Clovis’s sister, as his wife.

If I briefly explain who this Theoderic was and from where he derived his origin, do not consider it burdensome, especially since yesterday I promised to relate something about the histories of neighboring peoples.

This Theoderic, then, as Idatius reports, descended from the stock of the Macedonians—namely, those who, by a great stroke of fortune, had fled from Troy with our people, subdued Macedonia by force of arms, and further overrun it.

The Romans attacked them, as they did the other nations, wearing them down in many battles, bringing captives away with them, and carrying off much booty. Among the others they brought away a certain boy named Theoderic and a certain girl called Lilia.

By the lot of military booty, these two fell to the share of the patrician Idatius, and by faithfully serving him they fully won their master’s favor.

Idatius had a wife named Eugenia, very beautiful but barren. For this reason they adopted Theoderic as their son and Lilia as their daughter, and cherished them with extraordinary affection.

When they observed them, according to the customary law of love, clinging to one another with glances and whispers, jokes and embraces, they permitted them to be joined in marriage.

Eugenia then summoned the girl and said to her privately:

“When you have approached intercourse with your husband, report to me tomorrow everything that appears to you in a nocturnal vision.”

For those mad and foolish people believed that everything a betrothed woman dreamed on the first night of intercourse would come to pass. Many assert that this custom is still preserved by ignorant and rustic people as though it were truthful, although it is wholly empty and ought to be rejected.

The woman went away and fell asleep, and yet fictitious things were displayed to her in dreams as though they were present. In her dream she saw what seemed to be a tall and lofty tree emerging from her belly’s navel, so high that it appeared almost to equal the height of the clouds. This signified the son who was to be born from her womb.

When she awoke, terrified, she told her husband the dream; she also, without delay, disclosed her mistress’s secret. When Lilia had risen in the morning and had been instructed by her husband, she did not report the matter as it had happened but, deceiving her mistress, spoke to her differently:

“Behold, my lady, remembering your words, I fell asleep beside my husband last night, and in a dream I saw what seemed to be a horse and a mare, more beautiful than all others, enter the house of my masters. A well-formed and playful foal followed them, surpassing all herds of horses in beauty.”

When Idatius and Eugenia heard this, they thought that offspring would be born to them. For this favor they granted Theoderic and Lilia their freedom and enriched them with many gifts.

Lilia bore a son whom she called by his father’s name, Theoderic. The boy grew, was weaned, and Idatius adopted him as his son and ordered him to be brought up with every care.

He was handsome in appearance, tall in stature, equipped with worldly prudence and cleverness, and distinguished by extraordinary bodily strength.

After Idatius and Eugenia had died, Theoderic was ordered to serve as a soldier. In this way he won the favor of the emperor Leo and acquired a reputation and renown for nobility and daring at the imperial palace in Constantinople.

A certain Ptolemy of senatorial rank is said to have been bound to him in singular friendship, so that until the day of Theoderic’s death he attempted, by his counsel and prudence, to protect him from the dangers posed by his enemies.

While some admired Theoderic’s prudence, and while to others it seemed burdensome as a cause of envy, the Italians asked the emperor, through intermediaries and by common agreement, that Theoderic be appointed patrician over them, so that Roman freedom might be protected from its pressing enemies by his exceptional prudence.

This pleased the emperor. He sent Theoderic to Rome, where he was raised to the dignity of the patriciate. He fought many battles with the Heruli and destroyed them utterly.

Thus it happened that one day, when they had stirred up battle against their king and a great multitude of men from both armies had been laid low by mutual wounds, Theoderic, perceiving that the swords of his men had failed, turned his back and, fleeing with his companions, entered Ravenna.

When his mother Lilia unexpectedly saw him, she began to rebuke and mock him, provoking him with these words:

“What madness, my son, is compelling you to flee so precipitately? You have nowhere to flee now except into my womb, entering beneath my raised garments—the womb from which you emerged as a little child at your birth.”

When he heard this and was overcome with immense shame, he gathered a few soldiers. Preferring to die rather than live any longer, and finding the enemy already scattered for plunder, he suddenly confronted them. Finding them unprepared, he defeated them as though they were an ignoble mob, killed their king with the sword, and also killed his wife and children. He reduced the kingdom, people, and name of the Heruli to nothing and enriched himself with their spoils, so that he believed he had surpassed the wealth of Croesus.

When this was reported to the emperor, he immediately feared that Theoderic might someday take up arms against him in the same way, deprive him of life, and strip him of the empire.

Certain rivals, displeased by Theoderic’s generosity and prudence, also persuaded the emperor against him; they had accused him of the worst crime. They urged the emperor to order Theoderic to come to him quickly and to deprive him of life.

Theoderic, suspecting no treachery, hastened to Constantinople with twelve thousand exceptionally brave warriors and thus presented himself before the emperor.

The entire senate had decreed that, when Theoderic entered the palace alone, he should be torn limb from limb and removed from the world of the living. But he was preserved and freed by the counsel and cunning of his friend Ptolemy.

Ptolemy approached the emperor and addressed him in these words:

“It is altogether unworthy of your majesty, my lord emperor, that this man should be deceitfully killed without law or judgment; that he should be separated from his own men and oppressed by ours. First let the charge be laid out before everyone; first let men, nobler even than those of our curia, be sent to his senators to examine the matter carefully—men who have learned to multiply the charges of offenses. When he has been judged deserving of death by both sides, he may then more properly and freely be thrown to the beasts, punished by decapitation, or perish by hanging. In the meantime let him be held alive and bound. Behold, I am prepared to depart with your envoys.”

Finally, five of the nobler men of the emperor’s court were chosen to carry the emperor’s commands to the Goths in Italy. By the emperor’s order Ptolemy went with them. He secretly sent ahead a boy who would report everything to the Goths and tell them that all the envoys, including Ptolemy, were to be bound and terrified by the prospect of various punishments unless the emperor quickly returned their lord Theoderic safe and unharmed and allowed all who were with him to return home in safety.

What more is there to say? The senators who had been sent had not yet finished speaking when, behold, they were bound on every side; crosses were prepared for hanging them, swords were sharpened, and various forms of death were made ready. They were threatened with being killed together unless their lord were returned to them and the emperor swore that he would permit all those who were with him to return home unharmed.

Pressed by these difficulties, the emperor, whether he wished it or not, returned Theoderic to the Goths and allowed all of them to return to their homeland safely.

When Theoderic had returned home with his companions, he learned that the Avars had entered Italy, devastated the people and country, leveled many cities to the ground, and wished to extend their advance as far as Rome.

At last, taking up his arms and strength again, he expelled all of them from the country, pursued them as far as the borders of Pannonia, and pitched his tents near their army.

On the following day he took six soldiers with him—making seven in all—and left the camp to reconnoiter the Avar camp personally.

In the same way, a certain Avar named Xerxes left his own camp alone, wishing to investigate for himself the power of those pursuing him, as though he were a most powerful warrior.

When Theoderic saw him wandering alone, he sent three of his companions to capture him. The Avar, pretending to flee and repeatedly turning back, killed them one by one.

Theoderic ordered three others to go. As soon as he had deceived the first group, the Avar tried to deceive the others as well; before Theoderic’s eyes he struck them down with spear and sword.

After this Theoderic fought him alone, wounded him in the arm, and finally defeated him and personally led him back to his own camp.

Delighted by his prudence and courage, Theoderic urged him with gentle words to remain with him in peace, promising many gifts and honors.

But the Avar, making light of the requests and gifts, asked only this each day: that Theoderic allow him to return to his own land.

Since he could not retain him in any way, Theoderic at last allowed him to leave and followed him as far as the river Ister.

When the Avar had swum across it, he looked back and addressed Theoderic from the opposite bank:

“Since you have restored me to freedom of my own accord, I will now return to you and will be utterly faithful to you.”

Theoderic brought him back with him and, after bestowing many gifts upon him, often kept him as a companion in campaigns against the Vandals and Suebi, since he saw that everything prospered for him.

After these events, and after the Avars had been put to flight, Theoderic returned victoriously to Rome.

About this time Theoderic sent his envoys to Clovis, requesting that he give him his sister Landechildis in marriage and that from then on they should maintain a most firm treaty of peace between them.

Our lord Clovis agreed to his requests and, with the greatest honor, handed his sister over to him. Theoderic received her graciously and took her as his wife.

She bore him two daughters and conducted herself most graciously with him until she married one of them to the blessed King and Martyr Sigismund.

The other remained at home with her mother after Theoderic’s death. When she wished to be joined in an illicit marriage with a certain low-born man, her mother prohibited her.

But turning over in her mind the resentment she had conceived, she repaid her mother for the injury she had suffered and killed her, as though she were a criminal woman, with poison.

When the king who had succeeded his father learned of this, he decreed that the evil of so great a crime should be punished by a fitting vengeance, and ordered her to be suffocated by the heat of a bath.

But enough has been said about these matters. Let us now return to the order of the history, especially since we still consider the history of this Theoderic necessary to complete the sequence of our narrative.

In the second year after his baptism, Clovis took up arms against Gundobad and Godegisil. Directing his army against them, he inflamed the courage of the Franks to avenge the ancient injuries done to his wife, resolving either to slaughter all the Burgundians by the sword or to subjugate them under a heavy tribute.

Against him Gundobad and Godegisil prepared a large army. To defend themselves, although their conscience reproved them and they deserved punishment for fratricide, they caused men of every age to gather together with every apparatus of war.

Thus, having assembled the entire multitude, they hastened as far as Dijon. When they fought with all their strength on both sides, the Burgundians turned their backs, and the army of the Franks ravaged them with such ferocity that it is scarcely possible to compile the number of the slain.

Gundobad, fleeing from the battle, shut himself up and fortified himself in the city of Avignon, as though he could resist so great a king.

But perceiving that he could not ultimately escape Clovis’s hand and fearing the measure of his offense, he sent a certain councillor of his, a wise and moderate man named Aredius, to Clovis. By his very temperate eloquence he [lacuna]. The anger of the king was calmed by the wise man, and Gundobad gave our lord the king many immense measures of gold and silver, in view of the crime he had committed, so that the king’s anger might not be stirred further.

They established this condition between them: every year, throughout the ages to come, the Burgundians would pay tribute to the Franks, present and future.

Clovis, laden with booty and honored with these gifts, returned victoriously to his homeland. Gundobad had two sons, Sigismund and Godegisil.

At that same time a very great earthquake occurred in the city of Vienne, and many churches were overturned. Very many houses are also reported to have been shaken by the same movement so violently that even their foundations were loosened from their deepest seats.

Soon afterward wolves and other savage beasts followed the earthquake. Bursting through the city gates with terrifying force, they cruelly tore apart anyone they happened to encounter and dragged some children into the wilderness to be divided among their cubs.

The city and the entire surrounding region were devastated by this plague for almost a year.

In that same year, when the solemn feast of Easter arrived and Saint Mammertus, the bishop of that city, was offering the sacrifice to the Creator on Holy Saturday according to the solemn rite, the royal palace of that city was consumed by divine fire.

When the aforementioned bishop saw that divine fury had blazed forth against the wretched inhabitants of that district, and that, by the permission of almighty God, irrational wild beasts were ravaging human beings with irrational ferocity, he warned that a remedy for so great a misfortune should be sought from the Lord.

He ordered the entire people, with groaning and contrition of spirit, to abstain from food for three days, after the manner of the Ninevites. Covered in sackcloth and walking barefoot, they were to go around the sacred places weeping and praying, crying out, “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”), in the hope that the Lord, appeased by this humiliation, might change so terrible a sentence of destruction into benevolence.

He also established that every year litanies should be held in the same church for three days, to which the entire people would come and pour out humble prayers to the Creator, so that they would not be devoured savagely again.

The Lord saw the affliction of his people and spared his creation, so that it would not be destroyed to the point of annihilation; he was greatly pleased by this devotion.

Thus the raging wolves were driven back; thus, with the Lord restoring favor, heavenly vengeance subsided. Thus general mourning was changed into joy, when the tribulation ceased and the beasts’ ferocity was transformed into gentleness.

The holy mother Church was pleased by this sacred custom, and with the authority of the Roman pontiff it was established throughout the world that on these three days—Monday before the Sunday of the Ascension, namely Tuesday and Wednesday—the people should gather in church and celebrate the litanies.

Thus, just as at that time the Viennese people were defended by God’s grace from the wolves that attacked them, so now may God’s mercy drive spiritual wolves—that is, demons—far from us and deign to defend his holy Church, lest the crafty enemy stain by his ferocity what is known to have been redeemed by the Lord’s blood.

There prayers are offered for the state of the Church, for the safety of rulers, for fair weather, for the fruits of the earth, and for the various troubles of the people, so that God and our Lord Jesus Christ, in his goodness and mercy, may preserve the state of his holy Church in complete prosperity; may protect and preserve the Catholic rulers of the people so that, girded with spiritual strength, they may drive all barbarian nations far from us; may grant us a favorable climate; may himself transform the barrenness of the fields into rich fertility; may protect, multiply, and bring the crops to maturity; and may drive away the ailments of our bodies by healing power and deign to preserve us sound and unharmed in his holy service.

The south wind has driven away the dreadful cloud of spiders; the webs have been torn apart; the harmful air has been dispersed. The little sheep must be led to pasture, lest I be struck and beaten by the scourge of an impertinent tongue.

But you, who know the name, follow me cautiously. If you take pleasure in hearing more, beware that my lords do not learn of this as well, for they will be exceedingly angry with me if they catch me idling and chatting with you.

# [BOOK FOUR]

## PROLOGUE OF THE FOURTH BOOK

[Col. 0607]

The third hour of the day has now passed. With the Lord’s help, I shall begin the fourth little book of this work, since we have avoided the heat of the sun by sitting beneath a leafy tree, and the wolf that was lying in wait for the sheep has gone away in fear.

For they have constricted the jaws with which he was lying in wait for them. He no longer howls like a wolf but yelps like a little fox; he has lowered his eyes, bent his neck, altered his voice, and walks like a sick creature—not to lay aside his ferocity, but to deceive the unwary.

Whether he is watching the hens or thirsting for lambs remains uncertain. And if an Ethiopian had changed his skin, I would likewise believe that this one had changed himself into a sheep.

But if he casts off his false disguise and again attacks our sheep with his customary ferocity, we have filled the shepherd’s bag, which you can see nearby, with stones and prepared the sling. He will not find us sluggish or unprepared: we shall await him boldly, and he will be struck down by sling and stone.

And since you are looking toward the south and, rather than speaking, indicate by nods that, just as you suggested the Romans were worn down and expelled by the Gauls, I should likewise touch upon the Goths and demonstrate in plain speech how their fury was suppressed, I shall do what you urge—provided you promise not to trouble me any further and conceal my rusticity along with me, lest my poorer speech offend the cultivated ears of noble men. For I have rashly ventured to taste the history of so great a king, which some sensible person ought to have extolled with countless praises.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0607]

[Col. 0607D] Clovis, therefore, whose religious spirit had been breathed upon by divine fervor, inflamed with zeal for the faith, not only drove heretics from his own territories, but also, whenever he discovered that some of the neighboring peoples were less religious, either subdued them by repeated incursions or violently oppressed them with the harsh bonds of slavery. Hence it came about that he took up arms against Alaric, king of the Goths, whom he had learned, according to the opinion of the whole people, to be defiled by Arian wickedness.

This Alaric was bold and powerful, a man of exceedingly great spirit, always renowned for prosperous outcomes and girded with excessive savagery. King Clovis had often warned him through envoys to abandon his Arian perversity and believe that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit possess equal divinity in three persons, if he wished to retain Clovis as a friend. But Alaric, relying on his accustomed ferocity, began to trust in his own strength; and, indignant that Clovis dared to speak thus, he repeatedly insulted him and, instead of thanks, inflicted insults.

For this reason, as has been said, Clovis often raised arms against him and harassed him with many incursions of war, until at last a certain Paternus, Clovis’s envoy, a wise and modest man, almost bent Alaric’s savage spirit toward belief. He wished to establish permanently between the two of them the laws of peace and friendship, had not the faithlessness of the others stood in the way.

The modest man had requested that Alaric become Clovis’s sponsor at the cutting of his beard; thereafter, while persevering in the confession of the true faith, they would secure a treaty of mutual peace under this provision: whenever both armies met either to establish the treaty or to confer, the Franks and Goths alike would lay down their arms.

The Goths, therefore, wishing to disturb the treaty of peace in their accustomed faithlessness and plotting to deprive our king of life and rule, concealed beneath their cloaks enormous knives, which in the vulgar tongue we call *hantsaccos*, by a corrupted name. Thus, disguised in cloaks, they could without hindrance cut down Clovis’s unsuspecting army.

When the envoy Paternus perceived this, astonished at the kind of conspiracy, he pretended that the Franks should return to their own people, and himself attacked Alaric with these words:

“Since I had resolved, by providing for the interests of our peoples, to establish the laws of peace and friendship between the two kingdoms, and since it has become evident that you are using your customary lying and deceit, wishing to strike down our men beneath cloaked weapons, let this arrangement not be rejected so suddenly and unexpectedly. Let us jointly consult, through messengers, whatever neighboring kings we can; and whatever he himself decides, let it be carried out without frustration.”

Paternus ordered the peoples to fulfill what he had requested, proposed that Theoderic, king of Italy, be consulted on the matter, and commanded that whatever he decreed should be carried out.

When Paternus and Alaric’s envoy had gone there together and the affair had been disclosed, Theoderic considered that if he separated these two very powerful kings from one another and sowed among them the seeds of quarrel and hatred, while they attacked one another with the successive outcomes of war and each army cut down the other with mutual wounds, he himself, placed between them, could rest in peaceful security.

Finally, he established and decreed this, as though it had been issued by common judgment: the two battle lines, those of the Franks and the Goths, should meet and surround the place from either side. In their midst, Clovis’s envoy, seated on horseback, would raise his spear upward; and the Goths would bring gold and silver around him as compensation for their crime until the entire spear was covered by a heap of these two metals.

Burdened by this condition, Alaric chose hatred rather than peace and attempted to deceive Paternus by another kind of fraud, in case he should happen by some accident to be wounded fatally and the dispute should thus be ended, since there would be no one to report the truth of the matter to our lord Clovis.

He ordered Paternus to lodge in an ancient upper chamber. As Paternus walked carelessly through it, the wood broke beneath his feet, and he fell headlong to the ground. His arm was broken, but, under the Lord’s protection, he was preserved alive.

When he had scarcely recovered, while the wound was not yet healed, Alaric one day led him to display his treasures. Opening his chests, he showed him the immeasurable quantity of his riches. Paternus leapt toward them and, jesting, stretched his hand toward a chest in joy and snatched as much gold as his fist could hold. Looking back at Alaric, he boldly addressed him:

“Unless you quickly assemble the battle lines, gather an innumerable army, arm their right hands and their spirits, and sharpen your sworn legions for our blood, you will suffer the punishment deserved by your conspiracy without delay—when I bring our Franks to divide this gold, when I inflame our descendants to possess this dignity, and when I cause our pens or ropes to be extended for the division of these territories.”

Having finished this speech, he mounted his horse and hurried back to the Franks. He reported everything as it had happened to his lord Clovis and powerfully inflamed his spirit to enlarge the glory of the Franks, urging him to go to see the Pyrenees or to behold the Ocean Sea.

This was the beginning of the troubles; from it the cause of the conflict grew. This was the origin of the discord by which the ferocity of the Goths was crushed and Alaric was deprived alike of life and dignity.

And since we have recounted certain beginnings of King Theoderic that we hoped would suit our narrative, let us likewise disclose what his end was, so that by his terrifying example we may correct wicked judges.

Having been corrupted by the counsel of certain wicked men, he condemned by an unjust judgment and ordered the execution of Pope John and the patrician Symmachus, Christian men accused by conspirators, although they had lived entirely without offense. Afterward, when he was being led toward death and did not cleanse such a deed by repentance, divine vengeance descended upon him, violently snatched his wicked spirit from his body, and—as we learned from the blessed Pope Gregory’s account—on the very day when he departed this life, a certain man living in Sicily, who practiced the life of angels among human beings, was engaged, as usual, in prayer. Caught up in spirit and presenting his supplicatory petitions to the Creator, he saw Theoderic, stripped and barefoot, his hands bound behind his back, being dragged toward the places of punishment.

These two men, namely John and Symmachus, were shamefully reviling and dragging him along by force. Just as he had condemned them to an unjust death, so they brought him after death to punishment and, without pity, threw him into the abyss of Vulcan. Let this suffice concerning them. Let us return to the order of the history.

Clovis, therefore, encouraged by the counsel of his envoy Paternus and strengthened by his prudence, ordered the Frankish nobles to assemble at Paris. He addressed the wiser men in these words:

“Since the vigor and confidence of your spirits are well known to me, I have summoned you, judging that I should disclose the secrets of my heart to those whose will and singular friendship are united with mine. I wish you to know that my spirit is inflamed more intensely whenever I consider how the course of our life declines daily toward its setting without any title of glory; how the fierce spirits of our soldiers are softened by idleness; and how I fear that, once sluggish spirits have been seized by disuse, we may find their swords blunted and corrupted with rust when necessity should perhaps demand them.

“Our weapons must now be taken up again; our swords must be sharpened; our bodies must be restored to the labor of military service. Let not the blandishments of women entice you; let not the cries of little children frighten you. Although our parents were held in the error of paganism, by arms and repeated efforts they subdued the proud.

“And we, who have already begun to adore Christ, who delight in his praises and enjoy his friendship, ought most fittingly to hate his enemies. Behold, an unfaithful people—namely, the senseless Goths—seems to be staining with blood a great part of Gaul, which they call Aquitaine. Through their Arian perversity they separate the Son from the Father and do not acknowledge that the Holy Spirit possesses equal divinity with the Father and the Son; and by this they are proved to be enemies of God.

“If, with one mind, you assent to our words and show yourselves, in Christian name, to be friends of God, raise your right hands upward and draw your happy swords to crush this wretched people. Equip the less cautious with weapons and good exhortations. He will certainly grant victory—the one who has dedicated your minds to his worship.

“They stripped fortunate Rome alike of wealth and liberty; nor will lesser glory be prepared for us if, by waging war, we overcome their most savage king and subject his kingdom and fortune to our rule.”

All alike embraced the king’s prudence, admired his courage, and especially revered his faith. They all raised their right hands on high, declared that the king’s command would be hastened, and bound themselves by vows; they professed that their beards were not to be shaved again unless the unbelievers were no more.

Without delay the proclamation flew through the peoples: both sexes were ordered to prepare for such an undertaking. Children and mothers were brought forth; when the thorns of heretical perversity had been torn out and uprooted, shoots of virtue were planted in their place, so that the new plantation might bear a hundredfold fruit for the Lord, whom shameful contrivance had defrauded.

At this Queen Clotildis rejoiced exceedingly in the Lord and applauded the fact that through baptism she had offered the Creator such a precious offspring, which had resolved to subdue by arms even the minds of unbelievers that the ecclesiastical plowshare could not furrow.

She therefore approached the king and said to him:

“Listen, I beg you, my lord king, to your handmaid, and order a church to be built in honor of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, so that he may be your helper in war; and surely the Lord will grant victory into your hands.”

The queen’s speech pleased Clovis. He raised the double-headed ax that he held in his hand, hurled it away from him with all the force he could muster, and said:

“On this spot, with the Lord’s help, the church of Saint Peter shall be established when I return victorious from battle.”

He then moved his army and resolved to hurry as far as Poitiers. At that time Alaric, king of the Goths, was staying there.

As Clovis’s army passed through the district of Tours, the king ordered, out of reverence for Saint Martin, that no one inflict any violence in that province. Indeed, the army would not have presumed to take anything from there by force except grass that seemed necessary for their horses.

The king also sent many gifts and a very swift horse, which he greatly loved, through envoys to the basilica of blessed Martin, and said to them:

“When you have entered the oratory of the blessed man and presented our gifts, commit to memory whatever the church cantor first pronounces aloud, so that you may know how to report it to me. Perhaps you will receive from the holy utterance some sign of victory.”

After saying this, he prayed to the Lord:

“If you, Lord, deliver this unbelieving people into my hands, and grant [f., *dederis*] victory into my hands, and prove to be my helper and protector in war, may it happen that, upon entering the basilica of Saint Martin, our boys hear such words that I may discern in them some sign of victory and know that you have been favorable to me, your servant.”

He then sent the boys away, and they departed. When they reached the entrance of the basilica, the cantor pronounced aloud:

“You have girded me, Lord, with strength for war; you have brought down beneath me those who rose against me; you have given me the backs of my enemies; and you have destroyed those who hated me.”

After presenting the gifts and being strengthened by the divine oracle, they returned joyfully and exultantly to their lord and refreshed him with this report.

At that time the waters had overflowed because of the excessive rains, and the river Vienne had risen so greatly that no place could be found at all where it might be crossed without a boat. When the king reached it and could proceed no farther, he ordered tents to be erected, so that either a bridge might be laid or a boat prepared by which he and his army could cross that flood of water.

The mercy of our God removed this labor. On the following day, when the morning light had already spread, behold, from a distance they saw a doe of extraordinary size. It entered the river with slow steps and, by divine sign, showed the people—ignorant of the crossing—where they should pass.

Without delay the entire army crossed the river, and with exultant hearts glorified the Lord on high, who, just as he had enabled the Israelite people to cross the Red Sea, so wonderfully instructed the Frankish people to pass through the flood of such a great river by showing them a way.

When they reached the city of Poitiers, Clovis ordered the tents to be pitched far from the church of Saint Hilary. He threatened the whole people that they should take no one’s property in that district, plunder no houses, seize no livestock, and take no provisions by violence.

That same night a fiery beacon appeared to emerge, as it were, from the tomb of Saint Hilary and remained visible above Clovis’s tent for nearly half an hour. We believe it was sent to aid the Franks, so that, strengthened by this standard, they might be inflamed ever more intensely to crush the unbelieving people.

Alaric happened to be absent at that time. He had sent envoys everywhere to gather an innumerable army and, so to speak, had encouraged the spirits of his people not so much to resist as to fortify themselves, recalling their brave deeds. He said that our people were extremely few and declared that his empire was broad and spacious. Just as they had crushed Rome, so, he suggested, the glory of the Franks must be crushed.

He falsely claimed that they had come not to wage war but to plunder. He disgraced our men with a thousand insults and exalted his own with immense praises. He declared that weapons must be taken up lest the little ones be despoiled by brigands.

Thus, enraged, he came against our men not to strike but to swallow them; surrounded by the multitude of his soldiers, he yearned for the spoils of our people, greedily desiring that they be stained with shed blood.

The madman did not know that the one who was leading our army was he who does not trust in thousands, who thunders in the clouds, who moves the abyss, and who sits in heaven.

Clovis, therefore, emerged from the camp carrying Christ in his breast, and, surveying the entire army, arranged the ranks of the chosen. He urged the strongest soldiers to strike and encouraged the average ones not to fear with lively words.

As an outstanding soldier, he led the army before them; as a most faithful Christian, he repeatedly sighed toward heaven. He restrained the fiery spirits of the noble youths lest they burst from the line before the proper time, and, when they stood in battle, he urged them not to forget their swords.

He instructed the inexperienced in how to strike the enemy and likewise showed them how to make the blows of the enemy spring away harmlessly. He called upon Peter and Martin to come to their aid; and, looking toward Hilary, he implored him to take up the standard and lead the army.

Let him strike the Arians no less vigorously than their wretched leader Arius had been accustomed to strike an empty belly with his disputations. Leaning on his spear, he looked upon all the Franks, marked the faithful army with the sign of our faith, and prayed that they might strike in the name of the Lord.

Then battle was joined on both sides. With trumpets sounding everywhere, the sky was filled with shouting; missiles flew through the air, and the earth was stained with blood. Here you would hear the groans of the dying; there you would shudder at the shrieks of the wounded. One, bloodless and fluttering, dying, devoured the earth or stones.

Another, kicking because the slow process of death seemed too prolonged, constricted by the pain of his wounds, seized something from his shattered weapons with which to pierce his sorrowful breast and, by thus hastening death, ended the torment of his wounds.

Clovis, brandishing his spear, struck down everyone who came before him and repeatedly shouted the name of the Lord. While he encouraged the spirits of the Franks with continual cries toward the destruction of the hated people and strengthened some who were less attentive in battle, he caught sight of Alaric at a distance. Sending his horse after him, he struck him with his lance and then drew his sword.

Behold, the assembled people marveled at the two fiercest kings and offered them no assistance as they fought. Each searched for the place of the other’s wound and, often failing to find it, cut away the turned shield with his sword.

As each in turn, burning with fury, pressed against the other, and the flat surfaces of both helmets were cleft into pieces, Clovis, recalling the brave deeds of ancient ferocity, raised his arm and poised his sword for the wound. He struck away Alaric’s beard, chin, and left hand—the hand with which he held his shield—and then sprang back to one side, intending with a second blow to cut off his head.

[Col. 0614A] While they were fighting thus, two Goths sprang forward from the opposite side and struck our king with their lances with great force, intending to deliver him unexpectedly to death. But the almighty Lord protected him; covered by threefold glory, he regarded such blows as nothing. Seizing Alaric with his left hand, he brought down his sword with powerful effort and thus cut off his head.

Once again voices rose to the stars, and the Franks, their strength renewed, were again stirred to slaughter. But when the Goths saw the death of their king, they scattered here and there like whirlwinds and, throwing away their weapons, searched the hidden places in vain.

As it is written in the history of the ancient Fathers, one of our men pursued a thousand of them, and two put ten thousand to flight. You would have seen fulfilled what Scripture testifies concerning sinners: “As wax melts before the fire, so may sinners perish before the face of God; and may the righteous feast, rejoice before God, and delight in gladness.”

Thus Clovis defeated the enemy army and brought it almost to complete destruction. Those who escaped the swords of the Franks fled to Spain with Amalaric, Alaric’s son, and raised that same Amalaric to his father’s throne.

The great multitude of the Arverni, who had come with their leader Apollinaris to assist Alaric, was so crushed in that battle, together with many senators, that scarcely a messenger survived from so great a multitude to announce the event to their wives.

This battle was fought in the field of Vosaglinse, above the river Clain, ten miles from the city of Poitiers.

[Col. 0614C] After this victory had been accomplished, King Clovis sent his son Theoderic, whom he had fathered by a concubine, with part of his army into the territory of the Arverni, so that he might subject its cities and municipalities as far as the Rhône River.

Obeying his father’s commands, he skillfully subdued all the cities from the borders of the Goths as far as Burgundy and placed them under Frankish rule.

King Clovis then entered the city of Bordeaux, where he remained during the winter and restored his army, exhausted by the war. From there he advanced and seized Toulouse, ordering the treasures of Alaric to be divided among those who were going to possess that province.

When he approached the city of Ecolesina, which had dared to rebel, and resolved to conquer it by arms and siege, divine power granted him such favor that, at his arrival, the walls of that city collapsed.
