When the townspeople saw this and believed that the event had occurred by divine will, they surrendered themselves and their possessions to Clovis. They demolished the city’s fortification with siege engines and likewise offered the king the Gothic soldiers who had defended it.

He put all of them to death by beheading. Then, having subjected the region as far as the Pyrenees and Perpignan, demolishing cities and fortresses, and plundering every municipality, he distributed an innumerable quantity of booty and many spoils equally among his soldiers.

After these things had been accomplished, when he resolved to return to his own land, he left chosen and very brave soldiers, together with children and women, to guard the cities he had conquered and to restrain the savagery of the Goths, and he enriched them with immense gifts.

Thus exulting in the Lord and delighting in joy, he returned to Tours and humbly offered many gifts to the confessor. He ordered one hundred solidi to be given to the matricularii (church dependants) to redeem his horse. But the horse could neither be released nor moved from the spot.

He gave another hundred, and the horse could be moved and released. When he had recovered it, overcome with abundant joy and dissolved in laughter, he is said to have replied:

“Truly, blessed Martin is regarded as both prompt in assistance and gracious in business.”

He mounted the horse, dressed in purple and wearing gold and a royal diadem on his head. In celebration of the victory and out of reverence for Saint Martin, he scattered a great quantity of gold and silver in the courtyard between the church of Saint Martin and the city, in the presence of the people, and distributed it with royal generosity.

From that very day the emperor Anastasius received him into singular friendship, and ordered him to be called not only king or consul but also Augustus.

Raised to such glory, he knelt before the tomb of blessed Martin and prayed. Then, leaving the city, he returned to Paris and established that city as the seat of his kingdom.

He had the church of Saint Peter, which he had promised to build before setting out for war, constructed with fitting arrangement, and, once built, sufficiently endowed it with ornaments and revenues.

Afterward he led an army against Ragnerius and Richarius, who were staying at Cambrai, and resolved that they should be stripped alike of every secular dignity and of life.

This Ragnerius was unrestrained in lust and had a counselor named Pharo, equally filthy and befouled by the same depravity. The Lord hated them, and therefore they could not be loved by God’s people.

For this reason the Franks who had been subjected to them and oppressed by their unjust domination, bearing this subjection with the greatest indignation, approached Clovis. They requested gifts from him so that they might deceitfully incite Ragnerius to fight against our people, and thus bring his life to an end without great tumult and without blame.

The king therefore gave them bracelets, copper belts, and electrum ornaments skillfully made and covered above with gold. After receiving these gifts, they began to urge Ragnerius to take up arms against Clovis and go out to battle, falsely claiming that the king was approaching with only a few men while they were surrounded by many soldiers.

When Ragnerius heard this, he went boldly to battle and fought fiercely against our men. But with the Lord’s favor, since his wicked life was displeasing to him, Ragnerius was seized, bound, and presented to Clovis.

With him they also captured Richarius and Pharo and presented them, likewise bound, to the king. Clovis ordered them to be punished by beheading and thus put an end to their wicked crime. In addition, he restored their treasures and city to his own rule.

At the city of Le Mans, a certain relative of Ragnerius, named Ragnimirus, was also living. Clovis likewise deprived him of life and kingdom, so that no spark of the wicked offspring might remain that could rekindle a horrible crime among the peoples and, God forbid, condemn them to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah.

When Ragnerius’s traitors learned that, as the price of such a crime, they had received adulterated copper, they came to the king, complaining greatly and repenting too late, and disclosed how they had been mocked.

Clovis answered them:

“You rightly received such gold, since you delivered your lord to death. Let it now be enough for you that you have preserved your own lives and have not paid the punishment deserved for so great a crime.”

After these things had been accomplished, Clovis was seized by a fever. Feeling his illness grow worse from day to day, he summoned the Frankish nobles, divided his kingdom into parts, and distributed those parts among his four sons.

To his son Childebert, whom he loved uniquely, he gave Paris; he ordered Clodomir to reside at Orléans. He gave Soissons to Clothar, and to Theoderic, whom he had fathered by a concubine, he granted the city of Reims and Cambrai.

When great mourning arose among the Frankish nobles at the departure of so great a king, the faithful king sighed toward heaven and said:

“Behold, Lord God, have mercy on me, and govern this people, who has been purified in your name by the regeneration of holy baptism. Surround our heirs with perpetual protection. As for our Crochildis—indeed, yours, and because she is yours therefore more truly ours—I commend her to you in such a way that you may guard her as your own, as one of your household, as a daughter, or as a handmaid. You provided and entrusted her to me, your servant; I return her to you, through whom I came to know the decrees of your law.”

After saying these things, he gave up his spirit and was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, which he himself had built, in the thirtieth year of his reign. The Lord Jesus Christ reigns forever, and to him belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0616] End.

In the year of the Lord 1008. Aimoin, monk of Fleury.

[Col. 0617]

HISTORICAL NOTICE.

(From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. I, p. 33.)

[Col. 0617A] Aimoin, or Haimo, a native of Périgueux in Aquitaine, whose name has been variously transformed by copyists into Aumonius, Aimonius, Amonius, or Annonnius, was a monk from A.D. 970 onward of the monastery of Fleury, or Saint Benedict, on the Loire.

In A.D. 1005 he recorded the *Life and Miracles* of his abbot Abbo [Note: [Col. 0617B] Of the book of the Miracles, only one chapter now survives.]—whom the Gascons had killed the preceding year—and addressed it to Hervaeus, or Herivaeus, the treasurer-clerk of Saint Martin.

The *Life* appears in Jean du Bois’s *Bibliotheca Floriacensis*, Lyon, 1605–1608, p. 299; in Pithou’s *Twelve Writers*, p. 428; and in volume VIII of the *Acts of the Benedictines*, p. 682.

To the same Abbo he dedicated four books of the *History of the Franks*, which he intended to carry to the inauguration of King Pepin, that is, to A.D. 752, but stopped at the foundation of the monastery of Fleury [Col. 0617B] around A.D. 650 or 660.

The remainder, therefore, from chapter 42 of the fourth book, where Chesne’s edition ends, and the fifth book down to the year 1165, were added by some monk of Saint-Germain in Paris and by others.

See Labbe’s dissertation on Aimoin, volume II of *Sacred Ecclesiastical Literature*, p. 829; Cointius, *Annals of the Franks*, vol. I, p. 842; vol. II, p. 161; vol. III, p. 401; vol. IV, p. 117, and elsewhere; Launoy, *Inquiry into the Charter of Immunity*, p. 77 ff., and the *Assertion of that Inquiry*, p. 620 ff.; both works were reprinted in the third volume of Launoy’s *Works*.

Nicolas Jérôme Gundling, *Frag-Stücken*, XIV.

Aimoin’s *History* was published by Badius in Paris in 1514 folio under the name of Annonnius, restored to Aimoin, [Col. 0618A] and revised by Jean Nicot, Paris, at the press of Andreas Wechel, 1567–1568; afterward by Jacques Breul there in 1603 folio; in Jean du Bois’s *Bibliotheca Floriacensis*, Lyon, 1605–1608; and also in Marquard Freher’s *Frankish Writers*, Hanover, 1613 folio.

Finally, it appeared in the third volume of André du Chesne, Paris, 1641 folio. That volume also contains the poem *On the First Foundation of the Monastery of Fleury*, in hexameter verse, as well as another poem *On the Translation of the Relics of Saint Benedict into Gaul*, which is likewise found in Mabillon’s *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, second century, p. 359.

There is also a sermon for the festivals of Saint Benedict, with verses by Maurus and Paul, monks of Cassino, by Abbot Smaragdus, Bishop Aldhelm, and others, in the aforementioned Jean du Bois’s *Bibliotheca Floriacensis*, p. 270. In the same work, p. 79, there is also a *History of the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, in two books, addressed to Gauzlinus, or Gauslenus [Note: Trithemius, chapter 305, says “to the monk Renaldus.”], abbot and later archbishop of Bourges. These works are also found in Bollandus, under 21 March, p. 324, and in Mabillon, *Benedictine Century* IV, part II, p. 366.

Sigebert of Gembloux, in chapter 101, mentioning Aimoin’s *History of the Franks*, writes that he also described the situation of Gaul. He also produced an account of the translation of Saint Savinus the martyr from a temple already ruined and deserted to the abbey now called Saint Savinus in the territory of Poitiers. Read this account in Martène, *Ancient Monuments*, vol. VI, p. 806.

[Col. 0617]

LITERARY NOTICE.

(*Literary History of France*, vol. VII, p. 218.)

[Col. 0617C] Aimoin of Fleury wrote a *History of the Franks*, which he undertook to compose at the command of his abbot Abbo, as he himself declares in the dedicatory epistle by which he dedicates it to him and submits it to his judgment.

He therefore began it while Abbo was alive and consequently before 1004, the year of Abbo’s death. In the same epistle Aimoin himself set out the entire plan of his project.

He intended to gather into a single work and express in better style what was scattered and poorly written in various books concerning the nation of the Franks and the kings who had ruled it. He was to carry this out by taking up the history from the origin of the nation and continuing it to the reign of Pepin the Short, father of Charlemagne—an essential circumstance insufficiently observed. This alone would have been enough to prevent the attribution to Aimoin of a work that carries the history far beyond that point.

His work was to be divided into four books. In the first he would treat five kings of the Frankish nation, and six in the second. The third was to be devoted to the history of seven further kings, and the fourth to that of more than eight.

The historian promised to distinguish so carefully the names of the kings, which elsewhere were stated confusedly because of their similarity, that he would bring their genealogy into a new light.

And, in order to shed greater light on the whole work, he believed, on Abbo’s advice, that he should place at the beginning a notice of Germany and Gaul, where the events he intended to describe had taken place. He carried this out in a fairly long preface, in which he took Pliny, Orosius, and especially Julius Caesar as his guides, scarcely doing more than copy what they said about these vast regions and the customs of their inhabitants.

Although Aimoin’s fourth book was supposed to contain the history of more than eight Frankish kings, indeed down to Pepin the Short, as has just been seen, in the work as we possess it one finds only the history of three of these kings, extending to the sixteenth year of the reign of Clovis II.

Thus it must be admitted either that we do not possess the work in its entirety or that the author did not finish it. The principal sources from which he drew his account are Saint Gregory of Tours, of whose work Aimoin nevertheless possessed only the first seven books; Fredegar; the abridgment Fredegar had made of the first six books of the preceding historian; the *Deeds of the Franks*; the *Deeds of Dagobert*; Paul the Deacon; and several Lives of Saints (Valesius, *On Frankish Affairs*, book XV, p. 441; Mabillon, *Diplomatic Supplement*, p. 24).

As for the manner in which he carried out his project and put his materials to work, he did not succeed in giving us an accurate and complete history. Following Fredegar’s example, he does little more than designate or lightly indicate the events, without entering into appropriate detail (Valesius, ibid.).

He speaks of the wars individually only very briefly and develops neither their motives nor their causes nor their consequences, whatever their nature may be. Not only does he cite none of the authors from whom he drew, but he also adds various things of his own to what they say, reverses the order in which they report their material, and sometimes finds himself in contradiction with them.

When Aimoin published his history, he anticipated that he would have critics, even during his lifetime. We do not see that he had any at that time, but he has had many in recent centuries.

Pasquier, among others, devoted chapters 27 and 28 of the fifth book of his *Researches into France* to making known some of the errors into which our historian fell. He does not merely point them out; he verifies them by comparing Aimoin’s passages with those of the authors he used.

It is true that this critic sometimes cites passages that belong not to Aimoin but to his interpolators. At other times he also mistakes one chapter for another, taking, for example, chapter 99 of book III for chapter 98.

Father Le Cointe, for his part, likewise identified a good number of errors in the same historian (Cointius, year 654, nos. 25–27).

The famous Pierre Pithou, in his *Memoirs of the Counts of Champagne and Brie*, in turn observes that Aimoin, when speaking of the offices of the crown, often confuses them and thereby led many writers into error.

He adds that he would be able to show that Aimoin took several other liberties by abusing the terminology of the ancient historians and adapting it to his own time in order to make a display of his Latin.

Aimoin is no more accurate with regard to geography, as the learned Abbé Le Beuf has shown very well by detailing certain rather gross errors into which he fell in this branch of learning (Le Beuf, *Dissertation*, vol. I, pp. 16, 17, 94, 340, 341, 348–350).

There are two principal manuscripts of Aimoin’s *History*, very different from one another, which served as models for nearly all the others and for the [Col. 0620C] editions made from them. One belongs to the abbey of Fleury and contains Aimoin’s work only through the forty-second chapter of the fourth book; this carries the continuation of the history to the sixteenth year of Clovis II’s reign, corresponding to the year 654 of our common era. Thus, according to the author’s design, nearly a hundred years are missing, since—as has been seen—he had proposed to continue his work through the reign of Pepin the Short. We do not know whether Aimoin completed this plan; and, supposing that he did, we do not know what became of the continuation now missing.

The other manuscript, one of those of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, represents Aimoin’s *History* in a much fuller form. [Col. 0620D] Not only does its fourth book contain seventy-five chapters more than the first manuscript, but it is also followed—contrary to the author’s design—by a fifth book, divided into fifty-seven chapters, which carries the history to 1165. It also contains various additions and interpolations in the first four books that are absent from the Fleury manuscript. Those in the first book amount almost entirely to the epitaph of Clovis the Great. But those in the other books are substantial and quite visibly extraneous.

All critics now unanimously agree that everything read in this manuscript [Col. 0621A] from the beginning of the forty-second chapter of the fourth book onward consists of foreign additions that do not belong to Aimoin. It is the work of one or more monks of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, as can easily be demonstrated from the charters and the summary history of the abbots of that monastery, which were inserted into the second book and the two following books. We shall not pause to discuss the additions to the fourth and fifth books. Several able critics have already done so with great insight. On this subject one may consult Vossius, Father Le Long, and above all Father Labbe, in the learned and lengthy dissertation he composed on our historian (Voss., *Hist. Lat.*, book II, chapter 34, pp. 98–99; Le Long, *Bib. Fr.*, pp. 319–320; Labbe, [Col. 0621B] *Scri.*, vol. II, pp. 841, 850–877). Part of these additions—that is, those from chapter 58 of Book IV to the end of that book, comprising a continuation of the history from the year 741 to 829—was printed in sixteens at Cologne in 1562 under the name of an anonymous Benedictine monk (Wion, *Lig. vit.*, part I, book II, p. 398).

The first edition of Aimoin’s *History* came from the presses of Badius Ascensius in 1514. It is a folio volume dedicated to Guillaume Parvi, or “the Little,” the king’s confessor, who appears to have directed it (Bib. D. de Lorch). Failure to read the author’s name attentively caused him to be called *Annonius* there instead of *Aimoinius*. In a script without dots over the *i*s, it is easy to read one for the other. [Col. 0621C] At the end it is stated that the author was a monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, proving that the edition was made from the manuscript of that abbey. The editor had nevertheless been given access to the Fleury manuscript, since after chapter 41 of Book IV he warns that the latter manuscript extends only to that point and that the continuation was probably by another author.

Since this edition was full of errors, Jean Nicot, master of requests and the king’s ambassador in Portugal—not M. Pithou, as M. du Pin wrote—began work as early as 1557 on producing a new one (Bib. S. P. de Cult.). This appears from the privilege, which is dated the same year. Nevertheless, it was not published until ten years later, in 1567. [Col. 0621D] The volume is in octavo and was printed in Paris by André Wechel. Like the preceding edition, it contains Aimoin’s text with all its additions, but it is more accurate. After chapter 41 of Book IV it also contains the same remark as the earlier edition, though somewhat expanded. Wion and Possevin say that this same edition also appeared at Lyon in the same year as at Paris (Wion, *ibid.*; Possevin, *App.*, vol. II, p. 21), but we have seen no copy of it.

Dom Jacques du Breul next undertook to produce another edition, which the booksellers Ambroise and Jérôme Drouart published in Paris in 1602, in a very well-produced folio volume (Bib. Vin. Cen.). It is entirely astonishing that nearly [Col. 0622A] all our modern bibliographers, contrary to the facts, agree in assigning it to the following year, 1603. Among these are Fathers Labbe and Le Long, as well as Cave, du Pin, Fabricius, and others (Labbe, *ibid.*, p. 832; Le Long, *ibid.*; Cave, p. 472; du Pin, *ibid.*; Fabricius, *Bib. Lat.*, book II, p. 83). It is easy to see that, once the first person made the error, the others fell into it as well—an indication that they copied one another and did not themselves see the edition.

Du Breul based his edition on the manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, but, unlike the other editors, he did not warn that the Fleury manuscript does not extend beyond chapter 41 of Book IV. He did everything possible to transfer to Aimoin of Saint-Germain the honor of this history, with its interpolations [Col. 0622B] and even its additions through Book V exclusively. Not only did he adorn it with this writer’s name and attributes from the title page onward, but he also devoted almost his entire preface to trying to persuade readers of the same point. We now know how the matter stands. The editor appended several other writings by the same author, as well as the poem of Abbo, his disciple, which we have discussed in their proper place. He also added several other monuments that make his collection interesting—not so much for the text of the history in question, which is much more accurately available elsewhere, as for the shorter works accompanying it.

M. Fabricius wrongly supposes that Father Dubois included Aimoin’s *History* in the *Library of Fleury*, printed at Lyon in 1605. After du Breul’s edition, no other appeared until the one published in 1613 by Marquard Freher in the second part of his collection of historians of France, issued at Hanau in a folio volume. This editor followed Nicot’s edition as his model through chapter 41 of Book IV, inclusive. But he removed chapter 42 and the following fifteen chapters, replacing them with Einhard’s *Annals* and the same historian’s *Life of Charlemagne*. He then made further additions that do not concern Aimoin’s genuine writings.

In 1641 François Duchesne, continuing the collection of the historians of France begun by his father André, placed Aimoin’s work at the beginning of the third volume. [Col. 0622D] This edition presents our author’s text freed from all foreign interpolations and additions. It was made from a manuscript resembling the one at Fleury, though differing from it in that the fourth book of the *History* contains a forty-second chapter absent from the other. This chapter, which briefly treats the foundation of the abbey of Fleury and at greater length the transfer there of the relics of Saint Benedict, is important for identifying the true author of this history, who clearly presents himself in it as a monk of that abbey.

After all the editions of Aimoin’s *History* just enumerated, Dom Bouquet had it printed again at the beginning of the third volume of his great collection of the historians of France (Bouquet, *Script. Franc.*, vol. III, pp. 20–139). [Col. 0623A] This new editor used Duchesne’s edition as the most accurate text and took care to collate it with three manuscripts: the one at Saint-Germain-des-Prés already mentioned, and two others from the fourteenth century belonging to the King’s library. Another advantage of this last edition is that the editor took the trouble to mark in the margins the passages of Aimoin borrowed from the writings on which he drew—a thankless task for the person who undertook it, but useful and agreeable for the reader.

Aimoin’s work, which seemed to us to deserve so lengthy a discussion in order to make its merits and defects known, ordinarily bears the title *Historia* or *De gestis Francorum*. M. du Cange (*Gloss.*, index of authors) had nevertheless seen a manuscript entitled *De abbreviatione historiarum*—a reasonably suitable title, since the work is an abridged compilation of other historians. Among the manuscripts of John Selden there is an abridgment made by a certain Wilhelme, under the title *De gestis imperatorum, ex historia Haimonis abbatis Floriacensis collecta* (“On the Deeds of the Emperors, Compiled from the History of Haimon, Abbot of Fleury”) (English Library, manuscript, part I, no. 3362). Here Aimoin is incorrectly called Haimon and even more incorrectly described as an abbot.

**2.** At the end of Aimoin’s *History*, Duchesne and Dom Bouquet printed a poem of more than two hundred heroic verses by the same author, which forms part [Col. 0623C] of the work, since it is announced at the very end of the prose. Dom Mabillon also published it in the third volume of his collection of the acts of the saints, based on Duchesne’s edition. Aimoin describes in it the history of the translation of Saint Benedict’s body from Monte Cassino to Fleury. Since he begins by recounting the foundation of his monastery, Cave counts it as two separate poems (Cave, p. 518). We observed elsewhere (*Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 518) that Aimoin merely put into verse what Adalbert, another monk of Fleury, had written in prose on the same subject more than a century earlier.

**3.** Aimoin has left a very long sermon on Saint Benedict. This, together with his other writings on that saint, the patriarch of Western monks, shows how genuine was the veneration he professed for him. The sermon is essentially a panegyric, in which Aimoin gathered what the authors known to him had said most notably in praise of the saint. Sometimes the compiler gives only a summary. At other times he copies the text word for word. He does this especially with the poets: Gauzbert of Fleury, Mark of Monte Cassino, Paul the Deacon, Abbot Smaragdus, and Bishop Saint Adhelm. Aimoin proceeded in this way, as he himself says in his exordium, so that those who could not possess the writings of these various authors would find collected in a single discourse [Col. 0624A] the principal material concerning Saint Benedict. This sermon is printed in the *Library of Fleury* (part I, pp. 270–298), from which it was transferred to the end of the new Life of Saint Benedict in Greek and Latin, printed in quarto at Venice in 1723 (*Life of Saint Benedict*, part II, pp. 70–88). But the poems copied by Aimoin, already printed in the first part of that collection, were wisely omitted from this edition. It was also published in other collections following the poems of Mark of Monte Cassino (*Christian Poetic Sylloge*).

**4.** Aimoin’s veneration for Saint Benedict led him also to undertake a continuation of the *History of His Miracles*, already begun by Adrevald and Adeler, other monks of Fleury. Sigebert, who mentions this work (*Writers*, chapter 101), says that Aimoin resumed the sequence of miracles performed during the reign of King Odo and carried it through the reign of Robert the Pious. Thus his continuation, divided into two books, together with the collection of Adrevald and Adeler printed at the beginning, contains the miracles performed in various places through the invocation and merits of Saint Benedict, under thirty successive abbots who governed Fleury for more than 385 years. Aimoin had begun working on this composition while writing the *Life of Abbo*. Trithemius, who knew only this one work by our author (Trithemius, *Chronicle of Hirsau*, vol. I, p. 113), says that he undertook it at the command of that abbot and dedicated it to a monk named Renauld, whom Possevin (Appendix, vol. I, p. 67) calls Romuald. But it is dedicated to Gauzlin, abbot of Fleury, and to his entire community; and the author’s words suggest that he took up his pen at their urging.

Aimoin found a way to make his work interesting by incorporating a large number of details concerning public history and several others concerning the history of his monastery. Accordingly, the Duchesnes printed a substantial portion of it among the historians of France (vol. IV, pp. 135–142, 151–155).

Besides these detached portions, we have three editions of the complete work. The first was prepared by Father du Bois, a Celestine, who published it in the *Library of Fleury* after the work of Adrevald and Adeler, which forms the first book of the collection; consequently, Aimoin’s first book is counted as the second, and his second as the third (Fleury Library, *ibid.*, pp. 79–148). The successors of Bollandus then inserted Aimoin’s work, based on the preceding edition and on the manuscripts of Fleury and Peresi, into the *Monuments* they printed on 21 March for use in the history of Saint Benedict (Bollandists, 21 March, pp. 301–316, 334). Finally, Dom Mabillon produced a third edition based on that of du Bois and on the Bollandists’ edition (Mabillon, *Acts*, vol. VI, pp. 356–390).

Dom Matthieu Lauret, abbot of Saint-Sauveur of [Col. 0625A] Castello (Simonet, *Selected Letters*, vol. III, letter 12), having occasion to speak of Aimoin in the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, which he published at Naples in 1616 and which Dom Angelus de Nuce severely disparages in the preface to his own work, reproaches the monks of Fleury for carrying their veneration for his writings so far as to enclose them with Saint Benedict’s bones. He is doubtless referring to the collection of miracles directed by our author, and perhaps also to the poem on the translation of the same saint’s body from Italy to France. If the monks of Fleury actually do what they are here accused of doing, it is not clear why anyone should blame them. It is a long-established and hitherto irreproachable custom to preserve with the relics of the saints the records and other documents attesting the [Col. 0625B] truth of those relics and the sanctity of those whose remains they are. The writings of Aimoin in question are of this character with regard to Saint Benedict’s body. Dom Lauret is no better founded in promoting the supposed charge of heresy that Baronius tried to fasten upon Aimoin by calling him an iconomach—an opponent of images.

**5.** Another work by Aimoin that has earned the praise of all learned men [Note: [Col. 0625D] It is entirely astonishing that Du Cange (*Gloss.*, index of authors) transfers the credit for this work to a monk of York whom he calls Haimon.], is the *Life of Saint Abbo*, his teacher and abbot of Fleury, who was put to death, as has been said, on 13 November 1004. No one was better suited than Aimoin to succeed in this undertaking. He had been the holy abbot’s disciple; he had accompanied him on his final journey; he had been present at his death; and he possessed the ability to write well for his age. It would therefore be difficult to decide which of the two was more fortunate: Aimoin, in having Abbo as his teacher, or Abbo, in having Aimoin as the historian of his life (Mabillon, *ibid.*, vol. VIII, p. 30, n. 1). Aimoin began it immediately after Abbo’s death, at the request of Father Hervé, treasurer of Saint-Martin of Tours and another disciple of the holy abbot. This led the author to dedicate the work to him in a letter highly honoring his memory. A short preface follows, devoted particularly to justifying the title of martyr given to Saint Abbo because of the violent death he suffered on an occasion involving the reform of morals.

This work is valuable not only because it offers an accurate, well-ordered history, free of episodes, commonplaces, and extraneous reflections, but also because it contains several original documents presented as evidence, and because its particular events are connected with others concerning the general history of the Church and especially that of France. Duchesne showed that he held the same opinion by printing most of it in his collection of historians (Duchesne, *ibid.*, pp. 123–135). Father du Bois gave us the complete work in his *Library [Col. 0626A] of Fleury*, inserting in it laments—or a kind of lamentation—of his own composition concerning the decline of regular discipline in the Order of Saint Benedict (Fleury Library, *ibid.*, pp. 299–348). Dom Mabillon later published it on the basis of the preceding edition, which he collated with the Fleury manuscript from which it had been made. His edition is much more accurate and enriched with notes and learned observations (Mabillon, *ibid.*, pp. 30–58).

**6.** Aimoin himself tells us (*Life of Abbo*, no. 16) that he had written a history of the abbots of Fleury, but this work appears to exist nowhere any longer. Dom Mabillon greatly regretted its loss. It was not the same work that Trithemius mentions (*Chronicle of Hirsau*, cited above) under the title *Chronicle of the Same Monastery*, in which, according to that author, Aimoin had inserted several matters concerning the history of the Franks in the form of digressions. From this addition it is clear that Trithemius meant the *History of the Franks* written by Aimoin, of which he had not a sufficiently accurate understanding.

**7.** Besides the collection of the miracles of Saint Benedict, which we have discussed, our author intended to make a separate collection of the miracles that had occurred in Neustria through the intercession of the same saint. But it is unknown whether he carried out this projected plan, although he lived several years after announcing it (Aimoin, *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, Book II, chapter 22).

Helgaud, another monk of Fleury, reports in his history of King Robert a few verses in praise of that prince and of Queen Constance, his wife (Helgaud, *Life of Robert*, pp. 66, [Col. 0626C] 72). In truth, he does not name their author, merely describing him as a poet of the highest reputation. But since Aimoin practiced poetry, as we have seen from his poem on the translation of Saint Benedict, and as is also shown by several verses he placed at the end of the *Life of Saint Abbo*, one might think that he is the poet Helgaud has in mind here. Others, by contrast, believe that it was rather Gerard, his colleague and contemporary, or finally some other poet of that same century, which was fertile in versifiers.

Manuscript no. 101, preserved in the library of Fleury, contains on page 211 and following a commentary on the Apocalypse under Aimoin’s name. [Col. 0626D] But the character of this work is older than our author; and we have shown elsewhere that it belongs to Remigius of Auxerre. The error arose because, instead of *Raymon* or *Reimon*, the common name of Remigius, a copyist wrote *Heimon*, as it appears at the end of the same manuscript. Then another person, imagining that this was Aimoin, gave him that name at the head of the commentary.

Several bibliographers (Wion, *ibid.*; Possevin, *ibid.*) have also attributed other works to Aimoin of Fleury, such as a work on the discovery or translation [Col. 0627A] of Saint Vincent and another on the miracles of Saint Germain of Paris. But they assigned these writings to him only by confusing him with Aimoin [Col. 0628A] of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, to whom they belong.

[Col. 0627]

## Four Books of Aimoin’s *History of the Franks*

(From André Duchesne, *Contemporary Writers of Frankish History*, vol. III, p. 1.)

### Letter of Aimoin, Monk, to Abbo, Abbot of Fleury, Prefixed to the Book *On the Deeds of the Franks*

[Col. 0627B] To the venerable lord ABBOT ABBO, established in the love of Christ, AIMOIN, least member of the whole flock entrusted to him by God: the gift of perpetual blessedness.

Most blessed Father, I have obeyed the commands of your blessedness, by which you instructed me to exercise my small talent—which, through Christ’s grant, you judged to have made progress toward better things through the labour of your solicitude and of your disciples—and to reduce into the body of a single small work the deeds of the Frankish people and kings, scattered through various books and written in an uncultivated style, and to restore them to a more polished Latin form. I therefore applied myself as best I could—and would that I had done so as effectively as willingly! Moreover, let your fatherhood judge of the work, whether I have done rightly or otherwise. For my part, I am content with the testimony of obedience alone, if indeed I have adorned it by my willingness and effort.

[Col. 0627C] Accordingly, mindful of your admonition—by which you very often urged me not to omit the situation of Germany and Gaul, where the events to be recounted took place—I thought it fitting, by collecting what I could find in the authors Julius, Pliny, and Orosius and inserting it in this little work, suitably to satisfy the wish of your exaltedness. To this I added what Julius inserts in his historical book concerning the customs and institutions of the Germans and Gauls. From the departure of the Franks from Troy down to the time when Pepin, father of Charlemagne, began to reign, I resolved to divide the entire sequence of events into four books.

[Col. 0628B] I composed them on this plan: each succeeding book should always surpass its predecessor in its length and in the number of kings; for example, the first contains the acts of five kings, the second of six, the third of seven, and the fourth of eight and more. I also distinguished, with all the diligence I could, the genealogies of the kings, which were very confused because of the similarity of their names, distinguishing each from another either by his father’s name or by the designation Elder or Younger, as the attentive reader may observe in their proper places. I took particular care that in all these books mention should be made, for definite reasons, of Father Benedict, to whom, after God, I ascribe my knowledge, my ability, and my life.

Nor am I unaware that there will be many who, with their customary desire to disparage everything, will fasten their native tooth upon this volume. No one can avoid this except one who writes nothing whatever. For they will cavil at the dates, alter the order, criticize the facts, sift the syllables, and—as commonly happens—impute the copyists’ negligence to the author. They will also say: “Behold our historian and novel author, who uses other men’s words as his own.” I do not deny that I have done this, nor am I ashamed of it; indeed, I intend to do so again. I have the example of good men, by which I think myself permitted to do what they did. Nor am I greatly troubled by the opinions of detractors: to be instructed by your praise or blame is enough for me. Farewell, venerable Father, and flourish in prosperous success according to your desires.

[Col. 0627] Here ends the letter to Abbo the abbot.

### Begins the Situation of Germany and Gaul, Extracted by the Historian from Various Authors

[Col. 0629]

### First, Concerning Germany

[Col. 0629A] **Chapter I.** Germany as a whole is divided into the territories of five peoples: first the Vindelici, then the Cimbri, after them the Teutones, likewise the Peucini, and last of all the Basternae, who border on the Dacians. Germany extends 686 Roman miles in length and 548 in breadth. Its notable rivers flowing into the Ocean are the Guthalus, Visurgis, and Rhine. In the Rhine itself there are nearly a hundred islands along its course, the most famous being that of the Batavians and very many others, spread between the Rhine and the Flevus. Thus are called the mouths into which the Rhine disperses itself: northward into various lakes and westward into the river Meuse, while between these it preserves a middle channel, though only a small one, under its own name.

[Col. 0629B] It rises among the Lepontii, who inhabit the Alps, and, rushing through a long stretch of the territories of the Helvetii, Mediomatrici, and Treveri, it approaches the Ocean. There it flows out into several branches, forming many large islands, as has been stated; a great part of these is inhabited by wild and barbarous peoples, some of whom are thought to live only on fish and birds’ eggs. It enters the Ocean by many mouths. Within Germany no range of lower renown extends than the Hercynian ridge. Julius Caesar, in his history of the Gallic War, writes as follows concerning this ridge, namely that it is covered with forest and abounds in various kinds of wild beasts:

[Col. 0629C] “The most fertile regions of Germany around the Hercynian Forest—which I see is known by report to Eratosthenes and certain Greeks, who call it Orcynia—were named by the Volcae Tectosages, who settled there. This people remains in those settlements down to the present time and enjoys the highest reputation for justice and military valour. Even now they persist in the same poverty, want, and endurance as the Germans and use the same food and bodily dress. But proximity to the provinces and knowledge of things overseas provide the Gauls with much abundance and many conveniences.” Gradually accustomed to being defeated and vanquished in many battles, they do not even compare themselves with the Germans in valour.

The breadth of this Hercynian Forest, described above, extends over a nine-day journey for an unencumbered traveller. It cannot be defined otherwise, for they do not know measurements of routes. It rises from the territories of the Helvetii, Nemetes, and Rauraci, follows the straight course of the Danube, and reaches the borders of the Dacians and Anartes. From there it bends to the left, away from the river, and because of its size touches the boundaries of many peoples. [Col. 0630A] No one in this Germany says that, after advancing for a journey of sixty days, he has either heard of or reached the beginning of this forest, or learned from what place it rises. It is certain that many kinds of wild beasts are born in it which have not been seen elsewhere. Of these, the following are those that differ most from others and seem worthy of record.

There is an ox shaped like a stag, from the middle of whose forehead, between its ears, rises a single horn, taller and straighter than the horns known to us; from its top branches spread widely like a palm. The female and male are alike in nature; their horns have the same shape and size. There are also animals called elk. They resemble goats in shape and in the variegation of their hides, but are somewhat larger; they have no horns and legs without joints or articulations. They do not lie down to rest; nor, if they fall when disabled by some accident, can they raise or lift themselves. [Col. 0630B] Trees serve them as beds: they lean against them and, only slightly reclining, take their rest. When hunters have discovered from their tracks where they customarily resort, they either undermine the trees at their roots or cut them, leaving just enough that they appear to stand. When the animals lean on them as usual, they bring down the weakened trees with their weight and fall with them.

A third kind is called the urus. These are somewhat smaller than elephants, but have the appearance, colour, and form of bulls. Their strength and speed are great; they spare neither man nor beast upon which they set their eyes. Men zealously catch and kill them in pits. Young men harden themselves by this labour and practise themselves in this kind of hunting. Those who have killed the greatest number, displaying their horns publicly as evidence, win great praise. But not even when taken young can they become accustomed to people or be made tame. The size, shape, and appearance of their horns differ greatly from those of our oxen. [Col. 0630C] These horns are carefully sought out, rimmed at the lips with silver, and used as drinking-cups at the most splendid banquets.

### On the Customs of the Germans

**II.** [Col. 0631A] The same author also reports the following in the same book concerning the customs and way of life of the people. “The Germans,” he says, “differ greatly from the customs of the Gauls. For they have neither druids—whom we may call priests or diviners—such as those who preside over religious matters among the Gauls, nor are they devoted to sacrifices. Among the gods they count only those whom they see and by whose manifest assistance they are helped: namely, the Sun, Vulcan, and the Moon. Of the rest they have not even heard by report. Their entire life consists in hunting and military pursuits. From childhood they devote themselves to labour and hardship. Those who remain unmarried the longest receive the greatest praise among their people. Some think this makes their stature, strength, and sinews firmer. They consider it among the most shameful things to have known a woman before their twentieth year. [Col. 0631B] There is no concealment of this, because they bathe promiscuously in rivers and wear skins or small coverings of reindeer-hide, with a great part of the body naked.

“They do not practise agriculture, and the greater part of their food consists of milk, cheese, and meat. No one has a fixed measure of land or private boundaries. Rather, every year magistrates and chiefs assign to the tribes and kin-groups who have assembled together as much land and in whatever place seems fit, and after a year compel them to move elsewhere. They offer many reasons for this: lest, captivated by continual habit, they exchange the pursuit of war for agriculture; lest they strive to acquire broad estates and the more powerful drive the weaker from their possessions; lest they build too carefully to avoid cold and heat; lest desire for money arise, from which factions and dissensions spring; and so that they may keep the common people in an equitable temper, when each sees his own resources equalled with those of the most powerful.

[Col. 0631C] “For communities, the greatest glory is to have wide desolate tracts around them after devastating the adjoining lands. They consider it a special mark of valour that their neighbours, driven from their fields, withdraw, and that no one dares remain nearby. At the same time, they think they will thereby be safer, the fear of sudden incursions having been removed. When a community either defends itself against a war brought upon it or makes war, magistrates are chosen to preside over that war and to have the power of life and death. In peace there is no common magistrate; rather, the chiefs of districts and cantons administer justice among their own people and settle disputes. Robberies committed beyond the boundaries of each community carry no disgrace, and they declare that these are undertaken to exercise the young and lessen idleness.

[Col. 0631D] “When one of the chiefs has said in council that he will be leader, let those who wish to follow declare themselves. Those who approve both the cause and the man rise, promise their assistance, and are applauded by the multitude. Those among them who do not follow are counted as deserters and traitors, and thereafter are denied credit in every matter. They do not think it lawful to violate a guest. Whoever comes to them for any reason is protected from injury; they regard him as sacred, every house is open to him, and food is shared with him. There was formerly a time when the Gauls surpassed the Germans in valour, voluntarily made war upon them, and, because of their population and scarcity of land, sent colonies across the Rhine.”

[Col. 0632A] Thus far we have taken care to set forth what we could find concerning Germany in the ancient writers. We must now speak of Gaul.

### Concerning Gaul
### III

Orosius divides all Gaul into four provinces in the following manner: “Gaul,” he says, “Belgic Gaul has as its eastern boundary the river Rhine and Germany; to the southeast, the Pennine Alps; to the south, the province of Narbonensis; to the west, the province of Lugdunensis; to the northwest, the British Ocean; to the north, the island of Britain.”

Gaul Lugdunensis, extending lengthwise and curving broadly, almost encircles the province of Aquitania. It has Belgica to the east; to the south, part of the province of Narbonensis, where the city of Arelas is situated; and on the Gallic Sea it is received by the river Rhône. The province of Narbonensis, a part of Gaul, has the Cottian Alps to the east; Spain to the west; Aquitania to the northwest; Lugdunensis to the north; Belgic Gaul to the northeast; and to the south the Gallic Sea, which lies between Sardinia and the Balearic Islands. At its front, where the river Rhône flows out into the sea, it has the Stoechades Islands.

The province of Aquitania, along the oblique course of the river Loire—which is its boundary for the greater part—is enclosed in a circle. It has the Ocean to the northwest, which is called the Aquitanian Gulf; Spain to the west; Lugdunensis to the north and east; and it touches the province of Narbonensis to the southeast and south.

Julius Caesar, however, who waged war for ten years against the inhabitants of this same land, agreeing with Pliny and many other philosophers, wishes there to be only three provinces. Here we insert his writings in the same order that he used, interposing only certain details that he stated elsewhere in his History concerning cities or rivers, as well as matters about which Pliny held a different opinion from him.

### Gaul according to Caesar

### IV

“All Gaul is divided into three parts. The Belgae inhabit one; the Aquitani another; and those who in their own language are called Celtae, but in ours Gauls, the third. Pliny likewise asserts that this part is Gaul Lugdunensis. All these peoples differ from one another in language, institutions, and laws.

“The river Garonne divides the Gauls of Lugdunensis from the Aquitani; the Marne and the Seine divide them from the Belgae. Of all these peoples, the Belgae are the bravest, because they are farthest removed from the culture and refinement of the province, merchants seldom travel to them, and they import the things that tend to weaken courage. They are nearest to the Germans, who dwell across the Rhine, and with whom they continually wage war. For this reason the Helvetii also surpass the other Gauls in valor, since they contend with the Germans in almost daily battles, either keeping them away from their own borders or waging war themselves within the Germans’ territory.

“On one side the Helvetii are bounded by the very broad and very deep river Rhine, which separates Helvetian territory from the Germans; on another side by the very high Jura Mountains, which lie between the Sequani and the Helvetii; and on the third by Lake Geneva and the river Rhône, which separates our province from the Helvetii.”

One part of Gaul, which is said to be held by those who are specifically called Gauls, begins at the river Rhône, is bounded by the river Garonne, reaches the Ocean at the borders of the Belgae, and also extends northward from the Sequani and Helvetii toward the river Rhine. It contains many wealthy cities. The principal ones, and those better known in our own age, are: Lugdunum, Cabillonum, Hedua, which is also called Augustodunum, Senones, Autissiodorum, Meldi, Trecas, Parisius, Carnotum, Gennabum, where Aurelianis now stands, Rothomagus, Ebroas, Oximus, Cenomanni, Lexovium, Namnetis, Rhedones, Venetus, Abrincatina, Andus, which is also called Andegavis, Turonis, Bituriges, and Niviodunus, which some think is Nivernis.

Of these, Augustodunum and Senones were anciently cities of great authority and power among the Gauls. Indeed, one of them—Augustodunum, which Julius calls the Hedui—by embracing the friendship of the Roman people, became, supported by their favor, almost the ruler of all Gaul. Senones, moreover, trusting in its own strength, did not fear to besiege Rome itself, the capital of the world; indeed, it captured it.

The city of the Bituriges and that of the Turoni, according to Orosius’s definition—which determines Aquitania from the river Loire to the Pyrenean Mountains, and which modern writers follow—belong not to Celtic Gaul but rather to the province of Aquitania.

There are many rivers in Gaul Lugdunensis, but the chief among them is the Rhône, which forms its boundary on the eastern side. When we used Julius’s words, “which separates our province from the Helvetii,” we understood by “our province” the land that has received this proper name. Next comes the Arar, which flows into the Rhône through the territories of the Hedui and Sequani with such astonishing gentleness that it is scarcely possible to judge with the eyes in which direction it flows. We ourselves have observed this and marveled that so great a river should flow with such sluggish motion.

After it is the Loire, which makes the land lying between itself and the Seine almost an island. There are many forests, but the most outstanding is the Perticus. This much, then, concerning Celtic Gaul, which is also called Lugdunensis. Let us now consider the province of Belgica.

### Belgic Gaul

The Belgae originate at the farthest boundaries of Gaul. They extend along the lower part of the river Rhine and face toward the north and the rising sun. Its renowned and famous cities are Colonia Agrippinensis, Tungris, Treveris, Metis, which is also called Mediomatricum, Remis, Laudunus, Suessionis, Ambianis, Viromandus, Belvagus, Atrebatum, Lingonis, and the district of the Helvetii, which the Alamanni now inhabit.

The rivers of this province are the Scheldt, the Marne, and the Meuse, which flows from the Vosges Mountains, situated in the territory of the Lingones. Having received a certain branch from the Rhine, called the Vaculus but commonly known as the Vualis, it forms the island of the Batavi, which in the rustic language is called Battua.

[Col. 0634A] Another river in Belgic territory is the Axona, which flows past the outermost borders of the Remi. There is also the forest of Arduenna, the largest in all Gaul, extending in length for more than five hundred miles from the banks of the Rhine and the territory of the Treveri.

Let this suffice concerning the Belgae, provided that what deserves remembrance concerning Aquitania is also transmitted.

### Aquitania

Aquitania, in the opinion of Pliny and Julius, extends from the river Garonne to the Pyrenean Mountains and to the region that borders Spain, lying between the setting sun and the north. At the present time, however, Orosius’s definition, explained above by us, is more commonly followed.

According to this division, Aquitania contains the distinguished cities of Narbona, Arvernus, now called Clarusmons, Cadurx, Tolosa, Gavalis, Rotenus, Lemovix, Petragorica, Pictavis, Burdegalis, Santonia, and Engolisma.

There are also rivers of no little renown in this province. The Elaver, only slightly smaller than the Loire, is received into its channel. The Dordonia, too, which rises from a mountain called Dor in the territory of the Arverni, springs from two sources, one called Dor and the other Donia. These join not far from the mountain itself, and the river flows into the Garonne.

Finally, it is called Aquitania because, more than the other provinces, it abounds in springs and rivers. It also contains a forest called Leccenna, of considerable size, adjoining the territories of the Bituriges and Arverni. In it there is still shown the stone house of Brunichildis, once queen of the Franks, situated in a pleasant place, as we ourselves also observed. A small river flowing past it makes meadows fertile on one side, while on the opposite side fields of grain are enclosed by a forest suitable for hunting.

After the Franks had occupied all these provinces, dividing them into only two parts, they called the region extending toward the north and lying between the Meuse and Rhine Austrasia; the region extending from the Meuse as far as the Loire they called Neustria. Nevertheless, the part of Gaul Lugdunensis occupied by the Burgundians retained the name Burgundy. Aquitania likewise did not deem it worthy to change its ancestral name.

Having now set forth what we were able to investigate in the books of the ancients concerning the situation of Germany and Gaul, let us explain in Caesar’s own words what he thought about the ancient customs and practices of the Gauls.

[Col. 0634D]

### On the Institutions of the Gauls

### V

He says, then:

“In all Gaul there are two classes of those men who possess some rank and honor. For the common people are treated almost as slaves, undertake nothing on their own authority, and are admitted to no counsel. Most of them, when they are oppressed either by debt, by the burden of taxes, or by the violence of the more powerful, give themselves into slavery. The nobles exercise over them all the same rights that masters exercise over slaves.

“Of these two classes, one is that of the Druids, the other that of the knights. The Druids take part in divine matters, oversee public and private sacrifices, and interpret religious observances. A great number of young men gather to them for instruction, and they are held in great honor among their people. For they decide almost all public and private disputes. If any crime has been committed, if a murder has occurred, or if there is a dispute concerning an inheritance or boundaries, they are the ones who decide it and establish rewards and punishments.

“If any private person or community does not abide by their decision, they exclude them from the sacrifices. This is considered among them the most severe punishment. Those upon whom this exclusion has been imposed are regarded as impious and criminal. Everyone withdraws from them and avoids their company and conversation, lest they receive some harm from the association; justice is not granted to them when they seek it, and no honor is shared with them.

“Over all these Druids presides one who possesses supreme authority among them. When he dies, if any one of the rest excels, he succeeds to the dignity; or, if several are equal, the Druids choose by vote. Sometimes they even contend for leadership by arms.

“They assemble at a fixed time of year in the territory of the Carnutes, which region is considered to lie at the center of all Gaul, in a consecrated place. Hither all who have disputes come from every direction, and they obey their judgments and decisions.

“It is believed that this discipline was discovered in Britain and transferred from there to Gaul. Even now, those who wish to learn the matter more carefully generally travel there for the sake of study.

“The Druids habitually abstain from war, do not pay taxes together with the others, and possess exemption from military service and immunity from all burdens. Attracted by such great rewards, many come to the discipline of their own accord, while others are sent by parents and relatives. There they are said to learn by heart a great number of verses. Thus some remain in training for twenty years, and they do not consider it lawful to commit these teachings to writing, although in almost all other public and private matters they use Greek letters.

“They seem to me to have established this practice for two reasons: because they do not wish their discipline to be spread among the common people, and because they do not wish those who learn to rely on writing and therefore devote less attention to memory. This generally happens to most people: relying on the aid of writing, they relax their diligence in learning beforehand and their memory.

“Above all, they wish to persuade their pupils that souls do not perish but pass after death from one person to another, and they think that this belief most strongly excites people to courage by extinguishing the fear of death. They also discuss and transmit to the young much concerning the stars and their movements, the magnitude of the world and the earth, the nature of things, and the power and authority of the immortal gods.

“The other class is that of the knights. Whenever there is need, and some war breaks out—as generally happened every year before Caesar’s arrival, when they either inflicted injuries themselves or repelled injuries inflicted upon them—all take part in war. And the more distinguished each man is by birth and wealth, the greater the number of dependents and clients he has around him. They recognize this alone as influence and power.”

### On the Religion of the Gauls

### VI

The entire nation of the Gauls is exceedingly devoted to religious observances. For that reason, those who are afflicted with more serious illnesses or are engaged in battles and dangers either sacrifice human beings as victims or vow that they will sacrifice themselves. They employ Druids as administrators of these sacrifices, because they believe that the divine power of the immortal gods cannot be appeased for a human life unless a human life is offered in return. They publicly maintain sacrifices of the same kind.

Others possess images of immense size, whose woven-wicker limbs they fill with living human beings. When these images are set on fire, the people enclosed within them perish in the flames. They believe that the punishments of those caught in theft, robbery, or some other offense are more pleasing to the immortal gods. When a sufficient number of such offenders is lacking, however, they descend even to punishing the innocent.

They worship Mercury above all. They have very many images of him. They say that he is the inventor of all arts; they consider him the guide of roads and journeys and believe that he possesses the greatest power over the pursuit of money and commercial transactions.

After him they worship Apollo, Mars, Jupiter, and Minerva. Concerning these gods they hold almost the same opinions as the other peoples: Apollo drives away diseases, Minerva teaches the beginnings of crafts and arts, Jupiter holds heavenly rule, and Mars governs wars.

When they have decided to fight in battle, they generally vow to this god the things they have captured in war. They sacrifice whatever captured animals remain; the remaining objects they collect in one place. In many communities it is possible to see heaps constructed from these things in consecrated places. It rarely happens that anyone, having disregarded religious obligation, dares either to conceal captured objects among his own possessions or to remove what has been deposited. The severest punishment, accompanied by torture, has been established for such an offense.

### On the Origin of the Gauls

### VII

The Gauls all proclaim that they are descended from Father Dis, and say that this teaching was handed down by the Druids. For this reason they reckon all periods of time not by the number of days but by nights. They observe birthdays and the beginnings of months and years in such a way that the day follows the night.

In the other arrangements of life they differ from the rest chiefly in this: they do not allow their children to approach them publicly until they have grown up enough to be capable of undertaking military service, and they consider it shameful for a son of boyhood age to stand in public in his father’s presence.

Men add from their own property, after an equal valuation has been made, as much money as they have received from their wives under the name of dowry, and combine it with the dowries. An account is kept jointly of all this money, and its proceeds are preserved. Whichever of the two survives, that person receives the share belonging to both, together with the proceeds of earlier years.

Men have power over their wives, as over their children, of life and death. When the head of a household born into a more distinguished station dies, his relatives assemble. If the matter appears suspicious, they investigate the death and interrogate the wives in the manner of slaves. If the truth is established, they kill the women after subjecting them to fire and every form of torture.

Funerals, according to the wealth of the Gauls, are magnificent and costly. They cast into the fire everything that they think was dear to the deceased while alive, including animals. Until fairly recently, slaves and clients whom the deceased was known to have loved were also cremated together with him after the proper funeral rites had been completed.

Among those communities that are considered to administer their commonwealth more effectively, the laws provide that if anyone hears anything concerning the commonwealth from neighboring peoples through rumor or report, he must bring it before the magistrate and must not communicate it to anyone else. For it is known that reckless and unstable men are often frightened by false rumors, driven to crime, and induced to deliberate concerning matters of the greatest importance.

The magistrates conceal what seems appropriate to conceal and reveal to the multitude whatever they judge to be useful. No one is permitted to speak about the commonwealth except through the council.

### On Other Institutions of the Gauls

### VIII

The same author says elsewhere:

“It is a custom of the Gauls to compel travelers, even against their will, to stop and to ask each of them what he has heard or learned about any matter whatsoever. Merchants in the towns are likewise surrounded by the crowd, and they are compelled to declare from which regions they come and what things they have learned there.

“Moved by these reports and hearsay, they often make decisions concerning the most important matters, of which they necessarily repent immediately afterward, since they serve uncertain impulses and most people give fabricated answers according to their wishes.”

After placing these statements from Julius’s book before us, it should not seem burdensome to the reader to add two examples from two illustrious men, Orosius and Sallustius, concerning the valor attributed to the Gauls. Although the preface did not promise to treat this subject, it was nevertheless judged appropriate to insert the testimony of two or three writers, so that, while the great valor of the Gauls is demonstrated, the greater courage of the Franks who conquered them might be made clear.

Orosius says:

“Whenever the Gauls rose up against the Romans, with all their resources, Rome was so battered that under the present invasion of the Goths she ought rather to remember the Gauls.”

He calls the Gothic invasion “present” because in his time the Goths first captured Rome. The Franks later defeated them, as will be explained below.

Sallustius writes as follows:

“At that same time—there is no doubt that it was when the Romans were waging war against Jugurtha—our commanders, Quintus Scipio and Memmius Manlius, fought unsuccessfully against the Gauls. Italy trembled with fear at this. Yet from that time down to our own memory the Romans held that all other things submitted to their valor, while against the Gauls they fought for survival, not for glory.”

## THE PROLOGUE OF THE HISTORY OF THE FRANKS BEGINS

[Col. 0637]

The kingdom of the Franks, ennobled by the ancient lineage of the Trojan race, has plainly always flourished both through the fierce bodily and spiritual courage of its men and, above all, through the outstanding power of its kings. This nation, certainly, although it is known to be exceedingly fierce in the name by which it is designated, nevertheless displays such conspicuous signs of gentleness that it has preferred not so much to strike the necks of rebellious enemies with a sword of vengeance as to subjugate them to itself.

Indeed, as we have said, since the kingdom flourished through the most excellent authority and the powerful courage of its men, it sought not merely to enlarge the extent of its own borders but to acquire dominion over foreign peoples for itself. Holding forth a vigorous right hand in war, it knew both how to spare the subjected and how to defeat the proud.

Not undeservedly did it become mistress of many nations, since it did not long tolerate serving the worship of idols and demons. Judging it more right to submit to the Creator than to a creature, it preferred to dedicate the beginnings of its kingdom—so to speak, begun under Christ’s auspices—to his worship.

Raising itself from this point toward higher things, it ardently adopted the standard of the Catholic faith and eagerly worked to extend it together with the boundaries of the kingdom. Yet, stirred by the progress of its prosperity, it did not restrain its momentum; rather, it considered it by no means improper to annex neighboring peoples compelled by war, until the nation of the Alamanni, refusing to bear the yoke of domination, provoked a terrible war.

The illustrious king Clovis, who held the kingdom as the fifth king of that people, skillfully brought this war to victory. These matters, however, will be related in their proper place. Let the sequence of the History now be woven together.

[Col. 0637] The Prologue ends.

## THE FIRST BOOK BEGINS

### CHAPTER ONE  
### On the Deeds of the Franks, and First, on the Dispersion of the Trojans

[Col. 0637D]

After the Greeks had celebrated their triumph over the destruction of Troy, many citizens of the ruined city who had been able to escape the disaster of death sought to secure settlements for themselves wherever they could. One of them, named Antenor, a man of no low birth, set out onto the open sea in ships, accompanied by a large multitude of companions.

At last, after great and varied labors upon the sea, they entered the mouths of the river Tanais, crossed the Maeotian marshes, and encamped in the territory of the Pannonians. Delighted by the pleasantness of the place, they established their settlement there and built a city, which they called Sicambria.

After many years had passed, the obstinate nation of the Alans rebelled against Valentinian, who held supreme authority over the Roman Empire, with the audacity of traitors. He defeated them in battle and forced them to seek the hiding places of the Maeotian marsh.

He pursued them there as well with a large army, but the configuration and difficulty of the terrain prevented him from harming them as he wished. He therefore summoned the Trojans who inhabited Sicambria to his aid. He urged and instructed them to open for his troops a path by which they might invade and crush the enemy while secure and expecting nothing of the kind.

They promised that they would do not only this but would also drive the Alans from the region. The emperor granted them exemption from tribute for ten years if they accomplished it.

Encouraged by their confidence that they knew the terrain, and also attracted by the promise of rewards, the Trojans unexpectedly attacked the Alans, who trusted in the strength of their position. They cut down and overthrew many men and, having thrown the rest into flight, drove them into confusion away from the marsh.

The emperor, astonished at the valor and boldness of the people—because they had not hesitated not only to enter places that the Romans, conquerors of the whole world, had feared, but also to expel the most savage enemies—called them in the Attic language Franks, that is, “the fierce.”

### CHAPTER TWO  
### Another Opinion Concerning the Name of the Franks

Some authors, however, report that the Franks were called after a king named Francio. They say that, after departing from Troy, they established as their king a man named Friga.

Under his rule, they say, as they wandered through Asia, a certain part of them received a place of settlement among the Macedonians. Strengthened by their power, the Macedonians plainly waged many successful wars under the kings Philip and Alexander.

The remaining portion, together with the aforementioned leader, went to the regions of Europe and settled between the Ocean and Thrace along the banks of the Danube. Dividing themselves under two kings whom they had chosen, they separated into the names of two peoples. One nation acquired the name of the Torchi from King Torchotus; the other, from Francio, received the name of Franks and, as we have said, drove the Alans from the Maeotian marshes.

### CHAPTER THREE  
### On the Deeds of the Franks before They Came to Gaul

When the ten years had passed, the emperor sent men to collect the customary tribute from the Frankish people. They declared that they had been freed from tribute by the price of their blood and would not pay the tax for the remission of which they had endured the danger of death.

Angered by this, Caesar drew up his forces, which were both trained in strength and ready to confront so great a people. The Franks did not delay but went out to meet the Romans. Battle was joined immediately, without postponement, although one people had to fight against several peoples.

When the Franks saw that the strength of other nations had come to the Romans’ aid, they judged that it would be more advantageous to yield the ground. They left Sicambria and occupied the banks of the Rhine. After choosing as their leaders Marchomir, Sunno, and Genebaud, following the death of the aforementioned King Francio, they overran many towns of Germany.

Their number, which at the time of their original departure from Asia had scarcely been estimated at twelve thousand armed men, grew into such a multitude that they became a source of fear even to the Germans, who surpassed others in stature and bodily valor.

In the time of Theodosius, the generals Nannius and Quintinus attempted to drive them from Germany after gathering an army. At first they thought that they had defeated them in battle. Later, however, when larger forces, with Heraclius and Jovinianus, commanders of the Roman army, added to their ranks, marched against them, battle was joined. The Franks inflicted such slaughter upon the Romans, putting Heraclius and Jovinianus to flight, that they struck terror with the report of their valor into all the surrounding nations. Thereafter no people was found that could justly bring the Franks under the yoke of tribute by force of arms.

Arbogastes, a count of that same people, came over to the Romans and, defeated by the Franks in the first engagement, fled. Later, however, when battle was joined again, he put a considerable number to the sword and made peace with the survivors. This can be found more fully in the Life of Saint Ambrose.

At the same time the Franks seized the city of Treveris through the faction of Lucius the consul. Lucius, moved by indignation because he had learned that Avitus, the Augustus of Gaul, had dishonored his wife by adultery and had heard him jestingly say that he possessed warm baths but bathed in cold water, carried out these actions.

### CHAPTER FOUR  
### On Pharamund, the First King of the Franks

The Franks, choosing Pharamund, the son of Marchomir, as their king according to the custom of other nations, raised him to the royal throne. His son Clodio the Long-Haired succeeded him. At that time the kings of the Franks were customarily long-haired.

By provoking neighboring peoples to war and laying waste to the territories of the Thoringi, who inhabit Germany, they seized a certain fortress called Disbargum. King Clodio established the seat of his kingdom there.

### CHAPTER FIVE  
### On the Destruction of the Roman Empire and the Growth of the Franks under King Clodio

At that time, as the Roman Empire declined from iron strength into the fragile weakness of clay, the Burgundians had overrun Lugdunensis and the Goths the province of Aquitania. Only that part of Gaul remained subject to Roman rule which the waters of the Rhine and the river Loire bounded.

King Clodio, wishing to enlarge the narrow borders of his kingdom, sent scouts across the Rhine from Disbargum and followed them himself with an army. He captured the city of Cameracum and put to death every Roman whom he encountered.

### CHAPTER SIX  
### On King Meroveus

After this, when King Clodio departed this life, Meroveus, his kinsman, assumed the government of the Frankish kingdom. Clodio had reigned for twenty years.

At that time the Huns also crossed the Rhine, burned the city of Metis, plundered Treveris, and devastated the territory of Tungris. Thus throughout Gaul the savage fires of war broke out. Everywhere there was mourning, everywhere sorrow, and everywhere the image of death.

They also approached the city of Aurelianis and enclosed it in a siege. They took careful measures, barricading the gates with guards so that no one could safely leave.

At that time the bishop of the city was Anianus, admirable for his virtue. Through his merits and prayers, the omnipotence of Christ so crushed the monstrous phalanxes of the Huns that it remains unknown to this day in what lands those fugitives now dwell.

### CHAPTER SEVEN  
### On King Childericus

When Meroveus, king of the Franks, had been taken from this light, his son Childericus was raised to the royal throne. The beginnings of his reign were detestable to all good people.

For when he first acted wickedly against the Franks and did not cease to defile the daughters of nobles through incest, he was expelled from the kingdom. After his expulsion, he sought Bissinus, king of the Thoringi, believing that he would have a secure refuge with him. Nor was he disappointed in his hope. Throughout the whole period of his exile he lived with the king and was treated by him with honor.

There was a certain Frankish nobleman bound to him by ties of friendship, named Winomadus. Childericus had acted according to his advice in all matters while he still possessed the scepter of the kingdom.

Calling him, Childericus explained the hostility of the Franks, who were threatening to drive him from the kingdom, and asked what should be done. Winomadus advised him to yield to their anger, lest, if he thought he ought to remain, he increase rather than lessen their hatred. He said that it was characteristic of human nature to envy someone’s presence and pity his absence.

Meanwhile, while Childericus remained wherever he might be, Winomadus promised to test the feelings of the people and persuade them to be reconciled with him.

He divided a gold coin, kept one half for himself, and gave the other half to Childericus, saying:

“Take half of this gold coin. If I am able to reconcile the Franks to you, this will be a sign for you: when I send you this half and the two pieces happen to fit together, you will understand that the people’s desire for reconciliation corresponds to your own. Therefore hasten your return to your homeland, so that you may recover the kingdom of which you are now deprived.”

After these words Childericus went to Thoringia, as has been related.

The Franks, however, forgetting the injuries they had inflicted upon the Romans, established as their king Aegidius the patrician, who had received from the Romans the responsibility of defending Gaul.

O blind mind of mankind, which thinks that he is consulting its interests, though it itself does not cease to inflict evils upon him! For how could he wish them well whose lands they had crushed with fire, whose people with the sword, and whose cities with devastation?

Winomadus, skilled in crafty cunning and sufficiently ready to accomplish whatever he had set his mind upon, quickly attached himself to the friendship of Aegidius. Aegidius, considering him his most intimate friend, entrusted him with himself and all his affairs.

Winomadus, therefore, foreseeing that the power of the Franks would be suspect to Aegidius, did not cease to heap up against them, in every way he could, words of hatred and hostility. He therefore advised that they ought to be oppressed by the burden of tribute.

But when he considered that this injury did not bend them—indeed, since they had begun by hating Childericus, they continued to proclaim Aegidius worthy of honor—he addressed Aegidius as follows:

“Thus,” he said, “you will be able to break the obstinacy of the Franks if you kill some of their powerful men with the sword.”

Aegidius entrusted this task to him. Winomadus, finding a suitable opportunity, accused those whom he knew to have been especially hostile to Childericus and sent them to Aegidius for punishment. He ordered them to be punished with the sword as guilty of an offense against imperial majesty.

The Franks, moved by the king’s savagery and considering Winomadus innocent of this counsel, complained to him about their situation. He said that he marveled at the changeability of their minds [OCR: “men ium”], since they now complained of the cruelty of the man whom they had previously judged worthy of such great praise.

At the same time he addressed them in these words:

“What madness,” he said, “has taken possession of your frenzied minds, that, after expelling a citizen, you have submitted yourselves in pride to the rule of a foreigner? But you will say that his unrestrained lust was a disgrace to you. Why, then, do you complain about the savagery of the man whom you judged preferable to him?
