“You despised a king born from your own people, who by nature was kind and, had his lust been removed, could have been even kinder; and you chose a tyrant, all the more to be feared because his lineage is drawn from a foreign nation.

“Even animals, which lack reason, prefer the rule of their own kind to that of an alien species. Only storks welcome leaders of foreign blood, for, devoted to their bellies, they protect themselves at the peril of other birds.

“But if you have decided to follow my counsel, I think you should be reconciled and appease the spirit of the prince, offended by his expulsion. Certainly I judge it harsh that you cannot endure the lust of one man but can bear the destruction of so many noble citizens.”

Encouraged by these words and likewise moved by the atrocity of the deed, when they saw the leading men of the kingdom being ruined, they said to Winomadus:

“We repent of the injuries inflicted upon our own king. If we knew that he could be found anywhere among the nations, we would send suppliant envoys to beg him to return to his kingdom.”

Sensing that the feelings of the Franks corresponded with the king’s wishes, Winomadus sent Childericus half of the gold coin, the middle part of which he had given to him when he departed, as a sign.

He ordered the envoy to say this to him:

“Return now, as a desired lord, and enjoy your kingdom in happiness.”

After receiving this embassy, Childericus joyfully returned to his homeland. From the middle of his journey he sent a messenger to announce his arrival to Winomadus and to tell him to meet him with haste [the transmitted “fetinato” is evidently for festinato].

Winomadus promptly fulfilled this task, joining with himself the nobles of the Franks. He met Childericus at a fortress called Barrum.

The aforementioned leader had ordered the people of Barrum to receive the arriving king with the highest honor. Obeying his command, they went out to meet him and welcomed him with the greatest honor.

The king took this as a favorable omen and gratefully accepted their service. In royal generosity he remitted the tribute that they paid in those parts of his kingdom.

Joining forces with Winomadus, Childericus proceeded from there and compelled Aegidius, defeated in battle, to withdraw from the kingdom. Expelled, Aegidius sought the city of Suession, where he lived for the remainder of his life. When he had departed from this present light, his son Syagrius possessed the same city by hereditary right.

Childericus, moreover, being prompt in action and prudent in counsel, fought victoriously at Aurelianis against Adovagrius, king of the Saxons. Pursuing him in flight as far as Andegavis, he did not find him there, and so he attacked and captured the city itself. He killed Paul, count of the Roman forces.

Thus he diligently extended the borders of his kingdom as far as the city of Aurelianis and finally as far as Andegavis.

### CHAPTER EIGHT  
### On Basina, Wife of the King of the Thoringi, and Her Departure to Childericus
Basina, however, the wife of Bisinus, king of the Thuringians, learning that Childeric had recovered his paternal kingdom, hastened to go to him, abandoning her former husband. It was said that this same prince had maintained an illicit relationship with her while she was living in exile with the aforementioned king. When Childeric asked her why she had taken such pains to come to him, he received this answer from her [Col. 0643B]:

“Having learned of your courage and moderation, I resolved to seek you out. For if I hoped to find someone more useful to me at the farthest limits of the world, no hardship of travel would prevent me from hastening to him.”

When the king had received this answer from her, he, as a pagan, forgetful of the friendship and benefits bestowed on him by her husband, took her in marriage while Bisinus was still alive. When the secret silence of the marriage chamber had descended, the woman warned her husband that he ought to abstain from marital intercourse with her, and urged him to go outside the palace and report to her what he had seen. He, judging that the woman’s advice should not be disregarded, obeyed her word.

And behold, before the doors of the royal hall he saw the forms of great beasts, as though they were walking about—panthers, namely, unicorns, and [Col. 0643C] lions. Terrified, he hurried back to his wife and reported everything in order. She ordered him to trust her and commanded him to do the same thing a second and a third time.

When the king returned, he again saw images of bears and wolves running about. Going out a third time, he saw figures of dogs and smaller animals tearing one another apart. Astonished, therefore, and ignorant of the meaning of the vision, he returned to bed, disclosed the matter to the prudent woman, and anxiously asked what these things signified. For he knew with certainty that she had not sent him to look upon them without reason.

She warned her husband to behave chastely that night, promising that she would explain everything at dawn. When, therefore, the golden face of heaven and the sun’s radiant light adorned the day, the woman arose and relieved her husband’s mind, which had been suspended in uncertainty by the strange vision, with this speech [Col. 0643D]:

“Drive these anxieties from your heart, my husband, and listen attentively to what I shall say. For what has been shown is not so much a prophecy of present events as a presage of future ones. You ought not to ponder the forms of animals that you saw placed before your feet, but rather to discern in them the character and deeds of our descendants.

“From our seed the first son who will arise and be counted by the name of ‘son’ will be distinguished by great power; you saw him in the form of a lion or unicorn. In the shape of a wolf and bear are signified his descendants, exceedingly strong in courage and greedy for plunder. But the dog, incapable of restraining its lust, possessing no virtue, and unable to survive without human assistance, foretells the cowardice of those who in the final ages will possess the scepters of this [Col. 0644A] kingdom.

“Moreover, the crowd of smaller animals tearing one another apart is the people without fear of their rulers. While they attend too closely upon the leading men of the kingdom as those men attack one another with mutual hatred, the people entangle themselves in various tumults of lawsuits and disputes. And while the nobles strive to deprive one another of their honors, the ignoble multitude, by favoring them, lies exposed to innumerable killings.

“This, my lord king, is the clear interpretation of your vision and a sure indication of the future.”

Thus the king, setting aside his painful anxiety about his own vision, rejoiced that he had come to know the omens of the numerous offspring destined for him.

## CHAPTER IX. The reign of Anthemius and the prodigies during his reign

At that time, while Anthemius governed the Roman Empire and Leo governed Constantinople, blood flowed for an entire day in a very abundant stream from the middle of Toulouse, a city of Gaul. The prudent among the Goths, who then ruled in that city, said that this portended their destruction and the domination of the Franks.

In those same days Odoacer, who ruled over the Heruli and other nations inhabiting the banks of the Danube, elated by the victory he had won after defeating Feletheus, king of the Rugians, was considering invading Italy from the direction of Pannonia. When he entered the territory of Noricum, he sought an interview with a certain servant of God named Severinus, who had built a monastery for himself in that region.

After asking for and obtaining his blessing, Odoacer was about to leave the house. Since he was tall in stature, he bent down at the threshold of the door so as not to strike his head, and heard these words from the same man of God:

“Go, Odoacer, now clothed in the worthless skins of animals; soon you will be lord of Italy.”

When he had heard this prophecy from the man of God, Odoacer entered Italy and devastated everything with slaughter and plunder—not as he ought to have done, but as he wished. After the emperor Anthemius had been killed through the treachery of his son-in-law Ricimer, Odoacer began to threaten the highest citadels of the city of Rome even more fiercely.

For this reason the Romans, and especially the Goths, sent envoys to Leo, emperor of Constantinople, asking that some ruler be sent to them through whose assistance they might repel the attack of the enemy.

## CHAPTER X. The reign of Theodoric

There was at that time among the chief men of the imperial court a man named Theodoric, of remarkable wisdom. His father, Theodorus, born in Macedonia, had been the servant of a certain patrician named Idatius. He began to love one of his fellow-servants, a woman named Lilia, with passionate devotion.

When his master learned of this, he took the advice of his wife Eugenia and gave Lilia to Theodorus as his wife, knowing that she was descended from the same people. His mistress, who grieved that she had been deprived of the fruit of the womb, instructed Lilia to report to her whatever she saw in a dream on the first night of her marriage.

On that night, when she first sought the secret silence of the bedchamber with her husband, the woman saw a tree proceeding from her navel and growing up to the roof of the house. Awakened by terror at the vision, she told her husband about it and also about his mistress’s command. He marveled at the vision and began to praise the mistress’s instruction. But, fearing for the child’s life, he ordered her to alter the dream and gave her this command:

“When you come before our mistress and are ordered to reveal the dream, say that you saw a horse and a mare, the most beautiful of all, walking about, with another small one following behind them.”

Obeying her husband’s words, she reported to her masters the invented account of the dream. They rejoiced at the omen of the child who was to be born, granted freedom to the servants, and adopted the newborn boy as their son.

After Idatius and his wife had died, Theodoric, by order of the emperor Leo, was enrolled as a soldier in the imperial army. Since he stood out among the others in height of body, he was also superior in strength of limb and courage of spirit [Col. 0645B]. Hence he was held dear by the emperor himself and by many senators.

When the envoys of the Romans and Goths mentioned above arrived and explained the reasons for which they had come, the emperor sent Theodoric, distinguished by the honor of the patriciate, to defend the regions of Italy. Having entered Hesperia by sea, he fought against Odoacer and the Heruli with varying success.

On one occasion, defeated in battle, he was forced to flee toward Ravenna. His mother Lilia came to meet him and urged him to return to the battle. When he hesitated, she addressed him as follows:

“Believe me, my son: there is no hut into which you can withdraw as a fugitive, unless you remove your clothing and enter the house in the garment in which you were first brought into the light.”

Stung by these words and inflamed with shame [Col. 0645C], the young man gathered the small force of his men whom he found at hand—small indeed, but strong—and rushed upon the enemy, who were lying scattered across the field, confident in their victory.

He struck down and routed those who were surrounding him and captured Odoacer himself. Not long afterward he killed him and freed all Italy from the domination of the Heruli.

But envious Fortune changed the course of his success. For, as often happens, when an increase in the good fortune of virtuous men gives rise to envy among the wicked, certain senators living in the imperial city envied Theodoric’s successful actions. Therefore they attempted to disparage his achievements before the emperor. Approaching the emperor Leo, whose most merciful spirit habitually judged others by his own simplicity, they sought to turn him away from his love of Theodoric [Col. 0645D], falsely claiming that Theodoric wanted to seize the kingdom of Hesperia.

The emperor, believing their words, summoned Theodoric from Italy. Obeying the command, Theodoric went with the nobles of the Goths to meet him at Constantinople. But the prince, deceived by the cunning of the informers, was considering killing Theodoric after separating him from his people.

Ptolemy, however, a man of senatorial rank and prudent counsel, thwarted this plot. He was Theodoric’s most faithful friend and, bound to him from youth by the law of friendship, could not be diverted by any cunning into hatred of him.

When he perceived the crafty plans of Theodoric’s adversaries, he approached the prince and addressed him as follows:

“Although the glory of the Roman name [Col. 0646A] has been exalted by the triumphs of war, it has earned still greater distinction through the marks of unimpaired loyalty and splendid compassion. Our ancestors strove to conquer one another more through compassion than to conquer their enemies by the laws of war.

“It is certainly most glorious that Scipio is said to have triumphed over Carthage; but more glorious still that he is said not only to have attended the funeral of his most hostile enemy, but even to have carried the funeral bier upon his bowed shoulders.

“Pompey is also worthy of praise for destroying the forces of Mithridates and compelling him to die; but still more worthy of praise for raising Tigranes when he surrendered, prostrated himself on the ground at his feet, and placed his diadem upon Pompey’s knees, and for not only raising him but placing the crown upon his head and making him sit beside him.

“Why should I mention the remarkable fidelity of the consul Regulus [Col. 0646B], who, as a citizen devoted to Rome, preferred to perish by unheard-of punishments in the hands of his enemies rather than live by breaking his oath?

“Therefore, most merciful emperor, do not accept the words of those who wish to stain the honor of your empire with the blot of treachery. For what will be said throughout the world if you put such an outstanding commander to death by so unspeakable a death?

“But let my counsel please you: when Theodoric enters the palace, let him be bound and handed over to custody. After that, send some senators to report this answer from your clemency to the Goths: ‘Theodoric will not be released unless he clears himself of the crimes alleged against him.’”

The speech pleased the prince and the entire senate. Ptolemy was sent with other envoys to announce this to the Goths [Col. 0646C]. He had in fact sent a boy ahead to inform them, so that when he arrived with the others they might seize him and send this message to the emperor:

“The senators will not be sent back unless the nobles of the Goths have received their lord.”

They obeyed the advice that was most useful to them and threw the surrounded senators into chains. When Caesar learned of this, he feared the savagery of the people and prudently took precautions lest they should do something cruel to his men; he therefore returned Theodoric unharmed to the Goths.

Thus, through the prudent counsel of his friend, Theodoric was freed for the moment from the danger of death. When he had returned to Rome, he experienced various successes in war. He often defeated the Avars in battle, though he was also defeated by them.

One day, after slaughtering the aforementioned enemies along the roads as they fled after being defeated in battle, he established his camp not far from the river called the Hister [Col. 0646D]. Taking a few of his men, he went out to reconnoiter the enemy. And behold, a certain Avar named Xerxes was likewise approaching alone to inspect Theodoric’s tents.

When Theodoric saw him advancing alone, he sent three of his men to capture him and bring him quickly before him. The Avar Xerxes, pretending to flee, killed them one by one. He likewise delivered three others to death.

Then Theodoric attacked him while his companions hung back in fear. After struggling with him for a long time and with great effort, Theodoric finally captured Xerxes, who had been wounded in the arm, and had him bound and placed in the Gothic camp.

The aforementioned prince, admiring his courage, first tried by blandishments and then by threats to compel him to live with him. But when he saw that Xerxes could be shaken neither by terror nor bent by promises, he reluctantly allowed him, after inflicting many injuries upon him, to return to his homeland.

Xerxes, however, entered the river Hister by swimming. Looking back at Theodoric, he addressed him as follows:

“Stripped of your domination and restored to my freedom, I shall now return to you as my lord, promising that I shall be your faithful servant.”

After saying this, he returned to the bank he had left and placed himself under Theodoric’s authority.

While the aforementioned patrician was flourishing in Italy through these successes, he was being torn apart at Constantinople before the emperor by the slanderous reports of his detractors. For the minds of wicked men, wishing to increase their own advantages through the misfortunes of others, strive to turn the good deeds of virtuous men to the opposite [Col. 0647B].

At last the emperor, led into error by the cunning accusations of the informers and enraged because Theodoric was said to be plotting against the kingdom, ordered him to come to him again. After discussing his death with the senators, he bound them by oath that none of them would reveal his secret.

When Theodoric received the emperor’s embassy, he immediately sent a boy to Ptolemy, whom we mentioned above, to ask him to report whether it would be expedient to obey the emperor’s command. Ptolemy pretended that he did not wish to give an answer; but overcome by the insistence of the boy who had been sent and by his long-standing friendship with the old man, he finally gave Theodoric’s messenger these instructions:

“Since today is the emperor’s birthday and we senators are reclining at table with him, [Col. 0647C] you shall stand beside me in the role of an obedient servant. During the banquet, listen carefully to whatever subject is discussed with the senators or the prince, and report it to the one who sent you.”

The boy obeyed the command and became Ptolemy’s attentive listener at the banquet. Then, during the food and wine, when the hearts of the nobles had been heated by unmixed wine, Ptolemy encouraged them with this speech:

“Since this day is joyful with splendid feasts, it ought also to be made pleasant by delightful stories. Let the wishes of those who enjoy such things be satisfied, since the overflowing abundance of wine has increased their appetite for them.”

When everyone had been captivated by this speech, he began to say the following:

“At the time when the abundance of human eloquence [Col. 0647D] existed in all the living creatures of the earth, the beasts of the forest came together in a single agreement to choose a king for themselves, so that those who despised the rule of human beings might have an emperor chosen from their own kind.

“Encouraging one another with these words, they approached the lion and asked him not to reject their will. They said that they wished to have as their prince one whom they knew to be wise in counsel.

“The lion accepted the right of rule, and all the wild beasts raised him to the royal throne. They gathered in large numbers to greet him and worshiped him as their lord.

“Among the others there came a stag, outstanding in the beauty of his body and powerful with branching antlers. As he fell forward with lowered neck to worship, the lion seized him, intending to make him his meal. But the stag, sensing the trick and shaking his head with a mighty effort, lost his antlers and fled into the forest.

“The emperor, indignant at this contempt for himself and unable to restrain his anger, furiously threatened the stag with many punishments. The wild beasts mourned among themselves the insult to their prince, but none was found who dared pursue the stag and avenge this outrage.

“Although he appeared to be unarmed, the stag could nevertheless escape without the aid of night by leaping swiftly over the steep ridges of the mountain.

“Among them was a fox, skilled in ingenious devices. They sent her to approach the stag cunningly and bring him back to the lion. She obeyed the command, approached the stag, and said that she sympathized with his grief and that it seemed unjust to her that he had suffered such things without cause.

“He, on the contrary, heaped many curses upon the lion and complained that, while he had been obeying him, he had been badly punished.

“The fox said to him: ‘It must be considered whether what you regard as an injury may be proved to have been done by him out of love for you. For, as I suppose, when he wished to raise you as a suppliant to his mouth for a kiss, you perhaps mistook it for a bite and avoided his presence. But now he grieves that you are absent; he speaks about you in your absence, and his attention is fixed on you alone.’

“What more need be said? She persuaded the stag to approach the lion and entrust himself to his power. When he came, as before, with bowed head to worship the king, the lion seized him, fixing his claws into his neck, and the surrounding beasts immediately tore him apart.

“The fox, standing nearby, secretly took out and devoured his heart. The lion, seeking the stag’s heart and not finding it, roared angrily. The terrified beasts anxiously investigated which of them was responsible for this offense.

“There was suspicion that the fox was guilty of the theft, because they had seen her standing very close to the stag. When questioned, the fox denied that she knew anything about the crime. But when she was not believed and was handed over to torture, she burst into these words:

“‘Woe to me, miserable creature, who suffer such punishments undeservedly! Why is something being demanded from me that it is clearly known he did not have? For if he had had a heart, he certainly would not have returned here. First, after his antlers were torn away, he fled unarmed; second, he did not hesitate to expose himself to the danger of death. Therefore he certainly had no heart, since he did not know how to look after himself.’”

Ptolemy finished speaking and fell silent.

Theodoric’s boy, listening attentively to these things and understanding the words with keen intelligence, returned to his master, disclosed everything in order, and warned him to be more cautious against the deceits of those plotting against him [Col. 0648D].

Theodoric therefore disregarded the emperor’s commands ordering him to go to Constantinople and remained in Italy. Later he became king and lord of the Goths who had invaded Italy.

Each year he paid to the imperial authorities a *modius* of land. Consequently, those ignorant of the truth of the matter, when it was said that King Theodoric paid a *modius* to the public treasury, without any noun being added—of wine or oil, for example—thought that he was contributing a *modius* of coins.

## CHAPTER XI. The two popes and the punishment of the antipope’s supporter

At that time, after Anastasius, the Roman pope, had died, there was a shameful division among both the clergy and the people over his successor [Col. 0649A]. One party gave its support to a certain Laurence; but the larger party, using (as later became clear) the sounder judgment, had chosen the most holy Symmachus for itself.

Both were ordained on the same day: Symmachus in the Constantinian basilica, Laurence in the church of Saint Mary. But since neither party would yield to the other, they decided that the dispute should be settled by the judgment of the aforementioned king, Theodoric.

While he was at Ravenna, after hearing the envoys of both parties, he decreed:

“Let the one who was ordained first, or the one whom the greater part of both clergy and people elected, sit upon the apostolic throne.”

Accordingly, after Symmachus had become pope, he appointed Laurence bishop of the city of Nocera out of consideration for mercy. Whoever wishes to know more fully about these matters will find them in the *Gesta Pontificalia* [Col. 0649B].

In this dispute, as blessed Pope Gregory writes, the most holy Paschasius, a deacon of the Roman Church, supported the party of Laurence. Although he was a man who despised himself, loved the poor of Christ, and diligently distributed alms, he could never be bent to communicate with Symmachus. He loved and always preferred the man whom the Church, by the just judgment of the bishops, had rejected as its head.

During the pontificate of Symmachus, Paschasius reached the end of his life and was carried to the church to be committed to burial. When a certain demoniac touched his dalmatic, which had been placed upon his bier, he was immediately freed.

The physicians had prescribed to Germanus, bishop of Capua, that he should bathe in the baths of Angulanum in order to recover bodily health. When he entered those same baths, he found Paschasius standing in the same hot waters and ready to serve him.

When Germanus, trembling, asked what so great a man was doing there, he received this answer:

“I have been assigned to these hot waters for no other reason than that, favoring Laurence, I consented to his wicked actions against Symmachus. But if you deign to offer prayers to the Lord for me, know that you have been heard if, when you return here, you are unable to find me.”

The bishop returned to the church and offered a saving sacrifice to the Lord for him. When he returned to the baths, he did not find him at all.

## CHAPTER XII. The birth and reign of King Clovis

[Col. 0649D]

Childeric, king of the Franks, had by his aforementioned wife a son named Clovis. As he advanced in age day by day, so too he grew in uprightness of character.

At this time, when a severe famine was oppressing almost all Burgundy, one of the senators, named Edicius, pleasing to God and to human beings, undertook to perform a pleasing work. He sent out servants and gathered four thousand people who were being hard-pressed by the want caused by famine; throughout the entire period of their poverty he fed and supported them at his own expense.

One day, while he was devoted to this pious work, a voice was heard from above saying:

“Because, O Edicius, you have given food to me when I was hungry in my members, bread shall not fail your offspring for ever and ever.”

God is indeed faithful in his words and holy in all his works (Psalm 144:9); he wished his faithful servant to be secure concerning the reward of his righteous labor.

Meanwhile King Childeric, after ruling the kingdom of the Franks vigorously for twenty-four years, departed this life. The aforementioned Clovis succeeded him by hereditary right, a man vigorous in military affairs and second in courage to none of his predecessors.

He expelled Siagrius, the Roman patrician and son of Aegidius, from the city of Soissons and subjected it to his own authority. The army of the Franks, however, invading many churches of Gaul, plundered their treasures.

Among the other spoils they carried away from the church at Rheims a vessel of remarkable weight and beauty. For this reason blessed Remigius, bishop of that city [Col. 0650B], sent an envoy to Clovis, earnestly requesting that, if he deserved to receive nothing else, at least that vessel might be returned to him.

Then the king instructed the envoy, saying:

“Follow me as far as Soissons. There the things that have been captured will be divided by lot. If a fair lot gives me the vessel for which you are asking, you will encounter no delay in receiving it.”

The envoy obeyed the command and followed the king’s journey to the appointed place. When they arrived, all the goods were brought into the center by the king’s order to be divided by lot.

The king, fearing that after the lots were cast the vessel might fall into another’s possession, summoned the leaders and addressed them as follows:

“Although the order of reason requires a prince rather to command his subjects what he wishes than to ask them for it, I nevertheless, my most valiant fellow soldiers [Col. 0650C], prefer to demand something from you with favor rather than with severity.

“For it belongs to tyrants to command their subjects in every small matter with force and savagery; good princes, on the other hand, invite their subjects by the gentleness of their words even to endure grave and difficult things.

“Therefore the dignity of the royal name ought to follow the example of a pious father, so that it may demand more reverence for itself through kindness than fear through cruelty.

“I have therefore judged it more proper to ask you, with the benevolence of a gentle spirit, for what I could seize by royal authority without consulting you. Thus I ask all of you to grant me this vessel”—and he pointed to the vessel—“by your generosity, outside the portion assigned to me by lot. Let none of you doubt the reward of compensation, since I declare myself to be the one who will repay you if I am able to obtain this with your good will.”

The Franks replied to the king:

“We remember, illustrious king, that we once promised you our loyalty under oath, and we did not blush to profess that we were ready to undergo death for the preservation of your life. If, therefore, we have vowed to you life itself, which is dearer to all than wealth, what greater thing could we justly refuse?

“Indeed, we yield not a part but the whole of these spoils to your authority; do whatever you wish. Whether you order us to be drowned in rivers or handed over to devouring flames, it makes no difference to us, so long as your desire is satisfied.”

While the king admired and praised the army’s devoted will toward him, one of the Franks, moved by levity of spirit, struck the vessel with his sword and said to the king [Col. 0651A]:

“You, king, will receive nothing from here except what the true lot permits you to take.”

While the others marveled and at the same time blamed the man’s audacity, the king pretended not to take the matter badly and returned the aforementioned vessel to the bishop’s envoy.

After the course of the passing year had been completed, the same prince ordered the army to assemble in a field called the Campus Martius, issuing a general edict that they should appear armed as though they were about to fight against enemies.

The army came forward to the place where it had been ordered to assemble, renowned for its military exploits and conspicuous in the gleam of its weapons. King Clovis also advanced to inspect the ordered ranks of his men, and, circling through the formation, came to the man who had struck the vessel with his sword.

When he saw him, he addressed him as follows:

“Surveying the entire army, I have found no one more cowardly than you [Col. 0651B], nor have I seen anyone carrying more useless weapons. For neither spear nor shield, neither helmet nor sword, is of any use.”

He stretched out his hand and threw the man’s *francisca* to the ground; this is called a *spatha*. When the man bent down to retrieve it, the king drew his own sword from its sheath and struck him forcefully on the neck, saying:

“This is what you did to me at Soissons concerning that vessel.”

When the man had died, the king ordered each person to return to his own place. Great fear of the Franks seized them because of this deed and restrained anyone from opposing his will in the future. His face bore a gravity mingled with cheerfulness, so that the pleasantness of his appearance soothed the good and his severity terrified the wicked.

## CHAPTER XIII. The wooing of King Clovis

I shall briefly explain by what course he came to the bosom of Mother Church and to the unity of the Catholic faith [Col. 0651C].

He took a wife from the Burgundian people, named Clotilde, a Christian from the very cradle of her infancy. She came to the king’s attention for the following reason.

The prince had sent envoys to Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, to carry a peace proposal. While they remained at the palace, they saw the girl Clotilde and asked who she was. They were told that she was the king’s niece, born of his brother.

“She is,” they said, “deprived of her parents and is now being supported by royal charity.”

When the envoys returned, they reported that the matters for which they had gone had been completed.

“Among other things,” they said, “we saw a girl so beautiful in appearance that she could be given in marriage to any very powerful king. She is descended from royal stock; since her father has died, her uncle has raised her from early childhood” [Col. 0651D].

When he heard this, King Clovis fell in love with the girl, hoping that through this opportunity he might seize the kingdom of Burgundy. He immediately sent one of his most trusted companions, named Aurelianus, carrying gifts sent by him to the girl, so that he might observe her appearance more carefully.

He ordered him to approach the girl, learn the king’s wishes concerning marriage, and discover what she herself thought about the matter.

Obeying the command, Aurelianus entered Burgundy. As he approached the palace, he ordered his companions to hide in the woods. He himself, wrapped in the clothing of a beggar, hurried to the court and looked for a way to speak with his future mistress.

It happened that she had gone to church [Col. 0652A] to fulfill her vows of prayer to the Lord. It was a Sunday. Aurelianus stood among the other poor before the doors and waited for her to come out.

When the rites of the Mass had been completed, the girl came out to distribute alms to the needy, as was her custom. Aurelianus approached as a beggar to ask for a gift. When she extended a gold coin to him, he seized her hand, pulled back the cloak from her arm, and brought her bare hand to his mouth to kiss it.

Covered with the blush of maidenly shame, she returned home. She immediately sent a girl to bring before her the man whom she supposed to be a beggar.

When he had been brought into her presence, she addressed him as follows:

“What did you think you were doing, man, that, when you were about to receive alms, you uncovered and kissed my hand?”

He ignored the question and gave this answer [Col. 0652B]:

“My lord, the king of the Franks, having heard of your outstanding nobility, desires to have you as his wife. Here is his ring and the other bridal ornaments.”

But when he turned to take the sack that he had set down behind the door, intending to offer her the gifts he had brought, he realized that it had secretly been taken away. After an inquiry, the sack was found. He received it back as a traveler and offered the gifts to the girl, now confident of the marriage.

For when she heard about the union of the marriage bed, she replied to the envoy:

“It is not lawful for a Christian woman to take a pagan as her husband. But if God, the Creator of all things, has ordained that through me he should recognize his Creator, I do not reject the request; rather, may the command of the almighty Lord be fulfilled.”

When the envoy said that the king would consent in every respect to her desire, she asked him to keep this matter secret from her, lest her uncle discover it in any way.

After giving his word that he would not disclose it for any reason, he returned to the king and made him joyful with the good news. The girl, for her part, placed in the treasuries of her uncle the ring that Clovis had sent her for safekeeping.

## CHAPTER XIV. The betrothal of Clotilde

Clovis again sent the same Aurelianus to King Gundobad to request his bride, who was to be joined to him by a marriage covenant.

Approaching the king of the Burgundians, Aurelianus delivered Clovis’s message. Gundobad declared that he did not know who Clovis’s bride was and that he could give no answer.

“But you must beware,” he said, “lest, having come to spy out our kingdom, you be expelled from this court under the weight of public disgrace” [Col. 0652D].

The envoy replied:

“This is what your lord, our king Clovis, commands me to say: ‘If you wish to return my Clotilde to me as my bride, designate a place where I may come to receive her.’”

Gundobad was astonished that Clovis should be asking for his niece. He summoned the leading men of the kingdom and consulted them about what he should do.

Fearing the courage of the Franks, and lest they prepare an expedition against Burgundy if the girl were not handed over to their king, they gave their ruler this advice:

“Let our lord inquire what the girl desires and whether the ring of the Frankish king has been delivered to her. If she wishes what has been mentioned, and perhaps has already received the bridal gifts, you will not be able to resist; rather, you will hasten to hand her over to the envoys. The Burgundians protect their commonwealth more through counsel than through arms.”

When questioned, the girl confessed that she had received the gifts mentioned above and that she eagerly desired the king’s union. Although unwilling, Gundobad handed her over to Clovis’s envoys, giving her nothing from his own treasures.

Later, however, through the work and skill of Aurelianus, the greater part of those treasures passed into Clovis’s possession. After Clovis had enlarged his kingdom as far as the Seine and afterward as far as the Loire, he granted Aurelianus the fortress of Melun, together with the dukedom of the entire region, by right of benefice.

The aforementioned Aurelianus therefore hastened to escort Clotilde to the king [Col. 0653B]. When she approached the borders of her uncle’s kingdom, she ordered the Franks who were with her to seize plunder and set fire to the villages in the kingdom of Burgundy.

Without delay they did exactly what they had been ordered to do. After setting fire to the surrounding villages and turning away with their booty, they left Burgundy and returned toward Frankish territory.

When she saw this, Clotilde is said to have spoken as follows:

“I give thanks to you, almighty God, because I see the beginning of vengeance for my father’s death.”

For King Gundobad had killed her father by a most unspeakable death, as will be shown later in what follows.

King Clovis, meanwhile, celebrating his wedding with great splendor in the city of Soissons, took the aforementioned Clotilde as his wife. Joined to an unbelieving husband, this faithful woman tried to lead him to the faith [Col. 0653C]. But he denied that he could do so and declared that he did not wish to abandon the rite and custom to which the Franks were accustomed.

## CHAPTER XV. The conversion of King Clovis to the faith of Christ

Meanwhile the queen conceived a child and brought him to baptism, naming him Ingomer. Placed in white garments, he breathed out his spirit and passed into eternal life.

For this reason the king, filled with excessive indignation, said to the queen:

“Because the child was baptized in the name of your God, our gods have deprived him of the light of the present life.”

The queen replied:

“I give thanks to almighty God, who has deigned to receive the firstborn of my womb into his kingdom.”

She gave birth to another son, whom she named Clodomir after he was baptized. When he fell ill, the king began to reproach his wife, saying:

“This child too will incur the anger of the gods because of your superstition” [Col. 0653D].

But when the queen prayed, the child’s health was restored.

While the king remained in unbelief, however, at last—as was said above—the army was stirred up, and war was launched by the Franks and Alamanni with all the strength of their kingdoms.

Then King Clovis gave his men the signal and ordered them to engage in battle. But while the fighting continued, seeing his men being slaughtered grievously by the enemy’s sword, he cried out:

“Christ, most powerful God, whom my wife Clotilde worships with a pure heart, I vow to you the trophy of my faith, if you grant me victory and triumph over these enemies.”

When he had finished speaking, fear seized the Alamanni and the ardor of courage inflamed the Franks. Thus the enemy turned their backs and left the victory to Clovis. At last, seeing their king cut down by the sword, they willingly promised that they would serve the Franks under tributary obligation.

# CHAPTER XVI. Clovis’s Address to His People after His Conversion, and His Baptism

Afterward the victorious Clovis, returning, reached the city of Toul, and, finding there the blessed Vedast, later bishop of Arras [Atrebatum], took him as his companion on the journey. When he had arrived at Reims, the king related to his wife all that had happened to him and to his people. Together they gave thanks to God, and the king professed his belief. His rejoicing wife hastened to Saint Remigius, bishop of the city of Reims, announced the king’s faith, and asked what ought to be done. She urged the bishop [Col. 0654B] to hasten to the king’s court and, while his mind still hung in uncertainty, to open for him the way of truth by which one goes to God:

“She says that she fears lest, with his mind elated by his prosperous successes, he should despise the Giver of these things while failing to recognize him. For things granted to us at our pleasure are more easily removed from memory by the passage of time than things that have happened otherwise and contrary to our wishes.”

The bishop hastened to obey the religious woman’s admonitions and presented himself before the king, who had long been awaiting his arrival. The bishop expounded the faith and instructed him in the manner of believing. The king, recognizing the truth, devoutly promised that he would serve the one God, while declaring that he would first seek the judgment of the nobles of the kingdom and of the army. He confessed what had taken place, so that they might submit their necks to Christ all the more devoutly when they saw that they were being drawn by kindness rather than by threats. The proposal was approved, and by the king’s order a public summons of the people was issued. The leading men of the kingdom assembled, nor was the army absent.

When they had been brought before him, the king began as follows:

“Franks,” he said, “descendants of Troy—for you ought to remember your name and lineage—I ask you to recall to your minds and courage how long we have served the gods until now. It has seemed appropriate and useful first to show whose worship has enslaved us, so that, when they have proved useless, the acknowledgment of the one true God may be more readily accepted. This will be done most properly if the deeds of our ancestors are reviewed.

“Let us first contemplate that city, once the glory of the Trojan people [Col. 0654D], which, as was believed, was surrounded by the protection of so many divinities, yet was overthrown by the cowardly fickleness of the Greeks, while those gods offered no assistance—by deceit more than by courage. Certainly, we had heard that the defenses of its walls had been constructed by the hand of the gods. Images of the gods themselves are also said to have been placed upon the citadel, consecrated to them, so that it might remain impregnable against the attacks of its enemies. But what assistance, I will not say to human beings, but even to the structures of the walls themselves, did those gods provide, when they did not help their own images?

“Let us therefore cast aside those whom we have proved useless, and abandon their empty worship. Let us submit our minds and bodies to God the Father alone, and to his Son Jesus Christ, with the shared power of the Holy Spirit, venerating one in the Trinity and three in the Unity [Col. 0655A]. Know for certain that our lord Remigius is the patron and author of this religion or discipline. My consort Clotildis also professes herself to belong to this faith, and has persuaded me to hope for help from the omnipotence of this divine being—help which it would be a misfortune not to seek.

“This Christ God plainly struck down the arrogant obstinacy of the Alamanni in the battle we recently fought against them, and by the stimulus of your hearts roused the boldness of your renowned courage. Let us therefore lift our minds toward right hopes, raise humble prayers to the heights, and seek as our protector him who grants everything to those who hope in him.”

When the king, full of faith, had finished speaking, he persuaded most of the people to submit their gentle necks to Christ. The priest rejoiced that the king, though not yet initiated, had already become the apostle of his own people. The baptistery was adorned, and the king descended, like another Constantine, into the sanctified basin of the font. When the holy bishop had recited to him the account of the Lord’s Passion, the king said to him:

“If I had been there with my Franks, I would have avenged his injuries.”

The miracle that followed showed what a gracious and acceptable offering to God the faith of that king had been. For when the man carrying the chrism was unable to get through the crowd and was absent, behold, suddenly—without doubt no one other than the Holy Spirit—he appeared in the visible form of a dove. Carrying the chrism in its shining beak, it set it down between the hands of the priest, in the waters of the font that was being sanctified. Joy and rejoicing followed; many of the people were baptized; praises and thanks were proclaimed to God [Col. 0655C], and the joyful king returned from the church to his own residence.

And, to reveal his devotion to the faith more fully, he had a basilica built to God and to the chief of the apostles in the city of Paris, where his own seat was located. The guardianship of religion and the strength of justice remained in him until the end of his life.

# CHAPTER XVII. On the Remaining Expeditions and Victories of Clovis

The citizens of the city of Verdun rebelled against this king. But when the king had surrounded the city with a siege and the battering rams, brought up against it, were already striking the high walls, they obtained from the prince, at the supplication of the holy man Euspicius, then archpriest of that city, a promise of immunity; and the king recovered the city.

Later, when King Clovis had decided to go to the city of Orléans, he summoned Saint Euspicius and his nephew, the blessed Maximinus, and ordered them to accompany him on his journey. He also granted them the estate of Miciacum and, so that they and their descendants might possess that place, confirmed it by his Pragmatic Sanction.

# CHAPTER XVIII. On Saint Fursa

In those days Saint Fursa also came to Gaul and, with the king’s permission, built the monastery called Lagny. This blessed Fursa, coming from Ireland, had first been honorably received by the Saxon king Sigebert and had built a monastery in that same province of Saxony.

Concerning this king, Sigebert, we have been able to find nothing else in the ancient histories [Col. 0656A] except what is read in the Life of Saint Fursa: that he received this man of God as a guest. Yet in the Chronicle called Gregory’s, and believed to be by the bishop of Tours, it is reported that a certain King Sigebert sent his son Cloderic to the prince Clovis to bring the assistance of the Franks against the Goths. The same chronicler also records that they—the father and son—were killed by Frankish treachery, and that their kingdom and treasures were seized by the Franks.

But because the manuscript in which we found these things arranged had been corrupted through the fault of its scribes, we could not ascertain with certainty of what people that king had been king, or what just cause for this death had existed. It merely relates that his kingdom and wealth were seized by Clovis.

# CHAPTER XIX. On the War against Gundobad

[Col. 0656B]

Clovis waged war against Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, and destroyed his army utterly. The cause of this conflict was that Gundobad had killed his brother Chilperic—the father, namely, of Queen Clotildis—with the sword, and had caused his wife, the mother of the aforementioned queen, to be thrown into a river with a stone tied around her neck.

For this reason, when his wife had asked him, King Clovis entered Burgundy with the Frankish army and devastated it; he also compelled Gundobad himself, exhausted by a long siege, to pay tribute. Gundobad’s brother Godegisil had defected to the Franks and, joining forces with Clovis, was attacking his brother.

But through the skill and effort of Aredius, a wise man who had come from the city of Arles to bring aid to Gundobad, that king repelled with gold the enemy whom he had been unable to defeat with iron. For Clovis, having received gifts, returned to his own country, leaving five thousand Franks to assist Godegisil.

Then Gundobad, now secure in himself, surrounded his brother at Vienne with a siege. Entering the city through an aqueduct, he killed many people and killed his brother at the same time. He also slaughtered with the sword the Franks who had gathered in a certain tower.

# CHAPTER XX. On the War against Alaric, King of the Goths

Clovis also fought against Alaric, king of the Goths, and emerged victorious. He is known to have begun this war chiefly because the Goths, like the Burgundians, belonged to the Arian heresy, and held the greater part of Gaul, from the river Loire as far as the ridges of the Pyrenees.

There was also another just occasion for this war. Clovis had sent his envoy, named Paternus, to Alaric, king of the Goths, to discuss matters of peace with him and also to learn his wishes, so that he might determine where the two kings ought to meet for the advantage of both their kingdoms; and so that Alaric, following the custom of the ancients, might touch Clovis’s beard and become his adoptive father.

When the envoy arrived and explained the reasons for which he had come, Alaric designated a place and said that he would not fail to attend the conference. At last the envoy asked whether he would come with a few men or with a large army. Alaric replied that, taking only a few men, he would seek their meeting.

Paternus again asked whether they would be armed or unarmed. Alaric said that all his men would come unarmed, and that he would ask the Franks to do the same. Paternus agreed to all these conditions, returned to his lord, and reported that the Goths had approved what he had learned.

Clovis therefore set out from Francia and came into Aquitaine. Before he reached the place appointed by agreement, he sent the aforementioned envoy ahead to investigate what equipment the Goths would use.

While speaking with King Alaric, Paternus noticed that he was carrying an iron bar from a door in his hand as though it were a staff, and he discovered that the others were doing the same. Taking the king by the right hand, he said to him:

“What has my lord Clovis and the Franks done to offend you, O king, that you should plot to deceive us by treachery?”

When Alaric denied this, and the matter progressed as far as a quarrel, it was decided that the affair should be settled by the judgment of Theodoric, the king of the Goths whom we mentioned above. Accordingly, both kings sent envoys to him in Italy, where he also ruled.

After learning the cause of both parties, he decreed that the Frankish envoy should mount a horse and stand before the doors of King Alaric’s palace, holding a raised spear in his hand. Upon it Alaric and the Goths were to heap silver coins until the tip of the spear was covered; the total number of solidi was to pass into the possession of the king of the Franks.

Those who had been sent returned and reported King Theodoric’s judgment, which all the Franks praised. But the Goths said that they could not fulfill it; moreover, they insulted Clovis’s envoy.

For one night, when he had gone to sleep in the upper room of a certain house, the Goths destroyed the flooring that was before his bed. When he rose to attend to the needs of nature, his foot slipped and he fell, breaking his arm; he escaped scarcely alive.

He therefore hastened back to his native land, reported the whole sequence of events to the one who had sent him, and pitifully expressed his tearful complaint about his wretched suffering.

King Clovis, therefore, judging that such matters should not be delayed and unable to restrain his anger at the injury done to his envoy, assembled his army and encouraged it to battle with this speech:

“Confident in your courage, O strongest fellow soldiers, I judge your spirit to require no exhortation. Our enemies feared it so greatly that they sought to kill our envoy by a monstrous act of violence. They plainly show that they cannot endure the anger of the entire people, since they were terrified by the steadfastness of one envoy.

“I want you to know only this: your conflict against the most savage enemies is not for wives or children, nor even for the acquisition of wealth, but rather for the inseparable unity of the Holy Trinity, which they divide by their most wicked error; and finally, for the divine and human laws that decree that those who act as mediators of hostile arms ought to be immune from injuries. Among hostile arms, an embassy alone is the mediator of peace. He who performs an embassy lays aside the role of an enemy.

“Let us therefore hasten to battle, and, trusting in divine protection, attack the enemy ranks without fear.”

Inspired by this address from their leader, the brave men set out against the enemy with steadfast hearts, prepared either to conquer or to die.

# CHAPTER XXI. On the Sign of Victory and the Appearance of the Doe

That divine assistance had been present with him in this war was shown by signs displayed by God. For when he was sending envoys bearing gifts to the tomb of Saint Martin, he said to them:

“Go and bring me a sign of victory from the basilica of Saint Martin.”

When they entered the church to pray, the voice of a cantor sounded in their ears, saying:

“You have girded me, Lord, with strength for war, and you have given me the backs of my enemies” [Psalm XVII, 40–41].

Rejoicing, they completed their prayer, offered their gifts, and reported to the king the sign of victory granted to them by God, making him eager for the battle.

When he decided to cross the river called the Vienne, he could not find a ford because the river, swollen by the rains, had overflowed. He began to pray to the Lord in these words:

“Trinity in persons, God, and one in majesty, grant me victory against the adversaries of the Catholic faith and provide an easy crossing of this riverbed.”

The merciful ear of the Almighty granted his prayer. When they had moved the camp at daybreak, behold, a certain doe suddenly appeared before their eyes. They, as is the custom of the Franks, being devoted to the chase, thought it was prey and eagerly pursued it. But, after crossing the river, it showed them a ford and then disappeared from sight.

Thus the king crossed with his entire army, reached Poitiers, and pitched his tents not far from the basilica of Saint Hilary. By an edict he restrained the people who accompanied him from plundering anything in that province, not even the necessities of food.

Then, in the silence of midnight, a fiery beacon was seen to emerge from the church of Saint Hilary and extend over the tent in which the king was resting. Battle was joined, and the Goths were defeated and turned their backs.

In the midst of the most densely packed lines, Clovis engaged Alaric. When he had thrown him to the ground and was searching for a place to inflict a mortal wound, two Goths struck him from the side with spears; but they were unable to wound him because of his coat of mail.

# CHAPTER XXII. On Theodoric’s Expeditions

[Col. 0658D]

After King Alaric, who had ruled the Goths for twelve years, had been killed in this manner, Clovis sent his son Theodoric with a strong reinforcement of troops into the upper regions of Alaric’s kingdom. Theodoric traversed the entire province, subdued the Ruthenians, Cadurcians, and Arvernians, and returned victorious to his father, who was then wintering in the city of Bordeaux.

When the severity of winter had withdrawn and the mildness of spring had succeeded it, Clovis headed for Toulouse. From there, carrying off Alaric’s treasures, he hastened to Angoulême. At his arrival, the city wall, collapsing of its own accord by divine command, opened a way for the approaching king. He killed with the sword all the Goths whom he found there.

In the same way, killing his adversaries and establishing his own men in the neighboring cities, he compelled them to obey him. When everything had therefore been arranged according to his wishes, he directed his journey toward Tours.

While he remained there for a little while in temporary quarters, he received an embassy from Anastasius, the emperor of Constantinople, who sent him gifts and letters. These letters contained the following statement: that it had pleased the emperor and the senators that he should be a friend of the emperors and a patrician of the Romans.

After reading them, he was invested with the consular robe, mounted his horse in the courtyard situated between the basilica of Saint Martin and the city, and distributed very generous gifts to the people. From that day he deserved to be called both Consul and Augustus.

When he had decided to redeem the horse that, among his other gifts, he had sent to Saint Martin by giving one hundred solidi, and was unable by any means to move it from the place, he ordered another hundred to be given and said:

“Saint Martin is known to be good in assistance, but expensive in price.”

After receiving the horse and establishing peace throughout the surrounding area, the king returned to Paris.

# CHAPTER XXIII. On the Death of King Chararic and Clovis’s War against Ragnachar

As for King Chararic, who ought once to have assisted Clovis when he fought against Syagrius, but, breaking faith and withdrawing, had preferred to be a spectator of the battle rather than a fighter, intending afterward to follow the side of the victor—Clovis captured him and his son by deceit. He had them tonsured and ordered the father to be ordained a presbyter and the son a deacon.

When Chararic complained about his humiliation, his son said to him:

“These branches”—pointing to his beard—“cut from the top of the trunk while the tree is green will quickly grow again. If only the author of this deed would perish just as quickly!”

When this remark was reported to Clovis, he immediately ordered them to be punished with the sword and seized their kingdom together with its treasures.

After this he prepared an expedition against a certain leader named Ragnachar, who lived at the city of Cambrai. Blood relationship united him to Clovis, but the wickedness of his character made him hostile. For he was devoted to obscenity and luxury, and was hated even by all his own people.

He had also taken as his close companion a certain man named Faro, whom he considered to possess conspicuous prudence. This man, a master of deception, had so alienated Ragnachar’s mind that, if anyone offered him a gift, he would include Faro as a partner in accepting it, saying: “These things are for me and my counselor Faro.”

Moved by the leader’s cowardice, those who served in his court began to discuss among themselves how they might remove this injury from themselves. The idleness of a ruler is a reproach to his subjects. Therefore they secretly urged Clovis through intermediaries to seek an occasion for war against him, promising that they would withdraw from the battle before coming to blows and, if rewards were granted to them, would hand over their bound lord.

Clovis delayed no longer. He set out against him with a strong force of his own men, first sending the traitors gilded bronze bracelets and swords gilded in the same manner as gifts.

They came to the place of battle, and the men privy to the treachery pretended to seek safety in flight. While Ragnachar was trying to flee, his own men captured him and presented him bound to Clovis. Clovis, judging him a man of degenerate character, ordered him to be punished with the sword.

He likewise ordered his brother to be killed, reproaching him for having failed to bring assistance to his brother and thus allowed both himself and his brother to be disgracefully held. In the same way he handed many of his relatives over to death and seized their treasures, so that no one might remain who could plot against his kingdom or life.

For he had Ragnachar’s brother, named Rignemir [also Ricimir], whom he had noticed was more desirous of the kingdom, deprived of life by agents at the city of Le Mans.

For this reason he is said one day to have said in the presence of the leading men of the kingdom:

“Deprived of all my relatives, I fear danger to my life, since I have no close relation to guard my safety.”

Some judged that this had been said as a pretext, in case someone should come forward claiming to be close to the king by blood.

The traitors of Ragnachar, discovering that the gifts they had received as a reward for their treachery had been debased, brought a complaint to Clovis. Clovis said to them:

“You are ungrateful for the benefits bestowed upon you. For what punishments do you think those deserve to suffer who cause the death of their lord? Go instead back to your homes; let the unworthy life you enjoy be sufficient for you.”

Fearing the prince’s anger, they returned to their dwellings.

# CHAPTER XXIV. On Saint Severinus and Others

[Col. 0660C]

When this king had been suffering from a fever for nearly an entire year, the man of God Severinus—then the distinguished abbot of the monastery of the Agaunian martyrs—was summoned by him and restored him to health. Later, completing a praiseworthy course of life in the grove called Castrum Lantonis, Severinus departed to the Lord.

At that time, after Anastasius had died, Justin the Elder was administering the imperial majesty. In the territories of his empire, namely in the province of Nursia, Benedict—already then approaching childhood, venerable throughout the whole world in life and name—was being assigned by his parents to the schools of the liberal arts.

Hormisdas also took over the governance of the Roman Church after Symmachus. During his time, the often-mentioned king, the glorious Clovis, sent to the threshold of blessed Peter, at the urging of the supreme bishop Remigius, a golden crown of royal dignity adorned with the most precious gems.

By this deed he plainly showed that he would not be ungrateful to God, since he was sending a distinguished royal gift to the tomb of that apostle himself, knowing that he had been granted the throne of his kingdom by Christ.

For the Roman consul Sosius, after capturing the city of Jerusalem, also offered a crown in the temple of the Lord. But this man’s gift was more pleasing because his faith was superior. The former was a worshiper of idols, whereas this man was, to the best of his ability, a devoted worshiper of the Catholic Church. The former offered what was present, although he was hostile to the city and temple themselves; but this man, though absent, was a lover of the Roman house and no less devoted to the basilica of the apostle Peter.

# CHAPTER XXV. On the Earthquake and the Death of Clovis

In those days, in the Gallic city of Vienne, many houses and churches alike were shaken and collapsed in an earthquake. During the Easter festival, while the most blessed Mamertus, bishop of that city, was celebrating the solemn Masses, the royal palace located in the same city was consumed by heavenly fire.

Wolves and bears, driven from the forests, also began to become an innumerable threat to that city, to such an extent that, tearing apart the bodies of many people, they forced them to abandon their own dwellings.

Therefore, when the feast day of the Lord’s Ascension approached, the aforementioned priest summoned the people and warned them [Col. 0661B] to undertake a three-day fast and to seek the assistance of almighty God [Col. 0662A]. When the appointed day drew near, all the people gathered joyfully at the church, performing litanies while observing the three-day fast.

From that time, a most beautiful custom arose in the holy universal Church: wherever throughout the world the faith of Christ is spread, all the faithful perform these litanies with rejoicing.

The illustrious Clovis, king of the Franks, reached the limit of the time allotted to him and died in the fifth year after he had killed Alaric, king of the Goths. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, which he himself had built at the request of his wife.

He reigned for thirty years, leaving four sons as heirs to the kingdom. From the death of Saint Martin to the death of King Clovis, one hundred and twelve years are reckoned.

[Col. 0661] The first book ends.

# THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS

# CHAPTER I. On the Division of the Kingdom of the Franks among the Sons of Clovis

[Col. 0661B]

Accordingly, the four sons of Clovis—Theodoric, Clodomir, Childebert, and Clotarius—divided the kingdom among themselves with equal measure. Theodoric received the royal seat at Metz, Clodomir at Orléans, Clotarius at Soissons, and Childebert at Paris, where their father had also ruled.

At that time the most holy Pope John, who had succeeded Hormisdas [Col. 0661C], went to Constantinople to the emperor Justin, sent by Theodoric, king of the Goths.

For Justin Augustus, being a man of Catholic faith and attacking the heretics, had restored their churches to the orthodox, following the counsel of the aforementioned pope. Therefore Theodoric, who belonged to the Arian heresy, sent him, together with other Catholic men, to the emperor, commanding that, unless the churches were restored to the Arians, he would strike down and destroy the entire population of Italy with the sword.

The holy bishop, although ill, undertook the journey and traveled by ship to Constantinople. The emperor and all the clergy of the city met him, and the prince rejoiced that he had received the bishop of the apostolic see in the imperial city.

After he had delivered and obtained what he had gone there to accomplish [Col. 0661D], he placed the imperial crown upon Justin Augustus as the vicar of blessed Peter. Having received permission to return, he went back to Ravenna.

Because Theodoric had heard that the emperor had received him honorably, he subjected him to prolonged imprisonment and afflicted him with fasts and the squalor of confinement, finally forcing him to breathe out his last breath. As he died, he yielded his soul to Christ as a martyr.

He also killed the others who had been with him, some by burning them in fire, others by various punishments. Among them he ordered the patrician Symmachus and Boethius, his son-in-law, to be punished with the sword after their imprisonment.

How eloquent Boethius was in secular letters, and how Catholic he was, is demonstrated by his books. Arithmetic testifies to this, as does dialectic, and also music itself—most pleasing to the minds of all—which he translated and poured delightfully into the ears of the Latins who had long desired it [Col. 0662B].

Moreover, his book on the consubstantiality of the Holy Trinity clearly shows how distinguished a cultivator of the holy Church he would have been in his own time, if he had been permitted to continue.

Theodoric, however, immediately paid the price for so monstrous a crime. For on the ninety-eighth day after this deed, he died a sudden death and ended his unworthy life with a fitting end [Col. 0662C].

A solitary living on the island of Lipara saw his soul, led by the most holy Pope John and Symmachus, the former consul, being plunged into a nearby cauldron of Vulcan. It is so called because there it boils with fire like a bronze vessel.

In this way Theodoric perished, a man who in his beginnings had been distinguished for honorable character. For at first he annually provided the Romans with one hundred and twenty thousand measures of wheat as assistance. But when he approached the end, as is clear from what has been said above, he defiled everything.

His wife was Audefleda, the sister of Clovis, king of the Franks. Theodoric also joined his own sisters or daughters in marriage to the rulers of the nations surrounding him. There was no people neighboring Italy whose king was not related to him [Col. 0662D].

Let us now continue the sequence of our history that we began.

# CHAPTER II. On the War that Arose among the Brothers over the Division of the Kingdom

After the kingdom had been divided into four parts, as was mentioned above, the fierce fires of war were quiet for a short time.

But the Danes, a most restless people, boarded a great number of ships, entered the borders of the kingdom of King Theodoric, and ravaged them. Against them the aforementioned king sent his son Theodebert with an army into those regions. Theodebert routed the enemy, rescued the captives, and returned victorious.

# CHAPTER III. On Clotildis’s Address to the Kings

While King Theodoric was repelling the hostile attack, Queen Clotildis summoned her other sons—Clodomir, Childebert, and Clotarius—and addressed them in this speech:

“Almighty God, creator and ruler of the whole world, wished you to be heirs of your father’s kingdom for this reason: that he might make you avengers of your mother’s wrong.

“Therefore, beloved sons, happily born and more happily raised, if I have deserved anything good from you, I beg you to avenge the unspeakable and unjust killing of my father and mother. Let me rejoice, I say, that I have nourished the executors of their mother’s grief, though I lament that their grandparents—great founders of honor, had they lived—have perished.

“You must not regard lightly the cause of my complaints, since it has fallen to you to lack the protection of such great relatives, whom the cruel envy of your enemy took from you before you had received the pleasures of this life.

“Consider what hope remains. Do you think that those who spared not their brothers will spare their nephews? They removed those men from the midst of the living for the sake of a small portion of the kingdom. Do you think they will be gentler toward you, for whose removal the hope of great kingdoms will be present?

“For if you do not exact a just vengeance, they themselves will inflict a disastrous death upon you. But if compassion for the dead does not move you, at least contemplate the anxious feelings of my heart and entrails, when I saw my father condemned to the sword, my mother to drowning in a river, and my sister to exile.”

Moved by the pious emotions of their mother’s complaint, the sons gathered a very powerful Frankish army and entered Burgundy to fight against Sigismund and Godomar, the sons of King Gundobad.

# CHAPTER IV. On Sigismund’s Holy Magnificence in Building a Church of the Holy Martyrs and on His Victory

[Col. 0663C]

At that time Sigismund was constructing the basilica of Saints Maurice and his companions at great expense, in the place called Agaunum. In the vicinity of that same place he displayed the greatness of his devotion, being a man of excellent mind and an enrich­er of holy churches.

He bestowed an abundance of estates upon that place, established an order of clerics who sang the psalms, and secured the holy martyrs as favorable protectors for himself.

For he remembered that, deceived by the persuasion of his wife, he had lost his only son. While she pursued him with stepmotherly hatred, she had made him so detested by his father that, moved by anger, he ordered him to be punished with the sword.

Not long afterward, led to repentance for his deed and reflecting with himself on what crime he had committed, he often hurried to the tombs of the saints, prostrated himself on the ground, and begged that they would be most merciful toward him. He asked them that, if anything imperfect or contrary to the divine majesty were found in his actions, the just Judge might, through their intercession, punish it in this world rather than in the judgment of the future.

It is evident that this petition was fulfilled according to his desire. For when he heard that the Frankish army was approaching, he also equipped a large force of his own and drew up his battle line against them.

When the engagement took place, the Franks fought fiercely, but the Burgundians were defeated and entrusted themselves to the protection of flight. Sigismund, however, while hastening at speed to seek the protection of the Agaunian martyrs, was captured by Clodomir, king of the Franks, who was pursuing him, and was brought to Orléans and handed over to prison.

Then the blessed Avitus, who held the office of abbot in the territory of that city, began to ask Clodomir not to put such a man of outstanding nobility and distinguished goodness to death. Clodomir refused to listen to him and ordered Sigismund to be taken to a villa called Calumpnia, where he was beheaded with his sons and thrown into a well.

Later his body was taken from there and conveyed to the basilica of the holy Agaunian martyrs, where it was buried with due honor.

That Christ the Lord enrolled him among the company of the saints is considered beyond doubt for this reason: whenever people suffering from fever have faithfully caused a saving sacrifice to be offered for the remedy of his soul, they are immediately freed from the affliction of their illness.

The author of his death, however, did not long rejoice in this deed. For the following year Clodomir himself, having assembled an army, attacked the regions of Burgundy in order to devastate them.

The brother of the dead king met him and, eager to avenge his brother’s death, did not hesitate to join battle with him. But the Burgundians, as was their custom, unable to withstand the courage of the Franks, exposed their backs to the enemy.

King Clodomir, youthful and vigorous, protected by his armor and encouraged by the favorable outcome of the present battle, pursued the enemy more recklessly than he should have. Carried by the speed of the horse on which he rode, he passed ahead of the enemy line, paying too little attention to his own men.

When they saw that he had been abandoned by his own troops and surrounded by them, they began to press him from a distance with missiles. The very appearance of the man and the reputation of his renowned and energetic courage alone made the enemy hesitate, so that no one dared approach to strike him at close range.

When he saw himself surrounded by hostile wedges and realized that none of his own men was present, he placed the hope of his safety in his courage alone, turned his horse, and gathered himself for combat.

Yet the high-spirited young man began to grow agitated and, uncertain in mind, turned immense plans over in his heart. For a while he considered whether he should go to meet the enemy or yield to them.

At last he found a way through deliberation, and shame overcame his mind. Bursting among the most densely packed men of the opposing army, he attempted to open a path with his sword and struck down with his horse the first man who came against him.

But when he was surrounded, his sides pierced, he met the end of his life. He was indeed an energetic young man, swift with his hand but insufficiently prudent in counsel; in prosperity he had placed his love upon life. Yet, as far as he was able, he had avenged his mother’s wrong.

When the Franks learned of the king’s death, they did not, like other nations, seek safety in flight. Instead, burning with anger, they pursued the Burgundians, killing and striking them down with great force.

After devastating the entire province, they returned to their native land. Clotarius, Clodomir’s brother, received the kingdom of the slain king together with his wife, named Gundeuca.

His sons—Theodoald, Guntarius, and Clodoald—were taken in by their grandmother Clotildis and raised with maternal affection.

# CHAPTER V. On Justinian and Belisarius
In those very days at Constantinople, when Justin was taken from human affairs, Justinian succeeded him in the kingdom. While the aforesaid Justin was still alive, Justinian was superintendent of the sacred treasury and Belisarius prefect of the cavalry; they had pledged their right hands to one another in friendship. They had bound themselves by oath and faith “that, if either of them should attain the honor of a higher rank, he would raise his companion to equal dignity.”

One day, therefore, when they had entered a brothel with their peers, they saw there two little women from the nation of the Amazons, brought away as captives by lot and prostituted there. They seized them and led them to their own homes [Col. 0665B]. One was named Antonia, the other Antonina. Justinian took Antonia, and Belisarius Antonina. They were sisters.

One day, then, while Justinian was resting outdoors at midday, having laid his head in the lap of his beloved, an eagle arrived with outspread wings and tried to protect him from the heat of the sun. The woman understood this omen to signify the imperial power destined for Justinian. When he awoke, she addressed him in these words:

“Most beloved young man, I beg you that, when you have obtained the scepters of the kingdom, you will not judge me unworthy of the embraces of a most beloved wife.”

When he said that it was impossible for him to be raised to the imperial height, the woman begged him not to prove inexorable toward her concerning what she knew with certainty. When he gave his consent, and they exchanged rings, they parted from one another.

Belisarius, too, entered into the marriage bond with Antonina, who was joined to him, so that—since Belisarius did not doubt that he would attain the higher rank if Justinian gained the empire—he might take her as his partner in his bed. Not much time had passed when the emperor Justin prepared an expedition against the king of Persia. But, overtaken by illness amid the very preparations for war, he died in the eighth year after assuming the empire.

With the consent of the entire senate and of the army as well, Justinian was made Augustus. Without delay, he gathered an army and set out against the barbarians. When battle had been joined and the enemy put to flight, he rejoiced that he had captured their king. He made him sit beside himself on the royal throne [Col. 0665D] and ordered him to restore to him the provinces he had taken from the Romans. The king replied, “I will not give them.”

To this Justinian answered, “You will give them” [*Daras*].

Because of the novelty of this exchange, a city was built at that place and named Daras. The king of Persia, although unwilling, restored to him everything that had belonged by right to the Romans; and thus he was permitted to return to his own kingdom. Augustus Justinian likewise returned to Constantinople in great triumph.

Then Antonia, once his beloved and by no means forgetful of him, took five gold pieces and entered the palace. Of these she gave two to the doorkeepers, so that entry might be opened to her, and three to those holding the curtain, so that she might be allowed to state her case. Standing before the emperor [Col. 0666A], she addressed him as follows:
