“Since Scripture says, ‘The honor of a king loves judgment’ (Psalm 98:3), and again, ‘The king who sits on the throne of judgment scatters every evil by his gaze’ (Proverbs 20:18), I, most merciful emperor, understanding these words to have been spoken of you, have taken courage to approach you and to lay before you a matter of personal relationship.

“There is, then, in this city a young man who, after exchanging rings with me, pledged himself to a mutual love, declaring that he would join me to himself under the name of lawful wife. For this reason I have approached your serene presence, asking your judgment concerning this matter.”

The emperor replied, “If faith has been pledged, it ought not to be made void.”

When she heard this, she removed a ring from her finger and showed it to Augustus:

“Let my lord see,” she said, “whose ring this is” [Col. 0666B].

The emperor recognized it as the ring he had given her. He ordered that she be brought into his chamber, dressed in royal ornaments, and thereafter called Augusta and made one.

The entire populace and senate were vehemently horrified by this action, so much so that they openly cried out that the Augustus had committed a wicked deed by taking into marriage a prostitute of public disgrace. Stirred to anger by this insult, Caesar ordered many senators to be dragged away to their deaths. This act terrified the common people so greatly that, each fearing for himself, no one thereafter dared oppose his endeavors.

## CHAPTER VI. On Belisarius’s Success

After this he promoted his fellow soldier Belisarius to the province of Africa [Col. 0666C], appointing him patrician; and Belisarius married the aforesaid Antonina, the sister of Augusta. Since Justinian embraced him with the greatest affection, he strove to enrich him with great wealth. Belisarius was constantly present in the emperor’s counsels and was also admitted as a participant at his banquets.

But the more fortunate are always envied, and no one envies the poor; those abounding in wealth are torn by the bites of excessive slanderers. Thus many were offended by Belisarius’s prosperous success. They concocted a bitter accusation against him and prepared an even more bitter end for him.

At last, the most wicked men approached the king and aroused his envy, asserting that Belisarius desired the king’s death and the power to usurp the empire. The emperor was easily driven to regard as credible what was being affirmed as true. Thus, before any test of parricidal crime had been established for him, or any examination of the truth had excluded the suspicion of falsehood, he ordered Belisarius, at the calumniators’ prompting, to conquer the Vandals [Col. 0666D]. These Vandals had often overwhelmed the greatest forces of the Roman army and its commanders of the most illustrious nobility.

Having received this order from the emperor, Belisarius returned home mournful and sad. When his wife saw him weighed down by profound grief, she asked him the cause of the sadness that darkened his face. She begged him to reveal the secret, in case she might be able to offer some counsel or assistance. He told her that the matter concerned battle, not wool-working, and that men rather than women ought therefore to be consulted.

To this she replied:

“I trust in Christ that I shall offer a manly judgment if I can attain knowledge of this secret. For true is the saying of the Apostle: ‘The unbelieving husband is saved through the believing wife’ (1 Corinthians 7:14).”

She herself was a Catholic, although Belisarius was entangled in a detestable heresy.

Then the aforementioned patrician, after deliberating briefly within himself and considering that wisdom is also found in women and that the weaker sex is not deprived of understanding profound matters, told his wife that he had been ordered to conquer the Vandals. Casting aside womanly weakness, she began to exhort him to faith in these words:

“No one, as Holy Scripture testifies, has hoped in the Lord and been abandoned by him. Therefore, my husband, I advise you to abandon the blasphemies of the heretics and acknowledge the triune and one God who reigns in heaven. Make a vow, then, to the God of heaven, and you will be victorious more successfully than you have been before.”

Through Belisarius himself, the emperor Justinian had subjugated many fierce nations. When Belisarius had pledged his faith in Christ, she said to him again:

“Let not the beauty of your face be changed by anxiety over the difficulty of battle, and let the pallor that has taken possession of your face depart from you. Do we not have twelve thousand lads whom we support at our own expense, and eighteen thousand soldiers whom you acquired together with the dignity of the patriciate?”

When he answered, “We do,” she added:

“Take part of the soldiers—twelve thousand, that is—and four thousand of the lads, and attack the regions of Africa by land. I, however, with the remaining army—namely, six thousand soldiers and eight thousand lads—shall seek the borders of Libya by sea. This shall be our sign to one another: let your men kindle a large fire in the camp, while we display a light from torches on the ships” [Col. 0667C].

What more is there to say? Matching deeds to words, they set out for Africa in divided columns. When the Vandals learned of the land expedition, unaware of the naval force, they prepared for battle, stationing their wives and children in the camp to watch the fighting.

When battle was joined and neither army yielded ground to the other, a messenger came to the Vandals claiming that their wives and children had been slaughtered by the sword. For Antonina, having disembarked with her men [Col. 0667D], had overrun the enemy camp and left no one alive—not even the boys and girls.

When the Vandals learned of the death of their people while they were still fighting, they broke their formation. Fearing for their own, they neglected their safety and hastened back to the camp. Those who had invaded it met them as they came in disorder, struck them down, and pursued them as they scattered across the entire field.

King Childemerus, escaping the danger with only twelve Vandals, entered a very strongly fortified castle. Besieged there by Belisarius, and having no way out, he asked the patrician to lead him, freed from his bonds, into the emperor’s presence. Belisarius promised him that he would not be bound with a cord or ropes, nor constrained by iron fetters, nor tied up with *mastigia* [term uncertain]. When he surrendered, however, he was bound with a silver chain.

He was brought to Constantinople in triumph. But when he was placed in the palace and suffered insults from many courtiers, he asked the emperor to grant him the horse he had first possessed, and to allow twelve of those who were striking and spitting upon him to engage in single combat with him.

“There,” he said, “you will witness both the disgrace of my cowardice and the strength of their audacity.”

The emperor did not refuse his request and ordered twelve young men to fight him as a spectacle. Pretending to flee and casting spears behind him, he killed them all.

Afterward, by order of the emperor, Childemerus was made a eunuch and appointed patrician over the Roman frontier territories adjoining the province of Persia. He fought great and successful wars against the Persians and ended his life there.

But let us return to the order of the History.

## CHAPTER VII. On Clotarius and Childebert

After Clodomir, the firstborn of Clotildis’s sons, had been killed in the manner described above, his two remaining sons, Clotarius and Childebert, again set out with an army for Burgundy. Having put its king Godmar to flight, they subjected the kingdom of Burgundy to Frankish rule.

In this battle Theodoricus, whom Clovis had fathered by a concubine, refused to offer assistance to his brothers, because a daughter of King Sigismund—namely, a granddaughter of King Godmar—was married to him.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Goth Amalricus

Amalricus, son of Alaric, king of the Goths, had assumed the government of that part of his father’s kingdom which had not been overrun by the Franks. He sent ambassadors to Childebert and Clotarius, asking that, after making a treaty, he might be deemed worthy to receive their sister as his wife.

They did not refuse her—since that was worthy of kings of so great a nation—but sent her with the highest honor. Yet he, savage in both race and disposition, began to treat her carelessly. He did not love her as a queen but dishonored her with insults, as though she were a purchased slave.

For he himself was stained by the detestable treachery of the Arian heresy, as his father had been. He despised her because she was of the Catholic faith and heaped many insults upon her when she went to the church of the orthodox. He even threw excrement at her or in her path, provoking a violent stench [Col. 0668D] so as to turn her devout mind away from the practice of pure prayer.

Overwhelmed by these insults, Clovis’s daughter wrote to her brothers in tears, sending the letter by a trusted man. After setting out the injuries she had suffered, she concluded:

“Have pity on me, my most loving brothers, and be indignant at the circumstances of my suffering.”

At that time Childebert held the city of Arverna among his neighboring territories, having seized it by force from the rule of his brother Theodoricus. When the letter from his sister reached him, this experienced soldier, without waiting for the support of his brother Clotarius, arranged his ranks, moved camp, and unexpectedly poured armed forces into Spain.

Amalricus did not fail to meet the attack, being prepared to fight by land and sea. When both armies agreed to decide the matter in a field battle, Childebert, stronger in cavalry, put the enemy to flight. The Goths could not long resist, being thrown into confusion by the spears of the men and the neighing of the horses.

Some of them turned in different directions, while many fled to the fleet. The Franks also came against them from that side and, blocking their route, drove them all back from the sea. Amalricus himself, attempting to flee, was making for a Catholic church. Then one of the Frankish cavalry, pursuing him at a gallop, struck him at close range with a spear and threw him lifeless to the ground.

When his death was discovered, Childebert directed his march behind the Goths and attacked and captured the city of Toledo without delay, while its citizens were terrified by the very fear of war. After taking away many treasures and bringing his sister with him [Col. 0669B], he hurried back to his own territories.

But before they reached their desired homes, the king’s sister died, overcome by some illness whose nature I do not know. Her body was placed in a coffin, carried to Paris, and buried in the basilica of Saint Peter beside her father.

Among the treasures that Childebert carried away from Spain were found ecclesiastical vessels for sacred ministry, including, from vessels said to have belonged to Solomon, nine most precious chalices, fifteen patens, and twenty Gospel chests. Although all these objects had been made of solid gold and adorned with gems in inlaid work, the king, free from their temptation—for he was very generous—distributed them all among various churches.

But while he strove to seize what belonged to another, he lost what he thought was his own. His brother Theodoricus, grieving that the city of Arverna had been taken from him, invaded it again. After killing or driving out those whom Childebert had left to defend the city, he ordered Mundericus—who boasted that he was related to the king and that the kingdom was owed to him—to be killed, and ordered his property to be brought into the treasury.

For Mundericus had persuaded the citizens of Arverna and, having gathered a considerable band of country people, seized the fortress of Victuriacum against Theodoricus. When the king surrounded him with a siege and could not overcome him, he ordered one of his men, named Aregisilus, to persuade Mundericus to leave the castle after being given an oath of safety, so that he might be killed by those surrounding it.

Aregisilus obeyed the order and led the surrounded man out of the fortress. He then gave his men this signal:

“Why, O people,” he said, “are you looking at this man as though you had never seen him before?” [Col. 0669D]

When they heard this, they rushed upon Mundericus. Seeing it, Mundericus addressed Aregisilus:

“Because, O Aregisilus, you have deceived me with your perjuries, from this time forward no one shall see you alive with the eyes of the flesh.”

As he said this, he drove a spear between Aregisilus’s shoulders from behind and pinned him to the ground. Then, drawing his sword and encouraging his companions, he rushed upon the enemy and did not cease striking as long as the breath of life remained in him.

Arcadius, who had handed the city of Arverna over to Childebert, fled to Bourges. At that time that city was open to Childebert. His mother and aunt, however, were captured and exiled to the city of Cahors.

## CHAPTER IX. On Clotarius’s Expedition against the Thuringians

From there, after taking his brother Clotarius into partnership, he himself set out for Thuringia with his son Theodebert [Col. 0670A]. Hermenfredus ruled the Thuringians, having slaughtered two of his own brothers. Through his marriage he had acquired an empty arrogance of mind, because a daughter of Theodoricus, king of Italy—born of the sister of Clovis—was joined to him by lawful marriage.

Lifted up by womanly pride because she came from royal stock, she hated her husband’s brother, named Bertharius, with enormous cruelty. At last she persuaded her husband to deprive his rival brother of life and kingdom.

He carried this out without delay and, sending executioners, ordered him to be killed. In the same way he condemned another brother, named Baldricus, to a shameful death, accusing him on suspicion of seeking vengeance for his brother.

By this scheme Amalberga—for that was the woman’s name—made the royal court empty for herself while pretending that she wished to protect her husband’s safety. Wretched was the man who thought that she hated murderous designs against his brothers, and who did not perceive that his partners in kingdom and danger had been removed. Among the wicked, affection is held so cheaply that it is quickly torn away by evil suggestions.

Theodoricus, then, setting out for Thuringia, encountered Hermenfredus with an innumerable multitude of enemies. The Thuringians had dug a ditch and covered it with turf, so that the horses of the approaching Franks would be weakened there.

When the Franks learned of this, they were fiercely angered. They shattered the enemy with utter slaughter and pursued them as they fled all the way to the river Onestrude [Col. 0670C]. When the adversaries dared to resist there and tried to prevent the Franks from crossing, an even more serious battle began.

But when the Franks strengthened themselves through the practice inherited from the past and the habit of victory, they relied upon their ordered ranks, attacking and striking, driving the enemy back with their shields, and with all their effort and valor forcing the disorganized multitude into the river.

It was not difficult for many to be drowned in the stream, since the fighting was taking place not far from the bank. So great, it is said, was the slaughter then inflicted upon the Thuringians that, when the river was filled with the heap of the slain, the Franks crossed over to the farther bank over the bodies of the dead.

Hermenfredus himself escaped with a few men and withdrew into the fortification of the city. Later Theodoricus, after giving him a pledge of safety, ordered him to come to him at Tulbiacum [today Zülpich]. While they were walking along the city wall and conversing with one another, he drove him headlong down from it. Falling with his skull shattered, he died.

Nor did he spare Hermenfredus’s offspring. He ordered them to be strangled and subjected all the cities of the Thuringians to the Franks, commanding the Thuringians to inhabit their former homes.

## CHAPTER X. On the Origin of the Franks, as Cited from Saint Jerome

The statement above has already shown that the Franks formerly possessed the territory of the Thuringians. Blessed Jerome, too, in the little work he wrote on the Life of Saint Hilarion, asserts that this people—“not so extensive as it was strong”—once lived between the territories of the Saxons and the Alamanni [Col. 0671A]. He recounts that an illustrious young man of that nation was cured after the same man of God expelled a demon from him.

Nor will it be burdensome for us to set down the words of that most eloquent man, since, if inserted, they both adorn our subject and make known the strength and splendor of the nation. At the same time, they make it plainly evident that God’s power was at work even in a man of pagan origin.

Thus the interpreter of divine law says:

“A ruddy-haired candidate of the emperor Constantius, by the whiteness of his body indicating his province—for his nation, between the Saxons and the Alamanni, was not broad but strong, called by historians Germany and now ancient Francia—had been possessed by a demon from childhood. The demon compelled him at night to howl, groan, and gnash his teeth.

“He secretly sought from the emperor permission to travel, simply explaining the reason to him. After receiving letters also to the consular official of Palestine, he was escorted to Gaza with great honor and retinue.

“When he had asked the decurions of that place where the monk Hilarion lived, the frightened people of Gaza, thinking that he had been sent by the emperor, went to the monastery, both to show honor to the person entrusted to them and, if any offense from past injuries against Hilarion existed, to erase it through this new act of service.

“At that time the old man was walking on the soft sands and murmuring something from the psalms to himself. Seeing such a great crowd coming, he stopped, greeted everyone in return, and blessed them with his hand. After an hour he ordered the others to leave, but commanded the young man to remain with his servants and attendants. From his eyes and face he had recognized why he had come.

“Immediately, when questioned, the man was suspended in the air, scarcely touching the ground with his feet and roaring terribly, and answered in the Syrian language in which he had been questioned. You would have seen a barbarian mouth—and one that knew only the Frankish and Latin languages—sound out words perfectly in Syrian, so that neither the harshness of its aspirates nor any idiom of Palestinian speech was lacking.

“He confessed how the demon had entered him. So that his interpreters might understand—for they knew only Greek and Latin—Hilarion questioned him also in Greek. When he gave similar answers in the same language, they were astonished.

“At last, when the demon alleged many occasions and necessities for incantations and magical arts, Hilarion said: ‘I do not care how you entered; but I command you, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to come out.’

“When he had been cured, he offered ten pounds of gold with rustic simplicity and received from him a barley loaf, hearing that those who were nourished by such food regarded gold as mud.”

This was said by Jerome, a man worthy of every proclamation of praise in the holy Church. But let us turn back to the matter we began.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Remaining Deeds of Clotarius and Theodoricus

While they were delayed in Thuringia, Theodoricus secretly prepared a trap for his brother Clotarius. He stretched a curtain across part of the house and ordered armed men to stand behind it, so that they might unexpectedly kill Clotarius when he came to confer with him.

As Clotarius entered the house, the feet of the concealed armed men became visible [Col. 0672A]. When he noticed this, he ordered his men to take up their weapons and to go before him. Theodoricus immediately understood that his brother had detected the deception. To prevent the deed from becoming more obvious, he gave him a silver dish as a gift, thanking him for the assistance he had provided.

Thus, while his own men did not know what had happened, Clotarius returned to his camp. Afterward Theodoricus complained to his men, without cause, that he had lost his own dish. Calling his son Theodebert, he said:

“Go to your uncle and ask him for the vessel I gave him as a gift.”

The boy went and obtained without delay what he had requested. On his return, Clotarius took with him Radegund, daughter of King Bertharius, who later shone with many virtues in the city of Poitiers [Col. 0672B].

As we have said, discord separated Theodoricus and Childebert, whom nature had joined together. At last, through a domestic treaty, the contests of civil war were set aside. But through the schemes of certain wicked men, who rejoice in constant changes of affairs, the laws of the agreed peace were again violated.

Consequently, many sons of noblemen who had been given as hostages by both sides were subjected to slavery. Among them was the nephew of the blessed Gregory, bishop of the city of Langres. While he was being oppressed in the service of a certain barbarian, he was rescued by a servant of the aforementioned bishop named Leo, who performed the office of preparing banquets, and was restored to his former freedom in the following manner.

When the aforesaid priest heard that the boy was being detained at Trier, he sent servants who, after offering his master a price, were to bring him away. The barbarian replied:

“This boy, who is of so illustrious a family, will not be released unless ten pounds of gold are given to me.”

When they reported this to the bishop, Leo offered himself, saying:

“Permit me, and with God’s help I will free the boy.”

When permission had been granted, Leo sought out a certain man and asked him to sell Leo to the boy’s master as though Leo were the man’s own servant, and to keep the price as a benefit for his own use. The man obeyed his request and sold Leo to the aforementioned man for twelve gold pieces.

The captor then asked Leo what work he knew how to do. Leo replied:

“No one surpasses me in the skill of preparing banquets.”

His master therefore ordered him, when Sunday arrived—for that is how the barbarians call the Lord’s Day—to prepare such a feast that the friends coming to him would marvel at it. Leo gathered a multitude of roosters and hens and prepared them so well that the guests said they had never tasted anything like it even at a king’s table.

His master, delighted, placed Leo in charge of the pantry and granted him his highest favor.

After a year had passed, he went down into a meadow with Attalus—for that was the bishop’s nephew’s name—since the latter was the keeper of the horses. They spoke with their backs turned to each other so that they would not be recognized. Leo began to address Attalus:

“It is time, boy, that we think of our homeland. Therefore, tonight, when you have brought the horses back from pasture, take care not to be weighed down by sleep. When I call you, if you are wise, prepare our journey.”

That very night Leo accompanied his master’s son-in-law, who was returning home, and handed him wine. The man jokingly said:

“Tell me, boy, if you can, on what night you intend to return to your homeland.”

Leo likewise answered in jest, though speaking the truth:

“Tonight, if God permits.”

“Would that,” replied the other, “my servants guard me, lest you take anything from my house.”

Before the first rest of the night had passed, Leo hurried to Attalus and asked whether he had a sword. When Attalus said no, Leo took a shield together with a spear from beside his master’s head. When his master asked him about it, he replied that he was going to awaken Attalus, who was resting as though drunk, so that he might lead the horses to pasture.

When the master did not object, Leo went to Attalus. They mounted the horses, seized some garments or ornaments, and traveled for three days fasting. When they reached the Meuse and certain people tried to detain them, they abandoned the horses and crossed the river on their shields. They found a plum tree, took its fruit, and satisfied themselves with it while continuing their journey.

After entering the road to Champagne, one night they heard the sound of horses running behind them. Leo said to the boy:

“Let us throw ourselves to the ground so that we will not be seen.”

They hid behind a thornbush, having nevertheless drawn their swords so that, if necessary, they could defend themselves with them.

The horsemen stopped there, waiting until the horses raised themselves to urinate. One said to the other:

“Woe is me, for these detestable men are escaping! But if they were found, I would send one of them to the gallows and destroy the other with blows of the sword” [Col. 0673C].

The man speaking these words was their master. He moved on from the place with his companion and the horses.

That same night they reached Reims. They were refreshed for two days by the priest Paulellus and then returned to the blessed Gregory. Attalus was received with joy; Leo, together with his wife and children, was rewarded with freedom and a grant of land.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Plot against the Sons of Clodomir

Meanwhile Queen Clotildis, residing at Paris, diligently raised the sons of Clodomir, her grandsons. Childebert, however, was moved by jealousy because he saw that the queen had turned her maternal affection toward them. Thinking that whatever maternal love was poured out upon them was being lost to him, he stirred up Clotarius to seek an opportunity to remove the young men from among the living [Col. 0673D].

They devised deceitful plans together and sent someone to their mother to bring the youths, whom she had taken into her care, to them. They claimed that they wished to restore to them their rightful share of the kingdom.

The queen did not foresee the deception. She obeyed her sons’ command all the more eagerly because she rejoiced that provision was being made for the young men’s welfare. The messenger took charge of the youths in order to lead them to the kings.

As he departed, another arrived immediately, carrying shears and a sword. When the queen saw these, she asked what they meant. The messenger replied:

“Your sons command this: do you wish your grandsons to be tonsured, or struck with the sword? Decide. One of these two things must happen.”

When she heard this, she drew deep sighs from her breast, groaned [Col. 0674A], and said:

“Now it is good for me to die with my sons. Piety has died. Now indeed is the time when, even if everyone offered counsel, no one could find a remedy for this evil. This is a new kind of crime, in which uncles seek the lives of innocent nephews.

“I grieve, I confess, that I have borne sons who are parricides, who could not spare their own relatives. But I say nothing of those whom a just accusation had made hateful to them because of their mother’s calamity. In these boys, however, no cause for offense is found, except that, born into the kingdom and sons of a king, they are denied their due share of their father’s inheritance.

“They perish, then, to my sorrow and to their profit. But someone may ask why they wish to kill them. Let him understand that their death will benefit them for the present.

“Wretched am I, who have been preserved for such fruits of fertility, so that I might offer my unhappy breasts to those who would take away from me the dear pledges of my grandsons! Little ones, I am the cause of your destruction, for by heedless persuasion I exposed your father to the dangers of death. I had been an unhappy enough mother; I wished to be a more anxious grandmother.

“Seeing that age was advancing upon me, I tried to provide for my grandsons after my death—and would that I had succeeded! But now intolerable sorrow takes from me those whom nature and compassion had commended to me more and more.

“Most high God, do not count the souls of the innocent among the flocks of the guilty, nor let cruel punishments of the underworld torment them. Rather, as they journey from this world along the path above, may peaceful dwellings of eternal life immediately receive them.”

After these words, indignation and compassion together cut off the speaker’s voice. But when she had recovered her breath, she said:

“And what else remains? I am being offered the choice of whether I prefer them to be tonsured or struck with the sword. But whatever may happen, I will never allow them to become clerics.”

She said this, thinking that they would be moved by natural piety and desist from so great a crime. Although Clotarius’s ferocity was known to her, she could never have believed that he would persist as far as parricide.

But he acted in a manner entirely opposed to her judgment. Seizing the elder boy, he dashed him to the ground and, piercing his side with a knife, deprived him of life.

When the younger saw this, he went to Childebert. Covered with tears and displaying a pitiable appearance, he clung to his uncle’s feet, begging for mercy and imploring him to restore King Clotarius’s goodwill toward him.

Moved by compassion, Childebert begged his brother to soften his anger out of regard for nature and to spare his nephew, placing the law of nature above anger. He also promised that, in return for this favor, he would repay him with whatever benefit he wished.

His brother replied:

“Since you are the agent of this deed, why do you pretend that you wish to show mercy? Rather, drive the boy away from you, or die in his place.”

Childebert feared his brother’s words and was unable—or rather unwilling—to resist his will. He pushed the boy away from him. Clotarius killed him in the same manner as his brother.

The one brother who remained, intent on life and safety rather than the kingdom, used the ready assistance of his most faithful servants and escaped the danger by flight. His name was Clodoald. He later became a cleric and was ordained a priest, conducting himself worthily. After reaching the end of his life, he was buried at the villa of Novientum in the territory of the city of Paris, and by many signs of miracles he declares that he lives in heaven.

Clotarius, however, after handing the boys’ tutors over to the same death, mounted his horse and withdrew from that place with his men. Then Queen Clotildis gathered up the little bodies of her grandsons, embalmed them with spices, and had them buried in the basilica of Saint Peter.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Origin and Deeds of the Lombards
Theodoricus betrothed to his son Theodebert a wife named Wisegard, daughter of Wacho, king of the Lombards. This occasion prompts us, interrupting for a little while the sequence of the work we have begun, to unfold the origin of this people and, retracing earlier times, recall them [Col. 0675B]—especially since certain splendid deeds of the Franks are contained in the History of the Lombards.

The Winili, who are also called Lombards, having departed from the island of Germany called Scandinavia under the leadership of Ibor and Aio, entered the region called Scoringua as though intending to settle there. Compelled to leave it because of a shortage of food, they crossed into Mauringua. Proceeding from there, they settled in Gollanda. When their leaders had died, they appointed Agelmund, son of their leader Aio, as king; he ruled them for thirty-three years. Lamissio succeeded him; Lethu succeeded Lamissio; after Lethu, Hildehoc reigned. When he had died, Gudehoc, the fifth king, assumed the kingdom.

Then, after the battle between Odoacer and Feletheus which we mentioned in the preceding [Col. 0675C] book, the Lombards departed from Gollanda and reached Rugiland, which in Latin is called the homeland of the Rugii. For *land* in the language of the Germans means “homeland” in the language of the Romans.

When Gudehoc had been removed from human affairs, his son Claffo succeeded him. When Claffo also died, Tato held the kingdom. At that time the Lombards left the homeland of the Rugii and came into the broad open fields, which in the barbarian language are called *felth*, and remained there.

While they were lingering there, Radulf, king of the Heruli, broke the treaty he had made with Tato, because he had learned that his own brother had been most wickedly killed by Tato’s daughter, and he made war upon him. But he himself, together with his people, was defeated by the Lombards and deprived alike of life and kingdom. Such panic—and, to speak more accurately, such derangement of mind—seized his army that they imagined green crops, fields of flax, and rivers to be present. As they stretched out their arms as though they were about to swim, they were cut down without difficulty by the enemy who came upon them.

Wacho, the son of his brother, then attacked Tato. After killing him, Wacho himself became the eighth to rule over the Lombards. As was said above, Theodoricus betrothed Wisegard, Wacho’s daughter, to his son Theodebert. But after his father’s death, Theodebert abandoned her and, for the following reason, took as his wife Deutheria, a woman of Roman descent:

When, after Clovis’s death, the Goths had seized many of the things that he had taken from them, Theodoricus sent his son Theodebert to recover them. When Theodebert approached the city of Bituris [also Biterris], [Col. 0676A] he sent envoys to the fortress of Capraria so that the citizens might open it to him. Deutheria, a noble and intelligent woman whose husband had gone to the aforementioned city because of an enemy incursion, sent word to Theodebert that he would be received in peace if he came. As he approached, she went out to meet him. The king was captivated by her beauty and took her to his bed.

## CHAPTER XIV. Theodoricus and Theodebert.

In those days Theodoricus killed his kinsman Sigivald with the sword and secretly ordered Theodebert to kill his son, who had gone away with him. But because Theodebert had raised him from the sacred font, he showed him his father’s letter and advised him to flee until, after his father’s death, he could return to him when Theodebert himself was reigning. [Col. 0676B] The man fled and hid in Latium.

After this, Theodebert was informed that his father was gravely ill. Leaving Deutheria behind in Auvergne, he set out for him, putting all other matters aside. For Theodoricus, after holding the kingdom for twenty-four years, died and left the seat of his kingdom to his son Theodebert. The latter was gentle and modest toward everyone and was also an outstanding practitioner of justice.

Childebert and Clotarius, however, rose up and attempted to drive him from the kingdom. He appeased them and cleverly recovered the kingdom; then he sent a messenger to summon Deutheria from Auvergne and joined her to himself in marriage. When Childebert saw that he could not subdue him by force, he judged it more advantageous to bind him to himself in friendship. After summoning him, he presented him with threefold ornaments from all his possessions.

Givald, [Col. 0676C] son of Sigivald, meanwhile, hearing that Theodebert was reigning in his father’s place, returned to him. The king kissed him, restored all his paternal inheritances to him, and gave him a third part of all the gifts he had received from his uncle.

But Deutheria, seeing that her daughter by her former husband had grown very mature, feared that the king might desire her. She therefore ordered that the girl, placed in a carriage and dragged by untamed oxen, be thrown from a bridge into the Meuse at Verdun. Theodebert was otherwise a king of excellent character. When he recognized that Deutheria had killed her daughter, as was stated above, he repudiated her and once again took Visegard as his wife.

## CHAPTER XV. The remaining successes of Belisarius.

After the celebrated triumph that Belisarius, as we related above, celebrated at Constantinople over the Vandals, he was regarded as the closest of the emperor Justinian’s friends. And because of the distinction he had gained through their earlier association, he was repeatedly summoned as the first among the chief advisers on secret matters. This aroused against him the hearts of many who envied him. Grieving that he possessed greater power and supposing that what advanced him hindered themselves, they repeatedly warned the emperor, pretending to be concerned for his safety:

“Belisarius’s plots must be guarded against. Unless we ourselves had recalled you through the appearance of more faithful counsel, Justinian would long ago have been killed by Belisarius’s sword and the kingdom left vacant for an unworthy heir.”

By such words and others like them from the royal attendants and even from the leading men of the palace, the Augustus was gradually inflamed by envy. [Col. 0677A] Suspecting Belisarius’s power, he deprived him of the office of patricius. Released from public duties, Belisarius, deciding to lead the remainder of his life in security, lived in a private house.

But because it is difficult to be free of envy in prosperity, jealousy and accusation arose again, because he conducted himself beyond what is customary for private citizens. For he advanced wherever he had to go surrounded by twelve thousand young men. Some even wished to deprive him of life. When they could not bend the emperor’s mind to their own view, they plotted to strip the emperor himself of his royal dignity.

Finding a suitable opportunity, they seized the emperor as he was proceeding to the spectacle of the circus, held him in private custody, and stripped him of his crown and purple robe. [Col. 0677B] They led him into the middle of the theater and seated a certain Florian on the imperial throne.

Justinian, suffering such disgrace, sent to Belisarius men who were to say:

“Justinian Caesar, once emperor and Augustus, gives this command: ‘Having become forgetful of injuries, my Belisarius, and having been made *modernatum* [sic], I ask you to recall the former benefits and, if you have any power, help me.’”

Belisarius replied:

“If I possessed the power of my ancestors, I would bring aid to one who asks for it. But now he pours out prayers in vain, since my presence has been deprived of the consular fasces. Nevertheless, in obedience to the command of Christ my Lord’s Father, not returning evil for evil, I will prepare to bring him whatever help I can.”

With these words he hurried to the presence of the new ruler, ordering all his young men to follow him. Standing at the theater doors, he saw from a distance a crowd of those who hated him surrounding the chair of the emperor Florian.

Turning to those who were with him, he said:

“Behold, most faithful soldiers, the day awaited by all our prayers has arrived, for taking vengeance upon our enemies. The tyrant is surrounded by a throng of malicious men who have joined themselves to him, relying upon the wickedness of their character. There must be no doubt that those whom the same cause of evil has made alike ought to perish by an equal destruction. Therefore arm your avenging right hands, and whatever you see me do, do yourselves also.”

Afterward, entering, he bent his knee as though he were about to offer worship; then, drawing his sword, he cut off the head of the false ruler. When those who had come with him saw this, they drew their swords and began striking vigorously all around. [Col. 0677D] Those who had earlier applauded themselves over the change of rule in their favor were thrown into confusion and sought the help of flight rather than defense.

Belisarius lifted up Florian’s head together with the royal crown, and, coming to Justinian, addressed him as follows:

“The men who opposed my safety and yours appear to have sown discord between us with the greatest possible violence for this reason: so that they might both make me share no longer in honor and, with you deprived of my presence, subject you to insults, as is now openly evident. Nevertheless, setting aside the things that you know you did against me at the instigation of your adversaries, I return to you the grace of empire and life, which they wished to take away, and, recalling your former benefits toward me, I now deem you worthy of this gift.”

After saying this, he placed the diadem [Col. 0678A] of the kingdom upon Justinian’s head. Restored in this way to imperial power, Justinian again appointed the aforementioned Belisarius as patricius and sent him against the Goths, who, inhabiting Italy, were oppressing the Romans severely with their arms.

## CHAPTER XVI. The holy Benedict.

In those days the most blessed Father Benedict shone forth first at the place called Subiaco, which is forty miles from the city of Rome, and afterward at the fortress of Cassino, which is called Haruin, both through the merits of a great life and through apostolic virtues.

At that same time the most holy Agapitus, pontiff of the Roman see, went to the imperial city and brought the emperor Justinian, who had fallen into the sect of Eutyches, back to the true [Col. 0678B] and catholic faith. After condemning Anthimus, patriarch of Constantinople, the same pope died not long afterward in that city. Sylverius succeeded him in the pontificate.

Sylverius was elevated by the tyrant Theodorus, who had seized the kingdom among the Goths without waiting for an imperial decision. Having been corrupted by money, he inspired such fear in the clergy that anyone who did not consent was punished by the sword. After two months Theodorus was destroyed by divine will, and Withigis was raised as king.

Then the patricius Belisarius came into the region of Sicily. When he heard that the Goths had made themselves a king, he hurried from there through Campania to Naples, which he began to besiege because the Neapolitans refused to open the city to him. He entered the city by force of arms and put to death whatever Goths he encountered. After a great war [Col. 0678C] against Withigis, he entered the city of Rome and fortified it.

Withigis then gathered the multitude of the Goths and besieged Rome for one year so completely that no one could leave or enter. But while hunger oppressed the people inside the city to such an extent that water was sold at a price, great battles nevertheless took place, as Belisarius defended the Romans and the city against the Goths. He later forced the Goths to flee toward Ravenna.

## CHAPTER XVII. The efforts of the deacon Vigilius.

At that time the deacon Vigilius, who was an *apocrisiarius* at Constantinople, noticed that the emperor and empress were displeased by the condemnation of Anthimus, patriarch of Constantinople. Wishing to gain favor with the rulers of the world, he persuaded the empress to send a letter to Pope Silverius written as follows:

“Either do not hesitate to come to us,” she said, “or at least by your written command recall Anthimus to his place.”

When the blessed Silverius had read this, he groaned and wrote back to the empress in these words:

“Even if this matter brings about the end of my temporal life, nevertheless, Augusta my lady, I shall never do this: recall a man who remains in condemned error.”

The empress, angered by this, sent Vigilius to Belisarius and ordered him to take an opportunity to drive Sylverius into exile and to appoint Vigilius pontiff, since he had promised that he would recall Anthimus.

Belisarius, accepting the substance of this command, said:

“I do not dare oppose the will of the rulers. Although unwilling, I am carrying out the order. But the author of this crime will not escape the anger of the Judge who sees all things.”

Witnesses were therefore suborned to say that the lord pope had wished to hand over the city and the patricius to the Goths. He was ordered to appear for a hearing in the emperor’s palace. As he entered with Vigilius alone, the patrician Antonina addressed him:

“Tell us, lord Silverius, what have we done that you wished to hand us over to the Goths?”

While she was still speaking, John, the regional subdeacon of the first see, entered, took the pallium from his neck, and clothed him in a monastic garment. He was exiled to the island of Pontia, where he died as a confessor.

Vigilius, [Col. 0679B] meanwhile, took his seat on the pontifical throne. Belisarius again fought against Withigis, king of the Goths, shattered his army with a great slaughter, captured him, and led him in triumph to Constantinople.

## CHAPTER XVIII. King Childebert and the blessed Bishop Germanus.

King Childebert of the Franks resolved to set out to fight against his brother Clotarius, calling Theodebert, son of Theodoricus and his own nephew, to his aid. A messenger hurried to Chlotild, the mother of the aforementioned kings, who was then staying at Paris, reporting that the two brothers were gathering their armies for mutual destruction.

When the mother learned this, she grieved over the wickedness of her sons. Constrained by the bonds of maternal affection, [Col. 0679C] she hurried to the tomb of Saint Martin and, pouring out streams of tears, offered this prayer to the Lord:

“O good Jesus,” she said, “who join together the discordant courses of the elements in a holy covenant, grant that these brothers, violating the laws of nature through the evil of discord, may return to unity and peace. Let it not count against me that I bore and even raised such men, who do not recognize brothers and know nothing of affection for their relatives. They have killed uncles and slaughtered nephews; nevertheless, I did not think they would go so far as to forget what they were born to be. Now, almighty Father, who are the author and arbiter of nature, establish an honorable agreement between the brothers; by the power of your might, terrify those who disturb the peace.”

The Almighty heard her offering these prayers [Col. 0679D] for the safety of her children, and thunder sounded from the clear part of heaven.

For Clotarius, considering it dangerous to engage in battle against the forces of two powerful kings, took refuge in the district of Aurelianus, at a place called Combros. He remained there until either his brothers’ disposition toward him became more peaceful or he had a stronger force of his own men ready to resist them; these men were believed to be arriving at any moment.

His greater hope, however, rested upon the power of Christ the Lord. Suddenly, at the place where his adversaries had fixed their camp, thunder was heard roaring in the early morning, and rains poured down. Lightning hurled through the storm tore apart their tents and drove their horses in different directions.

The soldiers, sheltering themselves from the violence of the rain only with their shields, threw themselves upon the ground to implore the Lord’s mercy and prayed that they might be struck by a punishment of vengeance more moderate than they deserved. And what is more remarkable, in Clotarius’s camp no breath of wind blew, not a drop of rain fell, and no sign at all of lightning appeared.

At last those who had come to destroy him sent envoys to Clotarius to seek peace and enter into a permanent treaty. He willingly granted this, and, with the agreement of both armies, both sides withdrew.

Thus, through the prayers of that woman devoted to God—namely, their mother—the brothers were rescued both from the impending crime and from destruction. They were not permitted to complete the monstrous deed they had conceived in their minds. Many people rejoiced, for they were pleased by the brothers’ reconciliation.

## CHAPTER XIX. The remaining deeds of Childebert.

[Col. 0680B]

King Childebert, who, as was explained above, had earlier entered Spain and captured the city of Toledo, appealed to his brother Clotarius, with whom he had made a treaty, to assist him, so that, relying upon his alliance, he might undertake to subdue the same province for himself.

When Clotarius arrived with a strong reinforcement of troops, they joined forces and advanced as far as Zaragoza. Prevented from entering the city, they began a siege. The townspeople resisted, and the two sides fought with the greatest force. At last the Spaniards, terrified by the very arrangements of the siege and by the Franks’ fierce hostility, withdrew their courage [Col. 0680C] from battle. Turning their whole attention to imploring Christ’s mercy, they took up crosses and, accompanied by a litany, began to walk around the wall.

When the kings saw this, they suspected that the inhabitants were practicing some kind of magic. They seized one of the country people and carefully asked him of what religion the inhabitants of the city were, or what incantation they were performing by going around the city.

He replied:

“The citizens are Christians. Now they are praying that the Lord may have mercy on them.”

The kings said to him:

“Go and tell the bishop of the city to come to us without hesitation.”

When he arrived, Childebert addressed him as follows:

“Recognizing that you are worshipers of the Christian religion and of the one true God, we have decided to spare you, if you, who perform the office of bishop in this place, assent to our request and give us the relics of Saint Vincent, who, as the sincerity of many people and the words marked by truth attest, shone forth as an outstanding deacon in this city.”

The bishop, without delay, offered the kings the stole of that celebrated deacon and martyr. They received it with fitting honor and, as they had promised, lifted the siege. After devastating the entire province, they returned to their native land with spoils and immense booty.

## CHAPTER XX. The killing of the Gothic kings by their own people, and the deeds of Childebert, king of the Franks.

After Amalricus, Theodus held Spain. When he was killed, Theudegilus succeeded him. While he was indulging in excessive merriment during a meal, his own men killed him after the candles had been extinguished, and Agila seized the kingdom.

The Goths have long since turned this practice into a custom: whenever their own king displeases them, he is killed by his own people.

Childebert, meanwhile, brought the stole of Saint Vincent to Paris and had a basilica built from the ground up and dedicated to that holy deacon and martyr. In it he devoutly presented a considerable portion of the vessels which, as we mentioned above, he had carried away from Toledo, together with Gospel chests, crosses of marvelous workmanship, and other gifts of the highest excellence.

## CHAPTER XXI. Theodebert’s expedition into Italy.

While Childebert was attacking the regions of Spain with his brother Clotarius, Theodebert, son of King Theodoricus and nephew of the kings just mentioned, hastened into Italy with the greatest possible cavalry force. He overran it from the Alps as far as the borders of the coastal regions, made it tributary, and, hastening his return to his own territories, left the commander Bucellenus to overrun Sicily and the neighboring parts of Italy.

After crossing the Tyrrhenian Sea, Bucellenus subdued most of Sicily. Overrunning the camps and cities of Italy, he sent King Theodebert gifts taken from the booty of the conquered peoples.

## CHAPTER XXII. Saint Benedict.

During the reign of this prince, envoys from the city of Cenomani went to the fortress of Cassino and, with every kind of prayer, asked the most blessed [Col. 0681C] Father Benedict—who, as we have already related, was living in that holy monastery after his eremitical life—to send brothers proven in monastic conduct to the western regions, so that the Gallic stubbornness might be subjected to the gentle yoke of the rule he had given them.

With a joyful heart he sent his beloved disciple Maurus to these regions of ours. He foretold to him that the day of his own most holy death was near, making it very clear that his most sacred remains would be transferred to the place where he was sending the disciple united to him by the bond of charity.

The illustrious levite of the Lord Maurus, therefore, traveling to Gaul, reached the district of Auxerre. On the day when, according to custom, the sacred solemnity of the Lord’s Supper was celebrated on earth, he turned aside to the monastery of Saint Romanus, once the fosterer [or spiritual nourisher] of Father Benedict. Relieving the labor of his long journey through his gracious conversation, Maurus announced to him that the day was near on which the blessed Father would joyfully ascend to his heavenly homeland.

And behold, during the night preceding that holy Saturday on which the vigil of Christ’s resurrection is celebrated—namely, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—he was suddenly caught up in spirit. He saw a road spread with cloths and shining with countless lamps extending from Benedict’s cell all the way to heaven. He heard an angel saying to him that by this road Benedict, beloved of the Lord, was ascending to heaven.

When he returned to himself, he shed tears as witnesses of the vision he had been granted and disclosed what had been revealed to him to Saint Romanus. Sharing the heavenly joy with him, he celebrated the holy Pasch with him in rejoicing.

For God, glorious in his saints, continually glorifies the servants who please him through marvelous works. He rightly granted this distinguished Father a more excellent way of reaching him than that granted to others: placed in the valley of tears, he had arranged in his heart the ascents of virtue, setting before his followers the ladder of Jacob, by which angels were shown ascending.

In the passing of this man—speaking with the consent of all the saints, I will not say merely a martyr but even an apostle—such a road appeared, shining with innumerable lights of divine radiance and adorned with garments fit for a wedding. For one must not suppose that a woven cloak appeared upon that road by which he was being carried away to the kingdom of eternal incorruption.

There is nothing surprising, then, that this bearer of the divine law [Col. 0682B] earned such glory in the assumption of his spirit. While he was still clothed in the corruptible covering of flesh, he shone with such signs of miracles that, unless the man venerated throughout the world, namely Pope Gregory, had been the narrator and also an outstanding witness to his life, certain unbelievers would surely have disparaged his marvelous deeds.

To pass over the fact that, while still a little boy, he fearlessly sought the desert—a feat which, as a certain wise man says on his account, even Martin, renowned throughout the world, is not known to have accomplished—this certainly must not be omitted: after the Almighty had granted him many gifts of grace, he shone forth through three marvelous miracles previously unknown to the world.

For when, by a mere glance, he loosened the bonds of a bound peasant; when, in an instant, as though under the sun’s rays, the whole world was gathered before his sight; and when, carried upward, he was borne along the high road to the heavens, spread with cloths and shining with countless lamps, I think that no saint can be compared with him.

A great obligation of integrity has been laid upon us, if we do not wish to conceal it: we have been granted so great and such a patron in the present time that, as far as we are able, we must never depart from his teaching, but follow what we have heard from him and seen with the eyes of our mind in him.

He will certainly be present to us and, just as once he loosened the bodily bonds of a peasant, so he will loosen the bonds of our sins. Those whose dwelling places he is believed to have chosen in contemplation of the whole world, he will lead—if their souls adhere to him devotedly and follow his footsteps—with the great splendor of divine light into eternal habitations.

As was said above, the blessed Pope Gregory wrote the life of this Father; the flowers of his eloquence shine like gold throughout the holy universal Church. The venerable Odo, abbot of this monastery of Fleury, in which Father Benedict—so often to be named—rests bodily, also exalts his memory with marvelous praises in one of his sermons.

But we, for love of so great a patron, having offered these preliminary remarks, should return to the History.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The remaining deeds and death of Belisarius.

Belisarius, who, when crossing to Africa for the second time, had treacherously killed Vintharith, king of the Vandals, under the pretext of peace after accusing him of rebellion, and had subjected the remaining Vandals to the authority of the Roman state, hastened to return to Rome when he heard that the Franks were ravaging Italy.

As he approached the city, he was received with great joy by everyone, male and female alike. Through the hands of Pope Vigilius he offered Saint Peter a golden cross weighing one hundred pounds and adorned with the most precious gems, on which he had inscribed his victories.

From there he was recalled to war against the Franks. Despising the smallness of their nation and ignorant of its courage, he did not hesitate to engage in battle with only a few men whom he had taken with him.

But the Romans were fighting for their safety and freedom, while the Franks were fighting to win glory. Because they hoped to carry away a more glorious triumph if they defeated the Romans, the conquerors of the whole world, they chose to die rather than yield their position.

When the battle had begun and neither line gave way to the other, the Romans eventually realized that the safety for which they had held out for some time was slipping away, as they saw their bravest men falling in battle. They gradually began to withdraw from the contest.

Thus the most valiant man Belisarius, deserted by his own men and surrounded by the enemy, was killed while fighting bravely but in vain. He who had brought captive kings of many nations beneath his triumph was defeated by a commander—not of an emperor or king, but of a tetrarch of the Franks—and lost his life together with the glory of his name.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The blessed Gregory of Langres and the fortress of Dijon.

At that time the blessed Gregory was chief bishop of the city of Langres. Since we have mentioned this bishop, it is fitting that we describe the site of the fortress of Dijon, where he stayed most of the time.

That fortress stands on level ground, surrounded by extremely strong walls and adorned with thirty-three towers. It has fertile lands, through which the Ouche flows not far from the southern wall, rich in fish. From the north another river enters through a gate; running beneath a bridge and exiting through another gate, it turns mills with the greatest speed.

The wall, built of squared stones, extends for twenty feet; above it smaller stones have been placed. It is thirty feet high and fifteen feet wide. There are four gates, one on each of the four sides of the heavens.

Although it is of such great size, it is considered strange that it has not been given the name of a city. Antiquity asserts that it was built by the emperor Aurelian.

## CHAPTER XXV. The death of Chrotildis and the offspring of Clotarius.

Meanwhile Queen Chrotildis, of blessed memory, wife of Clovis, once a great king, devoted to pious works throughout her life, died at the city of Tours, full of days, and departed to the Lord.

Her sons, the kings Childebert and Clotarius, lifted her body from there with a great choir of those singing psalms and brought it to Paris, where she was buried in the sacristy of the basilica of Saint Peter beside her husband. The blessed Genovefa also lies buried and rests in that same house of prayer.

Theodebert, king of the Austrasians, afflicted by a severe fever, also ended his life in the thirteenth year of his reign. [Col. 0684A] At the petition of Desideratus, bishop of Verdun, he granted the citizens of that city, with the greatest generosity, eight thousand solidi, which were annually brought from there into his treasury, for the restoration of the city.

That king was of excellent character and affable in speech. He greatly honored the most blessed Maurus when he was building a monastery in a certain part of his kingdom, namely in the district of Angers, a place anciently called Glannafolium. He personally went to that place and most generously contributed extensive estates and other gifts of royal munificence.

His son Theobald succeeded him. He was devoted to God and loved his servants above all, but was cruel toward his own people. During his time a star coming from the opposite direction entered the moon. At that time grapes also grew on the tree called elder, and the flowers of those trees which ordinarily produce black berries produced clusters of grapes. A severe winter, harsher than usual, occurred at that time, so that frozen torrents provided passable roads over themselves for the people. Birds, too, restrained by the cold or hunger, were caught buried in the snow without any human trickery.

Theobald took as his wife Walderada, daughter of Wacho, king of the Lombards, who was the sister of his stepmother. After governing the kingdom he had undertaken for eight years with vigor, he died and left the rule of the people he governed, together with its treasures, to Clotarius.

Clotarius had seven sons born from different wives, and one daughter. By Ingund he had Guntharius, Childeric, Cherebert, Guntrannus, Sigebert, and a daughter, Clotsinda. By Charagund, Ingund’s sister, he had Chilperic. In love with Ingund, he had joined her sister Charagund to himself in marriage. By Gunsind he fathered Chrannus.

## CHAPTER XXVI. The Franks’ hatred of Parthenius.

At that time the Franks were pursuing with immense hatred Parthenius, once a powerful man in the palace of King Theodebert, because he had oppressed them severely with the burden of tribute.

When he realized that he could not escape, he asked two bishops to lead him to Trier and calm the rebellion of the raging people by their preaching. As they were traveling there with him, one night the aforementioned man began to utter cries in his sleep, saying:

“Alas! Alas! Help, you who are here!”

Those around him awoke and asked what had happened. He replied that he had seen Ausanius, once his friend, and Papianilla, his wife, whom he had killed long ago, driven by jealousy. They were calling him and compelling him by force, saying:

“Come, so that before God you may contend with us concerning our unjust killing.”

At last they arrived at Trier, and the bishops wished to soothe the disturbed people by their prayer. When they could not do so, they brought Parthenius into the church and put him into a chest, spreading the church’s curtains over it.

When the crowd had searched the basilica and was withdrawing, growling because he could not be found, one of them shouted:

“Behold the chest where our adversary, whom we have not found, is not being sought!”

Immediately he was pulled from the opened chest, tied to a column, and killed with stones.

He was greedy in consuming food. But whatever he ate, he immediately expelled after drinking aloe, so that he could take other food more quickly. He also emitted the noise of his belly in public without any sense of shame.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Clotarius’s edict and expedition against the Saxons.

Clotarius proposed an edict that all the churches of Gaul should pay a third part of their produce into the treasury. When Bishop Injuriosus resisted, the attempt was annulled at its very beginning.

After this the same king marched directly against the Saxons, who were continually ravaging the borders of the Franks. After subduing them in battle on the river Weser, he also devastated the Thuringians because they had given aid to the Saxons.

When the Saxons again prepared to rebel, Clotarius moved an army against them. But the Saxons, humbled by the wound inflicted in the earlier war, asked through envoys for pardon for their offenses and promised future correction. As a pledge, they offered half of all their possessions, except their wives and children.

The Franks regarded this with contempt and thought that battle should be undertaken. The Saxons were forced to join hands in combat and raged against the Franks with such slaughter that scarcely any men remained with King Clotarius, more as companions for flight than as support for fighting.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Chrannus and his deeds.

[Col. 0685C] Clotarius also had a son named Chrannus, handsome in body but light-minded, and second to none of the crafty in deceit. He had an restless spirit and ready boldness; his father had entrusted him with authority throughout Aquitaine. Yet the savage force of his character did not permit him to conduct himself as a king. Driven at last by tyrannical cruelty, he plundered the possessions of others by robbery. Therefore his father sent an embassy to summon him to his presence, so that he might rebuke with moderate admonition the insolence with which he was swollen.

Disregarding his father’s commands, he hastened with the greatest zeal to Paris, to Childebert, intending never to return to his father. He was eager to draw away the king’s friends and relatives, and especially Childebert, his father’s [Col. 0685D] brother. He had made him so hostile to his brother that he sought his brother’s life; and Chrannus, after touching the holy relics, voluntarily promised that he would remain his father’s perpetual enemy. A great and memorable crime would have been committed, with one brother conspiring against the life of another, if God had not intervened and Childebert had not died a timely death.

After making a treaty with Childebert, Chrannus returned to Aquitaine, intending to subdue everything through which he had first passed. His father, however, being occupied with the Saxon campaign and unable to go himself, sent his sons Charibert and Guntrannus there with an army. They followed him through the territory of Auvergne, and, when he had already reached the Limousin, established a camp on Mount Niger. They sent word to him that he should restore what he had seized. Although he promised to do so, he did not fulfill his promise; so they drew up their ranks to fight against him. When he advanced against them no less boldly, a storm arose and restrained them from this undertaking.

Afterward Chrannus, through agents secretly introduced among them, caused his brothers to be informed that their father had fallen in battle against the Saxons. Believing this to have been reported truthfully, they returned to Burgundy by a forced march. After they had departed, Chrannus followed them; having captured the city of Chalon, he hastened to the fortress of Dijon. There certain clerics, eager to learn what would happen to Chrannus, placed three books upon the altar: one of the Prophets, one of the Apostle’s Epistles, and one of the Gospels.

After praying to the Lord, they opened the book of the Prophets and found this verse first:

> “I will remove its hedge,  
> and it shall become a desolation;  
> because it ought to have produced grapes,  
> it produced wild grapes.”  
> (Isaiah 5:4–5)

When they also opened the Apostle’s book, they found this:

> “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’  
> then sudden destruction will come upon them.”  
> (1 Thessalonians 5:3)

But the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “Whoever does not hear my words will be like a foolish man who built his house upon the sand,” and so forth.  
> (Matthew 7:26)

And these things were indeed shown concerning Chrannus.

## CHAPTER XXIX. The death of Childebert after his attempt to obtain his brother’s kingdom

Childebert, believing that his brother had been killed by the Saxons, approached Reims and devastated everything with fire and plunder. Then two swarms of locusts passed through Auvergne and the Limousin into the plain of Romaniacum [Col. 0686C]. There they fought one another and left behind a great heap of dead locusts.

Childebert’s undertaking was cut short by a swift death. For that king, after having exercised his kingdom for a long time, was afflicted with fever and died. He was buried at Paris in the church of Saint Vincent, which he himself had built. By law, his kingdom and treasures returned to Clotarius.

## CHAPTER XXX. Chrannus’s efforts and Clotarius’s clemency and piety

When Chrannus realized that he had been deprived of so powerful an accomplice in his parricidal crime, he fled to Conabus, prince of the Britons, and attempted to renew the war. The nobility of his wife supplied him with material for hostility, since she surpassed others in the distinction of her lineage. Her name was Calte, daughter of Willecarius, duke of Aquitaine.

Willecarius, terrified by the threats of Clotarius, who accused him of having favored Chrannus, sought the protection of the basilica of Saint Martin; Austrabius, another duke, had previously sought the same refuge. When his pursuers sought to drag him out and were unable to do so, they set fire to the church. He was burned together with the house of prayer itself. Clotarius, with careful workmanship, adorned the church with a more beautiful finish and covered its roof with tin.

Believing that his son’s offenses should not be passed over in silence, Clotarius entered Brittany with as many of his men as he could muster. Chrannus met him there with Conabus, king of the Britons, leading a barbarian host. When they came to battle and each side had tested the other’s forces, they judged that the matter must be decided by arms: Chrannus had not seen the Britons whom he had hired with money abandon their allegiance, nor had Clotarius seen his son lay aside the hatred he had conceived against him and his readiness for battle.

Then Clotarius, uncertain of the battle’s outcome, his face covered with tears, entreated Christ in these words:

> “Christ,” he said, “God, who alone knows the hidden things of men, now be present to my prayers, exercising the judgment of a just judge. For I am quite certain that Chrannus’s wickedness could appear pardonable to no just man, least of all to you, who know all things. He forgot the grace of natural piety and rose up with hostile intent against his father’s life; and what he was unable to accomplish secretly by plotting, he now seeks to complete openly by bringing war upon me.
>
> “While he seeks to hasten the death of one decrepit old man, he has not hesitated to expose countless peoples to death. Indeed, I had given him hope of reigning when, while I was still alive, I entrusted him with the care of governing Aquitaine. But he could not bear to wait, nor would he await the kingdom unless he could obtain it by parricide.
>
> “Look down, therefore, Lord, from heaven, and judge justly; exercise the judgment that you once exercised against Absalom, who was most hostile to his father David. I am not David, certainly, but I am not degenerate from him in faith. He believed that the Redeemer of the world would come; I believe that he has come and will be the just arbiter and judge of the age.”

The almighty God heard him, intent upon these prayers. For, victorious in the battle, he pursued the Britons as far as the refuge of the ships which they had prepared for this purpose, so that they might flee there if the fortunes of war turned against them, and he inflicted a great slaughter upon them.

Chrannus himself, while eager to carry off his daughters and his wife into captivity, was captured by the army and brought before his father. By his father’s command, he was stretched upon a bench in the hut of a poor woman, strangled with a neckcloth, and there he was burned with his wife and daughters.

In this way the plotter against his father, who had emptied himself of all piety, paid the penalty of just vengeance. He perished, indeed, in a manner not to be wished by fathers, yet not one to be passed over in silence. Who would spare him who, as far as he was able, had not spared his father’s life? Thus Chrannus met the end of his wickedness.

## CHAPTER XXXI. The kings of the Lombards and Totila the Goth

While Clotarius held supremacy among the Franks, Alboin ruled the Lombard people. Not long afterward, he led the Lombards into Pannonia.

Among the Goths who inhabited Italy, after Withigis, Baduila—also called Totila—ruled. He came to the most blessed Father Benedict, whom we mentioned above. Benedict both reproved and admonished him, and softened him from the harshness of his cruelty. The same man of God foretold to him that he would cross the sea, enter Rome, reign for nine years, and die in the tenth.

## CHAPTER XXXII. The controversy between Pope Vigilius and the empress Theodora

Vigilius, bishop of the holy Roman Church, who had been appointed in the manner we have mentioned to replace the most holy Silverius, received an embassy from the empress Theodora, bearing this message:

> “Come and fulfill for us what you promised with willing intent concerning our father Anthimus, and restore him to the honor of his former rank.”

Vigilius replied:

> “Far be it from me, Lady Augusta,” he said. “I spoke wrongly and foolishly before. Now, however, I in no way agree to restore a heretical and anathematized man.”

When the empress heard this, she sent Anthimus, a scribon, to Rome with a strong force of soldiers, ordering him and saying:

> “We decree that you place Vigilius, the Roman pontiff who rebels against our ordinances, on a ship and bring him to our presence. He shall receive no assistance from the protection of any basilica of the saints, except the church of the Prince of the Apostles.”

Anthimus went to Rome and seized the pope while he was celebrating the solemn Mass in the oratory of Saint Cecilia on the tenth day before the Kalends of December—that is, on the feast day of the holy virgin herself—and distributing gifts to the people. He placed him on a ship to take him to Constantinople.

The Roman people accompanied him as he departed, all the way to the ship, and asked him to give them his blessing. After he had given it, the ship set sail.

There were nevertheless some whom the unjust expulsion of Silverius had aroused against Vigilius. Throwing stones and whatever kinds of weapons chance placed in their hands after him, they reviled him in these words:

> “May your hunger be with you; may your pestilence be with you. You brought evils upon the Romans; may you encounter evils wherever you are going.”

Some of his supporters, however, joined his company.

[Col. 0688C] Traveling through Sicily, Vigilius promoted certain men to the sacred orders in the city of Catania and entrusted them with responsibility for protecting the Roman Church. He himself was carried by ship as far as Constantinople, where he was honorably received by the emperor and the clergy of the city. He was detained there for two years.

When the emperor demanded from him a pledge that he would enter into communion with Anthimus and produced the document bearing his hand by which he had promised to do so, the dispute proceeded to the point that Pope Vigilius said:

> “I thought that I had come to Justinian and Theodora, joined to him, as to the most merciful rulers of the state. But I have found them more cruel in character than Diocletian and Eleutheria. Yet because Christ has handed me over to you on account of the sins I have committed, I will endure whatever is most wretched, so long as you command whatever is most savage.
>
> “For a recompense suited to my merits is not being paid me, since my crimes deserve things greater than these. The punishment of my wickedness is close at hand, and I am being confronted with the fitting price of Silverius’s expulsion. Nor could I escape the eye of God as the plotter of so impious a crime.”

One of the ruler’s household, standing nearby, struck the pontiff in the face and said:

> “Murderer, do you not know to whom you are speaking? Or do you think that we do not know that you struck your own notary in the face, and that he immediately fell dead; and that, by your command, you had Hasterius, the widow’s son to whom you had given your niece Vigilia, beaten with clubs until he was brought to the point of death; and that Pope Silverius was exiled through your faction?”

When he heard this, Vigilius was terrified. Entrusting his hope to God alone, he fled into the basilica of Saint Euphemia and seized one of the altar’s columns. Torn away from it, with a rope tied around his neck, he was ordered to be dragged throughout the city and, toward evening, shut up in a prison, where each day he was given only a small amount of bread and water.

Later, at the urging of Narses, commander of the Roman forces, the emperor relieved him of his chains and permitted him to return to Rome together with his clergy. When he reached Syracuse, he was weakened by the illness of a kidney stone and died. His body was taken to Rome and buried at Saint Marcellus on the Via Salaria. Pelagius succeeded him in the pontificate.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. The siege of Rome by Totila and the Romans’ appeal to Justinian

[Col. 0689B]

Totila, king of the Goths, returned after ravaging Sicily and surrounded Rome with a siege. The citizens then suffered such extreme scarcity of food that, compelled by hunger, they wished to eat the flesh of their own children.

The Romans, exhausted by prolonged fighting and famine and unable to defend the walls, were overwhelmed when Totila broke into the city from the Ostian side. But preferring to spare the Romans rather than destroy them, throughout the night in which he entered the city as victor he ordered some of his men to sound their trumpets:

> “Let the citizens protect themselves from the swords of the Goths either in the churches or by hiding themselves in whatever ways they can.”

He lived for some time among the Romans, showing them more paternal compassion than tyrannical [Col. 0689C] cruelty. This kindness of spirit in one who had previously been excessively cruel was granted to him by the admonition of the blessed Father Benedict, whom, as has been said, he had formerly heard.

Some of the senators—once the glory of the Roman name, but then the wretched remnants of a deserted city—went as suppliants to the emperor Justinian in Constantinople, asking for aid against the Goths. The emperor was troubled by the grave report, since affairs in the West had gone poorly, and appointed Narses, a eunuch and his chamberlain, an experienced soldier, over all the army that was in Italy.

Narses hurriedly—for there was no time for delay—with a picked body of young men. Crossing the Mediterranean strait, he made for Latium and, joining to himself auxiliary forces of the Lombards, defeated the Goths in battle. [Col. 0689D] After killing King Totila, he freed Italy from their rule.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. The war brought by Narses against the duke Bucellenus

Narses also made war against the duke Bucellenus, whom Theodebert, king of the Franks, as we mentioned above, had left in Italy with another duke, Amingus, to subjugate it when he himself had returned to Gaul.

After killing Belisarius, Bucellenus ravaged almost the whole of Italy by plunder and presented rich gifts to the Frankish kings from the spoils of the subjected enemy. While wintering in Campania at a place called Tannetum, and suffering from dysentery, he was overcome by Narses in a great battle and killed [Col. 0690A].
