Amingus, however, did not hesitate to assist Widin, count of the Goths, who was preparing to rebel against Narses; both were defeated by Narses’s valor. Widin was captured and exiled to Constantinople. Amingus, who had wished to assist him, was killed by Narses’s sword.

A third Frankish duke, named Leutharius, Bucellenus’s brother, was hastening home, heavily laden with much booty, when he died a natural death between Verona and Trent, beside Lake Benacus.

Narses also fought against Sisuvald, king of the Brentes, who was the last survivor of the stock of the Heruli whom Odoacer had brought with him into Italy. Sisuvald alone remained of the Herulian people. Narses first bestowed many benefits upon him because he had faithfully attached himself to Narses. [Col. 0690B] But later, when he had become arrogantly rebellious and wished to extend his kingdom throughout Italy, Narses defeated him in battle, captured him, and hanged him from a lofty beam.

This Narses had first been a *cartularius*; later, because of his merits and virtues, he earned the dignity of the patriciate. He was a very pious man, Catholic in religion, generous toward the poor, and especially devoted to recovering the basilicas of the saints. He was so intent upon vigils and prayers that he seemed to prevail in war more through the prayers he poured out to God than through arms.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Alboin, king of the Lombards

In those days Alboin, son of Aldoin, ruled the Lombards. While his father was still alive, he fought Turismod, son of Turisind, king of the Gepids. [Col. 0690C] When the two sides fought with the greatest force, Alboin struck Turismod with his sword through the neck and brought him down dead.

The Gepids were thrown into confusion when they saw that the king’s son, through whom the battle had been sustained for the most part, had been killed, and they turned to flight. Alboin, having achieved victory, returned joyfully to his father. Not long afterward, when his father was dying, he succeeded him in the kingdom.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The crime of Cautinus and the death and burial of Saint Medard

In those days Cautinus, bishop of the city of Auvergne, is said to have committed an unheard-of deed. In that city there was a certain man named Anastasius, a presbyter by office and freeborn by descent.

The bishop frequently compelled him, sometimes by prayers and sometimes by threats, to give him as a gift his property, which he possessed through documents of Queen Chrotildis, of glorious memory, together with those documents themselves. When Anastasius refused in every way, the bishop had him brought from his estate to the city and handed over to guards to be afflicted by hunger unless he complied with the demand.

But Anastasius resisted with steadfast courage, saying that it was better for him to suffer hunger for a time than, after surrendering his possessions, to disinherit his children.

Near the basilica of the martyr Cassius there was a crypt, and in it a sarcophagus made of Parian marble for a certain great man. At the bishop’s command, the presbyter was buried alive in this tomb with a dead man and covered with a stone. Guards were assigned to watch him.

But while the presbyter, like another Jonah, prayed to the Lord, the guards became drunk on wine and fell asleep. Understanding this, he used his arms—which alone were free because of the size of the tomb—to push the cover to one side. After opening the burial chamber slightly, he raised his head and thus made himself an opening large enough for his whole chest to pass through.

As he later stated, he was oppressed by a terrible stench that came from the decaying body. Once free of the tomb, he hurried toward the entrance of the crypt. These things were taking place at the beginning of the night.

Finding the entrance barred and looking through the cracks, he saw a man passing by with an axe. Calling him with a gentle whisper, he asked him to open the entrance with the axe. When this was granted, the presbyter came out free. He asked the man to tell no one about him, and then hurried to his own house and from there to King Clotarius [Col. 0691B].

When he had told the king his story, the king and his nobles said that nothing like this had occurred even in the time of Herod or Nero. The bishop was ordered to be brought before them. When he denied having ordered the deed, the presbyter convicted him, and the bishop withdrew in confusion. The presbyter retained his property.

At that time the blessed Medard, bishop of Vermandois, full of virtues, departed to the Lord. King Clotarius buried his body in a most honorable mausoleum.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. King Clotarius’s donations, pious works, death, and heirs

The illustrious Frankish king Clotarius went to Tours to seek the support and protection of the eminent confessor Martin. There he prayed frequently to the Lord and his saints for his own salvation and the forgiveness of his sins. Through royal generosity he bestowed splendid gifts upon that holy place and showed the greatest munificence in enriching other monasteries of the saints as well.

From there, to engage in hunting—for we have mentioned above that the Franks were devoted to it—he entered the forest of Cocia. While indulging in exercise beyond the strength of his body, which old age had weakened, he was stronger in spirit than in body; he exhausted all his remaining vigor and contracted a severe illness.

He suffered a violent fever and continuous pain in his internal organs without any interruption. While he was tormented, and his limbs were alternately shaken now by cold and now by heat, he repeated these words amid the anguished sighs which his troubled mind drew from him:

> “Woe, woe! How great is that heavenly King, who thus humbles the exalted kings of the earth. Since he is immortal, he is better than any mortal ruler of the world. And if he is better, he is also more powerful; and if he is more powerful, then he is also a giver of mercy.
>
> “He does not, like many human beings, delight in the deaths of the guilty; rather, being merciful and compassionate, he embraces the repentance of sinners. The gift of his clemency must therefore be desired with every affection, and one must never despair of his compassion.”

Amid such words and others like them, he brought his reign to an end, leaving his body to the earth and his kingdom to his sons. He had exercised power for fifty-one years, a power that had remained constant and had always increased.

His sons were named as heirs of the kingdom as follows: the first, Cherebertus; the next, Guntrannus; the third, Chilpericus; the fourth, Sigebertus.

He was buried in the basilica of Saint Medard, as he himself had ordered. It lay thirty thousand paces and more from the place where he had met the end of his life [Col. 0692C]. His sons and the chanting clergy escorted him there with great ceremony over that entire distance.

[Col. 0691] Here ends Book Two.

[Col. 0691]

# BOOK THREE BEGINS

[Col. 0691]

## CHAPTER I. Chilperic’s dispute with his brothers over their father’s inheritance

[Col. 0691C]

After Clotarius was buried, his sons ruled in different portions of the kingdom. Chilperic—for among the brothers his mind was the most enterprising—not content to share an equal portion with the other brothers, seized the treasures of their father stored in the city of Paris. Having won over the Franks, whom he perceived to be especially greedy for money, by payment, he seized the kingdom with their support.

But his brothers joined together and drove him from the city in an ill-considered attack. Then they summoned him after he had agreed to terms of peace, and the four brothers divided the entire kingdom equally into four portions.

To Cherebertus, also called Aribertus, fell the city of Paris, formerly Childebert’s. To Guntrannus was assigned Orléans, namely the kingdom of Chlodomer. Chilperic received the city of Soissons, itself the capital of his father’s kingdom. To Sigebert fell the territory of the Mediomatrici, also called Metz, formerly subject to the rule of their uncle Theodoric. It was a famous and illustrious city and therefore had always been held in no small esteem among the other cities of Gaul.

Let us briefly interrupt our present subject and bring forward what we have found concerning it in the books of the ancients.

When the nation of the Vandals, joining the Suebi and Alans to itself, had resolved to go and devastate Gaul, their king Chroco asked his mother what he should do to obtain the name of “Great.” She replied:

> “If, my son, you wish to be famous throughout the world, destroy the buildings of great houses erected by your ancestors, destroy distinguished cities, and extinguish their inhabitants with the sword. For you cannot build better dwellings than those of earlier times, nor by warfare spread the glory of your name more widely.”

He was not slow to carry out this answer, as though it had been spoken by a divine oracle rather than by a human voice.

For, crossing the Rhine by the bridge near Mainz, he first destroyed the city itself miserably, and then turned the course of his journey toward Metz. Its walls, collapsing of their own accord by divine will during the night preceding the day of his arrival, opened a way for those about to break in.

It is uncertain whether divine indignation brought this calamity upon the wicked and unrepentant citizens, or whether perhaps the destruction of the most unspeakable murderer was hastened justly, so that, believing that heavenly powers were aiding him, he might proceed to the place where he would suffer punishment worthy of his infamous deeds.

After nearly destroying the citizens of Metz to the point of annihilation, he hastened to Trier. The people of Trier, having stationed a defensive force in the city’s sandy terrain, resisted his efforts. Chroco, unsuccessful at Trier, attempted to capture Arles; but he was captured by a certain soldier named Marius. Led through the cities he had destroyed and tortured with punishments, he died. But enough has been said about these matters.

## CHAPTER II. Cherebertus, also called Aribertus

Cherebertus, also called Aribertus, king of Paris, took Ingoberg as his wife. She had two young maidservants. One was named Marcovefa, and the other was called Merofidis.

The king began to waste away so completely from love for them that he cast out his wife Ingoberg and substituted both maidservants in her place. For this he was rebuked by Saint Germanus, bishop of the aforementioned city, but he did not reform. He grieved when both women, together with the son whom one of them had borne him, were struck down by divine judgment and lost.

He himself, not long afterward, met the end of his life in Aquitaine at the fortress of Blavia and was buried in the basilica of Saint Romanus.

## CHAPTER III. The children and deeds of Guntrannus

Guntrannus had four sons by different concubines. I have chosen not to list their names, especially since none of these women had been joined to him in a lawful marriage and, while he was still alive, each reached the end of her life together with the child she had borne.

That king was otherwise exceedingly good and most observant of peace and justice. The only thing that clouded the glory of so great a man was that, softened by the allurements of prostitutes, he rejected lawful marriage.

One day he went hunting in a forest. After his companions had dispersed here and there as circumstances required, he himself sat down beneath a tree with one of his most faithful men to rest. He placed his head in the lap of his trusted friend and, wishing to steal some sleep from his labor, fell asleep.

Then, behold, an animal in the form of a reptile came out of the sleeping king’s mouth. It began to travel along the banks of a flowing stream and tried to cross to the farther bank. Seeing this, the man upon whose knees the king had laid his head placed his unsheathed sword over the little stream, and the animal crossed to the other side by this bridge.

It entered beneath the root of a certain mountain, returned after several hours, and used the same bridge to enter Guntrannus’s mouth.

The king awoke and, telling his companion about the dream, said that he had seen a marvelous vision:

> “I saw an enormous river crossed by an iron bridge. Carried across it, I entered a cave situated at the root of a certain mountain. There I found immeasurable treasures and the hidden wealth of the fathers of old.”

The other man reported what he too had seen, and the words of the dream and the visible vision agreed with one another.

What more is there to say? The place was dug up, and an enormous weight of gold and silver was found. From it Guntrannus intended to have a ciborium made, marvelous in both size and beauty, and to send it to Jerusalem for the tomb of the Lord Jesus Christ.

But when both the difficulty of the journey and fear of the Saracens who infested those regions prevented him from fulfilling his vow, he ordered it to be placed in the basilica adjoining the city of Chalon, which he himself had undertaken to build, above the tomb of Saint Marcellus. As long as it remained there and adorned the tomb of the holy martyr, no work in all Gaul could be found equal to it.

## CHAPTER IV. Sigebert’s marriage to Bruna, daughter of the Gothic king

Sigebert, having learned that his brothers were subjected to serious reproach because of their unfortunate marriages, sent the envoy Gogo to Spain, to Athanahild, king of the Goths, who had driven the emperor’s army from Spain, to request the marriage of his daughter, named Bruna.

Athanahild handed her over to him, with many riches, and Gogo brought her to Sigebert. Because she was devoted to the Arian heresy, Sigebert ordered that she be baptized by Catholics, called Brunichild, and instructed in the orthodox faith. He took her as his wife with a magnificent wedding feast.

Once she had been established as queen, she made Gogo, who had brought her from Spain, hated by Sigebert.

Later, when, during Sigebert’s minority, all the Franks had chosen Chrodinus—a good man and full of the fear of God—as master of the household for his kingdom, Chrodinus yielded the honor offered to him and addressed the king in these words:

> “All the powerful men of Francia are bound to me by the right of kinship, and I cannot endure their quarrels, since each one, relying on his relationship with me, becomes all the more ready to harm another because he does not fear my judgment, as though he were closer to me by affinity.
>
> “But you assert that it is good, out of regard for justice, to punish even relatives. Who denies this? Yet either Torquatus, who struck his son with an axe because he had disregarded his command, or Brutus, who in the same way killed the two sons born to him for the freedom of his country, are branded with infamy for all time. Thus the foremost of poets wrote of him:

> *Unhappy man, however his descendants may judge those deeds.*  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 6)

> “But let it be so: let it be better to be reproached for mercy than for cruelty. Why, however, should mercy be uselessly extended to wicked men, when the forgiveness granted makes them more insolent in practicing their vices everywhere? Therefore, let it not be my lot to undergo the sentence of eternal damnation for the sake of their temporary favor.”

After these words, when the king and all the nobles placed the choice of so great a succession at his discretion, Chrodinus remained silent that day.

At dawn on the following day, he rose early and hurried to Gogo’s house with certain leading men of the palace. He placed his arm around Gogo’s neck, giving him a sign of future authority, and said:

> “Our lord King Sigebert and the assembly of our state had designated me to be master of the royal household. I now yield this office to you. Use my privilege happily, since I freely profess myself to be without it.”

The other nobles who were present followed his example and acclaimed Gogo master of the household.

Gogo was regarded as vigorous in exercising his office until he was ordered to summon Brunichild from Spain. That day was the day of Gogo’s death. It would have been better for him to have changed his place of residence into exile before he brought this woman, more savage than any beast, to be placed upon his own neck.

For Brunichild, as has been mentioned, after obtaining a royal marriage, alienated the king’s mind from Gogo and finally compelled him to have Gogo’s throat cut. So much human blood was shed by her, and so many killings of powerful men and even kings took place in the Frankish kingdom, that it was reasonably believed that the Sibyl had prophesied about her many centuries earlier:

> “Bruna will come from the regions of Spain. Before her presence, peoples and the kings of peoples will perish. She herself will perish, torn apart by the hooves of horses.”

## CHAPTER V. Chilperic’s new marriages to women

King Chilperic also imitated his brother. He was surrounded by a very large crowd of women, more than was customary for a king, who were joined to him more for their beauty than for the nobility of their birth.

He sent men to ask Athanahild for his elder daughter, Brunichild’s sister, and in his name to promise that, if he were granted the opportunity to marry her, he would renounce his other wives. Trusting their words, Athanahild sent his daughter, named Galsonta, to Chilperic, richly endowed with a dowry.

Consecrated more fully by Catholic baptism [Col. 0695] [lacuna] [Note: The proper name of the place, which is missing in the manuscript codices.] she was joined to the king in the marriage bed.

The envoys of King Athanahild asked that, after touching the holy relics, Chilperic confirm by oath that Galsonta would not be expelled from the royal throne during her lifetime. Chilperic did not refuse. After the oaths had been given and peace agreed upon, he allowed them to return home.

But, being light-minded by nature, he violated the terms of the agreement. Fredegundis, who had once been called the wife of King Chilperic, was offended by the sight of the new bride. In a very short time she prevailed so greatly by her skill in flattery that she restored herself to the king’s marriage.

Then, lifted by womanly boldness to dare greater things, she placed herself above everyone who was in the royal court and did not cease to insult Galsonta, the daughter of King Athanahild.

Galsonta complained to her husband of these injuries, but he, whose affection for her had already been greatly diminished, mocked her with soothing words. Finally, driven by murderous furies and instigated by Fredegundis, he cruelly strangled her while she was resting in bed.

It was a monstrous crime, previously unknown to any tyrant, and especially to a Frankish man—above all to a king. It was utterly unfitting that he should not be ashamed to suffocate an innocent wife, one whom it would have been proper to avenge with the sword if she had been seized by enemies, or for whose sake he should have sought death, while she lay secure in their common bed.

He was mad to violate the honor of so great a marriage at the persuasion of that little prostitute, by whose treachery he himself was soon to be killed.

After Galsonta’s death, divine power deigned to display a great miracle at her tomb. A glass vessel in which oil was burned before the tomb fell to the ground; the pavement gave way, and the vessel sank whole into the earth as though into a measure of flour.

Her brothers could not tolerate having as their associate a man stained by so great a crime. They joined together and tried to drive him from the kingdom. Their plan, however, was dissolved—not so much by Chilperic’s cunning as by the very fickleness with which it had been begun.

## CHAPTER VI. Chilperic’s sons and their deeds
Chilperic had three sons, Theudebert, Merovech, and Chlodovech, born to Queen Audovera. Fredegund drove her from his side by the same deceitful contrivance by which she had removed Galswinth, and for the following reason. While Chilperic was campaigning with his brother Sigebert against the Saxons, he had left Queen Audovera at home pregnant. Fredegund, being a maidservant born of her household, attended to all her daily needs. She urged her mistress to bring the newborn girl to the grace of baptism, so that when the king returned he might rejoice that not only had a daughter been born to him, but that she had also been reborn in Christ.

[Col. 0696B]

The woman obeyed the little harlot’s advice all the more readily because she supposed that Fredegund was giving her good counsel. Then, when she asked which matron might receive the girl after the waters of holy baptism, Fredegund replied that no nobler woman could be found to perform this service than Audovera herself. Trusting these words as well, Audovera became the girl’s spiritual mother.

Afterward, when the king was returning, Fredegund went to meet him and addressed him: “How glorious,” she said, “King Chilperic appears today, returning victorious after triumphing over his enemies! A daughter has been born to him, Childechinda, of outstanding beauty. But alas! Tonight you will commit a crime—a crime that should indeed be avoided, if it could be avoided—lest my mistress Audovera enter with you into the secret silence of the bedchamber.”

[Col. 0696C]

Stunned by the novelty of these words, the king asked the reason. When she remained silent, he drew it out by persistent questioning and an impulse of indignation. When he learned that the queen, having borne the child, had become its godmother, he answered Fredegund in these words: “If I am now deprived of Audovera’s embraces, I shall take you as the companion of my bed.”

As he hurried toward the palace, the queen came to meet him, carrying in her arms the little girl whom, so to speak, she had twice given birth to—her daughter. The king said to her: “You have committed, O queen, an unspeakable act, one unbecoming royal majesty. Nor shall I be able to have you as my wife, since you have acquired the name of godmother.”

[Col. 0696D]

Afterward, he sent into exile the bishop who had baptized the girl, and shut the queen and her daughter, covered with the sacred veil, inside a monastery, granting them estates and property. Fredegund, however, he took as his wife.

At that time King Sigebert, Chilperic’s and Guntram’s brother, was compelled to lead an army against Cacanus, prince of the Huns, who was approaching in order to ravage the borders of his kingdom. In this encounter he proved superior in war and inflicted enormous slaughter upon the Huns. With the survivors, however, he established peace.

Chilperic took advantage of his absence and, in keeping with his restless character, disturbed the public peace of the Franks by domestic sedition. He suddenly seized Rheims, the wealthiest city of Sigebert’s kingdom.

[Col. 0697A]

Sigebert, enraged by the blow, invaded Soissons and himself entered Chilperic’s kingdom. After capturing the city’s people, he added them to his own authority and, when he found Theudebert, Chilperic’s son, handed him over to custody. Later, when his father asked for him, he returned him with the greatest clemency, after first receiving an oath that Theudebert would undertake nothing against Sigebert in the future. But, through the hindrance of the enemy of the human race, this oath did not remain inviolate for long. Chilperic too, defeated in war, accepted the terms of peace.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the Saxons, who invaded Gaul and were driven back by Mummolus

[Col. 0697B]

The Saxons, who had migrated to Italy at the command of the elder Theudebert, broke into Gaul with their wives and children. Mummolus, patrician of King Guntram, went out to meet them and compelled them to flee back to Italy.

The following year the Saxons again approached, intending to enter Gaul as far as the Rhône River. Mummolus, meeting them with his army, prevented them from crossing the river. But after accepting gifts, he granted them permission to pass through the borders of the kingdom he was defending and proceed to Sigebert. Received by him, they were ordered to settle in their own lands.

As they made their way there, they deceived many merchants along the road, selling plates of copper that they had colored by some art to resemble the appearance of fine, tested gold, and accepting gold in payment for them.

[Col. 0697C]

Many merchants later lamented that this affair had reduced them to poverty.

But the Saxons paid the penalty for their fraud through swift vengeance. For they were defeated in a threefold battle by the Suebi and other peoples who had invaded their homeland; nearly twenty thousand of their men were killed, and the survivors, though unwillingly, obeyed the conditions imposed by their enemies.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the Emperors Justinian and Justin

At that time Justinian, after ruling the empire for thirty-three years with good fortune, left the scepter and crown of the kingdom to Justin the Younger.

Justinian was a man of Catholic faith, distinguished in piety, and an outstanding cultivator of justice. Therefore everything worked together for his good. He successfully conducted civil wars through various commanders, especially Belisarius, and proved remarkable in settling civil cases and framing laws.

[Col. 0697D]

Because of his many victories, he earned the additional names Alemannic, Gothic, Alanic, Vandalic, and African. The same prince also built within the city of Constantinople a temple to Christ God, who is the Wisdom of God the Father. He named it, in the Greek language, Hagia Sophia—that is, “Holy Wisdom.” Its workmanship surpasses all other buildings to such a degree that those who have seen it testify that nothing like it can be found throughout the whole world.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning Cassiodorus and other distinguished men

[Col. 0698A]

In his time Cassiodorus became famous in both secular and divine learning; the abbot Dionysius was admired for his skill in calculating Easter; Priscian of Caesarea for grammatical art; and Arator for his metrical composition of the Acts of the Apostles. Benedict, too, shone more peacefully than the others in heavenly discipline.

These matters have compelled us to speak briefly of the good ruler and of those who lived in his time. Now let us touch briefly upon the deeds of Narses, so that afterward the course of the History may proceed continuously from where it began.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the renowned deeds of Narses

[Col. 0698B]

Narses, glorious in the many triumphs of the nations he had subdued, distinguished by the civic crown, exercised the highest authority of justice throughout Italy. But in these matters he discovered that envy had harmed him more among the wicked than favor had benefited him among the good.

For although he had very often exposed himself to the danger of death in order to free his fellow citizens, and had aroused against himself the hatred of the neighboring peoples, he suffered so much from the Romans that after the war he experienced greater danger from his own people than from the enemy during the war itself.

The Romans completed an abominable crime: they did not blush to accuse before a judge, even in his absence, the man whom they had regarded as the protector of their safety. Nor was this kind of disgrace new among them. For once the elder Africanus, Scipio, celebrated for the trophies of conquered Carthage, lived for a long time in exile from the ungrateful city of Rome and wasted away in his own fields from illness and grief.

[Col. 0698C]

The other Africanus, Scipio, no obscure descendant of the earlier Scipio, was compelled after subduing Libya to plead his case in the Senate against his accusers. He had learned that wicked and ungrateful men were denouncing him, although he had labored for his fatherland. In the middle of the following night he was killed by his rivals in his bedroom.

In the same way, a report by the Romans against Narses reached the emperor Justin and his wife Sophia. They complained that, after the Goths had been conquered, nothing had been granted to them in the way of freedom, while a still harsher master remained over them—namely, the eunuch Narses.

When this became known, Caesar, blazing with anger, sent Longinus as Narses’ successor and prefect. When Narses learned of it, he is said to have spoken as follows: “If I have dealt badly with the Romans, I shall receive what my deeds deserve. But if I have done good, and if they wish to repay me in kind, why do they slander me, sewing false accusations onto my head?”

[Col. 0698D]

Such indignation, especially on the part of the empress, was aroused against Narses that, among other insults, she ordered him in sufficiently abusive language to divide out the wool-workers’ task in the women’s quarters, since he was a eunuch, rather than hold the Roman consulship.

To this Narses replied: “I shall spin a thread from which a fabric will be woven—one that Justin and Sophia will be unable to cut apart throughout their entire life.”

[Col. 0699A]

Without delaying in fulfilling his promise, he sent to Alboin, king of the Lombards, urging him to abandon the impoverished fields of Pannonia and cross over to Italy, a land rich in soil. Alboin did not reject the advice; with all his people and their belongings, he hastened to Hesperia.

Narses, however, left the city of Rome and came to Naples. Pope John, who had succeeded Pelagius, followed him and asked him to return to Rome. Having obtained this, they both returned. The most holy John, however, did not survive long afterward. Narses died some time later, and his body, placed in a lead coffin, was carried to Constantinople with all his treasures.

But, to fulfill what we promised, we must return to the course of the History.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the Huns, or Avars, invading Gaul

[Col. 0699B]

The Huns, also called Avars, broke the treaty they had made with Sigebert, king of the Franks, and poured into unprepared Gaul. When he had gathered an army and intended to meet them in battle, the Huns, by magical arts and certain apparitions, terrified the Franks and compelled them to flee before the fighting began.

The king himself, having tried unsuccessfully to resist, was captured. But, through the cunning of his prudence, after offering gifts he was honorably permitted to return to his own people, and he secured a lasting peace with the Huns for the future.

He did not prefer the shortcut of death to safety, thereby condemning the wicked counsel of the Roman Crassus, once consul, who, in order to escape the disgrace of slavery, prepared not a payment for the enemy but destruction for himself.

[Col. 0699C]

For when, fighting by chance against the Thracians, he had fallen into the power of the enemy after thousands of his men had been killed, he did not wish to become a source of mockery to his enemies. He thrust into the eye of the Thracian who was holding him the staff he used to spur his horse. The barbarian, driven by pain and anger, pierced Crassus’ side with his sword.

Thus a man of great name and courage, while avoiding what he might perhaps have escaped through chance or even through the enemy’s mercy, fell into a death that not even an unwilling adversary can avert once inflicted.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the deeds of Chlodovech and Guntram

At that time Chlodovech, Chilperic’s son, invaded Bordeaux, which belonged to Sigebert’s kingdom. Duke Sigulf, commander of Sigebert’s faction, attacked him there and drove him out.

[Col. 0699D]

As though he were driving a stag before him, Sigulf pursued him as he hurried back to his own territory, sounding trumpets, as far as the refuges of the city of Paris.

When Chilperic learned this, he sent Theudebert, another of his sons, who had previously sworn to Sigebert that he would in no way harm him, into Neustria to seize the cities subject to his brother. After subduing several cities, Theudebert assigned tribute, by right of conquest, to the people of Tours, Poitiers, Cahors, and Limoges.

After ranging through the province of Aquitaine, he devastated monasteries of the servants and handmaids of God by plundering them, subjected monks and clerics to torture, and dishonored nuns with shameful abuses.

[Col. 0700A]

Finally, when some members of the hostile army were advancing toward the monastery of Saint Martin called Lata and wished to cross the river flowing between them, the monks shouted: “Do not, O barbarians, do not inflict injury upon this monastery of Saint Martin.”

When they heard this, some of them turned back, pierced in heart with remorse. Nevertheless, twenty of them boarded a ship, crossed the river, killed the monks, broke into the monastery, and plundered its goods. After loading their spoils, they returned to the ship.

But the power of the blessed confessor was not absent. When they entered the river channel and lost their oars, they tried to propel the ship with their spears; but the vessel sank beneath their feet. They themselves, pierced by their own lances, descended into the depths. Only one survived—the man who had urged them to abandon the undertaking.

The monks rescued them and their goods from the water, bringing the men to burial and returning the goods to the monastery.

[Col. 0700B]

At that time Theudebert appeared to the people of Aquitaine and to Christians as Diocletian once appeared to Catholics throughout the world.

In a battle at Poitiers against Duke Gundoald, he destroyed almost all his forces. Nor did Chilperic remain inactive. He was indignant that his armies had been made a laughingstock to his brother Sigebert. Not content with his son’s victory, he too came with a large force and ravaged Champagne and the region of Rheims.

Sigebert, however, was not entirely idle, nor did he suffer much loss in his kingdom for long. For, having opportunely laid an ambush, he destroyed Theudebert’s entire army together with Theudebert himself. While Theudebert tried to escape, he was overwhelmed and killed by the royal cohort.

Duke Arnulf gathered his body and carried it to Angoulême, where it was buried.

[Col. 0700C]

Then Sigebert assembled the leading Austrasian Franks and, gathering the assistance of their allies as well, directed his forces against his brother. He ordered the citizens of Auvergne to invade Arles unexpectedly.

Having learned of this beforehand, Guntram informed the people of Arles through messengers of the enemy’s approach. They, under Duke Celsus, occupied the places suitable for ambush and killed those who had come to kill them.

Guntram too, gathering forces from every direction, prepared to march against his brothers. When he had pitched his camp at a place called Viriacus, while Sigebert was staying at Archiacus and Chilperic repeatedly at the place where the twelve bridges over the Seine are reported to have been built, the three brothers came together in a treaty through the mediation of the best and wisest men, whose custom it is always to offer counsel to kings.

[Col. 0700D]

Then, joining right hands in the oratory of Saint Lupus at Troyes, Sigebert and Chilperic swore to Guntram that they would undertake nothing further against him in a hostile manner. Guntram was likewise seen to give them the same oath.

They departed in peace. After greeting one another, Guntram returned to his own territory, while Sigebert and Chilperic returned to their camps.

Then the Austrasians began to quarrel with Sigebert, demanding that the promises made to them be fulfilled. They remembered that they had been enticed into joining the war by the hope of enemy booty.

[Col. 0701A]

He ought either to distribute pay to them from his own resources or point out a public adversary from whose resources they might enrich themselves. Meanwhile, they complained that while the kings either sold peace to one another or pursued hostility, they were treated like mercenaries—first in danger, last in honor or rewards.

They declared that they did not wish to raise any complaint of offense against Guntram, with whom Sigebert had established a treaty by just agreement. But against Chilperic, they said, the hatred of all was blazing up in remembrance of the old hostility. He was one of those many men whose life was hateful and whose death would be welcome to everyone.

Compelled, therefore, by these arguments from his own people, Sigebert decided to pursue his brother. Chilperic, fearing nothing of the sort, had dismissed most of his army to winter quarters. When he received news of his brother’s pursuit, he fled with a few horsemen to the city of Tournai.

[Col. 0701B]

Sigebert followed and entered the city of Paris. Bishop Saint Germanus met him and said: “If you desire to shed your brother’s blood, you will experience, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words, the pit prepared for your brother as prepared for yourself; nor will you escape the name of fratricide, since the will itself is not free from punishment.”

Sigebert scorned these words as though they had been spoken by a bishop favoring his brother’s faction, and he intended to complete what he had begun.

When he came to a village called Victoriacus [elsewhere, Victoria], he encountered there a strong force from Chilperic’s kingdom, consisting of Neustrians who wished to surrender to him. When they saw the king, they came eagerly to him and submitted themselves to his authority.

[Col. 0701C]

No duke or nobleman of the Frankish kingdom remained with Chilperic except Ansoald, who preferred not to abandon his king’s fortune even in adversity rather than become, or be called, a traitor by violating his pledged faith.

Thus surrounded by such great bands of soldiers, Sigebert brought all the cities of Chilperic’s kingdom under his authority. He then advanced to the city called Tournai and besieged his brother there.

Seeing himself hard pressed, Chilperic was uncertain what plan would free his wife and sons, whom he had brought with him, from danger. But the woman, far more cunning than her husband in devising schemes, equipped two men whose audacity had brought them to despise death. She urged and instructed them to approach Sigebert and kill him while pretending to adore him as their lord.

[Col. 0701D]

If they succeeded, she promised rewards for their escape; if they were killed, she promised them fitting burial and alms at the shrines of the saints as an offering for so great a deed.

They did not delay in carrying out the command. Leaving the city, they advanced to the enemy’s camp. No men more audacious or more terrifying to the enemy emerged from the city in that war. Bursting into the midst of the adversaries, they neither trembled nor drew back. As though they were remaining among their own familiar companions, they did not consider returning until they had surrounded the king from the sides and, stabbing his flanks with their knives, delivered him to a most unspeakable death.

Immediately a cry and mourning arose throughout the whole camp, making it publicly clear that King Sigebert had been killed.

[Col. 0702A]

The soldiers then rushed upon the murderers and, with little difficulty, cut the two men to pieces.

When Chilperic feared to leave the city and did not know what had happened, his wife Fredegund came to him. When he learned from her that his brother had died, his spirit, as though brought back from the underworld, returned to hope for life and safety.

The next day he left the city. The Neustrians who had defected from him to Sigebert were reconciled with him, and he ordered his brother’s body to be buried in a village called Lambrus. Later, when the faithful brought it forward, it was buried in the church of Saint Medard at Soissons, beside his father Chlothar.

He had reigned for thirteen years.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning Bishop Fortunatus and his learning

[Col. 0702B]

During his reign, Fortunatus, who was considered famous in rhetorical and metrical art, passed from Hesperia into Gaul and was ordained bishop of Poitiers. He composed the lives and passions of many saints, partly in prose and partly in verse. He also wrote elegant individual couplets to his friends as an accomplished poet.

For this reason he sent the aforesaid king an elegiac poem, congratulating him on his marriage to Brunhild. I myself read it when fortune placed in my hands a book that he had written for various friends and associates. In it I greatly admired the man’s eloquence and his gracious warmth of expression.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning Brunhild’s skill in preserving her offspring

[Col. 0702C]

After Sigebert had been killed in this manner, circumstances changed, and many of his household sought the friendship of Chilperic.

Brunhild, whom Sigebert, when returning from the seizure of his brothers’ cities, had ordered to meet him at Paris, was living in that same city. When she learned of her husband’s death, she was tormented in mind, wondering how she might free herself and her offspring from the impending destruction.

Then Duke Gundoald seized the boy Childebert, placed him in a basket, and lowered him through a window to one of his faithful men, so that he might take him to Metz. When the boy had been brought there, all the Austrasians, with the support of the aforementioned Gundoald, raised him to his father’s throne.

Another concern seized Brunhild after she had been relieved of the burden of her son. For, fearing for herself, she could find neither sleep for her eyes nor rest for her mind. Although she wished to depart, she lacked the means.

[Col. 0702D]

Pressed by such anxieties, she was driven into exile at Rouen by the arrival of Chilperic. Her treasures were added to Chilperic’s wealth, and her daughters were sent to Meaux for safekeeping.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the deeds of Merovech and the other kings

Merovech, sent by his father Chilperic to bring the cities along the Loire River over to his side, disregarded his father’s command and hastened to Le Mans, as though he intended to visit his mother Audovera, who was exiled there.

From there he passed to Rouen and came to Brunhild, taking her in marriage. His father Chilperic could not tolerate this. Wishing to separate them, he went as far as Rouen.

[Col. 0703A]

They avoided his presence and entered the basilica of Saint Martin, constructed of wooden planks above the walls of the aforesaid city. Chilperic’s initial attempts would have been fruitless had he not sworn that he would not separate them, but, with God’s permission, would instead join them more closely.

Believing him, they went to him and were entertained by him with lavish banquets for two days. On the third day he departed, taking his son with him and making light of the oath he had given—a remarkable censor of morals, condemning an unlawful marriage in his son but not fearing the future judgment of God upon himself for perjury.

In truth, he feared the crafty designs of Brunhild more than he resented the injury done to divine law: he feared that she would fill his son with treachery.

As Chilperic returned, he was informed that the nobles of the district of Champagne around Rheims had seized the city of Soissons from him.

[Col. 0703B]

He immediately gathered his forces, defeated them in battle, killed many nobles, and restored the captured city to his authority.

He sent his son Chlodovech to Tours, ordering him to bring the districts of Périgueux and Agen under his control. He assigned Duke Desiderius to him so that Chlodovech might have his support in every difficulty.

Mummolus, patrician of Guntram, marched against them with an army, defeated them, and put them to flight, though not without enormous loss on his own side. For fifty thousand of his army were killed, while on the enemy’s side, although defeated, no more than twenty thousand were slain.

Afterward, at the instigation of his stepmother Fredegund, Chilperic ordered his son Merovech, whom he suspected of treachery because he supported Brunhild’s faction, to be tonsured, ordained a presbyter, and confined in the monastery of Aninsola.

[Col. 0703C]

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the passing, holiness, and miracles of the holy bishop Germanus

At the same time the most holy and truly God-worthy Germanus, bishop of Paris, departed to the Lord. His body was buried in the oratory of Saint Vincent.

I shall not omit what Fortunatus wrote about this most blessed man. “On one occasion,” he says, “the most excellent king Childebert the Elder sent him six thousand solidi to distribute among the poor. After spending three thousand, Germanus returned to the palace.

[Col. 0703D]

“The king asked him whether he still had anything left to distribute. He replied that half remained and that he had not found enough needy people on whom he could spend the whole sum.

“The king said to him: ‘My lord, give what remains. For, with Christ’s generosity, there is no lack of what may be given.’

“The king broke up golden serving dishes and smashed silver vessels, giving the priest whatever he first came upon, lest it be lost. Thus a contest between priest and ruler was to be expected. Within themselves they waged a battle over mercy and a contest over piety, scattering treasures so that the poor might grow rich from their resources.

“Again, on another occasion, when a horse suitable for the priest to ride was needed, the king gave him his own and asked him to keep it for himself. Meanwhile, the blessed man gave the forbidden horse to a captive who asked for it, because the poor man’s voice had greater weight with him than the king’s command.”

At that time Chilperic also received an embassy from his nephew Childebert the Younger, who asked that his mother Brunhild be returned to him. Chilperic did not reject his request but sent her back to the son who asked for her, together with a peace offering.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the affairs of the Spanish kings

After Athanagild, king of Spain, died, Leuva and his brother Leovigild assumed the kingdom. When Leuva died, Leovigild held the whole kingdom of Spain. He had Gadsuinda, Brunhild’s mother, as his wife.

Among the Lombards Alboin, whom we mentioned earlier, was reigning. Having gained possession of most of the cities of Italy, he established his own people in them and expelled the Romans, whom he regarded especially as his adversaries.

[Col. 0704A]

He besieged for three years the city called Ticinum, also known by the name Pavia, and at last captured it. Since he was a pagan and knew that its inhabitants were Christians, he intended to strike them down with the sword. But his horse collapsed in the middle of the gate.

Driven by spurs and beaten with clubs, it could not in any way be forced to rise. Finally, when his men urged him toward religion, the king relented and broke the vow he had made concerning the killing of Christians.

He was married to Clodsind, daughter of Chlothar, king of the Franks. After she died, he took as his wife Rosemund, daughter of Cunimund, king of the Gepids; Alboin himself had once killed her father.

[Col. 0704B]

After he had ruled the Lombards in Italy for three years and more, he was killed in the most disgraceful manner in revenge for her father’s death. A man most warlike and of the greatest courage perished through the counsel of a single little woman, although he had become famous in war through the slaughter of so many enemies.

She, however, paid the punishment she deserved for such monstrous wickedness with swift retribution. When she later offered, as he emerged from the bath, a cup of poison to her adulterous partner, Helmechis, who had been armed by her to kill the king, claiming that it was a health-giving drink, he realized that he had swallowed a deadly draught. Drawing his sword, he forced her to drink what remained.

Thus the most wicked murderers alike suffered the just retribution for their deeds.

[Col. 0704C]

After Alboin, Cleph, the most noble of the Lombards, held the leadership for one year and six months. Thereafter, dukes were elected among the Lombards for ten years, and each duke ruled his own city.

Some of them, desiring to plunder Gaul, entered Provence and fought against Amatus, patrician under Guntram, the king to whom he was subject. After inflicting a great slaughter upon the Burgundians, they killed the duke himself.

When Guntram heard this, he summoned Mummolus, a man of proven courage, and entrusted him with the office of patrician.

When the Lombards again burst into Gaul, Mummolus met them with a powerful force of Burgundians. In two battles he weakened the enemy almost to destruction and compelled the survivors to flee back to Italy. The Lombards did not afterward dare attempt to cross into Gaul.

[Col. 0704D]

Mummolus then sent a Frankish army in their rear, stormed and captured the fortress of Anagnis, situated on the borders of Italy. For this reason Ragilo, count of the Lombards, came to Anagnis and plundered it. As he hurried back to his own territory, he was killed by a Frankish duke named Chrannichis, who met him on the road.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the deeds of Justin the Younger

[Col. 0705A]

At this time, as we have said above, Justin the Younger was reigning at Constantinople. He was so devoted to avarice that he ordered iron chests to be made in which he could heap up the talents of gold he had seized.

When he turned the ear of his heart away from the divine commandments, he was made insane by God’s just judgment. Afterward he elevated Tiberius Caesar, a just, useful, charitable, wise man,

[Col. 0705B]

equitable in judgments, renowned in victories, and—what surpasses all these qualities—a most genuine Christian, to govern his empire.

Thus Justin, after reigning for eleven years, finally ended both his life and the madness he had incurred.

The wars against the Goths and Franks conducted by the patrician Narses, which we mentioned earlier in advance, began indeed during the reign of Justinian but were completed under Justin.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning Tiberius Constantine and his reign

After Justin’s death, Tiberius Constantine, the fiftieth Roman emperor, assumed the empire.

As we said above, while he was still Caesar under Justin and governing the state, he distributed many alms to the poor, and the Lord supplied him with a great abundance of gold.

[Col. 0705C]

As he was walking through the palace, he saw on the floor of a room a marble slab marked with the sign of the Lord’s cross. He said: “Why do we trample under unworthy feet the cross of the Lord, with which we ought to fortify our breast and forehead?”

At once, together with these words, he ordered the slab to be removed from the floor. When it had been taken away, they found another marked with the same sign. After this one too, they found a third. When these had been removed, a treasure of immeasurable value, long concealed, was brought to light.

Tiberius distributed it among the poor, according to his customary practice. The treasure of Narses, buried in the ground in a certain city of Italy, was likewise discovered when a decrepit old man revealed its location, and Tiberius distributed it for the same purpose.

[Col. 0705D]

The empress Sophia, however, forgetful of the promise she had made to Tiberius, plotted to remove him from the empire and substitute Justinian, Justin’s nephew. When the emperor learned of this, he placed the empress under guard.

He rebuked Justinian in gentle words but afterward loved him with such affection that he promised his own daughter to Justinian’s son and asked that his own son be joined in marriage to Justinian’s daughter. It is uncertain for what reason this arrangement did not come to completion.

Chilperic, king of the Franks, sent ambassadors to Tiberius and received from him many ornaments and also gold pieces each weighing a pound. On one side they bore the emperor’s likeness and the inscription around it: **TIBERIUS CONSTANTINE, PERPETUAL AUGUSTUS**. On the other they showed a four-horse chariot and its driver and bore the inscription: **GLORY OF THE ROMANS**.

[Col. 0705D]

The army sent by Tiberius defeated the Persians with great force. Returning victorious, it carried away such an enormous quantity of booty, together with twenty elephants, that it seemed sufficient to satisfy human greed.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning the affairs of the Britons and Guntram’s crime

While these events were taking place in the East, the following occurred in Britain.

Macliaus and Bodicus were then counts of the Britons. They had joined themselves in mutual friendship by oaths exchanged with one another. After Bodicus died, Macliaus drove his son Theodoric out of the kingdom of Britain.

[Col. 0706A]

Theodoric, having regained his strength, killed Maclianus and his son Jacob and recovered his father’s inheritance. Varocus, Macliaus’ son, succeeded his father in the countship.

At that time Guntram, king of the Franks, killed two sons of Magnacharius, formerly his father-in-law, and subjected their property to the royal treasury. Afterward the deaths of two of his own sons followed. For this reason, deprived of his children, Guntram adopted Childebert, his nephew through his brother Sigebert, as his son.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning Chilperic’s quarrel with Praetextatus

[Col. 0706B]

His brother Chilperic, another king of the Franks, sent Praetextatus, bishop of Rouen, into exile because he was said to have plotted against him while acting on the advice of Queen Brunhild.

[Col. 0706C]

His son Merovech, whom we have mentioned as having been tonsured and confined in a monastery by his father, was again made a layman. For Duke Guntram, about whom the following account will say more, sent messengers to entice him. Merovech left the monastery, was dressed in lay clothing by his attendant Gailenus, and was urged to seek refuge in the church of Saint Martin at Tours.

Guntram himself had also taken refuge in that church, fearing the threats of King Chilperic, because he was said to have killed his son Theudebert in the war mentioned above.

For this reason Chilperic had sent a certain Ruccolenus to Tours to drag him out by force. When Ruccolenus arrived at Tours, he ordered the blessed bishop Gregory to expel Guntram from the holy basilica. If Gregory delayed doing so, Ruccolenus said, he should know that he would come with a powerful force and carry it out himself.

[Col. 0706D]

The holy bishop replied that this had never been done and that he would in no way do it.

Meanwhile, the wretched Ruccolenus did not fear to destroy the church’s house in which he was lodging. He was seized by a royal illness and carried to the basilica of Saint Martin. Finding no relief there, he died a few days later.

Merovech then came to the aforesaid church while the bishop mentioned above was celebrating Mass. He asked Gregory to give him the *eulogiae*, the blessed loaves. When Gregory refused, Merovech threatened to kill some of the people, since he was being deprived of communion without a judgment of the priests.

The bishop then gave him the *eulogiae*, but informed the king through a deacon of what had happened. The queen cried out that the cleric had been sent by Merovech as a spy, and the king banished him into exile.

[Col. 0707A]

Chilperic then sent word to the priest that he should expel his enemy from the church. When Gregory delayed, Chilperic ordered an army to be mobilized.

When Merovech heard this, he wished to leave the basilica. But Leudast, count of Tours, killed his servants, who had gone to a villa for necessary purposes.

For this reason Merovech, with the assistance of Guntram, seized Marileff, the physician who had come from the king. He took away the gold and silver he was carrying and would certainly have killed him had Marileff not sought refuge in the church.

Meanwhile, while Merovech was saying many things about the crimes of his father and stepmother, one day he invited Bishop Gregory to dinner and asked him to read something for his instruction.

The bishop then took up the Book of Solomon and found and read this first verse:

“Let ravens from the streams dig out the eye that mocks his father” (*Proverbs* 30).

Merovech did not understand what this meant, but the bishop was astonished that words of rebuke had been the first to meet his eyes.

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning Guntram’s consultation of a prophetess

[Col. 0707B]

After this Guntram sent to a woman prophetess who had once foretold to him not only the year but also the day and hour on which King Charibert would die. He sent to ask her about his own future.

She sent him this reply:

“This year, after Chilperic has died, Merovech will receive the kingdom after defeating his brothers, and he will appoint you duke. After holding that office for five years, in the seventh year you will become a bishop.”

He reported this to Bishop Gregory and received from him the following reply: “They ought rather to have sought these things from God than from the devil [Col. 0707C].” Nevertheless, Fredegund, who secretly favored Guntrannus because of the death of Theodebert—for he had not been born of her—sent to him, asking him to persuade Meroveus to leave the church. Thinking that assassins would be at hand, he did not delay; but this did him no harm. Finally Chilperic sent two little documents by a deacon to the tomb of Saint Martin. One of them instructed that a reply be written divinely upon the other, which was blank, stating whether it was lawful for Guntrannus to be dragged from the church. The deacon waited three days and departed without an answer. But when the king’s envoys arrived, Guntrannus publicly gave a pledge at the altar under oath, boastfully promising that he would never leave the church without the king’s knowledge.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Meroveus Seeks an Oracle from the Divine Books

[Col. 0707D]

At last Meroveus, setting aside the Pythoness’s answers, kept vigil for three days and received the following response from the divine books. In the Book of Kings: “Because,” it says, “you have abandoned the Lord your God, God has delivered you into the hands of your enemies.” In the Psalter: “You cast them down while they were being exalted” (Ps. LXXII). In the Gospel: “You know that after two days Passover will take place,” and so forth (Matt. XXVI).

When he saw these passages, he departed weeping for the tomb of Saint Martin with five hundred men and more, taking with him also Guntrannus as commander. Passing through the city of Auxerre, he came to the fortress of Dijon, and from there crossed into the Champagne of Reims. When he was surrounded by men from Tarvanna at a certain estate and realized that he was about to be captured, he feared that, if he were brought before his father, he would suffer severe punishment. He therefore asked a certain Gailenus, his associate, to strike him with a sword. Gailenus pierced him through the entrails with a knife, and he died. Gailenus, after his hands and feet had been cut off, together with his nose and ears, ended his life disgracefully. After this, Sanson, Chilperic’s son, died. The same king accompanied his funeral with excessive mourning. That year a star was seen shining in the middle of the moon.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The Daughters of Guntrannus-Boso Are Freed through Their Father’s Valor, with Saint Martin’s Aid

A certain most powerful nobleman of Chilperic, called by the single name Guntrannus-Boso, left his daughters in the church of Saint Hilary and went over to Childebert [Col. 0708B]. In the third year of the reign of the younger Childebert, which was the seventeenth year of Chilperic and Guntrannus, Guntrannus Boso wished to remove his daughters from Poitiers. He attempted to turn aside by entreaties and gifts a certain Dracolenus, who was extremely hostile to him and was pursuing him.

Dracolenus, carried away by pride of mind, replied arrogantly, declaring that he had the cord ready with which he was accustomed to destroy those whom he had deceived, so that he might bind Guntrannus with it. Guntrannus could not tolerate his arrogant boasting. Raising his hands to heaven, he invoked the Lord, who performs wonders, and prayed that God would have mercy on him through the intercession of blessed Martin. Engaging his adversary, he thrust a spear through his throat as he uttered words of defiance, then lifted him from his saddle and threw him lifeless to the ground. [Col. 0708C] Taking advantage of this fortunate event, he brought away his daughters, who had been removed from the city of Poitiers, and led them wherever he wished.

## CHAPTER XXV. The Discord between the Pictavians and the Britons

The Pictavians and the Bagassians—now called Arbassians—joined with the people of Angers and attempted to overwhelm Varocus, count of the Britons, by a sudden attack. Varocus forestalled their ambush, rushing upon them around midnight and inflicting a great slaughter upon them. On the third day he made a treaty with Chilperic’s commanders, giving his son as a hostage and returning what he had seized. He also restored the city of Vannes on the condition that, if he deserved to retain it by the king’s favor, he would not delay paying the annual tribute.

After some time had passed, however, he abandoned his allegiance and sent Eunius, bishop of Vannes, to the king to bring back an answer concerning certain matters. The king rebuked him angrily and sent him into exile.

## CHAPTERS XXVI–XXVII. Chilperic’s Accusation against Bishop Praetextatus and Praetextatus’s Defense

After these events, King Chilperic assembled a council of bishops in the church of Saint Peter in the city of Paris. He brought before them Praetextatus, bishop of Rouen—whom we have already mentioned—having recalled him from exile, and presented the following accusation:

“Although, venerable bishops, royal power may condemn a person guilty of treason under the laws of majesty, I nevertheless present to your hearing this man, who falsely assumes the name of shepherd and is the author of the conspiracy made against me, without contradicting the sacred canons.”

Then, turning to Praetextatus, bishop of Rouen, he said: “Why, bishop, did you distribute gifts to the people against my welfare? And for what reason did you unite my son Meroveus with his uncle’s wife? Were you unaware of what the sacred canons decree concerning this matter? Why, moreover, did you arm my son against his father in such a way that he wished to deprive me both of my life and of my kingdom?”

When the king had fallen silent, the Franks who were standing outside, growling, tried to break down the doors of the basilica so that they might subject the bishop to punishment. But the king forbade this and granted Praetextatus an opportunity to defend himself. As he refuted the charges brought against him, certain false witnesses rose and accused the bishop of having given them gifts so that they might destroy the king by deceit.

The bishop said to them: “I confirm that you are telling the truth in this respect: you yourselves admit that you were bribed by me. For what else would I have been doing, enriched by your gifts, except returning like for like? But what you falsely allege—that I plotted evil against the king—is altogether false.”

As he was saying this, the king withdrew to the royal residence. The bishops remained in the church’s house, and Etius, archdeacon of Paris, arrived and addressed them as follows:

“Now is the time, most holy priests, when either you will be glorified for your great-hearted steadfastness, or, if you remain silent, you will henceforth be held in contempt for the degradation and dishonor of your brother and fellow bishop.”

When the others remained silent—because they feared the fury of the queen, at whose prompting these things were being done—and placed a finger upon their mouths, Gregory, bishop of Tours, began to speak:

“It is proper for us, dearest brothers, and especially for those who enjoy the ruler’s intimacy, to offer him salutary counsel, lest, overcome by anger, he become more enraged than is just against a priest of God and be punished more severely by God, the avenger of the innocent.”

Since they still gave no response, the bishop continued:

“We must fear, most holy Fathers, that terrible threat of the Lord which he foretold through the prophet: ‘If, when I say to the wicked, “You shall surely die,” you do not announce it to him, I shall require his blood from your hand’ (Ezek. III). Therefore, since we have been appointed watchmen in the house of God, let us not neglect to point out to the king his dangers. If necessary, let him be summoned to repentance by examples: let him learn how the emperor Maximus, who compelled Saint Martin to share in the company of the impious, was driven from the empire, and how Clodomir, who did not obey the priest Avitus, perished.”

When none of them even then offered a reply, some flatterers informed the king that no one resisted him more stubbornly than Gregory of Tours. He was immediately summoned by a court official. The king stood beside a tent covered with branches, with Bertrannus, bishop of Bordeaux, clinging to his right hand and Ragnemodus, bishop of Paris, to his left. The king addressed the bishop as follows:

“Tell me, lord bishop, you who preserve the path of justice for everyone else: why do you deny it to me? But, as I see, you agree with the wicked, and the common proverb is fulfilled in you: ‘A crow does not pluck out a crow’s eye.’”

The priest replied: “O king, many will correct me if I abandon equity. But who will correct you when you do wrong, except the one who confesses himself to be the avenger of sins? Therefore, if you disdain to listen to us when we admonish you concerning justice, you will be condemned more by God than by us.”

The king answered: “I always prevail in the cause of justice with others, but never with you. Yet I have found an excellent means of taking revenge. If I persuade the people of Tours to cry out that you deny them the rights of equity, I too shall proclaim that I, although I possess royal dignity, am unable to obtain from you anything they themselves demand. Thus, when hatred of the people has arisen against you, you will be branded as unjust.”

The bishop replied: “Whether I am unjust is known more to God than to anyone else. But if you reject our admonitions, take up the sacred canons and, at least by agreeing with them, issue just decrees.”

At last the king, crafty as he was, began to soothe the bishop’s spirit in the following manner. A table stood before them, with bread and various dishes laid upon it. The king said to the priest:

“Look, I have prepared a dish for your sake, containing nothing but chickpeas and the flesh of birds. Now eat of it gladly with me.”

Blessed Gregory replied that no food was more pleasing to him than doing the will of his Father who is in heaven. He asked the king to promise that he would do nothing contrary to the canons. Chilperic raised his hands and swore by the One who lives forever that he would not transgress the decrees of the holy Fathers.

At dawn on the following day, envoys of Queen Fredegund came to the lodging of the aforesaid bishop. They asked him to consent, together with the other bishops, to the deposition of Praetextatus, and offered him two pounds of silver as a gift. They claimed that they had already secured the agreement of the others. He refused, declaring that he would in no way consent even if a thousand pounds were offered to him. When they pressed him more insistently, he finally promised that he would give his brothers his assent in accordance with the decrees of the canons.

Thinking that they had obtained what they wanted, they withdrew with thanks. Then certain priests arrived asking for similar concessions. The bishop gave them the same reply as he had given the others.

When the bishops assembled in council, King Chilperic arrived and said that he had found in the decrees of the canons “that a bishop liable for theft ought to be deprived of his sacred orders.” The king was educated in letters. When the bishops asked which of them was being accused of theft, the king said:

“Have you forgotten how much I showed you that Praetextatus stole from me?”

The previous day the king had displayed various ornaments, valued at three thousand solidi, together with a purse filled with two thousand gold coins. He said that all these things had been stolen from him by the bishop.

But Praetextatus easily cleared himself of the charges and replied to the king as follows:

“Your Excellency, my lord king, may recall, if you deign to do so, that when Brunichild was leaving Rouen she entrusted many packages of various kinds to me. After some time she sent servants to reclaim them from me. When I consulted your will concerning this matter, obeying your commands I handed them one package, since they were unable to carry any more. When they came again, and a third time, I returned the rest at your order, your Magnificence telling me to get rid of these things so that anger might not again arise between you. Only these two packages remained with me. Now, then, of what theft do you accuse me of being guilty?”

The king replied: “If this is how matters stand and you accepted these things for safekeeping, why did you then tear away a golden border woven with threads of gold and distribute it, for our humiliation, to those whom you pleased?”

The priest replied: “I have already answered this once, and now I say again that I gave those things to them for no other reason than to return equal gratitude for the gifts they had granted me. As for taking some of the entrusted property when my own possessions had run out, confidence gave me the boldness to do so, because Meroveus—whose marriage she had sought—was physically begotten by you but, through baptism, was my spiritual son.”

Chilperic perceived that Praetextatus could not be overcome in this way. He left the council and summoned certain flatterers, saying to them:

“I admit that I have been defeated by the bishop’s words, and I know that what he says is true. But, to satisfy Queen Fredegund, go and, as though speaking on your own behalf, give her this advice: ‘You know that our lord Chilperic is a merciful king and quickly forgives those who confess. Go, therefore, fall at his feet, confess that you have sinned against him, and he will immediately forgive you.’”

When they carried out his orders, Praetextatus was deceived by their trickery. They also promised that they themselves would kiss the king’s feet so that he might forgive him.

On the following day, while the bishops were seated in council, Chilperic again began to dispute with Praetextatus, saying:

“If you returned gifts for gifts, why did you demand oaths on Meroveus’s behalf against my welfare?”

The priest replied: “I have made known to Your Highness that I received Meroveus from the saving baptismal font. Therefore, if it had been possible, I would even have summoned the angel of the Lord to his aid.”

What more is there to say? As the dispute continued at greater length, Praetextatus fell at the king’s feet, crying out:

“Have mercy, most merciful king, upon the murderer who wished to drive you from the kingdom and set your son in your place.”

As he spoke, the king himself prostrated himself at the feet of the other priests seated in the synod and said:

“Listen, most holy priests, to this utterly wicked criminal confessing an abominable crime.”

Nevertheless, while the bishops were raising the king from the ground, the king ordered Praetextatus to leave the church. He himself withdrew to the royal residence and sent to the synod certain canons, together with a newly added quire containing the following provision:

“A bishop found guilty of homicide or of other criminal sins shall be deprived of his sacred orders.”

When these words had been read and Praetextatus stood in astonishment, Bertrannus, bishop of Bordeaux, said to him:

“Listen, brother and once fellow bishop: unless you win the king’s favor, you will not be able to enjoy our fellowship.”

After this, Chilperic asked the bishops either to tear Praetextatus’s clothing, or to recite over him the one hundred and eighth psalm, which contains the curses against Judas Iscariot, or at least to deprive him of communion forever. But the bishops refused to do this, and Gregory of Tours resisted especially strongly. Praetextatus was expelled from the church and handed over to custody. When he attempted to escape from there by night, he was beaten and then exiled to a certain island in the sea adjacent to the city of Constancia.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. King Guntrannus of the Burgundians’s Address to Childebert

[Col. 0712B]

King Guntrannus of the Burgundians sent word to Childebert, king of the Austrasians and his nephew, asking him to meet him peacefully with the nobles of his kingdom at the bridge called the Stone Bridge. After lingering for a long time in the embrace of his arriving nephew, he spoke as follows in the hearing of everyone:

“It has happened, through the impediments caused by my sins, that I have been deprived of the sons born to me. Therefore, being bereft of heirs of my own, I must seek outsiders to whom I may leave the treasures I have acquired. I have judged it best to choose you, Childebert, nephew dearer to me than all human flesh, so that you might be both successor to my kingdom and possessor of the treasure I have accumulated. Therefore, I ask that the affection which ought to remain between father and son continue between us. May one shield protect us, and one spear defend us against our adversaries. From this day forward, may such love remain between us that, if God grants me sons, I shall nevertheless not exclude you from the hereditary right.”

After these words, and after Childebert’s nobles pledged themselves on his behalf, since he was still a child, they dined together, honored one another with gifts, and returned to their own territories. Nevertheless, they both sent envoys to King Chilperic, warning him either to return what he had seized from their kingdom or to prepare himself for war. At that time he treated the warning with contempt.

At this period an evil rumor arose against the bishops Salonius and Sagittarius. Saint Nicetius, bishop of Lyon, had brought them up and had first promoted them through the ranks of the diaconate and then of the priesthood. He appointed Salonius bishop at Embrun and Sagittarius bishop at Vapingus. But they did not devote themselves to the discipline proper to bishops; rather, like tyrants, they occupied themselves with homicides, invasions of other people’s property, and adulteries.

Their wickedness increased to such an extent that, when Victor, bishop of Troyes, was celebrating the feast of his birthday, they attacked him with a military troop, tore his clothing, beat and drove away his servants, seized all the provisions prepared for the banquet, and left him alone amid this humiliation. When this matter reached King Guntrannus’s ears, a synod was assembled by his order at Lyon. Saint Nicetius presided and expelled them from their own sees after they had been convicted.

They were deeply indignant at this. Securing the king’s favor, they received letters from him and went to Pope John at Rome. Persuading him that they had been condemned unjustly, they brought his letters to the king, ordering that they be restored to their sees. The king rebuked them in words and ordered them to return to their own cities.

They made peace with Victor, but sent him the men who had inflicted injuries upon him, so that he might take revenge upon them. Remembering the Lord’s command and not repaying evil with evil, Victor dismissed them unharmed to their homes.

Finally, Salonius and Sagittarius, adding worse deeds each day to their worst deeds, went on the expedition that Mummolus conducted against the Lombards and committed many homicides. They acted with equal cruelty toward their own fellow citizens, beating many of them until blood flowed.

When this was reported to King Guntrannus, he ordered them to be brought before him but kept them away from his presence until the hearing. Sagittarius took this so badly that, speaking shamefully of the king, he publicly proclaimed: “The king’s sons will not reign, because their mother belonged to the family of Magnacharius.” The king’s sons were in fact still alive.

For this reason the king was angered. He took away their horses and everything they possessed, and assigned them to do penance in two monasteries far apart from one another. He ordered his own judges, stationed around those places, to guard them with the utmost vigilance and armed protection, lest they escape.

At that time, when the king’s elder son happened to be ill, certain members of his household approached him and advised him to order the aforesaid bishops to return to their own churches, lest perhaps, because of their condemnation, God’s anger should fall upon the ruler’s house.

The king did not reject their request. Salonius and Sagittarius returned to their sees and presented themselves as such outstanding cultivators of holy religion that, reciting the entire Psalter in order every day, they seemed never to cease from psalmody. Yet shortly afterward they returned so completely to their own vomit that, devoting themselves to fornication and drunkenness, they remained at banquets and demanded wine while the clerics sang the morning hymns. At the beginning of dawn, wrapped in soft coverings, they slept until the third hour of the day. Since they lived in such ways, putting God behind their backs, they too were put behind by God and incurred his anger, as we shall show in what follows.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Chilperic’s Cruelty toward Ennodius and the Other Supporters of Childebert, and the Revolt of the Britons

[Col. 0713D]

In those days Chilperic seized the city of Poitiers, and the faithful men of his nephew, King Childebert, together with the commander Ennodius, were driven out by Chilperic’s men. Ennodius was sent into exile, and his property was confiscated for the treasury; after a year he was restored to his homeland and to his possessions.

Dacco, son of Gadaricus, abandoned Chilperic and wandered everywhere. He was captured by the commander Draccolenus, who was called Industrius, through treachery. Draccolenus swore to him that he would not kill him. But when he had brought him before the king, he arranged for him to be put to death.

When Dacco learned this while in custody, he confessed his sins to a certain priest and, without the king’s knowledge, asked for penance. After receiving it, he was killed. Draccolenus, for his part, was killed by the commander Guntrannus in the manner we have described.

At that time the Britons, devastating the region of Rennes with great severity, reached a village called Cornutus. Commander Bibolenus was sent against them and pursued them as they withdrew; he ravaged Brittany with sword and fire. This provoked the Britons to even greater anger, so that in the following year they attacked not only the region of Rennes but also that of Nantes. Although they promised, through envoys, to make amends to Felix, bishop of Nantes, they proved false to their word.

## CHAPTER XXX. The Violation and Restoration of the Church of Dionysius

At that time a certain woman was accused by a jealous husband at Paris of being an adulteress.
