She sought help from her relatives, who believed her innocent and swore on her behalf before the tomb of Saint Dionysius, either to the husband or to his relatives. They were then rebuked by the opposing party for having sworn falsely.

When the dispute broke out into a quarrel, neither side would yield to the other because of their nobility—for they were leading men in the palace of King Chilperic. They struck one another with swords and polluted the sacred basilica with blood.

Meanwhile the church remained without divine services. When these events were reported to the king, he declared under threat that he would show neither of them any favor until, through the reconciliation of Ragnemodus, bishop of Paris, in whose diocese these things had occurred, they earned forgiveness. The bishop restored them to communion after they confessed their crime and had been assigned penance, and he reconciled the church.

## CHAPTER XXXI. The Dreadful Death of Nantinus of Angoulême

[Col. 0714C]

At that time Nantinus, count of Angoulême, suffered a severe divinely inflicted punishment of death for the following reason. His maternal uncle Maracharius had long held the countship of the aforesaid city. Entering the clerical state, he became a bishop after not much time had passed. His adversaries wickedly murdered him by introducing poison into the head of a fish, but they did not long rejoice.

For Frontonius, on whose advice this crime had been committed, held the bishopric for only one year after him. When Heraclius, a priest of Bordeaux, succeeded him, Nantinus—who had purchased the countship from the king in order to avenge his uncle’s death—rebuked him most severely for retaining his uncle’s murderers.

As the dispute grew more serious, the count seized the church estates that his uncle had left by testament, asserting that he ought not to retain testaments whose testator had been killed by his clergy. After his anger blazed up still more cruelly, and after he had killed certain laymen as well, he ordered one of the priests, who had been wounded with a spear, to be hanged while still alive and compelled to confess his crime. He hung there for a long time with his hands bound behind his back; blood flowed from the open wound, and he gave up his spirit innocent.

For these many crimes Nantinus was excommunicated by Heraclius. Some priests gathered at the city of Saintes, and he asked them to intercede with the bishop on his behalf, promising that he would restore the church’s property and correct the wrongs he had committed. The bishop agreed to the brothers’ requests and restored him to communion.

But when the count returned to Angoulême, he destroyed the houses he had seized, saying: “If this church receives them, at least let them be found deserted.” When the bishop heard this, he again deprived him of communion and died.

Nantinus was also restored to communion by certain bishops corrupted by money, and then fell ill. When he was tormented by a violent fever, he cried out:

“Alas! Alas! What torments inflicted by Heraclius I suffer! He himself now torments me; I am consumed by his fire. I ask for death, lest I live long in misery.”

He died while uttering these words. Let those who inflict injuries upon priests or upon those who desire to serve God hear this. Let them understand that God is the avenger of those who are unjustly oppressed.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Chilperic’s Cruelty toward His Subjects through Fredegund

King Chilperic also, at the urging of Queen Fredegund, began to crush his subject people with the harshest proscriptions. For this reason many commoners, abandoning their native soil, preferred to seek new dwelling places in exile rather than perish in their ancestral territories under the unjust burden of taxation.

Among the other things they were compelled to pay, even those born of freer families had to bring to the royal table an amphora of wine from their own land, cultivated by their own labor. Marcus the referendary was placed in charge of this levy and was sent to urge, by words or threats, all the cities of Aquitaine that seemed to belong to Chilperic’s kingdom to pay it. When a revolt arose among the people of Limoges, he was slaughtered, and all the registers he was carrying with him were burned in the fire.

Chilperic, meanwhile, adding worse deeds each day to his worst deeds, was seized by a severe fever. When he recovered from this illness, his little son, who had not yet received baptism, began to fall gravely ill. After receiving the grace of baptism, the boy improved for a short time, but could not make his mother rejoice with complete joy. For as he recovered, she grieved that his older brother Clodobert had contracted a similar illness.

Thus the hidden plague spread through the entire royal offspring, as though passing from the father’s entrails into the limbs of the sons and seeking to claim for itself an inherited dwelling there. At last Fredegund, whose heart was torn by grief whenever she saw her children’s half-dead bodies, forgot her former savagery and assumed a human compassion of spirit. She approached the king and addressed him as follows:

“We ought, my husband, to respond with good deeds to the divine benefits bestowed upon us, since heavenly clemency has not punished us even though we have persisted in wickedness for so long. We have not endured the scourges of almighty God as criminals, but, chastened by the rod through our sons, we have experienced in ourselves the prophetic saying: ‘The Lord chastises every son whom he receives’ (Heb. XII).

“For behold, we have often been afflicted by fevers and various calamities, and in addition we are losing the embraces of our dearest sons, whom the tears of widows and orphans unjustly oppressed by us have brought near to death. Let us finally repent of the evils we have committed, and, turning to the Lord, let us beseech him to be appeased toward our wickedness. He will not reject us as we plead before him, unworthy though we are, because he is merciful and compassionate.

“Let us therefore burn the unjust tax assessments, and erase, for our salvation and that of our people, the assessments that we established to oppress the poor. We have nothing to fear if we truly repent, as though we were about to suffer severe things when we have already endured the most severe. What can be more grievous than losing what is dearer? And what could be sweeter to us than the affection of our children?

“For whom, moreover, are we preserving the treasures acquired over so many years, if we send ahead the heirs whom we had hoped would become our successors? We must be careful lest we incur the sentence of that rich man in the Gospel who, enlarging his barns and gathering great wealth, received the answer that he would not see the following day or know the heir of his possessions. But he who has exacted vengeance may now be favorable, and gentler than if he had not exacted it.”

By continually repeating words of this kind, Queen Fredegund led King Chilperic away from his anger and so softened his purpose that with his own hand he gave the documents containing the abominable law to the devouring flames.

After this had been done, their younger son died. His little body was buried in the oratory of the holy martyrs Dionysius and his companions. Not much time had passed when Clodobert, the other son mentioned above, also began to approach death. The terrified mother, groaning anxiously over her suffering son, carried him to the basilica of Saint Medard at Soissons. There both parents honored the saint’s tomb with vows and gifts of gold. But when night came, the sick boy breathed out his final breath.

The people of the aforesaid city, clothed all around in black garments and mourning greatly, accompanied his funeral to the church of Saints Crispinus and Crispinianus. There the king’s son received burial in a tomb.

In the following year another of Chilperic’s sons, named Theodoric, reached the end of his life. Chilperic, recognizing that the judgment of divine retribution threatened his own neck, gave many gifts to Christ’s poor or to the churches.

Only one member of the royal offspring still remained. At Fredegund’s prompting, Chilperic handed him over to the guards, consigning him to custody for punishment. Chilperic’s wickedness had become so inflamed that it was not enough for him that heavenly vengeance threatened his family; he had to increase it through his own crimes.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Floods, Storms, Earthquakes, and Many Portents

In the fifth year of King Childebert—which was the nineteenth year of Chilperic and Guntrannus—such floods occurred throughout all the regions of Gaul that the rivers passed beyond boundaries they had never previously exceeded. They brought destruction upon livestock and inflicted severe ruin upon buildings in every place. When the rivers returned to the limits of their channels and the rains ceased, the trees blossomed again around the month called September.

At that time lightning also seemed to run across the sky, and a sound like falling trees was heard over almost the entire land. The city of Bordeaux was shaken by an earthquake. Immense stones were torn from the Pyrenean mountains, and an immense multitude of animals and human beings was struck and killed by them.

A village of Bordeaux was set on fire by a divinely kindled blaze, increased by no human agency. It burned many people, suddenly seizing houses and courtyards filled with crops. The city of Orléans was devastated by a similar fire.

In the district of Chartres, blood flowed from broken bread. [Col. 0717B] In the city of Poitiers, a wolf came from the forests and entered through a gate. When the gate was closed along with the others, the citizens killed the wolf in the middle of the city.

The sky also appeared to burn, and the river Loire rose higher than usual. A south wind was so violent that it laid forests low, uprooted houses and hedges, and rolled people about to their death. The whirlwind covered a width of seven acres at the place where it was seen to pass, although its length could not be estimated.

But these portents were followed by grievous evils. Discord arose among the kings and stirred up civil wars, while an outbreak of dysentery seized almost all Gaul. Queen Austrigild, wife of King Guntrannus, suffered from this plague and brought a complaint against the physicians before her husband, as though her illness had become worse through their negligence.

By Guntrannus’s order, the physicians died under various punishments. She herself then weakened and died.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Envoys Captured and Released; the Praiseworthy Death of Bishop Maurilius, and Gregory of Tours’s Victory for the Catholic Faith

In those days Chilperic captured at Poitiers the envoys whom Mir, king of Galicia and ruler of the Suebi, had sent to King Guntrannus, and placed them in custody at Paris. Nevertheless, after a year he released them and sent them back to their own country.

Maurilius, bishop of Cahors, while applying heated iron to his shins or feet because of the illness of gout, contracted a severe sickness. As it grew worse, and while many were seeking the bishopric, he chose Ursicinus and, while still alive, had him blessed as his successor. Thus he departed from this world.

He was exceedingly generous in almsgiving and so learned in the divine Scriptures that he often recited the genealogies of the Old Testament from memory. He supported the poor of his church against the oppression of unjust judges, so that he might sing to the Lord the words of Job:

“I was a father to the poor, and I investigated their case with the greatest diligence” (Job XXIX).

At that time Gregory of Tours also engaged in a dispute concerning the faith of the Holy Trinity with Egila, envoy of Leovigild, king of the Spaniards, whom Leovigild had sent to Chilperic. Since Egila was an Arian, Gregory engaged him in controversy and wonderfully overcame him. Although Egila had denied that he would ever become a Catholic, illness nevertheless compelled him to embrace that religion.

## CHAPTER XXXV. The Death of Tiberius Constantine and the Succession of Maurice to the Empire

After Tiberius Constantine had ruled the empire for seven years, he perceived that the day of his summons was approaching. With the counsel of the empress Sophia, he chose Maurice, a Cappadocian by birth and an energetic man, for the empire, and gave him his daughter, adorned with royal ornaments. He said:

“May the empire be granted to you together with this girl. Use it successfully, bearing in mind that equity and justice are the chief insignia of an excellent emperor.”

After saying this, he laid aside his bodily burden and migrated to his eternal homeland, leaving the peoples subject to him in deep mourning for his death. He was a man of supreme goodness, prompt in almsgiving, most cautious in judgment, despising no one and loving everyone; he himself was also loved by all.

After his death, Maurice, clothed in purple and crowned with a diadem, proceeded to the circus. When praises had been shouted for him and he had distributed gifts to the people, as is customary, he was the first of Greek descent to be confirmed in the imperial office.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The First King of the Lombards
At that time, however, after the Lombards had been under the authority of dukes for ten years, they finally established Flavius Authari, son of the aforementioned prince Cleph, as their king by common agreement. To enable him to restore the kingdom, the dukes who then held office contributed half of their entire property, so that the king himself and those serving him in the various offices could be supported from it. This was indeed remarkable among the Lombard people: there was no violence, no ambushes were laid; everyone went wherever he wished, safely and without fear.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. How the Emperor Maurice stirred up the Franks against the Lombards

At this time the emperor Maurice sent fifty thousand solidi through his envoys to Childebert, king of the Franks, chiefly for this purpose: that he might invade the Lombards with an army and drive them from Italy. Without delay, Childebert suddenly entered Italy with an immeasurable multitude of Franks. The Lombards, however, abandoning hope of joining battle, entrusted themselves to the fortifications of their cities and, when envoys intervened and gifts were offered, made an agreement with Childebert. When he had returned to Gaul, the emperor Maurice learned that he had made a treaty with the Lombards and began demanding back the solidi that he had given him for the expulsion of the Lombards. But Childebert, relying on the power of his own forces, would not even give him an answer on this matter.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The persecution of Catholics in Spain

In those days a dreadful persecution of the Catholics arose in Spain, occasioned in the following way by Gadsunda, the mother of Brunichildis. Hermenegild, son of King Leovigild, had as his wife the sister of Childebert. Hermenegild had been converted from the Arian heresy—which afflicted his father—to the Catholic faith through the preaching of Leander, bishop of Seville, and through the exhortation of his wife. Gadsunda, however, tried to persuade her granddaughter Ingundis to have her husband killed by some sort of death. Since she could not accomplish this, she persuaded the king to order his son and his wife to live in another city, saying that she was offended because they belonged to another faith.

When Hermenegild was not at all moved by this insult to deny the sacraments of the true faith, his impious father shut him in prison. Later, on the very holy day of Easter, he had him struck with an axe and killed.

After the burial of her husband and martyr, Ingundis fled from Spain. While she was making her way back to the native fields of Gaul, she fell into the hands of soldiers guarding the frontier of Spain against the Goths. Captured with her little son and taken to Sicily, she there ended her life. Her son was sent to the emperor Maurice at Constantinople. When Childebert learned of his sister’s captivity and was informed of what had been done to her, he led an army into Spain, fought the Goths, inflicted a great defeat upon them, and returned victorious.

Again the emperor Maurice sent envoys to Childebert, asking him to send an army against the Lombards. Childebert, supposing that his sister was still living at Constantinople, agreed to Maurice’s envoys and again sent a Frankish army into Italy against the Lombards, so that he might recover his sister. But while the Lombards were preparing to draw up their battle line and meet their opponents, the Franks and Alemanni, who were at odds with one another, returned home without gaining any advantage.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Benedict and Pelagius, Roman bishops; Mummolus’s flight to Avignon; Childebert’s defection to Chilperic; Lupus, duke of Champagne; Chilperic’s expedition against the Petrocorii; the death of Baudastis; the holiness of the recluse Hospitius; the passing of blessed Martin of Galicia; and a comet and heavenly portent

After John, Benedict assumed the governance of the Roman Church. After him Pelagius was ordained without the prince’s authorization, because the Lombards were besieging Rome and no one could depart from Rome.

The patrician Mummolus, defecting from King Guntrannus, withdrew to the fortress of Avignon, where he prepared to defend himself with arms against his pursuers and to strengthen himself with other resources.

Childebert also, abandoning his peace with Guntrannus, joined Chilperic. Chilperic promised that, since he had no children, he would make Childebert heir to his kingdom. In this promise, as in other matters, he proved to be a liar.

Lupus, duke of Champagne, was put to flight by Ursio and Bertefridus. When he was already on the point of being captured or killed, together with his army, Brunichildis intervened on his behalf and rescued him from the impending danger. Nevertheless, the aforementioned dukes handed over his stronghold for plunder.

Chilperic sent the duke Desiderius with organized forces to invade the Aquitanian cities of Petrocorium and Agennum. After putting the duke Ragnoald to flight, Desiderius invaded those cities and stripped Ragnoald’s wife of all her possessions.

The duke Baudastis perished in Wasconia with most of his army.

At that time there was a certain recluse, a servant of God named Hospitius, near the city of Nice. He was bound in iron chains over his naked body and covered above with a hair shirt. On other days he ate plain bread and a few dates; during Lent he was nourished by the roots and herbs produced by the wilderness. Through him, while he still lived on earth in the body alone, the Lord deigned to display many miracles, to the praise and glory of his name.

At that time blessed Martin of Galicia departed to the Lord. He was born in Pannonia, traveled throughout the holy places in the East, and there richly instructed himself in learning. Returning through Galicia, he was ordained bishop in the basilica that was the first among the Spaniards to be dedicated in honor of Saint Martin, and he completed thirty years in this office.

In the seventh year of King Childebert, which was the twenty-first of Chilperic and Guntrannus, a comet appeared on the holy day of Easter. At the city of Soissons the sky seemed to burn. In the district of Paris, blood flowing from a cloud stained the clothing of many people. Various illnesses and a great mortality afflicted the people of the Franks that year.

## CHAPTER XL. The death and piety of the duke Rodinus

At that time the duke Rodinus also died. He was a true giver of alms, full of goodness, conducting himself justly in everything and loving the poor of Christ.

One day, when he wished to bury a dead man, he ordered his servants to open a certain tomb in which he could place the deceased. When they had promptly carried this out, they found a treasure of immense weight and a considerable quantity of solidi. They lifted it from the ground and carried it before their master.

Understanding it to be a heavenly gift, Rodinus distributed it all to the poor, as he was accustomed to do, sending back through the hands of the needy the talent entrusted to him, doubled, to the one from whom he had received it. Many signs and wonders were also seen in the sky that year.

## CHAPTER XLI. Chilperic’s lapse into the Sabellian heresy and his repentance

At the same time King Chilperic, wishing to promulgate the Sabellian heresy, wrote to the bishops of Gaul ordering them, after rejecting the Trinity, to say that there was only one God. He asserted:

> “The Father is the same as the Son or the Holy Spirit, and the Son and the Holy Spirit are the same as the Father; nor can any distinction of persons in God exist in any way.”

When he tried to persuade Gregory of Tours, who at that time surpassed the other bishops in holiness, and yet admitted that Hilary and Augustine were opposed to him in this matter, the blessed bishop said to him:

> “My lord king, you must beware lest the one whose servants those men were become angry with you, since, as you yourself admit, they disagree with this belief.”

When the king replied with a jest that wiser men than he should be consulted on this matter, the priest said:

> “No one is wise who thinks differently in matters of faith from the way he does.”

When Bishop Salvius of Albi came to the palace, Chilperic tried to persuade him to agree with him, reading aloud a document in which he had written the aforementioned heresy. The blessed man abhorred it so greatly that he threatened, if it should come into his hands, to tear it to pieces and burn it in the fire.

Finally, seeing that everyone thought differently from him, the king abandoned that intention. He added the Greek letter omega, ω, to our letters, as well as three others, whose characters he had himself invented; we have written them below with their respective sounds: χ, ch; θ, th; φ, ph. He then sent letters to the cities subject to him, ordering that boys be taught these letters and that books be rewritten after being smoothed with pumice.

## CHAPTER XLII. The saints Agricola and Dalmatius

In those days Agricola of Chalon and Dalmatius of Rodez, men outstanding in holiness and excellent administrators of the episcopate, departed from this world.

Agricola strengthened the church of his city with columns, embellished it with marble, and decorated it with mosaic. Dalmatius, however, repeatedly destroying his own church while trying to improve it, left it unfinished.

## CHAPTER XLIII. The expulsion of Count Leudastis for his tyranny

At that time Leudastis, count of Tours, was removed from the county because he oppressed the people unjustly and inflicted injuries upon Bishop Gregory, although he had often given him sworn assurances that he would never harm him.

When Eunomius succeeded him, Leudastis, inflamed with resentment against the bishop as though these events had occurred through Gregory’s counsel, went to the king. He accused Gregory of wishing to hand over the city of Tours to King Guntrannus and of saying many evil things about the queen, asserting that she was having an affair with Bertrannus, bishop of Bordeaux.

He had a cleric named Riculfus as an accomplice, who plotted many schemes against his master. The king therefore ordered a synod to be assembled because of what had been said about the queen.

When the bishops had assembled at the estate of Brittannicum, and Bertrannus complained that the charge had been unjustly brought against him, Gregory, by decree of the brethren, swore three times that he had never said such a thing. Although they recognized that this contradicted the authorities, they nevertheless carried it out in order to satisfy the king.

For this reason the bishops approached the king and said:

> “Our brother and fellow bishop Gregory has shown by his oaths that he is innocent. What do you now think should be done with you, or with Bishop Bertrannus, who brought this accusation against our brother, unless you too are deprived of communion?”

The king replied that he himself had not said these things but had merely reported what Leudastis had told him. Leudastis was sought but not found—for, fearing for himself, he had fled the hearing. The bishops excommunicated him and wrote to those who were absent, instructing them not to receive him into communion.

Those present on that occasion admired the king’s extraordinary patience. Although such a crime had been spread abroad concerning the queen that it would also bring disgrace upon himself, he was never so disturbed in spirit as to oppress anyone unjustly. This, however, was certainly not his usual practice on other occasions. He merely ordered that Leudastis, because he had given false testimony against the bishop, be expelled as an excommunicate from his entire kingdom.

Leudastis then transported from the city of Tours into the territory of the Bituriges all his possessions that had been granted to him through the king’s favor. After wandering for a long time here and there, he was eventually reconciled to the Church and restored to the king’s favor after a long period of years.

Bishop Gregory warned him to beware of the queen, whose anger against him was inflamed. Disregarding the warning, Leudastis, while she was praying in a certain church, threw himself at her feet. She scorned him. After he had left the oratory and wished to buy certain goods in order to win the queen over with gifts, her servants surrounded him.

After striking one of them with a sword, Leudastis was put to flight by the others. In the middle of the bridge of the city of Paris, his foot slipped between two timbers and he broke his shin. He was carried away and, by order of the king, transported to an estate for treatment. There, the queen’s agents smashed his throat between two poles, and he ended his wretched life.

Thus perished the man who, in order to bring a charge against his bishop, had thrown many people into chains and had even subjected some to beatings. Nor was he any less criminal in his own earlier offenses. Born among the fiscal slaves, he was first assigned to the royal kitchen. But because his eyes were bleary, he was transferred from there to the bakery. There, while pretending to enjoy himself among the masses of dough, he escaped from servitude. When he was repeatedly recaptured and returned, he was branded by the cutting off of an ear.

Unable to conceal this injury, he went to the wife of King Charibert. By flattery he became very intimate with her and was appointed keeper of the horses. From there, after obtaining command over the other keepers, he received the county of Tours from Charibert after the queen’s death. From this office he was removed with the disgrace mentioned above.

The cleric Riculfus, who had not hesitated to give false testimony against his own bishop, endured such scourging at the king’s command that, even if he had been made of bronze, he would still have presented a spectacle to those watching by enduring such torments. He was nevertheless rescued from capital punishment through the intervention of blessed Gregory.

Amid tortures and beatings, Riculfus confessed that he had invented such accusations against the queen so that, once she had been driven from the kingdom, Clovis—who alone of Chilperic’s sons remained—might receive the kingdom from his father and reign.

This Clovis, born to Chilperic by another wife, had been ordered by his father, at the queen’s instigation, to remain at the estate of Brenacum after the deaths of the king’s sons born to Fredegundis, so that he too might die of an illness like that of his brothers. At that time the plague of dysentery was raging in the same district.

When Clovis escaped the danger of death, he perceived his stepmother’s schemes and contemptuously reviled her, boasting that he alone had been left heir to the kingdom. Nevertheless, there were some who used the art of informing against him. They reported to the queen not only the insulting things he himself said about her but also certain lies, claiming that her sons had died through the magical arts of the mother of a certain little prostitute who was accustomed to sleep with Clovis.

When the queen heard this, she was moved to anger and ordered the girl to be beaten and impaled on a stake before Clovis’s lodging. She had the girl’s mother torn by beatings and forced her to confess that what had been reported was true.

When she demanded vengeance from the king, the king, having gone hunting, ordered his son to be bound and sent to him. The queen shut him in prison and questioned him about the truth of the matter and about which nobles supported him. He confessed none of the crimes but disclosed his friends and associates.

After two days she ordered him taken across the Marne to an estate called Nocetum and killed there in prison with a knife. She had it conveyed to the king through secretly introduced agents that Clovis had killed himself and that the knife still remained in the wound. When the king heard this, he felt no grief for his son’s death and ordered him to be buried there.

Clovis’s mother was cruelly killed, and his sister, abused by the queen’s servants, was forced into a monastery. The woman who had spoken against him was sentenced to be burned alive. Although she cried out in vain that she had lied, she was tied to a stake and burned alive.

Clovis’s treasurer, seized by Cupan, count of the Stables, from Bourges and sent bound to the queen, was released by her from his chains and punishments at the request of blessed Gregory, bishop of Tours.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Chilperic’s spectacles; Salvius’s vision and what followed

At the same time Chilperic ordered circuses to be built at Soissons and Paris and provided spectacles for the people.

After the aforementioned synod, while the blessed Gregory was returning to his own city and was engaged in familiar conversation with Saint Salvius in the courtyard of the royal house, the man of God Salvius said to him:

> “Do you see, brother, what I see above the roof of the hall?”

When Gregory replied that he saw nothing except the tiles that the king had recently ordered to be laid, and asked him to point out anything else he saw—he thought Salvius was joking in his usual manner—Salvius said again:

> “I see the sword of God’s wrath hanging over this house.”

His prophecy was not in vain. For twenty days later two of the king’s sons died; we shall speak of them shortly.

The archbishop Gregory himself, one night after the matins hymns, while lying on his bed, saw an angel of God flying above the church. In a clear voice the angel said:

> “Alas! God has struck Chilperic and all his sons. Of those now living, no one will succeed him in his kingdom.”

At that time four sons were still surviving.

At this time a synod assembled at Lyon and disciplined many bishops who were acting negligently.

## CHAPTER XLV. The blessing rejected by the Jew and sought by Chilperic; and the death of the recluse Eparchius

Meanwhile Chilperic, staying at an estate called Novientum and preparing to set out for Paris, asked the aforementioned Bishop Gregory to lay hands on a certain Jew named Priscus, who was very close to him.

The Jew resisted, protested that he did not believe, and moreover disparaged our faith. The blessed bishop rebuked him in a sufficiently appropriate disputation. The king then said:

> “Because this unbeliever rejects the blessing, it will surely withdraw from him as well. But I say to you in the words of Jacob, with which he addressed the angel wrestling against him: ‘I will not let you go unless you bless me’ (Genesis 32).”

The bishop therefore blessed the king, ate with him, and returned to his own city.

At that time Eparchius, a recluse at Engolismum, died. He was a man of magnificent holiness who restored to life a man hanged on the gallows for theft.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Theodorus, bishop of Marseille, and Lupus, a citizen of Tours; an eclipse of the moon, a miraculous flow of blood, and other portents

In those days Theodorus, bishop of Marseille, was unjustly arrested and mistreated by Dinamius, governor of Provence. While he was proceeding from there as a free man to King Childebert, he was again seized by King Guntrannus.

When his clerics, who hated him, heard this, they invaded the property of the Church and plundered its storerooms. They also falsely brought accusations against the bishop himself.

King Childebert then sent a message to his uncle, King Guntrannus, ordering that the part of Marseille which he had given him after the death of his father be returned to him; otherwise, he should know that he would lose still more.

When Guntrannus refused to agree and moreover ordered the roads in his kingdom to be guarded so that none of his nephew’s subjects might reach Marseille, Childebert appointed Gundulf, a man of senatorial rank and his own household officer, as duke and sent him to the city in question.

On his way through the city of Tours, Gundulf was recognized by the blessed Gregory, who was his maternal uncle, and was most hospitably entertained by him for five days. After receiving the necessities for his journey, he departed.

Dinamius and the clerics denied Gundulf entry into the city, and denied Bishop Theodorus—who, having been released from custody, had already joined Gundulf—entry into the church. Finally they persuaded Dinamius to come down and speak with them in the church of Saint Stephen, which stood near the walls.

When Gundulf arrived there, the doorkeepers admitted him alone and excluded the others who followed him. Gundulf and the bishop led him into the reception room and severely rebuked him.

After those who had come with him and were indignant at not being admitted had been driven away, Gundulf ordered the leading men to be seized, intending to take them into the city so that they would open the gates.

Meanwhile Dinamius, recognizing that he was being held captive, fell at their feet and promised that he would open the gates and thereafter remain faithful both to the king and to the bishop. Released on the strength of his pledge, he received the duke and the bishop into the city while all the people rejoiced.

The clerics who, at his instigation, had acted wickedly against their shepherd were compelled, after going to his house, to provide sureties that they would present themselves to King Childebert.

Gundulf, having recovered Marseille and restored the bishop to his see, returned to the king.

Dinamius, however, disregarding the faith he had promised the bishop, sent messengers to King Guntrannus to say that he wished to surrender the city, but that Theodorus was obstructing him; and that the citizens would not obey him in any way unless the priest were driven into exile somewhere.

Enraged by these words, the king ordered Theodorus to be brought to him in chains. Since the bishop, fearing for himself, did not readily leave the city, an opportunity arose when a suburban basilica had to be dedicated.

As he was hurrying there, his opponents suddenly burst from ambush, drove the clerics and the other attendants into flight after beating them, threw the bishop from his own horse, placed him on a lowly beast, and led him to the king.

When he reached the city of Aix, Bishop Plentius supplied the clerics with provisions and whatever else they needed for the journey.

After examining Theodorus, the king found him free of guilt and ordered him, honored with many gifts, to return to his own church. When the people received him joyfully, he found that the property of the Church and his own possessions had been seized by the clerics.

For these reasons the treaty between Guntrannus and Childebert was broken and immense discord arose.

Nevertheless, while the kings were thus divided from one another, a certain Lupus, a citizen of Tours, whose wife had died and who wished to enter the clergy, was prevented from doing so by his brother Ambrosius. Ambrosius promised that he would find him a wife suitable to his rank.

While he was trying to arrange this, both men were killed by an adulterer who was having sexual relations with Ambrosius’s wife. While each was trying to deprive the other of God and hand him over to the pleasures of the present life, he destroyed both himself and the other.

That year the moon suffered an eclipse, and true blood flowed from a broken loaf of bread within the territory of Tours. In the district of Senlis, the house of a certain man appeared, when he rose in the morning, to have been spattered inside with blood. The wall of Soissons was overturned by divine power. An earthquake occurred at Angers. Within the walls of Bordeaux, wolves entered and devoured dogs, and fire seemed to run across the sky.

## CHAPTER XLVII. The obstinacy and death of Priscus the Jew

At that time King Chilperic ordered many Jews to be baptized and himself received them from the sacred font. Yet he could not persuade his familiar Priscus, mentioned above, to believe.

He therefore ordered Priscus to be handed over to custody. Priscus bribed him to give him time to marry his son to a Hebrew woman from Marseille, promising that he would then fulfill the order. But he refused to confess Christ and, not long afterward, descended to hell.

For when a quarrel arose between him and a certain Patir, a convert from Judaism, Patir struck him with a sword and he died.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Chilperic’s vengeance upon Guntrannus for the killing of the guards at the Paris bridge

At the bridge of the city of Paris the aforementioned prince had stationed guards so that raiders coming from the kingdom of his brother Guntrannus might be kept away.

Asclepius, once an office-holder as duke, killed all of them in a single night and laid waste to the district near the bridge.

Therefore Chilperic wished to attack his brother with an army, but, warned by the counsels of good men, he refrained and sent envoys to his brother, asking him to make amends for the wrongs inflicted upon him.

Guntrannus, a lover of justice, did not delay in doing as he was advised. Nevertheless Chilperic, not satisfied with this, took certain cities from his brother, appointed new counts over them, and ordered that their taxes be brought into his own treasury.

## CHAPTER XLIX. The apprehension of the messengers of Bishop Charterius and the birth of Theodoric

In those days Count Nunnichius of Limoges detained two men carrying letters in the name of Charterius, bishop of Périgueux. Among other insults written in them against Chilperic, this was also read:

> “The bishop complained that he had been expelled from paradise and descended into hell.”

By this he clearly meant that the bishop had descended from Guntrannus’s kingdom into Chilperic’s dominion.

The men, together with the informers, were sent to the king, and the bishop was ordered to be brought to give an account of these matters. Since he could not easily be convicted, he was ordered to return unharmed to his own city.

Finally, after the funerals of his sons, a son was born to Chilperic. He had him baptized at Paris at Easter the following year and named him Theodoric.

## CHAPTER L. Childebert’s formal embassy to Chilperic

Childebert sent Egidius, archbishop of Reims, together with other nobles, to his uncle Chilperic to confirm the treaty they had made.

Egidius reported the substance of his embassy in these words:

> “The peace that your illustrious nephew established with you, glorious king, he earnestly asks you to make firm. In the end, he cannot make use of the goodwill of your brother because he unjustly retains part of his territory around Marseille and refuses to return his fugitives to him. Therefore, if you attack him with united forces and in agreement with one another, due vengeance for the injuries inflicted by him can easily be exacted.”

The king replied:

> “My brother’s guilt is so evident that it can scarcely be concealed. For if my most beloved nephew reviews in his mind his own wrongdoings, setting aside the rest, he will find that his father perished through Guntrannus’s treachery. Therefore I too promise that I will assist him in avenging his father’s death, since I lost a brother whom, if he were alive, I would love greatly.”

When the king had finished speaking, the treaty was confirmed by the exchange of hostages.

Immediately Chilperic ordered an army to set out from his kingdom. It was to besiege the cities subject to his brother and lay waste to the surrounding fields.

Berulfus, the duke of his party, attacked the Bituriges from one side with the men of Tours and Angers; Desiderius and Biadastis attacked from the other with a very large multitude. The king instructed them that, once the city had been captured, they were to exact oaths of allegiance in his name.

The people of Bourges, however, meeting the duke Desiderius near the fortress of Mediolanum, now called Magdunum, opposed him with fifteen thousand armed men and fought him. The other dukes surrounded the city with a siege.

Although Childebert’s army had not yet arrived, Chilperic nevertheless had some of his dukes with him. Leading all his forces through Paris and laying waste to everything, he reached Melun.

Guntrannus did not hesitate to go out to meet him. Placing his hope in God alone, he attacked at dusk the enemy wedge that had been separated from the others through greed and shattered it in utter ruin.

On the following day, when envoys intervened, brother made terms with brother, and each promised to correct the offenses that had been committed.

Chilperic urged his soldiers to abstain from theft and plunder. When they did not obey, he struck the count of Rouen with a sword. In this way he restrained the others, led them back to their own territory, first restoring all the plunder and releasing the captives.

Those who had been besieging Bourges, when they received the order to withdraw, seized everything their eyes saw and their hands could grasp as they returned to their own country.

## CHAPTER LI. The people’s revolt against Bishop Egidius

While Childebert was keeping all the companies of troops he had gathered in one place, a sudden murmur of the lower people against the dukes and Bishop Egidius arose during the following night. They said:

> “Let those who traffic in his kingdom among themselves, and who subject his cities to foreign rule, be removed from the king’s presence.”

At daybreak they hurried armed to the king’s tent in order to kill the bishop Egidius.

When the priest learned of this, he mounted a horse and fled with a few companions. Fear gave such speed to his flight that he did not bother to retrieve the bandage that had slipped from his shin. This, however, helped him, because his opponents did not have horses ready for pursuit.

While they delayed in following him, he took refuge inside the city of Reims.

After this Guntrannus returned to his nephew Childebert the part of Marseille that he had been retaining against his will.

Chilperic, deeply grieved by the death of the son whom, as we have said above, had been born to him, postponed the marriage of his daughter, whom he had at that time betrothed through envoys to the king of Spain.

For this reason, after sending mounted couriers, he recalled the envoy who was returning to Spain and said to him:

> “Burdened with mourning for the death of my son, I cannot celebrate the marriage at the time I had fixed.”

When the envoy persisted, Chilperic wished to send to Spain the daughter whom he had had by Audovera and had entrusted to God in the monastery at Poitiers. But blessed Radegundis prevented him.

## CHAPTER LII. Mummolus accused of magic and sorcery

While these events were taking place, a report reached Queen Fredegundis from certain people. They said that the boy who had recently died had lost his life through the devices of her prefect Mummolus, by means of certain little women’s sorcery and incantations.

Mummolus had long been hostile to the queen. When she heard these things about him, she ordered the prostitutes to be seized and punished. They confessed that they had killed many innocent people through spells and incantations and had sacrificed the queen’s son in exchange for Mummolus’s safety.

The queen then handed some of them over to the flames and fastened others to wheels.

She complained about Mummolus to the king. The king ordered him brought in chains, tied to a beam with his hands bound behind his back and suspended. He questioned him about what sorcery he knew.

Mummolus said that he knew nothing about the death of the king’s son. He confessed only that he had received various potions and incantations from the aforementioned women in order to win the favor of the king and queen.

At last, when he had been taken down, he told the king that he had felt none of the punishments. The king declared him a sorcerer and ordered him to be scourged with very hard thongs and struck with a sword. The queen obtained his life, though with difficulty.

Nevertheless, before long he died from the pain of those tortures.

The queen then took the boy’s treasure. She burned all his clothing in the fire, but melted the gold in a furnace and buried it in the earth, so that nothing might remain to recall her son to her memory.

## CHAPTER LIII. A certain cleric’s lust and detestable ingratitude

Etherius, bishop of Lisieux, had sentenced a certain cleric to death because he had seduced a girl. He redeemed him for twenty gold pieces. When the man claimed to be a teacher of letters, the bishop entrusted a school to him.

But when the parents of the boys whom he taught frequently invited him to dinner, he desired one of their mothers. She, being chaste, reported this to her husband. When the husband sought the cleric for punishment, the bishop again freed him and restored him to his former honor.

This wretched man, forgetting such great kindnesses, one day followed the bishop with an axe when the bishop had gone out to supervise the work of the farm laborers.

The priest turned and, seeing him, said:

> “Why are you following me with that axe?”

The man then fell at his feet and asked forgiveness, saying:

> “Forgive me, holy Father, a guilty man confessing his crime. The archdeacon urged me to dare such things. Three times I raised my hands to strike you, but suddenly I was covered with darkness and seized by a powerful trembling. As soon as I lowered my hands, my sight and strength immediately returned to me.”

When the bishop heard this, he gave thanks to God, ordered him to keep silent about it, and returned home.

The archdeacon, realizing that he could not harm the bishop through another person, invented an accusation himself. He asserted that he had seen a woman leaving the bishop’s bedchamber.

At once, rushing in with the cleric already mentioned, he ordered the bishop to be bound. The bishop was tied with the hands from which he had often cast off chains, and was handed over to the custody of the man whom he had frequently brought out of a filthy prison.

Meanwhile, seeing that human help was unavailable to him, the bishop sought divine aid through prayer. By divine power his bonds were loosened and the guards fell asleep. He escaped from custody and went to King Guntrannus.

Eventually the bishop’s opponents found an opportunity to tell King Chilperic that he was a traitor to the kingdom. But the people, grieving for their shepherd, sent men to beg the king to bring him back.

Chilperic therefore sent to his brother and asked him to release the bishop to return to his own city, saying that he had found no offense in him.

Guntrannus gave the bishop a large sum of money and sent him back to his own city. He also sent letters to the bishops of his kingdom instructing them to honor him with gifts.

As the bishop traveled, he received so many gifts from the faithful that he could scarcely bring them all into his city.

## CHAPTER LIV. The birth of Clotarius, son of Chilperic; the restoration by Mummolus of part of Marseille; and Chilperic’s fear

In those days another son was born to Chilperic, named Clotarius. Therefore Chilperic ordered all the prisons in his kingdom to be opened and people guilty of various crimes to be released.

The same king, however, entered the city of Paris by force, contrary to the treaty he had made with the Franks—namely, that he should never enter it by right of domination. For this reason he justly lost that portion of the city which seemed to belong to him.

Mummolus returned the part of Marseille that belonged to Guntrannus and Childebert, which he had seized for himself.

Fearing that Guntrannus and Childebert had conspired against him, Chilperic established his treasures and all the resources of his defenses at Cambrai. He frequently moved his army and, as though he were about to advance into battle, made it remain in its tents.

## CHAPTER LV  
### On Innocentius, bishop of Rodez, and Sulpicius, bishop of Bourges; and on the premature appearance of roses and trees bearing fruit twice

After Theodosius, bishop of Rodez, had died, Innocentius, count of Gévaudan, succeeded him by decree of Queen Brunhild. Likewise, when Remigius, bishop of Bourges, had departed this life, Sulpicius was appointed in his place by King Guntram. To the many competitors for the bishopric the aforesaid ruler said:

> “It is not,” he said, “the custom of our gentle disposition to sell the churches of Christ for money, lest we appear worthy of condemnation and you seem like Simon Magus.””

And indeed the king uttered a saying worthy of remembrance. In this year roses were seen in the month of January; and trees that had produced fruit in July produced more fruit again in September.

## CHAPTER LVI  
### On the betrothal of King Chilperic’s daughter through envoys

On the Kalends of this month, Chilperic betrothed his daughter to the king of the Spaniards through envoys, in the following manner. [Col. 0730A] Coming to Paris, he forcibly compelled many fiscal dependants, separated from their parents, to travel with his daughter to Spain. Some of them strangled themselves, so that they would not be separated from their relatives. Many others, compelled by violence to go there, made their wills, as though they were soon to lose their lives. There was then such mourning among the inhabitants of Paris as once existed among the Egyptians when their firstborn were killed.

They say, moreover, that one of Childebert’s envoys—whom he had sent to Chilperic, entreating him not to give his daughter anything from the treasures of the cities that they had seized from him, nor any slaves—was secretly killed. There was suspicion that Chilperic had been responsible for his death. Nevertheless, through the other envoys he sent word to his nephew that he would presume nothing of the things forbidden, and he gave his daughter many gifts from his own possessions.

Moreover, the queen produced such gifts in gold, silver, and various garments that the king thought he was being left impoverished. Seeing that the king was disturbed by this, she addressed the Franks standing around her, in such a way that Chilperic could hear:

> “Let none of us suppose that these are ornaments from the royal treasuries. Some of them the prince himself bestowed on me as a dowry; some my own labor acquired; and some were given by your generosity.”

Once this explanation had been accepted, the king’s concern subsided. The leading Franks also enriched the king’s daughter with splendid gifts. Finally, there was such an abundance of treasure that six wagons loaded with it preceded her.

As she departed from the city of Paris, after the kisses and tears of her parents, she was riding in a carriage when, at the very threshold of the gate, one of the wheel’s axles broke and she fell to the ground. Although many wished her an evil hour, the people accepted this as an omen.

When at last they had pitched their tents eight miles from the city, fifty men, having seized one hundred horses with their golden trappings, went over to King Childebert. Chilperic therefore feared that his nephew or brother was preparing some plot against his daughter, and assigned four thousand armed men to protect her, commanded by the generals Bobo and Wado. He also ordered that the necessities of the journey be supplied to them from the property of the poor, so that the revenues of the treasury should in no way be diminished.

With this pomp, then, and with a large household of both sexes, the daughter of King Chilperic set out for Spain. [Col. 0730D] Those escorting her left everything through which they passed devastated.

## CHAPTER LVII  
### On Fredegund’s cunning and allurements, and on Chilperic’s death and character; also on the expedition of the people of Orléans with the people of Blois against the people of Dunois

The aforementioned Fredegund was outstanding in beauty, shrewd in counsel, and—apart from Brunhild—knew no equal in deceit. Having brought Chilperic under the control of her desires, she had so obstructed his mind with passion for her that, unable to overcome feminine appetites, he obeyed womanly insolence like a worthless slave.

While he loved her with intense affection, one day, as he was about to go hunting, he descended from the palace to the horse-stables. The queen, thinking that the king had already gone out, was preparing to wash her head with water in an inner chamber. The king therefore returned to the palace, entered the chamber behind her, and, as she lay leaning over a bench, struck her buttocks playfully with a stick.

Thinking that Landeric had done this—he was then count and chief officer of the palace, and was accustomed to have an adulterous relationship with the queen—she said:

> “Why, Landeric, do you presume to do such things?”

When the king heard this, he immediately became as if mad. He was overcome by suspicion, raged with excessive indignation, and, no longer master of himself, sprang up and fled, shunning the pollution of such shameful corruption. The palace could not contain his fury. Accordingly, he sought the solitude of the forests, so that by concentrating on the hunt he might calm the anger he had conceived in his heart.

When the queen realized that the king had not received her words calmly and that her safety would be endangered if she awaited his return, she cast off her fear and assumed feminine boldness. She sent for Landeric and said to him:

> “Your life, Landeric, is now at stake. Unless you take care, you will soon have to think more about your burial than about your bed.”

She recounted to him everything that had been said and done. When he learned this, Landeric began to consider his crimes, and was tormented by the goadings of his conscience. No avenue of flight or means of escape remained to him; he was surrounded and held captive as if in certain nets. Finally, groaning deeply, he said:

> “Woe to the day on which I have come into such bitterness of heart! Miserable man that I am, I am tortured in mind, and I do not know what to do or where to turn.”

Fredegund said to him:

> “Listen briefly, and you will learn both what I want you to do and what will benefit us. When the king returns from hunting, as is his custom, assassins must be sent out under cover of darkness. Despising life because of the promise of rewards, they must pierce him with a fatal wound.” When this has been done, we shall be safe from danger of death and shall reign with our son Chlotar.”

Landeric praised the plan. When Chilperic returned from the forest, those who had come with him being distracted by another matter, the men sent at the queen’s command surrounded him and carried out their orders. They then leapt upon him as he dismounted, shouting that “assassins sent by King Childebert of Austrasia had killed their lord and had immediately fled on foot toward the forest.”

When those present heard this, they seized horses and tried to pursue the men they could not see. When they failed to find them, they returned home.

Madalulf, bishop of Senlis—who had already been staying in his tent for three days and had been unable to speak with the king because of the arrogant pride with which the king was swollen—came when he learned that Chilperic had been killed. He took away the king’s body, clothed it in his finest garment, placed it on a boat, and conveyed it from the village of Chelles, where these events had occurred, to Paris, where he buried it in the basilica of Saint Vincent.

Chilperic was devoted to gluttony; his god was his belly. During his reign few clerics were promoted to the episcopate, since he entrusted churches to neophytes. He believed that he surpassed all the learned men of his age in knowledge and composed two books, wishing to imitate Sedulius. In them many verses were scazons, and short syllables were used as long and long syllables as short.

When he also composed other little works, hymns, or Masses, which could not be accepted by any reasonable standard, those works, together with the aforementioned books, were erased from human memory. He did not readily allow the causes of the poor to reach him. He persecuted churches and monasteries with hostile hatred, so much so that, often sitting in the palace, he would say to those standing around him:

> “Behold, our riches have passed over to the churches; now the bishops alone reign, and honor is paid to them alone.”

He had also made the priests of the Lord a subject of mockery and a proverb to himself. But why should we enumerate more of his depraved character? He never truly loved anyone, and he was loved by no one. In this way he perished, hated by his own people and loved by no strangers.

After Chilperic’s death, the people of Orléans, joined with the people of Blois, undertook an expedition against the people of Dunois and unexpectedly overwhelmed them, carrying off their movable goods and burning their immovable property. But when they were returning home, the people of Chartres, allied with the people of Dunois, inflicted an identical blow of vengeance upon them in every respect, repaying like with like. As the anger increased further, peace was made through the intervention of the counts of both sides.

## CHAPTER LVIII  
### On the flight of Fredegund and Chilperic’s treasurers

Meanwhile, Queen Fredegund, widowed by her husband, went with the treasures she had with her to the basilica of the city of Paris dedicated in honor of Saint Mary, and was received by Bishop Ragnemod.

For Chilperic’s treasurers, with the treasures discovered at the village of Chelles and with the golden dish that the king had fashioned at great expense, went over to King Childebert. The same queen, however, acting with prudent counsel, sent envoys to King Guntram, announcing that she wished to place herself and her son—whom she had borne from Chilperic, his brother—under his protection.

When Guntram had been informed by reliable reports of his brother’s death, he hastened to Paris with the greatest zeal. Fredegund met him and received him inside the city. Afterward Childebert arrived; but when the citizens prevented him from entering, he sent to his uncle, asking him to confirm more properly the pact that they had made long before.

The aforesaid ruler reproached the envoys themselves for treachery, because through their wicked counsels the friendship once joined between him and his nephew had been broken; but he replied that he would make no treaty with them. When this was reported to Childebert, he again sent word that Guntram should withdraw from the kingdom of Charibert, which belonged to Childebert.

Guntram replied:

> “It is owed more to me, since I am the brother of the deceased, and I shall in no way yield the brotherly inheritance to another.”

Childebert sent other messengers and asked that Fredegund be handed over to him for punishment, since she had murdered his father through a wicked plot with his uncle. Guntram replied:

> “I shall soon hold a formal meeting with my nephew, and there I shall discuss these and similar matters.”

He sent the envoys back to the one who had dispatched them. In secret, he appeared to be protecting Fredegund.

When he repeatedly invited her to dinner, one day the queen rose from the middle of the meal, and the king invited her to take some more food. But she said that, as happens to women, she had to rise because she had conceived. The king was astonished, knowing that not yet four months had passed since she had given birth to another child.

## CHAPTER LIX  
### On the inauguration of Chilperic’s son Chlotar by the nobles, and on Guntram’s praiseworthy address to the people

The nobles of Chilperic, the first among whom was Ansoald, took his son Chlotar and led him through the cities of his kingdom. They received oaths in his name and in the name of Guntram.

Guntram, for his part, relieved all those whom Chilperic had unjustly oppressed and restored to the churches the testamentary gifts that Chilperic had taken from them. But, suspicious of the wickedness of those among whom he had come, he never went anywhere unless surrounded by armed men and guards.

Accordingly, one day, after silence had been established in the church, he addressed the multitude of people standing around him:

> “I entreat you, people who are present, to keep faith with me more firmly than you previously kept it with my brothers, so that I may be able peacefully to raise my nephews and rule you with justice. Otherwise, should God forbid that I be taken from you before my time, they will be deprived of a guardian and you of a ruler.”

The people marveled at his words and praised him, praying to the Lord for his safety.

## CHAPTER LX  
### On Rigund’s detention and the seizure of her dowry

While these things were happening, Rigund, daughter of King Chilperic—whom we have said was sent to Spain—came to Toulouse and began to delay her journey there.

When news of Chilperic’s death reached the ears of Desiderius, the city’s commander, she was seized and stripped of all her treasures, then fled for refuge to the basilica of Saint Mary. Desiderius assigned her a restricted allowance, entrusted the treasure, secured with a seal, to very strong men for safekeeping in a certain house, and himself went to Mummolus, who was staying at Avignon.

## CHAPTER LXI  
### On many matters concerning Theodorus of Marseille, who raised up Guntram’s false brother, and on the portents of that year

[Col. 0733D]

New quarrels again arose against Theodorus, bishop of Marseille, because he had received a certain Gundoald, who falsely claimed to be Guntram’s brother. It is pleasing to discuss briefly his origin.

This Gundoald was born in Gaul and, having been brought up by his mother in the manner of kings—for this was the custom of the ancient kings of Francia—wore his hair long and flowing. His mother therefore presented him to the elder Childebert, saying that he was the son of his brother Chlotar.

Because Chlotar hated him, he was brought to Childebert, whose nephew he was, so that Childebert might raise him. Childebert, who had no sons, took him in for rearing and, when Chlotar requested to see him, sent him to him. After looking at him, Chlotar ordered that his hair be cut, denying that he was his son.

After Chlotar’s death, while Gundoald was being raised by Cherebert, Chlotar’s son, in the place of a brother, Sigebert summoned him and, after his hair was again cut, had him confined at Cologne. Escaping from there, and allowing his hair to grow again, he first went to Narses, who was then governing Italy; from there he went to the emperor and became his most intimate associate.

After a short time had passed, Guntram Boso, whom we mentioned above, found him at Constantinople while proceeding to the Lord’s tomb for the sake of prayer. At his urging, as Boso himself later claimed, Gundoald returned to Gaul. Received by Theodorus, bishop of Marseille, and taking horses from him, he went to the duke Mummolus, who had rebelled against King Guntram and fled for refuge to Avignon.

When Guntram Boso learned this, he pretended that he wished to oppose Gundoald’s efforts and placed Bishop Theodorus in custody, accusing him of having dared to receive an enemy plotting against the kingdom. But while the bishop was praying to the Lord under harsh guards, an immense light suddenly filled the entire cell in which he was being held, so that the aforementioned duke was seized with extraordinary fear.

Nevertheless, the bishop was led to King Guntram together with Bishop Epiphanius, who had migrated from Italy to Marseille, and was again placed under guard. Epiphanius died there, but Theodorus was found innocent and returned to his own see. [Col. 0734C] For when letters were produced in the name of Childebert’s faithful men, bearing the instruction that Gundoald was to be received with the highest honor, he was released.

The duke Guntram, together with another duke of King Guntram, divided the treasures of Gundoald, who had moved to an island in the sea to await the outcome of events, and transported a considerable weight of gold and silver into the city of Clermont.

From there he went to Childebert. On his return he was captured with his son by King Guntram, who terrified him with threats; he often heard the king threaten that he would be consumed by punishments because he had invited Gundoald.

He said to the king:

> “I shall prove my innocence by handing over to you, after giving my son as a hostage, Mummolus, who by his plotting supported Gundoald, once I have captured him.”

The king believed his promise and, retaining the boy, allowed him to depart.

Guntram Boso surrounded Avignon with a large force of his men. After some of his followers had been drowned in the Rhône, he himself, wishing to speak with Mummolus, walked along the bank of the river branch by which the city was encircled.

At Mummolus’s urging, and after Mummolus promised that he would suffer no harm, Guntram Boso entered the river with one of his friends. When his companion was drowned, Boso was carried this way and that by the waves. Seizing a spear extended to him by a soldier, he escaped.

Finally, after Mummolus had heaped insults upon him and Boso had returned even harsher insults, while Boso was besieging him, Gundulf, whom we mentioned above and whom Childebert had sent, removed Boso from the siege and took Mummolus with him to Clermont.

Disliking remaining there for long, Mummolus returned to his own city, from which he had departed. He joined Duke Desiderius, who, as we have said, had come to him from the region of Toulouse. They summoned Gundoald and proclaimed him their king according to the custom of the ancient Franks, then raised him upon a shield.

When they had gone around the entire army with him for the third time, the shield suddenly collapsed with the king, and he could scarcely be lifted from the ground.

While these things were happening, it was the tenth month. Shoots appeared in the vineyards with fully formed clusters of grapes, and flowers appeared on the trees. A fiery meteor also, racing across the sky in the middle of the night, spread a bright light over the world far and wide. A column of fire was likewise seen hanging from the sky, with a great star above it.

People judged these to be signs of Gundoald’s destruction, since the earth also trembled and many other signs appeared.

## CHAPTER LXII  
### On King Guntram’s dispute with his co-heirs over the kingdom

In those days King Guntram sent his dukes to seize the cities that Sigebert had held from the kingdom of Charibert, the brother of both Guntram and Sigebert, and that Chilperic had forcibly taken from his nephew Childebert, the son of his brother Sigebert.

Gariricus, however, count of Childebert’s territories, had exacted oaths of loyalty from the people of Limoges in his lord’s name after Chilperic’s death. When he came to Poitiers intending to do the same, he was graciously received by the citizens. There he heard that the people of Bourges, who obeyed King Guntram, had made a hostile incursion into the territory of Tours, because the people of Tours too had already gone over to Childebert.

Accordingly, while the people of Bourges were devastating the territory of Tours, they burned the church of the village of Marolles, dedicated to Saint Martin. There the evident power of the blessed confessor appeared: he protected the altar cloth, together with the surrounding grasses, from the flames.

Marvelous to relate, enormous beams were consumed by fire, while the linen and the grasses remained untouched.

When Gariricus learned what was happening, he sent men to warn the people of Tours not to transfer themselves in any way to Guntram’s side. Bishop Gregory replied to this message:

> “After the death of his brothers, the whole kingdom of the Franks is owed by right to King Guntram, so that, just as his father Chlotar ruled over his own sons, so Guntram should rule over his nephews. We therefore shall not resist him; indeed, I consider him to be acting foolishly who thinks that he can resist so great a ruler.””

When the count saw that the people of Tours were doing not what he himself had wished but what the king had ordered, he left Eberon, Childebert’s chamberlain, in the city of Poitiers and departed as though he were going to assemble an army against the enemy.

Then the people of Poitiers, seeing their territory being devastated—for the people of Tours, together with the people of Orléans and their frequently mentioned allied enemies, were ravaging their fields by plunder and fire—sent envoys to them concerning peace. They asked that they cease hostilities until the formal meeting that the uncle had arranged with his nephew, and that afterward they would have as their lord the one whom God and fate should give them.

But when the others replied that they would not place the petitioners’ requests above the king’s commands, the people of Poitiers were compelled to promise by oath that they would remain loyal to Guntram, and drove Childebert’s supporters from their walls.

Yet they did not remain faithful for long.

At last, when the day appointed for the meeting of the kings arrived, Childebert sent Archbishop Egidius of Reims to serve as his envoy to his uncle. Egidius hastened to Guntram and began his speech with these words, intended to flatter the ruler:

> “Most excellent of kings, we give thanks to almighty God, who grants you daily not only tranquility in your kingdom but also its enlargement.”

The king replied:

> “Thanks must truly be given to Him who is the most gracious governor of all kingdoms—not to you, the most wicked of all men, by whose counsel the territories of my cities have been devastated, and who, beneath a sheep’s clothing, perform not the office of a priest of the Lord but that of the most savage traitor.”

When the priest remained silent at this, one of the envoys, overcome by indignation, said to the king:

> “Your glorious nephew, our lord King Childebert, commands you to restore to him in full his father’s inheritance.”

King Guntram replied:

> “I thought that I had already given a sufficient answer concerning this matter. I answered at another formal meeting, and I shall answer now as well: these things passed to me by agreement, and I shall yield them to no one except as a favor arising from friendship.”

Then another envoy addressed the king:

> “If, excellent ruler, these things seem difficult for you to grant, at least let him obtain this: that Fredegund be handed over to him for punishment, since she wickedly murdered his father with his uncle.”

The king gave him this answer:

> “She cannot be handed over to him in any way, because she has a son who is king and was born of a king; and I believe her innocent of the crime of which she is accused.”

After this, Guntram Boso—who, as has been said, had earlier gone over to Childebert and had now arrived there with the envoys—approached King Guntram as though he wished to offer him some suggestion. The king ordered him to be silent and forestalled him with these words:

> “What do you say, good man? Your prudence sought the kingdoms of the East for this reason: so that you might summon from there a certain ‘ballomir’—for that is what the king called Gundoald—who would invade our cities. O perpetual traitor, never remaining in anything you have promised!”

Boso replied:

> “No one dares contradict you, a king seated upon a royal throne. Nevertheless, if any of my equals laid this charge against me, I would refute it by arms and, with God’s help, overcome him powerfully in your presence.”

While the others remained silent, the king continued:

> “All who live piously ought to resent this and strive to remove this tyrant from the midst of men. His father was overseer of the royal mills—or, to speak more truthfully, he spent his life in the craft of wool-working.”

Although one man may indeed be skilled in both occupations, one of the envoys, wishing to insult the king, began to accuse him, saying:

> “Do not speak so crudely, O king. For how can it be possible for any man to have two fathers, except in spiritual matters? Such words are not fitting for royal dignity.”

When everyone burst into laughter at these words, another envoy said to the king:

> “We bid you farewell, O king. Since you reject the peace of your nephew, know that the axe is ready—the axe by which your brothers were struck—so that you may be cut down by it.”

After these words, the king ordered them driven from his presence and had excrement gathered from the streets thrown over the heads of those departing. Because of this great insult, violent discord arose between the kings.

## CHAPTER LXIII  
### On the cruelty of Queen Fredegund in the Parisian asylum, inflamed by Audon

At the same time, a certain Leonard, one of Chilperic’s nobles, came from the region of Toulouse and informed Queen Fredegund, who was still staying in the major church of Paris, that he had escaped from her daughter. He claimed that the girl was living in great poverty of food and clothing.

The queen, angered by these words, ordered the belt that he had earned as a gift from the aforementioned king to be taken from him, and deprived him of every dignity. In the same way she deprived many who withdrew from her daughter’s service either of their honors or subjected them to insults and punishments.

She did not fear the Lord or His Mother, in whose basilica she was staying, while committing wicked acts with Audon at her side as her accomplice in every evil. The people would then have killed him, had he not fled into the church.

## CHAPTER LXIV  
### On the restoration of Bishop Praetextatus of Rouen

King Guntram ordered that Praetextatus, bishop of Rouen, be brought back from exile. Since the king wished to convene a synod on his account, Ragnemod, bishop of Paris, said that Praetextatus had in no way been deprived of communion by the priests and that there was therefore no need to summon the bishops.

Thus at last Praetextatus was restored to his city.

## CHAPTER LXV  
### On Guntram’s careful protection of himself, and on Fredegund’s flight to the countryside and her deception

Meanwhile, while the king was staying near the city of Paris, a certain poor man came and suggested to him that he should beware of Faraulf, formerly Chilperic’s chamberlain. He said:

> “I have discovered the plan he conceived for killing the king.”

When he heard this, the king questioned Faraulf and, although Faraulf denied it, dismissed him. He himself, however, fortified himself so thoroughly with arms and guards that he went nowhere—not even to church—without the protection of weapons or guards.

He sent Fredegund to Rotojal, a village in the territory of Rouen, to spend whatever remained of her life there. Many of Chilperic’s nobles followed her and left her there with Melanius, who had been appointed by her after Praetextatus was deposed, and whom Guntram rejected after Praetextatus was recalled. They promised to obey her son Chlotar faithfully.

But she was indignant at being left without honor, and considered Brunhild more powerful, as indeed she was. She therefore sent to Brunhild a certain cleric trained in the arts of deception, so that, while pretending to serve her energetically, he might secretly strike a deadly blow.

Obeying his mistress’s orders, he pretended that, offended by Fredegund’s cruelty, he had hastened to Brunhild’s presence because he had heard of her benevolence toward everyone. At last admitted into her friendship, he flattered everyone, even escorting the mistress to the door of her bedchamber, presenting himself as friendly toward his equals and submissive to his superiors.

But he could not conceal who he was for long, since suspicion threatened him. Subjected to questioning, he revealed all the secrets of his wickedness. He was then subjected to dreadful punishments and sent back to his former mistress. He recounted to her what had happened to him, supposedly so that Brunhild’s suspicion might be removed from her mind, but in reality so that she might truly punish him for a crime not committed. She punished him by cutting off his hands and feet.

## CHAPTER LXVI  
### On the punishment of Eberulf, his hostility toward Saint Gregory of Tours, and Guntram’s deeds

After some days had passed, King Guntram returned from Chalon. Carefully investigating the author of his brother’s murder, he learned through Fredegund’s informants that Eberulf, who had been placed in charge of the chamberlains in Chilperic’s palace, was the principal author of the crime.

Fredegund had asked Eberulf not to abandon her. But when he refused to give her his support, she accused him of this before the king.

The king, moved by bitterness, swore before the friends around him:

> “I shall destroy not only the murderer but his entire family, so that anyone who dares to kill kings may be removed from the kingdom of the Franks.”

Struck by this terror, the aforementioned man fled to the basilica of Saint Martin with the clerics against whom he had frequently committed offenses.

The people of Orléans and the people of Blois then drew lots, by the king’s command, to take alternating turns guarding the basilica, so that Eberulf might not escape from it. As they went and returned, they committed much plundering.

Two of them, who had stolen the mules of the aforementioned confessor, came to the house of a certain peasant to ask for a drink. When the peasant denied that he had any, one of them extended his spear to strike him, but the peasant killed him with a blow of his sword. The other, terrified by the unexpected death of his companion, fled and returned the things they had wrongly seized.

After this, the whole property of Eberulf—which was very considerable—was distributed by the king to various people. The house that he possessed within the walls of Tours was also surrendered to plunder, so thoroughly that nothing remained except the bare walls.

For these reasons Eberulf brought accusations against the holy bishop Gregory, as though everything had been done at Gregory’s command. He threatened that, if he ever regained the king’s favor, he would repay Gregory with a similar turn of fortune.

The bishop, however, was moved more by compassion for Eberulf’s misery than by indignation over the injuries Eberulf had inflicted.
