The unfortunate man had a dwelling in the small oratory of Saint Martin, and the other doors were closed by the priest entrusted with the care of the oratory. Through the door of that oratory, boys and girls entered the church and searched through all the furnishings of the sacred temple.

When the guardian of the holy building noticed this and fastened the doors themselves with iron nails, Eberulf, in the middle of the night, during the very nocturnal hymns, assailed Bishop Gregory and the clerics with such abuse that they were forced to abandon the praises owed to God.

He also, already drunk, beat a certain cleric with whips while the man lay stretched across a bench, almost to the point of death, because the cleric would not give him wine. He inflicted violence upon many people in the atrium of the blessed bishop, not fearing to heap insults upon the man whose mercy he daily begged.

One night the same bishop had a dream, which he related to that man in the following manner:

> “I saw myself,” he said, “standing at the holy altar of Martin and celebrating the mysteries of the Lord’s sacrifice. King Guntram entered the same house of prayer and ordered his men to tear you away from the altar cloth to which you were clinging and drive you outside. When I interrupted the solemn rites of the Mass and went to meet him, even holding you back with my hands so that they would not touch you, you meanwhile wandered about in fear around the deserted sacred altar. Then, troubled by this, I signaled to you not to go anywhere, and I awoke, turning over in my mind the meaning of the vision.”

Eberulf replied:

> “My thought agrees very closely with your vision.”

The bishop asked:

> “What are you thinking?”

He answered:

> “I am thinking that, if King Guntram wishes to drive me out of here, I shall cling to the altar cloth with one hand and, with the other, cut you and the clerics down with my sword.”

The bishop understood that he was saying these things at the prompting of the devil.

Not much time passed before what had been revealed to the bishop in the vision began to become evident in reality.

When Guntram was seeking a man who could skillfully bring Eberulf out of the church, either to deliver him bound to the king or to leave him slain by the sword, a certain Claudius offered himself, promising to be a capable servant for this task.

After the price of so great a crime had been promised to him, he approached Eberulf. He swore by God and by all the holy things of heaven and earth that no one could or would more faithfully plead Eberulf’s case before the king than he could.

The wretched man considered that Eberulf could not be deceived more conveniently by any contrivance than by Claudius’s perjury.

What more is there to say? The unfortunate Eberulf believed the perjurer. On the following day, summoned by the clerics, he went with Claudius to a banquet.

When the meal was over, as Eberulf walked with him through the atrium of the basilica and promised mutual friendship by oath, Claudius said:

> “If it happened that more delightful wines could be found, I would admit that I am burning with desire for them.”

Eberulf replied that he would provide everything Claudius wished, provided that Claudius would visit his lodging. He sent all the boys out to seek a draught of better wine.

When Claudius saw that Eberulf was sitting alone—he thirsted more for Eberulf’s death than for any other drink—he raised his hands toward the tomb of Saint Martin and prayed to him as follows:

> “Holy confessor, I beseech you to let me return safely to my wife and son.”

With these words, he drew his sword and attacked his adversary. One of the servants, recognizing the attempt, seized Eberulf around the arms and threw him backward. Eberulf, already wounded by Claudius, drove the sword he had drawn from its sheath into his enemy’s sides.

Then Claudius was attacked by the man’s surrounding followers and killed by many blows of weapons.

Claudius, conscious of his guilt in so enormous a crime, fled to the abbot’s cell with his side pierced and his thumb cut off, asking the abbot to hide him.

But when Eberulf’s guards rushed in, the house was surrounded with weapons, and javelins were thrown through the windows. The abbot himself was scarcely brought out unharmed by two clerics after the doors had been opened.

The attackers entered through them, found Claudius hiding beneath the bed, and slaughtered him and his companions as well. Their bodies were dragged from the house and left lying on the bare ground; their relatives and friends gathered them and buried them.

To avenge the murder committed in the atrium of the sacred building, even the possessed and the poor, keeping watch before the doors, hastened there with clubs and stones.

When this matter was brought before him, King Guntram at first took it very hard. Once he learned the sequence of what had happened, however, he turned his attention to other affairs. Those to whom the royal authority had granted Eberulf’s property took it away, leaving his wife destitute.

## CHAPTER LXVII  
### On the ransom of the bishop of Poitiers and the reconciliation of the people

In the tenth year of Childebert’s reign and the twenty-fourth of Guntram’s, the same ruler mobilized an army against Gundoald from all the cities subject to him.

Among them, the people of Orléans together with the people of Bourges attacked the city of Poitiers. They attempted, by force, to bring back into their former alliance the citizens who had already abandoned their allegiance, and they sought to mistreat the bishop.

But he redeemed himself from exile and the people from captivity by breaking up one golden chalice belonging to the ecclesiastical monastery.

## CHAPTER LXVIII  
### On Gundoald’s deeds and certain other matters
In those days, Gundoaldus, having set out for Poitiers, turned aside toward Angoulême when he heard of the expedition. There he was gladly received by the bishop and leading men; having rewarded their attentiveness, he proceeded toward Périgueux. He left its bishop severely punished because he had not received him favorably. From there, making for Toulouse, he sent soldiers ahead and ordered Bishop Magnulfus to come out to meet him. Therefore Magnulfus summoned the people and exhorted and warned them to resist bravely, lest they again be subjected to the calamity they had once experienced under Sigulfus. They should also remember how Desiderius, the city’s duke, would suffer the fate of that aforementioned man if he attempted anything similar.

These words indeed stirred the people to revolt. But the strength of the approaching army persuaded them to open the gates. Gundoaldus was therefore admitted into the city, and, while dining with them, the bishop addressed him in these words:

“Although you assert that you are the son of Chlothar and that the kingdom is owed to you, it nevertheless remains incredible in the minds of our people that you will be able to accomplish what you have begun.”

Gundoaldus replied:

“I confess that I was born of Chlothar, and, having now obtained the portion of the kingdom owed to me, I shall establish my proper seat there, once the city of Paris has been captured.”

“Never,” said the bishop, “with Christ preventing it, will you accomplish these things, so long as anyone of the royal stock remains alive.”

Then Mummolus struck the priest of the Lord across the face, saying:

“Are you not ashamed, most foolish man, to contradict our lord the king with such ridiculous words?”

Desiderius also, having recognized what the bishop had advised the people against his own safety, beat him with fists and clubs together with the others. Afterwards he bound his feet with a rope and sent him into exile, seizing both his possessions and those of the Church.

The Franks, therefore, who had been stirred from every direction to pursue Gundoaldus, advanced as far as the river Dordogne and waited there to see whether they could detect any movement of his, as rumor reported. Waldo, Rigundis’s chamberlain, had joined him. He was a man of considerable power, while the other attendants of the girl had dispersed in flight. Desiderius, too, together with Mummolus and Bladaste, as well as Sagittarius—who had already extracted from him a promise of the bishopric of Toulouse—were among his intimate advisers, and affairs were conducted through them.

In those days Gundoaldus sent letters to friends living in northern Gaul, entrusting them to two clerics to carry. One of them, a resident of the city of Cahors, hollowed out the wooden tablet he was carrying, inserted the letters, and covered it with wax. Yet this deception did him no good: he was detected by Guntrannus’s loyal men, and, once the embassy had been exposed, he and his companion were flogged and handed over to custody.

Gundoaldus, meanwhile, crossed into the city of Bordeaux, where Bishop Bertrannus received him with the greatest kindness, and remained there for some time. When he asked what made him invincible to his enemies, one of his household told him that a certain king of the East, who carried relics of the holy martyr Sergius bound to his arm, always prevailed over his adversaries.

As Gundoaldus diligently investigated who possessed the patronage of this witness of the Lord, Bishop Bertrannus said that there was in the same city a Syrian merchant named Eufron, who had once brought the relics from the East.

“This man,” he said, “in his own house, which he consecrated as a church, among the other miracles accomplished through the merits of that beloved servant of God, also deserved to witness this: when the city was consumed by fire, that very basilica remained untouched.”

Mummolus the duke was immediately sent with the bishop to investigate the aforesaid relics. When he pressed his inquiry more forcefully, Eufron replied:

“I beg you, do not weary an old man exhausted by age, nor inflict injury upon that saint. Rather, accept one hundred gold pieces and desist from this purpose.”

The other, however, declared that even if two hundred were offered, he would not abandon what he had begun. Then, seeing a small chest hanging from the wall, he placed a ladder against it and ordered a deacon to climb up and lower the case. The deacon obeyed; but as he touched the sacred relics with his hand, he was seized by such a violent trembling that everyone thought he would immediately fall. Nevertheless, after lowering them, he handed them to Mummolus.

Mummolus found a bone of the precious martyr and, with rash boldness, struck it with a knife and divided it into three pieces. When these sprang away and could nowhere be seen, great terror seized those standing by. But after they had prostrated themselves in prayer, and especially after the old man had wept—lamenting that he had been deprived of so great a protection—the fragments appeared lying not far away. Mummolus took one of them and departed.

The blessed martyr showed especially by this that what had been done was not pleasing to him: he refused to be a help to the man by whose command these things had been carried out.

Nevertheless, Gundoaldus again sent two envoys to King Guntrannus, following the custom that had formerly prevailed among the Franks for envoys. He ordered them to carry consecrated rods, so that, when these were produced, they would be immune from every injury. But the men who had been sent unwisely made their embassy known to the common people before they were presented to the king. Therefore the king ordered them to be brought before him in chains and strictly questioned them about where, by whom, and by whom else they had been sent.

They related the whole matter in order, just as it had happened: they had been sent by Gundoaldus, the son of King Chlothar—as he himself claimed—to demand the portion of the kingdom owed to him.

“This,” they said, “should be restored without delay, for soon he will devastate the surrounding cities. They also said that he had immediately gathered no small band of warriors and, in addition to the forces of Aquitaine, hoped to have powerful supporters from Austrasia. They added that the mighty dukes of Childebert’s kingdom knew whether they were pursuing the truth.”

The envoys disclosed these things during the first interrogation. Afterwards, however, when they had been stretched upon the racks and beaten for a very long time, they revealed that Rigundis, the daughter of Chilperic, had been sent into exile with Magnulfus, bishop of Toulouse. Finally, they were assigned to custody and ordered to be kept there until another hearing.

## CHAPTER LXIX  
### On the Reconciliation of Childebertus and Guntrannus, the Counsel Given by Guntrannus to Childebertus, and the Party of Gundoaldus

[Col. 0742C]

Meanwhile Childebertus, urged on by messengers from his uncle, left the place where he was staying and came to confer with him. Then, at Guntrannus’s command, the men mentioned above were brought into the presence of both kings. After first repeating what they had reported, they added that Gundoaldus had seized all Rigundis’s treasures and that he himself was accustomed to say that he had crossed from the East into Gaul at the invitation of Guntrannus-Boso.

When they asserted that Childebertus’s leading men knew these things, suspicion arose that some had therefore delayed coming to the present conference. Then at last King Guntrannus handed to his nephew the spear that he was carrying and said:

“By this sign, dearest nephew, know that you will succeed me in the kingdom. Therefore, since I have transferred power to you, govern all the cities of my kingdom as though they were your own, remembering that you alone survive from our line.”

Thus the king spoke before all the people. Then, taking his nephew aside from the gathering of the others, he warned him not to reveal to anyone what he was about to say to him. Finally, he instructed him which of the faithful should be consulted about affairs to be undertaken, whom it would be necessary to exclude from counsel, and to whom the care of protecting his own person should be entrusted. He warned him in advance to beware of the frauds and perjuries of Bishop Egidius and of the cunning of his mother Brunichildis.

When their conversation had ended, both kings sat down to a banquet. During the abundant feast, the most serene prince Guntrannus addressed the guests:

“I exhort you, illustrious leaders of Francia, to regard my nephew as worthy of the highest honor and to show him the devotion of your loyalty, since he has now passed beyond the age of childhood and gives reason to hope better things of him. Do not despise him as a boy; revere him as a lord.”

After this, Childebertus, having received back from his uncle the cities that his father had held, hastened to return to his own possessions.

## CHAPTER LXX  
### On Gundoaldus’s Deception at Convenae

At that time Gundoaldus, abandoned by Desiderius, entered the city of Convenae together with Mummolus, Bladaste, and Waddo, or Sagittarius. That city lies on the summit of a lofty mountain beyond the Garonne, far removed from the other mountains. At the foot of the cliff a spring rises, and above it stands a very high tower, which protected the citizens from enemy assault when they descended through a passage to obtain water.

When the aforesaid man had persuaded the inhabitants of that city to hide their possessions within the walls because of the approaching army, and they had obeyed his advice, he deceived them by the following trick. Pretending that the enemy was already close at hand, he addressed them:

“Look! The enemies are here. Go out to resist them.”

When they had gone out, he expelled the bishop as well, shut the gates behind them, and prepared to resist with his followers.

How blind is the human mind, ignorant of the future! Afterwards there certainly came a day for him—the day that, by a similar sequence of events, showed him expelled from the city to mortals—when he would wish to see those who had been driven out received back, though those thought most trustworthy had been rejected, and only after they had been purchased at a great price.

## CHAPTER LXXI  
### On the Letter Sent by Guntrannus to Gundoaldus, the Seizure of Gold, the Plundering of the Monastery of Vincentius in the Territory of Agen, Its Punishment, and Gundoaldus’s Cunning Complaint and Other Deeds

In those days King Guntrannus sent Gundoaldus a letter in Brunichildis’s name, advising him that, after dismissing the forces he had gathered for winter quarters, he should withdraw to spend the winter at Bordeaux.

But the hostile commanders of the army, whom we have already said had encamped beyond the Dordogne, learned that Gundoaldus was holding the farther bank of the Garonne. They gathered a large and well-equipped force of brave men and decided to cross the river by swimming. Some of them, riding weak horses, perished under the force of the river’s waters. The rest, carried by swimming to the opposite bank, encountered on their way a great number of camels and mules laden with gold and silver, which the fleeing enemy had abandoned.

After capturing these animals and leaving behind the remaining common people because of the impediments they caused, the commanders themselves pursued Gundoaldus with the greatest speed possible. When they came to the basilica of Saint Vincent in the territory of Agen, those who had brought their possessions there resisted them. They applied fire to the doors; when these had been consumed, they carried away everything found inside, including the vessels used for sacred ministry.

Divine vengeance immediately followed. The hands of some burned with the sacred fire; others were filled with demons, and some killed themselves.

At last the survivors reached Convenae and pitched camp in the open country. First the entire suburban region was devastated. Some men, inflamed by an even keener desire for plunder, withdrew too far from their comrades and were slaughtered by guards from neighboring cities.

Meanwhile, when the siege had begun, the bolder men climbed the steep slopes of the hill and hurled insults at Gundoaldus:

“Whence, you old corpse [silicernium], comes this great presumption of yours, that, accustomed to spend your life in the art of painters, you now dare to call yourself king? Indeed, for such attempts you have often been tonsured by the lords of the world—the kings of the Franks—and condemned to exile. All Gaul calls you by the nickname *ballomirus* [buffoon]. Come now, fool; answer us: who compelled you to presume such things? Or declare what helpers of strength you possess. For soon, caught in our trap, you will suffer the punishment deserved for your foolish obstinacy.”

Although they shouted these and many other things, Gundoaldus was not moved to anger. He merely lamented and said that the insults in question had been inflicted upon him by his father; that he had been unjustly driven from his homeland by his relatives but mercifully received by strangers; and that, while his kinsmen pursued him with hostile hatred, strangers received him with friendly affection.

“Moreover,” he said, “when I was prospering greatly in the wealth of kings and was intimate with the friendship of the emperor of Constantinople, Guntrannus Boso deceived me by his treacheries. For when I had gone to the East, ostensibly on a mission of piety, and was asking anxiously about my father’s welfare, I also inquired how the kingdom and my brothers were faring.”

Then he said to me:

“Are you asking about your father? He has died. Your brothers, following their father in death, have scarcely left any of their own alive. Guntrannus alone remains, and he too, deprived of children, has only a little nephew born of his brother Sigibertus.”

I replied:

“And what, dearest friend, do you think I should now do?”

Then that man urged me to come to Gaul and declared that the Franks, longing for me, wished to hand the kingdom over to me—especially those who judged the age of my nephew Childebertus useless for protecting the state.

“Therefore,” I said, “acknowledge me also as your lord, abandon this siege of me, and, by supporting me, recall my brother Guntrannus to reconciliation.”

While Gundoaldus continued speaking in this manner, his adversaries frightened him with curses and also threw weapons at him. The fifteenth day had already passed since they had arrived there when Leudegisilus, superintendent of the royal horses—commonly called the constable—and placed by the king in command of the expedition, ordered the siege engines constructed for overthrowing the walls to be brought forward.

There were carts covered with wicker hurdles and wooden boards, in which soldiers concealed themselves to undermine the foundations of the walls. But this device accomplished little, especially because the enemy impeded them with sharpened stakes and massive stones. The walls also seemed unsuitable, since, once fire had been thrown upon them, they could easily be burned. For the besieged threw down from above vessels filled with pitch and dry wood, set alight; these burned the attackers’ works and prevented their approach.

When the day had been consumed in this struggle, those who were besieging the city devised another means of harming it for the following day. They made a bundle of astonishing size from branches and the twigs of trees and wished to fill the valley with it. But both the depth of the valley and the fire cast by the defenders from above, together with stones, resisted their efforts.

As Leudegisilus watched all his endeavors prove fruitless, it occurred to him that it would be more advantageous to test the besieged through the prospect of betrayal. He therefore summoned Mummolus for a conversation and began to reproach him for abandoning the most merciful King Guntrannus and joining himself to a most unjust tyrant.

“What, then, do you expect?” he said. “That you should perish miserably when the city is captured? Rather, come to your senses and return to your gracious lord, abandoning that most foolish man, who will shortly be punished.”

Mummolus replied that he would consult with the others. When he returned to the city, he summoned Sagittarius and Waddo. Bladastes, however, fearing that the city would be captured, had set fire to the church building and, while the others hurried to extinguish the blaze, secretly fled.

They had also joined their faction to Cariulfus, a citizen of the same city, whose many storehouses supplied their needs. Mummolus therefore approached him together with the men mentioned above. He showed them how disastrously their affairs stood, and how hateful they had become to all peoples because they supported a king of uncertain origin. Finally, he urged them to yield to the circumstances flowing against them and, if security for life and safety were granted them by oath, to hand over to the enemy the city, which was on the point of being captured, together with its false king.

His companions agreed. The aforesaid duke sent word to Leudegisilus to come to a conference and explained what he and his comrades had decided. Leudegisilus praised their decision and swore that he would obtain their lives from his king. If, however, the prince’s will remained obstinate, he promised that he would shut them up in any church until Guntrannus’s anger cooled.

Deceived by this cunning, Mummolus repeatedly ensnared Gundoaldus in the following trap:

“I have shown,” he said, “that I am faithful to you with a willing heart and devoted mind, not only by fighting against your enemies, but you yourself have also proved it by experience. You know better than anyone how often, when you have used my counsel, you have always enjoyed prosperity. Now also I retain the same desire to give advice, as you have well deserved.

“For this reason I spoke with the adversaries, so that I might discover what their attitude toward us was. As far as I could judge, they are by no means opposed to your advantage. Indeed, they say that they wonder why you so greatly avoid the presence of your brother. They suppose that, ignorant of your genealogy, you avoid disputing with petty scholars and do not present yourself to your brother, who longs to see you recognized.

“If, therefore, you are now willing to listen to me and hurry with these men and with me into the presence of King Guntrannus, you will both free yourself from this suspicion and provide for yourself and for peace.”

Gundoaldus was not deceived: he understood that Mummolus was about to betray him. He gave him this answer:

“Although unwillingly I have now abandoned these regions, and although, urged on by you, I came to Europe, I nevertheless always supported your cause with goodwill and complete loyalty, nor did I place my interests before your advantages. Even though the treachery of the man who enticed me to come here became plainly evident—since he both abandoned me in flight and stole part of my treasures—I nonetheless honored you continually and loved you as the authors of my safety, in the place of brothers.

“Therefore, if you act against me contrary to what is proper, indeed contrary to what is right, especially since I have placed my body and soul, together with my counsel and resources, in your hands, may God, the searcher of hearts, take notice of it.”

After saying this, he consented to descend with them to the enemy.

Mummolus, however, advised him not to go to them wearing splendid clothing. Rather, he should replace the gold-worked belt that he had received from Mummolus with his own belt, which lacked the brilliance of that metal.

“In this,” he said, “your deceit is already evident, since you are demanding back the things that I have possessed from you up to this very time.”

When Mummolus denied that he would use any treachery against him, they came to the gate, where the enemy commanders were waiting in full strength—Boso, that is, together with Bollon, count of Bourges—surrounded by a considerable crowd of followers.

When they received Gundoaldus, Mummolus returned to the city and secured the gates most firmly. Gundoaldus, seeing that he had been abandoned by his own men, surrounded by the enemy, and barred from entering the city, raised his hands to heaven and prayed to the Lord with a groan from his heart:

“Eternal Judge and avenger of the innocent, God, to whom every secret is open, who embraces no deceit and takes no pleasure in the frauds of the wicked, hasten to avenge my sufferings, turning back upon those who betrayed me to my enemies the snare of their own deception.”

After these words, signing himself with the Lord’s cross, he began to depart with those who had captured him toward their camp. He had not yet passed beyond the hill overlooking the city when, struck by Bolo, he fell forward and was carried toward the depths of the valley. When he rose and struggled toward the opposite mountain, Boso struck him on the head with a stone; he collapsed and breathed out his spirit.

His feet were then bound with a rope, and he was dragged about. His coat of mail was stripped from him, and, pierced with spears, he was carried around the entire army.

Mummolus, meanwhile, seized all the treasures and concealed them in various places. On the following day he opened the city’s gates to the enemy. They became so frenzied with slaughter that they killed even the priests of the Lord at the very altars and burned the remaining citizens together with the city itself.

Their commander Leudegisilus had secretly sent messengers to Prince Guntrannus to ask what judgment should be imposed upon the city’s traitors. Guntrannus ordered that all of them be punished by the sword,

“so that such attempts might be removed from the Frankish kingdom, and no one would dare thereafter to support tyrants of this kind.”

When this became known, Cariulfus and Waddo escaped from the camp in flight.

Mummolus, seeing some men running to arms and understanding that they intended to attack him, went straight to Leudegisilus’s tent and reproached him for breaking the faith that had been promised him.

“I,” said Leudegisilus, “will go out and calm everything.”

After saying this, he placed one foot beyond the threshold and gave his men a signal to hand Mummolus and Bishop Sagittarius over to death.

As they hastened to carry out the order, Mummolus’s servants, at his command, tried to defend the entrance to the building until their master could arm himself. But when some of them had fallen dead and others had been wounded, Mummolus armed himself and confronted the doorway. With every exertion of his strength he struck down the adversaries and drove them away.

When he incautiously pursued them as they withdrew, he left the building, was surrounded from the sides, pierced by weapons, and fell lifeless.

Sagittarius, once a bishop, was thrown into confusion by his fall. As he stood there in amazement, someone said to him:

“Why, bishop, are you standing here as though you were mad? Rather cover your head so that you will not be recognized, and hasten to the forest.”

The bishop obeyed and committed himself to flight. But as he hurried along, someone swiftly overtook him and cut off his head together with its covering.

Leudegisilus hastened to return to his own country with the victorious army. Since he did not restrain his soldiers from plundering, he left everything through which they passed devastated.

## CHAPTER LXXII  
### On the Return of Rigundis to Her Mother

In those days Fredegundis sent her chamberlain Cuppanes to Toulouse to discover how affairs stood with regard to her daughter. She also charged him to bring her back to her native land by whatever means he could devise.

He obeyed her instructions, went to Toulouse, and found the queen’s daughter in a state of profound humiliation. As far as he was able, he quickly brought her back to her mother.

## CHAPTER LXXIII  
### On the Confiscation of Mummolus’s Property, the Great Flood and Pestilence in Italy

Guntrannus ordered Mummolus’s treasures to be brought before him. Because of the nobility of her lineage, he granted Mummolus’s wife what she had received as her pledge.

The aforesaid duke’s treasures amounted to thirty talents of gold and two hundred of silver. Guntrannus and his nephew Childebertus divided all of these and excluded Chlothar from the partition. The things that had come to King Guntrannus himself were distributed by him for the benefit of God’s churches.

Among the gifts presented to him from the household of the aforementioned prince was a man of such immense bodily size that he exceeded the height of three ordinary men by the measure of his feet.

At that time, while Authari was reigning over the Lombards, there was a flood in the regions of Venetia and Liguria and in the other regions of Italy such as is believed not to have occurred since the days of Noah. In this violent storm of waters the Tiber rose so greatly at the city of Rome that its waters flowed over the city walls and occupied its largest districts.

Immediately after this inundation came a very severe pestilence, which they call bubonic. It first struck Pope Pelagius and quickly killed him. Then, after the shepherd had been slain, it spread among the people.

## CHAPTER LXXIV  
### On the Election of Blessed Gregory as Pope and the Conversion of the English, or Britons, to the Catholic Faith

While such great tribulation was afflicting the wretched city, blessed Gregory—then a levite and serving under Pope Pelagius in the office of *apocrisiarius*—was unanimously elected pope.

At his ordination, nothing was lacking except the emperor’s command. For at that time no one in the Roman state could be promoted to the pontificate without the order of the emperor of Constantinople. Therefore Gregory, the man of God, sent an envoy to the emperor Maurice, begging him not to give his consent to the people’s choice of himself.

The prefect of the city intercepted and destroyed his letter, and sent the emperor the people’s approval instead. The emperor was greatly pleased to have found an appropriate occasion for conferring honor upon the deacon, who had formerly been most dear to him in the intimacy of friendship—for Gregory had stood as sponsor at the baptismal font for the emperor’s son—and he ordered him to be ordained without delay.

Once ordained, Gregory conducted himself with such prudence and humility in all his actions that, as can be recognized from his deeds and writings, scarcely any of his successors can be found comparable to him in the flowering of eloquence, the purity of doctrine, or even the holiness of life.

At that time blessed Gregory sent Augustine and Mellitus, as well as John and other servants of God, to Britain. In letters of his own, he commended them to the bishops and kings of the Franks, through whose territories they would have to pass.

When their preaching had converted the nation of the English to faith in Christ, he rejoiced so greatly that, mentioning the matter in his books of the *Moralia*, he gave thanks, among other things, for the fruit of his good works and said:

“Behold, the tongue of Britain, which had known nothing except to growl barbarously, now knows how to resound with the Hebrew ‘Alleluia’ in the praises of God.”

## CHAPTER LXXV  
### On the Punishment of Mummolus, Unseasonable Weather, the Patriciate of Leudegisilus, the Birth of Theodebertus, and the Flooding of Burgundy

In the twenty-fifth year of Guntrannus’s reign, Mummolus the patrician, convicted of rebellion, was killed at the royal estate of Senonia by order of that king. His wife Sidonia, together with the entire abundance of his treasures, was presented to Guntrannus by Domnulus the chamberlain and Wandalmarus, prefect of the king’s treasury.

In the twenty-sixth year of the same prince, his army set out for Spain but, afflicted by unseasonable weather, returned without accomplishing its purpose.

In the twenty-seventh year, Leudegisilus was appointed patrician in Provence by the same Guntrannus. A son was also born to King Childebertus, named Theodebertus.

That year there was excessive flooding in Burgundy, and the rivers overflowed their banks. A sign also appeared in the sky: a fiery globe, sparkling amid a tremendous crash of thunder, fell to the earth.

In that same year Count Syagrius, sent by order of Guntrannus to Constantinople to make peace with the emperor, attempted by deceit to assume the patriciate there. The attempt was begun but by no means brought to completion.

Leovigildus, king of Spain, also died and left the kingdom to his son Reccaredus.

## CHAPTER LXXVI  
### On the Birth of Theodoricus, Son of Childebertus, and the Confirmation of Childebertus in the Succession to the Kingdom

In the twenty-eighth year of the aforesaid king, the prince was informed that another son had been born to his nephew Childebertus, named Theodoricus. He therefore summoned him and his mother Brunichildis to his presence and once again designated him in his testament as the future heir of his kingdom.

These events took place at a place called Andelot. his sister and Childebertus’s wife were present, together with many powerful men from Francia and Burgundy, so that it might be openly recognized by everyone that, after the death of his uncle Guntrannus, the kingdom of Burgundy was owed to Childebertus.

## CHAPTER LXXVII  
### On Childebertus’s Leading Men Convicted of High Treason; the Marriage of Authari the Lombard to Theudelinda; Reccaredus’s Catholic Faith; and the Army of the Burgundians Sent into Spain

At that time Setacechingus and Boso-Guntrannus, as well as Ursio and Bertefredus, leading men of King Childebertus, were killed by his order because they had plotted to murder him.

Leudefredus, duke of the Alamanni, incurred the displeasure of the aforementioned king. Escaping by flight so as not to be condemned to death, he remained in hiding, and Uncelenus was appointed duke in his place.

In Bavaria, after Garibaldus, Tassilo was appointed king by Childebertus. Soon afterwards, entering Provence with an army of Slavs, he won a victory and returned to his own land with very great booty.

Garibaldus, whom we have just mentioned, was the father-in-law of Authari, king of the Lombards, through his daughter Theudelinda. Authari went in person to her father’s house under the appearance of an envoy, saw her there, fell in love with her, and afterwards took her as his wife.

At that time Reccaredus, king of the Goths, followed not the impiety of his father Leovigildus but the Catholic faith of his brother Hermenegildus. He was first baptized secretly by Bishop Leander. Then he ordered all the books of the Arian sect at Toledo to be gathered together in one place and burned them in the fire, bringing the Goths into the unity of the true faith.

In the twenty-ninth year of Guntrannus’s reign, the army of the Burgundians again entered Spain. But through the negligence of Boso, commander of the army, some of his men were severely cut down by Gothic swords, and the army scarcely returned to its homeland.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII  
### On the Discovery of the Lord’s Seamless Tunic, the Eclipse of the Moon, and the Battle with the Britons, in Which One Frankish Commander Was Killed and Another, on Whom a Heavy Fine Was Later Imposed, Was Reduced to Wretched Poverty

In the thirtieth year of the aforesaid prince, a report spread throughout all the lands of the Franks that the tunic of our Lord Jesus Christ, which had been taken from him during the Passion and assigned by lot to one of the soldiers, in accordance with the prophet’s prediction, “For they cast lots over my garment” (Psalm 21), had been found. A certain Simon, descended from Jacob as his father, made this confession.

After he had been subjected to punishments for nearly two weeks, he finally admitted that the tunic had been placed in a marble chest in the city of Zaphat, far from Jerusalem.

Gregory of Antioch, Thomas of Jerusalem, and John, bishop of Constantinople, together with many other bishops, after completing a three-day fast, transferred it with the greatest devotion and placed it in the place where the Lord’s cross is venerated, together with the same marble chest in which it had previously been kept.

When it was being carried out, it appeared to be so light that those bearing it felt no weight at all.

That year the moon was eclipsed. War also arose between the Franks and the Britons near the river Vixona. There Beppolenus, a Frankish duke, was killed by the Britons through the treachery of another duke, Ebrecharius.

Afterwards Ebrecharius was compelled to pay the substantial compensation that the law requires to be paid to the relatives of the slain, and he fell into the misery of poverty.

## CHAPTER LXXIX  
### On the Embassy of Authari the Lombard to the Frankish Kings and His Death

In the thirty-first year of King Guntrannus, Theodefredus, duke of the Upper Jura, died, and Wadalmarus succeeded him.

Meanwhile Authari, king of the Lombards, sent an embassy to King Guntrannus with peaceful words. The envoys were received by him graciously and sent on to Childebertus, so that peace with the Lombard people might be established through his decision.

While King Authari’s envoys were staying in Francia, Authari died at Pavia, as they relate, after taking poison. Immediately the Lombards sent a messenger to Childebertus, king of the Franks, to announce the death of King Authari and request peace from him.

When Childebertus heard this, he received the envoy in a friendly manner but promised that he would grant peace in the future. Nevertheless, after a few days he dismissed him after promising peace.

## CHAPTER LXXX  
### On Theudelinda, Authari’s Widow, Marrying Agilulfus

After Authari’s death, Queen Theudelinda, who was highly esteemed by the Lombards, with their permission chose Agilulfus—also called Ago—the duke of Turin, a vigorous and warlike man, as both her husband and king of the Lombard people.

To this queen the most wise Pope Gregory sent the four books of his *Dialogues*, which he had written about the lives of the saints, knowing that she was devoted to the faith of Christ and outstanding in good works.

About this time the monastery of blessed Father Benedict, situated in the fortress of Cassino, was attacked at night by the Lombards. Although they plundered everything, they were unable to seize even one monk, so that the prophecy of the venerable Father Benedict, which he had foreseen long before, might be fulfilled. He had said:

“With difficulty I was able to obtain from God that souls should be handed over to me from this place.”

The monks fleeing from that monastery went to Rome, carrying with them the book of the holy Rule that the aforesaid father had composed, along with certain other writings, a weight of bread, a measure of wine, and whatever household goods they had been able to carry away.

After blessed Benedict, the congregation of the monastery of Cassino was governed by Constantine, then by Simplicius, next by Vitalis, and finally by Bonitus. It was under the latter that this destruction took place.

In the thirty-second year of Guntrannus’s reign, the sun was diminished from morning until midday to such an extent that scarcely a third of it could be seen.

## CHAPTER LXXXI  
### On the Death of King Guntrannus and His Monastic Foundation
In the thirty-third year of that same king, the king himself was taken from the body, [Col. 0751B] exchanging—as is believed—an earthly kingdom for a heavenly one, and was buried in the church of Saint Marcellus at Chalon. He himself, as we have said, inflamed by divine love, had built this basilica with great devotion in the suburb of the aforesaid city, though in the territory of Segon and in the Brexian forest. There, gathering monks, he constructed a monastery, which he enriched with numerous estates and possessions.

He ordered a synod of forty bishops to be convened, and ensured that the order of psalmody instituted at the monastery of the holy men of Agaunum in the time of King Sigismund by Avitus and the other bishops of that period should be observed in the coenobium he had built. This same order had also been celebrated from ancient times at the tomb of Saint Martin and, as will be explained later, [Col. 0751C] had been ordered by King Dagobert to be practiced in the monastery of Saint Denis; and when we investigated what its character was, it was found to be as follows.

During the summer days, six antiphons were performed with two psalms each. Throughout August, because of the frequent feast days, *manicationes* were performed. *Manicare* is said to mean “to rise in the morning.” In September, seven antiphons were sung, with two psalms assigned to each; in October, eight, with three psalms; in November, nine, likewise with three psalms; and in December, ten, similarly with three psalms. In January and February, however, they observed this rule as circumstances permitted: at vigils they were not to recite fewer than twelve psalms during the night. At the sixth hour, six psalms with the Alleluia were sung; at the twelfth hour, twelve, likewise with the Alleluia, [Col. 0751D] were sung.

But let this suffice concerning these matters. Guntrannus was outstanding in goodness and generous in distributing nourishment to the poor. He showed himself humble toward the priests of Christ, kindly toward his *leudes*, and peaceful toward foreign peoples. Possessing such virtues, and with many nations proclaiming his praises, he left his present kingdom to his nephew Childebert and himself departed to the heavenly realm.

## CHAPTER LXXXII. Concerning Childebert’s Plan to Take Vengeance on Fredegund for His Father and Uncle

Childebert, surrounded by the support of two kingdoms, was planning vengeance for his father and uncle, whom he knew from reliable indications to have perished through Fredegund’s conspiracy. [Col. 0752A] Accordingly, after assembling all the Austrasians and strong auxiliaries from the kingdom of Burgundy, he placed the dukes Gundoaldus and Wintrio in command and ordered them, as they advanced into hostile territory, to seize booty, spread fires, and carry away as many captives as possible.

They departed from the Campania of Reims and set out to devastate the district of Soissons. Meanwhile Fredegund, having summoned the Franks who obeyed her and also called upon Laudericus—who, as we have recalled, had been appointed guardian by Guntrannus for his son Clotarius—addressed them all in an assembly. Carrying the child before her, she urged them not to despise the infancy of their orphaned king and leave his lands to be ravaged by the enemy. They should remember that they had not promised contempt for his childhood, but reverence for royal majesty. They should cherish the honor which [Col. 0752B] they had judged worthy to be conferred upon him while he still lay in his cradle, lest, when he reached maturity, the king should remain empty of power and full of disgrace. For her part, she would in every possible way ensure a reward for her son, since, stationed in a prominent place, she would watch the battle from above as the observer of all things and the witness of each person’s cowardice or valor.

When she had made them more eager for battle by these exhortations and also by gifts, she concluded: “Let none of you,” she said, “be frightened by the multitude of our opponents. If you engage them face-to-face, I have found a way to deceive them that will bring you victory. You need only follow me as your guide, and whatever you see Landericus, acting in the king’s place, do at my suggestion, do the same yourselves.”

All approved what the queen had said [Col. 0752C] and, in accordance with the plan, armed ranks followed the king, who was still suckling at his mother’s breast. The army rose in the dead of night and entered the forest under Landericus’s leadership. He seized an axe and cut off a branch of a tree; then, carrying a bell suspended from the neck of the horse on which he was riding, he urged his companions all to follow his example. They competed in cutting branches from the trees and, taking bells at the same time, imitated the deed of their leader. At dawn they stood before the enemy camp.

Meanwhile Fredegund, carrying her son Clotarius in her own arms, went ahead of the armed army as far as the place of battle, so that pity for the child might inflame them: if they were defeated, they appeared likely to make a captive of him, though he was king.

But one of the enemy, who with his companions [Col. 0752D] was stationed to perform guard duty, saw them approaching in the still incomplete daylight, without understanding what was happening. Turning to a companion, he said: “What sort of forest is this that I see, when yesterday evening not even the smallest shrubs appeared here?”

His companion replied: “Still belching up yesterday’s meal and loosened by wine, you have committed to forgetfulness that we found suitable pasture for our horses in the neighboring woodland. Do you not hear the bells hanging from the necks of the grazing horses?”

For it had become customary among the ancient Franks, and especially among the Austrasians, to place bells on grazing horses, so that, if they happened to wander farther away while feeding, they could be recognized by their sound.

While the sentries exchanged such remarks, the forest that had first appeared dense, [Col. 0753A] as its branches fell away, seemed to have very sparse foliage but to be extremely dense with the gleam of weapons. The guards were thrown into confusion and hesitated over what to do. When the army descended upon them, some were still resting, exhausted by the previous day’s great labor, on their beds, while others had awakened and cast off sleep; they paid the penalty. Many men were killed, and the rest were put to flight. The commanders themselves mounted their horses and barely escaped death.

Landericus tried in vain to pursue Wintrio, but could not catch him as he was carried along at speed by a swift horse. After this great and wholly unexpected victory, Fredegund, with her son Clotarius and a very large body of armed men, invaded the Campania of Reims, filling everything with fire and blood. Everything was ravaged by day and night; buildings were burned, estates plundered, [Col. 0753B] all who were fit for war were killed, and the weak were kept for the work of slavery. When slaughter and plunder had satisfied them, Fredegund led her army back to Soissons. These events took place in the district of Soissons, at a place called Trueco.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. Concerning the Mutual Slaughter of the Franks and Britons, the Destruction of the Varni, Grippo’s Embassy, and the Franks’ Expedition into Italy

In the second year after Childebert had assumed the kingdom of Burgundy, the armies of the Franks and Britons, intent upon one another’s destruction, struck each other down in mutual slaughter. In the following year, many signs appeared in the sky, and a comet became visible.

That year, [Col. 0753C] Childebert’s army fought against the Varni, who were attempting to rebel; it brought them almost to total destruction. At the same time, Grippo, Childebert’s envoy, returned from Constantinople and reported to the king how honorably he had been received by the emperor Maurice, and that the emperor had promised, according to Childebert’s wishes, that he himself would avenge the injuries Grippo had suffered at Carthage. Childebert therefore once again sent twenty dukes, with a select body of young men, into Italy to destroy the Lombard people. Among them, Andoaldus, Olo, and Cedinus were the most prominent.

But Olo, when he imprudently approached the fortress of Bilitio, was struck by a javelin beneath the breast and fell dead. Andoaldus and six Frankish dukes, however, came to the city of Milan [Col. 0753D] and pitched camp on the plain.

There the emperor’s envoys came to them, announcing that an army was on its way to assist them. They said: “Because we shall come together with them after three days, this will be your sign: when you see the houses of this village, which is situated on the mountain, being consumed by fire and smoke rising to the heavens, know that we are approaching with the cohorts we have promised.”

But the Frankish dukes waited six days beside the place as agreed and saw none of those whom the envoys had promised arrive. Cedinus, entering Italy on the left with thirteen dukes, captured five fortresses and exacted oaths from them. In the territory of Trent, [Col. 0754A] the Franks also destroyed ten fortresses and led away captive all who lived in them.

For the fortress of Ferruge, however, through the intercession of Bishop Ingenuinus of Savio and Agnellus of Trent, a ransom was paid: one solidus for each man, amounting to six hundred solidi. Meanwhile, because it was summer and the air was unaccustomed to them, the Frankish army suffered severely from dysentery. After roaming through Italy for three months and being unable to reach the king whom they had come to defeat, since he had shut himself up within the city of Ticinum, they returned home, weakened—as we have said—by the unhealthy climate.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. Concerning the Death of Childebert and His Wife, and the Succession of His Sons Theodebert and Theodoric

[Col. 0754B]

In the fourth year of the kingdom of Burgundy assumed by Childebert, but the twenty-third of his paternal kingdom, and in the twenty-fifth year of his age, King Childebert himself, as is reported, died with his wife by the force of poison. This was Childebert, the son of Sigebert, who was also called the Younger.

He was succeeded by his two sons, still little boys and placed under the guardianship of their grandmother Brunechildis. The kingdom of the Austrasians fell to Theodebert—namely, the kingdom which their father Childebert had received from his own father Sigebert and which had been left to him. To Theodoric fell Guntrannus’s kingdom, which Childebert had held by right of adoption.

They also established their residences in the places where the earlier kings had established theirs. Letters of the blessed Gregory, Roman [Col. 0754C] pontiff, survive addressed to these brothers and to their grandmother Brunechildis, in which he commends to them Augustine, the bishop whom he had sent to the Anglo-Saxons. In them the same man of God confesses, in response to the aforesaid queen’s request, that he had sent relics of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

## CHAPTER LXXXV. Concerning the Incursion of the Huns into Thuringia, and the Embassy of Agilulf, or Agon, into Gaul

At that time the Huns, who are also called Avars, came out of Pannonia and waged very serious wars with the Franks in Thuringia. Nevertheless, after receiving money from Brunechildis or from her grandsons, they returned to their own land.

Agon, king of the Lombards, also sent Agnellus, bishop of Trent, into Francia [Col. 0754D] on behalf of those who had been carried away captive by the Franks from the Trentine fortresses. On his return, he brought back with him some of the captives whom Brunechildis had ransomed at her own expense.

Evuin, duke of the Trentine people, was likewise sent by the aforesaid prince and went to Gaul to obtain peace. Having secured it, he returned to Italy.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. Concerning Fredegund’s Ravaging and Death, the Slaughter of Quintrio, Colenus’s Patriciate, the Bubonic Plague, the Cooking of Fish in a River through Excessive Heat, and Warnecharius’s Generosity

In the year, then, in which Childebert died, Queen Fredegund, elated by the triumph of her earlier victory, swept through Paris and the other cities with barbarian violence, together with her son Clotarius. Their army attacked Kings Theodebert and Theodoric, and at a place called Latopha [Col. 0755A] severely weakened the military forces they had assembled, inflicting great slaughter and putting the survivors to flight.

In the second year of the reign of Theodebert and Theodoric, Queen Fredegund, old and full of days, died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Vincent in the suburb of Paris. In the third year of the aforesaid kings, the duke Quintrio was killed at Brunechildis’s instigation. In the following year Colenus, a Frank by birth, was appointed patrician.

In those days, at Marseille and in the other cities of Provence, a very great mortality arose when certain swellings, like nuts, developed in the groins of human beings and in the more delicate parts of the body. In Lake Dunus, into which the Arula River flows, the water also boiled so fiercely that it cast onto the shore a large quantity of cooked fish. When Warnecharius, mayor [Col. 0755B] of the palace of King Theodoric, died, he distributed all his possessions as provisions for the poor.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. Concerning Brunechildis’s Downfall, Her Remarkable Wandering, Her Gratitude toward a Poor Guide, and Celestial Portents

Brunechildis was expelled from the kingdom of the Austrasians by her grandson Theodebert and the nobles who obeyed him. She was found and recognized alone by a certain poor man in the plain of Marciac. At her own request, she was led by him to her other grandson, Theodoric.

Theodoric received his grandmother Brunechildis with the honor she deserved and kept her with him for as long as she lived. The poor man, whom the often-mentioned queen had used as her guide, obtained the bishopric of Auxerre as [Col. 0755C] a reward for this reciprocal service.

In the fifth year of the aforesaid kings, the signs that had appeared in earlier years appeared again: fiery globes moving through the sky in the western regions, resembling a multitude of stars.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. Concerning the Most Savage Conflict between the Kings, the Vision of an Angel, and the Flight and Losses of Clotarius

Theodebert and Theodoric at last brought forth the quarrel they had long conceived against their uncle Clotarius. With their grandmother Brunechildis urging them on, they engaged him in battle beside the River Arvenna, not far from the village of Doromellus.

There such slaughter took place on both sides, especially on Clotarius’s, that the river itself, filled with human bodies, [Col. 0755D] could no longer complete its course. In that battle an angel of the Lord was seen standing with a drawn sword.

When Clotarius saw his men being slaughtered with terrible violence, he fled. Passing through the fortress of Milidunum, situated on an island in the Seine, he hastened to Paris. Theodebert and Theodoric pursued him from behind, overthrowing a large part of the cities in his kingdom and subjecting the inhabitants to slavery.

Although unwilling, Clotarius was compelled to confirm the terms proposed by his enemies: Theodoric’s kingdom was to extend between the Loire and the Seine as far as the Ocean and the boundary of the Britons; the whole duchy of Dentelen between the Seine and the Isère, and likewise the territory extending to the sea, was to belong to Theodebert. Only twelve districts between the Seine and the Isère, [Col. 0756A] reaching as far as the shores of the Ocean, remained to Clotarius.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. Concerning the Slaughter of Catinus, the Birth of Sigebert, the Death of Egila, the Subjugation of the Basques, the Elevation of the Lombard Adaloald, and a Battle with the Saxons

In the sixth year of the reigns of Theodebert and Theodoric, Catinus, duke of Theodebert, was killed. In the following year, Theodoric had a son by a concubine, named Sigebert.

Egila, the patrician, although no fault of his was apparent, was killed solely because of the prompting of avarice, through Brunechildis’s counsel, and his possessions were added to the treasury. At that time Theodebert and Theodoric subdued the Basques and appointed over them a duke named Genialis.

In those days, [Col. 0756B] Adaloald was raised as king over the Lombards at Milan in the presence of his father, King Agilulf, while envoys of Theodebert, king of the Franks, stood by. The daughter of King Theodebert was betrothed to the royal boy, and perpetual peace was established with the Franks.

At the same time, while the Franks were fighting with the Saxons, great slaughter took place on both sides.

## CHAPTER XC. Concerning the Discovery of the Body of Saint Victor, the Death of Etherius, Archbishop of Lyon, the Birth of the Younger Childebert, the Deposition of Bishop Desiderius, the Appointment of Dommilus, and a Solar Eclipse

The blessed Econius, bishop of Maurienne, discovered the body of Saint Victor, who had suffered martyrdom at Solodorum together with Saint Ursus, in the following manner.

One night, [Col. 0756C] while resting in his city, he was warned in a divine revelation through a vision to rise and go as quickly as possible to the church that Sedeleuba, once queen of the Burgundians, had built in the suburb of Genava. There, in the middle of the basilica, he was shown the place where the holy body had been buried.

When the bishop hurried to the city of Genava, taking with him the bishops Rusticus and Patricius, and after a three-day fast had been completed, a heavenly light appeared on the following night at the place where the limbs of the glorious martyr rested. Then these three priests of the Lord lifted the stone beneath which it was covered and found the saint lying in a silver coffin. His face, illuminated by divine radiance, shone seven times more brightly than that of any living human being. [Col. 0756D]

Theodoric the prince was present at this wondrous discovery of the illustrious martyr. He bestowed upon that place a very large portion of Warnecharius’s property, which, as we have said, Warnecharius had assigned for distribution in alms. Thereafter, at the tomb of the most blessed Victor, the power of Christ displayed many signs of miracles.

That year Etherius, archbishop of Lyon, died, and Secundinus was ordained in his place.

In the eighth year of Theodebert’s reign, another son was born to him by a concubine, bearing the name of his grandfather Childebert. A synod was also convened at Chalon and deposed Desiderius, bishop of Vienne. He was driven into exile through the conspiracy of Brunechildis and Aridius, bishop of Lyon, who had succeeded Secundinus, and Dommilus was appointed [Col. 0757A] in his place to the priestly office. That year a solar eclipse occurred.

## CHAPTER XCI. Concerning the Birth of Corbus, the Death of Bertoaldus, the Insolence of Protadius, Brunechildis’s Lover, and the Conflict of the Kings

In the ninth year of the aforesaid king, another son was born to him, named Corbus.

At that time Bertoaldus was count of the palace of the prince. He was a wise and cautious man, suited in character to the king, brave in battle, and faithful in entrusted matters. A certain Protadius, however, was a Roman by birth, extremely intimate with Brunechildis for the sake of sexual relations, and for this reason she appointed him duke in the district of Ultrajura after Wandalmarus.

As Protadius’s habit of vice increased, so too did his desire to increase his honor. Brunechildis, having secretly considered this plan, presumed [Col. 0757B] to ask her grandson to have Bertoaldus killed and Protadius appointed mayor of the entire royal household.

At that time Bertoaldus had been sent by Theodoric with three hundred men into Neustria to defend part of his kingdom, and was engaged in hunting at the estate of Arenaunus [variant: Arelaunus]. When Clotarius learned of this, he sent his son Meroveus and the duke Landericus, with able men given as auxiliaries, to crush Bertoaldus.

When Bertoaldus learned from reliable messengers that the enemy intended to attack him, and knew that he would be too weak to resist them, he turned his back and withdrew to Orléans, where he was received by Saint Austrenus, bishop of that city. Landericus led his army before the gates of Orléans and challenged Bertoaldus to come out for battle.

[Col. 0757C] Bertoaldus replied: “You trust in the numerous soldiers surrounding you and believe that I, with only a few men, cannot resist you. But, if you agree, let the two of us engage in single combat, while the armed multitude remains at a distance and awaits the outcome. Let no retinue offer assistance; let the judgment of the just judge alone be awaited.”

When Landericus refused to engage, Bertoaldus said to him again: “Since fear now prevents you from joining battle with me, it is fitting that our masters, because of your rash ventures—in which you presumed to seize part of my lord the king’s kingdom—should decide the matter among themselves with their armed forces. Then, if you wish, you and I, clothed in patterned garments, may engage amid the packed ranks. There you will be able to experience both the disgrace [Col. 0757D] of my cowardice and the proof of your own valor.”

Landericus did not reject these conditions. Each of them invoked certain curses upon the other if he abandoned what he had undertaken.

These events took place on the feast day of Saint Martin. When Theodoric learned for certain that part of his kingdom had been invaded by Clotarius, on the very day when the birth of the incarnate Word is devoutly celebrated by all the faithful, he moved his army and drew up his battle line at Stampae on the River Junna against Clotarius, who was preparing no less energetically to meet him.

Because the crossing of the River Junna was narrow, battle began before the entire army of Theodoric had crossed. Amid the most densely packed battalions, eager for mutual destruction, [Col. 0758A] Bertoaldus repeatedly called Landericus by name and did not cease challenging him to engage according to their agreement.

When Landericus refused and gradually withdrew from the place, Bertoaldus rose with the sole intention of facing death. Since he already knew that Brunechildis intended to remove him from his former rank of honor and appoint Protadius in his place, he judged it better to meet death honorably in battle than to spend whatever life remained to him in disgrace.

As he strove to drive back the scattered ranks, press the retreating enemy, and strike down those who confronted him with the sword, he was surrounded and overwhelmed by many men and killed. In that battle Meroveus, Clotarius’s son, was captured. Landericus fled with Clotarius, while the victorious Theodoric [Col. 0758B] entered Paris.

Afterward Theodebert made peace with Clotarius at the estate of Compiègne; their armies returned home unharmed.

## CHAPTER XCII. Concerning the Shameful Avarice of the Roman Protadius, Who Became Mayor of the Royal Palace, by Which He Became Hated by All and Was Finally Killed by the Nobles; the Reconciliation of the Kings; and the Succession of Claudius, a Prudent Roman

In the tenth year of Theodoric’s reign, Protadius was appointed mayor of the palace at Brunechildis’s wish and by Theodoric’s command. Although he was extremely sharp-minded and considered energetic in counsel, he was stained by a savage greed toward the wealthy, wishing to fill the treasury and enrich himself.

By persecuting the Burgundian nobility and wishing to subject everyone to himself, [Col. 0758C] he attempted unjustly to take away their property, lest anyone be able to deprive him of the honor he enjoyed. Consequently, no powerful person could be found who wished to enjoy his intimate conversation or friendship.

Meanwhile Brunechildis, remembering her former enmity and plotting vengeance for her expulsion, urged Theodoric to seek his father’s treasures from Theodebert’s hands, asserting that Theodebert was not the son of Childebert but of some gardener. Protadius began urging the king more zealously to carry this out.

At last Theodoric set out with his army and pitched camp at Cariciacum, prepared to engage his brother on the following day. Theodebert had encamped not far away with a strong force of Austrasians.

Meanwhile [Col. 0758D] Theodoric’s *leudes* began urging him “to be reconciled with his brother and not place the honor of brotherhood below a most empty desire.” Protadius, on the contrary, resisted vehemently, saying: “Peace ought not to be made.”

The other nobles realized that he alone was opposing their counsels and discussed among themselves that it would be more expedient to hand one man over to death than to endanger the entire army.

By chance the king left his tent for exercise. When rumor brought him word that certain men wished to kill Protadius, he tried to rush out to remove them from injuring the aforesaid man, but his own men restrained and forcibly detained him. He sent a certain man named Uncelenus, who, invoking the authority of his command, was to forbid the leaders of the faction to undertake such an act.

Then [Col. 0759A] Uncelenus came to those who had already surrounded the king’s tent, where Protadius was sitting and playing at tables with Peter, an expert in medicine, and addressed them as follows: “My lord King Theodoric commands that Protadius, who is opposed to peace, be killed.”

At these words, all rushed together and cut down the tent with their swords, killing Protadius there.

Although compelled by his men, Theodoric was reconciled with his brother Theodebert, and both armies returned safely and in full strength to their own territories.

In the eleventh year of Theodoric’s reign, a certain Claudius, likewise Roman by birth, was appointed mayor of the palace in place of Protadius. He was a prudent man, full of faith, entertaining in conversation, farsighted in all things, but extremely heavy because of the bulk of his body. Frightened by the example of his predecessor, he maintained friendship with everyone and showed himself gentle and [Col. 0759B] gracious.

## CHAPTER XCIII. Concerning Brunechildis’s Vengeance upon the Enemies of Protadius and the Stoning of Bishop Desiderius

In the twelfth year of Theodoric’s reign, Uncelenus, who through his deceit had been responsible for Protadius’s death, was ambushed by Brunechildis, had his foot amputated, was stripped of his possessions, and was reduced to poverty.

The patrician Wolfus, because he had consented to the killing of the aforesaid Protadius, was also killed at Fariniacum by Theodoric’s command, at Brunechildis’s suggestion.

A son was also born to Theodoric by a concubine, named Meroveus. King Clotarius lifted him from the sacred font.

The often-mentioned King Theodoric, deceived by the persuasion of Aridius, bishop of Lyon, and of his grandmother Brunechildis, ordered the holy [Col. 0759C] Desiderius, bishop of Vienne, to be stoned after he had been recalled from exile. Miracles were frequently displayed at his tomb.

## CHAPTER XCIV. Concerning the Unfortunate Marriage of Hermemberga, Daughter of the King of Spain, with Theodoric

At that time Theodoric sent the bishop Aridius and the prefects of the horse, Rocconus and Eborinus, to King Bettricus of Spain. They were to ask that his daughter be joined to Theodoric in marriage and, if the father wished, to offer an oath “that throughout the days of his life he would not deprive her of royal honor.”

Bettricus gladly agreed and handed the girl over to the envoys. Theodoric received her joyfully and at first loved her above all others. Yet, through Brunechildis’s sorcery, she did not know her husband [Col. 0759D].

Then, at the instigation of the same grandmother, Theodoric stripped Hermemberga—for that was the maiden’s name—of her treasures and ordered her to return to Spain.

Bettricus, angered by this, sent envoys to King Clotarius, who was born of Theodoric’s uncle. They explained the reasons for the injury and sought to persuade him to join them in war. When he appeared to have granted their request, they went directly with his envoys to Theodebert.

Having learned that he too would provide them assistance, they proceeded directly to Agon, king of the Lombards, together with the envoys of the kings mentioned above. Their purpose was that these four kings should attack Theodoric, deprive him both of life and kingdom, and exact vengeance for the insult inflicted upon the king of Spain [Col. 0760A].

When Theodoric was informed that such a plan was being organized against him, he despised it as futile. Bettricus’s envoy, however, believing that he had obtained everything for which he had come, returned to Spain by sea.

## CHAPTER XCV. Concerning the Freedom of Speech and Miracles of the Irishman Columbanus, the King’s Feigned Repentance, the Construction of the Monastery of Bobbio, and Columbanus’s Departure

In the fourteenth year of the reigns of Theodebert and Theodoric, the blessed Columbanus came from Ireland, an island in the Ocean, and was first received by Theodebert.

Later, because crowds of people were flocking to him, he departed from that place, wishing to lead a solitary life. He crossed into [Col. 0760B] the kingdom of Theodoric and, at the command of the aforesaid king, was ordered to live in a place called Luxeuil.

The king frequently came to visit him. When the man of God rebuked him for abandoning his lawful wife and devoting himself to adulterous unions, and when the king inclined the ear of his heart toward obeying the saint’s salutary admonitions, his grandmother Brunechildis, inflamed by the viperous instigations of the ancient enemy, began to turn more fiercely against Saint Columbanus.

The holy man, preparing to confront her wickedness, hurried to the villa called Bruchariacum, where she was staying. The queen, meeting him with her grandsons, the sons of Theodoric, asked him “to bless the royal offspring.”

He replied that “they would by no means receive royal scepters, since they had emerged from brothels.” [Col. 0760C]

The indignant queen ordered the boys to leave and followed shortly afterward. As the man of God hastened to return to his own place and set foot on the threshold of the royal palace, the entire structure of the house suddenly shook with a crash.

But the mind of the most wicked woman was not shaken; rather, it was inflamed with an even greater fire of anger. She feared that she would be expelled from the kingdom and stripped of all dignity if the king, setting aside the charms of prostitutes, took a royal woman in marriage.

She therefore forbade both the holy man and the brothers living with him to leave or return to the monastery. She ordered her nobles, who occupied the places near the coenobium, to allow no one to depart or to receive anyone who arrived as a guest.

Again the holy man went to the palace to warn her to desist from such obstinacy. By chance, on that day Theodoric was staying with his grandmother at the villa of Spinsia [Col. 0760D]. He was informed that the man of God was standing outside the doors and did not wish to lodge in the same building.

Then the king, fearing that the Lord’s anger threatened him, said that it was better to honor the man of God with suitable provisions than to provoke God to anger through an offense against His servants. He therefore ordered that everything necessary for food be prepared in royal fashion and delivered to the servant of the Lord by his own ministers.

When they had promptly fulfilled this order, the blessed Columbanus, looking at them with the stern expression customary to him, asked what these things meant. They told him that the king had sent the food for his own use and that of his companions.

He replied: “No,” [Col. 0761A] he said, “according to the testimony of Scripture,” the gifts of the impious are not acceptable to God. Therefore His servants ought not to receive what He himself is shown to hate.”

After these words, all the vessels were smashed to pieces, the wine and *sicera* were poured out on the ground, and everything else was scattered separately.

The royal ministers, terrified, returned to the king and reported the sequence of events. Struck by immense fear, the king hurried at dawn with his grandmother to the man of God. They begged forgiveness for what they had done and promised to correct their conduct thereafter.

Pacified by these promises, he returned to the monastery. But this promise produced no fruit of effective action. Theodoric continued to wallow in the mire of lust, as he had previously been accustomed to do, and Brunechildis’s mind, once steeped in wickedness, was not changed at all by the persecution of the holy man.

Rather, [Col. 0761B] the savage spirit of cruelty proceeded so far that she persuaded her grandson to exile the holy man of God to the city of Vesontio and, after he had returned from there, to lead him as far as the shores of the British Sea, so that, once he had crossed the strait, he would never again see the fields of Gaul.

Since the man of God had resolved, in accordance with his purpose of mind, never to return to his native land, he passed through the kingdom of Theodebert into Italy, constructed the monastery called Bobbio, and, full of holiness and years, departed to the Lord.

## CHAPTER XCVI. Theodoric Makes a Pact with His Brother Out of Fear of Him

In the fifteenth year of his reign, Theodebert prepared to add some of his brother Theodoric’s possessions [Col. 0761C] to his own and thereby provoked him against himself.

Nevertheless, on the prudent advice of wise men, a place called Saloissa was selected [formerly Saletio, today Seltz, near the Rhine], so that the brothers, meeting at the appointed place with only a few of the leading men of Gaul, might determine the terms of peace.

Theodoric arrived there with only ten thousand men, while Theodebert came with a large force of Austrasians; he was also ready to disturb the peace by war if his brother did not agree to his demands [Col. 0761D].

Terrified by the sight of so great a multitude, Theodoric granted what Theodebert wanted, though unwillingly. The brothers’ agreement was as follows: Theodoric was to cede Alesatio, Sugitensi, the county of Tours, and the Campanian county, and authority over all these territories was to pass to Theodebert.

They departed from there with goodwill, though it was feigned, and, greeting one another, each returned to his own kingdom.

## CHAPTER XCVII. Concerning the Alemanni’s Ravaging of the Ultrajurane Territory

In those days the Alemanni entered the territory of the Veneti. They defeated in battle the Ultrajurani who attempted to resist them under the leadership of Cambelenus and Erpinus, pursued them as far as their mountain refuges, and struck them down.

Afterward, with no one troubling them, they traversed the Jura forest, filling everything through which they passed with slaughter and fires. After carrying away many captives, they returned home with booty and immense plunder.

## CHAPTER XCVIII. Concerning Theodoric’s Plans, Theodebert’s Disgraceful Marriage, Berto Leunisius, and His Fable about the Wolf and the Conflict of the Kings

[Col. 0762A]

Theodoric, desiring to avenge the injuries he had received, was considering with his men by what means he might crush his brother. That year Theodebert killed Bilechilda—whom Brunechild, having bought her from merchants because she was exceptionally beautiful, had given him as a wife—and took a girl named Theudechild as his own wife. Theodoric, as we have said, pursuing Theodebert with hostile hatred, sent to Clotaire men who, as though speaking in his name, were to say:

“Having been subjected to insults by my brother, I intend to repay him what he deserves, if I learn that you will not come to his aid. Therefore I ask you to remain quiet and bring him no assistance, promising that, if I emerge victorious and am able to take both his kingdom and his life from him, I shall restore to your authority the duchy of Dentelin, which he unjustly retains after having taken it from you.”

Clotaire agreed to this pact. In the seventeenth year of his reign, in the month of May, Theodoric ordered all the most war-ready men under his authority to assemble at Langres. Proceeding by way of the fortress of Vervona, which at that time had begun to be built, he reached Toul. There he encountered Theodebert, who had come with reinforcements from the Austrasians, and did not hesitate to join battle. Having engaged his brother in the Toul countryside, he severely battered his army.

Theodebert nevertheless escaped and, fleeing from the battle through the city of Metz and the Vosges forest, sought the refuges of the city of Cologne. Theodoric, hastening to pursue his brother without delay, met the blessed Leunisius, bishop of Mainz, who came to him and offered the following counsel:

“Continue what you have begun,” he said, “and, with God’s help, you will bring this undertaking to completion. A rustic tale relates that a wolf, leading his cubs out to hunt, called them to himself on a mountain and gave them these instructions: ‘Know that no one should seek what is advantageous for you, my sons, except among the few who are of your own kind. Therefore I warn you not to abandon the duties you have undertaken, and to seek what is necessary for your sustenance.’”

Theodoric, a diligent executor of this advice, obeyed it, especially since he knew that Leunisius favored his interests and opposed Theodebert’s folly. Crossing the Ardennes, he advanced as far as Tolbiacum [today Zülpich].

Meanwhile Theodebert, who had prepared for flight, delayed. He summoned the Saxons and the other peoples of Upper Germany to his aid and set them against Theodoric at the place mentioned above. The struggle was fierce for as long as Theodebert remained in the fight. He resisted, although his army was being slaughtered like cattle.
