But when he himself, unable to endure the burden of the battle, sought safety in flight, all who had stood to fight turned away. Most of them, scattered in the uncertainty of flight, perished; the survivors hurried with the king toward Cologne.

At the first clash of battle, the two sides came together with such fierce determination that the corpses of the slain, because the masses of the peoples pressing together prevented them from falling to the ground, were carried around together with the living, just as the men had sat upon their horses. But after the defeated phalanx exposed its back to the enemy, the roads and the pathless places of the forests were filled with the bodies of the dead.

When word was brought to Theodoric that Theodebert had escaped, this gave him an additional incentive to hasten his journey, since he considered the war’s cost to have been wasted if the leader and the people most ready for battle were not intercepted. Thus, arriving with his men in the territory of the Ripuarians, he devastated or burned everything that came in his way.

The inhabitants of that land came to him to plead that he not bring destruction upon them because of one man’s guilt—men whom he knew, by the right of victory, would be his own. He replied:

“Destruction is being prepared not for you, but for Theodebert. If you wish to earn my favor, you must either take his head or bring him to me alive and bound.”

They entered the royal palace at Cologne and addressed Theodebert as follows:

“Your brother Theodoric sends this message: ‘If I deserve to receive back the paternal treasures which Theodebert still unjustly holds after seizing them, I shall promptly return to my own homes.’ Therefore we urge you, lord king, to restore to him the portion owed to him and not allow him to molest our homes.”

Theodebert believed these words and considered what they had said to be true. He entered with them the place where the royal treasure was kept. While he was examining what might most suitably be restored to his brother without loss to himself, one of those standing nearby struck his neck with a drawn sword, cut off his head, and carried it around the walls of Cologne.

When Theodoric saw this, he immediately took possession of the city itself and seized the royal treasures. He compelled the leading men of the city to swear allegiance to him. While he was exacting their oaths in the basilica of Saint Gereon, he thought that someone had struck him in the side with his fist. Turning to his men, he said:

“Watch the doors, so that no one may leave, because I do not know which of these Ripuarians [French: Ribaroles], guilty of perjury, has attempted to wound me.”

While they were keeping watch, the chamberlains removed the king’s clothing and examined his side, but no wound was found. Only a certain purple mark appeared, which I believe was an indication of his swift death.

Having arranged matters according to his wishes, Theodoric departed from there with much booty. He took with him his brother’s sons, together with his daughter, who shone with a beautiful appearance. When he arrived at Metz, he found that his grandmother Brunechild had come there to meet him. She seized Theodebert’s sons and immediately handed them over to death. The younger one, Meroveus by name, still dressed in white, she forced to breathe out his innocent spirit after dashing him against a stone.

Thus Theodebert reigned for seventeen years. Certain authors [FREDEGARIUS, ch. 38] have written that, after Theodoric’s victory and his own calamity, Theodebert crossed the Rhine, and that Theodoric, after capturing Cologne, sent his chamberlain Bertarius to seize him. Having been captured by Bertarius, brought before Theodoric, and stripped of his royal garments, he is said to have been banished into exile at Chalon. In recompense for so distinguished a deed, Bertarius is also said to have received from Theodoric Theodebert’s horse with its royal trappings.

## CHAPTER XCIX. On Clotaire’s recovering the duchy of Dentelin and Theodoric’s anger against him

In accordance with the agreement that Clotaire had made with Theodoric—in the manner mentioned above—the duchy of Dentelin was restored to its rightful lord. Therefore Theodoric, seeing that the kingdom of the Austrasians obeyed Clotaire, was moved by immense indignation and sent him this message through ambassadors:

“He must withdraw from the aforesaid duchy. If he does not do so, Theodoric will not lack whatever means may be available to avenge the injury of the insult inflicted upon him.”

## CHAPTER C. On Theodoric’s seeking his brother’s daughter, his rebuke by Brunechild, his anger against Brunechild, and Brunechild’s cruelty in killing him with poison

Meanwhile, while Theodoric was staying at Metz, he began to waste away from love for the daughter of his brother Theodebert, whom he had taken captive at Cologne. When he wished to join her to himself in marriage, his grandmother prohibited him from doing so. He said to her:

“What offense shall I incur if I take her as my wife?”

Brunechild replied:

“It is not lawful for you to have as a wife one descended from your brother.”

When Theodoric heard this, he was stirred to fury and answered her in these words:

“Did you not, hateful to God and detested by all good people, tell me that he was not my brother? Why did you impose upon me so heavy a burden of brother-murder?”

He drew his sword and wished to strike her. But those standing nearby rescued her and carried her out of the house in their arms. She escaped the danger of death, but with feminine recklessness devised treachery against her grandson. When he was leaving the bath, she had a cup of poison brought to him by the hands of servants whom money had corrupted. After drinking it, he received the end of life as though repenting of the crimes he had committed—the life he had stained with his offenses.

The authors mentioned above (FREDEGARIUS, ch. 39) report, however, that he died of dysentery in the aforesaid city of Metz, while preparing an expedition against Clotaire, in the eighteenth year of his reign.

[Col. 0763D] Here ends the third book.

# THE FOURTH BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0763]

## CHAPTER I. On Clotaire’s struggle, at Brunechild’s instigation, with Theodoric’s illegitimate sons over the succession to the kingdom, and on Brunechild’s death

After so many Frankish kings had been extinguished or had met death by various fates—kings under whom rule had continued for nearly fifty-one years—Clotaire, born of King Chilperic, appeared to be the only heir of legitimate succession left from the royal line, and to him the right of ruling ought above all to pass.

Brunechild, however, was working, if possible, to place Sigebert, Theodoric’s son, over the kingdom of the Austrasians. Theodoric had fathered four sons by concubines, whose names were Sigebert, Corbus, Childebert, and Meroveus. But because they were less noble on their mother’s side, they were considered unfit to govern the kingdom as well. It was also understood that Brunechild wished, after selecting one man merely for the appearance of kingship and not for the actual power, to reserve for herself the administration of the supreme affairs of state. At the same time, the leading men of Francia were indignant at being subjected for so long to female domination.

Accordingly, with the support of Arnulf and Pippin, the chief men of Austrasia, Clotaire advanced as far as Captonnacum. Brunechild, residing in Warmatia, heard of his arrival and sent to him, entreating him to withdraw from the kingdom that Theodoric had left to his sons.

Clotaire replied that she ought to assemble a gathering of the nobles of the Franks and, through common deliberation, consult about common affairs; he himself promised to obey their judgment in everything and not to oppose their decisions.

Brunechild perceived that she was being deceived by these words. She sent Sigebert, Theodoric’s firstborn son, into Thuringia and attempted to invite the peoples living beyond the Rhine to join the war. She also arranged for Warnarius, the mayor of the palace, and Alboin, one of the most eminent nobles of Austrasia, to be sent with him.

But because she suspected Warnarius of planning to defect to Clotaire, she sent letters after them ordering that Alboin be punished. Alboin tore the letters he had read into pieces and threw them to the ground. Nevertheless, one of Warnarius’s household discovered them, copied them onto a wax tablet, and showed them to him. When Warnarius saw them, he understood that his life was in danger. He began to gather himself and mentally prepare how, after destroying Theodoric’s sons, he might hand over the kingdom to Clotaire together with himself. First, therefore, he alienated from Brunechild the peoples to whom he had been sent to summon reinforcements for the war.

Then, having entered Burgundy with Brunechild and Sigebert, he brought all the leading men, together with the bishops of that people, over to his opinion, privately using among them the following argument. Since they all hated Brunechild’s arrogance and cruelty, they promised that they would not fail to support his will.

After accomplishing this, he sent messengers to Clotaire and instructed him to come with an army, promising that, if security of life and honor were granted to him in complete good faith, he would hand over the kingdom of Burgundy together with the entire military force of the Austrasians.

When Sigebert came with the Burgundians, Clotaire met him in the Catalaunian plain beside the river Axona with the Neustrians. He had with him a number of Austrasians, among them the patrician Aletheus, and the dukes Rocco, Sigoaldus, and Eudilanus.

While armed divisions on both sides stood ready for battle, Warnarius and his men, as he had arranged, withdrew from the fight at the given signal before the armies engaged. Those whose desire to fight was equal did the same.

Clotaire gradually followed them, since he wished to destroy none of those whom he trusted would become his own. He reached the river Arar, now called the Saône, and, having captured three of Theodoric’s sons—Sigebert, Corbus, and Meroveus—returned to the village of Riona, situated on the river Vincenna. The fourth, Childebert by name, escaped from the battle with the help of a swift horse and was never found afterward.

There, at the urging of Warnarius and the other nobles who favored him, Brunechild was presented to Clotaire, together with Theudelana, Theodoric’s sister. Theudelana had been dragged out from the village of Urbana in the Upper Jura by Erpone, overseer of the royal horses.

In Clotaire’s presence, he ordered Sigebert and Corbus, his nephews born of Theodoric, to be killed. Meroveus, however, for whom Clotaire himself had served as spiritual father at baptism, he entrusted to the count Ingobodus and ordered him to be taken to Neustria and raised with the utmost kindness.

Then he ordered Brunechild to be brought before him. A multitude of soldiers had assembled, not only from Neustria but also from Austrasia and Burgundy. Having received authority to conceal no longer the hatred they had long harbored against her, he ordered that she be subjected to various tortures for three days and carried around the entire army mounted on a camel.

At last, recalling that ten Frankish kings had perished partly through her counsel, partly by her hand, or even through her sorcery, he addressed her as follows:

“Why, accursed among women and deviser of the worst arts, did you burst forth into such obstinacy that you were not ashamed to destroy so many generations of a glorious stock? Perish, then, as a cruel example of punishment, you who were not afraid to stain yourself with so great a murder.

“For, to say nothing of the others, we know that my paternal uncle Sigebert, your husband, rose against his brother at your advice; because of this he met an unforeseen death. Meroveus, my brother on my father’s side, hated by his father because of you, was killed by a most wicked form of cruelty.

“Why should I recall Chilperic, the father of my birth, whom, as is reported, you put to death through officers sent for that purpose, although he feared no such thing? I cannot recount the end of so great a father without tears, nor express the sorrows of my orphanhood.

“I am ashamed to recall the fraternal armies and alternating wars fought out in profane hatred—wars that you, the storm of the entire palace, aroused, encouraging your grandsons to mutual slaughter, so that brother might kill brother and no just compassion might move their minds.

“Finally, Theodoric, believing your persuasion that Theodebert was not his brother, became a shedder of fraternal blood, although he already bore upon his hands the stain of the blood of Meroveus, his own son.

“It is known that Theodebert’s son, still clothed in the white garment of new birth, was dashed by you against a stone and breathed out his innocent spirit together with his brother.

“Nor must the recent atrocity be omitted: namely, that Theodoric was killed by your sorcery with poison, and that his sons, persuaded by you to make war against me, were handed over to death—three of them, as though they were guilty.

“I prefer to be silent about the innumerable slaughterings of leaders. Whether they were carried out justly or unjustly is not for this time to explain, provided that you, my dearest fellow soldiers and foremost nobles of Francia, decide what punishment one so guilty of such crimes should suffer.”

When everyone shouted that she ought to be subjected to unheard-of punishments, Clotaire ordered an untamed horse to be brought. The hair of the wretched queen was tied, together with her arms, to its tail, and the horse was finally urged into a gallop. At the first charge of the running horse, her brain was scattered by its hooves. Her remaining limbs were dragged through every rough place, among thorns and rocks, and were torn apart.

Such was the end Brunechild suffered—a woman especially practiced in the slaughter of her relatives. After killing them, she had added their possessions to her own as spoils. Prosperity increased her arrogance, so that feminine weakness lifted itself beyond measure.

Nevertheless, she was not so completely foolish that she failed reverently to honor the memories of God and his saints, which her predecessors had established; indeed, she devoutly multiplied them by building new structures. In the suburb of Laon she built a basilica in honor of Saint Vincent; and at Autun she ordered another dedicated to Saint Martin, employing for this work the necessary services of the venerable Siagrius, bishop of that city.

In many other places she founded magnificent churches under the name of Saint Martin, trusting that he would be her helper above all others and appealing to him with that trust. The buildings constructed by her, still standing to this day, are shown to be so numerous that it seems incredible that one woman, reigning only in Austrasia and Burgundy, could have caused so much to be built in so many different parts of Francia.

While she governed the kingdom with her son and grandsons, the following men shone in Gaul, illuminated by the grace of divine power like lights: Etherius, archbishop of Lyon; Siagrius of Autun; Desiderius of Vienne; Aunarius of Auxerre, together with his brother Austrenus of Orléans; and Columbanus the abbot.

## CHAPTER II. On the holy bishop Austregisilus, falsely accused and miraculously cleared, and on his holiness

Austregisilus, archbishop of Bourges, had for a long time lived at the palace with King Guntrannus and was accustomed to offer him a napkin with which to wipe his hands.

On one occasion he was falsely accused by a man of the worst disposition of having composed certain writings without the prince’s order. Although he persistently denied this, the king ordered him to repel the charge by combat.

Rising at dawn, he had all his military equipment carried into the field by a servant boy and went to the church of Saint Marcellus to pray to the Lord. On the way he met a poor man asking for alms, to whom he gave a triens (a third-solidus coin). He then devoted himself to prayer.

Nor was the prayer without effect. While he was traveling with the king to the place of combat, a messenger met them and said:

“His adversary, while hastening to meet him at the appointed place, fell from his horse and has met the end of his life.”

Then the king turned to the blessed man and said:

“Rejoice, most beloved young man, because the Lord is your defender, so that your enemy cannot harm you.”

Afterward Austregisilus obtained the episcopal chair and shone in the world through the remarkable excellence of his virtues.

## CHAPTER III. On the slaughter of the emperor Maurice and his sons, his evil character, and his saving repentance revealed from heaven through the Egyptian anchorites, and on the deeds of Philippicus

While these events were taking place in Gaul, Maurice Augustus, after ruling the empire for twenty-one years, was killed by Phocas, who had been the groom of the patrician Priscus, together with his sons Theodosius, Tiberius, and Constantine.

He had been useful to the state. Indeed, fighting against its enemies, he often won victory. The Huns, who are also called Avars, were likewise defeated through his valor.

In the middle of his reign, while he was issuing commands contrary to the divine law and, although frequently admonished by the blessed Gregory, refused to correct them—in fact, he did not cease to insult that man of God with words when he could not do so by deeds—he deserved to be restrained by the Lord through the following rebuke.

A certain man living at Constantinople in the guise of a monk carried a drawn sword from the city gate to the statue of a gladiator standing in the middle of the Forum and declared that the emperor ought to be punished by the sword.

When Augustus heard this, he was greatly terrified. He summoned a man of prefectural rank, his closest associate, and sent him with every expression of devotion to the holy men living in the desert of Upper Egypt, bearing gifts of candles and incense. He asked them to pray to the Lord’s mercy on his behalf.

He himself also did not cease day and night to strike the pious ears of his Creator with prayers. He continually begged that God punish his sins in the present life rather than preserve them for the fires of everlasting punishment.

The prefect returned from the holy solitaries and announced to the emperor:

“The holy men living in the desert told me that, because God heard the prayers of your humility, he would not deprive you of eternal glory. Nevertheless, he would take from you, with great disgrace, the honor of the temporal empire that you now enjoy.”

The emperor rejoiced, because, although he could not escape transitory evils, he would not lose the rewards prepared for the just. The heavenly kindness also wished to console him through a vision of this kind.

One night, overcome by deep sleep, he saw himself standing before a bronze image of the Savior that had been placed before the palace doors. A voice came from the likeness of the incarnate Word and said:

“Hand Maurice over.”

Certain servants of unknown form and radiance seized him and placed him before the presence of the speaker. The voice sounded again and asked him:

“What would you choose: to receive in this world the things you have wickedly done, or to preserve them for judgment in the world to come?”

Maurice replied:

“O good Jesus, who redeemed the human race with your blood, command that I rather pay now for the evil deeds I have committed, and not fear the day of the coming judgment; indeed, make me a participant in the company of your elect.”

Then the speaker said:

“Let Maurice be handed over to the soldier Phocas, together with his wife and two sons.”

The emperor awoke from sleep and pondered the visions within himself. He ordered his son-in-law Philippicus to be summoned, whom he had once suspected on the accusation that he intended to seize the tyranny.

Philippicus, fearing that the emperor’s anger against him had reached its completion, said farewell to his wife as though he would never see her again and hurried to the palace. Maurice met him, fell at his knees, and begged him, for the Lord’s sake, kindly to forgive the wrongs he had committed against him under the compulsion of a false suspicion.

Philippicus was astonished and marveled at what had happened to him beyond expectation. He raised Augustus from the ground and prayed that Maurice would forgive him still more, if he retained any ill will against him.

Maurice replied:

“You must forgive more generously. If there is anyone in the army who holds an office and is called Phocas, order him to be summoned.”

He then recounted the entire vision in order.

Philippicus answered that he knew of no soldier named Phocas. There was, however, among the common soldiers a groom of the patrician Priscus named Phocas, and that man possessed a frightening recklessness.

The emperor replied:

“If he is frightening, then he is bloodthirsty as well.”

A few days later, wishing to set out with the army against those who, having violated the agreed pact, were attacking the Roman garrisons assigned to them, Maurice began his march. Once he was in enemy territory, he compelled the soldiers to refrain from theft and plunder, yet did not distribute their customary pay. Moreover, he forced them to spend the winter in deserted places. By this conduct he aroused no small amount of mutiny against himself.

Offended by the severity of this old military commander, the soldiers began to confer with one another and to complain that an emperor who had no parent of noble Roman descent wished to oppress them so wickedly. They said that they could no longer endure a foreign tyrant, since they had in the army a ruler worthy of the Roman race.

Shouting these words among themselves, the soldiers attacked Phocas, then a centurion, and asked him to assume the government of the Roman Empire. He obeyed their commands and put on the purple.

When Maurice learned this, his spirit collapsed in despair. He yielded to the events flowing against him and fled to an island near the sea. There he was struck with the sword by the officers whom Phocas had sent to pursue him, together with his wife and two sons, and thus, through a temporal death, fulfilled his dream.

## CHAPTER IV. On the succession of the Roman pontiffs and the primacy of the Roman Church

When the most blessed Pope Gregory learned that Phocas had obtained the empire, he sent a letter to him or to his Augusta Leontia, filled with words of congratulation.

During the reign of that prince, the same beloved Gregory of the Lord departed from the labors of the present life into eternal rest and left the pontifical see to Sabinian.

His successor Boniface asked and obtained from the aforesaid Augustus the following decree:

“That he should establish the see of the Roman and apostolic Church as the head of all Churches, since the Constantinopolitan Church was writing that it was first among all Churches.”

At the request of another Pope Boniface, that prince also ordered that, in the ancient shrine called the Pantheon, after the filth of the idols had been removed, a basilica be made for the blessed and perpetual Virgin Mary and for all the martyrs. Thus, where worship had once been offered to all—not gods, I will not say, but demons—thereafter the memory of all the saints would be celebrated.

## CHAPTER V. On Cacan of the Avars, or Huns, and his war with the Lombard Gisulf, and on Romilda’s disastrous desires

[Col. 0770B]

At that time the king of the Avars, whom they call Cacan in their own language, fought against the Lombards of Forum Julii and killed their duke, Gisulf, together with many of his men.

The wife of this duke, named Romilda, admired the beauty of King Cacan, who was besieging her in the aforesaid city, and handed the city over to him in return for a promise that he would satisfy her lust.

After the city had been captured and its people taken prisoner, the same king took her to himself for one night, as though in marriage, because of the oath he had given. Afterward he handed her over to twelve Avars, who, taking turns with one another, abused her as though she were a cheap prostitute.

Finally, ordering a stake to be fixed in the middle of the field, he commanded that she be impaled upon its point, adding this word of reproach:

“She deserves to have such a husband.”

The same king certainly left to posterity a memorable example of treachery. Although he embraced treachery, he showed that the author of treachery displeased him—perhaps fearing that she who had spared no one close to her would show him no mercy either if she obtained his embraces.

Thus that dreadful betrayer of her homeland perished by such an end, because she had cared more for her own lust than for the safety of her citizens and relatives.

Her daughters, however, following not their mother’s licentiousness but their love of chastity, placed raw flesh from chickens between their breasts under a bandage, so that the pieces, rotting from the heat of their bodies, would drive the Avars away from intercourse with them by their stench. And so it happened. For whoever wished to touch them with obscene contact was repelled by the enormity of the odor and withdrew far away, saying with curses that all Lombard women were foul-smelling.

One of them is said afterward to have married the king of the Alemanni, and another the prince of the Bavarians; thus they obtained marriages worthy of their preserved modesty.

Her sons, whom she had borne by her aforesaid husband Gisulf, fled on horseback after the city had been devastated. The youngest of them was captured by one of the enemy bands, which had run more swiftly than the others.

The man who had captured him did not wish to kill him because of his small body. Rather, he preferred to preserve him for service because of his exceptional appearance. For the boy had shining eyes, and nature had adorned him with milk-white hair. The captor began to lead him to the camp.

But the boy, harboring immense courage in his narrow breast and groaning that he was being dragged away captive, drew the small sword with which he was girded according to his age, so that he might become accustomed to using it. With all the strength he possessed, he struck it against the neck of the man dragging him.

When the man had been thrown to the ground, the boy turned his horse and, following a backward path, returned to his brothers, bringing them no small joy.

Now let us return to the order of our history.

## CHAPTER VI. On the deeds of King Clotaire and his monarchy in Francia

Therefore Clotaire, king of the Franks, in the thirtieth year of his reign, after he had begun to reign following the death of his father and had obtained sole rule of the kingdom, appointed Warnarius—through whose efforts he had obtained the kingdom of Burgundy—mayor of the palace in that kingdom. He exacted an oath from him that he would never accept a successor for as long as he lived.

For the Austrasians he appointed a certain Rado, a man of commendable life, and granted him the same rank. For the people of the Upper Jura he appointed Erpone, a Frank by birth and a patrician.

Because Erpone loved the things that make for peace and suppressed the frivolity of evil men, he was killed by the very inhabitants of the district, at the instigation of the patrician Aletheus and Leudemundus, bishop of Sion.

At that time Clotaire came with Queen Bertetrude to a villa called Maurolegicum [Maurolegium, in Alsace, today Marley]. Under the pretext of justice, he ordered many people acting unjustly to be punished by the sword.

Leudemundus, bishop of Sion, at Aletheus’s urging, came to Queen Bertetrude and summoned her privately. He advised her to transfer her treasures to Sion, saying that he knew perfectly well that Clotaire would depart from this world that year, and that Aletheus was prepared to abandon his wife and take the queen, together with the kingdom, as his own, since Aletheus himself was of noble Burgundian descent.

When the queen heard this and was deeply offended that she had been judged a woman to whom such proposals could be made, she rushed swiftly into her chamber.

Leudemundus, realizing that he would be accused because of his words, hastened through the city of Sion to the abbot of the Austrasians at Luxeuil, so that through the abbot’s prayers he might obtain the king’s forgiveness. This was indeed done. After immunity had been promised him, he was permitted to return to his see.

At Clotaire’s command, Aletheus came to the villa of Massolacum and was ordered to plead his case before the nobles. Since he could not clear himself of the charges brought against him, he was condemned to death.

In the thirty-fourth year of his reign, Clotaire summoned Warnarius, count of the palace, from the kingdom of Burgundy to the villa of Bonogilum, together with all the bishops and leading men. By granting their requests, or by agreeing to their petitions, he made them all completely loyal to him.

## CHAPTER VII. On the tribute that the Lombards paid to the Franks

The occasion now requires that we explain how the Lombards paid twelve thousand solidi as tribute to the Frankish kings for many years. We must also explain why they surrendered two cities—namely, Augusta and Seusium—to Frankish rule.

After the most noble King Cleph had died, as has been shown above, and dukes had been appointed over the Lombards, they invaded Gaul and carried away herds of captives together with booty.

Because of the rash audacity of this presumptuous act, they handed over the aforesaid cities to the territory of King Guntrannus.

Then, by common agreement, they sent twelve ambassadors to the emperor Maurice and made peace with him. They also sent twelve other ambassadors to Guntrannus and Childebert. These men begged for their friendship and alliance and promised on their behalf that they would pay him twelve thousand solidi.

They gave their envoys this particular instruction: that, among those whose goodwill toward treaties of friendship they observed to be the more favorable, the envoys should strive above all to unite their concord with them.

At last, after hearing the position of both sides, the Lombards placed themselves under the protection of the Franks. They also handed over to King Guntrannus the valley called Ametegis. Thus they continued to pay the aforesaid tribute until the time of their king Agilulf.

Agilulf sent chosen ambassadors of his people to Clotaire, prince of the Franks. Their names were Agilulf, Pompeius, and Gauto. They asked that the tribute paid to him every year be remitted.

They bribed those whom they knew to be closest to the king’s council, giving each of them one thousand solidi, and offered as much as three thousand solidi. To the king himself they offered thirty-six thousand solidi together with their prayers. The burden of the customary payment was thus remitted, and they returned to their own country.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the death of Queen Bertetrude, the marriage to Sichild, and her son Aribert; and on Dagobert’s being admitted to a share in the kingdom

[Col. 0772C]

In the thirty-sixth year of the same prince, Queen Bertetrude died. Clotaire had loved her with a unique affection, and all the common people, seeing her goodness, had loved her intensely.

After her death, King Clotaire took another wife named Sichild, by whom he had a son named Aribert.

In the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Clotaire made his son Dagobert, whom he had fathered by Queen Bertetrude, his partner in the kingdom and established him as king over the Austrasians. He retained for himself the lands bounded on the side of Neustria and Burgundy by the Ardennes and the Vosges.

## CHAPTER IX. On Samo’s being made king among the Slavs, his success, and his offspring

[Col. 0772D]

In the eleventh year of Clotaire’s rule, a certain man named Samo, a Frank by nationality and from the district of Sens, led many merchants with him into the land of the Slavs, who are also called Wends, for the purpose of trade. The Slavs had long been subject to the Huns, who are also called Avars, and were attempting to reject the yoke of their domination. For although at first they paid them tribute as their masters, guarded the camps of those engaged in battle, and supplied assistance to those fleeing in order to resist, they endured such great insults inflicted by them that you might have thought that not human beings ruled over human beings, but wild beasts over any worthless pack animals. For among the other things they cruelly—indeed, horribly even to speak of—practised against them, there was one unspeakable crime, unheard-of in all previous ages: as though preparing to winter, they would approach their dwellings and take their wives as companions to their own beds.

But those who had been born from Slavic women and Huns, unwilling to endure the evil that their stepfathers had long inflicted upon them, raised up a terrible war against their masters and fathers. Samo happened to set out with his companions to support the Wends. When the battle was joined, the Wends defeated the Huns. In this conflict Samo gave a splendid demonstration of military prowess. Throwing himself into extreme danger, he destroyed many of the enemy.

As a result of this success, Samo was sought by the Slavs as their king, because they delighted in his outstanding courage. From being a merchant he was made king, and for thirty-six years he governed the kingdom energetically amid the countless upheavals of the wars that he waged against the Avars. In all of them he consistently emerged victorious through his prudent cunning. He also had twelve wives from the Wendish people, by whom he fathered twenty-two sons and fifteen daughters.

## CHAPTER X. On Adaloald, king of the Lombards, his successor, and Queen Gundeberga

Adaloald, son of Agilulf, also called Ago, king of the Lombards, succeeded his father in the kingdom. After he had ruled for ten years with his mother Theudelinda, he received a drink after bathing from a certain man named Eusebius, who had been sent to him as an envoy by the emperor of Constantinople, and was driven into madness. When, persuaded by that envoy, he ordered twelve Lombard nobles to be put to death, he was expelled from the kingdom by the others.

In his place they installed Arioald, duke of Turin, to whom Gundeberga, the sister of King Adaloald, had been married. This queen, who was both beautiful in appearance and outstanding in the goodness of her mind, and who also possessed the grace of chastity, one day began to praise a certain man named Adalulf, born among the Lombards in no lowly station, who was serving her, because he was exceptionally handsome. He, supposing that the queen had fallen passionately in love with him, said in her ear:

“Since it has pleased your goodwill to exalt my position by your praise, please, I beg you, take me as your bedfellow.”

She considered these words not to be endured lightly and spat in his face. Fearing that, if he did not himself disclose the matter, the queen would reveal everything, he approached the king and declared that, if he were granted a safe opportunity to speak, he would disclose something important to him.

When the king withdrew privately with him, Adalulf began to obscure the truth with falsehood in the following manner:

“Taso,” he said, “governor of the province of Tuscany, has now for three days been plotting your destruction with the queen, so that she may kill you with poison and take him as her husband.”

The king believed him and confined his wife in an Italian fortress called Amelium. When Clotaire learned of this, he began through envoys to rebuke Arioald, saying that he had acted wrongly in judging a queen—and one descended from the royal stock of the Franks—deserving of such dishonor without a legal examination.

Although Arioald admitted that he had just cause for imprisoning his wife, one of the envoys, named Ansoald, addressed the king as follows:

“You will readily find an examination of this matter convincing if one of the queen’s household is allowed to contend in battle with her accuser.”

When Arioald had granted and approved this proposal, and despair of life compelled Adalulf not to decline the proposed challenge, a certain Aribert, the queen’s cousin, sent a man named Pitto to fight in his place against Adalulf. Pitto defeated the accuser without delay and punished him with the sword. After nearly three years of confinement, Queen Gundeberga was restored to her former royal dignity.

## CHAPTER XI. On the prudence of King Dagobert among the Austrasians and the insolence of Rodoald

In the forty-first year of Clotaire’s reign, while Dagobert was energetically governing the affairs of Austrasia, he had advanced to high honors a certain Rodoald, distinguished among the Austrasians by his noble birth, at the urging of the most blessed Bishop Arnulf and Pippin, mayor of the palace. But this man, his mind becoming deranged through a change of character, began to provoke the king’s anger against himself.

For he devoted himself to seizing other people’s property, was given over to pride, and was filled with arrogance; thus he gave those who envied him an opportunity to speak against him. For this reason Dagobert, angered, contemplated killing him. Terrified, Rodoald went to Clotaire, begging him to deign to preserve his life with his son.

When Clotaire saw his son, he entreated him, among other things, not to kill Rodoald. Dagobert promised that, if Rodoald corrected whatever he had done wrongly, he could hope for his life. But when Rodoald had come with Dagobert to Trier, without any delay, by the king’s order he was beheaded by Bertarius of Scarpone before the door of the royal bedchamber.

## CHAPTER XII. On Dagobert’s marriage to Gomatrude, his dispute with his father Clotaire, and their reconciliation concerning the kingdom of Austrasia

In the forty-second year of Clotaire’s reign, Dagobert, furnished with every royal ornament and adornment, came at his father’s command to Clichy, not far from Paris. There his father gave him in marriage Gomatrude, the sister of Queen Sichilde.

On the third day of the wedding, a serious disagreement arose between father and son. Dagobert was asking that the consolidated kingdom belonging to the Austrasians be returned to him. Clotaire, however, opposed him, unwilling to grant him anything of it. At last twelve Franks were chosen, among whom was a man pleasing to God, Arnulf, bishop of Metz. Through their salutary counsel, the father was reconciled with his son and returned to him what he had requested. He retained under his own authority only what lay on this side of the Loire, or in the region called Provence.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the courage and faith of Sisebut, king of Spain, his subjugation of Cantabria, and the consequent expansion of the Gothic kingdom

[Col. 0775A]

In Spain at that time, after Bettricus had been removed from human affairs, Sisebut succeeded him in the kingdom. Energetic in war, sound in counsel, and more ready in faith than all the former kings of Spain, he subjected Cantabria to himself. It had once been possessed by the ruling Franks. Indeed, the Frankish duke Francio, who governed that province for some time, paid tribute to the Frankish kings.

After his death, soldiers of the emperor residing at Constantinople, to whom, as we have mentioned above, the task of guarding the frontier of Spain against foreign peoples had been entrusted, seized the same region. As we have just recalled, Sisebut took it from them by force, capturing many coastal cities and destroying them to their foundations.

When soldiers of his army were slaughtering those found in the aforementioned cities, Sisebut, moved by pious compassion and wishing to rescue many from death, gave them confidence to flee to him and urged them, with a promise of immunity, to save themselves by flight. Groaning, he said:

“Woe to me, wretched man, in whose kingdom’s time so much human blood is being shed!”

Thus the kingdom of the Goths inhabiting Spain was extended along the seacoast as far as the ridges of the Pyrenees.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the death of Warnacharius; the incestuous marriage of his son Godinus with his stepmother; his repudiation of her; the repudiated woman’s rage and deception against Gogo; Gogo’s oaths of fidelity sworn in several churches and his death; and also the exile of Palladius and Sedecus and the killing of Boso

[Col. 0775C]

In the forty-third year of King Clotaire, Warnacharius, who was in charge of the royal palace of Burgundy, ended his life. His son Godinus, moved by the fickleness of his mind, took his stepmother as his wife. Provoked by this outrage against divine law, King Clotaire ordered Duke Arnobert to kill Godinus as quickly as possible.

Overwhelmed by fear, Godinus abandoned Burgundy and crossed into Austrasia. He implored Dagobert to intervene, so that he might turn his father away from carrying out the harsher command toward something milder. Dagobert did not refuse.

Although reluctantly, Clotaire granted his pleading son’s request: out of regard for the honor that Warnacharius, Godinus’s father, had held, and in supreme gratitude for his devoted service to the king, the sentence of death was to be mitigated. This was on the condition that Godinus put away the wife whom he had married contrary to the decrees of the canons.

After repudiating her and securing his life, he returned to Burgundy. But the woman, bearing the injury inflicted upon her with a resentment far different from what might have been expected, used deceitful accusations against Gogo. She approached the king and brought forward the following story: if Gogo came into the king’s presence, he had decided to kill him with the sword.

Believing her, the king required Gogo to guarantee by oath the security of his life, safety, and honor. Although he had sworn, at the insistence of the king’s household officials Crannulf and Wandelbert, in the basilica of Saint Medard at Soissons and that of Saint Vincent at Paris, that he would plot no treachery against the king, he was nevertheless not trusted. He was compelled by the same men to repeat the oaths in the church of Saint Aignan at Orléans and in that of Saint Martin at Tours.

As he proceeded toward the places already mentioned in order to satisfy the royal command, he was most wickedly slaughtered at Chartres during a banquet, together with many of his men, who wished to resist but were utterly unable to do so, through the ambush of the aforementioned men, the king not forbidding it.

In that same year, a certain Palladius and his son Sedecus, bishop of Toulouse, were accused by Duke Aynan of having been accomplices in the rebellion of the Gascons and were driven into exile. Boso too, a native of Étampes and son of Audolenus, was killed by Duke Arnebert on Clotaire’s order, because Clotaire attributed to him the commission of adultery with Queen Sichilde.

## CHAPTER XV. On Clotaire’s consultation concerning a successor to Warnacharius, prefect of the palace of Burgundy, with the princes and nobles of the kingdom; and on the uprising caused by Aginanus’s killing of Hermarius

Clotaire ordered all the more powerful nobles of Burgundy to assemble at Troyes and discussed with them Warnacharius’s successor, carefully investigating whom they wished the king to appoint as governor of the palace. When they declared that they wished to endure the authority of no one except God and the king, the king gladly received their words and also satisfied their desire.

In the forty-fourth year of Clotaire’s reign, he convened at Clichy an assembly of the king’s sons and relatives, as well as of the bishops of Gaul, so that whatever measures were conducive to peace in the kingdom or to the welfare of the Church might be established.

Among the leading men of France who had assembled, a certain Hermarius, governor of the palace of Aribert, the king’s son, and his attendant from childhood, was killed when Aginanus attacked him. He was a Saxon by birth and one of the nobles of the royal court.

Because of this, a serious uprising arose, and the quarrel had nearly reached bloodshed, had Clotaire not recognized the cause and suppressed the disturbance by royal authority. He granted Aginanus the opportunity to withdraw to a mountain called Marcomirus, together with a considerable number of warriors who could serve as his protection if circumstances required it.

Brunulf, however, Aribert’s maternal uncle—that is, the brother of Queen Sichilde—gathered a force of nobles and companions and attempted to defeat Aginanus. When Clotaire learned of this, he summoned the leudes who were especially indignant at the unjust killing of so great a man and declared that, if they wished to remain in his favor, they should not go to war.

In this way he recalled their attack, and the civil conflict came to an end.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the death of the younger Clotaire, his miraculous healing from fevers through Saint Sulpicius, the sanctity of Sulpicius’s life, and the innocence and work of the goldsmith Saint Eligius

In the sixteenth year of his acquired monarchy, but the forty-fourth year of his paternal kingdom, King Clotaire died and was buried in the suburb of Paris, in the basilica of Saint Vincent.

This Clotaire was called “the Younger” because of his grandfather, who had been called by the same name with the addition “the Elder.” He may also be called the first, since the present one was the second, followed by another, who will be described later.

The blessed Sulpicius—at that time an archdeacon, but later bishop of Bourges—had earlier freed this Clotaire from a serious affliction of fever after completing a seven-day fast. Clotaire was patient, educated in letters, full of the fear of God, giving the poor what they needed, and caring for the welfare of the churches of the Lord and of the priests.

Nevertheless, through the deceitful cunning of malicious people, he was induced to expel the blessed Bishop Lupus of Sens from his own see and drive him into exile. From the written accounts of his deeds it is openly shown that Lupus was a man of such great sanctity that, one day, while he was celebrating the sacred rites of the Mass, a jewel fell from heaven into the holy chalice.

At last the king repented of his action and ordered him to be recalled from exile and brought to him. After asking for and obtaining forgiveness for the offenses committed, he sent him back to his own place with gifts.

The blessed Eligius, a most distinguished goldsmith, likewise left his native soil in the territory of Limoges and went to the same king. From him he received both the order and the funds to make a golden seat suitable to royal dignity.

Keeping his hands pure from every stain of greed, he divided the gold that he had undertaken to use for a single work into two parts. From one he completed a saddle no smaller than he had been ordered to make. With the gold remaining from the funds assigned to him, so that he would not lose it through negligence or appear to retain it in order to satisfy his own desire, he cast a smaller seat.

When the ruler saw this, he praised and rewarded him and ordered him to live in the palace residences. But let this suffice concerning these matters.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Dagobert’s actions after Clotaire’s death was announced to him; the faction of Aribert and Brunulf against him; the miraculous discovery of the bodies of Dionysius and his companions; and Sadregisil, acting as governor in Aquitaine

The report of the deceased Clotaire reached Dagobert—as is customary with the human mind, which, once it has received the main facts, is content not to inquire into the rest. Therefore Dagobert sent into Neustria and Burgundy those men of the Austrasian kingdom whom he found most trustworthy, so that they might secure for him the favor of the dukes and bishops of those peoples.

Everyone received this with joy, because they recognized that the kingdom was owed to him. The people of Reims were the first to receive Dagobert when he arrived, while the leaders of the aforementioned nations gathered there with the greatest joy.

His brother Aribert was eager for some public office to be entrusted to him. Likewise Brunulf, Queen Sichilde’s brother and Aribert’s uncle, gradually sought out the more powerful men and attempted to arrange that, with Dagobert rejected, supreme control of everything should be entrusted to his nephew.

But they judged him to be more intent on acquiring power for himself than on the common good, and also more sluggish in character, and considered that he should be avoided. Nevertheless, once Dagobert had obtained what he desired, he later took care to repay Brunulf with a fitting return for his deeds.

When matters concerning himself had been settled, and he had gained the support of all who either administered military affairs or were conspiring around his authority, his heart was touched and, out of regard for brotherly compassion, he was moved to mercy. On the advice of his friends, he made his brother a partner in the kingdom in part.

He granted him the province extending from the bank of the Loire toward Gascony as far as the ridges of the Pyrenees, which separate Gaul from Spain. He also made a written agreement with him:

“That, content with the status of a private man, he should hope for nothing further from his father’s kingdom.”

Once he had obtained power, he chose Toulouse as the seat of his kingdom. His judgment was not, as had been thought, sluggish; rather, by nature he was keen in carrying out affairs, and he immediately found material for exercising his abilities.

*(What follows is taken from the deeds of Dagobert, which appear in Volume I.)*

In the third year after he had begun to reign, he subdued the whole land of Gascony and enlarged his kingdom. All Austrasia together with Burgundy, and Neustria as well, obeyed Dagobert’s rule.

Although some people possess separate accounts of his deeds, we have nevertheless thought it worthwhile to touch upon them, so that his actions may not remain unknown to those among whom the writing mentioned above is not found.

Dagobert had been entrusted by his father Clotaire to the venerable Arnulf, bishop of Metz, for instruction, and he spent the years of his boyhood in literary studies. He trained his adolescence in hunting—a practice that, as we have often said, was familiar to Frankish rulers—and one day he set out to hunt a stag.

The stag was easily discovered through the skill of the horsemen and the keen scent of the dogs. With the speed customary to that animal, it crossed woods and mountains and any rivers that happened to lie in its path, and raced to a village called Catulliacus.

In this village was a small chapel that sheltered the bodies of the martyrs Dionysius and his companions. The stag, finding a secure refuge, entered it. The dogs followed close behind but, unable to enter through the open doors, barked at the entrance.

Dagobert arrived and regarded the matter as worthy of wonder. The rumor of this miracle moved the neighboring people, and Dagobert above all, to reverence for the saints.

Furthermore, Clotaire had placed a certain man named Sadregisil in charge of affairs under him, entrusting him especially with the dukedom of Aquitaine. This man, seeking to despise the king’s son because of the pride with which he was swollen, did not bear his success with an even temper. The excuse was that Dagobert was still young, so that he would not acquire arrogance from ruling over princes.

By chance Clotaire went hunting and, becoming separated from his son by a considerable distance, provided Dagobert with an opportunity to summon the duke to a banquet, reproach him for his insolence, and order that he be beaten with lashes and disfigured by the cutting off of his beard.

Conscious of this bold deed, Dagobert himself withdrew into the hiding place where he had seen the stag take refuge while fleeing from its pursuers.

Afterward Clotaire returned and, learning of the insult to the duke, furiously threatened his son with many punishments and sent men to summon him, so that he might pay the penalty deserved for his actions.

Meanwhile, while Dagobert lay prostrate before the martyrs with a humble heart and was overcome by sleep, a certain man of venerable and kindly appearance stood beside him and commanded him not to fear. He promised that Dagobert would be delivered not only from his present danger but also from eternal punishment, and would moreover be granted the royal throne, if only he promised that their memorials would be adorned.

The promise did not fail. Indeed, so that he might understand that these were not empty dreams—by which we are often deceived—the men sent to lead him away from the sacred building were prevented by divine power from advancing when they were no more than a mile from the sanctuary.

They returned in confusion and reported to the one who had sent them what they had suffered. He accused them both of laziness and of lack of faith and sent others to accomplish what the first men had neglected.

When these too suffered the same fate, he despised them as though they had been born to support his cause. Wishing to drag his son away from the martyrs’ tombs himself, he went in person. But because God’s power prevails no less over kings than over other men, the man who had called others lazy became lazy himself.

At last, recognizing the power of Christ and of his servants, he granted pardon and was reconciled with his son. Having received permission to depart, Dagobert returned to the blessed chapel and invited the glorious martyrs, through devoted prayers, to be his aid.

Yet, as later became clear, no place was more pleasing to Dagobert.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Dagobert’s dangerous battle with Bertoald, duke of the Saxons; Clotaire’s remarkable assistance; and the death of the fleeing Bertoald

[Col. 0779C]

After his father had appointed him king over the Austrasian Franks, Dagobert took up arms against the Saxons, who had attempted to rebel. Having crossed the Rhine and engaged Bertoald, duke of the Saxons, in battle, he was struck on the head with a sword. He sent his father, by an armor-bearer, locks of hair cut off together with part of his helmet, and requested that he hurry to his aid before the entire army fell.

By a stroke of fortune, Clotaire was nearby. He had gone to the forest of Longolaria for the sake of hunting. When he received news of his son’s danger, he was shaken by deep grief. He seized the young men who were at hand, sent envoys to summon others to follow him, and covered a long journey in a short time—for he also traveled by night—until he reached his son.

That night they rested with their tents pitched above the river Weser. At daybreak, while the Franks were raising applause and joyful cries at the arrival of King Clotaire, Bertoald, the duke of Saxony, who was awaiting battle on the riverbank, heard the commotion and asked what caused such a great disturbance in the Frankish camp.

He was told that King Clotaire had arrived and that the Franks were therefore celebrating a festival. But he replied:

“Deceived by a false hope, they dream in fear of the desires they cherish. For reliable report has made known to us that the king whom they rejoice to have among them is already dead.”

Clotaire, armed and standing on the nearer bank, heard him uttering such arrogant words. Saying nothing, so that his silence might inspire the enemy with even greater fear, he swiftly removed his helmet from his head. His hair was beautifully streaked with white, and by its appearance he was especially recognizable to his adversaries.

Bertoald immediately recognized him, and Clotaire received the following insulting reply from the duke of the opposing side:

“So you were the mute beast who was here?”

The king was provoked by this insult and burned with indescribable anger. Replacing his helmet on his head, he drove his spurred horse toward Bertoald, intending to cross the river and take revenge on his enemies.

The Franks, likewise moved by the duke’s insult and encouraged by the king’s example, crossed the river swimming behind him. The king pressed fiercely after the fleeing Bertoald.

He was hindered in the pursuit both by the weight of his armor and by the fact that, while he was swimming across the river, the water had filled his bosom and his boots. Nevertheless, as he retreated, Bertoald called out to the king:

“What you are doing is neither fair nor right in pursuing me. You are doing it only because you are driven by a desire for glory and wish to be regarded as so great that, separated from your men, you compel an enemy to turn his back on you. Beware lest this affair, turning against you, destroy you instead.”

As he said these things, he did not cease fleeing. He often declared that he was the king’s servant and that the king was his master, and that it seemed unjust for either a servant to be killed by a most merciful master or a master by a servant, even if unwilling and compelled.

But Clotaire knew that Bertoald was cunningly prolonging these words and paid no attention to what he said. At last, through the speed of the horse on which he rode, he caught up with him and killed him.

He took off his head and returned to his son and the other Franks, who, saddened because they had been unable to catch up with him and fearful for his safety, were hastening after him as quickly as they could.

Having lifted their spirits from grief, he entered Saxony with them and ravaged it so completely that he left no living man there who was taller than the length of the sword he happened at that time to carry.

Such was Clotaire’s deed.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Dagobert’s journey to Burgundy after his father’s death to raise up the oppressed, his subsequent travels, his repudiated wife, his marriage to Vestal, and his good counselors, Bishop Arnulf, Pippin, and Bishop Chunibert

[Col. 0780D]

After Clotaire’s death, Dagobert, having acquired the government of the entire people, set out for Burgundy with the intention of assisting the oppressed and those suffering injustice by administering justice.

His arrival inspired confidence among the good, especially the poor. But fear and a certain disturbance of mind seized the seditious and those intent on plunder. When he reached Langres, he granted the poor and widows access to him and, without showing preference to anyone, had each person’s rights settled according to the laws, maintaining the equity that the Most High loves.

After this he went to the fortress of Dijon, where he intended to act in the same way. From there, as he was about to set out for Chalon, he entered the baths in the morning and ordered the dukes Amalgar and Arnebert, together with the patrician Willebald, to kill Brunulf, the maternal uncle of his brother Aribert, whom he suspected of disloyalty.

Then, from the city of Chalon, he directed his journey through Autun to Auxerre; afterward, passing through the city of Sens, he came to Paris. While staying at the estate of Romilly, he abandoned Queen Gomatrude—the sister of his stepmother Sichilde—because she was barren, following the advice of certain Franks, and took a certain young woman named Nantild, seized from a monastery, as his wife.

Until that time he had followed the counsel of the blessed Arnulf, bishop of Metz, and of Pippin, who held the office of mayor of the palace in the kingdom of Austrasia. For that reason he appeared so energetic and effective in administering the kingdom that the surrounding peoples feared his name and pledged, with the utmost loyalty, to provide assistance in subjecting foreign nations.

But after the departure of the aforementioned bishop, he obeyed the counsels of Pippin and Chunibert, bishop of Cologne. At their urging, he devoted himself to equity and justice.

## CHAPTER XX. On Dagobert’s son by Ragnetrude, who answered “Amen” when baptized by the blessed Amandus; his subsequent fall into shameful greed, the plundering of the church of Saint Hilary, and his lust; and his repentance on Pippin’s advice

In the eighth year of his reign, while he was traveling through the northern parts of France, as was customary for kings, he was saddened because he had not fathered a son who would reign after him. He took a certain girl named Ragnetrude into his bed, and by her he had a son that year.

Later, when the venerable Amandus, bishop of Maastricht, was marking the child according to the custom of the faithful in the city of Orléans, with his father present and King Aribert of Aquitaine also in attendance, the prayer was finished and no one among the vast multitude of the army answered “Amen.” Then the Lord opened the mouth of the child, who was no more than thirty days old, and he answered before everyone: “Amen.”

Immediately the holy bishop regenerated him through baptism, and King Aribert lifted him from the sacred font. This event filled not only the kings but all those standing around with great astonishment and rejoicing.

After this, while Dagobert often strove to visit his ancestral kingdom of Neustria, he forgot his former goodness. He became an unscrupulous plunderer, coveting not only the possessions of churches but also those of wealthy people generally.

Among the other spoils taken from the churches of Gaul, he is said to have carried off from the church of Saint Hilary at Poitiers, on the pretext of adorning the basilica of Saint Dionysius, doors worked in cast bronze. When he ordered them to be transported by sea into the Seine and carried along it as far as Paris, one of them was swallowed by the river and, it is said, was never afterward found.

He gave himself over to lust so unrestrained that, apart from three women who were supported not only by their names but also by royal attire, a very large number of concubines attended him. His heart was therefore thought to have turned wholly away from God and to have become completely alienated, unless, returning to himself, he had decided to redeem his sins through almsgiving.

There was in his kingdom a certain Pippin, one of the most powerful of the Austrasians, who remained close to him in friendship. He hated wicked men and did not associate with the depraved. Certain malicious people attacked him and attempted to make him hateful to Dagobert.

But, protected by the mercy of the Lord—whose commandments he followed in observing justice—he escaped the plots prepared against him and proved most faithful by giving the king useful advice.

Another man named Ega was associated with him in sound counsel and in a relationship of intimacy with the ruler scarcely different from Pippin’s. Ega was from Neustria and possessed considerable power.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the envoys to the emperor; the deeds of the emperors Phocas and Heraclius; Heraclius’s successes against Chosroes, the tyrant of the Persians; his death; and the recovery of the Lord’s Cross

At that time Servatius and Paternus, who had served as envoys to Heraclius, the successor of Phocas, returned and presented themselves to Dagobert, saying:

“We have established perpetual peace with Heraclius.”

The emperor Phocas was then killed by Heraclianus, the governor of Africa, after he had been entirely abandoned by the senate. He had become deranged as though his mind were corrupted and was throwing the wealth of the empire into the sea, saying that he wished to appease Neptune with gifts.

Heraclius, the son of Heraclianus, was installed in his place as emperor. In the ninth year after he had assumed the purple, this Heraclius restored to the state many provinces seized by the Persians and recovered others that had been gravely weakened.

For Chosroes, ruler of the Persians, devastating everything through which he passed, came to Jerusalem and, among the other ecclesiastical and public spoils, carried away a portion of the life-giving Cross that Helena, the mother of Constantine, once Augustus, had left there.

After handing over the kingdom to his son, Chosroes himself sat on a golden throne in a silver tower that he had prepared for this purpose and placed the standard of our redemption at his side as though it were his partner in the kingdom.

When this was reported to Heraclius, he went toward Persia with a strong force of soldiers. He encountered Chosroes’s son with a very large Persian phalanx, which followed him because fear compelled it to do so, rather than from any desire to help him.

When the forces of both sides had made their preparations, the emperor and the Persian commander engaged in single combat, under the following condition:

“No one from either army is to advance to bring assistance to his commander. If anyone should dare to violate this decree, his own ruler will have his hamstrings cut and will plunge him into the neighboring river.”

After they had fought for a long time and with great courage, Heraclius said to his opponent:

“Why are your men violating the agreement we established?”

The Persian turned his neck to see which of his own men was coming to help him, and Heraclius struck him. He was thrown from his horse and died.

Immediately the Persians submitted themselves as suppliants to Heraclius. Advancing farther with his men, Heraclius found Chosroes seated in the aforementioned shrine, with the Lord’s Cross beside him.

He asked him whether he wished to accept the faith of Christ and adore the saving wood—which, although unworthy, he had nevertheless treated honorably according to his own manner. When Chosroes answered that he would absolutely not do so, Heraclius immediately killed him.

After traversing the whole of Persia, Heraclius ordered the young son of Chosroes, whom he had found with him, to be baptized and placed him in charge. He assigned the silver of the tower to the army and the gold to the restoration of the churches. With abundant booty and seven elephants, and having also taken up the Cross of the Savior, he returned to Jerusalem and from there to Constantinople.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Heraclius’s appearance and his mistaken interpretation of the omen by which he had seen himself driven out by a circumcised people; why he persecuted the Jews and arranged for them to be expelled from France, although he was to be expelled by the Saracens; and on their battle and Heraclius’s death
He was handsome in appearance, cheerful in countenance, of medium height, and of exceptional strength; he often killed lions in the arena and, by himself, killed several of them. Since he was abundantly versed in letters, he eventually became an astrologer. Recognizing from the signs of the stars that his empire was destined to be ravaged by a circumcised people, and supposing that this had been foretold concerning the Jews, he asked Dagobert, king of the Franks, through intermediaries to order all those of Jewish descent who lived in the provinces subject to him to become Christians, and to condemn those who refused either to exile or to death. Dagobert willingly carried this out, expelling from the borders of France all who refused to receive baptism.

But to Heraclius this had been foretold not concerning the Jews but concerning the Saracens. For the Hagarenes—also called Saracens—a faithless people who derived the practice of circumcision from Abraham through their ancestry, advancing from the root of Mount Caucasus, came to ravage Heraclius’s lands. Against them a selected force of soldiers, sent by the Emperor, was severely defeated by the enemy. It is reported that 150,000 soldiers perished. The victors sent the spoils of the slain to Augustus to be received through envoys. But he, who was considering vengeance rather than accepting them, not only rejected the offerings but, through that very embassy, brought the Alans to his aid by opening the gates that Alexander the Great had set upon Mount Caspius; for a price he led out nearly 150,000 armed men.

There were two commanders of the Saracens, leading 200,000 armed men into battle. When each army had set up camp far from the other, on the night preceding the day of battle fifty-two thousand fighters were suddenly found lifeless in their beds in the Greek camp. At this, the survivors, struck with fear, fled in different directions, abandoning their kingdom to be laid waste by their adversaries. The latter, as though they had received an insult because the enemy had dared to oppose them, pursued the devastation with even greater violence.

When Heraclius received news of so great a disaster and lost confidence that he could resist—since the enemy had already overrun a great part of Asia and was preparing to attack Jerusalem—he fell ill. As his bodily illness grew worse, even to the sickness of his soul, he evidently fell into the sect of Eutyches. Having also entered into a lawful marriage with his sister’s daughter, he ended his life in the twenty-sixth year of the power he had assumed. [Col. 0784A] His son Heraclona succeeded him, together with his mother Martina. After holding supreme power for two years, he left the rights of the empire to his brother Constantine.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the death of Aribert, king of Aquitaine, and of his son Chilperic; on the merchants who were badly treated by the Slavs; on the embassy to Samo, king of the Slavs; and on the battle fought with them and its disastrous outcome for the Franks

In the ninth year of King Dagobert, his brother Aribert, king of Aquitaine, died, leaving a young son named Chilperic. He did not long survive in this human life. The suspicion of his death was attributed to Dagobert. When Dagobert learned of it, he sent the duke Barontus to seize his kingdom or bring its treasures to him. Barontus is said to have suffered a serious loss as a result. [Col. 0784B]

At that time, merchants of goods from Francia entered the territory of the Slavs. The Slavs stripped them of their possessions, and those who had attempted to resist were killed. Therefore a certain man named Sicharius was sent by Dagobert to Samo, prince of that people, to demand justice for what had been done. Knowing that Samo did not wish to see him, he put on the clothing worn by the Slavs so that he would not be recognized, and presented himself before the king, who was reluctant to receive him.

After stating the instructions entrusted to him, he said that Samo ought not to hold the Frankish people in contempt, since Samo himself and the people subject to him were liable to servitude under Dagobert, their king. Provoked to anger by these words, Samo replied that he and his people, together with their land, would gladly obey Dagobert, “provided,” he said, “that he is willing to preserve friendship with us.”

To this Sicharius replied: “It is impossible for the servants of Christ to make treaties with dogs.”

Samo answered: “Since you profess that you are servants of God, and we are his dogs, therefore, because you wickedly do against his will those things which you do, as useless servants, we are frequently granted permission to avenge them with our bites.”

Sicharius was immediately expelled from his presence.

Aggravated by this insult, Dagobert sent military forces selected from Austrasia to wage war against the people of the Wends. The Alemanni under Duke Rotbert, as well as the Lombards, came to their assistance. The side on which they engaged the enemy won the victory and, returning home, carried away a very large number of captives. The Austrasian Franks, meanwhile, besieged the Wends who had taken refuge in the fortress of Vogast. When they conducted the siege carelessly, the enemy attacked them and inflicted a severe defeat. Abandoning their camp and tents, they fled.

Made more confident by this victory, the Wends poured into Thuringia and the neighboring Frankish territories, so that Dervanus, the duke who governed the Slavic cities that had until then obeyed the Franks, despairing of the situation, transferred himself to the other Slavs. In truth, this disaster befell the Franks not so much through the valor of the Wends as through the cowardice of the Austrasians. Otherwise, they would have exacted upon the Slavs under Dagobert the very vengeance that they had exacted under Clotaire against the Saxons—

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the dispute between the Avars and Bulgars over the choice of a king; on the Bulgars expelled from their homeland and preparing to invade Francia; and on their massacre in a single night

[Col. 0785A]

In those days a great dispute arose between the Avars, also called Huns, and those who are called Bulgars, over which people should provide the succession to the kingdom: whether it should come from one born among the Bulgars or from the seed of the Avars. The quarrel was carried as far as armed conflict, and victory fell to the Huns.

The defeated Bulgars, exiles from their own lands, sought Dagobert, king of the Franks, asking that vacant land be granted to them for settlement. He sent them to spend the winter in Bavaria until he could deliberate with his friends about what he should do with them. While they were being lodged in the houses of the Bavarians, the king held a council with his advisers. Fearing that they might be plotting something new, he summoned the Bavarians and gave them this order: “Let each man slaughter the one lodging with him, together with his wife and children.” This was done; and in a single night, appointed for so cruel a deed, they were all delivered to death.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the kings of Spain, the war brought against them by Dagobert through the Burgundians, and the demand, seizure, and compensation for the great dish

In Spain, after the death of the most merciful king Sisebut, Sentila succeeded to the kingdom. While he was perpetrating many cruel acts against his own people, a certain Sisenand, a man of no insignificant Spanish birth, went to Dagobert, asking him to assist him in expelling Sentila from Spain. Dagobert ordered the entire military force of the Burgundian kingdom to go there and bring aid to Sisenand.

When it became known throughout Spain that Sisenand was leading a Frankish army to his support, everyone immediately abandoned Sentila, whom they had long hated, and without a battle followed the other man, who was better prepared for war, and raised him to the throne. The dukes Abundantius and Venerandus, with only the army from Toulouse, accompanied Sisenand as far as Zaragoza. There the Gothic nobles surrendered to him; and, having themselves been rewarded by him with gifts, they returned home.

After this, Dagobert sent the envoys Amalgarius and Venerandus to demand that what had been promised him be paid. Sisenand had promised to give him a golden dish from the treasures of the Goths, which Torsimodus, who had once ruled among the Goths, had received as a gift from Aetius, the Roman patrician. When the king had willingly handed it over to the envoys, the Goths, observing that the route by which it would be carried passed through their territory, seized the dish and did not allow it to be carried away into the public treasuries. Therefore, afterward Sisenand paid King Dagobert, as compensation for the dish, 200,000 solidi of silver. Dagobert gave these to the basilica of Saint Denis; how greatly he displayed his generosity in its construction will be explained below.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the war Dagobert prepared against the Slavs, which the Saxons falsely undertook on the pretext of relieving the tribute, but which was successfully conducted by the king’s son Sigebert

[Col. 0786A]

In the tenth year after the aforesaid Dagobert had begun to reign, remembering the evil deeds of the Slavs against his people, he assembled a picked troop of warriors from Francia, which we may call a squadron or wedge. As it hastened to take vengeance on the enemy, envoys of the Saxons met it, promising that they would avenge the insults inflicted upon the Franks if they deserved to be relieved of the tribute they paid for the king’s use.

For they had been ordered by Clotaire the Elder, son of Clovis and father of Chilperic, to deliver 500 taxable cows to the royal table. They were called “taxable” [inferendales] because they were delivered each year. Dagobert therefore, following the wise counsel of the Austrasians, did not refuse their request, on the condition that in all succeeding times the Saxons should defend the Frankish frontier adjacent to them against the attacks of enemies.

This agreement was indeed confirmed by an oath over weapons, as was their custom when swearing. But it was not established with any effectiveness in deeds, although they had been released from the payment which they were accustomed to render.

In the following year, when Thuringia was suffering from continual incursions by the Slavs, Dagobert, after consulting with the bishops and elders of the people, placed his son Sigebert over the Austrasians, so that he might exercise the office of ruler with the dignity of a kingdom. He appointed two guardians for his son: Chunibert, bishop of the city of Cologne, and Adalgis, master of the palace. [Col. 0786C] He also gave them an adequate treasury and ordered that everything he granted be entered in a testament and authenticated by the impression of a seal. Thereafter, for as long as Sigebert lived, the incursions of the Wends were restrained through the care and industry of the Austrasians.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the birth of Clovis, Dagobert’s son; on the division of the kingdoms between Sigebert and him by their father; and on the recovery of the duchy of Dentelin

In the twelfth year of King Dagobert, a son was born to him by Queen Nantildis, named Clovis; he is also found called Ludovicus. Therefore the king, at the urging of those who seemed concerned for the interests of the kingdom, decided to divide the kingdom equally between these two sons.

Accordingly, he established Sigebert, the elder of the children, as king of Austrasia, as was mentioned above; but Clovis, the younger, he placed with equal dignity over Neustria and Burgundy. He also restored the duchy of Dentelin, which until that time had been unjustly retained and possessed by the Austrasians. Although the Austrasians bore this with difficulty, through fear of Dagobert they confirmed it for the present and promised that it would remain stable in the future.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the killing of the duke Sadregisilus and the disinheritance of his sons for cowardice and negligence concerning their father’s murder; and on the successful war against the Basques, except that Duke Arembertus perished

In the thirteenth year of Dagobert’s reign, the duke Sadregisilus of Aquitaine was slaughtered by certain men who rose against him with murderous intent. [Col. 0787A] This is the Sadregisilus whom the preceding account declared to have been defeated by Dagobert, while Dagobert was still in his boyhood, beaten with whips, and disfigured by the shaving of his beard.

His sons, although they could have become avengers of their father’s shed blood, preferred to live sluggish and idle lives rather than exact blood from the murderers by pressing the matter with arms.
