Therefore, in a public assembly of the Franks, certain nobles appealed to the Roman laws, which decree that those who refuse to avenge the death of the slain ought to be deprived of their paternal inheritance. The sons were stripped of all their father’s goods and left destitute. From their possessions Dagobert bestowed many gifts upon those who cared for the services of the church of Saint Denis.

In the fourteenth year of Dagobert, when he had been informed that the Basques wished to revolt from his authority, he sent an army of the Burgundians there with twelve dukes. After engaging the enemy in battle, they defeated them in the field, took many of them captive, and laid waste their land with plunder and fire.

Finally, the entire army returned home with complete success and unharmed, except that Duke Arembertus, together with the greater part of the nobles and also of the veterans among those whom he had brought with him, was killed by the Basques in the valley of Robola. The commander of this great force, which subdued Vasconia by war, although it had many leaders, was Audoen. He had proved himself vigorous in many battles under Theodoric, and every prerogative in the most important matters was reserved to him.

The leading men of the Basques approached him and asked that they be spared, promising that they would present themselves to King Dagobert and make satisfaction for the charges brought against them. Understanding these claims to have been made without deceit, he led back the army from where it had come.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the embassy to Judicael, king of Brittany, with whom the good man Eligius made a treaty, and on the piety of Judicael and Audoen

After these events, Dagobert sent an embassy to Judicael, king of Brittany, so that the wrongs the Britons had committed against the Franks might be corrected. Otherwise, he threatened that he would send all the forces that had returned from Vasconia into the territory of the Britons.

Eligius, a man of proven faithfulness, as has been shown above, was added to undertake this embassy. After discussing peace at length with Judicael, he persuaded him not only to obey the king of the Franks but also brought him with him to the estate of Clichy, where Dagobert was then staying. There the aforesaid prince offered both correction for the wrongs committed and the submission of himself and the Breton people, and entered into perpetual peace with him.

When Dagobert withdrew, according to custom, to refresh himself with royal banquets, Judicael left the palace and went to the house of Dado the referendary, also called Audoen, because he bore witness to a religious life. He dined there. Judicael himself was indeed very devout, and he had heard that the aforementioned Dado was devoted to holy conduct.

The next day, after taking leave of King Dagobert and receiving royal gifts from him, he returned to his own kingdom.

## CHAPTER XXX. On Dagobert’s generosity toward the churches; on his speech at the council of the kingdom’s nobles; and on his testament and donations

[Col. 0788A]

In that year, King Dagobert, having made peace with all the surrounding peoples and nations subject to him, turned his attention to piety. To show himself grateful for the heavenly benefits that flowed upon him beyond measure, he made almost all the churches of Gaul heirs to his patrimony.

After summoning his sons and a crowd of friends, he proclaimed a general assembly at a place called Bigargium. When all the leading men of Francia had hastened there, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, the king, seated upon a golden throne, addressed them in this manner:

“My most beloved sons, and all you powerful men of the Franks who are present: the purpose and intention for which I have summoned you now appears useful and fruitful, so that I alone may not applaud myself for what I have decided to do for the salvation of my soul.

“Since we bear mortal bodies and immortal souls, a great obligation of uprightness has been imposed upon us, if we do not wish to ignore it. For if, which God forbid, we are insufficiently attentive, we may hand over not only the bodily corruption for which we hope but also the very eternity of our souls to perpetual fires.

“Therefore, remembering the rewards prepared for the just and the punishments prepared for the wicked, and also mindful of the evils I have committed, I have decided to write a testament by which we shall make all the famous basilicas of the saints in our kingdom at this time heirs of the possessions that have been given to them by us.

“I have also arranged for four copies to be made in one form and signed below not only by my hand but also by those of my sons Sigebert and Ludovicus, whom I establish as kings today, and by your hands as well, most holy bishops who are present, together with the leaders of our people. Of these copies, we are sending one to Lyon in Gaul, another to Paris, and a third to Metz, to be kept in the archives where the churches’ records are preserved. The fourth, which we have here before us, we order to be preserved in our treasuries.

“When, after we have laid aside the burden of the flesh, each bishop who presides over the places named in the document has received what is assigned to him, we ask and adjure them, by the terrible name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to commemorate us on three days each week in the years to come, to offer a saving sacrifice for the repose of our soul, and, holding our name as a perpetual memorial, to enter it in the book of life.

“But you, good sons, first considering the reverence owed to nature, whose power even binds wild beasts, remain brothers and do not cast off what you were born to be. Next, revere me as your father. I prefer to ask, although I could command, that you preserve our decrees unshaken, if you wish your own decrees to be preserved by your successors. Know for certain that if you hold the sanctions established by us in contempt—which I do not think you will do—your own decrees will likewise be despised by later generations.”

After he had spoken these words, and everyone had wished him a long and happy life in this world and one enduring in the next, he greeted them all and dismissed the assembly, so that each might return to his own affairs.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the pledge of loyalty given to the Franks by the Basques

In the fifteenth year of his reign, nearly all the leading men of Vasconia, together with Duke Amando, came to him at Clichy. Fearing his presence, they took refuge in the oratory of Saint Denis. Although he had judged them deserving of death, out of respect for the saints whose memory they had sought, he spared their lives.

After giving an oath of loyalty that henceforth they would remain faithful to Dagobert and to the other Frankish kings who came after him, they were permitted to return to their homeland.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the deeds of Grimoald, king of the Lombards, and the murder of his brothers; on the Emperor Constantine, also called Constans, besieging Beneventum; on his cruelty and death; on the tyrant Mezentius; and on the reign of Constantius

[Col. 0789B]

While Dagobert was reigning peacefully in Gaul, Grimoald ruled the Lombards. After killing Godipert, son of King Aripert, and driving his brother Bertharit from Italy, he had seized the kingdom.

This is the Grimoald of whom we stated above that, after the aforesaid city had been overthrown, he killed the Avar by whom he had been carried captive while still a boy, as has been said. His brothers Taso and Caco were treacherously killed by Gregory, the Roman patrician, in the city of Opitergium.

For Gregory promised Taso that, after cutting his beard according to the custom of the ancients, he would adopt him as his son, and persuaded him to come to him with his brother and a few loyal men. When Taso entered the city, Gregory ordered the gates to be closed behind him and sent armed soldiers to kill him.

When those who had entered noticed this, bidding one another a final farewell, they scattered through the streets of the city and slaughtered everyone they encountered. After causing a great massacre, they were at last surrounded and cut down by the greater number.

Gregory had promised that he would cut off Taso’s beard. He cut off not only his beard but also his head; nevertheless, so that he would not be called a perjurer, he pointlessly cut off the tip of the beard as well.

Therefore, once Grimoald had obtained the kingdom, he utterly destroyed Opitergium in revenge for his brothers who had been killed there.

In his time the Emperor Constantine Augustus, also called Constans, wishing to drive the Lombards from Italy, crossed the Adriatic Sea and besieged Beneventum. Terrified by Grimoald’s sudden arrival, he withdrew, leaving behind with the army a certain nobleman named Saburrus, who engaged Grimoald in battle.

Then one of the Lombards, named Amalongus, who was accustomed to carry the royal staff, struck a certain Greek with that same staff and lifted him from his riding saddle over his own head. He compelled the rest, terrified, to flee.

When the Emperor learned of this, he turned the anger he had conceived in his heart against his own people—that is, the Romans. He immediately hastened to Rome and was honorably received by Pope Vitalian. On the first day he offered blessed Peter a pallium woven with gold; but on the following day, and throughout the twelve consecutive days he remained there, he ordered all the ancient bronze objects that had been made as ornaments of the city to be removed.

He even stripped the basilica of Blessed Mary, anciently called the Pantheon, and removed from it the bronze tiles, sending them to Constantinople with the other ornaments.

When he reached Sicily, however, he paid the deserved price for such great wickedness. For he afflicted the inhabitants of that island, as well as those of Calabria, Sardinia, and Africa, with such grievous sufferings that wives were separated from husbands and children from parents and forced to endure harsh slavery.

Thus the Emperor, more hostile to his own people than to his enemies, was killed in a bath by soldiers who detested his cruelty. After him Mezentius seized tyrannical power in Sicily. He was punished in the same way without delay, and his head was carried to Constantinople. Constantine, the son of Constantius, whom we mentioned earlier, then held the reins of the Roman Empire for seventeen years.

It should be noted that in the time of his father, Pope Vitalian sent Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Hadrian to Britain to strengthen the harvest of the Christian faith that blessed Gregory had sown among the English.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the praiseworthy death and burial of Dagobert, and the construction and adornment of the church of Saint Denis

The illustrious Dagobert, king of the Franks, after administering his glorious reign for sixteen years, began to suffer from a discharge of the bowels at the estate of Spino(g)ilo, situated on the Seine not far from Paris. From there he was carried by the hands of his attendants to the basilica of Saint Denis.

When he realized that the illness of his final sickness was pressing him toward death, he ordered his adviser Ega to come to him with the greatest speed. He announced that he was about to depart from the present world, entrusted his wife Nantildis and his son Clovis to Ega’s protection, and admonished him to raise his son according to the wisdom granted him by God and to govern the kingdom piously.

After summoning the other nobles and bishops of Neustria and Burgundy, entrusting the son to them and them to the son, he ended his life on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February. His body, embalmed with spices, was buried in the church of Saint Denis, on the right side of the tomb of that martyr.

Finally, as was shown above, since he had promised to adorn the memorial of that saint and his companions, he built for them all a church more excellent than any churches then existing in Gaul. Setting no limit on expense, he adorned it with marble columns and a matching pavement, constructing it at immense cost and with exquisite workmanship.

He showed no less concern for its other ornaments. He surrounded the entire interior of the church with garments woven with gold and silk hangings. There he established an order of singers such as was maintained at Saint Martin of Tours and at Saint Maurice of Agaunum.

He also bestowed so many estates upon the brothers serving God in that place and upon the church officials that his devotion of spirit was greatly worthy of admiration. For King Dagobert was extremely cautious, shrewd in intelligence, gentle toward those who were well disposed and faithful to him, but very terrible to rebels and traitors. He was devoted especially to bodily exercises and hunting, vigorous in every physical agility, and exceedingly powerful in knowledge and courage in war.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On a vision shown to a hermit concerning the condition of the dead King Dagobert; on the benefit of adorning churches; and on the harm of stripping them

At the time when Dagobert reached the end appointed for his life, a certain distinguished man named Ansoald, defender of the church of Poitiers, was traveling through the regions of Sicily. While returning by sea, he came to a certain small island made illustrious by the presence and merits of a hermit named John.

While Ansoald was speaking with him about the salvation of the soul, he asked whether the hermit had known King Dagobert. The hermit replied that he had known him very well. The old man then asked him to describe the king’s character and life.

The hermit said:

“After I had surrendered my limbs briefly to sleep, weighed down by much vigil and fasting and also by the fatigue of old age, someone appeared before me, venerable and handsome with white hair. He urged me to rise quickly and pray for the mercy of the Lord on behalf of the soul of King Dagobert, which had departed from the body at that same hour.

“When I hastened to do this, I suddenly saw, not far away in the open sea, demons of hideous appearance and savage faces. They were driving the bound King Dagobert across the stretches of the sea and, in addition to inflicting blows upon him, were dragging him toward the regions of Vulcan.

“Stretched out amid torments, between the tossing and the blows, he was heard asking for the assistance of certain saints. Suddenly the sky opened, and amid lightning bolts crashing down upon the waves, men of wondrous radiance appeared to descend.

“I began to ask who they were. They said that they were those whom Dagobert had called to his aid: namely, the martyrs Denis and Maurice, and Martin the confessor. They rescued the soul from the demons and lifted it with them to the heavens, singing this psalm:

‘Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken, O Lord; he will dwell in your courts’ (Psalm 64).”

That venerable man John related to Ansoald that he had seen these things. When Ansoald returned to Gaul, he told Saint Audoen these things. Audoen wrote it down on a single sheet so that posterity might arrange it in the order of history.

From this it may be understood that the adornment which devout men offer to the saints in honor of their memories is in no way despised by them. Although this is the statement of certain slanderers who wish to devour everything—“Gold or silver attached to wood, or hangings suspended from walls, benefit neither God nor his saints”—nevertheless it was not without cause that divine vengeance punished either Belshazzar, who converted the vessels stolen from the Lord’s temple to shameful uses, or Heliodorus, who attempted to plunder God’s treasury. Antiochus too, because he stripped the temple of the city of Jerusalem, consecrated to the Most High, later died covered with worms.

Dagobert, however, specifically asked those saints to assist him whose basilicas he remembered enriching with more resources than the others.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On Clovis under the just rule of Ega, and on the pavement of the Roman Paradise; and on the Gothic kings Tolga and Risicind in Spain

After Dagobert’s death, his son Clovis—whom we have also said was called Ludovicus—began to reign with his mother Nantildis over the regions of Neustria and Burgundy, while Ega, the royal adviser, governed the palace and the kingdom.

Ega was devoted to patience, rich in possessions, an outstanding cultivator of justice, and descended from a distinguished family. He was criticized by many only because he was devoted to avarice [French: *était blâmé*—“was blamed”]. Nevertheless, whatever possessions belonging to the poor had been seized under Dagobert and unjustly added to the treasury, he restored to their owners with complete integrity.

In those days the lord pope of the Roman Church magnificently paved the place called Paradise [vulgate, *le Parvis*] before the basilica of Blessed Peter the Apostle with large white marble slabs.

In Spain, after the death of Sisenand, his son Tolga was made king at his father’s request. When the Goths took advantage of the king’s youth and committed many crimes according to their accustomed practice, a certain Cintasind, the most distinguished of the Goths, expelled Tolga from the kingdom, compelled him to become a cleric, and seized the throne.

Recognizing the custom of his people in killing or expelling their kings, he put to death many whom he knew to be devoted to this vice. He killed nearly 200 of the more powerful and about 500 of the common people, condemning the rest to exile. After holding the kingdom peacefully, he established his son Risicind as king while he was still alive. Risicind repented of the evils he had committed and gave many alms; he ended his life, as is reported, in his ninetieth year.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the division of the royal treasury, and on the counsels Pippin gave to Sigebert

Since we have shown above in what order Dagobert, while still alive, divided the kingdom among his children, we must now explain how, after his death, his treasures were divided among them.

Accordingly, Pippin, who under Dagobert had continually lived at the palace with certain leading men of Austrasia, went to Sigebert after Dagobert’s death. Joining himself, as before, in a bond of friendship with Bishop Chunibert, he supplied the aforesaid king with useful counsel.

Following their advice, Sigebert sent a messenger to his brother Clovis to demand the portion due to him from their father’s treasures. A definite place and date were appointed for its return.

On the appointed day, Chunibert and Pippin went as far as the royal estate of Compiègne. There, through the agency of Ega, who governed King Clovis’s palace, all the contents of Dagobert’s treasury—various kinds of objects and gifts formerly kept hidden—were brought out and divided equally between the brothers. A third part of everything Dagobert had acquired after taking Nantildis as his wife was nevertheless reserved for the queen herself.

Chunibert and Pippin carried Sigebert’s portion to him.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the death of Ega, the appointment of Erchinoald, and the killing of Ermenfred

In the third year of Clovis’s reign, Ega, master of the palace, died at the estate of Clichy, stricken by fever. After his death, Erchinoald, related through his mother to King Dagobert, was appointed master of the household in Neustria.

He was humble, peaceful, and adorned with every virtue. He honored the priests of the Lord by loving them, and was loved by them and by all the nobles.

A few days before Ega’s death, a certain Ermenfred, who had married his daughter, killed Count Ainulf at the village of Albioder during a public assembly. Therefore, with the permission and also the command of Nantildis, he suffered a serious loss of his possessions at the hands of Ainulf’s relatives. Fearing the king as well, he remained for many days at Reims in the basilica of Saint Remigius.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On Pippin’s death, mourned by many, and the succession of his son to the office after much contention and faction

After a year had passed, Pippin died, leaving the Austrasians in the deepest grief because of his death, since he was loved by everyone for the gentleness of his spirit and the equity he had maintained in justice.

His son Grimoald, a very vigorous young man, was greatly loved by both the people and the nobles because of his father’s exceptional merits.

Otto, however, son of Bero, hoped that he could become count of the palace because he had been King Sigebert’s tutor during the king’s early youth. Therefore, when he gradually began to despise Grimoald and no longer conceal the hatred he had conceived against him, but instead repeatedly revealed himself as his adversary through his contempt, Grimoald—who had long been bound in friendship with Bishop Chunibert through the privilege of his father’s friendship—sought to drive Otto from the palace.

When he could not accomplish this, he made Otto hateful to Leutherius, duke of the Alemanni. Otto was killed by him in the tenth year of King Sigebert, and Grimoald was appointed master of the household in the kingdom of Austrasia in his father’s place.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On Flaucatus, master of the household of Burgundy, and his conflict with Willibad

[Col. 0793D]

In the fourth year of his reign, Clovis went with his mother Nantildis to Orléans, the capital of the kingdom of Burgundy. When the bishops and nobles of that people arrived and surrendered themselves to Clovis’s authority, Nantildis treated them with the greatest kindness and admonished them to remain faithful to her son.

On their advice, she appointed Flaucatus, a native of Francia, master of the palace, joining her niece Ragneberta to him in marriage.

Thereafter Erchinoald and Flaucatus—one governing the palace of Neustria and the other that of Burgundy after the king—gave each other their right hands in a mutual partnership, so that, acting in common deliberation and with equal agreement, they might pursue the things that made for peace and preserve the rights of justice and equity among their subjects.

Flaucatus crossed into Burgundy and diligently performed the duties entrusted to him. The patrician Willibad of Transjurane opposed his efforts. Exalting himself through the nobility of his lineage and the abundance of his wealth, Willibad considered it beneath him to be subject to Flaucatus or to obey his commands.

Although Flaucatus concealed from him that he had taken note of this, he did not delay in May to hasten with Clovis to a general assembly decreed to be held at Chalon. Willibad also proceeded there with a sufficiently hostile-looking retinue, one that seemed to threaten war.

He refused to enter the palace, evidently fearing that Flaucatus might catch him off guard and overpower him. When Flaucatus noticed this, he left the palace and wished to kill him. His brother Amalbert came forward to meet him and rescued Willibad, who was vainly preparing to resist, from death.

From then on Flaucatus sought an opportunity to take final vengeance on Willibad.

## CHAPTER XL. On the death of Queen Nantildis, the killing of Willibad, and the not undeserved death of Flaucatus shortly afterward
That year Queen Nantildis died and was buried in the church of Saint-Denis, in the same tomb as Dagobert. In that same year Clovis set out from the city of Paris in September with the dukes Erchinoald and Flaucatus and several leading men of Francia. He proceeded through Sens and Auxerre toward the city of Autun. From there he sent a messenger to Willibad, ordering him to come to him as quickly as possible.

Although Willibad knew that he had to beware of the ambushes being prepared for him, he nevertheless considered it dangerous not to obey the king. He therefore complied with the commands, which he did not dare to challenge, but came surrounded by a strong multitude of armed men. A certain Ermenric, sent by the king with others from among the nobles to urge him to hasten without delay to the palace, met him. Ermenric was also to give him his word that he would suffer no harm either on his way there or on his return. Willibad did not entirely reject belief in Ermenric’s assurances and proceeded. He also honored him with generous gifts and asked him to go ahead to the city.

Yet even then he did not feel sufficiently secure. He ordered Agilulf, bishop of Valence, and Count Wisco to go ahead of him to the royal palace, learn what was being planned concerning him, and quickly report back to him what they had learned. [Col. 0794D] Flaucatus had them detained in the city; then, rising early with his men, he left the city and set out to fight against Willibad.

Erchinoald the duke, with the Neustrian forces, supported him, as did Amalgarius and Ramelenus, young men of no obscure birth, accompanied by a considerable multitude of retainers. Ramelenus and Amalgarius, together with those who obeyed them, brought assistance to Flaucatus in the battle line, while the rest of the multitude stood at a distance awaiting the outcome of the fight.

A messenger who had hurried ahead announcing the enemy’s arrival made Willibad aware of it. He encouraged his companions not to allow their opponents an unbloody victory and received the advancing forces. In the first line he himself was struck down dead, since, already contemptuous of his life and despairing of his safety, he had thrown himself entirely against the enemy.

Bertarius, too, on Flaucatus’s side, while vigorously pressing the opponents, encountered a certain Madalulf, a Burgundian who had formerly been very well known to him through their close friendship. When Bertarius called out to him and promised that, if he came over to him, he would rescue him safely from the battle, he raised his shield to protect him; but, ungrateful for the proffered kindness, Madalulf struck him in the breast with a spear.

His son Aubedo, roused by the danger to his father, ran to him and pierced Madalulf’s breast with a lance. He either struck down or put to flight all who had attacked his father. Thus filial devotion protected his father, although gravely wounded, so that he did not suffer the death that threatened him.

Those who had refused to take part in the battle, seeing that Flaucatus was on the point of gaining the upper hand, invaded the tents of Willibad and his companions and carried away whatever equipment they found there. They also drove off the horses of the slain, which were wandering in various directions.

The next day Flaucatus left Autun and came to Chalon. On the following day, when he entered the city, Chalon was accidentally consumed by fire. Flaucatus, suffering from a fever, was carried by boat along the Saône to the fortress of Dijon, where he breathed his last and was buried in the basilica of Saint Benignus.

Many believed that these two men, Flaucatus and Willibad, had suffered punishments worthy of their deeds, because they had been entangled in many perjuries which they had committed after exchanging oaths at the holy places.

## CHAPTER XLI  
### On King Clovis’s distribution of alms to the poor in an assembly, and on the exemption of the church and monastery of Saint-Denis from episcopal jurisdiction; and on the holy men who were present and their pious works

[Col. 0795C]

In the fourteenth year after assuming the government, King Clovis ordered the silver which his father had placed over the projecting apse above the tombs of the martyrs Denis, Rusticus, and Eleutherius to be removed and handed over to Aigulf, the abbot of that place, so that he might distribute it to the poor and those suffering want—for at that time famine had occupied almost the whole of Francia.

Because that same place was still under the authority of the bishop of Paris, the God-beloved prince devised the following plan.

In the sixteenth year after he had assumed the royal scepter, he ordered the bishops and the leading men of the whole nation to assemble at Clichy. Sitting on a throne among them, he began his speech as follows:

“Although, fellow citizens of Francia, the care of earthly rule has prompted us to summon you as counselors in public affairs, nevertheless it is fitting first for us to arrange the things that belong to God and his saints, so that afterward, with God’s help, the things that belong to us may proceed according to our desire.

“For he who deigned to promise this through his own mouth, saying, ‘Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you’ (Matthew 6), will bestow his promises upon us when we obey his commands.

“Let us therefore inquire what pleases the saints who now dwell in the kingdom of the eternal Father; and all things will turn out prosperously for us on earth if we take care to fulfill those things in our deeds. You, priests, who are called gods and all sons of the Most High (Psalm 81), attend to and hear the intention of our heart; and, if you approve what you have heard, strive together with us to bring it to completion.

“Our devotion therefore rests upon this purpose: that we should release entirely from every dominion of mortal men the monastery of our patron, the lord Denis, in which he lies buried with his companions in bearing witness to the truth, and in which our parents of pious memory—namely, Lord Dagobert and Lady Nantildis—ordered themselves to be buried.

“Thus the abbot and the brothers who dwell there may possess without disturbance from any ruler the estates handed over to them by our parents or by other faithful Christians, and may pray to God more freely for our salvation and for the stability of our kingdom.

“Our suggestion is supported by the venerable Landeric, bishop of the city of Paris, in whose diocese that monastery is situated and to whom it has been subject until the present time.

“Once the servants of God established there have obtained this liberty, and have suffered the dominion of no one except God, his saints, and us—whose authority the entire nation of the Franks also obeys—let them know that they will thereby be obligated to our parents and to us, and to those who, as we hope, will arise from our seed by God’s grace, so that they may never cease to entreat God for our present and future rest and for that of those whom we have mentioned.”

After those surrounding the king had listened attentively to him speaking before the assembly, they proclaimed his praises and wished him enduring joys.

Almost all the bishops of Gaul attended this gathering. Among them were certain holy men whom the holy Church honors with due reverence, because those afflicted by various illnesses are healed at their tombs: blessed Audoenus, and Saint Rado his brother, as well as Lord Eligius together with blessed Sulpitius and Saint Eucherius.

Among these, blessed Audoenus—also called Dado—was the referendary of King Dagobert and the son of the most distinguished man Autharius. He was called a referendary because all public documents were brought to him, and he authenticated or confirmed them with the king’s ring or with the seal entrusted to him by the king.

He had two brothers, Ado and Rado. Ado, rejecting worldly pomp, built a monastery in the forest of Iodre on the river Marne, and called it Iodrum. There he served God under the rule of Abbot Columbanus until his final day.

Rado, likewise inspired by zeal for fraternal devotion, while he was in charge of the royal treasures, built a monastery on his paternal inheritance and called it Radolium, after his own name.

Blessed Audoenus, moreover, lest he seem inferior to his brothers in good works, also built a monastery within the forest of Brie. He named it Jerusalem, but it is now called the monastery of Rebais, after the little river on which it is situated.

I think these brothers were inspired to such glorious undertakings by the example of Saint Eligius. While he was living a life pleasing to God and to men at the palace, he had asked King Dagobert to grant him an estate situated in the district of Limoges, called Solignac. There he built a monastery and established a community of monks serving God.

## CHAPTER XLII [Note: This chapter, which proves that Aimoin was a monk of Fleury, has now been added for the first time from manuscript codices.]  
### On the foundation of the monastery of Fleury

Since we have mentioned other places and described how and by whom they were founded, it seems appropriate that we should not omit the foundation of our own monastery. In it the venerable Father Benedict, renowned for his virtues, lies buried in body; and we, nourished, so to speak, from our very cradles by him, have received from God—through the intercession of the merits of that patron—whatever good or useful thing exists in us, if indeed there is anything.

Thus, while the glorious King Clovis, son of Dagobert, was governing the Frankish kingdom, a certain man named Leodebodus, noble by birth and no less distinguished for the uprightness of his character, held the office of abbot in the monastery of Saint Aignan, in the suburb of Orléans.

He approached the aforementioned prince and asked that the royal estate of Fleury be exchanged. Since the king was kindhearted, he willingly granted the request. He accepted from the abbot the estate which had come to him through his paternal inheritance, and transferred the aforesaid royal estate of Fleury into the abbot’s ownership.

Having obtained what he desired, Leodebodus did not allow the place to remain vacant for long. He built two churches, one in honor of Peter, prince of the apostles, and the other in veneration of Mary, the Mother of God; he soon also constructed dwellings suitable for the use of monks.

After gathering together noblemen and others who desired to serve God, he appointed as abbot a man named Rigomar. After completing five years, Rigomar departed from this world and was succeeded by a man named Mummolus.

This good shepherd, seeking to increase the flock entrusted to him by God, the supreme and true shepherd, received into the service of Christ a man of innocent life named Aygulf, born of a family of no little distinction in the fortress of Blois.

In time, after testing him in monastic conduct, Mummolus sent him to the province of Benevento so that he might bring from there to Gaul the body of the holy Father Benedict, revered by all mortals.

Aygulf obeyed his command without delay and brought to Gaul the most holy limbs of the aforementioned Father, together with the bones of his sister Scholastica. Anyone who wishes to know this more fully may find it in the book entitled *The Translation of Father Benedict*. We have rendered that account, as far as we could, in heroic verse, out of the ardor of love with which we burn toward that same father.

## HERE BEGINS THE TRANSLATION OF FATHER BENEDICT  
### Composed in heroic meter by Aimoin, monk of the monastery of Fleury

[Col. 0797]

My spirit urges me to loosen my tongue in singing measures,

In graceful praise of the excellent Father Benedict,

So that I may reveal to all peoples by what ordered course

The glorious limbs of his body were brought to us.

His own venerable limbs, joined in the tomb’s urn to those of his sister, who was united with him in merits.

Now, Father Benedict, grant strength to your servant who asks,

And begin with me, my pipe, the pleasing verses

With which your humble disciple may praise you.

While Clovis, king of the Franks, ruled in the royal court,

The illustrious offspring of the exalted prince Dagobert,

There lived a man distinguished by outstanding moral character,

Leodebodus, born from a renowned lineage,

Governing the monastery of the holy Anianus,

Which looks toward the walls of neighboring Orléans.

[Col. 0797D]

His heart was drenched with the Lord’s abundant grace.

He sought King Clovis, whom I mentioned at the beginning of my song,

A man adorned with supreme goodness,

And not unlike himself, to whom he spoke these words:

“King, by whose government the Gallic land depends,

Under whom the Franks rejoice to be powerful,

I possess a small estate, yet dear to my mind,

Which I have learned by report to be held under royal jurisdiction.

They commonly call this estate by the name Fleury.

I ask that you grant it to me to be governed as my own.

[Col. 0798C]

“Do not think that, if you grant it, this will bring you any loss,

Since, I confess, I shall give you back my own estate.

Nor do I wish to receive the royal estate from you for nothing;

I promise to return from my own property a similar piece of land.”

The prince graciously assented to these prayers

And rejoiced to lose his own royal estate,

Content that a field no different from it would be returned to him.

When these matters had been arranged, the venerable Leodebodus,

Having put aside the biting cares that had weighed upon his mind,

At last obtained the land he had long desired.

He laid foundations for buildings suitable for habitation,

Taking care to construct dwellings for the monk-servants of Christ,

And worked diligently until the highest completion

Showed the work finished and brought his labors to an end.

At last he built two small churches for the time being,

[Col. 0798D]

And dedicated the smaller one to Christ’s mother, Mary,

While he consecrated the other in the name of Saint Peter.

At that time this second church was larger and somewhat more spacious.

For now, after the body of Benedict,

The excellent Father, has been brought to the western land

And entered the sanctuary of the Mother,

This church has been made broader in extent

And higher than the many basilicas gathered into one.

Meanwhile, glorious Leodebodus took care

To lead a great flock to the enclosures

And gather together countless bands of men,

So that he might unite to Christ the companies

That had willingly sworn themselves to his service.

Then, seeking one whom he might deem worthy

To receive the office of shepherd,

And finding a monk pleasing to God and to the people

For his vigorous and blessed merits,

He placed him over the other brothers by deliberate choice.

His name was Mummolus, and he too was of noble lineage.

He himself later ascended to the heavenly heights

When he had passed beyond the limits of life.

But the shepherd, wisely caring for the holy flock

Entrusted to him, relieved his mind with writings

Rich in honeyed words, knowing how to join himself

To the sayings of the Fathers.

His chief devotion was to rereading the books

Which blessed Pope Gregory had poured forth from his sacred heart,

Gregory, whose words conveyed the meaning of delightful speech.

The Holy Spirit taught Gregory—he who, in a cave beside the familiar waters, honored Christ in the form of a dove.

While devout Mummolus continually turned these writings

With his hands, he found that in the deeds of the Father

Who must always be remembered, Benedict had declared,

While he dwelt in the lofty stronghold of Monte Cassino,

That savage peoples would destroy all the enclosures

Of the flock without any delay.

Recognizing that the predicted time had now passed,

The saint turned his mind to what he had previously foreseen,

In case an opportunity should arise to carry away

The sacred body of the aforesaid disciple.

Aygulf was sent to the great city of Diomedes

To bring the limbs desired by all mortals—

[Col. 0799C]

Your limbs, O Benedict, radiant with the lamp of virtues,

Brought down from the lofty summit of Monte Cassino.

For Mummolus said that, while the servant of God

Had surrendered his limbs to sleep, this had been shown to him from heaven.

At that time, some men from the city of Le Mans also arrived.

A similar vision in sleep had warned them

To seek, in a distant region, the tomb

Where holy Scholastica, joined to her pious brother,

Had been buried, so that they might carry her protection

Back to their own city.

Therefore they happily joined Aygulf on the same blessed road.

After crossing the Alps, they reached

The city of Romulus and the revered seat of Peter.

There the holy Aygulf, while his companions

Were occupied in the sacred places, left them

And hastened without delay along the road

That leads to the stronghold of Monte Cassino.

At that time it was surrounded by a vast wilderness.

Because the Lombards had once devastated everything around it,

And had not feared to lay their impious hands

Even upon the holy buildings, every inhabitant had departed.

A diligent investigator came there and searched carefully

With attentive eyes for the place where the tombs

Of the holy men lay buried, or for any stronghold.

He saw only deserted places, without even the appearance of tombs.

An old man, dwelling in a secluded part of the mountain,

Saw him examining everything and asked him in these words:

“Alas, stranger, from what distant people have you come

To investigate and visit our borders?

What are you seeking?”

When Aygulf hesitated, the old man again said:

“Do not fear to reveal to me the secrets of your heart.

I promise to keep your words concealed in my breast

And to lend my strength to the request you make.”

[Col. 0800A]

The old man had spoken, and Aygulf followed his words,

Answering him as follows:

“No greater desire occupies my heart

Than to possess the sacred body of Father Benedict.”

At last the old man, mature in age, replied,

Speaking these words from his hidden heart:

“What you seek can indeed be accomplished,” he said,

“But it must be redeemed by a great gift,

If you wish, with me as your guide,

To see before your eyes the treasure sought throughout so many lands.”

The hero replied to the old man:

“You will receive a great reward if you show me

What I ask; and I promise that I shall cause you no delay.”

The man, full of God, poured forth from a sound heart

Words worthy of what he held silently in his mind:

“When dark night has covered the sky

And Phoebe, borne in her flashing chariot,

Has reached the middle of her course,

Then keep watch with attentive eyes along the mountain paths.

Look toward the place where the radiance sent forth

By the shining light overcomes the immense darkness.

There you will find what you burn to possess with such love.”

Aygulf obeyed the old man’s instructions.

When the first rest of night had passed, he rose

And searched for the direction in which the kindly light shone.

He saw a place brightly radiant with a new light.

A stone inscribed on the outside with the names of the brothers

Covered it. The venerable man gently moved it aside.

Suddenly the discovery was revealed:

The blessed bones of Father Benedict,

And also those of his distinguished sister,

Which a venerable thief soon placed

In a basket woven with green palm leaves,

While he prepared to make his way to his homeland.

[Col. 0800C]

At once he saw the companions whom he had left at Rome

Approaching along the road and climbing the mountain.

When he came near them, he asked why they had come.

Only then did they reveal the secrets of their hearts

To Aygulf, the servant of Christ.

He told them that everything had now been accomplished,

And quickly instructed them to hurry along the road

By which the fields of Gaul are reached.

They did exactly as commanded.

As they hastened away and eagerly left Italian soil,

A voice sent from heaven sounded through the air over the earth.

It forbade them to advance or move from the place

Where they had stopped.

At that time an angel sent from heaven,

Terrifying the bishop of the Roman see in sleep

By his face and threatening words,

Broke his slumber and rebuked him:

“Why,” he said, “does sluggish torpor keep you,

Lying idle in bed, and allow the fields of the Latins

To be ravaged?

For the Gauls, once hostile to your territories,

Now mindful of their former anger, are striving

To deprive you openly of the aid of the righteous,

Secretly carrying away the bodies of the servants of God.”

[Col. 0800D]

The bishop, shaken in heart by this vision,

Rose from his bed and gathered his forces for battle.

Relying on the strength of the Lombards, he pursued them.

They looked back over their shoulders and saw

An innumerable host of enemies running behind them.

When they saw this, fear drained the heat from their bones.

[Col. 0801A]

Nor were their cheeks without tears.

They fell prostrate and entreated Christ,

Who had deemed them worthy of so great a gift,

To preserve it, lest it become booty for those peoples

And they be stripped of their glorious honor.

God surrounded them as they traveled through the dark air,

So that no one could see or touch them.

Meanwhile they seized the road that had been shown to them,

And rejoicing, reached their native fields.

They call the field Bonodium, in the district of Orléans.

There the bearers of the holy ashes first rested,

Wearied by their journey.

The Lord desired to glorify himself in his saints.

A blind man, cast from his mother’s womb,

Perceived, as day came and night departed,

And a lame man rejoiced to walk on straight feet.

They reached a place called by the name of New Ville.

[Col. 0801B]

Here another man, born into this light without light,

Received sight and praised Saint Benedict.

Fleury is a village not far away from the monastery

To which the bearers carried the precious limbs.

The servant of God Mummolus went there with the rejoicing flock

So that he might convey the fear-inspiring relics

In a solemn procession.

After him, nearly the entire people of Le Mans hurried,

Hoping that the bones of the distinguished virgin

Would not be denied to them.

But Aygulf firmly declared that he was unwilling

To surrender them, since he had redeemed them

By his own sweat.

Nevertheless, overcome by their constant prayers,

He did not persist against his will,

But allowed the body to be restored to those who requested it.

Then the thought arose in his mind to separate

The limbs that had been mingled together.

But he did not know how this could be done,

Until Christ, by showing him, granted him the knowledge.

[Col. 0802A]

Finally he placed the larger limbs beside

The already dead limbs of a boy.

Immediately the boy was restored to life: he rose from where he lay and learned to walk on his feet.

A girl who was already lifeless and destined for burial

Soon touched the slender limbs and awoke.

Thus, by a like means, the two holy siblings were decisively separated.

Then the people of Le Mans joyfully returned

To their own land with the virgin.

From that point Abbot Mummolus,

And Aygulf as well, having earned this privilege,

Carried away great and sweet joys from the gift.

They rejoiced that at such a time they had borne

Upon their shoulders to the dwelling of blessed Peter,

The keeper of the keys, until divine power should indicate

Where it commanded them to bury its beloved Benedict, after the joyous celebration of his birthday.

The author of piety granted this not long afterward.

[Col. 0802B]

Therefore the servant of God, rejoicing in so great a gift,

While anxious care moved through the hidden places of his heart,

Climbed the twin heights of heaven by vigilant prayer,

Asking God, in his compassion, to grant a suitable tomb.

At once, as he prayed, the lofty gate of heaven opened, and a humble messenger of the heavenly choirs entered and stood visible before his eyes after earthly things [the compressed poetic phrasing is uncertain].

Without delay, the King granted him whatever he desired.

For soon a radiance was sent down from the heavenly court,

Marking the place where the remains of Benedict were to be buried.

When Mummolus saw this and believed it with a faithful heart,

He rejoiced as he built the church;

He rejoiced as he transferred the Father’s bones,

So that he might protect his own servants under Christ the prince and grant them everlasting life after this life.

Amen.

[Col. 0801] Here ends the *History of the Franks* by Aimoin, monk of Fleury.

[Col. 0801]

# TWO BOOKS ON THE MIRACLES OF SAINT BENEDICT  
### Written by Aimoin, monk of Fleury

*(Mabillon, Acta Sanctorum of Saint Benedict, IV, II, 356, from the Library of Fleury and the Bollandist March.)*

## PROLOGUE TO GAUZLIN, THE ABBOT

[Col. 0801D]

To the honorable Fathers, Gauzlin, most reverend abbot, and the entire holy congregation of the monastery of Fleury entrusted to him: Aimoin, the least of them all, wishes eternal reign with Christ.

From your teaching, reverend lords, I have learned how worthy of reward is the good of obedience. Therefore, at the command of certain among you—who preferred to persuade me by paternal admonition rather than by imperious authority—I willingly bowed my neck, so that I might commit to writing for the memory of posterity certain things concerning the miracles of our common patron, the most holy Benedict.

I therefore applied myself as best I could, taking care to record in writing not only the deeds performed at the most holy tomb of that same Father, but also those which the Lord deigned to perform in other places dedicated to his memory, in order to make his merit known. I have divided the whole work into two books.

Receive, then, most holy Fathers, this slight but faithful fruit of a slender branch growing from the great tree of your harmonious community. May you not regret having labored for the progress of one who strives above all to proclaim the praises of his beloved nourisher Benedict and to satisfy your wishes in every respect.

And you, most beloved brothers, with whom in the first flower of my age I learned to bear Christ’s gentle yoke, I ask you to rejoice with me that, with your assistance also, I have advanced far enough that some useful service may be assigned to my unworthiness.

For although no usefulness exists in me in comparison with you, whatever good there is in me comes entirely from almighty God, through the intercession of the glorious Virgin Mary and of our lawgiver Benedict, and through the labor of his servants.

[Col. 0803B]

2. Finally, I fittingly ask all those whose hearts are possessed by love for that same confessor of Christ not to seek in this work the persuasive eloquence of rhetoric. Rather, among the humble baskets of our rustic table, let them admire and draw up the gleaming and sweet-smelling honey of the miracles.

Let them remember that people often take pleasure in using more elegant dishes served in earthen vessels.

Having offered this preliminary account of the poverty of our small talent—

[Col. 0804A]

3. At the end of the prologue we thought we should not omit the fact that divine mercy granted our shepherd, among its other gifts, this particular favor: whenever worthy things that had been reported about him were to be brought forth, he never needed the assistance of any outsider.

Indeed, the pupils themselves who had been educated and instructed by his help in his monasteries were found capable of entrusting to the memory of posterity whatever had to be proclaimed in his praise—apart from blessed Pope Gregory alone. Gregory himself, subject to the disciplines of his rule, eloquently explained how greatly the same Father shone with virtues.

Finally, the poet Marcus and Paul, in the monastery of Monte Cassino, composed many elegant accounts of his miracles in verse.

The order of the translation of his sacred body to this venerable place, as well as the signs accomplished here and throughout Gaul through his merits, was committed to writing by the most eloquent man Adrevaldus, a monk of this monastery. [Note: The Patriciacensis manuscript, used by the Bollandist collaborators, inserts here: “who is also thought to have been called Adalbertus,” etc.; on this matter, see above.]

To this work Adelerius, likewise a monk of this congregation, added only two chapters.

Following in their footsteps, although with unequal steps, and wishing you health and prosperity, I now give this beginning to the matters I have proposed to relate.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0803]

## CHAPTER ONE  
### The ravages of the Northmen in Gaul under Charles the Bald, Louis, Charles the Simple, Odo, and Robert; the site of the palace of Cassinogil, etc.

[Col. 0803C]

4. The ancient and modern histories, for all who carefully reflect upon them, reveal the inhabitants of the Gallic regions, weakened by the repeated incursions of foreign nations.

The ten-year struggle of Julius Caesar exhausted them; the sudden invasion of the Huns tore them apart; the presumptuous invasion of the Goths, who sought to establish settlements, overturned them. Finally, the vigorous right hand of the Franks in war—both conquered and conquerors—subjugated them to its rule by an equal destiny.

The fierce power of the Franks, both in subduing barbarian peoples and in keeping them away from their borders, flourished through the strength of concord until the time of Charles the Bald, of blessed memory, son of Louis, who was surnamed the Pious.

Against him, the accusation of fraternal hostility stirred up the hatred of neighboring peoples, especially the Northmen, who, practicing piracy, devastated the maritime regions of his kingdom by the most grievous plundering.

At first Count Robert of Anjou resisted their savage attempts. He was a man of Saxon origin and had been entrusted by the king with supreme authority in those regions, with the support of the most distinguished men of Neustria, Rainulf and Lambert, as the most eloquent author Adrevaldus relates in his first book.

But when these men met different fates, the Danes obtained an unhindered opportunity for their raids. The text of the work that follows will disclose to the diligent reader what and how great a loss they inflicted upon the cities in two expeditions through devastation and the burning of monasteries and other churches.

5. When the august Charles had been removed from human affairs, his son Louis succeeded him. He acquired the surname “the Do-Nothing,” either because he held the kingdom for scarcely two years and accomplished nothing energetically, or because, as we have received from our ancestors, he took a certain nun, removed from the women’s monastery of Cala, and joined her to himself in marriage, thereby committing the sin that is known as “nothing.”

In his days that savage nation of the Danes arrived, intending to inflict a third disaster upon the Neustrians. It would have brought a greater calamity than the earlier ones had not Hugh, who held the dignity of abbot throughout Gaul, restrained their reckless assaults. [Note: John of the Wood adds, “as is reported, son of Robert.” These words are absent, and rightly so, from the Patriciacensis manuscript; for this Hugh was not the son of Robert, but of Count Conrad and Adelaide, as Herric testifies in book II, chapter 5, of *On the Miracles of Saint Germanus, Bishop of Auxerre*. He died at Orléans in 887 and was buried at Auxerre in the monastery of Saint Germanus. Another was Hugh the Great, son of Robert who styled himself king; he was slain in the battle of Soissons in 923, below.]

That he, aided by the manifest assistance of the most holy Father Benedict, routed countless enemy forces with a small band, so that scarcely a messenger survived, can easily be learned from the writings of the venerable Adelerius.

Humbled by this defeat, the Danes left Gaul in peace for some time.

6. But when Hugh was closing the final days of his life, and Prince Louis, after administering the kingdom for two years, died, his son Charles—later called the Simple—remained deprived of his father while still in the cradle.

The leading men of Francia judged his age unsuitable, as it was, for exercising rule, especially since reports were already announcing renewed movements among the Northmen. They therefore deliberated concerning the supreme government.

Two sons of Robert remained. The elder was called Odo; the other was Robert, who bore his father’s name.

Of these, the Franks, although Odo resisted, chose the elder to be guardian of the boy and governor of the kingdom. Kindhearted in disposition, he energetically defended the state against its enemies, cared for the child most carefully, and, when the young man came of age and reclaimed his own kingdom, patiently restored his rule to him.

The young king restored to him part of the kingdom, and Odo remained, as long as he lived, a terror to the enemies and always faithful to the king.

Robert, his brother, departed so far from this fraternal gentleness of spirit that, after Odo’s death, because the portion of the government which his brother Odo had held was not returned to him, he openly seized tyrannical power.

The northern peoples, judging that this would not harm them—for the inhabitants of the entire region, their zeal being directed in different ways, would not resist them with united purpose—decided to devote all their strength to plunder.

7. Since our present purpose is not to discuss the wars of kings or the disturbances of peoples, but rather to bring forth the miracles accomplished by God through Benedict, the most blessed fosterer of our unworthiness, we must proceed to explain those miracles.

We do not confess him to be the author of our unworthiness because he himself made us worthless, but because, when we were lowly and despised and of no account, he raised us by his intervention and assistance to the point where, after the Lord, we must attribute to him whatever we have been able to proclaim of his praises and whatever salvation or usefulness we recognize in ourselves.

8. Therefore, remembering the prophetic oracle which says that every evil comes from the north (Jeremiah 1:14), and as though it had been spoken especially concerning us, our minds are frequently compelled to recall the attacks of the aforementioned pagans. From their native land they have poured over our provinces, as we said above, like a swarm of bees—a swarm of plunderers.

In this final expedition, of which we are now speaking, they were led by a certain Rainaldus and attempted, as far as they could, to uproot the remains of our thorns.

Witnesses to this are not only, as the words of the aforementioned author Adrevaldus testify, the cities adjoining the banks of the Seine and Loire, by which Neustria is distinguished, and those along the Dordogne and Garonne, whose waters mark Aquitaine, but also the ruins of outstanding buildings.

Among these is the most distinguished palace of the prince Charles the Great at Cassinogil, once the glory and ornament of the cradle of his son, the aforementioned Louis the Pious. The God-hating people overturned it so completely that they made it uninhabitable, although it still clearly shows what it once was.

It is situated where the stream called the Codrot flows into the Garonne. A brick tower built on the bank of that stream allowed the approach of enemies to be observed and the entry of hostile ships to be prevented. It also enabled the royal fleet, built without interference from the enemy on the lesser stream, to be brought down to the waters of the greater river.

The site has a church joined to a larger church, built of brick with remarkable workmanship. In it, if I remember what I saw correctly, there is a very small sarcophagus in which the twin brother of Louis the Pious is believed to have been buried. [Note: His name was Lothair, as the ancient Frankish Annals relate. See also the *Life of Saint Abbo, Abbot of Fleury*, likewise written by Aimoin, where he mentions the matters related here: the palace of Cassinogil, Charles the Great, and the stream called Codrot or Aroth, commonly Drot, which, after passing by the river Dordogne, meets the Garonne.]

The book of his life also reports that Charles the Great crossed the Garonne there while bringing aid to the Christians of Spain, and that he returned by the same route.

But enough has been said about these matters; [Col. 0806B] let us now carry out our purpose.

## CHAPTER II  
### Rainaldus, king of the Northmen, stays at Fleury and is struck down by Saint Benedict; his corpse is thrown into the Seine; his image at Fleury
9. Accordingly, innumerable companies of Northmen, over whom Rainald had obtained kingship, using a great many long ships, ravaged everything as they sailed as far as the upper reaches of the Loire. At length Rainald, arriving with his men at the monastery of the thrice-blessed and God-beloved Benedict, which is called Floriacum, found it empty of inhabitants and stripped of all necessities, except only the buildings. For the monks, together with the body of our ever-to-be-named father Benedict, had withdrawn to safer places, while Lambert, then abbot, was piously caring for them. The aforesaid king therefore arrived there and, learning from captives what sort of people inhabited such a place, chose the monks’ dormitory as the site of his encampment. There, being a pagan, he committed various outrages. One night, as he lay resting, Saint Benedict appeared to him accompanied by two monks: one, as Rainald thought, possessed the strength of middle age; the other had the appearance of a boy. The most blessed Father, with snow-white hair upon his head and a staff in his hand, addressed the adversary as he lay there:

“Why,” he said, “have I offended you, Rainald, that you disturb me and mine from our own dwellings? But henceforth I shall take care both to restrain you from what you have begun and to restore the desired rest to Christ’s servants and to my bones as well.”

Having said this, he touched the already-awakening king’s head with the curved staff he carried and foretold that the end of his life was near; then he withdrew. Troubled by this vision, Rainald summoned his attendants with a loud cry to aid him. When they came running and asked what had happened to him, he said:

“A certain monk—none other, I think, than that old man Benedict, the guardian of this place—touched my head with his staff, threatening me with death, and inflicted immense pain upon me.”

He immediately ordered everyone to abandon the dwellings they had seized and return to their native land. He himself departed with them, but when he reached his homeland, weakened by repeated torments, he died. At his sudden death such a violent storm arose that it overthrew not only the roofs of houses but also the great masses of lofty trees. The captives’ bonds were broken, and the horses and other beasts of burden, led out to pasture more than twelve miles and even farther from the city of Rouen, burst their fetters and fled in different directions.

We have learned that the pyramid erected over his grave was overturned by a most powerful earthquake and that the earth cast his corpse out of its bosom. Since the ground could not contain it when covered, it was sewn into a sack with a mass of stones and sunk in the Seine. The memory of this wicked man would have been erased by such a death, had not the ancient inhabitants of Floriacum, curious about posterity, caused a marble likeness of his head to be made [Note: [Col. 0807D] In place of the marble one, there is now visible a likeness of his head, carved in stone as a mockery; the inhabitants say that it is the head of the king of the Northmen.]. It can now be seen inserted into the far end of the wall of the church of Holy Mary, Mother of God, and of her servant Benedict, toward the north, so that all present and future generations might recognize what severity of vengeance Almighty God exercised against His adversaries through the intercession of these same saints.

Finally, this vengeance so terrified the future insolence of the Northmen that, above all the other saints of Gaul, they revere our most blessed father Benedict [Note: [Col. 0807D] The same is attested by Dudo the dean, Quintinianus, and William, a monk of Jumièges, as stated above; yet I nowhere find that they mention this King Rainald.].

## CHAPTER III. Robert slain. Herbert, Charles’s betrayer. King Rudolf. An example of his justice.

[Col. 0807C]

10. Meanwhile Robert, wishing openly to exercise the power of the tyranny he had undertaken, extorted from certain bishops—partly by flattery and partly by threats—that he be crowned with the royal diadem and invested with the kingdom’s scepter. But the outcome of this presumption was by no means joyful for him. At last, having been confronted in battle on the fields of Soissons by Charles’s commanders and stripped of his life, although his army won the victory, he nevertheless paid the price of his wicked temerity.

Yet his associates in rebellion were not terrified by his death into abandoning their insolence and treachery. Rather, Count Herbert of Vermandois, by an unspeakable crime, captured his lord and king, Charles, king of all France, by deceit, bound him in chains, and sent him to Péronne [Col. 0807D] to be shut up in a dark prison. Since the kingdom was being conducted without a ruler and was therefore drifting into uncertainty—especially because the youthful age of Hugh, Robert’s son, who later earned the name “the Great” through his worthy deeds, prevented him from assuming the royal insignia—and because everyone hated Herbert, particularly those whom compassion for the prince’s misfortune moved, a certain Rudolf, born in Burgundy, was finally placed in charge of the Frankish realm.

How severe he was in restraining the plunderers of the holy Church of God will be made clear by this single example.

11. A landed estate situated in the regions of Burgundy, called Diacum [Note: [Col. 0808D] Diac, Die: a village in the diocese of Langres, in the district of Tonnerre, according to Rudolf Tortarius, below, in chapter 22, *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict*. The provost of Diacum was required, by order of Abbot Macarius, to pay ten solidi each year for the library, in the Floriacum Library, p. 410.], had once been given to Saint Benedict by the illustrious Hugh [Note: [Col. 0807D] Hugh, namely the son of Drogo, later archbishop of Rouen; read his *Acts* in the first part of the second century.], a man who lived in the time of the younger Dagobert, for the support of the brothers of Floriacum. A soldier of perverse mind seized it for his own use and refused to submit it to legal judgment when the abbot or the brothers demanded it. When the complaint was brought before the king, he ordered the usurper to cease this obstinate presumption. The man heard the king’s command but delayed granting obedience to the one who commanded him.

It was reported to the prince that he was not only retaining what he had seized but was also preparing for himself, in a nearby forest, a feast from the property of the monks and inhabitants. The king happened at that time to be residing in the dwellings of the city of Auxerre when news of this reached his ears. Mounting his horse with an unexpected escort of soldiers, he hurried as quickly as possible to the place, leaving orders in the city that companies of armed men should follow him as he departed.

The royal attendants, stirred by the report that the king was setting out, hastened after him in emulation. He feared that someone in the army, once he learned what had happened, might make the offender more cautious. When they reached the forest, the prince ordered it to be surrounded by armed men, threatening that anyone from whose assigned section the usurper of the Church’s property escaped would pay with his head.

He himself, searching the hidden parts of the forest with picked young men, found the man he was seeking, who intended to resist with weapons. King Rudolf himself pierced him with a lance and threw him dead to the ground, while forcing his attendants, who had escaped the imminent danger, to flee in different directions.

As we received this from the fathers, so we have reported it in plain faith. We hold it certain that thereafter our father Benedict, of venerable memory and singular intelligence, granted Rudolf his aid against his adversaries, especially when he was waging war against the army of the Northmen.

## CHAPTER IV. Succession of the abbots of Floriacum. The testing of the novice Drogo, his withdrawal into the desert, his temptation, and Saint Benedict’s visitation.

[Col. 0808D]

12. After Abbot Lambert had been relieved of the burden of the flesh, some time having passed, Odo, a man of outstanding holiness, came from the monastery of Saint Géraud, which is called Aurillac, and was placed over this sacred monastery [Note: [Col. 0808D] John the monk relates how Saint Odo succeeded Lambert in Book II of *On His Life*, chapter 11; this occurred under King Rudolf, about the year 930. Archembald succeeded Odo in 942. Ulfald, Archembald’s successor, is praised in the aforementioned passage of Odo’s *Life*.]. What the Lord deigned to accomplish in those days at the tomb of His holy confessor Benedict, or in other places under his name, remains unknown to us until now, having been consigned to oblivion partly by antiquity and partly by the negligence of writers. Nevertheless, in the discourse that his most eloquent speech composed in praise and honor of that same Father, Odo records that this legislator of monks shone in his own time through many signs of miracles.

13. When Odo departed and Archembald [Note: [Col. 0809D] This is Ercamboldus, who is said, according to Frodoard in Book IV, chapter 32 of his *History*, to have restored the monastic rule in the monastery of Saint Remigius at Reims.] assumed responsibility for this sacred flock, a certain Drogo came to conversion. He was involved in the world not merely in body but with his whole mind. Wishing to test with certainty whether his spirit, long devoted to worldly vanity, still belonged to God, the same abbot exceeded the usual path of probation.

For, when Drogo was about to set out for Rome, the abbot ordered him to drag by hand, without the assistance of any vehicle, an animal carrying the provisions necessary for the journey, while he himself wore out his feet along the road. Thus, he who was thought to have surpassed the others who renounced worldly vanities through the depravity of his conduct was also to surpass them through the outward display of a more abject humility. He used that insult as a kind of whetstone to sharpen his virtues; and after obtaining admission, he strove to surpass the others in holiness of life.

14. When the aforesaid abbot reached the limits of monastic governance and the venerable Wlfald succeeded him—he who later became bishop of the city of Chartres [Note: [Col. 0809D] In the eighth year of King Lothar, as is clear from a fragment published by Chesne in volume III of the *History of the Franks*, p. 343, corresponding to the year of Christ 962. There it is said that he fortified the monastery of Floriacum with a rampart and wall, and that Oswald, nephew of Odo, bishop of Canterbury, entered the monastic life at Floriacum. Nevertheless, the writer of that fragment must be corrected where he substitutes Wlfald for Abbot Richard, since Richard succeeded Wlfald, according to Aimoinus below, chapter 7.]—the aforementioned Drogo earnestly requested and with great difficulty obtained permission from him, after having been tested by long monastic observance, to undertake the solitary combat of the desert.

At the place called Balma [Note: [Col. 0810D] Is this Balma in the borders of Burgundy, where Abbot Berno founded a monastery through his followers, according to Book I of the *Life of Saint Odo*, abbot of Cluny, chapter 10?], he bravely took up the struggle against the snares of the ancient enemy. How many and what sorts of contests of temptation he endured is not for this work to unfold. Certainly, while he spent his whole life in the mortification of body and spirit, joining vigils to fasts and fasts to vigils in alternation, he began to suffer more severe attacks from the enemy of the human race.

15. One night, on the eve of one of the feasts of Benedict, the most excellent legislator of monks, the hermit rose early from his vigilant rest. Beneath the open sky he watched the movement of the stars, awaiting the proper hour at their rising, when he would offer hymns of praise to God, his holy protector Benedict.

But the devil, envious of every good, wishing by his customary cunning to turn his mind away from the good purpose he had begun, approached the roof of the poor hut in the form of a bronze oak, which seemed to be burning with flames that vomited fire. Then the soldier of Christ resorted to his familiar defenses, armed his forehead with the sign of the cross, and set himself wholly against the phantasmal fire. He evidently remembered, as may be inferred, the deeds of his lord and master Benedict, who, anticipated by the gift of divine grace, summoned his disciples to his eyes and declared that the burning flames were imaginary (Gregory, *Dialogues* II.10).

At this man’s steadfastness, the enemy’s deception was defeated and disappeared. Immediately there appeared a gracious consolation of heavenly visitation, and, surrounded by immense brightness, he saw that someone had arrived together with the radiance: a man adorned with an excellent appearance and clothed in a white robe. He opened his beautiful mouth with these words:

“Greetings,” he said, “first inhabitant of this vast solitude, who daily offer to Christ the acceptable libations of a contrite heart. The obstinacy of the treacherous tempter has indeed seemed intolerable, but after the winds and clouds, believe me, calm serenity will follow for you. Therefore, do not cease to continue steadfastly in your purpose and to celebrate the praises of your foster-father Benedict. It will henceforth be yours to decide what you wish to request; it will be his concern to grant what you ask. Henceforth he will be at hand, so that you will need to ask for nothing; rather, even before your invocation, he will arrange that it be present for you.”

That solitary man undoubtedly suspected that the author of this most delightful kindness was none other than the most blessed Father Benedict. He therefore strove, according to his ability and understanding, to repay him with acts of thanksgiving. Here one may discern how great and how powerful is the favor of this protector of ours toward those who devoutly keep watch at his most sacred tomb, since his consolation appears in this way even to those who live far away in a remote land and humbly devote themselves to his service [Note: [Col. 0810D] Bucelinus included Drogo, with the title “Blessed,” in his *Menologium* under 2 April. That Drogo was a devout man is clear from this passage; I would not call him blessed without an authority, nor assign him a day of death that is unknown.].

## CHAPTER V. King Louis, successor of Charles; his two sons. Arnustus suffers punishment from Saint Benedict.

16. After King Rudolf died—while he had restrained the incursions of the violent Danes by force of arms and had thus far caused Gaul to remain largely tranquil from their attack—affairs changed. For Charles, shut up in prison, was released by custody of his soul, not his body, leaving Louis, born of Ileadtgiva [Note: [Col. 0810D] His funerary stone can be seen in the crypt of the monastery of Saint Medard at Soissons, with an epitaph published in volume I of the *Analecta*.], the daughter of the king of the English.

Fearing that the storm of his father’s misfortune might engulf him, Louis withdrew to the Anglo-Saxons, invited by his maternal kinship. He judged that he would remain safer in lands across the sea than among his own people, if he were a lord in a chamber or a king at a banquet. After King Rudolf’s death, however, Hugh the Great recalled him, and he was outwardly restored to his ancestral kingdom.

His administration was difficult for one who wished to exercise the right of dominion: first because he was captured by Theobald, count of the people of Chartres, and later because, even after recovering the kingdom, he experienced the varied and unstable outcomes of fortune. He died leaving two sons, Lothar and Charles, whom Gerberga, sister of Otto, later emperor of the Romans, had borne him. Charles, the younger in age, grew old in private houses; Lothar succeeded to the whole inheritance and exercised royal power for thirty years and more without interruption.

[Col. 0811B] 17. In his days, many miracles were performed by that same excellent confessor, through God’s favor, both at the most sacred bones of our father Benedict and in other places where his venerable memory is held. With Christ’s help, we shall undertake to transmit them to the knowledge of posterity.

There was a certain Arnustus, a man distinguished by the rewards of secular military service, who possessed, by right of benefice, certain properties of the monastery that Abbot Archembald of this place had granted him. Forgetting the favors he had received, and also the faith that he had pledged by a sacred oath to Benedict and to the monks serving him as best they could, he continually exhausted an estate of the parish of Pauliacum (Pouilly in the Nivernais; see Adrevald, chapter 37) by quartering his men there [that is, by lodging them].

When the brothers ordered him to cease this presumption, and he scorned to obey, the brothers were compelled to begin imploring the mercy of the almighty Lord and the aid of their patron Benedict. While they earnestly prayed to the Lord and their adversary persisted in his wickedness, it happened that one day the aforesaid man ordered a meal to be prepared for himself at the estate in question. During the banquet, with its lavish table, he ordered pears to be brought for eating.

Holding one of them in his hand, after uttering many blasphemies against the monks of Floriacum, he made a lying oath, saying:

“I call this pear to witness,” he said, “that this year I shall inflict many hardships upon them.”

After saying this, he put part of the cut fruit into his mouth. Immediately it blocked the blasphemer’s throat so completely that, his voice cut off, he could utter no words. His attendants carried him as though lifeless to a bed and urged him, in repentance for the injustices he had inflicted upon those who served the most blessed Benedict, to ask forgiveness. But unable to speak, he leaned his head against the wall and breathed out his spirit. The Lord Christ did not permit the prayers of His humble servants to fall fruitlessly, prayers presented through His glorious mother Mary and His beloved Benedict.

## CHAPTER VI. The feast of Saint Remigius. The man who placed a sword upon Saint Benedict’s altar is punished.

[Col. 0812A]

18. We now undertake to set forth one notable deed of that man—of Father Benedict, I mean—which we have not happened to learn from any brother’s account or writings. A certain brother testified that he had learned it from faithful men of the holy Church of Reims and that it had occurred in the territory of that city.

The anniversary of the blessed confessor of Christ, Remigius, was being celebrated on earth according to custom: a festive day full of reverence, on which crowds usually gather at his venerable basilica. On that same day, when the hour was already late, Queen Gerberga came to the church surrounded by her retinue and found that the offices of evening praise had already begun with the choir of singers.

Ashamed of her lateness, she left the customary station and entered the crypts of the church, where the oratory of the precious Father Benedict is located. While the royal attendants were bowing their heads in prayer, one of them, in an act of insolent recklessness, placed the sword he was carrying upon the altar.
