His companions condemned the deed, removed the sword, and addressed words of reproach to the perpetrator of such foolishness. He answered them arrogantly:

“What new religion,” he said, “has come upon us, that you judge a heap of lime and sand, together with a mass of stones, to be made holier by my sword?”

And with these words he did not hesitate to place the sword he had taken up once more upon the Lord’s table. He did this a third time and could not be restrained by the arrogance of his defiance. But because he refused to be corrected by the gentle words of men, he experienced upon himself a sharper rebuke from divine severity.

When the queen departed from the sacred building, he too departed. Then, excessively confident and presumptuous about himself, he happily joined those dining and dined with them. During the food and drink, as a knife slipped across his groin, he was wounded. Then, carried away from the table in the hands of his attendants, he breathed out his wretched soul immediately, unrepentant and greatly to be mourned by his own people.

Thus God showed that He is displeased by the profanation of His altar, which is said to belong to Him under the names of His servants and which, because of the offering of Christ’s most sacred body, bears the form of a cross.

## CHAPTER VII. Herbert, invader of the estates of Floriacum, is struck by Saint Benedict’s staff.

[Col. 0812D]

19. A certain Herbert was known as the possessor of the castle of Soliacum (Suilly), which lies three miles from the village of Floriacum. His father was Herchenald, and he had a brother named Archembald, now archbishop of the Church of Tours [Note: [Col. 0811D] From this word “now,” the Bollandist associates correctly infer that Archembald survived into the year 1005.].

The venerable Abbot Richard, successor of Lord Wlfaldus [Note: [Col. 0812D] Abbot Richard assumed the administration in 962, when Wlfaldus was raised to the see of Chartres, as stated above.], had granted Herbert certain estates belonging to ecclesiastical jurisdiction as a benefice. Not content with these, he wickedly and audaciously plundered the remaining properties assigned to the monks’ needs.

Then the father of the monastery and the whole community sent messengers to him, asking him to remember the faith he had promised them by oath and to cease invading their property. When he disregarded their admonitions, they went to King Lothar and to Duke Hugh to lament before them the grievous distress of their complaint.

When they made little progress with them, they approached the man of treacherous mind themselves and begged him to have mercy on them by ceasing his oppression. But when he turned a deaf ear, they returned to their familiar defenses. For nearly the entire Lenten season of that year, during the solemn litanies, they poured out their prayers to the Lord concerning their tribulation and struck two bronze bells, so that those who heard their sound might be invited to undertake a similar work.

[Col. 0813B] Meanwhile, the aforementioned Herbert persisted in the obstinacy of his wickedness, daily adding worse deeds to the worst. One night he had decided to go with certain attendants into the district of Wastina. For, as Truth says, “he who walks in the night stumbles, because the light is not in him” (John 11:10). Lacking the light of virtues and surrounded by the darkness of vices, every wicked person also tries, in the darkness of worldly night, to conceal himself and his actions. Yet although he avoids human eyes as far as he can, he cannot in any way escape the eyes of the Lord, which are upon the ways of men and observe all their steps. For, as blessed Job testifies, with the Lord there are no darknesses or shadows of death in which those who practice iniquity may hide (Job 34:22).

Thus the light was taken from this wicked Herbert, and he himself was suddenly taken away, because he had been long awaited. As he rode on horseback with his men, making his way beneath the darkness of night, he suddenly saw someone standing beside him, bearing the marks of monastic habit. His clothing, as he later reported to his men, shone with heavenly brightness.

He was struck between the shoulders by a staff that the figure seemed to hold in his hands, and he uttered a terrible cry. Then the vision vanished from his eyes. Those riding around him, overcome by the horror of his cry, anxiously asked what had happened to him. He replied:

“Saint Benedict, who is now standing beside me, has afflicted me with a powerful blow. I am suffering terribly from the resulting pain. But you, my most faithful comrades, take the road back and carry me home. From there, hasten to the glorious tomb of the confessor and ask forgiveness for me.”

They obeyed his commands and brought him back, supporting him on either side, to the place from which he had departed. While still in the hands of his servants, almost at the threshold of the doorway, he gave up his spirit.

The devout faithful brothers of the monastery of Father Benedict came to them and informed them of what had happened, asking that they receive at least the lifeless body for burial. Although they feared the displeasure of their abbot, who happened then to be absent, they granted their assent and covered the body with earth.

Although they rejoiced in the peace thus obtained for themselves, they nevertheless pitied the dead man with pious compassion, since, deprived of the gift of this life in the first flower of his youth, he had not been able to correct the depravity of his conduct.

## CHAPTER VIII. Romaldus likewise struck down by death.

20. Romaldus was a citizen of Chartres. His forest, situated beyond the Loire in Sologne, is known to have bordered the forest that devout men assigned to the aforementioned church. He was one of those about whom Scripture says: “For they have moved the boundaries; they have seized the flocks” (Job 24:2). He was trying to divide equally between himself and the monks the herd of pigs gathered for pasture both in Saint Benedict’s forest and in his own.

Because the monks’ woodland was larger than his, this seemed a serious matter to the brothers. Therefore, by common counsel, they sent certain members of their community to Arnulf, then bishop of Orléans, whose authority this man obeyed because of the benefice he had received, so that Arnulf might recall him to the bounds of justice.

But, stuffed with the spirit of obstinacy, he answered the bishop’s exhortation to keep to the path of justice with arrogance. He said that he would give his answer to those who questioned him on the day when the pigs were to be driven from the forest. He thought, poor man, that he would deprive the servants of God of what they demanded, forgetting the rich man of the Gospel, whose barns he enlarged and to whom the Lord said: “Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20).

Indeed, before the aforementioned Romaldus had moved his foot from the place where he had told the envoys that he would respond, he was seized by a violent fever. He languished until, on the very day when he had hoped to have the herd of swine taken away from Christ’s poor, he was condemned to death and carried away for burial.

Meanwhile, the brothers sent by the others according to their agreement went to the forest and awaited his arrival. When they learned that he had died, they returned home with the portion owed to them, blessing the Lord, as well as Mary, the holy mother of Christ, and praising Benedict, the servant of God.

## CHAPTER IX. The fire at Floriacum; another fire.

21. In the time of the abbot Richard, whose name must often be spoken with reverence, a decree proceeded from the severity of the heavenly King, the emperor, because of the enormity of sins: this venerable place, namely Floriacum, was to be purified by devouring flames. It is pleasing to recall briefly what prodigies occurred—things to be despised by the faithless but to be marveled at by us and by all who think soundly.

The first and most astonishing thing was that, when a chance fire consumed the basilica of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, the treasure dedicated to the most holy Mother of God and perpetual Virgin Mary, which all who fear the Lord ought to love greatly—the body, namely, of the most holy Father Benedict—remained unharmed.

Not only that building, which stood sixty and scarcely more paces away, but all the buildings constructed within the very narrow circuit of the fortress also remained untouched by the flames, except for a single granary attached to the wall of the burning church. A heap of grain, which in common speech we call a *metam* (in French, *méteil*), likewise escaped the greedy flames. It stood only a bridge scarcely nine paces long away from the oratory.

This calamity ought to have moved the hearts of mortals. But alas! The human mind, too ignorant of the future, does not consider the adversities that threaten it, does not fear them, and falls into worse things.

22. For not many years later, through the industry of the excellent Abbot Richard, a cast-bronze vessel was being prepared for summoning the faithful to the oratory. The workers on this project, exhausted by their labor, had surrendered their limbs to sleep on the night preceding the octave of Saint Lawrence. They had forgotten to extinguish a burning candle attached to the doors and left it there.

When it fell, it set fire to the straw with which the beds were constructed. The house became filled with flames and, burning more fiercely, spread the fire to the adjoining hall of Saint Mary, Mother of Christ, and of the most beloved lord Benedict.

Suddenly the brothers raised a cry and lamented, fearing that, once everything was caught up in the flames, they would lose the ability to carry out the sacred body of Father Benedict. They did have hope that the excellent Father could keep his own limbs undefiled, but the human mind, shaken by the wind of its own frailty, was driven into uncertainty.

At last, with the hands of the grieving and sorrowful, that miraculous pearl was carried out and borne around with the cloth [Note: [Col. 0815D] They call it a *corporale*, which at that time was customarily carried against fires. Read Book II, chapter 30 of the *Customs of Cluny*; Book V, chapter 1 of Rudolf Glaber’s *History*, where it is called a *chrismale*; and Abbot Rupert’s account of the fire at Deutz.], upon which the most sacred body of Jesus Christ had been prepared the day before.

Then suddenly, when the north wind—which had been driving the flames toward the brothers’ granaries—ceased to blow, the whole mass of fire, forming itself into a sphere, extended its peak toward the sky. There a miracle equal to the former appeared: the church of Saint Benedict, which had previously been burned and restored, remained standing, together with its hospice and kitchen, and also its bakery, as though the Lord were saying to His servants not in words but in deeds:

“Although I seem angry with you because of the iniquities you have committed, nevertheless, appeased by the prayers of my faithful servants whom I have appointed guardians of this place, I leave you some dwellings in which to live.”

## CHAPTER X. The unburned table. Restoration of the monastery. The fire of the year 974.

[Col. 0815D]

23. The Lord also displayed another sign, previously unknown through the ages, which there is no doubt was obtained through the merits of the glorious Virgin Mary and the most holy confessor of Christ, Benedict, for the consolation of the grieving monks.

There was a small three-legged table prepared for the use of travelers who might happen to arrive and require refreshment. It had been raised beneath the tower from which the bells hung when it was surrounded by falling, charred beams. Then God renewed the ancient miracles: as under Moses He preserved the bush unburned amid the flames, so the wooden table felt no fiery heat.

The tripod therefore seemed to burn without burning, and the material touching the heat did not supply it with fuel, so that it became plainly evident that the one who acknowledges that whatever is given to the needy and beggars is given to him (Matthew 25) had once reclined at this very table.

A great crowd gathered to witness the spectacle. Those who were granted the sight saw what seemed to be a whirlwind rising from the aforementioned table and scattering a heap of coals here and there. Faces that had shortly before been sorrowful because of the impending calamity of so many people were suddenly changed by the joy of this marvel.

When everything else had been consumed, the table remained unburned. The spirits of the good were not broken by these hardships. Indeed, through the care of the venerable worshiper of God, Abbot Richard, within the space of three years this sacred monastery, so pleasing to those devoted to the monastic life, was prepared in the condition in which it is now seen.

The year of the burning was the year said to be 974 from the Incarnation of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0815D] The anonymous chronicler in volume III of Chesne, p. 355, agrees.].

## CHAPTER XI. The architect unharmed by a fall. A woman freed from a demon.

24. Around the time when its restoration was being completed with the greatest zeal, a certain architect named Dominic, who is still alive, was laboring to roof the brothers’ refectory. As he stood at the highest point of the roofing and leaned farther than necessary toward someone offering him a cup, his foot slipped and he fell to the ground among the immense mass of beams.

The brothers ran together, thinking that he had been killed by the blows of the timbers and the hardness of the ground. They found him not only alive but also completely sound in every limb. There is no doubt that this was obtained through the merits of the holy man Benedict, so that a man devoted to his service would suffer no loss of life or limb.

25. At that same time, while labor was still being diligently devoted to the restoration, and while the most sacred bones of his father Benedict were being preserved with devoted filial love in the church of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 0815D] This oratory still survives for the most part within the monastery cloister, separate from the principal church, which is dedicated to the blessed Mary, although the high altar was also consecrated in honor of Saint Peter, as I infer both from the letters of Count Eckard cited above and from a certain small wooden chest. When that altar was recently restored on a grander scale, the chest was found at its base; it contained these words inscribed on a sheet of brass: “Mummolus ordered this to be made in love of Saint Mary and Saint Peter.” He was the second abbot of the place, whose eulogy is reported in the Second Century.], it is said that our protector displayed the following event at the earlier place of his burial.

A woman possessed by a demon was brought to the monastery and admitted into the inner crypt so that she might be healed there. After some delay spent in the frenzy of her possession, she was brought out and stood before the altar of Saint Mary, Mother of God. From her mouth, as it was reported to us, three demons fell in the form of beetles, with green bile, into a bronze basin; striking the bronze, they made a sound. Thus the woman was cleansed through the intercession of the glorious Mother of the Lord and her renowned confessor Benedict.

## CHAPTER XII. A cripple made upright. Twelve poor people maintained at Floriacum.

26. There was a certain man, a native of the Wastinensis district, who had been deprived from his mother’s womb of the use of his feet. He traveled with the aid of little stools, sweeping the ground before him. Having heard of the fame of our thrice-blessed Father Benedict, he approached his venerable shrine. He was received into the house assigned to the support of the poor, and asked to be sustained by the brothers’ charity until, through the intervention of his holy confessor, the Lord should grant him the effect of the healing he desired.

Abbot Richard consented to his request and ordered that he be counted among twelve needy men whom the careful and charitable concern of the good ancient Fathers had decreed should be fed and clothed daily from common resources in this monastery of ours at Fleury, on account of the number twelve, corresponding to the Apostles. Striking the ears of the most merciful Creator with daily sighs, he asked for the gift of the health he desired. And because, according to the saying of Truth, “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:12), by asking to receive, seeking to find, and knocking so that an entrance to mercy might be opened for him (Luke 11:40), he deserved to obtain it.

At last, first through the intercession of Christ’s gracious Mother Mary, in whose court he kept vigil, and then through that of Benedict, the most eminent lawgiver of monks, whom he had chosen as mediator of his prayers between himself and the Lord, his withered sinews began to be moistened and his contracted legs to relax. When the sick man perceived this, he too, eager for health, attempted to tread the road in an unfamiliar manner. Gradually raising himself, and in the course of time acquiring the firmest strength for walking, by the merits of the outstanding confessor he resolved to recover the natural property of the earth—his ability to stand and walk.

After requesting permission to depart, and giving such thanks as he could to God his liberator and to Saint Benedict, he returned to his own home with the brothers whom he had summoned for this very purpose. Thereafter he devoted himself to agriculture.

## CHAPTER XIII. Three Lamps in the Church of Blessed Mary. A Candle Kindled from Heaven.

27. In the time of the often-mentioned Abbot Richard, a certain monk named Benedict, surnamed Niger, had been entrusted by that abbot, together with several others from the community of brothers, with the care of the sacred building dedicated to God under the name of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God. It preserves within itself, to everyone’s wonder, the pearl of the heavenly treasure—by which I mean the most holy body of our Father Benedict.

One day, while the diligent watchfulness of his turn of duty required him to exercise especially attentive care, it happened that the lamp lit before the altar of the perpetual Virgin Mary in her honor went out. The custom established by the ancient Fathers and habitually observed was that the church mentioned above should be illuminated both by day and by night with the light of three lamps. The brother therefore carried the extinguished lamp to another, which was accustomed to shine before the tomb of the blessed confessor, so that he might light it, but found that this one too had failed. When he inspected the third, which ordinarily illuminated the chapels of the crypt, he found that it also was dead.

Disturbed in spirit, he hurried out to restore light to the basilica. On returning, he saw that one of the larger candles, which are customarily placed beside the altar of the Queen of Virgins and lit only on feast days, had been kindled by divine power and was glowing with flashing flames. Greatly astonished at this, he gave thanks to God, understanding that the extinguishing of the lamps had occurred not by chance but by divine providence, to show mortals that heavenly visitation was by no means absent from this most sacred place.

## CHAPTER XIV. A Contemner of the Saint Is Punished.

28. Once, while traveling, a certain knight came to a village belonging to the jurisdiction of the monastery of Saint Benedict, called Vitriarias. Entering the house of a widow, he found a measure of oats. Wishing to take them for his horses’ fodder, he was prevented by the woman, who said:

“If you hold me in contempt by taking away the poverty of my widowhood, at least revere the most holy Benedict, whose jurisdiction is this countryside in which I dwell.”

The knight replied: “For Saint Benedict’s sake I leave as much as I leave for you.” He then called his squire and handed over the oats, which he himself had poured into the poor woman’s sack, to be carried at the horse’s neck; and so he departed.

He had not traveled far when, suddenly, although no spur was urging it, the horse, inclined toward a run, fell headlong. The charger died with its throat torn open, while the knight, disabled by a broken leg, languished for a long time. By his own punishment he learned, and gave others an example, that the saints ought not to be despised and that the tears of widows ought not to be held in contempt. As Solomon says, they fall from the eyes to the cheeks, from the cheeks to the ground, and the Lord is their protector (Ecclus. 35:19).

## CHAPTER XV. Many Predators Routed by a Few. Saint Benedict’s Banner.

29. Caput-cervium (Sacerge) is an estate of Saint Benedict. With God’s favor, we shall relate more fully below how it came into the possession of this monastery of Fleury, or how the monks’ settlement was transferred from there to the fortress of Salense (Book II, Chapter 5; see Adrevald, Chapter 38).

[Note: On the site of the fortress of Salense, commonly Saint-Benoist du Sault, see below, Book II, Chapter 6, no. 15.]

A little earlier, the venerable monk Benedict mentioned above (no. 27) had been placed in charge of administering this estate. At that time about one hundred and forty armed men from the fortresses, which are extremely numerous throughout that region, had spread into the fields of Argentomagus, which lie near that place, in order to carry off plunder.

[Note: Argentomagus—Argenton, and by others Argentomum—was formerly a fortress which Waifer, duke of Aquitaine, is said to have destroyed and Pippin, king of the Franks, to have restored; it is now a town in the district of Bourges on the river Creuse, below the confluence of the lesser Creuse with the greater, La Creuse.] For this reason they had also driven away the herds and flocks from the villages belonging to the aforesaid estate.

When news of the Argentomagans’ losses reached them, the men of the fortress immediately rushed out through the gates to fight the raiders. But when they gathered together and saw that they were inferior in number to the enemy, they were afraid to engage them. Then one of them, divinely inspired, said to his companions:

“Now, most faithful comrades, let us allow the adversaries to enter and plunder the land of Saint Benedict. Since our lord Giraldus is his advocate, let us defend it in his place and attack the enemy bravely and confidently. First, however, let a messenger be sent to bring swiftly from the monastery of Salense, which belongs to Saint Benedict, the banner of that precious confessor, so that it may serve as our protection.”

All agreed and followed his counsel. After receiving the banner, forty young men alone, invoking Saint Benedict with all their strength, suddenly fell upon the raiders, who were fearing nothing of the kind. Almighty God had so terrified the hearts of the adversaries through the merits of his beloved Benedict that they dared in no way to resist. Thus one hundred and forty enemies were routed or captured by only forty young men, with no bloodshed or scarcely any.

The victors, having gained possession of all the booty and captured the more distinguished men in the enemy force, came to the monastery of Salense. They asked the aforementioned provost Benedict to accept freely whatever property belonging to their own poor might be recognized among the spoils. He gladly accepted it, restored their plunder to his own people, and allowed the rejoicing warriors to return home.

Two other miracles, not greatly different from this one, follow, performed by the Lord through the supreme confessor Benedict in the same places. One of them occurred during the tenure of this same provost; we shall connect it with this account, while relating the other, entirely similar to it, more suitably in its own place.

## CHAPTER XVI. Another Incident. The Argentomagans Strengthened by Blessings of Bread and Wine.

[Col. 0819D]

30. While Lothair still ruled the kingdom of the Franks, the leading men of the kingdom of Aquitaine happened to be disturbed by a serious rebellion. Giraldus, viscount of the city of Limoges, and Boso, who possessed the march of that region, were striving against one another with concentrated hatred.

Therefore Elias, Boso’s son, persuaded his lord William, count of Poitiers, by gifts and entreaties to join him in besieging Giraldus’s fortress, called Brucia (see Book II, Chapter 6). As a result, not only the villages subject to Giraldus but also the possessions of the monastery of Salense were grievously devastated.

A messenger came to Giraldus, who was then residing in the city of Limoges, and told him that not only his territory but also the fields of Saint Benedict—because they had been entrusted to his protection—were being ravaged by the enemy. He judged that there should be no delay in such circumstances. Especially confident that Father Benedict would assist him because of the devastation of his possessions, he sent his son Guido with a chosen troop of cavalry, ordering him to restrain the enemy from plundering and, after joining forces with the Argentomagans, to deter them from the siege by force of arms if this could safely be done.

The Argentomagans, remembering through whom, after the Lord, they had been victorious in the earlier battle, came to the monastery of Saint Benedict, already mentioned, to pray. They asked the brothers to give them blessings of bread and wine, declaring that they had such faith that they believed without hesitation that, through this food and the merits of the glorious Confessor Benedict, they would be victorious in battle and immune from the danger of death. Nor was their hope disappointed.

When the battle was joined, they inflicted such slaughter upon their adversaries that, after the victory, the monks—wishing, out of human compassion, to bury even their enemies—could scarcely bury them. Nevertheless, they ordered plows to turn the earth here and there in the manner of plowmen and buried the corpses, as best they could, beneath the clods.

No Argentomagan who had been fed with the bread and wine of Saint Benedict for the aid of his safety suffered any danger of death. All returned home victorious and in full number, praising the Lord and exalting his confessor Benedict with the highest praises. They openly declared that through his merits they had been delivered from danger and that their enemies had been put to flight.

## CHAPTER XVII. A Beam Moved from Its Place.

31. Amalbert succeeded Abbot Richard.

[Note: I am uncertain in what year this occurred. In the Chartary of Patricia I find two charters addressed to Abbot Richard, namely the twenty-fifth and the twenty-eighth. The former was issued in the tenth year and the latter in the fifteenth year of King Lothair, and therefore in the year of Christ 969. See document 9 of that Chartary, and Book 12 of *The Miracles of Saint Maximinus, Abbot of Micy*, where Richard is said to have attended the funeral of Abbot Anno, and Amalricus, dean of Fleury, is recorded as having succeeded Anno after the monk Hermenaldus had been rejected.]

By nature kind, he proved still kinder through the gentleness of humility implanted in him. He had received the government of our monastery from Lothair, son of Louis, who had formerly been captured by Count Tethbald, with the consent of the brothers.

In his days, at an estate of the monastery of Fleury called Hervini-curtis (see Tortarius, Chapter 6), the following event occurred by divine action. Gauzlinus, the monk then placed in charge of the estate, had hired workers and ordered wooden steps to be made at the entrance of the basilica dedicated to God in that village under the name of the outstanding confessor of Christ, Benedict.

A carpenter, applying himself to this task, was preparing to remove with his axe whatever was superfluous from a tree felled in a nearby forest. When he tried to turn it to the other side and could not, he said: “Come, Saint Benedict: since I cannot, you turn it.” He spoke these words neither with the desire of one praying nor with the devotion of one asking, but rather, so to speak, in a spirit of disbelief.

He went to the neighboring houses of the forest to summon assistance. When he returned with them, he found that the timber—which the hands of scarcely six men could have moved—had been turned by divine power toward the side he wanted.

What do you think this outstanding Father of ours can bestow upon those who invoke him with their whole mind and with purity of heart, if he granted so much to one who addressed him with what I might call a certain frivolity of spirit? Nor should we, to whom God has granted, although unworthy, such a great Father in the present life, despair entirely if we implore his help with a pure and simple prayer. He does not disdain the most humble sighs of strangers, and he very often hears servants who are far away.

Finally, I would like briefly to explain what Benedict, ever worthy of being named, bestowed upon a certain monk of his flock named Anno (below, Book II, Chapter 6), who even now survives, although he was at some distance from this place—a consolation for sorrowful hearts.

## CHAPTER XVIII. A Little Boat Supplied from Heaven.

32. After the death of the shepherd Amalbert, from whom in tender youth I received the habit of the monastic life—and would that I had received it with a corresponding purpose of mind!—Oilboldus, by the election of the brothers and through the royal appointment of Prince Lothair, rose to the leadership of the brothers of Fleury.

[Note: It is not clear to me in what year Oilboldus became abbot. He died in 988 or the following year; see below.]

With pious care he provided for both the spiritual and temporal needs of his subjects. As the solemn feast of the celebrated passing of Father Benedict approached, he thought it appropriate to send one of his men to regions rich in an abundant supply of fish. He therefore sent the aforementioned brother, along with enough money for the undertaking, and urged him to devote himself diligently to the work entrusted to him.

Obeying the command, the brother sought out the produce of the rivers with careful attention, bought what he had found, and, after purchasing it, anxiously pressed on to carry it back to the Father by whom he had been sent. But the Aquitanian rivers, swollen by the abundance of rainfall, delayed his hasty journey.

Among them was the Andria, a rather unimpressive little stream in appearance, but difficult to cross because its channel was repeatedly divided into many branches and marshes intervened in several places. When the brother reached what one might call its mother-stream, he found the ford flooded with water and therefore impassable for horses. He also found two little boats: one half-submerged in the middle of the river, the other held fast by a rope on the farther bank.

He looked all around but was unable to find the help of any boatman or assistance from any passer-by. Thus, while he was in a state of anxiety and understood that his journey was obstructed and the feast day approaching, he gathered his courage, drew boldness from desperation, and devoted himself entirely to prayer.

“May your helping right hand now assist me, Lord God, your unworthy servant. If our holy Father Benedict has ever done anything pleasing to your majesty, or if any of his little servants serving you in the presence of his sacred body has done so, show it now. May it please you to exercise, in whatever manner pleases you, the same power that you once exercised through the merits of your beloved servant, when you granted his disciple permission to tread the waters with dry feet.

“I did not approach to ask these things presuming upon my own merits. Rather, because I trust that the outstanding confessor Benedict can obtain greater things from you, I too, relying on his patronage because of my weakness before your mercy, have dared to presume upon things greater than my strength.”

Moved by this prayer, by the gentle simplicity with which the monk was endowed, and above all by the preceding merits of the most blessed Benedict, the Lord granted him the swift assistance of his grace.

For the boat which, as we said, was situated on the opposite bank was divinely released and crossed the river without any mortal helmsman to the side where the monk and his companions were staying. It was an immense prodigy to behold: a boat that at another time, when its helmsman resisted unwillingly and in vain, had followed errant courses upon the current, now seemed to keep without hindrance to a line shown to it from heaven, passing from bank to bank until it came alongside the monk’s servants and was drawn to them with spears. Using their spears as oars, they transported all the loads, entrusting the horses to their ability to swim.

The aforementioned monk returned to the Father—or rather to the brothers, who were preparing to begin the solemn office of the already-arrived feast day—and filled them with great joy. They rejoiced not so much in the arrival of the provisions as in devout exultation at the power of the signs through which their most holy lord Benedict shone throughout the world.

## CHAPTER XIX. Bishop Arnulfus Seizes the Vineyards; Relics Are Carried There; A Sick Man Is Healed; A Little Shrine Is Built.

33. The grace of that holy man Benedict is also generous toward the sick. I shall therefore relate one miracle which the aforementioned Abbot Oilboldus rejoiced had occurred in his time.

Arnulfus, bishop of Orléans,

[Note: I think there were two bishops of this name, with Manasses between them. One was the nephew and successor of Ermentheus, who greatly loved the monks of Fleury and Micy, as is clear from Book 12 of *The Miracles of Saint Maximinus, Abbot of Micy*, in Volume I. The other came after Manasses. It is of the latter that the present account speaks, as also in the *Life of Saint Abbo, Abbot*.]

otherwise a good man, and one who observed ecclesiastical rules most excellently in knowledge and practice, never wholly loved the prelates of this place of Fleury. The principal reason was that, although they were subject to royal authority, they did not depend upon his nod and will in the submission which he desired beyond measure.

For this reason he gave permission for his satellites to invade the vineyards of Saint Benedict situated in the suburb of the city of Orléans, in a place called Boaria (the enclosure of Bourie). When the aforementioned abbot sent messengers to him to recover them but obtained nothing, he consulted the elders and decided that, taking the relics of the saints, he would hurry to the place with several of the brothers as the vintage approached and gather their produce. Since it was difficult for him to resist that man by force of arms—although he is known to have frequently resisted many kings endowed with secular power—he resolved at least to meet him by this strategy. The bishop, who in matters belonging to Jesus Christ surpassed almost all the bishops of Gaul living in his time in wisdom, could not oppose this without regard for divine judgment.

[Note: This concerns spiritual subjection, which abbots promised to the bishop when they were blessed; that matter will be discussed elsewhere. Here the question seems to concern temporal subjection.]

The bodies of the two martyrs Maurus and Frongentius having been lifted up under the name of the renowned confessor of God, Benedict, they proceeded to the place.

[Note: A certain bishop from Brittany, named Hedrem, who assumed the monastic habit at Fleury, brought with him the body of the blessed martyr Maurus, who is known to have suffered at Rome under the prefect Celerinus, during the reigns of the emperors Carinus and Numerian. Another man, Otto by name, likewise came to that monastery and offered Saint Benedict the body of a certain holy Frotgentius, as is read in the previously cited Chesnian fragment. The Life of the martyr Maurus was written in verse by Rodulfus of Tortarius, as was the account of his translation, and both are held in the library of Fleury. The catalogue of the Petavian Library attributes a metrical Life of the same martyr to the monk Framberto; is it different from Tortarius’s poem?]

[Note: The diploma of Charles the Bald is apparently to be understood of this Saint Frongentius or Frotgentius: at the request of Erispoë, duke of Brittany, it grants to Hilbold, abbot of Deas, a cell in the district of Le Mans, at Bussogilum, founded in honour of Blessed Peter by Saint Trogetius—probably to be read Frogetius. See Chifflet, proofs to the *History of Tournus*, p. 206.] As they traveled, neighbors and those who lived in houses close to the road asked whose such celebrated procession of passers-by might be. They were told: “Saint Benedict’s.”

Among them was a certain sick man, worn down by the heat of fever and by a long wasting of his strength. He asked those passing by in whose service such a crowd was making its way along the road with so many crosses. He was told that Saint Benedict, beloved of the Lord, was traveling that road to the suburbs of Orléans in defense of his vineyards.

When he heard this, he conceived hope of obtaining health. Supporting his weak limbs with a staff, he followed the blessed relics. Then, prostrate beneath the silver shrine in which they were enclosed, he fell asleep.

After one night had passed, he rose early in the morning and felt himself restored to his former health. Giving thanks to God, he extolled Saint Benedict with whatever praises he could proclaim, calling him the provider of his recovery. His opinion did not depart far from the truth. It is established that through Benedict’s aid and prayers he was restored to his own strength, since he had hastened to that place trusting in the saint’s merits or summoned by his fame. Nevertheless, we do not exclude the witnesses of truth mentioned above from participation in this miracle; indeed, we judge them equal in every respect both in merit and in action.

The brothers and the aforementioned abbot, having completed without hindrance from any petitioner the business for which they had gone, returned home rejoicing in a double joy. The poor man in spirit who had been healed, however, built a little hut of wooden boards at the place where he had lain, with the limbs of the saints placed above his head. Those who rest beneath it while suffering from a similar illness—provided that their full faith has demanded this—receive very swift assistance from the three saints mentioned above, as the inhabitants of those places testify.

# BOOK TWO

## CHAPTER ONE. Fleury, the Golden Valley. The Author Relates What He Knows. The Kings of the Franks. Abbo, Successor of Oilboldus.

1. By a favorable omen of heavenly graciousness, this monastery in which, by God’s authority, we serve him received the name Fleury; in ancient times it was called, by a privilege of grace not unlike this, the Golden Valley.

For it contains within itself the golden flower of paradise, the most holy Father Benedict, who by the most delightful fragrance of his virtues invites even those who are farthest away to reverence him. If we wished to explain the character of his works one by one, we would understand for certain that our parchment and our speech would run out before the subject of our speech did.

But lest we seem ungrateful for the benefits of his loving fatherhood, bestowed upon us unworthy people by him, we shall undertake to commit to the memory of posterity those matters that have come to our knowledge, insofar as the merciful intercession of that kind patron has obtained from Christ the strength for our feeble little intellect—even though in rustic speech. First, let us briefly touch upon how the commonwealth of the Franks endured in these times, so that afterward we may pursue more freely what we have proposed.

[Note: This place was known by this name even before the monastery was founded, as is clear from the testament of Abbot Leodebodus. John a Bosco testifies that he had read the inscription on the arch of the chapel of Blessed Mary at Fleury: “THIS IS THE GOLDEN VALLEY.” After the foundation of the monastery, the place was sometimes called Old Fleury; where the town now stands, the monastery was called Fleury. The monastery of Paredo, discussed below in Tortarius’s book, was likewise called the Golden Valley at its beginning.]

2. When King Lothair exchanged, as we believe, an earthly kingdom for a heavenly one, his son Louis succeeded him. Overtaken by premature death, and being without a legitimate marriage, he left the leadership of the Frankish people without an heir of his own.

His uncle Charles, whom we mentioned earlier as having grown old in retirement, tried, if he could, to claim for himself the imperial power long possessed by the founders of his lineage; but his intention achieved no result. For the leading Franks, abandoning him, turned to Hugh, who at that time was vigorously governing the duchy of France—the son of that great Hugh already mentioned—and raised him to the royal throne at Noyon.

In that same year he chose his son Robert as his associate in the kingdom. Since, insofar as concerns the cause we have begun to treat, we have spoken of the kings, we must now proceed with it.

3. When Abbot Oilboldus had come to rest in Christ, Abbo, a man beloved by God and human beings, was elected by the brothers with the assent of King Hugh and succeeded to the office of monastic government.

In the year preceding the year in which I write this—namely, the year 1004 from the Lord’s Incarnation—he was innocently killed in the regions of Gascony by the treacherous men of that nation. Crowned with the blood of martyrdom, he was called by Christ to the eternal kingdoms.

During his days, since we had already reached the limits of mature age and had been present for some of these events, we set down in a more reliable style the wonderful things performed by the almighty Lord through our most eminent Father Benedict.

[Note: In 988 Abbo succeeded Oilboldus. He governed the monastery of Fleury for sixteen years and died in 1004, according to Aimoinus in his *Life*.]

## CHAPTER II. The Fire at Fleury. Preparations for the Feast of the Translation. The Fire Extinguished by Divine Power.

4. In the summer months the festive day of the annual translation of that glorious Father returned in its appointed season. To behold its joys, there flowed together not only the country people—as a certain wise man says in his praise of him (Saint Odo, *Sermon on the Translation of Saint Benedict*)—but also the urban populace, adorned with the honorable persons of the clergy.

While they were devoted to the vigils of nightly praise, and the devout company of monks, arriving from every direction in repeated groups because of the joy of so great a solemnity, was joining with us in celebrating the service of its lawgiver, suddenly the light of a destructive fire shone horribly through the northern windows of the basilica.

For a fire, accidentally falling upon a certain hayloft and fed by dry fuel, spread itself through the surrounding buildings. The flame had no difficulty increasing its strength, since the heat of summer had already scorched the roofs and the houses, joined closely to one another, readily offered one another an opportunity for burning.

Meanwhile, abandoning the morning hymns, everyone rushed out from the sacred shrines, each intent with all his mind on protecting his own property. A few of the elders, together with us, who were still in the years of boyhood, completed the morning praises as the situation required, though with a less fitting conclusion. Then willing hands turned to removing whatever was necessary from the flames.

The hall of the holy Mother of God Mary was adorned within and entirely surrounded with silk coverings and curtains of such varied beauty that many of those who had gathered for the feast admitted that they had never before seen that basilica decorated so splendidly.

Adding to this beautiful ornament was what might be called a starry expanse of lamps and candles, as well as a bier shining with gold and gems at its front. It contained a treasure more precious than Arabian metal and the topaz stone.

This was the first thing carried out, together with the relics of the other saints, upon the grieving shoulders of their servants, and placed in the cemetery of the brothers on the eastern side of the church.

Then everyone turned his face toward removing the adornment of the sanctuary, which the diligent care of the sacristans had elegantly arranged over a period of eight days. We removed it in the space of three or, at most, four hours of the night.

It was possible to see and lament that royal hall of the Mother of the Lord—bearing in its night praises the marks of the road by which Benedict, once beloved of the Lord, had ascended to heaven—made after a short while to resemble a deserted building.

[Note: That is, the principal basilica, which was dedicated to Blessed Mary the Mother of God, although “royal” sometimes signifies the doorway of a church.]

Since it was thought that the lead in the glass windows might already be melting from the fiery heat, especially as the devouring victorious flame was consuming everything, hope in human assistance having collapsed, various goods were hidden some distance from the monastery among dense woods.

Suddenly, however, a vision of heavenly consolation appeared to one of the abbots who had come from neighboring monasteries to serve his veteran commander, the name of this abbot being Rainardus.

[Note: At that time two abbots named Rainardus were living in neighboring monasteries, at Ferrières and at Saint Peter’s in Sens. Rainardus of Sens had indeed been abbot of the monastery of Saint Columba near Sens. But Sevinus, archbishop and restorer of the monastery of Saint Peter, had brought regular monks there from the monasteries of Saint Benedict and Saint Peter of Cluny, according to the monk Clarius in his *Chronicle*, where this Rainardus is said to have died in 1025.]

For he saw, together with others who were granted the sight, two doves whiter than snow. Flying three times around the circuit of the church, they directed their flight toward the southwest, where the violence of the fire had already halted near the brothers’ barns. The fire did not dare to pass beyond the boundary divinely marked out.

By then human skill had ceased and human labor had come to rest, so that the greater power of divine mercy might shine forth through the most blessed Benedict, whom we wretched people had accused of having gone to sleep.

None of the things enclosed within the circuit of the cloister suffered any loss, as though they had been surrounded and protected by the angelic appearance of those birds in flight.

## CHAPTER III. A Contracted Man Raised Upright. An Ungrateful Man Falls Ill Again and Is Healed Again.

5. In our own time we knew a certain Archembert, a resident of the territory of Auxerre, who was severely afflicted by a prolonged illness. Since the diligent care of friends or relatives had failed him, his knees were so continually bent by lying down that his thighs and shins adhered to one another, and the flesh growing beneath them exceeded the width of a man’s palm.

His relatives had decided to carry him to the tomb of a certain Saint Simeon, which rumor had taught them was famous for healings, since it was said to lie within their own region.

[Note: I have not yet been able to discover who this Saint Simeon was.] But the sick man refused and asked to be taken to the monastery of Fleury.

For he said that during sleep he had seen himself standing before the most sacred tomb of Father Benedict, before the altar of the exalted Virgin Mary, standing upon straight feet and gazing upon a basilica of immense beauty, from which he was denied the ability to depart.

Those dreams, with which we are often deceived, were not empty. With God’s help and through the merits of the Queen of Virgins and the most eminent confessor, they produced a healing effect.

At last, having been carried on a donkey to the desired place, he was set down by those who had brought him near the monastery gates. Since he had not yet used little stools, he crawled on his buttocks and hands toward one of the public bakeries and was received by its keeper out of humane compassion.

After waiting there a long time for the arrival of his cure, he was inflamed with the desire to approach the hall of the Mother of Christ, in which Saint Benedict, the hope of his restoration, rested. When he entered it, he wished to place upon the altar, dedicated to God under the honor of Saint Mary and all the holy virgins, a small coin sent to him by the vicar of that same village, Ermenfredus, as an offering.

He felt his sinews begin to relax. Looking around to see who might help him, he was lifted up by the church’s sacristan and placed his little stools against the sanctuary railings; but his offering, scarcely the equivalent of the widow’s farthing in the Gospel, he placed upon the altar as acceptable to Christ.

Then, having prostrated himself upon the ground and devoted himself to prayer, he fell asleep, drenched in salty sweat. When he awoke, he no longer asked for his little stools. Supporting himself with a staff handed to him by one of those standing nearby, he went to the guesthouse and gradually acquired the firmest strength for walking.

6. When he realized that he was sufficiently able to continue his journey, ungrateful for his recovery, he secretly departed without the permission of his host or of the saints who had granted him the power of healing. Coming to a village called Dominipetri (Dompierre), he was again reduced to weakness. The priest Teudo, who had granted him a place to lodge in his own house, addressed him as follows [Col. 0827D]: “What evil,” he said, “have you committed, man, that you cannot escape your former illness?” He replied that he had left the saints who had provided for his healing without giving thanks.

Meanwhile, on the following night, as he slept, he seemed to be standing unharmed at the sacred places from which he had departed, holding before him a candle [Note: [Col. 0827D] That is, a wax candle. Thus it was customary to fashion candles according to the height of a sick person.] equal in length to his own stature. Therefore, at the advice and with the assistance of the aforesaid priest, he was placed upon a cart and taken back to the places he had wickedly abandoned. Finally, having purchased wax according to the vision previously shown to him, he carried it to the memorial—that is, the church—of the illustrious Virgin Mary [Col. 0828A] and lit it before the tomb of the glorious confessor of Christ, Benedict. Clinging to the pavement, he asked pardon for the guilt he had incurred, together with the restoration of his health. Having therefore made a vow never again to leave that same village, he deserved to be granted back the full strength of his legs.

We happened to hear this from his own mouth on the very day on which we began to write these things. The priest Constantinus [Note: [Col. 0827D] Is this Constantinus the schoolmaster, to whom several letters of Gerbert are extant? Constantinus the priest is praised in the *Life of Saint Abbo*, chapter 10, where he is said to have been the companion of Abbot Bernard of Beaulieu on his Italian pilgrimage.] and Letherius, a deacon by rank and a monk by habit, then assigned to the service of receiving guests, were also present at this account.

## CHAPTER IV. The site of Sacerge. Otherius the paralytic vows Caputcervium to Saint Benedict; after the gift is made, he is immediately healed. Another account of the transfer of that estate.

[Col. 0828B] 7. And since, as blessed Pope Gregory reports (*Dialogues*, book II, final chapter), the holy martyrs display more frequent miracles where only their memory is preserved than where their sacred bodies are kept, it is clear that the same may be understood of other saints, and especially of our most holy father Benedict, who is to be honored in many ways. Our mind eagerly desires to hand down to posterity knowledge of his most excellent signs, performed by God through his merits in other places.

There is an estate called Caputcervium (Sacerge), situated on the borders of the Bituriges and adjoining the Limousin; from it the neighboring region is called, in corrupted form, Capcergensis. We have learned from the account of very ancient elders that it came into the possession of the monastery of Floriacum, dedicated to almighty God under the name of the perpetual Virgin Mary and of the most holy Benedict, for the following reason [Col. 0828C].

8. The owner of that possession was called Otherius, a man distinguished among the Aquitanian nobles and possessing a renowned lineage. Struck by paralysis from the flower of his earliest youth, he had been deprived of the use of his hands and feet; only the functions of his tongue, hearing, and sight remained to him, and even these only partially. Suffering for a long time from this illness, and having understood that the empty efforts of physicians, applied to him with the greatest diligence, had contributed nothing to his health, he heard of the miracles that the omnipotence of our Savior was then frequently working at the most sacred bones of our common patron, Benedict. He said to his attendants:

“You see, my most faithful companions, dearer to me than life itself, the miserable life that I now enjoy: despite the expense of medical treatment, I make no progress; indeed, the duration of my sickness is prolonged day by day. Therefore, if any concern for your Otherius touches you, and if you pity my sufferings, I beg you to hasten by the quickest road to the tomb of the glorious confessor of Christ, Benedict. And lest unfamiliar roads trouble you, know that the banks of the river Loire (the Loire), and the district of Orléans, are illumined by this splendid treasure.

“A divine oracle foretold this to me when I had entrusted my weary limbs to sleep: I was to send petitioners for my health there with vows, because from there I would obtain a remedy for my sickness [Col. 0829A]. And because I live alone with my sweetest mother, deprived of my father and brothers, and because she herself not only does not refuse but diligently urges this very act, I vow to God and to the aforesaid illustrious Benedict my portion of the inheritance, called Caputcervium, together with everything belonging to it. The condition is that, while we both survive and retain the usufruct and the income of the present life, after our dissolution we shall cause everything to be restored to the brothers of Floriacum.

“For, having been deprived by the revelation mentioned above of the hope of receiving offspring, I have completely cast aside the intention of taking a wife. Therefore, make haste, and by your prayers and those of the servants of God who dwell there, seek help for this wretched man.”

[Col. 0829B] 9. Having received these instructions from their master, his faithful servants, carrying gloves ornamented with his gold, by means of which they were to place the donation of the aforesaid possessions upon the sacred altars [Note: [Col. 0829D] The rite of investiture or transfer by means of gloves—*wantos*, that is, gloves—is frequently encountered among authors.], went without delay to the venerable monastery and made their master’s commands and prayers known to the assembled brothers.

Memorable to relate! On that very day, and at the very hour when those who had been sent presented the gift with their prayers before the holy tomb, the sick man, who lay ninety miles distant from the place, obtained perfect health. Giving proclamations of praise to God and songs of thanksgiving to Saint Benedict, he went into the hidden parts of the forests for exercise or hunting.

While he was engaged in this activity, he met his servants returning from our monastery. When they saw him riding through the woodland, they were struck with immense astonishment: they saw a man who shortly before had been unable to rise from his bed without another’s assistance now not only walking firmly but even exhausting a horse at a gallop [Col. 0829C]. As they hesitated and thought that they had been deceived by the resemblance of his face, he joyfully presented himself to them. He then carefully asked on what day they had fulfilled their vows for him, and discovered with complete certainty that it was the very day on which he rejoiced to have received his health.

10. This ancient account handed down by the elders conflicted with an older edict of King Clotarius III [Note: [Col. 0829D] He was the son of Clovis II, during whose reign the body of Saint Benedict was transferred to Gaul.]. It states that the aforesaid Otherius was ordered by that king to be killed for treachery, and that, after all his possessions had been confiscated, the estate was bestowed by the same ruler upon Saint Benedict. [Col. 0829D] This is what is read in a passage of the first book (*V. Andrevald.*, chapter 38): that the brothers of Floriacum obtained Caputcervium through royal generosity.

It may nevertheless have happened that, after the donation that we have just related, Otherius was accused before the king of disloyalty and ordered to be killed, and that the same king, as though acting on his own behalf, granted the same village to our monastery. [Col. 0830A] As for the fact that in the royal order he is called Aotharius [Note: [Col. 0829D] Neither Aotharius nor Otherius, if I am not mistaken, is mentioned by the older historians of Frankish history.], the alteration of the ancient words accounts for it, as we shall show more fully below. After his death, all the neighbors attempted to take this estate away from them and compelled them to resort to a course of action advantageous to themselves.

## CHAPTER V. Ademarus, invader of Bruccia and Caputcervium. Otherius the appointed superior urges Hugo; Hugo approaches when he sees the opportunity. The site of the castle of Salis. Ademarus is finally defeated and captured through heavenly favor; his companions are likewise punished.

11. Finally, as is contained in the preceding sequence of the book (chapter 15), after dwellings suitable for the monastic order had been constructed there, the adversaries’ hope of possessing those estates was removed until the time of King Rotbert, son of Hugo. When he assumed the burden of governing the kingdom [Col. 0830B], a certain Ademarus, elevated by both youth and bodily beauty—his father Wido held the office of viscount in the city of Limoges—attempted a wicked crime.

For, not content with the resources that were rightfully available to him from his paternal inheritance, and seeing the numerous family of his brothers, his coheirs, increasing, he turned his mind toward stealing the possessions of others. Skilled in deceit, he entered a castle that the peasants called Bruccia [Note: [Col. 0830D] The monk Ademarus calls this castle Brocia in volume II of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca*, where its siege is described. It seems to be none other than this one, although the account says that it was not relieved by Ademarus but by his father Wido, without mentioning Ademarus. See Aimoinus, book I, chapter 16 above. Brocia, commonly Brousse, lies beside the castle of Salis, mentioned below.], and acted as its lord.

In that region there was a man of no contemptible power named Hugo, to whom half of that castle had come by hereditary succession. Ademarus rashly invaded this half, as well as the portion that belonged to Hugo’s father. Thus, having gained possession of the entire castle, he shut within it for fifteen days the forces of two counts who were trying to expel him—namely, William of Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0830D] This was William called Ferabrachia, fourth of that name.] and Boso of Périgord—and forced them to raise the siege.

Released from this danger, and daring greater things, he entered, like a bandit, the town of the Father Benedict, situated four and a half miles from the castle just mentioned, taking advantage of the absence of its superior, Otherius. Antiquity had given that town the name Salis, and the monks had transferred their permanent residence there from Caputcervium, because the site was for the most part naturally fortified.

The aforesaid Ademarus attempted to seize it, as he later himself reported, in order to relieve Bruccia’s scarcity of grain and wine by taking the supplies that inhabitants of the surrounding area had gathered there for the protection of the holy places [Col. 0830D]. In reality, however, he was working to enlarge the extremely narrow boundaries of his own possessions.

12. Meanwhile, when the aforementioned superior of the place, Otherius, received news of so great a calamity, he was inwardly struck with grief because he seemed to have completely lost the place entrusted to him by the venerable Abbot Abbo, then ruler of the brothers of Floriacum. He was swept up in a turmoil of conflicting thoughts [Col. 0831A]. At last, realizing that the time had come not for mourning but for counsel, he went directly to the Hugo mentioned above.

He informed him that an opportunity had arisen to attack the enemy: Ademarus had abandoned Bruccia’s very strong defenses and moved his residence to the town of Salis. Otherius urged Hugo to set out to forestall his attempts. Hugo did not delay, understanding that it would serve his interests if he could take Ademarus by surprise in a less secure place.

What more is there to say? He attracted to his aid all the neighboring inhabitants whom he knew to cherish a reverent love for the place of the Father Benedict. At dawn on Tuesday he warned them to meet the enemy.

13. Meanwhile, during the night preceding the day of battle, a vision of the following kind appeared in sleep to a certain soldier among the auxiliaries on our side [Col. 0831B]. He seemed to be traversing a forest with Ainard, the superior of the church of Saint Stephen in the see of Limoges. At suitable places they had spread nets and were driving before them a multitude of wild boars. Some they led into prepared snares and captured alive; others they pierced with hunting spears and handed over to death.

When he awoke and had related what he had seen to one of his companions, he received this answer:

“The clear meaning of your vision,” he said, “with God’s help and through the supporting merits of the most holy Benedict, will soon be revealed. For what was shown to you concerning wild swine, you will see enacted with regard to treacherous men. And what you dreamed you were doing under the direction of Ainard, you will accomplish at daybreak, with Otherius, the monk of the holy man Benedict, as leader, together with us and with Christ’s help.”

When the man who had seen the dream asked that its meaning be explained more clearly—for he was unaware of what was taking place—the interpreter said to him:

“Has it not yet reached your ears that Ademarus, son of Wido, has invaded the monastery of the illustrious confessor Benedict, and that Otherius, its superior, has therefore sought the aid of our lord? Gaufredus was called by the nickname Asinus because of his bodily strength. The aforesaid monk happened to be in his castle when this soldier related the matter to his comrade.”

He added:

“We too, if God wills and holy Benedict assists us, shall either strike the invaders of the sacred place with the avenging sword or proclaim them, once captured, in a noble triumph.”

This statement strengthened the wavering hearts of many men. It seems to me that this dreamer and his interpreter resembled the two easterners, one of whom dreamed of Gideon’s victory and the other interpreted it.

14. It was Friday of the second week of Holy Lent [Col. 0832A] when the band of robbers seized the monastery mentioned above. Then, at twilight on the Tuesday of the following week, auxiliaries summoned from every direction unexpectedly appeared at the gates.

At that time, while certain men of our company were still some distance from the castle together with the superior Otherius, a divine marvel appeared. Although the sun was illuminating the rest of the earth with great brilliance, they saw the circuit of the castle surrounded by a dense, wall-like fog. It caused no impediment to their fighting, but obscured the enemy’s sight.

This day seems comparable to that of which the ancient legislator writes: “For the Egyptians there was thick darkness, tangible darkness, but for the children of Israel there was light throughout all their borders” (Exodus 10:22–23).

Strengthened in spirit by this sign, they decided to attack the enemy in battle. They sent the superior ahead, who, while approaching the walls that had previously been loyal to him but were now hostile, loudly proclaimed the name of blessed Benedict. Then they themselves, raising their voices on high, invoked Benedict, the Father of the monks. The hollows of the valleys resounded with “Benedict,” and the hidden depths of the neighboring forest answered, “Benedict.”

Because of that tumult, it seemed to them that the surrounding mountains had drawn together and that the underworld had opened before the enemy. Since mention has been made of the mountains, it will not burden the listeners if we now describe the site of the aforementioned castle of Salis.

15. There is a mountain of moderate height, on whose slope the castle was situated. From the eastern and southern sides it offered difficult access to those approaching it [Col. 0832C]. On the northern side, the downward slope of the mountain prevented the transport of every kind of siege engine. Toward the west, however, where an easy advance by the enemy was feared, stood a house built extremely solidly of stone and extending lengthwise toward the south, sufficiently suitable for repelling attackers.

This fortification became the occasion of the adversaries’ destruction: because of excessive confidence, they became aware of the enemy’s presence before they had anticipated it.

16. The first to attack the northern side was Gaufredus, nicknamed Asinus because of his strength, not because of his laziness. He ordered the fire to be brought forward, as he had pledged the previous day over drinks among his men in honor of Father Benedict [Note: [Col. 0831D] Such drinking toasts made in honor of the saints—if indeed it is honor—are still preserved in the custom of drinking during the vigil of Saint Martin, a custom handed down to our own time. On this, see Spondanus, year 580, no. 2, and, following him, Cointius, year 577, no. 45. From this arose in former times drinking oaths by Saint Stephen and other saints, and even by kings and their sons—practices forbidden by Charlemagne in the Capitulary of 789, *On Various Matters*, chapter 10, and by Hincmar of Reims in *Capitularies* 1, chapter 14, and, before both of them, by Augustine in sermon 232, *On Time*, cited by Canisius in his note to Alcuin’s letter 22. See Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book II, chapter 35.].

After him came the other auxiliaries: Giraldus, lord of the castle of Cluis, Hugo of Gargilesse, and the rest, whose names I have decided not to state. Protected by a company of two hundred armed men, they began to repel the adversaries with spears and stones from the battlements they were attempting to defend. The adversaries trusted in equal numbers but were inferior in steadfast courage.

And behold, through divine providence and the intervention of the illustrious confessor, a north wind arose. It drove the flames of the fires against the gates, while forcing the enemy’s missiles backward [Col. 0833A]. When the townsmen saw the fire growing stronger and their own missiles falling uselessly, they became afraid and fled inward.

As the rebels made for the church, our men followed more closely from behind. After killing several at the entrance to the gate, they pursued those who were seeking the basilica. Ademarus, realizing that it would not provide him a safe hiding place, fearfully climbed a wooden tower from which the bells hung, together with six of his faction’s companions.

Distrusting even that hiding place, he walked across the roofs like an architect until Hugo, who was searching for him more diligently than the others, caught sight of him and captured him after promising security for his life and limbs.

Five of his more prominent comrades-in-arms were captured with him: Hugo and Archembaldus of Buciacum; Rainardus and his brother Americus, sons of Heldegarius, a man of some distinction from Argenton; and Giraldus of Tirinus. I omit those whom either lesser power or less distinguished noble ancestry has kept from our knowledge; their number is said to have been twenty or more.

One hundred and twenty horses were captured, apart from those secretly carried off by the victors or taken away by the defeated as they sought safety in flight. From these figures the size of the enemy force may be inferred, and the heavenly power and the outstanding merit of Father Benedict may likewise be clearly recognized: adversaries protected by numbers and by the natural strength of the place were so easily overcome by so few men trained in warfare.

We nevertheless believe that by God’s free grace it was granted to us that, although thirty of the enemy’s soldiers were killed, none of our men was even wounded, except three. One of these was a professional soldier who, having received a mortal wound, died while returning home. The other two were engaged more in agriculture than in war; they had come with many other men skilled in their trades, aroused by the fame of the battle, to assist our side. While they were too intent on plunder, it is uncertain whether they were killed by their comrades or by outsiders.

In this way the castle was recovered within the sixth hour of the day on which our men had first arrived there and was restored to our possession, in the year 1000 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

17. And lest anyone think that so great a victory ought to be attributed more to human strength than to divine generosity, let him know that the adversaries themselves made known to us that they had been so deprived of strength that, although they saw themselves well supplied with a mass of missiles and stones, they nevertheless felt that they possessed no effectiveness in throwing them.

The souls of the slain also, resting by night in the same village, very often forced people to break their sleep, wandering about and crying lamentably that they were wretched because they had not hesitated to invade the possessions of the most illustrious Father Benedict.

18. Nor were Ademarus’ father Guido or his brother Giraldus, the godfather of the young man mentioned above, free from misfortune. Just as they had shared in his plan, so also, by the most just ordering of God’s providence, they shared in his dangers [Col. 0834A].

Guido went to Rome under the pretext of prayer rather than of concealment, as though he did not know what his son was doing. There an illness of vitiligo so weakened him that he could return home only in a litter.

Giraldus, meanwhile, remained at Poitiers under the same pretext of pretending innocence and awaiting the outcome of the affair. A fierce horse seized him by the thigh with its teeth and forced him to lie in bed for several days.

Hildebertus of Argenton [BOSCIO Argensis], a local inhabitant and standard-bearer of this faction, publicly appeared to be an intermediary for peace but secretly fostered treachery. He was burned on the jaw by divine fire and remained incurable until the day of his death, so that, after the flesh had been consumed, his teeth were exposed in a wretched spectacle.

Blessed in all things is God, who continually glorifies the saints pleasing to him [Col. 0834B].

## CHAPTER VI. Ademarus’ castle destroyed. A horse drawn from a well.

19. Since we have once entered Aquitaine, it does not seem out of place to relate a miracle that occurred there and that the sequence of events connected with what happened a few years earlier. Ademarus, captured by Hugo as related above, was led to the castle of Bruccia.

A certain Giraldus, favorable to Ademarus’ party, held the castle, having excluded Hugo’s supporters, who were deeply indignant that Ademarus had seized the portion of the same castle belonging to Hugo. Hugo therefore ordered the captured young man to be led before the walls, where his own men could see him, and threatened to cut off his head unless they promptly surrendered the fortifications to him.

This greatly terrified Giraldus and those inside, especially when they saw their lord, together with so many excellent warriors trained in warfare, suddenly overthrown by this reversal of circumstances. Consequently, terrified, they surrendered not only the town but also themselves and all their possessions.

After Hugo took possession of the castle, he immediately demolished the tower that appeared to have belonged to Ademarus. Beside it was a cistern excavated to collect rainwater, extending forty-five or more cubits in depth.

20. Some time later, two of our brothers residing at the aforementioned monastery of the holy Father Benedict at Salis visited the aforesaid Hugo, who was then living at Bruccia, for the monastery’s benefit [Col. 0834D]. Since they were going up to the upper part of the tower to converse with him, they left below two horses tied together by tethering straps.

One of them, unable to remain still, dragged its companion while wandering here and there. With the hind part of its body it slipped into the cistern mentioned above and, unable to be helped by the other horse, fell all the way to the bottom.

The onlookers immediately raised an outcry that the monks’ horse had fallen into the well. Hugo carefully inquired into the cause of the commotion and, when he discovered the damage suffered by the fallen animal, was deeply distressed that the monks who had come to visit him—for he was ill—had suffered so great a loss.

He therefore ordered his wife to summon the stronger young men and have the half-dead carcass of the horse removed from the well [Col. 0835A]. Shortly afterward, having put on his clothes, he followed her and, leaning over the mouth of the well, saw only the horse’s head rising above the water, while the rest of its body and the saddle were covered by the water. Turning to those standing around, he said:

“This horse will never again feel the burden of a saddle.”

The woman replied:

“Is that old Benedict, who obtained victory for you from the Lord over your enemies, so powerless that he cannot obtain that his monk be carried back on his own animal?”

Doubtfully he answered:

“If he obtains this, I shall entrust myself to his protection above that of all the other saints.”

A ladder was then brought down, and a man trusting in the boldness of youth descended to bind the horse with ropes around the appropriate parts of its body, so that it could more easily be drawn out. But when he had come back up, it seemed difficult, because of the narrowness of the well, to extract an animal of such immense size together with the ladder. They therefore first drew out the ladder and then began to pull out the horse.

But almighty God, to show not only the aforementioned Hugo but also every person of sound judgment that the illustrious leader of the monks, the supreme Benedict, possessed no small merit before him—indeed, more than any mortal could imagine—doubled the miracle. When a large group of young men had already raised the horse to the very rim of the well, and the brothers standing at a distance were offering prayers to the Lord in the litany, as soon as they began to invoke Benedict, beloved of the Lord, the ropes suddenly broke and the horse slipped back into the depths [Col. 0835C].

Despair seized everyone. They no longer believed that it could be brought back alive, especially since it would be difficult to descend again to bind it, they did not have a sufficient supply of ropes, and they thought that its fall from above had crushed its limbs.

One of the brothers then approached the aforementioned Hugo and urged him, trusting in the power of Christ’s confessor Benedict, to undertake the attempt once more. Some of the young men agreed with this advice, wishing to test what their strength could accomplish, especially the wife of that most noble man Hugo, who burned with the fervor of faith and devotion toward our most blessed Father Benedict.

The ladder was again lowered into the well. No other equipment of ropes could be found except the interconnected and twisted cords that they used for nets intended to catch wild goats [Col. 0835D]. With these, therefore, they bound the horse as they had done before and pulled it up, loudly invoking Saint Benedict.

And behold, when it was almost within their hands, the bindings failed again and it began to slip back into the depths. Then one of the crowd asked to be tied with broad and very strong straps cut from deer hides, which the Aquitanians use. He was lowered inside, took hold of the straps around the horse’s legs, and fastened the animal most securely by the head. He instructed his companions to pull him out first and the four-footed animal afterward.

They promptly obeyed his instructions and brought both of them back up. The horse was laid upon the ground as though dead [Col. 0836A]. The honorable Hugo approached it, touched it with a staff, and said to those standing around:

“This horse will never come back to life.”

Then, when some men lifted it from the ground, the horse raised itself, shook its body, and discharged through the urinary passage the water it had unwillingly swallowed.

The woman immediately rebuked her husband joyfully:

“Learn from this proof,” she said, “that Benedict, the servant of God, is faithfully present to those who invoke him, especially to his own servants.”

At once applause and cries of joy arose throughout the castle. They praised Benedict and gave thanks to Benedict because the horse was now alive and now walked on its own feet.

Since it was winter, the devout woman herself led the horse into a sunny house and covered it with soft bedding until it began to sweat [Col. 0836B]. Shortly afterward it was brought out, rolled upon the ground, and shook all its limbs; neighing, it sought its companion.

The brothers who were present joyfully took it back and returned it home unharmed, with no limb weakened. One of them was named Anno (mentioned above, book I, chapter 17), who performs the office of priest; the other was Remigius, who remained in the order of the diaconate. From their account I learned that these things had happened within the past fifteen years. They also showed me the saddle that had fallen with the horse; its stirrups, although new, and its front-piece had been torn apart by the horse’s restless feet.

21. Let anyone who boasts that these things do not seem miraculous now determine which of them is greater: to bring iron back from the depths of a lake, or not only to preserve the life of a four-footed animal in a terrible plunge but also to bring it back alive to the upper world.
