Because our own lawgiver accomplished both, I acknowledge that in both he was not merely powerful but supremely powerful. In this event, however, there is something worthy of admiration: the horse that the restraints of ropes could not pull out was drawn back by fragile straps, as by reins (*Gregory*, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 6). It was as though the pious Father Benedict were plainly warning them, not by words but by deeds, that this should be attributed not to human strength but rather to divine action and to his intervention.

But if anyone judges that his marvelous deeds should be despised because of the lowliness of our person, we ask him not to read our account but at least not to provoke the exceedingly gentle countenance of that same Father by his ingratitude [Col. 0836D]. If, God forbid, he is offended, no one should doubt that he will show himself harsh and unyielding; but, when softened by prayers of humility, he will show himself gracious and gentle.

## CHAPTER VII. Soldiers fed with Saint Benedict’s bread remain unharmed in battle.

22. It seems appropriate to insert into this account also what the Lord deigned to accomplish in the same province, under the aforementioned superior Otherius, through the merits of his saint, Benedict.

Hildebertus, son of the aforementioned Boso, having obtained the county of the city of Périgueux through the succession of his maternal grandfather, took up arms against William, count of Poitiers. After assembling an army, he set up camp two miles from the city of Poitiers [Col. 0837A].

Among the other auxiliaries whom he had summoned for that war was Hugo, whom we mentioned earlier, lord of the castle called Gargilissa. Knowing that our most blessed Father Benedict is accustomed to assist everywhere, and especially in war, those who invoke him with complete faith, he asked the aforementioned superior Otherius to give him at least two loaves of the bread on which the monks fed. He intended to eat them with his men as he entered the battle, possessing no small faith in believing that by this food he could be more strongly protected against every danger than by all weapons.

Meanwhile, while Hildebertus awaited both Hugo and the rest of the auxiliaries, especially Fulk, count of Anjou [Note: [Col. 0837D] Concerning this Fulk, called Nerra, see Rodulfus Glaber, book II, chapter 3, and book III, chapter 2. See also the *Deeds of the Counts of Anjou* in volume X of the *Spicilegium*.], the Poitevins assembled and attempted to overwhelm him by a sudden attack. Their purpose was to crush the commander of the war before all his forces had gathered and thereby frighten the remainder away from assisting him [Col. 0837B].

Hildebertus was no slower in meeting them. With the few men he had with him, he received the attackers and engaged them twice in open battle. When he was on the point of being overcome by the enemy’s multitude, and even his veterans were not ashamed to flee, the aforementioned Hugo suddenly arrived.

Seeing the spirits of his allies cast down by their misfortunes, he quickly broke up the loaves he had received from the monastery of Saint Benedict. He himself ate some and distributed the rest to those whom he had brought with him. Then, together with Hildebertus, he attacked the Poitevins, who were already on the verge of victory and overly confident in themselves, and defeated and routed them.

Indeed, among the soldiers who had eaten even a small amount of Saint Benedict’s bread, no one received a mortal wound; all escaped unharmed.

## CHAPTER VIII. When a soldier had entered the monastery of Abbatisvilla by force and, in contempt of Saint Benedict, had made himself drunk on the brothers’ wine, the abbot prayed that God would show himself the protector of the place; the soldier was consumed by fire, as were his two boy accomplices, his horses, and all his possessions.

23. Now, moving forward in our narrative from Aquitaine, let us return to Francia. After relating what seems pertinent concerning the condition of the kingdom and its kings, let us recount the miracle performed by almighty God through our most blessed Father Benedict at a place called Abbatisvilla [Col. 0837D], and then, for definite reasons, pass through the monastery on our way toward Burgundy.

24. Hugh, duke of the Franks, having obtained the royal insignia, possessed it for ten continuous years together with his son; but when he died, he left the monarchy of his principate to his son Robert. Robert, the Hughson, had long been considering marrying and wished to take as his wife a woman from the region of Arles [Note: namely Constance, daughter of William, count of Arles, and of his wife Blanche or Adela]. He gathered an army to meet his bride, who was already on the point of arriving.

While the army was on the march and held the farther bank of the Loire, it happened that William of Bellême chose, for the purpose of pitching camp, a courtyard belonging to the above-mentioned estate of Abbatisvilla [Col. 0838A]. One of his attendants, a young man of perverse mind, anticipating his master, furiously ordered the monk in charge of the courtyard, named Theoderic, to open the gates to him, since he intended to pitch his tent there.

The monk replied: “Have patience with me, excellent soldier, while I await the arrival of your lord, for these gates will be opened to him alone.”

When the soldier perceived that he was being denied entry, he turned to anger and said to his companions: “Look at this monk, swollen like a puffed-up toad, sitting arrogantly on an equally swollen horse, and unwilling to open the gates to me.”

Moved by these insulting words, the monk turned toward the eastern quarter, where the monastery is situated, and said [Col. 0838B]: “I suspect that you, O most holy lord Benedict, have either fallen into everlasting sleep or, offended by our sins, have departed from these dwellings once so dear to you, since you allow the injuries done to your people to remain unavenged.”

Why delay with many words? The vengeance for the blasphemy was not long postponed, divine providence hastening it, as we believe, through the merits of the blessed confessor, so that the brother, overcome by faintheartedness, might not fall into a greater offense in speech.

For when William arrived, that wretched man who had scandalized the brother and had also despised Benedict the Father—boasting that, without Benedict’s favor, he would fill his own belly and those of his companions to drunkenness with the wine of his servants—entered a house some distance from the courtyard. There, to carry out his threats, he drank wine beyond measure and, together with the unmixed wine, drained the Lord’s cup of wrath to the dregs.

Rising from the table, he placed himself beside the fire, joining temporal sleep to eternal sleep. The fire seized the bedding and raised globes of flame aloft, easily setting the roof of the house alight. The wretched man did not awaken until, when everything had been caught, he was overwhelmed by the weight of the beams. Thus he was consumed in the fire together with two of his attendants—for a third escaped half-burned—and five horses, as well as all his traveling equipment.

A man who had escaped the danger of death because his clothing and the hair of his head had been singed was brought into William’s presence and related the matter in the order in which it had occurred. Then William said [Col. 0838D]: “This punishment deservedly befell these wretched men, who, in the malicious madness of their minds, thought they could drain all the monks’ wine and devoted themselves so completely to drunkenness that they could not avoid the danger hanging over them.”

By this event the brother’s suspicion was erased: he had falsely accused our most blessed Father Benedict of having fallen asleep, though Benedict keeps constant and vigilant watch over the flock entrusted to him. Henceforth none of us can be deterred from visiting these places pleasing to him by any crime, however monstrous, since the gracious presence of his bones invites us. Nevertheless, we must be all the more careful not to offend the gaze of so kindly a visitor with the dark cloud of our sins [Col. 0839A].

## CHAPTER IX. The flooding of the Loire in the year 1003. A herdsman rescued from the waters.

25. Concerning that flooding of the Loire which the inhabitant of the riverbank experienced as more extensive than usual, while the farmer living far away sensed it as something unprecedented, I shall undertake to transmit to the memory of posterity—since I happened to be absent—the miracle accomplished through the merit of our frequently named patron Benedict, as I learned it from the account of our elders.

The Loire, the greatest of those rivers which, through Gaul, carry the courses of their channels into the Ocean under their proper names, exceeded its ancient boundaries in a manner never before heard of in the ages, in the year 1003 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the sixteenth year of King Robert’s reign jointly with his father, and in the seventh year of his sole monarchy [Note: This chronology concerning the reign of King Robert should be noted. The first year of his joint reign with his father is compared with the year of Christ 988, and his sole monarchy with the year 997. Both chronologies are confirmed by many documents, but especially the first, which will be discussed in its proper place. Yet Hugh was called king in 987 and in that same year chose his son as his associate in the kingdom, as Aimoinus testifies above, Book II, chapter 1—namely, in the same year of Hugh, but in the following year according to Christ’s era, and indeed on the Kalends of January, which, according to the ancient custom, belonged to the preceding year] [Col. 0839B].

Its outpouring was so great and so sudden that it engulfed farmers at work and horsemen traveling, bringing sudden ruin upon them. Thus Virgil’s lines about the Po may appropriately be applied to it:

> The king of rivers, Eridanus,  
> swirling forests in his mad whirlpool,  
> swept away the herds with their stalls  
> across all the fields.  
>   
> *(Virgil, Georgics I)*

So too this river, with an unforeseen surge, carried away not only livestock with their folds and human beings with their houses, but also heads of households with their sons and daughters, together with all their household goods.

Fearing that the herdsman responsible for the cattle assigned for the use of the monks of Father Benedict dwelling in the monastery of Fleury might be caught in this flood of waters, he led the herds away to the safer mountain pastures. Returning from there, he hurried to escape the impending danger by taking refuge within the enclosure of the fortress, but he encountered the hostile river from which he wished to flee.

He therefore turned back and hastened on foot toward a bridge over a stream which, because of the breadth of the surrounding marsh, is called Longumrete—a bridge he had perhaps already passed. There, too, he found himself confronted by the swirling floodwaters and fell into despair for his life. Unsure what to do, he unwound the bands from his legs and tied himself to two planks of the bridge.

Nevertheless, he began to invoke Christ and pray to Saint Benedict [Col. 0839D], asking him to have mercy on him by bringing aid. But when the bridge was loosened by the force of the swollen river, he too was carried headlong away.

Then he repeated the name of the most blessed Benedict more frequently, with his whole heart’s devotion. Believing that he had already been handed over to death, he asked only that his soul might be saved. When the waters had driven him onward and carried him to the place where the little river Bonodia flows into the Loire, he was borne nearly three miles through the waters. Since the holy name of Benedict was always in his mouth and always in his heart [Col. 0840A], he deserved to be heard.

For when the winds changed, a west wind began gently to bring him toward the bank. Some of his own people, sailing nearby in small boats, recognized who he was, loosened the bonds with which he had tied himself, and brought him back unharmed with them to a safe landing place.

The man himself was named Constantius. He also relates that he was surrounded by a multitude of serpents and reptiles of various kinds, yet by God’s providence and through the intervention of the outstanding confessor of Christ, Benedict, none of them harmed him.

This is considered all the more astonishing because some men who had climbed to the very tops of trees, believing that they could not safely breathe in the presence of the surging torrent, were followed by snakes as they crawled after them; the snakes forced the men, torn by pitiful bites, to fall into the depths [Col. 0840B]. But although the snakes encircled this man, who was situated below, as though forming a belt around him, they did not harm him in the least. Divine grace, through the merits of its holy confessor Benedict, protected him so that he might render devoted service to Benedict’s servants.

It is also certain that another benefit of divine generosity was granted to him. The flood had torn up enormous trees by their roots, and their force overturned even trunks hardened by long age. Yet under the impact of these trees he could not merely avoid being submerged: with only his hand or arm he pushed them away as they approached him, as though they were light stalks of straw.

## CHAPTER X. A man who reduced the land of Saint Benedict perishes by an evil death.

[Col. 0840C]

26. A certain field belonging to the authority of the church of Saint Stephen in the city of Auxerre borders the land of Saint Benedict, which adjoins the marsh mentioned above. A certain Walter, who had received this field by right of benefice, wished to seize a portion of the same land for his own use. Fabricating the accusation that it belonged to his benefice and had been unjustly occupied by our peasants, he brought his complaint before the venerable abbot Abbo.

At a certain time he had been sent by one of his lords to attend, on his behalf, the abbot mentioned above as he traveled to the royal palace. When the two were returning together and had reached the place where the dispute seemed to have arisen, the same man turned to the abbot and said [Col. 0840D]: “Now, lord abbot, if you please, I shall show you the boundary of my possession.”

The abbot warned him not to mark out anything beyond his rightful property, lest the act somehow go unpunished. But the man drove his spurs into his horse and hurried toward the boundary he had chosen, while nearly everyone who was with the abbot urged him not to cross the limit of the rightful division.

As he tried to restrain the horse with the reins, he said [Col. 0841A]: “From this place I shall vindicate for myself all the right to that side”—pointing to it with his hand—“even if it is necessary to do so in single combat.”

The horse, driven into its course, could not be held back by him. Instead, plunging forward against its rider’s will, it slipped on its offended foot once and then a second time.

Then the most reverend abbot Abbo turned to his attendants and said: “You will now very quickly behold the just judgment of the most righteous Judge.”

After these words, the horse fell a third time and threw its master over its back. The man fell, his internal organs torn and his shoulder broken. Carried weakened to the monastery estate, he died as that same day was growing late. Thus he alone fought the single combat he had proposed, while God made manifest the judgment carried out through the merits of his beloved confessor Benedict [Col. 0841B], whose property he had wished to alienate.

The honorable abbot Abbo, taking pity on his death because the man had served him most devotedly on the journey, buried him with the brothers in the cemetery of the church with the greatest honor.

## CHAPTER XI. The translation of the body of Saint Paul to Fleury.

27. Osa (Huessant) is an island in the Ocean Sea, separated from the mainland of the Armorican region—which they call Cornwall—by sixteen miles of open sea stretching across the intervening space. From the book of his Life we have learned that the blessed Paul, surnamed Aurelianus, led the life of a hermit there [Note: This book survives, though mutilated, in the library of Fleury].

This Saint Paul was eventually made bishop in a place in Britain called the town of Saint Paul [Note: The Bollandist associates restored the text in this way; Boscius erroneously has “which is called a town.” It is now called Leonium, or Leon, and is an episcopal see]. Having become famous there for many virtues during his life, he deserved by divine designation to receive burial in that same place [Col. 0841C].

After a long period had passed since his death, his body was transferred from there by Mabbo, the bishop of that place, to this monastery of ours at Fleury [Note: Mabbo presided over the Church of Leon from 940 to 945, according to Albert of Monterelaxo, who also attributes this translation of Saint Paul’s relics to Fleury to Bishop Liberalis under Charles the Bald] [Col. 0842D].

Since an opportunity has presented itself, we have thought it worthwhile to relate the course of this translation, although it took place long ago, just as we learned it by hearsay from our predecessors.

The venerable bishop Mabbo mentioned above, inflamed by divine love for the contemplative life, was uncertain where he might most suitably fulfill his purpose. It was divinely inspired in him that nowhere could he accomplish it more appropriately than in the presence of the body of our most holy Father Benedict, who was the leader and standard-bearer of the discipline he himself desired to follow [Col. 0841D].

Taking the Gospels and a respectable array of sacred vestments, he arrived, together with the most sacred body of the outstanding bishop Paul, at the dwelling he desired. The abbot of this holy monastery, Wlfaldus—named in the preceding book [Note: The author of the historical fragment already cited, in Chesnius, volume III, page 343, also bears witness to the same]—and the entire congregation received them with the most joyful service of affection and honorably kept them among themselves for as long as he lived.

When he had completed the course of his praiseworthy life, he obtained burial before the altar of Saint John the Evangelist, in the basilica of Saint Mary, the Mother of God [Col. 0842A].

They placed the body of the aforementioned confessor Paul, together with its own coffin, behind the coffin of the most holy Father Benedict, enclosing both in a single larger chest, which was also covered with silver.

Now let us return to completing what we began.

## CHAPTER XII. Felix the anchorite rescued from shipwreck. The bishop of Leon learns of it from heaven. Felix thereby becomes more devoted to Saint Benedict. He is rescued again.

28. On the island mentioned above, out of love for so great a bishop, a certain citizen of the aforementioned region of Cornwall, named Felix, moved there to live. Together with other men of his province, he earnestly led a life pleasing to God for several years [Col. 0842B].

But when truthful report informed him that the body of the saint mentioned above was being kept with us, he resolved to hasten to his most sacred remains. The rumor of our most holy Father Benedict, which had filled even the most remote shores of Britain, also encouraged his good intention.

He therefore boarded the one ship he could find at that time and resolved to go to the above-mentioned town of Saint Paul, in order to consult the bishop of that see about whether it would be expedient for him to carry out what he had conceived.

But the sea passage which, as we said, lies between the island and the mainland is often difficult for sailors to cross because of its narrowness and the roughness caused by the rocks projecting within it [Col. 0842C]. When the man mentioned above wished to cross it, an unexpected surge of waves overturned the ship and shut him in between itself and the sea, together with all his companions.

Some of them did not know how to swim. The wave seized them and set them unharmed upon one of the projecting rocks. Felix, however, boarded the ship, which had righted itself, with only one companion. Bailing out the waves that had filled it with a piece of cloth from his gathered garment, he approached the rock with the two oars that alone remained, in order to recover his companions.

After taking them aboard, he saw at a distance the book with which he was accustomed to offer praises to God being tossed about by the waves but not sinking. Then the ship, proceeding on a straight course, lifted it up, so completely free of moisture inside that it seemed not the waves to have carried it through the sea but the wind through the land.

After they had taken aboard some oars and a small amount of equipment [Col. 0842D], they finally reached the place to which they were bound.

29. When the man mentioned above wished to relate to the bishop of the place, in a familiar conversation, what had happened to him, the bishop anticipated him and said:

“Do you, my lord Felix, not know what was revealed during the night in sleep about you to a certain monk well known both to you and to everyone?”

When Felix said that he knew nothing whatever about it, the bishop continued [Col. 0843A]:

“That same monk reported it to me before many witnesses, saying: ‘It seemed to me that Felix, who lives on the island, was here among us. When he wished to return to his own place and had boarded a ship, the devil came in the form of a vulture. The mass of his body seemed capable of reaching the height of a mountain. I seemed to see him sink into the depths, together with the ship, all those who were traveling in it.

“When they had been submerged in this way, a certain man suddenly appeared, clothed in a monastic garment. Like an abbot, he carried in his hand a staff curved at the top. Walking upon the water, he used that same staff to draw the ship, with the men unharmed and all their possessions, from the depths to the shore.

“After rescuing them, he ordered them to wait for him there. He pursued the vulture, which had already prepared to flee, struck it with his staff, and plunged it into the abyss of the deep [Col. 0843B].

“Then he returned to Felix and his companions, and with the cheerful expression he had before, he urged them to board the small boat and sail safely wherever they wished, saying: ‘There is your adversary. By God’s grace I have drowned him, and he has lost all power to harm you.’”

30. When the servant of God heard these things from the bishop, he too explained all his experiences to him, asserting that the vision had been fulfilled in him not only figuratively but also in bodily fact.

Understanding from the apparition mentioned above that our most holy Father Benedict had brought aid to his salvation, he began to burn with an even greater love for that pre-eminent confessor and to insist on reaching his most sacred tomb.

[Col. 0843C] 31. After a short delay, he gathered the things he thought necessary and prepared to return to the mainland. Indeed, almighty God doubled the miracle so as to inflame his heart still more with love for the saints whose presence he desired.

When the anchor had been lifted from the shore and the ship was heading toward the open sea, the waves suddenly rose. A steep mountain of water, lifted high, surrounded the entire boat so completely that there seemed to be no way of escape from any side.

Then Felix, the servant of Christ mentioned above, struck with terror at the danger hanging over him, poured forth within his heart prayers of the deepest supplication:

“Renowned confessors of Christ, Benedict and Paul, whose most sacred ashes I long to approach, bring aid to me, wretched as I am, for now I fear only the peril of death” [Col. 0843D].

After this prayer, the swollen waters subsided more quickly than words can tell, and the sea stood calm in the winds, offering sailors a safe passage.

Thus Felix, so often mentioned, was rescued from the imminent shipwreck [Note: This is that Felix, praised at length in the book on the Life of Abbot Gildas in the First Century, who was sent by Gauzlin, abbot of Fleury, to Armorica in the year 1008 to restore the monasteries in that region]. He came to the monastery he had long desired and related to us the manner of his salvation.

## CHAPTER XIII. An evil advocate perishes.

32. We ought indeed to have aimed at brevity, lest an excess of words generate in our hearers a distaste for the subject [Col. 0844A]. But since the flow of speech could not be restrained, being driven by the force of love for the most holy Father Benedict to set forth his deeds more fully, pardon must be granted if the loquacious page has exceeded what was permitted.

From now on, we shall endeavor to encompass the miracles of that beloved lord in a more concise style of narration, both to proclaim his praises and not to burden the reader.

33. In the region of Burgundy, in the territory of Troyes, there is an estate of Saint Benedict called Tauriacus. Its advocate, a man named Gauzfredus, although he was supposed to defend it against outsiders, devastated it more violently than any outsider would have done.

The monks frequently admonished him to cease his wrongdoing, but he did not obey. Therefore the merciful Father Benedict obtained from God that he should first be struck by the scourge of correction, before his wickedness was completely destroyed [Col. 0844B].

One day, while Gauzfredus was sitting in his own house within the walls of the aforementioned city of Troyes and conducting a judicial proceeding among the peasants, a black dog full of rabies appeared. Without harming any of the bystanders, it rushed at him, tore apart his nostrils and face with its bites, and departed.

He was driven into madness and was taken by his friends to the basilica of Saint Denis. There he recovered his senses to some extent, though not completely. Returning home, he added worse deeds to the evils he had inflicted upon the poor men of Saint Benedict. Then a demon seized him; he was chained and shut away in a certain room, where he breathed out his final spirit.

All who knew him declared that he had suffered these things because of his cruelty toward the peasants of the precious confessor Benedict.

To this fearsome vengeance let us attach another sign of mercy and healing.

## CHAPTER XIV. A monk abandoned by everyone at the point of death finds Saint Benedict favorable.

34. In the lower parts of this Neustria [Note: Neustria once comprised all the territory between the Loire and the Seine as far as the Ocean], specifically in the city of Angers, a certain Ainfredus, formerly a cleric at the monastery of Saint Albinus, voluntarily became a monk.

For the sake of improving his life, he moved to this venerable place at Fleury, remained with us for some time, and then returned to the monastery mentioned above. While he was staying there, he was afflicted by a serious illness involving a swollen hip and was pressed by a double anguish.

For the abbot of that monastery, hostile to him because of certain disputes, had forbidden all the brothers to visit him, even at the point of death. As his illness grew worse and the pain spread toward his vital organs, he asked the brothers to come to him and commend his departure to the Lord.

One brother alone had been permitted to visit him, and from him Ainfredus learned what the abbot had ordered. He took the news badly and sent word through the nobles of the city of Angers—who, because they loved him, could not be prevented from visiting him—to ask the abbot to have mercy on him, since he was prepared to make satisfaction if he had done anything wrong against him [Col. 0845A].

But because the abbot delayed, the sick man was forced to seek consolation elsewhere. Seeing that his temporal abbot despised him, he turned with his whole mind to the one who, for many ages, had devoted the care of his solicitude to legions of monks. Recalling how much affection he had found among the fathers of this monastery of Fleury during his pilgrimage, he turned his head toward the wall, his face covered with tears, and burst into these words:

“O holy Benedict, have mercy on me, who anxiously implore your help and promise you that, if you obtain bodily health and a prosperous life for me from God, I shall humbly seek your most sacred bones and offer thanks as far as I am able” [Col. 0845B].

After he had finished this prayer, he suddenly saw—as he later reported—a man of unknown appearance, covered in a monastic habit, who extended his hand toward the side of the ulcer and then seemed silently to depart.

At once the sick man fell asleep. He had spent three nights and more without sleep, but now enjoyed the most peaceful rest for the space of an hour. When he awoke, he carelessly pressed with his fingertips the wound which the violence of the disease had opened. A piece of rotten flesh, like a mushroom, burst out from it, together with much of the pain. In a short time he regained his strength and devoutly fulfilled what he had vowed, not without making an offering.

## CHAPTER XV. Patriciacus (Pressy) in Burgundy. The relics of Saint Benedict and others are carried there against raiders. Candles twice rekindled from heaven; relics given as a reward for learning.

[Col. 0845C]

35. Patriciacus is the name of an estate situated in the territory of Autun, in the region of Burgundy. Echardus, the wealthiest count of the Burgundians, generously granted it to Saint Benedict and the brothers of the monastery of Fleury for their support and expenses.

After Echardus died and was buried at the monastery of Fleury beside the church of Saint Mary, the brothers established a dwelling for themselves on the aforementioned property. Relics of the holy Father Benedict were also brought there from Fleury, and a church was built in honor of God, the glorious virgin Mary, and that outstanding confessor himself.

Christ the Lord, through the merits of his holy Mother and of his beloved servant Benedict, has very often made this church illustrious through miracles [Col. 0845D]. Since many of them have been consigned to oblivion through our negligence, we shall commit to the memory of posterity, for the praise of almighty God and his saints, the few that have come to our unworthy notice.

36. Certain men of perverse mind were attempting to invade the estate of Solinarius, which was subject to the monastery of Patriciacus mentioned above. The monk Robert, then in charge of that place, wished to resist their wickedness. As the time of the grape harvest approached, he hurried there with the relics of the saints [Col. 0846A].

As they traveled, the bearers of the holy relics reached the monastery of Cluny and rested there for the night. On the following day, as they were about to take up the road, the brothers of that monastery led them forth with a great procession. Then, as they were leaving the basilica of Saint Benedict, rain arose with the wind and completely extinguished the candles that had been lit in honor of God and his saints.

But before they had left the gate of that monastery’s fortress, the sky cleared, the candles were rekindled by divine power before everyone’s eyes, and for some distance along the road they could not be extinguished by any blasts of wind.

In the same way, when they had completed the business for which they had gone and had taken the holy relics from the tabernacle beneath which they had remained, the extinguished lamps were illuminated by divine power. They did not lose their light through any breath of air until the relics had departed from the land of Saint Benedict [Col. 0846B].

The relics carried with the protection of our holy Father Benedict were those of the most blessed confessors Eucherius and Veranus, as well as of the martyrs Cyprian, Speratus, and Pantaleon.

As we learned from the account of our elders, a certain bishop of Lyons had once given these relics to a monk of this holy congregation as a reward for his diligent service, because the monk had instructed him in the liberal studies [Note: Leidradus arranged for the relics of Saint Cyprian to be brought from Arles to Lyons, as Ado testifies in his Martyrology. Charles the Bald later brought them to Compiègne, into the basilica he had built, where they are preserved to this day. But this passage cannot refer to Leidradus, because the donation of Patriciacus to Fleury took place later] [Col. 0846D].

The monk deposited them in the oratory of the same estate of Patriciacus, so that the place might thereby become more renowned.

## CHAPTER XVI. A threatening blasphemer against Saint Benedict perishes. Two women are healed of four diseases.

[Col. 0846C]

37. A certain Bernard, an illustrious man of the same region of Burgundy and lord of the castle called Uzon [or Vizon], was at odds with a certain kinsman by marriage, no less powerful, named Lotboldus.

While devastating the latter’s possessions by raids, Bernard also wished to drive away cattle from estates belonging to the monastery of Patriciacus mentioned above. When certain servants of Saint Benedict resisted him, he killed them.

For this reason Robert, the aforementioned prior, approached him and humbly asked him to make lawful amends to Saint Benedict and his monks for the wrong he had inflicted upon their servants in violation of the law.

Full of the spirit of defiance, Bernard replied in these words [Col. 0846D]:

“I am amazed, lord Robert, that so wise a man has fallen into such folly that you demand compensation from me for this matter, when you ought rather to ask me not to add worse things.”

Then he added: “I call upon the Lord who caused me to be born as witness that, before fifteen suns have passed from this day, I shall prove by experiment whether Saint Benedict can prevail over fire, or whether fire, set by me against his houses, will prevail over Saint Benedict, who is trying to defend my enemy within his own castle.”

The monk, moved by these words, said [Col. 0847A]: “I trust in the Lord and in the merits of his saints that you will neither accomplish these things nor live beyond the limit you have set for yourself.”

The truth of events followed this statement. After the venerable Robert had returned to the monastery, and before the appointed days had passed, the aforementioned Bernard was pierced by a lance and killed by the enemy he encountered, the aforesaid Lotboldus. He was certainly destined to undergo with fire that prolonged contest which he had falsely sworn he would bring against Saint Benedict within a short time.

38. To this miraculous vengeance let us add four notable healings granted by Christ in the same monastery of Patriciacus to only two persons of the female sex, through the merits of his holy Mother, the renowned confessor Benedict, and the other saints whose protection is present there [Col. 0847B].

## CHAPTER XVII. A mute and lame woman is healed.

39. A certain woman named Adelais, deprived of the use of her tongue and feet, came to the monastery mentioned above, crawling on her hands.

She lay for some time before the monastery gates. From the brothers she asked, by gestures of her hands, for the support of life; from the saints she sought, with the voice of her heart, the aid of healing.

One day—namely, the Tuesday before holy Pentecost, whose feast that year fell on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June [Note: That is, in the year 1005, when holy Easter fell on the first of April and Pentecost on 20 May]—she perceived that the hour of her cure had arrived.

Coming before the church, she asked by whatever signs she could make that the entrance be opened to her. When this had been granted, she dragged herself across the ground and entered the oratory. At the very entrance, before the altar of the holy and undivided Trinity, she suddenly stopped and began gradually to raise herself from the ground [Col. 0847C].

Why delay with more words? Within a brief moment she was standing completely upright. She proceeded with straight steps to the altar of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and of the confessor of Christ, Benedict, and prostrated herself as though in prayer.

A little later she rose, lifted her hands on high, and burst into these words:

“I give thanks to you, my Lady, holy Mary, Queen of virgins, and to you, Saint Benedict. Through your intercession almighty God has granted me, crooked and mute as I was, uprightness of limbs and speech.

Nor do I offer less thanksgiving to you, saints of God, Eucherius and Veranus. I do not doubt that, often entreated, you have been helpers of my healing” [Col. 0847D].

She spent nearly the whole night in these words. That day was the feast of the blessed Romanus, disciple and fosterer of our most holy Father Benedict [Note: You see that in ancient times the feast day of Saint Romanus the abbot, the pupil or fosterer of the holy Father Benedict, was celebrated. His Life is preserved in the First Century]. The brothers were singing hymns to God at Compline, and, when the bells immediately rang out, they joyfully rendered praises to God for the miracle that had been displayed.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Another woman unable to walk. Disabled again, and healed again.

40. Since Christ ordained that he should continue to make his saints illustrious through miracles, on the ninth day after this sign had occurred—namely, on the third day before the Kalends of June—another woman was brought there [Col. 0848A].

Her name was Alexandra. Two men carried her on a litter of the kind customarily used to transport stones, and she asked to be brought into the basilica.

At the same place where the earlier woman had been restored to standing, Alexandra inclined herself in prayer and shortly afterward began gradually to raise herself. The brothers who had gathered for so wondrous a spectacle wished to assist her and supported her by lifting her among their hands.

At about the third hour of the day, the hour at which she had been brought there, she was granted complete health and remained in the service of the church for several months.

41. After asking and obtaining from Robert, the aforementioned prior of that place, permission to return home, she promised that she would return to the service of the shrine she had begun. But while she delayed her return, she fell again into her former illness.

Meanwhile, as she sought someone to carry her back to the place of her healing and found no one, she began to be anxious and sorrowful. At last necessity found a solution: she vowed to God and to Saint Benedict that, if the health granted to her were restored so that she could return to the monastery mentioned above, she would never again depart from it.

As soon as she made this vow, she immediately regained the firmest strength to walk in the place where she was staying. Setting aside every reason for delay, she returned to the monastery of Saint Benedict at Patriciacus, where she had previously been healed.

When she related to the brothers everything that had happened to her and promised that she would never leave them again, they together blessed the Lord and his servant, our most holy Father Benedict. They gave thanks to him who, by deeming his little servants worthy of a spiritual visitation, gladdened them with miracles—servants whom the absence of his sacred body might perhaps have saddened [Col. 0848C].

And so that no doubt might remain concerning the miraculous benefits bestowed, they carefully questioned the neighbors of both women. They also questioned the host of the woman who had first been healed, asking whether he had ever seen her speaking or walking properly.

From him and from the others who knew both women, they learned that the women had truly been disabled and had truly been healed by Christ through the merits of his holy Mother and of his beloved Benedict.

## CHAPTER XIX. A fire is extinguished on the feast of the translation.

[Col. 0848D]

42. When our venerable Father Abbo, in the order related above, departed to the heavenly realms, certain misfortunes immediately befell us, especially those of us who had remained attached to his service. Passing over the other troubles, it may not seem burdensome to our hearers to commit one to memory—the one that would almost have overwhelmed this sacred monastery with an intolerable loss, had the pious clemency of Christ, the heavenly King, moved by the intercession of his holy Mother and our Father Benedict, not withdrawn the hand raised to avenge our crimes. For since it has been demonstrated in the preceding signs [Col. 0849A] how powerful this outstanding leader of ours, Benedict, ever to be named, proved himself separately in the two elements, water and fire, it will here become clear how powerful he was in both at one and the same time—or, to speak more accurately, in a single instant.

43. A day renowned throughout our world had dawned: the feast of the translation of that supreme confessor, which returns to us every year on the fifth day before the Ides of July [July 11] as a joyful and welcome festival. When the entire night of the vigil, together with the following day, had suitably been spent in the praises owed to God out of devotion to so great a Father, after the appointed meal and the evening service the hour of rest arrived. As we desired to steal our eyes away from the day’s labor, the ancient enemy’s deceptive ambushes appeared. [Col. 0849B] For, instigated by him, certain men of perverse mind—out of a desire to commit robbery, as some report—set fire to the buildings outside; according to others, however, fire accidentally broke out in those same buildings.

As a result, when an uproar had been raised, the brothers awoke and hurried to extinguish the ravenous flames. First they removed, wherever opportunity allowed, all the furnishings of the basilica, which adorned the interior of the church no less—indeed, in every respect more—than in the earlier fire. Then they turned unanimously to the work just mentioned; but their labor was fruitless. For as the fire rose upward, driven by the breath of the winds, it suddenly seized the guesthouse kitchen, which stood near the hall of holy Mary, Mother of God, where the precious confessor of the Lord, [Col. 0849C] Benedict, rests.

Then great fear seized everyone, for they dreaded that, because of that building, the church venerable to all who fear the Lord might be burned. Therefore some of our number, with the voice of the inner person, begged holy Mary, Mother of God, and her illustrious servant Benedict to aid them with pious prayers, repeatedly invoking the name of his sister Scholastica. Others repeated the same plea aloud, though in plaintive words.

At last the Almighty heard the prayers of the saints just mentioned, and thundered from the clear part of the sky. Then, although the sky had been completely serene, a sudden shower poured from the clouds and utterly extinguished the flames that were consuming the inner buildings of the fortress. [Col. 0849D] The winds changed direction, and forced the falling embers—which were being carried inward in such abundance that they resembled falling snow—to turn back upon themselves.

Thus, through the merits of our outstanding protector Benedict, not only did the monastery remain unharmed, but not even as much of the village was burned as had perished in the earlier fire, which had occurred on the same feast and in the time of the aforesaid venerable abbot Abbo. Therefore, quite appropriately, legions of monks can apply to their lord Benedict the following commendation of a certain wise man, without distortion or embellishment: [Col. 0850A]

“O one exceedingly beloved by God, heaven serves you,  
and the winds, conspiring together, come to your trumpet-call.”  
(From Claudian, *Panegyric on Honorius*.)

Let us say a few words about this matter by way of a brief prelude. It seemed fitting, I think, for our lawgiving saint, when the elements were in turmoil, to call upon the assistance of his venerable sister, whom he remembered as having opposed the storms when she wished to retain him with her. Thus, intending vigorously to resist the aerial powers that were trying to overturn the places dear to them, he wished that same sister to be invoked together with him by his servants, since he knew that her prayers would be effective in obtaining from the Lord an outpouring of rain.

## CHAPTER XX. A crippled woman is made upright.

[Col. 0850B]

44. We have recently learned that a certain girl named Adelaide, of long-standing noble birth, was crippled in her legs. Her father and mother had taken her through many holy places, but they could obtain no remedy for her from the saints. Having despaired of her recovery, they brought her home and remained in sorrow, not knowing what to do with her.

For they had taken her to Paris [Note: [Col. 0849D] That is, in the suburban territory of Paris, a single location sufficient to explain certain passages of ancient authors who place the basilica renowned for the tomb of Saint Denis at Paris. For no one who has read the *Life of Saint Abbo*, chapter 9, will deny that in Aimoinus’s time it stood five miles from the city. See the *Eulogy of Abbot Fulrad* in Part II of the third century.] to the tomb of Saint Denis, and to Limoges, to the tomb of the lord Martial, both of whom at that time shone forth through miracles; yet they had achieved absolutely nothing.

While her mother was sleeping, however, a heavenly voice came to her and said: “What madness,” it said, “has driven you to waste such great expenses in vain, so that you might seek the patronage of saints far away, while leaving here your own neighbor, the most holy and beloved of the Lord, Benedict? His most sacred bones have been divinely transferred from the province of Italy to this region for your salvation—and that of many others—if only you seek it in faith. Know for certain, therefore, that your daughter cannot be healed unless she is taken to him.” [Col. 0850C]

The woman awoke and related the dream to her husband, who was lying beside her. He said to her: “I had already conceived the same idea in my mind; but I fear that, angered by our contempt, that saint may not wish to entreat the Lord for her.”

She replied: “Let her be taken to the saint’s tomb; and if he heals her, let him possess her as a servant forever. But if he is unwilling, let her be brought back, retaining her freedom along with her disability.” For they were not only free, but also extremely distinguished by birth and wealthy.

At sunrise, therefore, they set out for the monastery, which was no more than eighteen miles from their home, taking their disabled daughter with them. The celebrated feast of that most holy Benedict was approaching, and on the very day of the feast they presented her to the holy Father Benedict to be healed. The following morning, when they arose and wished to return, they found their daughter healed and sound in all her limbs. [Col. 0850D]

For this reason, they offered immense thanks to God and to his most blessed friend Benedict, and entrusted their daughter to him to serve him perpetually. Later she married and bore children; some of her descendants still remain in the service of the brothers, not without usefulness. [Col. 0851A]

[Note: [Col. 0851C] That is, servants devoted to monasteries; if they had children, those children too were bound to the monasteries.]

## CHAPTER XXI. Two blind men received their sight.

45. A recent event, which I am about to relate, also took place. A certain blind man, a resident of the fortress of Argentomagus, received his sight immediately when he touched the reliquary as the brothers were carrying the relics of that pre-eminent confessor of Christ, Benedict, from the cell of Salense to Saint Marcellus the Martyr. [Note: [Col. 0851C] Saint Marcellus is said to have won the palm of martyrdom at the fortress of Argentomagus, according to the *Life of Saint Genulfus, Bishop*; nevertheless, the village of Saint-Marcel lies below Argentomagus.]

The body of that holy martyr rests in a church built not far from the fortress. When the reliquary had repeatedly been carried from there to the monastery of Salense by its own people, another blind man from a village belonging to that monastery, named Modicia, arrived there, invoking Saint Benedict in a loud voice. For the report of the aforementioned miracle had already reached his ears. He too, not long after arriving there, through God’s mercy and by the saints’ merits, was deemed worthy to receive the sight he requested.

In that monastery of Salense, therefore, Benedict, the Father of monks venerable throughout the whole world, shines with such great and such continual miracles, especially in avenging enemies, that if someone wished to commit them all to memory, they would require a volume of their own.

## CHAPTER XXII. The author omitted many things.

[Col. 0852A]

46. These miracles, which God has deigned to perform through the merits of his saint Benedict in various places, we have published in an inept style and rustic language. Nevertheless, as we bring the work to a close, we warn the reader that we have deliberately passed over many things. In every matter all excess must be avoided; the attention of listeners should be invited by agreeable brevity, not driven away by wearisome talkativeness.

This, then, will be the end of the book—although, if the Lord wills and life remains with us, those things that faithful report has spread through nearly all Neustria will by no means be left unspoken through our negligence. Our friends [f., enemies] also compel us to keep silent, for they consider it a lavish feast if they can sink a tooth into the work of others. Nevertheless, no detraction of theirs will frighten us away from recounting the praises of God and of his beloved, namely our most blessed Father Benedict.

All these things, therefore, together with the miracles described by other authors in the earlier work, Jesus Christ our Lord has deigned to perform through the merits of his holy confessor Benedict in various places, under the rule of thirty [Note: [Col. 0851C] Thus five are missing from the commonly circulated catalogues, in which Gauzlinus, to whom Aimoinus dedicates these books, occupies the twenty-fifth place.] abbots who governed this monastery of Fleury from the beginning of its foundation for three hundred and eighty-five [Note: [Col. 0852C] Aimoinus, followed by Helgaudus, dates the establishment of the monastery of Fleury to the year 620 of Christ, through an erroneous comparison of the year of the Incarnation with the second year of Clovis the Younger, son of the great Dagobert; in that year the foundations of the monastery were laid. See the *Dissertation on the Translation of the Body of Saint Benedict into Gaul* in Part II of the second century.] years and more. He lives and reigns as God, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, in the perfect Trinity, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0851]

# AIMOINUS OF FLEURY’S SERMON ON THE FEASTS OF SAINT FATHER BENEDICT

(First published by John a Bosco, *Bibliotheca Floriacensis*, vol. I, p. 271.)

[Col. 0851D] At the annual birthdays of earthly emperors, it was once customary for subject kings to present them with the greatest gifts. Each man therefore exerted himself on his own behalf, striving to ensure that another would not appear superior to him in offering presents.

By this example, it is fitting for each of us, on the solemn feasts of the saints, to offer God pleasing gifts. If someone lacks an abundance of gold or silver, let him at least display the service of devotion and pour out prayers to the Lord, asking him graciously to accept his vow in due form. And although praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner (*Ecclesiasticus* 15), each of us ought nevertheless to strive, in accordance with the Psalmist’s admonition, to praise the Lord in his saints (*Psalm* 150).

Therefore, moved by the gentle kindness of our most beloved patron Benedict—who never ceases to help us through his holy intercessions—we have thought it appropriate to gather together, in summary, all that various authors have scattered through their writings about his praise, and to offer it, however small yet faithful, as a gift of our service at his sacred solemnities. [Col. 0852D] In this way his praise may be seen to spread among many, and whoever has been unable to possess all the authors’ volumes may rejoice to find the praises of his nursling collected in one place. This, then, will be the beginning of the promised undertaking.

The goodness of the heavenly Majesty, rewarding its chosen ones with heavenly gifts, also enriches them on earth with exceptional proclamations of praise. By spreading these praises among the peoples through its servants—men of supreme eloquence—it grants that their great merit before God may be illuminated in eloquent writings.

Thus it bestowed upon Benedict, a servant of outstanding merit, such a privilege above the other Fathers of the holy Church that Gregory, the foremost of teachers and apostolic bishop of the holy see, expanded the praises of his life in honeyed speech. Of many saints he extracted only two or three miracles; but he proclaimed with sweetest eloquence what Benedict’s life had been from his earliest years and how wondrous his passing had been.

In the book of his *Life*, among the other praises of this saint, Gregory compares him with certain ancient Fathers in particular miraculous deeds. Above all, he compares him with the holy prophet Elisha in the matter of the iron that both of them, as he records, drew back from the depths of the water.

Yet, without detracting from the authority of that holy pope Gregory, we may say that the deeds of the holy prophet Elisha are almost entirely similar to the deeds of our holy Father Benedict. Let us therefore speak a little about both of them, as though preaching.

When the disciples asked the Lord in the Gospel about the coming of Elijah, he replied: “Elijah has already come” (Matthew 17:12); and shortly afterward: “If you are willing to understand, he himself is Elijah” (Matthew 11:14). It is therefore clear what merit Elijah possessed, since he is equated with John, of whom Truth itself testifies that “among those born of women no one has arisen greater than he” (Matthew 11:11).

When Elijah was about to be taken by the Lord into heaven, he had Elisha as his disciple and instructed him to ask whatever he wished before Elijah was taken away. Elisha replied: “I ask that your spirit may be doubled in me” (2 Kings 2:9). Elijah agreed, saying: “If you see me when I am taken from you” (ibid., 10). Elisha saw him and obtained what he had asked.

We have recounted this because we wish to show how great was the merit of our holy and blessed Father Benedict, whose deeds are entirely like those of the man who possessed Elijah’s spirit—that is, Elisha. When the deeds of that venerable Benedict are compared with Elisha’s deeds, they appear as follows.

After the translation of his master, Elisha divided the Jordan with the mantle that had fallen from him and crossed over (ibid., 14). Blessed Father Benedict, by the power of his merits, caused his beloved disciple Maurus to walk upon the waters and restored the boy Placid to life after he had already been submerged. It is not for this work to discuss which of these deeds is greater, especially since the venerable Odo has given this miracle its own interpretation, comparing it with Moses’ deed in the division of the Red Sea.

It is enough briefly to indicate that in Elisha one sign was performed in the division of the water, whereas through blessed Benedict a double benefit appeared: the crossing of the water and the salvation of the brother. There, the master’s garment accomplished the deed; here, the rescued boy saw the abbot’s *melota* [sheepskin cloak] carried upon him and himself snatched from the waters by it.

When Elisha returned after Elijah’s translation, the sons of the prophets insisted, even against his will, that he permit them to search for his lord, lest he had perhaps been carried away and hidden in one of the valleys or on one of the mountains. They searched, therefore, but found nothing (2 Kings 2:16–17).

By contrast, blessed Father Benedict, abandoning human society for the love of God and seeking the hollows of the rocks, was sought by a priest who had been divinely warned—through underground passages and over the precipitous slopes of the mountains—and was found. He was informed that it was Easter and was refreshed with food.

As Elisha was ascending into the mountains, boys mocked him, saying: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead” (2 Kings 2:23). The demons, who are indeed infants in goodness, attacked Father Benedict, whose spirit continually yearned upward toward heavenly things, with curses, saying: “Accursed one, not Benedict; what have you to do with us? Why are you persecuting us?” But bears came out of the forest and devoured the mocking boys. The cursing demons are perpetually burned by the fires of eternal Gehenna.

When three kings—the king of Israel, the king of Judah, and the king of Edom—were conducting a campaign against the king of Moab and were suffering from thirst, Elisha ordered them to dig pits in the dried bed of the torrent. Water flowed from them and satisfied the exhausted army (2 Kings 3:18).

The venerable Benedict instructed monks from three monasteries founded by him, who had come to him because of a shortage of water, to dig into the rock on which they had found three stones placed by him. When they had done so, a spring immediately emerged, which still flows as a stream today (2 *Dialogues*, chapter 5).

A certain woman, suffering accusations from the creditor of her deceased husband, approached the prophet Elisha, seeking both counsel and assistance from him. Through his merits, the oil that the woman declared she possessed increased so greatly that she could repay the creditor and still have enough left over to live abundantly with her children (2 Kings 4:6).

In the same way, a man oppressed by debt approached Benedict, beloved of the Lord, owing twelve solidi. The compassionate Father helped him by giving him thirteen solidi, which he had received by divine provision, instructing him to repay twelve to the moneylender and retain the thirteenth for his own use (2 *Dialogues*, chapter 27).

Likewise, when a cleric requested a glass vessel, Benedict gave it together with oil; at the cleric’s prayer, he filled an empty barrel so completely that the overflowing oil wet the floor.

Elisha’s power restored the Shunammite woman’s son from the dead to life through prayer. The merit of the venerable Benedict, through holy prayers, restored a peasant’s son alive to his father.

When Elisha was staying at Gilgal, and the sons of the prophets who lived there with him had eaten something poisonous cooked in a pot, they escaped the danger of death when Elisha’s hand healed it (2 Kings 4:40). Similarly, Father Benedict reduced to nothing, by the sign of the cross, the cup of poison offered to him by false brothers. [Col. 0855A]

He also taught a boy who had furtively hidden a flask sent by a faithful man to avoid the serpent’s poison, for by prophetic spirit he knew that a serpent had already entered the vessel (2 *Dialogues*, throughout).

A third instance of the power of our holy Father Benedict shone forth in this single deed of Elisha, when he had a bread infected with poison thrown far away by a raven so that the pestilence would not spread to others.

Behold, it is clearer than daylight how great a merit Benedict, the shining jewel of monks, possesses before the Lord. In one deed of Elisha, whom the Holy Spirit had clothed with a double gift, Benedict shone forth with a fourfold miracle: the poison poured out, the flask discovered with the serpent, the obedient raven, and the poisonous bread thrown far away.

Although in these miracles he may also be compared with other Fathers, especially the holy Elisha, our sole purpose here has been to compare the life of this saint with the deeds of the righteous Elisha.

Elisha provided food for one hundred men from twenty loaves, and bread remained over (2 Kings 4:42, 44). Benedict, the servant of God, obtained divine assistance for brothers suffering from want through the provision of two hundred measures of flour, brought from an unknown source.

When Naaman the Syrian was afflicted with the destructive contagion of leprosy, Elisha ordered him to wash seven times in the Jordan. He went, washed, and returned cleansed to the kingdom of Syria (2 Kings 5:10–19).

A small boy struck by elephantiasis was brought to Benedict, the man of God; after recovering his former health, he returned home unharmed. Another man, who had acquired a discolored skin through drinking poison, was restored by the same man of God, Benedict, to his former appearance.

Gehazi, the servant of Elisha, the man of God, was detected by prophetic spirit in having received clothing and gifts from Naaman, and he too was given leprosy (ibid., 22, 27). A monk, likewise recognized through the prophetic spirit of Benedict, the man of God, as having received handkerchiefs from nuns and put them in his bosom (see the entire book of Gregory’s *Dialogues*), confessed his fault and was immediately granted not punishment but the most indulgent pardon.

We must remain silent about the iron that returned from the depths of the water, so that due honor may be given to the supreme bishop Gregory, who in this sign equated our most blessed Father Benedict with the holy Elisha.

Moreover, the fact that Elisha announced to the king of Israel, through messengers and by prophetic inspiration, the plans of the king of Syria is comparable to the occasion when venerable Benedict sent word to brothers building a wall and warned them to beware, because an evil spirit was coming to them in ambush.

Elisha, surrounded by Syrians, showed his servant, who could not see them, the army of angels sent from heaven to help him. Our Benedict, although in a different matter, did something similar when he showed his beloved disciple Maurus an unclean demon dragging a monk out of the oratory.

Elisha did not permit the Syrians who had surrounded him and whom he had struck blind to be killed after leading them into Samaria before the king of Israel. [Col. 0856A] Instead, he restored their former sight, fed them with bread and water, and allowed them to return to their own people.

The venerable Benedict terrified Zalla, who was raging and stubbornly threatening him, merely by looking at him; he refreshed him with food and made him less cruel thereafter by a simple command.

When Elisha foretold to the king of Israel that famine—which had afflicted the people while the Syrians besieged Samaria—would be followed by an abundance of grain, one of the officers, on whose hand the king leaned, remained incredulous and opposed to the prophet. He heard these words from the man of God: “You will see it, and afterward you shall not eat” (2 Kings 7:19). Remaining in his unbelief, he saw the abundance of food, in accordance with the man of God’s word, but was trampled by the people at the entrance of the gates and died (ibid., 20).

A case not very different from this occurred when a certain cleric, freed from a demon by Benedict, the servant of the Lord Jesus Christ, received from him the command neither to eat meat nor to dare approach sacred orders; if he presumed to do so, he would immediately be handed over to the devil’s jurisdiction. As long as he obeyed Benedict’s commands, he remained unharmed. But when, disobedient and as though incredulous toward the mouth of God, he entered the sacred orders, he was immediately persuaded by the demon and remained in the same punishment until the end of his life.

When Azael, who later became king in Syria, consulted Elisha about the welfare of his lord Ben-hadad, the man of God said among other things: “I know the evils that you will do to the children of Israel: you will capture their fortified cities, tear open their pregnant women, and kill their children with the sword” (2 Kings 8:12).

In similar fashion, the Gothic king Totila came to Benedict, the man of God, prostrated himself before him, and was raised from the ground by him. He heard Benedict say to him: “You do many evils; you have done many evils. At last, restrain yourself from wickedness. Indeed, you will enter Rome, you will cross the sea, you will reign for nine years, and in the tenth you will die.”

Although, as already stated, it had not been our intention to do anything except compare the deeds of our holy Father Benedict solely with the deeds of blessed Elisha, the mention of King Totila has provided a suitable opportunity to recall a memorable saying about another holy prophet, which may be compared with one of the deeds of this illustrious confessor.

The wife of Jeroboam, who caused Israel to sin, went to consult the prophet Ahijah about her sick son. Because the prophet’s eyes had grown dim with old age so that he could not see, she changed her clothing so that she would not be recognized. But when the venerable prophet perceived her not with bodily but with spiritual eyes, he said to her: “Enter, wife of Jeroboam. Why do you pretend to be someone else?” (1 Kings 14:6.)

The corresponding event is that, when King Totila was informed that the man of the Lord Benedict possessed the spirit of prophecy, he wished to put this to the test and announced that he himself would come to him. Instead, he sent his sword-bearer, named Rigo, dressed in royal clothing and accompanied by a great crowd of attendants, so that the king might be thought to be present both from the garments and from the service of the leaders.

When Rigo approached, the man of God went out to meet him and, while he was still some distance away, shouted and commanded: “Put down, my son; put down what you are carrying. It is not yours.” Rigo returned to his lord in shame, and Totila himself approached the man of God. From him he heard the words that had been foretold by the prophet.

But let us return to our Elisha—ours, certainly, because we consider him worthy of special affection above the other prophets, since his deeds resemble those of our holy Father Benedict.

Let us therefore compare the last of Elisha’s miracles with one of Benedict’s miracles, though by no means the last among the wonders he performed. After that servant of God had departed from this present life, some men were burying a corpse. When they saw robbers, they threw the body into Elisha’s tomb. As soon as it touched him, the dead man rose and returned to his own people.

Likewise, through the most blessed Benedict and his venerable sister Scholastica, when their most sacred bones were being joyfully carried from the regions of Italy into Gaul, two dead persons were restored to life.

These, then, are the things that our blessed Father Benedict and the holy prophet Elisha share. We fear, however, that some admirer of this distinguished confessor may object that, while wishing to exalt him with praises, we may seem to have diminished him by comparing him with only one prophet.

Whoever he may be, let him know—and let him consider this our answer—that we have not equated Benedict with just any prophet; rather, we have equated him with the one in whom the double spirit of Elijah came to rest.

And lest this objection prevail, let him, if he pleases, briefly compare Benedict with both new and ancient Fathers: in the restoration of the sieve, with John, beloved of the Lord, who joined fragments of jewels into a whole; in his desert life from childhood, with Elijah or John the Baptist; in relinquishing leadership, with Samuel or John the Baptist himself, who, born of a supreme priest, preferred to inhabit the deserts of the wilderness rather than hold the pre-eminence of the priesthood; in prophesying the destruction of his monastery, or the overthrow of the city of Rome, with Isaiah, or rather Jeremiah, who mourned the ruin of the city of Jerusalem in a double alphabet.

In this deed he also imitated the example of his Lord, the Redeemer of all, Jesus Christ. For the gracious Jesus, weeping, foretold the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, which hated him. His true servant Benedict, grieving and lamenting, foretold that the dwellings dear to him had been divinely handed over to destruction by the nations.

Indeed, ravens once served Elijah as providers of food; they followed blessed Father Benedict as he traveled, flying around him. They served Elijah only for the provision of food; but they served Father Benedict not only in carrying the poisoned bread, but also as companions on his journey.

Let him be compared, as is fitting, in legislation with Moses. Although Moses gave the law to only one people, the chosen of God, scattered everywhere among tribes, languages, and nations through the venerable Father, were called sons with paternal gentleness and admonished to submit their necks to Christ’s gentle yoke.

We pray that these things, which we have expressed in an abbreviated manner, will not displease the supporters of so illustrious a confessor. As for what has been written by blessed Gregory, we leave it to his excellence. We openly acknowledge this about ourselves: the glory of our holy Father is not spread by our praises to the extent that the sweet eloquence of that bishop proclaimed it.

That blessed pope Gregory, as John, the more extensive author of his *Life*, testifies, sent preachers to the English people and instructed them to observe especially, after the holy Gospel, the teaching of this most gentle lawgiver. In his *Dialogues*, after explaining the life of that most holy Father—which he placed second—he introduced certain additional matters in the third book, chapter 16, as though they had escaped his memory.

Speaking of a certain holy man named Martin, he said:

“This man of the Lord, undoubtedly Martin, when he first withdrew to that same mountain, before living in a closed cave, fastened his foot with an iron chain and attached the other end to a rock, so that he could not go farther than the length of that chain allowed. When the venerable Benedict, whose memory I have mentioned above, heard this, he arranged to send him a message through his disciple: ‘If you are a servant of God, let an iron chain not hold you, but the chain of Christ.’ At these words Martin immediately removed the fetter. But afterward he never stretched his freed foot beyond the place to which he had been accustomed to extend it while it was chained.”

In the fourth book, while speaking about the departure of souls, Gregory recalled a miracle that he had described in the *Life* of our lawgiver Benedict—one that, because of its greatness, might perhaps have become doubtful in the minds of the weak—and added another incident that he had not previously reported. He said in chapter 8:

“In the second book of this work I already mentioned that the venerable Benedict, as I learned from his faithful disciples, while staying far from the city of Capua, saw in the middle of the night the soul of Germanus, bishop of that same city, carried to heaven by angels in a globe of fire. As he watched that soul ascending, the breast of his mind opened, and he saw the entire world gathered before his eyes, as though beneath a single ray of the sun.

“I also learned from the disciples of blessed Benedict that two noble men, educated in secular studies, were brothers, one named Speciosus and the other Gregory, and that they devoted themselves to a holy way of life under his rule. The same venerable Father had them live in the monastery he had built near the city of Terracina. They had possessed much money in this world, but gave everything to the poor for the redemption of their souls and remained in that monastery.

“One of them, Speciosus, had been sent near the city of Capua for the monastery’s benefit. One day his brother Gregory was sitting at table and eating with the brothers when, lifted up in spirit, he saw the soul of his brother Speciosus, who was so far away, depart from his body. He immediately told the brothers and ran there. He found that his brother had already been buried, and at the very hour when he had seen him leave his body, he found that he had died.”

Nevertheless, a certain wise man of this place, named Gausbertus, who had been thoroughly trained from childhood in the liberal arts, added the following preface to the life of this outstanding Father:

“Renowned by lineage, learning, merits, and name,  
this book contains the life of an abbot.  
God, making him powerful in his eternal dwelling,  
granted him to be heir to his own name.  
For Benedict was, is, and will rightly be called Benedict:  
as you reread his deeds, you can prove it.  
So that no one might be allowed to doubt them,  
they obtained an outstanding witness to themselves.  
For the Roman bishop, known above the heavens,  
Gregory, joyfully made these things public to the world.  
He varied them honorably in a dialogic form,  
so that the discourse would be more pleasing to the reader.  
Then follows the gift divinely accomplished for us:  
the conveyance of the body of that same Father by the mouth of the leader.  
At his birth, his mother Nursia is adorned;  
Rome, his pious nurse, marvels at the child.  
At his maturity, Subiaco venerates his cave;  
Benevento possesses the fruits of the shepherd.  
Fleury flourishes with his limbs,  
and behold, the soil of Orléans covers them.  
Gaul, rejoice enough, endowed with so great a patron;  
raise yourself above the stars through his examples.  
Glory to you, Christ, who ennoble your servants  
with such a lineage and cherish them so fatherly.”

After blessed Gregory, Faustus, the author of the life of holy Maurus, relates in the following manner a miracle performed by our compassionate Father Benedict but omitted by that pontiff:

“Once Saint Benedict was entreated by a man of the highest nobility according to worldly rank to deign to come in person to his house, so that he might free the man’s wife and son—whom she had recently borne—from the demon by which both were being gravely tormented, through his holy merits and prayers. Since the man was familiar to the saint because of certain religious works he had performed, the saint did not delay going; and he restored both of them completely to health.”

After this, a certain poet named Marcus came to the same venerable Benedict and entrusted himself to his instruction. As his deacon, he composed some verses in his praise, which read as follows.

## CHAPTER I. On the oratory that Saint Father Benedict founded on the summit of the mountain, where pagan error had sacrificed to Jupiter.

While the blind crowd worshiped profaned images  
and believed that gods were made by human hands,  
it had once built temples here beside ruined altars,  
where it offered bloody sacrifices to obscene Jupiter.  
But Benedict came by command and settled in the lofty wilderness;  
the saint purified this ground,  
threw down the sculpted marble with its broken images,  
and made the temple belong to the living God.  
Let the one who desires to see the heavens opened hasten here,  
and here, mindful of his vow, preserve his devout, difficult path.  
Great things are always sought through difficult labor;  
blessed life always has a narrow way.  
When I, weighed down, had begun to climb this burdened path,  
I felt the weight laid down and removed from me.  
I believe that I shall also enjoy that blessed life,  
if you pray for your Marcus, Benedict.

The foolish people once called this place a citadel  
and made it sacred to marble gods.  
If anyone had then marked it with its true name,  
he could rightly have called it Tartarean chaos.  
To it the deluded came with blinded minds.

Improperly returning votive offerings to deadly Jupiter.

But, I think, it had marked the summit of a perverse court.

Now modern temples call it by the name “citadel.”

In them was the gate of the eternal punishments of Gehenna,

and the citadel of life is now what formerly was the citadel of death.

From it the gate of starry heaven is knocked upon,

while the blessed throng sings in angelic melodies.

From it you converse with the Thunderer, O Benedict,

dweller on the mountain and leader of the sacred choir of hermits.

## CHAPTER II.—The angels who showed him the road by which he ought to travel

[Col. 0860C]

When, warned by another, you came from that mountain,

God himself was your guide through the wilderness.

For he led two young men to every fork in the road,

so that they might assure you which path you should follow.

Here too, while you were alive, he had said to one of the righteous:

“Spare these places; another friend is here.”

## CHAPTER III.—The three ravens whom he was accustomed to feed, and who followed him from Subiaco to Benevento, for nearly fifty miles

And you would think it a fabricated tale—unless he had gone away alone—

when suddenly three ravens earned the right to follow you.

Here too the peoples call for you, who seek you as their witness,

when you await the holy festivals of the night.

[Col. 0860D]

Like those bereaved, they persist in weeping for you with hoarse utterances,

because they have been deprived of your companionship.

With you taken away, the Caelian hill shudders in darkness,

and, itself of the same color as its own mists, is strong.

## CHAPTER V.—The monks who, gathered to him from three monasteries because of the need for water, deserved to obtain abundant water flowing from the rock

The caves mourn and drip with abundant streams,

and together with their wild creatures they lament their dry haunts.

But then the rocks and thorn-bushes yielded to the well-instructed man,

and the dry earth disclosed wondrous waters.

It is certain that Christ’s mountain rules over the mountains themselves:

the mountain itself, their head, lies beneath your feet.

[Col. 0861A]

So that you, holy Father, may flourish as the highest summit,

[Note: [Col. 0861D] An obscure word.]

it flattens the swelling earth with its lowered peak,

and, lest those who seek you, Benedict, be wearied,

everywhere it lays down its sloping side gently.

Now the mountain itself rightly returns honor to you,

since, when you adorned it, it deserved so great a blessing.

You whose dry places you arrange into pleasant gardens,

and whose bare rocks you cover with fruitful vines.

The mountains, the crags (*scopula* [*scopuli]), and the seas now marvel at your gifts,

and the lovely forest flourishes with fruit-bearing branches.

Thus you direct the swift limbs of human beings toward fruitfulness;

thus you water dry hearts with a life-giving stream.

Thus, I beg, now turn the evil thorns into crops,

the thorns that torment the brutish heart of your Mark.

[Col. 0861B]

And these things Marcus, in praise of his spiritual teacher, playfully composed in verse. After him Paul, a monk of the sacred monastery of Cassino, makes mention of this holy Father of ours in the sixteenth book of his *Roman History* as follows:
