“At these very times—without doubt, at the time when the patrician Belisarius subdued the Vandals in Africa by war—the most blessed Father Benedict, dwelling after his solitary life in the holy monastery at the fortress of Cassino, shone forth in wondrous holiness and, no less prescient of future events, in virtues. Moreover, intending in the history of his own people, that is, of the Lombards, to describe the life of this same man, our protector after the Lord, in elegiac meter, he took the following as his beginning:

‘In the times of the emperor Justinian, who ruled the Roman Empire with fortunate success, who waged wars successfully and proved outstanding in civil affairs, the most blessed Benedict first shone forth at the place called Subiaco, forty miles from the city of Rome, and afterward at the fortress of Cassino, which is called Harum, both through the merits of a great life and through apostolic virtues. His life, as is known, the blessed pope Gregory set down in his *Dialogues* in gracious language. I too, Paul, his monk, according to the smallness of my ability, have woven together, in honor of so great a Father, each of his miracles in individual couplets, in elegiac meter, as follows:

Where shall I begin your triumphs, sacred Benedict?

Where shall I begin the accumulation of your virtues?

Well done, blessed Father, who emerge in accordance with your name!

Shining light of the age, well done, blessed Father!

Nursia, rejoice sufficiently, exalted by so great a child;

Nursia, bearing the stars to the world, rejoice sufficiently!

O youthful glory, surpassing your years in character,

and exceeding the old in virtue, O youthful glory!

Your flower, O paradise, despised the world’s flowering things;

your flower, O paradise, spurned the wealth of Rome.

The nurse [Note: An antiquated expression requiring excuse.] carried away the broken vessel, sorrowful at heart;

the nurse brought back the vessel restored, rejoicing.

The one bearing a name from the city [Note: St. Romanus.] hides the novice among the rocks;

he brings the help of devotion, the one bearing a name from the city.

The caves hidden from all mortals resound with praises;

the caves known to you, Christ, resound with praises.

For three tireless years he endured cold, winds, and snows;

out of love for God you despise cold, winds, and snows.

A venerable deception pleases; pious thefts are approved;

where the sacred man was lofty, a venerable deception pleases.

He signals that food is present, food for love, but the envious man resists;

nevertheless, generous faith signals that food is present.

He duly celebrates the sacred rites who lends his ear to Christ;

feeding the abstinent man, he duly celebrates the sacred rites.

Eager swineherds bring welcome food to the caves,

and with joyful hearts they bring welcome food.

Fire perishes through fire while the thorns tear the flesh;

the fleshly man is consumed by the heavenly fire; fire perishes through fire.

The hidden, wicked pestilence was detected by the watchful eye;

the hidden, wicked pestilence did not withstand the weapons of the cross.

[Col. 0862B]

Gentle scourges restrain the wandering mind by discipline;

they drive out the pestilence, gentle scourges restraining the wanderer.

A perennial stream of water flows from the native marble;

a perennial stream of water moistens dry hearts.

Iron (*Chalybs* [*Calybs*]), torn from its hilt, you sought at the bottom of the whirlpool;

you abandon the heights while seeking the depths, O iron.

Carrying out the father’s command, he slips and runs into the sea;

carried along by the waters, he runs, carrying out the father’s command.

The wave opened a path for the swimmer who was prompt to obey his master’s commands;

for the swimmer ignorant of the way, the wave opened a path.

You too, little boy, are carried away by the waves and do not perish [you are submerged];

you are a true witness, you too, little boy.

[Col. 0862C]

Faithless hearts groan, driven by wicked goads;

faithless hearts groan amid Tartarean flames.

Corax brings food offered by wicked fingers;

ordered far away, Corax brings food.

Sacred hearts grieve for the enemy destroyed by a fall.

The sacred hearts of the disciples grieve over his death.

Seeking the lovely Liris, you are accompanied by excellent guides;

you are drawn from heaven as you seek the lovely lyres (*lyris*).

Wicked serpent, you rage in the place [grove], stripped of its shrine and altars;

with the peoples lost, wicked serpent, you rage.

Away with you, wicked rider; let the marble be given to the walls;

you are compelled by command: away with you, wicked rider.

The devouring fire is seen rising in false flames,

and, shining jewel, the devouring fire is not seen for you.

While the wall is being built, the brother’s entrails are torn;

the brother is safe while the wall is being built.

Hidden deeds are exposed; the greedy are revealed openly,

and the hidden deeds of the gift received are exposed.

Savage tyrant, the nets of your deceit are frustrated;

you receive the reins of life, savage tyrant, your own.

The lofty walls of Neuma will not be overthrown by any enemy;

the whirlwind says: “It will overturn the lofty walls of Neuma.”

You are punished by a grievous enemy, lest you quarrel at the altar over the offering;

while you carry the offering to the altars, you are punished by a grievous enemy.

All the enclosures of the flock, as was foreknown, were handed over to the nation;

the same nation restores all the enclosures of the flock.

The boy, friend of deceit, is ensnared by the serpent’s persuasion;

you are not caught by the serpent, boy, friend of deceit.

Swollen mind, be silent; do not secretly censure the seer;

everything is exposed to the prophet; swollen mind, be silent.

Black hunger is driven away by food brought from heaven;

nevertheless, the black hunger of the mind is driven away.

All hearts are amazed that you were present without a body,

that you give warnings after seeing through everything; all hearts are amazed.

At the command of your voice they are not permitted to be absent from the sacred rites;

they are present at the sacred rites, at the command of your voice.

The gaping earth thrusts the human body from its bosom;

the earth holds the body by command, the gaping earth.

That treacherous dragon soothes the fugitive’s haste;

that treacherous dragon halts the forbidden journey.

The deadly evil cut off the head’s honor;

far from your dominions be that deadly evil.

The pious man has no yellow metal, yet promises it to the needy;

from heaven the pious man received the yellow metal.

You pitiable one, whose skin the serpent’s gall discolors,

you recover your skin unharmed through his compassion.

The harsh rocks seize the glass but cannot break it;

the harsh rocks preserve the glass unbroken.

Why, O steward, do you fear to provide a drop to Lechitius?

See, the jars are flowing; why, O steward, do you fear?

What remedy is there for you, whose hope of salvation is none?

You who are always afraid, what remedy is there for you?

Ah, weeping old man, you fall beneath an enemy’s blow;

but through the blow you recover, ah, weeping old man.

Barbarous reins restrain hands innocent of crime;

of their own accord the barbarous reins flee from the hands.

[Col. 0863C]

That proud man, thundering on horseback with threatening cry,

lies stretched upon the ground, that proud man on horseback.

A father’s neck bears the entrails of his dead son;

a father’s neck bears his living son.

Love conquers all; the blessed sister conquered through rain;

sleep is absent from the eyes; love conquers all.

Pleasing in simplicity, he seeks the heights like a dove;

pleasing in simplicity, he seeks the realms of heaven.

O one exceedingly well suited to God, to whom the whole world is opened!

You who examine hidden things, O one exceedingly well suited to God!

A fiery sphere bears the righteous man swimming above the ether;

the fiery sphere bears him, whom devout love commanded [or, in the variant, burned: *jussit* {*ussit*}].

Called three times, he appears as a witness to be received as a sign of novelty;

called three times, he appears, beloved through his father’s love.

Good leader, warning of battles, you strengthen hearts by examples;

you rush first into arms, good leader, warning of battles.

He gave fitting signs, leaving the fellowship of life;

hastening toward life, he gave fitting signs.

Constant psalmist, he never gave his plectrum rest;

singing sacred songs, he died, a constant psalmist.

Those who were of one mind are held in the same tomb;

equal glory holds those who were of one mind.

A splendid road appeared, glittering with torches;

the road by which the holy man ascended appeared splendid.

Seeking the rocky enclosure, she found salvation through her error;

she escaped error by seeking the rocky enclosure.

As a suppliant servant, an exile, needy and insignificant, he offered little poems (*poemata* [*carmina*]) as a gift;

an exile, needy and insignificant, he offered little poems.

I pray that they may be suitable for you, guide of the heavenly path;

O Father Benedict, I pray that they may be suitable for you.’

We also composed a hymn containing the individual miracles of that same Father, in iambic Archilochian meter, as follows:

Brothers, with joyful heart,

come with equal song:

let us enjoy the joys

of this illustrious festival.

On this day Benedict, the Father,

revealer of the narrow path,

ascended to the realms,

seeking the rewards of his labors.

[Col. 0864B]

He shone like a new star,

driving away the world’s clouds;

he resplended with miracles,

foretelling what was to come for the age.

About to bring food to several people,

he restores the little vessel.

Giving a narrow prison,

he extinguished fires with fires.

By the weapons of the cross he broke

the poison-bearing cup;

with a gentle bodily scourge

he restrained the wandering mind.

Rivers pour forth from rocks;

Chalybs returns from the whirlpool.

The ruin crushes the enemy;

the roaring lion yields, burdened.

The mass becomes light though immovable;

the phantom pyre departs.

Health returns to the broken;

the departure of the absent is revealed.

[Col. 0864C]

The crafty ruler [you are detected], wicked possessor, flees;

you are forewarned of the future;

the secret does not touch the heart.

A building is founded at a distance;

the earth vomits up corpses.

The fleeing man is restrained by the dragon;

the ether rains down coins.

[Col. 0864D]

The glass withstands the rocks;

jars flow with oil.

The vision releases the bound;

it restores life to the dead.

The power of so great a light

is conquered by the sister’s prayer.

The more anyone loves, the more powerfully he can

relate what he beholds in heaven.

Not previously known through the ages.

At night a radiance shines [shines again];

through it the whole world is seen,

and the pious man is carried upward through the flames.

These wonders, like [lacuna] nectar,

shone clearly through the plectrum;

for he suitably painted the line

[Col. 0865A]

of sacred life for its followers.

Now, leader of your disciples, sufficiently powerful,

be present to the sighs of the flock;

let him flourish in good things, avoiding the serpent,

and let the path be such as follows you.

Moreover, he took care to make known, in the briefest manner of narration, the desolation of the most sacred Mount Cassino itself, which the blessed Father Benedict had foreseen long beforehand with spiritual eyes, as well as its restoration. Yet in the very *History of the Lombards* he unwillingly bore witness to the translation of the body of that same holy Father and of his sister Scholastica to this venerable place, Floriacum (Paul of Cassino). Since all these matters have been set down almost in his own words in the first book of the *Miracles*, it is sufficient for us meanwhile to have given this preliminary account in a concise manner. One thing certainly must not be passed over: the abbot Odo, beloved of God, delivered a speech in eloquent language in praise of that same Father, and in the sermon he composed about Saint Martin he did not remain silent about this man’s praises. Smaragdus too, having composed a commentary on his Rule, prefaced it with these verses:

Whoever wishes to ascend to the eternal kingdom

must rise in mind toward the star-bearing heaven,

must seek through devout religion the path of life

by which he may swiftly climb to the golden realms.

The Rule of the holy Father Benedict is for monks

a perfect, level, gentle, and broad way,

rough for boys and narrow for novices,

whom a nursing life long nourished in its bosom.

This is the holy way, the shining path of heaven,

which God’s blessed camps desire to tread.

This lofty Rule admonishes all monks

to be free from possessions and seek the heavenly kingdoms;

to abandon what is their own, so that they may possess all things as their own—

the prosperity of the heavenly kingdoms that awaits their companions.

In the sacred song of the Law, from our fathers,

this is called the royal way for those who walk straight.

This is life for the good, and also the rule of salvation;

a bow and weapons for the devout, cold arrows for the wicked.

No one unwillingly fulfills it, but everyone who desires it does;

it is burdensome to the burdensome, gentle and suitable to the good.

This flower-bearing Rule shows the monks [the heavenly paradise commands and teaches them]

to desire the light-filled place (desire the place).

[Col. 0865D]

It chastises its children with good maternal love,

rebuking as it instructs and admonishing without bitterness.

It patiently nourishes them with a tender beating,

and after death it will give many bright rewards.

It opens the road to the upright and the heavens to its friends;

let them not be reluctant to run, but let them proceed patiently.

It examines lives, composes and adorns conduct.

It weighs and balances, and by moderating threatens [and diminishes while moderating].

It annihilates what is small, and melts the just man like gold (*conflascit* [sic; *conflat*]).

It files and examines him, and balances him by polishing.

[Col. 0866A]

For all it is a slender rod, just moderation,

a pious file [piously], receiving them and preparing the blessed kingdoms.

It rebukes, pleads, reproves, and willingly corrects

those whom it joins to itself in brotherly covenant.

It knows how to lead monks to the eternal kingdom

and gently join them to the angelic choir.

Although it leads its companions upward to heaven’s heights,

it is nevertheless a narrow path and a confined way.

The narrow path leads the devout to the lofty halls of the kingdom;

the broad path plunges the wicked into the depths of the black pit.

Let no one fear to enter the monks’ narrow way;

they lead to the blessed camps of the star-bearing heaven.

[The blessed camps lead to the star-bearing heaven.]

He will be able easily to ascend the heights of heaven

whom no harmful guilt burdens with any weight.

[No harmful guilt burdens him with any weight.]

No winged being in the ether, with a burdened body,

strikes his way while flying often through the heavenly paths.

For no monk weighed down by the burden of sin

will be able to enter the realms of the starry heaven.

Every monk must wash away his transgressions with tears

and suffer no further need of washing.

Meanwhile, let the monk’s discretion temper his mind,

and let it guide him along the royal middle way.

Let him carefully avoid the right and fear the left:

the duties of sacred law urge him to do this.

Let him not fear sad things [lacuna] but the prosperous things of the world;

then he will be able to climb to the blessed realms of heaven.

Whoever loves to gather the shining fruits of the saints

must be joined to them in all his deeds.

Adorned in character and arrayed in a chaste body,

he will live and will always be loved by the Lord.

Thus let him be silent, humble, very gentle, and kind;

let him be patient, sober, prudent, and devout;

of teachable disposition, wise, and humble in mind;

let him proceed composed, calm, and very cautious.

Meanwhile, let remorse of heart awaken the guilty man,

so that he may wash away the filth and uncleanness of his soul [the filth of his mind].

The outpouring of tears is likened to a font infused with chrism;

like that font, it wipes away black stains.

It also cleanses the purified inhabitants of paradise,

and makes them seek citizenship there without end.

There they can continually render *laudes* [*lautas*]—praises [abundant praises]—in thanks,

live forever with the Lord and be his own.

Nevertheless, Adhelmus the Englishman, first made abbot and afterward bishop, remembered this holy Father in the book he published *On the Praise of the Saints* as follows:

When flourishing Rome held the empire of the world

and governed the boundaries of kingdoms throughout the earth,

Benedict the Fortunate shone forth in the time of Faustus. He was the one

whom God, the merciful creator, had granted to Ausonia,

so that he might lead the Lord’s people, traveling along the straight path,

to the footsteps of the ruler of the eternal kingdom.

Previously, hidden error had thrust him

through savage winding paths into the black Tartarus of the infernal torrent.

He first often crushed the temples of former tyrants,

who denied the Lord of light with darkened hearts.

Soon, planting there his victorious signs of salvation,

as Christ’s soldier he triumphs over the conquered enemy.

Restoring a basilica to the Lord in a renewed building,

what method, number, or reckoning could possibly explain

his abundant virtues?

[Col. 0867A]

They exceed measure and number through the greatness of his deeds,

for he restored light to dead bodies,

which the power of cold death had deprived [rather: denied] of it.

He gives hearing to the deaf and adorns the lame with steps;

he strengthens the sick, increasing the powers of their limbs;

he drives away the weapons of demons and also breaks their darts;

[Col. 0867B]

expelling enemies, he restores wounded hearts.

This man renews the sieve, broken by the fracture of its openings,

while the nurse poured forth streams of tears.

With his outstretched right hand, through signs of salvation,

he broke the deadly cup that held the poisonous draught.

Thus too he ordered the Chalybs, fallen into the whirlpool, to return

again to its own limbs.

He was the first to establish the contests of our life,

the way in which monasteries strive toward the desired rule,

and the manner in which the holy man hastens along the direct path,

climbing as a worshiper toward the summits of the heavens above.

Gregory the bishop once described his splendid life,

revealing it from its beginning in written pages,

until the blessed man migrated to the heavenly citadel.

[Col. 0867C]

His rejoicing pupils are gathered into his number,

citizens whom fertile Britain bears in her bosom.

From him the grace of baptism has now flowed to us,

and a venerable company of teachers has proceeded.

Likewise, in praise of his sister, namely the blessed Scholastica,

he inserts several verses into the same poem as follows:

In the time of the Goths a certain young girl shone forth,

who took the name Scholastica from her own school

[Note: In this, an antiquated expression must be excused.]

God richly endowed her with a heavenly gift,

as she won golden rewards through her virginal vow.

About her this nourishing branch of life is accustomed

to spread a particular account wherever the world extends:

that the virgin, joined to her brother by a bond of kinship,

earnestly sought to persuade him with prayers,

so that he might receive by night the sweet fare of sacred books

and the banquets of the holy word.

From these the hearts of the common people are abundantly filled,

and the hearts of holy men are fattened.

But her faithful brother was moved by no prayers;

indeed, he despised his holy sister with his words.

Then the Virgin knocked with a kindly heart at Christ,

asking that he deign to heal the wound of her grief.

Immediately the whole sky grew dark with a rainy storm,

and the vault of heaven blackened with dusky air.

Vast rumblings thunder, mingled with flashing flames,

[Col. 0868A]

and the trembling earth trembled with a mighty crash.

Moist fleeces were drenched with dew-bearing drops,

and the air irrigated the earth with dark rains.

The valleys were filled and abundant streams overflowed.

Then he who previously had freely denied what his sister requested

remained unwillingly, grieving, anxious with cares.

Thus God listens to those who pray with devout minds,

even when they receive words of consolation from no one.

And this was Adhelmus.

Finally, the dependents of that most beloved patron of ours, Benedict, who had been specially educated in the presence of his precious body at Floriacum, did not appear slow to praise their alumnus—particularly in describing the translation of his holy relics, as well as the miracles that Christ has deigned to perform through him in ancient and modern times. We too, according to the measure of our ability, having recounted the miracles mentioned above, have undertaken this work in his praise. Let us see with which holy Fathers he may still be compared.

Certainly let him be compared with the strong man Gideon, who, about to attack the enemies of the Israelite people in battle, first destroyed the altar of Baal from his father’s house and uprooted the grove dedicated to it. Thus this strong soldier of Christ too, about to declare war on the aerial powers at the fortress of Cassino, overturned Apollo’s oracle, cut down his grove, and made his shrine a temple for the living God.

Let that strongest of men, Samson, envy his wondrous virtues. For Samson, having brought down the roof, destroyed three thousand enemies together with himself, in requital for the tearing out of his eyes; but this Benedict, beloved of God, supported by the weapons of patience, both avoided his enemy Florentius while the latter was alive and, when the roof collapsed and crushed him, wept that he had died.

Samson broke the sinews and bonds with which his enemies had tied him, as though they were threads of tow; the gentle Father Benedict broke the bonds of another—and, what is more wondrous, by a mere glance.

The younger Tobias deserved to have the archangel Raphael as his guide on his journey; two angels appearing in the likeness of young men showed the blessed Father Benedict the road by which he ought to travel to the fortress of Cassino.

Daniel, the man of desires, by the keen insight of his shrewd mind detected the priests’ secret banquets to Bel; Benedict, an energetic man enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, recognized and exposed the costly banquets of absent brothers at their expense.

Daniel extinguished a dragon; Benedict presented the appearance of a dragon to a fugitive brother and mortified in his heart the crafty persuasions of the ancient enemy, who is represented in the serpent.

Enough has been said concerning the ancient Fathers to whom he was either equal or superior in miracles. Now, examining the Fathers of the New Testament, let us consider whom he equaled or surpassed in the power of signs.

Let Peter, first in the order of the apostles, be placed first in this discussion; the blessed pope Gregory did not hesitate to compare this illustrious confessor with him, both in the matter of water on a journey and in the excommunication of nuns.

Indeed, he compares him with the Teacher of the Gentiles when, having learned by divine revelation of the desolation of the Cassinese monastery, he says that Benedict obtained the souls of the inhabitants of that place, speaking as follows:

“I see Benedict taking Paul’s place: when his ship suffered the loss of all its goods, he himself received the lives of all who accompanied him in consolation.”

That distinguished Preacher himself writes that he asked the Lord three times for the thorn of the flesh to be taken away from him, but did not obtain this. Gregory, however, relates that this blessed man, after conquering the temptation of the flesh amid thorns and nettles, never afterward—or only very rarely—experienced anything of the kind.

That Martin, renowned throughout the whole world, does not at all begrudge the virtues of our Father; he rejoices that he reigns with him in the heavenly seats of the kingdom.

Martin drove away by a mere breath a demon who had been sitting on the neck of Anicianus. Benedict rescued two monks from the domination of the ancient enemy, one by a blow of his rod, the other by the impact of a slap.

Martin, although absent, heard Brictius disparaging him. Benedict, watchful and divinely instructed, understood a monk speaking arrogantly in his thoughts.

A glass vessel containing oil sanctified by Martin fell onto the marble pavement and was not broken at all. A glass vessel containing oil, which venerable Benedict had ordered to be thrown through the cellar window onto a heap of stones because of disobedience, remained unbroken.

Nor is our patron found unequal to the choir of the anchorites. In the triumph of signs, the wondrous Macarius, persevering in prayer, saw a demon in a perforated garment carrying to the hermits cups filled with various vices. When he questioned him—“Ho, great one, where are you going?”—he received the answer that the demon was going to the brothers and wished to offer them various tastes of the passions.

Benedict, chief of monks, while going to prayer, encountered the same ancient enemy in the form of a physician and asked where he was going. He replied that he was going to the brothers and wished to give them a potion.

Macarius restored Theoctistus, corrupted by demonic deceit, to a better way of life by his exhortations. Benedict, because the devil had been despised, gave an old man who had been hunted by him only a single slap, and immediately made him well.

Antony, distinguished among the anchorites, saw the soul of Paul the first hermit carried to heaven by angels. Father Benedict’s clear-sightedness not only saw the spirit of his sister Scholastica ascend to heaven in the form of a dove [Col. 0869D–0870A], but also saw the soul of Germanus of Capua penetrate the heights of heaven in a sphere of fire.

Let us consider whether he was judged by God to be no less than that most ancient and therefore first of hermits, Elijah, although he has already been compared with him because of the ravens that obeyed him.

Elijah was carried into heaven in a fiery chariot. The beloved Father Benedict ascended to the heights of heaven by a road spread with cloths and glittering with innumerable lamps.

As Elijah was taken away from him, Elisha cried out in tears: “My father, my father, chariot of Israel and its charioteer” (*2 Kings* 2).

While the disciples of the venerable Benedict marveled at the road by which their joyful master was going to the Lord, a distinguished man standing nearby—undoubtedly an angel—spoke these words of consolation:

“By this road,” he said, “Benedict, beloved of the Lord, ascended to heaven.”

Thus far we have discussed the saints to whom this blessed Father of ours, Benedict, appeared equal in miracles. Now let his admirers briefly consider in discussion the signs in which he should be believed to surpass others.

For in this respect—that while still a very young boy he fearlessly sought the desert, and that in adolescence he so subdued the impulses of the flesh that afterward examples of struggles with lust among others are either extremely rare or nonexistent; and because, by the laying-on of the Lord’s Body, he caused burial to close over one whom the earth did not retain after death, and he released rustic bonds by a mere glance; and because he appeared to the brothers to whom he had foretold that he would come to build a monastery; and because he saw the whole world in a moment of a single hour; and because he ascended to heaven by a road spread with cloths—in order to speak peacefully of all the saints, I see no one who can be compared with him.

Although we seemed to compare him with Elijah in his passing, this is nevertheless believed to be more excellent to human understanding: that this most beloved Benedict of the Lord is said not to have been subjected to being carried away or snatched up, but to have ascended.

For the rest, we who, weighed down by the great burden of sins, have dared to undertake the praises of so magnificent a Father, shall meanwhile be silent, because a mind conscious of its own guilt fears that it has attempted such great praises. Therefore, by the light itself that we enjoy and by the life dearer to us, we earnestly implore the goodwill of this alumnus of ours, the most holy Benedict, that he may obtain for us forgiveness of our sins from the mercy of almighty God, and eternal glory throughout infinite ages. Amen.

**In the year of the Lord 1008. John the Deacon, Venetian.**

[Col. 0871]

# HISTORICAL AND LITERARY NOTICE CONCERNING JOHN THE DEACON AND HIS WRITINGS

(*In Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae Historica* VII, 1.)

[Col. 0871A]

The most ancient surviving chronicle of the Venetians, begun at the end of the tenth century and carried down to the year 1008, is attributed by some to John Sagorninus, an ironworker, because we read at the end of the work a notice said to have proceeded from him. This is incorrect, however, since that notice, inscribed in a vacant space twenty-four years after the book had been completed, indicates not the author of the *Chronicle* but perhaps the owner of the manuscript.

The author, although he wished his name to remain hidden, appears to have been none other than John the Venetian deacon, minister of Doge Peter Urseolus. Below we read that he undertook more than once the embassy to Otto III and secretly brought the emperor to Venice. [Note: Lebret asserts that he also accompanied John, the doge’s son, to Constantinople to fetch Maria as his wife; I do not know the basis for this assertion.]

The history of this embassy is so constructed that either John himself or a man extremely close to him must have written the *Chronicle*. He was therefore a man of the highest reputation among his people, devoted to the doge and admitted by him to the secrets of government; the narrative itself in the history of his own time provides abundant testimony to this.

He used as sources ancient narratives and the fabulous legends of the saints, annalistic books—among them Bede’s *On the Six Ages of the World* and Paul the Deacon’s *History of the Lombards*, as the many excerpts drawn from them demonstrate—catalogues of Venetian doges and Gradensian patriarchs, and also public documents worthy of greater or lesser confidence. That very many such documents were preserved among the Venetians may be inferred from the great number of them that still exists today at Vienna and Venice.

He used these aids in such a way that in the older material one sometimes misses both a correct reckoning of time and sound judgment, whereas in the more recent material he deserves considerable praise.

He seems to have laid the first hand to the work around the year 980. [Note: In the year 979 he calls Doge Peter and Abbot Warinus “lords,” and the catalogue of Venetian doges appended to the Venetian *Chronicle* ends under the tribune Meni after one year and four months, that is, in the year 980.] Then, as the autograph manuscript shows, he extended the narrative as time passed, [Note: See below the history of the year 1004, which evidently was written at that very time, certainly before the year 1007.] and finally laid down his pen in the year 1008.

His style of writing is for the most part simple and clear, but his Latin displays the Venetian dialect. [Note: For example: *Serzi* for *Sergii*; *circumscepti, viscere, scita, posce, obscula* for *circumsepti, visere, sita, posse, oscula*. *Consendentes, siphus, justa, estitit* for *conscendentes, scyphus, juxta, extitit*. We also find *dequoritas, quomoda, Venetiquorum, Teutoniquorum* for *decoritas, commoda, Veneticorum, Teutonicorum*; and *condam* for *quondam*. The letter *h* is often omitted, for example *illaresco* for *hilaresco*. We also find *mollitur, pallacium, cessar* for *molitur, palacium, cesar*; *Vergelensis, Belonensis* for *Vercellensis, Bellunensis*; *Federicus*; *Arripdanus, Eripdanus* for *Eridanus*.]

It also contains numerous violations of grammatical rules and forms of words that almost foreshadow the Italian language. [Note: Compare, for example, the faulty case forms: *a Ausonia* for *ad Ausoniam*; *suo sceptrui, episcopati, praeconi* in place of *praeconis*; *illo* for *illum*; *filia* for *filiam*; *filium* for *filius*; *adventum* for *adventus*; *unus* for *unum*; *ditatus* for *ditatum*; *tanti* for *tanto*; *duci* for *ducis*; *capacitate* for *capacitatem*; *subditos* for *subditi*; *cunctos cleres* for *cunctus clerus*; *perversos* for *perversi*; *dies* for *die*; *multitudine* for *multitudo*; *Mediolensem rurem* for *Mediolanense rus*; *patre* for *pater*; *Gradensem castrum*.

Faulty verb forms include *diferabatur* for *differebat*, *largivit*, and *expugnaturam* for *expugnandam*; *vento imperatore*; *auderet* for *auderent*. Verb constructions include *Quem successit Petrus*, *ab aliquis*, *ab ipso infortunium*, the indicative following *ut* where the subjunctive is required, and accusatives absolute for ablatives. I omit *turim* for *turrim*, words used with alien meanings—for example *interim* for *donec*, *reciprocare* for *repetere*, *repetere* for *redire*—and similar examples. Adverbs more often end in *-ae*.]

The book became famous not only at Venice but appears to have been carried beyond the Alps as well, since in the twelfth century we see an excerpt from the *Gradensian Chronicle*, and, toward the end of that same century, certain portions of the Venetian chronicle excerpted by the Saxon Annalist. [Note: See *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores* VI, p. 567 (vol. CXLVII of Migne’s *Patrologia*).]

By that time, however, the autograph manuscript had suffered damage and had lost its final leaves, namely the second part of the *Gradensian Chronicle*. Transcribed in the thirteenth century, the book—both the Venetian and the Gradensian *Chronicles* complete—was used in the fourteenth century by Andrea Dandolo, the most celebrated doge of Venice, in his own history, and became known to the authors of the books *On the Lives of the Patriarchs of Aquileia*. [Note: Muratori, *Scriptores* XVI, p. 8; and the other author, Antonio Bellono, in the same volume, p. 30.]

In later centuries too the work was copied again and remained known to learned Venetians. [Note: For example, Flaminio Cornelio, who in 1749 published fragments of the *Gradensian Chronicle* in *Ecclesia Torcellana*, pp. 5–11, 15 ff.] Yet it was not published at Venice until 1765, by Zanetti; today it is appearing again with the assistance of the best manuscripts. Among these, one outstandingly deserves to be named first—
[Col. 0873B] 1) The Urbino codex in the Vatican, marked with the number 440, is a parchment manuscript in large quarto. Our colleague Boehmer examined it, and at my request the distinguished scholar Giesebrecht copied it out with the greatest care. It consists of five quires. The quire that now occupies the first position, but certainly stood last in the thirteenth century, contains the Chronicle of Grado; the remaining quires present the Venetian Chronicle. Both chronicles are written in the same hand. From the words *of the Greek emperors* on folio 22 onward, the necessity of the subject caused the scribe to continue in slightly smaller and more even writing. The first part of folio 27 is blank; on the latter part, the history of the year 991 continues in larger letters and paler ink. From folio 32, beginning with *But having departed from there*, the script becomes less broad and more cursive; on folio 35 verso it again becomes larger, after lines had been omitted; [Col. 0873C] and in the middle of folio 37, at *Meanwhile, while Duke Peter was seeking for himself the fulfillment of his wishes*, the writing returns to that of the opening pages. On folio 38, line six, the Chronicle ends; on the following page and on folio 39 there is a catalogue of the Venetian dukes. The blank portions of the later pages were filled by an eleventh-century scribe with two sheets and catalogues of the Lombard kings and of the emperors of the West, from Charlemagne to Berengar I, and of the East, from Julius Caesar to Probus. That the codex is an autograph is demonstrated by the very variation in the handwriting, which accompanies the chronological sequence of events and exhibits the characteristics of the late tenth and eleventh centuries. Many corrections made by the same hand and at the same time confirm this conclusion; a few additions made at a later date, especially in the numerals, are easily distinguished. The present order of the pages is shown by several considerations to be disturbed: both the fact that the much more substantial part of the book, namely the Venetian Chronicle, may be judged to have occupied the first place, and the arrangement of the codices copied from ours, in which the Chronicle of Grado occupies the last place, provide strong evidence. If one supposes that the autograph too was formerly bound in this manner, the loss of the first and last pages—the beginning of the Venetian Chronicle and the other part of the Chronicle of Grado—is more readily explained. Nor does the condition of the codex contradict this, since the present order of the quires was established in recent times, as the revealing numerals show; and the first page of the final quire, marked only with the old numeral X, is so worn that one may readily infer that it was once the first page of the entire Chronicle.

It was copied from the Urbino manuscript.

2) The Vatican codex marked with the number 5269 is a parchment manuscript in large octavo, written in the thirteenth century, specifically between the years 1237 and 1261. Folios 1–40 contain the Venetian Chronicle; folios 41–48, the Chronicle of Grado; [Col. 0874B] folios 49–96, the Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs down to Gregory II, which Lucas Holstenius formerly used [Note: [Col. 0873D] *Codex minor* (“the smaller codex”).]; and folios 97–99, a catalogue of the emperors of the West and East [Note: [Col. 0873D] *Codex minor* (“the smaller codex”).] extending down to Baldwin I. This book preserved the lost earlier part of the Urbino codex, which the distinguished Giesebrecht used in correcting the text.

3) The codex formerly belonged to Apostolo Zeno, later to the Dominicans’ library [Note: [Col. 0874D] Cornelius, *Ecclesia Torcellana*, p. 5.], and is now in the Library of Saint Mark at Venice, among the manuscripts of Class X, marked number 141. According to our colleague Koepke, it is a parchment manuscript in folio, written in a beautiful hand of the late fourteenth or early fifteenth century. Its origin from the Vatican is indicated by its readings. Zanetti used it, and in his edition printed a text badly copied from it, while assigning to the margin various readings from the Urbino and [Col. 0874C] Vatican codices, which he states that he had taken from the copy of both codices

4) made for the use of Marco Foscarini, Duke of Venice, while he was staying in Rome. That copy by no means faithfully reproduced the actual readings of the codices, as Giesebrecht recognized after examining them again and again. You should therefore know that our reading often differs from Zanetti’s marginal notes. This copy was recently mentioned in the catalogue of the Foscarini Library [Note: [Col. 0874D] *Archivio storico Italiano* V, p. 283.] and passed into the Imperial Library at Vienna [Note: [Col. 0874D] Another codex, dated to the eleventh century, about which we had formed some hope—the Mediomontanus, which we recently examined at the home of the distinguished Sir Thomas Phillipps—was copied from Zanetti’s edition and therefore cannot be taken into account.].

4*) After our edition had already been completed, through the kindness of Leopold Ranke, the celebrated professor of history at the Royal University of Berlin, we were able to use a copy [Col. 0874D] of the critical apparatus compiled by P. Pellegrino in 1806 for the use of a new edition. It consists of Zanetti’s text, with the readings of codices 3, 2, and 1 recorded in the margin; a preface explaining Zanetti’s carelessness and reviewing the resources for a new edition—namely, the Venetian codex placed as the foundation and a copy of both Vatican codices sent to him through Borgia [Col. 0875A]; critical and historical notes containing passages omitted by Zanetti; the Chronicle of Grado, extended from the Venetian codex down to the election of Patriarch Primogenius; and an index of the clerics and laymen who occur in the Venetian Chronicle.

5) The codex of the Barberini princely library, marked no. 247 and written in the twelfth century, bears the following title: *Chronicle of the individual patriarchs of New Aquileia, which is called the Church of Grado, from the time of Lord Elias, patriarch of that church*. On four parchment sheets it presents excerpts from the Chronicle of Grado beginning as follows: “In the time of Tiberius Constantine Augustus, Elias, patriarch of Aquileia, ordered the church of Saint Euphemia to be built in the fortress of Grado.” Beyond the material found in codices [Col. 0875B] 1–4, it extends the catalogue of the archbishops of Grado down to Ursus II, who was appointed to the see in 1012 and occupied it for thirty-seven years. By means of this codex, therefore, it is possible to restore that part of the Chronicle. Since the Venetian Chronicle proceeds down to [Col. 0876A] the year 1008, one may infer that only the years of Vitalis, who died about 1012, and the succession of Ursus were added by some later scribe. Moreover, Ughellus used our codex in his account of the patriarchs of Grado, and Giovanni Francesco Bernardo Maria de Rubeis, having obtained a copy by Filippo della Torre, used it in the *Monuments of the Church of Aquileia* [Note: [Col. 0875B] p. 241 ff.]. For our use, the distinguished Roestell, professor of civil law at the Royal University of Berlin, copied the codex again twenty years ago while he was living in Rome, and recorded various

6) readings of the Vatican codex no. 3922, which contains the same excerpts.

With these resources, we arranged our edition as follows: codex 1 was placed as the foundation, its lacunae were filled with the assistance of codex 2, and the second part of the Chronicle of Grado, as it appears in codex 5, was appended, corrected in several places with the help of Andrea Dandolo’s Chronicle. We judged that the readings of the less important codices and of Zanetti’s edition should be reported only rarely.

[Col. 0875]

# THE VENETIAN AND GRADENSE CHRONICLE OF JOHN THE DEACON

(*Pertz, Monuments of German History, Historical Writers VII, 1*)

## THE VENETIAN CHRONICLE

[Col. 0875C] There are indeed two Venices. The first is that which is contained in the histories of antiquity and extends from the borders of Pannonia to the river Adda; its capital was the city of Aquileia, where blessed Mark the Evangelist, enlightened by divine grace, preached Christ Jesus the Lord. The second Venice is the one that we know to be situated among the islands, gathered within the bay of the Adriatic Sea and inhabited happily by a multitude of people amid the remarkable arrangement of the surrounding waters [Note: [Col. 0875] Thus the edition; codex 2 has *habitant*, “they inhabit.”]. That people, as may be understood from its name and is confirmed by the annalistic books, derives its origin from the former Venice.

The reason why it inhabits the islands of the sea was as follows. The people of the Winuli [Note: [Col. 0875] I correct this to *Winuli*; codex 2 has *Winilli*.], who are also called Lombards, emerged from the shores of the Ocean in the northern regions and, after passing through the struggles of many wars [Col. 0875D] and traversing various lands [Note: [Col. 0875] The edition has *transitionum*, “of passages.”], finally reached Pannonia. No longer daring to advance farther, they established there a permanent dwelling for themselves (Paul, *History of the Lombards* II, 7). After they had lived there for forty-two years, during the time when Justinian, the most glorious Augustus, governed the Roman Empire at Constantinople, Narses the patrician, a eunuch, was sent by him to the city of Rome so that, with God’s help, he might crush the army of Totila, king of the Goths, who was ravaging Italy (ibid., ch. 1). When he arrived, he first established complete peace with the Lombards; then, advancing to war, he destroyed the entire Gothic people and their king Totila to the point of annihilation and gained possession of all the borders of Italy.

### (3.) This Narses was first a *cartularius*—an official of the imperial records—and afterward, because of his valor, earned the honor of the patriciate. He was a just man, Catholic in religion, generous toward the poor, and very zealous in recovering basilicas. He devoted himself so greatly to vigils and prayers [Col. 0876D] that he obtained victory more through the supplications poured out to God than through weapons of war (ch. 5). But when he had acquired from the spoils of the peoples whom he had crushed a great amount of gold and silver and immense wealth of various kinds, he suffered great hostility from the Romans, for whom he had labored much [Col. 0877A] against their enemies. They made the following accusations against him to the Emperor Justin, who had succeeded Justinian, and to his wife Sophia: “It would have been better for the Romans to serve the Goths rather than the Greeks, when the eunuch Narses rules and oppresses us with servitude; and our most pious emperor does not know this. Now either free us from his hand, or certainly we shall hand over both the city of Rome and ourselves to the nations.”

When Narses heard this, he briefly replied: “If I have acted wrongly toward the Romans, I shall find evil.” Then the emperor was so enraged against Narses that he immediately sent Longinus to Italy as prefect, to take Narses’ place. When Narses learned of this, he was greatly afraid, and he was especially terrified by that empress Sophia [Col. 0877B], so that he no longer dared to leave Constantinople. Among other things, because he was a eunuch, she had ordered him to work with the girls in the women’s quarters, dividing out the quantities of wool. Narses is said to have replied: “I shall weave for her a web such as she will be unable to lay aside while she lives.”

Thus, driven by hatred and fear, he withdrew to Naples, a city of Campania, and soon sent envoys to the Lombard people, instructing them to abandon their impoverished land and come to possess Italy, filled with every kind of wealth. At the same time he sent them many kinds of fruit and examples of the other products in which Italy is fertile, so that he might entice their minds to come. The Lombards gladly received the embassy, its message, and the things they desired [Col. 0877C], raised their hopes by the advantages that lay ahead, and, departing with their king Alboin, arrived to take possession of Italy (in the year 568).

### (Paul the Deacon II, 10.) At the same time the most holy Benedict was governing the Roman Church as pope. Blessed Paul the patriarch presided over the city of Aquileia and its people. Fearing the fury of the Lombards, he fled from Aquileia to the island of Grado, carrying with him the bodies of the most blessed martyr Hermagoras and the other saints who had been buried there. He laid them to rest with the greatest honor in the fortress of Grado and called the city itself New Aquileia.

At that place, shortly afterward, the outstanding patriarch Elias, who was the third after Paul to assume responsibility for governing the church, with the agreement of the most blessed Pope Pelagius, convened a synod of twenty [Col. 0878A] bishops and established that the city of Grado should be the metropolitan see of all Venetia. To strengthen this decision, the Emperor Heraclius later sent, supported by his love for the saints, the seat of blessed Mark, which Helena, the mother of Constantine, had formerly brought from Alexandria. It is still venerated there together with the chair in which the blessed martyr Hermagoras had sat.

### (Cf. Paul, *History of the Lombards* II, 14.) But when 540 years had elapsed from the Incarnation of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0877D] Rather, 568.], the Lombards entered Venetia, the first province of Italy, and, after attacking, captured Vicenza, Verona, and the remaining cities, except Padua, Monte Silicis, Oderzo, Mantua, and Altinum [Note: [Col. 0877] The edition has *penetrarunt*, “they entered,” rather than *penetrarent*.]. The people of that province, however, utterly refusing to submit to Lombard rule, [Col. 0878B] sought the nearby islands. Thus they gave those islands the name of Venetia, from which they had come. They themselves, still dwelling there today, are called Venetians. The Eneti, although the Latins add one letter, are called in Greek [Note: [Col. 0877] Codex 2 has *Greci*, “Greeks.”] “praiseworthy.”

But after they decided to establish on these islands a permanent place of habitation, building several strongly fortified settlements and cities, they recreated for themselves a new Venice and an outstanding province. It is now necessary to set out in due order the names of the individual islands.

The first of them is called Grado [Note: [Col. 0877D] Grado.]. Since it is provided with high walls, adorned with an abundance of churches, and strengthened by the bodies of saints, just as Aquileia was the head of ancient Venice, so this place too is recognized as the head and metropolis of all New Venice.

The second is called Bibiones [Note: [Col. 0877D] That is, the island later called Bibione, where a very high tower stood for a very long period of years; its traces and ruins survived down to the present day, from which the place received the name Torre delle Bebe. An old document in my possession, dated 1478, contains the following: “Likewise, from the communal tower of the Bibiones, annually on the feast of the Nativity, fourteen hens, and at the feast of Easter another fourteen.” The document begins: “Example. The following are the regalia of the Lord Duke found in the old promise.” Zanetti. The author does not here mean the Tower of Bebe situated south of Capo d’Argine; the order of the narrative, which proceeds from north to south, proves this. It is therefore clear that an island formerly existed between Grado and Caorle.].

The third is called Caprulas [Note: [Col. 0878D] Caorle.]. The bishop of Concordia, terrified by fear of the Lombards, came there and, by the authority of Pope Deusdedit [Note: [Col. 0878D] He held office about the year 615.], confirmed that the see of his bishopric should henceforth remain there and resolved to live there.

The fourth island is Heracliana [Note: [Col. 0878D] Heracliana no longer exists.], [Note: [Col. 0877] Codex 2 has *estat*, “exists.”] on which a city had formerly been built on a grand scale by the Emperor Heraclius. After it had been destroyed by age, the Venetians rebuilt it on a smaller scale. But after the city of Oderzo [Note: [Col. 0878D] Oderzo.] had been captured by King Rothari, its bishop, by the authority of Pope Severinus, wished to go to Heracliana and establish his see there. [Note: [Col. 0878D] In the year in which the Emperor Heraclius died, King Rothari captured Oderzo; consequently, this account of the city of Heracliana cannot stand.]

The fifth island is called Equilus [Note: [Col. 0878D] Jesolo.]. Since the people living there lacked an episcopal see, a new bishopric was established there by divine authority.

The sixth island is Torcellus [Note: [Col. 0879D] Torcello.]. Although it is not distinguished by the walls of cities [Note: [Col. 0879] The edition has *munita*, “fortified.”], it is nevertheless surrounded by the defenses of the other islands and enjoys a very secure position at their center.

The seventh island is called Morianas [Note: [Col. 0879D] Murano.].

The eighth island is Rivoaltus [Note: [Col. 0879D] Rialto.]. Although people came to it only at the end to settle there, it remains the wealthiest and most elevated of all. It is distinguished not only by the beauty of its churches and houses, but also appears to possess the dignity of a duchy and the seat of a bishopric.

[Col. 0879B] The ninth island is called Metamaucus [Note: [Col. 0879D] Malamocco.]. It needs no fortification of cities, but is enclosed on almost every side by a beautiful shore; there the people obtained, by apostolic authority, the right to have an episcopal see.

The tenth island is Pupilia [Note: [Col. 0879D] Poveglia.].

The eleventh is called Lesser Clugies [Note: [Col. 0880D] Chioggia.]. The monastery of Saint Michael is situated there [Note: [Col. 0879] Codex 2 has *scitum*, “situated.”].

The twelfth island is called Greater Clugies [Note: [Col. 0880D] On the two Chioggias, see what we noted in the observations to the *Ravennate Papyrus*, published at Venice in 1752, p. 29. Zanetti.].

There is also, at the extremity of Venetia, a fortress called Caput Argilis [Note: [Col. 0880D] Capo d’Argine.]. There are, in fact, very many habitable islands in that province.

### (Paul the Deacon III, 11.) During these times, as stated above, Justin the Younger ruled at Constantinople. He was wholly devoted to avarice, a despiser of the poor, and a plunderer of senators. His greed was so frenzied that he ordered iron chests to be made in which he could heap up the talents of gold that he stole. He is also said to have fallen into the Pelagian heresy. When he turned the ear of his heart away from the divine commandments, by God’s just judgment he lost the understanding of reason and became insane.

He elevated Tiberius Caesar [Note: [Col. 0879] Codex 3 has *Tyberim*.], who governed his palace and the individual provinces—a just, useful, energetic, wise, charitable man, fair in judgments, renowned in victories, and, surpassing all these qualities, a most genuine Christian. When Tiberius distributed much of the treasure that Justin had amassed to the poor, the Empress Sophia frequently rebuked him for reducing the state to poverty, saying: “What I gathered over many years, you squander prodigally within a short time.”

But he replied: “I trust in the Lord that money will not be lacking in our treasury, provided only that the poor receive alms or captives are redeemed. [Col. 0880A] For this is a great treasure, as the Lord says: ‘Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal.’ Therefore, from what the Lord grants us, let us gather treasures in heaven, and the Lord will deign to increase them for us in this world.”

Thus, after Justin had reigned for eleven years, he ended the madness into which he had fallen together with his life. The wars waged by the patrician Narses against the Goths and Franks, which we have mentioned in advance, belong to this period. Finally, when Rome in the time of Pope Benedict was suffering from severe famine because the Lombards were devastating everything around it, Tiberius sent many thousands of measures of grain by ship from Egypt and relieved the city through the care of his mercy [Note: [Col. 0879] That is, *relevavit*, “relieved.”].

### (12.) After Justin died, Tiberius Constantine, the fiftieth of the Roman rulers, assumed the empire. As stated above, while he was still Caesar under Justin and governed the palace and performed many acts of charity every day, the Lord supplied him with a great abundance of gold. For while walking through the palace, he saw on the pavement of the building a marble slab on which the Lord’s cross had been carved, and said: “We ought to fortify our foreheads and breasts with the cross of the Lord—and behold, we are trampling it under our feet!” He immediately ordered the slab to be removed.

When they dug it up and set it upright, they found another slab beneath it bearing the same sign. He ordered that one removed as well. When it had been taken away, they found a third; and when this too had been removed at his command, they discovered a great treasure containing more than a thousand hundredweights of gold [Col. 0880C]. He took the gold and gave it to the poor even more generously than was his custom (ch. 25).

When the patriarch Paul died, after governing the church of Grado for twelve years, Probinus succeeded him.

### (12.) The patrician Narses of Italy also had a large house in a certain city within Italy. With many treasures, he had come to the city mentioned above and secretly dug a great cistern in his own house, in which he deposited many thousands of hundredweights of gold and silver. After killing all those who knew of it, he entrusted the secret to only one old man, having first exacted an oath from him.

After Narses died, the old man came to Tiberius Caesar and said: “If it is of any benefit to me, I shall tell you, Caesar, something of great importance.” He replied: [Col. 0880D] “What do you want? It will benefit you if what you report will benefit us.”

“I possess,” he said, “a treasure hidden by Narses, which at the end of my life I can no longer conceal.”

Then Caesar Tiberius, rejoicing, sent his own servants to the place. The old man went ahead, and they followed, astonished. When they reached the cistern, they entered it, uncovered. So much gold and silver was found there that it could scarcely be removed by those carrying it away even over many days. He distributed almost all of it to the needy in lavish generosity, according to his custom.

When he was about to receive the imperial crown, and the people were waiting, as was customary, for the spectacle in the circus, the Empress Sophia prepared a plot against him in order to raise Justinian, the grandson of Justin, to imperial rank. Tiberius, however, first proceeded through the holy places; then, summoning to himself the bishop of the city together with the consuls and prefects, he entered the palace, clothed in purple, crowned with the diadem, and seated on the imperial throne. Amid immense acclamations he was confirmed in the glory of the kingdom.

When his opponents heard this, [Col. 0881B] and were unable to harm him who had placed his hope in God, they were covered with deep shame and confusion. After a few days Justinian arrived and threw himself at the emperor’s feet, offering him fifteen hundredweights of gold in gratitude for his favor. Tiberius, accepting him according to his customary patience, ordered him to remain in attendance at the palace.

The Empress Sophia, however, forgetting the promise she had once made regarding Tiberius, attempted to plot against him. When he went to his estate, intending, according to imperial custom, to enjoy thirty days of the grape harvest, she secretly summoned Justinian and wished to raise him to the throne. When Tiberius discovered this, he quickly returned to Constantinople, seized the empress, and stripped her of all her treasures, leaving her only the food necessary for daily sustenance [Col. 0881C]. He separated her attendants from her and placed other loyal servants of his own around her to obey her, ordering absolutely that none of the former attendants should have access to her.

As for Justinian, although he rebuked him only in words, he afterward loved him so greatly that he promised his daughter to Justinian’s son and in turn sought Justinian’s daughter for his own son. But this matter, for some reason unknown to me, never came to fulfillment.

An army sent by Tiberius defeated the Persians with overwhelming force. Returning victorious, it brought back such a mass of booty, together with twenty elephants, that it seemed sufficient to satisfy human greed.

### (Paul the Deacon III, 14.) When the patriarch Probinus died at Aquileia, after governing the church for one year [Note: [Col. 0881D] These words agree almost verbatim with the Chronicle of Grado down to “they confirmed the place.”], the priest Heylas was placed over that church (below, col. 950). He arranged the matters written above and built a house for himself from its foundations. He also placed the aforesaid bodies of the saints in a marvelous manner, declaring in the synod the following decision:

“Dearest brothers, beset by our misfortunes, we suffer the hostile scourge every day. Long ago Aquileia, our city, was utterly destroyed by Attila, king of the Huns; afterward it was laid waste by the advance of the Goths and the other barbarians [Col. 0882A], scarcely able to draw breath; and even now it cannot endure the scourges of the Lombards, that unspeakable nation. Therefore our gentleness considers it fitting—if it pleases your holiness—that we confirm our metropolitan see in this fortress of Grado.”

When he had said this, all the bishops approved. Having drawn up a document of their decision, that is, concerning the aforesaid Council of Chalcedon and this very see, they wrote it below with their own hands: first Elias, the patriarch; then Marcianus, bishop of the holy church of Oderzo; Leonianus, bishop of Tiburnia; Petrus, bishop of Altinum; Vindemius, bishop of Cissa [Note: [Col. 0881D] In Istria.]; Bergullus, bishop of the church of Padua; Johannes, bishop of Celeia [Note: [Col. 0881D] Cilly in Carinthia.]; Clarissimus, bishop of Concordia; Patricius, bishop of Emona [Note: [Col. 0882D] Ljubljana.]; [Col. 0882B] Adrianus, bishop of Pola; Maxentius, bishop of Juliensis [Note: [Col. 0882D] The fortress of Julium in Carniola.]; Severus, bishop of the church of Trieste; Solatius, bishop of Verona; Johannes, bishop of the church of Poreč; Aaron, bishop of Avoncia [Note: [Col. 0882D] Perhaps Auronzo near Cadore.]; Ingenuus, bishop of Second Rhaetia; Agnellus, bishop of Trent; Vigilius, bishop of Scarabantia [Note: [Col. 0882D] Scarabantia on the Danube.]; Fontegius, bishop of Feltre; Martianus, bishop of Pedenatis; Laurentius, Marinus, and Emeritus, provincial presbyters; and the other presbyters, both metropolitan and parish priests.

All those named above gave their consent and confirmed everything in that same place.

### (Paul the Deacon III, 15.) After Tiberius Constantine had ruled the empire for seven years, sensing that the day of his death was approaching, he chose, with the counsel of the Empress Sophia, Maurice, a Cappadocian by birth and an energetic man, for the empire. He adorned his daughter with royal ornaments and gave her to Maurice, saying: “May my empire be granted to you together with this girl. Use it happily, always remembering to delight in equity and justice.”

After saying this, he departed from this light to the eternal homeland, leaving the people in great mourning at his death. For he was exceedingly good, ready in almsgiving, just in judgment, extremely cautious in administering justice, despising no one but embracing all in goodwill, and loving everyone. He too was loved by all.

After his death, Maurice, clothed in purple and crowned with the diadem, proceeded to the circus. When the people had acclaimed him and he had distributed gifts to them, he was the first of Greek descent to be confirmed in the empire.

### (17.) At this time the Emperor Maurice sent fifty thousand solidi through his envoys to Childebert, king of the Franks, so that he might invade the Lombards with an army and drive them out of Italy. The envoys presented the gifts and made peace with Childebert. When he had returned to Gaul, the Emperor Maurice learned that he had entered into a treaty with the Lombards [Col. 0883A] and began to demand back the solidi that he had given him for the harm of the Lombards. But relying on the strength of his own power, Childebert refused to give any answer on the matter.

### (20.) Finally, after Pope Benedict, Pelagius was ordained pontiff of the Roman Church without the emperor’s command, because the Lombards were besieging Rome on every side and no one could leave Rome. This Pelagius sent a very useful letter to Elias, bishop of Aquileia, who refused to accept the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon. Blessed Gregory wrote it while he was still a deacon.

### (23.) Around this time, because of the outpouring of a flood, the river Tiber rose so greatly near the city of Rome that its waters flowed over the city walls and occupied its largest districts [Col. 0883B]. Then, along the bed of that same river, together with a great multitude of serpents, a dragon too, borne through the city by the tremendous volume of water, passed across it and reached the sea.

Immediately after this inundation there followed a very severe pestilence, which they call the groin-plague. It devastated the city with such a slaughter of the people that, from an immeasurable multitude, scarcely a few remained. It first struck Pope Pelagius, a venerable man, and killed him without delay. Then, after the shepherd had been slain, it spread among the people.

### (24.) In this great tribulation, the most blessed Gregory, who was then a deacon, was unanimously elected pope. When he had ordered a sevenfold litany to be performed, within the space of one hour, while they were praying to God, eighty of them suddenly fell to the ground [Col. 0883C] and breathed their last.

The litany was called “sevenfold” because blessed Gregory divided the entire population of the city into seven groups to pray to the Lord. In the first choir was all the clergy; in the second, all the abbots with their monks; in the third, all the abbesses with their communities; in the fourth, all the children; in the fifth, all the laymen; in the sixth, all the widows; and in the seventh, all the married women.

We omit saying more about blessed Gregory because, several years earlier, with God’s help, we had already composed his life [Note: [Col. 0883D] That is, Paul, not John.]. In that work we recorded everything that had to be said, according to the limits of our modest ability.

### (25.) At this time the same blessed Gregory sent Augustine [Col. 0883D], Mellitus, and John, together with several other God-fearing monks, to Britain, and through their preaching converted the English to Christ.

### (26.) In those days, when the year from the Incarnation of the Lord was 588, Elias, patriarch of Aquileia, died after having held the priesthood for fifteen years. He was buried at the metropolitan church of Grado, in the church of Saint Euphemia [Note: [Col. 0883D] The name of the patriarch Severus has dropped out.].

Patrician Smaragdus, coming from Ravenna to Grado, personally removed him from the basilica and took him to Ravenna together with three other bishops from Istria—namely John of Poreč, Severus, and Vindemius—and also with Antonius, already an old man and defender of the church. Threatening them with exile and inflicting violence upon them, he compelled them to communicate with John, bishop of Ravenna, who condemned the Three Chapters and had defected from communion with the Roman Church in the time of Pope Vigilius or Pelagius [Note: [Col. 0883] That is, *desciverat*, “had separated himself.”].

When a year had passed, they returned from Ravenna to Grado. The people refused to communicate with them, and the other bishops would not receive them. Patrician Smaragdus, justly struck by a demon, accepted Romanus as his successor in the patriciate and returned to Constantinople.

After this, a synod of ten bishops was held at Marano [Col. 0884B]. There they received Severus, patriarch of Aquileia, after he had presented a written confession of his error, because he had communicated at Ravenna with the condemnors of the Three Chapters.

The names of the bishops who held themselves aloof from this schism are as follows: Petrus of Altinum, the distinguished; Ingenuinus of Sabione; Agnellus of Trent; Junior of Verona; Horontius of Vicenza; Rusticus of Treviso; Fonteius of Feltre; Agnellus of Asolo; and Laurentius of Belluno.

The following bishops, however, communicated with the patriarch: Severus of Poreč, John the patrician, Vindemius, and John.

### (Paul the Deacon IV, 4.) In this year the groin-plague was again extremely severe at Ravenna, Grado, and in Istria, just as it had been thirty years earlier.

### (26.) The Emperor Maurice, after ruling the empire for twenty-one years with his sons Theodosius, Tiberius, and Constantine, was killed by Phocas, who had been the groom of the patrician Priscus. He had been useful to the state, often engaging the enemy and winning victories. The Huns, who are also called Avars, were defeated by his valor.

### (33.) In those days, after Patriarch Severus died, John the abbot was ordained patriarch in his place at Old Aquileia, with the consent of the king and Duke Gisulf. At Grado, Marcianus was ordained bishop by the Romans [Note: [Col. 0884D] The bishop Candidianus; Paul.].

### (36.) As stated above, after Phocas had killed Maurice and his sons, he invaded the Roman kingdom and ruled for eight years. [Col. 0884D] In the second year of his reign, in the eighth indiction, Pope Gregory departed to the Lord.

At the request of Pope Boniface, he established that the Roman and apostolic Church should be the head of all the churches, because the Church of Constantinople was writing that it was first among all the churches. At the request of another Pope Boniface, he ordered that the old temple called the Pantheon, after its idolatrous filth had been removed, should become the church of the Blessed and Ever-Virgin Mary and of all the martyrs, so that where formerly the worship not of gods but of demons had been practiced, there might henceforth be a memorial of all the saints.

In his time the Blues and Greens throughout the East and Egypt waged civil war and laid one another low in mutual slaughter. The Persians too, waging extremely serious wars against the state, took many Roman provinces and Jerusalem itself. Destroying the churches and profaning the sacred things, they carried away, among the ornaments of holy and public places, even the standard of the Lord’s cross.

Against this Phocas, Heraclius, who governed Africa, rebelled. Coming with an army, he deprived him of both kingdom and life, and Heraclius, his son, assumed responsibility for governing the Roman state.

After Marcianus died, having governed the church of Grado for three years and five days, Candidianus succeeded him.

### (c. 49)

In those days Heraclius died, after governing the empire for twenty-five years. Heraclonas [Note: “raclones” in manuscript 3], his son, assumed the rights of kingship together with his mother Martina and ruled the empire for two years. When he died, Constantine, his brother, another son of Heraclius, succeeded him and ruled for six months.

### (c. 33)

Again, in November and December, a comet appeared. When Candidianus [Note: “Candidianus” in manuscript 3], the patriarch, died at Grado—he had governed the church of Grado for five years—Epiphanius was ordained patriarch. He had been first secretary of the notaries, and was ordained by the bishops who were under the Romans. From that time onward there began to be two patriarchs. [Col. 0885C]

### (c. 49)

When the aforementioned Constantine, the son of Heraclius, had died, Constantine, his son, ascended to the dignity of the kingdom and held the kingdom for twenty-eight years.

### (c. 50)

Around this time, the wife of the king of the Persians, named Cesara, left Persia with a few of her faithful companions. Wearing private clothing, out of love for the Christian faith, she came to Constantinople. She was honorably received by the emperor and, after some days, obtained baptism as she desired; the empress lifted her from the sacred font.

When her husband, the king of the Persians, heard this, he sent ambassadors to Constantinople to the emperor [Note: “augustam,” “the empress,” in manuscript 3], asking him to return his wife to him. When they came to the emperor, they announced the words of the Persian king, who was seeking his queen.

The emperor, hearing this and knowing nothing at all about the matter, replied to them:

“We confess that we know nothing about the queen whom you seek, except that some woman in private clothing came here to us.”

The ambassadors replied:

“If it pleases you, we wish to see this woman whom you mention.”

When she came at the emperor’s command, the ambassadors immediately recognized her, threw themselves at her feet, and reverently informed her [Col. 0886A] that her husband was seeking her.

She replied to them:

“Go and report to your king and lord that, unless he believes in Christ as I have now believed, he will no longer be able to have me as his wife.”

Why say more? The ambassadors returned to their homeland and reported to their king everything they had heard. Without delay, he came peacefully to Constantinople with sixty thousand men. He was received by the emperor with gratitude and fitting honor. Believing in Christ the Lord together with all his people, he was washed with all of them in the waters of sacred baptism; he was lifted from the font by the emperor and confirmed in the Catholic faith. After being honored by the emperor with many gifts and receiving his wife, he returned joyfully and happily to his homeland.

In the year 602 from the incarnation of the Lord [Note: 612, according to Pellegrin], the patriarch Epiphanius died. He had ruled the church of Grado for five years and three months. Cyprian succeeded him as patriarch. [Col. 0886B]

### (Paul the Deacon, Book V, chapter 6)

In those days the emperor Constantine, also called Constans, wishing to free Italy from the hands of the Lombards, left Constantinople. Traveling along the coast, he came to Athens; from there he crossed the sea and landed at Tarentum. Beforehand, however, he went to a certain hermit who was said to possess the spirit of prophecy, carefully asking him whether he could overcome and subdue the nation of the Lombards, which lived in Italy.

Around this time the patriarch Cyprian put off the human condition. He had governed the church of Grado for twenty-five years, three months, and twenty days. Primogenitus, a regional subdeacon of the Roman see, succeeded him.

Since the servant of God had asked Emperor Constantine for the space of one night in order to pray to the Lord about this matter, he replied to the emperor in the morning as follows:

“The nation of the Lombards cannot now be overcome by anyone, because a certain queen, coming from another province, built a basilica of blessed John the Baptist within the territory of the Lombards. For this reason blessed John himself continually intercedes for the Lombard people. But a time will come when his oracle will be held in contempt, and then that nation will perish.”

We have found that this happened in precisely this way [Note: namely, Paul], for before the destruction of the Lombards we saw that the same basilica of blessed John—which is certainly situated in the place called Modicia—was entrusted to base persons, so that the place was granted to unworthy and adulterous men, not for the merit of their lives but in exchange for payments. [Col. 0886D]

### (Paul the Deacon, Book V, chapter 7)

As we have said, when the emperor Constantine had come to Tarentum, he departed from there and invaded the territory of the Beneventans. He captured nearly all the cities through which the Lombard people had come. He also attacked Luceria, a wealthy city of Apulia, with great force, destroyed it, and levelled it to the ground. He was entirely unable to capture Arentia, however, because of the exceptionally strong position of the site.

Then, with his entire army, he surrounded Beneventum and began to attack it fiercely. At that time Romuald, the son of Grimoald, still a young man, held the duchy there. As soon as he learned of the emperor’s arrival, he sent his foster-father, named Sesuald, to bring the news to his father Grimoald, begging him to come as quickly as possible and powerfully assist his son and the Beneventans whom he himself had raised.

When King Grimoald heard this, he immediately set out with an army toward Beneventum, intending to bring aid to his son. Many Lombards abandoned him on the journey and returned home, saying that he had plundered the palace and would return no more, but would reclaim Beneventum.

Meanwhile the emperor’s army attacked Beneventum fiercely with various siege engines. Romuald, on the other hand, resisted bravely with the Lombards. Although, because his army was small, he did not dare to engage such a large force in hand-to-hand combat, he frequently broke into the enemy camp with lightly armed young men and inflicted great losses on them everywhere.

When his father Grimoald was already hurrying to him, he sent to his son the foster-father mentioned above, so that he might announce his arrival. When Sesuald had come near Beneventum, he was captured by the Greeks and brought before the emperor. The emperor asked him where he had come from. He replied that he had come from King Grimoald and announced that the king would arrive shortly.

The emperor was immediately terrified and took counsel with his men [Col. 0887C] about making peace with Romuald, so that he might be able to return to Naples.

### (c. 8)

Taking Romuald’s sister as a hostage—her name was Gisa—he made peace with him. He ordered that Romuald’s foster-father, Sesuald, be led to the walls, threatening him with death if he said anything to Romuald or the citizens about Grimoald’s arrival. Rather, he ordered him to insist that Grimoald could not come at all.

Sesuald promised that he would do as commanded. But when he came near the walls, he said that he wished to see Romuald. When Romuald came quickly, Sesuald spoke to him as follows:

“Be steadfast, lord Romuald, and, having confidence, do not be troubled, because your father will soon be here to bring you aid. Know that tonight he is staying beside the river Sangro with a strong army. I ask only that you show mercy to my wife and children, because this treacherous people will not allow me to live.”

After he had said this, the emperor ordered that his head be cut off and thrown into the city with the war machine called a stone-thrower. Romuald ordered that the head be brought to him; he kissed it while weeping and commanded that it be buried honorably in a small coffin. [Col. 0887D]

### (c. 9)

Fearing the sudden arrival of King Grimoald, the emperor abandoned the siege of Beneventum and departed for Naples. His army, however, was severely beaten by the count Mitola of Capua beside the waters of the river Calor, at the place that is still called Pugna today.

### (c. 10)

When the emperor had reached Naples, one of his nobles, named Saburrus [Col. 0888A], requested from the emperor, as the story goes, twenty thousand soldiers. He promised that he would fight Romuald and emerge victorious.

After receiving the army, he came to a place called Fornitus and set up camp there. Grimoald, who had already arrived at Beneventum, heard this and wished to march against him.

His son Romuald said to him:
