“There is no need. Give us only a portion of your army; with God’s favor I shall fight him, and when I have won, the greater glory will certainly be attributed to your power.”

And so it happened. Having received a portion of his father’s army, Romuald marched against Saburrus together with his own men. Before engaging him in battle, Saburrus ordered trumpets to sound from the four sides, and then boldly rushed upon them.

When both battle lines were fighting with fierce determination, one of the king’s soldiers, named Amalongus, who was accustomed to carry the royal spear, struck a certain Greek with that spear, using both hands with great force. He lifted the Greek from the saddle on which he was riding and raised him into the air above his head.

When the Greek army saw this, it was terrified by immense fear and turned to flight. It was slaughtered with the utmost ruin as it fled, thereby winning victory for Romuald and the Lombards.

Thus Saburrus, who had promised his emperor that he would win a victory over the Lombards, returned to him with only a few men and brought disgrace with him. Romuald, having achieved victory over his enemies, returned triumphantly to Beneventum and brought joy to his father and security to everyone. [Col. 0888B]

### (c. 14)

But when the emperor Constans saw that he had accomplished nothing against the Lombards, he turned all the threats of his cruelty against his own people, that is, the Romans. He left Naples and proceeded to Rome.

At the sixth milestone from the city, Pope Vitalian, together with the clergy and the Roman people, met him. When the emperor reached the threshold of blessed Peter, he offered there a pallium woven with gold. Remaining at Rome for twelve days, he removed all the ancient bronze objects that had been placed as adornments of the city.

He even stripped the basilica of blessed Mary, which had once been called the Pantheon and had been built in honor of all the gods, and which, by concession of earlier rulers, had become a place dedicated to all the martyrs. He removed its bronze tiles and sent them, together with all the other ornaments, to Constantinople. [Col. 0888D]

Then the emperor returned by land to Naples. He proceeded through the city of Rhegium and, entering Sicily during the seventh indiction, lived at Syracuse. He imposed such afflictions upon the people, inhabitants, and landowners of Calabria, Sicily, Africa, and Sardinia as had never previously been heard of, to such an extent that wives were separated from husbands and children from parents.

The peoples of these regions also suffered many other unheard-of hardships, so that no one retained any hope of life. Sacred vessels and treasures of the holy churches of God were likewise removed by imperial command and through the greed of the Greeks.

The emperor remained in Sicily from the seventh indiction until the twelfth. At last, however, he paid the penalty for such great iniquities: while bathing, he was killed by his own men. [Col. 0889A]

### (c. 12)

After the emperor Constans had been killed at Syracuse, Mezezius seized the kingdom in Sicily, but without the consent of the eastern army.

Against him, some soldiers from Italy came through Istria, others through the regions of Campania, and still others from Africa and Sardinia. They came to Syracuse and deprived him of life. Many of his judges were mutilated and taken to Constantinople, together with the head of the false emperor.

### (c. 13)

When the Saracen people heard this—they had already overrun Alexandria and Egypt—they suddenly came with many ships, invaded Sicily, and entered Syracuse. They inflicted a great slaughter upon the people, with scarcely a few escaping; these fled for refuge into very strongly fortified camps and onto mountain ridges.

They also carried away immense booty, including all the bronze ornament and various objects that the emperor Constans had taken from Rome. Thus they returned to Alexandria. [Col. 0889B]

In the year 647 from the incarnation of the Lord, the patriarch Primogenitus departed from this life. He had governed the church of Grado for twenty years, three months [Note: manuscript 3 reads “four”], and seven days. Maximus succeeded him.

During his time, Maurus, bishop of Altinum, unable to endure the madness of the Lombards, came to the island of Torcello by the authority of Pope Severinus [Note: From Dandolo, Book VI, chapter 7, page 11. “Paul, the Catholic bishop of the city of Altinum, with the Catholic people … came to Torcello … and there first chose a place of habitation; after one month had passed, he died.” [Col. 0890D] Others agree. Perhaps our author omitted him because of his very brief life there and began with Maurus, his successor—Mauritius according to Dandolo and others. Pellegrin.]. There he decided to establish his see firmly and to remain there in the future.

He governed the church of Altinum for four years and died. Julian, a bishop, succeeded him.

### (Paul the Deacon, Book V, chapter 30)

As we have said, after Mezezius the tyrant, who had succeeded him, had been killed and punished, Constantine, the son of the emperor Constantius, assumed the government of the Roman kingdom.

The Saracens invaded Sicily and, carrying off immense booty, soon returned to Alexandria.

### (Idem, Book VI, chapter 4)

At the request of Constantine, Heraclius, and Tiberius, the most pious rulers, Pope Agatho sent his legates to the imperial city. Among them was John, then a deacon of the Roman Church and not long afterward its bishop. They were sent to bring about the union of the holy churches of God.

### (Bede, On the Six Ages of the World)

They were received with the greatest kindness by Constantine, the most reverend defender of the Catholic faith. They were ordered, setting aside philosophical disputations, to inquire into the true faith through peaceful discussion.

The books of all the ancient fathers that they requested were given to them from the library of Constantinople. One hundred and fifty bishops were also present, with Gregory, patriarch of the imperial city, presiding, and Macarius of Antioch.

Those who asserted that there was one will and one operation in Christ were convicted of having falsified the statements of the Catholic fathers in many places [Note: Thus I correct the text; “falsa se” in manuscript 3].

When the dispute had ended, Gregory was reprimanded. Macarius, together with his followers and with his predecessors Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter, was anathematized. Theophanius of Sicily was appointed bishop of Antioch in his place.

Such grace accompanied the legates of Catholic peace that John, bishop of Porto, one of their number, celebrated the public Mass in Latin on the Sunday of the octave of Easter in the church of Holy Wisdom, in the presence of the emperor and the patriarch.

This was the sixth universal synod, celebrated at Constantinople and written in the Greek language, during the time of Pope Agatho. The most pious emperor Constantine both carried it out and presided over it within his palace, while the legates of the apostolic see and 150 bishops sat together.

The first universal synod was assembled at Nicaea against Arius [Note: a word is missing in the manuscript], with 318 fathers, during the time of Pope Julius and the emperor Constantine.

The second was held at Constantinople with 150 fathers against Macedonius and Eudoxius, during the time of Pope Damasus and the emperor Gratian, when Nectarius was ordained bishop of that city.

The third was held at Ephesus with 200 fathers against Nestorius, bishop of the imperial city, under the emperor Theodosius the Great and Pope Celestine.

The fourth was held at Chalcedon with 630 fathers, under Pope Leo and during the reign of the emperor Marcian, against Eutyches, the most unspeakable leader of the monks.

The fifth, likewise, was held at Constantinople during the time of Pope Vigilius and under the emperor Justinian, against Theodore and all the heretics.

The sixth is the one about which we have just spoken.

The holy and perpetual virgin of Christ, Æthelthryth, daughter of Anna, king of the English, was first given in marriage to another very distinguished man and afterward to King Ecgfrith. After preserving her marriage bed undefiled for twelve years, she became, after her queenship, a consecrated virgin and religious nun when she took the sacred veil.

Without delay she also became a mother and pious nurse of virgins, after receiving a site on which to build a monastery, a place called Ely. The vitality of her merits is also attested by her dead flesh, which, sixteen years after burial, was found incorrupt, together with the garment in which she had been wrapped.

At this time Maximus also died. He had governed the church of Grado for twenty years. Stephen succeeded him as patriarch. [Col. 0890D]

### (Paul the Deacon, Book V, chapter 17)

Around this time Lupus, duke of Friuli, entered the island of Grado with a cavalry army by way of the causeways that had formerly been constructed through the sea. After plundering the city itself, he carried away the treasures of the church of Aquileia.

### (Book VI, chapter 12)

Meanwhile the emperor Constantine died at Constantinople, and his younger son Justinian assumed the government of the Roman kingdom. He held its reins for ten years.

He took Africa from the Saracens and made peace with them on land and sea. Because the pontiff Sergius had refused to favor and subscribe to the synod that Justinian had held at Constantinople in support of that error, Justinian sent his protospatharius Zacharias and ordered Sergius to be taken to Constantinople.

But the army of Ravenna and the neighboring regions, scorning the emperor’s wicked command, drove the same Zacharias from the city of Rome with insults and injuries.

Because of his treachery, Justinian was deprived of the glory of the kingdom and withdrew as an exile to Pontus.

In the year 672 from the incarnation of the Lord, the patriarch Stephen departed from this life. He had ruled the church of Grado for five years. Agatho succeeded him. [Col. 0891B]

### (c. 13)

Against the aforementioned Justinian, Leo seized the imperial dignity and deprived him of the kingdom. He ruled the Roman kingdom for three years and kept Justinian in exile in Pontus.

Then Tiberius rose up against Leo, invaded his kingdom, and kept him in custody in that same city for the entire period during which he himself ruled.

### (c. 31)

But Justinian, who was living in exile in Pontus after losing the imperial power, regained the kingdom with the assistance of Terebellus, king of the Bulgars. He killed those who had expelled him from power.

He also captured Leo and Tiberius, who had usurped his position, and had them slaughtered in the middle of the circus before the entire people. He sent Gallicius, the patriarch of Constantinople, to Rome after having his eyes torn out. He appointed Cyrus the abbot, who had supported him during his exile in Pontus, as bishop in Gallicius’s place.

He ordered Pope Constantine to come to him, received him honorably, and sent him back. Prostrating himself on the ground, he asked the pope to intercede for his sins and renewed all the privileges of his church.

When Justinian sent an army to Pontus to seize Philippicus, whom he had exiled there, the venerable pope strongly urged them not to do this. Nevertheless, he was unable to prevent it.

### (c. 32)

The entire army turned to Philippicus, made him emperor there, and returned with him to Constantinople. He fought Justinian at the twelfth milestone from the city.

After Justinian had been defeated and killed, Philippicus assumed the kingdom.

At this same time the patriarch Agatho died. He had governed the church of Grado for ten years. Christophorus succeeded him.

Around this time Julian, bishop of Altinum, died. He had governed the church for forty-eight years. Bishop Deusdedit succeeded him; he had most devoutly renovated and adorned with various marbles the church of the holy Mother of God. [Col. 0892A]

### (Paul the Deacon, Book VI, chapter 34)

Philippicus, also called Bardanes, was confirmed in the imperial dignity. He ordered Cyrus, whom we had mentioned, to be removed from the pontificate and to return to Pontus to govern his monastery.

Philippicus sent Pope Constantine a letter containing an erroneous doctrine. The pope rejected it together with the council of the apostolic see.

For this reason he caused paintings to be made in the portico of Saint Peter, depicting the proceedings of the six holy universal synods. When such paintings were displayed in the imperial city, Philippicus had ordered them to be removed.

The Roman people decreed that no one should receive the name, letters, or image of the heretical emperor on solidi. Consequently, neither was his likeness introduced into the church, nor was his name proclaimed during the solemn celebrations of Mass. [Col. 0892B]

After he had ruled for one year and six months, Anastasius, also called Artemius, rose up against him, expelled him from the kingdom, and deprived him of his eyes, though he did not kill him.

This Anastasius sent a letter to Pope Constantine at Rome through Scholasticus, patrician and exarch of Italy. In it he declared himself a supporter of the Catholic faith and a preacher of the holy Sixth Council.

While they were remaining in that same province amid a multitude of people [Note: Zanetti writes in the margin that here “nota,” which our author interprets, is said to be present. But it is a well-known sign, frequently occurring in manuscripts 1 and 2: NOTA], they preferred to be subject only to tribunes.

Thus it happened that, over a period of 150 years, each year they raised someone to the highest office of this position, someone who would strive to examine their cases with judicial scrutiny.

Because they were deeply grieved that their ancestral territories were held by barbarians, great quarrels arose between the two sides, so that they competed with one another in inflicting troubles and devastation by turns.

In the time of the emperor Anastasius and Liuprand, king of the Lombards (713–716), all the Venetians, together with the patriarch and bishops, assembled and decided by common agreement that from then on it would be more honorable to remain under dukes than under tribunes.

After deliberating for a long time about whom they should elevate to this dignity, they finally found a highly experienced and distinguished man named Paulicius. Giving him an oath of loyalty, they appointed him duke at the city of Heracliana.

He was so moderate that he judged his subjects with even-handed restraint. [Note: manuscript 2 reads “cujusjurandi,” “of whose oath.”] With King Liuprand he confirmed an unshaken bond of peace and obtained from him the terms of the agreement that still exist between the Venetian and Lombard peoples.

He also established, together with that king, the boundaries of the New City, which are still held by the Venetians: that is, from the greater Piave [Note: Piave] according to the places marked out as boundaries, as far as the Piavesella. [Col. 0892D]

In the year 717 of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: 712 in the edition], Patriarch Christophorus departed from this life. Donatus succeeded him.

Around this time Deusdedit, bishop of Torcello, died. He had governed the church for twenty-four years. Bishop Honoratus succeeded him.

### (c. 36)

Theodosius, year 1.

He was elected, defeated the emperor Anastasius in a serious battle at Nicaea, and, after receiving an oath from him, made him a cleric and had him ordained a priest.

As soon as he himself received the kingdom, since he was a Catholic, he immediately restored in the imperial city to its former place the venerable image depicting the holy six synods, which Philippicus had removed.

The river Tiber left its channel and caused great destruction to the Roman city. It rose in the Via Lata to a height of one and a half men, and the waters flowing down from the gate of Saint Peter reached and joined the Milvian Bridge.

It remained for seven days, until, when litanies had been conducted repeatedly, it returned on the tenth day. [Col. 0893B]

### (Bede, On the Six Ages of the World)

In these times many English people—noble and low-born, men and women, leaders and private persons—were accustomed, moved by divine love, to come from Britain to Rome.

Among them was the most reverend abbot Ceolfrith, seventy-four years old. He had been a priest for forty-seven years and an abbot for thirty-five. When he reached Langres, he died there and was buried in the church of the blessed twin martyrs.

Among the other gifts that he had planned to bring, he sent to the church of Saint Peter a pandect, translated by blessed Jerome into Latin from the Hebrew or Greek source. [Col. 0893C]

At the same time Honoratus, bishop of Altinum, died. He had governed the church for seven years. Vitalis assumed its governance.

### (Paul the Deacon, Book VI, chapter 47)

Leo, eight years.

The Saracens came to Constantinople with an immense army and besieged the city for three years. At last, while the citizens were crying out to God with many urgent prayers, very many of the Saracens perished from hunger, cold, and pestilence, and thus, wearied by the siege [Note: “thus” (sic), according to the Patristic edition], they withdrew.

On their return, they attacked in battle the people of the Bulgars, who live beyond the Danube. They were defeated by them as well, fled, and regained their ships. When they put out to sea, a sudden storm arose, and many of them were killed when their ships sank or were smashed along the shore. [Col. 0893D]

### (c. 48)

When Liuprand heard that the Saracens, after devastating Sardinia, had also desecrated the places where the bones of Saint Augustine the bishop had once been transferred and honorably buried because of the barbarian devastation, he sent envoys and, after paying a great price, obtained them. He transferred them to Pavia and reburied them there with the honor due to so great a father.

In the year 727 from the incarnation of the Lord, Duke Paulicius died at the New City. He had ruled as duke for twenty years and six months. Marcellus succeeded him as duke.

At this same time the emperor Leo departed from the world; Constantine succeeded him. [Col. 0894A]

Around this time Patriarch Donatus departed from this life. He had ruled the church of Grado for seven years. Patriarch Antoninus succeeded him.

At the same time the aforementioned Duke Marcellus died. He had governed the duchy of Venice at the New City for twelve years and twenty days. Ursus succeeded him as duke; he had ruled the aforementioned duchy in the same city [Note: manuscript 2 reads “cade”] for eleven years and five months.

Afterward the Venetians killed him out of fierce hatred and decided to remain subject only to masters of the soldiers for five years.

The first of these was named Leo, whose authority over them lasted one year. The second was called Felix, surnamed Cornicula, who likewise ruled them for one year.

After him the third was called the master of the soldiers Deusdedit, the son of the aforementioned slain duke Ursus. He held that office for one year [Note: namely, he was its possessor].

Afterward the fourth was named Julian, surnamed Hypatus, who likewise possessed that office for one year [Note: omitted in manuscript 2].

In his time, in the year 729, the exarch of Ravenna came first to Venice and urgently asked the Venetians to defend with their assistance their own city, which had been captured and held by Hildebrand, nephew of King Liutprand, and Paradeus, duke of Vicenza.

The Venetians approved his request and hurried by sea with an army toward the aforementioned city of Ravenna. One of the two men, namely Hildebrand [Note: “Ilderandus” in manuscript 2], was captured alive by them; the other, called Paradeus, was killed in battle.

The city was suitably restored to the aforementioned exarch. For this reason Gregory, the apostolic bishop of the city of Rome, moved by complete eagerness to assist the aforementioned city, sent his own letter, which is read below, to Antoninus, patriarch of Grado, so that he might induce the Venetians by loving entreaty to come and defend that city:

“To Antoninus, our most beloved brother, Gregory.

“Because, through sin, the city of Ravenna, which was the head of all, has been captured by the unspeakable nation of the Lombards, and because our distinguished son, the lord exarch, as we have learned, is staying among the Venetians, your fraternal holiness ought to join him and, in our place, fight together with him, so that the city of Ravenna may be restored to its former condition and to the imperial service of the holy commonwealth of our lords and sons, the great emperors Leo and Constantine.

“Thus, through zeal and love for our holy faith, we may be able, with the Lord’s cooperation [Note: manuscript 2 perhaps reads “quoque,” “also”], to remain steadfast in the condition of the commonwealth and in the imperial service. May God keep you safe, most beloved brother.”

After these events, following the departure of the four aforementioned masters of the soldiers, a fifth was appointed to the same prefecture. He was called John Fabriacus. His rule likewise lasted one year, as had that of the others, and the Venetians also tore out his eyes. [Col. 0895A]

At this time also Antoninus, patriarch of Grado, departed from this present life. His rule had lasted twenty-two years, ten months, and twenty days.

In those same days the church of Friuli was governed by Bishop Serenus. Having no experience of justice, he was the first to acquire from the apostolic see, solely for the purpose of usurpation, the pallium by royal authority. It is known that he received the following letter from Gregory, the Roman bishop:

“A person is enriched by so great a gift in proportion as, placed in a position of eminence, he humbly understands what he is by command of the Lord Redeemer.

“For pastoral dignity is adorned above all by humility. The apostolic reading declares that the proud are to be despised: ‘If you have received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?’

“Since, in order to increase your honor, I was bent by the prayers of our distinguished son the king, and since I was also strongly moved by our knowledge that you and your church hold and embrace the rectitude of the faith, we sent you the pallium. Among other instructions, we forbade you ever to invade the rights of another or to usurp anyone’s jurisdiction through a reckless act of presumption. You were to be content with what you had possessed until now.

“Now, however, as we have learned, you are attempting to invade the rights of the bishop of Grado and to usurp what he has possessed until now.

“Therefore, so that you may not be found to be a violator in any respect, we command by apostolic authority that you in no way exceed the boundaries possessed by him. Let it be sufficient for you to remain within what you have possessed up to now. Do not presume to extend your steps beyond the boundaries undoubtedly existing within the territory of the Lombard people, so that you may not show by your presumption that you received the gift of the pallium unjustly [Note: “collata,” feminine, in manuscript 2]. Otherwise, by the force of an apostolic council, if you are disobedient, you will be rejected and judged greatly unworthy.” [Col. 0895C]

At the same time Patriarch Emilianus, who had governed the church of Grado for eight years and five days, ended his life in peace. Vitalianus succeeded him in the same see.

At this time also the aforementioned Vitalis, who had ruled the church of Altinum for nine years and six months, was taken from this life. Severinus was subsequently ordained as his successor in that dignity.

In those same days the Venetians, detesting the dignity of the master of the soldiers of the aforementioned prefecture, once again created for themselves a duke, namely Deusdedit, the son of the aforementioned Ursus Hypatus, on the island of Metamaucum. His rule lasted thirteen years.

Afterward, with the grace of honor and distinction, he wished to build the fortress called Brundulus—not in the place where it now appears to stand, but beyond the present bank of the river. There, a certain unbeliever named Galla tore out his eyes, and, having deprived him of the duchy, possessed it for one year.

Then the Venetians attacked him and, conspiring with one accord, likewise tore out his eyes. In his place they made Dominicus, surnamed Monegarius, a duke of Metamaucum.

As is the custom of the populace, which never persists in the decision once adopted [Note: manuscript 2 reads “presistens”], but, through a certain superstitious folly, continually devises one plan after another, in the first year of that duke’s rule they placed over themselves two tribunes who were to serve under ducal authority. They also attempted to do this in each successive year of the aforementioned duke’s life.

Afterward the Venetians conspired and tore out the eyes of the same Duke Dominicus. The years of his duchy numbered eight. [Col. 0896A]

After his death [Note: manuscript 1 continues here; it reads “dicessum,” “departure”], the entire assembly of the Venetians gathered together and elevated a certain citizen of Heracliana, named Mauricius, to the honor of the duchy on the island of Metamaucum. He was highly experienced in secular affairs.

While he wisely and honorably managed the affairs of the Venetians in every respect, in the eleventh year of his duchy he decreed, by apostolic authority, that a new bishopric should exist on the island of Olivolo [Note: Olivolo]. He ordained there as bishop a certain cleric named Obelliebatus.

After he had governed the dignity of the duchy for thirty-one years and had become an old man, when the people requested it, he was pleased to make his son John a partner in his honor. He remained with his son for two years and thus peacefully ended his final day.

Moreover, when the years from the incarnation of the Lord numbered 823, John, the son of the aforementioned Mauricius, began to govern at the same island the dignity of the office. We have learned neither from writing nor from report that he managed the welfare of his homeland well.

He had a son named Mauricius [Note: the word is written above the line in manuscript 1], and in the eighteenth year of his duchy he granted him a share in the same dignity.

During their time the sea rose so high at Venice that it covered all the islands beyond measure.

Around this time, moreover, the eyes of the emperor Constantine were torn out by some of his own soldiers, and the empress Irene seized control of the empire and began to govern it (797).

After Bishop Obelliebatus, who had governed the bishopric of Olivolo for 23 years, died, Christoforus succeeded him [Col. 0896D]. In the twenty-third year of the aforementioned John’s duchy, having found an opportunity, he sent his son Mauritius with a naval force to the city of Grado, so that he might kill the most holy patriarch John. When he arrived there, striving to obey his father’s commands, he cruelly killed that most holy man. His death left the citizens in the deepest grief, since he had been slain though innocent. The aforesaid man of God governed the church of Grado for 36 years [Note: [Col. 0897] I supplied the number with the aid of the Chronicle of Grado; it is absent from manuscript 1 and the edition], and was buried in the chapel of Saint Mark [Note: [Col. 0897D] In the church of Saint Euphemia, according to the Chronicle of Grado], behind the mausolea of the holy martyrs. Fortunatus succeeded him in governing the church.

At the same time, Charles, king of the Franks, went to Rome (in the year 800, December 25), and there was crowned and anointed emperor by the pope. The empress Irene died, for she had ruled the empire for eight years, and Nicephorus attained the imperial dignity. A certain tyrant, named Turchis, accompanied by a large expeditionary force, attempted to challenge him to battle. But although the emperor defended almost all the places of his empire against the tyrant, he was able to destroy only the place of Tarsatica [Note: [Col. 0897] The preceding word is written above the line in manuscript 1]. Afterwards, however, the aforesaid tyrant, repenting that he had committed some offense against the imperial majesty, humbly and reverently sought his favor.

The aforementioned patriarch Fortunatus, deeply grieving the murder of his predecessor and kinsman, devised a plot against the dukes Mauritius and John [Note: [Col. 0897] Added above the line in manuscript 1], and, abandoning his see and city, departed for Italy [Note: [Col. 0897] Above the line in manuscript 1]. A certain tribune named Obellierius of Metamauco, the tribune Felix, Demetrius, Marinianus or Fuscarus, son of Gregory, and several other leading Venetians also followed him (in the year 803). Of these, only the patriarch went to Francia. The others remained in a certain city not far from Venice, called Treviso. After staying there for only a short time, and having been advised by those who remained in Venice, they elected the tribune Obellierius as duke [Note: [Col. 0897D] Einhard calls him Wilharenus or Willeri].

When the dukes John and Mauritius learned of this, they were overcome by fear and fled. One of them—Mauritius—went to Francia; the other went to Mantua. They remained there so long that neither returned to Venice, but each ended his life there. Christoforus, bishop of Olivolo, likewise, not daring to await the arrival of Duke Obellierius, fled with the aforementioned dukes. Then Obellierius boldly entered Venice. Since the people received him with devotion and honor, he made his brother, Beatus by name, his associate in the dignity. At this time also, Civitas Nova, which is called Eracliana, was destroyed by the Venetians. Thereafter the aforesaid dukes sent a naval force to ravage the province of Dalmatia [Col. 0897D]. The see of Olivolo, which appeared to be without its own shepherd, had been assigned by the people to John the deacon.

After some time, Patriarch Fortunatus returned from Francia with Bishop Christoforus. Since they were not permitted to enter Venice, they were received and stayed for some time in the church of Saint Cyprian, belonging to the people of the bishopric of Altino [Note: [Col. 0897] The abbreviations “p. s. A. e.” were added in the margin of manuscript 1], which is situated at Mestre [Note: [Col. 0897D] Mestre]. But when Lord Fortunatus learned that the see of Bishop Christoforus had been unjustly usurped by John the deacon, he was profoundly grieved and began most diligently to consider how he might assist him and restore him to his own see. One day, while the aforesaid deacon John was walking unawares, he was captured by Patriarch Fortunatus and held for a long time. But while he was considering what he ought to do with him [Col. 0898B], John escaped by fleeing at night and immediately went to Duke Obellierius. When he recounted in order all that he had suffered at Fortunatus’s hands, he stirred the duke’s mind against the patriarch into greater hatred than before. Nevertheless, at the patriarch’s urging, Christoforus eventually recovered his see [Note: [Col. 0897] Above the line in manuscript 1], while the deacon John returned to his own house.

Thus, while Patriarch Fortunatus remained an exile from his own see for some time, he decided to return to the city of Grado. But because he greatly feared awaiting the arrival of the patrician Nicetas, who had then been sent by the emperor with an army and was coming into the regions of Dalmatia and Venice, he abandoned his see and native city and again went to Francia (in the year 806). John the deacon, who had been elected to the bishopric of Olivolo [Col. 0898C], was ordained patriarch. Duke Obellierius received from the patrician Nicetas the dignity of spatharius [Note: [Col. 0897D] Spatharii and protospatharii—or, as others write, spatharii and protospatharii—were at that time almost the equivalent of what we today call knights, or cavaliers. Their insignia were the scaramangium, a type of garment, the sword, and the torque. See the *Ceremonial of the Byzantine Court*, book I, chapter 59. There is a notable passage concerning the protospatharii [Col. 0898D] in the extracts of the laws in the editions of the emperors Leo and Constantine, from about the year 870, in Leunclavius, *Basilica*, p. 99. There they are called μεγαλοπρεπέστατοι, that is, “most magnificent.” ZAN.]. Beatus, his brother, went to Constantinople with the aforesaid Nicetas, taking with him the Venetian hostages, Bishop Christoforus, and the tribune Felix (in the year 807). The emperor condemned them to exile. The aforementioned Christoforus governed the church of Olivolo for twelve years. Christoforus the presbyter succeeded him; he had been parish priest of the church of Saint Moses. At the same time, the city of Eracliana was again ravaged and burned by the Venetians.

Then Duke Beatus, who had gone to Constantinople with the patrician Nicetas, returned to Venice and was adorned by the emperor with the honor of hypatus [Note: [Col. 0898D] *Hypatus*, that is, “consul,” though an honorary consul—or, if you prefer, a consular; and, as in Procopius, *Gothic War*, book III, a consul in name only, called ὕπατος καλούμενος μόνον, “called hypatus only.” Greek authors frequently mention such men after the founding of Constantinople. Combefis rightly noted, however, in his notes on Theophanes, that the word ὕπατος does not always mean “consul” in Greek authors, but sometimes “excellent,” “pre-eminent,” “a notable person,” and the like. For the insignia of these honorary consuls, see Cassiodorus, *Variae*, book VI. See also the celebrated Pagi, *Dissertatio de Hypato*, chapter 8, p. 71, from which we have drawn this note. ZAN.] [Note: [Col. 0897] The preceding word is written above the line in manuscript 1]. Thereafter, the dukes Obellierius and Beatus wished to have Valentinus, their third brother, as their associate in the dignity of the duchy [Col. 0899A].

Meanwhile, the treaty that the Venetian people had once had with the king of Italy was broken at that time (in the year 810), when King Pepin was acting; and that king advanced a huge army of Lombards to seize the Venetian province. After crossing, with great difficulty, the channels that divide the shores of the islands, he finally reached a place called Albiola [Note: [Col. 0899] Supply *sed*, “but,” or read: “and finally he reached a place … and had arrived.” ZAN.]. From there he was unable to advance any farther. At that place the dukes, accompanied by a large Venetian force, boldly attacked the king, and God granted the Venetians a triumph over their enemies; thus the aforesaid king withdrew in confusion.

Therefore, in the year of the incarnation of our Redeemer [Col. 0899B] … King Pepin died (in the year 810, June 24), and the envoys from Constantinople, who had then been coming to him on a diplomatic mission, returned after his death. Patriarch John, who had usurped the see of Grado for four years while its shepherd was still alive, was deposed by synodal judgment. Although he had invaded the see unjustly, he nevertheless took care to construct, before the bodies of the holy martyrs Hermagoras and Fortunatus, or Hilary and Tatian, and also before the chapel of Saint Mark, choirs honorably adorned with marble columns and panels. In the church of Saint Mary, the Mother of God, he constructed a ciborium above the altar.

Fortunatus thereafter returned to his own see. Since I do not think that I can set down the whole extent of his works in writing, I have endeavored to record in my style the portion that I have learned from the report of certain persons [Col. 0899C]. He adorned the altars of the churches of the city of Grado with silver plates and constructed silver shrines above the martyrs’ altars. He himself most devoutly caused the church of Saint Agatha the martyr to be built from its foundations. There he placed forty-two bodies of martyrs in the crypt of the same church [Note: [Col. 0899] Thus in manuscripts 1 and 2, contrary to Zanetti’s assertion]. As for everything else that he did in the treasuries or in the adornment of the churches, no one can specify it individually.

At this time a Constantinopolitan envoy named Ebersapius came to Venice. Through the counsel and strength of the Venetians, he brought it about that both dukes lost both their dignity and their homeland [Note: [Col. 0899] The preceding word is in manuscript 1]. One of them, Obellierius, went to Constantinople; the other went to Jadera [Col. 0900A] [Note: [Col. 0900C] Zara]. They had governed the Venetian duchy for five years.

Then, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0899] The abbreviations “c. e. a. ab i. D.” are written above the line in manuscript 1] 8. [813] [Note: [Col. 0899] “VIIIe” and “VIIII” were later added in the margin, by a more recent hand; before the number, an erasure can be seen in the margin. In manuscript 2, “eight hundred four” was added in the margin, in the same hand in which the entire book was written], the Venetians preferred by common decree to establish the seat of the duchy on the island of Rialto. They raised to this honor a certain man named Agnellus [Note: [Col. 0899] Thus in manuscript 1] [Note: [Col. 0900C] A document from the year 819 survives—the oldest, if I am not mistaken, of all Venetian documents—in which the transfer of the monks of Saint Servulus to Saint Hilary, carried out by this same duke, is recorded. See the distinguished Cornelius on the church of Saint Servulus. ZAN.], who had been the builder of the palace that still remains. Under his authority they also established that two tribunes should be appointed each year.

In that same year, when the emperor Michael had undertaken to conquer the Bulgarian people, he was so terrified by the multitude of the enemy that, abandoning his army, he fled to Constantinople. Since he considered this conduct exceedingly shameful, he went not to the palace but to a monastery. Then Leo, who had been commander and standard-bearer of that army, did not fear to engage in battle and, with God’s favor, returned to the city in triumph. Everyone acclaimed him as emperor. Afterwards he wished to have Constantine, his son, as his associate in this dignity.

The aforementioned Duke Agnellus had two sons. He sent one of them, Justinian, to Constantinople; the emperor received him honorably and bestowed upon him the honor of hypatus. He advanced the other, John, to become duke. Not long afterwards, however, Justinian, the hypatus of the emperor [Note: [Col. 0899] It should be written *imperatoris*: this is an apograph corrected by Giesebrecht’s hand; I conjecture that the reading should be *impr*.], returned from Constantinople to his homeland. Grieving and scorning his brother, who had been raised to the pinnacle of honor, he refused to enter the palace and lodged with his wife in the church of Saint Severus [Col. 0900C]. His father could not long endure the distress and absence of his son, for he loved him greatly. He deprived John of the honor and, expelling him from his homeland, confined him in exile at the city of Jadera. Then, wishing in every respect to satisfy his son Justinian, he made not only Justinian but also his grandson Agnellus, the son of that same Justinian, his associate in the duchy.

As a result, John, who was in exile at Jadera, escaped and first reached Sclavenia, then Italy and the city of Bergamo. Meanwhile, when the father and brother heard this, they sent envoys to Emperor Louis, imploring him to return to them their son who had fled [Note: [Col. 0899] The preceding word is written above the line in manuscript 1]. The emperor willingly complied with their pleas and returned the fugitive to them; without delay they sent him, together with his wife, to Constantinople.

At that time Emperor Leo was murdered at Constantinople (in the year 820). He had governed the imperial office for seven years, and Michael acquired the empire. The aforesaid Duke Agnellus sent his grandson and namesake to Constantinople on a diplomatic mission; the latter died there. Patriarch Fortunatus did not wish to remain continually in his own see, but, against the will of the Venetians, repeatedly returned to Francia. Since this now displeased the dukes, they removed him from his see and ordained John, abbot of Saint Servulus, in his place.

Around this time construction began on the church of Saint Peter on the island of Olivolo. The aforementioned Patriarch Fortunatus, having lost his own see, returned to Francia with the Greek envoys, as we have said [Col. 0901B]. After remaining there for some time, he ended his life (in the year 824). He had governed the church of Grado for twenty-seven years.

At that time certain Venetians attempted to conspire against the dukes. Two of them were hanged near the church of Saint Gregory: John Tornaricus and Bonus Bradanisso. John the moneyer escaped to King Lothair. Nevertheless, everything he possessed—his house and property—was ravaged. Meanwhile, John the abbot, who had been elected to the pontificate of Grado, voluntarily abandoned his see and went to the church of Saint Hilary. Together with the community of monks who lived in the monastery of Saint Servulus, he decided thereafter to establish and maintain a monastery there [Col. 0901C] [Note: [Col. 0901] “and maintain it for the future” is written above the line in manuscript 1].

Venerius thereafter obtained the see of Grado. He was the builder of the church of Saint Maurus, which is situated in the suburb.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 822, Duke Agnellus died. He had governed the Venetian duchy for eighteen years, and the dignity of the duchy remained with his son Justinian.

At this time (in the year 827), Emperor Michael sent an army to Sicily and sought Venetian assistance. Duke Justinian endeavored to send him certain warships, but neither army was able to achieve any triumph. At the same time John, the son of the aforesaid Duke Agnellus and the brother of Justinian, who had been in exile at Constantinople [Col. 0901D], returned to Venice. With the support of his brother Justinian, he became duke. Again, at the emperor’s request, they prepared an army for Sicily, but it too returned without a triumph.

Duke Justinian died (in the year 823). He had governed the duchy together with his father for seventeen years and, after his father’s death, had held the dignity alone for one year. The dignity then remained with his brother [Note: [Col. 0901] “after the death of his brother” was added in the margin of manuscript 1]. The aforesaid Justinian had been a great patron of churches [Note: [Col. 0901] “The aforesaid Justinian” is written above the line in manuscript 1]. He was a most devoted builder of the monasteries of Saint Zacharias and Saint Hilary. In the final year of his life he was privileged to receive the body of the most holy evangelist Mark, brought by the Venetians from Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0901] “from Alexandria” is written above the line in manuscript 1]. Receiving this gift of so great a treasure with honor, he caused a chapel to be made in a corner of his palace, where it could be placed and preserved until the church he had begun was completed. But death overtook him, and his brother John brought the work to completion.

Around this time an envoy of the Slavs from the island of Narenta [Note: [Col. 0901D] Norrenta or Nurenta, to which belonged the islands of Corcyra Nigra, Lesina, and others] came to Lord Duke John. He was baptized by him and established peace with him, although it did not last long [Col. 0902B].

Meanwhile Duke Obellierius, who had been condemned to exile at Constantinople, returned to Venice and shut himself up in the city of Vigilia, at Curidum [Note: [Col. 0901D] Curidum—or perhaps Curiclum—is today Cornichia, on the island of Veglia, near a town of the same name]. When Duke John heard this, he advanced with an army to capture him. After surrounding the aforesaid city with a siege for a long time, the Metamaucans finally divided from the army and fled to Obellierius. The troops that remained faithful to their lord stormed the island of Metamauco and utterly burned it.

Then Lord Duke John again prepared an army. Coming with it, he stormed the city of Vigilia, captured Obellierius, and ordered him to be beheaded. His head was taken to the island of Metamauco and hung beside the bank of Saint Martin on Holy Saturday [Col. 0902C]. At that time the church of Saint Peter of Olivolo, which had been built over a period of nine years, received its consecration.

In the year of the incarnation of our Redeemer … the bishops of Istria, who customarily received the gift of consecration from the patriarch of Grado, were compelled by the power of the king of the Lombards to submit to the metropolitan of Aquileia. Meanwhile certain Venetians—namely the tribune Carosus, Victor, and several others—formed a conspiracy, drove Duke John from Venice, and Carosus usurped this dignity. Lord Duke John then went to Francia, to King Charles [Note: [Col. 0902D] Andreas Dandolo writes “Louis”], who received him devotedly and arranged to provide him with honor and assistance.

In the following year, the tribune Basil, John Marturius, and thirty others of the nobility, departing from their homeland out of loyalty to the aforesaid Duke John, lodged in the church of Saint Martin at Mestre, in the place called Strata [Col. 0902D]. They remained there until a multitude of Venetians gathered to them, so that they could enter Venice without obstruction and endanger Duke Carosus. Thus it happened that one day, while the aforementioned Duke Carosus was living securely in the palace, he was captured by these men, had his eyes torn out, and was confined in exile. His followers—namely Deusdedus Grurus, the patrician Marinus, Dominicus the moneyer, and Tritulus of Grado—were also killed.

Afterwards they preferred to appoint no duke, but, in the duke’s absence, were governed for one year by Ursus, bishop of Olivolo, and the tribunes Basil and John. Then Lord Duke John returned from Francia on the feast of Saint Demetrius. The Venetians received him promptly and endeavored to restore the duchy to him. Dominicus, bishop of Torcello, abandoned his bishopric and sought a monastery; John was ordained in his place.

Around this time, while the Venetians were returning from Benevento on business [Col. 0903B], they were captured by the Narentine Slavs, and almost all were killed. Lord Duke John arranged for the church of the most holy evangelist Mark to be consecrated and for the blessed body to be honorably placed in it.

Moreover, certain Venetians surnamed Mastallici, deceived by diabolical suggestion, seized the same John as he was coming from the church of Saint Peter on the saint’s feast (in the year 836). Having shaved his beard and hair, they had him consecrated a cleric at the city of Grado. He remained there as long as he lived. He had presided over the Venetian people for seven years. A certain most noble man named Peter succeeded him and wished to have his son John as his associate in the honor.

In the third year of his duchy, Peter went with warships to conquer Sclavenia. When he reached the place called the Court of Saint Martin, he concluded peace with their prince, named Muisclavus. Then, proceeding to the Narentine islands, he likewise established a treaty with Drosaicus, judge of the Mariani, although it did not hold; thus he later returned to Venice. He was not permitted to remain there long, however, but again prepared an army against the Slav Liuditus. More than one hundred Venetians were killed, and he returned without a triumph.

Then (in the year 840), at the sixth hour of the day in the month of May, the sun was darkened and an eclipse occurred. At this time the patrician Theodosius came from Constantinople to Venice and conferred upon Duke Peter the investiture of the dignity of spatharius [Col. 0903D]. He remained there for an entire year, urging the duke on behalf of the emperor not to refuse to undertake an expedition against the Saracens for him. The duke willingly agreed.

He then hastened to prepare sixty warships and sent them as quickly as possible to Tarentum, where Saba, the prince of the Saracens, was stationed with a very large army. But almost all the Venetians were captured and killed by the multitude of the Saracens. When those same Saracens saw that they had gained victory over the Christians, they did not hesitate to reach the city of Absarus [Note: [Col. 0903D] Ossero, on the island of Cherso in the Gulf of Flanaticus]. They devastated it by fire on Easter Monday and proceeded to the city of Ancona. Burning it likewise with fire, they carried many captives away with them.

Afterwards, sailing widely over the sea here and there [Note: [Col. 0903] “here and there” is written above the line in manuscript 1], they reached the port of Adria [Note: [Col. 0903D] At the mouth of the Po], which lies near Venice. When, after careful investigation, they realized that they would capture no booty there, they set out on the return journey to their homeland [Note: [Col. 0903] “return” is written above the line in manuscript 1]. But after they had reached the outlet of the Adriatic Gulf [Note: [Col. 0903D] That is, the gulf], all the Venetian ships returning from Sicily or other regions were seized by those same men.

In the second year, the aforesaid Saracens again reached the Gulf of Quarnaro with a very large army [Note: [Col. 0903D] The gulf in which the islands of Cherso, Lussin, Arbe, and Pago lie]. The Venetians attacked them with a naval force and fell upon them fiercely near the place called Sansagus [Note: [Col. 0903] The letter “g” is written above the line in manuscript 1] [Note: [Col. 0904D] Sansego, a small island west of the island of Lussin] [Note: [Col. 0903] The preceding word is written above the line in manuscript 1]. But eventually the Venetians turned their backs, were defeated, and retreated.

The aforesaid Saracens also dared to go to Rome (in the year 846, August) and plunder the church of Saint Peter. But when they reached Saint Paul’s, almost all were killed by the Roman citizens [Note: [Col. 0904D] Prudentius also testifies to this in the *Annals*].

Around this time Slavs came to attack the Venetian territories and plundered only the fortress of Caprula.

Meanwhile Louis, king of the Franks, went to the principality of Benevento (in the year 848). After capturing the enemy Abomasale [Note: [Col. 0904D] He is called Amelmassar or Massar in the *Chronicle of Cassino*, and by Andrea of Bergamo and Erchempert], he returned with his men to Rome [Note: [Col. 0903] The preceding word is written above the line in manuscript 1]. There he was crowned and anointed king by the pope (in the year 850, April 6).

It is also reported that at that time the city of Ragusa collapsed for the most part through the force of sea and wind. The city of Ancona was again plundered in those days [Note: [Col. 0903] Added in the margin]. Venerius, patriarch of Grado, who had ruled the pontifical chair for 24 years and eight months, died, and Victor became his successor as patriarch.

It must also not be omitted that, at that time, the aforementioned dukes took care to build two warships for the defense of their territories, of a kind never before seen at Venice. In the Greek language they are called *zalandriae* [Note: [Col. 0903] “from the language” is written above the line in manuscript 1].

In those days Ursus, bishop of Olivolo [Col. 0905A], who had governed the episcopal see for 32 years, departed this life [Note: [Col. 0905] Added in the margin by a more recent hand: “He died in the year 860.”]. Bishop Maurus succeeded him. In that year (860), it is said, there was such ice at Venice as had never been seen either before or afterwards [Note: [Col. 0905D] See Rudolf’s *Annals*, year 860].

When Victor, patriarch of Grado, died—he had governed the church for six years, three months, and four days—Vitalis obtained the see.

In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0905] The words “in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ” were later written into the lacuna, as the paler ink shows] … Louis, king of the Lombards, came with his wife to a place called Brondolo [Note: [Col. 0905D] Brondolo] and was honorably received by both dukes at the monastery of Saint Michael. When they remained there together for three days, in order to strengthen the bond of affection and peace, Duke John presented his child from the sacred font to the king to be received as godfather. After this, the king and his wife returned to Italy, while the dukes returned to the palace.

At that time the people of the Normans dared to approach Constantinople with 360 ships. Since they were unable by any means to harm the impregnable city, they fought a vigorous battle in the suburbs and did not refrain from killing very many there; then that people returned home in triumph.

In those days the death of Charles, king of the Franks and son of Lothair [Note: [Col. 0905] “his” is written above the line, incorrectly] [Note: [Col. 0906D] King of Provence], was announced to Louis, king of the Lombards (in the year 863). When the Franks appealed to him, he hastened to go there, acquired them as subjects who would remain under his rule, and thereafter became emperor of two kingdoms.

Then, when Maurus, bishop of Olivolo, died—he had held the episcopal honor for ten years—Bishop Dominicus succeeded him [Col. 0905C].

Meanwhile, when the years from the incarnation of our Redeemer were …, Duke John ended his life, and the duchy remained solely with his father. One year after his son’s death, while he was celebrating the feast at the monastery of Saint Zacharias, wicked men cruelly murdered him as he was leaving the church after vespers, although he was innocent. The holy nuns carefully arranged for his body to be buried in the atrium of that church.

He governed the Venetian people for … years. Thereafter they raised to the same pinnacle of dignity a certain man named Ursus (in the year 864). The names of the murderers who committed this crime are these: John Gradonicus with one of his nephews; Peter, son of Stephen Candianus; Stephen of Sabulo; Dominicus, son of Faletrus; Ursus Grugnarius; the two brothers, sons of Salbianus; and many others whose names we do not know [Note: [Col. 0905] “whose names we do not know” is written above the line in manuscript 1].

But divine mercy did not wish to leave this crime unpunished for long. On the feast of Saint Sixtus, John Gradonicus with his two sons, Stephen of Sabulo, and John Labresella were killed. Peter Candianus, Peter Cletensius, Peter Flabianicus, and Dominicus Faletrus were sent into exile at Constantinople by Peter, bishop of Equilio, John, archdeacon of Grado, and Dominicus Massonus. The others—namely Stephen Candianus with the nephew of John Gradonicus, and all the remaining accomplices in the aforesaid crime—were expelled from their homeland and condemned to exile in Francia; they were never able to find a way back.

One of them, however, who remained at Venice—Ursus Grugnarius—died after being tormented by a demon. The aforementioned Duke Ursus hastened with a naval expedition against Dommagous, prince of the Slavs. But when he saw the multitude of the Venetians, he forbade battle and sought peace. Then, after receiving hostages, the duke returned to Venice.

At that same time Deusdedus, bishop of Torcello, was killed by two of his servants at Altino and ended his life. When the duke heard this, he permitted one to be hanged beside the river called the Sile, and the other in the lagoon of Torcello. The aforesaid bishop had presided over the church of Altino for … years.

The church of the holy Mother and Virgin of God, Mary, which had been almost consumed by age, was strengthened by the sons of the patrician Marinus. At this time the emperor Michael was murdered (in the year 867). Basil and his son Constantine became emperors [Note: [Col. 0905] The preceding word is written above the line in manuscript 1] [Note: [Col. 0905] So manuscript 3; the edition and manuscripts read “were murdered”?].

In those days it was announced to Ursus, duke of the Venetians, that a Saracen army was stationed near Tarentum [Col. 0906C]. He then went against them with warships to fight them. After they had fought one another for a long time [Note: [Col. 0905] The second *se* is written above the line in manuscript 1], and the Saracens had been defeated and fallen, the Venetians returned victorious.

Meanwhile the city of Bari, belonging to Lord Louis, king of the Franks and Lombards, was captured by his army (in the year 871, February 2). The Saracen people had held that city for approximately thirty years, under the administration of Bandone, the *gastald* of the same city. In the thirty-first year, by the favor of divine grace, the impiety that they had formerly inflicted upon the Christian inhabitants was repaid to them. The city was captured on the fourth day before the Nones of February, the day on which the Purification of the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, is celebrated.

In the following year (872), in the month of May, the Saracens likewise emerged from the island of Crete and ravaged certain cities of Dalmatia [Col. 0906D]. They also invaded the city of Bracia in that province [Note: [Col. 0905] “of that province” is written above the line in manuscript 1]. When this was reported to Lord Duke Ursus, he hastened to send a small boat with fourteen men as far as Istria, so that they might investigate whether the Saracens perhaps intended to attack Venice, or what their strength might be [Col. 0907A].

When they had set out from the city of Grado to make for Istria, Slavic pirates [Note: [Col. 0907] The preceding word is written above the line in manuscript 1], who were hiding concealed in the harbor of Silvodis, swiftly attacked that boat. While the two sides fought bravely and many Slavs were struck down and killed, at last the Slavs captured the Venetian boat, and all the Venetians who were aboard were killed. The aforementioned Saracens, after devastating the cities we have mentioned, returned home with immeasurable booty.

At the same time, while Emperor Louis was still staying at Benevento and his army was besieging the city of Tarentum, which the Saracens had captured and held, Adelchis, prince of the Lombards, attempted to kill the emperor (in the year 871, August 25). But since he could not easily accomplish this crime, he bound him by oath that thereafter he himself would not come into that region except when summoned, nor send an army there. Then, as Louis was returning to Benevento, he attacked and vigorously defeated the Saracens who were staying at Terracina in Campania (in September), killing eleven thousand of them; thus he returned to Italy.

At this time Patriarch Vitalis died. He had governed the church of Grado for … years [Note: [Col. 0907] A more recent hand supplied the number in manuscript 3] [Note: [Col. 0907D] Nineteen years, one month, and six days, according to the Chronicle of Grado]. Lord Peter the deacon, a man eminent in holiness and skilled in the grammatical arts, was elected in his place. Since he considered himself unworthy of so great an honor, he fled to Italy before he was elected; but at last, brought back by entreaties, he unwillingly ascended to the pontifical dignity [Col. 0907C].

The pious emperor Louis died then at Verona [Note: [Col. 0907D] Rather, in the territory of Brescia, according to the testimony of Andreas the presbyter. *MGH*, SS III, 237] (in the year 875, August 12). At Torcello, after Bishop Senator died—he had governed the church of Altino for … years—Dominicus, abbot of the monastery of Altino, was appointed to that see [Note: [Col. 0907] “to that see” is written above the line in manuscript 1]. He had formerly been a monk of Saint Hilary; after leaving there, because of a charge brought against him, he had his genitals cut off and afterwards remained for some time at Spoleto.

When the distinguished Patriarch Peter placed him under the bond of anathema because he had acted against the duke’s decree, Dominicus lost the duke’s favor, departed, and went to the province of Istria.

Around this time the Saracens arrived and attempted to capture the city of Grado. But since the citizens fought bravely, the Saracens’ impiety did not prevail. Nevertheless, after they had besieged the aforesaid city for two days, this was reported to Lord Ursus the duke, who promptly sent his son John against them with a naval force. When the Saracens learned of this by chance, they immediately withdrew from the city and plundered the village of Comacchio [Note: [Col. 0908D] Comacchio.].

Lord Peter the patriarch, however, abandoning the city of Grado, came to Rialto and lodged at the church of his patrimony of Saint Julian [Note: [Col. 0907] “of his patrimony,” as written above in 1.], where he remained for a full year [Note: [Col. 0907] “for a full year,” as written above in 1.]. Yet he did not have complete peace with the duke on account of the election at Torcello. At last, unable to resist the duke, the patriarch secretly left Venice and decided to go to Rome. Lord Pope John received him devotedly and compelled him to remain with him for a full year.

At that time Lord Ursus the duke made his son John his associate in the dignity. Then the most wicked peoples of the Slavs and of Dalmatia began to ravage the province of Istria. They devastated four cities there, namely Umag, Civitas Nova, Sipiares, and Rovinj [Note: [Col. 0908D] Umago, Cittanuova, Cervere, Rovigno.]. It was then announced to Lord Ursus the duke that they wished to cross over to the city of Grado. He came to that city with thirty ships. From there, crossing into Istria and boldly attacking those same Slavs, he struck them down in such a slaughter that none of them was able to escape and return to his homeland.

Because this ruler had obtained victory from heaven, he released the Slavs whom he had captured in this battle and restored the property of the churches that had been seized in the aforesaid province. Thus he returned to the palace in triumph and glory. For this reason the treaty that had formerly existed between the Slavs and the Venetians was broken.

At that time Saudan, the ruler of the Saracens, who had long ago been captured in the city of Var [Note: [Col. 0907] Thus in 2 and 3.] [Note: [Col. 0908D] Bari.] and had remained confined in prison until this time, was released by Aldegis, duke of the Lombards [Col. 0908C] (in the year 876). After some time he returned to Taranto and later inflicted much harm upon the Christians.

Afterward, when Domagoj, the most wicked duke of the Slavs, had died, Lord Ursus the duke and his son John made peace and concord with the Slavs. Nevertheless, he sent an army against the Narentines, with whom he was in conflict.

At this time Dominic, bishop of Olivolo, died. He had governed the see of Olivolo for . . . . . years; Lord John, archdeacon and son of the patrician Marinus, was ordained in his place. The patriarch Peter, who had been in Rome, came to Ravenna together with Pope John. There, with a synod of seventy bishops assembled, he summoned the two bishops of Venice—Peter of Equilo and Leo of Caprula—and those who had been elected in the same province to that council, so that the cause of the dispute between Duke Ursus and the patriarch might be settled with the greatest care.

But when the bishops arrived at Ravenna with the elected men, late and after the synod had already ended, they were deprived of communion. Nevertheless, when the duke intervened, they were released [Col. 0909A]. Around this time Charles, king of the Franks, whom Pope John had formerly anointed king of Italy (in September 877), came to Pavia and seized the kingdom. The pope went to him and was received with due honor.

Peter the patriarch, meanwhile, came to Bologna and remained there for some time. He then went again to Parma and afterward, out of love for the lord pope, went to Pavia. During these days Carloman, king of the Bavarians, entered Italy with a great army and drove out Charles. When that Charles wished to make his way to Francia, he was overcome by illness and died on the road, on October 6.

The lord pope returned to Rome, but left the patriarch Peter at Pavia. After remaining there for several days, Peter came to Treviso and was received with the greatest reverence by Landon, bishop of that city. When, through envoys traveling between him and the aforesaid duke, the former peace had at last been restored, that distinguished pontiff returned to Venice. At the duke’s request he remained for several days in the palace, on the following condition: Dominic, the presbyter elected to the church of Torcello, on whose account discord had arisen between them, was to remain without episcopal consecration during the lifetime of the patriarch Peter; nevertheless, while residing in the episcopal house, he was to have permission to enjoy the property of that church.

After a few days, when Dominic had regained the favor of the aforementioned pontiff, he invited him to a banquet in the church of Torcello. The patriarch then returned to the city of Grado and consecrated three elected bishops: John of Olivolo, Leo of Metamauco, and John of Civitas Nova.

After a short time the patriarch Peter came to Rialto [Note: [Col. 0909] “to Rialto,” as written above in 1.] and lodged in the basilica of Saint Julian. Since he did not long retain bodily health, he was overcome by illness in that same church, and his holy soul departed to glory. He governed the church of Grado for four years and six months. He was of dignified stature and handsome appearance, and was no more than forty years old. The Venetians carried his body with the greatest honor to the city of Grado [Note: [Col. 0909] “to the city of Grado,” as written above in 1.] and buried it in the atrium before the church of Saint Euphemia.

After him Victor, presbyter of the basilica of Saint Silvester, succeeded to the governance of the church of Grado. During these days Sedesclavus, descended from Tibimir, came to Constantinople with imperial support and seized the dukedom of the Slavs [Note: [Col. 0909] Read “of the Slavs.”], driving the sons of Domagoj into exile.

At that time Lord Ursus the duke was made protospatharius by the imperial envoys and was enriched with very generous gifts. He gave his daughter, Felicia by name, in marriage to Rodoald, son of John, duke of Bologna. Likewise, Johanna, abbess and daughter of Lord Ursus the duke, undertook to restore from its foundations the monastery of Saint Zacharias, which had almost entirely perished through age.

Then Victor, the elected patriarch, was consecrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, January 25. He also consecrated Dominic, the elected bishop of Torcello [Col. 0910A], against his will, because on the day of his own election he had been bound by an oath imposed by the ruler to consecrate whichever elected man the ruler himself directed to him. The patriarch nevertheless said to him:

“Woe to you, because you rashly approach this honor! Do you not know where it is said: ‘If anyone has cut himself off, let him be cast out from the clergy’? And so that you may believe that I am doing this under compulsion, on the day of judgment you will give an account for this honor, unless you repent, because you did not spare yourself the amputation of your penis.”

Around this time, on May 22, blood rained from the clouds. Then John, prelate of the church of Olivolo, died; he had governed that church for . . . . . years. He was succeeded in ruling that see by Laurence the presbyter.

During these days a certain Slav named Brenamir, after killing Sedesclavus, usurped his dukedom. At that time Lord Ursus the duke, at the request of the emperor Basil, sent twelve bells to Constantinople. The emperor placed them in the church that he had newly built, and from that time the Greeks began to have bells.

When Lord Ursus the duke died during this period (in the year 888), the dignity remained with his son John. The aforesaid Ursus was a man of great wisdom and piety and a lover of peace. He had a palace built at Civitas Nova of Heraclea. In his time, at Rialto, people were also granted permission to cultivate the marshes and to build houses toward the east. The island called Dorsoduro [Col. 0910C] had been laid out with his advice.

He governed the aforesaid dignity for seventeen years and died and was buried in the monastery of Saint Zacharias. Duke John, wishing to acquire the county of Comacchio through the largesse of the Roman pontiff, sent his brother Badovarius to Rome. While Badovarius was traveling toward Ravenna, Marinus, count of Comacchio, sent armed men against him. He was wounded in the leg and captured there. Then the aforesaid count, binding him by an oath so that he would not seek redress for this injury, released him. But after returning to Venice, he immediately ended his life.

For this reason Lord John the duke hastened with a naval force to the fortress of Comacchio and took possession of its people. After appointing judges there according to his will, he returned to the palace and ordered the people of Ravenna to be plundered in revenge for his brother’s death.

Around this time, in the month of July, a star was seen to pass from the east in the form of a torch, illuminating almost the whole world. After it had passed, people seemed to hear in the sky a sound like that of gates when they are opened and closed, and for this reason they said that the sky had been opened and closed.

Then Victor the patriarch departed from this light. He had governed the church of Grado for eighteen years and was buried in the atrium of Saint Euphemia. George, his brother, succeeded him; he lived no more than one year, six months, and twenty-one days. Vitalis the Younger succeeded him in governing the church.

Lord John the duke, held down by bodily illness, chose his younger brother Peter as his successor, with the people acclaiming him. Later, when he recovered, he wished to have Peter as his associate. But Peter himself, overcome by illness, did not remain long with his brother before dying. He was buried beside his aforesaid brother Badovarius, who had been no more than twenty-five years old.

Lord John the duke had the church of Saints Cornelius and Cyprian built from its foundations in the place called Vinea Contra. Then the emperor Basil departed from this life (in the year 886).

The aforementioned Duke John made another of his brothers, Ursus by name, his associate [Col. 0911B]. Lord Ursus the duke had four sons—John, Badovarius, Ursus, and Peter—and all except Badovarius became distinguished in the dignity of the dukedom.

At the same time there were floodwaters throughout the territory of Venice, to such an extent that they entered all the churches and houses. Then, while Lord John the duke was still held by illness and his brother refused the dukedom, the Venetians appointed as their duke Peter, surnamed Candianus, within his own house, on April 17 (887). Lord John the duke graciously summoned him to the palace, handed him the sword, staff, and seat [Note: [Col. 0911D] On our ancient silver coins, commonly called grossi or matapans, the duke holds a standard in his right hand and a staff, or scepter, in his left. ZAN], and, appointing him his successor, returned to his own house [Col. 0911C].

Having thus assumed the dukedom, Duke Peter treated Lord John the duke and his brother with considerable honor, and immediately sent an army against the Narentine Slavs. When the army returned without result, he himself went out to sea in August with twelve ships to attack the enemy. Reaching the mountain of the Slavs, he disembarked at a place called Mucules, although he had only a few men with him.

The Slavs resisted him, but he first put them to flight, killed many of them, and broke apart with axes five of their ships that were there. At last, however, when the Slavs attacked, he was killed there together with seven others on September 18; the rest returned unharmed. That Duke Peter held the dukedom for five months.

He was a warlike and courageous man, wise and exceedingly generous. He attended church so regularly that he was never without the divine office. Andreas the tribune secretly took his body from the Slavs and sent it to the city of Grado, where it was buried in the atrium of the church. He was of medium height and forty-five years old.

Then Lord John the duke, although still ill, returned to the palace at the people’s request [Col. 0912A].

*(In the year 888.)* But unwilling to remain any longer, he gave the people permission to appoint whichever duke they wished. Then they all together elected for themselves Peter, a nobleman and son of Dominic the tribune. This Peter had been born to Agnella, niece of the earlier Duke Peter, whom we said had been killed in the monastery.

At that time the patriarch Vitalis died. He had governed the church of Grado for three years, three months, and fourteen days. Dominic the patriarch succeeded him. Lord John the duke again returned to his own house, where he remained until the end of his life.

Meanwhile (in the year 899), the pagan and most savage people of the Hungarians came into Italy, devastating everything with fires and plunder, killing an enormous number of people and also keeping some as captives. King Berengar sent an army of fifteen thousand men against them. But only a few of these returned.

The Hungarians, passing through Treviso, Padua, Brescia, and the other territories, came to Pavia and Milan and as far as Mount Jove [Note: [Col. 0912D] Jovis; Saint Bernard.], laying waste to everything. When they entered Venice with horses and ships made of hides [Note: [Col. 0911] Thus in 1; the corrected reading is “with warships.”] [Note: [Col. 0912D] Ships made from hides.], they first burned Civitas Nova, since its people had fled. Then they set fire to Equilo, Fine, Chioggia, and Capo d’Argine, and ravaged the shores along the sea.

They also attempted to enter Rialto and Metamauco through the places called Albiola, on the feast of the passion of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. Then Lord Peter the duke, protected by God’s aid, put the aforesaid Hungarians to flight with a naval force.

This persecution lasted for one year in Italy and Venice. King Berengar therefore gave hostages and gifts and compelled the aforesaid Hungarians to withdraw from Italy with all the booty they had taken.

At this time Dominic the patriarch departed from the world. He had governed the church of Grado for seven years and eleven months. Laurence succeeded him.

Around this time Lord Peter the duke, together with his people, began to build a city at Rialto [Note: [Col. 0912D] The beginning of the city of Venice. ZAN.] in the ninth year of his dukedom. Thus the emperor Leo conferred upon him the rank of protospatharius.

The wall of the aforesaid city extended from the head of the stream by the fortress as far as the church of Saint Mary called Jubianico. A massive iron chain had been installed there, with one end attached to the extremity of the aforesaid wall and the other to the edge of the church of Saint Gregory, which stood across the bank. Its purpose was that no ship should have the ability to enter unless the chain had been undone.

The aforementioned Duke Peter lived in the dukedom for twenty-three years [Note: [Col. 0913] “lived,” as written above in 1.] and died in the year 912. He was buried in the monastery of Saint Zacharias. The Venetians grieved deeply at his death, because he had governed the dukedom honorably and with every virtue.

Ursus, surnamed Particiacus, succeeded him in this dignity. As soon as he became duke, he sent his son Peter to Constantinople to the emperor Leo. The emperor received him honorably, made him a protospatharius [Note: [Col. 0913] “Him” has been added, but the signs placed beneath indicate that it should not be read.], enriched him with the greatest gifts, and allowed him to return home.

When Peter wished to cross the territory of the Croats on his return, he was deceived by Michael, duke of the Slavs, through treachery, deprived of all his possessions, and handed over to the Bulgarian king, Simeon, for punishment by exile. His father, grieving bitterly over his loss, was unable to recover him, until he ransomed him through his envoy Dominic, archdeacon of Metamauco, who later became a bishop.

During these days the emperor Leo died (in the year 912), and his son Constantine obtained the empire. At the same time the patriarch Laurence departed from the world. He had governed the church of Grado for twelve years, nine months, and twenty-four days, and was buried in the atrium of Saint Euphemia. Marinus succeeded him as patriarch.

The aforementioned Duke Ursus, after holding the dukedom for twenty years and having become an old man, utterly despised earthly things. Devoutly taking the monastic habit in the monastery of Saint Felix, he ended his life there. He had been distinguished in intelligence, endowed with holiness, a lover of justice, generous in almsgiving, and supported by every virtue.

After his departure, a certain very noble Peter, surnamed Candianus, assumed the dukedom and likewise attempted, following the example of his predecessor, to govern the people subject to him. When some men of Venice had rashly seized certain inhabitants of the island of Comacchio, Peter, unable to endure the insult of so great a disgrace, sent an army there, burned their fortress with fire, killed some of them, and led the rest, men and women alike, to Venice. There he detained them until they submitted to his authority by oath and promised thereafter to obey him in everything as his own subjects.

During these days a certain bishop of Olivolo named Dominic died. Peter, son of the tribune Peter, succeeded him.

The aforesaid Duke Peter Candianus sent his beloved namesake son to Constantinople to the emperors Constantine and Romanus [Col. 0914A]. They made him a protospatharius, and he returned to Venice with very great gifts. But the aforesaid duke lived no more than five years after his son’s arrival and was taken from this life.

Peter, son of Duke Ursus [Note: [Col. 0913] Added by a more recent hand: “1437.”] [Note: [Col. 0913] Added above by a more recent hand: “Badovarius.”], succeeded him. He was the man who had been exiled to the Bulgarian king.

It does not seem inappropriate to insert here how the aforesaid Romanus usurped the imperial throne. The emperor Leo, whom we mentioned above, was sending a naval force against the Saracens in the customary manner. He appointed that Romanus, who at that time held the office of *delongarius*, as the first commander of that army.

Meanwhile, after the emperor Leo died, his son Constantine obtained the empire by the unanimous choice of all. He immediately sent envoys to Romanus, ordering him to return to Constantinople together with the army.
