Romanus is said to have replied that he would in no way return to Constantinople or submit to Constantine’s authority unless Constantine honored him in the palace as chief counselor and almost as a father. Otherwise, he promised that he would undoubtedly resist his empire with all his strength.

He soon fulfilled his words by deeds. He went to the city called Abydos [Note: [Col. 0913D] Abydos.], and there strictly prohibited anyone from bringing provisions to Constantinople. As a result, when the citizens had almost been consumed by hunger, they received him into the palace, at the imperial council’s request (in the year 919). He immediately gave his daughter in marriage to the emperor Constantine.

Then he placed the imperial crown upon himself and upon his three sons—Christopher, Stephen, and Constantine—so that five emperors lived together in one palace. Christopher, Romanus’ eldest son, did not live long and lost the empire together with his life (in the year 920).

During these days Duke Peter Badovarius died. He had governed the dukedom for three years. Peter Candianus, son of the aforementioned Duke Peter, succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0913] Added by a more recent hand: “940.”].

The four aforesaid emperors, hostile in spirit toward one another, were plotting to kill their kinsman Constantine. When Stephen and Constantine, the brothers, sought to kill him, they violently made their father Romanus a monk, because he had tried to prevent them, and condemned him to exile on the islands called the Paonariae [Note: [Col. 0913D] “The islands of the princes” today. Zonaras, book 16, writes that the emperor Romanus was exiled to the island of Prota.].

After perpetrating this crime against their father, I shall now explain how they again attempted to destroy the aforesaid Constantine. It is said that an ancient custom existed in the palace at Constantinople: each emperor had soldiers there who performed palace guard duty by lot. The Aeolic language calls them *littoriae* [Note: [Col. 0914D] Perhaps from the Latin word *lictor*, inflected according to Greek usage in those centuries, like καμπιδοὔκτωρας (*campiductores*), καντάτωρας (*cantatores*), and other hybrid words of that kind. Although Latin, they were written in Greek letters and with Greek inflection and were commonly used by Greeks of the later period. In the manuscript, however, *lictoras* should be restored in place of *littoras*. I interpret them as *somatophylaces*, bodyguards. ZAN.].

Since three men were governing the empire together at that time, each of them had his own soldiers in the palace under this arrangement. A certain eunuch named Gallus was in command of all of them. One day the two brothers, Stephen and Constantine, secretly conferred with him in the following manner: when they had gathered together at the usual time for a meal and had provoked their kinsman Constantine with harsh words, as soon as the master received the agreed signal from them, he was to open the exit for his own soldiers, so that they might either kill Constantine or disgracefully expel him from the palace. He was also to block the passage for Constantine’s soldiers, so that they could not come to his aid.

Gallus gladly promised to carry this out. But God’s providence, which had determined that Constantine should rule, did not allow this wicked conspiracy to remain hidden from him. The same Gallus, under divine inspiration, immediately sought to reveal the plan entrusted to him to Constantine. He promised that, when the brothers gave him the signal, he would open the passage for Constantine’s soldiers, whom he had promised to shut in, and would shut in the soldiers whom he had promised to release.

This was done. On the following day, when they gathered at the table and the aforesaid brothers heaped insults upon their kinsman, Constantine, confident in Gallus’ loyalty, began firmly to return the insults inflicted upon him. Then the brothers signaled and said:

“Gallus, can we perhaps have anyone who might avenge our injuries against this arrogant man?”

He replied, “You can,” and at once brought Constantine’s soldiers forward to aid their lord. They came and immediately seized both brothers. At Constantine’s command they were made clerics and brought to their father, the monk whom they themselves had exiled.

When the father saw them coming, he mocked them and said:

“And from where, in this solitude of my exile, have such devoted and handsome clerics been brought? But you who were not ashamed to exile your father shall not undergo the punishment of exile together, so that you may not have as a consoler in sorrow the one whom you scorned to have as a partner in honor.”

Then, through messengers, he addressed his son-in-law Constantine as follows:

“Please do not allow your sons to remain with me in a single exile, because those whom one palace could not contain should not be contained by one exile either.”

Then the emperor Constantine ordered one of them, Stephen, to be exiled to the island called Proconnesus [Note: [Col. 0915D] Proconnesus.], and the other, Constantine, to the island of Samothrace [Note: [Col. 0916D] Samothrace.]. That Constantine was beheaded on the same island shortly afterward by one of the emperor’s soldiers [Note: [Col. 0915] From this point the lettering is slightly smaller and more even, but by the same hand.].

The account of the Greek emperors compelled us to depart somewhat from the sequence of our history. Now it is necessary to resume it in order.

Duke Peter Candianus, whom we mentioned above, in the sixth year of his dukedom sent thirty-three ships, which the Venetians call *gumbarias*, against the Narentine Slavs. Ursus Badovarius and Peter Rosolus commanded them. They returned without result. He again attempted to send the same number against them. After establishing a treaty, these ships returned home.

At that time Bishop Peter of Olivolo died; he had governed the bishopric for . . . . . years. Ursus succeeded him.

The aforementioned Duke Peter had three sons. At the people’s urging, he chose one of them, named Peter, as his associate (in the year 959). But, scorning his father’s admonitions [Note: [Col. 0915] Thus below; in 1, *flo. .*, with the ending pending; in 2, *flocipendens*.], he attempted to rise against him. Matters reached the point that one day the soldiers of both sides assembled in the forum at Rialto to fight.

But since most of the people obeyed the sick and aged father and wished to destroy the son, the father was finally moved by mercy and began to plead that he not be killed [Note: [Col. 0915] A *t* has been added afterward in 1.]. Nevertheless, wishing to satisfy the people, he ordered him to leave the homeland. Then all the bishops, the entire clergy, and the whole people, having formed a sworn agreement, swore that they would never have him as duke, either during his father’s life or after his death.

That Peter, who had been driven from his homeland, accompanied by the deacon George and a certain presbyter Gregory, together with twelve personal servants, reached Hwidon, marquis and son of King Berengar. Hwidon received him devotedly and presented him to his father, King Berengar. The king likewise received him with honor and invited him to accompany him in fighting against the march of Spoleto and Camerino.

After returning, and having received permission from the king to take revenge upon the Venetians, Peter went to Ravenna. There he learned from someone’s report that seven Venetian ships were in the harbor called Primarius [Note: [Col. 0916D] Porto di Primaro, at the southern mouth of the Po.], laden with merchandise and preparing to sail for the city of Fano. Then, having obtained six Ravenna ships, he attacked them as an enemy and captured them without difficulty. He then returned to Ravenna.

Meanwhile his father, Duke Peter, died. He had governed the dukedom for seventeen years. It is said that after the expulsion of his son he lived no more than two months and fourteen days.

In the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 959, the entire Venetian population, together with the bishops and abbots, assembled. Renouncing their oaths of oblivion, they prepared nearly three hundred ships and hastened to Ravenna to restore the aforesaid Peter to the dignity of the dukedom [Col. 0916D]. Receiving him, they brought him to the palace with such an array and, by an oath of allegiance, reestablished him as their ruler [Col. 0917A].

Not long afterward, taking advantage of an opportunity, he forbade his wife Johanna the marital bed and compelled her by force to receive the monastic habit in the monastery of Saint Zacharias. He dedicated the son whom he had by her, named Vitalis, to the clerical state and later advanced him to become patriarch of Grado.

Then he took in marriage Hwalderada, the sister of the marquis Hugh [Note: [Col. 0917D] Hugh, king of Italy and duke of Provence. [Col. 0918D] See Guichenon, *Histoire généalogique de la maison royale de Savoie*, p. 164, and Grandi, *Life of Saint Peter Urseolus*, where there is more about Waldrada, or Gualdrada, daughter of the marquis Uberto. ZAN.]. From her he received, by right of dowry, large numbers of male and female servants and great estates. With these he sought to acquire foreign soldiers from the kingdom of Italy, by whom he could defend and possess the aforesaid estates.

He is said to have been of such great audacity that he oppressed his subjects with the severity of his authority more than was customary and overcame foreign opponents by taking revenge upon them. He waged a most powerful war against the people of the fortress of Ferrara. He ordered the fortress of Opitergium to be burned and devastated. He inflicted harsh treatment on many others who reproached him.

But since I cannot explain all his deeds, let us demonstrate his end by writing it down. In the eighteenth year of his rule (977), he was killed together with his young son, whom he had by the aforesaid Hwalderada, in the following manner.

For a long time the Venetians had hated him on account of his severity and had diligently sought an opportunity to destroy him [Note: [Col. 0918D] That is, “him.”]. One day, after forming a conspiracy, they began to rise against him. Yet they did not dare to enter the palace by any means, because they knew that he was surrounded by warlike soldiers, although they were few.

At last, devising a wicked plan, they attempted to set fire to the nearby houses, which stood opposite the palace on this side of the stream, using fire mixed with pitch as fuel, so that the flexible peaks of the flames might reach and burn the neighboring palace. As a result, not only the palace but also the churches of Saint Mark, Saint Theodore, and Saint Mary of Jubianico, as well as more than three hundred dwellings, were burned that day.

The duke, unable to endure the heat of the fire and the suffocation of the smoke for long inside the palace, attempted to escape with a few companions through the doors of the atrium of Saint Mark. There he found several leading Venetians, together with their relatives, awaiting his destruction. When he saw them, he addressed them as follows:

“And you, brothers, have wished to come to complete my destruction? If I have done anything wrong in word or in public affairs, I beg you to spare my life [Note: [Col. 0917] *insperate*, corrected to *inspirate* in 1.], and I promise to make amends for everything according to your will.”

But they declared him utterly wicked and deserving of death and cried out in dreadful voices that there was no possibility for him to escape. Then they repeatedly wounded him cruelly on every side with blows of their swords [Col. 0918A]. His holy soul, leaving the prison of the body, went to the customary dwelling above.

His son, whom his nurse had rescued from the danger of the fire, was pierced through by a spear wielded by a certain utterly wicked man. The soldiers who had tried to support him were likewise killed.

They first carried the frozen bodies of the father and son, for the sake of dishonor, in a small boat to the market of the butchers. Then, after a certain most holy man named John Gradenicus intervened, they carried them to the monastery of Saint Hilary [Col. 0918D].

After this heinous crime had been perpetrated [Note: [Col. 0917] Superscribed by a recent hand: 974.], they assembled in the church of Saint Peter. There, by common consent, they resolved to elevate to the dignity of duke a certain man, namely Peter, surnamed Orseolo, distinguished by nobility of birth and character. From childhood he had striven for nothing other than to please God, and he shrank from ascending to so great an elevation, fearing that through ambition for worldly honor he might lose his resolve to pursue holiness. At length, when the people insistently pressed him, he did not refuse to accept the summit of this principate—not out of human favor, but for the advantage of the entire commonwealth.

Then, after all had confirmed him by oath, he wished to reside in his own house, so that in the meantime he might restore the church of Saint Mark and the palace. He had a wife, Felicia by name and by merit, and she was the mother of only one child. The child, his father’s namesake, proved no less distinguished in conduct. After his conception—which the blessed mother is said to have learned through an angelic revelation—she and her husband mutually vowed thereafter to preserve their marriage bed inviolate, with the husband’s consent.

For this same duke had begun to administer the affairs of the Venetians well and usefully, to observe the rigor of the law most conscientiously in every matter, and to excel in the grace of every virtue. He diligently undertook to restore, at his own expense and with due honor, the burned palace and the church of Saint Mark.

Meanwhile Vitalis, patriarch of Grado and son of the aforementioned Peter who had been killed, hastened to Saxony to the second Emperor Otto on the advice of certain Venetians. The emperor received him devoutly and said: “Why, father, after undertaking so long a journey, did you wish to come into my presence?” He replied: “Driven by the destruction of my own parents, I have come to your clemency, so that you may become the comforter and supporter of my misfortune and my poverty.”

Then the emperor, having learned the circumstances and sequence of this crime, asked the patriarch to remain with him for some time, and compassionately and mercifully mourned his complaints. At the same time, the venerable lord Hwarinus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael, which is situated in the region of Aquitaine, at a place called Cussanus [Col. 0919A] [Note: [Col. 0919D] Saint-Michel de Cusan, in the diocese of Perpignan.], set out for Rome to visit the thresholds of the Apostles.

On his return, supported by the fear of God and by devotion to blessed Mark, he entered Venice, where he remained for several days, compelled both by his devotion to prayer and by the entreaties of Duke Peter. While the lord duke honored him with due veneration and they frequently engaged together in divine conversation, the abbot perceived that the duke utterly despised earthly things and held his dignity not through ambition but for the consolation of his subjects. Nevertheless, he admonished him, saying: “If you wish to be perfect, abandon the world and this pinnacle of dignity, and hasten to serve God in a monastery.”

The duke replied: “Excellent father, and gainer of my soul, I eagerly desire to obey your admonitions. But I ask for a period of time, so that I may dispose of my property. Thereafter, subjected to the monastery and bound by your governance, I desire to serve as a soldier of God.”

Having settled these matters, they fixed a definite day on which the abbot would return to Venice to receive him. Then, having obtained permission, he returned to his monastery.

The aforementioned duke, meanwhile, did not cease to labor diligently for the safety of his country, although certain men—through whose counsel, as we have said, the patriarch had gone to the emperor—had become perverse opponents of his rule, to such an extent that they plotted to bring about his death by a cruel end. Yet such was the strength of his goodness and divine virtue that whatever they secretly determined against him by wicked conspiracy, he learned without anyone investigating. He did not wish to repay any resister with evil, but endured and bore everything with an even spirit in the fear of God.

Meanwhile, on the appointed day, the aforementioned abbot returned to Venice, intending to go to Jerusalem (976). Duke Peter gladly received him. On the first night of the Kalends of September, he secretly departed from Venice together with John Gradonicus and John Maurecenus, his son-in-law, without the knowledge of his wife, his son, or any of his faithful followers.

After mounting horses not far from the monastery of Saint Hilary, and with their beards already shorn, they began to travel at the greatest speed. So rapidly did they proceed that on the third day, after crossing the countryside of Milan [Note: [Col. 0919D] *Rus*, land.], they caught sight of the city of Vercelli [Note: [Col. 0920D] Vercelli.].

On the following day the Venetian people mourned their lost shepherd. When they could not find him, they languished in the deepest grief [Col. 0919D]. He had indeed been a nourisher of the poor, a restorer of churches, a supporter of clerics and monks, and benevolent toward everyone. From his own resources he gave a thousand pounds for the relief of the Venetians at the palace, and another thousand for feeding the poor. For the altar of Saint Mark he ordered a panel of marvelous workmanship to be made at Constantinople from silver [Note: [Col. 0919] *argen*, 1.] and gold. He also carried with him a very large quantity of treasure for the restoration of the aforementioned monastery.

Thus he ruled the duchy for two years and one month. For he was no more than fifty years old when he laid aside worldly glory.

After his departure [Note: [Col. 0919] Superscribed by a recent hand: 976.], Vitalis, surnamed Candianus, a man of every kind of prudence and goodness, was substituted in the dignity of duke (976). When the patriarch Vitalis, who was staying near the Veronese march, heard this, he entered Venice. When the duke appealed to him, he went with his messengers to the German region in order to consolidate peace between the emperor and the Venetians [Note: [Col. 0919] An *r* superscribed.], since he regarded them as especially accursed and hateful because of the killing of Duke Peter. After the treaty had been confirmed, he returned to his own country.

The aforesaid duke, when bodily illness came upon him, arranged to become a monk four days before ending his present life and to be carried to the monastery of Saint Hilary. He governed the duchy of the Venetians for one year and two months, and was buried in that same monastery (977).

He was succeeded in dignity by Tribunus, surnamed Menius [Note: [Col. 0919] Superscribed by a recent hand: 977.]. Although he lacked worldly skill, he nevertheless abounded in the greatest resources of fortune. During his time golden Venice was dishonored by several perilous disgraces.

It happened that the leading men of Venice first laid an ambush against the duke, and afterward, falling into mutual discord, became infected in turn with the wickedness of hatred. Meanwhile, a great quarrel arose between the Maureceni and the Coloprini, nobles of Venice. It reached the point that one day Stefanus Coloprinus, together with the kinship of his sons and relatives, rose up to destroy the Maurocenian family, with the consent and assistance of the aforesaid duke.

But by God’s power all the prudent men involved obtained the means of escaping this perilous outrage. One of them, however—namely Dominic Maurecenus—was seized in the square of Saint Peter of Olivolo and cruelly mutilated for a very long time. His body, shamefully stripped and still half alive, was carried by a small boat to the monastery of Saint Zacharias. While he lay in the church and was mourned by the relatives standing around him, he gave up his breath within the space of two hours. His death caused his family the greatest grief, so that they awaited a suitable time to avenge this crime.

About this time the second Emperor Otto, coming to Italy, attempted to break the treaty with the Venetians on account of the death of Duke Peter Candianus. The aforementioned Duke Tribunus sent messengers to him and sought to appease him with gifts. He also granted the duke and his people a renewed written agreement at Verona, to be held perpetually [Col. 0920D] [Note: [Col. 0920D] The author seems to reverse the sequence of events. On his first arrival Otto prohibited provisions from reaching the Venetians at Verona in December 980; after two years had elapsed, he returned to Verona and renewed the treaty on 7 June 983.].

Then, passing through Ravenna, he hastened to Rome (981, March), where he learned that the fearsome people of the Saracens had invaded the regions of Calabria and were already wishing to direct their steps toward Apulia. He attempted to attack them in warfare. But while he imprudently approached the nearby places where the Saracen multitude was stationed, the grim host suddenly tried to challenge the Christian army to battle (982, July 14).

The emperor, unaware that all the Saracen leaders were concealed among the mountain ravines, began the battle boldly, supposing that he could easily defeat those whom he was able to see. With Christ’s favor he overcame them most courageously. But when the Christian army, with triumphant glory, wished to pitch its tents, a multitude of pagans leapt down from the mountains and unexpectedly fell upon them, beginning to slaughter them fiercely. Those who were denied any avenue of escape fell cruelly wounded.

The emperor, although with immense difficulty, barely reached the shore through the enemy lines. Terrified by the attackers’ pressure, he entered the wave-tossed sea. Two Greek ships were anchored there not far from land; in their language these are called *zalandriae*. They took him aboard with two of his servants, without recognizing him.

It is said that they kept him bound for three days. Although he utterly denied that he was the emperor, the Greeks, highly skilled in their craft, were nevertheless able to identify him by certain signs. Once they had recognized him, they decided to carry him to Constantinople. He replied:

“And I desire this with all the affection of my heart, since I would rather live in exile near the footsteps of the holy emperors than remain here, deprived of all my possessions, bearing the disgrace of my misfortune. Only promise that, before you depart, you will allow me to receive my wife and the remnants of my fortune.”

Then twelve chests filled with a great quantity of treasure were carried to the edge of the shore. When the Greeks saw this, all hesitation removed, they firmly believed that he wished to go with them. While these things were being done, in the presence of Bishop Cessone of Metz [Note: [Col. 0921D] Deoderic; unless perhaps the punctuation should be: “While these things were being done, at Cessone, at Metz, etc.,” with *Cessone* written in place of Rossano.] and several others standing on the shore [Note: [Col. 0922D] Liupone and Richizone. Compare Alpert, *SS*, vol. IV (*Patrologia*, vol. CXL).] [Note: [Col. 0921] The words *littori a. i. a. g. i. m. p. et v. n. d.* are absent in witnesses 2 and 3.], he seized a sword and leapt into the sea. Swimming bravely, he reached the desired shore unharmed. Thus freed from two dangers, he arrived in Rome with his wife.

Afterward, traversing Pavia and the other cities of Italy, he came to Verona (983, June). The aforementioned Stefanus Coloprinus, together with his two sons and certain relatives, having learned that the violence of the Maureceni intended to avenge their kinsman’s death at the duke’s instigation, secretly departed from Venice and hastened to reach the emperor.

When the emperor took leave of him, he asked why he had wished to abandon his homeland. As Stefanus solemnly recounted the disasters of his journey, he persuaded the emperor that, if he were willing to heed his counsels and admonitions, he could acquire long-desired Venice in an easy campaign. Moreover, to inflame the emperor’s spirit still further toward completing this wicked crime, he promised to give him one hundred pounds of pure gold if, after conquering the country, he granted him the dignity of duke.

When the emperor heard this, he issued an edict and unavoidable command to all who were subject to his scepter: no one, relying on any presumption, was thereafter to permit any Venetian to leave for any part of his empire, nor was any of his own people to dare enter Venice. He then firmly ordered each Venetian living with him to guard diligently, together with his messengers, the places where they knew that provisions flowed for the relief of the Venetians.

Thus it came about that Stefanus Coloprinus and his son Dominic stayed at Padua; Ursus Badovarius watched over the river Adige; Dominic Silvo and Peter Tribunus occupied the region of Mistrina; John Bennatus hurried busily among them all like a purveyor of trifles; Marinus Coloprinus performed this duty in the Mistrian county; and Ravenna was assigned for guarding to the younger Stefanus, son of the aforementioned Stefanus.

The aforementioned Duke Tribunus, unable to endure for long the wickedness of his rebellious and faithless enemies without retaliation, permitted their houses to be devastated and ordered their wives to be guarded so that they could not flee. But the emperor persisted with such severity and harshness in the destruction of the Venetians that they could appease him neither with prayers nor with any gifts. Instead, he imposed his command upon all once more, ordering that no one dare spare any Venetian who reached any part of his empire.

With these matters settled, he planned to visit Rome. He did not remain there unharmed for long, however, for when a violent fever attacked him, he died and was buried in the courtyard of Saint Peter, not far from the church of Saint Mary (983, December 7). Hence there is no doubt that a certain spiritual monk learned, through an angel’s revelation, that he had suffered an unexpected death because of his persecution of the Venetians.

Venice, after suffering this misfortune for two years, was freed by the favor of God. The aforementioned Stefanus Coloprinus, together with his sons and the others, hastened to the city of Pavia. There they began continually to entreat Augusta Adelaide, who was staying there, on bended knees, so that they might be preserved unharmed in the kingdom, since almost all the princes of Italy had judged them worthy of death for betraying their own homeland.

Then, when Stefanus Coloprinus suddenly died at Ticinum, the empress, compelled by the prayers of the margrave Hugo, sent his sons, together with certain others and preceded by her messengers, to Duke Tribunus, so that whatever offense they or anyone else had perversely committed against him, they might deserve to obtain Venice through his favor [Note: [Col. 0923] Zanetti prefers to read *veniam* (“pardon”); but the reading of the manuscripts, supported by what follows—*patriam illis concessit*—can be defended.].

Although unwilling, Duke Tribunus nevertheless, at the empress’s command and request, granted them both his favor and their homeland. Moreover, so that they would not be rashly killed by any of their enemies, they remained safely in their country, protected by four guarantors on the security of their oaths.

The Maureceni, silently observing all this, firmly resolved to avenge their kinsman’s death. Therefore, one day, as the three brothers born to Stefanus Coloprinus wished to return home from the palace in their usual small boat, they were killed by four Maurocenian men, and the stream’s waters were stained with their blood.

Their bodies were lifted from the water by one of their own men and carried to their bereaved mother and wives. On the following day they were buried in the monastery of Saint Zacharias [Note: [Col. 0923] This sentence—“On the following day they were buried”—is found in witness 1 but is absent from the printed editions.]. Two of them were laymen; the third, namely John, held the office of a cleric.

Although the duke declared himself innocent of this crime, some nevertheless asserted that he was guilty of it. In the thirteenth year of his dukeship, he sent his son Maurice to Constantinople. While he himself was held by the same illness, six days before his final hour was darkened, he became a monk in the monastery of Saint Zacharias—not of his own will, but under compulsion from the people. He ruled the Venetians for thirteen years and five months, and was buried in the same monastery [Col. 0923C] [Note: [Col. 0923] Here the Urbino manuscript has a lacuna of one page. What follows appears to have been written amid the account of these events.].

In the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 991, the Venetian people elevated Peter, the son of the aforementioned lord Duke Peter Orseolo, to his father’s dignity when he was thirty years old. In character and conduct he was not degenerate from his saintly father; yet in the practical knowledge of both men he surpassed almost all the ancient dukes.

This man not only restored the advantages of his country by consolidating its former condition, but so increased the commonwealth that in his time Venice was said to have been elevated above all the neighboring provinces in splendor and wealth. At the beginning of his reign, through his embassies, he secured the favor of the emperors of Constantinople and of all the Saracen princes, making them devoted friends bound by firm stability.

He also sent messengers to Saxony to King Otto III, a boy of outstanding character. With him he bound himself by so strong a bond of love and friendship that, without delay, he thereafter obtained at will whatever was possible and appropriate for him [Note: [Col. 0923D] The treaty renewed on 19 July 991 is preserved in the *Liber Blancus* and in Andrea Dandolo’s *Chronicle*, pp. 223–225.].

By his power this duke freed his people from the oppression of the Croatian Slavs. He was also the first to forbid them to pay their customary tribute [Note: [Col. 0924D] Compare Andrea’s *Chronicle*, book IX, part III, p. 225. Zanetti.]. He is shown always to have remained joined by a treaty of friendship with the Italian princes. Yet if any of them, emboldened by rashness, wished to impose upon his people some burdens greater than those established by the treaty, he resisted manfully and remained master of himself in every respect.

Why say more? He strove to rule his own people with balanced moderation and the scales of justice; toward outsiders who resisted his authority, he repaid them in kind. I shall attempt to set forth in order the prosperity through which Venice flourished in his days.

At that time the city of Grado, recognized as the metropolis of all New Venice, appeared to have been largely consumed by age. The aforementioned prince rebuilt it with the strongest fortifications, from its very foundations to the summits of its battlements. He also had his own house built there beside the western tower, and willingly undertook to restore the walls and the ceilings of the churches.

At New City, which is called Heracliana, he had a house of beautiful design built, together with a chapel, at that same time.

Meanwhile John, bishop of Belluno, had violently usurped and continued to hold the estates of the duchy of Venice within the territory of New City, seized during the time of Duke Tribunus. Neither a royal command nor any promise made by the bishop could frighten him into returning what he unjustly retained and making peace with Lord Duke Peter.

Although displeased, the duke resolved to tolerate this for the time being, while Duke Henry of the Veronese march was present. When the duke arrived, Peter arranged through his messengers to petition him. Henry, pretending to act under a bond of friendship, promised that he would administer justice according to his will concerning Bishop John and the others who opposed him. Yet what he had promised with his mouth he quickly exchanged for an intention to act otherwise.

Therefore Duke Peter, perceiving such deception, without any delay sent his envoy to the most renowned King Otto at the palace of Aachen, so that he might explain these matters to him in due order. When the king learned of this, he wholly censured the conduct of the aforementioned Duke Henry and, by royal command, granted Duke Peter all the aforesaid estates to possess. He also sent Bruno, his noble knight, who was to settle this dispute between the duke and the bishop by the authority of law and of the king.

The bishop held Bruno in such contempt that he would neither meet him in conversation nor agree to see him. When Lord Duke Peter observed this, and after receiving sound advice from the royal envoy and his own men, he imposed an unavoidable decree upon his subjects: no one, relying on any presumption, was to dare enter the aforementioned or the Istrian march, nor was anyone to sell or purchase any merchandise there.

After these matters had been carried out, the royal envoy returned to his own country. The quarrel begun by the duke continued for a very long time, to such an extent that not only were the resources of that march consumed by a shortage of salt, but its inhabitants, deprived of Venetian supplies and suffering wretched calamity, repeatedly and humbly begged the duke for the peace they could not obtain [Note: [Col. 0925] A recent hand has superscribed *f*].

(996.) When the duke heard that King Otto was going to come to Italy, he delayed making peace with the people of the aforementioned march. He then decided to send his messengers to Germany once more (March). They found the king amid the Alpine passes, already coming from Ausonia.

The king received them honorably and willingly heard whatever wickedness the duke’s enemies had inflicted upon him. Moreover, he promised never to compel him in any way to make peace unless he himself wished to do so.

Then, before he reached the plain of Italy, he sweetly and earnestly requested the same duke to send his son, who still lacked confirmation in the Christian faith, to Verona without delay. On the advice of his faithful men, the duke agreed to do this.

When the boy reached Verona, the king received him ceremoniously. He strengthened him with the anointing of chrism, embracing him in his own arms, and, taking away his paternal name, called him Otto—that is, the king’s namesake.

The aforementioned Bishop John and Rozo, bishop of the see of Treviso, together with several others, gathered there to seek peace. The king forbade them to obtain it until they had promised to recover Lord Duke Peter’s favor by making satisfaction. He also compelled Bishop John by law to return the duke’s land, which he unjustly possessed.

At this time a quarrel had arisen between the citizens of Verona and the German army. Some of the Germans were killed by the citizens and fell in the streets of the city. Among them a very noble young man named Charles was killed; his death had left the king and his countrymen in the deepest grief. The king resolved to avenge it severely upon the citizens. Nevertheless, they escaped through the intervention of Odbert, bishop of that city.

Otto, the aforementioned Lord Duke Peter’s son, returned to Venice from the king with various gifts. Then the lord duke granted the long-sought peace to his enemies, although the severity of Bishop John continued over the loss of the estate.

At that same time, when Marinus, bishop of Olivolo, died at Rialto after governing the bishopric for … years, Dominic surnamed Gradonicus succeeded him.

King Otto, after traveling through Brescia and the other cities of Italy, reached Pavia (April). There the Italian princes, pledging faith upon the sacred Gospels, praised the king. When he heard there that John, bishop of the apostolic see, had died, he decided to raise Bruno, his nephew—namely, the son of Duke Otto—to this summit of dignity, which he afterward accomplished.

Then he traveled by ship through the waters of the Eridanus [Note: [Col. 0925D] That is, the Po.] and went to Ravenna. After remaining there for some time [Note: [Col. 0925D] On 1 May he granted Duke Peter the liberty of establishing three ports.], he ordered the eyes of Rudolf, count of Rimini, as well as those of Herimund and of his brother Raimund, to be put out, on account of the estates of churches and of the poor which they had usurped and possessed (May 1).

Having settled these matters, he made for the city of Romulus, where he was anointed and consecrated emperor by the aforementioned Bruno, the apostolic bishop later called Gregory, at the appeal of the Roman multitude (May 21).

From there, departing not far from the city of Rome, he stayed for some time among the Alps of the march of Camerino, so that he might endure the heat of that region more easily. Later, returning by way of Tuscany toward the city of Pavia (August 1), he imposed an edict upon all who obeyed him [Note: [Col. 0926D] It does not survive.]: wherever Venetians were found within his empire, they were to live unharmed and without any burden imposed upon them. He then set out by way of Lake Como on his journey beyond the mountains.

About this time the Croatian judge, because the duke had forbidden the payment of tribute, attempted to inflict harm upon the Venetians. Therefore the lord duke sent six prepared ships there, under the command of Badovarius, surnamed Bragadinus. He seized one of their cities, called Issa [Note: [Col. 0926D] Today Lissa.], and carried captives of both sexes to Venice. As a result, the hatred between the Venetians and the Slavs grew still greater.

They began once more to demand the duke’s tribute insistently [Note: [Col. 0926D] That is, *exigere*, “to demand.”]. To their disgrace the duke replied: “I do not intend to send this through just any messenger; rather, so long as life remains, I will not refuse to come in person to make this payment” [Note: [Col. 0925] *ipse*, “in person,” superscribed.].

At that time John the Greek, bishop of the church of Piacenza, returned from Constantinople with an envoy of the Greek emperor and went to Rome. When he found the apostolic see vacant, its shepherd having been expelled through the audacity of John Crescentius, he did not fear to seize it in defiance of the imperial decree. Gregory, the spouse of that church, was meanwhile moving mournfully through the cities of Italy, awaiting the emperor’s arrival.

During these events the aforementioned duke sent his son John to Constantinople. The emperor not only rewarded him with various gifts but also elevated him with distinguished honors.

(998.) When the emperor heard of this most wicked crime perpetrated by John the Greek, he did not delay hastening back to Italy. Planning to descend by ship from the city of Ticinum to Ravenna (January), he requested his beloved countryman, Peter, Duke of the Venetians, not to refuse to send his son Otto to meet him beyond the fortress of Ferrara.

The duke gladly agreed and sent his son with decorated ships. Among them was one ship outstanding in size and beauty [Note: [Col. 0927] *pulchritudine*, “in beauty,” superscribed.]. The emperor boarded it with the boy and reached Ravenna. Remaining there only a short while, he allowed the duke’s son, enriched with an abundance of gifts and possessions, to return to Venice (February).

He himself proceeded to Rome in order to abolish the arrogance of his enemies. When they heard that he was coming to Rome, one of them—namely, John Crescentius—shut himself up with his followers in the fortress of Saint Angel. The other, John the Greek, entered an impregnable tower far from Rome, but was not permitted to remain there long once the emperor had arrived.

Captured by the emperor’s soldiers, he had his eyes put out and his ears cut off; he also lost his nose and tongue. His head disfigured, he was carried to Rome and placed in a certain monastery. Since this was not considered sufficient vengeance for so great a crime, he later suffered a sentence of deposition from a sacred council and lost his priestly office. The Romans then placed him, disfigured, on the back of a donkey, facing its tail [Note: [Col. 0927] *ad cuidam* in witness 1; *ad cauda* in witness 2.], and led him through the Roman territories amid the herald’s proclamation.

Afterward all the Roman citizens, together with the German army, began to besiege the strongly fortified castle of Saint Angel. They captured it only with great difficulty and beheaded John Crescentius at the summit, where all could see him, while he cried out for mercy in a pitiful voice (April 29). The others who lacked the means of escape were cast to the ground and hanged on Mount Gaudio by imperial decree.

Having completed these deeds, the emperor ruled the Italian kingdom for three years, during which he accomplished many things and visited the German kingdom.

In those times, in the territory bordering Dalmatia, no more than the citizens of Iater—were subject to the authority of the Venetian doge. The princes of the Croatians and Narentines regularly harassed them, to such an extent that the Narentines, having captured forty of them, carried them away as captives [Note: That is, bound men.]. Therefore all the peoples of Dalmatia, assembling almost as one, instructed Peter, the doge of the Venetians, through their envoys that, if he wished to come or send an army to free them from the harshness of the Slavs, they and their cities would remain subject in perpetuity to his authority and that of his successors.

When Doge Peter heard this, without any delay, strengthened by the counsel of his people, he completed preparations for a naval expedition. In the seventh year of his dogeship, on the feast of the Lord’s Ascension (May 26), he wished to assemble with his men in the church of Saint Peter of Olivolo to receive the services of the Mass. Dominicus, bishop of that place, presented him with a victorious standard, and, boarding the fleet together, they entered the port of Equilium on that day. Then, with the sails set and a westerly wind blowing, they reached the city of Grado.

Lord Vitalis, the patriarch, receiving them with the people preceding him and with the clergy in procession, rendered services worthy of his prince; he also adorned his right hand with the victorious sign of Saint Hermagoras. From there, plowing through the waves of the open sea and crossing over to the province of Istria [Note: “to” is written above the line in manuscript 1.] [Note: “crossing over” is written above the line in manuscript 1.], they decided to spend the night beside the city of Parentium [Col. 0928B], after lowering their sails near the island. The venerable Bishop Andreas came to meet them and bestowed many services upon Doge Peter [Note: “many” is written above the line in manuscript 1.]. He humbly begged him not to refuse to visit the shrine of Saint Maurus. Granting his request, Peter entered the city [Note: Parenzo.] escorted by a large force, and, after completing the sacred services in the church of Saint Maurus, he then set out. With the sailors rowing, they wished to find welcome hospitality at the monastery on the island of Saint Andrew, which lies near the city of Pola [Note: Pola.]. Bertaldus, the distinguished bishop of Pola, hastened there with a multitude of clergy and citizens and honored the same doge with every mark of respect.

Then, sailing across the vast sea, they were carried to the city of Absarus [Note: Ossero.]. There not only the citizens but also all those who came together from the neighboring Roman and Slavic strongholds rejoiced that they had anticipated the arrival of so great a guest. After all had completed their oaths, they resolved to remain under the authority of that prince. Having accomplished this, they solemnly celebrated the holy day of Pentecost (the year 998, June 5) and sang songs of praise to the aforesaid prince.

Then he ordered all those who had reached the full strength of adulthood to come with him. After receiving their pay, they began the planned crossing. On the following day, before he approached the city of Iatera, the prior of that city, together with the bishop and the others, received their lord with rejoicing. Once they had entered the city, the leading men of that region assembled there [Col. 0928D] and eagerly desired to be subject to the authority of the same prince. Among them were the bishops of Veglia and Arbe [Note: The islands of Veglia and Arbe.] with the priors of their cities. With one accord they swore upon the sacred words of the Evangelists that, to the best of their knowledge and understanding, they would henceforth observe faith toward Lord Peter, the doge.

Moreover, the bishops confirmed to them by those same sacred texts that, on feast days, when they customarily proclaimed the pomp of praise in the church, they should glorify the name of this prince after the proclamations of praise for the emperors [Col. 0929A].

When the king of the Croatians learned that the doge had come to lay waste to his nation, he tried through the efforts of envoys to appease him with peaceful words. Lord Doge Peter, however, making no account of them at all, sent the envoys back. He then began to consider, together with the army of both peoples, how he might enter the approaches of the enemy and by what means he could capture their heavily fortified places without harm.

Then he learned from the report of certain men that forty Narentine nobles, having completed their business in the regions of Apulia, wished to return home. He sent ten ships loaded with men, with all haste, to the island called Cazza [Note: Caza.]. While they were sailing, they captured the Narentines in an easy engagement and wished to hasten to the city of Traù [Note: Traù, west and north of Spalato.].

Lord Doge Peter, surrounded by soldiers both from Dalmatia and from Venice, left the aforesaid city on the sixth day and reached an island not far from the city of Belgrado [Note: Formerly Belogrado, now Zara Vecchia.]. From there he decided to send the citizens this message: if they wished to render voluntary service and swear loyalty to him, they could obtain his favor; otherwise, they should know without doubt that he would capture them by force.

When they heard this, they feared bringing danger upon their lord, namely the king of the Slavs, and were unable to resist so great a prince. Thus placed between two dangers, they were entirely uncertain what to do. At last, worn down by fear of Lord Doge Peter, while the soldiers of that same king were present, they rendered both their oaths and their service [Col. 0929C].

After leaving there, the colonists of the island of Levigrada [Note: Is this the fortified city of Novigrad, or the island of Grossa, on whose shore the town of Neligrad stands?] came to meet the excellent doge and promptly swore their oaths. As he proceeded toward the city of Traù, the bishop and the citizens strengthened him with their oaths. There he found victorious his men whom, as we said earlier, he had sent from the city of Iatera.

The brother of the king of the Slavs, named Surigna, was also present. Once deceived by fraternal treachery, he had lost the royal diadem. He not only joined himself to that doge by the bond of an oath, but also entrusted to him as a hostage his little son Stephen, his dearest offspring.

From there the aforesaid prince came to Spalato [Note: Spalatro.], a most noble and powerful city, which is recognized as the metropolis of all Dalmatia. The archbishop, clad in his sacred vestments, received him with a multitude of both clergy and laity from the city. While celebrating the solemnities of the Mass, they all strove, according to their vow, to appease him by the faith of an oath.

The prince of the Narentines, having learned that forty of his men had been enslaved, begged Lord Doge Peter through his envoys, in continual prayer, to return them to him [Col. 0930A]. This was the agreement: before the doge departed from those borders, both the prince of the Narentines and all his leading men would come before him to make satisfaction for their men according to his wishes; he should not in any way evade the aforesaid tribute, nor should he molest any traveling Venetian.

Then the doge ordered the captives to be returned, but retained only six of them, so that he himself would not violate the peace. Having settled these matters, he began to direct his steps toward subjugating the other peoples of that region.

When he wished to take lodging at the church of Saint Maximus, he seized the inhabitants of the island of Curzola [Note: Curzola.], who refused to obey his commands, by force of arms and subjected them to his authority.

Furthermore, while the same doge, with God’s favor, was achieving whatever he desired according to his wishes, he attempted to attack the wicked inhabitants of the island of Ladaestina [Note: Lesina.]. The Venetians, sailing through those waters, had often escaped naked from their fury, deprived of their possessions.

That island was indeed surrounded by rocky promontories. Although it did not deny access to those entering, it was nevertheless displayed in the height of its mountains. One of these, fortified with walls, towers, and buildings, was believed by everyone to be impregnable.

Then the aforesaid prince, having gathered a multitude of ships, entered a certain harbor of the island and ordered the citizens to abandon their obstinacy and come to him, or else know that they would be attacked in battle. Constrained by fear, they offered peaceful words.

Afterward, they were told that they could obtain peace from the doge on no condition unless they themselves destroyed the city and left it destroyed, beyond repair, and uninhabitable. They refused to do this with all their strength and began to resist so great an army.

Then the same prince ordered his men to prepare for battle and attack them fiercely. But because the steep location made entry difficult for those approaching, the defenders tried for some time, with such courage as they could, to hold the enemy at a distance by the blows of their javelins.

Nevertheless, by the dispensation of almighty God, the greater part of the army made an assault from the place where the entrances of that stronghold were open, while the rest climbed the mountain by difficult paths and seized the towers where the water vessels were kept. Taking up positions in them, they pressed the defenders so hard that, at last, their courage cast down and their arms laid aside, they knelt and begged for nothing more than to escape the hated danger of death [Note: “until” in manuscript 1.].

Accordingly, the doge, a lover of mercy, resolved to preserve all the living [Note: “to preserve” is written above the line in manuscript 1.] and ordered only the city to be devastated. When this had been done, the victorious prince returned to the church of Saint Maximus [Note: That is, he revisited it.]. There the archbishop of Ragusa [Col. 0931A], assembling with his people, all swore oaths to the same prince and rendered him many services.

From there, revisiting the aforesaid cities, he eventually returned to Venice with such a triumph.

(Year 1000.) Meanwhile, the Emperor Otto, preparing to visit the kingdom of Italy for the third time, wished to gain access by way of the waters of the vast Lake Como (late June). A multitude of Lombards received him in the city of Como. Among them came John the deacon, envoy of the aforesaid Doge Peter. Although he was unaware of his lord’s triumph, he announced to the emperor only that his lord had advanced in order to fight against the stubbornness of the Slavs.

When this same John went with the emperor to the city of Pavia (beginning of July), he learned from the reports of several people of his lord’s arrival and triumph [Col. 0931B]. When John was now wishing to return to his own country, the emperor entrusted him with this secret message for his lord: if it were possible, he would like, for the sake of affection, to come secretly to some place under his authority, so that he might enjoy the presence and wisdom of so great a man and his godfather.

Although the doge eagerly heard such a message, he nevertheless never believed that this could be done, since the ruler of so many kingdoms could not, without his subjects’ knowledge, enter another’s jurisdiction without difficulty. Yet, unwilling to share the matter with any of his men, he kept it silently in his heart.

The aforesaid emperor, leaving the city of Pavia (November), sought the Roman throne by way of the Alps of Tuscany. Then, during the fast preceding the Easter solemnity [Col. 0931C], he arranged to descend to Ravenna (year 1001). Doge Peter sent the same John the deacon to him. The emperor received him graciously, and John persistently strove to repeat the very message he had delivered earlier.

Thus it came about that, with the aforesaid John the deacon frequently traveling back and forth between the two parties, this matter was discussed. Finally, after receiving sound counsel from the doge, the emperor celebrated the holy Easter day with the greatest devotion and announced to all his leading men that he wished to take a medicinal draught at the monastery of Saint Mary on an island called Pomposa and remain there for several days.

That island lies not far from Venice: on one side it is enclosed by the seashore, and on the other sides by the flowing waters of the Eridanus. After this announcement, a day was fixed [Note: Namely, the day] on which he would visit both the shrine of Saint Mark and his long-desired godfather [Col. 0931D].

Then, entering a ship with a few men to whom he had entrusted this matter privately, he sought the aforesaid monastery. He did not spend the night there at all. With the abbot and monks standing by, he arranged for a certain small lodging of the monastery to be prepared [Col. 0932A]. In it he pretended to keep himself for three days on a medicinal drink.

When night had come, he boarded a small boat in which the aforesaid John the deacon lay hidden in wait at the edge of the island. Count Hecelinus, who later became duke of the Bavarians [Note: In 1004; Thietmar, book VI, chapter 3.], Count Raimbald of Treviso, Teupernus, a most warlike man, Rainardus, Tamo, the chamberlains, Walter, the sole chaplain, and Frederick, who later became archbishop of Ravenna [Note: The word is missing.] [Note: In the years 1001–1003], all boarded the aforesaid ship together.

After the sailors had navigated restlessly through the whole night and day, they reached, in a storm during the following night, the church of Saint Servulus, which is judged to lie not far from the doge’s palace. There the powerful Doge Peter awaited the secret arrival of so great a man [Col. 0932B].

Since they could scarcely see one another in the darkness of the dreadful night, amid embraces and the sweetest kisses for the new guest, the doge addressed him as follows:

“If you wish to visit the monastery of Saint Zacharias, you must go there immediately, so that before the dawn you may be received most honorably within the walls of my palace.”

Then they both boarded a ship: one sought his own palace, while the other sought the aforesaid monastery. After the emperor had entered that monastery and revealed himself there, he entered the church, but did not remain there long [Note: “with” is written above the line in manuscript 1.]. Instead, as had been agreed, he came to the palace. After inspecting all its decorations, he wished to be shut up and guarded with two of his men in the eastern tower.

He was dressed in a shabby garment so that he would not be recognized. Meanwhile, the aforesaid Hecelinus and the others received the doge, as he came from the morning office, before the threshold of Saint Mark [Col. 0932C]. From the imperial side they delivered words of greeting, so that those standing around would not perceive the secret.

The doge asked them how the emperor was faring and where he was. They replied that they had left him safe and sound at the monastery of Pomposa. After exchanging kisses and ordering them to lodge near the palace, the doge himself went to the emperor.

It was not permissible for the doge to remain with the emperor in the aforesaid tower throughout the day, lest any Venetian become aware of such a thing. He came openly with the others for the midday meal; in the evening, he refreshed himself with the emperor through food and conversation [Note: That is, with the emperor.].

To confirm the bond of perfect faith, the emperor received the doge’s daughter, still a catechumen, from the sacred baptismal font.

The pallium, which, as a bond of the agreement, had been paid by the Venetians at more than fifty pounds [Note: Such a payment had been renewed everywhere by emperors since the time of Charlemagne; see the account of them in our Annals, vol. III, pp. 578–579, 598 ff.], he granted by a perpetual written deed to that doge, his godfather. He also promised henceforth to grant him all advantages firmly according to his wishes [Note: “advantages”; manuscript 1 reads “all benefits.”].

But the doge wished to demand nothing from him except that he preserve intact, securely, the estates of his churches and of all the Venetians, in the condition in which they stood in his own time.

On the following day, when he already wished to have permission to return, the doge wanted to honor him with gifts of various kinds. The emperor wished to accept none of these, saying:

“I do not wish to incur that charge against myself, lest anyone claim that I came here out of greed and not because of Saint Mark and my affection for you.”

Nevertheless, constrained by persistent pleas, he accepted, although unwillingly, an ivory seat with its footstool, as well as a silver cup and pitcher, executed with rare craftsmanship. After a kiss had been given, they separated in tears on both sides.

Hecelinus and the other men mentioned above received permission to leave not on that day but on the next. The emperor, entering a ship with only two men and John the deacon, secretly returned by night to the monastery. In the morning he unexpectedly presented himself to those waiting to see him. Then, hurrying to Ravenna in the ship of the aforesaid John the deacon, he made it known to everyone that he was returning from Venice. Those who were reluctant to believe this marveled greatly thereafter.

After three days, the doge ordered the entire Venetian people to assemble in the palace. Revealing this deed to them, he praised no less the emperor’s faith than the skill of his own lord [Note: Namely, the people.]. (Late March of the year 1001, beginning of April.)

At the same time, the emperor heard that the citizens of Benevento were rebelling against him. He attacked them, subjected them forcefully to his authority, and killed many. After this, he came again to Ravenna and then sought the city of Pavia [Col. 0933C]. There he heard that the citizens of Rome, having cast off the yoke of his rule, intended to resist him.

Against them he sent his patrician named Zazon with an army, while he himself hastened down by ship to Ravenna (November). At that time the emperor sent through John the deacon two imperial ornaments, made of gold with marvelous workmanship, to Peter, his godfather, the doge: one from the city of Pavia, the other from Ravenna.

In return, the doge sent an elephant-seat, artistically carved from ivory panels, through the same deacon to Ravenna. The emperor received it eagerly and left it to be preserved in that city.

Afterward, when he wished to revisit the strong city of Rome, fearing ambushes by the citizens, he climbed to a certain fortress called Paternum (year 1002, January). There the unfortunate man, not remaining safe for long, lost his earthly life amid his sweet years (January 24) [Col. 0933D]. At that time, peoples everywhere could scarcely refrain from lamenting his funeral. His little body, carried by the archbishop of Cologne together with the others, was brought to the palace at Aachen, so that, with his predecessor Charles of pious memory, he might await the judgment day appointed for him.

After him, Henry [Note: Below, “Heinricus.”], a royal duke born from royal lineage, properly received the diadem of the kingdoms (year 1002, June 6), although Arduin, son of Count Dado, usurped the crown of the kingdom at Pavia with certain Lombards supporting him. Nevertheless, the greater part of them awaited the arrival of King Henry.

In the year of the incarnation of our Redeemer, 1004, and in the tenth year of the dogeship of Lord Peter, doge of the Venetians and Dalmatians, John, the distinguished son of that doge, was made his father’s associate in dignity.

While his third age was nurturing him as an eighteen-year-old youth, he flourished notably in his father’s character and goodness. He strove to obey his pious parent’s ways [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “so he strove”; edited text: “he strove.”] so faithfully that the whole homeland remained under one covenant through the twofold government [Note: Since our author reports John’s death before 1007, he should be considered to have written this at the time when these events occurred.].

In that same year, a multitude of Saracens invading the borders of Apulia surrounded the city of Bari, where Gregory, the imperial catepan, was in command, with a siege on every side. When the powerful Doge Peter heard this, he ordered a very large expedition to be prepared.

Leaving Venice on the solemn feast of Saint Lawrence (August 10), he set out to attack them. As he sailed across the vast sea and passed various regions, he was approaching the aforesaid city on the eighth day before the Ides of September (September 6).

When both Saracen armies saw unexpected salvation coming to the Christians, some stood armed on horseback along the shore, while others boarded ships and boldly challenged the Christians to battle. But by divine favor, Lord Doge Peter entered the harbor of the aforesaid city safely with all his men [Col. 0934C].

The citizens, together with Gregory, the imperial catepan, received him suitably and arranged for him to lodge in the palace of that city. Then Lord Doge Peter began to consider how he could protect the city from the harshness of the pagans.

First, however, he adequately refreshed the citizens, who were suffering from hunger, with supplies of food. Then he exhorted them to wage war manfully against the most wicked people. Ordering the victorious standard to go before him, he stationed some men in the suburb for battle, while taking others with him and beginning to wage a naval war.

Thus it came about that for three continuous days they pursued the Saracens fiercely, now with sword blows, now with fiery darts. In the silence of the third night, the pagan army fled [Col. 0934D]. The others who held the neighboring regions by cruel domination withdrew in confusion not long afterward.

From then on the citizens held the name of Lord Doge Peter famous and honorable. Bound by no earthly fear but by fear of God, he had freed them from the persecution of their enemies.

I do not think the prodigy should be omitted that was divinely shown to a certain Saracen on the day when the faithful celebrate the festive Assumption of the Mother of God [Col. 0935A].

While he was staying in the monastery of Saint Benedict, not far from a certain extremely well-fortified tower, he saw a shining star come at headlong speed from the western region and fall into the harbor of that city. When this was revealed to Jerome, the spiritual father and abbot of the aforesaid monastery, he immediately understood that the future help of Saint Mary—whose name is interpreted as “star of the sea”—was coming to the citizens.

The undefiled Mother, in the arrival of Peter, doge of the Venetians, undoubtedly fulfilled this sign. She allowed him to come from the western regions and, on the feast of her birth, granted him triumph over the enemy.

The same doge sent his envoys from that place to Constantinople [Col. 0935B], and, enriched with many gifts by the imperial catepan, returned safely to Venice.

At this same time King Henry, sending Otto, the duke [Note: Duke of Carinthia and margrave of Verona. See Thietmar, V.16.], to Italy with an army, fought with the usurping king Arduin near the Alps, in the field called Vitalis [Note: Thus in manuscript 1.] [Note: In the plain of Verona.], and many fell on both sides.

When this became known to King Henry, he entered Italy the following year (1004), accompanied by a very large expedition. After expelling Arduin from the city of Verona, he forcefully subjected all the Lombards to his rule.

Peter, the doge of the Venetians, also honorably sent his own son, a boy of marvelous beauty, to the king in the aforesaid city, moved by his request. Henry had him anointed according to custom with the holy liquid of chrism and sent him back to his father richly rewarded [Col. 0935C].

Then, preparing to hurry to the other cities of Italy, he was crowned at Pavia by the archbishop of Milan (May 14). There, learning that the citizens were plotting against his rule, he devastated almost the whole city with fire and slaughter, and then sought the transalpine kingdom by way of Lake Como (June).

At this same time the famous Doge Peter, compelled by the persistent requests of the emperors Basil and Constantine, sent John, his beloved son, to the imperial city for the purpose of marriage.

The emperors received him graciously and decided to betroth to him the daughter of a most noble patrician named Argyropoulos, born of imperial stock [Note: See Cedrenus, vol. II, p. 452, Bekker edition.]. To hasten the wedding day of so great a woman, namely the granddaughter of the emperors [Col. 0935D], the aforesaid young doge and the imperial girl were permitted, by imperial decree, to meet in a certain chapel. There they received the gift of sacred blessing from the shepherd of that city and golden diadems from the emperors upon their heads.

With each emperor placing his right hand upon them, they reached the hall where the assembled banqueters appeared to be staying, in such splendor [Col. 0936A]. The aforesaid emperors strove to conduct this marriage so magnificently and joyfully that for three days they themselves did not absent themselves from the banqueters’ celebrations as intimate guests.

After this ceremony had been completed in the palace called the Oeconomium, each of them withdrew, returning after receiving gifts. The new doge decided to live with his beautiful bride in the palace which he had recently acquired by right of dower.

Emperor Basil instructed and warned him not to leave the city until he returned, with God’s help, from the borders of the Bulgarians, whom he was attempting to attack and conquer by force of arms [Note: That is, “until.”]. The doge obeyed his instructions and eagerly awaited his return.

When Basil returned, he raised the same doge to the dignity of the office of patrician. He honored his little brother Otto, who was present, only with gifts [Col. 0936B].

Then the doge, having received the bridal dowry—that is, riches of various kinds—together with imperial gifts, obtained permission to return to his homeland. For the parents of the noble girl, weeping as she departed for a foreign region almost as an exile, were not lacking.

The doge, having obtained everything according to his wishes, boarded a ship with his illustrious bride and ordered his men to plow through the waves of the sea. Throughout the journey, inhabitants of Greek and other peoples everywhere did not fail to render them services until they reached their homeland.

When the arrival of their two children was announced to the worthy and long-expectant father, he gave thanks to the King of Heaven and sent a multitude of ships to receive them far from the shore. Surrounded by such a procession [Col. 0936C], they were restored safely to their parents’ embraces before the palace tribunal.

The father did not cease to hold frequent banquets of this kind, not only for his own people but also for foreigners. Indeed, no one among our people remembers such equal joy having shone forth in our lands.

Lady Maria, the Greek duchess, after not many days gave birth at Venice to a boy begotten in Constantinople. The distinguished Doge Peter received him from the sacred baptismal font and named him Basil, after his imperial maternal uncle.

About this time the aforesaid Doge Peter, for the remedy of his soul, gave one thousand and fifty pounds of money for the benefit of his entire homeland, Venice, and brought the work of the palace he had begun to completion.

Among its other works of decoration, he had a chapel built with Daedalian craftsmanship, and adorned it marvelously not only with marble but also with gold.

Meanwhile, as Doge Peter observed that almost everything was being supplied to him according to his wishes, he strove to govern the people subject to him with a stricter-than-usual standard of justice. But divine providence, arranging all things with equitable governance, struck down with severity the man it had placed at the summit of such happiness, in proportion to the height of his virtue [Col. 0937A].

At that same time (year 1006) a comet-star appeared in the southern sky, whose sign human experience always declares to portend disaster [Note: See the Greater Annals of Saint Gall and the Annals of Liège.]. A very great pestilence followed throughout all the territories of Italy and Venice [Note: Greater Annals of Saint Gall.] [year 1007]. Many human beings of both sexes fell in an unexpected death.

Among them, Lady Maria, the Greek duchess, and John, her distinguished husband, were, within the space of sixteen days, alas, enclosed in one mausoleum in the monastery of Saint Zacharias. Their death was mourned not only by their grieving parents, as though by a brotherhood, but the whole homeland wasted away in tears and sorrow.

They were indeed so famous for every virtue that both pleased God and human beings by their goodness. For only six years did he govern the people of Venice under his father’s rule.

But so that some support of consolation might be present amid so great a grief, the Venetians, with one accord, made petition and raised the other son of Lord Peter, their prince—namely Otto, the royal boy—to the dignity of the dogeship.

Although he flourished in the tender age of fourteen years, he nevertheless possessed such eloquence of intellect that he was said to be second to his other brother not in virtue but in age.

Moreover, Doge Peter wished to bestow the paternal gift upon all his children, so that each might receive his portion by testamentary right. I wish to record their names, as I properly remember them.

The first received the name of his lordship, and he corresponded sufficiently in form and strength to his noble birth [Col. 0937C]. The second was named Orso; he exercised the office of the clergy in such a way that he could deservedly be called the glory of clerics.

The third in order was Otto, the aforesaid boy, sharing his father’s name and dignity. The fourth was named Vitalis; through the vigor of his intellect he attained an ecclesiastical calling. The fifth bore the name Henry; his childlike appearance shone like the radiance of the sun.

The same excellent father also had four daughters. The first of them, named Hicela, he honorably joined in marriage to Stephen, son of the king of the Slavs, whom I mentioned earlier. He devoted the other three to Almighty God in a monastery.

After arranging these matters properly, he decided henceforth to keep himself apart from the bed of his noble wife Maria [Col. 0937D], specifically so that there would be no separation in the companionship of their familiar life.

Then, distributing everything that remained of his resources to churches and the poor, he reserved nothing for himself except his dignity.

In the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1008, when Valerius, bishop of the church of Altinum, died—he had ruled the episcopal see for twenty years, lacking only fifteen days—Orso, the aforesaid son of Lord Doge Peter, was appointed to the same see with the clergy and people consenting [Col. 0938A].

I wish in my account to sketch the character of this young man [Note: “adulentis” thus in manuscript 1; “eius” (“his”) in manuscript 2.]. He was devout in faith, handsome in appearance, prudent in intellect, and so skilled through literary training that everyone declared him worthy of so great an honor.

At the beginning of his ordination, Peter, the doge and his illustrious father, most zealously caused the whole house and church of Saint Mary, already almost consumed by age, to be restored [Note: At the beginning of page 38 in manuscript 1, a blank space contains this charter, written in the year 1032. In the margin of manuscript 3 is written: “John Sagorninus, author of this little book.” Zanetti has already observed that this conjecture by a fifteenth-century scribe carries no weight:

“One day we, John Sagorninus the smith, together with all our relatives, assembled in the time of Lord Peter Barbolanus, the doge. He and his gastald required of us that we should work iron in the court. But we opposed this in every way, except that we should work in our own houses whatever necessity required, and should at all times work for the aforesaid palace as much iron as its jailer brought to us.

“Therefore, at that time, we established this with witnesses, and it was adjudged for us that we should swear upon the four holy Gospels of God. But during the days of the aforesaid lord we did not perform the said oath [Note: ‘We did not perform it’ is written above the line in manuscript 1.].

“Now we have come before the presence of Lord Dominicus Flabianus, our most glorious doge and lord, while he was sitting in the palace with his judges, and while the greater part of his faithful men stood there. We began to complain about the force [Note: Virtus = force.] that the gastaldus of the smiths was inflicting upon us.

“Finally, they judged and confirmed that, just as we should have sworn at the time of the aforesaid Peter Barbolanus, so now we should fulfill it; and so we did. But our most merciful and glorious doge and lord gave us a written notice thereafter that we should not work iron in the courts of the palace, nor remain under the yoke of the gastaldus of the smiths, but should work iron only in our own houses, as much as the prison-keeper of this palace transported to us, with all our cost and expense, so that the other smiths paid from their own resources. And it should be permitted for us to work all iron according to the way in which the other smiths work.”)]

[Col. 0938C] Paulicius ruled as doge for 20 years, 6 months, and 9 days. Marcellus ruled as doge for 9 years and 21 days. Orso ruled as doge for 11 years and 5 months.

After the killing of Doge Orso, there were no doges in Venice for 6 years. But a master of the soldiers governed it; namely, Lord Leo, master of the soldiers, held office for 1 year; Felix, master of the soldiers, held office for 1 year; Deusdedit for 2 years; Jubianus, hypatus, for 1 year; and John Fabriacus for 1 year [Col. 0938D].

Deusdedit, hypatus, ruled as doge for 13 years. Galla ruled as doge for 1 year and 2 months. Dominicus ruled as doge for 8 years. Mauritius ruled as doge for 23 years. John ruled as doge for 25 years. Obelerius and Beatus held office for 5 years. Agnellus ruled as doge for 18 years. Justinian ruled as doge for 1 year and 2 months. John ruled as doge for 8 years. Peter ruled as doge for 29 years.

[Col. 0939A] Orso ruled as doge for 17 years. John ruled as doge for 5 years and 6 months. Peter ruled as doge for 6 months. Peter Trondominicus ruled as doge for 23 years and 23 days. Orso ruled as doge for 20 years.

Peter Candiano ruled as doge for 5 [Note: The word is written twice in manuscript 1.]. Peter Badoario ruled as doge for 3 years. Peter Candiano ruled as doge for 23 years. Peter Candiano, his son, ruled as doge for 18 years. Peter Ursoylus ruled as doge for 2 years and 20 days. Vitalis Candiano ruled as doge for 1 year and 2 months. Tribunus Meni [Note: Thus in manuscript 1; manuscript 2 reads “duke.”] ruled as doge for 1 year and 4 months. [Note: [Col. 0939A]

In codex 1 this is added:

“An inquiry was conducted concerning the *pallia*—the cloaks or mantles—that were carried through the various parts of Italy. I, Duke Otto, appeared in a public assembly with the chief judges of our land, as well as the intermediate and lesser judges. Badovario Bragadino, Mauricius Maureceni, and Dominicus Florencius Flabianicus testified [Col. 0939: He later expelled Duke Otto in 1028] that the *pallia* ought not to be carried or sold in any part of Italy except from Pavia and from the market of Saint Martin [Col. 0939B] and Olivo.”

In Italy Alboin ruled for 3 years and 6 months. Cleph ruled for 1 year and 6 months. The Lombards had no king for 10 years. Authari ruled for 6 years. Agilulf ruled for 25 years [Col. 0939: Agdulf, 2]. Adaloald ruled for 10 years. Arioald ruled for 12 years. Rothari ruled for 16 years and 4 months. Rodoald ruled for 5 years. Aripert ruled for 9 years. Grimoald ruled for 9 years. Bertari ruled for 17 years. Cunipert ruled for 12 years. Liuperto ruled for 8 months [Col. 0939: Gomberto—Lauperto, 2]. Aripert ruled for 12 years. Ansprand for 3 months. Liutprand ruled for 31 years and 7 months. Hilprand ruled for 7 months [Col. 0939: Idprand, 2]. Ratchis ruled for 4 years and 9 months. Aistulf ruled for 7 years. Desiderius ruled for 17 years and 3 months.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 774 [Col. 0939: thus, 1; 2], King Charles entered Italy and conquered it. He ruled for 46 years. When King Charles had died [Col. 0939: thus, 1; 2], Louis succeeded him; he ruled the kingdom for 59 years and died. Charles succeeded him and ruled the kingdom for 2 [years?]. When Charles had died, Karlmann succeeded him [Col. 0939: thus, 1; 2]; he ruled the kingdom for 3 years. When the aforementioned Karlmann had died, his brother, the younger Charles, succeeded him; he ruled the kingdom for 9 years. Berengar the emperor succeeded him.

The following was written in another hand at the end of the eleventh century:

The first to rule in the Roman seat was Julius Caesar, for four years and six months. Octavian Caesar ruled for fifty-six years and six months. Tiberius Caesar ruled for twenty-three years. Gaius, surnamed Caligula, ruled for three years, ten months, and eight days. Claudius Caesar ruled for thirteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days. [Col. 0940A] Nero Caesar ruled for thirteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days. Vespasian Caesar ruled for nine years, eleven months, and twenty-two days. Titus Caesar ruled for two years [Col. 0939: thus] and two months. Domitian, the younger brother of Titus, ruled for fifteen years and five months.
