Nerva Caesar ruled for one year, four months, and eight days. Trajan Caesar ruled for nineteen years, six months, and fifteen days. Hadrian Caesar ruled for eleven years. Antoninus Caesar, with his sons Aurelius and Lucius, ruled for twenty-two years and two months. Marcus Antonius Verus, with his brother Lucius Aurelius Commodus, ruled for nineteen years and one month [Col. 0939: in 1 the text continues in a high hand]. Lucius Antonius Commodus ruled for thirteen years after the death of his father [Col. 0940B]. Aelius Pertinax ruled for six months. Severus Pertinax ruled for seventeen years. Antoninus, surnamed Caracalla, ruled for seven years. Macrinus Caesar ruled for one year. Marcus Aurelius Antoninus ruled for four years. Aurelius Alexander ruled for thirteen years. Maximinus Caesar ruled for three years. Gordian ruled for six years. Philip, with his son Philip, ruled for seven years. Decius Caesar ruled for one year and three months. Gallus, with his son Volusianus, ruled for two years and four months. Valerian, with his son Gallienus, ruled for fifteen years. Claudius Caesar ruled for one year and eight months [Col. 0940C]. Aurelian Caesar ruled for five and a half years. Tacitus Caesar ruled for half a year. After his murder, Florian ruled for eighty-eight days. Probus Caesar ruled for six years and four months.

A catalogue of the eastern emperors continues to the end of the eleventh century, namely: Alexius seized the imperial kingdom in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1081, in the fourth indiction, on the first day of April, on which the Lord’s Supper was then celebrated, and he ruled for … years. From there another hand has extended the text to the middle of the thirteenth century; codex 2 displays it, ending with this sentence: “After the death of John, his son-in-law Baldwin, son of the aforementioned Peter, ruled for … years.” This Baldwin ruled from 1237 to 1261.]

.

# CHRONICLE OF GRADO

[Col. 0939]

[Col. 0939C] (Folio 1.) After the destruction of many cities and the devastation of Aquileia, when a most savage multitude of pagans had directed its battle line against the city of Altinum, and, finding no one there because the inhabitants of that city had fled, they plundered the entire city and set it on fire; they also utterly destroyed its walls and towers. A large part of the population of that city, seized by fear, lived for a long time in the marshes and islands while fleeing the ambushes of the pagans. By divine providence it happened that a certain most holy man named Geminianus, a priest enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit and wishing to aid the needy, after carefully exploring many places, reached the aforementioned marsh. There, together with a certain Arius and Arator, he found a great multitude of Christians. When he saw them, and was greatly rejoiced at finding them [Note: [Col. 0941D] That is, “rejoicing”], he announced to them that, by the will of divine mercy, that wicked multitude had been destroyed and reduced to nothing. They gave thanks and glorified God, who does not abandon those who hope in him. Then Arius and his son Arator, together with all who were with them, looking toward certain neighboring islands situated in the same marshes and examining those they had chosen as the better ones, began to build houses and churches on them. While building them, they recalled the beauty left behind in the city of Altinum and the destruction of its many towers. Although deeply grieved, they nevertheless named the islands they inhabited [Note: [Col. 0941] Thus, codex c.] after the aforesaid towers. Thus, because of the name of a particularly eminent tower of that city, all the aforesaid islands came to be called Torcello by Arius.

Accordingly, Arius and some of his servants claimed a certain island for themselves, so that they might live there. There, changing their former name, all who belonged to their tribe were called Aurii. Together with these, all those who had been in the city of Altinum, residing at the gate that looked toward the north (folio 1′), established that the settlement of Burianum should be called “of the Aurii” after that gate. The tribune Aurius, together with the armed band called the Macinii Celires [Note: [Col. 0941D] That is, *massa*, a troop or group of armed men], and with certain others whose names are unknown, chose the place nearest to this island for habitation. With them remained all those who had been in the aforementioned city at their gate, beside which there had been a great and very high tower, through which they had their entrance and exit. Since they inhabited this place, Aurius established that it should be called Vicus Majoribus [Note: [Col. 0942D] Mazzorbo], after that gate and great tower.

There Aurius appointed Maxum as judge. The same tribune Aurius, together with the Frauduni, who are also called Faletri, Rusticus, who is called Luthoitus, and the Calciamiri, whom they named “Silken Legs,” together with travelers and certain others whose names are unknown, jointly chose certain neighboring islands [Col. 0942A]. From these, Aurius established the settlements of Constanciacum and Amianarum, naming them after the gates from which the people had come.

After the entire multitude of this people had occupied the sites of the neighboring islands, they gathered together and, with wondrous form and shining splendor, founded a basilica in honor of holy Mary, the Mother and Virgin of God. It was adorned with a most beautiful pavement, whose center was especially embellished by a certain wheel because of its beauty. Thus every dwelling nearest to that church was called Rota, after the tribune Aurius. The tribune Aurius established that church as a bishopric. The aforesaid Aurius claimed that bishopric as a duchy under his own right of lordship, with the approval of the people of Metamauco and Rialto [Col. 0942B], and with the confirmation of Obelierius [Note: [Col. 0941] Now erased; in its place a later hand has written “the tribunes and nobles.” Codex 3 preserved the ancient reading], and [Note: [Col. 0941] Now erased; in its place a later hand has written “the tribunes and nobles.” Codex 3 preserved the ancient reading] Beatus [Note: [Col. 0941] Now erased; in its place a later hand has written “the tribunes and nobles.” Codex 3 preserved the ancient reading], the dukes who at that time governed Venice.

When all these matters had been arranged and ordered, the aforementioned tribune Aurius, together with the entire multitude of the people who had fled from the aforesaid city of Altinum, submitted and subjected themselves to the dukes Obelierius [Note: [Col. 0941] Now erased; in its place a later hand has written “the tribunes and nobles.” Codex 3 supplies the ancient reading] and [Note: [Col. 0941] Now erased; in its place a later hand has written “the tribunes and nobles.” Codex 3 supplies the ancient reading] Beatus [Note: [Col. 0942D] See above, cols. 897–899] [Note: [Col. 0941] Now erased; in its place a later hand has written “the tribunes and nobles.” Codex 3 supplies the ancient reading], in the same order in which they had formerly been subject in the aforesaid city to the dukes who had held its government.

After these things had been accomplished, as was mentioned above, certain shores were granted to the authority of the aforesaid tribune Aurius by the concession of the aforementioned dukes and with the approval of the people. On the first of these he found a certain priest named Maurus, who had fled from the city of Altinum. Maurus explained everything to him in due order: how God had revealed to him a certain deserted place in which the holy martyrs Hermes and Erasmus had ordered him to build a church in God’s honor and under the title of their names, promising him a reward for doing so.

On the next shore, he said, an exceedingly white cloud had appeared to him, from which he had seen two rays of brightness shining like those of the sun. When he approached it, he heard it speaking to him in a very clear voice: “I am the Lord God, Savior and ruler of the whole world. The land on which you stand: take care that, in the very place that I shall show you, you build a basilica in my name.” Then that cloud, together with the aforementioned rays, moved not far away to another place. There another sweet-sounding voice came from the cloud, saying: “I am Mary, Mother of the Lord Jesus Christ. In this place I wish you to build a church in honor of my name.” He said that she also pointed out the place to him.

When he had reached the third shore, he said that he saw half of that shore occupied by a diverse multitude of nations and people. Its other half was covered with very dense herds of oxen and buffaloes [Col. 0943A]. In the middle of the shore that exceedingly white cloud stood with its rays. When he approached it, he saw beneath the cloud an old man with shining white hair seated on a most beautiful throne; with him was a certain young man, and they were conversing together.

Then the old man said to the priest Maurus: “I am Peter, chief of the apostles, appointed shepherd of the Christian flock so that I might feed its sheep and lambs. Now, for the remission of your sins, I command you to make every effort to found in this place, for the honor of God and under the title of my name, a church worthy of honor, so that on the day of my feast the entire people of Torcello may gather in it.”

The younger man who was with him said: “I am a servant of God named Antoninus, who suffered for the name of Christ. Therefore I command you to build a small church beside the basilica of my master, in honor of God and under the title of my name. Yet do not dare to make any work of another kind between the two. If anyone should ask anything in it with a just and devout mind, he will not doubt that he shall obtain it from God through my prayers. Take care to have these churches built as we have shown you.”

When he reached the fourth shore, it seemed to him that the entire shore was full of vineyards bearing very ripe grapes. And behold, that cloud of which we spoke a little earlier appeared to him. When he approached it, he saw a young woman of beautiful appearance seated on a precious throne. She said: “I am the virgin Justina, who suffered for the name of Christ in the city of Patavium. For love of him I beg you to have a small church built on this shore in God’s honor and in commemoration of my name.”

After all these things had thus been revealed, it seemed to him that he remained at the site of a very small tomb [i.e. mound]. There the bright cloud appeared to him again, and above it he saw the sun with rays that illuminated it. In that same cloud was a man of wondrous appearance, who said to him: “I am John the Baptist, the Lord’s forerunner. By his name I beg you to have a church built for me according to the form that I shall show you at this place.” He charged him to devote himself there day and night to prayers and vigils, and he also granted him an investiture through a ring and a written document.

After all these things had been completed, it seemed to him that he was standing above the roof of the church of Saint Mary. There, awakened from the sleep of this quiet vision by the great clatter of the mills that seemed to be situated beside the aforementioned church, he found the written volume and the ring in his hands. After he had explained all these things in sequence, the tribune Aurius and the other nobles who were with him, seeing the ring and the written volume that Maurus had found in his hands, became convinced of the vision of this revelation [Col. 0944A]. They built, with wondrous beauty, a small church in honor of God and Saint John, just as the same holy Baptist had shown Maurus, beside the atrium of the bishopric.

They also placed baptismal fonts in it and, in a marvelous manner, caused bronze images of animals to pour out water through hidden channels into those same fonts. When these things had been accomplished, the aforementioned priest Maurus led the tribune Aurius with him to the shore where the holy Justina had appeared to him. There he had a small church built, according to what had been revealed to him in the vision.

Then, when they came to the shore where the multitude of pagans and oxen had appeared to him, they built, as he had been commanded in the revelation, a church in honor of Saint Peter and another small church in honor of Saint Antoninus [Col. 0944B], the martyr. The tribune Aurius established that the shore of the oxen should be called by this name.

Then, wishing to cross over to another shore, they saw an exceedingly white cloud above the shore toward which they were heading. When they arrived there, the cloud vanished; according to the signs they found there, they built a church in honor of the Lord Savior. Because of the vision of the aforesaid white cloud, the tribune Aurius established that this should be called the White Shore.

Proceeding toward the right-hand part of this shore, just as had been shown to him in the aforesaid vision and designated by the holy martyrs, they built a church in honor of the holy martyrs Hermes and Erasmus [Col. 0944C] [Note: [Col. 0943] “edifficerunt,” 1.]. There they found a great deal of gold, at the place that had been designated by the promised reward, while digging the foundations for the altars. For this reason the tribune Aurius established that this should be called the Shore of the Reward.

When all these things had been completed, the aforesaid Aurius, together with the other leaders of the same bishopric, received all the shores mentioned above under the right of their own authority, within the same bishopric. On them they also settled many farmers or tenant cultivators, with the following arrangement: no one was to dare to plant vineyards or undertake any kind of cultivation on those shores without the bishop’s permission or sale.

They also established that every year, from each *sulcus* of every vineyard, two vine shoots with all their clusters should be paid to the aforesaid bishopric as a rent; and that, for each house, eight coins should be paid to the same bishopric as payment for the fisc [Col. 0944D] [Note: [Col. 0943] “prosisci,” 1; “pro fischi,” 3]. They also subjected all the fisheries of the pools and marshes to the aforesaid bishopric. Moreover, certain other portions of that bishopric paid eggs and chickens as the rent due [Note: [Col. 0943] “eisdem,” 3]. They entrusted all the revenues of the things mentioned above to the priest Maurus [Note: [Col. 0943] Changed to “Magno”; see the following note] for as long as he held episcopal office.

At that time the Frauduni, together with the Willareni *mastalici* [Note: [Col. 0943D] That is, *massalici*, inhabitants], honorably built a church in honor of God and Saint Lawrence, deacon and martyr [Col. 0945A]. After constructing its foundations all around, they ordered a certain castle to be built there. From that castle they built a bridge and made a road as far as Amiana.

The tribune Aurius and the priest Maurus granted the aforementioned Frauduni the tribunal authority in the settlement of Amiana. With the permission of the tribune Aurius and also of the priest Maurus, the Frauduni took possession of most of a certain shore, so that they might plant vineyards for the benefit of the same church. The same tribune Aurius and the priest Maurus also granted fisheries and marshes so that he might establish mills for that church [Note: [Col. 0945] It was first written thus; afterward the *u* was changed to *g* and the *n* to *r*, so that the codex now reads “Magnus.” The traces of the first reading can nevertheless easily be recognized. Giesebrecht].

In the same settlement of Amiana the aforementioned Frauduni built the church of Saint Mark [Col. 0945B], and, subjecting it to the church of Saint Lawrence, placed it under its authority. Not long afterward those Frauduni, together with the Calciamiri, received certain relics of the holy martyrs Sergius and Bacchus from a certain Stephen Scopacalle and built, in honor of God and of those saints, a church at the head of the settlement of Constanciacum. They subjected it to the aforesaid parish of Saint Lawrence.

Again, they acquired certain other relics of the holy martyrs Marcellianus and Maximus from certain castellans. Building a church in their honor, they subjected it to the aforementioned parish. By a written charter they subjected these three churches to that parish, with the provision that every year, on their feast days, they should honorably prepare a meal for the parish priest of the aforementioned church [Note: [Col. 0945] “prepare,” codex c]. In return, they established that the same parish priest should provide a meal for the clergy of those churches on the feast of the parish itself.

With the approval of the tribune Aurius, prince of Torcello, and of the priest Maurus, who had been elected to the episcopal office, they decreed by a testamentary document that, if any suitable cleric from their tribe were found, he should, after receiving investiture from the bishop of Torcello, be appointed parish priest in the church of Saint Lawrence without anyone’s opposition. But if no such cleric remained from the aforesaid lineage, the neighbors of that parish were to have the power freely to elect another person of their choice.

The remaining churches that had been built in various parts of Torcello, the tribune Aurius and the aforementioned priest Maurus, who had been elected, established and confirmed with the approval of the entire people [Col. 0945D] [Note: [Col. 0945] Thus in codex 3; “of the tribunes and nobles” and, in a place erased and written by a later hand, codex 1], and subjected them under the authority of the church of Saint Mary. They decreed that the church of Saint Mary itself should be the bishopric of all the churches mentioned above.

Near this church the aforementioned Frauduni built, in honor of God and of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist, a basilica not far away. By the concession of Obelierius and Beatus, dukes of Metamauco, by the approval of the tribune Aurius, and also by the confirmation of the priest Maurus, who had been elected to the episcopal office, they established that the church of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist should perpetually be a convent of nuns [Col. 0946A].

When these matters had been established as stated above, at the same time the entire population of Venice, having taken counsel together, came to the fortress of Grado. There, according to the form of the church of Saint John the Baptist at Torcello, they built a basilica in honor of the Virgin Saint Mary. They also built another church in honor of Saint Agatha the virgin and arranged a crypt in it with marvelous workmanship. In it an altar was erected in honor of Saint Vitalis the martyr [Col. 0946B].

At that time, a certain priest named Geminianus was commanded by divine revelation to search carefully, in the ruined city of Tergeste, between the walls of the church and the walls of the destroyed city, for the bodies of forty-two holy martyrs. When these had been found, he came with certain fellow countrymen [Note: [Col. 0945] “with” seems to need to be supplied. G.] to the destroyed city of Aquileia. While searching for the relics of the saints, they found there the bodies of the holy martyrs Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla, as well as the bodies of the holy virgins Euphemia, Dorothea, Thecla, and Erasma. Carrying all these relics with him, as had been revealed to him, he buried them with the greatest honor and in the most fitting manner inside the churches of the fortress of Grado.

[Col. 0946C] At those same times Beatus [Note: [Col. 0945] Thus in codex 3; “the nobles,” and in an erased place, “1”], duke of Metamauco, set out with certain of his tribunes and nobles (folio 5) to the universal pontiff of the Roman See, named Benedict [Note: [Col. 0945D] No Benedict occupied the see at the beginning of the ninth century]. When they reached him, they earnestly petitioned him, pouring out their prayers, to establish the fortress of Grado as the new Aquileia and to make it the metropolitan see of all Venice and Istria.

They also recited the names of the patriarchs who, after the destruction of the city of Aquileia, had sat in the aforementioned fortress of Grado without the authorization of any apostolic pontiff, saying:

“Patriarch Marcellinus was the first to sit in that same new Aquileia for 19 years [Note: [Col. 0945] Read: “sat”]. He had previously founded the monastery of Beligna in destroyed Aquileia, and he retained that monastery under his own authority for as long as he lived. Marcellinus succeeded him and governed the church of the new Aquileia for 15 years. After him Stephen sat in the church of the same fortress for 12 years, 3 months, and 15 days. His successor was Maurus, who presided over the same church for 4 years and 5 months. After him Macedonius remained there as patriarch for 16 years, 5 months, and 6 days; he founded the church of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist in the same fortress [Col. 0947A].

“We believe that these men should be counted among the bishops who existed from the time of blessed Mark until Nicetas, who presided over the church at the time of the destruction of Aquileia. Moreover, they were sent to this new Aquileia by the pontiffs of the apostolic see with the blessing of the pallium, which we request.”

Then that most holy man Benedict, supreme pontiff of the Roman See, moved by the merciful kindness of his character, yielded to their worthy petitions. After taking counsel with a synod of thirty-nine bishops, he established the city of Grado as the new Aquileia and, with the approval [Col. 0947B] of the bishops mentioned above and of all the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, constituted it the metropolitan see of all Venice and Istria.

Having summoned the duke and those who were with him, he said: “By a privilege of the Holy Roman Church and [Note: [Col. 0947] Thus it was first written; another hand later changed it to “by”] by the approval and confirmation of all these brothers, both bishops and cardinals, we establish the church of Grado as the metropolitan see for you, for all Venice and also for Istria. We grant the clergy and people the freedom to make the election of the same bishop. Moreover, after the election has been made, we entrust the power of investiture to the duke of the aforesaid region; once he has received investiture from the duke, we grant his suffragans permission to consecrate him. When these matters have been completed, we command him to hasten to the seat of this Holy Roman Church to receive the blessing of the pallium.”

He granted all these things by a document of privilege to the duke [Note: [Col. 0947] Another hand has “to the dukes,” 1] and to all his successors [Note: [Col. 0947] Another hand has changed “his” to “their,” 1]. In confirmation of this matter, following the proper order as stated above, he consecrated as patriarch a certain Paul, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. After the election had been made by the noble tribunes who were with Duke Beatus [Note: [Col. 0947] Thus in codex 3; “the aforementioned,” in an erased place], and after he had received investiture from the aforementioned duke, Benedict sent Paul back with them to the new Aquileia with the blessing of the pallium.

That most holy patriarch honorably deposited the bodies of the saints in the churches of the new Aquileia. In the church of Saint Vitalis he buried with the greatest distinction the bodies of forty-two martyrs; in the church of Saint Mary he carefully placed the bodies of the holy virgins Euphemia, Dorothea, Thecla, and Erasma [Col. 0947D]; and in the church of Saint John the Evangelist he placed with great honor the bodies of the holy Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla.

(Folio 6.) When the same venerable patriarch was preparing to go with a multitude of people to the destroyed city of Aquileia, it was made known to him by divine revelation that the citizens of Aquileia, fleeing the savage fury of the Lombards into the fortress of Grado, had carried with them the bodies of the most blessed saints Quirinus, Hilary, and Tatianus, and of the others. Rejoicing greatly at this revelation, he wrote an account of their translation and established the day of their feast.

He instituted the feast of the forty-two martyrs on the eighth day after Pentecost; the feasts of Saints Hilary and Tatianus on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March; that of Quirinus the priest on the fourth day before the Kalends of June; that of Saints Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla on the day before the Kalends of May; and the feast of the holy virgins on the third day before the Nones of September.

Paul, the most merciful patriarch and the first to hold office by apostolic concession, governed the church of the new Aquileia for 12 years.

[Col. 0948B] Probinus succeeded him and governed the metropolitan church in the same new Aquileia for 2 years and 8 months.

Then the distinguished patriarch Elias undertook the governance of the church of Grado. In it he ordered the church of Saint Euphemia to be built, in accordance with the meaning of its name. For what is called *euphemia* in Greek means “good form” in Latin [Note: [Col. 0947] Read: “good fame”]. In that church [Note: [Col. 0947] “quoquoque,” 1.], after a multitude of bishops had assembled from Verona as far as Pannonia and the entire people of Venice had been summoned, he celebrated a general synod.

At that time, searching for the bodies of the holy virgins according to what had been written by the revered patriarch Paul, he revealed everything to the assembly. When all who were present at the aforesaid council had seen them [Col. 0948C], they venerated the bodies with the greatest honor.

Then the distinguished patriarch Elias, with the approval of the entire multitude of bishops, clergy, and people, established sixteen bishoprics among the regions of the people of Forum Julii, Istria, and Dalmatia, namely at Vegla, Apsaro, and Pathena. In Venice he decreed that six bishoprics should be established. Entrusting the elections of each parish to its clergy and people, as had been ordained by blessed Benedict, bishop of the Holy Roman See, and confirmed in writing by a privilege, he granted investiture to the duke.

He established the first of these bishoprics at Torcello, just as it had first existed in antiquity in the city of Altinum; the second at Metamauco; the third at Olivolo. The latter was given this name because, before the door of the church of Saint Sergius, there was a huge olive tree [Note: [Col. 0947] Thus in codex 1; that is, *Sergi* or *Sergii* in Venetian, in which, for example, San Giorgio is pronounced San Sorso]. After summoning the people of that parish, the venerable patriarch ordered a large church to be built in honor of God and Saint Peter, and established a bishopric there. By written confirmation and under threat of anathema, they bound themselves to assemble there every Saturday, and there they conducted many commercial transactions.

He established the fourth bishopric in the city of Equilio. He ordered the fifth to be located in the city of Heracliana. At the same time the venerable patriarch built a church in honor of God and Saint Peter, which he called Opitergium. He ordered the sixth bishopric to be established at Caorle, where he founded a fortress and built a church in honor of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. Beside it he ordered an episcopal residence to be built quite honorably, in accordance with the character of the site.

The bishopric of Metamauco originated from the city of Padua. Just as the entire population had departed with its bishop, so it resolved to live on the same island of Metamauco (folio 7).

[Col. 0949B] The bishopric of the new city, which was called Heracliana, is attested to have come from the city of Overdecina [Note: [Col. 0949D] Oderzo]. Thus the duke and a large part of the nobles of that city, fleeing, established the aforementioned bishopric in the city of Heracliana.

The bishopric of Caorle was constituted here from Concordia by the fleeing clergy and people, just as it had existed there.

The same most holy patriarch Elias also had certain churches built on the shores that extend from the city of Grado as far as the bishopric of Caorle. On the first shore, which is known to lie beside the city of Grado, he ordered a basilica to be built in honor of God and Saint Peter, chief of the apostles [Note: [Col. 0949] “of the apostles,” 1], and he also ordained that a convent of girls should be located there [Col. 0949C].

On the second shore, whose length extends for six miles, two men were found living in a deserted place on that same shore. One was called Barbanus, while the other was called Tardessus. These men, fleeing the fury of the pagans, had hidden there from Treviso with all their belongings.

The aforementioned patriarch ordered a church to be built for them in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, just as had been revealed. When the same patriarch reached the place, he laid the foundations of that church according to the signs they had found there. He also ordained that a monastery of monks should be located there and that Barbanus should become abbot. His companion, however, returned to his own home.

(fol. 7′) In that same synod which we mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0949] Compare de Rubeis, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Aquileiensis*, p. 235 ff.], whatever had been in doubt concerning the Council of Chalcedon was confirmed after all ambiguity had been removed. There it was also decreed that the church of Grado should be the head and metropolitan church of the whole province of Istria and Venetia; the boundary of Venetia extends from Pannonia as far as the river Adda. They received a letter concerning these decrees [Col. 0950A] from the most blessed Pope Pelagius, with all the bishops of the aforementioned provinces consenting.

Paul, his predecessor [Note: [Col. 0949] *processor* (for *precessor*) in c.], unable to withstand the hostile danger, had withdrawn to Grado with all the church’s treasure when the Lombards arrived, bringing with him the bodies of the holy martyrs Hilary [Note: [Col. 0949] *hylari* in witness 5], Tatian, and the others. After Paul died and was buried in the church of Grado—his tomb remains there to this day [Note: [Col. 0949] *modo* (“now”) in witness 5]—Probinus governed the church of Grado, that is, of New Aquileia. When the aforementioned Patriarch Elias succeeded him, he arranged the matters written above (see above, col. 881), and placed the bodies of the saints already mentioned there in a wondrous manner. He also ordered a house to be built for himself from its foundations, declaring in the synod mentioned above:

> “Dearest brothers, because of our sins, hostile scourging afflicts us daily; and long ago Aquileia, our city, was utterly destroyed by Attila, king of the Huns [Note: [Col. 0949] *unorum* (“of the Huns”) in witness 5; see also the *Venetian Chronicle* above, cols. 881–883], and, devastated by the incursions of the Goths and other barbarians, it scarcely breathes. But now it cannot endure the scourges of the abominable Lombard people. Therefore our gentleness considers it fitting, if it pleases your holiness, that in this fortress of Grado we should establish our metropolitan see.”

This statement pleased all the bishops. After a document of his decrees had been drawn up—that is, concerning the aforementioned Council of Chalcedon, this see itself, and all the matters mentioned above—they wrote it out beneath their own signatures (fol. 8): first Elias, patriarch; then Marcellus [Note: [Col. 0949] *Marcianus* in witness 5; see also above, cols. 881–883], bishop of the holy church of Opitergium; Leonianus, bishop of Tiburnia; Peter, bishop of Altinum; [Col. 0950C] Vindemius, bishop of Cissa; Bergullus, bishop of the church of Padua; John, bishop of Caelia; Clarissimus, bishop of Concordia; Patricius, bishop of Aemonia; Adrianus, bishop of Pola; Maxentius, bishop of Iulium Carnicum; Severus, bishop of the church of Trieste; Solacius, bishop of Verona; John, bishop of the church of Parentium; Aaron, bishop of Aequum; Ingenuus, bishop of the second Rhaetia; Agnellus, bishop of the church of Trent; Vigilius, bishop of Scarabantia; Fonteius, bishop of Feltre; Marcianus, bishop of Pedena; Laurentius the presbyter, Marinus the presbyter, and Emerius the presbyter, all provincials; and the remaining presbyters, both metropolitan and parish clergy. All those written above consented and confirmed everything in that same place [Col. 0950D] [Note: [Col. 0949] *edem* for *eodem* in witness 1].

Five years after all the matters written above had been completed at the metropolitan see of Grado [Note: [Col. 0949] Witness 5 corrects this to: “after all the matters written above had been carried out”], the aforementioned Patriarch Elias died. He had governed the patriarchate for fourteen years, ten months, and twenty-one days, and was buried in the church of the blessed Euphemia.

He was succeeded by Patriarch Severus, to govern that same church of Grado [Col. 0951A]. He left in the aforementioned church of Saint Euphemia all the property which he had possessed by hereditary right, commending it by testamentary declaration to the priests of that metropolitan church of Grado, so that they, or their successors, might specifically celebrate Masses for him every Saturday on account of those possessions and offer oblations. He also established a table for the poor (fol. 8′). His testamentary document remains with the church of Grado, and the possessions which he bequeathed to it are still held by that church. When that most blessed man died, he was buried at the metropolitan church of Grado, in the basilica of the blessed Euphemia. He governed the patriarchate for twenty-eight years [Note: [Col. 0951] Thirty-one years in witness 5] and thirty-one days.

Patriarch Marcianus succeeded him. He governed the church [Col. 0951B] of Grado for three years, one month, and five days. When he died at Grado, that is, New Aquileia [Note: [Col. 0951] “that is, New Aquileia” is absent in witnesses 5 and 6], he was buried in the church of the blessed Euphemia.

Candidianus succeeded him in that metropolitan church of Grado. During his time, with the consent of Agilulf, king of the Lombards, Duke Gisulf forcibly appointed John, an abbot, bishop at Forum Iulii [Col. 0952A]. Three bishops, acting contrary to God, consented to this and consecrated him.

Nevertheless [Note: [Col. 0951] In the margin, in the same hand as the text: “At this point the letter of Pope Boniface is needed”], afterward, through a letter from Lord Boniface, pope of the city of Rome, they submitted themselves to the same metropolitan church of Grado. When Patriarch Candidianus died at the fortress of Grado, after governing the church for five years, Epiphanius succeeded him. He governed the holy church of Grado for one year, three months, and eleven days; he died and was buried in the church of the blessed Euphemia.

Cyprianus succeeded him in governing the church of Grado. He governed it for fifteen years, three months, and twenty days. When he too died, he was buried in the same basilica where his predecessors mentioned above had been buried.

That same pope, taking thought for the welfare of the holy church of God, sent the aforementioned Primogenius, subdeacon and regional officer of the apostolic see, to govern that metropolitan church.

## Supplement to the Grado Chronicle [Note: [Col. 0951] From manuscripts 5 and 6]

[Col. 0951]

[Col. 0951B] A certain heretic named Fortunatus seized the patriarchate. Since he did not believe in the Fifth Council, and feared punishment for his error, he stripped the entire metropolitan church of Grado of its gold, vestments, and ornaments; likewise [Note: [Col. 0951] *simul* (“together”) in witness 6], he stripped the baptismal churches of the province of Istria [Note: [Col. 0951] *hystoriae* in witnesses 5 and 6] and the *sinochagia* [Note: [Col. 0951] That is, hospices or xenodochia], which seemed to belong to that same church of Grado. He then fled to Lombardy and took refuge at the fortress of Cormons, fifteen miles from the city of Aquileia.

Against his wickedness and heresy, the bishops of Venetia and Istria and the clergy of Aquileia, who also belonged to the church of Grado, sent their written statements to Pope Honorius [Note: [Col. 0951] “The same pope … sent” already occurs above at the end of manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and 4]. That same pope, taking thought for the welfare of the holy church of God, sent Primogenius, [Col. 0951C] a deacon and regional officer [Note: [Col. 0951] *ragionarium* for *regionarium* in witness 6] of the apostolic see, to govern that metropolitan church, and also gave him a letter of apostolic authority condemning the heresy of the aforementioned Fortunatus. The same Primogenius, having been warned by a vision, brought into the city of Grado the bodies of the blessed Hermagoras, martyr and bishop, and of Saint Felix and Fortunatus, which lay three miles away, and deposited them there with careful attention. To this day the bishop of the city of Grado has obtained the blessing of the pallium from the highest apostolic see.

The aforementioned Patriarch Primogenius sent his representative to the imperial city, to the most devout Emperor Justinian [Col. 0952B] [Note: [Col. 0951C] “Read Heraclius with Dandulus”], to investigate how the baptismal churches had been stripped, how the Lombards had wished to withdraw their bishops from his diocese, and how they themselves had retained the treasure. Then the most devout emperor sent back more gold and silver than they had lost [Note: [Col. 0951] *quoniam* (“because”) in witness 6], and in addition sent the seat of the blessed Mark the Evangelist, which the Emperor Heraclius had brought from Alexandria to the imperial city.

When the most blessed man Primogenius died (in the year 649), after governing the patriarchate for twenty years, three months, and seven days, he was buried beside the body of his predecessor, the most blessed Cyprianus, in the basilica of the blessed Euphemia. Maximus the prelate succeeded him (in the year 670); he governed the patriarchate for twenty years and was buried in the same basilica.

Then the prelate Stephen succeeded him in governing the church. He was a bishop for five years. When he died (in the year 675), he was buried in the same fortress beside the basilica of the blessed John the Evangelist [Note: [Col. 0952C] Ughelli inserts Agatho here]. The prelate Christopher then assumed responsibility for governing the church of Grado. He lived in the patriarchate for thirty-two years and died and was buried in the same basilica (in the year 685).

Donatus the bishop succeeded him (in the year 717). During his time, the Lombards forcibly obtained the pallium for Serenus, archbishop of the church of Forum Iulii, from the highest apostolic see for the first time [Col. 0953A] [Note: [Col. 0953] This is absent in witness 5]. The most blessed Pope Gregory sent him a letter forbidding [Note: [Col. 0953] *interdicentem* is absent in witness 6] him, among other things, ever to invade another’s rights or, through a rash act [Note: [Col. 0953] *au* for *aut* and *ausi* for *ausu* in witnesses 5 and 6], to usurp anyone’s jurisdiction; rather, he was to remain content with what he had possessed up to that time [Note: [Col. 0953] “be content” is the explanation of the transmitted *contemptus*]. By apostolic authority the most blessed pope himself ordered that he should in no way exceed the boundaries possessed by Bishop Donatus of Grado; he should be satisfied with what he possessed and should not presume to extend his step farther than the lands unquestionably within the boundaries of the Lombard people. If he were disobedient, he was to be judged unworthy of apostolic authority.

When Patriarch Donatus died, after governing the patriarchate for seven years, he was buried in the basilica of Saint Euphemia.

[Col. 0953B] The letter of the blessed Pope Gregory sent to Serenus, bishop of Forum Iulii, begins here. In it he forbids him in these words:

> “Each person is enriched by as great a gift as he humbly understands himself to possess, placed as he is in a position of eminence, by command of the Lord Redeemer. Indeed, pastoral dignity is adorned above all by humility. The apostolic reading rightly condemns the proud; and if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?
>
> “Since, then, I bowed to the petitions of our distinguished son, the king, for the increase of your honor, and since we were greatly moved by the uprightness of the faith which we know that you and your church hold and embrace, we sent you the pallium, while forbidding you, among other things [Note: [Col. 0953] Dandulus adds “prohibiting” in his chronicle, p. 132], ever to invade another’s rights or, through a rash act, to usurp anyone’s jurisdiction [Note: [Col. 0953] *usu* (“by use”) in witnesses 5 and 6]; but to remain content with what you have possessed up to now [Col. 0953C].
>
> “Now, however, as we have learned, you are attempting to overrun the rights of the prelate of Grado and to usurp from him what he has possessed until now. Therefore, lest you prove yourself rash in any respect, we command you by apostolic authority not to exceed in any way the boundaries possessed by him, but to be satisfied only with what you have possessed until now and to confine yourself to it. Nor should you presume to extend your step farther than the lands unquestionably lying within the boundaries of the Lombard people, lest by your presumption you show that you have received the grace of the pallium bestowed upon you unjustly.
>
> “Therefore, by the force of the apostolic council, if you were proved disobedient, you shall be judged unworthy.
>
> “Given on the Kalends of December, in the seventh indiction.”

The same Gregory, concerning this matter, sent the following letter to the bishops of Venetia and Istria:

> “Gregory, servant of the servants of God, bishop, to all the bishops of Venetia and Istria and to the people of the same region.
>
> “Although, by virtue of the ministry which we govern through heavenly mercy, it is fitting that whatever we undertake after prudent deliberation should proceed without hindrance, nevertheless, lest we appear to have exercised judgment in vain [Note: [Col. 0953] The words “lest we appear to have exercised judgment in vain” are absent in witnesses 5 and 6; they have been restored from Dandulus, p. 133], we desire to pursue matters which do not [Note: [Col. 0953] *non* is absent in witnesses 5 and 6] tend toward anyone’s injury but rather toward protection [Col. 0954A], and to strive for those things [Note: [Col. 0953] *et illa* (“and those things”) is absent in witnesses 5 and 6] from which not [Note: [Col. 0953] *non* is absent in witnesses 5 and 6] punishments, through the power divinely granted to us, but rewards may be hoped for. For it is fitting that, when we comply with one person’s wishes, another’s rights should not be defrauded.
>
> “Since, therefore, after a report had been sent, your community, preserved by God [Note: [Col. 0953] Witnesses 5 and 6 read *c. et v.*], petitioned us against the bishop of Forum Iulii, alleging that he desired to invade the jurisdiction of the patriarch of Grado [Note: [Col. 0953] The text from *invadere* through the following *invadere* is missing in witnesses 5 and 6], and asking that he should never exceed the boundary or invade another’s rights, while he was unwilling to be content with what he had possessed until now, know, dearest ones, that we have forbidden him by apostolic authority at the present time to attempt these things, and that the pallium granted to him was granted under this condition. We have again ordered him not to presume to exceed the boundary.
>
> “Therefore, lest through some negligence or division their people should invade by stealth—as they are accustomed to do—be vigilant in guarding against it; rather, be solicitous and consider your safety after the divine protection [Note: [Col. 0953] Dandulus, p. 133, reads *cogitare* (“to consider”)]. For this is not being done by chance, but they strive to accomplish whatever they can, despite the power of God resisting them [Note: [Col. 0953] Dandulus reads *eis* (“them”) instead of *ejus* (“his”), and *obtemperare* (“to obey”) instead of *perpetrare* (“to accomplish”)].
>
> “We wish you henceforth to flourish in the love of our Lord Jesus Christ and to remain free from every adversity. Farewell.”

Meanwhile the blessed Gregory died at Rome, and the most blessed Pope Gregory III succeeded him. After the death of Donatus, patriarch of Grado, he sent his letter to all the people of Venetia and Istria, instructing them to elect a patriarch of Grado. At the command of that same Pope Gregory, they elected Antoninus, a man of the highest reputation, to the holy patriarchal church of New Aquileia (in the year 725) [Col. 0954C]. The blessed Pope Gregory III granted him, following the example of his predecessors, a privilege together with the blessing of the pallium.

This Patriarch Antoninus [Note: [Col. 0953] *Antonius* in witnesses 5 and 6] was summoned by the aforementioned Pope Gregory to come to Rome for a synod. Archbishop John of Ravenna was also summoned to that synod because of the images which the emperors Leo and Constantine were ordering to be removed in the imperial city, and because of the illicit marriages which were taking place in various places.

After this summons, Patriarch Antoninus went to Rome with his suffragan bishops for the synod. At that synod a definitive division was established between Antoninus, patriarch of Grado, and Serenus, bishop of Forum Iulii, in accordance with the decree of the blessed Gregory II. The entire synod confirmed it and pronounced a sentence of anathema against those who violated this confirmation.

When Patriarch Antoninus died, after governing the patriarchate for twenty-two years, ten months, and twenty days, he was buried in the same fortress, in the church of Saint Euphemia. Aemilianus succeeded him as patriarch (in the year 749); he governed the patriarchate for eight years and six days. When he died, he was buried in the same church [Col. 0955A].

Vitalianus succeeded him (in the year 757). He governed the metropolitan church for twelve years, two months, and fifteen days, and was buried in the same basilica.

Patriarch John succeeded him (in the year 766). He governed the metropolitan church for thirty-six years and was buried in the same church of the blessed Euphemia.

Fortunatus succeeded him (in the year 803) [Note: [Col. 0955] *Fornatus* in the text]. From Pope Leo he received a privilege together with the blessing of the pallium, following the example of his predecessors. He was so renowned that the Emperor Charles, of blessed memory, desired to have him as his spiritual father. For the enlargement of the church, that most reverent emperor granted him very many charters. Fortunatus governed the church for twenty-seven years.

Venerius, restorer of churches, succeeded him (in the year 825) [Col. 0955B]. He governed the patriarchate for twenty-four years and eight months and was buried in the church of Saint Euphemia.

Victor succeeded him (in the year 848). He governed the church for six years, three months, and four days and was buried in the same church of Saint Euphemia.

Patriarch Vitalis succeeded him (in the year 854). He governed the patriarchate for nineteen years, one month, and six days and was buried in the church of the blessed Agatha.

Patriarch Peter succeeded him (in the year 873). He governed the church for four years, six months, and eight days and was buried before the church of Saint Euphemia.

Victor the Younger succeeded him (in the year 878). He governed the church for seventeen years, eleven months, and thirteen days and was buried before the church of Saint Euphemia.

Patriarch Gregory succeeded him (in the year 896). He governed the patriarchate for one year, six months, and twenty-two days.

Patriarch Vitalis the Younger succeeded him (in the year 897). He governed the church for three years, three months, and fourteen days and was buried in the church of Saint Euphemia beside the bodies of the holy martyrs Hermagoras and Fortunatus.

Patriarch Dominic succeeded him (in the year 900). He governed the patriarchate for seven years, eleven months, and three days.

Patriarch Laurence succeeded him (in the year 921). He governed the church for twelve years, nine months, and twenty-four days.

Patriarch Marinus succeeded him (in the year 955) [Col. 0956B]. He held the patriarchate for thirty-four years, three months, and seven days.

Patriarch Bonus succeeded him (in the year 967). He governed the church for nine years, six months, and two days.

Vitalis succeeded him. He governed the patriarchate for fifty years and six months [Note: [Col. 0955] It is clear that the remainder was added by the continuer of the Chronicle].

Urso succeeded him (in the year 1012). Full of every virtue, he governed the church for thirty-seven years and forty-five days.

# In the Year of the Lord 1008: Heriger, Abbot of Lobbes

[Col. 0955]

## Historical Notice on Heriger

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis, book VIII.)*

[Col. 0955C] Hariger or Heriger, abbot of Lobbes or Laubach, of the Benedictine order, in the territory of Liège, from the year 900 to 1007, is mentioned by the author of Fulcuin’s continuation *On the Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, published by Luc d’Achery in volume VI (new edition, volume II, p. 744). He wrote the *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*; he wrote, in verse, the *Life of Saint Ursmar*; he also wrote a letter to Hugh concerning certain questions and composed many other works, but did not publish them.

In the persons of himself and Adelbold, a cleric of Liège and later bishop of Utrecht, he wrote a dialogue, *On the Discordance of the Church, on the Advent of the Lord*. He also assembled against Ratbertus many writings of the Catholic Fathers concerning the body and blood of the Lord.

These are Fabricius’s words. The same statements are also found in Sigebert, chapter 138, and in Trithemius, chapter 360, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and book II, chapter 63, *Illustrations of Benedictine Writers*. Trithemius also adds a book *On the Divine Offices*, which Oudinus, volume II, pp. 487 ff., thought was the work published under Alcuin’s name by Melchior Hittorp among the writers on this subject, p. 225, and in a version thirteen chapters fuller among the *Works of Alcuin*, [Col. 0956C] p. 1007.

The first twenty-seven *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*, from Saint Maternus to Saint Remaclus, were published by Chapeaville in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren, Utrecht, and Liège*, volume I, pp. 1–98, Liège, 1612, quarto.

Henschenius, volume I of the *Acta Sanctorum*, April 18, no. 558, says that he did not wish to publish the *Life of Saint Ursmar, Bishop and Abbot in Belgium*, who died in the year 713, written in leonine hexameter verse and in six books, because it contains nothing historical that is not related more briefly in the *Life of that same Ursmar*, which Abbot Anso wrote in prose. Nevertheless, he did not fail to provide some specimens.

Cave notes that Heriger’s books were published by Gilles Waulde among other monuments of the monastery of Laubach. The title of the book is: *The Life and Miracles of Saint Ursmer and of the Seven Other Saints, together with the Chronicle of Lobbes, collected by Gilles Waulde*, Mons, 1628, quarto.

Edmund Martene published the letter to Hugh in volume I of the *Anecdota*, pp. 112–118, Paris, 1717, folio. In this letter Heriger subtly argues against Dionysius Exiguus’s reckoning of the years of Christ, [Col. 0957A] and in turn proposes seven questions to Hugh for explanation. I see no reason not to agree with Edmund Martene that this letter is complete; on p. 117 he also published the beginning of Hugh’s letter to Hariger from a manuscript.

The dialogue with Adelbold, which Miraeus noted in his annotation to Sigebert, chapter 137, was preserved in manuscript at Gembloux; as far as I know, it has not yet been published by anyone.

The book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* was not directed against Ratbertus (Paschasius), whom Heriger praises and follows, but against Ratherius—see Oudinus II, 486—a monk of Lobbes and subsequently bishop of Verona. Sigebert, chapter 127, mentions his book on the same subject, which, in my opinion, is different from his letter to Patricius, published by D’Achery in volume XII of the *Spicilegium*, p. 37 (new edition, volume I, p. 375).

Cellotius was the first to publish Heriger’s book, but without the author’s name, at the end of the *History of Gottschalk*, Paris, 1655, folio. Mabillonius was the first to observe that it was Heriger’s work, in volume I of the *Analecta*, p. 211 (new edition, pp. 496 ff.), and in the preface to the fourth century of the Benedictine history, sections 2 and 3.

The *Life of Saint Landoald, Archpriest of the Seventh Century*, which Surius published under the name of Notger, bishop of Liège, on March 19, Vossius vindicates for Heriger on the testimony of Notger himself, p. 353 of *On Latin Historiography*. Henschenius presents the same work, with notes, in volume III of the March volume, pp. 35–42, stating that it was written by Heriger at Notger’s command.

Finally, Mabillonius also attributes to Heriger, in volume III of the Benedictine *Acta Sanctorum*, p. 14, the *Life of Saint Berlendis the Virgin*, who lived around the year 700 in Brabant; Bollandus had published it without the author’s name in volume I of February, February 3, p. 378 [Col. 0958A].

The *Method of the Abacus according to Heringer*, mentioned in the catalogue of the library of Leiden published in 1674, quarto, by Friedrich Spanheim among the manuscripts of the Scaliger bequest, p. 393, no. 31, I do not find in the catalogue of the same library, which Casimir Oudinus later published in a much fuller form in 1716, folio, but on p. 339 there is the *Teaching or Rules of the Abacus* of Adolard, the last of the philosophers’ followers.

That this author should in fact be credited with a book *On the Method of the Abacus* is proved by the testimony of Alberic in his *Chronicle*, who attributes this book to Heriger under the year 990. Heriger’s *Rules of Numbers concerning the Abacus* are preserved under the name of Gerbert, archbishop of Reims, later of Ravenna, and finally Roman pontiff under the name Sylvester II.

The *History of Gallic Literary Affairs* reports much that is worth knowing about this author. In the first place, the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* was written entirely against Paschasius Radbertus; Sigebert expressly affirms this. Moreover, the book published by Cellotius under this name is entirely different from the work composed by Heriger himself. For the same authors of the *History of Gallic Literary Affairs*, volume VI, p. 587 and elsewhere, established by arguments of no small weight that Cellotius’s work is genuinely the offspring of Pope Sylvester II. It follows that Heriger’s book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* has not yet seen the light of day. See the same *History of Gallic Literary Affairs*, volume VII, p. 201, where some of his poetry in honor of the saints and of the holy Virgin is also identified.

## Heriger’s and Anselm’s Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren, Utrecht, and Liège

Edited by the distinguished scholar Rudolf Koepke, Ph.D.

*(In Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica, Scriptores, volume VII, p. 134.)*

[Col. 0957]

## An Inquiry into the Life and Writings of Heriger and Anselm

[Col. 0957C] Everyone knows, and the very nature of things confirms, that the art of writing history seems to follow the same course as the events of kings and peoples and to obey the same laws implanted and innate in them. Thus, when the kingdom of the Carolingians had emerged from the transformation of all things, there arose along with it, after those illustrious writers of the Germanic peoples, the annals of kings and emperors, which are known to have flourished in the eleventh century through the considerable skill of their authors.

But at the same time that the German empire seemed to be falling apart amid the conflict between emperors and Roman pontiffs, another kind of historical writing gradually began to grow. Authors writing ecclesiastical histories, so to speak, had already become more numerous; in these they described the lives of bishops and abbots. This kind of book gained all the more strength among the clergy as bishops and monasteries, joined together by the common bond of the Church, perceived more clearly that they enjoyed their own particular genius.

Since the first example of this kind had been placed before people’s eyes in the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs* [Col. 0959A], and since Paul the Deacon in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Metz*, the writer of Fontenelle, and Bertarius of Verdun had already gone before them on the same path, a new host of writers now emerged. Alongside Folcuinus of Lobbes, Heriger and Anselm lead the narrators of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren, Utrecht, and Liège*, which we are about to publish.

At that time there was scarcely another episcopal see which shone with the names and glory of so many and such distinguished rulers as Liège, where one holy bishop welcomed another. After Saints Remaclus, Amandus, and Lambert, no one surpassed the two bishops Notger and Wazo in the excellence of every virtue; their greatness inspired Heriger and Anselm to write [Col. 0959B].

They also attained this great glory above all others: although they themselves had received no slight taste of learning, they prepared at Liège a most peaceful refuge for the Muses. In that academy, when more distinguished pupils had been instructed and educated by distinguished teachers, Liège began to be celebrated throughout Germany and Gaul, almost as Athens, under the auspicious name of a great school, so that the writers of that age could scarcely do justice to its educational achievements.

[Note: [Col. 0959B] Adelmannus, the adversary of Berengar and later a schoolmaster at Liège after Wazo, has these verses about the illustrious men of his own time in his alphabetical poems:

> “Liège, once the nurse of great arts,
>
> under Wazo and under him whose verses these are.”

See Mabillon, *Analecta vetera*, p. 382.

Since the name of Liège occurs in innumerable places in the books of Heriger and Anselm, and Liège is almost the stage on which those bishops acted, I cannot persuade myself to pass over in silence an accurate description of that city and the praises which Gozechin, a contemporary of Anselm and schoolmaster of Liège, poured forth with a full hand.

Shortly after the death of Liupold, archbishop of Mainz, in the year 1060, when he had resigned his office, Gozechin wrote the following to Walcher, likewise schoolmaster of Liège. Mabillon, same work, p. 438:

> “Above all other places, however, that corner smiles upon me which Mother Liège, knotty with the strong fiber of virtues, displays to her natives as delightful and pleasant. For, as you know, rising gently on its western side by no sudden slopes of hills and bending in a double curve of the public mountain—which on its not very daring ridge carries the four herds of the regular road—she is softly hollowed out by that same double curve. Like a hen gathering her chicks beneath her wings, she gathers her children beneath hers, warms and nourishes them, and shapes and instructs them for everything that is civil and conducive to good morals. She allows nothing to be lacking that could either govern abundance or moderate want.
>
> “The two-horned Meuse also pleases and washes around the city’s defenses and supplies its abundance. It is not undeservedly preferred to the rivers of our Belgium. It flows generously, supplying fish not only to the citizens but also to the native inhabitants of the land; it is convenient for the varied traffic of merchandise and useful for every kind of advantage, except that . . . when at times it is summoned into the banquet of the gods, together with all its cloud-born brothers, with King Aeolus and his winds, into Juno’s palace, then, exhausted by long labors and intoxicated by Aeolus’s pouring more than usual, it returns after bringing snow or rain.”

After this witty description of the flooding of the Meuse, he continues:

> “Our suburbs also have, on every side, pleasantly fragrant vegetable gardens and groves of trees, sweetly red. Extending its branches toward regions more suited to our vineyards, it has put the finishing touch to the highest shoots of the vines, sprinkling them with a few thyrsi. Enriched abundantly by these and many other advantages, our Liège still possesses things far more valuable and far superior to these.
>
> “Finally, it flourishes as the flower of threefold Gaul and a second Athens, nobly devoted to the study of the liberal disciplines; and—what is more excellent than these—it is outstanding in the observance of divine religion, so much so—if I may say it without offending the churches—that, as regards the study of letters, you would desire nothing from Plato’s Academy, while as regards religious worship, you would miss nothing from Leo’s Rome.”

Elsewhere, on p. 444, the same Gozechin wrote:

> “From the days of Lord Notger, bishop of our city, preeminent among the bishops who flourished contemporaneously with him in the Church, until these two lustra which have now slipped away in misery, mercy and truth met one another; justice and peace kissed one another. But now, and so forth.”

See also Nicholas’s *Life of Saint Lambert*, chapter 16, in Chapeaville I, p. 399.]

[Col. 0960A] From this same school, in the second half of the tenth century, Heriger of Lobbes, the first writer on the history of Liège, emerged. For the monastery of Lobbes, too, in the time of Richarius, bishop of Liège [Note: [Col. 0960C] A.D. 945. II, 20–22.], had already given the happiest promise of the fruit it was to bring forth for letters, as the names of learned men preserved in literary records demonstrate and the records themselves confirm. Among them, Fulcuin, abbot of Lobbes, mentions Scaminus and Theoduinus as men “highly esteemed in the study of letters” [Note: [Col. 0960C] C. 19.], his predecessor Aletramnus, a man “eloquent and learned in every respect” [Note: [Col. 0960C] C. 27.], and, above all, Ratherius, whom he declares to have been the most perceptive of them all, later bishop of Verona, whom we know to have produced many works of intellect.

If you remember that at almost the same time Fulcuin the abbot wrote a little book on the deeds of the abbots of Lobbes [Note: [Col. 0960C] Mon. SS. IV, 53.] and other Lobbes and Liège [Note: [Col. 0960D] Whether the Annals of Lobbes, Mon. SS. II, 209, were written at Lobbes may be doubted; that they were written about A.D. 982, in the time of Notger, is certain. The Annals of Liège, Mon. SS. IV, 9, were composed in part about A.D. 1000; compare the years 867 and 872; the Annals of Lobbes printed there were composed later.] annals, and if you enroll among those Lobbes men who shone among pupils in the middle of the tenth century but among teachers toward its end our Heriger, you will see that the times of Notger, who governed the affairs of Liège from 971 to 1008 [Note: [Col. 0960D] II, 25–30.], are rightly celebrated for literary distinction.

Among these men Heriger occupies by no means the lowest place: first a teacher, then abbot of Lobbes [Note: [Col. 0960D] Many have devoted themselves either to ecclesiastical or to literary history and have discussed the life and writings of Heriger and Anselm, some at greater length, others more briefly, as the purpose of their books required. Very few, however, provide material on which one can rest with confidence. Among these are Mabillon, Annales Ordinis Benedictini IV, 60, 178; and the authors of the Histoire littéraire de France VII, 194–208, 472–476, who must be named both here and repeatedly below. It is enough to mention the rest: the authors of the Magdeburg Centuries X, c. 10; Possevinus, Apparatus sacer I, 86, 735; V. Andreas, Bibliotheca Belgica, p. 149, 396; Sweertius, Athenae Belgicae, p. 129, 340; Miraeus, Bibliotheca ecclesiastica [Col. 0961B] p. 151, 156; Vossius, De Historicis Latinis II, 41; Oudinus, Commentarius de Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis antiquis II, 483, 610; Dupin, Nouvelle bibliothèque des auteurs [Col. 0961C] ecclésiastiques VIII, 51, IX, 109; Cave, Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum Historia Literaria II, 112, 135; Pagi, Critica on Baronius, 1007; Spanheim, Historia Ecclesiastica, Opera II, 1, 1495; Olearius, Scriptores Ecclesiastici, p. 60, 318; Fabricius and Mansi, Bibliotheca Scriptorem Latinorum Medii et Infimi Aetatis I, 114, III, 189; Foppens, Bibliotheca Belgica, p. 65, 471; Berthollet, Histoire de Luxembourg I, 301; Ceillier, Histoire générale des auteurs sacrés XX, 54, 397; Hamberger, Zuverlässige Nachrichten III, 760, 821; Villenfagne, Mélanges pour servir à l’histoire de Liége, 1783, a book I have not seen; de Windt, Bibliotheek der Nederlandsche Geschiedschryvers I, 1, d. 19, 20.], whose devoted labor in teaching letters, to the immense benefit of posterity, is demonstrated by the illustrious names of the pupils whom he educated.

For Heriger’s example and instruction were preserved down to the middle of the eleventh century, when the very fruitful seed he had planted in the minds of boys flourished in Olbert [Note: [Col. 0961C] Gesta Abbatum Gemblacensium, Dachery II, 763: “Brought up from childhood in the monastery of Lobbes according to monastic discipline and thoroughly trained in the study of the Scriptures, he displayed, as his character developed, what kind of man he would become. After drinking from the lips of Heriger, abbot of Lobbes, the most eloquent man of his age, something of the savor of the seven liberal arts, he could not quench his thirst for study.””] the illustrious abbot of Gembloux, and in Wazo, bishop of Liège [Note: [Col. 0961D] II, 30, 70. Olbert is called Wazo’s contemporary and colleague from the very years of childhood. Gesta Abbatum Gemblacensium, l.c., p. 766. On others educated in the discipline of Liège in Notger’s time, see II, 29; among them was Adelbold, a cleric of Lobbes and later bishop of Utrecht; see Mon. SS. IV, 680.], and reached the happiest fruition.

But let us now see what traces of Heriger’s life have been left by other writers. One testimony has been handed down to us that was written not very long after his time. Since it seems to provide a virtually firm foundation for the question, I think it should properly be incorporated into the text, and the very words ought to be set out lest I reproduce the witness’s opinion less accurately. They are the words of an anonymous writer who continued Fulcuin’s book into later times. Everyone can see that, if it is not the earliest testimony about Heriger, it is at least the most important; for, unless I am mistaken, the brief account Sigebert gave in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers was borrowed from this other one [Note: [Col. 0961D] Although I see that others have embraced a different opinion, I would hardly persuade myself, after comparing the wording of the two authors, that Sigebert’s meager passage in On Ecclesiastical Writers, c. 137, is the source from which the Lobbes anonymous writer derived his fuller narrative. Chapeaville, in the preface to the Deeds of the Bishops of Liège, rightly asserts that the writer to whom we owe the text of our Lobbes continuation lived about A.D. 1160; see Dachery II, 7. But I would not venture either to affirm or to conjecture that the first continuation of Fulcuin, in Dachery II, 743–746, which he copied, was committed to writing in the very time of Sigebert, under Othert, bishop of Liège, and Fulcard, the abbot. The words of Sigebert of Gembloux, c. 137, in Miraeus’s Ecclesiastical Library, are these: “Heriger, abbot of Lobbes, distinguished in literary learning, wrote the Deeds of the Bishops of Liège; he wrote, commendably in verse, the Life of Saint Ursmar; he wrote a letter to Hugh concerning certain questions; he wrote, in the person of himself and Bishop Adelbold, a dialogue on the dissonance of the Church and the coming of the Lord. He also collected, against Ratbert, many writings of the Catholic Fathers concerning the body and blood of the Lord.” Let me add the other testimony of Trithemius from On Ecclesiastical Writers, c. 306, in Fabricius’s Ecclesiastical Library: “Heriger, abbot of the monastery of Lobbes, of the Order of Saint Benedict, exceedingly learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly educated in secular letters, outstanding in verse and prose. Abbot Berno of Reichenau mentions him in a certain book addressed to Aribo, archbishop of Mainz. He wrote a notable dialogue in the person of himself and Adelbold, then a cleric and monk residing at Rome, later bishop of Utrecht, one book on the dissonance of the Church; one book, in verse, on the Life of Saint Ursmar; one book to Hugh concerning questions; one book on the divine offices; one book on the Deeds of the Bishops of Lobbes” (read: Liège); “one book on the body and blood of the Lord, and many other works.” He flourished under the Emperor Otto III, in A.D. 990. Trithemius repeated the same account in almost the same words in his Chronicle of Hirsau, under the year 979, adding: “He is also said to have written several other works that have not come into our hands.” How little he had even read what did come into his hands is adequately shown by what he rashly wrote there about the Deeds: “On the deeds of certain abbots of Lobbes who ruled the bishopric of Liège.”]

After him [Note: [Col. 0962D] Fulcuin, who seems to have died at the beginning of A.D. 990. I have not copied Dachery’s text, but have presented it from the collation of the Brussels manuscript made by the distinguished Waitz.] Heriger was appointed. I consider it unnecessary to enumerate his virtues, since even among foreigners he was renowned both for his life and for his learning. He was so dear and familiar to the venerable bishop Notger that the bishop always counted him among his foremost associates, not only in domestic or ecclesiastical affairs but also in courtly business, of which he was then the principal executor [Note: [Col. 0962D] He seems to have had before his eyes a letter of Otto III in Chapeaville I, 211.]. Not only in Lotharingia but also in Italy, where he was preparing the kingdom for Otto II [Note: [Col. 0962D] Rather, Otto III; this is a scribal error.], still a boy, he made use of Heriger’s services and counsels.

After he had been ordained abbot, he built this oratory on the western side of the church in honor of Saint Benedict. He had it dedicated by the same bishop Notger and, by the bishop’s authority, assigned it so that thereafter, every year on the day of the translation of the same blessed Benedict, a suitable food allowance might be provided for the brothers. He also took care to record in writing how much he increased the ecclesiastical furnishings, both while he was still a monk serving the bishop’s court and after he had become abbot.

He wrote the Deeds of the Bishops of Liège; he wrote in verse the Life of Saint Ursmar; he wrote to Hugh concerning certain questions, as well as certain other works that he composed but did not publish. In the person of himself and Aelbo, a cleric of Liège and later bishop of Utrecht, he wrote a dialogue on the dissonance of the Church and the coming of the Lord. He also collected, against Ratbert, many writings of the Catholic Fathers concerning the body and blood of the Lord.

He died in a good old age in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1007, on the day before the Kalends of November, and was buried before the altar of Saint Thomas the Apostle in the church of Saint Ursmar. This altar he had built for that apostle on the day on which he was ordained abbot. In his honor, too, he is said to have composed two antiphons, “O Thomas Didymus” and “O Thomas Apostle,” and a hymn on the Blessed Virgin Mary, “Hail, through whom,” together with certain other works. There were those who said that fever sufferers were healed at his tomb. Just as we do not disbelieve in the holiness of his life, so we do not doubt that he rejoices before the Holy of Holies in the reward of his holiness.

No one can deny that the author has placed before our eyes a sketch of Heriger’s figure, rough indeed but sufficiently expressive. You see a man adorned both with virtue and with literary learning, admitted among the friends of Bishop Notger, devoted not solely to ecclesiastical affairs or hidden away in the shadow of the monastery, but active in the public light and at court; even before he attained the office of abbot, he had advanced to a more important position both in rank and in the conduct of affairs. Learned men have already conjectured that he had earlier stayed in Rome [Note: [Col. 0963C] Histoire littéraire de France VII, 196.]. But whether this happened at the very time when he was elected abbot, I scarcely dare say. Nevertheless, the authority of the Annals of Lobbes seems to establish no less clearly that in 989, the year before Fulcuin’s death, Heriger accompanied Notger when the latter was about to travel to Italy [Note: [Col. 0963D] Annals of Lobbes, Mon. SS. IV, 18, under 989: “Bishop Notger goes to Rome, and H. with him.” I would not rely on the letter H. as standing for Heriger’s name unless the narrative of the Lobbes continuator removed every doubt as to whether Heriger reached the borders of Italy.].

In administering the office of abbot, an educated man succeeding an educated man, he was consecrated on 21 December 990 [Note: [Col. 0963D] Annals of Lobbes, 990, l.c.: “Fulcuin died; Heriger was appointed in the Nativity of the Lord.”], held the helm of his little vessel with a vigorous hand until 31 October 1007 [Col. 0963C]—through the reigns of the emperors Otto III and Henry II [Note: [Col. 0963D] Annals of Lobbes, l.c.]. But a letter of the monks of Lobbes to Notger and Rothard, bishop of Cambrai, has been preserved, in which, “having long been deprived of a shepherd” [Note: [Col. 0963D] That this interregnum did not extend beyond the end of 990 is confirmed by the explicit words of the Lobbes writers; the opinion of others, refuted in Gallia Christiana III, 84, was rejected in Histoire littéraire de France, l.c.], since they could find no one more suitable than Heriger, they asked that he be made their abbot. That letter is read in the Chronicle of the Bishops of Cambrai and Arras. Here I shall present only the words that express the principal judgment concerning Heriger:

“For undertaking this charge [Note: [Col. 0963D] I, 105.] we could find no one at this time more suitable than the lord Heriger. Yet, with God as witness, this is not according to his own assessment but according to ours: for many years he has lived among us in brotherly fellowship and has been of great benefit to us, while for many of our people he has diligently fulfilled the office of teacher and educator. … Know that our unanimity is not lacking in his election, etc.”

From the fact that we hear that Heriger died “in a good old age” in 1007, and that in 990 the monks of Lobbes wrote that he had lived with them “for many years,” it is evident that, when he undertook such a charge of governance, he had already passed middle age. Hence I think it can be established without controversy that Heriger was born before the year 950 [Note: [Col. 0963D] That he was born at Merbes, not far from Ninove, cannot be proved from the rather ambiguous passage that the authors of Histoire littéraire de France VII, 194, drew from the miracles of Saint Berlendis. Nor is it established whether the Life of Saint Berlendis itself was written by Heriger; on this see below.]. We must stop with these testimonies concerning the time during which he presided over the monastery as abbot; nor is it permissible to describe from other sources how he discharged the office. But there is something else I should add.

What we have brought forward thus far makes it abundantly credible that Bishop Notger and the abbot of Lobbes were joined by the bond of an unusually close association. Yet an even greater intimacy existed between them, as is apparent from the fact that later writers, unable to distinguish what each had accomplished in letters, assigned one man’s books to the other and doubted whether one or both of them had worked together on the composition of the same books.

I believe that the letters of Bishop Notger prefixed to another work of Heriger, the Life of Saint Landoald, shed sufficiently clear light on this question. In 954, the earlier Life of Saint Landoald and his companions had perished in the flames, together with other things, when the Hungarians invaded. Later, the monks, wishing to repair this loss as far as they could, collected whatever the memory of Sarabert, an aged priest, and others supplied concerning the earlier translations of those saints. They then asked Notger to arrange the material, once collected, as it were into proper order, and to confirm it by his authority. How he satisfied their request is shown by the letter dated 19 June 980, which we have appended in a note [Note: [Col. 0964D] Henschenius published the letters prefixed as a prologue to the Life of Saint Landoald from the Ghent manuscript, Acta Sanctorum, March III, 35; compare also what Bollandus said about the same Life, Acta Sanctorum, February I, 369, and Surius, Acta Sanctorum II, 281. Notger’s letter is as follows:

“Notger, whom, although unworthy, they nevertheless proclaim to be a servant of Saint Mary and Saint Lambert, yet a bishop, to Womar, venerable father in Christ, and to all the brothers of Ghent, and to all the faithful wherever they may be who will read this with an unprejudiced eye, wishes the perpetuity of heavenly life.

“You have not hesitated, most reverend fathers, to request—indeed, to exhort—the little capacity of our modesty, so that, from the miracles proclaimed among all ages and peoples and manifested in our own days, though we are unworthy, and especially from those revealed at the translation of Saint Landoald the archpriest and his companions, since they proceeded from our diocese and by God’s foreordination passed into your jurisdiction, we might satisfy, as far as report could be conveyed, the request of all—indeed, especially your own.

“Your request is just, and your exhortation worthy; according to a certain wise man, it joins the honor of the present undertaking with the usefulness of the age to come. For if the deeds of these men had not perished through the negligence of our predecessors, they would still suffice for us today. But whatever we have heard and learned, our fathers also told us—namely, what our memory still retains—and you ask that it be committed to writing, lest we likewise be condemned by the posterity that follows.
