“Since we were placed in uncertainty, because it is agreed and believed that the episcopate among you is the art of all arts, a suspended mind was balanced by silence; and the poetic saying, ‘Do not carry wood into the forest,’ offending our spirit, conveyed a certain lack of confidence. But since the mind is at fault when it never escapes itself, the sluggishness of distrust yielded, your appeal prevailed—except that speed, which according to Socrates makes a benefit more welcome, compelled us to hasten more than the matter required. For it had been said before us: ‘The strength that inexperience denies, charity supplies’; and since only the beginning requires effort, the rest will be facilitated by the matter itself.

“Therefore we began, lest we should seem to evade your authority. Authority is granted to one who presumes, when he believes that the person whom he asks can accomplish what is requested; and, conversely, obedience is an equal glory for the one who knows how to obey the commander.

“But if some future detractor should not fear to polish these things with a crooked eye and should presume to poison them with a dark bite of hatred, we call Jesus, his holy angels, and the coming judgment to witness, in his satisfaction, that we have contributed here little beyond what we either heard from the priest Sarabert, solemnly swearing to it and—as he himself related—having been strongly adjured by you through God and the merits of these saints, or faithfully found committed to writing in the document you delivered to us. The only exceptions are those matters gathered during our episcopate which, in view of the time available, seemed suitably to be placed before this little document.

“Farewell. Given on 19 June, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 980, indiction 8, while the lord Otto was reigning, in the eighth year after his father’s death, and in the ninth year of our episcopate.”

John of Thielrode also read this letter and adapted it for his own use in his Chronicle of Saint Bavo at Ghent, c. 14, Ghent edition, 1835.] The final words above all must be retained, in which Notger confirms that, apart from the accounts of the people of Ghent, he contributed nothing else except those matters gathered during his episcopate which, in view of the time available, seemed suitably to be placed before this document.”]

But we cannot stop at this one passage; another must be added. For an anonymous monk of Ghent, whom the narrative itself shows to have been an eyewitness present at the translation and elevation of Saint Landoald in 982, committed to writing at about the same time what he had seen [Note: [Col. 0966C] Henschenius published from the Ghent and Corsendonk manuscripts the history of the translation of Saint Landoald together with the Life, Acta Sanctorum, March, l.c.; see c. 15.]. Among other things, he wrote this about Heriger:

“But when the lord abbot—Womar [Note: [Col. 0966C] He presided over the monastery of Ghent from 965 to 982. Annals of Ghent, Mon. II, 188; he is the same person to whom Notger addressed the letters praised above.]—had seen such benefits, he gave thanks to almighty God. Not long afterward, inspired by the Lord, for the protection of the future and, more truly, for the greater glory [Col. 0965B] of the saints, he arranged for our predecessors named above to be sent to the venerable bishop of the Church of Liège, humbly entreating him to investigate through his clerics whatever seemed worthy concerning the relics of the translated saints and to report to them in writing the truth about all these matters. By God’s gift this was immediately accomplished.

“For when priests and clerics from every quarter had been summoned and assembled in a full synod, they unanimously recounted before their bishop how many miracles they had heard of and seen performed by our saints. Accordingly, at the command of that distinguished pontiff, the miracles they had made known were collected there, briefly indeed but with sufficient eloquence and in lucid language, and described by the lord Heynger [Note: [Col. 0966C] It is plainly evident that Heriger should be read; the Ghent Chronicle confirms this, in which the same words recur, as Henschenius says. They are absent, however, from the other Ghent Chronicle, Mon. II, 188.] the teacher, a man skilled in the musical art. They were also strengthened by the authority of the bishop himself, secured by the impression of his seal, and faithfully sent to the lord abbot and all the brothers of Ghent.”]

From this it is clearer than daylight that in 980 Heriger, schoolmaster of Lobbes and skilled in the musical art, composed the Life of Saint Landoald from the notes of the people of Ghent [Note: [Col. 0966D] Nevertheless, John of Thielrode, in his Chronicle of Saint Bavo, c. 14, attributed the Life of Saint Landoald to Notger, as did not a few later writers on literary history.], whereas Notger supplied him with the facts and the material for writing and thus became, as it were, the guarantor of the Life as it was genuinely and fully written by Heriger.

Then—and this is of the greatest importance—the Deeds of the Bishops of Liège had already been published at that time; they must therefore be judged to have been written before 980. Consequently, they were composed by Heriger while still a monk, not while he was abbot, contrary to what someone might conjecture from Anselm’s words in his letter to Archbishop Anno [Col. 0966B] [Note: [Col. 0966D] At the beginning of Heriger’s book.]. For I certainly do not see what Notger’s words—that he had inserted into the text of the Life of Saint Landoald certain matters extracted from his diocese—can mean unless, with Bollandus, you refer them to Heriger’s History of the Bishops [Note: [Col. 0966D] In the preface to the Life of Saint Hadelin, Acta Sanctorum, February I, l.c.]. You see that this is in fact proved, since certain passages taken from the Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren recur in the Life of Saint Landoald in almost the same words.

To use one example only: the letter to Werinfrid, abbot of Stavelot, which precedes the Deeds, Heriger incorporated in part into the other letter to Womar of Ghent, but he incorporated it in such a way that he omitted words here and there and compressed the discourse as though into a narrower space [Note: [Col. 0966D] The author also incorporated chapter 41 of the Deeds into the first chapter of the Life of Saint Landoald, but omitted some material in accordance with the purpose of the little book. Let no one hope that the date when the Deeds were written will be illuminated by new information under the name of Werinfrid, abbot of Stavelot; for new darkness arises instead. We first find mention of Werinfrid, abbot, in a charter of Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, written in 953, in Martene, Collectio amplissima II, 46; then in the letters of Everacrus, bishop of Liège, and in the charters of the Ottos from 961, 966, and 974, ibid. II, 47–50. But in that very year 980, when Notger sent a letter to Werinfrid, it was not Werinfrid but Ravenger who presided over the monastery, as the privilege of Otto II, drawn up on 4 June, demonstrates; Martene II, 50. Nevertheless, in a bull of Pope Gregory V the name of Werinfrid, abbot, occurs again, and then again the name of Ravenger; ibid. II, 52.

Others have taken different paths toward resolving this difficulty. Mabillon held that two Werinfrids and two Ravengers presided over the monastery, Annales Ordinis Benedictini III, 616; Martene and Durand followed him, Collectio amplissima II, p. V. Roderique, however, in his book Discussions concerning the Abbots of the Abbeys of Malmedy and Stavelot, Würzburg, 1728, tried to prove that Gregory’s bull was spurious and, on the authority of the manuscript catalogue of the abbots of Stavelot, to establish that Werinfrid ruled the monastery for twenty-four years; see pp. 38, 120. This seems scarcely compatible with the letters cited above.

That affairs at Stavelot were troubled in Werinfrid’s time is sufficiently apparent from a passage in a charter of Bishop Everacrus from 961, which it is useful to set out: ‘How Abbot Werinfrid and the other brothers of the Church of Stavelot, approaching our gentleness, earnestly begged us that, because of the various and manifold disasters of persecution in this kingdom, we should bestow some refuge of our city where those coming from different regions might flee,’ and so forth. In the year 966 of Otto I, the monastery was restored to Werinfrid by privilege. See also Fulcuin’s Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes, c. 28.]

[Col. 0967A] Yet even so the difficulty that has greatly troubled learned men has not been unraveled [Note: [Col. 0968C] Chapeaville in the preface to the Deeds of the Bishops of Liège; Valerius Andreas; Miraeus; Bollandus, Acta Sanctorum, February I, 369; the authors of Histoire littéraire de France VII, 198; and the others whom we named above.]: whether the Deeds were written by Heriger himself or rather had Notger as their author. For in one manuscript—and a sufficiently ancient one—of Saint Martin’s at Liège, which we shall discuss in its proper place, the name of Notger, not Heriger, is read as the author of the Deeds.

But how did that doubt about the author arise, when Anselm, the Lobbes continuator, and Sigebert expressly attributed our little book to Heriger, not to Notger? It is true that the author of the book wished to remain modestly hidden. He disclosed neither his name nor the place where he wrote to posterity, or indicated it only faintly; and unless it were established by the witnesses praised above that the book was written by a monk of Lobbes, one could scarcely infer as much.

The first doubt was raised by the Life of Saint Remaclus, which we see, as with Anselm’s Life of Wazo, to comprise nearly half of the whole little book [Note: [Col. 0968C] I, 40–56.]. For Surius published the same Life separately from some unknown manuscript [Note: [Col. 0968C] Acta Sanctorum V, 17.] under the name of Notger.

In this matter, contrary to his usual practice, he did not indulge his own ingenuity. Both the character of the book itself and the author’s admission in the letter to Werinfrid, prefixed as a preface, show that the Life of Saint Remaclus was written separately from the other Lives. For the abbot of Stavelot, complaining that the Life of Saint Remaclus, his own patron and that of the people of Liège, which we possess, was dry and meager, urged the author to compose a Life more worthy of the holy man [Note: [Col. 0968C] Acta Sanctorum, September I; it was written toward the end of the ninth century.]. Having found such an opportunity, he committed the Lives of the other bishops to writing as well, and published that fuller Life of Saint Remaclus separately from them, or, to use his own word, excerpted it.

But the letter, which in our manuscripts bears neither the name of Notger nor that of Werinfrid, has the following inscription at its head in the manuscript used by Surius:

“Notger, whom, although unworthy, they nevertheless proclaim to be a servant of Saint Mary and Saint Lambert, yet a bishop, to Werinfrid, venerable father in Christ and fellow priest, the aid of eternal salvation.”

“What, then, could be clearer?” someone might say. “Notger wrote the letter, and he also wrote the book to which the letter is prefixed.”

But it is not so clear. For, unless I am mistaken, Notger wrote neither the Deeds of the Bishops nor the Life of Saint Remaclus, nor, finally, the letter. Whoever gave that letter plainly writes in the person of the author of the book, as is evident from the very words he used [Note: [Col. 0968C] He uses such expressions as: “I undertook the task”; “I accepted that charge”; “this labor which has been undertaken”; “I collected and presented the deeds”; “the task undertaken through the presumption of friendship”; “I fear the bite of envy,” and so forth.].

Yet he is inconsistent with himself. In one passage he speaks in the person of the man who had impelled the author to write, in these words:

“At the same time you seemed—not, let me say, to request, but rather to exhort me—to have it committed to writing not in the usual manner but somewhat more elegantly polished, both because an abundance of material concerning his deeds, drawn from elsewhere, is available and because knowledge of the times, whose diversity now especially needs to be known, is not lacking in your chartulary.”

Who, I ask, commissioned the work? Was it the same person who wrote the book? Not at all. One person commissioned it; another wrote it.

That Bishop Notger commissioned the book to be written, while Heriger the scholasticus wrote it, is demonstrated by the example of the Life of Saint Landoald that we have before our eyes and is established by the authority of the witnesses cited above. Unless someone should prefer to resolve the difficulty in this way: holding fast to the actual words of the preface, he might conjecture that Notger entrusted the writing of the Life of Saint Remaclus to someone else [Note: [Col. 0968D] Two manuscripts of the Life of Saint Remaclus, the Trier and Saint Gall manuscripts, seem to oppose this view, since the name of Notger appears at their head as author; in one Saint Gall manuscript he is called Notger the priest at Saint Lambert. If this inscription could be trusted, Notger would have written the Life of Saint Remaclus before 972. But when he was raised to the bishopric of Liège, he was among the people of Saint Gall, being himself an Alemannian by birth. Compare the Annals of Hildesheim, 1008, and below, II, 25. Moreover, the considerations we are about to present concerning the style found in the Deeds oppose it, as do the above-mentioned words of the preface, “I should have it polished.”], while he himself composed the Lives of the remaining bishops.

But there is another obstacle. If you examine somewhat more carefully the style of writing found in the *Gesta*, you will hardly be persuaded that the letter to Werinfrid [Col. 0968C] was written by one person, the *Life of St. Remaclus* by another, and the remaining works by yet another. When you read the final chapters of the *Life of St. Remaclus* [Note: [Col. 0968D] I, 55–56], does that letter not come back to your mind, or the *Life of St. John the Bishop*, which has been taken from the series of the other bishops [Note: [Col. 0968D] I, 29–31. Vossius had already observed nearly the same thing, *De historicis Latinis* II, 41]? The author certainly did not write more meticulously or [Col. 0969A] compose his book in a more polished style. Rather, his manner of expression is rough and harsh; he is bold in his translations; and although the book is filled with passages from ancient authors, it is often so obscure that at times you might think you were hearing some sort of oracle [Note: [Col. 0969C] Herigerus elegantly proves that the art of writing consists in a certain learned obscurity. In his letter to Hugh—written with sufficient clarity, and discussed shortly below—he says, in Martène, *Thesaur. anecd.* I, 117: “I paid less attention to urbane gracefulness, knowing that those who wrote about the arts before us worked only to make themselves understood, while they entirely neglected eloquence.” That the other writers who emerged from the discipline of the Liège school pursued the same urbanity is sufficiently clear from the books of Fulcuin, Ratherius, and Everaclus; from the letter of Everaclus to Notgerus [Col. 0969D]; and from the works of Notgerus, Adelboldus, Anselm, and Gozechinus.]. The same manner of expression is found in the letter, in the *Life of St. Remaclus*, and in the remaining *Lives*. And if the same person is the author of those three works, who else wrote them except the man whom Anselm, the continuator of Lobbes, and Sigebert unanimously identify as Herigerus? They do not utter a single word about Notgerus.

But how, then, did Notgerus’s name make its way into this book? Unless I am mistaken, the difficulty can be unraveled in only one way, namely the way pursued by Chapeaville [Note: [Col. 0969D] In the preface cited above. Nearly the same course was followed by Andreas, Miraeus, and afterward Foppens; somewhat differently by Bollandus, Oudinus, and Lelong, *Bibliothèque historique de la France* I, 584; by Laguille, *Histoire d’Alsace*, p. 47; and by the authors of *Hist. litt. Franc.*; Ceillier also thought the matter could be explained in the same way: that Notgerus was the true author of the *Gesta*, but had handed over to Herigerus what he had written to be polished, corrected, and published. Hirsch, *V*, on the class of Sigebertus, p. 85, reached nearly the same conclusion as I have proposed concerning Herigerus.]. In the name and at the command of the bishop, Herigerus [Col. 0969B] composed that letter to Werinfrid like a secretary; and the letter itself shows that Notgerus supplied Herigerus with the material for composing the *Gesta* of the bishops, drawing it from the archives and from other sources.

Nor do I think that I have indulged my imagination beyond what is reasonable if I infer that Herigerus prefixed the same letter to the whole work in order to honor the friend who had been the instigator and assistant of his writing, and if I believe that, out of gratitude, he preferred to let his own name remain concealed. Thus this book too had almost the same origin as the *Life of St. Landoaldus*.

One point still remains on which I must offer a warning. The letter to Werinfrid expressly proves that the *Gesta* of the bishops had been brought down to Notgerus’s time [Note: [Col. 0969D] “And lest this labor, undertaken at your urging, should prove fruitless, I have collected down to our own times not only the times and deeds of the saint whom we have mentioned—namely Remaclus—but also those of the other pontiffs of our see, gathered from whatever sources they could be scraped together.”]. I would deeply lament that the portion of the book dealing with these matters—whether stolen from us by the hostility of the times or already buried in oblivion [Col. 0969C]—had been lost, unless I persuaded myself that it had never even been written. Some have thought [Note: [Col. 0969D] Bollandus, *Act. SS.* February I, and *Hist. litt. de France*, vol. VII.] that the *Lives* of the successors of St. Remaclus were among the works which, as the continuator of Lobbes says, Herigerus composed but did not publish. But why, I ask, would Anselm have [Col. 0970A] undertaken to write the *Lives* of the bishops down to Notgerus’s time if he knew that Herigerus had written them? Why would he have testified clearly in the preface that the deeds of the bishops had been committed to writing by Herigerus down to St. Remaclus? Unless one prefers to suppose that, seventy years after Herigerus, that book had entirely perished and vanished from human memory, this is the only way in which the difficulty seems capable of being resolved. The plan of bringing the book down to his own time had taken such firm possession of Herigerus’s mind that he presented the matter as though it had already been completed; but the author was prevented by some misfortune of the times from actually carrying it through to the end.

Now let us see how Herigerus discharged the actual task of writing [Col. 0970B], and with what aids he approached his work. There is one thing whose absence you will scarcely be willing to tolerate in him: he wrote nothing at all of what he himself had done or seen while serving in public affairs, and very little of what he had heard from others. Thus he could not adequately demonstrate in his book what sort of talent he had brought to the writing of history; he therefore procured other support for himself from the books and writings of others. Among these, as the subject of the little work required, the *Lives of the saints* clearly occupy the first place.

His sources are these: Eusebius’s *Chronicle* [Note: [Col. 0970C] Since Herigerus himself cites Eusebius as a witness in his letter to Hugh, in Martène, cited above, there can be no doubt that he followed him in chapters 3 and 4 of the *Gesta*, even if with considerable freedom.], in Jerome’s translation; the *Ecclesiastical History*, by which title he apparently means Eusebius’s work translated into Latin by Rufinus and, unless I am mistaken, the history of Sulpicius Severus [Note: [Col. 0970C] I, 3, 4, 16]; Jordanes [Col. 0970C] [Note: [Col. 0970C] I, 17–19]; the book of the Ravennate Geographer, apparently [Note: [Col. 0970C] I, 26]; the *Deeds of the Franks* [Note: [Col. 0970C] I, 26, 41, 5 [lacuna]]; Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne* [Note: [Col. 0970C] I, 26]; Bede’s *Book of Times* [Note: [Col. 0970C] I, 17; he cites it in his letter to Hugh]; and the *Martyrology* [Note: [Col. 0970D] It seems that he took from this, rather than from the hymn itself concerning St. Lupus, the two verses in I, 21]; the *Passion of the Apostles Saints Peter and Paul* [Note: [Col. 0970D] It is uncertain which *Passion of the Apostles Peter and Paul* this is. From the material that Herigerus owes to that little book, it is clear that it is not the *Passion* circulated under the name of St. Linus, of which two recensions exist that do not agree well with one another, in *Bibliotheca maxima Patrum* I, 67, and *Act. SS.* June V, 424. Several things found in Herigerus are missing from them. I therefore infer that the author followed another *Passion of the Apostles*, falsely attributed to Marcellus, the disciple of St. Peter, which Sigebertus mentions in *De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis*, chapter 1, and which the Bollandists had in their papers from the manuscripts of Gladbach and Trier. I have not seen this little book, published twice by Nausea and Florentinius. See *Act. SS.*, cited above, p. 399]; the *Life of the Saints Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus* [Col. 0971A] [Note: [Col. 0971A] I have firmly convinced myself that the relationship must be understood in this way, by which everyone sees Herigerus and the author of the *Life of those three holy men* to have been connected. In fact, unless I am mistaken, all doubts are removed. That Herigerus did not fabricate his account of those three holy men from unknown sources or derive it from his own imagination is contradicted by the very style of writing; rather, he himself explicitly testifies that he had before his eyes a certain *Life of Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus*, in the passage of his letter to Hugh quoted shortly below, where we read: “A certain place in the district of Alsace, bearing the name Elegia, agrees with their”—Eucharius’s, Valerius’s, and Maternus’s—“history.” That such a book had already been published before Herigerus undertook the *Gesta of the Bishops of Tongeren*, and before his patron Notgerus ascended the episcopal chair in 972, is as clear as daylight from the papal bulls collected by Hontheim on this subject. For it seems that news of such a little book reached Rome at the beginning of the year 969. In a letter of Pope John XIII, dated 22 January 969 and addressed to Theoderic, archbishop of Trier, Honth. I, p. 305, we find these words: “As we also learned long ago by hearing and indeed by reading, that very Church of Trier, more than the other churches of Gaul, received the beginning of the Christian religion and the first rudiments of the Catholic faith through the evangelical teaching of the most holy men Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus and the others, whom the blessed apostle Peter mentioned above ordained and instructed in their own time and also sent there to preach.” Finally, another argument of the greatest weight may be added. During the time of Egbert, archbishop of Trier, whom we know to have occupied the see from 975 to 993, Remigius, abbot of Mettlach, composed a chant about those three holy men, at Egbert’s command, in a sweet and regular melody, as Trithemius testifies in his *Chronicon Hirsaugiense* 122. This is also proved by the manuscripts themselves: he wrote homilies about them, concerning which Hillarius reports the following in his book against Hontheim, entitled *Vindiciae historiae Trevirensis de tribus primis Trevirorum episcopis, Euchario, Valerio et Materno, contra impactam recentius crisin* [“Vindication of the History of Trier concerning the first three bishops of Trier, Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus, against the criticism recently brought against it”], Metz, 1763, quarto, p. 132: “We too preserve in our library a large parchment volume of various homilies and sermons. On folio 15 and following I find a homily of this Remigius, abbot of Mettlach, on the feast of St. Eucharius, the first bishop of Trier.” That Remigius copied the same *Life of the saints* which is falsely printed under the name of Golscherus in *Acta Sanctorum*, January II, 922, is sufficiently demonstrated by the fragments of the homilies published by Hillarius. It is useful to quote one of them, from folio 18 of the manuscript: “He”—St. Eucharius—“did not fear to approach those who were attempting to bury him under stones; for the text of his most pleasing life to God contains the following: one day, when he entered this city together with his companions in order to offer the people instructions for salvation, the assembled crowd of the entire populace began to rush upon him, preparing to kill him by blows of stones. But, filled with God, he held out the weapons of prayer together with his most holy companions, and bound them all with such wondrous power that each one stood immovable according to the direction of his movement, in which he had prepared himself to cast the stone, until the holy bishop, after pouring out prayers to the Lord once more, restored their former strength.” The words printed in prominent type, recurring at I, 8, will prove that the same *Life* was the guide of both Remigius and Herigerus; no one, surely, will persuade me that the latter borrowed his homilies from the former. Hillarius also published the *Life* itself, I, pp. 146–159, from a manuscript of St. Ghislain; he had another, from Saint-Matthias, in his hands, p. 56, which shows that Bollandus had earlier given only the first half of that epilogue on which Hontheim relied. Bollandus himself testifies that this conclusion is missing from several manuscripts; hence a strong suspicion arises that it was added later, and nothing about the date when the *Life* was written can be inferred from it. One doubt nevertheless remains: from where did Herigerus take what is read in I, 5–6 concerning the three men and is absent from their *Life*? Perhaps a fuller account, built upon that *Life* as its foundation, was found in Herigerus’s manuscript. From the seventeenth century down to our own time, I should not pass over in silence the fact that the question of the *Life of Saints Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus* troubled learned men, partly because those men were said to have been the disciples of St. Peter who first preached the faith of Christ to the Gauls. Bollandus, cited above; Laguille, *Histoire d’Alsace*, p. 47; Bertholet, *Histoire de Luxembourg* I, 113, 301; Hontheim, *Historia Trevirensis* III, 965; de Marne, in the clearly written little work entitled *Sur l’époque de la prédication de S. Materne* [“On the date of St. Maternus’s preaching”], in the appendix to *Histoire du comté de Namur* II, 482; Perier, in his inquiry *De praedicata primum in Belgica Evangelii epocha* [“On the period when the Gospel was first preached in Belgium”], no. 23; and *Act. SS.* September IV, 354 ff., have rightly judged that Herigerus copied that *Life* into his book. Oudinus, in *Commentarius de scriptoribus ecclesiasticis antiquis* II, 1136; Schöpflin, *Alsatia illustrata* I, 332; and in our own day the distinguished de Sybel, in the engaging book *De tunica Domini*, fasc. II, 67, adopted the contrary view. Against those who attempted to defend the legends concerning those first bishops of Trier and Tongeren stood Bucherius, in his historical dissertation on the first bishops of Tongeren, in Chapeaville I, appendix, p. 16; Browerus, *Annales Trevirenses* I, 143; Gelenius, *De magnitudine Coloniae* I, 29; Fisen, *Historia Ecclesiae Leodiensis* I, 16; Laguille, cited above; Foullon, *Historia Leodiensis* I, 25; Bertholet, cited above; Hillarius, cited above; and Hartzheim, in his critical dissertation in Ghesquierus, *Acta Sanctorum Belgii* I, 53. Launoy, in his dissertation *De tempore quo primum in Galliis suscepta est Christi fides*, in *Opera* II, 1, pp. 72 ff., examined the *Lives* of Martialis, Memmius, and other saints who are said to have restored the dead to life; Calmet, *Histoire de Lorraine* I, p. III; Longueval, *Histoire de l’Église Gallicane* I, 50, preliminary dissertation; Tillemont, *Mémoires pour servir à l’histoire ecclésiastique* IV, 499; Hontheim; Perier; Sollier, *Acta Sanctorum*; Marne; Schöpflin, cited above; and Grandidier, *Histoire d’Alsace* I, 14, wrote learnedly and acutely on the question. Hillarius, pp. 139–145, and Hartzheim, cited above, offer a far greater harvest of books written on this question, which I have not seen.];

the most ancient *Deeds of St. Servatius* [Note: [Col. 0972C] Herigerus seems to have preserved a large part of the most ancient *Life of St. Servatius*, apparently word for word. It seems either to have perished or still to lie hidden in the shadow of libraries. Henschen already lamented its loss in the preface to the *Life of St. Servatius*, *Act. SS.* May III; but at nearly the same time Ruinart, in his edition of Gregory of Tours, indicated a remedy for the loss in a note on II, 5, p. 52, in these words: “Among other Corbie manuscripts brought into our library of St. Germain, I came across one written partly in Merovingian script and partly in Roman script, at least nine hundred years old, in which this entire narrative of Gregory, and indeed a somewhat fuller one, is contained under the title of the *Life of St. Servatius*.” That those *Deeds of St. Servatius* are rightly called “the most ancient” is proved by the fact that Gregory of Tours used them in II, 5 and in *De gloria confessorum*, chapter 72, and did so in such a way that in one or another passage Gregory’s text agrees word for word with Herigerus’s. Henschen had already observed this, cited above, and in our own day the distinguished Haupt confirmed it in *Zeitschrift für deutsches Alterthum* V, 73 ff. I scarcely dare say whether that most ancient *Life* is among those whose numerous manuscripts are listed in *Archiv* volumes VII and VIII (see the index). That it is not preserved in the single Paris manuscript of the thirteenth century, no. 5320 (*Archiv* VII, 59), is proved by the description of the manuscript owed to the distinguished Bethmann. The remaining *Lives* either derive from Herigerus’s book (see *Archiv* VIII, 481) or were joined to the miracles of St. Servatius written by Jocundus the priest in 1088. Concerning those miracles, in which Henschen did not hesitate to say that the fantasies of a fabulist were being reported, see his preface to the *Life of St. Servatius*, chapters 3–4, *Act. SS.*, cited above. The author of a German poem from the end of the twelfth century, which the distinguished Haupt published from a Viennese manuscript in the work cited above, seems to have followed a similar book.];

the later *Life of St. Lupus of Troyes* [Note: [Col. 0971D] I, 26; Boschius published it as a work of the end of the ninth century, *Act. SS.* July VII, 77. It too contains quite a few passages concerning St. Servatius.], [Col. 0972A] Baudemundus’s *Life of St. Amandus* [Note: [Col. 0972D] I, 32–39, 42], the *Lives of Saints Bavo* [Note: [Col. 0972D] I, 6], Chlodulf [Note: [Col. 0972D] I, 44], and St. Trudo, by Donatus [Note: [Col. 0973A] [Col. 0973D] I, 44–45], the earlier *Life of St. Remaclus* [Note: [Col. 0973D] I, 1, 41–54, 56], the *Life of St. Remigius*, by Hincmarus [Note: [Col. 0973D] I, 1, 27, 41], and the *Life of St. Lambertus*, by Stephanus [Note: [Col. 0973D] I, 53].

In some cases he preserved the text word for word, as the subject seemed to require—for example, in the *Lives of Saints Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus*, Jordanes, and Baudemundus; in others, he took the subject matter from them and developed it in his own style. But Herigerus also mentions other books which he did not turn to his own use, but merely cited. Besides Jordanes, he possessed many historians who wrote about the Huns [Note: [Col. 0973D] I, 17]. In his letter to Werinfrid he cites Hilduinus’s *Passion of St. Dionysius*; and in the same place he proves that he had read very many *Lives of the saints* written by others and had considered their manner of composition in relation to his own.

To these books he added the charters and public records [Col. 0973B] of Kings Sigebertus and Childericus, the letters of bishops [Note: [Col. 0973D] I, 3, 46, 48, 54], and the canons of councils [Note: [Col. 0973D] I, 28]. Elsewhere he testifies that what he has said can be supported by many documents preserved in the archives of Liège and Stavelot [Note: [Col. 0973D] I, 1: “Let the information not be lacking from your cartulary”—that of Stavelot. I, 41: “For many documents concerning the same matters, possessed by us over the course of many years, are still retained in the archives of both churches.”].

Nor did he despise that source which flows from the living imagination of the people—the common rumor circulating on human lips—which he described in the *Life of St. John* as follows: “We have received it solely by hearing and by the report of our elders and of those advanced in age” [Note: [Col. 0973D] I, 29]. Elsewhere he confirms that he received it from the inhabitants who reported it, and calls the reputation or antiquity of the report [Note: [Col. 0973D] I, 17, 46; and I, 48: “As anyone will be able to hear from the inhabitants who report it.”].

Finally, he made the events themselves witnesses to what their condition had been in his own time [Note: [Col. 0973D] I, 30. “The estates granted by that man to our church by our ancestors and still possessed by us bear witness”; I, 48: “The place of his prayer still exists to the present day, cut into the rock by his work.”].

Finally, there is another aid which, if you examine it more carefully [Col. 0974A], you will not deny that Herigerus possessed to a degree far surpassing that of others. From the writings of the ancients and of the Church Fathers he acquired a rare erudition for those times; he read much and reflected upon it. He did not merely touch the ancient authors with his fingertips, but—to use the expression—in such a way that he turned them into nourishment and substance, so that the thoughts of the ancients came to his memory spontaneously as he wrote. At times you may think you are reading not a medieval chronicle but some kind of cento [Note: [Col. 0974C] I, 1, 55].

He displays an exceptional knowledge of authors whose mention is rarely encountered in that period. Among the ancient writers are Cicero [Note: [Col. 0974C] He read *De oratore* and the speeches against Catiline, but above all turned the *Tusculan Disputations* to his own use, I, 1, 20, 55], Sallust [Note: [Col. 0974C] I, 22, 55], Pliny [Note: [Col. 0974C] *Natural History* I, 7], Terence [Note: [Col. 0974C] I, 1, 55], Horace [Note: [Col. 0974C] He read the *Odes*, *Satires*, *Epistles*, and *Art of Poetry*, I, 1, 55], Virgil [Note: [Col. 0974C] I, 30, 55], Tibullus [Note: [Col. 0974C] I, 55], Persius [Note: [Col. 0974C] I, 29], and Martial [Note: [Col. 0974C] I, 1]. Add to these Jerome [Note: [Col. 0974C] The letters against Vigilantius and the letter to Ageruchia; I, 7, 21], Augustine [Note: [Col. 0974C] I, 2] [Col. 0974B], and, among Christian poets, Arator [Note: [Col. 0974D] *History of the Apostles*, I, 3] and Prudentius [Note: [Col. 0974D] The book *Peristephanon*, I, 3. But I know well that, even with the names of the ancient writers I have mentioned, I have not penetrated into the more hidden recesses of Herigerus’s learning. Both in his letter to Werinfrid and in the *Prayer of St. Remaclus*, I, 55, some passages have been left which everyone sees to have been drawn from ancient writings, but from where they were taken is not equally clear. I gladly leave their investigation to those more learned than I. There is one point, however, on which I must offer a warning. Bucherius, in Chapeaville I, appendix, p. 9, and in our own day the distinguished Haupt, cited above, thought they had detected a trace of Tacitus’s *Germania* in Herigerus’s chapter 7; but that reading, which seemed to smell of Tacitus, arose from Aegidius’s error. Nothing of the kind occurs in the genuine text of Herigerus.].

Nor is there any reason to be surprised that other elements are also present which bear the flavor of that superstitious learning that flourished in monasteries [Note: [Col. 0974D] Compare what he says in I, 7 concerning the origin of the names of the cities Metz and Toul]. Nevertheless, in writing about the events themselves, the author was by no means reluctant to undertake the risk of exercising criticism. He did not himself deny credence to miracles; yet, with sound judgment, he refutes those of his contemporaries who complained that miracles did not occur in their own times [Note: [Col. 0974D] I, 26].

He does not hesitate to reject the claim that St. Servatius descended from the family of the Savior, which may perhaps have been inserted into his *Life* out of piety. And certainly he displays an open and candid spirit in the confession he makes: it is better modestly to acknowledge ignorance than irreverently to lie in the name of piety [Col. 0975A] [Note: [Col. 0975C] I, 20].

Thus, concerning the earliest history of the people of Tongeren, he openly acknowledges in more than one passage that, amid such obscurity of events, nothing certain can be stated [Note: [Col. 0975C] I, 15: “Let no inquiry on the part of any reader demand that we say under whose emperors or consuls these men flourished.” I, 26: “It is uncertain, as it is also recorded concerning the bishops of many other cities, for how long an interval the church of Tongeren was without a bishop.” I, 43: “It is likewise unknown for how long an interval the people of Maastricht were without a shepherd,” etc.].

To make his method of exercising criticism still more evident, I shall quote another passage from his letter to Hugh, in which we see Herigerus doubting whether those first bishops of Trier—Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus—were really sent by St. Peter to preach the Gospel. Here are his words [Note: [Col. 0975D] Martène and Durand, *Thesaurus anecdotorum* I, 117]:

> Concerning our men of Trier, Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus, who are said to have been sent by the apostle Peter, a certain place in the district of Alsace bearing the name Elegia agrees with their history. But from the passion of blessed Peter—which occurred in the thirteenth year of Nero, if he—namely Peter—perhaps sent Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus to Trier, he did so several years before his own passion—the years are reckoned as 263 up to the twenty-fifth year of Constantine, when St. Sylvester died. At his command the synod was held at Arles, where St. Maternus, bishop of Cologne, is read to have been present with Maurinus, his archdeacon; St. Agricus, bishop of Trier, was also present there.

But he did not confine himself merely to recounting events. Attempting to perceive their character and nature, he proves in his book that he possessed a more elevated spirit and had been imbued with a certain philosophical taste. For he attempted to resolve questions concerning the world, created by the eternal God but not itself eternal, and concerning the reconciliation of human free will with divine providence [Note: [Col. 0975D] I, 2, 40]. Elsewhere he undertook to explain the difference between antiquity and more recent times [Col. 0975C], deriving from that very difference the necessity of writing history [Note: [Col. 0975D] I, 1].

I would now pass to Anselm’s book, were it not that I think a few things should be added concerning Herigerus’s other little works, lest I seem to have taken anything away from so learned a man. We have already seen above that he composed the *Gesta of the Bishops* no later than 979 [Col. 0976A], and that in the following year he composed the *Life of St. Landoaldus*. He tested what he could accomplish in verse in another book, written in hexameters, concerning the *Life of St. Ursmarus*, which he published before undertaking the office of abbot. Of all the little works of Herigerus that we possess, this was, unless I am mistaken, the first to be composed; for in the *Gesta of the Bishops* he transcribed certain verses from it.

He himself is the metrician whom he says composed not inappropriate verses concerning St. Servatius [Note: [Col. 0975D] I, 21. Aegidius Waulde published the whole *Life of St. Ursmarus*, together with other Lobbes materials, in 1628; I have not seen the book itself. Mabillon published from a manuscript of St. Vanne of Verdun a fragment of the poem containing the same verses that are read in I, 21; *Act. SS.*, third century, II, 2. On p. 557 he testifies that it bore this inscription: “In the name of Christ begins the *Life of St. Ursmarus, confessor and bishop*, honorably composed in hexameter meter through the industry of the venerable Herigerus, abbot.” From what has been said above it is sufficiently clear that these words were added at a later time. Henschenius had another manuscript of the same *Life*, from Gembloux, in his hands. Besides some verses, he supplied the following summary of the poem, in which you will not fail to recognize Herigerus’s talent (*Act. SS.* April II, 558): Herigerus begins with the fall of the angels, the creation of the world and of Adam, Adam’s fall, and his restoration through Christ’s coming and triumph on the cross. He then proceeds to the Gospel proclaimed throughout the whole world by the apostles and apostolic men, and especially in the neighboring regions.].

That Herigerus devoted himself not only to narrating historical events but also applied his great learning to illuminating other questions is shown by catalogues of his books and confirmed by witnesses. Among these the first place certainly belongs to the little work entitled *Letter of Herigerus the Abbot to a Certain Hugh, a Monk* [Col. 0976B] [Note: [Col. 0976C] Martène, *Thes. anecd.* I, 112. Mabillon wished this Hugh to be the same man whom we know to have been appointed Herigerus’s successor among the monks of Lobbes in 1033. *Ann. ord. B.* IV, 317; *Ann. Lob. Mon.*, *SS.* IV, 19. This, without doubt, is the little work whose manuscript, Sanderus says, was preserved in the monastery of St. Lambert at Liège, *Bibliotheca Belgica manuscripta* II, 24; the authors of *Hist. litt. Franc.* VII, 207 rightly recognized it. The manuscript was entitled: “An epistolary response concerning the Easter cycle and related matters against Abbot Dionysius.”].

The fact that it was written after 990 and before 999 is persuaded to me by the title of abbot given to Herigerus and by the mention of Lord Gerbertus [Note: [Col. 0976D] Martène, *Thes.* I, 117], with the title of supreme pontiff suppressed. That Herigerus was already advanced in age at that time is shown by these words found in the same place: “These matters, dearest brother, I have set out briefly and summarily because, with illness intervening and the sight of my eyes already dimming, I could not write them myself.”

That Hugh had proposed certain questions concerning chronological calculation, and concerning the manner in which the authority of Dionysius was to be reconciled with the truth of the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0976D] Martène and Durand, *Thesaurus anecdotorum* I, 117. They also testify that they had read Hugh’s letter, whose beginning is: “To the lord abbot H., Brother Hugh. What Bede and Dionysius appear to hold differently in their little works, a matter that sometimes confuses many people, we ask to have corrected by your examination.”], is clear. Having thus obtained a kindly opportunity to display his learning by resolving these questions, Herigerus sufficiently confirmed the judgment he had made of himself in the *Gesta of the Bishops*. He made Eusebius, Jerome [Note: [Col. 0976D] Among other things, the following is read there, Martène I, 112: “According to the chronicle of Eusebius or even of Jerome, who, unless he had approved it, would not have translated it in this way”], Augustine, Fulgentius, and Bede—whom he cites by name—witnesses to his learning.

Finally, at the end of the letter, as a kind of repayment for Hugh’s questions, he gives him seven chronological questions to solve, and I very much doubt that Hugh actually resolved them. We have already brought forward the third question [Col. 0977A], and in its proper place we shall give the seventh, which likewise concerns Liège.

Another book, which later writers say was a dialogue between Herigerus and Adelboldus, later bishop of Utrecht, concerning the celebration of Advent, seems to have been snatched from us by the hostility of the times. This is scarcely surprising, since not long afterward Herigerus’s work had still not emerged into the light it deserved. Berno, abbot of Reichenau, who devoted himself to the same question in several little books, gave this testimony concerning that work in a letter to Aribo, archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0977C] *The Book on How the Advent of the Lord Is to Be Celebrated*. Pez, *Thesaur. anecd. nov.* IV, 2, p. 46; see there also the introductory dissertation, p. VII.]:

> But Abbot Herigerus too, a man of no small authority, composed in our own times a little book of his own on this subject. In it, as those who have read it assert, he proves with probable arguments [Col. 0977B] that those act against the institutions of the Fathers who insist on celebrating more than four Sundays of the Advent of the Lord.

Nor did Herigerus wish to regard mathematical disciplines as alien to him. He wrote rules concerning the abacus, about which Albericus, monk of Trois-Fontaines, wrote bitterly under the year 990 [Note: [Col. 0977C] Leibniz’s edition, p. 32]:

> Herigerus becomes the seventh abbot of Lobbes, distinguished in literary knowledge; his rules of numbers on Gerbertus’s abacus are extant. For the ancients devoted themselves to many things that are regarded as objects of ridicule today.

Pez had in his hands at Regensburg a manuscript of the same book from the twelfth century [Note: [Col. 0977C] It is a quarto parchment manuscript, and bears this inscription at the beginning: “Here begin Herigerus’s rules for the abacus.” Pez copied its opening verses in *Thes. anecd. noviss.* I, introductory dissertation, p. XXXVIII: “If the greater is divided by the lesser, the dividend receives denominations either from the whole dividend, or from its parts, or from neither; but they are denominated by the differences of the divisor.”]. Oudinus reports that another is preserved at Leiden [Note: [Col. 0977D] The Leiden manuscript is inscribed on the folio: “The method of the abacus according to the divine Harigerus.” It is Scaliger manuscript no. 31; see Oudin II, 486.].

The books which we have enumerated are truly shown to have been written by Heriger—by manuscripts or witnesses whose testimony cannot be called into question [Col. 0977C]. I shall add one more, concerning whose author learned men have embraced differing opinions. It is the little book in which, as the Lobbes continuator records, he gathered together many writings of the Catholic Fathers against Ratbert concerning the body and blood of the Lord. I am convinced, with Mabillon, that it was written by Heriger.

After Cellot, who first published this book [Note: [Col. 0977D] In *Historia Gotteschalci*, Paris, 1655, fol., p. 541 ff., from a manuscript of Sirmond, in which the book is called *De Eucharistia*; and afterward Pez published it under the name of Gerbert, *Thesaurus anecdotorum novissimus* I, 2, p. 133 ff.], Mabillon found the same work in a sufficiently ancient Gembloux manuscript [Col. 0978A], bearing an inscription which seems to remove all doubt, in these words [Note: [Col. 0977D] *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedicti*, sixth century, part 2, p. 591, and p. XXI, “On the name and age of Cellot’s anonymous author.” See also Mabillon, *Vetera Analecta*, p. 496; *Annales Ordinis Benedicti* IV, 178.]:

> “Sayings of Lord Abbot Heriger concerning the body and blood of the Lord.”

And when shortly afterward he examined the Lobbes library, he read in an old catalogue of books, entered under the year 1049, the following words:

> “Abbot Heriger’s amplification concerning the body and blood of the Lord.”

Finally, Oudinus saw another manuscript of the same book inscribed with Heriger’s name [Note: [Col. 0977D] In the library of Sigy, of the Cistercian Order in the archbishopric of Rheims; see Oudinus, *Commentarii de Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis* II, 486, who also testifies that a manuscript exists at Saint Martin’s in Leuven [Col. 0978C].].

I rely upon these credible testimonies, nor does their authority seem to be overturned by Abbot S. Gerald, who says that Heriger wrote a letter on this subject [Note: [Col. 0978C] In the prologue to the *Life of Saint Adelhard of Corbie*, Mabillon, *Acta Ordinis Benedicti* IV, 345, has the following concerning Paschasius: “What sort of man and how great he was is attested in a certain letter by Heriger, abbot of Lobbes, who at that time was regarded as the most distinguished among the learned.” Gerald was undoubtedly mistaken; both the book and the Gembloux catalogue prove that Heriger’s work was a treatise, not a letter [Col. 0978D].]. Nor am I swayed by the Gottweig manuscript found by Pez [Note: [Col. 0978D] It is an eleventh-century manuscript; see Pez, *Thesaurus anecdotorum* I, 2, p. LXIX. Pez also invoked Gerald’s words in support; his view was defended by the authors of *Histoire littéraire de la France* VI, 587; VII, 201, by Ceillier I, at the indicated place, and by Mansi in his edition of Fabricius III, 191. Nearly all the others have followed Mabillon.], in which the same book is read under Gerbert’s name.

For although no certain indication of the author can be obtained from the book itself [Col. 0978B], I seem to have detected traces both of Heriger’s learning and of his manner of writing. The author did in fact gather passages from the ecclesiastical Fathers on this subject: Eusebius, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Leo, Hilary, Cyril, Basil, and Fulgentius. The dialectical arguments which he himself advances [Note: [Col. 0978D] Chapter 7.] rest upon the same biblical passage concerning measure, weight, and number, upon which he constructed the first chapter of the *Gesta* as upon a foundation. We have already seen that Heriger had this practice in composing books: he copied suitable material from one book into another [Note: [Col. 0978D] He incorporated several passages from the *Gesta* into the letter to Werinfrid and chapter 41 of the *Life of Saint Landoaldus*, and repeated others in the letter to Hugh; see above and I, 1, 16. From the *Life of Saint Ursmar* he transcribed several verses into the *Gesta*; see I, 21.].

Finally, everything that he gathered in this little work is directed toward a single end: it seeks to refute the decrees of Paschasius Radbertus [Note: [Col. 0978D] The claim, repeated by others after Possevinus and Miraeus, that Heriger composed this book not against Radbertus but against Ratherius or Berengar is unsupported by any argument and has been refuted by Andreas, *Bibliotheca Belgica*, at the indicated place, and by the authors of *Histoire littéraire de la France* VII, 201.].

Another little work might give rise to greater doubt. Trithemius included it in his catalogue of Heriger’s books under this title:

> “Two books on the divine offices.”

Learned men have been surprised that the Lobbes continuator passed it over in silence. But either I am mistaken, or the Lobbes writer did not omit this book at all. For it is the same book which Trithemius either saw or had in mind, and concerning which the following is read in the Lobbes writer:

> “He also took care to record in writing how much he had increased the ecclesiastical adornment, both while still a monk serving the episcopal court and after he had become abbot” [Col. 0979A].

[Note: [Col. 0979C] Oudinus II, 486. Oudinus thought he had found this book of Heriger in an anonymous tenth-century treatise falsely circulated under Alcuin’s name; the authors of *Histoire littéraire de la France* VII, 207, have adequately refuted his opinion.]

Other books are of such doubtful origin that I shall offer no judgment concerning them; still others have plainly been falsely attributed to Heriger.

Among the former I place the *Life of Saint Berlendis*, which Mabillon, and after him others, conjectured to have been composed by Heriger [Note: [Col. 0979C] Bollandus first published it from manuscripts at Lobbes, Merbes, and elsewhere, omitting the prologue, *Acta Sanctorum*, February I, 377; on account of the mention of the duke of Lorraine, he dated the book to around the year 1000. From his own manuscript Mabillon restored the prologue in *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedicti* III, 16. It is inscribed: “To his lord and friend Gerard, H., the last monk of Lobbes”; hence arose the conjecture which Mabillon appended, apparently making Heriger the author. The same opinion was accepted by the authors of *Histoire littéraire de la France* VII, 194. If the book really is Heriger’s, it must have been written by him before 990 [Col. 0979D].].

But apart from a single preface composed by a certain monk of Lobbes whose name is marked by the letter H, there is not even a word which seems to point to our author; nor can the time when that little book appeared be determined with greater precision. I therefore do not by any means attribute it to Heriger as certain.

The same is true of the metrical *Life of Saint Landelin*, which has not yet been printed. Mabillon was chiefly persuaded that it was by the same author because he had read it, with the author’s name suppressed, attached to the *Life of Saint Ursmar* in the same manuscript of Saint Vitonus [Col. 0979B] [Note: [Col. 0979D] *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedicti* III, 2, p. 557. Mabillon further confirmed his conjecture by noting that the same account of the origin of the name of the Crispian monastery—derived from *crispantes aquae*, “rippling waters”—which occurs in the *Life of Saint Ursmar* also appears in the *Life of Saint Landelin*, and this does indeed seem to reveal Heriger’s character. But in the Gembloux manuscript of the *Life of Saint Ursmar*, which Henschen saw, the *Life of Saint Landelin* is lacking; see above. The authors of *Histoire littéraire de la France* VII, 202, and nearly all the writers on literary matters whom we have named followed Mabillon.].

This question can scarcely be settled unless one examines the book itself.

Finally, the *Life of Saint Hadelin*, which some have thought to have been written by Heriger because Heriger’s preface to the *Life of Saint Remaclus* appears again at its beginning, is not Heriger’s but the work of Bishop Notger [Note: [Col. 0979D] The manuscripts of Malmedy and Liège omit Notger’s name, but the author himself confirms that he was a bishop with these words in chapter 10, *Acta Sanctorum*, February I, 368: “When this had been learned, the prelate who was then in office, whose name we now serve, God so granting, not—shame upon it!—according to his merit, issued a prohibition by the authority of his episcopal see.” That he was bishop of Liège is indicated by the name of the village mentioned in chapter 10, which lay in the diocese of Liège. Elsewhere the author commends the *Life of Saint Remaclus*: “Whoever wishes may find it in the book of his life.” All doubt is removed by the fact that the author borrowed from chapter 40 of Heriger’s *Gesta* concerning Saint Remaclus the material for the preface to his *Life of Saint Hadelin*, and thereafter for chapters 43 and 49 [Col. 0980C].]. Bollandus demonstrated this sufficiently, and the others agreed [Note: [Col. 0980C] Compare Bollandus’s preface to the *Life of Saint Hadelin*, at the indicated place; his opinion was approved by Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedicti* II, 1013, and *Histoire littéraire de la France* VII, 214.].

There is, however, one matter which chiefly concerns Heriger and which may appropriately be mentioned at the end of this discussion of the abbot of Lobbes.

Besides the question concerning Saint Maternus and his successors mentioned above, another dispute had arisen. After Bucherius, who was the first to open the way for critical investigation into the most ancient affairs of the Tongeren people [Note: [Col. 0980C] *Disputatio historica de primis Tungrorum seu Leodiensium episcopis*, in Chapeaville I, in the appendix.], this controversy greatly exercised learned men at Liège in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

Literary battles were fought over the succession of the bishops and over the time when the see was transferred from Tongeren to Maastricht and from Maastricht to Liège. But because of the intense rivalry between Tongeren and Maastricht, the fiercest dispute concerned the name of the bishopric: was it called Tongeren or Maastricht?

Bucherius was the first properly to break through the succession of bishops which Heriger had drawn from older catalogues and from popular memory [Note: [Col. 0980C] Thus, in I, 29, in the *Life of Bishop John*, Heriger admits that he owed his account to popular memory; this is also proved by his saying in I, 36 that John was the predecessor of Amandus, although Baudemundus, an author two centuries older than Heriger, could not produce John’s name [Col. 0980D].]. Bucherius denied that a bishopric of Tongeren had existed before Saint Servatius, and attempted, with remarkable boldness for his age, to establish that afterward it had been buried in oblivion until the time of Clovis, and that nothing certain could be discovered concerning Tongeren before Saint Amandus [Col. 0980B] [Note: [Col. 0980D] At the indicated place, pp. 38, 47, 49. See Albericus on the bishops of Tongeren, whose words, drawn from some source unknown to me, we appended at I, 27.].

All this was true and correct, but exceedingly bitter to the people of Liège. Yet it did not anger learned men so much as Bucherius’s other opinion: that after Saint Servatius those bishops were nowhere called bishops of Maastricht, but everywhere bishops of Tongeren [Note: [Col. 0980D] p. 48.].

This was what first called the standard-bearer of hagiographers, Godfrey Henschen, to arms. In 1653 he composed a discussion [Note: [Col. 0980D] *Diatriba de episcopis Tungrensibus*, Antwerp, 1653.] supported by very extensive learning, in which he vindicated the episcopal name for Maastricht. It was published again at Antwerp in 1688 [Note: [Col. 0980D] *Exegesis historica de episcopatu Tungrensi ac Trajectensi*, by Michael Cnobbaert.], and after Henschen’s death, in the same year, Papebrochius incorporated the author’s revised version into the *Acta Sanctorum* [Note: [Col. 0980D] *Acta Sanctorum*, May, vol. VII, p. XVIII.].

Since, besides others, Fisen [Note: [Col. 0980D] *Sancta Legia Romanae Ecclesiae filia, sive Historiarum Ecclesiae Leodiensis partes duae*, Liège, 1696, fol.] and Foullon [Note: [Col. 0980D] *Vindiciae Ecclesiae Tungrensis*, Liège, 1653, and *Historia Leodiensis per episcoporum et principum seriem digesta*, fol., 2 vols.]—historians of Liège—had taken Bucherius’s side [Col. 0981A], while others defended Henschen’s opinion [Note: [Col. 0981B] Laurentius Ludovici, Michael Seneschal, and Jacobus Platel, professors of theology at the university of Douai, delivered an opinion on the same question and sent it to Henschenius bearing their signatures. See *Exegesis historica*, chapter 26 [Col. 0981C].], a singular literary contest was finally joined by Baron de Crassier, then counsellor to the prince-bishop of Liège, who attacked Henschen in 1738 [Note: [Col. 0981C] *Brevis elucidatio quaestionis Jesuiticae*—so called, without doubt, because nearly all the disputants belonged to the Jesuit order—“concerning the alleged bishopric of Maastricht on the Meuse.”], and Peter Dolmans of the Society of Jesus [Note: [Col. 0981C] *Observationes apologeticae pro episcopatu Trajectensi ad Mosam*, Antwerp, 1741. Crassier opposed another book to it, *Additamentum ad brevem elucidationem*; Dolmans replied in a pamphlet, *Observationes alterae pro episcopatu Trajectensi ad Mosam*, 1742.]. Bertholet joined them in 1743 [Note: [Col. 0981C] “Dissertation on the alleged bishopric of Maastricht,” in *Histoire de Luxembourg* VI, 313.], and de Marne in 1754 [Note: [Col. 0981C] “Dissertation on the episcopal see of Maastricht,” in *Histoire du comté de Namur* II, 534.]. Joseph Ghesquier summoned the opinions once more for examination in 1783 [Note: [Col. 0981C] *Acta sanctorum Belgii selecta*, Brussels, 1783, quarto; he arranged for those books to be partly reprinted, vol. I, pp. 221 ff. See also *Essais historiques sur le département de la Meuse inférieure*, p. 184, 1803 [Col. 0981D].].

Thus the war could not be brought to an end in a single century. I have no intention here, either in the text or in the notes, of proving or refuting matters which those writers have certainly repeated six hundred times.

Heriger already clearly understood, as the tenth century was drawing to a close, how deeply the most ancient history of the Tongeren people lay buried in darkness [Col. 0981B], and he did not hesitate to state openly that there were three sufficiently obscure intervals in the succession of the bishops: after Saint Maternus, after Saint Servatius, and before Saint Amandus [Note: [Col. 0981D] I, 15, 26, 43; see above.]. This frank confession of ignorance can certainly never be refuted by us, living eight centuries later; and when other supports are lacking, we may not go beyond Heriger’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0981D] There was very little that Aegidius, writing three centuries after Heriger, could add concerning the bishops whose names alone Heriger transmitted; he has almost nothing except barren eulogies. The first, unless I am mistaken, to set later writers upon the path of superstition was John of Warnans, whom we shall discuss shortly. He was a fourteenth-century continuator of Heriger and Anselm. Bucherius read his manuscript at the indicated place, p. 19, and copied the following about him: “In his account of Valentine, the ninth bishop of Tongeren, he writes that he knows Heriger did not record the years of the first eight bishops who succeeded Saint Maternus, because all their deeds perished in the persecutions of the Huns. Yet John himself thinks otherwise, believing that peace always reigned tranquilly at Tongeren while the other churches of Gaul were shaken by storms of persecution; indeed, he says, religion flourished there so greatly that seventy-two congregations arose there, as we believe, of religious communities and orders, or of churches. Hence it is not true that all the deeds of the earlier bishops perished” [Col. 0982B–C].].

Whoever wishes to subject their arguments to critical scrutiny should consult the discussions of the learned men themselves. It is useful to repeat here one point which Henschen and Dolmans correctly observed: even at that time the bishops of Liège were called bishops of Tongeren in public documents, although the see had already been fixed at Liège for three centuries [Col. 0982A] [Note: [Col. 0982C] Walcand is called bishop of Tongeren in a charter of Louis the Pious from 831, in Chapeaville I, 154. Franco is called bishop of the church of Tongeren or Liège in a charter of Charles the Fat from 884, ibid. I, 161; and likewise in another charter of Zwentibold, ibid. I, 162: “bishop of the Church of Saint Lambert established at Liège,” 898. The possessions of the Church of Tongeren were confirmed by Louis in 908, ibid. I, 167. Stephen “venerable bishop of the Tongeren people” appears in letters of Charles the Simple from 915, ibid. I, 169. The see of Liège occurs in a privilege of Otto I from 949, ibid. I, 175; Bishop Notger of Liège appears under Otto II in 981, ibid. I, 209; Notger, bishop of the Tongeren people or of Liège, in 985 under Otto III, ibid. I, 215, and likewise in another privilege, I, 211; Notger, bishop of Liège, in 997, ibid. I, 210; Notger, bishop of Tongeren or Liège, in 1006 under Henry II, ibid. I, 212; Balderic, bishop of Liège, in two charters from 1008, ibid. I, 224–225; Durand, bishop of Liège, under Conrad II in 1021, ibid. I, 263; Nithard, bishop of Liège, under Henry III in 1040, ibid. I, 279. At the council of Toul, Franco signed as bishop of Tongeren; at Ingelheim, Farabert as bishop of Tongeren. Stephen, bishop of the Tongeren people, sent his *Life of Saint Lambert* to Herimann, archbishop of Cologne. Chapeaville I, 351. In 961 Everaclus calls himself bishop of the Church of Saint Lambert of Liège; Martène and Durand, *Amplissima Collectio* II, 47. But this too must be conceded to the opposing view: the name “bishops of Maastricht” occurs hundreds of times in the writers of that period [Col. 0982D].].

Let us now pass to the second part of the *Gesta*, appended to Heriger’s book seventy years later by Anselm. As an eyewitness whose account of events extends down to his own time, he seems deserving of no small gratitude. Yet there is something to be missed in both authors.

We rightly lamented that Heriger—whom many witnesses prove to have been extremely learned—did not produce a greater monument of his intellectual ability in composing works. We may equally justly regret that the life of Anselm, who left a work yielding great historical benefit, is supported by far fewer witnesses than one might wish.

Only a few things are recorded about him by others; concerning his own life he himself handed down some information to posterity, though not with a full hand. Our first testimony comes from an author contemporary with Anselm, in the *Life of Saint Theodoric of Andage*. If we listen to him, Anselm was noble by birth, but nobler in character and ecclesiastical devotion [Note: [Col. 0982D] Chapter 16. Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedicti* VI, 557.]. Elsewhere we read that when Theodoric was setting out for the Holy Land, he happened by chance to meet Bishop Theoduin of Liège at Rome, together with several of his friends, among them Anselm, a canon of Saint Lambert, already from childhood made especially intimate with him in friendship on account of his intellectual distinction and nobility of character [Note: [Col. 0982D] Chapter 15, at the indicated place.].

Anselm himself testifies that he was an unprofitable pupil of the Muses of Liège [Col. 0983A] [Note: [Col. 0983D] II, 74: “O nurse of a leader, in whose lap, among so many initiates of true philosophy, I alone grew up as an unprofitable little slave!”]. The work he left to posterity shows with extraordinary clarity that this was said more modestly than truthfully.

It is not sufficiently certain when he was born. I shall conjecture that he was born in the final years of Notger or shortly after Notger’s death, because Anselm confirms that he had seen several men who had been educated during that bishop’s time [Note: [Col. 0983D] II, 30.].

As is clear from another passage of the *Gesta* [Note: [Col. 0983D] Prologue to Book II. I have searched in vain for the years during which Ida held her office.], he was received from the sacred baptismal font by Ida, abbess of the monastery of Saint Cecilia among the people of Cologne. He was then admitted among the canons of Saint Lambert [Note: [Col. 0983D] The claim made by the above-mentioned writers on literary history that Anselm was dean of Namur is an invention which one accepted from another in good faith.], and first entered into Wazo’s close association and intimate friendship [Note: [Col. 0983D] II, 51, 52, 67, 68.]. He enjoyed no less the companionship of Wazo’s successor, Theoduin.

When he had accompanied Theoduin to Rome in 1053 [Note: [Col. 0983D] As we are told in the *Life of Saint Theodoric*, at the indicated place, Hugh of Lobbes had died and Adelard had succeeded him; this occurred in 1053, as the Lobbes annals attest, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores IV, 20.], Anselm at Rome dissuaded Theodoric, then a monk of Lobbes and Anselm’s very dear friend, from a plan which that religious man had undertaken and which could not have been carried out without the greatest danger to his life: a journey to Jerusalem. Anselm brought him back with him to his homeland.

A few years later, in 1055, when Anselm himself had been raised to the dignity of dean and possessed the highest authority in administration, he arranged for this man, after the death of Abbot Adelard, to be placed in charge of the monastery of Saint Hubert at Andage [Note: [Col. 0983D] *Life of Saint Theodoric*, chapter 16. *History of Saint Hubert of Andage*, in Martène and Durand, *Amplissima Collectio* IV, 923 [Col. 0984D].].

In March of the following year, Anno was consecrated archbishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0984D] Lambert’s *Annals*, 1056.]. In that same year Anselm wrote to him the letter in which he dedicated to him the book on the deeds of the bishops of Liège.

The fact that the author did not complete that book before 1052 is established by the mention of the heretics who were sentenced to death at Goslar on the Nativity of the Lord in 1051 [Col. 0983C] [Note: [Col. 0984D] II, 64. Herman of Reichenau, *Chronicle*, 1051.].

The period in which the *Gesta* was committed to writing can therefore certainly be bounded by the years 1052 and 1056; but whether this took place before Anselm’s journey to Rome in 1053 or afterward cannot be determined conclusively from arguments drawn from the book itself.

Someone might conjecture that it was written before 1053, and that this very fact could prove it, since the book itself contains no mention of the Roman journey. No one, so far as I know, has transmitted to posterity the year in which Anselm died. There are, however, certain arguments which seem to persuade me that he died in the year 1056; whether others too will be willing to accept them will become clear from what follows [Col. 0983D].

[Col. 0984A] Having set forth the testimonies concerning the author’s life, I seem to have shown plainly that I have no hesitation in attributing the second part of the *Gesta* to Anselm.

To others, however, the question did not appear so free from doubt. For, by some strange fate, the origin of this book too was burdened by nearly the same obscurity as that of the author of the first part of the *Gesta*. There had been uncertainty whether the first part was written by Heriger or by Notger; after Martène and Durand, the question arose whether the second had Anselm or the canon Alexander as its author.

These scholars were the first to restore the genuine text of the book from their Andage manuscript. They showed that no one had yet seen the true Heriger and the true Anselm, and they brought that Alexander out of the shadows [Note: [Col. 0984D] Martène and Durand, *Amplissima Collectio* IV, 836: “While we were examining the library at Liège of the distinguished man, Lord Baron de Crassier, an ancient manuscript of the monastery of Saint Hubert at Andage, written more than six hundred years ago, fell into our hands. It contained the works of Heriger and Anselm. When we carefully compared it with that edition, we found it not only different in many respects but also much fuller. Moreover, we observed that Alexander of Liège, a canon of Saint Lambert, after extracting from Heriger’s work the deeds of the first bishops, committed to writing the acts of the subsequent bishops after Saint Remaclus, and so forth.”].

We must now see how the difficulty can be resolved [Col. 0984B]. It turns upon a single passage in the prologue to the second book, which the editors printed from their manuscript as follows:

> “From this point onward, what follows was annexed to this work by order of the elders of this place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1056, from the little book of another work, which one of the canons of Saint Lambert, named Alexander, composed at the prompting of the venerable Ida, abbess who governed the monastery of Saint Cecilia the Virgin in Cologne” [Note: [Col. 0984D] At the indicated place, p. 843. Chapeaville read “Anselm” instead of the name “Alexander.”].

Thus it was certainly not Anselm who is thought to have written these words; Alexander is the true author of the book, if one is willing to rely upon this single manuscript.

But that this opinion is not so firmly established that it cannot be overturned is proved by the manuscripts underlying our edition. It is true that in one of our three manuscripts—namely the most recent, the Hagen manuscript of the thirteenth century—the name Alexander is read. Yet little authority should be attributed to it; and, unless I am mistaken, it is the same manuscript which Martène and Durand themselves followed, as I shall attempt to prove in its proper place.

The other two manuscripts are very different. One of them, the Wolfenbüttel manuscript, was written in the eleventh century, not very long after Anselm. In neither manuscript is the name of either Anselm or Alexander expressed in writing. Here too, however, the author modestly wished his name to remain hidden, and in the passage just cited that canon of Saint Lambert is indicated only by the single letter A.

Nor did the author mention himself differently in the letter to Anno, but only in these words:

> “To Lord Anno ... A., the least of the priests,” and so forth.

A strong suspicion therefore arises. Since Alexander rests upon that one passage alone, perhaps some pedantic scribe who did not know the author’s true name introduced a false name into the text, indulging his own ingenuity [Col. 0984D–0985A]. This one argument would remove the difficulty, were it not that it seems to be increased and, as it were, to flare up again at another point.

The most certain traces are found in the book itself that two books concerning the deeds of the bishops of Liège were written after Heriger, and learned men have been pleased to attribute one to Anselm and the other to Alexander [Note: Martene and Durand IV, 838; *Histoire littéraire de la France* VII, 472 ff.]. For that A. the priest, whom we heard above confessing that he had drawn one part of the book from Alexander’s work, expressly attests the following in his letter to Anno:

“Of these, the first part was written by Heriger, abbot of the monastery of Lobbes, without chapters; and, prefacing chapters to it, we have endeavored to join our little work, composed with its own chapters, to his. And since that earlier *Gesta* had arranged the deeds of those same bishops from the first to the twenty-seventh—that is, from Saint Maternus to Saint Remaclus—we too, cutting off the beginning of our work, which we had written at the request of the lady abbess Ida, so as not to weary the reader by repeating the same material, began with Blessed Theodard and continued the order of the bishops up to Lord Wazo, who is known to have been the fifty-second. We have included nothing except what we either read, learned from the reliable report of trustworthy persons, or ourselves saw and heard while present.”

Thus A. the priest himself also wrote the earliest history of the people of Liège, but suppressed the first part of his book in favor of Heriger. To these two writers, in the preface placed before Book II of the *Gesta*, a third is added—Alexander—if one follows the Hague manuscript and Martene. From that preface it is useful to add the following words from the passage quoted above:

“And he is not ashamed to confess that he compiled the first part of that same little work from the present *Gesta* of the twenty-seven bishops”—that is, Heriger’s, which there above are called the “first volume of the *Gesta*”—“speaking in this way.”

There follows a passage from the preface addressed to the same abbess Ida, in these words [Note: Ida’s name does not occur in this fragment of the preface; nevertheless, no one will doubt that she is the bride of Christ to whom the letter was written, and this is confirmed in explicit words in the earlier part of the prologue.]:

“From the *Gesta* of the bishops of Tongeren, which extend from Saint Maternus to Saint Remaclus, it pleased us to weave, as though plucked from the pleasant abundance of a flower-bearing meadow, a garland from various flowers. Thereafter we endeavored to append what we had either read here and there concerning the later bishops or learned from the reliable report of the ancients; and, in a kind of abridgment, we have briefly touched upon the names of each, together with a few deeds of some of them, down to Lord Wazo.”

Thus it may appear that this one portion of the letter to the abbess Ida was rescued from the ravages of time from Alexander’s own book; the rest of the work, whoever that compiler A. may be, turned to his own use. For the compiler testified in these words that he had cut away the other part of the book, in which Alexander too had committed to writing, following Heriger, the deeds of the first twenty-seven bishops:

“Since these things are so, we too, not inappropriately removing the beginning of the same little work, so that we may preserve the order of the episcopal deeds with an unobstructed step, shall make a new beginning with the successor of Saint Remaclus, namely Blessed Theodard.”

From this it seems clear that the compiler preserved Alexander’s book for us intact, except for the removal of one beginning extending to Saint Theodard—a conclusion which, unless I am mistaken, is also confirmed by the words quoted above: “what follows, taken from the little book of the other work, has been appended to this work.”

But let us recall what that A. testified about his own time and authority in his letter to Anno. He handed down to posterity what he had heard and seen in person concerning Wazo. Can we believe that a man who had taken part in the actual conduct of affairs, either as an eyewitness or as a servant and assistant, when writing about those same matters contributed nothing of his own, but copied another man’s book word for word? Can we believe that, promising one thing and actually presenting another, he lied disgracefully? And what are we to conclude about that other author [Note: The editors Martene and Durand attempted, without much success, to unravel these complications; nor can the difficulty really be explained if they rely upon the single Hague manuscript. At first they proposed the view that, after Wazo’s death in 1048, Alexander immediately applied his hand to writing the deeds of the bishops of Liège; then, when Alexander was taken from the living shortly afterward, Anselm offered Alexander’s abridged work to Anno, archbishop of Cologne, in 1056. Shortly afterward they thought they could take this course: in the Hague manuscript and in Chapeaville’s recension, both Anselm’s and Alexander’s books had been presented with Anselm’s preface, but it could not be sufficiently determined which text was Anselm’s and which Alexander’s.
