Seeing that this could not stand, the authors of *Histoire littéraire de la France* VII, 475 conjectured that, because Alexander’s little book had displeased the men of that place, Anselm had undertaken the same work at their command. Cellier adopted Martene’s opinion. I scarcely need point out that Chapeaville’s recension, which the authors of *Histoire littéraire de la France* rightly recognized as nothing other than an epitome of Martene’s text, must be entirely excluded from this question.]?

Alexander no less clearly shows in his preface to Ida that he had seen the face of the bishop Wazo and had enjoyed his company, and he sufficiently plainly indicates that what he wrote about Wazo flowed from that source, since he wished to hand down his image to posterity. Thus there are two authors who, living at the same time, carried the history of the bishops of Liège down to Wazo. Each, in the earlier part, wrote what he had read or learned from the reliable report of the ancients; in the later part, what he himself had seen. Each appended his own work to Heriger’s book. Nevertheless, each also committed to writing again the period covered by Heriger; but later this part of the book was suppressed. Finally, each composed his book at the urging of the same abbess Ida and dedicated it to her.

Alexander sent Ida a genuinely original work, actually composed by himself; shamelessly, indeed, the other man also wished his own book, in which he had compiled Alexander’s, to be regarded as dedicated to her. Nor did he rest there: he tried to deceive Archbishop Anno by the same falsehood, and he was so shameless—or, if you prefer, so demented—that in the preface to the second book he freely confessed that he had borrowed from another what he had solemnly affirmed in his letter to Anno to be his own.

For what, after such a proud and magnificent preface concerning his work, did that A. finally attempt to send to his metropolitan? The first book of the *Gesta* was composed by Heriger, the second by Alexander, and the latter half of the preface to Book II likewise belongs to Alexander. If each of these two claimed what was his own, nothing would remain to the priest A. except that lying letter to Anno, the first half of the preface to Book II, and the chapter headings—miserable scraps, as it were, of those fictitious riches, with which scarcely anyone could believe that he had behaved so arrogantly.

When I consider all these things—so contradictory and scarcely reconcilable with one another—I cannot persuade myself otherwise than to conclude that Alexander is one person and that priest A. who wrote to Anno another. Yet if we adopt that conclusion, then, in view of what we have said above about our manuscripts, no one will easily persuade us that the author’s name was Alexander.

That Anselm alone wrote the *Gesta of the Bishops of Liège* is expressly established by Sigebertus [Note: *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chap. 163: “Anselm, a cleric of Liège, wrote the deeds of the bishops of Liège, and in that book he fully described the life of Bishop Wazo, which was truly known to him.”], by Aegidius of the Golden Valley in 1251 [Note: In his letter to Maurice, canon of the Hague, Chapeaville II, 1: “Imitating the zeal of the venerable fathers Heriger, abbot of Lobbes, and Anselm, a religious man, who successively, one after the other, faithfully though briefly described the earlier parts down to their own times.”], by John of Stavelot [Note: Cod. Hamburg. Hist. Germ. f., knowledge of which the distinguished scholar Waitz shared with me. These are John of Stavelot’s words: “The first writer was Heriger, abbot of Lobbes. Beginning his part with Blessed Maternus, the first bishop of Tongeren, he continued the order of the bishops from that point through the twenty-seventh, of whom Blessed Remaclus was the last; thus that saint is said to be the boundary of the book of Abbot Heriger. Afterwards the priest Anselm wrote; beginning his book with Blessed Theodard, who became bishop after Remaclus, he continued the bishops in due order and ended with the twenty-fifth bishop, who was called Wazo.”] c. 1450, and by others [Note: John of Liège, Placentius, Brusthemius, continuators of Liège history. See Chapeaville’s preface.] in explicit words; concerning the other, not a word. Let that ill-omened Alexander, then, finally depart—the man who introduced such confusion into literary history.

With the twofold authorship now removed, a new question arises: how could a double book concerning the same events, the *Gesta* of the bishops of Liège, have been written by one and the same person? For those two books concerning the bishops of Liège written after Heriger remain even so, and cannot be eliminated. One of them—the book we have before our eyes—was composed in its entirety from Heriger’s little book and Anselm’s own work, and Anselm sent it to Archbishop Anno. The other little book he sent to the abbess Ida; in its first part he continued, in his own style, only the most important excerpts from Heriger, as the letters themselves show.

Thus the books differ in their first part; no one can deny that the second part, carried down to Wazo’s death, was the same in both. Anselm therefore published two versions of his book: one complete and unaltered, as it were the body of Liège history, which he dedicated to Anno the metropolitan; and another abridged version, which he sent to the abbess Ida in order to satisfy her exhortations [Note: Chapeaville had already proposed a similar view a hundred years earlier, before Alexander was discovered under an ill omen, in the preface to volume I, p. 3, in these words: “Accordingly, the words quoted above from the preface to Anselm’s book mean nothing other than that Anselm took these deeds of the bishops from the book that he himself had written concerning the deeds of all the bishops down to his own time, cutting off the deeds of the first twenty-seven bishops and the preface to Ida, and appended it to Heriger’s book, which already contained the previously written deeds of the first twenty-seven bishops.”].

Ida had requested two things from him: that he write something about Saint Ebergisus, bishop of Tongeren, whose ashes had been preserved in that very monastery since the time of Saint Bruno, and likewise about Wazo, his illustrious contemporary, whose great reputation had reached her [Note: See the prefaces to Books I and II.].

It might seem sufficiently clear which of those editions we possess; yet it appears that we possess neither. Rather, our little book has been rather awkwardly composed from the two. For what that fragment of the preface addressed to Ida is doing in the book that the author sent to Anno, I certainly cannot see. Nor do I understand why Anselm would have placed at the beginning of Book II the same preface which, as the very words prove, he ought to have published at the front of the entire work. I can scarcely persuade myself that, having prepared two editions, the author himself so thoughtlessly confused them into one.

A further doubt is raised by the fact that in the preface to Book II the author says that a certain canon of Saint Lambert composed that little work, although Anselm did not hesitate either in his letter to Anno or in the *Gesta* themselves to speak of himself and his affairs under his own name [Note: See the passages which we shall cite below. Chapeaville conjectured in the preface to volume I that Anselm spoke under another’s name in the prologue to Book II out of modesty.].

Finally, what is read in the same place—that the second part of the *Gesta* was appended to the first at the command of the leading men of that place, that is, of Liège—cannot be reconciled with Anselm’s own words. For he sent the book to Anno of his own accord, so that Anno might draw examples of good living from it and be further inflamed to virtue; the other book he composed after being urged by Ida.

I see only one possible way of explaining this difficulty. The preface to Book II, except for the fragment of the letter to Ida, was written by some unknown compiler. Anselm, however, was prevented by some adverse fate from completing the *Gesta* himself in every respect and joining the later part to the earlier with a suitable transition. This is sufficiently proved, unless I am mistaken, by the text of that preface itself. For if you examine it somewhat more carefully, you will find that it is frequently copied in the very words of Anselm’s letter to Anno [Note: Compare the following passages taken from the preface to Book II: “the earlier … successors”; “thereafter, what … has been appended”; “since these things are so … the order,” with the corresponding passage in the letter to Anno: “and since that earlier … we heard”; and “the place rests … affirm,” with “what also, apart from … the tomb.”].

Nor is it clear why this author briefly repeated here what he had stated more plainly and fully at the beginning of the entire work. Anselm had therefore prepared the first edition for Ida, as the letter to Anno proves; while preparing the second, perhaps overtaken by death, he left his book to someone else, who, omitting the first part, composed it together with Heriger’s little book in a single volume. And for that reason it cannot be believed that the author really sent his work to Anno. No one will say that the anonymous compiler, who confused and disturbed everything by his interpolation, performed his task successfully.

In Anselm’s book one does not find the more abundant learning that was present in Heriger; nevertheless, he undertook the work equipped with by no means contemptible resources both for recording events and for scholarship. For writing about earlier times, he called upon the Lives of the Saints as aids: Theodard’s [Note: II, 2.], Hubert’s [Note: II, 16.], and Lambert’s, composed by Godescalc and Stephen [Note: II, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 20. See the acute discussion by the distinguished Hirsch, in his commentary on Sigebertus, p. 288, concerning the various recensions of the Life of Saint Lambert composed by Godescalc. Anselm appears to have had before him a text corresponding to Mabillon’s edition.]; Ruotger’s Life of Saint Bruno [Note: II, 24.]; and the Life of Bishop Balderic by an anonymous monk of Saint James of Liège [Note: II, 31.]. From works of wider scope he added Regino’s *Chronicle* [Note: II, 8, 19.] and Fulcuin’s *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes* [Note: II, 19–22.], as well as a passage taken from some writer unknown to me concerning Saint Lambert [Note: II, 8. Neither Mabillon nor Suyskens, *Acta Sanctorum*, September V, 541, nor anyone else has investigated where this was taken from; I confess that I have not been more successful.].

Yet in assembling his material he did not, following the customary practice of writers of those times, submit himself to the servitude of copying. With very few exceptions, he followed a freer method and tried to adapt the events to the purpose of his book. Nevertheless, he preserved in full other testimonies of great value, which he introduced into the text intact from the archives of Liège. These include Wazo’s letters, which even today, in their native form, move the reader’s mind: to John the provost [Note: II, 38.], to Robert, king of France [Note: II, 58.], and to Roger, bishop of Châlons [Note: II, 60. II, 62 also appears to have been taken from Wazo’s letter to the emperor Henry.]. To these are added letters of that same Roger and a charter of Richarius, bishop of Liège [Note: II, 59, 21.].

Of the greatest importance, however, are the matters which he either saw himself as an eyewitness or heard at Wazo’s court, for nearly half of the book that he wrote about Wazo is built, as it were, upon this foundation. In 1041 he was present as a witness at Wazo’s solemn inauguration [Note: II, 51: “Unless I had seen it myself, I would in no way have believed it,” etc.]; he saw the bishop bestow twenty-five prebends in a single day [Note: II, 67: “We saw them given by him,” etc.]; and when Wazo undertook to construct a house, Anselm was assisted by money supplied by him [Note: II, 68: “This I myself experienced,” etc.].

Many passages testify that he drew no little material from conversations with Wazo [Note: II, 24: “As I heard Wazo relate,” etc.; II, 52: “as he himself admitted”; II, 68: “Wretched man that I am … he would deign to address me,” etc.]. Whether he also stood beside the dying bishop, I hesitate to say. In other matters he followed other witnesses, among them Poppo, abbot of Stavelot and a friend of Wazo [Note: II, 48: “As Abbot Poppo regularly used to testify,” etc.], and clerics who were connected with him through daily association [Note: II, 48, 57: “Through his deacon, who had learned the same thing from his mouth,” etc.; II, 71: “The priests and chaplains who assisted him testified,” etc.]. Indeed, he did not reject the testimony of opponents [Note: II, 56: “They themselves still commonly testify,” etc.], and he no less gladly praised matters that, being exposed before everyone’s eyes, were known to all [Note: II, 25: “As it is at the present time”; II, 38: “It is permitted to see among us”; II, 46: “Almost all who have known Liège are witnesses”; II, 53: “It is still possible to see the traces.”].

From these sources he acquired such a wealth of narrative material that he testifies in more than one place that he omitted many things worthy of mention, lest he exceed the limits of the abridgment he had promised [Note: II, 53: “While reporting a few things, I pass over more, some of which I am aware that I neglect for the sake of brevity”; II, 61: “Desiring brevity, I feared that I might succumb to the abundance of material, and I passed over many things that ought to be said”; II, 68: “If we wished to enumerate these things one by one, it would no longer be an abridgment, as we promised, but …” Compare the preface to Book II and II, 69: “Passing over many things both said and done,” etc.].

Nor, in writing the history of earlier times, did he disdain to draw from the memories of the living and from common report whatever he judged not foreign to his purpose. Concerning the miracles of Saint Lambert, he calls Bishop Thietwin and the clerics who affirmed that they had seen them as witnesses [Note: II, 6–10, 13, 14.]. He himself saw other miracles of Saint Lambert and Wolbodo [Note: II, 14: “We saw him first contracted and then standing upright”; II, 33: “I have experienced this both personally and through others.”]; and in the latter’s Life he owes part of his narrative to a servant or friend of the bishop [Note: II, 33.].

Nor are witnesses to his learning lacking—those lights drawn from the writings of the ancients, with which he filled his book, though not as generously as Heriger. He inserted sayings of Sallust [Note: II, 61.], Virgil [Note: II, 24, 37, 39, 59, 61, 73.], and Horace [Note: II, 26, 52.], and cited Cicero, Donatus, and Priscian by name [Note: II, 52.]. Among the Fathers of the Church, he read the works of Sulpicius Severus [Note: The Life of Saint Martin, II, 55, 64.] and Gregory the Great [Note: II, 50.] and adapted their words for his own use.

Finally, if one asks how Anselm performed the task of recording events, one will scarcely deny that he handled everything with sound judgment and completed the work with the discernment that appears in distinguishing truth from falsehood. For he indulged less than the spirit of his age in the superstitious celebration of miracles; the stories he tells are of a simpler kind and do not conflict with the nature of things [Note: II, 11–14.]. Nor will you fail to find evidence of critical judgment. In his letter to Anno he tries to prove that Evergisilus and Ebergisus were not one and the same person; and he thinks he has discovered why the writers of Saint Lambert’s life passed over the true cause of his passion in silence [Note: II, 8.].

He takes care not to report uncertain matters as certain [Note: II, 20, 64: “When we investigated carefully, we could learn no other cause.”], and he shows particular caution in avoiding the narration of miracles not yet approved by common report [Note: II, 35: “We have avoided inserting these things into this little work … because we avoid judging accounts of miracles that have not yet become generally known, but leave them to be faithfully written for posterity.”]. He does not hesitate frankly to indicate matters that he has not sufficiently investigated [Note: II, 53: “Some things unknown to me must necessarily be left unspoken”; II, 60: “By whom or from whom the letters were sent is not sufficiently known to us.”].

The character of those times is most clearly visible in the way he portrayed Wazo, whom alone—and not undeservedly—he undertook to celebrate in his little book and to place before the eyes of posterity. Wazo is the model and, as it were, the standard of those bishops of whom quite a few occupied sees in the time of Pope Gregory VII: men radiant with the devotion of a holy life, who strove with all the fervor of their souls to free the Church from the power of emperors and entrust its government to the one supreme pontiff.

Anselm celebrates Wazo as a man of this kind, and dedicated his book to Anno, the leader of all those men. He therefore censured even more sharply those bishops and clerics who, casting off the yoke of monastic discipline and involving themselves in the affairs of kings, cared for the concerns of the world and, after stripping their own churches, maintained mimes and other palace dogs [Note: II, 28, 34.]. Anselm’s attitude is no less evident in what he wrote about the conflict between Wazo and the emperor [Note: II, 57, 60.].

Finally, the style of expression he used is neither pure nor polished; indeed, you will not deny that more serious faults also occur. Yet no one will demand purity of language from a writer of those times or judge it by a stricter standard. Compared with Heriger’s, his manner of writing is clearer and more transparent, neither so ponderous nor so covered with the learned obscurity which we saw Heriger pursue. Even so, it is often inflated and affected, and bolder than it is accurate; by these very faults Anselm sufficiently shows that he was trained in the Liège tradition.

Not many writers of the more recent period employed our authors in composing their own books. Most of them appear to have been Liège writers, as is evident from the book’s limited scope. Notger used Heriger in the Life of Saint Hadelin [Note: See above.]; so did the *Gesta of Trier* [Note: C. 16. The genuine text has been copied, not the mutilated type of manuscript C which we found in Aegidius. I have no doubt that the names of those eight bishops who, according to I, 15, are said to have succeeded Saint Maternus and to have presided over the Churches of Tongeren and Trier in both the catalogues and the *Gesta of Trier*, were copied into the Trier books at a later time, so to speak, out of horror of a blank. For it is clearer than daylight from Heriger’s own narrative that it never occurred to him that those bishops had been prelates of the two Churches; Aegidius, in the middle of the thirteenth century, thought that this could not be passed over in silence. I see that Henschenius in *Exegesis* no. 6, Calmet in *Histoire de Lorraine* I, VII, Hontheim, Marne in his dissertation p. 503, and Perier in *Disquisitio* no. 53 adopted nearly the same view.], the anonymous author of the Life of Saint Servatius [Note: See shortly below what we have said about the sources used for the edition.], and Nicholas in the Life of Saint Lambert [Note: C. 16, Chapeaville I, 399.].

Sigebertus used Anselm in his *Chronicle* [Note: More rarely than one might expect; see the entries for the years 903, 960, and 972, *Monumenta Germaniae Scriptores* VI, 275.] and in the *Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux* [Note: What is read there about the deaths of Wazo and Olbert, Dachery II, 767. Hirsch demonstrated this by an exact collation, *On Sigebertus*, p. 263; he also showed that Sigebertus had before him both the complete text of the *Gesta* and the abridged version.]. Rupert used him in the *History of Saint Lawrence of Liège* [Note: In the Lives of Euraclius 1, 2, 5; Notger 7; Balderic 1; Wolbodo 2, 3, 4, 8; Wazo 14, in Martene and Durand, *Amplissima Collectio* IV, 1033. There can be no doubt that Rupert read both texts of the *Gesta*—or, what I find more plausible, a less mutilated manuscript of type B. This is proved by chapter 7 of Notger and chapter 3 of Wolbodo, which sometimes agree word for word with the genuine text at II, 26 and 33; whereas in chapter 2 of Euraclius there are traces of the abridged text, for example:

Rupert: “At midday, an eclipse of the sun suddenly occurred.”

Abridged text: “Suddenly the eclipse, the darkening of the sun … scarcely an hour after midday had passed.”

Complete text: “A sudden darkness struck the sun … while much of the day still remained.”], Reinerus in the *Lives of the Bishops*—Euraclius [Note: C. 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, Pez, *Thesaurus anecdotorum novissimus* IV, 3, p. 155 ff. Reinerus appears to have had the complete text.], Reginard [Note: C. 1, 8, Pez, same work I, p. 267 ff.], and Wolbodo [Note: *Acta Sanctorum*, April II, 857 ff.]—and the anonymous author of the Life of Wolbodo [Note: See below.].

Both authors were adapted for their own purposes by Alberic of Trois-Fontaines in his *Chronicle* [Note: See the years 546, 577, 595, 617, 626, 647, 651, 994, 1014, and 1016. He copied the complete *Gesta*.] and by Aegidius of the Golden Valley [Note: Compare Hirsch, p. 424. The other continuators of Liège history—John Hocsemius, John Warnantius, John of Liège, John Brusthemius, and John Placentius—took not Heriger but Aegidius as their guide in writing the earliest history of Tongeren. Both a certain method of copying and Chapeaville, who saw their manuscripts, testify to this in his preface. The same testimony is given concerning Hocsemius, whose book he published only in part at II, 272: “Gathering from the books, monuments, and charters of the Church of Liège the matters that preceded his own time, he wrote them briefly.”

In John of Stavelot’s manuscript the following is written about John Warnantius: “John, invested with the church of Saint John of Warnans, wrote beginning with Henry, bishop of Gertruydenberg, who was made bishop after the aforementioned Robert, and ended his writing with Engelbert of Marck. After him a certain monk of Saint Lawrence, called John of Stavelot, wrote and continued the catalogue of the bishops of Liège in due order, as is clear from his writing.”

John of Warnans certainly did not omit the history of Tongeren, for Bucher, in Chapeaville’s appendix I, 19, testifies that he saw a manuscript of his written in 1378, in which the author admits that he interpolated the narratives of Heriger, Anselm, and Aegidius. Thus Hocsemius and John of Warnans wrote precisely the same events at the same time. Compare Villenfagne, *Mélanges*, etc., 1810, p. 290 ff., who conjectured that the two Johns who continued the work were the same person; but unless one examines the manuscripts, nothing certain can be established.

John of Stavelot, who died in 1449, also, if his epitomator may be trusted, went back to events beginning with Saint Maternus; see Andreae and Foppens, *Bibliotheca Belgica*, pp. 734, 753. The same was done by Brusthemius, who carried the history of Liège down to 1505; see Sanderus, *Bibliotheca Belgica manuscripta* I, 24; and by Placentius in Boxhorn’s little book *On the Liège Republic*, Amsterdam, 1633, p. 209. Compare also Villenfagne, same work.], who incorporated the abridged text of the *Gesta* into his history of Liège and inserted his own additions.

But now we must examine the manuscript basis on which our edition of Heriger and Anselm has been established. We have called upon two manuscripts for assistance which no one has hitherto used, and a third—the same one, unless I am mistaken, that Martene and Durand followed. The others have come to our attention in such a condition that their importance, which is certainly not great, can be discerned in restoring the text.

They must be arranged in the following order according to the nature of the manuscripts themselves. We have marked with the siglum A those manuscripts that preserve the complete and genuine text of Heriger, now published for the first time [Note: Passages restored or supplied by the German editor in Heriger’s text have been reprinted in the smallest type; we enclose the same passages in brackets. Editor of the *Patrologia*.], and of Anselm, presenting a narrative neither abridged nor disfigured by later interpolations. All the manuscripts contain both Heriger and Anselm, closely joined to one another in the eleventh century; but no manuscript has come to our attention that transmits the book of only one of them while omitting the other [Note: I do not know what conclusion should be drawn concerning the manuscript of the *Gesta* which Foppens, *Bibliotheca Belgica*, p. 471, says was preserved at Arras among the monks of Saint Vedast.]. Thus we do not possess a manuscript older than Anselm.

**A 1.** Codex Guelferbytanus, on parchment, eleventh century, in a small folio format, from which the Life of Bruno by Ruotger and the works of Alpert have already been published [Note: See what has been said about the same manuscript in *Archiv* VI, 6; VII, 439.]. On folios 49–63 it contains the books of Heriger and Anselm. They were written in two quires, with the final leaf and half of the preceding one left blank. The text is written in two columns; the lines are set down in a very narrow spacing. The letters are extremely small but elegantly and cleanly formed, written first in dark-brown ink and then in lighter brown, almost faded ink.

I judged that the orthography displayed by this, the oldest of our manuscripts, ought to be retained. The text is neither pure nor corrected; indeed, it is open to many faults arising from the negligence, or rather the ignorance, of the scribe, who in quite a few places scarcely understood what he was writing. At times, however, he preserved the true reading [Note: For example, at I, 21, instead of the corrupt word *quod*, manuscript A 1 correctly reads *Quadus*; at II, 11, instead of the inept *latam*, correctly *latera*; at II, 30, instead of *licet*, correctly *lucis*; at II, 41, instead of *celebratione*, correctly *celebri statione*; instead of *dedere*, *ledere*; at II, 51, instead of *maturam*, *inaratam*. But faults are not lacking: at II, 2, *occidi domesticorum* for *acciti*; II, 7, *persuasores* for *pervasores*; II, 15, *bellare rideat* for *bella derideat*; II, 33, *in pectoris* for *inspectoris*.], so that this manuscript can provide a remedy for the corruptions of the other manuscripts.

**A 2.** Codex Parisinus suppl. Lat. 812, on parchment, quarto, early twelfth century [Note: *Archiv* VIII, 309.] nine quires and four leaves, written on folios 46–122. Its variant readings were supplied by the distinguished Waitz. It is written in letters as elegant as they are clear. Very frequently the scribe used “oe” in place of *e*; for example, he writes *aequitare, aebrietas, caeleriter, aecclesiae, rabiae, progeniae, urbae*, etc.; likewise *aput, aliut, quit*, etc., and accents are frequent.

Nor is this text more correct; indeed, new and more serious corruptions are added, in some of which the scribe’s pen slipped. The scribe himself attempted to remove some errors, and a contemporary corrector attempted to remove others, though not always with a successful hand. It cannot be doubted that this manuscript flowed from the same source as A 1; many errors in which they agree, as well as the sounder readings preserved in A 2, prove this.

### A 3, 4

Of these, 3 is the Hagen codex A 23, on parchment, from the twelfth century, from the library of G. I. Gerard [Note: [Col. 0994D] *Archiv* VIII, 569. A fragment of a seventeenth-century copy of Anselm’s *Gesta*, taken from Wilthemius’s papers, is preserved at Brussels. *Archiv* VII, 36; VIII, 503.]; the other, 4, is the one followed by Martène and Durand in their edition.

A 3, consisting of 143 leaves, contains only the *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*. In many corruptions, as well as in the corrections that a contemporary hand added to A 2, it agrees with that codex so closely that one must necessarily believe A 3 to have been copied from A 2. This is confirmed even by the errors that the scribe added on his own account, having falsely read letters that were written less clearly here and there in A 2 [Note: [Col. 0995D] A 2 reads, I, 17, *ex Cain generatis* (“begotten from Cain”); A 3, *ex ea ingeneratis* (“engendered from her”). A 2, I, 19, falsely has *Alantis* for *Alani*; A 3, thinking the reading to be *Al esse M*, made it *Mantis*.]. The scribe removed a few of A 2’s errors and quite often slightly altered the arrangement of the words.

[Col. 0995A] The Andage codex supplies a pleasing remedy for almost all the corruptions of A 3; from it Martène and Durand published Anselm alone, passing over Heriger [Note: [Col. 0995D] *Amplissima Collectio* IV, 843: “As for Heriger’s work, although here and there we could present it in a more corrected form, the matter nevertheless did not seem important enough to us, since nearly all the deeds of the earliest bishops of Tongeren are sprinkled with fables,” etc.].

Yet these codices are closely connected with one another. In both the same arrangement of words recurs, and the same words have fallen out in both [Note: [Col. 0995D] For example, the following are missing in A 3 and 4: II, 2, *dicina ... tantum*; II, 5, *coelo*; II, 9, *Dei* in *Dei miracula*; II, 10, *sed ejus*; II, 14, *preme*; II, 23, *quatuor quadragesimus* (“the forty-fourth”); II, 26, *futuram*; II, 11, both codices read *in rabiem verso* (“turned into madness”), whereas A 1 and 2 have *converso* (“having been turned”); II, 12, *ignotumque* (“and unknown”), whereas A 1 and 2 have *ignotum est* (“it is unknown”); II, 15, *congregavit* (“he gathered”); II, 21, *struentes* (“building”); II, 24, *percutit* (“he strikes”); II, 26, *jubet, coeperit* (“he orders,” “he will have begun”); II, 27, 12, *congregati* (“gathered”); II, 30, *in se* (“into himself”); II, 33, *inspirante, inspectoris* (“inspiring,” “of the inspector”); II, 34, *crediderat* (“he had believed”). Nor is this the least significant evidence: the name Alexander is falsely written in both codices; see above on this point.].

These agreements, which it would scarcely be possible to explain in any other way, lead one to suppose that the Andage and Hagen codices are one and the same, and that Martène and Durand removed its errors by conjecture. They removed them so successfully, however, that no one will readily deny that their readings ought to be admitted into the text in quite a few places.

For the sake of brevity, the codices of this class are designated only by numbers, so that 4 indicates Martène’s reading. Since these codices present, if not a corrected, at least a genuine text, there is no reason why we should regret not having seen the remaining codices, in which the text has been both abridged and interpolated, as is sufficiently clear from the description and notes supplied by Chapeaville [Note: [Col. 0996D] In the preface to the *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren, Maastricht, and Liège* I.].

I have marked with B two codices whose text is abridged but not yet interpolated.

### B1

The Alne codex, which Chapeaville obtained on parchment from the abbot of the monastery of Alne, is today preserved in the library of the very learned Sir Thomas Phillipps of Middle Hill. In 1844, however, when Pertz was present, it could not be shown to him, hidden as it was among a very large collection of precious codices. [Col. 0995C]

### B2

The codex of the collegiate church of Saint Martin of Liège, extremely old and written on parchment, which Chapeaville owed to Raymond, a canon of Liège, is in every respect similar to the other codex [Note: [Col. 0996D] On this codex see Sanderus, *Bibliotheca Belgica manuscripta* I, 24, 26.].

As he testifies, both codices have in certain places a fuller and more elaborate diction; all the other copies that it was possible to see follow, in those places, a shorter wording more suited to historical narrative, while preserving in every respect and in all copies the same account of the events. From these words it is clear that Chapeaville did not deal at all with Heriger’s and Anselm’s genuine text. For it is even clearer from the various readings he cites that the text of the *Gesta* is mutilated in these codices as well.

They are certainly not of great importance. In chapters II, 15–18, however, Chapeaville proves by the following words that he followed only these codices [Note: [Col. 0996D] I, 128, note]: “In separating Anselm’s text from the additions of Giles of Orval, we have thus far used the codex of the Cross-bearers, which is mutilated here; for four chapters, 14–17, are missing from it (15–18). We restored them from the Alne and Saint Martin codices.”

Yet in both codices the end of chapter 15 and several other passages are missing [Note: [Col. 0996D] See the critical notes appended to the text; two lacunae are detected in chapter II, 15.]. Anyone who knows this will not be at all moved by the fact that Saint Martin’s is the codex that presents Heriger’s book under the name of Notker.

[Col. 0996B]

### C

The third class contains only one codex, which later continuators read more than the others and adapted for their own use: the codex of the convent of the Cross-bearers of Liège. According to Chapeaville, it has a text conforming to Giles’s text but without Giles’s additions.

It is a paper codex of the sixteenth century, entitled *The Book of the Brothers of the Holy Cross at Liège*, which the very learned Bethmann saw at Liège [Note: [Col. 0996D] *Archiv* VII, 439; VIII, 478.]. Copies of the same kind seem to be preserved by the distinguished Th. Phillipps [Note: [Col. 0996D] Nos. 435 and 1130; *Archiv* VII, 96, 97. Codices of this kind, much older, are attested by Sigebert and Rupert.].

The text found in this codex is very different from, and much more abridged than, that in B. The above-mentioned chapters II, 15–18 are entirely absent. That the text has been abridged and falsified is proved both by Giles’s text and by the readings of codex C that occur here and there in Chapeaville.

The same errors and lacunae recur for the most part in the codices of the fourth class, which unquestionably derives from this one [Note: [Col. 0996D] I, 38, *vita* (“life”) is missing in C, and the word is likewise absent in the codices of class D; II, 53, C reads *conculcandum* for *inculcandum*, and class D has the same reading; II, 55, in both classes, *nominibus daemoniosis* occurs instead of *nominibus portentuosis*.].

### D

The codices of class D are abridged and interpolated, and were continued by later writers.

### D1

The Aurea Vallis codex presents an abridged text of Heriger and Anselm, interpolated by Giles. Chapeaville conjectured that it was Giles’s autograph. He therefore requested this codex from the monastery of Saint-Hubert in the Ardennes and used it as the foundation of his edition, though hardly with good judgment.

### D1*

The codex of the convent of the Capuchins of Liège must be joined with this one; Chapeaville asserts that it corresponds to D1 word for word.

[Col. 0997A]

### D2

The parchment codex that he owed to the nobleman Théodore de Groesbeek presents a mutilated text of Heriger and Anselm, interpolated by Giles, together with the continuation of John of Hocsem, canon and scholastic of Liège. Hocsem began writing at the beginning of 1334 and laid down his pen under Engelbert of Marcka, bishop of Liège, in 1348 [Note: [Col. 0997D] Chapeaville II, 272, 274.].

### D3

Finally, the Tongeren codex must be placed last. Chapeaville received it from Willem Herkenroede, prior of the canons of Tongeren; in it Radulf of Rivo, dean of the Church of Tongeren, added his own continuation, extending to the year 1389, to the continuations of Giles and Hocsem [Note: [Col. 0997D] Chapeaville III, from the beginning. Sanderus records two codices of Radulf of Rivo, one from Alne and the other from Leuven, *Bibliotheca Belgica manuscripta* I, 27.]. To this may perhaps be added:

### D4

The Hamburg Codex, Historical German Folio 31b, from the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth centuries [Note: [Col. 0997D] *Archiv* VI, 240.], by John of Stavelot, which must be presumed likewise to have received the Giles-like text of Heriger and Anselm.

Other aids are added to these codices, supplying quite a few corrections to the *Lives* of certain bishops. Among them the first place belongs to:

### 1

Liège codex 260, collated by the distinguished Bethmann. In this codex is found the *Life of Saint Servatius*, which, apart from its final lines, is nothing other than Heriger’s text, chapters 22–28. It is greatly to be regretted that this codex of Heriger has perished, since this *Life of Saint Servatius* derived from it.

The codex, being neither mutilated nor interpolated, is to be assigned to class A; yet it is another codex of the same family. Its sound readings prove this wherever A 1, 2, and 3 contain corrupt errors [Note: [Col. 0997D] It is useful to give a few examples. I, 22: A 1, 2, and 3 perversely read *salutem* (“salvation”); the *Life of Servatius* correctly has *saltem* (“at least”). I, 23: A 1, 2, and 3 have *genu inculcantes* (“pressing the knee”); the *Life of Servatius* has *incurvantes* (“bowing”). I, 24: A 1, 2, and 3 falsely have *per nanus*; the *Life of Servatius* correctly reads *perimmanis* (“enormous”). I, 25: A 1, 2, and 3 falsely have *irriguit*; the *Life of Servatius* correctly has *irrugiit*. In the same place A 1, 2, and 3 falsely read *invenire*; the *Life of Servatius* has *invenires*. A 1, 2, and 3 falsely have *ingeminantius*; the *Life of Servatius* correctly reads *ingeminantium*.].

### 2

To a similar class of codices must be assigned the one in which only the *Life of Saint Remaclus*, together with the letter to Werinfrid, was read, and which Surius used as his authority in his edition of the *Life of Saint Remaclus*. It has neither an abridged nor an interpolated text, and we owe quite a few corrections to it. But I neither know which codex Surius followed nor have I seen the codices that came to my attention.

As far as I know, there are four. The oldest seems to be the Bern parchment codex of the tenth century [Note: [Col. 0997D] *Archiv* V, 483.]. Chapeaville saw the very ancient Stavelot parchment codex. The Trier parchment codex of the eleventh century is entitled *The Life of Saint Remaclus by Notker* [Note: [Col. 0997D] *Archiv* VIII, 608.]. The Saint Gall parchment codex of the eleventh century, quarto, likewise bears this title: *The Life of Saint Remaclus by Notker of Liège, priest at Saint Lambert* [Note: [Col. 0998D] *Archiv* IV, 334.].

### 3

The *Life of Wolbodon* published in the *Acta Sanctorum* is, unless I am mistaken, of nearly the same character. The chapters of Anselm 30–36 concerning Wolbodon, bishop, were taken from the genuine text. Although it is close to codices A 1 and 2, it nevertheless preserves some better readings [Note: [Col. 0998D] II, 32: A 1, 2, 3, and 4 falsely read *vitae* (“of life”); the *Eulogy of Wolbodon* correctly has *viae* (“of the way”). II, 33: A 1, 2, and 3 falsely have *prioris* (“of the former”); the *Eulogy of Wolbodon* correctly reads *pejoris* (“of the worse”). II, 35: A 2, 3, and 4 falsely have *licet* (“although”); the *Eulogy of Wolbodon* has *lucis* (“of light”).].

### 4

A codex of another character is the one whose fragments Henschen published in the *Acta Sanctorum* with the *Life of Saint Servatius*, Heriger, chapters 20–25, according to the collation made by Rosweyde, his colleague [Note: [Col. 0998D] Preface, chapter 3: “These acts of Servatius, after omitting the interpolations of Giles of Orval, we wish to present here verbatim, according to the correction and emendation made by our Rosweyde’s own hand on the authority of an ancient copy.”].

If these fragments are examined more carefully, one will scarcely doubt that the codex belongs to class C, since, except in one or two places, it agrees with Chapeaville’s text. Thus no help at all is to be sought from it.

Finally, there are aids of a third kind, which we have drawn from the sources of Heriger’s text or from copies of those sources in order to restore the text; these likewise provide remedies for corruption. Among them are chiefly the following:

1. We consulted the *Life of the Saints Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus* in Heriger’s chapters 8–14.

2. Here and there we also called upon the *Life of Saint Landoald*, written by Heriger himself, and Notker’s *Life of Saint Hadelin* [Note: [Col. 0998D] See above concerning these works.].

Only a few things need be said about the editions of Heriger and Anselm. They first appeared in print as the *Chronicles* in the book of John Chapeaville, canon and vicar of Liège, *The Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren, Maastricht, and Liège*, Liège, 1612, quarto, pp. 1–98 and 99–318 [Col. 0998C]. The same book, scarcely corrected or altered, was published again at Liège in 1618 as a new edition, with only the opening leaf newly printed [Note: [Col. 0998D] *Histoire littéraire de la France* VII, 198.].

From what we have said above about the codices, and what becomes apparent to anyone who reads them, it is sufficiently clear how unsuccessfully Chapeaville attempted to exercise criticism: he took an interpolated codex as his guide. Everything is thrown into confusion, and there is nothing on which one can rest. This is the only edition of Heriger.

Anselm’s genuine text was later published by Martène and Durand in volume IV of their *Amplissima Collectio of Monuments*, pp. 843–911, from the Andage codex. Surius published the individual *Life of Saint Remaclus* in *Acta Sanctorum* V, 17; fragments of the same *Life* are found in Duchesne I, 642, and Bouquet III, 544–547. Individual *Lives* drawn from Heriger are found in the *Acta Sanctorum*: the *Lives of Saints Servatius, Amandus, Monulphus,* and *Remaclus*, on 13 May, 6 February, and 16 July [Col. 0999A].

Finally, in the fragments of Anselm found in Bouquet’s continuing *Collection*, volume XI, pp. 9–12, the editors followed Martène [Note: [Col. 0999D] There is scarcely any need to repeat what Papebrochius clearly recognized already in 1688 in the *Paralipomena* to the *Conatus chronico-historicus de catalogis pontificum Romanorum*, *Acta Sanctorum*, May VII, 65: namely, that the passage which some ignorant person attempted to force upon Heriger in the *Life of Saint Gundulf*, as though it were a fragment preserved from the wreck of a letter, is merely the fabrication of a forger.

When, at that time, a dispute had broken out between Hadrianus Jordanus and others concerning the genealogy of Saint Arnulf of Metz, the fragment attributed to Heriger emerged from its darkness. Its entire purpose is to prove that Saint Arnulf was the son of Duke Bodegisil. To make this credible, the shameless forger invented the following story, which I shall reproduce in Papebrochius’s own words [Col. 1000D]:

“How these things were inserted by Chapeaville into the history of the bishops of Tongeren, Maastricht, and Liège, and later removed not only from the printed copies but also from the original parchment codex of the Church of Liège; and by what route I came to possess a copy of that parchment, thus removed and still preserved at Dijon, there is no need to explain at greater length.”

Papebrochius rightly saw that Heriger’s actual text contradicted this spurious offspring, and all our codices make the fraud abundantly clear.].

Finally, in establishing the chronology of the most ancient periods, I considered it safest, amid such great obscurity, to follow the Bollandists [Col. 1000A]. In Anselm, after the imperial privileges and public records, the *Annals of Lobbes* and the *Annals of Liège* served as reliable guides.

I was writing in Berlin in July 1845.

**RUDOLPHUS KOEPKE**

[Col. 0999]

# Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren, Maastricht, and Liège

## Preface

[Col. 0999A]

To Lord Anno [Note: [Col. 0999] Codex 1 lacks the inscription. Codex 2 prefaces these verses:

“Here is written this book, made illustrious by the zeal of its reader,

concerning the deeds of fifty-two bishops

of the see of Tongeren, Maastricht, and Liège.”

Codex 3 is entitled: “In this book are contained the deeds of fifty-two bishops of Tongeren, Maastricht, and Liège”; a fifteenth-century hand adds: “Chronicle of the bishops of this diocese. The prologue to Saint Anno, archbishop of Cologne, begins in the Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren, Maastricht, and Liège.” So also D 1 and D 1*.], venerable archbishop of Cologne, A., the least of priests, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and faithfully to distribute his provision to Christ’s household.

Glory to almighty God, who has deigned in our times so to glorify his name that he has placed you, whom we have come to know as his servant and as the bridegroom of holy Cologne, over the Church of Liège as archbishop. Of these two churches, namely Cologne and Liège, the latter rejoices greatly that you so faithfully watch over the advancement of her venerable mother, Cologne; and, yearning with the whole desire of her heart to embrace your charity, she earnestly wishes to be helped and at the same time nourished by the supports of your fatherhood [Note: [Col. 0999] Chapeaville has “of holy.”].

And so that your kindness may owe this to her all the more readily [Note: [Col. 0999] d: *beata* (“blessed”); b, Chapeaville: variant reading as printed.], through me she sends you the deeds of her bishops, so that you, who by your own efforts strive diligently enough toward the summit of the better life, may by these examples be inflamed still more toward virtue [Note: [Col. 0999] Manuscript 1 has *per* (“through”).].

The first part of these deeds [Note: [Col. 0999] Manuscript 3 has *pras* for *pars* (“part”).] was written by Heriger [Note: [Col. 0999] Chapeaville has “Hariger.”], abbot of the monastery of Lobbes, without chapters. We, setting the chapters before it, have endeavored to join our little labor to his chapters. Since that earlier work arranged the deeds of the same bishops from the first through the twenty-seventh [Note: [Col. 0999] Manuscript 1 has *vicesimus* (“twentieth”).], namely from Saint Maternus [Col. 1000A] to Saint Remaclus, we too, cutting off the beginning of our work, which we had written at the request of Lady Ida, abbess [Note: [Col. 1000D] Of Saint Cecilia in Cologne.], so as not to weary the reader by repeating the same material, began with Saint Theodard [Note: [Col. 0999] Chapeaville reads *coepimus*, “we began,” for *incepimus*, “we began/started.”] and followed the succession of bishops up to Lord Wazo, who is known to have been the fifty-second.

We have included nothing except what we have either read, learned from the certain report of trustworthy persons, or ourselves seen and heard while present. Indeed, holy Cologne, your mother, ought not to be unaware how many and what sort of humble rulers Lethgia has had [Note: [Col. 0999] Chapeaville omits “humble”], among whom [Note: [Col. 0999] Chapeaville reads *ut si quos eorum*, “so that if any of them,” for the printed transition.], if she should learn that some have pleased God [Note: [Col. 0999] Corrector 2 has *placere*, “to please”; witnesses 1 and 3 read *placeret*, “might please”; Chapeaville reads *placuisse*, “to have pleased.”] [Note: [Col. 0999] Chapeaville then reads *inveniat*, “may find,” for *habebit*, “will have.”], she will have grounds for rejoicing more abundantly. For it belongs to mothers to regard the achievements of their daughters as their own.

Besides the thousands of crowned martyrs, she should also know that she preserves the ashes of one of our patrons, namely the blessed Ebergisus [Note: [Col. 0999] Chapeaville has “Ebregisus”]. According to these same deeds, his remains were buried in Trutmonia [Note: [Col. 0999] Chapeaville has “Trumonia”], a village of our bishopric [Note: [Col. 0999] Witnesses 1, 2, 3, B1, and B2 read *ita*, “thus”; witnesses 1 and 3 read *episcopatu*, “in the episcopate,” for *episcopatus*, “of the bishopric”; Chapeaville reads *episcopi*, “of the bishop.”]; Archbishop Bruno, who, as they say, was also duke, transferred them from there to the monastery of Saint Cecilia, as both the notable abbess and the inhabitants [Note: [Col. 0999] Chapeaville: “all the inhabitants of the same Trutmonia”] of the aforementioned Trutmonia report [Note: [Col. 0999] Compare I, 28; II, prologue. But Bruno ordered the transfer not of Ebergisus’s body but of that of Evergisilus, archbishop of Cologne, as Ruotger testifies in his *Life of Bruno*, chapter 31.]. There his empty tomb is held in the greatest honor to this day.

Yet because your people call him Evergislus, we suppose that this name was attributed to our Ebergisus from some bishop of that name, whose mausoleum is perhaps unknown, through similarity of names. Some, however, contend that this same man was both the bishop of Cologne and ours [Note: [Col. 1001] Codex 3 omits “the same man”], and assert that he was identical with the blessed Severinus, his predecessor, as they add [Note: [Col. 1001] Chapeaville has “they say”], who, during the passing of blessed Martin, heard angelic voices singing [Note: [Col. 1001] Codex 1 has “the passing”] [Note: [Col. 1002D] Gregory of Tours, *On the Miracles of Saint Martin* I, 4; on Severinus, see *On the Confessors of the Martyrs* 45.].

If this were so, the man who was fourth among the bishops of Cologne would have been twenty-fourth among ours. But that is altogether impossible, as is plainly gathered from the calculation of the times [Note: [Col. 1001] Chapeaville omits “altogether”]. At the passing of blessed Martin, it was the second year of Arcadius and Honorius, which is the four hundred and first year from the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 1001] One manuscript has “four hundredth.”].

From that point, 252 years are counted up to King Dagobert [Note: [Col. 1001] The manuscripts give the ordinal form “two hundred fifty-second”; this is the reading of A 1, 2, and 3.], around whose time this Ebergisus of ours presided over the see of Tongeren. They must therefore say either that their Evergislus lived for those same 252 years after the passing of Saint Martin, up to the time of Dagobert, so that it might appear credible that your bishop and ours could have been the same man at one time—which exceeds belief—or else they must agree with us that the two men were altogether different.

This follows both because, since the time of the Flood, no one is recorded to have lived for 200 years [Note: [Col. 1001] The text is lacking in manuscripts 1, 2, and 3; a supplement appears necessary.], and because between our blessed bishop Servatius, who was a contemporary of blessed Severinus, and this Ebergisus, we read that thirteen bishops presided over us [Note: [Col. 1002D] Only eleven, if one follows Heriger.].

It therefore depends upon your judgment, my lord archbishop, whether you command these things that concern us to be consigned to the flames or not [Note: [Col. 1001] Chapeaville has “discretion”]. Nevertheless, since this material has been dictated in some fashion, it is expedient that it be preserved, so that it may serve as an example of good living.

# Book One

[Col. 1001]

## The Chapters of Book One Begin

[Col. 1001B]

1. Prologue to the following little work.  
2. That God established all things in number, weight, and measure, and concerning the mystery of the cross.  
3. That the Lord deigned to enlighten the western regions through the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul [Note: [Col. 1001] The numeral IIII is inserted in error in manuscript 1.].  
4. When Peter came to Rome [Note: [Col. 1001] Manuscripts 1 and 2 number the chapters from this point one higher.].  
5. That he sent Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus to Trier [Note: [Col. 1001] Manuscript 2 has “to Treves.”].  
6. How blessed Maternus, after dying, was raised again through his staff.  
7. That these three men preached at Trier, Cologne, and Tongeren, and concerning the distinguished fountain of Tongeren.  
8. How Saint Eucharius bound the resisting people by prayer and released them.  
9. That he raised the widow’s son.  
10. That it was revealed [Note: [Col. 1001] Manuscript 1 has “reported.”] to a certain senator that everyone ought to be baptized [Note: [Col. 1001] Manuscript 2 has the spelling “baptized.”].  
11. On the death of blessed Eucharius.  
12. On the life and death of blessed Valerius, his successor.  
13. That blessed Maternus was bishop for as many years as he lay in the tomb [Note: [Col. 1001] Manuscript 3 has “was” instead of “had been.”].  
14. How Eucharius and Valerius called him from this world in a vision.  
15. On the eight bishops who succeeded blessed Maternus in the see of Tongeren [Note: [Col. 1001] Manuscript 2 has “who may have succeeded.”].  
16. How orthodox men in various places resisted the Arian heresy.  
17. On the Huns spread throughout the entire Roman Empire.  
18. That they are said to have been begotten by unclean spirits and by magical women [Note: [Col. 1001] Manuscript 3 omits this phrase.].  
19. How, led by a hind, they left the island and first invaded the Goths, then other peoples, and finally Gaul [Note: [Col. 1001] Manuscripts 1, 2, and 3 read “by the direction” rather than “led by.”].  
20. On Saint Servatius.  
21. That many holy men were his contemporaries, and concerning the destruction of many cities.  
22. That Saint Servatius went to Rome, to see whether he might free Gaul from the Huns by his prayers.  
23. How, in a vision before the tomb of blessed Peter, he was informed of the destruction of all Gaul and of his own death.  
24. On his return, what he saw he explains to the flock entrusted to him.  
25. His prayer and the lamentation of the clergy and people, and concerning his death.  
26. That the Huns overthrew many cities of Gaul, together with Tongeren; the Franks then expelled them from Gaul [Note: [Col. 1001] Manuscript 3 has “at that time.”].  
27. On Saint Remigius and the nine bishops of Tongeren.  
28. On Saint Domitian, and likewise on Perpetuus and Ebergisus.  
29. On Saint John.  
30. That someone from overseas foretold to him that he would become bishop of Maastricht.  
31. What he replied to this, and how his staff, fixed in the earth, blossomed; also concerning his episcopate, life, and death.  
32. On Saint Amandus.  
33. On the serpent driven away by his prayers, and how, after becoming a cleric, he went to Tours, then to Bourges, then to Rome, and from there again to Gaul.  
34. That, after being ordained bishop, he performed many good works.  
35. That he converted the people of Ghent [Note: [Col. 1003] Manuscript 1 has “Gaudent.”], enclosed Bavo, and raised a dead man.  
36. He catechizes King Dagobert’s son [Note: [Col. 1003] Manuscript 3 has “catechizes” in a variant spelling] and, after three years, leaves the bishopric of Maastricht.  
37. That divine vengeance struck those who despised the word of God from his mouth, and that a blind man received his sight from water poured by his hands.  
38. He strikes his persecutors with blindness, likewise gives sight to a blind woman, and frees a disobedient monk struck by paralysis. Enumeration of his miracles and his death.  
39. Prologue to the life of blessed Remaclus.  
40. On the kingdom of the Franks and Aquitaine, from which Saint Remaclus originated.  
41. That he first became known to the leading men of the palace after being educated by Saint Sulpicius and later under Eligius.  
42. That he succeeded Saint Amandus in the see of Maastricht, and how he lived there.  
43. Which holy men gathered around him.  
44. What he foretold to Saint Trudo, still a boy, that he ought to do.  
45. How far removed he was from greed.  
46. That Sigebert, on his advice, first built a monastery on the river Semoy [Note: [Col. 1003] Manuscripts 2 and 3 have “Sesmara”], and then another in the Ardennes.  
47. On the construction of Malmedy.  
48. On the construction of Stavelot [Note: [Col. 1003] Manuscript 3 omits the number.].  
49. That, after appointing a successor for himself, he desired the eremitical life [Note: [Col. 1003] Manuscript 3 numbers this chapter XLVIII.].  
50. The reply of his sons, who opposed this from happening [Note: [Col. 1003] Manuscript 3 numbers this chapter XLIX.].  
51. The same holy man’s excuse [Note: [Col. 1003] Manuscript 3 omits the number.].  
52. That many abandoned the world after his example [Note: [Col. 1003] From this point manuscript 3 numbers the chapters beginning with L.].  
53. That, as religious devotion grew, the resources of the Church grew.  
54. The holy priest’s exhortation to the brothers as the day of his calling approached.  
55. His death.

[Col. 1003] **The Chapters End.**

# Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren, or of Liège

## Prologue to the Following Little Work

[Note: [Col. 1003] Manuscript 2 has “of the book.”]

[Col. 1003C]

“All antiquity,” as the greatest of orators says, “the nearer it was to its origin and divine ancestry, the better perhaps it discerned those things that were true” [Note: [Col. 1003D] Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I, 12. The same words recur in Heriger’s letter to Hugo; compare the preface.].

But we know, from the angel Daniel’s report, that “many shall pass to and fro, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Daniel 12:4): among the ancients, reason was in force as the investigator of truth and the discerner of future things; among modern people, faith based on belief, though formerly it flourished together with extensive knowledge of the past [Note: [Col. 1003] The reading of manuscripts 1 and 3, “which seems to have had cruelty,” appears to be intended here.].

For them, length of life, drawing over them the callus of age [Note: [Col. 1003D] *Tusculan Disputations* III, 22.], supplied knowledge of all things. For us, by contrast—because hot blood and ignorance of affairs trouble us [the surviving syntax is irregular]—would that, because life is brief and cares press upon us, the task of remembering the discoveries of ancient men might not fly away. [Note: [Col. 1003] Read *calidus*, “hot,” for *callidus*, “clever”; witness 2 corrects it. Surius and Chapeaville preserve a corrupt alternative. They also read *quos* for the second *quod*. Witness 2 corrects *inscientia*, “ignorance,” to *inscitia*, likewise “ignorance.” The accepted reading is *vexat*, “troubles”; *versat*, “turns about,” occurs in the first Venetian edition of Horace. Col. 1003D cites Horace, *Epistles* I.3.33.]

> Many brave men lived before Agamemnon,
>
> but they are unwept [Note: [Col. 1003] The source omits *omnes* (“all”).],
>
> and are pressed down beneath a long night,
>
> because they lack a sacred poet [Note: [Col. 1003D] Horace, *Odes* IV, 9, 25.].

Reflecting on this, as I believe, most reverend abbot [Note: [Col. 1004D] Werinfrid of Stavelot; see the preface.], and because it is necessary that the younger be all the more discerning, you offered a little book on the life of the special patron shared by both our communities, namely Lord Remaclus [Note: [Col. 1004D] Compare what we said in the preface.].

You complained, however, that through the negligence of your predecessors [Note: [Col. 1003] Manuscripts B 1, B 2, and C have “our predecessors,” as do Surius and Chapeaville.] it had been published more briefly than the magnitude of his deeds required [Note: [Col. 1003] Surius reads “elaborated.”]. At the same time, you seemed—not, I should say, to beg, but rather to exhort me—that I should not have it copied as an exemplar in that manner [printed *examplari*, corrected by manuscript 2 to *exemplari*, “to copy/as an exemplar”], but should have it polished somewhat more elegantly [Note: [Col. 1005] Witness 1 has misspelled *lipidius* for *lepidius*, “more elegantly.”], both because there was an abundance of material concerning his deeds drawn from elsewhere and because your cartulary contained no lack of information about the times, whose differences now especially require careful knowledge [Note: [Col. 1005] Surius has “knowledge.”].

But while I was reflecting that you, together with your companions, were acknowledged to be the foremost master of every art, and while this line of Pierian poetry came to mind:

> Do not carry wood into the forest [Note: [Col. 1005D] Horace, *Satires* I, 10, 34.]!

and:

> Why bring fish into the sea, or water into rivers [Note: [Col. 1005] Manuscripts 1, 2, and 3 have “into the river.”]?

my mind began meanwhile to weigh the silence [Note: [Col. 1005] The first manuscript corrects this to “knowledge.”], when suddenly I remembered that charity supplies the strength that inexperience denies, and that once a work has been begun, the rest will take care of itself [Note: [Col. 1005] Manuscript 3 has “may take care of it.”].

Therefore I undertook the task, and, to use the words of a certain wise man, I shall take from him as much as the matter requires [Note: [Col. 1005] Surius and Chapeaville read “from the heap, as much as the matter requires”]: “I considered nothing more important than your exhortation, which is joined both to the dignity of the present undertaking and to the usefulness of the future age” [Note: [Col. 1005] Manuscript 1 has “more ancient”].

And, lest I seem to evade authority, I more willingly submitted to that task [Note: [Col. 1005] The second manuscript corrects the reading; the third seems to have had “of the matter,” while the first has “to be numbered.”]. Authority is granted to one who presumes, when he believes that what is requested can be accomplished; and knowing how to obey is a glory equal to that of commanding.

The venerable Hilduin, abbot, did the same long ago in his *Passion of Saint Dionysius* [Note: [Col. 1005D] He has before him Hilduin’s letter to Louis the Pious, prefixed to the *Passion of Saint Dionysius*. Surius V, 636.], as did Archbishop Hincmar in the *Life of Saint Remigius* [Note: [Col. 1005D] Preface to the *Life of Saint Remigius* 7, *Acta Sanctorum*, October I, 132.], and very many others in compiling the deeds of not a few saints.

With such authorities [Note: [Col. 1005] Manuscript B 1 has “authorities”], we can obtain something excellent [Note: [Col. 1005] Thus corrected in manuscript 2; manuscripts 1, 3, B 1, C, D 1, and D1* have variants meaning “to be obtained”], which in every matter both customarily and properly ought to carry the greatest weight. For:

> No one has ever so carefully reckoned out a way of life
>
> that circumstances, age, and experience did not always bring something new [Note: [Col. 1005D] Terence, *Adelphi* V, 4, 1.].

And lest this labor, undertaken at your urging, become unproductive [Note: [Col. 1005] Thus corrected in manuscript 2; manuscripts 1 and 3 have “unproductively,” while Surius and Chapeaville have a related form], I gathered not only the times and deeds of the saint whom we have mentioned, namely Remaclus, but also those of the other bishops of our see, as far as I could, from every quarter down to our own times [Note: [Col. 1005D] The printed phrase *quae undecumque potuere Conradi* is materially uncertain].

The life for which you especially longed, selected from that series of lives and published separately [Note: [Col. 1005D] That is, selected from the sequence of the *Lives* and issued separately.], I have placed before your wishes [Col. 1006A].

In my own judgment, I am far removed from the excellence of the best orator [Note: [Col. 1005] Surius has “the first”], who can dispatch much in few words, spin little out into many, diminish great things, make the greatest things out of the smallest, treat broad matters narrowly and narrow matters broadly, set forth familiar matters fittingly [Note: [Col. 1006D] That is, appropriately and with propriety.], matters to be expressed intelligently, new things in familiar fashion and familiar things anew, and in this way touch upon very many subjects [Note: [Col. 1005] The manuscripts variously read “and thus he may touch upon many things.”].

To him the poet also gives this instruction:

[The supplied source ends here, with the sentence incomplete.]
