Either follow the received account, or invent things consistent with themselves. Nor, like schoolboys given a theme and asked what words the man who suffered the wrong, or the one who inflicted it, might have used, have we invented anything frivolous—or even dubious. Even if I were to strive to follow a certain most eloquent speaker who said, “Even if neither of them said these things, nevertheless he held them in mind and showed them in action,” I would fear the judgment of no one. But more of this elsewhere.

I have sent, then, to your affection a gift undertaken with less confidence in my ability, but especially with the presumption of friendship. For the contemplation of friendship supplies great strength in the course of a very difficult work, and the abundance of the subject often provides much that is pleasing. Hence, although I fear that I may not be equal to the task [the printed phrase *imperator muneri* is uncertain], let the fault of my failure fall as a reproach upon the one who encouraged me, nevertheless, when I consider your goodwill, everything becomes straightforward and easy—or, so to speak, pleasurable —that is spent according to the prescription of your delight.

By offering this gift I wish to place you under an obligation, because if at some time I should ask for any of your works, you will wrong me if you refuse.

[Col. 1006C] Whoever gave great things wished great things to be repaid to him. But I do not claim great things, since they are unequal both to your merits and to our wishes. Therefore I fear the bites of barking envy, because in a difficult matter malice easily brings prejudice.

Finally, not everyone admires and loves the same things. Therefore:

> Let no one here with sidelong glance scrutinize my words, 
> nor poison them with hidden hatred and a bite.

But you, most blessed father, defender of my labor and of your own encouragement, take care lest completing the task leave me complacent: if it displeases you, it would better befit you to put your friend to shame [Col. 1007A].

## 2. That God established all things in number, weight, and measure, and concerning the mystery of the cross

God, supremely good, whose divine nature reigns from eternity and endures forever without any change, providently foreseeing all things and wisely ordering them, established the universe in number, measure, and weight (Wisdom 11:21).

He, most beautiful, also created the beautiful world of the universe, when it did not yet exist, so that it might exist, by his own free will, known only to himself. He did not bring it forth from his own substance, lest it be believed coeternal with him; for from his own essence, in a manner known only to himself, he had uttered from his heart the Word alone, coeternal with himself, through whom all things were to be formed [Col. 1007B].

Nor, in order to create the same world, did he labor with material from elsewhere, lest there already be something either in matter or in cooperation from another source that might assist his all-powerful will by external and insufficient supports in accomplishing the work, and so something might exist that had not been made by him and yet existed. No: by the Word, with the Spirit giving life together with him, he brought forth the revolving heavens, and he stretched them over everything like a skin (Psalm 103:2). He placed the earth in the midst of all things, with the elements balancing it on every side, making beings worthy of heaven for the heavenly habitation, and from the earth compose earthly things.

For he is the most powerful of all, alone supremely good, alone naturally one; and, being of such a nature that he alone is nothing other than good, he created all things from nothing, from things that did not exist—he alone existing—and created them very good.

Since these things are not simple—for they did not come forth by themselves, nor could they exist at all unless he who alone is naturally good had wished them to exist —therefore, because their goodness came forth from the highest good, it is necessary that their being too should be good.

He established all things, I say, to come forth at their appointed times in number, measure, and weight. He also, by a predetermined arrangement, gave the whole world of the universe, consisting of four elements, its fourfold arrangement in the four quarters, in an order whose arrangement, as may be believed, already prefigured that the human being whom he was to create, and for whose sake he fashioned all visible things, and the human body itself which he was to assume for our salvation, would be perfected in fourfold solidity; and that the sign of the life-giving cross, so that it might be a defense against the snares of all enemies, would be marked out by a four-sided extension.

The apostle appears to commend this in the fullness of charity, the most perfect of all virtues: “Rooted and founded in charity,” he says, “so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height and depth” (Ephesians 3:17).

[In the breadth, he signifies the good works of charity; in the length, perseverance in perfection; in the height, the rewards of the heavenly kingdom; in the depth, the inscrutable judgments of the Almighty; and he adapts the mystery of the saving cross to this interpretation.]

The author of our redemption willingly chose to undergo this, so that, with his hands spread out upon the cross and the rest of his body extended, he might be believed, by the very position of his limbs, to have drawn all things to himself.

[In the breadth, where the hands are extended across, because of the display of good works according to charity. In the length, because of the crucifixion of the whole body,] he assigned the northern region to his knowledge by sending ministers, and likewise the southern region, through the will’s patience in the exercise of charity. [In the height, where he wished the head to project upward, because of the expectation of heavenly promises,] he wished the eastern region to be illuminated by the many lights kindled by preachers. [In the depth, however, where the part of the cross beneath the feet lay hidden, fixed in the earth, because of the hidden calling of human beings according to God’s will,] he graciously devoted the western region to his will.

Nor did he turn his most merciful gaze there without reason, for “those who are well have no need of a physician. He came to call sinners to repentance, not the righteous” (Luke 5:31). For among certain eastern peoples who feared the name of the Lord, the sun of justice seemed in a certain way to have risen, whereas the western peoples, always covered by the darkness of ignorance, had chosen until then to serve the creature rather than the Creator.

## 3. That the Lord graciously chose to enlighten the western regions through the apostles Peter and Paul

[Col. 1008D] I say, then, that it was not without reason that, while hanging on the cross, he graciously directed his most benevolent gaze especially toward the western regions, since he wished to illuminate them through such great teachers as Peter [Col. 1009A] and Paul, the leaders of the apostles, like twin lamps.

After they had wonderfully provided many peoples and nations with numerous examples of virtue and instruction in various languages, Paul—who labored more than all the others (1 Corinthians 15:10), preaching the gospel of Christ from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum—finally, two years before the triumph of his most victorious death, joined Peter at the Roman citadel in opposition to Nero and Simon Magus.

Peter himself, after establishing certain churches and then firmly founding the church of Antioch, had many years earlier illuminated by his saving arrival that same city [Rome], which claimed primacy over the whole world. Their struggle’s outcome is sufficiently known from the account of their most triumphant passion.

It will be enough to remind those who do not know that, for two years before their consummation, they jointly contended against Simon Magus; and after the magician’s exposure and defeat, Agrippa and Nero condemned them both to death—one by crucifixion, the other by the sword. Peter indeed died at that time. Paul’s triumph, however, because Nero was occupied with other matters, was postponed for a year, although to the same day, by the soldiers to whom he had been handed over and whom he had immediately converted. He himself seems to indicate this in the letter written from Rome to Timothy: “And all the nations shall hear,” he says, “because I have been delivered from the mouth of the lion” (2 Timothy 4:17), signifying Nero.

This is also sufficiently attested by the letters of many Greek as well as eastern bishops, written to various recipients, as anyone can discover in ecclesiastical histories. Arator, too, a Roman subdeacon of the Church, confirms it in his book on the Acts of the Apostles:

> Yet it was not one and the same day; when a year had run its course,
> their martyrdom consecrated the returning day.

And the most distinguished scholar of the Spaniards, Prudentius, reports:

> A single day, renewed only after the full year had passed, 
> saw both crowned with the laurels of a glorious death.

But, to turn our attention back to the point toward which we directed it, let us briefly recall what we had set aside.

## 4. When Peter came to Rome

It was the second year of the emperor Claudius, the eleventh year after the Lord’s Passion, when Peter, having appointed Evodius in his place at Antioch, came to Rome. There, preaching Christ for twenty-five years—that is, until the thirteenth year of Nero and the thirty-sixth year after the Lord’s Passion (compare Eusebius, *Chronicle*; Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*)—he perceived that his own preaching alone could not suffice to occupy in advance the whole western region, which had been specially assigned to his apostolate.

For in the great city, the capital of the whole world, there was an immense influx from every surrounding nation, and the worship of every kind of idolatry flourished greatly. He also knew that he had to oppose the errors both of Simon Magus and of many philosophers, especially of the Jews who constantly defended the Law of Moses. Therefore, having selected good cultivators of Christ’s vineyard, [Col. 1010B] he sent them to carry out the duties of so great an embassy throughout all the regions of Italy and Gaul.

Among them, in the second year after his arrival, he sent Mark to Aquileia and several other cities of Italy, with the Gospel dictated by Peter and written down by Mark himself; finally, he sent him to Alexandria and Egypt. He sent suitable preachers and truthful witnesses of Christ to the other parts of Gaul, whom our account, hastening elsewhere, does not permit us to name individually (compare Rufinus II, 16).

To Gaul, then, which is called “Comata” [Long-haired Gaul], he had sent blessed Clement as bishop to the city of the Mediomatrici. This was not the Clement who was fourth after Peter in administering the pontificate of the Roman see and who later sent, together with many other defenders of the truth, the holy Dionysius to the city of Paris, Lutetia, in Gaul called “Bracata” [Trousered Gaul].

## 5. That he sent Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus to Trier

At that very time, blessed Peter had sent to the metropolis of the Treveri —that is, the city—three confessors of the one Trinity, concordant in the unity of faith, in heart and mind, and equally in courage: Eucharius, namely, Valerius, and Maternus.

[He bestowed upon Eucharius the honor of the pontificate, upon Valerius that of the diaconate, and upon Maternus that of the subdiaconate.] After giving them the apostolic blessing, he said:

“You see, brothers and fellow soldiers, how great is the harvest of the Lord’s sowing and how many laborers it needs. Since, therefore, you have been sufficiently instructed by me in the sanctions of catholic doctrine, and have been strengthened by a thoroughly Christian devotion, go forth in the name of the Lord, enter the western regions, and, like good soldiers of Christ, wage the battles of the Lord our God.

“Pierce with the spear of the divine word the strongest wall of unbelief with which the people of all Gaul and Germany are enclosed; attack it with the battering ram of the Lord’s faith. May the power granted to us by the Lord Jesus Christ in the authority of binding and loosing always be with you, accompanied also by our prayer, together with the portion assigned to our apostolate.”

Thus, having equipped this brotherhood with such a blessing, he released them to depart. After leaving Rome and undertaking their fortunate journey, they proclaimed without hesitation, everywhere around them, the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. When they had scarcely completed a few days’ journey, they suffered the loss of so great a fellowship.

## 6. How blessed Maternus, after dying, was restored to life through Peter’s staff

[For when they had reached a certain fortress called Elegia, and had remained there for some time, earnestly urging everyone toward belief, Saint Maternus was suddenly struck down by a severe fever and taken from human affairs.] (*Life of Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus* 3.)

From this the devil increased his joy, whereas Christ turned it to glory. The others, struck by unexpected grief but not doubting God’s mercy, decided that the body should not be left unburied and that, retracing the road by which they had come, they should return as quickly as possible to blessed Peter.

When they arrived unexpectedly, panting and drawing sighs from the depths of their hearts, they said: “Behold, Lord, the man whom you deigned to give us as a colleague and fellow worker. Having reached the very end of human life, he has deprived us of his companionship in the life we undertook and frustrated our work at its beginning.”

But the apostle consoled them kindly, saying: “Return as quickly as possible, take with you the badge of our pontificate, and, without losing confidence in God’s mercy or our authority, place it upon the body of the dead man, commanding him at once to rise, to accompany you on the journey already begun, to perform the work of an evangelist, and to complete the ministry entrusted to him. Behold, I say, the pontifical staff, a most effective performer of signs, the support of every mighty work and the relief of your labor. Just as the Lord was always with me in everything, so may he everywhere graciously assist your prayers.”

Strengthened again by this apostolic consolation, they finally returned to the body of the dead man, without hesitation, on the fortieth day after they had departed from that place. They removed so great a treasure from the earth, so that the Lord’s promises might be confirmed: “The one who believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John 15:12). And so that their minds might be strengthened to perform signs, their feet being directed to preach peace, the staff of him whose shadow had healed every kind of disease recalled blessed Maternus from death.

When they saw this power, they were strengthened. What joy do you think accumulated in their hearts over the recovery of their companion? What wonder at the depth of God’s inscrutable judgments and at the ineffable power of his divinity? Although he had seen things among the heavenly beings which the human tongue could not fully express, by recounting them he both lightened the labor of his companions on the journey and further encouraged their minds to proclaim Christ’s mighty works (*Life of Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus* 5).

[The inhabitants of that place, moreover, lifted immense praises to heaven, and many pagans, having obtained the grace of baptism, joined themselves to the unity of the faith. And the occasion of his death became for many a resurrection to life. Later, the Christians built a church in that place and, because of what had happened there, gave it the name Resurrection (*Life* 6).]

After they had instructed many in the faith of Christ and now saw that it was time to migrate to other places, they said farewell to the brothers and, scattering the seed of the divine word throughout Gaul and wherever they passed, finally reached the most ancient city of the Treveri, the metropolis of three cities.

Of these, the middle and mother city was that of the Mediomatrici. The Romans, who had brought under their empire whatever was good anywhere among the nations, called it Metz in memory of Mettius Fafeceus, king of the Albans. Likewise, in memory of Tullus, the third king of the Romans, they had named the populous city of Leuchum of the Aulerci Tullum. Mettius was Tullus’s contemporary and at first his ally, but was later severely punished for breaking their treaty.

I say that the city of Metz had already been illuminated by a certain ray of divine brightness, namely blessed Clement, who had earlier been sent to that city by blessed Peter. When he first arrived there and, since he had no other lodging, had taken shelter beneath the theatrical arena, he dedicated there a small church in the name of blessed Peter, in which he converted to Christ many people devoted especially to theatrical games and brothels.

## 7. That those three men preached in three cities, and concerning a remarkable spring

Since, then, as has been said, a ray of the true sun had already penetrated that region near Trier, leaving that place aside, the three men mentioned above entered the city of the Treveri, so that everywhere the Trinity they preached might truly become known under the worship of the one true God. Under the pontificate of one of the three, they added to themselves the other two neighboring cities: Agrippina, also called Cologne, and the city of the Tungri.

Pliny the Second, who flourished in the time of the emperor Trajan, more than four hundred years before its destruction, mentions it in his *Natural History*, in the book on the properties of waters, in these words :

> The city of the Tungri in Gaul has a remarkable spring, bubbling up in many streams, with an iron-like taste, which is perceived only at the end of drinking. It purges the body and drives away tertian fevers; it assists against the disease of stones. When exposed to fire, the water becomes cloudy and finally turns red.

They say that it was named Octavia in honor of Octavian, Augustus, or of his mother, the sister of Julius Caesar, who first brought Gaul and Germany under Roman rule.

In these cities, then, the three men mentioned above, as good cultivators of Christ’s true vineyard, sowing the seeds of the divine word, accompanied by the grace of every mighty work, recalled many people through the staff of blessed Peter that they always carried with them to the worship of the living God, casting aside the worship of idols.

The ferocity of the Gauls was bent beneath Christ’s gentle yoke; the stiff-neckedness of the Germans bowed before the authority of faith. And the Gallic buskin, which, as blessed Jerome testifies, had no monsters but always abounded in strong and most eloquent men, submitted its heart favorably to the disciples and teaching of fishermen. Christ’s inheritance from the Father rejoiced, because the portion of the devil mourned as it diminished day by day.

## 8. How Saint Eucharius bound and released the resisting people through prayer

[Col. 1014A]

[When blessed Eucharius warned the people every day to cease worshipping vain idols and to turn to the true God, creator of heaven and earth, and they in no way listened to his words, one day he entered the city with his companions, intending to deliver the same sermon to the people (*Life of Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus* 6).]

Therefore, the priests of the Capitol, inflamed with zeal against them, stirred up most of the people against them. They drove the saints outside the city and wished to overwhelm them with stones.

When blessed Eucharius saw this (*Life* chapter 7), he and his companions turned to the weapons of prayer, beseeching with tears the mercy of almighty God: that he might offer them his pious aid against the unbelievers, and open an understanding capable of recognizing the truth of the faith to the mad crowds of the infidels.

Meanwhile, the entire raging crowd was bound from heaven in a wondrous manner, so that some of them stood rigid with arms outstretched, relying in vain on their attempted throws, while others, bent down to gather stones, clung to the earth with their necks bowed toward the ground. All remained motionless and rigid in the posture each person’s body had assumed and continued in that state.

When this had continued for nearly an hour and all were held fast by bonds imposed by the heavenly power in various ways, they began, exhausted by excessive pain, humbly to ask for the release of their limbs, and cried out that they would believe if they were released.

Then Saint Eucharius once more poured out a prayer to the Lord, released the entire rebellious crowd from the bond of pain, and, restoring their health, returned them to their former condition (*Life* chapter 8). When they saw this miracle, all of them together fell at the feet of the saints and begged them not to delay showing them the way of salvation, but to explain as quickly as possible what they ought to do for their recovery and what they ought to avoid.

## 9. That he restored the son of the widow Albana to life

When Saint Eucharius preached, they were pierced in their hearts and testified that they had never before heard or learned such things (*Life* chapter 13). This saving admonition was also accompanied by a confirmation of divine power, and an attestation of a wondrous miracle immediately followed it.

For among those present at the spectacle was a certain widow named Albana, illustrious by birth and extremely wealthy in possessions. She received from servants who came running in haste the sad news that her only son, whom she had left at home ill, had died when the pain returned to his vital organs.

When she heard this, she immediately threw herself in tears at the feet of Saint Eucharius, saying: “I beg you, renewer of our city and illuminator of the whole people, to have pity on me, who am now twice bereaved, and to deign to show your compassionate heart toward me, the most wretched of women. Recently I was widowed of my husband, and alas, today I have been miserably deprived by the death of my only son. If you restore him to life, know with certainty that thereafter I will most willingly obey your commands and believe in your Christ together with my son and my entire household.”

Moved by these lamentations, blessed Eucharius went with her, accompanied by a large crowd because of the novelty of so great a miracle. When he arrived there, he took blessed Valerius and Maternus with him and entered the house, while the people waited outside for the outcome.

First he bent his knees and devoted himself to prayer. Then, rising from prayer, he approached the lifeless body, took the young man’s hand, and confidently said: “I say to you, young man, that in the name of Jesus Christ, who by his own power restored the widow’s only son to life, you too should return to the present light and thereafter, abandoning the error of demons, recognize your Creator with right faith.”

When his soul returned, he immediately rose and, although he had not yet been instructed in the faith, began to give thanks to God. Saint Eucharius took him and led him outside the house; in the presence of all the people he restored him to his mother alive and free from every infirmity.

Then all who were present began to cry out with loud voices, saying: “Truly the God of the Christians is shown to be great and all-powerful, because through his servants he performs such signs and wonders.”

That same day Albana was baptized together with her son and her entire household, along with a considerable crowd of the people. After not many days, Saint Eucharius consecrated her house as a church.

## 10. That it was revealed to a certain senator that everyone ought to be baptized

After this, a noble senator of the same city saw a dream that would benefit the salvation of all the citizens (*Life* chapter 14).

One night he saw in a dream a certain man standing before him, handsome in appearance, shining in the most splendid garments and carrying in his hand a cross of marvelous magnificence. The man said to him:

“These men who have come here are servants of God Most High, and they have been sent here for your salvation. Therefore, if you wish to escape death and reach eternal life, do everything they tell you and obey their commands with complete devotion.”

Having said this, he was taken from the senator’s sight.

When morning came, the senator summoned the citizens and related in order what he had seen and heard in the dream. Relying on this revelation, they began to run eagerly to the saints of God and thirstily to seek the water of sacred baptism.

For three days the rush to them was so great that they baptized the people in the river flowing through the middle of the city, since they were unable otherwise to bear the pressure of the crowds. Hence it is believed that from that time the stream itself, because of the infusion of holy oil, came to be called Olevia by derivation.

Meanwhile the city was cleansed from the pollution of idols, superstitious error was cast aside, the altars of demons were destroyed, and churches of Christ were built throughout the various places. The saving trumpet sounded broadly through the city, inviting and summoning everyone to the grace of faith. The city was fortified on every side with the weapons of faith against the snares of spiritual enemies. A new hymn was publicly sung in it, and she who previously, by failing to know her Creator, had been adulterous, was transformed through faith into Christ’s most sacred bride.

Meanwhile (*Life* chapter 16), they preached the word of life throughout all the surrounding regions and were powerful far and wide both in speech and in miracles: they illuminated the blind, restored the weak, raised the dead, drove out demons, and cured every illness.

## 11. Concerning the death of blessed Eucharius

## Textual notes

[Note: 1. Col. 1006D; at *Aut famam sequere, aut sibi convenientia finge*. Horace, *Art of Poetry*, 119.]

[Note: 2. Col. 1006D; at *intulit, aliquid finximus frivolum, immo nec creperum*. That is, “doubtful.” The word *creperum* occurs in Festus, Varro, and Lucretius.]

[Note: 3. Col. 1005; at *Misi, inquam, karitati tuae munus, quod minus*. *minus*, “less,” is Surius’s reading; it is absent from all the manuscripts. The note also records *non*, “not,” as a correction in 2.]

[Note: 4. Col. 1005; at *securitate, maxime autem susceptum amicitiae praesumptione. Magna*. Surius has *magnas*, “great,” feminine plural agreeing with his added “strengths,” for neuter *Magna*, “great things.”]

[Note: 5. Col. 1005; at *praesumptione. Magna etenim in difficillimi operis cursu*. Surius adds *vires*, “strength.”]

[Note: 6. Col. 1005; at *Magna etenim in difficillimi operis cursu amicitiae*. 1 spells *amicitiae*, “of friendship,” as *amiticiae*.]

[Note: 7. Col. 1005; at *copia suppeditat. Unde licet verear nedum imperator*. 1 has the altered form *impato* at *imperator*, “commander/emperor”; the syntax of the printed passage is uncertain.]

[Note: 8. Col. 1005; at *suppeditat. Unde licet verear nedum imperator muneri*. 3 has *numeri*, “of number,” for *muneri*, “to the task/gift.”]

[Note: 9. Col. 1005; at *par nequeam esse, deficientis culpa in adhortantis*. 3 has *adhortandis*, “to those to be encouraged,” for *adhortantis*, “of the one encouraging.”]

[Note: 10. Col. 1005; at *et facile, et ut ita dicam voluptuarium*. 3 and Surius have *voluntarium*, “voluntary,” for *voluptuarium*, “pleasurable.”]

[Note: 11. Col. 1005; at *quia si quid operum tuorum quandoque postulavero*. Surius has *expostulavero*, “I shall have demanded,” for *postulavero*, “I shall have asked.”]

[Note: 12. Col. 1006D; at *Quisquis magna dedit, voluit sibi magna remitti*. Martial, *Epigrams*, V, 60, to Stella.]

[Note: 13. Col. 1005; at *sibi magna remitti . Set non arrogantur*. 2, 3, and Surius have active *arrogant*, “they claim,” for passive *arrogantur*, “are claimed.”]

[Note: 14. Col. 1006D; at *importare. Denique non omnes eadem mirantur amantque*. Horace, *Epistles*, II, 2, 58.]

[Note: 15. Col. 1005; at *Non istic obliquo oculo mea famina quisquis*. 2 and 3 have the abbreviation *quisq* for *quisquis*, “whoever”; Surius has *quisquam*, “anyone.”]

[Note: 16. Col. 1006D; at *quisquis Limet, non odio obscuro morsuque venenet*. “Anyone scrutinizes advantages,” and so forth—*Commoda quisquam limat*—are Horace’s words, *Epistles*, I, 14, 37. The main text substitutes *mea famina*, “my words.”]

[Note: 17. Col. 1005; at *pater beatissime, mei laboris tuaeque adhortationis assertor*. 2 and 3 have *afferior*; 2 corrects to *assertor*, “defender”; 1 has *asserior*. The alternative forms are corrupt spellings at this word.]

[Note: 18. Col. 1005; at *laboris tuaeque adhortationis assertor , caveas securum*. Surius has *securum*, “secure/complacent”; 1, 2, and 3 have *insecurum*, “insecure/anxious.”]

[Note: 19. Col. 1007; at *pudor amici dignius possit convenire, si displicet*. Surius adds “Farewell,” then these verses: “Always possess with joy what wishes cannot encompass nor dreams imagine. Tender little ears rejoice at the name; your virtue has made me your friend. Farewell again.”]

[Note: 20. Col. 1007; at *dignius possit convenire, si displicet . 2.*. The chapter number 2 is absent in 1, 2, and 3.]

[Note: 21. Col. 1007; at *aeternum sine aliqua mutabilitate perdurat, omnia providens*. Ch. has adverbial *provide*, “providently,” for participial *providens*, “foreseeing/providing.”]

[Note: 22. Col. 1007D; at *in numero et mensura et pondere constituens*. Augustine says much the same in his book *On Genesis*, Venetian edition, III, 1, p. 168.]

[Note: 23. Col. 1007; at *ne coaeternus crederetur, quippe ex propria essentia*. Ch. has *substantia*, “substance,” for *essentia*, “essence.”]

The apparatus marks the ending *-us* in 2 and 3, by correction in 2, for *summe*, “supremely,” yielding *summus*, “supreme”; Ch. has *-e*, retaining the adverb. This is an ending variant at *summe*, not a variant replacing the separate word *solus*, “alone.”]

[Note: 28. Col. 1007; at *ut nihil aliud sit nisi bonus, qui*. 2 erases *qui*, “who,” at this point.]

[Note: 29. Col. 1007; at *ut nihil aliud sit nisi bonus, qui*. The supplied source repeats the notice “erased in 2” at the same point, after *qui*. No additional erased wording is supplied.]

[Note: 30. Col. 1007; at *creavit valde bona. Quae quoniam non sunt*. 1 omits *sunt*, “are.”]

[Note: 31. Col. 1007; at *ea is, qui solus naturaliter bonus est*. 3 omits *est*, “is,” after “naturally good.”]

[Note: 32. Col. 1007; at *omnibus sanctis quae sit latitudo, longitudo, sublimitas*. Ch. omits *sublimitas*, “height.”]

[Note: 33. Col. 1007D; at *quae sit latitudo, longitudo, sublimitas et profundum*. Augustine, *To Honoratus*, Venetian edition, II, p. 446.]

[Note: 34. Col. 1007; at *et profundum (Ephes. III, 17). [In latitudine*. 1 and 2 have *Latitudo*, “breadth,” for *In latitudine*, “in the breadth.”]

[Note: 35. Col. 1007D; at *omnipotentis, huicque intellectui coaptans mysterium salutiferae crucis*. The author here draws from the letter to Paulinus *On Seeing God*, *Works*, II, p. 486, the allegorical interpretation of the cross that Augustine favors—for example, *Expositions on Psalm* 103, *Works*, IV, p. 1140 [Col. 1008D], and *Sermons* 53 and 166, *Works*, V, pp. 317 and 798. Such things, contrary to what one might suppose, do not occur in the little work *On the Praises of the Cross*, which Hrabanus Maurus composed with more ingenuity than truth.]

[Note: 36. Col. 1007; at *mysterium salutiferae crucis .] Quod in eo*. Ch. reads *ideo*, “therefore,” for *in eo*, “in that/on it.”]

[Note: 37. Col. 1007; at *altitudine, quo capud voluit eminere, propter supernorum*. Ch. has *superiorum*, “of higher [things],” for *supernorum*, “of heavenly [things].”]

[Note: 38. Col. 1007; at *praedicantium luminaribus irradiari voluit partem. [In profundum*. 2 corrects accusative *profundum* to ablative *profundo*, giving “in the depth.”]

[Note: 40. Col. 1007; at *delegissent eatenus creaturae potius quam creatori deservire*. Ch. has perfect infinitive *deservisse*, “to have served,” for present *deservire*, “to serve.”]

[Note: 67. Col. 1011D; at *[Nam cum in quoddam castellum nomine Elegia*. “A certain place in the district of Alsace named Elegia”: Heriger’s letter to Hugo; compare the preface. Today it is the village of Ell, on the stream Ill, between Kogenheim and Ernstein, opposite Benfeld. See Calmet, *Histoire de Lorraine*, I, p. 3; Laguille, *Histoire d’Alsace*, p. 47. The same place occurs in the Ravenna geographer in these words: “A city called Alaia, near the city of Strasbourg.” It is called Alege in Pope Leo IX’s bull, Grandidier, I, p. 261. In the letter of Frederick, bishop of Strasbourg, of 1387, the following words occur [Col. 1012D], cited by Grandidier, I, p. 14: “In that place, Elley, many Christians from different regions flock throughout the whole year to our most blessed father Saint Maternus.”]

[Note: 75. Col. 1011; at *efficacissimus signorum, tocius virtutis solamen et alleviatio*. 1 writes *alleuiatio*, “relief”; 2 corrects *alleuato* to *allevatio*, also “relief,” for the printed *alleviatio*.]

[Note: 81. Col. 1011; at *potentia divinitatis ejus inenarrabili? Quaeque apud superos*. 1 corrects *superbos*, “the proud,” to *superos*, “those above/the heavenly beings.”]

[Note: 83. Col. 1011; at *gratiam indepti unitati fidei se conjunxerunt. Et*. 3 omits “And the occasion of his death became for many a resurrection to life,” from *Et* to *resurrectio*.]

[Note: 84. Col. 1011; at *multos ad fidem Christi imbuerunt, et jam*. Ch. omits “and now seeing that it was time to move to other places,” from *et jam* to *videntes*.]

Ch. omits “who had brought whatever was good anywhere among the nations under their empire,” from *qui* to *imperio*, and then “his contemporary, at first allied to him, but afterward severely punished for breaking the treaty,” from *eidem* to *multati*.]

[Note: 86. Col. 1011; at *ob memoriam Mettii Fafecei Albanorum regis, Mettim*. 3 has *metum*, “fear,” where the place-name *Mettim*, “Metz,” is printed; 2 apparently corrects to *mettim*.]

[Note: 87. Col. 1011; at *et ob memoriam Tulli, Romanorum tercii regis*. 3 reverses *tercii regis* to *regis tercii*, “of the third king,” abbreviated *r. t.*]

[Note: 88. Col. 1012D; at *memoriam Tulli, Romanorum tercii regis eidem contemporalis*. Compare the *Deeds of the Bishops of Metz*, in d’Achery, II, p. 224.]

[Note: 89. Col. 1013; at *hospicium accepisset, aecclesiam sub beati Petri nomine*. The note gives the order *Nomine Petri*, “in Peter’s name,” rather than *Petri nomine*. No witness is specified.]

[Note: 90. Col. 1013D; at *ludis et lupanaribus deditos ad Christum convertit*. See Paul the Deacon’s *Deeds of the Bishops of Metz*.]

[Note: 91. Col. 1013; at *lupanaribus deditos ad Christum convertit . 7.*. The chapter number is absent also in 1 and 2.]

[Note: 92. Col. 1013; at *jam penetraverat radius, ea neglecta jam dicti*. Ch. omits the beginning, through the introduction of “the three men already mentioned.”]

[Note: 93. Col. 1013; at *alias sibi duas contiguas civitates addidere, Agrippinam*. *Agrippinam*, the name Agrippina, seems to have been corrected to the spelling *Agripinam*. No witness is specified.]

[Note: 94. Col. 1013D; at *aquarum, mentionem facit in haec verba: Tungris*. Pliny, *Natural History*, XXXI, 8.]

[Note: 95. Col. 1013D; at *hic corpora, tertianas febres discutit, calculorum vitio*. Pliny’s words are *Calculorumque vitia: eadem aqua igne admota*, “and diseases of stones; the same water, when put to the fire,” and so forth.]

[Note: 96. Col. 1013; at *rubescit. Et octaviam eam ob honorem Octaviani*. 3 spells *Octaviani*, “of Octavian,” as *octoviani*.]

[Note: 97. Col. 1014D; at *Galliam Romano subegit imperio et Germaniam, ferunt*. The later *Life of Saint Lupus*, chapter 33, reads “Octavia, which is called Tungri”; *Acta Sanctorum*, July, VII, p. 77.]

[Note: 98. Col. 1013; at *Romano subegit imperio et Germaniam, ferunt fuisse*. 3 omits *fuisse*, “to have been.”]

[Note: 99. Col. 1013; at *ferunt fuisse nominatam. In quibus civitatibus ut*. Ch. omits two separate stretches: *ut … agricolae*, “as good cultivators of Christ’s true vineyard,” and *comitante … bacillum*, “with the grace of every mighty work accompanying them, through the staff of blessed Peter that they always carried with them.” The intervening clause about the three men sowing the divine word is not included in this omission notice.]

[Note: 100. Col. 1013; at *civitatibus ut boni verae vineae Christi agricolae*. The supplied source repeats the same two-span omission notice at *agricolae*, “cultivators”; see note 99 for both complete English spans.]

[Note: 101. Col. 1013; at *tres viri semina verbi serentes divini, comitante*. The supplied source repeats that notice at *comitante*, “accompanying”; see note 99 for the actual omitted readings.]

[Note: 102. Col. 1013; at *quem semper secum beati Petri ferebant bacillum*. The supplied source repeats that notice at *bacillum*, “staff”; see note 99 for the actual omitted readings.]

[Note: 103. Col. 1013; at *qui monstra non habuit, sed viris semper*. 1 has *septem*, “seven,” for *semper*, “always.”]

[Note: 104. Col. 1014D; at *sed viris semper fortibus et eloquentissimis habundavit*. Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*, *Works*, Vallarsi edition, II, p. 387.]

[Note: 105. Col. 1013; at *magisterio favorabiliter corda submittit. Laetabatur a patre*. 2 corrects *a patre*, “from the Father,” to *apte*, “fittingly.”]

[Note: 106. Col. 1013; at *patre hereditas Christi, quia portio cotidie minorata*. 2 corrects to *minorata*, “diminished”; 1 and 3 have *imminorata*, also “diminished.”]

[Note: 107. Col. 1013; at *populum resistentem orationibus ligaverit et absolverit. [Cumque*. Ch. omits the opening from *Cumque* to *Quapropter*: Eucharius’s daily warnings, the people’s refusal to listen, and his entry into the city to preach. What follows is worded somewhat differently there.]

[Note: 108. Col. 1013; at *habiturus (Vita E., V., M. 6). Quapropter*. The supplied source repeats the notice at *Quapropter*, “therefore”; the exact omitted episode and subsequent variation are described in note 107.]

[Note: 109. Col. 1013; at *lacrimis omnipotentis Dei clementiam, ut et illis*. Rather, *sibi*, “to themselves,” as in the *Life of Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus*, instead of *illis*, “to them.” This is the object receiving divine help, not God offering himself.]

[Note: 110. Col. 1013; at *in modum ita coelitus obligata est, ut*. 3 has *et*, “and”; 1 and 2 write *ut*, “so that,” above the line.]

[Note: 111. Col. 1013; at *coelitus obligata est, ut alii ex eis*. 1 and 3 have *nexeis*, an altered form; 2 corrects to *ex eis*, “of them,” also the reading of Ch. and the *Life of Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus*.]

[Note: 112. Col. 1013; at *ex eis incassum jactui innitentes, brachiis extentis*. 3 has *extensis* for *extentis*, both “outstretched.”]

[Note: 113. Col. 1013; at *deorsum inclinati, terrae pronis cervicibus inhererent, et*. Ch. omits “and all remained motionless and rigid in the posture each person’s body had assumed,” from *et* to *perdurarent*.]

[Note: 114. Col. 1013; at *pronis cervicibus inhererent, et omnes secundum uniuscujusque*. 1, 2, and 3 add *rei*, “of the thing,” after “each”; it is erased in 2 and absent in the *Life of Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus*.]

[Note: 115. Col. 1013; at *Praedicante sancto Euchario, conpuncti sunt corde, ac*. Ch. omits “and testified that they had never heard or learned such things,” from *ac* to *sunt*.]

[Note: 116. Col. 1015; at *infirmum, redeunte ad vitalia dolore esse mortuum*. Ch. reads *subita morte defunctum*, “had died a sudden death.”]

[Note: 117. Col. 1015; at *lacrimis ad pedes sancti Eucharii dicens: Obsecro*. Ch. lacks Albana’s whole speech from *Obsecro* to *credere*: “I beg you, renewer of our city … to believe in your Christ,” including her two bereavements and her promise of obedience and faith with her son and household.]

[Note: 118. Col. 1015; at *ac tota familia in Christum tuum credere*. The source repeats the same omission notice at the closing *credere*, “to believe”; see note 117 for its full scope.]

[Note: 119. Col. 1015; at *flectens genua, in orationem se dedit, et*. 1 omits *et*, “and,” before his rising from prayer.]

[Note: 120. Col. 1015; at *famulos suos operatur. Eadem die baptizata est*. 1 omits *est*, the auxiliary “was” in “was baptized”; 2 inserts it above the line in the same hand. The note does not omit Albana’s baptism as a whole.]

[Note: 121. Col. 1015; at *urbis senator vidit somnium ad salutem cunctorum*. 3 and the *Life of Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus* have *multorum*, “of many,” for *cunctorum*, “of all.”]

[Note: 122. Col. 1015; at *cunctorum civium profuturum (c. 14). Quadam autem*. 2 corrects *autem*, “however,” to *enim*, “for.”]

[Note: 123. Col. 1015; at *virum quemdam coram se stantem, vultu elegantem*. 1 and 2 have *eligantem*; 2 corrects to *elegantem*, “handsome.”]

[Note: 124. Col. 1015; at *elegantem , splendidissimis vestibus corruscantem, crucemque mirae*. 1 omits *mirae*, “marvelous”; 2 adds it afterward. The omission concerns that adjective, not the whole phrase about the cross’s splendor.]

[Note: 125. Col. 1015; at *mane convocatis civibus narravit per ordinem quae*. Ch. partly omits and partly changes the account from *quae* to *expetere*: what the senator saw and heard in the dream, the people’s reliance on the revelation, and their eagerness to seek baptism.]

[Note: 126. Col. 1015; at *ad sanctos Dei currere et sacri baptismatis*. The source repeats that same notice beside “of sacred baptism”; see note 125 for its scope.]

[Note: 127. Col. 1015; at *currere et sacri baptismatis undam sicienter expetere*. 2 spells *baptismatis*, “of baptism,” as *baptysmatis*.]

[Note: 128. Col. 1015; at *rivulus ob infusionem sancti olei derivative Olevia*. 3 omits the name *Olevia*.]

[Note: 129. Col. 1015; at *credulitatis, armisque fidei contra spiritualium hostium insidias*. Ch. has *nequitias*, “wickednesses,” for *insidias*, “snares.”]

[Note: 130. Col. 1015; at *et quae antea creatorem suum non cognoscendo*. Ch. has *fugiendo*, “by fleeing,” for *cognoscendo*, “by knowing,” in the phrase “not knowing [her Creator].”]

And when blessed Eucharius had held the episcopate of the city of Trier for twenty-three years and had the ecclesiastical affairs firmly established and well founded [Note: [Col. 1015] “had administered them energetically,” Ch.]; and when he himself had already advanced in age (c. 16), an angel appeared before him one night [Note: [Col. 1015] Apart from a few exceptions, this is absent in Ch.] and said:

“Eucharius, you have labored faithfully in the Lord’s commands; valiantly you have fought in the contest of this present [Col. 1016C] life. Come now into the rest promised to you, and receive the incorruptible crown of your struggle.”

Having learned this through the vision, Saint Eucharius rejoiced greatly and awaited the time of his departure without fear. But when he foresaw that the day of his passing was drawing near [Note: [Col. 1015] Apart from a few exceptions, this is absent in Ch.], he summoned his disciples and said:

“I know, dearest brothers, that I shall soon depart from this world and fulfill the debt of human existence. Therefore I ask you to maintain among yourselves firm faith, unshaken hope [Note: [Col. 1015] “shaken,” 1.], and true charity [Note: [Col. 1015] Absent in 1.; supplied above the line in 2.], and never again to consent to diabolical errors. Commit to the earth whatever in me is earthly, and provide spiritual obsequies also for whatever is spiritual” (c. 17).

To blessed Valerius he said:

“I commend to you, dearest brother, the bride of Christ—namely, his church [Note: [Col. 1015] From ‘namely’ through ‘acquired’ absent in Ch.]—which by his power I acquired in these regions [Note: [Col. 1015] From ‘namely’ through ‘acquired’ absent in Ch.], so that you may guard her chastely and not allow her to be defiled by any deceptions of error during your days. Distribute generously the measure of the evangelical household [Note: [Col. 1015] ‘Of spiritual nourishment,’ Ch.]; faithfully multiply among them the talents entrusted to you, so that when your judge comes to settle accounts with his servants, you may not be punished like a wicked and idle servant [Col. 1017A] for burying the talents, but rather may happily be brought into the joy of your Lord for the treasures doubled.”

As Saint Eucharius was saying these things, suddenly, in the sight of all who were present, a bright light flashed like lightning and illuminated his entire cell for almost the space of an hour. Then, having said farewell to the brothers and reverently lowering his eyes, he left this sorrowful world and, together with that light, on the fifth day before the Ides of December [Note: [Col. 1017] “Sixth,” Life of E., V., and M.] joyfully departed to Christ (c. 17). Then the disciples celebrated sacred funeral rites for his passing and committed his body to burial with hymns and devout tears in the church situated outside the city walls, toward the south.

## 12. The life and death of blessed Valerius, his successor

After his venerable death, blessed Valerius succeeded him in the priestly ministry [Col. 1017B] [Note: [Col. 1017] “Priestly,” 3.; corrected to “priestly” in 2.] (c. 18), and governed it with the highest distinction for fifteen years, living holily and preaching the word of life [Note: [Col. 1017] “illutque,” corrected to “illudque” in 2.]. During that period [Note: [Col. 1017] 1. corrected to “during that period of time.”], by performing great signs and astonishing miracles, he converted many peoples to the Lord and led them, through the most salutary exhortation [Note: [Col. 1017] Absent in Ch.], to recognition of the Catholic faith [Note: [Col. 1017] Absent in Ch.].

He also devoted himself most diligently to the ministry of preaching, so that by that time Christians throughout nearly all Gaul and Germany [Note: [Col. 1017] “Christians,” 1. and 3.; corrected from “Xpi.” in 2.] surpassed the pagans both in number and in religion. His teaching was suited to each person and sweet and most pleasing to all who heard it. Thus, because of the honey-flowing eloquence [Note: [Col. 1017] Corrected from “soft-flowing” in 2.] of his speech, peoples streamed to him from every direction and desired to hear at least some word [Col. 1017C] [Note: [Col. 1017] “Several,” 1.] from his mouth (c. 19).

As for his personal conduct, to speak briefly: he was most pure in thought, useful and discerning in speech, and likewise blameless and outstanding in action [Note: [Col. 1017] 1 corrected from “especially”; “especially,” Ch.]. Through the active life he became a neighbor to each person in compassion, while nevertheless being more than others suspended in contemplation [Note: [Col. 1017] “Devoted,” Ch.]. While engaged in this contemplation, he did not abandon fraternal condescension in the active life; nor, when humbled in action, did he withdraw from the sublimity [Note: [Col. 1017] Ch. differs considerably.] of contemplation. Following the salutary counsels of his teacher along the straight path, he faithfully distributed the Gospel wheat of the Lord’s household and multiplied the talents entrusted to him through spiritual increase.

But when he had reached venerable old age by stages of perfection [Note: [Col. 1017] Corrected to “stages of progress” in 2.] and the completion of his course was already approaching (c. 20), blessed Eucharius appeared to him one night in a vision [Col. 1018A] and said [Note: [Col. 1017] Absent in Ch.]:

“The time of your departure, brother Valerius, is now at hand, and the joys of eternal recompense have been prepared for you. The gate of the heavenly kingdom stands open for you; after this hour, on the fifth day, you will enter it joyfully and rejoice without end in the benefits granted by your Lord. Therefore appoint Maternus, our companion in the struggle [Note: [Col. 1017] “Cooperation,” 2.], as successor in your office, and make him utterly certain of our visitation before the day of his departure.”

Having said this, he withdrew. Saint Valerius awoke and immediately related the dream he had seen to blessed Maternus and the other brothers who were present, and with a most joyful countenance foretold to them that the day of his death was near [Note: [Col. 1017] Absent in Ch.]. On the following day [Note: [Col. 1017] “On the day following,” 2.], he advanced the venerable Maternus to the priestly rank and carefully instructed him in the exercise of the ministry entrusted to him [Col. 1018B] (c. 21).

During the aforesaid period, as faithful people came because of the report of his impending death, he earnestly instructed them by salutary admonition in the practice of holy conduct [Note: [Col. 1017] “Exercise,” 1.] and urged them toward the salvation of their souls with sweet-flowing exhortation and fatherly compassion. When the fifth day was dawning, he entered the oratory, received the viaticum that he himself had consecrated, and afterward, with his sacred limbs extended among the hands of his disciples [Note: [Col. 1017] Thus in the Life of E., V., and M.; absent in 1., 2., and 3.], on the fourth day before the Kalends of February, returned his spirit to heaven.

The disciples gathered his body, joined it to the most sacred body of Saint Eucharius, and buried it with divine praises in the same sarcophagus. We believe that this was done by heavenly providence, so that, since their minds had always been one in the Lord, their bodies too might not be separated from one another even by the grave [Note: [Col. 1017] The remainder is absent in Ch.].

## 13. That blessed Maternus was bishop for as many years as he lay in the tomb

(Ann. 314.) Then blessed Maternus, receiving the summit of the episcopal office [Note: [Col. 1017D] That a certain Maternus truly presided over the Cologne Church in 214 is taught by Optatus of Milevis, *On the Schism of the Donatists* I, 23, and by Constantine in a letter preserved in Eusebius X, 5. He took part in the Council of Arles. Mansi II, 476. Compare Perieri, *Disquisition on the One First Preached the Gospel in Belgium*, *Acta Sanctorum*, September, part IV, pp. 354 ff.], began to preach steadfastly throughout the cities and regions the true faith that is in Christ, to summon all by constant admonition to the way of salvation, to increase through great virtues, and to become renowned far and wide through signs and miracles. The more he saw the multitude of the faithful increase daily, the more diligently he strove to order the ministry entrusted to him according to rule.

Although he was a man of great authority and prudence [Note: [Col. 1017] Absent in Ch.], he exercised nothing by his own command [Col. 1018D] as though using free power [Note: [Col. 1017] Absent in Ch.], but did everything humbly and simply and, through the zeal of holy love, presented himself as a companion to his subjects. In everything he commendably accomplished, he sought not his own glory but Christ’s.

Among his other exercises of holy virtues [Note: [Col. 1019] Absent in Ch.], he applied himself most gently [Note: [Col. 1019] “Being,” corrected in 2.] to consoling the afflicted, fed the needy from what was available, clothed the naked, redeemed captives, welcomed strangers, mercifully showed the way of salvation to those who had gone astray, and gently promised the despairing the hope of obtaining pardon. He always urged those running along the way of God’s commandments onward toward what lay ahead [Note: [Col. 1019] “Toward what is within,” 3.; “toward better things,” Ch.], encouraged those lingering on that same way by exhortatory speech [Note: [Col. 1019] Absent in Ch.], and, now by teaching, now by exhorting, now by enduring, now by exposing himself to dangers [Note: [Col. 1019] Erased in 2.], continually came to everyone’s aid with pious consolation (c. 23).

Supported by these and other such works of goodness, he reached a holy and praiseworthy old age. And just as he lay in the tomb for forty days, so he remained for an equal number of years in the priestly ministry.

## 14. How Eucharius and Valerius called him from this world in a vision

He was accustomed during the night’s rest to visit silently the place where the bodies of the saints rest and to remain there alone for a long time in prayer [Note: [Col. 1019] The beginning is absent in Ch.; what follows differs considerably.]. Thus, when one night he entered the same church according to his custom and celebrated divine praises there at greater length, around midnight he began to be weighed down by sleep and to be hindered from the persistence of prayer by his tongue, which repeatedly stumbled.

As he sat on a bench that was there, he placed his elbows upon his knees [Note: [Col. 1019] “With his elbows fixed upon his knees,” corrected in 1.] and rested his holy head between both hands. Yielding briefly to sleep, he quickly fell asleep. Immediately Saint Eucharius and blessed Valerius appeared to him in a vision, shining with radiant faces [Note: [Col. 1019] Corrected from “most radiant” in 2.], gleaming in priestly vestments, wearing upon their heads individual crowns woven with marvelous artistry from roses, lilies [Note: [Col. 1019] “And,” 3.] and other fragrant flowers [Note: [Col. 1019] “Gems,” Ch.]. Showing him a similar garland, they said:

“Behold, Maternus, just as we once promised you, so we have come to you before the day of your sleep, to visit you. Therefore rejoice and be glad, because on the third day you will depart from this world and enter into the indescribable joys of your Lord.

“Behold [Note: [Col. 1019] The Life of Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus reads “Certainly.”] the incorruptible crown of your reward, taken from the paradise of perpetual delight [Note: [Col. 1019] Corrected from “delightfulness” in 2.] and sent to you by Christ through us, his servants. Its flower will never wither; its fragrance will never cease to be sweet; its permanence knows no end. After this corruptible present life, you will possess it incorruptibly, and with it you will remain eternally crowned before the King of kings.”

After saying these things, they immediately disappeared (c. 24).

Waking from his very light sleep [Col. 1020A], he was indeed exceedingly happy at the vision shown to him, but immediately felt that bodily distress was present [Note: [Col. 1019] “His distress,” 1.]. He summoned a servant, returned to his cell with his assistance [Note: [Col. 1019] Corrected to “assistance” in 2.], and privately related to his familiar disciples what had been shown to him (c. 24).

On the following day he summoned a company of brothers and began earnestly to admonish them concerning the integrity of faith, to kindle their souls toward heavenly desire with delightful words, and, without ceasing to give them salutary counsels throughout the day, prolonged his exhortatory discourse until the eighth hour of the following night. He spent the remainder of the night with the brothers in psalms and hymns [Note: [Col. 1019] “Hymns,” 2. and 3.].

After the cockcrow, when day was already approaching, a clear voice came from above, heard by all who were in that cell, saying:

“Maternus, beloved of God, come.”

As though hearing a familiar voice [Note: [Col. 1019] Absent in Ch.], he immediately turned to the brothers standing around him and said:

“Farewell, my little sons [Note: [Col. 1019] “My sons,” 2. and 3.], my inmost being. For I am now departing, and I shall no longer be with you in this present world [Note: [Col. 1019] “I shall not be with you,” 3.].”

Having said this [Note: [Col. 1019] “They completed,” 2. and 3.], he received communion in the Lord’s sacrament and immediately breathed out his holy soul. For his absolution, the faithful who were present completed fitting funeral rites [Note: [Col. 1019] “Seven,” 1.; but the heading of the chapters has “eight.”], and they honorably placed his body not far from the relics of Saints Eucharius and Valerius.

## 15. The eight bishops who succeeded blessed Maternus in the see of Tongeren [Note: [Col. 1019] Absent in Ch.]

After Maternus had been taken from human life, Navitus occupied the chair as his second successor, Marcellus as the third, Metropolus as the fourth, Severinus as the fifth, Florentinus as the sixth, Martinus as the seventh [Note: [Col. 1019] Absent in Ch.], Maximus as the eighth, and Valentinus as the ninth.

As for the times of which emperors or consuls they flourished in, what the end of each man’s life was, how many years each administered the episcopal office, where each one’s tomb is, or how much each increased the revenues of his church: since the devastation wrought by the Huns throughout Gaul destroyed not only our records but those of other churches as well, no reader should demand an exact account from us [Note: [Col. 1019] “Demands,” 1. and 3.; corrected to “should demand” in 2.].

We hold this certain: that the resources of all the churches flourished abundantly around the time when Constantine Augustus, of blessed memory, ruled the Roman world [Col. 1020D], and afterward his sons Constans and Constantius.

## 16. How orthodox men resisted the Arian heresy in various places

At that time also, when the rulers of the world had inclined toward the Christian religion [Col. 1021A] [Note: [Col. 1019] Absent in Ch.; what follows is expressed differently], and consequently the storm of persecution had ceased [Note: [Col. 1021] “Persecutions,” 1.], while the resources of the churches were overflowing, the more the abundance of wealth increased, the more it supplied fuel for luxury [Note: [Col. 1021] “Luxis,” 3.] and lust [Note: [Col. 1021] Supplied above the line in 2.]. These evils were especially surpassed by the treachery of the Arian heresy, which had sprinkled the entire Roman world with the offspring of its error [Note: [Col. 1021] The remainder is absent in Ch.].

Against this pest, which was spreading everywhere, stood especially those who hung from the neck of the Church and the tower of the true David, which was built with battlements, from which hung a thousand shields, every shield of the mighty (Song of Songs IV, 4): Silvester of Rome, Athanasius of Alexandria, Ambrose of Milan, Maximus of Trier, Hilary of Poitiers, Martin of Tours, Anianus of Orléans, Severinus of Cologne, Eusebius of Vercelli, and other likewise Catholic and distinguished bishops of that time [Col. 1021B] [Note: [Col. 1021D] Compare Sulpicius Severus II, 36, 37–45.].

Among them Athanasius was driven into exile throughout the world, but was fearlessly received by Maximinus, archbishop of Trier [Note: [Col. 1021D] Compare the seventh question that the author posed to Hugh in his letter: Arius’s shameful death could not have occurred, according to ecclesiastical history, under Alexander, his own bishop, in the time of Constantius, Constantine’s son. Alexander died eight years before Constantine’s death. Athanasius, who succeeded Alexander, endured his first exile at Trier by order of Constantine, not Constantius. At that time he took part, together with Maximus, bishop of Trier, Servatius of Tongeren, and many others, in the Council of Cologne, where Euphratas, bishop of that city, was condemned. Compare also Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History* X, 13, 18 ff.].

After him, the bishop Paulinus, together with Rhodanius [Note: [Col. 1022D] Of Toulouse.] and Hilary, likewise bishops of Gaul, was condemned to exile in Phrygia, where Paulinus of Trier died in exile (Ann. 364).

When this filth had subsequently sprouted under many emperors throughout the Christian empire, up to the time of Emperor Valens, the Most High saw that human wickedness was great and that every thought of the human heart was inclined toward evil at all times (Gen. VI, 5). He who had first cleansed the whole earth by the flood of waters [Note: [Col. 1021] Corrected from “flood” in 1.] so that the offspring from the intermingling of the sons of God—namely, those descended from Seth—with the daughters of men born from Cain [Col. 1021C] [Note: [Col. 1021] “Born from it,” 1. and 3.] might not be polluted, the offspring from which he had decreed to take flesh for our salvation, had in those times prepared destruction for the Roman world, so that the Church, redeemed by his blood and whitened above snow by the water of baptism, might no longer be stained by Arian treachery.

## 17. The Huns spread throughout the whole Roman empire

In the time, therefore, of the emperor Valens, who, last of all, did not fear to inflict persecution upon the Catholic churches [Note: [Col. 1021] “In the last persecution,” 1.], and who had been rebaptized by Eudoxius, arch-heretic [Note: [Col. 1021] “Arch-heretic,” corrected in 2.], according to Arian doctrine, the savage nation of the Huns emerged from its hiding places [Col. 1022A] and spread throughout the Roman world [Note: [Col. 1021] “Throughout the Roman world,” corrected in 1.; 3. reads “spread throughout the whole world.”].

Let us briefly relate the origin of this previously unknown people, as the ancient account presents it. Some say that at the time of the famine [Note: [Col. 1021] “Famine,” 1.] which, according to Bede [Note: [Col. 1021] “Bede attests,” Ch.], occurred in the tenth year of Claudius Caesar (Acts XI, 28) [Note: [Col. 1022D] This is derived in part from Bede’s *On the Six Ages of the World*, who writes that it was Claudius’s ninth year.], whom Luke also mentions in the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 1022D] This is taken in part from Bede’s *On the Six Ages of the World*], when Peter had entered Rome and was completing his ninth year there and Paul was urging all the churches to send alms for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem—for a measure of grain was being sold in Greece for six gold drachmas—when, I say, at that time, as Luke relates [Note: [Col. 1021] Absent in Ch.], Claudius, because of the scarcity that threatened the whole world, ordered not only the Jews to be expelled from the City but also all the weaker persons [Col. 1022B] [Note: [Col. 1021] Corrected in 1 to “the weaker”; original form in 1.], together with the Jews, to be shut up in a certain hidden place in the earth, so that at least the stronger might be supported by the remaining bread. It is said that they grew there into a great nation until the times mentioned above. It is well known, moreover, that the Hungarians wish to lend their support to this story, since they also boast that they derive their origin from the Jews.

As for the Huns, although many historians are available, the most trustworthy witness is especially Bishop Jordanes, who set out their origin most clearly in his history of the deeds of the Goths, or Getae, in these words:

## 18. That they are said to have been begotten by unclean spirits and by magical women

[Afterward [Note: [Col. 1021] Absent in Ch.], not after a long interval of time, as Orosius relates, the nation of the Huns burst forth with extraordinary ferocity against the Goths [Note: [Col. 1021] Absent in Ch.]. For we have learned from antiquity that their origin was as follows (Jordanes, 24):

Filimer, king of the Goths [Note: [Col. 1021] “Filime,” 1 and 3, and B 1; corrected to “Filimer” in 2; “Filimeth,” B 2.], son of the great Gadaric [Note: [Col. 1021] Erased in 2.], who, after the departure from the island of Scandia, was already the fifth to hold the sovereignty of the Getae [Note: [Col. 1021] Corrected from “held” to “was holding” in 2.] and had entered the Scythian lands with his people, as we have said, found among his people certain magical women. In his native language he himself called them Haliorunnae. Suspecting them, he drove them away from his midst and, having expelled them far from his army, forced them to wander in the wilderness.

When unclean spirits saw them wandering through the desert, they joined themselves to them in sexual intercourse, and they produced this most savage race. At first it was among the marshes, small, hideous, and stunted, resembling a human race, known by no other voice except that they gave an imitation of human speech. Thus created from such a stock, the Huns came to the borders of the Goths.

Their nation, savage—as the historian Priscus relates—dwelling on the farther bank of the Maeotian swamp, experienced nothing but hunting and no other labor, except that, after it had grown numerous among the peoples, it disturbed the borders of neighboring nations by fraud and plunder [Note: [Col. 1023] “Hunting,” corrected from “capture” in 2; “no other labor,” corrected in 2 from “another labor”; the phrase concerning growth among the peoples is corrected in 2 from “having grown into peoples”; the final phrase is transmitted variously: B 2 and D 1* read *fide*, 1 and 3 *fidem*, C and D 1 another form.].

## 19. How, led by a doe, they left the island, invaded the Goths first, then other peoples, and finally Gaul [Note: [Col. 1023] “The Gauls,” 3.]

While the hunters of this people were searching for game on the farther bank of Maeotis [Note: [Col. 1023] Various readings: “the farther bank of Maeotis,” 1; “the farther Maeotian bank,” 2 and 3; corrected to the present reading in 2.], they observed how suddenly a doe presented itself to them. Entering the marsh, now moving forward and now stopping, it offered itself as a guide to the way. The hunters followed it and crossed on foot the Maeotian swamp, which they had considered impassable like a sea [Note: [Col. 1023] “Like cattle,” 1, 2, and 3; Jordanes reads “sea.”].

As soon as Scythian land appeared to them, unknown as it was, the doe disappeared. I believe that the evil spirits from whom they derive their origin did this out of hatred for the Scythians [Note: [Col. 1023] Some witnesses add “the evil”; in C the word “spirit” is absent.]. But because they utterly did not know that any other world existed beyond Maeotis [Note: [Col. 1023] “Maeotis,” 1; “Maeotis,” corrected in 2 to another form.], they were filled with wonder at the land of Scythia. Being clever, and judging that what no one had previously known in that age had been divinely shown to them [Note: [Col. 1023] Erased in 2; absent in Jordanes.], they returned to their own people, reported what had happened, and praised Scythia. Having persuaded their nation, they hastened to Scythia by the route they had learned from the doe as guide [Note: [Col. 1023] “Their way” is absent; C reads “the route.”], and sacrificed in victory all whom they encountered at the entrance to Scythia; the rest they subdued and brought under their power.

For as soon as they had crossed that vast marsh, they immediately swept away, like a certain whirlwind of peoples, the Alpidzuri, Ildzuri, Itimari, Tuncorsi, and Boisci, who occupied the bank on that side of Scythia. They also subdued the Alans [Note: [Col. 1023] “Alantis,” 1; corrected to “Alanos” in 2; another form in 3.], equal to themselves in battle but different in civilization, food, and appearance, wearing them down through frequent conflict. Those whom they perhaps could not overcome in war they put to flight by inflicting immense fear through the terror of their appearance, for their appearance was terrifying in its blackness, like a shapeless lump, if one may say so, rather than a face, having points instead of eyes.

Their troubled appearance reveals the confidence of their spirit. They are also savage toward their own children on the very first day of their birth. For males they cut the cheeks with iron, so that before they receive the nourishment of milk they are forced to endure the endurance of a wound [Note: [Col. 1023] C and D 1 read “they become accustomed to harshness”; other witnesses have related readings.]. They grow old beardless and are effeminate without beauty [Note: [Col. 1023] “Without age,” 1, 2, and 3.], because the face furrowed by iron removes the grace of hair through its scars [Note: [Col. 1023] The readings vary between “removes the grace through scars” and “takes away grace by means of scars.”].

They are small in stature but sharp, swift in movement, and extremely ready for riding; broad-shouldered and prepared for bow and arrows; strong-necked and always holding themselves erect in pride. Yet they live under the appearance of human beings with the savagery of beasts.]

Finally, they began to attack the Gallic world.

## 20. Saint Servatius

At that time Saint Servatius presided as the tenth bishop over the see of Tongeren [Col. 1024B], a man angelic in appearance, most eloquent in speech, and distinguished by every moral excellence. Although some maintain [Note: [Col. 1023] “q. f. ex d. e.,” corrected to “coaeva” in 2.] that his origin and lineage descended from the family of the Savior’s relatives [Note: [Col. 1023C] In the later Life of Saint Lupus of Troyes, written at the end of the ninth century, Servatius is called the son of Emmuus, son of Eliud, who was a cousin of the blessed Virgin Mary, *Acta Sanctorum*, July VII, 77.], since we have by no means learned the place of his birth, nor have we heard anywhere else the reasons for his coming, we may be readily disposed to believe what we have heard [Note: [Col. 1023] “We have heard,” 1; the Life of Servatius adds “readily.”], nor do we think that an opinion of such magnitude, which perhaps arises from piety, should be altogether rejected.

But whoever does not object to the claim that, nearly three hundred years after the stoning of the protomartyr Stephen, the discoverer of the holy cross, Judas surnamed Quiriacus [Note: [Col. 1024C] On him and his apocryphal acts, see Papebroch’s commentary, *Acta Sanctorum*, May I, 439.], was the nephew of that protomartyr through his brother Simon [Col. 1024C], may likewise accept that, nearly four hundred years after the birth or passion of the Lord, blessed Servatius was a great-great-grandson of the holy Mother of God through his mother’s maternal aunt [Note: [Col. 1023] Absent in 3.].

However the matter may stand [Note: [Col. 1023] “However the matter stands,” 2 and 3.], those men did not labor excessively to persuade us, nor should we be excessively eager to reject them, since, in Cicero’s words, we ought not to be ashamed to admit that we do not know what we do not know [Note: [Col. 1024C] *Tusculan Disputations* I, 25.]. It is more fitting for them to confess their ignorance modestly than, irreverently in the name of piety, to lie [Note: [Col. 1023] “In the name of propriety,” 1, 2, and 3; Ch. reads “in the name of piety.”].

## 21. That many holy men were his contemporaries, and concerning the destruction of many cities [Note: [Col. 1023] “Subversion,” 3.]

This man, as is read in his earlier acts [Note: [Col. 1024C] Compare the preface, p. 143.], was born from the noble stock of great men [Col. 1025A], nobly born and more nobly conducted. He wore the episcopal mantle [Note: [Col. 1025D] Servatius, bishop of Tongeren, took part in the Council of Sardica in 347, Mansi III, 67, and afterward in that of Ariminum in 359. He was a vigorous opponent of the Arians, as Sulpicius Severus II, 44, testifies. Compare Henschenius’s commentary on Saint Servatius, *Acta Sanctorum*, May III, section VII.], protected the Lord’s sheep from the ambushing wolf and roaring lion, and was prepared to endure martyrdom on their behalf, even though the sword of their persecutors did not fall upon him.

Clearly, in the days of his priesthood he was pleasing to God and was found approved, righteous in the time of impending wrath (Ecclus. XLIV, 17), seeking reconciliation in view of the barbarian invasion. For at that time the Lord had kindled many such lamps, which could drive away the darkness of worldly error and calm the storms of raging tribulation amid so great a tempest.

Thus a certain poet, not inappropriately, said of them and of that time:

> With such protectors of the Church standing firm everywhere,
>
> they withstand the rain-bearing storms shaken by the wind from above,
>
> nor can they make the rock tremble to its ruin.

And specifically of this blessed man, among other verses:

> Servatius, by preserving the faith, preserves the perishing people,
>
> and by prayer stoutly preserves the people of Trajectum. [Note: [Col. 1025D] These verses are taken from the author’s own metrical *Life of Saint Ursmer*, Mabillon, cited work, p. 609.].

And blessed Lupus, bishop of the city of Troyes:

> While all wars were destroying everything,
>
> by prayer he fortified Troyes [Note: [Col. 1025D] As it is sung in his hymn: “While all wars…” These words are Bede’s in the *Martyrology* on the fourth day before the Kalends of August.].

Jerome too, writing a letter to Geruntia [Note: [Col. 1026D] Letter 123 to Ageruchia, whom the editors note is called Geruntia in some manuscripts. Jerome’s works, edition of Vallarsi, vol. 89.], concerning contempt for the world [Note: [Col. 1026D] It is entitled *On Monogamy*.], also took up a tearful lament over such a calamity. His words are these:

> That a few of us remain here to this day is due not to our merit but to the mercy of the Lord. Innumerable and most savage nations have occupied all Gaul. Whatever lies between the Alps and the Pyrenees, whatever is enclosed by the Ocean and the Rhine, the Quadi [Note: [Col. 1025] “Quod,” 2 and 3.], the Vandals and [Note: [Col. 1025] Absent in 1; added afterward in 2 and likewise in 3.] the Sarmatians, the Alans, the Gepids, the Heruli [Note: [Col. 1025] The witnesses give variant forms, including “Alanigi pedes herculi.”], the Saxons, the Burgundians, the Alemanni, and—O mournful disaster for the state!—the enemies of Pannonia have laid waste; indeed, Assur has come with them.
>
> Mainz, once a noble city, has been captured and destroyed, and many thousands of people have been slaughtered in its church. The people of Worms have been wiped out by a long siege. the most powerful city of Reims, Amiens, Arras, the remotest of peoples, the Morini, Tournai, the Nemetes, and Strasbourg have been transferred into Germany. The provinces of Aquitaine, of the Nine Peoples, of Lyon, and of Narbonne have been devastated almost entirely, except for a few cities [Col. 1025D] [Note: [Col. 1025] “Populated,” corrected from “papulated” in 2.]; and even these are ravaged from without by the sword and from within by famine.
>
> I cannot mention Toulouse without tears [Col. 1026A] [Note: [Col. 1025] “Dolosae,” corrected to “Tolosae” in 1.], whose survival to this day was secured by the merits of its bishop, Saint Exuperius. Spain itself, already trembling on the verge of destruction, remembers the invasion of the Cimbri [Note: [Col. 1025] Jerome reads “Cimbric.”] and trembles; whatever others have suffered once, Spain suffers continually through fear.
>
> I say nothing of the rest, lest I seem to despair of God’s mercy. Formerly, from the Pontic Sea to the Julian Alps, the lands that are now ours did not belong to us; and for thirty years, after the Danube frontier had been broken, battles were fought in the heart of the Roman Empire. Tears have dried up through age. Except for a few old men, all were born in captivity and siege and did not desire the liberty they had never known.]

And because the pious do not perish on behalf of the impious, it also happened that many holy men—clerics as well as monks and nuns—fell in this destruction. Heavily fortified cities were overthrown despite long sieges; the churches of the saints were burned; the altars were polluted with the precious blood of slaughtered priests; children and unmarried girls were strangled; virgins dedicated to God were violated [Note: [Col. 1025] “strupabantur,” 1.]; monks and clerics were exposed to mockery and public spectacles; and every kind of death was inflicted indiscriminately upon all.

And because such a portion of the people deserved this on account of its wickedness, the sword of the Most High raged as far as destruction. Thus it happened that Saint Nicasius, bishop of the city of Reims, together with Saint Eutropia, a virgin and his sister, like many others, caused the church’s marble to be stained by a shower of precious blood during this invasion of the Huns [Note: [Col. 1026D] The *Passion of Saints Nicasius and Eutropia*, *Surius* VII, 1011, is later than Herigerus.].

Nor were only our people punished by this penalty. The Goths, defenders of the Arian heresy, who alone seemed to resist and oppose Emperor Valens and the Romans in Gaul, were also cruelly devastated by the Huns. Athanaric, their king, because he had not feared to shed much innocent Catholic blood, was driven from his kingdom and deserved to go into exile.

But when the Huns were compelled by famine, through the avarice of Maximus, the prefect of Gaul appointed by Valens, they were forced to oppose the Roman side, and soon afterward to occupy Gaul again, laying waste cities and fortresses together with their inhabitants in a cruel slaughter [Note: [Col. 1026D] Compare below, c. 26, where the author reports the same thing, no less falsely, about the Franks.].

## 22. That Saint Servatius went to Rome to see whether he might free Gaul from the Huns by prayer [Note: [Col. 1025] “From,” 3.]

[Col. 1026D] When Saint Servatius, bishop of the church of Tongeren, heard of their arrival (*Deeds of Saint Servatius*; cf. Gregory of Tours II, 5), and at the same time feared the invasion and destruction of his city, he afflicted his body with many vigils and fasts, and, pouring himself out in frequent tears [Note: [Col. 1027] *profundens* (“pouring out”): text; *perfundens* (“drenching”): 1 and *vit. Serv.*], begged God’s mercy, asking that God never permit this unbelieving nation, which was always unworthy of him, to enter Gaul [Note: [Col. 1027] Absent in Ch.] [Note: [Col. 1027] Everyone agrees that this in fact occurred only a hundred years after Servatius.] and allow the nation dedicated to his worship to be defiled in some way [Note: [Col. 1027] *quomodo* (“in what manner”): 1, 2; corrected to *quodammodo* (“in some way”) in 2; *quoquomodo* (“in any way whatever”) in *vit. Serv.] [Note: [Col. 1027] Absent in Ch.]. But when he perceived through the Holy Spirit that this was in no way being granted to him because the sins of the people were intervening [Note: [Col. 1027] *interpellantibus* (“intervening”): text; *interpellentibus* (a different inflection of the same verb): 3], he resolved to visit the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul, so that at least, through their intercession, he might be deemed worthy to be heard concerning the salvation of his city [Note: [Col. 1027] *salvatione* (“concerning the salvation,” ablative): text and *vit. Serv.*; *salutem* (“salvation,” accusative): 1, 2, 3].

And because [Note: [Col. 1027] *Et* (“and”) is absent in Ch.], before anything is begun, it is necessary to deliberate, but once deliberation has taken place, action must follow promptly [Note: [Col. 1027] Absent in Ch.; cf.
