Sallust, *Catiline* 1], having prepared suitable provisions for the journey and taken with him the necessary companions, he also gave his citizens a blessing and announced that, in view of so great a danger, they must persist together in vigils and prayers, fasts and almsgiving. He decided also to confer about this matter with the blessed Auctor, bishop of Metz, both in name and in merit, who [Note: [Col. 1027] Absent in Ch.] was then regarded as outstanding in the affairs of God, but was exceedingly anxious about the destruction of those entrusted to him and about the invasion of his own city as well [Note: [Col. 1027] Absent in Ch.].

After deliberating with blessed Servatius, Auctor judged that his intention was sound, while at the same time asking him to pour out a more abundant prayer on his own behalf and that of his city before the threshold of the apostles. Since he himself could not visit Rome, he asked that, through the intercession of that most holy man, he too might be deemed worthy to obtain what he desired.

Having therefore undertaken so great a journey [Note: [Col. 1027] The following passage is expressed very differently in Ch.], and disregarding all the hardships of the road—both during the vast crossing of the Alps [Note: [Col. 1027] The text has *tum* (“both/then”); *dum* (“while”) in 1, 2, 3], and in passing over the rivers [Note: [Col. 1027] The text has *tum* (“both/then”); *dum* (“while”) in 1], and also amid the attacks of robbers [Note: [Col. 1027] *dum* (“while”) in 1 was corrected to *tunc* (“then”)]—provided only that he could attain what he had vowed, he finally made his way to Rome.

### 23. How, before the tomb of blessed Peter, he learned in a vision of the destruction of all Gaul and of his own death

Coming, therefore, to the tomb of blessed Peter (cf. Gregory of Tours II, 5), he implored the aid of his intercession. Since the Almighty had honored the western world through Peter’s apostolate [Note: [Col. 1027] Absent in Ch.; the following is otherwise expressed], he asked that he at least restrain the unspeakable nation of the Huns from the cities of Tongeren and Metz [Note: [Col. 1027] Absent in Ch.; the following is otherwise expressed].

Persisting without respite in this prayer, he weakened himself by great austerity, consuming his body with the severest hunger, so that for the span of three days, and sometimes two [Note: [Col. 1027] *ita* (“thus”): *vit. Serv.*; *interdiu* (“during the day”): 1, 2, 3], he remained without food or drink, with no interval in which he was free from prayer. By day he frequently sought the patronage of other saints, but by night he returned to the tomb of blessed Peter. At last, because he did not cease to knock without interruption at the ears of the most merciful God, he was deemed worthy of consolation through the following vision [Note: [Col. 1027] the difficult printed *solari* and *consolari* (“to be consoled”) in *vit. Serv.*].

He saw—and behold, as if before the altar of blessed Peter, a throne had been set; and the Most High was seated upon the throne, with a chorus of holy souls [Note: [Col. 1027] *sanctarum* (“holy female souls”): 1, 2, 3; *sanctorum* (“holy souls”): *vit. Serv.*] and angels all around. Two men of distinguished appearance were bending their knees before the throne [Note: [Col. 1027] *genu incurvantes* (“bending the knee”): *vit. Serv.*; *inculcantes* (“pressing or urging repeatedly”): 1, 2, 3], alternately imploring the majesty of the Lord and alternately seeking the intervention of the holy Mother of God. These were evidently the chief apostles, Peter and Paul, and they were earnestly pleading for the preservation of the Gauls.

Since the same holy man [Note: [Col. 1027] *idem* (“same”) is absent in 3] to whom these things were being shown had also presented, together with his own supplication, the prayer of blessed Auctor, bishop of Metz, he saw, standing on the opposite side toward the north, a certain faithful man splendidly clothed in white garments. Without doubt this was the protomartyr Stephen [Note: [Col. 1027] *martirem*, corrected to *martyrem* in 2]. The holy apostles were conveying certain responses to him, and he in turn was presenting certain supplications to the majesty of the Almighty [Note: [Col. 1027] *iterum* (“again”) is added in *vit. Serv.*].

Saint Peter then approached Saint Servatius, astonished by this vision, as he stood, so to speak, upon the steps of the church:

“Why,” he said [Note: [Col. 1027] The text has *quit*; *inquit* (“he said”) in 3 and *vit. Serv.*], “do you trouble me, most holy man? Behold, it has been decided by a most just decree before the Almighty that the Huns will attack all Gaul, level all its towns and fortresses in Europe to the ground, and that your city, because the sins of the people demand it, will be utterly destroyed [Note: [Col. 1027] Likewise in the *Life of Servatius*].

“The one whom you see speaking with us in the northern part [Note: [Col. 1027] *interloquentem* (“speaking with [us]”): text; *loquentem* (“speaking”): *vit. Serv.*]—know that he is Stephen the protomartyr [Note: [Col. 1027] *esse* (“to be”) is added in *vit. Serv.*], humbly pleading for the city of Metz [Note: [Col. 1027] *subplicius* (“more humbly”): text; *suppliciter* (“humbly”): *vit. Serv.*] [Note: [Col. 1027] The following explanation is absent in Ch.]. Although he was the first to offer God, before all others, the dew of precious blood which he received from him in common with the whole human race, we could scarcely obtain for him [Note: [Col. 1027] *habere* (“to have”): text; *optinere* (“to obtain”): *vit. Serv.*] that at least the oratory in the city of the Mediomatrici, where his blood is known to spring forth, might escape the flames and destruction of the rest of the city. You have this also to convey in your replies to Auctor, your fellow bishop [Note: [Col. 1027] *coepiscopo* (“fellow bishop”): text; *episcopo* (“bishop”): 1; the following wording is absent in Ch.].

“But you [Note: [Col. 1027] *Tu* (“you”): 1, 2, and *vit. Serv.*; corrected to *Tua* (“your”) in 2 and 3], most holy soul, already chosen for a place among the saints, because you have become pleasing to God and beloved during the days of your priesthood, are now and presently to be taken away while living among sinners, because righteousness has been found in you. Now, I say, you are to be gathered to your fathers [Note: [Col. 1027] I did not hesitate to adopt from the *Life of Saint Servatius* the words “to be taken away … to your fathers,” lacking in our manuscripts. Their reading, “seeing that, while living among sinners, you are now and presently to be gathered,” persuades us that something has fallen out; the repeated words “now” and “are” likewise support this. Aegidius also preserved the words “and shortly to be taken away.”], lest your eyes see the evils which the Huns will inflict throughout Gaul, and especially in your city [Note: [Col. 1027] Absent in Ch.].

“For Tongeren, just as in name, so also in deed, having been cut down and destroyed, will remain so to the end [Note: [Col. 1029] *finem* (“end”): text; *aeternum* (“forever”): *vit. Serv.*]. Therefore hasten your return without delay; put your household in order; seek clean linen [Note: [Col. 1029] The words *nitida linteamina quere* (“seek clean linen”) are absent in *vit. Serv.*], and prepare your burial [Note: [Col. 1019] Absent in Ch.]. You will not have a grave in that wicked city, and therefore doomed to perish, because it has pleased the Most High to preserve the town of Maastricht [Note: [Col. 1029] *reservare* (“to preserve/save”): text; *servare* (“to preserve”): 3], so that your little body may be buried there.”

Having received this oracle [Note: [Col. 1029] *oraculo* (“oracle”): text; *miraculo* (“miracle”): 3], the venerable bishop Servatius hastened his return and made his way back to Gaul as quickly as possible [Note: [Col. 1029] *citissime* (“as quickly as possible”): text; *citius* (“more quickly”): 2, 3]. Passing through the city of Metz, he told blessed Auctor what he had received in the responses.

### 24. Returning, he explains to the flock entrusted to him what he had seen

At last, greatly wearied both by the difficulty of the journey and by the haste of his return, he reached the city of Tongeren [Note: [Col. 1029] The wording is either absent or expressed differently in Ch.], which was anxiously awaiting the arrival of its shepherd. Taking with him on the road priests and Levites devoted to the Lord, he made arrangements for everything that seemed appropriate for a burial, and also consulted the whole community, so that, in view of the danger threatening them, they might be prepared for the salvation of their souls.

After concealing his departure for three days, he finally addressed them all, gathered in the greater Catholic church of the blessed ever-virgin Mary [Note: [Col. 1029] The wording is either absent or expressed differently in Ch.]:

“Now I can no longer conceal from your brotherhood [Note: [Col. 1029] *vestrae* (“your”): *vit. Serv.*; *nostrae* (“our”): 2, 3] what I have concealed for three days and am at last compelled to say [Note: [Col. 1029] This opening of the address is absent in Ch.]. From this day onward you will not see my face, nor will you see me remaining any longer in this city with you [Note: [Col. 1029] *morantem* (“remaining”): text; *commorantem* (“remaining”): 3], because I am going the way of all the earth and will not return here again [Note: [Col. 1029] Absent in Ch.].

“Some time ago I visited the tomb of blessed Peter concerning your salvation. After first offering my supplication, I asked for the preservation of this city. Since I did not deserve this on account of your sin [Note: [Col. 1029] *peccato non merebar* (“I did not deserve [it] because of the sin”): text; *peccatum ... merebatur* (“the sin ... deserved”): *vit. Serv.*], I received this response:

“‘For everlasting destruction threatens this city, and your own immense destruction also [Note: [Col. 1029] *perimmanis* (“immense”): *vit. Serv.*; *per manus* (“through hands”) in 1], unless a conversion of conduct precedes it from the whole heart.’

“Therefore I too have been forbidden to dig a grave for myself here, and I have been ordered to go from here to the village of Maastricht [Note: [Col. 1029] *jussus* (“ordered”): text, 1, and *vit. Serv.*; *missus* (“sent”): 2, 3], so that my final day may overtake me there before I can either see or endure with you the evils that will befall you.

“But this much I promise you, as far as lies within me: if [Note: [Col. 1029] *pro* (“for”) is absent in 3 and *vit. Serv.*], because your sins outweigh my prayers, I cannot be heard when I plead for the salvation of your bodies, then, when I have died and reign with Christ, I shall intervene more effectively and obtain at least the salvation of your souls [Note: [Col. 1029] *saltem* (“at least”) is added in *vit. Serv.*], which God has entrusted to me.”

### 25. His prayer, the lamentation of the clergy and people, and his death

[Col. 1029D]

After consoling them with much exhortation, he raised his eyes to heaven [Note: [Col. 1029] *surrectis* and the *vit. Serv.* reading *levatis* both mean “raised”], together with his hands, and said [Note: [Col. 1029] The introductory *Et* (“and”) is absent in Ch.]:

“Lord, these sheep whom you have redeemed with your precious blood—this flock, I say, because it is yours, I deliver to you today, and I commend myself wholly to you [Note: [Col. 1029] Absent in Ch.]. I beseech you, most righteous judge, with humble and tearful prayer: do not let ravening wolves overthrow your sheepfold, sparing none of the flock; do not let them consume the flesh of your sheep by devouring it [Note: [Col. 1029] *neve* (“and do not”): text; *nec ve* (the same words written separately): 2, 3, with *ve* erased in 2]. You, Lord Jesus, who laid down your life for them in death, rescue their souls from the ravenousness of wolves [Note: [Col. 1029] *voracitate* (“ravenousness”): text; misspelled *voratitate*: 1, 2] and from the roaring lion, so that I may bring back to you some sheaves from them [Note: [Col. 1029] *de eis* (“from them”) is added in *vit. Serv.*].”

When blessed Servatius had tearfully finished these words [Note: [Col. 1029] *His ergo* (“when these things, therefore”): text; *igitur* (“therefore”): 3 and *vit. Serv.*; *flebiliter* (“tearfully”) is added in *vit. Serv.*], the entire crowd standing there immediately broke into a great roar [Note: [Col. 1029] *irrugiit* (“roared out”): *vit. Serv.* and Ch.; *irriguit* (“drenched”): 1, 2, 3], and mourning and wailing increased among both sexes [Note: [Col. 1029] *ejulatio* and the form *julatio* in 3 both mean “wailing”; the transition *At* (“then/but”) is absent in Ch.].

Then the man of God, taking with him what was necessary for his burial, went on foot toward the eastern region and exited through the gate of Tongeren, taking the road that leads to the town of Maastricht [Note: [Col. 1029] The printed wording through *oppidum* (“town”) is likewise in 1, 2; the following wording is absent in Ch.].

Then everyone followed his footsteps with shouting and tears [Note: [Col. 1029] *persequuti* (“followed”): text; *prosecuti* (“followed”): *vit. Serv.*], leaving the city in sorrow and adding these humble words:

“Do not abandon us, holy father; do not forget us, most watchful shepherd—we are your people and the sheep of your flock. Do not leave us in the jaws of the raging enemy.”

The monks and consecrated maidens of God, whose monasteries were very numerous there [Note: [Col. 1029] *perplura* (“very numerous”): text; *plura* (“more numerous”): 3], together with the entire clergy, came out from the monastery and followed his journey. They beat their breasts and, after all this, threw themselves to the ground [Note: [Col. 1029] *post* (“after”): text and *vit. Serv.*; *per* (“through”): 1, 2, 3], and repeatedly cried out:

“Why, good shepherd, are you abandoning us so quickly, or where are you now rushing away to go [Note: [Col. 1029] *iturus* (“about to go”) is added in *vit. Serv.*]? Take us with you, so that, dying with you, we may be buried with you—our only misfortune is to be left behind you.

“We rejoiced at your arrival [Note: [Col. 1029] The words beginning with *Adventu* (“at [your] arrival”) are absent in Ch.], because, having returned from a distant pilgrimage [Note: [Col. 1029] *longinqua*, corrected from *longuinqua* in 1], you had deigned now to be with us [Note: [Col. 1029] *esse* (“to be”): text; *esses* (“you might be”): 1], yet you are unwilling to remain with us even for the space of three days [Note: [Col. 1029] *nec* (“not even”): *vit. Serv.*].

“Tell us what must be done, and what counsel we should take when you depart [Note: [Col. 1029] *quidve* (“and what”): text; *quidque* (“and what”): *vit. Serv.*; this clause is absent in Ch.]. What, then, will become of us, now that the presence of so great a father is taken from us [Note: [Col. 1029] *ergo* (“therefore”) is added in *vit. Serv.*]? What shall we wretched people do, who cannot live without you but are destined to be handed over to the worst death [Note: [Col. 1029] *vivere* (“to live”): text; the misspelling *vivivuere*: 2]? Woe to us, who are deprived of your presence because we are exposed to heavenly vengeance, and are not worthy to be freed from this punishment by dying with you [Note: [Col. 1029] *tibi* (“with you”) is added in *vit. Serv.*]. It is far too unworthy of you to be entangled with us in our destruction.

“Ah, ah [Note: [Col. 1029] *O, o* (“Ah, ah”) is absent in Ch.]—the name of shepherd which you always bore before you! You preferred to die for those entrusted to you rather than expose the sheep of your flock to wolves that would tear them apart [Note: [Col. 1029] At “your flock,” witnesses 2, 3, and *vit. Serv.* have the unexplained abbreviated reading *gr. t.*]. But we are exposed not merely to be torn apart, but to be utterly devoured.

“At least [Note: [Col. 1029] *Saltem* (“at least”): text; spelling *saltim*: 2, 3], perhaps on this occasion [Note: [Col. 1029] *hac* (“on this”): text and *vit. Serv.*; *his* (“in these”): 1; *hic* (“here”): 2, 3], you may find the martyrdom that you have always thirsted for [Note: [Col. 1029] *invenires* (“you might find”): text and *vit. Serv.*; *invenire* (“to find”): 1, 2, 3], and your death, witnessed before our eyes, may somehow be a consolation for our own death [Note: [Col. 1029] Absent in Ch.].”

[Col. 1031A] “We beg you [Note: [Col. 1031] *quaesumus* (“we beg”) is abbreviated *qs.* in 1, 2, 3] to abandon the intention you have proposed, making some delay in your departure, so that, by postponing it for three days, two days, or at least one night, he who deigned to spare the Ninevites may deign to accept the fruit of our repentance.”

Moved by their pursuit [Note: [Col. 1031] The transition beginning *Quorum* (“by whose [pursuit]”) is absent in Ch.] and likewise tormented by the tearful cries of those repeating such words [Note: [Col. 1031] *ingeminantium* (“of those repeating”): *vit. Serv.*; *ingeminantius* (“more repeatedly”): 1, 2, 3], blessed Servatius gradually proceeded, then resisted again, dissolving in tears, and, as one must suppose, endured martyrdom [Note: [Col. 1031] Likewise in 1, 2, 3, and *vit. Serv.*]. While, in compassionate affection [Note: [Col. 1031] *compassionabili* (“compassionate”): text; *compassibili* (“capable of suffering/compassion”): 3], he was being refined beyond gold [Note: [Col. 1031] *exquoquebatur* (“was being refined”): text and *vit. Serv.*; *exquoquatur* (“may be refined”): 1, 2, 3], he was tortured by natural affection for those already about to be abandoned, and was compelled to depart because of the irretrievable destruction of his people, as he had said [Note: [Col. 1031] Absent in Ch.].

But the weaker and lame [Note: [Col. 1031] At *inbecilliores et claudi* (“the weaker and lame”), *ut* is written above *et* in 2; hence 3 reads *utque*], the poor and pilgrims, widows and orphans, standing upon the towers and battlements, scattered dust toward heaven [Note: [Col. 1031] *spargentes* (“scattering”): text; *aspergentes* (“sprinkling”): 1], and with weeping and sobbing cried out:

“Who will give us food? Who will provide nourishment [Note: [Col. 1031] *alimentum* (“nourishment”): text; *indumentum* (“clothing”): Ch.]? We are naked and hungry; who will console us?”

But since he could not be called back by these tears [Note: [Col. 1031] *fletibus* (“tears”): *vit. Serv.* adds *his* (“these”)], he gave them his episcopal blessing, kissed and encouraged them, and compelled them to return.

When he approached the village of Maastricht, he was struck by a slight fever, released from his frail body, carried out in a public funeral [Note: [Col. 1031] *elatus* (“carried out”): text; *elevatus* (“raised”): *vit. Serv.*], and buried by faithful men beside the public embankment on 13 May.

### 26. How the Huns destroyed many cities of Gaul, including Tongeren [Note: [Col. 1031] *Tungris* (“with Tongeren”): text; *Tungri* (“the people of Tongeren”): 1, 2], and how the Franks [Note: [Col. 1031] *Franci* (“Franks”) is written over an erasure in 1] in turn expelled them from Gaul

After his death [Note: [Col. 1031D] *Life of Saint Lupus of Troyes*, ch. 36], the Huns, after destroying many cities of Gaul, also demolished the city of Tongeren. When they reached the city of Metz [Note: [Col. 1031] *Mettensem* and the form *Mettense* in 1 both designate Metz] on the eve of Easter, they surrounded it with siegeworks. Exhausted by the long siege, when they had already begun to discuss returning, the city walls collapsed of their own accord and opened a passage for those returning.

Then they entered the city without delay and killed everyone, as they had at Tongeren, by the edge of the sword; they committed the rest of the city to fire, except for the oratory of blessed Stephen, which they believed was being defended by a certain most splendid man standing above it [Note: [Col. 1031D] Paul the Deacon gives a somewhat different account in *Deeds of the Bishops of Metz*, MGH II, 263. See also Hirsch’s discussion of this story in his study of Sigebert, p. 229].

After this vengeance, therefore [Note: [Col. 1031] *eam* (“this”) is absent in 1], which they inflicted by the slaughter of Gaul, while the cruelty of the Vandals followed [Note: [Col. 1031] *prosequente* (“following”): text; *persequente* (“pursuing”): *vit. Serv.*], or rather preceded it, as is clear from the fragment of Jerome’s letter in chapter 21 [Note: [Col. 1031D] Rather, it preceded it, as is clear from the fragment itself of Jerome’s letter in chapter 21], it is uncertain—as is also recorded concerning the bishops of many other cities—how long the church of Tongeren remained without a bishop, while the few surviving Christians hid themselves in secret places among the mountains and in rocky caves [Note: [Col. 1031] *Tungrensis* (“of Tongeren”): text; misspelled *trungrensis*: 2; *fuerit* (“may have remained”): text and *vit. Serv.*; *fuit* (“was”): 1, 2, 3].

For the Franks [Note: [Col. 1031] *Frangi* is the spelling in 1], who traced their origin to Antenor (*Deeds of the Franks* I), and Venetia [Note: [Col. 1031] *Vinetia*: text; *Venetia* (the place-name Venetia): *vit. Serv.*]—or [Note: [Col. 1031] *vel ut* (“or as”): text; *velud* (a spelling of *velut*, “just as”) in 1, 2], as others report [Note: [Col. 1031] This wording follows *vit. Serv.* and is absent in 1, 2, 3], Mauretania [Note: [Col. 1031D] The author seems to have derived the name Antenor in this direction, mindful of Livy’s narrative.] [Note: [Col. 1031D] Thus, by an unsuccessful effort, he interpreted the name *Maurungani*, which he found in the Ravenna Geographer I, 11: “The homeland of the Albis Maurungani was most certainly so called in ancient times; in that homeland the line of the Franks remained for many years.”]—had grown into a great nation, and the Sicambri [Note: [Col. 1031] *Sicambri*: text; *Sicabri*: 1, 2, 3], or, as they were called after a leader of their people, Merovingians, since their own homeland could no longer suffice for them because of their numbers [Note: [Col. 1031] *eis* (“for them”): text; *ejus* (“its”): 1, 2, 3], wandered here and there and were devoted to plunder and robbery [Note: [Col. 1031] *intenti erant* (“were intent”): text; *intenderant* (“had devoted themselves”): *vit. Serv.*]. They had not yet found a permanent settlement; only Thuringia was their refuge.

The emperor Valens, to whom supreme authority belonged, gave them both a proper name—“Franks,” as they were called in the Attic language—and part of Gaul, permitting them to use and inhabit it without the exaction of taxes [Note: [Col. 1032D] With a hurried pen, the author took this from *Deeds of the Franks* II. It was not the emperor Valentinian, but the Franks who were called by this name in the Attic language]. He also compelled the Huns to go to the Maeotian marshes or to Pannonia [Note: [Col. 1031] *ire* (“to go”): *vit. Serv.*; *iterum* (“again”): 1, 2, 3] [Note: [Col. 1031] At “compelled,” *compulit* is the text; *compellere* (“to compel”) in 1, 2, 3; *compullere* in Ch.], where, after many years, they perished completely, even in name, at the hands of the emperor Charlemagne and his son Pippin [Note: [Col. 1032D] This seems to have been taken from Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne*, ch. 13.].

But because of the greed of the succeeding emperors, who demanded taxes from them, the Franks were compelled both not to keep faith with the Romans and to seize the cities of Gaul which they still hold [Note: [Col. 1032D] See chapter 21]. These people, I say, still served pagan rites, and therefore many cities lacked bishops [Note: [Col. 1031] *vacabant* (“were vacant”): text; *carebant* (“lacked”): Ch.].

### 27 [Note: [Col. 1031] The chapter number is *XXVI* in 1, 2]. Concerning Saint Remigius and [Note: [Col. 1031] *et* (“and”) is absent in 1] the seven bishops of Tongeren

[Col. 1032C]

At last, when this had been foretold from heaven to Saint Remigius, and he had been born through a promise so that he might convert that people to the worship of the living God and the people of Gaul might come together in the unity of the Catholic faith—for [Note: [Col. 1031] The passage beginning *jam* (“now”) is absent in Ch.] the mercy of the Most High was flowing forth, despite the corrupt or uncertain reading *ablato* [Note: [Col. 1031] The reading *stillabat* (“was dripping”) in 1 appears as *still: bat* in 2; *stillebat* (“was dripping”) seems to have been the original, corrected to *stillabat* in 3], and the spirits of the blessed angels and human beings were already demanding that mercy be shown to Gaul, saying: “It is the time to have mercy on her, for the time has come” [Note: [Col. 1031] Absent in Ch.; cf. Hincmar, *Life of Saint Remigius*, ch. 2]—at that time, then, the eleventh bishop to preside over the church of Tongeren was Agricolus; thereafter came:

12. Ursicinus  
13. Designatus  
14. Resignatus [Note: [Col. 1033] *Resignatus*: text; *Renatus*: *vit. Serv.*, 1, 2, 3]  
15. Supplicius [Note: [Col. 1033] *Supplicius*: text; corrected to *Sulpicius* in *vit. Serv.*]  
16. Quirillus  
17. Eucherus [Note: [Col. 1033] *Eucherus*: text; *Eucherius*: 3]  
18. Falco [Note: [Col. 1033D] Falco was presiding over the people of Tongeren in Saint Remigius’s time, if we may trust the letter sent by Remigius to Falco in Sirmond I, 205.]  
19. Eucharius.

### 28. Concerning Saint Domitian, and likewise Perpetuus and [Note: [Col. 1033] *itemque Perpetuo et* (“and likewise Perpetuus and”) is absent in 1, 2] Ebergisus

The twentieth bishop was Domitian [Note: [Col. 1033D] The lives of Saint Domitian preserved in the *Acta Sanctorum*, May II, were written after his translation in 1173; nor is the other life of Saint Monulfus, in *Acta Sanctorum*, July I, of greater importance]. When the Christian religion was already flourishing everywhere, during the reign of the most glorious King Hildebert (in the year 549), he is recorded as having attended the Council of Orléans [Note: [Col. 1033D] The fifth council, held in 549, whose acts Domitian signed. Mansi IX, 135. In Alberic’s *Chronicle* under the year 511 we read: “It is said that from the death of blessed Servatius until the Council of Orléans the see of Tongeren was vacant for eighty years and more.”].

Disdaining the city of Tongeren, which had already been destroyed [Note: [Col. 1033] *dirutae* (“destroyed”): text; corrupt *diruputae*: 1, 2, 3], he frequently visited the tomb of Saint Servatius at Maastricht. Around that tomb, even if a great quantity of snow had fallen, so that sometimes the surrounding ground was covered to a depth of two or even three feet [Note: [Col. 1033] At “sometimes,” *ita* (“thus”): *vit. Serv.*; *interdiu* (“by day”): 1, 2, 3], his mound was never covered by it (*Deeds of Saint Servatius*; cf. Gregory of Tours, *The Glory of the Confessors*, ch. 72). It was a wonder to see the mountains all around covered with snow, yet not to see Saint Servatius’s grave touched by it [Note: [Col. 1033] Ch. reads “not touched by the snow”].

Christ also performed many miracles in that place, clearly showing that the merits of the holy man were continually precious in his sight. For this reason the devotion of the faithful brothers and the zeal of the frequenting people often attempted, as far as possible, to make a little oratory for him [Note: [Col. 1033] *oratoriolum* (“little oratory”): text; *oratorium* (“oratory”): *vit. Serv.*]. But because such a structure was not worthy of so great a man—being made of smoothed wood and fitted boards—it was quickly either [Note: [Col. 1033] First *aut* (“either”): text; *ut* (“as/that”): 1] carried away by the wind or [Note: [Col. 1033] Second *aut* (“or”): text; *ut* (“as/that”): 1] collapsed of its own accord to the ground [Note: [Col. 1033] *subruebant* (“they collapsed”): text; *subruebantur* (“they were brought down”): *vit. Serv.*].

After Saint Domitian had been taken from human affairs [Note: [Col. 1033] *humanis* (“from human affairs”): text; *hominum* (“of human beings”): 1] and buried at Huy [Note: [Col. 1034D] Huy on the Meuse], in the greater church of holy Mary, Mother of God [Note: [Col. 1033] *theotocos* (“God-bearer/Mother of God”): text; *Dei genetricis* (“Mother of God”): *vit. Serv.*], blessed Monulfus, the twenty-first, succeeded him in the governance of the church of Tongeren in the course of time. He erected, completed, and adorned an honored temple in memory of the holy man, transferred his body there with due reverence, and henceforth established the episcopal seat at Maastricht [Note: [Col. 1033] *eo modo* (“in that manner”): 1, 2, 3; *ita* in *vit. Serv.*], where he also ordered that his own body be buried in the middle of the church.

There too blessed Gundulfus, who succeeded him as the twenty-second bishop, has a place of burial [Note: [Col. 1034D] The bodies of Monulfus and Gundulfus were raised in the presence of King Henry III by Nithard of Liège and Gerard of Cambrai in August 1039. See *Chronicle of Cambrai* III, 51. Concerning their tomb, opened in 1623, and the inscriptions found in it, see the *Acts of the Elevation*, *Acta Sanctorum*, July I.].

Saint Perpetuus, who presided as the twenty-third bishop, rests at Dinant [Note: [Col. 1033] *aput Deonantum* (“at Dinant”): text; *Dionantum requiescit* (“rests at Dinant”): 3; [Col. 1034D] Dinant].

Blessed Ebergisus, who succeeded as the twenty-fourth bishop, was buried at Trutmonia, a village of that same bishopric [Note: [Col. 1033] *episcopatus* (“of the bishopric”): text; *episcopatu* (“bishopric,” ablative): 1, 2, 3; [Col. 1034D] See Anselm’s letter to Anno].

### 29. Concerning Saint John

After these men had been called by succession to other things, John, the twenty-fifth, succeeded—a man of complete holiness. Since we have received his life and deeds only by hearsay and by reports from our elders and those advanced in age, we too shall dispose of them in very few words.

Nor should it be thought impossible [Note: [Col. 1033] The difficult printed form is *difficere*; *difficile* (“difficult/impossible”): Ch.; [Col. 1034D] *difficere* is interpreted as *deficere* (“to fail”)], however unusual the matter may be, for God—who is wonderfully able to accomplish all things—to glorify his saints [Note: [Col. 1033] *suos* (“his”) is absent in 3] beyond telling in whatever ways he chooses. He is powerful enough [Note: [Col. 1033] *potens* (“powerful”) is absent in Ch.] to accomplish even more wondrous things, adapting times to circumstances and bringing timely interventions to the untimely and unbelieving.

For, as the Apostle says, tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers (1 Corinthians 14:22), so that those who do not heed the Omnipotent working daily in the making of the world, in the harmony of the elements, in the governance of the heavenly mechanism, and in the annual renewal of seeds, crops, and living creatures may at least be stirred to faith by unseen miracles [Note: [Col. 1033] *excitentur* (“may be stirred”): text, corrected in 1 from *excitente* (“stirring”)].

We have often heard certain people foolishly muttering that martyrs no longer deign to perform miracles in their time [Note: [Col. 1034D] That is, “for a long time,” meaning in our own times], plainly ignorant that it was necessary for them to become known through miracles then, when, because of human weakness, they could succumb to their enemies in death and, when their persecutors reproached them, they seemed for a time to become contemptible, as though their God were nowhere.

But now, since due reverence is rendered to their honor according to what is fitting, there is no need for them to shine through miracles, but rather to admit the vows and prayers of the faithful into the sanctuary of their hearing [Col. 1034C] and graciously to command that they be offered upon the altar of the Most High [Note: [Col. 1033] *vota* (“vows”): text; *nota* (“note”): 1, 2].

He, therefore, who calls things that are not as though they were, who chooses the foolish things of the world in order to confound the strong, and the contemptible, lowly things and things that are not in order to destroy the things that are, chose fishermen rather than philosophers—poor and lowly men—and made them apostles. And since, according to the Apostle, he made the wisdom of this world foolish (1 Corinthians 3:19), he nevertheless chose, through the simple rusticity of the apostles, to save those who believe.

He opened the mouth of the mute [Col. 1035A] [Note: [Col. 1035] *mutum* (“mute”): 1, 2; corrected to *muti* (“of the mute”) in 2], and he made the tongues of infants eloquent. When the prophet said, “Behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am a child” [Note: [Col. 1035] Only *puer ego* (“I am a child”) is absent in 1], he replied: “Do not say, ‘I am a child,’ because you will go wherever I send you, and you will speak whatever I command you” (Jeremiah 1:6–7).

And so that the Almighty’s design might be proclaimed still more wonderfully even among disorderly peoples, he clothed Quintius Serranus, wearing down plowshares in the furrow, as dictator [Note: [Col. 1035] *sulco* (“furrow”): text; *fulco* (“furrow”): 3; [Col. 1035D] Persius I, 73–75]:

> The trembling wife clothes the dictator before the oxen,
>
> and the lictor carries your plows home. [Note: [Col. 1035] The text should be restored from Persius as *dictatorem* (“the dictator”); *dicturam* (“she would dictate”): 1, 2, 3. *dum aratur* (“while it is being plowed”): 1, 2, 3.]

And he not only opened the mouth of a foreigner [Note: [Col. 1035] *alienigenae* (“of a foreigner”): text; corrected in 2 to the misspelling *aligenigene*], who still possessed his sight, to speak the prophet’s praises, but—what was even more wondrous—when the rider fell and was hastening to utter a curse, he opened to speech the tongue of the she-ass on which the man sat [Note: [Col. 1033] Absent in Ch.].

He, I say, who makes himself known to all peoples through signs so wondrous and ineffable, wondrously glorified blessed John, perhaps because of the unbelievers of his own time, so that he who was most fully known to the One who alone knows all things, because of the good work known to him, might be wondrously displayed to the people of that time.

### 30. How a certain man from overseas foretold to him that he would become bishop of Maastricht [Note: [Col. 1035] *Trajecti* (“at Maastricht”): text; *trajectensi* (“of Maastricht”): 1, 2]

The see of Maastricht was vacant [Note: [Col. 1035] Absent in Ch.], and clergy and people had gathered to appoint another in his place. The majesty of the king had approved whom they wished; the dignity of the priests and nobles had summoned a public assembly. By chance—
The crowd is divided, uncertain, into opposing factions [Note: [Col. 1035D] Virgil, *Aeneid* II, 39], because another was being wondrously provided for by the Lord [Note: [Col. 1035] *mirificissime* (“most wondrously”) in 2 and 3; absent in Ch.]. Blessed John [Col. 1035C], whose name at that time was Agnus (“Lamb”), corresponded to so auspicious a name through the merits of his simplicity and his chaste works. For he devoted himself to agriculture, the one occupation, almost alone, that can be practiced without the stain of every kind of crime. He pursued this work not compelled by the poverty of want or constrained by hunger arising from necessity, but rather, in accordance with the custom of that time, by applying himself diligently to it. Yet he did not work with his own hands; for he was noble and abounded in the revenues of many large estates [Note: [Col. 1035] “possessions” misspelled as “posions” in 1 and 2]. Lest this seem doubtful to anyone, the estates granted by him to our church also testify to it: our predecessors and we still possess them, and from them the church retains the tithe owed to the Lord for Saint Cosmas, on account of the burial of that holy man.

While he was engaged in such labors, a certain pilgrim from overseas regions arrived. He had been warned by an angelic vision to cross the sea, proceed to the well-built city founded by the Emperor Antonius, and instruct a holy man, designated by name, concerning the great works of God [Note: [Col. 1035] *instrueret* (“instruct”) corrected to *institueret* in 1; *instrueret* in 3.]. Accordingly, he had traveled through many surrounding lands, seeking the well-built city. At last he reached Huy, and found a city corresponding to the name that had been indicated [Note: [Col. 1035] “he found the city with the indicated name”; in 2, “he found the city with the name indicated,” corrected in 3]. Proceeding farther east, he rejoiced that he had found blessed John, laboring beside his estate at Tietantia [Note: [Col. 1035] *Tutantia* in Ch.] in a rational activity worthy of the angelic message [Note: [Col. 1035D] This is a village near Huy, called Tyhange in the modern French language. — Chapeav]. And lest any doubt remain in his mind, he tested whether the remaining indication corresponded to the name. “Hail,” he said, “excellent man, Agnus.” When John assented and returned the greeting, the overseas traveler, now more certain, said:

“You are devoting yourself to a good work, and you yourself are recognized by God as good. I have been sent to you as a good messenger—unless, God forbid, you prove unbelieving toward my words. Your works and almsgiving have pleased the Most High; your frequent prayer has also penetrated the heavens, and your intention, which remains hidden, is pleasing to him to whom all things are known. And because you serve the Lord magnificently, you will be magnificently honored by him. You have presented a wondrous spectacle of service to the angelic spirits; a marvelous example of you will be offered to human beings. The town of Trajectum has been deprived of its own shepherd; the Lord has determined to raise you to it in the dignity of this office.”

At these words the holy man was first struck with amazement, and his hair stood on end; his voice stuck in his throat [Note: [Col. 1036D] Virgil, *Aeneid* III, 48; IV, 280]. Terrified by the novelty of the matter, at last he recovered his voice and said:

“You proclaim marvelous things indeed [Note: [Col. 1035] Omitted in 3], and I am not altogether unbelieving of what you tell me. The town of Trajectum is indeed without a bishop, but it seems very far from appropriate that I should be admitted to it. For I am bound by the tie of marriage, and, according to the Apostle, must consider ‘the things of the world, how I may please my wife’ (1 Corinthians 7:33). But no one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs, and it is necessary that the one who desires to see how sweet the Lord is (Wisdom 12:1) should be free from these things. The canons do not appoint a bishop, nor do the statutes of the Fathers even admit such a man to the clergy. I have had children [Note: [Col. 1035] The passage from “I have had children” to “are absent” is absent in Ch.], whose prosperity [Note: [Col. 1035] *prosteritate* in 1, 2, and 3; corrected to *posteritate* in 2] and needs the law of the world commands me to attend to; and although the Apostle commands that they be subject in all chastity (1 Timothy 3:4), the canon has nevertheless ordered that the household be arranged beforehand. And suppose all these requirements were supplied: what is nevertheless necessary for me to perform this office is entirely lacking.

“The highest qualities of character, selected by the Apostle for a bishop [Note: [Col. 1035] *indotis* in 1, 2, and 3], are absent from me; the privileges of holiness are wholly lacking [Note: [Col. 1035] “I have children … are absent” is omitted in Ch.]. I do not consider myself blameless (1 Timothy 3:2) [Col. 1036D] [Note: [Col. 1035] *inauctumo* in 1]; conscious of being ensnared in many vices, I condemn myself. I have not stood by those who labor; I have not sympathized with those who suffer. Like Martha, I have not ministered to Christ’s poor [Note: [Col. 1035] “in spirit” in 1 and 2]; like Mary, I have not attended to the divine words [Col. 1037A]. Therefore I confess that I am very far removed from the active life [Note: [Col. 1037] Omitted in 1, C, D, 1*, and 2], while I have never even tasted the beginnings of the contemplative life. The Apostle, he says, requires one who puts forth a sound discourse in accordance with the faith [Note: [Col. 1037] The passage from *Proferentem* to *ullum* is absent in Ch.]. But who will utter a sound discourse who has scarcely ever learned anything [Note: [Col. 1037] The reading in 1 is corrupt: *rumpepat*]? I did not learn letters, never studied, never attended school, and never withdrew my hands from the schoolmaster’s rod: ‘not a recent convert’ (1 Timothy 3:6), says the Apostle. And how should one who has not been able to administer each rank individually ever ascend so unexpectedly to the episcopate? How, finally, can one preside who has never known how to be subject?”

So many complaints did he break forth from his breast [Note: [Col. 1037D] Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, 553].

At last the elder added these words:

“Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised, and of his greatness there is no end (Psalm 144:3). He who can do all things as he wills is not unable to accomplish this as well. He created all things from nothing; who can resist his power? He who can raise up children for Abraham from stones [Note: [Col. 1037] “Abraham” spelled *Habrahae* in 2 and 3] can himself fill your mouth with knowledge. Only do not suppose that anything is difficult for his majesty; rather, trusting, open your faithful tongue in praise of the Creator.

“Although the prophet was considered worthy to beget the herald of supreme truth, he was nevertheless condemned to silence because he appeared doubtful of the divine promise. He considered his own body dead and the condition of his wife barren, and did not reflect upon the majesty of the almighty Lord. For if he had sufficiently understood that God made all things from things that did not exist, he would have doubted less that he could bring something into being from things that already stood—even if he considered himself unworthy, because he saw that his wickedness outweighed his worth. He ought not, however, to have judged God’s mercy by his own unworthiness.

“‘Behold,’ says the Lord to another prophet who was accusing himself of his crimes and therefore timidly withdrawing from the vision of God and from announcing his mighty works, ‘behold, I say, the stone with which I touched your lips, and your iniquity shall be taken away’ [Note: [Col. 1037] The passage beginning ‘Although the prophet …’ and ending ‘your iniquity shall be taken away’ is omitted in Ch.].

“Do not doubt, I beg you, but diligently examine the histories of the ancients—for perhaps you have at least heard some of them. What else do the ancient miracles resound with than this: that nature, by the marvelous commands of almighty God, changed the state innate to it?”

### 31. What he replied to this, and how his staff, fixed in the earth, blossomed

Blessed John replied:

“None of these things is doubtful to me; but in comparison with those through whom or by whom such remarkable deeds were accomplished, I am greatly inferior.”

Then, fixing in the ground the staff that he happened to be holding [Note: [Col. 1037] *infigens* is misspelled *infingins* in 1], he said:

“Just as it is exceedingly difficult for this dry piece of wood, which you see, to cling to the earth by its roots, produce shoots, blossom, and likewise bear fruit, so it seems inconsistent that the words you speak should be fulfilled in me.”

Immediately, in a marvelous manner, the wood changed its surface. It clung to the earth by its roots, put on bark, at once became green, blossomed, and bore fruit [Note: [Col. 1037] Through some error, the words “it clung to the earth by its roots … and bore fruit” were omitted in 1].

“O marvelous power of the Creator, O ineffable grace of the Maker, O acceptable time, day to be proclaimed everywhere! Happy are those who deserved to see these things; happy also are we if we do not pretend not to believe [Note: [Col. 1037] *si* in 1]; happy the king in whose time these things occurred; happy the members of the royal court who were permitted to be present! Happy the clergy with such a bishop, happy the peoples with so great a shepherd!

“The ancient miracle is renewed; Aaron’s rod, that glorious prodigy, is restored. The former was an indication of a legitimate priesthood; this one has proved an indication of an unexpected and doubtful episcopate, yet one wonderfully provided by God. The difference is that the former was granted the delay of one night, whereas this one, bearing fruit in a moment, allowed no postponement. The former silenced unbelievers; this one brought to the task the man appointed from heaven [Note: [Col. 1037] The passage beginning “The ancient miracle …” and ending “the man appointed from heaven” is omitted in Ch.].

This celebrated event was spread abroad to everyone’s ears and reported to many nobles throughout the kingdom. The king did not remain unaware of this report; it reached the people assembled at Trajectum. They immediately hastened, a delegation was sent to Huy, and blessed John was found with the overseas traveler. They were brought to Trajectum amid everyone’s amazement.

Dagobert, still a young man, governed the kingdom of Austrasia (in the year 622), while his father, the great Lothair, energetically ruled alone as monarch over the four kingdoms [Note: [Col. 1037D] He died in the year 628]. Royal orders were therefore issued, the matter that had been in doubt was resolved, and blessed John was appointed to the episcopate (around the year 625). Everyone agreed, all approved, and all rejoiced. Although the holy man still wished to resist, nevertheless, when he saw that he was favorably received by everyone, he rejoiced that he was being overcome by so marvelous and ineffable a disposition of God.

Thus he was received by everyone with praises, elected and enthroned, brought forward and exalted, sanctified by acclamation, placed upon the episcopal seat and obeyed with reverence, and his name was changed to John [Note: [Col. 1037] The passage beginning “Thus he was received …” and ending “his name was changed to John” is omitted in Ch.]. What sort of man he made himself, and how great he became, by the merits of holiness; how he clothed himself in the armor of faith; how he adorned himself with the finest virtues; what he fulfilled by his pious work; and whatever worthy commands he imposed upon his subjects to be fulfilled—all this is and will be clear to everyone who does not consider it doubtful that the marvelous things announced beforehand by the Almighty concerning him were accomplished.

For it is established that he himself was perfect in every moral excellence and that he had many perfect disciples. From among them we have learned that one in particular, namely blessed Monon [Note: [Col. 1037] *in unum* (“into one”) in 1]—who, while busily engaged under him in ecclesiastical duties, was shown to be a perfect martyr [Col. 1039A] [Note: [Col. 1038D] *Life of Saint Monon*, in Surius VII, 783. It is later than Herigerus]—was among them. The lord and holy John, having completed the course of his present life, obtained rest in a good old age, departed from this human life, received the prize of an everlasting crown, and was buried in the church of Cosmas situated on the mountain at Huy [Note: [Col. 1039D] If you accept Aegidius, this was John’s epitaph:

“Through the flower of his pointed staff, the farmer received honor.”].

### 32. On Saint Amandus

After these events Saint Amandus is appointed as the twenty-second successor. Since his life is known to have been written out in full of virtues, it seemed fitting here merely to pluck out and present a few passages from it, and to trace back more fully the beginnings of his deeds before his episcopate.

[Note: [BAUDEMUNDUS, *Life of Saint Amandus*, chapter 2.] Aquitania was therefore the land of his birth; his father was named Serenus and his mother Amantia. They were distinguished not only according to the dignity of the world but also as Christians. While he was still a boy, he left his homeland and parents and sought the island of Oga, westward in the Ocean Sea [Note: [Col. 1040D] Now the island of Oye, opposite La Rochelle. See *Acta Sanctorum*, February I, 816]. There he was received by the spiritual brothers with great joy, and because he had learned the sacred writings, he burned with a greater desire each day in the service of God [Note: [Col. 1039] “sacred” abbreviated as “l. s.” in 2 and 3; “daily” misspelled in 3].

### 33. How he drove away a serpent by prayer, visited holy places, and returned to his homeland

[Note: [Col. 1039] Chapter XXXII in 1, 2, and 3.]

[Note: The heading in A reads “The first indication of his signs.”]

The first indication of his miracles was this: while he was walking through that same island at the command imposed by a duty of obedience, he encountered a serpent of enormous size [Note: [Col. 1039] “he has” in 1]. At first, as his childish age permitted, he was afraid; then he prostrated himself and poured out a prayer. He rose, made the sign of the cross, and by the power of his words ordered it to return to its hiding place. It obeyed his command, immediately returned, and did not appear again anywhere on that island.

Then his father came to the same island. He advised him that he ought to leave the monastery and urged him to resume secular dress; he added that, unless he obeyed, he would deprive him of his inheritance [Note: [Col. 1039] “obey” is misspelled in 1; “he obeys” in 2 and 3]. But he replied:

“You threaten me idly with what I have always wished to lack: the Lord is the portion of my inheritance.”

After this he sought Tours and the tomb of Saint Martin. There he prayed for the aid of Martin’s intercession, asking the Lord to grant him this grace, namely, that he might be permitted to continue the course of his entire life as a pilgrim.

He rose from prayer and cut off the hair of his head. He attained the honor of the clerical state and advanced through every rank of the clergy.

Proceeding from there, he came to Bourges, where he was received honorably and courteously by Saint Austrigisilus, bishop of that city, and by his archdeacon, blessed Sulpicius [Col. 1039D]. At their urging he built a cell there, which he inhabited for nearly fifteen years. Clothed in a hair shirt and ashes, he continually afflicted himself with vigils; worn down by fasting and hunger, he was content with barley bread, abstained from wine, and sustained rather than nourished his body with weak water.

Next he was inflamed with a heavenly desire to go to Rome, visit the thresholds of the Apostles, and seek the support of their prayers. When he had accomplished this, one night, as the guards were going out, he entered the church. He was discovered, mistreated, and expelled from the church. For this reason, while he was sitting sorrowfully at the doors, Saint Peter appeared to him, suddenly rapt in an ecstasy of mind, and gently and graciously comforted him [Note: [Col. 1039] “comforted” in 2 and 3], urging him to return to Gaul to preach. Restored to greater joy, he returned to Gaul.

### 34. How, after becoming a bishop, he performed many good works

[Note: [Col. 1039] Chapter 33 in 1; absent in 2 and 3.]

He was then compelled by the king and the priests to be ordained bishop for preaching, as was customary at that time. He fulfilled this office energetically, announcing the word of the Lord throughout the surrounding regions. He built many monasteries and supported them with estates and resources received from the king and the nobles, placing people there to inhabit them and serve Christ. If he found any captives or people from overseas, he redeemed them at a price obtained from the king or the faithful, instructed them in the sacred writings [Note: [Col. 1039] The words “instructed them in the sacred writings … bishops” are absent in Ch.], and sent them to various churches for their support. Some of these were later seen as abbots, many as priests, and some even as bishops.

Again he conceived the desire to attempt a journey to Rome, and on his return from there it happened that he reached Centumcellae. While he was spending the night in prayer [Note: [Col. 1039] “while he was making a note” in 1, 2, and 3], the devil was dragging one of the servants toward the sea in order to drown him. As the man kept repeating, “Christ, help me,” the devil mocked him: “Who is Christ?” Blessed Amandus replied: “The crucified Son of the living God.” At these words the devil disappeared [Col. 1040C], and the man was rescued.

As they sailed across the same sea, they caught a fish, and its capture had increased the sailors’ joy. A storm that suddenly arose disturbed this happiness; it drove everyone into despair, forced them to throw everything necessary into the sea, and finally made them flee to the servant of God. Again Saint Peter appeared, passing along the stern of the ship. He ordered them to have confidence and promised that everyone’s lives would be saved. The storm calmed and the tempest was driven away. When morning came, they all went ashore unharmed.

### 35. How he converted the people of Ghent

[Note: [Col. 1039] Chapter XXXIIII in 1, 2, and 3.]

Meanwhile he undertook the town of Ghent, situated on the flowing Scheldt, which was so entangled in the devil’s snares that its people called trees and wood gods. Although all the surrounding peoples had inclined toward the faith of Christ, they themselves still served idols, either because of their savage customs or because of the barrenness of their soil. With the support of Aicharius, bishop of Noyon [Note: [Col. 1039] Corrected from *Achario* to *Aichario* in 1], and with royal authority bearing upon the undertaking, he dared to confront so great a danger without hesitation.

How often he was insulted, how often beaten with whips, how often driven away by dishonorable women, how often thrown into the river! At last, when the other companions had been driven away, he alone remained constant in preaching [Note: [Col. 1041] “how often” misspelled in 1].

He built there the monastery of Saint Peter, converted Saint Bavo, formerly a robber from Hasbania, and, after building a cell across the river, shut him away there as a penitent.

In the same district, a certain accused man was brought by lictors before a count who was sitting to settle cases. He was severely beaten and condemned to the stake. The holy man Amandus arrived and wished to intercede for the accused, but obtained nothing from the judge. He immediately returned home. The accused was fastened to the gallows, and at once appeared to be dead. The judge departed with the others, but blessed Amandus found the man dead. He had him carried to the chamber where he used to pray, spent the night in prayer over the body, and in the morning summoned the brothers. They washed the man and restored him alive, so that no trace of his wounds remained [Note: [Col. 1041] “any trace” in 1, 2, and 3].

When this miracle had been widely proclaimed far and wide, people came to him of their own accord. They destroyed their idols with their own hands and built churches of Christ and monasteries from their remains.

Thus rejoicing that his preaching was bearing fruit, he crossed the Danube and began to preach to those peoples. He regenerated a few in Christ, but because he did not gain the fruit he had expected and did not attain the martyrdom he hoped for, he eventually returned to his own country.

### 36. He catechizes the son of King Dagobert

[Col. 1041C] Meanwhile King Dagobert had a son. He ordered that blessed Amandus be sought to receive him from the sacred font. Since that same bishop had previously reproved the king for capital crimes and had been expelled from the kingdom not without insult, Dagobert wished humbly to pray that this be forgiven him and to reconcile Amandus to himself through the birth of his son.

Blessed Amandus was found and came. He forgave the offense, but nevertheless humbly refused to receive the king’s son from the sacred font and avoided doing so by fleeing. The king then sent for the holy men Eligii [Note: [Col. 1041D] Bishop of Noyon] and Audoen [Note: [Col. 1041D] Bishop of Rouen], who later became bishops, and only with difficulty obtained his consent. Amandus catechized the child, who was not yet more than forty days old. When those standing around were occupied elsewhere and did not respond, the infant answered “amen” in a clear voice [Col. 1041D], and thus, having been baptized and named Sigebert, brought joy to everyone.

After this, as stated above, blessed John, bishop of the people of Trajectum, happily departed to Christ (around the year 646). The king summoned many priests and called Saint Amandus, appointing him over the people of Trajectum. For three years he traveled through villages and fortified places, announcing the word of life. Then, seeing that he was accomplishing nothing, and observing that the priests and levites were even mocking him [Note: [Col. 1041] “and further” in 1], he shook the dust from his feet against them and afterward departed for other places [Note: [Col. 1041D] Compare the letters of Pope Martin I to Saint Amandus, written in the year 649; Mansi X, 1183] (in the year 649).

For the rest, we shall aim at brevity, since we reserve ourselves for writing the deeds of other bishops.

### 37. How divine vengeance struck those who despised the word of God from his mouth

Afterward he found the island of Canalaus on the Scheldt River [Note: [Col. 1041D] Called Chavelaus, Chanalaus, Chalelaus, or Calolo in the *Life of Saint Amandus*. It is an island in the Scheldt, at Calloo, two leagues from Antwerp. *Acta Sanctorum*, February I, 820]. There he served Christ with his spiritual brothers. For two years a great plague afflicted those who despised the word of God, so that no one remained in that place who had despised the man of God while he preached.

Next he went to the people called the Vaccei, who are called Wasconia. They lived in the mountains and worshiped idols as God. A certain Mimilogus [Note: [Col. 1041] Corrected from *Minilogus* to *Mimilogus* in 1] mocked the servant of Christ and nullified the Gospel; immediately seized by a demon, he miserably died while tearing himself with his own hands [Note: [Col. 1042D] He is called *Jocularis* in certain manuscripts of the *Life of Saint Amandus*. *Acta Sanctorum*, same volume].

### 38. He strikes his plotters with blindness and likewise restores sight to a blind woman

There too he made little progress, and while returning he entered a certain city. There he was honorably received by the city’s bishop. While water was being poured over his hands [Note: [Col. 1041] “was being poured over their hands” in 1 and 2], the bishop discreetly preserved some of it and gave it to a certain blind man. When the man bathed his eyes with it, he immediately saw.

### 39. He frees a disobedient monk struck by paralysis. Enumeration of his virtues

[Note: [Col. 1041] “and his death” is added in the index of 1.]

[Col. 1042C]

Next he returned to Francia, chose a place where he would live thereafter, approached King Childeric, and asked for a district in which he might build a monastery.

He obtained this, but Mumolus, bishop of the city of Ozidinum [Note: [Col. 1042D] That is, Uceticum in Narbonese Gaul], took it very badly. He immediately sent officers who would pretend to show him a more suitable place and, after leading him to a certain mountain, secretly kill him. The holy man was not unaware of this, since the Holy Spirit revealed it to him; nevertheless, because of his ardor for martyrdom, he continued on his way.

When they reached the mountain, the officers were struck with blindness; but when they repented, they were again illuminated through blessed Amandus’s prayer.

On the return journey he received lodging from a certain blind woman in the territory of Beauvais. Having asked the cause of her blindness, he learned that she worshiped a tree consecrated to demons. He immediately had the tree cut down, and the woman, having recovered her sight, saw at once.

[Note: [Col. 1041] In 1 and 2 this passage is marked as chapter 39; in 3 some erasures appear; it is absent from the index.]

He ordered the superior of a certain monastery to prepare wagons for transporting the brothers’ wine [Col. 1043A]. The man, as though he could not have wagons, neglected the order with excuses for sins and proved disobedient at that moment. But as soon as he began to go, he was immediately struck with paralysis, and, with such words as he could utter, revealed that he was suffering this because of disobedience.

Placed on a boat, he was taken to the man of God at Elnone [Note: [Col. 1043] Omitted in 1]. Receiving wine and bread from him, he was restored to complete health and thereafter corrected his perverse conduct.

He performed many other wonders, built countless monasteries, enriched them with resources [Note: [Col. 1043] “resources” omitted in 2 and 3], and filled them with people serving God. Finally he inhabited the monastery of Elnone [Note: [Col. 1043D] Situated between Tournai and Valenciennes. — Chapeav], where he also received his holy death (around the year 684).

### 40. Preface to the life of blessed Remaclus

[Col. 1043B]

The almighty Lord, who is rich in mercy, whose nature is goodness, whose will is efficacy [Note: [Col. 1043] “efficacy” in 2], and whose work is mercy, endured the vessels of wrath, prepared for destruction, with great patience (Romans 9:22). At last he came for the salvation of all, because he found no one free from the guilt of the first transgression. He bestowed upon all the riches of his goodness and forbearance and exercised most effectively the omnipotence of his will even toward the ungrateful and those unworthy in view of his grace, because in mercy he had provided beforehand that the work of saving mercy should be recoverable.

He took away from the strong man the weapons in which he trusted and distributed the vessels he possessed, so that, just as they had previously been vessels of wrath because sins called for it [Note: [Col. 1043] “because sins call for it” in 3], thereafter by divine grace they might become vessels of mercy [Note: [Col. 1043] The passage beginning “He took away from the strong man …” and ending “vessels of mercy” is omitted in Ch.].

For just as one must not believe that anyone comes to salvation unless God invites him, so no one who is unwilling can work out his salvation unless God assists him. No one perishes by God’s will, but only through the permission of free choice, according to his own election, lest the freedom of power once attributed to humanity be forced back into servile necessity [Note: [Col. 1043] The passage beginning “He took away from the strong man …” and ending “servile necessity” is omitted in Ch.].

Thus we possess the beginning of our salvation through God’s mercy. To consent to a saving inspiration lies within our power; to attain what we desire by consenting when admonished is a gift of God. To stumble lies within our power and negligence; not to stumble, once the gift of salvation has been received, is in some way our concern, but wholly the work of heavenly assistance [Note: [Col. 1043] The passage beginning “Thus we possess …” and ending “heavenly assistance” is omitted in Ch.].

Relying upon this strongest hope [Note: [Col. 1043] The passage beginning “To consent …” and ending “strongest hope” is omitted in Ch.], we discover in reality that those are blessed who, although they did not see Christ in the flesh offering so great a foretaste of salvation, did not hesitate faithfully to believe what they heard. For not only do those nearby acknowledge that many of them performed the works that Christ himself performed, and even greater works, according to his promise (John 14:12); those who live beyond the Sarmatians, frequent the frozen Ocean, and inhabit the Fortunate Islands also proclaim it [Col. 1043D–1044A].

And therefore let it delight us all the more to submit to goodness, let it be all the more a pleasure to be subject to the Lord, who is not only the supporter and helper of those who progress as they grow, but also mercifully provides a remedy to meet the falls of those who are collapsing. He ensures that the assistance of angels is not lacking to us, and grants us the patronage of the saints, whom we do not hesitate to implore as intercessors for our offenses.

Although it is fitting to honor these saints collectively, since they have been bestowed upon many different provinces, he has nevertheless mercifully assigned particular saints to each place, whom he wished to be embraced especially and entreated more earnestly. From among them he sent us blessed Remaclus. Since we rely greatly upon his intercessions, we begin to relate his life and deeds as far as our ability permits.

### 41. On the kingdom of the Franks and Aquitania, from which Saint Remaclus originated

[Col. 1044B]

From its beginning the kingdom of the Franks had always appeared vigorous, and at that time it seemed to flourish above all the peoples bordering it [Note: [Col. 1043] “bordering” appears as *collimitanus* in 1 and *collimitans* in 2 and 3],

“when it wished to bow its neck beneath the yoke of the Lord’s faith, to burn what it had previously worshiped, and thereafter to worship what it had burned” (*Hincmar, Life of Saint Remigius*, chapter 64; compare *Deeds of the Franks*, chapter 40).

The holy Church of God received its greatest increase and a firm condition under King Clothar, who by lawful succession was the fourth to rule this single monarchy of three kingdoms [Note: [Col. 1043] “this” appears as “then” in 2 and 3], when he was forty years old (in the year 613), the same year in which the Emperor Heraclius, bearer of the holy cross, was in his fourteenth year.

He did not allow the scepter of any ruler around him to oppose his own [Note: [Col. 1043] The wording follows the *Life of Landoald*, chapter 1: “with the surrounding scepters”; 1 reads “scepter,” 2 and 3 “scepter with the surrounding scepters”] [Col. 1044C]. Rather, he strove to restrain with his own reins nearly everything that Gaul and Germany contained in the way of kings and peoples.

He had appointed his illustrious son Dagobert over the Austrasians and had joined the kingdoms of Germany to his dominion (in the year 622). During their most fortunate time, the name of Christianity flourished everywhere to such an extent that even today scarcely any church, if any, can be found among the neighboring regions that does not present to us the patronage of some saint of that age [Note: [Col. 1043] The wording follows the *Life of Saint Landoald*, chapter 1: “presents” in 1].

But, to say nothing for the moment of countless others, the holy men Eligius and Audoenus were then beginning to devote themselves to courtly duties; blessed Arnulfus and Romaricus were already taking part in royal councils; while Saint Amandus, blessed Remaclus, and Saint Goar were illuminating Aquitania with the auspices of their birth [Col. 1044D].

Aquitania is considered by some to be almost the third part of Gaul. It takes its name from the winding waters of the Loire River, which bounds it for the most part and nearly surrounds it in a circle. To the northwest it has the Ocean, called the Aquitanian Gulf; to the west, the Spains; to the north and east, the province of Lugdunensis [Note: [Col. 1045] “Lugdunensis” appears as *lugdiniensem* in 1 and 2]; and to the southeast and south, Narbonensis [Note: [Col. 1045D] These boundaries are found in Aethicus’s *Cosmography* and thereafter in Orosius I, 2. I freely confess that I do not know where the author obtained what follows; I can scarcely, if at all, persuade myself that it should be attributed to Herigerus].

It is rich in fish through its streams and rivers, exceedingly fertile in the soil of its fields, nectar-bearing in its vineyards, planted with forests, abundant in fruits, fully sufficient in pastures for livestock, extremely rich in supplies of gold, silver, and other metals, profitable through the traffic of ships and customs dues, but more fruitful than the other provinces in the luxury produced by every pleasure. It is also warlike and turbulent, with men whose character is more savage than that of others.

Apart from its municipalities and the fortified camps of its other fortifications, it possesses fourteen very famous, very large, and likewise populous cities. Among these are two metropolitan cities: one, Bordeaux, always distinguished by the titles of its great men [Col. 1045B]; the other is Bourges, which at this time has Saint Austrigisilus as archbishop and blessed Sulpicius as archdeacon, soon afterward elevated to episcopal honor [Note: [Col. 1045D] In the diocese of Bourges].

In their parish blessed Remaclus most happily received the beginning of his birth in those days. His father was Albucius, and his mother was called Matrinia. Both were wealthy according to the dignity of the world, distinguished by the nobility of their lineage, as is testified by the tradition of his great estates, which were transferred both to the church of Tongeren and to our monastery, whether by him himself, by his heirs, or even by royal highness [Note: [Col. 1045] The remainder is absent in Ch.; “to us,” according to the *Life of Remaclus*]. For many documents concerning these properties, possessed by us over the course of many years, are still retained in the archives of both churches [Col. 1045C].

### 42. How the same man, afterward educated by Saint Sulpicius under Eligius, became known to the leading men of the palace
But, to return to the point from which we have strayed for a short while [Note: “inde” (“from there”) in witnesses 2 and 3], let us resume the thread [Note: “flectamus” (“let us bend”) in witness 3]. [The boy Remaclus, endowed with excellent character, was nobly educated (*Life of Remaclus* 1), insofar as his parents’ abundant resources allowed.] Under Saint Sulpicius [Note: This is passed over in silence in the contemporary *Life of Saint Sulpicius*, *Acta Sanctorum*, January III, 167], in whose honor it is established that many churches were later dedicated by that same holy man in our diocese. Then, when he had grown up and was fully virtuous, as befitted his age, already [bearing fruit, they report that] they entrusted him to Saint Eligius, a man who, by the grace of his merits, surpassed all the men of his time. He placed him in the monastery of Solemniacum [Note: “sollemniaco” (a spelling of Solemniacum) in witness 1; “cum sollempniaco” (“with Solemniacum”) in witness 3] [Note: Solignac in Aquitaine and in the diocese of Limoges. Compare the *Life of Eligius* I, 16; Surius VI, 636], which he himself was building through pious labor on his own inheritance [Col. 1045D], and instructed him thoroughly in the sacred disciplines of monastic observance [Note: “apprime” (“thoroughly”) in the main text; “ad primum” (“at first”) in witnesses C and D1].

[The good youth adhered so closely to the holy man’s admonitions that he became not merely a diligent executor of the divine word [Note: “exesutor” (a misspelling of “executor,” “doer”) corrected to “executor” (“doer”) in witness 1] [Col. 1046A], but heavenly grace overflowed in him so greatly [Note: absent in witness 3] that he became an example and standard of religious conduct for all who served under the same discipline. For he spent the nights in continual vigils; he continued his prayers throughout the night [Note: “pernox” (“lasting through the night”) in witnesses 2 and 3 and in the *Life of Remaclus*]; he was outstanding in abstinence and distinguished in every moral excellence [Note: “honestate” (“honor” or “uprightness”) in witness 3].]

When Saint Eligius, to whom he had been entrusted, observed this, and at the same time eagerly rejoiced in his spiritual progress, [he did not refuse to entrust to him the care of the flock committed to himself, nor hesitate to divide the burden and responsibilities, but surrendered himself again to the service of the palace, as he was compelled to do. (Chapter 2.) After these events, as the years passed and report spread throughout the neighboring provinces of all Gaul, news was heard everywhere of the holy man’s life and deeds. The reputation of his achievements reached the ears of the nobles who at that time were occupied with the concerns of the palace [Col. 1046B] [Note: absent in witness 1]; namely, that such a great and flourishing branch answered the planting of the supreme vine. By the ordinance of the Most High, a divine lamp kindled by grace could not be hidden beneath the bushel of private contemplation; rather, so that it might become a supplement to those sluggish in their purpose of faith, the light was placed upon a lampstand [Note: The passage from “After these events” through “lampstand” is absent in manuscript Ch.]. Thus it was announced in the royal court that such a man ought not to be absent from the king’s presence, so that the affairs of the kingdom might be arranged by one whose great and distinguished merits were already being heard of. Accordingly, he was honorably summoned, as befitted him, and brought to the threshold of the palace, destined thereby to become a great consolation to all, as the subsequent course of events clearly demonstrated.] [Note: “ea” (“those things”) in witness 1.]

About this same time, blessed John, who was successfully governing the bishopric of the Tongrians or Trajectensians [Col. 1046C], departed this life [Note: “exiuit” (“departed”), corrected to “exuit” (“put off”), in witness 2]. The renowned King Dagobert, who had auspiciously succeeded his deceased father [Note: Nearly all that follows is absent in manuscript Ch.] and alone skillfully administered the monarchy of the realm, had summoned blessed Amandus, who had been made bishop in order to preach, as was then customary [Note: Compare chapter 34]. [Because he had earlier rebuked him for capital offenses and had been insulted and expelled by him (*Life of Saint Amandus*, chapter 16), and then had been reconciled with him to some extent through the rebirth [Note: Witnesses 1, 2, and 3 read “peregrinationem” (“pilgrimage”); witness 2 corrects this to “per regenerationem” (“through rebirth”)]—that is, the baptism [Note: Specifically, baptism]—of his son Sigebert, he attempted, and succeeded, in binding him more closely to himself and elevated him to the see of the Trajectensians. (Chapter 18.) After traveling for three years through villages and forts and spreading the word of life, and seeing that he was accomplishing nothing, while grieving that the priests and Levites even mocked him [Col. 1046D], he shook the dust from his feet against them as a testimony, according to the Lord’s command, branded them thereafter with such an accusation, and then moved on to other places to preach, as he had done before.]

### 43. How he succeeded Saint Amandus in the see of Trajectum, and how he lived there

[Col. 1047A]

It is unknown how long the people of Trajectum remained without a shepherd [Note: “pleps” (a spelling of “plebs,” “people”) in witness 1], until his father appointed Sigebert king over Austrasia and established his seat in the city of Metz (in the year 632). Then the people of Trajectum, together with the clergy in a common election, with an assembly and hearing of the nobles [Note: The *Life of Saint Remaclus* reads “magnatum” (“of nobles”); the *Life of Hadrian* reads “magistrorum” (“of masters”); witnesses 1, 2, and 3 read “magnarum” (“of great [women]”)], and even with the cries and acclamations of every order, presented this petition: no one ought to preside over them except blessed Remaclus, a man acceptable to God and to human beings, second in holiness [Note: “secundum” (“second”) is absent in witness 1] to no one of his age [Note: Witness 1 reads “aet. acceptum” (“acceptable in age”); “acceptum” is deleted], pleasing to the angelic spirits, revered by those dwelling on earth, and one whose manifold benefits they had experienced [Col. 1047B]. They had often felt the support of his intercessions both with the king and with the nobles; they had observed his skillful wisdom when he frequently took part in royal counsels. He did not lack knowledge of the Scriptures, from which he could bring forth things new and old; he possessed the entire catalogue [Note: Witness 2 corrects “omne” (“the whole,” neuter) to “omnem” (“the whole,” masculine, agreeing with “catalogue”)] of qualifications, together with the fullness of the gift which the Apostle requires in a bishop [Note: The passage from “this man” through “deflowered” is absent in manuscript Ch.] (1 Timothy 3:2).

The king favorably assented to such petitions and courteously agreed with such earnestness. Since they were making a just request, he resolved to grant their petition and at the same time to confer with the holy man about it. But who could adequately recall how greatly the most gracious king softened him toward consent by the sweetness of his words? Who, finally, could recount how much the holy man appeared, to the best of his ability, to struggle and resist [Col. 1047C]? The king, relying on the counsel of the priests and nobles, did not abandon his proposed intention [Note: “destituit” (“abandoned”) in witnesses 1 and 3; corrected to “destitit” (“desisted”) in witness 2 and in the *Life of Saint Remaclus*].

The holy priest, however, fearing to oppose the divine decree, though unwillingly, was appointed the twenty-seventh bishop of the Church of the Tongrians or Trajectum (in the year 650) [so that he might thereafter spread among many the seeds of the word which he had until then kept hidden within himself for a long time (*Life of Saint Remaclus*, chapter 3)].

Now, what was the extent of his merit and integrity of religious life in that office is beyond the power of our humble ability to unfold, since at the very beginning of his ordination the Lord bestowed upon him such grace in preaching that everyone very quickly inclined an ear to obedience [Note: The reading follows the *Life of Remaclus*; the word “desideratur” (“is desired”) is lacking in witnesses 1, 2, and 3] [Note: The passage from “when” through “obedience” is absent in manuscript Ch.], and there was no one who did not love him affectionately; each person diligently strove, for his own part, to adhere to his teaching [Col. 1047D]. For arrogance claimed nothing from his character [Note: The *Life of Remaclus* has “arrogantiam” (“arrogance”); witnesses 1, 2, and 3 have the form in the main text]; complete humility possessed him. The proud revered him [Note: Witness 1 reads “revertebantur” (“they were turning back”) for “reverebantur” (“they revered”)] as their superior; the humble embraced him as a brother.
