In general he was good and certainly benevolent toward everyone; though placed on earth, he showed himself heavenly in appearance and conduct: angelic in countenance, pure in his bearing, radiant and holy in action, entirely upright in body, most skillful in mind, circumspect in work, excellent in intelligence, great in counsel, catholic in faith, most patient in hope, and abundant in charity. He demonstrated by his deeds what sort of merit he possessed, being exceedingly compassionate and easy in every gentleness.

He always stood between rich and poor, so that the poor regarded him as poor and the rich counted him as rich. For he did not consider the persons of the powerful, but weighed the elegance of their conduct; he honored each one more generously in proportion as he recognized that the person lived more holily. What he affirmed with his mouth he never destroyed by his actions, demonstrating through his conduct what ought to be taught by his words [Col. 1048B]. And what divine grace granted him, he transmitted to those who came after. For not only do his deeds continue to benefit us even today, but also the works of his disciples and of those who were faithfully instructed [Note: “educati” (“educated”) in the *Life of Remaclus*] by him continue to benefit us through their example and imitation [Note: The passage from “not only” through “imitation” is absent in manuscript Ch.].

He was the founder and ruler of many monasteries, where even to the present day the ranks of those serving Christ increase through his example. He was the father and teacher of many disciples, whose souls he won for Christ and whose souls are still won through them and through their successors. Through the daily use of his talent, he earns interest in its repayment [Note: The *Life of Remaclus* has “tali” (“such”)]; and it is credited to his merits that their increase is multiplied [Note: The passage from “whose” through “increases” is absent in manuscript Ch.]. Among these was blessed Theodardus, undoubtedly instructed by him in ecclesiastical disciplines [Col. 1048C], since he had been designated by him as his successor [Note: absent in witnesses 2 and 3], and who ultimately obtained the crown of martyrdom.

### 44. How many holy men gathered around him

[Note: “LIII.” in witnesses 1 and 2.]

Saint Lambert was also one of his disciples, and he too proved himself a distinguished martyr in his own time. Likewise blessed Badelinus [Note: “Hadelinus” (a spelling of Badelinus) in witness 3], who is also said to have been born in Aquitaine and to have been his companion in pilgrimage [Note: “fuisse” (“to have been”) is repeated in witness 1], at a certain time when he was performing works worthy of God in the place where he had withdrawn, saw in a vision that the same father appeared to him, handsome in face, venerable in his hair, and outstanding in the rest of his stature. He showed him a place for his future way of life [Note: “cumversationis” (a misspelling of “conversationis,” “way of life”) in witness 1] and perpetual rest, and pointed out a spring suitable for human use [Note: Now called Celle, not far from Dinant. Chapeav].

This is still clearly demonstrated to all: his body rests there to this day [Note: “dum et” (“while also”) is absent in witness 3] [Col. 1048D] [Note: “corporenus” in witness 3], while in spirit he remains present and does not cease to bestow innumerable benefits daily upon those who believe there.

From the work and choice of the holy man Trudo also, one must discern with what intention the holy priest watched over the folds and guardianship of the Lord’s flock [Note: The passage from “In the holy man” through “exhorted” is absent in manuscript Ch.], [and that, filled with the prophetic spirit, he was at times aware beforehand of future events (*Life of Saint Remaclus*, chapter 4)], and, burning with love of divinity, had cooled toward every incentive to desire.

### 44. He foretells to the still-young Saint Trudo what he ought to do

With pastoral skill blessed Remaclus customarily went around his parish [Note: “circuiebat” in witnesses 1 and 2; corrected to “circuibat” in witness 2; “circuibat” in witness 3]. He rescued as many as he could from the wolves’ greed and strove to win them for the supreme Shepherd. He supported the good so that they might progress toward better things, and exhorted the negligent and sluggish to come to their senses [Note: See the variant readings].

Meanwhile Saint Trudo, still flourishing in boyhood, was putting forth the first fruits of good flavor [*Life of Saint Remaclus*, chapter 4; Donatus, *Life of Saint Trudo*, chapter 1]. Although he was greatly distinguished by the nobility of an illustrious family [Col. 1049B], he longed still more for the pursuit of divine love and virtues, [and therefore was touched by the ardor of the Holy Spirit, so that he bound himself by a vow that, if at some time, with Christ’s help, he should learn the sacred letters, he would build a church on the estate belonging to him [Note: Sarchinium in the territory of Hasbania; Col. 1049D] and serve there perpetually, gathering there, as he could, co-workers [Note: “cooperatores” (“co-workers”) is absent in witness 3] and fellow servants of the Lord [Note: Witness 1 reads “conservaturos” (“those who will serve together”)].

[(The *Life of Saint Remaclus*, chapter 5.) Burning with such desire, he was seized by a nocturnal vision and was fully instructed by angelic consolation in these words: “Know [Note: “paginae praecedentis,” “of the preceding page,” marks the continuation of the note in the source] that the vows by which you bound yourself, brother, from childhood, while watching over all things, have been accepted; the prayers which you humbly offered to the Almighty—he who, by going before, inspired you has, by helping, brought them to fulfillment—and he who first tasted your affection will powerfully supply its fulfillment. He will fill [Note: Witness 1 reads “inplevit” (“has filled”) for “inplebit” (“will fill”)] your heart with his wisdom [Col. 1049C] and instruct you in his commandments, and he will inscribe his admonitions in the inner chamber of your breast. You will also be advanced to the degrees of ecclesiastical dignity [Note: “promoveheris” in witnesses 1, 2, and 3]. You will beget many children for Christ and the Church by your example. And, so that you may be made more certain of these things, rise and visit blessed Remaclus, who is now not far from this neighborhood. The Lord has revealed to him what you must do [Note: “debes” in witness 3]; he himself will direct your steps toward what your soul desires” [Note: The passage from “The vows” through “your soul desires” is absent in manuscript Ch.] (Chapter 6.)]

The man of God rose quickly. He did not doubt the angelic vision and hastened toward the place to which he had been ordered to direct his steps. Saint Remaclus was meanwhile laboring in the care of feeding the sheep. Blessed Trudo approached and drew near, when suddenly, just as the Holy Spirit had earlier revealed to his ear, he said to his attendants: “Rise quickly [Note: The passage from “Rise” through “bring him in” is absent in manuscript Ch.], go as quickly as you can to meet the man of God who has come to visit us; receive him with reverence and bring him honorably to me. Look, he is close by; hasten to meet him.” They carried out his commands and brought him to the bishop, who was staying at home with his companions [Note: “manebant” in witnesses 1 and 2; corrected to “manebat” in witness 2] [Col. 1050A] [Note: The passage from “Rise” through “bring him in” is absent in manuscript Ch.].

When the compassionate father saw him, he rose and, weeping for joy, rushed to kiss him. He supported him as he tried to throw himself at his feet and immediately lifted him from the ground. Then he offered these thanks to God from the depths of his heart:

“Good Jesus [Note: The passage from “Good Jesus” through “foreknowing” is absent in manuscript Ch.], visitor of souls through the Holy Spirit with the eternal Father, to you be glory, praise, and jubilation. You have wished to console us on this day through the arrival of your servant, in whom you dwell” (Chapter 7).

“And you, my son, be blessed by God Most High, who has deigned to direct you to us and to signify to us, by hidden inspiration, the desire of your heart. Know, therefore, my son, in advance [Note: The passage from “Good Jesus” through “foreknowing” is absent in manuscript Ch.], that from this hour you will be my son by the bond of charity, and I shall perpetually fulfill for you the rights of a spiritual father. For the Lord has deigned to reveal to me, his servant, whatever you ought to do concerning the disposition of your heart [Col. 1050B], and through me you will be fully instructed how you may accomplish your desire.

“I have learned that in your childhood, under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, you vowed that, if with Christ’s assistance you should ever learn the sacred letters, you would build a church on your inheritance and serve him there for the rest of your life. Know that you will fulfill all these things in the following order: you must give to the protomartyr Saint Stephen the possessions that you have near the city of Metz [Note: “to be added”; absent in witnesses 1, 2, and 3], and learn the divine Scriptures fully from those who dwell there. Afterwards, having fulfilled your vow, you will return to me and build the church wherever you wish, just as you promised.”

Accordingly, he gave him a little letter of introduction, fortified with his blessing, and sent him to the bishop of the city of Metz, so that, according to what the saint had indicated to him [Note: “indicaverit” in witnesses 2 and 3], he might be instructed by the Spirit [Note: absent in witness 3]. At that time Chlodulfus presided over the city of Metz [Note: “Choldulfus” in witness 1] [Note: Compare the *Life of Saint Chlodulfus*], the worthy heir and successor of blessed Arnulf—not only as his son according to the flesh, but also in the merits of his virtues and in the insignia of the episcopate [Note: The passage from “blessed” through “commanded” is absent in manuscript Ch.].

He received blessed Trudo most kindly and humanely, rejoicing not only in the choice of the one who was being received, but also in the most reverent recommendation of the one who had sent him, namely Saint Remaclus [Note: absent in witness 1]. He learned the reasons for his arrival and ordered that he be instructed in the sacred letters and divine law [Note: The passage from “blessed” through “commanded” is absent in manuscript Ch.]. He accepted the transfer of his possessions on behalf of Saint Stephen and treated him kindly while he remained there for many years. Having been instructed in what he had come to learn and promoted even to the dignity of the priesthood, he sent him back to his holy father and fellow bishop Remaclus.

[(Donatus, *Life of Saint Trudo*, chapters 9 and 13.) When Remaclus asked what the Lord had done for him, and whether his journey and return had been prosperous [Note: “prosperatum” in witnesses 2 and 3], and approved that he had been instructed in divine law, he gave immense thanks to God: “Praise [Note: The passage from “Praise” through “you have brought him back” is absent in manuscript Ch.] be to you, Lord, Father of heaven and [Note: “and” in witness 3] earth, because you have deigned to fulfill the word that you revealed to me, insignificant though I am, concerning your servant; and because you have returned him safely to me, properly ordered according to your commandments [Note: “ornatum” in Donatus’s *Life of Trudo*] [Note: The passage from “Praise” through “you have brought him back” is absent in manuscript Ch.].” And he granted him permission to proclaim the divine word in his diocese, to celebrate Mass in whatever churches he wished, and, as he had promised in childhood, to build an oratory on his own property.] (Compare chapter 15.)]

After remaining there for some time in the holiest manner of life, he at last received an episcopal and paternal blessing and returned to his native land. He accomplished what he had long held in his heart: he founded an oratory on his estate, filled it with servants of God, and finally requested consecration from blessed Remaclus, which he also obtained. After the many labors of this life, he was buried there; and through many benefits and miracles, he still provides suitable dwellings for the monastic order to this day [Col. 1051B].

### 45. How far he was removed from greed

It is worthwhile here to dwell at some length on the fact that, as we said above, all the fires of greed had died down in blessed Remaclus; that he surpassed the merits of all the priests of our age; and that, by comparison with him, he condemned all the bishops of our time. If the same choice were perhaps offered to them as to this holy man [Note: “opinio” in witness 3], they would doubtless do something else in order not to do that: while they should direct devoted donors to bequeath their gifts to another church rather than to their own, they would themselves discourage such action, indeed make the gifts bequeathed to themselves, and—to speak with their permission—supplant others.

The more this must be impressed upon us, the more the merit of blessed Remaclus, who rejected such things, must be proclaimed with magnificent praises [Col. 1051C]. For this reason we thought the entire account of blessed Trudo ought to be inserted [Note: The passage from “The entire” through “provided” is absent in manuscript Ch.], so that we might also demonstrate that the gift of prophecy and knowledge of future events were not lacking in the holy priest Remaclus.

[When Trudo, the servant of Christ, was first departing from him, and Remaclus’s attendants mocked him because he had taken such a person to himself dressed in such wretched clothing, Remaclus learned this through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, rebuked them most severely for it, received their repentance, and thereafter admonished them to amend their ways.

“But more of this elsewhere. Who, finally, could adequately describe how holily and religiously blessed Remaclus lived thereafter, or how great his solicitude was for the flock entrusted to him? He warned everyone to beware of the allurements of the flattering world [Note: “lenotiis” in witness 1; the *Life of Remaclus* reads “blandimentis”], to draw back their steps from secular concerns, to maintain the harmony of brotherly peace, and to run without offense along the path of God’s commandments. They should not love the world and its desires [Col. 1052A], but should trample them without resistance in their hearts, like the flower of hay that quickly passes away; they should desire heavenly things in mind and deed.]

In this work he began to burn with still greater intensity of mind, so that he might more freely be at leisure for contemplation [Note: The gloss *i. q. desiduo* identifies the unusual *desidius* with a form connected with leisure/rest; it should not be pressed into an unsupported “more continually”] and might see how sweet the Lord is; and he earnestly desired that the reasons enabling this to happen more easily might be supplied to him [Note: “quo” in witnesses 2 and 3].

### 46. How Sigebert, on his advice, first built a monastery on the Sismara and afterward one in the Ardennes

Sigebert, the glorious king of that time, founded with the greatest devotion places to be dedicated to the worship of the saints in regions where there were none. He supported those already founded, whether by himself or by preceding kings, with the greatest generosity and resources; and, so that the worship owed to God might not be lacking, he provided for it through the vigilance both of this holy father and of the other priests [Note: See the variant readings].

[At a place called Casecongidunus [Note: Cougnon, between the towns of Bouillon and Chiny], situated above the river Sesmarus [Note: “Sesomiris” in Sigebert’s table] [Note: The Semoy], that same king had built a monastery, on the advice of his nobles, in honor of the apostles Peter, Paul, and John, because the site appeared to offer suitable dwellings for servants of God. He enriched it with his generous gifts and gathered there persons approved as servants of God. He appointed blessed Remaclus as its administrator and commissioned him to accustom its inhabitants to live according to the tradition of the Fathers [Note: These details are taken from the foundation charter of King Sigebert, which, lacking all chronological indications, is conjectured to have been written between the years 644 and 648. See J. Veldius’s commentary on Saint Remaclus, *Acta Sanctorum*, February I, 234].]

A place of prayer, cut into the rock through his work, remains there to the present day, from which benefits still come to the sick. There he himself for some time offered himself as a victim upon the altar of the supreme God, worn down by fasts and vigils; more intimately united to God, he devoted himself to holy contemplation and poured the streams of his teaching into the hearts of those subject to him.

At length he grew weary of that place, though it is uncertain for what reasons. Yet, according to the report of tradition, the place was pressed on every side by the attacks of the neighboring and more powerful inhabitants, and the king had no nearby [Note: The remainder is absent in manuscript Ch.] place from which any expansion could be made for it [Note: “ullu” is deleted in witness 1; “fieret” in witness 1; “fieri” in witness 2; witness 3 has “possit dilatio”]. The holy man therefore resolved to approach the king about the matter.

“Renowned prince,” he said, “I have decided to test your highness, because although you have many monasteries dedicated by your generosity to the worship of God and the saints, the Ardennes alone, situated in lofty mountains and set apart beyond the boundary, is known to have few—or rather no—monasteries. Therefore let your serenity command that some be built there. With God’s favor, the means for building will be available, and the proximity of our see will supply what is needed. It will not be impossible to enlarge them and provide what is necessary, since it is clear that all the surrounding lands belong to your authority.”

“You [Note: Witness 3 reads “Tunc” (“then”) for “Tuum” (“your”)], most blessed father,” replied the king, “must advise us in this matter; it will be ours to lend our ears as quickly as possible to your counsel [Note: Witnesses 1, 2, and 3 read “uestrae” (“your”) for “nostrae” (“our”)], to assent to your serenity, and to see that the work is carried out promptly.”

“It is for you, I say, to arrange the matter and devote yourself to the work; it is for us to assign the sites you select as suitable for it and to provide from our resources whatever assistance you may need” [Note: “indigneris” in witnesses 1, 2, and 3].

The king then summoned his faithful men: Saint Cunibert, archbishop [Note: Of Cologne], Atellanus [Note: Of Laon], Teodefridus [Note: Of Toul], and Gislochardus [Note: Of Verdun], likewise bishops; also his nobles, Grimoaldus, mayor of the palace, Fulchoaldus, Bobo, and his household officers Chlodulfus [Note: “choldulfo” in witnesses 1 and 2; “clodulpho” in witness 3; “Flodulfo” in Sigebert’s table; “Chlodulfo” in Childeric’s table], Ansigisilus, and Betselinus [Note: The author preserved, with a few omissions, the order in which the names occur in King Sigebert’s charter. See *Acta Sanctorum*]. “By the will of God,” he said, “and with your agreement and that of our other faithful men [Note: “vestr.” in witnesses 1, 2, and 3; “nostr.” in the *Life of Remaclus*], we are deliberating about founding two monasteries within our forest [Note: “forensem” in witness 3], situated in the woodland of the Ardennes [Note: “vestr.” in witnesses 1, 2, and 3; “nostr.” in the *Life of Remaclus*], in which religious men devoted to the monastic order may be gathered. For the safety of ourselves and our successors, for the stability and peace of our entire kingdom, and for the watchful observance of those who attend to the kingdom’s affairs, they ought to beseech almighty God with abundant prayer. With blessed Remaclus before us as the adviser and instigator of this undertaking, we have appointed him administrator and master of the work [Note: “ministrum” in witnesses 2 and 3].”

### 47. On the construction of Malmundarium

Having received royal authority and the assistance of the necessary counts, the holy priest undertook the vast woodland of the Ardennes, full of marshes and rugged mountains [Note: “confrogasis” in witnesses 1, 2, and 3] [Col. 1053C]. He crossed the Fagnes [Note: “Les hautes Fagnes,” “die hohe Veen”], approached the stream of Warchinne [Note: The Warchienne, a brook that overflows into the Warche. See the description of that region given by Roderique, p. 93, in the book mentioned in the preface] [Note: “peraccessit” (“approached”) in witness 3], and found there indications that those places had once been devoted to idolatry: stones fashioned with images of Diana and monstrous names [Note: “daemoniosis portentis” (“demonic monstrosities”) in sources C, D, 1, 1*, and 2], and springs suitable for human use but polluted by pagan error and consequently still exposed to demonic infestation.

Having invoked the name of Christ and extended the sign of the holy cross, he purified the place from demonic attack, and immediately the water, trickling drop by drop from its own channel, disappeared. Seeing that the place was suitable for habitation both because of its fish-filled waters and its abundant pastures, he increased the blessing of prayer abundantly over the springs, carved the sign of the cross into a stone, and poured lead over it [Note: The *Life of Remaclus* adds “with holes”]. At once copious waters flowed back, which still today give proof to those who see them [Col. 1053D]. And because he had cleansed the place from the infestation of evil spirits [Col. 1054A], it pleased him to call it Malmundarium [Note: Malmedy], as though it had been cleansed from evil.

There he built an oratory, constructed dwellings for the use of the servants of God [Note: “adversus” (“against,” for “ad usus,” “for the use”) in witness 1], and increased everything pertaining to the worship of God.

### 48. On the construction of Stabulaus

Because that place lay in the parish of Cologne, he took care to begin another one that would be enclosed within the limits of his own diocese [Note: “statuit” (“decided”) in witness 1, corrected in another ink to “studuit” (“strove”)]. Proceeding from there about two miles toward the west [Note: “militibus” (“soldiers”) in witness 1, for “milibus” (“miles”)], he crossed the stream called Calla, which is [Note: The passage from “Proceeding” through “foresaw” is absent in manuscript Ch.] a boundary between parishes, and stopped at [Note: “ad” (“at”) is absent in witness 3] the river Amblava [Note: Ambleve] on the border of a certain mountain [Note: The words “which … river” were inserted in the same hand in witness 1].

After remaining there for some time, he accomplished many things conducive to a disciplined way of life, as anyone may learn from the inhabitants who recount them [Col. 1054B]. But because the same place was confined by the narrowness of the terrain [Note: The *Life of Remaclus* adds “although it abounded in springs”] [Note: “angustus” (“narrow”) in witness 1], and therefore was less adequate for the needs of necessary workshops, he returned again toward the east and searched out a more spacious place, more suitable for the work to come [Note: Corrected in another ink in witness 1] [Note: See above, variant note 597].

He began to devote himself more attentively to the proposed labor. As usually happens in such matters, divine power cooperated, and the result followed the will with prosperous success. Because, on account of the convergence of wild beasts from every direction, whether to drink or to feed, as though they were running together to a stable, the place had long been called Stabulaus, he did not think it worthy to change the name. Rather, he wished it always thereafter to be called and to be a stable of faithful souls hastening there as to the pastures of eternal life.

For the great herd of various wild beasts often making noise there caused no small terror to the brothers whom the holy man had gathered there at that time [Note: The *Life of Remaclus* has “the noise”]. They therefore ran back in fear to blessed Remaclus, who was engaged in that work, and urgently asked what protection and defense they should employ against these snares of the devil.

He consoled them kindly and encouraged them all together:

“Believe faithfully in the Lord, little sons; embrace his commandments without violation. Keep your minds unharmed by thoughts that are without understanding; purifying your souls, offer pure service to the Lord. Pray without ceasing; at evening, morning, and midday sing psalms; devote yourselves to reading as often as possible. Fortify your foreheads with the sign of the cross; hide its power in the deepest chamber of your hearts, and immediately the snares and machinations of the invisible enemy [Col. 1054D] will be reduced to nothing. The terror of these beasts [Col. 1055A], through which he hopes to have found an entrance for attacking us, will be in vain.

“For in this way he attacked [Note: The words “Taliter enim inpugnabat” (“For in this way he attacked”) are absent in manuscript Ch.] those who inhabited the vast deserts of Egypt, the Thebaid, and Nitria before us [Note: The *Life of Remaclus* adds “before us”]; may God grant that we may become even faint imitators of them. He has a thousand arts of doing harm and innumerable deceitful ambushes. But we are not ignorant of his cunning, since he has sometimes even begun an assault through his flies.

“But we, servants of Christ, the more we are pressed by his attacks, the more we rise when we resist. Satan, experienced in these matters [Note: The *Life of Remaclus* reads “sanitas” (“health”); witnesses 1, 2, and 3 have the printed “satanas” (“Satan”)], fears those who begin to live rightly: vigils, prayers, fasts, gentleness, patience, voluntary poverty, contempt of empty glory, humility, mercy, and especially pure love toward Christ. Therefore, like a lion, he lies hidden in ambush in his den, so that he may frighten us away from our purpose [Col. 1055B] [Note: The *Life of Remaclus* has “vos,” “you,” instead of “nos,” “us”; the words “ut nos deterreat a proposito” (“so that he may frighten us away from our purpose”) are absent in manuscript Ch.].”

By exhorting them with these and similar words [Note: The *Life of Remaclus* has “exhortatur” (“he exhorts”)], he made their minds more ready for the service of God and rendered them more steadfast against every temptation. After appointing overseers for the works, he delegated to each the tasks that had to be done. Then, returning to Tongrians or Trajectum, he again occupied himself with the duties of pastoral care.

Not much time had passed when the king heard that monasteries had been built in his forest. He gave immense thanks to almighty God. Because the churches, newly adorned with building material, required episcopal blessing, he sent for blessed Remaclus and ordered him, with the consent of the venerable Cunibert, metropolitan of the same city, to solemnly consecrate both the church subject to the diocese of Cologne and the one adjoining our diocese. Since they had been built through his direction [Note: “expositioni” (“at the arrangement,” dative) in witness 1; “dispositione” (“by the arrangement”) in the *Life of Remaclus*] and greatest effort, they were also to receive episcopal blessing through his diligence.

The holy man immediately fulfilled this, since he was so dear to the king and nobles that nothing important was done without his advice. Thus it happened that, because he was held by them in such honor and dignity, after the solemn celebration of the Mass, Grimoaldus, mayor of the palace, handed both monasteries over to the blessed man to govern thereafter with his skill, and ordered that everything necessary for the monastic order be supplied from the royal authority at his recommendation and through his care.

### 49. How, after designating his successor, he longed for the hermit’s life

### Precise apparatus by passage and source lemma

The following passage-keyed notes supplement the inline notes above. They retain the actual source form, its English force, and the witness or editorial scope.

- **Cols. 1045–1046, Remaclus’s education.** Witnesses 2–3 read *inde* (“from there”) for *unde* (“whence”); witness 3 *flectamus* (“let us bend”) for *reflectamus* (“let us turn back”). The silence about Sulpicius is specifically in the contemporary *Life of Sulpicius* (*Acta SS.*, Jan. III, 167). At Solemniacum, manuscript 1 has *sollemniaco* and manuscript 3 *cum sollempniaco*; the editorial identification is Solignac in Aquitaine, diocese of Limoges (*Life of Eligius* I.16; Surius VI, 636). C and D have *apprime* (“very thoroughly”) and D1 *ad primum* (“at first”).
- **Cols. 1045–1046, youthful conduct and court call.** Manuscript 1 corrects *exesutor* to *executor* (“doer”); manuscript 3 omits *ita* (“so”); manuscripts 2–3, Ch., and the *Life* read *pernox* (“all-night”) for *per noctem* (“through the night”), while manuscript 3 has *honestate* (“uprightness”) for *probitate* (“moral excellence”). Ch. omits exactly the material from *Post haec* (“After these things”) to *candelabro* (“lampstand”); manuscript 1 omits *gestorum eorum opinio* (“report of their deeds”), and reads *ea* (“those things”) for *eo modo* (“in that manner”).
- **Cols. 1046–1047, Amandus and the vacancy.** Manuscript 2 corrects *exiuit* (“went out/died”) to *exuit* (“put off”); Ch. lacks almost all that follows *Inclitus rex Dagobertus*. The Life of Amandus requires *per regenerationem* (“through the rebirth”), correcting the manuscripts’ *peregrinationem* (“pilgrimage”); the editor explains that this is baptism. Manuscript 1 has *pleps* for *plebs* (“people”); the *Life of Remaclus* has *magnatum* (“of nobles”), the Life of Hadrian *magistrorum* (“of masters”), and manuscripts 1–3 *magnarum* (“of great [women]”).
- **Cols. 1047–1048, election and character.** In *aetatis acceptum*, manuscript 1 writes *aet. acceptum* but deletes *acceptum*; it omits *secundum* (“second”). Ch. omits from *hunc* (“this man”) through *deflorata* (“set out”). Manuscript 2 corrects *omne* to *omnem* so that “whole” agrees with *catalogum*; manuscripts 1 and 3 have *destituit* (“abandoned”), corrected in manuscript 2 and the Life to *destitit* (“desisted”). The Life reads *accommodarent* (“they might apply”), while the manuscripts’ *desideratur* means “is desired”; Ch. omits from *cum* to *obaeditionis*. The Life’s *arrogantiam* is accusative “arrogance,” whereas the printed *arrogantia* is nominative; manuscript 1 has *revertebantur* (“were turning back”) for *reverebantur* (“revered”).
- **Cols. 1048–1049, disciples and chapter 44.** The Life reads *educati* (“educated”) for *edocti* (“instructed”), and *tali* (“such”) for *usuratu* (“use”). Ch. omits exactly the clauses *Non … opera* and *quorum … augmentis*; manuscripts 2–3 omit *utpote ab ipso sibi successor designatus* (“as having been designated by him as successor”). The chapter number is LIII in manuscripts 1–2. Manuscript 3 calls Badelinus *Hadelinus*; manuscript 1 repeats *fuisse* (“to have been”); *cumversationis* in manuscript 1 is a misspelling of *conversationis* (“way of life”). The editorial topographical note identifies the place as Celle near Dinant (Chapeav). Manuscript 3 omits *et* in *dum et* (“while also”) and has *corporenus* for *corpore tenus* (“as to the body”). Ch. omits exactly *In sancti … hortabatur*.
- **Cols. 1049–1050, Trudo’s call.** Manuscripts 1–2 read *circuiebat*, manuscript 2 corrects it to *circuibat*, and manuscript 3 has *circuibat*: all mean “went about.” The editorial note at Sarchinium identifies it as in Hasbania. Manuscript 3 omits *cooperatores* (“co-workers”); manuscript 1 has *conservaturos* (“those who will serve together”) for *conservituros* (“fellow servants”). The note *paginae praecedentis* means “of the preceding page,” marking continuation, not source text. Manuscript 1 has *inplevit* (“has filled”) for *inplebit* (“will fill”); manuscripts 1–3 have *promoveheris* (“you will be advanced”) for *promoveberis*; manuscript 1 corrects *illic* (“there”) to *illi* (“to him”), and manuscript 3 has *debes* (“you ought”) for *habes* (“you have”). Ch. omits exactly *Vota … anima tua* (“the vows … your soul”).
- **Cols. 1049–1050, reception and instruction.** Manuscript 1 has *quos* (“whom”) for *quo* (“where/to which”), and manuscripts 2–3 *propinquabat* (“was approaching”) for *appropinquabat* (“drew near”). Ch. omits precisely *Surgite … introducunt* (“Rise … they bring [him] in”), including its repeated close after *introducunt*. Manuscripts 1–2 write *manebant* (“they stayed”), corrected in manuscript 2 to *manebat* (“he stayed”). Ch. omits *bone … praenoscens* (“good … foreknowing”), both when it first occurs and when it is resumed. Manuscripts 1–3 read *novisse* (“to have known”) for *vovisse* (“to have vowed”); the editor says an object after *quas* (“which possessions”) seems required but is absent from manuscripts 1–3. Compare Donatus, *Life of Trudo* 6 and 9.
- **Cols. 1050–1051, Metz and return.** Manuscripts 2–3 have *indicaverit* (“will have indicated”) for *indicaverat* (“had indicated”); manuscript 3 omits *Spiritus* (“Spirit”). Manuscript 1 has *Choldulfus* for *Chlodulfus*; compare the *Life of Chlodulfus*. Ch. omits *beati … mandavit* (“of blessed [Arnulf] … he ordered”), and manuscript 1 omits *sancti* (“holy”) before Remaclus. In Donatus manuscripts 2–3 have *prosperatum* (“prospered”) for *prosperum* (“successful”), manuscript 3 *et* (“and”) for *ac* (“and”), and *ornatum* (“adorned”) for *ordinatum* (“ordered”). Ch. omits *Laus … revocasti* (“Praise … you brought [him] back”).
- **Cols. 1051–1052, greed and ascetic purpose.** Manuscript 3 has *opinio* (“opinion”) for *optio* (“choice”); C, D, 1, 1*, and 2 have *conculcandum* (“to be trampled down”) for *inculcandum* (“to be impressed”). Ch. omits *Totum … providebat* (“the whole [text] … he provided”). Manuscript 3 has *ejus* (“his”) for *illius* (“that man’s”), manuscript 1 *lenotiis* for *lenociniis* (“allurements”), and the Life *blandimentis* (“enticements”) for *blandientis* (“flattering”). The gloss *i. q. desiduo* relates the unusual *desidius* to leisure/rest in the contemplative context; it does not establish “more continually.” Witnesses 2–3 have *quo* (“by which/so that”) for *quod* (“that”).
- **Cols. 1051–1053, Sigebert and the Ardennes.** Manuscript 1 has *Ssismara* and Sigebert’s charter *Sesomiris* for the river Semoy; Cougnon lies between Bouillon and Chiny. The foundation details derive from Sigebert’s privilege, thought to have been written 644–648 because it lacks chronological marks; see Veldius, *Acta SS.*, Feb. I, 234. Ch. lacks the remainder after *nec* (“and not”); manuscript 1 deletes *ullu* (“any”), has *fieret* (“might be made”) while manuscript 2 has *fieri* (“to be made”), and manuscript 3 *possit dilatio* (“an enlargement may be possible”).
- **Cols. 1052–1053, royal dialogue and charter.** Manuscript 1 has *arduentia* for *Arduenna*; the Life has *sanctificando* (“consecrating”) where manuscripts 1–3 have *aedificando* (“building”). Manuscript 3 reads *Tunc* (“then”) for *Tuum* (“your”); manuscripts 1–3 *uestrae* (“your”) for *nostrae* (“our”). The printed *indigueris* is the legitimate future-perfect form from *indigere*, “whatever assistance you may need”; witnesses 1–3 have *indigneris*, a corrupt form, not an uncertainty in the meaning. Cunibert is Cologne’s archbishop, Atellanus Laon’s, Teodefridus Toul’s, and Gislochardus Verdun’s. For Chlodulfus: manuscripts 1–2 *choldulfo*, manuscript 3 *clodulpho*, Sigebert’s charter *Flodulfo*, Childeric’s *Chlodulfo*. The author retained, with few omissions, the charter’s order of names (*Acta SS.* cited above). Witnesses 1–3 have *vestr.* (“your”) and the Life *nostr.* (“our”); manuscript 3 *forensem* (“outside/market-place”) for *forestem* (“forest”), and manuscripts 2–3 *ministrum* (“minister/servant”) for *magistrum* (“master”).
- **Cols. 1053–1054, Malmedy.** Manuscripts 1–3 have *confrogasis* for *confragosis* (“rugged”); the Fagnes are the Hautes Fagnes / hohe Veen, and Warchinne is the Warchienne stream flowing into the Warche (Roderique, p. 93). Manuscript 3 has *peraccessit* for *peraccedit* (“approaches”); C, D, 1, 1*, and 2 read *daemoniosis portentis* (“demonic monstrosities”) for *portentuosis nominibus* (“monstrous names”). The Life adds *cum foraminibus* (“with holes”) to the lead; Malmundarium is Malmedy; manuscript 1 has *adversus* (“against”) for *ad usus* (“for the use”).
- **Cols. 1053–1055, Stavelot.** Manuscript 1 first wrote *statuit* (“decided”) and corrected it in another ink to *studuit* (“strove”); it has *militibus* (“soldiers”) for *milibus* (“miles”). Ch. omits exactly *Procedens … prospexit* (“Proceeding … he looked out”); manuscript 3 omits *ad* (“at”), the words *qui … fluvium* (“which … river”) are inserted by the same hand in manuscript 1, and Amblava is the Amblève. The Life adds *licet afflueret fontibus* (“although it abounded in springs”); manuscript 1 has *angustus* (“narrow”), and marks *aptiorem* (“more suitable”) corrected in another ink. The reference “see above variant note 597” is retained as such.
- **Cols. 1054–1055, beasts, exhortation, and consecration.** Manuscripts 1 and 3 have *portum* (“harbor”) corrected in manuscript 2 to *potum* (“drink”); the Life has *strepitus* (“noise”) for *caterva … perstrepens* (“a herd … making a din”). Ch. omits *Taliter enim inpugnabat* (“For in this way he attacked”); the Life adds *ante nos* (“before us”). The Life’s *sanitas* (“health”) stands against manuscripts 1–3 *satanas* (“Satan”), and its *vos* (“you”) against printed *nos* (“us”); Ch. omits exactly *ut nos deterreat a proposito* (“so that he may frighten us from our purpose”). The Life has *exhortatur* (“he exhorts”) for *exhortans* (“exhorting”). At the consecration, manuscript 1 has *expositioni* (dative “for the exposition/direction”), while the Life has *dispositione* (“by arrangement”); the point is his direction in building, not a generic ‘exposition’.

Therefore the holy priest, in this way, by God’s assent, obtained an opportunity for what he had always desired: namely, the solitude of a more secluded life [Col. 1055D].

> [Life of Remaclus, ch. 12:] At last, although with the greatest difficulty, he nevertheless obtained from the king that another should succeed him and that he might be permitted to enter the long-desired wilderness, where, withdrawn from secular cares, he might more freely aspire to heavenly things.

> [Note: At col. 1055, *remotis* (“removed”) was corrected to *remotus* (“removed,” masculine singular) in manuscript 1 in a different ink.]

He presented the life of Saint Theodard as sufficiently worthy of approval to the king and nobles, and designated him by name to take his place and to be installed after him in his see [Col. 1056A] (661).

> [Note: At col. 1055, *remotis* was corrected to *remotus* in manuscript 1 in a different ink. On the time of his abdication, see Veldius’s commentary cited above.]

[Oh, what great mourning arose at his departure! How sorrowfully he left those to whom he had imparted the seeds of life, when they saw themselves left without such a father and so great a teacher!] Every age and both sexes testified to the grief of their hearts with tears and, as they accompanied him, expressed it with loud cries [Col. 1056C].

> [Note: Absent from Ch.]

[Alas, wretched ones, what are we to do, since we are losing so great a shepherd? Where shall we receive consolation, when he himself was the chief relief of our troubles? Who will heal us henceforth, when he alone was the medicine of our sorrows? What place of salvation finally remains for us, since we are deprived of the presence of so great a father?]

> [Note: Manuscripts 1–3 have *quid*; Ch. omits the passage.]

Moved by their lamentation, the holy man consoled them as follows:

> [Note: From “Do not” through “endure” in chapter 51, almost everything is absent from Ch.]

“Do not, I beg you, little sons, pursue the purpose of my mind with such persecutions. You have God above all as your shepherd and father, eternally a kindly comforter in your difficulties. For your external needs we have provided our son Theodard, approved in every respect, a most discerning overseer and, according to his capacity to distribute, a most faithful dispenser of grain to his fellow servants in due season.

> [Note: At col. 1055, *commodis* is found in manuscripts 1 and 3; manuscript 2 corrected *incommodis* to *commodis*.]

“Since I do not doubt that his provision will suffice for you, I have resolved to go to the place of my beloved solitude and strive to dwell alone with myself in the sight of the heavenly Watcher.”

### 50. The response of the sons opposing this action

> [Note: The number is absent in manuscript 2.]

Then the more prudent among those present addressed him at length [Col. 1056C]:

“See, most blessed father, see what you are doing; consider to what disgrace you are exposing us. As the decrees of the fathers determine, once you have undertaken the governance of a flock, you may not resign it unless compelled by illness, nor may you voluntarily renounce it.

“For as long as a bishop lives, when necessity arising from illness—not crime—removes him from his office, no ordination permits another to take his place unless he himself refuses and confirms his request in writing. Even if he is mentally incapacitated but is accustomed to have intervals of illness, another must not succeed him unless he gives his consent by submitting a request. But if he never returns to the office of a sound mind, a faithful person of worthy life must be chosen to discharge his duties only while he lives, so that, when he dies, a successor may rightly be ordained.

“According to this rule promulgated by the fathers, if anyone acts otherwise, he unquestionably makes the woman he has dismissed into an adulteress and gives the name ‘adulterer’ to the man who marries her. By this reasoning, most holy father, consider how greatly your judgment is burdened; consider how much damage our reputation will suffer as disgrace follows.

“No crime is being charged against you, by which you might be convicted and deposed; no condition of illness aggravates your case, by which you might be suspended from office for presenting a repudiation [Col. 1057A]. Therefore we reject your request for renunciation, even if it is supported in writing; and we wholly disapprove both one who would discharge your duties and, still more, one who would become your successor while you live.

“We admitted you as our father through a lawful succession; we ardently desire to be called and to be sons, not adulterers. You have already perceived where your judgment is most heavily burdened; hear, we beg you, where our reputation suffers damage amid the disgrace that follows.

“You have no reason for abandoning us. First, we are not fornicators, so that by right you should leave us. You received us into the bosom of the Catholic mother; we have never readily lent our ears to perverse doctrine, and if we had perhaps gone astray in such a manner, you ought certainly to have come to our aid.

“Next, your departure elsewhere is not forced by persecution from us [Col. 1057B]. Even if this consultation of the weak and imperfect is conceded by the Lord, many saints patiently endured the perversity of evil people, and their endurance became a discipline for them. Finally, the wicked are to be fled rather than borne with equanimity only where no good people remain who can in some way be won over.

“But woe to us, who, deprived of your presence—which is acknowledged to be most perfect—are exposed to such infamy that we are said not merely to weary you through our zeal, but to drive you away by our evil actions, since your departure will be taken as proof that no good person remains here.

“Now let the malicious speak evil; let the slanderers make predictions that your successors will perhaps not merely have to be driven away but even exposed to death, while you evade our governance and blessed Amandus, who preceded you, departed from us shaking the dust from his feet [Col. 1057C].

“Yet almighty God, ready and merciful to show favor, suddenly rebuked the grieving prophet over the withered ivy (Jonah 4:10). He thereby shows that he is even more concerned over the work of his creation if it perishes, and that he prefers repentance to the death of sinners.”

> [Note: Manuscript 1 has *propitiendum* for *propitiandum*.]

### 51. The same holy man’s defense

> [Note: This heading was added by a later hand in manuscript 1 and is absent from manuscript 2.]

At last Saint Remaclus, shaken by the remonstrances of those who opposed him, weighed his thoughts for a while in measured silence and then burst forth in these words:

“Do not, my brothers, do not accuse me in this way, fathers. To lament your welfare before me is not something from which I should shrink; but to press this injury in such a way is not something I can endure.

> [Note: At col. 1057, manuscript 1 has *nos* for *non*.]

“I do not affirm that you are fornicators, as though you had been placed in my heart to be abandoned; nor do I condemn you collectively in such a way that all of you must necessarily be fruitless. When I consider that my labor here is without fruit, I wish to depart elsewhere where it may bear fruit.

“No, I say: it is clear that I am not perfect; to call me most perfect is far from the truth. But, to use your own judgment rather than my own, it belongs to the perfect both not to shrink from what they have begun and to extend themselves toward further perfection: to persist with Martha in the active life, to sigh ardently with Mary for the contemplative life, and, if the opportunity is given, to withdraw from the active life rather than fail to correspond most eagerly to contemplative reflection.

“I have governed the flock entrusted to me among you, with the Lord’s cooperation, as I was able. I have heaped desire upon desire that my labor might bear fruit. I am not sated with your pursuits, nor am I offended by any perversity in your actions, for there is none.

> [Note: Manuscript 1 has *nostra* for *vestra*.]

“It remains for me to carry elsewhere, to be multiplied, the talent which, to my joy, I see accumulated in you in accordance with my desires, so that your abundance may supply the poverty of others.

“The saints acted similarly before your time. Would that we might prove equal to them in merit—or even to the least among them! Some, for the sake of greater usefulness, allowed themselves to be transferred to other churches; others, trusting in a superior merit, departed voluntarily. When they perceived that they were accomplishing little or were not greatly needed, they withdrew and offered themselves to greater labors. As God’s most courageous warriors, they did not wish to be held within the enclosure of rest, but willingly leapt into the open field of battle. They did not become deserters from spiritual warfare, nor were they comparable to hirelings who flee at the sight of wolves. Rather, when they saw that some were fighting weakly or that enemies were pressing close upon them, they thrust themselves forward to engage there bravely.

“And I, little sons, do not exalt myself by displaying these examples, nor do I, as a vain comparer of merits, rank myself alongside them.

“If the name of successor is repugnant to you, let the commendation of a co-worker and fellow administrator give you strength. Do not think yourselves deprived of my presence; for, although I shall go to instruct others, I shall not be able to go beyond your diocese.

“Soon there will be access to me, so that I may offer counsel if any event befalls you. You will have me as an intercessor for your transgressions and as one mindful of all your needs, the more diligently attentive to you the more clearly it is established that I have withdrawn from popular cares and aspire more earnestly to contemplation of divinity.

> [Note: At col. 1057, manuscript 1 has *vestra* for *nostra*.]

“And Moses stood on the mountain and fought not with weapons but with prayers, while Israel fought against Amalek (Exodus 17:9). Israel was superior in the battle to the extent that Moses was nearer to God in prayer and more distant from the tumult of the fighting enemies.

“And for me, dearest ones, it is settled that I should cling more closely to the divine gaze there, where I need not endure the tumult of worldly affairs [Col. 1058D].”

> [Note: Almost everything up to this point is absent from Ch.]

“Blessed John the Baptist inspired me to this hope (Matthew 3:1). Even in the tenderness of his years, he chose to be a dweller among beasts, including sharing their food, rather than contaminate his life among citizens even with a mild speech.

> [Note: Manuscript 2 has *letu* or *saltu*; manuscript 1 has *saltem*; manuscript 3 and Ch. have *levi saltem*. The correct reading may perhaps be *Jerusalem*.]

“Moses approved this life: in the desert of a vast solitude he preferred to enjoy conversation with God rather than be weakened by the Egyptians’ divinations (Exodus 3). Elijah and Elisha (2 Kings 2), and the other prophets, dedicated themselves to it; distinguished by contemplation of this way of life, they subdued themselves to it.

“Abraham, made by faith the father of all believers (Genesis 12; Romans 4:16), urged me toward these deeds. I imitated his example: leaving my native land, I renounced all the profits of worldly desires.

“The deed of the Savior himself led me to this purpose. Intending to defeat the devil, he resolved to enter the wilderness alone (Matthew 4). May his mercy grant and his loving-kindness permit me there to trample the cunning of the ancient enemy, to gather gains from those whom I instruct there, and here to serve your needs by my prayer.”

Thus Saint Remaclus concluded his speech; thus he addressed the grief of those who opposed him; thus he satisfied their complaints. Then he hastened toward the purpose he had set and reached it [Col. 1059A].

### 52. How many people left the world following his example

> [Note: Manuscript 2 has *reliquer* for *reliquerunt*.]

Devout men, hearing these things either from the neighboring regions or from distant parts, whose hearts God had deigned to touch, began to flock to him from every direction like bees to their hives. Some devoted themselves to the service of the Almighty and submitted their necks to Christ’s gentle yoke; others entrusted their children to be instructed there in liberal monastic disciplines and to serve there perpetually; many also shared their property and revenues with the needs of the saints [Col. 1059C].

Among them came the lord and father Papolenus to visit him, but he strove to remain under his instruction rather than return. Saint Remaclus therefore received him with the greatest courtesy. He lived there without causing offense, and although he had come to be instructed, he edified many others by his example.

The holy man, considering within himself whether the Lord had perhaps sent him for this very purpose, not only asked him not to depart but also appointed him, with full authority, over the brothers established at Malmedy, for the sake of their discipline.

> [Note: The Life of Remaclus adds: “according to the institution of Saint Benedict.”]

He himself returned to Stavelot and thereafter girded himself for greater works of virtue, encouraging many others to follow his works by his example.

Who was there who did not change sadness into joy in his presence? Who did not turn anger into peace? Who did not moderate the grief of bereavement when he saw him? Who, forgetting the sorrow of poverty by which he was oppressed, did not despise the wealth of the rich and rejoice in his own poverty? Who, weighed down by the burden of labor, was not relieved by his encouragement? What young man, inflamed by the incitements of vice and the tickling of the flesh, did not immediately become a practitioner of chastity through his most salutary admonition?

He healed those tormented by the devil; likewise, he restrained those distracted by unlawful thoughts from their deeds, having dashed them against Christ the rock. He knew what difficulty afflicted each person and, making a judgment from the merits of their life, applied correction according to the nature of their illnesses.

> [Note: The Life of Notger adds *interea* (“meanwhile”).]

There the ardor of divine fervor increased, as did the inflexible rigor of monastic discipline. How thoroughly the opportunity for sin was prohibited in the other buildings of the enclosure is shown by the dormitory of that place; Saint Lambert the martyr is also a witness. Driven from his episcopal office, he decided that this place in particular should be sought because he had learned that the path of holy religion was observed there with greater rigor.

> [Note: Compare Stephen’s *Life of Saint Lambert*, chapters 5–6.]

The cross near which he stood is also a witness.

> [Stephen’s *Life of Lambert*, ch. 6:] “When he rose for prayer in the middle of the night, because the slipping of his shoe disturbed the brothers’ rest with a noise, he was sentenced to stand until dawn. He devoted himself to psalmody and prayer, repelled the cold, restrained the snow, and made known to everyone that he was holy.”

But these matters belong elsewhere.

### 54. As religion increased, so too did the property of the church

> [Life of Remaclus, ch. 14:] “As religion increased, the revenues of the church also increased. For the renowned King Sigebert, hearing of such fervor for the worship of Christ, sent for Saint Remaclus.”

In addition to what he had previously given and what the illustrious Grimoald had acquired—namely Germigny, a village in the diocese of Reims—and from which they had hitherto lived, King Sigebert, with the consent of his faithful men, both bishops and the nobles mentioned above, granted it to Saint Remaclus for the honor and worship of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and Saint Martin, to whom those places were dedicated, and for the use of the servants of God, so that thereafter they might live more peacefully and devote themselves more freely to God alone, without oppression from their neighbors.

> [Note: Germigny was in the diocese of Reims; see Grimoald’s charter in Miraeus I, 281.]

The boundaries of both monasteries were measured in a circuit of twelve Gallic leagues.

> [Note: This is taken from King Sigebert’s charter; see *Acta Sanctorum*, February I, 235. The charter says: “We granted … to avoid the company of women, so that, measuring the circuit by going around it, the spaces on both sides of both monasteries should be measured to the right through forest tracts, no more than twelve miles, so that God alone might be served without oppression from the people or secular disturbance.”]

Within those boundaries, whatever was contained there was cultivated solely by the tenants of both monasteries.

> [Note: With a few exceptions, the remainder is absent from Ch.]

It is said that a Gallic league is reckoned in that language as two thousand paces, or sixteen stadia.

> [Note: The Life of Remaclus has one thousand five hundred paces; manuscript 2 has seventeen stadia, corrected to sixteen; the Life has twelve stadia.]

The holy man willingly accepted this grant, confirmed by a testament and marked with the impression of the royal ring, and reverently retained it.

As time proceeded—specifically, in the fourteenth year of his reign—the same king added to the grant and confirmed by testament certain possessions in Aquitaine for Saint Remaclus.

> [Note: See *Acta Sanctorum*, cited above. The places whose names follow are not identified as being in Aquitaine in Sigebert’s letters.]

These were the customs revenue at the port of Vetraria on the rivers Taunacus and Itta, also the port called Sellis, and likewise Vogatio on the river Loire, with everything attached to those places.

> [Note: The Life of Remaclus has *Taunaco*; manuscripts 1–3 have *Tannaco*. The words of the charter itself follow in Notger’s Life of Remaclus.]

He also gave tithes from the royal estates adjoining the monasteries.

After these events, the same king, having gloriously governed the kingdom of Austrasia, ended his life (655). Compare the *Deeds of the Franks*, chapter 43.

Grimoald, mayor of the palace, was summoned to Paris by Clovis, his brother, under the pretext of receiving gifts, but he was not permitted to return. For he had made a cleric of the son of his lord Sigebert, whom he had received in faith, although he was to be installed in his father’s kingdom, and had arranged for his own son to reign.

> [Note: Manuscript 1 has *Chodoveo* for *Clodoveo*. Manuscript 2 adds *postea* after eight—or ten—years of reign.]

When Clovis died, his son Lothar ruled in the West, while his brother Childeric ruled the kingdom of Austrasia (656).

> [Note: Manuscript 2 corrects *Hildricus* to *Childericus*.]

> [*Deeds of the Franks*, chapters 44–45:] “The holy man approached him and asked that what his uncle had granted be confirmed. The king readily agreed and, at the request of the man of God, ordered the successor of that uncle, Saint Theobard, and Odo, his household official, to have the same measured tract surveyed. He reserved half of it for his own authority and reconfirmed the other half by testament for the use of the servants of God.”

The man of God clearly acted prudently and wisely, so that, if it should at some time prove difficult for his successors to retain all of it, they might more easily retain what remained without provoking the envy or disturbance of their neighbors.

> [Note: The Life of Remaclus has *inquietudine* for *inquietate* and *vicinorum* for *viciorum*. Compare the *Deeds of the Franks*, chapter 45.]

King Lothar died (670), and his brother Childeric obtained sole rule. Afterward, he too was killed and met his death because of his arrogance of character (673). Their brother Theuderic then succeeded to rule the western territories together with Ebroin.

> [Note: Manuscript 2 corrects *Hebruinus* to *Hebroinus*, as does manuscript 3.]

The Austrasians, renouncing their tyranny, were sufficiently active on behalf of Prince Pippin.

> [Note: Manuscript 2 adds “son of Ansegisus.” It later adds: “Theuderic reigned for seventeen years.”]

### 55. Exhortation of the holy priest to the brothers as the day of his calling approached

At that time blessed Remaclus was already advanced in age, but more mature in character than in years. Realizing that the day of his calling was approaching—the day when heavenly honor would repay the labor he had worn away on earth—he resolved to fulfill his duty toward his subjects.

He summoned them and, as they mourned the departure of their father and their own desolation, consoled them with these final words [Col. 1062A]:

“Behold, most holy fathers; behold, dearest brothers, bound to the inmost parts of my heart, half of my soul [Horace, *Odes* I, 3, 8]—I am about to enter upon the way of all the earth and shall not return to you thereafter.

“It is your solitude, the solitude of those whom I am leaving, that troubles me—not my own, for I am strengthened by God, my comforter. I am not terrified by the end common to every mortal, since the whole commendation of the life of the wise ought also to be a meditation on death.

“Death cannot be shameful for a brave man; it cannot be premature for one who has held public office; it cannot be wretched for one who looks ahead [Cicero, *Against Catiline* IV, 2].

“Rather, the tenderness of your minds—your minds which must still be formed through harsher disciplines—holds me back more strongly. I fear for you: should the rage of wolves assail you, there may be no one to drive them away.

“I dedicated these monasteries to God and the saints, and assigned them to serve your needs. For this purpose I have relied upon your strong and faithful labor, and I fear what may happen when minds must often hang in uncertainty.

“You see where our possessions lie and understand with me that this world is placed in wickedness (1 John 5:19). Therefore, if anything is of concern, take care that you never be led astray by any error from the integrity which I have placed in you, but remain joined by the unanimous bond of peace in Christ, according to what you have learned both from the tradition of the fathers and from reading the sacred Scriptures, as well as from the admonition of my vigilance.

“Let sacred reading never depart from your hands, and let continual meditation upon it be yours.

> [Note: The Life of Remaclus reads “from your ears and hands.”]

“For just as a field, however fertile, cannot be fruitful without cultivation, so the mind cannot be fruitful without instruction [Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* II, 5]. To a learned and educated person, to live is to think [Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* V, 38].

“You must frequently devote yourselves to prayer; you must pray for the transgressions contracted through human frailty, and not only supplicate concerning those yet to be contracted, but also watch over them with cautious diligence. For when anyone gives himself over to carelessness and sloth, he calls upon God in vain.

> [Note: These are Cato’s words in Sallust, *Catiline* 52.]

“Let this be your virtue: to flee vice, and your first wisdom: to lack foolishness [Horace, *Epistles* I, 1, 41].

“Modesty, the sister of justice, uncorrupted faith, and naked truth [Horace, *Odes* I, 24, 6–7] must hold a place in your hearts, so that those who see your works may be stirred to imitate them.

“Offer a true confession of your sins to God and to your superiors. Reveal the attacks of temptations at their very entrance, because the shameful modesty of fools conceals incurable sores [Horace, *Epistles* I, 16, 24], and by concealing them supplies them with strength [Virgil, *Aeneid* XI, 71].

> [Note: Manuscript 3 has *celando* for *tegendo*.]

“Show obedience to your superiors and imbue your minds with their teachings, because everyone then lives rightly if he takes care to be what he hears [Horace, *Epistles* I, 16, 17].

> [Note: Manuscript 3 omits *id*.]

“Abstain from everything that anger loves to do, because it is true that the sole triumph of innocence is not to sin when one has the power to do so.

“Be moderate even in good things and in your judgments, because there is a measure in things; there are, in the end, fixed boundaries beyond which and short of which the right cannot stand [Horace, *Satires* I, 1, 105–106].

> [Note: Manuscript 1 has *verum*; the editions of Horace have *rectum*.]

“To measure each person by his own standard and foot is right [Horace, *Epistles* I, 7, 98].”

> [Note: Manuscript 1 has *sese*; manuscript 1 also has *pete* for *pede*.]

“No one should wrong another, because it is better to receive than to inflict an injury [Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* V, 19].

“Embrace patience, which is the harbor of miseries, since no one is so savage that he cannot be softened, if only he lends a patient ear to cultivation [Horace, *Epistles* I, 1, 39–40].

“Do not be frightened by any labor imposed by your superiors, because all illustrious and ennobling labors become bearable even through striving [Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* II, 25].

> [Note: The printed text reads *contentu*; the cited editions read *contendendo* (“through striving”).] Habit makes the endurance of hardships easier [Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* II, 15].

“Avoid sluggishness, because virtue does not readily accompany slow minds.

“Trample pride above all things, so that you may be endowed with true freedom. For he is not free whom a proud spirit inflames.

“Love chastity, because all sacred Scripture says: Nothing comes before it; nothing is better than the celibate life [Horace, *Epistles* I, 1, 88].

> [Note: Manuscript 1 has *celibet*.]

“Do not delight in prosperity, which exhausts the minds of the wise [Sallust, *Catiline* 11]. For the man whom favorable circumstances have delighted beyond measure, when they change, they will shake [Horace, *Epistles* I, 10, 30].

“Above all, I urge you to maintain peace and unanimity. Just as you have been gathered into two monasteries, so may you burn with a twofold love of God and neighbor; and since you are governed by one shepherd, may you never be separated by any scandal or schism.

“Do not allow envy, which consumes the bones, to tear you apart, because the envious man grows thin at another’s prosperous fortunes; the tyrants of Sicily found no greater torment than envy [Horace, *Epistles* I, 2, 58–60].

> [Note: The reading in manuscript 2 is corrected from another form.]

“Do not complain about having lesser possessions, for he is not poor to whom the use of things is available [Horace, *Epistles* I, 12, 4]. Nature herself daily reminds you how few, how cheap, and how coarse are the things that she needs [Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* V, 35]. For wealth does not lift the minds and cares of human beings [Tibullus, *Elegies* III, 3, 21].

“These, then, are the admonitions of my exhortation, which I ought now to communicate to you as I am about to depart and bid my final farewell, so that they may be impressed upon your hearts all the more firmly, since it is established that my departure weighs upon you so heavily.

“If they produce some fruit, that will be my chief reward [Terence, *Eunuch* V, 4, 8]. If this comes to pass, I shall triumph in earnest, and my spirit will rejoice exceedingly.

“You too, dearest ones, must know that you will die. Therefore, I beg you, do not allow the time granted for repentance to pass in vain. The day will come—most certainly it will come—when you will desire in vain the use of a single hour [Cicero, *Against Catiline* I, 12].

“While you have time, do good to everyone, because the fleeting years slip away and day is driven on by day [Horace, *Odes* II, 14, 2; II, 18, 15].

“The year, and the hour that snatches away the white day, warns that immortal things are not to be hoped for [Horace, *Odes* IV, 7, 7–8].

> [Note: Manuscripts 1–3 have *Jam mortalia* (“Now [there are] mortal things”) for *Immortalia*; Horace has *immortalia* and *almum* rather than *album*.]

“Death is the final line [Horace, *Epistles* I, 16, 79].

“Perpetual enjoyment is granted to no one, and an heir succeeds another’s heir, as wave follows wave [Horace, *Epistles* II, 2, 175].

“We are dust and shadow [Horace, *Odes* IV, 7, 16].

“One death awaits us all, and one road must be trodden once, gladly [Horace, *Odes* I, 28, 15–16].

“But we shall be blessed when we finish in a good work, once we have left our bodies and become free from every desire and rivalry [Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I, 19].”

### 56. His death

> [Note: The number is absent from manuscripts 1–2.]

After these sweet admonitions of paternal affection and final words of charity, he quieted their grief over his departure and ceased speaking [Col. 1065A].

Then, struck by a slight fever and strengthened by the viaticum of the most holy body and blood, he returned his soul to its Creator among the hands of his dearest sons, around the year 667, in the place where he had labored most greatly in God’s service.

A true Israelite, he left Egypt and plundered his neighbor (Exodus 3:22), returning to his Creator the talent put out at interest.

> [Life of Saint Remaclus, ch. 16:] “His body was honorably prepared, amid the melodious singing of psalms and hymns,”

and was buried in the oratory of Saint Martin, which he himself had founded [Col. 1066A]. There he lay for some time and, through miracles, gave evidence that he was living with the Lord.

The lord apostolic man Papolenus, whom we mentioned above, succeeded him. Then Sigilinus was approved by the equally authoritative judgment of the blessed father.

> [Note: The Life of Remaclus has *Sigolinus*.]

Afterward came Godwinus, advanced in years and mature in character.

> [Note: King Dagobert II gave him a letter concerning the monastery in 677.]

He also transferred the body of the holy man and placed it in the church of Saint Peter, adorning his bed with gold and silver.

There, through his merits, the Lord continues to the present to perform many miraculous acts. A multitude of them has been collected and recorded there for the praise and glory of his name, which is blessed forever. Amen.

> [Note: Manuscript 1 omits *Amen*. Manuscript 2 adds: “Here ends the first book with the holy death of Remaclus.” Manuscript 3 has: “The first book ends.”]

## Book Two

### Chapters of the Second Book of the Deeds of the Bishops of the Church of Tongeren, Maastricht, or Liège

> [Note: *Ecclesiae* is absent from manuscript 1. Manuscripts 2–3 read: “Here begin the chapters of the following book.”]

[Col. 1065]

## Source-grounded textual apparatus

The following notes preserve every remaining source note, keyed to its source lemma and location; paired forms are retained where an English gloss alone would conceal the variant.

### Opening and chapter 50

- **Col. 1055, *remotis / remotus*.** Manuscript 1 corrects *remotis* (“removed,” plural/ablative) to *remotus* (“removed,” masculine singular) in another ink. On the date of the abdication, see Veldius’s commentary cited above.
- **The mourners’ lament.** Ch. omits the sentence beginning “Every age and both sexes.” In the question “What place of salvation,” manuscripts 1–3 have *quid* (“what”) for *qui* (“who”); Ch. omits the end of the lament.
- **Remaclus’s initial answer.** From *Nolite* (“Do not”) through *tollerare* (“endure”) in chapter 51, nearly everything is absent from Ch. At *exterioribus vestris commodis*, manuscripts 1 and 3 have *commodis* (“advantages”); manuscript 2 corrected *incommodis* (“troubles”) to *commodis*. Manuscripts 1–3 have *vestrum* (“your”) for the printed *nostrum* (“our”).
- **Chapter 50 heading.** The number is absent in manuscript 2. At *convictus*, manuscripts 1–3 read *convictis* (“having been convicted”); at *quaesumus*, they abbreviate *qs*. The word *quem* is marked corrected in manuscript 1. Manuscript 3 has *malivoli* (“malevolent people”) for *maliloqui* (“evil-speakers”). Manuscript 1 has *propitiendum* for *propitiandum* (“for appeasing/showing favor”), and marks *marcida* (“withered”) corrected in another ink.

### Chapter 51

- **Heading.** Added by a later hand in manuscript 1 and absent from manuscript 2.
- **Opening reply.** Manuscript 1 has *nos* for *non* (“not”); the source glosses *devoto* as equivalent to *devoveo*, “I affirm/avow.” Manuscripts 1–2 have *eccum* for *et cum* (“and when”). Manuscript 1 reads *nostra* (“our”) for *vestra* (“your”), and manuscript 2 *satias* for *sacietas* (“satiety”).
- **The saints as warriors.** Manuscript 2 has *pungnae* for *pugnae* (“of battle”). In the following assurances, manuscript 1 has *vestra* (“your”) for *nostra* (“our”), *nostris* (“our”) for *vestris* (“your”), and lacks *que* (“and”) from *omniumque* (“and of all”).
- **Withdrawal and examples.** Up to this point almost everything is absent in Ch. The difficult *leni saltem sermone* is *letu saltu saltem* in manuscript 1, *letu* in manuscript 2, and *levi saltem* in manuscript 3 and Ch.; the editor asks whether *Jerusalem* should be read. *Enervari* (“to be weakened”) is marked corrected in manuscript 1. At *exemplum*, manuscripts 1 and 3 have *est*, while manuscript 2 has an erasure.

### Chapter 52

- **Heading.** The numeral LIII was added by a later hand in manuscript 1; manuscript 2 lacks the number. Manuscript 2 has *reliquer* for *reliquerunt* (“they left”).
- **Gathering at Remaclus.** The bracketed clause is from *Life of Remaclus*, chapter 13: “whose hearts God deigned to touch.” Manuscript 3 omits *se* (“themselves”) in “some devoted themselves.” The Life adds “according to the institution of Saint Benedict” to Papolenus’s appointment at Malmedy.
- **Miracles and discipline.** Ch. lacks the remainder after “Who … changed sadness into joy?” Manuscript 3 has *orbatus* (“bereaved”) for *orbitatis* (“of bereavement”); the Life omits *quo premebatur* (“by which he was oppressed”). Manuscript 1 has *sucessus* for *succensus* (“inflamed”) and *abhibebat* for *adhibebat* (“applied”); the Life of Notger adds *interea* (“meanwhile”). Compare Stephen’s *Life of Saint Lambert*, chapters 5–6.
- **Stephen’s citation.** In “the slipping of his shoe disturbed the brothers’ rest with a noise,” manuscript 1 has *lalsu* for *lapsu* (“slipping”); manuscripts 1–3 have *quietum* for *quietem* (“rest”) and *sonitum* for *sonitu* (“with a sound”).

### Chapter 54

- **Heading and grant.** Manuscript 2 has *crever* for *creverunt* (“increased”). Germigny was a village in the diocese of Reims; see Grimoald’s charter in Miraeus I, 281. The twelve-league clause is drawn from Sigebert’s charter (*Acta Sanctorum*, February I, 235): “We granted … to avoid the company of women, so that, measuring the circuit by going around it, the spaces on both sides of both monasteries should be measured to the right through forest tracts (*dextrorsum saltibus*), no more than twelve miles, so that God alone might be served without oppression from the people or secular disturbance.” With a few exceptions, Ch. lacks what follows.
- **Measures and later grant.** The Life of Remaclus has 1,500 paces for 2,000, and twelve stadia for sixteen; manuscripts 2–3 have XVII, corrected in manuscript 2 to XVI. See *Acta Sanctorum*, cited above, for the confirmation. The editor warns that Sigebert’s letters do not say that the named places lie in Aquitaine. The Life has *Taunaco*; manuscripts 1–3 have *Tannaco*. The charter’s own words follow in Notger’s *Life of Remaclus*.
- **Royal names and succession.** Manuscripts 1–2 have *sustitueret*, corrected in manuscript 2 to *substitueret* (“might install him”). Manuscript 1 has *Chodoveo* for *Clodoveo*; manuscript 2 adds *postea* (“afterward”) after “eight (and ten) years of reign.” Manuscript 2 corrects *lotharius* to *clotharius* and *hildricus* to *childericus*. The cited *Deeds of the Franks* has **Saint Theobard**, not Theodard; consult its charter in *Acta Sanctorum* cited above.
- **Later reigns.** The Life has *inquietudine* for *inquietate* (“disturbance”) and *vicinorum* (“neighbors”) for *viciorum*; compare *Deeds of the Franks* 45. Manuscript 2 corrects *lotharius* to *clotharius* and adds “He reigned four years”; it corrects *hildricus* to *hildericus*, as does manuscript 3. Manuscripts 2–3 correct *hebruino* to *hebroino*. Manuscript 2 superscribes “son of Ansegisus” after Pippin and later adds “Theuderic reigned seventeen years.”

### Chapter 55

- **Opening.** Manuscript 3 omits *et* (“also”) and *sibi* (“for himself”); Ch. lacks the remainder after “those whom he summoned.” *Sapientium* (“of the wise”) is marked corrected in manuscript 1; manuscripts 2–3 and the Life read *commentatio* (“meditation”) for *commendatio* (“commendation”). Manuscript 1 has *accedere* for *accidere* (“happen”). The source cites Horace, *Odes* I.3.8, and Cicero, *Against Catiline* IV.2.
- **His fear for the community.** The Life has *quas* (“which”) where manuscripts 1–3 have *quam*; manuscript 1 has *nobis* (“for us”) for *vobis* (“for you”), and the Life’s *nemo* (“no one”) is *nemo qui* (“no one who”) in manuscripts 1–3. Manuscript 1 has *ancillarum* (“of maidservants”) for *ancillari* (“to serve”). The Life omits *in* in *in commune* (“together”), and has *ullo unquam* (“by any ever”) where manuscripts 1–3 have *inquam* (“I say”). The Life reads “from your ears and hands.”
- **Prayer and quotation sequence.** The Life has *si* (“if”) where manuscripts 1–3 read *se* (“himself”); manuscripts 2–3 normalize *nequicquam* (“in vain”) to *nequiquam*, while manuscript 1 reads *nequaquam* (“by no means”). These are Cato’s words in Sallust, *Catiline* 52. Horace’s *Virtus sit vitium fugere … Stulticia caruisse* is *Epistles* I.1.41.
- **Confession, obedience, and judgment.** Manuscript 2 reads *vestri cordibus vestris* and manuscript 3 *vestris c. vestris* for *in vestris cordibus* (“in your hearts”); manuscript 1 has *temptatio* for *temptationum*. Manuscripts 2–3 abbreviate/reorder the preceding Horatian words as *ulc. inc. p. m.* for “the harmful shame of fools conceals untreated sores”; manuscript 3 reads *celando* (“by hiding”) for *tegendo* (“by covering”). Manuscript 3 omits *id* (“that”) in “be what he hears.” The editor judges *adjudicantes* (“in judging”) correct; manuscripts 1–2 read *adjudicantis*, manuscript 3 *adjudicandis*, and the Life *adjudicatis*. *Consistere* is marked corrected in manuscript 1; printed *verum* (“truth/right”) is *rectum* (“right”) in Horace’s editions.
- **Measure, discipline, and wealth.** Manuscript 2 has *meriti*, corrected from *Metiri* (“to measure”); manuscript 1 has *sese* for *se* and *pete* for *pede* (“foot”). The printed *contentu* is *contendendo* (“through striving”) in Cicero’s editions. Manuscript 1 has *celibet* for *celibe* (“celibate”). In *Invidia Siculi*, manuscript 2 corrects the final *-a* to *-e*. Manuscript 1 has *malefacturum* (“about to do evil”) for *valefacturum* (“about to say farewell”), and the Life has *serio* (“in earnest”).
- **Mortality.** The printed line is “*Immortalia non speranda monet annus et album quae rapit hora diem*”: “The year and the hour that snatches away the **white** day warn that immortal things are not to be hoped for.” Manuscripts 1–3 read *Jam mortalia* (“Now [there are] mortal things”), while Horace has *immortalia* and *almum* (“nourishing”) in place of *album* (“white”). Citations: Horace, *Odes* IV.7.7–8; *Epistles* I.16.79 and II.2.175; *Odes* IV.7.16 and I.28.15–16; Cicero, *Tusculans* I.19.

### Chapter 56 and transition

- **Death.** The number is absent from manuscripts 1–2. Manuscript 1 omits *super* (“over”) in the grief clause; manuscript 2 has *redidit* for *reddidit* (“returned”). In *vicinum conditori suo foeneratum reportans talentum*, *vicinum* is the object of *spoliavit* (“he plundered his neighbor”); *conditori suo* means “to his Creator,” and *foeneratum talentum* is “the talent put out at interest.”
- **Successors and ending.** Manuscripts 1–3 have *cui* (“to whom”) for *cujus* (“whose”) concerning Papolenus; the Life has *Sigolinus*. King Dagobert II gave Godwinus a letter concerning the monastery in 677. Manuscript 1 lacks *Amen*; manuscript 2 adds “The holy death of Remaclus brings the first book to its end,” and manuscript 3, “The first book ends.” In the next heading manuscript 1 omits *ecclesiae* (“of the church”), while manuscripts 2–3 read “Here begin the chapters of the following book.”

## I. [Note: 2 and 4 omit this.] PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING LITTLE WORK

[Col. 1067C]
