In the preceding volume the deeds of the bishops of Tongeren were arranged, faithfully preserving the order of those things among their deeds that were worthy of reporting or relating, by the twenty-seven bishops of that remembered see, whose first was blessed Maternus [Note: 1 and 2 read “Martinus”; 2 corrects this to “Maternus”]. Blessed Munulfus, however, who was the twenty-first, removed the episcopal see from Tongeren by the authority of the canons and established it at Trajectum, where at that time there was a more suitable place; and that place preserved the episcopal see until Saint Hubert.

Because of the patronage of Saint Lambert the martyr, he wished it to have its episcopal head at Liège, a public settlement where it still remains to this day. The material that follows was subsequently appended to this work, at the command of the leaders of this place, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1056, from the little book of another work, composed at the prompting [Note: 1 and 2 have the reading printed here; 3 and 4 read “Alexander”; Ch. reads “Anselm”] by a certain canon of Saint Lambert, [Col. 1068C] at the prompting of the venerable abbess Ida, who governed the monastery of Saint Cecilia the virgin in Cologne. [Note: The words from “whose” through “we endeavored” are absent in Ch.] As he himself testifies, the reason why he undertook this labor was as follows.

In that same monastery of the holy virgin rests the body of blessed Ebergisus, who presided over the church of Tongeren for the twenty-fourth time [Note: In 1, an entry in different ink is written in the margin opposite this passage]. They assert that he was transferred there by Archbishop Bruno, who is said to have been a duke, from Trutmonia, a village of the bishopric of Liège, where his tomb is still visible. [Note: See Anselm’s letter to Anno and I.28.]

Since nothing about his life was available there, the same venerable abbess Ida approached the exceedingly chaste canon of the church of Liège with whom she was especially familiar—for she had received him from the sacred font as a spiritual mother—and asked him that, if anything concerning that holy man were preserved in the church of Liège, he should write it down and not delay sending it to her. [Note: 4 reads “dispatching.”]

She also frequently and at length asked about the life and character [Col. 1069A] of Lord Wazo, the bishop remembered by us [Note: 1, 2, and 3 read “by you”], and sometimes, while listening, she was accustomed to utter devout sighs and tears of pious remembrance at some, even the final, details concerning that blessed man.

He says that the importunity of this splendid handmaid of Christ moved him to attempt, with excessive boldness, a work beyond his strength.

He does not shrink from confessing that he compiled the first part of this same little work from the extant deeds of the twenty-seven bishops, saying:

“From the deeds of the bishops of Tongeren, which extend from Saint Maternus to blessed Remaclus, it pleased us to weave a garland from various flowers, as though gathered from the pleasant richness of a flower-bearing meadow. To this we then endeavored to append [Note: See note 392] what we have either read here and there [Col. 1069B] or learned from the reliable report of the ancients; and, in a kind of abridgment, we have touched upon the names of each, together with a few of the deeds of some of them, down to Lord Wazo.

“Concerning whose life and character, by speaking of certain final matters, we have lingered somewhat longer: first, so that knowledge of so great a man might not be denied to posterity, if anyone should deign to read these things; but above all because I could not refuse this to the tears of your devotion, with which you are accustomed to embrace the sweetest memory of that venerable man, whom you never knew by sight but only by reputation. By those tears you were able to extort from us what was beyond our strength, unless the will to obey had been aided by divine assistance.

“Thus it happened that I, an unskilled painter, was compelled by you [Note: 4 omits “by you”] to portray a most beautiful man. If, through the defect of a feeble intellect or a slight style, I have diminished in any respect the praises of so great a man [Col. 1069C], let the ignorance of one who obediently and favorably complied with the bride of Christ be overlooked.

“Since this is so, we too, not inappropriately, after removing the heading of that same little work [Note: Ch. omits the words from “which” through “removed”], so that we may preserve without stumbling the order of the episcopal deeds, shall enter upon a new beginning with the successor of Saint Remaclus, namely blessed Theodard.”

## 2. [Note: 4 has I, and so thereafter.] On Saint Theodard

*(Around the year 661.)*

Blessed Theodard, therefore, having been thoroughly trained by blessed Remaclus in ecclesiastical disciplines, succeeded his teacher in the see of Tongeren or Trajectum, when the teacher voluntarily declined the honor of the episcopate out of a desire for a stricter life (Acts of Saint Theodard, ch. 8).

While he was proceeding to address royal ears concerning the affairs entrusted to him and to request help against those who had seized the church’s estates, in a certain forest called Biwalt, not far from the city of Nemetum, now commonly called Speyer [Note: 1, 2, and 3 omit this], he was suddenly surrounded on every side by the very plunderers of his church. His companions fled in all directions, while he, innocent, was slaughtered there *(around the year 668)*.

Immediately, the mercy of almighty God declared how highly this man had been regarded by him (Acts of Saint Theodard, chs. 12–13). For when a certain girl, in pious boldness, had taken from her mistress some threads of under-warp with which the martyr’s head, shattered into pieces, was to be gathered, she returned with the livestock [Note: 2 corrects *peccore* to *pecore*, “livestock”]. Because she had not completed her assigned task, her mistress was greatly angered and, driven by fury, attacked her with fists and blows.

But suddenly, while she was striking, she herself was struck by God with a more grievous blow—namely blindness. At once the grieving household raised an uproar, and the neighbors, summoned by the lamentation of the household [Note: 1 and 2 read “the grieving household and those summoned”; 1 reads “slain” for “summoned”], arrived.

The cause of such sudden blindness was carefully investigated, and she hastened to the priest’s corpse [Col. 1070B]. The guilty woman was brought there with faith and the prayers of those who flocked together; she confessed her crime, asked for pardon, and obtained it. She learned to seek mercy from the one whose funeral she had shortly before refused to allow a servant-girl to honor piously.

Thus the concern of the local people, confirmed by so clear a sign of the priest’s powers, led them to take care that his bones be committed to the earth there with the greatest reverence.

As time passed, however, his successor, our venerable patron Lambert, very often attempted to transfer his teacher’s bones from there to us. Since this long remained impossible, because the peasantry strongly objected and, as they said, defended the bones of their martyr with weapons [Note: 1 reads “as theirs”; 3 omits the words from “and” through “grace”], divine mercy finally granted its servant such favor in the sight of those dwelling there [Col. 1070C] that they gave the priest permission to transfer so great a treasure.

Leaving each of them enriched with very generous gifts of money [Note: Ch. omits the sentence from “whose” through “leaving”], Saint Lambert brought the pledge of the sacred body to his church. The fellow countrymen of that province still habitually celebrate the day of his passion every year with the greatest festivity. Although he is absent in his bones, they rejoice that they possess him as present through his merits and through the signs that frequently occur there.

## 3. On Saint Lambert [Note: 2 has “The Passion of Saint Lambert, Bishop and Martyr” written in the margin.]

His successor in the twenty-ninth place was our ever-remembered and venerable patron Lambert (Life of Lambert by Godescalc, book 1). To summarize much about his life in very few words: blessed Lambert was born of the most noble stock of the people of Trajectum at that time [Note: “at that time” was erased in 2; omitted in 3 and 4; it is preserved in 1 and Ch.].

From his earliest age he conducted himself nobly in holy religion, and, because of the merit of his excellent life, he was taken up—rather than elected—to supply the place of the aforementioned predecessor and pious teacher (Life of Lambert by Stephen, ch. 3).

While in the height of the episcopate the grace of his blameless life shone forth in him for good men to imitate, it was so hateful to the depraved conduct of certain men that they eventually fell into such madness as to murder their innocent king, named Childeric [Note: In 2, “in” was later corrected; Kilderic is identified as the son of Clovis and the daughter of Dagobert], in the year 673, and did not shrink from driving this holy man from the episcopal see (Life of Lambert by Godescalc, ch. 2).

## 4. That, expelled from the episcopate, he went to a monastery

He accepted this insult most gladly, since he had long eagerly desired to escape transient honors voluntarily. He went especially to the monastery of Stavelot, founded by Saint Remaclus [Note: The name was erased in 2], where it was known that holy men were fervent in the pursuit of monastic conduct.

Because he knew well how to govern, he desired and obtained permission to be subject to the authority of the abbot [Note: “of Godwinus,” if it is permissible to establish anything amid such uncertainties] and remained there for seven years, carrying out a holy and angelic [Note: 4 reads “evangelical”] way of life amid labors [Note: Ch. omits the words from “in labors” through “indeed”], fasts, vigils and prayers, charity, patience, and indeed every observance of the virtues (Life of Lambert by Godescalc, ch. 3).

## 5. How he was tested there

*(The same source.)*

One night, when a winter storm raged with an unusually harsh horror of cold and snow, the man of God was proceeding, in keeping with his most cherished custom, to anticipate the brothers’ vigils in the praise of God. From the hand of one who was piously hastening, a shoe suddenly slipped, and a somewhat loud sound was consequently heard by the father of the monastery.

He immediately, without knowing whom he was ordering, sentenced the one who had thus broken the brothers’ silence [Note: 1 reads “was adjudged”; 2 has “was adjudged” written above the line and later corrected to “he adjudges”; 3 and 4 read “was adjudged”; Ch. omits it] to stand at the cross set up beneath the open sky—for this was the discipline there for correcting such offenses [Note: 4 and Ch. have this reading; 1, 2, and 3 omit it].

He carried out the abbot’s commands more quickly than if favorable orders had been given. Wearing only a hair shirt and barefoot, he remained before the cross, crucified to the world and to the desires of the flesh, praying and singing psalms. He stood like the cross placed before him; plainly, he stood as a living victim of Christ, offering heaven the sweetest fragrances of obedience, while bravely despising the snow that lay upon his freezing little body despite the cold, and nevertheless performing the service of psalmody [Note: 3 and 4 omit “to heaven”].

I would truly believe that our martyr was inflamed by the same spirit even in this punishment as that Laurentius, broiling on the gridiron, who, burning inwardly, trampled upon the outward flames and conquered. Their equal faith, intensely kindled by the fire that the Lord Jesus sent upon the earth, rendered their bodies almost insensible to unlike punishments (Life of Saint Lambert by Stephen, ch. 6).

Thus, while contempt for fire sent one of them to heaven, the fierceness of the cold mercifully spared the life of the other for the greater labors of future struggles.

Although he was delayed for a little while from heavenly glory for the salvation of many, he was not ultimately deprived either of the precious death common to holy martyrs or of the fruit of manifold struggle.

His most sacred body was covered by snow rather than clothing, as has been said [Note: Added above the line in 2], remaining fixed and motionless before the cross until the brothers, after completing their vigils, withdrew into a chamber suited to this purpose in order to warm their chilled bodies [Note: 1 reads *clavis*; 2 corrects it to *conclave*; 3 reads *clavis*; 4 and Ch. read *conclave*].

When everything had been considered, the abbot alone discovered that blessed Lambert was absent (Life of Lambert by Godescalc, ch. 3). Inquiring into the reasons for his absence [Col. 1072B], he learned from those reporting it that he was the one who, at the abbot’s command, had gone to the cross in the dead of night, and who, almost barefoot and unshod, had long been suffering amid snow and intolerable cold even for those clothed.

They hurried there. The priest of God, scarcely recognizable, was pulled from that mass of snow, and his sacred limbs, stiff with cold as though in death, were brought near abundant fires—not without the great repentance especially of the brothers and the abbot, who repeatedly called himself guilty and sacrilegious for having presumed to judge such things against a holy man [Note: 2 corrects the wording; 4 and Ch. agree].

Nor did the diligence of fraternal piety cease until, with God’s help and by applying many remedies, the afflicted body was restored to its former health.

## 6. How he was forcibly recalled to the episcopate, lived in it, and preached in Texandria

[Col. 1072C]

Not long afterward (Life of Lambert by Godescalc, ch. 4), the devotion of the sons of the church of Trajectum belatedly remembered the loss of their shepherd, who was lost but still alive [Note: 1, 2, and 3 read “but living”; 2 later corrects the wording].

At last, rejecting the yoke of the most wicked usurper [Note: 1 reads “usurper” in another form], who had harassed the Lord’s sheep most outrageously for seven years, they unanimously demanded Lord Lambert as their bishop [Note: 2 later corrects the singular to the plural].

After he had resisted for a long time, they dragged him from the monastery and restored him to the episcopal see with greater force than that by which he had earlier been expelled. Received with an extraordinary triumph both of those serving God and of Christ’s poor, they again raised him to the episcopal throne [Note: 1 and 3 read “truly”; 2 later corrects this to “again”].

How great a perfection he attained in both forms of life, contemplative and active, is clearly shown by the Life written by our predecessors. For those who have not read it, we set down its substance here, lest we seem to have passed over in silence our most glorious patron, to whom we owe far more than this.

He attacked Texandria, until then devoted to idolatry, with a more steadfast and powerful courage than when he stood beneath the snow (Life of Lambert by Godescalc, ch. 6). Like a brave warrior, he began to pierce it with that word which is sharper than every sword (Hebrews 4:12).

Immediately, with God’s grace consenting, the wildness of those human hearts was tamed; and the vast solitude, which previously had known nothing but brushwood [Note: Ch. omits the words from “which” through “field”], rejoiced, by the Lord’s blessing, to receive cedar, fir, pine [Note: 1, 2, 3, and 4 read “thorn,” following the Vulgate] and boxwood (Isaiah 60:13).

The field lying amid the marshes, long sterile and unfruitful [Note: Ch. omits the words from “which” through “field”], yielded fertile fruits to the Lord: one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, another thirtyfold (Matthew 13:8).

## 7. How he was killed by treacherous men

Through such exercises of virtue [Note: 1 reads “exercises”; 2 corrects the form], he came to the glorious martyrdom by which, as a victor, he found the entrance of life and the exit of death (Life of Lambert by Godescalc, ch. 7).

Some of Saint Lambert’s relatives, without his knowledge, killed two brothers who had violated and seized church property. Dodo, their close kinsman, at that time exceedingly powerful in the royal household, judged that vengeance should be taken for this against the bishop himself [Note: 1, 2, and 3 read “judged”].

Having gathered not a few troops of soldiers for this crime, he leapt upon the bishop, who happened then to be staying at Liège with only a small band of his household, as a wolf leaps upon sheep.

At first light, the boldest aggressor surrounded the bishop’s house with an armed siege. Some had seen the entire house marked throughout the night with heavenly light in the form of the Lord’s cross.

The man of God, asleep within, having rested his weary limbs after the vigils [Col. 1073C], was awakened by the sudden din of the rioters. He sought neither to resist nor to oppose them, although he could have done so—for he knew that Christ’s warriors, following their teacher’s example, know how to conquer by dying rather than by fighting. Prostrating his whole body in prayer, he awaited death steadfastly.

Soon the enemies broke through the walls of the house from every side, and many martyrs were sent to heaven by the sword of those slaughtering the shepherd [Note: 1 reads “before”; 2 corrects “martyrs”].

At last the venerable father himself, fixed to the ground as he was, was struck down by a deadly wound; thus, in prayer, he breathed forth the spirit of life *(around the year 709)*.

There is no doubt (Life of Lambert by Godescalc, ch. 11) that angelic praises received the holy martyr’s soul. His corpse was not without heavenly obsequies, which reliable witnesses perceived at the place where he first received burial, namely Trajectum (ch. 13).

Dodo, however, the most savage perpetrator of the crime, was deprived of life before the year was complete, his intestines being shamefully expelled [Note: 1 reads “you expelled”], and was condemned to eternal death.

All the others who had taken part in the bishop’s killing likewise suffered divine retribution before human eyes: some, fighting among themselves, killed one another; others, tormented by demons, became a pitiable spectacle.

After several years, it was revealed by the Lord to priests and many other God-fearing people that the most sacred body should be transferred to the place of his passion, namely Liège. Blessed Hubert, his successor, faithfully fulfilled this.

For when the most sacred body was dug from the earth, it was found uncorrupted and suffused with wonderful fragrances. It was lifted from there onto a bier and carried with every honor to the place where it is now venerated [Note: Ch. omits the sentence from “for” through “carried”].

As they proceeded, the Lord deigned to declare the power of his martyr more fully to crowds flocking from every direction by giving sight to the blind and healing the lame. From that time innumerable miracles were displayed at his tomb, both before our time and in our own memory; because of their number they have not been written down.

How, then, does he live there where he lives—he who lives through so many miracles—while his dead body rests there?

Therefore, may holy Cologne, distinguished by many thousands of martyrs, not hesitate to venerate this patron of her daughter also, so that it may consider itself indebted to him before God in prayer [Note: 4 reads “to be present in prayer”], since he has had such standing with the church that presides over its city [Note: 4 reads “her city”].

## 8. Another account concerning the same man [Note: Ch. lacks this chapter.]

The abbot Regino of Prüm bears witness to this most blessed man, writing the following among other things in his chronicle, which extends from the first year of the Lord’s incarnation to the year 908 of the same Lord:

“During the time of Pope Vigilius,” he says [Note: 2 adds “once” after this], “a synod was held at Aquileia against the heretics who asserted that blessed Mary had given birth only to a human being, not to the God-man. At that synod it was established in accordance with Catholic teaching that Mary, ever virgin, should be called Theotokos (printed *Theodocos*), ‘God-bearer,’ because she gave birth not only to a human being but to the true God and man.” [Note: 2 adds this sentence afterward.]

“At that time [Note: 2 adds ‘under Justinian the Younger, Leo, and Tiberius’] Lambert flourished as bishop of the church of Tongeren.” [Note: The author has rendered Regino’s words less accurately; Suyskens already noted in his commentary on Saint Lambert that the Synod of Aquileia was held in 698, during the time of Pope Vigilius: *Acta Sanctorum*, September, vol. V, p. 541.]

“When, inflamed by zeal for religion, he rebuked the royal household”—so another account preserved for us by our predecessors relates [Note: Compare what Hirsch established on this matter in his study of Sigebert of Gembloux, p. 298]—“King Pippin [Note: 2 corrects the spelling], then holding sole rule over the kingdom, had brought in as a concubine the sister of the aforementioned Dodo, while setting aside his lawful wife; and, persuaded by the devil, had preferred illicit loves to lawful ones.

“For this reason he alone, by priestly authority, did not fear to accuse the ruler publicly of adultery. At one moment he threatened him with the terror of divine judgment; at another he commended the honor of the lawful marriage-bed and denounced the disgrace of adultery. By these means the apostolic man had brought it about in the savage heart of the king that he was already becoming less and less madly attached to the fornicator.

“When she first perceived this, burning with fury and lust, like Jezebel against Elijah or Herodias against John, she went sorrowfully to her brother and reported the insult inflicted upon her by the priest. She said that the king’s heart had been turned away from her at his instigation; that she would rather die than be deprived with disgrace of such honorable fires; that he should ensure the priest’s death, so that thereafter there would be no dissolution of the royal marriage-bed.

“He drank in the deep recesses of his heart the poison poured forth by his sister’s viperous tongue. He immediately armed auxiliary soldiers from the royal household for the killing of the bishop. Wretched man: while he cruelly raged toward the priest’s death, he did not know that he was preparing eternal death for himself, but for the priest an end to his labors and everlasting life.

“I think that the writer of his Life concealed the cause of his passion for this reason: so that, as often happens, he might not incur the offense of those whose ancestors had been marked by such infamy [Note: 1, 2, and 3 read “incurred offense”].

“Since we approve the holiness of his life and the dignity of his glorious passion both by the evidence of events and by the authority of so many testaments, we dare confidently to persuade the Christian religion that he is truly a fellow citizen of the angels and a fellow heir of the martyrs. The glorious Mother of God deigns to associate him with herself among us in the greater church and in all its apparent dependencies.”

## 9. That miracles frequently occur in Bavaria and in the district of Würzburg in memory of him

[Col. 1075C]

In various regions of the earth, certainly, wherever chapels have been built in honor and memory of the venerable martyr, God’s miracles frequently occur through his merits [Note: Ch. reads “quite differently”; 3 and 4 omit “God’s”], so that it is equally clear to the faithful that his prayers are no less powerful where his ashes are seen to be absent than among us, where he is present in body.

In Bavaria there is a lake that gently laps an island lying within it in a calm circuit of water. On this island stands a monastery dedicated to Saint Lambert. It was built by the predecessors of Lord Piligrin, archbishop of Cologne, together with its cloister and the offices necessary for a monastery, and was endowed by them with extremely wealthy revenues from estates. We have frequently heard that miracles of Christ very often take place there in memory of our holy martyr and bishop.

Not far from the city of Würzburg, a village called Duckelinhusen [Note: “Dünkelhausen”] has a church in honor [Col. 1076A] of the same holy martyr. On the anniversary of his passion, crowds of people from the surrounding region customarily flock there from every direction, and abundant gifts of grain, wine, and cattle come to the holy martyr.

While they devoutly strive to offer material things, they frequently rejoice that, in addition to invisible aids for their souls, they also carry away remedies for whatever parts of their bodies have been injured.

Lord Thietwinus, the bishop [Note: Martène identifies him as the bishop of Liège, Wazo’s successor, a Bavarian by birth from Noricum; Alberic gives this account], is witness, as are all the clerics and laypeople from those regions who customarily come to us.

## 10. What happened at Lovinion in memory of him [Note: 4 omits the chapter; 1 reads “what”; 4 reads “Loviniol”; 2, 3, and 4 read “at” instead of “in”; Ch. has “at”; Ch.’s chapter is much shorter.]

I do not think that certain miracles of this same holy martyr should be passed over. Two years ago I happened to hear about them from a certain priest named Wirinus [Note: 2 gives no name; 3 reads “Warino”; 4 reads “Waritio”].

A small estate of this church lies very near a town, whose name gives the neighboring little village its diminutive name: the town is called Lovanium, and the village is called Loviniol.

Within that estate there is a church which, because it was wooden, had long been preserved through the religious devotion of the fathers; but now they are trying to improve its walls with a structure of cement and stone [Note: 3 and 4 omit “but its walls”].

The priest mentioned above reported that he had heard and seen many miracles of Christ the Lord performed in that place. Since most of them have slipped from memory, I have decided to recall briefly the few that come to mind [Note: 1 and 3 read “briefly”; 2 corrects the form; 4 and Ch. read “I have decided”].

## 11. On a horse that became rabid and died [Note: 4 has IX, and thereafter the chapter numbers are two lower.]

A young, untamed horse once rubbed its sides against the wall of that very church [Note: 2 and 3 read “the broad side”]. Immediately it became rabid and, not long afterward, fell dead.

## 12. On a certain man who struck his foot against the doors of his church and lost it after it had putrefied

A reckless young man, wishing to violate a certain girl, pursued her at a swift run as she fled. She wore out the young man who followed her with her nimble feet [Note: 1, 2, 3, and 4 read “while she was pursuing”; Ch. reads “pursuing him”]. Finding no other place to escape, she fled into the church mentioned above and carefully barred the doors.

He quickly followed her. Burning with both love and fury, he struck his foot against the sacred doors with great force. It is unknown whether he broke the doors, but his foot was struck so severely for such recklessness that thereafter, afflicted by a pain that grew worse every day for an entire year, it finally putrefied and fell away miserably from the joint of the shin.

Thus that wretched man gave everyone a conspicuous example of how dangerous it is not to reverence sacred places.

## 13. On the man who revealed a theft by vomiting
The people of this same parish, as well as of the neighboring districts, are accustomed to steal from one another whatever they can—grain, clothing, or any other household article; where they cannot do so openly, they secretly carry things off and drive away livestock for themselves. Moreover, they are accustomed to fear neither the priest’s ban nor the terror of any authority for restraining crimes of this kind—an authority which is rare, not to say wholly nonexistent. [Note: Col. 1077: the words “not to say” (*ne dicam*) are absent in 4. In Ch., everything from this point onward is missing.]

A certain ringleader among such men had cooked and eaten a pig stolen from a neighbor, together with others accustomed to practice similar deeds with him. On the following day, which was observed as Sunday, while the people were flocking to the church, this man, though conscious of his deed, stood shamelessly nearer the altar, by the chancel railing, where he would be within everyone’s view. A complaint about the loss of the stolen pig was brought before the priest, who immediately pronounced a ban against anyone guilty of the matter either in deed or in knowledge of it.

While that robber and the others who knew of the deed were pretending ignorance, the entire people, together with the priest, cried out, praying that the mercy of almighty God, because of the present memory of the saints, would not long allow the wickedness of such robbers to remain hidden from human beings. They had scarcely finished these words when, behold, that reckless robber began to vomit up the prey he had abjured, with obscene retching. For those who saw it report that many pieces of swine’s flesh, together with part of the foot which, having been consumed the previous day, could already have been digested, flowed from his mouth.

With nausea more disgraceful than the deed, exposing the man who had committed a disgraceful act, they drove him from the church; nor did they desist until he confessed more clearly where, when, and with whom he had driven away that pig. [Note: In 1, *abierit* (“had gone away”) is read instead of *abegerit* (“had driven away”).]

Because of miracles of this kind performed by the Lord, considerable reverence is preserved for that place, and they believe that nothing indecent which would remain unpunished can occur around that same church or its atrium. [Note: In Ch., what follows is missing.] The same priest had made that atrium accessible as pasture for his sheep and other livestock, out of fear of neighbors eager for plunder; but he denied that any of those animals could live for long, because they had repeatedly worn an illicit path through the atrium.

### 14. On a crippled man visibly made upright

[Note: The beginning is missing in Ch.; the remainder differs altogether.]

May I still recount one event to the praise and glory of the Lord and of his precious martyr? Our memory preserves it as having occurred in the present church, where his venerable body rests; and there may be as many witnesses to it as there are survivors who saw the same thing. A certain adolescent had been lame from his earliest childhood. He used to crawl about the church and wherever we went, with little stools; and for seven continuous years he was accustomed to be diligent in ringing the bells, opening and closing the doors, and performing such tasks. [Note: In 3 and 4, “from his earliest childhood” is absent. Col. 1077: 4 has *perreptare* as printed; 1, 2, and 3 read *pertemptare*.] He was fed each day from the brothers’ alms, and knew no other way of living.

Accordingly, when conversation arose among the brothers about certain vagrants who falsely claimed that signs had been performed upon themselves, it was asserted that, if this boy were made upright, this should unquestionably be believed—since, in his extreme simplicity, he would be much more likely to be deceived than to deceive, let alone invent anything. [Note: Col. 1077: 4 reads *se* rather than *sese*.]

After he had lived among us in this manner for approximately seven years, once, being cheerful and ready to perform such duties as these, but otherwise entirely lame and weak, he hurried to meet the brothers at table and went to close the crypt in which the shrine of the holy martyr is located. He came to the door on the left side and, while leaning with the tips of his fingers and attempting to fasten the bolt, felt his sinews gradually relax and his shins separate from his thighs, so completely that he no longer needed the support of his joints to raise himself; rather, if he believed himself capable of it, he was able to rise fully upright. [Note: Col. 1077: “his sinews” is absent in 3 and 4; 4 has *sic* for *si*.]

The simple boy was amazed and astonished at the new power he possessed of walking upright. Unable to understand how this had happened to him, he kept the matter secret from everyone—I do not know whether out of fear or shame. Thus, for some time he continued uselessly with his stools, now much more truly weak and helpless than before. [Note: Col. 1077: 1 and 2 read *contigeret* rather than *contigerit*; 4 has *it* as printed, whereas 1, 2, and 3 read *ut*; 4 reads *ac* (“but”) instead of *at* (“yet”).]

At last, however, he secretly summoned one of the members of the matricular body and showed him what, by God’s gift, he could do. At first the man fled in fear of this extraordinary event; but then, recovering his strength, he returned and inquired about the time and sequence of the healing. From the boy’s simple account he learned what had happened, told us, and from then on, leaving the stools before the martyr’s tomb as testimony to the miracle, he learned to direct his steps, supported by a new staff.

We saw him first crippled and afterward upright; we saw him live for several more years; and we retain the stools as testimony to his restored strength. We do not say these things in order to diminish the daily benefits which God grants us through the merit of the holy martyr—for they are so many and so great that the human mind can scarcely comprehend them—but to satisfy those accustomed to marvel at new and unusual things, and so that, by recalling new events, diligent inquiry might be stimulated into the daily ones.

### 15. Prayer to Saint Lambert

Now let our discourse turn to you, illustrious martyr of Christ; I beg you, do not oppose the prayers of your servants. [Note: Col. 1077: 4 and B 1–2 have *vertatur*; 1–3 have *veneratur*. Chapters 15–18 are missing in manuscript C; Ch. says that it restored them from B 1–2. Manuscript 1 reads *adversaris*.]

You watered the hearts of our forebears with the Gospel fountain, and likewise irrigated the earth with your precious blood. [Note: In 4, “with his precious blood” is read.]

The spirit possesses heaven; the earth preserves the ashes. We venerate those ashes, who are ourselves earth and dust, so that by your prayer you may blot out the sins of your servants, which surpass the sands in number and weight. [Note: The words “which … in weight” are absent in B 1 and 2.]

By your blood, pastor, whereby you founded this church—for you raised it from an almost insignificant beginning nearly to equality with the greater churches—we pray: protect more earnestly by your prayers what you nourished. [Note: Col. 1077: 4 reads *tuum* (“your”); 1–3, *te* (“you”); B 1–2, *eum* (“him”). Col. 1079: 4 has *ipsam*; 1–3, *ipsa*.]

We do not ask that the estates be increased from their revenues; let it have been the practice of our forebears, endowed with possessions and excelling in learning, to enlarge the commonwealth. [Note: Col. 1079: 4 reads *non*; 1–3, *nos*; the words from *non* to *praesule* are absent in B 1–2. In 2, both occurrences of *e* (“from”) are written over an erasure.] For us lesser men, let it suffice to follow, however distantly, the footsteps of such men beneath you as father, you as protector, and you as our gracious bishop.

Do not allow any of your sheep to be diseased by the contagion of sin; and if one has been afflicted by a mortal stain, make that sheep once more worthy of your fold through the lamentations of repentance. Drive away first swollen pride with her livid daughter. [Note: B 1–2 read *repelle* (“repel”) for *depelle* and *prurigine* (“itching”) for *contagio* (“contagion”).] Let anger be absent, and hatred absent; let discord have no place in fraternal hearts. Let external conflicts and internal quarrels be quieted; through your intervention let everything be at peace. [Note: B 1 and 2 add “be put to rest.”]

Let shameful drunkenness flee together with its companion, gluttony; let luxury and avarice, which fight against each other, yield in turn; and let lust also yield, bringing about the shipwreck of a thousand souls. Obtain, we ask, by your prayer for those who serve you true humility together with the kindness of patience from God. Let unfeigned charity reign among us together with fraternal harmony; let inner peace mock external wars. [Note: 1 reads “let peace within laugh at waging war”; B 1 and 2, “let peace laugh at wars.”] With sincere sobriety, let moderation in food be present, and by God’s help let the flesh be subdued by the laws of chastity.

In place of the desire for earthly things, let the longing for heavenly things arise; in place of love for the present age, let fear of judgment never sleep. Blunt the visible robber’s sword; [Note: B 1 and 2 read “hide” instead of “blunt.”] and press down, much more, invisible enemies. [Note: In 3 and 4, this is absent.] For these kill souls; those others accomplish nothing more unless they take external possessions. [Note: 4 reads “the soul.”]

We earnestly beseech you not to allow anyone from your flock to be swallowed down the throat of that most savage *Vehemoht* [Behemoth] (Job 40:10). [Note: 1 reads “to be swallowed.”] But if he should seize one of your own in his teeth, may the grace of the bracelet that encircles him, on account of your merits, free that person through the opening of his jaw. [Note: The following differs greatly in B 1 and 2; the ending is missing.]

Pray for the spirits of those whom the Lord joined to you in this same church in former times. [Note: 3 and 4 read “gathered” instead of “joined.”] Finally, pray for all who have entered upon the way of all flesh, for those of the present who are traveling toward the same destination, and for the descendants of the age to come, so that all together we may be delivered from an evil report at the coming of the Judge.

That you may be able to do this, may Theodoche, the most excellent God-bearer, help you beside her Firstborn; for she is indebted to you and to her servants together with you. May he grant that we live for him in such a way, through your merits, that he may appear reconciled to us on the final and severe day of judgment; to him, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, be praise and glory through infinite ages of ages. Amen. [Note: The ending is missing in Ch.]

We have now wandered for some time beyond the purpose of the work we undertook. With pardon requested, let us return to our subject.

### 16. On Saint Hubert

Accordingly, the venerable father Hubert succeeded Saint Lambert in the episcopal order, the thirtieth bishop (708). Those who wish to know his life more fully should consult the Life of him preserved among us, written as a work full of miracles. [Note: See the Life of Saint Hubert written by a contemporary author in Surius, VI, 45.] But lest we seem to have passed him over in silence, let us say about him only as much as will not burden those who know, nor be wholly obscure to those who do not.

When he transferred the bones of blessed Lambert to Liège, he moved the episcopal see, which until then had been at Maastricht. With God’s help, he first laid the foundations of religious life at humble Liège, establishing only one church and adorning it, as the time required, with buildings and other distinctions. He granted the townspeople civil law and regulated their lives and morals with the bridle of discipline. He wisely established the pound of bread, the pound of wine, and the bushel, which remain with us to this day. [Note: B 1 and 2 read “instituted” instead of “established.”]

At last, full of many virtues, he departed to the Lord in a good old age (727) and received burial among us in the church, now that of the prince of the apostles, which he himself had ordered. [Note: Col. 1079D: this was in the thirteenth year of his episcopate, according to the Life of Saint Hubert.] When, after seventy years, he was found there with his body transformed by the glory of the future resurrection, he was transferred, at the request of Louis, son of Charlemagne, to the Ardennes region (825). [Note: Compare Surius, VI, 56.] There, from sufficiently ample revenues offered by the devotion of the faithful, a monastery of his own was founded for him (817). [Note: Col. 1079: *ex* (“from”) is absent in 4. Compare the *History of the Monastery of Saint Hubert of Andage* in Martène and Durand, *Collectio amplissima* IV, col. 918.]

### 17. On Saint Florebert

After him, Florebert assumed the episcopate, the thirty-first bishop, said—as tradition has it—to be the son of his holy predecessor. [Note: This is attested by the author of the Life of Saint Hubert, a contemporary of Florebert. Surius, at the same place, p. 52.] If the same natural father begot him before adopting the habit of holy religion, neither man’s dignity can be diminished by this; but if one was the other’s spiritual son, it is no hindrance—indeed, it is greatly advantageous—when spiritual sons happen to succeed good fathers.

His body was placed in one tomb with Peter and Audolecus, who were killed together with blessed Lambert (746). [Note: B 1 and 2 read “Andoleto.” See the *Acta Sanctorum*, April, III, 377.]

### 18. On seven other bishops

[Col. 1080D]

The thirty-second was Fulgaricus, who held the see (769). [Note: B 1 reads “Fulcarius.” Pope Zacharias sent a letter to Fulcarius, bishop of Tongeren, around 751.] The thirty-third was Agilfridus, to whom Charlemagne sent Desiderius, king of Italy, into exile at Liège (787). [Note: Compare the Annals of Lobbes and Liège, 774; but the Annals of Saint Gall, which report that the king died at Corbie, seem more trustworthy.]

Gerbaldus succeeded him as the thirty-fourth bishop. [Note: Martène and Durand published some letters written by him, *Collectio* VII, 16.] After him Walcaudus assumed the episcopate as the thirty-fifth (810). [Note: 4 reads “Walcandus.” In 2, the following is added in the margin: “This Walcaudus restored from the foundations the monastery in the Ardennes, at the place called Andage, which monastery had been founded by … Beregisus, the contemporary of Saint Hubert; canons had inhabited it until the time of this same Walcaudus. But Walcaudus placed monks there, and transferred the body of Saint Hubert there from Liège with the consent of Louis the Emperor, son of Charlemagne. Enlarging the place itself with possessions, he also transferred to that monastery the bones of Saint Beregisus, buried nearby, and placed them in a little shrine.” [Note: Compare chapter 5 of the History of the Monastery of Saint Hubert of Andage. A letter of Louis the Pious written on April 19, 831, and preserved in Chapeaville I, 154, confirms that Walcaudus was still alive on that date.]]

In his fourth year, which was 814 from the Lord’s Incarnation, Charlemagne died. Walcaudus was succeeded in the see by Eirardus, the thirty-sixth bishop (831), and then by Harcarius, the thirty-seventh (842). [Note: B 1–2 read *Pirardus* for *Eirardus* and *Hircarius* for *Harcarius*.]

### 19. On Franco, the bishop

[Note: The heading is absent. Ch. supplied an entirely different chapter.]

Franco, the thirty-eighth bishop, held Liège (854), the episcopal see having been transferred from Maastricht. He prudently endeavored to govern it for approximately forty-eight years, amid the harshest storms of a turbulent age.

For in his time, we read (Regino, year 881) that the savage race of the Northmen, with their most cruel leader Godefridus, burst into our territories from across the sea; and that from the Ocean so great an army suddenly poured partly into the channels of the Rhine and partly into those of the Meuse that, leaving their boats in the rivers, they traversed the land on both sides with incredible speed, laying waste everything with slaughter and fire, and then returning unharmed to the ships with whatever they wished. [Note: The author follows Regino somewhat freely in what follows. This is apparent not from his exact words but from the events. Regino likewise records that in 881 Liège, the fortress of Maastricht, and the city of Tongeren were burned by the Northmen under Duke Godefridus. Compare also Folcuin, *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter 16.]

So great, I know not what, fear of divine vengeance had invaded the minds of those whose concern was to defend their freedom by arms that, placing no hope in weapons, they preferred to serve rather than rebel (Regino, year 882). [Note: 1 and 3 read “mind”; 2 corrected this to “minds”; 4 reads *rebellare* rather than *rebellari*.] Yet whenever any attempted such resistance, it was often discovered that the numerous forces of our countrymen shamefully turned their backs before a few of them.

The crime of Prince Lothair entangled the once unconquerable Lotharingia in such great misery. While he preferred the illicit embraces of a concubine to the honorable love of his lawful wife, he pitifully drove the priests themselves—an unspeakable thing to say—into agreement with his most pernicious error (Regino, year 863). [Note: 4 reads *dictu* rather than *dictum*.] [Note: Whether Franco was among them escaped the author, or he deliberately concealed it in silence. Franco attended the councils of Aachen and Metz in 860 and 862, as the acts of those councils and Letter 45 of Pope Nicholas I attest; Mansi XV, 314, 547, 611. Compare also Hincmar’s annals for 869, where Franco is called bishop of Saint Lambert. He later served at the court of Charles the Bald; Hincmar and Regino, years 869 and 876.]

For they convened an adulterous synod and gave a hearing to false accusers, so that they might summon Queen Tietbirga on a charge of adultery. While she sought to defend herself against the accusation, she was judged, as though she were a rejected prostitute, unworthy of the royal marriage-bed; meanwhile the adulterer pretended to grieve at the judgment of the bishops, as though he were being deprived of his beloved wife while concealing and thereby doubling his crime.

Not long afterward, after an unjust divorce from the lawful marriage-bed, the adulterer did not conceal what he had plotted in his wicked heart; with Waldrada he wallowed in shameful adultery. This was heard of at Rome, and a messenger was immediately sent here by blessed Pope Nicholas to investigate carefully the whole truth of the matter. [Note: The messenger was Romualdus, bishop of Porto, and Johannes, bishop of Ficocle; afterward Arsenius, bishop of Orte, the pope’s *apocrisiarius*, that is, his representative.]

The representative of the apostolic lord therefore came. He found the matter true, just as it had been reported at Rome. They discovered that the archbishops Guntharius of Cologne and Tietgaudus of Trier were both promoters and authors of so great an evil: they had shamefully stained the Council of Metz (862) by the unjust dissolution of the royal marriage.

By apostolic authority, both archbishops were summoned to Rome (863) together with King Lothair. The king was charged under the canonical laws with the unjust dissolution of a lawful marriage. The king confessed that he was a layman and ignorant of the canons, but declared that in this matter he had obeyed the episcopal judgment in every respect. He did not deny that, after losing his wife, he had taken another, because the youthful heat of his age had demanded it. [Note: These words are not found in Regino. They seem to have been taken from the defense Lothair sent to Rome; compare Hincmar, 864.]

What more need I recall? Thietbirga was adjudged the lawful queen, while the other—Waldrada, namely—was declared an adulteress; and the archbishops who had consented to such a disgrace were deprived of their priestly dignity (865).

But the wretched men—the king and the other archbishop, Guntharius—despised apostolic authority. The king despised the oath by which he had promised to preserve faith with his lawful queen, and took greater pleasure in the mire of adultery; the archbishop, with presumptuous arrogance, dared to celebrate the divine office. For this reason both of them, and those who consented with them, were condemned by the pope with anathema.

Because of this guilt, the peoples of Gaul were made so wretched that, as we recalled above, the anger of almighty God allowed the barbarian Northmen entirely to prevail over our countrymen (867–869).

At last divine vengeance struck the king and the archbishops. [Note: 1 reads “the archbishop.” Theutgaudus of Trier died in 867; Guntharius of Cologne resigned his episcopal office in July 869, according to the Annals of Saint-Bertin. Lothair died that same year.] While they falsely sought pardon from the pope and then, having experienced the humanity of the supreme priest, returned, they died as exiles within Italy (Folcuin, *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter 17).

In that period, it is said, our bishop Franco, unwilling to endure any longer the devastation of the natives by foreign plunderers, finally took up arms to defend the church’s possessions and to vindicate the causes of widows and orphans; he fought the barbarian enemies bravely and very often, until with God’s help he freed his homeland from so great a plague of invaders. [Note: 4 reads “he freed” instead of “he had freed.”] And because he had frequently participated in the shedding of human blood for this necessity, they say that he voluntarily renounced the office of the altar.

He bestowed the pleasant estate of Lustinum upon our church. [Note: 1 reads “Justinum”; 4, “Lustinium.”] He also acquired the abbey of Lobbes and the provostship of Fosses. [Note: Col. 1083C: on the abbey of Lobbes, see the annals of Lobbes and Folcuin, *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*; Arnulf’s royal charter of donation, issued at Frankfurt on 15 November 889, is printed in Miraeus I, 650. Until Notger’s time the bishops of Liège administered the abbey, a burden the monks bore badly; see the *Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux*, in d’Achery II, 762, and the continuation of the *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, p. 743. Regarding the kings who made other donations—Charles the Fat, Charles the Simple, and Zwentibold—see their charters dated 884, 894, and 898 in Chapeaville I, 160ff.] Almighty God, as a loving father, wished to correct him with his rod and to smelt away completely whatever displeased him in that man (Isaiah 1:25). [Note: In 4, *apurum* is printed; in 1, *a* is deleted; 2 and 3 also read *apurum*.]

For before the end of his life he was wearied by a long bodily illness; but, as we believe, his soul was restored to health, and, worn down by many tribulations, was stored up in the heavenly treasuries. The house of Saint Mary and Saint Lambert preserves his ashes committed to the earth. [Note: 1, 2, and 3 omit “committed to the earth.” From the Liège book of commemorations, Chapeaville quotes: “On the fifth day before the Ides of January, the commemoration of our brother, the priest of the lord, Bishop Franco, who gave us two manses at Merhein.”] (901, January 9.)

Around the same time, after the city had been devastated by the Northmen’s fury and the churches of the saints by slaughter and fire, the see of Cologne, which had been without a shepherd for seven years, at last, through the favor of God, received Willebert as archbishop (870). [Note: In 863, Guntharius had gone to Rome. Compare the Cologne Annals, MGH, *Scriptores* I, 97.] In his time the church of Saint Peter, which still stands there, was dedicated by him and several other bishops. On the day before its dedication, enormous noises of demons were heard, complaining that they were being driven out of their familiar dwelling.

### 20. On Bishop Stephen and Richarius

We had Stephen as our thirty-ninth bishop (901). Because he had been a canon of the church of Metz and a pupil of the protomartyr, he is said to have composed the responsories that are sung about the discovery of the saint. (Folcuin, chapter 18.)

But, to leave uncertain matters aside, this same man polished the Life of Saint Lambert, simply dictated in ancient times, with the graces of refined speech, and composed the responsories that we sing on his solemnity. [Note: The Life had been written by Godescalcus; see *Acta Sanctorum*, September, vol. V, and *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. VI, 168.] He wrote to Lord Herimannus, archbishop and successor of the aforementioned Willebert.

He was also the author of the responsories sung about the Holy Trinity. [Note: The rest is missing in Ch.] We, however, had not known this, believing, as rumor had it, that some Hubaldus—I do not know who—had composed them. But less than a decade ago, while certain documents were being turned over in the archive, one of them was unexpectedly found, written by the successor of the venerable Stephen mentioned above, a man named Richarius. We think it appropriate to insert a copy of it into this little work, so as to establish the truth for all who wish to know the facts of the matter. It runs as follows:

### 21. Copy of the testament in which Richarius testifies that Stephen composed the responsories on the Holy Trinity

[Note: The heading is absent in 2 and 3. In Ch., the text is given in an abridged form.]

To all who confess the Holy Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; the Father, fully God in himself; the Son, fully God, begotten from the Father; and the Holy Spirit, fully God, proceeding from the Father and the Son, yet not three Gods but one God—Richarius, bishop of the church of Tongeren, sends grace and peace from God the Father, his Son our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit.

If we are able to arrange anything useful or fruitful in the ecclesiastical matters entrusted to us, we ought to hasten to do so without delay. Therefore, let the diligence of the faithful, both present and future, know that the venerable man Stephen, namely our predecessor, undertook to establish, in honor of the Holy Trinity, certain responsories with nocturnal, matutinal, and vespertine antiphons, and indeed the entire office in a complete and most pleasing melody. He believed that it would clearly benefit himself and his church if he offered particular praises to the One to whom nothing can be added or taken away, because he is always what he is; to whom belongs that which is eternal; and whose living and understanding are the same. [Note: 1–3 read *cui* (“to whom”); this word is absent in 4. Compare Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* V, 38.]

Following firmly in the path of the aforementioned man’s footsteps, we have likewise taken care to build an oratory in the church of Saint Lambert, where he rests, and, having established an altar there, [Note: Col. 1085: 3 and 4 read *struentes* (“building”) for *statuentes* (“establishing”).] although God and Lord—the true and eternal unity—is faithfully worshiped everywhere by all the faithful in one substance, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one substance, we have hastened to dedicate it in honor of that Holy Trinity.

What follows is the transfer of a certain estate to the same altar, so that, as the document states, lamps and the remaining solemn observances of divine service may continually be maintained there; [Note: Col. 1085: *ut* (“so that”) is absent in 1–3.] I have judged it superfluous to insert them here. [Note: That is, I have judged it so; *extimavi* is a scribal form for *existimavi*.]

This was enacted at Liège on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the year of the Lord 932, in the fifth indiction, while the most glorious King Henry was reigning in his fifteenth year. [Note: In 1, “nine hundredth” is written above the line in a different ink. 2, 3, and 4 read “eleventh” instead of “fifteenth.” In fact, Henry’s fourteenth year was in progress.] (932, November 16.)

But let us return to our subject. This same venerable man Stephen (Folcuin, chapter 18) contributed several useful things to the holy church. Among them is that little book in which he arranged, for each season throughout the whole circle of the year, readings appropriate to the time, together with responsories, versicles, and prayers called collects, to be recited at the duly appointed canonical hours. He wrote the aforementioned book to Ropertus, bishop of Metz. [Note: He was abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael in the Verdun region; *Chronicle of Saint Michael of Verdun*, MGH, *Scriptores* IV, 81. For the estates acquired by the church through donations of Kings Louis the Child and Charles the Simple in 908 and 915, see Chapeaville I, 167. He is called “a relation of our kinship” in a diploma of Charles the Simple.]

### 22. Also on Bishop Richarius

When Stephen happily departed to the Lord (920, May 19), [Note: The fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, as Aegidius reports and the obituaries of the Lambertian college confirm; Foullon, *History of Liège* I, 162.] Richarius, mentioned shortly before, was ordained our bishop, having previously been abbot of Prüm. [Note: On the dispute between Bishops Richarius and Hilduinus, omitted by our author, see Flodoard’s *Annals* from 920 onward; Folcuin, *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter 19; and the letters of Pope John X and King Charles in Bouquet IX, 215, 297.]

He enlarged the church in which Saint Hubert first rested and consecrated it in honor of the prince of the apostles (922). [Note: In the month of May, on the feast of Saint Maximin, according to Aegidius.] He assigned to it enough estates to provide, down to the present, sufficient food and clothing for thirty brother-canons.

### 23. On four other bishops

[Note: The heading is absent in 2 and differs in Ch.; it is absent in 3 and 4.]

(Folcuin, chapter 21.) This bishop, the fortieth, had Hugh as his forty-first successor (945, July 23). [Note: He died on the tenth day before the Kalends of August; compare Aegidius and the Liège book of the dead, cited by Foullon I, 167.] Hugh was succeeded by Farabertus, the forty-second, formerly abbot of Prüm (947, January 24). [Note: He attended the Council of Ingelheim in 948. According to Flodoard, the continuation of Regino, and Folcuin, he was abbot of Saint Maximin; the Liège book of the dead gives his final day as the ninth day before the Kalends of February, while Aegidius gives the third day before the Ides of April.]

After him, Ratherius, a countryman of ours, first expelled from the bishopric of Verona, was elevated to the Liège episcopal see as its forty-third bishop (953, August 28). [Note: 4 reads *Leodiensis* for *Leodicensis*. See Liudprand, *Antapodosis* III, 42, 52.] Yet he did not retain that honor until the end of his life. For when he attacked human morals in writing and speech with somewhat excessive sharpness, and the insolence of the powerful could not endure this, he was nevertheless expelled from our see. [Note: On the Nativity of the Lord, Folcuin, chapter 23; compare the *Life of Bruno* by Ruotger.] He was granted several small estates from the bishopric for his lifetime. [Note: See Folcuin, chapter 28.] The forty-fourth was Baldrico (954, December 25). [Note: Nephew of Rainer, count of Hainaut. “He seized the bishopric of Liège,” according to the Annals of Lobbes, MGH, *Scriptores* II, 210.]

Some little works by this Ratherius, seasoned with much wit, are preserved among us; even today he is accustomed bitterly to rub the consciences of his hearers raw. [Note: Regarding the books of Ratherius that came to the attention of the people of Liège, see Folcuin, chapters 20 and 24, and Aegidius in Chapeaville I, 477. On Ratherius’s Lobbes manuscript, see the same work, p. 179.]

### 24. On Bishop Everacrus

[Note: 2 reads “Everhardus”; 3, “Everardus”; 4, “Everaclus”; C, “Everacus.”]

[The supplied source ends here.]

[Col. 1086B] (FOLCUIN, ch. 27.) After Balderic had died, a few years after administering the episcopate [Note: [Col. 1085] “administrating” in witnesses 1, 2, and 3.] [Note: [Col. 1086D] The Necrology of Liège gives 20 April; Chapeav., I, 187; Aegidius gives 18 October.], Everacrus [Note: [Col. 1085] Everardus in witness 3; Everaclus in witness 4.] [Note: [Col. 1086D] Of clear Saxon descent, as Reinerus relates in the Life of Everaclus, ch. 1; Pez, *Thesaurus anecdotorum novissimus*, IV, 3, p. 157.] 45, provost of Cisalpine Verona, which is commonly called Bonn [Note: [Col. 1085] “Nerone” in witnesses 1, 2, and 3.], was appointed bishop for us (30 April 959), with the approval of Archbishop Bruno, who, as they say, was also duke and whose responsibility at that time it was [Note: [Col. 1086D] He followed Ruotgerus, *Life of Bruno*, ch. 38.] to administer all the affairs of this kingdom, while Emperor Otto I was occupied with other regions of the kingdom.

Though distinguished by an elegant moral character and by a generous knowledge of liberal learning of the highest excellence—having long before, among our countrymen of that age, thoroughly completed the course of liberal study with full mastery [Note: [Col. 1086D] That the celebrated learning of the people of Liège had already shone forth in Everacrus is proved by his letters to Ratherius; Chapeav., I, 190, from the Lobbes manuscript; *Works of Ratherius*, ed. Ballerini, p. 459. Compare *Life of Balderic II, Bishop of Liège*, ch. 18, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS IV, 731.]—he took care to establish schools throughout the cloisters. He himself, in turn, did not consider it beneath him to attend them, to teach the lessons in large classes, and, whenever the students understood something less well in their reading, to explain it to them again and again with the greatest kindness, promising that what was not easily comprehensible he would unravel for them even a hundred times.

Whenever it happened that he had to leave this city and travel either to the palace or on a distant expedition, he used to encourage by letters the teachers whom he had left in charge of the schools. He often addressed them in a sweet song, and, since he could not rejoice with them in person because he was bound by imperial commands, he frequently sent from Italy, frequently from Calabria, as though they were dear sons, messages to kindle their zeal for study [Note: [Col. 1087] Witness 4 omits “frequently.”] [Note: [Col. 1087] Witnesses 1 and 2 read “from” instead of “to.”]. Nor did he desist from so distinguished an undertaking until he had made many who were untrained perfect within a short time in both spiritual and secular disciplines.

And since Calabria has just been mentioned, I shall not hesitate to recall something that happened there in his presence. The emperor was holding the borders of Calabria with his army spread far across the countryside [Note: [Col. 1087C] Boehmer, *Regesta Imperii*, p. 19], when suddenly a solar eclipse struck everyone with enormous terror [Note: [Col. 1087] Witnesses 3 and 4 read “strikes” instead of “struck.”] [Note: [Col. 1087C] In 968, on 22 December, eleven days before the Kalends of January, with the moon twenty-eight days old and at the third hour of the day, according to the greater *Annals of St. Gall*. Compare Liudprand, *Embassy*, 64.].

For, as I heard Bishop Wazo relate, while much of the day still remained, they saw the sun gradually failing, although it was still early in the day, and the daylight grow black as though evening had already come. As if night were approaching, flocks of sheep left their pastures for the stalls, and birds sought their aviaries. Accordingly, our countrymen who happened to be present there at the time [Note: [Col. 1087] Witnesses 1, 2, and 3 omit “who.”], terrified by an unbelievable fear [Note: [Col. 1087] Witness 4 reads “terrified” instead of “struck with fear.”], thought of nothing except that the day of judgment was imminent. A powerful body of armed men, which had destroyed many cities by its outstanding strength and subdued many rebellious peoples by the sword, was so frightened by this alien night, with its glittering stars, that it sought, in incredible anxiety, various hiding places as though to preserve its life.

Some hid shamefully in wine vessels, others in chests, others beneath carts; each counted it a gain for his life [Note: [Col. 1087] Witness 4 omits “for his life.”] if he could find some hiding place for himself during this extraordinary night [Note: [Col. 1087] Witness 4 reads “reckons” instead of “counts.”]. The prudent bishop was astonished at this—not at the eclipse of the sun, whose natural cause he understood perfectly, but at the irrational fear of so many strong men, whom he supposed would be of the slightest terror to the enemies among whom they were encamped, if those enemies heard that they had been so frightened by a natural event.

And so, while each of them lurked happily in his own camp, believing the danger small, he went around to them one by one, striving to accuse their cowardice and remind them of their innate courage. He reproached them severely, asking why men born of ancestors none of whom had ever yielded to any adversity, and who themselves had often been accustomed to overcome harsher difficulties, could so easily have their spirits shaken by this natural failure of the sun [Note: [Col. 1087] Witness 4 adds “these men.”].

“Most courageous warriors,” he said, “who, through a thousand forms of danger, have so often won victories worthy of your illustrious name, rise, I beg you; rise without fear. Recover the manly strength that you shamefully lost while lying asleep. Be ashamed to dread the natural alternations of the elements. No danger threatens life; no blood flows from a wound inflicted by an enemy’s right hand. Only harmless darkness envelops this air, and shortly afterward you will see it begin to brighten as the light is restored [Note: [Col. 1087] Witnesses 1, 2, and 3 read “you see” instead of “you will see.”]; everything else is safe.”

At last, awakened by these words, the hearts of so many heroes, lulled by a groundless terror, recognized after a short while the shining disk of Phoebe’s lamp [Note: [Col. 1087C] Virgil, *Georgics* I, 459; *Aeneid* IV, 6.] gradually being restored to its proper condition [Note: [Col. 1087] Witnesses 1, 2, and 3 read “to restore” instead of “being restored.”]. They saw the day returned to the earth, which shortly before they had watched disappear with hearts trembling far too much; and afterward their terror became a pleasant object of mockery to them.

The same bishop often endured many things at the hands of his own people, and, although he could have repaid them, overcame them through patience, wishing to take no revenge for the injury done to him. Thus it happened that when the citizens of Liège had broken into his house by force and led streams of red Worms wine from the hill on which the church of Saint Martin now stands [Note: [Col. 1087C] The Public Hill, Publemont; Bouille, *History of Liège*, I, 65.] down to the Meuse, he bore this calmly and did not seek to repay his adversaries for their rashness.

Although he was burdened by innumerable troubles and great financial hardship—for he had been deprived by military men of the villages belonging to the episcopate [Note: [Col. 1087] Witness 1 omits “by.”] [Note: [Col. 1087] Witnesses 1, 2, and 3 read “the bishop” instead of “the episcopate.”] [Col. 1088C]—he nevertheless founded two churches with us [Note: [Col. 1087] Witness 4 omits “with us.”] (in 963), consecrating one in honor of blessed Paul [Note: [Col. 1087C] Compare *Life of Balderic II, Bishop of Liège*, ch. 18, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS IV, 731.] and the other in honor of blessed Martin [Note: [Col. 1087C] He did so because he had recovered his health through the aid of Saint Martin at Tours, according to Aegidius, who inserted in his *Chronicle* a little book written by Everacrus himself about that miracle; Chapeav., I, 194. Foullon proved that this book is spurious, I, 188. Compare the diploma of the canons of Liège from 963—thus corrected on the basis of the remaining chronological notes—Martene, collection I, 320.]. He assigned thirty canon brothers to each. He began a third in honor of blessed Lawrence but did not complete it. After twelve years of episcopacy, his body was committed to the earth in the church of Saint Martin (27 October 971) [Note: [Col. 1088C] The day of his death is recorded as 27 October in the Necrology, six days before the Kalends of November.].

## 25. On Bishop Nokero [Note: [Col. 1087] “Nochero” always in witness 3; Ch. has a fuller text than this passage.].

Nokerus 46 was substituted for Everacrus [Note: [Col. 1087] “Everardus” in witness 3.] [Note: [Col. 1088C] He was appointed by Archbishop Gerona of Cologne in April, on the octave of Easter and nine days before the Kalends of May, at Bonn; *Annals of Lobbes*, I, 1. The name Rotgerus is read on his surviving coins; see Renesse-Breidbach, *Numismatic History of Liège*, p. 2.]. He was by birth an Alamannian [Note: [Col. 1088C] He had previously been provost at Saint Gall; *Annals of Hildesheim*, 1008.], but was highly distinguished by every refinement of character. He strove to become toward the sons of our church what a father’s love would be.

To summarize much in a few words, he improved and enlarged everything among us, both externally and internally. He renewed the house of Saint Mary and Saint Lambert, as it exists at present, with its ornaments, cloister, and episcopal buildings; he enlarged and repaired the city walls [Note: [Col. 1089D]

For praises of Notger, see Folcuinus, ch. 29, which later writers enclosed in these verses found in Aegidius:

“Liège, binding laws with its prelates,  
owes Notger to Christ, and everything else to Notger.”

Compare also the letters of Gozechin; Mabillon, *Analecta veterum*, 444; *Literary History of France*, VII, 208.

What the condition of the Church of Liège was shortly before Notger’s death is clear from the privilege of Henry II, written in 1006; Chapeav., I, 212. See there also the other privileges granted to Notger, and Fisen, *History of Liège*, I, 168 ff.].

Removing many disadvantages, he brought even more advantages to our church. Among these, he strove to free the unfortunate people of Liège from the strongly fortified castle of Mont-Capra [Note: [Col. 1089D] Chèvremont.], always fertile in factious men. How ruinous that fortress was to Liège itself can be attested by the ruins of that town, which lie before the faithful eyes not far from here [Note: [Col. 1089] “Town” corrected from “settlement” in witness 2.].

For, in addition to the natural defenses provided by the site [Note: [Col. 1089] Witnesses 1, 2, and 3 read “exit” instead of “site.”], it had been built with lofty structures and adorned with three churches [Col. 1089B] [Note: [Col. 1089D] They were dedicated to Saint Mary, Saint John the Apostle, and Saints Cosmas and Damian, according to Aegidius.]. In one of them twelve priests had been assigned to serve God. For their use, portions of tithes from some neighboring villages were designated, together with the usufruct of certain fields in their entirety.

After the destruction of the town [Note: [Col. 1089D] This did not occur before 987, when the castle was besieged by the army of the empress Theophanu. [Col. 1090D] Compare Wilmans, *Otto III*, 46. For how the castle was captured, see *History of Saint Lawrence of Liège, Life of Notger*, ch. 6.], he could have diverted all these resources to the advantage of himself and his church [Note: [Col. 1089] Witnesses 1, 2, and 3 read “their” instead of “his.”] [Note: [Col. 1089] Witness 1 omits “and his.”], since he was both bishop of that diocese and one of the chief counselors at the court of the still-minor Otto III [Note: [Col. 1090D] Some donations were made to Notger by Otto in 997, namely in recompense for the service rendered to my grandfather, father, and myself, and for the devotion which I always found in him, above all others, ready to carry out my will and justice: these are Otto’s words in the charter of 997; Chapeav., I, 210. In another diploma of Otto III he is called “the most ready executor of our fidelity,” ibid. See also the letters of Gerbert to Notger, 30, 39, 42, 49, 66, and 67.]. Yet, so as to transfer resentment over the deed from his own position, he preferred to honor the royal seat [Note: [Col. 1090D] That is, Aachen.] with what had previously belonged to the aforesaid town.

Accordingly, in the oratory of Saint Mary at Aachen, he increased by the same number the company of those serving God there as the number of clerics that had previously been there [Note: [Col. 1089] Witnesses 3 and 4 omit “there.”], believing that he and his church would have enough if only his faithful people might be free from the exceedingly troublesome oppression of wicked men, by which they had until then been harassed, and which had been caused entirely by the refuge provided by that town.

## 26. How wisely he outwitted the desire of a certain powerful man [Note: [Col. 1089] Almost the entire chapter is cut out in Ch.].

That distinguished man, whose eyes were as sharp as a lynx’s when providing for the welfare of his sons [Note: [Col. 1090D] Horace, *Satires* I, 2, 90.], took care to guard against anything that might in some way harm his descendants. Thus, in the one case I shall relate [Note: [Col. 1090D] Compare *History of Saint Lawrence of Liège, Life of Notger*, ch. 7.], he wisely thwarted human treachery and malice, and devoutly honored the magnificence of the Creator.

In a very elevated place in this city [Note: [Col. 1090D] On the Public Hill, midway between the collegiate churches of Saints Peter and Martin; Fisen, *History of Liège*, I, 150.] there was an area that seemed large enough for a building from which the rest of the city could be violently attacked by the inhabitants of the proposed fortress [Note: [Col. 1089] “Attacked” is misspelled in the source.]. When some exceptionally powerful man in arms sought permission to build there, supposedly so that he might defend the entire city and all the resources of the episcopate against enemy attacks, the prudent bishop understood the man’s crafty wickedness. If he granted what was being requested, he saw that the whole matter would be turned upside down: the man who had promised to defend the church would himself use force against the bishop, oppress the clergy and people, and finally seize for himself at will everything belonging there [Note: [Col. 1089] “Belonging” instead of “hanging” in the variant.]—relying on that ruinous fortification.

Accordingly, adopting the cunning of the evangelical serpent, he outwardly pretended for the time being to lend a most kindly ear to the man’s requests, while inwardly deliberating with deeper counsel how to counter the plots of an enemy within the household. Meanwhile, by postponing the matter until some fixed day, he kept the man suspended, having already brought him to hope that his wish would be fulfilled.

Not long afterward, he summoned the archdeacon and provost of the major church, a man named Rotpert, and secretly disclosed to him the schemes of the hidden invader. He urged, advised, and even commanded him to have a church founded there instead, in honor of the most victorious cross, certain that by its power he and all that belonged to him could be kept safer than by the arms of all mortals [Note: [Col. 1089] Witness 4 reads “all” instead of “all mortals.”]. He further insisted that the foundations of that church be laid promptly, before the appointed day. He also supplied quite generous funds to hasten the work, promising that if Rotpert either did not wish or was unable to spend what was necessary for this purpose, he himself would not fail to provide any required assistance [Note: [Col. 1089] Witnesses 3 and 4 read “orders” instead of “provides.”].

Instructed by the good bishop’s methods, Rotpert took care to lay the foundations of the church in honor of the holy cross before the agreed day. He directed there the benefice that he held from the bishop, adding a vow that he would contribute whatever he possessed or might later possess of his own.

But when the impious invader learned that a church was being founded at the place where he had vainly hoped that a fortress would be built for him [Note: [Col. 1091] Witnesses 3 and 4 omit this phrase.], he returned to the bishop with many complaints and insults. He accused him of treachery and Alemannic fraud, saying that the bishop had changed his decision and that, where he himself had requested a house, the deceitful promiser had ordered a church to be founded.

The bishop, however, wishing rather to accommodate the armed man’s character than to serve his deceit, continued for a long time to conceal his knowledge of the affair. To satisfy the man whose character he had to accommodate in such a difficult circumstance, he ordered the aforesaid provost to be summoned in his presence, and questioned him with considerable feigned indignation: what was he building, with what hope, by whose authority, and at whose command had he begun it [Note: [Col. 1089] The additional “and” in witness 1 is written in another ink; witness 4 reads “and by the same authority.”]?

With complete humility and no desire for presumption or hatred of anyone [Note: [Col. 1091] “Desire” corrected from “hatred” in witness 1.], Rotpert replied that he had been led to do this in order to obtain more earnestly the intercession of the Redeemer and of his revered cross [Note: [Col. 1091] Witnesses 1, 2, and 3 read “from” instead of “to.”].

“I found,” he said, “the land there vacant for many years and exempt from any useful purpose. It seemed to me especially suitable for the church of the holy cross, whose foundations I also began to lay. But if, lord bishop, your judgment is otherwise [Note: [Col. 1091] Witnesses 1, 2, and 3 omit “if”], whether you prefer the foundations of God’s house to be changed into a refuge for robbers, it will make no difference to my good will [Col. 1091C] [Note: [Col. 1091] Witnesses 1, 2, and 3 read “matter” instead of “make a difference.”]. Nothing will be lacking on my part in good will; if there is any reward due me, God will not withhold it. But whoever prevents this church from being completed in honor of God [Note: [Col. 1091] Witness 4 reads “might be completed” instead of “from being completed.”] will not be able to remain free of sin because of it.”

Hearing this, the bishop, his expression now calm as though restraining anger, said: “If you had begun anything else there, it would certainly have been in vain, and my faith in the promises made to my friend would have remained unshaken. But now, since the Savior has wished through you to dedicate this place to the banner of his cross, we shall preserve what you have begun without disturbance; indeed, we shall supply whatever additions we can. For we do injury to the Creator if, having set him aside [Note: [Col. 1091] Witnesses 1, 2, and 3 read “his”; *dolus* was falsely omitted after the word.], we place our hope of a false salvation in human arms.”

Thus the deceit of the man whose mind had already been seized by ecclesiastical plunder was commendably restrained—not by fraud, but by the bishop’s ingenuity.
