The church building, together with a cloister and suitable buildings for the site, was completed [Note: [Col. 1091] Witness 4 reads “strengthened” instead of “completed.”]. It was dedicated in honor of the holy cross and endowed with fields and tithes, from which food and clothing could be provided for fifteen brothers.

## 27. On the churches of Saint Dionysius and Saint John

Another church was likewise founded with his assistance by Nithard, custodian of the major church, in honor of the blessed martyr Dionysius. At first twenty canons were assembled there [Note: [Col. 1091] Witnesses 3 and 4 read “twelve were gathered” instead of “twenty were assembled.”]; as time went on, ten were added, and their number grew to thirty.

He himself also built and dedicated, in his own name, a church in honor of blessed John the Evangelist [Note: [Col. 1091D] The monastery of Saint John on the Island, newly built before the city, is mentioned in the privilege of Otto III dated 9 April 997; Chapeav., I, 210.]. He appointed thirty canon brothers to serve God, assigned them estates acquired by him from which sufficient food and clothing could be provided, and ordered that his body—just as we now see has happened—be buried there.

## 28. How great his concern was for educating boys [Note: [Col. 1091] Witness 2 omits this; Ch. differs entirely.]

[Col. 1092B]

He was extremely concerned with educating boys. He had them instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines, to such an extent that wherever he went, whether to nearby or distant places [Note: [Col. 1092D] For example, he traveled to Rome in 989; *Annals of Lobbes*, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, IV. Compare *Life of Saint Adalbert*, ch. 22, ibid.], he took with him adolescent scholars who obeyed one of the chaplains under the strictest discipline, no differently from pupils in a school. He also had a supply of books and the other weapons of scholarship carried with them.

Thus it happened that those whom he had often taken from the cloister as crude and illiterate, and even those whom they had previously had as teachers, were surpassed by them when they returned perfected in letters. But I fear that those who seek to break out from the schools into the courts of kings and bishops, and who, rejecting the yoke of discipline, strive to give their minds over to frivolity, may defend themselves by an example of this kind. I would judge them fortunate if they deviated in no respect from the discipline of this example [Note: [Col. 1091] Witness 4 reads “thus”; witness 1 reads “therefore”; witnesses 2 and 3 read “so.”].

For if, in our own time, the study of the liberal arts remains no less vigorous amid the bustle of courts than in the quiet of the cloister [Note: [Col. 1091] Witnesses 1, 2, and 3 read “cloisters” instead of “cloister”], we do not deny that one ought to pass from the less demanding path of learning to the stricter one. But if the reality is entirely the opposite—indeed, because it is so—let frivolous youth cease to advance false excuses for its instability. What it neglected in the tranquillity of the cloister, it is true, it can in no way attain amid the turmoil of the restless world.

Would that, in our time, those golden ages could be recalled, so that in the chapels of both emperor and bishops nothing might be sought more eagerly than the discipline of character together with the study of letters! But since matters are now far otherwise [Note: [Col. 1091] Witness 4 reads “because” instead of “since”], let us return to our Notger.

## 29. Who and what sort of men flourished under him [Note: [Col. 1093] Ch. omits a considerable amount.]

[Col. 1093A]

Since he considered it necessary, for the honor of his church, to nourish with such care both those of noble birth and those who came from the church’s faithful household—some of whom he often requested even from pregnant mothers—he also gladly received the sons of other churches, whom learned fellow bishops or parents entrusted to him.

Through God’s gift, many of them attained such perfection under him that they became suitable rulers of souls. Several churches rejoiced to have them as pastors. The church of Salzburg had Gunter as archbishop; the church of Cambrai had two, one succeeding the other, Ruothard [Note: [Col. 1093D] *Chronicle of Cambrai* I, 101.] and Eclewinus [Note: [Col. 1093] Herluinus in witness 4.] [Note: [Col. 1093D] He had previously been archdeacon of Liège; ibid., I, 110.]; Verdun had Haimo; Toul had Hezelo; Utrecht had Adebold. Besides these, although they were not bishops, many others who had likewise flourished under him corrected a great many churches.

Among them, our Durandus later illuminated the church of Bamberg [Note: [Col. 1093] “Banimberg” in witness 2; “Baumberg” in witness 3; “Bamveberg” in witness 4.] through the discipline of religion and the liberal arts. Otbertus, together with several others whom he took away with him from here, strove to restore to the holy standard of religion, as far as he could, the life of the clerics of Aachen, which had previously been corrupted by the highly destructive contagion of license [Note: [Col. 1093] Witness 1 omits this.].

What shall I say of Hupaldus? When, as a young man, he had fled from the discipline of the school here, he came to Paris, attached himself to the canons of Saint Genevieve, and in a short time instructed many students. While he remained there for some time, during which Lord Bishop Notger did not know where he was, he was at last compelled by the canonical execution of an episcopal sentence to return. When he departed, his friends, whom he had quickly won for himself, followed him with much weeping, and he left behind there some traces of his learning [Note: [Col. 1093] “Of study” in witness 1.] and moral character.

Not long afterward it happened that Bishop Notger came to Paris to reconcile the friendship between Ruopert, king of the Franks, and our emperor, Henry [Note: [Col. 1093D] Doubtless shortly before the conference held by the emperor and King Robert at the Meuse in 1006; see Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, IV, 185; compare Thangmar, *Life of Saint Bernward*, ch. 41, and *History of Saint Lawrence of Liège, Life of Notger*, ch. 10.] [Note: [Col. 1093] Witness 4 reads “then” instead of “when.”]. The canons of the aforesaid blessed virgin Genevieve hastened to him with the greatest devotion and humbly asked that Hupaldus be allowed to remain among them for one month each year.

The bishop, gladly receiving their good testimony concerning the canon’s conduct, readily granted their request—indeed, he allowed him to remain with them for three months if he wished. When Hupaldus returned here, he rewarded him with favor and gifts and kindled him to even greater virtue. Later, under Balderic, he was sent to Prague, a city of Bohemia; after offering there various teachings of the Christian religion, he returned to us with the greatest honor.

Many others, brought up under so great a father, shed light through religion and liberal studies upon various places, while he strove to make everything of learning or religion that existed anywhere flourish in his own place [Note: [Col. 1093] “Alone” in witnesses 2 and 3.]. With prudent counsel he divided the estates of the church into three equal portions [Note: [Col. 1093] Thus in witness 4; “as before” in witnesses 1, 2, and 3]. One he assigned for the use of himself and his successors, another to those serving God in churches and monasteries, and the third to those who practiced military service.

He left behind many men trained in counsel and the liberal arts, imitators of his life and character; the transmitted wording concerning the disciples’ knowledge and the master’s refinement is corrupt, but does not allow doubt about the master’s excellence [Note: [Col. 1093] Witness 4 reads *quos qui* instead of *quas*].

## 30. That he was gentle toward the humble and terrible toward the proud

[Col. 1094B]

He was gentle toward the poor, terrible to the proud and rich, meek toward all good people, feared by wicked and factious men, venerable to the powerful, loved by those of moderate rank, admirable to the wise, and a most compassionate teacher to the unlearned. He was a staff to the old and weak, a diligent corrector of the young and adolescent, prudent in counsel, circumspect in action, eloquent in speech, and restrained in silence.

The highest magnates—the prelate, I mean, of the city of Rome, and likewise the emperor—held him in such honor [Note: [Col. 1093] Witnesses 1, 2, and 3 read “held” instead of “have held”] that one of them, namely the pope, often ordered him to act in his stead as arbiter (*sequestrum*) in the disputes of the Cisalpine bishops [Note: [Col. 1094D] The same as *equester* or *aequester* at Pavia: one who intervenes in the middle of contests and through whom both parties pursue the right judgment.], while the emperor gave him first place in arranging the affairs of the kingdom.

Though held in such honor externally, he was of such a character inwardly that he never allowed room for sluggishness either in himself or in those who were more closely attached to him. He himself was most joyfully occupied with the clerics in reading and rereading the pages of divine Scripture, while at the same time he engaged lay youths, whose education he maintained separately, in studies appropriate to their age and rank.

Devoting himself to these and similar labors, this venerable father spent thirty-six blameless years in the episcopate [Note: [Col. 1094D] The Necrology of Liège and Aegidius agree on the date of his death, four days before the Ides of April. Compare the *Annals of Quedlinburg*.] (30 April 1008), and left behind many sons in no way unworthy of his nobility.

We remember having seen some of them, among whom the lord Wazo, of blessed memory, shone like Lucifer among lesser stars. He had first grown up in the bishop’s chapel as a very lowly and almost despised carrier of books and of the abacus [Note: [Col. 1093] *abacis* in witness 4.]; but as his vigorous intellect gradually advanced, he finally rose to govern the schools of the major church when the lord Bishop Rother ordered it [Col. 1095A]. Formed by his example and instructed by his teaching, and endowed in addition with virtues granted by God, Wazo also strove to represent a teacher to our own age. Of him, in his proper place, we shall have more to say as much as God grants us.

## 31. On Bishop Balderic

Balderic, the forty-seventh, assumed the episcopate. He was distinguished by nobility of birth and character [Note: [Col. 1095C] Previously vicedominus at Regensburg; *Annals of Hildesheim*, 1008. Brother of Count Gislebert of Los, as he himself states in a letter written in 1016 concerning the church of Saint James; Martene and Durand, collection II, 377.].

Since he often strove to follow in many matters the footsteps of his good predecessor [Note: [Col. 1095] Witness 4 reads “is said to have striven” instead of “strove.”], he is held to have been magnificent in honoring the churches of God and managing their affairs. Thus he passed over no church or monastery in the episcopate (the *Life of Balderic*, ch. 3) without granting it some usufruct from fields or tithes [Note: [Col. 1095C] See some donations made by Emperor Henry II in 1008; Chapeav., I, 224–225.].

And although, as the number of brothers and other relatives increased, the narrowness of an inheritance that had to be divided into many portions might have caused him, in the flesh, to fear for his kindred descendants, he nevertheless preferred to make the church and the poor of Christ heirs to a large part of his estates.

Thus it happened that he granted Pannard, his allodial estate, to the major church for the use of the brothers, and a church for the support of twenty-four poor persons [Note: [Col. 1095] “Thirty-four” in Ch.; “twenty-four” in witnesses 1 and 4.]. Moreover, he persuaded Count Arnulf [Note: [Col. 1095C] Of Lassa.] and his most noble wife Liutgard to do likewise: since they were without children, they made the church their heir for the remedy of their souls.

During his time, Gerhard, bishop of the church of Cambrai [Note: [Col. 1095C] The first of this name.], together with his brother Godefrid, handed over to the Mother of God and to the holy martyr Lambert the monastery of Florennes [Note: [Col. 1095C] Florennes. Compare the *Chronicles of Cambrai and Arras* III, 13, and the letters of Arnulf, archbishop of Reims, dated 1012; Fisen, I, 171.]—built in honor of Saint John the Baptist and endowed, suitably enough for its circumstances, with a portion of estates [Note: [Col. 1095C] *Authors of Gembloux* in the continuation of Sigebert, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, VI.]. So that nothing might be lacking for those serving God there, the same lord Bishop Balderic gladly added to it two churches from his own possessions [Note: [Col. 1095C] The church of Liers near Liège and Saint Mary’s at Rovera, as Aegidius notes.].

In the presence of Saint Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, he dedicated the house of Saint Mary and Saint Lambert, built by his blessed predecessor Notger. On the third day thereafter he dedicated another church [Note: [Col. 1096C] Saint Bartholomew’s; *History of Saint Lawrence of Liège, Life of Balderic*, ch. 2.] which the distinguished Godescalc, provost of the major church, endowed from his allodial estates so that sufficient food and clothing would be available for twelve canon brothers (28 October 1015).

Seeing that, given the modest size of the place, the eight canonical churches constructed by his predecessors were sufficient, he also considered it fitting to build a monastery where a stricter life could be led under the rule of blessed Benedict, so that the minds of those who lived there might be all the more intent upon prayer the freer they were from the turmoil of secular concerns (chs. 19, 20, 29, 27).

Accordingly, with faithful devotion he began to lay the foundations of a monastery in honor of blessed James the Apostle (1016). After completing its crypt, in which his body now rests, and dedicating it in honor of blessed Andrew the Apostle, he assigned a few estates for the use of those serving God there. He left the remaining work unfinished and no higher than the windows, since the final day had overtaken him.

On that same day and at the same hour when the battle at Flardenges [Note: [Col. 1096C] Vlaardingen. Compare Alpert, *On Various Times* II, 21; Thietmar VIII, 13. The date of his death, four days before the Kalends of August, is recorded in the manuscript Necrology of Stavelot and by Aegidius.] was being fought—a battle in which a great slaughter of our people occurred—he breathed out his vital breath (29 July 1018) [Note: [Col. 1095] Witness 4 reads *vitalem* rather than *vitale*.].

## 32. On Bishop Wolpodo [Note: [Col. 1095] “Wolbone” in witnesses 2 and 3; “Wolbodone” in witness 4.]

Walpodo, a man of God, succeeded him as the forty-eighth bishop. At Utrecht [Note: [Col. 1096C] He was provost of the church of Saint Martin; *History of Saint Lawrence of Liège, Life of Wolpodo*, 1. If one follows Reinerus in the *Life of Wolpodo*, *Acta Sanctorum*, April II, 857 ff., the bishop was born of a noble family of Flanders.], he grew up under highly religious fathers in the ecclesiastical disciplines of cloistered life. Later, having become an excellent teacher from a good pupil, he strove to train the life of his subjects by the same disciplines.

Although, once made provost, he undertook responsibility for external matters [Note: [Col. 1095] “Had undertaken” in witness 1.], he nevertheless remained constantly vigilant above all in governing internal affairs. Submitting himself before all else to the most gentle yoke of Christ, he restrained others together with himself within the boundaries of that narrow way which leads to life (Matthew 7:14) [Note: [Col. 1095] Thus in the epitome of Wolpodo’s life in witnesses 1, 2, 3, and 4], both by example and by instruction.

He showed himself a son to the older men, a brother to the young, and a father to the adolescents. On the one hand, he restrained their frivolous age by stricter discipline [Note: [Col. 1095] “Frivolity” in witnesses 2 and 3]; on the other, he personally instructed them through readings from sacred Scripture. Under him there was no opportunity for anyone to wander off or to stray in any direction from the path of holy religion.

## 33. How he lived after becoming bishop
For this exceptional merit of life, the emperor Henry embraced him with wondrous affection; he even drew him unwillingly away from the quiet of the cloister and wished him to remain for some time with him in the chapel. When, therefore, the seat of this bishopric had been deprived of its shepherd, he—[Col. 1097A] so we believe, at God’s prompting—confidently entrusted its governance to this blessed man, who had not expected it, indeed who was weeping most bitterly (1018). Once he had reached this high office, he relaxed nothing of the discipline of his former life; rather, with still greater rigor he persisted in subduing his body, lest, as the Apostle says, while preaching to others he himself should become disqualified (1 Cor. 9:27). Besides the most certain discipline that he imposed upon his afflicted body under the eyes of the heavenly Inspector, he was an indefatigable observer of fasts and vigils. Nothing was dearer to him than to discover whether anyone else was similarly devoted to such practices; and if he ever found some of them either in corners or around the altars, he was accustomed to esteem them highly and honor them with gifts. He neglected no one whom he knew to fear God, but regarded as worthless anyone by whom the service of God was neglected.

He possessed a tall stature and a bulk that was venerable not because of flesh but because of the mass of his bones; nevertheless, as we see in men of this kind, he required twice as much nourishment as any man of slender build. Yet he restored such a huge body with coarse bread and other ordinary foods, far short of satiety. When richer and more exquisite foods were set before him, he would handle them with his hands as though he were about to devour them in an instant, but he refused to indulge himself in any of them and distributed everything to the poor, accusing himself of being gluttonous and greedy because he had not yet attained the frugality of many even among secular people, although, as has been said, he accepted nourishment far less than sufficient for his immense body.

Indeed, while he was exceedingly sparing at table and most humane toward the poor, in all other matters as well he was so lavish a giver to the needy of every kind that, whatever he could secretly take from himself by a faithful theft, he scarcely retained anything for himself but continually returned everything to Christ through the hands of the poor. Consequently, it was often necessary for the chamberlains to redeem from the poor, at whatever price they could pay, cloaks, carpets, or any other ornaments of the episcopal household that they had received from the lord bishop during the night.

What shall I say of the vigils and prayers to which he was so devoted that he would continue sleepless through many winter nights, visiting the thresholds of the saints and abundantly filling the hands of the poor, who had divided themselves among the familiar byways? One of those who were more closely attached to him is accustomed to testify that, while washing his feet, he saw them scorched by the cold and the icy harshness of the roads; indeed, it was evident that the blood drawn from within by such constant walking had congealed in both feet.

## 34. What he did to appease the emperor Henry



To appease the anger of the emperor Henry against him, he had, on the advice of his associates, gathered some money, intending to meet the emperor at Cologne and offer it to him in order to obtain his favor (1020). But afterward, reconsidering in his mind why it should not rather be given to the Giver of all things, in whose hand are the hearts of kings, he reflected that, if the Ruler of heaven were offended, it was useless to appease an earthly prince; and that, if the Creator were appeased, the threats of any man, however exalted, ought to be disregarded. [Translator’s note: the printed *minus*, “less,” appears here to stand for *minas*, “threats.”] Therefore, on the very night before he was to set out, he began faithfully to distribute what he had collected and, as he went along, to spend everything, so that he did not retain for himself even a single coin from the sum mentioned for the purpose of appeasing the prince.

Thus, when the report had run ahead to the emperor’s ears, brought by certain informants, that Bishop Walpodo had gathered a considerable quantity of gold and silver in order to win his favor, the emperor was waiting for it to be brought to his chamber. Then he heard that the money which he had believed was intended for him had instead been distributed to the poor. Although some maintain that this orthodox man, otherwise truly excellent, had taken insufficient precautions against avarice, in this action he nevertheless upheld the venerable bishop’s just decision against himself. [Translator’s note: “this orthodox man” here refers to the emperor; he approved the bishop’s disposal of the money at his own expense.] The emperor, who, if he had followed carnal feelings, might have been angered, found in that splendid contempt of his something for which to love him even more, and was openly delighted that his own vain power had been mocked in this matter by a good priest.

Thus the name of this bishop became more celebrated at the royal court through his giving nothing than did the names of other bishops who, despoiling the churches entrusted to them, strive to enrich jesters and the other palace dogs, and are themselves not ashamed to serve kings with buffoonish foolish talk and the most shameful flatteries. Entirely free from this old and new disease, our bishop trampled courageously upon the seductions of the world’s evil blandishments, sighed with his whole heart for heavenly things, and during the two and a half years that he lived in the episcopate, besides the voluntary affliction by which he continually subjected his body to servitude, suffered from a persistent illness of the stomach. [Col. 1099A] And by this means he strengthened the powers of his soul all the more, and increased among his subjects the rigor of ecclesiastical discipline both by admonitions and by example. Many who had previously pursued frivolity were converted to seriousness of conduct and endeavored to follow in the footsteps of his holiness.

## 35. His calling

After celebrating, as he was accustomed, the days of Easter in spiritual joy (1021, April 2), he perceived that, as God was calling him, he was being invited to the joys of the everlasting Passover. As his illness grew heavier and his already dying limbs could no longer support him, he strengthened his spirit, intent upon heaven, with psalmody and meditation on the divine law, lying naked upon a poor mattress and a cilice spread over it. He earnestly exhorted the brothers who attended him to learn, from his present example, to dread the hour that they saw approaching for him.

When he had repeated this several times, he turned to John the archdeacon, later provost, and repeatedly impressed the same lesson upon him. He wished no one to be kept from the doors of the house in which he lay; admitting everyone, he offered the spectacle of himself dying, so that each person might esteem his own flesh, destined to return to dust, the less as he saw it die so abjectly in a bishop.

Meanwhile, the snares of that ancient dragon were not absent. According to his custom, wishing to investigate whether he might find anything belonging to him in the holy soul that was departing, he stood at the feet of the man lying there. When the bishop recognized him, he immediately drove him away by prayer and the sprinkling of blessed water, saying:

> “By no means, most wicked inhabitant of darkness! With God granting it, I shall be no prey for you. I am confident that I shall have no part with the left, but shall enjoy a dwelling of light with the right.”

He then asked those standing around him to sing psalms without interruption as they awaited his departure. He himself supplied the antiphons for the psalms they were beginning and the collects for those they were ending. To make this possible more effectively—or rather, to make it possible at all—he ordered that his mouth and tongue, already dried by the nearness of death, be moistened with water poured into them.

At last, when an image of the crucified Savior had been brought forward, he asked that his head be brought close to the feet of that image. While greeting the crucified Lord and kissing him with inexhaustible sweetness, whose image he was embracing outwardly, he gave up his spirit (1021, April 21).

At his body, buried in the monastery of Saint Lawrence the martyr, whoever asks in faith finds remedies there for illnesses of every kind. I have experienced the efficacy of his merits with God both in myself and in others whose known faith and authority do not permit doubt about the truth of what occurred. We have refrained from inserting these accounts into this little work, partly because we are hastening on to other matters, and partly because we are unwilling to pass judgment on reports of miracles that have not yet become widely known; rather, we leave them to posterity to record faithfully.

## 36. Bishop Durandus

[Col. 1100B]



The forty-ninth bishop appointed was Durandus (1021). He was born of humble stock, from the servants of the aforementioned provost Godescalcus, but he possessed a remarkably noble intellect. It is related of him that, when his master wished to give him his hand, as was customary, and to make the oath, Durandus rose from the episcopal seat with great reverence and humbly refused to allow this to be done, asserting that he would rather render to his master the service owed by a servant.

## 37. Bishop Reginhard

[Col. 1100C]

After Durandus died and was buried at Saint Lawrence, Reginhard succeeded him (1025, January 14).

He had attained perfection in ecclesiastical discipline as a fellow student of Archbishop Heribert, a man of exceptional holiness. Heribert also appointed him head of the canonical institution established at Verona, more commonly called Bonn, and he governed it energetically for many years.

He was good toward the good and deliberately troublesome to the perverse; he showed himself gentle toward the poor and extremely harsh toward wicked rich men. In his time a considerable number of exiles from the western region flocked to this city. Abandoning their homeland and their sweet fields, which, as they reported, had been reduced to desolation by plunder and fire, they were compelled to beg alms from unknown peoples while carrying their little children about in misery.

The crowd of these people who came daily became somewhat burdensome to the local inhabitants, who sought their food by hand and labor, because of the difficulty of buying bread, which could scarcely suffice for so large a multitude. Therefore this lord bishop addressed our fellow citizens with paternal admonition: each person should strive, according to his ability, to show mercy to such needy people; but whoever was unable to give anything should at least inflict no annoyance upon them. The human mind ought to be moved by their example, since a similar misfortune might one day overtake them, and in that reversal of circumstances they might perhaps have to ask those same people for bread.

To provide the first example of the mercy he had recommended to the people, he undertook to support three hundred of them at his own expense, and encouraged others to perform similar works of compassion as far as they were able.

At the church of Saint Bartholomew the apostle, he added eight canons to the twelve who had previously served there, from the goods he had acquired. Among his other notable works, he built a bridge over the Meuse at great expense (1026). He renovated the monastery of Saint Lawrence, increased its estates, and established thirty monks to live according to a rule under an abbot who still survives. He also had Archbishop Piligrinus consecrate the monastery.

There, after his death (1037, December 5), he received a place of burial.

## 38. Bishop Nithard

[Col. 1102B]

In his place Nithard succeeded him, keeper of the greater church, unanimously elected by clergy and people.

Though young in age, he was old in character. He lived four and a half years in the episcopate and, in so short a time, added to our basilica a great adornment that may still be seen among us. After his death (1041, August 16), he obtained his tomb in the same church.

## 39. Lord Bishop Wazo



We have given the life of this bishop, which concludes Anselm’s book, under the year 1048, in *Patrologia*, volume CXLII, column 725.

[Col. 1103]

# Life of Saint Berlendis, Virgin of Merbecca in Belgium

By Heriger, apparently, abbot of Lobbes.

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, Century III, part I, p. 16, from a manuscript and the Bollandists’ February volume.)*

## Preliminary observation

John Bollandus published this life of Saint Berlendis, or Bellendis, without a prologue and illustrated it with notes; he attributed it to an anonymous author who lived in the eleventh century. We obtained the prologue from a handwritten codex in which the author’s name appears only in abbreviated form, with the initial letter H. I interpret this as Heriger, abbot of Lobbes. This conjecture is supported both by Heriger’s date and by the title expressed in the prologue, in which the author acknowledges himself to be the least of the monks of Lobbes.

The author’s date is inferred from the name of the duke of Lorraine, which he uses in chapter 3. I have heard that the name *Lotharienses*, from King Lothair, began to be used as the ninth century turned; the designation *Lotharingi* was heard later. According to the continuator of the *Chronicle of Lobbes*, Heriger succeeded Abbot Fulcuinus in 990 and died in 1007; he was renowned for the monuments of his intellect listed there.

## Author’s prologue

[Col. 1103]

### 1

To his lord and friend Gerard, H., the least of the monks of Lobbes, wishes that he may walk with Bellendis, crowned in the heavenly court.

I know that I have completed later and more sluggishly what I promised you long ago, but a friend must be forgiven. I always had the desire to do it, but I did not have a model suited to my purpose [Col. 1104A]. Take care, therefore, to read and reread it, so that, instructed by the example of the Virgin’s good way of life, you may be able to rejoice with her in the heavenly kingdom.

# Here begins the life

[Col. 1103]

### 2

Since everywhere the faithful worshipers of Christ of all nations, trusting in and protected by the patronage of all the saints, venerate them and ask their intercession for help from heaven, and since they honor with greater affection the saints whose relics are kept in their own places, I do not think it inappropriate to retell, according to the modest capacity of my humble style and in words admittedly unpolished, the memory of this virgin, through whose patronage we can be protected before God, and to commend it to the minds of those who hear it as a model of both kinds of life [Col. 1103B].

This virgin, named Bellendis, although according to the dignity of the world she is remembered as having been born not of the lowest but of the noblest parents of the entire kingdom, must nevertheless be honored by us with more excellent reverence, since she shines before Christ, worthy of veneration because of her merits and glorious in the holiness of her chastity. In her virginity she built for her heavenly Bridegroom a pleasing dwelling, and, laboring at sacred deeds, laid for herself in heaven the foundation of an eternal home.

This virgin ought rightly to be honored by those to whom she was joined in this life by blood relationship or familiarity, by those who trace their genealogy from her family, and by those who, being subject to the service of her and her ancestors, devoted themselves to her service. For she was a native [Col. 1103C] and the lady of this place, and therefore, watered by the dew of divine assistance through her prayers, it has always flourished and will continue to flourish.

### 3

In the time of Dagobert, king of the Franks, the father of this virgin, named Odelardus, served under Wiger, duke of the Lotharingians. He commanded the army of the entire duchy and, more closely attached than anyone else to the duke and enjoying his intimate friendship, arranged with prudent and useful counsel everything that had to be done in the duke’s household and army.

His possessions were two castles, Huniberth [also Grimbergh] and Ascum [also Ascia, between Brussels and Aalst]. One of them, Ascum, had been destroyed by the Huns; the other, fortified by nature and defended by a large number of soldiers, remained impregnable.

Since this man was powerful through his noble ancestry, his wealth and estates, and the dignity of his honors—for he governed the county from the port of Antwerp to Condacum (Condeck, between Antwerp and Mechelen)—he took in marriage a most noble girl, the sister of the blessed bishop Amandus, named Nona.

She was a virgin of exceptionally attractive appearance, composed in honorable conduct, chaste in purity, Catholic in faith, and thoroughly instructed in every kind of learning. By her he fathered a son named Eligardus, who was killed by the Huns when the aforementioned castle was destroyed. By the same wife he also fathered a daughter, a virgin exceedingly beautiful in face, conspicuous for her beauty, elegant in person, and brilliant in every virtue and skill, named Bellendis.

### 4

Four times three years after their first union, the aforementioned Nona, his wife, died in the Lord Jesus Christ. In accordance with the obligation of human custom, she was entrusted to the bosom of the first mother, to be preserved for the blessed resurrection. The man himself no longer wished to become further entangled in the world, desiring to fulfill what the blessed Apostle says: “Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife” (1 Cor. 7:17).

For a long period he persisted in pious works with his aforementioned daughter, the virgin. He showed the compassion of his heart toward all through almsgiving and good works, but especially toward those of the household of faith. God, the rewarder of all good things, who chastises the sons of light, not yet purged of the rust of sins, with the blows of holy correction, so that, when the chaff has been shaken away, he may receive pure wheat into a clean threshing floor, and who wishes to test gold purified in the furnace, struck this man, as a son, with the paternal blow of a manifold illness. A lingering sickness seized him, and during that illness leprosy also afflicted him severely.

### 5

After he had been ill for a long succession of years, and the servants had gradually drifted away, weary of the burden, it happened one day that he remained alone in the house with his daughter. When he asked her for a drink, she immediately rose, quickly washed a cup, poured in the drink, and carried it to her father. He drank and returned the cup to her.

But the ancient serpent, always envious of the human race and ignorant of kindness, stained the virgin a little with the dye of pride, the root of all evils. For, being thirsty, she disdained to drink after her father. She poured out the drink, washed the cup again, filled it, and then drank from it.

Her father saw this but said nothing to her. Silently, he bore it with astonishing indignation; disturbed by violent anger, he summoned the servants and immediately ordered his carriage to be prepared. Mounting it, he went to Nivelles. There he gave to Saint Gertrude whatever estates he possessed, together with his entire household of male and female servants, using a sod, a branch, and a knife with a white handle as tokens of the transfer. He deprived his daughter of every right to her paternal and maternal inheritance.

### 6

During this same transfer there occurred, to the praise of Him who created all things, an astonishing event, marvelous beyond human expectation. When the man approached the bier, he firmly declared that he would never give the estate to her unless the blessed virgin received it with her own hand.

Three or four times he cried out:

> “Saint Gertrude, receive this little gift from my hand, and do not disdain me, a sinner, weeping and lamenting before you; unless you would rather have me go away and give it elsewhere.”

Immediately, at the command of the supreme Thunderer, the shrine in which the blessed virgin lay opened itself. Her lifeless body extended a hand and, before all the people who were present and watching, received from the man’s outstretched hand the branch with the sod and the knife into the shrine [Col. 1106A]. It then remained closed and sealed as it had been before.

A cry was then raised to heaven. The Creator of all things, who never turns away the ears of his mercy from the groaning of his servants, was worshiped, and his handmaid, through whose merits he had deigned to display such an unexpected and joyful miracle in the presence of sinners, was venerated with the utmost devotion.

But while the aforementioned man was purified for some time in the fire of tribulation, following the example of blessed Job, it pleased Him who leaves nothing unrewarded to reward his patience and, after the exhaustion of his labors and sufferings, to place his soul in eternal rest.

### 7

The blessed virgin Bellendis, therefore, deprived of every right to her paternal and maternal inheritance, recognized that she had been stripped of her family’s goods because of the guilt of her offense [Col. 1106B]. She thought little of the honors of this world and feared the anger of the heavenly Judge, because she had presumed to disdain her father. For she had often heard what is written: “Whoever has inflicted injury upon father or mother shall be subject to the sentence of eternal death” (Deut. 27:16).

She put worldly things aside with such concentration of mind that she not only rejected the delicacies of food and clothing but even refused to possess things that were cheap and contemptible. Soon she was clothed beneath her garments with a cilice next to her flesh; she desired to suffer martyrdom through hunger and the burning cold; she afflicted her body with fasts, prayers, and frequent vigils; and she often poured out showers of tears. By this she deserved not only to be cleansed from sins but also to find the grace of the heavenly Bridegroom.

Whatever good her hands could find, she gave to the poor, so that she was scarcely ever, or never at all, free from almsgiving; often, when no poor person could be found, what she held would become wet with sweat in her hand. [Translator’s note: the subject of *desudaret*, “would sweat,” is left implicit in the Latin.]

### 8

It happened that this same virgin received, at the place called Morsella, in the monastery of the blessed Mary, Mother of God, the habit of the sacred veil and led a celibate life for many years.

While the same virgin was in the monastery, diligently devoting herself to holy works, one night, when the signal for matins was sounding, she heard the voices of holy angels carrying her father’s soul to heaven with melodious rejoicing. This virgin proved to be full of remarkable holiness and heavenly grace. Like the most glorious Severinus, archbishop of the city of Cologne [Col. 1106D], who, while attending the soul of blessed Martin, deserved to hear angelic choirs, she too was granted to hear them.

Lifted above herself, as if into an ecstasy of mind, by the sweetness of such great delight and the gentle harmony of the music, she listened intently toward heaven. Refreshed with joy by so blessed a consolation, she asked the maidservant standing beside her whether she heard what the virgin heard and understood what she understood.

When the maidservant replied that she heard and understood nothing of the kind, the blessed virgin explained to her that her father’s soul, released from the bonds of the body [Col. 1107A], was being crowned for his patient endurance of tribulation and carried on high by the angels who were singing.

Having received permission from the mother of the monastery, the nun went to Merbecca to bury her father. In the little church that he himself had built in honor of blessed Peter, she buried him beside his wife, the mother of the virgin, according to the custom of nobles and as was fitting.

### 9

After her father’s death, since the monastery in which she had been professed had previously been utterly destroyed and burned by the Huns, and had been rebuilt only in poverty, it lacked the appurtenances and resources by which the handmaids of Christ could be supported. Indeed, it could scarcely maintain six girls on bread and water.

Compelled by the servants and by necessity, she remained at home. Living day and night in the aforementioned little church, she devoted herself to the service of the Lord. Her foot never rested from visiting the sick, nor did her hand ever cease caring for the poor. The praise of God was always constant in her heart, and the singing of psalms and hymns never departed from her mouth. Singing to herself, in accordance with the Apostle, she sang spiritual songs, psalms, and hymns in the Lord.

At no time, whether in winter or summer, would she allow anything to be placed beneath her except the cilice that she wore over her naked body, a little mat, and a stone placed beneath her head. She weakened her body with constant vigils, prayers, and continuous fasts. She took nourishment only twice a week, apart from Sunday and the feasts of the apostles [Col. 1107C]. From the day of her consecration she did not eat meat; she touched fish or any other food besides bread and water only on the most distinguished solemnities.

### 10

Because of the merit of her blessed life, the Lord had granted her such grace that whenever she laid her hands upon sick or feverish people, she restored them to their former health.

As she advanced from day to day and rose from virtue to virtue, after fifteen years had already been spent in the austerity of life, it happened during the solemnities of Easter that a small piece of fish was placed before her as she sat at table.

This piece, which is astonishing to relate and almost incredible, changed into flesh between her hands. It greatly frightened her, and with intense astonishment she indignantly said to the servant:

> “May God forgive you! Why did you wish to mock me in this way? You knew that I would not eat meat, and yet you placed it before me.”

When the servant denied this and swore emphatically that he had not done it, she understood that it had happened by God’s command. She tasted a little of it, pushed it away from herself, immediately rose from the table, and gave herself over to the Church and to prayer in praise of her Creator.

### 11

I consider it unworthy to suppress this also in silence: He who never delayed to glorify and magnify his servants once changed a cup of water placed before her on a certain solemn day into the taste of wine.

### 12

After three times five years and two more had been completed since her father’s death, she sensed through divine revelation that the final days of this light were approaching for her. She summoned priests and asked for holy oil. Having received it, she consecrated her departure with the body and blood of her Redeemer, and thus returned her final breath to heaven.

## Textual notes

[Note: 1. Col. 1095; at *capella aliquandiu commorari voluit. Hujus ergo episcopatus*. 1, 2, and 3 have *episcopatu*, “in the bishopric,” ablative, for *episcopatus*, “of the bishopric.”]

[Note: 2. Col. 1097; at *Hujus ergo episcopatus sede pastore viduata, inspirante*. 1 and 2 have *insperante*, “not expecting,” corrected to *inspirante*, “inspiring,” in 3 and 4. It is God’s prompting in the text; *insperante* does not mean “unprompted.”]

[Note: 3. Col. 1097; at *cujus nimirum gradus culmine nil de prioris*. 4 and the *Eulogy of Wolbodo* read *prioris*, “former,” describing his life; 1, 2, and 3 have *pejoris*, “worse.” The apparatus’s *ita* means “so,” confirming the printed reading; it is not a variant meaning “thus.”]

[Note: 4. Col. 1097; at *praeter certissimam qua sub oculis superni inspectoris*. 1 and 2 have *in pectoris*, literally “in … of the breast,” for *inspectoris*, “of the observer.” The former is grammatically broken in this phrase.]

[Note: 5. Col. 1097; at *Nil illi dulcius erat, quam si cui*. 4 reads *sicut*, “as,” for *si cui*, “whether anyone.”]

[Note: 6. Col. 1097; at *illi dulcius erat, quam si cui itidem*. 4 adds *aliis*, “to others.”]

[Note: 7. Col. 1097; at *cordi esset explorare; quorum aliquos si quando*. 4 has *aliquando*, “sometimes,” for *si quando*, “if ever.”]

[Note: 8. Col. 1097; at *nullum a quo Deum timeri sciebat negligere*. 2 and 3 spell *negligere*, “to neglect,” as *neglegere*.]

[Note: 9. Col. 1097; at *necessaria, ut videmus in hominibus ejusmodi. Quod*. 4 has *qui*, “who,” for *quod*, “which,” shifting the relative from the body to the man.]

[Note: 10. Col. 1097; at *atque aliis cibis communioribus longe citra saturitatem*. 1, 2, and 3 have *saturnitatem* for *saturitatem*, “satiety”; this is an altered form, not a distinct reading meaning “saturation.”]

[Note: 11. Col. 1097; at *ut dictum est, longe minus quam inmenso*. 4 and the *Eulogy of Wolbodo* have *inmenso*, dative “immense,” agreeing with “body”; 1, 2, and 3 have *inmensum*, the accusative or neuter nominative form.]

[Note: 12. Col. 1097; at *sibi parcissimus, pauperibus esset humanissimus, tum alias*. 4 reads *aliis*, “to others” or “in other things,” for *alias*, “on other occasions.”]

[Note: 13. Col. 1097; at *occaluisse. 34. Quid placaturus imperatorem Heinricum fecerit*. 3 and 4 place *iratum*, “angry,” after *fecerit*, “he did,” at the end of the heading, qualifying Emperor Henry.]

[Note: 14. Col. 1097; at *suorum aliquantum pecuniae contraxerat, quam ut eidem*. 4 places *eidem*, “to him,” after *Coloniae*, “at Cologne.”]

[Note: 15. Col. 1097; at *contraxerat, quam ut eidem pro gratia ejus*. 3 and 4 read *ei*, “to him,” for *pro gratia ejus*, “to obtain his favor.”]

[Note: 16. Col. 1097D; at *pro gratia ejus offerret, Coloniae occurrere deliberaverat*. From Wolbodo’s time we possess one charter of Emperor Henry II issued at Cologne on 18 February 1020: Böhmer, *Regesta*, p. 61. Reinerus, *Life of Wolbodo*, chapter 8, wrote that this happened at Cologne at Christmas, but the Hildesheim Annals contradict him, showing where the emperor celebrated the Lord’s Nativity in those years. The note continues into col. 1098D.]

[Note: 17. Col. 1097; at *fama, quibusdam deferentibus, ad aures imperatoris praecurrerat*. 3 and 4 read *percurrerat*, “had run through,” for *praecurrerat*, “had run ahead.”]

[Note: 18. Col. 1097; at *ipsius non parvam auri argentique copiam coegisse*. 3 and 4 have *collegisse*, “to have collected,” for *coegisse*, “to have gathered.”]

[Note: 19. Col. 1097; at *afferretur, iterum audit deputatam sibi ut, crediderat*. 1 and 2 read *credideret*, “he might believe” or “was believing,” subjunctive, for *crediderat*, “he had believed.”]

[Note: 20. Col. 1097; at *Et licet in aliis sane perfectum aliqui*. 3 has *aliquid*, “something,” for *aliqui*, “some people.”]

[Note: 21. Col. 1097; at *Et qui, si carnales sequeretur affectus, succensere*. 3 reads *succendere*, “to set on fire,” for *succensere*, “to be angry.”]

[Note: 22. Col. 1097; at *carnales sequeretur affectus, succensere habebat, ex splendido*. 1 has *spendido*, an altered spelling of *splendido*, “splendid.”]

[Note: 23. Col. 1098D; at *duos semis annos quibus in episcopatu vixit*. “He held the episcopate for three times ten months” is read in the very short *Life of Wolbodo*, written in Latin, French, and German verse. Chapeaville printed the Latin verses from the Saint Lawrence manuscript, I, p. 256.]

[Note: 24. Col. 1099; at *cessabat afflictionem, continua stomachi infirmitate laboravit, eoque*. 3 and 4 omit the suffix *-que*, “and,” in *eoque*, “and thereby.” They do not omit a word meaning “for.”]

[Note: 25. Col. 1099; at *valens sustentare membra, spiritum coelo intentum psalmodia*. 4 reads *psalmorum*, “of psalms,” instead of *psalmodia*, “psalmody.”]

[Note: 26. Col. 1099; at *Johannem archidiaconum, postea praepositum, ipsi identidem inculcabat*. 3 and 4 have *inculcare cepit*, “he began to impress upon him,” for *inculcabat*, “he kept impressing upon him.”]

[Note: 27. Col. 1099; at *explorare volens si quid suum in egrediente*. 1 and 2 have *suum ingrediente*, “his own … entering”; 3 and 4 have *suum egrediente*, “his own … departing”; Ch. has *in egrediente*, “in the departing [soul].” *suum*, “his own,” supplies what the dragon might find; the changes concern the following participial construction.]

[Note: 28. Col. 1099; at *ero; nullam partem habiturus cum sinistris, lucis*. 1, Ch., and the *Eulogy of Wolbodo* read *lucis*, “of light”; 2, 3, and 4 have *licet*, “although.”]

[Note: 29. Col. 1099; at *et inter salutandum et inexplebili dulcedine adosculandum*. 4 and Ch. read *deosculandum* for *adosculandum*, both “kissing.”]

[Note: 30. Col. 1099C; at *Domino, cujus imaginem foris amplectebatur, reddidit spiritum*. The eleventh day before the Kalends of May: the Stavelot Necrology, Liège Necrology, and Aegidius.]

[Note: 31. Col. 1099C; at *corpus in beati Laurentii martiris monasterio tumulatum*. The following epitaph is inscribed in letters of gold: “Your imposing bodily dignity, but still greater grace of character, places you in the bishop’s office and throne. Rich man and needy man felt how you were present for each need: from you salvation flowed to the former, food to the latter. Here that same compassion is now present for all of us, and here we honor the tomb that brings salvation.” These verses are in Reinerus’s little book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, I, 3; Pez, *Treasury of Unpublished Writings*, IV, 3; and Aegidius. Molanus, in *Feasts of the Saints of Belgium*, notes that he found the commemoration of this most illustrious bishop’s burial in more than thirty martyrologies. The note continues into col. 1099D.]

[Note: 32. Col. 1099; at *dubitare. Quae nos huic opusculo inserere devitavimus*. 1 corrects *deputavimus*, “we assigned,” to *devitavimus*, “we avoided”; 3 and 4 read *deputavimus*.]

[Note: 33. Col. 1099; at *huic opusculo inserere devitavimus , partim quia*. 4 reads *quod* for *quia*, here both “because.”]

[Note: 34. Col. 1099; at *partim quia ad alia festinamus, partim quia*. 4 again reads *quod* for *quia*, both “because,” in the second reason for omitting the miracle accounts.]

[Note: 35. Col. 1099D; at *dijudicari devitamus, sed posteris fideliter scribenda relinquimus*. Besides Reinerus and Aegidius, an anonymous author wrote about Wolbodo’s miracles after 1454: *Acts of the Saints*, April, II, p. 862. On the opening of Wolbodo’s tomb in 1656, see the same place. Chapeaville, I, p. 257, published a verse prayer to Wolbodo from the Saint Lawrence manuscript.]

[Note: 36. Col. 1099D; at *Durando episcopo. Quadragesimus nonus subrogatus est Durandus*. On Durandus see the *History of Saint Lawrence of Liège* and Reinerus’s *Life of Wolbodo*, chapters 17–19, in *Acts of the Saints*, April, II, p. 861, where we read that he did not escape an unfavorable reputation among later generations. Compare also Anselm, chapter 29.]

[Note: 37. Col. 1099; at *cum magna reverentia de sede episcopali eidem*. 4 reads *eidem*, “to the same man”; Ch. has *ipsi*, “to him”; 1, 2, and 3 have *ejusdem*, “of the same man.”]

[Note: 38. Col. 1100C; at *exhibiturum. 37. De Reginhardo episcopo. Huic defuncto*. He died on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February (14 January), according to the Stavelot Necrology. Aegidius, from the Liège Necrology, gives the tenth day before those Kalends (23 January). That this date belongs with 1025, as in the Liège Annals, rather than 1024 as in the Lobbes Annals, is shown by Conrad II’s privilege concerning the church’s property, given to Bishop Durandus at Liège on the sixth day before the Nones of October (2 October) 1024: Chapeaville, I, p. 264. The letter against Berengar of Tours printed there under Durandus’s name was certainly written by Theodwin, Wazo’s successor. Compare Mabillon, *Old Analects*, p. 446. The note continues into col. 1100D.]

[Note: 39. Col. 1100D; at *Huic defuncto et apud Sanctum Laurentium tumulato*. Aegidius preserved these verses inscribed on the tomb by Stephen, abbot of Saint Lawrence: “Here lies Durandus, who nobly governed the see of Tongeren for a little more than three years. Born and reared in the nest of a poor inheritance, through his intellect he soars to the highest nobles. Enjoying as servants the very men whom he had borne as masters—what a story he was in the theater of the world! The seventh day of the Water-bearer was passing in the heavens when the lord bade a sorrowful farewell to earthly things.” Stephen seems to indicate, rather obscurely, some other day of death, which the editor cannot identify.]

[Note: 40. Col. 1100D; at *et apud Sanctum Laurentium tumulato successit Reginhardus*. He obtained the bishopric by simony, if one follows the *History of Saint Lawrence of Liège*.]

[Note: 41. Col. 1101C; at *Reginhardus (an. 1025, Jan. 14), qui conlitteralis*. A canon of Cologne. Reinerus, *Life of Reginhard*, chapter 1, in Pez, IV, 3.]

[Note: 42. Col. 1101; at *tempore non parva exulum copia ex occidentali*. Ch. reads *orientali*, “eastern,” for *occidentali*, “western.”]

[Note: 43. Col. 1101C; at *confluxit, qui patriam et dulcia arva linquentes*. Virgil, *Eclogue* I, 3.]

[Note: 44. Col. 1101; at *est ammonitione, ut unusquisque hujusmodi egenis studeat*. 1 and 2 have *studeant*, “they should strive,” for *studeat*, “he should strive.”]

[Note: 45. Col. 1101; at *egenis studeat pro posse misericordiam impendere, qui*. 4 reads *ut*, “so that,” for *qui*, “who.”]

[Note: 46. Col. 1101; at *tangi debere, quod similis casus quandoque ingrueret*. 4 reads *ingrueret*, “might overtake,” for *ingruere*, “to overtake,” in 1, 2, and 3.]

[Note: 47. Col. 1101; at *ab eisdem forsitan panem expetitum iri. Ut*. 4 and Ch. read *Ut*, “so that”; 1, 2, and 3 have *et*, “and.”]

[Note: 48. Col. 1101C; at *quam populo suggesserat, prior exemplum praeberet, trecentos*. The author of the *History of Saint Lawrence of Liège* states that there were twelve hundred.]

[Note: 49. Col. 1101C; at *insignia, pontem super Mosam magno sumptu extruxit*. Compare Dewez, *History of Liège*, Brussels, 1822, I, p. 38. The editor has not seen the *History of Liège* recently published by Polain.]

[Note: 50. Col. 1101C; at *extruxit (an. 1026), monasterium sancti Laurentii renovavit*. Liège Annals.]

[Note: 51. Col. 1101C; at *triginta monachos sub abbate, qui adhuc superest*. Stephen, who died in 1061; compare the *History of Saint Lawrence*.]

[Note: 52. Col. 1101C; at *constituit, ipsumque monasterium Piligrinum archiepiscopum consecrare fecit*. Rupertus, in the *History of Saint Lawrence of Liège*, attests that the monastery was consecrated in the year of the Lord 1034, indiction II, the tenth year of Reginhard’s episcopate, in the presence of Piligrinus, archbishop of Cologne, and John, bishop of Porto.]

[Note: 53. Col. 1101C; at *post obitum suum (an. 1037, Dec. 5)*. Besides the Lobbes and Liège Annals, a lead tablet found when Reginhard’s tomb was opened in 1569 shows that the bishop died in 1037. According to Fisen, *History of Liège*, I, p. 180, it read: “I, Reginhard, bishop of Liège, departed this life in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation one thousand and thirty-eight, indiction five, on the Nones of December, and was buried in the basilica of Saint Lawrence, which I built with God’s help.” On retaining indiction V, that is, 1037, see below, chapter 49. The inscription’s differing year is retained. The note continues into col. 1101D.]

[Note: 54. Col. 1101C; at *(an. 1037, Dec. 5) locum sepulturae accepit*. Two funerary inscriptions survive. The author of the *History of Saint Lawrence* preserved one in these verses: “This house bears witness to him, and all its furnishings; nor is the church’s adornment an inferior testimony to his episcopate. Here he is taken away, having completed his course, as it happened on the Nones of December; equal was his entrance, equal his return.” It continues: “In the year of the Lord 1036 died Lord Reginhard, venerable bishop of Liège.” The other, by Abbot Everlinus, is recorded by the same author and also by Reinerus and Aegidius: “Flower and glory of the Church, bishop and mirror of wisdom, here, Reginhard, you lie; your body is now ashes. Because you fill us with the sweet richness of grain, may heaven’s pastures be multiplied a hundredfold for you! The fifth day of December snatches you from the world’s darkness; may the Sun of Righteousness shine for you in your rest. Amen.” The note continues into col. 1102C.]

[Note: 55. Col. 1102C; at *Nithardo episcopo. Hujus in loco successit Nithardus*. Called Nizo or Nitho by others; Reginhard’s nephew. Reginhard’s foundation charter reads: “Nizo, treasurer of the cathedral, of my lineage.” Mabillon, *Annals*, IV, p. 442.]

[Note: 56. Col. 1102C; at *nos fas est cernere, nostrae addidit basilicae*. In 1040 he obtained the county of Haspinga for the church of Liège from Henry III, “for the constant and faithful service with which he served our father and us most faithfully.” Compare also above, II, 28; Chapeaville, I, p. 279. The note continues into col. 1102D.]

[Note: 57. Col. 1102D; at *1041, Aug. 16) postea adeptus est sepulchrum*. “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1042, indiction X, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, Nithard, bishop of Liège, died.” Foullon, I, p. 225, gives this inscription from the lead tablet taken from the tomb in 1568 more accurately than Chapeaville at the cited place. The Lobbes and Liège Annals agree; the Stavelot Necrology has the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September. Four and a half years indicate 1041, certainly not 1042; see confirmation from Anselm himself, chapter 50.]

[Note: 58. Col. 1101; at *sepulchrum . 39. De domno Wazone episcopo*. This chapter is absent in Ch.]

[Note: 59. Col. 1103C; at *obnoxii, obsequiis ejus deservierunt. Indigena namque istius*. That is, Merbecca; this explanatory place-name has slipped into the text in Bollandus’s edition. More on this below.]

[Note: 60. Col. 1103C; at *virginis, Odelardus nomine, sub Wigero duce Lotharingorum*. Neither the name of the Lotharingians nor that of their duke was known at that time. The author followed the usage of his own day. Duke Wiger is said to have been Amalberga’s husband and the father of the virgin Saint Gudila. The note continues into col. 1104C.]

[Note: 61. Col. 1105D; at *servorum ancillarumque, cum cespite et ramo cultelloque*. Observe this noteworthy rite of conveyance. The same is related in the miracles of Saint Gertrude, abbess of Nivelles; for her see Century II, under 658.]

[Note: 62. Col. 1105D; at *eamdem virginem in loco qui dicitur Morsella*. Morsella, Morselle, is a village near Dendermonde, a town on the Scheldt. This passage shows that Charlemagne did not first found the Morsella monastery but enlarged or restored it. Saint Gudila’s withdrawal there had given the occasion or origin of the monastery. The note continues into col. 1106D.]

[Note: 63. Col. 1107D; at *matre monasterii, ad sepeliendum patrem suum Merbeccam*. Merbecca, Merbeke, is a village in Brabant in the diocese of Mechelen, not far from the Flemish town of Ninove, according to Miraeus in his *Belgian Calendar*. In the division of Lothair’s kingdom in 870, Merrebecchi is named among the monasteries of Belgium; it is now a parish and collegiate church with seven chaplains.]

[Note: 64. Col. 1107D; at *quo ordinata fuerat, quod prius ab Hunnis*. Perhaps the Frisians, who often ravaged the regions adjoining their own; other barbarian peoples are sometimes included under the name “Huns.” The note continues into col. 1108D.]

13. Accordingly, his relatives and friends, male and female servants, and also the leading men of that region gathered to bury her, and they laid her to rest in the proper manner beside the tomb of her parents. But since they had no stone sarcophagus in which to place her—for such things are scarce in that region—they felled a large oak standing beside the church and fashioned from that oak a container in which she was placed. Yet how many wonders the Lord deigned to perform through her at that place, neither can our mind recount nor our tongue adequately explain. For many blind people, restored to sight, returned home without a guide; many lame people, their limbs made firm, were raised upright; hearing was restored to the deaf; the tongues of the mute were loosed; and demons were expelled from possessed bodies at her burial.

14. When, therefore, her holiness, endowed with so many and such great miracles, had become renowned far and wide, after seven years her friends and neighbors decided to inspect the sarcophagus and, if possible, change it for a better one in her honor. At that place an extraordinary event occurred, a miracle unfamiliar and unheard-of among human beings. For when they were removing from the earth the sarcophagus in which the holy virgin lay, although it had previously been wooden, it was found to be made of stone. When knowledge of this event spread throughout the region and raised the hearts of all who heard it to the praise of God and of Saint Bellendis, a certain woman from the neighborhood, remaining incredulous and insisting that it was a fabrication, came, perversely distrustful, to see it. But as soon as she saw the sarcophagus, she was seized by a demon and fell to the ground. There she lay for three days as though lifeless, neither hearing nor seeing, until the most holy virgin, moved by the prayers of those present, restored her to her former health.

15. Stirred by such joyful and wondrous miracles, the entire region came together and built, in honor of the blessed Mother of God Mary and of the holy virgin Bellendis, the church in which she now rests. In the thirtieth year after her burial, the whole population of the neighboring regions, moved by divine inspiration, assembled with two bishops—namely, Ausbert of Cambrai and Norbert of Tournai—who raised her from the tomb and placed her in the shrine in which she now rests.

[Note: A mistake, as Bollandus correctly observed. For Autbertus, who seems to be intended here, had died before Bellendis; nor is any bishop of Tournai named Norbertus or Florbertus known.]

16. When God wished to increase the glory, honor, and renown of his servant, it happened that, in the city of Toul, a certain monk of the monastery of the blessed protomartyr Stephen [Note: Thus there were then monks in the cathedral church of Toul, dedicated to Saint Stephen.] saw in a vision a most beautiful young man standing before him and saying: “Rise and go to the province of Brabant, to a place called Merbecca, and try to obtain some relics of the holy virgin Bellendis, so that, in her honor, you may build a church at the place that God will show you. When he comes to the aforesaid place, he will be received with great honor, held there in great veneration, and eventually made keeper of the church.”

One night, when everyone was overcome by sleep, he opened the shrine and took from the virgin’s relics as much as he wished; then, at a suitable time, he departed. Guided by God, he came into a wilderness to a place called Tin, shown to him from heaven. He remained there and built a basilica for the blessed virgin, in which she continues to shine, glorious in signs, powers, and miracles, admirable even to this day. For a community of religious monks was established there to serve the Lord, and through the patronage of that virgin the region is sustained by the Lord.

It is therefore fitting that those who worship, love, believe in, and serve the Lord should praise, glorify, and bless him, since he works such great and almost innumerable miracles gloriously and laudably in his saints. And, so that we may deserve to be preserved and blessed by him, let us ask, with the whole intention of pious devotion, through the prayers of this virgin whose Life, with the Lord’s help, we have described in words admittedly unpolished, that we may deserve to reach the homeland of the heavenly inheritance.

[Note: A place of this name exists in the county of Rethelois, called Tin-le-Monstier, not far from Charleville, situated on the River Thin, which bears the same name. A monastery was once built there by Count Stephen and his wife Freduida in honor of the blessed Mary; later it was united by Adalbero, archbishop of Reims, to the abbey of Mouzon, as is recorded in the Mouzon Chronicle in volume VII of Acher’s *Spicilegium*. It is now a priory subject to that abbey, and Saint Bellendis is venerated as patroness in its church.]

17. Saint Bellendis departed happily from this life in the Lord on the third day before the Nones of February [3 February]; and she rejoices, reigning eternally with Christ among the saints, with him who reigns everywhere without end.

[Note: That is, about the year 702, as we conjecture.]

[Note: She survived her father by seventeen years. Her father was also the father of Saint Gertrude of Nivelles, to whom he handed over his possessions after she had already been received into heaven. Gertrude, moreover, departed to heaven in the year 658, as we determine, or certainly, as others maintain, in 664. The body of Saint Bellendis is preserved at Morsel in her sacred church. Read other miracles of Saint Bellendis in Bollandus.]

[Col. 1109]

# LIFE OF SAINT LANDOALD

Written by Heriger at the command of Notger, bishop of Liège

(*In Bollandus, March, vol. III, day 19, p. 35, from various manuscripts and Surius.*) (G)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1109C] Notger, whom they nevertheless call bishop, though he is an unworthy servant of Saint Mary and Saint Lambert, sends eternal life in heaven to Womar, venerable Father in Christ, and to the Gandavian brothers, and to all the faithful living wherever they may be who will read this with an unprejudiced eye.

[Note: Womarus was made abbot of Ghent in 965 and died in 982. See Sanderus’s *Ghent*.]

You did not hesitate, most reverend Fathers, to request—or rather to urge—the small ability of our mediocrity to satisfy your petition, insofar as the report of what could reach us allowed, concerning events that ought to be proclaimed by all ages and peoples: events manifested to us in our own days, though we are unworthy, and granted especially to you, namely those revealed at the translation of Saint Landoald, archpriest, and his companions, who, having been raised from our diocese, passed by God’s foreordination into your jurisdiction.

[Note: The sense remains suspended for too long and must finally be joined to the end of the period in this manner: “so that from the marvelous events … we ought to satisfy your petition, since they arose from our diocese,” and so forth.]

It is a just request and a worthy exhortation, one that, according to a certain wise man, is joined both to the propriety of the present undertaking and to the usefulness of the age to come. For if the deeds of those men had not perished through the negligence of our predecessors, they would still suffice for us today. But since we have heard and learned many things, and our fathers have related them to us—things that our memory still preserves—you ask that they be committed to writing, lest we too be condemned by posterity.

Since we were placed in a dilemma by the fact that your episcopate is acknowledged and believed to be the citadel of every art, silence balanced our hesitant mind; and that poetic line, “Do not carry wood into the forest” (Horace, *Satires* 1.10.34), brought with it a small measure of diffidence. But since “The mind is at fault when it never escapes itself” (Horace, *Epistles* 1.14.13), the torpor of diffidence yielded and your insistence prevailed—except that our haste, which according to Socrates makes a favor more welcome, compelled us to hurry more than the matter required.

For we had before us the saying: “Charity supplies the strength that inexperience withholds”; and, “Once the undertaking has begun, the rest will take care of itself” (Sallust, *Catiline* 21). Accordingly, we undertook the task, lest we seem to evade your authority. Authority is granted to one who presumes to act when he believes that the person he summons can accomplish what is requested; and, conversely, for the knowledgeable person to obey is an equal glory to that of commanding.

But if some future detractor should not fear to polish these things with a sidelong eye (Horace, *Epistles* 1.14.37) and should presume to poison them with obscure hatred and a biting tooth (ibid.), we call Jesus and his holy angels, and the coming judgment, to witness on his behalf that here we have set down little beyond what we either heard from the priest Sarabert—who swore to it as sacred truth and, as he himself reported, was earnestly adjured by you and invoked the merits of these saints—or faithfully found recorded in the written account delivered to us by you, except only for those matters extracted from our episcopate that, in view of the circumstances, seemed appropriately to be placed before this little document.

Farewell. Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July [19 June], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 980, in the eighth indiction, in the eighth year of the reign of the Lord Otto after the death of his father, and in the ninth year of our episcopate.

[Note: Otto I, emperor, died on 7 May, a Wednesday before Pentecost. From that time this is called the eighth year of Otto II; nevertheless, Otto II had been crowned by the Roman pontiff while his father was still alive, toward the end of 967, and thus the year commonly called 980 is often reckoned as the thirteenth year of his empire.]

# BOOK ONE

The deeds, translations, and miracles of Saint Landoald and his companions performed at Wintershoven

[Col. 1111]

## CHAPTER ONE

The arrival among the Franks in Belgium of Saint Landoald and his apostolic companions

[Col. 1111B]

1. From its beginnings the kingdom of the Franks had always been indefatigable, but at that time it seemed to flourish above all its neighboring realms, when it allowed its neck to bend beneath the image of the Lord’s faith, and to burn what it had previously worshiped, while thereafter wishing to worship what it had burned.

[Note: The beginning and development of the Frankish kingdom, with an accurate calculation of its kings, were set out by us on 1 February in the Life of Saint Sigebert, king.]

[Note: Clovis I was baptized in 494.]

The holy Church of God received its greatest increase and a firm condition under him, when King Clothar, fourth in succession from that point, singularly governed the monarchy of three kingdoms, and was in his fortieth year, while Heraclius Augustus, bearer of the holy cross, was in his fourteenth.

[Note: After Chlothar I and Childeric intervened, the son of the latter, Chlothar II, succeeded and became sole monarch in 613.]

[Note: Heraclius became emperor after Phocas was killed on 27 March 610; consequently, his fourteenth year and Chlothar’s fortieth fall in the year 623.]

He allowed no scepter of any surrounding ruler to confront his own; rather, he strove to restrain with his reins almost everything in Gaul and Germany that belonged to kings and peoples. He had placed his illustrious son Dagobert over Austrasia and joined the kingdom of Germany to his dominion.

[Note: In the thirty-eighth year of his reign, A.D. 621, or, according to others, in the following year.]

During their most prosperous time, the name of Christianity flourished everywhere to such an extent that even today scarcely any church is found beyond the neighboring regions, or none at all, that does not present to us the patronage of some saint of that age.

But, leaving aside for the moment the innumerable others, the holy men Eligius and Audoen had begun to devote themselves to courtly duties, while the blessed Arnulf and Romaric were already taking part in royal councils.

[Note: These two were ordained bishops together on 4 May 646. Eligius of Noyon is commemorated on 1 December, and Audoen of Rouen on 24 August.]

[Note: This is Saint Arnulf, formerly bishop of Metz and later a dweller in the Vosges wilderness; he is commemorated on 18 July. Romaric, however, abbot of Luxeuil, is commemorated on 8 December; but he had lived at the court of King Theudebert long before.]

Saint Amandus was illuminating Aquitaine by the auspices of his birth. While still a boy, he left his homeland and parents and sought the island of Ogie, situated to the west in the Ocean Sea. There he was received with great joy by spiritual brothers; and because he had learned the sacred writings, he daily burned with a greater desire in the service of God.

Afterward, more mature in age but more fervent in purpose, he sought the tomb of Saint Martin at Tours. There he prayed for the help of Martin’s intercession and begged the Lord to grant him the grace to undertake the course of lifelong pilgrimage. Rising from prayer, he had the hair of his head cut off, received the dignity of the clerical state, and, though continuing his pilgrimage, advanced through every rank of clerical grace.

[Note: We have treated Saint Amandus’s Life extensively on 6 February and corrected the errors of Notger and others. Saint Austregisilus is commemorated on 20 May and Saint Sulpitius on 17 January.]

He then went to Bourges, where he lived in the greatest holiness with the blessed Austrigisilus and his archdeacon, Saint Sulpitius. In a cell that he had built himself, he devoted himself for fifteen years to the strictest life.

2. He then returned to Rome, where he was warned in a vision by Saint Peter to return to Gaul for the sake of preaching. At last, compelled by the king and the priests, he was ordained bishop for preaching, as was customary at that time. Since the error of paganism still prevailed everywhere, it was necessary for both devout rulers and the priests of the Lord to appoint others to proclaim the word of God, baptize the people, and confirm them.

To ensure that this may seem doubtful to no one, Taxandria bears witness: many years later it was completely freed from the worship of idols by the blessed Lambert.

[Note: We have discussed the location and extent of Taxandria at length in book 1, chapter 2, of our treatise *On the Bishops of Tongeren*.]

[Note: Saint Lambert is commemorated on 17 September.]

Brabant too, entangled in many pagan errors, was partly corrected by his successor, Saint Hubert.

[Note: Saint Hubert transferred the see from Maastricht to Liège, and the name of the bishopric of Tongeren was resumed, as we have shown elsewhere. We shall treat Saint Hubert on 3 November.]

Almost all Germany was not only newly converted but also illuminated and enriched by new bishoprics and churches. Of these men, we know that some persevered in preaching until death; others were afterward appointed to vacant bishoprics or abbeys; and still others established new bishoprics for new churches.

[Note: This is abridged from the Acts of Saint Amandus. Consult chapters 4 and 5, together with our notes on them and the preliminary commentary.]

The blessed Amandus diligently fulfilled the office he had undertaken and proclaimed the word of the Lord throughout the surrounding regions, extending his journey as far as Vasconia—called Vacceja here—and beyond the Danube. At last, seeing that his strength was insufficient for so arduous a task, he resolved to visit Rome again.

3. At that time Pope Martin was administering the universal Roman pontificate. The blessed Amandus disclosed to him the purpose for which he had come and asked that helpers be sent to him for carrying out that work.

[Note: Here there is a very serious chronological σφάλμα (*sphalma*, “error”), explained in the Life of Saint Amandus. This was his third Roman journey, undertaken after he had left the bishopric of Maastricht in the year 650, when Saint Martin was Roman pontiff.]

Several assistants were assigned to him, though their names have been lost. Among them were Saint Landoald, archpriest, and Amantius, deacon. They were also accompanied by the holy women Vinciana and Adeltrudis, together with seven other men and women.

At approximately the same time, the blessed John, who was successfully governing the bishopric of Tongeren and Maastricht, died.

[Note: Saint John Agnus had already died several years earlier, namely in 646, on 25 July.]

King Dagobert, who had auspiciously succeeded to power after his father’s death, summoned the blessed Amandus and made him preside over the see of Maastricht.

[Note: Dagobert had already departed this life on 19 January 644, three years before Saint Martin became pope. Saint Amandus was bishop of Maastricht during the reign of Saint Sigebert among the Austrasians.]

For three years Amandus traveled through villages and fortified places, proclaiming the word of life. But when he saw that he was accomplishing nothing, and grieved that priests and deacons were moreover insulting him, he thereafter moved to other regions. How long the people of Maastricht remained without pastoral blessing until the blessed Remaclus is unknown, except that, as report has reached us, the blessed Landoald remained there and administered the bishop’s functions for nine years.

[Note: Once this error is removed, several others follow. Saint Remaclus succeeded Saint Amandus immediately, as is clearly demonstrated in his Life.]

4. We were easily led to accept that opinion because it is reported that the same blessed Landoald nurtured our special patron, namely Saint Lambert, from his earliest childhood.

[Note: The earlier writers of Saint Lambert’s Lives, Godescalc and Stephen, bishop of Liège, do not mention this instruction; but Nicholas the canon and Reinerus the monk later affirmed as certain what is related here in this Life. We stated in the Life of Saint Amandus that Saint Lambert does not seem to have been born before the year 650, that he was consecrated bishop in 677, and that Saint Landoald could have been counted among the wise men from whom Godescalc and Stephen say that Saint Lambert learned the sacred writings.]

For that reason the illustrious man Aper, father of that boy, granted him in perpetuity the estate called Wintershoven, situated on the River Archa, so that he might inhabit it and build a church there; and he arranged for the boy to remain with him so that he might be instructed in divine teachings.
