[Note: Wintershoven is also called Windohaim or Widohaim in the Salic Law promulgated there. It is still a village between Tongeren and Hasselt, somewhat distant from the river. Nicholas, Reinerus, and Aegidius describe what follows without mentioning a river.]

While the craftsmen were laboring at the work and were displeased with the muddy water, which came from marshes, blessed Landoald, invoking the name of Christ and making the sign of the cross, caused a most clear spring to bubble forth for everyone’s use by striking the ground with his staff. It still gives credence to his words today.

5. At another time, when it seemed that the necessary fire was lacking, the holy man summoned the boy and ordered him to bring in fire. The boy began to resist the command and openly explained why he had not immediately obeyed:

“You see, lord, that there is no vessel in which the fire may conveniently be carried; and in what way do you now command it to be brought? My mind is ready to obey you, but the lack of a vessel itself prevents me from seeming to oppose your wishes.”

But when the pious Father perceived the boy’s hesitation, he said: “My son, is it pleasing to delay your father’s command, when the garment with which you are clothed can carry the fire quite adequately?”

Moved by this rebuke, and compelled also by the example of obedience, the boy obeyed the Father’s command without hesitation. After going a short distance, he hurried to find the fire. When he had found it and saw that there was nothing with which he could carry it more conveniently, he opened his lap to the burning coals, placed them inside without hesitation, and carried them all the way to the Father with his garment unharmed.

Then the holy man reflected more deeply on the novelty of the miracle and did not hesitate to compare the merit of the fortunate boy even with the virtues of the perfected. Indeed, the fiery element either feared to display its nature or was compelled entirely to conceal it. But when the still-fresh miracle reached the ears of the people, the boy was exalted by everyone’s voice, and the divinely accomplished deed was attributed both to the merit of the obedient boy and to the command of the one who ordered it. Thus the same power was believed to have been performed through the holiness of both. Christ also worked many other miracles there through their merit.

## CHAPTER TWO

Various translations carried out at Wintershoven

When King Childeric heard reports of these events, he was then residing at Maastricht and, moved to repentance, sent him the necessary provisions every day.

[Note: Childeric began to reign as a child with Imnechild, the widow of his paternal uncle Sigebert, from the year 664; he became sole ruler in 676 and was killed in 679.]

[Note: Diplomas of Childeric signed at Maastricht are extant, and he seems often to have been there. His seat, and that of the other Austrasian kings, was chiefly the city of Metz.]

[Note: Wintershoven is about thirty miles from Maastricht.]

On one occasion, however, a certain Adrian, believed to be carrying excessive amounts of gold and silver as the blessed man’s messenger to the king, was intercepted by robbers and obtained martyrdom midway along the road at a place called Villers.

The blessed Landoald, having completed the course of his present life, attained rest in a good old age, put off the human condition, and received the prize of an everlasting crown. He was buried in the church that he himself had built and dedicated in honor of blessed Peter on the Kalends of December [1 December]. He died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April [19 March].

The companions of his pilgrimage, mentioned above, were likewise summoned from this light at times appointed by Christ and were buried around him in the same church. Only Amantius, blessed in name and merit, the deacon, was content to be buried in the same coffin with him, because, as report has it, he had been Landoald’s son in baptism.

7. After many years had passed, Saint Florebert, who governed the bishopric of Maastricht or Liège in the third place after Saint Lambert, heard of the multitude of miracles there and, being likewise warned by the responses of visions, transferred them from that place with due reverence and ordered their tombs to be adorned as far as he was able.

This translation took place on the Kalends of December [1 December], the same day on which, as we stated above, the dedication of that church was commemorated. Honor, worship, and reverence remained attached to the bodies of the saints until the savage race of the Normans, dissatisfied with its own settlements, disturbed almost the whole of Gaul. Out of fear of their invasion, lest the saints’ tombs be violated, the faithful returned them to the earth.

[Note: The invasion seems to be the one that occurred in the year 881, when Maastricht, Liège, Tongeren, the county of Hasbaye, and the neighboring regions are recorded in the Fulda Annals as having been devastated and burned.]

A certain Frangerus took part in this reburial, a man extremely old in our time, who before the pagan invasion had also been administrator and steward of that same village for nine years.

[Note: The manuscript of the Abbey of Rood refers to the Hungarians.]

The priest Hildebrand, whom the priest Sarabert buried with his own hand a few years ago, was likewise a most faithful reporter of this information. He stated that he had heard the foregoing from that same Frangerus, with many witnesses confirming it, and that he had also seen a little book about their lives. Since he says that it was written in an antiquarian hand and was almost completely soaked through by dripping wax, we recognize that readers of it must have been exceedingly rare.

But what we have so far touched upon briefly in words, he said that he had gleaned from that book; more recently, however, during the invasion of the Hungarians, the same book, through the negligence of its custodians, was burned together with other possessions.

[Note: In the year 954 the Hungarians ravaged Hasbaye with fire and plunder, having been summoned by Conrad, duke of Lorraine, as Frodoard, Sigebert, and others testify.]

But enough of this.

8. After the expulsion of the Normans, a certain man named Tietbold was the first to receive by right of benefice from the count of Flanders, who held the abbey of Saint Bavo the confessor, the aforesaid place where the bodies of the saints had been deposited; Adelgandus succeeded him.

[Note: After the monks had been scattered by the Norman invasion, when Elias, abbot of Laon, died in 895, he was buried there in the church of Saint Vincent. Saint Gerard, abbot of Brogne, later gathered the monks again and rebuilt the monastery about 940.]

These men, thinking more about the things of the world than about the things of the Lord, considered that little reverence remained to be shown to the saints; consequently, the place gradually began to be held in contempt. When Aper, a man close to our own age, obtained the place on a precarious tenure together with his sons, the church itself, through the abandonment of the fear of God, was not only deprived of the honor due to the saint but entirely stripped of its adornment.

Wandoldus afterward succeeded to ownership of the same village and there received a place of burial. On account of his burial, his son Lambert [Note: Below, and in the preceding account, he is called Lantzo.] was then moved by devotion to cultivate this place, and he was also prompted by the report of the miracles that occurred there.

For, while the Lord was then claiming the estate for himself, and the family of its owners had become divided from the neighbors because of certain hostilities, the household, fleeing to the church, threw the village’s tapestries and other cloths upon the saints’ tombs. The priest Sarabert, on the other hand, removed them from there. But when the household brought them back again and frightened the priest so that he would not resist them any further, night came on, and the household settled down around the place to sleep. When they awoke in the morning, they saw, unexpectedly and without having suffered any injury, that the tapestries and whatever else they had deposited had been burned.

9. There is also a phylactery said truly to have belonged to Saint Landoald; whoever presumes to swear falsely upon it does not escape unpunished. A household of more than twelve men and one woman was bound by an oath sworn by the brothers Witger and Lambert upon that phylactery, so that it should not flee. Treating the oath as void, and moreover violating and carrying off a treasure of its lords stored in that same church, the household fled. In the morning, after its pursuers had searched all around in vain, it was found by those returning, asleep beneath a tree near the church, with the treasure unharmed.

Another man, truly entangled in a certain crime, swore falsely upon the same object; that very night the wretch was burned together with his house and his only son. Other miracles also happened there, which I now pass over.

10. For this reason that same Lantso approached our venerable predecessor, namely Lord Euraclus, as a suppliant, asking that either he himself or his representatives transfer the bodies of the saints and remove them from the place where they had been deposited before the Norman invasion.

[Note: Euraclus is Eurapus in the manuscript of Ghent and in Surius; in the manuscript of Rood Abbey he is Everardus. Anselm discusses him in chapter 47 of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège* as printed by Chapeauville and calls him Eraclius; other manuscripts read Everacus and Euraclus. He held the see from 959 to 970. The ecclesiastical Office of Ghent is said to have set down the Life and translation of Landoald in a proper book, though we have not read this elsewhere.]

After repeating this request many times, he finally obtained his wish. The archdeacon Bono, together with two archpriests, trustworthy men indeed, Thietbold and Uhodon, and also with others from the monasteries of Saint Trudo, Belisia, and Tongeren, came to the place and, with a solemn litany, lifted the saints from the tombs in which they had been lying in excessive neglect.

[Note: Belisia, called Bilsena by others, is a town five miles from Wintershoven. It has a very large monastery of canonesses.]

They found several coffins. One contained Saint Landoald, the archpriest, and his deacon Amantius together. There was also a stone at their heads, carved with their names. Other coffins contained Saints Adeltrudis and Vinciana, as was indicated by a small silver cross found upon the breast of Saint Vinciana.

After these other coffins had been set aside and restored, while the bodies of the saints were being washed with wine and water, a little bird slipped through the window into the bier of the saints. It repeatedly and most intrusively plunged itself among those engaged in the rite, then repeatedly flew down into the excavation from which the bodies of the saints had been lifted. This caused both a miracle and horror among all who stood by and witnessed it.

Its coloring was of an extraordinary beauty, but one never previously seen; and its voice had a sweet, shrill sound, but one never previously heard. Although it could have been caught by those present, no one dared to touch it. Flying here and there as though with certain clappings of joy and whistling of its voice, and then settling again upon the bier of the saints, it did not cease its activity until everything had been completed according to the proper rite.

11. On the same day a certain blind woman from the nearby village of Hasbaye, having heard the report that the bodies of the saints were being brought out, hurried there with a candle. After waiting for two days and continually seeking the patronage of the saints, she departed on the third day seeing clearly.

12. In the following year the wife of the aforementioned Lantso, named Sigeburgis, was suffering from a disease of dropsy, and her legs and feet had swollen so greatly that for almost an entire year she could scarcely enter even the church unless she were carried in a sedan chair. She neither shared her husband’s bed nor attended his table; she found all food repulsive and rejected every drink except water.

During the deep night, while half awake, she was suddenly seized by a vision and addressed in these words: “When you have raised up our lords and ladies, why do you allow us, their faithful servants, to lie hidden in the mud? I am Landrada; the martyr Adrian and Julian are also members of our company.”

She disclosed this vision to her husband and asked that either the bishop or the bishop’s authority be invited to raise them. In the previous year he had spent so lavishly on the elevation of the others that undertaking this seemed to him exceedingly difficult.

After several days the same vision appeared again. She was rebuked for negligence by the same nun, in the same form as before, and confounded for her contempt: “You have spent so much and so greatly on physicians, yet have not deserved to be cured. If you had raised us from the mud, you would already have deserved to be healed.”

“And where,” she asked, “shall we find you?”

“Your chair,” the apparition replied, “in which you are carried to church, irreverently presses down our tombs; and the chest placed behind it is excessively burdensome to us. And if you claim that you cannot obtain the bishop or his representatives, you at least have the nearby priest Sarabert, as well as other faithful men to complete the work.”

The next morning, while she was considering what ought to be done about these matters, a young woman from her women’s quarters came to her, reporting that she too had been warned in the same vision by these same signs. At that time she was living in the village of Godenghove.

Her mistress Sigeburgis, to whom these things were revealed, still lives; I mean that she lives, enjoys the present light healthy and unharmed, and takes nourishment. A noble person and the grandeur of her household do not permit the matter, which we have learned faithfully from the mouth of one who swore to and affirmed these things, to remain concealed.

She immediately sent with all haste for priests to accomplish these things. Meanwhile, unable to remain inactive while seeking the restoration of her health, she had herself carried to the church and began meanwhile to remove the earth gradually from the designated place.

They had scarcely dug out half a foot of earth when, behold, the saints’ coffins appeared almost at the surface itself. The priests who had been summoned arrived, uncovered the saints’ tombs, and found their names written on little slips.

While they completed as best they could everything proper to the translation, the aforementioned matron, who was attending the work most carefully, suddenly turned and saw streams of poison and foul matter, amounting to a sextarius, pouring from her legs.

Amazed and made more joyful by the recovery of her health, she returned home on foot, prepared an abundant feast for her guests and household, and took part in it herself. She found no food repulsive and no longer recoiled from wine or any other drink.

The report of many people, both before our time and at present, further states that this blessed woman, while presiding over the nuns at Belisia and gathering the sweetest fruits of heavenly contemplation, instructed the most holy virgin and woman of illustrious nobility, Amelberga, in holy conduct and pursuits.

[Note: Saint Amelberga is commemorated on 10 July.]

This translation took place on the third day before the Nones of March [5 March].

[Note: The Life of Saint Landrada was inserted here in the manuscript of Ghent.]

## CHAPTER THREE

Miracles performed at Wintershoven
13. [Note: [Col. 1119D] This entire chapter is lacking in the manuscript of Rooden Valley, as is the following chapter of Book II.]

Nor do we think that this miracle, likewise astonishing in the novelty of its nature, should be passed over in the memorable glorification of the saints. After the aforementioned Lantso had inherited by lot the basilica, or estate, of the most sacred resting place of the saints after some others, he, being well aware of the situation, deliberately resolved—with a fixed and reasoned purpose, since the charter had established that his right of possession should end with him—that the offspring of his line who would succeed him should be deprived of the aforesaid estate. He therefore prudently decided to provide for himself, with the intention that, although deprived of the rural estate, he might at least not be defrauded of the solace of the saints’ relics. Seeking the favor of the bishop of that diocese, he disclosed to him the secret of his great devotion. Immediately marked by the bishop’s blessing and strengthened by his authority, he entered the repository of the precious treasures and selected from the sacred bodies such portions as he judged suitable.

But behold, on the very chief feast of paschal joy, with the bearers’ necks bent beneath their burden, they undertook the arduous labor of the journey and, hastening onward, reached the doors of the sacred church. Yet—wondrous to relate!—unable in any way to cross them, they remained fixed and stuck in place, their steps suddenly and unexpectedly arrested. After long striving in vain with every effort, they finally understood that they were being barred by divine power, and thus, unwillingly, yielded to the difficulty that brought shame upon them. [Col. 1119B]

The illustrious Lantso, however, did not in the least abandon his purpose. Continuing throughout that day and the following night with frequent distributions of alms and repeated petitions of prayer, he was frustrated again on the next day, just as before. Indeed, for all the intervening days of the week, the same attempts were followed daily by the same repulse from the obstacle at the threshold. Since this had achieved so little, then, at the eighth dawn he undertook another course without delay. Although all the prayers he had previously poured forth had been entirely ineffective, he now accumulated heartfelt vows with every effort of his strength, promised many services, and assigned to that very basilica of their resting place a ninth portion of his crops, since the tenth was known to belong to another church. To the place where he was striving to bring the fruit of his devotion, he also generously gave a substantial possession from his inheritance, together with the cost of other gifts.

Thus at last, through the intercession of the saints, he merited the merciful attention of the kind God. Having obtained what he had vowed and gained the hope he desired, he regarded the losses caused by his former failure as insignificant, having acquired, through the magnificent compassion of the Lord, the gains he sought.

14. Subenmenha is the name of an estate. A certain man named Manimius was so contracted in every power of his limbs that he could not bring his hand to his mouth to take food, nor could he even go to attend to the necessities of nature unless someone else carried him. He was conveyed by cart to the patronage of the saints; but when they had granted him complete health, he returned home on foot and well.

In the village of Lewa [Note: [Col. 1120D] Lewa, or Leuwa, is a town of Brabant on the borders of the territory of Liège, four miles from Sint-Truiden. Surius reads Lena.], there was a woman named Geyla, attached to a certain leading man named Hubert, who had received a benefice from the bishop of Liège. She was full of a demon—something that subsequently became clear. For her relatives had led her through various monasteries of men of God, namely those of Saints Gervasius, Lambert, Trudo, and Gertrude; and since she could nowhere be cured, she was brought there in utter despair, because the saints who were newly to perform wonders were awaiting a fuller triumphal praise over the enemy.

When she had been placed in a tub overflowing with blessed water, she immediately began to call out the name of Blessed Landoaldus in a terrifying manner and to emit from her mouth a great swarm of flies. In the middle of Easter week she merited purification. [Col. 1120B]

15. Another woman, a servant of Saint Bavo who had until then lived at Andresburg, was deprived of her eyesight because she had neglected the annual payment for several years. Having suffered blindness for four years, she promised to amend her conduct, brought a candle to the saints’ lights, and paid the neglected due. She immediately departed healed and enlightened.

Zubleva is also the name of another village. There a certain woman had suffered from dropsy for the course of six years. In a nocturnal vision she saw herself being brought there with an offering and returning in restored health. On awakening, she immediately fulfilled what she had seen: she ordered herself to be taken there in a wagon; and after recovering her health, she was handed over by her master Hildrad to the jurisdiction of the saints, and then departed. [Col. 1120C]

16. A certain man named Hildico, utterly reckless in his conduct and repeatedly clearing the Church’s forest, was finally reproved one day in the name of the saints and told at least to desist. When he further insulted his admonishers and the saints with vile words, he went out the following day to do the same thing. In his arrogance he immediately climbed a beech tree with an axe, but at once fell backward onto his neck, crushing his throat—the throat that had breathed blasphemy—and thus ended his wicked life by a death he deserved.

The priest Sarabertus had lost a horse when thieves secretly stole it one night. When he discovered this in the morning, he ran to the well-known shrine and hastened to make a candle. As soon as he brought it to the saints and expressed the vows of his prayers, he found the horse returned and standing at the doors. [Col. 1120D]

17. Thus, fearing that we might bind ourselves through sluggish silence and fail to record the abundant miracles which the Lord has deigned to perform through their merits, we have set down these memorable events, though with somewhat extended prolixity. Even now many more deeds performed among us remain available, which you asked to have inserted here, likewise entrusted to our authority for confirmation, as briefly as possible. But, mindful of the needs of our readers’ and hearers’ powers of attention, and unwilling that the magnificent benefits of the great Lord should be forced into a narrow space, we have judged that this discourse should be closed at this point, postponing what follows. Thus, when strength has meanwhile been restored through silence, the remaining material—since it clearly requires a volume of its own—may be given a more suitable and distinguished title with a fresh beginning. [Col. 1121A]

# BOOK TWO. The Translation of the Relics to Ghent

[Col. 1121]

1. As we are about to relate the wondrous works of the all-powerful Lord, by which in our own times he has graciously made Blessed Landoaldus, the confessor of his name, and his companions wonderfully known, we consider it fitting and not superfluous to place first the memorable joy of the translation of these same saints. Through it, some of their signs also shone forth, and your place or region was happily honored by the gracious presence of their relics.

After the passage of time, when the inexorable determination of mortal life required it, the aforementioned illustrious Lantso, namely the appointed possessor of the estate mentioned above, paid the common debt owed by all the living, and deprived his offspring of the succession to that possession by hereditary right. But, under the governance of the clemency of imperial serenity—which, through the praiseworthy vow of devotion, naturally inclined a benevolent mind to care greatly for the lowliness of God’s servants—the same possession, without obstruction or resistance, was transferred into the jurisdiction of your authority, namely that of the prelates of the saints, especially the chosen soldier of Christ, the distinguished confessor Bavo. [Col. 1121C]

2. Since the wise person always acts wisely, you examined with discerning diligence the possession restored to your jurisdiction and understood, with deeper counsel, that the honorable deposit itself outweighed everything else, and that the reliquary of so precious a treasure ought not to be hidden there beneath so small a measure.

After long weighing the matter in mutual discussion among yourselves, and with the agreement of archbishops, bishops, and prudent men, you resolved that the relics of the saints should be transferred to the eminence of your place, which was evidently the more powerful site. But while the journey was being undertaken—while, that is, the fulfillment of this holy devotion was finally being celebrated and the saints’ most precious relics were being carried across a considerable stretch of road—it happened, as was natural, that very many of the neighboring people were seized by the report of so happy an event. [Col. 1121D]

3. Among several of those who heard it there was found a certain weak woman, weighed down by the burden of illness and confined to her bed, who for many days had been unable to rise from it except when carried. But, when she was likewise raised to good hope by the welcome pleasure of hearing the news, she was confidently assured that her lost health would be recovered through the saints’ assistance. Without delay, therefore, through a neighbor who shared her purpose, she asked that a little candle-offering be promptly presented to the saints in recognition of their merits and presence.

He faithfully agreed and hastened to fulfill this holy duty. But behold—a wondrous thing to relate!—the abandoned and sick wife experienced the saints’ sudden aid. Immediately she sent someone to remove her husband, who had gone ahead to meet the saints, since she herself would soon follow, seeking the saints’ presence and offering in person what she was sending. But because the narrowness of place and time did not permit the saints’ procession to be delayed, the bearer of the little offering presented himself bodily to the saints’ mercy; and, after displaying before them the work of their compassion in the presence of all who were there, he proclaimed and testified it to the praise and glory of the all-powerful Lord. [Col. 1122B]

4. Furthermore, since the suitability of the journey required it, a ship was hired with its crew and arranged to serve the saints’ joyful conveyance. But one of the men assigned to the oars, upon whom a certain misfortune had recently fallen, driven on by the loss of his property and wearied by the labor he had undertaken, presumed, unfortunate man, to withdraw from this holy service before the appointed cost of the journey had been paid.

But because the saints’ biers were not to be despised or subordinated to private advantage, he soon perceived this, without any lengthy interval. Voluntarily and inexorably torn away from the service of God’s chosen ones, he not only failed to benefit the advantage he had intended, but unwillingly suffered a deserved rebuke.

On departing, he did not travel far, nor did he reach the distance he desired. Instead, deprived of soundness of mind and likewise of his former bodily strength, he scarcely reached the fence of the neighboring place—which had been offered to him sooner and lay close at hand—before stumbling against it with his feet and falling there in a daze. Indeed, for the remainder of that day and the entire course of the following night he remained stunned, undergoing the punishment he deserved. [Col. 1122C–D]

After being worn down for some time by so severe a blow of correction, he finally, through the pious intercession of the saints whom he had despised and by the kindly visitation of the merciful God, understood from the depths of his heart the offense of his guilt. As soon as delayed repentance had crossed the threshold of his mind, his body, which had likewise been sunk in stupor, recovered its sluggish strength. Abandoning the bitter cares of his former intention and now burning with eager devotion to the saints’ service, previously neglected, he retraced the journey with hurried steps so that at last he might joyfully present himself before them.

This recent chastisement and his true conversion to repentance had made his steps swift; nor did he rest until, having obtained his desired wish, he reached the saints’ glorious presence. Before them and in the presence of many people, he testified to the correction and clemency he had experienced. [Col. 1123A]

5. On that very day—namely, the eighth day before the Kalends of April—when the monastery mentioned above was entered with those relics, a woman named Lenekin [Note: [Col. 1123D] The Ghent manuscript reads Levekin.] recovered the sight she had long lost. This occurred on the Ides of April [Note: [Col. 1123D] In the stated year 980, when the lunar cycle was 12 and the solar cycle 4, with Dominical Letters D and C; Easter was celebrated on 11 April.], namely on the Tuesday of Easter week.

A certain blind girl came from the village of Ostholta [Note: [Col. 1123D] Surius reads Schult.], named Teudsmudis. She remained while the brethren were celebrating the evening synaxis and returned seeing clearly, with no further need to seek a guide for the road. [Col. 1123B]

6. In that same village there was another girl who, within the years of childhood, had become so weak that before reaching one year of age she could neither walk on her feet nor even rise from her bed. Her mother, stirred by the miracles mentioned above, carried her outdoors in her arms early in the morning, made a vow to the saints for her recovery—namely, that she would come there with her child and bring with her a devout offering.

When she had fulfilled this, the girl gradually raised herself onto her feet, stood, grew stronger, began to walk, and departed. In the same place there was another woman, called Lewich, likewise weak in every bodily power. When she had almost despaired of life, she heard the report of the miracles taking place there and vowed a wax candle to the saints’ lights. As soon as she sent it there, she immediately merited the restoration of the strength of her entire body. [Note: [Col. 1123D] The same as Wentiae.]

Wechtre is the name of a village. There lived there a woman named Riberta, afflicted by various sufferings and deprived of almost every function of her limbs. She came devotedly to the memory of the saints, stayed there for several days, and departed after receiving health. [Col. 1123C]

7. Moreover, a certain woman came on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May to pray for her son. She had left at home a son named Adelgerus, deprived not only of the light of his eyes but also entirely hunchbacked from rheumatic movement of the head and body. His mother prayed for his recovery and made a vow; but, afraid for the son whom she had left in despair, she returned quickly. When she reached home, she found her son seeing and rejoicing in assured health, and received him back happily. [Col. 1123D]

After this, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June, a servant named Egerin arrived. For many years she had suffered from whiteness or bleary disease [Col. 1124A] in her eyes. Having obtained health through the merits of the saints, she returned joyfully and exultantly to her own home without a guide.

8. Next, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, a poor woman from the village of Rothen, named Adalmudis, became blind through excessive illness and, having heard of the saints’ fame, desired to reach their patronage. But, while she could scarcely crawl with her legs swollen and her family, because of their poverty, had neglected to have her taken there [Note: [Col. 1123D] Here the Ghent manuscript ends, followed by three blank paper leaves, evidently, as one must believe, substituted for leaves that had been torn out.], and while she was wasting away in extreme despair, night came and she gave herself over to sleep. She recognized Saints Landoaldus and Vinciana standing beside her in splendid garments with lighted candles.

On awakening, she perceived that the strength of her entire body had been restored and learned that the pain of her whole illness had departed. On the following day, already certain of the restoration of her sight and confident of her remaining health, she attempted on her own, with many other admirers, to visit the saints’ shrine; and she did not cease to offer thanksgiving as best she could.

On the following day—that is, the fourth day before the Kalends of June—a woman named Frethunara, herself also blind, went to the saints’ shrine in order to pray and seek healing. But while she was still on the road and had not yet arrived there, behold, she received her former health and rejoiced as she walked. [Col. 1124B]

9. Finally, on the following day, the holy day of Pentecost, which is the second day before the Kalends of June [Note: [Col. 1124D] An error had crept in: III Kalends had been written instead of II, although the Dominical Letter was then C. This is clear from what follows, where Thursday is joined with III Nonas of June; and a new error had been printed for July, although the writing had been completed on XIII Kalends of July.], a certain Theodoricus, whose whole body had been contracted for many years, obtained complete health in the presence of many truthful witnesses.

Then, on the third day before the Nones of July, the Thursday of that same week, a blind woman from the district of Brabant [Col. 1124C] called upon the saints for aid and prepared, as best she could, a light to bring to them. No delay occurred: she recovered the sight of her eyes. [Note: [Col. 1124D] The neighboring territory of Aalst is indicated, where the Brabantine region was then situated.]

Another woman from the same district suffered from excessive kidney pain and for nearly a year, as she herself confessed, had been unable to rise for the convenience of any task. When she learned that the saints’ relics had been brought there and understood that miracles were being performed through them, she vowed a candle in order to regain her health. She prayed that the saints might take pity on her in so great a pain. Immediately restored to her former health, she reverently offered the candle to the saints and also brought a girdle, returning immense thanks to God through the merits of the saints for the health she had received. [Col. 1124D]

# [LIFE OF SAINT URSMAR]

[Col. 1125]

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING OPUSCULUM

(From Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, vol. IV, p. 557.)

[Col. 1125]

I shall relate certain fragments from Herigerus, abbot of Lobbes, who published two books on the life of Saint Ursmar, the abbot, in verse at the beginning of the eleventh century; he also rendered in verse the deeds of Saint Landelinus, founder of the monastery of Lobbes. I received both of these works of Herigerus from the library of the celebrated monastery of Saint-Vanne at Verdun, through the kindness of the religious and learned Bartholomew Senoc, a lecturer in theology and my friend, who, although occupied with serious studies, does not cease to lend assistance to our work.

In the manuscript codex sent to me there is this inscription:

“IN THE NAME OF CHRIST BEGINS THE LIFE OF SAINT URSMAR, CONFESSOR AND BISHOP, HONORABLY COMPOSED IN HEXAMETER VERSE THROUGH THE INDUSTRY OF THE VENERABLE HERIERUS” [to be read: HERIGERUS], namely in two books, one on the virtues and the other on the miracles of Saint Ursmar. The first book begins as follows:

> First, with wondrous revolution, the highest heaven,
>
> The wisdom of the most high God, breathing upon all things, made.

After the second book, the same copy immediately continues, in the same kind of meter, with the *Life of Saint Landelinus*, beginning:

> The Unbegotten Father, creator of all things through the Word,
>
> And the Begotten One, reigning by his will and governing what has been fashioned.

Although this *Life* does not bear the author’s name, I am convinced that it is by Herigerus, both because of the similarity of its meter and because of the same etymology of the monastery of Crispinien which the author gives in both places, deriving it from the waters of a spring “curling” [*crispantibus*], as he supposes, after the saint had drawn it forth there.

Certainly, it is established from the continuation of the Chronicle of Lobbes, which appears in volume VI of the *Spicilegium*, that Herigerus published the *Life of Saint Ursmar* in verse and wrote many other works. The reason I have not reproduced both of these works of Herigerus in full is that, apart from certain unwelcome moral digressions, they contain nothing different from the Acts—either of Saint Landelinus, which we presented in the second century, or of Saint Ursmar, which we present in this third century—except for certain verses that we give here.

[Col. 1125]

# LIFE OF SAINT URSMAR, ABBOT

(Fragment from Book I)

(From Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, Century III, Part I, p. 608.)

[Col. 1125A]

> But now let the remaining disciples of Christ be mentioned,
>
> Who were splendid lights of life to the world
>
> And filled all things everywhere with their teaching.
>
> To you, Rome, are sent two lofty columns:
>
> Peter together with Paul, upon whose triumph
>
> You extend the citadel of primacy, founded four-square throughout the world.
>
> From these, their distinguished followers,
>
> We have taken eminent teachers who came to us from there.
>
> Gaul, then trusting in Dionysius of Paris,
>
> Received the woman of the divine word.
>
> And Clement, sent to the city of the Mediomatrici,
>
> Teaches the neighboring people to believe in Christ alone.
>
> Three are sent to Trier, faithful in heart,
>
> To teach the people, renewed by baptism,
>
> To believe in the one Lord, three in persons
>
> But one in divinity:
>
> Eucharius, Martinus, and Valerius, namely.
>
> Agrippinus believes, and Tungri becomes a disciple of the faith.
>
> Strong champions fight through the power of Christ,
>

# LETTER OF HERIGERUS, ABBOT OF LOBBES, TO A CERTAIN MONK HUGO

[Note: [Col. 1129C] Sigebert mentions this letter in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. When reviewing Herigerus’ writings, he says: “He wrote a letter to Hugo concerning certain questions.”]

He responds to questions proposed to him concerning the disagreement that arises between Dionysius and Bede, and in turn proposes to Hugo other difficulties for him to unravel.

(From D. Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum* I, 112, from a manuscript of Lobbes written in the author’s time.)

[Col. 1129A] Brother Hugh, if you are asked whom you ought rather to believe when they disagree—the Gospel or Dionysius—I do not doubt that you will answer, “The Gospel.” Yet, while the truth of the Gospel remains constant, Dionysius is found to disagree with it in many respects.

The truth of the Gospel states that Christ was baptized in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, beginning his ministry when he was about thirty years old. According to the chronicles of Eusebius, and likewise of Jerome—who would not have translated it so had he not approved it—he came to his Passion in the eighteenth year of Tiberius, which could have been the thirty-third year of his Incarnation.

Again, the truth of the Gospel states that he celebrated the lawful Passover on the fourteenth day of the moon, that is, on Thursday, neither anticipating nor postponing it; that on Friday, namely the fifteenth day of the moon, he ascended the cross; that on the Sabbath, the sixteenth day of the moon, he rested in the tomb; and that on the Lord’s Day, the seventeenth day of the moon, he rose again.

Therefore, if you open Dionysius’s cycle and find that the year of his Incarnation was the thirty-second, thirty-third, or thirty-fourth—years which follow the great cycle of the return, 564, 565, or 566—give thanks to God, as Bede commands, though he said this ironically.

I have set down three possible years because some have thought that he suffered in the thirty-second year, others in the thirty-third, and others in the thirty-fourth; Bede seems more inclined toward the latter view. According to the truth of the Gospel, the Revelation of John, and the prophecy of Daniel, he preached for three and a half years. Some have regarded the first year of his preaching as the thirtieth year of his birth, so that he began his preaching immediately after his baptism and fast.

[Col. 1129C] We know, however, that the evangelist John, after returning from exile, wrote not only to refute the heresies that had arisen in his absence, but also because, when he read the other evangelists, he found that they had said much about Christ’s miracles but little about his divinity, and that they had omitted certain more remarkable matters: the wedding at Cana of Galilee, Nicodemus, the man born blind, the sick man at the pool, the woman at the well, Lazarus raised from the dead, the washing of the feet, and many other things. What they had related, moreover, they had set down confusedly and out of order—that is, placing earlier events later and later events earlier.

[Col. 1130A] Accordingly, John undertook to distinguish the number of years of Christ’s preaching by the feast-days of Passover, and chose to begin most beautifully with the very days themselves:

“The Jews sent from Jerusalem” (John 1:19);  
“On the next day John saw Jesus coming toward him” (ibid. 29);  
“On the next day John was standing, and two of his disciples” (ibid. 35);  
“On the third day there was a wedding at Cana of Galilee” (John 2).

Thus, in the first year of his preaching, when he was in Jerusalem for Passover, he drove the sellers and buyers from the temple. In the second year, on the feast of Passover, he healed the sick man at the pool. In the third year, after the miracle of the five loaves, “the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was near.” In the fourth year, six days before Passover, he came to Bethany, where he raised Lazarus from the dead and also suffered.

For if he suffered in the eighteenth year of Tiberius, which perhaps extended halfway beyond his three years of preaching, then the first year of his preaching was the fifteenth year of Tiberius, in which he was also baptized. But perhaps, according to Bede’s reckoning, the beginning of the nineteenth year of Tiberius Caesar could have been the fourth year of his preaching, which was also the year of his Passion—that is, the thirty-fourth year of his Incarnation—the preceding three years being the thirty-first, thirty-second, and thirty-third.

Whether, therefore, according to Dionysius’s cycle, he suffered in the thirty-third or the thirty-fourth year from his Incarnation, the account does not agree in any way with the truth of the Gospel. For in the thirty-fourth year the moon at Passover falls not on the seventeenth day, as stated, but on the twenty-first; nor does the fourteenth day of the moon fall on Thursday, but on the Lord’s Day.

His Passion would therefore occur neither on Friday nor on the tenth day before the Kalends of April according to the Greeks, nor on the eighth day before the Kalends according to the Latins. Likewise, his Resurrection would occur neither on the eighth day before the Kalends of April according to the Greeks, nor on the sixth day before the Kalends according to the Latins.

How inappropriate it is, moreover, to place his Passion or Resurrection in the thirty-third year from his Incarnation will become clear, since all these events fall in April rather than in March.

The Gospel prescribes, and we know, that John the Baptist was announced at the autumnal equinox. In the sixth month, that is, in March, after half a year, Christ was announced on the same Kalends; on that day he was conceived and on that day he suffered, according to the saying: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” (Exodus 23:19). That is: you shall not kill Christ on the day on which he was conceived. Although God forbade this, he nevertheless foresaw that the Jews would not obey, just as he forbade Adam the tree of the knowledge of good and evil while foreseeing that Adam would not observe the command. For this reason the Psalmist says: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin” (Psalm 31:2).

O how dangerous it is to hear such things announced beforehand either by God or by some holy man! Since the Spirit of prophecy is in him, it rarely happens that what he forbids does not come to pass. When the sick man at the pool had been healed, Christ sorrowfully warned him: “Go now, and do not sin, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14). Something worse did indeed happen to him when he struck Christ in the face during the Passion.

These matters being firmly established in truth, it is clear that Christ was both conceived and suffered on one and the same day.

Concerning the Calendar, and the years of the Lord’s Incarnation, there is much debate among chronographers because of ignorance about the times. For how could Abbot Dionysius, reckoning backward from his own time through the years of the emperors as far as the forty-second year of Augustus Caesar—which, according to Eusebius’s chronicles, was the first year of Christ’s birth—know with certainty how many emperors reigned for complete years, how many had additional months or days, and how long the interregnums lasted—that is, how much time elapsed between the death of one ruler and the installation of another?

The Greeks, however, should be followed more readily: they have the authority of the Council of Nicaea and of blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, and were both neighbors of the East and close in time to the apostolic men. For, as the greatest orator says, the closer antiquity was to its origin and divine ancestry, the better it perceived what was true.

The Greeks therefore reckon eight years fewer from the Incarnation of the Lord than Dionysius’s cycle. According to them, the first year from the Lord’s Incarnation is the ninth year in Dionysius’s cycle. That year is the thirty-fourth year, which is the forty-second year in Dionysius’s cycle. It has seven concurrent days, an epact of fourteen, and its term falls on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April—namely, Thursday—when the Supper took place and the celebration of Passover began in the evening, as the Lord says: “On the fourteenth day, toward evening, is the Lord’s Passover; and on the fifteenth you shall celebrate the solemnity under the moon,” when he also suffered—that is, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April.

The Sabbath, when he rested in the tomb, fell on the sixteenth day of the moon, the ninth day before the Kalends of April; and the Lord’s Day of the Resurrection fell on the seventeenth day of the moon, the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

Excellent indeed! For in the questions discussed by King Ptolemy with the Seventy Interpreters concerning the Book of Exodus, it was discovered that the equinoxes and solstices should be marked, also according to the reckoning of the hours, on the twelfth day before the Kalends rather than on the eighth.

When Constantine Augustus was baptized in the eighteenth year of his reign, a dispute arose among the newly built or restored Eastern churches—not only concerning the rivalry between Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, and his presbyter Arius, but also concerning the celebration of Passover, which the Easterners observed earlier than the Jews themselves.

The Jews, following lunar years, celebrate in certain embolismic years one month before us, and do so before the equinox. But this error is easily dispelled from Bede’s book *On Times*.

The Easterners, who boasted that they followed the successors of the apostles but had not thoroughly investigated the concordance of solar and lunar years, therefore limped on both feet. For this reason, at the request of Pope Sylvester, the emperor sent Hosius, bishop of Córdoba, to correct both matters and establish peace among the Alexandrians; but he returned without effecting anything.

Accordingly, at Sylvester’s request and by Constantine’s command, a synod was convened at Nicaea. It lasted two months. There the error of Arius was easily detected and was quickly condemned.

But difficult and almost inextricable questions concerning the observance of Passover were debated for a long time. Finally, after the questions of King Ptolemy with the Seventy Interpreters had been read out, and the fourteen paschal moons had likewise been confirmed according to Pachomius, it was decreed that whoever thereafter celebrated Passover with the Jews—that is, before the equinox—would be anathema.

Yet among Pachomius’s fourteen moons one finds dates before the equinox, which was thought to fall on the eighth day before the Kalends of April: the fourteenth paschal moon on the fifth day, that is, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April; or on the fourth day, the eleventh day before the Kalends, where both the term and sometimes the solemnity itself are found; or on the third day, the tenth day before the Kalends, where only the solemnity occurs; or on the preceding day, the ninth day before the Kalends, where both occur; or on the very day of the eighth day before the Kalends, where the same date is repeatedly recorded.

Thus one must either submit to anathema or celebrate Passover as was decreed at the Council of Nicaea.

It was therefore concluded, also on the basis of Egyptian science—for the Egyptians are more experienced in the art of calculation, since they have never had rain or clouds—that, according to the reckoning of the hours, the spring equinox falls on the twelfth day before the Kalends.

And how fittingly and appropriately this is so! For on the fourth day of the week, when the stars were created, at that very moment, as the sun and moon divided the heavenly sphere, with the sun possessing Aries and the moon Libra, it became clear that the spring equinox had fallen on the twelfth day before the Kalends.

Thus on the thirteenth day before the Kalends, Tuesday, the dry land appeared; on the fourteenth day before the Kalends, Monday, the firmament was made; and on the fifteenth day before the Kalends, Sunday, the first day of the world and the sun’s entry into Aries were established.

Since these matters are thus firmly grounded in truth, on Thursday, the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, the fish and birds were created; and on Friday, the tenth day before the Kalends of April, man was made, and Eve was brought forth from his side.

Where and when could man have been more authoritatively and more holily redeemed through Christ’s cross, and the Church baptized from the blood flowing from Christ’s side, than on that very day and under that same Calendar date?

And just as God rested from his works on the Sabbath, the ninth day before the Kalends of April, so Christ rested in the tomb. The Lord’s Day of his Resurrection followed, the eighth day before the Kalends of April, which is inscribed not only as the first day but also as the octave.

That Passover occurred after the equinox, in the third week, and on the Lord’s Day, as the angel communicated through the shepherd to Pope Victor of Rome, can easily be found in Bede’s book *On Times*, in the discussion of their observance.

For on whatever day after the Sabbath—that is, on the first day of the Sabbath, now called the Lord’s Day; or on the second, third, fourth, or fifth day of the Sabbath—the fourteenth day of the moon occurred, the Jews held Passover on that same day after evening had come and the fifteenth moon had begun. They extended it until the Sabbath for however many days remained, and sometimes celebrated Passover five days before the Sabbath, sometimes four, and so forth; sometimes only one or two days before the Sabbath, as happened at the Lord’s Passion.

Then, as Thursday evening came and the fifteenth moon began, they treated that night and the following day as Passover, as the evangelist says: “It was Passover, and the feast of Unleavened Bread was two days away” (Mark 14:1).

The following Sabbath, both on its own account and because of the paschal solemnity, was called, as it were, a double feast, “the Sabbath of Sabbaths.”

The distinction between Passover and Unleavened Bread—or whether the terms are used indifferently, as in another evangelist: “On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lamb was customarily sacrificed” (Matthew 26:17)—and how many days before us, or how many days together with us, the Jews celebrate Passover, can easily be found in Bede.

It is therefore clear that the Easterners celebrated earlier than the Jews themselves. Although the Jews sometimes erred concerning the equinox, they nevertheless followed the fourteenth moon.

The Easterners, however, entirely ignorant of the lunar cycle, while fixing the equinox on the eighth day before the Kalends of April—as did many of our own people, including Augustine, Fulgentius, John Chrysostom, and Pliny himself, who also assigned Christ’s conception and Passion to that day—had decreed that Passover should be celebrated on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, whichever day of the week it might be, just as they placed the Nativity of the Lord on the eighth day before the Kalends of January.

Pope Victor of Rome, warned by an angel through the shepherd, decreed that Passover should be postponed to the Lord’s Day, whatever day of the week the sixth day before the Kalends of April might fall upon.

His decision concerning Sunday was sound: the day on which the Lord rose should never be changed, and Passover should always be celebrated after the equinox. But whether it should be after the fourteenth day—that is, in the third week of this world—was either entirely unknown or not read until the Council of Nicaea fixed the equinox on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April and ordered that the paschal days thereafter be observed according to Pachomius’s fourteen moons.

This must be known with complete certainty: if the equinoxes and solstices had been fixed at the twelfth day before the Kalends, as they now are, the conceptions and births of blessed John and of Christ himself would never have been assigned to the eighth day before the Kalends, but rather to the twelfth.

Those who thought that the equinoxes fell on the eighth day before the Kalends assigned those same feasts there, on account of what John said: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

[Col. 1134A] But the truth is to be learned with the Greeks. The custom of the churches, if it is not contrary to the faith, must in no way be changed; nor should those who placed the date on the eighth day before the Kalends be entirely repudiated. Yet with the Greeks and Egyptians we should accept the twelfth-day reckoning.

This statement is highly effective against the heresy that has recently arisen, which our lord Gerbert derives from the Council of Toledo. Since there are five days from the twelfth day before the Kalends to the eighth, if the Lord’s Day of Passover, Holy Saturday, Good Friday, or the Lord’s Supper prevents the Annunciation of blessed Mary, the Mother, from being celebrated on any of those five days, it may be anticipated; and if you ask, you will be able to obtain our written ruling concerning this matter.

These matters, dearest brother, I have set down briefly and in summary because, hindered by illness and with my eyesight now growing dim, I could not write them out personally. I have paid less attention to elegant urbanity, knowing that those who wrote before us about the arts labored chiefly to make themselves understood and entirely neglected eloquence.

In return for this exchange, however, I wish to ask a favor: since there are many things in the divine Scriptures that seem to offend our understanding, may they, through your prayers and your traversing the fields of Scripture, become clearer.

First: how I may discern the great discrepancy found in Bede’s homily for Palm Sunday.

“‘The paschal lamb,’ he says, ‘by whose sacrifice the people of Israel were freed from Egyptian servitude, was ordered to be sacrificed five days before Passover, that is, on the evening of the fourteenth day of the moon. It signified him who was to redeem us by his blood five days before Passover and who, on this very day, was led into the temple of the Lord amid the great joy and praise of the peoples who went before and followed him.’

Second: concerning the decretal letters of James and Clement, sent to one another, in which Clement speaks of blessed Peter as though he had already suffered. It is therefore clear that Clement did not write them while Peter was alive. It is also clear that James died eight years before Peter’s Passion. After the Passion of blessed Peter, Linus held office for twelve years and Anacletus for the same period; they were Clement’s collaborators, and Clement truly succeeded Peter. Much less, therefore, could James have replied during their time. After their deaths, when Clement alone presided over the Roman Church for nine years, it is even less credible that he could have written a reply, since thirty-two years had elapsed from James’s Passion.

Third: concerning our Treveran saints Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus, who are said to have been sent by the apostle Peter. A place in the district of Elisatium named Eligia agrees with their history; but from the Passion of blessed Peter, which occurred in the thirteenth year of Nero—if he perhaps sent Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus to Trier several years before his Passion—there are reckoned 263 years to the twenty-fifth year of Constantine, when Saint Sylvester died. By Sylvester’s command the synod at Arles was held, where Saint Maternus, bishop of Cologne, is recorded as having taken part, together with Maurinus, his archdeacon; Saint Agricius, bishop of Trier, was also present.

Fourth: how Decius, who ruled for only one year or a little more and martyred Pope Cornelius, could have killed Pope Xystus together with his archdeacon Laurence, when Stephen and Lucius, Xystus’s predecessors, were martyred by Decius’s successors, Gallus and Volusian, or Valerian and Gallienus.

Fifth: concerning Constantine Augustus, who is said to have been baptized by Eusebius of Nicomedia according to the Arian doctrine. Heretics say that he wished to postpone his baptism until he could be baptized in the Jordan, but that death overtook him at Nicomedia and he was newly baptized there by the Arian Eusebius. The Greek historical account, however, is more credible. It says that the story of his being born of a concubine and rebaptized was fabricated by the heretics out of envy of the Christians, since the baptistery in which he was baptized by Sylvester can still be seen at Rome, and his *pragmatic decree* contains the whole truth.

Sixth: concerning the holy cross, which some think was not discovered until after Constantine’s conversion and in the time of Saint Sylvester. But Melchiades preceded Sylvester, and Eusebius preceded Melchiades; Eusebius ordered that the anniversary of its discovery be observed in his decretals, since it had been discovered in his own time, on the fifth day before the Nones of May.

Seventh: concerning the shameful death of Arius, which, according to ecclesiastical history, occurred in the time of Constantius, Constantine’s son. It could not have occurred under Alexander, his bishop. For Alexander’s death preceded Constantine’s by eight years. Athanasius, who succeeded Alexander, endured his first exile at Trier by order of Constantine, not Constantius, when he attended the Council of Cologne together with Maximinus, bishop of Trier, Servatius, bishop of Tongeren, and many others; there Ephrata, bishop of that same city, was condemned.”

[Note: [Col. 1135B] I do not think this letter is complete. Herigerus replies in it to questions put to him by Hugh in a letter, of which I possess only the following fragment:

“To the lord abbot H., brother Hugh.

Since Bede and Dionysius seem to differ in their works, a matter that sometimes confuses many people, we ask that it be corrected by your examination. For Bede, who in chapter 47, entitled *Concerning the Years of the Lord’s Incarnation*, authoritatively—indeed, evangelically—places the fifteenth lunar day on the eighth day before the Kalends of April ...” [Col. 1136B]]

# A.D. 1008. Notger, Bishop of Liège

[Col. 1135]

## Historical Notice

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. III, p. 845.)

[Col. 1135C] Notger, or Notker, as he is commonly called in charters, was Alemannic by birth and born of noble parents in Swabia. He was first provost of the monastery of Saint Gall, as the Saxon Chronicle relates. There he advanced so far in learning and piety that he deserved to be placed over the brothers. He was then summoned by Odilo, abbot of Stavelot, to educate his monks, as Bartholomew Fisen testifies. Finally, after Heraclius had been taken from this life, Notger was appointed in his place and consecrated by Saint Gereon, bishop of Cologne, in 974.

He was a man of extraordinary piety, singular learning for those times, supreme wisdom in action, remarkable shrewdness in handling affairs, and almost boundless benevolence and generosity toward everyone.

His first concern was to restore the people to their proper duty, judging that, unless restrained, they would soon infect the whole commonwealth with their poison. As soon as he took possession of his office, he summoned those who had shamelessly broken into the entire household of Heraclius; after investigating the case, he ordered the condemned to suffer their penalties.

He captured the fortress of Caprimont, situated less than two miles from the city, difficult of access, fortified with strong walls and towers, until then unconquered and even thought unconquerable, looming over Liège and serving as a den of brigands and tyrants of the district. He took it by a reprehensible and daring stratagem and utterly demolished it, with such ardor on the part of his men that no trace at all remained of the former fortification.

This destruction increased the prosperity of Liège and Aachen. After the basilica of the Mother of God had been demolished, he joined the twelve priests who served the Lord there, together with all their revenues, to the collegiate church at Aachen; adding revenues from his own resources, he established ten more priests. He transferred the collegiate church of canons dedicated to Saint Caprasius, situated on the same mountain, to Saint Paul’s at Liège.

[Col. 1136D] No force could destroy the third church of Saint John the Evangelist until he had vowed to build a similar one in the city; he fulfilled this vow in 981. Hence these verses were composed:

[Col. 1137A]

“Through me Liège grows rich; Mount Caprasius is stripped bare.  
Here one falls, there one rises; this remains, while that will never rise again.”

He then surrounded the city with a wall and adorned it with buildings. He renewed from the foundations and enlarged the greater church, which was leaning toward collapse because of age and the weakness of its construction, and decorated it with the richest ornaments. He newly built the cloister, houses, workshops, and episcopal palace; he erected many other churches throughout the city; and, by founding as many strongly fortified citadels as there were churches, he made the city completely secure against its enemies. Hence these verses:

“Liège, binding laws to itself together with its prelates,  
owes Notger to Christ, and all else to Notger.”

Nor did the bishop’s generosity remain within the city. It extended outward, and he not only adorned his diocese far and wide but also fortified it.

“Notger founded the church of Fosses,” says Giles, “and surrounded it for its defense with a wall and very strong towers.” He founded the city of Thuin, or Thudinium, and fortified it with solid works in a naturally strong location, steep on almost every side. He restored Mechelen, which had been devastated by the Northmen, and founded a college of twelve canons, adding the dignity of a provost. Finally, he acquired the county of Huy, which Ansfrid granted to Saint Lambert.

Notger cared not only for the temporal affairs of his church but also, and especially, for its spiritual welfare. He preached by example and by word. Giles says of him in chapter 57:

“He was gentle toward the poor and terrifying to proud rich men; mild and meek toward all good people, feared by the wicked and malicious; venerable to the powerful, beloved by those of moderate rank, admirable to the wise; toward the unlearned, most merciful in instruction; a staff of support for the old and weak; an earnest corrector of the young and adolescents. Prudent in counsel, circumspect in action, eloquent in speech, disciplined in silence.”

His eloquence was extraordinary. By it he persuaded people of everything right and honorable, attacked everything vicious and disgraceful, and vigorously overthrew heresies, though no one has recorded what those heresies were. He struck rebels against the divine word with anathema, never in vain, as the authors note.

Since the chief hope of the Church rests in the young, it is astonishing how carefully and ardently he labored for their education. He sought out teachers everywhere who were distinguished by knowledge of letters, diligence, and integrity of character. By the deeds and exhortations of teachers and students he kindled their spirits; he often discussed and settled difficult theological questions with them. He instructed the students by proposing subjects suited to each one’s capacity and by explaining somewhat obscure matters.

He could scarcely be drawn away from them, so much so that, while traveling on the road, as Anselm says, he carried schools and schoolmen about with him, together with his entire collection of books and a most learned provost.

This was a bishop’s care, crowned with marvelous fruits. Through this kind of discipline all the clergy of so great a diocese became more learned, and not a few emerged so distinguished in religion and wisdom that they spread piety and knowledge far and wide. Among these Anselm lists Otbert, Hubold, Durand, Wazo, Rothard, Erluin, and others, who either brought luster to various churches by teaching or governed them as bishops.

He also favored monks everywhere. He supported the monks of Gembloux so greatly that they elected him as their father and lord (*Anselm*, p. 206); thus, when imperial authority intervened, the abbey of Gembloux passed to the Church of Liège. He restored Fulcuin to Lobbes, with considerable benefit to monastic affairs, and after Fulcuin’s death appointed Heriger, a man renowned both for piety and learning, in his place.

His wisdom proved highly useful to the commonwealth and to imperial dignity. He was very dear to Otto II and was almost always among his counselors. After Otto’s death, Otto III succeeded him at the age of eleven. While the boy was maturing into kingship, the princes of Germany chose Notger as his tutor.

He assisted Henry, Otto’s successor, who became famous for his continence in marriage, in many matters and especially in the war against Baldwin, count of Flanders. When the emperor was unsuccessfully besieging Valenciennes, which Baldwin had occupied, Notger was summoned to give counsel and assistance. Drawing on his long experience of affairs, he advised that war be carried into Flanders. Henry followed his counsel and marched into Flanders, devastating everything. He besieged Ghent with such success that Baldwin sought peace, restored Valenciennes, and returned to his allegiance and duty.

It is therefore hardly surprising that he received many benefits from these emperors. In a charter, the emperor Otto II ordered that everything donated to the Church of Liège by Pepin, Charles the Great, Louis, and the other princes down to his own time be considered valid—specifically Huy, Fosses, Lobbes, Tongeren, and Mechelen.

The charter is reported as dated on the eighth day before the Ides of January, in the year 981 of the Lord’s Incarnation according to the modern reckoning, the nineteenth year of Otto II’s reign, the thirteenth year of his empire, and the sixth indiction. But the scribes erred in the chronological figures; the reading should be the year 990, indiction eight.

Notger obtained a similar charter from Otto III, who, in addition to the places already listed, transferred the county of Brunengerus, Maastricht, and the abbey of Gembloux into the jurisdiction of Liège. It is said to have been issued in 994.

Finally, in 1006, he obtained from Henry, Otto’s successor, an order confirming by his authority whatever the Church of Liège possessed through the beneficence of earlier kings.

He extended charity and beneficence even to the dead. When Saint Odilo had instituted a commemoration of the dead throughout the entire congregation of Cluny, Notger eagerly adopted the institution and, according to his tradition, ordered it to be observed in his own diocese.

When asked to have what he knew of the sanctity and miracles of Landoald and Amantius committed to writing, he ordered Heriger, a monk of Lobbes, to carry out the task. Heriger prefaced his work with a letter written in Notger’s name and addressed to Womar, the venerable father in Christ, and to the brothers of Ghent. As a result, Adalbero, archbishop of Reims, allowed the relics of those saints to be displayed and established their public veneration.

[Col. 1139A] In 995 he sat in the Council of Mouzon on the fourth day before the Nones of June, where the case was discussed of Arnulf, deposed from the see of Reims, and Gerbert, appointed in his place. See volume IX of Labbe’s councils.

In the same year he arranged for Erluin, archdeacon of the Church of Liège, to be promoted in place of the deceased Rothard, bishop of Cambrai, through the agency of Mathilda, daughter of Otto and abbess of Quedlinburg.

He was also present at the Synod of Frankfurt in 1006, where Saint Henry the emperor petitioned for the establishment of Bamberg as an episcopal church. In 1007, at Notger’s request, Henry, king of Germany, conferred a benefit on the college of noble canonesses at Thorn (*Miracula Notkeri*, chapter 78).

Finally, full of years, merits, and glory, after completing thirty-six years in government, he departed to Christ on the fourth day before the Ides of April in the year 1007—or 1008, says Mabillon (*Annals*, vol. IV, p. 201). He bases this on the authority of the author of the *Life of Saint Theodoric of Andagin*, or Saint Hubert, abbot, who was Notger’s contemporary and records his birth as follows:

“He was born in the year 1007 of the Lord’s Incarnation, when Henry was emperor among the Romans and Germans, in the sixth year after he had succeeded the younger Otto, while Notger, a man of great holiness and prudence, presided over the see of Liège, after he had been ordained bishop in the thirty-seventh year, and so forth.”

Another manuscript adds: “One year before he departed this life.”

This is also confirmed by the fact that the whole year 1007 appears to have elapsed. For Saint Henry the emperor, at Notger’s petition, conferred a benefit on the college at Thorn by a decree issued on the second day before the Nones of June. Then, in that same year, he subscribed to the establishment of the bishopric of Bamberg on the Kalends of November, as may be seen in Labbe, volume IX, column 785. He therefore cannot be said to have died before April of the following year.

Finally, this is confirmed by the authority of Lambert of Schafnaburg, who assigns Notger’s death to this year, as does the *Chronicle of Liège* (Labbe, *Bibliotheca manuscripta*, vol. I, p. 337).

Since what is possessed with love cannot be lost without grief, all the orders of the entire diocese lamented their bereavement. In the city, each collegiate body of canons took a separate day to mourn him as the father of his country. At last he was buried in the Church of Saint John, as he had directed in his will, beside the altar of Saint Hilary.

Besides the Anselm and Giles already mentioned, Alberic discusses him in his *Chronicle*. The *Chronicle of Centula*, book III, chapter 30, also mentions him. Some maintain that he composed the *Life of Saint Remaclus* at the request of Warinfrid, abbot of Stavelot. In *Marca Hispanica*, p. 994, Notger is reported to have subscribed the letter of Pope Benedict VIII concerning the Church of Urgell; this cannot stand.

[Col. 1139]

## Literary Notice

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latinitatis*, vol. V, p. 143.)

[Col. 1139C] Notger, Notheger, or Notker, born in Swabia, forty-sixth bishop of Liège from 972 to 1008, and favored by the emperor Otto III, to whom he was related, declares in a letter to Warinfrid, abbot of Stavelot, prefixed to the *Life of Saint Remaclus* in Surius under September 3, and to the *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren, Maastricht, and Liège* prefixed by Chapeaville, that he had collected, down to his own time, not only the periods and deeds of this Remaclus but also those of the other bishops of his see, gathering whatever he could from every source.

Those deeds of the first twenty-seven bishops, however, were published not under Notger’s name but under that of Heriger, abbot of Lobbes, by John Chapeaville in volume I of his *Collection concerning the Bishops of Liège* (1612, quarto), and Sigebert attributes them to Heriger as author in chapter 138.

Nevertheless, it seems likely that this was not a different work, but one undertaken by Notger and completed through the combined efforts of Heriger, Notger’s friend, and others, as Oudinus reasonably conjectures (vol. II, p. 484).

In the *Life of Saint Remaclus* in Surius and in Chapeaville, volume I, pp. 82 and following, many passages are identical word for word. Surius, under September 3, presents under Notger’s name both the *Life of Saint Remaclus*, the twenty-seventh bishop of Liège from 650 to 653, and two books concerning his miracles.

In the second of these books, the burning of the monastery of Stavelot by the Danes in 883 is described, and the author testifies that he was dismayed by the news: “And behold, the most grievous report is brought to us,” and so forth. These words therefore belong to an older author, but this does not mean that one should posit an elder Notger as the author of these books.

The *Life of Saint Landoald*, archpriest of the seventh century, and of Rotgan and his companions—Amantius the deacon, Adrian the martyr, Julian, Vinciana, and Adeltrudis—in two books, was written at Notger’s command by the same Heriger and consequently attributed to Notger as author; his letter, written in 980 to Womar, abbot of Ghent, is prefixed to it.

The work appears in Surius under March 19, and with Henschenius’s notes in the *Acts of the Saints*, volume III for March, pp. 35 and 41. The same *Acts* offer, under Notger’s name, the *Life of Saint Hadelin the priest*, who lived in Belgium around 690, in volume I for February 3, pp. 372 and 376. See also Mabillon, *Second Century of the Benedictines*, p. 1013.

[Col. 1141]

## Deeds of the Bishops of Liège

(See above, under Heriger.)

[Col. 1141]

## Life of Saint Hadalin, Confessor and Founder of the Monastery of Celle near Dinant on the Meuse

By Notger, bishop of Liège, as is understood from section 6.

(In Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. II, p. 1013; from a manuscript of the monastery of Andain and from Bolland.) (G)

[Col. 1141A] 1. Blessed Hadalin was born in the territory of Aquitaine, sprung from a noble lineage. In tender youth he was advanced in moral integrity, surpassing the years of childhood and always desiring to belong to the company of the elders of Solomon. As he daily strove to extend himself toward greater things, he also attempted to imitate the example of that famous patriarch to whom the Lord said, “Go out from your land” (Gen. XII, 1), and so forth. He had long since heard that many others had undertaken this very thing, and he did not wish to appear unequal to them according to his ability. Thus Saints Agricius, Maximinus, and Paulinus, exiles from that same homeland, had come to our land, that is, to the land of the Franks. Later elevated to the archiepiscopal dignity of the see of Trier, they died there and, through miracles attesting that they lived with the Lord, made this manifest. Likewise blessed Remaclus, the beneficent and God-worthy bishop of the Tungri, Goar, the comforter of those crossing the Rhine near his monastery, and many others from that same region are known to have happily visited our territories. [Note: [Col. 1141C] We have omitted here much material inserted from the Life of Saint Remaclus, to be repeated from his Acts of the year 664.]

2. When blessed Hadalin saw the man whom he loved with such extraordinary affection exalted by God and by men and raised to the episcopal chair, it is beyond our capacity to unfold how greatly his heart and tongue were filled with exultation. [Note: [Col. 1141C] From this Bollandus concludes that Hadalin attached himself to Remaclus before Stavelot was founded, since Remaclus, already a bishop, laid the foundations of that monastery.] What his merit and unblemished religion were in that administration, and how he built the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy through pious labor, anyone who wishes may find in the book of his Life. But after he had gathered an observance of servants of God in those monasteries and had also arranged, for the most part, dwellings suited to the practice of religion, he obtained, with God’s favor, the opportunity he had always desired: solitude for a more remote way of life. At last, though with the greatest difficulty, he obtained from the king that another should succeed him and that he might be permitted to go to the desert he had long desired, where, removed from worldly cares, he might more freely yearn for heavenly things. He presented the life of Saint Theodard as sufficiently acceptable to the king and nobles, and by name designated him to take his place after him and be appointed as his successor in the episcopal chair. Thus, having blessed the people, Remaclus set out upon the long-appointed road with blessed Hadalin accompanying him. [Note: [Col. 1142C] We stated in the Acts of Saint Remaclus that the withdrawal of Saint Remaclus with Hadalin took place about the year 660.]

3. But when the Lord was preparing to place the radiance of blessed Hadalin’s holiness upon a lampstand (Matt. V, 15) for public recognition, it happened, while they were traveling, that both lay down to rest. While the saint in question slept and the other—namely, the kindly Remaclus—kept watch, he saw a ray of sunlight that had fallen upon the sleeper’s face being covered by an angelic shade. When he awoke, the blessed bishop said to him: “Dearest brother, if you recognize any vision now shown to you in sleep, do not delay to tell me, most beloved.” But the other at first resisted with downcast face; then, obeying the voice of the one commanding him, he said:
