“I had decided, most blessed Father, to conceal for the present what I had seen and, after several days had passed, to disclose it with humble devotion, face bowed low. But since it is not permissible to refuse anything to your command: I saw, I say, while I rested in gentle sleep, a dove descend from heaven upon me, unworthy as I am, with wings spread out (John I, 32), and fly around my eyes for a little while. Then it remained above my head. I confess that I do not know what good this omen signifies.”

But blessed Bishop Remaclus, looking upon him with an even cheerful countenance, said:

“O Hadalin, your dignity surpasses my lowliness, and I confess myself unworthy of such a companion, whose service I saw overshadowed by an angelic ministry. ‘The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night,’ says the Psalmist (Ps. CXX, 6), because you shall not surpass the Church—neither in Christ nor in the Church enlightened through him. The dove signifies the Holy Spirit, who rested upon the Lord at his baptism in the river Jordan and anointed him with the oil of gladness above his companions (Ps. XLIV, 8). He himself has illumined your heart with the grace of the gentlest devotion and has appointed you perpetually to his service.”

These and similar words of sacred instruction, Hadalin, chosen by God, heard with the ear of his heart, and thereafter he considered girding himself for greater works of virtue.

4. Again the kindly Bishop Remaclus, foreseeing the future, said to him: “Hasten, then, my son; depart elsewhere as swiftly as possible, following Christ as your guide. Seek out the valley adjoining the forest beside the river which the inhabitants call the Letia [Note: [Col. 1143D] The Letia or Laetia, commonly called the Lesch or Les, rises in the Ardennes not far from Bouillon. There it is swallowed up by the earth for two leagues, then emerges from a rock in the district of Han and joins the Meuse half a league above the town of Dinant. From that town the village called Celles—named after Saint Hadalin’s monastery built there—is a journey of an hour and a half. In the course of time the monks yielded the place to canons; they too, harassed by the oppression of the lords of Celles, were transferred to Visé, as we shall say below. At present a church and the title of a provostship remain at Celles; but on the slope of a hill, not far from the principal church, there is another small building where Hadalin first constructed a cell and lived the eremitical life, and where his tomb is seen. This account is taken largely from Bollandus, who rightly rebukes the error of Philip Ferrarius, who in his general catalogue confused the monastery of Laetias, Lutosas, and the Cella of Saint Gislenus in Hainaut, as well as the town of Lessines in Flanders, with Hadalin’s Celles on the river Letia, under 3 February.] Go to the place called ‘Between Four Mountains,’ inquire for it, and there, with God as your fellow inhabitant, build for yourself a dwelling and an oratory, where, with angels as your leaders, you may worthily serve the Lord Christ.”

He received these predictions with a cheerful mind and tried to throw himself at the bishop’s feet. But the latter raised him with kindly encouragement and advised him to go to the place with a few companions and, as time went on, to return frequently to him for a visit. Having therefore obtained the desired blessing, he went forth in eagerness to investigate the matter and reached the house of a man named Beo. With difficulty, through the assistance of Beo’s wife, he obtained lodging and, while staying there, began to inquire.

The saint at last found the place mentioned above. Having obtained a gentle guide, he discovered the site, gave thanks to God, and sang, “Our help is in the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXXIII, 8). Thereafter he built a dwelling and completed a little oratory, as far as the circumstances of that time allowed. There he devoted and surrendered himself entirely to the service of Christ and the protection of the angels.

Thus, in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness, in labors and various anxieties, hardships, and afflictions, the athlete of God lived soberly, quietly, and piously for the Lord, not for the world. There he awaited the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ (Tit. II, 12). Chastising his own body daily and subjecting it to the service of his soul, he continually assigned his very soul to heavenly vigils. By daily sacrificing on the altar of his heart the pleasing offering of his former deeds, he enriched the king seated at his banquet with the nard of wondrous fragrance (Song I, 11).

5. Hearing of the fame of the holiness and holy way of life of his teacher, blessed Remaclus, in the aforementioned monastery of Stavelot—where people strove to flock to him from every direction like bees to their hives; where some added themselves to the service of the Almighty and submitted their necks to Christ’s gentle yoke; others entrusted their children to be instructed in liberal, indeed monastic, disciplines and to serve there perpetually; and many shared from their possessions and revenues for the needs of the saints—Hadalin himself also strove to visit him frequently, driven by an immense ardor of charity, and to feast there in converse upon the fruits of God’s paradise, as is continually recorded in the catalogue of illustrious living men displayed there above the altar.

“These,” it says, “are the names of those who began to inhabit the monastery of Stavelot with blessed Remaclus: Saint Remaclus, Saint Hadalin, Saint Theodard, Saint Lambert—without doubt his spiritual son in baptism—Saint Hubert, Christian the most wise, and many others.”

6. But to return to the matter from which we briefly digressed: blessed Hadalin began to cultivate the place of his dwelling and adorn it through the work of a holy way of life, becoming from day to day the good fragrance of Christ before God in every place (II Cor. II, 15).

Certainly, because a heavenly lamp could not remain hidden for long beneath the shadow of a bushel (Matt. V, 15), nor could a city set upon a mountain be concealed (Matt. V, 14), the fame of his holiness reached the ears of Pippin, the most glorious king of that time. Just as the Queen of Sheba came to Solomon of old, so he humbly hastened to the modest dwelling of this peaceful and most wise servant of God. From his honey-flowing speech he received salutary counsels about submitting himself to Christ, the King of kings, and governing his kingdom according to Christ’s command; and, having granted the support of certain estates—still held by the administrators of that place—he returned rejoicing to the palace after conversing with the blessed man.

And because nothing is lacking to those who fear God, many wished to supply from their possessions and revenues the voluntary poverty of the saint, so that his devotion to the religious life in that place might increase. For there were three brothers living near him: the aforementioned Beo, another named Triclinus, and a third named Balduin. Each of them devotedly granted whatever he possessed there.

7. His name therefore became known to everyone in the neighboring regions, and from that time many began to visit him. He himself led there a celibate life worthy of God. He made all who came to him not only gentler in soul through the sweetness of his words, but also most willingly performed for them, according to his ability, the duties of charity.

Since the pious Lord had consecrated that place through his holy conversion, he wished to demonstrate in this servant the words he had spoken earlier: “Whoever honors me, I will honor” (I Kings II, 30). When the narrowness of the little place had begun to expand, two knights, accompanied by two trained Umbrian hunting dogs and coming there by chance, unaware of the dignity of the little valley, learned in their own persons what ought to happen to other newcomers. For when they rose in the morning, they found the steeds on which they had arrived lifeless, and the dogs lying dead upon their corpses.

When the bishop who was present at that time learned of this—the bishop whose see we now serve, God willing, in name though, alas, not in merit—he forbade by episcopal authority that any knight should thereafter approach the boundaries of that oratory. He also assigned to it from his revenues, as an estate of our Church, a village called Mons Francheri [Note: [Col. 1145D] This is a village between the towns of Charlemont and Mariembourg, still belonging to the canons of Celles.]—where the miracle that occurred and whose memory has now intervened took place; we consider it wrong to pass over it in silence.

8. Once, when reapers were laboring in the fields belonging to their lord, they sent one of their number to the saint, complaining and humbly begging him to provide a remedy. He replied that he had already sent them drink, but that it had been delayed through the messenger’s negligence.

So that those suffering from thirst would not be endangered by the delay, the saint came to the place, planted in the ground the staff with which he had traveled, and prayed with the deepest feeling of his heart. The searcher of hearts heard the words of his prayer, and immediately a spring burst forth, gushing abundantly. It satisfied the thirsty and revealed the man’s merit.

9. At about the same time, as he was passing through the marketplace called Dinant, a certain woman came running up, uttering a bellowing sound with her voice, and kissed his footprints. But what she was panting to say in her heart she could not express with her voice.

He therefore stopped and asked the people standing around him who she was and how this had happened to her. They informed him that a great deal of time had already passed since she had become mute, and all begged him to deign to have compassion on her misfortune and unhappiness.

But he said: “This does not belong to us, but to the holy Fathers. Would that we might prove to be their equals in merit, even at the lowest degree.”

The people, however, urged him with loud cries that he, who had always taught pity and clemency, should himself deign to display them in the misery of that poor woman. Moved by compassion and trusting in the Lord’s words, which he had promised to his disciples—“Whatever you ask for in prayer, believing, you will receive” (Mark XI, 24)—he devoted himself entirely to the Lord. Prostrated upon the ground, he prayed with tears.

When his prayer was completed, he impressed the sign of the holy cross upon her mouth. Immediately she gave thanks to God in the hearing of everyone, raised her voice in praise, and thereafter remained devoted to God.

10. Moved by wonder at this event, a certain powerful matron named Aquila, as the story goes, whose famous estate at that time was Anthegia [Note: [Col. 1145D] Anthegia, commonly Anthée, lies midway along the road from Dinant to Florennes, says Bollandus.], gave to God, for the support of the saint, an estate called Russina, namely, a mansus.

Following this example, another woman named Guiza wished to give to God through the hand of that same most blessed man, Hadalin, an estate called Veltz. Deriving its new name from the saint’s name, she arranged that it should thereafter be called Mount Saint Hadalin, for she had learned that a man’s riches are the redemption of his soul.

[Col. 1146A] After these events had taken place, she was overtaken by her final illness. When a crowd of many faithful surrounded her bed, she complained to them in a sorrowful voice about the saint’s absence. When our people asked her to whom she wished to entrust the estate, she repeatedly answered: “To Hadafino, to Hadalin, to Hadalin, I say, the blessed one.”

While she held a glove in her hand, as is customary, ready to transfer the property legally, and the man’s arrival was delayed, she died. A messenger hurried to blessed Hadalin, who happened to be absent at the time, and informed him both of the dying woman’s grief and of the reason why she was transferring the possession to him.

When the saint arrived and examined with his hand the beating of her heart to see whether she was already entirely dead, her stiff fingers, which had become rigid in the manner of death, opened—as astonishingly as if she were alive—and, in the sight of everyone present, she transferred the estate to him. There are as many witnesses to this event as there are inhabitants of that region. The matter is also made clearer than daylight by the fact that the inhabitants still appear to possess the same place, thereby confirming the story to this day.

[Note: [Col. 1146D] *Wantos*, or gloves—called *gants* in the vernacular by the French. Jerome Bignonius, in his notes on Book I, chapter 13 of the *Formulary of Marculf*, records various ancient rites for transferring possession: by a straw, reed, or rush; by a turf or clod; by a rod or staff; by a glove; by a knife together with a turf and straw; and by other means.]

11. Some time later, a wayward bull happened to break down the door of a certain woman’s house. When its inhabitant filled the whole place with the most lamentable wailing, the kindly hero arrived and asked her what had happened to her and why she was gathering everyone with such cries.

After learning the facts, he consoled her, saying: “Do not be troubled, poor woman, by the ruin of your little cottage. Rather, labor at good works, so that in that place where there are many dwellings you may deserve to become an inhabitant.”

As he said this, he marked the door and restored it to its former soundness by his word. He filled everyone with wonder and, avoiding vainglory, quickly withdrew and concealed himself.

12. Thus poor in spirit, since by circumstance he could not purchase the kingdom of heaven, he strove to purchase it by devotion; and with the gentlest mind he diligently desired to possess the land of the living. Since he hungered and thirsted for righteousness, he longed to be satisfied when the glory of Christ should be revealed, and he regarded worldly fame as nothing.

To receive God in his mind, he strove to preserve the clearest eye of his heart from malice and from the dust of worldly cares. Although “the flesh is against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V, 17), and although, while the earthly dwelling weighs down the understanding, it is accustomed to desire many things while reflecting upon them, he established a wondrous peace. By the force of a master, he compelled the spirit to rule the flesh and God to rule the spirit, so that he might deserve to see the God of heaven in Zion, adhere unceasingly to his vigils, and be called and be a son of God—not by nature, but by grace.

Indeed, just as no one could fully behold the forms and appearances of his inward virtues, so no one is capable of describing them. Just as he strove to cultivate them, so he labored to conceal them. When he desired these virtues to increase, he did not wish to be recognized as one who despised repose, fled pleasure, and sought labor; patient under humiliation, impatient of honor; poor in money, rich in conscience; humble in regard to merits, proud in regard to vices. Among all things he had no more earnest concern than either to speak about God in reading and conversation or to speak with God in prayer.

13. After remaining there for many cycles of years [Note: [Col. 1147C] The Andain manuscript reads: “For more than thirteen cycles of years.” Yet Hadalin lived for a longer period in the monastery he had founded, since he was known to Pippin the Mayor of the Palace. This Pippin, whom the author calls king, did not peacefully hold the office of prefect of the palace before the year 687. Accordingly, we date Saint Hadalin’s death to about the year 690. His sacred body rested there until the year 1338, when it was carried to the town of Visé in the diocese of Liège, on the right bank of the Meuse, after the canons of Celles had been transferred there because of the harassment of the lords of Celles. This translation is celebrated on the fifth day before the Ides of October.], after the many varied labors of this life had run their course, he was shown to be dear to men and to God through many benefits and miracles. Understanding that the day of his calling was approaching, when the honor he had earned in heaven would repay the labor that had worn him down on earth, he resolved to fulfill his duty toward his subjects.

He summoned the faithful, many in number, and placed them before him, grieving at his departure. He consoled them with these final words:

“Behold, dearest fathers and most loving brothers, the time of my dissolution is at hand, when my failing limbs will leave the spirit and it will hasten to be presented before its Judge. I am not frightened by the outcome of the condition common to every mortal, since the whole life of the wise ought to be a meditation on death. Rather, I fear for you, whom I desire by every means to be saved.

“Behold, I am about to enter upon the way of all flesh, and shall not return to you thereafter. Know, dearest ones, that you too will die; therefore, I beg you, do not allow the time granted for repentance to pass in vain. Whoever among you feels himself stained by the commission of any crime or swallowed up in the pit of a greater sin, let him quickly apply a saving medicine to his wound.

“While the Judge extends the hand of mercy to the penitent, behold, the door of mercy stands open while you are alive; after death it is closed, and only the gate of Gehenna remains open to receive those who despise the Lord’s commandments and are to be punished as deserters. I therefore beseech you through Christ: in whatever matters you know that you have hitherto strayed from the truth, strive to be reconciled to God.

“Pray, as the Gospel reading admonishes you, that your flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath (Matt. XXIV, 20). You see together what our condition is in this place; and because this world lies in the power of the evil one (I John V, 19), you all understand this together with me.”

After these sweet admonitions of paternal devotion and final words of charity, he was afflicted with a slight fever and strengthened by the viaticum of the most holy Body and Blood of the Lord. While they grieved and wept, he himself rejoicing, on the third day before the Nones of February he came to Christ, whom he had always desired.

His body was honorably tended and buried with the singing of psalms and hymns in the place he himself had appointed. There, through his merits, the Lord continues to perform benefits of miracles to the present day, to the praise and glory of his name, which is blessed forever.

[Col. 1147]

NOTGER’S PREFACE TO THE LIFE OF SAINT LANDOALD

(See above under HERIGER, col. 222.)

[Col. 1147]

LIFE OF SAINT REMACLUS, BISHOP OF MAASTRICHT

By NOTGER

(Surius, *Acts of the Saints*, 3 September.) (G)

DEDICATORY LETTER OF NOTGER, BISHOP OF LIÈGE, TO WERINFRID, ABBOT

[Col. 1147C] NOTGER, whom, although unworthy, they nevertheless proclaim a bishop, the servant of Saint Mary and Saint Lambert, sends the aid of eternal salvation to Werinfrid, venerable father and fellow priest in Christ.

[Col. 1149A] All antiquity, as the greatest of orators says, because it was nearer its origin and the divine race, perhaps saw more clearly those things that were true. Yet, as the angel told Daniel, we know that “many shall pass to and fro, and knowledge shall be multiplied.” In the ancients, reason was vigorous—the investigator of truth and the discernment of future things; in modern people, by contrast, the faith of belief is strongest, together with abundant knowledge of the past.

For them, the length of life, laying a hard crust over the ancient past, provided knowledge of all things. For us, on the contrary—whom hot blood and ignorance of affairs agitate—if only, because of our brief life and our burden of anxieties, we would not allow the discoveries of ancient men to fly away from memory! “Many brave men lived before Agamemnon,” but all are pressed by a long night without tears and without recognition, because they lack a sacred poet.

Considering this, as I believe, most reverend abbot, and since it is necessary that the younger be more discerning in proportion as they are younger, you offered me a little book concerning the life of the special patron both of our community and of yours, namely our lord Remaclus. You complained that, because of the negligence of your predecessors, it had been written more briefly than the subject required in view of the greatness of his deeds [possibly: “edited more briefly than the subject required”].

At the same time, you seemed not so much to ask as to urge me to have it not merely copied but polished somewhat more attractively: first, because there was an abundance of material concerning his deeds drawn from elsewhere; and second, because information about the times—whose differences are now especially important to know—was available in your chartulary.

But while it was clear that you and your companions were masters of every art, and while that saying of Pierius came to mind, “Do not carry wood into the forest!” and, concerning the sea, “Why pour water into rivers?”, my mind began to waver in a silence suspended between these considerations. Then suddenly the thought came to me that charity supplies the strength which incompetence denies, and that once the work has merely been begun, the rest will be arranged by circumstances.

Therefore I undertook it. To use the words of a certain wise man, I would take from that heap as much as the matter demanded. I considered nothing more important than your exhortation, which is joined both to the honor of your present purpose and to the benefit of the future age; and, lest I seem to shrink from authority, I willingly accepted the task.

For authority is granted to one who presumes to act when he believes that what is requested can be accomplished; and knowing how to obey is a glory equal to that of the one who commands.

Venerable men had done this very thing long ago: Abbot Hilduin in the *Passion of Saint Dionysius*, Archbishop Hincmar in the *Life of Saint Remigius*, and many others in compiling the deeds of numerous saints. Through these authors we can obtain what, in all matters, has always been and ought to be of the greatest value. For no one has ever so carefully calculated a life that circumstances, age, and experience did not always bring something new.

And lest this labor, undertaken at your urging, prove fruitless, I gathered not only the times and deeds of the saint whom we have mentioned—Saint Remaclus—but also those of the other bishops of our see, wherever they could be collected, down to our own times. From these materials I extracted the Life for which you most eagerly desired and offered it to fulfill your wishes.

In my own judgment I am far from the excellence of the greatest orator, who could express much in few words, extend little at great length, diminish great things, make the greatest things out of the smallest, present broad matters narrowly and narrow matters broadly, render common things elegantly and elegant things intelligently, express new things familiarly and familiar things newly, and undertake many other such tasks. To him the poet also gives this injunction: “Either follow reputation, or invent things suited to it.”

Nor have I, like schoolboys after a theme has been assigned, invented some frivolous or even absurd expression about what words the man who suffered an injury might have used, or the man who inflicted it. Even if I wished to follow a very eloquent speaker who said, “Even if neither of them said these things, nevertheless he had them in mind and showed them in action,” I would fear no one’s judgment—but that is for another time.

I have sent, I say, to your charity a gift undertaken with less confidence in its effectiveness than in the presumption of friendship. For the contemplation of friendship supplies great strength in the course of a very difficult work, and those who desire to please are often provided with abundant material.

Thus, although I fear that, because I cannot make myself equal to the task imposed, the fault of my inadequacy may rebound upon the one who urged me to undertake it, nevertheless, when I consider your goodwill, everything becomes easy, straightforward, and—as I may say—willing, when it is devoted to your delight according to your direction.

Having bestowed this gift, I wish to make you solicitous: if at some time I ask for any of your works, you will wrong me if you refuse. Whoever has given great things wishes great things to be returned to him. Yet I do not arrogantly call them great, since they are unequal to your merits and to our wishes.

Therefore I fear the bites of envious slander, because envy is accustomed to bring prejudice against difficult matters. In the end, not everyone admires or loves the same things. Let no one therefore look askance at my work there, nor poison it with hidden hatred and biting criticism.

But you, most blessed father, defender both of my labor and of your exhortation, must take care that the completion of my task does not leave me secure, since, if it displeases you, the modesty of a friend may more fittingly suit you.

Farewell.

Whatever neither prayers can endure nor dreams invent,

always keep joyfully; for soft ears rejoice

at your name. Your virtue has made me your friend.

Farewell again.

PREFACE OF THE AUTHOR

[Col. 1151]

[Col. 1151A] The almighty Lord, who is rich in mercy, whose nature is goodness, whose will is power, and whose work is mercy, endured with great patience the vessels of wrath, prepared for destruction. At last, however, just as he found no one free from the guilt of the first transgression, so he came to set everyone free. He bestowed upon all the riches of his goodness and patience, and exercised the omnipotence of his will most effectively upon the ungrateful and those unworthy of consideration by his grace, when, in his clemency, he first prepared the work of saving mercy so that humanity might be restored.

He took away from the strong armed man the weapons in which he trusted; he distributed the goods that he possessed, so that just as they had previously been vessels of wrath because of sins, so through his grace they might become vessels of mercy.

For just as it must not be believed that anyone reaches salvation unless God invites him, so neither can one who has been invited work out his salvation unless God assists him. No one perishes by God’s will, but by his permission and according to the choice of free will, lest the freedom and natural liberty once attributed to humanity be reduced to a kind of servile necessity.

Thus, by God’s mercy, we have the beginning of our salvation. But to consent to saving inspiration belongs to our free choice. To attain what we desire after consenting to the divine admonition belongs to God’s gift. To fall belongs to our power and negligence. Not to fall, once the gift of salvation has been obtained, is indeed in some way a matter of our vigilance, but in every respect it depends upon heavenly assistance.

Relying firmly upon that hope, we discover in reality that those are blessed who, although they did not see Christ accomplishing such great things in the flesh, did not hesitate steadfastly to believe what they heard. Among these there are also many who performed the works he performed and, in accordance with his promise (John XIV), performed even greater works. This is confessed not only by those nearby, but also proclaimed by those beyond the Sarmatians, who reach the Glacial Sea and inhabit the Fortunate Islands.

We have therefore gladly submitted ourselves to so great a good, and it delights us to serve so great a Lord, who is not only the supporter and helper of those who advance, but also provides remedies for those who fall. He ensures that angelic assistance is not lacking to us and grants us the patronage of the saints, whom we do not hesitate to implore as intercessors for our sins.

Although he has distributed these saints generously among different provinces, so that they are to be honored generally and communally, he has nevertheless assigned certain ones to particular places, to be embraced especially and entreated more earnestly. Among these he has given us blessed Remaclus. Just as we rely greatly upon his intercession, so we undertake to narrate his life and deeds according to the measure of our strength.

HERE BEGINS THE LIFE

[Col. 1151]

[Col. 1151C] I. From its very beginnings the kingdom of the Franks always appeared invincible, but it seemed to flourish above all its neighboring kingdoms when it submitted its neck to the yoke of the Lord’s faith, burned what it had previously worshiped, and worshiped what it had burned.

It received enormous growth, and the Church of God acquired a firm position under it, when King Clotarius, fourth in legitimate succession, became monarch of three kingdoms. He was then in the fortieth year of his reign, while Heraclius, the restorer of the Holy Cross, was in the fourteenth year of his imperial rule.

This Clotarius allowed none of the neighboring kings to bring arms against his dominion. Rather, he strove to restrain all the kings and peoples of Spain, Gaul, and Germany with his reins. Moreover, he placed his illustrious son Dagobert over the Austrasians and wished the regions of Germany also to be subject to him.

During their most prosperous times Christianity grew to such an extent that today scarcely any church, or only a rare one, is found within the boundaries of their kingdom that is not illumined by the patronage of some saint of that age.

To pass over countless others: the holy men Eligius and Audoenus served in the ministries of the palace; blessed Arnulf and Romaric were admitted to the king’s councils; Saint Amandus, most blessed Remaclus, and Saint Goar illumined Aquitaine by their birth.

Some hold that Aquitaine constitutes nearly a third part of Gaul and received its name from the winding waters of the Loire, which irrigates most of it and nearly surrounds it in a circle. On the northwest it has the Ocean, called the Bay of Aquitaine; on the west, Spain; on the north and east, the province of Lyon; and on the southeast and south, Narbonensis.

It is famous for its streams and fish-filled rivers, its extremely fertile soil, abundant pastures for livestock, nectar-bearing vineyards, extensive woods, and great abundance of fruit. It is rich in gold, silver, and other metals, wealthy in the revenue of taxes, but more devoted than other provinces to the luxury of every pleasure. Finally, it is furnished with brave, warlike, and fierce men.

Besides forts and fortified places, it has fourteen very large cities, populous and highly renowned. Two of these are metropolitan sees: one is Bordeaux, always distinguished by great men; the other is Bourges, whose archbishop at that time was Saint Austregisilus, while blessed Sulpitius was archdeacon and succeeded Austregisilus in the episcopate.

It was in their ecclesiastical district that Remaclus was born into this world at that time, to a father named Albutius and a mother named Matrinea [Matrinia]. Both possessed wealth and noble birth in accordance with the dignity of the world.

His great estates testify to this: some were given to our Church and some to your monastery, whether by Remaclus himself, by his ancestors, or even by royal elevation. This can be demonstrated from letters that are still preserved in the archives of both Churches.

## II

The boy Remaclus, of good character, was educated under Saint Sulpitius [Col. 1153A]; in his honor, it is established that this same holy man dedicated very many churches in our diocese. When Remaclus had grown older and, as befitted his age, had produced the fruits of complete integrity and goodness, he was commended to Saint Eligius, a man easily foremost among those of his age by reason of his merits. Eligius, in the monastery at Sollemniacum (Solemniapcum), which he was himself building on his own estate, thoroughly instructed him in the sacred teachings of monastic discipline.

The pious youth obeyed his admonitions so completely that, with divine grace overflowing in him, he offered to all who were serving Christ in that monastery an example of religious conduct. He was constant at the Vigils, watchful throughout the night in prayer, outstanding in abstinence, and distinguished by complete integrity of character. [Col. 1153B] Saint Eligius, seeing this—he had been entrusted with the boy by his parents—and rejoicing with a certain eagerness of spirit at his progress, transferred to him the care of the flock committed to him, entrusting his duties to him and appointing him as his substitute. For Eligius was being compelled to return to the royal palace and serve the king there.

Afterward, the fame of Remaclus’s holy life spread far and wide and reached even the leading men of the court. Thus, by the action of divine providence, a lamp kindled by the fires of divine grace could not remain hidden beneath the bushel of self-regard; rather, so that the sluggish might receive light from it in their commitment to the faith, it was set upon a lampstand. It was proclaimed in the royal court that so great a man ought not to be absent from the king’s presence, so that the affairs of the kingdom might be arranged by the wisdom of one whose remarkable marks of merit were evident. He was therefore honorably summoned, as was proper, and brought into the royal palace, destined thereafter—as subsequent events showed—to be a great consolation to all.

## III

At approximately this same time, Saint John, who had successfully governed the Church of the Tongrians, or of Maastricht, departed this life. The illustrious King Dagobert, who had succeeded his father Chlothar as sole ruler, had summoned Saint Amandus, who had been made bishop for the purpose of preaching, as was then customary. Because he had expelled Amandus with an affront and had been rebuked by him for certain crimes, Dagobert sought to bind him more closely to himself through the baptism of his son Sigebert [Col. 1153D] and to place him in the see of Maastricht.

That holy man traveled through villages and fortified places for three years, sowing the word of life. But when he saw that he was achieving nothing, and indeed observed that even the priests and Levites themselves were mocking him, he shook the dust from his feet against them, as the Lord commands, and went, as he had done before, to other places for the purpose of preaching.

It is unknown how long the people of Maastricht then remained without a shepherd, until Sigebert’s father made him king of Austrasia and wished him to have his seat in the city of Metz. The people of Maastricht then presented the following petition to him, through the common election of the priests, with a great gathering of nobles and the request of every order: that no one but Saint Remaclus should be appointed bishop over them. He was dear both to God and to human beings; in holiness he was second to no one of his age; he was pleasing to the angelic spirits and worthy of being welcomed and revered by all mortals.

They recalled that they had experienced many benefits from him, and that his intercessions had often been of great assistance to them both with the king and with the nobles. Nor, they said, was his wisdom obscure, since he had frequently been called upon for royal counsels. He possessed knowledge of the Scriptures, by which he could bring forth both the Old and the New. In short, none of those qualities was lacking in him with which the Apostle wished a bishop to be equipped.

The king courteously assented to these words with a favorable disposition of mind and complied with their wishes; he decided to grant what they requested. He therefore summoned Saint Remaclus to him, conferred with him on the matter, and employed—one can scarcely say how great was—the persuasive sweetness of his speech. The holy man resisted him in every way. But the king, relying on the counsel of the priests and nobles, did not abandon his purpose.

At last the man of God, fearing that he might resist the divine will, was appointed, though unwillingly, the twenty-seventh bishop of the Church of the Tongrians, or of Maastricht, so that he might share with many the seeds of the divine word that until then he had kept hidden within himself.

## IV

We cannot adequately explain with what religious devotion and integrity he carried out that office, since, from the very beginning of his ordination, Christ bestowed upon him such abundant grace of speech that everyone showed himself ready to obey, and no one failed to love him sincerely; each person strove, as far as possible, to conform himself to his teaching.

There was no arrogance in his character; holy humility claimed him wholly for itself. The proud revered him as a superior; the humble embraced him as a brother. His goodwill and love were shared equally toward all. Though dwelling bodily on earth, he declared himself heavenly in dress and conduct. Angelic in appearance, composed in his bearing, holy in his actions, utterly pure in body, exceptionally diligent in spirit, circumspect in his work, outstanding in intellect, great in counsel, Catholic in faith, most patient in hope, and abundant in charity.

His deeds testified to the merit he possessed before God. An extraordinary sweetness and graciousness of character could be observed in him, and he knew how to conduct himself among rich and poor with such moderation that the poor regarded him as belonging to their condition, while the wealthy regarded him as belonging to their rank. He did not weigh the status of powerful persons but the elegance of their character, honoring each one more readily the holier he had learned that person to be.

What he said with his mouth and affirmed, he never overturned by conduct or deed; rather, by his actions he showed what ought to be taught by words. What divine grace had conferred upon him, he transmitted to those who came after him. Hence it followed that not only his deeds benefit us even today, but also those of his disciples and of those who were faithfully educated by him; their acts and works are examples for us and invite us to imitate them.

## V

He was both founder and rector of many monasteries [Col. 1155A], in which the ranks of those serving Christ continue to increase to this day. He was the father and instructor of many disciples. As he won their souls for Christ, so they and their successors brought many souls to Christ; and their merits, certainly, redound to his credit.

Among them was Saint Theodard, without doubt formed by him in ecclesiastical disciplines, since he designated him as his successor; he eventually departed this life as a martyr. Likewise there was Saint Lambert, who in his own time likewise showed himself an outstanding martyr.

There was also Saint Adelinus, born in Aquitania and, as the story goes, a companion of Remaclus on his pilgrimage. At one time, while Remaclus was engaged in works and pursuits worthy of God in a secluded place, Adelinus appeared to him in a vision: handsome of face, venerable in his hair, distinguished in all other respects by his stature, and indicating the place of his future religious life and perpetual rest, as well as a spring suitable for human use. This fact is by no means obscure today, since his body rests in that same place and, present in spirit, he never ceases to bestow innumerable benefits there each day upon believers.

## VI

In the election of Saint Trudo, one can readily discern with what purpose the holy man watched over the affairs and guardianship of the Lord’s flock, how the spirit of prophecy was not lacking in him, and finally how, burning with a great love of Christ, every desire had been extinguished in him.

With pastoral concern he customarily visited his parish and drew from the jaws of wolves [Col. 1155C] as many as he could, striving to make them a gain for the chief Shepherd. He assisted the good so that they might become better; the idle and sluggish he exhorted to return to a better way of life.

Meanwhile Saint Trudo, still a boy, was already producing the first fruits of virtue. Although he possessed great nobility of proud blood, he nevertheless had within him so much greater a fervor and devotion for divine love and the virtues that at one time he bound himself by a vow: if, with Christ’s help, he learned the sacred writings, he would build a church on his own estate, serve the Lord there perpetually, and gather to himself as companions as many as he could for the worship and service of God.

Burning with this desire, he was visited by a nocturnal vision and strengthened by angelic consolation in these words:

“Know, brother,” said the angel, “that the vows which as a boy you have made to Christ are pleasing to him, and that he has admitted your prayers. Do not doubt that he who, anticipating you, inspired this desire in you will also, by helping you, follow through and bring your intention to fulfillment. He, I say, will imbue your heart with his wisdom, instruct you in his commandments, and inscribe this law upon your breast.

“Moreover, you will also be raised to the duties of ecclesiastical dignity, and by your words and example you will bring forth many sons for Christ and his Church. To make you more certain of these things, visit Saint Remaclus, who is not far from here. God has revealed to him what you must do. He will direct your steps toward that for which you aspire so greatly.”

## VII

Saint Trudo rose immediately, having no hesitation about the angelic vision, and hastened to the place to which he had been directed. Saint Remaclus was then occupied in feeding and caring for his sheep. As Saint Trudo approached, Remaclus, instructed by divine revelation, said:

“Rise quickly and go to meet the man of God who has come to visit us. Receive him reverently and bring him to me with honor. Look, he is near; hurry to meet him.”

They did as they had been ordered and brought Saint Trudo to Saint Remaclus, who was staying at home with his companions. When the pious father saw him, he rose and, weeping for joy, rushed to embrace him. He restrained Trudo when he wished to throw himself at his feet, immediately raised him up, and, giving thanks to God from the depths of his heart, said:

“May glory, praise, and rejoicing be yours, good Jesus, through the Holy Spirit with the eternal Father, visitor of souls, who have willed to console us today by the arrival of this servant of yours, in whom you dwell.” [Col. 1156B]

He added:

“And you, my son, may you be blessed by the Lord, who has deigned to send you to us and, by a hidden inspiration, to make known to us your heart’s desire. Know, therefore, that from now on you will be my son by the right of charity, and that I shall always perform for you the duties of a spiritual father.

“For the Lord has revealed to me, his servant, what must be done for the salvation of your soul; from me you will learn how you may obtain the fulfillment of your vow. I have learned, with the Lord as my teacher, that in your childhood you vowed that, if knowledge of the sacred writings should ever be granted to you, you would build a church on your estate and serve the Lord there for as long as you lived.

“Know that you will fulfill this in the following order. You will offer your possessions to Saint Stephen the protomartyr near the city of Metz, and you will be taught the divine writings by the inhabitants of that place. When you have attained this, you will return to me and build a church wherever you wish, as you promised.”

## VIII

After blessing him, Remaclus gave him a letter of his own to the bishop of the city of Metz, who was to instruct and educate him, as had been divinely revealed to Remaclus. At that time Clodulphus presided over the Church of Metz. He was the son of Saint Arnulf according to the flesh and, in the merits of his virtues, his most worthy successor in the episcopate.

Clodulphus received Saint Trudo with the greatest kindness. Once he had learned the reasons for his arrival, he arranged for him to be instructed in the sacred writings and divine law—not only for Trudo’s own sake but also because of Saint Remaclus’s distinguished recommendation—and he accepted the possessions that Trudo offered to Saint Stephen.

He treated Trudo well during the many years he remained there, carefully instructed him, ordained him to the priesthood, and sent him back to Saint Remaclus. Remaclus asked him what the Lord had granted him and whether he had made the journey there and back safely. When he learned that Trudo had been well educated in the sacred writings, he gave immense thanks to God, saying:

“Praise be to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have deigned to fulfill what you revealed to me concerning your servant and have brought him back safely to me, instructed and adorned with your commandments and the teaching of your law.”

He permitted Saint Trudo to preach the word of God in his diocese, to celebrate Mass in whatever churches he wished, and finally to build an oratory on his own estate, as he had promised. Trudo therefore remained with him for some time, living most holily. At length, having received the episcopal blessing, he returned to his native land and accomplished in reality what he had long conceived in his mind: he built an oratory on his own estate, where he gathered many who would serve God.

Finally, he both requested and obtained from Saint Remaclus the consecration of that oratory. He was also buried there after the many labors of this life, and, performing very many miracles there, he continues to provide a fitting dwelling place for monks to this very day.

## IX

Here we may briefly consider how, as we have said, the fire of every desire had been subdued in Saint Remaclus; how he surpassed the merits of all the priests of our age; and how, by comparison with him, he condemned all the bishops of our time. If the circumstance that was offered to that most blessed man were to arise for them, they would plainly act otherwise: they would not merely fail to encourage pious people to give their possessions not to their own church but to another church; they would even dissuade those who wished to do so voluntarily and persuade them to give the possessions to themselves—something I say without wishing to offend them.

Since this fault is all the more blameworthy in us, the merit of Saint Remaclus, who entirely rejected such a course, must be exalted with correspondingly greater praise and commendation.

We have wished to recall these matters concerning Saint Trudo at somewhat greater length [Col. 1157C], in order also to show that the gift of prophecy was not lacking in Saint Remaclus. When Trudo first departed from him to go to Metz, the household of Saint Remaclus, despising him because of his shabby clothing, were displeased that the bishop had taken in a man so poorly dressed. Learning this through divine revelation, Remaclus rebuked them most severely. But when they regretted what they had done, he received them back into his favor, warning them to be more careful in the future. But more on this elsewhere.

## X

Who could adequately recount how holily and religiously Remaclus lived after these events? Who could explain his concern for the flock entrusted to him? He warned everyone to keep themselves from the seductions of the flattering world [Col. 1157D], to withdraw from the cares of this world, to strive for brotherly peace and concord, to tread the path of God’s commandments with an unoffending step, to despise the world and its desires, and, with ready hearts, to trample underfoot the flower of hay that quickly withers; he urged them to pursue and desire heavenly things in mind and action.

While he was engaged in these matters, he began to burn with a greater desire to devote himself more freely to God, so that he might taste how sweet the Lord is. He wished that some means might be shown him by which he could more easily attain this.

At that time King Sigebert was founding, with great devotion of spirit, places to be dedicated to divine worship wherever there were none; he supported with the greatest generosity and resources those founded either by himself or by kings of earlier times; and, so that the worship owed to God might not be neglected there, he took care, through the vigilance both of Saint Remaclus and of the other priests.

## XI

In the place called Coesecongidunum, beside the River Sesmarus, that same king, on the advice of his nobles, founded a monastery in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul and of John. The site seemed suitable for the habitation and way of life of monks. He enriched it through his generosity and brought into it outstanding servants of God. He wished Saint Remaclus to be its administrator, and also its master and instructor, so that they might learn from him to live in accordance with the tradition of the holy Fathers.

To this day there remains there a place of prayer, cut into the rock through his work, where benefits of healing are still granted to the sick. There the most holy man had for some time offered himself to God as a victim worn down by fasts and vigils [Col. 1158B]. More closely united with Christ, he had devoted himself to divine contemplation and watered the hearts of his subjects with the rains of saving doctrine.

Eventually he grew weary of that place, for reasons unknown—unless it was because, as rumor spread, the place had suffered many disturbances from the powerful men who lived around it. Since the king had no nearby territory from which the site could be enlarged, Remaclus approached him and said:

“I have judged it necessary to advise your Highness, illustrious prince, that although many monasteries throughout your realm have been dedicated by your munificence to the worship of God and his saints, only the Ardennes, situated among rugged mountains, still possesses no monasteries. Let your serenity therefore order some to be built there also. By God’s kindness, resources will be available to one who wishes to undertake this, and the nearness of our see will not be lacking. It will not be difficult to enlarge them and furnish them with the necessities, since there can be no doubt that all the neighboring places there are subject to your authority.”

The king replied:

“It is your task, most blessed Father, to give us counsel in this matter; it will be ours to give our assent in accordance with your counsel and to carry it out at the proper time. You, therefore, undertake responsibility for this affair and apply yourself to the work; we shall not deny you the suitable places that you select, nor the expenses.”

The king then summoned the faithful men Saint Cunibert the bishop, Atetlanus, Theodefridus, and Bishop Gislochardus; his nobles as well, Grimoald the Mayor of the Palace, Folcoudus, and Bobo; and also his household officers Clodulphus, [Col. 1158D] Ansigisilus, and Berselo. He said to them:

“By the will of God and with the consent of you and of our other faithful men, we have decided to establish two monasteries within the borders of the Ardennes. Religious men, devoted to the monastic life, will dwell in them and pray to almighty God for our safety and that of our successors, for the stability and tranquility of the entire kingdom, and for the preservation of those who are assigned to the affairs of the kingdom. We wish Bishop Remaclus, its administrator and promoter, to preside over the undertaking itself.”

## XII

Thus, equipped with royal authority and provided with the necessary companions, the holy bishop set out for the forest of the Ardennes, obstructed by marshes and mountains. He came to the stream called Vuarchinna and found there clear indications that those places had once been devoted to idolatry. There were stones inscribed with the name of Diana and with other monstrous names of that kind, or bearing their images. There were also springs suitable for human use but polluted by pagan errors and, for that reason, still subject to the attacks of demons.

Accordingly, after adjuring them through the name of Christ and making the sign of the holy Cross, he freed and purified that place from demonic assault. Immediately the water, which had trickled drop by drop from its own channel, disappeared.

Seeing that the place offered a convenient habitation both because of its fish-filled waters and because of its abundant pastures, the holy man prayed at length over the spring and blessed it. He carved the sign of the Cross into a stone, pouring lead into the grooves. And suddenly immense quantities of water burst forth, which to the present day bear witness to the truth of our words for those who see them.

Since he had cleansed that place from the infestation of evil spirits, he decided to call it Malmundarium, as though “cleansed from evil.” There he built an oratory and dwellings for the use of the servants of God, and enlarged whatever pertained to the worship of God.

## XIII

But since that place lay in the parish of Cologne, he undertook to establish a monastery that would be contained within the boundaries of his own diocese. Proceeding from there about two thousand paces toward the west, he crossed the stream called Calla, which forms a boundary between parishes, and stopped at the edge of a certain mountain beside the River Amblava.

He remained there for some time and gave many examples of holy conduct, as those who wish to know can learn from the reports of the inhabitants. Although that place had many springs, it was narrow and insufficient for the necessary buildings. He therefore turned his steps toward the east and, proceeding a short distance, saw a more spacious place, more suitable for the work that was to be undertaken.

There he began to devote himself more attentively to the labor, and, as ordinarily happens in such matters, divine power was present with him. Through it, the will was brought to fulfillment. Since wild animals from every direction used to gather there, whether for stabling, drinking, or feeding, the place had been called Stabulaus from ancient times. The holy man did not think that name should be changed; rather, he wished it both to be called and to be a stall for faithful souls, who would henceforth hasten there as to the pastures of eternal life.

The noise of the beasts rushing there in herds often caused no little terror to the brothers whom the man of God had gathered there at that time. In a state of horror they fled to Saint Remaclus, who was laboring at the undertaking, and asked what protection they ought to take against the devil’s schemes directed against them.

He looked upon them kindly and reassured them:

“Believe faithfully in the Lord, my little children,” he said. “Follow his commandments without violation. Keep your minds free from thoughts that lack understanding. Purifying your souls, offer the Lord a pure service. Pray without interruption; at evening, morning, and midday sing psalms. Devote yourselves very frequently to reading. Fortify your foreheads with the sign of the Cross and impress its power upon your souls. Immediately the snares and devices of the grim enemy will be reduced to nothing, and all the terror of the beasts through which he thinks he has found a way to attack you will depart.

“For by these same methods he formerly harassed those who inhabited the deserts of Egypt, the Thebaid, and Nitria—would that we might be found, however imperfectly, to be their followers! He possesses a thousand arts of harming, nor does he lack innumerable ways of deceiving. But we are not ignorant of his tricks and frauds; he sometimes attacks us even through flies.

“We, the servants of Christ, the more frequently we are pressed by his assaults, rise up all the more strongly, resisting him with courage. Satan, by experience, fears the beginnings of those who undertake to live rightly: vigils, prayers, fasts, gentleness, patience, voluntary poverty, contempt of empty glory, humility, mercy, and, above all, pure love toward Christ.

“Therefore, like a lion in its lair, he lies in wait unseen, seeking to frighten you away from your purpose.”

By these and similar words he made their minds more ready for the worship of God and strengthened them against every temptation.

## XIV

After the works had been established and completed, he explained what they were to do. Then, returning to Tongres, or Maastricht, he devoted his attention to the duties of pastoral office.

Not long afterward, the king learned that the monasteries had been built and gave immense thanks to almighty God. Since the newly built churches needed episcopal blessing, he summoned Saint Remaclus and wished him solemnly to consecrate both the one that belonged to the parish of Cologne, with the consent of the venerable Bishop Cunibert, and the one that belonged to our diocese [Col. 1160C], so that those churches founded by his direction and through his great zeal might also receive pontifical blessing through his work.

The holy man caused no delay in these matters. He was so dear to the king and the nobles and held in such high esteem by them that nothing of importance was done without his advice.

For this reason, after the solemnities of the Masses had been completed, Grimoald the Mayor of the Palace entrusted both monasteries to his careful management and diligence, while also informing him that, if the monks lacked anything, the king would supply it once Remaclus had made him aware of their needs.

Thus, with God’s approval, the holy priest obtained the opportunity he had always desired to pursue and seek a more secluded life. Although with the greatest difficulty, he finally obtained from the king that another successor should be given to him, while he himself might go to the long-desired desert, where, removed from secular cares, he could more freely yearn for divine and heavenly things.

He proposed Saint Theodard to the king and the nobles, a man whose life had been tested, and asked that Theodard fulfill his duties and be substituted for him as bishop.

It is scarcely possible to say how great the mourning was at his departure, or how sorrowful and afflicted he left those to whom he had given the seeds of life. They saw that they were being deprived of such a father and so great a teacher. Every age and both sexes testified to the grief of their souls with tears, and, escorting him as he departed, they cried out:

“Alas for us miserable people! What are we to do, [Col. 1161A] deprived of so great a shepherd? From where will consolation come to us after losing him who was the chief relief of our miseries? Who will heal us when he abandons us—the one who knew above all how to provide medicine for our sorrows? What hope of salvation remains for us, who will lack the presence of so great a father?”

## XV

Moved by their tears and complaints, the man of God consoled them in words much like these:

“Please do not, my little children, delay the purpose of my heart by your lamentations. You have God as your shepherd and father among you; he will console you most kindly in difficult and adverse circumstances.

“So that you may not lack anything even outwardly, we have provided you with our son Theodard, approved in every respect. He will watch most diligently over your salvation and distribute the measure of wheat to you with the greatest fidelity.

“Since I do not doubt that his prudence will suffice for you, I desire to give myself to the solitude I have longed for and to dwell in the presence of that Majesty who contemplates all things. I wish to remain with him.”

Those among them who were wiser replied:

“Consider very carefully, most blessed Father, what you are doing; reflect on the disgrace to which you are subjecting us. Once you have undertaken to feed a flock, the statutes of the holy Fathers do not permit you to abandon it unless compelled by illness and unless you do so of your own accord.

“For while a bishop lives, if weakness of health rather than crime recalls him from his office, no principle permits another to be substituted for him unless he himself first refuses and confirms his petition in writing. Even if he has lost his mind, if his illness has periods of remission, another ought not to be substituted unless he himself consents. If he never regains possession of his mind, a faithful person of tested character must be chosen to fulfill his duties while he lives and to succeed him after his death.

“If anyone refuses to follow this path of the Fathers, he makes the wife who has been dismissed commit adultery and brands the man who marries a woman so dismissed with the charge of adultery.

“Therefore, most holy Father, consider by this reasoning how greatly your judgment is burdened and what damage our reputation suffers. No crime is alleged against you for which, if convicted, you should be deposed. No illness weighs upon you for which, as though presenting a repudiation, you should be suspended from your ministry.

“Therefore, although you confirm in writing the petition by which you wish this office to be taken from you, we reject it. We absolutely do not admit another to exercise your duties; far from allowing another to succeed you while you live, we cannot do so. Father, you were given to us by legitimate succession; we greatly desire both to be called and to be legitimate sons, not illegitimate ones.”

## XVI

“You have now understood where your judgment is burdened. Hear, we ask, how the mark of disgrace is branded upon our reputation.

“You have no grounds on which you may rightly and properly abandon us. First, we are by no means illegitimate, so that you may lawfully leave us. We were received by you into the embrace of the Catholic Mother; we have never lent credulous ears to perverse doctrine. And if perhaps we have sinned in that respect, you ought to have healed us.

“Next, no persecution by us compels you to go elsewhere. If the Lord permits one to flee while the persecutor rages, that may indeed be a consolation for the weak and for those who are not sufficiently perfect; but many saints patiently endured the wickedness of evil people and healed them by their patience.

“Finally, evil people should be fled rather than endured only when there are no good people present whom you might benefit.

“But alas for us miserable people! While we are deprived of the presence of the most perfect of men, we are brought under the suspicion of infamy: that you have grown weary not only of our efforts but also that you are driven away by our evil actions. Your departure, as such a great man, plainly signifies that no good remains among us.

“Nothing now remains except for slanderers to defame us and for malicious people to predict that your successors must not only be expelled but even put to death, since you are withdrawing from us and Saint Amandus, your predecessor, departed from us after shaking the dust from his feet against us.

“Yet almighty God, easy to forgive, when he rebuked the prophet for being displeased at the sudden withering of the ivy (Jonah 4), made it sufficiently clear that he would bear the destruction of his creature much more grievously and that he prefers the repentance of the wicked to their death (Ezekiel 18).”

## XVII

Moved by these words, the man of God remained silent for some time, reflecting within himself. At last he burst forth in these words:

“Do not, my brothers, reproach me with words of this kind. I do not take it amiss that you mourn your losses before me, but I cannot bear that you wish to quarrel with me as though you had suffered an injury.

“I do not wish you to be regarded as illegitimate, nor have I departed from you for that reason. Nor do I think so badly of you as to suppose that I can bear no fruit among you and that I am therefore transferring myself elsewhere, where the hope of greater fruit shines forth.

“Nor do I claim this for myself. Far from being perfect, I do not even wish to appear most perfect. Nor do I judge it characteristic of the perfect to refuse to depart from what they have begun and to stretch forward toward what lies ahead; to persist with Martha in the active life and not fervently aspire with Mary to the contemplative life; and, when the opportunity presents itself, to renounce the active life rather than fail to devote oneself most eagerly to contemplation.

“With the Lord’s help I governed you, entrusted to me, as best I could, and I earnestly prayed that my labor might be fruitful for you. Your pursuits do not weary me, nor does the wickedness of your actions offend me—for there is none.

“One thing remains: that I should transfer elsewhere the talent which I rejoice to see multiplied among you, so that it may be multiplied still further and your abundance may supply their poverty.

“Holy men before us did this as well—would that we might be able to equal even the least of their merits! Many of them allowed themselves to be transferred to other churches for the sake of greater usefulness; some moved of their own accord in the hope of greater merit.

“Afterward, if they felt that they were making little progress or that their services were not particularly necessary, they withdrew and offered themselves for the undertaking of greater labors. Like the strongest champions of Christ, they did not wish to be held within the enclosure of quiet but leapt willingly into the open field of battle—not becoming deserters from spiritual warfare, nor fleeing like mercenaries at the sight of wolves, but preparing to engage them courageously. They willingly placed themselves where either the number of those fighting against the enemy was smaller or the enemies themselves threatened more fiercely and more closely.

“Yet, my little children, I do not claim their virtue for myself, nor rashly assert that I am equal to their merits.

“If you cannot bear the name of successor, let Theodard be my cooperator. Do not think that I shall be absent from you. Although I am departing to instruct others, I shall not go outside this diocese. I shall not be far from you. If any circumstance should arise, you will be able to come to me for counsel; there you will have me as an intercessor for your sins and as one who remembers all that you need and all that troubles you, all the more earnestly the farther I am removed from popular concerns and therefore the freer and more devoted to contemplating divine things.

“Once Moses stood on the mountain while Israel fought against the Amalekites. He fought not with weapons but with prayers, and he brought it about that the people of Israel were superior in the conflict to the extent that he himself was nearer to God in prayer and farther removed from the noise of the combatants.

“Likewise, my dearest ones, I have resolved to cling more attentively to divine contemplation in a place where secular disturbances will scarcely interrupt me.

“Saint John the Baptist urges me toward this life. Even in tender youth he preferred to live among wild beasts and eat their food rather than remain among his fellow citizens, lest he contaminate himself even with idle speech.

“I also have Moses as an outstanding guide to this life. He preferred to enjoy divine conversations in the vast desert rather than be enervated by the wealth and pleasures of the Egyptians.

“Elijah and Elisha, too, and the other prophets distinguished by their devotion to contemplation, even subdued kings.

“Abraham, made the father of all believers through faith, invites me here. Following his example already, I have despised my native land and cast away all my possessions and resources.

“Finally, I am stirred by the example of the Lord himself, the Savior, who, when he was about to contend with the most terrible enemy, withdrew alone into the desert.

“By his mercy and kindness, may it come to pass that there I may crush the deceits of the wicked enemy, gather spiritual gains from those who are to be instructed there, and bring some benefit to your salvation through my prayers!”

Thus Saint Remaclus eased the grief of his people and quieted their complaints. Then he continued on his journey.

### XVIII

After this matter became known to religious men living both near and far, whose hearts God had moved, they began to flock to him from every direction, like bees to their hives. Some devoted themselves to the service of almighty God and submitted their necks to the Savior’s easy yoke; others offered their children to be instructed in liberal, or rather monastic, disciplines and to serve Christ there perpetually; many supplied the saints with necessities from their own possessions and revenues.

Among these was also the lord and father Papolenus [also Babolenus], who came to him indeed to pay a visit, [Col. 1164A] but preferred to remain under his direction rather than return home. Blessed Remaclus received him with the greatest courtesy, and he lived with him without causing offense. Although he had come to be instructed by him, he stirred many others by his example to pursue virtue. Blessed Remaclus, observing this and reflecting that perhaps the Lord had sent him for this very purpose, asked him not to leave him. Then, especially so that the brothers might be kept in discipline, he placed him over the monastery of Malmundarium, whose monks lived according to the rule of Saint Benedict, while preserving in every respect his own authority. Returning thence to Stabulaus, he devoted himself to still greater works of virtue and drew very many to imitate him by his example.

### XIX

Who did not change sadness into joy in his presence? Who did not drive away anger of mind through tranquility and peace? Who, at the sight of him, did not restrain the grief of bereavement? Who, oppressed by poverty, was not so relieved by his words that he despised worldly riches and rejoiced in his own want? Who, weighed down by the burden of labors, was not raised up by his encouragement? What young man, inflamed by the fire of raging lust, did not immediately, in response to his salutary admonition, become a devotee of chastity?

He cared for those tormented by demons; he drew those burning with unlawful thoughts away from evil action, teaching them to dash [such thoughts] against Christ the rock. He knew what illness afflicted each person and, judging each according to the merits of his life, applied reproofs in proportion to the diseases.

Meanwhile his devotion to and ardor for divine love increased, as did the inflexible rigor of monastic discipline. [Col. 1164C] That every opportunity for sinning was forbidden in all the other offices of his monastery is attested even by the dormitory alone. Saint Lambert also bears witness: driven from his own seat, he fled especially to that place because he knew that the practice of holy religion flourished there above all. The stone cross is another witness. Because the sound of a slipping shoe had interrupted the brothers’ rest, he was ordered to go to it in the middle of the night; he stood beneath it until dawn, occupied with psalmody and prayers, despising the cold and trampling the snow, and thus gave sure indications of his holiness. But more on these matters elsewhere.

### XX

As religious observance grew, so too did the revenues of that church. When King Sigebert heard of the brothers’ fervor for the worship of Christ, he summoned blessed Remaclus and, in addition to what he had previously given and what the most illustrious Grimoald had obtained—by which the brothers had until then lived—with the consent of his faithful men, both the bishops and the aforesaid nobles, in honor of God and in worship of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of blessed Martin, to whom those places had been dedicated, he permitted blessed Remaclus to designate, for the use of the servants of God, so that henceforth they might live more peacefully and devote themselves more freely to God alone without pressure from their neighbors, twelve leagues around both monasteries. Within those boundaries, whatever land there was would be cultivated only by the tenants of the two monasteries.

Among the Gauls, a league is said to be a distance of one thousand five hundred [Col. 1165A] paces, that is, twelve stadia. The holy man willingly accepted this donation, confirmed by a testament and authenticated by the impression of the royal ring, and reverently preserved it.

Then, in the fourteenth year of his reign, the same king bequeathed by testament to blessed Remaclus certain properties in Aquitaine: namely, the customs station at the port of Vetraria on the rivers Taunacus and Itta; likewise the port of Sellis and Vogatium on the river Loire, together with everything belonging to it. A document, subscribed by his own hand, bears witness to this. It says:

“Those holy and venerable monasteries called Stabulaus or Malmundarium, where the venerable man Remaclus, bishop and abbot, appears, with Christ’s favor, to preside; monasteries which the illustrious Grimoald, mayor of the palace, built by his own work in the vast forest of the Ardennes in honor of Saint [Col. 1165B] Peter and Saint Paul, and Saint Martin, and the other saints; just as we granted those places for the construction of the monasteries by our command from our forest; although they have been enriched by Christ’s grace, they are seen to possess only a small amount of worldly substance. Therefore, warned by divine inspiration, we have decided to direct and provide some portion of our fisc toward those monasteries.”

And so on, as follows in that same document—which the author calls a “command.” Finally, from the royal estates adjoining those monasteries he gave them tithes, which those monasteries still possess.

### XXI

After this, that king, having governed the kingdom of Austrasia with distinction, ended his life. Grimoald, the mayor of the palace, or prefect of the palace, or, as some wish, master of the cavalry, was summoned to Paris by Clovis, Sigebert’s brother, under the pretext of receiving gifts, and was detained there because he had made a cleric of his master Sigebert’s son—whom he had taken under his protection in order to substitute him for his father in the kingdom—wishing to make his own son king.

After Clovis died, his son Chlothar ruled in the West, while Childeric, Chlothar’s brother, ruled in Austrasia. Blessed Remaclus therefore approached him and asked him to confirm what his uncle had donated to him. The king willingly agreed and, as the man of God had requested, ordered his successor Theodard and Odo the domesticus to remeasure land of the same extent [Col. 1165D]. The king retained half of it for himself and assigned and confirmed the remainder by testament for the use of the servants of God. It is clear that the man of God acted with great prudence, so that, if his successors should perhaps at some time be less powerful, they could more easily claim for themselves what was lacking, without the envy or harassment of their neighbors.

King Chlothar also died, and the monarchy devolved upon Childeric. But when he was later killed because of the insolence of his character, he had his brother Theodoric as successor in the western parts of the kingdom; Ebroin was Theodoric’s master of the cavalry. The Austrasians, detesting their tyranny, supported and obeyed Prince Pippin. When he learned that the observance of religion was increasing in the aforesaid monasteries, he assigned, for the support of the table of God’s servants, two villas from his royal estates—one in Harbanium and the other in the Ardennes—in reverence for God and Saint Remaclus [reverence. *Patrologia edition*].

During their time, it is said, he went to Rome to seek the intercession of Saint Peter and the other saints, and remained there devoted to prayers and fasts until, strengthened by divine and angelic consolation, he deserved to obtain a portion of the relics of that most blessed apostle. These relics, adorned with gold and gems, are preserved among us with the greatest honor. Although this may perhaps seem incredible to some, we who venerate that incomparable treasure have witnessed many benefits divinely granted in its presence. Whoever wishes may read of them in his Book of Virtues, or Miracles.

Now blessed Remaclus was advanced in age, though more mature in character than in years. Sensing that the day of his calling was near and that the time was approaching when the honor he had earned through labor on earth would be repaid in heaven, he summoned his subjects to him. They were grieving both over his death and over their own desolation, and he consoled them as follows:

“Behold, most holy fathers; behold, dearest brothers, whom I hold fast in my inmost being, half of my soul: I am entering upon the way of all flesh, and shall not return to you again. Thus it is your loneliness, you whom I am leaving, that troubles me—not my departure, for I am strengthened by God, who consoles me.

“The common condition of all mortals does not frighten me, since even the whole life of a wise man ought to be a kind of meditation on death [Note: Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I, 30]. Ugly death cannot befall a brave man, nor untimely death a wise man, nor miserable death one who foresees it.

“Your tenderness moves me greatly, since you still need to be formed by more solid disciplines. I fear for you altogether, lest, if ravening wolves attack, there should be no one to repel them. Indeed, I dedicated these monasteries to God and his saints, and adapted them to your use; in this matter I employed your strong and faithful assistance. But what will happen in the future is unknown to me. You see clearly the condition of our affairs and how this world lies in the power of evil.

“If, therefore, my prayer has any influence with you, I beg you to take care never to be led astray from that integrity which I wished to produce in you. Rather, remain always joined together and of one mind in Christ, as you have received both through the tradition of the Fathers, through reading the Holy Scriptures, and through my anxious exhortation.

“Let sacred reading never be put down from your hands, but let constant meditation be yours in it. For just as a field, however fertile, cannot be fruitful without cultivation, so neither can the mind be fruitful without instruction [Note: Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* II, 5]. You know that for a learned and educated person, to live is to think.

“Devote yourselves frequently to prayer. Beg God’s pardon for sins committed through human frailty; watch carefully so that you do not commit such sins again. For if anyone gives himself over to carelessness and laziness, he will have called upon God in vain.

“Let it be your virtue to flee vice, and your first wisdom to have escaped folly [Note: Horace, *Epistles* I, 1, 41]. Modesty, and incorruptible faith, the sister of justice, and naked truth [Note: Horace, *Odes* I, 24, 7–8], should claim a dwelling in your hearts, so that those who see your deeds may be summoned to imitate you.

“Make true confession of your sins to God and to your superiors. Reveal the impressions of temptations at their very first entrance. For the perverse shame of fools, while concealing their wounds, supplies them with greater strength.
