“Show obedience to your superiors; conform your minds to their instruction. For then each person lives rightly if he takes care to be what he hears [Note: Horace, *Epistles* I, 16, 17].

“Restrain yourselves from everything anger suggests; for it is the sole triumph of innocence not to sin when one has the power to do so. Exercise moderation even in the best things. There is a measure in all things; there are, finally, fixed limits beyond and short of which right cannot exist [Note: Horace, *Satires* I, 1, 107]. Each person must measure himself by his own foot and his own standard [Note: Horace, *Epistles* I, 7, 98].

“Let no one wrong another. For it is better to suffer wrong than to inflict it. Embrace patience, which is the harbor of sufferings; no one is so barbarous that he cannot be softened, provided he lends a patient ear to cultivation [Note: Horace, *Epistles* I, 1, 39–40].

“Do not shrink from any labor imposed upon you by your superiors, because every hard labor becomes bearable through exertion, and use or habit in labor makes even pains more endurable.

“Flee laziness altogether, for virtue does not easily accompany sluggish minds. Reject pride above all, so that you may possess true freedom. For a man whose mind is occupied by pride must not be considered free.

“Pursue chastity, for, as divine Scripture says, no weighing is worthy of a continent soul.

“Let prosperous successes—which weary even the minds of the wise—not delight you; for one who rejoices excessively in good fortune will be shaken when circumstances change in the opposite direction [Note: Horace, *Epistles* I, 10, 30].

“Above all, I admonish you to preserve peace and concord. Just as you are gathered in two monasteries, so let a twofold love of God and neighbor burn within you. Since one shepherd has been placed over you, never allow yourselves to be divided by scandal or schism (Ecclesiasticus XXVI).

“Let no envy, which consumes the bones, lay you waste. For the envious person wastes away at another’s prosperity, and the Sicilian tyrants found no greater torture than envy [Note: Horace, *Epistles* I, 2, 57].

“If your resources should perhaps be smaller, do not complain. For the person who has the use of things at his disposal is not poor [Note: Horace, *Epistles* I, 12, 4]. Nature herself daily reminds us how few, how cheap, and how small are the things we need. Wealth does not lighten the minds and cares of human beings [Note: Lucretius].”

“These are the matters, dearest ones, about which I wished to admonish you, as though saying my final farewell, since I am about to depart from life. Take care of them, and let them cling all the more closely to your hearts the greater the distress you suffer from my departure. If they produce any fruit among you, you will render me the greatest joy.

“At the same time, remember that you too will die, and do not, I beg you, allow the time granted for repentance to slip away in vain. The day will come—indeed it will come—when you will desire the use of an hour in vain. Therefore, while there is time, work what is good toward all (Galatians VI).

“Death is the final boundary of things [Note: Horace, *Epistles* I, 16, 79]. No one is granted perpetual possession, and heir follows heir as wave comes upon wave [Note: Horace, *Epistles* II, 2, 175–176]. We are dust and shadow [Note: Horace, *Odes* IV, 7, 16]. One death awaits all, and once only must the road of death be trodden [Note: Horace, *Odes* I, 28, 15–16]. But if we depart from here in good works and righteous deeds, we shall be blessed, freed together with our bodies from every desire and rivalry.”

By these most gentle and final words he eased their sorrow. Then, seized by a slight fever, after strengthening himself with the viaticum of the most sacred body and blood of the Lord, he returned his soul to the Creator in the hands of his dearest sons, after a long service rendered to Christ.

The old Israelite, having departed from Egypt and despoiled his neighbor, brought back increased talents. His body was honorably prepared and buried with much melody of psalms and hymns in the oratory of Saint Martin, which he himself had built. There he also lay for some time, meanwhile giving testimony through miracles that he lived with the Lord.

The lord Papolenus, an apostolic man whom we mentioned above, succeeded him. Papolenus was succeeded by Sigolinus, equally approved by the judgment of the blessed father; Sigolinus by Godwinus, advanced in years and maturity of character. Godwinus transferred the body of the holy man and placed it in the Church of Saint Peter, and arranged for his tomb to be adorned with gold and silver. There, through his merits, the Lord continues to perform many signs of miracles even to the present day. They have been written down there for the praise and glory of almighty God, who is blessed forever. Amen.

**In the year 976–1018. Thietmar, Bishop of Merseburg.**

[Col. 1169]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THIETMAR: AGE, HOMELAND, BIRTH, DEEDS, WRITINGS

*(Lappenberg, Preface to Thietmar’s Chronicle, in Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Historical Writers, vol. III, p. 723.)*

[Col. 1169A] Thietmar, a Saxon by nationality, was the son of Count Sigifrid and Cunigunda. Born of distinguished parents, he had the counts of Walbeck as his ancestors on his father’s side and the family of Stade on his mother’s side.

Both of his great-grandfathers [Note: He himself says “great-great-grandfathers” at I, 6. Thietmar’s genealogy is described on the following page], each named Liutherus [Note: Or Liutharius, Liuthardus; the same name], followed King Henry’s army and were killed by the Slavs near Lunkini on the same day. One of them had a son, Liutharius, the paternal grandfather of our Thietmar and founder of the monastery of Walbeck.

When Liutharius was handed over for custody to Count Berthold of Bavaria because of his participation in the conspiracy made against King Otto in 941, Liutharius later gave his daughter Eila, Thietmar’s paternal aunt, to Berthold in marriage. From this marriage was born Henry the Margrave [Note: *Annals of Saxony* under 977; it nevertheless, in a serious error, considers Henry, the son of Margrave Berthold, and Henry called the younger duke to be the same person; Mascov and Scholliner supported this view].

Of Liutharius’s sons, the eldest received both his father’s name and his county, to which the Brandenburg margraviate was later added. The second, Thietmar, was abbot of Corvey, from whom we may suppose that our Thietmar drew much useful material for his work. The third, Sigifrid, went to Poland in 972 with Udo, Margrave of Brandenburg, against Mieszko [Note: II, 19]; in 979, together with his brother Liutharius, he received Count Gero as a prisoner to be guarded [Note: III, 7]. In 983 he fought against the Obodrites [Note: III, 11] and was present at the defeat at Tangermünde; but he was so weakened by a fall from his horse that he could no longer bear arms [Note: IV, 9]. Later he took part in the embassy which the empress sent to Poland around 988 to reconcile Mieszko and Bolesław [Note: This embassy must have taken place before 990, since Sigifrid had already died at the beginning of that year].

He died at Walbeck on the Ides of March, 990 [Note: The Saxon annalist gives this year of death; it is confirmed by Thietmar himself, who speaks at IV, 11 of his father’s death and at VI, 30 of the time when Thiedricus was abbot of Walbeck. The year 996 might seem to be indicated by what Thietmar himself wrote in the margin of the manuscript at IV, 11; but the context clearly shows that this date of the year belongs rather to the following period], leaving by Cunigunda the following sons: Count Henry; Frederick, prefect of Magdeburg, who frequently showed himself an associate of men acting ferociously [Note: IV, 26; VI, 29]; Sigifrid, abbot of Berge in 1009 and placed over the see of Münster in 1020, to whom Thietmar dedicated his work; Bruno, educated at Corvey, [Col. 1170A] abbot of Berge in 1025 and consecrated bishop of Verden in 1034; and our Thietmar, born at Halberstadt, apparently, on July 25, 976 [Note: III, 4]. Bishop Hilliward baptized and confirmed him there [Note: IV, 12].

As a boy he was instructed in the first elements of letters at Quedlinburg by Emnilda, his father’s maternal aunt. In his twelfth year his father entrusted him to Ricdag, abbot of Saint John in Magdeburg, whose school was then flourishing among the most distinguished. Thietmar devoted three years there to study. He apparently did not reach Greek letters, since no trace of them appears throughout the entire work; he seems to have read almost only the poets of Latium, since he neither names the others nor brings from them passages quoted or expressed in imitation.

In his fourteenth year, when his father could not secure him a place among the canons of Saint Maurice, he was received with great ceremony, his father being present, among the vicars who performed sacred offices there [Note: I understand the words at IV, 11 thus: “There I spent three years; on the feast of All Saints, at Saint Maurice, because he could not give me to this altar, I was joined by him to the fellowship of the brothers.” Most say that Thietmar was a canon of Magdeburg; but the *Deeds of the Bishops of Merseburg* also say: “At Saint Maurice in Magdeburg, a servant and spiritual brother”], on November 2, 989.

The following year, deprived both of his father and of his grandmother Mathilda, he seems to have suffered many hardships with his mother Cunigunda at the hands of his uncle Liutharius because of the inheritance, until the emperor came to their aid in 996 [Note: IV, 11].

In 994, when his mother’s relatives had been captured by the Northmen at Stade, they wished to give Thietmar as a hostage for their ransom. But on the very day when he, intending to set out toward the pirates, had already left the school in lay clothing, his uncle Sigifrid escaped from custody; the other captives, their limbs cut off, were thrown outside by the Northmen. Thus Thietmar, after visiting his uncles at Stade and Hersefeld, soon returned safely to Magdeburg [Note: IV, 16].

In 998, after his mother Cunigunda died [Note: IV, 25], when the brothers divided the inheritance, Thietmar received half of the property. His ancestors held this property from the church of Walbeck by feudal right; most of it had been transferred by them to that monastery. For this reason he says that he himself “was then, by paternal tradition, a servant of the church of Walbeck” [Note: VI, 30. He praises his estates: Retmerslevo I, 7; VI, 27, 31; Egisvilla VI, 29; Heslinge VIII, 8].

The reason he received this share of the inheritance seems to have been that it enabled him to attain the dignity of provost at Walbeck. But his uncle Liutharius had long before granted it, in exchange for ten hides, to a certain noble and wealthy cleric named Thiedricus. Therefore Thietmar could succeed to the dignity he had long desired only after many prayers and after giving an estate to his uncle, when his predecessor withdrew, on May 6, 1002 [Note: VI, 30. Wedekind incorrectly places this in the year 1000, relying on the fact that a custodian already existed at that time in the church of Walbeck and that Thietmar gave up the dignity of provost on the very day of his episcopal anointing. But Thietmar explicitly says that he gave it up only when he was staying at Walbeck between Ascension and Pentecost—May 26 to June 5—in 1009, after having been provost there for seven years and twenty-four days. This calculation falls precisely in 1002].

That he had obtained it by payment subsequently caused him considerable regret, since he accused himself on that account of simony. When he soon afterward fell ill, he went immediately after recovering to Cologne, both to cleanse himself of that fault and to do penance for a violated tomb [Note: VI, 30].

On his return, he was ordained priest in the city of Altstadt by Tagino, archbishop of Magdeburg, apparently in 1003, on December 21, with King Henry present and giving him a chasuble [Note: VI, 31]. In 1004 he accompanied the king, who was setting out for Italy with Tagino, as far as Tingen near Kempten [Note: VI, 3], where he seems to have attended the dedication of the Church of Blessed Mary on March 19 [Note: As may be conjectured from the Merseburg calendar for that day]. Returning from there, he celebrated Palm Sunday at Gernrode and Easter itself at Magdeburg [Note: VI, 3]. In 1008 he accompanied the king, setting out with Tagino against Bolesław; but when they had reached as far as Jüterbog, they thought it safer to return home [Note: VI, 24].

Tagino’s friendship was of the greatest benefit to our Thietmar. While Wigbert, bishop of Merseburg, was still alive, Tagino had already recommended Thietmar to the king as his future bishop. Although the king at first agreed and later appointed Ethelgar to that see, Tagino nevertheless, after summoning Thietmar to Augsburg, arranged for him to receive there, with the election of those present, the episcopal dignity and staff entrusted to him by the king on April 21, 1009.

On the third day afterward he was anointed with chrism at Neuburg by Tagino, with the king present [Note: IV, 27; Merseburg Calendar, the eighth day before the Kalends of May]. He accompanied the king as far as Regensburg. But then, hastening to his own see, he summoned at Eitra the clerics subject to him, many of whom had fled, in order to strengthen them and bring back the absent to their office.

After being honorably received at Merseburg and enthroned by Eric, bishop of Havelberg, he celebrated Ascension at Magdeburg. From there he proceeded to the monastery of Walbeck and, by the common counsel of the monks, entrusted its governance to his half-brother Willigis, born of another mother, perhaps a concubine.

He celebrated Pentecost at Merseburg with the king and accompanied him from there to Magdeburg [Note: VI, 31].

In 1010 his name occurs in a royal charter dated at Merseburg on July 28 [Note: Höfer, *Zeitschrift* I, 160]. At the end of January 1011 he went with the king to Liubusua, for the city to be newly built; on that occasion he recognized there a great work of the Romans [Note: VI, 39].

On May 6, 1012, he was present at the consecration of the church at Bamberg [Note: VI, 40 ff.]. On June 1 he celebrated Pentecost with the king at Merseburg, where he himself sang Mass in place of the sick Tagino. When Tagino soon afterward died, Thietmar immediately hurried to Magdeburg so that he might exercise his church’s rights in the election of a new archbishop. From there, summoned by the king, he went with the elected Waltherd to Grona on June 14 and spoke at length to the king about the needs of his church. Returning to Magdeburg on June 22, he attended Waltherd’s anointing [Note: VI, 44].

Soon afterward, on July 25, he went to the army assembled near Schrenz [Note: VI, 45]. But he returned to Merseburg already on August 3, early enough to assist the dying Archbishop Waltherd and, with the other bishops, to elect his nephew Theodoric as his successor.

On August 22, while consecrating two altars at Magdeburg, he was frightened by news of the great defeat inflicted by the Poles and immediately hurried to the queen at Merseburg. She sent him with the provincial forces toward the Mulde, and on September 21 he met the king at Seehausen. He did not neglect again to remind the king of the needs of his see, whose claims had been raised by the archbishops of Magdeburg.

The following day he came with the king to Magdeburg. There, at the king’s persuasion, Gero was appointed archbishop in place of Theodoric. Thietmar then went to Merseburg for a court to be held there [Note: VI, 50; Höfer I, 161].

After it had been completed, he was summoned to his beloved cousin Liudgarda, who was ill at Wolmirstedt. He received her final breath on November 13 and accompanied her body to Walbeck [Note: VI, 51]. He celebrated Christmas at the royal estate of Palithi.

In 1013, while the king stayed at Merseburg three times, Thietmar obtained from him on September 22 a certain donation for his church [Note: Höfer I, 163]. On November 1, 1014, the emperor was again at Merseburg, and in 1015 he celebrated Easter there [Note: VII, 6; Böhmer, *Regesta* II, nos. 1129, 1140].

In that year Thietmar began to build a new episcopal church. He himself laid its foundation in the form of a cross on May 18, with Archbishop Gero present [Note: VII, 9]. In September the emperor again stayed at Merseburg [Note: VII, 15; Böhmer no. 1141] and sent our Thietmar with Gero to Meissen on October 8 to repair and guard that fortress.

When they returned fourteen days later, Thietmar persuaded Gero on the journey to confer upon him four of the nine towns claimed by the see of Merseburg. Gero did so, and Thietmar accepted them. Then, going to Walbeck, he celebrated the feast of All Saints there [Note: VII, 16].

On March 1, 1016, the recently elected bishop of Meissen was consecrated by Gero at Merseburg, with Thietmar supporting him [Note: VII, 20]. We see Thietmar again at Magdeburg before Easter and around the feast of John the Baptist [Note: VII, 25].

There, on February 22, 1017, the emperor, who had come there from Merseburg, settled a dispute between the churches of Merseburg and Meissen, though not in the manner Thietmar had hoped [Note: VII, 37]. At the end of March Thietmar himself went to Meissen, apparently at the emperor’s command [Note: VII, 39]. On October 1, while present at Merseburg, the emperor richly endowed Thietmar and his church with gifts and estates [Note: VII, 48].

In May 1018 [Col. 1175A] Thietmar visited the part of his diocese situated around Rochlitz because of disputes that had arisen with Count Ekkehard. Ekkehard harassed him so severely that he was forced to seek the emperor’s assistance [Note: VII, 10].

These are the matters which he himself relates about himself in the *Chronicles*. He died on December 1, 1018 [Note: The Quedlinburg Annals under 1018, above p. 84; the Merseburg Calendar. Since the Saxon Annalist and the Saxon Chronographer assign his death to 1019, this must be understood to refer to the consecration of his successor Bruno. [Col. 1175C] Höfer, *Zeitschrift* I, 167, and Köhler, *Fragmente zur Geschichte Leipzigs*, 1787, p. 51, have already shown that two charters from the years 1021 and 1022, in which he is mentioned as living, are spurious], before completing his forty-third year.

His body was buried in the church at Merseburg [Note: At the head was inscribed:

> The reverend lord Saint Ditmar, bishop

To the left and right:

> What those who follow the right path think, do, and teach,  
> Thietmar’s deeds declare through heart, hand, and tongue.

At the feet:

> By the grace of God I am what I am.

But after another sarcophagus was placed over it in 1760, these inscriptions were erased. See Wagner’s edition, p. 276].

He says that he was short in stature, deformed in his left jaw and the corresponding side, and ridiculous because his nose had been broken in childhood [Note: IV, 51].

Thietmar began to write the Books of the *Chronicles* [Note: This is what he himself calls them in the prologue, verse 39. Codex 2 calls them *Deeds of the Saxons*. He never wrote anything else] when he already held the episcopal see [Note: I, 1]. Yet he did not complete all of them in a continuous act of composition [Note: He first composed the work at the end of 1012 [ [Col. 1175C] This is apparent from the words at I, 7: “this year, etc., I saw,” referring to the death of Lady Liudgarda, who died on November 13, 1012. Bethmann]; he seems to have written the following books through approximately chapter 52 of Book VI in that same year [ [Col. 1175D] The words at VI, 39—“which in this year, alas, recognize that it is not false”—refer to the disaster narrated at VI, 48 and could not have been written correctly except in 1012, when that disaster occurred. The same]; he added the end of Book VI in 1014 [ [Col. 1175D] The verses at VI, 61—

> Now twelve times two years have passed since he ruled,

—and the words that follow at VI, 57, compared with VII, 3, show that he did not write either earlier or later; they concern the period after Easter 1014. The same].

He completed Book VII only at the end of 1017 or the beginning of 1018 [ [Col. 1175D] VII, 48: “In the month of December”; and shortly afterward: “Before I bring this year to its conclusion.” The same]. Finally, almost foreseeing his death [ [Col. 1175D] It contains, in chapter 7 and 8, something like a confession and testament of the author], he applied his hand to the last book during the final period of his life. He wrote its first seven chapters around April 1018 [ [Col. 1175D] VIII, end of chapter 4, compared with the beginning of chapter 8. The same], and the last chapter no earlier than September [ [Col. 1175D] VIII, 17: “He held a conference concerning the state in Swabia.” The same].

Thus, after different intervals, he added the remaining portions to the earlier part of the *Chronicles*, whenever swift rumor brought him something new to write [ [Col. 1175D] As he himself says at VIII, 4. See also IV, 35. This is shown especially by Book VIII, both by the whole method of composition and by the state of the author’s manuscript, where a blank page was left between the very place at which we said above that the author stopped around April 16 (chapter 7, end) and the following chapter. The same].

It is therefore clear that the entire work can be called neither unfinished nor complete, since the author himself had not set a definite end for it [ [Col. 1176C] I, 1: “To whose unknown clemency I humbly entrust how this writing may be concluded.” The same], unless perhaps he intended to conclude it with the death of Emperor Henry [ [Col. 1176C] *Life of the Kings of Saxony*, prologue V, 7], if he had lived long enough to accompany him to that point.

But, perhaps led by some foreboding of death, shortly before his death he seems to have wished to complete his book: he himself corrected, supplemented, and enlarged the whole work after it had been written out by others [ [Col. 1176C] See below the description of the Dresden manuscript. The same]. At that time, I believe, he also added the prologue addressed to his brother [ [Col. 1176C] Prologue, verses 25 ff., compared with VIII, 14. The same. Bethmann]. He remained occupied with writing the book even in the last year of his life.

[Col. 1176A] Thietmar wrote in a sufficiently rough and unpolished style, using many words intermixed with barbarisms and others employed with a different meaning—so that one might suppose he had never handled the ancient writers, had he not incorporated into his work, sometimes verbatim and sometimes by imitation, individual words and longer passages from Horace [Note: [Col. 1176C] I, 1, 7; II, prologue 2; III, 7, 16; IV, 10, 11, 26; V, 16; VI, 12, 23, 46.], especially, and Lucan [Note: [Col. 1176C] II, 21; V, 15, 24; VI, prologue 39; VIII, 4.], but also Juvenal [Note: [Col. 1176C] IV, 51.], Persius [Note: [Col. 1176C] II, 2, 18; IV, 41, 51; VI, 1, 27.], Virgil [Note: [Col. 1176C] IV, 5, 11; V, 20; VI, 9; VII, 5, 6; VIII, 4.], Ovid [Note: [Col. 1176C] VI, 61; VII, 12.], Martial [Note: [Col. 1176C] VI, 10, 61 at the end. But perhaps he took these from a commentator on Persius.], Terence [Note: [Col. 1176C] II, 4; V, 6; VII, 51.], Ausonius [Note: [Col. 1176C] II, 2, unless he also took this from a commentator on Persius.], Statius [Note: [Col. 1176C] I, 13.], Cato [Note: [Col. 1176C] I, 5; VI, 26.], Macrobius [Note: [Col. 1176D] V, 1, 10; VIII, 3.], and, among the Fathers, Augustine [Note: [Col. 1176D] VI, 14.] and Gregory [Note: [Col. 1176D] I, 1; II, 28; VII, 41; VIII, 14.]. From the poems of a more recent age, there can be no doubt that he had read *Ecbasis captivi* [Note: [Col. 1176D] VII, 21.]. Besides these authors, whose sources we know, he here and there inserted poetic cento-like passages into his prose; whether he took them from others or pieced them together himself is not entirely clear [Note: [Col. 1176D] For example: I, 1, “as far as bold or skillful confidence permits”; 6, “the glory and consolation of the fatherland”; 7, “as the day is granted to the living, so the night is granted to the dead.” II, 15, “he supplicatingly struck the divine ears.” III, 16, “an unconquerable wall for the entrusted flocks.” IV, 15, “envious, mocking others, himself to be mocked”; ibid., “sparing no one according to his due, a glutton and a hypocrite.” V, 1, “Heinricus wished to reign against God’s will.” VI, 6, “may the unstable course always roll downward”; ibid., “thus, by alternating, [he granted] rest friendly to all”; 39, “taming minds tossed by waves with the bridle of wisdom.” VII, 13, “a monk in habit, but a deceitful fox in conduct”; 27, “the Scythians, who carry their houses with them and are nourished by wild animals and horse’s milk.”]

Although he did not excel in elegance of language, abundance of learning, or literary craftsmanship, he nevertheless must not be said to have approached the history of his own time unequipped. For, joined both by the nobility of his birth and by his episcopal dignity to the highest-ranking men, and frequently himself involved as a participant in the conduct of public affairs, he was, if anyone was, our man: one who could acquire knowledge of people and events in many ways and preserve a judgment free from every kind of authority and fear. And although we cannot deny that here and there he allowed himself to be carried away in judgment by a certain partisan inclination [Note: [Col. 1176D] For example, concerning the Slavs and Bavarians (V, 11), the Lotharingians (IV, 10; VI, 32, 39).], this never happened in such a way that he knowingly concealed the truth or distorted it by narrating it perversely. Rather, it must always be kept in mind that there the bishop is speaking about the pagan invaders of his homeland, the Saxon about the Bavarians, who had been hostile to Saxony from the time of Heinricus I, and about the turbulent Lotharingians, the authors of many troubles for the empire.

Throughout the work as a whole it is entirely apparent that the author wished everywhere to tell the truth, so that he did not even spare himself or his relatives when accusing them of actions that seemed to him less than correct [Note: [Col. 1177C] Compare what he himself says at the end of V, 20.]. And when he sometimes seems to pass over some matters in silence and to emphasize others more strongly, this may have arisen, without his knowing it, from the defective condition of the sources from which he drew them. Most of the few errors that we detect here and there [Note: [Col. 1177C] For example, I, 5, 9, 13; II, 1, 3, 15; VII, 28, 29; VIII, 4.] arose from the same cause; others originated in the fact that he was not sufficiently skilled in the Slavonic language.

As sources for his chronicle, besides what he himself saw, he had reports from others [Note: [Col. 1177C] Such as those of Husward (III, 7), Waltherd (III, 9), Avico (III, 11), Meinsvitha (IV, 12), a certain more important man (IV, 23), Merquard (IV, 45), Tagino (V, 25), Sewald (VII, 28, 29), and Gezo (VII, 51); of the emperor Heinricus (VII, 23), and doubtless of other eminent men with whom he associated. Compare also the truthful testimony at VIII, 12; I, 7, “swift rumor” at VIII, 4; “he informed me from the report of his predecessors” at IV, 47; “I learned truly” at I, 7; “I heard” at VII, 50; “I heard from credible men” at VII, 53; “the shrewd memory of the ancients” at I, 2; “I learned from the most ancient men” at I, 7.], and in the earlier part he also made use of written books: Widukind’s *Deeds of the Saxons*, from which he very often copied the actual words [Note: [Col. 1177C] There is no reason, with Wedekind (*Not.* I, 302), to suppose that these passages were not taken from Widukind himself but from the same source from which Widukind drew. Compare especially the Sallustian passage at II, 3.]; the Quedlinburg Annals [Note: [Col. 1177C] Compare *Archiv.* of the Society VI, 647, 689.]; Ruotger’s *Life of Bruno* [Note: [Col. 1177D] II, 15.]; the *Life of Saint Othmar* [Note: [Col. 1177D] I, 5.]; the Merseburg Calendar [Note: [Col. 1177D] He himself entered certain material in it, VIII, 7. Compare *Archiv.* of the Society IV, 280.]; the decree of the Dortmund synod [Note: [Col. 1177D] VI, 13.]; and documents of the churches of Merseburg, Magdeburg, and Walbeck. He also appears to have used the Magdeburg and Halberstadt Annals [Note: [Col. 1177D] I have no doubt that Thietmar used such materials; but it is difficult to say what he took from them, since we can judge on this matter only from those writers who, besides those sources, already possessed Thietmar’s *Chronicle*.]. Finally, he used letters and other information committed to writing, which we seem especially able to recognize where the narrative is more elegant than usual, particularly in what he relates about Italian affairs.

This work, so useful for learning the history of its time, was both known and valued by later writers. It was used by Adelbold in the *Life of Heinricus II* [Note: [Col. 1177D] From IV, 31, through VI, 8, he reproduced both the sequence of the narrative and often the actual words of our author.]; by the Saxon Annalist [Note: [Col. 1177D] He excerpted everything from the year 908 through 1018, using not the genuine Thietmar manuscript but a manuscript that was the source of the Brussels copy, as the variant readings clearly show.]; by the Saxon Chronographer [Note: [Col. 1177D] That he drew this material from Thietmar himself—and from the genuine manuscript—not from the Saxon Annalist is shown above all by the passages for the years 1014, 1016, and 1021, which approach Thietmar’s wording more closely than the Annalist’s. Besides these, compare the years 955 and 965 (from II, 10); 968 (from II, 14; VI, 30); 971 (from II, 16; III, 2); 982 (from III, 10, 11). It is not entirely clear whether he took several other passages from Thietmar or from the Quedlinburg Annals and some Magdeburg chronicle.]; the Magdeburg Chronicle [Note: [Col. 1178C] Where a certain venerable bishop is mentioned without his name being added.]; the Halberstadt Chronicle; Gobelinus Persona in the *Cosmodromium* [Note: [Col. 1178C] *Aetas* VI, chapter 49, from our III, 4–15; and chapter 52 from III, 3, 4, 7, 10, 12, 13; V, 16; VI, 5, 6, 13, 22, 40, 49; VII, 26, 28, 31; VIII, 4.]; the *Life of Meinwerk* [Note: [Col. 1178C] Chapter 24 in the manuscript was added afterward from VIII, 12.]; the Merseburg Chronicle; Paulus Lange in the 1515 *Chronicle of Zeitz* and the 1536 *Chronicle of Naumburg*; and perhaps also Honorius Solitarius in the *Image of the World* [Note: [Col. 1178C] A manuscript of this work preserved at Stendal in the Alvensleben Library contains, under the year 919, a passage from Thietmar I, 7, collated by Vignoles; this passage is not found in the Speyer edition of 1583. What Jordanus relates about Poppo in his *Chronicle* (*Muratori, Antiquities of Italy* IV) he took neither from Thietmar nor from Widukind, but from Sigebert of Gembloux.].

Only two manuscripts of Thietmar are extant:

1. The Dresden Royal Library manuscript, on parchment, quarto, donated to the monastery of Saint Peter at Merseburg by Wernher, bishop of Merseburg (1073–1101), and subsequently lent to Siegmund of Lindenau, later bishop of Merseburg (1535–1544) [Note: [Col. 1178C] Brotuf, *Merseburg Chronicle* II, 7, 385.], transferred to Wittenberg in 1574 and to Dresden in 1579. It was accurately collated for our use by the distinguished Mauricius Haupt, and we have based our edition on that collation. The manuscript is an autograph [Note: [Col. 1178C] “I believe it to be Dietmar’s autograph,” Albinus had already written in the manuscript; that this is Albinus’s hand and conjecture is shown by Mader in the preface to the *Walbeck Chronicle*. But Haupt was the first to establish the matter conclusively.], consisting of 207 folios [Note: [Col. 1178D] Not 211, as Haupt believes. See *Archiv.* VII, 421 ff., where he describes our manuscript.]—of which 15 are now missing—with 21 lines on each page. It was written by several scribes at different times, from the author’s dictation [Note: [Col. 1178D] In the subsequent dictation, I, 14.] or from autograph sheets. Shortly before his death Thietmar himself corrected it continuously, supplied gaps left by the scribes, and enlarged the book in a second revision, adding names, more precise descriptions of times, and matters expressed in greater detail—things which, when he first composed the work, he either omitted or did not yet know [Note: [Col. 1178D] For example, II, 2; III, 3, 5, 11; VI, 23, 31, 40, 46, 55; VII, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 13, 16, 17, 30, 35, 37, 39, 45, 48; VIII, 1, 4, 8.].

In addition, he himself wrote many other portions of the manuscript in his own hand, especially at the ends of folios, but also entire pages, when the book was first committed to writing [Note: [Col. 1178D] The places where this is most certain are these: III, 14 (manuscript fol. 46); VI, beginning, in the poem (end of fol. 96′); end of 40 (end of fol. 123′); 45–46 in the middle (fols. 128′, 129, and beginning of 129′); end of 61 (fol. 141); VII, 25 (end of fol. 157′); middle of 44 (end of fol. 168′). It cannot be asserted with equal certainty of the end of I, 17 and the following poem (end of fol. 14), III, 7–8 (end of fol. 38′), IV, 43 (end of fol. 74′), and 47 (end of fol. 76′). The statements found in *Arch.* VII, 424 must be restricted accordingly. BETHMANN.]. The separation of words is very often neglected. He generally left unchanged the scribes’ orthography, which frequently varies within the same word—*avinculus* and *avunculus*; *incolumis* and *incolomis*; *ecclessia*, *eclesia*, and *ecclesia*; *letus* and *laetus*; *egregius*, *egreius*, and *egrius*; *imperator* and *inperator*; *succipere* and *suscipere*; *comitissa* and *cometissa*; *Libusua* and *Liubusua*; *Bozlavus* and *Bolizlavus*; *Lusizi*, *Luzici*, *Liutici*, *Liuticii*, and *Liuzici*; *Gisillerus* and *Gisilerus*; *Herimannus* and *Hirimannus*—although Thietmar himself was not everywhere consistent in this, and here and there corrected what he had written himself.

After 1073 another hand—the same hand that subscribed several folios with the words “Werner, bishop, to Saint Peter at Merseburg”—corrected and erased much in the manuscript. Yet these changes, made entirely at the writer’s discretion, can almost always be distinguished from Thietmar’s genuine corrections. From Book VI onward, traces of this hand appear only rarely. The same hand frequently added the marginal sign *NOTA*; in other places, however, this seems to have been added by the first scribe. Besides these, much was written in the margins in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, of absolutely no importance [Note: [Col. 1179A]

Since the autograph itself could be of the greatest usefulness in reproducing Thietmar, I begged the distinguished Karl Falkenstein, most learned director of the Dresden Royal Library, to send me the manuscript for a time. Through the generosity of this most gracious man, I immediately obtained my wish, and I have not hesitated to set forth my conclusions about it.

It is established that the book was written at the beginning of the eleventh century in twenty-five quires, although the twelfth is missing and a bifolium was inserted between the fourth and fifth. Each book, with the sole exceptions of the second and seventh, is completed in its own quires, so that only the third and eighth begin with incomplete quires; these therefore must have been attached with a single stroke of the pen to the preceding ones. Each book—especially the first, second, third, and fourth, which deal with individual kings—must be regarded almost as a separate work. In almost every case, after one had been completed, another narrative was added or inserted, making it clear that Thietmar devoted attention to the work at different times.

Thus Book I was written in one hand through the words *scriptis confirmavit* in chapter 11; the remainder of the chapter through *consuluit* was written later; chapter 12 at another time; chapters 13 and 14 in another hand; chapter 15 again in another hand; then, after two blank pages had been inserted, chapters 16 and 17 through *exaltata*; and afterward the remainder was written [Col. 1179C]. In Book II the text was written in one hand from beginning to end, but folios 31a, 31b, 31c, and 31d were inserted into the completed work—namely, chapters 22–26, by which the thread of the narrative taken from Widukind is interrupted. Verses were also prefixed after the book had been completed.

Book III was written by the same hand as the preceding books. On folios 38′ and 46′, Thietmar’s hand wrote the words “For whose sake … until he visited more fully.” After this, chapter 8, and in chapter 13 the words “alone until it was burned” and “and in the year until he is chosen,” were inscribed in previously blank spaces. Book IV was written in a hand different from the earlier ones; chapters 35–39 were written in another hand; and, beginning with quire X, chapters 40–48 through “to bring about” were written in a third hand. The remainder, beginning with “You see,” is in a fourth hand.

Book V consists of quires XI and XIII, with XII missing, and is the work of one hand. The verses of the preface beginning with the tenth, and the verses of the epilogue 27–34 and again 35–39, were added by other hands at other times.

The first quire of Book VI was added by the scribe of Book V; folios 105–123 were added in another hand, which may be regarded as Thietmar’s, since he wrote the final lines of page 123′, chapter 40: “After this synod takes place here … it is to me.” Perhaps the remainder of the book, through folios 128, 128′–129′, 129′–133, 133–138, 138′–141, and 141–141′, was also added by him, though at different times.

In Book VII, folio 153′ from “The agreement of these same men is made,” and the remaining folios of the quire, 154–157, as well as folio 167′ from “to himself in the place called Paderborn,” together with the folios completing the quire, 168 and 169, were written in another hand. Folio 173, from “Because every rare thing …” through folio 175, “fled to his father-in-law”; then folio 175, from “The aforesaid king …” through folio 176, “I hope to avenge”; and thereafter, in Thietmar’s hand, “In the year of the Lord DCCC …” through “lost the power of speech,” and “Among the Bavarians …” through “buried,” were added at yet another time.

Book VIII was written at first through folio 183′, from “I fear that it will perish.” [Col. 1180A] Thietmar’s hand added the remaining lines of chapter 7; then page 184 was left blank; folios 184′ through 185′ contain “they were reconciled”; then “Bertoldus …” through folio 190′, “I desire”; and again “Baldericus …” through “on that same day”; then folio 191, “In those days …” through “is not heeded,” were added in Thietmar’s hand [Col. 1180B].

The work, therefore, having been written largely by quires, was unified by Thietmar through words added, altered, or deleted at the beginnings and ends of the quires [ [Col. 1179D] Compare fols. 39, 40, 59, 60.], and through innumerable corrections and new insertions throughout the text itself, so that it is unmistakably apparent that a copy completed in his own hand now exists. Thietmar’s hand, exactly the same as that which the distinguished Hesse first presented in the facsimile of the Merseburg Calendar, can be recognized in many places; but I am convinced that a much larger portion of the manuscript is his work, written at different times and shaped differently according to the writer’s state of mind. It is therefore the first form of the work preserved in the Merseburg Church, later corrected in many places in the time of Bishop Wernher, and copied by the Saxon and Halberstadt chroniclers.

One might easily regard as a second copy of the same work a manuscript perhaps copied from the first during Thietmar’s final months and sent to Sigefrid, abbot of Magdeburg. Since certain passages [Col. 1180C] erased or altered in the authentic manuscript, either at that time or by Bishop Wernher, survive in genuine form in the Brussels manuscript and in the Saxon Annalist, the manuscript from which these were copied must certainly have been derived from the authentic one before Wernher’s time. But that this was done under Thietmar’s supervision cannot be maintained on the basis of the character of the text.

Nevertheless, the fact that this manuscript, or a copy of it, was interpolated at Corvey and was well known through the bishopric of Paderborn is clearly proved by the *Life of Meinwerk*, by Gobelinus Persona of Bielefeld, and by a manuscript written around the year 1400 and transferred from Paderborn to Belgium in the seventeenth century. All of these, together with the Saxon Annalist, diverge in the same way from the reading of the Merseburg manuscript.

Since, therefore, after our Lappenberg’s edition had already been completed, the autograph manuscript came into my hands, I myself consulted it again in many places, so that nothing would be lacking in the work of the most important historian of his fatherland. When I thus saw that some matters which had been doubtful could be established with certainty [Col. 1180D], it seemed appropriate that the entire book should be carefully collated a second and third time by the distinguished Bethmann and Waitz, and that the passages peculiar to the Brussels manuscript should be copied out again by Bethmann, who had gone to Belgium for that purpose. When the work of the distinguished Haupt is added to these efforts, the extent to which the genuine reading has been restored will be shown by comparison of the earlier editions with ours. PERTZ.]

If this manuscript had been preserved intact for us, we would have needed no other; but since eleven of its folios have completely disappeared [Note: [Col. 1180D] Containing the prologue; I, 1–2 at the beginning; IV, 18 in the middle–25 at the beginning; V, 9 in the middle–19 at the end; VI, 26 in the middle–27 in the middle.], while only two others survive in mutilated form [Note: [Col. 1180D] In which I, 15 and VI, 13–15 are read.], in these passages we had to call upon the following manuscript for assistance:

[Col. 1180A] 2. The Brussels Library manuscript, formerly no. 5815, now no. 7513, on parchment, folio, which was donated to the college of the Society of Jesus at Paderborn in 1612 and later belonged to the Society of Jesus at Antwerp. Among other materials [compare *Archiv.* VII, 426], it contains Thietmar, written at the beginning of the fifteenth century.

The manuscript from which this one derives was not the Dresden manuscript, but a copy of it made before 1137 [Note: [Col. 1180D] For in that year the Saxon Annalist ends, and he had already used this exemplar.], by a Corvey monk, as is shown by several additions relating to that monastery [Note: [Col. 1180D] I, 10; II, 26; IV, 48; VII, 10, 25, 53.]. Besides these materials which he received from his fellow monks at Corvey, the scribe also added other matter of his own [Note: [Col. 1180D] VI, 13, 15, 23, 41, 43, 53; he inserts verses in VI, 31; VII, 5.]. Yet all these additions are of such a kind that he must be thought to have drawn them solely from his own invention, not from another source or from a second recension of Thietmar.

In general, he altered and revised the Thietmar text in an excessively arbitrary fashion, rather than copying it; this adulterated form of our author’s text passed from him into the Saxon Annalist and other writers. From this manuscript we have taken only what is lacking in the Dresden manuscript. For the rest, the collation prepared by the illustrious Leibniz, preserved in the Royal Library at Hanover, was sufficient [Note: [Col. 1181C]

How Thietmar’s words have been altered in the Brussels manuscript is shown better by passages published from it in the *Acta Sanctorum* than by the few readings recorded by Leibniz [February II, p. 798; June I, p. 923; etc.]. One example here will suffice:

**Dresden manuscript**

V, 25. “When the course of this exile had then been completed in admirable holiness, the venerable bishop, having already begun to suffer illness even unto death, summoned his beloved Tagino to him and said: ‘Place, my son, your mouth over my mouth, receiving from God the breathing of my spirit.’”

**Brussels manuscript** (*Acta Sanctorum*, June I, p. 923)

“Therefore the venerable pontiff, when the course of this exile had been completed in admirable holiness and he had begun to suffer illness even unto death, summoned his beloved Tagino and addressed him as follows: ‘Place, my dearest son, your mouth over my mouth, and receive from God the inspiration of my spirit.’”

Compare what we have cited at IV, 48; VI, 15; and especially VI, 46, where Thietmar’s words are transcribed in verse [Col. 1182C].]

Some fragments of Thietmar are said to be preserved in the Imperial Library at Vienna and others in the monastery of Rajhrad near Brno [Note: [Col. 1182C] Wagner, preface, p. VIII.], but this is false. Another manuscript was still preserved in 1516 at the monastery of Neuwerk near Halle; where it has now gone is unknown [Note: [Col. 1182C] *Archiv.* V, 679.].

The following editions have appeared. Reinerus Reineccius first published Thietmar, very seriously corrupted by errors, at Frankfurt by Andreas Wechel in 1580; it was reprinted in 1600 from the Dresden manuscript. He complained greatly that he had searched in vain for the autograph, unaware that he already had it in his hands.

J. J. Mader, Helmstedt, 1667, quarto, presents only Reineccius’s text, further corrupted through negligence, together with several marginal notes and genealogical tables.

G. W. von Leibniz, in *Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium* I, 1707, was the first to publish Thietmar in full, supplying the gaps in the autograph from the Brussels manuscript. But he was misled by an error: believing the Brussels manuscript to be more genuine, he neglected the Dresden one. He also presents several notes by Alphonsus de Vignoles, chiefly concerning chronology.

P. F. Laitenberger, Merseburg, 1753, published the first book, enveloped in a cloud of notes.

J. A. Wagner, Nuremberg, 1807, quarto, revised the *Chronicle of Dithmar* anew according to the Dresden manuscript, adding here and there notes by Ursinus, Kinderling, and Wedekind, as well as some of his own. The editor used the Dresden manuscript only carelessly and sometimes even reports its readings incorrectly; but the notes he presents are full of useful material. Compare Ebert on this edition in *Archiv.* II, 55–71.

[Col. 1181C] The following German translations exist: that of Georg Hahn, Leipzig, 1606, folio, made from Reineccius’s edition; and that of J. F. Ursinus, Dresden, 1790, octavo, who translated our work from the Dresden manuscript and added a commentary on Thietmar’s life and work, together with exceptionally good notes. Ursinus also prepared an edition, but did not complete it; Wagner later completed the one he had begun.

Our method in editing Thietmar’s work was to reproduce literally the text of the autograph manuscript as Thietmar himself established it in his second revision. We also presented the orthography as we found it, by no means consistent. Since Thietmar had not altered it, we did not think that we should do so either.

To make clear how the author proceeded in writing—what he first gave, what he later judged should be added or removed, and what he recognized as false and corrected—we indicated in the notes all his corrections and additions incorporated anywhere into the text. The sign 1a denotes the first scribe of the manuscript, while 1b denotes Thietmar’s own hand. We omitted only the very slightest matters and those in which the first reading can no longer be determined with certainty [Note: [Col. 1182C] For the same reason we did not report errors which the first scribe himself appears to have corrected.], so that anyone may now learn the complete history of the work—its origin, development, and completion.

Only one difficulty could arise: in erasures it is not always certain whether they were made by Thietmar himself or by the third hand that appeared after 1063. For the most part, however, comparison with other passages, the authority of what Thietmar himself wrote, or the readings of Manuscript 2 and the Saxon Annalist leaves no doubt about what should be read in each place. All passages in which Manuscript 2 or the Saxon Annalist preserves not the altered but the original reading of the manuscript must have been corrected only later, not by Thietmar.

Nevertheless, in places where the scribe made an obvious slip of the pen and Thietmar himself failed to remove the error—for example, *blanciis* for *blandiciis*, *propietatem* for *proprietatem*, *triburarium* for *tributarium*, and similar cases—we had to depart from the reading, whether the third hand had already supplied the correct form, whether the editors had corrected it, or whether we ourselves had to restore it. We always indicated the first reading in the notes. We called the third hand 1c; we do not present each of its corrections individually, but we do present all those that may be of some importance, so that the present form of the manuscript may be more easily understood.

What has been lost from Manuscript 1 we supplied from Manuscript 2, following in these passages not the orthography of the fifteenth century but Thietmar’s [Note: [Col. 1182C] Thus *proch* and *michi*, as found in Manuscript 2, could not be accepted. BETHM.]. Where Manuscript 1 has been preserved, we have only occasionally given the readings of Manuscript 2 as copied by Leibniz, chiefly in passages where it enlarges and amplifies Thietmar’s narrative. We entirely disregarded the editions in recording variant readings.

We retained the division into books established by Reineccius. Although the Dresden manuscript contains absolutely no division into books or chapters, it is sufficiently clear that this division belongs to Thietmar himself [Note: [Col. 1182C] I, 17: “I have a little book inscribed”; ibid., “let this first little booklet be closed by the death of Heinricus.” III, 1: “Otto the Second is to be the subject of my second little book.” III, 15: “I now begin the sequence of the third volume.” IV, 34: “and let this one [Heinricus II] also mark the title of the fifth book.” Ibid. and in the preceding books. Since, however, the sixth, seventh, and eighth books are nowhere mentioned, while at the end we read “Here begins the little book of the second emperor Heinricus” (compare chapter 8, where he calls this a book), Thietmar seems rather to have intended Book V, or the first book of Heinricus, to include our Books V, VI, and VII; then Book VI, or the second book of Heinricus, would follow. BETHMANN. The fifth is the first book of King Heinricus, the sixth the second of King Heinricus, the seventh the first of Emperor Heinricus, and the eighth the second of Emperor Heinricus. P.]. We added the chapter numbers, since these too are not found in the manuscripts.

[Col. 1183]

# Thietmar’s Chronicle, edited by the distinguished Johann M. Lappenberg, Doctor of Both Laws, archivist of the Republic of Hamburg

(Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*)

## Here begins the prologue of the venerable lord Thietmar, bishop of Merseburg, on the deeds of the Saxons [Note: [Col. 1183] The prologue and the beginning of Book I, lost in Manuscript 1, have been supplied from Manuscript 2.]

[Col. 1183A]

Joined to you by the sweet love of brotherly kinship,  
and dear to me, Sigefrid, I humbly ask you:  
now I, Thietmar [Note: [Col. 1183] *thitmarus* in Manuscript 2, once in this place.], ask that you look kindly upon my writings,  
adding whatever pleases you and removing whatever is superfluous.  
[Note: [Col. 1183C] Sigefrid: abbot of Berge, elected in 1109.]

These things do not shine with any ornament of composition,  
but merely run across the open field in a plain order:  
the life and character of the pious kings of Saxony.  
Under their rule our kingdom shone forth  
like a lofty cedar, feared far and wide.

They speak of the structure of the Church and of our losses,  
of her joyful years, in which she is restored,  
and of all her guardians together.

Let no blame fall upon me if anything in this book varies  
or is lacking, since I have only a little testimony [Note: [Col. 1183C] That is, rare testimony, few witnesses. Compare II, 25.].

Change, dearest brother, the blemishes born of ignorance [Note: [Col. 1183] Leibniz corrected this to “correct the blemishes born of ignorance.” But our Thietmar always uses the noun *naeva*, never *naevus*.],

[Col. 1183B]

believing that I would never have begun to write anything  
if I had not had what I have already mentioned to you [Note: [Col. 1183C] Namely, the lack of witnesses or annals.].

Therefore, kindly pour forth such prayers with me from my groaning heart:

Christ, glory of kings, ruler of realms,  
be gracious to your kingdom entrusted to you,  
so that glory of praise may be rendered to you, not to us,  
and so that your sheepfold [Note: [Col. 1184C] That is, flock.] may never be subject to outsiders [Note: [Col. 1183C] That is, obey them or be subjected to them.] [Col. 1184A].

O you who worship Christ, now pray with the voice of your hearts  
that the majesty of the Lord may deign to have mercy,  
lest the evils we deserve in abundance seize and afflict us—  
evils which the sure voice of coming future evils  
foretold would be manifested in our times—  
alas, already manifest in many ways and certainly still to be manifested.

And whoever you are who must care for my see,  
read this writing and love this little work diligently,  
which briefly unfolds the many things your mind desires.

Flourishing composition surpasses all mortals.  
What is now scattered everywhere, gather gradually.  
Be no slave to fame; watch that you may receive  
the gifts of the life above,  
and strive that you may deserve them.

[Col. 1184B]

Remember me, I pray, who have committed many crimes,  
behold, the worst of my predecessors.  
I entrust myself to you; I ask and implore your pardon.

The chronicles of Thietmar ask you, reader, to love them;  
through constant use they drive sorrow from the mind.  
Prefer them to games and various vanities:  
praise the just and pray for sinners.

[Col. 1183] **The prologue ends.**

# BOOK ONE [Note: [Col. 1183] “Here begins the first book, concerning the first emperor Heinricus,” Manuscript 2.]

[Col. 1183C]

### 1

All who are distinguished by some useful achievement have it in mind to benefit themselves in the present and the future and, insofar as ability or skillful confidence permits, to advance the matters entrusted to them and commend them to everlasting memory. For this reason I, Thietmar, unworthy not only of episcopal honor but even of the episcopal name, greatly fear that, while eagerly attempting to uncover the once-renowned history of the city of Merseburg, now growing dim with the old age of oblivion, I may produce smoke from brightness through ignorance [Col. 1184C] and, like an inferior craftsman, fail in the final result of the work [HORACE, *Satires* II, 3, 143 and 32, 34].

But since good will is sufficient for anyone [Note: [Col. 1184C] That is, when anyone has sufficient good will.], and, as blessed Gregory acknowledges, since Christ inspires this undertaking, I begin. I humbly entrust to his unknown mercy [Note: [Col. 1184C] The most merciful Christ, whose purpose concerning this book and this city is unknown to us.] how this writing, or indeed the whole history of the aforesaid city, will be brought to completion.

### 2

Diligent reader, learn that its foundation from the beginning, and its superstructure upon the earth, were begun by the Roman race that once followed Julius Caesar, the son-in-law of Pompey [Col. 1185A], a man powerful in all things and distinguished by strength in both respects [Note: [Col. 1185D] It is established that Julius Caesar was Pompey’s father-in-law.]. Receive, reader, the account that the foundation and superstructure of this city of Merseburg were begun by those Romans who followed this Caesar, mighty in every respect and distinguished in both kinds of strength—that is, of body and mind; compare I, 15; VI, 45; VII, 33 [Note: [Col. 1185D].].

And because at that time this place was suited to wars and always triumphant in all things, it was marked, according to the ancient custom, with the name of Mars (fol. 1, Manuscript 1). Later generations called it *Mese*, that is, “middle of the region” [Note: [Col. 1185D] Our author found the name *Mesaburii* in Widukind II, 3. He derives *Mese* from the Italian word *mezzo*, “middle.”], or they named it after a certain maiden so called.

But who its rulers were, or what their achievements may have been, before or after the incarnation of Christ, since I cannot establish this with the sure inquiry of the shrewd memory of the ancients [Note: [Col. 1185] *Sagati* in 1a, and so often elsewhere, for *sagaci*.] and do not find it in written records [Note: [Col. 1185] *indare* in 1a, corrected by 1c.]—lest I be found to be a liar—I omit entirely.

Let the account begin with Heinricus, who then united the rights of many persons pertaining to the dependencies of the aforesaid city and subjected to his power, through his own ability and diligence, territories much greater than these.

He, born from the most noble lineage of Otto and Hatthui [Note: [Col. 1185D] Hathuwi, mother of King Heinricus. Merseburg Calendar, 9 Kalends of January.] (compare HORACE, *Odes* I, 12, 45), grew from childhood like a hidden tree [Note: [Col. 1185D] Compare the Quedlinburg Annals, year 913.], and, as a young man of good character, gradually shone forth like a flower in fresh spring.

His father sent him with a large army into the province which we call *Deleminci* in German, but which the Slavs call *Glomaci* [Note: [Col. 1185D] The Lommatsch district.]. After devastating and burning it extensively, he returned victorious [Note: [Col. 1186D] Widukind I, 17.]. But how this district came to bear this name, I shall explain.

### 3. Glomuni

[Col. 1186D: Glomuni is a small place, the Poltzscher See, half an hour from the town of Lommatzsch. URS.] Glomuni is a spring situated no more than two miles from the Elbe. It produces from itself a marsh and often performs remarkable things, as the inhabitants assert as fact and many have confirmed with their own eyes. When there is a good peace beneficial to the natives, and this land does not lie about its fruit—being equally filled with wheat, oats, and acorns—it frequently makes glad the hearts of neighboring people who flock to it. But when the savage storm of war has broken out, it foretells with blood and ashes a certain indication of the future outcome. Every inhabitant venerates and fears it more than churches, however doubtful his hope may be. This province, extending from the Elbe as far as the river Chemnitz [Col. 1186D: the Chemnitz], derives its name from it.

[Col. 1185: *terraena* at first hand.] But not far from the aforesaid river, in the district called Chutizi [Col. 1186D: eastern Chutizi, where the present towns of Chemnitz, Freiberg, Pirna, and Annaberg are situated], Arn, bishop of the holy church of Würzburg [Col. 1185: *virciburgiensis* at first hand; *VIIII* (“the ninth”) added by 1c], returning from an expedition against the Bohemians, pitched his own tent on a hill beside the road, on its northern side. While he was celebrating Mass, he was surrounded by a hostile army; and after all his companions had gone before him through martyrdom, he offered himself to God the Father in the year 892 of the Lord’s incarnation, during the reign of Emperor Arnulf [Col. 1185: *et* (“and”) erased in 1; *DCCCXCIIo ... imp.* (“892 ... emperor”) added by 1b]. With the consecrated offerings he offered a sacrifice of praise. Even today lights are often seen burning there, and the Slavs too do not doubt that these are the holy martyrs of God. [Col. 1186D: This is likewise recorded in the Annals of Hildesheim and Regino’s Chronicle, while the Würzburg Annals give the year 891. The Merseburg Calendar gives his day of death as 29 June.]

During the days of his office in the city of Würzburg [Col. 1185: *wirciburgiensis* at first hand; the initial *i* in these names seems always to have been erased by the first corrector], this bishop built one church for the Lord and, in his diocese, nine churches modeled on it within ten years. When he blessed the largest of these, and when the relics of Christ’s martyr Kilian were carried around [Note: [Col. 1185] *circumferrentur* (“were carried around”): text; misspelled *circumfrererentur*: 1a]—Kilian, who, coming here from the Scots, first preached Christ to Duke Gozbert, his wife Geilan, and the other inhabitants of the province, and who, at the instigation of a second Herodias, was martyred there together with his companions Colomannus and Totmannus [Col. 1186B]—the Lord performed seventy miracles through him.

When the master of the cooks saw this [Col. 1185: the reading is erased or changed into “of their number” at a later hand; another witness has “of all”] [Col. 1186D: Concerning the master of the cooks, compare J. Grimm and A. Schmeller, *Latin Poems of the Tenth and Eleventh Centuries*, p. 386], he exhorted his disciples as follows:

“Do not delay, but diligently and without hesitation perform what has been entrusted to you. For our lord Kilian is now performing glorious signs through himself, without any delay.”

I am altogether unable to encompass in writing how great the virtue of the bishop mentioned above was; but I believe from my heart that he was held in great merit before God.

### 4

Meanwhile, when Heinricus [Note: [Col. 1185] *Heinricus* is added in 1b] learned of the reputation of a certain noblewoman named Hatheburg, he burned with youthful love, wondering how he might make her his companion. She was the daughter of the elder Etvinus, who held a very large part of the aforesaid city, which we call the Old City [Col. 1186D: the Altstadt of Merseburg]. Since he had no son, he left his two daughters a great inheritance when he died [Col. 1185: *hereditatem magnam* (“a great inheritance”) added by 2].

Because of her beauty and the advantage of her inheritance and wealth, Heinricus sent messengers as quickly as possible. Although he knew [Note: [Col. 1185] *h. e.* is added in 1b after *hanc esse* (“that she was”)] that she was a widow and veiled [Col. 1186D: Falke, *Corvey Traditions*, p. 521, asserts that she had previously been married to Count Osdagho], nevertheless, to satisfy his desire, he sought her hand with a promise of fidelity.

Then, overcome by the entreaties and advice of many, she accompanied him. Honorably received and treated affectionately by his people, as was fitting, she was joined to him. When the wedding had been celebrated according to custom, the bridegroom came to Merseburg with his wife. Calling together all the neighbors, and being an illustrious man [Col. 1187: *industris* (“industrious”): 1a; *illustris* (“illustrious”): 1c], he so attached them to himself through familiarity that they loved him as a friend and honored him as a lord [Col. 1187: manuscript 1c has *ita* (“thus”); manuscript 1a has *honerarent*, an orthographic variant of “honored”].

At that time Conradus, once an excellent duke of the Franks and then the successor of the boy Luthuwicus, held the stronghold of the kingdom [Col. 1187D: that is, he held the kingdom. Bede uses a similar expression, *History of the English* III.3: “The monastery of Hii held the stronghold among all monasteries”]. For his merit, the aforesaid Otto, elected king by all the leading men of the kingdom, had placed him over himself, although he considered himself unworthy of such a position, and had submitted himself and his sons to Conradus’s fidelity and authority.

The spiritual father and shepherd of the eastern peoples at that time was Sigimundus, the distinguished bishop of the holy church of Halberstadt, an ingenious man who surpassed all his contemporaries [Note: [Col. 1187] *tunc* (“at that time”) is added in 1b] in every kind of knowledge relating to spiritual and even worldly matters [Col. 1187B]. He was filled with the greatest piety and, what is the highest summit of perfection, burned with zeal for Christ. As soon as he heard of the crime of the marriage that had been committed, he mourned the guilt of his sheep. Through a messenger and a letter, he forbade any further intercourse between them under the ban of apostolic authority and summoned both of them [Note: [Col. 1187] *ambos* (“both,” accusative): text and 1c; *ambo* (“both,” nominative): 1a] to a designated synod [fol. 3].

Heinricus, disturbed by this report, hurried to the emperor. He explained the whole matter in order and sought his help. Since he was the emperor’s intimate, he obtained it through the trust and faithful service that he had inherited from his father. The emperor quickly sent an envoy to the bishop, requesting that he release those under ban and allow them to be brought into his presence [Col. 1187D: *concite* here means *citissime*, “very swiftly”].

After this, Otto entered the way of all flesh on 30 November [fol. 3; Col. 1187: “30 November” added at a later hand; Col. 1187D: the Merseburg Calendar gives 30 November. Otto was Count, father of King Heinricus of Saxony. He died in 912; according to the Annals of Hildesheim, in 914], and the young man often mentioned, succeeding to his position as though it were vacant, received the inheritance by right and a very large part of the benefice as a free gift from the king. He bitterly resented what he and all his people had not received; and afterward, just as darnel grows hidden among wheat, so a thread of concealed hatred grew from this [Col. 1187D: compare Widukind I.21].

The king, carefully considering the matter, pretended not to know it. Since he did not dare to overcome the man by force, he tried to deceive him by the familiar cunning of Archbishop Hattho. Hattho’s predecessor had defeated Count Aethelbertus of Teresi by cutting off his head, and Hattho attempted to deceive Heinricus in the same way [Col. 1187: “Hattho” at a later hand; “Teresi” perhaps “Tereti”]. [Col. 1187D: Concerning Aethelbertus’s beheading, see Widukind I.22 and the Corvey Annals for 906 and the Hildesheim Annals for 907.]

But wise God made this counsel foolish. For the craftsman who, at the bishop’s command, was preparing with remarkable skill a golden collar in which Heinricus was to be killed, inquiring from the grieving old man how the deed was to be carried out, completed the work exactly and presented it. Then he secretly escaped, encountered the aforesaid duke, and revealed the whole matter to him in order.

The duke returned and sent a messenger to the bishop, who disclosed what had been hidden [Col. 1188D: *patesceret* is interpreted as *patefaceret*, “would disclose/make manifest”] and declared that he would swiftly keep watch to the bishop’s disadvantage. For he ordered everything that belonged to the bishop in Saxony or Thuringia to be seized for himself, driving away the king’s friends after plundering them completely in all these regions [Col. 1187: “from all these regions”].

Soon the archbishop expired by a sudden death, and Fortune, which until then had favored the king, quickly yielded to Heinricus [Col. 1187: one manuscript first read “had favored the king,” then “favored the king”; another reading runs: “the archbishop expired, and Fortune, which until then had favored the king, quickly yielded to Heinricus”]. But since I am hastening on to other matters, it would take too long to relate how often they met [Note: [Col. 1187] *mutuo* (“in turn/mutually”): text; *mutua* (feminine form): 1a], alternately yielding or conquering, and how at last, through the prompting of good men, they were reconciled in friendship.

### 5

Meanwhile, Conradus, held by a long illness, and having forgotten all the hostility that had arisen against him on Heinricus’s part,

“After hostilities, to remember angry wrongs is wrong.”

—Cato, *Distichs* 2.15—

gave this counsel to his brother Everhardus [Note: [Col. 1187] *Everhardo*: text; misspelled *ewrhardo*: 1a] and to the leading people gathered together: whenever he should surrender himself to the common destiny of nature—*se concederet* is interpreted as *moreretur*, “he should die” [Col. 1188D]—they should choose Heinricus [Note: [Col. 1187] 1c deleted *eum* (“him”) and added *Heinricum* (“Heinricus”) in the margin], suitable in every respect to govern the kingdom, and entrust his soul, together with the remaining company of his kinsmen and retainers, to Heinricus’s firm fidelity. He urged them to consent to this without any delay [fol. 4; Col. 1187: the manuscript originally read “him”; “Heinricus” was later added in the margin].

They received this final request with great mourning and lamentation, promising, as long as life remained, to fulfill it. After his swift death, which occurred in the eighth year of his rule, on 19 October—alas!—[Note: [Col. 1188D] The author here confuses the death date of Conrad, king of Burgundy, with that of Conrad, king of the Germans, which was 23 December; see the Merseburg Calendar under both dates], and after the funeral rites had been completed at Viliniburch [Col. 1188D: the same place is mentioned by Widukind I.25; the Continuation of Regino gives another account under 919], they were present at the assembly quickly convened at Fridisleri [Col. 1187: *frideslari* at a later hand]. They crowned Heinricus and, under the testimony of Christ and the whole Church, commended to him as king and lord the people entrusted to them in faithful allegiance, not without tears.

Heinricus first received with humble devotion the gift of divine mercy and afterward the universal affection of such great charity; he gave thanks to God and promised that he would consent to this and to everything else that they should request by common counsel. He did not desire the episcopal anointing of blessing, offered by Archbishop Herigerus according to the custom of his predecessors, nor did he wish to receive it; rather, he declared himself altogether unworthy of it [Col. 1189D: compare Widukind I.26].

Nevertheless, I fear that he was at fault in this. For in the Life of the holy father Othelricus, whom this same king later promoted to the priestly order, I read that the holy martyr of Christ, Afra [Note: [Col. 1189] *Afram*: text; misspelled *affram*: 1], showed many things in a vision to her beloved bishop. Among them were two swords, one with a hilt and the other without one [Col. 1189: *capulo ... ea* (“with a hilt ... it”): text; uncertain *capulo ... eo*: 1]; through these she demonstrated King Heinricus, deprived of consecration [fol. 4′; Col. 1189D: compare Gerard’s *Life of Saint Udalricus*, bishop of Augsburg, chapter 3, ed. Welser, and Berno’s *Life of the same saint*, chapter 9. From this vision Heinricus was called “the Sword without a Hilt” in the Prüm Necrology for 919, *Archiv für ältere deutsche Geschichte* III.24].

But leaving this hidden judgment of God aside, I shall proceed further.

### 6

The fame of the new king, spread in every direction, gladdened the hearts of his friends and, conversely, saddened those of the rebellious, because he was such a man that he knew how to treat his own wisely, while overcoming his enemies with cunning and courage.

Meanwhile Tammo was born [Col. 1189: also called Tanckmarus], and the king’s affection for his wife diminished. Because of the beauty and property [Note: [Col. 1189] *pulcritudinem et rem* (“beauty and property”): text; *in amorem* (“into love”): 2] of a certain maiden named Mathildis, his heart secretly burned. At last the ardor of his hidden mind broke forth. He finally confessed that he had long been gravely at fault in an unlawful marriage, and through his relatives and envoys he approached the daughter [Note: [Col. 1189] *filiam* (“daughter”) stands in an erased space in 1] of Theodricus and Reinilda, sprung from the tribe of King Widukind [Col. 1189: one manuscript has *widuinni*, another *widikindi*], asking [Note: [Col. 1189] *interpellat* (“he solicits/approaches”): text; erased *pellare* in 1 was corrected, apparently by the same hand, to *interpellare cepit* (“he began to solicit”) in 2] whether she would consent to satisfy his desire. [Col. 1189D: “Queen, daughter of Thiadricus … of the stock of the great Duke Widukind,” Widukind I.31. Reinhild, mother of Queen Mathildis, who died on 2 May, is praised in the Merseburg Calendar.]

Since a woman’s mind is pliable, and since she knew him to be distinguished in every respect, she consented. Joined to him, she benefited him in both divine and human affairs. In due time she bore three sons—Otto [Col. 1189: “emperor” added at a later hand], Heinricus, and Bruno [Col. 1189: “archbishop” added at a later hand]—and brought them up successfully; the sweetness of offspring from so great a lineage overcame the pain of childbirth. [fol. 5; Col. 1189D: this second marriage was celebrated in 909; compare Waitz, *Yearbooks of the German Empire*, I, p. 11.]

Since my subject is Otto, I do not think it necessary to examine all his father’s deeds individually, since the son himself reveals how great his father’s dignity was and the writings of many sufficiently display the glory of his life. Nevertheless, I shall insert certain matters that I judge especially necessary to relate [Col. 1189: *necessaria* (“necessary things”): text; *necessario* (“necessarily”): 1a].

He made these regions tributary to himself: Bohemia, the Deleminci [Col. 1189: *delemencici* at a later hand], the Obodrites, the Wilzi, the Hevelli, and the Redarii. Soon afterward they rebelled, incited others to do the same, and attacked, destroyed, and burned the city of Wallislevo in the year 929 [Col. 1189D: from Widukind I.36].

To avenge this, our army assembled. Besieging the city of Lunzini [Col. 1189: the second *i* in *Lunzini* erased in 1], it attacked their allies, who wished to defend them, and struck them down, while only a few escaped. It also captured the aforesaid city.

Among our men, two of my great-grandfathers, both bearing the same name, which sounded like Liutherus [Col. 1189: two *i*s in the associated name erased in 1], excellent soldiers and most distinguished by birth, the honor and consolation of their homeland, perished on the Nones of September together with many others [Col. 1189D: Widukind and the Quedlinburg Annals record that Count Liuthardus died with many others at Lunzini on 5 September 930; the Corvey Annals state that the battle occurred on 4 September 929].

### 7

So that no Christian may distrust the future resurrection of the dead, but may hasten through holy desires toward the joys of blessed immortality, I shall relate certain events that I truthfully learned had occurred in the city of Wallislevo after its destruction and rebuilding [fol. 5; Col. 1189: “its” erased at a later hand].

At the very dawn of day, the priest of that church was accustomed to sing Matins. But when he came to the cemetery and saw a great multitude in it offering gifts to a priest standing before the doors of the church, he first stopped. Then, fortifying himself with the sign of the holy cross, he tremblingly approached the oratory through all these people, without recognizing even one of them.

One woman, recently departed from this world and well known to him, asked what he wanted there. When he explained why he had come, she told him that all these things had been completed by the dead and foretold that he himself would live only a short time [Col. 1189: “she narrated” added by Honorius, *Imago mundi*, under 919]. He later reported this to his neighbors, and its truth was confirmed [Col. 1189: Honorius adds “by his death”].

In my own time, at Magdeburg—as I learned from truthful witnesses, while I myself was continually residing there—the guards of the merchants’ church, keeping watch that same night, perceived by sight and hearing things corresponding to what I have just related and brought the city’s leading men. While they stood some distance from the cemetery, they saw lamps placed upon candelabra, and heard two men sing the invitatory [Col. 1190D: that is, Psalm 99] and all together perform the Matins praises in due order. But when they approached, they understood nothing at all.

The following day I related this to my niece Brigida, who was suffering from bodily illness [Note: [Col. 1189] *laboranti* (“suffering,” dative): text; *laborante* (“suffering,” ablative): 1a] and governed the monastery of Saint Laurence with pastoral care [fol. 6; Col. 1190D: this seems to have been a convent of nuns in the new city of Magdeburg, entirely destroyed in the Thirty Years’ War. There was also a convent of nuns at Calbe in the suburb, dedicated to Saint Laurence and already destroyed by the Bohemians in the tenth century; it is mentioned below. KIND. She was the daughter of Count Lotharius of Walbeck; see J. L. Levin Gebhardi, *Northern Margraves*, p. 29. WED. Abbess Brigida died on 30 December; see the Merseburg Necrology], she, not at all astonished by the matter, immediately gave me this answer:

“In the time of Bishop Baldricus, who governed the see of Utrecht for eighty years or more [Col. 1190D: so the manuscript and the *Annals of Saxony* under 929 say. More correctly, our author should have said forty-eight. Baldricus governed the see of Utrecht from 928 to 977. Wagner therefore conjectured wrongly that Brigida meant eighty years earlier. Perhaps she said that he was already eighty years old], he renewed and blessed at the place [Note: [Col. 1191] *qui* (“which”): text; *que* (“and”): 1a] called Deventer a church ruined by age and entrusted it to his priest.

“One day, going to it very early, the priest saw the dead offering gifts in the church and in the cemetery, and heard them singing [Note: [Col. 1189] *audivit* (“he heard”) is added in 1b]. As soon as he reported this to the bishop, the bishop ordered him to sleep in the church. But on the following night [Note: [Col. 1189] *casu* (“by an occurrence/chance”) is added in 1b] the dead drove him, bed and all, from the place on which he had rested.

“Because of this, trembling, he complained of these things to the bishop. The bishop ordered him, signed with the relics of the saints and sprinkled with holy water, not to cease guarding his church. Following his lord’s command, he again wished to sleep in the church; but, overcome by the spur of fear, he remained awake as he lay there [Note: [Col. 1191] *evigilavit* (“he remained awake/awoke”): text; *vigilavit* (“he kept watch”): 1a].

“And behold, at the customary hour, they came, lifted him up, placed him before the altar, and reduced his body to ashes with fire. When the bishop heard this, he was moved to penitence and proclaimed a three-day fast, so that he might aid both himself and the soul of the dead man [Col. 1191: one manuscript has *defunti*].
