“I could have said much more to you about all these things, son, if illness had not prevented me. As day is granted to the living, so night is granted to the dead [Col. 1191: this sentence is erased in one manuscript].”

A mortal ought not to know more than is proper, as Saint Paul exhorts: “unto sobriety” (Romans 12:3). But since two or three witnesses suffice for one testimony, I have written down these events that occurred in our own recent times, so that the unbeliever may learn that the prophets’ oracles are true. One of them testifies:

“Your dead shall live, O Lord!”  
(Isaiah 26:19) [Col. 1189: “shall live” added at a later hand.]

And another—correctly supplied in the note as Daniel 12:2—says: “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake”; and the Lord himself says:

“The dead who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of God and shall rise and rejoice.”  
(John 5:28) [Col. 1191: Honorius, *Imago mundi*, correctly emended Thietmar: “and another,” namely Daniel 12:2.]

Whenever such things are heard or seen by the living, they signify something new [Note: [Col. 1191] *aliquid* (“something”): text; abbreviated *aliqd*: 1, repeatedly], as a trustworthy testimony proves in many cases. I know a large part of it, but the greater part I do not know; nevertheless, I believe the testimony of truthful witnesses.

I was at my estate called Retmerslevo [Col. 1191: *ratmaerslevo* at a later hand] [Col. 1191D: Rotmersleben. This chronological description fits only the year 1002, when Friday fell on 18 December, unless Thietmar himself made an error. BETHM.], where, on 18 December, a Friday, at the first crowing of the cock, a great light shining out from the church filled the entire cemetery, and an immense sound like the grunting of swine was heard [Col. 1191: “like the grunting of swine” added at a later hand]. My brother Frithericus saw this with my retainers [Note: [Col. 1191] *satellitibus* (“retainers”): text, corrected in 1a; *satellibus*: 1b] and the others [Note: [Col. 1191] *c.* was added after *caeterisque* (“and the others”) in 1b and later erased] who had gathered there; and the chaplain who slept before me heard it [Col. 1191: “saw it” added and later erased].

The next day, when I inquired whether anything of this kind had ever happened there before, I learned from the oldest inhabitants that similar things had once occurred. And I saw this sign grievously fulfilled in this year in the death of the illustrious Lady Liudgardis [Col. 1191: the manuscript seems to have read this, though after four letters had been erased a later hand corrected it to *Lukardis*; Col. 1191D: namely Liukiard, daughter of Ekkehard, margrave of Meissen, wife of Count Werner, and Thietmar’s cousin; she died on 13 November 1012], my niece on one side and my daughter-in-law on the other [Col. 1191: this phrase added at a later hand], and, among friends, the person closest to me. I shall speak of her more fully below [Col. 1191: *edisseram* (“I shall explain”): text; *edissero* (“I explain”): 1a and 2].

It often happened to me that at night I heard wood being cut. On one occasion, while all the others were asleep, my companion and I plainly heard the dead speaking together. From these two signs I understood on the following day [Note: [Col. 1191] *crastino* (“on the following day”) is added in 1b] that a funeral was about to occur.

Although I serve as the whetstone that sharpens iron but does not sharpen itself,

“I perform the office of a whetstone, which sharpens iron but not itself.”

—Horace, *Epistles* II.3.304—

nevertheless, so that I may not be branded with the reproach of a mute dog, I speak these things to the unlearned, and especially to the Slavs, who think that everything ends with temporal death. I firmly proclaim to all the faithful the certainty of the resurrection and of future recompense according to the quality of one’s merit [Col. 1191: the manuscript’s *certitudinem* is a later correction for *certitudine*. The construction means “the certainty of the resurrection and of future recompense according to merit”].

There are three kinds of souls, which do not begin equally and do not end simultaneously [Col. 1192B]. The first is that of incorporeal angels, which exists with them without beginning or end. The second is that of human beings, which begins with them but has no share in an end. It is immortal and, as certain pagans believe, will not in the future possess the office that it has in this world. The third kind is the soul of beasts and birds [Note: [Col. 1191] *pecudum* (“of beasts”): text; misspelled *paecudum*: 1a], which receives the same beginning and end as the body.

Therefore, just as it is commanded in the law given by the Lord through Moses [Note: [Col. 1191] *data* (“given,” feminine): text; *date* (variant spelling): 1], so the true Christian is forbidden by canonical authority [Note: [Col. 1191] *auctoritate* (“by authority”): text; misspelled *actoritate*: 1] to pollute himself with their blood [fol. 7]. For there are many poor people who habitually eat it and, ignorant that they sin in doing so, resist everyone who contradicts them.

Therefore you, human being, crowned by God with glory and great honor and placed above all his works, give thanks above all to the Most High, repaying him according to your ability for what he has done for you through his mercy. And I shall return to matters from which I have wandered too far.

[Col. 1191D: This passage was discussed by J. E. Wüstemann, “The Error concerning the Eternity of Angels in Thietmar, Book I of the Chronicle,” in his program on the early origins of philosophy in Saxony and on Bishop Thietmar of Merseburg the philosopher, Wittenberg, 1760.]

### 8

The king drove away the Avars, who frequently rose against him [Col. 1191: “that is, the Hungarians,” added above the line; Col. 1192D: concerning the defeat of the Hungarians, see the Corvey and Quedlinburg Annals under 933]. When on one occasion he tried to injure them in an unequal engagement, he was defeated and fled into the city called Bichni [Col. 1192D: Pichen or Püchen, near the river Mulde, between the towns of Wurzen and Eilenburg]. There he escaped the danger of death and honored the townspeople with greater glory than they had previously possessed or than their fellow provincials possess today, rewarding them with worthy gifts.

Whenever, during his life, he proudly rose against God and his own lord, his power having been humbled each time, he inclined himself toward fitting amendment [Col. 1192D; Col. 1191: “for suitable amendment” added at a later hand].

I heard that when he went to Rome for the sake of prayer, he labored more on foot than on horseback. When many asked him why he did this, he confessed his fault.

### 9

In the year 931 of the Lord’s incarnation he became emperor [Col. 1193: “in the year … he became emperor” added at a later hand] [Col. 1193D: No one is unaware that Heinricus was not adorned with the imperial crown. Our author had Widukind I.39 before his eyes].

He cultivated a certain mountain situated beside the Elbe [Note: [Col. 1193] *et* (“and”): text; *ex* (“from”) in 1a was corrected to *et* in 1b; 2 has both *et* and *ex*], which at that time was covered by dense woods [Col. 1193: *densitate* (“density”): text; misspelled *denscitate*: 1a]. There he built a city and gave it the name Meissen from a certain stream [Note: [Col. 1193] letters in 1, including *et ua*, are erased; 2 reads *Lubuzuam*] flowing on its northern side [Col. 1193: the manuscript’s letters were erased; a later witness has *Lubuzua*]. As it is still used today, he fortified it with garrisons and other defenses [fol. 8]. He subdued the Milzeni to his authority and compelled them to pay tribute in the year 932 [Col. 1193D: The Milzeni lived in Upper Lusatia and its borders; their cities were Bautzen and Görlitz. See the Hildesheim and Weissenburg Annals under 932, where *Lonsicin* or *Lousicin* and *Losicin* seem to refer to Lusatia].

He also long possessed the city of Liubusua [Note: [Col. 1193] *Liubusuam*: text; letters in 1, including *et ua*, are erased; *Lubuzuam*: 2], about which I shall speak more fully later [Col. 1193D: Lebusa, situated between the towns of Dahme and Schlieben in the Schweidnitz district of Saxony], and forced its inhabitants to flee to a small fortress situated within it and to surrender themselves. From the day on which that city justly perished by fire until our own time, it remained without inhabitants [Note: [Col. 1193] *habitatore* (“inhabitant”): text and 1c; *habitore*: 1a]. If he plundered anything in his kingdom, as many say, may merciful God forgive him.

Moreover, he made the Northmen and Danes obey him by force of arms [Col. 1193: *obtemperantes* (“obeying”): text; misspelled *opterantes*: 1; Col. 1193D: compare Widukind I.40; concerning the subdued Danes, see the Annals of Augst under 931, the Corvey Annals under 934, and Adam of Bremen I.48ff.]. After recalling them from their former error, he taught them, together with their king Cnut [Col. 1193: *Cnittone* in another witness] [Col. 1194D: Harde Cnut, according to Adam of Bremen I.47], to bear the yoke of Christ.

But because I have heard remarkable things about their ancient sacrifices, I do not wish to pass over them without examination [Col. 1193: the text’s reading is marked *ita*, corrected by 1b; 1a has *non placet* (“it is not pleasing”)]. There is a place in those regions, the chief place of that kingdom, called Lederun, in the district known as Selon [Col. 1193: *Lederun ... dicitur* (“Lederun ... is called”) was added by 1b in a blank space] [Col. 1194D: Lejre near Roskilde in Zealand]. Every ninth year [Note: [Col. 1193] *VIIII* (“ninth”) stands in an erasure made by an uncertain hand], in the month of January, after the time when we celebrate the Epiphany of the Lord, they all gathered there. They sacrificed to their gods ninety-nine men [Col. 1193: *LXXXX* (“ninety”): 1a; *VIIII* (“nine”) added by 1b] and an equal number of horses, together with dogs and roosters offered in place of hawks [Col. 1193C], firmly believing, as I have said, that these victims would serve the gods among the dead and appease them for crimes committed [Col. 1193: “among them” and “for crimes committed among them” were added at a later hand] [Col. 1194D: compare Adam of Bremen, *On the Situation of Denmark*, chapter 27, and J. Grimm, *German Mythology*, p. 28ff.].

How rightly our king acted when he prohibited them from such an abominable rite! For he offers an acceptable sacrifice to God the Father who spares human blood [Col. 1193: *sanguini* (“blood,” dative): text; *sanguine* (“blood,” ablative): 1a]. The Lord commands:

“You shall not kill the innocent and the pious.”  
(Exodus 23:7) [Col. 1193: *pium* (“pious”): text; *impium* (“impious”): 1a.]

### 10

The aforesaid king adorned the ancient Roman work at Merseburg with a stone wall [Col. 1193: *in Mersburg* (“at Merseburg”) added by 1b after correcting *in mesburg*]. Within it he ordered the church—which is now the mother of other churches—to be constructed of stone and dedicated on 19 May [Col. 1194D: the Merseburg Calendar gives 22 May: “At Merseburg, the dedication of the church constructed within the monastery”]. He also built the other cities for the security of the kingdom and temples for the Lord as a remedy for his soul, with devout intent [Col. 1193: a second manuscript and the *Annals of Saxony* add: “At New Corvey he wonderfully adorned the altar of Saint Vitus the martyr with gold and various gems, at the urging of his wife Mahtildis”; Col. 1194D: compare Widukind I.35].

After countless distinguished deeds [Col. 1194D: “distinguished deeds” occurs in the Saxon chronological record under 974 and in the Quedlinburg Annals under 999], when the course of his life had run its course, in the sixteenth year of his reign and the sixtieth year of his age, on the sixth day before the Nones of July, he died at Miminlevo. He was buried at Quedlinburg, which he had built from its foundations, and was rightly mourned by all the leading men. This occurred in the year 936 of the Lord’s incarnation [Col. 1193: the following passage, through “for good imitation,” is written in an erasure filling half of folio 8′ and the recto of folio 9, but by the same hand as the preceding text].

The character [Note: [Col. 1194D] *indolis* stands for *indoles* (“character”); such forms occur often] of the posterity he left behind gladdened the sorrowful hearts of the leaders [Note: [Col. 1193] *principum* (“of the leaders”): text; *principium* (“beginning”): 1a, repeatedly] and made them certain of a voluntary election. Woe to the peoples who are left without hope of a ruler among the succeeding offspring of their lords, and who, divided among themselves and engaged in prolonged contention, do not quickly provide some counsel or consolation [Col. 1193: one manuscript has “will be provided,” later erased].

If no one worthy of such an office is found in the line of consanguinity, at least let someone of good conduct from another family be chosen, with all hatred removed; for it is the greatest disaster for foreigners (*alienigenos*; manuscript variants *aligeninos* and *aligenienas*) to reign. From this comes oppression and the great endangerment of liberty.

From the Heinricus of whom I have spoken and from his successors down to the present, the Saxons have been elevated and honored in every respect [Col. 1194D: compare Widukind I.39]. Whatever [Note: [Col. 1193] *Quicquid* (“whatever”): text; abbreviated *quicqd*: 1] is praised in these men is carefully preserved in the life of his namesake, about whom I am going to write as long as life lasts, and afterward, I fear, it will come to an end.

Therefore, whatever I now pass over [Note: [Col. 1193] *ullatenus* (“in any respect”): text and 1c; *ultenus* (“further”): 1a] in these matters, or leave unexamined because life fails me, dearest successor, complete; and preserve in the memory of writing the qualities of the times.

I, a sinner and negligent in everything, have until now been idle in good works and devoted myself to evil. I turned to these matters and to better things only late, and in no way practised saving remembrance for my soul. After I became a shepherd, I taught my subjects by words alone, not by examples. Outwardly I appeared good, while violating my inner self with the worst thoughts. Conceived from unclean seed, I wallowed in the mud like an unclean sow.

Someone may say, “You have spoken badly about yourself!” I answer that this is true, for I know no one worse than myself [Col. 1195: *aliquis* (“someone”): text; *aliquem* (“someone,” accusative) added by 1c]. Therefore I accuse myself in this way so that, recognizing my wounds, you may come to my aid with the necessary medicines [Col. 1193: “come to my aid” added at a later hand] and, since you are in large part my companion in these things, help me in everything as you would wish to be helped in your own case.

### 11

I shall briefly encompass the illustrious and venerable deeds of Mahtildis [Col. 1195: variant spellings include *machtildis* and *mechtildis], which she performed with the greatest zeal after the death of her lord, for the good imitation of all the faithful. For, as Scripture teaches (2 Maccabees 12:46), it is a holy and salutary thought to pray for the dead and to obtain release for them through almsgiving [fol. 9; Col. 1195B].

We read [Note: [Col. 1195] *quod* (“that”): text; *ut* (“how/that”): 1a] that the bonds of a certain captive, whom [Note: [Col. 1195] *et* (“and”) after *quem* was deleted in 1b] his wife believed dead and for whom she continually arranged funeral rites, were released as often as acceptable sacrifices [Note: [Col. 1195] *hostiae* (“sacrifices”): text; *ostias*: 1a; *hostias*: 1b; *hostie*: 1c] were offered by her [Note: [Col. 1195] *ab ea* (“by her”): text; *hab eo*: 1a] to God the Father for him [Note: [Col. 1195] *offerrentur* (“were offered”): text, 1b, and 2; *offererentur*: 1a; *offerri procurarentur* (“were caused to be offered”): 1c]. He himself later reported this to her when he returned home free.

Following this example, Lady Mahtildis [Col. 1195: variant spellings as above] aided her husband, oppressed by the bond of momentary death, supplying food not only to the poor but also to birds [Col. 1195D: compare the *Life of Mathildis*, chapter 4].

On the thirtieth day, she also founded a community of holy women in the aforesaid city. From her own property she granted it whatever was sufficient for the necessities of food and clothing, and confirmed the grant in writing, with her sons praising this action [Col. 1195D: this was the monastery of Saint Servatius at Quedlinburg; see its foundation charter of 13 September 937. The city of Quedlinburg formed part of Queen Mathildis’s dower; compare the charters of King Heinricus dated 16 September 929 and of Emperor Otto dated 15 July 961].

Some assert that she had long striven [Note: [Col. 1195] the *e* in *enisam* (“striven”) is erased in 1] with the greatest zeal for this: that her younger son Heinricus should possess his father’s throne. But God, who always predestines his chosen ones for their several purposes, did not will this, nor did the best part of the leading men consent [Col. 1195: *nec summatum optima pars consensit* (“nor did the best part of the leading men consent”): text; *summa optimatum pars concessit* (“the chief part of the nobles permitted it”): 2]. Rather, through prudent reasoning, and therefore with arguments easily persuasive, they inclined the mind of the deserving queen somewhat away from her purpose and advised her to assign the Bavarians to her younger son [Note: [Col. 1195] *huic* (“to this [son]”): text; *hunc* (“this [son],” accusative): 1a and 2] for more suitable protection, while giving precedence to her elder son.

12. (fol. 10) In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 723, indiction II, and in the fifth year of the reign of the first King Heinricus, the venerable Sigimundus, sixth bishop of the holy church of Halberstadt, placed there by King Arnulf in the seventh year of his reign, died on 14 January (the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February). [Note: [Col. 1195] “died” was added in manuscript 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1195] The ending *-us* in manuscript 1b is in an erased place.] [Note: [Col. 1195] “from Arnulf … seventh year” was added in the lower margin of manuscript 1b; the words previously written above the line were erased.]

Bernhard, his chaplain, succeeded him, just as the holy man had previously foretold to him. For, having long been ill, he saw in a dream that the pastoral staff had slipped from his hands and that Bernhard, following behind, lifted it and carried it openly. When he awoke, he summoned him and said:

“Go to the royal court, taking from my resources whatever you need for this purpose, and there acquire the favor and assistance of those who are most influential, so that you may succeed me without any offense or hindrance. For God will provide all these things for you, beloved son!” [Note: Added in manuscript 1b.]

Bernhard immediately fulfilled the command of his beloved master with humble obedience. When he was returning from King Heinricus, he learned that his lord and father had departed from this light to Christ in the thirtieth year of his episcopal office. Returning at once, he obtained from the aforesaid king the grant that he had requested.

The body of the aforesaid bishop was placed on the right side of the altar of Christ’s protomartyr, on the step before it, [Note: [Col. 1195] “on the preceding step” was added in manuscript 1b.] just as he had previously indicated—not lying down, but sitting above the chair—in the hope that, through the holy intercession of his patron and priestly blessing, he would be eternally protected.

13. (fol. 10) How merciful God regarded the aforesaid king during his lifetime, although I have never drunk from the Pierian spring, [Note: [Col. 1196D] “The Pierian springs”: Statius, *Silvae* I, *Epithalamion* 6, I, 30. See G. Waitz, *Jahrbücher*, under the years 921 and 923.] I shall nevertheless make known to all the faithful. [Note: [Col. 1195] Added in manuscript 1b.]

There was in the western regions a certain king, whom the inhabitants ironically called *Karl Sot*, that is, “Charles the Fool.” [Note: [Col. 1195] Manuscript 2 has *ita*; in manuscript 1, the entire little phrase between “king” and “who” is almost erased, though the space makes it likely that it contained the same words as manuscript 2. The word begins with *ab* and the final letter of the sentence is visibly preserved.] He was captured by one of his dukes [Note: [Col. 1196D] Heribert, count of Vermandois; compare Widukind.] and shut up in a prison of darkness.

Appealing for the aid of our King Heinricus, who was his nephew, he promised under oath that, if he were freed, he would hand over to him the right hand of Christ’s martyr Dionysius, and with it the whole kingdom of the Lotharians. [Note: [Col. 1196D] Widukind I, 33.] Without delay, the renowned warrior girded himself with invincible arms, visited the man in distress, and, in rescuing and restoring him, earned the reward due to a worthy deed; he also greatly increased the former honor of himself and his successors.

14. But because every human being is more inclined to fall than nature equips him to stand, I shall not remain silent about how pitiably this man once sinned, as a warning and to enable the devout to avoid such conduct.

On the Lord’s Supper he became excessively drunk, and on the following night, through diabolical instigation, he unlawfully joined himself to his wife, who strongly resisted him. Satan, the author of so great a crime and the snarer of human salvation, disclosed this deed to a certain venerable matron in these words:

“Queen Mahtild, having recently consented to marital pleasure at my urging, has conceived a son—beyond all doubt mine. Take care that you conceal so great a deed completely.” [Note: [Col. 1197] Manuscript 1c has *mechtild*; manuscript 1a reads *manitalit sentiens*, evidently corrupt.]

The matron, becoming deeply and secretly troubled by this, quickly reported it to the aforesaid queen, urging her always to keep bishops and priests with her and, at the child’s very birth, to wash away in the water of holy baptism whatever the ill-fated demon might boast had happened to him as pleasing to itself. [Note: [Col. 1197] Manuscript 1a reads *effectum*, with *m* erased and *u* written above it, for *effecta*. Manuscripts 1 and 2 read *quicquid*, “whatever”; manuscript 1c falsely corrects it to *ne quid*, “lest anything.” Manuscript 2 reads *delictum*, “offense,” rather than *dilectum*, “pleasing/beloved.” Manuscript 1c and manuscript 2 read *accidisset*, “had happened.”]

And so she gave thanks to God. [Note: [Col. 1197] Manuscript 1a reads *populo*, “to the people,” for *Deo*, “to God.”] But when the demon—that is, the one who knows everything—saw that he had been wholly deceived, he rebuked the aforementioned woman and added:

“Even if my will has now been frustrated by your blasphemies, [Note: [Col. 1197] Manuscript 1 reads *frustata*.] I have nevertheless achieved this much: from him, and from all who shall ever proceed from his loins, my companion Discord will never be absent, nor will firm peace arise for them.”

That liar and enemy of truth spoke these words according to his own desire, not, I hope, according to their fulfillment. Many, however, affirm—as appears in the account that follows—that during the times of this man and of his son frequent upheaval occurred and there was little certainty of peace.

But in these days, when Heinricus, third in the succession of dukes and second in the order of scepter-bearers, began to reign, that flint of iniquity dried up and the flourishing flower of good peace appeared. If anything resembling the earlier troubles now occurs, it is not his fault but that of the impious instigator. [Note: [Col. 1197] The reading *q* occurs repeatedly.]

We read that “all times have a time” (Ecclesiastes 3:1), but not every time is such a time—that is, from the beginning God established no time as a place for vices. And because the weakness of the flesh cannot exist without some stain, let a person abstain from capital crimes and preserve purity on all solemn occasions. [Note: [Col. 1197] Manuscript 1 has the abbreviated form *sollepn.*]

Scripture testifies that there is no sin in lawful unions (1 Corinthians 7:28); when these are honored with observance of the festivals, no threatening storm of danger disturbs them.

To confirm this further, I offer one example. A certain man named Uffo, a citizen of Magdeburg, driven by excessive drunkenness, compelled his wife Gelsusa to consent to him on the holy feast of the Innocents. [Note: [Col. 1197] Manuscript 1a has *cives*, “citizens.” Manuscript 1b has “on the holy feast” in an erased place.] That same night, bound by her husband, when she gave birth at the proper time to an infant whose toes were twisted backward, she was struck with amazement. [Note: [Col. 1197] Manuscript 1 first read *obstipuit*, “was stupefied”; manuscript 1c has *obstupuit*.]

She immediately summoned her husband and showed him the miracle. Lamenting that this had happened through the guilt of them both, she said:

“Did I not warn you not to do this? Behold, the wrath of God has revealed itself to us, and it terribly urges us not to act in this way again. It is a great sin for you to command me unjustly, and for me to render you obedience.” [Note: [Col. 1197] “It is a great sin” was added in manuscript 1b. Manuscript 1a omits *non* in the phrase “to render you obedience,” thereby altering the sense.]

After the infant was baptized, he was led from this exile among the company of the Innocents.

Blessed forever is the man who has such a companion in marriage, one who tirelessly prays for her absent husband and, forgetting her sex, urges him, when present, to guard himself. [Note: [Col. 1197] Manuscript 1c may read *illi*, “for him,” rather than *illo*, “to that man.”]

15. (fol. 12) [Note: In manuscript 1, folio 12 contains nineteen lines from the words “custodiat” to “mox furit”; the first sixteen lines are mutilated at the damaged margin. We have supplied what was cut away from manuscript 2. After this chapter, the verso of folio 12 and the recto of the following page were left blank in manuscript 1; nevertheless, nothing is missing and the hand does not change.]

At the time when the aforesaid king was at the height of his power, there was in Bavaria a certain duke named Arnulf, distinguished equally in mind and body, who possessed exceptional authority to distribute by his own hand all the bishoprics established in those regions. [Note: [Col. 1197] The apparatus repeatedly prints the following mutilated fragments after many words in this passage: *oratus rex, dam dux ar, corpore qui, stribuere ma, ic post varios, ss non suc, uin potius, ris vice in hac, dinant meri, quia incongru, hujus terrae, ominio absque, et coronae, ivi tamen non, itum po, il li ex 2.* Read consecutively, these fragments correspond to the passage translated here; the mutilated text is supplied from manuscript 2.]

But when, adorned with various virtues, he had ended this life, he did not leave this honor solely to his successors. [Note: This is how the passage must be supplied, as indicated by a space sufficient for three letters; manuscript 2 reads *successorum suorum nulli*, “to none of his successors.”] Rather, our kings and emperors, appointed in place of the supreme Ruler over this pilgrimage, alone regulate these matters, and rightly preside over their other shepherds, because it is exceedingly improper that those whom Christ established as the princes of this land, mindful of him, should be subject to the dominion of anyone except those who, following the Lord’s example, surpass all mortals in the glory of blessing and the crown. [Note: [Col. 1197D] *Absque* means “except” or “apart from.”]

Yet I have heard that some endure great abuse under the authority of dukes—and, what grieves me more, under that of counts—although nothing is permitted to them except what benefits lovers of the world. For when impious power oppresses those who rule rightly with God’s consent, it soon rages with expanded cruelty.

16. (fol. 13) In the palace of the aforesaid king a marvelous event occurred. In the sight of the whole people present, a certain dog, recognizing from a distance its seated enemy, approached more closely and, with a swift bite, unexpectedly tore away his right hand. Then, as though it had done something entirely proper, it immediately returned, wagging its tail.

Everyone marveled and was greatly astonished. The unfortunate man was asked what he had done. He immediately replied that this had deservedly happened to him as divine punishment, and continued:

“I found the master of this dog sleeping, exhausted in body, and, wretched man that I was, killed him. At that time I suffered many attacks from this very persecutor who has now wounded me. I barely escaped him then; now, with that hope wholly forgotten, I came forward guilty.”

I know that thereafter, whether here or at the future judgment, no guilty person will in any way remain hidden without subsequent punishment. [Note: [Col. 1199] The letter *o* was erased in manuscript 1.]

17. My dearest reader, many deeds of our aforesaid king and emperor are eminently worthy of ever-living remembrance. But because I cannot set them down exactly as they occurred, I sadly pass them over, [Note: [Col. 1199D] That is, preserve them in the memory of Scripture, as above, chapter 10.] since he, as I said, justly obtained preeminence in title and in every virtue among our kings.

I have written a small book about some of his greater deeds. [Note: [Col. 1199D] That is, “I wrote it.”] But I hope that his memorial is inscribed in the book of life. He was the faithful servant of Christ’s forerunner, who, as Christ our Lord and God affirmed, was the greatest among those born of women; and he was the first to lay in our city the foundation of the cultivation that followed. Whatever has ever been built upon it in any way is, deservedly, marked to his praise.

An excellent beginning and a good end agree most fittingly wherever this can happen. If this cannot be fulfilled in every respect, let us praise the Lord for what he has done, and let all the faithful, especially you, illustrious Merseburg, with your spiritual offspring, humbly implore his goodness, that he may deign to bring his majesty to its highest point. In the time of your beloved master you were raised above your other neighbors like a cypress. [Note: [Col. 1199D] Apparently a slip of the pen for “cedar.”] [Note: [Col. 1199] The following passage to the end of the poem appears to have been written by Thietmar himself, though this is not beyond doubt.]

Give continual thanks to God, and always eagerly desire that every good thing in you may be perfected under divine governance. [Note: [Col. 1199D] That is, *exoptato*, “desire earnestly.”] For it is the custom of the wicked to be forgetful of good things and to turn for the worse what the Almighty has graciously deigned to create for the better.

If I can ever add anything to the work mentioned above, I shall never cease to do so. But if not, if anyone remembers even somewhat favorably so great a ruler of ours, may the Hearer of all who exist be gracious to him!

Let this first little book be closed with the death of the first Heinricus.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 1199]

*(fol. 14)*

Otto, the glory of the kingdom, born from the noble lineage

of his father Heinricus, shone everywhere with glittering deeds

and thereby ascended to his father’s throne. [Note: [Col. 1199D] Compare the *Annals of Quedlinburg* under the year 937.]

At first many malicious men opposed him,

through envy—all those proud men whom he had conquered

by divine hunger, which always seeks from above.

There had not been so great a patron since the death of Charles,

nor, I think, would the kingdom receive a shepherd like him.

At last he built six bishoprics.

[Col. 1199C]

Here, having overcome the proud Berenger by his valor,

he subjected to himself the raging necks of the Lombards.

Rome made him a powerful emperor,

and distant peoples living by the sea paid him tribute. [Note: [Col. 1199D] These may be peoples living on the seashore, such as the Frisians, or those situated beyond the sea, such as the Greeks. See the *Annals of Quedlinburg* under the year 944.]

He was a friend of peace and kept war far away.

He pacified the western peoples and the fierce Danes.

At that time no enemy appeared in the eastern regions. [Note: [Col. 1200D] Compare Horace, *Odes* I, 35, 31.]

Greatest among scepter-bearers, he sat for thirty-eight

years in the kingdom. [Note: [Col. 1200D] More correctly, thirty-seven years, namely from 8 August 936 to 7 May 973.]

Then Otto departed, [Note: [Col. 1199] Manuscript 1b reads *discerat*. The poem appears to have been written in Thietmar’s own hand, and he seems to have corrected it to *disceserat*.]

alas, mourned by his homeland, yet at the same time unconquered,

leaving here behind him the pledge of a son for his beloved wife,

in whom his friends rejoiced.

1. (fol. 15) All the princes of the realm, wishing to lighten the great sorrow of Queen Mathild, [Note: [Col. 1199] Manuscript 1c frequently has *mechtildis*.] chose Otto, her son, as their king and lord, by the decree and request of his father, with one voice, raising their right hands and crying out: “May the victorious king live and prosper forever!” [Note: [Col. 1200D] From Widukind II, 1.]

Together with him they then set out for Aachen (936). When they approached it, the whole senate went out to meet him, promised faith with submission, and, leading him to the imperial throne, established him in the place of his predecessors, acclaiming him as their king and then giving thanks to God.

Hilbertus, who cared for the see of Mainz, did this with the permission of Wigfrid, archbishop of the holy see of Cologne, in whose diocese the event took place, and with the assistance of the archbishop of Trier. [Note: [Col. 1199] Manuscript 2 has *curator*, “curator,” rather than *cura*, “care.” Manuscript 1c adds *sedis*, “see.”] He blessed Otto in the church of Saint Mary Ever-Virgin in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 936. [Note: [Col. 1199] Manuscript 1b adds the full date in Roman numerals.] The great Charles had built that church with every care.

Then Otto, strengthened in God and the greatest among scepter-bearing rulers, [Note: [Col. 1200D] “Greatest of kings” concerning Otto appears in Widukind II, 1; the same expression is used concerning Heinricus I in I, 41.] ordered his wife Edith, a God-fearing woman whom he had married while her father was still alive, to be consecrated. [Note: [Col. 1200D] More correctly, she was the daughter of Eadward and sister of Eadmund; this error probably derives from our Widukind I, 37.] Edith was the daughter of King Eadmund of the English.

Many favorable events were disturbed by adverse ones. For the wicked Bolizlavus killed his brother Ventizlavus, duke of the Bohemians, who was faithful to God and the king, [Note: [Col. 1199] Manuscript 1c has *uuenzlaum*.] and boldly resisted for a long time. Later he was vigorously defeated by the king and handed over to his own brother Heinricus, duke of Bavaria, to serve him. [Note: [Col. 1199] Two letters preceding *traditus* were erased in manuscript 1.]

The Avars, too, formerly hostile to his father but pacified for a long time, rose again and, swiftly routed, returned (938).

A considerable dispute also arose among fellow citizens and allies. It stirred up Tammo, the son of the king and Liudgerda, [Note: [Col. 1201] Manuscript 1a has *tommonem*; manuscript 2 correctly has *Hateburgae*.] because the legation of Count Sifrid of Merseburg, which he had claimed for himself, was granted to the margrave Gero, [Note: [Col. 1201] Added in manuscript 1b.] and his maternal inheritance was completely taken from him.

The king besieged him at Eresburg and tried, by threats and persuasion, to remove the son from his unjust presumption. [Note: [Col. 1201] Manuscript 2 rightly reads *fratremque*, “the brother,” rather than *filiumque*, “the son.”] But after the army entered the captured city, it drove the aforementioned young man, exhausted by battle, as far as the church of Saint Peter, [Note: [Col. 1201D] See Widukind II, 11.] where the ancient Irminsul had previously been worshiped.

Finally, on 28 July, the young man was pierced from behind beside the altar by the spear of Maginzo, a recruit thrusting it through a window, and died. [Note: [Col. 1201] *a. m.* was added by manuscript 1b in an empty space.] [Note: [Col. 1201D] “At Mainz … pierced from behind by a lance through a window, he killed Thancmar beside the altar”: Widukind I, 1.] The king later avenged him with a cruel death in the second year of his reign. [Note: [Col. 1201] Added in manuscript 1b.]

2. Whatever harmful things happened to him publicly or secretly, he safely escaped through the grace of divine mercy and the continual intercession of his most holy wife Aedith. [Note: [Col. 1201] The *a* in *Aedithae* was erased in manuscript 1.] At her urging he began to build the city of Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 1201] The *a* was erased in manuscript 1, and likewise often elsewhere.], to which he brought the relics of Christ’s martyr Innocentius with great honor. [Note: [Col. 1201D] The city of Magdeburg is already mentioned in Charlemagne’s capitulary of 805. Here, therefore, “city” means a church or monastery. Compare Otto’s charters concerning the foundation and endowment of the churches of Saint Peter, Saint Maurice, and Saint Innocentius at Magdeburg, dated 21 and 27 September 937. The *Chronicon Saxonicum* under the year 929 attests that Otto offered this city to his wife Edith as her dowry.]

For the sake of eternal reward and the salvation of their common homeland, he both acquired and built this city. [Note: [Col. 1201D] Compare above, I, 10, “for the salvation of the kingdom”; compare II, 14.] Blessed Edith helped him in this with all the means at her disposal. Endowed with innumerable virtues, as signs made clear after her death, she spent the time granted her in this life acceptably to God and to human beings.

She was with her husband for nineteen years [Note: [Col. 1201] Manuscript 1 writes this as *X et VIIII*.] and died in the eleventh year of her consecration, on 26 January (946), leaving one son named Liudulfus, radiant with every virtue. She was buried in the aforesaid city, in the principal church, in the northern oratory. [Note: [Col. 1201D] From Widukind II, 41.]

The king, however, while hunting, by which he had hoped to refresh himself somewhat, was afflicted by a mortal wound and endured unheard-of grief; at the arrival of his beloved son he checked it. [Note: [Col. 1201] Manuscript 1c has *compescitur*, “is restrained.”]

The boy, in praiseworthy simplicity, traversed the branching letter of the Samian Pythagoras, which signifies the movements of human life, to the fork in the road, [Note: [Col. 1201D] Compare Persius, *Satires* III, 56, and Ausonius, *Idyll* XII, 9.] and, having entered the right-hand path, the shorter yet better branch, rose from day to day like flourishing ivy, imitating his father in everything, and adorned his nobility with such distinction of character that he pleased all the leading men—an honor by no means insignificant. [Note: [Col. 1201D] The same image occurs in the *Annals of Quedlinburg* under the year 999. The Samian letter is the letter Y. See Forcellini, *Lexicon*, under “Pythagoras.” The author appears to have known the following lines of Persius III, 54:

“And the letter that divided the Samian branches

showed you the rising path along the right-hand boundary.”

He also appears to have known Persius V, 34–35:

“When the road is uncertain and error, ignorant of life,

divides anxious minds at the branching crossroads”;

and Ausonius’ *Idyll* on one-syllable letters:

“Pythagoras’ forked road, with its ambiguous branches,”

where the manuscript has the corrupt sequence *r mis pateo ambiguis*, perhaps referring to “the shorter, yet preferable, branch.”]

Therefore his father’s favor smiled upon him so greatly that, by the common election of the entire senate, he appointed him his partner in honor and labor and confirmed him as his successor. [Note: [Col. 1202D] Having made his will, he created him king after himself: Widukind III, 1.]

He also betrothed to him Ida, daughter of Duke Hirimannus, who surpassed all in beauty and virtue. When the father joined her to him in the bond of marriage, after a short interval he gave him the duchy and inheritance of his deceased father-in-law. [Note: [Col. 1202D] Widukind I, 6.]

How powerful the kingdom was during the time of such a father and son is difficult for anyone to explain fully. [Note: [Col. 1202D] “It is not within the capacity of our weakness to relate how magnificently he enlarged the empire with his son”: Widukind I, 63.]

The venerable Queen Mathild, however, after building the monastery at Quedlinburg, as I have said, [Note: [Col. 1201] Manuscript 1b has *ut p.*, apparently an abbreviation of *ut praedixi*, “as I said,”] and gathering a congregation of holy women there, earned through faithful service to God that her son’s virtue flourished in all things.

### 3

Meanwhile (951), Berengar, the invader of Louis’s kingdom [Note: [Col. 1201] *ludhuuici* in 1c?], captured Ethelheida [Note: [Col. 1201] *adhelheidam* in 1c.], his widow [Note: [Col. 1202D] Widukind (book I, chapter 7), and Thietmar, following him here, erroneously calls Ethelheidis’s former husband Lothar “Louis”], on 12 Kalends of May at Como and plundered her [Note: [Col. 1201] “12—Como” added in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1202D] Merseburg Calendar: “12 Kalends of May. On the same day Empress Aedelheid was captured at Como by King Berengar. 13 Kalends of September. On the same day the Lord freed Queen Aethelheida (m) from chains (m).”], and afflicted her pitiably with confinement and hunger [Note: [Col. 1202D] From Widukind, book I.].  

Observing this woman’s admirable beauty and reputation, our king [Col. 1202C] pretended to be going to Rome. On that very journey he reached Lombardy and, through envoys [Note: [Col. 1201] *legatas* in 1a.], addressed the aforesaid lady, who had by then escaped from custody [Note: [Col. 1201] “Flight—from custody” added in 1b.]. Having been placated by the gifts previously sent, he compelled her to consent to his will; together with her he also claimed the city of Pavia (folio 17).

Concerning this matter Dudo [Note: [Col. 1203] “Ludolfus” here and shortly afterward in 1c.] [Note: [Col. 1203C] Dudo seems to be nothing other than a contracted form of the name Liudolfus—perhaps originally, as Lappenberg suggests, *Thiodulli*, which means the same as *Liudolfus*. Thus the bishop Liutolius or Liutoldus of Augsburg (cf. the Augsburg Annals, 989) is called Tuto and Toto in the Einsiedeln Annals, 988 (above, p. 143); Liudgardis, Liudolf’s sister, is called Dudicha in the genealogical table (p. 215). Waitz.], her son, becoming extremely distressed, hastened to our people and concealed himself in hidden places belonging to Saleveldun, suitable for concealment and treachery [Note: [Col. 1203D] From Widukind, chapter 9.].

After this the king, having fortified Pavia with a garrison and arranged the necessary affairs there, returned (952). Berengar followed him with Duke Conrad [Note: [Col. 1203D] From the same source, chapter 10.], and earned the king’s favor by surrendering the city of Augsburg, himself, and his son; at the same time, by humbly seeking pardon, he appeased the queen’s anger and returned peacefully to his homeland [Note: [Col. 1203D] From the same source, chapters 10–11.].

As the king traveled through Francia governing it, he discovered the hidden ambushes being prepared by his son and his son-in-law Hugh [Note: [Col. 1203D] This son-in-law is related to our Thietmar, being the husband of his sister. Here, however, he confuses Hugh, duke of the western Franks, who had married Hathuwin, King Henry’s daughter, with Conrad, duke of the eastern Franks, to whom Otto had given his daughter Liudgard in marriage.] [Note: [Col. 1203D] Widukind, book I, chapter 13.]. Immediately, in anger, he sent them this message through intermediaries [Note: [Col. 1203] “These things” added in 1b.]: either they should send him the perpetrators of so great a crime, or they should know for certain that they were enemies of royal power [Note: [Col. 1203D] From the same source, chapter 15.].

When they refused to comply with such an embassy [Note: [Col. 1203] *connivere* in 1c.], he gathered an army and pursued them as far as Mainz (953), capturing or compelling the surrender of all the cities which his son possessed [Note: [Col. 1203] “Son” added in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1203D] Same source, chapter 18.]. Having surrounded them with this powerful force [Note: [Col. 1203] *circumseptam* in 1.], he wearied the rebels greatly through continual warfare.

Then, after selected hostages had been exchanged by both sides [Note: [Col. 1203D] Same source, chapter 19.], the father spoke with his son and promised that he would grant him his favor if he disclosed and handed over for punishment his associates who were plotting such things (folio 17 verso) [Note: [Col. 1204C] Same source, book I, chapter 18: “He demands the supporters of the ambush.”] [Note: [Col. 1203] *sposponsdit* in 1a.]. Since the young man could neither do this nor wished to do it, unwilling to violate under oath the trust he had with his own people [Note: [Col. 1204C] “But they, bound by reciprocal oaths …, denied this entirely.”], he was insulted by his uncle Henry [Note: [Col. 1204C] “Henry, moved against the young man,” in the same source, book I.], entered the city intending to rebel [Note: [Col. 1204D] Same source, book I: “the young man … entered the city.”], and joined Count Ekbert and many of his uncle’s soldiers to himself [Note: [Col. 1204D] Same source, chapter 19.].

Then, secretly going out with all his men in the silence of night, he seized Regensburg—which is called Reinesburg—the capital of the Bavarian kingdom, together with its very strongly fortified towns, driving the lady Ivuthita alone, with her children, from those territories [Note: [Col. 1204D] Same source, chapter 20.].

Moreover, when Duke Thiedricus and Count Wigmann were moving their forces to recover Mainz once more, with the father following behind [Note: [Col. 1204D] Same source, chapter 21: “the king following his son into Bavaria”], the king attempted to remove them through envoys and money. When Thiedricus showed no inclination at all, he quickly corrupted Wigmann, won over by flattering words [Note: [Col. 1204D] Same source, chapter 24.].

Meanwhile, the king, setting out for Bavaria with troops prepared for the expedition, returned after all the gates of the walls had been closed against him and the region itself had been devastated and burned [Note: [Col. 1204D] Same source, chapter 26.].

Then Dudo [Note: [Col. 1203] “Ludolfus” in 1c.]—despairing of resisting his father and king—brought the quiver-bearing Avars in as allies (954); this did not escape the king’s notice. For he marched with military standards to meet the enemies rising against him [Note: [Col. 1204D] Same source, chapter 30.], but a different grief befell him than anyone might have expected. For these men, directed by wicked leaders along another route, invaded Francia and *pitiably ravaged it [Note: [Col. 1204D] Same source.].

But if anyone asks privately in his mind or aloud where such audacity among foreigners arises, so that they dare to violate regions so far inhabited and so remote, let him hear our answer: insofar as we have ever learned from writings or know by our own experience, these men are inflamed by divine consent to avenge our crimes as God’s vengeance. We, greatly terrified, flee cowardly from the injustice of our own deeds; and so it happens that those who, in prosperity, despised fear of God deservedly endure the Lord’s scourge, and, though we call upon God, are not heard, because we made no effort at all to appease the heavenly offense.

Hence it happened that Germany, unequal in strength to the other provinces of its region, succumbed to these forces; for a wall is said to be whatever is able to withstand arrows [Note: [Col. 1203] “Thus” in 1 and 2. The reading *quicumque*, corrected by erasure, is certainly from 1c, with 2 presenting our reading.] [Note: [Col. 1204D] Similarly Widukind, III.46, who followed Sallust, *Catiline* 54: “Boldness is regarded as a wall.”].

At last God, moved by the merits of the righteous and the groaning of the afflicted [Col. 1204C], put the multitude of the faithless to flight. The king pursued them when they again turned aside in a direction other than they had expected, and invaded Bavaria once more. They soon negotiated for peace and, seeking a truce, obtained it [Note: [Col. 1204D] Widukind, book I, chapter 31.].

But always uncertain and faithless toward their own lords, when they could not excuse themselves before the king, they sought Reinesburg with their elder lord Liudolf, revealing its known garrisons [Note: [Col. 1203] “Fleeing” in 1a; the reading “revealing” appears in 1b.] [Col. 1205A]. The king followed them with a powerful army and occupied the aforesaid city (folio 18) [Note: [Col. 1205C] Same source, chapters 34 and 36.]. After a long mutual struggle, he finally compelled the son and his men, to the great enhancement of his reputation [Note: [Col. 1205] “Great” added in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1205C] Same source, at the end of chapter 36.], to seek peace [Note: [Col. 1205C] Same source, chapter 37.].

After this Dudo [Note: [Col. 1205] “Ludolfus” in 1c.] came to his senses together with Hugh [Note: [Col. 1205] Read “Conrad”], threw himself at his father’s feet, humbly asked forgiveness for the past and correction for the present, and promised caution for the future [Note: [Col. 1205] *spospondit* in 1a.] [Note: [Col. 1205C] Same source, chapter 40.]. Overcome by the counsel of his leading men, the king received him and, remitting his offenses, firmly restored him to his favor [Note: [Col. 1205C] Same source, chapter 41.]. He then restored to his brother the kingdom he had long lost; and, after all his adversaries had been reconciled, as he hoped, he returned victoriously to Saxony [Note: [Col. 1205C] Same source, chapter 43.].

### 4

And [Note: [Col. 1205] Added in 1b.] behold, once again the Avars—that is, the Hungarians [Note: [Col. 1205] “That is, the Hungarians” added in 1c.]—as though they had forgotten the crime already committed, took up arms against us* [Col. 1205B] (955). When Duke Henry announced their approach to the king, he recalled him from the routes he had begun to take [Note: [Col. 1205C] Same source, chapter 44, beginning.].

The king, however, summoned all his retainers to himself at the city of Augsburg, declaring that he would rather die than endure any more such great evils [Note: [Col. 1205] Read “Conrad.”] [Note: [Col. 1205C] Terence, *Eunuchus* I.1.3: “not to endure insults”; 7: “where you will not be able to suffer”; 21: “I would rather die.”]. He exhorted [Note: [Col. 1205] *hortaturque* in 1c.] his men, promising rewards with his favor to all who supported him and punishment to those who fled [Note: [Col. 1205] *sibi* for *se* in 1c.] [Note: [Col. 1205] The letter *o* has been erased.].

He gathered from every direction only eight legions [Note: [Col. 1205C] Same source, chapter 44, middle.], and consoled them when they had been drawn up against the enemy, encouraging those who were to die with eternal rewards and those who were to conquer with present delights.

The fierce enemy, secretly circling around their exposed flank beside the swift Lech River (folio 19), attacked them while they were off guard [Note: [Col. 1205] *celerem* added in 1b.], killing and stripping many of them. When the king learned of this, he sent Duke Conrad with his men behind them; Conrad snatched the captives, together with all the booty, from the jaws of the wolf-like robber, and, having won the victory [Note: [Col. 1205] *que* added in 1b.], returned to the camp [Note: [Col. 1206C] Same source, chapter 44.].

On the following day, that is, on the feast of Christ’s martyr Laurence (10 August), the king alone confessed himself guilty before God above all others, prostrated himself, and made this vow amid abundant tears: if Christ would deign on that day, through the intercession of so great an advocate, to grant him victory and life, he would establish at Merseburg a bishopric in honor of the victor over the fires and would make his own great, newly begun building into a church [Note: [Col. 1205] *domum suimet* added in 1b.].

Without delay, rising from the ground after the celebration of Mass and after receiving holy communion from his distinguished confessor Othelric, the king took up his shield and sacred lance [Note: [Col. 1205] *sumpsit* added in 1b.], preceded his soldiers against the enemy, and was the first to break through the opposing line. He then struck down and drove the fleeing enemy into flight until evening [Note: [Col. 1206C] Same source, together with the *Life of Saint Udalric*, chapter 12.].

When the slaughter had finally been completed [Note: [Col. 1205] Added in 1b.], the king sat with the victorious host on the green meadows and carefully asked whether anyone from his army was missing [Note: [Col. 1205] *a suo* added in 1b.]. He then learned that Duke Conrad, his son-in-law and distinguished soldier [Note: [Col. 1205] *generum sui* added in 1b.], had perished. Having properly mourned and carefully prepared Conrad’s body, he sent it to Worms for burial [Note: [Col. 1206C] Widukind, book I, chapter 47.].

He had also sent messengers in advance to his holy mother, who, explaining everything in order, would relieve her anxiety and at the same time kindle the minds of the faithful to praise Christ (folio 19). All Christendom, and especially the people entrusted to the king, received so great a gift of divine mercy with indescribable rejoicing [Note: [Col. 1206C] Same source, chapter 49.] [Col. 1206B], unanimously singing glory and grace to God in the highest.

### 5

In this year Duke Henry, the king’s brother, died [Note: [Col. 1205] “In this year … died” added in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1206C] Quedlinburg Annals, 955.].

Meanwhile, as the king joyfully revisited Saxony and his homeland, all the princes who came from afar to meet him received him with the greatest enthusiasm [Note: [Col. 1205] Added in 1b; cf. Virgil, *Aeneid* I.415.]. Long awaited by his venerable mother, he embraced her with tears pouring forth from joy.

Immediately revealing his promise to them and explaining how he intended to carry it out exactly, he earnestly sought their counsel and support for the undertaking. When they praised this plan and approved his pious petition, the king decided to establish an abbey in the city of Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 1206C] That is, he built it. This abbey was founded in 937. See above, chapter 2.], beginning a church of marvelous construction at the place where Saint Edith rests [Note: [Col. 1205] The initial *a* has been erased in 1.], beside which he himself had desired to rest after his death [Note: [Col. 1205] Added in 1b.].

He also attempted to establish a bishopric there, but throughout his life he could not obtain this from Bernard, the seventh bishop of the holy church of Halberstadt [Note: [Col. 1205] Added in 1b.], in whose diocese the aforesaid city lies [Note: [Col. 1205] “Lay” in 1c.]. Whatever he acquired in estates or other possessions by permission [Note: [Col. 1205] “Granted” in 2; “granted to him” in A.S.; “by promise” in the Saxon Chronicle, 955.] during that period [Note: [Col. 1206C] That is, by permission granted to him by providence. Compare II.16 and VIII.7], he granted in its entirety to God and to His heir, Saint Maurice [Note: [Col. 1206C] That is, he acquired it.].

### 6

While these things were taking place, a terrible war broke out from the side of the Slavs*; it arose at the instigation of Counts Wigmann and Ekbert, but under the leadership of Nacco and his brother Stoinneguus. Duke Hermann, despairing of overcoming them, sought the king’s aid [Note: [Col. 1206C] Widukind, book I, chapters 50 and 52.].

The king, as energetic as ever, invaded the northern regions with a powerful army [Col. 1207A] [Note: [Col. 1207D] Same source, chapter 53, beginning], where they very often revealed evil, as Scripture says (Jeremiah 1:14). There he ordered Stoinneguus, who had been hiding in a grove and was captured while his companions were fleeing, to be beheaded [Note: [Col. 1207D] Same source, chapter 35, beginning]. He drove away his fellow conspirators, the perpetrators of so great a crime—Wigmann, the king’s maternal aunt’s son [Note: [Col. 1207] “The king’s maternal aunt’s son” added in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1207D] Compare the Quedlinburg Annals, 955, which say this of Ekbert. On this relationship, compare Wedekind, *Notes*, vol. II, p. 67.]—and Ekbert [Note: [Col. 1207D] Same source, chapter 55, end.].

But Liudolf, the king’s son, corrupted by the counsel of evil men, again resisted. Leaving his homeland, he went to Italy (956), and, after remaining there for nearly a year, died, alas, on 8 Ides of September [Note: [Col. 1207D] Widukind, book I, chapter 57; Quedlinburg Annals, 956 and 957; Merseburg Calendar, 6 September.]. His companions brought his body to Mainz (957), where it was mournfully buried in the church of Christ’s martyr Alban [Note: [Col. 1207D] Widukind, book I.].

When the king, on campaign against the Redarii, heard this sorrowful news, he was deeply distressed and mourned his son as David mourned Absalom [Note: [Col. 1207D] Same source, chapter 58.] [Col. 1207B].

After Thietherd, bishop of Hildesheim, had died, Adwin, abbot of the Magdeburg church, succeeded him [Note: [Col. 1207] “Thietherd … succeeded” added in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1207D] Hildesheim Annals, 954; Quedlinburg Annals, 955.].

### 7

After this, when the violence of the wars had subsided (961), he again pretended to be going to Rome, entered Lombardy with a powerful army, and finally cunningly captured the aforesaid Berengar—who had held the Mount of Saint Leo for two years—with his wife Willa, sons, and daughters [Note: [Col. 1207] In 1b the words “on Mount Saint Leo, and afterward Willa, and daughters, cunningly, with [him] in Bamberg” are added.]. He sent him into exile at Bamberg, where he later died [Note: [Col. 1207D] Widukind, book I, chapter 63; Hildesheim Annals, 964. Compare the continuation of Regino, 962 and 964, and there see the account of Berengar’s death under 966.].

Then, going armed with soldiers toward Rome [Note: [Col. 1207D] Not “then,” but earlier: Otto had gone to Rome to receive the imperial crown.], he defeated its citizens twice when they resisted him (folio 20) [Note: [Col. 1207] *resistens* in 1.] [Note: [Col. 1207D] Widukind, book I, chapter 63.], and entered the city gloriously in the year 961 of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 1207] The source reads DCCCCXLI, 941; “of the Lord’s incarnation” and shortly afterward “whose kingdom he had held” are added in 1b.].

Moreover, together with his wife, he earned the imperial blessing from Lord Pope John, at whose request he had come there, in the twenty-ninth year of his reign [Note: [Col. 1208D] He was crowned in Rome in 962, on 2 February, but in the twenty-sixth year of his reign.]. Having become the protector of the Roman Church, he claimed Benevento, Calabria, and Apulia for himself after defeating their dukes [Note: [Col. 1208D] Widukind, book I, chapter 63.].

### 8

During his reign a golden age dawned; among us a vein of silver was first discovered [Note: [Col. 1208D] Same source.]. Wigmann was also defeated [Note: [Col. 1208D] Same source, chapter 64.].

At that time, while Harold was reigning among the Danes, Christianity, which had been despised, was renewed through the priest Poppo. For Poppo rebuked both king and people, who had strayed [Note: [Col. 1207] Thus in 1c; *deinuantem* in 1a.] into the worship of their ancestors and were devoted to gods and demons, affirming that there is one God in three persons.

When the king asked him whether he wished to prove his words with a red-hot iron, Poppo cheerfully replied that he was ready to do so. The next day he carried a blessed iron of immense [Note: [Col. 1207] *ingenti* in 1.] weight to the place designated by the king and fearlessly raised his unharmed hand. Greatly rejoicing at the miracle, the king, together with all his people, immediately humbly submitted himself to the yoke of Christ and thereafter obeyed the divine commandments in the manner of the faithful [Note: [Col. 1208D] From Widukind, III.65. Compare the *Life of Bruno*, brother of the Emperor Otto, chapter 35. Let the reader beware of confusing this Poppo, a cleric and later bishop—perhaps of Aarhus—with the younger Poppo, bishop of Schleswig from about 1011 to 1016.].

When the emperor heard this, he summoned the venerable man Poppo and asked whether he was Christ’s champion; then he raised him to priestly dignity [Col. 1208B].

### 9

Gero, margrave of the Eastern March, subjected the Lusizi [Note: [Col. 1208D] Widukind, book I, chapter 67.] and the Selpuli [Note: [Col. 1208D] The district of Selpuli lies in the territory between the towns of Lübben and Storkow, beside the River Spree.], as well as Mieszko with his subjects, to imperial authority (963). Duke Hermann made Selibur and Mistui, together with their people, tributaries of the emperor [Note: [Col. 1208D] Widukind, book I, chapter 68.].

The emperor’s namesake—young Otto, I mean—whom the illustrious mother Ethelheid bore [Note: [Col. 1207] *adhelheidis* in 1c.], was made emperor at Rome on the Nativity of the Lord (967), at his father’s command, while his father was then residing in Campania [Note: [Col. 1207] *capania* in 1.] near Capua [Note: [Col. 1208D] Same source, chapter 70; the error arose from its wording.].

Desiring to arrange a marriage for his son with a wife from the Constantinopolitan emperor, Otto entrusted his faithful leading men with this embassy when messengers from that emperor had been sent to him for another reason [Note: [Col. 1207] *ad* for *ab* in 1a, more often.]. Along the journey the Greeks, attacking them unexpectedly with their customary cunning, killed some and captured others, whom they presented to their own lord, the Augustus. A few of the men escaped and revealed the outcome of the affair to their emperor [Note: [Col. 1208D] Same source, chapter 71. See especially Liudprand’s *Embassy*.].

Taking this loss of his men very seriously, Otto quickly sent the excellent soldiers Gunther and Sigifrid to Calabria to avenge such an outrage [Note: [Col. 1207] “And” added in 1b.]. They killed the Danes, elated by their earlier victory, when they came to meet them [Note: [Col. 1207] “And” added in 1b.]; they cut off the noses of others whom they caught in flight, exacted tribute from the Greeks in Calabria and Apulia, and returned joyfully enriched with spoils [Note: [Col. 1209D] Same source, chapter 72.].

The people of Constantinople, saddened by the death and captivity of their countrymen (folio 21), conspired against their lord and, on the advice of the deceitful empress, killed him through a certain soldier [Note: [Col. 1209] *peremerunt* in 1c.], appointing this man in his place as administrator of the entire empire [Note: [Col. 1209D] Same source, chapter 73.].

Soon afterward, sending across the sea to our emperor magnificent gifts and an outstanding retinue—not the desired virgin, but his own niece, named Theophanu—he freed his men [Note: [Col. 1209D] Same source.] and gained the hoped-for friendship of the august Caesar.

Some people tried to prevent this union before the emperor and advised that the woman be sent back. He did not listen to them, but gave her in marriage to his son (972), with all the leading men of Italy and Germany expressing their approval [Note: [Col. 1209D] Widukind, book I. The marriage contract of Otto II, emperor, dated at Rome on 14 April 972, still survives.].

### 10

The emperor sent many bodies of saints from Italy to Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 1209] *magaburg* in 1, as below in chapter 23.] through his chaplain Doddo [Note: [Col. 1209D] On these relics, see Wedekind, *Notes*, vol. I, p. 115.].

Nor should this, too [Note: [Col. 1209] “However” added in 1b.], be passed over: what I heard about his cleric [Note: [Col. 1209] “About his cleric” in 1b; “about him” in 1a.], named Poppo, the brother of Count William [Note: [Col. 1209D] The Saxon Annals, 965, add “of Weimar.”] [Note: [Col. 1209] “Named … brother” added in 1b.], is worthy of remembrance.

After serving the emperor faithfully for a long time, Poppo became seriously ill and, falling into an ecstatic state, was taken to a high mountain, where he saw a great city and its beautiful buildings [Note: [Col. 1209] Added in 1b.]. From there he came to a lofty tower and began to climb its arduous ascent. At its summit he was granted a vision of Christ seated with all the saints [Note: [Col. 1207] “Great” added in 1b.].

There the archbishop Bruno of Cologne [Note: [Col. 1209] Added in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1209D] 953–965. Brother of Otto I.] was accused by the supreme judge because of his vain pursuit of philosophy, but, defended by blessed Paul, was enthroned again [Note: [Col. 1209] Added in 1b.].

Then Poppo, summoned for a similar reason, was rebuked; supported by the humble intercession of the saints, he heard this voice: “After three days, when you come to me, you will possess this chair, which I now show you.”

When the priest awoke, he explained all these things after summoning the emperor to him. Affirming that it was not a dream but a true vision, he gave thanks to the emperor for all the good things he had ever done for him. As had been announced to him, after making his confession and receiving remission from those present, he abandoned what belonged to others and reclaimed what was his own; and, in good peace, he consoled his grieving lord at so happy a death (folio 22).

### 11

The emperor also ordered precious marble, together with gold and gems, to be brought to Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 1209] “To Magdeburg” in 1b (*magdurc* in 1c); “he ordered it to be brought there” in 1a.]. He commanded that relics of the saints be carefully enclosed in all the capitals of the columns [Note: [Col. 1209] “Which” added in 1b.].

He placed the body of the distinguished [Note: [Col. 1209] *egrei* corrected to *egregii* in 1.] Count Christinus [Note: [Col. 1209D] The Lüneburg Necrology records, under 15 June: “Count Cristin, Eppo, and Verlef, killed.” Another count of the same name appears under 5 November. He seems to be the same man who in certain charters dated 937–945 is called Christianus, count in the district of Serimunt—where Grimsleben and Rosenburg lie beside the River Saale—and who is called Christianus margrave in the Saxon annalist under 945.] and those of others beside the church mentioned above. There he desired throughout his life to have a burial place prepared for himself.

In the year 961 of the Lord’s incarnation, and the twenty-fifth of his reign, in the presence of all the nobles, on the eve of the Nativity of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1210D] It is established from both the continuator of Regino and a charter issued there by the emperor that he was at that time in Regensburg.], the body of Saint Maurice and some of his companions, together with other portions of the saints, was brought to him at Regensburg [Note: [Col. 1209] Added in 1b.].

It was then transferred with the greatest honor, as was fitting, to Parthenopolis [Col. 1210B] and received there by the unanimous gathering of the inhabitants and neighboring peoples [Note: [Col. 1209] Added in 1b.]. It has been venerated there ever since for the salvation of the entire homeland.

### 12

Meanwhile Bernard, a venerable bishop, full of days, died in the Lord in the forty-eighth year of his ordination (968), on the very day itself, that is, 3 Nones of February (folio 22) [Note: [Col. 1209] Corrected from XLVIIII.].

Moreover, William, holy archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 1209] *archipre presul* written on two lines in 1.], to whom the emperor—his lord and kinsman—had entrusted the administration of Parthenopolis and the governance of the other necessities of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 1210D] Widukind, book I, chapter 73.], while awaiting the end of the ailing Queen Mathilda [Note: [Col. 1210D] Same source, chapter 74. Compare the Hildesheim Annals, 968.], died at Redulwerothe on 6 Nones of March.

The venerable queen, overcome by great bodily weakness, announced his death to everyone present without yet having received any reliable report: “My son William [Col. 1210C] [Note: [Col. 1209] *uuillehellmus* in 1.], alas, is already dying [Note: [Col. 1209] Thus in 1b; “has died” in 1a.] and needs the aid of prayer” [Note: [Col. 1209] “Needs the aid of prayer” added in 1b.].

Liudolf, abbot of Corvey [Note: [Col. 1209] *corbeiensis* in 1c.] [Note: [Col. 1210D] Liudolf was abbot from 965 to 983.], seeing him bodily [Note: [Col. 1209] *carporaliter* in 1a.] appear to him on that same night on which he died, was astonished [Note: [Col. 1209] *obstipuit* in 1a; *obstupuit* in 1c.] and announced to his fellow brothers that he was dead [Note: [Col. 1209] Added in 1b.].

After this Saint Mathilda departed from this exile on 2 Ides of March, entrusting her spirit and returning it to God, her Creator. She was buried before the altar of Christ’s bishop Servatius beside her husband, because, having loved him while he lived, she had always prayed, throughout her life, that after death she might be joined to him [Note: [Col. 1209] “To him” added in 1b.].

### 13

Gero, likewise, the defender of the homeland, disturbed by the death of his only illustrious son Sigifrid [Note: [Col. 1211] Added in 1b.], went to Rome. Already an honored old man, he laid down his victorious arms before the altar of the chief of the apostles, Peter [Note: [Col. 1211] Added in 1b.], and, obtaining from the lord pope the holy arm of Cyriacus, fled to God with all his possessions.

Returning to his homeland, he appointed as abbess his son’s widow, previously veiled, named Hathui, in the monastery built in the forest (folio 23) and marked by his own name [Note: [Col. 1211] *Gerinrod* added in 1c.], after she had been consecrated by Bishop Bernard. After establishing all these things, he preceded them in a blessed death on 13 Kalends of June.

### 14

The emperor, having learned of the grievous deaths of his mother, his son, and the other leading men (965) [Note: [Col. 1211D] Widukind, chapter 75, beginning.], lamented with profound sorrow the irreparable loss of the entire commonwealth. Fear of approaching death was pressing him toward this, as was the promise he had made to God in his anxieties [Col. 1211B] [Note: [Col. 1211] The *c* has been erased in 1.], which he now strove to fulfill at the appropriate time [Note: [Col. 1211] *stud[it]* in 1.].

He ordered Hilliward, chosen by all the clergy and people of the holy church of Halberstadt, then provost and previously designated for this purpose by his own lord Bernard, to come to Rome [Note: [Col. 1211] Added in 1b.]. He then disclosed the secret intention that he had long kept hidden in his mind: namely, that he had always intended to establish an archbishopric in the city of Parthenopolis [Note: [Col. 1211D] Compare the statutes of the synod held at Ravenna in 967, the Saxon Chronograph, and the Magdeburg Chronicle.], for the sake of hope for eternal reward and the defense of the common homeland [Note: [Col. 1211D] Nearly the same words occur in II.2.]. He promised that he was prepared to do anything that Hilliward had ever requested of him [Note: [Col. 1211] *expitisset* in 1.], if Hilliward would consent to fulfill this vow.

As he was wise, Hilliward agreed to the pious request [Note: [Col. 1211] *conniuebat* in 1c.]. He granted to God, Saint Maurice, and the emperor the portion of the diocese situated between the rivers Ora (the Ohre) [Note: [Col. 1211] Corrected from *oram* in 1c.] and Elbe and the Bode [Note: [Col. 1211] *bodam* in 1c.], together with the road called Frederick’s Way [Col. 1211C] [Note: [Col. 1211] Added in 1b.].

Moreover, when the august Caesar asked him charitably, he gave to God and Saint Laurence the diocese lying between the rivers Willerbezi and the Salt Sea, and the Saale, Unstrut, and Helme, as well as the ditch that is beside Valeshusun [Note: [Col. 1211] *uualenhusun* in 1c?] [Note: [Col. 1211D] The *Wildbach*, or “wild stream,” flows into the Helme not far from the town of Kelbra; the Salt Lake lies near Seeburg in the county of Mansfeld, and from it flows the River Salza. The Saale and Unstrut are well known; the Helme flows past the village of Wallhausen at a short distance. Urs. On Frederick’s Way, see also Emperor Otto’s charter of 9 July 965.].

Rejoicing at such a gift, the emperor received Hilliward by the hand and entrusted the pastoral care to him with a staff: “Receive,” he said, “the compensation for your father!” [Note: [Col. 1211D] That is, the composition or wergild; added in 1b.]

For he had ordered this man’s father, named Eric, together with Baccho, Hermann, Reinward, Wirinus, Eseric [Note: [Col. 1211] “Hermann, Reinward, Wirinus, Eseric,” and immediately afterward “on the solemn feast” are added in 1b.], and the others who had attempted to kill the king at Quedlinburg on the solemn feast of Easter, to be beheaded [Note: [Col. 1211D] Quedlinburg Annals, 941.].

He also willingly wished to destroy my grandfather Liutharius, who had taken part in the same plot [Note: [Col. 1211D] On him, see VI.30.]. But, overcome by the counsel of the leading men among his household, he sent him, after capturing him, to Bavaria to Count Bertold, after confiscating all his possessions and distributing them widely [Note: [Col. 1211] Added in 1b.], for an entire year. Then Liutharius secured the king’s favor and all his possessions, along with a large sum of money and estates located at Sonterslevo and Vodenesvege [Note: [Col. 1211D] Sandersleben and Gutenswegen in the Magdeburg district. Urs.].

But I shall continue along the path I began.

The emperor summoned Richarius, the third abbot of the Magdeburg church—for Anno and Otwinus, then bishops, had presided over it [Note: [Col. 1212D] Anno, bishop of Worms, 950–978. Adwin, bishop of Hildesheim, 954–984.]—intending to adorn him with priestly dignity. But after seeing a certain letter secretly brought to him [Note: [Col. 1211] Added in 1b.], he abandoned the plan and promoted to the summit of the archbishopric, by apostolic authority, the illustrious and thoroughly approved father Aethelbert [Note: [Col. 1211] *adh* in 1c.], of Trier, a monk by profession, previously ordained bishop in Ruscia [Note: [Col. 1212D] Not in Ruscia, but among the Rugi, Adalbert had been ordained bishop, as is shown by the emperor’s mandate cited shortly afterward, the Saxon Annals under 968, the Saxon Chronograph under 969, and the continuation of Regino under 991.], and expelled from there by the pagans [Note: [Col. 1211] “And expelled from there by the pagans” added in 1b.], in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 970 [968], on 15 Kalends of November.

Then he sent him to his own see with great honor, ordering all the princes of Saxony to be with him at the coming Nativity of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1212D] See *Laws*, vol. II, p. 561, for the emperor’s mandate concerning the installation of the archbishop of Magdeburg.].

The archbishop was magnificently received by the clergy and the entire people. During those festive days he consecrated Boso, the first shepherd of the church of Merseburg [Note: [Col. 1211] “First” is added everywhere in 1b.], Burchard, the first bishop of the church of Meissen [Note: [Col. 1211] *misnesis* in 1.] [Note: [Col. 1211] “First” is added everywhere in 1b.], and Hugh, the first bishop of the church of Zeitz [Note: [Col. 1212C] The letters *ti* have been erased in 1c? The same spelling occurs throughout this word.] [Note: [Col. 1211] “First” is added everywhere in 1b.]; to these he joined Tundo, previously consecrated, as the first guardian of the church of Havelberg [Note: [Col. 1211] “First” is added everywhere in 1b.].

All of them promised submission to him and to his successors, and he assigned to each his own distinct diocese [Note: [Col. 1211] Added in 1b.]. Thietmar was added to these fellow bishops as the first pastor of the church of Brandenburg [Note: [Col. 1211] “Dudelinus” in the Saxon Annals, 969.] [Note: [Col. 1212D] He is called Duodelinus in the emperor’s mandate cited above, as in the Saxon Annals under 969 and the Saxon Chronograph under 970. Below our author calls Dodilo the second bishop of Brandenburg. Thietmar was the first bishop of Brandenburg, appointed by the emperor in 949.], having been anointed previously [Note: [Col. 1211] “Previously anointed” added in 1b.], together with Jordan, the first bishop of Poznań [Note: [Col. 1211] “First” is added everywhere in 1b.].

### 15.

It is worthwhile, although the order may rightly be charged against me as inverted, to add how the emperor [Col. 1213A] gave to his brother, the lord Bruno—named after his paternal uncle, Duke Bruno [Note: *Luthuwigo* (“Louis”): text; misspelled *luduuuico*: witness 1c], who, sent by King Louis on an expedition against the Danes, perished with three bishops [Note: Manuscript 1a reads *tribus*, “three”], Thiadric and Marquard and the other soldiers, in a flood of the river on 2 February [Note: Manuscript 1b adds “the fourth day before the Nones of February.”]—after Wigfrid, administrator of the see of Agrippina, had died, that same episcopate and, in addition, the duchy of Lotharingia [Note: See the Annals of Fulda and Corvey under 880, and Widukind I.15.].

Afterward, although he was most wise, Bruno was corrupted by the counsel of wicked men and contemplated repaying evil for good to his king and brother. (953.) For he summoned to himself Hugo, his son-in-law, whom, as we mentioned above [Note: See above, chapter 3, note 227. Cuno or Conrad, Otto’s son-in-law.], he knew to be excessively disloyal to the king, to a banquet. Forgetful of kinship and his oath, he endeavored to entrust the kingdom to him with a crown skillfully adorned with jewels [Note: Manuscript 1c reads *ipsi*, “to him,” for *ipso*.].

When, on the holy day [Col. 1213B] of solemn Easter, with all the royal insignia prepared, he wished to crown his son-in-law, who sought the promised gift with a woman’s longing, the bridle of hatred having been somewhat loosened through the grace of divine mercy and of Wisdom, which governs all things, he was ashamed of and repented his undertaking.

He secretly summoned his secretary Wolcmer, whom we mentioned earlier [Note: The author is mistaken: he had not mentioned Wolcmer earlier in these books.], opened to him the wound hidden in his mind, and carefully asked how it might be healed [Note: In witness 1 the first *u* of *Wolcmero* was erased; the same spelling intervention occurs repeatedly].
