But God, who is ready for every turn of events, sent this man a heavenly thought, by which he softened his lord’s anxiety through the following reply:

> “[f. 25] The Holy Spirit, dearest lord, has suggested to you that the enemy, the author of so great a crime, should no longer prevail against us. I think that he can be confounded in this way, while you can be honored. The crown that you promised to give your son-in-law [Col. 1213C] tomorrow I shall present while you are seated with him, so that your fidelity may shine before everyone; and, falling upon it unwillingly, I shall shatter it, so that fraternal love, now grown cold, may afterward grow warm again.”

This pleased the archbishop, and so, with exultant prayers, he humbly knocked at the divine ears. When morning came, and these words had been fulfilled in deed, the archbishop pretended great sorrow. Hugo and his companions, frustrated in so great a hope [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *fustrati*], endured inconsolable grief; and, when the festive days had been completed, Hugo returned, honored with gifts other than those he had expected.

After this, the brothers—that is, the king and the bishop—having been reconciled and persevering toward one another in a spirit of piety, took care thereafter to remove every scruple of hostility. But the archbishop, powerful in every divine and human advantage [Col. 1214A], having completed the thirteenth year of his ordination, fell asleep in the sleep of peace on 11 October [Note: Manuscript 1b adds “the fifth day before the Ides of October.”] [Note: See the Merseburg Calendar. He died in 965; compare the continuation of Regino.], leaving his brother sorrowful [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *reliqit*].

Otto, mentioned above, spent nearly forty-nine years engaged in such snares of conspirators [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *insiandicium*] and in many other affairs of the kingdom and the administration of the empire; yet, with Christ protecting him in all things, he escaped them safely (965) [f. 23′] [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *omibus*, “all,” without the *n*]. I have said little about the innumerable noble deeds of this great man, better than the one just recounted [Note: Witness 1a reads *histo*; the editor takes it to mean “this one,” namely the conspiracy just narrated], because an entire book has been written in full about his noble way of life [Note: Namely, Ruotger’s *Life of Bruno*], and this prevents me from adding anything further.

### 16.

The emperor, shaken by his brother’s death, faithfully entrusted the episcopate and the care of his soul, out of affection for him, to Wolcmer, his familiar chaplain [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *capellana*, “chaplaincy”]. While he held the see for the time granted him by God [Col. 1214B] [Note: Manuscript 1a reads *permissam*, “granted to her”], conducted himself excellently in all things, and departed this life on 18 July (967) [Note: See the Merseburg Calendar. He died in 967. Compare Regino’s continuation and Lambert’s *Annals* under 965. In the Cologne Annals his name is given as Poppo.], Gero, the brother of Margrave Thietmar [Note: Manuscript 1a reads “Thiadmar”], was elected by the clergy and by the whole people; this was immediately reported to the emperor.

Since he was angry with his aforementioned brother for many reasons, the emperor did not wish to give Gero the episcopate. Meanwhile, Wolcmer, who was then a chaplain, was celebrating Mass one day in the city of Pavia. There he alone saw Saint Peter and Saint Ambrose blessing him with holy oil. He disclosed this to no one at the time, but bore the gift of divine mercy with an even mind [Note: Witness 1 reads *Imperatore*, “the emperor” in the ablative, where the text has dative *Imperatori*, “to the emperor”] [Note: Manuscript 1c reads *nulli*, “to no one,” for *nullo*].

On the holy day of the Lord’s Resurrection, however, when the emperor had drawn his sword and, already prepared except for the crown, was about to go to the church [f. 26], an angel appeared to him with a bared sword and said:

> “Unless today you complete the election [Col. 1214C] of Gero, you will not escape this see safely.”

The emperor was terrified by this and said:

> “Call Lord Gero.”

When Gero came immediately, the emperor entrusted the pastoral office to him with the staff and humbly begged his forgiveness [Note: Witness 1a reads *cumque*, “and when,” rather than the text’s *eique*, “and to him”]. Later blessed by his suffragans, Gero carried the name and office, acceptable to God and to men, with complete devotion of mind throughout his life, as the signs still declare today [Note: Gero occupied the see until 975].

His holy mother, named Hidda [Note: *Ida*, corrected by an uncertain hand], journeyed to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer. There she fell ill and entrusted the following message to her attendants:

> “When my soul departs after the prolonged dwelling of this exile, quickly deliver my body to mother earth. Then go at once and report this to my son Gero: let him not deny his pilgrim mother on earth the honor that pious God has deemed fit to grant her in heaven [Col. 1215A], and let him establish an altar for me in the church of Saint Cecilia.”

[Note: Concerning this Ida or Hidda, see the *Chronicle of Mount Soren*, under the year 1171. From it we learn that she was the sister of Margrave Gero and Count Siegfried and was married to Count Christian.]

The devoted servants obeyed these commands, buried their mistress after she had happily expired, and immediately departed, unaware of the misery that was about to follow [Note: Manuscripts 1c and 2 add *non*, “not”]. For when the Saracens invaded Jerusalem at that time [Note: This occurred under al-Muʿizz, the first caliph of the Fatimid or Alid dynasty, around the year 970.], they left the defeated nothing. The matron Hidda [Note: Witness 2 adds the name *Hidda* here] had secretly foretold this to them when she ordered herself to be buried hastily and commanded them to depart.

When they reached Cologne, they reported everything in order to the archbishop [f. 26′]. He received them kindly, gave thanks to God, and fulfilled her just request. Since I have said little about the praise due to so great a bishop, though it is not widely known, I wish in what follows to discuss the rest, so that his virtue may appear more clearly in these matters. [Col. 1215B]

### 17.

When the emperor heard of the death of the bishop of the church of Regensburg [Note: Namely Isangrim, who died in 942; see the Annals of Saint Emmeram of Regensburg under that year.], he went there (942). In a dream he was warned not to give the episcopate to anyone other than the first person who should meet him [Note: Witness 1c reads *alii*, “to another,” for *alio*, “to another person,” and *ei*, “to him,” for *eo*, “that person”].

At earliest dawn on the following day, the emperor came with a few companions to the monastery of Christ’s martyr Emmeram, without the monks’ knowledge. Knocking gently at the door, he was admitted by a certain Gunther [Note: The letter *i* was erased], the church’s vigilant custodian and in every respect a venerable father.

When the emperor saw him, he first humbly approached to adore him, and then addressed him as follows:

> “What will you give me, brother, in order to obtain the honor of the episcopate?”

The old man smiled and replied:

> “My shoes.”

The emperor brought him, together with the other brothers, to Saint Peter [Col. 1215C] for the election of a bishop [f. 27]. There, after explaining the dream and all that had subsequently occurred, he established him as priest with the counsel of all the clergy and the entire people [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *cuntis*, “all,” without the second *n*; another reads *cuni*, perhaps *communi*. The Saxon Annals under 952 have *cum*.].

After receiving the blessing, Gunther occupied the see for only six months [Note: Gunther died thirty weeks after his ordination. See the Annals of Saint Emmeram under 942.]. Overcome by a severe illness, he recovered briefly [Note: Witness 1c reads *convaluit*, “recovered”; compare the Saxon Annals]. Taking ashes into his hands [Note: Witness 1 reads *manis*, a misspelling of *manus*, “hands”], he himself rose and marked with the sign of the holy cross the place where he wished to depart from this world. Then, lying on the ground, he blessedly sang the following words of blessed Job:

> “By the hearing of the ear I heard you, Lord; but now my eye sees you. Therefore I rebuke myself and do penance in dust and ashes” (Job 42:5).

Immediately, after completing his confession with tears, he gave up his spirit. In him was fulfilled what his predecessor, a man of similar character, had foretold:

> “You must govern this church, brother, as my successor [Col. 1215D]; but you will live only a short time, since God will mercifully crown you [Note: Witness c confirms *ita*, “thus/as written”]. [Col. 1216A]”

As long as he lived as a pilgrim here, he always desired this to come about according to God’s will. I have related these sayings concerning two bishops so that you may know, reader, how often heavenly grace revealed to the emperor what it wished to be done in human affairs.

When he heard of the death of so great a father, the emperor appointed Michael as his successor [f. 27′] [Note: Witness 1a adds *huic*, “to him”]. Michael governed the charge entrusted to him very well for a long time [Note: The first manuscript originally read: “who governed what had been entrusted to him,” which the scribe himself seems to have changed to the present reading. Manuscript 1c corrected it likewise; the Saxon Annals also have this reading.].

When the eastern Hungarians again stirred up trouble, Michael came with the other princes of Bavaria to aid them. But a battle soon broke out among them [Note: Witness 1a reads *exorta duella* (“battles having arisen”) across the phrase for “when a battle had arisen”], and, alas, our men were defeated and struck down by the enemy.

The bishop, with one of his ears cut off and wounded in his other limbs, lay among the slain as though dead. An enemy who was lying near him, seeing that he alone was still alive and then secure from the snares of his attackers, took up a spear [Col. 1216B] and tried to kill him. Then, strengthened in the Lord, Michael, after a long struggle of mutual combat, overcame and threw down his enemy. Through many hardships of the journey, he reached familiar territory unharmed.

From this arose joy for his flock and for everyone who knew Christ. He was welcomed by all as a good soldier in the clergy and preserved among the people as an excellent shepherd. His mutilation was not to his disgrace but rather to his honor.

Now I shall return to explaining the sequence of the narrative.

### 18.

The mighty emperor and Augustus of the Romans [Note: Witness 1a adds *sibi*, “than himself,” to the following comparison] consented to the deposition of the lord apostolic Benedict [Note: Witness 1a adds the words identifying him as the lord apostolic named Benedict], who was more powerful than himself in Christ and whom no one but God could judge, although, as I hope, he had been unjustly accused (964). And—would that he had not done so—he ordered him to be confined [Col. 1216C] in exile at Hamburg [Note: Witness 1a reads *religiri*, “to be bound/confined,” for *religari*] [Note: Thietmar seems here to have confused Otto I’s second expedition to Italy (961–965) with his third (966–972). In the former the emperor deposed Benedict; during the latter Aethelbert obtained the archbishopric of Magdeburg.], as I shall explain more clearly later.

[f. 28] Meanwhile Duke Hermann ruled Saxony. When he had set up an assembly at Magdeburg [Note: Witness 1c reads *Magadaburg*, a spelling of Magdeburg], he was received by the archbishop and led by the hand into the church, with lights kindled and all the bells sounding.

There the duke tried by deceit to capture my grandfather Heinricus, who resisted such great arrogance [Note: Through his mother, he was the son of Count Heinricus of Stade.], but he could not, because Heinricus was surrounded by a great troop of soldiers [Note: Witness 1a adds *hunc*, “him,” as the object of the attempted capture]. Nevertheless, the duke ordered him to travel to Rome after the emperor.

He fulfilled this most willingly. After crossing the Alps, when he first came to the emperor and saw him from a distance, he prostrated himself on the ground. When asked why he had done this, he replied tearfully [Col. 1216D] that he feared that, having been accused before the emperor, he had lost his customary favor and mercy.

[Col. 1217A] The emperor immediately raised and kissed him. Carefully questioning him about everything, he learned how the duke had been received and how he had sat [Note: Witness 1b adds *is*, “he,” in this clause] in the emperor’s place among the bishops at table and slept in his bed.

Inflamed by manly anger at this, the emperor Augustus sent a letter to Bishop Aethelbert [Note: Witness 1c reads *Adelberto*, “to Aethelbert”], ordering him [Note: Witness 1c reads *Adhelberto*, “to Aethelbert,” for the name at this point] to send as many horses as the duke had ordered bells to be rung or crowns to be lighted [Note: The Saxon Annals read “as he had ordered.”].

The archbishop, carrying out the imperial commands, tried by every means available through his envoys to excuse himself [f. 28′]. The aforementioned count was so resourceful that he was able to placate the angry emperor more easily than the other princes. Since he was also the emperor’s kinsman, he faithfully retained imperial favor until the end of his life [Note: Witness 1b adds *suimet*, “of his own,” to “the end of his life”].

The emperor dismissed him to return, after presenting him with a golden torque, and thus brought joy to his own companions, who had been saddened by the hostility. [Col. 1217B]

### 19.

Meanwhile the venerable Margrave Hodo [Note: [Col. 1217] in witness 1c, *Odo* is corrected to *Hodo*; the same form occurs below] marched out with a gathered army against Miesco, who was faithful to the emperor and paid tribute as far as the river Warta. My father, Count Siegfried, then still a young man and not yet joined in marital love, came to his aid alone with his own men.

On the day of Saint John the Baptist they fought against Miesco and at first prevailed; but then, except for the aforementioned counts, all the excellent soldiers were killed by his brother Cidebur and perished at a place called Cidini [Note: Perhaps Zehden on the Oder].

Disturbed by the report of this disaster, the emperor sent messengers from Italy, ordering Hodo and Miesco—if they wished to retain his favor—to remain at peace until he himself came and investigated the matter.

[Col. 1217C]

### 20.

After subjecting all the enemy’s bands to himself, the emperor crossed the difficult Alpine road and visited the region of Bavaria. Having arranged everything wisely there [f. 29], he proceeded by a direct route to the city of Magdeburg and celebrated Palm Sunday there with festive honor (973, 16 March).

On all solemn occasions he customarily allowed himself to be escorted to the church at Vespers, Matins, and Mass by a venerable procession of bishops, followed by the other ranks of the clergy, with crosses, the relics of the saints, and censers [Note: In witness 1 the first *r* of *turribulis* was erased].

There, standing and sitting with great fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom (Prov. 1:7), he remained until everything was completed, speaking of nothing except divine matters. Then he returned to his chamber with many lights and a great retinue of priests, dukes, and counts.

At dawn on the following day, [Col. 1217D] for the remedy of his soul, he presented unspeakable gifts to God and to his unconquerable duke Maurice: estates, books, and other royal furnishings. [Col. 1218A] He confirmed everything lawfully through advocates and by the delivery of written instruments, in the presence and with the approval of the empress and his son, and before the testimony of all Christ’s faithful.

Then he went to Quedlinburg, where he celebrated the approaching Easter with divine praises and human rejoicing [Note: See Widukind, *l. l.*, ch. 75]. At the emperor’s command, Miesco and Boleslav came there [f. 29′], together with the dukes and envoys of the Greeks, Beneventans, Hungarians, Bulgarians, Danes, and Slavs [Note: Witness 1b adds “and the envoys of the Greeks, Beneventans, Hungarians, Bulgarians, Danes, and Slavs,” apparently from the Quedlinburg Annals] [Note: Compare the Hildesheim Annals under 973], along with all the leading men of the entire kingdom.

When everything had been peacefully concluded, they returned home rejoicing, enriched with great gifts [Note: Witness 1b adds *magnis*, “great,” modifying the gifts]. On 1 April [Note: Witness 1b adds *Kalendis Aprilis*, “on the Kalends of April”], Duke Hermann died there and disturbed the emperor’s joy [Note: See Widukind].

While his body was being carried [Note: Witness 1a reads *defereretur*, “was being carried,” for *deferretur*] to Lüneburg by his son Bernhard [Note: In witness 1 the first *i* of *Liuniburg* was written and then erased], it happened that Bruno, bishop [Col. 1218B] of the church of Verden, was nearby. Since he had kept Hermann under the ban while he lived, the son humbly begged him both to release the dead man from it and to permit him to be buried in the church.

But he obtained none of what he requested.

### 21.

Since I have mentioned this bishop, I am pleased to say more about him [Note: Witness 1c reads *voluntas*, “will,” for *volupe*, “it is pleasing”]. He was a kinsman [Note: That is, a brother.] of the aforementioned duke [Note: Witness 1b has *predicti*, “the aforementioned”; witnesses 1a and 2 have *prefati*, “the aforesaid.” Compare the Saxon Annals under 973.], a novice monk at Corvey. Because of his reverence, the emperor appointed him bishop after Amelung.

He governed the church at Verden rationally and well. Because stone was unavailable to him [Note: Witness 1b adds *quia lapis defuit ei*, “because stone was lacking for him.”], he built it of wood, made it splendid, and consecrated it so that it surpassed the other churches in both size and quality. Advancing in a good old age, he died on 5 May [Col. 1218C] [Note: In witness 1 the abbreviated words *frater predicti ducis*, “brother of the aforementioned duke,” were erased; witness 2 reads *frater ipsius Herimanni ducis*, “brother of Duke Hermann himself.” Compare the Saxon Annals.] (962).

When he was greatly weakened by old age and continual illness and was moving very slowly, the emperor asked him whether he would be willing to nurture Hermann [Note: The name is *Hirrimannum* in witness 1a and *Herimannum* in witness 1c, both meaning Hermann], his own chaplain, the brother of Bishop Wolcmer [Note: Bishop of Cologne.], as a son and choose him for himself as an assistant and heir [Note: Witness 1a reads *nutrire*, “to nurture,” for the infinitive at this point.].

He accepted this embassy with a grieving heart and replied:

> “I have diligently governed the charge that my lord has deigned to entrust to me, unworthy as I am. As long as I must remain here, I desire, if permitted, to live without such a command [Note: *Famine*, that is, an order—specifically, an imperial order.]. Humility and pride do not make an equal partnership (compare Lucan 1.92), nor does power ever tolerate a partner. Whatever pleases my lord in another, I shall obediently fulfill.
>
> “Let the young man place no hope in the death of a decrepit old man, for that is a sin. Let him remember that a calfskin is often hung [Col. 1218D] upon a wall [Note: That is, young men die very frequently].”

Having begun with these words, he ordered himself to be carried to the church of Christ’s virgin Cecilia [Col. 1219A]. There he prostrated himself on the ground and complained, with tears poured forth, that he had served her unworthily until that time:

> “I, unhappy man, know that I have been rejected by God and by you, since a stranger is preferred to me and is taken into your service as more worthy [Note: Witness 1b adds *Unde*, “therefore,” introducing the next sentence]. Therefore I now wish to depart from here [Note: Witness 1b adds *hinc*, “from here”] in sorrow and to await in this place Christ’s grace and your holy intercession. I would that, just as I did not unjustly desire what belonged to another, so no one might ever presume to rejoice at my loss.
>
> “Now I humbly beseech God to show what is pleasing to him and beneficial to my church [Note: Witness 1 reads *quod*, “that/what,” for *quid*, “what”] [f. 30].”

When this prayer had been completed, he rose and departed. He remained in his own parish until he became certain of the death of the young man mentioned above [Note: Witness 1 reads *effititur*, a spelling of *efficitur*, “became”]. Then, calling his companions together, he said:

> “You have no new lord. But carry me to my monastery [Col. 1219B], where I shall await the day of judgment without wandering, with great attentiveness [Note: Witness 1b adds *cum magna sollicitatione*, “with great attentiveness”].
>
> “And learn, you mortals, that everything beneficial to you for salvation comes not from the one who runs or flies, but rather from the merciful God [Note: Witness 1c reads *volentis … miserentis*, “of the one willing … of the one showing mercy,” instead of *currentis … miserantis*, “of the one running … of the one showing mercy.” Compare Romans 9:16.].
>
> “Let us be an example to you: no one who trusts in God is abandoned, nor is anyone who hopes in himself exalted to any good purpose [Note: Witness 1b adds this preceding maxim, from “Let us be an example” through “good purpose”]. Place your hope, children, in God the Father, and, with the help of his Only-Begotten Son and consubstantial Comforter, overcome harmful fear.
>
> “Pray to the propitious God that whatever I have sinned against you, or you against me, through human frailty may henceforth be amended for the better. May you afterward have an elder dear to God and useful to you, and times that smile upon you prosperously [Note: In witness 1 the abbreviated words *et t. p. a.* (“and …”) stand in an erased place; their expansion is uncertain].”

After these words he reached the place appointed for him. Although many hardships surrounded his old age, he nevertheless remained affable and exemplary in his conduct [Note: Witness 1b adds *fuit*, “was”].

[Col. 1219C]

### 22. [f. 31a]

Having briefly dispatched the famous deeds of the aforementioned emperor, I am inclined, before committing his death to writing, to say something about those who, in his time, expired after having been useful to the church and to him, and to renew what happened meanwhile.

Archbishop Hillibert, who anointed him, fell asleep in Christ on 31 May during the second year of his reign. His successor, Fritheric, pleased both God and the world [Note: From the Quedlinburg Annals under 937 and the Merseburg Calendar: “the second day before the Kalends of June.”].

At the end of his life he gave thanks to God that he had never unjustly acquired or lost anything belonging to his church [Note: Witness 1b adds this sentence in the lower margin].

In that year the Hungarians [Note: [Col. 1219] the second *i* in *Ungarii* (“Hungarians”) is erased], ravaging Thuringia and Saxony (937), perished [Col. 1220A] in very strong places [Note: Witness 1b adds *firmissimis*, “very strong,” modifying the places], while some of them, fear supplying them with wings, returned to their homeland [Note: From the Quedlinburg Annals under 937].

Everhard, duke of the Franks [Note: Witness 2 reads *Francorum*, “of the Franks”; witness 1 has an erasure where this word would stand], long disloyal to the king [Note: Witness 1b adds *infidelis*, “disloyal”], was degraded, while Count Wigmann was reconciled through humble supplication [Note: From the same source].

In the following year (938), the king’s brother Heinricus was captured by Count Everhard [Note: [Col. 1219] *Everhardo*, “by Everhard”: text and witness 1c; apparently first written *Euuarhardo*, the same name] (939) and held in chains [Note: From the same source, under 938].

In the third year of the aforementioned king, his brother Heinricus [Note: [Col. 1220] *Hericum*, “Heinricus”: witness 1a; *Henricum*, the same name: witness 1c], Duke Everhard [f. 31a′] [Note: Witness 1 corrects *Euurhardus* to *Euerhardus*, both spellings of Everhard, and makes the same correction below], and Count Gisilbert [Note: Witness 1 corrects *Isilbertus* to *Gisilbertus*, both spellings of Gisilbert, and makes the same correction below], count of the Lotharingians [Note: Witness 1a reads *Luthuringorum*, “of the Lotharingians”], together with the other supporters of their wickedness, plundered many places west of the Rhine.

When Udo, the king’s friend, immediately learned of this, he killed Everhard and drowned Gisilbert with his companions in the Rhine [Note: Witness 1a originally reads *dimergi*, “to be drowned”; witness 1c corrects it]. He compelled Heinricus to seek the king’s favor [Note: From the same source, under 939].

After this, envoys of the Greeks [Col. 1220B] twice brought gifts from their emperor to our king (944), suitable to both parties [Note: From the same source, under 944].

Archbishop Fritheric [Note: [Col. 1220] *Fridericus*, the same name as Fritheric: witness 1c], a temperate man [Note: Witness 2 reads *abstinentissimus*, “most abstinent,” for *abstemius*, “temperate/abstinent”], died in the seventeenth year of his ordination (954). Willehelmus, though born of a captive and Slavic mother [Note: Witness 1b adds *et Sclavonica*, “and Slavic”], yet a noblewoman and descended from the aforementioned king, was ordained in his place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 954 [Note: From the same source, under 954; compare Widukind III.74].

Then, in the fourth year of that number (958), the sign of the life-giving cross, shining wondrously—and even more miserably—on men’s garments [Note: *vestimentis*, “garments”: text; misspelled *festimentis*: witness 1a], benefited those who received it worthily and harmed those who mocked it [Note: From the same source, under 958; witness 1b adds *sibi*, “for their benefit”].

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 963, following the aforementioned deposition and exile of Pope Benedict, a savage mortality, after his death, overtook the emperor’s army and destroyed Archbishop Heinricus [Col. 1220C] of Trier, Duke Godefrithus [Note: Witness 1c reads *Godefridum*, the accusative form of Godefrid/Godfrey, for the text’s *Godefrithum*], and innumerable others [Note: Compare the Hildesheim Annals under 963].

In the third year, on 31 March, the church of Halberstadt collapsed. The emperor, returning from Italy, came to Frankfurt [Note: [Col. 1220] the place-name *Francanavord* contains an uncertain hand’s correction of the earlier written form *francanu ord*]: remaining for a long time in these regions, he established peace and harmony among his people [Note: Compare the same source under 965 and the Saxon Chronograph under that year, apparently from the Quedlinburg Annals].

In the following year the emperor again visited the Roman territories [f. 31b] [Note: The same source, under 966].

In the fourth year, the emperor’s namesake, accompanied by Willehelmus, archbishop of Mainz, came to Rome (967) and, through the venerable lord Pope John, was made like his father in blessing [Note: The same source, under 967].

In the seventh year, the Lord’s temple at Thornburg was burned (971) [Note: The same source, under 971. Thornburg, once a fortress and palace of Otto I and the succeeding emperors, stood on the left bank of the Elbe. After the river changed its course, it was situated on the right bank near the town of Barby and has now been almost entirely swallowed by the Elbe, so that scarcely any ruins can be seen. See the *Chronicon Gottwicense*, vol. I, p. 512; Leuckfeld, *Antiquitates Halberstadenses*, p. 247. URS.].

[Col. 1221A]

### 23.

I also wish to add that Boso, my predecessor, appointed by the aforementioned emperor, governed the charge entrusted to him for one year, ten months, and three days. He died in his homeland, Bavaria, on 1 November (970), and was buried at Merseburg in the church of Saint John the Baptist before the high altar [Note: Witness 1b adds *summo*, “high,” specifying the high altar].

He had been raised in monastic life at the monastery of Christ’s martyr Emmeram [Note: Witness 1c adds *quod construxit Arnulfus imperator*, “which Emperor Arnulf built”], situated outside the city of Regensburg on its southern side. From there he was taken into the emperor’s service and received the benefice [Col. 1221B] of the church of Zeitz as the due reward for his great labor.

Near that city, in a certain woodland [Note: In witness 1 the abbreviation *qd.* is corrected to *qc.* at the relative *quod*, “which/that”] that he himself had built up [Note: In witness 1 the *c* of *construcxit*, “built,” is erased] and named after himself, he had a church constructed of stone and caused it to be consecrated. Before his ordination [Note: Witness 1 reads *anquam*, a defective form of *antequam*, “before”] he had obtained every benefice belonging to the churches situated at Merseburg and at Imenlevo, as well as to Thornburg and Kirberg [Note: Witness 2 supports singular *pertinens*, “belonging”; witness 1 and the Saxon Annals read plural *pertinentes*, “belonging”].

Because he had claimed an innumerable people for Christ in the East through constant preaching and baptism, he pleased the emperor, who gave him the choice among three bishoprics to be established: Meissen [Note: Witness 1c supports *Misnensis*, “of Meissen”; witness 1a reads the misspelling *misnessis*], Zeitz, and Merseburg.

Since Merseburg was peaceful, he requested that church [f. 31b′] from the Augustus, and governed it diligently as long as he lived. To instruct those entrusted to him more easily, he had words written in the Slavic language and asked them to sing *Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”), explaining its usefulness to them.

But those dull-witted people mockingly turned this into something evil, saying *Ukrivolsa* [Note: *Ukrivolsa*: text and witness 1b; witness 1a reads *kriolosso*, an alternative form whose sense is not established here] [Note: [Col. 1221D] The alder is called *olsa* by the Poles and *volsa* by the Bohemians. The first syllables are uncertain. The cited Slavic/German example is “Die Eller steht im Busche,” meaning “The alder stands in the thicket”; how that meaning is contained in *Ukrivolsa* is unclear.]—which in our language [Col. 1221C] means:

> “The alder stands in the thicket” [Note: Witness 1c adds *i.* (*id est*, “that is”); the Saxon Annals read *alnus quae stat in frutectis*, “the alder that stands in the thickets.”].

They said:

> “This is how Boso spoke,”

although he had said something else.

The emperor also granted him a few villages belonging to the aforementioned city and a certain castle situated in the district of Chutizi, called Medeburu [Note: Below, IV.5, the same name is written more correctly as *Medeburun*] [Note: Magdeborn near Rötha, not far from Leipzig. URS.]. Its interpretation is:

> “Forbid honey.”

His son and namesake [Note: Witness 1c adds “Otto II”] also granted him the church situated at Helpithi [Note: The monastery of Helfelde or Helfte in the county of Mansfeld], which his father had built in honor of Saint Radegund. While present, the father ordered Bishop Bernhard to dedicate it.

When the first father of our church, as I have said, died, the emperor, through the intercession of Anno, bishop of Worms, gave the episcopate to Gisiler, noble in character and by birth [Note: That is, by lineage. *Kind*.]. He was consecrated at Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 1221] *Magadaburg*: text; *Magaburg*: 1, as above in chapter 10] by Archbishop Athelbert [Note: [Col. 1221] *archiantistite* (“archbishop”): text; *Athelbert*: text; *Adelberto*, “by Athelbert,” in witness 1c; *archiantistite*, “by the archbishop,” is supported by 1c, while witness 1 reads *archiantiste*] in the month of June. [Col. 1222A]

### 24.

Since I have said little [Note: [Col. 1222] *Equidem* (“indeed”) is added in witness 1b] about Duke Conrad, who was the emperor’s son-in-law and was killed near the river Lech, I think it appropriate to disclose certain matters that I left unexamined at that time.

After a long interval, when the emperor came to Merseburg [f. 31c], he learned from a certain traitor that the Slavs were keeping Conrad’s remains at Zuencua [Note: Zwenkau near Leipzig], under Cuch, an elder very dear to him [Note: The scribe of witness 1 first wrote *suchanico* and then corrected it; witness 2 and the Saxon Annals read *Euchauico*.].

With the elder’s help, the emperor defeated them in single combat, ordered them to be hanged, and recovered most of the plunder [Note: That is, he retrieved it. KIND.].

But I do not know whether Conrad’s killers took this plunder, or whether, by some accidental circumstance, those innocent of his death found it. Since they had dared to conceal this in any way, they paid the penalty by a deserved death [Note: The *o* was erased at this point].

As for his daughter, Conrad’s wife [Note: Liutgard, who had already died in 953. See the continuation of Regino under that year.], a certain Cono [Note: Witness 1c reads the ablative *Conone*, “by Cono,” at this occurrence] had widely defamed her because she had refused to gratify him [Col. 1222B], and had secretly called her his wife. The emperor took this very seriously and cleared her in the following manner.

He summoned all the princes of his kingdom [Note: Manuscript 1a reads *conculcatis* for *convocatis*, “having summoned”]. First, in private conversations, he carefully inquired whether she was guilty of this matter. Then, when he saw her, with Christ as her witness and by oaths, making every effort to clear herself, he declared before everyone that if anyone from among his household wished to defend her by arms, he could thereby secure the emperor as a firm and perpetual friend.

Count Burchard, hearing this, stepped forward and declared before everyone [f. 31c′] that Cono had lied in every respect. When Cono [Note: Witness 1c reads the accusative *Cononem*, “Cono,” at this occurrence] affirmed the truth of his claim by oaths [Col. 1222C], Burchard engaged him in combat. At the first encounter he cut off the liar’s right hand, and, after being defeated, Cono made his own injustice known [Note: That is, he made it known by confessing it. URS.]. Thus the merciful Lord freed her from a false accusation, and made her pleasing to himself through the innocence of her life [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *innocia* for *innocencia*].

While her husband was still alive, although she was often despised and wearied by repeated labors, she nevertheless endured these things with manly patience and tried to preserve her innate honor. When she ended this life, she was buried sorrowfully in the church of Christ’s martyr Alban at Mainz [Note: Witness 1b adds the preceding burial clause, *in aecclesia Christi martiris Albani*, “in the church of Christ’s martyr Alban”]. A silver spindle belonging to her was hung there in her memory.

25. 25. Concerning the aforementioned duke Henry, I relate certain things that he wickedly did in his own kingdom, and in which it may be profitably considered that he cannot be contradicted in any of the matters mentioned above. He ordered the patriarch of Aquileia [Note: [Col. 1222D] Leo?] to be castrated and the archbishop of Salzburg [Note: [Col. 1221] Thus in 1c.; “Salb.” in 1a.] [Note: [Col. 1222D] Named Herold, in 954. See the Continuation of Regino, under that year.] [Col. 1223A] to be blinded. I do not wish to state the reasons, because I know in truth that they were not sufficient to merit such things. When, at the end of his life, he was admonished by Michael, bishop of Regensburg, concerning such a deed [Note: [Col. 1223] “amm.” in 1c.], he confessed only that he had sinned in the former matter [Note: [Col. 1223] “pecasse” in 1.], and not at all in the case of the archbishop—unaware how small a thing it is in which guilt is absent [Note: [Col. 1223D] That is, a rare matter, a matter of little consequence. Compare the preface, line 14.]. Hence David speaks as a suppliant: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults!” (Psalm 18:13).

His wife, named Judith, was present and heard this confession. Soon afterward, when her husband died, she placed his body in the church that he himself had built in honor of Saint Mary Ever-Virgin, with great sorrow; and whatever she herself knew, or learned from others, concerning any sin he had ever committed, she expiated with tears and unspeakable almsgiving [Col. 1223B]. Living chastely in her widowhood, she loved Abraham [Note: [Col. 1223] The initial *h* is erased.], bishop of Freising, above all others; yet she was savagely torn apart by the envious tooth of common gossip, although she was entirely without blame.

When she departed from this life, she was thus vindicated on the day of her burial, while that same bishop was celebrating Mass. Before Communion, he turned toward the people and declared to those standing by what her merits had been:

“If she ever committed this offense [Note: [Col. 1223] “Debt” in 1a.], on account of which she was defamed, may almighty God cause the saving remedy of the body and blood of his Son to become for me, at the judgment, a punishment and the condemnation I deserve [Note: [Col. 1223] “Condemnation” in 1.], but for her soul, eternal salvation.”

Then, with innocence of mind and body, he received the one remedy available to all the faithful. The people believed, although late; and the unjust slander benefited her all the more, since it had sought to harm her.

### 26. (f. 31d′)

In the days of the aforementioned emperor there was a certain count named Hed. Since he had no heir, he endowed with the greater part of all his property the church built at Heslingen [Note: [Col. 1223D] Heslingen, in the prefecture of Zeven, in the duchy of Bremen. See Adam of Bremen II.6; Albert of Stade, under the year 1136.] in honor of Christ’s athlete Vitus [Note: [Col. 1223] Vitus, the seven-year-old boy who rests at New Corvey.], and, after establishing there a community of nuns, subjected the abbey to the protection of Etheldag, archbishop of Bremen [Note: [Col. 1223] “Subdidit” in 1c.].

But the two venerable matrons placed over this see, both of whom were called Windilgerd [Note: [Col. 1223] The scribe seems to have corrected *uuinnilgerd* to *uuindilgerd*. “Windilgard” in 2; Annals of Saxony.], soon—alas!—died. When my grandfather [Note: [Col. 1223D] His maternal grandfather, Count Henry of Stade.] had asked the archbishop to allow his daughter Hathui, who had first been educated there and then entrusted to the matrons, to succeed them, he could not obtain this from the aforementioned archbishop [Col. 1224A].

Later, however, at the emperor’s request—for the emperor was his godfather—the archbishop veiled her when she was already twelve years old, on 2 Kalends of May, a Sunday [Note: [Col. 1223D] “Sunday” here seems to mean the Ascension of the Lord, which in 973 fell on the Kalends of May.], and on the following day appointed her abbess in the presence of her father. This afterward caused him great regret. For, as I am about to relate, five days later Otto I, the glory of Italy and the salvation of Saxony, died (in 973).

My grandmother Judith [Note: [Col. 1223] “Aua” in 1.], whose name had a second *t* erased [Note: [Col. 1223] “Juthita,” mother of the aforementioned Hathui.], rests in the church that her daughter later built with extraordinary effort from stones, which are scarce in this land [Note: [Col. 1223] The *c* is erased.]. She departed this world on 7 Kalends of November. The church of Fulda, alas!, having been burned [Note: [Col. 1224D] Concerning the burning of the monastery of Saint Boniface, see the Continuation of Regino, under 937, and the Annals of Hildesheim, under 930], was restored under the same emperor.

### 27. (f. 32)

The emperor was in Merseburg for the Ascension of the Lord, and with devout mind he strove to complete there whatever remained of his promise. Thereafter, arriving at Miminlevo on the Tuesday before Pentecost [Note: [Col. 1223] *Mimnlevo* in 1a; *mimnieue* in 1c.], he sat cheerfully at table on the following day. When the meal was finished and evening was already being sung, he began to fall ill and sink down. Those standing nearest received him and laid him down; and, quickly refreshed by the divine Viaticum, while everyone prayed for his departure, he paid the debt owed to nature [Note: [Col. 1224D] From Widukind III.75.] in the thirty-eighth year of his reign [Note: [Col. 1223] “XXXVIII years of his reign” added in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1224D] It was in fact the thirty-seventh year.], on the Nones of May (May 7), a Wednesday [Note: [Col. 1224D] Widukind I.1, chapter 76.].

On the following night his entrails were buried in the church of Saint Mary; his body, embalmed with spices, was transferred to Parthenopolis [Note: [Col. 1224D] Ibid.], where it was received honorably and tearfully, placed in a marble sarcophagus, and buried by the archbishops Gero and Aethelbert [Note: [Col. 1223] Perhaps *Athelbert* in 1c.], with the assistance of the other bishops and all the clergy.

### 28.

His namesake, the younger Otto, who had been elected and anointed while his father was still alive, was again acclaimed by everyone as lord and king [Note: [Col. 1224D] From the same source.]. But how diligently the elder’s empress, Aethelheidis [Note: [Col. 1223] *Atelheidis* in 1c.], watched over the liberation of his soul until the end cannot be comprehended either in words or in deeds. For whatever honor or secular advancement ever came to her, she attributed not to any merit of her own but to Christ, in David’s words of praise:

“Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Psalm 115:1).

If eloquence, knowledge, and memory were united in me, they would fail in setting forth the emperor’s praise [Col. 1225A]. As was the lord, so also were his princes [Note: [Col. 1225] “And”; “et” in 1a.]. They were not delighted by excessive variety of foods or other things, but in all matters by golden moderation. All the virtues that are read about flourished while these men lived and withered when they died. Although they do not live bodily, their immortal souls survive, rejoicing in blessed eternity through the advancement of good works.

But, to conclude my speech [Note: [Col. 1225] “Conclaudam” in 1a.], after Charlemagne no one so great as a king and defender of his homeland ever occupied the royal throne. Since many nobles had preceded him in death, as I have said, all who survived—though not forgetful of such great joy—neither wished for nor followed the new rule that came afterward; rather, until the end of their lives they did not willingly deviate from the straight path of ancient truth and justice.

For they then saw being fulfilled what a certain wise man, prescient of future events, had written: “The first is the golden age; afterward comes the bronze, and then the iron age” [Note: [Col. 1225D] That is, thereafter.] [Col. 1226A].

Let every faithful person hear the truthful admonitions of blessed Gregory:

“As gifts increase, so do the accounts demanded for those gifts. Let him shudder at having sinned exceedingly in the matters entrusted to him, and let him beseech God with suppliant mind on behalf of the emperor’s soul, that the innumerable crimes of the sinful servant—crimes that could not be prevented in the many things subject to him—may be mercifully forgiven, and that the ruler of all kingdoms may stand by present and future peoples as an ever-watchful and gracious guardian.”

And you, whoever may succeed me, mindful of so great a benefit, preserve the memory of his soul with faithful devotion, especially on the feast of Christ’s athlete Lawrence. Earnestly pray for his intercession, so that, just as on that day victory over visible enemies was divinely granted to this man through Lawrence’s merits [Col. 1226B], so he may deserve, through the remission granted him by God—the remission he always desired—to escape the snares of invisible enemies and, separated from the left, be placed on the right hand of God the Father on the day of judgment [Note: [Col. 1225] “To” in 1; the words “of God the Father” are erased.].

## BOOK THREE

[Note: [Col. 1225] “Here begins the preface of the third book concerning Otto II”; at the end of the poem: “The preface ends. The third book begins.”]

### [Col. 1225B]

Let Otto, third in the number of kings but second in name,

be written down and placed in a seat worthy of praise,

in the seat of his great father, living through the ages in the second succession [Note: [Col. 1225] *felici* in 1, but corrected by the author.],

he who aided all the wretched at every hour.

His beginnings rejoice in good things; at his end there came

sadness, brought upon us everywhere by our great crimes.

Then this world paid the penalty for what it wickedly despised:

the straight path. Many perished beneath the avenging sword

throughout the kingdom.

No certain cause is evident to us; yet all learned men

thought that the mournful disaster at Merseburg,

from the time it endured it, was the reason that holy peace

departed far from our borders and the enemy ruled widely.

Who can tell how fiercely this man raged in cruel slaughter,

since he did not even spare the holy temples of benevolent Christ?

Men confronted one another and fell in mutual combat;

many of our people were overcome by the Saracens.

Truly happy are those who, always loving Christ,

retain the peace they desire—calm, entirely ignorant

of the malignant fear that strikes the heart,

who has now troubled our forebears for more than thirty years

and, alas!, armed our enemies, who now also shatter our lands.

May he who joined heaven to earth put an end to these sufferings;

let every faithful person pray for this.

### 1. (f. 34)

Let Otto II, the third ruler of our kingdom, be the subject of my little book. While still young, renowned for exceptional bodily strength, he first pursued whatever things are reckless; and, having been granted many things through an act of piety [Note: [Col. 1225D] Compare V.25. *Largitus* has a passive sense. The meaning seems to be: many things were granted to him by his parents.], he fled mature counsel without restraint. Later, corrected by many and restrained by the bridle of praiseworthy virtue imposed upon him, he conducted himself nobly during his days, as I shall explain in what follows.

At the urging of his pious mother, whose governance prevailed, he obtained Miminlevo [Note: [Col. 1225] *Miminleue* in 1c.], where his father had died, by a just exchange, together with the tithes belonging to Herevesfeld [Note: [Col. 1225] 1 wrote *Hereues fel.* but corrected it to *Heresfeld*.]. After gathering monks there, he made it a free abbey, supplied it with the necessary goods, and confirmed it by an apostolic privilege [Note: [Col. 1225] “Decree” in 1a.] [Note: [Col. 1226D] Concerning this charter of 979, see Böhmer, *Regesta*, no. 544.].

Moreover, by an imperial decree issued at Magdeburg in the presence of Archbishop Aethelbert, he gave the brothers serving God permission to elect an archbishop [Note: [Col. 1225] *Magadaburg* added in 1b; *Adhelberto* in 1c.]. Together with one book, which is still there and in which his own image and that of the empress Theophanu shine, formed in gold, he confirmed the gift [Note: [Col. 1225] *quod* in 1a.][Note: [Col. 1226D] Charter issued at Walbeck, December 19, 979.].

The archbishop, by the emperor’s favor and in his presence, prepared to celebrate Mass. After preaching most fittingly, as was customary, once the Gospel had been read, he recited before the congregation the imperial decree containing the election; he showed it publicly, and condemned with terrible excommunication anyone rash enough ever to violate it. With everyone responding, “Amen! Let it be so! Let it be so!”, he confirmed the act.

He regarded the still-impoverished bishopric of Merseburg with generous piety. Because he loved its administrator Gisilher greatly, he first gave him the abbey at Palithi [Note: [Col. 1227D] Pölde, September 24, 981. In 981 Emperor Otto II gave this abbey to the archbishop of Magdeburg.], and afterward the city of Suencuam [Note: [Col. 1227D] A charter of Emperor Otto, issued at Frosa on August 30, 974, concerning the donation of the city of Zuenkouua, in the region of Chutizi and the county of Count Gundher, to the church of Saint Lawrence, was published by L. F. Hoefer in *Zeitschrift für Archivkunde* I, p. 153.], with all its appurtenances, for the service of Saint John the Baptist.

He also gave him everything enclosed within the walls of the city of Merseburg, together with its Jews and merchants, its mint and forest, the forest lying between the rivers Saale and Mulde and the districts of Siusuli and Plisni [Note: [Col. 1227D] A charter concerning the donation of this forest, issued at Allstedt in 979, August 30, is found in Wideburg, *Res Misnenses*, p. 85. The district of Siusuli lay around the river Mulde and the city of Eilenburg. The district of Plisni lay between the rivers Pleisse and Elster.], and the places Chorin [Note: [Col. 1227D] Today Kohren, a village near Borna; Nercha, a small town near Grimma; Poetsche, not far from Magdeborn; Gautsch, between Leipzig and Zwenkau; and finally the small town of Brandis. *Cothug* or *Cotowe* seems to be the village of Katow, commonly Kadau, near Löbejün.], Niriechua, Bucithi, Cothug, Borintizi, and Gunthorp [Note: [Col. 1227] “And Gunthrop” was erased in 1 and supplied from the Annals of Saxony by Ursinus.]. He confirmed all these things for him in documents strengthened by his own hand [Note: [Col. 1227] “These” added in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1227] “All” added in 1b.].

### 2.

Meanwhile Gero, the distinguished administrator of the see of Agrippina, died [Note: [Col. 1228D] In 975; see the Cologne Annals, vol. I, p. 98.] [in 975]. Since I previously touched only briefly upon him, reserving certain matters for that time, I shall now relate them briefly.

He ordered a crucifix, which now stands in the middle of the church where he rests [Note: [Col. 1227] Added in 1b.], to be carefully made from wood. When he saw that its head was split, he treated it as the work of the supreme Craftsman and, presuming nothing about himself and therefore trusting in a more salutary remedy, did the following: he joined a portion of the Lord’s body—the one comfort in all necessities—and a piece of the life-giving cross, placed them in the fissure, prostrated himself, and tearfully invoked the name of the Lord. Rising, he obtained its restoration through a humble blessing.

When he entered his chapel in full daylight, he saw Saint Victor fighting with and conquering the devil, as he later reported to his faithful.

The devil, envious of all good things, revealed Gero’s impending death to an abbess named Gerberga [Note: [Col. 1227] *Gerbergae* in 1.], whom he greatly loved for her purity of mind and body and often kept with him, just as he had formerly done with others:

“I would like to reveal my secret to you, if I did not know that you have never yet kept anything entrusted to you. But if you promise me that you will faithfully keep this secret, I will tell you, on the condition that, whenever you wish to reveal it to anyone, you may be sure that I shall take your life. Gero, your intimate companion, will this year fall into such a serious illness for three days that he will be believed dead; and if the period is guarded by someone, he can safely escape this danger” [Note: [Col. 1227] “So” added in 1c.].

But the handmaid of Christ, stunned by such words, promised faithfully to conceal this from everyone. When she saw him disappear, she went immediately by the direct route and told the archbishop everything.

When the devil realized this, he caused her to fall into such a condition that, after many days [Note: [Col. 1227] “A few days,” according to the Annals of Saxony under 974 and the Saxon Chronicle under 971.], she exchanged this fragile life for eternal life.

The archbishop, celebrating Mass on the day of her burial, declared her merit to all who stood by, asked them to grant her forgiveness, and himself did so.

Afterward, burdened by the illness foretold above, Gero entrusted himself to Evurgerus [Note: [Col. 1227] *Euergero* in 1c., and likewise below.] for care. The latter ordered him, exhausted by sharp pain and apparently dead, to be washed, placed on a bier, carried to the church, and buried on the following day.

According to the report of the people, on the third night Gero awoke as though from a deep sleep, heard a bell ringing, and asked three times that they open the door for him. The man who heard him, astonished, summoned Evurgerus, the aforementioned keeper of the church, so that he might assist the suffering bishop. Evurgerus declared that he had been lying in every respect and struck him hard with a staff. Thus the bishop rested in the memory of the faithful on 3 Kalends of July.

He soon appeared to Liudulf, abbot [Note: [Col. 1228D] Abbot of New Corvey, according to the Annals of Saxony, under 975.], saying, “Sing eternal rest for us!” Then he vanished from his sight. In his place Warinus was immediately anointed by election and imperial appointment.

### 3.

In the second year of the middle Otto (974), Henry [Note: [Col. 1228D] Son of Henry, son of King Henry and brother of Emperor Otto I.], duke of the Bavarians, was captured and taken to Gilhiem [Note: [Col. 1228D] Compare the Saxon Chronograph, under 974, and the Annals of Hildesheim, under 974, where Gilhiem is called Ingelheim.], where he was carefully guarded.

That year the winter was long, harsh, and dry, and great snow poured down from heaven [Note: [Col. 1227] The words “In that year … from heaven” were added by 1b at the bottom of the page. In the margin he first wrote DCCCCLXXV, then immediately erased that number and placed it at the upper margin of the following page, before the word “When Robert died.” Manuscript 2 placed the number after *Anno* in this form: “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 875 and of the middle …”].

In 975, when Robert, archbishop of the see of Mainz, had died, the emperor appointed as chancellor and head of that church a man named Willigis [Note: [Col. 1228D] Ibid., under 975.], although many rejected him because of the lowliness of his birth. For he knew, as Peter testifies, that God is not a respecter of persons (Acts 10:34), but loves above others all who love him from the heart, rewarding them with incomprehensible honor.

How divine mercy marked out this future shepherd must not be left unmentioned. While carrying him in her womb, his mother, although poor, yet—as what follows shows—a good woman, saw in a dream that the sun, shining from her womb, filled the whole earth with fiery rays [Note: [Col. 1229] *Essinu* in 1a.]. On the night when she gave birth to this child, all the livestock that she possessed in her house likewise responded, as though rejoicing for their mistress, with a similar birth.

He who was then born was the sun, because by the rays of his holy preaching he illuminated the hearts of many who were sluggish in the love of Christ. Therefore, at his birth a marvelous multitude of the male sex is brought forth in a corresponding generation, because the man of God, destined by the highest predestination to rule for the salvation of the entire homeland, arises.

Happy is the mother whom the Lord visited above all her contemporaries, so that she bore offspring equal to the noblest, or even better than some of them, and proved by her eyes and by reality itself that the hope of the vision shown to her was true. But I shall speak of these matters elsewhere.

### 4. (974)

In his first expedition the emperor captured the city of Buschuth [Note: [Col. 1229C] Bossut, on the river Haine in Hainaut. See Balderic of Cambrai, *Chronicle* I.94; Sigebert of Gembloux, under 973; the Annals of Weissenburg, under 974.] [Note: [Col. 1229] “The emperor … captured” was begun in an erased place and supplied in the second margin.]. In his second, seeking the Danes who had rebelled against him, he hastened to Schleswig [Note: [Col. 1229] “He came” in 1a.] [Note: [Col. 1229C] See Lambert’s Annals under 975 and the History of Theodoric, monk of Trondheim, in Langebek, *Scriptores rerum Danicarum* V, p. 316. This passage was very well explained by J. Asmussen in *Archiv für Staats- und Kirchen-Geschichte der Herzogthümer Schleswig, Holstein und Lauenburg* I, p. 252 ff.].

There he saw that his enemies had occupied with arms the ditch prepared for the defense of their homeland [Note: [Col. 1229] “Fortified” in 1a.] [Note: [Col. 1229D] Commonly called the Danevirke.] and the gate called Wieglesdor [Note: [Col. 1229] *Heggedor* in manuscript 2 and in the Annals of Saxony under 975.] [Note: [Col. 1229D] In Icelandic writers, for example in the *Jomsvikinga Saga*, it is called Aegisdor. Concerning this gate, compare Einhard’s Annals under 808; J. Grimm, *Deutsche Mythologie*, pp. 147 and 197.]. With the counsel of Duke Bernhard and my grandfather Count Henry, he courageously overcame all these fortifications [Note: [Col. 1229] In manuscript 1 there is here a blank space of half a line and two lines, the last of which was erased.].

On this expedition the first cry of mocking derision against the clergy was raised, and it is preserved by wicked men even today. It is exceedingly lamentable when something good discovered by the righteous is retained in use only briefly, then immediately rejected by the greater multitude as utterly detestable. What displeases God and leads a person toward meriting the penalty of his guilt, that person learns and strengthens by repeatedly chewing over it [Note: [Col. 1229] “And” added in 1b.]. Although many do not make such mockery seriously, nevertheless they perform it in no way without the stain of sin [Note: [Col. 1229] “Although many” added in 1b.].

The emperor built a city in these regions and secured it with a garrison. Bishop Brun, mentioned above [Note: [Col. 1229D] Above, II.20 ff.], died on 7 Ides of March, and Erp, provost of Bremen, was appointed through the intervention of Archbishop Aetheldag [Note: [Col. 1229] *Atheldag* in 1c.]. At this time I was born, on 8 Kalends of August, in the month of July.

### 5.

In the year 976 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 1229] The manuscript makes this division.], Henry, duke of the Bavarians, deprived of his honor and communion, fled to Bohemia [Note: [Col. 1229D] Compare Chron. S. and the Annals of Hildesheim, under 976. Concerning the excommunication of Duke Henry, see *Leges* II, [Col. 1230C] B. 171.].

The emperor pursued him there with a powerful army, while he remained with Duke Boleslav [Note: [Col. 1229] In 1a *Bolislavo*; afterward a *v* was placed above the *u*, and finally both letters were erased. The *u* was likewise deleted thereafter.]. He achieved absolutely nothing there against either of them. But he destroyed by the treachery of one of Boleslav’s soldiers a great host of Bavarians who had come there to aid him and had pitched camp beside the city of Pilisini [Note: [Col. 1230C] Pilsen.].

When evening came, the Bavarians washed themselves and enjoyed no security from their guards. Suddenly an armored enemy arrived and struck down the naked men as they rushed out among the tents and the green meadows; then he returned safely and joyfully with all the booty.

When the emperor heard of the slaughter of so many men and saw that no route of return was open to him, he went directly to his city called Camma [Note: [Col. 1230C] Chamb.], and in the following year (977) subdued the aforementioned duke, who had fled to Padua [Note: [Col. 1230C] Compare the Chronicle of Saint Andrew, the Annals of Hildesheim, and Lambert, under 977.].

In the following year (978), Duke Henry, Count Ekbert, and Bishop Henry, accused before the emperor, were captured at Magdeburg and condemned to lengthy exile [Note: [Col. 1229] “In the following year … lengthy exile” added in 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1230C] Annals of Hildesheim and the Saxon Chronicle, under 978. Our author seems here to have confused Henry the margrave, concerning whom see chapter 13 below, with Henry, bishop of Augsburg. The latter spent only three months in the custody of Werden. See the Life of Saint Ulrich, chapter 28; Hermann the Lame, under 978; and what the learned Hormayr reports concerning Margrave Henry in his book *On Duke Liutpold*, p. 27.].

### 6. (f. 37′)

After this the emperor devoted every effort to preparing his expedition (978) against Lothair [Note: [Col. 1229] Added in 1b.], king of the Carolingians [Note: [Col. 1230D] This expedition took place in 978. See the Annals of Hildesheim, Lambert, and the Cologne Annals, as well as the fuller account in Balderic’s Chronicle of Cambrai I.96 ff.]. Lothair had presumed, with a powerful army, to invade the palace and royal seat at Aachen—which always faced toward our dominion—and to turn the eagle there so as to point toward himself. It stands on the eastern part of the building, and it had been the custom of all who possessed that place to turn it toward their own kingdoms.

The emperor pursued him as he quickly departed, laying waste to everything and consuming it by fire as far as Paris, the royal seat. During that expedition, when many were overcome by severe illness, Brun, count of Harneburg, a soldier praiseworthy in every respect, died on 2 Kalends of December [Col. 1231A] [Note: [Col. 1231D] In the Merseburg Calendar Count Brun’s name is entered on 3 Kalends of December; in the necrology of Saint Michael of Lüneburg, on 5 Kalends of December.].

Returning from there in triumphal glory [Note: [Col. 1231] *Triumphali* in 1a; *thriumphali* in 1c.], the emperor inspired such terror in his enemies that they never afterward dared to begin anything of the kind. Whatever dishonor they had previously inflicted upon our people was repaid to them [Note: [Col. 1231] “Honor” in 1a.].

Meanwhile Othelric, shepherd of the church of Augsburg, a jewel among priests, departed from this world in the fiftieth year of his episcopate (973), receiving the fruit of his labor as Christ rewarded his devotion, on 4 Nones of July [Note: [Col. 1231] “Fourth Nones” was added in an empty space by 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1231D] The Merseburg Calendar gives this as Odelric’s day of death. The year was 973.].

Henry, who succeeded him, occupied the see only briefly, as I shall explain below [Note: [Col. 1231D] Our author nevertheless omitted this. Compare above, chapter 5, note, and below, chapter 11, note.].

### 7. (f. 38)

Count Gero was accused before the emperor by Waldo. At the place called Sumeringe [Note: [Col. 1231D] Groß-Sömmeringen, a small town in Thuringia not far from Weissensee, near the bank of the Unstrut. Ursinus.], he was captured at the instigation of Archbishop Aethelbert [Note: [Col. 1231] *Adhelberti* in 1c; likewise frequently below.] and Margrave Thiedric, and was firmly entrusted to my father and my uncle [Note: [Col. 1231D] To Count Siegfried and his brother Lothair, sons of Lothair of Walbeck. Ursinus.].

Then, when all the princes of the kingdom had been summoned to Magdeburg (979), these two met in judgment on a certain island for single combat [Note: [Col. 1231] “These two” in manuscript 2 and the Annals of Saxony under 979.]. Waldo was wounded twice in the neck, but pursued his opponent more fiercely, struck him on the head with a powerful blow, and felled him.

When Count Gero was asked by Waldo whether he could continue fighting, he was compelled to admit that he had already become exhausted. Waldo then came out, refreshed himself with water after laying down his arms, and fell dead on his back.

Gero was then ordered, by the judges’ decree and the emperor’s command, to be beheaded by an executioner on 3 Ides of August [Note: [Col. 1232D] Compare the Annals of Hildesheim and Lambert, under 979.].

No one approved this combat except Archbishop Aethelbert and Margrave Thiedric [Note: [Col. 1231] “No one” in 1c.]. The emperor was reproved on the same day by Otto, duke of the Bavarians [Note: [Col. 1231] *Bauvariorum* in 1c.], son of Liudulf, who arrived, and by Count Bertold, because so great a man ought never to have been condemned for so trivial a cause [Col. 1231C].

I wish briefly to explain the merit of Liudulf, father of the Corveyan [Note: [Col. 1231] *Corbeiensis* in 1c.] abbot [f. 38′], who, laboring greatly through vigils and fasts, was honored by God with many revelations.

On the day of the aforementioned combat, when at dawn he was humbly and reverently celebrating Mass, as he always used to do, he saw Count Gero’s head above the altar. When that Mass was finished, he celebrated another for the dead. After removing his priestly vestments, he went out silently, gathered the brothers, announced Gero’s death, and humbly asked that common prayer be offered for him.

His beheading took place at sunset that very day.

For his memory, his sister Tetta and his wife Aethela [Note: [Col. 1231] Perhaps *Athela* in 1c.] built a monastery at the place called Eleslevo [Note: [Col. 1232D] The Saxon Chronographer correctly reports that Count Gero himself had already founded a community of nuns in his own city of Alsleben, situated on the Saale, in honor of Saint John the Baptist. This is also confirmed by a charter of Emperor Otto issued on May 20, 979, by which he confirmed the foundation.], where he rests. They gave to God and to his beloved precursor [Note: [Col. 1231] In manuscript 1, four letters are missing before *partem*; the Annals of Saxony read “a tenth part,” while the Saxon Chronicle under this year reads “all his inheritance.”] [lacuna] a portion of all his inheritance, confirming this by a privilege and imperial decree, so that the abbey, freely established there, might remain under the authority and protection of the emperor and his successors.

After three years, when his wife was to be buried beside him, the body of the aforementioned count was found intact, together with his clothing.

At that time, when the aforementioned Otto had been emperor for six years [Note: [Col. 1232D] That is, from the death of his father.], King Lothair came to him with his son and magnificent gifts (980). Having made satisfaction to him, he firmly secured his friendship [Note: [Col. 1232D] Saxon Chronicle and Annals of Hildesheim, under 980; compare Sigebert of Gembloux, under the same year.].

In that same year our emperor went to Italy and, alas!, never again visited these regions [Note: [Col. 1232D] Ibid.].

**Additional apparatus (keyed to the relevant passage).**

25: [Col. 1221] *heinricho* in 1a; *considerare* in 1a. “I do not wish to state the reasons”: *preponere* in 1a. “How small a thing it is in which guilt is absent”: thus in 1c?; *flacium* in 1a and in the Annals of Saxony under 955. Judith’s account begins at (f. 31d).

26: “Soon—alas!—died”: *proch* in 1c, repeatedly.

28: The praise of Aethelheidis begins at (f. 42). “As was the lord, so also were his princes”: *et. et* in 1a. “Though not forgetful”: *haud* is erased in manuscript 1 but occurs in the Annals of Saxony. “The new rule”: *hac* in 1. “Truthful admonitions”: *veridica* in 1c. “Matters entrusted to him”: *commissis* in 1. “Innumerable”: *innuma* in 1; a line above an erased *u*.

Book III, chapter 1: “First … afterward”: *primo—dein* added in 1b. “Together with its Jews and merchants”: thus in 1b and the Annals of Saxony; *cum* in 1a.

Book III, chapter 2: “Distinguished administrator”: *egrius* in 1. “The crucifix which now stands”: added in 1b; “in the middle church where he rests”: also added in 1b. “In all necessities”: *cuntis* corrected to *cunctis* in 1. “As he had formerly done”: *pius* in 1a; thus in 1c. “I will tell you on the condition”: *ut* added in 1c.

Book III, chapter 6: “After this”: added in 1b. “Against Lothair”: added in 1b.

Book III, chapter 7: “Who arrived that same day”: added in 1b. The note beginning with Tetta and Aethela is followed, through the words “the aforementioned bishop,” by text apparently written in Thietmar’s own hand at the end of the folio.

## 8.

After these events, the aforementioned bishop Aethelbertus [Note: [Col. 1231] 1a has “Gresatus, however.”] [Note: [Col. 1231] 1 has *aethlbertus*.]—the emperor now residing at Rome—in the thirteenth year of his ordination [Note: [Col. 1231] 1a has “consecration.”], namely 981, instructed and strengthened his people. Since Bishop Gisilerus [Note: [Col. 1231] 1a almost always has *gisillerus*, but it appears to have been corrected by 1b.] was then with the emperor, Aethelbertus travelled through his diocese and celebrated Mass [Note: [Col. 1231] 1a has *caelebravit*.] at Merseburg on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July [Note: [Col. 1231] Thus the manuscripts, and also A. S., under the year 981. It should nevertheless be read, with the Saxon Chronicler, “June,” since Aethelbertus died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June.], and spent the following night joyfully with Hemuzon, a venerable layman, at Chruvati [Note: [Col. 1231] 1c has *choruueti*; the Saxon Chronicle under 981 has *Cruwati*; the Saxon Annals under the same year have *Crowate*; 2 has *Erderwate*.].

On the following day he rose sadly, complaining of an exceedingly severe headache, yet departed nonetheless. When he had passed the village of Cirmini, wishing to proceed to Frekenlevo [Note: [Col. 1231] 1c has *frankenleue*.] [Note: [Col. 1232D] Freckleven.], he would have fallen from his horse to the ground, gradually sagging from the saddle, had he not been quickly supported by his attendants. He was placed upon a carpet, and when everything [Note: [Col. 1231] 1b adds *que* (“and”).] that the clergy were required to say had been completed, he faithfully departed to Christ on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June [Note: [Col. 1233] The Saxon Annals have “July.” Aethelbertus’s date of death is also attested by the Lüneburg Necrology.].

His body was carried to Ivikanstem [Note: [Col. 1233] 1c has *gevikensten*.] [Note: [Col. 1233D] Giebichenstein.], clothed in priestly vestments, and conveyed by boat as far as Magadaburg. It was received amid lamentation by his fellow brothers, especially by the monks, and was entrusted by the distinguished Bishop Hilliwardus of the holy church of Halberstadt, with the support of the venerable Abbot Hardingus, to the middle of the church before the altar of the apostles Philip and James.

Reader, pay attention to how diligently this man watched over the flocks entrusted to him! Very often, in the silence of night, he came to the sheepfold of Saint John the Baptist and Saint Maurice, accompanied by only two men, and unexpectedly observed how the brothers assembled for Matins and who remained behind in the dormitory. If all was well, he gave thanks to God; but if not, he rebuked the guilty with suitable punishment.

The clergy and people, however, shaken by the death of so great a father, unanimously elected their fellow brother Othtricus [Note: [Col. 1233] The *h* is erased in 1; this is always the case.]—who at that time was faithfully serving the emperor—as their lord and archbishop, although the aforementioned archimandrite, while still alive and in good health, had publicly foretold to many of them that this could in no way happen.

For, since the bishop and Ohtricus never agreed in disposition, Ohtricus—having gathered a large and well-trained company of brothers and guests because he was master of the school—preferred to depart rather than remain in the monastery. When the emperor, while at the archbishop’s residence, could scarcely obtain permission for him to serve him [Note: [Col. 1233] 1b adds *vix*.], it happened that on the holy day of the Resurrection, while the bishop was prepared for Mass and the subdeacon, as was customary, held the holy cross before him, he embraced it with both hands and, with abundant tears, begged that Ohtricus and Ico [Note: [Col. 1233] 2 has *Leo*; the Saxon Chronicle under 982 has *Hico*.] should never possess his see.

When the divine service had been completely performed and he had sat down at table, he openly made known to all who were present that the aforementioned men would never succeed him. He did not reveal how this had been disclosed to him, nor has anyone ever been able to explain it to me.

After his death, the same things that he had foretold while alive were confirmed in a dream to Walterdus, his beloved associate, who was also called Dodico, as he himself related to me as a fact. While lying in bed, Walterdus saw in a trance the archbishop standing at the southern door of the church, which faces the cemetery, and wishing, as it were, to travel to Rome with his staff. He addressed him angrily in these words [Note: [Col. 1233] Thus in 1c, apparently; elsewhere 1b has rejected the *i* following the *h*.]: “My Dodico, why will you offer my honor to another?” [Note: [Col. 1233] 1 has *q l*.]

He replied: “Can you not, senior most beloved, discern from my mournful appearance that I have only obedience, not my own will?” [Note: [Col. 1233] The *o* is erased.] The archbishop then continued: “Know for certain,” he said, “that Ohtricus will never possess my see.”

After the clergy and people had completed the election, as I have related above, they sent Ekkihardus, called Rufus, together with other brothers and soldiers, to announce it to the emperor and remind him of his promises. When they reached the regions of Italy where the emperor was then staying [Note: [Col. 1233] Thus 1c; 1a has *antingerent*.], they implored the support of Gisilerus, who at that time wielded great influence with the emperor, and disclosed to him the secret purpose of their embassy [Note: [Col. 1233] 1b adds “to him.”].

He promised them faithful intercession, and every matter was soon brought to a favourable conclusion for them [Note: [Col. 1233] 1c? *beniu.*]. As soon as he had poured the news into the emperor’s ears, he fell suppliant at his feet, seeking the promised and long-awaited reward for his long labour; and, with God consenting, he immediately obtained it (981).

When he came out, the envoys, especially Ohtricus, who had firmly entrusted himself to his good faith, asked whether he had accomplished anything in the matter entrusted to him. He replied that what he had accomplished would scarcely meet their needs in this affair. Having then corrupted with money all the leading men—especially the Roman judges, to whom everything is always for sale—Gisilerus first considered secretly how he might in some way attain the archbishopric. Then he publicly and earnestly sought the help of Lord Pope Benedict VII, so called as the seventh of his predecessors bearing the same name [Note: [Col. 1233] 1a has *quia*.]. The pope promised that, if it could be granted with the counsel of the whole senate, it would be ready on his side.

A general council was convened at Rome. The wisest men assembled, and that prophecy of Jeremiah was fulfilled: “How the gold has become dim, the finest color has been changed” (Jeremiah 4:1), and so forth. For when the judges were asked by the apostolic authority whether Gisilerus might be promoted to the archbishopric—since he did not then possess a definite see, but had been deprived of the one he had held, unjustly, as he always complained, by Bishop Hildiwardus—they affirmed in words and by examples that he could rightly and deservedly obtain it by canonical authority, thereby transgressing the Davidic admonition: “Judge rightly, sons of men” (Psalm 57:2). They also cited the following:

> A corrupt judge cannot discern what is true.  
> *(Horace, II.2.8.)*

Reader, believe me: I am ashamed and grieved, though I am far inferior to these men, to set forth in words what they, because of present and future shame, were unwilling to omit.

Merseburg, which until then had ruled freely [Note: [Col. 1233] 2 and A. S. have *libera*.], was subordinated to the church of Halberstadt after its episcopal see had been destroyed [Note: [Col. 1233D] The bull of Pope Benedict VII concerning the abolition of the bishopric of Merseburg was issued in 981, September 11. [Col. 1234D] See Schöttgen, *Direct. diplomat.*, vol. I, p. 109, no. 117.]. Gisilerus, however, not its shepherd but its mercenary, always reaching for greater things, received what he desired on the fourth day before the Ides of September, forgetful of that proverb: “The higher the rank, the more grievous the fall” (cf. Proverbs 16:8).

Certainly, if he had wished to persist in the charge entrusted to him, he could, with the emperor’s aid, have driven away every obstacle that ever opposed him and secured great safety and abundance of all things for himself and his successors. But because God’s judgments are hidden from human beings and never unjust, I attribute this not only to him but also to our common sins, to which whatever adversity befalls our household is justly ascribed.

Ohtricus later came to Beneventum and fell ill. My fellow brother Huswardus, as he reported to me [Note: [Col. 1235] 1b adds “as he related to me.”], saw Aethelleken [Note: [Col. 1235] *athelleken* in 1c?], once our provost [Note: [Col. 1235D] Of Magdeburg.], but then already dead, standing beside him and offering him from a distance the grain of Saint Maurice.

Terrified by this vision, he said: “Do you see anything, brother?” And when he explained everything to him in order, Huswardus said: “Woe to me, miserable sinner, because I ever abandoned my monastery and obedience for ambition! If divine generosity deigns to grant me any health, I shall come here as a suppliant and never depart.”

After continuing in this manner, he was overcome by a more severe illness and, a few days later, died and was buried in the aforementioned city on the Nones of October [Note: [Col. 1235D] The Merseburg Calendar likewise has this date.], leaving no one equal to him in wisdom and eloquence.

## 9.

Gisilerus, having received permission from the emperor, came to Magadaburg on the second day before the Kalends of December, accompanied by Thiedricus, bishop of the church of Metz [Note: [Col. 1235D] See the Life which Sigibertus wrote about him.]. He was a friend of the emperor and very dear to him, and one of the corrupt men who received a thousand talents of gold and silver from the archbishop in exchange for obscuring the truth [Note: [Col. 1235] 1a has *milia*.].

When, at the emperor’s command, this man jokingly blessed a certain person at Matins, the man said to him: “May God satisfy you in the future with what here we are all unable to give you in gold.”

Then everything that had previously concerned our church was miserably divided, in the manner of a Slavic household; it, having been condemned [Note: [Col. 1235D] Here *accusata* means the same as “condemned.” KIND.], was scattered by sale [Note: [Col. 1235D] Lambert of Hersfeld assigns the destruction of the bishopric of Merseburg to the year 982, and the author of the Life of Godehard, bishop of Hildesheim, calls this destruction ill-considered.
