See more on the matter in Sagittarius, *Antiquitates Magdeburgenses*, p. 192 ff., who cites two bulls of the Roman pontiff clearly demonstrating that Gisilerus carried out this destruction with papal authority. Compare Dreyhaupt, *Saalkreis*, vol. I, p. 21 f. URS.].

The portion of our bishopric lying between the rivers Saale, Elster, and Milde, and comprising the districts of Plisni, Vedu [Note: [Col. 1235D] Apparently a district between the Saale and Elster, named after the small river Wietav, which flows into the Saale near Naumburg.], and Tuchurini [Note: [Col. 1235D] Teucheren.], together with the villages of Passini [Note: [Col. 1235D] Possenhain, not far from Naumburg.] and Piscini [Note: [Col. 1235D] Pissen near Lützen.], was given to Frithericus, bishop of Zeitz.

That part belonging to Gutizi [Note: [Col. 1235] 1a has *guntizi*, but the author himself corrected it.] in the east, distinguished by the rivers Caminici and Albis, together with its dependent villages Wissepuig and Lostatawa [Note: [Col. 1236D] Wiesenburg and Lostau near the river Mulde. Compare the charter of Emperor Henry II, March 5, 1004.], was granted to Wolcoldo [Note: [Col. 1235] *volcoldo* in 1c?], bishop of the church of Meissen.

For himself he retained nine cities, whose names are: Scudici, Cotug, Vurcin, Bigni, Hilburg [Note: [Col. 1235] The *h* is erased in 1.], Dibni, Paug [Note: [Col. 1235] The *a* is erased in 1.], Liubanici, and Gezerisca [Note: [Col. 1236D] Skeudiz, Gautzsch, Wurzen, Püchen, Eilenburg, Düben, Pouch, Löbnitz, and Gerichshayn. URS.].

He either burned the charters that held royal or imperial grants or had them designated for his own church under an altered name [Note: [Col. 1236D] We saw an example of this in the abbey of Pöhlde; see above, chapter 1.]. He voluntarily scattered the slaves and everything that ought to have belonged to Merseburg, so that it might never be reassembled. He established an abbey there [Note: [Col. 1236D] Concerning the foundation of the abbey established by Gisilerus at Merseburg, Sagittarius publishes in *Antiquitates Magdeburgenses*, p. 202, the bull of Benedict VII, written by the Roman pontiff in April, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the second indiction and the sixteenth year of his pontificate, which was the year 983. URS.], and placed over it Ohtradus [Note: [Col. 1235] The *h* is erased in 1.] [Note: [Col. 1236D] The date of death of the monk Ohtradus is recorded in the Merseburg Necrology on the seventh day before the Kalends of June.], a venerable monk of Saint John. Afterwards he appointed Heimo from the same monastery.

But, reader, pay attention to what events followed this destruction!

## 10.

These peoples, who after accepting Christianity had served kings and emperors as tributaries, provoked by the arrogance of Duke Thiedricus, took up arms in a unanimous uprising (perhaps in 983). This was revealed to my father, Count Sigifridus, before it happened.

In a dream he saw the sky gathered into a dense cloud. When, amazed, he asked what this might be, he heard a voice uttering these words: “Now that prophecy must be fulfilled: ‘God rains upon the just and the unjust’” (Matthew 5:45).

This crime first broke out on the third day before the Kalends of July, when the garrison at Havelberg [Note: [Col. 1235] In 1, the first *u* in *hauuelberg* is erased, and three letters before *presidio* have also been erased.] was attacked and destroyed and the episcopal see there abolished.

After a period of three days had passed, the united force of the Slavs attacked the bishopric of Brandenburg, established thirty years before that of Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 1236D] Since the bishopric of Brandenburg was founded in 949, whereas the archbishopric of Magdeburg was founded in 967, it is evident that Thietmar was mistaken in this number of years.], when the first canonical hour was already being sung [Note: [Col. 1235] 1b adds *magadaburgiensem*, with the *i* subsequently erased. In place of *XXX* one should read *XIX*.].

Its third bishop, Wolcmerus [Note: [Col. 1237] *uolcmero* in 1c?], fled first, while its defender Thiedricus and the soldiers barely escaped that very day [Note: [Col. 1237] 1b adds “and its defender.”]. The clergy there were captured. Dodilo, the second bishop of that see [Note: [Col. 1237] 1b adds this phrase.], who had lain unburied for three years after being strangled by his own people, was then dragged from his tomb. Although his body and priestly vestments were still intact, he was devoured by greedy dogs and then carelessly reburied.

The entire church treasure was sold off, and the blood of many was miserably shed. In place of Christ and his fisherman, the venerable Peter, various forms of worship belonging to demonic heresy were henceforth honored, and this lamentable change was exalted not only by pagans but also by Christians [Note: [Col. 1237D] The Hildesheim Annals, the Saxon Chronicler, and the Saxon Annals assign these events to the year 983.].

## 11.

At this time the church of Zeitz was captured and plundered by an army of Bohemians [Note: [Col. 1237] In 1a, *bemiorum*, with an *o* written above but erased again.], under the leadership of Dedo [Note: [Col. 1237] *Dedone* in 2 and in A. S. under 983.] [Note: [Col. 1237D] See below.], while Hugo, then its first bishop, was driven out [Note: [Col. 1237D] Frithericus had already succeeded Hugo at the end of 981, as may be inferred from chapter 8. All these events therefore seem to belong before 983, the year to which the annalist assigned them. Compare especially Book IV, chapter 36.].

Afterwards they desolated the monastery of the martyr Saint Lawrence, situated in the city called Calvo [Note: [Col. 1237] *calue* in 1c.], and pursued our people like fleeing deer [Note: [Col. 1237] *ceruuos* in 1a.]. For our crimes inspired us with fear and gave them courage.

Mistui, duke of the Abodrites, burned and devastated Hômanburg [Note: [Col. 1237] *Hammanburh* in the Saxon Annals; *Hamanburch* in the Saxon Chronicler under 982.], where there had once been an episcopal see. Let the devotion of the entire Christian world attend to what marvelous things Christ performed there from heaven!

A golden hand came from the heavenly dwelling, descended into the midst of the fire with its fingers spread, and returned full before the eyes of all. The army marveled at this; the fearful Mistuwoi [Note: [Col. 1237] 1a has *mistuiuoi*; 1b has *mistuvuoi*.] was struck with amazement. Avico, then his chaplain and later my spiritual brother [Note: [Col. 1237D] His date of death is recorded as October 7 in the Merseburg Necrology.], reported this to me.

I explained it to him in this way: the relics of the saints, divinely carried along the road to heaven, had departed, terrifying and driving away the enemies.

After this, Mystuwoi was driven mad and held in chains. When he was immersed in holy water, he said: “Saint Lawrence has burned me!” Before he could be released, he died miserably [Note: [Col. 1237] The words “After this … he died” were added by 1b in the lower margin of the page.].

At that time, after all the cities and villages had been desolated by plunder and fire as far as the water called the Tongera, more than thirty legions of Slavic infantry and cavalry assembled. With their trumpeters marching before them [Note: [Col. 1237] 1b adds “with trumpeters marching before them.”], they did not hesitate to devastate whatever remained without suffering any injury, relying upon the aid of their gods [Note: [Col. 1237] 1b adds “then.”].

This did not escape the notice of our men. Bishops Gisilerus and Hilliwardus assembled with the margrave Thiedricus and the other counts: Ricdagus, Hodo [Note: [Col. 1237] *hovdone* in 1c.], Binizonus, Frithericus, Dudo, my father Sigifridus, and many others [Note: [Col. 1237] *ceterisque* corrected to *aliisque* in 1.].

As soon as Saturday dawned, they all heard Mass, fortified body and soul with the heavenly sacrament, and confidently attacked the enemies who appeared before them. The enemies were routed, with only a few escaping to a certain hill [Note: [Col. 1238D] At a place called Belxem, according to A. S. under 983.].

The victors praised God, marvelous in all his works, and the saying of Paul the teacher was shown to be true: “There is no wisdom, nor strength, nor counsel against the Lord” [Note: [Col. 1238D] This is not Paul, but Solomon, Proverbs 21:30.].

Those who had previously presumed to despise God were abandoned, and in their folly had preferred handmade and utterly worthless idols to their Creator.

As night approached and our men were encamped some distance away, those whom I mentioned above secretly escaped—alas! All our men, except three, returned rejoicing the next day, while everyone whom they encountered on the road or found at home applauded them [Note: [Col. 1237] 1c has *applaudaentibus*.].

## 12.

Meanwhile the emperor ruled the Roman Empire in such a way that he retained everything that had previously belonged to his father, and bravely resisted the Saracens who attacked his territories, driving them far from his borders.

When the emperor learned that Calabria was suffering greatly from the frequent incursions of the Greeks and the plundering of the Saracens (982) [Note: [Col. 1237] 1 has *III*.], he summoned the Bavarians and the warlike Alemanni to reinforce his army [Note: [Col. 1238D] Compare the Hildesheim Annals and Lambert under 982; Balderic, *Chronicle of Cambrai*, Book I, chapter 103; Alpert, *On the Variety of Times*, chapter 24.].

He himself, together with Duke Otto, son of his brother Liudolfus [Note: [Col. 1237] 1c has *ludulfi*, with the *e* perhaps corrected.], hastened to the city of Tarentum, which the Greeks had already secured with a garrison, and after besieging it vigorously for a short time, defeated it [Note: [Col. 1238D] In March and April of 982.].

As he sought to overcome the Saracens, who were ravaging his territories with a powerful army, he sent out cautious scouts to bring back reliable information about the enemy [Note: [Col. 1237] Thus 1c; 1a has *contendas*.]. At first he drove them, defeated, from inside a certain city [Note: [Col. 1237] 1a has “in a certain city.”] [Note: [Col. 1238D] Scylacium; see the Cavense Annals in Prat, vol. IV, p. 420. W.]. Then, when they had drawn themselves up in formation on the plain, he attacked them courageously [Note: [Col. 1237] 1 has *ad ejus*; 2 has *ad ejus interitum*; Wagner conjectured *adiens*.], slaughtered an innumerable multitude of them, and believed that they had been utterly defeated.

But they gathered themselves unexpectedly, advanced united against our men, and, after offering a little resistance, routed them. Alas! On the third day before the Ides of July they killed Richarius, the standard-bearer [Note: [Col. 1237] Between *Julii* and *Richarium* 1 leaves a space of six or seven letters without erasure.], and Duke Udo, my mother’s uncle; and the counts Thietmarus, Becelinus, Gevehardus, Gunterius [Note: [Col. 1239] The *i* is erased.], Ecelinus and his brother Becelinus, together with Burchardus, Dedo, Conradus, and countless others whose names God knows [Note: [Col. 1239D] The Lüneburg Necrology, on the second day before the Ides of July, records Gunther, Udo, and many others as having been killed. Lambert’s Annals place the battle on the Ides of July and include among the dead Duke Otto, Bertoldus, Werner, abbot of Fulda, and Heinricus, bishop of Augsburg. On Otto’s death in this year, see the Hildesheim and Einsiedeln Annals under 982. The Merseburg Necrology, on the third day before the Ides of July, records the name of Bishop Heinricus; compare the Life of Saint Ulrich, chapter 28. Under the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August it reads: “Bishop Heinricus was killed by the Saracens with many others.” The counts Irmirid and Arnold are mentioned, among others, in the Fulda Necrology. Compare the Augsburg Annals. The Chronicle of the Bishops of Metz reports that this was the day of the battle.].

The emperor, however, fleeing with the aforementioned Otto and the others, reached the sea. Seeing from a distance a ship called a *salandria*, he rode toward it on the horse of a Jew named Calonymus. But the ship passed by and refused to take him aboard.

Seeking the protection of the shore, he found the Jew still standing there, anxiously awaiting the fate of his beloved lord [Note: [Col. 1239] 1a has *euuentum*.]. When he saw the enemies approaching and, saddened, asked what might ever happen to him [Note: [Col. 1239] Thus perhaps 1c; 1a has *dente*.], he noticed that he had a friend among them whose aid he might hope for. He therefore leapt again into the sea with the horse as his companion and made for another *salandria* that followed [Note: [Col. 1239] Thus 1c; 1a has *sequabatur*.].

He was recognized only by one of its soldiers, a man named Heinricus in German—*Zolunta* in the Slavic tongue—and was admitted aboard. Placed on the bed of the ship’s master, he was eventually recognized by the master himself, who asked whether he was the emperor.

After trying for a long time to conceal this, he finally confessed: “I am the one who, deserving this through my sins, has come into such misery. But listen carefully to what we must now do together. Miserable man that I am, I have just lost the best men of my empire. Because of this sting of grief, I can neither enter these lands nor ever wish to see their friends. Let us go only to the city of Rossano [Note: [Col. 1240D] Rossano, a town in Citerior Calabria.], where my wife awaits my arrival. Taking with us all the immeasurable wealth I possess, let us visit your emperor—my brother, that is—who, as I hope, will certainly be a friend to my necessities.”

Delighted by this pleasant conversation, the shipmaster agreed and hurried day and night toward the appointed place.

When they drew near, the emperor’s advance envoy, sent ahead by his command, summoned the empress and Thiedricus, the aforementioned bishop, who was with her, together with many pack animals loaded, as it seemed, with money.

When the Greeks first saw the empress departing from the city with such gifts, they dropped anchor [Note: [Col. 1239] Thus 1c; 1a has *ponens*.] and allowed Bishop Thiedricus to board with a few companions.

At the bishop’s request, the emperor removed his shabby clothing and put on better garments. Trusting in his own strength and his skill at swimming, he stood at the prow and quickly plunged into the sea. When one of the Greeks standing nearby presumed to seize him by his clothing and hold him back, he was pierced with the sword of Liuppo, a distinguished soldier, and fell backward.

The others fled to the opposite side of the ship, while our men, whose ships had brought them there, followed the emperor unharmed. They awaited him in the security of the shore, wishing to fulfill with great gifts the rewards promised to the Danes [Note: [Col. 1240D] The emperor was still staying in the city of Rossano on July 31.].

The Greeks, however, greatly terrified and distrustful of the promises, departed for their ancestral lands. Those who had always conquered all nations by deceit now felt that they themselves had been deceived by a similar stratagem.

I cannot describe how great was the joy with which the emperor was later received by those present and by those who arrived afterward.

## 13.

But so that you may be fully informed about everything, dearest reader, I shall briefly explain what a *salandria* is [Note: [Col. 1240D] It is called a *chelandria* by Liudprand, Book V, chapters 9 ff.], and why it came to these shores.

As I have said, it is a ship of remarkable length and speed [Note: [Col. 1239] *aclaritatis* corrected to *claritatis* in 1.], carrying two rows of oars on each side and one hundred and fifty sailors.

Two ships bore this single name. By order of the basileus Nicephorus, they went to Calabria to collect tribute. Although Calabria specifically belongs to the Roman Empire, it voluntarily pays the annual tribute in gold to the Constantinopolitans so as to avoid suffering any harassment from the Greeks [Note: [Col. 1239] 1a has *paciantur*.].

When the emperor encountered these ships, carrying an unquenchable fire that consumed everything except vinegar, he joined them to his forces and sent them out to burn the Saracen ships hired for that purpose.

One of them, as I said, refused to receive the defeated emperor, whether through ignorance of his identity or fear of the enemy pursuing him. The other, which received him at Heinricus’s urging [Note: [Col. 1239] Thus 1b; 1a appears to have written *susceperat* (“had received”).], returned him, as I have said, against its will.

## 14.

My mind has now strayed a little from its undertaking; I shall resume it and bring it to completion.

When all our princes learned this most sorrowful news, they assembled in grief and unanimously asked, through the bearer of a letter, that they might be permitted to see him. When the emperor heard their embassy, he agreed with a willing heart.

An assembly was convened in the city of Berna [Note: [Col. 1240D] We find the emperor at Verona in June 983.], and the entire principality was summoned there [Note: [Col. 1239] 1b has “and the entire principality was summoned here,” in an erased passage.], so that many necessary matters might be discussed (983).

Duke Bernhardus alone turned back halfway along the route. One of his cities [lacuna], which the emperor had fortified against the Danes by construction and a garrison, was treacherously recaptured by them; after its defenders had been killed, it was burned [Note: [Col. 1239] A space of several syllables is left between *suis* and *quam* in 1.] [Note: [Col. 1241] Here, after a verse and a half had been left blank, Thietmar himself wrote the following text through the end of the chapter, which is also the end of the folio.] [Note: [Col. 1241C] Compare Adam of Bremen, II.18.].

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 983, the emperor held an assembly at Verona, and the younger Heinricus, released from exile, was made duke of the Bavarians [Note: [Col. 1241C] From the Quedlinburg Annals. Compare the Hildesheim Annals under 983; also the same under 977 and 978 and above, chapter 5. In the peace concluded with the Venetians on June 7 of this year, Ezelo—also called Hecil and the younger Heinricus—already appears among the witnesses [Note: [Col. 1241D] The younger Heinricus.].

In this year the Slavs unanimously resisted the emperor and Margrave Thiedricus [Note: [Col. 1241D] See the same source.]. The emperor’s son was elected lord by everyone (983).

## 15.

After a few days they departed, saying their final farewell. For when the emperor came to Rome [Note: [Col. 1241] 1a has *venirent*.], leaving his venerable mother in the city of Pavia, he fell gravely ill. Sensing that his end was near, he divided all his wealth into four parts [Note: [Col. 1241D] Compare the Saxon Chronicler under 983.]: one for the churches, a second for the poor, a third for his beloved sister Mahtilda, who, as a devoted servant of Christ, held the abbey at Quedlinburg, and a fourth for his sorrowful servants and soldiers.

After making a full confession in Latin [Note: [Col. 1241D] “With full voice,” according to the Saxon Chronicler under 983.] before the apostolic authority and the other co-bishops and priests [Note: [Col. 1241] 1 has *ceterisque*.], and having received from them the desired remission, he was taken from this light on the seventh day before the Ides of December.

He was entrusted to the earth where the eastern entrance to the paradise of Saint Peter is open to all the faithful, and where an honorably fashioned image of the Lord stands blessing all who come [Note: [Col. 1241D] He was buried at Saint Peter’s, in the paradise, near the oratory of Saint Mary, according to Alpert, Book I.].

For my part, mindful of the human lot and greatly in need of mercy, I humbly beseech the God and Lord of heaven and earth mercifully to forgive whoever may at any time have sinned in my church here, and to grant a hundredfold in return for good deeds. By the authority undeservedly granted to me, I grant pardon, earnestly asking you, my successor, always from your heart to bestow this forgiveness—which is to be denied to no one at the last—upon him.

## 16.

His illustrious offspring, born to him in the forest called Ketil [Note: [Col. 1241D] The forest of Ketil, where today the parish village of Kessel lies beside the river Niers near the castle of Gennep in the district of Cleves. See Scheid, *Origines Guelficae*, vol. IV, preface, p. 96.], on the day of the approaching Nativity of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1241] 1b adds this phrase.], was consecrated king at Aachen by John, archbishop of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 1241] In 1, the second *u* in *rauuennate* is erased.], and by Willigisus of Mainz.

When this ceremony had been completed, a messenger immediately arrived with a sorrowful report, disturbing such great joy. An unspeakable grief moved the hearts of many; they lamented that virtue had been taken away—the virtue that frail and uncertain human beings so often pursue while they are still unharmed (cf. Horace, III.24.31).

This emperor had sat for twice five solar years after his father’s death, guardian of kingdom and empire, dreaded by all enemies, and an impregnable wall for the flocks entrusted to him [Note: [Col. 1241D] A hexameter: “An impregnable wall for the flocks entrusted to him.”].

The anxious judgment of the people wavered amid such events [Note: [Col. 1241] The words *peratoris … qua* occur in a passage erased in 1.], but divine mercy quickly established it.

Duke Heinricus was released from custody at Utrecht, and he took the tender young king from Warinus, archbishop of Cologne, for upbringing—or degradation. The boy had been entrusted by the aforementioned emperor to Warinus’s steadfast loyalty [Note: [Col. 1241] 1b adds “by the aforementioned emperor.”].

Now I shall close the sequence of the third book with the hard bolt of the death of our third emperor—a death to be mourned—and shall endeavour with a joyful pen to open up the certainty of the gracious piety by which he removed every ambiguity [Note: [Col. 1241] “The third book ends. The fourth book begins, concerning Otto III, emperor.” 2.].

# BOOK FOUR

## 1.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 984, the empress Theophano, mother of Otto III and, alas, the last in this succession [Note: [Col. 1241] Thus 2 and A. S. under 984; 1 has *di*.], stricken by the novelty of this terrible wound and by the absence of her only son, came to the empress Adelheid at the city of Pavia [Note: [Col. 1241] 1c consistently has *Adhelheidam*.]. She was received with great mourning and consoled by affectionate sympathy.

The aforementioned duke, who had long been kept under the authority of the venerable Bishop Poppo [Note: [Col. 1242C] The Saxon Annals add “of Utrecht.” This cannot refer to the bishop of Utrecht, who was Ansfridus from 976 to 1008; nor could Poppo have been the bishop of Würzburg, since that bishop had died shortly before Emperor Otto II. Perhaps he was the bishop of Kraków; see below, chapter 28.], came to Agrippina with Count Ekbertus, who had one eye [Note: [Col. 1241] 2 and the Saxon Annals have *monoculo*. The phrase is marked in a more recent hand in the manuscript; nothing is missing.]. As the king’s lawful guardian, the duke received the king from Archbishop Warinus, as I have said above [Note: [Col. 1242D] See above, Book II, chapter 15.], and firmly secured his support together with that of all whom he could turn to his favor [Note: [Col. 1242D] At first pretending that, by right of kinship, he would most faithfully defend the cause of the infant king; Quedlinburg Annals under 984.].

After arranging everything according to his wishes, the duke came with them to Corvey. There he refused to accept the penance of the counts Thiedricus [Note: [Col. 1242D] Count palatine.] and Sicco [Note: [Col. 1242D] In chapters 2 and 13 he is called Sibertus; Sigibertus in a document cited by H. A. Luntzel, *The Older Diocese of Hildesheim*, p. 345. In the Quedlinburg Annals under 995 he and his brother are called Saxons.] when they came barefoot to ask forgiveness.

They took this badly and departed, striving with all their might to remove their kinsmen and friends from the duke’s service.

When he wished to celebrate Palm Sunday at Magadaburg, he invited and ordered all the princes of that region to assemble there, considering how they might submit themselves to his authority and raise him to the royal dignity. Most of the nobles assented to this scheme on the understanding that he should first seek permission from his own lord, the king to whom he had sworn allegiance, and that they should afterwards serve the new king without fear.

But some, having departed because of his indignation, secretly devised cunning means by which this might never happen [Note: [Col. 1243D] Compare the Hildesheim Annals under this year.].

## 2

After this Heinricus departed and celebrated the following Easter at Quidilingeburg with festive rejoicing. [Col. 1243B] The great leading men of the kingdom assembled there; but, since some were unwilling to come there, a messenger was sent to inquire carefully into everything. At this festival he was publicly called king by his men and exalted with divine praises.

Miseco, Mistui, and Bolizlovo, the dukes, together with countless others, gathered there, affirming under oath that henceforth they would render him assistance as king and lord. Many of them, not daring through fear of God to violate their sworn faith, escaped after a short time and hurried to the city of Hesleburg, where their associates, already openly conspiring against the duke, were assembling.

These are their names. From the east came these counts with Duke Bernhard and Margrave Thiedricus: Ekkihardus; Bijo; Esic; Bernwardus, a count, and the cleric; Sifrith, count of Nordheim, and his namesake son; Frithericus; and Ciazo, brothers.

Among the men of the same province were the brothers Thiedricus and Siber; Hoico; Ekkihardus and Bezeco, brothers; Brunig and his men; and the soldiers of Saint Martin, at the command of the archbishop Willigis. A very large multitude of men from the western regions adhered to them.

When the duke learned this, he dismissed his men, richly rewarded and with his favor. He himself, hastening with a strong force to Werlu, to disturb or pacify this conspiracy, sent Bishop Poppo to try to separate his opponents or reconcile them.

Poppo persisted in his journey and, finding the enemies assembled and already prepared to attack the duke, scarcely secured a mutual peace, for an appointed day, at the place called Seusun.

[Folio 52] The duke then departed immediately for Bavaria. Since he either did not wish to come or was unable to do so because of Duke Heinricus, who at that time governed the Bavarians and Carentanians by the authority of the aforesaid emperor, the hostile force seized the city of Count Ekbert called Ala. They immediately destroyed the walls, entered, seized Ethelheidis, the emperor’s daughter, who was being raised there, together with the great quantity of money collected there, and returned rejoicing.

## 3

[Col. 1244B]

The duke, having won over to himself all the Bavarian bishops and several counts, entered the territory of the Franks, relying upon these allies, and settled in the pastures belonging to Bisinstidi, in order to address the leaders of that region.

At that time Willigisus, administrator of the church of Mainz, came there with Duke Conradus and the other nobles. The duke tried by every possible means to attach them to himself, but learned from their unanimous reply that they would never, as long as they lived, withdraw from the promise made under oath to their king. Compelled by fear of the coming battle, he affirmed under oath that he would come on the third day before the Kalends of July to the place called Rara and would return the boy to his mother and to them.

Then each man returned to his own place, with minds divided between joy and sorrow.

## 4

After this Heinricus and his men went to Bolizlavus, [Col. 1244C] duke of the Bohemians (984), who was always ready to assist him in all his needs, and was honorably received by him. With Bolizlavus’s army he was led from his borders through the districts of Niseni and Deleminci as far as Mogelini.

[Folio 52′] From there he proceeded to Medeburun with our men, who were coming to meet him. Wagio, a soldier of Bolizlavus, duke of the Bohemians, accompanied Heinricus with the army. When, returning through Misni, he reached that city, he spoke briefly with its inhabitants and, through a messenger, asked Frithericus to come to the church outside the city and speak with him. This Frithericus was the friend and retainer of Margrave Ricdagus, who was then residing at Merseburg.

When Frithericus came out, the gate was closed behind him. Ricdagus, guardian of that city—that is, its burgrave —and a distinguished soldier, was treacherously killed beside the river called Tribisa.

The aforesaid city, promptly secured by Bolizlavus’s garrison, soon received him as its lord and inhabitant.

## 5

The bishop Wolcoldus was expelled by him at the instigation of the fickle populace. He went to the archbishop Willigisus and was kindly received by him. For the bishop had brought Willigisus up as a son; when the bishop was appointed to the eastern regions, he carefully commended Willigisus to Otto II, whose tutor he had been, to be treated as his own representative.

[Col. 1245B] Willigisus always kept this in mind and acknowledged it with the greatest honor, especially now, when the bishop needed him. Willigisus ordered that he be provided for with the utmost care at Erpesfordi, where he himself wished it.

After living there for a long time, following the death of the distinguished Margrave Ricdagus, when Ekkihardus succeeded him and Bolizlavus returned to his own country, Wolcoldus revisited his own see in the year 985.

Afterward he firmly acquired Bolizlavus’s friendship. While celebrating the Lord’s Supper at Prague, and on the following day, Good Friday [folio 53], properly commemorating the divine Passion, he was struck by paralysis and carried away. He remained in this illness until the end of his life, although for a time he recovered.

He had occupied the see for twenty-three years. On the tenth day before the Kalends of September, he was led out of the prison of this flesh. [Col. 1245C] In his place Eid, a brother of our congregation, a just man of great simplicity, was ordained at the urging of Archbishop Gisilerus. When the time comes, I shall relate much about his distinguished conduct that is useful for our edification; for now I continue with what I have begun.

## 6

Meanwhile the king’s supporters were besieging Count Willehelmus, a close associate of the duke, at Wimeri. When they learned of the duke’s arrival, they hurried toward him and, assembling near the village called Iteri, pitched their camp, intending to fight him the next day in the year 984.

When the duke immediately learned this, he sent the archbishop Gisilerus there to inquire into their intentions and, if peace could be made by any means, to establish it. When Gisilerus revealed the secret of his embassy to the assembled elders, they said:

“If he is willing to restore their king and lord to them, and to retain none of the king’s possessions for himself until the appointed day except Merseburg, Walbizi, and Frasu, and if he confirms this with credible oaths, then, once security had been guaranteed on their side, he may depart safely. Otherwise, no opportunity for going or returning will remain for him while he lives”.

What more is there to say? On the following day they obtained everything they demanded, and permitted him to go to Merseburg, where Duchess Gisla [folio 53′] sat in sadness because of his long absence.

He, discussing every matter with his faithful men and truthfully declaring that, for fear of God and for the salvation of his homeland, he would withdraw from his undertaking, rendered worthy thanks for their assistance and goodwill and earnestly asked them all to go with him on the appointed day.

The empresses, who had been humbly awaiting divine consolation at Pavia, and all the princes of the empire and kingdom, came to Rara. The duke’s faithful promise was fulfilled: favor and permission to depart were granted to all who belonged to the kingdom.

At midday, a bright star of the ruler predestined by God shone forth before the eyes of all. A single chorus of laymen and clerics arose in praise of Christ, and the suppliant devotion of those who had previously resisted was heard; the discordant crowd was brought together under one rule.

The king, carefully received by his mother and grandmother, was entrusted to the guardianship of Count Hoico.

Peace was established between the king and the duke until their meeting in the aforesaid meadows of Bisinstidi, and both returned to their own territories. When they came together, however, they departed in hostility at the instigation of evil men, and thus a long interval ensued.

A great discord then arose between this man and the aforesaid Heinricus, who was called “the Younger.” It was later ended through the counsel of Count Herimannus, and, by submitting, he won the king’s favor at Francanafordi and received the duchy of Bavaria.

## 7

[Folio 54] The following Easter solemnity was celebrated by the king at Quidilingeburg. There four dukes performed the customary offices: Heinricus served at the table, Conradus in the chamber, Hecil in the cellar, and Bernhardus took charge of the horses.

Bolizlavus and Miseco also came there with their men. After everything had been properly completed, they departed richly rewarded. During those days Miseco surrendered himself to the king and presented him, among other gifts, with a camel; he took part with him in two expeditions.

In the first year of the king’s reign, Adwinus, bishop of Hildesheim, died on the Kalends of December, and Osdagus, provost of the same monastery, succeeded him.

After Osdagus had held the see for five years, he died, and Gerdagus, then the cellarer, was ordained.

In the third year of his ordination, Gerdagus went to Rome for the sake of prayer. On his return he died on the seventh day before the Ides of December. His body, divided limb by limb, was sorrowfully carried by his associates to his monastery in two chests.

The archbishop Gisilerus, who happened to arrive there, committed both bishops to the earth. Then Bernwardus, the king’s teacher, was elected and consecrated.

## 8

The king did not cease to harass the Slavs with many harsh wars. [Col. 1247B] He also defeated the eastern peoples who dared to rise against him. On the western side, many repeatedly took up arms and plundered many places; he strove to overcome them by force and strategy.

There is no need to enumerate childish matters, and it would be tedious to recount all that he accomplished through prudent counsellors. A comet announced the losses that would follow in pestilences in the year 989.

The emperor, having now become a man, “put away the things of a child,” as the Apostle says (1 Corinthians 13:11). He constantly mourned the destruction of the church of Merseburg and carefully revolved in his mind how it might be restored. As long as he lived in the body, he strove to fulfil this vow, in accordance with the exhortations of his pious mother.

As Meinsvith later reported to me, having learned it from the woman herself, she saw the following in a dream. [Col. 1247C] In the silence of the dead of night, Saint Laurence, an athlete of Christ, appeared to her with his right arm mutilated.

“Why,” he said, “do you not ask who I am?”.

She replied, “I do not dare, my lord.”

He continued, “I am”—and he made his name known. “What you now see in me was caused by your lord”—that is, Emperor Otto II —“who was led astray by the persuasion of the man whose guilt has caused a great multitude of Christ’s chosen to be divided”—that is, Gisilerus.

After this she entrusted to her son the charge that, by restoring the bishopric, whether this could be done while Gisilerus lived or after his death, he should bring his father’s soul to eternal rest on the last day.

Although fragile in sex, she possessed modest confidence and—something rare in Greece—an outstanding way of life. She guarded her son’s kingdom with manly care, soothing the pious in all things and wearing down and overcoming the proud.

From the fruit of her womb she offered tithes to God: her daughters, the first, named Aethelheidis, to Quidilingeburg; the second, called Sophia, to Gonnesheim.

## 9

[Col. 1248A]

At that time, in the year 990, Miseco and Bolizlavus, being at odds with each other, inflicted much harm upon one another.

Bolizlavus invited the Liuticians, who were always faithful to his parents and to himself, to aid him. Miseco, however, sought the assistance of the aforesaid empress. Since she was then at Magadaburg, she sent there the archbishop Gisilerus, together with the counts Ekkihardus, Esico, and Binizo, my father and his namesake, Bruno, Udo, and many others.

Setting out with barely four legions, they came to the district called Selpuli and encamped beside a marsh over which a long bridge extended.

Then, in the silence of the night, one of Willo’s companions, who had gone ahead the previous day to inspect his own estate and had been captured by the Bohemians, escaped and first reported the imminent danger to Count Binizo.

At his warning our men quickly rose and prepared themselves. In the first twilight of the approaching dawn they heard Mass, some standing and others seated on horseback; at sunrise they went out from the camp, anxious about the outcome of the coming battle.

Then Bolizlavus came with his men in organized bands on the third day before the Ides of July, and messengers were sent from both sides.

From Bolizlavus’s side a certain soldier named Slopan approached to inspect our army. When he returned, his lord asked him what sort of army it was and whether he could fight it. His retainers were urging him to let none of our men depart alive.

He answered him as follows:

“This army is small in number, but in quality it is excellent, and wholly made of iron. You can fight it; but if victory comes to you today, you will be so overthrown that, while fleeing, you will scarcely—or not at all—escape Miseco, your enemy, who will pursue you continuously, and you will acquire the Saxons as enemies forever.

“But if you are defeated, it is the end of you yourself and of the whole kingdom belonging to you. No hope of resistance will remain against an enemy surrounding you on every side.”

Such words calmed his fury. After peace had been made, he addressed our princes, asking that those who had come there against him should go with him to Miseco and assist him with Miseco in recovering his possessions.

Our men promised to do so, and the archbishop Gisilerus departed with him, together with the counts Ekkihardus, Esico, and Binizo; all the others returned home in peace.

As evening approached, their weapons were taken from all these men and then returned as soon as an oath had secured their safety. Bolizlavus came with our men to the Oder. A messenger was sent to Miseco to tell him that Bolizlavus held his auxiliaries in his power.

“If you return to me the kingdom that was taken from me,” he said, “I will let these men depart unharmed; otherwise I will destroy them all.”

[Col. 1249B] Miseco replied:

“If the king wished to recover his men safely or avenge those who had been lost, he should do so; but if this did not happen, he would not be willing to lose anything whatsoever because of them.”

When Bolizlavus heard this, he allowed all our men to remain safe, but plundered and burned whatever he could from the surrounding places.

[Folio 56] Returning from there, he seized a city whose name is missing in the manuscript: a space of about six letters is left. The name appears to have been Nimptsch, a city of Silesia in the principality of Brieg, as is apparent from Cosmas of Prague. He acquired the city, together with its lord, while the townspeople offered no resistance, and handed the lord over to the Liuticians to be beheaded.

Without delay, with “the gods favoring him”—the phrase *diis fautoribus* is erased in manuscript 1, though A. S. still read it—this victim was offered before the city, and everyone discussed the return.

Bolizlavus knew that our men could not reach home safely from Liutician territory without him. Therefore, on the following day, at dawn, he dismissed them, and they hastened on as they had been advised.

When the aforesaid enemies learned this, they immediately tried to follow them with a very large multitude of chosen men. Bolizlavus scarcely restrained them with these words :

“You who came here to my aid, see that you complete the good undertaking which you began. Know for certain that I will not allow any harm to come today, while I live, to those whom I have received into my protection and dismissed in good peace.

“It is neither honourable nor wise for us, who have until now been close friends, to become open enemies. I know that there is great enmity among you; opportunities much better than this will come for you to avenge it.”

Calmed by these words, the Liuticians were detained there by him for two days; then, greeting one another and renewing their ancient treaty, they departed.

Then those faithless men chose two hundred soldiers to pursue our men, since our men were few. This was promptly reported to our men by one of Count Hodo’s retainers.

They hastened forward at that very hour and, thanks be to God, reached Magadaburg unharmed, while the enemies laboured in vain to overtake them.

## 10

[Folio 56′; col. 1250A]

When the empress first heard this, she rejoiced in their success. But since little of her excellent conduct has come to my knowledge, I have briefly described above her immense nobility.

She inhabits the western regions, which are rightly called by this name because there the sun and every equity, together with obedience and mutual charity, turn toward the setting.

Night is nothing other than the shadow of the earth, and all that these native inhabitants do is nothing but sin.

Here the holy preachers labour in vain; here kings and other princes possess little power. Plunderers and persecutors of the just hold dominion.

Many bodies of saints rest in these regions, but as I see it, the saints despise these transgressing inhabitants. Yet lest anyone think me a disciple of bleary-eyed Crispinus (Horace, Satires I, 1, 120), I remain silent about these matters, because, on account of unlawful unions and other unspeakable deceits, I do not doubt that they are near destruction.

They have despised countless excommunications of bishops, and for this reason they will not be able to stand for long.

Pray this one thing together with me, I ask you, faithful followers of Christ: that these people may be changed for the better, and that such a custom may never come to us.

Now, as I am about to speak of the end of the aforesaid empress, I shall relate the signs that preceded it.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 989, the sun was eclipsed on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, at the fifth hour of the day.

But I urge all worshippers of Christ to believe truly that this did not occur through any incantation by evil women or through the sun’s being devoured, nor can it be remedied in any way by worldly means; rather, it occurs as Macrobius testifies and the other wise men assert, and they should be persuaded that the same is true of the moon.

[Folio 57] In the following year, after completing the course of her life in good works, the empress fell ill at Niumagun. She departed this life on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July and was buried by Ewergerus, archbishop of the holy church of Cologne, in the monastery of Saint Pantaleon.

Archbishop Brun, who rests there, had supplied funds and ordered the monastery to be built. Her son was present and gave many gifts to these brethren for the salvation of his mother’s soul.

When the distinguished empress Ethelheidis learned this, she immediately became sad. She then consoled the king, who had been reigning for seven years, by visiting him, and kept him with her in place of his mother until, corrupted by the counsel of reckless young men, he dismissed her in sorrow.

## 11

[Col. 1251A]

To this woman, well-born and adorned with virtues (compare Horace, *Odes* 4.4.36), my father, Count Sigifridus, faithfully rendered service at home and in war. During the expedition to Brandanburg, in which he served for the last time, he fell from his horse and began to suffer severe bodily pain.

He also perceived that his eighth year was approaching, as this had been foretold to him in a dream. While sleeping in Cologne, he was awakened again by these words:

“Sigifride, keep watch, and know for certain that from this day, after the course of eight years, you will end your present life.”

He always foresaw this appointed day with a vigilant mind and did not cease to anticipate it through whatever fruits of virtue he could produce.

As for me, my father took me—then still well trained in letters—from Quidilingeburg, where I was with his maternal aunt Emnilda, who had long suffered from paralysis, and entrusted me to Ricdagus, the second abbot of Saint John at Magadaburg.

I lived there for three years. On All Saints’ Day, since he could not offer me to that altar, my father secured my admission to the brotherhood at Saint Maurice [folio 57′]. On the following feast of Saint Andrew, a great and highly acceptable banquet was held for everyone for two days.

After leaving there, with Lent approaching, my father fell ill in the city called Wallibizi. On the Ides of March, that defender of his homeland and true man paid the debt owed to each nature.

His mother, Mahtildis, venerable in every virtue and soon to follow him in death herself, mourned him together with his wife Cunigunda. Deprived of such great comfort, she awaited her final day with immense sorrow and, in that same year, on the third day before the Nones of December, faithfully departed to Christ.

In the year 996 of the Lord’s Incarnation, my paternal uncle, named Liutharius, to whom this inheritance had fallen equally with us, inflicted many injuries upon my mother, renewing her ancient grief (compare Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.3). Although his own mother had firmly entrusted her to his care, he nevertheless attempted to deprive her of all the possessions of that inheritance. [Translator’s note: *haec*, “her,” could instead refer to “this inheritance”; the mother who entrusted it or her is Liutharius’s own mother.]

Why delay with many words? With the emperor’s assistance, everything was restored to her.

## 12

Meanwhile Atheldagus, archbishop of Bremen, died in the year 988, and Liaevizo succeeded him. Liaevizo had followed the exiled Pope Benedictus here from his own homeland on the borders of the Alps and the Swabians; by his service to God and the king he earned advancement to this honor.

The Slavs, attacked again, were subjected to the king. Fortresses were rebuilt along the Elbe, and in winter an overflowing river and a violent wind caused great damage.

An excessively hot summer harmed the crops greatly, and a severe mortality harmed human beings greatly.

[Folio 58′] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 991, Hilliwardus, the venerable bishop of the holy church of Halberstadt, who baptized and confirmed me, dedicated the temple of the Lord on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November. He had built it from its foundations and now completed it down to the last detail.

Present there were the king with Empress Ethelgida, who was also his grandmother; Abbess Mahtildis; and these archbishops [col. 1252B]: Willigisus, Gisilerus, and Liewizo, with sixteen of their brethren.

The festival was also the feast of Saint Gallus, confessor of Christ, in whose monastery the aforesaid bishop had been educated. For this reason he had always striven to fulfil his desire on this solemnity; it was then the twenty-fourth year of his ordination.

His faithful chaplain Hildo assisted him in everything and arranged all matters with great prudence. All the leading men of Saxony who assembled there were received with affection.

As trustworthy men affirm, never before or afterward was everything—both in divine praises and in secular affairs—carried out so completely and so acceptably to everyone.

In the following year, 993, at the first cockcrow, a light like day shone from the north. It remained for one hour, while the sky reddened on every side, and then vanished.

There were some who said that in the same year they had seen three suns and three moons and that the stars had fought with one another.

After this, in the year 994, Ekbertus, archbishop of Trier, died, and Liutdulfus succeeded him. Dodo of Minden also died, after whom Suitgerus was ordained. Erp of Verden likewise died, and Bernharius, then provost there, was appointed in his place.

A severe famine also oppressed our regions.

[Col. 1252C] In the third year after the aforesaid dedication, in the year 995, my maternal uncles were captured by pirates, as will be clear in what follows.

In the fourth year, pestilence, famine, and war descended upon the eastern peoples, and the king attacked the Apodriti and devastated the Wilzi.

## 13

[Col. 1253A]

After this the king held an assembly at Magadaburg with his princes. Heinricus, the distinguished duke of the Bavarians, came to it.

Since there had long been a dispute between him and Gebehardus of Regensburg, it was ended there by good counsel.

That pious duke, who had cleansed all his sins through continual almsgiving, then went to Gondesem, where his sister Lady Gerberg was abbess. He was suddenly overcome by illness.

He then summoned his namesake son and instructed him as follows:

“Go quickly to your homeland, arrange the kingdom, and never resist your king and lord. I greatly regret ever having done so. Remember your father, for you will never see him again in this world.”

As soon as his son had departed, the illustrious duke, continually crying “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”) from his heart during his illness, departed to Christ on the fifth day before the Kalends of September. [Col. 1253B] He was buried there in the middle of the church, before the altar of the holy cross.

When his son learned this, he obtained his father’s possessions from the king through the election and assistance of the Bavarians, as well as the duchy.

In the same year Count Thiedricus, the palatine, and his brother Sibertus departed from this world.

## Textual notes

[Note: 1. Col. 1243; at *egressus Heinricus, proximum (f. 51') pascha Quidilingeburg*. 1a spells Quidilingeburg *quidelingaeburg*.]

[Note: 2. Col. 1243D; at *presumentes, paululum evaserunt, et ad civitatem Hesleburg*. Asselburg, a now ruined castle near Burgdorf in the Saldern jurisdiction.]

[Note: 3. Col. 1243; at *adversus ducem jam palam conspirantes conveniebant, festinavere*. 1b adds *festinavere*, “they hastened.”]

[Note: 4. Col. 1243D; at *cum Bernhardo duce et Thiedrico marchione, Ekkihardus*. Count of Thuringia, son of Gunterius.]

[Note: 5. Col. 1243D; at *duce et Thiedrico marchione, Ekkihardus , Bijo*. Counts of Merseburg.]

[Note: 6. Col. 1243D; at *Thiedrico marchione, Ekkihardus , Bijo , Esic*. Counts of Merseburg; the same identification is repeated for Esic.]

[Note: 7. Col. 1243D; at *, Esic , Bernwardus, comes, et clericus*. Apparently later the king’s teacher and bishop of Hildesheim.]

[Note: 8. Col. 1243D; at *comes, et clericus , Sifrith ejusque filius*. Sifrith, count of Nordheim, and his son of the same name. Compare Schrader, *Die älteren Dynastenstämme zwischen Leine, Weser und Diemel* (“The Older Dynastic Houses between the Leine, Weser, and Diemel”); this passage, however, escaped him.]

[Note: 9. Col. 1243D; at *clericus , Sifrith ejusque filius , Frithericus*. Count of Eilenburg.]

[Note: 10. Col. 1243D; at *ejusque filius , Frithericus , et Ciazo*. Also called Ziazo and Zazzo. See below, chapter 28.]

[Note: 11. Col. 1243D; at *confratres. Conprovincialium autem Thiedricus et Siber confratres*. See note 419 to the preceding chapter.]

[Note: 12. Col. 1243D; at *autem Thiedricus et Siber confratres , Hoico*. See below, chapter 6.]

[Note: 13. Col. 1243D; at *et sui, militesque sancti Martini jussu archipraesulis*. The archbishop of Mainz.]

[Note: 14. Col. 1243D; at *perturbandam hanc conjurationem seu pacificandam ad Werlu*. The royal palace Werla near Burgdorf in the Hildesheim territory, with the Schaladen prefecture there, near Goslar. See C. U. Grupen, *Observations on German and Roman Affairs and Antiquities*, pp. 1–30, and F. D. Haeberlin, *Dissertation on the Site of Werla*, Helmstedt, 1786. The note continues into col. 1244D.]

[Note: 15. Col. 1244D; at *vix pacem mutuam in loco, qui Seusun*. Seesen, between Goslar and Gandersheim; called *Sehuson in Ambergo* in a charter of Emperor Otto II issued at Gruhonaha on 11 June 974, but *Seusi* in 1007. Compare Wedekind, *Notes*, I, p. 40.]

[Note: 16. Col. 1243; at *Bawariam continuo proficiscens, cum venire aut noluissed*. 1 corrects *noluisset*, “had been unwilling,” to the printed spelling *noluissed*.]

[Note: 17. Col. 1244D; at *ducem qui tunc Bawariis atque Carentis prefuit*. See above, book III, chapter 12.]

[Note: 18. Col. 1244D; at *hostilis immanitas urbem comitis Ekberti, quae Ala*. This seems to have been Ala, Oelsburch, beside the Fusa River in the Brunswick prefecture of Lichtenberg or the Saldern jurisdiction. Compare Wedekind, book I.]

[Note: 19. Col. 1244D; at *sociis adiit, et in pascuis ad Bisinstidi*. Bisenstatt near Worms, not far from the Rhine, formerly a royal estate. Compare the *Annals of Fulda*, I, p. 382.]

[Note: 20. Col. 1244D; at *tunc provisor aeclesiae Willigisus cum duce Conrado*. Conrad, duke of Franconia and Swabia.]

[Note: 21. Col. 1244D; at *Kalendas Julii ad locum qui Rara vocatur*. Gross-Rohrheim in the Hesse-Darmstadt prefecture of Zwingenberg.]

[Note: 22. Col. 1243; at *atque tristicia. 4. Post haec Heinricus Bolizlavum*. 1 has *bozlauum* for *Bolizlavum*, the name Bolizlavus in the accusative.]

[Note: 23. Col. 1244D; at *exercitu ejusdem a finibus suis per Niseni*. A district between the Elbe and Mulde, near Dresden and Freiberg.]

[Note: 24. Col. 1244D; at *Niseni et Deleminci pagos usque ad Mogelini*. Mugeln beside the Delnitz River, near Oschatz.]

[Note: 25. Col. 1245D; at *et satellitem, ad aecclesiam extra urbem positam*. The church of Saint Nicholas in the new market of the suburb of Misni, beside the Trubische River.]

[Note: 26. Col. 1245D; at *eum clauditur, et Ricdagus, ejusdem civitatis custos*. That is, the burgrave of Misni; perhaps the man whom the Luneburg Necrology records as killed on 11 October.]

[Note: 27. Col. 1245; at *et habitatorem succepit. 5. A quo Wolcoldus*. 1c (?) spells Wolcoldus *uolcoldus*.]

[Note: 28. Col. 1245; at *antistes vulgi instinctu varii expellitur, et ad*. 1b adds *et ad*, “and to.”]

[Note: 29. Col. 1245; at *Willigisum archiantistitem veniens, benigne ab eodem succipitur*. 1c has the beginning *susc.* in the verb *succipitur*, “is received,” indicating the spelling *suscipitur*.]

[Note: 30. Col. 1245; at *cum ad eoas ordinaretur regiones, secundo Ottoni*. 1a has *ottone* instead of *Ottoni*, the name Otto with a different case ending: ablative rather than the dative “to Otto.”]

[Note: 31. Col. 1245; at *cum sibi fuit necesse; et in Erpesfordi*. 1c has the place-name *erfordia* for *Erpesfordi*, Erfurt.]

[Note: 32. Col. 1245; at *in Erpesfordi , quo ipse desideravit, procurari*. 1a has *procurrari* for *procurari*, “to be provided for.”]

[Note: 33. Col. 1245D; at *diu conversatus, post mortem Ricdagi marchionis incliti*. Ricdargus, margrave of Misni, died in 985. See the Quedlinburg Annals and the Fulda Necrology.]

[Note: 34. Col. 1245; at *Bolizlavi amiciciam firmiter acquirens, cum in Pragu*. 1b or 1c has *praga* for *Pragu*, Prague.]

[Note: 35. Col. 1245; at *est parasceve, (f. 53) cum memoriam divinae*. 2 and A. S. have *dominicae*, “of the Lord,” instead of *divinae*, “divine,” qualifying the Passion.]

[Note: 36. Col. 1245; at *parasceve, (f. 53) cum memoriam divinae passionis*. 1b adds *passionis*, “of the Passion.”]

[Note: 37. Col. 1245; at *vitae, quamvis ad tempus evalesceret, permansit. Sedebat*. 1c has *Sedebat*, “he held the see”; 1a has the defective form *Sebat*.]

[Note: 38. Col. 1245D; at *permansit. Sedebat 23 annos, 10 Kal. Septembris*. The Merseburg and Luneburg Necrologies also give this day of death.]

[Note: 39. Col. 1245; at *Kal. Septembris ex hujus carnis ergastulo eductus*. 1b adds *eductus*, “led out,” in the release from the prison of the flesh.]

[Note: 40. Col. 1245; at *ergastulo eductus . In hujus vice Eid*. 1a writes the name Eid as *id*.]

[Note: 41. Col. 1245; at *ordinatur ortatu Gisileri archipresulis, de cujus inclita*. *inclita*, “distinguished,” describing his conduct, is erased in 1.]

[Note: 42. Col. 1245; at *persistens. 6. Interim fautores regis Willehelmum comitem*. A. S. adds *de Thuringia*, “of Thuringia.”]

[Note: 43. Col. 1245; at *comitem , duci nimis familiarem, in Wimeri*. 1c and A. S. spell Wimeri *uuimari*.]

[Note: 44. Col. 1245D; at *festinant, ac juxta villam quae Iteri dicitur*. The castle of Ittern on the borders of Saxony and Franconia.]

[Note: 45. Col. 1246D; at *nilque de rebus suis preter Merseburg, Walbizi*. Walbeck in the county of Mansfeld.]

[Note: 46. Col. 1246D; at *rebus suis preter Merseburg, Walbizi et Frasu*. Frosa, a town on the bank of the Elbe beyond Magdeburg.]

[Note: 47. Col. 1245; at *abire liceret; sin autem, quod eundi redeundique*. 1 has *reundique* for *redeundique*, “and returning.”]

[Note: 48. Col. 1246D; at *impetrant, eumque ad Merseburg, ubi ductrix Gisla*. Wife of Heinricus, duke of Bavaria, and daughter of Conrad, king of Burgundy, who was the brother of Empress Adelheidis. URS.]

[Note: 49. Col. 1245; at *ob Dei timorem patriaeque salutem a proposito*. 1c has *proposito*, “undertaking”; 1a has the abbreviated or defective *pposito*.]

[Note: 50. Col. 1246D; at *rectoris media die cernentibus universis clara refulsit*. The sentence from *Stella* to *refulsit*, “The star of the ruler predestined by God shone brightly at midday for all to see,” comes from the Quedlinburg Annals, 984.]

[Note: 51. Col. 1245; at *convenitque in unum dissona turba dominium. Rex*. 1a reads *ab :::: suimet ex matre*: “by [gap] his own … from the mother.” The supplied reading is fragmentary; it does not say “by his mother alone.”]

[Note: 52. Col. 1245; at *malo discesserunt, sicque multum temporis stetit intervallum*. 1a has *interuuallum*, the spelling of *intervallum*, “interval.”]

[Note: 53. Col. 1245; at *qui minor dicebatur, magna sedicio quae Herimanni*. The *i* in *Herimanni*, “of Herimannus,” is erased in 1.]

[Note: 54. Col. 1245; at *consilio postmodum finita, regis gratiam in Francanafordi*. 1c (?) reads *francinfordi* for *Francanafordi*, Frankfurt.]

[Note: 55. Col. 1246D; at *gratiam in Francanafordi et ducatum dedicius promeruit*. That is, he received the duchy of Bavaria.]

[Note: 56. Col. 1245; at *54) in Quidelingeburg a rege, ubi quattuor*. The first *t* in *quattuor*, “four,” is erased; no witness is specified.]

[Note: 57. Col. 1247D; at *presentavit, et duas expediciones cum eo fecit*. The same source, the Quedlinburg Annals, for 985 and 986. The printed *Indid.* appears to be a defective “ibid.”]

[Note: 58. Col. 1247D; at *ejus antistes Hillinessemensis Adwinus Kalendis Decembris obiit*. So also the Merseburg Necrology, concerning Bishop Otwinus.]

[Note: 59. Col. 1247D; at *Quo sedente quinque annos et tunc expirante*. Quedlinburg Annals, 989; Hildesheim Annals, 990. He died on the sixth day before the Ides of November, according to the Merseburg Calendar.]

[Note: 60. Col. 1247; at *et tunc expirante , Gerdagus tunc cellerarius*. 1c reads *cellerarius*, “cellarer”; 1a has *cellenarius*.]

[Note: 61. Col. 1247D; at *orationis petens reverteretur, 7 Idus Decembris obiit*. Quedlinburg Annals, 992; Hildesheim Annals, the same year; Merseburg Calendar, seventh day before the Ides of December.]

[Note: 62. Col. 1247; at *archipresul, casu ibidem adveniens, terre commendavit. Tunc*. 1b adds the whole sentence *Tunc … consecratur*: “Then Bernwardus, the king’s teacher, was elected and consecrated.”]

[Note: 63. Col. 1247; at *casu ibidem adveniens, terre commendavit. Tunc Bernwardus*. The *n* in *Bernwardus* is erased in 1.]

[Note: 64. Col. 1247D; at *Bernwardus , magister regis, facta eleccione consecratur*. See the Hildesheim Annals, 993. Compare his *Life*, written by the priest Tangmarus, chapter 2. The note continues into col. 1248D.]

[Note: 65. Col. 1248D; at *bellorum asperitatibus Sclavos lacessere rex non desistit*. See the Quedlinburg Annals for 986, 987, and 990.]

[Note: 66. Col. 1248D; at *damna in pestilenciis subsequutura (f. 54') indixit*. Quedlinburg Annals, 989.]

[Note: 67. Col. 1247; at *factus vir, ut ait Apostolus, evacuavit quae*. 1 writes *qae* for *quae*, “the things which.”]

[Note: 68. Col. 1247; at *quomodo haec renovaretur, sedula mentis intentione volvebat*. 1a writes *uuoluebat* for *volvebat*, “he pondered.”]

[Note: 69. Col. 1247; at *corpore vixit, hoc votum perficere studuit monitis*. 1c has *monitis*, “exhortations”; 1a has *monotis*.]

[Note: 70. Col. 1247; at *piae matris. Quae talia, ut mihi Meinsvith*. 1a gives the name Meinsvith as *meinsuth*.]

[Note: 71. Col. 1247; at *Laurencius, dextero mutilatus brachio: Cur, inquiens, quis*. 1c has *quis*, “who”; 1a has *quid*, “what.”]

[Note: 72. Col. 1248D; at *me modo ipsa consideras, tuus effecit senior*. That is, Emperor Otto II.]

[Note: 73. Col. 1248D; at *tuus effecit senior ejus persuasu seductus, cujus*. That is, Gisilerus.]

[Note: 93. Col. 1249; at *restituendis suimet rebus se apud Miseconem adjuvare*. 1 has the defective *auuuare* for *adjuvare*, “to assist.”]

[Note: 97. Col. 1249; at *talibus respondit: Si voluisset rex suos acquirere*. 1c reads *acquireret*, “he might recover,” for *acquirere*, “to recover.”]

[Note: 98. Col. 1249; at *voluisset rex suos acquirere salvos aut ulcisci*. 1a has *ulcissi* for *ulcisci*, “to avenge.”]

[Note: 100. Col. 1249D; at *Inde reversus urbem unam . . .*. The missing name seems to be Nimptsch, a town in Silesia in the principality of Brieg, as appears from Cosmas of Prague. URS.]

[Note: 101. Col. 1249; at *ad decollandum dedit. Nec mora, diis fautoribus*. *diis fautoribus*, “with the gods favoring,” is erased in 1, but A. S. still read it.]

[Note: 107. Col. 1249; at *eligerunt. Quod nostris mox a quodam Hodonis*. 1c has *hovdonis* for *Hodonis*, “of Hodo.”]

[Note: 108. Col. 1249; at *optima ejus conversacione parum mihi ad noticiam*. 1c has *noticiam*, “knowledge”; 1 has the defective *nociam*.]

[Note: 109. Col. 1249; at *et o nis equitas cum obedientia et*. 1b adds *obedientia et*, “obedience and,” abbreviated *o. et*.]

[Note: 110. Col. 1249; at *Nox nil aliud est, nisi umbra terrae*. 2 reads “earth, by which the sins of the faithless are understood,” expanding *terrae*, “of the earth.”]

[Note: 111. Col. 1249; at *in melius, et ad nos numquam veniat*. 1a has *ueniant*, plural “may they come,” for *veniat*, singular “may it come.”]

[Note: 112. Col. 1249D; at *precesserint signa narrabo. Anno Dominicae Incarnationis 989*. Quedlinburg Annals, but under 990, which is more correct.]

[Note: 113. Col. 1249; at *12. Kalend. Novembris et 5. diei hora*. 1b adds *et V diei hora*, “and at the fifth hour of the day.”]

[Note: 114. Col. 1250D; at *non aliqua malarum incantatione mulierum vel esu*. Compare J. Grimm, *German Mythology*, p. 401.]

[Note: 115. Col. 1250D; at *modo seculariter adjuvari posse; sed sicut Macrobius*. Macrobius, *On the Dream of Scipio*.]

[Note: 116. Col. 1250D; at *sapientes fieri asserunt, et id de luna*. That is, they should be convinced that it happens in this way also to the moon.]

[Note: 117. Col. 1249; at *luna . (f. 57) Et sequenti anno*. In 1, *Et sequenti anno*, “And in the following year,” is written over an erasure; 1c has *In sequenti anno*, “In the following year.”]

[Note: 118. Col. 1249; at *in bonis vitae suimet cursu, in Niumagun*. 1c adds *teophanv*, the name Theophanu.]

[Note: 119. Col. 1249; at *vitae suimet cursu, in Niumagun infirmatur imperatrix*. 1b adds *imperatrix*, “the empress.”]

[Note: 120. Col. 1249; at *Kal. Julii discedens, sepulta est ab Ewergero*. 1c (?) spells *Ewergero*, “by Ewergerus,” as *euegero*.]

[Note: 121. Col. 1250D; at *Coloniensis aecclesiae archiepiscopo, in monasterio sancti Pantaleonis*. Quedlinburg Annals, 991.]

[Note: 122. Col. 1249; at *remedio matris his confratribus largiente. Quod cum*. 1b adds *cum*, “when.”]

[Note: 123. Col. 1249; at *effecta, regem tunc septem annos regi antem*. 1b adds *tunc septem annos regnantem*, “then reigning for seven years.”]

[Note: 124. Col. 1251C; at *fructibus valuit, preoccupare non desistit. Me autem*. Compare the preface, p. 724.]

[Note: 125. Col. 1249; at *adhuc instructum, sumpsit et Ricdago abbati secundo*. 1b adds *secundo*, “second,” referring to the abbot.]

[Note: 126. Col. 1251; at *migravit ad Christum. 996 Dominicae Incarnacionis anno*. 1b adds the entire date phrase, “in the year 996 of the Lord’s Incarnation.”]

[Note: 127. Col. 1249; at *multa intulit mala. et quamvis haec firme*. 1b adds *firme*, “firmly.”]

[Note: 128. Col. 1251; at *mala. et quamvis haec firme suimet fidei*. 1c reads *fidei*, “to the care” or “faith”; its *e* is corrected.]

[Note: 129. Col. 1251; at *contendit. Quid multis moror? Inperatoris auxilio cuncta*. 1 has the defective *cuu ta* for *cuncta*, “everything.”]

[Note: 130. Col. 1251; at *multis moror? Inperatoris auxilio cuncta ei restituuntur*. 1c reads *restituuntur*, “are restored”; 1a has *resistuntur*, formally “are resisted.”]

[Note: 131. Col. 1251; at *auxilio cuncta ei restituuntur . 12. Interea*. In 1, the passage from *Interea* to *Alpium* is written over an erasure: Atheldagus’s death, Liaevizo’s succession, and his following the exiled Benedict from his homeland as far as the words “the Alps.”]

[Note: 132. Col. 1251D; at *. 12. Interea Atheldagus, archiepiscopus Bremensis, obiit*. He died in 988.]

[Note: 133. Col. 1251D; at *aqua inundans et ventus ingens multum nocuit*. From the Quedlinburg Annals, 987.]

[Note: 134. Col. 1251D; at *frugibus, et seva mortalitas hominibus nimis nocuit*. The same source, 988.]

[Note: 135. Col. 1251; at *. Anno Dominicae (f. 58') Incarnationis 991*. After an *I*, some letter may have been erased. The editor thinks it was another *I*, making the year 992, the number in the Quedlinburg Annals.]

[Note: 136. Col. 1251; at *Halverstidensis aecclesiae venerabilis antistes, qui me baptizavit*. 1 has *bapzavit* for *baptizavit*, “he baptized.”]

[Note: 137. Col. 1251D; at *unguem usque perduxit, 12 Kalendas Novembris dedicavit*. Thietmar incorrectly wrote the twelfth instead of the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, perhaps because he failed to notice that the Quedlinburg Annals under 992, from which he took this account of the Halberstadt dedication, separately relate quite different matters about a phenomenon seen on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November.]

[Note: 138. Col. 1251D; at *Gisilerus et Liewizo, cum suis confratribus 16*. For their names see the Quedlinburg Annals and the *Halberstadt Chronicle*, 992. The note continues into col. 1252D.]

[Note: 139. Col. 1251; at *hic tunc convenientes caritative succipiuntur. Numquam fuit*. 1c has *fuerunt*, plural “were,” for *fuit*, singular “was.”]

[Note: 140. Col. 1252D; at *manens horam, undique celo interim rubente, evanuit*. From the Quedlinburg Annals, 993.]

[Note: 141. Col. 1251; at *Fuere nonnulli qui dicerent eodem anno vidisse*. 1a has *se*, “themselves”; 1b adds *vidis*. Perhaps the intended reading was *vidisse se*, “that they had seen.”]

[Note: 142. Col. 1252D; at *Ekbertus Treverensis archiepiscopus, cujus successor Liutdulfus fuit*. The same source, 993 and 994.]

[Note: 143. Col. 1252D; at *Dodo Mirmigendensis, post quem Suitgerus ordinatus est*. The same source, 990.]

[Note: 144. Col. 1252D; at *Bernharius (f. 58') tunc ibi prepositus subponitur*. The same source, 994.]

[Note: 145. Col. 1251; at *, obiere. Fames quoque valida nostras oppressit*. 1 reads *oppressit*, “oppressed,” as in the printed text.]

[Note: 146. Col. 1252D; at *obiere. Fames quoque valida nostras oppressit regiones*. The same source.]

[Note: 147. Col. 1251; at *valida nostras oppressit regiones . In tercio*. 1 has *tertia*, feminine “third,” for *tercio*, masculine “third,” qualifying “year.”]

[Note: 148. Col. 1252D; at *anno avuncuti mei a piratis capti sunt*. The same source.]

[Note: 149. Col. 1251; at *ut in sequentibus patet. In quarto pestilencia*. 1 writes *pestilecia* for *pestilencia*, “pestilence.”]

[Note: 150. Col. 1252D; at *et rex Apodritos petit et Wiltios vastavit*. The same source, 995. The king’s charters show that he was on this expedition in September and October.]

[Note: 151. Col. 1253; at *inclitus, venit. Et cum inter hunc et*. 1b adds *et*, “and.”]

[Note: 152. Col. 1253; at *venit. Et cum inter hunc et Ratisbonensem*. 1a reads *ratisbonensem*, “of Regensburg,” as in the printed text.]

[Note: 153. Col. 1253; at *continuis mundavit elemosinis, inde pergens ad Gondesem*. 1c gives the place-name Gondesem as *Gandesem*.]

[Note: 154. Col. 1253D; at *continuis mundavit elemosinis, inde pergens ad Gondesem*. Gandersheim.]

[Note: 155. Col. 1253; at *, ubi domna Gerberg soror suimet erat*. 1a has *fuerat*, “had been,” for *erat*, “was.”]

[Note: 156. Col. 1253; at *regi ac domino resistas tuo. Multum enim*. 1b adds *enim*, “for.”]

[Note: 157. Col. 1253; at *in medio aecclesiae coram sanctae crucis altari*. 1a has *altare* for *altari*, “altar,” with a different case ending after *coram*, “before.”]

[Note: 158. Col. 1253D; at *comperiret, electione et auxilio Bawariorum patris bona*. And also the duchy; see the Quedlinburg Annals.]

[Note: 159. Col. 1253D; at *Sibertus frater ejus, de hoc seculo transierunt*. From the Quedlinburg Annals, 995. Compare the Merseburg Calendar, 14 October.]

### 14

At that time my nephew, Margrave Henry [Note: [Col. 1253D] He was not the nephew of our Thietmar, but his cousin, namely the son of his father’s sister. See above.], seized Ewerker [Note: [Col. 1253] *Euerkerum* in 1 c.?], (f. 59) an outstanding knight of Bernward, bishop of the church of Würzburg [Note: [Col. 1253] The *n* has been erased in 1.], but excessively proud, and blinded him at a place called Lindinlog [Note: [Col. 1253D] Lindloch in the district of Altötting, or Lindenlohe in the district of Burglengenfeld, seem to us much too far away.], on account of injuries inflicted upon him. When the king learned of this through messengers sent by the bishop to complain about it at length, and took the matter very seriously, he banished the aforesaid count into exile. Afterwards he restored his favor to him and reconciled him with the bishop by a worthy compensation.

After this, the aforesaid prelate summoned Margrave Liutpold of the Eastern March and his nephew Henry to himself for the Mass of Saint Kilian, which is celebrated on 8 July (994). He received them with great affection. During the sacred night, after Matins, the count was playing with his knights, when an arrow shot through an opening by a friend of the blinded man [Note: [Col. 1253] Added in 1 b.] wounded him. After making his confession, he died on 6 July [Note: [Col. 1253D] The Merseburg Calendar has “Liudbold, margrave” on 6 July; compare 8 July and 11 July. The Quedlinburg Annals place it on 1 June in the year 994.], innocent both in the deed described above and in the counsel behind it. He was buried there the following day [Note: [Col. 1253] Thus in A. S. for the year 994: *vallonte* in 1 a., *vallante* in 1 c.], and deservedly mourned, since he left behind no one wiser than himself or better in all his deeds [Note: [Col. 1253] “No one remained”: added in 1 b.].

The winter that had preceded was full of severity, pestilence, excessive cold [Note: [Col. 1253] *-que* added in 1 b.], wind, and unusual dryness [Col. 1254A] [Note: [Col. 1254D] Quedlinburg Annals, year 994.]. During it the Slavs were defeated [Note: [Col. 1254D] Compare the Hildesheim and Quedlinburg Annals, year 994.].

### 15

But since above I mentioned the destruction of the Brandenburg church, I shall now briefly explain how it was temporarily subjected to the aforesaid king [Note: [Col. 1253] Added in 1 b.].

There was in our neighborhood a certain distinguished knight named Kiza [Note: [Col. 1254D] Kizo, in whose county lay the district of Helmingowe, is praised in a charter of Emperor Otto II, 30 July 977 (in Höfer, *loc. cit.*, I, 155).]. Margrave Thiedricus treated him in a manner displeasing to him. For this reason, and because his resources were in no way sufficient for his impiety [Note: [Col. 1253] “In no way remained”: added in 1 b.], he went over to our enemies [Note: [Col. 1253] Thus 1 c.; *super* is written over an erasure.]. Recognizing that he was exceedingly loyal to them in all things, they entrusted the aforementioned city to him as a means of harming us [Note: [Col. 1254D] Compare the Hildesheim Annals, year 991.]. Later, softened by the flatteries of our people, he surrendered it, together with himself, to royal authority [Note: [Col. 1254D] Compare the same source, year 993.].

Therefore the Liutici [Note: [Col. 1253] *Liustici* in 1.] were inflamed with tremendous fury and immediately attacked him [Note: [Col. 1253] Added in 1 b.] with all the bands they possessed [Col. 1254B] (991–993). Meanwhile the king was at Magdeburg. When this became known, he quickly sent there the men he then had with him: Margrave Ekkihard [Note: [Col. 1254D] Of Meissen.], my three maternal uncles [Note: [Col. 1253] Henry, Udo, and Siegfried, counts of Stade.] together with Count Palatine Fritheric and my paternal uncle [Note: [Col. 1253] “And my paternal uncle” added in 1 b.] [Note: [Col. 1254D] Lothar, margrave of the North.].

All of these men came there with their forces, but were broken by the enemies, who made a fierce incursion against them [Note: [Col. 1253] *Irrumpentibus* in 1.]. One part of our men entered the city; the other, which remained outside, returned after several soldiers had been slain. Then the king, having gathered allies from every direction, hurried there. When our enemies, inflicting great violence upon the city’s defenders, saw the last army approaching, they quickly [Note: [Col. 1253] Added in 1 b.] removed their camp and fled [Note: [Col. 1253] The *i* has been erased in 1.].

Our men, rejoicing within at their rescue, sang *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy”—and those arriving responded with one accord. After securing the city with a garrison, the king departed and retained it under his authority for a long time.

After this, when Kizo came to Quedlinburg, he lost his own city, his wife, and his retainers. He later recovered all of these except the city [Note: [Col. 1253] Added in 1 b.]. One of his knights, however, named Bolibut [Note: [Col. 1253] *Boliuut* in 1 a.; *Boliwit* in A. S. under the year 992.], whose counsel had directed the whole affair, although he was then absent, ruled there. When Kizo later wished to cause harm secretly in these regions, the excellent knight was killed together with his men [Note: [Col. 1253] In the margin, after the gathering of four leaves was completed, there is added: “He was killed.” Below, in 1 c., it is written: “Here follows: And as I said, my three uncles”; and at the beginning of fol. 60, in an erased place, are the words “and as I said.”].

### 16

(f. 60) And, as I said above [Note: [Col. 1254D] Above, chapter 12. Compare the Quedlinburg Annals, year 994.], my three maternal uncles, Henry, Udo, and Siegfried, together with Ethelger and many others, encountered on 9 Kalends of July (23 June 994) the pirates who were ravaging their lands in ships. After they had fought one another, Udo was beheaded [Note: [Col. 1255D] The Lüneburg and Merseburg necrologies, 23 June.].

Henry, however, together with his brother Siegfried and Count Elerger, was defeated and—miserable to relate—captured and led away by the worst of men [Note: [Col. 1255] *Dedicutur* in 1; *deducuntur* in 1 c.; *abducitur* in A. S., year 994.]. This misfortune quickly spread among Christ’s faithful, as rumor carried it abroad. Duke Bernhard, who was nearby, sent messengers as quickly as possible to promise them a ransom for their release and to request a peaceful meeting and a place for negotiations. They were ready, and concluded a firm peace [Note: [Col. 1255] “To grant a firm peace” in 2 and A. S., *loc. cit.*] for an unspeakable sum of money.

What the king first did in response to this, and then what the abundant generosity of all Christians in our regions contributed in the proper exercise of human kindness, I am unable to explain fully. My mother, deeply shaken inwardly by such grief, gave everything she possessed or could in any way acquire for the rescue of her brothers [Col. 1255B] [Note: [Col. 1255] *Attribuit* in 1 a.].

But when the accursed band of pirates had received the greater part of the money collected, of immense weight, they accepted, in place of Henry, his only son, named Siegfried, together with Gareward and Wulferem [Note: [Col. 1255] “And Wulferem” added in 1 b.]; and, in place of Ethelger, his maternal uncle Thiedricus and his aunt’s son Olef. They allowed these men to depart, while Siegfried alone remained, so that what still remained of the treasure promised to them might be collected more quickly [Note: [Col. 1255] Thus 1 c.; *colligetur* in 1 a.].

(f. 60') Since Siegfried had no son, he asked my mother for one of her sons as a substitute. Wishing to fulfill so necessary a request, she quickly sent a messenger to Abbot Rigdag [Note: [Col. 1255D] Abbot of Saint John’s near Magdeburg.] to bring back my brother Siegfried, who was then living there in monastic habit, after obtaining permission.

He, being a very prudent man, investigated everything carefully and resisted this unjust mission [Note: [Col. 1255] Thus 1 c.; *insistit* in 1 a.; *restitit* in A. S., *loc. cit.*]. He replied that, because of the responsibility entrusted to him by God, he would not presume to do this.

The messenger, as he had been ordered, went to Ekkihard, who was then custodian of the church of Saint Maurice and master of the school, and humbly begged him to send me back to my mother on account of the urgent necessity. I came, and, still wearing the clothing I had previously worn, I set out on Thursday in the secular clothing in which I was to live as a hostage among the pirates.

On that very day Siegfried escaped, by divine assistance, from the pirates’ vigilant guard, in which he had been held after suffering many wounds. While he was in great distress, he was constantly considering with Nodbald and Edico how he might escape.
