He ordered them to bring in a swift little boat as much wine and other necessities as they could reasonably provide to those who were detaining him [Col. 1255D–1256A].

When these orders had immediately been carried out, the greedy dogs were filled with drink [Note: [Col. 1255] “Will be filled” in 1; “are filled” in A. S., *loc. cit.*]. When morning came, the priest prepared for Mass. The count, approaching the prow alone and without guards in order to wash himself, while all the others were weighed down by the previous day’s wine, leapt into the prepared stern. An outcry arose; the priest, as though he were an accomplice [Note: [Col. 1255] *Consiliator* in 1.], was seized; the anchors were raised; and the rowers rapidly pursued the fugitives.

The count barely escaped them. When he reached the safety of the shore, he found the horses prepared, as he himself had previously ordered, and hurried to his city called Hersevel [Note: [Col. 1255D] Harsefeld.], where his brother Henry and his wife Ethela, unaware of such joy, were staying.

The enemies followed behind, attacked a city near the shore called Stethu [Note: [Col. 1255D] Stade.], and searched for him carefully in its most hidden places. Not finding him, they violently tore the women’s earrings from their ears and departed sadly.

Inflamed with such fury, on the following day they cut off the noses, ears, and hands of a cleric, my nephew [Note: [Col. 1255D] Siegfried, son of Count Henry.], and all the other hostages, and threw them outside into the harbor. Then, as the fugitives escaped, each man was seized by his own people, while unheard-of grief arose.

As for me, after visiting my maternal uncles, I returned safely by Christ’s generosity and was received affectionately by my household.

### 17

At that time Liudolf, the venerable bishop of Augsburg, died on 8 Kalends of August (25 July 996), and Gevehard was ordained abbot of Ellwangen [Note: [Col. 1255] The manuscript has an erased place in 1.] [Note: [Col. 1256D] Quedlinburg Annals, compared with A. S., year 996.].

Meanwhile (995), in a certain village called Horthorp [Note: [Col. 1256D] Hordorf, on the Bode River in the territory of Halberstadt. URS.], a child was born who was half human and resembled a goose in its hind parts. It had a smaller right ear and left eye, teeth like saffron, and a left arm without four fingers, retaining only the thumb. Before baptism it looked about in astonishment, but afterwards it saw nothing, and died on the fourth day. This monster brought great pestilence upon us because of our crimes [Note: [Col. 1256D] From the Quedlinburg Annals, year 995.].

The aforesaid bishop Hilliwardus had governed the church and the flock entrusted to him for twenty-nine years with the utmost glory, a true Israelite. He died on 7 Kalends of December and was buried outside the church, within the cloister, where he had previously prepared a dwelling for himself.

When his brothers could not agree upon an election, Arnulf, from the king’s chapel, was appointed over them and ordained on the Ides of December. This occurred just as his holy predecessor had foretold to all who were present while he was still in good health:

“Honor this guest [Note: [Col. 1257] Thus 1 c.; *honerate* in 1 a.],” he said, “and serve him as much as you can. For he must provide for you after me.”

When that same holy man was already lying in the agony of his death, he saw the glory of God. Calling to himself his chaplain Wulfharius, he said: “Brother, do you see anything?” When the latter replied that he saw nothing, he heard him say that this chamber, in which he was then lying and in which his two predecessors had died, had been filled with divine majesty. Saying this, he passed from this prison into unfailing light [Note: [Col. 1257D] Compare the same source, year 996.].

### 18

The king spent the Nativity of the Lord in Cologne (996). After pacifying everything in those regions, he went to Italy, long desired, and celebrated Easter at Pavia [Note: [Col. 1257D] Quedlinburg Annals, year 996.].

Then he came gloriously to Rome and, with the praise of all who were present, installed his nephew Bruno, son of Duke Otto [Col. 1257B] [Note: [Col. 1257D] Bruno was related to the king, since his grandmother was Liutgard, daughter of Otto the Great and wife of Conrad, duke of the Franks. Her son Otto, duke of Carinthia and margrave of Verona, was Bruno’s father. See Mascov, *Commentarii de rebus imperii Romani Germanici*, p. 22. URS.], in the place of Pope John, who had recently died. On the Ascension of Christ, which then fell on 12 Kalends of June, in the fifteenth year of his age, the thirteenth of his reign, in the eighth indiction [Note: [Col. 1257D] More correctly he should have said “in the ninth indiction.”] (996), Bruno received imperial anointing from him and became advocate of the church of Saint Peter.

After this he governed that empire according to the custom of his predecessors, surpassing his age in character and diligence.

### 19

In the first part of the summer, Adalbert, bishop of the Bohemians, received at baptism the name which sounds like “Woytech” [Note: [Col. 1257] I have corrected this thus. See the life of Saint Adalbert in the *Acta Sanctorum*, 23 April: *uuortech* in 2.], and received another at confirmation from the archbishop of Parthenopolis. In that same city, he had been instructed in letters by the Othricus mentioned above [Note: [Col. 1257D] See above, Book III, chapter 8.].

Since he had been unable, through admonitions based on the divine commandment, to remove those entrusted to him from the error of their ancient depravity, he excommunicated them all and went to Rome to explain himself to the pope. With the latter’s permission, he humbly lived for a long time under the strict rule of Abbot Boniface, dwelling there as a good example.

Afterwards, with the permission of that father, he attempted to tame the minds of the Prussians [Note: [Col. 1257] “Of the few”: *paucorum* in 2, wrongly.] alienated from Christ by the bridle of holy preaching. He was pierced by a spear and, on 9 Kalends of May, received the martyrdom he had always desired by the cutting off of his head [Note: [Col. 1257] Thus A. S., year 996; *optavit* in 2, where Leibniz supplied the word.]. Alone among his companions, he received it without any groan, just as he himself had seen in a dream that night and foretold to all the brothers:

“I thought,” he said, “that I was celebrating Mass and receiving Communion alone.”

But when the authors of that wicked crime saw that he had already expired, to increase their own crime and divine vengeance they plunged the blessed man’s body into the sea, impaling his head upon a stake with insults and returning in triumph.

When Bolizlav, son of Misecon, learned of this, he immediately purchased the renowned martyr with money, together with his head and limbs [Note: [Col. 1257] “Heads” in 2.] [Note: [Col. 1257D] See the Quedlinburg Annals, year 996.].

When the emperor in Rome became certain of what had happened, he humbly offered worthy hymns to God because in his own time God had taken such a servant to himself through the palm of martyrdom.

At that time Bernward, of the holy church of Würzburg, was sent to Greece by order of the emperor and died in Achaia [Note: [Col. 1258D] See the same source.] with a very large company of his companions. Many affirm that God performed numerous miracles through him.

### 20

[Col. 1258B] As the emperor departed from Romania, he visited our regions (997). When he learned of the rebellion of the Slavs, he marched against Stoderania, which is called the land of the Hevelli [Note: [Col. 1257] *Hevellim* in 2; *Heveldun* in A. S., year 997.], with an armed force, devastating it by fire and extensive plunder. He returned victorious to Parthenopolis.

For this reason our enemies attacked Bardengau [Note: [Col. 1257] *Berdangan* in 2.] in bands, but were defeated by our men [Note: [Col. 1258D] The same source, year 997.].

Ramward, bishop of Minden, took part in that battle. Holding a cross in his hands, he went before the standard-bearers who followed him and powerfully encouraged them to undertake these deeds. On that day Count Gardulf died with a few men [Note: [Col. 1258D] 8 November. See the Merseburg necrology.], while a very large number of the enemy also perished. The rest abandoned their booty and fled.

### 21

While the aforesaid pope—who, after his blessing, was called Gregory—was absent, Crescentius installed John of Calabria, a favorite count of the empress Theophanu and then bishop of Piacenza [Note: [Col. 1258D] John, bishop of Piacenza, was present on 16 October 992 at the dedication of the church of Halberstadt. See the *Chronicle of Halberstadt*. Compare Arnulf of Milan, Book I, chapter 2, concerning him.], and usurped the empire for himself in such presumption, forgetful of the oath and of the great favor bestowed upon him by Otto Augustus.

Moreover, the messengers of that same pope were captured by the aforesaid usurper and handed over to strict custody [Note: [Col. 1258D] Quedlinburg Annals, year 997.].

As soon as the emperor heard this, he hurried there and asked the lord pope through messengers to come out to meet him. John, the usurper, fled as the emperor’s men approached. Later, however, he was captured by faithful servants of Christ and of the emperor, and lost his tongue together with his eyes and nostrils.

Crescentius entered the Leonine fortress [Note: [Col. 1257] “Castle” in the Quedlinburg Annals.] [Note: [Col. 1258D] Fortified by Pope Leo IV; commonly called the Leonine City.] and attempted in vain to resist the emperor.

The emperor celebrated the Lord’s Resurrection in Rome. After the festive days, he prepared weapons of war and, after the Easter octave, ordered Margrave Ekkihard to attack the house of Thiedricus [Note: [Col. 1259D] A very powerful tower of the Emperor Hadrian, which had also been the work of the tyrant Theodoric. It seems to have endured in the world without any injury against every siege engine. *Chronicle of Saint Pantaleon*, year 1001. The castle of Crescentius, commonly called the House of Theodoric. Ekkehard of Aura, year 1083; compare Florence of Worcester, year 1084. Today the Castel Sant’Angelo.], where that wicked man was sitting.

Ekkihard did not cease harassing it day and night. At last he climbed up by means of machines constructed to great height, beheaded Crescentius, and, by imperial command, suspended him by the feet from a noose [Note: [Col. 1259D] Compare the emperor’s charter of 29 April 998.]. He thereby inspired all who were present with unspeakable terror.

Pope Gregory was enthroned with great honor [Note: [Col. 1260D] “John ... was enthroned,” from the Quedlinburg Annals, year 998.], and thereafter the emperor ruled without any opposition.

### 22

It seems best to me to recall certain events of that same period. Some people considered them childish and very astonishing, but they are recognized as works predestined by God through his powers.

The count Ansfrid, of blessed memory, was certainly a man conspicuous for every virtue. He sprang from a noble line of ancestors [Note: [Col. 1260D] Ansfrid’s father was named Lambert, as A. Miraeus demonstrated in his *Belgian Chronicle* from the book of donations made for the monastery of Gembloux. Compare Aegidius of Liège, monk of the Val-des-Roses, additions to Anselm’s *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège, Tongeren, Utrecht, and Liège*, chapter 53. URS.]. While he was still a little boy [Note: [Col. 1259] “While he was still a little boy” in 2, after “with all worldly law,” in 2.], he was thoroughly instructed both in all worldly law by his paternal uncle Rodbert [Note: [Col. 1259] *Rutpert* in 2.], bishop of the city of Trier, and especially in divine matters.

Thereafter his uncle—namely, his namesake, the energetic lord Bruno, archbishop of Cologne and count of fifteen counties—handed him over to military affairs [Note: [Col. 1259] *Tradetur* in 2.]. Thus the young man of good character progressed daily under his direction, until he was assigned to the service of the first Otto the Great, who was already preparing to acquire Rome with his army.

At the beginning of his military career, Otto ordered him to set up his tent every day directly opposite the imperial tent and to draw his sword, in order to test whether he was beginning to train himself nimbly for service at court. He undertook this task all the more gladly because, while following him through byways as though for amusement and secretly lying in wait for little birds, he could more privately practise the exceedingly sweet psalms from his own mouth [Note: [Col. 1259] Ursinus wished to supply *caneret*, “he might sing.”] [Note: [Col. 1259] Ursinus restored *sequens* from A. S.] without being distracted [Note: [Col. 1259] Thus A. S., *loc. cit.*; *detritione* in 2.].

When the aforesaid emperor entered Rome, placing no small confidence in the young man, he made him his sword-bearer and said:

“While I pray today at the holy threshold of the apostles, hold the sword continuously above my head. For I know that Roman loyalty has often been suspect to our predecessors. It is the mark of a wise man to foresee by reflection every adversity that still lies far away, lest unforeseen dangers should prevail.

“Afterwards, when you are returning to the Mount of Joy, pray as much as you wish.”

After returning from there, he built from his own inheritance the abbey called Torna [Note: [Col. 1260D] Turne, in the diocese of Liège.], where, with the consent of the bishop, he installed his daughter as abbess and mother of many holy women devoted to God [Col. 1260A]. He handed the abbey over in its entirety to Saint Lambert for the salvation of his soul.

### 23

Since we have mentioned this servant of almighty God, we shall not pass over in silence what the Lord worked through her in our time.

Not forgetting hospitality, she showed such generosity toward the poor and strangers that one day she left no wine for herself or for the sisters, either for the sake of kindness or for sharing [Note: [Col. 1259] *Beneficientiae* in 2.].

When the cellarer reported this to her, she said: “Be of good cheer, dear one, and take courage. For God’s grace will be able to give us enough.”

Immediately, as was her custom, she prostrated herself before the cross in the oratory of Saint Mary and began to pray. The wine vessel, which had been completely emptied the day before, began to fill until it overflowed [Col. 1260B]. Not only the holy women but also many of the people living nearby or arriving from elsewhere drank from it for a long time, to the praise of the Lord.

Meanwhile it happened that the countess Hereswit [Note: [Col. 1259] *Hersuit* in A. S.; *Heresuint* in 2.], namely the wife of that venerable man, began to fall ill at her estate called Gilisa. Immediately, as though foreseeing her future death, she hastened to go to Torna.

Because she was unable to reach it on account of excessive pain, she remained on the road in the house of a certain mayor. As he himself later told us, he possessed dogs of extraordinary ferocity, whose barking the sick woman endured with great difficulty. When the host heard this, he urgently begged her and most willingly wished to seize the dogs or, if possible, even kill them.

When he could accomplish neither of these things, something marvelous occurred: none of the dogs was able to bark thereafter, until the holy handmaid of God fell asleep in peace.

She was buried beside the monastery by her companion in the common labor of holy simplicity, in the sacristy [Note: [Col. 1259] “Her own companion,” in A. S., year 995.].

Her chambermaid had been dropsical for many years. On Christmas Eve she dreamed that she ought to bring candles to her mistress’s tomb, and she did so. As soon as the morning praises were being celebrated, she went out, experienced a discharge, and returned healthy before all the people.

### 24

After the departure of that lady, the fortunate count, not despairing because an earthly undertaking had failed, but lifted up by that very event in the flight of virtue, resolved to embrace the monastic life wherever he could find a rule of greater obedience.

While this intention was still only beginning to take shape, he was summoned by Emperor Otto III to the bishopric of Utrecht through Notger, bishop of Liège, out of the greatest necessity (995). When he heard this, he entered the chapel at Aachen and prayed to the Lady of the World that, if it were from God, the matter might be canonically completed, but that, if not, it might mercifully be annulled.

But after Everger, archbishop of Cologne, had consulted the emperor and himself, with the agreement of the suffragans [Note: [Col. 1261] “With himself” in 2.] [Note: [Col. 1261D] Ansfrid was ordained bishop in 995. He died in 1010. See also Alpertus, *On the Diversity of Times*, I, 11–18.], he was acclaimed bishop whether he wished it or not.

Not long afterward he gave five estates from his own property to blessed Martin, as a faithful guarantor of those estates.

In his old age, when his eyes had already grown dim, he became a monk. Every day he fed seventy poor people with his own hand. For the weaker among them, while the chamberlain went ahead, the blind man himself carried a bath from the bottom of the valley to the summit of the mountain during the night and prepared it, providing changes of clothing and everything else necessary for the body. He ordered them to depart in peace, so that he might thereby conceal his good works [Col. 1261B].

On that same mountain he established a community of monks [Note: [Col. 1261D] The place where he founded this Benedictine abbey was called Hohorst, near Amersfoort. He himself inaugurated it on 18 November 1006, under Henry II, in the fifth year of his reign, and gave it the new name Saint’s Mountain—Heiligenberg. See the *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. I, May, p. 430. URS.]. He was frequently chastised by its superiors with blows from rods because he dared to resist their commands.

Whatever he was ultimately able to acquire, he gave to the hands of the poor. Out of compassion, he also had bundles placed on the trees of his mountain in winter so that the little birds might eat them [Note: [Col. 1261] *Poni* in A. S.].

He continually wore a hair shirt hidden beneath his cloak. From the Nativity of the Lord until the Invention of the Holy Cross, he was ill; during that period he ate no more than three loaves.

As the dissolution of his flesh drew near, he saw a cross in the window that had been made there after the loss of his sight, and he declared to those standing around him that he could see it. He praised God and said:

“Surrounding you, O Lord, there is a light that will never fail.”

At last, strengthened by receiving the most holy Viaticum, he had learned to love the Judge with complete expectation and, so to speak, by fearing him in the present, refused to fear him eternally.

Trusting greatly in the intercession of the holy Mother of God, to whom he had given himself and all that he possessed, he continued to sign himself with the sign of the holy cross until, falling asleep in peace, he came to rest in hand and mind alike.

After his death, the people of Utrecht came barefoot and armed, weeping and praying, and said to his household:

“For God’s sake, give us our shepherd, so that he may be carried to the tomb of his own see.”

The abbess of venerable life—namely, his most holy daughter—answered them with her chaplains and soldiers:

“He ought to be buried in the same place where God permitted him to be stripped of this present life.”

The matter reached the point that the armed men on both sides were about to meet in the greatest danger and many would have had to lose their lives, had not the lady abbess thrown herself down between them and begged them to make peace, even if only for a moment [Col. 1261D–1262A].

Meanwhile the soldiers seemed to see that the sarcophagus was being dragged from the side where the brothers’ workshops were, from the water called the Ema to the summit of the mountain [Note: [Col. 1261] Thus A. S., year 1010; *traheret* in 2.].

As they attempted this, the body was lifted up by the people of Utrecht and, as they still swear, was carried with the greatest ease beyond the water. Thus, by the Lord’s will, the stronger party of soldiers was deceived.

After the translation of the sacred body, a fragrance of wondrous sweetness was perceived along the road. According to the testimony of the most truthful men themselves, it filled the noses and breasts of those who smelled it for more than three miles.

### 25

Let us recall the loss that, miserably through his own negligence, befell Archbishop Gisilerus] (f. 63) [Note: [Col. 1261] Here manuscript 1 continues.].

For the defense of the homeland, the emperor was fortifying the city of Harnaburg [Col. 1262B] with the necessary works and entrusted it to Gisilerus for four weeks to defend. Summoned by the Slavs through an unknown deceit to a conference, he went out with a small force. Some had gone ahead, and he left several men in the city.

Then one of his companions suddenly burst out of the forest and revealed that the enemy was emerging. When soldiers from both sides engaged, the archbishop, who had come in a wagon, fled on a winged horse [Note: The allusion is to Ovid, *Fasti* III, 416.], escaping death while only a few of his men survived.

The victorious Slavs safely enjoyed the booty of the slain on 6 Nones of July [Note: [Col. 1261] “6 Nones of July” added in 1 b.] [Note: [Col. 1262D] Many of the dead are recorded in the Merseburg necrology, 2 July.], and complained that the archbishop had escaped in this way.

Although he had been so grievously mutilated, Gisilerus nevertheless kept the city until the appointed day. Returning in sadness, he encountered my paternal uncle, Margrave Liuthar, whose responsibility the aforesaid city then was. He firmly entrusted it to him and departed.

The count approached, and when he saw the city smoking with fire, he vainly asked through a messenger that the archbishop return. He himself attempted to extinguish the fire, which was already rising high in two places. When he accomplished nothing at all, he left the gate open to the enemy and sadly returned home. Afterwards, accused before the emperor, he cleared himself by oath of the guilt imputed to him.

Nine days after the aforesaid slaughter, my mother, named Cunigund [Note: [Col. 1261] *Gunigund* in 1 a.], died in the city of Germersleben on 3 Ides of July [Note: [Col. 1262D] See the Merseburg necrology, 12 and 13 July.].

## 26. (f. 63r)

Ekkihardus, sprung from the noblest ancestry of southern Thuringia [Note: [Col. 1261] “Margrave of Meissen” added by 1c.], tracing the origin of his genealogy from this line [Note: [Col. 1262D] “of this” in place of “of his own”], when he gradually reached manhood, honored his entire family, illustrious in the dignity of its character and deeds [Note: [Col. 1261] *grauite* in 1.; or *inclitam* is to be read. Compare below, V.16, *inclitum* in 1.], since, as we read: “Faults disgrace those nobly born” [Note: [Col. 1263] Thus 1c.; *benata* in 1a.], [Note: [Col. 1263] We read: “Very evil morals disfigure the nobler” (Horace, *Epistles* IV, 4, 36).]

After enduring many hardships of war with his father Guntherius [Note: [Col. 1263] The *i* is erased in 1.], who had long been suspended from his honor, he returned honorably to the favor of the second emperor Otto [Note: [Col. 1263] “Otto” added by 1c.] and to his homeland. There he took in marriage Suonehilda, the widow of Count Thietmar and sister of Duke Bernhard [Note: [Col. 1263] “of Lüneburg” added by 1c.], and by her acquired a firstborn daughter named Liudgerda. [Note: [Col. 1263D] She was the daughter of Duke Herimann Billung.]

Liutharius, born of a distinguished lineage of northern Thuringia, when he became a man and surpassed his age in virtues [Note: [Col. 1263] This seems to be the correct reading. 1a. and 1c. have *superare*; 1a. reads *cum vir factus esset, aetatem superare nitebatur*; A. S. reads *cum vir factus esset, aetatem superavit*.], and when he was especially dear to Otto the Second, with the emperor’s assistance betrothed and acquired as his wife a certain noblewoman named Godila [Note: [Col. 1263] A. S. correctly reads *matronam* (“noblewoman”) in place of *matrimonium*.], nobly born in the western region [Note: [Col. 1263D] She was the daughter of Werinharius. Compare Meibom, *Chronicon Walbeccense*.], with the permission of her cousin Wigfrid, bishop of Verdun. She bore him, in the thirteenth year of her age, a firstborn son, whom she named Wirinharius after his father [Note: [Col. 1263] 1a. apparently has *uuurinharium*; 1c. has *uuerinharium*.]

But when these two offspring—this boy and this girl—had emerged from the root of so noble a vine, they now strove gradually to reach the ripeness of their fruit by the distinguished ladder of virtues. When Count Liutharius first perceived that girl’s beauty and good conduct, he continually revolved in the secret chamber of his mind how he might unite her with his son. At last, breaking forth, he revealed through trustworthy intermediaries to Ekkihard, then margrave, the desire long hidden [Note: [Col. 1263] Thus A. S.; elsewhere *lateris* in 1.], and quickly obtained his agreement.

When the members of both households had then assembled, Ekkihard lawfully promised Liutharius that he would give the girl to his son in marriage, affirming this in the presence of all the nobles according to custom and law. But because Ekkihard was very dear to Otto the Third and possessed great influence with him among the other leading men, I do not know for what reason he was led astray and tried with all his might to break the firmly established agreement.

This soon became known to Liutharius, who anxiously considered how it might be prevented. While the emperor and Ekkihard were then staying in Romania (998), the care of that kingdom had been entrusted to the venerable abbess Mathild, whom I mentioned above. The girl was being brought up in her city called Quidilingaburg [Note: [Col. 1263] *quidilingabur* in 1.].

A public assembly of the abbess and the entire council took place at Darniburg [Note: [Col. 1263D] Derenburg, a small town on the river Holtemme between the cities of Halberstadt and Wernigerode, two leagues from Quedlinburg. URS.]. Meanwhile Wirinharius, as I believe, not with his father’s approval but out of love for the maiden and fear of manifest disgrace [Note: [Col. 1263] *manifasti* in 1.], climbed the aforesaid city with my brothers Heinricus, Frithericus, and the other excellent soldiers. Seizing his betrothed by force, although she resisted and cried out, he reached Wallibiki happily and unharmed with his companions.

When the abbess learned this with certainty from a reliable messenger, she was deeply angered and complained of it to all the princes with tears in her eyes (f. 64r), asking and commanding that all the armed men should immediately pursue the public enemies and should try to bring the maiden back, whether by capturing or killing them [Note: [Col. 1263] Added by 1b.]. Without delay the armed soldiers hastened to carry out these orders. Before they reached the fortified city, they sought eagerly to capture, kill, or drive away the fugitives, cutting across the shorter routes.

Travelers reported that those whom they were pursuing were rejoicing in strong forces and closed gates, already secure in familiar defenses [Col. 1264B]; that they admitted no one; and that they were determined either to die or to defend themselves there [Note: [Col. 1263] Added by 1b.] and never to return the bride [Note: [Col. 1263] *illi* corrected to *ulli* in 1.]. On hearing this, he became exceedingly sad and returned.

Count Liutharius, together with the elder Alfricus and Count Ekkihard’s soldier Thietmarus, then set out to ascertain the bride’s wishes. They learned from her with sufficient certainty that she preferred to remain there rather than return, and they reported these answers to the lady abbess and the others [Note: [Col. 1263] *abbatise* in 1a.].

When the abbess’s leading men were consulting about this matter, some advised that an assembly should be held at Magadaburg, that the bridegroom should come there with his wife, and that all their helpers should either present themselves there as guilty or flee as condemned men. And so it was done (999).

When a very great multitude had gathered there, Wirinharius and his associates threw themselves down barefoot and returned the wife. Through the assistance of the princes, he obtained forgiveness for his own offense and that of his companions by promising suitable correction [Note: [Col. 1263] Thus 1b.]. But the venerable Mahtild, in every respect exemplary, took Liudgerda [Note: [Col. 1263] Thus 1., in place of *Liukerdam*] away with her—not to retain her, but to confirm her great fear [Note: [Col. 1263] “Love” in 2 and A. S., under the year 999.].

## 27. (f. 65r)

Her resolve to do good, however, was interrupted by the sudden onset of death [Note: [Col. 1263] *Autem* is erased in codex 1; it appears in A. S.]. A few days later, when she reached the place prepared for her by God, she immediately fell ill. She summoned Bernwardus [Note: [Col. 1263] The *n* is erased in 1.], then pastor of the holy church of Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 1263] *hillinessemensis* in 1a., repeatedly.], and, having received from him the indulgence she requested, on the eighth day before the Ides of February put off the inner man [Note: [Col. 1263] Read: “the outer man”]. She was buried in the church at the head of her grandfather, King Heinricus [Note: [Col. 1264D] Compare the *Annals of Quedlinburg*, under the year 999, where Mathild’s day of death is nevertheless said to have been the seventh day before the Ides of February. The same appears in the *Necrology of Lüneburg*; the *Necrology of Fulda* gives the sixth day before the Ides of February.]

Because of this funeral, the empress Aethelheidis, mother of the same emperor [Note: [Col. 1265] *aehelheidis* in 1a.; *adhelheidis* in 1c.], was exceedingly distressed. She sent a messenger to the emperor both to make her death known to him [Note: [Col. 1265] Thus 1c.; *innoceret* in 1a.] and to request that her namesake sister should succeed her.

The emperor, granting assent to these pious wishes, mourned the death of his aunt and, through the bearer Becelinus [Note: [Col. 1265] *p. B. p.* added by 1b.], from afar entrusted the abbey to his beloved sister by means of a golden staff, and ordered that she be blessed by Bishop Arnulf. [Note: [Col. 1265D] Count Becelinus, in the district of Chutizi, appears in a charter of Emperor Otto dated 18 September 991, in Höfer, vol. I, p. 531.]

Meanwhile [Note: [Col. 1265] Added by 1b.] the empress Aethelheidis [Note: [Col. 1265] *aetheldis* in 1a.; *aethelheidis* there; *adhelheidis* in 1c.] built the city called Celsa [Note: [Col. 1265D] Selz in Alsace, given to Adelheid by Emperor Otto I on 16 November 968.]. After gathering monks there and completing everything, in that year, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, she joyfully departed to those from whom she had sprung [Note: [Col. 1265] Compare the *Annals of Quedlinburg*, under the year 999.]. Because God repays her faithful service with fitting rewards, he performs many miracles at her tomb even to this day.

Pope Gregory, too, having put everything in Rome in good order, died on the second day before the Nones of February, and Gerbert immediately succeeded him [Col. 1265B]. [Note: [Col. 1265] “Pope … succeeded him” was written by 1b in the blank space left by the scribe.]

## 28

After this the emperor accused the archbishop Gisilerus at a Roman synod because he held two dioceses. Having suspended him from office by judicial sentence, he ordered that he be summoned there through messengers from the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 1265D] See the statutes of this council, held in 998, in d’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. I, p. 603.]. But since Gisilerus had then been struck by paralysis and could not come, he sent the cleric Rotmannus, who was to excuse him on oath if he were not otherwise believed.

A postponement was then granted, and the matter was deferred until the emperor could examine it with the bishops of the surrounding provinces. Later, after hearing of the miracles that God had performed through his beloved martyr Aethelbertus, the emperor hastened there for the sake of prayer.

When he came to Ratisbon, he was received with splendid honor by Gebehardus, bishop of that church (1000), accompanied by Ziazo, then a patrician [Note: [Col. 1265D] Zazzo, Roman patrician, is praised in a charter of the chapter of Merseburg granted by Emperor Otto at Regensburg in 1000, on the second day before the Kalends of February, in Höfer, vol. I, p. 157. Compare above, chapter 2, where he is called Ciazo.], and by Robertus the almoner, together with the cardinals. No emperor ever departed from Rome or returned to it with greater glory.

Gisilerus went to meet him, earned his favor, although it was not secure, and accompanied him. When the emperor reached the city of Citicium, he was received, as befitted an emperor, by the second Hugo, the third administrator of that see. Then, traveling by a direct route toward the city of Meissen, he was honorably received by the venerable Egedus, bishop of that church, and by Margrave Ekkihard, who was counted among the emperor’s foremost men.

After crossing the boundaries of the Milcini, the emperor first came to the district of Diedesis [Note: [Col. 1266D] A district between the rivers Oder, Bober, and Katzbach.]. There Bolizlavus—whose name is interpreted as “greater praise,” not according to its meaning but according to ancient custom—met him with great joy at a place called Ilua [Note: [Col. 1266D] Halbau or Eilau, near the Bober], having prepared lodging for him there (f. 66r).

How the emperor was received by him and escorted through his territories as far as Gnesin [Note: [Col. 1265] The earlier *e* in *genesin* is erased in 1.] is incredible and beyond description [Note: [Col. 1266D] Compare the *Annals of Quedlinburg*, under the year 1000, and the *Life of Meinwerk*, chapter 11.]. When he saw the desired city from afar, he approached it humbly with bare feet. Venerably received by its bishop Ungerus [Note: [Col. 1265] “of Poznań” added by 2.], he was led into the church, and the martyr of Christ was entreated with abundant tears to obtain Christ’s favor for him.

Without delay he established an archbishopric there, as I hope lawfully, though without the consent of the aforesaid bishop, to whose diocese the entire region was subject. He entrusted it to Radimus, the brother of the aforesaid martyr [Note: [Col. 1265] “the brother who is also called Gaudentius,” *Annals of Saxony*, under the year 1000.], and subjected to him Reinbern, bishop of the church of Kolberg [Note: [Col. 1266D] Perhaps near the sea? P.], Poppo of Kraków [Note: [Col. 1265] The word is erased in 1.], and Johann of Wrocław [Note: [Col. 1265] *uuratizlaensem* in 1c.], excluding Ungerus of Poznań [Note: [Col. 1265] *posnaniensem* in 1a.]. Having made an altar there, he honorably placed holy relics within it.

When everything had been completed, the emperor was presented with splendid gifts by the aforesaid duke, especially three hundred armored soldiers [Note: [Col. 1266D] They seem to have been those whom he later calls *Slavic guests*—*Goscie*—in Book VI, chapter 55; Book VII, chapter 41; and Book VIII, chapter 16. The word is commonly used not only of foreign merchants but also of soldiers serving without pay, attracted only by the hope of booty.]. As the emperor departed, Bolizlavus magnificently escorted him as far as Magadaburg, where the Palm Sunday ceremonies were celebrated.

On Monday the archbishop of that place, at the emperor’s command, was asked to resume his former see. By sending messengers a large sum of money, he scarcely obtained a postponement until Quidilingeburg. A great gathering of senators took place there; the paschal celebrations were also held there; and, when a synod was held on Monday, Gisilerus was summoned again.

Overcome by severe illness, he was excused by the aforementioned Rotmannus and defended in many matters by Waltherdus, then provost. A council was summoned for him at Aachen [Note: [Col. 1265] *aqisgrani* in 1.]. When he came there with his companions, he was again addressed by the archdeacon of the Roman see. Following wise counsel, he requested that a general council be granted to him. Thus all these matters were postponed without investigation, until God, in his mercy toward our times, deigned to bring them to an end.

## 29

The emperor, wishing in his own time to renew the ancient custom of the Romans, which had largely been obliterated [Note: [Col. 1265] Added by 1b.], did many things that different people judged differently. He alone sat at a table made almost semicircular, in a place more elevated than the others [Note: [Col. 1267] *caetaeris* corrected to *ceteris* in 1.].

When he was uncertain where the bones of Emperor Charles rested, he secretly broke through the pavement and ordered the place where he thought they were to be excavated until they were found seated on a royal throne. Taking the golden cross that had hung around his neck, together with part of his clothing that was still undecayed, he reverently replaced the remainder [Note: [Col. 1267D] Compare the *Annals of Hildesheim*, under the year 1000.].

But why should I recount each of his arrivals and departures through all his bishoprics and counties? “Through the Transalpine lands all things being well ordered, he visited the Roman empire and reached the citadels of Romulus” (Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* II, 766), where he was received with great praise by the apostolic bishop and the other fellow bishops [Note: [Col. 1267] See the variant reading at 674.].

## 30

After this (1001), Gregory, who was very dear to the emperor, tried by treachery to seize him and laid hidden snares. When these men had gathered and unexpectedly risen against him, the emperor escaped through a gate with a few companions, while the greater part of his followers remained enclosed. The populace, never content with its lords, repaid him for his ineffable piety with evil [Note: [Col. 1267D] Compare throughout Balderic, *Chronicon Cameracense* I, 1, chapter 114, and the *Life of Bernward*, chapter 23 and following.].

Then, through his own messenger, the emperor summoned and ordered all his friends and household to come to him there, charging each one that, if they had ever cared for his honor or safety, they should hasten to him with armed forces to avenge him and protect him more fully.

The Romans, ashamed of the guilt of the crime now exposed [Note: [Col. 1267] 1a. has *culpa se*; A. S., under the year 1001, has *culpam*.], and rebuking one another severely, released all those who had been enclosed unharmed. They humbly sought the emperor’s favor and peace by every means.

Wherever the emperor could injure them, whether in their persons or their possessions, he did not delay to do so, distrusting their lying words. He held all the regions associated with the Romans and Lombards faithfully subject to his rule, except Rome alone, which he loved and always cultivated above all others.

When a very large crowd of the faithful gathered with Heribertus, archbishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 1267] “of the holy see” added by 1c.], the emperor rejoiced. Although he always pretended an outwardly cheerful expression, he nevertheless groaned in the secrecy of his conscience over very many sins and did not cease, in the silence of night, to wash them away with streams of tears while devoting himself to vigils and prayers (f. 67r). He very often passed the entire week fasting, except Thursday, and was extremely generous in almsgiving.

Many troublesome events preceded his approaching death. For our dukes and counts, not without the knowledge of the bishops [Note: [Col. 1267] Thus 1c.; *conscientia* in 1a.], sought to conspire against him [Note: [Col. 1267] *netuntur* in 1a.], requesting for this purpose the assistance of Duke Heinricus, later his successor.

He, preserving in his heart the final admonitions of his father and namesake, who died and rests at Gonneshem [Note: [Col. 1267] *Gandenshem* in 1c.], and remaining faithful to the emperor in all things, gave them no assent.

The emperor immediately learned of this and bore it patiently. In the city of Paterna [Note: [Col. 1267] The scribe himself perhaps corrected *paterno* to *paterna* in 1.] he fell ill, with pustules pressing upon his internal organs and at times gradually breaking out [Note: [Col. 1267D] Landulf the Elder II, chapters 18–19, gives a different account. Compare Sigebertus and the *Chronicle of St. Pantaleon*. Also compare Adelboldus, *Life of Emperor Heinricus II*.].

Distinguished in appearance and outstanding in faith, on the ninth day before the Kalends of February [Note: [Col. 1268D] The same day of death is recorded in the *Annals of Quedlinburg*, under the year 1002.] he departed this world wearing the Roman imperial crown (1002), leaving behind for his people an inconsolable grief, for at that time there was no one more generous or in every respect more merciful than he.

May Alpha and Omega (Revelation 1:8) have mercy on him [Note: [Col. 1267] 1c. has *ei*], granting great things in place of small and eternal things in place of temporal ones.

## 31

Those who had been present at his final moments continued these observances until the army, then dispersed in every direction, could be gathered through messengers. Then the sorrowful company accompanying the body of their beloved lord endured seven continuous days of great hardships of war. The enemy granted no assurance of safety, except only when they reached the city of Berna.

From there, when they came to Polling [Note: [Col. 1268D] Polling near the river Ammer, below Weilheim.], the estate of Sigifridus, bishop of Augsburg, they were received by Duke Heinricus and again deeply moved by his tears. He urged them one by one, with many promises, to choose him as their lord and king.

He took possession of the emperor’s body and imperial regalia, with the sole exception of the holy lance, which Heribertus the archbishop secretly sent ahead and took into his own power [Note: [Col. 1267] *supsit* in 1c.]. After being held for a short time under guard, the archbishop departed with permission, leaving his brother there as surety, and soon returned the sacred lance.

The archbishop, together with all those following the emperor’s funeral except Bishop Sigifridus, did not then consent to the duke, yet did not refuse him altogether [Note: [Col. 1267] Manuscript 2 does not include *non*; 1a reads *consentiebant, neque omnino denegabant*.]. Rather, he declared that he would willingly agree wherever the better and greater part of the whole people inclined.

When the duke and these men reached the city of Augsburg, he honorably buried the beloved lord’s intestines, which had first been carefully placed in two small vessels, in the southern part of the monastery of the holy martyr Afra, in the oratory of the holy bishop Othelricus. Liudulfus, bishop of that church, had built it in his honor. For the remedy of his soul he also granted one hundred manors of his hereditary property [Note: [Col. 1267] Added by 1b.].

Then, dismissing the great multitude in profound peace, he followed the emperor’s body to his own city, which is called Nova [Note: [Col. 1269D] Neuburg near the Danube.]. Afterwards, earnestly entreated by his namesake Heinricus, whose sister he had already married while the emperor was alive (f. 68r), he finally sent the body on to its appointed destination, bidding farewell to each person [Note: [Col. 1269D] Namely, Aachen. See Adelboldus and the *Annals of Quedlinburg*.].

## 32

Meanwhile the princes of Saxony, having learned of the untimely death of their lord, gathered sadly at the royal estate of Frasa, which Count Guncelinus then held from the emperor as a benefice. Gisilerus, archbishop of Magdeburg, came with his fellow bishops; Duke Bernhardus; the margraves Liutharius, Ekkihardus, and Gero; and the nobles of the kingdom, to deliberate about the condition of the commonwealth.

As soon as Count Liutharius perceived that Ekkihardus wished to exalt himself above him, he called the aforesaid archbishop and the better part of the nobles aside for a private discussion. He proposed to them all that they should swear not to elect any man jointly or individually as their lord or king before the assembly scheduled to be held at Werlo.

Everyone praised and approved this proposal except Ekkihardus. Taking it hard that he had been delayed, even briefly, from the summit of royal power, he burst out:

“Count Liutharius,” he said [Note: [Col. 1269] Added by 1b, but later erased], “why do you oppose me?” And he replied:

“Do you not notice that your chariot is missing a fourth wheel?” [Note: [Col. 1269] Thus 1c.; 1a has *curru*.] [Note: [Col. 1269D] By the fourth wheel he seems to mean nobility of birth and close kinship with the royal family. This privilege at least belonged to Heinricus; see Adelboldus, chapter 1. KIND.]

Thus the election was interrupted. The truth of the ancient saying was fulfilled: that the interruption of one night causes a delay of one year—and that delay continued until the end of this man’s life [Note: [Col. 1269] See the variant reading at 689.].

During the reign of the aforesaid emperor, the monastery at Hilleslev was burned by the Slavs (1002), after the nuns had been led out; and on the same day many of our men were killed [Note: [Col. 1269] The words “and they … were killed” were written by 1b at the end of the page.].

## 33 (f. 69r)

Having strayed far from my beginning, I shall at last return and briefly touch upon the emperor’s funeral. When his body came to Cologne, it was first received by Heribertus, archbishop of that city.

On Monday after Palm Sunday it was carried to the monastery of Saint Severinus; on Tuesday to Saint Pantaleon [Note: [Col. 1269] *albanum* in 1a.]; on the fourth day to Saint Gereon. On Maundy Thursday it was carried to Saint Peter, where penitents were introduced according to ecclesiastical custom and released from their penance. The archbishop granted remission for the soul of the present body, while the fellow priests asked for its commemoration [Note: [Col. 1269] Added by 1b.], and the people tearfully offered their supplication.

At dawn on Good Friday [Note: [Col. 1269] *illusessente* in 1a.], the funeral bier was lifted up and carried to Aachen on Holy Saturday. On Sunday it was buried in the middle of the choir of the church of Saint Mary ever-virgin.

The piety he had shown to all earnestly urged them to continue their prayers and weeping aloud. The feasts of the Lord’s resurrection, in which the joys of angels and human beings rejoice together, could not be completed with fitting reverence because of the weakness of those assembled [Note: [Col. 1269] Thus 1c.; *fragitatem* in 1a.]. They recognized together that this was God’s vengeance, deserved by their sins.

May his soul obtain pardon with tears from whoever, by profession, is faithful to God [Note: [Col. 1269] Thus 1b.; *coram* in 1a.], because he strove with the utmost effort of his mind to renew our church [Note: [Col. 1269] Added by 1b.]. May he receive in the land of the living the ever-adopted communion of the pious together with the unfailing good things of the Lord—he who always strove to have mercy on the miserable.

## 34

Most of the nobles who had attended this funeral promised Duke Herimannus assistance in acquiring and defending the kingdom [Note: [Col. 1270D] Duke of Alamannia, son of Duke Udo, who was killed in Italy in 982.], judging Heinricus unsuitable for this on account of the many circumstances involved.

But the Lombards, having heard of the emperor’s departure, unconcerned about what would follow and not eager for worthy fruits of repentance, chose Hardwigus as their king [Note: [Col. 1270D] Arduino, margrave of Ivrea and count palatine in Lombardy], a man more skilled in the art of destruction than of rule—as became clear in divine judgment to the very authors of this deed.

Leaving these matters to be explained later [Note: [Col. 1269] *exponendo* in 1a.], I shall begin writing about the man who, by divine mercy and his own virtue, humbled all who ever rose against him and forced them, with bowed necks, to render him honor.

He was the fifth in succession and the second in name. Let him mark the title of the fifth book [Note: [Col. 1269] 1a. has “fourth.”].

## 35

Since I cannot set down in orderly fashion everything that must be written on the present page of this work, I do not blush to gather it gradually in what follows [Note: [Col. 1269] In 1 the text continues in another hand. In 2 the following is read: “Prologue of the book. Since I shall explain all … the remaining deeds” (thus). “An inserted little book concerning certain omitted matters: Miesco, illustrious duke of the region of Bohemia, etc.”].

For I enjoy the varied alternation of a traveler who changes the course of a straight path, now because of roughness, now because of ignorance, through the winding variety of roads and paths [Note: [Col. 1269] *itinerantis* in 1c.; *semite* in 1c.]. Thus I shall explain the remaining deeds of Miesco, the illustrious duke of the Poles, already marked out for the most part in the earlier books (f. 70r).

He had taken as his wife from the region of Bohemia a noblewoman, the sister of the elderly Duke Bolizlavus. As her name suggested, so she truly appeared in reality. For she was called Dobrawa in the Slavic language, which in the German tongue is translated as “Good.”

When this woman, faithful to Christ, perceived that her husband was entangled in various errors of paganism, she carefully deliberated in the narrow chamber of her mind how she might unite him with herself in faith [Note: [Col. 1271] *et* added by 1c.]. She strove by every means to please him, not because of the threefold desire for this harmful world, but rather because of the praiseworthy reward of the future—a fruit greatly desired by all the faithful.

For a time she willingly did wrong, so that later she might be able to do good for a long time. During the Lent immediately following the marriage mentioned above, when she was trying to offer God an acceptable tithe of abstinence from flesh and bodily affliction, she was asked by her husband, with a sweet promise, to abandon her resolution.

She consented for this reason: so that on another occasion she might more easily be heard by him. Some say that she ate meat during one Lent, others during three.

You have now heard, reader, of her offense; consider at this point the fruit of her noble piety (f. 70v). For she labored for the conversion of her husband and was heard by the kindness of her Creator. By his infinite goodness, her zealous persecutor came to his senses: at the frequent urging of his beloved wife, he vomited out the poison of his inborn unbelief and washed away the stain of original sin in holy baptism.

Immediately his head and his beloved elder, followed by the formerly weak members of the people, came after him [Note: [Col. 1271] *subsequntur* in 1.]. Receiving the nuptial garment, they were numbered among Christ’s adopted people [Note: [Col. 1271] *adoptiunos* in 1a.].

Jordan, their first bishop, labored greatly among them, diligently inviting them by word and deed to cultivate the heavenly vineyard. Then the married couple—the aforesaid man and the noble woman—legitimately rejoiced together, and the whole household subject to them rejoiced that it had been married to Christ [Note: [Col. 1271] *nubsisse* in 1.].

After this the good mother bore a son greatly unlike herself and destined to destroy many mothers. She named him Bolizlavus after her brother [Note: [Col. 1271] *bolizlaum* in 1c.], that man who first revealed the evil lying hidden in the same family and then sowed it into its very entrails, as I shall make clear in what follows.

## 36

When his mother died [Note: [Col. 1271D] Dobrawa died in 977, according to the Saxon annalist under the year 986.], his father took as wife, without canonical authority, a nun from the monastery called Calva, the daughter of Margrave Thiedricus.

Her name was Oda, and her presumption was great. For she had rejected her heavenly bridegroom, preferring to him a military husband (f. 71r)—a deed displeasing to all the governors of the Church, and especially to her own venerable bishop Hilliwardus [Note: [Col. 1271D] What Thietmarus already related in Book III, chapter 10, seems to refer to this matter.].

Yet, for the salvation of the homeland and the strengthening of the necessary peace, this did not lead to a breach. Rather, it became a salutary means of continual reconciliation [Note: [Col. 1271D] Compare the *Annals of Hildesheim*, under the years 985 and 986.]. Through her, the service of Christ was greatly increased: a multitude of captives was restored to its homeland, those bound were released from their chains, and the prison was opened to criminals. And, as I hope, the magnitude of the offense committed was forgiven her by God, since such love of piety was recognized in her.

We read that the person who does not entirely abandon the purpose of the wickedness he has begun strives in vain to placate the Lord [Note: [Col. 1271] *domini* in 1.; A. S., under the year 986, has *Deum*.].

She bore her husband three sons: Miesco, Suentepulcus, and [lacuna] [Note: [Col. 1271] In codex 1, as also in A. S. at the same place, space was left blank; an early-seventeenth-century hand supplied the name Bolizlavus.]. [Note: [Col. 1271D] This third son seems to have been that Wolodowei about whom our author writes in Book V.]

She lived there with great honor until the end of her husband’s life, having been received with those among whom she had lived and with the offspring from which she had come [reading uncertain: *accepta cum quibus fuit et prolicua de quibus venit*].

## 37

But in the year 999 of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 1271] 1 has “892.”] [Note: [Col. 1271D] The *Annals of Hildesheim* also give the year 992.], in the tenth year of the reign of Otto the Third, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of June [Note: [Col. 1271] “The tenth … of June” added by 1b.], the aforesaid duke, now old and feverish, passed from this exile to his homeland [Note: [Col. 1271] “To the heavenly homeland” added by 2 and A. S.] [Note: [Col. 1271D] *Necrology of Fulda*, under the year 992: “Miesco, margrave, count, and layman.”].

He left his kingdom to be divided among many. Later his son Bolizlavus [Note: [Col. 1272D] Boleslaus I, duke of the Poles, called *Chrabry*, that is, “the Brave”], after expelling his stepmother and brothers [Note: [Col. 1271] “Three” added by 2 and A. S.] and blinding his retainers Odilienus and Pribuvojus, gathered it into one by foxlike cunning.

To rule alone, he set aside justice and every law. He married the daughter of Margrave Rigdagus [Note: [Col. 1271] Thus 1b.; *ricdagi* in 1a.], later putting her away. Then he took a wife from Hungary, by whom he had a son named Besprim, likewise expelling her.

His third wife was Emnildis [Note: [Col. 1271] *erminildis* in 2 and A. S.], born to the venerable elder Dombremirus. Faithful to Christ, she turned her husband’s unstable mind toward every good work and did not cease to cleanse the stains of both of them by immense generosity in almsgiving and by abstinence [Note: [Col. 1271] *utrisque* in 1a.].

She bore two sons, Miesco and another, whom the father named after his beloved elder. She also bore three daughters: one is an abbess; the second married Count Hirimannus [Note: [Col. 1272D] He was the son of Ekkihard, margrave of Meissen.]; the third married the son of King Wlodemirus, as I shall relate.

38. [Col. 1272D] Through the favor and urging of the aforementioned Emperor, Waic, the son-in-law of Heinric, duke of the Bavarians, established episcopal sees in his own kingdom and received a crown and blessing. 

Nor will I pass over a certain miracle that arose from heaven at Rome in the time of the aforementioned emperor. For when the soldiers of Duke Herimann seized by force the meadows of the monks of Saint Paul, they refused to withdraw, although those monks repeatedly entreated them to do so. Immediately various clouds rose, lightning flashed, displaying the terror of the Lord; dreadful thunder followed at once, killing four of the best men from their number and driving the rest into flight. By this it was shown that Christ’s poor are not to be despised in this world. For God is the merciful protector of such people; he advances with a fitting reward those who honor them and heed them in their need, while he punishes their persecutors either here—which is considered the lighter punishment—or in the future—which is the more serious.

The emperor’s sister, named Mahtild, married Ezo, son of Herimann, count palatine. This displeased many; but since it could not be legally remedied, her only brother patiently endured it, giving her very much so that the glory inherited from her eminent parents would not be diminished. 

In his time Conrad, the distinguished leader of the Suevi, and his brother Heribert, count, as well as Hodo, the renowned margrave—alas!—were overwhelmed by sudden death. 

Sigifridus, however, the son of the aforementioned margrave, had long lived among the monks at Nova Urbs, where his father rests, observing the same habit; but he cast off his cowl and took up secular clothing. Summoned to a synod by his abbot Ekkihard and by Gisilero, archbishop, he came to Parthenopolis and, although unwilling, put on his former habit. By judicial sentence, with himself as the twelfth, he cleared himself by oaths, following the example of one who at Rome had purged himself by a similar sentence before the aforementioned emperor. Their spiritual fathers had full testimony against them; but, as I fear, because the judges were corrupt, they lost the same men without any fault of their own.

39. [Folio 72′] I would also like briefly to recall the life of Francho, bishop of Worms. As a young man, distinguished by every virtue, he pleased the august emperor; and when the emperor had taken him into his intimacy and carefully observed his excellence in divine matters, after the death of Hillibald, bishop of that city, he caused Francho to succeed him. After sitting for only one year, he died in Italy and was buried there. 

I would most gladly have wished, if it could ever have happened, that the memory of any of the best men should have flourished among the present and future through some novelty produced by the works of my useless hands, so that all these men, even if not pleased by this, might nevertheless, because of their piety, remember me before almighty God. For I know myself, though less than I ought, and, placing no trust at all in the frailty of a reed staff, humbly commend myself, a sinner, to righteous intercessors. 

The emperor also wished to raise his chaplains Herpo of Halberstadt and Raco of Bremen to episcopal rank. While they lay sick in bed, he gave them the pastoral staff; but each departed without priestly anointing. What I could say about this, I do not know, since I have never read or even heard anything about such matters. God, who knows all things, alone ordained and can know this.

40. (f. 73) Those two men, although pious, ought nevertheless not to be counted among the bishops, because they were unable to become sharers with them in the blessing.

Razo, however, at the command of his beloved lord, brought back from Hamburg to Rome the bones of the aforementioned Pope Benedict, just as he himself had foretold. For that venerable father, the lord apostolic—as I call him—while he was in exile and devoted to the service of Christ, when this northern region still enjoyed the peace it desired, said:

“Here my fragile body must be dissolved; and afterward this entire region must be devastated by the sword of the pagans and left to be inhabited by wild beasts, and before the translation of my remains the native inhabitants will not see lasting peace. Once I rest at home, however, I hope through apostolic intercession that the pagans will be at rest.”

41. [Col. 1274C] During the time of the aforementioned emperor many pious people died, whose lives I do not know, and therefore I am silent about them. Among their number was a certain countess named Christiana, who gave a large portion of her estate, which she possessed in the city of Stuwi, to Saint Maurice in Magdeburg. 

As she passed through the swift course of this life while living in Christ, she joyfully came, on 8 March, to the long-desired bridal chamber of her Bridegroom. This was revealed in the following manner to Gisilero, then archbishop of Parthenopolis, who was at that time staying in Quedlinburg. A certain man appeared to him and said:

“Do you know that the entire heavenly army is preparing for the arrival of the soul faithful to Christ and for the worthy reception of such a bride? For she has now come to her reward and to the blessed hope of an eternal dwelling.”

When he awoke, he first made this known to Waltherd, then provost. As soon as Waltherd heard that the venerable lady had departed this life that same night in which these things had been seen, he reported it to his superior and said that his vision had been fulfilled.

Keeping every good deed hidden in the secrecy of her conscience, she was quite unlike the other married women of our day. A great part of them, improperly dressed in every limb, openly displays to all lovers what it has in itself for sale. Since in these things there is an abomination before God and a disgrace to the world, without any shame she comes forward as a spectacle for the whole people. It is shameful and exceedingly pitiable—compare Persius I, 3—that every sinner does not wish to hide away, but presumes to come forward as an object of ridicule to the good and an example to the wicked.

42. [Col. 1275B] In those days Mahtild, a religious woman, daughter of Thiederic, the margrave, married a certain Slav named Prebizlav. Later she was captured by Bolibut, the unjust governor of the city of Brenneburg, and was so strictly confined that she could neither prepare for the Lord’s Nativity or any other solemnity by an appropriate fast nor celebrate it with festive joy. There she gave birth to a boy, whom she raised in sorrow. Later she received release from such great misery and, undeservedly, the abbacy at Magdeburg. 

Her husband had earlier died at the hands of the twin brothers Ugio and Uffico, on the fifth day before the Kalends of January. 

Her brother, named Liudulf, laid aside his clerical status and took up weapons of vengeance; he did much harm to our people. But after being captured by the emperor, he was restored once more to his former rank.

43. [Col. 1275C] In the time of the aforementioned emperor there was in the city of Parthenopolis a certain dean named Hepo, a cheerful man and very useful in the monastery, especially in the choir. When he had become old and mature in all his actions, he was suddenly struck by paralysis and became mute. Yet, with the help of the supreme Physician, he was able to sing the psalms very well with his brothers; but he could scarcely utter other words. In this wondrous matter the virtue of Christ is recognized and praised, for it is shown in many instances that he supplies strength to those who faithfully serve him.

But when the venerable father had groaned after making confession, lamenting that he had sinned greatly by abandoning the monastic habit, and when he had wished, at the urging of the brothers, to amend this at the time of his readmission, he died not long afterward, after the Nones of January. He was buried at Saint John with the other brothers, with whom he ought to have lived, if such a thing could have been accomplished amid human frailty. 

Ekkihard, surnamed Rufus, the custodian of the church mentioned above, a grammarian by training and at that time master of the school, once wished to examine the great altar—of gold, adorned with gems and with excellent electrum—to see whether anything was missing from it. Unexpectedly, he was crushed by it. Disabled by this blow, he entrusted to Waltherd, the provost, money that he had long accumulated, to be distributed with a generous hand. A few days later, on the second day before the Nones of September, he breathed out his faithful spirit. 

I do not accuse him of anything; but I know this truthfully: if anyone offends Saint Maurice, let him not be unaware of the danger of the punishment that follows.

A certain young man, prompted by the devil, wished to steal this man’s treasure during the dark night. As he began to tremble at the first entrance and was already trying to desist, he later reported that he heard a voice encouraging him boldly to carry out the deed. But the wretched man took a crown from that place and was immediately caught in the church itself, had his legs broken, and was placed upon a wheel. 

44. (f. 75) Nor should you, reader, be unaware of the steadfastness of a certain brother of mine, Husward. While he was sleeping beside me at that time, the devil—our crafty enemy—often approached him during the night and repeatedly tried in vain to lie down near his sleeping place. At last he humbly begged Husward to serve him in exchange for a reward.

That pious man, mindful of his vow to the Lord, asked him first to show him the prize he had promised, and afterward to receive his answer. [Col. 1276C] Then the devil said: “With a similar prize”—that is, a reward—“with which I recently enriched my servant in the west, I will reward you if you consent to me.” 

Hearing such words, this venerable priest, as he had often done before, drove him away with the sign of the holy cross and harsh rebukes. When he discovered that a certain cleric in the western regions had been hanged because of the enormity of his crime, he made known to all of us both what had preceded and what followed. It is astonishing that, although the true cross of Christ was carried every Sunday to that dormitory, the evil one dared to do such things.

In that same year, therefore, the aforementioned brother—victorious, as I hope, and moved to repentance for his offenses—escaped the danger of the world on the seventh day before the Kalends of March. His mother, Berhta, already extremely old, comforted him as he struggled in his final agony, patiently bearing a double grief. For it was then the anniversary of the death of her son Bevo, an excellent soldier, whose eyes Margrave Ekkihard had earlier taken away. 

45. Nor will I keep silent about the vision of our brother Merquard. As he himself reported to me with groans, he was led into a common cemetery, where he saw a grave burning intensely. His guide addressed him as follows:

“You must soon be cast into this burning pit; and Rodulf ought to follow you, had he not now turned back and remained at Ludger’s threshold.”

For both of these men had been monks in the monastery of the aforementioned confessor, who built this place, called Helmanstidi, from his own property in the time of the great Emperor Charles. He was the brother of Hildigrim, bishop of Châlons and first ruler of the holy church of Halberstadt; Hildigrim governed it for forty-seven years. He departed this world while the pious Emperor Ludwig was reigning, in the year 827 of the Lord’s incarnation. 

Liuderus was made by Emperor Charles the first pastor of the church of Mirmingerdevord. After he had excellently ordered his parish and had built the place called Wirdunun at his own expense, he received his heavenly reward in the year 808 of the Lord’s incarnation. After him the aforementioned emperor lived only five years, giving up his spirit on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the seventy-first year of his age, the forty-seventh of his reign, and the fourteenth of his imperial rule. 

In the year in which he saw these things, the aforementioned priest vowed to resume his former habit and obedience, and not long afterward he died, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May. 

I have spoken these things about my brothers not to accuse them, but rather to exhort us to be watchful and to imitate the good.

46. [Col. 1277C] During the reign of the third Otto, Albi, son of Guncelin, was killed by one of his own retainers in a certain forest for a pointless reason. Gisilero, the archbishop, received his county, together with the benefice lying near the Milda.

His chamberlain and my brother Gunterus, after the death of Dodo, bishop of the church of Asanbrun, came to Italy. He was dear to the emperor and had often served him faithfully. Since he was kindly received there and was heard in every matter, on the following night he saw Christ’s martyrs Crispinus and Crispinianus coming to him and asking whether he wished to accept their bishopric. 

When he answered them, “God wills it, and it is pleasing to you,” he was pierced by them with two spears. Immediately awakening, he was utterly unable to rise by himself. The next day, when the emperor learned of his illness, he fulfilled his faithful promise. After this, Gunterus recovered and returned home. Having received consecration, he lived in great suffering for nearly four years, and on the eighth day before the Kalends of December exchanged these temporal things for those that endure eternally.

I do not know whether anything in him displeased God or his holy martyrs. I saw this, and heard it from others, that he was a just and devoutly God-fearing man, gentle and chaste; and, as those with whom he now rests assert, he is now of great influence with God, as is proved by many signs. This I know truly: God does not exact punishment twice from one guilty person for the same thing.

47. Reader, so that you may learn from me about the reverence for the aforementioned martyrs, which shines forth clearly in the older books, I shall relate one matter that my brother Brun told me. Educated at New Corbie and serving at its altar, he learned it from the report of his predecessors.

In the time of the aforementioned abbot Liudulf, a man worthy of great remembrance for every virtue, there was a certain young man, his fellow brother and a regular monk. While carrying the relics of the aforementioned martyrs with him in the customary manner during the duty then entrusted to him, he handled them carelessly. He soon perceived through the punishment that followed that he had sinned against Christ’s martyrs. For he dies carnally who has neglected to serve God’s saints spiritually.

[Col. 1278B] To make this known to the aforementioned abbot, the holy martyrs themselves met him at the church doors as he was going out that night. When he first saw them, he was struck with great fear, stopped, and kept silent. Immediately they said to him:

“Why do you not ask, father, who we are, or for what reason we have come here?”

When he replied that he did not dare to ask, he immediately heard from them their names and the reason for their coming, and that this would not be left unpunished.

When they departed, the abbot told these things to his brothers, saying:

“That young man who was under our obedience has died because he failed to observe due reverence for the saints whom he carried with him. Woe to me for ever having consented to such things!”



Not long afterward a messenger came, affirmed that these things were true, and announced that the young man’s body was being brought. The venerable man neither wished to go out to meet it nor allowed the brothers to receive it in their customary manner. Instead, he angrily addressed the corpse:

“Why, insolent one, have you dared to bring negligently with you those who are held in great honor with the only-begotten Son of the living God, or, after such a crime, to come here without any humble appeal for mercy?”



The dean, excusing the dead brother as far as he could, received this answer from his father:

“My beloved brother, you know what this man did in your presence as one who served only under his master’s eye; but what he has done in your absence, you do not know. I, however, understand it fully, and inwardly lament it deeply, for I now understand that he is in severe torments. And now I humbly ask the intercession of our patron saints, so that through them divine mercy may make known to me when, once God has released him, I, a sinner, may grant him absolution and communion. It is exceedingly harsh to kick against the rack [the variant *aculeo* reads “goad”], and it is unbecoming for human beings to offer pardon when Majesty is angered.”

After these words the pious abbot went barefoot to the oratory, his special refuge in anxious circumstances. As was his custom, he mourned there for human frailty, both his own and that of others, appeased God, and released the guilty man. Then, rising immediately with many acts of thanksgiving, he remitted the crime of the deceased by divine authority before all the brothers and granted his body communion with the church and burial.

48. [Col. 1279B] Now, reader, you have heard of the grave punishment for contempt of the saints; you will now receive a healing medicine arising from continual love.

Long ago, in the time of Abbot Godescalc, there was a certain monk named Alvricus. A migraine greatly afflicted his head; it is of two kinds, arising either from gout or from worms.



But when his brothers were watching over him, already almost at the point of death, it happened by chance that they went out separately and left him alone. Then demons emerged from the sewer, carrying individual books in their hands; by reading from them gravely, they vainly terrified the sick man with his deeds written therein. But the renowned martyr of Christ, Vitus, entered immediately, drove them away with a gesture of his hand, stood beside the sick man, and consoled him. He promptly told him who he was, gave him a blessing, ordered him to rise, and commanded him to deliver these instructions quickly to the aforementioned abbot:

“See to it that you do not receive so carelessly all our admonitions, lest afterward you groan with empty lamentation. For I truly declare to you: if you are any longer disobedient to me, you will be despised by God, and while you are still alive you will see another lord in your seat.”

When the holy boy had foretold this through the sick monk, the negligent abbot afterward understood it. 

It is therefore exceedingly salutary to observe the frequent exhortations of good men—how much more those of men who, by their merits, have happily been counted among the children of God and know his will in the outcome of future events. Whoever is reckless and does not rely on wise counsel will see what he is in himself. We have many examples of such people, which lead their imitators to a hard-earned prize when the final things arrive.

49. [Col. 1280A] Gisilero, the archbishop, was very dear to the often-mentioned Augustus a fact which at first secretly stung Margrave Ekkihard; later Ekkihard’s resentment gradually emerged, when he realized with great pain that Gisilero was preferred to him in everything.

Meanwhile, the subjects of the aforementioned count committed a theft in a town called Goresin. Our people did not leave the matter unpunished. They accused the culprits before their fellow countrymen and hanged them; they had failed to notify the aforesaid lord as justice required.

Because of this the count’s anger, not yet extinguished, was inflamed, and his soldier was ordered to arm himself to exact vengeance. Rambaldus, uniquely beloved by him, gathered a great multitude, surrounded the aforesaid village, seized all the men together with the goods they possessed, and led them away with him to his own city. He released none of them unless a heavy ransom subsequently redeemed him.

When I asked our people, who were complaining to me about the matter, how such a crime could be reconciled, I heard from them that no satisfaction followed, and I groaned bitterly. If divine law had any authority in this province, secular power would not rage in such a manner. I declare to those living now and to those yet to come that this case cannot grow old or be lawfully concluded without priestly correction. Everyone may remain silent as much as he wishes, but he cannot transfer to his successor an unexamined account. Wherever anything of this kind arises, it is there brought to an end by canonical authority.

If the will of the co-bishops agreed—as is read in the Acts of the Apostles—the stubborn presumption of the wicked would not be strengthened in this way. When one of those wrongdoers is rightly opposed by someone else, he is defended by whatever means possible. This is not an excuse, but an unjust strengthening of something much worse, harmful to themselves in the future.

Therefore let those who faithfully believe in unity return to unanimity, so that they may more forcefully confound the poisonous conspiracy of the perverse. Let these words suffice.

50. [Col. 1281A] Now I shall say a few things about a certain brother of mine named Conrad, lest he be in any way forgotten by me; he loved his neighbors in obedience to the divine command. He was the maternal uncle of Archbishop Gero, and in him will and ability came together equally for the perpetual service of Christ, insofar as this can occur in a human being. 

I very often heard him say that, after he had publicly completed something by singing or reading, he eagerly wished to do it again. He was never disobedient to his superiors, but with continual charity he subjected them, together with the other brothers, to himself. But as soon as this most venerable person first became known to the aforementioned emperor, he was immediately loved by him and joined to his intimacy.

Premature death prevented him from receiving the dignity that he desired and that the Augustus had proposed for him, and carried him away from this light on the fifth day before the Kalends of September. Born in Saxony, he rests in Italy; illustrious Parthenopolis weeps for him as a spiritual son.

51. What excellent nobles I saw in this city, whose praiseworthy life I neither imitated as duty required nor duly commemorated them after the dissolution of their flesh. (f. 80) Woe to me, wretched man! I, who undeservedly have been joined in brotherhood with so many and such great men, am nevertheless far different from them in a worthy manner of life.

[Col. 1282A] I, already almost dead in sins, hope to live in the radiant presence of God, refreshed by their merits, because, although I have done little good in this world, I have nevertheless always remembered the dead. My will is sometimes good; but because I do not take care to supply it with suitable strength, it accomplishes little. I always accuse myself, but I do not discharge my guilt as I ought. I therefore need correction in everything, because I do not turn to him who is praiseworthy above all.

Recognize, reader, the nobleman [*procerem*]—and you will see in me a little human being, deformed in the left jaw and on that same side, for from there a constantly swelling fistula burst forth long ago.
