My nose, broken in childhood, makes me ridiculous. I would have complained about none of this if something within me shone.

Now I am wretched, exceedingly irascible, and inflexible toward better things; envious, mocking others while myself deserving mockery; sparing no one as duty requires; a glutton [*glutto*]——and a pretender; greedy and a slanderer. To conclude these insults deservedly directed against me, I am worse than can be said or in any way estimated. 

Let it be permitted for everyone not merely to mutter, but rather to speak openly, because I am a sinner; and after fraternal correction it is fitting humbly to pray. Many are praised by the people; only a few things stand in their way, so that they would be counted among the best. Since it is true that human beings fall far short of due perfection, what benefit is there in proclaiming such a thing about those who are inferior?

All praise is sung at the end, and moral conduct is tested by fire. 

# BOOK FIVE



[Col. 1281C] After overcoming boyhood, Heinric, sprung from royal stock, 
ascends the heights of virtue.

His father was Duke Heinric, and his mother was Gisla, 
who by her merits equaled the footsteps of King Conrad, 
her father, who held the kingdoms of Burgundy.

Bishop Wolfgangus nurtures his illustrious pupil, 
and he follows Christ the Lord with all his strength.

After his father’s death, he succeeded to hereditary rule, 
and also looks afar toward the helm of empire. 

A great part of the kingdom, devastated by the cruel Slav, 
rejoices greatly because, in the abodes it desired, 
it enjoys his peace and justice, 
the haughty plunderers utterly driven away 
and subdued under a dreadful law. 

He crushes all the enemies who rise against him, 
and wins over all his allies with joyful speech.

If he errs in anything slight, he immediately comes to his senses; 
with worthy fruits he tended the wounds of the flesh.

Useful to the Church, he has compassion everywhere for all. 
O Merseburg, if you knew this ruler’s pious desires, 
you would thirst for the arrival of so great a leader, 
praise the illustrious gifts of Christ, 
and offer worthy rewards.

## Textual notes

[Note: 1. Col. 1271; at *et hortatu gener Heinrici, ducis Bawariorum, Waic*. 1b adds the name *Waic*.]

[Note: 2. Col. 1272D; at *et hortatu gener Heinrici, ducis Bawariorum, Waic*. The Saxon Annals under 999 add *Rex Pannoniae*, “king of Pannonia.”]

[Note: 3. Col. 1273; at *occidens, caeterosque fugans, pauperes Christi in hoc*. 1b adds *hoc*, “this,” in “this world.”]

[Note: 4. Col. 1273; at *misericors (f. 72) Deus, et hos honorantes*. 1a writes *honerantes* for *honorantes*, “those honoring.”]

[Note: 5. Col. 1273; at *Mahtild nomine, Herimanni comitis palatini filio Ezoni*. 1a has *ezone* for *Ezoni*, “to Ezo,” with an ablative rather than dative ending.]

[Note: 6. Col. 1273D; at *vilesceret innata sibi a parentibus summis gloria*. On these matters compare the monk of Brauweiler in Leibniz, *Writers on the History of Brunswick*, I, p. 313 and following.]

[Note: 7. Col. 1273D; at *In temporibus suis Conradus, Suevorum ductor egrejius*. Conrad died in 997; see Hermann the Lame and the Fulda Necrology. Specifically on 15 December; see the Merseburg Necrology.]

[Note: 8. Col. 1273D; at *frater Heribertus comes, necnon Hodo inclitus marchio*. Hodo died on 13 March 993, according to the Luneburg Necrology. Compare Leutsch, *Margrave Gero*, p. 136 and elsewhere. The note continues into col. 1274D.]

[Note: 9. Col. 1273; at *marchio , pro dolor! morte momentanea depressi*. 1c has *depressi*, “overwhelmed”; 1a writes *depresi*.]

[Note: 10. Col. 1274D; at *autem, predicti marchionis filius, in Nova urbe*. Munchen-Nienburg in the duchy of Anhalt.]

[Note: 11. Col. 1273; at *et Gisilero archipresule vocatus ad sinodum, Parthenopolim*. 1 has *parthepolim* for *Parthenopolim*, the name Parthenopolis, Magdeburg, in the accusative.]

[Note: 12. Col. 1274D; at *sedulo vidisset, mortuo predictae civitatis antistite Hillibaldo*. Hillibald died on 4 August 998; see the Fulda and Merseburg Necrologies. The Luneburg Necrology gives 3 August.]

[Note: 13. Col. 1274D; at *annum sedens, in Italia obiit, ibidem sepultus*. Francho died on 28 August 999, according to the Fulda Necrology.]

[Note: 14. Col. 1273; at *pietate tamen sua apud Deum omnipotentem recordentur*. 1a reads *recordarentur*, “might remember,” imperfect subjunctive, for *recordentur*, “may remember,” present subjunctive.]

[Note: 15. Col. 1273; at *sua apud Deum omnipotentem recordentur mei. Agnosco*. The entire passage from *Agnosco* to *potest* is written in another hand: the narrator’s self-knowledge and appeal to righteous intercessors, the two chaplains’ proposed appointment and death without consecration, and his acknowledgment that God alone ordained and knows these things.]

[Note: 16. Col. 1273; at *quam debeo ac in baculi fragilitate harundinei*. 1 has *harundei* for *harundinei*, “of reed.”]

[Note: 17. Col. 1273; at *relinquitur, et ante translationem meam non videbit*. 1b adds *non videbit*, “will not see.”]

[Note: 18. Col. 1273; at *De quorum numero quaedam cometissa, nomine Christiana*. The printed name *Christiana* is attributed to 1b (?) and the Saxon Annals. The note records *cristina* in 1a and again *cristina* as the reading after correction by erasure; that apparent repetition is in the source.]

[Note: 19. Col. 1273; at *Christiana , predii suimet, quod in Stuwi*. 1a spells Stuwi *stuui*.]

[Note: 20. Col. 1274D; at *Christiana , predii suimet, quod in Stuwi*. Stoeben, a Thuringian village near Camburg on the Saale. URS.]

[Note: 21. Col. 1273; at *thalamum sponsi gaudens venit; quod Gisilero archipresuli*. 1a reads *archipresule*, ablative “archbishop,” for *archipresuli*, dative “to the archbishop.”]

[Note: 22. Col. 1273; at *sponsi gaudens venit; quod Gisilero archipresuli tunc*. 1b adds *tunc*, “then,” before “of Parthenopolis.”]

[Note: 23. Col. 1275; at *esse completam. Haec bona quaeque conscientiae tegens*. 2 has *legens*, “reading” or “gathering,” for *tegens*, “concealing.”]

[Note: 24. Col. 1275; at *conscientiae tegens secreto suae, fuit caeteris matronibus*. 1c has *matronis* for *matronibus*, both intended as “married women” in the dative/ablative plural.]

[Note: 25. Col. 1275; at *fuit caeteris matronibus , quae apud modernos*. 1a has *modernas*, feminine “contemporary,” for *modernos*, masculine “contemporaries.”]

[Note: 26. Col. 1275; at *circumcincta, quod venale habet in se, cunctis*. 2 reads “dishonorably dressed, and [showing] her shame to all as though she had it for sale”: *inhonesta circumcincta turpitudinemque suam quasi eam venalem habeat cunctis*. The following verb completes the construction in the base text.]

[Note: 27. Col. 1275; at *omni pudore coram procedit speculum tocius populi*. 2 reads “she comes forward and irreverently puts on display before the whole people what she ought to be ashamed of.”]

[Note: 28. Col. 1275; at *3.), quod peccator unusquisque non vult delitescere*. 1c has *delitescere*, “to hide”; 1a spells it *delitiscere*.]

[Note: 29. Col. 1275; at *diebus illis nupsit Mahtild sanctimonialis, filia Thiederici*. The first *e* in *Thiederici*, “of Thiederic,” is erased; no witness is specified.]

[Note: 30. Col. 1275; at *marchionis, cuidam Sclawo, nomine Prebizlavo. Quae post*. 1b adds *Quae post*, “She afterward.”]

[Note: 31. Col. 1275; at *Sclawo, nomine Prebizlavo. Quae post a Brennebrugensis*. 1c has *brandeburgensis* for *Brennebrugensis*, “of Brandenburg.”]

[Note: 32. Col. 1275; at *Brennebrugensis injusto provisore (f. 74) civitatis Bolibuto*. 1 corrects the name *boliuuto* to *bolibuto*, “by Bolibut.”]

[Note: 33. Col. 1275D; at *injusto provisore (f. 74) civitatis Bolibuto ,*. Compare above, IV, 15.]

[Note: 34. Col. 1275; at *tantae solutionem miseriae et abbaciam in Magadaburg*. 1b adds *et abbaciam in Magadaburg*, “and the abbacy in Magdeburg.”]

[Note: 35. Col. 1275D; at *tantae solutionem miseriae et abbaciam in Magadaburg*. The abbey of Saint Lawrence in the new city of Magdeburg, formerly governed by Brigid, mentioned in Book One. KIND.]

[Note: 36. Col. 1275; at *in Magadaburg indigna percepit. Cujus vir antea*. 1b has *antea*, “earlier”; 1a has *post hec*, “after this.”]

[Note: 37. Col. 1275D; at *Ugione ac Ufficone 5 Kalendas Januarii occubuit*. The Luneburg Necrology reads: “The third day before the Kalends of January: Prebeszlaus, our brother.” As son-in-law of Dieteric, margrave of the northern march, he must be regarded as related by marriage to the Billungs. WED. The note continues into col. 1276D.]

[Note: 38. Col. 1275; at *re laudanda virtus Christi cognoscitur, quae servienti*. 1a has *servientibus*, “to those serving,” plural, for *servienti*, “to one serving,” singular.]

[Note: 39. Col. 1275; at *monachico se nimis peccasse, facta confessione tunc*. 1b adds *tunc*, “then,” at Hepo’s confession and lament.]

[Note: 40. Col. 1275; at *post Nonas Januarii obiit, sepultus ad sanctum*. 1a has *sanctam*, feminine “saint,” for *sanctum*, masculine, before John.]

[Note: 41. Col. 1276D; at *dies 2 Nonas Septembris spiritum fidelem exalavit*. See the Merseburg Calendar. The printed *V.* means “see,” not a date “fifth day before the Kalends.”]

[Note: 42. Col. 1275; at *Mauricium, dampni subsequentis non ignoret periculum. Hujus*. The entire passage from *Hujus* to *superpositus*—the youth’s attempt to steal the treasure, the encouraging voice, theft of the crown, capture, breaking of his legs, and exposure on the wheel—is written in another hand.]

[Note: 43. Col. 1275; at *post retulit, vocem quandam ad haec audacter*. 1b has *audacter*, “boldly”; 1a has *fiducialiter*, “confidently.”]

[Note: 44. Col. 1275; at *ibidem corona, celeriter in ipsa est captus*. A. S. under 999 adds *ecclesia*, “church,” after “in that very.”]

[Note: 45. Col. 1275; at *constantia Huswardi; ad quem juxta me tunc*. 1b adds *me tunc*, “me then,” in “beside me then sleeping.”]

[Note: 46. Col. 1276D; at *perciperet, postulavit. Tunc is: Consimili, infit, bravio*. That is, *brabeo*, a prize or reward.]

[Note: 47. Col. 1275; at *esse comperiret, nobis omnibus et antecedens ac*. 1b adds *ac*, “and,” between the preceding and subsequent events.]

[Note: 48. Col. 1275; at *cum omni dominica die ad dormitorium illud*. 1b adds *illud*, “that,” qualifying the dormitory.]

[Note: 49. Col. 1275; at *Quem agonizantem mater sua, Berhta nomine, jam*. 1b adds *jam*, “already,” before “very old.”]

[Note: 50. Col. 1277D; at *militis, cui prius oculos abstulit marchio Ekkihardus*. Compare the Quedlinburg Annals, 780 and 827. These are the years as printed in the supplied note.]

[Note: 51. Col. 1277; at *sequi deberet, ni modo in limine Ludgeri*. 1a spells *Ludgeri*, “of Ludger,” as *luderi*.]

[Note: 52. Col. 1277; at *confessoris predicti, qui locum hunc, Helmanstidi vocatum*. 1b adds *Helmanstidi vocatum*, “called Helmanstidi.”]

[Note: 53. Col. 1277; at *qui locum hunc, Helmanstidi vocatum , proprietate*. 1b and A. S. have *proprietate*, “property”; 1a has *pietate*, “piety.”]

[Note: 54. Col. 1277; at *Halverstedensis aecclesiae rectoris primi, quam tenuit 47*. 1 reads *XL et VI*, “forty-six,” instead of forty-seven.]

[Note: 55. Col. 1277; at *aecclesiae rectoris primi, quam tenuit 47 annos,*. 1b adds *annos*, “years.”]

[Note: 56. Col. 1277; at *imperatore pio, Dominicae incarnationis 827 anno. Liuderus*. 1c reads the name *Liudigerus* for *Liuderus*.]

[Note: 57. Col. 1277; at *Wirdunun ex propriis constructo inpensis, anno dominicae*. Supply *incarnationis*, “of the Incarnation,” after “of the Lord.”]

[Note: 58. Col. 1277D; at *inpensis, anno dominicae 808 praemium coeleste recepit*. Quedlinburg Annals, 809.]

[Note: 59. Col. 1277; at *coeleste recepit . Post quem predictus imperator*. 1c adds *Karolus sanctus*, “Saint Charles.”]

[Note: 60. Col. 1277; at *vixerat annos, emittens spiritum 5 Kalendas Februarii*. 1c adds “that is, the octave of Agnes”; in the margin it adds: “The translation of Saint Charles is on the sixth day before the Kalends of August.”]

[Note: 61. Col. 1277D; at *vixerat annos, emittens spiritum 5 Kalendas Februarii*. From the Quedlinburg Annals, 814.]

[Note: 62. Col. 1277; at *imperii vero 14. Predictus autem presbiter in*. 1b (?) has *in*, “in,” after another word was erased.]

[Note: 63. Col. 1277; at *obiit. Haec quae de confratribus meis dixit*. 1a has *dix* for *dixit*, literally “he said”; in context the narrator means “I have said.”]

[Note: 64. Col. 1277D; at *locutus sum. 46. Regnante tertio Ottone, Albi*. Perhaps the Alwi named in the Merseburg Necrology under 17 December. The note continues into col. 1278D.]

[Note: 65. Col. 1277; at *Regnante tertio Ottone, Albi , filius Guncelim*. 1a gives the name as *guncelino*, rather than *Guncelim*; the printed apparatus reads *guncelino ab 1a*. Both refer to Guncelin.]

[Note: 66. Col. 1277; at *accepit. Hujus camerarius et confrater meus Gunterus*. An *i* is erased in the name Gunterus in 1.]

[Note: 67. Col. 1277; at *confrater meus Gunterus , mortuo Dodone Asanbrunensis*. 1a writes *asanbruniensis* for *Asanbrunensis*, “of Osnabrück.”]

[Note: 68. Col. 1278D; at *Gunterus , mortuo Dodone Asanbrunensis aecclesiae episcopo*. Dodo died on 12 April 996.]

[Note: 69. Col. 1275; at *et si suum vellet accipere episcopatum interrogantes*. 1b adds *interrogantes*, “asking.”]

[Note: 70. Col. 1277; at *est ab hiis duabus hastis; et mox*. 1b (?) has *mox*, “immediately,” after another word was erased.]

[Note: 71. Col. 1277; at *caesar ut ejus infirmitatem comperit, fidele promissum*. 1 writes *promisum* for *promissum*, “promise.”]

[Note: 72. Col. 1277; at *temporalia in aeternaliter manentia. Nescio, si quid*. 1 abbreviates *quid*, “anything,” as *qd*.]

[Note: 73. Col. 1277; at *vindicat Deus in id ipsum. 47. Predictorum*. 1b wrote the entire passage from *Predictorum* through *more secum*: the introduction to the martyrs’ reverence, Brun’s report, Liudulf’s time, and the monk carrying the relics with him in the customary manner. *more secum* means “in the manner … with him”; these are the end words marking the span, not a reading inserted after *Predictorum*.]

[Note: 74. Col. 1278D; at *suorum mihi indicavit. Tempore predicti abbatis Liudulfi*. See above, II, 12.]

[Note: 75. Col. 1277; at *qui sanctis Dei servire neglexit spiritualiter. Et*. 2 and A. S. add *ipsi martyres sancti*, “the holy martyrs themselves.”]

[Note: 76. Col. 1277; at *spiritualiter. Et ut hoc predicto abbati innotescerent*. 1a has *et notescerent*, “and they might become known,” for *innotescerent*, here “they might make [it] known.”]

[Note: 77. Col. 1277; at *abbati innotescerent ante januas aecclesiae exeunti illo*. 1c has *illi*, “to him,” for *illo*, “he,” in the ablative construction describing his going out.]

[Note: 78. Col. 1277; at *in nostra nunc erat obedientia, de incustodita*. 1a has the defective *inta*, corrected by 1b by writing *custodi* above to form *incustodita*, “not observed.” From this 1c made *de neglecta custodia sanctorum quos secum habuit et reverentia*, “because of neglected care and reverence for the saints whom he carried with him” (abbreviated *s. q. s. h. et r.*). A. S. under 990 has *ob incustoditam sanctorum quos secum habuit reverentiam*, “because due reverence was not observed for the saints whom he carried with him” (the relative clause is abbreviated *s. q. s. h.*).]

[Note: 79. Col. 1277; at *haec vera esse affirmaret et corpus ejusdem*. 1b adds *ejusdem*, “of the same man,” qualifying his body.]

[Note: 80. Col. 1277; at *Venerabilis autem vir nec huic obviam exire*. 1a spells *exire*, “to go out,” as *exhire*.]

[Note: 81. Col. 1277; at *illud suscipere sinit; sed iratus ad truncum*. 1a has *tractum*, “dragged,” for *truncum*, “trunk” or “corpse”; 2 and A. S. at the cited place have *truncum corporis*, “the trunk of the body.”]

[Note: 82. Col. 1279; at *absentialiter fecerit, ignoras; ego autem optime perpendo*. 2 and A. S. at the cited place add *et intime ingemisco*, “and I groan inwardly.”]

[Note: 83. Col. 1279; at *et communionem dare. Asperum nimis est eculeo*. 2 and A. S. at the cited place have *aculeo*, “goad,” for *eculeo*, “rack.”]

[Note: 84. Col. 1279; at *salubrem medicinam. Fuit olim sub tempore Godescalki*. The *c* in Godescalk’s name is erased in 1.]

[Note: 85. Col. 1279D; at *medicinam. Fuit olim sub tempore Godescalki abbatis*. Abbot of Corvey, 890–913.]

[Note: 86. Col. 1279; at *monachus nomine Alvricus, cui in capite suo*. 1b adds *suo*, “his own,” qualifying the head.]

[Note: 87. Col. 1279; at *est, aut ex gutta, aut ex vermibus*. 2 gives the following, agreeing with A. S. under 891: “Worms. Some advised that, as a remedy, his head should be cut open. This was done, but day by day the pain increased until he despaired. But … it happened that, as they went out one by one, they left him lying there alone. Then he saw seven exceedingly hideous demons emerge from the sewer. Six of them each carried six books in their hands, thirty-six in all. The seventh carried a volume of immense size and sat down; by its grave reading he tried in vain to terrify the sick man with his actions, everything he had ever done from infancy to that hour in thought, word, or deed. For the precious martyr Vitus, clothed in a shining garment and glorious with an angelic face, entered from the church adjoining the cell where the sick man lay, and with his hand ordered the unclean crowd to flee.” The abbreviated *singuli e. h. d. s. jacentem r.* is expanded from the parallel text as “going out one by one, they left him alone, lying there.” The same manuscript continues AFTER THE WORDS *dominum videbis*, “you will see a lord,” with: “The boy had said these things as he stood there, and soon disappeared. What the precious martyr—the boy Vitus, I mean—announced through the sick monk, the negligent abbot later experienced. For while he was still alive, at his own request the venerable Abbot Bovo, a man most worthy of all praise, was appointed in his place. Hence, therefore, the frequent exhortations of good men …” The abbreviations *p. m. e.*, *a. n. p. p.*, and *c. h. h.* stand respectively for *per monachum egrotantem*, “through the sick monk”; *abbas neglegens postea persensit*, “the negligent abbot later experienced”; and *crebros hortatus hominum*, “the frequent exhortations of men,” completed by the adjacent *bonorum*, “good.” These are abbreviated parallels to the base narrative, not lost sentences.]

[Note: 88. Col. 1279; at *demones, libros speciales in manibus habentes, eorumque*. The suffix *-que*, “and,” is erased in *eorumque*, “and of them,” in 1.]

[Note: 89. Col. 1279; at *inclitus Christi martir Vitus ilico ingressus, eisdem*. 1a has *easdem*, feminine “the same,” for *eisdem*, dative “to the same [demons].”]

[Note: 90. Col. 1279; at *haec mandata predicto abbati celeriter deferre: Videsis*. *-sis* in *Videsis*, “see to it,” is erased in 1, leaving *Vide*, “see.”]

[Note: 91. Col. 1279; at *mihi eris, a Deo contempneris, et te*. 1c adds *te*, “you.”]

[Note: 92. Col. 1279; at *tua sede dominum videbis. Haec ut puer*. 1a has *vir*, “man,” for *puer*, “boy.”]

[Note: 93. Col. 1279; at *sanctus per monachum egrotantem prenotavit, abbas neglegens*. 1c (?) spells *neglegens*, “negligent,” as *negligens*.]

[Note: 94. Col. 1279; at *78') computati voluntatem ejus sciunt in eventu*. 1c has *eventu*, “outcome”; 1a has the defective *cointu*.]

[Note: 95. Col. 1279; at *temerarius sapienti non innititur consilio, videbit quis*. 1 spells *quis*, “who,” as *qis*.]

[Note: 96. Col. 1279; at *sine gravi dolore persensit. Interim predicti comitis*. 1c writes *ek.* above *comitis*, “of the count,” identifying the count as Ekkihard. It is not written over Goresin.]

[Note: 97. Col. 1280D; at *subditi quoddam furtum in oppido Goresin dicto*. Görschen.]

[Note: 98. Col. 1279; at *Ob hoc furor comitis nondum extinctus accenditur*. 1 spells *accenditur*, “is inflamed,” as *acenditur*.]

[Note: 99. Col. 1279; at *ejusdem haec ad vindicanda armari jubetur. Rambaldus*. 1c (?) spells Rambaldus *ramboldus*.]

[Note: 100. Col. 1279; at *lex divina, non sic insaniret secularis potentia*. 1 has the defective *potentencia* for *potentia*, “power.”]

[Note: 101. Col. 1279; at *nequaquam valet abalienare; et in quocumque loco*. 1a reads *loca*, plural “places,” for *loco*, “place,” in the ablative.]

[Note: 102. Col. 1279; at *valet abalienare; et in quocumque loco aliquid*. 1 reads *aliquid*, “anything,” as in the text.]

[Note: 103. Col. 1279; at *oritur, ibi canonica auctoritate finitur. Si consentiret*. 1 has *sic sentiret*, “he might think thus”; 1c corrected it by putting a line above the *c*. 2 has *si consentiret*, “if [the will] agreed.”]

[Note: 104. Col. 1279; at *alio, quolibetcumque id fieri potest modo, defenditur*. 1 has *descenditur*, “one goes down,” apparently corrected by 1c to *defenditur*, “he is defended.” 2 gives the passage as: “he is opposed by one of the bishops; by whatever means it can be done, the others give way to him. And this is not compassion, but …”]

[Note: 105. Col. 1281; at *Nunc (f. 79') autem de quodam confratre*. 1a has *confre*, an abbreviated or defective form of *confratre*, “brother.”]

[Note: 106. Col. 1281; at *confratre meo, nomine Conrado, pauca loquar, ne*. 1 has *ni*, “unless,” for *ne*, “lest.”]

[Note: 107. Col. 1281; at *fuit, et ad peragendam jugem Christi servitutem*. 1c has *servitutem*, “service”; 1a has the defective *servitem*.]

[Note: 108. Col. 1281; at *prepositis suimet erat, sed eos charitate continua*. 1a has *continuo*, “continually” or masculine/neuter “continuous,” for *continua*, feminine “continuous,” agreeing with “charity.”]

[Note: 109. Col. 1281; at *mors inmatura inpedit, eundemque ab hac luce*. 1 has *lucem*, accusative “light,” for *luce*, ablative, after “from.”]

[Note: 110. Col. 1281; at *carnis (f. 80) assequutus. Heu me misero*. 1c has *miserum*, accusative “wretched,” for *misero*, dative/ablative, in “Woe to wretched me!”]

[Note: 111. Col. 1281; at *est; sed quia eidem vires aptas suggerere*. 1c has *suggerere*, “to supply”; 1a has *suggere*.]

[Note: 112. Col. 1281; at *non solvo; sumque ideo in omnibus corrigibilis*. 2 has *incorrigibilis*, “incorrigible,” for *corrigibilis*, “needing correction” or “capable of correction.”]

[Note: 113. Col. 1281D; at *eum qui est super omnia laudabilis. Agnosce*. Taken from Juvenal, *Satire* VIII, line 26, *Agnosco procerem*, “I recognize the nobleman,” and applied ironically to himself. Uns.]

[Note: 114. Col. 1281; at *super omnia laudabilis. Agnosce , lector, procerem*. 1c has *proceritatem*, “tallness” or “stature,” for *procerem*, “nobleman.”]

[Note: 115. Col. 1281; at *eodem, quia hinc olim erupit semper turgescens*. 1c has *turgescens*, “swelling”; 1a has *turgencens*.]

[Note: 116. Col. 1281D; at *ipse deridendus, nulli pro debito parcens, glutto*. *Gluto*, “glutton,” is taken from Persius, *Satire* V, line 112.]

[Note: 117. Col. 1281; at *sum quam possit dici vel ullatenus estimari*. In 1, nearly two and a half lines after *simulator*, “pretender,” through *estimari*, “to be estimated,” have been erased. The words *avarus* through *ut haec*—“greedy and a slanderer, and to [conclude] these …”—cannot be clearly distinguished, but survive in 2, which ends *q. d. p. v. estimari*: *quam dici potest vel estimari*, “than can be said or estimated.”]

[Note: 118. Col. 1281; at *. Unicuique sit fas non solum muttire*. 1a writes *mutture* for *muttire*, “to mutter.”]

[Note: 119. Col. 1281; at *solum muttire , quin pocius in aperto*. 1c has *aperto*, “openly”; 1a has *apto*, “fitting.”]

[Note: 120. Col. 1281; at *hominibus de perfectione justa nimis deesse, quid*. 1 reads *quid*, “what,” as in the text at “what does it profit?”]

[Note: 121. Col. 1281; at *quid prodest de inferioribus hiis tale quid*. 1 reads *quid*, “something,” as in the text at “such a thing.”]

[Note: 122. Col. 1281; at *fine canitur, et moralis conversacio igne probatur*. After *probatur*, “is tested,” Thietmar’s own hand added the following, all subsequently erased: “Virgin without equal, gentle among all, free us from our faults and make us gentle and just.”]

[Note: 123. Col. 1281; at *moralis conversacio igne probatur . LIBER QUINTUS*. 2 has “Here begins the prologue of Book Five,” and at its end, “Here begins Book Five.”]

[Note: 124. Col. 1281; at *scandit, postquam puerilia vicit, Ardua virtutum cretus*. 1b or 1c has *cretus*, “sprung”; 1a has *natus*, “born.”]

[Note: 125. Col. 1281D; at *patris, Burgundia regna tenentis. Nutrit preclarum Wolfgangus*. Wolfgang, bishop of Regensburg.]

[Note: 126. Col. 1282D; at *Christum. Postque necem patris ductor successit herilis*. In the duchy of Bavaria, namely in 995.]

[Note: 127. Col. 1282D; at *Ejus et imperium longe spectat quoque clavum*. That is, the helm of the kingdom.]

[Note: 128. Col. 1282D; at *ab hujus pace potitur Sedibus optatis justoque*. That is, justice.]

[Note: 129. Col. 1282D; at *potitur Sedibus optatis justoque , rapacibus altis*. Proud and rapacious men.]

1. (f. 81r) The bountiful regard of divine mercy, overflowing toward human need—not because of our merit, but through the free gift of its compassion—kindles the hearts of its faithful to love its praise and to render thanks to it. It compels me also, foolish in understanding, impeded in speech, negligent in all things [Note: 1c perhaps reads *negligentem*], and excessively idle, to imitate the good in this respect. For “Great is God” [Note: 1a reads *Magnum*, “great”], as David testifies, “and greatly to be praised” (Psalm 95:4); no number can be found for his wisdom, by which he created all things from nothing and fashioned man alone [Note: literally, “man only,” or “man in particular”; cf. 2 Maccabees 7:28]. Whoever, forgetful of benefits, does not consider such things is rightly called an animal rotting in its own dung [Note: *inmemor beneficiorum*; 1c reads *inmemor beiciorum*]. But whoever strives to retain within himself in memory the saying “Know yourself” (*γνῶθι σεαυτόν*; *gnoti seauton*) [Note: 1 reads *gnotis eaucton*], anciently inscribed upon the temple lintels [Note: Our author seems to have consulted Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.6], and diligently endeavors to fulfill in the name of the Lord all that must be done in word or deed (Colossians 3:17), as holy Paul exhorts—that person is the one whom God the Father has chosen for the Son and rewards with the daily denarius, even though he comes late (Matthew 20:2).

Considering these things, and since I am wholly unable to respond with fitting recompense to the Holy Trinity and undivided Unity, I humbly implore the intercession of Saint John the Baptist (f. 82), so that I may be made fit for this in heart and body. Concerning these times, however, in which God looked upon our church and deigned to remove its reproach, I endeavor, with a more joyful mind and a more flowing pen, to reveal the piety of Duke Heinricus, chosen for the kingdom by the highest ordering [Note: “by divine predestination,” 1a].

Concerning him, after the emperor’s death, this was said by divine revelation to a certain venerable father:

“Do you remember, brother, how the people sang: ‘Although God did not will it, Duke Heinricus wished to reign’? But now Heinricus must, by divine predestination [Note: 1b has the words *divina predestinacione* inserted in a blank space], provide for the care of the kingdom.”

Everything pertaining to divine or human affairs promoted him above all his contemporaries toward the kingdom, whether they wished it or not. But lest anyone from our region should raise an objection against him, I shall briefly set forth and unravel the unjust presumption of the Westerners, who were able to achieve nothing against God by counsel, prudence, or courage.

2. Herimannus (1002) [Note: in manuscript 1, an *i* is erased, repeatedly], duke of Alamannia and Alsace, a God-fearing and humble man, was led astray by many who admired his gentleness and took up arms against Heinricus. Theodericus, however, duke of the Liutharians [Note: perhaps *Liuthariorum*, with the initial *L* missing in 1c], a wise and military man, confidently awaited the outcome, since the greater and better part of the people was inclining toward him.

Meanwhile my uncle, whom I mentioned above [Note: Margrave Liutharius; see above, Book IV, chapter 25], secretly set out for Bavanberg with his own uncle Ricbertus [Note: Count Ricbertus in the Hartgau; see the emperor’s charter of April 15, 1003. His date of death is given in the *Necrology of Lüneburg*, February 9], whom the emperor had removed from his county, giving that county to Liudgerus, the soldier of Bishop Arnulf [Note: of Halberstadt]. He had thereby obtained the duke’s favor [Note: namely, Heinricus’s] and the hope of retaining and enlarging his benefice. Although, while still observing his oath, he had not yet laid hands upon him [Note: this is the reading required by the *Annals of Saxony* for 1002; manuscript 1 has *quam* followed by a lacuna], he nevertheless achieved this with the aid of his nephew Heinricus [Note: the verb *est* is to be supplied, as in the *Annals of Quedlinburg*].

At his counsel, the duke sent a certain soldier to the city called Werlu, to his nieces, the sisters Sophia and Ethelheidis [Note: They were daughters of Emperor Otto II, and thus cousins of the quarrelsome Duke Heinricus], and to all the leading men of the kingdom who had then gathered there [Note: 1a reads *primatis*]. When all had assembled together, the soldier disclosed his embassy and, with the help of their own lord, promised them many good things if they would assist him in obtaining the kingdom. At once a single voice came from the very great multitude:

“Heinricus will reign by Christ’s assistance and by hereditary right; and we are ready for everything that we have ever known to be his will.”

They confirmed this by raising their right hands.

3. Since Ekkihardus and his men were not present, they endured this at the time with feigned patience, because, as Scripture testifies, whatever is sinned by many goes unavenged [Note: *in ultum* is apparently corrupt for *inultum*]. But when evening had already come, and the ladies mentioned above [Note: 1 and 2 read *dominis*; 1c and the *Annals of Saxony* read *dominabus*, “ladies”; the *Annals* also read *sororibus*, “sisters”] were seated in a great house, with the seats of the hall adorned with tapestries and the table laden with various foods, Ekkihardus forestalled them and dined there with Bishop Arnulfus and Duke Bernhardus (f. 83).

“For before ruin the heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled” (Proverbs 18:4).

This greatly disturbed the minds of the sisters, who had earlier been saddened, and of many others who were present. Hatred of him, long concealed, was renewed—though, alas, it was soon to end.

When the aforesaid margrave saw that everything there had turned out otherwise than he had ever hoped, he judged it best to visit the western regions and speak with Duke Herimannus and the other nobles about the welfare of the commonwealth and his own advantage. After greeting his retainers the next day and carefully noting his enemies, he came with Bishop Bernwardus [Note: the *n* was added in 1b and erased again] to Hildesheim [Note: the printed manuscript reading is *Hillin[lacuna]s[lacuna]em*; 1c reads *Hildenshem*], where he was received like a king and treated with honor.

Then, proceeding to Pathelbrunnan [Note: Paderborn], he found the gates closed. Admitted at the command of the venerable Bishop Retharius, he first entered the church for prayer. Afterwards he came to the house where the bishop was dining and was received affectionately. There he was told [Note: 1a and 2 read *interdictum*; 1c reads *dictum*, “said”; the *Annals of Saxony* have the same reading] that the meeting at Diusburg, on account of which he had come there, could in no way take place. Moreover, he perceived that the bishop was greatly displeased by his ill-considered undertaking [Note: 1a has *antisti*, corrected in 1b].

Departing for this reason, when he came to Northeim, the estate of Count Sigifridus, he was carefully received and was asked to spend the night there. Countess Ethefindis had secretly informed him that Sigifrith and Benno, her lord’s sons, together with their brothers Heinricus and Udo [Note: *of Katlenburg* is added by the *Annals of Saxony*. They seem to have been sons of Count Sigefridus from his second marriage to Ethelinda; see Schrader, *Dynastenstamme*], and other conspirators of theirs, were plotting his death and had laid ambushes for him. She earnestly begged him either to remain there until the following day or to turn aside elsewhere.

The count received this information kindly but replied that he neither could nor would interrupt his journey because of them. Immediately departing from there, he kept careful watch over his men throughout the entire day and, being an excellent soldier, warned them not to be frightened. The enemy, observing this from a distance while hidden in ambush, postponed the attack because it did not then seem advantageous to him; but on the following night he confirmed with an oath that he would persist in his undertaking.

4. The count reached the appointed place [Note: 1c reads *predestinatum*; 1a, *predistinatum*], called Palithi [Note: 1c reads *Polithi*]. When evening came, he ate and went to sleep with a few men in a wooden chamber [Note: 1c reads *paucis*; 1a, *pacis*]. Very many of the others rested in a nearby upper room.

When deep sleep weighed heavily upon them, exhausted as they were, an enemy band attacked the unsuspecting men and compelled the count, awakened by immense shouting, to rise quickly from his bed (f. 84). He supplied strength to the fire with his own breeches and with whatever else he could find. Since he could not then deliberate in advance, by breaking the windows he opened the enemy a greater means of attacking than of defending himself [Note: 1c reads *quam se defendendi*; 1a, *quam se defendi*].

Without delay the soldier Herimannus was killed before the doors [Note: 1 reads *heriman’*], and Athulfus, hastening outside to bring help to his lord—both brave men and faithful unto death—was also killed. Erminoldus, the emperor’s chamberlain, was additionally wounded [Note: He is mentioned in the *Necrology of Merseburg*, May 9]. Only Ekkihardus then resisted, a man praiseworthy at home and in war. Sifridus, with a spear hurled forcefully, broke the vertebra of his neck and compelled him to fall to the ground.

As soon as all saw what had happened, they rushed in, cut off his head, and—most pitiable of all—plundered his corpse. These events took place on the second day before the Kalends of May, that is, April 30 [Note: This date is given in the *Annals of Quedlinburg*, 1002, and in the *Necrology of Lüneburg*]. At last, after completing their monstrous crime, the killers returned joyful and unharmed [Note: *incolumes*, corrected from *incolomes* in 1]. Those who had been in the upper room were cowards: they neither helped their lord in any way while he was struggling nor attempted to avenge the dead [Note: 1c reads *ulcisci*; 1a, *ulcissi*]. The abbot of that place, named Alfkerus, visited the body and performed the commendation of the soul with the greatest devotion (f. 84r).

5. What cause persuaded these men to commit such a deed, I cannot truthfully explain. Some say that Heinricus, at the instigation of the aforesaid count, had been beaten with rods by the emperor and had often contemplated this action against him. Others maintain that, as I said earlier, because of the insult inflicted upon the sisters at Werlu—for these men gladly served them—and because of the feasts and threats he had openly made against them [Note: 1 reads *conuiua*, 1b *conniuia*, while the *Annals of Saxony* read *conuicia*, “insults”], they began this undertaking.

This alone I know: he would have been the glory of the kingdom, the consolation of his country, the hope of those entrusted to him [Note: *add.* 1b], the terror of his enemies, and in every respect most perfect, if only he had been willing to remain in humility. How admirably he conducted the course of this life, by which he acquired the greatest part of his lord’s benefice as his own property [Note: 1c reads *proprietatem*; 1a, *propietatem*]! He subjected the Milzian people, previously accustomed to freedom, to the yoke of servitude.

By flatteries and threats he won over the Bohemian duke Bolizlavus, surnamed the Red [Note: 1 reads *cognomitatur*], making him his soldier and another [Note: namely, Boleslaus, duke of Poland] his friend and intimate associate. By the common election of the entire people he earned the dukedom over all Thuringia. He held the eastern counts [Note: that is, the counties], with only a few exceptions, and the kingdom in expectation (f. 85). All these things dragged him down to such a miserable end.

When news of his death had soon spread far and wide, Lady Suonehildis came to meet him, and it disrupted the joy of her son Herimannus. For the latter, by his father’s command, had occupied Wimeri [Note: 1c reads *Wimari*] with a strong force in order to avenge the death of Widukindus and Herimannus, inflicted by his own son [Note: apparently his namesake]. He had compelled the meritorious old man to come into the presence of the aforesaid count and, by oath, to fulfill whatever the count himself demanded of him. But when he received the unexpected news of his parent’s death, he hurried with his mother to meet him. Receiving his father’s body amid immense grief, he had it buried in the city called Geni [Note: 1a reads *geniun*, which may perhaps be preferable] [Note: Grossjena, a village situated where the river Unstrut flows into the Saale]. After the thirtieth day had been completed [Note: cf. *Sachsenspiegel* I.22], Lady Suonehildis set out for Meissen with her sons.

6. Meanwhile Bolizlavus, son of Miseconis, far inferior to his father, rejoiced at the death of Count Ekkihardus. He immediately gathered an army and occupied all of Count Gero’s march lying beyond the Elbe [Note: the march meant is Lower Lusatia, which writers of that period also called the Eastern March]. Then, sending hostages ahead and taking the city of Budusin with all its dependencies, he at once attacked the city of Stricla [Note: the *i* was erased], secretly attempting to bribe the people of Meissen with money.

They, always delighting in novelty, learned one day that the greater part of the garrison had gone out to acquire fodder for the horses. They rushed in at the eastern-facing gate, at the point where the guards called in Slavonic *Vethenici* lived [Note: among the Poles, *Wodnik* or *wodnicy*, “castellan”], with Guncelinus of Cukesburg leading them for this purpose [Note: this is the correct reading; 1 reads *cukesburgiens*] [Note: Ursinus explains the Cukesburgenses as scouts or guardians of the fortress. Ciuskesburg was a *burgward* in the county of Margrave Eggihardus and later in the county of his son Count Herimannus. See the diplomas of Otto III, July 5, 993, and Heinricus II, October 17, 1012, in Hofer’s *Zeitschrift* I, 534 and 161].

They first killed Bececio [Note: this is the correct reading; 1 reads *beccionemque*, and the *Annals of Saxony* *Beccionemque*], a guard of Count Herimannus. Then all armed men gathered at his chamber, attacked the window with great stones, and loudly demanded that the lord of the city, named Ozerus [Note: the castellan of Meissen], be handed over to them for killing.

But the soldier Thietmarus, from the sole protection of the bedchamber, said:

“Why are you acting so? What madness has led you astray, that, forgetting the benefits of Count Ekkihardus and his voluntary invitation, you rise up in this way to the destruction of his son? If any one of you wishes to disclose, publicly or secretly, the cause of so great a crime, I promise firmly, on behalf of my lord and of all of us, that we will make amends for the offense and secure you against future fear, in whatever manner you wish.

“This man, whom you cruelly demand to be handed over to you for death, you shall not receive while we remain alive [Note: 1a reads *degentibus*; 2 and the *Annals of Saxony*, *quamdiu supersumus*, “as long as we survive]. We are few; know for certain either that we shall all die together or that we shall leave this city unharmed.”

Then, after hearing these words, they conferred with them [Note: 1 reads *colloquntur*]. Granting them permission to depart, they invited Duke Bolizlavus through messengers and received him with the gates open. Thus was fulfilled what is written: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in wicked things” (Proverbs 2:14); and again [Note: 2 adds, “but truly what is also written will happen to them”]: “Their beginnings are as honey, and their end as wormwood” (Proverbs 5:4) [Note: the *c* was erased].

Elated by this success, Bolizlavus occupied all the borders of that region as far as the river Elster and fortified them with his garrisons [Note: 1c reads *elatis ... Bolizlavum*; 1a apparently has the same wording]. When our people then gathered unanimously to prevent this, that deceitful man sent an envoy to meet them. The envoy declared that he had undertaken these actions with Duke Heinricus’s favor and permission; that he would harm none of the inhabitants; and that, if Heinricus ever held power in the kingdom, he would assent to his will in everything, but otherwise would gladly do whatever pleased the inhabitants at that time.

Our people, observing this, believed his embellished words [Note: from Terence, *Phormio* III.5.15, “with embellished speeches you lead me”; the same expression occurs below, VII.51], and, dishonorably, as though going to their lord, proceeded to him and exchanged their innate honor for supplication and unjust servitude [Note: *Sclavi*, “Slavs,” added in 2 and in the *Annals of Saxony*, under 1002].

How shamefully our predecessors and our contemporaries are to be compared! While the excellent Hodo was alive, the father of this Miseconis never dared enter the house where he knew Hodo to be wearing a fur cloak [Note: from the Slavonic *crusina*, “fur garment”], nor did he ever presume to sit when Hodo rose.

May God forgive the emperor for having raised a tributary subject [Note: 1 reads *triburarium*; 2 adds *sclavum*, “slave”] to the point of making him a lord, so that, forgetting the rule of his father, he dared gradually to draw into subjection those who had always been placed over him, catching them with the hook [Note: that is, a hook] of worthless passing money and taking them to the detriment of servitude and freedom (f. 86r).

7. The other Bolizlavus, governor of the Bohemians, surnamed the Red, and author of immense impiety, after the ancient custom had been somewhat restrained, aspired to Duke Heinricus. At the beginning of June, Heinricus came to Worms with the chief men of the Bavarians and Eastern Franks [Note: 1c reads *Francorum*; 1, *francium*], in order to cross the Rhine there and receive the blessing at Mainz.

Duke Herimannus tried to prevent this and, with the Rhine under his control, opened no entrance across it. Duke Heinricus, however, after taking counsel with his men about these matters, pretended to return to Bavaria and to have abandoned hope of crossing. He came to the city of Larsem [Note: Lorsch], where Saint Nazarius rests. Then, hastening quickly to Mainz (f. 87), he sailed safely across the Rhine.

There, on the eighth day before the Ides of June (June 6), he was unanimously elected king through the common devotion of the people. Having received royal anointing from Wiligisis, archbishop of that see, with the assistance of his suffragans, he was crowned while all present praised God together [Note: *Annals of Quedlinburg*, 1002]. The leading men of the Franks and of Muselen [Note: 1a reads *muselesnensium*] then pledged their hands to the king and thereby earned his favor [Note: 1a reads *applicatis*, “having pledged”].

When everyone from every direction had flocked there and been received by the king into military service, the new king again crossed the overflowing Rhine. Passing through Eastern Francia, which was faithful to him, he invaded Alamannia and, while laying waste to that land, attempted to turn Herimannus, who resisted him, away from his undertaking.

When the duke heard that his lands had been plundered by the king, he still refused to humble himself [Note: 1a reads *humiliare*] and, alas, raised himself against his lord and king. He attacked the chief city of his duchy, Argentina, called Strazburg [Note: Bishop Wernerus had succeeded Alawicus in May 1001], together with his son-in-law Conradus [Note: 1 reads *genero*; 2 and the *Annals* read *germano*], a mounted soldier, and climbed the walls. He left nothing to the defeated [Note: *reliquid*, corrected in 1c].

But the accursed Alemannic mob, exceedingly eager for plunder, entered the great church of the holy Mother of God without fear, unbeknownst to the duke, and robbed all its treasure. What was the greatest crime, they consumed the house of the Lord with fire.

If the duke had truly been fortunate, he would have been deterred by the bitterness of his first entry and would never have presumed to undertake greater things. For, while the bishop’s soldiers, at Reinwardus’s instigation, offered treacherous resistance, a very great throng of enemies rushed in, fell pierced by its own spear, and miserably ended this life through divine vengeance.

Herimannus departed lamenting these events in unconsolable grief [Note: 1a reads *insolabli*], and left the matter unavenged because numbers afforded him protection.

8. While the king was staying on the island of Augia for the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist [Note: 1c reads *in nativitate*], swift and often doubtful rumor announced that Duke Herimannus was coming to end the quarrel by single combat. The same rumor caused the king to depart from there and await the duke’s arrival and the judgment of battle in broad green meadows.

There, while celebrating the feast of the apostles (June 29) and awaiting certainty for a long time [Note: 1c perhaps reads *longamque*], he learned for certain that the duke neither wished nor was able to persist in his undertaking. His ill-advised supporters counseled him that the damage inflicted at Argentina should be repaid by Constance. For the bishop of that city, named Lanbertus, was assisting Herimannus together with the bishop of Chur, Othelricus (f. 88), though not so much from his heart as because of the proximity of his city [Note: literally, “on account of the closeness of his city”].

But the king, concerned as he was with the fear of God and certain of acquiring what he sought, rejected their profane counsels. He went about ravaging the duke’s estates and, finally overcome by the outcry of the poor, decided to return to Francia.

Then Count Heinricus, son of Bertoldus and of my aunt, who had until then been the king’s faithful helper in acquiring the summit of the kingdom, noticed that his lord’s mind was becoming somewhat alienated from him [Note: the word is absent in 1 and supplied in 1c; the *Annals* read *dignationem*, “favor”]. Through the king’s best soldiers he requested that the long and firmly promised dukedom of Bavaria be granted to him.

The king is said to have answered:

“Do you not know that this cannot possibly be done during this expedition? From the beginning, the Bavarians have had the free power to choose their duke. It is not fitting to cast them aside so suddenly, nor to violate the right of the ancient constitution without their consent. If you had been willing to wait until I myself came to these regions, I would gladly have satisfied you in this matter with the common counsel and consent of their leaders.”

When Heinricus learned this from the messengers, he fell into even greater despair of receiving the promised gift (f. 88r) and gradually withdrew from the king’s familiarity. Nevertheless, he accompanied the king as he departed from Alamannia for Francia, and afterwards to Thuringia.

9. There Willehelmus, at that time the most powerful of the Thuringians, went to meet him, received the approaching lord with great rejoicing, and became the king’s man [Note: *miles*, “soldier,” is added in 1c]. There the king, through the aforesaid count and the leading men of that region, was praised as lord. At the request of the entire people, he remitted to them the due tax on pigs [Note: this word was erased in 1; the *Annals of Saxony* and 2 read: “he was asked to remit to them the due tax, and he did so”].

From there he came to Merseburg, where he was received by Abbot Heimo and by his faithful count Esico, who had bravely guarded this city, Alstidi, and Thornburg with their dependencies, while Ekkihardus was alive and grievously resented it, until the presence of the desired lord.

Archbishops gathered there: Lieviso [Note: 1c perhaps reads *Luuizo*], of Bremen, and Gisilerus, of Magdeburg, together with their other brothers; and the bishops Retharius of Paderborn [Note: 1a reads *patheburhgiensi*], Bernwardus of Hildesheim [Note: the *n* was erased in 1], Arnulfus of Halberstadt, Ramwardus of Minden, Eiddo of Meissen [Note: the enclosed words, absent from the manuscripts, should be supplied, as Ursinus has already noted], Bernharius of Verden, and Hugo of Zeitz. The dukes were Bernhardus [Note: 1c reads *Bernhardus*; 1a *Berhardus*] and Bolizlavus, and the margraves Liutharius and Gero, together with Count Palatine Frithericus [Note: an entire quire is missing at this point in manuscript 1; the gap has been supplied from manuscript 2], as well as very many others, both bishops and counts [Codex Br., f. 238], whose names it would take too long to recount individually.

All these men received the king with humble devotion. On the following day, July 24, the eighth day before the Kalends of August, Duke Bernhardus [Note: *Annals of Quedlinburg*, 1002], with everyone present and in agreement, disclosed before the king the will of the assembled people and explained in detail their needs and law. He carefully asked what mercy the king wished to promise them in words or grant them in deeds.

He asked such questions, and the king replied:

“I am wholly unable to render fitting thanks first to God and then to all of you. Therefore I reveal to you the secret of my will: through your effective assistance I desire to benefit you all. For I know how faithfully you have always and everywhere striven to offer obedience and support to your kings. Therefore I wish to honor and love you above all in every respect, and to preserve you for the advancement of the kingdom and for our safety.

“And so that you may be certain of this, I affirm, as you wish, while the honor of the kingdom is preserved, that I appear invested with this royal dignity not because you reject or oppose me, but rather as though you applaud me and have invited me here.

“Therefore I prefer, as long as I live, mercifully to fulfill your law in everything and, insofar as I am able, everywhere to give heed to your reasonable will.”

Thus spoke the king, and a single voice rose at once from the people standing there, rejoicing for the king, with praises and thanks for such great acts of mercy.

Then Duke Bernhardus, taking the sacred lance in his hands, faithfully entrusted the care of the kingdom to him on behalf of everyone.

Again voices were raised, and praises were sung everywhere:

“Christ, for such great gifts, we give you praise for these good things.”

Moreover, their pious hearts poured forth joyful tears.

“Rejoice, illustrious Merseburg; rejoice with these things. Give worthy jubilation to Christ beneath this sun.”

Honor this sun, I say—that is, this day—reverently: on it he was elected in you, the one who thereafter always planned to raise you from your rejected state and restore you to your former condition.

Blessed be God, who exalts those who honor and love him from the heart, to the horror and disgrace of those who curse him. The end of your mourning has come, because the saving south wind has breathed upon you a friendly mildness. You will not remain long in servitude, for you will be renewed to rule freely, O Zion. But let us proceed further.

10. All who had served the former emperor, with Liudgerus alone remaining [Note: see above, chapter 2], joined hands with the king and confirmed their faithful assistance by oaths.

Bolizlaus, however, strove only to acquire the city of Meissen with an incalculable sum of money. Since the opportunity to obtain the kingdom was lacking, he could not secure it from the king, barely managing to obtain that it be given to his brother Guncelinus [Note: he seems to have been Boleslaus’s uterine brother], after the regions of Liudizi and Milizieni had been restored to him.

Count Heinricus, my nephew, who loved Bolizlaus exceedingly, willingly and amicably assisted him in every way he could. While accompanying him as he departed, richly rewarded and with the king’s permission, he saw an armed multitude rushing against him—by God I testify, rising against him without the king’s counsel or knowledge.

When Heinricus wished to investigate the cause of so great a disturbance and restrain it lest more harm arise, he scarcely managed to lead his companion to safety through the broken outer gate. Some of the soldiers who followed were plundered by the restraining crowd; others, severely wounded, escaped death through the aid of Duke Bernhardus.

These men had entered the royal court armed and, when ordered to leave it, refused. They therefore deservedly suffered such danger because of their own fault.

Bolizlaus, however, supposing that this deed had been done through the deceit of evil counsel, was consumed by deep grief and blamed the king for what he had not deserved. After bidding Count Heinricus farewell [Note: namely, the count and margrave of Bavaria], and firmly promising him his assistance should he ever need it, he quickly returned to his homeland.

When he reached the city of Strela, he immediately set it on fire and led away with him a great multitude of its inhabitants. He also sent back certain messengers and tried to turn away from the king as many people as he could. As soon as this reached the king’s ears, he kindly asked his retainers to investigate the Slav’s secret ambushes and, if possible, attempt to seize his spies.

11. Having arranged everything as the time then required, the king set out to seek the realm of the Liutharians. When he came to the city called New Corvey—so named from the place whence it originated, namely the Frankish Corvey, where the holy child and martyr Vitus rests—his illustrious wife Cunegundis came to meet him.

There both were received with every honor by the venerable Abbot Thietmarus [Note: the reading *Thoitmarus* occurs in manuscript 2 and the *Annals of Saxony*. This appears to be a singular error, doubtless introduced by an interpolator who seems to have added the entire Corvey passage, since Adelboldus, who follows Thietmar, says that the queen met Heinricus at Gruona. Abbot Thietmar, our Thietmar’s uncle, had already died on March 12, 1001; see the *Fasti Corbeienses* and the necrologies of Fulda and Lüneburg. Abbot Hosed succeeded him. See also Henry’s charter of August 24, 1002.] and, honored there in divine and human matters, they joyfully proceeded to Paderborn [Note: cf. the *Annals of Quedlinburg*, 1002].

On the following day, which shone festively upon the world because of the martyrdom of blessed Laurence (August 10), Lady Cunegundis humbly received blessing and crown from Archbishop Willigisis, while Sophia, the emperor’s sister, already appointed abbess by the king, received consecration [Note: cf. the same source].

From there public joy arose, but, shamefully, the insatiable greed of the Bavarians greatly disturbed it. At home these men were always content with little, but abroad they were almost without limit in their greed. When they violently seized the crops of their neighbors and beat those who defended them [Note: the *Annals of Saxony* read “those who prohibited them”], a very serious battle arose between them [Note: see the same source].

The king’s household troops went out [Note: the *Annals* read “arrived”]; the natives advanced with the newcomers and followed after them. A great clash took place among the combatants, and the defeated Bavarian force fled into the royal court.

There Heinricus, brother of Chancellor Eilbertus [Note: he later became bishop of Freising], who regularly served the king at table, fell dead after being wounded by a spear. Therefore the Saxons who had previously been absent gathered and pursued them again. Had Duke Bernhardus not intervened in the middle with a stronger force, an innumerable number of soldiers would have fallen by one another’s hands.

After this, all who could be found to have been authors of so great a crime were punished. The gift of Bockenevorde, handed over by the king [Note: Bockenförde, a parish village in the district of Arnsberg, prefecture of Lippstadt. A charter of the emperor concerning this donation exists, dated at Corvey, October 21, 1005], afterwards appeased the bishop’s grief.

12. The king then reached Diusburg by the direct route (around the middle of August) and waited for the Liutharians, who arrived late. The bishops of Liège and Cambrai, however, came here first and waited a long time for the archbishop of Cologne, who was delayed.

Although he inwardly resented the restraint by which, as I have already said, he had been detained somewhat more deeply than anyone would have believed, he pretended that he had approached the king’s favor so late because, in receiving the blessing at Mainz, the king had wished to place the archbishop of Mainz before him.

Accordingly, these brothers—the bishops—jointly elected the king and confirmed their loyalty by oaths; they accompanied him as far as Aachen. There, on the Nativity of Saint Mary (September 8), he was acclaimed king by the leading men of the Liutharians and was raised and honored in the royal seat according to the custom of his predecessors.

Meanwhile he endeavored to revisit Francia and to spend the harshness of winter there, so that, with the beginning of spring, he might compel by force Duke Herimannus—the only man resisting him in the Cisalpine regions—to yield.

Herimannus, however, greatly afraid of the vengeance of God that he had merited at Argentina, and no longer able to endure the people’s suffering on his account, asked through trustworthy intercessors, both for himself and for his supporters, that he be restored to the king’s favor.

13. But before that had been decided by him, we must not pass over something perpetrated by the Alamanni. Gerhard, count of Alsace [Note: [Col. 1293D] Gerard I, son of Eberhard, count of Alsace, who had married Eva, daughter of Count Siegfried of Luxembourg and sister of the Empress Cunegund.], [Col. 1293B] having received from the king a certain county belonging to the aforesaid duke, pitched camp beside one of the cities as he was returning home. The townspeople, having scarcely obtained peace from him for a single night, went out deceitfully as though to a conference, but in reality to reconnoiter. One of them, often proved equally for cunning and speed, approached more closely and, lifting the standard-bearing lance—which that same count had received from the king as the duke’s benefice and which had been fixed before his tent—looked around. Finally, carrying it with him, he entered the city safely, while all those following behind him in vain. Great rejoicing immediately arose in the city; the gate was closed, and the count was mocked as though deprived of his honor. He first tried unsuccessfully to recover it by sweet promises; but when they refused to return it, he departed sadly, as empty of his benefice [Col. 1293C] as of his military standard.

14. In another extremely well-fortified city, called Brisach, there were two bishops, the bishops of Strasbourg and Basel, stationed there for its defense. Their soldiers used to go out daily in arms to procure fodder for the horses. The duke’s friends, carefully observing this, at the time when these men had gone a little way ahead, proceeded toward the city in similar clothing and with pack-laden horses, singing; the guards admitted them as comrades. Immediately throwing down their loads, they declared themselves enemies in loud voices and, while the bishops barely escaped, plundered everything.

After this, Duke Herimann, my mother’s uncle’s son, was humbly presented to the king at Bruchsal on the Kalends of October [Note: [Col. 1294D] Bruchsal, where the king was on October 3]. Having mercifully obtained the king’s favor, and making satisfaction in his benefice and in every matter of rightful desire—except for the damage at Strasbourg, which, by the king’s order and counsel, he repaired from his own property, together with the abbey situated in that city—he became the king’s soldier and faithful friend.

These matters having been arranged, the king proceeded to Bavaria so that, by his arrival and every expression of affection, he might make it known to them that he loved them especially above all others. When he came to Regensburg, Gebehard, its excellent bishop, received him amid the rejoicing of all the clergy and people, and honored him greatly there as he celebrated the feast of Saint Martin.

15. Meanwhile, the duke of the Bohemians, Bolizlaus, because the power of a consort and successor is always fearful (*Lucan, Pharsalia* I.92), castrated his brother Jaremir and, wishing to suffocate the younger Othelric in a bath [Note: [Col. 1293] *otelricum* in manuscript 2], expelled both of them from their homeland together with their mother. Reigning alone in place of a harmful basilisk, he oppressed the people beyond description.

Unable to bear the burden of the crime inflicted upon them any longer, the people secretly summoned from Poland Wlodoweius, whose name is interpreted as “power of the army.” They unanimously elected him, out of kinship and affection, to the seat of that basilisk, namely Bolizlaus, after expelling the latter—a venomous asp who treated his own people without any mercy required by law [Col. 1294B].

Of him I shall tell one incredible thing, though not one to be imitated by any Christian: he was never able to endure a single hour without drinking.

But Bolizlaus, fleeing by the only route that lay open, took refuge with Margrave Heinric, who was then his nearest neighbor, and was captured by him because of the injuries he had inflicted. Later, because he had come to him as a guest, he was released and went, merely for love of life, to his namesake and his aunt’s son, his equal in crimes though unequal in resources. The latter, however, following the better counsel, set out for the king, who was still staying at Regensburg. With humble submission and a faithful promise, he chose him as his lord, obtained from him as a benefice what he had requested, and, departing with affection in every respect, returned in good peace.

16. While these things were taking place, Hartwig, whom I mentioned above, being extremely eager to learn about the prosperity and arrival of King Heinric, strengthened all the entrances into Lombardy—which the inhabitants call *clusae*—with vigilant guards. As I said above, he did not cease treating the advisers and supporters of his election as they deserved. Among them, when the bishop of Brescia said certain things displeasing to him, Hartwig seized him by the hair and threw him flat on the ground like a herdsman [Note: [Col. 1293] Thus manuscript A and S., at the cited passage], revealing to everyone his unbridled anger.

But why do I try to enumerate him through his individual vices, when it is apparent in the kingdom and among the people what a throng of wickedness armed him to perpetrate? Hence some of the leading men whom he had placed under himself [Note: [Col. 1294D] That is, the leading men subject to him.] regretted having submitted to him [Note: [Col. 1293] *tunc*—“then”—is added in A. S.] and, through intermediaries and letters, asked King Heinric either to come and deal with him or, if he were occupied with other affairs, to send his princes [Note: [Col. 1293] *mittere*—“to send”—in A. S.].

To come to the aid of their necessity, Duke Otto of Carinthia and count of Verona was sent by the king, together with Otto, son of Count Heribert, and Ernastus, son of Margrave Liupold [Note: [Col. 1295] *Arnesto Liuppoldi* in manuscript 2], along with a few others, in hope of the greater assistance promised by the Italians.

But who that Duke Otto was, since I passed over him above, I shall briefly explain. Born of Duke Conrad and Liudgarda, daughter of the great Otto, he adorned his family by the gravity of his conduct and the integrity of his deeds [Note: [Col. 1295D] A nearly similar expression is found above, Book IV, chapter 26]. After the emperor’s death, when Heinric was then duke and, by right of kinship, age, and maturity of virtue, was being chosen as king, Otto humbly excused himself from so great a burden. He placed Heinric before himself, both through intermediaries and personally, as more suitable for the task, and always faithfully assisted him.

When Otto came on the king’s behalf, and Archbishop Fritheric of Ravenna, together with Margrave Thiedolf [Note: [Col. 1295D] Leibniz judges this to be the same person as Theobald, grandfather of the famous Matilda, countess of Tuscany, and of the most famous friend of Hildebrand, the supreme pontiff. See Ursinus below, VI.9. In manuscript I he is called *Tiedoldus*.], and the king’s other faithful men came to meet him in support, Hartwig, stationed between them and examining everything with lynx-like eyes [cf. Horace, *Satires* I.2.90], discovered what was happening. He came to Verona with a large force to break them up and, by assaulting and capturing Lucca, which the bishop of that city had fortified until then, took it.

Hearing that the Germans had settled on the plain of Trent, he hurried there; but, failing to find them, he swiftly returned again to the Veronese Campania [Note: [Col. 1295D] An unusual expression. Liudprand II.11 called this region the Veronese Fields; Thietmar himself calls it the Veronese plain in VI.4].

While he was celebrating the feast of the Lord’s Nativity in a certain castle [Note: [Col. 1295] *celebranti*—“celebrating”—in manuscript 2], Duke Otto, as soon as he learned of all his actions, sent envoys asking permission either to pass through or to receive permission on his behalf. Hartwig replied to these requests with profound cunning of mind [Col. 1295C]:

“Spend the night here, so that tomorrow, after taking counsel with my friends, I may send you back informed about all these matters.”

But, without our envoys’ knowing this, he spent the whole night making a particular inspection of his men stationed in the camps everywhere around, strengthening their resolve to fight the Germans in the morning and ordering them to prepare their arms [Note: [Col. 1295] A lacuna occurs here in manuscript 2; the text is supplied from A. S. under the year 1003.].

At the first light of the following dawn, the duke’s envoys, setting out to approach the king for an answer, saw the Lombards preparing for battle with military force. When they asked what this signified, they received the order to depart, having learned that a definite engagement against the duke was intended. Hartwig followed them with his army and reached Mount Hungarian at midday, where the duke was awaiting the envoys with his men [Col. 1295D]. He found the enemy, although divided into detachments for forage and for guarding the roads on every side, nevertheless prepared to resist.

Thus the brave forces on both sides clashed with violent impetus [Col. 1296A]. And unless the flight of Otto, brother of Bishop Gebehard, had thrown into confusion and impeded the German line, which was inferior to the enemy in numbers, the Lombard enemy would have experienced it as victorious. Then, however, after it had been mutilated to a considerable extent—shame upon it!—it was put to flight and deprived of the honor of victory, but not without the greatest loss to Hartwig [Note: [Col. 1295] *cum*—“then”—in manuscript 2].

17. Meanwhile, after the king had departed from Bavaria and was celebrating the Lord’s Nativity at Frankfurt [Note: [Col. 1295] *Franckenforde* in manuscript 2; *Franconevorde* in A. S. under the year 1003], delegations from many people were brought before him. The envoys were first received kindly and then generously rewarded, and all returned joyful.

There also Duke Herimann humbly served the king and was treated by him affectionately, as was fitting for such a person [Note: [Col. 1295] *heremannus* in manuscript 2, frequently]. Leaving there, the king visited the district of the Moselle and, coming to Thionville [Col. 1296B] [Note: [Col. 1296D] Thionville, Diedenhofen. A charter of the king shows that he was there on January 15], held a general assembly there with the people of the surrounding region (1003).

Since the king desired to administer justice kindly to all who were suffering from some necessity, Merimannus and Theoderic—dukes in name alone, but not in reality—tried to prevent this, but in vain [Note: [Col. 1295] *nam*—“for”—is added in A. S.], immediately perceiving that they were deservedly succumbing to the author of justice. For, because of the pressing need of the entire people, the king firmly ordered that a certain castle of the duke, called Mulsberg, be destroyed and never rebuilt [Note: [Col. 1296D] On this castle, see *Chronicon Gottwicense*, vol. I, p. 694. Ursinus.].

After all this had been completed without delay [Note: [Col. 1295] *dilatione*—“without delay”—in A. S.], the king set out for Aachen (January 24), in order there to complete with the greatest diligence the anniversary of his lord and predecessor, the emperor [Note: [Col. 1296D] That is, January 24], and so that the Lotharingians might assemble unanimously.

Although an illness that arose meanwhile delayed him somewhat [Col. 1296C], the ineffable piety of Christ granted him strength to accomplish the purpose of his rightful desire. Then, coming to Utrecht [Note: [Col. 1296D] Utrecht on the Meuse] out of love for the holy bishop Servatius, he learned there with certainty of the unfortunate battle fought by our men (*Horace*, I.24.19). And because every misfortune that cannot be corrected is softened by patience [Note: [Col. 1295] *leniter*—“gently”—in manuscript 2], although he heard the distressing news gravely, he endured it wisely.

From there he came to Liège to obtain the patronage of Christ’s athlete Lambert. There he was severely afflicted by colic, but was freed through the suffrages of the aforesaid martyr’s intercession. Returning from there to Aachen, he reverently celebrated there the Purification of the Mother of God.

From there he proceeded to Nijmegen [Note: [Col. 1296D] Charters establish that the king was at Nijmegen on February 23 and 28] and remained there for several days of Lent [Col. 1296D], seeking first the kingdom of God and his justice, and afterward, concerned for human weakness, providing what was necessary.

18. Meanwhile, after Wlodoweius the duke had died, the aforesaid brothers, expelled together with their mother, were recalled by the Bohemians, who had been moved to repentance. Bolizlaus, ruler of the Poles, however, gathered an army from everywhere, attacked them, expelled them again, and placed his own namesake, the former exile, in his previous honors. He then withdrew home, with his plots concealed in the depths of his mind.

For he knew that his nephew would take excessive vengeance on those who had supported his expulsion, hoping that he himself might then perhaps be introduced under better circumstances. And so it happened.

Indeed, when the Bohemian Bolizlaus saw that his people, devoted to an accursed rite, were living in the greatest security, he so armed his impiety to break the treaties of peace which he had confirmed by oaths that, after gathering all the nobles into one house before him, he himself first killed his son-in-law by plunging a sword into his head. He then killed the others, unarmed and in the very holy season of Lent—this man of blood and deceit, never worthy to touch even half the days granted to him [Note: [Col. 1297D] That is, “to reach even half of the days granted to him”—or, “to be granted half as many days as he had been granted”]—together with the supporters of his wickedness.

The surviving people, greatly afraid because of this, secretly sent messengers to Bolizlaus the Pole, to declare the magnitude of the crime that had been committed and ask him for deliverance from the fear of what was to come. Having willingly heard them, he immediately sent a faithful envoy to request that the younger Bolizlaus come with a few men to meet him face to face in a certain fortress, so that they might discuss with him certain matters necessary for the common good [Note: [Col. 1297] *nepotem*—“the nephew”—in A. S.].

The younger Bolizlaus immediately agreed and went to the appointed place [Note: [Col. 1297] A. S. reads: “He, agreeing at once, went to meet his maternal uncle at the appointed place”]. At first he was received affectionately by him; but during the following night he was prevented by his attendants from ever again perpetrating such a deed against his own people or continuing to reign there: they tore out his eyes and condemned him to a long exile.

On the following day, therefore, he hurried to Prague and was admitted by the inhabitants, who were always delighted by a new rule; they commonly praised him as their lord. As his secular power increased there, the defiance of his unbridled mind rose much higher than usual.

Attend to this, reader, and know that the person whose spirit becomes more elated in prosperity will often be more humble in adversity; Scripture testifies that this is not the way of the wise.

19. Learning all these things as rumor reported them, the king bore them with the honorable dignity of a patient spirit, attributing solely to his own sins whatever misfortune occurred in the kingdom during his time [Col. 1297D]. Accordingly, doing what then seemed most expedient, he sent messengers to Bolizlaus, concealing everything that had happened to them. He instructed him that, if he wished to retain the land he had recently occupied by the king’s favor, as ancient right demanded [Note: [Col. 1297] *possit*—“might be able”—in manuscript 2; A. S. reads *more antiquorum*, “according to the custom of the ancients”], and to serve him faithfully in every respect, the king would assent to his will in these matters; otherwise, he would oppose him with arms.

Although this embassy was just and well composed, Bolizlaus received it indignantly and thereby rightly earned future vengeance. When the Lenten fast had ended, as I began to relate, the king honorably celebrated the Easter festival at Quedlinburg according to the custom of his predecessors [Note: [Col. 1297D] Compare the *Quedlinburg Annals* under the year 1003] [March 28].

There, concealing Bolizlaus’s unjust presumption and Heinric’s aspiration [Note: [Col. 1298D] Heinric, margrave of Bavaria], he smiled upon his attendants as such a great festival required. There too he honored Duke Otto and Ernastus [Note: [Col. 1297] *arnestum* in manuscript 2], returning from the badly fought battle, with royal gifts, and consoled them with paternal assistance.

He also mercifully received the messengers of the Rederarii [Note: [Col. 1297] Manuscript 1 continues here with *redariorum*; manuscript 2 reads *redariorum] and of those called Liutici. Until then they had been rebels, but he calmed them by the sweetness of gifts and the charm of promises and made them most intimate friends from enemies [Col. 1298B] [Note: [Col. 1298D] See the *Quedlinburg Annals*, at the cited passage].

20. After this, while celebrating at Merseburg the Rogation days, which Christ’s faithful must continually observe [Note: [Col. 1297] *rogatianum* in manuscript 1], the king was informed of the open rebellion of Duke Bolizlaus and Margrave Heinric. The king celebrated the approaching feast of Pentecost at Halberstadt (May 16).

Afterward, proceeding toward Bavaria, he first tried to overcome Heinric, who was resisting with Bolizlaus’s assistance, and then to remove the ambushes that had been laid at a distance [Note: [Col. 1297] *positos* in manuscript 1a.]. He also learned that Ernastus, whom he had recently honored, and Lord Bruno, his brother [Note: [Col. 1298D] Bruno later became, in 1007, bishop of Augsburg], had unjustly conspired with him, not knowing what was written:

> “A strength lacking counsel collapses under its own weight.”  
> (*Horace*, *Odes* III.4.65.)

To calm their arrogance, the king gathered his retainers from every side. As August began [Note: [Col. 1297] *augusta* in manuscript 1a], he invaded and devastated the aforesaid count’s property, compelling him to hide unwillingly wherever he could outside the city [Col. 1298C].

Someone who knows the cause of such great presumption might say that he necessarily did this: it is not fitting for higher powers to withdraw so firmly promised loyalty from anyone serving them faithfully and to alienate the devotion of others [Col. 1298D]. I answer them in turn: there is no domination in this world except from God, and whoever rises against it incurs an offense against divine majesty. The sudden inflation of an unjust mind must be restrained by the reins of patience, and with humble supplication one must await consolation that will truly profit him. I consider it preferable to rise higher day by day than suddenly to incur an insurmountable fall [Note: [Col. 1297] Witness 1b adds *subito*, “suddenly,” to the clause about incurring the fall.].

I would gladly defend my nephew to some extent, if I dared pollute the truth, which all the faithful ought to honor. The proverbs of the ancients, approved in many places, are true: the long-standing crimes of a people give birth to fresh losses of shame. For this man’s father often resisted the king’s father, not as a soldier but as an enemy, and, as he himself testified, supported the imperial party in order to confirm the favor established by oaths.

Likewise, this man remained faithful to him until the end of the last Otto and served his lord vigorously until these unhappy times. But the king secretly kept buried in the depths of his mind an endless hatred of his father and of himself [Note: [Col. 1299D] “It remains buried in the depths of his mind.” Virgil, *Aeneid* I.26]. I hope, however, that he would always have left all this unavenged for the love of Christ, if he had not seen him, together with the others opposed to him, resisting him openly and with such cruelty [Note: [Col. 1299] *saepius*—“repeatedly”—in manuscript 1].

Although Margrave Heinric appeared alone culpable in this crime, he did not first undertake it without the counsel of others. And because a traitor is considered a great disgrace in this world, he preferred to conceal the matter with a groaning conscience rather than increase his own loss by the damage of others.
