Thus the man who had previously tried manfully to defend his homeland from this enemy then opened it to him for plunder, and secret assistance was sent to him by Bolizlaus, though it profited him nothing at all.

21. When the king was then coming to the place called Hatheresburgdi [Note: [Col. 1299] Thus manuscript 1a, though a second *r* has been erased. A. S. reads *Hatheresbrugge.] [Note: [Col. 1299D] Perhaps Haderesbrugge in the district of Nordgau, today IIrspruch, beside the River Regnitz, between Nuremberg and Amberg], Maganus, a soldier of the aforesaid count, seized all his treasure that preceded him, together with his men. After dividing it among themselves, he returned joyfully to the city of Amardela [Note: [Col. 1299D] Amerthal, a district not far from Amberg [Col. 1300D]. See *Chronicon Gottwicense* I, p. 716. Ursinus].

The king pursued them and took possession of them [Note: [Col. 1299] *possedet* in manuscript 1a]. Having prepared the instruments of war, he compelled them to seek only their lives, with the city and booty restored, through the intercession of those who pleaded for them. Then, after completely destroying that city and dividing the Polish multitude among his men [Col. 1299C], the king proceeded to the fortress of Crusni [Note: [Col. 1300D] Creussen, below Bayreuth], in which Bucco, the brother of Count Heinric, was supposed to guard his lady Gerberga with her sons [Note: [Col. 1299] Witness 1a reads *proficissitur*, a malformed spelling of *proficiscitur*, “he proceeds/set out.”].

Count Heinric, however, attacked from outside with his men the army that was besieging the fortress on every side, wounding some and killing others who were carelessly gathering grain for the horses. So that this might not happen again, the king made careful provision: he stationed four hundred soldiers and forced the enemy to seek the more secluded parts of a certain valley [Note: [Col. 1299] *cuidam* in manuscript 1].

When the enemy was encamped there, the uncontrolled tongue of a peasant betrayed him to the guards. They moved secretly against the camp at midday and, as soon as they recognized the tents, called their comrades together in a loud voice with the *Kyrie eleison*. The enemy abandoned everything there except Ernastus, whom they captured, and fled [Col. 1299D].

When those who had gone out returned, they were for the most part sad, while their comrades were extremely joyful. The captive was presented to the king, and the judges pronounced a capital sentence [Col. 1300A]. Through the humble intercession of Archbishop Willigis of Mainz and a ransom acceptable to the king, however, the sentence was revoked.

Then, hearing of his lord’s flight, Count Bucco was shaken by deep grief and consulted his companions about what he should do [Note: [Col. 1299] The words *a. q. s. t.* are added in manuscript 1b]. He received different answers from them. Some said that, out of fidelity promised to their lord and because of the disgrace that would forever be imputed to them, they would rather die than ever surrender the city with such a hostage to the king. As long as their lord survived, they hoped that assistance would always come.

Others, who were wiser, declared that it was difficult to resist a rushing torrent and a powerful man; that the conquered rarely or never obtained pardon; and that, unharmed and not then delayed by any wound, they would seek from the king permission to depart with their lady and the other goods and guests [Col. 1300B].

Following the counsel of the latter, as I think, Bucco, guardian of that city, spoke with Otto, his own brother and lord, and through his support surrendered the city to royal authority. He himself then departed safely with all those entrusted to him.

Immediately the king ordered the city to be destroyed from its foundations. But because the authors of this act showed mercy, it was preserved for the most part, together with its buildings.

22. Meanwhile, while King Heinric held the city of Count Heinric called Crusni, Bolizlaus, striving with all his might to injure him in some way, secretly gathered an army. Through his messengers he urged his brother Guncilin, remembering his firm promise, to restore the city of Meissen to his authority and renew their former friendship.

But Guncilin, knowing that by Bolizlaus’s entry he had been entirely excluded from the king’s favor and from his demesne—or dominion and dignity [Note: [Col. 1299] Thus manuscript 1, that is, *demanio* or *dominio*. A. S. reads “from his dignity”—], replied to such instructions:

“Everything else that you ask of me, brother, I will gladly provide; and if an opportunity ever arises for doing this, I will not refuse. The retainers of my lord are with me, and they will not tolerate such things. If this becomes known, my life, together with everything I possess, will be in danger.”

After receiving this embassy, Bolizlaus ordered the envoys to be kept under guard and the army to hurry to the Elbe. There he secretly investigated the nature of the fords. At daybreak he himself followed [Note: [Col. 1299] Witness 1b adds *ipse*, “he himself”] and sent word to the city of Strela, since it was the dowry of his daughter [Note: [Col. 1300D] Compare above, Book IV, chapter 37], that they should fear nothing for themselves and should not, by raising an alarm, inform their neighbors of this matter.

Without delay the army, at the duke’s command, was divided into four parts, and it was ordered to assemble in the evening at the fortress of Cirin [Note: [Col. 1300D] Now Zehren, a district not far from Meissen. The fortress was destroyed long ago. Ursinus]. Two phalanxes were sent ahead to ensure that their men suffered no disturbance from the margrave [Note: [Col. 1299] The reading *e* is in a place erased in manuscript 1b?].

The entire district called Zlomizi [Note: [Col. 1301D] Above, Book I, chapter 3, it is called Glomuci, where there can be no doubt about the reading], then extremely well cultivated, was lamentably laid waste in a single day by fire, sword, and the removal of its inhabitants.

But how the man who was accustomed to deceive everyone was himself deceived by certain people who were sitting in the city of Mogilina [Note: [Col. 1301D] Mügeln, near Hubertusburg and Oschatz], I am pleased to relate. When they were attacked by the detachment sent against them, they said:

“Why are you doing this? We know that your lord is an excellent man, and we wish to place him above our own. Only go ahead, and do not doubt that we shall follow with our families and all our possessions.”

While they were making these pleas, the enemy no longer harassed them, and they reported with certainty to their lord that these men were coming [Col. 1301A]. But when the comrades assembled late at the appointed place and the duke saw that these men were sitting at home [Note: [Col. 1301] *has* in manuscript 1a], he became extremely angry and threatened punishment against his lying companions [Col. 1301B] [Note: At *poenas*, “punishments,” the *o* seems to have been added by witness 1b and later erased by witness 1, as often happened with *a* and *o*.]. The following day, once the sun had risen, an innumerable amount of booty was sent ahead, and a large part of the enemy was thrown into the Elbe. The rest returned home unharmed, divided the booty, and assigned the best portions to their lord [Note: [Col. 1301] *optimo*—“best”—is repeated in manuscript 1a]. The number of captives was no fewer than three thousand and, as those present asserted, considerably more.

23. Count Heinric [Note: [Col. 1301] Witness 1b adds *Heinricus vero*, “Count Heinric, however”], realizing that his strength had now failed [Note: [Col. 1301] In an erased place witness 1b has *s. i. d.*, abbreviating the adjoining *se iam defecisse*, “that his strength/self had now failed”], hurried to the city called Crana [Note: [Col. 1301D] Kronach in Bavaria]. There he found Sifrid, the young son of Count Siegfried, waiting for him with assistance. He promised neither himself nor Sifrid any hope of rebellion in those regions.

After speaking at length with him [Note: [Col. 1301] *ea*—“these things”—in manuscript 1a], he burned the city and withdrew to Bolizlaus, then the invader of Bohemia, together with Lord Bruno and the remaining supporters [Col. 1301C] [Note: [Col. 1301] *eccessit* in manuscript 1].

Sifrid, disappointed in his declared hope of resistance, did not accompany them but returned, assured that he would make amends in the future for the charge entrusted to him.

The king pursued the fleeing enemy to Crana and softened his own anger in this respect by recognizing that he had anticipated the enemy in destroying the place. He then sent Heinric, bishop of Würzburg, and Erkanbald, abbot of the monastery of Fulda, to burn and destroy the fortress of Suinvordi.

When they arrived, the illustrious mother of Count Heinric, named Eila, received and greeted them as was fitting for such persons. When she understood the royal orders, she was disturbed and hurried to the church. There she declared that she would rather endure the burning of the fire than leave alive after the church had been burned.

Therefore the aforesaid leaders, out of love for Christ [Note: [Col. 1301] *amore*—“out of love”—in manuscript 1], setting secular fears aside, changed the sentence they had determined. They broke down the city walls and buildings to the ground and consoled the grieving matron with these promises: if this could ever be done with the king’s favor, they would rebuild the whole thing on her behalf [Col. 1301D].

After devastating all the count’s property [Note: [Col. 1301] *propietate* in manuscript 1] and dividing it widely together with his benefice, the king came to Bamberg. There, dismissing his army in good peace, he celebrated the Nativity of the Mother of God (September 8) with solemn rejoicing.

From there he set out for the forest called Spessart [Note: [Col. 1301D] Spessart], softening the labor of the expedition with the pleasure of the hunt (f. 93). After completing the autumnal enjoyment there, he crossed through Francia into Saxony and announced to them his expedition against the Milceni in the coming winter [Note: [Col. 1301D] Compare the *Quedlinburg Annals* under the year 1003, which report an expedition in this year; according to Thietmar, Book VI, chapter 2, the expedition was undertaken in 1004].

After this he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Pöhlde [Note: [Col. 1301] *polithi* in manuscript 1c?], honoring it divinely and humanly according to the custom of his predecessors [Note: [Col. 1301] *honerando* in manuscript 1, as above] [Note: [Col. 1302D] Compare the *Hildesheim Annals* under the year 1004].

24. Then, coming to Thornburg (1004), he sent Archbishop Willigis, together with his other attendants, to Archbishop Giselher, who was then extremely ill, so that, mindful of the Lord, he might wish at least at the end of his life to correct whatever he had hitherto done wrong in the destruction of the bishopric of Merseburg [Note: [Col. 1301] *merseburgiensis episcopatum* in manuscript 1a], by restoring it and abandoning the unjust see [Note: [Col. 1301] Witness 2 reads *hunc archiepiscopum Gislerum rex*, “the king [hated] this Archbishop Giselher”; *rex* is the subject of the next sentence, not a title applied to Giselher.].

At first the king hated him because of Herimann, whom Giselher had always tried with all his might to place before the king in the realm. Later, after granting him his favor, the king counted him among his most intimate attendants. Having entrusted to him all his properties in Saxony, he found him a faithful administrator in these matters and accomplished through him many things that then pleased his will.

At last, unable to bear such great zeal for God any longer, he pursued him with perfected hatred and sent him the aforesaid messengers [Col. 1302C]. Giselher barely replied to them in these words:

“Grant me three or four days’ respite and allow me to leave; when they have passed, I shall give you a definite answer.”

Having obtained this from the king, he went out in a wagon, as he had long been accustomed to do, and came to his estate at Thriburi [Note: [Col. 1302D] Otherwise called Troibern, a now-ruined castle which I suspect lay not far from Thornburg, both from this account and from Feller’s *Monumenta inedita*, p. 18. Ursinus]. He stayed there for two days and, on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, departed from this world.

When the king heard this, he followed the body of the archbishop as far as Magdeburg, sending his chaplain Wigbert ahead to obtain the unanimous will of the brethren for the election of Tagino [Note: [Col. 1301] *taginone*, corrected to *tajone*, elsewhere *tainone*, but almost everywhere restored by another hand to *taginone* in manuscript 1].

The provost of that city, named Waltherd, summoned all the brethren together and announced both the death of their senior and the king’s arrival. He urged them to seek among themselves someone with whom they might preserve the ancient custom of election. Everyone immediately replied that, with God’s favor, they commonly wished to have Tagino as their lord.

He received this with great humility, as was fitting, and, prostrating himself, asked forgiveness.

The archbishop’s body was carried to Saint John [Note: [Col. 1303D] The monastery of Berge] and was kept there during the following night with due honors. On the next day, when it was being carried to Saint Maurice, the king arrived there and received it together with all the clergy and people; it was carefully guarded for a second night.

At daybreak the king sent Bishop Arnulf [Note: [Col. 1303D] Bishop of Halberstadt] to the brethren and the ministerial knights [Note: [Col. 1303] *ministeriales* in manuscript 2 and A. S.], who were greatly distressed, to secure the election of Tagino. Waltherd, setting out his embassy point by point, replied above all:

“We know what your senior intends. We wish, if it can be done, to have the power of electing; and all those present here wished me, though unworthy, to succeed to the vacant place, as you yourselves can establish. We greatly fear that our church may suffer loss. To prevent this, we ask the royal piety and your intercession. We are not forgetful of a certain saying of a wise man (*Lucan*, *Pharsalia* III.145–146):

> “The liberty of a people constrained by kingship perishes through the ruler’s liberty; only the shadow of the people’s liberty remains if it chooses to obey all that ruler’s commands.”

After saying this, the bishop departed and reported everything into the king’s ears. The king immediately summoned the provost, made him many promises, and obtained both his permission and that of his colleagues for Tagino’s election.

At once, when all had gathered in the greater church, the king, by the staff of Bishop Arnulf, entrusted the clergy and people to the venerable father Tagino, who would have to render an account before the supreme Judge; and he himself installed Tagino in the episcopal chair, while everyone stood by and sang praises to God [Note: [Col. 1303] Witness 1b adds *et*, “and,” linking “while everyone stood by” with “singing praises to God.”].

After the commemoration for the dead, the archbishop’s body was buried before the southern altar [Note: [Col. 1303] *altare*—“altar”—in manuscript 1a].

## Source-grounded apparatus and folio anchors

- **Chapter 16, Hartwig and the Italian campaign.** At *nunciis nostris*, “our messengers,” manuscript 2 instead has singular *nuncius*, “messenger.” In the next sentence the text has *regem*, “the king,” while A. S. reads *tyrannum*, “the tyrant,” which changes the characterization. Manuscript 2 has *carrentorum* (“of Carinthians”) with Duke Otto; *collustrans* (“surveying/looking about”) occurs in A. S. at the assault on the *clusae* (barriers), not Lucca. Manuscript 2 has *pene* (“almost/closely behind”) in Hartwig’s pursuit and A. S. *Ungarium* (“Hungarian”) for the mountain; it has *thetunicorum* (“of the Germans”) for the German battle-line and *cum* (“when”) in the defeat clause.
- **Chapters 17–19.** Manuscript 2 has *bolislaus* for Bolizlaus; A. S. *incommodi* (“of inconvenience/misfortune”) in the sentence on the unhappy battle. At the Rederarii, codex 1 continues with the reading *redariorum*, and manuscript 2 also has *redariorum*; this note belongs to the Rederarii, not to the preceding Merseburg passage. The source folio boundaries in this run are **(f. 89)**, **(f. 89')**, **(f. 90)**, and **(f. 90')**; they mark the manuscript’s successive leaves and do not indicate a textual omission.
- **Chapter 20.** The source resumes at **(f. 91)** and passes **(f. 91')** and **(f. 92)** during the Bavarian expedition. Witness 1b adds *subito*, “suddenly,” to the warning about incurring an insurmountable fall. The source pairs *sep* with *saepius* (“often/repeatedly”): it is a scribal abbreviation or reading, not an added adverb in the translation.
- **Chapter 21.** The source crosses **(f. 92')** in the Hatheresburg/Crusni campaign. Witness 1a has *proficissitur*, a malformed spelling of *proficiscitur*, “he proceeds,” at the clause in which the king goes to Crusni; witness 1 has *cuidam*, “to a certain one,” for the text’s *cujusdam*, “of a certain,” at the valley. At *poenas*, “punishments,” the letter *o* seems to have been added by witness 1b and later erased by witness 1.
- **Chapter 22.** Folio **(f. 93')** occurs in the Bolizlaus campaign and **(f. 94)** before the later movements. Manuscript 1a has *his* (“these”), *deludetur* (“will be deceived/mocked”), *subsequituros* (“about to follow”), and *has* (“these”); manuscript 1 has *hasque* (“and these”). The reading at *Duae* is erased and uncertain in the source; it must remain an uncertain erased reading rather than a supplied word.
- **Chapters 23–24.** Witness 1b adds *Heinricus vero*, “Count Heinric, however.” Its erased *s. i. d.* abbreviates the adjoining *se iam defecisse*, “that his strength/self had now failed,” and manuscript 1 has *eccessit* for *excessit* (“departed/withdrew”). Folio **(f. 94')** precedes the opening of chapter 24. Manuscript 1 reads *quicquid* (“whatever”) in the Merseburg sentence. Witness 2 reads *hunc archiepiscopum Gislerum rex*, “the king [hated] this Archbishop Giselher”; “king” is the subject, not part of Giselher’s title. Witness 1b adds *et*, “and,” between those standing by and singing praise at Tagino’s installation.

### 25

But before I come to the restoration of our see [Note: *renovationis* in witness 1a, with the *s* erased], I wish to discuss something concerning the aforesaid man who was then about to be ordained. He was an outstanding cleric of Wolfgang, the pious pastor who had governed the church of Regensburg, a monk in habit and conduct. This man was so dear to him that, having raised him from childhood in place of a son, he placed him, when grown, over all his own possessions. Moreover, he secured for him such favor with the duke and the emperor that, if ever he should withdraw from this life at God’s command, he had no doubt that this man would succeed him. [Note: *si* (“if”) is absent in witness 1.]

When the course of this exile had then been completed in remarkable holiness [Note: In witness 1, *in* is written over an erasure of three or four letters; after it, *antistes* is written with eight or nine letters erased], the venerable bishop, having begun to suffer from an illness reaching almost to death, summoned his beloved Tagino [Note: *Tagione* in witness 1a, with the *g* erased and not restored] and said:

“Place your mouth, son, upon my mouth, receiving from God the inspiration of my spirit, so that wherever you grow warm with the ardor of youth, you may remain temperate in the twofold love, receiving moderation from the supreme power and from my goodwill; and if perhaps you are deprived of my honors, after twice five solar years, when I have atoned before God for my sins, you will certainly rejoice in greater ones.”

After this, when the holy man foresaw in spirit that his end was near, he ordered himself to be carried into the church [Note: *portari*, “to be carried,” in witness 1?]. Having completed the prayers and the other things that the brothers had to perform, and commending himself and those entrusted to him to God, he peacefully sent forth his holy spirit on the day before the Kalends of October (994).

The man who had been elected by everyone came to the emperor, but did not receive what had been promised, since the emperor had given the bishopric to his own chaplain Gebehard. Tagino was faithfully entrusted to him, and although he was treated honorably by him, nevertheless, because good and evil do not accord with one another [Note: That is, they are incompatible], he did not remain with him long, owing to the inequality of their characters [Note: One witness has *suarum*, “of their character”; another has *inequalitate*, “inequality”]. For he immediately attached himself to Duke Heinrich, pleased him by the chastity of his mind and body, and until the day I have mentioned served him day and night—troublesome to the wicked, welcome to the good—striving especially to spend himself for God and human beings. Thus, because of the king’s love for the holy man, whom he loved uniquely [Note: One witness adds: “since he had been the king’s foster-father”; another: “for he had been the king’s nurse”], that holy man’s truthful prophecy was fulfilled after ten years had run their course, as Lord Tagino himself often related to me. [Note: *Veridicum*, “truthful,” is the reading of witness 1c?]

He honored his dearest lord and the queen, together with all their companions, with many gifts, as was fitting, although his own resources in no way sufficed for such generosity.

### 26

From there the king went with him to his own castle, called Givikansten (1004) [Note: *Giuikanstaen* in witness 1a], and carefully inspected everything that Bishop Gisilher had collected there, declaring it excessive. Then he went to Merseburg, which had long been deprived of its pastor, in order to bring consolation, and strove with all his might to restore it to its former honors.

There, on the fourth day before the Nones of February—that is, on the Lord’s Hypapante, the “meeting” of the righteous Simeon—venerable Tagino, having received permission from Bishop Hilderic [Note: Of Havelberg], who was first among these brothers in rank, was consecrated by Willigis, archbishop of Mainz, in the presence of the king and the Roman legate, with all the co-bishops supporting the act.

Since, as his own writing testifies, he was to be ordained only by the apostolic bishop, and that bishop could not come here [Note: That is, to Magdeburg] because of the pressing necessity, Tagino there completed the third number by the anointing with sacred chrism, entrusting the whole bishopric afterward to Waltherd [Note: One witness adds: “Waltherd … the bishopric”; another reads, “and he entrusted it to Waltherd”; compare below, Book VI]. [Note: Compare below, Book VI.]

The king, who had always hungered and thirsted for it and was then eager to be satisfied with the food of justice, knew that this could not otherwise be done with Archbishop Arnulf; therefore, by an exchange of one hundred manses, he redeemed the episcopal ban over the Merseburg burgward alone. [Note: One witness adds this sentence.] Whatever he had requested from his beloved Tagino, he received, since Tagino bestowed it with abundant goodwill.

By royal authority he decreed that what antiquity had been able to demonstrate as having been taken away from the bishoprics of Meissen and Zeitz should be restored to them in full. Therefore I begin with these verses, singing odes to Christ [Note: Here the sixth book begins in witness 2, which adds in the lower margin: “The prologue of Book VI begins”]:

> O Christ, sun of justice, shining above all,  
> At your first advent redeeming the world, and at your second,  
> Sole creator with the Father, destroyer and examiner,  
> Distributing rewards for various deeds  
> To the human race, which slips headlong into crime:  
> True day, bless now such light,  
> By which, merciful, you visited the despoiled Church.  
>
> Let Mersburg praise you, rejoicing in your gift;  
> Let its sons and its restored shepherds  
> Faithfully render thanks to you now from the heart.  
>
> Illustrious King of kings, now receive the speech of your servants  
> [Note: *Fasma*, that is, *sermo*, “speech,” from *fari*, “to speak”].  
> Mercifully look down from heaven upon your servant Heinrich,  
> And defend his faithful wife,  
> Upon these, for their small gifts, bestowing your greatest blessings.  
>
> May Tagino’s spirit live in the heavenly palace.  
> May Waltherd and Gero [Note: Gero was elected archbishop of Magdeburg in 1012] prevail in blessedness at the end.  
>
> May all be saved by Christ and assigned  
> To seats in Elysium [Note: “Seats in Elysium,” from Lucan, *Pharsalia* III.12]—all whom you, Mersburg,  
> With the kindly affection of piety  
> Raised up with benevolent hands.  
>
> O God, who first and supreme rule all things,  
> Govern this place, so that it may stand by your oar;  
> May its guardians follow your commands,  
> May its enemies have no power, but, converted, render good in return.  
>
> Be gracious, I pray, to the one who was its destroyer.  
> Moreover, grant pardon to all who assisted the wicked,  
> So that, rejoicing, they may await the certainties of the future.

[Note: At the middle of the last page of the final quaternion, the hand that wrote these two quaternions, comprising Book V and the first eight leaves of Book VI, comes to an end. The following verses were apparently added shortly afterward by another hand resembling Thietmar’s; Thietmar himself added the last five. It is therefore evident that the final thirteen verses are later than the others.]

> The city of Worms rejoices in these times  
> In its freedom, in whose shadow it had hitherto remained,  
> And had been under the law of its own dukes. [Note: Heinrich II granted very many privileges to the church of Worms. Our author is referring especially to the king’s privilege of 29 July 1014, by which he protected it against the unjust claims of the counts.]  
>
> Bishop Burchard rejoices among the noble lords  
> From the heart, because he no longer fears enemies  
> From nearby, being now far removed from that one.  
>
> The duke’s lordly palace is now a glorious house of Christ,  
> And the clergy now suppress the various judges.  
>
> King Heinrich, radiant with piety, did this,  
> Releasing this church from his own possessions  
> And restoring it to Christ.  
>
> The pious Duke Otto approved this, and, generous,  
> Granted by royal gift that it be held in abundance. [Note: See the king’s charter of 3 October 1002.]  
>
> From this let all the faithful rejoice forever.

[Note: “The prologue ends. Book VI begins,” added in witness 2.]

## BOOK SIX

### 1

After the line of the millennium had been completed following the saving birth of the undefiled Virgin, and in the fifth place of the cardinal order (February 1004) [Note: Ursinus and others have already observed that this should read “in the fourth [place] of the cardinal order … at the beginning of that fifth [week],” as is clear both from the sequence of the narrative and from the charters of King Heinrich dated 5 and 6 March 1004], at the beginning of that fourth week, in February, the month called purgatorial, a bright morning dawned upon the world [Note: *Loc* is written over an erasure in witness 1b]. Heinrich, king by God’s grace, wishing to cleanse the stain of his predecessors and earn eternal forgiveness for himself, having arranged everything relevant to this according to his own pleasure, went to his residence, where he always used to refresh himself bodily [Note: *Corporaliter* is the reading of witness 1a], so that there he might be somewhat restored in spirit by the nourishment he had long desired.

Calling all the leading men of the kingdom to himself, he gave the bishopric of the holy church of Merseburg to a certain chaplain of his own, named Wigbert [Note: In witness 1, the words *cuidam* (“to a certain [man]”) and *nomine* (“named”) are erased; *quidam* seems to have stood there]. He gave him Archbishop Tagino’s pastoral staff; with it Wigbert, desiring that church’s restoration, restored whatever his predecessor had presumed unjustly to take from it [Note: This restoration of the bishopric of Merseburg was confirmed by the king’s charter of 4 March 1004], with Bishop Arnulf consenting, as did Bishops Eido and Hilliward, among whom that diocese had been divided, and with all the people applauding.

Wigbert was then led with divine rejoicing to his see and, on the same day, was consecrated by his archbishop Tagino and by the brothers Hilleric and Wigo, together with the aforesaid co-bishops.

### 2

Meanwhile Bolizlav, at the instigation of Count Heinrich, inflicted great violence upon all the Bavarians and his other fellow citizens. For this reason the king, having first announced an expedition, invaded the territory of the Milceni as an enemy; and, had not an excessive fall of snow quickly melted and hindered him, the whole region would have been left devastated and without inhabitants.

Returning from there, he sadly stationed auxiliary garrisons to assist Margrave Guncelin and the other defenders of the homeland. Then, coming to Merseburg, he learned from trustworthy intermediaries that his brother had fled to the king of the Hungarians [Note: That is, Stephen] to obtain pardon, while Heinrich had deeply repented of his undertaking.

Although unwilling, he accepted the petitions of those sent to him as intercessors—especially those of his beloved Tagino [Note: One witness has *Daginonis*, as often elsewhere] and Duke Bernhard—and granted his count Heinrich pardon on the condition that he restore the estate and right of residence to him and to his supporters, while he might keep the count in custody for as long as he wished.

Heinrich, tearfully acknowledging that he was exceedingly guilty in all respects, surrendered himself to the king in the dress and manner of a penitent. By the king’s command he was then thrust by the aforesaid archbishop into the castle of Ivicansten and carefully guarded day and night by his soldiers. There, in addition to other good works, he sang the psalter with 150 acts of penitence (*veniae*) in a single day [Note: “There … he sang” is added in witness 1b].

### 3

Meanwhile the king, mindful of the wrong done in Italy, urged all his faithful to avenge it and, as Lent was approaching, prepared to go there himself with an armed force.

Leaving Merseburg, he sought at Magdeburg the intercession of Saint Maurice before God and prosperity for his journey [Note: He was there on 24 February, as a charter attests]. From there, passing through the borders of eastern Thuringia and Francia [Note: Witness 1 has *inper*], he came to Regensburg. Having held a royal assembly there, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, amid the acclaim of all present, he granted the duchy, with a banner-bearing lance, to his soldier and son-in-law Heinrich [Note: Duke Heinrich, who became duke of Bavaria, was the brother of Queen Cunigund].

Then, reaching the city of Augsburg on his journey, he was honorably welcomed and received by its bishop, Sigifrid. After staying there only two nights, he gave the queen careful greetings and permission to depart for Saxony, entrusting her to his beloved Tagino [Note: One witness has *her*]. He himself advanced with the army as far as a place called Tinga [Note: So in witness 1, in an erasure; *Tonga* in another witness] [Note: Now Thingau, near the city of Kempten. It may be inferred from the Merseburg Calendar that Thietmar attended the dedication of the church of Saint Mary in this city on 19 March].

There Lord Brono, his brother, was presented to the king together with Hungarian intercessors, and was mercifully received into favor by him. At the request of Archbishop Tagino I came to the aforesaid city and returned with him (March).

We came to Gero’s grove [Note: Gernrode in the duchy of Anhalt], where, together with the venerable abbess Hathui, we solemnly performed the palm rite. On the fourth day of the week the queen came to Magdeburg and celebrated there the Lord’s Supper and the solemnity of the Lord’s resurrection that followed.

### 4

The king, after many hardships on the journey [Note: One witness has the singular, “of hardship”], came to the city of Trent and there celebrated Palm Sunday (9 April). He allowed the army, afflicted by the necessity of excessive labor, to breathe for a little while during this solemn festival [Note: One witness repeats “of hardship”].

King Hardwig, foreseeing his arrival and greatly fearing it, sent trusted messengers to the fortifications mentioned above. He himself, having gathered his forces and sitting on the plain of Verona [Note: One witness has *Veronensi*, corrected from *Uveronensi*], hoped that the present situation might perhaps correspond to his former successes.

King Heinrich discovered that this passage was blocked and could scarcely, if at all, be forced. Turning elsewhere, he discussed with his intimate advisers whether he might in any way seize the closed passes far away, with the Carentanians assisting him.

This was accomplished by prudent counsel, although it seemed difficult to many. The Carentanians immediately obeyed the royal commands and divided into two legions. One, before dawn, secretly occupied with infantry the mountain above the passes; the other [Note: The words “one … the other,” missing from one manuscript whose greater part of the line is cut away, are supplied from another witness] followed at daybreak to attack them, after hearing from their comrades who had gone ahead a signal so loud that it could be heard from the enemy’s hidden ambushes.

Those who believed themselves secure behind the enemy’s rear hastened out armed to meet them. But our men, attacking them from the side, drove some to flight, while forcing others to perish over precipices and in the flooding of the river Brenta.

Thus, as victors, they carefully guarded the passes until the king’s arrival [Note: One witness has *clausas*, “the closed passes”]. When the king heard this from the messengers, he abandoned all impediments except his best companions, crossed the passes with great difficulty, and pitched camp beside the bank of the aforesaid water on a pleasant plain, so that there he might most devoutly venerate the Lord’s Supper, the consecration of the chrism, the Lord’s Passion, and his holy resurrection (13–16 April).

By royal ban, the count palatine forbade everyone to flee, and future assistance was promised to those who resisted bravely. On the third day of the week the king crossed the aforesaid river, pitched his tents again, and rested while awaiting scouts who were diligently seeking information about the enemy Hardwig’s movements [Note: One witness has “to acquire”].

### 5

The minds of the Lombards, hitherto united in evil [Note: After the syllable *clan*, a major part of the line is cut away in witness 1; “the purpose … the mind” is supplied from another witness], were divided by the prompting of divine mercy. Separated from the unjust usurper, by their flight they opened a safe entrance for Heinrich, the king crowned by God [Note: One witness has *rege*, “king”].

Verona first received him and rejoiced in the Lord that the defender of the homeland had arrived and that the author of all its misery had departed. Margrave Thiedoldus, together with the aforesaid auxiliaries, came to meet him, rejoicing that the time had arrived when he could reveal to him the secret of his good will [Note: One witness has *qua*, “by which”].

The king then came with such an escort to Brixna [Note: Brescia] and was received by the archbishop of Ravenna and by Ethelberon, administrator of that see [Note: Added in witness 1b], together with the provincial clergy. From there, reaching Bergamo, once conquered by Emperor Arnulf [Note: See the *Annals of Fulda* and Regino’s *Chronicle* under the year 894, and Liutprand I.23], he received the archbishop of Milan after his faith had been confirmed by oaths.

After this he visited the city of Pavia (May). Received by that archbishop and by the leading men of the region, he was led with remarkable acclaim into the church and, by common election, was raised and placed upon the royal throne.

### 6

On that same day it was revealed how, through the mutability of the whole unstable world, its course is always rolled downward. For amid so much joy, discord, the enemy of peace, suddenly arose; and through excessive drunkenness, from a base cause, the bond of faith and oath was pitiably broken.

The townsmen armed themselves against the newly elected king and hurried to the palace, especially those who disliked Heinrich’s claim but were pleased by Hardwig’s release. When the king heard the uproar, he immediately ordered an inquiry into its cause.

He was promptly told that commoners, inflamed by sudden fury and animated by servile presumption [Note: One witness has *servile*], had first begun this disturbance, while all the others had gathered to his harm or disgrace.

Heribert, the distinguished administrator of the see of Agrippina [Note: “Of the see” is added in witness 2], tried to calm those who were already breaking in and asked from a window the cause of so great an invasion. He was driven back by a shower of stones and a discharge of arrows.

The palace, heavily attacked by the enemy, was bravely defended by the king’s household troops, whose number was easily counted [Note: One witness has *domestis*, “household troops,” rather than *domesticis*]. Since our men had been divided among several necessary tasks, the enemy’s strength increased.

At last, when our men heard the sound of the immense uproar, they hurried in groups to the king and drove back the still-maddened enemy for a little while. But night was now approaching, and they were delayed by the arrows and stones hurled against them. To provide for this, our men then set fire to the city walls. Our men who were outside bravely climbed the city’s defenses, while the others resisted them more effectively in this way.

There a certain distinguished young man named Gisilbert, the queen’s brother, died after being wounded by the Lombards [Note: The Merseburg Calendar records that Gisilbert, brother of Queen Cunigund, died between the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June and 14–25 May; the same charters show that the king was staying at Pavia], greatly increasing the grief of his companions.

The soldier Vulfer, leaping into the midst of the battle and striking one of them through the helmet as far as the throat, avenged him without fear. Thus, by turns, they exchanged moments of rest, friendly to all, for the harshness of war [Note: So in witness 1b; another has “the rest of battle, friendly to all”; witness 1a has a reading apparently meaning “the quiet of war was changed”].

Our men captured some of the enemy by force and presented them alive to the king. Suddenly a house that had sheltered our exhausted men collapsed after being set on fire by the Lombards; but this made those who had gained no certainty of hope more eager for battle.

Meanwhile the Alemanni, with the Franks and Lotharingians [Note: The *i* is erased in witness 1], at last learning of these disasters and entering through the broken walls, pursued the townsmen so fiercely that not one of them dared leave the fortification of his own house (1004, May).

Those men, striking our forces with the arrows they shot from the summit of the walls, perished when the fire was brought against them. It is difficult for anyone to describe the extent of the slaughter there, produced in various ways.

The king’s soldiers, now victorious, used without hindrance the spoils of the slain. Moved by this pitiable sight, and firmly ordering them to spare the survivors [Note: Witness 1a has the spelling *firmater*], the king withdrew to the fortress of Saint Peter and mercifully granted pardon to the enemies who humbly begged for it.

Then all those who had been absent, having heard of the king’s victory, either came themselves to avoid such things or sent hostages, promising the king faith, assistance, and the duty of submission [Note: One witness has the singular *promittens*].

### 7

When the disasters at Pavia had been settled, the king came to the Long Bridge [Note: Perhaps the town of Sponte in the region of Novara, near Pavia], and took charge of the remaining Lombard forces. After holding a conference there with everyone and prudently arranging matters of the greatest importance, he sought Milan for love of the most holy bishop Ambrose.

Soon returning to the meadows of the aforesaid place [Note: One witness has *pratam*, “to the meadow”; another has an abbreviation apparently for *pontem*, “bridge”], he appeased the people who complained about his sudden departure by promising a speedy return and offering them many other consolations.

Then, as Pentecost was approaching, he celebrated the solemnity (4 June) at a place called Grommo [Note: Apparently the city of Crema]. Proceeding from there, he received the Tuscans who came to meet him into the company of those who would serve him faithfully [Note: One witness reads *Induntuscos*; another, *Duntuscos*; another, *Tuscos*, “Tuscans.” Compare also Adelbold’s *Life of Saint Heinrich*].

Hastening thereafter to revisit his homeland, he invaded the territory of Alemannia, recently deprived of the support of Duke Herimann and still devoted to his son and namesake, who was yet a little boy, in order to govern and secure it.

From there he went to Strasbourg, situated in Alsace, and devoutly celebrated there the nativity of Christ’s precursor. On its vigil I must not pass over the miracles that the Lord performed through him, for these things are spoken for the delight of the pious but for the terror of the reprobate.

The house in which the king was administering justice to the people of the law [Note: So in a passage written over an erasure in witness 1b] suddenly collapsed, injuring only one priest who was constantly staying there with a woman unjustly excommunicated [Note: One witness has the feminine form, “of an unjust woman”].

That man, more culpable than the others in this crime, paid the penalty for his offense by his death, his legs first being broken.

How sweet are the deeds of the pious, which we read for the building up of the soul and learn from others by sight and hearing—and yet, miserable people, we act foolishly with hardened hearts. We are not moved from our ingrained wickedness by the certain punishments of evil, nor are we delighted by the immeasurable rewards of the just [Note: Another witness reads: “nor are we turned toward correction of life, delighted by the ineffable rewards of the just”].

Departing from there [Note: Another witness adds: “from Strasbourg”], the king humbly visited at Mainz the threshold of Saint Martin, the bishop, and there devoutly celebrated the nativity of the apostles [Note: That is, Peter and Paul] (29 June).

### 8

After this, traveling through eastern Francia, he revisited Saxony, which, as he often declared, was like a flower-bearing paradise, a court of security and complete abundance.

There he vomited forth from his guileless heart the long-hidden secret of his concealed zeal and, in order to restrain the savage arrogance of Bolizlav, announced an expedition for mid-August to all the faithful of Christ and of himself within his jurisdiction [Note: Compare the *Quedlinburg Annals* under the year 1004].

When the appointed time had been set, an army was assembled at Merseburg and at last secretly advanced against the enemy. Pretending to be traveling into Poland, they amassed ships at Boruz [Note: Boritz, not far from Riesa beside the Elbe] and Nisani [Note: So in witness 1b; witness 1a has “ships at Citiza-Nicici”], so that no disclosure of an encircling movement would be made to the enemy through the feigned goodwill of his own men.

Meanwhile a great fall of rain caused the army ineffable delay in crossing the rivers. When no one could have guessed it, the king rapidly proceeded into Bohemia.

A lion roaring and striving to impede his advance with its pursuing tail fortified a certain mountain with archers in the forest called Miriquidui [Note: *Miriquidui*, that is, “the Black Forest”—a name also found as *myrkviðr* in the Icelandic poem *Atlakviða in grœnlenzka*. The mountainous region now called the Erzgebirge is meant here. See also the charter of Emperor Frederick I dated 26 February 1162].

The king, learning of this, secretly sent ahead selected armored soldiers. Against the enemy’s will they broke through the difficult route, preparing an easy path for those who followed [Note: One witness has *parentes* instead of *parantes*, “preparing”].

Meanwhile, while Bolizlav was dining one day, one of our men, a chaplain of Bishop Reinbern [Note: That is, of the bishop of Kolberg; see above, Book IV.28], spoke about the arrival of our army. Bolizlav immediately heard him and asked what he was saying. When the man replied, Bolizlav said: “If they were hopping like frogs, they would already have arrived here.”

And this would indeed have been true, had divine mercy not favored the king and had the man’s proud arrogance not inflated him; our victory would not have come so quickly.

The king was also helped by the exiled Jaromir, whose name means “firm peace.” The Bohemians were softened by the arrival of their adopted ruler. At their counsel and invitation he opened the way for the king’s entrance, and at the very gateway of that region he voluntarily surrendered a castle to him.

Because the Bavarians had not yet arrived, the king delayed his journey slightly and came to the city called Saaz [Note: *Satzi*, Saaz]. The townsmen immediately opened their gates to him, killed the Poles stationed there as a garrison, and made it known that they were his own friends.

Seeing such slaughter, the king was moved and ordered the survivors to be shut up together in one church. There also arrived a man who reported with certainty that Bolizlav had been killed by his fellow countrymen.

The king’s household rejoiced in God, while the corrupt supporters of the false duke grieved. Whispering among themselves, they spewed from the secret chamber of their unjust hearts this lie: that if the king ever stood in a secure position, they would then count for nothing and would have to suffer many adversities at his hands.

Because of this spark hidden beneath the ashes, on this journey and afterward they very often preferred to their own king an enemy of all the faithful, worse than brute animals, unaware that the unbegotten Father, God, the observer from above, was about to free from heaven his earthly vicar from their fraud.

### 9

Then, by the king’s command, Jaromir was sent ahead to Prague with the best of our soldiers and with the inhabitants attached to him, to capture or kill the poisonous serpent [Note: Compare also the celebrated poem of the Königshofen manuscript].

The messengers of the aforesaid persons forestalled him and reported the matter in due order [Note: Compare Virgil, *Aeneid* III.179] to Bolizlav, who had previously felt secure from such danger.

Warned by this embassy, Bolizlav secretly prepared himself. In the middle of the following night, hearing in the nearby city called Vyšehrad the citizens ringing bells to urge one another to battle, he went out with the first legion and returned to his homeland by flight.

Zebizlav, the brother of Adalbert, bishop and martyr of Christ, pursued him and was killed after being wounded on a bridge. He left great joy to the enemies but immeasurable grief to his own men.

On the following day Jaromir arrived and, before the gate, granted the people who asked for their rights and pardon for their offense what they sought. Immediately admitted, he was enthroned with great joy in his former honors, and then, having put aside his shabby garments, was clothed in more precious ones [Note: One witness has *preciosoribus*, “more precious,” in another form].

There he was presented with whatever each of the soldiers had taken as booty from the fleeing or slain enemy. Delighted by many gifts, he was escorted into Vyšehrad, where he was acclaimed as lord. He promised the king’s pardon and a reward long labored for to those who had persevered with him up to that point.

An immeasurable crowd of both common people and nobles [Note: Another witness has “nobles”] gathered from every direction to receive the favor of the new duke and to await the arrival of the glorious king.

When the king finally arrived, Bishop Thieddego and Duke Jaromir received him with immense rejoicing from all the clergy and people and led him to the church of Saint George. Before everyone, with the native inhabitants assembled, the king honored Jaromir with all the dignities that had belonged to his father.

### 10

While the king was there venerating the nativity of the holy Mother of God, celebrated throughout the world (8 September), Goddescalcus [Note: One witness has *Goddescalce*], the venerable pastor of the holy church of Freising—possessing in deed the name he bore [Note: That is, “servant of God”]—was ordered by the king to sing Mass and instruct the people, and was granted permission by the bishop of that see.

After the Gospel had been read [Note: Another adds: “he ascended the steps”; another: “ascending the steps”], he admonished those present concerning the fear of God, the preservation of the bond of twofold love, obedience to God and the honor due to higher powers.

Finally he addressed the king gently, urging him to recognize himself and to wish to attribute everything he had ever received from the first cradle of his life up to that time—whether honor or any advantage—not to his own merits but rather to divine generosity.

Moreover, he spoke of mercy, which is the sole safeguard of salvation, the venerable ornament of faith, and the great remission of sins [Note: One witness has *magno*, the masculine form]. In preserving this work, every Christian must always desire three things: to be able, to wish, and to accomplish.

Since these things must be fulfilled by everyone, they must especially be fulfilled by those who, injuring no one, desire similar things to be repaid them by the Lord. And in order that their vow may be acceptable to God, each person must give from the heart and forgive all his debtors, lest, in the place of the wicked servant [Note: One witness has the abbreviated form *seru*], they be bound by terrible torments.

Concluding in this way, he said:

“I appeal to you by the name and love of him [Note: Another witness reads: ‘I appeal to you, glorious king’] who forgave his debtor ten thousand talents, and forgave the Jews—*recutiti* (‘circumcised again’) [Note: *Judaei recutiti*, from Martial VII.29.5; one witness has *recucitis*, another *recusatis*]—for their transgression of his commandments: have mercy, most beloved lord, on Heinrich, formerly margrave, but now, as I hope, truly penitent; loose his bonds and grant him favor, so that with a freer spirit you may today address God: ‘Forgive us our debts,’ and so forth.”

The king, moved and appeased by this tearfully delivered exhortation, firmly promised that he would do so [Note: One witness has the duplicated form *spopondit*]. Afterward, returning home, he mercifully fulfilled his promise.

### 11

When everything had then been arranged there, he sent the Bavarians home. He himself, however, with the new duke of the Bohemians, entered the neighboring territory of the Milceni [Col. 1314A] by an indescribably difficult route and besieged the city of Budusin.

But when one day he was urging each of his own faithful men to storm it, he would have been unexpectedly wounded by one of the archers on the fortifications, had divine providence not guarded him. The arrow injured the man who was standing closest beside him and accomplished the enemy’s intention in another person. The king, raising his humble heart toward God in prayer, praised Him who had shown His customary watchful mercy to him, undeserving though he was.

The aforementioned city would have lain burned, since fire had already been brought to it, had not the unfortunate order of Margrave Gunzelin prevented this. Many were wounded on both sides, and some were killed. Among our men there was one noble both by birth and by manly conduct, named Hemuza. After repeatedly provoking the townsmen to battle, he pursued them almost to the walls; struck on his helmeted head by half a millstone (f. 105), he was thrown down and, dead, was dragged into the city by his jeering enemies. Count Heinricus, my brother, whose man he was, bought back his body for a price and brought it home.

Another man, called Tommo, untamed because of his constant practice of hunting, was bravely resisting the enemy in the river Sprewa. He slipped on the stones in the torrent and fell; although his excellent coat of mail had long protected him, he at last died, alas, from a delayed wound. When one of his own retainers tried to prevent his body from being carried away, he was pierced by a spear-point and fell upon him.

When the harshness of the aforesaid battle had nearly been overcome, at Bolizlavus’s command, delivered through a messenger, the city was surrendered to the royal power with its defenders unharmed and was fortified with a new garrison. After this the king returned home with his army, already exhausted by the journey and by hunger, assisting the margraves wherever necessary with their customary supports.

### 12

While he was giving himself over to the desired tranquillity at Merseburg, he learned that the venerable Count Esico, long afflicted by illness, had ended this life at Liubizici (November 22).

When the body arrived, he himself received it and ordered it to be honorably buried beside the church of Saint John the Baptist on its northern side. For the remedy of his soul, he gave to the holy altar and to the brethren serving God there a certain estate called Uppusun together with two silver candlesticks (f. 105′).

Moreover, he restored to Bishop Wigbert the merchants and Jews called *Appellas* (Horace, *Satires* I.5.100), whom Gisilher had originally acquired and long ago exchanged away.

He granted Burchard the county over Merseburg and the benefice belonging to it, and to Thiedbernus a benefice over the four cities situated beside the river Mulda. He retained every other estate for himself by his own judgment. He ordered Count Heinricus, released from custody, to depart with his favor.

### 13

Just as the prosperity of holy mother Church should be proclaimed to her spiritual offspring to increase Christ’s glory, so her losses must be recounted to provoke repentance. Her offspring should celebrate the former with unanimous joy, lament the latter with shared sorrow, and bear these losses with gentle patience.

In Pathelbrunn, the monastery and all its equipment were consumed by the avenging flame of our iniquity, moving the hearts of many of the faithful; love of divine recompense kindled them together to restore what had been destroyed.

A great synod was also held at a place called Throtmunni (1005). There the king complained to the assembled bishops and all those present of many abuses in holy Church. By their common counsel he decreed that these things should thereafter be forbidden, and by the excellent decree of a new institution he sought to lighten the heavy burden of his own sins (f. 106).

> In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1005, and in the fourth year of the reign of our lord Heinricus II, on the day of the Nones of July, this decree of that most glorious king and of his consort, Queen Chungunda, was enacted at Throtmunni (July 7), together with, and the archbishops Heribert of Cologne, Lievizo of Bremen, and Daginus, third archbishop of Magdeburg; and the bishops Notger of Liège, Suithger of Minden, Ansfrid of Utrecht, Thiederic of Metz, Thietmar of Osnabrück, Berenhar of Verden, Bernward of Hildesheim, Burchard of Worms, Rethar of Paderborn, Wigbert of Merseburg, Ekkihard of Schleswig, and Othinkerd.

> On the death of each of the aforesaid bishops, each bishop shall celebrate a mass for the deceased within thirty days, unless illness prevents it; and each presbyter in the monastery shall likewise do so. The presbyters outside the monasteries shall celebrate three masses. The deacons and the other lower orders shall recite ten psalters. The king and queen shall, within thirty days, distribute 1,500 denarii for the redemption of the departed person’s soul and feed an equal number of poor people. Each bishop shall feed 300 poor people, spend 30 denarii, and light thirty lamps. Duke Bernhard shall feed 500 poor people (f. 106′) and spend 15 solidi.

> We decree that the vigils of Saint John the Baptist, of the apostles Peter and Paul, of Saint Laurence, and of All Saints shall be fasted on bread, salt, and water; the vigil of the Assumption of Saint Mary, and all the vigils of the other apostles, as during Lent. The four Ember seasons shall be observed as during Lent, except for the Friday before the Nativity of the Lord, which we decree shall be fasted on bread, salt, and water.

### 14

The king approached the Frisians with a naval force and compelled them to desist from their rebellious undertakings, and to appease the great zeal of Liutgard, the queen’s sister. He also ordered that throughout his palace and all the counties of his kingdom, both an expedition against Poland and an assembly at Liezca should be proclaimed by royal command.

The army assembled at the appointed time, namely on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, at the agreed place. While the king was celebrating the Assumption of the holy Mother of God at Magdeburg, he crossed the Elbe on that very day, after mass and the completion of the customary almsgiving, accompanied by the queen, and set out.

### 15

During these days Ricdag, abbot of the Mount of Saint John the Baptist, was deposed from his abbacy by Bishop Tagino because of some crime, and Alfkerus, administrator of the monks serving Christ at Palithi, was appointed in his place. The rule of holy conduct that had until then remained firmly established was miserably destroyed and changed into the name of a provostship, and thus became the first indication of future misery.

Would that what came about through the passing of time had been a change of the right hand of the Most High! (Psalm 76:11.) The authors of the holy institution, who far surpassed the men of our own age in every form of piety, had prudently ordered what they built with the greatest zeal and completed, as it seemed to them, even to the point of perfection. In our unhappy time this has, through the instigation of evil men, as I fear, been changed not for the better but for the worse.

Would that this result had not arisen for the sake of our particular advantage. It is true that those whose new way of life is praiseworthy both in clothing and in food are often not what they pretend to be. Scripture says: “Pretended equity is not equity, but a double iniquity”.

Every fruit of human beings acceptable to God, consisting in a good heart, is sometimes concealed by good people under fine clothing and the golden mean in food and drink. But on whom is what is withheld from abstainers and those clothed in the *diplois* [a double cloak] spent? If it passes into the enlargement of those churches, it benefits twice over: the souls of the brothers, if they endure these things for God’s sake, and the acquisition of alms for their household resources. But if everything is bestowed outwardly, with what security does that increase whose growth causes the diminution of many to groan? Certainly it is not raised with firm stability but is eventually brought down in lamentation.

If Christ, who is Truth, keeps silent and all his heralds bite their tongues, is this whole affair faultless in every respect? The evangelical trumpet sounds that nothing will remain covered which will not be revealed (Matthew 10:26).

After we had satisfied our will in everything, we endured an unspeakable evil while concealing the crime. We are fellow mortals of a fragile nature, and we cannot fail to know that all weights tend toward the earth by their own inclination. Let us turn back and look again, and let us not despise those who admonish us; let us obtain the rewards promised to all the faithful through observance of the divine commandments.

Let us not appear better than our predecessors, since, being similarly deceived by various appearances of what seemed right, we are very unequal to them. Let no one become angry when he is familiarly reproved by someone for God’s sake. Let charity be kindly received by everyone, and let naked truth be endured for the sake of heavenly recompense.

Let the humble prayer of the faithful ask Christ for the necessary forgiveness of all these matters and of other crimes. And I, having wandered far from my subject, shall return to the course of the narrative I began.

### 16

After arranging the troops, the king proceeded from there. When the queen had quickly returned, she anxiously awaited in Saxony the desired arrival of her beloved lord.

Our army was advancing successfully toward the place called Dobraluh, in the district of Luzici. Duke Heinricus and Duke Jarimirus, hastening with their men to reinforce it, brought joy to the army and strengthened it with greater hope of counsel and courage.

There, because the guides had been bribed and wished to protect their own country, the army was led around through wildernesses and marshes, suffered severe hardship, and, through their envious malice, was delayed so that it could not quickly reach the enemy to injure him (f. 108).

Reaching the province called Nice, it pitched camp beside the river Sprewa. When Thiebernus, an excellent soldier, learned that the enemy was harming our men from a concealed flank, he secretly chose and summoned the best of his companions, wishing to seize the enemy by cunning for the sake of claiming special glory for himself.

The enemy, being sufficiently prudent, fled through the density of the fallen timber, so that he might injure his pursuers more effectively. Having, as usual, released the arrows by which they are chiefly defended, he first struck down Thiebernus, and afterward Bernhard, Isin, and Benno, famous retainers of Bishop Arnulf, together with many other comrades, on the eighth day before the Ides of September, catching them off guard and stripping them.

Because of this the king and his entire company were shaken with grief; and because of this, some truthful witnesses report, Bolizlavus also grieved. Afterward, on the day before our men came to the river Oder, the Liutici joined them, following their gods as they went before them.

Although I shudder to say anything about these matters, nevertheless, beloved reader, so that you may know their empty superstition and the still emptier practice of this people, I shall briefly explain who they are and where they came from.

### 17

[Col. 1319A]

There is a certain city in the district of the Riedireri called Riedegost, three-cornered and containing three gates. It is surrounded on every side by a great forest, untouched and revered by the inhabitants.

Two of its gates stand open to all who enter. The third, which faces east and is the smallest, displays a path to the nearby lake, a sight exceedingly terrible. Within it there is nothing except a temple skillfully constructed of wood, supported at its foundations by the horns of various animals.

Its walls are externally decorated with images of various gods and goddesses, wonderfully carved, as it appears to those who see them. Inside stand handmade gods, each with his name carved upon him, terrifyingly dressed in helmets and breastplates. The first of them is called Zuarasici, and he is honored and worshipped above all the others by all the pagans.

Their banners are never moved from this place except when necessary for an expedition, and then they are carried by foot soldiers. Special attendants have been appointed by the natives to care for these things diligently. When the people assemble here to sacrifice to the idols or appease their anger, the attendants alone sit while the others stand around, whispering secretly to one another. They dig into the earth with trembling, seeking certainty about uncertain matters by casting lots.

When this has been completed, they cover the lots with green turf. They then lead, with humble reverence, a horse regarded as the largest among the others and venerated by them as sacred over two spear-points fixed in the earth and crossed with one another (f. 109). After the lots by which they previously investigated the matter have been cast, they use this horse to divine again as though through a god.

If the same omen appears in both procedures, the undertaking is carried out; if not, the saddened people abandon it altogether.

The same antiquity, deceived by varied error, testifies that whenever the savage harshness of a long rebellion threatens them, a great boar emerges from the aforesaid lake, its white tusk shining through the foam, and shows itself to many with a terrifying shaking, delighting in wallowing.

### 18

As many regions as there are in these parts, so many temples are held, and individual images of demons are worshipped by unbelievers. Among them, the city mentioned above holds the chief dominion.

When they are hastening to war, they salute it; when they return successfully, they honor it with the appropriate gifts. What offering should be made to the gods by their attendants to render them propitious is carefully investigated by lots and by the horse, as I have said. Their unspeakable fury is appeased by human blood and the blood of cattle.

Yet none of all these people, who are commonly called Liutici, has a particular lord presiding over them. By unanimous counsel, discussing what is necessary at their assembly, they all agree on the matters to be carried out.

If one of their countrymen contradicts them at the assembly, he is beaten with clubs. If he openly resists outside it, he either loses everything through fire and continual plundering or, in their presence, pays a sum of money appropriate to his status. These unbelievers and changeable men demand immutability and great loyalty from others.

They affirm peace by shaving the top of the head, by grass, and by giving their right hands. Yet they are easily corrupted by money into disturbing it. These soldiers, once slaves but now free because of our iniquities, set out in such company to assist the king.

Flee, reader, their fellowship in worship. By listening to and fulfilling the commands of the divine Scriptures, learn the faith that Bishop Athanasius professed and retain it in memory; then you will truly prove that the things I have mentioned above are nothing.

### 19

[Col. 1320C]

From there, under unequal leaders, unequal squadrons soon reached the river Oder and pitched their tents beside the stream called Pober in the Slavic language and Castor in Latin.

Bolizlavus, seated with a large army at Crosno, after fortifying the banks of the aforesaid river, prevented them from crossing by every means.

But when the king had remained there for seven days and was preparing ships and bridges, divine providence showed his scouts, who had been sent out, an excellent ford. Six legions entered it at daybreak on the king’s command and crossed safely.

When Bolizlavus’s guards recognized this from a distance, they quickly carried the sad and unbelievable news to their lord (f. 110). At last, after he had been informed with certainty by three or more messengers, he hastily struck camp and fled with his men, leaving behind many possessions.

The king and his men carefully considered this. With the clergy and all the people he sang praises to Christ aloud, and crossed the river in safety. Those who had gone ahead would have overwhelmed the enemies, caught unawares in their tents, had they not waited for the long-delayed Liutici. Our men pursued them eagerly; but since they could not chase them like fleeing deer, they returned to their companions.

### 20

The king departed from there and reached the abbey called Mezerici. He strove to celebrate there, with the greatest reverence then possible, the annual feast of the Thebaid Legion (September 22). He also took care that neither this monastery nor the dwellings of the absent monks should suffer any annoyance from his men.

Thereafter he pursued the enemy, who dared spend the night in none of his cities, devastating everything nearby. At the request of his leading men, he settled no more than two miles from the city of Posnani.

While the army was divided among the gathering of crops and other necessities, it suffered great loss from enemies lying in ambush. Meanwhile Bolizlavus sought the king’s favor through trustworthy intercessors and soon deserved to be heard.

Archbishop Tagino came to the aforesaid city at Bolizlavus’s request with other members of the king’s household. With oaths and appropriate reparations, he concluded with him a firm treaty of peace.

Our men then returned joyfully, for they had endured great hardship from the length of the journey and excessive hunger, combined with the harshness of war.

### 21

After this, in our regions, the king strove with the greatest zeal to secure the prosperity of the desired safety, once the authors of every evil had been uprooted. He ordered the famous retainer Bruncio to be hanged at Merseburg; and, among the Slavs, he ordered Borisen and Nezemuisclen, the best men, together with their other supporters, to be hanged at Welereslevo.

Often holding an assembly with the Slavs at Wiribeni, situated beside the Elbe, he discussed and powerfully settled the necessary affairs of his kingdom, whether they wished it or not.

He rebuilt the previously devastated Arnaburch for the defense of the homeland, and restored whatever had long been unjustly taken from that place. By synodal judgment he himself, using canonical and apostolic authority, prohibited unjust marriages and the sale of Christians to pagans, and ordered those who despised God’s justice to be slain by the spiritual sword.

### 22

Meanwhile youth, abundant wealth, and the wicked incitement of evil men armed Baldwin, duke of the Flemings, against the king and persuaded him to seize the city of Valentia and subject it to his own power.

When the king first learned of this, he himself approached with military standards and tried through constant fighting to recover it. Achieving nothing, he departed, firmly announcing to the easterners and westerners that his expedition against Baldwin would take place in the following summer.

The desired time arrived, a large army was gathered, and the king with it reached the river Scheldt (1006). There Baldwin appeared with armed troops and tried, with vain confidence, to prevent the king’s crossing. But, by the prudent counsel of certain men, our forces were secretly transported elsewhere in ships; falling upon him unexpectedly, they confounded his excessive presumption.

When he fled, the king rejoiced in Christ the victor, crossed the river, and ravaged the adjoining region. When he came to the abbey called Ghent, he was received by the brethren of that church and spared the place and all its appurtenant possessions.

At last Baldwin, compelled by great necessity, obtained pardon through humble supplication. Not long afterward, having been made the king’s man, he received Walecorn and the aforementioned city as a benefice.

### 23

[Col. 1322B]

In the month of July, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, Gisela, the venerable matron and illustrious mother of our king, died and was buried at Regensburg.

When these regions had then been pacified, the king held a general council at Fronkenevordi, and it was attended by all the bishops on this side of the Alps (1007). Reader, listen with your ears to the cause that preceded it.

From childhood the king had cultivated above all others, with unique affection, a certain city of his called Bavanberg, situated in eastern Francia. After taking a wife, he gave it to her as a dowry. When, by divine mercy, he was elevated to the administration of the kingdom, he always desired silently in his heart to establish a bishopric there.

But since, as Flaccus testifies (*Epistles* I.2.40), “he who has begun has half the deed,” he began a new church there with two crypts and completed it. Gradually gathering everything that pertained to the divine service, he often asked Heinricus, bishop of Würzburg, who was very close to him, whether he would be willing to assist his purpose and grant him the parish situated in the district named from the river Radinzca, so that the king might claim it for himself in exchange.

The bishop received his beloved lord’s just requests graciously and consented on condition that the king obtain the pallium for his church and subordinate the pastor of Babenberg to him. He privately confirmed this by giving his staff to the king, with a certain estate handed over for the agreed exchange.

But when he realized that he could in no way attain the archbishopric, he refused to fulfill his promises and, summoned to the council mentioned above, declined to come.

When the archbishops were seated there in order with all their suffragans, the king prostrated himself to the ground. Raised up by Bishop Willigis, in whose diocese the synod was being held, he addressed everyone present as follows (f. 112′) :

> For the sake of future recompense I have chosen Christ as my heir, because no hope remains for me of obtaining offspring. Whatever was most precious to me, myself together with what I have already acquired or shall acquire, I offered long ago, secretly in my heart, as a sacrifice to the unbegotten Father.

> Until now I have desired to establish a bishopric at Babenberg with the permission of my bishop, and today I wish to fulfill this just desire. Therefore I appeal to your most serene piety, lest the absence of the man who sought from me what I was not permitted to grant him should be able to obstruct my purpose, since his staff, the sign of our mutual confirmation, makes clear that he fled not for God’s sake but because of his grief at being unable to attain the dignity.

> Let what he has presumed to do through his ambitious and trifling embassy move the hearts of everyone present: to annul the enlargement of the holy mother Church. The generous goodwill of my present consort and of my only brother and fellow-heir supports the firm establishment of this matter. Let both know for certain that I shall repay them with a settlement acceptable to them.

> If at any time the bishop deigns to come and accept the promises, he will undoubtedly find me ready to do whatever seems good to you.

When this address had ended, Beringer, Bishop Heinricus’s chaplain, rose. He testified that his lord had not come because of fear of the king and that he had never approved any injury being done to the Church entrusted to him by God. He begged all those present, for the love of Christ, not to allow such things to be done in his absence, since this would set a precedent for themselves in the future.

His privileges were then read aloud. Whenever the king saw that the anxious judgment of the judges was wavering, he repeatedly prostrated himself and humbled himself.

At last, when Archbishop Willigis was investigating by judgment what ought to be done in this matter, Tagino was the first to reply that the matter could legally be carried out according to the king’s speech.

All those present then affirmed and endorsed his statement. The pastoral office was entrusted by the king to Everhard, then chancellor, and on that same day he was consecrated by the aforesaid archbishop.

After this, Bishop Heinricus, with the assistance of his fellow bishop Heribert, obtained the king’s favor and the fulfillment of the arrangement pleasing to him.

Liutgard was then the widow of Arnulf, called “of Ghent,” count of Holland. The note continues into col. 1316C.]

[Note: 47. Col. 1317; at *caritatem* expletam comitante regina* Albiam* transnavigans* proficiscitur*. 1 writes *proficissitur* for *proficiscitur*, “he sets out.”]

[Note: 48. Col. 1317; at *Albiam* transnavigans* proficiscitur . 15. In hiis*. 2 reads *Diebus hiis*, “In these days,” rather than *In hiis diebus*, with the same meaning.]

[Note: 49. Col. 1317; at *de* monte* sancti* Johannis* Baptistae* ob* crimen*. The cut-off lines in 1 preserve these fragments: *crimen quoddam*, “a certain crime”; *none episcopo deposito Alfkerus mo*, “…none, bishop; upon the deposition, Alfkerus mo…”; *servientium provisor in va*, “overseer of those serving, into the va[cant place]…”; *sanctae conversationis rel*, “the rel[igious observance] of holy conduct…”; *tens miserabiliter dest*, “…tens, miserably dest[royed]…”; *mutatur unde et miseriae fut*, “is changed, whence also of fut[ure] misery…”; *Hoc etiam quod*, “This also, which…”; *si fuisset dextrae*, “if it had been of the right hand…” The broken *none* is retained as a name ending; “bishop” is the only office word surviving there, not an alternative “bishop or abbot.” Brackets identify partial words or context supplied only to make the fragment intelligible.]

[Note: 50. Col. 1317; at *monte* sancti* Johannis* Baptistae* ob* crimen quoddam**. 2 supplies the reading *crimen quoddam*, “some crime,” although there was scarcely room for it in 1. 2 omits *ab abbacia suimet*, “from his abbacy,” abbreviated *ab a. s.* in the note.]

[Note: 51. Col. 1317; at *consistens*, miserabiliter destruitur* et in nomen prepositurae*. 1 spells *prepositurae*, “of a provostship,” as *propositure*.]

[Note: 52. Col. 1317; at *Hoc* etiam*, quod* per labentia accidit tempora*. *tempora*, “times,” is erased in 1.]

[Note: 53. Col. 1317; at *vereor, non in melius, sed in pejus*. 1b adds *sed in pejus*, “but for the worse,” not the whole preceding contrast.]

[Note: 54. Col. 1317; at *habitu et in victu laudabilis extat, vero*. 1 has *vero*, “in truth”; 1b mistakenly changed it to *conversacio*, “way of life.” The word *inde* in the note means “from it,” describing that alteration; it is not part of the variant.]

[Note: 55. Col. 1317C; at *sunt sepe quod simulant. Dicit namque scriptura*. Augustine, *On Psalm 63*, p. 650.]

[Note: 56. Col. 1317; at *equitas non est equitas, sed duplex iniquitas*. 1 has *iquitas* for *iniquitas*, “iniquity.”]

[Note: 57. Col. 1317; at *firma stabilitate exaltatur, sed lugubriter quandoque degradatur*. 2 gives this passage as follows: “It will be exalted … it will be brought down, and the institution of the holy fathers will be restored. Let Truth, which is Christ, be silent, and let all his heralds bite their tongues: the stones will cry out that all these things are not well ordered. The evangelical trumpet sounds that nothing is covered which will not be revealed.
