The time will come, I say, it will come, when their hypocrisy will be exposed and the ancient institution of the fathers will be recognized as more praiseworthy in every respect than these varied innovations. We sinners, after …” The source abbreviates *veritas quae est Christus, precones ejus omnes linguam mordeant* as *v. que est C. p. e. o. l. m.*, and *nihil opertum esse quod non revelabitur* as *n. o. esse, q. n. r.*; their sense is supplied by the adjoining full wording.]

[Note: 58. Col. 1317; at *pondera in terram ferri non nesscimus. Resipiscenda*. 1 has *resipiscanda* for *resipiscenda*, “things to be reconsidered/amended.” 2 reads: “Let us consider everything that ought to be abandoned; let us not despise our admonishers, but, converted, let us obtain the rewards promised to all the faithful by observing God’s commandments. Let us not seem better than our predecessors, for, departing from their most approved conduct, we are far inferior to them. Let no believer be angry when someone admonishes him charitably for God’s sake. Charity …” Its *f. c. p. c. o. m.* condenses *fidelibus cunctis praemia cum observatione mandatorum*, “rewards [promised] to all the faithful, with observance of the commandments”; *Non v. m. a. n.* means “Let us not seem better than our predecessors.”]

[Note: 59. Col. 1317; at *in varia specie recti hiis sumus nimis*. 1b adds *nimis*, “greatly,” before “unequal.”]

[Note: 60. Col. 1317; at *narrationis cursus. 16. Ordinatis legionibus, rex inde*. 2 reads *rex a Liezka inde*, “the king from Liezka, from there.”]

[Note: 61. Col. 1317; at *sui in Saxonia sollicite prestolabatur adventum. Excercitum*. 1c (?) has *exercitum*, “army,” for the spelling *excercitum*.]

[Note: 62. Col. 1317C; at *cum prosperitate ad locum, qui Dobraluh dicitur*. Dobrilugk in Lower Lusatia.]

[Note: 63. Col. 1317; at *qui Dobraluh dicitur , in pago Luzici*. 2 reads *luidere* and A. S. *liudice*, variants of the district name Luzici.]

[Note: 64. Col. 1317; at *ex latere abdito nocentem Thiebernus, miles egreius*. 1 has *egrius* for *egreius*, “excellent.”]

[Note: 65. Col. 1317; at *comperiret, ob laudem sibi specialiter usurpandam optimos*. 1a has *a*, “from,” beside *optimos*, “the best”; the isolated reading does not supply a complete alternative construction.]

[Note: 66. Col. 1317; at *presulis inclitos satellites, cum aliis commilitonibus multis*. 1b adds *multis*, “many,” qualifying the fellow soldiers.]

[Note: 67. Col. 1317C; at *commilitonibus multis 8. Idus Septembris incautos prostravit*. Merseburg Calendar, 7 September: “Esi, layman, Odo, layman, were killed with others. Thiederic, bishop; Adala, count[ess]; Benno, layman; Bernhaer [gap], h. V.,” that is, “at the fifth hour.” Compare the Quedlinburg Annals, 1005. The note continues into col. 1318C.]

[Note: 68. Col. 1317; at *Idus Septembris incautos prostravit et despoliavit. Ob*. 1b adds *Ob*, “because of,” introducing the king’s grief.]

[Note: 69. Col. 1319; at *fluvium venirent, sotiantur, deos suimet precedentes subsequuti*. 1 corrects *subsecuuti* to *subsequuti*, both “having followed.”]

[Note: 70. Col. 1319; at *17. Est urbs quaedam in pago Riedirierum*. 1b has *Riedirierum*, “of the Riedireri”; 1a has *riedirerum* and 2 *Rederivi*.]

[Note: 71. Col. 1319D; at *17. Est urbs quaedam in pago Riedirierum*. This district occupied the greater part, namely the eastern and southern parts, of the duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, or the Strelitz and Stargard prefectures. See Lisch in the *Yearbooks of the Association for Mecklenburg History and Antiquities*, III.]

[Note: 72. Col. 1319; at *urbs quaedam in pago Riedirierum , Riedegost*. 2 spells Riedegost *riedegast*.]

[Note: 73. Col. 1319D; at *urbs quaedam in pago Riedirierum , Riedegost*. The city is generally called Rethra and lies near Prillwitz. Compare Adam of Bremen, II, 10 and IV, 13.]

[Note: 74. Col. 1319; at *tricornis, ac tres in se continens portas*. 2 adds “each one at a separate corner,” referring to the three gates.]

[Note: 75. Col. 1319; at *juxta positum et visu nimis horribile monstrat*. 2 adds “which is not readily accessible to anyone,” referring to the third gate.]

[Note: 76. Col. 1319; at *est nil nisi fanum de ligno artificiose*. 1c (?) reads *artificiose*, “skillfully,” as in the text.]

[Note: 77. Col. 1320D; at *atque loricis terribiliter vestiti, quorum primus Zuarasici*. The same name, Zuarasici, occurs in Saint Bruno’s letter to Emperor Henry II.]

[Note: 78. Col. 1319; at *iram eorundem placare conveniunt, sedent hii dumtaxat*. 1 writes *duxtaxat* for *dumtaxat*, “only.”]

[Note: 79. Col. 1319; at *dubiarum perquirant. Quibus finitis, cespite viridi eas*. 1b adds *eas*, “them,” referring to the lots.]

[Note: 80. Col. 1319; at *veneratur, super fixas in terram duarum cuspides*. 1 has *cupides* for *cuspides*, “points,” of the spears.]

[Note: 81. Col. 1319; at *obsequio ducunt, et premissis sortibus, quibus id*. 1b adds *quibus id*, “by which this,” not the entire clause about the previous divination.]

[Note: 82. Col. 1320D; at *autem, a tristibus populis hoc prorsus omittitur*. Compare Grimm, *German Mythology*, p. 380 and following.]

[Note: 83. Col. 1319; at *. Testatur idem antiquitas errore delusa vario*. 1a reads *varia*, feminine “varied,” for *vario*, masculine, qualifying “error.”]

[Note: 84. Col. 1319; at *si quando his seva longae rebellionis assperitas*. The first *s* of *assperitas*, “harshness,” is erased in 1.]

[Note: 85. Col. 1319; at *pecudum ineffabilis horum furor mitigatur. Hiis autem*. 1b adds *autem*, “however,” in the introduction to the Liutici’s government.]

[Note: 86. Col. 1319; at *Infideles ipsi et mutabiles ipsi, immutabilitatem ac*. 1b corrects the words *immutabilitatem ac*, “constancy and”; *e corr.* means “from a correction,” not “the letter e was corrected.”]

[Note: 87. Col. 1319; at *gramine datisque affirmant dextris. Ad hanc autem*. 1b adds *autem*, “however,” before the account of breaking peace.]

[Note: 88. Col. 1320D; at *servi, nostrisque iniquitatibus tunc liberi, tali comitatu*. That is, in the company of their idols. URS.]

[Note: 89. Col. 1319; at *quae supra memoravi, nil esse, probabis veraciter*. 2 repeats what it has already said: “These soldiers mentioned above, formerly slaves and now free because of our iniquities, came in such company to the king to bring assistance.” Its initials *n. q. i. t. l. t. c. a. r.* abbreviate *nostrisque iniquitatibus tunc liberi, tali comitatu ad regem*, the words translated here.]

[Note: 90. Col. 1320D; at *prefati fluminis, cum exercitu grandi in Crosno*. Crossen, a town in Silesia on the borders of Lower Lusatia. URS.]

[Note: 91. Col. 1319; at *pontes pararet, divinus respectus missis speculatoribus suis*. 1b adds *suis*, “his,” referring to the scouts.]

[Note: 92. Col. 1319; at *diei crepusculo jussu regis intrantes, incolumes eo*. 1b adds *eo*, “it,” referring to the ford.]

[Note: 93. Col. 1321; at *tardantes exspectarent, hostes in tentoriis inprovisos opprimerent*. The printed imperfects *exspectarent*, “were waiting,” and *opprimerent*, “would overwhelm,” stand for pluperfect subjunctives *exspectassent* and *oppressissent*, “had waited” and “would have overwhelmed.” This is a grammatical explanation of the past counterfactual, not a new alternative episode.]

[Note: 94. Col. 1321D; at *rex, et usque ad abbaciam, quae Mezerici*. Meseritz on the Obra River, in the province of Posen.]

[Note: 95. Col. 1321; at *qua maxima tunc veneracione potuit, complere studuit*. 1b adds *studuit*, “he endeavored.”]

[Note: 96. Col. 1321; at *regis gratiam Bolizlavus peciit, et exaudiri mox*. 1b adds *mox*, “soon.”]

[Note: 97. Col. 1321D; at *securitatis prospera solidare sumopere nititur, et Bruncionem*. “Brunzio, killed”: Luneburg Necrology, 21 September.]

[Note: 98. Col. 1319; at *et Bruncionem inclitum satellitem, in Merseburch, e*. 1b adds *e*, “from” or “among,” before the Slavs.]

[Note: 99. Col. 1321; at *e Sclavis autem optimos, Borisen et Nezemuisclen*. 1a gives Nezemuisclen as *uezemusclen*.]

[Note: 100. Col. 1321D; at *Nezemuisclen , cum caeteris fautoribus in Welereslevo*. Wallersleben.]

[Note: 101. Col. 1321D; at *suspendi precepit. Sepe cum Sclavis in Wiribeni*. On the assembly at Werben see Helmold, I, 18.]

[Note: 102. Col. 1321; at *patriae renovavit, queque diu hinc injuste ablata*. 1a has *ablatorum*, “of things taken away,” for *ablata*, “things taken away.”]

[Note: 103. Col. 1321; at *apostolica prohibuit, Deique justiciam spernentes spirituali mucrone*. 1 writes *mutrone* for *mucrone*, “sword.”]

[Note: 104. Col. 1321; at *interfici precepit. 22. Interea Balduinum ducem Wlandariorum*. *Wlandariorum*, “of the Flemings,” is erased in 1 but still legible. A later hand wrote *Flandrie*, “of Flanders,” in the margin.]

[Note: 105. Col. 1321D; at *inflacio adversus regem armavit, et Valentinam urbem*. Valenciennes.]

[Note: 106. Col. 1322D; at *Valentinam urbem possidere potestatique suimet subdere suasit*. Compare Balderic, *Chronicle*, I, end of chapter 214; Sigebert of Gembloux, 1006; Quedlinburg Annals, the same year.]

[Note: 107. Col. 1322D; at *indicens. Advenit optatum tempus, exercitus grandis colligitur*. Compare Balderic, I, 115; Sigebert, 1007; Quedlinburg Annals, 1006.]

[Note: 108. Col. 1322D; at *a rege cum eodem ad Scellam fluvium*. The Scheldt.]

[Note: 109. Col. 1321; at *autem ad abbaciam, quae Gent dicitur, veniret*. 1a has the split form *veni rent*, “they came,” for *veniret*, “he came.”]

[Note: 110. Col. 1321; at *a confratribus illius aecclesiae susceptus, loco eodem*. 1c (?) has *eidem*, “to the same,” for *eodem*, “the same,” in the phrase about sparing the place.]

[Note: 111. Col. 1321; at *susceptus, loco eodem et bonis appertinentibus cunctis*. 1b adds *cunctis*, “all,” qualifying the appurtenant possessions.]

[Note: 112. Col. 1321; at *et non longe post per manus regis*. 2 and A. S. add *miles*, “vassal” or “knight,” after his becoming the king’s man through homage.]

[Note: 113. Col. 1322D; at *longe post per manus regis effectus, Walecorn*. Walcheren. Compare Balderic, III, 2.]

[Note: 114. Col. 1321; at *post per manus regis effectus, Walecorn et*. 2 has *et Valencinam*, “and Valenciennes”; A. S. gives the name as *Valentinianam*. This belongs to Baldwin’s receipt of the city as a benefice, not to the possessions of Ghent abbey.]

[Note: 115. Col. 1321; at *regis nostri inclita, obiit et Ratisbone sepelitur*. 1b adds the whole notice from *Mense* through *sepelitur*: Gisela’s death on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August and burial at Regensburg.]

[Note: 116. Col. 1321; at *tunc partibus hiis, generale concilium in Fronkenevordi*. 1c (?) spells Fronkenevordi *frankenuordi*.]

[Note: 117. Col. 1321; at *Rex a puero quandam suimet civitatem, Bavanberg*. 1c (?) spells Bavanberg *babanberg*.]

[Note: 118. Col. 1321; at *autem ad regni curam divina miseratione promovetur*. 1 has *promotur* for *promovetur*, “is promoted.”]

[Note: 119. Col. 1322D; at *parrochiamque in pago, qui a Radinzca fluvio*. The Rednitz.]

[Note: 120. Col. 1323; at *positam concederet, sibi concambio vendicandam sepe rogavit*. 1b adds *sepe rogavit*, “he often asked.”]

[Note: 121. Col. 1323; at *ibidem ordine archiepiscopis cum omnibus suimet suffraganeis*. 1 has *suffra ::: aneis*, the word “suffragans” with a gap; *ne* appears to have been erased.]

[Note: 122. Col. 1323; at *elevatus, (f. 112') cunctis presentibus talia fatur*. 2 and A. S. preface the speech with: “Glorious lords and fathers, summoned here by my humble self, you have assembled today; I shall explain to your ears why I summoned you. I beg the kindness of you all, that you may favor me, inflamed with love of Christ, in these things which I hope divine grace has inspired in me. For no hope of obtaining offspring remains to me.” *inflammanti*, “inflamed,” describes the speaker asking for their favor.]

[Note: 123. Col. 1323; at *dudum secreto mentis optuli. Episcopatum in Bavanbergae*. The final *e* in *Bavanbergae*, “Bamberg,” is erased in 1.]

[Note: 124. Col. 1323; at *sanctae matris aecclesiae augmentum anullare, cum nugigerula*. 1 has *nuigerula* for *nugigerula*, “carrying trifles,” describing the embassy.]

[Note: 125. Col. 1323D; at *presentis et unici fratris et coheredis mei*. That is, Bruno, bishop of Augsburg.]

[Note: 126. Col. 1323; at *mei larga benignitas asspirat, et sibi placita*. 1a has *placito*, masculine/neuter “pleasing,” for feminine *placita*, agreeing with “settlement.”]

[Note: 127. Col. 1323; at *commissae in aliquo fieri numquam laudasse testatur*. 1b corrects to *testatur*, “he testifies.” The previous reading is not supplied.]

[Note: 128. Col. 1323; at *ibi alta voce recitantur. Inter haec quocies*. 1 corrects *quociens* to *quocies*, both “as often as.”]

[Note: 129. Col. 1323; at *nutare prospexit, toties prostratus humiliatur. Tandem archiantistite*. 1 writes *architistite* for *archiantistite*, “archbishop.”]

[Note: 130. Col. 1323; at *toties prostratus humiliatur. Tandem archiantistite Willigiso, quid*. 1 abbreviates *quid*, “what,” as *qd.*]

[Note: 131. Col. 1323; at *judicio perscrutanti, Tagino primus respondit, haec tunc*. 1b writes *haec tunc*, “these things then,” over an erasure. 2 and A. S. read: “This just will and petition of the king can now legally be fulfilled with the consent of you all.”]

[Note: 132. Col. 1323; at *ejus sermonem tunc affirmantibus et subscribentibus, Everhardo*. 1a spells Everhard *aeuerhardo*.]

[Note: 133. Col. 1323D; at *haec autem Heinricus antistes auxilio confratris Hiriberti*. Heribert, archbishop of Cologne.]

[Note: 134. Col. 1321; at *confratris Hiriberti regis gratiam et adimplecionem sibi*. 1b adds *sibi*, “to him,” referring to the settlement acceptable to Bishop Henry.]

24. But since serenity rarely dawns without being followed by the darkness of a gloomy cloud, while the king was celebrating Easter at Regensburg [Note: [Col. 1323D] Thietmar appears to place these events in 1008; the *Annales Quedlinburgenses* assign them to 1007. The *Annales Hildesheimenses* say that from 1008 the king celebrated Easter at Merseburg.] [Note: [Col. 1323] *illusessit* corrected to *illucēscit* in 1.], envoys from the Liutici, from those who had been sent by the city called Liuilni [Note: [Col. 1323] Thus in 1b; 1a has *liulni* or *luilni*; A. S. has *Luvirm.*], and from Duke Jaremir asserted that Bolizlav, eager to devise many things against him, was doing so, and affirmed that they themselves had been induced by him through words and money to carry these things out (fol. 113). They also informed him that, if he continued to keep this man in his peace and favor, he would not firmly maintain their servitude.

The king, carefully considering these matters with his princes [Note: [Col. 1323] *princibus* in 1.], and receiving different answers from them in counsel, agreed to their wicked desire only in this respect: he sent there his son-in-law Hirimannus [Note: [Col. 1324D] He was then margrave of the Milzeni, that is, of the Budissin march, and from the year 1010 of Meissen.], ordering him to interrupt the peace treaties that had been agreed [Note: [Col. 1323] 1a has *faedera*, with the *a* erased.]. When Bolizlav learned of this embassy from the intermediaries, he did not receive the aforesaid count kindly, although he had previously invited him; and, after hearing his account, he excused himself in many respects:

“Let Christ, witness of all things, know,” he said, “that whatever I shall do henceforth, I shall carry out unwillingly.” [Note: [Col. 1323] *quicqid* in 1a and 1b.]

After this, having gathered an army, he ravaged the district called Morezini, lying near Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 1324D] Mortsani, a district situated between the rivers Elbe, Stremma, Havel, and Nuthe.], and broke with hostile harshness the brotherhood in Christ that he had previously joined with the people of the Parthenopolitan city. From there he came to the city called Zirwisti [Note: [Col. 1324D] Zerbst.], and, having overcome its citizens by great terror and gentle persuasion, led them away with him.

Our men, learning all this, came late and pursued them even more slowly [Note: [Col. 1323] Added in 1b.]. Their first commander was Archbishop Tagino, who, although he had known all these things beforehand, did not make adequate preparations. I was there with him. When we had all arrived at the place called lutriboc, the wisest men decided that it was not advisable to pursue the enemy with so small a force, and we turned back (fol. 113′).

Bolizlav, however, occupied Luzici, Zara [Note: [Col. 1325D] A district situated in Lower Lusatia and Silesia, around the city of Sorau.], and Selpuli again; and not long afterward his envious father-in-law took possession of the city of Budusin, fortified by Count Hirimannus [Note: [Col. 1325] *herimanni* in 1c.]. He sent his messengers to the citizens, asking them to surrender this city to him without labor on either side and not to hope for rescue from their lord. A mutual peace was made for seven days.

He prepared attacks; they, through their own envoy, humbly sought help from the lord and from the princes of the kingdom, promising to resist the enemy for seven more days [Note: [Col. 1325] The number VII was erased and replaced by V in 1.]. Margrave Hirimannus [Note: [Col. 1325] *h* in 1.] came to Magdeburg, appealing to Walterdus, then provost, and summoning all the leading men individually through envoys. He complained bitterly that they had delayed so long there [Note: [Col. 1325B] *hic tunc* occurs in an erased place in 1b.], yet he encouraged his soldiers through intermediaries.

While they were suffering under Bolizlav’s continual attacks and resisting bravely for a long time, they saw that some of their companions were wavering and that their lord had not come to free them. They therefore obtained from the aforesaid duke permission to leave unharmed with all that they possessed, surrendered the city to him [Note: [Col. 1325] Added in 1b.], and returned sadly to their homeland.

25. After the venerable Liudulf, archbishop of the church of Trier, died after Easter [Note: [Col. 1325] *post Pascha* added in 1b.] (in the year 1008), his chaplain Aethelbero [Note: [Col. 1325] 1a has *aethelberto*; 1c perhaps *athelbero*.], the queen’s brother and an immature young man, was commonly elected more out of fear of the king than out of love of religion.

When the king heard this, remembering the earlier unpremeditated appointment of his brother Thiedricus [Note: [Col. 1325D] Bishop of Metz.], he rejected his beloved wife and his other relatives, who were eager to obtain this bishopric, and gave it to Meingaudus [Note: [Col. 1325] 1a has *meingozo*], chamberlain of Archbishop Willigisus [Note: [Col. 1325] 1a has *uuilligiso*], a nobleman according to the flesh. Because of this, the fury of a treacherous generation was kindled.

The Palas [Note: [Col. 1325D] Under this name is understood the palace of the archbishop of Trier, called Palz or Pfalz: a very ancient building, constructed of hard stones, with other walls and large, prominent windows. It was called a palace because it had been the most ancient seat and residence of the Frankish kings, and the counts palatine also had their dwelling there. See Browerus, vol. I, *Annales Trevirenses*, book X, p. 500; also Schekmann, *Medulla Gestorum Trevirensium*, chap. 2. This great palace is distinct from the suburban town and castle on the left bank of the Moselle, somewhat below the city of Trier, which today is called Palatiolum, or Pfalzel; see *Chronicon Gottwicense*, vol. I, pp. 501, 515. The *Palas* mentioned by Ammianus Marcellinus XVIII, 2, is entirely different from these. URS.] was fortified by the people of Trier [Note: [Col. 1325] Abbreviated *trever.* in 1c.] against the king, and this land, peaceful until then, was shaken by frequent burnings. Whatever these harsh men had previously done against their gentle lord, they received back on an equal scale [Note: [Col. 1325] 1 has *lancea*.].

What will all these men say here and at the future judgment, through whose unspeakable guilt the incorrupt mother Church, so often groaning over the slaughter and despoiling of her children, pours before the sight of the avenging God tears descending from her cheeks? [Note: [Col. 1325] 1 has *aecclesiae*.]

Moved by such presumption, the king hurried there with an army, ordering the enthroned archbishop to be consecrated there and Aethelbero [Note: [Col. 1325] 1c more often has the abbreviation *ath.*] to be excommunicated. By a continual siege he also so constrained those who defended the Palas that, exhausted by constant hunger and attack, they had either to perish inside or unwillingly come out into the king’s power [Note: [Col. 1326D] Compare the *Gesta Trevirorum*, chap. 46, and the *Annales Quedlinburgenses*, under the year 1008.]. To prevent this, Duke Henricus, by unforeseen cunning, secured from the king permission for them to leave unharmed. But after the king investigated the truth of these matters, he bore it heavily in mind and, as I shall relate below, took revenge.

26. Meanwhile my predecessor [Note: [Col. 1325] *Wigbertus* added in 2.] is confined by a long illness [Col. 1326B] and anxiously awaits his final day. But before concluding, I wish to bring certain things about him to memory [Note: [Col. 1325] Added in 1b.].

He was descended from excellent parents of southern Thuringia, but at Magdeburg received his training under Ohtricus [Note: [Col. 1325] *oftrico* or *ostrico* corrected to *ortrico* in 1.]. Archbishop Gisilerus, having educated him exceptionally [Note: [Col. 1325] 1a has *egreie*.], took him into his service as a close associate [Note: [Col. 1325] *familiariter* in 1.] and kept him with him for a long time, winning him over by a singular benefice and the office of archpresbyter.

Finally, after taking certain things away from him because of the continual whispering of wicked men, he so alienated his mind that, abandoning all his possessions, he attached himself to King Henry, as I have said, and pleased him exceedingly. For he had been outstanding in stature and appearance, eloquence and a very beautiful voice, wise in counsel, pleasant in assembly [Col. 1326C], and immensely generous. Thus, through divine visitation and such virtue, he rose to the priestly rank [Note: [Col. 1325] The manuscript lacks *dignitatis*.].

During the days divinely granted to him, he acquired these things for his church: Sidegeshusun and Wiribeni; nine hides at Derlingun, seven at Daliwi, and three at Ninstidi. From his own property he granted seven hides at Uppusun and a woodland called Pulcher mons, “Beautiful Mount.” [Note: [Col. 1326D] If I am not mistaken, this is Sotterhausen in the district of Sangerhausen; Werben, or perhaps Werbelin, in the district of Delitzsch; Nieder-Röblingen in the district of Allstedt; Thaldorf in the district of Querfurt; and Nienstädt in the district of Sangerhausen. URS.]

He amassed many books and other things pertaining to the divine mysteries [Note: [Col. 1325] 1 has the OCR form *respicienstibus*.]. Injured by poisoned drink for no fewer than ten years [Note: [Col. 1325] A leaf was cut out here in 1; we supplied the text from 2.] (Cod. Br., fol. 248), he endured frequent bodily suffering and, in the month of March, the greatest hardship. If anything contrary ever appeared in him, whether toward his own people or toward strangers [Col. 1327A], this was caused by the spur of his immense illness.

By constant preaching he recalled those committed to him from the error of empty superstition. He uprooted from its foundations the grove called Zutibure [Note: [Col. 1327] A. S. has *Zudibure*, under the year 1009. It seems that *Scutibure* should be read. We learn from a charter of Emperor Henry II, dated October 17, 1012, published in Höfer, *Zeitschrift*, vol. I, p. 162, and in the *Gesta episcoporum Merseburgensium*, that the church of this village had already been granted by Henry II’s predecessors.], which the inhabitants honored as God in all things and which had never been violated since ancient times, and built there a church to the holy martyr Romanus. Besides this church, he dedicated a third and a fourth at Magdeburg, as well as many others.

If the fickle and often lying crowd chattered anything against him, I persuade good people that it is wholly incredible. For many, when they blame others, do not know that no one lives without sin (Cato, *Disticha*, I, 5).

This venerable man held the episcopate for five years, six weeks, and five days. After he had often completed his confession in tears, and had received absolution from Bishops Wigo [Note: [Col. 1327D] Of Brandenburg.] and Hericus [Note: [Col. 1327D] Of Havelberg, who had recently succeeded Hildericus.], who visited him in his final illness, he departed happily, as I hope, from this light to Christ at Merseburg on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, a Tuesday (the year 1009) [Note: [Col. 1327D] In the year 1009; see the *Annales Quedlinburgenses*. The ninth day before the Kalends of April was not Tuesday but Thursday, as Widekind has already noted.]. He was buried where one of Christ’s elect, his leader and companion during life, had previously shown him in a vision.

27. I, indeed, who write these things, was predestined to succeed this pious shepherd Tagino [Note: [Col. 1327] 2 always has *thaginone*.], though unworthy. While the king was celebrating Christmas at Palithi [Note: [Col. 1328D] That is, in 1007; compare the *Annales Hildesheimenses*.] [Note: [Col. 1327] 2 has *palithe*.], he himself discussed with his companion (*simmista*) Tagino [Note: [Col. 1327] 2 has *simpnista*; A. S., under 1009, has *simmista*.] [Note: [Col. 1328D] If I am not mistaken, he was the provost of the church of Halberstadt, who died in 1018; concerning him, see the *Chronicon Halberstadense* and the *Annales Quedlinburgenses* under that year.] how, after Bishop Wigbertus’s death, he might commend the church of Merseburg to a good administrator.

Tagino said to him: “There is in my monastery a certain brother named Thietmarus, whom you yourselves [Note: [Col. 1327] 2 has *ipse*.] know well. I hope that, wisely arranging matters in his own way, he will, with God’s generosity, be suitable for this.”

The king replied: “Would that he were willing to accept it! He would certainly not hesitate to regard me as his most reliable supporter for whatever he might need.”

My nephew Thidericus was immediately sent to me to report these things to me on behalf of the king and the bishop [Note: [Col. 1327] A. S. has *archiepiscopi*.], and to persuade me as far as possible to undertake them.

I was at Magdeburg when I received this embassy, and I replied as follows: “May almighty God repay our pious lord and father with a fitting return, since he deigns to mention me somewhere for good. In this matter I consider myself unworthy, and therefore I do not yet dare to praise it. God is able to snatch a living bishop from the hand of death. But if I refuse outright, I fear that I shall be rejected from his accustomed favor. I have no other help than this man, from whom I may obtain either this opportunity or greater ones. After the bishop’s death, whatever is pleasing to God in the powers established by him, while life remains, I shall gladly fulfill.”

When the king, at Frankfurt [Note: [Col. 1327] 2 has *franckenvort*.], heard of the bishop’s death, he ordered the memorial observance owed for him. By then, indeed, at the prompting of certain people, he was turning his mind toward better things concerning me; for he wished to bestow this honor upon a certain Ethelgerus, who had deserved well.

When the king’s familiar Tagino learned this, he strongly opposed it, and, with constant supplication, summoned me to the king’s favor through Provost Gezo [Note: [Col. 1327] Here codex 1 continues.]. He came to me at my court, called Retmerslevo. That night I saw an episcopal staff standing beside my bed, and someone asked me:

“Do you wish to receive the church of Merseburg?”

“If God wills,” I replied, “and if the archbishop who commands me orders me to come.”

He continued: “Beware, for whoever shakes the brains of the holy Lawrence immediately goes mad.”

I answered him at once: “May Christ, guardian of human beings, protect me, lest in this or in anything else I offend the divine majesty and turn away the intercession of the saints.”

When I awoke, I was astonished [Note: [Col. 1327] 1 has *obstipui*.]. Leaping up immediately, I saw the bright daylight entering through the windows (Persius, *Satires* III, 1). And behold, the man of whom I had just been speaking entered. Showing me two letters, he asked and ordered me to come to Augsburg on Holy Saturday (April 10) [Note: [Col. 1327] 1 reads *rogauit*; *Aet* was corrected to *Et* in 1.].

I came to Parthenopolis. On Palm Sunday, with the permission of the provost and my fellow brothers, I departed from there, and on the Tuesday after the Lord’s Resurrection (April 19) I reached the appointed places. Although the archbishop was angry that I had come so late, he received me mercifully.

The next day I was summoned and asked by his command, on the king’s authority, whether I wished to assist my church with any part of my inheritance. I replied:

“I came here at your command, and concerning this matter I can and wish to give no definite answer now. If, by divine consent and through your will, which has always been kind toward me, and by the king’s generosity, this is accomplished here, whatever I can devoutly do in this or in other matters for the remedy of my soul and in fulfillment of the duty entrusted to me, I shall perform.”

The archbishop received and praised these words kindly. He led me to the chapel of Bishop Bruno, where the king was awaiting him, and, ready for Mass [Note: [Col. 1327] 1a has the abbreviation *p. sum*.], handed me over to the king. The king, with the consent of those present, undeservedly entrusted the pastoral care to me with the staff. I prostrated myself and asked pardon, and the cantor began the introit: “Come, you blessed of my Father.”

Meanwhile, in the greater church, all the bells were rung for Mass. Although this happened by chance and not at anyone’s command or because of my dignity [Col. 1328D], the king nevertheless declared that it was a good omen.

After the great banquet held there by the venerable Bishop Bruno, we came the following Saturday to Nova Urbs [Note: [Col. 1329D] Neuburg on the Danube.]. There, on the eighth day of the Lord’s solemnity, I was anointed as a priest by the aforesaid archbishop in the presence of the king, with our fellow bishop Hilliwardus assisting and no fewer than four co-bishops attending, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May. From there we were conveyed by boat to Regensburg on the river Danube [Note: [Col. 1329] 1 has *perducim’*.].

28. In those days there was a great famine in this region [Note: [Col. 1329] The words *In ... fuit* are added in 1b.]. Meanwhile Duke Heinricus, attempting secretly to enter Bavaria on account of his rebellion, immediately turned back in flight when he first perceived that the king’s prudent vigilance had blocked his access.

For this reason the best of the Bavarians assembled at Regensburg by royal edict. Although they all voluntarily swore that for three years they would not choose another duke for themselves, they were nevertheless rebuked by the king for this [Note: [Col. 1329] 1a has *ab*.] and were drawn away from his service and assistance by flatteries and threats, and were taken into his personal following.

There, the brothers from the monastery of Christ’s martyr Emmeramus—which Emperor Arnulf built in his honor and which the king chose as a place for his bodily repose [Note: [Col. 1329] 1a has *corparaliter*, and so repeatedly.]—fell unanimously at the king’s feet. On behalf of their bishop Gebehardus, they made many tearful complaints, which I myself heard [Note: [Col. 1329] 1 has *flebiter*.], and the laymen present followed them with great lamentations.

It is difficult for me to recount, or for anyone to believe, how much the people subject to him said about this, concerning empty superstition and the ruin of the soul. I know only this: I have never seen anyone like him in conduct and unusual equipment, nor heard of such a person among those of earlier times [Note: [Col. 1329] 1a has *et*.]. If his inner qualities correspond to his outward appearance, he is either better than the rest or much worse [Note: [Col. 1329D] That is, if they do not correspond.].

Destroying what had previously been cultivated with the greatest care, he devotes himself to immense new labors. He abandons his homeland and those entrusted to him, and cultivates foreign things—even though they are far away—with superfluous attentions.

I call God as witness that I do not say these things merely to criticize him—for our weakness must be overlooked in those close to us and corrected for their improvement—but because, with truth itself powerfully persuading me to this, I greatly wonder at it with many others.

May God be favorable to him, so that, if he does these things with good intention, he may walk without reproach through the course of this pilgrimage in the justifications of God. But if, more inflated by some swelling of pride than kindled by the fuel of spiritual love [Note: [Col. 1329] 1a has *quam et* or *quamque*.], he performs so much merely to disparage the conduct of those living now, may he turn from his wickedness and, by pursuing the building up of the faithful through the acquisition of worldly things, suffer no harm to himself.

Blessed in Christ is the one who, by cultivating eternal righteousness, earns a lasting memory and, keeping himself aloof from evil reports, merits the divine summons to the right hand [Col. 1330A].

29. While the king was examining these matters, which I have now described at length, I proceeded by royal command to take possession of the episcopal seat. First I came to my court, called Malacin in the Slavic language [Note: [Col. 1329] 1a has *malauin*.] and Egisvilla in German [Note: [Col. 1329D] Eisdorf in the district of Leipzig.]. At daybreak the next day, beside the river Elster and the town called Iteri [Note: [Col. 1330D] Eythra.], I spoke to the assembled servants of my church [Note: [Col. 1329] *famulus* corrected from *familis* in 1.], to console those present and summon those absent.

For most of them had fled because of their own inconstancy and the excessive illness of my predecessor [Note: [Col. 1329] 1 has *harum* instead of *horum*.]. Proceeding from there to Merseburg, I was first honorably received by Bishop Ericus [Note: [Col. 1330D] Of Havelberg.] by my fellow brothers and was enthroned.

The following day, Sunday, dawned. I sang the Mass for sinners, instructed the people who came, needy of admonition [Note: [Col. 1329] 1 has *egens*.], and, by divine power but in my weakness, absolved those who confessed their sins (fol. 117).

Monday of Rogation Week began (May 23) [Note: [Col. 1329] 1 has *rogantionum*.]. From there I went to Magdeburg at the request of my archbishop, and on Wednesday I was received by my spiritual brothers with immense affection—not according to the quality of my merit but according to the greatness of their love. With common devotion and according to our ability, we celebrated the glorious and royal mystery of the Ascension [May 26].

30. From there I went to Wallibizi, where, as provost, I had governed for seven years, three weeks, and three days the brothers serving God and the ever-virgin Mary as provost. There I undertook, alas, so great a Simonian burden—not in money, but in an estate given to my paternal uncle [Col. 1330C].

In this I am very culpable, yet I hope for the forgiveness of the strict Judge, because I did it chiefly to defend the Lord’s flock and observe the arrangements of my ancestors. Therefore, reader, I call upon you before God to examine the text of this account, discern according to the quality of my merit, and forestall the dreadful face of the coming Examiner with tearful supplication.

My grandfather Liutharius, of whom I spoke earlier [Note: [Col. 1330D] II, 13.], after offending his lord and king, earnestly considered how to wash away this stain. Therefore he built a monastery in a wooded place called Rivus [Note: [Col. 1329] *qui rinus* added in 1b.] in honor of the holy Mother of God, and appointed Willigisus provost there, granting these brothers a tenth part of his inheritance for the necessities of food and clothing.

After he departed, his wife Mahtildis, encouraged by their two sons, eagerly sought to fulfill the vow of her beloved lord. After the death of Willigisus, that excellent father [Note: [Col. 1329] 1a has *egrii*.], she caused Reginbertus, born in eastern Francia, to succeed him.

After many years had passed, my father and his mother died [Note: [Col. 1331] 1 has *mortua*.], and, through the assistance of my uncle Liutharius, who had been made bishop of the Old City [Note: [Col. 1331D] Aldenburg in Wagria.] by Otto III, he became provost. At that time there was in our vicinity a cleric noble by birth, named Thiedricus, who, at the urging of the aforesaid count, purchased this provostship for ten hides [Note: [Col. 1331] 1a has thirteen.].

After he had held it for that many years or more, my mother died, and I succeeded as the third heir. I received from my brothers [Note: [Col. 1331] 1 has *acfrib.*] half of the estate belonging to the aforesaid monastery [Note: [Col. 1331] 1 has *meditatem*.]. From then on I often addressed my uncle, asking that I might be permitted to undertake the aforesaid office; and, if it could not be obtained as a gift, that it might at least be obtained for a moderate price.

After a long deliberation of steadfast mind [Note: [Col. 1331] 1 has *longa animi constantis deliberatione*.], he [Note: [Col. 1331] *h* in 1.] set aside the duty of charity and kinship and demanded a large part of my property. Since I enjoyed no assistance from my brothers, I consented, alas, to his desire. Thus I became the guardian of that church, whose servant I then was by paternal tradition, on the second day before the Nones of May in the thousandth year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 1331] 1b adds *servus dominice* and, after *anno*, additional words.], with the approval of my predecessor because he had received the exchange that pleased him.

In this office I spent more time as an idle worker of iniquity than of divine justice, and for this I never attempted to perform the fruits of penance that were due. I accuse no one connected with me by blood, but I earnestly seek good in return for all these evils.

When my brother’s wife died, he asked me whether I would prepare for her the burial she desired [Note: [Col. 1331] 1b adds *rogatus ... ut* and *ei*.]. Since I knew that the venerable Willigisus was buried there, I first refused; but finally I placed what was right and honorable beneath his will [Col. 1331C], and, wretched man, undertook what I wish I had not done.

What seemed impious even to pagans, I, a Christian, carried out by disturbing the tomb and bones of my fellow brother [Note: [Col. 1331] 1a has *ossuum*.]. I ordered a silver chalice that I found there to be reserved for distribution to the poor, but afterward I could not find it at all. Later, during the illness that followed, I recognized that I had sinned too greatly against God [Note: [Col. 1331] Added in 1b.].

When I overcame this illness with divine assistance, I went to Cologne for the sake of prayer. One night I heard an immense cry and asked what it was. “It is I,” he replied, “Willigisus, who, wandering because of your guilt, am roaming about.”

I immediately awoke in amazement [Note: [Col. 1331] 1 has *obstipui*.], and to this day, and for as long as I live, I lament this guilt.

31. To receive the order of the priesthood, I was summoned by Lord Tagino to the city of Allstedt [Col. 1331D]. On the way I confessed the deed I had committed and promised to amend it, but I did not fulfill that promise as I ought.

I received the dignity of the priesthood from the aforesaid archbishop on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January, in the presence of King Henry, who generously gave me an excellent chasuble, though I was unworthy (the year 1008, October 11).

Before I was ordained bishop, during the week in which the commemoration of the brothers is universally celebrated by all the faithful, someone announced to me in a dream (fol. 118′):

“In this year Bishop Hillericus, Deacon Meinricus, and you must fulfill the command of God.”

I replied: “As it is the will in heaven, so may it be done.”

In that very month, on the third [Note: [Col. 1331] 1c perhaps has *tercia*.] day before the Kalends of November, which was then approaching, the aforesaid bishop breathed forth his life in Christ, as had previously been revealed to him [Note: [Col. 1332D] Hillericus, bishop of Havelberg, died in the year 1008; see the *Annales Quedlinburgenses*.].

Since almighty God often deigns to visit and console human weakness [Note: [Col. 1331] 1 has *dignitatur*.], it is fitting to make this known to posterity in praise and writing, so that the name of the Lord may be glorified and a fickle man may take heed for himself [Note: [Col. 1331] 2 has: “Praise and honor to Christ, by whom he may be magnified in this man.”].

The aforesaid bishop, while an excessive bodily illness was already growing strong in Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 1331] Added in 1b.], was thus admonished in a dream by an excellent man who appeared to him:

“Do not now be anxious about your end. You will await four years and two or three weeks, and whatever good things you can do, do not cease.”

[Note: [Col. 1331] 2 adds: “You, however, must not neglect the time granted to you by God, but whatever good you can do, do it earnestly, so that you may merit eternal life.” A. S., under the year 1008.]

After speaking these words, he vanished [Note: [Col. 1331] 2 adds: “He spoke, and immediately dissolved himself into empty air.”]. As this man had foretold, the bishop, vigilant in mind, as I hope, lived on, but by a sudden death, alas, he brought the supreme line of this life to its end. On the following night a great light appeared, seen by many [Note: [Col. 1331] *In ... apparuit* added in 1b.].

After the commemoration of all the saints (November 2), I, very fearful about myself, asked the dean for permission to depart and admonished him to make provision for himself.

I came to my court, called Retmerslevo [Note: [Col. 1331] 1c perhaps has *retmersleue*.], and during the following night humbly prayed God to deign to reveal some certainty about me. At the first twilight of the next day, that is, on the vigil of Saint Martin (November 10), while I was resting a little, Walterdus, then our provost, appeared to me, as it seemed, saying (fol. 119):

“Do you wish to know what will benefit you?”

When he perceived my desire in this matter, he immediately examined carefully the volume of a martyrology [Note: [Col. 1331] 1 has *martorlogii*.], silently inserted a plumb line [Note: [Col. 1331] 1 has *blumbum*.], by which a wall is measured and aligned, and after a long interval of time it came to rest.

“What is it now?” I asked him.

“Five,” he replied.

I clearly saw this number marked in ink, uncertain whether it signified days, weeks, months, or years. Immediately I asked him whether the time foretold would come earlier or later; but he silently departed.

I carefully noted the period shown to me, not without the greatest anxiety, but I did not anticipate it by good works at all [Note: [Col. 1333] 1 has the obscure reading *Nulfatus*.]. When the fifth month arrived—although I expected death more than this—the two dreams were fulfilled in the episcopate I received: in it I obeyed the divine commands and completed the number that had been marked.

Therefore it seemed improper to me that the church I had governed until then should be without a special rector. By the common counsel of the brothers, I appointed to it Willigisus, my brother on my father’s side, as servant of this altar. From there I came to Merseburg and celebrated the approaching Pentecost with my lord the king (June 5) [Note: [Col. 1333D] The king was still at Merseburg on June 9; see his charter in Höfer, vol. I, part I, p. 159.].

32. Thereafter we all came to Magdeburg. There my nephew, Margrave Wirinharius, was accused by the king on many counts and would have lost his favor and benefice through the instigation of Count Daedi [Note: [Col. 1333] Erased in 1.], if his sudden illness had not prevented it [Note: [Col. 1333] Added in 1b.], and if Count Palatine Burchardus had not postponed the matter by prudent counsel.

The king then proceeded to test the minds of the western peoples and tried to calm them, lest they be stirred up in their customary manner [Note: [Col. 1333D] Concerning the Lotharingians, compare Widukind I, 30.]. Some praise those who refuse to endure the injustice of their lords, while they in turn condemn us as though cowardly.

There are many who, enslaved to every bodily pleasure, pay no attention to the bridle of equity imposed by God upon the king. Instead, they defend whatever can be accomplished by force or craft, without concern for the future, and pursue with slander and insatiable hatred all who do not agree with them.

But I do not agree with these men or with their supporters. Rather, I incline toward those who humble and submit themselves to God and to the authorities established by him. They hold that it is more fitting to suffer everything for God than to offend the divine majesty through litigation [Note: [Col. 1333] 1a has *quas ligitios*, with two *s* erased.] and detestable perjury.

Our predecessors, always faithful to their lords, raged as excellent soldiers against foreign nations, not against their own flesh. Let posterity learn this and avoid other things; let it strive to transfer what must be changed not for the worse but always for the better. Let it willingly attend to the eighth beatitude, and, fleeing its opposite, strive to grasp it [Note: [Col. 1333] The manuscript reading *beatitudinem oct* is incomplete or uncertain.].

Why do I wish to rebuke the former any further or exalt the latter, when each person certainly receives the fruit of the future harvest according to the quality of his seed? (Matthew V.) Since we are always laboring to receive corruptible things, why do we not, casting fear aside, hasten somewhat toward the unfailing crown of honor (fol. 120)?

To seize this crown, our king, laboring greatly in journeys and other necessities, made friends into enemies, hating them justly, as I have said.

33. Meanwhile Count Daedi, inflicting great disgrace in words and deeds upon my aforesaid nephew, stirred up an evil that he had thought forgotten. By his counsel and aid, the city of his father and of our family, Walmerstidi [Note: [Col. 1333D] Wolmirstedt.], called in Slavic Ustiure because the rivers Ara and Elbe meet there, was burned and devastated.

This stirred the whole spirited heart of the excellent young man. When he learned for certain that the enemy was riding out from the city called Tongeremuthi [Note: [Col. 1333D] Tangermünde.], so called because the river Tongera falls there into the Elbe, he took with him my brother Frithericus and only twenty armed soldiers. From the summit [Note: [Col. 1333] 1a has *assummitate*.] of a field extending as far as the village of Mosum [Note: [Col. 1333D] Moss, a village near the aforesaid city.], which could be seen from a distance [Note: [Col. 1333] The first *s* was erased in 1.], he attacked him bravely.

When more than forty of his companions immediately fled, the enemy resisted firmly; but he killed him together with his own soldier Egilhardus. After this, he justly lost what he had previously, and almost irrationally, lost at his urging [Note: [Col. 1333] *pene* corrected to *poene*, but the *o* was later erased in 1.].

[Note: [Col. 1333D] The Merseburg calendar records on July 9 the death of Count Aeilherdus of Daedi; the Lüneburg Necrology records him on July 10. Compare the *Annales Quedlinburgenses* under the year 1009. It should nevertheless be noted that the Lüneburg Necrology records on November 13 a slain Tado and Eghillerdus the layman.]

> **Full witness additions:** Manuscript 2’s long expanded reading is: “He loved them, remembered them everywhere for good, and always praised them before the king, princes, and all peoples, within and without.” Its St Vitus addition reads: “the feast of the precious martyr Vitus, a boy and patron of Saxony, who rests at New Corvey.”

### 34

But if it pleases you, reader, to hear from what stock he came, you will learn that he derived his origin from the tribe called Buzici [Note: [Col. 1333D] As it seems to me, Thietmar here relates that Dedi was descended from the people who took their name from the village of Busci, today Pausitz, situated in his diocese not far from the city of Leipzig. Concerning the village of Busci, see the charter of Emperor Otto III dated 18 September 991, in Höfer, vol. I, part I, p. 531.], and from a father named Thiedricus. From childhood he served Margrave Riddag, his kinsman, and was endowed with a double strength of heart and body. As I said earlier [Note: [Col. 1334D] III, 10.], he led the Bohemians (f. 120') who had risen against us [Col. 1334C] to the church of Zitice [Note: [Col. 1333] *perdux* in witness 1: “he led.”]. While ravaging the surrounding region with them, he eventually brought back his own captive mother, an enemy rather than a son, together with the rest of the booty.

Afterward he was reconciled, became a man of King Otto III, and in a short time earned his favor and intimacy. Meanwhile Bio, count of Merseburg, died on campaign; and Archbishop Gisiler acquired for himself this county, which lies between the rivers Wipper, Saale, and Salza [Note: [Col. 1334D] Salza or Salzsee.], and the Villerbizi [Note: [Col. 1334D] Wildenbach. The rivers named here by Thietmar clearly indicate that this county included within its boundaries most of the land of Mansfeld.], [Note: [Col. 1333] *isto ac acquisivit* in witness 1: “acquired this.”] He also claimed for himself and his brother Fritheric the burgward of Zurbizi [Note: [Col. 1333] *curbizi* in witness 1a.], [Note: [Col. 1334D] Zörbig.], which his predecessors had held as a benefice.

He also married Thiedburga, daughter of Margrave Thiedricus [Note: [Col. 1333] *dux* in witness 1: “he married.”], and on account of this became so puffed up that he secretly caused annoyance to the king and offered it openly to many [Note: [Col. 1335] *offeret* in witness 1: “he offered.”]. At the following Christmas the king celebrated at Palithi, and there gave Thiedricus, son of the aforementioned count, the county and the entire benefice by right and at the prompting of his queen and princes [Note: [Col. 1335] *principum*; the first hand has *principium*, repeatedly. *Ortatu*, “at the prompting”; witness 1a has *interuentu*, “through intervention.”]. Moreover, whatever march and property Wirinzo held on the king’s behalf was all granted to Count Bernhard.

### 35

In those days Thiedricus, bishop of Metz, and Duke Heinricus, his brother [Note: [Col. 1335D] They were brothers of Empress Cunigunda.], together with the other conspirators, inflicted great trouble upon the king and his intimates and earned for themselves and their successors an insuperable loss [Note: [Col. 1335D] Compare Sigebert of Gembloux, under the year 1009.].

For one church that stood outside the city of Metz, together with the community serving there, was devastated by Slavs who did not fear God [Note: [Col. 1335D] Not so, but by Northmen. Compare Alpert, I, chapter 8 and following.]. But the king restored this damage for the most part by oaths and from his own property and, lest anything similar should happen to this church, ordered the entire army to take precautions. He damaged vineyards and buildings, together with grain and other useful goods.

Not long afterward I saw a letter in which eight hundred serfs of Saint Stephen were listed who, because of famine [Note: [Col. 1335] *fam* in witness 1: “famine.”] and another necessity, had left their native territory without the knowledge of their officials, apart from all those who had departed with their consent. It would have been better for this church if that man had never been born.

I shall also describe one of their deeds, which they perpetrated mournfully at Adram [Note: [Col. 1335D] Perhaps Odernheim, between Oppenheim and Alzey.] [Note: [Col. 1335] *lugub* in witness 1: “mournfully.”]. The king held an assembly in the city of Mainz, and these men were present. Since they could not answer everything there according to their own wishes, they returned in anger, although peace had been made for the time being. When Bishop Heimo of Verdun and Duke Thiedricus [Note: [Col. 1336D] Of Upper Lorraine.] followed them, expecting no evil, they suddenly fell upon them from an ambush [Note: [Col. 1335] *insidiantes* in witness 1a: “lying in wait.”], and, although a few escaped with the bishops, countless men were killed.

That duke, grievously wounded, was captured and led away because he had been their friend [Note: [Col. 1335] *et* “and” added in witness 1b.] and was kept under guard for many days. Afterward he was released when hostages had been given, and on this account was not removed from the king’s favor.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation one thousand … Duke Bernhard of Corvey died [Note: [Col. 1335] “In the year … died” was added in the lower margin by witness 1b. The numeral for the tenth or fortieth year is omitted; it is established that Duke Bernhard died in 1011.] (1011).

### 36

Meanwhile Count Herimannus and Margrave Guncelinus, contending with one another, engaged in battle in a manner unusual in these regions (1009). For Guncelinus, attempting to storm the city of Strela, which was guarded by Herimannus’s soldiers [Col. 1336A], and accomplishing nothing, ordered the city of Rocholenz [Note: [Col. 1335] Witness 1a has *rocholenti*; witness 1c has *rocholezi*; apparently *Rocholenci* in A.S.] situated beside the river Mulde and inadequately defended to be consumed by fire.

Moreover, he did not delay in doing whatever harm he could to the aforementioned count, since uncles always rage against their brothers’ sons [Note: [Col. 1335] Witness 1a has *seruiant*, “serve”; the intended reading is apparently *seviunt*, “rage.”]. Herimannus and Ekkihardus, brothers, surrounded by a strong force and taking by surprise a certain castle situated beside the Saale—which Guncelinus had fortified with walls and a garrison because he loved it above all, and had filled with innumerable goods [Note: [Col. 1336D] Perhaps this was the castle whose ruins can still be seen near Saalfeld.]—stormed it, divided all its stores, tore it down to its foundations [Note: [Col. 1335] Added in witness 1b.] and consumed it with fire [Note: [Col. 1335] Added in witness 1b.].

This reached the king’s ears, and he immediately hurried to Merseburg to investigate these matters [Note: [Col. 1335] *discuenda* in witness 1: “to be investigated.” [Col. 1336D] So also the Annals of Quedlinburg under 1009: “There, having spent the summer—namely, in Francia—he returned to Saxony.” On 3 November he was still at Worms.]. But when he had considered the opinions of the aforementioned counts there [Col. 1336B], he laid all the blame upon Guncelinus, because he had previously despised him in many matters and had not awaited an avenger for the disgrace inflicted upon him.

He added that Guncelinus had often sold the households of many people who complained to him about this to Jews, and had never taken care either to restore them at his command or to restrain the robberies that, under his authority, harmed many people. Moreover, he complained that Guncelinus had hitherto enjoyed greater favor with his brother Bolizlavus than was fitting or ought to have pleased him [Note: [Col. 1335] Added in witness 1b.].

Four men were present, who wished jointly to accuse him of being guilty of treason against majesty. Amid all these complaints and the excuses of Guncelinus and his men, the king sought the common counsel of the princes [Note: [Col. 1335] Witness 1a has *communice*; corrected to *communiter*, “jointly.”]. After they had long and secretly considered the matter [Note: [Col. 1335] Witness 1 has only *h*, which, as elsewhere in this codex, signifies *hoc*, “this.”], they answered as follows:

“We know that he is not without excuse before you [Col. 1336C]. But it seems good to us that, without any resistance, he should surrender himself entirely to your mercy. May merciful God admonish you to act in his case not according to the quality of his own merit, but according to the measure of your ineffable clemency, as an example to all who turn to you [Note: [Col. 1335] That is, *in eo faciatis*, “that you act in his case”; *f.* was added in witness 1b.].”

With the counsel of these men the king agreed, received Guncelinus, and handed him over to Bishop Arnulf for firm custody, strengthening Misni against its enemies by maintaining its garrison and entrusting it for the time being to Fritheric for protection [Note: [Col. 1335] Witness 1 has *comitens*; witness 2 has *commisit*, “entrusted.”]. At the following harvest, through the queen’s intervention and at the prompting of his beloved Tagino, he gave Count Herimannus the march, with the counsel and approval of those same princes [Note: [Col. 1335] *Laude*, “approval”; two letters were erased after it in witness 1.].

### 37

Meanwhile Count Brun, Guncelinus’s brother, was guarding the aforementioned city in his turn. And behold: on the day before Herimannus was to arrive, a great host of Poles crossed the Elbe at the first light of day and came silently as far as the gate of the city that had been promised to them [Col. 1337A]. But when the entrance was not readily open to them because soldiers had been stationed there, they turned back—sadly, alas!—unharmed and having harmed no one.

As was later revealed, two Wethenici [Note: [Col. 1337] Witness 1 has *uuetheni*.] from the suburb had been the leaders of this affair. For they paid the due price of such presumption with their own blood.

Bolizlavus, anxious between hope and fear, was awaiting them at Budusin [Note: [Col. 1337] Witness 1 has *busin*; A.S. has *Budizin*. [Col. 1337D] Bautzen.], and when he learned that his allies were approaching, he took it very hard that he had been deceived. On the following day [Note: [Col. 1337] Witness 1a has *Post adte* for *postera die*, “on the following day”; witness 1b has *ita*.] Count Herimannus was admitted by a royal messenger [Note: [Col. 1337] Witness 1a and 1b have *noccium*.], and he forgave his debtors whatever they had done against him, affirming this by his right hand.

During that summer and the following winter, the king, having pacified his enemies by counsel and strength, repeatedly reflected upon the insult and injury inflicted upon him by Bolizlavus, and after Easter announced his expedition by a harsh command [Note: [Col. 1337] *Jussione*, “by command,” in witness 1.].

### 38

An assembly was held at Belegori (1010), called “the beautiful mountain” [Note: [Col. 1337D] Belgern, beside the river Elbe.], on the estate of Margrave Gero. Then Duke Bernhard and Provost Walther went ahead in the hope of converting Bolizlavus, but, finding nothing there that pleased them, returned.

Jarimirus also came there, the illustrious duke of the Bohemians and in all things faithful to the king [Note: [Col. 1337] Witness 1 has *pro*, “for/on behalf of,” for *per*, “through” (in *per omnia*, “in all things”).]. I cannot pass over what happened there, a most grievous matter for the aforementioned count. We all—nor can I except anyone—became his enemies in place of friends; and, excepting only the serfs, we consumed everything, including some things by fire [Col. 1337C]. Neither the king nor anyone else was an avenger or restorer of this wrong [Note: [Col. 1337] “Nor anyone else who would make restitution” was added in witness 2.].

From there we went to the district of the Lusici [Note: [Col. 1337] Witness 1 perhaps has *luziti*.], at whose frontier stands a city called Jarina [Note: [Col. 1337D] Gaehren, a parish village at the extreme edge of the district of Luckau and of the lower Lusatian margraviate.], named after Margrave Gero, who was great and was therefore called “the Great” [Note: [Col. 1337D] He is also called “the Great” by Widukind III, 54, and in the Annals of Quedlinburg under 1013.].

There two brothers from the province of the Hevelli and from the city of Brandenburg were captured. They had come to Bolizlavus in order to turn him against the king, and on their departure they openly fell into the snare that had secretly been laid for them. Questioned about many matters [Note: [Col. 1337] Witness 1 has *interogati*.], and unwilling to confess anything concerning all these things, they perished together by hanging on a hill.

At that time the king and his beloved Tagino were becoming ill there. The princes anxiously turned over in their hearts what ought to be done about the expedition that had been undertaken [Note: [Col. 1337] Witness 1a has *exspeditione*.]. At last they decided that the king should return with certain bishops [Note: [Col. 1335] Added in witness 1b.] and the weaker portion of the army, while Bishops Arnulf and Meinwercus [Note: [Col. 1338D] Of Paderborn.] with Duke Jarimirus, the margraves Gero and Herimannus, and many others should ravage the districts of the Cilensi [Note: [Col. 1338D] This is also called the district of Silensis, situated around the city of Nimptsch. Compare below, Book VII.] and Diedesi.

And so it was done [Note: [Col. 1338D] Compare the Annals of Quedlinburg under 1010.]. When the aforementioned lords passed in a group and wearing cuirasses by the city called Glogua, where Bolizlavus himself was and could see them, the soldiers watching from the walls were provoked. Addressing their duke and asking why he allowed this, they sought permission to attack them.

He answered them:

“The army that you see, though small in number, is great in valor and chosen above the other thousands [Note: [Col. 1337] Added in witness 1b.]. If I attack it, whether I conquer or am overcome, I am ruined for the future. The king can immediately gather another army [Note: [Col. 1337] “And attack us” was added in witness 2.] It is much better for us to endure this patiently in this way, and on another occasion, if it can be done, to harm these arrogant men without great loss to ourselves [Note: [Col. 1337] “And avenge our injuries” was added in A.S. by witness 2].”

Thus the insolent spirit of the soldiers was calmed, and on this expedition their desire to harm us was not satisfied. Although our men were delayed by frequent flooding from the rains [Note: [Col. 1337] Witness 1 has *imundatione*.], they nevertheless inflicted great damage upon the enemy over a wide area.

At last, after ravaging everything lying around them, the Bohemians returned home, while our men joyfully returned through the territory of the Milzeni to the Elbe. They immediately sent messengers to the king [Note: [Col. 1337] A.S. has *veredarii*, “couriers.”], announcing that they would come with good success.

By God’s grace the king had by then recovered well; he received this embassy and the friends who followed it afterward amicably at Merseburg. Archbishop Tagino, who had earlier been separated from the king at Strela [Note: [Col. 1337] Added in witness 1b.], celebrated the solemn feast of the holy Theban martyrs at Magdeburg (22 September), and came safely to the king.

### 39

After attending to the many needs of his suffering country, the king again visited the western regions. Subduing the wavering spirits of the inhabitants with the bridle of wisdom, he celebrated Christmas with festive joy at Palithi [Note: [Col. 1338D] This did not take place at Palithi but at Frankfurt, according to the Annals of Hildesheim.].

Then he again visited Merseburg, which was especially dear to him, and, after mutual peace had been confirmed there for five years [Note: [Col. 1337] The word *pace* was written here by witness 1b after the first hand had written it following a few words.], he ordered, with the counsel of a few men, that the city called Liubusua [Note: [Col. 1338D] See above, Book I, chapter 9.] should be built and fortified. Many had foretold that something would come from it which, alas!, in this year they recognize was not false.

We came to it at the end of January (f. 123'), and there, on 2 February, we duly celebrated the Purification of the holy Mother of God (1011). Within fourteen days we completed the work that had been imposed upon us [Col. 1338D], fortified the city with a garrison [Col. 1339A], and returned.

Near it, on the northern side, stands a city separated from the aforementioned one by nothing but a single valley [Note: [Col. 1339] Witness 1a has *uualdis*.]; it has twelve gates. When I carefully surveyed it, I discussed the work of Julius Caesar and the great Roman construction, with Lucan as my guide [Note: [Col. 1339D] He refers to what Lucan reports in *Pharsalia* VI, verses 29–65, concerning the camp built by Julius Caesar near Dyrrachium.]. It could have held more than ten thousand men.

The smaller city, which we then completed, had remained empty from the time of King Heinricus I until this period [Note: [Col. 1339] Added in witness 1b.]. How lamentably and swiftly it collapsed, I shall explain by enumerating the events that occurred in the meantime.

### 40

In the preceding summer [Note: [Col. 1339D] That is, 1011. Since the church of Bamberg was consecrated in 1012, when Thietmar later himself added this note concerning Wallibizi in the margin, he could not have meant by “the preceding summer” any other than the summer before that consecration.], on 10 August, the monastery at Wallibizi, together with four churches, all their bells, and the associated buildings, perished by fire on account of my sins [Note: [Col. 1339] “In the preceding … perished” was added by witness 1b.].

After the major church at Bamberg had been completed, when it was the king’s birthday and he was beginning his thirty-fifth year (1012) [Note: [Col. 1339] “And … year” was added by witness 1b.], on 6 May, the second day before the Nones of May, all the chief men assembled there for the dedication of this hall. This bride of Christ was consecrated through the ministry of John, patriarch of Aquileia, and more than thirty other bishops [Note: [Col. 1339] The words “by the ministry … was consecrated” are absent from witness 1 and supplied from the *Saxon Chronicle* under 1012. The name appears as *iohanni*, written in a scraped area and above the line.].

I, a sinner, was present at these proceedings, and I saw it adorned in every respect as befitted the supreme king [Note: [Col. 1339] Added in witness 1b.]. After this a great synod was held there [Note: [Col. 1339] *Magnus* was corrected to *magna* in witness 1.]. At it Gevehardus, bishop of the church of Regensburg, was reproved by his archbishop [Note: [Col. 1339] *Accusatur*, “is accused,” corrected to *arguitur*, “is reproved,” in witness 1.], and Thiedricus, bishop of the church of Metz, was rebuked by the king [Note: [Col. 1339] *Incraepatur* corrected to *increp.*, “is rebuked,” in witness 1.], because in his letter he had unjustly accused the king before the pope.

But all these matters and many others were settled by prudent counsel, and the restoration of my parish was then promised to me.

### 41

When all the affairs in eastern Francia had been completed, the king revisited the city of Merseburg. There he celebrated the holy feast of Pentecost. At the first hour of the Lord’s Day on which the Holy Spirit filled the holy apostles (1 June), Archbishop Tagino began to fall ill and could not sing Mass. I, unworthy as I was, was then ordered to take his place in this office [Note: [Col. 1339] Added in witness 1b.].

On the following day the chief archbishop improved somewhat and, walking to the king, became greatly agitated. After this he was so weakened that he could no longer do anything by himself. My brother, Abbot Sigifridus [Note: [Col. 1339] Sigifridus, newly abbot of Corvey, according to witness 2. [Col. 1340D] Sigifridus, abbot of the monastery of Saint John the Baptist at Magdeburg, elected in 1009. See the *Saxon Chronicle*.], and Bishop Ericus were then summoned to him; he made his confession to them. On Thursday, when he had already wished to depart, he was carried on a chair near the king’s chamber. Raising the cap from his head, he addressed the sleeping old man:

“May almighty God repay you with worthy thanks, my dearest lord, for all your mercies, by which you have visited and consoled me, a stranger, until now [Note: [Col. 1339] Witness 2 adds: “And may he grant your goodness, in repayment for them, the reward in the heavenly Jerusalem which he himself has prepared unspeakably for those who love him. For you will not see me alive again from now on, because now, as I hope, I am entering upon the way of all flesh. Farewell, therefore, my dearest lord; farewell in the Lord!”].”

Then he came to the church and heard Mass, blessing those who were present [Note: [Col. 1339] Added in witness 1b.]. From there he was carried to a boat [Note: [Col. 1339] Witness 1 has “he was carried.”], and by it was brought to Ivicansten. There he rested on Saturday, and on Sunday he came by boat to his city called Spiutni [Note: [Col. 1340D] In charters of Otto I dated 29 July 961 and 12 April 965 it is called Zpiutneburg, in the district of Nuditzi. It lies on the river Saale and is still called Rothenburg.].

On Monday, while still on the journey and almost completely exhausted, he summoned Provost Walther to him. Entrusting himself and his people to Walther’s fidelity, on 9 June, the fifth day before the Ides of June, he did not die, but joyfully departed to Christ, whom he had always loved.

The brothers offered prayer amid mingled tears, and the soldier Bodo was sent to the king to report these things. The archbishop’s body arrived at Frasam that same day, and there, prepared in priestly vestments, it was transferred to his see and received by everyone with immense sorrow.

### 42

I learned all these things late at Merseburg, and on the day of his burial, after the sun had already risen, I arrived. Having poured out a few words of prayer in the major church, I went to the refectory, where the provost was sitting with all the brothers and soldiers and discussing the election.

Standing in their presence, I wept bitterly, troubled by overwhelming grief. After greeting everyone, I sat down and asked what they had then decided [Note: [Col. 1339] Added in witness 1b.]. Walther answered:

“I sent my representative to the king to inform him of the evils that had befallen us and to inquire about his will concerning the things that were to be done. He sent Bishop Hericus to us, so that we should not conduct an election, but only express unanimous consent and report it to him. Now, however, the devotion of all those present determines me, although I am unworthy of this, if God consents and if the king wishes it.”

I immediately replied:

“I am one of those who ought to participate in this election and consecration. I give you this counsel, and I wish to assist it insofar as I can. Let my lord command what he wishes [Note: [Col. 1339] The first hand has *imperat*, “commands.”]; but see to it that you do not lose what you have received from God and from his predecessors. As for you, brother, I choose you first for myself as chief archbishop—not because of your affection for me, but because I have recognized a certain advantage in you [Note: [Col. 1340D] “That is, in you” was added in witness 1b.]—and now I especially desire to know the mind of those present.”

From them I received this one answer: “We choose Walther as our lord and chief archbishop.”

When this had been confirmed, Walther arose and, prostrating himself, asked pardon. He called upon divine mercy to grant that these things be repaid to all of us, and for his part promised everything good.

Then I bowed and asked him, in the name of the Lord and for the love of true brotherhood, that, if he attained this dignity, he should restore to my greatly impoverished church the parish that rightly belonged to it, and that he should confirm this to me by oath together with the other things taken away from it. He firmly promised me this in the presence of everyone.

Meanwhile Bishop Hericus, wearied by the journey, fell asleep. Bishop Wigo came and confirmed our election. Then we all sent the church’s custodian, Redingus [Note: [Col. 1341] Witness 1 has *reedignus*, with the second *e* erased.], to the king, so that, mindful of the Lord and of his ancient promise, if such an event should ever occur, he might wish to console the bereft and exceedingly sorrowful household of Saint Maurice with so great a father.

### 43

At the sound of the first bell Ericus awoke and sang the Mass for the dead. After the Gospel it became clear to those present why the king had sent him there. For the deceased archbishop, he performed the absolution with us and asked that everyone should do so.

For it was then the third day since the aforementioned priest had died. This day, together with the seventh and the thirtieth, is to be commemorated at the death of every faithful person because of the mystery contained in it—namely, the faith of the Holy Trinity and the sevenfold Spirit [Note: [Col. 1341] Added in witness 1b.].

After this the blessed body was carried with song and lamentation [Note: [Col. 1341] Witness 1 has *plantu*, “lamentation.”] to the place of burial. It was placed on the western side, in the choir before the crypt which he himself had built and consecrated, and in which, as long as he lived, he had asked to be buried before the altar. There he had often poured out tearful prayers.

But Walther provided for his beloved lord this place, where he now rests, because it had not been consecrated [Note: [Col. 1341] Witness 1 has *qan*; the reading may also have been *quod*, “which.”], so that it might be salutary for his soul and visible to all who entered.

Since all the blessed live with Christ through their virtues, and since in this world they live on through writings, it is not good to conceal in silence the renowned conduct of so great a father, but to make it known to everyone for their benefit in the light of truth:

He was just and God-fearing, of extraordinary charity, generous and faithful, chaste and gentle, prudent and steadfast; canonical in his dress, but a monk in all his conduct. He sharply reproved vices in everyone for the sake of improvement, while praising every good quality.

Among modern pastors there was none more familiar to his brothers. He loved them and praised them publicly [Note: [Col. 1341] Witness 2 adds: “He loved them, remembered them everywhere for their good, and always praised them before the king, the princes, and all the people, both inwardly and outwardly.”].

In the first year of his episcopal ordination he began to build a temple for the Lord. He increased the clothing allowance of priests and deacons to eight *sicli*, and that of subdeacons and children [Note: [Col. 1341D] Choirboys.] to four.

Unless illness prevented him, he sang Mass and the Psalter every day. Since he could not fast because of weakness, he redeemed this through a multitude of almsgiving. He labored excessively in vigils, and, because he could eat little on account of the weakness of his teeth, he was easily satisfied with a moderate drink.

He loved those noble in birth and character, but did not despise the ignoble, although he did not keep them in his intimate circle [Note: [Col. 1341] *Sed* was erased in witness 1 but remains in witness 2.]. He loved those who served Christ, but pursued his despisers with just hatred. He cultivated everything divinely entrusted to him and strove to make it fruitful.

Before he performed the divine mystery [Note: [Col. 1341] Witness 2 has *officium*, “office,” instead.], he was severe; afterward he smiled cheerfully upon everyone, and often sang “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*) with his own people.

For my part I cannot count how much he strove to bestow upon me, unworthy as I am, as a gift of mercy. I know only this: I never repaid him for these things with worthy recompense. The obedience that I promised him and his successors during my examination I did not at all fulfill [Note: [Col. 1341] Witness 1c may have *eo*, “to him,” rather than *ei*.].

He acquired for his church the cities of Harnaburg, Frasam, and Pretini [Note: [Col. 1341D] Prettin, on the northern bank of the Elbe between Wittenberg and Torgau.], together with an estate that had belonged to Count Eseco [Note: [Col. 1341D; Col. 1342D] See the king’s charters dated 7 April 1006 and 21 January 1012.].

He gathered a sufficiently excellent and abundant episcopal apparatus. For eight years, four months, and eight days he sat as a pillar of the church, falling, as I said earlier, visibly; but, transferred to the invisible temple of the Lord, he remains forever [Col. 1342C].

On the same day Vungerus, pastor of the monastery at Poznań, his fellow priest and suffragan, died in the thirtieth year of his ordination [Note: [Col. 1341] Added in witness 1b.].

Let these words now suffice, and I shall speak further about the subject of my present discourse.

### 44

When Redingus came to the king, he humbly presented his embassy. Although he obtained the desired result only with difficulty, he summoned me through Walther as intermediary, who had been diligent at the obsequies of his beloved lord and who also bestowed on Thiedricus, my nephew, twenty talents of silver as alms, apart from provisions.

Ordered to come, I set out with him, and we arrived late on Saturday at Grona [Note: [Col. 1342D] Gronau near the river Leine, close to Hildesheim, one of the five royal palaces in Saxony. See Wedekind, *Noten*, II, pp. 360 and following.].

When we soon came into the king’s presence, we were received mercifully. After speaking a few words, the king allowed us to go to our lodging. We had encamped outside the city and beside the grove where the church of Saint Alexander now stands [Col. 1343A].

The next day was Sunday and the feast of Christ’s martyr Vitus (15 June) [Note: [Col. 1343] “The solemnity of the precious martyr Vitus, a boy and patron of Saxony, who rests at New Corvey.”]. Very early I sang Mass for my brothers. Afterward, summoned into the city, we went as far as the king’s chamber. There Walther alone was admitted, and they spoke privately until the third hour.

Then Walther came out, carrying a ring in his hand, and showed it to us:

“Behold,” he said, “you have the pledge of the mercy that is to follow!” [Note: [Col. 1343] Witness 2 has: “Behold the pledge, the sign of the future dignity mercifully promised to me.”]
