Then we all came into the king’s presence. After the king himself had first praised Walther, and following his examination, we elected the aforementioned father, and all the best men gave their support. Immediately the king gave him the pastoral staff [Note: [Col. 1343] Added in witness 1b.].

After he had sworn the oath to the royal power, he was introduced into the church which the king had built there and which his predecessor had blessed. Those present sang “Praise to the Lord” (*Laus Domino*) [Col. 1343B].

Then I appealed to the king’s mercy, asking him to permit me to speak with Walther about the needs of my church [Note: [Col. 1343] “With him” added in witness 1b.]. As I requested, he entrusted me firmly to Walther’s faith. The king also handed over to him my nephew Thiedricus, as Walther himself had desired.

When the king again wished to attack his in-laws [Note: [Col. 1343D] That is, his wife’s brothers.], he discussed with the princes present how Bolizlavus was to be invaded by them [Note: [Col. 1343] Witness 1a has *intravit*, “entered,” rather than *tractavit*, “discussed.”]. He entrusted all this to the newly appointed archbishop, together with his estates situated in Saxony [Note: [Col. 1343] Witness 1 has *positos*, masculine, rather than *posita*, agreeing with estates.].

That same day we all departed, each to his own destination.

On the following Saturday (21 June), Bishop Arnulfus, by the king’s command [Note: [Col. 1343] Added in witness 1b.], enthroned Archbishop Walther, and both men were received there with honor and great joy.

On the following day (22 June), Walther was anointed by Eido, the venerable third bishop of the church of Meissen [Note: [Col. 1343] Witness 1 has *misnessis*.], with the assistance of his fellow bishops Wigo, Hilliwardus, and Hericus—and of me, far inferior to them in all these things. Bishop Arnulfus also assisted us.

On Monday we all departed with good fellowship and a great gift [Note: [Col. 1343] Witness 1 has *magna*, “great,” rather than *magno*, “great,” agreeing with gift]. It had been the vigil of Saint John the Baptist, and Redingus was then appointed provost by the archbishop through the common election of the brothers.

On the holy day he was led to the Mount with the customary honor and received by me and my brother Sigifridus [Note: [Col. 1343D] “The monk of Saint Vitus” was added by witness 2.]. There he sang Mass, instructed the people first, and afterward, although greatly urged by the abbot to hold a charitable feast there for the crowd attached to him, he omitted it [Note: [Col. 1343D] Added in witness 1b.].

He was in his own see on the feast of the Apostles (29 June), and then gave salutary admonitions to those entrusted to him.

## Source-grounded textual apparatus and folio anchors

- **Chapter 34 (cols. 1333–1335).** The source begins on **f. 120'**. Manuscript 1 has *perdux* for *perduxit* (“led”), *isto ac acquisivit* (“acquired this also”) for *isto acquisivit*, and *dux* for *duxit* (“married/took”). Manuscript 1a has *curbizi* for *Zurbizi*; the editorial note identifies the latter as Zoerbig. Manuscript 1 has *offeret* for *offerret* (“might cause”), *at* for *ac* (“and”), and repeatedly *qicquid* for *quidquid* (“whatever”); manuscript 1a has *interuentu* (“intervention”) for *ortatu* (“prompting”) and *principium* (normally “beginning,” here apparently a misspelling of *principum*, “of princes”) for *principum*.
- **Chapter 35 (cols. 1335–1336).** Folio **f. 121** begins the Metz account. Manuscript 1a has *mettensis* for *Metensis* (“of Metz”); manuscript 1 *qd* for *quid* (“anything”), *fam* for *fames* (“famine”), and *lugub* for *lugubre* (“mournfully”). Manuscript 1a has *insidiantes* (“lying in wait”) for *latentes insidias* (“hidden ambushes”); *add. 1b* after the duke’s wounding means the clause is added in manuscript 1b. The marginal notice “year … Bernhard died” is added at the foot of the page in 1b and lacks the numeral X or XI by which the duke’s year of death is known.
- **Chapter 36 (cols. 1335–1336).** Folio **f. 121'** marks the burning of Rochlitz. Manuscript 1a reads *rocholenti* and 1c *rocholezi* for Rocholenzi; A. S. apparently has Rocholenci. It has *seruiant* (“may serve”) for *seviunt* (“are savage/rage”), *communice* for *communiter* (“jointly”), and a letter-form *h* that in this codex signifies *hoc* (“this”). *Pervenit hoc* (“this came”) is added in 1b; 1a has *idem* (“the same”) for *id* (“this”), and *discuenda* for *discutienda* (“to be examined”). The *ei* (“to him”) after Bolizlaus is added in 1b. In the mercy formula, manuscript 2 and A. S. have *vestre, que magna esse expertum est*: “your [mercy], which he has experienced to be great.”
- **Chapter 37 (cols. 1336–1337).** Manuscript 1 has *uuetheni* for Wethenici, *sollicit* for *sollicitus* (“anxious”), and *busin* while A. S. has Budizin; Bautzen is the place. The words *in* (“in”) and *hos* (“these”) are additions in 1b. Manuscript 1a has *Post adte* for *Post haec* (“after these things”), while 1b retains the printed reading; manuscript 1a/1b have *noccium* for *nuncium* (“messenger”), and 1a *reuuoluit* for *revolvit* (“reviewed”).
- **Chapters 38–39 (cols. 1337–1339).** Folios **f. 122**, **f. 122'**, and **f. 123** mark the campaign narrative. Manuscript 1 has *pro* (“for/on behalf of”) for *per* (“through”), *luziti?* for Luzici, *interogati* for *interrogati* (“questioned”), and 1a *exspeditione* for *expeditione* (“expedition”). The phrase “with certain bishops” is added in 1b; in the reply at Glogów *et* is added in 1b, while manuscript 2 adds “and attack us,” and 2/A. S. add “and avenge our injuries.” Manuscript 1 has *imundatione* for *inundatione* (“flooding”); manuscript 2 and A. S. *veredariis* (“couriers”) for *nunciis* (“messengers”); and “from Strela” is added in 1b. Folio **f. 123'** introduces Liubusua; manuscript 1a has *uualdis* for *vallis* (“valley”), and the smaller fort’s earlier state is added in 1b.
- **Chapters 40–41 (cols. 1339–1340).** The Wallibizi fire entry, the king’s age, the long consecration phrase, and the presence of Thietmar are additions in 1b; *ministerio consecratur* (“is consecrated by ministry”) is absent in manuscript 1 and supplied from the Saxon Chronographer. Manuscript 1 corrects *magnus* to *magna* (“great,” changing masculine to feminine to agree with “synod”), *accusatur* (“is accused”) to *arguitur* (“is reproved”), and *incraepatur* to *increpatur* (a spelling correction, “is rebuked”). Folio **f. 124** begins Pentecost; *Tunc jussus sum* (“Then I was ordered”) and *ac presuli Erico* (“and to Bishop Eric”) are additions in 1b, as are the words *quibus* (“to whom”), *peregrinum me* (“me, a stranger”), and *ipse* (“himself”) in the farewell. Manuscript 1 has *portatus est* (“was carried”) for *portatur* (“is carried”). Folio **f. 124'** marks Bodo’s embassy.
- **Chapters 42–44 (cols. 1340–1343).** Folios **f. 125**, **f. 125'**, and **f. 126** are preserved at the election, burial, and character sketch. Manuscript 1a has indicative *imperat* (“he commands”) for jussive *imperet* (“let him command”); *i. t. a.* abbreviates the added *in te agnita*, “recognized in you,” referring to Walther’s demonstrated usefulness, in 1b. Manuscript 1 reads *reedignus* for Redingus, with a second *e* erased. The word *quid* appears for *ad quid* (“for what purpose”); the day-number clause is added in 1b. Manuscript 1 has *plantu* for *planctu* (“lament”), *qan* for *quam* (“than/as”), either *cum* (“with”) or *tum* (“then”) where the printed text has *cum* (“with Christ”), and *canicus* for *canonicus* (“canonical”). Its long expanded reading is translated above: “He loved them, remembered them everywhere for good, and always praised them before the king, princes, and all peoples, within and without.” “Choirboys” glosses *infantibus*. In the later clause about admitting men of low birth into his intimate circle, *non*, “not,” is erased in 1 but survives in 2. Manuscript 2 has *officium* (“office/service”) for *misterium* (“mystery,” here the sacred rite); the uncertain 1c *ei* is retained as uncertain. The thirtieth year of Vungerus is added in 1b. In chapter 44, 1b adds Arnulf’s royal command, *is* (“he”), *ab* (“by”), and *fuit in* (“he was at”); manuscript 1 has *misnessis*, *magna*, and *viilia* as spelling forms, witness 2 adds “the monk of Saint Vitus,” whose fuller addition is translated above.

### 45

Meanwhile, summoned by envoys from Bolizlav [Note: [Col. 1343] “bozlavi” in witness 1.], he came to Sciciani [Note: [Col. 1343D] Seitsh, not far from the town of Glogau. URS.] to make peace. There he was magnificently received, stayed only two nights, and, accomplishing nothing there, returned with great gifts. The appointed day of the expedition soon arrived, namely 9 Kalends of August [July 24]; we assembled near the place called Zribenz [Note: [Col. 1344D] Schrenz, in the prefecture of Zörbig. URS.], and from there climbed upward as far as near Belegori [Note: [Col. 1343] “p. b.” added in witness 1b.]. Then it seemed to the princes [Note: [Col. 1343] “that this had already happened several times” added in witness 1.] that it was not good to complete our journey, but that the march should be secured with the best possible garrisons.

On the following night the archbishop became seriously ill in the head. When I came to him in the morning, I waited a long time while he lingered in his tent. At last he came out and complained to me that he had been very ill. He promised that he would come to the queen, who was then staying at Merseburg, and speak with me there. I then departed, while he at first refused; nevertheless, because it was then the Sunday of the Invention of Christ’s protomartyr [Stephen] (August 3) [Note: [Col. 1343] “e. d. d.” added in witness 1b.], he sang Mass—alas! his last.

On Thursday (August 7), when I came to Merseburg and was preparing, with my brothers, for his arrival, I heard from messengers that he was coming by wagon to Ivicansten, in poor health. The next day, riding there, I found Bernward [Note: [Col. 1343] Erased in witness 1.], bishop of the church of Hildesheim, summoned for the purpose of giving a blessing and, as he well knew, for the sake of healing; Fritheric the count was also there, whose brother was Count Dedi. When I entered, the archbishop was sitting on a throne, and received me most affectionately. He then looked at his own feet, which had been relieved of their usual swelling, and grieved because, while these had swollen, his belly had been easier [Note: [Col. 1343] Added in witness 1b.]. He had then told me that, if he survived this danger in good health, no friend could have been more faithful to me.

I remained there until evening, and then returned unwillingly, because the next day was the vigil of Christ’s athlete Lawrence, whose festival was approaching on Sunday (August 10). When I preached briefly to the people who had come, I earnestly asked them all to pray for the sick archbishop.

On Tuesday (August 12), before Prime, I came to the place where he was. Bishop Eido was there, laboring greatly for him in continual prayer. When I entered the chamber where that holy man lay, I neither heard him speaking nor saw him recognizing anyone properly [Note: [Col. 1343] “cognocentem” in witness 1.]. Arnulf and Hilliwardus also arrived while he was still alive, together with their fellow bishops Meinwerc and Erico; they all blessed him together and granted him absolution.

But I, a sinner, anointed him with consecrated oil on the places that hurt him most [Note: [Col. 1343] “hunc si” in witness 1a. Such are the indications that Thietmar himself dictated the book.]. Duke Jarmirus was also present [Note: [Col. 1343] Added in witness 1b.] [Col. 1345A]. His own brother Othelricus, together with a retainer who remembered no debt at all, had expelled him from the kingdom of Bohemia on Holy Saturday before the following Easter [Note: [Col. 1345] Added in witness 1b.], and had forced Bolizlav, although he was his friend by blood-relationship, yet had hitherto been regarded by him as an enemy in the persecution, to seek flight. Since Jarmirus knew that the archbishop was exceedingly faithful to all who suffered, he hoped for his recovery and sought his intercession to obtain the king’s favor. When he saw that the archbishop had now grown weak, he tearfully begged that he be entrusted to his right hand and, through it, to us [Note: [Col. 1345] Added in witness 1b.].

But when the archbishop’s end was already near, I do not know what he saw on his left. He firmly fortified himself with the sign of the holy cross using his right hand, and, turning his body and face away, contracted his features as if about to weep; then he relaxed them, appearing joyful.

Seeing this, I went out in grief. Meanwhile, those present, observing that he was already half-dead, immediately lifted him from the bed and laid him upon a carpet. When the lights had been kindled, I was summoned, and saw him dressed in a stole and struggling in his final agony. A holy cross had been placed upon his breast; in his hands he held ashes, and beneath him he had a hair shirt, as Bishop Eido showed us.

When the sun was already declining after midday, with incense applied to him, on the second day before the Ides of August (August 12), his soul passed to its Creator, whence it was, leaving behind what it was not. While all those present prayed with tears, I, unhappy man, did not help them as duty required. What then came into my mind I cannot disclose to anyone; but only this, faithful Christians: pray with me that the Lord, from whom no secret is hidden, may charge neither him nor me with this.

After his bowels had been removed and buried inside the church and the chamber, the body was prepared and presented at the holy altar. There a commemoration for the dead was made; we then dined there and accompanied the body that same day as far as Coniri [Note: [Col. 1345C] Coennern, reckoned among the prefectures of Giebichenstein in the district of Saale. URS.]. On the road a weeping household came out to meet us.

The next day, when we had come to a village situated beside Saint John’s mountain, all the clergy arrived weeping. A great number of Jews [Note: [Col. 1345] “the synagogue of the Jews” in witness 2; “a part of the Jews” in A. S.] also assembled, as did a multitude of orphans whose father he had been; they expressed their grief with lamentation. As we entered the principal church with the funeral procession, the friends, together with all the hereditary dependants, received us miserably, raising their hands in mourning.

Who would not have wept then on seeing such things? Yet no lamentation equaled this new loss.

### 46

All of us brothers then came to the chapter and chose my nephew [Note: [Col. 1345C] That is, Theodoricus.] except Bennus [f. 129]. We did not hope that this could be carried out on account of his youth, but acted especially out of regard for preserving the election and from affection for Archbishop Tagino [Col. 1346B] [Note: [Col. 1345] The words “we did not hope … out of regard” are absent from witness 1, whose first leaf was cut away at folio 129; we supplied them from witness 2.].

When evening came, Bishop Arnulf arrived, striving for this office with whatever advantages he possessed. On the following day, the election having been renewed, the body of the archbishop was buried to the right, before his predecessor, in the southern side-chapel [Note: [Col. 1345] “apse” in witness 2.] [Note: [Col. 1345C] Among architects of that age, *manica* means the side or broader part of any building, especially a church. URS.], on the vigil of the Assumption of Saint Mary.

As soon as the queen learned this, she informed the king through her cupbearer Geconus. The king was then withdrawing with his army from near the city of Metz [Note: [Col. 1346C] On the siege of the city of Metz in 1012, see Balderic, *Chronicon Cameracense*, book III, chapter 3.]. He was greatly astonished, asked how matters stood with us, and quickly sent Geconus back to her, with instructions concerning the kingdom as she was administering it [Note: [Col. 1345] “her; quickly he sent him back” in witness 1.].

But, reader, hear the epitaph of the archbishop, to be inscribed not on some stone but in a remembering heart:

Walthardus [Note: [Col. 1345] In witness 2 the following is greatly altered and reads as follows (Acta Sanctorum, June I, p. 926): “Walthardus, although his power is interpreted as harsh—severe in public, he was perceived as most gentle in private. He was a temperate man, well-mannered; he possessed a twofold love and flourished in supreme religion. Constant in vigils, he prayed in tears; generous in alms, he brought aid to the wretched. Honored for his virtues, he pleased the king and the leading men; he was loved by the former and revered by the latter. His predecessor surpassed him in blessing and in name alone. He was the strongest defender of his church in all things. Without any boastfulness he bestowed very much upon his neighbors. In my hearing he swore and affirmed as truth that he had not sought this honor through ambition, but for the benefit of the suffering and now almost failing church. ‘I know,’ he said, ‘that I am unworthy to undertake this office. There are two brothers whom I would gladly have chosen, if I had known that this could in any way have been done. He was a just man, steadfast in his purpose. He did not desire to be praised by others, nor did he himself disparage others. He traced his descent from the noblest birth, which he elevated by good conduct. His father was called Erp, a man adorned with a praiseworthy life and dear to all his contemporaries. His mother was named Amulradis; flourishing in chastity and good works, she surpassed other matrons in good repute.”]—although his name is interpreted as “harsh in power”—was severe in public but most gentle in private [Col. 1346C]. In continual fear and righteous love he acknowledged God and his neighbor. He dissolved the frailty of the flesh through the bitterness of frequent weeping and through an ineffable generosity in almsgiving.

Strong in both virtues [Note: [Col. 1346C] See above, book I, chapter 2.], he was acceptable to the king and greatly worthy of honor to all the leading men. His predecessor surpassed him in blessing and in name alone. Truthful and compassionate, he was also a strong defender of his own church. Without any boastfulness he gave very much to those living near him; he alone was known to have sufficed for everyone.

I heard him swear repeatedly that he had sought this honor not out of ambition but for the benefit of the suffering and almost failing church. He said that he was unworthy of it, and that there were two brothers there whom he would gladly choose if he hoped this could in any way be done.

This man was just and steadfast in his purpose [HORACE, III.3.1]. He did not desire praise from others, nor did he himself disparage others. Descended from the noblest lineage, he in no way dishonored the noble character he had inherited [Note: [Col. 1347] The words “he did not desire … noblest lineage” are missing from witness 1; we supplied them from witness 2, which reads: “He did not desire to be praised by others, nor did he himself disparage others. He traced his descent from the noblest birth …”], but adorned it with greater diligence.

His father was the elder Erp, a man of praiseworthy life, dear to all his contemporaries. His mother was named Amulred [Note: [Col. 1347D] Concerning her, see the *Saxon Annals*, year 1040. URS.]; distinguished among other matrons by devout chastity and womanly good works. She carefully expended all the good she could for his memory.

Walterdus had previously been told in a dream that he was to receive the archbishopric of Magdeburg and possess it for a short time [Note: [Col. 1347] Added in witness 1b.]. In the year when this was to be fulfilled, the deceased mother of a venerable matron appeared to her in a vision. When the matron greeted her and asked how she was then faring, she replied, “Well!” Then she added:

“Do you know,” she said, “that our Archbishop Tagino is to depart from this world and that Walterdus is to succeed him—not to reign here for a little while, but to sit among the judges at the Last Judgment? A tablet of silver is almost completed for him in heaven; and when it is completed more quickly, he will be taken from human sight to receive his rewards.”

He himself, as his lay sister informed me—for he had another sister who was a nun—knowing this very thing beforehand, summoned her and said:

“Do you now remember how you once promised me that, if you should ever succeed to my inheritance, you would give to Saint Mauritius, for the remedy of my soul, the estate that I possess at Osulfstidi [Note: [Col. 1347D] Olvenstedt in the duchy of Magdeburg. URS.]?”

When she acknowledged all this and confirmed it with her finger, as he had requested [Note: [Col. 1347D] Compare *I Grim, Rechtsalterthümer*, p. 140.], he replied tearfully:

“It is not permitted me to live. You, however, do as you said, and know for certain that I shall alienate nothing from what remains for you, my sisters.”

He knew that all these things had to be fulfilled, but he hoped for a longer period.

He had been provost for twenty-eight years, and held that name and office more honorably than all his contemporaries [Note: [Col. 1347] Added in witness 1b.]. He made a huge silver sarcophagus for enclosing the relics of the saints [Col. 1348A] [Note: [Col. 1347] “artento” in witness 1.]. After the great fire, he rebuilt from the foundations the round church that had fallen into ruin. There he proposed to establish a congregation of canons and wished to give them the aforementioned estate from his own property.

He was not talkative, but concealed the secrets of his conscience, to be revealed at appropriate times [Note: [Col. 1347] So perhaps in witness 1b? The passage is in an erased place.]. The only charge made against him above all others is that he did not bless the churches and clergy; but he felt no grief about the pallium [Note: [Col. 1347] “This”—through “felt no grief”—added in witness 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1347D] For the bull of Pope Benedict VIII was not written until the sixth day after the archbishop’s death, namely August 18, in the tenth indiction and the first year of Benedict’s pontificate. See Sagittarius, *Historia ducatus Magdeburgensis*, book III, chapter 5, p. 271; Dreyhaupt, vol. I, p. 249. URS.].

He amassed an ineffable abundance of books and priestly equipment, together with many things pertaining to secular affairs [Note: [Col. 1347] “priest” in witness 1.]. At his sudden death all these things were dispersed by many unworthy hands [Note: [Col. 1347] “distracserunt” in witness 1.]. For he had occupied the seat for only seven weeks and two days.

### 47

I have said all this so that no one, either openly or secretly, may marvel at his swift death or suppose that it happened through some particular fault of his own. For many before him occupied such seats for more than thirty years, yet were deserving of no greater reward either here or in the future.

Woe to those who live long in this pilgrimage and waste that span by evil deeds; but blessed are those who spend the days granted to them with cautious diligence in Christ’s service. Those who do evil increase their punishments through long life [Note: [Col. 1347] “long life” added in witness 2.]; conversely, if those whose present life is shortened are guilty, they quickly pay the penalty for their misdeeds. But all the good, even if they do not live equally in bodily circumstances, nevertheless rejoice in one eternity of blessedness.

He was not the only one to hold office for so short a time. We read that Tertulinus received the dignity of the presbyterate from Pope Saint Stephen [Col. 1348C], and four days later received martyrdom from a tyrant because of his love for Christ and steadfastness of faith [Note: [Col. 1348D] Tertulianus, or Tertullinus, a Roman presbyter, died under Valerian on August 4, about the year 260.]. He remains forever in both ranks.

This man indeed paid for his sins, and in a short time received from God a reward for his righteous labors [Note: [Col. 1347] “brauiuiu” in witness 1.]; and this was immediately made known to many [Note: [Col. 1347] “and this” added in witness 1b.]. To recount all these things would take too long. But how these matters came to me I shall explain, with God as my witness, for I do not lie.

He was at the fortress of Meissen. On the feast day following the feast of the apostles Simon and Jude (October 28), after Matins, that venerable man appeared to me. Since I knew clearly that he was dead, I immediately asked how matters stood with him. He replied:

“I was in punishments according to the quality of my merit, but I have now entirely overcome them.”

I then said, greatly rejoicing: “May I ring the bells and stir the people to the praise of God?”

He answered: “Yes, because it is true.”

Then I continued the conversation and said: “Is it known to you that, through the whispering of many, the king’s mind has been alienated from you, because after your ordination you endeavored to do many things against him?”

He replied: “Believe me, I beg you—believe me,” repeating the words, “for I am not guilty in this matter.”

When I wished to ask him why he had died so quickly, I awoke, and it was not permitted me to know this.

I later learned from truthful men [Note: [Col. 1349] “veratibus” in witness 1.] that, in the commemoration of all the saints, he was deemed worthy to be presented mercifully before the divine gaze [Note: [Col. 1349] Added in witness 1b.].

Everything I have said about him I have not said because of some special affection of my own. It is true that, before his blessing, he loved me only moderately [Note: [Col. 1349] Added in witness 1b.] and, in defending his church, obstructed many of my affairs. For the sake of truth, and because of the reproach that would follow from this change, I have said these things in terms less serious than they were, because he left no one better behind him.

After his burial, Bishop Hericus was sent from our side to the king with the election. I entrusted to him a letter entitled “Concerning the Loss of My Church,” urging the king’s clemency.

### 48

Meanwhile Bolizlav [Note: [Col. 1349D] Duke of Poland.] learned of the archbishop’s death, assembled an army, and marched against Libusuam, which I mentioned earlier. Since he knew that, because of the Elbe’s flooding, no townsman from our side could come to its aid, he encamped there.

His soldiers advanced, encouraged to battle, and the defender resisted for a short time. For this great city was defended by no more than one thousand men, while scarcely three times that number would have been sufficient [Note: [Col. 1349] “would have surpassed them” in witness 1a.].

Bolizlav sat at dinner and joyfully watched his retainers, already victorious, enter the city. The gate was opened, and the blood of many was poured out. Among those captured were the excellent Guncelinus and Wiso [Note: [Col. 1349] “wisso” in witness 1a, with the first s marked by a point.], and its unfortunate guardian Scih, who was wounded [Note: [Col. 1349] “cih” in witness 1a; “Isich” in A. S.]. He had always lost every city entrusted to him for defense—not through his own cowardice but through miserable misfortune.

All these men were led into the presence of the proud victor, by whose command they were immediately taken away into custody. Of the aforementioned duke’s associates, no fewer than five hundred remained there [f. 132]. This miserable slaughter took place on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September (August 20) [Note: [Col. 1349D] *Necrologium Merseburgense*, August 20: “Many were killed at Liubusua.”]. The enormous booty was then divided, the city was burned, and the victorious host returned joyfully with its lord.

### 49

The queen, who was then staying at Merseburg, learned this from hastening messengers. I, meanwhile, at the urging of Provost Redingus, had unworthily dedicated two altars in Magdeburg on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September (August 22)—one where the archbishop rests, and the other in the northern part of the same church [Col. 1350A]—and there I first learned of the event. I immediately hurried to the queen.

She ordered all of us who belonged to the province to sit beside the Mulde and make all preparations for the king’s arrival. Meanwhile the king returned from his western expedition and attempted to place his own chaplain Gereno in the vacant office [Note: [Col. 1349] The “ua” is missing, cut away, in witness 1.]. Bishop Hericus met him, presented his embassy [Note: [Col. 1349] Above “legation” is written “ciui.”] [Note: [Col. 1349] Added in witness 1b.], and was not heard.

My nephew Thiedricus [Note: [Col. 1349] Added in witness 1b.] was then summoned to Grona. He came, was received by the king, and thereafter was treated as Gereno’s replacement.

On the feast of Saint Matthew the apostle (September 21), the king came to Sehusun. I approached him, and when the time was right, I urged him before all those seated there to discuss with him something concerning the parish belonging to me and other possessions unjustly taken away before the archbishop’s appointment [f. 132′] [Col. 1350B]. There he entrusted himself to my firm faith, so that these matters might be settled either by justice or by some other wholesome means.

The next day the king came to Magdeburg and ordered all of us to assemble in the brothers’ refectory. There, at the king’s request, and with the election preserved for the future, Gero was unanimously elected (September 22) [Note: [Col. 1349] Added in witness 1b.]. After first presenting himself at the altar in the church and acquiring the brothers’ fellowship with ten manses [Note: [Col. 1349] “acquirans,” corrected to “acquirens” in witness 1.], he received the pastoral staff from the king. He was then enthroned and anointed bishop by Eido, with us, the aforementioned brethren, assisting him.

The king celebrated there with great solemnity the feast of the martyrs of Thebes. After this, the archbishop honored the king himself and all his companions with magnificent gifts. From there they hurried to Merseburg and remained there for a long time, handling the administration of the kingdom with the highest officials [Note: [Col. 1349] The passage is cut away in witness 1; so reads A. S.].

This year Erluvinus, bishop of Cambrai [Note: [Col. 1349] The ending “ra” is cut away in witness 1.], and the outstanding dukes Conrad and the boy Hermann died [Col. 1350D] [Note: [Col. 1350D] From the *Quedlinburg Annals*, year 1012.].

A certain monk, weighed down by a grave illness, saw many things revealed to him in a vision. Meanwhile, while he himself was speaking of these matters, they were recorded in writing by those present and regarded as a very great miracle [Note: [Col. 1350D] “Indid.”].

In those days two brothers were born with teeth, alike in the mouth of a goose; one of them had half of his right arm shaped like a goose’s wing [Note: [Col. 1349] Added in witness 1b.]. On the third day after their birth, while laughing at one another, they died in civil dissension [f. 133] [Note: [Col. 1350D] See the *Quedlinburg Annals*, under this year, where the better reading is “in civil agreement.”].

A certain soldier, when he had forcibly taken the property of Saint Clement and refused to make restitution for it, was one day attacked in his chamber by innumerable mice. At first he seized a stick and tried to drive them away; afterward, drawing his sword, he attacked them. When this accomplished nothing, he was enclosed in a chest, at his own request, and suspended by a rope in the middle of the room. When the external assault had subsided and he ought to have been released, he was found gnawed to death by the others [Note: [Col. 1351] “by them” or “by his own people” in witness 1a.] [Note: [Col. 1351D] From the *Quedlinburg Annals*, under this year.].

Then it became clear to all who were present, and afterward to those who came, that the wrath of God, avenging the aforementioned crime, alone had consumed him [Note: [Col. 1351] “made this clear” in witness 1a.].

### 50

Meanwhile Jaremirus, whom I mentioned earlier, humbly sought the king’s favor and received, as an act of mercy and restoration, the exile and custody of Bishop Ethelbolus, the successor of Ansfrid. Ethelbolus had deserved such punishment by traveling to Bolizlav, without the permission of the king or his own superior, with gifts carried by travelers, amid the immense slaughter of the Bavarians, and by the massacre of those entrusted to him—not through any disloyalty to the king [Note: [Col. 1351] “without the king’s and his own permission” added in witness 1b.].

When our enemies heard this, they mocked us; but our fellow citizens feared that it would prove advantageous to them [Note: [Col. 1351] Added in witness 1b.]. Let those who once gave such counsel to our king recognize this deed in themselves.

After this Othelricus, his brother [Note: [Col. 1351] “his brother” added in witness 1b.], was summoned by the king and came to Merseburg. He received as a free gift the kingdom that he had previously usurped unjustly.

At the same time, the overflowing rains and the pirates rising up with them caused great harm—alas! [Note: [Col. 1351D] From the *Quedlinburg Annals*, under this year.]. At that time the Danube flooded in Bavaria and the Rhine stood stagnant. So vast was the number of people and livestock that perished, together with buildings and forests uprooted by such force, that all the inhabitants of those regions affirmed that nothing like it had ever happened within their own or their ancestors’ memory. They groaned that this had then occurred because of their various crimes and, fearing something greater, expected another calamity to come upon them.

I have wandered far from my subject; it is time to return [Note: [Col. 1351] Witness 2 adds: “It is time to return to what I began.”].

### 51

Leaving Merseburg, the king came by boat to Harneburg. There, after discussing many matters with the Slavs who had gathered, and after peace had been established, he returned and celebrated All Saints’ Day at Helmanstidi. Then he hastened to visit the western regions.

Meanwhile Lady Ludgerd, having become exceedingly ill, summoned me through a messenger because she loved me uniquely and, as I mentioned above, was related to me by a bond of blood. But when I came after dusk to Walmerstidi, where she lay, I entered the chamber and saw her suffering greatly, though she did not cease reciting psalms.

Among them she repeated only these words with her lips and mind:

“Your right hand has received me, O Lord; but they have sought my soul in vain” (Psalm 63:9–10).

When she said nothing at all to me, although I asked her whether she wished to be anointed with holy oil, she replied: “Gladly, because after this Christ’s will will soon be fulfilled in me.”

She then summoned me after being dressed in new garments. When everything properly belonging to the anointing had been completed, I said to her: “How beautiful you are now!” And she replied: “Look at the handsome young man on the right,” indicating him with her eyes.

After this I departed and, exhausted by the journey, slept for a long time. When I awoke, I heard her groaning heavily from excessive pain. Approaching her, I sang the Psalter until those present testified that she was at the point of death. Then, after everything that had to be said on that occasion had been completed, her blessed soul passed away, at the invitation of the saints, on the Ides of November (November 13), to the chamber of her heavenly Bridegroom [Note: [Col. 1351D] *Merseburg Calendar*, November 13: “Countess Liudgerd died.”].

A certain layman, a citizen of Partenopolis, foretold her death while lying ill: “Lady Liudgerd is about to depart from this world,” he said, “and truly blessed is the one who is worthy to follow her path.”

When it first began to grow light, the body was carried to Wallibizi with us accompanying it. On the following day it was laid down beside the monastery, on the northern side, where Father Liutherdus [Note: [Col. 1351D] This refers to Liudgerd’s father-in-law, the founder of the monastery.], enclosed there as a recluse, had rested for twenty-six years [Note: [Col. 1351] “inculsus,” corrected to “inclusus,” in witness 1.]. Her husband Wirinharius mourned her beyond words.

For she had been the careful guardian of his life and soul. Laboring especially in divine service, she had protected him, more than herself, from every ambush of the enemy by fasts in the cold, continual prayer, and almsgiving.

I say to all present and future generations: whatever good the faithful offer in this world for someone’s memory [Note: [Col. 1351] Added in witness 1b.], if it is not permitted to benefit the person for whom it is done [Note: [Col. 1351] “if it is not permitted to profit him” in witness 1.], is never rendered void by God for the one who diligently strives to do it [Note: [Col. 1351D] “it is rendered void” in witness 1.].

In the first year of the reign of King Henry, the aforementioned Liudgerd returned, after her father’s death, to her husband, from whom she had unjustly been separated for so long, in the month of January [Note: [Col. 1351D] See above, book IV, chapters 11 and 25.].

### 52

After the marriage, Margrave Liutharius fell ill in the West and, having been intoxicated with a potion called *Paulina* [Note: [Col. 1351D] In Leyser’s *History of Medieval Poets and Poems*, pp. 502–692, there is a poem by Aegidius, a physician who lived toward the end of the twelfth century, concerning the virtues and qualities of compounded medicines. Among other remedies, on p. 629 there appears, as Adelung first observed, the potion of Saint Paul:

> Those whom the violent storm of apoplexy shakes,  
> whom madness attacks, whom the soporific power  
> implanted in the nerves dissolves—the force  
> of sensation—the potion restores, rejoicing in Paul’s name.  
> It restrains asthmatics’ breathing, loosens menstruation;  
> you can preserve it unharmed for two years.

On the following page, p. 630, where the same medicine is called *Paulinum* and Paulinus’s potion, and where its powers against a head and stomach covered with phlegm are extolled, it is added at the end that it can be kept intact for four years. From this one may conclude that it was different from the *Paulina* potion mentioned on p. 629. In any event, Adelung adds, I do not know whether it derived its name from the apostle Paul, although he did instruct his Timothy how it might remedy a weak stomach. WAG.], died unexpectedly on the eighth day before the Kalends of February (January 25) [Note: [Col. 1353] “on the eighth” in witness 1a.]. He was buried at Cologne, in the same place where he had earlier requested: on the southern side of the church, where penitents are admitted on the Lord’s Supper.

His widow, named Godila, did not cease doing whatever good she could for his memory. For her son Wirinharius she acquired his father’s benefice and the margraviate [Note: [Col. 1353] “and the margraviate” added in witness 1b.] at the price of two hundred talents, remaining chaste for four years.

Then she married her kinsman Hirimannus [Note: [Col. 1353D] Namely, the margrave of Meissen, brother of Wirinharius’s wife, Godila’s son. See the *Chronicle of Walbeck* in Meibom, p. 71. Godila ceased to live among the living in 1015. URS.], caring nothing about the ban imposed by Bishop Arnulfus or about having deceived three bishops whose right hands had forbidden this to her in God’s name. For this she was struck down by the aforementioned bishop with the sword of excommunication, and thereafter obtained no hope of bearing children.

But I am wandering like a madman—that is, deviating somewhat from my subject—and shall undertake the celebrated conduct of King Henry.

### 53

He convened a great synod for the condemnation of Thiedricus, bishop of Metz. At this same council all the bishops who had gathered there forbade him to sing Mass before his purification [Note: [Col. 1353] The passage from “Huic” through “caneret” was written in witness 1b.].

After this he celebrated Christmas at Palithi with festive rejoicing. There Walkerus, a servant of the church of Trier [Note: [Col. 1353] “Client” in witness 2.], and a prudent guardian of his chapel, fell ill and was left there when we departed. On the third day before the Ides of January (January 11), he died—alas! [Col. 1353].

Meanwhile Lievizo, archbishop of Bremen, weighed down by a long illness, devoutly and anxiously awaited his final day. On the night preceding that last day, he comforted his companions, already wearied by frequent vigils, with these words:

“O sweetest brothers and sons, let none of you distrust heavenly clemency. And so that your labor may now be somewhat relieved, I shall offer you a highly credible example from my own life.

“I sought Lord Pope Benedict, an exile in these regions [Note: [Col. 1353] Emperor Otto consented to his deposition after he had been unjustly accused. Added in witness 2.]. To prevent me from reaching him, many people repeatedly delayed me [Note: [Col. 1353] Added in witness 1b.], but I yielded to none of their flatteries [Note: [Col. 1353] Added in witness 1b.]. When I reached him, I devotedly attached myself to him and, after his death, served my elder Aedtheldagus in the capacity of a servant. When he perceived this, he entrusted his poor to my care. I then became his chamberlain.

“But when that holy man departed for the heavenly homeland he had always desired, I, unworthy, succeeded him through your common election and the king’s gift. Let us forgive one another from the heart whatever we have sinned against one another, so that, now separated in good peace, we may deserve to be reunited on the last day.

“This salutary counsel I give you at my end: choose Oddo, who is a participant in your brotherhood [Note: [Col. 1353] “partipes” in witness 1.], by the common agreement of us all, to restore our church and to serve the interests of our homeland. Let us beseech the divine mercy, in whose hand is the king’s heart, so that this may be accomplished in a manner pleasing to him.”

Everyone heard him as he gave this exhortation, and they unanimously praised his goodwill and administration.

The next day, Sunday, dawned. That blessed father, with raised hands and spirit, entrusted the flock subject to him to the supreme Shepherd. On the second day before the Nones of February (February 4) [Note: [Col. 1354D] He died January 4, according to the *Lüneburg Necrology* and Adam of Bremen; that is also what Thietmar appears to have intended to write, as the following makes clear. This day was also a Sunday in the year 1013.], he died and proceeded to the place toward which he had lived.

For he had been one of the number of those whom the prophet marvels at as flying like clouds and like doves to their windows (Isaiah 60:8). Because of his constant vigils and fasting, while he was still strong he appeared almost dead to those who did not know him. He never approached the Lord’s altar without offerings. He was a constant admonisher of the people and smiled cheerfully upon everyone as a generous giver.

Toward God he earned this distinction: amid the continual incursions of the raging pirates, his see remained untouched until that time.

[Additional apparatus omitted above: 45: at *causa pacem faciendi*, witness 1a has *faciendam*, “to be made”; at *duas ibi*, “there,” is added in 1b; at *juxta locum*, 1a reads *i. in loco*, “indeed, in the place”; at *principibus*, witness 1 reads “to the princes; as had already happened several times”; *quam* in “as he well knew” is added in 1b; 1a has *attumore*, “from swelling”; *hunc*, “him,” is added in 1b; at Bolizlav, 1a reads *oste actenus*, “hitherto as an enemy”; “his,” at “right hand,” and “his intercession” are additions in 1b; *archipresul*, “archbishop,” is added in 1b. Thietmar himself wrote the passage from here through the words “shone among other matrons” in chapter 46 in codex fols. 128v, 129, and the beginning of 129v.

46: 1a spells *mitissimus*, “most gentle”; after *inhonestavit* (“dishonored”), the letters *nho* are cut away in 1; in the prophecy, “and possess it for a short time” contains two additions in 1b; the statement that he concealed his conscience is “so perhaps in 1b,” in an erased place.

48: “his” at “soldiers” and “among them” are additions in 1b.

49: at Gereno’s embassy, *et* is cut away in 1; above *legationem* is written *ciui*; *suam*, “his,” is added in 1b; 1 reads *aliqit* for *aliquid*; “him” at the brethren’s assistance and “they” at their departure are additions in 1b; the monk’s revelations are *notata*, “recorded,” not *nota*.

50: the source says “the flooding rains and the pirates rising up” caused harm; the insertion in witness 2 is *a ceptis tempus est ut*, “it is time to return to what I began.”

51: 1a has *prima* for *primo*; 1 reads *canatur* for *conatur*, “strives.”

53: *Is* is corrected from *his/Iis* in 1; the reading “day” is corrected from *tempus*, and *pius* is corruptly written *pus*; “already wearied by frequent vigils” is added in 1b. The variant in witness 2 at the account of Pope Benedict reads: “I yielded to his persuasions. At last, reaching him and seeing him most devoted to the divine offices, I attached myself to him for as long as he lived.” *Aedtheldago* is written *etheld.* in 1c; “now” and “again” are additions in 1b; 1 reads *eligamus*, “let us choose,” for *eligatis*, “choose.”]

54. Meanwhile, the king departed from Alstidi, where he had celebrated the Epiphany of the Lord. He had heard envoys from Bolizlav asking for peace and promising that a confirmation would be made with Miesco, his son. He came to Merseburg and there learned of the aforesaid bishop’s death (fol. 136), grieving on account of the present loss but rejoicing because of his subsequent intervention, and recalling him with the greatest honor. After this he moved on from us and celebrated the Purification of the holy Mother of God at Magdeburg. On that very day the aforesaid Oddo came humbly, accompanied by clergy and laymen, and, as before, through faithful intercessors requested the king’s favor for the completion of the election.

The king did not listen to them at all. Instead, amid praise of the visitors—though not spontaneous praise—he gave the bishopric to his own chaplain Unwan, taking Oddo by the hands and soothing him with the mercy he had promised him. Then, at the king’s command and in his presence, Unwan was anointed archbishop by Archbishop Geron, with the consent and assistance of the bishops Ekkihard [Sleswicensis, “of Schleswig”] and Thurgat [Scarae, “of Skara”]. A few days later Miesco, Bolizlav’s son, came with magnificent gifts, became the king’s man, and confirmed his allegiance by oath. He was then sent back with great honor, and the king expressed his pleasure that he should come again.

During these days a great storm occurred after sunset and greatly disturbed us all. For it destroyed a church situated outside the city, built of red wood during the reign of the first Otto. A fire also consumed many possessions of the archbishop. Moreover, it reached the king’s ears that my nephew Wirinharius was going without permission to Bolizlav with Ekkihard, brother of Margrave Hiriman (fol. 136′), that he was speaking there many things contrary to the king’s favor, and that he was frequently receiving Bolizlav’s envoys here in secret.

[Note: The readings *pergerent—loquerentur—haberent* have been corrected to *pergeret—loqueretur—haberet*.]

The king took all this very seriously and ordered both men to come into his presence. Since they did not dare to do so, they were publicly accused of resisting royal authority, and all their property was seized. At last my nephew bought back the king’s favor and his residence, together with his own estate, by payment in gold. The other, much later, was restored through the faithful intervention of others.

In the same year Wonlef, a hermit and a true Israelite, died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.

[Note: “In the same year Wonlef … died” is an addition in witness 1b.]

[Note: The Quedlinburg Annals, under the year 1013; the Merseburg Calendar; and the Lüneburg Necrology give March 18.]

55. In the following Lent the king came to Werla and was ill there for a long time from a colic attack.

[Note: *Ibi* (“there”) is an addition in witness 1b.]

[Note: Compare the Hildesheim and Quedlinburg Annals for this year.]

Many things were revealed to him in a vision.

[Note: The words *multa … per visionem sibi revelata sunt* (“many things were revealed to him in a vision”) stand in a passage erased in witness 1b.]

Finally, recovering through the tears and prayers of many, and being unable, in so short an interval, to reach the appointed place—

[Note: That is, Aachen; see the Quedlinburg Annals.]

—he celebrated Easter with Meinwerk, who was especially close to him, at Paderborn, with fitting reverence (April 5). He celebrated Pentecost (May 24) with us.

On its eve Bolizlav came under the protection of the hostages left in his keeping, and he was received most favorably. On the holy day, with hands joined, he was made a knight; afterward, when the king proceeded to the church in ceremonial attire, Bolizlav served as his armed attendant. On the second day of the feast (May 25), Bolizlav appeased the king with magnificent gifts offered by himself and his wife. Then, through the king’s generosity, he received gifts better and much greater, together with the long-desired benefice, and sent his hostages back with honor and joy.

[Note: “Together with the long-desired benefice” is an addition in witness 1b.]

(Fol. 137) After this he set out for Rus’, with our people assisting him. Having devastated a large part of that region, and when a quarrel arose between his own men and his guests, the Pechenegs, he ordered all the latter—even though they were his supporters—to be killed.

[Note: The Byzantines call them *Patzinatzi*. Liudprand and other writers of that period call them *Pizenaci*, *Piczinegi*, or *Petschinegi*. They inhabited the lands along the Volga and the Jaik and had the Rus’ as their neighbors. — URS.]

56. During those days Bronhag, abbot of Fulda, was deposed.

[Note: Concerning him, later bishop of Halberstadt, see the *Chronicle of Halberstadt*.]

Poppo, a convert and at that time pastor of Lorsch, succeeded him. As the brothers of this monastery dispersed widely, its condition was changed from what it had previously been.

[Note: Compare the Quedlinburg Annals, under the year 1013.]

In the city of Duke Bernhard, called Lüneburg, a remarkable change and movement of the air occurred in that same year, together with an immense chasm in the earth.

[Note: See the Quedlinburg Annals.]

The local inhabitants were astonished and declared that they had never seen anything like it before.

The king, meanwhile, proceeding toward the western regions, planned his journey to Lombardy and then returned to us again. Departing from there on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, he hurried through the territories of the Bavarians and the Swabians to a place whose name has been omitted.

[Note: The name of this place seems to have been omitted through the copyist’s negligence.]

An army gathered there from every direction, and the goodwill of those who came to assist became evident. From there the king came all the way to Rome without any hindrance, accompanied by the queen.

Bolizlav, who had previously been invited to support the completion of this journey, made no effort to do so and, as usual, proved false to his promises. Moreover, he had earlier complained to the lord pope through the bearer of a letter that, because of the king’s hidden ambushes, he was unable to pay the tribute he had promised to the prince of the apostles, Peter.

Then he secretly sent envoys there to investigate how the king was faring in those parts, and tried through them to remove from the king’s favor as many people as he could. Such was his regard for God, and so he sought the intervention of the pious; so conspicuous was the steadfast faith of this renowned warrior, and so greatly did he care about solemn oaths!

Reader, consider what he does amid so many crimes. Whenever he himself senses that he has sinned greatly, or perceives it through some faithful correction, he orders the canons to be placed before him and commands that inquiry be made into how the offense ought to be corrected; then he immediately strives to purge the crime he has committed according to these writings. Yet his habit of sinning dangerously is stronger than his perseverance in salutary repentance.

57. Hardwigus, his equal and almost his associate, falsely called king by the Lombards, was distressed by the arrival and power of the great king and his army. Since he distrusted his own strength to harm him, he immediately withdrew into the fortifications of a castle, lamenting only that, having been summoned to a greater honor, the king had then advanced.

After a long deliberation of his troubled mind, he sent envoys to the king to ask that a county be granted to him (fol. 138), and they truthfully promised that he would restore his crown to the king together with his sons. Although the king, after consulting certain men, had been unwilling to agree to this, as I shall explain in what follows, he later perceived that this had produced great harm for his intimates.

[Note: The reading *provenire … dampnum … persensit* (“he perceived that … harm had resulted”) is corrected from *provenire … dampnum … sensit* (“he perceived that … harm resulted”).]

But before I undertake this subject, I shall try to insert what I previously passed over in forgetfulness without discussing it.

58. There was a certain man named Brun, my contemporary and fellow student, born of a most illustrious family but, through divine mercy, chosen among the sons of God above his other relatives. Loved uniquely by his venerable mother Ida, he was entrusted to the instruction of the philosopher Geddon, and everything he ought to have had was supplied to him abundantly.

[Note: Geddon was a Magdeburg schoolmaster; see below, Book VII, chapter 25.]

His father was Brun, an eminent elder, praiseworthy in every respect, related to me by blood and close to me in every kind of intimacy.

[Note: Concerning him, see the Saxon Annals, under the years 1009 and 1106 at the end.]

When his son and namesake was supposed to go to school in the morning, he asked permission before leaving his lodging and, while we were playing, was at prayer.

[Note: “And namesake” is an addition in witness 1b.]

He preferred business to leisure and, thus bearing fruit, reached maturity. Otto III sought him out and received him. Not long afterward he left Otto, sought a solitary life, and lived by his own work.

[Note: “And lived” is an addition in witness 1b.]

After the death of the most glorious emperor, while the second Henry was reigning by the grace of God, he came to Merseburg and asked him, with the permission of the lord pope, for an episcopal blessing. At the pope’s command he received consecration from Archbishop Tagino, and there also received the pallium that he himself brought here.

Afterward, for the salvation of his soul, he undertook the labor of a long and difficult journey, chastising his body with hunger and tormenting it with vigils. He received many gifts from Bolizlav and other wealthy men, which he immediately distributed among churches, his companions, and the poor, retaining nothing for himself.

In the twelfth year of his conversion and distinguished religious life, he went to Prussia and endeavored to make those barren fields fruitful with divine seed. But, since thorns sprang up everywhere, the harsh land could not easily be softened.

When he was preaching on the border of that region and Rus’, he was first forbidden by the inhabitants; but when he evangelized more insistently, he was captured. Then, for love of Christ, who is the head of the Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March (1009), he was beheaded gently as a lamb together with eighteen of his companions.

[Note: The reading *suis* (“his own”) is corrected from *suis sociis* (“his companions”).]

[Note: The Quedlinburg Annals and the *Chronicle of Halberstadt* give the seventh day before the Ides of March, 1009. A letter of Brun to King Henry, written during his final journey, survives; it was copied from a manuscript in the Cassel library.]

The bodies of so many martyrs lay unburied until Bolizlav learned of the matter, purchased them, and acquired them as a future consolation for his household. These events occurred during the reign of the most serene King Henry, whom almighty God honored with the triumph of so great a bishop and, as I greatly hope, saved.

Long afterward the father of the aforesaid bishop fell ill and, as he himself told me, received the monastic habit at his son’s command. He died in peace on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November.

[Note: The Merseburg Calendar gives October 19: “Brun the convert died.”]

[Col. 1358A] 59. Nor should the great presumption of the margrave Gero’s followers be thought insignificant, a presumption that a faithful man should shudder at and avoid through love of piety. Let the matter be brought forward, and then let the deed be weighed: is it praiseworthy, or detestable to all good men?

Bishop Arnulf was invited by Hathawi, the venerable abbess of Gero’s forest, to a banquet on the feast of Christ’s martyr Cyriacus, and he came. On the holy day, as he was walking from the church after Mass, he saw a cleric holding a hawk in his hand. Moved by zeal, he seized the cleric by the arm and led him away with him—not to punish him, but to reprimand him in moderate words.

Rumor, flying swiftly, gathered the aforesaid soldiers. The first of them, a man named Hugal, came to the bishop and asked why he had wished to dishonor their lord in this way.

[Note: The name is written *huga* in witness 1a.]

The bishop replied: “What have I done?” I saw an abomination of Christ, and because I saw that it had been committed in my episcopate, I could not endure it. No evil has been done. Let us appoint a day agreeable to you; and if I am found blameworthy by our common friends, I shall make suitable restitution.”

The other continued: “It must not be so, nor can it be done in that way. Today either clear yourself by oath, or promise me and my lord that you will make amends.”

The bishop replied: “The holy solemnity forbids me to swear, and forbids you to accept such an oath. It seems exceedingly pitiable to me that justice alone is denied me by you.”

After this, the man departed angrily, and an armed force of soldiers gathered, without the margrave’s knowledge.

[Note: “Without the margrave’s knowledge” is an alternative reading.]

When the bishop was now about to dine, he saw them approaching. The house in which he was staying was firmly secured by his men and fortified in every possible way, lest it be easily accessible to the enemy. But when they were already intending to attack it, they were truthfully told that the priest had gone elsewhere and could not be found there.

He was then sought in the cloister and finally in the monastery, but by God’s grace, although he was hiding without any disgrace to himself and observing all these events, he was nowhere found.

[Note: The reading *nullatus* is corrected to *nullatenus* (“in no way”).]

At last, once their fury had subsided, they went to the lodging and returned sadly to their homes.

At daybreak the following day, after summoning his soldiers, Arnulf returned to his own see and consoled the abbess, who was weeping bitterly.

[Note: *Propria* (“own”) is corrected from *propria*; the manuscript readings are defective.]

When the king learned all this, he ordered these conspirators to be brought before him. When the aforesaid margrave saw that the king was extremely angry, he tried to appease him through faithful intermediaries.

The king listened to them on the condition that they first pay three hundred pounds of gold to the bishop’s jurisdiction, and that those judged guilty in this affair either clear themselves by the oath of eleven of their friends or satisfy the bishop according to canonical authority.

[Note: *Auttoritatem* is an orthographic variant of *auctoritatem* (“authority”).]

[Note: “To him” is an addition in witness 1b.]

A mutual peace was then made between them, and a truce was established until after Easter. Our friends and theirs gathered here, and I was present with them (fol. 140). When the aforesaid money had been paid, the bishop came to the western monastery and sat there on the throne of the highest rank.

There the margrave alone cleared himself by a highly credible oath. His followers, individually, received fasting from the hand of the aforesaid bishop in the manner of penitents, on the condition that, whenever they were admonished, they would undertake the burden imposed upon them.

60. It should also be added how Othelricus, duke of the Bohemians, interpreting “the mammon of iniquity” (Luke 16:9), ordered the illustrious soldier Bosio and many others to be killed because he had heard from false accusers that they were helping his exiled brother. Through these calamities everyone was to learn cautiously how they ought to guard against such dangers in the future.

Ambition, always blind, prevents these regions from observing firmly what the Lord commands in both Testaments. For Othelricus feared his brother, whom he ought rightly to have loved above all these others, and carefully tried to ensure that he would never come to him.

The Bohemians were once princes of our people under Duke Zuetepulcus.

[Note: Swatopluk, or Zwentibold, the most powerful duke of Moravia, died in 894.]

An annual tribute was paid to him by our forebears, and he had bishops in his region called Marierun.

[Note: *Marierun* means Moravia; compare Palacký, *Geschichte von Böhmen*, vol. I, p. 140.]

All this he and his successors lost through their pride and arrogance, because, as the Gospel testifies, all humility grows while the height of arrogance is brought low.

[Note: The reading “and he had bishops in his region called Marierun, all of which …” appears in witness 2.]

No one rules these provinces without the greatest fear. Pure charity groans, excluded, because perjury reigns there together with its companion, fraud.

61. (Fol. 140′) Since above, while discussing the universal pope Bruno, I merely mentioned his successor Gerbert in order to write something more extensive about him, it is not inappropriate to do so now.

He was born in the western regions, educated from childhood in the liberal arts, and finally promoted unjustly to govern the city of Reims (991).

[Note: The reading is supplemented in witness 1b and in the Saxon Annals under the year 999. In witness 1 the word stands in an erasure.]

[Note: Compare above, pp. 616–694, and C. F. Hock, *Gerbert und sein Jahrhundert*, Vienna, 1837.]

He was exceptionally skilled in discerning the courses of the stars and surpassed his contemporaries in knowledge of various arts. At last, expelled from his own lands, he sought the emperor Otto. After spending a long time with him, he made a sundial at Magdeburg, setting it up correctly after observing through a tube a certain star that guides sailors.

[Note: “Sundial.” Compare Ersch and Gruber, *Encyclopaedia*, s.v. “Compass”; Hüllmann, *Städtewesen*, vol. I, pp. 123–137; Capmany, *Quaestiones criticas sobre varios puntos de historia económicas*, etc., Madrid, 1807, quarto, pp. 73–132; and *Complainte d’amour*, a thirteenth-century manuscript, cited by Wolf in *Jahrbücher für wissenschaftliche Kritik*, July 1837, p. 142.]

After the aforesaid Pope Gregory died (999), Gerbert, through the emperor’s favor, succeeded him and occupied the see until the time of King Henry, under the name Sylvester.

In his place John Phasan—meaning “rooster”—

[Note: “That is, rooster” is an addition in witness 1b.]

—was installed (1003) and governed the apostolic see for the days entrusted to him. During his pontificate the church of Merseburg was restored and strengthened by the authority of its privilege.

He was succeeded by Sergius (1009), who was called “Pig’s Snout,” and Benedict (1012), both distinguished men and restorers of our church.

[Note: The addition reads: “who was called ‘Pig’s Snout.’” The Saxon Annals under 1009 give *bucca porcus*, “pig’s snout.”]

All these supreme priests greatly desired the king’s arrival, but the opposition of various enemies delayed it for a long time.

Blessed in all his works be almighty God, who deigned to console and pacify Rome, long oppressed for many years by many people, through such a shepherd! For Pope Benedict prevailed over a certain Gregory in the election.

[Note: The reading may be *cuidam*, “a certain [Gregory].”]

For this reason he came to the king at Palithi on Christmas with the entire apostolic retinue, announcing to everyone with lamentation his expulsion. The king took his cross into his own protection and ordered the others to refrain from violence, promising that, when he himself came there, the matter would be carefully settled according to Roman custom.

[Note: That is, according to Roman law. Compare *Laws*, vol. II, part B, p. 159 ff.]

The long-awaited time soon arrived, and in February (1014), in the city of Romulus, King Henry was received by Pope Benedict, who at that time exercised greater authority than any of his predecessors, with indescribable honor; and he deserved to become the advocate of Saint Peter.

[Note: “Who at that time exercised greater authority than any of his predecessors” is an addition in witness 1b.]

Since I am about to speak of his second coronation, it is fitting that I first praise him, through whose gracious gift this came about, as the teacher of the nations, Paul, exhorts us: “Give thanks to God the Father above all and in all things, brothers” (Ephesians 5:20); “for this is his will in Christ Jesus our Lord” (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

He is rightly to be praised by us, for he benefited us greatly through the gift and grace of the eternal King. King Henry increased our church’s resources in many ways, especially in sacred furnishings, and from all the estates that he possessed in Thuringia and Saxony he gave us two households.

[Note: See the emperor’s charter issued at Merseburg, July 28, 1010, in Höfer, vol. I, p. 160.]

He gave us a Gospel book adorned with gold and an ivory cover, a golden and jewel-encrusted chalice with a paten and a fistula, two crosses and two silver ampullae, and a large chalice of the same metal together with a paten and a fistula. Whatever had been neglected in the estates by my predecessors, he renewed by command.

(Fol. 141′)

Whom the heavenly ones praise, let us servants also venerate,

bringing forth worthy hymns from our hearts.

For here is the triune God, yet one in divinity,

that gracious God without whom no one reigns.

The supreme good, driving away everything harmful,

grants from high heaven what benefits all.

He has now confounded the lying witnesses

who said that King Henry would not undertake

the imperial office, nor reign for a long

time, but would be crushed by a savage death.

Now twelve years have passed since he assumed the kingdom,

after the illustrious ruler ascended into the imperial palace,

in that month in which he himself freed my chair.

Let this day be marked brightly with a beautiful stone (Martial 9.53),

the day on which Rome submits herself to our gracious king,

and rejoices, suffused with sacred liquid and nourishing grace.

He gives thanks to the Lord, who visited him from on high,

and who visited from on high both him and his beloved wife Cunigunda.

The supreme shepherd rejoices, and his choir also sings,

because they are secure, having obtained so great a ruler.

Merseburg, you too, sing fittingly to all in deed.

[Note: Another witness adds: “Give a hymn to the Lord, through whom you appear to flourish.” In that witness the line reads “and you too.” The poem is also preceded there by the rubric “Prologue.”]

## BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 1361]

1. (Fol. 142) After thirteen years had elapsed from the Lord’s Incarnation beyond the completion of the thousand-year number, and in the second month and third week of the following year, in the thirteenth year of his reign—

[Note: More correctly, our author should have said “the twelfth year.”]

—and on Sunday, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March (February 14, 1014), Henry, illustrious king by the grace of God, came with his beloved wife Cunigunda to the church of Saint Peter, accompanied by twelve senators, six of whom proceeded shaven and the others with long hair, mystically carrying staffs.

[Note: The phrase “six of whom … carrying staffs” is an addition in witness 1b.]

[Note: Witness 2 adds “with the clergy”; the Saxon Annals under 1014 have the same.]

The pope was awaiting him. Before he was admitted, the pope asked him whether he wished to be the faithful patron and defender of the Roman Church, faithful in every respect to the pope himself and to his successors. He replied with a devout profession of faith, and then received from him, together with his wife, anointing and a crown.

[Note: “Royal anointing” is an alternative reading.]

[Note: Compare Glaber, Radulfus, Book I, chapter 5.]

He ordered his earlier crown to be hung above the altar of the prince of the apostles. On that same day the pope prepared an abundant dinner for them at the Lateran.

On the eighth day (February 21), a great disturbance arose between the Romans and our countrymen on the Tiber bridge, and many fell on both sides. Night eventually put an end to the conflict.

Three Germans were responsible for this affair: Hug, Hecil, and Ecilin.

[Note: They were Lombard brothers, as our own Thietmar records at the beginning of Book VIII.]

They were later captured and held in custody. One of them escaped to these regions, a second was taken to Fulda, and the third was held for a long time in the castle of Ivicanstene.

[Note: The names are uncertain in the manuscript. One appears to have been written as Hug or Hecil; the second is in an erased passage. The additions concerning Fulda, Ivicanstene, and the third brother occur in witness 1b.]

2. The emperor ordered his brother Arnulf, whom he had previously placed over the church of Ravenna, to be enthroned again and consecrated there by the pope. He first wished to degrade Aethelbert, the usurper who had long been sitting there unjustly, but, overcome by the continual intercession of pious men, he placed him over another church, called Aricia.

[Note: “Aethelbert” is an addition in witness 1b.]

The pope deposed two men at Ravenna and as many at Rome by synodal judgment; they had been consecrated by Archbishop Leo, who was already mute—that is, dead.

[Note: “Mute” means “dead.”]

He restored and renewed, under excommunication, the institutions of the holy fathers concerning the sacred orders, which had long been neglected there and among us, alas! For the canons prohibit ordaining a deacon before the age of twenty-five, and a priest or bishop before the age of thirty. Because we have not observed this, we are wretched transgressors and have incurred excommunication.

[Note: The phrase concerning Aricia through “have incurred excommunication” is an addition in witness 1b.]

3. The emperor celebrated the Lord’s Resurrection in the city of Pavia (April 26) and strengthened the unstable disposition of the Lombards by displaying affection toward everyone. After calming all the disturbances, the emperor returned from Italy. Hardwigus, greatly rejoicing at this, invaded the city of Vercelli, while its bishop Leo barely escaped.

He also seized the whole city and began again to grow arrogant. As I explain below, divine majesty compelled him, after he had been excessively humbled, to acknowledge his guilt.

[Note: “Whom … compelled” was written in an erasure in witness 1b.]

In these regions the emperor built a bishopric at Bobbio, the third adornment of his devout works, by common counsel and with the permission of the neighboring bishops. In that city the holy worshipers of Christ and renowned confessors Columbanus and Attala rest bodily. Supreme necessity, and Christ’s charity, which surpasses it, impelled him to do this.

With the greatest prosperity and glory he overcame the Alpine difficulties and entered the peaceful regions of our land, since the climate and inhabitants of that country do not agree with ours. There are many ambushes, alas, in Romania and Lombardy; little kindness is shown to anyone who comes here; everything that guests require is for sale, and sold deceitfully, and many perish here after being given poisoned food.

[Note: “Poisoned food” is an expanded reading in witness 2.]

4. (Fol. 143) In the same year, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, Count Charles, son of Margrave Riedag, died.

[Note: The Lüneburg Necrology gives the same date.]

He had previously lost all his benefice through the inflated accusations of his accusers, although he himself was guilty of nothing, and he bore the offense inflicted upon him with equanimity.

On that same day my niece Mathildis died.

[Note: See the Lüneburg Necrology.]

She had long been brought up in Gero’s forest with the abbess Hathawi, the lady of that place, by right of kinship. Since the venerable matron had always hoped that Mathildis would succeed her, she mourned her death with inconsolable grief and followed her herself in the following month, July, on the fourth day before the Nones.

[Note: *Eandem* (“the same woman”) is corrected from *eidem* (“to the same man”) and then from *eandem* to *eadem* (“the same woman”).]

I shall briefly recount some things concerning Mathildis’s praiseworthy life. She was the illustrious niece of Queen Mathildis, and in the thirteenth year of her age had married Sigifridus, son of Margrave Gero. She remained joined to him for only seven years.

After his death, for love of God and to console the grieving elder, she received the sacred veil and soon afterward consecration from Bishop Bernhard.

[Note: Bernhard was bishop of Halberstadt.]

As I said, she remained there for fifty-five years, as constant in Christ’s service as Anna the widow, as generous as the woman of Sarepta, like Judith in chastity and abstinence, adorning the church entrusted to her with various ornaments.

[Note: Witness 2 adds “the widow,” referring to Anna.]

[Note: The name “Judith” filled the space left in the manuscript in witness 1b.]

The following signs foretold her death. The fishpond situated on the eastern side of the city appeared bloody until midday, and afterward changed to a green color. Many people believed that my niece, by virtue of her merits, had gone before them with the palm of virginity.

She was buried by Bernhard, bishop of the Old City, the distinguished bride of Christ (fol. 143′), not where she had requested, but where her grieving congregation asked, in the middle of the church before the altar of the holy cross.

[Note: The Old City was Aldenburg in Wagria.]

There, afterward, through her noble merit, almighty God granted an easy walk to a certain man who had long been infirm and had long walked with crutches.

[Note: “To a certain man” may reflect the reading *cuidam*.]

[Supplemental textual apparatus: 54. *Unwan* is written *unuuano*, corrected to *unuano* in witness 1, and similarly below; *archiantes* is corrected to *archiantites* in 1. At each of the three clauses concerning Wirinharius, 1 corrects plural *pergerent—loquerentur—haberent* to singular *pergeret—loqueretur—haberet*.

56. Witness 1a reads *lareshirsemensi* for *Laressemensi*. The added identification of the emperor as Henry II is by 1c; the words “returned from Italy” stand in an erasure in 1.

57. “Of his agitated mind” is added in 1b.

58. Witness 1a reads *abire* for *habere*; 1 reads *habuncia* for *habundancia* and *debuiset* for *debuisset*. “And namesake” is added in 1b (at both relevant places). Witness 1 reads *rengante* for *regnante* and *prohibitur* for *prohibetur*. The witnesses read respectively *suis* (1a) and *suis sociis* (2): the text does not present one as a correction of the other. The clauses “and, as he himself told me” and “at his son’s command” are additions in 1b.

59. Witness 1 has *floccipendaenda*; apparently Thietmar himself elsewhere deleted the intrusive *a* in words of this kind. “On the holy day” is added in 1b. Witness 1 reads *hospicum* for *hospitium*; 1a reads *propria*, corrected by 1b to *propriam*. Witness 1a has *nostrique eorundem* for *nostri eorundem* and *sedit* for *sedens*; “there” is added in 1b. The source reads *auttonitatem* in 1 for *auctoritatem*; *ei* (“to him”) is added in 1b.

60. Witness 1a reads *murmutaribus*, with *to* superscripted and corrected in 1b; witness 2 has *criminatoribus* (“accusers”). The name *Germanum* is retained: “For Germanus, whom he should rightly have loved above these men, he feared, and carefully tried to prevent him ever coming to him.” “Princes, and to him … bishops … are erased in codex 1, though still legible”; witness 2 reads: “and he had bishops in his region called Marierun, all of which …”. The editor notes that *solvitur* stands for *solvebatur*. Witness 1 reads *exculsa* for *exclusa*.

61. Witness 1a reads *parte* for *arte*; witness 2 has *naturalibus artibus*. Witness 1 reads *remensam* for *Remensem* and *nautorum* for *nautarum*. The word *papa* was added above *Gregorio* in 1b; “and” before the following clause is also added in 1b. The following prose through the verses is written in Thietmar’s own hand; the poem fills the verso of this final page of the quire. The spelling *adauxit* has a superscript *g* over *u* and *x*, apparently intended as *adaugxit*. The editor’s note on the *fistula*: it was also called a suction-tube; communicants drew wine from the chalice through it, indicating communion under both kinds. A deacon held the tube in the chalice while each faithful person sucked from its other end; the Roman pontiff still used such a tube when receiving the sacred synaxis. Gobelinus Persona recounted a pious tale concerning Henry’s chalice in *Cosmodromium*, Meibom, I, p. 259; Ursinus seems not to have known J. Vogt, *Historia fistulae eucharisticae—ex antiquitate ecclesiastica et scriptoribus medii aevi illustrata* (Bremen, 1772, 4°).

Book VII, 1. Witness 1 reads *incarcione* for *incarnacione*; “after … number” is added in 1b. The manuscript first had XVI before Kalends of March, but its X was erased; the Hildesheim Annals also give VI Kalends of March. Witness 1a reads *uuallatus* for *vallatus*. The addition concerning the twelve senators is in 1b.

Book VII, 3. Witness 1 corrects *langobarum* to *longobarum*; “Henry II” is added in 1c. “Poisoned food” is the expanded reading of witness 2.

Book VII, 4. Witness 1 corrects *sua* to *sui*, though *sua* was later restored, perhaps by 1c. “Soul” is added in 1b. Witness 1a first had *eidem*, then *eandem*, corrected finally to *eadem*.
