Witness 1a reads *uuarium*; 1b *vivuarium*, with its first *u* erased. Witness 1a reads *virido* for *viridi*. “Was seen by many” and “had long walked with crutches” are additions in 1b; *altare* is the reading of 1a.]

### 5.

But the emperor, having crossed the Alps and traversed the other adjoining provinces in the course of his rule, celebrated the Nativity [Col. 1364B] of the Lord at Palithi. After this, coming to Merseburg, he made known to his faithful men the loyalty and support of Bolizlavus, and unanimously requested that Bolizlavus be summoned by them either to offer an excuse or to make amends for the offense charged against him.

Meanwhile my nephew, Count Wirinharius, prompted by the ill counsel of youth [Note: Witness 1a has *instintu*, a misspelling of *instinctu*, “prompting/impulse.”] and the contrivance of deceitful women, came with a few men [Note: *pacis* in manuscript 1; compare the note that *pacis* was corrected to *paucis* in manuscript 1; manuscript 2 and A. S.: “he came under a pretext of peace... with a few men”] to the city called Bichlingi on Sunday (November 7), and seized against her will the lady Reinilda, whom he had previously desired for himself, after deceiving her guards. For she had earlier firmly promised the emperor that she would never associate with any husband without his knowledge and counsel [Note: *nulli*, “to no one,” in manuscript 1c.]; and for this reason she was led away amid shouting and lamentation.

When the retainers and guards heard this, they assembled armed. One of them, named Vullerd, was delayed by a [Col. 1364C] grievous wound. But when one of the maidservants likewise asked to be carried away [Note: *duci*, “to be led,” in manuscript 1a.], and the nobleman Alwinus wished to take her at the command of his lord, he was surrounded on every side and recalled my nephew, who had by then gone out [f. 144], to his aid. Before help could reach him [Note: manuscript 1b reads *ita* in a scraped place; manuscript 1 has *succurretur* for *succurreretur*]—alas!—he was killed. His lord, arriving, was shut inside and wounded by one of the servants [Note: Witness 1a has *servuorum*, a misspelling of *servorum*, “servants.”]. He immediately pierced that man with a lance and fastened him to the wall, terrifying the others so that they did not dare approach him more closely [Note: Witness 1b adds *et*, “and,” linking this action to the next]. When he saw that his men had already [Note: Witness 1b adds *jam*, “already”] gone far away with the lady, while no avenue of escape lay open to him, he at once abandoned his horse, lowered himself from the wall, and, badly crushed by the stone that followed, scarcely reached his sorrowing companions.

They carried him as far as Wi [Note: *Vui* is added in manuscript 1b.; the name of the village is unknown to us], to the house of the [Col. 1364D] emperor’s steward. There he was left with a few men [Note: *paucis* corrected from *pacis* in manuscript 1]. They carried the lady away in great haste, hiding with her now here, now there, and anxiously awaiting their lord’s arrival.

But the steward of iniquity [Col. 1365A] soon [Note: Witness 1b adds *mox*, “soon”] betrayed his sick guest to the emperor and made his mind exceedingly joyful. For he hoped that, once the man came into the emperor’s power, he would either perish as an example to others [Note: *exsemplum* is the source spelling; witness 1b adds *aliis*, “to others”], or redeem himself from him at an immeasurable price.

It was already night [Note: “It was night, and the stars were shining throughout the sky, when behold” is added in manuscript 2; compare Virgil, *Aeneid* III.147, IV.522, VIII.26], and Counts Bernhardus, Guncelinus, and Willehelmus, sent by the emperor with their soldiers, came to the place where the sick man lay. Wirinharius, having learned from his men that they were present [Note: More correctly, *adesse*, “to be present,” rather than *adfuisse*, “to have been present”], greeted Willehelmus, who was close to him, and declared to the other two that, if he had been able to raise his sword, he would never have wished to come alive into their power [Note: Witness 1a reads plural *uoluissent*, “they would have wished,” for singular *voluisset*, “he would have wished.”].

Willehelmus, however, binding his wounds and understanding that he could in no way come to Merseburg as he had been ordered [f. 144′], had him carried by his men to the nearest village, called Elerstidi [Note: Allerstaedt, near Memleben. URS.], and ordered him to be guarded there [Col. 1365B] in a house strongly fortified with stones, while he himself returned with his men to the emperor.

On the same day we [Note: Witness 1b adds *nos*, “we”] were summoned into the emperor’s presence, and heard from him, amid tearful lamentation, with what presumption my nephew had violated his oath. For when Brun was killed by his enemy Milo in his own house, where all should enjoy peace, and this was sorrowfully reported to the emperor by all the inhabitants, he was earnestly asked to forbid such wicked men the possession of property together with residence, after the manner of his predecessors, and ordered to confirm this on his own part by oaths. With hands raised to almighty God and to all who were present, he promised that he would fulfill this for as long as he lived.

And because we know that it is far better not to make a good vow to God [Col. 1365C] than afterward to turn away from it, let us beseech him to whom these promises were made that, if he has broken them anywhere through human kindness or at evil instigation, he may repent and make fitting amends.

After the emperor’s lamentation, all the best men gave counsel that, once all his property had been seized, the lady should be brought back, and that the authors of this deed should either be presented as prisoners or, if they fled, suffer pursuit until death. The count himself, once he had recovered from his illness, was to lose his head if he were found guilty [Note: Witness 1 reads *efficiretur*, a nonstandard form of *efficeretur*, “were found/made.”]; but if all these things had been done with the lady’s consent [f. 145], he was to make the best use of his bride.

My brother Count Heinricus was immediately sent to carry this out, and was ordered that they should come to Alstidi for a public conference. As he was then departing, [Col. 1365D] the aforementioned counts arrived and reported to the emperor what had happened.

On the following day, that is, on the feast of Saint Martin, Wirinharius, who had until then endured every adversity with patient spirit, died [Note: *Merseburg Calendar*, November 11: “Count Wernicho died”], leaving no gain to his enemies but an [Col. 1366A] unconquerable loss to his own people. Therefore the king grieved, and his enemy Thiedricus wept.

When I learned this, I asked my nephew Thiedricus for permission to depart, and brought the body of my friend by my retainers from Miminlevo, where the abbey then stood [Note: See below, chapter 22], and where Reinoldus, its excellent administrator, had arranged this with due kindness, back to Helpithi [Note: Helfta in the county of Mansfeld. URS.], where I was then waiting for it.

But since it was already giving off an exceedingly foul odor, I immediately ordered the entrails to be removed and ordered him buried beside my church. I followed the funeral procession as far as Wallibizi, placing him on the left of my beloved wife [Note: Liutgerdis. URS.]. Fourteen days later, the lady Swonehild, his mother-in-law, died a sudden death on the sixth day before the Kalends of December [Note: Witness 1b adds the entire preceding report, from “Fourteen days later” through her death date] [Note: *Merseburg Calendar*, November 26: “Suonehild, countess, died.”].

### 6.

Meanwhile the emperor was administering justice to the people at Alstidi [Col. 1366B] [Note: Compare Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.246] and, as those present asserted, denying these things to my friends. Because of the island called Porei [Note: *Porci* in the Saxon Annals under 1014; Parey is an island of the Elbe near Jerichow and Genthin], since Count Bernhardus had earlier wished to kill the aforesaid Wirinharius, the emperor ordered it assigned to him through unjust judges. Count Vicmannus prevented this and declared it unjust [Note: *justum*, “just,” in manuscript 1a.]; all the people murmured and secretly proclaimed that the Lord’s anointed was sinning.

There, in the middle of the day, a star appeared to many (December 7) [f. 145′] [Note: *Ibi tunc* is added in manuscript 1b.]. On the octave of Saint Andrew, the priest Rigmannus [Note: so also in the *Merseburg Calendar*, December 7; witness 1 abbreviates *presbiter*, “priest,” as *pr*], who had presided over his church for eighty-five years, died in Christ [Note: “On the octave he died” is added in manuscript 1b.].

Departing from there, he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Palithi, and on the fourth feria before Easter (1015) he came to Merseburg. On Maundy Thursday I, unworthy as I am, blessed the chrism in his presence. On the vigil of the holy Resurrection [Note: Witness 1b adds *In vigilia autem*, “but on the vigil”], which then fell on the fifth day before the [Col. 1366C] Ides of April, Redbald, abbot of Werden, died, and Hethenricus, provost of the same monastery, was elected [Note: *ita*, “thus,” in manuscript 1b, in an erased place]. On the holy day the archbishop Gero sang Mass; meanwhile Othelricus, duke of the Bohemians, arrived, and we spent these solemn days exceedingly joyfully.

Meanwhile Margrave Hirimannus celebrated Easter with his father-in-law [Note: *Bolislavo Polono*, “the Pole Bolizlavus,” identifies his father-in-law], and, scarcely released from there, came to the emperor with that same Stoignewo, his envoy, for whom the emperor had long waited. This envoy, always accustomed to lie, had been sent by his fickle elder to the emperor in the western region, more to cause disturbance than, as he pretended, to make peace.

The emperor entrusted him and his companions to his intimates. He mercifully received his sons-in-law, who sought his favor with bare feet, and [Col. 1366D] only then ordered the babbler to be brought forward to see these things; he replied publicly to his lord. Since he had reported at home matters other than those the emperor had commanded, he was sent back by order of his ill-fated duke with the aforementioned count [Note: Witness 1 reads dative *comiti*, “to/for the count,” rather than the text’s ablative *comite*, “with the count”], who wished to establish peace. In the presence [Col. 1367A] of the emperor and his princes, he was exposed as deceitful and as one who stirred up discord between them.

Then Bolizlavus [Note: Witness 1b adds the abbreviated name *B.*, meaning Bolizlavus] was again summoned by the emperor either to offer an excuse or to amend his disobedience. He refused to come into the emperor’s presence, but requested that these matters be conducted before his own princes [Note: Witness 1 reads misspelled *princibus* for *principibus*, “princes”]. [f. 146] But, reader, consider how much kindness the emperor had previously shown him!

### 7.

The aforesaid duke, full of knowledge of a thousand arts, sent his son Misecon to Othelricus, ruler of the Bohemians, so that, remembering their mutual kinship, they might reconcile one another and together resist all their enemies, especially the emperor.

But Othelricus, learning from truthful men that all this had been arranged to his own detriment, seized Misecon, killed the best [Col. 1367B] of his companions, brought the others back to Bohemia together with their captured elder, and threw them into prison.

When the emperor learned this, he sent my nephew Thiedricus there, so that Othelricus might return his retainer to him and, if he cared at all for the emperor’s favor, might in no way destroy him. He is said to have given him this reply:

“It is absolutely necessary for me both to be able and to wish to follow my elder’s orders in everything. Almighty God recently snatched me, unworthy as I am, from the lion’s mouth, and delivered his cub, sent for my destruction, into my hands. If I allow this man to depart free, I shall always have confirmed enemies in father and son; but if I retain him, I may hope to gain some advantage for myself through him. Let my lord consider all these matters and decide what pleases him [Note: Witness 1 reads abbreviated *qd* for *quid*, “what”] and may in some measure benefit me [f. 146′] [Col. 1367C]; I, as his devoted servant, will fulfill it all.” But when Thiedricus returned from this embassy, another man was immediately sent back, asking that Misecon be released and firmly commanding Othelricus to do so [Note: Witness 1b adds the abbreviated *B.* after *ei*, probably identifying Bolizlavus; the compressed syntax is uncertain], while promising on the emperor’s behalf to remove all his anxiety and establish a good peace.

Then Othelricus, unwilling or willing, returned the captive and greatly appeased the emperor. Bolizlavus, however, rejoicing beyond measure at the recovery of his son, gave the emperor fitting thanks through his intermediaries, asking that the emperor return him to his father’s honor and to the sorrow of his enemies, and that he himself truly recognize the future recompense of both sides.

The emperor replied that this could not then be done, but promised that, when he came to Merseburg, he would satisfy his wishes with the common counsel of his princes. [Col. 1367D] When Bolizlavus heard this, he did not receive it well; he continually revolved in his silent mind, and through frequent embassies, how he might bring his son back under his own power [Note: Witness 1a reads *reuuoluit*, a spelling of *revolvit*, “he turned over/revolved.”]. [Col. 1368A]

### 8.

When the emperor came to the appointed place [Note: *condictum*, “appointed,” corrected from *conditum*, “founded,” in manuscript 1], he consulted all the leading men about what ought to be done in this matter. Among them Archbishop Gero spoke first [Note: Witness 1 abbreviates *loquitur*, “speaks,” as *loqt’*]:

“When the time was right and this could be done with your honor preserved, you did not heed me when I urged it [Note: Witness 1a reads *hista* for *ista*, “these things”]. Now Bolizlavus’s mind has been turned away from you by the long retention and custody of his son, and I fear that, if you send him back without hostages or other guarantees, you will afterward lack faithful service from both father and son [f. 147].” A very large part of those present followed the speaker in such arguments, while the bribed faction repeatedly insisted that this could not be done with great honor. Money prevailed over counsel. So that this might cost Bolizlavus more dearly, Bolizlavus received Misecon back from the emperor into his allegiance, together with all that they possessed, and received the promised assurances [Note: *succipiens* in manuscript 1a.]. [Col. 1368B] He admonished father and son, reminding them of Christ and of God’s firm oath [Note: that is, an oath-bound obligation], not to inflict any further harm upon the emperor and not to allow his friends to be deceived.

To this sweet exhortation, however, they immediately replied in the manner of a flattering flute [Note: *ortatu*, “exhortation,” in manuscript 1], but afterward fulfilled it in no respect. For although they had little or no good faith, they nevertheless blamed us because, on the emperor’s and our side, the man who had been counted among the soldiers was sent back so late. This was always in their minds, and for that reason they declared that they would not come into the emperor’s presence.

And it is true what the evangelical voice testifies: that a certain excuse is sought by one who is contemplating departure from a close friend (Luke 14:18).

Recognizing this, the emperor departed from us and spent the following Rogation days at Capungun [Col. 1368C] [Note: Not far from Kassel is the monastery of Kaufungen, founded there by Empress Cunigunda and, in the sixteenth century, converted by Landgrave Philip into a collegiate foundation for noble virgins]. There he transferred his court from the city called Cassalun [Note: Witness 1a reads *cassulun*, another spelling of Cassalun; the place is Kassel], and there, with the counsel of his archbishop Heribertus, entrusted the aforesaid Hethenricus with this responsibility.

Meanwhile our church was begun in the presence of Archbishop Gero, and I laid its first stones in the form of a holy cross on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June [Note: “Meanwhile... June” was added in the margin of manuscript 1b; manuscript 2 inserted it after “the solemnity” and continues: “while the king remained at Immedeshusen there”].

After the necessary matters had been dealt with there [Note: that is, at Kaufungen], he came on the vigil of Pentecost (May 28) to Immedeshusun [Note: A town situated between Minden and Geismar, today Immshausen, an estate of the noble family of Steinberg. WAG.], and there, together with Bishop Meinwerc, he solemnly celebrated this holy festival (May 29) [f. 147′].

### 9.

There Val, abbot of Corvey, previously suspended from office, was deposed, and one Druhtmer [Note: Witness 1b adds the name *Druhtmer*] from the monastery of Lorsch was appointed in his place without the consent of the aforesaid brothers. [Col. 1368D] When he came to his seat in the following week, the entire congregation, except for nine, departed weeping; and, as Abbot Liudulfus had foretold [Note: Witness 1b adds *u. L. a. p.*, abbreviating *ut Liudulfus abbas predixit*, “as Abbot Liudulfus foretold.”], it left this place almost empty, though unwillingly.

[Note: Codex 2 adds: “But since I have often mentioned this monastery, I wish to say briefly something about its foundation and its rulers, because it is one of the most ancient. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 822, the emperor Augustus Liudowicus, son of Charlemagne, in the tenth year of his reign, founded this monastery through the venerable Adelhardus, former abbot of Old Corbie, in memory of the place from which it had originated, giving the place the name New Corbie. He bestowed upon that place many estates, namely the village of Huxeri and the abbeys of Eresburg and Meppia. His son Liudwicus, however, presented a noble gift, namely the abbey at Visbike and tithes in the bishopric of Osnabrück, together with the tithe-paying churches. He also granted the fishery on the Wisera called Hocwar. The emperor Lotharius came with the eastern Franks into Sclavia, killed their king Gestimulus, subdued the others [Col. 1369B], and gave them to the church of Corvey in the very year of its dedication, as the chronicle testifies. Moreover, kings, princes, and other nobles enriched that place with many riches and estates, while the Roman pontiffs raised it still higher through privileges and honors. Here rests the illustrious martyr Vitus, a seven-year-old boy, transferred there from Francia by Warinus, the place’s first abbot. Through the patronage of this martyr, Saxony grew immeasurably in the prosperity of its affairs. This place is situated on the river Weser, in the bishopric of Paderborn.”]

Manuscript 2 repeats the same account again near the end of Book VII. Compare A. S., year 822. [Note: The material concerning Lotharius through the dedication of the monastery is taken from the *Annals of Quedlinburg*, above.] [Col. 1369B]

### 10.

During these festive days Ernost [Note: Witness 1c appears to read *ernest*, another spelling of Ernost], the illustrious duke of Alemannia and successor of the boy Herimannus, was hunting unlawfully in a certain forest when, alas, he was wounded [Col. 1369C] by one of his soldiers [Note: Witness 1a reads subjunctive *vulneretur*, “might be wounded,” for indicative *vulneratur*, “is wounded”], more through ignorance than deliberate intent, just as the man was supposed to shoot a hind [Note: Witness 1 reads misspelled *sagitare* for *sagittare*, “to shoot.”].

When he perceived that death was threatening him, he summoned his companions and begged them to spare the guilty man. Since he did not then have a priest to whom he could confess his sins [Note: Witness 1c may read *cui*, “to whom,” for *quo*, “to whom,” here], he ordered one of the soldiers to approach in the priest’s place [Note: *propius*, “nearer,” abbreviated as *propu’* in manuscript 1].

When he saw that the man was present, he said:

“Come closer, all of you, and receive with the ear of your heart the deeds of your fellow-mortal and sinner, and unanimously help to heal them [Note: Witness 1b adds *-que*, “and,” to *absentibusque*, which begins the next request]. I ask you to commend my sinful soul to all the faithful who are absent, and admonish my wife to preserve her honor and not forget me.”

Saying this, he made known to all who were present everything that he could remember ever having done wrong. Then he departed from this light [Note: Witness 1b adds *hac*, “this,” to *de luce hac*, “from this light”] on the second day before the Kalends of June [Note: see the *Annals of Hildesheim*, year 1015; *Merseburg Calendar*, May 31], and was buried [Col. 1369D] at Würzburg beside his father, Margrave Liupoldus, as he himself had requested.

This young man, I hope, has a blessed soul, since, as he himself testified while alive, he preferred to be put to shame before many people here rather than remain hidden before almighty God [f. 148]. [Col. 1370A] Take an example from this, brothers in Christ, and open to the heavenly physician [Note: Witness 1a reads *celeste*, “heavenly,” for the dative *celesti*] the disease lying hidden within. Do not in any way reject his healing antidote [Note: Witness 1a reads *antitodum*, a misspelling of *antidotum*, “antidote.”]. And whoever our confessor may be at the end, let the sinful man not delay in mournful confession, so that in heaven he may be found by him as a merciful forgiver.

### 11.

To the aforementioned solemnity and place, a certain peasant coming from the western regions brought the emperor a new message, which he wished never to disclose to anyone except the emperor alone [Note: The source repeats witness 1’s *antitodum*, “antidote,” apparatus from the preceding paragraph here; it does not modify the message. Witness 1c may read *nulli nisi ei*, “to no one except him,” for *nullo nisi eo*, “with no one except him.”]. He still carried the goad [Note: Witness 1b supplies *stimulum … minavit*, “the goad … with which he drove,” in an erased place.] with which, while plowing, he had driven livestock, when he received a command from heaven through a dove [Note: “through a dove” is added in manuscript 1b.; *fuet* corrected to *fuit*, “was,” in manuscript 1]. It [Note: Witness 1a reads feminine *hec* and *eam* (“this” and “it”) for masculine *hic* and *eum*, referring to the goad] was of such great length that all who saw it were exceedingly amazed. [Note: The remainder of the sentence, “But on his return... he perceived,” was added by manuscript 1b in a blank space.] [Col. 1370B] On his return, when questioned by everyone, he declared that, by the emperor’s command, he himself would come to Aachen after the expedition and receive an answer from him there.

And because the emperor spurned this admonition, as well as countless others repeatedly given, he experienced vengeance. On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, which was then near at hand, the emperor came to Goslar and gave Ernost’s duchy to his niece and her son. From there, proceeding to Magdeburg, he devoutly prayed for the intercession of the soldier of Christ, Saint Maurice, to overcome the insolence of the enemy Bolizlavus.

Next he advanced with a gathered army to the place called Sclancisvordi [Note: A place unknown to us, to be sought not far from Torgau], and inflicted great damage on the people of the region and on their margrave, Gero [f. 148′] [Note: *damnum*, “damage,” is missing in manuscript 1].

Our assembly took place on the eighth day before the Ides of July, and there was great [Col. 1370C] plundering for the rightful defense of these inhabitants.

After our men crossed the Elbe, the empress and I, traveling with her toward Merseburg, awaited the emperor’s arrival in these regions. But when our men came to the district called Lusici, they were attacked by a garrison that had come out from the city of Ciani [Note: Witness 1 reads *egreso*, a spelling of *egresso*, “having come out”; Ciani is Zinnitz, between Kalau and Luckau in Lower Lusatia]. Recognizing this, they killed a great number of them and captured Hericus, called “the Proud,” who had fled there from our region because of a homicide, and presented him in chains to the emperor.

From there the emperor proceeded as far as the Oder. At the place called Crosna [Note: Crossen, where the Bober flows into the Oder], he sent the best men from the army [Note: Witness 1 reads *exertitu*, a misspelling of *exercitu*, “army”] to Misecon, who was sitting there in formation, so that they might remind him of the faith he had promised and unanimously ask him not, because of himself, to cause them to lose their possessions to the emperor, since the emperor wished to forestall them [Col. 1370D] through their surrender.

He replied to them as follows:

“I acknowledge [Note: Witness 1 reads accusative *gratiam*, “favor,” for ablative *gratia*, “by favor”] that I was rescued from the power of my enemy by the emperor’s favor and promised you my loyalty; and I would gladly fulfill it in everything if I were free. [Col. 1371A] But now, as you yourselves know, I am subject to my father’s authority [Note: manuscript 1 has *domino*, “lord,” instead of *dominio*, “authority”]. Since he forbids this, and his soldiers presently here do not allow such things to be done, I unwillingly refrain.

“I wish, if I can, to defend the homeland you seek until my father arrives; then I hope to incline him toward the emperor’s favor and toward your friendship.”

Hearing this, our men returned and reported these answers to the emperor. [f. 149] Meanwhile Duke Bernhardus, with his supporters—bishops and counts—and a multitude of pagan Liuticians, advanced against Bolizlavus from the north and held him there, surrounded on every side by fortifications along the Oder.

### 12.

On the Finding of Christ’s Protomartyr (August 3), the emperor crossed the Oder and utterly defeated the resisting multitude of the Poles. None [Col. 1371B] of our men fell except Hodo, the illustrious young man, together with Ekkrico and another retainer of Count Guncelinus [Note: *Merseburg Calendar*, August 3: “Hodo and Ekkricus were killed with many others.” Compare the *Annals of Quedlinburg*, year 1015, and the *Lüneburg Necrology*.].

Hodo and Sigifridus, son of Margrave Hodo, had been accused by the emperor because they had until then been excessively intimate with Bolizlavus [Note: Witness 1 reads *bolizlovo*; witness 1a has plural *familiares* and *fuissent*, “they had been intimate,” for singular *familiaris* and *fuisset*, “he had been intimate”]. On that same day they bravely cleared themselves of the charge [Note: Thus in manuscript 1; A. S. reads *expurgavit*, “he cleared himself”]. Hodo then went far ahead of his men and, while pursuing the fleeing enemies alone, was struck by an arrow through the head: first he lost an eye, and afterward this life.

When Misecon recognized the body, since Hodo had been his guardian and companion among us, he wept greatly and sent it, properly cared for, to the army [Note: *et*, “and,” in manuscript 1, apparently instead of *ad*, “to”]. The number of those who fell on the enemy’s side was no less than six hundred, leaving an indescribable amount of booty to our men.

When Bolizlavus, who remained there, quickly [Col. 1371C] learned this from hastening messengers, he wished gladly to go there, but, because enemies were present, did not dare make the way in open. Wherever our men turned in their ships, he followed there with his men on a winged horse (compare Ovid, *Fasti* III.415).

At last, when our men quickly raised their sails, they sailed for an entire day, and, since the enemies could no longer accompany them, safely reached the desired shore [f. 149′] and set fire to the nearby places. When the aforesaid duke saw this from afar, he fled in his usual manner and unwillingly granted our men confidence and an opportunity to inflict harm.

Duke Bernhardus, unable to come with his men to the emperor’s aid as he had previously been ordered, secretly sent foot soldiers [Col. 1371D] to report to him the outcome of the affair and the necessity that had caused his disobedience. After laying waste to the surrounding places, he returned home.

Othelricus likewise, who was supposed to come to the emperor with the Bavarians, failed to do so because of the many circumstances of his affairs [Note: Similarly II.16, “many kinds of circumstances”]. [Col. 1372A] Although these men did not accompany the emperor, they nevertheless demonstrated faithful service by their proximity [Note: That is, the proximity of Bohemia].

For Othelricus attacked a certain large city called Businc [Note: The same place as above, VI.37, it seems; *Busin*, Budissin], and, capturing in it no fewer than one thousand men, without women or children, burned it and returned victorious.

Heinricus, however, margrave of the East, learning that Bolizlavus’s soldiers had taken booty near him, immediately pursued them and killed eight hundred of those who offered stout resistance [Note: Witness 1b adds the preceding clause reporting the killing of eight hundred], recovering all the booty.

### 13.

Meanwhile Redingus, provost of Magdeburg, died in Christ on the Nones of August [Note: See the *Merseburg Calendar*, August 5]. In the same month, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, Eila, the venerable countess, died [Note: *Merseburg Calendar*, August 19. Compare the *Saxon Annals*, year 1015] and was delivered [Col. 1372B] to burial by Bishop Everhardus [Note: *Bambergensi*, “of Bamberg”; he held the see in 1007–1039] in the monastery that she herself had built [Note: that is, at Schweinfurt]. [Note: Witness 1b adds the whole preceding report from Redingus’s death through Eila’s burial.]

But before the emperor learned all these things, he was greatly troubled. Although his army was small, he nevertheless remained in these regions with full authority for as long as he wished. Then, returning to the district called Diadesisi, he arrived and, alas, camped in a narrow place where no one sat except the master of the bees, who was killed there at that time [f. 150].

When Bolizlavus heard that the emperor would leave by a different route from the one he had entered, he fortified his own position in every way beside the Oder [Note: Witness 1b adds the preceding statement about fortifying beside the Oder]. But when he learned that the emperor had already departed, he sent ahead a large multitude of foot soldiers to the place where our army had encamped, ordering them, if any opportunity arose, to attempt to injure at least some part of it.

Moreover, he sent his abbot, named Tuni [Col. 1372C], to the emperor under the pretense of peace. The emperor immediately recognized him as a spy and detained him there until almost the entire army had crossed the marsh lying ahead, bridges having been built during the preceding night (September 1).

Then that man, a monk in appearance [Note: *Gero*: text and witness 1b; witnesses 1a and 1 write *Jeroni*, another form of the name Gero, at its two following occurrences] but a deceitful fox in conduct, and for this reason beloved by his lord, returned. The emperor proceeded, entrusting the remainder to Archbishop Gero, the illustrious Margrave Gero, and Count Palatine Burchardus [Note: Witness 1b adds the preceding mention of Burchardus], and urged them to keep watch around themselves more cautiously than usual.

After this, a great shout was raised by enemies hiding nearby in the forest, with three bellowing blasts. Immediately they attacked our column, mingling archers among those who advanced. Our men resisted them bravely in the first and second engagements [Note: Witness 1b adds *-que*, “and,” joining the first and second engagements] and killed [Col. 1372D] many of them as they scattered.

But when some of our men fled, the enemy, taking courage, gathered together, charged our men again, dispersed them, and killed those who had been separated by means of their deceptive arrows [f. 150′].

Archbishop Gero [Col. 1373A] and Count Burchardus, wounded and barely escaping, reported these events to the emperor. The young Liudulfus was captured with a few men, while Counts Gero and Folcmarus were killed and stripped, together with two hundred excellent soldiers [Note: *Merseburg Calendar*, Kalends of September: “Counts Gero and Wolcmarus were killed with two hundred of their companions.” Compare the *Annals of Quedlinburg*, year 1015].

May almighty God mercifully regard their names and souls, reconcile to himself through Christ us, whose guilt caused them then to perish, and in his clemency preserve us from suffering anything of this kind again.

### 14.

When the emperor heard this sorrowful news, he wished to return and retrieve the bodies of the slain. But, delayed by the counsel of many, he abandoned this almost unwillingly and sent Bishop Aeidus to obtain permission from the ill-fated duke to bury them and to request the body of Margrave Gero.

The venerable father [Note: Witness 1b adds *venerabilis*, “venerable”], willingly agreeing with the emperor [Note: manuscript 1a reads *cesare* for *cesari*], returned at a swift pace. [Col. 1373B] When he saw the pitiable slaughter, he groaned tearfully and prayed earnestly for them [Note: Witness 1b adds *pro*, “for,” and *hiis*, “these men/them,” in two separate apparatus entries].

When the victors, who were then lingering alone over the booty, saw him from afar, they first fled in fear of those who might follow. Then, when he approached more closely, they greeted him and allowed him to depart without any offense.

Having obtained from Bolizlavus, who was greatly rejoicing in our destruction, what he requested, he returned without delay and buried the bodies of his companions [f. 151] with great [Note: Witness 1a reads feminine *magna* for neuter *magno*, both meaning “great”] labor, the enemy allowing it [Note: that is, with the enemy’s favor; *fav.* in manuscript 1a].

He had the funeral of the aforesaid margrave and his companion Widredus brought as far as Meissen. There Count Hirimannus received it tearfully and accompanied it as far as the New City, where Gero, archbishop of Cologne [Note: Witness 1a appears to have had *Agripinensis*, “of Cologne”; witness 1c reads *Coloniensis*, likewise “of Cologne.”], and Thietmarus the margrave, his brother, stepfather of this man but father of the slain [Col. 1373C] count, had built an abbey in honor of the Mother of God and Saint Cyprian the martyr during the reign of Otto II [Note: Compare the *Saxon Chronograph*, year 971]. He accompanied it with his brothers Guntterius and Ekkihardus [Note: the *i* is erased in manuscript 1].

At that place Archbishop Gero then committed the body to the earth and consoled the lady Aethelheida [Note: *ath.* in manuscript 1c], her son Thietmarus, and their grieving friends and soldiers.

### 15.

Meanwhile the emperor arrived with his men at the city of Strela. Knowing that Misecon was following with an army, he ordered Margrave Herimannus to hurry to the defense of the city of Meissen. He himself proceeded directly toward Merseburg.

Misecon, instructed by his wicked father, crossed the Elbe beside the aforesaid city [Col. 1373D] at sunrise on the Ides of September with seven legions, ordering some to ravage the surrounding places and others to attack the city. [Col. 1374A] When the Weneinici [Note: *Wenenici* in A. S. Perhaps the author intended *Wenetnici* or *Wethenici*] [Note: *Weinenici*, that is, the same as the Wethenici above, or from the Slavic word *Vojnik*, Polish *Wojownik*, “warrior”] saw this and despaired of being able to defend themselves, they climbed onto the fortification of the upper city, abandoning almost all their possessions [f. 151′].

The enemy therefore entered the abandoned suburb with great joy, removed the goods they found, and burned it. They attacked the upper castle tirelessly after setting fire to it in two places.

Count Hirimannus [Note: Witness 1b adds the name *Hirimannus* here], seeing that his auxiliaries had already become very few [Note: *defesisse*, “had failed,” in manuscript 1a], prostrated himself and invoked the holy mercy of Christ and the intercession of his illustrious martyr Donatus. He urged the women to come to the rescue.

When they reached the battlements, the women helped the men with stones. Since the water had run out [Note: Witness 1b adds the preceding clause about the water having run out], they extinguished the fire that had been set with mead; and, thanks be to God, they diminished the enemy’s fury and boldness. [Col. 1374B] Seeing all this from the nearby mountain, Misecon awaited the arrival of his companions. After ravaging everything as far as the river Gana [Note: *Granam* in manuscript 2 and A. S.; the Jahna, a small river flowing into the Elbe near Riesa], wherever fire was found, they returned late on weary horses. They would have spent the night there with their elder, intending to fight at the city on the next day, had they not seen the Elbe rising.

For this reason the army, exceedingly exhausted, returned in unexpected safety and relieved its anxious commander’s heart through this success [Note: Witness 1 reads *prosperate*, the adverb “successfully,” for the noun *prosperitate*, “success”].

When the emperor heard this, he quickly sent to the aid of his margrave all whom he could then gather, and shortly afterward ordered the suburb to be restored. To complete and guard this work, Archbishop Gero and Bishop Arnulfus, together with counts and many others, assembled on the eighth day before the Ides of October [f. 152].

I, far inferior [Col. 1374C] to all these men, was present. After completing in fourteen days, down to the last detail [Note: *per unguem*, “to the fingernail,” is added in manuscript 1a], the work we had begun [Note: Witness 1b adds *nos*, “we,” as the subject of completing the work], we departed, entrusting the city to Count Frithericus for four weeks.

### 16

Archbishop Gero [Note: “of Magdeburg” is added in witness 1c.] and I, his companion, came to the place called Mucherini [Note: Mokrehna, a village between Torgau and Eilenburg.]. There, reminding him of his gracious promises, I received from him, together with his staff—which I hold today—the parish over these four cities: Scudizi, Cotuh, Bichini, and Vurcin. As for the remaining five—Ilburg, Pauc, Dibni, Liubanizi, and Geserisca [Note: “Gezerisca” in witness 1c.] [Note: Compare above, Book III, chapter 8.]—he deferred the matter, saying that he would leave it for the future [Note: “the remaining five … would leave it” is added in witness 1b.; some words in the text have been erased.], on 25 October, in the presence of these witnesses: Heribald, Hepo, Ibo, Cristino, and Seberto.

On that same day we came to the city called Curbici [Note: Zörbig.]. When the soldiers of the archbishop assembled there, I told them how mercifully their lord had acted toward me. There we also learned of the illness of the venerable Fritheruna, at whose lodging we then were; and she, alas, on the following day—that is, 27 October—“put off the inner man” [Note: Read “the outer man.” (But Thietmar always writes it this way.)] [Note: The Merseburg and Lüneburg calendars record: “28 October: Countess Fritherun.”].

From there the archbishop set out for Magdeburg [Note: “and” is found in witness 1.] and celebrated the feast of All Saints, while I remained at Wallibici.

### 17

Meanwhile Hardwig, king in name only, having lost the city of Fercelli, which he had long unjustly possessed after expelling Bishop Leo, fell ill. He shaved his beard, became a monk, and died on 30 October; he was buried in a monastery. The emperor, meanwhile, visiting the western regions, corrected whatever there required correction [Note: “Hardwig … western …” is added in witness 1b. The words “Hardwig, king in name only” are in an erasure, and the rest is in the margin; witness 1a seems to have read: “Meanwhile the emperor was visiting the western regions.”].

### 18

After this, Aeid, an excellent bishop, returned at last from Poland with great gifts and began to fall ill; and in the city called Libzi he gave his faithful soul back to Christ on 20 December [Note: The Merseburg calendar records: “20 December: Bishop Aeid died.”]. Hilliward, bishop of Zeitz, summoned to take charge of this matter, promptly arrived. Entering the house from which the holy man had departed, he recognized that it was fragrant with the finest scents; and he accompanied his body as far as Meissen. He buried it before the altar [Note: “the altar” in witness 1a.], with the assistance of Count William, who at that time guarded the same city in accordance with his office.

But since I earlier promised that I would speak of his life in what follows, I shall mention a few of his great qualities. The man in question was noble by birth and wealthy in estates, but in spirit of poverty he regarded these things as nothing. Before his blessing [i.e. episcopal consecration], he lived regularly and most commendably with the other brethren at Magdeburg; afterward, rising more vigorously to win souls in the divine flocks, he imitated the apostolic life as far as he was able.

He never wore a shirt or breeches except when he celebrated Mass; indeed, he often omitted Mass for this reason, because he judged himself unworthy of it. Many wondered how he could ever endure the harshness of winter. Frequently, when his own people had almost given up hope for him, he could scarcely be revived in a heated room. He afflicted his body excessively with fasts, working more often barefoot than on horseback.

Whenever he saw that food had run out for himself and his companions as they wandered widely, or that some difficult situation had arisen, he gave thanks to God and ordered everyone to do the same. In baptizing, continuous preaching, and confirmation, he was useful not only to his own church but to many others as well.

From the resources on which he and his companions were to live, withholding them from himself, he acquired for his own church nearly two hundred hides. He rarely consecrated chrism and clergy, but willingly consecrated the Lord’s temples, and often did so without celebrating Mass. His eyes were already growing dim from the constant outpouring of excessive tears [Note: “without … growing dim” is added in witness 1b.].

We, his contemporaries, disliked his way of life because of our sin, and he disliked ours. Living for twenty-three years and more amid indescribable labor, he foretold his end and repeatedly begged never to be buried at Meissen. He had always desired this in his heart, through fear of future desolation: he wished to deserve burial at the place called Colidici [Note: “Coldic” in witness 1c?], where the great martyr of Christ rests bodily. But Count Hermann, hoping that the place prepared for him by God would be aided by the man’s prayers, as I have said, had him buried there.

### 19

On Christmas Eve, Meingaud, archbishop of Trier, died in his own city, called Cophelenci [Note: Koblenz.], after having held office for eight years and seven months [Note: “after having held office … seven months” is added in witness 1b.]. His body was then carried to his proper see and honorably placed beside his predecessors.

When the emperor heard this, he was troubled by the loss of so many fathers and discussed with his familiars how he might properly fill the vacant places. He celebrated Christmas at Paderborn with festive joy [Note: “and” is added in witness 1b.; “at Paderborn” is inserted in a space previously left blank]. After this he appointed Poppo, son of Margrave Liupold and then provost of the church of Bamberg, to the city of Trier.

When Poppo was to be consecrated by Erkanbald, archbishop of Mainz, at the emperor’s command and with the permission of the bishop of Verdun—who was first in rank among these brother-bishops—Thiederic, bishop of Metz, repeatedly and humbly protested in vain, arguing that this ordination ought more properly to be carried out by him. For the emperor did not heed Thiederic, who displayed the written authorization and forbade the act under penalty of ban, but ordered that the anointing [Note: “unction” in witness 1a.] be completed.

During these days, in place of Bishop Aeid, Eilward, chaplain of Margrave Thietmar, was appointed by the emperor at the urging of our brother Hermann. On the Sunday before Palm Sunday, he was blessed at Merseburg by Archbishop Gero, with our support (18 March 1016).

### 20

The emperor, together with Henry, the venerable bishop of the church of Würzburg [Note: So in witness 1; the *i* is not erased.], completed the next Palm Sunday celebration and came to Bamberg on Wednesday. There he honorably celebrated the Lord’s Supper and the Passion with paschal rejoicing (25 March, 1 April).

Since Rudolph, king of Burgundy, his maternal uncle [Note: That is, the brother of Gisela, daughter of Conrad, king of Burgundy. See above, Book V, chapter 4 and following.], could not come there as he had been summoned, he asked his beloved nephew to travel to meet him. Their meeting took place in the city of Strasbourg [Note: Witness 1 reads *Pergit* (“he proceeds”); this is the hand responsible for many errors. “Argentiva” in witness 1.], and abundant mutual kindness born of affection pleased both parties [Note: Witness 1 reads *consosociis*, written over two lines.].

Rudolph’s illustrious wife was also there. As an aid to this friendship, she commended to the emperor her two sons, who were her husband’s stepsons. The emperor granted all this as a benefice to his beloved followers: both what had then been granted to her by her uncle and what William of Poitiers [Note: This was Count Otto William I, son of Adalbert, king of Italy, and Gerberga of Burgundy; the ancient counts of Burgundy descend from him. —The editor] had hitherto held by royal grant.

Using wise counsel, the emperor wished through these men to secure more firmly for himself what the aforementioned king had previously confirmed to him by oath for after his death. He received from his uncle the primacy of the whole region of Burgundy and a firm assurance that no important matter would be undertaken without his counsel. He gave a bishopric in this region to a certain nobleman [Note: “to a certain” is uncertain in witness 1c?], from whom he afterward scarcely escaped unharmed.

For when William, a powerful man in those parts, learned of this, he ordered the bishop to be pursued and ultimately, as he fled alone, to be hunted down by dogs. When the already exhausted bishop heard them barking, he made the sign of the holy cross over his tracks—the only consolation he then possessed—lay down as though dead, and made himself ready to be prey. But behold, the swift dogs, sniffing the marked places from a distance, were driven back as if by a great whirlwind; they turned and retreated. Thus the true servant of God made his way through unknown woodland paths to the territory of his friends.

The emperor gave an immeasurable sum of money to the king, his wife, and all his own princes. After once again confirming the ancient treaty, he allowed them to depart; then, having assembled an army, he set out for the city of Basel [Note: The emperor was at Basel on 25 June of this year, as is shown by a charter issued there.].

When he heard that William was resisting from fortified cities and wishing to bar his entrance, he, mistrusting his small force, gathered friendly troops from every direction. He confidently laid waste by widespread, blazing fires the provinces that dared to rebel against him [Note: “rebel” is written *repallare* in witness 1a, corrected to *rebaellare* in witness 1b.]. Since he knew for certain that he could conquer none of those cities, he returned sadly, having inflicted no harm on his enemies either here or in the eastern region.

### 21

Meanwhile the empress, staying in our provinces, considered with our princes the defense of the homeland. Our enemy Bolizlav, however, did not harm anything belonging to us during this time, but fortified his own possessions; and, confident of the emperor’s outcome, he rejoiced and became excessively elated.

Many who knew the situation truthfully maintained that, if the emperor had then come against him with a massed army, he could have restored the fear which Bolizlav had felt regarding our forces and, once peace alone had been granted, could have made him ready and faithful for his service.

But the king of Burgundy, soft and effeminate, wished at their instigation to obstruct the good things he had promised his nephew. These men, with the bridle of justice loosened, delighted in running freely through the open field like an unhappy calf [Note: Compare *Ecbasis captivi* (“The Escape of the Captive”), edited by J. Grimm, *Latin Poems of the Tenth and Eleventh Centuries*, verse 66 and following: “And like the wretched calf … I was restrained by the reins of my fathers,” verse 88: “He strives … that he may run freely,” and verse 248: “The unhappy calf.”].

When he again tried to persist in his undertaking, he could not do so because of their collusion and wicked resistance. For, as I hear, there is no one who rules in that kingdom in such a manner [Note: Witness 2 reads: “as I hear, there is a king who …”]: the king has only the name and crown, and he grants bishoprics to those chosen by these princes. Holding little for his own use, he lives from the expenses of the bishops and cannot rescue either them or others laboring abroad in any matter. Hence these men, with hands folded, serve all the chief nobles as though they were their king, and in this way enjoy peace.

The only reason such a ruler dominates among them is that the fury of evil men may roam more freely against one another, and that the law of another king may not enter there and break their established custom. Count William, whom I mentioned above, is a king’s soldier in name but a lord in fact [Note: So in witness A.S.; the reading *ire* (“of the land”) was changed to *ire* in witness 1.]. In these regions no one is called a count unless he possesses ducal rank; and lest William’s power in this region be diminished even slightly, he resists the imperial majesty in counsel and action, as I have said.

### 22

In the preceding summer (1014), Bernhard, pious father and bishop of the holy church of Verden [Note: “bishops” in witness 1.], seeing that he was already inclining toward the appointed end of this life [Note: “life” is abbreviated and partly defective in witness 1.], gently summoned all his debtors to him. He admonished them that they had humanly transgressed against God and against the church entrusted to him, and mercifully forgave all who confessed.

But to all who denied that they were in any way guilty toward him [Note: Witness 1 reads: “they denied, thus he rebuked them”; it further has the corrupt reading *nequoso f. s. faciasti*.], he said:

“Please, sons, do not act in this way! I do not desire that you should in any respect be deceived through my portion or that of my successor. Rather, I now wish you to be released from such things and to part from you in sincere peace.”

He enlarged his church by three hundred hides lawfully acquired. He loved his emperor and all the faithful of Christ from his heart, and especially loved those subject to him, following the example of the supreme shepherd.

That venerable man held office for twenty-four years [Note: “years” is written “year” in witness 1a.]. He began to build beside the church of Verden a tower of stones, which are scarce in this land. Then that radiant one was taken away from our sight on 25 July [Note: Not in the year 1015 but in 1014. See the Annals of Corvey and Quedlinburg. The day is also confirmed by the Merseburg calendar.].

When the emperor learned this, he wept over the death of so great a lord as a son weeps over the absence of his father. In his place, on 24 August, he appointed Vidzier, formerly provost of the church of Cologne but then deposed by Archbishop Heribert, after Vidzier had long resisted. Consecrated by Archbishop Erkanbald, he sent him back with great honor to his proper see.

It must also be noted—and expressed not without heavy sobbing—that the monastery established at Miminlevo was reduced from a long-strengthened freedom into servitude. For after its abbot Reinold was deposed and the brethren there were scattered far and wide [Note: “there” is added in witness 1b.], it was subjected to the church of Hersfeld and to Arnold, its administrator at that time.

### 23

In a certain province of the region of Swabia, in the county of Count Becelin, a remarkable and exceedingly terrifying event occurred. A married woman, overcome by the bonds of sudden death, died. After her body had been washed and properly prepared, her grieving companions carried it to the church.

There she suddenly rose from the bier, drove away everyone present, summoned her husband and the rest of her household to her, and assigned to these persons in particular a special gift, consoling them with sweet words. After this she rested in peace.

What I say is marvelous, but I recognize this as solely a wondrous work of the Lord. And lest anyone doubt that it is true, I offer testimony that cannot reasonably be rejected. The aforementioned count reported it as fact to the emperor, and the emperor revealed it to me in the presence of many brethren.

It often happens that the cunning enemy appears to a person in the likeness of the dead, attempting to deceive him in various ways; and fools commonly suppose that this is what has happened. But I truthfully make known to all the faithful that, after the commendation of the soul and the proper Christian rite of burial have been carefully completed, that lifeless body never rises before the resurrection of all flesh, which will unquestionably take place, unless it is raised temporarily through the merits of the righteous. This happened only when the world flourished through their renowned way of life.

I think that the aforementioned woman had great merit [Note: That is, before God.]. After tasting death, she was permitted to fulfill her righteous desire and then, without a groan, to fall asleep once more in the sleep of peace.

Blessed is the person who completes a good work with continual haste and does not suspend it through prolonged delay. Conversely, the place of the wretched is assigned to the one who either utterly despises what is just or tries to postpone it so that it cannot be completed. I have often been guilty in both respects; for now I mention only two matters in which I severely accuse myself.

### 24

After the decision carried out at Dortmund [Note: See above, Book VI, chapter 13.], Richarius, priest of the church of Magdeburg and my spiritual brother, fell ill. Because I was not there, I did not visit him. When I came on the day before that just man died [Note: “departed” in witness 1a.], I did not go to him but postponed it until the following day; and then he died without receiving my charity.

His body was carried to the church by our brethren. Since I could not endure keeping vigil, it was guarded by my vicar. Not long after his burial, Richarius appeared to me in a dream and said:

“Why did you not visit me, sing the psalter, or perform the commemoration established at Dortmund?”

When he heard my excuse, he replied:

“You did badly; you abandoned these duties.”

I then asked him how he was faring. He answered:

“As I fell asleep on the Sabbath, I passed over into another state to the joys of sweet rest” [Note: “another” is written “the other” in witness 1a.].

I asked him how things stood with my father and mother. He replied, “Well,” and continued:

“Your mother has commanded me to tell you that you will join her on either the second or the fifth day.”

With a groan I awoke, knowing for certain that the holy and salutary discipline common to the righteous is beneficial if observed, but a great danger if neglected. Although in this matter I accuse no one except myself, I fear that a very great multitude are transgressors of this covenant and of the other one as well; and the more we despise the commands of our superiors, the more guilty we are at their judgment [Note: Witness 1 has *exanime* (“lifeless”) for *examine* (“judgment”).].

### 25

I also sinned in another matter, something I regret from my heart ever having done. During the Lent that preceded his death (1015), Reding, provost of the community at Naples, received me hospitably when I came here and asked to speak with me privately. At once tears came to his eyes, and he began:

“I greatly fear that I shall be struck by sudden death, and I shall disclose to you the circumstances that have preceded it. Once in the city of Arnsburg and twice here, this happened to me unexpectedly: I could neither see nor hear anything; I overcame this through the swift aid of Christ.

“From that time I have been exceedingly anxious, and I have exposed the wound of my iniquity to my brethren, whom I hope to be suitable for this purpose. Since I have always recognized you as faithful to me, I humbly ask you to bear witness to my confession, because I do not think I shall live long.”

I devoutly accepted this request and promised to satisfy him in every respect. Afterward he admonished me about such matters; but because the time was not then suitable, he did not receive from me the fulfillment of his laudable desire. Although, because of the tireless stench of my sinful conscience, I willingly avoid looking upon and despair of treating the wound of any convert [Note: “willingly” is added in witness 1b.], I would gladly have taken upon myself this brother’s burden if I had seen any opportunity for us to respond to these matters.

On the next Good Friday, Rotman, priest and provost of Archbishop Gero, was overcome at night by the force of an unexpected death and was found dead in his bed. This seemed marvelous and exceedingly frightening to all who heard it. But thanks be to God: the day before, he had distributed alms and had made his confession publicly and not without abundant tears.

On Holy Saturday [Note: That is, of Easter.], I came here and solemnly celebrated this holy feast with my archbishop (10 April). At that time Reding [Note: “Rediggus” in witness 1a.], a prudent and entirely cautious man, divided his possessions between his brother and his beloved sister, saying:

“Keep these things for yourselves, so that, when you soon lose me bodily, you may recognize that I have been faithful to you in this love” [Note: “when you soon …” is added in witness 1b.].

On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist [Note: “on the Nativity” is added in witness 1b.], with my brother Abbot Sigifrid, a monk of New Corvey [Note: This phrase is added in witness 2.], I bade the often-mentioned provost farewell with a final greeting; alas, I made no effort to receive reconciliation from him [Note: This clause is added in witness 1b.]; I did not sense that he wished to seek me again; and when I discovered that he had died, as I have said, I then lamented too late what I had previously neglected to consider [Note: “after” is added in witness 1b.].

He presided over his brethren for three years and six weeks, a pious, wise, and exceedingly faithful man. He was buried in the southern portico beside the monastery.

In the following year (1016?), on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, Geddo, a venerable father, formerly master of the school but then custodian of the church, succeeded him. On the vigil of that feast, Esico the recluse had first died; for the love of Christ he had changed his residence many times [Note: The words from “He presided” through “many times” are written in Thietmar’s own hand and conclude the final page of the quire; he also wrote “Zeal” at the beginning of the following quire.].

Zeal for the Lord’s house—which is our spiritual mother in Christ—though rarely, nevertheless sometimes consumes me. For this reason, what I have just said compels me to insert myself into the work of the provost.

### 26

I have often heard that the English—called *Angli* because of their angelic, that is, beautiful, appearance, or because they are situated in a corner of this earth [Note: Compare Widukind I, 8.]—suffered indescribable misery at the hands of Swegen, son of Harald, the savage king of the Danes.

They were compelled, although previously tributaries, to pay every year to the unclean dogs [Note: That is, the Danish pirates.] the tribute imposed upon them, even though they were spiritual sons of the prince of the apostles Peter and of their holy father Gregory. They were also forced, after their inhabitants had been captured and killed, unwillingly to leave the greater part of their kingdom for the enemy to inhabit with confidence.

With the Lord consenting to this and stirring up the aforementioned enemies in order to chastise the sins of certain of his unfaithful people [Note: The *in* is erased in witness 1.], the persecutor sowed such devastation that he had never learned to spare even his own people. This man, I mean, mentioned above—not a ruler but a destroyer—had been captured after his father’s death by rebellious Northmen [Note: “Northmen” is misspelled in witness 1.]. When he was ransomed by the people then subject to him at an enormous price, he learned that, because of the secret whispering of wicked men, he was for this reason being called a slave. What he could have avenged beneficially upon a few, he planned, impatiently, to avenge to the common harm—which, had he understood it, was chiefly harmful to himself [Note: Compare Adam of Bremen, Book II, chapter 21.]—

Then, abandoning his own power to foreign enemies, he exchanged security for wandering, peace for war, a kingdom for exile, and the God of heaven and earth for the devil [Note: “exchanged” in witness 1a.]. Laying waste every inhabited place, he repeatedly boasted that he was not a master purchased or desired by his people, but their voluntary enemy, reigning everywhere—alas!

This impious man remained for a long time among the pious, to the great hardship of himself and his contemporaries; then, by divine judgment, the death of many was brought low by his lingering death. His companions soon fled, and he was buried there [Note: Swegen, king of the Danes, died in England in 1014, on 2 February.] [1014].

When Æthelred, king of the English, who had long been driven into exile by him, learned this with certainty, he gave thanks to God, joyfully returned to his homeland, and, gathering all his soldiers together, tried to remove the enemy’s body.

To prevent this, a certain noblewoman, having first been warned by her attendants, raised the preserved remains from the ground and, although a native of the country, sent them by ship to the northern lands—that is, toward the region of the north [Note: That is, Roskilde in Zealand. Compare throughout Lappenberg, *History of Great Britain*, vol. I, pp. 449 ff.]. This name derives from the two *Arcturi*, that is, the lesser and greater bears, which, as astrologers assert, are encircled and divided by a single serpent.

### 27

That land is as cold as it is removed from the sun’s warmth, and the minds of its inhabitants are devoid of the twofold charity. There are Scythians [Note: “Scythians” is written *scithi* in witness 1a.] who carry their houses with them and feed on wild animals and horse milk [Note: Compare Horace III, 24, 9, and Virgil, *Georgics* III, 463.].

In those regions there is a king named Gutring [Note: “Gulring,” corrected to “Gutring,” with a line drawn across the *l* and later erased in witness 1.] [Note: Guthrun. Perhaps one of the kings of Uppland, such as Gudröd, king of Gudbrandsdal, who was defeated around 1018 by Olaf the Saint, king of Norway, and was ordered into exile after his tongue had been cut out. See Snorri Sturluson, *Saga of Olaf the Holy*, chapters 34, 73, and 74.]. He was raised in clerical service at the monastery of Verden under Erpo, bishop of that place, and unworthily attained the rank of deacon.

But after the aforementioned bishop died [Note: He died in 993.], this man escaped, cast aside his name and rank, and, like another Julian [Note: “and rank … another Julian” is added in witness 1, evoking Julian the Apostate, the emperor, as a model of the demon.], abandoned them. He professed only the name of Christianity, but in many respects he is found to be far removed from it.

As soon as he was recognized by his own people, he was immediately received and elevated to hereditary kingship. Let no one praise what displeases God; let no one imitate it. Let the present fruit be despised because of the future terror. That king, a slave of sin and son of death, does not rule, as he supposes, but is weighed down by a daily burden. Concerning him the Lord cries out through Isaiah [Note: “Isaiah” is corrected from “Isaias” in witness 1.]:

“I nourished sons and exalted them, but they themselves despised me” (Isaiah 1:2).

For his conversion, and that of his companions, and for their worthy correction and perseverance, let all Christendom pray, and let it implore God never again to allow such a thing to befall its members. Although I have spoken here only of this man, there are, alas, others who have followed a similar course, not attending to Paul’s saying:

“For it is better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn away from it” (2 Peter 2:21).

### 28

But since no one is capable of describing all the varieties of the northern region, which nature produces there as more marvelous than elsewhere, or the cruel practices of that people, I shall pass them over [Note: “I pass over” is corrected to “I shall pass them over” in witness 1.] and briefly discuss the brood of vipers [Note: It should have been *geniminibus* (“offspring”), but the form was taken from the Vulgate, Matthew 23:33, and is likewise found in Jerome’s commentary on Isaiah 30.]—that is, the sons of the persecutor Swegen.

His sons were born to him by the daughter of Duke Miseco, sister of Bolizlav, Miseco’s successor and son. Long driven away by her husband [Note: That is, King Eric. She was called Sigrid the Haughty. Compare Adam, Book II, scholion 22 and chapter 28.], she endured no small controversy with the others.

Her offspring, closely resembling their father in all things, sorrowfully received and buried the body of their beloved parent after it had been brought to them. Whatever insult the English had proposed to inflict upon their father, they sought to avenge with prepared ships.

I shall pass over their many deeds, since they are unknown to me, and briefly record in writing what Sewald reported to me as known to him as fact [Note: That is, Sewald, as is clear from the following chapter.].

Æthelred [Note: “Ath.” in witness 1c.], king of the English, died in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1016. In July of that year the aforementioned brothers Harald and Cnut, together with their duke Thurketil [Note: His name was Thurkil. See *History of Great Britain*, vol. I, p. 450.] and with him [Note: “and with him” is added in witness 1b.], set out with 340 ships [Note: “Three hundred and forty” in witness 1.]. They surrounded a certain city called London, where the queen, grieving over the death of her husband and defender, was stationed with her sons Æthelstan and Edmund, two bishops, and the other leading men.

They led each ship, each carrying eighty men, along the river called the Thames and attacked the city for six months. At last the queen, exhausted by continual warfare, sent messengers to ask them for peace and carefully inquire what they demanded from her [Note: Witness 1 has *qd* for *quid* (“what”) and *eis* (“from them”) for *ea* (“from her”).].

The enemies, who could not be satisfied, immediately answered that, if the queen wished to give her sons over to death; to ransom herself with fifteen thousand pounds of silver; the bishops with twelve thousand; and all the coats of mail, whose number was an incredible twenty-four thousand; and, in addition, to give three hundred chosen hostages in expectation of these payments, then she and her companions could obtain peace and their lives. Otherwise, they all shouted three times, they would perish by a single sword [Note: “all” is added in witness 1b.].

The venerable queen, greatly disturbed by this message together with her people, after long deliberation by her heated mind, promised that she would do this [Note: “would do this” is rendered differently in witness 1c and reads “would become” in witness 1a.] and confirmed it with the soldiers named above.

Meanwhile, two brothers, in the silence of night, escaping the danger that had been promised in a small boat [Note: “Edmund and Æthelstan, kings” is added in witness 1c.], gathered as many men as they could for the defense of their homeland and the rescue of their mother, while the enemy still knew nothing of it.

But one day, when Thurketil, the pirates’ leader, went out with a multitude to ravage the nearby territories, he unexpectedly encountered them and engaged them. As soon as he saw them from a distance, he encouraged his companions, boldly attacked them, and both sides fell: Edmund and Thurketil, together with a very great multitude of their companions [Note: “Edmund the king and Thurketil the leader” is added in witness 1c.].

Neither for these men nor for the others did any hope of the desired victory arise. Wounded, they withdrew voluntarily, lamenting only that this had happened through the accidents of fortune. Scripture, however, forbids us to believe that fate or chance is anything (Wisdom 2:2).

The Danes, though weakened, then visited their allied ships [Note: Added in witness 1b.]. When they learned that assistance was coming to the city from the surviving Æthelstan and from the Britons, they cut down the hostages and fled [Note: “cut down” is misspelled in witness 1.].

May the God who protects those who hope in him destroy and annihilate them, so that they may never again harm these or any other faithful people as they are accustomed to do! In the rescue of that city, let us rejoice; in everything else, let us mourn.

> **Apparatus correction:** §29 retains MS 1 *constringeret* (“might bind”), *duci* (“to the duke”), *effitia*, and *tt* with the first *t* erased; *Thurcil* is added in 1b, while 1b *potitus est* (“obtained”) and 1a *optata* (“desired things”) are distinct. §30 has MS 1 *subseqture*; §31 has 1b *p. i. e. t.* and uncertain 1c *eidem aut idem*. In §33, *Rotberti* is erased; MS 1 has *inexuperale* and *aninculus*, and 1a *bona*. In §34 MS 1 corrects *predictam* to *predicti* and has *tristis*, *thredricus*, and *subbere*; every *add. 1b* means “added in manuscript 1b” at its own locus. The Goslar note says only that the estate was also built by the emperor; the separate Capungun note identifies Cunigundis’s canonesses’ monastery as Confugium. Retain folio/page anchors and editorial references at their source passages; erased forms remain uncertain.

### 29

I also learned from the account of the aforementioned man Sewald of a pitiable deed, and therefore one worthy of remembrance: the treacherous hand of the Northmen, under a leader named Thurkilo, seized the distinguished bishop of the city of Canterbury—*Cantuarae* in manuscript 1c, with *cantare* in manuscript 1—named Dunsten, together with the others, and bound them in chains, hunger, and indescribable suffering, according to their foul custom. [Col. 1384C–D] The erased *o* in manuscript 1 occurs in this passage. Our author intended to speak here of Elphegus, archbishop, who died in this manner in 1012, not of Dunstan, his predecessor. Compare what I said in the work cited above, vol. I, p. 444.

Moved by human frailty, he promised them money and set a delay for obtaining it—manuscript 1 reads *petrandam* for *impetrandam*—so that, if by an acceptable ransom he could not escape immediate death, he might in the meantime cleanse himself through frequent groans, a living offering to be sacrificed to the Lord. When all the appointed periods had elapsed, the ravenous Charybdis of the pirates (*piratarum*; the supplied text appears to have OCR *picarum*) summoned the servant of God and demanded, threateningly, that the tribute promised to them be paid at once.

And he, like a gentle lamb, said: “I am here, prepared for everything that you now presume to do to me; and, for love of Christ, that I may deserve to become an example of his servants, I am not disturbed today. That I seem to you a liar is caused not by my will, but by cruel poverty.” [Col. 1384D–1385A; *mihi* “to me” is added in manuscript 1b.] “I offer you this body of mine, which in this exile I have loved beyond measure, as liable to punishment, and I recognize that what you do with it lies in your power” (*qd*, an abbreviation of *quod*, appears in manuscript 1). “But my sinful soul I humbly entrust to the Creator of all things, without regard to you.” [Manuscript 1 reads *suplex commito* for *supplex committo*: “I entrust humbly.”]

As he spoke these words, the crowd of profaners surrounded him and gathered various weapons to kill him. When their leader Thurcil saw this from a distance, he hurried up and said: “Please, do not act in this way! I willingly hand over to all of you gold and silver, and everything that I have here or can acquire in any manner, except only the ship; do not sin against the Lord’s anointed.”

The anger of his companions, harder than iron and stones, was not softened by this sweet speech but appeased by the spilling of innocent blood, which they immediately poured out upon him collectively, striking him with oxen’s heads and showering him with stones and pieces of wood.

Amid all the attacks of those who raged around him, he attained heavenly joy, as the effectiveness of the following sign immediately attests. For one of the chief men, having become weak in his limbs, recognized in himself that he had sinned against Christ’s chosen one, as it is written: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Romans 12:19).

In this triumph of Christ’s athlete, his wretched persecutors were defeated; they lost both the god and the money that their leader had supplied to them, and finally, unless they repented and made satisfaction, they lost their souls. But he, with his robe—white until then through the innocence of mind and body, and now dyed red with blood—appeased the divine gaze.

May we sinners obtain this man as an intercessor through constant prayers and believe that he has great power before the divine majesty. [Col. 1385B–C]

### 30

Of the evils that the leap-year, avenger of sin, inflicted upon Christian people during the course of the year mentioned above (1016), I shall speak with no small sorrow. Magadaburg was attacked at night by Margrave Bernhard with a great multitude; there an innocent soldier of the archbishop was captured and another wounded. [Col. 1385D; the addition “Magadaburg … was wounded” occurs in manuscript 1b.]

On the fourth day before the Ides of February and on the following Friday, signs of misery appeared: at the very twilight of night, thunder with lightning and great storms resounded terribly, causing destruction in various places. Some people died when their houses were shattered by such a force; others, wounded, barely escaped death. Great damage also occurred when the forests fell. [Col. 1385D; compare the Quedlinburg Annals, year 1016.]

Count Palatine Bernhard was struck by paralysis. [Col. 1385; manuscript 1b adds the abbreviated reading “P. c. B. p. p.” and “Burchardus A. S.”]

In the province called Hassegun, four brothers—whose names were Aelli, Burchard, Thiedric, and Poppo—were often despised by a certain free man and good soldier named Ber. They gathered their forces, attacked him, and killed him, although he had no fewer than one hundred shield-bearing men; some on both sides perished. [Col. 1385; manuscript 1 reads *contempti* for *contempti*—“despised”—and manuscript 1a *utrisque* for *utrimque*, “on both sides.”] [Col. 1385D; Ber was killed together with others. Merseburg Calendar, July 26.] (July 26.)

### 31

In Longobardia the Saracens, arriving by ship, attacked the city of Luna after driving away its shepherd, and with power and security occupied the borders of that region and abused the wives of its inhabitants. Luna, a city very frequently ravaged by Saracens and Northmen, stood near the Gulf of Spezia, between Lavenza and Sarzana. Robert Wace testifies to its ruins in *Le Roman de Rou*, and Albert of Stade calls it *Wostelune*—“the desolate, devastated Luna.”

When report of this reached the apostolic lord, named Benedict, he gathered all the rulers and defenders of holy Mother Church, asked and commanded them to break into the enemies of Christ who dared such things, to fight manfully with him, and, with the Lord’s help, to kill them. Moreover, he secretly sent ahead an indescribable multitude of ships to cut off their possibility of return. [Col. 1386A–B]

When the Saracen king noticed this, he was at first indignant, but finally escaped the impending danger with a few companions in a small boat. All his men, however, assembled and attacked the advancing enemy first; and when the enemy soon fled, they—miserable to relate—struck them down for three days and nights. At last God, appeased by the groaning of the devout, looked upon them, drove away those who hated him, and defeated them so completely that, with not one of them left behind, the victors could not count the multitude of the slain and of their spoils.

Then their queen was captured and put to death because of her husband’s audacity. [Col. 1386D; “of the man’s audacity,” that is, her husband’s; manuscript 1 lacks *deest*, “is absent,” before the phrase.] The capital gold ornament belonging to her, set with gems, the pope claimed for himself above all else, and afterward sent the emperor his share, which was valued at one thousand pounds. [Col. 1386C]

After all the spoils had been divided, the victorious crowd returned home with joyful hearts and offered worthy songs to Christ triumphant. But the aforementioned king, greatly distressed by the death of his wife and companions, sent the supreme pontiff a sack filled with chestnuts and announced through the bearer that in the following summer they would bring him so many soldiers.

When the pope received this message, he returned the same purse, filled with millet, to the messenger, saying: “If it is not enough for him to have injured the apostolic endowment so severely”—the manuscripts read either “to have injured the endowment” or “to have injured the see”—“let him come a second time, and let him know for certain that he will find here as many armored men, or more” (Proverbs 16:9).
