Man thinks and speaks; God judges. May every faithful person humbly pray that he mercifully remove such a scourge and, in his goodness, grant the security of the desired peace.

### 32

On the island called Augia—manuscript 1a reads *augeat*—on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, nine ships filled with people of mixed sex sank in the sea. [Col. 1385–1387A]

In the west, Lambert, son of Reinher, was defeated by the enemy Godefrid and fell together with his men, an enemy of many. [Col. 1387A; the addition “and fell together with his men” occurs in manuscript 1b.] This was in the battle near Florines, or Fleures, on September 12; compare Balderic of Cambrai, *Chronicle* III.9 and 12, and the Liège and Lobbes Annals. [September 12, 1016.]

For there was no worse man than he in that land at that time: he strangled many people in churches with bell ropes. No one can explain how many men he disinherited or killed. He never took care to do penance for the crime he had committed. Together with his brother Reinger he killed Wirinharius and his brother Reinzo as well. [Col. 1387D; concerning Warner and Raynold, see Balderic I.94.]

Their father, sent into exile in Bohemia by Otto, died there. [Manuscript 1a reads “brother” for “father”; see Balderic, book I.] Their native land itself mourned the living and rejoiced at the lost. This alone we must lament: that on that day, because of the guilty man, so many innocent people fell on both sides of those who engaged in battle.

### 33

Other massacres also occurred in these regions at that time, alas! For in the kingdom of the peaceful and wholly venerable King Robert, more than three thousand men of the same region were killed while fighting one another.

Nor must I pass over the immeasurable loss that occurred afterward. My maternal uncle, Count Heinrich, a man of great power in Christ and in this world, rejoicing, paid the debt of both natures in a ripe old age and with a good death, on the sixth day before the Nones of October. [Col. 1387; compare the Quedlinburg Annals, year 1016; the Lüneburg Necrology, October 2; and the Merseburg Calendar, October 1.]

Moreover, Count Wigmann, useful to his homeland in every respect, fell pitiably through the urging of a second Herodias and through servile presumption. [Col. 1387C; compare Alpert II.12 and the Quedlinburg Annals, year 1016.] How this came about I shall reveal in a mournful account.

There had long been strife between the aforementioned man and Count Baldric; this had so humbled Baldric, who had often been defeated in battle, that he moved among the other nobles in great disgrace. Wigmann bore all his prosperity with an even spirit and ascribed it to divine mercy. He considered how to calm the long-raging discord by a treaty of peace. Calling his enemy amicably to his house, he appeased him with a banquet and a gift, and was invited by him to confirm the bond of the affection that had begun. But the ancient serpent, hissing through his wife, urged this plan: the man who could never be captured by force should at least be overcome by the deceitful nets of cunning.

Then the praiseworthy simplicity of the noble spirit was unguarded, as was the feigned fairness of the deceiving friend. At first he was received with great honor, but immediately afterward he was afflicted by a drink infected with poison. As excessive pain rapidly grew worse, he scarcely awaited the following day there. When he departed, having been well rewarded and greeted with affection, while his soldiers were deceitfully detained there, a certain servant secretly struck him down, in the presence of his lord Baldric, who did not avenge this in any way. [Col. 1387D–1388A; Merseburg Calendar, October 5; Hildesheim Annals, October 6; Lüneburg Necrology, October 9.]

Then one of his companions killed the perpetrator of the wicked crime, but was immediately killed himself. Baldric then fled, thereby revealing his guilt. As report spread, the misery became widely known, and Thiedric, bishop of the holy church of Mirmingend, my aunt’s son [the word “son” is supplied editorially, although more may seem to be missing], who had been waiting nearby, arrived first. He mourned the death of his beloved friend with inconsolable grief, accompanied the body as far as the city of Fretheni, and took the greatest care to lay it among his forefathers. [Col. 1388D; Fretheni is Vreden in the district of Münster.]

### 34

Thereafter, sending his messengers throughout this entire region, he himself stirred up the men of the same land and his relatives to avenge these things. With a strong force he seized the city of the aforementioned enemy, named Upplan, devastating and burning the neighboring places. [Col. 1388A; Upplan, Uplun, Uflahun, or Ubladium lay in the district of Hamaland, where the county of Zutphen was later situated, near the former abbey of Elten; it is now deserted. See the *Life of Meinwerc*, chapter 34; *Chronicon Gottwicense*, vol. I, p. 619; and Alpert II.13.]

At last my nephew, Duke Bernhard, arrived. By right of the son of the aforementioned count, who was still a child, he had become guardian of the whole inheritance and avenger of the wicked crime. [Col. 1388D; this was Wichmann IV; concerning him, see Wedekind, *Notes*, vol. II, p. 75; vol. III, p. 56.] He consoled the grieving soldiers as much as he could, while, together with his other supporters, he harassed the townsmen night and day.

Meanwhile the emperor departed from Burgundy, where he had spent much of the summer, and, as soon as he learned the entire course of events, hurried by ship to that place. On that journey my nephew Gevehard, son of Count Heribert, who was then greatly favored by the royal majesty and outstanding in every virtue, died, leaving the emperor and all who were stationed in those regions sorrowful behind him. [Col. 1388D; see the Merseburg Calendar, November 8.] [November 8, 1016.]

Archbishop Heribert of Cologne, greatly concerned on behalf of his soldier Baldric, repeatedly petitioned the emperor that he should subject the city, which had long been held, to his own authority. Overcome by his persistent request, the emperor consented.

When the enemy had then departed from the emperor, the city called Upplun was utterly destroyed, while the countess, long agitated there, was preserved, alas, together with everything she possessed. [Col. 1388D–1389A; “the city called Upplun” is added in manuscript 1b.]

May every curse that blessed Job invoked upon himself befall this woman, who deserved such a fate. Let her experience so much evil in the present time that she may at least hope for pardon in the future. Whoever should ever rise to her aid in this matter, let him turn to God, confess that he has sinned grievously, and hasten to worthy amendment; for the Church lacks the hiss of the poisonous asp of so great a defender.

In this same year Bishop Thiedric [“of Münster” is added by the Saxon Annals, year 1017] and Count Hirimannus, son of Gerberga, contending with each other over an empty matter, ravaged their own possessions. Thereafter, at the persuasion of their friends, and especially by imperial command, they were pacified and both awaited the emperor’s presence. [Col. 1389B; thus in the Saxon Annals; manuscript 1 reads *prestobantur*.]

### 35

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1017, on the Kalends of January, Archbishop Gero, by order of the emperor, received Margrave Bernhard, who promised to make amends, barefoot, and presented him to the Church, after all the bans imposed upon him had been lifted. [Col. 1389B; manuscript 1b adds “the year 1017 … imposed upon him.”]

The emperor departed from Palithi, where he had celebrated the Nativity of the Lord, and solemnly celebrated Epiphany at Alstidi. [Col. 1389; manuscript 1 reads *exigens*, “demanding,” for *exiens*, “departing.”] On that same holy night Count Frithericus, faithful to Christ and to his lord, died in his city called Ilburg.

Because he was wise and saw that the end of this life was already approaching, he gave the aforesaid city to the son of his brother, named Thiedric, on the condition that, since the latter was his heir and the transfer could not otherwise be legally effected, he would be permitted, to his own credit, to hand over to his three daughters all the property that remained.

That Thiedric afterward received the county and authority over the district of Siusili as a gift from the emperor. A public assembly of the princes was held at Altstidi. The dispute between Margrave Bernhard and the sons of my paternal uncle was settled by the amendment accepted by Bernhard and by an oath. The long-standing enmity between Bishop Thiedric and Count Hirimannus, and the hatred between Eggihard and the brothers, sons of the elder Udo, were settled by the emperor up to the third day before the Kalends of October. [Col. 1389C; the reading “third day before the Kalends of October” is in a scraped-away passage of manuscript 1b.]

There Bernhard the margrave also promised Archbishop Gero five hundred talents of silver as compensation for the damage inflicted. The emperor did many excellent things during his long stay there. Peace was made between Counts Gevehard and Willehelm. The envoys who had come from Italy returned joyfully to their own country. The emperor’s journey toward the west was postponed because of the difficulty of the road. [Col. 1389D]

The emperor approved the request made to him on behalf of Bolizlav and said that his princes should come to him; if Bolizlav wished to offer him anything good, he would gladly accept it with their counsel. [Col. 1389; “the emperor praised this” is added in manuscript 1b.] Envoys were sent back and forth, and a truce was established.

### 36

Meanwhile the emperor came to Merseburg and awaited certainty concerning this matter. At that time many robbers, defeated in single combat by gladiators, perished by hanging.

Two archbishops, Erkanbaldus [manuscript 1a reads *erkinbaldus*] [of Mainz] and Gero, together with Bishop Arnulf, Counts Sigifrid and Bernhard [“and Bernhard” is added in manuscript 1b], and the other princes, sat beside the river Mulde for fourteen days, asking through their envoys that Bolizlav come to the Elbe for the conference they had long desired.

He was then at Sciciani. [Col. 1389D; see Book VI, chapter 45.] When he heard the embassy, he said that he did not dare come there at all because of his enemies’ hostility. The envoys said: “What will you do if our lords come to the Black Elster?” He replied: “I do not even wish to cross this bridge.”

They returned after saying these things and reported all this to their lords. The emperor celebrated with us the Purification of the holy Mother of God.

Afterward the bishops and counts arrived sorrowfully because Bolizlav had scorned and deceived them, and they inflamed the emperor’s mind with their open reports. There the future expedition was discussed, and every faithful man was urged to prepare for it. The emperor firmly prohibited anyone from thereafter sending or receiving an envoy between us and the public enemy, and carefully investigated who had previously dared to do this. [Col. 1390B; manuscript 1 reads *prohibitur* for *prohibetur*.]

### 37

Thereafter the emperor departed from us and came to Magadaburg (February 9, 1017), where he was received with great honor. On the following day, Sunday (February 10), because Septuagesima was then approaching, he laid aside flesh—that is, he ceased eating meat and began to fast. [Col. 1390C–D]

On Monday (February 12), the archbishop blessed the northern chapel in the emperor’s presence. On the following day a disturbance arose between the archbishop’s companions and those of Margrave Bernhard; it was settled without danger and ended honorably for the bishop. By order of the emperor, thieves gathered there, but were defeated by those who engaged them and handed over to the noose. Many matters affecting the safety of the homeland were concluded there.

From there Gunther turned and went to preach to the Liuticians. [Col. 1390C; “From there … went” is added in manuscript 1b.] Compare the *Life of Gunther* in Canisius, *Lectiones antiquae*, vol. III, pp. 185–189, and the *Acts of the Saints* under October 9; also the Saxon Annals, years 1006 and 1008.

But although I had often complained to the emperor about the part of my parish unjustly taken away by the church of Meissen and restored by written decree, and although I hoped that useful property would come to me from it, I learned that the matter would turn out otherwise than I had thought.

For, when the emperor was seated on the feast of Saint Peter, which falls on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, and the bishops present were Gero, Meinwerc, Wigo, Ericus, and Eilwardus, I rose and made my complaint. Then the emperor and the archbishop, from whom I had hoped for assistance, ordered me—God knows against my will, since I did not dare resist them—to grant Eilwardus the parish situated on the eastern side of the river Mulde, namely in the burgwards of Bichni and Vurcin, while he would leave me the parish that he then held on the western bank, although I had never desired it. We confirmed this exchange by mutual staffs.

I testify before God and all his saints that I in no way abandoned what remained. The emperor also ordered that the three villages which lay under the aforementioned bishop should either be retained under oath by Margrave Hirimannus or by the church of Meissen, or be returned to me. [Col. 1391A–B; manuscript 1a reads *uuillas*, “villages.”]

### 38

On the same day the emperor and his consort were honored with great gifts by Archbishop Gero. On the following day (February 24) they departed from there and, on the third day, that is, Sunday, reached Halverstidi. There Bishop Arnulf received them magnificently and kept them with him for two nights. On Tuesday they set out for Quidilingeburg, where the venerable abbess Ethelhida adorned them with no less glory.

On the fourth day the monastery situated on the western hill, where nuns serve the heavenly Bridegroom in monastic clothing, was dedicated by Bishop Arnulf in the presence of the emperor, on the third day before the Kalends of March (February 27), with Archbishop Gero and the other brothers assisting him. [Col. 1391B–C; “situated on the western hill” is added in manuscript 1b; manuscript 1 reads *monachito* for *monachico*. According to the Quedlinburg Annals, year 1017, and the Saxon Chronicle, the dedication occurred on the eighth day before the Kalends of March.]

There the emperor gave a talent of gold to the altar. From there, having received great affection from his niece, he proceeded to Goslar and remained there for four weeks. [Col. 1391C; manuscript 1c adds “which he afterward built and which is called the church of Confugium.”] For at that time he greatly cultivated the place.

Because it was then Lent, he strove to carry out the things suitable for Christ and the many necessities of the world. Afterward Bertold, son of Liuthar, with his supporters, entered the city of Munna at dawn on the Kalends of April (April 1), with a hired guard, and killed Baldric, the renowned follower of Count Wigmann, who had long resisted him together with his companions; victorious, he took possession of the city. [Col. 1391D; Alpert gives a different account of these events, book II, chapter 15 and following.]

### 39

The day before, I had come to Meissen for protection. During that week our princes assembled at Goslar by command of the emperor. There the county of Heinrich, brother of my uncle Count Sigifrid, was entrusted to Sigifrid, and an expedition was organized in our regions; other matters useful and greatly necessary for the endangered homeland were also discussed. [Col. 1391D–1392A; a charter of the emperor testifies that he was at Goslar on March 26.]

When the emperor departed from there, he first learned of the evil I have mentioned and became concerned about the coming disturbance.

In that spring, in the territory of Margrave Bernhard, a sheep was born with five legs. In April, on the sixth day before the Ides, when it was already full moon, the moon was seen by many as though it were new—that is, as it is when it is first visible—and it glowed red for a long time at the third hour of the day. [Col. 1391; “In April … glowed” is added in manuscript 1b; the Saxon Annals add “namely, as when it is first seen.”]

The king celebrated Palm Sunday (April 14) at Mainz and Easter at Ingilnen; never in those regions had he been present with greater honor or authority. [Col. 1391; “at Mainz and in Ingilnen” is added in manuscript 1b in a scraped-away passage.] Because many important matters could not be concluded there amid so great a solemnity (April 21), an assembly was arranged at Aachen, and there, with the counsel of Archbishop Heribert, he reconciled Bishop Thiedric of Metz and his brother Heinrich.

The queen, departing from the emperor at Franconofurd, fell ill when she came to a place called Capungun. There she promised God that, for his praise, she would establish a monastery. [Col. 1392A–B; manuscript 1c adds “of canonesses, which she later completed and which is called the church of Confugium.”] But what happened in the meantime is not unfittingly attached to these events.

### 40

In the city of Parthenopolis there were two sisters in religious life, the elder called Alwred and the younger Irmingerd. Both led highly praiseworthy lives. They did not associate with the other nuns, but served Christ and his beloved Mother individually and diligently in the church called the Rotunda.

The younger, having lost the outward light of her eyes, enjoyed eternal brightness with her inward sight and not long afterward passed to her ever-desired homeland, on the sixth day before the Ides of February.

Her elder sister, leaning upon her niece Fritheruna, and wasting away from the repeated grief of losing her sister and from constant illness, survived no more than fourteen weeks and three days. [Col. 1392C; her name is entered in the Lüneburg Necrology on March 18.]

On the day before she paid the debt of the flesh, she fell into ecstasy and was brought into the presence of the holy Mother of God. There she was deemed worthy to see Tagino and Walter, archbishops, and the venerable bishop Aeidus, shining with great honor and showing her favor. She also recognized the maternal aunts of Archbishop Gero, named Miriswida, Emnilda, and Eddila. [Col. 1392D; “Miriswida … Eddila” is added in manuscript 1b.] One of them, leaving her abbey, was enclosed for love of Christ beside the monastery of Paul, teacher of the nations, at Rome. She also saw another named Odd. [Col. 1391; manuscript 1a reads *odila*, and the Saxon Annals *oda*.]

All the psalm-singers were singing: “I will please the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 114). [Col. 1391; “All … in the land of the living” is added in manuscript 1b.]

Meanwhile she appeared dead to everyone present. At last she awoke, lifted her eyes, and made known to all what she had seen: “Until now,” she said, “I have gladly remained with you. But now, considering these things, which are far better, I am sorry to remain any longer in this house of clay. I tell you truthfully that tomorrow I shall leave you and, by divine gift, possess the place prepared for me.”

And so it happened. Her soul, blessed in Christ, departed on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June. [Col. 1393A; See the Merseburg Calendar under May 22. [The source abbreviation *V.* means “See.”]]

Brothers in Christ, believe me that this is true, and know for certain that these women are extremely useful helpers of our church. They received me, a sinner, into their holy prayers, and, alas, never received any good from me in return.

### 41

When the emperor heard that his consort was somewhat better and had made a vow to the Lord, he offered heartfelt thanks to Christ and devoutly celebrated Pentecost (June 9) at Wirthunu, which the holy priest of God Liudiger had first built at his own expense, with Abbot Hethenric fully serving him there. [Col. 1393A–B; manuscript 1a reads *Heinrico*.]

On the following day, the fourth day before the Ides of June, Thieddegus, bishop of Prague and successor of Christ’s martyr Adalbert, faithfully went the way of all flesh. [Col. 1393B; manuscript 1a reads *antistites*; manuscript 1c gives an abbreviated form of Adalbert.]

He had been educated at New Corbie and was excellently instructed in the medical art. When the elder Bolizlav was struck with paralysis for disobeying the herald of Christ, he summoned him with the permission of Abbot Thietmar and began to feel better under his care.

But when the burning lamp Woitegus, as I have related, was removed from the darkness of this world, this man, with the assistance of the aforementioned duke, received his seat from Otto III to govern it. After the death of the elder Bolizlav, he was often expelled from it by Bolizlav’s namesake and son; as often, Margrave Ekkihard restored him, and he suffered great injuries.

He invited guests to himself, as Saint Gregory commands, and even drew them to him. He had this great fault, however: because of an illness that was not his fault, he drank beyond measure. For he was paralyzed and, because of the continual trembling of his hands, could not sing Mass without the assistance of the attending priests. Thus he languished until the end, caring for his soul, as I hope, with good medicines. [Col. 1393C; manuscript 1 reads *tremorem assiduum*; the corrected reading is *tremore assiduo*, “with continual trembling.”]

### 42

Meanwhile the Moravians (*Mararenses*; perhaps an OCR-corrupted form), soldiers of Bolizlav, deceitfully surrounded and killed an unsuspecting great troop of Bavarians, taking considerable revenge for the injury previously inflicted upon them by the Bavarians. [Col. 1393; the erased text in manuscript 1b is uncertain; manuscript 1 reads *ulcisciscentes*, “avenging.”]

As the emperor was traveling eastward, he ordered the empress to come to him at a place called Pathrebrunnun. [Col. 1393D; an imperial charter testifies that the emperor was already there on June 10; manuscript 1a reads *pathelb*.] From there the two proceeded as far as Magadaburg and were honorably received by Archbishop Gero.

On the following night, that is, Sunday, the day before the Nones of July, a dreadful storm arose, consuming men together with cattle, buildings, and crops over a wide area. An immense crash, shaking the forests, occupied all the roads with terrible force.

On the following day the emperor crossed the Elbe with his wife and army and came to Liesca, to the former estate of Bishop Wigo, then inhabited by innumerable wild animals. [Col. 1394A; see above, Book IV, chapter 14. Concerning the assembly held there, see the *Life of Meinwerc*, chapter 42, and an imperial charter of July 10, 1017. Wigo seems still to have been alive at that time, although the Lüneburg Necrology records his death on January 14; he had died by the time Thietmar wrote this.]

He remained there in camp for two nights, awaiting the delayed company. After this, when the empress and several others had returned, he advanced in separate groups.

On that same day Heinrich, a certain Bavarian duke, who had gone to Bolizlav for the sake of securing peace, returned with Bolizlav’s envoys. The emperor, having heard his report, sent him back with another embassy, and, since he accomplished nothing there, allowed him to depart to his lady and sister.

### 43

Meanwhile, on the mountain of Saint John the Baptist, situated beside Parthenopolis and subject to it together with all its appurtenances, a most pitiable event occurred on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, on a Sunday night.

A lamp in the brothers’ dormitory shone more brightly than usual. It caught what was nearby and, while those resting there realized it too late, consumed it in a devouring flame. Although everyone else escaped such danger, they lost one man who had suddenly turned back to rescue the priestly vestments and was caught in the middle of the fire while confessing his sins. His name was Hemico. [Col. 1394B–C; the Lüneburg Necrology calls him Hemmo; manuscript 1a reads *heumuco*.]

Thereafter the monastery, which its abbot Sigifrid had labored to improve for eight years, burned and troubled the hearts of those present and of those who came afterward. In addition, the fire, spreading widely, swallowed two chapels belonging to it, together with the refectory and the other adjoining workshops. From its greedy jaws, however, divine mercy and the supreme devotion of those who came running rescued all the relics of the saints and the greater part of the treasure. [Col. 1394C; manuscript 1a reads *tesauri*, manuscript 1b *teshauri*, “of the treasure.”]

When morning came, the inhabitants of the aforementioned city and those whom the emperor had left there as a garrison assembled and lamented such a loss with profound grief.

In the morning the brothers took the thin ashes of the burned body and carefully gathered them, placing them with their predecessors. Through his own messenger they announced the pitiable event to their absent abbot. [Col. 1394C–D; manuscript 1 has the malformed or divided reading *per in nuntium* for *per internuntium*, “through a messenger.”] When he learned of it, recognizing that it had happened especially because of his own sins, and since he could not remedy it, he bore it with dignified gravity.

[Col. 1395A] **44.** While these events were taking place, Miseco, son of Bolizlav, invaded Bohemia, which in the absence of its duke Othelric was resisting less than usual, with ten legions; he plundered it for two days and, returning with an innumerable multitude of captives [Note: [Col. 1395] “multitude” is written *militudine* in witness 1.], filled his father with immense joy.

But the emperor, devastating everything in his path with his army and an immense retinue of Bohemians and Luticians, came anxiously on 9 August to the city of Glogau, where Bolizlav with his men was awaiting him [Note: [Col. 1393] “avenging themselves” is read in witness 1.]; he prevented our men from pursuing the enemy, who was challenging them while hiding among the archers.

From there he sent twelve picked legions from the strong army [Note: [Col. 1395] “strong” is read as *valida* in witness 1a.] to the city called Nemzi [Note: [Col. 1395D] Nimptsch, beside the Lohe River, between Reichenbach and Ohlau.], because it had formerly been founded by our people [Note: [Col. 1395D] *Nox Niemez* in Slavic means “mute” or “foreigner,” one who does not understand their language; hence especially a German.]. These troops were sent ahead so that they might forestall the assistance that was coming to the inhabitants [Note: [Col. 1395] “which had formerly been founded” is added in witness 1b.].

When they had pitched their camp, rumor announced that the enemy was approaching. Since they were quite unable to harm them in the dark night and amid a great downpour of rain, they drove some away, while they unwillingly allowed others to enter the city.

This city lies in the district of Silesia, a name once given to it from a certain exceedingly high and large mountain [Note: [Col. 1395] Thietmar himself wrote “This city lies in the district of Silesia …” in the final lines of folio 168.]. Because of its character and size, and because the accursed pagan religion [Note: [Col. 1395] Thus A.S.; witness 1 reads *exequanda* (“to be carried out”).] had once been worshiped there, it was held in exceedingly great honor by all the inhabitants. [Note: [Col. 1395D] Mount Zlenz, the “Mountain of Silence,” now called Zobtenberg after the village of Zobten. Compare K. Zeuss, *Die Deutschen und die Nachbarstämme*, p. 663.]

After three days the emperor came to it with a strong army and ordered the city to be surrounded on every side by camps, hoping thus to block every approach to his enemy. His wise plan and good will in all matters would have been of great benefit there, if the devotion of those assisting him had supported him in carrying out these undertakings.

But now, during the silence of the night, a large force had arrived at the city through all the guard posts. Then our men were ordered to prepare every kind of siege engine [Note: [Col. 1395] Witness 1 reads *omnigenarum*.], and very similar devices were soon seen on the opposite side. I have never heard of people who tried to defend themselves with greater patience and wiser counsel.

The pagans raised a holy cross on their side and hoped to defeat our men with its aid. If anything favorable happened to them [Note: [Col. 1395] Witness 1 reads *quod* (“that which”).], they never shouted; nor did they disclose adversity by any deepening groan.

Meanwhile the Mararens entered Bohemia, captured a certain city, and came out unharmed with enormous booty. When Margrave Heinric heard that they had attempted to attack with an army, he pursued them swiftly; after killing more than a thousand men from their number and putting the rest to flight, he sent all these captives home released.

Nor should it be passed over in silence that other soldiers of Bolizlav attacked the city called Belegori on 15 August and, assaulting it in a prolonged battle, achieved nothing—thanks be to God! A great multitude of Luticians who had remained at home attacked a city belonging to the aforementioned duke. There they lost more than one hundred companions and returned in great sadness; afterward they devastated much of his property. [Note: [Col. 1395] “and there” is added in witness 1b.]

**45.** To this I shall also add the deadly encounter between Duke Godefrid and Count Gerard. Since they had long been at odds with one another, they appointed a definite day on which they and their supporters would settle the matter by a formal judgment of combat.

In August, on 6 September [Note: [Col. 1395] “in August and on 6 September” is added in witness 1b.], they clashed on an appointed plain in a flowering meadow [Note: [Col. 1395] “on an appointed plain” is added in witness 1b.]. [Note: [Col. 1396D] Our author seems to have been thinking of the battle at Florines, concerning which see above, chapter 32. For this battle of Gerard, see Balderic, Book III, chapter 11.]

But the humility of Christ softened Gerard’s pride and suddenly put his companions to flight; it struck down no fewer than three hundred men among them. One of these was a man named Walter Pulverel [Note: [Col. 1395] Added in witness 1b.], so called because he had been summoned to reduce whatever opposed him to ashes. In appearance he was a cleric, but in reality an outstanding brigand.

This centurion was shut in with his men in a single lake (*lacu*; the reading is uncertain), and then lay wounded in the battle—he to whom no shedding of blood had ever been enough. For the people say that he alone counted as a joyful day the day on which he saw his own spear spattered with human blood and the houses of the Lord, which other wicked men had spared, burning and collapsing.

Born in Burgundy and once captured by the aforesaid count, he could not be released by him until he had sworn that he would always assist him and serve him as a devoted soldier in his place [Note: [Col. 1395] “to him” is read in witness 1c.]. Thus summoned, he came here; but, delayed by divine mercy so that he might not increase his customary crimes, he did not return.

At that time Sigifridus, his lord’s son and the nephew of our empress, was captured on his side, together with Balderic and many others. Cono was wounded there [Note: [Col. 1396D] The future Emperor Conrad II, who had married Gisela, daughter of Hermann, duke of Alamannia and widow of Duke Ernest.], he who had already unlawfully married his niece, the widow of Duke Ernest [Note: [Col. 1395] “Cono was wounded … the widow” is added in witness 1b.]. The aforementioned duke lost only thirty men, and these were picked soldiers.

**46.** When all the siege engines had been completed, and the emperor had already been encamped there for three weeks, he ordered the city [Note: [Col. 1396D] That is, Nimptsch.] to be attacked. He saw all these engines quickly set ablaze after fire had been cast from the fortifications.

After this Othelric attempted to climb into the city with his men, but accomplished nothing. Then the Luticians made a similar assault and were thrown down. The emperor, seeing that his army was weakened by illness and that he was laboring in vain to capture the city, directed his exceedingly difficult march toward Bohemia. There he was received by Othelric, the unjust duke of that province [Note: [Col. 1397] “unjust” is erased in witness 1.], and honored with a fitting gift.

Meanwhile Margrave Heinric, the son of my paternal aunt, worn down by a long illness, died on 18 September, the glory of the eastern Franks. He was placed in the northern part of the monastery in his city of Suinvord and, at his own request, was buried outside the church beside the door by three bishops—Heinric, Evurhard, and the venerable Riculf [Note: [Col. 1397D] Bishops of Würzburg, Bamberg, and Trier.]. [Note: [Col. 1397] “by three bishops” is added in witness 1b.] When the emperor learned of this at Meissen, he grieved greatly.

**47.** Bolizlav, anxiously awaiting the outcome at the city of Wortizlava [Note: [Col. 1397] Witness 1a reads *unordizlavo*.] and hearing that the emperor had departed and that his city stood unharmed, rejoiced in the Lord and shared the joy of his soldiers in this world [Note: [Col. 1397] The words “in the Lord” and “in this world” were erased in codex 1 and restored in a second hand.].

More than six hundred of his infantry [Note: [Col. 1397] Witness 1a reads *sixecenti*, with its *i* corrected to *e* in 1b.] secretly made for Bohemia, hoping as usual to obtain booty there, and fell into the trap that they had intended for the enemy, with only a few escaping.

But the returning Luticians, angered, complained that dishonor had been inflicted upon their goddess. For her image, formed upon their banners [Note: [Col. 1397] “that is, upon the banners” is added in witness 1b.], had been pierced by a single stone thrown by a companion of a certain Margrave Hermann [Note: [Col. 1397] The name *heramanni* was corrected to *herimanni* in witness 1a; an *i* was subsequently erased.]. When her attendants sorrowfully reported this to the emperor, they received twelve talents as compensation.

When they wished to cross the excessively swollen river beside the city of Vurcin, they lost a second goddess together with an excellent escort of fifty soldiers. Returning home under so evil an omen, the survivors attempted, at the prompting of their misfortunes, to withdraw from the emperor’s service; but after holding a common council of their own, they were turned back by their leaders.

Who could ever describe the toil of this journey and the common loss? [Col. 1397C] The entrance into the region of Bohemia was insurmountable, but its exit was much worse. This expedition was undertaken for the destruction of the enemy; yet through our crime it greatly harmed our victorious men. For what the enemies were then not permitted to do to us was afterward accomplished through our crimes.

I shall also lament that Bolizlav’s retainers committed a crime between the Elbe and the Mulde. For, having swiftly gone out at their lord’s command on 19 September, they seized more than a thousand serfs in those regions, consumed much else over a wide area by fire, and returned by a successful route.

**48.** On 1 October the emperor came to Merseburg. There he appointed Ekkihard, abbot of Nova Civitas (“New City”), who had presided over it for twenty-three years and five months, to the church of Prague; and, with the consent of Archbishop Erkaenbald, he ordered him to be consecrated on 6 October [Note: [Col. 1397] The following events show that this should be read as 6 October, not November, as the manuscripts have it.].

There Bolizlav’s envoy promised that the long-imprisoned young Liudulf would be sent back, and asked that his soldiers, who were being held in strict custody among us, be released in exchange for him. He also carefully inquired whether it would be permissible to send an envoy to the emperor to obtain his favor.

At the constant intercession of his princes, the emperor granted all these requests. Only then did he learn that the king of the Rus [Note: [Col. 1397] *ruszurum* in witness 1a, subsequently corrected by the author.] had asked Bolizlav, as he had promised him through an intermediary [Note: [Col. 1397] “as he had promised him” is added in witness 1b.], and had accomplished nothing there concerning the city he possessed.

Later the aforesaid duke invaded the Rus’ kingdom with an army and restored to the throne his son-in-law and that man’s brother, who had long been expelled; then he returned joyfully.

When the emperor departed from us, he gave three altar cloths and a silver pitcher [Note: [Col. 1397] “three altar cloths … From there” is added in witness 1b; “silver” is followed in codex 2 by “of our church.”]. From there he came to Alstidi, where he celebrated the memory of all the saints with fitting veneration. On that same day Herdingus, whom the emperor had appointed abbot of Nova Civitas there, was consecrated by Archbishop Gero.

On the following Sunday, that is, 3 November, the emperor gave to our brethren serving Christ at Merseburg a certain estate called Rogalici [Note: [Col. 1397D] Roeglitz near Schkeuditz.], which he had acquired in an exchange from Hathold, a soldier acceptable to him. He also assigned for their use a certain forest purchased from Hager, the brother of the aforementioned lord, for ten talents of silver [Note: [Col. 1397] “Hager” is written *hogero* in witness 1c?], and ordered these grants to be confirmed by his charter.

He also granted me the three churches situated at Libzi, Olscuizi [Note: [Col. 1397D] Oelschau near Leipzig.], and Gusua [Note: [Col. 1397D] A charter of the emperor’s donation of the church of Gusua, now Geusa, dated 3 November 1017, still survives.].

In this springtime [Note: [Col. 1398D] That is, in the spring of this year.], he had ordered the same golden altar to be made for the adornment of our church. For it I gave six pounds of gold from the resources of our old altar [Note: [Col. 1397] “of gold” is added in witness 1b.].

But after the emperor had remained in the aforesaid city for five weeks and four days, he visited Bavenberg, a place dear to him. There [Note: [Col. 1397] “where then, and … on the first [night] … remaining intact” is added in witness 1b.], then in December, on the first night following the emperor’s arrival, Guncelin, who had long been held in custody [Note: [Col. 1398D] Compare Book VI, chapter 36.], was released: the chain fell gently from his feet, constrained by divine majesty, while remaining intact. He also restored to his former honors on Sunday Heinric [Note: [Col. 1397] Added in witness 1b.], once duke of the Bavarians, who had been deposed through his own fault for eight years and almost as many months, to his former honors [Note: [Col. 1397] “to his former honors” is added in witness 1b.], just as Archbishop Poppo of Trier had previously guaranteed to him [Note: [Col. 1397] “on Sunday” is added in witness 1b.].

[Col. 1398D] (Folio 172.) But before I bring this year to its conclusion, I shall insert a few matters that must be said here.

[Col. 1399A] **49.** Thietmar, venerable bishop of the holy church of Asenbrunn [Note: [Col. 1399] Witness 1a reads *asenbrunniensis*.], servant of Saint Maurice at Magdeburg and formerly a useful provost at Mainz and Aachen, lost the visible light in the preceding year when a certain darkness obscured it [Note: [Col. 1399] “in the preceding year” is added in witness 1b.]. Now, with his inner eye shining more brightly, he contemplates Christ, the source of all light, with unremitting labor.

He succeeded at the hands of King Heinric to his predecessor Nonnonus, who was called Othilulfus [Note: [Col. 1399D] He is called *Wodilulphus* in an imperial charter of 28 July 1002; *Wotellolfus* in the *Life of Meinwerk*, chapter 12; and *Vthilolfus* in the Osnabrück necrology, under 17 February, the day on which he died in 1003.].

In this year the distinguished bishops Amulric [Note: [Col. 1399] *Amulric* was corrected to *Amalricus* in witness 1c; “and” is added in witness 1b.] [Note: [Col. 1399D] Compare the Lüneburg necrology, 5 February.] and Fermundus and Becelinus died, as did Altmannus, after sitting only a few weeks. He had been a monk of Saint John the Baptist at Magdeburg. From there Abbess Haethelheida [Note: [Col. 1399] *hath.* in witness 1c?], because he belonged to her household, gave him to Arnulf, the king’s brother and now archbishop of the church of Ravenna, for service. He was later consecrated by Arnulf and was injured by a poisoned drink administered by his own men [Note: [Col. 1399] Added in witness 1b in a blank space.].

**50.** In my neighborhood, in the town called Silivellun [Note: [Col. 1400D] Selben near Delitzsch?], a certain miracle occurred in the second week of December.

There was a woman whose husband was not at home. She had bolted her house upon herself and her children, and behold, before cockcrow an immense sound was heard by her. Astonished at such things, she summoned her neighbors with continual shouting and disclosed her distress [Note: [Col. 1399] Witness 1a reads “calling upon” instead of “summoning.”]. When they wished to help her, they were repeatedly driven back by blows.

At last they broke down the door and entered with drawn swords, carefully investigating what had rebelled so violently against the mother of the household or against them themselves. Finding no enemy—for it was a monstrous thing—they went out sadly.

The woman, expecting an anxious day, summoned a priest early the next day. He purified the whole house with relics of the saints and blessed water. On the following night she was shaken only slightly by the terror mentioned above and, thanks be to God, was freed through the priest’s frequent visits [Note: [Col. 1399] Witness 1a reads “on the next night.”].

Whenever something of this kind occurs, it portends some new event. Let every believer not fear that terror for himself, but recognize in his heart that he is a sinner; and, continually fortifying himself with the sign of the holy cross, let him completely exclude every hostile power. The enemy thus mocks the unwary and finally deceives those who believe in him.

Where there is then desolation, or a crime is about to follow, or some change is impending, such a thing precedes it as a sign [Note: [Col. 1399] Added in witness 1b.]. Since it is good for us to cling to God and place our hope in him, let us anticipate his holy face with continual prayers, so that, whether something is signified to us or concealed from us [Note: [Col. 1399] Witness 1 reads “is concealed” rather than “be concealed.”], his most merciful kindness may be fulfilled in us sinners.

It is not surprising that such a portent appears in these regions. For those inhabitants rarely come to church and pay no attention to visiting their guardians. They worship household gods and, hoping that these will be of great benefit to them, offer sacrifices to them.

I heard of a certain staff, at whose top there was a hand holding an iron ring. It was carried with the shepherd of the village where it had been through all the houses, and at his first entrance the bearer would greet it in this way: “Watch, Hennil, watch!”—for that was its name in the rustic language. The fools who feasted there luxuriously believed that they were protected by its guardianship [Note: [Col. 1400D] See J. Grimm, *Deutsche Mythologie*, pp. 286 and 699.].

They did not know the words of David: “The idols of the nations are the work of human hands, and so forth.” [Col. 1400B] “Let those who make them and all who trust in them become like them” (Psalm 113:4, 8).

**51.** Since everything rare is necessarily worthy of wonder, and often causes one to be amazed as at a portent [Note: [Col. 1399] A different hand continues.], I shall explain an event that occurred in our own time.

While the most serene King Heinric ruled [Note: [Col. 1399] Erased in witness 1.] and my predecessor Wigbert was active, it happened in a certain village called Rotlizi [Note: [Col. 1399] A *t* and a second *i* are erased in witness 1.], that is, Rochlitz [Note: [Col. 1400D] Rochlitz.]. The provost Gezo then held it as a benefice; the venerable matron Ida, daughter-in-law of the first Otto, had transferred it to our church [Note: [Col. 1400D] See above, Book II, chapter 2.]. I learned this truthfully from him.

During a difficult harvest, when on one of the days his workers, already exhausted, wished to refresh themselves, they saw blood flow from a loaf that had just been cut. Astonished, they showed it to their lord and to their fellow citizens.

[Col. 1400C] (Folio 173.) In my opinion, this portent signified beforehand the outcome of the war that was to come and the blood of many people that would flow in it.

I shall also describe another event, much more praiseworthy though nevertheless marvelous and worthy of remembrance. In the Romulean citadel, which is the head of all cities because of the diverse kinds of matters found there, oil flowed for an entire day from a hole in the pavement in one church, on the right side of the altar, with many people seeing and marveling at it.

John, son of Crescentius, sent some of this oil in a little flask to his lord, the elder Heinric, then our king. Since oil is now understood as mercy, as in the words, “May oil not fail from your head” (Ecclesiastes 9:8), and now as flattery, as in: “May the oil of the sinner not anoint my head” (Psalm 140:5) [Note: [Col. 1399] “Oil … as in” is added in witness 1b.], I discerned in this sign the abundant clemency of our ruler and the hidden wantonness of that patrician.

For he, the destroyer of the apostolic see, often openly honored the king established by God with his gifts and lavish promises [Note: [Col. 1401] “his” is erased in witness 1.]. Yet he greatly feared that the king would ascend to the height of imperial dignity and secretly tried by every means to prevent it. For, as blessed Gregory says: “Earthly exaltation is confounded when heavenly majesty is revealed.”

Our king, although he was a human being, possessed zeal for God and, strongly armed, avenged the violent plundering of holy churches. He would not have possessed this kindness unless it had been granted to him from heaven [Note: [Col. 1401] Added in witness 1b.]. But that earthly man, earthly by nature and by his deeds, dragged into plunder through a filthy abyss what many devout hands had heaped upon the altar of the apostles as an offering for sins [Note: [Col. 1401] Witness 2 reads “granted” instead of “heaped”; A.S.].

When he died not long afterward, he was, as I fear, confounded by a double punishment, and greater security was opened to the lord pope and greater power to our king.

**52.** I shall proceed further in my discussion and briefly touch upon the unjust action of Wlodemir, king of the Rus.

Having taken a wife from Greece named Helena [Note: [Col. 1401] Added in witness 1b.], betrothed to Otto III [Note: [Col. 1401] Witness 1a reads “in the third year, to Otto.”] but taken from him by deceitful cunning [Note: [Col. 1401D] Compare the Hildesheim Annals, year 995. The matters Thietmar relates here seem to concern Wlodemir, king of the Rus. Yet Wlodemir married not Helena but Anna, sister of Basil and Constantine; and this marriage had already been contracted in 998, therefore long before this embassy, as Pagius noted under the year 987, no. 6. URS.], he accepted the faith of holy Christianity at her urging, but did not adorn it with righteous works.

For he was an unrestrained fornicator and a cruel man, and inflicted great violence upon the effeminate Danes. Having three sons, he married one of them to the daughter of Bolizlav, our duke and persecutor [Note: [Col. 1402D] Zentopulc or Swaetopolc. See below, Book VIII, chapter 16.]. Reinbern, bishop of the Salsae-Cholberg church, was sent with her by the Poles.

Born in the district called Hassegun and educated in the liberal arts by prudent teachers, he rose to the episcopal rank, worthy, I hope. How much he labored in the pastoral care entrusted to him, neither my knowledge nor my eloquence is sufficient to say.

He destroyed and burned the temples of idols; he purified the sea worshiped by demons by casting into it four stones anointed with sacred chrism and by means of blessed water; and he brought forth a new planting of sacred preaching for almighty God on an unfruitful tree—that is, among a very foolish people.

Afflicting his body by constant vigils, abstinence, and silence, he fixed his heart upon the mirror of divine contemplation.

When the aforesaid king heard of him, he seized him, together with his son and wife, at the secret urging of Bolizlav, who was to resist him, and shut him in solitary custody. There the venerable father diligently performed in secret the praise of God that could not be performed openly.

When he reconciled himself to the supreme priest as an offering through continual tears and prayer poured forth from a contrite heart [Note: [Col. 1401] Witness 1 reads “was reconciled” instead of “reconciled himself.”], he was released from the narrow prison of the body and joyfully passed into the freedom of everlasting glory.

The name of the aforementioned king is wrongly interpreted as “power of peace”; for that peace which impious men hold among themselves or the inhabitants of this world possess, since it always totters [Note: [Col. 1401] Witness 1a reads “they totter.”]. True peace belongs only to the one who, composing every movement of his own spirit, earns the kingdom of God through the consolation of conquering patience amid distress.

That bishop, seated in heavenly security, laughs at the threats of the unjust man, possesses a twofold chastity [Note: [Col. 1402D] Compare Book V, chapter 25, “twofold charity,” and Book VIII, “twofold innocence.”], and watches the avenging flames of that fornicator; for, as our teacher Paul testifies, “God judges adulterers” (Hebrews 13:4).

Bolizlav, learning all these things, did not cease to avenge them as far as he could.

After this that king, full of days, died, leaving the integrity of his inheritance to two sons, while the third was still in prison. The latter later escaped, left his wife there, and fled to his father-in-law.

The aforesaid king possessed a lascivious girdle [Note: [Col. 1401] *venereum* was corrected from *venerium* in witness 1.], a great increase of inborn weakness. But Christ, the teacher of our salvation, when he ordered our loins, filled with an abundance of harmful lust, to be girded (Luke 12:35) [Note: [Col. 1401] Added in witness 1b.], made known continence, not any provocation.

And because the aforesaid king had heard from Christ’s preachers about the burning lamp, he cleansed the stain of his completed sin by the continual generosity of almsgiving. For it is written: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.”

When he had reached an extremely advanced age and had long possessed the aforesaid kingdom, he died. He was buried in the great city of Cujewa [Note: [Col. 1402D] Kiev.], in the church of Christ the martyr and Pope Clement, beside his aforementioned wife, their sarcophagi standing openly in the middle of the church.

His power was divided among his sons, and Christ’s saying was confirmed in every respect. For I fear that what the voice of Truth declares will follow and be fulfilled: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated” (Luke 11:17), and so forth. May all Christendom pray that God may wish to change this sentence in those regions.

Since I have now digressed a little, I shall return and briefly disclose what occurred in the aforementioned year but was left unexamined above.

**53.** The greater part of the imperial palace at Palithi, the major church in the city of Trajectum with all the residences of Bishop Ethelbaldi, and the city of Count Thiedric, Ilburg, were accidentally destroyed by fire [Col. 1403A] (in the year 1017).

The emperor, departing from Bavenberg [Note: [Col. 1403] Witness 1a reads *bauvanberge*.], first came to Würzburg and then to Frankfort, where he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord with festive rejoicing.

But lest the authority of this name remain further hidden from you, reader, I wish to explain it to you as I heard it from trustworthy men.

When the Emperor Charles the Great, son of King Pippin, was reigning, war broke out between his men and our predecessors. In that battle the Franks were defeated by our people. When they were forced to cross the river called the Main while wandering about without any certain ford, they followed a hind going before them and, by divine mercy, showing them a kind of road; thus they joyfully reached the safety of the desired bank. From this event the place was called the ford of the Franks.

During that expedition, when the aforesaid emperor realized that he had already been overcome by the enemy, he went ahead saying: “It is more acceptable to me that the people should say, reproaching me, that I fled from here than that I fell here; for while I live, I hope to avenge the weight of the injury inflicted.”

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 800 [Note: [Col. 1403] In the year 800, the individual letters *p* were written in an erasure by witness 1a rather than 1b; after *DCCC* a blank space was left.], the aforesaid emperor [Note: [Col. 1403] “Charles” is added in witness 1c.] established eight bishoprics in Saxony, subject to Christ, with individual parishes, thereby gilding the glory of his virtue and good work.

[Col. 1403B] Codex 2 adds the following [compare above, p. 840, and A.S., year 822]:

“His son, the lord Luduwicus, selected the most proven monks from Gaul together with the venerable man Adelhard, gave them the relics of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, built the monastery of Corvey for him, and had it dedicated. The emperor himself then granted that monastery donations, namely the abbeys of Eresburg and Meppen and many estates in the north, as well as the village of Höxter with all its boundaries.

His son also, the younger Ludowicus, gave the abbey of Visbek, as well as tithes with the tithes-paying churches in the bishopric of Osnabrück, and the fishery on the Weser called Hocwar; these matters have already been mentioned above.

In this monastery monastic discipline first flourished in Saxony, and afterward in many places of that land. Corvey is rightly regarded as the head and mother of all of them and, in a certain sense, the glory of the whole country, together with its Saint Vitus. From the time he came into this land, Saxony has held the chief place in the Teutonic kingdom, because, as we hope, it is assisted in all things before God by his prayers and merits.” [Col. 1403D] Compare Widukind I, 34.

**54.** Four large Venetian ships, laden with various spices, suffered shipwreck in the aforementioned year [Note: [Col. 1403] “in the aforementioned year” is added in witness 1b.].

And, as I said earlier, in the western regions, which had rarely been peaceful before, everything remained peaceful, thanks be to God!

Ekkihardus, my fellow brother, a monk of Saint John the Baptist at Magdeburg, was afflicted by paralytic illness and lost the power of speech.

On the border of Bavaria and among the Mararens, a certain foreigner named Colomannus was seized by the inhabitants as though he were a spy. They compelled him by dreadful tortures to confess a crime he had not committed.

When he protested his innocence too vehemently and affirmed that he wandered in this way as a poor man of Christ, he was hanged while innocent from a tree that had long been dry. For his flesh [Note: [Col. 1403] The manuscript note reads: “Although he affirmed it, fixed by evil intent, the flesh could not be torn away. For they hanged him innocent upon *a. d. a.* [abbreviation uncertain]. But the Lord showed what the wicked had done to him. For his flesh …”] was later slightly cut by someone and shed blood; his fingernails and hair continued to grow. The tree itself also blossomed and showed that he was a martyr of Christ.

When Margrave Heinric learned of this, he buried his body at Mezilecun [Note: [Col. 1403D] Melk on the Danube, a monastery in Lower Austria. Compare the *Passion of Saint Colomannus* in Pez, *Scriptores rerum Austriacarum*, I.].

# BOOK EIGHT

## HERE BEGINS THE SECOND BOOKLET OF THE EMPEROR HEINRIC II

[Note: [Col. 1403] Written in red by the scribe on the last line of the page in codex 1; perhaps by Thietmar himself.]

[Col. 1403C] **1.** (Folio 176.) In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1018, indiction 2, in the sixteenth year of the lord Emperor Heinric Augustus and the fourth year of his empire, the Circumcision of the Lord and the Epiphany were reverently celebrated by him in the aforementioned city.

Ecelinus the Lombard was released from four years of imprisonment on 25 January [Note: [Col. 1403] “Ecelinus … was released” is added in witness 1b; *quadringenni* was corrected to *quadrienni*.]. [Note: [Col. 1403D] See above, Book VII, chapter 1.]

Afterward, at his command and after the repeated supplication of Duke Bolizlav [Note: [Col. 1403] The *u* is erased in witness 1.], peace was confirmed by oaths in a certain city called Budusin by Bishops Gero and Arnulf and by Counts Hirimann and Triedric. It was confirmed by Fritheric, his chamberlain, on 30 January—not as was fitting, but as could then be done. After selected hostages had been received, the aforementioned lords returned.

Four days later Oda, daughter of Margrave Ekkihard [Note: [Col. 1404D] Of Meissen. Oda was the fifth wife of Bolizlav; see above, Book IV, chapter 37.], long desired by Bolizlav and then summoned by her son Otto, came to Cziczani [Note: [Col. 1403] Witness 1a reads *zizani*, with two superscript *c*s.]. [Note: [Col. 1404D] Perhaps Zitzen in the district of Luckau in Lower Lusatia. URS.]

Since it was night, she was received with many lights by an immense multitude of both sexes, and after Septuagesima she married the aforesaid duke without canonical authorization. Until then she had lived without the customary life of a married woman, and she was altogether worthy of so great a union [Note: [Col. 1403] The *o* is erased in witness 1.].

## 2.

In the kingdom of this bridegroom there are many different customs; although dreadful, some are nevertheless at times commendable. For his people must be pastured like oxen [Col. 1405A] and chastised in the manner of a sluggish ass, and they cannot be dealt with safely for the ruler without severe punishment. If anyone presumes in this matter to abuse the wives of others or thus to commit fornication, he immediately experiences the following penalty of vengeance. He is led to the market bridge and nailed through the scrotum [Note: [Col. 1405] *claue*, manuscript 1]. With a razor placed nearby, he is given the harsh choice either of dying or of freeing himself from this condition. Whoever is found to have eaten meat after Septuagesima is severely punished by having his teeth knocked out. For the divine law, newly arisen in these regions, is reinforced by such authority more effectively than by the fast instituted by the bishops [Note: [Col. 1405] *ienuio*, manuscript 1].

There are also other customs among them, much inferior to these, which neither please God nor benefit the natives except by inspiring terror; I have dealt with them in part above [Col. 1405B] [Note: [Col. 1405] *illi duci*, manuscript 2]. I do not think it necessary to discuss further a matter whose name and practice, if almighty God so willed, would be better hidden from us. All this—that his father and he have been joined to us in marriage and close association—has brought, and continues to bring, more ensuing harm than preceding good. For although he loves us for a time under a pretended peace, nevertheless he does not cease, through secret varieties of temptation, to lead us away from mutual charity and our innate freedom, and, whenever time and opportunity come to him, to rise up in open destruction.

In the time of his father, when he was still a pagan [Note: [Col. 1405] *jam*, erased in manuscript 1], each woman, after her husband’s funeral and cremation, followed it by being beheaded. If any prostitute was found, she was circumcised on her genitalia, in a shameful and pitiable punishment; and, if one may say so, that foreskin was hung at the doors, so that the eye of anyone entering, offended by it, might be all the more watchful and prudent in future matters [Col. 1405C] (f. 177′). The Lord’s law commanded such a woman to be stoned, while the institution of our own carnal parents urges that such women be beheaded. But among people today, because the freedom to sin dominates everywhere more than is right or customary, some portion of married women, more numerous than the suppressed crowd of maidservants, itch with sexual desire as a harmful irritation scratches beneath them and commit adultery while their husbands are alive [Note: [Col. 1405] *add.*, manuscript 1b]. Nor is this enough for them: through the adulterer, by secretly inspiring a plot, a woman hands her husband over to death; and afterward, with the same man publicly accepted, she abuses him, alas, as an example of evil to the others [Col. 1405D] [Note: [Col. 1405] *add.*, manuscript 1b].

Their lawful, albeit detestable, husband is repudiated, and his soldier is preferred by these women—as sweet Abro and gentle Jason are. [Note: [Col. 1405] Manuscript 1a reads *amabo* (“I shall love”); manuscript 2 reads *Absolon* (“Absalom”). Ursinus notes that Thietmar meant Abro, a lecherous Greek whose dissolute life became proverbial; see Erasmus, *Adagia*, p. 1176, Wechel edition, 1599.] Because this is not now avenged by severe punishment, I fear that, as a new custom, it is cultivated by many more and more each day.

O priests of the Lord [Col. 1406A], rise up manfully and, with nothing hindering you, repeatedly tear this newly sprung bramble out by the roots with a sharp ploughshare. You also, laymen [Note: [Col. 1405] *religiosi* (“religious men”), manuscript 2], do not assist such people [Note: [Col. 1405] “You also … do not assist such people” is added in manuscript 1b]. May Christ permit married people to live innocently and, once these adulterous subverters [Note: [Col. 1405] *mechis* (“adulterers”), manuscript 2] have been uprooted, to lament forever with unfailing chastity.

May our helper [Note: [Col. 1405] manuscript 1a perhaps reads *uestri* (“your [helper]”)] Christ destroy them by the mighty Spirit of his holy mouth, unless they repent [Note: [Col. 1405] “unless they repent” is added in manuscript 1b], and scatter them through the great illumination of his second coming. For now, let it suffice that I have said this about them (f. 178), since something remains to be narrated concerning the misfortune of the aforementioned duke.

## 3.

He possessed a certain city situated on the border of his kingdom and that of the Hungarians. Its guardian was the elder Procui, maternal uncle of the Pannonian king, who had previously been expelled from his own domains by that same king, as he had recently been. Since he could not free his wife from captivity, he received her as a gift through the generosity of his nephew, although the latter was his enemy. I have never heard of anyone who spared the conquered so greatly [Note: [Col. 1405] *aliquaem*, manuscript 1a]; and for this reason God granted him diligent victory in the city mentioned above, as in the others.

His father was named Dewix, exceedingly cruel and killing many because of his sudden rage. When he became a Christian, he sowed violence to strengthen this faith against his resisting subjects, and, burning with zeal for God, washed away his former crime. He used to sacrifice to almighty God and to various illusions of the gods; when his bishop accused him on this account, he declared that he was rich and sufficiently powerful to do such things.

His wife, Beleknegini—that is, “beautiful lady,” as she is called in the Slavonic language—drank excessively and, traveling on horseback like a soldier, killed a certain man in the excessive heat of her anger [Col. 1406C] [Note: [Col. 1405] *iracudiae*, manuscript 1]. This polluted hand would have been better at drawing thread from a spindle than at drawing a sword from its sheath, and patience would have restrained her deranged mind [Note: [Col. 1405] “This polluted hand would have been better at drawing thread from a spindle than at drawing a sword from its sheath,” and so forth, manuscript 2].

## 4.

At that time the Liutici, always united in evil, attacked in a great troop Mistizlav, their elder, who in the preceding year had given no assistance to the imperial expedition [Col. 1405D; see above, Book VII, chapter 44]. They devastated a very large part of his kingdom and forced his wife and daughter-in-law to flee, while he gathered himself with chosen soldiers inside the fortification of the city of Zuarina. Then, by their own perversely counselled cunning, through natives rebellious against Christ and their own lord, they compelled him scarcely to escape from his paternal inheritance [Col. 1406D; it is uncertain whether this should be connected with Adam of Bremen, Book II, chapter 30 and scholion 25 concerning Mystivoi. Thietmar, chapter 33, and Helmold, Book I, chapter 18, agree better with Thietmar].

This abominable presumption took place in February, a month revered by pagans for purification and the presentation of the required offering; it received its name from the infernal god Pluto, who is called Februus [Col. 1407A; see Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book I, chapter 13].

Then all the churches erected in these regions in honor and service of Christ fell through fires and other destructions; and, most lamentably, the image of the Crucified One was mutilated [Note: [Col. 1407] “and, most lamentably, the image of the Crucified One was mutilated, and …” is added in manuscript 1b]. The worship of idols was set up in place of God, and the mind of this people, who are called Abotriti and Wari [Col. 1407D; Wari, or Wairi, means Wagrien, where Aldenberg was Bishop Bernard’s see], was hardened for these things like Pharaoh’s heart.

They claimed liberty for themselves through the notorious deceitful practice of the Liutici [Note: [Col. 1407] *mota*, manuscript 1a], but, having shaken off Christ’s gentle yoke, they voluntarily subjected their neck to the heavy burden of the devil’s domination, although previously they had used a better father and a nobler lord in everything [Note: [Col. 1407] *patre ac mobiliori*, “a father and one more changeable/mobile,” alternate reading]. Let the members of Christ mourn this weakness of theirs and complain to their Head, continually asking in their minds that it be changed for the better [Col. 1407B] (f. 179), and, for their part, insofar as possible, refusing to let these things continue [Note: [Col. 1407] “and” is added in manuscript 1b].

Bernard [Note: [Col. 1407] “Bernard, fellow brother of Parthenopolis,” appears in a passage erased in manuscript 1b], my fellow brother of Parthenopolis and at that time bishop of this apostate people [Col. 1407D; Adam of Bremen, Book II, chapter 34, calls him Benno], as soon as he learned of it, did not cease to report it to our emperor, moved not by immense grief over his secular loss but rather over his spiritual loss. Having heard this embassy, the emperor sighed heavily, but deferred his response concerning such matters until Easter [Col. 1407D; in March of the year 1019 we find Bennon of Slavonia with the emperor; see above, Book II, B. 173], so that, through prudent counsel, what had been joined together by an ill-fated conspiracy might be annulled. May almighty God favor this prayer and salutary secret [Note: [Col. 1407] *decretum* (“decree”), manuscript 2].

Let no faithful heart fall into despair because of this misfortune, or say that the day of judgment is approaching. For, according to the true admonition of Paul, before the dissension [Note: [Col. 1407] “the secession of the Roman Empire,” manuscript 2] and the accursed coming of Antichrist [Note: [Col. 1407] *antechristi*, corrected to *antichristi* in manuscript 1] (2 Thess. 2:1), no such speech ought to arise from these events, nor should sudden agitation come among Christians, since their unanimity ought to be steadfast in the highest matters [Note: [Col. 1407] *sumis*, manuscript 1]. Let mortal diversity waver as much as it wishes, and let the manifold inequality of its ways do the same. Every human being, a flower of the field, must first be reborn by Mother Church into the innocence of Christ the Savior. Unexpected calamity is then to be feared when firm peace and tranquility are proclaimed everywhere.

For this reason we are always admonished to be attentive and watchful, since we cannot be certain about the future or endure permanently in our frailty. Let no one distrust that the last day will come, nor desire that it arrive quickly [Note: [Col. 1407] “or come” is added in manuscript 1b], because it is to be feared by the just, and much more by all who need correction.

## 5.

Now I shall turn away from these matters and speak of the prosperity that has recently arisen for our emperor. For his maternal uncle, Rothulf, king of the Burgundians, granted him his crown and scepter, together with his wife, stepchildren, and all his nobles, and the confirmation of the oath was renewed; this was done at Mainz in the aforementioned month. An omen occurred at Malacin on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March.

In the same month, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, a great synod was held at Nijmegen. My nephew Oddo [Col. 1407D; according to the *Saxon Annals*, he was one of the leading Franks, Count of Hammerstein; he is mentioned in the *Life of Saint Godehard, Bishop of Hildesheim*, chapter 4; compare the *Quedlinburg Annals*, year 1020, and the *Life of Meinwerk*, chapters 62 and 75], and his wife Irmirgerd, who had long been unlawfully joined in a close degree of consanguinity [Note: [Col. 1407] “unlawfully” is added in manuscript 1b], were excommunicated for disobedience to the continual summons. Their accomplices, however, were summoned by the bishops to make satisfaction [Col. 1408B].

There it was established, after an ancient exemplar had been read through, that the Lord’s Body should be placed on the left and the chalice on the right [Note: [Col. 1407] “the priest’s chalice,” manuscript 2] [Note: [Col. 1407] this passage is added in manuscript 1b, although the words “on the left” are lacking there].

At that time the archbishop of Milan died [Col. 1408D; Arnulf], and his provost, Hiribertus, succeeded him. In England, thirty shiploads of pirates were killed by their king, the son of King Swein—thanks be to God! [Col. 1408D; see *Geschichte Großbritanniens*, vol. I, p. 464]. The man who had previously been an invader and constant destroyer of the province alongside his father now sat as its sole defender, like the basilisk on the Libyan sands, which are empty of inhabitants (Lucan, 9:726).

During this Lent, and within my episcopate, a certain man killed his brother, alas. But when the emperor discovered at the aforementioned place that Baldricus, who had offered no legitimate excuse concerning the killing of Count Wigmann, was resisting with his conspirators, he celebrated Palm Sunday and holy Easter there (1018, March 30 and April 6). Wolcmarus, abbot of Fulda and Lorsch, died [Col. 1408D; our author was deceived by this name. In 1018, on April 7, Abbot Bobbo died; see above, Book VI, chapter 56]. (f. 180) In those days the sun appeared portentously to some people as half-diminished before its setting [Note: [Col. 1407] “Wolcmarus—appeared,” with the second *u* erased, is added in manuscript 1b].

## 6.

Meanwhile, while swift rumor might bring me some new matter to write, I now burn to explain the life of a pious woman, which earlier I, guilty and exceedingly forgetful, passed over without discussing [Note: [Col. 1407] the preceding words occur in an erased passage in manuscript 1b].

In the time of King Henry II there was a certain solitary woman named Sisu, in a place called Thrubizi [Col. 1408D; Traubitz], of immense piety and therefore indescribable to me. When she was already grown and was betrothed by someone during the time of Otto the Great, she hastened swiftly to Christ, whom she had impressed as the special seal of faith upon her heart above all others [Note: [Col. 1409] a note appearing at the foot of column 1049 states: “This note appears at the foot of column 1049, but the callout number ‘1830*’ has not been printed in the text,” added in manuscript 1b].

In the solitude of the aforementioned city she strove to offer herself as a chaste virgin to her heavenly Bridegroom for sixty-four years [Note: [Col. 1409] “seventy-two years,” manuscript 1a], and endeavored to preserve herself undefiled, beyond what human frailty permits.

During so long an interval she never warmed the harsh cold by any fire. Instead, this was her greatest comfort: she revived her feet or hands, which were then almost failing, with a slightly warmed stone. Through continual prayers and intermittent tears she adorned the interior of her cell; outside, she greatly benefited the people who flocked to her through frequent instruction and necessary consolation. She did not throw away the worms that continually devoured her, but replaced those that fell, after the manner of the monk Symeon, who stood for a long time on a column [Note: [Col. 1409] the sentence concerning the worms is added in manuscript 1b].

Whatever she continually received from the people’s offerings, she withheld from herself and generously distributed to Christ’s poor, thereby redeeming the sins of those who offered them [Col. 1409B]. This woman was kind to my mother and firmly promised that her remembrance would be maintained by her descendants [Note: [Col. 1409] the associated note is absent from Migne’s printed edition].

Striving amid the struggle of this faltering world, she abstained from every illicit thing, not for the sake of receiving corruptible glory, but for the flowering crown of the heavenly prize, with which she deserved to be divinely clothed on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March [Col. 1409D; compare the Necrology of Lüneburg, February 16].

On that night, when the lamp beloved by Christ had been set in the starry heavens, I, a sinner, was sleeping in the dormitory at Magdeburg. God is my witness that I do not lie: before matins I dreamed that two boys came forth from the ancient treasury, which still stood there, singing this antiphon [Col. 1409C]: “Martin is joyfully received into Abraham’s bosom,” and so forth.

These infants proclaimed her twofold innocence and reward [Note: [Col. 1409] another reading has “The infants proclaimed her twofold innocence and first,” namely piety in poverty of spirit and humility of heart, and the heavenly harmony that she deserved]. In her piety, poverty of spirit, and humility, all this was present, and she merited what follows [Note: [Col. 1409] the sentence concerning the infants is added in manuscript 1b]. I then announced this to my brothers: “Know for certain,” I said, “that a soul dear to God has now departed from this light.” Six days later it was reported to us that, just as I had seen, the true servant of God had indeed passed from the prison of the flesh.

## 7.

I shall now take up the remembrance of my fellow brother Bernarius, who, through the friendship he showed me, won from me sincere affection and, if that had benefited him even a little, would have deserved diligent commemoration [Note: [Col. 1409] *exhibite*, manuscript 1]. He was related to me by blood, and—what is now the greater thing—was joined to me in friendship [Note: [Col. 1409] “was joined to me in friendship” is added in manuscript 1b].

He was very dear to Otto III (f. 181), because he faithfully served him and his venerable aunt, the abbess Mahtild [Note: [Col. 1409] the initial *h* is erased; Quedlinburg], and whatever he held as a benefice in the village of Salbozi [Col. 1409D; the village of Salbke, situated on the Elbe between Magdeburg and Salza], he acquired from them as hereditary property [Note: [Col. 1409] “from them” is added in manuscript 1b]. He served Archbishop Aethelbert [Note: [Col. 1409] *ath.*, perhaps *Aethelbert*, manuscript 1] and his successors down to Lord Gero, and received worthy recompense from them.

At last he was weighed down by illness and was joined to almighty God, whom he had always loved above all. Out of love for him and in reverence for him, he built a church on the property he had acquired, mentioned above, and summoned me, unworthy as I am, to bless it [Note: [Col. 1409] “and summoned me” is added in manuscript 1b]. Before its consecration he opened to me a long volume inscribed with his sins, which he had first shown to his other confessors; he read it aloud before me with groans and humbly sought pardon from me.

I took this letter and, by divine authority, granted him absolution for the offense. On that same day, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, since it was then the anniversary of his father’s death, I consecrated the aforementioned church. Above the box filled with the relics of the saints I placed the aforesaid book, so that, through their continual intercession, remission and the long-desired abolition of guilt might be granted to one who confessed his sins with true contrition.

I have never seen or heard of anyone doing this. But because I feared that my weakness would benefit him nothing, I took refuge with the holy intercessors. After this, the venerable father lived thirteen weeks and, longing to be released, died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June (f. 181′).

[Col. 1409D–1410D: *Buxis* seems to be formed from *pyxis*. It signifies a small chest or box, sometimes made of ivory, sometimes silver, sometimes wood, in which the relics of saints were placed. It was deposited, together with four crosses made with chrism, in a chapel or “sepulcher”—properly so called because it was a quadrangular hole cut into the stone slab of the altar—along with three grains of incense and a parchment slip inscribed with the name of the consecrator, sometimes also of the founder, and with the day and year of the consecration. Finally it was closed or sealed with the altar’s seal, that is, with a small stone. See Durandus, *Rationale*, Book I, chapter 6, §34.]

## 8.

Furthermore, I offer as an example worthy of imitation a remarkable deed of the pious abbot Alfker [Col. 1410D; compare above, Book IV, chapter 14. He died in 1009; see the *Saxon Chronography* for that year]. Among his other virtues, he had this practice: he wrote his name upon every altar. When he himself sang Mass, he wept so much that a great part of his body was moistened. He had no doubt that, as it is written, “Tears poured out from the depths of the heart for sins not only ask for divine forgiveness but also obtain it” (Judith 8:12) [Note: [Col. 1409] “but also” is added in manuscript 1b].
