And so that he might be able to implore heavenly assistance more freely for himself, he was merciful toward all his debtors.

Woe to me, an unworthy priest, who have never attained any of the virtues of these brothers mentioned above! I have read and very often seen the examples of many good people, but I did not apply them to my own mind. I succumbed voluntarily and without strong resistance to the various temptations against which I ought to have struggled. Those whom I ought to have helped I harmed more, alas, and, as though I were the best keeper of a hidden treasure, I always concealed my crime.

It is unnecessary, dear reader or successor of mine, for you to believe—because of the favor of the fickle crowd—that I was useful. Rather, by the continual medicine of prayer and almsgiving (f. 182), come to the aid of me, long festering, and snatch me, torn apart, from the jaws of the ravenous wolf. I, who am conscious of myself, tell you things much more credible than anyone else could.

There are indeed some whom I treated unjustly, though gently; and when they are corrected by you according to their merits [Note: [Col. 1411] “by you” is added in manuscript 1b], why should it be surprising if they deceitfully say something against me? Stand midway between my detractors and my various praisers, and be a continual intercessor for me before God [Note: [Col. 1411] *suffrator*, manuscript 1]. I know that, as is commonly the case, much about me displeases you; may this be turned to better ends, pleasing both God and human beings.

Whatever I acquired or did with permission [Note: [Col. 1411] “or did” is added in manuscript 1b] at that time [Note: [Col. 1411] a word is erased; compare above, Book II, chapter 5, note 238], I have affirmed in writing. Nor should you be elated by your great honor, since you are all the heavier under the burden imposed upon you [Col. 1411B]. As a careful steward, inspect the charge of the flock entrusted to you, and strive greatly to set divine things before secular ones.

Increase, as far as you can, what I gave to my spiritual brothers, and, when asked under Christ’s witness, diminish nothing. These are the fellow workers of your sacred order and the future helpers of your hope. As far as you are able, I ask you to be so concerned for laymen who can stagger and be transferred here and there that the clergy may not be destroyed [Note: [Col. 1411] a word is absent in manuscript 1].

If you carefully guard what is yours, you will have God and pious people as supporters. Otherwise, you will lose both your subjects (f. 182′) and incur opposition in the present and future. Listen to me, your excessively undisciplined teacher and predecessor, who lacked a useful example [Note: [Col. 1411] *meum* (“my”), corrected to *tuum* (“your”) in manuscript 1], and willingly endure poverty in yourself so that your flock may become rich through you. Christ did this for us, so that we might do the same for his sheep.

Do not be ashamed of this before the people [Note: [Col. 1411] “of this” is added in manuscript 1b], so that you may be able to stand confidently before God. I was sufficiently open-handed toward this world, but often for the sake of my own people; to those who did not know me I appeared contemptible. If anyone strives to exalt himself above himself, he falls beneath himself through a shameful fall, late and sorrowfully.

Treat your rich with honor, but your poor with grace and good charity [Note: [Col. 1411] “and good” is added in manuscript 1b]. For the ancient proverb declares that these always go together with a great multitude. Guard your poor household, entrusted to you by the supreme Shepherd and scarcely gathered by me, and do not lend a pious ear to wicked whisperers who persuade you badly about it [Note: [Col. 1411] manuscript 1a reads *nec* (“and do not”)]. Your resources are small and should by no means be managed in the manner of great men; it is much better gradually to rise, increasing day by day, than finally to fail with the loss of many [Col. 1411D].

These times, inferior to all those before them, take more away than they add to anyone [Col. 1412A] (f. 183). Through grave guilt and dreadful poverty, inherited and bestowed honor becomes worthless. I do not ask you to be stingy, because that is disgraceful; but I earnestly urge you not to be excessively generous, because that is neither prudent nor suitable [Note: [Col. 1411] “because this” is added in manuscript 1b].

Take care also of the soul of the pilgrim Godebert, who was greatly useful to our church, and of as many others as possible [Note: [Col. 1411] “Take care … of as many others as possible” was written at a different time in manuscript 1b]. You have enough books—those I found collected here by our predecessors, as well as those I acquired. In them you will find wholesome instruction; heed them, and then you can be saved.

I acquired the relics of the saints and their clean containers, together with many other useful things, both estates and slaves, and, lest they perhaps remain unknown to you, I entered them in my martyrology [Note: [Col. 1411] *martorlogia*, corrected to *martirologio* in manuscript 1].

But your piety ought to know the emperor and our king Henry’s manifold benevolence shown to our church. I dealt with part of it above, but left the greater part unexamined; now I have thought it best to write it for you [Col. 1412B]. See to it that he remains in your continual remembrance as our renewer and unfailing helper. Woe to those times when this hope is absent from the wretched and from the Church of Merseburg! (f. 183′) Now is the time above all to pray, for then above all there will be cause to weep.

For she has received the following things from him, and while he lives she will rejoice in a gratuitous increase much greater than these. For he has already determined in his lofty mind how he will exalt her with varied endowments. I now speak of what has preceded, and humbly entrust the perfection that will follow to almighty God, to whom all things are present.

Since there is not time to recount individually the things which you will be able to see confirmed by his charters, I identify only those things which, lacking written authority, I fear may perhaps perish in the future [Note: [Col. 1411] *auctoritate*, corrected to *auctoritati* in manuscript 1].

A portion of the holy and most victorious cross, together with other relics of the saints; a golden altar honorably adorned with gems [Col. 1412D; concerning it, see Brotuf, *Chronicle of Merseburg*, p. 581]; a golden box [Note: [Col. 1411] *capsellam* (“small reliquary”), manuscript 2] decorated with precious stones; and a book of collects adorned at his own expense and also at ours, together with two censers and a silver cup—these the emperor gave to our church with a generous hand [Note: [Col. 1411] after *bicario*, one word and one verse-space are left blank in manuscript 1. The end of the page beginning with *Sanctae* appears to have been written by Thietmar himself]. We must not merely preserve these things but also increase them.

But since I am wholly unable to say enough about his honey-sweet piety, I eagerly hasten to explain his conduct in orderly fashion, as I proposed [Note: [Col. 1411] page 184a was left blank in manuscript 1; nothing is missing].

## 8.

This year (1018), in which I titled this book, is the forty-first year of my birth, or a little more [Note: [Col. 1411] manuscript 1 adds “I” between *est* and *vel*]. In April, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May [Col. 1413D; more correctly, the eighth day before the Kalends of May; see above, Book VI, chapter 27], the tenth year of my ordination began. On the preceding day, the church of that archbishop in the suburb of Gniezno was burned together with the other buildings [Note: [Col. 1413] “On the preceding day, in the suburb of Gniezno, the church of that archbishop was burned with the other buildings,” added in manuscript 1b].

And because every human affair is always uncertain, I wish to vomit up that dangerous antidote which I once swallowed in misery and have since felt harming me greatly. One night, while I was resting in one of my estates called Heslinge, I dreamed that a great crowd was standing there, compelling me to eat something from a dish placed before me. At first, realizing that these were enemies, I despised them [Note: [Col. 1413] *contepsi*, manuscript 1]; but finally I answered that, in the name of God the Father, I would partake of it. When this greatly displeased them, and that hateful assembly saw that it could not be otherwise, it seemed, as though groaning, to approve that I must be utterly lost. And unless I had then invoked the Lord’s name, I would have remained without eternal salvation.

From this food, as it seemed to me, mixed in the form of every kind of herb, I took on varieties of the worst thoughts. Although these greatly disturb me in divine praises, nevertheless, with God’s help—whom I have placed above them—they have rarely or never led me to an ill-fated deed. It is enough for their wicked will that they think they possess some share in me.

Thus, at another time, these same beings again surrounded me from a distance, as though marked out: “You have guarded yourself well,” they said. I replied that I hoped so. They continued: “But it will not be so at the end.” I neither fear their threats nor believe their flatteries, since these things, together with their authors, are vanity.

I greatly fear the extent of the charge entrusted to me, and I know truly that such a phantasm, although it appears bodily [Note: [Col. 1413] *corparaliter*, manuscript 1], does not by itself harm human beings [Note: [Col. 1413] *nocent* (“they harm”), manuscript 1]. But when, by sinning, the divine face is turned away from us, we miserable people fall into their insane hands, which spare no one; and we are immediately freed from them when either we ourselves turn back or we are strengthened by the frequent visitation of God’s chosen.

If anyone, possessing self-command, meditates on God’s law, such beings do not attack him; rather, they fear him—not because of him, but because of the holy power of the one whom he loves. For God is the guardian of all who always love him with their whole heart.

I am a sinner, fully conscious of my frailty; since I do not rest upon the highest consolations, what wonder is it if I am shaken by the lowest? I have said these things so that you, reader, being like me in mortality and innate humanity, may know that I have sinned gravely in this matter and may assist me with unfailing supports.

Woe to me, wretched man, who ought in this world to have helped many spiritually, yet neither benefit them nor can protect myself! From where this temptation came upon me (f. 185′), I pour into your faithful ears. I have tried to aid many people suffering from the harassment of the aforementioned enemies, and for this reason I stirred them up vehemently to lie in wait for me, although they are always inclined toward evil. But I hope in almighty God that he will not hand me over to them for my destruction, but, after a harsh purification, will mercifully rescue me.

## 9.

In the aforementioned month, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, Archbishop Gero and Margrave Bernhard were reconciled at Wonclava [Note: [Col. 1413] *in uuonclava* (“at Wonclava”), added in manuscript 1b; Col. 1413D: Wanzleben]. The priest Liudherdus also died [Note: [Col. 1413] “and the priest Liudherdus died” is added in manuscript 1b; Col. 1413D: see the Merseburg Calendar, under this date]. Duke Godefridus and Count Gerhardus were likewise reconciled by imperial authority.

Bertoldus, however, the invader of the city of Munna, voluntarily surrendered himself with his supporters to imperial authority; and that city was immediately burned, as punishment for many. May God, the peaceful King, ensure that this never rise again. How good it would be if the inhabitants of that kingdom, always united in evil, had no means of fortification for its completion! But now, alas, the situation of these places is as the minds of the natives demand.

After a long residence at Nijmegen, the emperor departed and diligently celebrated the solemn days of the Rogations at Aachen. When these had passed, Lambert, bishop of the Church of Constance [Note: [Col. 1413] *cosstanciensis*, manuscript 1a], died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June [Col. 1413D; see the Merseburg Calendar, under this date]. When the emperor learned this after celebrating Pentecost with great solemnity at Ingelheim, he appointed his chaplain Rotherdus to that see.

After these events there was a great assembly of princes at Birgilum [Col. 1413D; Birgeln, Birgel, or Bürgel, on the left bank of the Main between Offenbach and Hanau. *Pargilla* appears in Böhmer, *Codex Franconiae*, pp. 4, 5, and 9. Concerning the estate of Pirge, property of Saint Peter’s Church at Mainz, see Kindlinger, *Horigkeit*, no. 159. At the same place Otto III was present in 993, June 2, according to a charter of his issued there], so that through judicial proceedings what had long been corrupted by the negligence and great rashness of that people might be corrected.

After this the aforementioned Count Oddo came humbly into the presence of the emperor and Archbishop Erkanbald, and lost his unlawful wife through three oaths. Balderic was reconciled, and the divine promise was forgotten. A few days later, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July [Note: [Col. 1413] the date is absent from manuscript 1], Heinrich, who held the march situated between the Hungarians and Bavarians, died fully armed and bravely.

Meanwhile the emperor came to the city of Basel, gathered an army, and hastened into Burgundy. The empress, coming to Capunga, which she loved, established a monastic life there. From there she proceeded through eastern Francia, made for Bavaria, and enthroned her brother, Duke Heinrich, at Regensburg. In June, irregular weather greatly harmed many people and their various interests.

Additional apparatus and source-boundary details not otherwise noted inline: the scrotal punishment begins at f. 177; f. 178′ begins §4. At Procui’s designation as the king’s maternal uncle, manuscript 1 reads *auinculus*. In §4, manuscript 1 reads *pondere* for *ponderi*; the report to the emperor (*id nuntiare*) is added in manuscript 1b; and manuscript 1 corrects *veredici* to *veridici*. The repeated manuscript-1a reading *patre ac mobiliori* is the alternative to both “better father” and “nobler lord.”

In §5, a word following “his maternal uncle and” is erased in manuscript 1. In §6, manuscript 1 reads *aliqd* for *aliquid*; “second” in “King Henry II” stands after an erasure; manuscript 1 reads *antiqo* and *antiphanam*; and an *h* is erased in *Habrahae*. In §7, manuscript 1 reads *aliquatinus*; “to him” is added in manuscript 1b; an *h* is erased in *Mahtildi*; and “before whose” is added in manuscript 1b.

In §8, manuscript 1 reads *egriam*; the continuation at “Your poor household,” “Through grave guilt,” and “The holy and most victorious cross” is in another hand; a word is erased after “take more away”; “and” before “much better” and “you” before “finally” are added in manuscript 1b; *satis* is added in manuscript 1b; manuscript 1 reads *cu* for *cum*; *maximum* for *maxime*; *sequntur* for *sequuntur*; and manuscript 1a reads *habeo* for *ab eo*. In “the perfection that will follow,” the second *u* of *subsequuturam* is erased. In §8’s vision passage, “from them” is added in manuscript 1b. In §9, the continuation beginning “Bertoldus” is in another hand.

These notes preserve the remaining scribal additions, erasures, alternate spellings, and hand changes from the supplied apparatus.

10. At that time the church entrusted to me, unworthy as I am [Col. 1415: at an erased place in 1b], suffered great loss (fol. 186′), my own guilt demanding it [Col. 1415: *exgente*, 1]. For the merciful and patient God did not wish to leave unpunished what frequent chastisement had been unable to prevent; He struck her in gentleness, not with the deserved retribution of His wrath. She lost ministers useful to Him and daily laments my crime.

In the aforementioned month, great disgrace was inflicted upon her and upon me [Col. 1415: “and upon me” added in 1b] by the half-breed Aethelbert [Col. 1415: *ath.*, 1c?], who presumed to invade my estate and break it up by a servile levy [Col. 1415: *servile*, 1a]. I shall truthfully explain what inflamed them to undertake these things [Col. 1415: “them” added in 1b].

The generous kindness of Otto II, smiling fully upon everyone, granted to our church a forest lying between the rivers Saale and Mulde and the districts of Siusili and Plisni, in the time of Bishop Gisiler and Margrave Gunter [Col. 1415: the second *i* erased in 1] [Col. 1415D: See the emperor’s charter of 30 August 974]. After the lamentable destruction of our see, when Otto III was reigning, Margrave Ekkihard acquired a forest at a place called Sumeringi and exchanged it with ours. King Heinrich, restorer of our dignity, then restored this one by judicial law, together with most of its appurtenances, in the presence of all his nobles, while our confrères Herimann and Ekkihard were unable to defend it [Col. 1415: “these,” added in 1b].

When it had remained in the domain of our church for more than twelve years (fol. 187), and Count Herimann had been wholly unable to redeem it from my authority for sixty hides, it seemed to him that he and his brother should claim it for themselves, by imperial charters, as belonging to the property of the two *burgwardi*, Rochelinti [Col. 1415: *rochelinti*, as below *rochelenzi*, 1; the letter *n* erased in both] and Titibutziem [Col. 1415D: The district of Teitzig, lying between Rochlicium and Colditium. URS.], hoping that our earlier confirmation had long since been abolished.

When he disclosed this to me, he realized that it would accomplish nothing. For at Magdeburg, and in the presence of our emperor, the charters of both sides are displayed, and it is proved that our grants are earlier in every respect [Col. 1415: *convinciuntur*, 1].

At last the aforesaid count, with his own brother present and hearing this, said: “Whatever we have done in these matters until now was not out of any rashness, but because of the justice we hoped to possess. Now, however, let us abandon it.”

Not long afterward the young Ekkihard—and therefore immature—prepared, in his own *burgward* called Rochelenzi [Col. 1416A], lofty fortifications for the capture of wild animals there, at the prompting of his soldier Budizlav. When I later learned of this, I bore it patiently, and through my messenger, his brother [Col. 1415: “his brother,” now erased in codex 1, present in 2], I asked him not to act in this way. I also quickly complained of this to his brother Herimann, but accomplished nothing in all these matters; and so it remained (fol. 187′) until after Easter.

Since at that time the weather was clear and the roads convenient, and I had never before come to these parts of my bishopric, I decided to go there and carefully investigate matters hitherto unknown [Col. 1415: *-que* added in 1b]. In May (1018), on the sixth day before the Nones of that month and on a Friday, I came to Chorum [Col. 1415D: Today it is called Kobren, a small town a short distance from Rochlitz. URS.], and there confirmed the assembled people.

Then, as I saw on the very road that the aforementioned work had been secured with great snares and nets, I was astonished [Col. 1415: *obstipui*, 1] and considered what I should do about it. Finally, since I could not carry these instruments away with me, I immediately ordered part of them to be cut down. Proceeding by the direct road toward Rochelinzi [Col. 1415: the *n* and final *i* erased], I confirmed a few people there; and, forbidding everyone by a ban to enter the forest, I assigned to our church the tithe unjustly taken from me and the forest, peace having been made.

Then I returned to the estate mentioned above and, while staying there for seven days, heard that Ekkihard’s soldiers were threatening my companions. The chancellor [Col. 1415D: This was Guenther, kinsman of the margraves Herimann and Eccard. From 1008 until 1024 he held the office of imperial chancellor, and later attained the archbishopric of Salzburg. See the *Saxo* under 1029 and Hansiz, *Germania sacra*, II, p. 167. URS.] spent the night there with me, and, learning these things from me, gave a good answer.

Afterward many gatherings were organized against me by the aforesaid satellites to do me harm, but our guards forestalled them at a favorable moment. Meanwhile, in May 1018, I sent my messenger to the emperor at Mainz and humbly begged for his peace (fol. 188). Although Ekkihard promised this peace on his side, and his brother, long desired by me, came from Poland and promised peace with his right hand, neither of them kept it well. For six men, flogged and shorn, together with buildings shamefully mutilated, demonstrate how such great lords ought to beware of others. Their satellites, according to their custom, not only burned against me but also harmed better men.

For they attacked Archbishop Gero at Wirbini and Count Sifrid at Nicici [Col. 1416D: The name Nicici seems to conceal the village Nischwitz, in whose place, toward the end of the seventeenth century, the neat and cultivated city of Oranienbaum, near Dessau, arose. URS.], and took away as much as pleased them.

11. The pride of the lords [Col. 1415: *servorum*, “of servants,” 1a] stirs up the fury of their satellites; and, because it suffices them, does not allow others equal to them to exist in these regions [Col. 1415: variant 2, *his non sufficit*, “it does not suffice them”]. If some neighbor, without intending it, unexpectedly commits an offense against them, a fitting correction is not acceptable to them, and afterward there is an irresistible recompense.

By this scourge the neighbors are severely shaken, so that no one may rise up against them, whether the others possess what is right or not. The bishoprics established in these regions are excessively oppressed by their power. And we, their agents, if we satisfy their will in everything against God and His justice, have honor and some advantage; but if not, we are despised and, as though no lord ruled or commanded us, we are plundered (fol. 188′) [Col. 1417: “and thus,” added in 1b].

A new horned assailant now breaks apart the ancient law and the good custom that had flourished until now, and boldly shows himself to be more exalted than the others [Col. 1417: *ceteris*, 1]. Unless he is quickly humbled from heaven, intolerable insolence will become too firmly established [Col. 1417: *inimis*, 1].

He does not know David’s saying, which sweetly admonishes him: “Do not lift up your horn on high” (Psalm 74:6), and so forth [Col. 1417: *cetaera*, 1]. The same holy psalmist prays for such people: “You take away their spirit, Lord, and they perish, and they return to their dust; You send forth Your spirit, and they are created” (Psalm 103:29), and the rest.

He greatly lacks self-knowledge who in no way recognizes himself, since the one who continually considers himself is worth nothing without a good reputation (*fama*). Therefore let all sinners repent, and let them strive with all their strength to guard themselves and show mercy to the poor [Col. 1417: *-que* added in 1b].

I am wretched in my offenses and poor in possessions; although in both respects I surpass all men of the same order [Col. 1417: *viris*, 1a], nevertheless I do not alone suffer the insult mentioned above without them [Col. 1417: *illos*, 1]. Of my fellow bishops established in various parts of this world [Col. 1417: *institutis*, “established,” 1a] and suffering unspeakable harm, I introduce nothing into these examples, because I deeply lament that they possess nothing except blessing, without any honor. It is now time for me to discuss only how, among our contemporaries, they have suffered at the hands of their fellow citizens a similar—or, alas, worse—vengeance (fol. 189) [Col. 1417: *aciucibus* in 1].

12. Bernward [Col. 1417: the *n* erased in 1], venerable pastor of the church of Hildesheim [Col. 1417D: See the *Life of Bernward*, chap. 34], was so hated by Count Bruno that he saw his soldier, named Rim, disfigured in hair and back, and afterward saw the same man, while traveling with him, lying dead after being killed by the young Altmann.

Swithger, distinguished bishop of the gracious church of Minden, was attacked in his own estate by a certain freeborn recruit [Col. 1417: *quadam*, feminine, in 1a], and was stained by the blood of his steward [Col. 1417: *uuillici*, 1a], who was killed before him.

What had such men ever deserved? Both were pious fathers, yet they suffered this disgrace undeservedly. But since in the preceding account, because of the lethargic plague that prevented me, I said nothing about Bishop Swithger, it is fitting now to make amends.

Born in Saxony and brought up from childhood at Halberstadt and Magdeburg, he was appointed provost of the aforesaid city by Otto III. After he had governed it with every diligence [Col. 1417: a *c* added by a later hand after erasure], supported by divine grace, he excelled in various virtues. Of these I shall relate only two matters, which I can establish by truthful testimony.

When his chamberlain wished to conceal a certain cap that he had secretly stolen, and, carefully questioned by the pious old man, confessed nothing, he was forced to take a knife lying on the table, which had been blessed from the heart [Col. 1417: *coatus*, 1—i.e. *coactus* or *conatus*; he ordered him to take it, according to A.S., under 993]. He immediately threw it away as though it were burning, and openly confessed before everyone that he was exceedingly guilty.

At another time, a certain man seized by an evil spirit was captured with great force and brought into the presence of the aforesaid father. Ordering him at once to be released, and courageously fending off with a staff the man violently rushing upon him, he made the sign of the holy cross and, by divine power, caused him to depart unharmed (fol. 189′) [Col. 1418B; Col. 1417: “the enemy,” 2, A.S.].

Such a man, attributing these things not to himself but to Him who accomplished such great deeds through him [Col. 1417: *tantum*, “so much,” 1a], lived out the days granted to him in this life in Christ, serving Him, a faithful servant, with every devotion [Col. 1417: *illi*, “to Him,” 1c]. He held office for sixteen years, always weighed down by a great weakness that perfects every virtue, and then died in the place where he had been born, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, while our emperor Heinrich had been reigning for ten years [Col. 1417D: 1011].

His successor Thiedricus, the son of my maternal aunt [Col. 1417: *memet*, 1], suffered great disgrace from Heinrich, the son of Count Herimann [Col. 1417: the second *i* erased in 1], as I have related above [Col. 1418D: See above, book VII, chapters 34 and 35]. But in this year the same agitation, having been quieted for a time, rises again.

Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, endured many hardships from the aforesaid count for a long time; and this is not surprising, since the count held his own mother in prolonged captivity. Moreover, Bishop Meinwerc was despoiled by my nephew Thietmar, the brother of Duke Bernard [Col. 1418D: Compare the *Life of Meinwerc*, chapters 32 and 70].

13. But why do I explain all this, since in none of these matters do I recognize either a good example [Col. 1417: *in e.*, 1a] or any relief for myself [Col. 1417: *nullatenus*, “in no way,” 1a]? It is better for me to persist in my own undertakings; and while I treat this subject, I have in mind that vision of blessed John: “The first woe has passed, and behold, two more after this!” (Revelation 9:12).

For it is exceedingly pitiable that I have often reviewed the matters related above [Col. 1417: *reuuolui*, 1a]. Nothing of this kind ever occurred in the days of our reader and unconquered defender Heinrich such as the loss that has now emerged from our crime.

For in the month of July, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, and on the fourth day of the week—29 July [Col. 1417: the date in an erasure; *IIII*, 1a]—Mars raged into her very entrails, a deed that Mother Church will lament forever.

Aethelbold, bishop of Utrecht [Col. 1417: *ath.*, 1c], attacked, with Duke Godefrid and the aid of his own companions and friends, Thiedricus, our empress’s nephew, who had often inflicted great harm by killing his soldiers. An assembly of the gathered army took place on a certain island. There, swiftly prepared for battle, he suffered, alas, the death he threatened for the enemy.

For when the Frisians burst forth from ambush on every side, and he was unexpectedly surrounded by the satellites of the aforesaid young man, he ended this life—terrible to say!—by sword [Col. 1419: “sword” added in 1b] and water, without loss to those resisting. The bishop barely escaped in a small boat, while the duke was rescued from the enemy [Col. 1419: “rescued from the enemy,” added in an erasure in 1b]. According to reliable reports, more than three legions were slain [Col. 1419: “three” in an erasure in 1b].

The whole region, deprived of a strong defender, fears the invading pirates and mourns daily. Count Godefrid was killed, and the excellent soldier Johannes lies dead, whom his homeland always mourns [Col. 1419D: Merseburg Calendar, 29 July: “Counts Godizo, Johannes, and Godefrid were killed together with an innumerable multitude of their companions.” Compare the Lüneburg Obituary, 30 July. Compare also Alpert, book II, chapter 21, where this battle is assigned to 29 July, and Balderic, book III, chapter 19].

Their noble and renowned companions, who until now had fought with victorious right hands, now rest in an unhappy lot (fol. 190). Their bodies pay the penalty deserved for the stain of our offenses; but, as I hope, their souls will rejoice, cleansed by so grievous an ordeal.

But, reader, do not marvel at such a disaster; consider also its origin. That unfortunate Thiedricus had been a satellite of the aforesaid bishop. In a certain forest called Mirwidu [Col. 1419: Above, the *u* appears first to have had a *c* erased, so that 1b may have intended *Mircuuidu*] [Col. 1420D: In the district now called Merwe, near Dordrecht], he possessed a large estate, which all the inhabitants of the region complained to the emperor at Nijmegen had been unjustly taken from him.

Therefore, on the advice of the best men, the emperor ordered the bishop of Utrecht to have these places burned and returned to those who were loudly demanding them. When the wicked young man could not restrain his lord from such commands, he asked permission to leave and promised that he would prevent this from happening. Without delay, what I have related was done—more because of our crime than in proportion to the merit of the victor.

A multitude of birds, gathered here from every direction and killing one another with their claws, long foretold this unspeakable and utterly overwhelming disaster; it occupied beforehand the very place where these men later perished.

What holy David invoked against Mount Gilboa (2 Samuel 1:21), I, though deserving nothing, continually wish upon this island. Balderic, bishop of Liège [Col. 1419: the *c* erased in 1], died at Tiel on the same day [Col. 1420D: Merseburg Obituary, third day before the Kalends of August].

14. (Fol. 191.) In those days, in my bishopric, seven bondsmen ate improper mushrooms and, consumed by a sharp fever, quickly died. In August (1018), a certain star newly appearing near the Wagon [Col. 1419: near the constellation of the Great Bear, commonly called the Wagon, 2], sending rays from afar, terrified everyone who saw it [Col. 1420D: On this comet, see the Quedlinburg Annals under 1018 and Alpert, book II, chapter 19].

Never, within the memory of our people, had such a thing arisen; therefore everyone marveled at it. The common people fear that this is a portent, but the faithful populace hopes that it will end in mercy. Concerning such matters the truthful Jeremiah cries: “He who knows all things knows them, and by his own wisdom devised them” (Baruch 3:32).

This star that shone was visible for more than fourteen days. In the province called Northuringun, three wolves, always found together and never previously seen by those inhabitants, caused unspeakable harm to many people and animals. Every native, greatly terrified by this, fears greater losses still to come.

For blessed Gregory says: “Many evils must come first, so that they may announce what is to come without end.” In all the things mentioned above, heavenly anger is revealed to us from above; but through vigilant watchfulness [Col. 1419: “watchfulness” added in 1b] it is not perceived by human frailty.

15. (Fol. 191.) This year may truthfully be called, by a new designation, an earthquake or a great destruction [Col. 1419: *terrae*, “of the earth,” 1]. For an unspeakable tribulation arose in the unstable world and disturbed its inhabitants everywhere. I have already related part of it; now I explain with deep groaning what I had passed over.

Nearly all the soldiers of Bishop Balderic and of the bishop of Cambrai perished on the aforesaid island, and in the three neighboring provinces no house remained in which at least one inhabitant was not missing. Since the times of Charles, no such event had occurred in these regions in a single day or year, as antiquity asserts [Col. 1419: *t* corrected to *I*, 1].

How could such men ever have fallen without hostile loss? Yet no one who rightly considers the matter is surprised, because no one can fight whom the grave vengeance of God for his guilt seeks to crush [Col. 1419: *deprimire*, 1].

May this unconquerable disaster soon be forgotten afterward, for through the assistance of Duke Godefrid, Bishop Athelbold was reconciled with the enemy Thiedricus; and this came not from his own will but from the greatest necessity. There was no powerful defender of that region if a more violent enemy should rise again.

If this loss occurred with divine consent, who can avenge it? But if not, who could be more unrelenting than its avenger [Col. 1419: Codex 1 has *uindica . . . insanabilius*, leaving a space for four or five letters]?

Now, as the holy abbot Columbanus did at the death of the great emperor Charles, let us also restrain our tears and pour out useful prayers [Col. 1419: *fundimus*, “we pour out,” 1].

16. Nor must the grievous loss that occurred in Russia be left unmentioned. For Belizlav went against it with a large army and inflicted great harm upon it through our famine (*nostro famine*).

In July, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, the aforesaid duke came to a certain river [Col. 1420D: namely, the Bug] (fol. 192) and ordered his army to camp there and to prepare the necessary bridges. Near it, the king of the Russians [Col. 1421: *rurorum*, 1] [Col. 1421D: Jaroslav] sat with his men, anxiously awaiting the outcome of the duel they had mutually agreed upon.

Meanwhile, at the provocation of the Poles [Col. 1421: *provocacione*, 1], the enemy present was roused to battle and, from the river he was guarding, was driven away by an unexpected success. Encouraged by this report, Bolizlav, asking his companions to prepare and hasten, crossed the river swiftly, although with difficulty.

The hostile battle line, arranged in troops opposite him [Col. 1421: *tuimatim*, 1], strove in vain to defend its homeland. For it yielded in the first conflict and afterward never resisted bravely. There an innumerable multitude of the fleeing were cut down, while only a few of the victors were lost.

The renowned soldier Hericus from our side perished, whom our emperor had long kept in chains [Col. 1421D: Compare above, book VII, chapter 12]. From that day Bolizlav, with the desired success, pursued his scattered enemies and was received by all the inhabitants and honored with many gifts.

Meanwhile, a certain city that was then obedient to his brother [Col. 1421D: Sviatopolk] was forcibly captured by Jaroslav, and its inhabitants were carried away. The city of Kitava [Col. 1421D: Kiev], exceedingly strong, was shaken by frequent attacks from the enemy Pechenegs, at Bolizlav’s instigation, and diminished by a great fire.

It was defended by its inhabitants, but quickly became exposed to foreign forces. For, after its own king had been turned to flight [Col. 1421: thus A.S.; *agere*, 1], and the city had been abandoned, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September it received Bolizlav and Zentepulcus, his former lord whom it had long lost [Col. 1421: *habeo*, 1a, and likewise below]. For his sake, and out of fear of our people, the whole region had been transformed.

The archbishop of that city, with the relics of the saints and various other ornaments, honored these arrivals in the holy monastery of Sophia, which in the preceding year had been disastrously burned in an accident [Col. 1421D: Compare book IV, chapter 37] [August 1018].

There were the stepmother of the aforesaid king, his wife, and his nine sisters. One of them, previously desired by him, the old fornicator Bolizlav had unjustly taken as his wife, forgetting his own consort.

An unspeakable amount of money was displayed there; much of it was distributed among his guests and supporters, while some was sent to his homeland. Three hundred men from our side had been in aid of the aforesaid duke, five hundred from Hungary, and one thousand from the Pechenegs. All these men were then sent home, while the aforesaid lord rejoiced that the natives were approaching and appearing loyal to him [Col. 1421: *domum* appears twice on two lines in 1].

In this great city, which is the capital of that kingdom, there are said to be more than four hundred churches and eight markets. Its population is an innumerable multitude, drawn—as is that of the whole province—from the strength of fugitive slaves flocking here from every direction, and especially from the swift Danes. This population had hitherto resisted the Pechenegs, who inflicted much harm upon it, and had defeated others.

Elated by this success, Bolizlav sent the archbishop of the aforesaid church [Col. 1421: “namely, of the church”] to Jaroslav, to ask that his daughter be brought back by him and to promise that his own wife, together with his stepmother and sisters-in-law, would be returned.

After this he sent his beloved abbot Tum [Col. 1421: *Thuni*, “in whom all hypocrisy reigned,” 2, A.S.] to our emperor with great gifts, in order to obtain more fully his favor and assistance and to indicate that he would do everything pleasing to him [Col. 1421D: See the Quedlinburg Annals under 1018].

He also sent messengers to nearby Greece [Col. 1421: *gram*, 1; *urbem*, “city,” 2], who would promise that kingdom’s emperor good things if he wished to be regarded as a faithful friend; otherwise, they would announce that he would become a most steadfast and invincible enemy.

Amid all these things, may almighty God stand in the midst and mercifully show what is pleasing to Him and beneficial to us.

In those days Count Udo, my nephew [Col. 1421: *oms*, 1], seized Herimann, his equal in both nobility and power, and led him unwillingly into his own fortress. Because of this I fear that a dangerous fern-shoot may arise, one that could scarcely, or perhaps not at all, be uprooted.

17. Let my discourse now turn to our emperor, who, having returned from the hated expedition [Col. 1422D: Namely, from Burgundy. Compare above, chapter 9. On 9 September, in the city of Zurich, he donated to the monastery of Meinradszell the forest in which it is situated, as the charter of that monastery attests], received none of what had been promised to him (1018, September), but harmed those who resisted him only slightly.

His excellent and faithful soldier, Duke Thiedricus [Col. 1422D: Of Upper Lorraine], wishing to return home after separating from him, was attacked in hidden places by a certain lord named Stephan [Col. 1421: *stphano*, 1], who, as became clear, was an enemy both of the emperor and of Thiedricus. Although Thiedricus had already emerged victorious, when his soldier fell into the hands of the enemy he was attacked again and, alas, overcome; he escaped with a few men [Col. 1421: *pauos*, 1].

This was his second trial in such circumstances; may God ensure that a third danger does not befall him.

When our emperor was informed of all these matters [Col. 1421: *omibus*, 1], he held an assembly in Swabia concerning the affairs of the realm and soon descended anxiously along the Rhine. For his associates and the chief pillars of his kingdom had, alas, fallen for the most part, and a grave hidden burden threatened him [Col. 1421: “threatened in secret,” 2, A.S.]. Pretenders to loyalty were striving through outsiders to resist him by secret plots, so that he might not rule with the freedom appropriate to him and might not in any way lessen their unjust rashness and insolence of liberty [Col. 1421: “and the insolence of liberty,” 2, A.S.].

[Col. 1421: Codex 2 adds at the end: “This book contains the deeds of five emperors: namely, Heinrich I and his three sons, Otto, who was called the Red, and Otto II, and also Otto III, who was called the beautiful boy, and Heinrich II, to whom the name ‘the Pious’ adhered. These emperors vigorously ruled the Roman and German Empire for one hundred and seven years. Thietmar, bishop of Merseburg, composed this work; and because he was a Saxon, he seems chiefly to describe what these emperors did in Saxony.”]

# In the Year of the Lord 1008. Bridfertus, Monk of Ramsey

[Col. 1423]

## Historical Notice Concerning Bridfertus

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis.)*

Bridfertus, or Britfrithus—called Brightefertus by Leland, chapter 136—a Saxon, disciple of Abbo and monk of Ramsey, wrote around the year 1000 commentaries on Bede’s *On the Nature of Things* and *On the Times*, published in volume I of Bede’s works.

To the same author belongs Britfertus’s *Computus of the Latins, Greeks, Hebrews, Egyptians, and English*, which exists in manuscript in the Bodleian Library. Henschenius published his *Life of Saint Dunstan, Archbishop of Canterbury*, who died in 988, in the *Acta Sanctorum*, 19 May, volume IV, p. 345. Moreover, John Bale, century 2, chapter 35, mentions his book *On Mathematical Principles* and another, *On the Institution of Monks*.

[Col. 1423]

## Life of Saint Dunstan

By B., a contemporary priest and eyewitness.

*(In Bollandus, May, volume IV, 19 May, p. 346, from a manuscript at Saint-Vaast in Arras.)*

## Notice

Several distinguished writers composed accounts of Dunstan, and we have labored tirelessly to obtain them. Among these, the oldest is the work written for Alfric, archbishop of Canterbury, by a certain Saxon priest in England who designated his name only by the letter B. Mabillon conjectures that he was Britfertus, a monk of the monastery of Ramsey who lived around the year 980.

Alfric had been promoted to that see in the eighth year after the death of Saint Dunstan and died in 1006. In his prologue, this author asserts that he is writing what he himself learned either by seeing or hearing it from Dunstan, or from Dunstan’s pupils, whom he personally brought up from tender youth to mature manhood, properly instructed with the nourishment of learning.

And in section 39, when about to discuss Dunstan’s death, he says: “I consider it right that, urged by a just admonition from God, I should unravel, insofar as I can in charity, those things that I myself either saw or heard.”

But, sadly, when the account reaches the exhortation delivered three days before Dunstan’s death, on the feast of the Ascension, the remainder was missing from the very old manuscript which, after returning from Rome in 1662, we found and transcribed at the celebrated monastery of Saint-Vaast in Arras.

## Prologue

[Col. 1423A: The style, obscure through a certain affected strangeness of phrasing, seems in the prologue to have twisted the scribes and driven them into various errors. So that these may not trouble the reader excessively, I shall attempt to correct some of them conjecturally, reporting here the original reading of the Arras manuscript, in case someone may be able to extract from it a more coherent sense. Where the matter could be handled merely by transposing one word or another, I have not thought it worthwhile to warn the reader of the alteration made.]

[Col. 1423A]

To the most prudent lord and archon Alfric, B. [Bridfertus], least of all priests and a lowly native of the Saxons, sends the lofty joys of heaven.

Because of the enormity of your widely celebrated learning, and because of the magnificent and gracious dignity of your privilege, I receive you, before all others, however distinguished they may be in doctrine, for invincible protection [Col. 1424B: Manuscript, “safer”]. I would attempt, with the brilliant pen of suitable eloquence, to extend the worthy memorials of the accomplished guardian of the house of God, the gracious Dunstan; but, as you see, I have stained the praises of his glorious life, begun by me, and the whole structure of this little work, by a degenerate style full of faults [Col. 1424B: *praemia*, “rewards”].

Therefore, before all others, I openly confess such disgrace to your serenity, and, prostrate at your knees, I afflict and burden myself with the blows of my own words, after the manner of winged creatures that seem to beat themselves with the clapping of their wings before they utter the sound of departure.

So much so, I say, that whatever you find in this work employed contrary to the rule of orthography through the fault of its composer, may you order, by your authority, to be scraped away and corrected from error into something better by the weeping little quill of the flowing ink.

Moreover, I urge the perceptive men and women of both orders, as they pass with the feet of their letters across this slender field, this little harvest of our booklet [Col. 1425A; Col. 1425D: “earthly,” perhaps], to do the same, with the full attention of their hearts and, rather, with your support [Col. 1425D: *potitus*], but cautiously, lest they crush the nurseries of the rare growth by heedlessly trampling them; and lest, while they strive to uproot completely the vegetables that have sprung up in the pressed-down grain, they cut away the proper plants as well, intercepted together with the weeds by the same sickle.

Rather, let them eradicate and cut away these detestable tares of the surface, scattered here and there carelessly across the spaces of the text, with a light effort, down to the roots.

If I perceive that these preliminary measures [Col. 1425D: *precamina*; the following words are added: “These words were added by someone who, from the little hearts of the clouds, thought they might be omitted until a more fortunate conjecture should discover an intelligible sense”] . . . are granted to me in my undertaking, I shall bring forth sufficiently gracious benefits in return.

But if they are rejected and despised through the envious dismissals of rivals, I know not what better course I can undertake than to proceed, with my own little sickle, however rough, covered over by thin mutilation, to cleanse as far as my strength permits the harvest of my labor, provided that a correcting finger should point out to me where in the text I, provoked by the blame of the corrupted field, should cut.

Therefore, since what I wish cannot be done because of ignorance, I am compelled at last to wish what I can do.

This is what I shall do: after mentioning the theologian whom I desired as the desired preface [Col. 1425D: He seems here to name Saint Dunstan, whom above he called “the worthy guardian of the house of God”], to discuss the capitals and the whole tall sequence of this texture with a charmingly facile encomium—or, if I can, having examined it summarily [Col. 1425D: *summorum rimatum*]—and to set it forth like a jeweled work in a golden design [Col. 1425D: *chrysidineus*: perhaps meaning “golden” or “woven with gold”], with the color of twofold amber [Col. 1425D: namely, in prose and verse; henceforth you will find various verses, though in a very wavering meter, woven into the structure of the *Life*; he seems soon to call this “satirical folly”], I shall now walk, as though less wise, with satirical folly and a stumbling gait.

Nevertheless, I reserve the beauty of so great a life for suitable authors to write down—unless I fear the imminent anger of the blessed bishop—because no one is superior anywhere in the arrangement of this universe if he makes no great claims; but he is more contemptible than all persons if he lacks divine doctrine.

For you scarcely know any wise person liberally educated in genius who seems to abuse eloquence in writing prologues in so deformed a fashion as I do.

Nevertheless, cleanse the following little pages, composed somehow with a small spark of ability, by the most trustworthy testimony of the faithful [Col. 1426D: “I shall cleanse”], if you doubt that I have inserted in them any distinguishing marks through my own rashness—unless they are things that I myself learned from him by seeing or hearing, however dull my understanding, or from his pupils, whom he personally brought up from tender youth to mature manhood, properly instructed with the nourishment of learning.

I beg you, surrounded only by the bond of charity, to receive this slender heap of little letters, compacted with scarcely an ink-black title and darkening style [Col. 1426D: *ebenina* is thought to indicate writing in ink, since ebony is black in color; thus he earlier used “the weeping quill of flowing ink”], and to defend it with unconquered protection against all envious rivals—not devoted to flattering rumor, but specifically offered to your exalted dignity.

In this literal plain, I ask that the mind be examined as more spontaneous than the sluggishness of a rustic composer. And, without causing you offense, I admonish you to be shaped by the virtues of so great a Father, instructed by his examples, fortified by his conduct, and justified by his disciplines, so that, since you were his successor on earth, you may deserve to be his perpetual confessor in heaven.

This may the Lord Jesus Christ grant, who with the coeternal Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# CHAPTER ONE  
## His birth, education, studies, residence at the king’s court, and expulsion from it

[Col. 1426B]

### 2

After the course of many years had passed during which the nation of the English, empty of the true worship of the Christian religion, chose to be enslaved more to its ancient error and pagan ritual than to Christ, the Creator of all things, the merciful Lord—so that His handiwork, ensnared in the devil’s traps, might not perish eternally condemned—provided a remedy of eternal salvation for that same blindness. In His compassion He sent to these regions Augustine, a venerable Father, chosen by the blessed Pope Gregory. [Note: [Col. 1426D] Saint Augustine is commemorated below on 26 May, and Saint Gregory on 12 March; the latter sent him to England in the year 597.] Augustine was to unite the people converted through the keen intelligence of his mind to the blessed fellowship of the angels.

Accordingly, as soon as the man of God drove the furrow of his renowned teaching and the ploughshare of God’s visitation into the thickets of that ignorant nation, and planted the wheatlike seed of the holy Trinity, he uprooted from it the serpentlike growth of the destructive darnel, so that thereafter he prevented the ruins of the thorny field from sprouting there and demonstrated, alike by instruction and example, that worthy fruits of repentance ought to be offered to God. Thus the whole people of the Britons, which had previously despised Him, believed in the Lord and, through recognition of the true faith, was joined to its God.

He, without whose providence even the little sparrows do not fall, thereafter applied himself to the care of this excellent crop, in accordance with the condition of his office. For he chose as future nurturers of the children who would come to him kings, bishops, commanders, deans, provosts, and the other rulers of his Church, [Col. 1426D] so that, after each had completed his allotted course, they might govern the flock reborn for God under the protection of peace and with justice.

### 3

Among these distinguished men of royal authority—whom many most Christian and orthodox rulers had preceded in governing, though difficulty now prevents us from investigating their names one by one—the glorious King Athelstan was numbered among the kings of the English in successive years.

Among these distinguished men of royal authority—whom many most Christian and orthodox rulers had preceded in governing, though difficulty now prevents us from investigating their names one by one—the glorious King Athelstan was numbered among the kings of the English in successive years. [Note: [Col. 1427D] Athelstan succeeded his father Edward the Elder, who died in the year 924. Thus all authorities commonly report the matter. Only the Saxon Chronicle, appended to Bede’s History, assigns it to the following year.]

In the time of this king there arose in the territory of the West Saxons a vigorous boy. [Note: [Col. 1427D] Following the Worcester, Durham, Westminster, and other sources, these words read: “In his time there arose a vigorous boy, Dunstan, in the territory of Wessex, namely in the county of Somerset.”]

His father was called Heorstan, and his mother Cynedrida. [Note: Heorstan is called Herstan by some; Cynedrida is also found as Kynedrida, Kinedritha, and Chinedrita.] When the pious parents had caused him to be reborn in the waters of holy baptism, they named him Dunstan. The boy grew and became dear both to God and to human beings.

There was a certain royal island adjoining the territory of this aforementioned man. In the ancient language of the inhabitants it was called Glastonbury. It extended over broad expanses of land, was enclosed by fish-filled waters and stagnant rivers, was suited to many human needs, and—what is most important—was consecrated to the sacred gifts of God.

There, indeed, the first neophytes of the Catholic faith, guided by God, discovered an ancient church constructed by no human art, but rather prepared from heaven for human salvation. [Note: [Col. 1427D–1428D] We discussed this ancient tradition of the church of Glastonbury, situated in the aforesaid county of Somerset, on the Kalends of March before the Life of Saint David, Archbishop of Menevia, no. 12.] Later the Maker of heaven demonstrated by many miraculous deeds and by many manifestations of mysteries that this church had been consecrated to Him and to His holy mother Mary. They also added to it a stone-built oratory, which they dedicated to Christ and to His apostle Saint Peter.

From then onward, a multitude of faithful from all around venerated it and humbly frequented the precious place on the aforementioned island. It happened, therefore, for such reasons, that the aforesaid Heorstan, accompanied by the blessed boy Dunstan, passed through Glastonbury. When they spent the night there for the sake of prayer, behold, a blessed period of repose covered the boy in exceedingly sweet sleep. In a state of mental ecstasy he saw an old man dressed in snowy white, leading him through the pleasant courts of the sacred temple and showing him the monastic buildings that were later to be constructed under his pastoral care, in the arrangement in which they are now said to have been established.

### 4

Afterward the parents of the religious boy Dunstan devoted him to the sacred leisure of literary study. The Lord immediately deigned to bestow upon him such abundant grace in these studies that he surpassed all his contemporaries and passed through the periods of his studies with an easy stride:

> But what sign the Supreme Majesty had bestowed upon him,  
> In these very studies I shall briefly reveal, as far as I can.
>
> It happened that he suffered long from severe fevers,  
> So that he endured the bitter illness of delirium,  
> Forgetful of himself and babbling foolish things,  
> He spewed many words from his empty mouth.
>
> Worn out by these afflictions, he was entrusted to a certain woman,  
> Who at that time was to provide for the tender boy  
> And take care that he did not perish beneath that disease.
>
> But the illness mentioned pressed heavily upon the boy,  
> So that he lay as though lifeless, stretched out to the point of death,  
> And all his limbs became as if he were already dying.
>
> When for a long time he was thus weighed down by the burden of the hidden illness,  
> Suddenly, moving, he departed [Note: Adalard of Blandigny says that he was restored to his former health by a heavenly—or, as one may rightly believe, angelic—cure.], and quickly rose.
>
> He seized a staff and a small branch that happened then to be at hand;  
> Striking the air with it on both sides,  
> He went along as though defending himself from savage dogs.
>
> They say that at night he hurried alone as far as the outer limits of the church,  
> And from there came to the high flights of steps  
> By which the craftsmen who built the summit of the church  
> Climbed, at great peril—alas, the timid men!  
>
> There, as though strong, he climbed to the highest tower  
> And stood and walked upon it most carelessly.
>
> But the mercy of the Lord snatched the innocent one from falling  
> From the heights, and placing him below  
> Set him down unharmed in body, safe and sound,  
> Carried from the roof into the interior of that same church.
>
> There two keepers were accustomed to sleep together,  
> So that the third might rest among them.
>
> He himself, however, did not know by what means he had come there;  
> No living person beneath the sky could devise an explanation.
>
> For the doors of the church opened to no one entering,  
> Yet the same hard iron bolt beneath its covering barred them.  
> [Note: The same Adalard adds: “But the matron, in whose care the sick boy had been entrusted, kept watch tirelessly, observing everything until he had crossed the roof’s ridge, and by this heavenly marvel bore faithful witness. It was plainly a divine miracle; since the pious man denied that he knew anything of it, it is clear that the whole event was accomplished from heaven and was entirely divine.”]
>
> Now, excellent reader, quickly declare in speech  
> What seems truthful to you in this little boy:
>
> If you doubt that such a one could climb the temple above,  
> He who here, with the doors closed, is placed in the temple  
> To be saved from the danger of a fall,  
> So that afterward he may redeem very many from corrupting defilement  
> And send companies to heaven, distributing teachings and also leaving examples.

Let the patient and humble rise, and let the proud fall. For the more exalted he became as he grew, the richer he was in sharpness of understanding; the more mature he became through the turning wheels of the years, the more fervent he was in love of God; and the more accustomed he became to divine praises, the more earnestly he persevered.

### 5

When the aforementioned parents saw such excellence in their son, they imposed upon him the discipline of the clerical office [Note: Manuscript: “of the clerical state.”] and associated him with the celebrated monastery of the Church of Glastonbury, so that there he might serve God and God’s mother Mary continually, by day and by night.

Bound now to divine disciplines, he passed beyond youth and trod down the flourishing years of his adolescence. As a just man in the house of his God, he blossomed with the strength of virtues like a cedar of Lebanon; planted in the divine courts, he extended the strength of his growth toward the stars day by day.

Meanwhile the fame of his great steadfastness became known at the king’s palace, so that it was proclaimed far and wide by magnificent reports of his praiseworthy deeds. He did not seek the empty favors of this world; rather, enriched beforehand by the abundance of virtues, he bore within himself the glory of the eternal King. His powerful wisdom had inscribed that glory with the learned finger of spiritual gifts, with a variety of studies, and also with the jeweled brilliance of golden ornaments.

For he swiftly traversed many meadows of sacred and divine books, like an ingenious bee, with such rapidity of capacious understanding that he refreshed his mind rather than his body with divine readings and devoutly filled the receptacle of his chaste little heart, suffused by the breath of the Holy Spirit, with nectar-like taste.

Moreover, Irish pilgrims venerated the place I have mentioned, Glastonbury, with great affection, as did the other crowds of the faithful, especially in honor of the younger Saint Patrick, who is said to have happily rested there in the Lord. [Note: In the Life of Saint Patrick, apostle of Ireland, which we elucidated on 17 March, Jocelin lists among his disciples who wrote his deeds Saint Patrick his little son. After the death of his paternal uncle, he returned to Britain, died there, and was honorably buried in the church of Glastonbury.]

Dunstan diligently cultivated their books, which philosophized along the path of right faith; and he constantly investigated the writings of other wise men whom, through his innermost discernment, he perceived to be established by the testimony of the holy Fathers.

He so disciplined the practice of his life that whenever he examined the books of sacred Scripture, God seemed to speak with him; and whenever, released from worldly cares, he refreshed himself in the leisure of prayer, he himself seemed to speak with the Lord.

### 6

While these exercises of good works were taking place within him, certain of his companions and courtiers—especially his relatives, who envied his saving deeds—tried to gnaw at or cut down the blessed Dunstan, the vine and branch of the holy vineyard reaching toward the heavenly kingdom and flourishing in Christ, with sharp serpent tongues and the bites of dreadful teeth, like bristly goats.

For beneath the livid cavern of their blemished hearts they forged against him an unexpected rash of falsehood, saying that from salutary books and learned men he had learned not what would benefit the salvation of souls, but the utterly vain songs of his ancestral paganism, and that he cultivated the frivolous dirges of magical stories.

Against this disease of falsehood the blessed novice always set Christ, who knows all things before they happen. In His person the kindly prophet David, His most faithful witness, forestalling them by the oracle of the Holy Spirit, speaks thus against the false witnesses of the Lord’s Passion:

> “Unjust witnesses rose up against me, and iniquity lied to itself” (Psalm 26:12).

And again:

> “Those who sought evil for me spoke vanities, and all day long they meditated deceit” (Psalm 37:13).

The Lord Himself also says in the Gospel:

> “Blessed are you when people hate you,” and so forth (Luke 6:22).

And to His hearers:

> “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of the world, and I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you” (John 15:19).

Likewise:

> “Blessed are you when people curse you, persecute you, and speak every evil against you falsely for my sake. Rejoice on that day and exult, for your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matthew 5:11).

Thus strengthened by this most firm promise, God’s servant Dunstan became like a deaf man who paid no attention to a voice of reproach, scarcely ever opening his mouth in bitter rebuke against the dogs barking at him.

But they persisted in their malicious plotting, accused him before the king by a certain false charge, and obtained that he be expelled from their company—though, if they had been of sound mind, they would have loved him above all.

Then, when the most atrocious rage of their impiety prevailed, they seized the innocent man by his four limbs, like a patient sheep, bound his hands and feet, and threw him into the muddy places of the marshes. To make him more contemptible in the madness of their fury, they trampled upon him until, according to the malice of their will, they had dishonored him in the stinking mire.

When they had gone away, he himself scarcely rose from the river marsh, covered with mud; and he resolved to go to a certain friend a mile away, so that he might wash himself there.

But his own fierce dogs met him. Since they thought him, disfigured by mud, more a monster than a human being, they attacked him with savage barking. Yet as soon as they heard his caressing voice, they immediately recognized that it was he and thereafter fell silent.

Then he groaned within himself with a deep sigh from his heart and said:

> “O savage madness of my relatives, transformed from human affection into canine ferocity! The irrational nature of dogs has shown me human affection by wagging its tail in friendliness; but my relatives, forgetting their humanity, have inflicted upon me the severity of dogs attacking me. Thus the perverse order of both has changed the rightful way in each.”

# CHAPTER TWO  
## Saint Dunstan’s monastic life; the deeds and pious death of the widow Aethelflaed; an antiphon produced from a harp

[Col. 1430D]

### 7

The ancient enemy of the human race therefore understood that the aforementioned young man, through the wicked messengers of the envious companions whom he had sent, had yielded little to his evil desires. He began to engage him in battle with the weapons of ambush; how many struggles of temptation he inflicted upon him, the following pages of this little book will partly reveal.

First he injected into him a love of women, so that through familiar embraces with women he might enjoy worldly pleasures.

Meanwhile his kinsman Elphegus, surnamed the Bald, also a faithful bishop, urged him with many petitions and spiritual admonitions to become a monk. [Note: We gave the Acts of Saint Elphegus on 12 March, though not this author’s account, but those of others. He presided over the Church of Winchester from the year 935 to the year 951.]

Rejecting this through the prompting of the deceiver mentioned above, Dunstan preferred to become betrothed to a young woman, whose daily caresses might comfort him, rather than to be clothed, in the manner of monks, in garments made of rough wool.

When the man of God heard him refusing these words, he immediately asked, with a sigh from the depths of his heart, the Ruler of the heavenly kingdoms to bring upon him the judgments of correction, so that he might sharply recognize the one whose counsels he had despised. By God’s merciful favor, this was proved to have happened within a very short time.

For an intolerable pain from swelling blisters covered his entire body, so that he thought he was suffering from elephantiasis and had no hope whatsoever of his own life.

Then, seized by great anguish, he sent in haste and summoned to himself by humble prayer the bishop whom he had previously despised. He announced that he wished to obey his salutary counsels. The bishop came to visit him and, after comforting and correcting him, consecrated him to God as a monk.

### 8

Thus the pious and merciful Lord, in His compassion, drew His servant Dunstan back from the love of women, just as history relates that He recalled the apostle and evangelist John, whom He specially loved, from the bridal chamber.

Through this correction by God and the salutary instruction of the blessed bishop Elphegus, Dunstan became a lover of understanding. Thereafter he often remained in diligent attendance upon the revered bishop, both for the sake of very salutary teaching and because of their kinship.

Meanwhile the religious citizens of Winchester invited the same bishop of God to the dedication of a new church that they had built in their city of Winchester, where he held episcopal authority, in honor of the Supreme Divinity. It stood in the southern part of the public street, which is now said to be nearer to all the churches on the western side.

Among many others, Dunstan was present with the bishop at its consecration, as one of his chief companions. After its dedication they compelled the venerable man and his companions, in the customary manner of hospitality, to attend the prepared feast of charity. They spent a joyful day in honor of so great a man and in celebration of the consecration.

But when night was already approaching, the bishop rose with his companions after giving thanks. Having blessed the men and women at the feast, he returned to his own dwelling, blessing God as he went.

As they proceeded along the road, they came to a church consecrated to the blessed Pope Gregory. There the bishop stopped and said to Saint Dunstan:

“Let us complete here, at the oratory of our holy father Gregory, our hour of Compline.”

After the spoken prayers they approached and joined their heads together, as was customary, so that they might disclose their confessions to one another in turn.

When this had been done, and the bishop was granting remission of sins, a very large stone fell from the high air and, by the Lord’s mercy, crashed violently to the ground between their two heads. It merely touched the hair of both heads and injured neither of them. Unless I am mistaken, that malignant one, the enemy of every good work, hurled it down in fury from the missiles of his wickedness, as though he intended to avenge a double anger upon both of them.

### 9

At the same time it happened that a deacon of the Church of Glastonbury named Wulfred suffered temporal death. During his lifetime he had been both Dunstan’s superior and his intimate friend. [Note: Is the reading “most precious” or “approved”?]

Not long after his departure, he appeared to Dunstan rejoicing. He revealed many things unknown concerning heavenly matters; moreover, he set out the whole course of Dunstan’s life, defining the fate of his future years and the outcomes, whether good or evil.

When the blessed man heard such great lights of mysteries and such unavoidable events in his life, he said, in a state of mental ecstasy:

“If the things you affirm with such certainty are true and must be believed, how shall I know them? By what signs will those matters be revealed to me through evident demonstration?”

Then Wulfred led him into the courtyard of the temple, where the bodies of the dead lie buried. He pointed with his finger to an undisturbed place on the southern side of the church and said:

“Because the things I have told you are true, know clearly that within three days a certain priest will be buried in this place, although he is not yet ill; and his little body will be brought from the western side of the present church to be buried here.”

At these words of the vision the blessed Dunstan awoke. After the first hour of the day, remembering the marvelous revelation, he came with certain companions to the place in the cemetery that had been spiritually indicated to him. He also picked up a stone that could be thrown and cast it into the place, adding:

“If the things I saw in my sleep are true, a certain priest must be buried here within three days.”

After they had departed, the teacher and priest of a certain Aethelflaed, a most noble and religious matron, came with another group of companions and, amid various words of conversation, obtained that same place for his burial, saying:

“When I have died, I beg you to bury me here.”

According to the testimony of many, he was still physically healthy. But after they had gone away from there a short time later, he was stricken with a severe illness bordering on death. Then, during the following night, he commended his last breath to Christ the Lord, and within three days he was buried in the very place of his choosing that had previously been assigned by Saint Dunstan.

> Then the servant of the Lord, blessed throughout the ages, understood  
> That by such signs all future things had been foretold—  
> Those things that the aforementioned Wulfred had conveyed to him in speech.  
> Through these visions the humble and wise blessed man,  
> Happy, strong, prudent, and chaste, shone forth  
> Before God and before human beings throughout his life.

### 10

Now, by gradually postponing it, I interrupt the discourse I have begun, until I briefly set forth a few short statements that I do not think should be omitted.

There was a certain exceedingly wealthy matron, born of royal lineage [Col. 1433A] but bound by the tight bonds of divine religion. We recently touched upon her name in a brief mention. After losing her husband, she desired to lead a widow’s life according to her strength. [Note: Ethelfleda—called Elfleda by the author of the Westminster account—is also said to have been a widow. She is recorded as a saint in the English Martyrology on 13 April, but is wrongly called a virgin. Since we do not find her entered in the older calendars, we referred the reader to this Life. This also refutes the Westminster account, which assigns the event to the year 929, when Saint Dunstan was still a little boy.]

She therefore established little dwellings for herself beside the sacred temple on its western side, so that, out of desire for the heavenly kingdom, she might not cease serving the Lord Jesus Christ there day and night.

The blessed Dunstan was always attached to her. He loved her above others in marvelous ways and diligently relieved her poverty, both for the sake of religion and because of their kinship.

It is beyond our ability to relate in detail how great and how extensive she made her preparations for divine service. Yet the Lord, examiner of all secrets, revealed what her merit was, both at the final limits of her life and while she dwelt in this world.

She loved with the innermost ardor of charity all the royal stock from which she herself had derived her noble origin. Therefore, through the grace of her kindness, she often supplied kings from her own resources.

Following this pious custom, she prepared for the glorious King Athelstan whatever meal she could provide, since she had learned that he had come to Glastonbury for the sake of prayer.

The royal officials responsible for overseeing the king’s arrangements knew that the king had promised his niece that he would visit her. They came on the preceding day to see whether all the provisions and preparations were suitable and sufficient.

When they had inspected everything, they said to her:

“You have sufficient provisions for the entire service, provided that you do not lack a supply of mead.” [Note: *Medo* means mulled wine or hydromel; the word is Saxon and likewise Germanic.]

But she replied:

“May my lady, the holy Mother of my Lord Jesus Christ, Mary, not permit me to lack that or anything else appropriate to royal dignity.”

Saying this, she entered as quickly as possible the ancient church of Mary, the Mother of God, prostrated herself there to pray, and for a long time begged that the most abundant provision of the heavenly King might be present for her, so that the king’s entertainment might be increased.

What more need be said? At the appointed time the king arrived, accompanied by a great retinue. After the prayers and Masses had been celebrated, he gladly entered the banquet to which he had been invited.

At the first serving they emptied the vessel of mead to the measure of one palm’s breadth. Thereafter, by God’s increase and through the merits of the blessed matron, it remained undiminished, while the cupbearers, as is customary at royal feasts, poured throughout the entire day from split horns and other vessels of unmeasured capacity.

When the king himself heard of this miracle from those who had served, he said, his mind changed, to his attendants:

“We have sinned by burdening this servant of God with the excess of our multitude.”

He rose, greeted his niece, and immediately went on his way.

### 11

When this servant of God had completed the course of her blessed struggle and her end was already approaching, she became gravely ill according to the human condition.

Saint Dunstan carefully provided for her needs and guarded her as though she were his own mother. It happened, however, that these duties kept him away during the evening hours, so that he was not present with the choirs that were singing the psalms as usual.

Yet at the twilight of the day, he went with the students following him to the church he had already observed, in order to complete the delayed office.

As he stood outside before the church door for the sake of psalmody, he saw from afar, bursting forth from the regions of the eastern sky, a snowy-white dove shining with marvelous beauty and an unfamiliar appearance.

The tips of its wings resembled blazing fire, and sparks like lightning were scattered through the air from its wings as they struck in flight. [Note: The manuscript reads “they poured forth a lightning-like flight”; here *ictuare* appears to mean “to strike.”] It flew swiftly to the dwelling of the blessed matron.

The blessed Dunstan, mindful of his sick friend, returned immediately after completing the psalms. When he arrived, he heard her within the enclosure of her curtains conversing in solemn speech, as though with an intimate friend, alternating words with him.

He therefore approached the confident maidservants who watched over their mistress and courteously asked them, wondering with whom she was speaking.

They said that they did not know, but added:

“Before you came, a ray of immense brilliance filled this whole room with radiance. Then, when the light ceased, she herself—as you now hear—did not cease speaking to the one who was speaking with her.”

He himself gradually sat down while watching, until she somehow ceased speaking. When she too had fallen silent, he entered by pushing aside the folds of the curtains and asked her familiarly with whom she had been speaking.

She said to him:

“You too saw him coming before you came here, and now you ask with whom I was speaking? It was he who was speaking with me, the one who appeared to you while you were singing psalms as you stood before the church door. He has now announced to me, in order, the whole course of my departure.

“Nevertheless, you, my friends, need not grieve greatly for me, because the mercy of my God will meet me as I die and will mercifully grant me entry into the joys of paradise. [Note: The same source reads *obibit*, ‘he will die,’ instead.]

“But to you, as the servant of your special friend, I assign this task: tomorrow morning, as early as possible, have baths prepared for me and prepare the funeral garments that I shall wear with me. After the washing of my body, celebrate Masses, and then, at the time of participation, let me receive Communion of the holy blood and body of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that at that same moment, with the Lord as guide, I may enter upon the way of all human beings.”
