He fulfilled this most earnestly, obeying all the commands of the blessed matron, lest he entrust the final observance of her foresight to sluggish care, further weakened by the burden of delay.

She too most certainly fulfilled, in the order she had foretold, what had been shown to her during the night as destined to happen that day. Thus, I say, after the mystery of the Mass and after the saving taste of the Eucharist, she ended her blessed life in the Lord Jesus Christ at the very completion of the Mass.

> Then the watchful man, rejoicing, commended her soul, with its imminent destiny,  
> To the Lord, and buried the body with honor.  
> He gave her possessions to the saints, as she herself had wished  
> While she lived in the body.  
> The freed attendant too departed,  
> Wishing that she might rest in the sweetness of the Lord.

### 12

Amid these studies of sacred letters, so that he might be competent in every respect, Dunstan diligently cultivated the art of writing, as well as skill in playing the harp and in painting. Thus, so to speak, he shone as a vigilant inspector of all useful things.

For this reason a certain noble matron named Aedelpyrm summoned him for a brief while through a familiar request, asking him to paint for divine worship a certain stole for her with various patterns and designs, which she could later embellish by varying it with gold and gems.

When he had come and done this, he took with him, as was customary, his harp, which in his native language we call a harp, so that at intervals he might delight himself and those whose minds were directed toward him.

Then, one day after dinner, while both he and the aforementioned matron with her female workers were returning to their repeated work, a marvelous event occurred. The harp of the blessed novice, hanging on the wall of the bedroom, sounded aloud of its own accord, without anyone touching it, and in the hearing of all performed a melody of rejoicing.

It sang the melody of this antiphon and carried it through to the end in an ordered song:

> “The souls of the saints rejoice in heaven,  
> Those who followed the footsteps of Christ;  
> And because they poured out their blood for love of Him,  
> Therefore they will reign with Christ forever.”

When they heard this, both Dunstan and the matron mentioned above, together with all her workers, were terrified. Completely forgetting the work in their hands, they stared at one another in astonishment, wondering greatly what new example this marvelous event might foreshadow.

# CHAPTER THREE  
## Deeds performed under King Edmund; the abbey of Glastonbury undertaken; the snares of demons avoided

[Col. 1435D]

### 13

After King Athelstan had died [Note: King Athelstan died in the year 940, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November. He was succeeded by his brother Eadmund, or Edmund.], and the condition of the kingdom had changed, the majesty of the succeeding king, namely Edmund, ordered the blessed Dunstan, who was of exemplary life and learned speech, to appear before him, so that he might be chosen and numbered among the royal nobles and court officials.

Dunstan did not rashly resist these commands. Rather, mindful of the Lord’s precept, he hastened to render to Caesar what was Caesar’s and to God what was God’s (Matthew 22:21).

Likewise, instructed by the command of the blessed apostle James [Note: Rather, the blessed Peter is meant here.], he did not cease submitting himself to every human authority, especially to those in power: to the king as the one who excelled, and to governors as those sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good, and so forth (1 Peter 2:13).

Nor, if I am not mistaken, did he fail to remember the blessed apostle Paul, who says:

> “Let every soul be subject to higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been established by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance; and those who resist will bring condemnation upon themselves” (Proverbs 13:1).

And again:

> “Therefore, brothers, render to all what is due: tribute to whom tribute is due, taxes to whom taxes are due, fear to whom fear is due, honor to whom honor is due” (ibid., 7).

Again, to this same apostle, at the time of his own calling, the Lord said:

> “It is hard for you to kick against the goad of my power” (Acts 9:5).

These and similar commands of sacred Scripture the blessed Dunstan carefully hid in the bosom of his heart, lest he sin against the Lord. He set the words of His commandments, sweeter in his mouth than honey and the honeycomb (Psalm 18:11), as a lamp of true light for his feet, by which he might walk in the ways of the Lord. [Note: I remove two superfluous words: “might mercifully minister.”]

After he recognized that he had been more deeply instructed and enlightened by the commands of his God, he swore to himself and firmly resolved in the secrets of his heart to keep the judgments of God’s justice to the end, as the same Lord says elsewhere concerning this sentence:

> “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22).

And again:

> “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation 2:10).

Thus, although with difficulty, he lived for a long time with the nobles in the royal palace, holding two reins under sacred guidance: namely, those of the law and of theoretical as well as practical life.

When some of the soldiers residing there saw this steadfastness in his conduct [Note: [Col. 1435D] Manuscript: “conversion.”], they began to love him with the singular sweetness of charity or the affection of brotherhood.

Many others, however, covered by minds shrouded in darkness, began to detest the same man of God with the bitterest hatred of vanity and to envy his prosperity to the point of death.

These detractors, to increase their wickedness, urged everyone they could to persecute the servant of God. For so long did they twist the cord of their iniquity around him—more likely to bind themselves in it than him—that they might stain the king himself with their vices and make him credulous toward their deceptions.

The king, immediately instructed by the wicked as he had been before, was moved to great fury. He ordered that Dunstan, stripped of his office, also be deprived of every honor and seek for himself, wherever he wished, a dwelling apart from the king and his people. [Note: *Moratus* means “a dwelling” or “habitation.”]

At Ceodrium [Note: [Col. 1436D] I suspect that *Seorsium* should be read, and that it is the same place which, under a compound name, is commonly called Windsor: a royal castle, also called Windefora by some, with a hunting park and an extensive forest. Shortly afterward the text reads *Ceoddis*, which departs still further from this form.], where these things had happened, there were venerable men—namely, messengers of the eastern kingdom [Note: [Col. 1437D] By “the eastern kingdom” I understand Essex, or eastern Saxony.]—who were then staying as guests with the king.

Dunstan, as though already condemned to exile and unaware of any other course, approached them and begged them not to abandon him, now that he had been left by the king, but to take him with them to their homeland, even if only for residence there.

They sympathized with his sorrow and promised him whatever advantages their kingdom possessed, if he would accompany them there.

14. Accordingly, the next day the king went out, as usual, to enjoy himself with his men by hunting. When they reached the forests, they eagerly took different paths through the wooded tracks. And behold, amid the varied uproar of the horn-blowers and the baying of the hounds, many stags took flight. From among them the king alone selected one for himself to hunt with his pack of dogs; and for a long time he wearied it through various byways, pursuing it with the agility of his horse and the chase of his hounds.

Now, near Ceoddis, there is, among several other places, a precipice formed by a severed mountain, sloping down with extraordinary and immense depth. The same stag, I do not know by what chance—unless by the hidden will of God—fled to it; and it plunged headlong into the depths of that precipice together with the pursuing dogs, and, mangled limb by limb, they fell together to their deaths.

The king likewise, following the stag and the dogs, came on with the great rush of his flying horse. At once, when he saw the precipice, he tried with all his strength to restrain the horse as it quickened its course. But because the horse had a stubborn neck and rigid nape, he could not. What more is there to say? With every hope of life taken away, he commended his soul into the hands of his God, saying inwardly:

“I give you thanks, Most High, because I do not remember having harmed anyone in these past days except Dunstan alone; and this I shall repair by my willing disposition, if my life is spared, by being reconciled to him.”

At these words, through the merits of the blessed man, the horse stopped on the last patch of ground at the edge of the precipice—something I now shudder to relate—where the horse’s forefeet had almost plunged into the bottomless chasm.

Then the king, in heart and voice alike, offered God the greatest thanks and praises for restoring his life. He clearly understood within himself, and repeatedly reckoned in the secret places of his heart, that on account of vengeance against so great a man he had been brought almost to the point of death.

When he returned home, he ordered Blessed Dunstan to be summoned to him immediately and with all haste. When Dunstan came at the summons, the king said to him:

“Hurry and prepare a horse for yourself, so that you may go with me, with the small company with which I shall be travelling.”

They mounted their horses at once and took the road leading directly to Glastonbury. When they arrived there under guidance, they entered the churches of God to pray, as was fitting. Immediately after their prayers had been completed and their eyes wiped of streams of tears, the king again called the servant of God Dunstan to him. Taking him by the right hand, he kissed him as a gesture of reconciliation and also of restored dignity; then he led him to the priestly chair and seated him in it, saying:

“Be the powerful master and rightful occupant of this seat, and the most faithful abbot of this present Church. Whatever you lack from your own resources for the advancement of divine worship or the completion of the sacred rule, I shall devoutly supply from royal generosity.”

15. After these events, the servant of God Dunstan accepted the aforesaid dignity by the king’s command, for the purpose of governing. Following, in the manner described above, the most salutary institution of Saint Benedict, he became the first abbot of the English nation.

[Note: That is, as Osbern states in the following *Life*, no. 4, the monks then at Glastonbury observed a monastic practice proper to their nation, utterly different from the Benedictine one; Osbern himself describes it.]

Thus he devoted himself to rendering spontaneous service to God, out of the affection of his heart. Then the very wise shepherd first fortified on every side the enclosure of the cloister with monastic buildings and other defenses, just as long before an old man had indicated to him in a revelation. There he might enclose the Lord’s sheep, gathered together in flocks from far and wide, lest they be torn apart by the invisible wolf.

Next, this same teacher of God began to nourish the assembled monastery entrusted to him with the nourishment of the divine word, and to give it drink from the heavenly fountain—that is, from the honey-sweet teaching of Holy Scripture—teaching that through the narrow paths of this life one must pass to the eternal delights of the heavenly banquets.

It is now evident to almost all the faithful throughout the surrounding regions that, after the interval of a few years, the disciples whom he had grafted, by his exhortations, as tender shoots into the vine of true faith, namely Christ the Lord, grew abundantly and bore the fruit of good works with disciplined beauty.

Moreover, afterward many pastors of Churches, instructed by his teachings and examples, were sought out for various cities and other holy places. They were chosen to be teachers there of sacred government and the rule of justice: namely, provosts, deans, abbots, bishops, and even archbishops, pre-eminent among the other orders.

[Note: These are discussed at length in volume I of the *Monasticum Anglicanum*, p. 8: archbishops and bishops from the Glastonbury community were elected to various sees. Among them are reckoned the immediate successors of Saint Dunstan, Athelgar, or Edelgar, and Siric, or Sigeric; and, after these *Acts* had been written, Saint Elphegus and Elnoth, or Egelnot. Several other bishops are also listed there.]

Whoever, in those same times, among his disciples, was released from the bonds of the body at the end of life and underwent unavoidable death, undoubtedly sought the lofty joys of heaven.

16. When the ancient enemy, with his penetrating intelligence, realized that Blessed Father Dunstan had snatched such great companies from his hands and wrested them away, he did not cease day and night to oppose him by every fraud he could devise, as we have already begun to relate.

One night, while the athlete of God remained steadfast within the cloister, occupied with psalmody and vigils, the enemy of God and humanity appeared to him, bristling and terrifying in the form of a bear. He wished in some way, through a grim apparition, to frighten him and, by the cunning of deceit, to draw him to some extent away from a work so contrary to himself.

But when God’s champion perceived this hostile monster more by spiritual than by bodily sight, he remained all the more securely, like an unconquered man, at the praises of God he had begun.

A short while later the enemy appeared again—not in the likeness of his earlier sport, but in a canine form entirely suited to him, since his deceits are wicked in everything. He hoped that by imitating the ferocity of dogs he might hinder and deceive the saint and, by whatever means he could, separate him from his devotion to prayer.

Yet that persistent tempter raged against the servant of God in vain with the abominable deceits of his trickery. He found him protected on every side with the weapons of faith and was therefore struck back and destroyed by the same point of the holy cross which he always carried with him in his right hand.

[Note: *Chira* means “hand”; in Greek, χείρ.]

Nevertheless, the saint remained undaunted in praise of his Christ, despising the adversary’s assaults. The same treacherous dragon added a third attempt, creeping forward in viper-like fashion to discover whether he might perhaps still find the man of God less resolute in overcoming him.

On that occasion, by an evil contrivance of his heart, he changed himself into a foul little fox, hoping even so to turn the servant of God away from his purpose toward his God by wagging his tail and darting about in various directions. When Blessed Father Dunstan saw him transformed so many times, he smiled and said to him:

“Go now, enemy, for you have appeared in a form sufficiently like yourself.”

And when he made the sign of the cross, the enemy disappeared.

17. With these and similar spectral weapons the ancient deceiver often wearied Blessed Father Dunstan, though always in a fruitless struggle. On one occasion, for example, he was laboring in prayer before the altar of Christ’s martyr George, keeping vigil.

It is unknown in what manner this happened—whether through the injection of the aforesaid deceiver or through prolonged wakefulness—but amid the words of the psalm a gentle sleep suddenly stole over him. It seemed to him, although he was not, so to speak, completely asleep, that a shaggy, enormous, and terrifying bear was coming with great force. It placed its dreadful feet, prepared to tear him apart, upon both shoulders of the seated man and hovered over him with its jaws gaping greedily, as if to devour him.

When the man of God awoke completely from the terror inflicted upon him, he quickly seized the staff which he always carried in his hand and attempted, in human anger, to strike the wicked monster. But with a wasted blow he struck the wall of the church, producing a tremendous crash that resounded throughout the building.

Coming to himself, he entered upon a stronger contest, chanting this psalm of spiritual battle:

“Let God arise … thus may sinners perish from the face of God” (Psalm LXVII, 3), as above.

For in that place, overcome by sleep, he had abandoned his devotion to psalmody; and immediately, when he resumed this psalmody, the shadowy deceiver was recognized and withdrew, confused like an exceedingly black shadow in the form described above.

18. This same man of God had, by human descent from his parents, a certain brother named Wulfric. Dunstan appointed him as a powerful external administrator in the affairs of his estates, so that neither he himself nor anyone belonging to the monastic profession would wander outside in the foolish management of secular business.

After he had completed the span of his life, Wulfric was overtaken by a fatal condition and underwent temporal death. For this reason it happened that all the monks of the aforesaid church went out for his funeral. No one remained at home except the abbot and a young scholar, who later became a bishop and disclosed these events to us, so that they could convey the lifeless body with the sacred funeral rites to the monastery where it was to be buried.

Meanwhile the abbot was walking with the same scholar, apparently to see whether the brothers had by then drawn near with the body of the deceased. As he continued walking and singing psalms according to his custom, a stone missile suddenly came from beyond the old church, flying violently toward the blessed Father’s head in an attempt to strike it. But, because God protected him, it could not do so. Nevertheless, it knocked off and hurled far away the cap with which he covered his head, almost a rod’s length from him.

Turning around, he said to the scholar walking with him:

“Hurry, then, and quickly pick up this rolling stone, so that you may bring it for me to see.”

When the scholar, at the Father’s command, brought it back with difficulty because it was so heavy, the venerable Father Dunstan said:

“O hostile enemy! For a long time you have been deliberately lying in wait and maliciously preparing the blow of this stone against me. For, as many people testify, there was no stone of this kind, large or small, in these parts of Somerset, except perhaps in buildings made of stone. It is therefore plain from whose wicked hand it was hurled.”

Nevertheless, afterward he ordered that the stone, although it had been thrown to harm him, should be fastened in safekeeping and preserved as a witness.

[Note: Somerset is the county among the West Saxons in whose territory the Glastonbury abbey, commonly called Glassenbury, is situated. Ferrarius wrongly confused it with another monastery of a similar name in Kent, near the borders of the South Saxons.]

## Chapter IV. Events under Kings Eadred and Edwy. The Episcopate Refused. Exile

19. When King Eadmund had been killed by an unjust assassin,

[Note: King Eadmund was killed in the year 946, on 26 May, a Monday.]

[Note: *Cleptor*, “thief,” is called Leof, “a little robber,” by William of Malmesbury, book II, chapter 7. The king had expelled him because of his robberies; after six years he returned and secretly drove a dagger into the king’s breast, but he himself was cut limb from limb.]

his nearest heir, namely Eadred, immediately succeeded him and assumed the hereditary kingdom.

Strengthened in his high position, Eadred loved Blessed Father Dunstan with such ardent affection that he placed almost no one before him in rank. In return, the man of God, wishing to repay from the depths of his heart the love shown by one who loved him so devotedly, habitually acclaimed the king as his dearest of all.

Because of this confidence of affection, the king entrusted to him the best of his possessions for faithful safekeeping under the protection of his monastery: numerous rural charters, the ancient treasures of preceding kings, and various riches acquired by the king himself.

After some time had passed, the blessed man—namely, the aged Aethelgar, bishop of the Church of Crediton—was compelled by the law of human nature to bring his life in Christ to an end.

[Note: Crediton, or Credition, a city of Devon commonly called Kirton, became an episcopal see in 609; the see was later transferred to Exeter. Bishop Aethelgar died there in 953, as the Westminster writer asserts.]

The king repeatedly urged the man of God Dunstan to accept the bishopric, deprived of its father, and undertake its pastoral care himself.

But Dunstan immediately put forward the ready excuse that he had not been appointed for this pastoral charge and was not yet suited to such a great dignity, so that he could guard so extensive a flock of Christ with prudent care without bringing about his own ruin.

He sometimes opposed the king with these and similar arguments, until, by wholly refusing, he restrained all his persuasion. Yet the king could not thereby alter the secret purpose of his will, for he wished the man whom he loved more deeply than all others to become a man of still higher distinction.

Therefore he placed the words of his will in the mouth of his own mother, saying to her:

“I wish, dearest mother, that at your midday meal you invite our special friend Dunstan to dine with you. While, amid the cheerful feast, you exchange pleasant conversation, make every effort, with feminine eloquence, to persuade him to become, in accordance with our proposal, bishop of the Church so recently widowed.”

When she had done everything in her power, she could not turn him from his former declaration of refusal. Nevertheless, on her advice, the venerable Aelfwold, because of his eminent excellence, obtained that same bishopric.

[Note: Aelfvold, or Alfwold, governed the aforesaid Church from 953 to 973.]

20. On the following night, it seemed to him in a nocturnal revelation that he was to hurry to Rome with a ready company. Along those same roads Peter and Paul appeared to him together with Andrew, revealing various unexpected secrets about his future experiences.

When the familiar conversation with the apostles had ended, Andrew struck him with the staff he was carrying in his hand, giving him a fairly strong blow, and said:

“Take this as your reward, because yesterday, by refusing, you scorned association with our apostolate.”

Immediately after this saying he awoke and asked the monk lying before him who had rashly struck him with such a sharp little rod.

The monk replied:

“No one, so far as I know, touched you while you were resting with any blow.”

Then Dunstan, having reflected, said:

“Now, my son, now I know; I recognize from whom I have been struck.”

Alas, it was King Eadred, Dunstan’s beloved, who throughout the whole period of his reign suffered from excessive illness. At mealtimes, after swallowing the juice of his food, he would reject from his mouth the remainder, only partly chewed by his teeth, and would often cause the soldiers dining with him to experience a foul nausea by spitting it out.

Although he dragged out this diseased life for a considerable time in his failing body, the worsening illness repeatedly attacked him with thousandfold weight and miserably brought him to his death.

Then, uncertain of his own life after so long an illness, he sent everywhere to gather his possessions, so that while he was still alive he might distribute them among his people by his own spontaneous and free decision.

For this reason the man of God Dunstan, like the other guardians of the royal treasures, was travelling to return to the king whatever he had held with him for safekeeping.

As he was returning after several days along the road by which he had come, carrying the burdens of those possessions, a voice was sent from heaven and said to him:

“Behold, King Eadred has now died in peace.”

[Note: King Eadred died in the year 955. In his will, published by Michael Alford, he bequeathed two hundred pounds to Dunstan, abbot of Glastonbury, and to the monastery of Glastonbury, to be paid from the counties of Somerset and Devon.]

At this voice the horse on which the man of God was riding suddenly collapsed and died, because it could not endure the presence of an angelic majesty.

When Dunstan arrived, he found that at the very time when the angel had announced it to him on the road, the king had ended his life in final death. The assembled companies of the faithful commended his departed spirit, and likewise his lifeless limbs, to the Lord their Creator for burial in the peace of rest, according to mortal custom.

21. After him Eadwig arose, the son of King Eadmund. He was young in age and possessed little wisdom for ruling, although he had been chosen to fill the number and names of kings among both peoples.

A certain woman, though of exalted birth, but foolish, clung to him by the shameful allurements of intimacy, together with her grown daughter. Her purpose was to bind both herself and her daughter to him as wives. He, as they say—though it is now shameful to relate—handled them alternately with lustful and shameless touching.

When, at the appointed time, he was anointed and consecrated king by the common election of all the princes of the English, on that very day, after the royal anointing of the sacred rite, he suddenly sprang away, wanton, abandoning the cheerful feast and the distinguished gatherings of his nobles, to seek the caresses of the aforesaid harlots.

When the supreme pontiff Odo saw the king’s insolence, especially on the day of his consecration, displeasing the entire senate seated around him, he said to his fellow bishops and the other princes:

“Go, I beg you, each of you, to bring the king back, so that he may be a suitably cheerful companion of his retainers at this royal feast.”

But they feared incurring the king’s displeasure or the women’s complaints, and one by one they withdrew and began to refuse. Finally, from among them they selected two whom they knew to be most steadfast in spirit: Abbot Dunstan and Cynegius, bishop and a kinsman of Dunstan,

[Note: The man here called Cynegius is called Kinsinus by Osbert in Surius. He was bishop of Lichfield and presided from 948 to 966.]

so that, obeying the command of all, they might bring the king, willing or unwilling, back to the seat he had abandoned.

Entering according to the order of their princes, they found the royal crown—shining with the varied brilliance of gold, silver, and gems, and fashioned with marvelous workmanship—carelessly torn from his head and lying on the ground some distance away. They found the king himself repeatedly rolling about between the two women, as though in a filthy swine’s wallow.

They said:

“Our nobles have sent us to you with a request: come immediately to the dining hall appropriate to your dignity and do not disdain to take part in the joyful feast of your nobles.”

Dunstan first rebuked the women for their foolishness. When the king refused to rise, Dunstan pulled him away with his own hand from the adulterous couch; then, having placed the diadem on him, he led him by force, though he had been forcibly dragged away from the women, to the royal assembly.

[Note: Saint Odo, archbishop of Canterbury, consecrated him king at Kingston.]

22. Then that same Aedelgyw—such was the name of the dishonorable woman—turned the empty circles of her eyes toward the venerable abbot in blazing fury, saying that a man of this kind was excessively bold to enter uninvited into the king’s private chamber.

We have heard in the books of the ancient kings that Jezebel, steeped in the error of paganism and the venom of a serpent, raged day and night in bitter hatred against the prophets of God and did not cease persecuting them even to the point of death.

So too, from that day onward, this shameless virago, infected by the same poisonous breath of Jezebel—although unworthy to bear a Christian name—did not cease persecuting the man of God Dunstan with hostile schemes until she fulfilled the plague-bearing desire of her hatred, together with the king’s intensified hostility.

Then, with the aforesaid king’s consent, she subjected all the honor of Dunstan’s order and all his property to her own laws. Indeed, under pressure from the king’s command, she herself swiftly banished him into exile and misery.

The madness of this raging woman was not, however, as deserving of attention as the secret plotting of the disciples whom he was tenderly nourishing and instructing with nectar-like teaching. For they too were accomplices and secret supporters of the wicked conspiracy; if they were able to deplore his unjust losses, they ought to have done so.

While those who were expelling him were arranging to inventory all the ecclesiastical property, a harsh sound of the laughing devil was heard in the western part of the church, resembling the voice of a clapping maidservant.

When the man of God perceived in his mind who it was, he said to him:

“Do not rejoice so greatly, enemy, for as much as you now rejoice at my departure, so much again, when I return, will you grieve, with God condemning you.”

23. Afterward, whenever any of his friends received this same man of God into their hospitality out of affection or compassion, after he had been expelled by the unjust judgment of the accusing woman, they incurred the king’s raging anger severely.

For this reason Dunstan was compelled to cross the mad waves of the turbulent sea in a dangerous voyage and to enter the uncertain exiles of Gaul.

When he had gone about three miles out to sea in a swift vessel under sail, messengers came from the wicked oppressor—so it is reported—to put out his eyes if he were found on those shores.

But he swiftly crossed the watery roads of the blue sea and reached an unknown region of the aforesaid Gaul, whose language and customs he scarcely knew.

Yet, with the mercy of his God accompanying him, he found favor with a certain ruler of that land,

[Note: Count Arnulf of Flanders, as will be related in the following Life.]

who cared for him with fatherly affection during his exile.

Although he was daily treated kindly under the protection of this ruler, his mind nevertheless remained constantly in his homeland, from which he had been removed without just cause. Often, too, he drew down an abundant shower of tears from his flowing eyes with groans, whenever, established in exile, he remembered the great height of religious observance he had left behind in the monastery.

While he was long meditating on this matter in the sadness of his heart, behold, one night as he slept he saw in a familiar vision what he had eagerly desired while awake. It was as though, in his usual manner, he was in the monastery with the assembled company of the brethren, singing and completing the evening praises.

After the final canticle, “My soul magnifies the Lord” (*Magnificat anima mea Dominum*), they began this antiphon:

“Why do you disparage the words of truth? You compose words for reproof and strive to overthrow your friend? Nevertheless [lacuna].”

At this point, in the vision, they all simultaneously abandoned the chant and became completely silent. They could not in any way finish it with word or voice, although with fruitless effort they repeatedly sang it up to the same point; they never allowed the two neighboring words to be sung together.

Then, in the same vision, he rebuked them:

“Why,” he said, “do you not say the words that complete the antiphon: ‘Fulfill what you have devised’?”

Immediately he perceived a divine answer coming from another side in these words:

“Because they will never accomplish what they plot in their minds; and so they will also tear you away by removing you from the authority of this monastery.”

When he awoke after the vision, he gave thanks to the Most High who had consoled him. It was made clear by this most certain revelation that, as we have mentioned above in various passages, some of those men had secretly become his persecutors.

[Note: In all the ancient breviaries of various Churches that we possess, the Book of Job is prescribed for reading in the first and almost also the second week of September. But on the preceding Saturday another antiphon is prescribed, namely the one found in the Roman use. What is called an antiphon here is, in those books, the responsory after the third lesson of the First Sunday.]

## Chapter V. The Bishoprics of Worcester and London; Then the Archbishopric of Canterbury. The Roman Journey

24. It happened that, as the years passed, the aforesaid king was entirely abandoned and despised by the northern people,

[Note: Namely, by the Mercians and Northumbrians, as the writers of Worcester, Durham, and others assert; they assign this event to the year 957.]

because he had acted foolishly in the government entrusted to him. He drove away the shrewd and wise out of a vain hatred, while deliberately attaching to himself all the ignorant who resembled him.

After he had thus been abandoned through the conspiracy of all, they chose for themselves, at God’s direction, Eadgar, the brother of that Eadwig, as king. He would justly strike the unjust with the imperial rod, while peacefully protecting the kind and upright beneath the same little rod of equity.

Thus, as the whole people bore witness, the commonwealth of the two kings was separated by the decision of the wise, so that the famous River Thames would divide the kingdoms of the two.

Then Eadgar, having been chosen for kingship by the aforesaid people, sent by God’s will to recall the venerable abbot from the hated exile in which he lived. He did not forget the great reverence Dunstan had enjoyed among his predecessors, whom he had served faithfully and tirelessly with salutary counsel. After bringing him back from exile, Eadgar treated him with every honor appropriate to his dignity.

Meanwhile Eadwig, Eadgar’s brother, because he had abandoned the right path by straying from God’s just judgments, breathed out his last breath in a miserable death.

[Note: The writers generally assert that Eadwig died in the year 959.]

Eadgar himself, chosen as the rightful heir by both peoples, assumed his kingdom and joined the divided rights of the kingdoms together under a single scepter.

He restored Blessed Dunstan to the honor of his former dignity from which he had been deprived. He likewise restored his great-grandmother and several others whom his brother, previously established in the same position of power, had ordered to be despoiled by an unjust judgment.

25. A great assembly of wise men was afterward held at a place called Bradanfoort. There Dunstan was unanimously appointed bishop, especially because he had continually attended the royal presence on account of his prudent counsel.

[Note: Two places called Bradford are found in Dorset, two in Devon, and one in Wiltshire. The last is the more famous and the head of a hundred; it lies about two days’ journey from Glastonbury.]

After the king had been suitably instructed in godly conduct by Blessed Dunstan and the other wise men, at the king’s summons, he began to suppress the wicked everywhere, to love the just and the temperate with a pure heart, to subject the surrounding kings and tyrants to himself, to renew or enrich the churches of God that had been destroyed, and to gather companies of servants for the praise of the supreme God. He guarded his entire region as a king beneath the protection of peace.

Then he became pastor of the Church of Worcester. Cynewald, having been taken away by the course of mortal life,

[Note: Cynewald, called Kinewold by others, is said to have died in 957, and Saint Dunstan was ordained, as is also read below in Osbern.]

succumbed; and Blessed Bishop Dunstan, appointed by the king, took over that same Church to guard it with pastoral vigilance.

There he immediately planted the vine of true faith and the branch of justice with discerning cultivation, and sowed the wheat-like seed of the Holy Trinity in the hearts of believers, uprooting the thorns of error, so that after the end of the present age they might reach, unharmed, the life that endures forever through good works.

When the aforesaid king saw that the vigilant shepherd was properly governing and guarding the Church entrusted to him, he entrusted him with the Church of London, which had been widowed of its pastor,

[Note: After Brithelm, bishop of London, died in 958, King Eadgar of Mercia also entrusted that Church to Saint Dunstan.]

so that he might prepare a bridge for the great population of that city and also for the remaining multitude of the East Saxons, by which they could climb to the lofty summits of heaven.

For many years Dunstan carefully governed these two Churches under the authority of his episcopal dignity. To each flock alike, by example and teaching, he showed the way leading to the true sheepfolds of Christ.

[Note: The Westminster writer adds under the year 959: “Immediately afterward, having built at Westminster a monastery for twelve monks, in the place where Bishop Mellitus had once built a church for Blessed Peter, he appointed Saint Wulfius abbot there, with the support of Saint Dunstan,” as is read in his Life on 8 January, the day on which he is commemorated.]

26. When greedy death, with insatiable devouring, had brought venerable Odo—archbishop of the metropolitan city and ruler of Christ’s Church—to an end, consuming him according to Adam’s condition,

[Note: Saint Odo died in the year 958; his feast is kept on 4 July.]

Aelfsinus, pastor of the Winchester people, was appointed to the same supreme priestly see.

Following the custom of the supreme pontiffs, he hastened toward the Roman city to request the pallium of the chief dignity. But he was hindered in the Alpine mountains by a terrible obstacle of snow. It had bound him with such a severe frost that he perished there in death. His young companions returned after burying the bishop and reported with tears that such misfortune had befallen them in those mountains.

After his death they chose Byrhtelm, overseer of the Dorset people, as supreme priest of the holy Church of Dorobernia. He was a gentle, moderate, humble, and kind man, so much so that he did not restrain the arrogant and rebellious under the rod of correction as he ought to have done.

It is the duty of rulers to guard the good well and, with all the strength they possess, to guide them toward better things; but they must rebuke the wicked and rebellious with strict correction until they turn them away from the paths of vanity.

When the king learned that the aforesaid bishop was failing to fulfill these prescribed duties among the people entrusted to him because of excessive mildness, he ordered him to return by the roads through which he had come and to take up again the dignity he had relinquished.

Thereafter, with divine regard and on the advice of the wise, he appointed Dunstan, whom he knew to be steadfast, supreme priest of the aforesaid Church.

27. Immediately, after accepting the priesthood, he undertook the lengthy journeys customary for supreme priests and proceeded by a prosperous route toward the city of Rome.

[Note: The Worcester, Durham, and other writers likewise say that this took place in the year 960.]

The Lord accompanied him on his journey and did not abandon him as he journeyed in pure faith, just as he promised through the Prophet to every faithful person:

“I will give you understanding and instruct you in this way in which you shall walk; I will fix my eyes upon you” (Psalm XXXI, 8).

And again:

“I shall go before you, and I shall humble the glorious ones of the earth” (Isaiah 45:2).

After he had hurried through a long journey, all the provisions they had carried, whether on horseback or by other means of transport, had been entirely consumed by their own people or by others. He said to his steward:

“What provision do you have to contribute toward sustaining us through this night?”

The steward replied angrily:

“Absolutely nothing. You took no care to reserve anything for yourself; whatever food we seemed to have, you distributed by your generous command to our own people and to outsiders.”

The bishop said to him:

“Do not, I beg you, be excessively troubled about this, for our Lord Jesus Christ is sufficiently generous and rich toward all who believe in him.”

The steward replied again:

“Now you will see what your Christ will give you to eat during this night.”

The bishop rose, since evening time was approaching, in order to complete the fitting offices of evening praise in that remote place.

The aforesaid steward continued to shout after him in foolish complaint:

“Go and worship that Christ of yours as much as you like, paying no attention to any other aspect of our need.”

There were in that same village, where the man of God and his companions were then staying as guests, messengers of a certain venerable abbot who had been awaiting the blessed bishop’s arrival for three days.

Before Dunstan had finished singing the offices of evening praise that he had begun, the messengers arrived with rich gifts of thanks and all the delicacies of that region. They greeted the bishop affectionately in the name of the abbot and the faithful company of his brothers.

Gratefully accepting these tokens of blessing and affection, Dunstan returned the greeting to the gracious abbot, together with the devoted fellowship of the brothers who were staying with him.

Afterward they lived for a long time, hastening onward in comfort, from the gifts provided through the affection of those brothers. Thus the foolish complaint of the insolent servant, overcome by the bishop’s firm faith, fell silent.

28. At last, with the Lord guiding him, he reached the Church of the Roman See, which he had desired to visit, and there, under the privilege of his episcopal office, he gloriously received the principal pallium together with the apostolic blessing. After visiting the shrines of the saints and bringing comfort to Christ’s poor, he returned by peaceful roads all the way to his homeland. When the supreme pontiff of the English had returned, endowed with spiritual grace, he first began—since he was higher than the other orders of priests—to subject himself to the higher services of Christ, lest, while supplying others with the nourishment of the true faith or showing them the straight way to heavenly things by salutary speech, he himself should—as the Apostle says—become disqualified (1 Cor. 9:27) and contrary to his own preaching. Then he set about restoring what had been destroyed, justifying what had been neglected, enriching holy places, loving the righteous, recalling the erring to the way, building churches of God, and fulfilling in everything the name of a true shepherd.

29. Indeed, if day and night I were to utter thousands of sounds with an iron tongue, contrary to nature, I would still be unable to recount all the beneficial works of virtue that he performed, whether openly or secretly. I do, however, profess that I can report one thing about him: although here below he lived enclosed in a bodily covering, in mind—whether awake or resting under the hold of sleep—he always remained above, as the Apostle Paul said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20).

This was especially often evident when he composed divine songs of sacred melodies, which he had never received from human beings but had learned with receptive understanding from the blessed citizens of the heavenly realm through revelation during sleep [Col. 1448D] [Note: “Sopitalis,” from the participle *sopitus* (“lulled to sleep”), is used of a vision granted through sleep.]. The following account makes this clear.

One night, following devout prayer and the final office of Compline, when he had committed his blessed limbs to rest, he saw with unmistakable clarity how his own mother—who had brought him forth into this world—was joined in marriage to a certain most powerful king as his wedded bride, in the presence of the highest of his princes and under the title of a dowry. And at these royal nuptials there arose such joy among the singers that the rejoicing hosts resounded on every side with a most sweet hymn, to be sung with sonorous praise in honor of that king.

While these events continued for a long time, a certain young man, clothed in snowy whiteness, approached amid the voices of the singers and said to the bishop within the vision:

“Do you not see and hear how all this exultant multitude glorifies the great king in its companies by loudly acclaiming him, while you alone remain silent? Why do you not, with open voice, sound forth with us worthy praises in celebration of so great a king, when above all others you ought especially to rejoice over so great a union of your parent?”

He replied that he did not know such songs, and that he was entirely unaware of what they were singing in praise of the king. But the other said:

“Do you wish me to teach you what you ought to sing?” [Col. 1448D]

When he humbly declared that he did, the young man immediately instructed him in the following model of an antiphon:

“O King, ruler of the nations, lord of all: because of the throne of your majesty, grant us pardon, O King Christ, for our sins. Alleluia.”

After this had been repeated several times and firmly impressed upon him in the same vision, upon waking he uttered a repeated refrain. He immediately ordered it to be written down, before it slipped from his memory, and instructed a certain monk to learn it while it was still fresh. In the morning he had all those subject to him, monks and clerics alike, make it resound as they learned it. He himself continually said amid the voices of those singing, with an abundant shower of tears [Col. 1449A]:

“For he is true and no deceiver, the one who taught and showed me this sonorous antiphon in the vision of this night.”

Thus, without doubt, as we have already said above, it became clear in what regions he himself remained in spirit while his body rested.

30. Now, before I hasten farther in my reading, I should like to find a learned interpreter to fit the mystery of this wondrous vision to its meaning—or, if by some effort I were able, to unfold its interpretation myself as far as my strength permits, although it has been melted by a lukewarm fire.

I think that the mother of the holy bishop, joined in marriage to a great king, signifies the holy Church [Col. 1449D] [Note: Osbertus adds to the foregoing: “He who wrote about these matters before me wishes this to be understood mystically as referring to Mother Church,” and so on, evidently alluding to the author of this Life.]. She regenerated him, and many others as well, in the maternal manner, through the spiritual womb of holy baptism, from the transgression of the first parent [Col. 1449B] [Note: Here “privilege” is understood as a violation or transgression of the law.].

Thus this same holy mother Church, now joined through recognition of the true faith and the embrace of divine love to the supreme King—namely, Christ the Lord—seems to cling to him as a bride to her husband. She cries out in the Song of Songs:

“The king brought me into his chamber; we shall exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts more than wine; the upright love you” (Song 1:3).

And again:

“The king brought me into the wine cellar; he ordered love toward me. Sustain me with flowers, surround me with apples, because I languish with love. His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song 2:4–6), and so forth.

Alternatively, I think that the mother of this same holy bishop, joined in marriage to the exalted King [Col. 1449C], may signify the Church of his own episcopate, which he had received to be guarded in the place of a mother under the hand of the eternal King—namely, Christ the Lord—and to be comforted in the unimpaired purity of virginity [Col. 1450D] [Note: *Solatura* is used for *solanda*, “to be comforted”; this expression, as you may already have noticed, seems to have been familiar to this author. For below, in no. 14, we find *venaturus*, that is, “to be captured by hunting,” in no. 18; and *tumulaturus*, that is, “to be buried.”].

Thus the same Lord, fastened to the cross on the gibbet for the sins of the peoples, entrusted his mother, the Virgin, to the virgin disciple, saying: “Behold, I commit my Mother to you as a mother.”

The military companies that exultantly resounded with a song of praise to their king, I do not doubt, were the heavenly citizens of the angels. Although at some time they had been enemies of human beings because of the discordant separation caused by sins, they now see that the inhabitants of heaven and earth have been joined into one household under a father. Therefore they do not cease to sing such songs day and night to God, the true King:

“Give praise to our God, all his saints, and you who fear him, little and great, because the Lord our almighty God has reigned in heaven and likewise on earth. Therefore let us rejoice and exult and give him glory” (Rev. 19:5).

The multitude of the heavenly army sang this same glory when the Lord was born, announcing peace in heaven and on earth to people of good will (Luke 2:14). It was that very peace for which the blessed Apostle pleaded, saying:

“He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2:14), and so forth.

As for the young man whom he saw shining in a garment white as snow, rebuking him somewhat harshly for remaining silent in praise of the aforesaid prince, I have no doubt that he was his guardian angel. By instructing him with spiritual words, the angel warned him not to imitate the silence of a mute dog and thereby permit the hidden enemy—the thief, namely, the devil—to steal away the souls entrusted to him or the talent of his God. Rather, he was to preach with open mouth and resound with devout confession that Christ is King and ruler of all things, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and he was to implore and beseech him, because of the throne and name of his majesty, first for his own sins and then for the sins of the peoples, so that he might mercifully forgive them, for whom he did not delay to offer himself once in obedience to his Father’s command.

## Chapter VI. Various Visions. Preparation for Death.

31. In these and similar ways, he had often learned by his ever-watchful spirit, from divine teachers, the melodies of sacred songs and other praises pleasing to God, even though his human limbs lay overcome in the sleep of slumber. Thus runs the saying of Solomon: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5:2). Again the prophet Isaiah says: “By night my spirit watches for you, O Lord, for your commandments are my light” (Isa. 26:9).

While still in the world, he also clearly saw the very enemies of the human race, as was made evident when the wretched death of King Edmund was approaching.

This king, while making his customary circuit with his men to visit the places of his own domain where he intended to dine, happened to have blessed Dunstan, then still an abbot, accompanying him. He was traveling beside a certain leading duke, namely Elfstan, and was keeping pace with him. Suddenly, as he looked ahead at the road before him, he saw a dreadful enemy running about among the king’s trumpeters in a playful manner.

After gazing at him in astonishment for a long time, he said to the aforesaid nobleman who was accompanying him:

“Do you think, my dear friend, that you can see what I see?”

The other replied:

“I see nothing except what I ought to see.”

Then he said:

“Therefore mark your eyes with the sign of the holy cross and test whether you can see what I see.”

When, at the command of blessed Father Dunstan, the man marked his eyes with the light impression of the holy cross, he immediately saw—as confirmation of so great a man’s testimony—the same enemy of God and human beings whom the blessed Father had seen, leaping about in the form of a little black man. From this hostile manifestation of the wicked demon he was then able to perceive that certain serious misfortunes were destined to befall some of them. When the sign of the cross had been made, the enemy disappeared.

32. After they had ceased speaking about this wicked apparition of the deceiver they had seen [Col. 1451A], the aforementioned prince asked the man of God to loosen and interpret for him the dreams of his vision, which had recently been revealed.

He said that, through the indications of visions, he had seen the king in his palace dining hall, seated with his princes and all his nobles according to customary practice. Amid the cheerful feasts of the servants and revellers, the same king whom I have mentioned had fallen asleep, overcome by slumber. Then, after the heavy burden of his sleep, nearly all his princes and wise men had been changed into he-goats and she-goats, abandoning their human form.

Blessed Dunstan, immediately replying with prophetic eloquence, said:

“The king’s sleep is an indication of his death. As for what you saw—his magnates and wise men changed into dumb or senseless animals—this signifies a future time in which nearly all the princes and rulers of this region will voluntarily stray from the way of truth, of which they themselves are supposed to be wise, like foolish animals without a shepherd.”

33. When these things had happened, they reached the royal settlement, continuing to speak about them throughout the journey. At the twilight of that day, the man of God Dunstan again saw, at the king’s evening feast, the same enemy—or perhaps another—moving about among the numerous servants.

Then, if I am not mistaken, three days later, on the very day when the aforesaid king was destined to perish by the sword, he saw for the third time an unknown person. He did not know whether this figure was hostile or spiritual, but the man carried in his hand a large roll of an elongated sheet, densely written with characters. This occurred at the moment when the king, after the celebration of Mass and about to take his final meal, was returning to the hall.

When Dunstan asked who he was, the figure replied in the Saxon language that he came from the regions of the eastern kingdom and that, together with the king, he possessed certain secrets concerning a nuptial word.

When he was announced to the king and was to be brought into his presence, as is customary with visitors, he was nowhere to be found. But on that same day, as we have said, the bitter anguish of death entered secretly into the king’s heart through the dagger of a treacherous robber.

Behold how promptly the holy man’s foreknowledge concerning the king was revealed. As for the princes, it did not become apparent until the time of King Eadwig—if one may rightly call him a king who governed neither himself nor anyone else well [Col. 1451D–1452A].

Since blessed Father Dunstan was moved by the Spirit of God, as the Apostle says (Rom. 8:14), he had deserved these and similar mysteries as a son of God. Yet many people claimed that he was uttering the most senseless ravings of words when, instructed by a prophetic mouth and the Holy Spirit, he foretold many things that we afterward saw come to pass with the clearest signs [Note: Osbertus, in Surius, reports another vision that occurred under King Edgar in these words:

“On another occasion the king went hunting early on a Sunday morning and asked Dunstan, who happened to be with him, to defer his Mass until he returned. As the third hour approached, the man of God proceeded to the church. Clothed in sacred vestments, he waited for the king, as he had promised. He stood leaning on his elbows against the altar, devoted to prayer and tears. Suddenly, lightly overcome by sleep, he was carried up into heaven. Joined to the blessed hosts of angels, he heard them singing praise to the highest Trinity in melodious voices: ‘Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison, Kyrie eleison.’ Having been instructed by the contemplation of their heavenly melody, he returned to himself.

“The king turned to his attendants and asked whether he had come or not. When he learned that he had not yet come, he returned to his prayers. After no great interval, he was again carried outside himself and heard a loud voice in the heavens saying: ‘Go, the Mass is ended.’ When the response ‘Thanks be to God’ was given, the king’s clerics came running and cried out that the king was present; they begged the priest to celebrate Mass more quickly. But he turned from the altar and declared that he had already celebrated Mass and would not celebrate another that day.

“After he had removed his sacred vestments, his attendants asked him about the matter; he revealed what had been hidden. From that time onward, therefore, he prohibited the king from hunting on Sundays. He also taught his people the ‘Kyrie eleison’ that he had learned in heaven, and today the holy Church sings it in many places during the solemn celebration of Mass.”]

34. He also saw and heard, without any obstacle of difficulty, certain wondrous mysteries of spiritual secrets, which I shall now set down.

As we have said, this venerable man was always inflamed with the love of God and therefore carefully visited the sites of holy monasteries for the edification of souls. In accordance with this salutary custom, he came to the place of the baths, where hot water bubbles up in vaporous drops from the hiding places of the abyss. The inhabitants, in their native tongue, customarily call the place Bath [Col. 1452D] [Note: Bath, or Bathonia, is a celebrated episcopal city in the county of Somerset.].

After he had been charitably received and was staying there among the brothers of that place, after the hour of the midday meal he saw the soul of a certain young student from the monastery of Glastonbury being carried by God’s angels, amid hymnal praises, to the heights of heaven, accompanied on every side by the great funeral procession of the heavenly citizens.

On the following day, as though to confirm this wondrous vision, a certain provost from the aforesaid monastery, named Ceolwy, arrived. He wished, as was customary, to seek the bishop’s advice concerning monastic matters and the affairs of his brethren.

As soon as the bishop had given him his blessing, he anxiously asked whether everything was going well with his brothers. Not imagining the boy’s death, the provost replied that everything was in complete and sound condition.

But the bishop, more perceptive than he because of his own vision, said in a restrained tone:

“I do not think that everything among everyone will prove beneficial in the human sphere of departures.”

The other replied:

“Everything is indeed so, except that yesterday, around midday, a little boy from our community underwent unavoidable death as he died.”

“This is what I meant,” said the holy bishop. “May his blessed spirit, according to our vision, rest in peace.”

35. Again, while he was staying at his own monastery, namely Glastonbury, that diligent guardian of Christ’s flock was walking with one of the monastery’s monks from house to house, inspecting the provisions and other necessities of the common brothers. As he was returning and approached the western regions of the ancient church [Col. 1452D–1453A], he heard from a distance a voice suddenly sent from heaven as an unexpected omen. In gentle speech it invited the monk walking with him to the delights of heaven, saying:

“Come, come, Aelfsige, come”—for that, I believe, was the brother’s name.

Then the blessed man, understanding that the summons was an invitation for his servant, said:

“Hasten bravely, then, brother; prepare yourself as quickly as possible, for within a very few days, called by the Lord, you will depart from the refuse of this world to him.”

This was fulfilled concerning him, as Dunstan had foretold, after not very many days had passed, with credible indication.

Afterward, in the same place, he ordered a square church with equal angles to be built in the form of a little shrine [Col. 1453B], and when it had been built he solemnly consecrated it in honor of the holy and gracious Baptist John.

O great merit of the glorious bishop, who while still living was worthy to behold visions of angels and to hear their wondrous voices!

36. While he was therefore residing in the city of his own episcopate, among his other lofty practices of holy custom it was his habit, during the secret hours of night [Col. 1453D] [Note: In the Life of Saint Ethelbert, king of Kent, on 24 February, no. 3, we read: “Coming frequently by night to the monastery of Saints Peter and Paul to pray, Saint Dunstan was deemed worthy to see a vision of the heavenly citizens and to participate in heavenly hymns. He is said often to have remarked that wherever anyone set foot in a church or cemetery, he would tread upon the foot of some saint, so full were these places of the bodies of saints.”], to go around the holy places, continually singing sacred psalmody, because of the many crowds of people who clung to him and the occupation of many others.

Bound by this rule of religious practice, he came to the little church of the blessed Father Augustine, as I have said, to pray during the night. When he had completed his sacred prayers there, he proceeded to the eastern church of the divine Mother [Col. 1453C] [Note: Concerning this church of the Virgin Mother of God, the following revelation is reported in the Life of Saint Adrian the Abbot, 9 January, no. 6:

“When the church in which he rests had been burned, he appeared in a vision to a certain man and said: ‘Go and tell Bishop Dunstan: Christ’s servant Adrian commands you thus. You rest carefully beneath well-covered roofs, while the Mother of our Lord and we, his servants, endure every assault of heaven.’ Hearing this, Dunstan repaired the church of Saint Mary, which, carried away by eternal sweetness, he used to visit every night. One night, when the same bishop entered the church, he saw Saint Adrian praising the Lord together with the Lady of the world amid the choirs of the heavenly beings.”], intending to pray there for an equal length of time.

When he had approached it and had arrived there while singing psalms, he unexpectedly heard unusual voices of musicians [Col. 1453C] [Note: “Sonorita” seems to be used for “citharist,” or harpist.], resounding in that same basilica with subtle melody.

Immediately, looking through an opening in a broad aperture, he saw that the aforementioned church was suffused with radiant light, and that companies of virgins were circling in the choir while singing this hymn of the poet Sedulius:

“Let us sing, companions, let us sing honor to the Lord:

[Col. 1453D] May Christ’s sweet love resound from the pious mouth,” and so forth.

He also perceived that, after each verse, they sang back the first little verse of the same hymn in alternating voices, as though in harmony with their circling, in the manner of human virgins, saying:

“Let us sing, companions, let us sing honor to the Lord.”

These venerable marks of spiritual gifts, and countless others which neither I nor any other inhabitant of this life could recount in human speech, the outstanding Bishop Dunstan was worthy to receive because he walked in the ways of justice [Col. 1454A].

37. Now, since I cannot explain all the exercises of his good works—even if I were to devote myself day and night to the highest keenness of meditation, deprived of natural sleep—I nevertheless think it right, spurred by God’s admonition, to unravel at least those things that I myself either saw or heard, as far as charitable ability permits.

While he laboriously endured the tedious dwelling of this life, his greatest concern was to devote himself constantly to sacred prayers and to the psalmody of David’s ten-stringed instrument; to spend successive nights in vigils, overcoming sweet sleep; to labor fervently and continually at ecclesiastical works; or, whenever he could behold the first light of the rising day, to correct corrupt books by erasing the falsity of their writing.

He also devoted himself to discerning truth from falsehood with a keen mind when judging between one person and another; to making all who were hostile or quarrelsome peaceful and reconciled through calm speech; to helping widows, orphans, strangers, and newcomers in their needs with pious assistance; to separating unsuitable or unjust marriages through rightful dissolution; to strengthening every human order, arranged in three divisions, in its proper steadfast purpose by word and example; to supporting the churches of God, so that they might be enriched from the just revenue he had acquired; and to seasoning the unlearned of either order, men and women alike, whoever he could reach day and night, with heavenly salt—that is, with instruction in saving wisdom [Col. 1454B].

Therefore all this English land was filled with his holy teaching, shining before God and human beings like the sun and moon.

Whenever he judged that he ought to render to Christ the Lord the due hours of his service [Col. 1454C] [Note: *Vernulitas*, that is, “service”], and the other celebrations of Mass, he carried them out in singing with such integrity of mind that he seemed to speak with the Lord himself face to face. Although previously he had been deeply entangled in the conflicts of the tumultuous crowd, his eyes and hands, like those of blessed Martin, were always directed toward heaven, and he never relaxed his spirit from prayer.

Whenever he performed any other work worthy of perfection or praise—whether in the sacred ordinations of priests, the consecrations of churches or altars [Col. 1454D], or any other institution of divine matters—he always did so with an abundant shower of tears. The invisible inhabitant, the Holy Spirit, who continually dwelt in him, powerfully drew those tears from the streams of his eyes.

[Col. 1455A] 38. When the heavenly observer had contemplated these pious practices and all the labors of the blessed man for a very long time, gazing upon them from the lofty heights of heaven, he finally decided in his mercy to bring his arduous struggles to an end, so that Dunstan might receive in heaven, together with the blessed hosts of angels, the reward he had so often earned by sweating while bearing Christ’s light burden on earth.

The day of the Ascension of the Lord our God was approaching, and with it the day of his departure. Nevertheless, on that day, at the Lord’s command, he completed the solemn celebration of Mass without any impairment, and he ministered to the people entrusted to him the final nourishment of the word of God amid many showers of tears.

He continually taught that the Son of God had descended from the highest seats of heaven to earth for the salvation of humanity, so that by his manifest love he might reveal that he and his Father, together with the Holy Spirit, are one God [Col. 1455B]. He also taught that on the same day of which I have spoken, after conquering the devil and liberating his people, he ascended into the heavens from which he had appeared to come [Col. 1456A].

When he had brought this exhortation to its conclusion, with immense love of heart he asked for what he himself first obtained through swift petition: namely, that the almighty Lord, in paternal mercy, would grant all the faithful—members, that is, of Jesus Christ—the ability to ascend, since Christ, their source and head, had powerfully ascended on that day.

With these exhortations and other salutary teachings, he earnestly admonished the hearts of those entrusted to him three times during the celebration of that one day: first, as the ecclesiastical order properly declares after the reading of the Gospel; second, after the blessing of the authority freely bestowed upon him; and third, after the bestowal of holy peace, when we sang together:

“Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.”

Then he too, having first lightened the little lambs entrusted to him of the burdens of their sins, with pious [lacuna]; the remainder is missing.

[Col. 1455]

## In the Year of the Lord 1006. Saint Aelfric, Archbishop of Canterbury

[Col. 1455]

## Historical Notice on Saint Aelfric

(Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, vol. VIII, p. 55.)

[Col. 1455C] 1. The name of this holy bishop is written in various ways by English authors. They call him Alfric, Aelfric, Elfric, Alvric, Alvred, and sometimes, in Saxon, Alrio. No one records his lineage, parents, or homeland; nevertheless, he is said to have been born of noble stock in a letter to the people of Canterbury, which we shall reproduce below.

All agree that he lived the monastic life in the very celebrated monastery of Abingdon, or Abbendon, situated in the county of Berkshire, and he is also said to have been abbot of that monastery. Certainly, after William of Malmesbury, in Book I of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, nearly all more recent historians grant him this title. Henry Wharton, however, denies it in volume I of *Anglia Sacra*, in a special dissertation on the two Elfrics, where he assembles much information about our Aelfric that is not unworthy of notice; he considers it more than probable that this man was abbot of Saint Albans.

Moreover, in the decree of his election, which we shall present below, he is called a monk, not an abbot; nor has anyone committed to writing what an abbot he was or for how long he held that office. The letter that we reproduce here in full from Nicholas Harpsfield’s *History of England*, century ten, chapter seven, bears witness that he flourished in many virtues at the monastery of Abbendon.

“To all the sons of the holy Church of Canterbury, the clergy and people of that same Church offer devout prayers.

“It is known to your whole community how long it has been, through various events and successive occurrences, since the mother Church of England was deprived of her shepherd and left without a ruler [Col. 1457A]. This is recognized as harmful not only to us but also to you and to the whole of this island, since it is clear that the care of the entire country has been entrusted to the metropolitan.

“Therefore we have chosen the monk of the holy Church of Abbendon, named Elfric, whom we know most fully: noble in birth and character, instructed in apostolic and ecclesiastical discipline, Catholic in faith, prudent by nature, teachable, patient, temperate in conduct, chaste in life, sober, humble, affable, merciful, learned, instructed in the law of God, versed in the meanings of Scripture, practiced in ecclesiastical doctrines, and understanding with sound judgment—and teaching and observing with sound judgment—the ecclesiastical rules according to the course of Scripture, the tradition of the orthodox, and the constitutions of the bishops of the apostolic see expressed in canons and decrees.

“He embraces the faithful word that accords with doctrine and is able with modesty to correct those who resist; he is capable of opposing and refuting those who contradict sound teaching; he is hospitable, modest, and well ordered in his household; he is not a recent convert; he has a good reputation; he ministers in each rank according to ecclesiastical tradition; and he is prepared for every good work and to give an answer to everyone who asks for an account of the hope that is in him [Col. 1457B]. Him, therefore, we …”

2. Menardus, in Book II of his *Observations on the Benedictine Martyrology*, and Harpsfield, in the place cited above, assert that this letter was sent by the people of Canterbury to the monks of Abbendon, although its heading says that it was issued by the clergy and people of Canterbury to the sons of the Church of Canterbury.

I, however, strongly suspect that it was not written by the people of Canterbury, but rather by the people of Wilton to the people of Canterbury themselves, or to the archbishop of Canterbury, requesting that he confirm the election made by them [Col. 1457C]. For Aelfric was bishop of Wilton before he obtained the see of Canterbury.

The decree of election was to be sent to the people of Canterbury, or to their archbishop, since he was the metropolitan to whom, as the words of the letter itself state, responsibility for the whole province had been entrusted. This will be clear to anyone who reads the letter attentively, since it contains several statements that are entirely unsuitable for a bishop but properly applicable to a monk or abbot being sought as a bishop.

“We have chosen,” they say, “the monk of the holy Church of Abbendon, named Elfric.” Why would they not have called him a bishop if this letter concerned the translation of Alfric from the see of Wilton to Canterbury? It is certain that Alfric was transferred from the see of Wilton to Canterbury.

No less incompatible with a bishop is what is added at the end of the letter: “ministering in each rank according to ecclesiastical tradition” [Col. 1457D]. Who would say this of a man who was already a bishop?

Finally, other passages could be brought forward that seem to support this position, although it must be admitted that, apart from the heading attributing the letter to the people of Canterbury, there are also other features that are not free from difficulty. Since these matters, however, do not concern our present purpose, I gladly pass them over. It is enough for us to learn from this letter that our Alfric was noble in character and birth and adorned with many distinguished virtues, which prepared the way for him to attain episcopal dignity.

3. In the year 989—or, as others hold, 1191—when Siricius, bishop of Wilton, had been elevated to the see of Canterbury, as we shall prove below, our Alfric was appointed bishop of Wilton. No one records what he accomplished in that see, although it is a strong indication of his outstanding merit that he was transferred to the primatial see of all England [Col. 1458A] at a time when the English Church was richly endowed with most holy bishops.

This occurred, by the agreement of nearly all historians, in the year 996, and he held the see for ten years. There is no controversy about these matters.

There is, however, disagreement among the authors as to whom he succeeded in the see of Canterbury. Some assert that Siricius succeeded Alfric, while others say that he preceded him. William of Malmesbury, in Book I of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, in the chapter on the bishops of Canterbury, places Alfric before Siricius. Nearly all the others, however, place Siricius between Alfric and our Elphegus; and we willingly follow this latter opinion.

Nor should the sole authority of William seem so weighty that what he once stated—indeed, outside his immediate subject—ought to be preferred to the unanimous judgment of all other writers. Against him we set not only Godwin, Henschenius, and other recent authors, but also ancient charters and English historians nearly contemporary with Alfric himself: namely, Roger Hoveden, the Chronicle of Melrose, recently published at Oxford together with Ingulf, and Osbern, a witness beyond exception, who shortly after Alfric’s death was a monk of the Church of Canterbury, along with many others [Col. 1458B].

Osbern, in chapter 3 of the *Life of Saint Elphegus*, asserts that Elphegus was appointed to the see of Canterbury in the year of Christ 1006, in which same year, or the preceding one, Alfric unquestionably died. To Osbern we add Gervase of Canterbury, who deliberately composed a short work on the archbishops of Canterbury, as well as other authors whom it would serve no purpose to list individually.

We therefore hasten to the deeds that Alfric performed once he had become archbishop.

4. That Alfric went to Rome barefoot in order to obtain the archiepiscopal pallium is attested by an anonymous monk, the author of the *Chronicle of Abingdon*, cited by Harpsfield; he adds that the cloak which the holy bishop had worn on that journey was, in his own time, still preserved at Abingdon as a memorial of his piety. How ardently he labored to promote ecclesiastical affairs, and especially monastic ones, is demonstrated by his various subscriptions, through which he either confirmed the liberties of monasteries or contributed his efforts to the construction of new ones.

He confirmed in 1001 the donation made by King Ethelred to the nuns of the church of Saint Edward at Shaftesbury, in volume I of the *Monasticum Anglicanum*, p. 217. Likewise, he confirmed the charter of the same king for the foundation of the monastery of Evesham in Oxfordshire, which Ethelman erected in 1005 under the rule of our holy father Benedict, in honor of our holy Savior and of all the saints. He himself declares that he composed the charter for the erection of another monastery, which Wilfric had built at Burton in the preceding year, namely 1004, under the same rule of Saint Benedict. This charter is found in volume I of the *Monasticum Anglicanum*, and also in the *Burton Chronicle*, which was recently published at Oxford together with the complete *Ingulf*.

But the charter praised above is superior to the others: in it, King Ethelred, after expelling the clerics from Christ Church, permanently established monks there. It seemed worthwhile to present its opening here, since it contributes greatly to commending the pastoral care of our Alfric:

> “In the name of the Lord God Almighty. I, Aethelred, by the gift of God king of the English peoples and ruler of the other surrounding islands, make known to all Christian Englishmen that the venerable Archbishop Aelfric, through his wisdom and pastoral care, has repeatedly brought me to occupy myself with the commandments of God, and that I myself have determined diligently to learn whatever belongs to the commandments of God and whatever sacred teaching is necessary,” etc.

We owe this version of Ethelred’s charter, which had been issued in Saxon, to Henry Spelman. He also presents another ancient Latin version, which commends our Aelfric no less. From it it also appears that the charter was issued not in 1006, as the commonly circulated copies have it, but several years earlier, namely in 1002 or 1003. Not before 1002, because Godwin, who subscribes to this charter among the other bishops, obtained the see of Rochester in 1001; and not much later, since Wlfranus, another witness, died in 1003 or 1004 according to Savile’s chronological tables.

Moreover, since monks had already been established in the Canterbury monastery of the Savior before Alfric’s time, as William of Malmesbury maintains in Book I of *On the Bishops of the English*, this charter was either issued to confirm what had already previously been established, or, indeed, to expel the clerics who, after perhaps driving out the monks, had occupied this church; or finally—and this seems more plausible to many—the monks were not established in this church after clerics had then been expelled, but the monks themselves who were performing the divine offices there were reformed and recalled to a better life.
