5. Alfric was made illustrious not only by his virtues but also by exceptional learning and singular erudition. Hence some are said to have called him “the Grammarian,” a name under which he gained a place among England’s distinguished writers. Pitseus lists his works, following Leland, in *On the Illustrious Writers of England*, under the eleventh century:

> “One book of Grammar. Two books containing one hundred and eighty sermons in the Saxon language. One letter on the customs of monks. He also translated the canons of the Council of Nicaea into the Saxon language. A Saxon chronicle, chiefly concerning the Church of Canterbury. One book of a Latin dictionary. One book of a translation of Genesis. Four books on the Dialogues of Pope Saint Gregory. One translation of Donatus. Excerpts from Donatus, and many other works.”

Most of these still exist in manuscript in the celebrated public library at Cambridge.

The translation of the Nicene canons mentioned here by Pitseus seems to be none other than the canons addressed to Bishop Wllino by Aelfric, which Spelman includes in volume I of the *Anglican Councils*, p. 582; and he argues that these, as well as the two books of sermons, can scarcely be attributed to our Alfric of Canterbury. The author of volume I of *Anglia Sacra* holds the same view and supports it in a special dissertation on the two Aelfrics, where he argues that most of the short works commonly attributed to our Alfric belong to another Aelfric, who was surnamed “the Grammarian.”

Other learned men disagree. Yet, as evidence for Alfric’s learning, one may cite the Prologue—although written in a rough hand—to the *Life of Saint Dunstan*, which its contemporary author addressed to our Alfric. Its beginning was published in the previous century in the preliminary observations to the *Life of Saint Dunstan*, where it reads:

> “To the most prudent lord archon Albric, B., the least of all priests and a humble native of the Saxons, sends the high joys of heaven. You, indeed, illustrious shepherd, because of the extraordinary extent of your widely renowned knowledge, and through the magnificent, gracious dignity of your privilege, [are] an invincible protection to me,” etc.

Concerning the *Life of Ethelwold*, written by Alfric, see volume I of *Anglia Sacra*, p. 128.

6. After completing the ten years during which Alfric governed the Church of Canterbury, he died on 28 August 1006. His body was buried in the monastery of Abingdon, where he had lived the monastic life, and was later brought back to Canterbury. This translation seems to have been recorded under the heading “depositio” in the obituary book of the archbishops of Canterbury, in volume I of *Anglia Sacra*, where, on p. 54, we read:

> “16 Kalends of December. At Canterbury, the burial of blessed memory, Alfric, archbishop and confessor of that city.”

This translation is said to have taken place under King Cnut, according to the *History of the Monastery of Abingdon*, which appears in the volume of *Anglia Sacra* cited above.

Menardus asserts in Book II of his *Observations on the Benedictine Martyrology* that Alfric was renowned for miracles both before and after his death. Certainly the anonymous author of the *Chronicle of Abingdon*, whom we have already cited from Harpsfield, gives a lengthy account of the miracles of this same saint. He reports not only those which Alfric performed as a boy or later in the course of his life, but also many others that occurred at his tomb in the monastery of Abingdon. Thus, renowned for miracles, he is commemorated in the Benedictine calendars on 28 August. Pitseus calls him a pious man and one learned beyond the ordinary standard of humanity. Nearly all who have written commentaries on the affairs of the English Church remember him.

[Col. 1459]

# Dissertation on Aelfric or Elfric, Archbishop of Canterbury: Whether He Was Aelfric the Grammarian

*(Henry Wharton, Anglia Sacra, I, 125.)*

[Col. 1459D] We discussed above the order which Elfric held among the archbishops of Canterbury, and asserted that he succeeded Siricius and occupied the see from approximately 995 until 1005 or the following year. Another and much more difficult question concerning Archbishop Elfric remains to be examined: namely, whether this man was that learned Elfric whom they commonly call “the Grammarian,” to whom we owe almost all that survives of Saxon literature. I would readily believe this, since it is always desirable that the primacy of learning should be joined to the primacy of the Church. But I fear that, after the arguments on both sides have been weighed, the Archbishop of Canterbury must be judged to have been someone other than the Grammarian.

Bale, Pitseus, and, after them, nearly all our native writers believed that they were one and the same person; nor do I deny that I was once carried away by that error. Indeed, there are arguments of no little weight in favor of this opinion. To set aside the unanimous authority of all the more recent writers: both Elfrics were pupils of Ethelwold and achieved an outstanding reputation for learning in their own age; both were vigorous opponents of married clergy; and both are said to have died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December. No one has hitherto noted the agreement of their death dates; yet Leland, Bale, Pitseus, Usserius, and others, who investigated the antiquities of our nation with the greatest diligence, concur in the same opinion.

The most distinguished Usserius assembled many arguments in his manuscript theological library. From all of these he constructed a certain hypothesis, the epitome of which the very learned William Cave transferred into his *Literary History*, p. 588: namely, that before 956 Elfric had been abbot of some small monastery and had at that time written letters to Wulfstan, Archbishop of York, and Wulfino, Bishop of Sherborne. He then succeeded his teacher Ethelwold in the abbey of Abingdon, after the intervening abbot Ordgar. Soon afterward, around 969, he was appointed abbot of Saint Alban’s by Oswald, and in 974 was transferred to the governance of the monastery of Malmesbury. Next he was made Bishop of Crediton, then Bishop of Wilton after Siricius, and Bishop of Devon after Sideman. Finally he was raised to the archbishopric of Canterbury and died in 1006.

Thus the most reverend primate reconciled chronologically everything that seemed established in the accounts of Elfric. Yet, with all due respect to so great a man, I may adopt another opinion, relying on indisputable evidence concerning the matter which he either did not know or considered insufficiently. I do not, however, think it necessary to attack his hypothesis first. Its error will become apparent of its own accord in nearly every one of its parts from what I shall say below.

[Col. 1461B] We have already stated the order of Archbishop Elfric among the bishops of Canterbury: namely, that around 995 he succeeded Siricius in the archbishopric and died in 1005 or the following year. Nor does it seem more doubtful that, after Siricius had been elevated to the archbishopric, Elfric succeeded him in the see of Wilton, from which he was eventually transferred to the see of Canterbury. This is reported by William of Malmesbury, Gervase, Ralph de Diceto, and the Saxon Chronicle, among others.

The Latin version prepared by Wheloc, however, presents him as having first been Bishop of Winchester. This is plainly contrary to the testimony of the Saxon chronicler. The Saxon text reads:

> “Elfric, bishop of Wilton.”

Bale is no better, for he writes that Elfric was transferred from the see of Wells to Canterbury. Whatever certainty should properly be assigned to this matter, some statements in our historians disturb Elfric’s succession to the bishopric of Wilton.

To take the matter somewhat further back: after the translation of Bishop Odo to the archbishopric of Canterbury around 938, Osulf succeeded him, according to the unanimous opinion of all. Osulf died in 970 according to Florence; according to William of Malmesbury, Algar succeeded Osulf and Elfstan succeeded Algar; more correctly, however, Florence places Alfstan as successor to Osulf and Wulgar as successor to Alfstan. Both authors report that Elfstan was a monk of Abingdon and a disciple of Saint Ethelwold. William’s Algar is none other than Florence’s Wulgar. In the list of bishops appended to his history, he calls Alfstan’s successor Alfgar.

That Alfgar succeeded Alfstan is indicated by Florence’s account: King Ethelred assembled a great fleet and appointed as its commanders Alfric and Theored, and as bishops Alfstan of Wilton and Aescwin, who was Bishop of Dorchester. The fleet ultimately suffered the loss of a great victory through Alfric’s treachery in 992. Florence narrates the outcome in that year, although the commanders may have been placed over the fleet several years earlier, and that Bishop of Wilton may have died before the event. Certainly, by 989 Alfric occupied the see of Wilton, and Siricius had preceded him there, as we proved in the preceding dissertation.

The printed manuscript of Florence calls the man Alfstan; the oldest manuscript instead calls him Aelfgar. Alfgar therefore succeeded Alfstan, and Alfstan succeeded Osulf. Alfstan died in 980 and was buried at Abingdon, according to the ancient *History of Abingdon* mentioned below, perhaps late in the year after the Kalends of January. For Florence reports that he died in 981. Certainly Alfstan was present at the consecration of Winchester Cathedral on 20 October 980, according to Wulstan in chapter 40 of the *Life of Ethelwold*. His successor Alfgar held the see until 988. For, if William Thorn is to be trusted, Siricius, formerly abbot of Saint Augustine’s at Canterbury, was made Bishop of Winchester—read “Wilton”—through the agency of Dunstan in 988.

[Col. 1462A] William of Malmesbury and the Westminster historian write that before assuming the bishopric of Wilton, Elfric had been abbot of Abingdon; and among all recent writers this is regarded as certain. Yet they have all gone astray. The *History of Abingdon*, first published by me, follows; it deserves complete confidence. For an introduction concerning its venerable antiquity, consult the preface. This work carefully sets out the succession of the abbots of Abingdon from Ethelwold to 1131, but gives no place to Alfric. Osgar succeeded Ethelwold in 963—a fact also confirmed by Wulstan in the *Life of Ethelwold*; Edwin succeeded Osgar in 984; Wulgar succeeded Edwin in 990; Adelwin succeeded Wulgar in 1017; and Siward succeeded Adelwin in 1030.

What nevertheless gave rise to the error was that Alfric of Canterbury had first been a monk of Abingdon, according to the authority of the history cited above, under the year 1006. He had been raised in that monastery under Ethelwold, the outstanding restorer of the monastic order, as were many other bishops of that age. From the beginning of King Edgar’s reign until approximately the year 1000, nearly all the bishops and abbots of England were selected from the monasteries of Abingdon, Glastonbury, and Winchester. So powerful had the monastic order become, and so much influence did Dunstan, Ethelwold, and Oswald possess over our kings: they had introduced monks into these three monasteries above all others after expelling the clerics, and had established them as virtually three nurseries of the monastic order.

We noted above that, after expelling the clerics, Elfric of Canterbury introduced monks into Christ Church at Canterbury. He died in 1005—according to others, 1006—and was buried at Abingdon, where he had been a monk; under King Cnut he was transferred to the Church of Canterbury. The *History of Abingdon* teaches us these things. The manuscript Canterbury Martyrology gives the day of his death as the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December. A poem prefixed to his glossary, published by Somner, reports that Aelfric the Grammarian died on the same day. I nevertheless suspect that the author of the poem, deceived by the similarity of the name and of the dignities held by the two men, wrongly assigned to the Grammarian the day belonging to the Canterbury archbishop. We shall show below, on probable evidence, that the Grammarian died on another day; and it is by no means appropriate to withdraw credit from the Canterbury Martyrology on this matter.

In any case, the reputation for learning enjoyed by Elfric of Canterbury is supported not only by his education under the learned bishop Ethelwold, but also by the testimony of Bridferth, a contemporary monk of Ramsey. In the *Life of Saint Dunstan*, dedicated to Elfric himself, Bridferth praises his name on account of the extraordinary extent of his widely renowned knowledge (*Acts of the Saints*, May, volume IV, p. 346).

These are the only things established concerning Elfric, Archbishop of Canterbury. That he had previously been abbot of Saint Alban’s is, however, highly probable. I shall explain the reasons.

Thus John Capgrave writes in the *Life of Oswald*, Bishop of Worcester and later Archbishop of York. When Edgar the king and Dunstan the archbishop assigned Oswald the task of expelling secular canons from the monasteries and introducing monks—a task which he vigorously fulfilled—he appointed, among others, Elfric as abbot in the church of Saint Alban’s; Elfric was later elevated to the archbishopric of Canterbury. In the church of Ely he appointed Brithnot as abbot. (*Legendarium Novum*, fol. 252.)

I do not know where Capgrave obtained this information. Certainly John of Tynemouth, from whom he derived nearly everything else, says nothing of the kind in his manuscript *Golden History*. Yet tradition lends it credibility: among the monks of Saint Alban’s there was a tradition that a certain Alfric or Leofric, their abbot, eventually ascended the throne of Canterbury.

This is apparent from Matthew Paris’s *History of the Abbots of Saint Alban’s*, although he seems to have arranged the dates and succession of the abbots incorrectly. We have noted some of the chronological discrepancies admitted in this work in the notes to the *Chronicle of the Bishops of Lichfield*. Perhaps a similar error can also be detected here. He numbers Ulsin as the sixth abbot, Alfric as the seventh, Ealdred as the eighth, Eadmer as the ninth, Leofric as the tenth, Alfric as the eleventh, and Leofstan as the twelfth; Leofstan succeeded Alfric during the reign of Edward the Confessor.

If one reconciles the dates, one will find that the seventh abbot, Alfric, flourished during the reign of King Edgar. This agrees perfectly with Capgrave. For he appears to assert that Alfric was placed over the monastery of Saint Alban’s and Brithnot over Ely at approximately the same time; and the *History of Ely* reports that Brithnot was placed in charge of the monastery of Ely in 970. The matter is confirmed by the subscription of Aelfric the abbot to a charter of King Edgar granted to the monastery of Ramsey in 974 (*Monasticum Anglicanum*, volume I, p. 236).

This Alfric could very well have later obtained the see of Canterbury. Of his end Matthew tells us only that he, full of days and distinguished for holiness, departed to the Lord—or rather, if the truth must be confessed, that he does not know what became of him. He assigns the honor of the archbishopric, however, not to the seventh abbot but to the tenth, namely Leofric.

He arranges the matter as follows. Leofric was the son of the Earl of Kent, and Alfric was his uterine brother. When Leofric was elected archbishop of Canterbury, he did not consent, asserting that his brother Alfric was more worthy of the office. Later, however, he consented. For, when elevated to the archbishopric, he left his household overflowing with every kind of good. Alfric, his brother, succeeded him; supported by his brother the archbishop, he suppressed many insurgents, and by his authority caused the office of Saint Alban’s, composed by himself, to be published in many places throughout England, etc.

William Watts, the editor of Matthew Paris, therefore added this marginal note rather ineptly:

> “Leofric, elected archbishop, did not consent, asserting that his brother Alfric was much more worthy. Alfric therefore became Archbishop of Canterbury.”

This Alfric, while still a secular cleric, had been King Ethelred’s chancellor; afterward, when he became abbot, he purchased certain properties for his monastery from that same Ethelred. Under King Ethelred, therefore, Leofric relinquished the abbacy and Alfric succeeded him. Thus Alfric could not have been abbot of Saint Alban’s before the year 978, which Usserius assigns. But neither could he have obtained the abbacy much later.

For this Leofric, whom Matthew raises to the archbishopric, was none other than Leofric, Bishop of Crediton. He received the bishopric of Crediton from King Edward, whose chaplain he was, in 1046, as is written on the front of the Missal which he himself gave to the Church of Exeter. He transferred the see to Exeter in 1050 and died in 1071. We find no other bishop of this name among the English bishops of the same period.

If, therefore, Alfric was abbot during the reign of King Ethelred, it must be said that he preceded Leofric in office. Ralph de Diceto certainly supports this opinion (*Abbreviation of the Chronicle*, p. 446). He lists the abbots of Saint Alban’s as follows:

> “Wlsin, the sixth; Elfric; Eldred; Edmar; Aluric, the tenth. This man,” he says, “became Archbishop of Canterbury. Leofric, the eleventh abbot, brother of Eluric, succeeded him in the abbacy of Saint Alban’s.”

Ralph therefore arranged the order more cautiously, although he too was mistaken in assigning the archbishopric to Alfric, the tenth rather than the seventh abbot.

He likewise confirms that Leofric the abbot was the Bishop of Exeter, when he reports that Leofstan, the twelfth abbot, was appointed in 1047. For Leofric had obtained the see of Exeter in the preceding year. I do not know whether Matthew may have altered the offices and order of the brothers alike. The Westminster and Worcester historians report that Leofric was the king’s chancellor; no one says this of Alfric.

To state my view: if Alfric of Canterbury was previously abbot of Saint Alban’s, he was the seventh in order. I do not assert that he was, though I readily concede it. I had written this before reading Eadmer’s *Life of Oswald*. On its authority it is established with complete certainty that Archbishop Elfric of Canterbury had first been abbot of Saint Alban’s, placed in charge of that monastery recently restored by Oswald.

We must now pass from Alfric of Canterbury to the Grammarian, and first examine what William of Malmesbury reports about him. In William’s *History of the Deeds of the Kings* (Book II, chapter 8), as well as in the *Life of Aldhelm*, first published by me, p. 32, there is a charter of King Edgar granted to the monastery of Malmesbury in the year of the Lord 974, the fourteenth year of his reign. In it Edgar says that he had appointed as abbot Elfric, “a man ecclesiastical in all things”—thus in the book *On the Deeds of the Kings*. In the *Life of Aldhelm*, however, the reading is “a man most experienced in ecclesiastical conduct”; I suspect it should be read, “most experienced in all ecclesiastical duties.”

To this abbot William attaches, in the *Life of Aldhelm* (p. 33), characteristics which belong specifically to the Grammarian. He writes:

> “Unless deceptive antiquity misleads us, he was skilled in letters and, above all, a most elegant translator. At his death he left behind several books, no small monuments of his intellect: the *Life of Saint Adelwold* before Wulfstan had fashioned it with greater elaboration; an abridgment of the Passion of Saint Edmund; and many books translated from Latin into the native language.”

Everyone recognizes that these works belong to Aelfric the Grammarian. For in the public libraries we still possess almost innumerable sermons, treatises, and books of Holy Scripture translated by him from Latin into the Saxon language.

A manuscript copy of the *Life of Ethelwold* composed by him—transcribed from the Fécamp library—is in the possession of the learned Mabillon, who published its prologue in the *Benedictine Acts*, century V, p. 608, in the notes to Wulstan’s *Life of Ethelwold*. Let me note in passing that this passage of William establishes for the first time that Wulstan was the author of that *Life*, a matter about which the distinguished Mabillon had remained uncertain. What William says about Wulstan’s work agrees exactly with the *Life of Ethelwold* published there by Mabillon.

No one else has mentioned the abridgment of the *Passion of Saint Edmund* prepared by Elfric. I do not know whether it survives today. A *Life of Saint Edmund the King* in Saxon, written by Elfric, is found in the Cottonian Library, Julius E. 7.

William further adds concerning Elfric, abbot of Malmesbury, that when he was already advanced in age, he was elevated to the bishopric of Crediton and survived scarcely four years.

He was therefore entirely different from Alfric of Canterbury, who, according to William himself and everyone else, held the archbishopric for eleven years and previously held Wilton for five. The distinguished Usserius was therefore mistaken in making them one and the same person.

Moreover, in conjecturing that this great man had become Bishop of Crediton in 978, Bishop of Wilton after Siricius in 990, and likewise Bishop of Devon after Sideman at the same time, Usserius fell into error several times more. For Sideman died in 977, according to Florence, and there was no other Bishop of Devon apart from the Bishop of Crediton. William himself was no less mistaken in identifying Elfric the Grammarian with the Bishop of Crediton.

The Grammarian wrote the *Life of Ethelwold* for Kenulph, Bishop of Winchester, in 1006. But Elfric of Crediton had already been gone for a considerable time: he held the see for only four years and had four successors in the abbacy of Malmesbury before 991—Ethelward, Kineward, Brichtelm, and Brithwold. For Brithwold paid the Danegeld, according to William (*Life of Aldhelm*, p. 35). It is established that this tax was imposed in 991.

We might approach the truth still more closely if the charter of King Ethelred granted to Abbot Ethelwerd, in the place cited, presented genuine chronological indications; these have been corrupted through an error in the manuscript. William nevertheless states beforehand that the charter was issued by Ethelred while he was still a young and inexperienced king. He began his reign on 18 March 978.

The witnesses were, besides Elfric, Aescwin, Bishop of Dorchester, and those who had subscribed the preceding charter—the one by which Elfric was appointed abbot—namely Dunstan, Oswald, Ethelwold, and three Elfstans: the bishops of London, Rochester, and Wilton. Of these, Elfstan of Wilton died in 981, as we observed above. Accordingly, Elfric of Crediton died before 985. This is sufficient.

Since the authenticity of charters is rightly regarded as suspect, it will not be unhelpful to examine the succession of the bishops of Crediton. William of Malmesbury lists them as follows in Book II of *On the Deeds of the Bishops*: Edulfus, Edelgar, Elfwold, Sideman, Elfric, Elfwold. Florence preserves the same order and also supplies the years of many of them.

Ethelgar died in 953, in the twenty-first year of his episcopate. Alfwold succeeded him in 953—952 according to the *Florilegus*, although that author is inconsistent with himself, reporting his accession in exactly the same words under the year 976—and held the see for nineteen years, dying in 972. In 968 King Edgar appointed Sideman abbot of the monastery of Exeter, and in 972 made him Alfwold’s successor. Sideman died in 977. Florence’s manuscript adds that he was buried at Abingdon. Sideman’s death is confirmed by the acts of the synod held at Kyrtlington in 977 (*Anglican Councils*, volume I, p. 493). For the acts say that he died at the synod itself.

Elfric therefore succeeded him around 977 and died around 981. I believe that this is the bishop referred to in the *History of Glastonbury* (*Monasticum Anglicanum*, volume I, p. 9):

> “Elfric the bishop, monk and abbot of Glastonbury, died in 988.”

The year does not fit well; nevertheless, the conjecture is no less plausible. For the chronology usually turns out most unfortunately for the author of that history.

Having rejected William of Malmesbury’s opinion, we must investigate what is more certain about Elfric the Grammarian. It is established above all that he was a pupil of Ethelwold, first abbot of Abingdon and later Bishop of Winchester. He himself testifies to this repeatedly in his writings, praising both his teacher’s virtue and his learning.

Thus, in the first preface to his Saxon grammar, he says:

> “As we learned in the school of the venerable bishop Athelwold, who instructed many in goodness.”

In the second preface he says that Archbishop Dunstan and Bishop Ethelwold revived among the English letters that had long been buried in the monasteries.

Wulstan, another of Ethelwold’s pupils, gives clear testimony to Ethelwold’s distinguished zeal in this matter in his *Life* of him, chapter 31:

> “For it was sweet to him,” he says, “always to teach adolescents and young men, to render Latin books into English for them, to impart the rules of the grammatical art and of metrical composition, and to encourage them toward better things through pleasant conversation.”

Ethelwold had pupils among the monks of Abingdon before becoming a bishop and among the monks of Winchester after assuming the episcopate. Elfric belonged to the Winchester group. In the letter to Kenulph prefixed to the *Life of Ethelwold*, he calls himself a “Winchester alumnus.” Bishop Elphegus of Winchester also sent this Elfric to the monastery of Cerne, so that the monastery in which he lived must properly be considered to have belonged to the jurisdiction of the Bishop of Winchester.

Nevertheless, Elfric could have been subject to Ethelwold’s authority in either monastery, provided that his age allowed it. For, to use the words of John of Tynemouth in his manuscript *Golden History*, Book XXI, chapter 58:

> “After expelling the clerics from the old monastery of Winchester, he introduced monks from Abingdon, over whom he himself was both abbot and bishop.”

But the fact that Elfric was one of these monks is precluded by his not yet mature age. For in 963, when Ethelwold was transferred from the abbacy of Abingdon to the bishopric of Winchester, Elfric had not yet completed his eleventh year. This must now be demonstrated.

Abraham Wheloc published the Saxon chronology from Julius Caesar to the year of Christ 1070, using two manuscript codices: the older one from the library of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, and the more recent one from the Cottonian Library. The author of the entire work is sought in vain, for it was written by different people. The Cambridge codex, however, bears an attached note stating that this chronology was written by Elfric in the twenty-third year of his age.

It is quite clear that this cannot be understood of the latter part of the work. The earlier part, therefore, has Elfric as its author. This section pursues the affairs of the Church of Winchester with such greater diligence than the rest that at first sight it appears to have been composed by some Winchester monk.

It ends in the year 975, namely the first year of King Edward the Martyr. This will readily be apparent to anyone who consults the passage. There, after narrating Edward’s accession, the historian prays that many years may be granted to him. But in the next year whose events this chronology records—namely 977—it is related that King Edward was killed. These statements certainly could not have proceeded from one and the same author.

Elfric therefore brought his chronology to an end in 975, at the age of twenty-three; accordingly, he was born around 952.

The same Ælfric, after the year 908 and before he had yet been raised to the dignity of abbot, wrote to Wulfin, bishop of Sherborne, a very famous letter, which was published on several occasions, together with ecclesiastical canons found in Spelman, *Councils of England*, vol. I, p. 572. Spelman indeed argues (in his notes on these canons, p. 583) that Ælfric was then a bishop, deriving this conclusion from the fact that he seems to present himself as Wulfin’s equal, beginning his canons in this manner: “Ælfric, humble brother, to the venerable Bishop Wulfin.” Furthermore, there were only two bishops named Wulfin in this century: one of Sherborne from 940 to 958; the other of Dorchester from 1053 to 1067; yet no bishop Ælfric contemporary with either of them can be found. The dates of the sole Ælfric Putta, archbishop of York, come closer to the matter. For he held the see of York from 1003 to 1031, so that, if Wulfin had entered the see of Dorchester somewhat earlier, or Ælfric had held that of York somewhat longer, Archbishop Ælfric could suitably have inscribed the canons to his fellow bishop Wulfin. Spelman inclines to this opinion.

Or, if it could be granted that Ælfric, the author of the Canons, was not a bishop at that time, nevertheless, since it is established from other evidence that Ælfric, the author of the canons, was the Grammarian, and that the Grammarian was a pupil of Æthelwold, who entered upon the see in 963, it is altogether impossible that these canons could have been inscribed to Wulfin, Bishop of Sherborne, after Wulfin’s death in 958. This amounts to the position of the learned Spelman, which has almost as many errors as arguments.

As for the statement that Ælfric Putta obtained the see of York in 1003, I think it is a typographical error. The very learned man could not have failed to know that Ælfric was raised to the archbishopric of York in 1023. Nor is it worthwhile investigating the year in which Wulfin entered the episcopate. For it is perfectly clear from the preface of Ælfric the author to the manuscript codex in which the Catholic Homilies and these same canons were preserved in Saxon that these canons had been written at least before 1006. Spelman gives the beginning of the preface in the same place. In it Ælfric says that he was sent by Ælfheah, bishop of Winchester, to the monastery of Cerne and translated this book from the Latin language into the English tongue. Thus it was before 1006, the year in which Ælfheah ceased to be bishop of Winchester, and after 983, when he began to hold that office.

Ælfric could nevertheless have written the canons in Latin to Wulfin of Sherborne many years earlier and later translated them into Saxon in this place. It was not unusual for him to translate his books from Latin into Saxon and from Saxon into Latin. He could also have composed the canons before 1006 and inscribed them to Wulfin of Dorchester after 1053, as Spelman wishes. Yet it seems excessively unlikely that Ælfric composed the canons for the benefit of a prelate whom he had foreseen would exist roughly fifty years later.

If we say that they were inscribed to Wulfin of Sherborne, everything fits perfectly. Wulfin and Ælfric shared the same manner of life and devotion to the same religious party, which could easily have enabled them to form a friendship. The former was brought up under Æthelwold at Winchester, the latter under Dunstan at Glastonbury—according to the *History of Glastonbury*, p. 9. Ælfric everywhere attacked secular clerics, especially married ones, with the deepest hatred, and he pursues this subject above all others in the canons addressed to Wulfin. Wulfin, a devotee of the same party, immediately after receiving the episcopate, expelled the clerics from the Church of Sherborne and installed monks in the episcopal see, according to William of Malmesbury (*De gestis pontificum*, book II, fol. 141).

In the letter prefixed to the canons, however, Ælfric is so far from implying that he is Wulfin’s equal that he rather indicates the contrary quite clearly. Thus he addresses Wulfin:

“We willingly obeyed your command; but we did not dare to write anything concerning the episcopal rank, because it is your responsibility to know how you ought to become an example to all in the best conduct and to exhort your subjects to salvation by continual admonitions, which I speak of in Christ Jesus; especially since you ought more frequently to address your clerics and rebuke their negligence, because through their perversity almost all the established canons, the discipline of the Church, and its teaching have been destroyed.”

That he calls himself “brother” signifies nothing more than that he was a monk, the term being extremely common among monks, including those of earlier times. Moreover, it is Ælfric’s customary practice, more than anyone else’s, in all his writings to add to his proper name the name of his order or dignity. Thus almost all his works begin with “Brother Ælfric,” “Ælfric, abbot,” or “Ælfric, bishop.”

Finally, this Wulfin was Ælfric’s contemporary. For in 958—according to Spelman—he was so far from having died that he had not yet obtained the episcopate. In 962 Wulfin was appointed abbot of Westminster by Dunstan, bishop of London, according to the testimony of Ralph de Diceto (*Abbreviatio Chronicorum*, p. 456, and *Historia de praesulibus Angliae*, chapter 3). It is clear from William of Malmesbury (*De gestis pontificum*, book II, fol. 141) that he later became bishop of Sherborne, for in recounting the deeds of Wulfin of Sherborne, Malmesbury relates the same facts as Ralph concerning the abbacy of Westminster entrusted to him by Dunstan while Dunstan was bishop of London, omitting only the year.

I would readily believe that Ralph was mistaken about the year. For in the preceding dissertation we proved that Dunstan was transferred from the see of London to Canterbury toward the end of 959. According to Florence, he had become bishop of London in the preceding year, so that Wulfin was appointed abbot of Westminster in 959 or 958. Florence expressly states that he was appointed in 958, as does John Flete in his *History of Westminster*.

It remains to investigate Wulfin’s death. It occurred before 978, if Florence and Malmesbury are to be trusted together. For in that year, according to Florence, Ælfwold died; according to Malmesbury and others, he succeeded Wulfin in the see of Sherborne.

A certain Wulfin, bishop of Wilton, is recorded in the *Evidences of Christ Church, Canterbury* (col. 2223) as having subscribed a grant of Ætheric and Leofwenna together with Ælfheah, bishop of Winchester. This must therefore have taken place after 984, the year in which Ælfheah entered the episcopate. It is nevertheless easy to suppose that “Wulfin” entered incorrectly for “Wulgar.” For we proved above that Wulgar held the see of Wilton after 981.

Whatever the truth of the conjecture may be, I think the authority of these evidences deserves very little weight. I do not know whether a charter of King Æthelred, issued to Wulfsin, bishop of Sherborne, and to his monastery in 998, surpasses the authority of Florence. It is found in a very old manuscript in a half-Saxon hand and is copied below in this volume. In the midst of such disagreement among the witnesses, when I was entirely uncertain what conclusion ought chiefly to be adopted, the manuscript *History of Westminster* by John Flete fortunately came into my hands. Drawing from Sulcard, a Westminster monk who flourished about fifty years after Wulfsin, Flete reports in chapter 17 that Wulfsin was made bishop of Sherborne by King Æthelred shortly after 980 and died about 998.

I am therefore led to the opinion that the Ælfwold mentioned by Florence had presided over the see of Sherborne before Wulfsin, and that Malmesbury and his followers made an error in constructing the catalogue of the bishops of Sherborne. In the place where Malmesbury puts Wulfsin, Florence places Alfsin and the *Florilegus* Ulsin, who places his succession to Ælfred in 940.

Our Wulfsin must be sought below, approximately in the position occupied by Æthelric and Æthelsius in the commonly circulated catalogues of the bishops of Sherborne.

The authority of John Flete is supported by very ancient Saxon charters in the manuscript history of the monastery of Abingdon in the Cotton Library, Claudius B. 6. Wlfsin subscribed many of these at approximately this time. For example, charters dated 995 are subscribed by Ælfric, bishop of Wilton, and Wlfsige, fol. 96; a charter dated 995, indiction 8, by Ælfric, archbishop-elect of Canterbury, and Wulfsige, bishop of Sherborne, fol. 95; a charter dated 996, indiction 9, by Ælfric, archbishop of Canterbury, and Wulfsige, bishop of Sherborne, fol. 99. Indeed, many charters issued there after 998 are found for almost every year; yet in none of them does the name Wifsin appear.

After 987 Ælfric was sent by Ælfheah, bishop of Winchester, to the monastery of Cerne in Dorset in order to establish monastic discipline there, at the request of Earl Æthelmar, who had recently founded the monastery. Ælfric records this in the preface to the Catholic Homilies and the canons mentioned above. The foundation charter of that monastery exists (*Monasticum Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 254), dated 987.

While residing in this monastery, he translated into the Saxon language many homilies, which he calls “Catholic”; he himself reveals this in the passage cited. Thus, after 987, he composed his grammar. For in the second preface to the grammar he says that he had rendered eighty books of homilies into the vernacular. We possess exactly that number, and no more, including the homilies translated by him in the Cerne codex.

He was still a simple monk, since in the preface to the said codex he calls himself merely a monk and a mass-priest. Nor should it seem surprising that the care of instructing a newly founded monastery was entrusted to a simple monk, since, besides Ælfric’s outstanding reputation for learning, he also possessed the distinction of having been a pupil of Æthelwold. At that time scarcely anyone was considered worthy to govern or organize monasteries and churches unless he had emerged from the schools of Dunstan, Æthelwold, or Oswald.

Hence we also read that Ælfric was sent as an emissary to other monasteries. In a manuscript codex of the Saxon translation of the Gospels, in Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, the following words are found at the end of the Gospel of Saint Matthew, written in Saxon characters:

“I, Ælfric, wrote this book in the monastery of Bath”—

I think he was sent there by Bishop Ælfheah, who had himself first been abbot of Bath—

“and gave it to Prior Brithwold.”

So reports Mareschall in his *Observations on the Anglo-Saxon Version*, p. 490.

After 1002 Ælfric wrote an important letter, which survives, *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, to Wolstan, archbishop of York. There were two archbishops of York named Wolstan in this century. The first died in 956, on 26 December, according to Florence and the *Chronicle of Mailros*. The second succeeded Aldulf in 1002, according to Florence and the Westminster historian; he died in 1023, on 28 May, a Tuesday, according to Florence and Thomas Stubbs.

That Ælfric was an abbot when he wrote the letter is demonstrated by his having assumed the title “abbot” at the head of the letter. It therefore could not have been addressed to the elder Wolstan, since in 987, more than thirty years after Wolstan’s death, Ælfric had not yet been honored with the dignity of abbot.

Nevertheless, there are those who maintain that it was written to the elder Wolstan. It is sufficient to oppose them by observing that Ælfric was a pupil of Æthelwold, and that Æthelwold himself had become abbot not long before Wolstan’s death and had taken pupils to himself—not to mention that Ælfric was still a simple monk after 987 and, if we have correctly conjectured his age, was still in his cradle when Wolstan died.

In 1005 Ælfric, now an abbot, composed the *Life of Æthelwold*, his teacher, and dedicated it to Kenulf, bishop of Winchester. Kenulf succeeded Ælfheah, whom we showed in the preceding dissertation to have been transferred to the see of Canterbury in 1005. Kenulf died before July of the following year, according to Florence of Worcester.

I have assigned the composition of the *Life of Æthelwold* to 1005 rather than 1006 so that Ælfric’s calculation may accord more closely with the truth: in the preface he says that twenty years had elapsed since Æthelwold’s death. Æthelwold died in the middle of 984. If others prefer the year 1006, I do not object.

It is less certain which monastery Ælfric was abbot of. It nevertheless appears to have been Winchester, both because he dedicated the work to Kenulf, bishop of Winchester, and because he had previously been a Winchester monk, as we showed above. In the dedicatory letter, when he calls himself both abbot and a Winchester alumnus and identifies the place of his education, he says nothing about the location of his abbey; this suggests that the place was the same for him as both abbot and monk.

Florence of Worcester, Ralph de Diceto, and Thomas Stubbs will put the matter beyond doubt: they report that Ælfric Putta, archbishop of York, had previously been prior of Winchester. We shall demonstrate by one single and most certain argument that our Ælfric was that archbishop of York.

It is finally established from a manuscript letter of his in Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, entitled “Ælfric the Bishop to Those Recently Ordained,” that Ælfric was raised to episcopal dignity. It is clear that he was an archbishop among the English from an ancient poem prefixed to his glossary:

“Here the relics of the supreme prelate Ælfric breathe forth their fragrance,

He who remained ruler of the English people.

Among pontiffs, shining like a mystical lamp,

Defender of the kingdom and likewise the people’s salvation.”

Finally, it is evident from an ancient letter, appended in an old codex to Ælfric’s glossary and published by Somner together with the glossary, that he was archbishop of York. In it a certain religious man, asking Ælfric to secure the king’s favor for him in some matter of little importance, addresses him in these words:

“Thus you, excellent priest Ælfric, are always present before the eyes of our King C.; his secret counsels are not hidden from you, but through the diligence of your wisdom they are examined and discerned. In his presence you assist the troubles of many, both rich and poor. Therefore with all my strength I implore the serenity of your benevolence,” and so forth.

There was no other king C. in this century except Canute, and in the time of King Canute there was no other Archbishop Ælfric except the archbishop of York.

[Col. 1470A]

The case is further strengthened by the surname of Ælfric, archbishop of York, whom some call Putta and Florence of Worcester calls Puttoc. I had long suspected that the word was corrupt and that the letter *p* had been wrongly substituted for a Saxon letter, which would have been very easy because of the similarity of the letters. At last an ancient manuscript codex of Florence at Lambeth most happily provided assistance: instead of *Puttoc* it reads *pittunc*.

This word is derived from the Saxon word *pitt*, which means “understanding” or “learning.” Hence also *pittiz* and *pittol*, “learned” or “wise.” Thus *Ælfric pittunc* means nothing other than “Ælfric the learned” or “Ælfric the wise.” The surname was rightly given to him, since he alone contributed more to letters than all the English of his age taken together.

Ælfric therefore succeeded the younger Wolstan in the archbishopric of York. Wolstan died in 1023, on 28 May, a Tuesday, according to the testimony of Florence of Worcester and Thomas Stubbs. Ælfric himself died at Southwell in 1051 and was buried at Medeshamstede, that is, at the monastery of Peterborough.

The same authors and Ralph de Diceto report this, but omit the day of his death. The poem mentioned above, prefixed to the glossary, states that he died on 16 November. We previously noted that this death-day more certainly belongs to Ælfric, archbishop of Canterbury.

It is preferable to seek the death of Ælfric of York among the monks of Peterborough. If he was buried among them, they would have celebrated his death-day, which they call his anniversary, every year.

There is therefore a manuscript in the Lambeth Library, the *Customary of the Monastery of Peterborough*, prefixed by a calendar. Inserted in the calendar, in separately arranged columns, are the anniversaries of each month to be celebrated in that monastery. In these, Ælfric’s death is recorded in the following words:

“9 February: the deposition of Lord Ælfric, archbishop.”

The obituary of the monastery of Ramsey likewise says—extracts from which exist in the *Monasticum Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 235:

“On the ninth day before the Kalends of February, Ælfric the archbishop died.”

[Col. 1469]

# ÆLFRIC’S CANONS TO WULFIN, BISHOP

(Edited by Labbe, *General Councils*, vol. IX, col. 1003. These canons are found at the end of the book of Catholic Homilies, to be recited in English in church, in the celebrated library of Corpus Christi—commonly called Saint Benedict’s—at Cambridge, as follows.)

## LETTER ON THE CANONS

[Col. 1469D]

ÆLFRIC, humble brother, to the venerable Bishop WULFIN, greetings in the Lord.

We willingly obeyed your command; but we did not dare to write anything concerning the episcopal rank, because it is your responsibility to know how you ought to become an example to all through the best conduct and to exhort your subjects to salvation by continual admonitions, which I speak of in Christ Jesus. This is especially so because you ought to address your clerics more frequently and rebuke their negligence, since through their perversity almost the whole body of the canons’ ordinances, the discipline of the Church, and its teaching have been destroyed.

Therefore save your soul, and tell them what must be observed, to priests and ministers of Christ, lest you too perish if you are regarded as a mute dog. We, for our part, are writing this letter, which follows in English, as though it had been dictated from your mouth and as though you were speaking to the clerics subject to you, beginning in this manner:

## I

I myself say to you priests: I will not tolerate your negligence in your ministry, but I will announce to you truthfully what has been established concerning priests. Christ himself gave us an example of Christian instruction and purity of life, that is, chastity. Therefore all who have walked with him in his way left everything worldly behind, without looking back at wives. Hence he himself says in one of his Gospels: “Whoever does not hate his wife is unworthy to be my disciple” (Luke XIV).

## II

[Col. 1471A]

After Christ’s ascension into the kingdom of heaven and the departure of his venerable apostles, such persecution arose throughout the world that the ministers of God could not gather in council, because pagan peoples lay in wait for their lives, until Caesar Constantine, having attained the rule of the world, became a Christian.

## III

Then he assembled at the city of Nicaea 318 bishops from all nations to confirm the Catholic faith. In this council there were many bishops distinguished by remarkable miracles, and they struck a certain mass-priest named Arius with the weapon of anathema, because he did not believe that the Son of the living God was eternally equal in power to his glorious Father. They therefore all delivered him to Satan; but he refused to repent until he had seen his intestines poured out with his belly into a latrine.

## IV

In this council the liturgy of the holy Church and the Creed which we use at Mass were established, together with certain other matters pertaining to the worship and service of God.

## V

They then unanimously decreed that neither a bishop, nor a mass-priest, nor a deacon, nor anyone who is truly a canon, should keep any woman with him in his house except his mother or sister, his paternal aunt or maternal aunt; and whoever acted otherwise was to be deprived of his order and rank.

## VI

Consider, then, these matters worthy of hearing. For when you have the care of your church, on the other hand [lacuna] brought [lacuna] as though it were not dangerous for a priest to live in the manner of a married man [or of a common layman]. But you will say that he cannot do without women’s services.

I answer: How did the holy men of old pass their lives without a woman or wife, who now enjoy eternal life as the reward of their chaste spirit? To this priests will say that Peter had a wife. It is true; under the Old Law, before he had yet entered Christ’s service, this was permitted him. But as soon as he became a disciple of Christ, who provided an example of chastity, he abandoned his wife and all worldly things.

## VII

Under the Old Law the high priest was permitted to take a pure virgin as his wife and raise children by her until the appointed time, because the high priest was to be chosen from one family alone and never from another kindred. Yet he was not permitted to marry more than once, nor to marry a widow or a divorced woman, but, as we have just said, a pure virgin.

In those ages they could rightly enjoy a wife; for they did not celebrate Mass or administer the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, but offered oxen, until Christ sanctified that sacrament before his Passion and instituted the Mass. [lacuna]

## VIII

It was also established in the same council that a man who had married a widow or a divorced woman, or had entered into a second marriage, should never thereafter be admitted to holy orders or consecrated as a priest. But a man who had been the husband of one chaste wife was to be chosen for the chaste order, according to what the Apostle Paul delivered in writing in his epistle.

## IX

[Col. 1472B]

No priest may attend celebrations of weddings in which either a second husband is joined to a wife or a woman to a second husband; nor may he bless such marriages, as he admonished him [lacuna] so that they may live in chastity. Thus the teachers have written, although the Apostle granted permission for a man to marry again if his wife [lacuna]. The canons, however, already forbid the blessing and also impose penance upon those who enter such unions.

## X

Seven orders have been established in the Church: first, doorkeeper; second, reader; third, exorcist; fourth, acolyte; fifth, subdeacon; sixth, deacon; seventh, priest.

## XI

[Col. 1472C]

1. The doorkeeper is the guardian of the doors of the temple or church. By the sound of the bells he indicates the appointed times, opening the church doors to the faithful and closing them to unbelievers.

## XII

2. The reader is the one who reads in the Church of God and who has also been ordained for the purpose of preaching the word of God to the people.

## XIII

3. The exorcist is the one who, by adjuring them in the name of almighty God, compels evil spirits that torment people to depart from them.

## XIV

4. The acolyte is so called because he carries a lighted candle or taper while the Gospel is read in the service of God, or while the priest consecrates the sacrament of the Lord’s body at the altar. This is not primarily to drive away the darkness, but to signify by that light the blessedness of Christ and to honor him, who is our light.

## XV

5. The subdeacon is the one who hands vessels to the deacon and serves him with all humility at the holy altar, supplying the vessels pertaining to the sacrament of the body of our Lord.

## XVI

6. The deacon is the assistant in the ministry of the mass-priest. He places the offerings upon the altar and reads the Gospel in the celebration of divine worship. He may baptize and present the Lord’s Supper to the people [lacuna]; serve the Savior, cultivate the way of heavenly life in chastity, and perform everything [lacuna] as befits that order.

A priest who functions without a deacon has the name, but not the ministry.

## XVII

7. The presbyter is the mass-priest, or elder—not because of old age, but because he rejoices in the prudence of an elder. It belongs to him to consecrate the Lord’s body in the sacrament in the same manner in which the Savior himself instituted it. It is his duty to lead the people to faith, both by preaching and by carrying out the sacred ministries chastely, presenting himself as an example to Christians and living a life unlike that of laymen.

There is no greater difference between a mass-priest and a bishop than that the bishop is appointed to confer ordinations and to visit, inspect, and care for the things pertaining to God (*the rights of God*), since it would be considered too great a burden if every priest performed this same work. For both hold one and the same order, although the bishop’s portion is the more dignified.

## XVIII

No other order has been established among ecclesiastical ministries besides these seven mentioned above. The classes of monks and abbots are of another kind; they are neither counted among these nor given the name of any order. Yet these orders are holy and lead the souls of their priests to blessedness if they are observed purely.

## XIX

[Col. 1473C]

It belongs to priests and to all the ministers of God to cultivate their church with holy service and to sing seven hourly chants in it, as was established by the council: namely, the pre-dawn chant, the morning chant, the third-hour chant, or chant at the third hour of the day, the midday chant, the ninth-hour chant, or chant at the ninth hour of the day, the evening chant, and the night chant, which is the seventh.

## XX

They are also bound to offer earnest prayers for the king and for their bishop, as well as for their benefactors and for all the Christian people.

## XXI

Every priest, before he is ordained, shall also possess the weapons belonging to spiritual work, namely sacred books: a Psalter, a book of Epistles, a book of the Gospels, a Missal, books of Canticles, a Manual or *Enchiridion*, a *Gerim* [the term is uncertain], a *Passional*, a *Penitential*, and a Lectionary.

It is necessary that he possess these; and the priest must carefully see that they are all accurately corrected and free from the faults of scribes.

## XXII

He shall also have the vestments of the Mass, so that he may serve God honorably, as is fitting. They must not be mouldy, not even in the slightest degree [lacuna], and the altar cloths must also be skillfully woven.

His chalice must be made from a pure material not subject to decay [the source reading is uncertain], and the paten likewise. The corporal must also be clean, as is fitting for the ministry of Christ. Let no one presume to offer anything that has not always been worthy before God to serve him, whether in prudence or in purity.

## XXIII

The priest, or mass-priest, shall also on Sundays and feast days tell the people in English the meaning of the Gospel, and shall use the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed with them as often as he can, in order to instruct them, so that they may learn the Creed by heart and retain their Christian confession.

The Lord himself gives this warning, together with the prophet’s saying: “Mute dogs cannot bark” (Isaiah LIX). We must bark and exhort the lay people, lest through lack of instruction we lose them.

Christ says in the Gospel concerning the foolish teacher: “If the blind lead the blind, both fall into a pit” (Luke VI). The teacher who does not know letters is blind, and through his ignorance he deceives lay people and the unlearned. Therefore beware of this, as necessity requires.

## XXIV

The holy Fathers also decreed that everyone should contribute his tithes to the churches of God and that these should be handed over to the priest, who shall divide them into three portions: one for the repair of the church, another to be distributed to the poor, and the third to the ministers of God who care for the church there.

## XXV

They also established that no one should celebrate Mass in an unconsecrated house except in urgent necessity, or when someone is ill and unable to go to church.

## XXVI

If an unbaptized child is freely brought to a priest, let him take care to baptize it immediately, lest it die a pagan.

## XXVII

No priest shall sell his ministry for money or ask anything for it, whether for baptism or for carrying out any other ministry, lest he resemble those whom Christ himself drove from the temple with a whip because they were wickedly conducting business there.

The ministers of God should not perform ministries in order to obtain money for themselves, but in order to earn eternal glory.

## XXVIII

Likewise, no priest shall move from one church to another for any reason of profit or greed. He shall remain until death in the church to which he was first ordained.

## XXIX

No priest shall drink through folly more than is proper, nor provoke another to drink beyond what he desires, lest he should be entirely unfit when a child must be baptized or someone dying must be given the viaticum. Even if such a situation does not arise, he must not become drunk, because the Lord has forbidden drunkenness to his ministers.

## XXX

[Col. 1475A]

A priest must not be a merchant or greedy for trade. He must not abandon the study of theology and turn to worldly conversations. He must not bear arms, be a lawyer, or conduct lawsuits. He must not drink in wine-shops in the manner of secular people. He must not swear an oath. He must always speak the truth plainly and without falsehood, as the servants of God have taught.

## XXXI

He shall also assign penance distinctly to sinners, to each one according to the measure of his merit, in the manner by which he may most probably attain it.

He shall administer the Lord’s Supper to the sick and infirm, provided that they are able to swallow it. He shall not offer it to one who is half dead, because Christ says: “A human being eats this sacrament.”

## XXXII

The priest shall also possess two kinds of consecrated oil: one prepared for infants and the other for the sick. He shall always anoint the sick while they are lying down.

Some sick people, however, attach no importance to this and do not allow themselves to be anointed in their illness. I shall say what James, the apostle of the Lord, taught concerning them. To believers he says:

“Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray with a tranquil heart and sing psalms. Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the priests of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him. Therefore confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James V).

James spoke these words concerning the anointing of the sick. Before he is anointed, the sick person shall confess from the depth of his heart whether he has committed any sin for which he has not made appropriate satisfaction, as the Apostle has already admonished him above. No one should presume to anoint him unless he has been asked to do so and after confession has been completed.

If he was previously sinful and negligent, let him now, before his death, make confession, perform penance, and give alms, so that he may not be assigned to hell but may rejoice in divine mercy.

## XXXIII

There were four councils for the defense of the true faith against heretics who poured forth blasphemies against the Holy Trinity and the human nature of our Savior.

The first was at Nicaea, as we mentioned earlier. After it came the second at Constantinople, consisting of 150 holy bishops, servants of God. The third was at Ephesus, consisting of 200 bishops. The fourth was at Chalcedon, where many hundreds of bishops were present.

All these confirmed by unanimous agreement everything that had been established at the Council of Nicaea, and whatever had been violated they restored. These four councils must be observed by the Church of Christ as the four books of Christ.

Many councils took place after that time, but these four were the firmest. For they extinguished those heretical teachings which heretics had perversely set up against God, and they likewise established the ecclesiastical ministry.

## XXXIV

[Col. 1476B]

With what audacity, then, O priests, have you despised the ordinances of all these councils? Monks observe the ordinances of one man, namely the holy Benedict, and live according to his rule. If they violate it, they immediately correct themselves with all humility according to the judgment of their abbot.

You also have a rule. If only you would read it, you would see what has been established for you. Yet you delight in worldly conversations, in becoming sheriffs, provosts, or bailiffs, while neglecting your church and these ordinances.

## XXXV

The ordinances declare that we wish you to free yourselves more quickly, as befits Christians, and devote yourselves diligently to your church.

In the church, however, no one should be permitted to chatter or to speak [lacuna], for it is a house of prayer, consecrated by God for the exercise of spiritual speech. No one should drink or eat improperly in it, since it has been sanctified for those who there eat the Lord’s body in faith.

Although people do these shameful things—often carousing and drinking to madness in the house of God, playing there insultingly and disgracefully, and even polluting that very house with filthy speech—it would be better for them to remain quietly in their beds than to provoke God in such a manner.

*(The remainder is missing.)*

[Col. 1475]

Some small works of Ælfric the archbishop exist, translated from the Saxon language into Latin, but they are of unreliable authority and have been interpolated by an unorthodox hand. For this reason we shall refrain from presenting them.

# In the Year of Our Lord 1009: Pope John XVIII

[Col. 1477]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(Chacon, *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 283.)

[Col. 1477A]

John XVIII, called Fasanus or Fassanus, a Roman from the district of the Gate of Mathodius, under the emperor Henry the Younger Augustus, sat for five years, seven months, and twenty days. He was created on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December.

This John, whom Platina calls the twenty-first, calls himself the eighteenth in his diplomas and likewise in the instruments of public records made in his time. Accordingly, the Johns whom we call XXI and XXIII ought to be called XIX and XX.

When he entered the pontificate, he accomplished nothing worthy of remembrance—which is itself something that may be greatly celebrated. Some nevertheless write that he repaired several churches that had collapsed through age. He was a great lover of monks, especially the monks of Monte Cassino, to whom he granted many privileges.

There survives a letter to this pope, John XVIII, from Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, a very celebrated man. In it he complains that a certain Rudolph had invaded the property of his Church, killed one of his clerics with his own hands, and was holding two others captive.

The people of Siena in Etruria were first honored with a bishop by him, in the year 1009.

Burchard received the Church of Worms in the year 1008; he composed a volume of Decrees.

A German synod, convened by order of the emperor Henry from all the bishops of the empire in the year 1004, during the pontificate of Pope John XVIII.

Likewise, the Synod of Frankfurt, in the year 1006.

At last Pope John XVIII died at Rome on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August [18 July], in the year 1009; he was buried at the Lateran. The see was vacant for thirty days.

[Col. 1477]

## DIPLOMATIC NOTICE

The bulls of John were written by the hand of:

George, notary and scrinarius of the Holy Roman Church (1).

Peter, notary and scrinarius of the Holy Roman Church (2, 5, 10).

Benedict, regional notary and scrinarius of the Holy Roman Church (4).

Peter, abbot and chancellor of the sacred Lateran palace (6, 7, 9).

Stephen, notary and scrinarius of the sacred Lateran palace (11).

Ingilo (John?), scrinarius of the Holy Apostolic See (8).

Issued through the hand of:

Gregory, bishop of the Holy Church of Ostia and librarian of the Holy Apostolic See (3, 4).

[Col. 1477]

# LETTERS AND DIPLOMAS OF POPE JOHN XVIII

## I. John XVIII confirms the privileges and possessions of the monastery of Saint Florentius of Saumur. (Year 1004.)

[Dom Martène, *Veterum Scriptorum Collectio* V, 1104.]

[Col. 1477B]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Robert, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Florentius, confessor of Christ, situated in the place called Saumur, and to his successors and all the brothers dwelling in that place, perpetual greeting.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those endowed with devout religion through benevolent compassion, and to grant the requests of petitioners with willing devotion. For then the richest reward of gain is stored up with God, the creator of all, when venerable places have suitably been brought to a better condition. Therefore, since you have humbly requested from our apostolate that the monastery of Saint Florentius, confessor of Christ, situated in the place called Saumur, in the territory of Anjou, should be adorned with the privileges of the Apostolic See, we willingly grant our assent to your petition.

Since, however, this monastery had formerly been nobly constructed by the emperor Charles in the place called Glonna, where Saint Florentius, after a long life, surrendered his spirit to heaven, and had been strengthened and enriched by imperial charters and privileges with very extensive possessions; and since, likewise, by Louis, surnamed the Pious, his son, it had been endowed with immunity from every fiscal exaction and from every legal or official payment, as well as from the synodical due of all the churches subject to that monastery, we, favoring the same ancient monastery, at the prayers of the lady Queen Berta and of her sons Theobald and Odo, by apostolic authority confirm and establish these things perpetually. If anyone should become a reckless violator of these provisions, or should attempt to violate the possessions, churches, lands, or waters of the same place, let him be condemned under the pronouncement of anathema.

Concerning that new monastery which, after the Norman devastation, was constructed by the most noble Count Theobald in the place called Saumur, in the abbey of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and Saint John the Baptist, which had been granted to the same Saint Florentius by Charles, son of Louis: at the petition of the aforementioned sons of ours, we decree by apostolic censure, under the witness of divine judgment, that it shall not be subjected to the ownership or authority of anyone else, but shall be governed and defended perpetually by the successive heirs of Theobald and Odo.

If any one of them should transfer that place to any outsider, or if any person should attempt to demand or purchase the same place from them, let him be anathema with Judas the traitor at the final judgment. We likewise bind with the same anathema those who attempt to take away anything from what the same place presently possesses or may acquire in the future, or to add new laws, except insofar as has been established by Archbishop Arduino and Count Odo, son of Theobald.

We further decree that if, by episcopal decision, that district should incur a sentence of excommunication, the same monastery shall nevertheless be permitted to celebrate Masses and the other sacred rites, and shall not be compelled to suffer any prejudice from the bishops on that account. If any accusation or crime should be brought against the abbot of that place, he shall be permitted to plead his case before two or three bishops, and he shall not be harassed irreverently without their judgment.

Therefore, let the monks dwelling there, servants of God, be free from every disturbance caused by covetous persons; and, with God’s favor and our apostolic authority confirming it, let them be permitted to dispose of their own goods, so that no person of whatever rank may ever presume in any way to take away or alienate anything from the property or possessions belonging to them.

These are: the fiscal estate of Lentiliacus, with the church dedicated to Saint Mary and the chapels of Saint Hilary and Saint Vincent, and with everything situated in the castle or otherwise belonging to it; likewise, the village called Distriacus, with the church of Saint Julian the Martyr; another village called Ulmis, with the church of Saint Vincent; and the chapel called Mainiacus, with the lands belonging to them.

Also the possession called Capriniacus, with the church of Saint George and the chapels commonly called Saint Helerus and Savoya, with the lands belonging to them; likewise the village called Cadvernis, with Daneziacus and the church situated there.

Also the possession with the castle of Carnonis, and the churches of Saint Andrew and Saint Lambert, with the lands belonging to them; and the church of Saint Peter with the chapel of Saint John.

Likewise, another village called Alomna, with churches dedicated to Saint John and Saint Docelinus, with the lands belonging to them.

Also another village named Mironio, with a church dedicated to Saint Caesarius and the lands belonging to it.

All these possessions, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, before God and the fearful future judgment, through the confirmation of this our apostolic privilege, we sanction and decree for the same place. Whatever the faithful may subsequently grant to the same place, if any wicked person should presume to oppose, invade, or bring a legal claim against it, let him be bound by the chain of anathema and forever separated from the fellowship of Christians.

But whoever, moved by pious regard, observes and in every respect protects this our apostolic decree shall obtain in many ways the grace of blessing from the most merciful Lord our God and shall deserve to become a participant in eternal life.

Written by the hand of George, notary and scrinarius of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of April, in the second indiction.

## II. The privilege of John XVIII for the Church of Saint Mary of Isergia. (Year 1004.)

[Marini, *Papiri diplomatici*, vol. I, p. 238.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the sons of the Holy Roman Church.

[Col. 1480C]

It is our duty to consider generally the interests of all the holy Churches of God, and especially those which are under the jurisdiction and dominion of our Roman Church. If there is any disadvantage, it is our duty to remove it, lest, neglected because of their serious distress, they become insignificant, or lest they should, on any pretext, be deprived of the solemnity owed to them.

Among the many kinds of business brought to the Roman See from different parts of the world, and among the many matters on which we are consulted for establishment or regulation, this matter has also reached our ears: the parish church of Saint Mary, situated within the city called Isergia, near the fountain of Saint John the Baptist, had fallen into ruin and failed, partly through its antiquity and partly through the negligence of its pastor.

But, by the will of God and of his Mother, Count Landinolfus, son of Count Landolfus the Greek, together with his wife Gemma, of blessed memory, rebuilt and restored that ancient parish church from their own property, for the redemption of their souls, and dedicated it to the honor of Saint Mary. It had once been occupied by pastors who had not promoted its growth, but had brought upon it the reproach of utter diminution.

Therefore, although the example of the earlier Fathers teaches us that, for the love of Christ, we ought to benefit all the churches spread throughout the world, since he wished them to be subject to the ministry of our office, nevertheless this necessity also compels us to come to its aid.

Accordingly, we declare that the Church of Saint Mary, situated near the fountain of Saint John the Baptist within the city called Isergia, together with everything belonging to it, shall be such that the aforesaid Count Landinolfus, son of Landolfus the Greek, and his heirs may exercise ownership and authority in governing the servants of that church according to God and ecclesiastical order, so that the service of God may not diminish but rather increase and grow.

We decree also that the bishop of the same city of Isergia shall presume to diminish or remove nothing whatsoever from the property or ornaments of the aforesaid Church of Saint Mary, on any pretext or by any device; nor shall he dare to take anything from it as though it were private property. Let it be suitable and perpetually secure from every external authority.

If, however—which we do not wish—in some offense arising from an evil reputation the servants of that church should be found guilty, we decree that the bishop of that city shall correct them according to the rule. If the bishop should neglect to correct them, we decree that they are to be heard and corrected according to the rule before the Apostolic See.

But if anyone should presume to alter this privilege of our authority, let him be wholly frustrated; first, let him be deprived of the rank of his order, and then let him be subjected to the punishment of anathema. At the end, in the final judgment, let him have his portion with Judas the traitor. By the authority which blessed Peter earned in heaven and on earth—the power of binding and loosing—let him be excluded from participation in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and from our fellowship, unless he repents; and let him remain perpetually shut out, so that what has been established may remain by perpetual definition, and so that the violator of this present decree may suffer manifold punishments for his recklessness.

Written by the hand of Peter, notary of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of October, in the third indiction.

Farewell.

## III. John XVIII grants privileges to the Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian at the Golden Mica. (Fragment. — Year 1005.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, I, 57.]

[Georgius in Baronius, *Annales*, Luc. edition, XVI, 431.]

## V. John XVIII grants Benedict, bishop of Porto, half of the field of Stagnellum the Accursed. (Year 1005.)

[Note: [Col. 1481D] Ughelli incorrectly attributes it to John XIX. Jaffé.]

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, I, 119.]

[Col. 1482A]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our beloved spiritual son in Christ, Benedict, most reverend bishop of the Holy Church of Porto, and to his successors forever.

Whenever those things are expected to be granted by us which unquestionably accord with reason, it is fitting that we grant them willingly and offer suitable assistance to the desires of petitioners. Therefore you requested from us that, by our apostolic authority, we grant to you and to your successors forever the entire half of the field called Stagnellum the Accursed—that is, an integral half—where saltworks are now newly being constructed through our apostolic blessing.

We order that it henceforth be called Stagnellum the Blessed, together with half of the saltworks, half of the payments, and every public obligation annually arising from the whole aforesaid field, and together with everything generally and wholly belonging to the aforesaid field, which is called Stagnellum the Blessed. It is situated in the territory of Porto between the greater field and the plot called Ticoh.

All these things, belonging by right to our Holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, we grant, by our present charter, from this third indiction to you and your successors forever, to hold and enjoy, moved by your prayers.

If anyone, however, by reckless daring—which we do not believe will happen—should attempt to act against the terms of this our apostolic confirmation, let him know that, by the authority of our lord and of Peter, prince of the apostles, he is bound by the chain of anathema; and that he is to be burned in eternal fire with the devil and his most dreadful pomp, and with Judas, the traitor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and, cast into the Tartarean abyss together with the impious, let him perish.

But whoever proves to be the guardian and observer of this our privilege shall obtain from the Lord the grace of blessing and eternal life.

Written by the hand of Peter, notary and scrinarius of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of July, in the aforementioned third indiction. Farewell. We decree, therefore, etc. If anything, therefore, etc. But to all, etc. Amen.

## VI. Privilege of Pope John XVIII for the Church of Paderborn. (Year 1005.)

[Schaten, *Annales Paderbornenses*, vol. I, p. 375.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Ratarius, venerable bishop of Paderborn, and to his successors forever.

The Holy Apostolic See, while universally exercising the office of maternal piety and governance in the Churches of Christ, must continually offer them the assistance of confirmation, instruction, and authority. Therefore, most reverend son, in granting to you and to your see a privilege of apostolic authority, we both gladly assent to your petition and grant it with the greatest generosity of heart.

For the head can rejoice when it perceives that the members are sound and possess established strength. Therefore, just as the see of the ancient holy Church of Paderborn, over which you preside by God’s authority, was founded and endowed with property of various kinds, and as it has appeared to increase until now in abundance of wealth and possessions through the gifts of good men and faithful Christians, so we decree that it shall remain perpetually under apostolic right for you and your successors forever.

Let whatever the aforesaid Church—or rather, episcopal see—appears to have possessed until now, or whatever it may be able to acquire in the future through the gifts of faithful Christians, be safe from the attacks, deceit, and plunder of the wicked: namely, villages, possessions, estates, dioceses and the territories belonging to the dioceses; likewise, strongholds, castles, fields, vineyards, rivers, lakes, with all the instruments or installations made in them; also male and female slaves, and likewise tenant farmers, taxes or revenues, and payments.

All these things, and every possession which the aforesaid Church appears to have or may appear to have, we confirm and strengthen for that church by apostolic authority, and decree that they shall remain valid forever, so that they may not be taken away or alienated from it by violence or craft.

We also decree, by the authority of the apostle blessed Peter, that no episcopal appointment shall take place there—that is, that no bishop shall be consecrated in the aforesaid Church—unless he has been approved by the election of the sons of that Church.
