If any madman or presumptuous person should attempt to act against this privilege of our authority by devastating, plundering, or diminishing the property of that Church, or should disdain to observe it, unless he repents through suitable reparation, let him be subject to excommunication, bound by the chain of anathema, condemned by eternal cursing, and subjected with the reprobate to eternal punishments.

Given and written through the hand of Peter, abbot and chancellor of the sacred palace, in the month of December, in the fourth indiction [elsewhere, the third], in the third year, by the favor of God, of the lord Pope John XVIII.

## VII. John XVIII confirms a gift made by Bishop Rainaldus to the canons of Paris. (Year 1006.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XIX, 291.]

[Col. 1483D]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

By the institution of imperial reason, it is perceived to be useful in arranging and disposing all matters that the ancient and prudent authority of our predecessors should be followed, so that the subsequent effort of all posterity may respond to it by carefully obeying and wisely imitating it; and it is thoroughly strengthened by the sounder judgment of censure.

Since the very life which we enjoy is restricted by a lifespan of manifold brevity and is cut short prematurely for many, it is easy to see how salutary it is for each person to be urged day by day toward the palm of interminable endurance by the higher sails of virtues that bring salvation, and toward more fortunate increases in good works.

Moved by these considerations, in the name of God and in the peace of all the saints, I, Regenoldus, bishop of Paris, solicitous in vigilant care for the flock entrusted to me by virtue of my office, and mindful of the great day of fearful judgment and of the recompense of both the just and the unjust, judged it worthwhile to secure for myself, by a blessed exchange from the revenues of my patrimony, the aid of the citizens of heaven.

Inflamed by the fervor of this devotion, I wish it to be known to all, both future and present, that, for the sake of the rewards of everlasting recompense and to obtain forgiveness for the sins of my parents—namely, Count Burchard and his highly renowned wife Elisabeth—so that we may deserve to be cherished in the bosoms of holy immortality and perpetually rejoice in the delight of eternal light, it pleased me, with your reverence, in synodal assembly and with the favor and knowledge of the public community, to grant a certain allod, commonly called the Long Field, to the Church of Saint Mary of Paris, and to assign it to the property and uses of the brothers dwelling there and canonically serving God.

The aforesaid Long Field is situated in the district and county of Wastin, with woods, villages and hamlets, vineyards, meadows, cultivated and uncultivated lands, together with a church dedicated in honor of Saint Maturinus and all its appurtenances. We offer the entire possession of the aforesaid allod to Saint Mary and to the aforesaid members of the canonical congregation under this condition: that our memory be kept by all of them in the psalters, in the solemn celebrations of Masses, and in all evening and morning vigils, and that this arrangement remain perpetually valid by law.

Finally, we earnestly ask that our three anniversaries—namely, those of our father, our mother, and of the prelate Regenoldus himself—be celebrated each year with the devotion of the realm [E. P.: “with all devotion”] and solemn commemoration. If anyone, however, lacking reason and overcome by envy and the torches of avarice, should wish to take away this exceedingly generous pledge of our devotion or impede it by any right or injury whatsoever, let him be compelled by royal majesty to pay one thousand pounds of gold to the brothers or canons of Saint Mary; and, subjected and humbled in rustic fashion or by *paralitate* [uncertain reading], let him be punished by payment of the capital tax.

By the authority of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, let him be cursed and confounded, condemned to endure the perpetual torment of all eternity, and let him deserve no relief through the intercession of the saints; let him be joined to the devil and his angels in the lower hell, and perish forever.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of December [2 December], through the hand of Peter, abbot and chancellor of the sacred Lateran palace, in the third year of the pontificate of John XVIII, supreme and universal pope, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, in the fifth indiction.

## VIII. Privilege of Pope John XVIII for the monastery of Saint Benignus of Dijon. (Year 1006.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, old edition, vol. IV, p. 163.]

[Col. 1485A]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, greetings to Abbot William.

Since those things which are known to belong to reasonable desires ought to be granted, the authority of our apostolate must not refuse to strengthen the pious devotion of those who construct holy places by providing privileges.

Therefore, in the love of God, the request of your petition must be granted: through the venerable Walter, bishop of Autun, you have earnestly requested from us that the monastery which you have already begun to construct with the greatest desire, for the praise and glory of Christ our Lord, his most glorious Mother Mary, and Saint Benignus the martyr, in the county of Hiporium, between the two rivers, namely the Orgus and the Ancolis, situated in the place called Fructuaria, should be adorned with the privileges of the Holy Roman and Apostolic See and strengthened with the firmest stability.

Thus, under the protection and patronage of the holy universal Church which, by God’s authority, we serve, let it, once established, never be subjected to the right or authority of another church.

Therefore, favoring such just desires, by this our apostolic authority we decree that the aforesaid monastery of the Mother of Christ and Saint Benignus, which you are striving to construct, shall henceforth and until the end of the age remain under the patronage and protection of the Holy Roman and Apostolic Mother Church, together with everything belonging to it.

We establish, under the witness of divine judgment and by the prohibition of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of our humility, that no emperor, king, bishop, duke, marquis, count, or any person established in any rank or office should ever dare to interfere violently in the affairs or arrangements of that monastery, or, after learning of this privilege, presume to take away the possessions or ornaments granted or to be granted there by the faithful to the abbot and brothers living there according to the rule and now serving God.

Nor may anyone exact from them the revenue of tithes or, from the demesne lands hitherto lying outside cultivation, any payment on fields, meadows, vineyards, or any other goods or animals, or on all uncultivated lands which their labor has brought or may bring under cultivation, whether in the place of Fructuaria itself, where the monastery appears to be situated, or wherever they may appear to possess anything by right of the aforesaid monastery. We testify, etc.

We also establish that, after the death of the abbot who is to die, no one shall ever presume to appoint another abbot there except one whom the common consent and will of the brothers of that monastery, according to God, have chosen.

Once elected, the abbot shall at all times have the power to choose a prelate who, both for himself and for the other brothers who are to be promoted to sacred orders, may confer the insignia of consecration wherever they wish, with fear of God and with the restraint of the entire congregation, by the privilege of this our authority and without receiving any earthly payment as a gift.

We likewise enact the same concerning the oratories built or to be built in the aforesaid place of Fructuaria, and concerning everything requiring the ordering of consecration. The judgment of the aforesaid Guntardus, as well as the episcopal decree, confirmed by the subscriptions of numerous bishops for the strengthening of what is contained in the charter of that judgment, we confirm and strengthen by the authority of almighty God, who entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven to blessed Peter, the first of the apostles, and by the authority of that first shepherd and of ourselves, though unworthy, acting in his place, in the page of this present privilege, etc.

If anyone, however, etc.

John, apostolic prelate of the holy Church, commands the venerable bishops Leo, Gesso, Constantine, and Sigefredus to consecrate with the utmost diligence the abbey called Fructuariensis.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of December [2 December], through the hand of Ingilo, scrinarius of the Sacred Apostolic See, in the third year of the pontificate of the lord John XVIII, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the most sacred see of the apostle blessed Peter, in the fifth indiction.

## IX. John XVIII confirms the possessions of the canons of the Church of Pisa. (Year 1007.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, III, 356.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most beloved spiritual sons, the canons of Saint Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, and to you and your successors forever.

It is indeed fitting for our office that we show the greatest care toward the Churches of almighty God, and that our mind should always remain watchful over those whom we recognize as worshipers of Jesus Christ the Lord.

Therefore let it be known to all people, present and future, that the canons of the Church of Pisa devoutly petitioned our apostolate through John, the deacon of the aforesaid Church, that we should confirm for them and for all their successors everything which they now possess on behalf of the canonical community in which they have been established for the accomplishment of the divine work.

We, moved by divine inspiration, inclined our minds to carry out the desire of the aforesaid deacon and of the other canons serving God. Accordingly, we confirm for them whatever they presently possess, as well as whatever they may acquire in the canonical community in subsequent times: namely, tithes, vineyards, and lands, as well as the remaining estates.

Whoever should attempt to take away any of these things from the aforesaid canons shall know that he has fallen into the snare of eternal Gehenna. Moreover, by the authority of almighty God, of the apostle blessed Peter, and of ourselves, let him know that he is excommunicated and accursed, separated from communion and from the Church, and condemned with Judas and the devil.

Likewise, as stated above, by our apostolic authority we confirm for them the estate called Pedianum, and all the other things which they have canonically acquired without tenure, or which they may acquire in the future. If anyone should wish to take the aforesaid estate away from the canonical community of Saint Mary, let him know that he is perpetually condemned by the bond of anathema.

We also order by apostolic authority that the settlement which the aforesaid canons made with the archpriest Bonizo be respected, and that no duke, marquis, bishop, count, viscount, or person of high or low rank dare demand or reclaim it. For it has been reported before our apostolate, in the presence of the archpriest Bonizo, whatever he himself committed against them through the efforts of his malice. Whoever should presume to demand that settlement shall be subject to perpetual curse.

This decree was constituted and executed by us on behalf of the canons of Saint Mary, who are:

Peter, by the grace of God archpriest.

Peter, dean and cantor.

John, archdeacon.

John, priest and primicerius.

Andrew, priest.

Albizo, priest and custodian.

Dominic, priest.

Amalfredus, priest.

Ursus, priest.

Bonizo, priest.

John, priest.

Leo, priest.

Theudo, priest.

Uvinizo, priest.

Albertus, priest.

John, deacon.

Peter, deacon.

Albericus, deacon.

Dominic, deacon.

Leo, cleric.

Bonus, son of the cleric.

Orbertus, cleric.

So that it may be believed more truly and preserved by all forever, we have confirmed this privilege with our own proper articles, and in addition have ordered our papal bull to be affixed below.

John, by divine clemency proceeding before him, apostolic prelate of the holy Catholic Church.

[Note: [Col. 1487D] The closing clause shows that this document is to be attributed to John XVIII. Jaffé.]

Given and written through the hand of Peter, chancellor of the sacred Lateran palace, in the month of May, in the fifth indiction.

## X. Diploma of John XVIII by which he confirms the bishopric of Bamberg. (Year 1007.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XIX, 286.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

It is our duty to consider generally the interests of all the holy Churches of God, and especially those which specifically remain under the jurisdiction and dominion of our Roman Church; if there is any disadvantage, to remove it, lest, neglected because of their serious distress, they become insignificant or, having encountered any opportunity, be deprived of the solemnity owed to them.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, that our beloved spiritual son Henry, the most glorious and unconquered king, by the inspiration of divine clemency, established a bishopric in the place called Bamberg, from his own hereditary possessions, for the sake of his soul and those of his parents, with perfect faith and devotion of charity, in honor of the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. This was done through a lawful and legal exchange with Henry, bishop of Würzburg, of a certain part of the parish of his bishopric.

The aforesaid bishop also sent us his letters, asking that, with his consent, the newly established bishopric should be founded by the privilege of our apostolic authority.

For this reason, Henry II, the most glorious king, sent his messengers to us to report all these matters and to petition us to confirm this see. Regarding his most holy [reading uncertain: *imitationem* or *intimationem*] with paternal and heartfelt affection, we have decided to confirm, by the privilege of our authority, all the property which he legitimately gathered and bestowed upon blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in the aforesaid place.

This is to be done on the condition that the bishop of that place and all who shall perpetually succeed him may possess these things in secure tranquility and have free power to order, arrange, and even increase the property and possessions of that church; but they shall have no power to dissipate or disorder them.

[Col. 1488C]

By our authority we likewise decree that within the boundaries and possessions of the same church there shall be no attack by tyrants or by any other wicked persons, whether they are in the city of Bamberg itself or in its castles and villages, among male and female slaves, tributary persons, tithes, forests, woods, fisheries, hunting grounds, mills, fields, meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, or anything else that now belongs there or may be acquired in the future. All these things, strengthened by the privilege of our authority, shall remain in secure peace.

No count or judge shall presume to make law there except such law as the bishop of that place should choose to establish through the grant of the most glorious King Henry or of his successors. No foreign authority shall invade it by force.

Let that bishopric be free and secure from every external authority, subject only to Roman protection (*mundiburdium*). [Note: *Mundiburdium* means protection.] Thus the bishop may devote himself more effectively, with his canons, to the service of God and may continually preserve the memory of the first founder and restorer of that place.

Nevertheless, let the same bishopric remain subject and obedient to its metropolitan [in the Vienna manuscript: “the archbishop of Mainz”].

Whoever observes these decrees shall receive divine recompense and apostolic blessing. Whoever, however, proves to be their despiser and violator shall be subject to the condemnation of perpetual anathema, unless, repenting, he attains satisfaction.

[Col. 1489A]

Written through the hand of Peter, notary and scrinarius of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of June, in the fifth indiction.

## XI. Confirmation of the privileges and metropolitan right of the Holy Church of Toulouse. (Year 1007.)

[Coquelines, *Bullarium amplissimae collectionis*, I, 243.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son in the Lord Jesus Christ, Raymond, venerable bishop of the see of Toulouse, and to his successors forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance, endowed with devout religion, to come to the aid of those who seek it with benevolent compassion and to grant the petitions of those who ask with eager devotion. For from this the chief reward of merit is stored up with the Lord, the Creator of all, whenever venerable places, suitably ordered, have without doubt been brought to a better condition.

Therefore, since your devotion humbly petitions our apostolate that we should grant and confirm to you, the aforesaid bishop, the church of the protomartyr Stephen, and of Saint Saturninus, and of Saint Mary—called the see of Toulouse—with all their estates, farmsteads, and dependencies; that is, houses, vineyards, lands and woods, villages, fields, meadows, pastures, willow-groves, fruit-bearing trees, whether fruitful or unfruitful, of various kinds, wells, springs, streams, waters and watercourses, mills, fisheries, and also saltworks, cultivated or uncultivated; together with the male and female servants, and the male and female tenant-farmers belonging there, and with everything generally and wholly belonging to the aforesaid bishop [read: episcopate or bishopric], situated in the county of Toulouse, for you and your successors to possess—we ought to grant and confirm these things by issuing our decree.

Moved by your petitions, through the text of this privilege we grant and confirm to you and your successors, from the present fifth indiction and forever, the aforesaid bishopric [read: episcopate or bishop], with all its estates and farmsteads and with all its dependencies and appurtenances, as described above, to be possessed by you and your successors.

Moreover, we decree that no bishop in those regions shall have the right to perform any ordination anywhere within the entire boundary of your bishopric, unless it is with your consent.

Therefore, establishing this by apostolic censure and under the adjuration of divine judgment, we impose the prohibition of anathema, so that no one ever among our successor pontiffs, nor any other person of great rank, may inflict any trouble or loss upon you or your successors; rather, let everything remain forever in the possession and for the benefit of your bishopric.

If anyone, however, should presume with reckless audacity to act against this page of our apostolic decree promulgated by us, or should perform a consecration in the aforesaid bishopric without your consent, or should wish to diminish any property of that bishopric, let him know that, by the authority of Almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, he is bound by the bond of anathema under the judgment of our humility and is condemned without end with the devil and all the impious, “whose fire shall not be quenched and whose worm shall not die,” unless he hastens to make full reparation.

But whoever proves to be the guardian and observer of this apostolic privilege of ours deserves to obtain in all things the grace of blessing and mercy, and eternal life, from our most merciful Lord, forever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary and archivist of the sacred Lateran palace, in the month of June and in the fifth indiction.

Farewell.

## XII. John XVIII Defends the Privileges of the Monastery of Fleury. (Around the year 1008.)

[Gallia Christiana, vol. VIII, p. 18, from the Vatican Library.]

[Col. 1490B]

John, servant of the servants of God, to the most excellent king of the Franks, Robert: strength in ecclesiastical honor . . . . . . . .

Long ago, when rumor spread, we learned that Your Excellency, most excellent of kings, loved and upheld ecclesiastical honor. It is therefore necessary that, if you cultivate the honor of other churches, you honor that which is the head of all the more greatly, inasmuch as it is clear that the others took their beginning from it.

We have learned that certain bishops of your kingdom hold in such contempt the authority of the apostolic see—which the blessed Peter granted to his successors in the city of Rome—that they openly declare that they will in no way observe it. Hearing that such contumacy existed among bishops beyond the Alps, and scarcely believing it, we sent our brother and fellow bishop, Bishop Bip. [name uncertain], to discover the truth of the matter. He reported that he had indeed been honorably received by you and treated with great kindness for a long time, until he heard, in your presence, the authority of the holy Roman Church being despised.

For your reception of our brother we therefore give thanks to Your Excellency. But we are astonished that your magnificence could have endured the Roman Church’s being despised in your presence—for, as we have learned, you were present there. Since, however, you have until now concealed your displeasure at this, we exhort Your Excellency henceforth not to remain silent, but rather to ensure by royal authority that the decrees of the apostolic see remain inviolate.

For, as has been reported to us, the bishops mentioned above are attempting to destroy the privileges that our holy predecessors granted to the kingdom. This greatly grieves us, because if we do not observe the ordinances of our predecessors, we cannot expect ours to be observed.

Accordingly, by the omnipotence of the Lord, and also by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and by our own, we exhort and command you to have the authors of this presumption come to us at the coming Easter. They are Leterius, pseudo-archbishop of Sens, and his suffragan at Orléans, Fulco, who proceeded to such insolence that he ordered Gauzlin, abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict, to burn in the fire the privileges granted to his monastery by the apostolic see.

We also wish the abbot himself to come, so that the controversy may be settled before the holy see—which, by God’s permission, I, unworthy though I am, occupy—and that the despiser of Saint Peter may receive a fitting punishment.

But whoever, disregarding your most loving admonition or despising your command, refuses to come to Saint Peter and to us—unless bodily illness has weighed him down—should know that, by the judgment of God and of us, he is excluded from the divine mysteries. Your Excellency’s letters, sealed with the royal seal, should inform our concern of the nature of that illness.

Therefore, let the greatness of your honor strive to fulfill our admonitions, and let it permit those who have appealed to the apostolic see to suffer no loss of their property at the hands of their adversaries, lest, if—God forbid—things are done otherwise than we command, the censure of anathema be brought not only upon the contumacious but upon your entire kingdom.

May the eternal God guard you with his protection and, after the long course of your temporal kingdom, lead you to eternal kingdoms. Amen.

## XIII. Privilege of Pope John XVIII for the Monastery of Belloc. (1004–1009.)

[Gallia Christiana, first edition, vol. IV, p. 151.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all kings, bishops, dukes, counts, and noble peoples of the Franks, present and future: peace in the holy faith in Christ and apostolic blessing.

The holy apostolic see—that is, the Roman Church—because it receives from the most blessed prince of the apostles, Peter the chief, the power of binding and loosing, together with the strength of its holy authority over the Churches, earnestly strives to support its subordinate members in piety, to strengthen places of sacred worship wherever it sees them wavering, and to confirm what has been strengthened, so that, by God’s dispensation, the ecclesiastical order may peacefully carry out the practice of holy faith and religion, and wicked men may be deterred from tearing it apart.

Therefore let it be known to Your Highness that the most noble and energetic Count Fulco made known to us that he had built from the foundations a certain monastery in the name and honor of the holy and undivided Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and likewise in honor of the heavenly ranks upon which God is enthroned, namely, the Cherubim and Seraphim, for the redemption of his soul.

For this monastery he requests the perpetual protection of a privilege of holy apostolic authority against the wickedness of evil men. Accordingly, no violator, whether noble or lowborn, should presume to diminish what he has bestowed upon that place for the love of God and assigned to it by confirmation.

The aforesaid monastery is situated in the district of Tours, beside the river called the Andria, in sight of the castle called Locas. He has humbly placed and commended that place under the guardianship and protection of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of our successors, the pontiffs of this holy see, so that no authority of any king, prince, archbishop, bishop, or person of whatever rank may dare to trouble, disturb, or diminish the aforesaid monastery.

Nor should anyone, driven by greed, presume to take away its lands, waters, vineyards, meadows, woods, mills, villages and the revenues of its villages, male and female servants, churches, or any of those things that the count has presently granted, or ought to grant, or that the faithful may give to that place.

We establish this by our holy apostolic authority and wish it to remain confirmed forever, so that whoever proves in any way to be a violator of the things mentioned above and attempts to act against this sanction of ours and the protection of our jurisdiction may, by the authority of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and likewise of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and Paul, teacher of the nations—to whom the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth has been granted—and by our pastoral sentence, remain excommunicated and bound forever by the chain of anathema, condemned with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord, and with the devil to infernal punishments, unless he comes to satisfaction and suitable reparation.

We also establish for the same monastery, by apostolic authority, the privilege that it shall in no way suffer a sentence of excommunication from any archbishop or bishop, nor shall it be compelled by those bishops to endure any trouble on account of any right or any ordination. Thus may that place remain undisturbed, under the jurisdiction and protection of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of the pontiffs of their see, forever.

But if any rebellious archbishop or bishop should wish to excommunicate this place contrary to our authority, let him himself be excommunicated, and let this place be absolved, forever and unto ages of ages. Amen.

## XIV. Privilege of John XVIII for the Monastery of Saint Victor of Marseille. (Around the year 1009.)

[Marini, *Diplomatic Papers*, I, 64.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gifred, venerable abbot, and to all the brothers of the monastery of Saint Victor, our most beloved spiritual sons: greeting and grace, and moreover apostolic blessing.

It was the custom of our pontifical predecessors to assist all who came to them for the sake of good works. We have learned of that good custom by hearing and observing them, and we ought to preserve it with every effort of devotion, so that the Lord, recognizing that we are accomplishing his will, may repay us when he removes us from this present life.

We have therefore wished the monastery of Saint Victor, with all the monks and the other servants of God remaining there, always to continue honorably, so that it may hold peacefully and quietly all its possessions belonging to that monastery.

We also confirm to it, by apostolic authority, its dependent cells, estates and villages, and its other places and possessions, from now and forever, so that no person, great or small, may ever dare to inflict any trouble upon anything belonging to the aforesaid monastery. Whoever presumes to do so should know that, by the authority of Almighty God, the blessed apostle Peter, and our own, he is excommunicated and accursed, and moreover separated from communion and from the Church, and condemned forever with Judas and the devil to the most atrocious punishments.

John, apostolic bishop of the holy catholic and apostolic Church, granted this privilege so that no metropolitan, no bishop, no count or viscount, and no person, great or small, might dare to take anything away from the property of the monastery of Saint Victor, nor dare to conduct or hold any judgment or public assembly, either within the monastery or throughout the entire land of Saint Victor, which it possesses today or shall possess in the future. Nor may any abbot enter the monastery unless he has been elected by the entire community.

Whoever wishes to violate this privilege shall not prevail, but shall pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold as a penalty. Moreover, let him incur the anger of Almighty God and be excommunicated by the authority of the holy apostle Peter, of ourselves, and of the three hundred holy Fathers. Let this privilege remain firm and stable.

+ Farewell.

+ Peter the archivist wrote this.

## In the Year of the Lord 1011. Arnold, Bishop of Halberstadt.

[Col. 1493]

### Arnold’s Letter to Henry, Bishop of Würzburg, Concerning the Establishment of the Bishopric of Bamberg

(Edited by Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol. IV, p. 39.)

[Col. 1493B]

**To Henry, bishop, from Arnold.**

Long and diligently sought, my lord, allow yourself at last to be found. I do not know by what misfortune of mine it happens that, whenever I come into this region of the world through which you have traveled so extensively, and while I am seeking you—having been told that you are on the opposite bank of the river—you have already crossed to the other, never giving me the opportunity even to meet you by letter.

Letters addressed to you long ago still lie dormant in my archives. My messenger, returning the next day, testified that, having failed to find you, he had received them in vain.

Nevertheless, if I dared, I would have very much to suggest to you, both concerning this upheaval of your affairs, by which I perceive that you are disturbed beyond what could be believed, and concerning the defense of our own affairs, which—by God’s gift—you have pitied in their weakness and taken under your protection. With you safe, our affairs will sail into harbor.

Meanwhile, therefore, setting aside our own concerns, we must attend to your affairs, which now press more urgently, and see whether they can in any way be remedied. “Our help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

What is this, my lord, that causes you to afflict yourself with such grief? What has happened to you that you should torment yourself? Even if there were some danger, it would nevertheless have to be endured, since whatever it is wrong to correct becomes lighter through patience [Note: Horace, *Odes* I.24.19].

But this matter over which you now distress yourself—if you are willing to look at it more carefully—you will, with God’s favor, find no lack of reason for legitimate joy. Yet, as though something impossible to overcome had happened to you, you handle your affairs so feebly.

You refuse to come to the assembly of your brothers, with whom you ought to overcome your difficulties; instead, you flee and bring great hatred upon yourself. You avoid the sight of the king, as though you had committed some offense against him.

What is this burden you impose upon yourself? Where is that wisdom which we once saw keeping vigilant in you with such acuity? What you are doing appears to be the conduct not of a vigilant man but of one sunk in a deep slumber; not of one seeing clearly but of one suffering from severe eye-trouble.

Awake, my lord, for a little while, and take hold of yourself. I do not know by what enchantments you have been led outside yourself. Strive as far as you can to return to yourself.

The divine voice says: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5:14).

You were the first, or among the first, to choose that lord for yourself, even before he became king. Afterwards, you persisted as much as you could—and as magnificently as you could—in making him king. Accordingly, joined to one another with such mutual affection and bound by such love, no one was more devoted than you in serving him generously, and he was more ready than anyone to receive you as a friend. You were altogether bound together almost inseparably by a kind of glue and bond of friendship.

Finally, wherever or whenever necessity or pleasure demanded it, you were never absent from faithfully supporting him, even at the risk of your life.

Since you bestowed all these benefits upon him, and thereby rightly won great gratitude, friendship, and affection from him, what is this that you now impose upon yourself? Why, when you have earned good things, do you allow yourself to be repaid with evil?

It is difficult to be guilty of treason. Yet, as I hear, he cannot summon you to him either by letters or by messengers, whether by sparing you, promising, or pleading.

How can you hold a bishopric in his kingdom if you resist coming to him? What will the judges say when such matters are examined in court?

Take care lest what could previously have been made better become worse too late, and lest this sternness be judged not strength but rather hardness.

To be hard is one thing; to be strong is another. A hard man cannot be bent toward what is good.

Why do you turn a grateful man into an ungrateful one, a friend into an enemy, and the most generous man toward you into an ungenerous one? Whatever you wished, as seemed most advantageous, you could obtain from him. Has he not granted you such power in these regions that everything obeys your command?

To whom are you leaving us, or the others who depend upon you, to be defended?

Let your spirit be strong, but only to the point of moderation. Whatever exceeds the proper measure is immoderate; what is immoderate is intemperate; intemperance is a vice.

I shall go no further. If you do not fear for yourself, at least you must fear for your sheep. For the safety of your commonwealth is at stake. If you persist as you have begun, it may be so harassed or even plundered that it will either never be restored or will be restored only late.

Therefore remember, my lord, the holy Church over which you preside; remember all those who willingly serve you. Speak with those who wish your welfare no less than their own: with my venerable lord Archbishop W. [Wiligis], your spiritual father and brother; with my lord H. [Heribert], your uterine brother and likewise a venerable archbishop; with my lord B. [Burchard], bishop of Worms; and with your other faithful friends.

Do not reject the counsel they give you. For what concerns you concerns them equally with you. If, perhaps, you go astray following their counsel, the responsibility will be attributed to them.

Fortune has often found a way back [Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* XI.413 and 426–27]. What now threatens you may perhaps soon happen to another. Therefore you should not fear too greatly that they impose upon you now what they themselves will soon refuse to endure.

[Col. 1495D]

It displeased very many of your faithful men that, at the assembly of your brothers where the arrangement was made, you were unwilling to come to be heard. They thought that, if you wished to invalidate the arrangement at all, it could more effectively have been invalidated in your presence.

But since, by your gift—however you gave it—the parish was granted, and since the arrangement was made with the approval of many religious and venerable men, what has been strengthened and ratified by such authorities can scarcely be annulled and rendered void.

I ask, therefore, that your holiness yield to the holiness of those who, consenting to this arrangement, subscribed it. Let what the gathering of many religious men has already confirmed be strengthened through you alone. Write with your fellow bishops and brothers, so that division through schism may not arise within the walls of the holy Church, but rather that the unity of charity may reign in all things.

I already sense that you wish to oppose me and to brand me with the accusation of unjust persuasion, in words such as these:

“To holy and righteous men it must seem exceedingly unjust to fear the power of earthly rule more than the divine, and, through love of temporal sweetness, to provoke against oneself the anger of him who punishes without end. Nor is it lawful that the episcopal see on which you sit—which you found enlarged with ample honors and spread across wide tracts of land—should at your discretion be dishonored or restricted; and you are unwilling to undergo punishment on account of the destruction of ecclesiastical property.”

Far be it from me, unless I am foolish, to persuade you of such things! Rather, if I know how, I wish to lead you toward precisely these conclusions.

Let the Apostle come forward; let that vessel of love, the teacher of the nations, speak for me. Behold our teacher. For we are not from the Jews but from the nations. What does the Apostle say?

“Let every soul be subject to higher authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been ordained by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists the ordinance of God; and those who resist acquire condemnation for themselves” (Romans 13:1–2).

Behold what I urge; behold where I lead you—or rather, not I but the Apostle, and not he but God through him: that you do not resist God’s ordinance and do not yourself assume domination.

Perhaps assuming domination means setting aside what is imposed by those above.

But because, when you were with me, I knew you to be exceedingly acute and clear-sighted, I think you still retain in living memory what is read in the canons: that one must obey the person who commands what is honorable. You may bring this objection against me: that you refuse to obey the command because it seems dishonorable to deprive your Church of its diocese.

As we have heard, your holy father-predecessors did not regard it as dishonorable but as very honorable and useful, in places entrusted to them, after the Church had grown so large that they could no longer visit and oversee it themselves, to substitute other priests for themselves and to make two or three bishoprics from one, so that what one man could accomplish less fully might be supplied more abundantly by two or three.

But now everything is full of errors. They devoted all their labor to winning souls; we are chiefly concerned with how to nourish bodies. They argued for heaven; we argue for earth. Yet this would not be necessary. Earth will be enough for us. As for heaven, we shall see to it if we wish.

In all these matters, the temporal gain—which people value more highly and whose diminution you fear would damage your reputation—will not be reduced for you. Indeed, as I hear, it has already produced, and would produce still, much greater and more useful returns, and perhaps will continue to do so, if only you come to be heard and act according to the advice of your associates.

With your permission, let me whisper in your ear what you yourself once said to me concerning this same matter. Do you not remember that, as we were riding to that same place, B. [Bamberg], in the previous year, when you summoned me to you, you began a speech of this sort, almost as though you foresaw what would happen?

“If the king wished to establish a bishopric there, he could easily assign to your Church whatever would be more useful to you. You would gain little profit from it; almost the whole of that land is forest; Slavs live there; you have come to that distant region either never or rarely.”

Do you not recall that these things were said in this way? Why does what then seemed easy now seem difficult?

Behold, as I trust, you can now recognize that I am not suggesting anything unjust to you, nor urging you to fear the king more than God, but urging you, for God’s sake, both to love and fear him, and to grant an honorable request—not to one who commands, but to one who petitions and wishes to make recompense. It will be lighter for you to have the burden divided with another; you will also be able more easily to render an account to God concerning the care of fewer souls.

If you still refuse to yield, and because it is written that God makes a hypocrite reign on account of the perversity of the people (Job 34:30), you think that you must resist unless this position is overthrown by some argument, I shall say what I think about it.

The Apostle, Christ’s instrument, filled by the Holy Spirit, cannot deceive. Whatever he sounds forth is true, but it requires understanding.

Whenever, because of our wickedness, we are oppressed by an evil authority, whatever that authority commands us which does not depart from the faith and is not opposed to the catholic religion seems to me to be something that must be done. Even if harsh, difficult, and burdensome things assail us, we must obey. For those authorities that exist have been ordained by God. In such a case our perversity is to be blamed, not the justice of the one who strikes. For the hypocrite would not reign except because of our perversity.

But whenever that authority imposes something upon us that wounds religion or inclines toward sin, I judge that it must be resisted freely. Strictly speaking, however, this is not resistance but an improper use of the term: it is avoiding error and completing the course of justice by walking along the straight path.

Errors do not meet us on a straight course; coming from across it and by a crooked route, they seek to drive us from the right path. Indeed, they would not be errors unless they deviated from the straight road. Hence, in works of justice, we are commanded not to turn aside either to the right or to the left.

With this distinction established, you will find nothing, so far as I understand, among the things demanded by the king that harms religion or leads to wrongdoing. Rather, everything protects the piety of divine worship.

He himself touched upon this in a wretched but eloquent speech: if God were to deprive him of the fruit of his womb and disinherit him of human offspring, he would willingly make God his heir, if God would deign to accept it. For this purpose he humbly seeks the support of all those present.

If you attend, as I feel sure you will favorably, you will undoubtedly take pity on him.

Therefore, I beg you, let your spirit grow gentle; loosen the bosom of your compassion; spare yourself and have mercy on your own people [Note: This is closely modeled on Virgil, *Aeneid* XI, where Drances speaks; Arnold here alludes to those words, just as above he alluded to Drances’ reply to Turnus’ speech. Editor, *Patrologia*.].

What you ought to have done for the hypocritical king, do for this man who is upholding religion. He asks for honorable things and is ready to repay them fully and more than fully.

If some portion of your Church’s bodily space is taken away, it is supplied by spiritual edification. It will be much more honored as fruitful in a daughter than it would remain sterile and barren altogether without children.

Remove rust from your heart and henceforth show yourself cheerful in all these matters. Help will not come too late to one whom God wishes to aid.

What now saddens you will, when this trial has passed, bring you much joy by God’s favor. Human life upon earth is a time of trial. There is no one who does not drink from this cup.

May God turn your mourning into joy.

I am deeply distressed that it has been so long since I have either heard or seen you. I should therefore like to hear something about you, either by letter or in person. But let it be according to your judgment. You have enough work to do; I do not dare to tire you further.

## In the Year of the Lord 1012. Pope Sergius IV.

[Col. 1497]

### Historical Notice

(Ciaconius, *On the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 284.)

[Col. 1497D]

Sergius IV, son of Peter Martin, a Roman, formerly called Bucca porci [“Pig’s Mouth”], from the castle of Luna, formerly a Benedictine monk, sat for two years, nine months, and twelve days. He was elected on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September in the year 1009. He was a man of the greatest holiness of life and agreeable character, both before and during his pontificate: generous toward the poor, pleasant toward friends and household members, merciful toward offenders, and restrained toward the obstinate. He was also of such great prudence that throughout his pontificate nothing was done for which the negligence of the ruler could justly be blamed. Turning his whole mind toward God—for all pontiffs ought to do this—he governed everything justly and uprightly according to his own judgment, well endowed by nature and formed by the discipline of his way of life. [Col. 1498D]

Meanwhile, on his advice and at his exhortation, the princes of Italy, having formed an alliance, began planning to drive the Saracens from the island of Sicily, which they had held for many years; with equal determination and resources they set about the undertaking.

The year 1010 was made notable by the illustrious conversion of the Hungarians to the Christian faith. The beginning of this undertaking was initiated by the king himself. Since he could not obtain in marriage Gisela, the sister of King Henry, a maiden of exceptional beauty, unless he accepted the Christian rites, he willingly approached the sacred font and kindled his people to imitate this most excellent deed.

Romuald was a man distinguished by holiness, character, and piety. In the year 1009, the Camaldolese congregation founded by him arose in Italy. Pursuing the eremitical life, he settled in the territory of Arezzo and lived in the hermitage in a hut belonging to a certain Maldinus, in the year 1012.

It seemed right to Sergius, and to the cardinals and leading men of the city of Rome, to assign the imperial dignity to the German nation, because that people, with Spain afflicted and Gaul transferred to new kings, appeared the most powerful of all the provinces of Europe. It was decreed that henceforth only the worthiest man should be elected, and one whom the Roman Church approved; he would be called Caesar and king of the Romans, and would finally be regarded as emperor and Augustus if the Roman pontiff confirmed him.

Ptolemy reports that these men first possessed the authority to elect the emperor: the archbishop of Mainz for Germany, the archbishop of Trier for Gaul, and the archbishop of Cologne in the name of Italy. Four princes were added to them: the Margrave of Brandenburg, who became chamberlain of the emperor after the election; the count palatine, who served the dishes; the duke of Saxony, who carried the sword; and the king of Bohemia, established as the seventh elector and the emperor’s cupbearer. The seventh was added to the election to remove discord between the parties, for whichever side he favored was regarded as the stronger.

They therefore entrusted the election to seven men of that nation, who still possess supreme authority in this matter. Yet it was not believed that this had been done by the Italian people, who had always produced great men, unless Ricordamus the Etruscan, a serious and ancient writer, had transferred the account into his commentaries; John Willancus followed him.

There are, however, those who attribute this authority to create the emperor not to Sergius IV but to Sylvester II, because John Nauclerus writes that the institution of these electors of Germany is found in the records of the Church of Aquileia as having been made in the year of the Lord 1002, under Pope Sylvester II, who succeeded Gregory V. [Col. 1499C]

It is also plainly evident from the rescript of Innocent III, whose words clearly declare it, in the chapter *Venerabilem*, in *Extra*, “On Elections”:

“But,” he says, “we recognize, as we ought, that the right and power of electing the king who is afterward to be promoted to emperor belong to those princes to whom, by right and ancient custom, they are known to pertain; especially since such right and power came to them from the apostolic see. And he who [sic] preceded Gregory X by fifty years, more or fewer, …”

[Col. 1500A]

The sense appears incomplete here; something seems to be missing for a full and perfect meaning [Note: Editor, *Patrologia*.].

From these words it is clear that historians who hold the contrary opinion have strayed very far from the correct chronology. Accordingly, the institution of the seven men is shown either to have occurred during the pontificate of Sylvester II or to have been established by Sergius IV.

Before his pontificate Sergius bore an unbecoming name. For Ditmarus, in Book Six, says that he was called Bucca porci, “Pig’s Mouth,” a name not imposed upon him as a child, when parents give infants attractive names, but bestowed upon him as an adult because of an earlier incident. The same story is also related in the Victorine manuscript.

At that time it was instituted that all who were thereafter designated as supreme pontiffs should change their names at their consecration. For, says the same Ditmarus, although the names of some had been changed, this had not yet happened to all, nor had it arisen from a general institution.

There were three reasons for this institution. The first was that the Lord gave blessed Peter a new name when he chose him as an apostle. The second was that pontiffs ought to be changed in the perfection of their life and reputation, and therefore also in their name. The third was that it would be shameful for someone elevated to so honorable an office of dignity to be called by some disgraceful and dishonorable name.

Following these authorities, especially Ditmarus, who was a contemporary of Sergius IV, the change of name should be attributed to him, not to the earlier men who bore the same name as Sergius. [Col. 1499C]

Sergius IV died at Rome on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, in the year 1012, and was buried at the Lateran. The see was vacant for eight days.

## Diplomatic Notice

The bulls of Sergius IV were written by the hand of:

Benedict, regional notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church (1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14).

John, archivist of the Holy Roman Church (16).

They were issued by the hand of:

Gregory, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church (2).

Peter, bishop of the church of Palestrina and librarian of the Apostolic See (3, 13).

John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church (9).

Gregory, bishop and librarian of the Apostolic See (16).

## Letters and Diplomas of Pope Sergius IV

### I. Sergius IV Asserts to Andrew, Bishop of Poreč, Possession of the Parish of Rovinj and Two Castles. (Year 1010.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, V, 402.]

[Col. 1499D]

**Sergius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Andrew, bishop of the holy Church of Poreč, for you and your successors forever.**
It is altogether fitting that what our predecessors granted or confirmed according to the ordinances of the holy canons or laws should be strengthened and firmly corrected by [Col. 1500D] us, lest after the passage of many years, at the devil’s instigation, anyone should rise up against holy Mother Church and attempt anything against this our confirmation.

Therefore, since you have repeatedly informed us that John, formerly patriarch of Aquileia, had invaded the parish of Ruvini, where an episcopal see is said once to have existed, as well as two castles with a certain valley during the time of our predecessor Sylvester, and since you took care to show us the privilege that you received from him, in which it is also recorded how he had been summoned three times and how he had treated that triple citation as worthless, [Col. 1501A] and how Sylvester himself, of blessed memory, prelate of the Roman Church, had asked Henry, who at that time held the duchy of the Bavarians, to admonish the aforesaid patriarch to withdraw from his harassment of the holy Church of Parenzo. The aforesaid Henry could not do this, but had him summoned to his presence; he nevertheless postponed the matter.

For this reason Pope Sylvester himself, of blessed memory, declared that he had consulted the books of the canons and laws in which he found the following chapters, namely, in the eighty-seventh title of the African Council:

> “It is decreed that any bishops who think that certain parishes belong to their own see should not reclaim them in such a way that they bring their cases before the judging bishops, but should send them elsewhere, whether the parishes suffer loss willingly or unwillingly. [Col. 1501B]”

From secular law also he learned that he could rightly do this. For when the Emperor Justinian speaks of this matter in the eighth book of the *Institutes*:

> “If anyone has dared to seize property on his own authority: if it is his own, let him lose it; if it belongs to another, let him restore the value of the property itself.”

Therefore, supported by the authority of the holy Fathers and the laws, he ordered that a privilege be made for you and commended it to him as valid in a fatherly manner. Having learned this, I confirm for you the aforesaid places—namely, the parish of Ruvini, the two castles, and the valley—and the written text of the privilege, just as our predecessor Sylvester confirmed it; and I order that it remain valid forever.

But if any patriarch, bishop, or any person, great or small, should presume to oppose this, or should attempt to impose any unusual exaction upon your successors concerning the aforesaid places, let him be struck down [Col. 1501C] by the sword of my anathema; and, unless he quickly repents, let him groan eternally with Judas, the betrayer of my Lord.

Written by the hand of Benedict, by the grace of God notary of the regions and *scriniarius* of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of March, in the eighth indiction.

Farewell.

## II. Letter of Pope Sergius IV granting a certain Vedianus the castle of Scuria by emphyteusis. (Year 1010.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, I, 941.]

SERGIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son VEDIANUS, lord of the castle of Scuria: greetings and [Col. 1501D] apostolic blessing.

It is manifest that the castle called Scuria, in the time of our predecessor Pope Sylvester, of blessed memory—as we have now also learned from your report—was once presented to blessed Peter through his hands by royal munificence, and that you have now offered it anew under an annual rent of ten solidi in Raimundian coinage.

We therefore accept this same offering, since we have recognized that it is your will, and grant to you, who receive it from the hand of our blessedness with great devotion, and to all your posterity, the castle of Scuria with all its appurtenances and possessions, to hold forever. We also secure it by the protection of the apostolic see.

For we decree that no ecclesiastical [Col. 1502A] or secular person whatsoever shall have the power to diminish this castle, harass it, or claim it for his own use; rather, it shall be preserved for you, as it has been granted by us, undisturbed and intact. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person should rashly presume to act against these provisions—which God forbid!—and, after being admonished a second or third time, should fail to correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, let him suffer the jeopardy of his honor and office, or be punished by the penalty of excommunication. But whoever proves himself its protector shall mercifully obtain the grace of almighty God and of his apostles Peter and Paul.

I, Sergius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Gregory, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the year 1010 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the [Col. 1502B] eighth indiction.

## III. Sergius IV confirms the foundation of the parish church of Saint Michael near the monastery of Nonantula, in the territory of Modena, established by Rodulfus, abbot of that monastery. (Year 1011.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, V, 341.]

SERGIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

It is the proper duty of our apostolate that, whenever any holy church asks it for some assistance or confirmation, it should rejoice that it has obtained this with all eagerness. And so that in the future no wicked cunning or hostile malice toward the holy Church should presume to add any accusation against it, we have judged it right to confirm forever, not only by words but also in writing, whatever has been granted to it by us.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all Christian believers how Rodulfus, venerable abbot of the holy church of Nonantula, together with the entire community of the senior monk-brothers, through divine inspiration and the prompting of the Holy Spirit—which ineffably enkindles minds that it has filled for the service of almighty God and of his Bride, namely, the holy Church—and also through the preaching of the aforesaid faithful brothers, compelled the inhabitants and cultivators of the fields of our aforesaid abbey [lacuna] to give parish tithes to God, although until then they had by no means paid God the tenth of their possessions.

[Col. 1502D] [Lacuna.] They considered it a [lacuna] crime, because they remembered that in the Old and New Testaments it had been commanded [lacuna] not only [lacuna] to offer God tithes of days.

At the exhortations of the venerable abbot and the aforesaid community, all unanimously inclined their hearts, and with contrite hearts vowed to offer God each year tithes from everything they were to possess. They earnestly requested that the aforesaid tithes, which they gladly desired to return to God, should by our apostolic command be prohibited from being granted in benefice to laymen in the future.

For this reason the aforesaid abbot, together with the counsel of the brothers, implored our magnificence to establish, from our generosity, a canonry from the aforesaid tithes, subject also to his abbey, in which clerics might diligently perform divine services for the Lord during the day and night [Col. 1503A] and for the people who gathered there.

These are the boundaries of the tithes belonging to the aforesaid canonry: from the Claudia Road to Porciola; from Mucia to the Panaro River; and beyond it, whatever and however much is cultivated from the villages of the aforesaid river or by the inhabitants of Nonantula. Also, whatever the clerics jointly serving God in the aforesaid canonry may justly acquire.

We assented to his requests, recognizing that what he asked was just. Accordingly, a canonry was established in honor of Saint Michael, and clerics were appointed, together with an archpriest [lacuna]. To this archpriest we also granted the power to judge penitents concerning criminal offenses. Nevertheless, if necessity should arise, he is to seek judgment from a [Col. 1503B] bishop, lest he appear meanwhile to deny repentance to a soul desiring it.

The same archpriest is to have responsibility for everything: for divine offices, lights, buildings, guests, and the distribution of tithes and offerings among the others, in such a manner that he recognizes that he will render an account to God on the day of judgment. He was also granted, before the others, the tithe of one village called Salicetus, on account of his diligent care.

By apostolic authority we decree that whoever strives to enlarge or observe this arrangement—which, with God’s help, we ordered to be established for the salvation of the souls of the faithful and so that they might be freed from their former error—shall be strengthened by our blessing. But whoever attempts to violate it—which we do not wish—or gives counsel for its violation, or wishes to [Col. 1503C] withdraw the canonry from subjection to the holy monastery, or wishes to grant the tithe in benefice to laymen, shall be struck by the bond of anathema.

So that this may be believed more surely and observed more diligently by all, we ordered this decree to be written by our chancellor and, as we stated above, strengthened it with our letters and the impression of our seal. We also ordered the aforesaid abbot Rodulfus and all the brothers to subscribe to this decree, which they had unanimously established.

Farewell.

+ Given through the hand of Peter, bishop of the holy Church of Palestrina and librarian of the sacred palace, in the year of the Lord 1011, on the sixth day before the Kalends [Col. 1503D] of June, in the ninth indiction.

I, Rodulfus, abbot, subscribed this decree in my own hand by order of the apostolic see.

I, Frogerius, prior, subscribed in my own hand.

Laurentius, priest and monk, subscribed in my own hand.

Gulferius, monk, subscribed in my own hand.

Gregorius, priest and monk, subscribed in my own hand.

Liuzo, monk, subscribed.

## IV. Pope Sergius IV confirms all the properties belonging to the monastery of Cuxa. (Year 1011.)

[COCQUELINES, *Bullarum amplissima collectio*, I, 310.]

[Col. 1504A]

SERGIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to OLIVA, religious abbot of Saint Michael the Archangel and Saint Germanus, confessor of Christ, situated in the Confluent Valley beside the Literan River, in the place called Cuxa; to you and those dwelling with you, and through you to your successors and theirs: health, peace, and apostolic blessing, for as long as the world endures. Amen.

[Col. 1504B] Since it is evident that our Lord God continually increases the honor of the holy universal Church through the propagators of the blessed faith, it is necessary for him, by the authority of his entire governance, to grant them the generosity of just judgment and to drive far from it the intrusion of evils.

Therefore, since it accords with apostolic piety to assist those who ask with kindly compassion, we, assenting to your just requests—for they have been judged by us to be just—confirm by our privilege all the properties or possessions of that place, its boundaries and limits with the adjacent lands of its chief estates, together with all its churches, parishes, villages, estates, houses, farmsteads, lands, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, brushlands, plots, winepresses, waters, watercourses, roads, mills, mill-sites with their headwaters, and fisheries, cultivated and [Col. 1504C] uncultivated; and whatever the most glorious Archangel Michael appears to retain from the gifts of the faithful in the monastery of Cuxa.

We therefore grant to the aforesaid monastery the alod situated around it, with its boundaries and landmarks: on one side extending along the summit of the Serra de Bovaria to Jovis of Clerano and to the mountain called Lavarias; along Lavarias as far as Flamidinum; from there it proceeds to the place called Stella and as far as the summit of Mount Canigonis. From the southern face of Mount Canigonis it descends along the Serra of the Hill of the North to the rock commonly called Cherum Clerinti; it descends along the summit of the Serra to the Hill of Parabarius and as far as the Merdarius stream, and is carried on to the River Têt.

[Col. 1504D] On the northern side it reaches the public road called the Two Sisters, and along that public road as far as the Literan; from there, below Saint Felix, it extends to the alod of Saint Mary and ends at Petrafixa. It then extends along the same little valley, where there is a great rock in which Seniofredus, count of good memory, carved a cross to make the boundary of that alod recognizable. From there it goes to Lower Bovaria and along the summit to Upper Bovaria.

We likewise grant the alod of Tauriniani with the church of Saint Fructuosus, together with its tithes and first fruits, and the village with all its appurtenances; likewise the village of Clerano with the church of Saint Martin, its tithes and first fruits, and its alod with its boundaries and landmarks.

[Col. 1505A] Also, the alod of Avallanet and the alod of Arboca, with their boundaries and landmarks; and the Leche Valley with the church of Saint Savior, with its tithes and first fruits. This valley is bounded on one side by Portella, on another by the aforesaid Stella, on the third by Mount Stabello, on the fourth by Mount Caprario, on the fifth by Cabum Convivium, on the sixth by Mount Cogoll, and on the seventh by the village of Senarius.

This valley, enclosed by these boundaries according to the former definition of Count Seniofredus, the command of King Lothar, and the restoration made by our son Count Wifredus, we grant to you without disturbance from anyone.

Moreover, the village of Curtis, with its boundaries and landmarks, and the alod of Foliolus, which the aforesaid Count Guifred exchanged with you, together with everything he had been accustomed to possess there—namely, the fief and the woods belonging to the same village—and another alod that you possess in the same village and within its boundaries and landmarks.

[Col. 1505B] Also, the church of Saint Vincent and the alod of that place, with its boundaries and landmarks, and the alod of Vernet.

Whatever it has in the same valley in numerous places, we establish in the same manner: namely, the alod of Foliano; the alod of Bonohomine, which he transferred to you by written instrument; and the properties in the village of Pini, the village of Mentedo, and many other places; the village of Ciresago and the village of Arriano, as much as Count Seniofredus possessed there by any title, or as other people granted to the same monastery; the alod of Canolia; and the village of Castellani with the two churches founded there, namely Saint Andrew and Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin, with the tithes, first fruits, and alods belonging to those churches.

[Col. 1505C] The same village has boundaries or landmarks: on one side at Petrafixa, which lies within the boundary of the village of Mollegio; on another at the ark of Casalono; it runs along the ridge by which one goes to the River Têt; on the third side at the farmsteads of Mengono; on the fourth at the boundary of Canova or Petrafixa, and from there as far as the River Têt.

Beyond that river, whatever Count Seniofredus held on the day of his death: the village of Torrentis with its boundaries and landmarks; the village of Insula likewise; villages and farmsteads with their limits; the alod of Molegio and of the Mosset Valley; also at Planicolos, Stagnilios, Terradas, Marceval, and Erbocolo; and in the church of Saint Eulalia the portion that you ought to have, together with the tithes and first fruits belonging to it.

[Col. 1505D] The entire village of Taresag, with the church situated there, its tithes, first fruits, and everything belonging to it; the alod of the village of Ropidaria; and the alod called Wlcraria.

In the same Confluent Valley, in the valley of Secundianus and in the villages of Ortos and Juliolos, Flacano, Sodanias, Marazanos, Porcinianos, Agnes, Eune, Evulo, Oreliano, Cirlano, and Tubiro; in the village of Vetesano, Canabellas, Erola, Planos, Caprilios, and Tovegal, with the church of Saint Adrian, together with its tithes and first fruits; the village of Talantii with the church of Saint Stephen and its tithes and first fruits.

[Col. 1506A] Mozunculas and Uncinias; the alod of Exalata with the church of Saint Peter; the village of Intervallos; the villages of Tobes, Aquas, and Pratis; the Balagarius Valley with its boundaries and landmarks; the church of Saint Thomas with its alods, tithes, and first fruits; the place called Lar with the church of Saint Andrew, its tithes and first fruits, and the alod with its boundaries and limits.

In the village of Saltone, the church of Saint Maurice, with the tithes and first fruits belonging to it; and in the same village, the alod and the place called Algion, woods and pasture suitable for livestock; the church of Saint Peter called Inforcats, with its tithes and first fruits; and the village of Rivofrigidum with woods and pastures for livestock.

The village of Lacuna, with the church of Saint Vincent, its tithes, first fruits, and all the property belonging to the church or village, together with its boundaries and limits; the church of Saint Valentine with its tithes and first fruits, situated in the village of Sponda; the alod of Angulos with the market toll, together with its small villages, lesser hamlets, and the Ursaria Valley.

[Col. 1506B] These are the boundaries of Angulos: on one side at the stream or village of Furmicaria; on another at the village called Crux, or at the summit of the mountain called Scalibatus. Along the summit of that mountain one goes to the village of Quilianus, and from there reaches Melum; on the third side at the cleared field; on the fourth at the king’s field, or at Elpericus Hill. Also, the lesser hamlet called Odelon of Chero Ramatum.

In the county of Cerdanya: Vil-Vulcaria, Avizuno, Odelon, Egat, Turba, Ernas, Alcone, Salagosa, Bajande, Estavar, Upper Gurguja, the village of Nervice, the court of Floridius, Edors, Unozes, Callegas, the village of Ixi, and the village of Lubinti.

[Col. 1506C] In the same county, the village of Eragolisa with the church of Saint James, its tithes, first fruits, and everything belonging to it; the alod of Eucig and of Lora; and in Araone, Exenegia, the village of Saint Martin, Ysavals, Saint Eulalia, and the Cheirol Valley.

Also, in Palleriolos, the parish of Saint Thomas, which is in Ventajola, with its tithes and first fruits; and in the same village the alod; the village of Vulvirri with the church of Saint Cecilia, its tithes and first fruits; and the alod of that village, with servants and maidservants and everything belonging to the same place, together with the boundaries and limits of both the church and the alods.

[Col. 1506D] The church of Saint Eugenia with its tithes and first fruits, and with the alod of Sagano; the alod in the village of Albi; and vineyards in the territory of Isogal.

Also in the villages of Curtes, Juncarias, Cerconeda, and Aranfer; the alod in the village of Palazold; and in Anauga, Oloja, Palazio, the village of Coma, the village of Borco, Chrxanos, Estol, and the village of Adacio.

In the church of Saint Lawrence, the portion given by Wisadus and his nephew Willelmus; the alod in the village of Senovastre; the village of Brrizella with its boundaries and landmarks; in the village of Pratis, the alod, the village of Oruc, and the village of Rivi, with their boundaries, landmarks, and adjacent lands; the church of the village of Tarteria with its tithes and first fruits.

[Col. 1507A] The church of Saint Andrew in the village of Batturga, and the alod there; in the village of Telone, the church of Saint Vincent, situated on the hill, with its alod, and another alod in the same village.

In the Baritana Valley, in the village of Montelianus, the alod with its boundaries and adjacent lands; and in the village of Bar, the alod with its boundaries in numerous places.

In the county of Urgell, in the village of Cabrils, the alod that belonged to Undiscolus the monk.

Whatever the same monastery possesses in the aforesaid counties or places, we establish and decree that it shall possess by perpetual right and hold without disturbance from anyone.

[Col. 1507B] In the county of Cerdanya, the village called Rivolorto, with its boundaries and landmarks; likewise the village of Montenigro with the church of Saint Stephen, its tithes and first fruits; and in the county of Berguedà, the village of Spiojiola with the church of Saint Clement, its tithes, first fruits, and everything belonging to it; the alod of Cleirano; and in Petra Furno, Herenna, and Viver de Castraserras, the alod that belonged to Onia the monk.

In Wardia, the alod and the church of Saint Mary with its possessions; and the alod in the village of Crosilios.

Also in the Confluent Valley, in the villages of Astoer, Aspicano, and Penedes, the alod.

In the village of Fenestret, Saorla, Vincano, Vilella, Rigerdano, Vallils, Arenianes, and Ghuvianas, alods in all these places; and in the village of Erzillano, the alod that belonged to Durandus the priest; the Stabia Valley, with the church of Saint Andrew and its tithes and first fruits.

[Col. 1507C] In the same valley, villages with their boundaries and limits, woods and mountains; also the Great Valley with the church of Saint Vincent, its tithes and first fruits, and its boundaries and limits, woods and hills belonging to the same valley.

The alod of Bula with its boundaries and limits; the alod of Insula, or of Ragollella, of Nisiago, of the village of Milliarios, of Upper Saint Felix, and of Lower Saint Felix; also the alod of Valletorta, of Locas, and of Curbaria.

In the place called Insulas, lands and vineyards; the alod of Valleventosa; on Buscano Hill and in the Asper Valley, the alod of Vernedas; and in Molledil, the alods of Crodos, Salvaticos, and the village of Paladolo.

[Col. 1507D] In the county of Roussillon, in the village of Tiviro, the alod with its boundaries and landmarks; the alod of the Centuria spring and of Reliano; and in the village of Milano, the alod that belonged to Bonisilius.

Also the alod of Basoni with the church of Saint Vincent, its tithes, first fruits, and all its appurtenances, with its boundaries and landmarks; the alod of Caucanet; the alod of Petra-Calce with its boundaries and adjacent lands; and in the villages of Turilias, Saint Lawrence, Judegas, and Caldarios, the alod of Berchal.

[Col. 1508A] In the county of Fenouillèdes, in the Saurinian Valley, the village called Valletta in its entirety, with its boundaries and adjacent lands; the church of Saint Michael; and the church of Saint Peter, which is in Tabernullas, with its alod; and other alods in the same village.

Also the church of Saint Felicitas, situated in Castellione, with its alods; in the villages of Favarios, Regulella, Tiriliano, Cassanias, and Pleucios, alods; likewise the alod of the village of Saccaria, of Palmas, of Campo Ursino, of Petralas, of Curbones, of Uxone, of Coma-Calida, of Porcilianos, of the village of Pratis, of Pricilianos, of Cabannas, and of Virano.

In the Valley of Saint Mary, the alod; and also the Valley of the Holy Cross, and of the Archangel Michael, and of blessed John, which is situated in the Alba Valley, with its tithes and first fruits and all property belonging to it.

Also the castle of Saint Lawrence with the same church, together with everything belonging to the same valley; the alod of the village of Attendido; and in Chonosolo, Buliaco, and Conredo, alods.

In the county of Razès, in the village of Brevazello, the alod.

[Col. 1508B] In the county of Toulouse, the church of Saint Mary situated between two waters, with its tithes, first fruits, and all the alods belonging to the same church, together with waters, fisheries, and alder groves; the alod of Lower Algares; and in Upper Algares half of the church of Saint Julian, half of everything belonging to it, together with the alod and woods.

In the village of Texonarias, the church of Saint Martin with its tithes, first fruits, and all its appurtenances, together with the alod and woods; the alod of Cortevillica; in the village of Fagia, the alod; in the village of Bexano, the alod and mill; in Artennago, the church of Saint Quininus with its tithes and first fruits, and the alod in the same place; in Ambliago, the alod and mill with its headwaters and fisheries; in Viliago, the alod and mill; and in Miliarias, the church of Saint Saturninus with everything belonging to it, and the alod there.

[Col. 1508C] In the province of Narbonne, the alod of the village of Aldrado.

In the county of Besalú, the village of Centens with its boundaries and landmarks; the alod of Maliano; the church of Saint Michael of Ortomadario with its tithes, first fruits, and the same village; in Cantens, the alod that belonged to Odo; and the alods of Maneval, Monte Canuto, and Sallellas.

In the county of Empúries, the alod of Castellione and the church of Fluviano with its boundaries and appurtenances.

[Col. 1508D] In the county of Barcelona, in Lanaria, the alod that belonged to Abbarich; and in the same city, an alod with lands and vineyards; also in Orta, Romanet, and Fenestrellas, alods; and in Balneolos, the alod.

In the county of Vallès, in Mogoda, Galleches, Tenes, Olineto, Palaciolo, Petrafitta, and Aspicell, alods.

In the city of Manresa, the alods that belonged to Audesindus the monk.

In the county of Osona, the alod of the village of Paulus, which lies beside the castle of Salliforas, and the alods of Cheros; and at Saint Hippolytus, in the village of Palazol, the alod.

[Col. 1509A] All the estates that we have mentioned, and those that we have not mentioned—namely, villages, churches, parishes, estates, houses, farmsteads, cultivated and uncultivated lands, fields, woods, vineyards, meadows, pastures for livestock, plots, winepresses, waters, watercourses, roads, mills, mill-sites with their headwaters and fisheries, together with saltworks and pitch kilns—all property already acquired or still to be acquired belonging to the monastery of Saint Michael situated in the Confluent Valley, together with servants and bondsmen, are preserved for it by our apostolic authority.

We decree moreover that, when the abbot of that monastery dies, abbots shall not be installed there by kings, counts, or any other person for the sake of money, or for any empty display of favor; rather, abbots shall be elected by all the servants of God dwelling there, according to God and in accordance with the rule of Father Benedict.

[Col. 1509B] We also grant the abbots of that place permission to have their clerics ordained by whatever bishops and wherever they wish, and to receive chrism from whatever see pleases them. No bishop shall be able to excommunicate them, neither the bishop in whose diocese the monastery is situated nor any other bishop; nor shall he be able to excommunicate any church belonging to the same monastery.

We further decree that any penitent excluded from the church threshold shall, for as long as he remains there, have permission to enter and hear the entire divine office.

We also grant the abbot or monks, and all clerics belonging to the monastery, permission not to attend a synod unless they wish to do so voluntarily or are summoned.

Therefore we confirm and establish henceforth that no king, prince, margrave, count, judge, bishop, or any person, great or small, shall presume to inflict any force or invasion upon the same monastery or its appurtenances.
