[Col. 1509C] Therefore, proclaiming and decreeing under the attestation of divine judgment and of “tuo” [reading uncertain], and under the prohibition of anathema, that no person dare or presume to act unjustly in any matter against this privilege of ours, nor attempt to break it. But if anyone—which we do not believe—should treat our privilege lightly and attempt to violate it, we bind him, unless he repents, with perpetual bonds of anathema, in the name of almighty God, his holy apostle Peter, and ourselves, who exercise his office.

But whoever, as a helper of this holy monastery, chooses, enriches, and loves it in whatever way he can, may rejoice that, through the intercession of almighty God, he is filled with apostolic blessing and grows from virtue to virtue.

Written by the hand of Benedict, notary of the regions [Col. 1509D] and *scriniarius* of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of November, in the tenth indiction.

Farewell.

## V. Privilege of Pope Sergius IV for the monastery of Ripoll. (Year 1011.)

[COCQUELINES, *Bullarum amplissima collectio*, I, 312.]

SERGIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to OLIVA, religious abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary, our Lady, situated in the county of Osona, in the valley of Ripoll, between two rivers; to you and those dwelling with you, and through you to your successors and theirs: [Col. 1510A] health, peace, and apostolic blessing, for as long as the world endures. Amen.

Since it is evident that our Lord God continually increases the honor of the holy universal Church through the propagators of the blessed faith, it is necessary that he, by the full right of governance, bestow upon her the generosity of the censure of just moderation and drive far from her the encroachment of evils. Therefore, since it is fitting for apostolic compassion to assist those who petition with kindly sympathy, we, assenting to your just petitions—for, as they have been adjudged by us, they are indeed just—confirm by our apostolic privilege all the properties or possessions of that place, their boundaries or limits with the adjoining lands of the principal estates, together with all churches, parishes, villages, estates, farmsteads, small holdings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, fields, meadows, [Col. 1510B] pastures, woods, scrublands, yards, winepresses, waters, waterways, roads, mills, millworks with their headwaters, and fisheries, and whatever the blessed and glorious Virgin Mary appears to retain from the donations of the faithful in the monastery of Ripoll.

We therefore grant to the aforesaid monastery the allod situated around it: on one side extending along the Tamarice, which flows into the Tezer; on another side along the watercourse that runs beyond the village of Molas, together with that same village of Molas, and flows into the Tezer; then ascending along the torrent beyond Engordans, and ascending through Fornellos as far as the Serra above the wood of Ordina, and reaching the district above Vilarzellum. From that Vilarzellum it reaches as far as the hill of [Col. 1510C] Calvellum; then it reaches the Serra above lesser Guausago and flows into the stream of Saint Lawrence as far as the river Freber; then it ascends along the stream that runs toward the village of Babos and reaches the village of Stamariz, flows into the Tezer, and borders the village of Archamala; from there it extends to Solomon’s hill, as far as the village of Molas with its boundaries—wherever it has authority in that valley, in very many places.

In the same way we establish the possessions in the valley of Tentarios, the village of Aramancias, greater Stuiolo, Grivolosa itself, and others in very many places. Also, the fisheries in the waters of the Tezer, from Risbamala to Spata, and in the Freter, from the same bend as far as the Tezer.

We grant in full the market of the aforesaid place, its toll, [Col. 1510D] and all justice to be administered there. The parish of that valley, the church of Saint Peter together with the other churches subject to it, just as Bishop Gotmar granted them there, or his successors, Bishops Idalcherius and Georgius, together with the tithes and firstfruits, without tribute.

The allod called Matamala, with the church of Saint Mary, and the church of the hill of Machonosius, with tithes and firstfruits. Its boundaries are as follows: on one side at the hill of Transvadoni; it proceeds along that stream to another stream that runs through those places, and joins the torrents that flow from Serra Viniclos as far as Cinctum opposite Tremolosa; it proceeds along the Serra to the pass of Villalonga, descends into the torrent, descends through Lobaria, and joins the hill of Transvadoni.

And in that valley of Matamala, [Col. 1511A] the allod that belonged to Bishop Rodulfus, and the parish of Vineolas, with the tithes and firstfruits that Bishop Georgius granted to Saint Saviour without tribute, as is recorded in that endowment; and the allod itself called Campmanandati, with its boundaries and adjoining lands—that is, the whole village.

At Guausago, the allod that belonged to Guisallus and Seniofredus, with its church, boundaries, and adjoining lands. Also the allod that belonged to John, with its house, lands, and vineyards, and Libertinus’s wood. In the village of Stamariz, that allod itself, with its boundaries and adjoining lands. In the village of Aenove, that allod which belonged to Tellemar or to his heirs, with its boundaries, and the allod held by Peter the priest. In the very wood called Guvalosa, with its boundaries and adjoining lands.

At Salton, [Col. 1511B] the allod with the woods which the aforesaid lord Oliba gave, and the wood that belonged to Sperandeus and Ortes, with its boundaries and adjoining lands. Also the allod of Sasitos, the condaminae of Archamala themselves, the allod of Balbos, the allod of Monteliols, and the allod of Guidmondi, with lands, vineyards, woods, a church, tithes, and firstfruits, with their own borders and boundaries, without tribute.

The allod called Salselles, with the church of Saint Peter, tithes, and firstfruits, with its borders and boundaries, without tribute. In the district of Berguedà, at the place of Brositano, the allod as it is recorded in their judgment, and the parish of Saint Mary with its dependent churches—namely, Rodgarius’s palace and Pera itself—with tithes and firstfruits, without tribute.

The church of Saint Vincent, which is at Albiols [Col. 1511C] with its allod, tithes, and firstfruits. At the place called Suburbano, an allod with the churches in the village called Guargalam. At the place called Pontus, an allod with the churches which Count Guifred gave to Saint Mary, as well as another allod of Gargalam with its churches, tithes, firstfruits, and boundaries; the allod of Nabars with its boundaries; the allod of Nureo; the allod of Montesclau; the allods of Torrentis profundi; the allods of Folcunaria; the allods at the foot of the castle of Balzarens; the allods of Begua and Anzano; and the allods of La Doixosa, which belonged to Bonifilius and Lobatoni, or to others.

The valley of Marles itself, with its villages and mills, the church of Saint Mary with its tithes and firstfruits, and its allods with their boundaries and adjoining lands. Also the allods of Gaminacos, [Col. 1511D] the church of Monte Clauso, the allods of Benemide, the allods of Serra which belonged to Delanti, the allods of Spurigia and Callers, the valleys of Boscedano themselves with their villages or their boundaries, and the allods of Palam.

In the city of Manresa, an allod—that is, houses, lands, vineyards—and the allods that belonged to other men. At Montserrat, an allod with the churches of Saint Peter and Saint Martin, and at the summit of Montserrat the church of Saint Mary and Saint Asisellus, with lands, vineyards, mills, woods, and scrublands; also the allod called Evelosa, with lands, vineyards, mills, woods, and scrublands.

In the city of Barcelona, houses with courtyards, wells, gardens, lands, and vineyards that lie within the city and [Col. 1512A] its boundaries; and the allod of Camma, with its church, tithes, firstfruits, and boundaries; and Enoiosa with its appurtenances.

In the district called Vallès, houses with courtyards, gardens, lands, and vineyards, and the allod of Digno or Engelfredus, the allod of Canobellas, and the allod of Mationa.

In the district of Osona, the allod of the palace, the allod called Oligo, Daniel’s villar, the allod of Saniliare, the allod of Elzedelo with its boundaries, the woods of Rocha Felix, and the allod of Planezas.

And in the district of Osona, other allods in many places—namely, Devesa itself; and at Wistiliano, very many houses, lands, vineyards, and the allod that belonged to Count Borell of Pallars Mirallès, with its boundaries; the allods which Gualdus gave to Saint Mary, just as he held them and [Col. 1512B] caused them to be recorded as a donation; the allod which Guillelmus gave at Albedano, with lands, farmsteads, and vineyards, cultivated or uncultivated; the allod of Serra, which belonged to Gafredus; the allod of Juniolosa; the field-allod of Galinde, which belonged to Guiscafredus the cleric; the allods of Lociana, which belonged to Guillelmus, son of Ermenairus; the allod of Guisado with its mills; the allods of Ovalo, which Gandamurus, Honestus, Oliba the cleric, and all the people gave; the allods of Jonna; the allods of the stream of Peras; the allods of Saturanus with their boundaries; and the allod of the valley of Oriola with its boundaries.

In the district of Cerdanya, in the valley of Llívia, the village of Armonedo with its tithes and firstfruits, together with the allod called Lilledo and Genebredo, the hill of Maranegas, and Marola. At the place called [Col. 1512C] Guarexer, that allod itself with its church, tithes, and firstfruits.

In Cerdanya, the allod called Alozos, with its church, tithes, and firstfruits, and the allod of Bar. In that same Cerdanya, the allods of Arreguall, Nassobell, Monteliano, Bar, and Adoll.

At Labertells, an allod with mills; the allod of Villa-vetere with the churches themselves; the allods of Evall, Bellich, Masolio, Saint Eulalia, Engils, Ger, Palaciol, Villa-Lobs, Oligua, Anama, Salciep, Equaleges, Ur, Centaflorida, Angastuna, Estavar, Salagosa de Sed, Palaciolo, Valfamelica, Ezer, Esna, Psanezas, Saltegual, Miella, Ventolano, Closellos, [Col. 1512D] Obzello, Campancionos, Macana, Meramors, Urriols, and Cols, with pastures; and the aforesaid Armonedo, with its woods, calino [a term of uncertain meaning], pastures, and the church of Saint Romanus with its boundaries; the allods of the hill of Malello, which is there; and Gomses and Scurrigeres; and in that same Cerdanya, in many places, houses and courtyards with vineyards and lands.

In the district of Urgell, the allod called Exeduli with the church of Saint Michael. At the castle of Cardona, the allod called Pradis and the other possessions; the allods of Scorbario with their churches and boundaries; the allods of Cordinello with the church of Saint Cucuphas and its boundaries; and the allods of Lagno and Castrobono. [Col. 1513A] In that same district, other lands and vineyards.

In the valley of Conflent, the allod called Evol, with its willows and pastures. In that same valley, in many places, vineyards; the allod of Sodames; the allods of Wincedo and Macanos; and the allod of Sagamano with the church of Saint Clement and its allods; at Soliano, an allod; at Corneliano, lands and vineyards; at Arriano, houses, lands, and vineyards; and the allods of Monsedo, Vitamarias, and Fenestredo.

At the place called Bulla, lands, vineyards, and houses, with tithes and firstfruits. At Vintolano, lands and vineyards. At Campajonos, houses, lands, and vineyards; and at Rippas, lands, houses, and vineyards. At Macana, houses, vineyards, and lands.

In the district of Roussillon, the allod of Tason and Amasos of Petra-calce. In the valley of [Col. 1513B] Speri, the allod of Etaloris and the allod of Hermis.

In the district of Pallars, the allods situated at Basturcius, with their churches or their allods. In the district of Besalú, the allods that belonged to Corbo and Argilagarios, Valle-alta, and Juviniano, with houses, vineyards, and lands.

At the place called Judaicas, the church of Saint Peter with houses, lands, and vineyards, with tithes, firstfruits, offerings, and its boundaries and adjoining lands. At Vernedas, houses and lands; the allods of Fulgosa and Secundella; at Aqualia, the allod of Bag, which belonged to Ramardus; and Porrarias; the allod of Blacarder with woods, pastures, and mills; the allod of Brania; and the third part of the village of Palazol itself, with its boundaries and borders; the allods of Basso and [Col. 1513C] Viguilar, Rivocano, Villalonga, Pineda, and the allod of Bagonos.

In the district of Girona, in the village called Celiano, that allod itself and the allod of Emulano. In the district of Cerdanya, the allod that belonged to Viscount Gualdaldus, with the churches established above it, wherever they are; also at the place called Valle-vetere, the churches of Saint Martin and Saint Saturninus, with their borders and boundaries, tithes, and firstfruits.

Likewise, in the valley of Asperi, the village called Hermas, with its borders and boundaries and woods. At Roveraso, houses with lands, vineyards, and uncultivated places. Likewise, in Berguedà, in the village of Donegua. In the district of Empúries, the allod of the salt pond. In the district of Peralada, the allod of Castillione and that of Valle-mala, with their boundaries.

[Col. 1513D] Thus, all the properties we have mentioned, and all properties not mentioned, whether already acquired or yet to be acquired, belonging to the monastery of the holy Mother of God situated in the valley of Ripoll, are confirmed by us to it by apostolic authority.

We decree, moreover, that when the abbot of that monastery dies, no abbots are to be installed there by kings, counts, or any other person out of greed, for money, or for any empty glory of favor; rather, abbots are to be elected by all the servants of God dwelling there, according to God and in accordance with the rule of Benedict the Father.

We also grant the abbot of that place permission to have his clerics ordained wherever he wishes and by whichever bishops he chooses, and to receive chrism from whatever see he prefers; and we decree that he may not be excommunicated by any bishop, whether by the bishop in whose diocese his monastery is situated [Col. 1514A] or by any other bishop, nor may any church belonging to that same monastery be excommunicated.

We further decree that whoever has been excluded from the thresholds of the Church as a penitent may, for as long as he remains there, have permission to enter and hear the entire divine office.

We also grant the abbot or monks, and all clerics belonging to the monastery, permission not to attend a synod unless they wish to do so voluntarily or are summoned.

Therefore we henceforth confirm and establish that no king, no prince, no margrave, no count, no judge, and no person, great or small, presume to inflict any force or invasion upon that monastery or its possessions. Under invocation of divine judgment and proclamation of the prohibition of anathema, [Col. 1514B] we decree that none of our successors in the pontificate, nor anyone else, shall ever attempt to violate this.

But if anyone—which we do not believe—without fearing God and disregarding our privilege, which we grant, attempts by word or deed to break it, whoever he may be, we bind him, unless he repents, with perpetual bonds of anathema, in the name of Almighty God, of his holy apostle Peter, and of ourselves, who act in his place.

But whoever, as a helper of this holy monastery, chooses, enriches, and loves it to the extent of his ability, may rejoice that, through the intervention of Almighty God and filled with apostolic blessing, he will advance from virtue to virtue. May paradise be his portion, the Lord Christ his inheritance, and peace and consolation his—where there is always joy [Col. 1514C] and no sorrow.

Written by the hand of Benedict, regional notary and scrinarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of November, in the tenth indiction.

Farewell.

### VI. Pope Sergius IV confirms the foundation of the monastery of Saint Peter of Fenouillet and the possessions belonging to it. (Year 1011.)

[COCQUELINES, *Bullarum amplissima collectio*, I, 314.]

SERGIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

If we are compelled to take care of the house of the most excellent watchtower, our most holy mother Church, and if, out of zeal for divine worship, we are moved by religious duty to anticipate [Col. 1514D] the elevation and stability of sacred places, so that those who dwell in them may be able to offer service to God alone, it is fitting for us to accustom ourselves to this through devoted labor: so that souls dedicated to Christ, who have submitted themselves to his service throughout the days of their lives, may persevere undisturbed under his military service; and so that those things which Christians have devoted to the praises of God by the authority of our apostolic see may remain there securely, under the firm protection of the faith of him whose place we occupy.

Therefore, we wish it to be known to all present and future bishops, dukes, counts, and primates of the holy Church of God, that our beloved and special son, the glorious Count Bernard, informed our apostolate [Col. 1515A] that he wished to build, according to the institution of canonical authority, a monastery in the district of Fenouillet, at a venerable place consecrated in honor of the apostle Saint Peter. He asked that we fortify that monastery with the privilege of our apostolic command.

Desiring to fulfill his petition all the more beneficially for the love of God, we decree by the dignity of this privilege that all things of whatever kind which have formerly been devoted to that place—whether estates, tithes, firstfruits, or other ecclesiastical payments—we order to remain there perpetually as attached allods; likewise, those which the aforesaid count has transferred to that place, or which presently appear to belong to it, we transfer to the aforesaid place by the authority of this privilege.

Their names are these: the church of Saint Mary of the Valley; the church of Saint Andrew; the church of Saint Martin of the village of Prinianas; and the church of Saint James, with their tithes, firstfruits, allods, and payments; [Col. 1515B] likewise the allod of the village of Archanis, with its boundaries and borders; and the allod which Wadallus, abbot of that same place, acquired in the village of Saint Felix, whether through his parents or by any other claim; likewise the allod of the village of Regulella, and that which Pontius, brother of the aforesaid abbot, devoted there.

All these estates named above, donated there by the faithful, or acquired thereafter, we receive with that monastery under the protection of the holy Roman [Col. 1515C] Church and our apostolic see. We establish that henceforth no person placed in authority shall presume to subject the aforesaid church and monastery, with all the things listed above, to the jurisdiction of another church; nor shall he be able to hold public courts there, whether on account of homicides or any other offense, nor exact from that monastery any official service or temporal service.

Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors live peacefully in the service established by us. No person, great or small, shall have permission to take away any of its goods or anything belonging to it. Instead, by the authority of our privilege, everything shall remain perpetually endowed in that place.

[Col. 1515D] We also grant the aforesaid abbot and his successors the right to receive chrism from whatever see they prefer and to have their clerics ordained.

But if anyone—which we do not wish—should presume with criminal audacity to oppose or in any way transgress what we have granted in that holy place and established for the stability of the aforesaid monastery, let him know that he is bound by the bond of our anathema and is to be burned with the devil, his most atrocious pomp, and Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the punishment of eternal fire.

But whoever proves in all things to be a faithful observer out of pious regard, guarding the statutes of this privilege, may obtain abundantly the grace of blessing from our most merciful Lord God and deserve to become a participant in eternal life forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1516A] Written by the hand of Benedict, regional notary and scrinarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of November, in the tenth indiction.

Farewell.

### VII. Privilege of Pope Sergius IV for the monastery of Canigou. (Year 1011.)

[COCQUELIN, vol. I, p. 315.]

SERGIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

Since, by the assent of divine goodness, it has been the diligent custom of our predecessors to watch most carefully over all people in prosperity and adversity and to assist them in their needs, so that we may cut away evil from the heart and strengthen what is good with apostolic blessings, [Col. 1516B] therefore we, who bear their insignia, wish to follow in their footsteps. We desire that all people established by God in our times may rejoice and, with God’s help, continually bear the honor and advantages of so great a dignity.

Because Christ has appointed us to bear the place of Peter, chief of the apostles, we wish what we do to remain unshaken, so that no layperson, bishop, or cleric may obstruct or oppose our commands and thereby fall under many curses.

Therefore, since you, beloved Count Guifred, have asked us to grant you the church of Saint Martin so that you might build a monastery in it for the remission of your sins and those of your parents, and grant to that holy Church possessions from [Col. 1516C] your estates, this petition, dearest son, appears good to us. With the assent of the supreme King, we grant you the aforesaid church with all its appurtenances, confirm it by apostolic authority, and decree that it remain perpetually unshaken.

We also grant to the aforesaid church that it shall never be subject to the servitude of another; it shall always be free and exalted by apostolic privileges, and shall remain elevated in its own right forever.

Whatever possessions, estates, or boundaries, with all their appurtenances and every other thing acquired up to this time, or whatever it shall acquire perpetually—that is, estates, namely villages and churches with their appurtenances, parishes, estates, farmsteads, small holdings, cotals, cultivated or uncultivated lands, fields, [Col. 1516D] woods, vineyards, meadows, pastures for animals, yards, winepresses, waters, waterways, roads, mills, millworks with their headwaters, fisheries, saltworks, and pitch kilns—we decree that all these things, acquired or to be acquired, shall be held and possessed peacefully by the monastery of Saint Martin in the valley of Conflent, on Mount Canigou, without suffering harm from anyone’s disturbance.

We decree, moreover, that when the abbot of that monastery dies, no abbots are to be installed there by kings, counts, or any person for the sake of greed or money, or for any empty glory of favor; rather, abbots are to be elected by all the servants of God dwelling there, according to God and in accordance with the rule of Benedict the Father.

Therefore we confirm and establish henceforth that no [Col. 1517A] king, prince, margrave, count, judge, bishop, or abbot presume to inflict any force, invasion, or subjection upon that monastery or any of its possessions.

Accordingly, under invocation of divine judgment and proclamation of the prohibition of anathema, we decree that no person, great or small, of whatever order, shall ever dare by any device to violate this apostolic privilege of ours.

But if anyone—which we do not believe—disregarding our privilege attempts to break it, we bind him, unless he repents, with perpetual bonds of anathema, in the name of Almighty God, of his holy apostle Peter, and of ourselves, who act in his place.

But whoever, as a helper of this holy monastery, chooses, enriches, and loves it to the extent of his [Col. 1517B] ability, may rejoice that, through the intervention of Almighty God and filled with apostolic blessing, he will ascend from virtue to virtue.

Written by the hands of Benedict, regional notary and scrinarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of November, in the tenth indiction.

Farewell.

### VIII. Sergius IV receives the monastery of Arles under the protection of the apostolic see and exempts it from the jurisdiction of every person, including the ordinary bishop. (Year 1011.)

[COCQUELIN, *Bullarum amplissima collectio*, I, 316.]

SERGIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in the Lord, Gauzbert, the religious abbot of the venerable [Col. 1517C] monastery of Saint Mary, our Lady, the holy and perpetual Virgin, situated in the valley and district of Asperi: to you and your successors forever.

The summit of supreme apostolic dignity is recognized as shining forth with the brilliance of divine foresight when it devotes itself more earnestly to the struggle of exercising labor in the praises of God. For this reason, compelled by the proper care of pastoral solicitude for the apostolic Church, we are moved to proclaim abundantly whatever is recognized as pertaining to the stability of pious places, to confirm it by the censure of apostolic institution, and—since we read with the apostle Peter that the care of all, both clerics and laypeople, has been divinely entrusted by the Lord—to exercise his vicariate in the present ordering of the world, [Col. 1517D] protect everything, and assist all people in prosperity and adversity by apostolic authority.

Therefore we, who, although unworthy, act in his place, with God’s support, have determined henceforth to hold, defend, and protect the monastery of the aforesaid perpetual Virgin Mary under our jurisdiction and patronage. We have also determined that, adorned with the insignia of the privilege of the apostolic see, it shall remain under the jurisdiction and authority—of which we have spoken—of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, and shall not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other church.

For this reason we endeavor to comply with your own wishes. You have indeed asked us to grant and confirm by the authority of our privilege to the aforesaid monastery cells and [Col. 1518A] estates, together with the dwellings or possessions belonging to that place.

We also confirm for the aforesaid monastery the cell of Albanianus, with the two churches established there—namely the church of Saint Peter and that of Saint Michael the Archangel—with tithes, firstfruits, and offerings of the faithful, as their endowment documents are found to record. We grant or confirm the boundaries of this cell as they are set out in your royal charter.

The manses of the village of Ollarias, with their estates and possessions; also the allod of Custodia, with the church of Saint Mary, or the church of Saint Lawrence subject to it, with tithes, firstfruits, and offerings of the faithful.

At Giro, the estates belonging to that place: first, in the village of Pratis, manses with [Col. 1518B] estates, fields, vineyards, millworks or headwaters, and fisheries, cultivated or uncultivated, formerly transferred to that place by the faithful; and the villar of Cumquotus with vineyards and lands, together with the allod of Maures, Maniaches, or Madaloth, with cultivated or uncultivated lands and vineyards; and the manses of Bennatus.

We also confirm the pastures for your herds, including the summit of Vesias, as it is established that they were granted to you in royal charters.

Also the valley of Riviferrarius, which you obtained from the comital court, together with the old valley of Riviferrarius, which you obtained above and below, with the church of Saint Martin of Curtio Savini, with tithes, firstfruits, and offerings of the faithful; the cell of Saint Peter; and the churches of Saint Columba and Saint Stephen, with tithes, firstfruits, and offerings of the faithful; together with the [Col. 1518C] tithes of Frexenum; the allod of the crooked castle; the village of Cleranos or Bonabosco; and the manses of Beceda or Arlelas.

Also the baths and the villar of Cotaeleto, together with that entire old valley belonging to the same monastery, just as it was formerly granted to you by royal charters or through donations of the faithful, or as it has recently been willingly granted.

Likewise, the allod of Palandanus, with lands, vineyards, manses, mills, and headwaters. At Rivo-nigro, two manses, with the lands and vineyards belonging to those manses.

The church of Mount Auriolus, with tithes, firstfruits, payments, and offerings of the faithful, together with the allod of the aforesaid village of Mount Auriolus.

[Col. 1518D] Also the aforesaid church of Saint Michael the Archangel, with tithes, firstfruits, payments, and offerings of the faithful. We confirm to it the boundary on one side at the parish of Saint Fructuosus of Castro-camelos; on another side at the boundary of the parish of Saint John of the village of Ulmos; on the third side at the boundary of the parish of Saint Martin of Laurisione; and on the fourth side at the communal vineyard, together with the tithe of Poncio or of his sister Illiardis.

The allod of the village of Moletto or Molletello, together with the church of Saint Michael the Archangel.

By the dignity of our privilege we grant to the aforesaid church boundaries: on one side in the great valley of Ferraria, namely at the hill of Lebraria; on another side at the boundary [Col. 1519A] of the parish of Saint Peter, called Serra or Aquabula; on the third side at the boundary of Civennago; and on the fourth side in the parish of Saint Saturninus.

Whatever appears to be established within these boundaries, cultivated or uncultivated, together with the tithes and firstfruits of the aforesaid possessions and the offerings of the faithful, we grant in perpetuity for possession to these previously mentioned parishes.

We also command by apostolic authority that no bishop or person of any kind presume to build a new church for himself within the aforesaid boundaries of these two previously mentioned parishes, nor choose other clerics to perform their functions, nor establish other churches for the administration of worship; nor shall any clerical person exercise the sacred [Col. 1519B] ministry for those who appear to inhabit the aforesaid boundaries, except those who have been appointed by the hands of the abbot of the aforesaid monastery in these two parishes named above. Whoever presumes to act otherwise shall be struck by the sentence of our authority with the bond of excommunication.

Indeed, we also confirm in the aforesaid monastery all the other allods found to have been donated by the faithful of God to the aforesaid monastery: namely, the village of Tordarias with its borders; the village of Fullonica with the church of Saint Martin, with its tithes and firstfruits and the offerings of the faithful; and the villar called Kasti, with the church of Saint John, its tithes and firstfruits, and its borders.

Likewise, the allod of the village of Cassamolas, and the church of Saint Mary called Pannessiares [Col. 1519C] under the protection of Lord Count Bernard and the abbot of the aforesaid monastery, for construction and administration, together with the donations of the faithful that have been transferred there, without any reduction or deterioration.

Together with all these things, whatever the monastery henceforth appears to increase or lawfully acquire—in every respect, whatever the aforesaid monastery appears to possess or thereafter acquire—we receive entirely under the protection of the certainty of our defense.

Moreover, establishing this by apostolic censure under invocation of divine judgment, we decree that no bishop of the Church presume to impose any jurisdiction or excommunication upon the aforesaid monastery, or upon its churches or possessions.

We further command that all harmful ecclesiastical sales or exchanges [Col. 1519D] formerly made by abbots or bishops from that monastery shall, by our authority, remain altogether void and invalid, because it is written that what has once been offered to God may in no way be taken away.

We also grant the monks of that place the power, in accordance with the rule of Saint Benedict, to elect an abbot from their own congregation or from wherever they judge a suitable person to be found; and that neither they nor their clerics be obliged to attend a synod; to receive chrism from whatever place they prefer; to have their clerics ordained at whatever see they choose; and to allow every penitent, for as long as he remains there, permission to enter the church and hear whatever is said there.

All the things we have stated above are therefore [Col. 1520A] confirmed to it by us through apostolic authority.

But if anyone—which we do not believe will happen—attempts with reckless audacity to break the statutes of this privilege of ours, which we grant, let him know that, unless he repents, by the authority of Almighty God, Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, and ourselves, who act in his place, he is to be indissolubly bound with the bonds of anathema and shall recognize himself as excluded from the kingdom of God.

We choose the aforesaid monastery as tributary to us, at the rate of two bezants each year.

But whoever chooses this holy monastery, tributary to the holy see, to the extent of his ability, and proves himself an observer of our privilege, may peace and the mercy of blessing be upon him; let him know that, enriched by grace in all things, he will attain everlasting joys.

[Col. 1520B] Written by the hand of Benedict, regional notary and scrinarius of our holy Roman Church, in the month, in the tenth indiction.

Farewell.

### IX. Privilege of Pope Sergius IV for the monastery of Montmajour. (Years 1009–1012.)

[Gallia Christiana nova, I, 104.]

SERGIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

We wish it to be known to all, especially to Archbishop Amalric, Archbishop Poncio, Bishops Eldibert, Jocelin, Almerard, and Frodon, and to all the rest, both clergy and laity: greetings and apostolic blessing, etc.

Know that Abbot Archinric sent the monk Aubert to our apostolic see, so that, with our blessing, Bishop Stephen might consecrate and bless the church of Saint Mary, Saint John, Saint Peter, and Saint Benedict. Know that we grant at its consecration such a blessing and absolution that whoever comes to it as a penitent at the time of its consecration may receive the following remedy. There we remit a third part of his penance, and restore him to the Church until the end of the year; he shall have peace and permission to cut his hair. If death should occur at the end of the year, or within the year, let him remain absolved on our behalf; and if, desiring to come annually, he is unable to do so because of illness and dies meanwhile, the absolution shall remain in force for him.

Let Aldibert and Rainoard, who desire to assist in bringing this matter about within their authority for the love of God, be absolved from the penance over which they now sigh. Let them, and their people, have full license and power, insofar as they wish, to enlarge and develop both this place, newly built, and the monastery of Mont-Major, which belongs to the Roman Church, Saint Peter, and us, both in ecclesiastical privileges and in the authority they exercise, as well as in all other possessions, according to the pious request of the venerable abbot Archinric of the aforesaid place, both now and in the future, just as their father Lambert once caused to be written when he made an agreement.

Whoever does good to this place, Corteno, or Mont-Major, shall receive such a blessing as we have described. Whoever goes to this church shall go secure from all his enemies; and whoever offers it any impediment shall know that he is excommunicated and anathematized. If anyone, therefore—which we do not wish—should presumptuously attempt this, etc.

Sergius, prelate of the holy Catholic and apostolic Church. Peter, bishop; Crescentius, bishop; Peter, bishop; Gregory and Stephen, bishops.

Issued at the Lateran through the hands of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church.

### X. Pope Sergius IV rebukes Amalric, archbishop of Aix, for the mistreatment of the monastery of Mont-Major  
*(1009–1012)*

[Gallia Christiana nova, I, 63.]

**Sergius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all archbishops, bishops, dukes, marquises, and counts: greetings and apostolic blessing.**

A complaint has reached us from the most noble countess Adelaide and from the monks of Saint Peter against the sons of Nebelong—namely Rainald, William, and Lanfred—and against Amalric, archbishop of Aix, who are violently devastating the monastery of Mont-Major, which is under the authority of Saint Peter and of us. Moreover, by their power they have plundered and burned the village called Pertusus, so that it remains uninhabitable.

For this reason, by the authority of the apostles and our own, we admonish and entreat the aforesaid archbishop of Aix first to make satisfaction himself; then, together with the other archbishops and bishops of the province and the faithful Christians who live under the authority of Provence, let him summon the sons of Nebelong and admonish them to make appropriate amends for the grave injury they unjustly inflicted upon the monastery of Blessed Peter.

If they listen to you and make amends, thanks be to God. But if they despise obedience to you and to the apostolic commands, we excommunicate and curse them on behalf of God and Saint Mary, and by the authority of the blessed apostles, etc.

Moreover, I ask all of you who appear to have care for God to act just as I excommunicate: let those be bound by the chain of anathema who, by secular force, ravage and destroy without the consent of the abbot and monks, and retain the lands which we and our predecessors gave and confirmed to the aforesaid monastery.

### XI. Pope Sergius IV orders Abbot Gratian and all the inhabitants of the fortress and city of Corgnito to restore the churches of Peregrinus and Saint Michael to Abbot Guido of Farfa  
*(1009–1012)*

[Mabillon, *Annales ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, IV, 206.]

**Sergius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gratian, abbot, and to all the inhabitants of the fortress and city of Corgnito: very dear greetings with apostolic blessing.**

Our pastoral care, with Christ’s favor, is such that we recall clergy and laity who are at odds to concord. Therefore we admonish you, Abbot Gratian, and absolutely command that, according to the precept of the Rule of Saint Benedict, you humble yourself beneath Guido, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary situated at Farfa; that whatever you have unjustly done against the aforesaid monastery you promptly correct; and that you return to that abbot the churches over which you contend with him—namely, Saint Peregrinus and Saint Michael, with all their appurtenances.

If you refuse to do this, remain excluded from every priestly office. Likewise, we command all the aforesaid men, or any others who wish to offer you assistance against this command of ours, to remain outside the Church until they have corrected their actions through satisfaction.

### XII. Sergius IV grants privileges to the Church of Bamberg  
*(1009–1012)*

See the privilege for the same church under Benedict VIII, at the year 1013.

### XIII. Sergius IV confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Vincent of Vulturnum  
*(1012)*

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, VI, 390.]

**Sergius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hilary, venerable abbot of the monastery of Christ’s martyr Vincent, and, through you, to the venerable monastery and to your successors forever.**

Since great concern and care for all the Churches of God presses upon us, and since we watch lest any of them suffer loss through necessity but rather receive support for their proper benefit, it is therefore fitting that, with complete pastoral integrity of mind, we should provide for the greatest stability of those venerable places, diligently offer them assistance for their benefit, and offer to our almighty God whatever has been contributed to those venerable places for the honor of his holy name and for the praise and glory of his divine majesty. May whatever things bring the fullest mercy to that place be worthy, in our desire, of the reward of such a pious work in the heavenly strongholds.

Therefore, since you have asked us that the monastery of Blessed Vincent the Martyr, situated above the river called Vulturnus, in the Beneventan territory of the region of Samnium, together with its dependencies and monasteries, be confirmed—namely, the monastery of Blessed Peter the Apostle situated beside the river Sabbatus in Beneventan territory; also the monastery of Saint Mary, Mother of God, in the place called Locus Sanus; likewise the monastery of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ situated at Alife; and the monastery built in honor of Saint Mary in the Marsican territory, at the place called Apinianicus; further, the monastery of Saint Maurus within the county of Atina; also another monastery of Saint Mary, Mother of God, situated in the territory of Penne, at the place called Mosano; and yet another monastery consecrated in honor of Saint Mary, Mother of God, at the place called Two Basilicas; likewise another cell of Saint Mary beside the river Trinius; also the cell of Saint Sossius in Liburia; and the place called Pantano, with the whole Wald belonging to that monastery of Saint Vincent, whose boundaries are as follows:

On the first side, the old road that goes toward Duecenta, which marks the division between this land or Wald and the other land and Wald that belonged to the aforesaid monastery; then the other land of that monastery; and as the old road descends, it goes toward the pool of the aforesaid monastery, and the road itself descends between those lands and the Wald of the aforesaid monastery; then the other land of that monastery, called Tortora; then the land of the men who are neighbors there; and as it begins above the pool, it turns over the land of the same Wald and the same land of Tortora, and goes to the Pantano of the aforesaid monastery; it proceeds through that Pantano, and through the wood and marsh, as far as the cold stream. On the fourth side, the text reads uncertainly, “without the aforesaid cold stream and the aforesaid lane”—

together with the other monasteries and cells, houses and farmsteads, male and female servants residing there, and everything belonging to you and to your successors, the abbots who shall be there in their time: we grant that all these shall remain under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which, by God’s authority, we serve, and shall not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other Church.

Favoring your pious desires, therefore, and by our authority undertaking what is requested, we grant to you and to your successors, the abbots, by the license of our apostolic see, full power to summon to the aforesaid venerable monastery whatever bishop you wish, in order to confirm the churches or consecrate an abbot. Likewise, you shall have the power to arrange in due time for the ordination of subdeacons, deacons, and priests, and to complete every ecclesiastical rank there as circumstances require.

We also declare that no bishop shall thereafter summon a subdeacon, deacon, or priest from there to his council unless that person wishes it, nor shall he in any way judge or excommunicate an abbot or monk. We also will and enjoin by apostolic authority that you and your successors, the abbots appointed there in due time, immediately receive any priest or cleric from whatever Church who comes to live there, to share the brothers’ way of life, or to receive the monastic habit. You may obtain chrism and holy oil from whatever bishop you wish.

It shall always be permitted, as we have said, under our apostolic authority, for no priest of any Church to exercise any jurisdiction in the aforesaid venerable monastery; except for the apostolic see, we prohibit this entirely, so that, unless invited by the abbot of the monastery, no one shall presume to celebrate the solemnity of Mass there.

Moreover, establishing this by apostolic censure, under the invocation of divine judgment and by powerful and terrible prohibitions of anathema, we decree that no one, whatever his dignity or power, shall ever presume to interfere in this venerable monastery or in its affairs, or to take away or alienate anything from its possessions, lands, or subject churches, or anything that appears in any way to belong to them. Nor shall anyone inflict upon it any malicious injury or loss, whether in times of peace or in barbarian times. We decree that the aforesaid monastery shall remain perpetually, as has been said, in firm stability under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, in both peaceful and barbarous times.

We further promulgate and, by the authority of the blessed prince of the apostles, before God and his terrible judgment, sanction and decree for the future through this our apostolic privilege and constitution that the places which have been exchanged or granted to you by abbots of any kind in the aforesaid venerable monastery of Saint Vincent the Martyr, as well as the other possessions of those places which kings, dukes, castalds, and all Christians have given and offered to that holy place, or which shall hereafter be granted there, shall belong by firm right to the aforesaid venerable monastery and shall remain so forever.

Nor shall it be lawful, as has been said, for anyone, whether a great or a small person, to take away anything belonging to it or to the monastery; rather, in accordance with what has been established by the apostolic constitutions and privileges concerning those venerable places, this arrangement shall remain in force.

Let the same monks always have the right to elect an abbot from their own congregation. Let that abbot have the right to judge his monks, not only in the men’s monastery but also in the women’s monastery subject to him.

If anyone—which we do not wish—should wickedly presume to oppose or in any way violate these provisions established by us for the praise of God and the stability of the venerable monastery, let him be bound by the chain of anathema and condemned to be burned in eternal fire with the devil, with his most dreadful pomp, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But whoever, with pious regard, observes and in all things keeps this our apostolic constitution concerning the worship of God shall receive in abundance the grace of blessing and eternal life from our most merciful Lord God, and shall be deemed worthy to become a participant in eternal life.

Written by the hand of Benedict, regional notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of February, in the tenth indiction. Farewell.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, through the hand of Peter, by the grace of God bishop of the Church of Praeneste and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the third year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord Sergius IV, most holy pope, seated in the sacred see, in the aforesaid tenth indiction.

### XIV. Privilege of Pope Sergius IV for the monastery of Bellus Locus  
*(1012)*

[Gallia Christiana, older edition, I, 756.]

In the name of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. In the year …, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord Sergius, supreme pontiff, the fourth pope, in the most sacred see of Blessed Peter the Apostle; in his third year, in the tenth indiction, in the month of April, on the fourteenth day.

Since the human mind is always recognized to be occupied with thought, and the mind of each person wanders and runs here and there because of various causes and cares, and cannot express everything in speech or retain in memory everything that happens, it has therefore been discovered by prudent and free men skilled in letters that we should write down in letters what we investigate in our minds.

Therefore I, Sergius, by divine grace fourth pontiff of the holy Roman Church, servant of the servants of God, wish it to be known to the whole people of the Church, especially to our successors and to the sacred inhabitants of the Lateran palace, how a certain Hugh, venerable archbishop of the holy Church of Tours, came lamenting to our apostolic see concerning the monastery which Fulco had newly built and offered to Blessed Peter the Apostle and to us as a remedy for his soul. Hugh brought his complaint before us and began to set out the matter, saying:

“O lord pope, why do you wish to take from us the consecration of the monastery which Fulco offered to you, and which is known to have been founded within the parish of our archbishopric?”

When I had heard such words from Archbishop Hugh, we immediately summoned him into our presence. Cardinals who were bishops, priests, deacons, and subdeacons were present, together with not a few members of the clergy, Roman judges, and many noble men. Their names are written below in their own hands, and we now make them known in order:

The archbishop of the Church of Lyon; Peter, bishop of Praeneste; Benedict, bishop of Porto; John, also called the bishop of the Church of Labicum; Gregory, bishop of Silva Candida; Peter, bishop of the Church of Viperna; Amicus, cardinal priest; Stephen, cardinal priest; John, cardinal priest; Crescentius, cardinal priest; John, archdeacon of the holy Roman Church; Abbo, deacon; John, deacon, surnamed de Beno, a craftsman; Peter, deacon, from Chana by origin; Crescentius, subdeacon and alms-officer; Gregory, chief of the defenders; Peter, son of another Peter, one of the *dativi* judges; Stephen called “of Bernard”; Peter of Breperato; Berard, son of Crescentius, at Puteum Proba [reading uncertain]; Franco the chamberlain; another Franco, son of Deodatus; and many others.

Before all these, Benedict, bishop of Porto, rose and addressed the said archbishop, beginning as follows:

“Most holy Father and lord, to whom God has entrusted supreme power and governance of the entire most holy Church: your holiness is being addressed by this archbishop, who laments and appeals to the Church and asks for law and justice. Fulco built the venerable monastery within his parish and offered it to you. If it pleases you, let the archbishop himself consecrate it; for, according to the provisions of the canons and Justinian’s law, the consecration cannot in any way be taken away from the archbishop’s jurisdiction.”

Then Peter, by God’s will one of our judges and acting in our place, replied:

“Certainly the monastery which Fulco built was his own hereditary property, and he offered it to the Church of the blessed apostle Peter and to the power and dominion of our lord, together with the monastery and its consecration, forever, for the sake of his soul. Show us how it ought to be taken from his dominion, and make this known to us. I know only this: whose the inheritance is, his also is the consecration.”

When Archbishop Hugh saw that he had no true or just case, and could not show how we ought to lose the monastery, he immediately began to confess and say that he had sinned and erred, and that he had gravely offended against almighty God and our holy Roman Church by unjustly and without any reason bringing a lawsuit against us concerning it.

Then, from the hand of Gregory, bishop of Silva Candida, he received a staff. Holding that staff in his hand, with one voice and devout mind, in the sight of all who were present, he renounced to us the monastery itself, with its consecration and everything belonging to it, just as Fulco had offered it to Blessed Peter the Apostle, to us, and to our apostolic see for the sake of his soul. He affirmed that it had thereby been handed over to us forever.

When these things had been completed publicly, he established and firmly stabilized them for perpetual observance, declaring:

“If from this time forward any document or privilege should appear to have been made by me or by my successors, by anyone whatsoever, whether priest or layman, concerning the aforesaid monastery, its consecration, or its appurtenances, let everyone know that it was made in part through fear. And if—God forbid—the document which I have mentioned should appear to have been made by us, I wish it to be invalid and condemned. I affirm that this brief record of renunciation shall remain firm and stable for all time.”

Thereafter we sent there one of our fellow bishops, namely Peter of the Church of Viperna, and ordered that the monastery be consecrated in our place. Whoever should presumptuously attempt anything against the decree of this constitution of ours shall be held under the curse of anathema until, repenting and returning to make satisfaction to the aforesaid Church of ours, he returns to obedience to our command.

But whoever proves in all things to be an observant guardian of this record and brief of renunciation of ours shall receive in abundance the grace of blessing from our most merciful Lord God and shall be deemed worthy to become a participant in eternal life.

We ordered this brief document of renunciation to be written by Benedict, notary and archivist of our apostolic see, for future remembrance and testimony, and ordered it sealed with our seal, in the month and indiction written above, the tenth.

The sign of me, Sergius, prelate of the holy Catholic and apostolic Roman Church.

Peter, bishop of the holy Church of Praeneste and librarian of the sacred palace.

Benedict, bishop of Porto.

Gregory, bishop of Silva Candida.

Homo, bishop of the Church of Labicum.

Peter, bishop of the holy Church of Viperna.

Peter, *defensor* and *dativus* judge.

Peter, *dativus* judge.

Another Peter, *dativus* judge.

Richard, noble man.

Stephen of Bernard.

Franco Deodatus, lord’s chamberlain.

Berard, son of Crescentius “at the well,” the examiner.

John, archdeacon of the holy Roman Church.

Abbo, deacon of the holy Roman Church.

John, deacon of the holy Roman Church.

Peter, deacon.

Crescentius, subdeacon.

Benedict, deacon.

Amicus, cardinal.

Stephen, John, and Crescentius, cardinals of the holy Roman Church.

John, prior of the subdeacons.

Ramerius, deacon.

I, Benedict, archivist and writer of the holy Roman Church, completed and finished this record of brief renunciation after the subscriptions of all those mentioned above had been made.

### XV. Privilege of Pope Sergius IV for the monastery of Bellus Locus  
*(1012)*

[Gallia Christiana, older edition, IV, 150.]

**Sergius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all faithful bishops of the holy Church of God.**

We wish you to know that a certain count named Fulco built a monastery on his own hereditary land, and gave it to Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, submitting it forever by right to our gift and to that of our successors. Since I was unable to consecrate that place personally, I sent there one of our suffragan bishops to consecrate and bless the monastery in the place of Saint Peter and of us.

We have heard that many people envy that place. Therefore, once the blessing has been completed, if anyone should wish to inflict any accusation or trouble upon those who serve this place or belong to it, or if any bishop or archbishop should wish to excommunicate or curse them, let those persons, by the authority of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom Christ granted the power of binding and loosing, of all the saints, and by our authority and that of all the bishops and archbishops of the holy Roman Church, be excommunicated, anathematized, or cursed, etc.

But let that place, all those who serve it, and its helpers or friends be, by the same authority stated above, absolved and blessed. Let them never fear excommunication or cursing from that bishop—or even from that archbishop—who may live upon the earth.

### XVI. Sergius IV confirms the metropolitan rights of Michael, archbishop of Salerno  
*(1012)*

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, VII, 377.]

**Sergius, servant of the servants of God, to our beloved and deservedly honorable brother Michael, archbishop of the see of Salerno.**

Since we ought to remember the benefit you have bestowed upon us, and since we recognize that your fraternal reverence toward us and toward the holy Roman Church has been especially abundant, we have therefore decided, deservedly and justly, to repay your charity with a corresponding act of love, so that it may be clear to all Christ’s faithful that whoever diligently honors the vicar of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, is worthy of immense honor.

With the consent and will of our brothers, we grant and confirm you, Michael, our fellow brother, in the archiepiscopal order, just as formerly Amatus was granted the archbishopric of your see of Salerno by our predecessors. Thus, by our authority, may you peacefully possess and diligently guard it.

We have decreed that this shall be done in such a way that you and your successors shall forever have the license and power to ordain and consecrate bishops in the places subject to you: namely, the bishopric of Paestum, with its parishes and dependencies; the bishopric of Conza, with its parishes and dependencies; likewise the bishopric of Acerenza; also the bishopric of Bisignano; the bishopric of Malvito; and the bishopric of Cosenza, with all their parishes and dependencies, just as is contained in the earlier use of your pallium, in the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and of Blessed Matthew the Apostle and Evangelist, whose most sacred body you possess and which has been granted to you and to your successors.

After your departure, your successors shall come to the apostolic see to receive, according to the decrees, the use of the pallium and their consecration. If our successors should refuse to consecrate them, your holy Church shall have permission to have them consecrated by your suffragan bishops. Our successors shall not thereafter have the power to consecrate any bishop in any of the bishoprics subject to you, since this has already been granted to you.

Whoever presumes to violate this concession and command of ours shall be bound forever by the chain of anathema, and this concession of ours shall remain stable and firm forever.

Written by the hand of John, archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of June, in the tenth indiction. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, through the hand of Gregory, bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the third year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord Sergius IV, pope, seated in the most sacred see of Blessed Peter the Apostle; in the tenth indiction, in the month of June, on the sixteenth day.

## In the year of the Lord 1015. Henry, bishop of Parma

[Col. 1529]

[Note: Henry was alive around the year 1015; for he attended the Roman synod of that year. This sermon, however, comes from an ancient Vatican manuscript.]

### Sermon of Henry on the Lord’s Pascha

(Edited by Mai, *Scriptorum veterum collectio nova*, VII, 271.)

The day of our redemption, dearest ones, must be honored and commemorated with so much greater devotion as we recognize that it was dedicated to the joy of our salvation. Although the days of the other festivals were established for our joy and progress, this day, which contains the mystery of our resurrection, holds primacy by the privilege of salvation and exultation. As the Psalmist says: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it.”

This, I say, is the day on which joy is granted to the living and refreshment to the dead. This, I say, is the day which the Lord specially claimed for himself and dedicated by the price of his blood and the glory of his resurrection. For he died and rose again for us, never again to die, according to the statement of the apostle Peter, so that together with him we might rise from vices to virtue. “Christ,” he says, “having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over him.”

Therefore, brothers, we must rejoice with the greatest joy on this day; by the Lord’s favor we must exult spiritually on the day when Christ our head, having conquered death, rose again and, by rising, showed us the pattern of our resurrection. The Apostle bears witness when he says: “If we have been planted” [thus in the manuscript] “in the likeness of his death, we shall also be in the likeness of his resurrection.”

But in order now to reveal to you the mysteries of this solemnity, let us, so to speak, enter through the gates of the Old Testament and learn from where this celebration first arose, so that, knowing it well, we may love it more and observe it with greater reverence. Whatever may be spiritually disclosed here and ought to be received, we shall explain for your benefit.

When the Israelite people were freed from Egyptian slavery through remarkable signs, they were commanded to celebrate the Passover annually, lest posterity, as time passed, should fail to know the power of so many great miracles and, not knowing it, should celebrate it without any reverence of honor. There also, the lamb which had been their Passover was commanded to be sacrificed, so that that symbolic people might eat it according to an unfamiliar manner of eating, as the Lord demonstrated to them through Moses:

“Gird your loins, have sandals on your feet, and eat in haste.”

But what they observed according to the death-dealing letter of the law, we must observe in the grace of the life-giving Spirit. For “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.”

What, then, do we understand by Egypt except darkness? And what do we call Passover except passage? Therefore, although we take *phase*, from which *pascha* comes, from another language, we rightly celebrate Passover when we pass from the darkness of the old law to the light of the new grace and exchange the prisons of hell for the heavenly dwelling. The apostle Peter bears witness when he says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.” And shortly afterward he admonishes us, saying: “You are a people of acquisition; proclaim the virtues of him who called you into his marvelous light.”

This is also well demonstrated when the evangelist Luke says:

“A certain man, going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers. After they had stripped and wounded him, they finally left him half-dead. But a Samaritan compassionately received him, and he obtained the grace of life and salvation.”

This man is understood as the first-created human being, or rather the human race. Jericho expresses decline; Jerusalem is named as the vision of peace; the robbers signify evil spirits.

This man truly descended from Jerusalem when, in the paradise of his Lord, he despised the Lord’s commands. As he proceeded toward Jericho, he rightly encountered evil spirits, because, having abandoned eternal things and attending only to things subject to decline, he failed entirely to understand that destruction was being prepared for him.

Therefore, deservedly, he was stripped of the garment of immortality; deservedly, he was afflicted with the wounds of the many miseries in which he is here entangled; finally, deservedly, he was trampled half-dead on the road of this world, so that everyone might henceforth learn to desire eternal things and strive with every care to avoid transitory things.

And because the priest and Levite, the fathers of the Old Testament, were subject to the same wounds and were overcome by them, they could offer no remedy to the wounded man. For no one who is entangled in his own chains should be considered capable of freeing others from theirs. Thus the Lord says: “If a blind man leads a blind man, both fall into a pit.”

What then? Is he to be abandoned in the wounds that have been inflicted and in the danger of impending death? Far from it! The Samaritan is present—interpreted as “guardian,” namely, the Lord Jesus Christ—who, according to the apostle Peter, was not darkened by the shadows of any sin: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth.” He was so moved with compassion by the man’s calamities that, by dying, he rescued him from darkness and the shadow of death, and, by rising, joined him to life and everlasting light.

But let us see what follows:

“Gird your loins, have sandals on your feet, and eat in haste.”

By the loins, dearest ones, carnal pleasures are understood. Those who eat the Passover—that is, those who are nourished by the flesh of the spotless Lamb, namely the Lord Jesus Christ—are instructed to gird them, because those who rightly desire to celebrate the glory of the Lord’s resurrection must restrain impure desires and harmful inclinations of the flesh.

They must have sandals on their feet, so that they may be able to guard their lives by the examples of those who came before them. We do not doubt that sandals are made from the skins of the dead; we unquestionably wear them on our feet when we fortify the steps of our lives with the examples of the holy Fathers.

They are to hold a staff in their hands, because, just as we explore the paths of the blind night by means of a staff, so we may appropriately understand discernment by the staff. We hold a staff in our hands when, by the staff of discernment, we guard ourselves against the obstacles of vices.

Therefore, brothers, gird your loins; restrain the pleasures of the flesh. Guard the way of your life by the example of the holy Fathers and by the staff of discernment. Pass hastily from earthly things to heavenly things, so that you may behold Jesus in Galilee, which is interpreted as “migration.”

For we shall be deemed worthy to enjoy fellowship in his resurrection if we migrate from the corruption of vices to works of virtue.

That the Lord’s resurrection is announced to the disciples by a woman plainly shows that, just as through the female sex death was imposed upon the human race, so through it the resurrection of blessed life was announced. Through the one by whom death was prepared for the world at the prompting of the devil, life was revealed from the tomb at the prompting of an angel. And by the hand through which humanity received the cup of death, through that same hand it received the antidote of life.

Let us therefore sing praises on earth to him who descended from heaven for our redemption: Jesus Christ, our Lord.

## In the year of the Lord 1016. Bruno, bishop of Langres

### Historical notice

(*Literary History of France*, VII, 232.)

Bruno, bishop of Langres, left posterity a few works from his pen. He was of high birth and a close relative of King Lothair (Spic. vol. I, p. 429). His father, Ragenald, lord of Roucy, bore the title of count of Reims; and his mother was the daughter of Gerberge and Gislebert, duke of Lorraine (Gall. Chr. nov. vol. IV, p. 548). Bruno was first a canon of Reims (Spic. ibid.), where he studied under Gerbert, who at that time directed the schools of that church. In 981, when he was still only twenty-four years old, he was ordained bishop of Langres by Bouchard, archbishop of Lyon (HUG. FL. Chr. p. 157). From then on he devoted all his care to fulfilling the duties of a good shepherd. He discharged them so worthily that he was inferior to no other bishop of that see, and deserved to be regarded as an excellent prelate, *praesul eximius*. One of his first concerns was to restore, in both spiritual and temporal matters, the abbey of Saint-Bénigne at Dijon, where he introduced the reform of Cluny and appointed as abbot Blessed William, who later became the reformer of several other monasteries. The authors disagree about the year of this great bishop’s death (Gall. Chr. ibid., p. 552). But one may rely on the *Chronicle of Saint-Bénigne* (Spic. I, 456), which places it on 31 January 1016, after thirty-five years of episcopacy. The necrology of the same abbey (LAB. *Biblioth. nov.* I, p. 657), which praises Bruno in a few words, adds that he was then in the sixtieth year of his age and the thirty-sixth year after his ordination, confirming the chronicler’s calculation. Only imperfectly do we possess the few writings of Bruno.

1. Dom Martène and Dom Durand (*Anec.* vol. I, p. 107) have given us the beginning of one of his letters, addressed to Heldric or Hildric, abbot of Saint-Germain of Auxerre, and to his entire community. The fragment is so short that it is impossible to guess what the subject of the letter was. The manuscript of the priests of the Oratory at Troyes, from which it was taken, contained no more. The following letter makes one regret that this one has not survived in full. In it Bruno uses this formula, which later became so common: “By the grace of God, bishop.”

2. The same editors published, among the monuments of the tenth century, from a manuscript of the abbey of Saint-Allire in Auvergne, another lengthy letter. It bears no author’s name; but the characteristics of its script show that a bishop of Langres is speaking in it. Indeed, it is addressed not only to the young clerics being educated in the church of Saint-Mammès, under whose invocation the cathedral of Langres is dedicated, but the author also addresses those responsible for instructing them and forming them in piety. From all this there results a reasonable probability that it belongs to Bishop Bruno.

After giving some general advice, the author comes to his principal aim: the care these young men ought to take to have frequent recourse to the remedy of the sacrament of Penance. He urges them to this by every kind of motive, with fatherly tenderness and an unction capable of moving hearts. Thus the letter could bear the title *On the Confession of Clerics*, just as we already have a treatise *On the Singularity of Clerics*. The latter was not unknown to the author of the letter, who seems to have taken it as a model in some passages and who in fact imitated it by employing only the authority of Scripture and reasoning. There is no work of piety from those times that surpasses this one.

Bruno wrote several other letters that have not come down to us, as appears expressly from the two addressed to him by Pope Benedict VIII. A charter of his survives, dated 1008, by which he confirms the powers possessed by the monks of Saint-Bénigne to preach and hear the confessions of the faithful (Gall. Chr. IV, Appendix, p. 138).

[Col. 1533]

## Letter of Bruno of Langres to Heldric or Hildric, abbot of Saint-Germain of Auxerre. Fragment

(Edited by D. Martène, *Thes. Anecd.* I, 107, from a manuscript of the Oratory at Troyes.)

[Col. 1533A] Bruno, bishop of the people of Langres by the grace of God, sends to the venerable Heldric and to the entire congregation entrusted to him the practice of true religion and the benefit of eternal blessedness.

I speak, unlearned in philosophy and entangled in the vanities of the world, [to those] freed from worldly allurements by contemplation of heavenly things [syntax uncertain] [Col. 1534A]. Let equity therefore flourish, and let it not be blamed as frivolity that our letter speaks familiarly and without arrangement. The authority of our associated office gives me the boldness to speak, as does friendship, within which—as Boethius testifies—it is not unbecoming for an uninstructed person to chatter among his own people. [lacuna]

[Col. 1533]

## Letter of Bruno of Langres to the Clerics of Langres: On the Constant Confession of Sins

(Edited by D. Martène, *Thes. Anecd.* I, 79, from a manuscript of Saint-Allire of Clermont.)

[Col. 1533B] To the dearly beloved sons in Christ, the young men of good hope who appear to serve the Lord Jesus Christ in the church of Saint Mammès, the glorious martyr of Christ, and who are instructed by ecclesiastical teachers in the house of God: eternal prosperity and salvation in Christ God.

Desiring, dearest sons, that you should advance in the salvation of your souls, I have therefore endeavored to send you, with fatherly affection, certain admonitions in gentle speech, so that through them you may merit to possess the prosperity of the present life and, by God’s mercy, the eternal blessedness of the life to come, and, instructed in his service, bring the years of your fragile condition to the perfect day of old age. You, holy Fathers and lights of this fraternal community [lacuna] [Col. 1534B], I beg you, in all goodness, to admonish them—that is, your pupils—to learn diligently what pleases God and pertains to the salvation of their souls, so that from their progress and prosperity you may have an everlasting reward with God. Exhort them to serve God soberly, chastely, modestly, and with all humility and obedience, in good conduct, holy behavior, and religious chastity, and especially concerning the confession of their sins, because many are the devil’s snares against young men in carnal desire and the other vices of youth. Yet, by God’s gift, the devil gains nothing from his wickedness if the young wish to make their confession pure [Col. 1535A] and perform worthy works of repentance—that is, if they do not add wounds to wounds or reopen wounds that have been healed. For the remedy of repentance is salutary: not to commit again what requires repentance [Note: [Col. 1535D] F reads *poenitenda*, “things requiring repentance”]. For it is written: “God has given those who repent a share in righteousness.” Therefore, repentant one, confess your own crimes; bring forth what is hidden in your wickedness. God knows what you have done in secret; if your tongue does not speak of it, your conscience will not be able to conceal it. In vain, fearing punishment, do you hide your crimes between your walls: everything you think hidden is open to God; and although you may escape human eyes in your sins, nevertheless nothing you have done in secret can escape God’s sight. If through confession you disclose your sins [Note: [Col. 1536D] “If you disclose your sins through confession,” or something similar, is missing.] before you experience the judge’s anger, believe me, everything will be pardonable, if you are not ashamed to confess and take care to cleanse yourself through repentance [Col. 1535B], as the Psalmist says: “I said, ‘My injustices to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Psalm 31:5) [the printed text is elliptical].

The Lord expects from us the sacrifice of confession, so that he may grant us the delightful gift of forgiveness—he who wishes all people to be saved and no one to perish. Scripture says this in another place: “On whatever day the sinner confesses, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezekiel 21:28). O singular benefit of the most merciful Judge! O great and secure treasures of divine compassion! For this reason he wishes to receive the gift of confession from sinners, so that he may find nothing that he ought to punish. Let us not be ungrateful for so great a kindness shown by our Redeemer, who wishes rather to forgive than to punish, rather to save than to destroy. What is not punished in a servant is gained for the Lord, and great benefit is conferred upon the author if what is assigned to punishment is remitted for forgiveness. He who is ready to show mercy does not desire vengeance, as he himself says through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live” (Ezekiel 33:11). Behold the true author of life, who does not desire the death of the sinner but the life of the one who turns back. Hence the Truth himself says in the Gospel: “There will be joy in heaven before your Father and his angels over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:10); and in the prophet: “You yourself first declare your injustices, so that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43:26).

Behold the gracious giver of forgiveness, who grants the joy of eternity in exchange for temporal mourning, as he himself says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” [Col. 1535D] (Matthew 5:5). And in another place: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11). For, as we said, he says: “First declare your injustices, so that you may be justified and not condemned,” so that the reward of repentance, not the punishment of sins, may remain in you.

Does God, as though ignorant, urge us to confess sins that he knew before they were committed, whose providence reveals all hidden things? You will be able to obtain the perfect benefit of healing if you do not conceal from the physician the wounds of your conscience. For I think that unless the physician is summoned, the sick person is not cured. Your confession is the medicine of your wounds and the surest assistance of your salvation. [Col. 1536A] The sick man seeks medicine, though he often labors in uncertain toil over the sick person. But God heals without toil and provides remedies without delay, if repentance written in devotion with tears is read in the ears of his mercy. No one restores you, O man, better than the one who made you; nor does anyone heal except the one who scourges and cures. For he alone knows the frailty of your work, and he waits only for you to confess; there will be no delay in your healing. Through the prophet Ezekiel he says: “When you have turned back and groaned, then you shall be saved.”

The most kindly Judge gives us the opportunity to heal ourselves of our sins before the priest of God, so that the devil may not accuse us again before Christ the Judge concerning them. For he wishes us to be forgiven, lest we be punished in the future. Therefore, when the merciful Father sees us condemn our sins through repentance [Col. 1536B], he rejoices to show mercy and desires to exercise his proper office of mercy toward the penitent, as he testifies through the prophet Isaiah: “I am he who blots out your iniquities” (Isaiah 43:25). And again: “Turn back to the Lord your God, for he is merciful and gracious, patient and rich in mercy” (Exodus 34:6).

Knowing this, blessed David says: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not conceal my iniquities” (Psalm 31:6). Conversely, if someone denies the sin he has committed, he heaps up the penalties of his guilt, because obstinacy is punished for the denial of crime. But perhaps you say: “The greatness of my sins terrifies me.” On the contrary, sinner, you must apply yourself all the more diligently to the medicine of confession, lest you perish in the decay of your wounds. If you are ashamed to open them to the physician, you multiply the pains of the ulcers. The abundance of divine clemency can in no way be overcome by the number of your sins.

“Do not delay from day to day,” Scripture says, “to turn back,” because you do not know what the coming day may bring. For as the final day finds you, so you will be judged; and God did not wish you to know that day in advance, so that you might always be ready. Prepare yourself to stand before the Judge as you desire to stand, while you have time to work.
