Be a devout merchant: purchase for yourself the kingdom of God through the profits of repentance, remembering the Lord’s words: “Repent, for the kingdom of God will draw near to you” (Matthew 4:17). For your sake, O living man, God became man in order to redeem you. He handed himself over to death in order to save you for life.

[Col. 1536D] Why do you lie in the death of crimes? Rise and say: “Father, I have sinned against heaven.” Bring to yourself a faithful witness to your repentance. You wish to have clean clothing; why do you not much more seek to have a clean soul? You do not wish to appear dirty before human beings; why do you not much more fear appearing soiled by sins before God? Wash yourself in the fountain of tears, lest anything in you offend the eyes of that Majesty.

Who, I ask, when he falls does not seek to rise? Who, when he becomes ill, does not desire to recover? Who, when in danger, does not hope to escape? Later you will regret your delay, if you do not consider what benefits your soul toward salvation. Rise, son, [Col. 1537A] rise; appease through repentance the Father whom you offended by crime. Confess your fault, so that you may be healed by the physician. Be concerned for your own salvation. If you yourself do not care for yourself, who can help you toward salvation, or who will be faithful to you if you prove yourself unfaithful to yourself?

It is great unfaithfulness not to care for your salvation and not to resurrect yourself through repentance when you are dying in sins. The farther you have withdrawn from God because of the greatness of your crimes, the more vigorously you should strive to draw near through repentance. The merciful Father is ready to receive you, if you do not delay in returning.

Conversion seems harsh to you, because it means abandoning the desires of the flesh; but far harsher is the condition of burning in eternal flames and, for a brief period of lust, being handed over to everlasting punishments. How many of those now assigned to infernal torments would have wished to turn back, if time for turning back had been granted them? All the hardships of this world appear light, and in a certain sense pleasant, in comparison with infernal punishments.

You served the devil in lust; serve Christ in chastity. Consider the end of each. Lust, that is, sends a person into the flames; will chastity joined to charity not lead him into the kingdom of God? Return to the road from which you strayed. The body is afflicted by fasts, but the soul’s beauty is restored. Let the body’s clothing be humble, but this itself is the chief adornment of holiness. Constant vigils in prayers and the praise of God are an imitation of the angelic life. Little food is nourishment for the soul.

If you have the means, extend your hand to the poor, because the poor person’s hand is Christ’s treasury; nor will you be able justly to excuse yourself from the work of mercy, since the reward of a cup of cold water will be everlasting. To visit the sick, console the sorrowful, welcome guests, and refresh those suffering from hunger or thirst is possession of the kingdom of God in heaven, as it is read in the Gospel. In the performance of such works, son, forgiveness of sins is obtained, and in addition they provide entry into everlasting blessedness.

Do not be of a degenerate spirit. You were consecrated in baptism as a son of God, but so exalted a nobility can be preserved only by great dignity of conduct. The heavenly Father—indeed, the Lord of all—will disdain to have sinful subjects as sons. Shake from your neck the yoke of diabolical captivity. Return to the compassion of your Father’s love; return to the Lord, son, return, and rise from death to life, and be restored from being lost [Col. 1537D]. The good Shepherd seeks the wandering sheep, rejoices more over the one found than over the one previously lost, and carries it back on his shoulders amid the angelic choirs.

Observe the most merciful judgment of the Lord, who says: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” The Lord therefore calls sinners to repentance because he wishes rather to save than to condemn, and wishes us to rejoice with the saints more than to be punished with the devil. He calls us through himself; he calls us through the holy Scriptures; he also calls us through Catholic teachers, so that we may return to him, because he is ready [Col. 1538A] to receive us if we are not sluggish in coming to him.

We have heard the blessed evangelist John urging us to repentance, saying in his Epistle: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just, so that he may forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity” (1 John 1:8). If no one is without sin, who is there who does not need repentance, which can scarcely become fruitful without confession?

Let us consider the sentence of the blessed apostle James: “Confess your sins to one another” (James 5:16). Let us remember that our Redeemer preferred the confessing sinful tax collector to the Pharisee who praised himself for his own righteousness. Our Creator knows the frailty of our nature; therefore he has provided the medicines of repentance for our wounds [Col. 1538B]. Let us say with the prophet: “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed” (Jeremiah 17:14). Likewise: “Lord, heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Psalm 40:5).

Therefore, dearest sons, hasten to the medicine of confession; open your wounds in confession, so that you may be able to complete the medicines of salvation within yourselves. The days of this life pass away, and it is uncertain for each of us when dust will return to dust and the spirit return to the Lord who gave it, so that it may be judged according to its works. Then the soul will hear whatever it did here in secret while joined to the flesh, if now you are ashamed to confess your sins and amend them through repentance. The malicious accuser will stand against it—the one who once suggested that it sin—if we neglect to come beforehand into the presence of the Judge through confession. For whatever we humbly confess among our sins, the devil will have no power to bring against us at that fearsome judgment of our life.

Now act, young men, youths, and boys: free yourselves from diabolical servitude through repentance and turn to the most merciful compassion of almighty God. Do not lose the joys of heaven and the blessedness of the eternal kingdom amid the angelic choirs through the desires of your flesh. Rather, strengthen yourselves and fight manfully against your adversary, so that you may happily deserve to be crowned with God’s saints and possess everlasting glory with them.

And you, most holy teachers and Fathers of this household, teach your sons to live piously, soberly, and chastely before the Lord, in all humility, obedience, and holiness; teach them to make a pure confession of their sins to Christ’s priests and to wash away the stains of carnal lust with the tears of repentance, without repeating them, because later wounds are worse than the earlier ones. Know that you yourselves will have an eternal reward from God for the salvation of your sons, so that for those whose ministries you use on earth you may receive an everlasting recompense in heaven. Amen.

[Col. 1539]

## Charter of Bruno of Langres, granting certain things to the monastery of Bèze

(*Gall. Christ.*, IV, Appendix, p. 138.)

[Col. 1539A] I, Bruno, bishop of the people of Langres, considering that the negligence of my office would fall upon the condemnation of my soul, have, according to the measure of my understanding, labored to establish administrators for the churches of the Lord who, by disseminating in them the talent of the divine Word and gaining profit from it together with me for the Lord Jesus Christ, might be enriched by the reward of eternal life.

Therefore I wished the most religious man, Lord William, abbot, to preside over the church of Bèze. While he was arranging everything there according to rule and religion, recognizing that his own resources were insufficient in certain respects, he asked the church of Langres that something be contributed to the church of Bèze for the provision of lights.

Accordingly, recognizing that the petition of this man of the Lord ought not to be opposed, I decided, with the counsel of the entire chapter of Langres, that from the churches both beyond and within six leagues of Bèze [Col. 1539B], at the time of the Rogations, all men and women should come with offerings to the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

I also considered carefully that, since at the same time they ought to come to Langres, some, delayed by the length of the journey, others by bodily weakness or by certain other circumstances, were deprived of the nourishment of the Lord’s word and the remission of sins that they ought to receive there [Col. 1540A]. Let them therefore come at the appointed time and, asking pardon for their sins, be admonished concerning the salvation of their souls by those whose tongues have been made the keys of heaven—that is, by the monks serving God there. After absolution has been given and a blessing bestowed, let them return joyfully in peace, and so forth.

And so that this may remain unshaken through the ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and have asked that it be confirmed by many others.

Sign of Bruno, bishop. Sign of William, abbot. Sign of Lambert, provost. Sign of Gerald, archdeacon. Sign of Theuderic, archdeacon. Sign of Bruno, archdeacon. Sign of Theuderic, archdeacon. Sign of Theudo, archchaplain. Sign of Wido, archdeacon. Sign of Amelius. Sign of Wido, priest. Sign of Girald, subdeacon. Sign of Nivard. Sign of Gocelin, and of many others [Col. 1540B]. I, Airard, chancellor, wrote this and, together with the others, served as its approver and confirmer.

This was enacted in the year 1008 from the Incarnation, in the sixth indiction, with epact XI and concurrent IV, during the reign of King Robert and while Lord Bruno held the see of Langres.

## In the Year of the Lord 1023. Arnulf, Archbishop of Reims

[Col. 1539]

## Historical Notice

(Dom Marlot, *History of the Metropolitan Church of Reims*, vol. II, p. 39.)

[Col. 1539C] Ambition stirred the minds of many in their quest to obtain the archbishopric of Reims. Some prepared their way to it with gifts; Gerbert boasted that Adalbero had chosen him as his successor, with the vote of the entire clergy, the support of all the bishops, and the suffrage of certain soldiers. But Hugh, finding an opportunity to win the friendship of Prince Arnulf, who was of royal descent, acted with the authority he possessed, in the hope of securing peace, so that the young man might be invested with the episcopal dignity. As soon as Arnulf was informed of this by Adalbero of Laon, who had come to the king’s camp, he was soon reconciled with Hugh.

Arnulf, formerly a canon of the church of Laon, was not Lothair’s brother [Col. 1540C], as the Continuator of Aimo writes, but his natural son and the nephew of Charles, duke of Lorraine. Bishop Bruno of Langres, speaking in the Acts of the Council of Saint-Basle about Gilbert, son of Count Reginald, calls him his only brother and Count Guy of Soissons his cousin. From this it follows that Lothair first married Reginald’s sister; afterward, when the king repudiated her, she married Theobald of Montaigu. When that marriage was dissolved, Arnulf, who had been born to him, was regarded as the king’s natural son, together with a certain Richard, who enjoys the title of “brother” in the synodal acts. Whatever the truth may be, Hugh’s purpose in this election was to bind the prince to himself, since otherwise he could have become an obstacle to the beginnings of his new rule [Col. 1541A].

Before assuming the episcopal burden, Arnulf swore an oath of clientage or fidelity to Kings Hugh and Robert; as was customary, he confirmed it with his own hand and seal.

Once inaugurated at Reims, Arnulf immediately turned his attention to securing friends from every quarter. Knowing the goodwill that Exbertus of Trier had always shown toward his predecessor, Adalbero of blessed memory, he judged himself safer if, amid the turmoil of divided kingdoms and the novelty of his appointment, he preserved an unbreakable friendship with him.

Meanwhile, Charles was hiding at Laon like a snail in its shell. Since no alliance or truce could ease his resentment, he ravaged the whole region like the most hostile of enemies, seeking to recover his ancestral kingdom by force or deceit. First he treacherously seized Montaigu in the district of Laon; then, roaming through the lands of Soissons and Reims, he devastated everything with plunder, slaughter, and fire.

It is also reported that Arnulf the archbishop summoned Charles to Reims. Taking pity on the fate of his uncle, he considered how he might hand the city over to him. Since he had previously used the services of the priest Adalger, he reached an agreement with him again, giving him the keys of the city gates so that he might open them immediately when the armed duke arrived. This was done.

Accordingly, Charles entered the city through the opened gate, according to the agreement, and handed it over to his soldiers to plunder. He profaned God’s sanctuary and took captive the clergy and people together with the archbishop. Since there was considerable suspicion that the city had been handed over to Charles at the archbishop’s command, Arnulf, in order to remove this accusation from himself, pronounced the severest sentence of anathema against all who had plundered the city.

When King Hugh was informed of everything that had happened—for rumor had spread against Arnulf concerning the betrayal of the city of Reims [Col. 1541C]—and judged that there was no time for delay, he decided to subject him to synodal judgment so that he might pay the penalty for his infidelity. Since he knew that this could not properly be done without consulting the Apostolic See, to which episcopal judgments must be referred, he himself sent letters through messengers to Pope John. He also arranged for others to be written by the bishops of the province of Reims, asking that the same pontiff pronounce a sentence of condemnation against Arnulf for his notorious betrayal and for the other crimes laid against him.

At the same time, ambassadors were sent to Rome by Count Heribert, the father-in-law of Prince Charles. They perhaps arrived sooner and forestalled the pontiff with gifts—if Gerbert is to be believed in a matter concerning his own cause. Meanwhile, the king’s and the bishops’ ambassadors, having been wearied for three days before the palace doors and not admitted, were forced to return to Gaul with their business unfinished.

When they reported that they had returned from the Roman pontiff without being heard, it was understood, as though from that silence, that the power of judgment had devolved upon the bishops of France. Accordingly, both the king and the bishops summoned a council at Reims. Arnulf was repeatedly called to it; but while he excused himself on the ground that he was being held in chains at Laon by King Charles, the following occurred: through the betrayal of Azelin, bishop of Laon, the same city, together with Arnulf and Charles who were in it, was captured by King Hugh.

Some report that the aforesaid Azelin, also called Adalbero, obtained Charles’s pardon for having communicated with Hugh, was restored by him to his see, and was admitted among his counselors. When he had also imprudently been entrusted with the guarding of the city gates, he secretly informed Hugh that on the appointed day and hour he would open them, at a signal given by a whistle from the episcopal residence. He did so. In memory of this act—whether as a monument of treachery or of the service rendered—two statues can still be seen here and there in the vestibule of the house, one of them with a pipe hanging from its neck.

Guibert of Nogent speaks of Azelin as follows: “What could be more wicked than that he betrayed his lord, the innocent boy-king, to whom he had sworn an oath of fidelity, and transferred the course of Charlemagne’s lineage into a foreign race?”” He committed this crime on the day of the Lord’s Supper. For this reason he is called “the old traitor” by Eginaldus, Nangis, and John of Nesle, although some, such as Papirius Masson, do not lack doubts about this story.

Whatever the truth may be, Charles, captured by Hugh, was led into custody in the city of Orléans, says Hugh of Fleury; and then the kingdom of France was entirely cut off from his branch of the lineage. As for Arnulf, the king ordered him to be taken for judgment before the synod assembled at Reims, in which he was deposed.

Moreover, if no account is taken of the alleged synod’s acts—which are not so authoritative that suspicion could not arise that they were corrupted by heretics—hardly anyone can determine with certainty what should be thought of Arnulf’s betrayal. Eginaldus, suppressing the charge of infidelity, asserts that Arnulf was a pious and modest man and that Capet degraded him solely because of envy and the defect of his birth. Certain authors who were nearly his contemporaries agree with this, including Hugh [Col. 1542B] of Fleury and Guy of Basoches in Alberic.

Balderic, on the other hand, states in the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, book I, chapter 110, that Arnulf was deposed from the episcopal rank for many crimes, especially infidelity toward his lord. But because he had been degraded without the permission and authority of the pontiff of the Roman See, the way back to the same see was again open to him. Sylvester II made this sufficiently explicit in the privilege granted to Arnulf, and the author of the *Life of Abbo of Fleury* openly acknowledges it.

When the synod had ended, the bishops discussed replacing Arnulf with another prelate. There is no doubt that Gerbert, who was present, relying on the friendship of the kings, applied all the powers of his intellect vigorously to obtaining this dignity. He seemed to himself to have found the right moment, but the presence of Hugh and Robert proved still more opportune: it so drew the electors’ minds toward what they had long desired that, without any further choice, they named Gerbert to the archbishopric [Col. 1542C] of Reims with the unanimous agreement of all.

“When the Roman prelate heard this,” says the Continuator of Aimo, “he was greatly angered by what had happened and placed under interdict all the bishops who had deposed Arnulf and ordained Gerbert.” He also sent Leo, abbot and representative of the Apostolic See, to Lord Seguin, archbishop of Sens, instructing him to assemble a synod in the city of Reims on his behalf. He ordered him without delay to recall Arnulf from prison and degrade Gerbert.

Accordingly, when the council had been assembled, Arnulf was recalled from custody in the city of Reims by apostolic command and received with great honor into his own see. Gerbert, however, abandoning the kingdom of France, devoted himself entirely to Otto, king of Germany, and accompanied him to Italy. After Otto had remained for some time at Ravenna, the archbishop of that city soon died. At the request of the clergy and people, and with the king’s consent, Gerbert was appointed in his place. Thus, immediately after the death of Gregory V, compelled by the same emperor, with whom he enjoyed very great favor, he attained the supreme pontificate and, changing his name, was called Sylvester II.

Thus Arnulf, with the king’s consent, was at last released from custody and restored to the episcopate. He received the pallium sent to him by Gregory V, John’s successor, through Abbo of Fleury. Immediately after his inauguration, summoned by Abbot Baso, he consecrated the high altar of the church of Mouzon.

While he was there that year, he gave the monastery the right to fish in the River Chiers, which flows beside Douzy as far as the Meuse; he also gave it the altar of the same place at Douzy and that of Colredo, commonly Corroy, in the territory of Reims, together with two tunics from the diocesan revenues.

In the year 1018 likewise, he subscribed to the foundation of the collegiate church of Saint-Laurent at Rozoy by Hilgandus, the lord of that place. Then, mature in character and advanced in years, he completed the hardships of this world and died on the third day before the Nones of March, or on the day before the Nones. There are differing opinions, however, about the year.

Some, such as Colvenerius and [Col. 1543A] Demochares, think that he died in 1009; it is clear that they are entirely mistaken. The Sammarthani cite a privilege granted to the monastery of Lagny in 1019, to which Arnulf the archbishop subscribed as chancellor of the kingdom; I conjecture that this Arnulf was the archbishop of Reims. The author of the *Chronicle of Mouzon* reports Arnulf’s death in 1021; Alberic gives 1023, which I think should be accepted, since otherwise the see would have remained vacant for several years.

The date 1023 is plausible, because it is unlikely that the see of Reims was vacant when Fulbert of Chartres urged and advised Guy, bishop of Senlis, elected in 1024, to be present, as a suffragan of the province of Reims, at the consecration of Ebal, [Col. 1544A] Arnulf’s successor.

Arnulf therefore died and was buried in the church of Saint Remigius, which he had enriched with benefactions. A certain ascetic who followed him composed the epitaph below, which is still visible affixed to the stone opposite the high altar, on the Gospel side:

> Here lies Arnulf, sprung from royal lineage,  
> Bishop of Reims, second to none in piety.  
> Hope of the needy, support of the weak, shepherd of monks,  
> Defender of truth, strict guardian of upright honor,  
> Whom savage death seized, knowing no one whom it spares.  
> Weep for the Father, monks, with an everlasting fountain of tears.

[Col. 1543]

## Acts of the Election of Arnulf (989)

(*The Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims*, I, 629.)

[Col. 1543B] The sons of the metropolitan city of Reims offer greetings to the holy and universal Catholic Church.

When our father Adalbero, of blessed memory, relinquished his bodily senses, we lost the bright light of a shepherd and became prey to our enemies. Therefore, while we were striving to repair the ruins left by so great a man, the canonical period elapsed, and the laws were violated which provide that no see may remain vacant for more than thirty days. At last, as we knocked, divine light opened itself to us and showed us the path we were to follow: the Antichrist was driven away and the Simoniacal heresy condemned.

We, I say, who are called the bishops of the diocese of the metropolitan church of Reims, together with the entire clergy of the various orders, with the acclamation of the people and the agreement of our orthodox kings, choose for ourselves as bishop a man outstanding in piety, distinguished in faith, marvelous in steadfastness, prudent in counsel, and suited to the conduct of affairs. We name Arnulf, son of King Lothar, in whom these virtues shine so brightly that they indicate the others cannot be absent.

Although his lofty blood, through the fault of an age placed under anathema, infected him with some contagion [Note: [Col. 1543D] See the Council of Reims of the year 987], nevertheless Mother Church, purifying him, has washed him in the mystical sacraments. This man, I say, we call a son of the Church of Laon, and, to speak more truthfully, of Reims. For that city belongs to the territory of Reims and is a parish of Reims, nor was it so divided from blessed Remigius as to become alien to him. Indeed, that man, filled with God, desiring unity and not seeking division, divided it in such a way that it remained joined, like a part within the whole; and, understanding what and how great he would become, he blessed his native soil with the dignity of the priesthood.

We therefore choose this Arnulf, born here and educated here, free from the Simoniacal heresy, removed from the tyrannical faction, restoring to each person his due rights, and not dispersing the sanctuary of God. Let fraud and deceit stand far from our election; nor let the sons of Belial think that it belongs to them. Let the sons of peace and concord make it enduring and solid forever by confirming, strengthening, and subscribing.

[Col. 1543]

## THE OATH OF ARNULF

[Col. 1543C] I, Arnulf, by the prevenient grace of God archbishop of Reims, promise that I shall preserve the purest fidelity toward the kings of the Franks, Hugh and Robert, and that, according to my knowledge and ability, I shall provide counsel and assistance in all their affairs. I shall knowingly aid their enemies neither by counsel nor by assistance in their infidelity.

In the presence of the divine majesty, the blessed spirits, and the entire assembled Church, I make this promise, prepared to receive the rewards of eternal blessing if I observe it faithfully. But if—which I do not wish, and may it be far from me—I should deviate from these obligations, may all my blessing be turned into a curse; may my days be few, and may another receive my bishopric; may my friends depart from me and become my perpetual enemies. I subscribe this charter, issued by me as a testimony of my blessing or curse, and I ask my brothers and sons to subscribe it as well.

I, Arnulf the archbishop, have subscribed.

Done at Reims in the palace, in the year of the Incarnation of the Word [Col. 1544D] 989, in the second indiction, in the third year of the ordination of Lord Arnulf, archbishop.

[Col. 1545]

## ARNULF’S ADMONITION AGAINST THE PLUNDERERS

[Note: [Col. 1545B] Since there was no slight suspicion that the city of Reims had been handed over to Charles at Arnulf’s command, he himself, in order to remove this charge from himself, pronounced the severest sentence of anathema against all who had plundered the city [Col. 1546B–C]. See the Historical Notice above.]

*(Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims, I, 631.)*

[Col. 1545A] Arnulf, archbishop by the grace of God.

What do you want, criminal hand of the Reims plunderers? Do the tears of orphans and widows move you not at all, nor their advocate? Whether you wish it or not, your own Lord is himself witness, judge, and severe avenger; you will not escape his judgment. Consider what you have done before his eyes.

You were not ashamed of the holy chastity of virgins; you even left matrons, whom barbarians ought to respect, naked; you showed no regard for the orphan or the fatherless. You considered this a small matter: you approached the temple of the Mother of God, revered by all mortals; you broke into, polluted, and violated its atrium [Col. 1546A]. Whatever your eyes saw, you coveted; whatever your hands could touch, you seized.

And indeed, contrary to divine and human law, while abusing mercy, we do not pardon what you took in food and drink, but because of these impious times we do not demand it. We do demand everything else that you invaded with polluted hands and continue to retain. Therefore restore it, or accept upon yourself the sentence of condemnation promulgated by the sacred canons against invaders of ecclesiastical property—a sentence already pronounced against you and to be pronounced many times over.

[Col. 1545]

## ANATHEMA AGAINST THE PLUNDERERS

[Col. 1545B] By the authority of almighty God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, with the intervention and assistance of blessed Mary ever-Virgin, and also by the authority and power handed down to the apostles and left to us, we excommunicate, anathematize, curse, condemn, and separate from the thresholds of holy Mother Church you, the leaders, perpetrators, collaborators, supporters, and those who alienate property from its rightful owners under the name of purchase—plunderers of Reims.

May your eyes, which coveted, be darkened; may the hands that seized wither; may all the limbs that assisted be weakened. May you labor always and find no rest, and be deprived of the fruit of your labor. May you fear and tremble before the face of the pursuing—and even the non-pursuing—enemy, so that you waste away and perish. May your portion be with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord, in the land of death and darkness, until your hearts turn toward full satisfaction.

Let this be the manner of full satisfaction: restore in their entirety to their rightful owners everything unjustly taken, except food and drink, and humble yourselves in penitence before the Church of Reims, which you did not revere, though it is holy. May these curses, the pursuers of your crimes, not cease from you so long as you remain in the sin of invasion. Amen; so be it, so be it.

[Col. 1545]

## ARNULF’S BOOK OF ABDICATION

*(Labbe, Councils, IX, 1738.)*

[Col. 1545D] I, Arnulf, formerly archbishop of Reims, recognizing my weakness and the burdens of my sins, appointed as judges of my offenses the following witnesses and confessors: Archbishop Siguin, Archbishop Dalbert, Bishop Arnulf, Bishop Gotesmann, Bishop Herveus, Bishop Ratbod, Bishop Walter, Bishop Bruno, Bishop Milo, Bishop Adalbero, Bishop Odo, Bishop Guido, and Bishop Heribert. I gave them a pure confession, seeking a remedy through penance and the salvation of my soul, so that I might withdraw from the pontifical office and ministry, of which I acknowledge myself unworthy, and might disqualify myself on account of my offenses, which I confessed privately to them that I had committed and for which I was publicly accused.

This I did in such a way that they might be witnesses to another succeeding and being consecrated in my place, one who could worthily preside over and benefit the Church over which I have hitherto presided unworthily; and so that from that time onward I might have no power by canonical authority to make any claim or appeal, I confirmed this by subscribing in my own hand. After it had been read, he subscribed as follows:

I, Arnulf, formerly archbishop, have subscribed.

[Col. 1547]

## ARNULF’S LETTERS

*(See among Gerbert’s letters, nos. 163 and 164, in this volume, cols. 244–245.)*

[Col. 1547]

## THE PRIVILEGES OF ARNULF, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

*(The Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims, vol. I, p. 630, and vol. II, p. 1.)*

### I. Privilege for the Abbey of Saint Remigius  
*(Year 989.)*

[Col. 1547A] In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, of the holy and undivided Trinity.

I, Arnulf, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, wish it to be known to all that, mindful of the generosity and munificence which my parents faithfully showed toward our father and patron, Saint Remigius—namely, my father Lothar and my grandfather Louis, illustrious kings, as well as my glorious grandmother, Queen Gerberga—I wish to increase the possessions and authority of the aforesaid saint for the salvation of myself and my parents, so that he may intercede for us with the Lord [Col. 1547B] and we may deserve to rejoice in the kingdom of the living.

Therefore I grant to his jurisdiction and authority the suburb called the Borough, which is also subject to his castle, together with all that belongs to it—namely, mills, gardens, fields, and houses—so that from this day forward and thereafter they may not pass into another’s power.

Let no one exercise authority therein; rather, with their complete immunity preserved, let everything be subject to the authority of Saint Remigius and his monks: namely, taverns, ovens, the market, the ban, the butchery, and finally whatever may be seen to belong to the Borough. Likewise, let all jurisdictions belonging to me be subjected to the aforesaid authority.

If anyone should violate what has been established by this decree of our confirmation, let him incur, by the authority of almighty God [Col. 1547C] and of us, perpetual condemnation and curse. And so that this may remain fixed and confirmed, I myself have affirmed it with my own hand and strengthened it by the subscription of authoritative persons and the impression of our seal.

The sign of Arnulf, archbishop of Reims, who ordered this deed of donation to be written.

The sign of Arnulf, bishop of Orléans, acting in place of his lord, Lord King Lothar, who approved and confirmed this gift.

The sign of Guido, bishop of Soissons.

The sign of Adalbero, bishop of Laon.

The sign of Heriveus, bishop of Beauvais.

The sign of Gotesmann, bishop of Amiens.

The sign of Ratbod, bishop of Noyon.

The sign of Odo, bishop of Senlis.

The sign of Adalger, dean.

The sign of Rotfrid, archdeacon.

The sign of Count Brocard.

### II. Privilege for the Monastery of Mouzon  
*(Year 1015.)*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

Let it be known to all faithful people, present and future, that I, Arnulf, archbishop of Reims by the grace of God, having been asked by the entreaty of the venerable Abbot Boso and my other faithful men, granted to the Church of Saint Mary of Mouzon the fourth-parts of all the churches that belonged to the aforesaid place—not contrary to the statutes of Saint Remigius, who ordered that these be given to the needy, but to relieve the poverty of that place and [Col. 1548B] for the reception of pilgrims and the poor.

I also granted, for the support of the monks’ livelihood, the entire tithe of the pigs which the abbot and brothers of the aforesaid place might send into the Ardennes forest for fattening, as well as the tithe of those pigs which the men of my authority—that is, of the village of Bervilliacum (Brevilly)—might have in the aforementioned forest.

At the same time I donated the right of fishing in the River Chier, which flows beside Douzy, from the place where they hold the ban of Bervilliacum to the point where that river flows into the Meuse.

Let the monastery possess securely, perpetually, and without any claim being made by my successors, their prévôts, or officials belonging to the bishop of Reims or to any other person, all the things written above, whether granted by me or by my predecessor Adalbero, or donated or to be donated by any faithful persons, for the remedy of my soul, the souls of my predecessors, and those of the other faithful. We have confirmed these things under the bond of anathema, by Roman privileges and apostolic decrees, and now, at the present synod, we have caused our fellow bishops and the other faithful to confirm them.

If anyone, overcome by the gall of greed, should attempt to act against this deed of donation or wish to violate it, may he incur the wrath of almighty God and, with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, be burned in the eternal fire of Gehenna, unless he repent and flee for satisfaction before the abbot and brothers of that place. So be it, so be it.

[Col. 1549A] + The sign of Arnulf, by the grace of God archbishop of the Church of Reims.

+ The sign of Adalbero, bishop of the holy Church of Laon.

+ The sign of Fulco, bishop of Amiens.

+ The sign of Rotger, bishop of Châlons.

+ The sign of Rudolf, bishop of Senlis.

+ The sign of Gerard, bishop of Cambrai.

+ The sign of Rotger, bishop of Beauvais.

+ The sign of Harduin, bishop of Noyon.

+ The sign of Baldwin, bishop of Thérouanne.

+ The sign of Rayner, prévôt. The sign of Alulf, viscount.

Done at Reims, in the monastery of Saint Mary, in the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1015, in the [Col. 1549B] twelfth indiction, on the fourth day before the Ides of May, while the most glorious king of the Franks, Robert, was reigning.

I, Dario, vice-chancellor, have subscribed.

### III. For the Same Monastery  
*(Year 1018.)*

ARNULF, archbishop of Reims by the grace of God.

It is credibly true that Holy Scripture says that almsgiving is held in great confidence before the supreme God by those who practice it. Therefore we firmly believe that the mercy which is faithfully bestowed upon holy places, the churches of God, and the poor of Christ will receive the greatest reward.

For this reason I wish it to be known to all Christ’s faithful, present and future, and to our faithful people and their successors [Col. 1549C], that I, Arnulf, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, with the counsel of Robert, king of the Franks, and of many of our faithful, following also what had been most devoutly done by my predecessor Adalbero, mercifully granted certain possessions belonging to our jurisdiction to the Church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, at Mouzon, at the entreaty of Boso, abbot of that place. Thus our benefactions might support the monks serving God there, and the prayer of Saint Mary and her servants might assist toward the salvation of our souls and those of my successors.

Concerning the possessions that ought then to belong to that monastery, when I had previously gone to Rome after a long interval and had the aforesaid abbot with me, I humbly petitioned and obtained from the Apostolic See that the place of Mouzon should deserve to have privileges under Roman authority.

After these had been received and several years had passed, our officials from Mouzon and the judges of the castle began frequently to harass that place and, as though acting according to our jurisdiction, to inflict many injuries under our ban and authority, taking the opportunity that had arisen. For the men living under Saint Mary’s authority at Mouzon and Flaba were required to attend two courts, keep watches at the castle, and perform services by providing beds and undertaking other duties.

For this reason, when I was in the king’s presence at Laon at Easter [Col. 1550A], the aforesaid Abbot Boso approached our humility and presence, explaining his distress and the oppression of his poor dependents, and humbly begging that, for the remedy of my soul and those of my successors, I should show some mercy and relief to the monastery of Saint Mary in this matter and oppression.

When I presented the matter to the king, and after I had been approached by the entreaties of many good men, with the king’s counsel and goodwill, I granted to the aforesaid church the ban and jurisdiction over the property written above, with the authority I owed and the devotion I was able to offer. I made the transfer through the hands of Duke Godfrey, advocate of that church, in the presence also of Haceca, now a widow, and her son Dodo, who abandoned there the third-part that belonged to their benefice [Note: [Col. 1549D] *Werpire* or *guerpire*, “to abandon”], for Saint Mary to have and possess perpetually and peacefully.

Thus the men of Saint Mary living at Mouzon or Flaba, or those who in future might come to live there from anywhere, shall render no customary services [Note: [Col. 1550D] *Constumias*, “service established by custom”] to any man or authority except the abbot and monks of Saint Mary; nor shall they attend courts, keep watches, or provide beds except for the service of the church.

After this transfer had been solemnly made and the ban had been legally imposed in the presence of King Robert, so that no one might ever presume to violate it, and also to preserve the remembrance of posterity and the liberty of the church, I issued and caused to be signed a written instrument of our authority. I admonished our successors, on God’s behalf, that just as they wish their own ecclesiastically enacted statutes to remain inviolate, so they should in no way permit this donation and charitable ordinance of ours to be rescinded or violated for any reason.

To all whom the bond of Christ ought to subject to our authority—counts, judges, prévôts, and authorities of every kind—we issue this prohibition under the anathema of Christ and of the entire Church, and we admonish them not to presume to violate or remove this decree by any means, for any reason, or under the intrusion of any greed. If they should presume to do so, may they, with Judas the betrayer of the Lord, be subject to eternal curse. So be it, so be it.

+ The sign of Arnulf, by the grace of God archbishop of the Church of Reims.

+ The sign of Adalbero, bishop of the holy Church of Laon.

+ The sign of Fulco, bishop of Amiens.

+ The sign of Gerard, bishop of Cambrai.

+ The sign of Rotger, bishop of Châlons.

The sign of Duke Godfrey, advocate of that Church.

The sign of Dudo; the sign of Count Odo; the sign of Hilgaud; the sign of Alulf, archdeacon and viscount.

Done at Laon, in the monastery of Saint Mary, in the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1018, in the first indiction, while Robert, king of the Franks, was reigning.

I, Bardo, chancellor, wrote this in the name of God.

## In the Year of the Lord 1024. Constantine, Abbot of Saint Symphorian.

[Col. 1551]

# LIFE OF ADALBERO II, BISHOP OF METZ, BY CONSTANTINE THE ABBOT

*(Edited by Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica, Scriptores, vol. IV, p. 658.)*

## NOTICE

After Adalbero II, who had occupied the see of Metz from 984 to 1005, died, Duke Theoderic appointed his son Adalbero III as successor to his brother and entrusted the still-child Adalbero to the care of Theoderic, Queen Cunegund’s brother. Abusing his power, he himself seized the episcopal throne and, relying on the authority of his brother, Duke Henry, went to war against Archbishop Megingoz, appointed by the king, and against Duke Theoderic, in order to seize the see of Trier as well, which had become vacant after Liudolf’s death in 1008. The war continued amid varying fortunes until 1012 and appears to have been settled in genuine peace only in 1017.

Amid these disturbances, during which all Lotharingia was being devastated, Constantine [Note: [Col. 1551] In chapter 26 he names his predecessors Fingenius and Siriaudus], abbot of the monastery of Saint Symphorian outside the walls of Metz, undertook to write the Life of Adalbero II. He was moved by the memory of a better age and by his grateful affection for the deceased, whom he revered as the restorer of his monastery. Constantine himself had once been his constant companion, both at table [Note: [Col. 1551] Chapter 8] and in caring for the illnesses of the poor [Note: [Col. 1551] Moreover, without speaking himself, he orders others to speak of his almsgiving; chapter 14]. Through Adalbero’s favor he had been appointed abbot of the monastery of Saint Symphorian in 1004 [Note: [Col. 1551] Chapter 26]. He had attended him in his illness and at his death at Nomeny [Note: [Col. 1551] Chapter 31] and at Metz, and had religiously preserved the deceased man’s hair shirt and woolen garment as great treasures [Note: [Col. 1551] Chapter 22]. Finally, after Adalbero had been buried in the church of Saint Symphorian [Note: [Col. 1551] Chapter 36], Constantine had undertaken to commend him to God with continual prayers.

The work, composed with great devotion but sometimes in a rather diffuse style, contains many things worthy of remembrance and follows an arrangement based more on subject matter than on chronology. The author wrote it several years after the deaths of Adalbero and Liudolf of Trier [Note: [Col. 1551] He died in 1008], when the limbs of both were already dry [Note: [Col. 1552] In chapter 27 he says that the limbs of both were already dry], while Immo, abbot of Gorze, was still alive [Note: [Col. 1552] The year of his death is unknown] and peace had not yet been firmly established in the region [Note: [Col. 1552] Chapter 27], under King Henry II, not yet emperor [Note: [Col. 1552] Chapter 15]. It was therefore written about the year 1012. Shortly afterward, following his example, it inspired Alpert, then a monk of Saint Symphorian, to write the deeds of the bishops of Metz and dedicate them to our Constantine [Note: [Col. 1552] See that work, printed below in Patrologia, vol. CXL].

The year in which the good abbot died is not entirely certain [Note: [Col. 1552] See Gallia Christiana XIII, p. 846, where he is said to have lived until 1046. Rivet, Literary History VII, p. 248, relying on some testimony unknown to me, says that he died on 10 September 1024].

Three manuscript copies survive:

1. Codex of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 5673, parchment, small quarto, eleventh century, written by Constantine’s hand or copied from his dictation, and corrected in only a few places. I examined it at Paris in 1839 and had it reproduced in our edition. It contains nothing except the Life and a letter written by Hildeward, bishop of Halberstadt, to Adalbero.

2. Codex of the same library, no. 5294, parchment, eleventh century, folio, formerly belonging to the monastery of Saint Symphorian at Metz, written at the command of our Constantine by Betto with a reed pen. Here the Life was copied from the first manuscript and corrected in various places by another hand; like the first, it seems to bear the authority of Constantine. The following manuscript agrees with it very closely:

3. Codex of the Ducal Library of Wolfenbüttel, marked among the Augustei as 76, 14, parchment, eleventh century, folio, which our Waitz collated, like Royal Manuscript no. 5294, with the printed editions.

I used these aids in such a way that I altered the first manuscript, reproduced literally, with the help of the others only very rarely. Hildeward’s letter is reserved for publication in our collection of Letters.

At the end we present an epitaph of Adalbero composed by Kuonrad, apparently a monk of Saint-Nabor. Baluze had formerly published it in *Miscellanea* IV, 554, from Colbert Manuscript no. 1682, concealing the author’s name. We present it from the same manuscript, marked no. 8088 in the Royal Library of Paris, eleventh century, folio, together with unpublished poems by Kuonrad, in which he offers the epitaph to Abbot Ratramnus and sets forth the holy man’s life.

# HERE BEGINS THE LIFE

[Col. 1553]

[Col. 1553A] **1.** Adalbero [Note: [Col. 1553] “Here begins the Life of blessed Bishop Adalbero. Thus Adalbero,” chapters 2 and 3], venerable bishop of holy Metz, nephew of the great Adalbero [Note: [Col. 1553C] Son of Frideric, the brother], although later in time and born afterward, was, we truly confess, not inferior in merit and grace, a glory, light, and adornment both of his own people—we mean ours—and of the whole homeland, and indeed of all who dwell throughout the world. With a lineage noble from great-grandfathers and beyond [Note: [Col. 1553] Thus manuscripts 1, 2, and 3], he adorned and illuminated both himself and his lineage completely by his own merit. During his life he was a source of splendor and joy and, for preserving the commonwealth, a hope of salvation and life. When he died on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January, he left behind an indescribable grief for those whose darkness and perpetual gloom, from his departure onward, have continued, alas, forever.

This man, great in name and in the grace of his life, born for the advancement of the world and the strengthening of the Church, was begotten by his father Frideric [Col. 1553B], duke of Middle Gaul, who surpassed many of his predecessors in that office through the excellence of his nobility and the preeminence of his wisdom, and by his mother Beatrice, daughter of the great Hugh. He not only did not disgrace so great and illustrious a line of descent [Note: [Col. 1553] *linea*, “lineage,” manuscript 3], but made it honorable and distinguished beyond what can be expressed or worthily conceived, as the pure and glorious life of Adalbero is recounted to the peoples according to the circumstances of the time and proclaimed among the nations to the glory of God and of Christ his Lord, our Lord.

**2.** Wishing to say briefly what he did, for what purpose he was born, and how he lived, we make known to anyone willing to listen that from the cradle he was a lover of his Creator with complete devotion of heart and the greatest eagerness of spirit. In accordance with the divine commandment he loved his neighbor without reserve; he always showed the same consideration for the needs of those infirm in body or heart as for his own; and whenever necessary he constantly assisted at the burial of the dead.

To say much in brief, the blessed man established this rule for himself: wherever he went, it should seem that a certain light and a hope of salvation had arrived. Most mercifully, he always prepared himself and his spirit with the greatest attentiveness to preserve the divine commandments and to foresee what would benefit his brothers.

He was most chastely trained and instructed in the scholarly disciplines among the Gurgitenses [Note: [Col. 1553C] That is, the Gorzienses]. After the death of the second Otto, the divine emperor, in the year 983, when the whole West was languishing because of the accidental death of the father and the premature orphaning of the son, who had subsequently been created Caesar, amid the dissension of the lesser and the greed of the greater for kingship, and after the death of the memorable bishop Theoderic in 984, Adalbero—by birth and mind most noble [Note: [Col. 1553] “Most noble,” manuscripts 2 and 3]—was raised and established as bishop of Metz, the most famous fulfillment of the wishes of the people and of the age, through the efforts and initiative of his mother Beatrice, with the favor of the lady Augusta Adelheid, grandmother of the still very young child, and, what is first and last among good things, with God’s complete assent, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 984 [Note: [Col. 1553] Manuscripts 1 and 2 have DCCCC, with manuscript 2 adding, in dark ink, LXXXIIII], in the twelfth indiction [Note: [Col. 1553] The place is erased in manuscript 1; the number was added in dark ink in manuscript 2].

**3.** It is a wondrous grace of God and of our Lord, and an ancient manifestation of his power—marvelous to relate—that the princes’ discord, which they thought could never be escaped without great dangers and much bloodshed [Note: [Col. 1553] “Nor without bloodshed,” manuscripts 2 and 3], was so calmed and reduced to nothing that, although affairs had already been placed in arms, they returned most perfectly to unity under the chosen prince and to the duration of true peace, which lasted as long as that same prince lived, when Adalbero, in accordance with the wishes of the faithful, happily ascended to this degree of pontifical dignity.

These things took place under favorable auspices at Worms—once called Vangio—about 20 October, where part of the army of Gaul and Germany had gathered, some to support the youthful prince and others to resist him [Note: [Col. 1554C] The king was there on 20 October; Böhmer, *Regesta*, no. 625].

But after Adalbero had been invested with the honor of the pastoral staff, those who shortly before had resisted the king whom God had chosen, as could be seen, hastened afterward to press forward more eagerly in service because of the merits of this blessed man, and pledged themselves to remain faithful from that time onward.

What more is there to say? When royal affairs had been pacified and all the affairs of the new king had been brought to tranquility, Beatrice—who, with God’s assent, had been the promoter of this peace and through whose diligence so sudden a confederation of soldiers and princes around the king had been formed—herself joyful with her most fortunate offspring, and accompanied by that noble army of the people of Metz, hastened to go to the city given to her son. By every gesture of heart and body available to her and known to her, she magnified and praised God, God’s ancient mercy, supreme goodness, and virtue known among the nations.

There was a gathering of men and women; there was an unheard-of inrush of the people; there was an admirable, dutiful, and sweet applause of monks, virgins, and all the saints [Note: [Col. 1553] “And of virgins,” manuscripts 2 and 3], as they came and saw that the joys for which they had long waited were approaching, and received them.

How great was the rejoicing of the devout, how great the proclamations of their hearts, while the peoples’ praises resounded to God [Note: [Col. 1553] “Resound,” manuscripts 2 and 3], while the clergy, not merely of one city, produced the sweetest and loftiest melodies in song [Col. 1555A], while the throng of consecrated women raised voices worthy of God on high [Note: [Col. 1553] “Sacred,” manuscript 3].

**4.** Meanwhile the priestly blessing was postponed until the Nativity of the Lord Christ. Since Sunday had been appointed by the Fathers for the performance of this sacrament, the fifth day before the Kalends of January, on which the solemn feast of the Holy Innocents is celebrated, arrived—a Sunday consecrated and made holy by the Lord’s resurrection. And behold, bishops of the neighboring cities assembled at Trier, the ancient metropolitan see, presided over by the venerable Archbishop Ecbert. With equal prayers and equal assent, they consecrated and blessed Lord Adalbero as bishop in the see of the city of Metz.

Having now undertaken pastoral cares and the keeping of the Lord’s sheep, he girded himself entirely to become a model of the flock entrusted to him. He resolved to prepare both body and soul wholly for the work of God and took the greatest care to be an example and model of virtue to his subjects.

**5.** He was also approachable toward those inferior to him in age or poverty, and humble beyond what can be believed in our own time, so that the wicked and proud marked him as though he were excessively abject. He was gentler than all the men of his time, entirely free from anger [Note: [Col. 1555D] That is, from wrath], so much so that he said he wondered how or why the vice of anger rose up against human beings, since although he desired to exercise discipline toward evildoers, he could not become angry.

**6.** He was a most fervent lover of God’s servants, especially monks, to such a degree that, continually attacked and reviled by laymen, he was accused of caring about nothing except monks [Col. 1555C]. He certainly longed and earnestly desired to become an imitator of the Lord Christ. When he read that people reproached his Lord because he associated at table with publicans and sinners, and heard that the worst Jews called him a drinker of wine, he judged it an immeasurable treasure and a welcome gift to endure, for love of that same Lord—by whose love he burned—such reproaches, or perhaps even heavier ones.

**7.** He took such delight in the banquets of holy men, and especially of monks, that he confessed himself fortunate on the day when it happened that he dined with them—those for whom the world had been crucified and who had been crucified to the world. When he reclined with them, he often said: “Come, so that you may sit at the right hand of the son of Mother Church.”

**8.** I speak and confess these things truly, because, although unworthy and most despised among his people, I often sat first at the right hand of my lord and shared both his words and his table. I shared in his sacred conversations and very frequently took delight while dining with him. The food was mingled with the sweetest words of sacred exhortation and correction, which he took the greatest care to prepare adequately for the monks whom he always loved.

**9.** Therefore the blessed man, with whom, as we truly believe, God was present, became truly apostolic and “all things to all people,” so that he might win them all [Note: [Col. 1555] “All things to everyone,” manuscripts 2 and 3]. He was beloved by everyone, not only by clergy but also by laypeople, and even by Jews, so that even to this day, leaving Christians aside, he is mourned by daily lamentations and deep sighs by the most hostile Jews of our own religion [Note: [Col. 1555] That is, “of our religion,” manuscript 3].

Every sex and age revered and loved him with extraordinary devotion of mind; every order and condition; residents and newcomers; those within and those outside [Note: [Col. 1555] Omitted in manuscripts 2 and 3]; the known and the unknown.

**10.** In body, then, he was more handsome than all the men of his time: graceful in stature, elegant in appearance, most loving in his eyes, moderate in his nose, white-haired, with hair that was itself sparse and smooth, and corpulent by nature. In his hands, feet, and entire body he displayed God, marvelous in all his works, and showed those who saw him how beautiful the Maker is in his nature, whose works are so beautiful.

The beginnings and first fruits of his activities, devoted to divine purposes and to exercising minds in the things of piety, were found at the monastery of Saint Symphorian. Although, because of its antiquity, it could display nothing but ruins and collapses, and although its great nobility had fallen into the blackest degradation, its setting was most pleasant, its vineyards most abundant, and its proximity to the city honorable. It was most renowned for the multitude of its saints and, more fittingly still, for the numerous bodies of bishops buried there.

This place moved the heart and mind of blessed and most beloved Lord Adalbero [Note: [Col. 1555] “And,” manuscript 3] to restore it to the splendid beauty that can be seen there. With the greatest devotion he labored to raise it again to the grace of renewed beauty, and he did not cease until, by God’s blessed gift, he had fulfilled his most blessed hopes [Note: [Col. 1555] “Most devout hopes,” manuscript 3].

For the height of walls and masonry, the peaks of roofs, the graceful roundness of columns, and the splendor of gleaming metals are acquired through empty labor and accumulated through vain effort if everything gathered and amassed has not been collected solely with a view to divine reward, after every desire for worldly favor and all appetite for passing praise have been cast aside. And, just as the faithful soul devoted to God must prepare for itself divine and eternal dwellings, so it must construct and prepare these earthly buildings [Col. 1556D].

Perceiving this, the blessed man adorned the place he had prepared for God with a most fitting community of God’s servants, who, trained in the institutions of Saint Benedict, knew how to obey them perfectly. With the greatest diligence he gathered them together so that they might pray to God for the eternal salvation both of himself and of his predecessors, and for that of the whole world, which faced great dangers.

11. After he had duly established this place for God and made it most honorable with a splendid multitude of monks whom he had gathered from every quarter, he resolved that not only his spirit but also his soul and body should always serve God and his Christ, so that no part of him should remain idle even for a moment from the divine work of mercy, but should be active and useful, constant in labor. Desiring to wear himself down through many kinds of holy exercises, he undertook the journey to Rome, visited the thresholds of the apostles, and, with tears in which he surpassed all mortals, lamented and laid aside the transgressions of himself and his subjects.

Pope John was presiding over the holy see and was administering the office of blessed Peter with the utmost dignity. [Note: [Col. 1557D] John occupied the see from 985 to 996.] He received Lord Adalbero with such honor and treated him with such reverence as befitted a man of such lineage and nobility; indeed, he recognized that this was appropriate to a man of such holiness and devotion, and most honorably rewarded him with relics of the saints.

How arduous and difficult this journey was for the blessed man, with what labor and sweat he traversed the mountain passes and the trackless paths among rocks and forests—you who know how delicate and infirm he was, who know that in bodily strength and the powers of his limbs he was altogether weak and feeble, both by the delicacy of his noble nature and by the weakness of his spirit, will be able to weigh and judge.

Upon his return, he devoted himself entirely to the divine work [Note: [Col. 1557D] Witness 2 corrects *opere*, “work,” to *operi*, “to the work”] and diligently persevered in praising his Creator. He mortified himself and his body with almsgiving and the labors of vigils and prayers; he made it his chief concern to assist the needs of the sick and the burials of the dead; and he relieved the nakedness and poverty of pilgrims of every profession and rank. He did so tirelessly and diligently that, receiving them as guests in his daily practice, washing their feet and hands, restoring them with various kinds of food, and giving them gifts when they departed, he would send some away only to receive others at once, ready to provide with equal fervor of love and equal devotion of charity whatever he knew had been instituted by God’s command to be bestowed upon the brethren.

12. Within the city of Metz there was a very ancient hospice, a small, poor, and wretched place, apart from the fact that it was dedicated to the name of the blessed and ever-virgin Mary. The deed itself bears witness to how, through love of Christ and of Christ the Lord’s Mother, he raised it anew with the splendor of its buildings [the wording *in quem aedificiorum splendorum reerexit* is uncertain], and enriched the handmaids of God gathered there with such abundant wealth that they might perpetually celebrate the praises of the Creator of all things.

13. Lord Adventius, venerable bishop of holy Metz, had begun a small establishment in the Blisac district in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity. [Note: [Col. 1557D] The Pays de Blois, near Saint-Mihiel on the Meuse.] Overtaken by death, he was unable to complete it. Lord Rotbert, bishop of the same see, completed it on a small scale, in accordance with the modesty of its beginnings.

Our lord Adalbero, seeing that this place was most suitable for the practices of holy religion—for it extended into a hermitage amid vast stretches of forest, while the charm of the surrounding waters bestowed pleasantness on it—and, above all, being greatly pleased that it had been consecrated, as we have said, in honor of the supreme and undivided Trinity and was distinguished by the body of Saint Terentius, confessor and bishop of the same see of Metz, gathered women dedicated to God and settled them there, granting them the very ample resources necessary for their support.

14. Lord Deoderic, likewise the glorious bishop of the city of Metz, whose episcopal successor our lord Adalbero was, found in the Calvomont district a certain place between the Moselle and a mountain which, because it had a castle on its slope, was by the accidental usage of the peasants called Spinal. [Note: [Col. 1558D] Épinal; compare Sigebert’s *Life of Deoderic*, chapter 12.] Finding it suitable for divine service, he built a monastery there, consecrating it to God and Saint Goeric. He transferred the saint’s most sacred bones from the city of Metz, placed them there with fitting veneration, and prepared a most blessed protection for the region.

Lord Adalbero, his successor, having become bishop for the salvation of Christendom and at the request of those entrusted to him, understood that the lofty heights of walls were useless if there were no servants of God to inhabit the buildings, and that earthly things were of no benefit where heavenly things were lacking. First, therefore, he gathered a community of clerics for the honor of almighty God. Then, desiring with all his strength and every effort to increase the glory of the Godhead as far as is possible for man, he assigned handmaids of Christ, well instructed in the regular life and under the rule of our father, the blessed Benedict, to serve God and Saint Goeric the bishop, giving them estates and possessions from which they could live without poverty or want.

What humility and hospitality he possessed, what patience and generosity he showed toward pilgrims and all the poor, the events enacted in that same place bear witness. By revealing through many signs and wonders of miracles what Saint Goeric, Christ’s confessor, had merited in his life and what influence he possessed with God, the fame of the saint spread far and wide and became known among peoples and nations.

Therefore, so that the glory of God might become known and the magnificence of his goodness shine ever more clearly and openly in our times, a most grievous calamity befell a great multitude of people throughout all the regions of Burgundy. Their hands and feet burned with a pitiable affliction: one had lost a foot, another both feet, another was burned halfway, while another was only then beginning to burn. Coming soon after hearing the report of the holy bishop, they flocked from every direction, leaning on staffs or carried in carts.

While this was happening, Lord Adalbero—who, as long as he lived, was the light and joy of his people, since the castle overlooking the monastery was the episcopal residence—was very frequently present. Each day he received such men to dine, [Note: [Col. 1559] Witnesses 2 and 3 read “received.”] handled and washed those wounds with his own hands, caressed them with his mouth and eyes, and never ceased praising and blessing God in all his works.

I speak the truth: I took part for seven days as a helper in this divine service, and with my own hands I either washed or wiped them, while he himself washed and refreshed with food not fewer than one hundred and eighty each day, as we have said. [Note: [Col. 1559] Witnesses 2 and 3 read seventy.]

For when the wounds themselves were washed with water, such vapor and mist filled the house where this was done that scarcely could one person see another. [Note: [Col. 1559] Witness 1 reads *pualeret* for *praevaleret*, “could.”] There was also an intolerable stench, surpassing and overwhelming the smell of sulfur and everything that is unbearable among odors. The blessed man carried out these acts, as I have said, without disdain and with great devotion of heart.

We have said this in order to proclaim, in one and the same event, two deeds of two priests most worthy of remembrance, and to hand them down to posterity for imitation or admiration: in blessed Goeric, the distinction of virtues; in Lord Adalbero, the desire for and supreme love of humility, abasement, and every form of human lowliness. [Note: [Col. 1559] Witnesses 2 and 3 read *adjectionis* (“addition”) for *abjectionis* (“abasement”); witness 1 corrects *utilitatis* (“usefulness”) to *vilitatis* (“lowliness”), the reading of witnesses 2 and 3.]

Yet while we praise this great and exceptional man as a devotee of profound humility and of all the virtues nourished by holy Mother Humility with the gentle milk of her breasts, and while we describe him in such matters as worthy of narration [Note: [Col. 1559] Witness 2 corrects *praedicantes* (“praising”) to *enarrantes* (“narrating”).], lest posterity charge him with what his contemporaries—and especially his intimates—imputed to him, namely, that he was excessively humble and excessively abject, we have resolved to append certain matters to this work. Through them we shall show that at definite times and for definite reasons he submitted himself to the good through humility, but resisted the wicked with steadfastness of faith and the judgment of justice, also opposing them with timely firmness, and resisted vices and vicious men.

15. Lord King Henry, who had succeeded Otto III, the august emperor [Note: [Col. 1559] Witnesses 1 and 2 read *vivo* (“living”); witness 3 corrects *divino* (“divine”) to *divo* (“august”).], in ruling—but not yet in imperial authority—throughout Germany this side of the Rhine and in the kingdom of Lothair on this side of the Rhine, summoned a conference and synod in the year 1005. [Note: [Col. 1559D] Compare Thietmar, VI.21, MGH SS III, p. 113.] There he gathered almost all the chief priests of his kingdom. Raising various matters for discussion, he sharply confronted those same priests during the debate, asking why in their dioceses and among their diocesan clergy they did not cut away with the synodal—and therefore spiritual—sickle those things that ought to be cut down, and why they refrained from severing from the members of the faithful, with the sword of the Holy Spirit, what was rotten and diseased.

Everyone wondered what the king’s very stern words meant and where they were directed. The king relieved them of their uncertainty and openly disclosed what he had in mind.

16. “Among the many things,” he said, “that must be corrected in our kingdom and in your parishes, kinsfolk contract marriage with one another so closely that, fearing neither God nor respecting men, they do not shrink even from bringing a blood relationship of the third degree to the marriage bond—a thing it is abominable to mention [Note: [Col. 1559] Witnesses 2 and 3 transpose the words: *nefas dictu*]—and, more unfortunate than Jews and pagans, they do not fear breaking at its very beginning the line which the institutions of the sacred canons command to be preserved inviolate down to the seventh generation.”

The bishops sat here and there in silence for a long time. Some did not know of whom he was speaking; others, loving or fearing the person being discussed, were utterly ignorant of what answer to give the king’s words. For a guilty conscience, when compelled to hear what it does not wish to hear, becomes stupefied: the voice retreats, words slip away, and before a wise man it seems more honorable to remain silent than to speak.

The king, whom no one could deceive—for he was exceptionally learned, most eloquent, and held most firmly to rule through fear of God—restrained the movement of his heart with the reins of patience. Judging it more fitting to approach them through examples from Sacred Scripture, he said:

“Behold, behold: you occupy the seats of holy priests and sit in a better chair than that in which Moses sat, since you possess the place of the Lord. You ought to be called good dogs and holy rams according to the merit of your life; yet, in the contrary role and in an inverted order, you have become mute dogs unable to bark. Struck with blindness yourselves, while being compelled to guide your subjects, both guide and follower are thrown headlong into the pit.

“Behold,” he said, “Conrad, duke of the Austrasians, who is related to us by blood and joined by affinity to all the noblest men throughout the whole country, has taken a wife so close and so near to him that, as we fear, God’s offense seems to be approaching with the utmost speed—not only for him but for the entire country—and, as is said, already stands at the door. The guilt charged against us for remaining silent is scarcely less than that charged against the man who is seen to perpetrate the same crime boldly and without any sense of sin.”

17. Lord Adalbero, venerable bishop of Metz, was closely related by blood and affinity to the king seated there and to all who descended from the line of the great Henry. He was seated in this holy synod, and, being nobler and more distinguished than all his fellow priests, he stood out among them in a nobler and more elevated seat.

Unable to endure the king’s rebuke any longer, and judging it dishonorable to remain silent, he said:

“Meanwhile, granting precedence in speaking with our brothers to age, holiness, and learning, and showing the honor due to a gray head and to old age according to the divine command, which says, ‘You shall rise before a gray head’ (Leviticus 19:32), we see, my lord king, that your majesty’s power is causing your words increasingly to enlarge the rebuke and denunciation directed against the disgrace of our order. We truly confess that to remain silent any longer and not to speak what is right we regard as not merely folly but, more seriously, a great disgrace.

“Lord Otto, duke and father of this venerable Duke Conrad seated here beside us, was born from the daughter of the great Otto. [Note: [Col. 1561] Witnesses 2 and 3 read *m. o. e.* [an unexpanded abbreviation in the apparatus].] Otto’s sister Girbergia [Note: [Col. 1561] *Girbergia* corrected from *Gibergia* in witness 1.] gave her daughter to Conrad, king of the Burgundians. From Conrad’s daughter was born Lady Matilda, [Note: [Col. 1561] Witness 2 reads *Matilda*.] the wife of this Conrad [Note: [Col. 1561] Witness 1 has the Latin genitive form *Conradi*.] seated here. Therefore, according to this genealogical order—for a brother and sister are not admitted in the reckoning—their consanguinity cannot be removed by more than the second degree.”

As the blessed man unfolded these facts, such anger and hostility began to arise within the synod that, had it not been for the nobility by which Conrad’s fame shone throughout heaven, earth, and sea and beyond the sea, Duke Conrad, whose case was at issue [Note: [Col. 1561] Witnesses 1, 2, and 3 read *rex* (“king”) for *res* (“case”).], and all who belonged to his party would have seized weapons and fury, showing reverence neither for God nor for royal majesty, and honoring not at all the priests, whose very large and honorable assembly was present. To satisfy their madness, they would have omitted nothing that the strength and power of their hands could inflict.

18. Lord Theoderic was present at this gathering, which was more a sedition than a synod. He was the brother of our lord Bishop Adalbero, but the duke of those who dwell on both sides of the Meuse [Note: [Col. 1561] Witness 3 reads *scis* for *cis*, “on this side of.”] and the Moselle. [Note: [Col. 1561] Witness 2 spells *Mosellamque* as *mossellamque*.] He supported and strengthened by his authority the proceedings then taking place and the just decisions being made. Together with the other dukes, counts, and—what is more—the priests who favored God, righteousness, and royal justice, he condemned the unlawful marriages, feared no human anger, and freely decided matters belonging to God with the scales of equity.

Also present at this venerable synod were the foremost and chief priests: Willigis, bishop of Mainz; Heribert, likewise bishop of Cologne; the bishop of Worms; that of Strasbourg; Walter of Speyer [Note: [Col. 1561] Witnesses 2 and 3 spell the name *Vualterus*.]; Notger of Liège [Note: [Col. 1561] Witnesses 2 and 3 spell the name *Notgerus*.]; Hezel of Würzburg; [Note: [Col. 1561] That is, the bishop of Würzburg. The bishop of Worms at that time was Burchard, and the bishop of Strasbourg was Werinharius. The wording in witnesses 2 and 3 is “that of Worms, that of Strasbourg.”] Haimo of Verdun; Bertald of Toul; and many others, not only from the kingdom of Lothair but from all Germany.

Some were swayed this way and that by favor, others by fear of the noble person involved. Only a very few, themselves foremost among their peers, gave testimony to the truth on behalf of the beloved of God, Adalbero, and his most just statements. Thus a considerable dispute and discord arose between truth and falsehood, which even the king himself could not wholly calm. Indeed, had it not been for the incomparable nobility of our lord and bishop Adalbero, blind fury and wretched madness would have seized weapons and missiles, and the agitation of anger might have reached the point of homicide.

19. Thus they departed amid this hostility and these most bitter hatreds, and each person hastened to return home. But when the lord bishop had left his own homeland [Note: [Col. 1561] Witnesses 2 and 3 read *patria propria* (“his own country”) for *propria patria*.] and gone to the royal conference, he feared and esteemed none of these things, because he was the gentlest and most peace-loving of all men of his time. He used not a large military force but the sweetest company of clerics and most honorable laymen. Therefore, on the return journey, fearing that he might perhaps suffer an enemy ambush on the road, he judged it proper to deviate slightly from the route and preferred to withdraw for a time rather than give the madness of a raging prince an opportunity for slaughter or some other act of malice.

But the ineffable mercy and eternal clemency of almighty God and of his Christ, in pity arranging and by his providence ordaining the outcome otherwise than the bishop had expected, changed the spirit of fury and malice, the force of his bacchantic [Note: [Col. 1561] Witness 3 reads *vachantis*.] and turbulent frenzy [Note: [Col. 1561] Witnesses 1, 2, and 3 have *ita*, of uncertain force.], into such dread and fear that, with the same violence and strength by which he had previously tried to pursue the man of God [Note: [Col. 1561] Witnesses 2 and 3 read *servum*, “servant,” for *virum*, “man.”], he now attempted with all his power to flee and retreat, fearing capture more than striving to capture.

20. For two days, entrusting himself to flight until he believed himself safe, the aforementioned Conrad constantly thought that he was being pursued by the lord bishop and his brother, Duke Theoderic. Our men, however, were attempting nothing other than to return home, and were doing so with the greatest haste. Since the season required it, they attended to peaceful matters and the things belonging to peace—namely, harvesting and managing what was useful for their domestic affairs—while the bishop [Note: [Col. 1561] Witness 2 reads *pontifex*; witness 3 *fontifex*.] saw to his customary duties, either building new monasteries or restoring old ones.

I have said this on account of those who twisted the blessed man’s innocence and devotion into stupidity and dullness. Like the followers of the Jews who persecuted our head and principle with biting words, they continually shouted—an abomination even to recall—that he was a drinker of wine and possessed by a demon. Such people called God’s servant, the most honorable member of the supreme Head, dull and senseless because, when subjected to every kind of insult, he did not become insanely angry. [Note: [Col. 1561] “Did not become insanely angry” is corrected from “did not rage” in witnesses 1 and 2.]

But this blessed man had learned to be patient toward injuries inflicted upon him, and he always hastened to attend to the calamities of his subjects. Awaiting the proper opportunity, he became all things to all people: always submissive toward the holy, but constantly prepared to correct and exhort the wicked so that they might be converted. Through his kindness he frequently gained for himself the fruit of the conversion of the depraved, and rejoiced greatly that he had made profit from money entrusted to him.

He exhorted those whom he saw to require exhortation; he rebuked the hard-hearted and faithless; he entreated the pious and kind to advance toward better things. But those whom hardness of mind made incorrigible, after long patience, he hastened to pursue with the sword and weapons of divine punishment and with spiritual missiles, and, once they had been condemned by the laws, he proceeded against them. At times he ravaged their possessions; at times he overthrew their castles and leveled them with the earth, because these were too close to the ecclesiastical household, and whatever they could plunder they inflicted upon it, causing the continual cry of the poor to reach the ears of the most merciful bishop.
