He condemned to destruction the castle of the most wretched Theoderic at Altrich, the tower also called Lantfrid’s Court, [Note: [Col. 1563D] Lantfrocourt on the Saale.] occupied by the most wicked Everelmus, [Note: [Col. 1563] Witness 1 reads *Everelinus*; witnesses 2 and 3 read *Everelmus*.] and Vendœuvre, [Note: [Col. 1564D] Vendœuvre.] situated in the Calvomont district and belonging to Count Berald.

Let anyone who reads this know that he never avenged injuries inflicted specifically upon himself, but endured everything with an even spirit for Christ and for love of so great a name. Through the virtue of patience innate in him, he became an imitator of his Lord, who, as the blessed apostle says, “when he suffered, did not threaten; when he was insulted, he did not insult in return” (1 Peter 2:23).

He remembered that the same Lord, when delivered up, displayed complete patience. He did not quarrel, he did not cry out, and his voice was not heard in the streets. He remembered that he received the spittle of those who insulted him—the one who deigned by his own spittle to open the eyes of the man born blind. He was crowned with thorns—the one who crowns his holy martyrs with eternal flowers. He was struck in the face with palms—the one who grants true palms to the victorious. He was stripped of his garments—the one who clothes others with the garment of immortality. He was scourged—the one in whose name his saints and servants scourge the devil and the apostate angels.

He was fed gall—the one who gave and continually gives the heavenly food to the faithful, and who is the bread of the saints and of the angels. [Note: [Col. 1563] Witness 3 omits *est* (“is”).] He was given vinegar to drink—the one who daily offers Christians the saving cup of faith.

That innocent and just one—indeed, Innocence and Justice itself—was counted among sinners and the wicked. Truth was oppressed by false testimonies; he who will judge was judged; and the Word of God and God’s speech was led silently to sacrifice. At last he suffered and died the death of the cross, he who grants life to the world; rising again, he gives believers the hope of resurrection; ascending into heaven—since we shall ascend with him if we are found holy, joined and fastened to our Head by good works and deeds—we become members of Christ the Lord, who is the Head and principle not only of us but of all creatures.

21. All these things the Son of God [Note: [Col. 1563] Witnesses 2 and 3 read *Deus Filius Dei*, “God, the Son of God.”], impassible in his own nature but made passible in ours, deigned to endure for us through the power of patience, and he urged us to be patient not only by words but by examples.

This blessed man strove to follow and imitate him so closely that he never avenged or punished injuries inflicted upon him by anyone, however insignificant. With steadfast heart he carried out the Lord’s command by which he instructed blessed Peter: “I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times seven” (Matthew 18:22). Whatever wrong anyone might ever commit against him, he was able to forgive with the greatest patience; forgetful of injuries, he repaid evil with benefits rather than vengeance.

For a long time he patiently endured the plundering of churches and the injuries inflicted upon the sons of the Church. At last, wearied either by the enormity of the wickedness or by the excessive and continual cries of the poor, he acted because the discipline of his office required it and because the Lord’s command enjoined it. The command says that the wicked person is first to be reproved with God alone as witness, then with one or two witnesses present, and thirdly that the matter is to be told to the Church; thereafter, if he does not listen to the Church, he is to be treated as a heathen and a tax collector (Matthew 18:15, 17).

After all these measures had been offered to one who proved incorrigible, he would sometimes bind him with the bond of anathema, sometimes overthrow his wicked dwellings, and very often deprive him of his own possessions—not driven by greed, but compelled to do so for the correction of the wicked and the repose of the good. [Note: [Col. 1563] Witnesses 2 and 3 read “for the repose of the good.”]

Since he did these things from mercy rather than avarice, the fact was demonstrated by this: when he legally received anything from some wicked person, he never wished to mix any of it with his own uses. Instead, it was distributed either immediately to the poor or donated for the needs of restoring churches. [Note: [Col. 1563] Witnesses 2 and 3 read “rebuilding churches.”]

22. Since he never wished to reserve or accumulate what rightfully belonged to him either from his father’s and mother’s inheritance [Note: [Col. 1563] Witness 3 reads “matrimony.”] or from the treasures and great wealth of the Church entrusted to him, but spent and gave everything to the poor, widows, orphans, and especially the monks—who were in his care and were his supreme love—it is not credible that he would have desired to keep for himself anyone’s property, even property acquired lawfully, or to lock it away in ecclesiastical purses. [Note: [Col. 1563] Witnesses 2 and 3 read “reserve.”]

Truly blessed, truly a man in whom there was no deceit: he deceived no one, defrauded no one, but willingly shared his own, retaining for the next day either nothing or very little. A most devoted and constant executor of the apostolic command, he was content with food and clothing, saying: “We brought nothing into this world, and plainly we can take nothing out of it.”

He possessed humility in his conduct, steadfastness in faith, modesty in speech, justice in his deeds, mercy in his works, and discipline in his morals. He did not know how to inflict injury, but he knew how to endure injury. He knew how to maintain peace with his brothers, love God with his whole heart, love in him what is fatherly, fear what is divine, and place nothing at all before Christ, since Christ placed nothing before us.

He knew how to cling inseparably to Christ’s charity and to stand firmly and confidently by his cross, because he had learned that this was to become Christ’s fellow heir, that this was to fulfill God’s command, and that this was to accomplish the Father’s will.

What I am about to say may perhaps seem incredible to those who knew him only outwardly [Note: [Col. 1565] Witness 3 omits *his*], since by the nobility of his flesh and by nature he was more delicate and tender than all mortals, and altogether weak in enduring hard things. He never celebrated Mass or the divine sacraments without a hair shirt. He soaked the bread of the heavenly mystery with his innermost tears, and likewise always tempered the divine drink with weeping.

He always passed the vigils of the Nativity of the Lord, of holy Easter, of holy Pentecost, of all the holy apostles, and of the principal martyrs without any food, doing this in secret in the chamber of his conscience and heart while he entreated God. If he could remain in his homeland, he never kept the days of Lent without the monks. He was accustomed to do this especially at Gurgitensis, because that place, distinguished by the rigor of holy religion, rich in abundant wealth, and most agreeable in its setting and beauty, provided peaceful and quiet leisure for divine uses and the accomplishment of divine service.

During two Lents he repeated the journey to Rome solely for the love of God, and honored the most holy memorials and thresholds of the apostles with prayers and gifts.

If anyone slow to believe has denied or disputed that the blessed man wore a hair shirt, let him come to us. Let him see the hair shirt that he used and the woolen undergarment [Note: [Col. 1565D] An inner garment, a shirt.] that he wore throughout Lent—items obtained and preserved by us as great treasures [Note: [Col. 1565] Witness 3 reads “of the treasure.”] from those who were intimately acquainted with his secrets. Since nothing is impossible for God, what may be seen with the eyes must be accompanied by a faithful heart’s belief.

23. O how easy access the blessed man always provided for conversation, meals, and the seeking of every convenience—for every rank, every age, every profession, for the poor, the weak, the most insignificant person, the just, and the sinner! No one lacked his presence; his private chamber was open to all, his doors closed to none, his assistance was available to everyone, and no one lacked his gentle counsel.

Let those who very often assisted the holy bishop in celebrating Mass, refreshing the poor, and other works of devotion report, without my speaking, with what expense, what great almsgiving, and what devotion he honored and remembered the anniversaries of former bishops. Let them raise the just man with fitting praise for divine worship and service, recalling what is written: “All praise is sung at the end.” Let them remember also that the Wise Man said: “Do not praise a man during his lifetime” (Ecclesiasticus 11:30), because nothing true is established in this life: everything is full of falsehood, everything is fleeting. Praise cannot be certain where the end is not certain, until a person is joined to blessed life and united with him who is the way, the truth, and the life.

Then he is truly praised; then he truly enters human memory [Note: [Col. 1565] Witnesses 2 and 3 read “into memory”], because Christ is the praise, peace, joy, and honor of all the saints. Whoever begins here to praise and bless him, having been brought to completion by a good end [Note: [Col. 1565] Witness 2 reads *consummatus* (“brought to completion”); witness 3 corrects *consummatur* to *consummatus*.], on passing from here truly sees him face to face and truly praises and blesses him.

24. Some bishops of his time, through the arrogance of pride and others through simplicity of heart, disdained to admit the sons of secular priests to holy orders and were unwilling to receive them into the clergy. But this blessed man, despising and rejecting no one, received everyone freely, choosing or prejudging neither person nor lineage, while firmly retaining this principle:

“For God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation anyone who fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 10:34–35).

Scarcely a year passed during the whole period of his pontificate [Note: [Col. 1565] Witness 1 corrects *pertransiit* to *transiit*; witnesses 2 and 3 read *pertransiit*.] in which, either before the feast of the Lord’s Nativity or during Lent, on the Saturday appointed from ancient times for fasting [Note: [Col. 1565] Witness 3 reads *statuo* for *statuto*.], he did not ordain priests, deacons, and the other ministers belonging to ecclesiastical office, and earnestly commend himself to their prayers. The number of priests ordained by him advanced to nearly a thousand, while the multitude of those in the other orders cannot possibly be reckoned.

Who could say or describe the size of the crowds, the honor shown to God and all the saints, and the great joy of the people and the entire clergy whenever the blessed bishop either celebrated Mass publicly, performed the new dedication of a newly built church, or completed the blessings of the divine orders?

For the performance of such offices before the faces of men and in public, he was clothed and adorned with gold and every kind of precious pearl, gem, and stone. Yet inwardly, as we said above, he secretly wore the hardest and roughest hair shirt, offering the inner and spiritual things to the inner man, so that Christ might dwell in him through faith, while outwardly he fulfilled what belonged to customary worship without any appearance of pride or elation of empty glory.

25. Otto III, the august emperor, ruled almost until the final years of Lord Adalbero, the blessed bishop of Metz, and spent nearly all his life in the city of Rome. Consequently, the kingdoms and lands of his empire were devastated, so that scarcely even the foremost men, bishops, and leaders of the kingdoms had the means to endure or live.

From these most dangerous military expeditions and the pitiable hazards of plundering, this blessed and ever-memorable Adalbero continually escaped through the wisdom and intelligence given him by God. He regarded it as his greatest duty to rescue the people entrusted to him. Accepting whatever small assistance he could obtain from the sons of the Church, but selling and expending the greater part, indeed almost all, of his money and patrimony, he sent every year whatever could be gathered from every quarter for this scarcely bearable service and the unendurable gifts required. [Note: [Col. 1567D] A memorable example of money supplied to the emperor in place of military service; see Conrad II, chapter on military obligations, *Leges*, vol. II, 38**, chapter 2, with the gloss.]

He judged it more just and less burdensome to send lesser and fewer offerings than, being delicate and noble himself, to join the expedition and undertake every difficult journey, thereby burdening himself with greater expense for his own journey than for royal service, and with money granted to no one.

With wise intelligence he knew and foresaw that, although he was inferior by birth and blood to no mortal, and although he might have resisted, he ought not to resist authority [Note: [Col. 1567] Witnesses 2 and 3 read *restitere* for *resistere*], since the Lord says and commands: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” (Matthew 22:21)—namely, tribute, taxes, and census to Caesar, but works of devotion, the duties of prayer, and the fruit of almsgiving to God.

He knew [Note: [Col. 1567] Witnesses 2 and 3 read *Sciebatque* (“and he knew”)], that the apostle commands and exhorts: “Let every soul be subject to higher authorities” (Romans 13:1). Therefore he foresaw that it would be more beneficial for his own soul and for the souls of his subjects to surrender his possessions than himself, and to sell earthly things rather than spiritual ones. He remembered that the Lord had said that it profits a man nothing if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul (Matthew 16:26).

For when the soul is lost, nothing remains to be lost; when the soul is saved, even if bodily wealth is lacking, there will be no lack of riches which the thief cannot diminish, the moth cannot destroy, and rust cannot consume. His poverty will be enriched most abundantly. He will be as one possessing nothing yet possessing all things, and God will be everything to him in everything, so that he may be fulfilled in all things.

26. Fulfilling most perfectly the Lord’s command, “You have received freely; give freely” (Matt. 10:8), the venerable bishop also observed it most faithfully throughout his life. Never for ecclesiastical offices, never for ordaining ministers of his own cloister, and even less for abbots of monasteries—whom he consecrated in numbers approaching forty—did he accept money or any gift [Note: [Col. 1567] *quidpiam* (“anything”) 2. 3.]. He always shuddered at and fled from the Simoniac heresy as from deadly poison and a poisoned death.

If anyone should think that, in stating the number of abbots ordained by him, we have exceeded the truth in writing, let him remember that in some monasteries he promoted two men, in others three, to the place, name, and dignity of their father. This is shown by the holy place over which, by God’s authority, we preside, unworthy though we are. After the two holy and venerable fathers who preceded us—Fingenius from Ireland, for the Scots and the other holy pilgrims were always especially dear to him, and Lord Siriaudus, brought from the rods of Gorze to govern the monastery [Note: [Col. 1567D] Siriaudus died in 1004.]—we, who write these things, were compelled to succeed to its government as the third abbot through the blessing of this blessed pontiff.

He consecrated two abbots for Saint Trudo, two for Saint Adelfus, likewise two for Saint Felix, and two for Saint Martin beyond the river [Note: [Col. 1568D] The Moselle; Saint Symphorian was situated on the right bank of the river, Saint Martin’s monastery on the left.] Nor is there a monastery adjoining the holy city to which he did not grant the grace of his blessing to its appointed fathers, or to which he did not grant it twice or even three times, when one father entered upon the way of his predecessors and another succeeded him—apart from the fortunate house of Gorze. It is fortunate not only because of the man who now presides over it and serves it with the greatest holiness and kindness, but also because of those who, now blessed, have departed to the heavenly realms [Note: [Col. 1567] *transmigravit* (“departed”) 3.]. Their renowned and glorious life would demand books of its own, and their truly memorable deeds would require ample leisure for writing.

We would have judged it proper to insert much concerning the most honorable deeds of this man, greatly worthy of honor, in order to increase the distinction of our subject, and to give our pages grace from his exceedingly magnificent acts. But because, by God’s grace, he still survives for the benefit and advantage of his homeland [Note: [Col. 1567] homeland 3.], we fear being branded with the charge of flattery and reserve this for another time or person.

This Lord Immo, certainly a most venerable man [Note: [Col. 1567] lord 2. 3.], was appointed shepherd and abbot of the people of Gorze by Lord Theoderic, the holy pontiff, after the death of his father Odelbert. Of all the abbots and abbesses whom Lord Adalbero found presiding over the leading houses of Saint Stephen, he alone outlived that same holy bishop; and meanwhile—which gives us great joy—he still survives him.

27. Our blessed priest Adalbero, chosen by God, also consecrated Liudulfus as archbishop of Trier [Note: [Col. 1568D] He held the see from 994 to 1008.], a man distinguished by great simplicity of life and maturity of character. While these men lived and governed their churches, there were, we truly confess, times of peace; but after their deaths, the days were changed into the blackest appearance of night, displaying nothing but death and the dangers of death—not merely to the living, but to the dying and the truly dead.

Those whom excessive wealth and the great, prolonged insolence of peace had recently caused to be lamented after their death—and, as the common saying has it, whom the world did not know while they were green—are now mourned and bewailed with continual lamentations and tears, their dry limbs already reduced to ashes, in calamity and misery of every kind [Note: [Col. 1569D] He is writing about the wars conducted by Theoderic II, bishop, and his brother Duke Henry, against King Henry, Megingaud, archbishop of Trier, and Duke Theodoric from 1009 to 1012, wars not fully settled until 1017.].

Now, alas, these things have reached our own times—and would that these very times of ours did not exist! Life is hateful, and death is truly desired, since the person from whom the means of living is taken does not know how he might wish to live, while the one who lacks the expenses for the journey is wholly reluctant to undertake the road.

Cities have been depopulated; villages and estates have all been burned; men and women and the entire undifferentiated populace have been consumed by sword, famine, fire, and pestilence. Many nobles, too, have fallen into poverty and great misery; many have been slain by the sword, so that today it can truly be said: “The sword has reached even to the soul” (Jer. 4:10). Vineyards have been uprooted, trees and groves cut down, monasteries depopulated; and soon, when their inhabitants have been driven away, the dwellings of God’s servants and handmaids will be forced to become a vast solitude and wilderness.

Yet while the situation remains uncertain, while victory has been granted to neither side among those fighting and disputing, and while neither party knows how to yield to the other, we entrust the writing of these dirges and such immense laments to someone else. We have undertaken to place everything peaceful and everything most sweet into our pages, leaving those sorrowful matters, to be lamented more and more by our descendants day after day, for someone to describe in elegiac mourning—I will not say song.

28. When the time came for the blessed and God-worthy priest Adalbero to be rewarded according to the great precedence of his merits, and when he was to be brought to completion by a good end and the consummation of good perseverance—he who had lived well and was to die even better, although the departure of the saints is more truly called a passage from death to life, and no one who lives well can die badly—it happened that Theoderic, the brother of our pontiff, having taken certain properties from God and Saint Arnulf, after being wearied for a long time by prayers and legal proceedings, appointed an agreed day so that, by the judgment of wise men, whose right or wrong it was might be disclosed and made manifest [Note: [Col. 1569] “secretly,” 1.].

The appointed day arrived (May 1005), and the entire day was consumed by the necessity of investigating the case. Its excessive summer heat scorched everyone who had come, especially since, as we have often said, this blessed bishop, because of his lineage and nobility and also because of the excessive weakness of his own body, was considered more delicate and tender than words can express. He was impatient of every kind of labor. What he would neither have undertaken nor been able to bear for any advantage of this life, he endured for the love of God and Christ and for the benefit of the church entrusted to him: namely, to bear the burden of the day and the heat—of that particular day, whose excessive heat was so intolerable [Note: [Col. 1569] “intolerable”; the first *l* was erased in witness 1.] that no one could remember having seen such fervor or burning heat throughout the whole course of time or years. More grievously still, the day was consumed and prolonged by this oppressive condition until the evening was far advanced.

29. What more can be said? After the conference they departed. Though the day was already spent and three or four miles had been covered, he was compelled to continue the journey and reached Nomeny [Note: [Col. 1570D] Nomeny on the Seille.] almost at midnight, without food, in the middle of May, when daylight exceeds night in length by roughly threefold. At last, with a great company of soldiers, he allowed his greatly exhausted body to be refreshed.

But since he was a man to whom frugality in food and meals had always been contrary, while generosity and abundance had been friendly and familiar from his earliest years, they sat for a long time—almost until daylight—and he enjoyed immense happiness while dining with the clerics, whose company had been continuous and most delightful to him throughout his life, and with laymen of various ranks. Their excessive delay, as later became clear and as commonly happens, proved the cause of great loss, one to be mourned through all time.

For while they devoted themselves too excessively—far too excessively—to what belonged to another time, they eventually departed for their own lodgings and surrendered themselves to sleep later than was proper. The others made up in sleep during the following day what remained of the night. But since it is commonly said that death does not come without an occasion, the venerable pontiff, unwilling to depart from his customary practice or fail to offer God the nocturnal service that was due, had scarcely lowered his head to sleep and scarcely surrendered his most tender limbs to a little slumber [Col. 1570C] when, behold, he rose to confess God’s justice concerning his judgments and devotedly paid God the expenses of the nocturnal office, more fully than usual.

Then suddenly—let me relate the grief of his people, destined to endure forever!—so suddenly and so unexpectedly were all the blessed man’s limbs loosened by paralysis that, unable to perform any of their functions, they gave his whole body to the ground. The speed with which that most evil disease seized him was such that none of the clerics standing nearby could assist him before the blessed man’s body was thrown to the floor.

30. They therefore came as quickly as they could, and behold: under the force of so swift an attack, neither mouth nor foot, hand nor tongue, could perform any of its function. He was carried to bed in the arms of his disciples [Note: [Col. 1569] “by the arms of his disciples,” 2. 3.], and remained for three days unable to speak or attend to anyone. On the third day, however, the Lord was moved by the prayers of his people. For men and women, monks and nuns, even solitaries and hermits, came running from the corners not only of his own episcopal territory but of many regions, breaking down in extreme pain and indescribable grief; and they obtained from almighty God the restoration of voice and speech to his faithful servant.

Duke Theoderic, the pontiff’s brother, also hurried there. The leading counts and officers of his soldiers were present, nobles and commoners alike. Everyone from the city, its suburbs, fields, villages, and towns rushed in, crying out that they were wretched and unworthy of all good fortune, since they were being left bereft and abandoned by such a shepherd. They repeated in intolerable voices that wolves and every kind of evil beast were at the doors, and that they would be exposed to being torn apart by their bites even unto death [Note: [Col. 1571] “intolerable,” 2.].

31. When the venerable bishop heard these things, he was disturbed in mind and spirit and moved by the compassion innate in him. He dissolved into many tears. He predicted that many adversities would pursue the people after his death, just as he had often foretold while he was well; and now, being ill and, alas for us, sufficiently near his departure, he foretold them again.

He said that they should rather weep over their own misfortunes and lament themselves. Nothing unprecedented was taking place: the debt of the first parent must be exacted from everyone, since Christ our God and Lord, who was bound by no debt, had not refused to undergo and endure the most severe dangers of death.

Overcome by that illness, he lay for several days in the same village of Nomeny. Then, when a common decision had been reached and shared by clergy and people, he was carried to his own city: borne by many and received by still more. It is impossible to say how many voices and cries of widows, orphans, distinguished men, and most honorable women were raised into the upper air.

Monks and nuns, whose abundant harvest had grown into countless and innumerable sheaves through the long and unbroken labor and sweat of that same shepherd, came running—indeed, to speak more truthfully, burst in—setting aside, amid their excessive grief, the modesty owed to their order. Every sex and every age cried out:

“Alas! Alas! What will the people, the clergy, and the monastic order of both sexes do, deprived of so great a father and left without so great a shepherd? Everything that had understanding, everything that had life, loved you above all else: what will it do, where will it turn, to whom is it left to be subjected?”

32. The bishop himself, beloved of God, according to his customary practice, continually extended his hand in the sign of the cross. Not once, nor merely twice, but until he had been carried into the church of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, he did not cease to commend to God the people entrusted to him [Col. 1571D].

He had ordered that he first be carried before the altar of Saint Stephen and afterward through all the oratories of the house, so that he might entrust himself and his people to God and to the prayers of the saints. He did this as he was able, insofar as his strength or weakness permitted.

Then he was brought inside beneath the hands of episcopal bearers and laid upon his bed. As his illness required, the necessary and familiar assistance was provided for him. He began to distribute alms from his own possessions at Nomeny, but completed the work at Metz, so that he kept nothing of which he remembered himself to be possessed. If anything remained, it should be attributed rather to the greed of his people than to the negligence of the pious shepherd.

Whatever gold and silver, purple garments, and precious clothing he could possess, he took care to send not only to relatives and neighbors but also to servants of God living far away. He begged them to pray for the remedy of his soul and for his daily transgressions, without which scarcely anyone—or perhaps no one—lives, and to become intercessors for him before the merciful ears of the Godhead.

33. Sending the most honorable gifts to blessed Martin at Tours, Saint Dionysius at Paris, Saint Remigius at Reims, Saint Mary at Verdun, Saint Peter at Cologne, and many other saints throughout upper and lower France, he hastened, as best he could, to acquire patrons for the journey on which he was departing. He hurried to gain friends for himself from the mammon of iniquity [Note: [Col. 1571] “mammon,” 3.], so that they might receive him into eternal dwellings.

Thus, placed in such great weakness and weighed down by this burden of illness, he never ceased to seek heaven and heavenly things with continual sighs, earnestly directing his very eyes and spirit toward them. He always confessed with mouth and heart that he had deserved far greater things, since, according to the Apostle’s most sweet exhortation, the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in the saints who are striving for eternal glory and an everlasting crown (Rom. 8:18)—and may it be so in us also, unworthy and undeserving though we are.

Remembering the venerable patience and endurance of Saints Job and Tobit and of the other holy fathers of the Old and New Testament, who endured mockery and scourging, and moreover bonds and prisons, and were stretched out without accepting release, so that they might obtain a better resurrection [Note: [Col. 1571] Text lacking in witness 3.]—he also remembered the blessed little servant and always proclaimed his merits. In the very moment of this same fortunate man’s blessed death, when he was fixed in illness and joined virtues to his weakness, he deserved to be consoled by a visitation from Jesus Christ our Lord and to hear the voices of hymn-singing angels resound in heaven. He left to posterity, for imitation, what virtue perfected in weakness and what gentleness of patience can attain.

For the blessed and venerable priest Adalbero, so that the heap of his merits might reach perfection even through the burden of illness and grow fully into a perfect man, lay depressed by an illness so severe and so great, [lacuna; [Col. 1571] after *a*, witnesses 1 and 2 leave a blank space], with all the members of his right side dissolved by the gravest paralysis, and unable in any way to exercise the vigor of any function. Yet, through the ministry of his tongue alone, he unceasingly rendered praises to his Creator, God the Father; to his Redeemer, God the Son; and to his Illuminator, God the Holy Spirit.

34. After the spirit had long been commended to God through these fruits of good works and these practices and exchanges of blessed conduct [Note: [Col. 1573] Omitted in witnesses 2 and 3.], and after his soul had sought heaven, he happily departed to Him on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January. He departed to the One whom, thirsting for Him most devoutly throughout all the days he had lived, he had desired to have near him, and to whom he had labored to be joined by tireless prayers and cries and by the unwearied practice of good works.

It was the first hour of Friday, when the entire population of the city, both out of the customary reverence of faith and in honor of the Lord’s coming [Note: [Col. 1573] “of the day,” 2. 3.], had gathered in the churches of the saints in sacred and proper fashion and was attending to the rite and service of prayers and Masses.

Then, behold, the noise of those running together arose; a cry went up into the heights at the death of the pious shepherd. With tearful sighs, the wholly grieving and most sorrowful people hastened to commend him to God and followed his departure with fitting reverence and fitting ritual.

Prayers and praises were offered to God as duty required; mourning and weeping were offered to the most pious father out of affection. They owed this to the father, that they should pray for the absolution and commendation of his soul [Note: [Col. 1573] “for the absolution of the soul,” absent in witness 3.]; and they owed it to themselves, that they should grieve over the departure of one so loved and deeply beloved, and over the loss caused by his absence and departure.

Although, in leaving this world, he had obtained the heavenly things he had long sought, those whom he left behind cried out as loudly as they could that they were destined to descend into excessive mourning and bitter days because of the great sweetness of their daily conversations and the habitual mutual kindness they had shared with him.

35. Meanwhile, after the rites had properly been completed around the blessed man’s body, his holy limbs had been washed according to custom, and he had been clothed in pontifical garments, themselves precious beyond anything ever seen, he was carried to the mother church amid the lamentation and mourning of clerics, abbots, monks, and laypeople of various ranks and ages. He was laid before the altar of Saint Stephen, the most precious first martyr and chief of the Levites.

There, throughout the whole part of the day that remained and throughout the following night, he was attended with the customary vigils and psalms, celebrated with great devotion—not only by the city’s clerics, regular clergy, and household servants, but also by those from the suburbs and by outsiders, a great and abundant multitude of whom had gathered from every direction.

[Col. 1573D] 36. On the following day, which was called the Sabbath (December 15), after Masses had been celebrated and offerings given to God with great reverence, and after vows and prayers had been offered most dutifully until the ninth hour for the commendation of the blessed soul, they lifted the venerable body and carried it through the middle of the city toward the south, outside the walls, to the place that he himself had begun to build from its foundations as the first undertaking of his works, as soon as he became bishop. He had prepared it for God and Saint Symphorian [Note: [Col. 1573] “and Saint Symphorian,” 2. 3.], and had ordered that he himself be buried there.

That place was and is renowned and celebrated for the bodies of many holy predecessors of his, the bishops of Metz. Saint Aeplicius [Note: [Col. 1573] “Aepletius,” 2. 3.], sufficiently distinguished among his fellow bishops for holiness and antiquity, whose merit has been made known in our own times through the revelations of many people, rests there.

Lord Papolus, whom Saint Arnulf succeeded in the episcopate and who bestowed many estates as benefactions upon that place; blessed Goericus, a wonderful worker of miracles in our own times; Saint Godo, the brother of that same Bishop Goericus, who succeeded them in the episcopate and were related by blood and flesh even to Saint Arnulf; Lord Aptatus; Lord Felix; and very many other priests of the same city are honored there, buried with due respect.

Drawn by love for them and by the beauty of the place, this blessed bishop ordered that he be buried there [Note: [Col. 1573] “that he be buried there,” 2. 3.; *sepeliri* is corrected to *sepeliri* in witness 2.].

37. The body was finally laid before the altar of Saint Symphorian the martyr. On the Sunday that followed, throughout both night and day (December 16), and almost until the evening hour of the fourth day after his departure, which was reckoned as Monday (December 17), it was visited by a great throng of the faithful and with profound devotion. By a sweet rivalry, the congregations of the saints hastened to anticipate one another in keeping the vigils with the greatest zeal, by night and by day.

At last his brother Theoderic arrived, mourning deeply as though already present the losses that would soon result from his brother’s death. Lord Bertaldus, the venerable bishop of Toul, also hurried there. He recalled and repeatedly recounted with many words and tears how gently and sweetly he had been raised by the same man until he was advanced to the summit of the episcopate [Note: [Col. 1573] The words “but he removed him” were added and then erased in witness 2.].

After the solemn Masses had been celebrated, he entrusted the body of the man he loved to burial and commended his spirit and soul to God the giver with great care and devotion.

He was buried beside the altar of the venerable martyr Saint Symphorian, on the left, as he had ordered. As a wise man who always considered what was useful and reflected upon what was salutary, he had discovered and established this, among other holy practices: that his burial should be near the saints, so that the priest standing at the divine table to celebrate the sacred mysteries might continually remember him, whose venerable bodily tomb was kept and seen before his eyes.

He assumed the episcopal office in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 984, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November; he was ordained in the same year on the fifth day before the Kalends of January. He passed from this light to blessed life and true light in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1005 [Note: [Col. 1573] In witness 1, a blank space is left in place of these words.], in the third indiction [Note: [Col. 1573] In witness 1, a blank space is left in place of these words.], while King Henry was reigning, in the sixth year of his reign [Note: [Col. 1573] In witness 1, a blank space is left in place of these words.]. In heaven, on earth, and throughout the sea, however, God and our Lord Jesus Christ reigned and ruled. To Him, with the eternal God the Father and the eternal God the Holy Spirit, belong perpetual praise, unfailing honor, continual glory, ineffable splendor, incomparable greatness, and infinite dignity. He is the blessedness of all the saints, the salvation of the sick, the remission of sins, the salvation of the living, and the resurrection of the dead, now and always and throughout all ages of ages [Note: [Col. 1575] “of ages,” 2.]. Amen.

## Epitaph of Adalbero

[Col. 1575]

Reader, halt your step, you who strive upward by your desire;

Here read carefully, noting what has been written,

So that you may strive to preserve a peaceful life,

In the manner in which he lived, whom this brief urn contains.

Here lies an outstanding citizen [Note: [Col. 1575] “ashes,” correction.], adorned with royal stock,

Kept in the tomb until he rises from the earth.

Here a father, shepherd, and gentle teacher in all things,

By the illustrious name of Adalbero, shone forth.

For twenty-two years he happily presided

Over the church of Metz, the Lady’s church.

A follower of the laws, the most upright model for his inferiors,

He went before them in deed and urged them by speech.

Distinguished by the jewels of virtue, he led his life,

And treated everyone as his own children.

Here, a kindly father, he loved the virginal communities of monks,

And preferred them to slippery laymen.

He was a foot for the lame and a shining path for the blind,

Comforting the sorrowful and restoring the needy.

He was difficult for no one, except perhaps for those bent upon crooked paths;

Yet even these, in his goodness, he guided toward better things.

For the praise of the Lord and his own everlasting reward,

He raised up and built many churches.

Founding this temple, laboring with much sweat,

Here he established that the Lord’s service should be performed;

But it was not completed as he wished, because a devouring end took him away.

Alas, the dreadful lot of death, which carried him to the heavenly ones!

The people mourn him, as did much youth,

Fathers and children, and the servant of God.

On the fourteenth day of the month of December,

Departing from the world, he gave himself to the Most High.

Reader, say: “God, creator, have mercy on this guilty man!”

And let every person cry out: “May he live in Christ!”

O Father Ratramnus, venerable master in speech,

Sweet, dear, graceful, eloquent, kindly, and wise,

Standard-bearer in war, leader of citizens in time of peace,

Your fame for virtue is proclaimed through every remote region.

Look now with tranquil eye upon what has been written here [Note: [Col. 1575] “Look,” correction.].

I have written for you the forms of so many verses;

Choose from the many those which you may write upon the tomb

Of the elder beloved by you and by everyone.

If any sound graceful, may they please you, kindly father;

Let what sounds harsh be buried in enclosed silence [Note: [Col. 1575] A word is missing.].

O sweet elder, sweeter than every nectar and honey,

I, little Conrad, prostrate myself before you on high [Note: [Col. 1575] The codex reads *κουωνραδουμ*.].

And I ask you, holy father, than whom no other is holier:

When you have finished these not very polished verses,

Say with a kindly heart: “May he who made them live in blessing.” Amen.

[Col. 1576C] Words of the Book:

When I was a radiant young man, I used to approach as a borrower

The holy monastery consecrated to lofty Nabor,

In which many illustrious men, tested in virtue,

Labor in everlasting praise;

In which great peace shines and wisdom reigns.

Among them concord gleams together with holy conduct.

When I came there, I considered myself fortunate;

For I carried bare skins on both head and tail,

I was naked on every side; but soon I departed clothed.

I do not believe that you, Lucanus, were adorned like me,

Nor did Constantine, though possessed of honor, clothe you

As Conrad clothed me—may he always be blessed [Note: [Col. 1575] The codex reads *expnrbdxs*.];

Through whose efforts I shine with fresh signs,

And now, from the margin and from my own page,

I compose many more riddles.

Whoever reads these, say: “May those who serve Saint Nabor

Live forever in the heights, by an everlasting destiny.”

Whoever willingly looks upon these verses,

Placed here on every side, useful and rightly deserving to be read,

Say: “May life and salvation belong to Conrad, the poor wretch.”

## In the Year of Our Lord 1024. Pope Benedict VIII

[Col. 1577]

## Historical Notice

*(From Mansi,* Conciliorum amplissima Collectio, *XIX, 323.)*

[Col. 1577A] Benedict, a Tusculan by nationality, the eighth of this name, was made pontiff in the year of our Redeemer 1012, during the reign of King Henry. Against him, in schism and contrary to the sacred canons, Gregory was appointed. Relying upon the power of the Romans, he expelled Benedict from the City.

The pontiff, unable to endure this injury inflicted by the schismatic, went to King Henry, who was staying in Saxony. After laying before the emperor the violence and dishonor he had suffered, King Henry, assembling and preparing an army as quickly as he could, set out for Rome to avenge the injury inflicted upon the Apostolic See.

At his arrival, Gregory the schismatic pseudopope, terrified, abandoned the City and fled. Benedict, whom the king had sent ahead, recovered the same chair of Peter.

Since Benedict had decided to confer the imperial crown upon Henry when he came to Rome, he ordered, as Ditmarus says, that a golden orb be made as the imperial emblem for presentation to the king, that it be surrounded on all four sides by the most precious gems, and that a golden cross be inserted above it [Col. 1577B].

It resembled the appearance of this worldly structure, which is said to stand enclosed within a certain roundness. Thus, when the ruler of earthly power looked upon it, it would be a lesson to him that he ought to rule or wage war in the world in no other way than as one deemed worthy to be protected by the standard of the life-giving cross. The decoration of the various gems likewise signified that the summit of imperial power ought to be adorned with the forms of many virtues.

As the king approached and drew near the City, the pious pontiff went out to meet him. He offered him the emblem and insignia of empire that he had prepared; and shortly afterward, after Henry had been brought into the City, he adorned him with the imperial title and crown, together with his most holy wife Chunegund.

Desiring to consecrate the beginnings of his empire to God, Henry pursued the Roman Church with distinguished munificence, piously and holily.

He attacked the Saracens, who were invading the shores of the Church, drove them away in war, and successfully defeated them. As Glaber relates in Book III, chapter 8, he imposed capital punishment upon certain Jews living in Rome because, on Good Friday, imitating the deed of those who crucified Christ, they had subjected an image of Christ to the same injuries and insults that Christ himself had once suffered [Col. 1577C–1578A].

He adds that on that same day, after the cross had been adored, toward evening a whirlwind of winds shook the whole of Rome, and nearly all the Romans were killed; nor did the winds cease before the pontiff had imposed capital punishment upon the Jews accused by a Jew.

At his urging, the Normans defeated the Greeks in Apulia in several victories. When Emperor Henry asked him to confirm by his presence the bishopric of Bamberg, which the emperor himself had founded, Benedict came to Bamberg in Germany. There, after dedicating the church of Saint Stephen, he obtained, through the emperor’s donation, dominion over the city itself and all its rights.

For after that time, when it had paid an annual census to Rome as its mistress for some while, the younger Henry, in order to free it and remove it from Roman dominion, surrendered Benevento in its place, in the time of Leo IX, Roman pontiff. (Leo of Ostia, Book II, chapter 47.)

He urged the emperor to bring aid against the Greeks. For in the second year after the pontiff had come to Germany, the emperor, terrifying to his enemies, entered Italy with an army. By his arrival he captured some supporters of the Greeks and drove away others; he besieged and conquered Capua, Troia, and other cities belonging to the Greeks.

In the following year he returned to Germany and held a meeting with Robert, king of the Franks, concerning the condition of the kingdom, the Church, and the empire, and presented him with many gifts.

Pope Benedict departed this life on the third day before the Kalends of March in the year 1024, after having sat for twelve years. Two or more apparitions made after his death indicate that he suffered the punishments of purgatory. In them, as Peter Damian reports in his account of Odilo preserved by Surius and in his letter to Nicholas II, he asked to be released through the intercession of Odilo and the alms of his brother, his successor in the Apostolic See.

[Col. 1577]

## Another Notice

*(Cocquelines,* Bullarum, privilegiorum amplissima Collectio, *I, 317.)*

[Col. 1577C] Benedict VIII, a Tusculan by nationality, son of Gregory, count of Tusculum, formerly called John, bishop of Porto, was enthroned not long after the death of Sergius, as appears from the documents written below.

He sat in the pontificate for eleven years, eleven months, and twenty-one days. He lived during the reigns of the emperors Basil and Constantine in the East, and in the West during the reign of Henry II, whom he crowned at Rome in 1014.

He died in the year 1024, approximately in August or September. For it does not seem that one should depart from what is stated concerning Sergius IV: that his death was assigned to August 18, 1012, according to the Benedictine Menologium. From that date, it is clear to anyone calculating that nearly twelve years elapsed until Benedict’s death, which should be assigned approximately to the beginning of September, especially if only a few days are allowed for the vacancy of the see.

### The Nineteenth Schism

When Benedict had prevailed over a certain Gregory in the election, although he had to yield to the more powerful man, he went to King Henry in Saxony with all the apostolic equipment, making his expulsion known to everyone with lamentation.

Therefore, when King Henry hurried to avenge the injury inflicted upon the Apostolic See, Gregory the schismatic pseudopope, terrified, abandoned the City and fled. Benedict, however, the pontiff whom the king had sent ahead, recovered the same chair of Peter.

[Col. 1579]
