# Letters and Decrees of Pope Benedict VIII

## Genuine

### I. Letter of Pope Benedict VIII to Bruno, Bishop of Langres (1012)

*[Pérard,* Collection of Several Curious Pieces Serving the History of Burgundy, *Paris, 1664, folio, p. 172.]*

[Col. 1579B]

Benedict, bishop of the holy universal Church, to Bruno, bishop of Langres: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Of the monastery of the martyr Saint Benignus, where, as we have learned from you, Willelm, a monk devoted to his holy vocation, was ordained abbot, I have reread the privileges of my predecessors and also the commands of the kings of France, sent to me by you or by that abbot; and, as your goodness requested, I have decided that they should be confirmed. Therefore, whatever they decreed concerning the borough, cloister, cemetery, authorities, and all appurtenances known to belong to the aforesaid saint, and whatever your predecessors established by their decrees, these things they decided should be confirmed by the authority of God, of blessed Peter the apostle, and by the written instrument of our privilege. [Col. 1579C] If anyone should oppose or violate these provisions, let him know with certainty that he has been struck down by us with the sword of anathema. We also admonish you to defend the aforesaid place under your protection against the attacks of outsiders and against the importunities of your own people. And because we know that you—and we fear this of your successors—do not act out of zeal for the religious purpose of monastic life, and that you have built and loved this same place, we therefore prohibit you or your successors from forbidding divine worship to be celebrated there, when the designated abbot earnestly requests it. We confirm this also by the authority of blessed Gregory, who for this very reason rebuked and prohibited John, bishop of the Old City, from forbidding divine offices to be celebrated in monasteries, because whenever [Col. 1580C] anything unusual is done in a monastery, the regular order is thereby obstructed and the guardianship of religion is relaxed to no small degree. Following this example, we decree that divine worship is to be celebrated continually in the monastery of Dijon for the welfare of the holy Church, so that the frequent celebration of Masses and prayers may be able to calm the storms and tempests of those who attack it—unless, which God forbid, some breach, treachery by the prelate of the aforesaid see, or some form of captivity should befall the Church of Langres or the same monastery, in which circumstances they ought voluntarily to cease from the office. Farewell.

Issued on the day before the Kalends of December, by the hand of Peter, librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the tenth indiction.

## II. Privilege of Pope Benedict VIII for the monastery of Saint Benignus of Dijon (1012)

[PÉRARD, *Recueil*, etc., p. 273.]

[Col. 1581B]

BENEDICT, prelate of the holy universal Church, to his beloved son in Jesus Christ, WILLELM, abbot of the monastery of Dijon, and to his successors regularly appointed, greeting and apostolic blessing.

By the office entrusted to us, we ought to watch over the peace of holy places, so that the more peacefully the Lord is served in them, the more devoutly he may be served.

Therefore, dearest son Willelm, granting your petitions, we decree that your monastery is to be preserved under apostolic protection, and we prohibit the bishop of Langres or his successors from prohibiting divine worship in that monastery. We confirm this also by the authority of blessed Gregory, [Col. 1581C] who for this reason rebuked and prohibited John, bishop of the Old City, from forbidding divine worship to be celebrated in monasteries, because whenever this or anything unusual is done in monasteries, the regular order is thereby obstructed and the guardianship of religion is relaxed to no small degree. Following this example, we decree that divine worship is to be celebrated continually in the monastery of Dijon for the welfare of the holy Church, so that the frequent celebration of Masses and prayers may calm the storms and tempests of those who attack it—unless, which God forbid, some breach or captivity should in any way befall the Church of Langres or the same monastery, in which circumstances they ought voluntarily to cease from the office. You are also to correct, with paternal discipline and according to the fear of God and the rule of blessed Benedict, any excesses committed by any of your monks, [Col. 1581D] nor may any bishop pronounce a sentence of interdict against them, or harass them with any exactions or levies, so long as those monks wish to remain subject to your discipline and to be placed under regular institutions. Whatever privileges of my predecessors, whatever commands of kings or emperors, and whatever writings of the bishops of Langres or of other persons the same monastery is known to possess, we confirm by this present decree; likewise, we decree by the authority of blessed Peter and our own that the possessions, dignities, and liberties recorded in those documents are to remain perpetually whole and inviolate. If anyone should oppose or violate these provisions, [Col. 1582A] let him know with certainty that he has been struck down by us with the sword of anathema.

Issued on the Kalends of December, by the hand of Peter, librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the tenth indiction.

## III. Benedict VIII confirms all the rights and property of the Church of Urgell (1012)

[COCQUELINES, *Bullarium*, vol. I, p. 319.]

[Col. 1582B]

BENEDICT, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and spiritual son ERMENGAUD, bishop of the holy Church of Urgell, and to your successors forever.

The concern of our apostolic office urges us to provide for the welfare of all churches and, lest they collapse utterly, [Col. 1582B] to grant them perpetual support. Therefore we wish it to be known to all archbishops, dukes, marquises, counts, viscounts, and all the sons of the holy Church of God that, together with all our clergy—bishops, cardinals, priests, deacons, and subdeacons—we confirm and grant to the aforesaid bishop Ermengaud his already-mentioned bishopric of the holy Church of Urgell in its entirety, with all its buildings, castles, villages, estates, and holdings, with the churches situated therein, as well as vineyards, lands, meadows, pastures and forests, fruit-bearing and non-fruit-bearing trees, fertile and barren trees of every kind, marshes and swamps, willow groves, wells, springs, streams, mills, fisheries, and also [Col. 1582C] hunting rights, waters and watercourses, mountains and hills, tracts and plains, caverns, and their appurtenances, cultivated or uncultivated; likewise, the dependencies of the same bishopric, namely the counties of Cerdanya, Llívia, Berguedà, Pallars, Ribagorça, Josa, Cardós, Noguera, and Tírvia; the place of Saint Deodata with its boundaries; also the castle called Turres with its boundaries; Bescaran with its boundaries; together with the allod called Sor; the small estates called Letone and Colpedra with their boundaries; Aclo and Sardina with their boundaries; the small estate called Boscedera; Calbitiano with its boundaries; Lenztirdo with its boundaries; Submonte with its boundaries; the allods in the valley of Andorra [Col. 1582D] that belonged to Count Senifred; the fief of Archavello; the allod of Salellas with the fief of Saint Stephen; and the villages called Montaneo, Lello, and Cubilare, with their boundaries or borders; also the village called Salento with its boundaries; the castle of Sanguia with its boundaries; and the village called Tossen with its boundaries, which Count Borrell formerly gave to this bishopric for the sake of his soul and which was later confirmed to this bishopric by his son, Bishop Ermengaud.

We also confirm that same village with its boundaries as belonging henceforth to the place called the holy Church of Urgell, from the time when Count Raimund returned it to the power of the Lord God and his exalted mother, and into the hand of the aforesaid Bishop Ermengaud, for the remedy of his own soul and that of his wife Ermesinde, and for the remedy of the soul of his father and of his brother Ermengaud; also the allod called Castellione, with Guardiola and Solane, with their boundaries or borders; and the allod called Turrizella with its boundaries; and the inheritance which he gave to the aforesaid Bishop Ermengaud for the aforementioned holy see of Urgell, which came to him by succession from his father, with this arrangement: while Arnaldus, his brother, lives, he is to hold and possess it, but after his death it is to remain with the aforesaid holy see; likewise the allod at the place called Spongia.

We also confirm to him a third part of the market toll of the same bishopric, with its appurtenances, and everything generally and entirely belonging to that bishopric in all its places wherever they may be. The aforesaid bishopric is situated within the territories of Urgell, Cerdanya, Berguedà, Pallars, and Ribagorça.

We likewise confirm to you and your successors the first fruits and tithes of the places and dependencies of the aforesaid bishopric. We also establish in full that no person may presume unjustly to deliver the clerics residing in your bishopric to detention or secular jurisdiction.

For the aforesaid bishopric, with all things belonging to it wherever they may be, was granted by charter to the Frankish kings by the lord and most excellent King Charles of the region of France, and was confirmed by the writing bearing his name [Col. 1583C] and by the royal seal; likewise by the grant and donation of King Louis, the son of Charles; and by the confirmation of the king’s commands, marked and sealed with the personal seal of Lord King Charles Louis’s son. It was also secured by the privileges of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of Lord Pope Agapitus and the other apostles who served here and whose obligations they observed, the preceding bishops remaining under the yoke and service of the inviolate Mother of God.

Thus we too, by apostolic authority, confirm and establish that from now and henceforth whatever you and your successors shall lawfully acquire, in future times from the present year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1013 [Note: [Col. 1583D] Read: 1012.], in the eleventh indiction, moved by your prayers, through your royal commands and the text of this privilege, shall be held, possessed, administered with the fear of God, and governed by you and your successors forever. No king, prince, count, marquis, judge, or any person, great or small, may presume ever to inflict violence upon or invade that bishopric or its dependencies.

For this reason, invoking the divine judgment and promulgating the prohibition of anathema, we have decreed that none of our pontifical successors, as stated above, nor any person, great or small, may dare or presume to act unjustly against this apostolic privilege in any matter, or attempt to break it. Therefore, whoever robs, removes, defrauds, invades, retains, or devastates anything belonging to this holy Church, or suppresses it by wicked cunning, shall be held as a murderer and judged guilty in the sight of God’s just judgment; he shall be judged a sacrilegious person, and unless he is reconciled through pure, proven, and public penance and through satisfaction to the Church by the laying on of bishops’ hands, according to canonical sanctions, he shall not possess the kingdom of God. He shall not only be alienated from the kingdom of God but also expelled from the thresholds of the holy Church of God.

The perpetrators of such crimes, unless they make satisfaction, shall dare to communicate neither while alive nor after death, and, moreover, shall be condemned by the bond of anathema, made hateful to God and his saints [the text is defective: “odibiles,” or something similar], and expelled from communion with the Catholic Church. Following their examples, we anathematize all such presumptuous persons, expel them from the thresholds of the holy Church of God by apostolic authority, condemn them, and judge them to be sacrilegious—not only those who commit these acts but also those who consent to them, since not only the perpetrators are judged guilty, but also those who consent to the perpetrators. The same punishment indeed encompasses both the agents and those who consent.

But if anyone—which we do not believe—should attempt to violate this in any respect, let him know that, unless he repents, by the authority of God, of the holy apostle Peter, and of us, who exercise his vicariate, he is to be bound indissolubly by the bonds of anathema [Col. 1584C], alienated from the kingdom of God, and burned in eternal fire with the devil, his most atrocious pomp, and Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ; and, plunged into the abyss and Tartarean chaos, let him perish with the ungodly. But whoever proves to be the guardian and observer of this privilege shall obtain manifoldly from the just Judge, our Lord God, the grace of blessing and heavenly recompense, and may deserve to become a participant in eternal life. Amen.

Written by the hand of Benedict, notary, regional officer, and scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of December, in the eleventh indiction.

Giselbertus, by the grace of God bishop.

Sigefredus of Siena, clothed by God’s providence with the episcopal insignia of the Church of Parma.

I, Pontius, though unworthy, bishop of Arretium under the hand of almighty God, confirm and seal this document so that it may remain firm in God’s name for all time. I, Peter, bishop of Pavia, have subscribed. I, Sigefredus, guardian of the holy Church of Piacenza, consenting, have subscribed. I, Leo, bishop and, though unworthy, guardian of the Church of Vercelli, have subscribed. I, Hotkerus, bishop of Liège, have subscribed. I, Benedict, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida, was present and subscribed. I, Aimericus, bishop of Ribagorza, have subscribed. Peter, bishop of Maguelonne; Borrellus, though unworthy, bishop; Boniface, bishop of Turin: I have subscribed.

## IV. Benedict VIII confirms the privileges of the Church of Bamberg at the request of King Henry and Bishop Eberhard (1013)

[PERTZ, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, Scriptores IV, 808, in *The Life of Emperor Henry*, by Adalbert.]

[Col. 1585A]

BENEDICT, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved lord in Christ and most serene king HEINRICH, crowned by God, his spiritual son, and also to Eberhard, his brother and fellow bishop, the venerable bishop of the holy Church of Bamberg, eternal salvation in the Lord and apostolic blessing.

Among all the things arranged by the counsel of divine providence, it is especially worthy of the Creator’s praise that venerable places are elevated and rightly ordered through the resources of great and God-devoted men, in view of piety and in hope of eternal recompense; that they are enriched by the benefits of their possessions and, with Christ’s help, transformed into a better condition. Hence, dearest son in all things, since it is clear that you have devotedly and mercifully done everything for the praise and glory of our Redeemer, you could do nothing more perfect or better to merit the kingdom of heaven than to make him your heir from whom you are to receive an eternal inheritance, and to raise the holy Church of Bamberg through yourself to the summit of episcopal dignity. There you chose as patrons for yourself the most blessed Mother of God, ever-virgin [Col. 1585C] Mary; the most blessed apostles of Christ, Peter and Paul; and the holy martyrs Kilian and George. With Christ’s favor and a fitting return, they will provide perpetual assistance for attaining the heavenly kingdom.

For so great a service rendered to God and his saints, we first offer him due thanks and praise, for he inspired you to undertake so holy a work and, in his abundant mercy, resolved to help you complete it according to your desire. Moreover, since the holy Roman Church, well founded upon the firm rock, has always shown true charity by rejoicing in the advancement of other churches, it is fitting for our apostolic governance that we, who by God’s authority serve him, should rejoice fully in your holy zeal, hoping to have a share in your work if we make what is yours through labor ours through charity.

Therefore, since you, together with our brother Eberhard, the God-worthy bishop of that same holy Church of Bamberg, asked us to confirm by a privilege of our authority everything granted to him and to his Church by the authority of privileges from our predecessors, namely the supreme pontiffs Lord John and Sergius, we have considered the affection of your devotion and the purpose of your pious will and have most willingly decided to grant your petitions.

Accordingly, establishing and promulgating this before God and before his terrifying future judgment, through the text and constitution of this apostolic privilege [Col. 1586A] we decree and sanction, by the authority of the blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, of the holy martyrs Kilian and George, and of all the other saints in whose name the aforementioned Church has been dedicated, and we solemnly adjure both the future pontiffs of the apostolic see and those who administer ecclesiastical affairs, as well as all who bear the name of Christian, that no one shall have permission to tear away, destroy, harass, or alienate anything granted to that Church by privileges of our predecessors, or given or to be given by us, or handed over to the aforesaid Church by any faithful men or women, or to be handed over in future times—whether families, lands, or any possessions. If anyone—which we do not believe—should attempt with rash boldness to oppose what has been piously and faithfully arranged through this privilege with stable and unshakable firmness, or to resist or transgress in any way what we have established for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid Church, let him know that, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of all the apostles, and by our own authority, in whose place we act though unworthy, he is bound by the bonds of anathema and is to be burned with the devil, his most atrocious pomp, and Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the punishment of eternal fire—unless he repents and makes worthy satisfaction to that Church.

But whoever, with devout intention, proves to be an observer [Col. 1586C] of this privilege, which is directed toward the worship of God, may obtain manifoldly from the most merciful God and Lord the grace of blessing and may deserve to become a participant in eternal life. May the Holy Trinity preserve your charity undefiled.

Written by the hand of Herhardus, scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of June, in the eleventh indiction. Issued by the hand of Benedict, bishop of Porto and librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the first year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal Pope VIII.

## V. Bull of Pope Benedict VIII confirming all the property and rights of the monastery of Farfa (1013)

[MURATORI, *Script. Ital.*, II, 557.]

[Col. 1586D]

BENEDICT, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in the Lord, GUIDO, fellow angel, abbot of the monastery called Farfa, in the district of Acutianus, and to your successors forever.

Since you asked us to grant, from our generosity and gift, to your religious community, on the estate of Massa, the church of Saint Mary at the place called Formello, with all its furnishings, vineyards, and lands, as formerly held by the two priests named Benedict, who now appear to be your monks, together with its access and exit and everything generally belonging to it in every respect, therefore we grant it to you. Moreover, on the aforesaid estate of Massa we grant you three complete farmsteads: namely, the farmstead of Petroccio, the farmstead of Leo of Sabina, and the farmstead of Peter, son of Leo the smith, with houses, vineyards, lands, fields, meadows, pastures, forests and trees, fruit-bearing and barren, fertile and unfruitful, of every kind, cultivated or uncultivated, vacant or occupied. Their boundaries and borders are as they now are and as they were from the beginning, and as is contained in the charter of your acquisition, and as the heirs of the aforesaid men now appear to retain them for cultivation with their own hands.

Everything belonging to the holy Roman Church, over which by God’s authority we preside and which we serve, we grant to you to hold, by this present decree, from the present eleventh indiction, for you and your successors to retain perpetually without rent or census. Establishing this by apostolic censure and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, under solemn invocation of divine judgment and the prohibitions of anathema, we decree that no future pope among our successors, nor any other person, great or small, may ever remove or alienate the named places in any way from your power and jurisdiction, or from that of your successors and your monastery.

If any person, great or small, should presume with rash boldness to act against this privilege, let him know that he is alienated from God and condemned with all the ungodly to eternal fire and punishment. But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be the guardian and observer of this privilege shall deserve to obtain grace, mercy, and eternal life from our most merciful Lord God, forever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of Benedict, regional notary and scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the apostolic hand [Note: [Col. 1587D] Read: “in the month of April.” JAFFÉ], in the aforesaid eleventh indiction.

Farewell.

Issued on the eighth day before the Kalends of May by the hand of Benedict, by the grace of God bishop of the Church of Saint Silva Candida and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the first year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord Benedict, most holy Pope VIII.

## VI. Donation of lands made to the monastery of Farfa and its abbot Guido by Pope Benedict VIII (1013)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, IV, 799.]

[Col. 1587D]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. In the first year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal Pope VIII, in the most sacred see of blessed Peter; in the eleventh indiction, in the month of June, on the second day.

Since the law of divine majesty unquestionably requires that, for the attainment of the eternal joys of the heavenly kingdom, offerings be contributed to divine worship, and since we are able to strive so that all things may remain in venerable places with perfect and complete stability—not merely by a verbal declaration of firmness, but also so that the page may be attested by the text of written documents—we wish the following to be recorded, especially in places where praises are offered to almighty God. Thus, what is known to have been arranged for the glory of his holy name may be acceptable to our Redeemer; and what is written below is offered to Lord Gregory and Lady Maria, my parents, for whose love and forgiveness and for the sake of my sins I make this offering, so that recompense may be granted to them by the same Lord God through his most holy mercies in the heavenly citadels, and so that they may deserve to obtain forgiveness for all their sins.

Therefore I, the aforesaid Lord Benedict, prelate of Rome, from this day give, donate, cede, transfer, and irrevocably bestow, and at the same time grant, from my own property, of my own spontaneous and free will, to you, Guido, venerable priest, monk, and abbot of the venerable monastery [Col. 1588B] of Holy Mary, Mother of God and our Lady, in the Sabine district at the place called Acutianus, and to your successors, abbots, priests, and monks, both greater and lesser, who are to serve God in that venerable monastery, in return for your most holy, faithful, and daily prayers, which you do not cease to offer for the salvation of our souls.

Accordingly, I recompense, donate, and offer, for my soul and for the souls of my parents of pious memory named above, the whole and entire vineyard and land held for cultivation by Benedictulus, who was called “of Laxo,” and by his son Pecculus, who were our servants, together with houses, vineyards, lands, fields, pastures, forests, willow groves, fruit-bearing and barren trees [Col. 1588C] of every kind, streams, springs, perennial waters, cultivated or uncultivated, vacant or occupied, entirely and in the same condition in which the aforesaid servants of ours held them for cultivation with their own hands, in mountains and plains, in various places and under various names, wherever they appear to be situated, with their access and exit and with everything generally and entirely belonging to them, situated in the territory of Collina, on the estate of Flajano, just as their boundaries were from the beginning or can now be identified, according to the law under which they exist.

From this day we bestow these things upon you, so that we may receive continual prayers from you; for if we grant you temporal things, we ought to receive spiritual things from you. From this day, for the redemption of the souls of my brothers and sisters and of me, the donor named above, you are to have, hold, and possess them; and it shall be in your power and that of your successors to use, enjoy, possess, sell, donate, exchange, or do whatever you wish with them for the furnishing of lamps and for the benefit of the holy Church and your monastery.

At no time shall you or your successors ever have any dispute or claim from me, or from my heirs and successors, or from any great or small person sent by me. If you and your successors have need of it, I promise, together with my heirs and successors, to stand by you and defend you against everyone, at every time and in every place [Col. 1589A] where you may require it. I also promise inviolably to preserve and fulfill all the provisions expressed in the text of this charter of donation.

For, which God forbid, if we should presume to act against what is written or recorded above, and should fail to observe everything, then, before the beginning of any litigation, we promise to pay you, as a penalty, two pounds of the finest gold; and after the penalty has been paid, the text of this charter of donation shall nevertheless remain firm in its entirety.

Roccio, scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, was asked to write this. And I, the undersigned, have subscribed with my own hand; I also asked the witnesses who were to subscribe, and in the aforesaid month and indiction I delivered it to you, the persons named above.

+ T h F K I h C T X C, also called Benedict, bishop, [Col. 1589B] servant of the servants of God.

+ Hilperinus, son of Hilperinus.

+ Franco, son of Duranti.

+ John, who is called Paparone.

+ Octavianus, son of Sergius of Trastevere.

+ Crescentius, son of John of Lottecar.

+ I, Roccio, scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, the writer named above, completed and finished this charter.

## VII. Bull of Pope Benedict VIII for the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre at Nociati (1013, December)

[MITTARELLI, *Annales Camaldulenses*, I, Appendix, p. 212, from the monastery of Fonte Buono’s original document.]

[Col. 1589C]

BENEDICT, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, RODERICO, who appears to be called BONIZZO, abbot of the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre and of the Four Holy Evangelists, situated in the castle of Felicitas, at the place called Nociati, and to your successors forever.

Since, if we arrange anything for the honor of God and his holy monasteries, we do not doubt that we shall receive a reward from God in the future, therefore we, to whom the care of God’s churches has been entrusted, deem it right to establish for the future, from the property of our holy Roman Church, a privilege of our authority for the aforesaid church. For we judge that what appears capable of resisting the attacks of tyrants [Col. 1589D] and the strength of every kind of wicked person contributes greatly to the fruit of future usefulness.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, we establish the privilege concerning what is set out below, for the remedy of our soul and those of our pontifical successors, for the support of the brethren, the reception of the poor and pilgrims, and those gathered in the praises of Christ, since we do not doubt that we shall receive a reward from God in the future.

Accordingly, I grant to you and your successors forever the following: the estate called Corte dei Constantii, Sargonina, Nobule, Balzolo, Campo Dominico, Campo de Puzzo, and Flavelle, all in their entirety. Just as they belong to the Church of our holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, so we grant them to you and your successors forever to hold and enjoy. Bending to your prayers, we decree by our authority that from the present twelfth indiction you shall possess them freely and securely, beyond the power of every outsider, so that no duke, prince, count, viscount, or person, great or small, may exercise authority there or presume to inflict violence there. You shall, however, pay each year, without difficulty or delay, to the collector of our holy Roman Church a pension of two gold solidi.

Therefore, establishing this by apostolic authority under solemn invocation of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we decree that no future pontiff among our successors, nor any person, great or small, as written above, may ever dare to act against this privilege. But if anyone—which we do not wish—should attempt with rash boldness to oppose it and should not allow it to remain as it has been granted and confirmed by our apostolic authority, let him know that he is accursed and bound by the bond of anathema by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and that he shall have a share in eternal fires with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be the guardian and observer of this apostolic privilege shall deserve to obtain the grace of blessing from the just Judge, our Lord God, and to become a participant in eternal life forever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of Sergius, regional notary of the holy Roman Church, in the aforesaid month and twelfth indiction. [Col. 1590C]

+ Farewell. Signed.

In the name of the Lord, issued by the hand of Azzone, bishop of the holy Church of Ostia and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the second year, by God’s favor, of Lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal Pope VIII, in the most sacred see of blessed Peter, in the month of December, in the aforesaid twelfth indiction.

## VIII. Benedict VIII transfers three estates situated in the duchy of Bavaria to Emperor Henry, receiving the royal estate of Colle Calvo in exchange (1014)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XIX, 329.]

[Col. 1590D]

BENEDICT, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved spiritual son in the Lord, H., the invincible and triumphant Augustus.

Although an exchange can be made firm by the actual physical transfer itself, and what is legally carried out cannot be overturned by any opposition, nevertheless, lest there be any doubt about the transfer, the support of our authority ought to intervene.

Since our apostolic see has until now held in the right of the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, three estates with all their appurtenances, including male and female servants and tenants of both sexes residing there, our charity seeks and desires to exchange them. In compensation for them, we have received from you, beloved son H., Emperor Augustus, into our holy Roman Church, the royal estate called N., with all its appurtenances, situated within the county of Spoleto and appearing to belong to your empire. In exchange for it, we now transfer and exchange the aforesaid three estates to you forever, so that from this day you may have, hold, and possess them, and perpetually claim them as your right and property.

No future pontiff among our successors, nor any other person, great or small, may ever dare to remove or alienate the three aforesaid estates, with all their appurtenances, from your power and jurisdiction. Rather, you may hold and possess them forever, having received them from our holy Roman Church. If anyone—which we do not believe—should attempt to violate this apostolic command of ours, let him know that he must pay you one hundred pounds of the purest gold, and that this charter of exchange shall nevertheless remain perpetually firm.

## IX. Benedict VIII confirms the liberty and possessions of the monastery of Saint Peter of Bremetum [Note: [Col. 1591D] Bethmann, V. D., who examined this bull in the archiepiscopal archives of Turin, considers it to have been copied or forged, since it was written in a twelfth-century hand. JAFFÉ.] (1014)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IV, 1024.]

BENEDICT, etc., to his beloved son GOTTIFRED, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, founded in the territory of Bremetum between the Po [Col. 1591C] and the Ticino, and to his successors forever.

If what accords with pious desires must always be granted, how much more must those requests not be denied which are made for the stability of divine worship, and so forth. Therefore, because, through the intervention of our dearest son Adalbert, by the grace of God most glorious margrave, and at the petition of Emperor Henry, the brothers of the same monastery of Bremetum have petitioned … concerning that monastery itself—which had earlier been built for the honor of God and of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, in the time of King Theoderic by the patrician Abbo near the Alps, in a place called Novalesa, and was afterward transferred, when the persecution of the Saracens threatened, through the zeal of Adalbert, a margrave devoted to God, with a congregation of regular brothers gathered at the town called Bremetum [Col. 1591D] and strengthened by the privileges of our holy apostolic see—we, favoring their pious desires, grant by this our authority what has been requested.

Therefore we prohibit all priests of whatever church who possess any jurisdiction from celebrating the solemn rites of Mass there, unless they have been invited by the abbot of that place; nor may anyone presume to perform any ordination or consecration there.

We also confirm to the same monastery of Saint Peter the Apostle all the possessions and properties which, from the beginning of its foundation at Novalesa, the aforesaid most excellent and most Christian man Abbo gave and assigned to it either by an instrument of his will or by a conveyance made during his lifetime; and whatever the aforesaid Adalbert, margrave, afterward donated at Bremetum after its transfer, together with his wife.

We likewise confirm to the aforesaid monastery the church built in honor of the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, at Pollicino, with all its appurtenances; and the cell called Saint Andrew in the city of Turin, with all its appurtenances; and so forth.

Moreover, the cell which is called “of the Pagans,” with all its appurtenances, as it was assigned to it by charter; and also the court of Gabiano, with the entire territory that lies at Stupinico, Vallicella, Maridiago, Loretto, Roxaria, and Abrusiateo; and the little monastery of Gorgiano, all of which, together with the aforesaid court and its appurtenances, has been granted by charter to the aforementioned monastery.

Likewise the cell of Pollentia [Col. 1592B], recently built by the brothers of the same monastery; the court of Colonia; and the fortress of Manciano, with all its appurtenances, which Margrave Oddo, for the salvation of his mother’s soul, granted to the same monastery with his wife by a deed of offering.

Also Cavallarium, with the great court and all its other appurtenances, as it was bestowed on the same monastery by Margrave Arduino for the salvation of his mother’s soul.

The fortress of Saint George; the court of Casale; and the cell built in honor of Saint Peter in the valley called Ignaria, with all its entirety; likewise the cell of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and of Saint Michael the archangel; and the church consecrated in honor of Saint Stephen, with the fortress called Rodo and another named Verduno [Col. 1592C], together with all their appurtenances, including gates, river dues, and so forth.

But if anyone, and so forth.

Written by the hand of Leo, regional notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of February and the twelfth indiction, in the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal pope, the eighth, in the most sacred see of Saint Peter the Apostle, the second; while Lord Henry, crowned by God, great emperor, was reigning in the first year of his reign, in the month and indiction aforementioned, the twelfth.

Farewell.

## X. Privilege of Pope Benedict VIII for the Monastery of Monte Cassino. (Year 1014.)

[J. Tosti, *History of the Abbey of Cassino*, vol. I, p. 246.]

[Col. 1592D]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in the Lord Jesus Christ, Athenulf, venerable and religious abbot of the most sacred monastery of Blessed Benedict, confessor of Christ, situated in the monastery [on the mount] called Cassino, and to your holy congregation and your successors forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those who abound in pious religion with benevolent compassion, and to grant support to the requests of those who ask with eager devotion. For then, above all, we shall unquestionably deserve the reward of gain from the Lord, the creator of all, if by our authority we bring venerable places of the saints, properly ordered, to a better condition [Col. 1593A].

Therefore, because your Love has humbly petitioned our apostolate that we grant and reconfirm to you the aforesaid monastery of Christ’s confessor, blessed Benedict, situated in the territory of Aquino on the mountain called the fortress of Cassino, where his most sacred body is believed to have been buried, together with all its adjoining and appurtenant properties—both monasteries of men and of the handmaids of God, as well as cells and estates, wherever or however they are known to belong by right to the monastery—we confirm all these venerable monasteries in their entirety.

First, the monastery of the Lord Savior situated at the foot of that mountain, and the monastery of Saint Mary, holy Mother of God and virgin [Col. 1593B], called Plombarola.

Likewise the monastery of Saint Mary at Cingla, which has now been built within the city of Capua; similarly, in that same city of Capua, the cell of Saint Benedict and the monastery of Saint John of the maidens; indeed also the monastery of Saint Sophia, which has been built within the city of Benevento.

Furthermore, the monastery of Saint Mary situated in the territory of Benevento, in a place called Canneto beside the river Trinius; and also the monastery of Saint Mary of the handmaids of God within the city of Cosenza [lacuna: the names of lands, churches, and other properties subject to the abbey follow] … [lacuna].

For this reason, favoring pious desires, and committing to execution by our authority what is requested, we prohibit every priest of whatever church from exercising any jurisdiction in the territory of the aforesaid [Col. 1593C] monastery, except the apostolic see. Thus, unless he has been invited by the abbot of the same monastery, no one may presume in any way to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass there.

From this twelfth indiction onward, we irrevocably establish that it shall remain forever stable, and we decree that it shall be ruled, governed, and administered in the fear of God.

After the death of the abbot, no one shall appoint an abbot there except one whom the common agreement and will of the brothers from that congregation shall have chosen. Whoever wishes to introduce an abbot from elsewhere shall be under anathema.

Moreover, by apostolic censure, under invocation of the divine judgment, and also under strong and most terrible anathemas [penalties], we prohibit anyone, of whatever rank or power, or any person, great or small, from presuming to interfere in that monastery or in its affairs, or to take away or alienate in any manner its property, possessions, or churches subject to it, or anything whatsoever that appears to belong to it; nor may anyone inflict upon it any injury or loss, whether in times of peace or in barbarous times.

Indeed, we decree that it shall remain perpetually, as has been said, in firm stability in times of peace as well as of barbarism, under the jurisdiction of our holy Church.

We proclaim and establish, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, before God and his terrible [Col. 1594A] judgment, through the constitutions of this our apostolic privilege, that the places which, by the offering of any person, have been exchanged or granted to the aforesaid monastery, and likewise the other local possessions which have been given and offered to that holy place by kings, dukes, castalds, and other Christians, or which shall afterward be granted there, shall belong by firm right to the aforesaid monastery and shall remain so forever.

Nor shall anyone, great or small, have the license, as has been said, to take away any part of it or of anything belonging to the same monastery.

Rather, in accordance with what is contained in the apostolic constitutions and privilege concerning the aforementioned venerable place, it shall remain furnished without disturbance, and the same monks shall always be permitted to elect an abbot from their own congregation [Col. 1594B].

You shall also have the license to prepare the chrism, to offer and ordain priests, deacons, subdeacons, and others to be consecrated.

We also grant you, in the aforesaid venerable monastery and in all the Christian churches subject to it, the right to perform consecrations; to invite whatever bishop you wish; and to have the angelic hymn sung at the solemn celebrations of Mass on Sundays and feast days at all times.

You shall also be permitted to ring the bell, both during the daytime and at night, whenever you wish, in the aforesaid monastery and in any of its dependencies; and no bishop shall prohibit the people of God from entering its monasteries or cells to hear the word of God [Col. 1594C].

Moreover, we decree that no bishop shall presume in the aforesaid monastery or in its dependent churches to excommunicate a priest, summon him to a synod, or excommunicate the abbot or the monks who may be there at that time.

You shall also be permitted to receive for residence, or to receive into the monastic habit with their possessions, any cleric, priest, deacon, or subdeacon, from whatever diocese he may come, without the prohibition of any bishop.

You and your monks, and those subject to you, shall also be permitted to govern monasteries and convents of maidens without secular power and without the prohibition of any bishop.

But if anyone—which we do not desire—should presume with wicked audacity to oppose or in any way violate what we have established for the praise of God and for the stability of the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1594D], let him know that, unless he repents, he is bound by the chains of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and destined to be burned with the devil and his most terrible pomp, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the punishments of eternal fire.

But whoever, with pious regard, observes and in every respect guards this our apostolic constitution and whatever pertains to the worship of God shall receive manifold the grace of blessing from our most merciful Lord God through the intercession of blessed Benedict, and may deserve to become a participant in eternal life.

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary, regional notary [Col. 1595A] and archivist.

Issued on the third day before the Ides of March through the hand of Lord Grambosus, bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Lord Benedict, most holy pope, the eighth, in the second year of his pontificate, in the twelfth indiction, in the month of March, on the twelfth day.

## XI. Privilege of Pope Benedict VIII for the Church of Paderborn. (Year 1014.)

[Schaten, *Annals of Paderborn*, vol. I, p. 407.]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in the Lord, Minwerc, venerable bishop of the Church of Paderborn, and to his successors forever.

[Col. 1595B] A desire which is shown to pertain to a religious purpose and to the stability of holy places ought, with God’s help, to be fulfilled without any delay on our part. Whenever it seeks our consent and the support of the customary apostolic authority for certain of its needs, it is fitting for us, in view of our goodness, to assist it and to secure it by reason for complete safety, so that from this salvation and protection may flow to those venerable places, and so that for us also the highest reward of gain may be prepared by God, the creator of all, in the heavenly citadels.

Therefore, because you have petitioned us to confirm and strengthen by apostolic authority for your Church, for you, and for your successors whatever has been offered for the redemption of the souls of the donors by emperors, kings, dukes, counts, or persons great and small, whether exchanged or otherwise, as well as everything that you, moved by the love of God, have perpetually bestowed on the same venerable bride of yours from your own hereditary possessions [Col. 1595C], we, inclined by your prayers, confirm and strengthen by the tenor of this privilege for your Church and your successors forever all cultivated and uncultivated estates, and everything that has been offered to it for the redemption of the donors’ souls by emperors, especially by the most Christian and serene Emperor Henry, whether in counties or wherever they may be; and likewise everything offered to the aforesaid Church by kings, dukes, counts, and persons great and small.

In the same way we confirm all those places which you yourself, for the redemption of your soul and those of your parents, have bestowed from your hereditary possessions on the aforesaid bride of yours; and also those which have been exchanged by others.

We establish by apostolic censure, under the prohibition of anathema, that no person, great or small, shall ever be permitted to rise up against or oppose this our apostolic command.

But if anyone—which we do not desire—should attempt with reckless audacity to act against or violate the provisions of this apostolic command of ours, piously promulgated by us, let him know that he is bound by the anathema of our Lord’s prince of the apostles, Peter, and is to be burned with the devil and his most terrible pomp, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, in eternal fire [Col. 1596A].

At the same time, let him, plunged into the Tartarean abyss and chaos, perish with the impious.

But may those who, with pious regard, prove themselves guardians and observers of this salutary command of ours deserve to obtain from the Lord God our judge the grace of blessing, heavenly reward, and eternal joys.

Written by the hand of Benedict, notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of March, in the twelfth indiction.

Farewell.

## XII. Pope Benedict VIII confirms to the Monastery of Farfa the Castle of Buccinianum, recently recovered by him. (Year 1014.)

[Muratori, *Italian Historical Writings*, II, II, 518.]

[Col. 1596B]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

It is fitting for apostolic governance, and so forth. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, how we, enlightened by divine love, out of reverence for holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, and at the petition of our most glorious son, the emperor Henry, our lord, recovered for the monastery of the Lady Mary, Mother of God and virgin, which is called Farfa, the castle of Buccinianum, which it had recently lost, so that it might remain perpetually for the use and benefit of the aforesaid monastery, situated in the county of Sabina.

Then the venerable Hugh, abbot of the aforesaid monastery, approached our clemency, earnestly requesting that, for the love of God and for the salvation of the same venerable monastery, we might deign, from our apostolic generosity, to grant it the jurisdiction and public court of the estate of Buccinianum, which lies before that castle, together with all the appurtenances belonging or adjoining to that estate [Col. 1596C].

Granting his request, we concede and confirm in perpetuity to the same venerable monastery, to the aforesaid abbot and his successors, and also to the holy congregation of the servants of God dwelling there, the jurisdiction and public court of the aforesaid estate of Buccinianum, with all its appurtenances and adjoining properties, from the generosity of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of the holy apostolic see, whose right it is recognized to be, and by our apostolic authority.

This is granted so that the monks of the aforesaid monastery may at all times delight in pouring forth prayers to God on our behalf, and that the most glorious Virgin Mary, and so forth.

Let the violator know that he is bound by the chain of anathema and alienated from the kingdom of God. Moreover, let him know that he must pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold, half in the holy Lateran palace and half in the aforesaid monastery.

Written by the hand of Peter, archivist, notary, and regional notary of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of August, in the twelfth indiction.

Farewell.

Issued on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August through the hand of Lord Boso, bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see, by the grace of God. In the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Lord Benedict [Col. 1597A], supreme pontiff and universal pope, the eighth, in the most sacred see of blessed Peter the Apostle, the third; while Lord Henry, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in the first year of his reign.

## XIII. Roman Synod of Benedict VIII, at which the privilege of the Monastery of Fruttuaria was issued. (Year 1015.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XIX, 361.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

In the year counted from the incarnation of the Lord 1015, in the twelfth indiction, while the lord and glorious Pope Benedict was presiding in synod within the Lateran basilica, there appeared an abbot named William, humbly requesting from the maternal bosom of the universal Church something necessary and exceedingly useful: namely, that apostolic dignity should provide the monastery of Fruttuaria—which he had built on his paternal land in honor of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and his undefiled Mother—with the support of liberty [Col. 1597B].

The dignity of the Roman see, not to be despised, granted assent to his petition all the more readily because he had founded the aforesaid monastery in a deserted place, from which no bishop was ever known to have received any revenue, even of tithes, and because he had acquired apostolic regalia as well as imperial charters, with everyone piously assisting a just vow and a just labor.

Furthermore, Warmundus, bishop of Ivrea [better, “Eporedia.” But people spoke in that way in that age], in whose episcopal boundary this place appears to be situated, himself signed the charter with his own hand [Col. 1597C] and asked several bishops to sign it as well. In it, the rash audacity of all people is prohibited under threat of our excommunication: namely, that no royal or episcopal dignity, nor that of any secular or ecclesiastical order, under any pretext of secular ambition or guise of ecclesiastical religion, should be able to disturb the inhabitants of that place in any way.

Therefore the lord Benedict, universal pontiff, in confirmation of all the charters by which that place of Fruttuaria was strengthened, endowed it with his sacred privilege. Moreover, he ordered this decree to be written, to which the entire holy synod would lend its support by subscription.

Accordingly, unanimously and most willingly obeying the command of so great a Father and supreme pontiff, and submitting to his salutary desire, [f. lacuna: “if anyone …”], those who strive to corrupt the privileges of such great authority and to violate whatever charters have been granted to the holy monastery of Fruttuaria by the levite Guntard, by bishops, or by kings, this holy synod confidently strikes with the sword as people who contradict the rights of their forebears and despise the institutions of the holy Fathers, who decreed that from the time of the apostles the Roman Church was to receive complete obedience from every order.

Armed with such weapons, and turning the darts of excommunication back against them, we permit no perverse person to alter or infringe anything that has been granted by such and so many charters for the tranquility, liberty, security, and honorable dignity of the monastery of Fruttuaria and its rulers [Col. 1598A].

Whoever preserves, loves, magnifies, and increases these things may rejoice with those whose names are written in heaven. But those who despise, corrupt, and destroy them as far as they can should beware lest they themselves be erased from the book of the living and not be written with the just. For unless they repent of this wickedness, let them know that they too are excommunicated by all.

## XIV. Benedict VIII sends the pallium to Poppo, archbishop of Trier. (Year 1016.)

[Hontheim, *History of Trier*, I, 352.]

[Col. 1599D]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most blessed brother and venerable bishop Poppo, archbishop of the holy see of Trier: eternal salvation in the Lord and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting for apostolic concern always to show benevolent affection toward the brethren and to grant assent to their petitions when they appear valid and reasonable [Col. 1600A].

Therefore, dearest brother, because you have asked me that, according to the custom of your predecessors, we grant you the use of the pallium, we willingly assent to your desire. We earnestly admonish your fraternity to adorn the habit of the outward garment with integrity of conduct, and to show yourself in all things such that you always strive to administer with pastoral care the office of the stewardship entrusted to you.

For then you will appear conspicuous to all, like a lamp shining in the house of the Lord, if you are adorned inwardly as well as outwardly; if you resolve to carry inwardly in your mind the cross of Christ, which you bear bodily under the form of the pallium, crying with the Apostle: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world”; and adding with longing the prophet’s words: “Transfix my flesh with nails, because of your fear” [Col. 1600B].

Therefore, admonishing you with due charity, we send you the pallium from the apostolic see, establishing by the authority of this privilege of ours that, when celebrating Mass, you shall wear it only on these solemnities: on the Nativity of the Lord, the Epiphany of the Lord, the Lord’s Supper, Easter, Pentecost, and the Ascension of the Lord; on the feasts of holy Mary, Mother of God and perpetual virgin; on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; on the solemnities of all the apostles; and on the solemnity of All Saints.

You may also wear it on the feasts of those saints whose bodies and relics rest in your diocese; at the dedication of your church; on the anniversary of your ordination; and whenever you properly resolve to confer sacred orders.

We also grant, dearest son, that a cross may be carried before you.

May the almighty Lord preserve your fraternity, dearest brother, here and in the future, and strengthen our minds in his service, so that for the well-administered office of pastoral care he may reward our labor with eternal blessedness.

Farewell.

Issued on the sixth day before the Ides of April through the hand of Benedict, bishop and legate of the apostolic see. In the year [Note: It appears that Henry II used the title “king of the Romans” (perhaps the first of all the kings of Germany; see Hahn, *History of the Empire*, part II, chapter 6, § 9, in the note at title R, p. 20) in the Paderborn charter of the year 1013, in Lunig, *Ecclesiastical Miscellany*, vol. II, p. 704, as well as in the Fulda charter in Schannat, *Collection of the Traditions of Fulda*, no. 593, p. 243; but this was before Henry’s anointing [Col. 1600D] as Roman emperor and his Roman coronation. After that coronation, however, and indeed after it had been performed by Pope Benedict himself, Hahn, in the place cited, finds it astonishing, and almost suspect, that in this document the same Roman pontiff still calls him “king of the Romans.”] of the seventeenth year of the most invincible King of the Romans Henry, and the third of his empire, in the fifteenth indiction.

## XV. Benedict VIII grants the pallium to Benedict, archbishop of Salerno, and confirms the rights of his Church. (Fragment—year 1016.)

[Baronius, *Annals*, under the year 1012, no. 4.]

[Col. 1600D]

[lacuna] … Written by the hand of Benedict, regional notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of April, in the fourteenth indiction.

Issued on the seventh day before the Kalends of May through the hand of Peter, bishop of the Church of Palestrina and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal pope, the eighth, in the most sacred see of blessed Peter the Apostle, the fourth; in the third year of the empire of Lord Henry, Augustus; in the fourteenth indiction, in the aforementioned month of April, on the seventh day.

## XVI. Letter of Benedict VIII to the Bishops of Burgundy and Aquitaine—He orders that the invaders of the property of Cluny be excommunicated unless they make satisfaction. (Year 1016.)

[Duchesne, *Writings on the History of the Franks*, IV, 169.]

Benedict, by divine grace prelate and bishop of the Holy Roman Church, to all the brothers and fellow bishops established throughout Burgundy, Aquitaine, and Provence—namely, Burchard, archbishop of Lyon; the archbishop of Vienne of the same name; Walter, archbishop of Besançon; Walter, bishop of Autun, of the highest religious character; Stephen, bishop of Clermont; Fredelo, bishop of Le Puy; Geoffrey, bishop of Chalon; Lambert, bishop of Langres; Gauzlin, bishop of Mâcon; Wigo, bishop of Valence; Harmannus, bishop of Viviers; Pontius, archbishop of Arles; Aribald, bishop of Uzès; Odulric, bishop of Troyes; Gerald, bishop of Gap; Peter, bishop of Vaison; Hildebert, bishop of Avignon; Stephen, bishop of Carpentras; Almerad, bishop of Riez—greetings and blessing from almighty God and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and from me, who, although unworthy, appear to hold the office of prelate of the apostolic see [Col. 1601C].

It is clear that the monastery of Cluny, once built by William, the most noble prince of Aquitaine, in the region of Mâcon, through his own action with the pontiff of the apostolic see, the Roman emperor, and also the kings of the Franks and Burgundians, is so free from the subjection of any person—whether king, bishop, or count—that it owes anything to no one except God, Saint Peter, and the supreme prelate of the apostolic see.

This liberty has been strengthened and confirmed by written privileges of all our predecessors who, from the foundation of that place until our own time, have belonged to this holy Roman Church, and by charters issued by the aforesaid princes, concerning both that place itself and everything belonging to it in Burgundy, Aquitaine, and Provence—namely, monasteries, cells, cultivated and uncultivated lands.

Their intention and desire was that those who abandoned the world and wholly devoted themselves in that place to the service of Christ under regular discipline might adhere to God more freely, without anyone’s hindrance, and might serve hospitality and the care of the needy from what the faithful offered there to God and Saint Peter.

Up to now, by God’s favor, with the support of apostolic authority, and also with the assistance of the goodness of those living around them, they have devotedly done this as far as they were able.

But now, as we have learned in the presence of the God-devoted lord Robert, king of the Franks, and of his princes and nobles who came with him to the thresholds of the apostles, and from the formal complaint brought by our dearest son Odilo, abbot of that place, the greed and madness of evil men have risen against them and grown so fierce—invading their lands and plundering both their property and that of the poor entrusted to them—that, afflicted by manifold difficulties and sufferings, they are in no way able, as they have done until now, properly to render the service owed to God, nor can they carry out their customary care for visiting guests and the poor [Col. 1602A].

Therefore, since perpetual prayers, celebrations of Mass, and almsgiving are performed in that place for the state of the holy Church of God and for the salvation and repose of all the faithful, living and dead, its loss is the common detriment of us all.

Although all good faithful people ought to feel compassion for their distress [Col. 1602B] and disturbance, and with the greatest zeal assist the servants of Christ so that they may persist in their holy purpose without any hindrance, nevertheless I, to whom, after God and Saint Peter, the care and protection of the aforesaid place especially belong, shall not cease to provide them the help and consolation of apostolic authority.

The persecutors of the inhabitants of the aforementioned place are still more cruel. Ildinus, an enemy of every good quality, not only provokes them by taking away what belongs to them and to their people, but also, eager to turn his own wickedness against them, makes those living around him understand that he wishes to do them every kind of justice for the wrongs he has himself committed. Thus, in the very hearing and settlement, he continually deceives and mocks them, so that, instead of justice, they receive from him a still worse injury. There is also Wichard of Belioc, who takes from them the church of Tresdo with all its appurtenances. Bernard of Retorterio as well, Hugo of Mount Pavo, and his wife Arilina, who take from them the jurisdiction of Lasiaco with everything belonging to it, just as Count Leotaldus, of divine memory, first, and afterward Milo, a religious knight, formerly bestowed it by written testament upon Saint Peter and the aforesaid place. Falco, nephew of the cleric Iterius, and his brother, together with all their associates, take from them the jurisdiction of Oiadellis with all its appurtenances. Warulf of Branceduno and his brother Walterius, provost of Mâcon, oppose them concerning the precarial grant (*precaria*) which Leobald, bishop of blessed memory, their maternal uncle, held from Saint Peter; and concerning another parcel of land which the same prelate, restoring that benefice before his death, had given from his own portion to Saint Peter. [Col. 1602C]

Durandus of Caudiac, Aiminus of Caudiac, and Girard of Centurpennis oppose them concerning the village of Fontanedo. Robert of Islevee takes from them the plantations which Bernard Dolum, who was killed, had given to Saint Peter. There are also those who oppose them concerning the jurisdiction of Sarrianis, as well as those who carry out and demand plunder and unjust customary dues in the jurisdiction of Valentiola, in the jurisdiction of Tudelleta, in Podioodolenis, and in the other jurisdictions, villages, and lands belonging to the aforesaid place. There are also innumerable others whose names it would take too long to insert in this document. [Col. 1602D]

We, therefore, having, as did our predecessors, a special concern and care for the aforesaid place, which in a particular way belongs to us, summon the persons named above and all the other persecutors, plunderers, and invaders of the lands and possessions belonging to that place, in the name of God and Saint Peter and in our own name, to repent; and we admonish them to lay aside as quickly as possible the opposition and unjust complaints by which they harass and disturb the servants of God. Let them also restore in full the lands unjustly seized and the possessions plundered, according to the settlement which they shall be able to reach with them. Let them also suitably make satisfaction for the injury which, without cause, they have inflicted upon them, within the period extending from now until the feast of Saint Michael. [Col. 1603A]

If they do this, let them have the grace, blessing, and absolution of God and Saint Peter and of us. But if, within the time fixed by us, they do not consent to our admonition and summons, but remain contemptuous and disobedient, persevering in their wickedness, then, by the cautery of ecclesiastical judgment, let them be cut off from the body of Christ like rotten members; let them be driven far from the thresholds of the holy Church of God, separated from the fellowship of the faithful, and excommunicated. [Col. 1603B]

Let them be accursed whether standing or walking, awake or asleep, entering or going out. Let them be accursed while eating and drinking. Let their food and drink be accursed. Let the fruit of their womb and the fruit of their land be accursed. Let them endure the plagues of Herod until their entrails burst apart. And, having been destroyed with Dathan and Abiram from the land of the living, let them remain eternally condemned with the devil and his angels in the pains of hell, to be tormented without end. [Col. 1603C]

Let their children also become orphans and their wives widows. Let their children be carried away trembling and beg for alms. Let them be expelled from their dwellings and, accursed and anathematized, let them be subjected to every curse that appears to be contained in the Old or New Testament, until they repent and suitably make satisfaction to our summons and admonition.

To you also, my brothers and fellow bishops named above, I command and order by apostolic authority that you confirm this sentence of mine and likewise excommunicate them, and that you order all priests and the other ministers of the sacred order entrusted to you to excommunicate them. If any one of you—which I very much do not believe will happen—does not obey this command of ours, let him know that he will have to give an account before the tribunal of Christ for his contemptuous disobedience. For he himself said: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me.” [Col. 1603D]

To the venerable Lord Count Willelmus the Elder; likewise to the most excellent in goodness and sweetness, Lord Count Hugo; to Lord Rainald, count and son of the aforementioned Lord Willelmus, of good character; and to Lord Count Otto, a man of good disposition and worthy of embrace with the whole affection of love; also to the most worthy Lady Countess Adelaide, surnamed Blanche, and to her daughter-in-law, Lady Countess Gerberga; and likewise to the illustrious men Lord Wigo, viscount, and his brother Lord Willelmus, as well as Lord Odulric, Lord Ansold, and the other princes and nobles of all Burgundy, Aquitaine, and Provence, who are able to assist the inhabitants of the aforesaid place, we send the gift of apostolic blessing and absolution. [Col. 1604A]

To them, as they implore forgiveness for all their sins, we grant, in the name of God and Saint Peter and in our own name, a share and fellowship in all the good works that are daily performed by us and by the other faithful in this holy Roman Church, on the condition that they always prove themselves helpers and defenders of the aforesaid place and of everything belonging to it against all who oppose them. If they neglect this, they will not only be deprived of so great a benefit, but will also without doubt render an account on the day of the final judgment for the power given them by God for the defense of the faithful. [Col. 1604B]

Given on the Kalends of September.

## XVII. The Erection of the Church of Bisuldunum into a Bishopric (1017)

*[Coquelines, Bullar. Collect., I, 327.]*

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ Guifred, consecrated bishop by us, and to you and your successors forever.

The desire which is shown to pertain to a religious purpose and to the stability of holy places must, with God’s help, be fulfilled without any delay. Whenever our consent and the protection of holy apostolic authority are sought for the useful advancement of such a matter, it is fitting that we should willingly assist out of benevolent consideration. … to strengthen it securely and completely according to reason, so that safety and protection may thereby proceed to those venerable places, and that for us also the chief reward of gain may be assigned by the Creator of all things in the heavenly citadels. [Col. 1604C]

Therefore we wish it to be known to all, present and future, that Count Bernard, together with his son Guillermo, and through them Guifred, the count’s brother, all of them, having been abandoned to the sole protection and defense of the blessed apostle Peter and his vicar by Oliba, count of most noble and pious memory, came to the threshold of the apostles and to our presence. They humbly requested that, with our consent and by our judgment—under which alone they had been placed—they might, for the redemption of the souls of their parents and the forgiveness of their own sins, establish a bishopric on their hereditary property in whichever one of three places they preferred: either in the monastery of Saint John of Ripoll, or in the monastery of Saint Saviour and Saints Genesius and Michael the Archangel, which is within the walls of Bisuldunum [only two of the stated three places are named in the supplied text]. [Col. 1604D]

They also requested that, by our constitution, they might enrich the bishopric from their gifts and hereditary properties, so that those serving there might live and serve God in peace; and, kneeling and kissing our feet, they asked that a bishop be consecrated there by us. Since we recognize that it is necessary to incline those who fear the Lord toward such a great or similar work by our exhortation, and since we do not wish to remove these men or others like them from their good purpose, we judged it unworthy to oppose their most sacred petitions. Rather, agreeing to their wishes, we decreed that a bishopric should be established and endowed in whichever of the three aforementioned places they preferred, and we determine that it shall remain a bishopric forever. [Col. 1605A]

We consecrated you, Guifred, as bishop in accordance with their petition, on the following condition: you and your successors, the bishops, shall have the license and power throughout all the land which the aforesaid brothers have offered or appear to possess for the venerable bishopric from their own gift or inheritance, or which other Christians may in the future give there for the redemption of their souls, to consecrate churches, to confirm children, to bless clerics and priests, and to perform every episcopal function. [Col. 1605B]

We reserve forever to ourselves and our successors the consecration of your successors. For that consecration, following the statutes of the holy Fathers, we judge that nothing is to be offered to us or to our successors by your successors. But, so that the person who is to be consecrated may not appear empty-handed before us or our successors, not as a payment for consecration, as we have said, but as due obedience and to show that he always regards himself as subject to our Church, we order that after his consecration he offer one pound of gold.

Likewise, we command that you presume under no circumstances to take up arms against Christians, nor should any person, great or small, attempt to compel you to do so. Establishing this by apostolic censure, under the solemn warning of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we decree that none of our successors in the pontificate, nor any other person, great or small, may ever in any way overturn what has now been decreed and established by us; rather, it shall remain firm, stable, and unshaken forever. [Col. 1605C]

If anyone, however, with rash presumption, attempts to act against, violate, or break the sequence of this apostolic command of ours, piously promulgated by us, let him know that, unless he repents, he is bound by the anathema of our Lord and of the chief of the apostles, Peter; that he is to be burned in eternal fire with the devil and his most dreadful pomp and with Judas, the betrayer of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ; and that, together with the wicked, he will perish and be plunged into the chasm and Tartarean chaos. [Col. 1605D]

But whoever, with pious regard, proves himself the guardian, obedient servant, and observer of this life-giving command of ours, may he deserve to obtain from the just Judge, the Lord our God, the grace of blessing and the eternal joys of heavenly reward forever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of Benedict, regional notary and scriniary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of January, in the fifteenth indiction.

Peter, bishop of the Church of Sutri, consented to all these things and subscribed. Linoltus, bishop. Robert, bishop. John, bishop of Orte. Benedict, bishop of Carensis. Peter, bishop of the holy Church of Piperno. I, Benedict, bishop of Porto. John, bishop of the Church of Fondi. [Col. 1606A]

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, by the hand of Boson, by the grace of God bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see.

## XVIII. Pope Benedict VIII Receives the Newly Built Church of Bisuldunum, Built by Bernard, Count of Bisuldunum, under the Protection of the Apostolic See (1017)

*[Coquelines, vol. I, p. 326.]*

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son in Christ, Adalbert, rector of Saint Saviour, Saint Genesius, and Saint Michael, whose church has been built beside the fortress of Bisuldunum, and to you and all your successors forever.

The desire which is shown to pertain to a religious purpose and to the stability of holy places must, with God’s help, be fulfilled without delay. Whenever our consent and the protection of holy apostolic authority are sought for the useful advancement of such a matter, it is fitting that we should willingly assist out of benevolent consideration. … to strengthen it securely and completely according to reason, so that safety and protection may thereby proceed to those venerable places, and that for us also the chief reward of gain may be recorded by the Creator of all things in the heavenly citadels. [Col. 1606B]

Therefore we wish it to be known to all, present and future, that our beloved son, the illustrious Bernard, count of Bisuldunum, together with his son Guillelmo, kneeling and kissing our feet, earnestly petitioned the holy Roman curia that we should receive the aforesaid church of Saint Saviour, Saint Genesius, and Saint Michael the Archangel under the sole protection and defense of the blessed apostle Peter and his vicar, and fortify it with the privilege of our apostolic confirmation and authority. [Col. 1606C]

Therefore, beloved son Adalbert, for you and your successors, by the privilege of this apostolic authority, beginning with the present fifteenth indiction, we decree and establish, for the honor of Saint Saviour, Saint Genesius, and Saint Michael the Archangel and for the stability of the same place—which the aforesaid Count Bernard, together with his uncle Mivone, has subjected, for the love of almighty God and the reward of his soul, from his own county to its present right or jurisdiction—the following properties:

First, the church of Saint Vincent with its tithes, firstfruits, and cemeteries, on this side and beyond the torrent, with its offerings and its suffragan churches, namely Saint Martin of Juviniano, Saint Mary of Faxis, Saint Fructuosus of Ursiniano, and Saint Sylvester of Mor, as their boundaries are assigned in the endowment of its consecration, which our spiritual son Bernard, already mentioned, presented to our consideration. [Col. 1606D]

The first boundary of the said church of Saint Vincent with its suffragans is, to the east, Portello; to the south, the river of Tezer and Turno; to the west, Lidercha and Mount Augustinus; to the north, the royal hill and Mount Frigidus above Paleria, and Mount Calvus above Ligordanum.

Also, the church of Saint Mary and Saint John with all its allodial properties and possessions, situated near the walls of Bisuldunum, together with the property which the aforesaid church of Saint Saviour, Saint Genesius, and Saint Michael appears to possess in the town of Bisuldunum, in its surrounding area, and in all other places. [Col. 1607A]

All these churches mentioned above, with all their allodial properties and possessions, as the said Count Bernard himself gave them with his uncle Miró to the aforesaid church or shall give them, and everything else that he has given or shall give anywhere—whether houses, farmsteads, courts, manses, churches, estates, lands, vineyards, meadows, or pastures, together with everything belonging by right to the said church—we confirm and decree that they shall remain safe and entirely undisturbed under the protection of our apostolic see.

No emperor or king, nor any clerical or lay person, great or small, may presume to exercise any jurisdiction over the aforesaid churches or their parishes, whether for peace, truce, or ecclesiastical matters, within the boundaries already assigned. Rather, they shall judge and decide matters by the judgment of Adalbert, rector of that place, or of his successors, who now and in the future will dwell there forever in the said church of Saint Saviour, Saint Genesius, and Saint Michael; and judgment and authority shall always remain in their will and power. [Col. 1607B]

Let them—and their priests, clerics, and lay people—live quietly and peacefully. Let all of them be exempt and free from every public obligation and dishonorable service, so that no one may dare to trouble or harass them, except that they shall pay two solidi each year to the altar of Saint Peter as a rent, and shall provide Miró, bishop of Girona, and all his episcopal successors with annual hospitality for seven mounts and the same number of companions only.

Miró himself and all his successors as bishops shall give chrism without any service to the said Adalbert and his successors residing in the aforementioned church of Saint Saviour, Saint Genesius, and Saint Michael; and the inhabitants of that church shall give it to Saint Vincent and the other churches subject to it. [Col. 1607C]
