On the principal feasts—namely Easter, Pentecost, the feast of Saint Genesius, the feast of Saint Michael the Archangel, All Saints, and Christmas—all the clerics of Saint Vincent, together with all their parishioners, shall come in full attendance, with their offerings, to the solemn Mass at the church of Saint Saviour, Saint Genesius, and Saint Michael, forever. [Col. 1607D]

Establishing this by apostolic censure, under the solemn warning of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we decree that none of our successors in the pontificate, nor any other person, great or small, may ever overturn in any way what has now been decreed and established by us; rather, it shall remain firm, stable, and unshaken forever.

If anyone, with rash presumption, attempts to act against, violate, or break the terms of this apostolic command of ours, piously promulgated by us, let him know that, unless he repents, he is bound by the anathema of our Lord and of the chief of the apostles, Peter, and is to be burned in eternal fire with the devil and his most dreadful pomp and with Judas the betrayer; and that, together with the wicked, he will perish in the chasm. [Col. 1608A]

But whoever, with pious regard, proves himself the guardian, obedient servant, and observer of this life-giving command of ours, may he deserve to obtain from the just Judge, the Lord our God, the grace of blessing and the eternal joys of heavenly reward forever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of Benedict, regional notary and scriniary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of January, in the fifteenth indiction.

Peter, bishop of the Church of Sutri, consents to all these things and subscribed.

Robert, bishop.

John, bishop of Orte, subscribed.

Benedict, bishop of Arles.

Peter, bishop of the holy Church of Piperno.

I, Benedict, bishop of Porto. [Col. 1608B]

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, by the hand of Boson, by the grace of God bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see.

Farewell.

## XIX. Pope Benedict VIII Confirms the Property of the Monastery of Saint Stephen of Banyoles in the Diocese of Bisuldunum (1017)

*[Coquelines, cited above, I, 323.]*

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved in the Lord Bonisilius, religious priest and monk, and evangelical abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Stephen, protomartyr of Christ, situated in the county of Bisuldunum, in the valley of Sterria, at the head of the same lake, in the place called Banyoles; to you and those dwelling with you, and through you to your successors and theirs, greeting and peace and apostolic blessing, for as long as the world endures. [Col. 1608C]

Since it is evident that the Lord our God continually increases the honor of the holy universal Church through the propagators of the blessed faith, it is necessary for those who receive from him the rights of governing the whole Church to grant him the firm generosity of just administration and to drive far from it the invasion of evils.

Therefore, since it is fitting for apostolic piety to assist those who ask with kindly compassion, we, agreeing to your just petitions—for indeed they have been adjudged by us, since they are justly made—confirm by our apostolic privilege all the properties or possessions of that place, its boundaries and limits, with the adjoining lands of its principal estates, together with all churches, parishes, villages, estates, houses, farmsteads, lands, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, brushlands, strongholds, winepresses, waters, watercourses, vineyards, mills with their headwaters, and their fisheries, cultivated or uncultivated; and whatever, through the gifts of kings formerly made to the blessed protomartyr and levite Stephen, appears to be retained in the monastery of Banyoles. [Col. 1608D]

We grant to the aforesaid monastery what is held around it, namely whatever it is known to possess in the county of Bisuldunum:

In the parish of the valley itself, the church of Saint Mary and Saint Benedict, with tithes and firstfruits free from tribute, together with the offerings of the faithful, and with their boundaries and appurtenances.

The church of Saint Peter with the village of Agemal itself, with its boundaries, tithes, and firstfruits; the church of Saint Romanus with its cemetery, with tithes and firstfruits and the offerings of the faithful, and that half of those firstfruits, and of Salisparsa, and of Ermetanos, and of Agelage, together with the houses, lands, and vineyards, mills, which are in that parish or belong to that monastery. [Col. 1609A]

The village of Leon with its boundaries and appurtenances; Savarres with its boundaries and appurtenances; Starola and Figerolas with their boundaries and appurtenances; Erementanos and Agelaga with their boundaries and appurtenances and with their woods; Neserga and Frescaned with their boundaries and appurtenances; the village of Jafare and the hamlet of Paternus with their boundaries and appurtenances; Agemal, Millanicas, and Villa Alba with their boundaries and appurtenances.

In the parish of Porqueres, houses, lands, and vineyards with their boundaries and appurtenances, together with the tithes which Saint Stephen holds there.

Vallemala, which they call Merdant, with its tithes, boundaries, and limits.

Solerols with its boundaries and appurtenances, and with its tithes.

In the village called Adiliano, and in Sirinano and Albuciano, farmsteads, houses, lands, vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated, woods, and mills.

Usal with its woods, boundaries, and appurtenances.

In the village of Vendut, houses, lands, and vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated. [Col. 1609B]

In the valley of Miliarias, the church of Saint Peter; Saint Mary of Romzilia; and Saint Andrew in Rovilias, with tithes, firstfruits, and the offerings of the faithful, and, in their parish, houses, lands, vineyards, and woods with their boundaries and appurtenances.

In Falgons, or within its boundaries, houses, lands, vineyards, and woods with their boundaries and appurtenances.

In Saint Nazarius, houses, lands, vineyards, and woods with their boundaries and appurtenances.

In Biserga, houses, lands, vineyards, and woods with their boundaries and appurtenances.

In the district of Arivilfo, houses, lands, vineyards, and woods, cultivated and uncultivated, and waste land, with their boundaries and appurtenances.

In Calvas, cultivated and uncultivated lands.

In the valley of Saint Pata, at the place called Saint Vincent of Salente, or at the place called Corbos, the church of Saint Vincent and its parish, with tithes, firstfruits, and the offerings of the faithful, together with houses, lands, vineyards, mills, and woods, with the boundaries and limits of that parish. [Col. 1609C]

We also grant in full the market toll of the aforesaid place and all jurisdiction to be exercised there.

In Somer, houses, lands, vineyards, cultivated or uncultivated, and its woods, with its boundaries and borderlands.

On Mount Saint Julian, the church itself, with tithes, firstfruits, and the offerings of the faithful, together with houses, lands, vineyards, and woods with their boundaries or appurtenances.

In Camedello, houses, lands, vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated, and mills.

In Baso, houses, lands, and the little church of Herma.

In Agelager, houses, lands, vineyards, woods, cultivated and uncultivated, with their boundaries and appurtenances.

In Logordano and Malano, lands, together with Oliberes, the estates of Boscholos, and the vineyard of Vallealta.

In Bruger, the manse which belonged to Seniofred Marhot, with cultivated and uncultivated lands.

In Morzano, houses, cultivated and uncultivated lands, and vineyards with their boundaries.

In Cisteriano, which they call Villavert, the church of Saint Mary with its parish, its tithes and firstfruits, and the offerings of the faithful, together with houses, lands, and vineyards, cultivated or uncultivated, and its mills, with the boundaries and appurtenances of that parish. [Col. 1609D]

In the village of Oller, or in the village of Amelio, and in the village of Vendut, houses, lands, vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated.

In Turres, houses, lands, and vineyards, cultivated and waste.

In the village of Almires, or within its boundaries, houses, lands, vineyards, cultivated and waste, woods, and olive groves.

In Contens, houses, lands, vineyards, cultivated and waste, and olive groves.

At Saint Felix of Ledono, houses, lands, vineyards, cultivated and waste.

In the parish of Saint Columba, houses, lands, vineyards, cultivated and waste.

In the village of Abundanti, houses, lands, or, within its boundaries, houses, lands, vineyards, olive groves, cultivated and waste.

In the village of Fedanti, one vineyard.

In Orfanos, or within its boundaries, houses, lands, vineyards, cultivated and waste, mills and millworks with their headwaters, gardens and orchards with olive groves, and the allodial property with its mills and headwaters, with their boundaries and borderlands, which Bonfilius gave, as is recorded in the charters of Saint Stephen. [Col. 1610A]

In the village of Galdinarios, houses, lands, and vineyards, or, within its boundaries, cultivated and waste land.

In Pareds, lands and vineyards.

In Ordios, houses, lands, vineyards, cultivated and waste, or within its boundaries.

In the high district called Murriano, houses, lands, vineyards, woods, cultivated and waste.

In the county of Girona, in Matamors, or within its boundaries, houses, lands, vineyards, cultivated and waste, mills and millworks, woods, and the lake with its meadows.

In Gerundella, cultivated or uncultivated lands and woods.

In Costa Rabida and Bonecurto, lands, vineyards, and woods, and the vineyard of Cona.

In Biert or Gralloners, houses, lands, vineyards, and woods.

On Mount Calvus, or in Canneto, houses, lands, cultivated and waste.

In Borgoniano and in the courts, or in Cannellas, or within their boundaries, houses, lands, vineyards, cultivated and waste, mills and millworks with their headwaters. [Col. 1610B]

In Parazol and Pulgaz, houses, lands, vineyards, or within their boundaries.

In the village of Trader, or within its boundaries; in Leudenago, or within its boundaries; and the manse of Biancheto, which he gave to Saint Stephen, houses, lands, vineyards, cultivated and waste.

In Tomedo, Mediniano, Exchers, the river of Llutos, and the Cross itself, or within their boundaries, houses, lands, vineyards, cultivated and waste, and mills and millworks with their headwaters.

In Celrrano, Bibiano, Riurano, and Pubol, or within their boundaries, houses, lands, vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated, waste land, and the vineyards which Seridredus of Aquaviva gave to Saint Stephen. [Col. 1611A]

At the place called Mazamet, the allodial property which belonged to Aurichius the judge.

In the county of Barcelona, in the valleys, the allodial properties which Bella Femina left to Saint Stephen, as is recorded in her judgment.

In the parish of Saint Felix, called Buada, or within its boundaries; at the place called Torrentilio, or within its boundaries; at the place called Torrente, or within its boundaries; the exchanges which Crustarius made.

At Ricolfo, houses, cultivated and waste lands, enclosures planted with trees, and the vineyards which Saint Stephen ought to possess.

In Segalars, which Seniofred Wita holds, and the vineyard of Susanna with its boundary, with waste and cultivated land, as is recorded in the charter of Saint Stephen.

In Petralta and within its boundaries; in the land within its boundaries; in Docuinano or within its boundaries, as is recorded in the charter which Rannus the cleric made for Saint Stephen: houses, lands, vineyards, gardens, cultivated and waste land. [Col. 1611B]

In Jafar or within its boundaries; in Tonnano or within its boundaries; in Ciurana or within its boundaries; in the village of Dud or within its boundaries; in Ventajone or within its boundaries; in the village of Mocorono or within its boundaries; in Armentera or within its boundaries: houses, lands, vineyards with brushlands, meadows, pastures, mills, and millworks with their headwaters, cultivated and waste land.

In Castellione, houses and lands, cultivated or uncultivated.

In Fontanedo, which they call Vallemala, the church of Saint Martin with the rock, with tithes, firstfruits, and the offerings of the faithful, together with houses, lands, vineyards, cultivated and waste land, and woods. [Col. 1611C]

This allodial property is bounded on the east by the Cher, or by the allodial property which belonged to Count Suniarius; it extends along the mountain summits and reaches the pass of Gode; it reaches the allodial property of Leo; and it reaches the allodial properties of Betlono Malachana. To the south it is bounded by the ridge itself at the spring of Ilar, or by the waste land of Betlone, or by the allodial property which belonged to Ajo Femina, or by the rock. On the west it is bounded by the river called Budiga, or by the hamlet of Melandre. On the north it is bounded by the river which flows from the springs; it runs through the forest itself and reaches Moloculino, or the allodial property of John the priest; and it reaches the pass of Colaria or the ark itself.

And another allodial property which belonged to Seximundus the priest, together with other vineyards situated in other places. [Col. 1611D]

At Saint Sylvester, a manse with lands and vineyards, with the waste lands belonging to it, and with the tithes of that manse.

At Deredeldos, a manse with lands and vineyards, and with the waste lands which are there.

In the county of Cerdanya, one manse with lands.

In Purermano, one manse with lands.

In Arriano, houses, lands, and vineyards with their boundaries and appurtenances.

In Bulla, houses, lands, and vineyards, and in the manse itself the lands and vineyards which Landricus and his wife gave to Saint Stephen, with their boundaries and appurtenances.

In Olmera, cultivated and uncultivated lands.

In Lampage, one field.

In Bages and Merresa, lands and vineyards, cultivated and waste, with their boundaries and appurtenances. [Col. 1612A]

All these properties, therefore, whatever we have mentioned or not mentioned, acquired or to be acquired, belonging to the monastery of Saint Stephen, protomartyr and levite, situated in the valley of Sterria, are confirmed to it by our apostolic authority.

We establish, moreover, that when the abbot of that monastery dies, abbots are not to be appointed there by kings, counts, or any other person on account of greed for money or any empty favor; rather, they are to be elected by all the servants of God dwelling there, according to God and in accordance with the rule of Benedict the Father.

We also grant the abbot of that place permission to have his clerics ordained wherever and by whichever bishops he wishes, and to receive chrism from whatever see he prefers; neither he nor any church belonging to that monastery may be excommunicated by any bishop, including the bishop in whose diocese the monastery is situated, or by anyone else. [Col. 1612B]

We further establish that any penitent excluded from the thresholds of the church may, for as long as he remains there, enter and hear every divine office.

We also grant the abbot, the monks, and all clerics belonging to the monastery permission not to attend a synod unless they wish to do so voluntarily or are summoned.

We therefore confirm and establish from now on that no king, prince, margrave, count, judge, bishop, or any person, great or small, may presume to inflict any force or invasion upon that monastery or its possessions.

For this reason, under the solemn warning of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we promulgate and decree that none of our successors in the pontificate, nor any person, great or small, as we have said, may dare or presume to act unjustly in any matter against this apostolic privilege of ours, nor may anyone attempt to break it. [Col. 1612C]

If anyone—which we do not believe will happen—fearing neither God nor respecting the privilege which we grant, attempts by word or deed to violate it, whoever he may be, we bind him, unless he repents, with perpetual bonds of anathema, in the name of almighty God, his holy apostle Peter, and ourselves, who exercise his office. Let hell be his portion, the devil his inheritance, and that place where there is never joy but always weeping his share and consolation. Unless, as we have said, he repents, let every curse that can be imagined or spoken come upon him. [Col. 1612D]

But whoever, as a helper of this holy monastery, chooses and loves it in whatever way he can, let him rejoice that, through the intervention of almighty God, filled with apostolic blessing, he may grow from virtue to virtue. Let paradise be his portion, the Lord Christ his inheritance, and that place where there is always joy and no sorrow his share and consolation.

We also prohibit persons of every rank from taking from the aforesaid monastery pasture dues, exacting transport services, or distraining the legal proceedings of any person belonging to the monastery, whatever his offense may be, on pain of being subjected to the curses mentioned above—which may almighty God always avert from the helpers of this privilege of ours and bring severely upon those who desire to break it. [Col. 1613A]

Written by the hands of Benedict, regional notary and scriniary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of January, in the fifteenth indiction.

Farewell.

## XX. The Privilege of Pope Benedict VIII for the Monastery of Saint Peter of Campirotundo in the Same County of Bisuldunum (1017)

*[Coquelines, cited above, vol. I, p. 325.]*

[The supplied source ends here.]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Bonfil, beloved in the Lord, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Peter of Campi Rotundi, which is situated in the county of Besalú, in the valley of Laudar, between two rivers; and to you and those who remain with you, and through you to your successors and theirs: health and peace and apostolic blessing, for as long as the world endures. Amen.

Since it is evident that the Lord our God continually increases the honor of the holy universal Church through the propagators of the blessed faith, those who receive from him the rights of all governance must grant it firm liberality according to the judgment of just moderation and drive far from it the invasion of evils. Therefore, since it is fitting for apostolic piety to assist those who ask with kindly compassion, we, assenting to your just petitions—for such they have been adjudged by us, since they are justly made—confirm by our apostolic privilege all the properties or possessions of that place: its boundaries and limits, with the adjoining lands of the principal estates; with all churches, parishes, villages, estates, farmsteads, cottages, lands, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, scrublands, areas, winepresses, waters, watercourses, roads, mills with their *caputaqua* (headwaters) and their fisheries; cultivated and uncultivated land; and whatever the blessed apostle Peter appears to retain from the donations of the faithful in the monastery of Campi Rotundi.

We therefore grant to the aforesaid monastery the allodial property held or known to be held around it; also the fisheries of the waters of the Tezen, from the seven houses as far as the Kalkers themselves, and in the crooked stream from Mullione as far as the Tezer.

The parish of that valley, namely the church of Saint Mary, with tithes, first fruits, and the offerings of the faithful, without tribute.

The parish of Saint Christopher Crescentarius, with the allodial property itself and its cemetery, with tithes and first fruits, and the offerings of the faithful, without tribute.

The allod called Milandars; the allod of Frescanet; the allod of Paradella and of Rescat; and in Villa-longa and Castellars, with their boundaries and adjoining lands.

The allod called Pugna Francorum; the allod called Grado; the allod in Borloso; and the allod in Arza, with their boundaries and adjoining lands; and the allod called Reget, with Massana itself; the allod called Vallestir; the allod called Albet, with the water itself and the wood itself; the allod called Oliba; and Malo Pertuso, with their boundaries and adjoining lands.

The allod called Genebrel; Aquabella; Prunarias; Habinarios; and the allod called Carrera, with their boundaries and adjoining lands.

The allod in the parish of Tortelliano and in the parish of Agelager, with their boundaries and adjoining lands.

The allod in the parish of Monteacuto—that is, the palace—with the wood itself and Molino Beteret.

The allod called Artisces, with the wood itself; and in Capriol and Mauro; the mills at the palace; in Molino Vetere; and in Wadomalo, with its *caputaqua* (headwater), its course, and its elevated lands. And in the … manor, with its boundaries and adjoining lands.

In Boscols, the allod itself, with its boundaries and adjoining lands.

In the parish of Saint Felix at Lutuno, the village itself, with the allod of Luders and of Selvatella, with the wood itself and the olive groves themselves, with their boundaries and adjoining lands.

In the parish of Saint Matthew, the allod in the village of Damires and in Stella, with their boundaries and adjoining lands; and the valley itself and Romaniano, with its allod and its church, with tithes and first fruits and the offerings of the faithful, with their boundaries and adjoining lands, without tribute.

In Pontons, the allod itself, with its boundaries and adjoining lands.

In Parietes, the allod itself, with its boundaries and adjoining lands.

At Saint Eulalia, the manors themselves, with their allods, with their boundaries and adjoining lands.

In the valley of Biania, the *solaria* themselves, with their church, with tithes and first fruits, with its cemetery, and with the offerings of the faithful, without tribute.

At Cubilisco, or in the valley of Biania, the farmsteads themselves, with their allod, with their boundaries and adjoining lands.

At Bago, or in Serra, the manors themselves, with their allod and their tithes.

In the county of Roussillon, or in the valley of Asper, or in Palaldà, the manors themselves, with their allod, with their boundaries and adjoining lands.

At Miralias, the village itself, with its allod and its woods, with their boundaries and adjoining lands; and the village of Avellanotello, with its allod and its tithes.

In the county of Roussillon, or in the village of Malleolas, the manors themselves, with their allod, with their boundaries and adjoining lands.

In the village of Torrilias, the saltworks themselves, with the vineyards and its allod, with their boundaries and adjoining lands.

In the county of Peralada, the manors of the village of Sacas; and at Olibes, the manors themselves, with their allods; and at Terrers, the vineyards, with their boundaries and adjoining lands.

In the county of Girona, the manors of Flassano, with its allod, with their boundaries and adjoining lands.

In the county of Bergadà, the manors which Count Wifred gave, another which Count Oliba gave, and another which Bonfil, now deceased, gave. Likewise at Corpe, Ardariz, and Gardilanz, with their allods, with their boundaries and adjoining lands.

In the county of Cerdanya, or in the village of Alone, or in Volpellage, or in Ezer, the manors themselves, with their allods and their ovens, with their boundaries and adjoining lands.

In the county of Roussillon, or in the confluent valley, the village of Pino itself, with its church, its allod, its cemetery, tithes and first fruits, and the offerings of the faithful, with their boundaries and adjoining lands.

In the village of Saorra, the village of Trolano, the village of Vernet, the village of Vhitefano, Ascajone, Parcinianos, Evulo, Marignanos, and Campestres, the farmsteads themselves, with their allods and vineyards, with their boundaries and adjoining lands.

At Massaneto, the village of Novories, the village of Malaconjuncta, the houses of Lavajol, the hamlet of Bellone, and the village of Olibeta, with its church, tithes and first fruits, and the offerings of the faithful, with their allods; and at Tapies, the woods themselves, with their boundaries and adjoining lands.

All these estates which we have mentioned, and those which we have not mentioned, whether already acquired or still to be acquired, belonging to the monastery of the apostle Saint Peter situated at Campi Rotundi, are hereby firmly established for it by apostolic authority.

We decree, moreover, that when the abbot of that monastery dies, abbots shall not be appointed there by kings, counts, or any other person for the sake of monetary greed or empty glory of favor; rather, they shall be elected by all the servants of God dwelling there, according to God and in accordance with the Rule of Father Benedict.

We also grant the abbot of that place permission to have his clerics ordained by whatever bishop and wherever he wishes, and to receive chrism from whatever see pleases him; and no church belonging to that monastery may be excommunicated by any bishop—not by the bishop in whose diocese the monastery is situated, nor by any other.

We further decree that anyone excluded from the thresholds of the Church as a penitent may, for as long as he remains there, have permission to enter and hear the entire divine office.

We also grant the abbot, the monks, and all clerics belonging to the monastery permission not to attend a synod, unless they wish to do so voluntarily or are requested to attend.

Therefore we confirm and establish henceforth that no king, prince, margrave, count, judge, bishop, or any person, great or small, shall presume to commit any violence or invasion in that monastery or in its dependencies.

For this reason, and under invocation of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we promulgate and decree that none of our pontifical successors, nor any person, great or small, as we have said, shall ever dare or presume to act unjustly in any matter against this apostolic privilege, nor shall anyone attempt to break it.

If anyone—although we do not believe this will happen—not fearing God and despising our privilege which we grant, attempts to break it by word or deed, whoever he may be, we bind him, unless he repents, with the bonds of perpetual anathema, in the name of God almighty, his holy apostle Peter, and ourselves, who exercise his office. May hell be his portion, the devil his inheritance, and his share and consolation be where there is never joy but always weeping; and unless he repents, as we have said, may every curse that can be conceived or uttered come upon him.

But whoever, as a helper of this holy monastery, chooses and loves it insofar as he is able, may that person, filled through the intervention of almighty God with apostolic blessing, rejoice to grow from virtue to virtue. May paradise be his portion, the Lord Christ his inheritance, and may his share and consolation be where there is always joy and no sorrow.

We also prohibit authorities of every kind from taking pasture dues (*pascuarios*) from the aforesaid monastery, exacting haulage dues (*traginas*), or compelling anyone belonging to the monastery to appear before a court, whatever his fault may be—if he does not wish to be subject to the aforesaid curses [“not,” E. P.]—which may almighty God always turn away from the helpers of this privilege and impose severely upon those who desire to violate it.

Written by the hand of Benedict, regional notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of January, in the fifteenth indiction.

### XXI. Bull of Pope Benedict VIII by which he grants the monastery of Saint Lawrence in the county of Macri, in Campania, to the monastery of Farfa. (Year 1017.)

[MURATORI, *Script. Ital.*, II, II, 521.]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hugh, beloved son in Christ, religious priest and monk, and spiritual abbot of the venerable monastery of our Lady, Saint Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God, situated on the side of the mountain called Acutianus, above the river called Pharpha; and to your successor abbots and your venerable congregation, forever and in perpetuity.

Whenever we are expected to grant what plainly accords with reason, it is fitting for us to grant it with willing mind and to provide appropriate assistance to the desires of those who ask. Therefore, since your affection humbly requested of us that, for love of the almighty Lord and for the reward of our soul, we grant and confirm to you and your successors in perpetuity the monastery dedicated to the holy martyr and levite Lawrence, situated in the county of Macri in Campania, with houses, gardens, vineyards, lands, fields, meadows, pastures, and woods, as its boundaries are set out below:

On the first side, the road coming from the fountain of Palumba; on the second side, the irrigation channels that run toward the public road and toward Cerrus Jannarius; on the third side, another public road leading to the New Bath; on the fourth side, another road and irrigation channels running toward Acrifolium, and from there continuing to Arciones and coming to the road of the aforesaid fountain of Palumba, which is the first boundary.

And likewise all the other property, however much of it there may be, lying in different places, wherever near or far around Petiolum, and appearing to belong to the aforesaid monastery: all of it belonging by right to our holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, we ought to grant and confirm to you for possession, by issuing this order.

Moved by your prayers, therefore, by the tenor of this document we grant and confirm to you the aforesaid monastery of Saint Lawrence in its entirety, with everything belonging to it, as written above, from the present fifteenth indiction and forever, on this condition: that you foster, govern, direct, and administer the servants of God, the monks who are in that monastery or whom you are able to gather there, in chastity, moderation, and regular monastic discipline, with fear of God, as a father of a household; and that you cause them continually to offer to almighty God in the aforesaid church the preparation of its lights and daily praises.

Therefore, by our apostolic authority, we decree and confirm for you that no bishop, margrave, count, viscount, castellan, or any other person, great or small, dare molest you or your monastery concerning the aforesaid monastery, or dispossess you of it.

Whoever presumes to do this shall know that, by the authority of our Lord Jesus Christ, the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and ourselves, he is accursed, excommunicated, and anathematized. Moreover, he shall pay one hundred gold *mancosi*, half to our treasury and half to your aforesaid monastery.

But whoever, moved by pious concern, proves himself the guardian, obedient servant, and observer of this privilege of ours, may deserve to obtain from the just Judge, the Lord our God, the grace of blessing and the eternal joys of heavenly reward, world without end. Amen.

Written by the hand of Peter, regional notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of June, in the fifteenth indiction. Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of June, by the hand of Boso, bishop by the grace of God and archivist of the holy apostolic see.

Farewell.

### XXII. Benedict VIII confirms the privileges and possessions of the Church of Porto. (Year 1017.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 116.]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our revered brother in Christ, Benedict, bishop of the holy Church of Porto, and to his successors forever.

Whenever we are expected to grant what plainly accords with reason, it is fitting for us to grant it with willing mind and to provide appropriate assistance to the desires of those who ask. Therefore, since your affection humbly requested of the apostolic see that we grant and confirm to you and your successors forever the aforesaid bishopric with its dependencies, moved by your prayers, by the tenor of this document we grant and confirm to you and your successors forever the aforesaid episcopate of the Church of Saint Porto, which appears to be situated outside the aforesaid city of Porto and is called Saint Hippolytus.

It includes the vineyards and gardens surrounding that church, together with the enclosure; one complete vineyard situated at Cardeto; and at Finilia, two enclosures with vineyards and lands, all lying within them on the greater island.

It also includes the church of Saint Mary and likewise the church of Saint Lawrence, with the episcopal residence, cells, gardens, and vineyards; five enclosures: in one there are the churches of Saint Peter, Saint George, and Saint Theodore; in another, the church of Saint Vitus, bounded by the wall, the river Tiber, and the surrounding boundaries; the third above the riverbank; the fourth beside Saint Mary as far as Trajan’s; and the fifth beside Saint Lawrence and extending to the aforesaid Trajan’s.

Also included are the vineyard enclosure at a place called Scaraio; another parcel called the Enclosure; one parcel of vineyard at the Tower of Cocuzina; another at Monlon; and a complete estate called Bacatum, with its appendage called Scriptula, in which there are ancient cisterns situated beside the same city of Porto.

Its boundaries begin on the first side at a tree called the tamarisk, proceed to a small column standing at the head of the road, two miles distant from that city, then continue straight along the Salaria as far as the fishermen’s hut; from there they return toward the sea by the trumpet-shaped channel, follow the seashore around as far as Saint Nympha, and continue to the beacon of Miccina, with the places called Trunceta, as far as the baths, and as far as the place called Trajan’s Port; then to the palace called Praegesta; and as far as the ancient city itself, with Trajan’s Lake.

It also includes another smaller castle in its entirety, with everything belonging to it; and, in the city of Constantiniana, everything which the aforesaid bishop is known to possess there, together with the destroyed church of the blessed Peter and Paul, with the crypts where the animals belonging to that church appear to remain. These lands extend as far as Saint Mary, situated in the field called Cisterna, and as far as the house called the Bath of Venus, and as far as the public road within the castle itself; also the reed bed of that city, namely the monastery of Saint Agnes, with the saltworks and vineyards which it appears to contain.

Furthermore, a complete estate called Pallius, with houses, vineyards, lands, and pastures, extending as far as the ancient oven belonging to the aforesaid episcopate; and in the same estate there appears to be an ancient tomb situated on the Porto road, approximately ten miles from the city of Rome.

Likewise, the smaller island, with vineyards, houses, and lands, together with the place called Scaraio, formerly Trajan’s Port, adjoining the same estate of Baccanus, and with everything belonging to it; also the complete estate called Judaeorum, and the estate called Gualdus, with everything belonging to them, situated beside the aforesaid ancient city; and one complete salt-pool strip situated in seven strips.

Likewise, at Bacan and Genecula, nine strips: all the strips of saltworks known to belong to your episcopate; and the complete estate called Greater Gualdus, with the church of Saint Aurea, its tomb, and the land called Planura, in which cisterns appear to be situated below the river; and the land called Arcionum.

We also confirm to you the complete court called Galeria, in which there is the church of Saint Mary with its covered halls, small gardens, various chambers, and all the buildings which it is known to contain within and around itself; with all its boundaries, terms, and limits; lands, farmsteads, woods, and marshes; with the bridge; and the very village called Galeria, as far as the river.

It also includes fields, meadows, pastures, willow groves, fruit-bearing and fruitless trees of various kinds, wells, springs, streams, perennial waters, places suitable for making a watermill, and everything belonging to the aforesaid court called Galeria.

Likewise, a complete cultivated and cleared meadow situated in the field called Meruel, on the Porto road approximately twelve miles from the city of Rome. Its boundaries begin at the entire court, on the first side at the meadows of Caracus called Merul; it proceeds over the mountain formerly held by John of Miccina and the heirs of Stephen the Nomenclator; from there it runs through the farmstead formerly held by John of Sergius; crosses another cart road; and reaches the farmstead held by certain heirs of Franco across the Tiber, as marked by marble boundary stones.

From there it goes to the farmstead of the monastery of Saints Cosmas and Damian; continues along the ancient ditch which in spring carries water into the stream called Galeria, running toward the mill of the wood; turns back along the cart road as far as the middle valley of the mountain called Sunuel; continues as far as the hut standing among the mastic trees; and as far as the head of the valley enclosing the entire field; then to the parcel called Ticli and the Galiarda Pool, enclosing that parcel, where there are thirty strips.

It continues beside the strips belonging to the monastery of Miranda as far as the greater pond; along the bank of the pond to Borduzaria; from the foot of the strips as far as Baccanum; and as far as the land of the aforesaid bishop; then to the watercourse called Arcionum; along that watercourse to the stream called Galeria; and beyond Galeria, along the watercourse, to the aforesaid first boundary at the meadows of Caracus.

Within these boundaries, the following places and names are included: Saint Caesarius, Palinus, Sorbilianus, Greater Marsh, Old Enclosure, Medianum, Rusty Mountain, Cannaparius, Celsa, Greater Limit, Accursed Little Pond, Siocli, Galiarda Pool, Olibastrum, and Pilgrim’s Little Pond, with everything belonging to them.

We also confirm to you and your successors forever four complete principal *unciae*, which constitute one third of the whole Greater Pond of Porto, with all its fishing, revenues, and payments, and with everything belonging in its entirety to those four *unciae* of the pond, as they were granted by our predecessors to the holy Church of Porto. Everything stated above is situated in the territory of Porto.

Likewise, we grant and confirm to you and your successors the complete tower called de Albo, with houses, vineyards, gardens, lands, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, marshes, and cultivated and uncultivated streams, empty and full, together with everything generally belonging in its entirety to the tower.

Its boundaries are: on the first side, the stream called Galeria; on the second side, the river called the Tiber; on the third side, the *pulverinula*; and on the fourth side, the watercourse called Arcionum.

We also grant that the people who from time to time will inhabit the aforesaid tower shall be subject to no authority or jurisdiction, nor serve or render honor to any person except the bishop who is then in the said episcopate.

We further confirm to you and your successors forever all the movable and immovable property and resources of those people throughout the city of Porto, across the Tiber, on the island of Lycaonia, or wherever the rights of your episcopate appear to exist, who die without an heir, intestate, and suddenly overtaken by death, unable to arrange their property themselves.

We establish and confirm that the holy mother Church of Porto shall have the inheritance of those who from time to time have been ordained in the aforesaid episcopate, with permission to order and dispose of it as they please, so that they may perish forever—that is, insofar as they may always be aided by their prayers.

Moreover, from the right of our sacred Lateran palace, which belongs to our public authority, we grant to you and your successors forever the entire castaldy of Porto, and whatever until now your castellans have possessed from the whole city of Porto, whether from its gates or from its ships, as well as from the entire *burdunaria*, or whatever they possessed outside or within, anywhere, from the aforesaid office.

We grant all this to you and your successors to possess forever, so that it remains within your authority to appoint there whatever man you wish as castellan or agent; and whatever he acquires or is able to possess from that office shall be delivered to you and your successors, with the right to do with it whatever you please—provided that, if our count or the successors of our count so desire, he shall swear fidelity concerning whatever belongs to our palace.

The counts who from time to time are there shall in no way dare to appoint or establish another castellan or agent except those whom you or your successors appoint or establish. If they do so, or violently take away anything from the aforesaid castaldy, or wish to break or oppose what has been handed over by us to you and your successors, each of them shall pay four pounds of gold, half to your episcopate and half to our palace; and whatever they have appointed as castellan or agent shall be annulled. If he proves contumacious, he shall remain excommunicated until true satisfaction has been made.

Likewise, we grant and confirm to you and your successors forever, from the city of Porto, two fishermen and two curials, whom you or your successors may choose from among the people who are or may be found there.

We therefore grant and confirm all these things to your religious office in perpetuity. These two fishermen and two curials shall henceforth render no payment or service and shall not be compelled by anyone to attend a court who at any time holds dominion in that city of Porto. We place them under the authority of you and your successors.

We also confirm to you and your successors the complete farmstead called Genesianum and Malianum, with the small island beyond the stream situated in that place, with everything belonging to it, on the Porto road beside Malianum, belonging by right to the monastery of Saint Pancratius.

We also confirm to you and your successors forever the entire island called Lycaonia, on which are the church of the blessed John the Baptist and the church of Saint Adalbert, with houses and oratories within the same court, with gardens, watermills, and their dependencies, situated within this city of Rome, extending from one end to the other end of the island, where the river divides.

In the same way, we grant and confirm to you and your successors forever the entire episcopal ordination—the ordination of priests, deacons, deaconesses, and subdeacons, and of churches and altars—which may be necessary throughout the region across the Tiber, unless a cardinal priest, cardinal deacon, subdeacon, or acolyte of the sacred Lateran palace should be appointed.

Namely, we grant to you and your successors, or to whatever bishops may be invited by you, the power to ordain, bless, and consecrate all these things.

And so that your parish may not be invaded by any bishop, we have caused this to be made known and have taken care to confirm it to your Church. The first boundary begins at the broken bridge, where the current is divided by the wall of the city across the Tiber; namely, by the Septimian Gate, by the Gate of Saint Pancratius, and along the paved road of that gate as far as the marble bridge over the Arrone.

It proceeds along that paved road to the *paritorium*, then turns through the marshes as far as the sea; from there it comes by sea as far as two miles beyond the lighthouse and as far as the greater spring; then it returns through the middle of the greater river and comes as far as the branch of the broken bridge beside the Marmorata; then to the middle of the bridge of Saint Mary and to the middle of the bridge where the Jews are seen to dwell; and it returns through the middle of the aforesaid broken bridge, where we have already spoken of the current, which is the first boundary.

This is without the Catholic churches across the Tiber, namely Saint Mary’s, Saint Chrysogonus, and Saint Cecilia’s across the Tiber, or the monastery of Saint Pancratius and Saints Cosmas and Damian. Nevertheless, in the aforesaid churches and monasteries, whatever it is necessary for bishops to do there, we grant the bishop of Porto, or those invited by him, the power to do.

Likewise, we grant and confirm within the aforesaid episcopate the parish church of Saint Mary and Saint Apollinaris at Mola Rupta; the parish church of Saint Stephen at Panchi; the parish church of Saint Mary at Apruniana; and all small or large churches of whatever name which are or may be within the aforesaid boundaries, except those across the Tiber which we have already mentioned.

Meanwhile, we enact and order, as was ordered by our predecessors, that throughout the entire river flowing beside the city of Porto no one shall dare, after your order or that of your episcopal successors, to establish mills or a bridge in any manner contrary to ancient custom. Whenever mills or a bridge have been established or constructed by you or by others to whom you have assigned the task, the mills or bridge shall be administered at your discretion.

If a bridge is built at that city, no one shall dare cross over it in either direction with a wagon loaded with wine or provisions.

Again we enact and order that no priest or cleric of any order throughout the aforesaid episcopate shall dare compel them to appear before a court, force them to settle a dispute, or demand any service from them; the bishop of Porto, in whose parish they are, has that power.

Any presumptuous person—whether duke, count, viscount, chamberlain, envoy of our apostolic see, or any other authority exercising dominion over that city of Porto—whatever his rank, who wishes to take away or diminish from the right, power, and jurisdiction of the aforesaid bishop all the immovable places mentioned above, the aforesaid castaldy, the two fishermen and two curials, or all the clerics mentioned above; who attempts to violate the parish; or who recalls to public service the people living in the aforesaid tower or anywhere the property of the bishop has been mentioned, shall know that he must pay the bishop then in office twenty pounds of the purest gold.

Moreover, by apostolic censure, by the authority of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, under invocation of divine judgment and the prohibitions of anathema, we establish that no pontifical successor of ours, nor any other person, great or small, shall ever dare oppose, transgress in any respect, or diminish anything established by us for the praise of God and the stability or increase of the aforesaid episcopate. Rather, just as we have established or granted above, so shall it be permitted to remain forever, throughout all enduring and perpetual times, without any diminution.

But if anyone—which we do not wish—presumes by rash endeavor to act against this privilege of ours or to violate it in any respect, and does not allow what we have established above to remain firmly in force and does not observe it in all things, let him know that, unless he repents, by the authority of almighty God, of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of ourselves, who exercise his vicariate, he is bound by the chain of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and destined to be burned entirely in the fire with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with all his pomp.

But whoever, moved by pious concern, proves himself in all things the guardian and observer of this apostolic privilege of ours, may he deserve to obtain the grace of blessing and eternal life from the just Judge, the Lord our God, and from all his saints, world without end. Amen.

Written by the hand of George, regional notary and archivist of the holy apostolic see, in the month of July, in the first indiction.

Given on the Kalends of August, by the hand of Boso, bishop by the grace of God and archivist of the holy apostolic see.

Farewell. We decree, therefore, and so forth. If, then, anything, and so forth. To all, moreover, and so forth. Amen.

### XXIII. Benedict VIII grants Amatus, archbishop of Salerno, the use of the pallium and confirms the privileges of his Church. (Fragment—year 1019.)

[BARONIUS, under the year 1012, no. 5.]

[Col. 1623B]

[…] Written by the hand of Stephen, regional notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of December, in the third indiction.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of January, by the hand of Benedict, bishop of Porto and archivist of the holy apostolic see, in the eighth year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Lord Benedict, most holy Pope Benedict VIII; while the most pious Lord Emperor Augustus Henry was reigning in his sixth year; in the third indiction, in the month of December, on the fifteenth day.

### XXIV. Privilege of Benedict VIII for the nunnery of Saint Mary and Saint Andrew. (Year 1020.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XIX, 330.]

[Col. 1623C]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Cunigunda, venerable abbess: eternal salvation in the Lord.

The apostolic office is bound to assist those who are endowed with devout religion by benevolent compassion, and to grant the requests of petitioners with eager devotion. For by this means we chiefly earn a reward of profit before the Lord, the creator of all, if venerable places of the saints, suitably ordered, are brought into a better condition. And therefore, since you have petitioned us to grant and confirm by apostolic authority to you and to those who are to succeed you in perpetuity the monastery situated in honor of Saint Mary and Saint Andrew [Col. 1623D], in the place called Goffia, in the county of Liubana, begun by Aribo of blessed memory and his wife Adala and completed by their son Aribo, a venerable deacon, and entrusted in freedom to our most beloved son, the Emperor II: moved by your prayers, and especially by the petition of the aforesaid emperor, and by the intervention of that same Aribo, the venerable deacon and completer of this place, we grant and confirm to you and to those who are to succeed you in perpetuity the aforesaid monastery, with all its appurtenances and properties, whatever it now possesses or will possess in any manner forever.

Indeed, it is to be provided that in each indiction one gold solidus shall be paid as a pension to the Holy Roman Church. Therefore, establishing this by apostolic authority, we decree that no mortal person shall ever be permitted to rise against the terms of this privilege of ours by usurping or invading anything belonging to the monastery or anything ecclesiastical, whether among what it now possesses or what it will possess forever, or by troubling you or your successors. If anyone—which we do not wish—should attempt, with wicked audacity, in any respect to violate or nullify this privilege of ours, piously promulgated by us, let him incur the wrath of God and of the prince of the apostles, and let him be condemned with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord, in the lower Gehenna. But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be the guardian and observer of this privilege of ours, may obtain the grace of God and deserve the blessing of the prince of the apostles, and may rejoice forever with the elect in the heavenly tabernacle.

[Col. 1624B] Written by the hand of Stephen, scriniarius of the Roman Church, in the month of April, indiction III.

### XXV. Privilege of Pope Benedict concerning the confirmation of the Bishop of Babeberg. (Year 1020.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XIX, 327.]

[Col. 1624C]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son in the Lord Jesus Christ, the venerable bishop of the holy Church of Babeberg, and so forth: perpetual salvation.

Whenever the pious support of our apostolic confirmation is requested, it must be granted with prompt action. And if it is requested for matters that appear destined to endure forever [Col. 1624C], it must also be recorded in writing, lest the passage of time render them doubtful or uncertain to posterity. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the sons of the holy Church, present and future, how the matter concerning the bishopric which the most Christian Emperor Henry most devoutly established at Babeberg in honor of the prince of the apostles, Peter, was conducted in that same church in our presence.

For the aforesaid emperor repeatedly and earnestly begged us to approach Babeberg in order to confirm it by apostolic authority, being inflamed by an exceedingly great love for the bishopric which, moved by divine impulse, he had completed. Recognizing that his repeated petitions and unceasing insistence arose from a just desire, we judged it wrong to deny him our presence and to allow inhuman cunning to seize any opportunity against that venerable place [Col. 1624D].

Therefore we came to Babeberg, where we were received by that same emperor as well as he was able and knew how to do. He also presented to the Holy Roman Church, over which, by God’s authority, we preside, and to us, the church with the whole integrity of the bishopric. Seeing this, we considered it right to draw up the text of this privilege of ours, to confirm the bishopric forever, and to grant it to you, dearest son, and to your successors. This was to be done in the following manner and order: no living person, whatever his dignity or order, should ever dare to act against this confirmation of ours, or to proceed against you or your successors on this account; nor should anyone be permitted by force, fraud, or wicked cunning to diminish anything from all that the aforesaid bishopric now possesses or will possess, or in any way to trouble you or your successors concerning any of these things [Col. 1625A]. It is further provided that in each indiction he shall pay to us and our successors, under the name of a pension, one white horse with a saddle suitable for the Roman pontiff.

If anyone—which we do not wish—proud and arrogant, should attempt with rash audacity to act or proceed against this text of our decree, piously promulgated by us, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema, since the bishopric with all its appurtenances was offered by the aforesaid most Christian emperor to our Lord and to the prince of the apostles, Peter, from whom, through us and our successors, he awaits support and judgment [Col. 1625B]. With the devil and his most atrocious pomps, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord and Savior, he shall be assigned to be consumed in eternal fire.

But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be the guardian and observer of this life-giving decree of ours, may obtain from the Lord, the most just judge, the grace of blessing and the joys of heavenly reward.

Written by the hand of Raphon, regional notary and scriniarius of the Holy Roman Church.

### XXVI. Benedict VIII confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Sophia of Benevento. (Year 1022.)

[*Anecdota Ughelliana*, 489.]

[Col. 1625C]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gregory [Col. 1625C], venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Sophia, which remains within the city of Benevento and the old city, and, after you, to your successors in that same venerable monastery forever.

It is fitting for the apostolic office to assist those endowed with devout religion with appropriate compassion and to grant the requests of petitioners with eager devotion. For by this means we chiefly earn forgiveness before the Lord, the creator of all, if venerable places of the saints, suitably ordered, are brought into a better condition. Therefore, since your religious devotion humbly petitioned our apostolate that we grant and confirm to you and to your successors the aforesaid monastery of Saint Sophia [Col. 1625D], with its churches, estates, villages and hamlets, as well as vineyards and lands, male and female servants, and all movable and immovable property, and that it be adorned with the privileges and insignia of the apostolic see, so that, established under the jurisdiction of the holy apostolic see, which by the Lord’s authority we serve, it might not be subjected to the jurisdiction of anyone else: moved by your prayers, through the terms of this apostolic privilege of ours we grant and confirm to you and to your successors forever the aforesaid monastery, with all its property, whatever it now possesses or will possess forever.

It is specifically to remain subject to no father or lord except the Roman pontiff, and always free from every subjection and condition of the monastery of Cassino. This freedom was made by Urso, abbot of Saint Sophia, as was declared by Magilpert, abbot of Saint Benedict’s monastery of Cassino, in the declaration made by Urso, abbot of Saint Sophia, in the presence of the princes Jandolf and Pandolf, their sons, as well as their nobles and judges. Many years later John, abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Cassino, also declared this to you, Gregory, abbot of Saint Sophia, just as Magelpotus did to the aforesaid abbot Urso.

We establish, under apostolic censure and by the solemn appeal of divine judgment and the penalties of anathema, that no Christian living, whatever his dignity or power, may act or rise against this apostolic privilege of ours, or by any means or device remove or usurp anything from the property and possessions of the same monastery, so that, in accordance with what is contained below in the constitution and privilege of the apostolic see concerning this place, it may remain securely endowed [Col. 1626B]. The same monks of the congregation shall always be permitted to elect an abbot from among themselves. Nor shall any bishop be permitted there to celebrate or sing Mass, or even to perform an ordination, unless he has been summoned by the abbot of that monastery.

If anyone should attempt with rash audacity to act against this apostolic decree of ours, or should in any way seek or contend to invalidate the decisions which the aforesaid abbots made among themselves; or if any person should wish to offer or give his property to that monastery or to those churches subject to it, and any person should wish to withdraw it: let him be excommunicated and cursed by God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and anathematized and condemned by the blessed apostles Peter and Paul of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1626C]. On the day of judgment let him be hurled with the devil and his angels into eternal Gehenna, there to burn without end.

But whoever proves in all things to be the guardian and keeper of the salutary provisions of this apostolic decree of ours, may be filled with every blessing throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

Written by the hand of Stephen, regional notary and scriniarius of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of March, indiction V.

### XXVII. Bull of Pope Benedict VIII confirming all the privileges and rights of the monastery of Pomposa. (Year 1022.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, V, 1051.]

[Col. 1626D]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Wido, venerable abbot of the monastery of Holy Mary, Mother of God, our Lady, situated on the island called Pomposa, and to his successors forever.

Since whatever accords with reasonable desires must always be granted, it is necessary that devotion, and so forth. Therefore, since your holiness, with bowed knees, petitioned our pious will that the aforesaid monastery of Holy Mary, Mother of God, our Lady, situated on the island of Pomposa, should be strengthened by apostolic privilege, so that it might be subject to no human being except God and the king [Col. 1627A]: by that authority which Christ our Lord granted to the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to the rulers of the holy Church, we establish and decree that neither that place nor anything belonging to it may ever be subjected to anyone except God and the king.

No mortal, except the height of royal power, shall presume to exercise any ordinance, authority, power, or jurisdiction in the aforesaid monastery, or in its estates or castles, or in its parishes, cells, villages, waters and watercourses, banks, pastures, woods, fisheries, marshes, and all movable and immovable property belonging to it; nor over the servants of God or the household servants of either sex, or even over free persons residing on the lands of the same monastery. Nor shall anyone presume to impede or trouble the monks’ way of life, or to exercise jurisdiction or judgment in any of the monastery’s places, or to hold any court without the abbot’s permission, or to invade or alienate the monastery’s property in any manner, or to dare to demand or exact fodrum, paratae, or any public obligations [Col. 1627B].

We also remove it from the power of archbishops and from everyone else, subjecting it only to royal or imperial authority or protection. We further confirm for you the fishery which Volana possesses with its appurtenances.

If anyone—which we very much do not wish—should be found disobedient to and contemptuous of this privilege of ours, in whole or in part, or should presume to make an attempt on the pretext of any person, unless he repents, may he receive the curse of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and be consigned with the devil and his most atrocious associates to punishments and eternal fire. May he also be found unworthy of the future resurrection of the elect, and be separated from communion, from the bosom of holy Mother Church, and from the fellowship of the saints [Col. 1627C].

Written by the hand of Stephen, first scriniarius of the holy apostolic see, in the month of July and indiction V.

Farewell.

### XXVIII. Privilege of Pope Benedict VIII for the monastery of Cassino [Note: [Col. 1627] Gattula, *Historia Casinensis*, 56, reports the true closing clause of this bull, containing the chronological indications. Jaffé]. (Year 1023, July 1.)

[MARGARINI, *Bullarium Casinense*, II, 75.]

[Col. 1627D]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most beloved son in the Lord Jesus Christ, Theobald, venerable and religious abbot of the most sacred monastery of the blessed Benedict, confessor of Christ, situated on the mountain called the Castle of Cassino, and to his holy congregation forever: salvation in the Lord.

If we ought, compelled by the ministry with which we appear to have been invested, to grant the requested apostolic support to all churches, then matters that specifically concern our apostolate alone [Col. 1628A] ought to receive it all the more quickly and fully, insofar as we recognize that they need it more urgently, so that no harm may come to venerable places received under apostolic protection which is not averted by the resistance of our arm.

We believe that the Lord will repay these concerns of ours; we desire him to be praised peacefully in those same places. For the praises and prayers of those dwelling there will be more acceptable insofar as, with our support, their minds are free from every disturbance.

Therefore, since you have petitioned us to grant and confirm the monastery of Saint Benedict situated on Monte Cassino, whose abbot’s consecration we recently received as a gift from the most devout Emperor Henry, and to consecrate its abbots through us and our successors forever, without any simoniacal wickedness intervening, we grant and confirm it, with all its churches, monasteries, cells, castles, and so forth [Col. 1628B].

After your death, no one shall appoint an abbot there except the person whom the convent and the common will of the brothers from that congregation have elected. The elected person shall come to us or to our successors to be consecrated freely and without payment. But if he comes from elsewhere, or prefers to be consecrated by some other archbishop or bishop, then let both the consecrator and the consecrated be anathema.

And further: by apostolic censure, under the solemn appeal of divine judgment, we prohibit any bishop from presuming to excommunicate a priest in the aforesaid monastery or in the churches subject to it, or to summon him to a synod [Col. 1628C]. If anyone—which we do not wish—should presume with wicked audacity to oppose or violate in any way the provisions established by us for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid monastery, let him know that, unless he repents, he is bound by the bond of anathema and alienated from the kingdom of God. He shall be assigned to be consumed with the devil and his most atrocious pomps, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, in eternal fires and punishments.

But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be an observer of and in all things a keeper of this apostolic decree of ours and of the matters pertaining to the worship of God—so the text reads—may receive abundantly from the most merciful Lord our God, through the intercession of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of the blessed confessor Benedict, the grace of blessing [Col. 1628D], and may deserve to share in eternal life.

Written by the hand of Sergius, scriniarius and notary of our sacred palace, on the Kalends of July, indiction VI.

Farewell.

### XXIX. Letter of Pope Benedict VIII to Stephen, bishop of the Auvergne, on behalf of the Cluniacs. (Years 1012–1024.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, p. 7.]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Stephen [Col. 1629A], the most religious bishop of the Auvergne, greetings in the Lord.

You know that the monastery of Cluny was entrusted by its founder to the holy Roman Church for defense against the insatiable greed of secular persons. Therefore, as the rule of justice dictates, whenever that place suffers oppression from wicked men, we are bound to set against it the shield of our defense.

In this matter we wish your holiness to be our helper in breaking the stubbornness of those who wish to seize the properties assigned to that monastery. We ask you to hurl against them not a small stone, but the strongest missile of excommunication—against those who, with wicked audacity and having set aside the fear of the Lord, do not fear to scandalize or distress God’s servants by taking away their property [Col. 1629B].

Above all, let Tetardus and Girbertus, sons of Stephen, be struck at this time by that sword. They unjustly retain and possess the allod which Archbishop Amblard left to Saint Peter. Therefore, until they return the aforesaid allod, let them be bound by the bond of excommunication on our part and likewise on yours.

Farewell.

### XXX. Pope Benedict VIII to William, abbot of the monastery of Dijon. (Years 1012–1024.)

[PÉRARD, *Recueil*, etc., p. 273.]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to William [Col. 1629C], venerable abbot and beloved son in Christ: most dear greetings with apostolic blessing.

Having heard of the vigilant zeal with which you watch over the sons entrusted to you, we give thanks to almighty God. We have learned, moreover, that you have long been laboring under the frequent incursions of your enemies, and that your Church is now almost stripped bare by plunderers; and we sympathize with the misfortunes which you suffer from outside.

For the patient endurance which you have shown until now toward the adversaries of your Church should bring us to rejoice and to praise your goodness. But it has been enough to show this patience hitherto: the property of the Church must not be utterly reduced to nothing with impunity, nor the order of monastic religion, which is known to flourish there under your direction, weakened by scarcity and want [Col. 1629D].

You have with you our son Benignus, bishop, who, thanks be to God, has become a monk. We admonish him to conduct himself honorably and religiously, to observe his profession of obedience in conduct and action, and to remain in the vocation to which he has been called.

We then command him with full authority to pursue the enemies of the martyr Benignus with every zeal for justice and, with divine authority, to strike them with anathema. We also instruct you not to oppose him in this; rather, we grant him authority, and command and order him, to strike your invaders. Thus, through true obedience, we command you not to hinder or prohibit him from restraining those evildoers with the sword of the divine word.

And if our authority is thereby strengthened, whomever he binds shall be bound by apostolic authority and ours, and those whom he absolves shall likewise be absolved without our absolution [Col. 1630A]. We also give him the power to ordain whatever he is rightly asked to ordain in the holy Church, though with your command. (Without seal.)

### XXXI. Benedict VIII grants that Alleluia may be sung in the church of the monastery of Ripoll, and the angelic hymn at the feast of the Hypapante (that is, the feast of the Purification of blessed Mary), even if it falls after Septuagesima. (Years 1012–1024.)

[COCQUELINES, *Bullarium*, collected privileges, I, 318.]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved sons in Christ assembled for the feast of the Hypapante of the Lord in the monastery of Holy Mary, Mother of God [Col. 1630B]: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since we believe that the governance of the whole universal Church has been entrusted to us, though unworthy, according to God, it is therefore fitting for us to assent to the requests of all the faithful, and for benefit to flow thence to all, from the source from which the beginning of all acceptable religion is known to have arisen.

Therefore we make known to your charity that our most beloved son Oliba, abbot of the monastery of Ripoll, came to us, led by divine zeal and love for the blessed virgin Mary, and humbly requested that, if the aforesaid feast should occur after Alleluia had been discontinued, he be granted permission for Alleluia to be sung on that same day [Col. 1630C], together with “Glory to God in the highest,” only in the aforesaid monastery.

We were pleased to grant his request, and we have granted to him and to his successors forever the singing of Alleluia, if it has already ceased, and also the angelic hymn, whenever it is to be sung.

Therefore, whoever desires to take part in the joys of this feast in the place mentioned above should know that he will be granted the gift of divine protection and an increase of our blessing, with the assistance of Jesus Christ, the most benevolent Savior.

### XXXII. Letter of Pope Benedict VIII to Count William. (Around the year 1014.)

[MÉNARD, *History of Nîmes*, Documents, p. 20.]

[Col. 1630D] BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to William, count, and also to his mother Adelaide, countess: perpetual salvation and apostolic blessing.

It appears that an unheard-of crime and unspeakable injury have arisen in your regions, inasmuch as monasteries founded long ago by the decrees of the Fathers are now seen to have been almost destroyed by the wickedness of evil men. Therefore I, struck by hidden grief and marked with the apostolic stigma, together with the clergy of various orders of this apostolic see, whom by God’s dispensation I serve, command all those persons—namely, those who rashly seek to receive from you the allod of Saint Giles, without the will of the abbot of that place and without the consent of the monks, to the detriment of Saint Giles and of those who serve him—to be excluded from the bosom of holy Mother Church [Col. 1631A].

With Dathan and Abiram, and also Korah, Baal, and Beelzebub, and their like, I impose an eternal curse upon them and grant them enduring participation in their fate. I likewise excommunicate and condemn those who, wickedly invading the land of the most holy Giles, claim it and plunder it for their own use, knowingly, because they did not receive it from your authorities in former times.

But if, because those men maliciously wished to possess the allod of the aforesaid blessed Giles and sought in various ways to receive it from you, any harm should come to the monks dwelling there [Col. 1631B], let them receive a double penalty of excommunication and curse, and may they never be able to separate themselves from the company of Judas, the betrayer of the Lord, nor from the fellowship of Caiaphas, Annas, Herod, and Pontius Pilate.

Let them perish under the curses of the angels, and receive communion with Satan in the destruction of the flesh. Let them receive curses from above, and from below the curses of the fallen abyss. Let them receive a heavenly curse and an earthly curse.

Let them receive the present curse in their bodies, weakness in their souls, and destruction and torment. Let them be cursed with the accursed, scourged with the ungrateful, and perish with the proud. Let them be cursed with the Jews who, seeing the Lord in the flesh, did not believe but rather attempted to crucify him [Col. 1631C]. Let them be cursed with the heretics who sought to overthrow the Church of God. Let them be cursed with those who blaspheme the name of the Lord. Let them be cursed with those who despair of God’s mercy. Let them be cursed with those who have been condemned in hell. Let them be cursed with the impious and sinners, unless they amend and acknowledge themselves guilty toward Saint Giles.

Let them be cursed throughout the four quarters of the world: cursed in the east, abandoned in the west, prohibited in the north, and stripped by excommunication in the south. Let them be cursed by day, and excommunicated by night. Let them be cursed within their house and excommunicated outside their house. When they stand, let them be cursed, and when they sit, excommunicated [Col. 1631D]. Let them be cursed when they eat; let them be cursed when they drink; let them be cursed when they sleep and excommunicated when they keep watch. Let them be cursed when they work at anything and excommunicated when they rest for a little while. Let them be cursed in spring and excommunicated in summer; let them be cursed in autumn and excommunicated in winter. Let them be cursed in the present age and excommunicated in the age to come.

Let their possessions pass to others, their women go to destruction, and their children fall by the sword. Let their food be cursed, and let whatever remains of it be cursed; and let those who taste it be cursed. Let the priest who gives them the body and blood of the Lord, or visits them when they are ill, be cursed and excommunicated [Col. 1632A]. Likewise, let those who carry them to burial and presume to bury them be cursed and excommunicated.

Let them be cursed and excommunicated with every curse unless they amend and come to make satisfaction.

You must know with certainty that after our death no bishop, count, or secular authority will dare presumptuously to usurp the monastery of blessed Giles as his dominion. If they presume to do so, being bound by all the curses set forth above, may they never be able to enter the heavenly kingdom, because blessed Giles entrusted that monastery, with all its property, to Saint Peter as his dominion and possession. Nor may any of my successors dare to sell it or exchange it to anyone, or subject it under the protection of any authority [Col. 1632B].

Written by the hand of John, deacon and scriniarius of the holy Roman Church.

### XXXIII. Benedict VIII, at the request of Count Roger of Carcassonne and his wife Adalhaid, confirms the property and rights of the monastery of Saint Hilary. (Years 1012–1024.)

[BESSE, *History of the Counts of Carcassonne*, p. 81, citing BREQUIGNY, *Chronological Tables*, I, 530.]

### XXXIV. Benedict VIII confirms the possessions of the monastery of Saint Savin. (Years 1012–1024.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, II, 207.]

[Col. 1632C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, BENEDICT, prelate of the apostolic see, to all the servants of Christ, present and future.

It ought neither to seem burdensome to us nor altogether useless to anyone to provide the protection of the apostolic see to those who petition for it, since we may neither sell what is God’s gift to us nor should anyone be permitted to despise it. Therefore let every assembly of the one Mother Church, present and future, know that, in accordance with the petitions presented to us by our brother and fellow bishop, the lord Sigefred, prelate of the see of Piacenza, and by Wimpbert, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Savin—which appears to have been constructed by a pontiff under the subjection of his bishopric—we give and grant, and by this decree establish that there be inviolably preserved without any diminution in the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1632D] whatever appears to have been given and granted to that monastery by imperial or royal command, by episcopal decree, or by the offerings of the faithful, as well as whatever has been justly and legally acquired to the benefit of the aforesaid monastery up to the present, or whatever the Lord may give in the future.

Therefore no person of any authority—restrained by fear of God and veneration for the holy apostles, whether emperor, king, bishop, marquis, count, or anyone else—shall have permission to remove, diminish, or transfer into another right any of these things, whatever they may be.

In similar fashion we further decree, preserving the statutes of the Fathers, that the Simoniac heresy claim no advantage for itself at the time when divine vocation orders the renewal of pastors in that same Church. Rather, with due opportunity preserved, in the appointment of whoever is worthy, the command of holy institution shall be observed, with every form of greed set aside [Col. 1633A].

But if anyone—which God forbid—should attempt to violate this decree of ours, or rather of the blessed apostles, at the coming of our God, let him be accursed at the Lord’s coming (*anathema maranatha*), joined in punishment to Judas the betrayer and Simon Magus. May the blood of the Redeemer, which was poured out to wash away the stain of the first transgression, become condemnation for him. Let that accursed person, whoever he may be, receive the pool of fire and sulfur instead of the joy of eternal life throughout all ages of ages.

But so that no one may doubt that this page of the decree was completed at our command, let him see it marked with the impression of our seal.

Farewell.

### XXXV. Blessed Simeon, monk and hermit at the monastery of Padolinor in the Mantuan territory, is enrolled in the canon of the holy confessors. (Years 1017–1024.)

[COCQUELINES, *Bullarium*, expanded collection of Roman pontifical privileges, I, 322.]

[Col. 1633B]

BENEDICT, servant of the servants of God, to Boniface, illustrious marquis by the grace of God: most dear greetings with apostolic blessing.

You requested our judgment, as was proper, whether it was permissible for you to establish a church in honor of Simeon, recently sanctified, whose works prove his sanctity and whose countless and various miracles testify to it, and to place his venerable body there with due honor.
