Concerning this we reply: If he shines with miracles as brightly as your man has asserted to us, build a church and place him in it. Ask that an altar be consecrated beside him, at which the relics of the ancient saints may be placed together with the most sacred body of our Lord Jesus Christ, and only then let the divine offices be celebrated [Col. 1633C].

Treat him as a saint, so that the Holy of Holies may repay you with the reward of a saint, just as he himself said: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward” (Matthew 10:41). He himself is the examiner of kidneys and hearts; may he grant him a worthy recompense, and may he bestow his grace upon you for your holy desire.

### XXXVI. Benedict VIII grants the monastery of Saint Andrew to Richard, abbot of Fulda. (Year 1024.)

[DRONKE, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*, 347.]

[Col. 1633D]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Richard, abbot of the venerable monastery of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior and Saint Boniface, situated in the place called Bochonia beside the bank of the river called the Fulda, and through you to your successors in the same venerable monastery forever.

It is fitting for the apostolic office to assist those endowed with devout religion by benevolent compassion and to grant the requests of petitioners with eager devotion. For by this means we chiefly earn a reward from God, the creator of all, if venerable places of the saints are undoubtedly brought in an orderly fashion to a better condition.

Therefore, since you petitioned us to grant and reconfirm to you the aforesaid monastery of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior and Saint Boniface, situated in the place called Bochonia beside the bank of the river called the Fulda, with all the movable and immovable property belonging to it which it now possesses and which, with God’s help, it will possess hereafter, we again grant and give to you, the monastery, the monastery in honor of the holy apostle Andrew which is called Exaiulo, situated beside the church of Holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, called “from the Manger,” with all its dwellings, heated rooms, wine-cellars, and kitchen; with the vineyards and gardens beside it, together with various fruit trees; with its estate and well; with its entrance and exit through the main gate from the public road; and with everything generally belonging to it [Col. 1634B], whether situated outside the city or within the city, which is known justly and reasonably to belong to it.

Beginning with the present seventh indiction, we establish and confirm by decree that this most sacred monastery shall remain perpetually immune under the protection of our holy Roman apostolic see. Thus you and your successors may hold and possess all the places of that monastery with complete security and tranquility from now until the end of the age, so that, established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, it may not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other church.

Favoring your pious desires, we therefore bring this authority of ours and the matter requested into effect. Accordingly, we prohibit any priest of any church from exercising any jurisdiction or authority in the aforesaid monastery except the apostolic see [Col. 1634C]. No one shall presume in any way to celebrate the solemnity of Mass there unless he has been invited by the abbot of the monastery.

Thus, in accordance with what is contained below and established under the apostolic see by the firmness of privilege, it shall remain securely endowed in its places and possessions—both those which it holds or possesses at the present time and those which divine mercy may wish to increase in the future within the right of that monastery through the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful—enjoying perpetual security without the contradiction of any person.

We also establish by this page of our decree that whoever, whether a prelate of any church or a person endowed with any dignity, should attempt to violate this charter of our privilege, which we confirm by the authority of the prince of the apostles [Col. 1634D], let him be anathema. Incurring the wrath of God, let him be excluded from the company of all the saints; nevertheless, the dignity of the aforesaid monastery, granted by us, shall remain perpetually inviolate, supported by apostolic authority. Written.

+ Farewell.

Given on 8 February, by the hand of Piligrim, archbishop of Cologne and librarian of the holy apostolic see, who acted in place of Pope Benedict. In the twelfth year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal eighth pope; in the tenth year of the empire of the lord Henry II, Augustus; indiction VII.

### XXXVII. Benedict VIII sends the pallium to Unwan, archbishop of Hamburg, and grants to him and his successors the legation and archiepiscopal authority over all the northern kingdoms. (Year 1022.)

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburg Documents*, I, 66.]

[Col. 1635A]

BENEDICT, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy Unwan, bishop of the holy Church of Hamburg: paternal affection.

If shepherds of sheep are content to endure sun and frost, day and night, for the protection of their flock, and with ever-watchful eyes continually observe that none of them should perish by wandering or be carried off, torn apart by the bites of wild beasts, with how much labor and care ought we [Col. 1635B] to be vigilant—namely, we who are called shepherds of souls—and never cease to perform the duty entrusted to us concerning the guardianship of the Lord’s sheep, lest on the day of divine judgment the charge of negligence should torture us before the supreme Shepherd because of our indolence. [lacuna] Do not permit that which you have not avenged to be perpetrated. Let there be in you both the gentleness of a good shepherd and the severe strictness of a judge: the one, namely, to cherish those who live innocently; the other, to restrain the restless, who must be punished, from wickedness. Let your protection assist widows and orphans who have been unjustly oppressed. Behold, dearest brother, among the many other things, these are the duties of the priesthood; these are the duties of the pallium. If you diligently preserve them, what you have shown yourself to have received outwardly, you will possess inwardly.

We also grant to you and to all your successors, to be held perpetually, the legation and archiepiscopal authority [Col. 1635C] and archiepiscopal authority over all the northern kingdoms—namely, those of the Danes, Swedes, Norwegians, Icelanders, and all the islands adjoining these kingdoms.

If anyone attempts to infringe, alter, or violate these provisions, in whole or in part, let him be excommunicated forever, unless he repents and makes satisfaction to the Church of Hamburg.

Given by the hand of Peter, chancellor of the holy Church, in the month of April, in the fifth indiction.

### XXXVIII. On the election of the abbot of Monte Cassino

I, BENEDICT, bishop of the Catholic Roman see,

[Col. 1635D] hereby establish what my predecessors established: that they should never seek or demand a price, census, or payment for the consecration of the abbot of Monte Cassino, which today we have received from our most serene son, the emperor Henry. But if they act otherwise and treat the matter as a sale, whoever is discovered to have done this shall be accursed by God the almighty Father, by his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, and by the Holy Spirit. Let his portion be with Dathan and Abiram, who stirred up sedition in the Church of God. Let all the imprecations that Moses, the servant of God, pronounced against the despisers of the Law come upon him. Let him be condemned with Annas and Caiaphas, who condemned the Author [Col. 1636A] by an unjust judgment. Let him have a portion with Judas the traitor, who for love of money sold his Lord and Master. Let him be anathematized by the seven universal councils. Let him be alien from the fellowship of all the saints and from the whole Church of God; and, condemned with the devil on the day of judgment, may he not see the glory of God. Amen.

Enacted on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul.

I, Puppo, patriarch of Aquileia.

I, Belligrinus, archbishop of Nepi.

I, Boso, bishop of Tivoli.

I, Henry, chancellor of the lord emperor.

I, Everard, bishop and chancellor of the lord emperor.

I, Hugh, chancellor of Everard, archchaplain.

### XXXIX. Bull of Pope Benedict VIII, testifying that Henry’s health was restored by Saint Benedict, and declaring the gifts brought by the emperor to the monastery of Monte Cassino (1012–1024)

[TOSTI, *History of Monte Cassino*, I, 251.]

[Col. 1636B]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

We wish it to be known to all Christian believers, both prelates and subjects, that the lord Emperor Henry, our spiritual son, went to the monastery of Saint Benedict situated on the mountain called Castrocasino, where the most sacred body of that same most holy Benedict has been buried. Although he had great devotion toward that place, and declared that he had never seen an oratory more awe-inspiring or [Col. 1636C] venerable, he was nevertheless troubled by a scruple of doubt as to whether blessed Benedict physically rested in that Cassinese monastery.

Because of the pain by which the emperor was being most grievously tormented, most holy Father Benedict appeared to him when he was neither fully asleep nor completely awake and asked where he was suffering. When the emperor immediately confessed his affliction, Saint Benedict said to him:

“I know that until now you have doubted that I rest here. But so that you may doubt this no longer, and may believe with complete certainty that my little body rests in this place together with that of my sister, this will be a sign for you: as soon as you rise today to urinate, you will expel three stones, not small ones, with your urine; from that moment onward you will suffer no more from this pain. [Col. 1636D] And know that I am Brother Benedict.”

Having said this, he immediately disappeared.

The emperor awoke, rose at once, and, restored to his former health in accordance with the vision he had seen, gave great thanks to God and to Father Benedict. When morning came, the emperor entered the assembly of the brothers and said:

“What do you advise me, my lords, to give the physician who has cured me?”

When they replied that he should take from the monastery whatever pleased him and give it to the physician, he said:

“No, that is not fitting for an emperor. Rather, since most holy Father Benedict has plainly cured me this night, it is right—and indeed entirely just—[Col. 1637A] that he should be rewarded for his healing from my own treasury.”

As he said this, with tears mingled with joy, he recounted to everyone what he had seen and heard, adding:

“Now I have clearly learned for certain that this place is truly holy, and no mortal should any longer doubt that here most holy Father Benedict rests together with his holy sister.”

As proof of his words, he openly displayed to everyone the three stones that shortly before he had expelled in accordance with the vision.

Then the emperor rose and went to the body of blessed Benedict, to whom he offered the following gifts:

A Gospel book, externally covered on one side with the purest gold and very precious gems, and internally magnificently decorated with uncial letters and golden figures.

[Col. 1637B] A golden chalice with its paten, worked with gems, pearls, and the finest enamel, together with the napkin with which it is offered; an all-silk cloth, woven with gold, adorned with a diopistim pallium and the finest golden strips; an orarion, napkin, belt, and stole, each likewise woven with gold; and a purple *diasprum* cope with strips woven with gold, as well as a tunic of the same material, decorated with golden work.

Also, a bucket and a silver cup from which the brothers might drink on feast days.

A rose-colored *diarodina* chasuble decorated with golden strips, together with an alb, belt, stole, and maniple.

He also redeemed from Jews, who held it in pledge for five hundred gold pieces, a vestment from the altar of Saint Benedict, which had belonged to King Charles, as well as a larger Saxon silver chalice with its paten, which Theoderic, king of the Saxons, had once sent to blessed Benedict.

[Col. 1637C] For our part, rejoicing in the emperor’s recovery, we placed upon the altar of blessed Benedict a very fine chasuble of Venetian color, suitably decorated with golden strips, and a very fine stole, embroidered with gold, together with its maniple.

Likewise, Archbishop Belgrinus offered a very fine purple chasuble, decorated around its edge with golden strips bearing the signs of the twelve months, and a stole and one golden cope.

All these things we placed upon the altar of Saint Benedict, to remain there perpetually.

[Col. 1638A] Therefore I, the aforementioned Benedict, bishop and servant of the servants of God, together with the aforesaid emperor, beseech all who are called by the Christian name, by the Lord God the almighty Father, by Jesus Christ his only Son, our Lord, who for the salvation of the whole world willed to be born, die, and rise again, by the Holy Spirit proceeding from both, and by blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, who possesses the power of binding and loosing: let no one ever presume, by any means or device whatsoever, to remove the treasure or any of the things that the aforesaid emperor has previously bestowed upon the aforesaid church for the remedy of his soul.

But if anyone—which we do not desire—should regard this our protest or supplication as worthless and should rashly presume by any means to remove anything from the aforesaid church among those things [Col. 1638B] written above, let him know that he is bound by the chains of anathema and alien from the kingdom of God. Let him be appointed to be burned with the devil and his most dreadful pomp, and with Judas, the traitor of our Lord Jesus Christ, in eternal fires and punishments.

But whoever, with pious intent, observes and in every respect guards this our apostolic decree and the things pertaining to the worship of God, may he obtain manifoldly the grace of blessing from our most merciful Lord through the intercession of blessed Benedict, and may he be deemed worthy to share in eternal life. Amen.

The following were present at this matter: Puppo, patriarch of Aquileia; Belgrinus, archbishop of Cologne; and [Col. 1638C] nearly all the bishops and abbots of the whole of Gaul and Italy.

**Section II: Papal Letters and Decrees.** 269

I. Sylvester II confirms the monastery of Saint Lambert at Sens, at the request of its founder, Count Aribo, and Emperor Otto III, and enriches it with rights, on the condition that the monks pay twelve denarii each year to the Roman see. 269

II. Pope Sylvester II confirms the privileges of the monastery of Fulda at the request of Abbot Erkanbald. 272

III. Pope Sylvester II grants Arnulf of Reims, who had been deprived of his pontifical dignity for certain excesses because his abdication lacked Roman consent, permission to resume his staff and ring, exercise the archiepiscopal office, and enjoy all the insignia in the customary manner. He confirms the privileges of the Church of Reims. 273

**GOZPERT, ABBOT OF TEGERNSEE**
EPISTLES. 365

EPISTLE I.—To Ramuold, abbot of St. Emmeram at Regensburg: he announces that he will be there on the feast of St. Emmeram and asks that the book of the complete collation be sent to him. 365

EPISTLE II.—To Count Arnold: he offers abundant thanks for the favors bestowed, declares his grief at the death of the empress Adelheid, and records in detail what his monks performed for the repose of her soul. 365

EPISTLE III.—To the same: he gives the greatest thanks for the finely made windows provided for the Tegernsee church, and sends back the boys whom he has until now kept in the monastery for study, so that they may give proofs of their learning. 365

EPISTLE IV.—To Count Meginhelm: he asks that some grain be granted to him for the sustenance of those who serve his monastery in Austria. 367

EPISTLE V.—To the same: he gives thanks for the *husones*, a kind of fish, and explains how many prayers the people of Tegernsee offer to God for the soul of his wife. 367

EPISTLE VI.—To the same: he asks that *husones* be sent to him and his companions, since they abstain from meat according to monastic custom. 368

EPISTLE VII.—To Gerhard, bishop of Augsburg: he praises his religious devotion and piety and promises to visit him when the time of year permits. 368

EPISTLE VIII.—To Bruno: he asks him to order that tithes in the village of Tatinhusa be paid to the church of Tontinhusa. 369

EPISTLE IX.—To Count Otto: he commends a certain servant to him and asks that two little cloaks be returned to him. 369

EPISTLE X.—To Countess H.: he asks for money for the redemption of certain relatives of his. 369

EPISTLE XI.—To Abbot Otpert: he asks him to permit an exchange between the servants of the two parties. 369

EPISTLE XII.—To the brothers of the Eichstätt church: he asks them to write to him the date of their brother’s death. 370

EPISTLE XIII.—To Lord H.: he asks that he be allowed to use and copy the third part [Col. 1646] of the *Tripartite History*. 370

EPISTLE XIV.—To Count R.: he proves that Imma, a female servant, together with her sons, is owed to him by law, and asks that she be returned. 370

EPISTLE XV.—To P., his kinsman: he asks him to persevere in his resolve to help the distinguished Tegernsee household and to protect certain servants who have been driven from the city. 371

EPISTLE XVI.—To the same: he complains of being neglected and forgotten and asks him to send some copper, tin, and lead for casting a bell, as well as some incense for the worship of God and St. Quirinus. 371
